definition: An aardvark is a burrowing African mammal with a long snout, large ears, and a sticky tongue for eating ants and termites. It's nocturnal and solitary, emerging at night to raid insect mounds. The name comes from Afrikaans for "earth pig," though it's unrelated to pigs. Because it begins with two A's, aardvark often appears first in dictionaries and encyclopedias.

An abacus is a manual counting device consisting of a frame with rods or wires along which beads slide. Used for arithmetic calculations, it predates written numerals and remains in use in parts of Asia. {She learned to add and subtract on an abacus before using a calculator.}

Abandon means to leave behind or give up completely, whether a person, place, or pursuit. You might abandon a sinking ship, abandon a child, or abandon hope. The word carries a sense of finality and often implies desertion or surrender. When used as a noun, abandon describes reckless freedom from restraint: {dancing with wild abandon}. This sense suggests casting off inhibitions entirely, which connects to the verb's core meaning of letting go.

Abandoned describes something that has been left behind or given up entirely. An abandoned {building} stands empty, its occupants gone. An abandoned {child} has been deserted by parents or guardians. The word can also mean uninhibited or unrestrained: {She danced with abandoned joy}. To feel abandoned is to feel forsaken, left alone when someone should have stayed.

Abandonment is the act of leaving something or someone behind, typically with no intention of returning. A parent who walks away from a child commits abandonment; so does someone who deserts a spouse. Property left unclaimed falls into abandonment. The word also describes an emotional state—the feeling of being forsaken: {a deep sense of abandonment}. In law, abandonment has specific meanings regarding property rights, parental duties, and contractual obligations.

An abbey is a building or complex where monks or nuns live under religious vows, or the community itself. The term also applies to churches that were once part of such communities but continue as places of worship after the monastic community dissolved: {Westminster Abbey}. {The abbey's cloisters were peaceful in the early morning.} (Capitalized Abbey is a given name.)

An abbreviation is a shortened form of a word or phrase: {Dr.} for Doctor, {etc.} for et cetera, {FBI} for Federal Bureau of Investigation. Some abbreviations use periods, others don't—convention varies by style and type. Abbreviation also names the act of shortening: {Abbreviation saves space in formal writing}.

Abdication is the formal renunciation of a throne or high office. A monarch who abdicates gives up the crown, usually permanently: {Edward VIII's abdication to marry Wallis Simpson shocked the British Empire}. The word extends to abandoning any serious responsibility: {an abdication of parental duty}, {an abdication of leadership}.

To abduct is to take someone away by force or deception, typically for ransom, sexual exploitation, or political leverage. The word implies the victim is held against their will: {The child was abducted from a playground}. In anatomy, to abduct a limb is to move it away from the body's midline—the opposite of adduct.

Abducted means taken away by force or deception. A person who is abducted has been kidnapped or seized against their will: {She was abducted from a parking lot}. The term applies to criminal kidnappings, alien encounter narratives, and legal contexts involving children taken by non-custodial parents. In anatomy, an abducted limb has been moved away from the body's midline.

Abduction is the act of taking someone away by force or deception—kidnapping. The term appears in legal contexts and news reports: {The abduction occurred outside the school}. In anatomy and physiology, abduction means moving a limb away from the body's midline, the opposite of adduction. In logic, abduction is reasoning from effect to likely cause—inferring the best explanation from incomplete evidence.

Abductions are acts of taking someone away by force or deception, typically against their will. The term applies both to criminal kidnappings and to claimed extraterrestrial encounters where people report being taken aboard spacecraft. In legal contexts, abduction often specifically refers to taking a child or dependent person. {The abductions were linked to a human trafficking ring.} {He wrote about alien abductions in the 1990s.}

An aberration is a departure from what's normal, expected, or right. The word suggests something that stands apart from an established pattern: {The election result was an aberration, not a trend}. In optics, aberration refers to distortion in an image caused by a lens or mirror failing to focus light properly. A person's aberration is a lapse in judgment or behavior: {His outburst was an aberration—he's usually so calm}.

Ability is the capacity to do something—a skill, talent, or competence. You might have the ability to speak French, solve equations, or calm a crying baby. Abilities can be innate or acquired: {She has a natural ability for music}. The word often appears with modifiers: {athletic ability}, {cognitive ability}. To the best of {one's ability} means as well as one can manage.

Ablaze means on fire or lit up brilliantly: {The building was ablaze within minutes}. It extends to anything radiating intense light or color: {The autumn trees were ablaze with red and gold}. Figuratively, ablaze describes passionate intensity: {eyes ablaze with anger}, {a city ablaze with excitement}.

Able is closely related to a word ending that always has a different stress pattern—that is, -able—but whether as word or word ending, the letters able are always about the power, skills, or resources to do something. The meaning of able is closely related to the meaning of the modal verb can.

Ableism is discrimination or prejudice against people with disabilities. It encompasses both overt bias and subtler assumptions—that disability is inherently negative, that disabled people need fixing, or that able-bodied experience is the default. The term parallels racism and sexism: {The building's lack of ramps is architectural ableism}. Ableist is the adjective: {ableist attitudes}, {ableist language}.

Abnormal means deviating from what is typical, usual, or expected. An abnormal {test result} falls outside the normal range. Abnormal {behavior} breaks social norms or suggests psychological disturbance. The word carries clinical overtones—doctors speak of abnormal {cells}, abnormal {growth}. Unlike unusual or atypical, abnormal often implies something is wrong or requires attention.

Aboard is used primarily in reference to vehicles and vessels but has also developed a figurative use in relation to someone joining an organization, team, or project: He came aboard to develop next week’s presentation.

Abolish means to formally put an end to a system, practice, or institution, typically one that has been in place for a long time. It carries a sense of official or permanent elimination rather than gradual decline. The word most commonly appears in discussions of ending slavery, laws, or governmental bodies: {The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery in the United States}. Unlike cancel or eliminate, abolish implies deliberate action to dismantle something established.

Abolished is the past tense of abolish, meaning to formally end or do away with something—typically a system, practice, or institution: {Slavery was abolished in 1865}. The word carries weight, implying official or permanent elimination rather than casual discontinuation. Laws are abolished, customs are abolished, departments are abolished. {The death penalty has been abolished in most European countries.}

Abolition is the act of formally ending or eliminating something, typically a system, practice, or institution. The word most often refers to the movement to end slavery, particularly in 19th-century America and Britain: {Abolition became the defining cause of his life}. It applies to ending other practices as well: the abolition of the {death penalty}, abolition of {monarchy}. An abolitionist advocates for such elimination.

An abolitionist is someone who advocates for abolishing an institution or practice, most commonly slavery. The term is strongly associated with the 19th-century movement to end slavery in the United States and British Empire: {Frederick Douglass was a leading abolitionist}. In contemporary use, abolitionists may advocate ending prisons, the death penalty, or other systems they consider unjust.

Abolitionists are people who advocate for the complete elimination of a practice or institution, most often slavery. The term is strongly associated with the 19th-century movement to end slavery in the United States and British Empire: {Frederick Douglass was among the most influential abolitionists}. Today the word applies to campaigns against other practices: {prison abolitionists}, {death penalty abolitionists}.

Abominable describes something that inspires disgust or moral revulsion. An abominable {act} is deeply offensive to conscience; abominable {conditions} are shockingly bad. The word carries more weight than merely unpleasant—it suggests something worthy of condemnation: {The treatment of prisoners was abominable}. In casual use, it can mean extremely unpleasant: {abominable weather}.

An abomination is something that provokes intense disgust or hatred. The word carries moral weight—abominations aren't merely unpleasant but deeply offensive or wicked: {The torture of prisoners is an abomination}. Religious contexts often label forbidden practices abominations. More loosely, abomination describes anything shockingly bad: {That building is an architectural abomination}.

Abominations are things regarded with intense disgust or hatred. The word carries moral weight—abominations aren't merely unpleasant but deeply offensive to one's values or sensibilities: {The text calls such practices abominations before God}. In casual use, abomination can describe anything found revolting: {That building is an architectural abomination}.

Abort means to end something before completion. A pregnancy can be aborted, terminating fetal development—the noun abortion refers to this procedure or its spontaneous occurrence (miscarriage). Missions, launches, and operations abort when something goes wrong: {Mission control aborted the launch at T-minus ten seconds}. In computing, abort stops a process or program mid-execution. The word implies incompleteness by design or necessity.

Abortion is the termination of a pregnancy before the fetus can survive outside the womb. The term covers both induced procedures and spontaneous loss (miscarriage). Abortion is among the most politically divisive topics in American life, with debate centering on when personhood begins and whether women have a right to end pregnancies. {She had an abortion at eight weeks}. In extended use, an abortion is something badly botched or monstrous: {The building was an abortion of clashing styles}.

Abortions is the plural of abortion, the termination of a pregnancy before the fetus can survive outside the womb. The word covers both deliberate procedures and spontaneous losses (miscarriages). Abortion is among the most politically charged terms in American English, with {pro-choice} and {pro-life} camps fighting over its legal status for decades.

Whether as adverb, preposition, or adjective, about delivers on two fronts. One is to indicate proximity in time, space, or condition: Let’s meet at about 4. I’m about fed up with this waiting. Over time, a related meaning – on the verge of – has developed: That man looks like he’s about to jump. The other big task for about is to associate a subject or quality with someone or something else: He’s reading a book about the Middle Ages; She’s all about money. About can also be synonymous with around: There were dirty clothes scattered about the room. We went about the town, looking for a place to stay.

Above has a similar meaning to over and is interchangeable with it in some instances. It is used more often than over in relation to rank and fixed scales: above freezing, a general ranks above a colonel. The common phrase above and beyond is somewhat redundant and usually just means beyond.

Abracadabra is a word spoken by magicians when performing tricks, meant to sound like a mystical incantation: {The magician waved his wand and said abracadabra}. By extension, it describes any seemingly magical transformation or solution: {There's no abracadabra that will fix the budget overnight}. The word suggests that something complex has been glossed over with theatrical flourish rather than genuine effort.

Abrasive describes materials or surfaces that wear away other things through friction: {abrasive cleanser}, {abrasive sandpaper}. An abrasive person or manner is harsh and grating, rubbing people the wrong way: {His abrasive personality made him difficult to work with}. As a noun, an abrasive is any substance used for grinding, polishing, or smoothing surfaces.

Abroad means in or to a foreign country: {She studied abroad for a year}, {news from abroad}. The word once meant more broadly "out in the world" or "widely scattered"—a sense that survives in expressions like {There are rumors abroad that the company is failing}. To get abroad is to become known or spread.

Abrupt describes something sudden and unexpected, often jarringly so: {an abrupt change in plans}, {The music came to an abrupt stop}. Applied to manner or speech, abrupt suggests curtness or brusqueness—someone who is abrupt cuts interaction short without the usual social smoothing: {His abrupt dismissal left her stunned}. An abrupt slope or cliff rises steeply.

Abs is the informal term for abdominal muscles, especially when visibly defined: {She's been working on her abs at the gym}. The word appears constantly in fitness contexts—{six-pack abs}, {ab workout}, {killer abs}. Abs also serves as shorthand for the anti-lock braking system in vehicles, though that usage more commonly appears as ABS.

Absence is the state of not being present or the lack of something: {His absence from the meeting was noted}. It often implies that presence or existence is expected or normal: {the absence of evidence}, {an absence of leadership}. In the phrase {absence makes the heart grow fonder}, distance supposedly increases affection. An absence can also be a period of being away: {After a long absence, she returned home}.

Absent is typically an adjective that characterizes something that is not present: Four students were absent yesterday. It is usually a predicate adjective but when used before a noun it often denotes something that is normally present: an absent father. Absent can be used as a preposition, and is commonly used by journalists: Absent any legislative action, tax rates will be higher in 2013.

An absentee is someone who is absent—from work, from voting, from a place where their presence is expected. Often carries a note of criticism: an absentee {landlord} collects rent without maintaining the property; an absentee {father} has abandoned his responsibilities. An absentee {ballot} is cast by someone who can't be present on election day.

Absentminded describes someone so absorbed in thought that they neglect immediate surroundings or tasks. The absentminded professor forgets where he put his keys while pondering abstract problems. {She absentmindedly stirred her coffee, lost in thought.} The word suggests harmless distraction rather than serious negligence—a mind present elsewhere, not absent entirely.

Absinthe is a potent green liquor flavored with wormwood and anise. It was banned in many countries in the early twentieth century over fears—largely unfounded—that it caused hallucinations and madness. The ban has since lifted in most places. Absinthe is traditionally diluted with water poured over a sugar cube, which turns the liquid cloudy: {She prepared her absinthe with the ritual slowness of a connoisseur}.

Absolute very often implies the extreme end of a scale – the end characterized by fullness or completeness (absolute truth, absolute power). It may also suggest exclusivity or exclusion of everything else (absolute joy, absolute necessity). By designating an extreme, absolute is often subject to hyperbole: We had an absolute blast! The phrase the absolute is used to designate something that is free from restrictions or conditions, or something complete.

Absolutely is the adverb form of absolute, carrying its sense of completeness or totality. It most often functions as an emphatic intensifier meaning completely or utterly: {The whole evening was absolutely perfect.} Standing alone, absolutely serves as an emphatic affirmative, stronger than yes: {Are you coming to the party? Absolutely.} Like many intensifiers, it frequently appears in casual hyperbole where true absoluteness isn't meant.

Absolution is formal release from guilt, blame, or punishment—especially the declaration by a priest that sins are forgiven after confession. The word implies authority: someone with power to absolve grants it. Outside religion, absolution suggests being cleared of wrongdoing: {The investigation brought him absolution}. To seek absolution is to seek forgiveness from someone who can grant it.

To absorb is to take something in and retain it. A sponge absorbs water; a student absorbs knowledge. Materials that absorb sound or light prevent reflection. To be absorbed in something is to be fully engaged: {She was so absorbed in the book she didn't hear me come in}. Absorb also means to incorporate: {The company absorbed its competitor}. To absorb a cost or shock is to bear it without passing it on.

Absorbed describes being deeply engaged or engrossed in something, with attention fully captured: {She was so absorbed in her book she didn't hear the doorbell}. The word also means taken in or soaked up—a sponge absorbs water, a company absorbs a smaller competitor, costs get absorbed into a budget. Both senses share the idea of one thing being drawn completely into another.

Absorbing describes something that fully engages attention—a book, film, or task so compelling that time passes unnoticed: {an absorbing documentary about deep-sea exploration}. The word draws on the physical sense of absorb, where a sponge takes in liquid completely. What absorbs you leaves no room for distraction.

Absorption is the process of taking something in. A sponge absorbs water; the body absorbs nutrients; a company absorbs a smaller rival. Mental absorption means being fully engaged: {She was so absorbed in her book she didn't hear the doorbell}. In physics, absorption refers to energy being taken up rather than reflected or transmitted. The word often implies that what's absorbed becomes part of something larger and loses its separate identity.

Abstinence is the practice of refraining from something, especially something desirable. Most often it refers to avoiding alcohol, sex, or certain foods: {The program promotes abstinence from drugs and alcohol}. Sexual abstinence specifically means not engaging in sexual activity, a concept central to some religious teachings and sex education curricula. {Abstinence-only} programs teach avoidance rather than harm reduction.

The core meaning of abstract is of something separate from, but closely related to, an underlying thing. In most uses the abstract thing is not tangible, but is rather an idea. An idea criticized as being too abstract means it is too far removed from reality or practicality. When you abstract, you take away or pull out the essential elements or ideas of something. An abstract of an article or paper is a short summary.

Abstraction is the process of pulling away from concrete particulars to focus on general principles or essential features. In philosophy and logic, abstractions are concepts that exist independently of specific instances: {Justice is an abstraction}. In art, abstraction departs from realistic representation toward form, color, and pattern. The word also names the state of being lost in thought: {She gazed out the window in abstraction}. In computing, abstraction hides complexity behind simpler interfaces.

Absurd describes something so unreasonable or illogical that it defies serious consideration: {The idea that the earth is flat is absurd}. The word often carries a note of ridicule—absurd claims invite laughter or dismissal. In philosophy, the absurd refers to the conflict between humans seeking meaning and a universe that offers none. As a noun, {the theater of the absurd} presents existence as fundamentally meaningless.

Absurdity is the quality of being ridiculous, illogical, or contrary to reason. An absurdity is also a specific instance—something that makes no sense: {The absurdity of the situation finally hit me}. The word often carries philosophical weight, pointing to the fundamental meaninglessness some see in human existence: {Camus explored the absurdity of life}.

Abundance is a large quantity—more than enough. It suggests plenty, even overflow: {an abundance of natural resources}, {food in abundance}. The word carries positive connotations of generosity and sufficiency rather than mere excess. Something abundant exists in great supply: {Wildlife was abundant in the valley}.

Abundant means present in large quantities—more than enough. An abundant {harvest} yields plenty. {Abundant evidence} leaves little doubt. The word suggests not just sufficiency but overflow: {The region is abundant in natural resources}. What's abundant is plentiful, ample, freely available.

Abuse is true to its roots in nearly all meanings: it’s a mash-up of ab- (away, off) and use. The various senses of abuse, whether noun or verb, have to do with using someone or something wrongly, in a way that is bad for the abuser (substance abuse), the abused (animal abuse), or both. Where people are the object and without further context, abuse typically stands for physical or sexual abuse of a woman or child by a family member.

Abused describes someone or something that has been mistreated, harmed, or used wrongly. An abused {child} or abused {spouse} has suffered physical, emotional, or sexual harm. Abused {substances} are drugs taken improperly or excessively. An abused {privilege} has been exploited beyond its intended purpose. The word can also mean worn out from misuse: {an abused old couch}.

An abuser is someone who mistreats or harms another person, typically through repeated acts of violence, cruelty, or exploitation: {Her abuser had isolated her from friends and family}. The term applies across contexts—physical, emotional, sexual, or substance-related. A drug abuser misuses controlled substances. An abuser of power exploits their position for personal gain.

Abusers are people who mistreat others or misuse something. The word most often refers to those who inflict physical, emotional, or sexual harm: {domestic abusers}, {child abusers}. It also applies to those who misuse substances: {drug abusers}, {alcohol abusers}. Less commonly, abusers exploit systems or privileges: {serial abusers of the welfare system}.

Abuses is the plural of abuse—instances of cruel treatment, misuse, or corruption: {a long history of abuses by the regime}, {abuses of power}. As a verb (third person singular), it means to mistreat or misuse: {He abuses his authority}, {She abuses prescription drugs}. The noun stresses the first syllable; the verb stresses the second.

Abusive describes behavior that causes harm through cruelty, violence, or exploitation. An abusive {parent} mistreats children. An abusive {relationship} involves patterns of control or harm. Abusive {language} is harshly insulting: {The caller became abusive when told we couldn't help}. The word implies repeated or sustained mistreatment rather than isolated incidents.

Abysmal means extremely bad or severe, suggesting a bottomless depth of failure or inadequacy: {abysmal performance}, {abysmal working conditions}, {The food was abysmal}. The word derives from abyss, implying something so poor it seems to have no bottom. Less commonly, abysmal describes literal vast depths: {abysmal ocean trenches}.

An abyss is a chasm so deep it seems bottomless. The word evokes vast, dark spaces—oceanic trenches, underground caverns, the void of space. Figuratively, an abyss is any profound depth: {an abyss of despair}, {staring into the abyss}. The abyss between two positions suggests an unbridgeable gulf. In religious contexts, the abyss is hell or primordial chaos.

Academia is the world of colleges, universities, and scholarly research—the institutions, people, and culture devoted to higher learning. Someone {in academia} works as a professor or researcher rather than in industry or government. The term often carries connotations of ivory-tower detachment: {That theory sounds good in academia but fails in practice}. Academic politics, publish-or-perish pressures, and the job market for professors are all part of academia.

Academic relates to education, scholarship, and learning institutions. An academic {career} involves teaching or research at a university. Academic {standards} concern educational achievement. As a noun, an academic is a scholar or professor: {She's an academic specializing in medieval history}. When something is called academic, it may be dismissed as theoretical rather than practical: {The question is purely academic now that the decision has been made}.

Academics refers to scholarly pursuits and educational matters—coursework, research, and intellectual study: {She excelled in academics but struggled socially}. The word also means scholars collectively, the people who work in universities and research institutions: {Academics have debated this question for decades}. As an adjective, academic describes things relating to education or scholarship, or something theoretical rather than practical: {The question is purely academic now that the decision has been made}.

An academy is a school or institution for specialized training: a military academy, a police academy, a dance academy. The word also denotes learned societies that set standards or honor achievement in a field: the French Academy, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. {Academy Award} derives from the latter. In casual use, academy sometimes appears in school names without implying special status. (Capitalized Academy may refer to Plato's school or a specific institution.)

Acapella (also a cappella) describes singing without instrumental accompaniment—voices alone. The term comes from Italian meaning "in the chapel style," referring to unaccompanied church music. Acapella has gained popularity through vocal groups and competitions: {The group performed an acapella version of the song}. Beatboxing often substitutes for instruments in modern acapella arrangements.

To accelerate is to increase in speed or cause something to go faster. A car accelerates when you press the gas pedal; a process accelerates when it picks up pace: {The company accelerated its hiring plans}. In physics, acceleration includes any change in velocity—speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction. Figuratively, anything that hastens progress accelerates it: {Social media accelerated the spread of the news}.

Acceleration is the rate at which something speeds up. In physics, it's precisely defined as change in velocity over time—including slowing down (negative acceleration or deceleration) and changes in direction. The word extends to any quickening process: {the acceleration of urban development}, {career acceleration}. To {accelerate} is to increase speed or hasten progress.

An accelerator is something that speeds up a process. Most commonly, it's the pedal in a vehicle that controls engine power: {She floored the accelerator}. In physics, a particle accelerator propels subatomic particles to high speeds for research. In business and tech, an accelerator is a program that helps startups grow quickly through mentorship and funding.

Accent has its roots in the Latin word for song and that’s a clue to its many meanings, most of which relate to the sounds that come out of people’s mouths. In extended use, accent can refer to anything that stands out from its surroundings (accented syllable, the room’s decorative accent). When preceded by the name of a language or dialect, accent denotes the prosody and pronunciation typical of native speakers: He has a German accent.

Accents are distinctive ways of pronouncing a language, shaped by region, class, or native tongue: {a Southern accent}, {a French accent}. The word also means emphasis or stress: {The accent falls on the second syllable}. Accent marks are diacritical symbols above letters indicating pronunciation or distinguishing words. To accent something is to emphasize or highlight it: {The pillows accent the room's color scheme}.

Accept means to receive willingly or agree to something offered. You accept a gift, an invitation, a job offer, or an apology. Beyond physical receiving, accept means to regard as true or valid: {I accept your explanation}. To accept responsibility is to acknowledge it as yours. To accept something difficult—a loss, a limitation—is to come to terms with it: {She finally accepted that he wasn't coming back}.

Acceptable means good enough to be allowed or approved, though not necessarily excellent. Something acceptable meets minimum standards without exceeding them: {The work was acceptable but not impressive}. What counts as acceptable varies by context—acceptable {behavior} at a concert differs from acceptable behavior at a funeral. The word often implies settling: {We found an acceptable compromise}.

Acceptance is the act of receiving something offered or agreeing to something proposed: {acceptance of a job offer}, {acceptance of an apology}. It extends to approval or favorable reception: {The theory gained wide acceptance}. In a more personal sense, acceptance means coming to terms with difficult realities rather than fighting them: {acceptance of loss}, {radical acceptance}. An acceptance is also a formal agreement to pay a draft or bill of exchange.

Access is about permission, ability, or freedom to get or use something, or to go to a place: Most people in developed countries have access to the Internet. If you have access to an important person, you have the ability to easily communicate with him or her. As a verb, access is a more formal way of saying get or get at. When you access information, you get it in order to read or use it.

Accessible means able to be reached, entered, or used. A building is accessible if people can get into it; wheelchair-accessible means navigable by someone in a wheelchair. Information is accessible when it's easy to find and understand. An accessible {writing style} doesn't require specialized knowledge. A person who is accessible is approachable and easy to talk to: {Despite her fame, she remained accessible to fans}.

Accessories are supplementary items that complement something primary. In fashion, accessories are additions to an outfit—scarves, jewelry, bags, belts: {She has a whole drawer just for accessories}. For products, accessories are optional add-ons: {camera accessories}, {phone accessories}. In law, an accessory is someone who aids a crime without directly committing it: {accessory to murder}, {accessory after the fact}.

An accessory is something added to enhance or complete something else—a belt, scarf, or handbag that complements an outfit; a case or charger sold alongside a phone. In law, an accessory is someone who helps commit a crime without being the principal actor: {accessory before the fact}, {accessory after the fact}. The adjective means supplementary or aiding: {accessory muscles}, {accessory equipment}.

An accident is an unplanned event, typically one that causes harm or damage: {a car accident}, {an industrial accident}. The word implies lack of intent—if you do something {by accident}, you didn't mean to. An accident can also be a fortunate coincidence: {a happy accident}. Calling a child {an accident} suggests the pregnancy was unplanned.

Accidental describes something happening by chance rather than intention or design: {an accidental discovery}, {accidental death}. The word often implies no one is at fault—things simply happened that way. In music, an accidental is a sharp, flat, or natural sign that modifies a note outside the key signature.

Accidents are unplanned events, typically with negative consequences. A car accident involves a collision; an industrial accident causes injury. The word often implies no one is at fault: {It was an accident—I didn't mean to break it}. By accident means unintentionally: {I deleted the file by accident}. Euphemistically, an accident can be a child from an unplanned pregnancy, or a loss of bladder control: {The puppy had an accident on the rug}.

Acclaim is enthusiastic public praise or approval. A film receives critical acclaim; an athlete basks in acclaim after a record-breaking performance. As a verb, to acclaim is to praise publicly and enthusiastically: {The novel was acclaimed as a masterpiece}. Someone acclaimed is widely celebrated: {the acclaimed director's latest work}.

Accommodation is the act of making room for something or someone, literally or figuratively. A hotel provides accommodations—lodging and related services. To make accommodations is to adjust arrangements for someone's needs: {The school made accommodations for students with disabilities}. In vision, accommodation is the eye's automatic adjustment to focus at different distances. The word often implies compromise or adaptation: {We reached an accommodation on the disputed terms}.

Accommodations are arrangements made for someone's needs. Most often this means lodging: {We booked accommodations near the beach}. In educational and workplace contexts, accommodations are adjustments made for people with disabilities: {The university provides testing accommodations for students with ADHD}. The singular accommodation covers the same ground but sounds more British; Americans favor the plural even for a single hotel room.

An accompaniment is something that goes along with something else. In music, an accompaniment supports a melody or soloist: {piano accompaniment}, {singing without accompaniment}. Food served alongside a main dish is an accompaniment: {The steak came with a mushroom accompaniment}. More broadly, anything that naturally occurs with something else: {Controversy is an inevitable accompaniment to fame}.

An accomplice is someone who helps another person commit a crime or wrongdoing. The word implies active participation or assistance rather than mere knowledge: {Police arrested the robber and two accomplices}. Unlike a witness or bystander, an accomplice shares legal or moral responsibility for the act.

Accomplices are people who help someone commit a crime or wrongdoing. The term implies active participation or assistance rather than mere knowledge: {The getaway driver was charged as an accomplice to the robbery}. Unlike witnesses or bystanders, accomplices share legal or moral responsibility for the act.

To accomplish something is to complete it successfully, to bring it to fruition: {She accomplished everything she set out to do}. The word implies effort and achievement—you accomplish goals, tasks, and missions, not accidents. An accomplished person is highly skilled, suggesting mastery achieved through dedication: {an accomplished pianist}.

Accomplished describes someone highly skilled through training and practice: {an accomplished pianist}, {an accomplished diplomat}. The word suggests refined expertise, often in arts or social graces. It also means completed or achieved: {an accomplished fact}, {mission accomplished}. The past participle of accomplish functions almost exclusively as an adjective.

An accomplishment is something achieved through effort or skill—a completed goal, a notable deed, a task brought to fruition. {Graduating was her proudest accomplishment}. The word carries connotations of merit; accomplishments are worth noting, not merely finished. Accomplishment can also mean refined skill or ability: {a woman of many accomplishments} suggests cultivated talents in areas like music, languages, or social graces.

Accomplishments are things achieved through effort or skill—completed goals, notable deeds, or acquired abilities. The word implies work and merit: {She listed her accomplishments on the résumé}. An accomplishment can also be a refined skill or social grace, now somewhat old-fashioned: {Piano was considered an accomplishment for young ladies}.

Accord is agreement or harmony between parties. Nations sign accords to formalize treaties. If something happens {of its own accord}, it happens spontaneously, without outside force. To accord is to grant or give: {She was accorded the respect she deserved}. Something {in accord with} another thing matches or aligns with it.

An accordion is a portable musical instrument with a bellows, buttons or keys, and free metal reeds. The player squeezes and expands the bellows while pressing keys to force air past the reeds, producing sound. Accordions appear in folk music traditions worldwide—polka, tango, zydeco, klezmer. As a modifier, accordion describes things that fold in pleats like a bellows: {accordion doors}, {accordion folders}.

The essential meaning of the noun account is similar to the noun record. An account of an event is someone’s version of how it happened. When numbers are involved, an account is a record of changes in value or an arrangement between parties to make regular commercial transactions. The common phrase take account of, also expressed as take into account, means to consider. As a verb, account is usually followed by for and means provide an account of.

Accountability is the state of being answerable for your actions or decisions, especially when things go wrong. If you have accountability for something, you're expected to explain or justify what happened and accept consequences. The word often appears in discussions of leadership, governance, and workplace responsibility: {The CEO demanded accountability from her management team}. To hold someone accountable is to require them to answer for their conduct. Accountability implies that blame or credit will be assigned based on outcomes.

Accountable means responsible for actions and obligated to explain or justify them. Officials are {accountable to voters}, employees to supervisors, children to parents. The word implies consequences—someone who is accountable can be blamed or punished if things go wrong. To {hold someone accountable} is to demand they answer for their conduct.

An accountant is a professional who keeps, audits, or inspects financial records. Accountants prepare tax returns, track expenses, and ensure businesses comply with financial regulations. The work ranges from routine bookkeeping to complex corporate audits: {Our accountant found several deductions we'd missed}. Certified public accountants (CPAs) have passed licensing exams.

Accountants are professionals who maintain and analyze financial records. They prepare tax returns, audit books, and advise on fiscal matters. The term covers a range from bookkeepers to certified public accountants (CPAs) who must pass rigorous exams. {The accountants found discrepancies in the quarterly reports.} Accountant carries connotations of meticulous, numbers-focused work—sometimes invoked as shorthand for cautious or unimaginative: {Leave it to the accountants to kill the creative budget.}

Accounting is the practice of recording, organizing, and reporting financial transactions. Businesses use accounting to track income and expenses, prepare tax returns, and assess financial health. The field divides into specialties: tax accounting, forensic accounting, managerial accounting. To give an accounting of something is to provide a detailed explanation or reckoning: {She demanded an accounting of where the money went}.

Accounts is the plural of account, which at its core is a record or reckoning. Financial accounts track money: {checking accounts}, {savings accounts}, {accounts payable}. To give an account is to provide a description or explanation: {eyewitness accounts of the crash}. {By all accounts} means according to what everyone says. To {take into account} is to consider. Someone may be called to account for their actions—held responsible.

Accuracy is closeness to the true or correct value. A watch with good accuracy keeps time precisely. In measurement, accuracy differs from precision: a scale can give consistent readings (precise) without being accurate if it's miscalibrated. {The accuracy of his predictions was remarkable}. In broader use, accuracy means freedom from error or distortion: {historical accuracy}, {the accuracy of a news report}.

Accurate means correct, precise, or free from error. An accurate {measurement} matches the true value. An accurate {description} faithfully represents what it describes. An accurate {shot} hits its target. The word implies careful attention to facts or details: {The report was accurate in every particular}. Something can be roughly accurate or perfectly accurate depending on how close it comes to truth.

An accusation is a claim that someone has done something wrong or committed an offense. It ranges from informal blame to formal criminal charges: {The accusation of theft destroyed his reputation}, {She denied the accusations against her}. To {level an accusation} is to make one; to {face accusations} is to be accused.

Accusations are claims that someone has done something wrong or illegal. The word carries weight—an accusation implies seriousness beyond mere complaint. {The accusations against him included fraud and embezzlement.} To level or hurl accusations is to make them forcefully. False accusations can destroy reputations; credible ones can end careers.

To accuse is to claim that someone has done something wrong or committed a crime: {She accused him of stealing her idea}, {The senator stands accused of corruption}. The word implies a direct charge, not mere suspicion. An accusation may be formal (in legal proceedings) or informal (in personal disputes). The accused is the person charged.

Accused functions as both verb and noun. As the past tense of accuse, it means to have charged someone with wrongdoing: {She accused him of lying}. As a noun, the accused refers to a person or people facing criminal charges: {The accused stood before the judge}. In legal contexts, the accused is the defendant until proven guilty.

An accuser is someone who charges another with wrongdoing or a crime. The term often appears in legal contexts: {The accuser took the stand to testify}. It can carry skeptical undertones, implying the charge may be false or malicious: {His accusers never produced evidence}.

Ace has many associations with one and being first, starting with its designation for a playing card with one mark on it. The high value of an ace in many card games informs its use as an adjective for top quality (an ace programmer) and as verb to do something easily and well: She aced her physics test. In tennis, an ace is a legal serve that is not returned, resulting in a point for the server. In golf, it is a hole in one.

Aced is the past tense of ace, meaning to perform exceptionally well on something, especially a test or challenge: {She aced the interview}, {He aced his finals}. The usage comes from tennis, where an ace is an unreturnable serve—a perfect shot. To ace something is to nail it completely, leaving no room for improvement.

Aces is the plural of ace—the playing card, the tennis serve, the expert. But aces also functions as a predicate adjective meaning excellent or first-rate: {Everything's aces between us}, {I'm feeling aces today}. This use is informal and somewhat dated, with a cheerful, old-school ring to it.

An ache is a dull, persistent pain—distinct from sharp or stabbing sensations. Body parts ache: {My back aches}, {an aching tooth}. The word extends to emotional longing: {She ached for home}, {an aching heart}. As a noun: {a dull ache in my shoulder}, {the ache of missing someone}.

Aches is the plural of ache—dull, persistent pains rather than sharp ones. Body parts ache: {My back aches}, {aching joints}. The word extends to emotional longing: {My heart aches for her}. As a noun: {the aches and pains of getting older}, {muscle aches from the flu}.

The idea of achieve nearly always relates to accomplishing a goal: Students in his class achieved the highest scores ever recorded at this school. A failure to achieve something usually means that a desired result was not reached: Many artists never achieve the success they dream of in their lifetimes.

Achievement is the accomplishment of something requiring effort or skill: {a remarkable achievement in science}, {Her promotion was a major achievement}. The word implies overcoming difficulty—finishing a routine task isn't an achievement. In gaming, achievements are markers awarded for completing specific challenges or milestones. {What do you consider your greatest achievement?}

Achievements are things accomplished, especially through effort or skill. The word implies meaningful accomplishment rather than trivial completion: {Her achievements in medicine earned international recognition}. In gaming, achievements are specific goals that unlock rewards or recognition when completed: {I spent hours trying to get that achievement}.

Aching describes a dull, persistent pain—the kind that lingers rather than stabs: {My aching feet need rest}. The word extends to emotional longing or yearning: {an aching heart}, {aching for home}. Something achingly beautiful is so moving it almost hurts to witness.

Achoo is the conventional spelling of a sneeze sound, used both as an exclamation and a noun: {Achoo! Sorry, allergies}. The word attempts to capture the explosive exhale through nose and mouth. Also spelled ah-choo or atchoo.

Achy describes a dull, persistent pain—the kind that lingers rather than stabs. Bodies become achy from exertion, illness, or age: {My legs are achy after that hike}, {I woke up feeling achy and feverish}. The word suggests discomfort that's bearable but wearing.

Acid is a substance with a sour taste that reacts with bases and turns litmus paper red. The word extends to anything sharp or biting: {acid wit}, {acid remarks}. In chemistry, acids are compounds that donate hydrogen ions. Acid is also slang for LSD, the hallucinogenic drug: {dropping acid}. As an adjective, acid describes sourness or corrosiveness: {an acid taste}, {acid rain}. (All-caps ACID is a database acronym.)

To acknowledge is to recognize or admit that something exists or is true: {She acknowledged her mistake}. It also means to confirm receipt or respond to someone's presence: {He nodded to acknowledge the applause}, {Please acknowledge this email}. Acknowledge carries a sense of acceptance—when you acknowledge something, you stop ignoring or denying it.

Acknowledgement is recognition that something exists, is true, or has been received. A nod can serve as acknowledgement of someone's presence. {We never received acknowledgement of our complaint.} In books, the acknowledgements section thanks those who helped. The word also appears in legal contexts where formal recognition matters: {acknowledgement of paternity}. Also spelled acknowledgment.

Acknowledgment is recognition that something exists, is true, or has been received. A nod can be an acknowledgment of someone's presence; a reply email acknowledges a message. In formal contexts, acknowledgments appear in books thanking those who helped: {The acknowledgments section ran three pages}. Legal acknowledgment confirms authenticity before a notary. Also spelled acknowledgement.

Acne is a skin condition characterized by pimples, blackheads, and inflamed spots, typically on the face, back, and chest. It occurs when hair follicles become clogged with oil and dead skin cells, and is most common during adolescence when hormonal changes increase oil production. {Her acne cleared up after she turned twenty.} The term also applies to similar eruptions in adults, sometimes called adult acne.

An acorn is the nut of an oak tree, consisting of a smooth oval seed seated in a rough, scaly cup. Acorns were historically an important food source for both humans and animals, particularly squirrels and pigs. The phrase {mighty oaks from little acorns grow} expresses the idea that great things can have humble beginnings. Acorn also describes the shape of certain objects, like an acorn squash.

Acorns are the nuts of oak trees—small, oval seeds sitting in a cuplike cap. They're food for squirrels, deer, and other wildlife, and were historically ground into flour by various cultures. The saying {from little acorns mighty oaks grow} uses them as a symbol of small beginnings that lead to great things.

Acoustic describes sound or hearing. An acoustic {guitar} produces sound without electronic amplification. Acoustic {tiles} absorb sound. The acoustics of a space—a concert hall, a cathedral—determine how sound behaves there: {The acoustics in this room are terrible}. In music, an acoustic {version} of a song strips away electronic production, returning to unamplified instruments.

Acoustics is the science of sound—how it's produced, transmitted, and received. More commonly, acoustics refers to the sound qualities of a space: {The concert hall has excellent acoustics}. A room's acoustics determine how clearly you hear music or speech, whether sound echoes or absorbs. The singular acoustic works as an adjective: {acoustic guitar}, {acoustic tile}.

An acquaintance is someone you know but who is not a friend. If you make someone’s acquaintance, you meet them and get to know them slightly. Acquaintance with an idea or subject is shallow knowledge: I don’t have enough acquaintance with genetics to judge the merits of her book. There is no negative connotation with acquaintance as an introduction to a subject: The course is intended to acquaint students with the main branches of sociology.

Acquaintances are people you know but not well—somewhere between strangers and friends. The relationship implies recognition and perhaps occasional interaction without deep familiarity or emotional closeness: {We're acquaintances, not friends}. To {make someone's acquaintance} is to meet them for the first time. A {passing acquaintance} suggests only slight familiarity with a person or subject.

Acquisition is the act of obtaining something, or the thing obtained. Companies make acquisitions when they purchase other businesses: {The tech giant announced three acquisitions this quarter}. Museums boast new acquisitions. The word carries a formal, institutional tone—you acquire assets, not groceries. Language acquisition is how children learn to speak. An acquisition can suggest strategic accumulation rather than casual getting.

An acquittal is a formal judgment that someone is not guilty of a crime. It typically comes from a jury verdict or judge's ruling after trial: {The jury returned an acquittal on all charges}. Unlike a dismissal, an acquittal means the case was decided on its merits. Once acquitted, a defendant cannot be retried for the same offense.

Acquitted is the past tense of acquit, meaning to declare someone not guilty of a criminal charge. A jury or judge acquits a defendant when the prosecution fails to prove its case: {The jury acquitted her of all charges}. To acquit oneself is to conduct oneself in a particular way: {He acquitted himself well under pressure}.

An acre is a unit of land area equal to 43,560 square feet—roughly the size of a football field without the end zones. The word appears constantly in real estate and agriculture: {a forty-acre farm}, {five acres of woodland}. Figuratively, acres can mean a large expanse: {acres of parking lot}, {acres of bare skin}.

An acrobat performs feats of balance, agility, and coordination—walking tightropes, tumbling, swinging from trapezes. The word extends to anyone who displays similar nimbleness: a {political acrobat} who pivots positions without losing support, or {verbal acrobatics} that dodge direct answers. {The acrobats formed a human pyramid.}

Acrobatic describes movements requiring unusual agility, balance, or coordination—the kind associated with acrobats and gymnasts. An acrobatic {catch} in baseball involves a diving or twisting motion. Acrobatic {feats} demand physical skill most people lack. The word often carries admiration: {an acrobatic save by the goalkeeper}. Figuratively, acrobatic can describe mental or verbal nimbleness: {acrobatic reasoning}, {linguistic acrobatics}.

Acrobatics is the performance of gymnastic feats requiring agility, balance, and coordination—tumbling, flips, aerial maneuvers, and the like. The term covers both the activity itself and the skills involved: {The circus troupe's acrobatics drew gasps from the audience}. Figuratively, acrobatics describes any impressive display of nimbleness or dexterity, whether physical or mental: {The lawyer's verbal acrobatics confused the jury}. Political or rhetorical acrobatics suggests contorted maneuvering to avoid a difficult position.

Acrobats are performers who execute gymnastic feats requiring agility, balance, and coordination—walking tightropes, tumbling, swinging from trapezes. The word extends to anyone displaying similar physical dexterity: {The waiters were acrobats, weaving through the crowded restaurant with loaded trays}. Figuratively, verbal or political acrobats perform impressive feats of maneuvering: {rhetorical acrobats who never give a straight answer}.

An acropolis is a fortified hilltop citadel in an ancient Greek city, typically containing temples and public buildings. The word combines Greek roots meaning "high city." Many Greek cities had an acropolis serving as both defensive stronghold and sacred center: {The ruins of the acropolis overlooked the modern town}. (Capitalized Acropolis usually refers to the one in Athens.)

Across works as both a preposition and an adverb with similar meanings. Its core idea is from one side to the other. A closely related meaning is on/to the other side, as in they live across the street. Figuratively, it is similar to throughout, the idea being that from one side to the other includes everything in between: people across the nation are finding the new service helpful.

Act is the most common noun used to designate something that you do—even though the word deed is arguably more accurate, as it is actually related to do. Since act is so general, it is often modified by a preceding adjective (a terrible act, a random act) or a following prepositional phrase (an act of terrorism, an act of kindness). An act can also be a division of a dramatic work, such as a play or opera, or a piece of legislation. Act is also a verb that is more specific than do because it suggests awareness or intention when the subject is a person (he acted like a gentleman), and power or effect when the subject is inanimate (geological forces act on mountains). Act can also suggest a disconnect between reality and appearance: She acted surprised but she knew I was already here.

Acting is performing a role, especially in theater, film, or television. It's both the craft and the activity: {She studied acting in New York}, {His acting was wooden}. Acting also describes someone temporarily filling a position: an acting {director}, an acting {president}. The word can suggest pretense: {All that sympathy was just acting}.

Action is a general verbal noun related to act. It is usually more about the doing than the thing done (for which we use the noun act). Action is often associated with movement, since the perception of movement is often our best clue that someone has acted. When action is used before a noun, this association with movement is strongest (action figure, action sequence). The verb action is relatively new, can be considered jargon, and means cause to be acted upon.

Actions are things done—deeds, behaviors, or movements as distinct from thoughts, words, or plans. {Actions speak louder than words.} In law, an action is a lawsuit or legal proceeding. In storytelling, the action is what happens—the events that drive the plot. The call {Action!} signals actors to begin a scene.

To activate something is to make it active or operational—to set it in motion or trigger its function: {Activate the alarm before you leave}, {The card activates automatically after your first purchase}. In biology, enzymes or genes are activated when switched on. In military contexts, to activate a unit is to call it into service. The word implies moving something from a dormant or standby state to a working one.

Active describes something in motion, operation, or engagement rather than at rest. An active {volcano} may erupt; an active {member} participates regularly. Active contrasts with passive or dormant: {She took an active role in the negotiations}. In grammar, the active voice has the subject performing the action rather than receiving it. Active can also mean currently in effect: {an active warrant}, {active duty}.

Activism is organized effort to bring about political or social change. Activists campaign, protest, march, and advocate for causes—civil rights, environmental protection, labor conditions. The word can carry positive connotations of principled engagement or negative ones suggesting disruptive agitation, depending on the speaker's sympathies: {Her activism got her arrested twice}. {Keyboard activism} or {armchair activism} dismisses online advocacy as inadequate substitute for real-world action.

An activist is someone who campaigns vigorously for political or social change. The word implies sustained effort beyond voting or casual opinion—organizing, protesting, lobbying, or direct action: {She's been a climate activist for years}. Activist can modify nouns to suggest aggressive pursuit of an agenda: an activist {judge} interprets law expansively rather than deferentially.

Activity is doing something, as opposed to remaining passive or at rest. The word covers both the general state of being active and specific things people do: {outdoor activities}, {extracurricular activities}, {criminal activity}. Physical activity means exercise or movement. Brain activity refers to neural functioning. When there's {activity} in a place, things are happening there—people moving, events unfolding.

An actor is a person who performs in plays, films, or television, portraying characters through speech, gesture, and movement. The word applies to performers of any gender, though actress persists for women. Beyond entertainment, actor extends to anyone who takes action or plays a role: {a bad actor in the industry}, {state actors in international affairs}. In legal and political contexts, an actor is any entity capable of action.

An actress is a woman who performs in plays, films, television, or other dramatic productions. The word distinguishes female performers from actors, though actor increasingly serves as the gender-neutral term for performers of any sex. Some women prefer actress; others find the distinction unnecessary or diminishing. {She's a trained actress with years of stage experience.}

Acts are things done—deeds, performances, or segments of a play or show. An act of {kindness} is a kind deed. A circus has multiple acts. Someone who puts on an act is pretending: {Her confidence was just an act}. In law, an act is a statute passed by a legislature. To act is to do something, perform a role, or behave in a certain way: {She acted surprised}. (Capitalized Acts is the biblical book.)

Acupuncture is a medical practice originating in China in which thin needles are inserted into specific points on the body. Traditional Chinese medicine holds that this regulates the flow of life energy (qi) through pathways called meridians. Western medicine uses acupuncture primarily for pain management, though evidence for its effectiveness varies. {She tried acupuncture for her chronic back pain.}

Acute means sharp or intense. An acute angle is less than 90 degrees—sharper than a right angle. Acute pain is severe; acute hearing is highly sensitive. An acute illness comes on suddenly and intensely but briefly, unlike a chronic one that persists: {acute bronchitis}. Acute awareness or acute observations are penetratingly sharp. The accent mark (´) is called an acute accent.

Adamant describes an unwillingness to change one's mind or position, regardless of arguments or appeals. Someone who is adamant about something refuses to be persuaded otherwise: {She was adamant that we leave by noon}. The word suggests firmness that borders on stubbornness, though it can be used approvingly when the position seems justified. Originally adamant was a noun referring to an impossibly hard substance, which explains why the adjective conveys such unyielding resolve.

To adapt is to adjust to new conditions or make something suitable for a new purpose. Organisms adapt to environments; people adapt to circumstances; books are adapted into films. The word implies modification rather than wholesale replacement—keeping the essential while changing what's necessary. {It took months to adapt to the new time zone.} {The novel was adapted for television.}

Adaptable describes someone or something capable of adjusting to new conditions. An adaptable person handles change without difficulty: {She's remarkably adaptable—she thrived in three different countries}. The word applies to things designed for flexibility: {an adaptable floor plan}, {adaptable software}. In biology, adaptable species survive environmental shifts that doom others.

Adaptation is the process of adjusting to new conditions, or the result of that adjustment. In biology, it refers to evolutionary changes that help organisms survive in their environment: {The camel's hump is an adaptation for desert life}. More broadly, anything modified to fit new circumstances is an adaptation: {The film is an adaptation of her novel}. To adapt is the verb; adaptable describes something capable of change.

Adat is customary law or traditional practice in Southeast Asian and Indonesian societies, governing social behavior, rituals, and community relations. The term encompasses unwritten rules passed down through generations, often existing alongside formal religious or state law: {The village settled disputes according to adat rather than the courts}. In Malaysian and Indonesian contexts, adat carries strong cultural weight, representing indigenous tradition distinct from Islamic law.

To add is to combine or include—putting numbers together to find a sum, or putting things together to make more: {Add two cups of flour}. To add is also to say something further: {I have nothing to add}. Adding to something increases it: {The news only added to her anxiety}. Something that {adds up} makes sense or accumulates meaningfully.

An addict is someone who cannot stop using a substance or engaging in a behavior despite harmful consequences. The word most often applies to dependency on drugs or alcohol, but extends to gambling, gaming, shopping, or anything that produces compulsive engagement. As a verb (stressed on the second syllable), addict means to cause someone to become dependent: {Video games addicted him to screens}. In casual use, people claim to be addicted to things they simply enjoy a lot: {I'm addicted to this show}.

Addicted describes a state of compulsive dependence. The core meaning involves physical or psychological reliance on a substance: {addicted to heroin}, {addicted to nicotine}. The word extends to behavioral compulsions: {addicted to gambling}, {addicted to social media}. Casual use describes strong enthusiasm: {I'm addicted to this show}. Someone who is addicted is an addict.

Addiction is compulsive engagement with something despite harmful consequences. The term traditionally applied to substance dependence—alcohol, heroin, nicotine—where the body develops tolerance and withdrawal symptoms. Usage has expanded to behavioral patterns: {gambling addiction}, {social media addiction}, {addiction to drama}. The looser sense risks trivializing clinical addiction, but reflects genuine experiences of feeling unable to stop. Someone can be {addicted to} exercise or {addicted to} approval. An addict is one who suffers from addiction.

Addictive describes something that creates dependency or is hard to stop once started. Drugs can be physically addictive, altering brain chemistry until the body craves them. But addictive also applies to compelling experiences: {This show is addictive}, {addictive gameplay}. The figurative use suggests something so pleasurable or engaging that you keep coming back.

Addition is the mathematical operation of combining quantities: {What's the addition of seven and five?} More broadly, it means anything added: {The new wing is an addition to the library}, {She's the latest addition to our team}. The phrase {in addition} means also or furthermore. {In addition to} means besides: {In addition to his salary, he receives bonuses}.

Technology has considerably increased the workload of address, since everything that lives on a computer must have an address. In addition, address denotes the particulars of a place where someone lives or works, and also serves as a synonym for speech in some contexts: Who gave the address at your graduation ceremony? The meaning of the verb address varies according to its subjects and objects. If you address a package, you write its destination on it. If you address an audience, you speak to them, usually in a formal way.
Adios is an exclamation or noun meaning goodbye or farewell. It is a single word in Spanish, but is a combination of two words: a dios, which translates as to God.

Adjacent means next to or nearby in space. Adjacent rooms share a wall; adjacent properties share a boundary. The word often implies direct contact without anything between: {The park is adjacent to the school}. In casual use, adjacent has loosened to mean closely related or associated: {His interests are adjacent to mine}. Online, X-adjacent describes proximity to a category without full membership: {podcast-adjacent content}, {theater-adjacent careers}.

Adjust means to change or move something slightly to achieve a better fit, position, or result. You adjust a thermostat to change the temperature, adjust your grip on a tennis racket, or adjust the rearview mirror before driving. The word extends to non-physical contexts: you might adjust your expectations, adjust to a new time zone, or adjust your strategy when circumstances change. {It took me a few weeks to adjust to the new job.} An adjustment is an instance of adjusting.

Adjustment is the act of making something fit better or work more effectively. You make adjustments to a plan, a thermostat, or your expectations. An adjustment can be a small correction: {a minor adjustment to the recipe}. It also names the process of adapting to new circumstances: {The adjustment to college life took a few months}. In insurance, adjustment is the settlement of a claim.

To adlib is to speak or perform without preparation, improvising in the moment. The term comes from Latin *ad libitum* (at pleasure). An adlib is an unscripted remark or action: {The best line in the movie was actually an adlib}. As an adverb, it means freely or spontaneously: {She spoke adlib for twenty minutes}. Also spelled ad-lib.

Adlibbing is speaking or performing without preparation, improvising in the moment rather than following a script: {The teleprompter broke, so she spent the last five minutes adlibbing}. Musicians adlib when they depart from written arrangements. The term comes from the Latin phrase ad libitum, meaning "at pleasure."

Admin is short for administrator or administration—someone who manages systems, organizations, or online spaces, or the work of doing so. In computing, an admin has elevated privileges to configure settings and manage users: {You'll need admin access to install that}. The word functions as noun or adjective: {Ask the admin}, {admin rights}, {admin duties}.

Administration is the management or direction of affairs—running an organization, institution, or government. In American politics, an administration is a president's term and the officials who serve under them: {the Biden administration}, {the Reagan administration}. The word also covers the act of giving or applying something: the administration of {justice}, the administration of {medicine}. Administrative work handles logistics and paperwork rather than core activities: {administrative duties}, {administrative assistant}.

An administrator manages or directs the affairs of an organization, institution, or estate. School administrators oversee operations rather than teach. A court may appoint an administrator to handle a deceased person's estate. In computing, an administrator (or admin) has elevated privileges to configure systems and manage user accounts: {You need administrator access to install that software}.

An admiral is a high-ranking naval officer, typically among the highest grades in a navy's command structure. The rank appears in compounds indicating relative seniority: rear admiral, vice admiral, fleet admiral. Extended to non-military contexts, admiral can denote leadership of any fleet: {the admiral of the yacht club}. A red admiral is a common butterfly with distinctive wing markings.

Admirals is the plural of admiral, a high-ranking naval officer. The word extends to certain butterflies with bold wing markings, particularly the red admiral and white admiral. In casual speech, admirals may refer collectively to naval leadership: {The admirals opposed the budget cuts}.

Admiration is a feeling of warm approval and respect for someone or something impressive. You might feel admiration for a person's courage, talent, or accomplishments: {She spoke of her grandfather with great admiration}. The word suggests looking up to rather than down on—genuine esteem, not mere tolerance. {I have nothing but admiration for what you've done}.

To admire is to regard with respect, approval, or wonder. You admire someone's courage, a painter's technique, or the view from a mountaintop. The word suggests looking at something with appreciation: {She stood back to admire her work}. Admiration can shade into romantic interest—an admirer may be a suitor—but the core meaning is esteem without possession.

An admirer is someone who regards another with respect, approval, or affection. The word often implies romantic interest, especially when unspoken: {She has a secret admirer}. More broadly, admirers are fans or appreciators: {He attracted admirers wherever he performed}. {I'm an admirer of her early work}.

Admission is the act of being allowed entry or the fee required for it: {Admission to the museum is free on Sundays}. It also means acknowledgment of something typically unfavorable: {His silence was an admission of guilt}. By extension, admission covers acceptance into an institution: {college admissions}, {hospital admission}. To {gain admission} is to be let in, physically or figuratively.

Admissions is the process or department handling entry into institutions—colleges, hospitals, theaters. {The admissions office reviews applications}. A university's admissions rate indicates selectivity. The word also means acknowledgments of truth, especially uncomfortable ones: {His admissions in court damaged his case}. An admission is a single instance; admissions names the ongoing function or multiple instances.

Admit means to allow entry: {The ticket admits one person}. It also means to confess or acknowledge something, often reluctantly: {He admitted he was wrong}, {She admitted to the crime}. A third sense involves accepting something as valid: {The evidence was admitted in court}. To admit of something is to allow for its possibility: {The situation admits of no delay}.

Adobe is sun-dried brick made from clay mixed with straw or other organic material, used for building in arid climates. The term extends to structures built with such bricks: {an adobe house}, {adobe walls}. The material has been used for thousands of years in the American Southwest, Mexico, and the Middle East, where the dry climate prevents the unbaked bricks from dissolving. (Capitalized Adobe is the software company.)

Adolescence is the period of life between childhood and adulthood, roughly the teenage years. The transition involves physical, emotional, and social changes—puberty, identity formation, increasing independence. {Her adolescence was marked by rebellion and experimentation.} The adjective is adolescent, which as a noun refers to a person in this stage.

Adolescent describes the period between childhood and adulthood, roughly the teenage years. As a noun, an adolescent is a person in this stage: {The clinic treats adolescents ages 12 to 18}. The adjective often carries connotations of immaturity or awkwardness: {adolescent behavior}, {adolescent insecurities}. Used dismissively, it suggests someone acting younger than their years: {His adolescent jokes weren't funny}.

Adolescents are young people in the transitional stage between childhood and adulthood, roughly the teenage years. The term emphasizes developmental change—physical, emotional, and social—more than a specific age range. {The program targets at-risk adolescents.} {Adolescents are particularly susceptible to peer pressure.} The singular adolescent also functions as an adjective: {adolescent behavior}, {adolescent angst}.

Adopt means to take something as your own. You adopt a child by legally becoming their parent, or adopt a pet by taking it home from a shelter. More abstractly, you adopt a {policy}, an {attitude}, a {strategy}, or a {way of life}—choosing to embrace something that wasn't originally yours. A legislative body adopts a {resolution} by formally accepting it. {We adopted a wait-and-see approach.}

Adopted describes someone or something taken as one's own. An adopted child has been legally made part of a family not biologically their own: {She was adopted at age three}. The word extends to anything chosen rather than inherited: an adopted {country}, an adopted {name}. To call a hometown one's {adopted city} suggests chosen belonging rather than native roots.

Adoption is the legal process of taking another's child as your own, with all the rights and responsibilities of a biological parent: {They finalized the adoption last month}. The word extends to accepting or taking up something new: the adoption of new {technology}, the adoption of a {resolution}, the adoption of foreign {customs}. A country or city of adoption is one you've chosen as home rather than being born there.

Adorable describes something that inspires immediate affection—typically because it's cute, endearing, or charming. Babies, puppies, and kittens are reliably adorable. The word applies most naturally to small, vulnerable things but extends to behavior and objects: {What an adorable little cottage}. When directed at adults, adorable can feel patronizing, though it's often meant warmly: {You're adorable when you're flustered}.

Adoration is intense love, devotion, or worship. The word suggests reverence beyond ordinary affection—the adoration of a deity, a parent's adoration of their child, or a fan's adoration of a celebrity. {She looked at him with adoration}. In religious contexts, adoration specifically means worship of the divine.

Adore means to love deeply or regard with the highest affection: {She adores her grandchildren}. It can also mean to worship, as in religious devotion: {They gathered to adore the sacred relics}. In casual use, adore expresses strong enthusiasm: {I adore this restaurant}, {He adores Italian cinema}. The casual sense is lighter than the romantic or religious ones.

Adoring describes a feeling of deep love, admiration, or worship toward someone or something. An adoring {fan} gazes at their idol with visible devotion; adoring {parents} beam at their child's every accomplishment. The word suggests warmth and tenderness rather than distant reverence. {She gave him an adoring look across the room.} Adoring can shade into excessive or uncritical devotion, as when critics dismiss an adoring {audience} as too easily pleased.

Adrenalin is a hormone released by the adrenal glands in response to stress or excitement, triggering the body's fight-or-flight response—increased heart rate, heightened alertness, surging energy. Figuratively, adrenalin describes any rush of excitement or intensity: {The adrenalin was pumping as we approached the finish line}. Also spelled adrenaline.

Adrenaline is a hormone released by the adrenal glands in response to stress or excitement, triggering the body's fight-or-flight response—increased heart rate, heightened alertness, surge of energy. The word often describes the feeling itself: {an adrenaline rush}, {pure adrenaline}. Thrill-seekers chase it; performers channel it. An {adrenaline junkie} craves dangerous or exciting activities.

Adrift means floating without direction, not anchored or moored: {The boat was set adrift}. Extended meanings preserve the sense of lacking guidance or purpose. A person adrift is without clear direction in life: {After graduation, she felt adrift}. Plans that go adrift fail or go astray. To come adrift is to become unfastened or detached.

Ads is the plural of ad, short for advertisement. These are promotional messages designed to sell products, services, or ideas: {The Super Bowl ads cost millions to produce}. Online ads appear as banners, pop-ups, or sponsored content. {I can't watch anything without sitting through ads first}. (All-caps ADS is a technical acronym.)

An adult is a fully grown person or animal, past the stage of childhood or adolescence. The line between child and adult falls somewhere in the late teens, though legal definitions vary by context—voting, drinking, contracts. As an adjective, adult describes things intended for or involving grown-ups: {adult responsibilities}, {adult content}. The latter often euphemizes sexual material: {an adult bookstore}, {adult entertainment}.

Adultery is voluntary sexual intercourse between a married person and someone who is not their spouse. The term carries strong moral and legal weight, appearing in religious prohibitions and historically in criminal statutes. In many jurisdictions, adultery remains grounds for divorce. The person who commits adultery is an adulterer (or adulteress, though this gendered form is increasingly dated). {She filed for divorce after discovering his adultery.} The adjective adulterous describes relationships, affairs, or behavior involving such infidelity.

Adulthood is the state of being fully grown—physically mature and legally responsible. The transition from childhood through adolescence to adulthood happens gradually, though law draws sharp lines: {She reached adulthood at eighteen}. Adulthood carries connotations of independence, responsibility, and self-sufficiency: {The responsibilities of adulthood hit him hard}.

Adulting is the practice of handling responsibilities associated with adulthood—paying bills, doing laundry, scheduling appointments, cooking meals.
