The term emerged from younger generations and carries self-aware humor about finding basic adult tasks challenging or tedious: {I spent all Saturday adulting—groceries, cleaning, taxes}. It often implies that maturity is something performed rather than achieved.

Adults are people who have reached full physical maturity and legal majority—typically eighteen in most contexts. The word often implies responsibility, independence, and the capacity to make binding decisions. As an adjective, adult describes things intended for mature audiences, especially sexual content: {adult entertainment}, {adult bookstore}. To adult as a verb, recent slang, means to handle grown-up responsibilities: {I spent Saturday adulting—laundry, taxes, the whole thing}.

As both noun and verb, advance is associated with forward movement or progress and is the opposite of retreat or setback. In some fixed phrases and as an adjective, advance has the sense of beforehand. You can plan a meeting in advance or give someone advance notice of an event. If you advance money to someone, you give it to them before it is expected or due, and often as a loan.

Advanced describes something beyond the basic or elementary level. Advanced {math} requires prior knowledge. Advanced {technology} represents the cutting edge. An advanced {student} has progressed past beginners. Advanced can also mean far along in development or time: {advanced age}, an {advanced stage} of disease. To pay {in advance} is to pay beforehand.

Advancement is forward movement or progress toward a goal. Career advancement means moving up in position or status. The advancement of knowledge or technology refers to its development and improvement over time. An advancement can also be money given before it's due: {She received an advancement on her salary}. To work for the advancement of a cause is to promote it.

Advances covers forward movement in multiple domains. Troops advance on a position; technology advances over decades. An advance is progress or improvement: {recent advances in medicine}. Advances also means money paid before it's due—an advance on your salary, or the advance a publisher pays an author. In the plural, advances often means romantic or sexual approaches: {She rejected his advances}. These may be welcome or unwelcome; {unwanted advances} is a common phrase in discussions of harassment.

Advantage is a favorable position or circumstance that increases chances of success: {Her experience gave her an advantage over other candidates}. In tennis, advantage is the point scored after deuce. To {take advantage of} something is to make use of it; to take advantage of someone is to exploit them unfairly. The verb advantage means to benefit: {The new policy advantages larger corporations}.

Advent refers to the arrival or emergence of something notable or long-awaited: {the advent of the internet}, {the advent of spring}. The word carries a sense of momentousness—you wouldn't use it for ordinary arrivals. It suggests something that changes circumstances or marks a new era. (Capitalized Advent is the Christian season before Christmas.)

Adventure is an exciting or risky undertaking, typically involving the unknown: {an adventure in the mountains}, {her adventures abroad}. The word suggests both danger and possibility—something out of the ordinary that tests you. As a verb, to adventure is to venture forth boldly, though this use is now rare. An {adventure story} features daring exploits. To seek adventure is to court the unpredictable.

An adventurer is someone who seeks out exciting or risky experiences, often involving travel to unfamiliar places: {The adventurers set off into uncharted jungle}. The word can carry romantic connotations of boldness and discovery, but historically it also meant someone who lives by their wits—a fortune hunter or schemer willing to take chances for personal gain. In gaming, adventurer is the standard term for a player character who explores dungeons and completes quests.

Adventurers are people who seek out exciting, risky, or unusual experiences. The word often suggests boldness and a willingness to face danger: {Renaissance adventurers sailed into uncharted waters}. It can carry a negative shade—implying recklessness or fortune-seeking at others' expense: {political adventurers}, {financial adventurers}. In gaming, adventurers are player characters who explore dungeons, complete quests, and battle monsters.

Adventures are exciting or unusual experiences, often involving risk, danger, or the unknown. The word carries a sense of venturing forth—leaving the familiar behind. A person might recount their adventures abroad or seek adventures in the wilderness. Children's stories often center on adventures. In a looser sense, any undertaking with uncertain outcome qualifies: {Starting the business was quite an adventure}. The singular adventure works as both noun and verb: to adventure into unfamiliar territory is to explore it boldly.

Adventurous describes a willingness to take risks or try new things. An adventurous {traveler} seeks out unfamiliar places; an adventurous {eater} samples exotic cuisines. The word implies excitement rather than recklessness—adventure as opportunity, not danger. {She's always been adventurous, the first to suggest we try something new.}

Adversaries are opponents or enemies—those who stand against you in conflict, competition, or disagreement. The word carries more weight than mere competitors; adversaries actively oppose each other's interests or goals. {The two lawyers were longtime adversaries in the courtroom}. The singular is adversary.

An adversary is an opponent or enemy—someone who stands against you in conflict, competition, or dispute. The word carries more weight than opponent, suggesting genuine opposition rather than mere competition: {The two lawyers were longtime adversaries}. In religious contexts, the Adversary (capitalized) refers to Satan.

Adversity is hardship, difficulty, or misfortune. The word typically describes challenging circumstances rather than momentary setbacks: {She showed remarkable strength in the face of adversity}. People speak of overcoming adversity or thriving despite it. The phrase {in adversity} suggests difficult times generally: {True friends reveal themselves in adversity}.

To advertise is to make something publicly known, typically to promote a product, service, or event: {They advertised the sale in the local paper}. Companies advertise to attract customers; individuals advertise to sell belongings or find jobs. The word extends to unintentional disclosure—you {advertise your intentions} when your behavior reveals them, or {advertise your ignorance} by speaking carelessly.

An advertisement is a public announcement promoting a product, service, or event—typically paid for by whoever wants attention drawn to it. Advertisements appear in newspapers, on television, online, on billboards, and anywhere else people might see or hear them. Often shortened to ad or, in British English, advert. {I saw an advertisement for cheap flights}. The word sometimes extends to anything that showcases qualities: {His behavior was not a good advertisement for the company}.

Advertising is the practice of promoting products, services, or ideas through paid messages in media. The word covers both the industry and its output: {She works in advertising}; {I hate the advertising on this site}. To advertise is to make something publicly known, whether through formal campaigns or casual mention: {He's always advertising his accomplishments}.

Advice is most commonly used with verbs of giving, receiving, seeking, and following because that’s what people do with it. Advice has a predictable relationship with its related verb advise for British spellers who have other such pairs, such as license and licence, but this rule does not hold in U.S. English. Advice does not have a plural, so if you need to break it into separate bits, the phrase piece of advice comes in handy.

When you advise someone you give them a recommendation about what to do or not do. In other words, you give them advice. The typical way to use advise is preceding an infinitive phrase: I advise you to shop around before you settle on a doctor. When advise is followed by a clause beginning with a question word, its meaning is not so much about advice as it is simple information: We were advised that the road to the park was still closed. The same is true when an of phrase follows: The suspect was advised of his rights.

Someone who gives advice, especially in a professional or official capacity. An adviser may guide students on academic matters, counsel executives on strategy, or help individuals with finances. The spelling advisor is equally common and carries no difference in meaning. {She served as a foreign policy adviser to three presidents.}

An advisor is someone who gives advice, especially in an official or professional capacity: a financial {advisor}, a campaign {advisor}, a faculty {advisor}. The role implies expertise and ongoing consultation rather than casual suggestion. Also spelled adviser, with no difference in meaning—both are standard.

Advocacy is the act of publicly supporting or arguing for a cause, policy, or person. An advocacy {group} works to influence public opinion or legislation. The word implies active effort beyond mere agreement—advocates speak up, organize, and push for change: {She devoted her career to advocacy for disability rights}.

Advocate has two pronunciations that distinguish the noun from the verb. The verb has a long ‘a’ in the last syllable. To advocate something, or advocate for something, is to promote it and work for it to succeed or prevail: They advocated the use of force. The organization advocates for pay equality. An advocate (unstressed vowel in the last syllable) is someone who promotes a particular idea, cause, or course of action: Sojourner Truth was a women’s rights advocate. In legal contexts an advocate is someone who pleads the cause of another.

Aequorin is a protein from jellyfish that emits blue light when it binds calcium ions. It revolutionized cell biology by allowing researchers to track calcium movement inside living cells—a breakthrough that earned its discoverers a Nobel Prize. {The team used aequorin to visualize calcium signaling in neurons.}

Aerial describes things relating to the air or atmosphere, or things that occur in the air. An aerial {photograph} is taken from above, typically from an aircraft. Aerial {acrobatics} happen high off the ground. The word also functions as a noun for an antenna, especially in British English: {the TV aerial on the roof}. In sports like skiing and skateboarding, an aerial is a maneuver performed in midair. The adjective can suggest lightness or ethereal quality: {the aerial grace of the dancers}.

Aerobics is vigorous physical exercise designed to strengthen the heart and lungs by increasing oxygen consumption. The term typically refers to structured workout routines—often set to music—involving sustained rhythmic movement: {She teaches an aerobics class at the gym}. The adjective aerobic describes any activity requiring increased oxygen intake: aerobic {exercise}, aerobic {fitness}.

Aesthetic is a formal adjective that is used mainly to talk about beauty and the role it plays in art. The nouns that keep company with aesthetic are typically abstract, such as value, experience, quality, and appeal. When aesthetic modifies words like theory or principle it is about the various ideas that thinkers have had about how and why it is that we perceive, understand, and appreciate beauty. The spelling esthetic is sometimes used in U.S. English.

Aesthetics is the branch of philosophy concerned with beauty and taste—what makes things pleasing to perceive. More practically, aesthetics refers to the visual principles or style of something: {The restaurant's aesthetics are minimalist}, {She has great aesthetics}. In casual use, aesthetic (singular) now works as both noun and adjective: {That's very aesthetic}, {cottagecore aesthetic}. The word implies attention to how things look and feel rather than how they function.

An affair is a matter or concern requiring attention: {affairs of state}, {put your affairs in order}. It can mean an event or social gathering: {The wedding was an elegant affair}. Most distinctively, an affair is a romantic or sexual relationship outside marriage or a committed partnership: {He's having an affair with his secretary}. The word implies something ongoing rather than a single encounter.

Affairs are matters requiring attention or management: {business affairs}, {foreign affairs}, {put your affairs in order}. The word often implies complexity or importance—financial affairs, affairs of state. In the singular, an affair is an event or occasion, often elaborate: {a black-tie affair}. An affair is also a romantic or sexual relationship outside marriage: {He's having an affair with his secretary}.

Affected describes something influenced or changed by external forces: {The affected areas were evacuated}. More commonly, affected means artificial or pretentious—behavior or speech that feels put on rather than natural: {an affected British accent}, {Her laugh seemed affected}. The two senses come from different meanings of the verb affect: to influence versus to put on airs.

Affection is warm feeling toward another person—fondness short of passion but beyond mere liking. It implies caring attachment: {She felt deep affection for her grandmother}. The word suggests tenderness expressed through small gestures rather than grand declarations. In older or medical usage, affection could mean any condition affecting the body or mind: {a nervous affection}.

Affectionate describes someone who readily shows warmth and fondness through words, touch, or attention: {an affectionate child}, {an affectionate gesture}. It suggests tenderness without intensity—gentler than passionate, warmer than friendly. {She gave him an affectionate squeeze on the arm.}

In scientific writing, affinity refers to the attractions between substances or particles: The drug has a high affinity for the estrogen receptor. Affinity also is used to characterize attraction or liking for a person, subject, or pursuit: The new composition reflects the composer’s lifelong affinity for Russian music. Perhaps the most modern use of the word is in the compound affinity card, a credit card that provides some benefit for an organization that the card’s user wishes to support.

Affirm means to state positively or declare something to be true: {She affirmed her commitment to the project}. In legal contexts, to affirm is to uphold a lower court's decision or to make a formal declaration without swearing an oath. More broadly, affirm suggests validation or support: {The results affirmed what we already suspected}. To affirm someone is to express approval or encouragement of them.

Affirmation is a statement declaring that something is true, or the act of making such a declaration. In legal contexts, an affirmation serves the same function as an oath but without religious reference, for those who object to swearing. In popular psychology and self-help, affirmations are positive statements repeated to oneself to encourage confidence or change thinking patterns: {She starts each morning with affirmations about her worth}. To affirm something is to state it positively or to validate it.

Affliction is suffering or distress, or the condition causing it. The word carries weight—afflictions are serious troubles, not minor inconveniences: {chronic pain was her greatest affliction}, {the afflictions of poverty}. Disease, grief, and hardship are typical afflictions. The word often appears in religious or literary contexts, suggesting trials to be endured.

Affluence is wealth, especially the comfortable kind that allows for ease and luxury. The word often describes a general state of prosperity rather than specific riches: {suburban affluence}, {an era of affluence}. Someone living in affluence has more than enough money to meet their needs and desires.

Afford means to have enough resources—usually money or time—for something: {Can we afford a vacation this year?} {I can't afford to wait any longer}. The word implies weighing cost against capacity. Afford also means to provide or supply: {The balcony affords a view of the harbor}. This older sense survives mainly in formal contexts.

Affordable means priced within reach—not necessarily cheap, but manageable given one's resources. {Affordable housing} is priced for moderate incomes. {An affordable luxury} is an indulgence that won't break the bank. The word often appears in marketing to suggest value without implying low quality.

An aficionado is someone with keen interest and knowledge in a particular subject—originally bullfighting, but now applied broadly: {a jazz aficionado}, {an aficionado of fine wines}. The word carries more weight than "fan," suggesting genuine expertise and discriminating taste rather than mere enthusiasm.

Afloat means floating on water rather than sunk: {The ship stayed afloat through the storm}. By extension, it describes staying solvent or viable: {The business barely stayed afloat during the recession}. Rumors or ideas that are afloat are circulating: {There's a rumor afloat that the company is being sold}.

Afraid describes the state of feeling fear or apprehension. You can be afraid of something specific {(afraid of heights, afraid of the dark)} or afraid that something will happen {(I'm afraid we'll miss the flight)}. In polite speech, {I'm afraid} softens unwelcome news: {I'm afraid the doctor can't see you today}. Unlike scared, afraid rarely appears before a noun—you wouldn't say "an afraid child."

An afro is a hairstyle in which naturally curly hair—especially Black hair—is grown out and shaped into a rounded mass. The style became a cultural and political statement during the Black Power movement of the 1960s and 70s, signaling pride in natural Black features: {She's been growing out her afro for two years}. The word also functions as an adjective: {afro hairstyle}, {afro pick}.

Afros is the plural of afro, a hairstyle in which tightly curled hair grows out from the head in a rounded shape. The style became a symbol of Black pride and identity in the 1960s and 70s: {The old photos showed everyone rocking afros}. The name comes from African American.

After is frequent in expressions about both time and space. With reference to time, after is similar to past and later than. With reference to space, after is similar to behind. In figurative use, after relates to the idea of a goal, somewhat like at or toward: he came after me with a gun. After is also used to point out similarities between things that came before and things that came after: the boy is named after his grandfather; a painting styled after van Gogh. Though mainly a preposition, after can also be used as a conjunction to introduce a clause describing action before the main clause: She left after we had breakfast.

Aftercare is the support or treatment provided after a primary intervention. Medical aftercare follows surgery or hospitalization: {The clinic provides aftercare for knee replacement patients}. In BDSM contexts, aftercare refers to the emotional and physical attention partners give each other after intense sexual activity—checking in, cuddling, or tending to any discomfort. The term also applies to services for people leaving institutions like rehab or prison.

Afterglow is the light remaining in the sky after the sun has set, or the lingering glow from any faded light source. By extension, it describes the pleasant feeling that remains after a positive experience: {basking in the afterglow of victory}, {the afterglow of good sex}. The word suggests warmth slowly fading rather than abruptly ending.

Afterimages are visual impressions that persist after the original stimulus has been removed. Stare at a bright light, then look away—the lingering spot you see is an afterimage. They can appear in the same colors as the original (positive) or in complementary colors (negative). The term extends figuratively to any sensory or emotional impression that lingers: {The afterimages of war haunted him for years}.

The afterlife is existence after death—whatever form that takes in various belief systems. Heaven, hell, reincarnation, and ghostly persistence are all versions of an afterlife. The word also describes a later phase of something's existence: {The building had an afterlife as a community center}. {She didn't believe in an afterlife}.

Aftermath originally meant a second crop of grass growing after the first has been mowed—the "after-math" (math being an old word for mowing). Now it refers to the period or consequences following a significant event, usually a destructive or turbulent one: {the aftermath of the hurricane}, {in the aftermath of the scandal}. The word carries connotations of dealing with damage or sorting through what remains.

Afternoon is the part of the day between noon and evening, roughly from 12 PM to 6 PM. It appears in greetings {(good afternoon)} and time expressions {(this afternoon}, {tomorrow afternoon)}. In British English, afternoon tea is a light meal. As an adjective: {the afternoon sun}, {an afternoon nap}.

An afterparty is a gathering that follows a main event—typically held after a concert, wedding reception, awards ceremony, or club closing time. It's usually smaller, more intimate, and less formal than the preceding event: {The real fun happened at the afterparty}. Also spelled as two words: after party.

Aftershave is a scented liquid applied to the face after shaving. It typically contains alcohol or other astringents that tighten pores and prevent infection from small cuts. The term covers everything from medicinal-smelling drugstore staples to expensive colognes marketed as aftershave: {He slapped on some aftershave before his date}.

An aftershock is a smaller earthquake that follows a larger one, occurring as the earth's crust adjusts after the main seismic event: {Aftershocks continued for weeks after the initial quake}. Figuratively, aftershocks are the secondary effects or repercussions of any disruptive event: {The political aftershocks of the scandal were still being felt months later}.

Aftershocks are smaller earthquakes that follow a major seismic event, occurring as the earth's crust adjusts to the shift. They can continue for days, weeks, or even months after the initial quake. Figuratively, aftershocks are the secondary effects or repercussions of any disruptive event: {The political aftershocks of the scandal lasted for years}.

An aftertaste is a flavor that lingers in the mouth after eating or drinking something: {The wine left a bitter aftertaste}. The word extends to any residual impression or feeling that persists after an experience has ended: {The argument left an aftertaste of resentment}.

An afterthought is something thought of or added later, after the main matter has been settled or completed. The word often carries a dismissive edge—to call something an afterthought suggests it wasn't important enough to consider initially: {The garage was clearly an afterthought, tacked onto the house years later}. A person treated as an afterthought feels overlooked or secondary.
The core idea of again, an adverb, is more than once. Its other, less frequent uses all grow out of this idea. The common adverbial phrase again and again means repeatedly.

Against conveys the idea of opposition and is the commonest preposition after words suggesting conflict or competition such as game, war, fight, case, charge, and attack. Uses of against that aren’t nuanced with conflict refer to physical contact: lean the ladder against the wall. Against can also be used in comparing and contrasting two things: how do the benefits stack up against the risks?

Age is a noun that designates a length of time in which something existed or flourished: the age of dinosaurs, the age of steam engines. The age of a person or object is how old they are in years: At what age did you begin to date? If the unit is not years, it is usually specified: Babies ages newborn to 18 months. Middle age is a vague term applied to people from about 45 to 65 years old. Age or ages can also mean a very long time: We haven’t been back there for ages. As a verb, age refers to allowing something to reach maturity: I don’t think this beef was aged properly. When a person or something else ages, they get older.

Aged describes something that has grown old or been allowed to mature over time. Wine and cheese are aged to develop flavor; aged {beef} hangs to tenderize. An aged {person} is elderly. The word has two pronunciations: one syllable when describing matured products {(aged whiskey)}, two syllables for elderly people {(an aged widow)}. With a number, aged means having reached that age: {a child aged six}.

Ageing is the British spelling of aging—the process of growing older or the changes that come with time. Wine and cheese improve with ageing; skin and joints typically don't. As an adjective, it describes something showing signs of age: {an ageing infrastructure}, {an ageing population}. The spelling with the e is standard in British English and common in scientific literature worldwide.

Ageism is discrimination or prejudice based on a person's age. The term most often describes bias against older people—in hiring, healthcare, or social attitudes—but can apply to any age group: {Mandatory retirement policies are a form of ageism}. The word parallels racism and sexism in structure and meaning.

Ageless describes something or someone unaffected by age or the passage of time. An ageless {beauty} retains youthful appearance; an ageless {truth} remains valid across generations. The word suggests timelessness—neither old nor young, but somehow beyond such categories: {Her style is ageless}.

Agency is the capacity to act or exert power. A person with agency can make choices and influence outcomes: {The new policy gives employees more agency over their schedules}. An agency is also an organization that performs services—a government agency, a talent agency, an advertising agency. These senses connect: an agency acts on behalf of others, exercising delegated power.

An agenda is a list of items to be addressed, typically at a meeting: {What's on the agenda for today?} More broadly, it means a plan or set of goals: {The administration's policy agenda}. When someone is said to have {an agenda} or {a hidden agenda}, the implication is ulterior motives—purposes they haven't openly declared.

The many meanings of agent might be summarized as person in charge or doer, and range from general (one who acts, rather than being acted upon) to particular (one who represents an agency). The idea of representation is pervasive, where an organization or other entity is implied by the existence of an agent, or named (real estate agent, FBI agent).

Agents is the plural of agent—someone or something that acts or produces an effect. In business and entertainment, agents represent clients: {Her agents negotiated the contract}. In espionage, agents gather intelligence or conduct operations. Chemical agents cause reactions; cleaning agents remove dirt. In computing and AI, agents are autonomous programs that perform tasks: {The company deployed AI agents to handle customer inquiries}.

Ages is the plural of age, but more commonly appears as an informal intensifier meaning a very long time: {I haven't seen her in ages}, {It took ages to get through security}. The expression suggests duration that feels excessive or noteworthy, though the actual time varies by context—ages might be weeks, months, or years.

Aggravate means to make worse: {The medication aggravated her symptoms}, {His comments only aggravated the situation}. In common usage, aggravate also means to annoy or irritate: {Stop aggravating your sister}. This second sense, though widely used, is considered incorrect by some traditionalists who insist the word should only mean "worsen."

Aggravated intensifies wrongdoing or injury. An aggravated assault involves circumstances that make it more serious than simple assault—use of a weapon, intent to commit another crime, or attack on a protected person. Aggravated can also mean irritated or annoyed: {I was aggravated by the constant delays}. Legal and informal uses coexist, though purists sometimes object to the irritation sense.

Aggravating means making worse or more serious: {Smoking aggravated his asthma}. More commonly, it means annoying or irritating: {an aggravating habit of interrupting}. Purists insist on the first meaning, but the second dominates everyday speech. {Stop being so aggravating!}

Aggravation is the act of making something worse, or the state of being made worse: {The construction noise was an aggravation of an already stressful situation}. More commonly, aggravation means irritation or annoyance: {I don't need this aggravation right now}. The informal sense dominates everyday speech, while the formal sense—worsening of a condition or problem—persists in legal and medical contexts: {aggravation of a preexisting injury}.

Aggression is hostile or violent behavior toward others, often unprovoked: {an act of aggression}, {military aggression}. The word implies the aggressor initiates conflict rather than responding to it. In psychology, aggression covers a spectrum from verbal hostility to physical attack. {His aggression on the basketball court earned him technical fouls.}

Aggressive describes behavior that is forceful, hostile, or ready to attack. An aggressive {dog} may bite; an aggressive {driver} cuts people off. The word extends to any pushy or assertive approach: aggressive {marketing}, aggressive {treatment} of a disease. In sports and business, aggressive often carries positive connotations of boldness and competitive drive: {She took an aggressive approach to expanding the company}.

An aggressor is the party who initiates conflict or attack. The term implies fault—the aggressor started it, whether in a schoolyard fight, a war, or a legal dispute. {Russia was widely condemned as the aggressor in the conflict.} International law distinguishes aggressors from those acting in self-defense.

Agile describes quick, nimble movement—the ability to change direction easily and gracefully: {an agile climber}, {agile fingers on the keyboard}. The word extends to mental quickness: {an agile mind} adapts rapidly to new information. In software development, Agile (often capitalized) names a methodology emphasizing iterative progress, collaboration, and flexibility over rigid planning.

Agility is the ability to move quickly and easily, with nimble coordination: {The cat leaped with surprising agility}. The word extends beyond physical movement to mental quickness—the capacity to think and adapt rapidly: {intellectual agility}, {The startup's agility let it outmaneuver larger competitors}. In business contexts, agility often describes organizational flexibility and responsiveness to change.

Aging is the process of growing older or showing the effects of time. Wine ages in barrels; cheese ages in caves. An aging {population} has an increasing proportion of elderly people. The aging {process} refers to biological decline over time. As an adjective, aging describes something or someone showing signs of age: {an aging rock star}, {aging infrastructure}. Also spelled ageing, especially in British English.

Agitated describes a state of nervous excitement or troubled restlessness. Someone who is agitated may pace, fidget, or have difficulty staying calm: {The agitated passengers demanded answers about the delay}. The word applies equally to emotional upset and physical disturbance—water can be agitated by stirring, just as a person can be agitated by bad news. In clinical contexts, agitated often describes patients experiencing confusion or distress.

Agitation is a state of anxious unrest or troubled excitement. Someone in agitation paces, fidgets, or can't settle down: {She waited in agitation for the test results}. The word also means the act of stirring up—agitation of a liquid keeps particles suspended, while political agitation stirs up public sentiment for change.

An agitator is a person who stirs up public opinion or discontent, especially for political change: {union agitators}, {outside agitators blamed for the protests}. The word often carries negative connotations—implying troublemaking rather than principled activism. In machinery, an agitator is a device that shakes or stirs, as in a washing machine.

Agnostic can function as either a noun or an adjective, to denote a person or characterize a belief or point of view. An agnostic is someone who is either not firmly committed to a belief in God, or who holds that God is unknowable. Agnostic is sometimes used in contrast to atheist, which is a firm denial of the existence of God. Outside of religious contexts, agnostic is a way of characterizing their opinion about something that is not known with certainty: He is agnostic about whether early painters might have used mirrors to project images.

Agnosticism is the position that the existence of God or gods is unknown or unknowable. Unlike atheism, which denies the divine, agnosticism suspends judgment: {His agnosticism prevented him from joining either the church or the atheist society}. The term extends beyond religion to any stance of principled uncertainty: {scientific agnosticism about untestable claims}.

Ago marks time elapsed from the present backward: {three days ago}, {years ago}, {not long ago}. It always follows the time expression it modifies. The reference point is usually now, but in narrative can shift to a past moment: {She had arrived two hours ago}. {Long ago} reaches into the distant past; {a moment ago} barely precedes the present.

Agonising is the British spelling of agonizing. It describes something that causes intense physical or mental suffering: {an agonising wait for test results}, {the agonising pain of a broken bone}. It also characterizes difficult decisions or processes that involve great struggle: {After agonising deliberation, she chose to leave}.

To agonize is to suffer intense mental distress or to struggle painfully with a decision: {She agonized over whether to accept the job offer}. The word emphasizes prolonged inner turmoil rather than physical pain. Someone who agonizes dwells on a problem, turning it over repeatedly without resolution. Agonizing as an adjective describes something that causes such distress: {an agonizing wait for test results}.

Agonizing describes something that causes intense physical or mental suffering: {an agonizing decision}, {agonizing pain}. The word often applies to difficult choices where every option hurts: {After agonizing deliberation, she chose to end the relationship}. Something agonizing may also be unbearably slow or drawn out: {The agonizing wait for test results lasted two weeks}.

Agony is extreme physical or mental suffering—pain so intense it dominates consciousness. A person in agony writhes, cries out, can think of nothing else. The word applies to both bodily torment {the agony of a kidney stone} and emotional anguish {the agony of watching her marriage fall apart}. To {agonize} over a decision is to struggle painfully with it. {The agony of defeat} has become a sports cliché.

Agree means to share an opinion or reach a common understanding: {We agreed that the plan was too risky}. Two parties agree when they consent to terms: {They agreed on a price}. Things that agree are consistent or compatible: {Your story doesn't agree with the evidence}. Food that doesn't agree with you causes digestive trouble. In grammar, words agree when they match in number, gender, or case.

Agreed functions as an affirmation—a way of confirming that parties share the same understanding or have reached consensus: {We meet at noon? Agreed.} As an adjective, it describes something already settled or accepted by all involved: {the agreed price}, {the agreed-upon terms}. The word often closes negotiations or confirms mutual understanding.

Agreement is a state of harmony or accord between parties. When people reach an agreement, they've arrived at a shared understanding or decision: {We finally came to an agreement about the terms}. An agreement can be a formal arrangement—a contract, treaty, or settlement. In grammar, agreement refers to correspondence between words: subjects and verbs agree in number. {There was general agreement that changes were needed.}

Agriculture is the practice of cultivating land and raising animals for food, fiber, and other products. It encompasses farming crops, raising livestock, and the broader systems of production that feed populations. {The region's economy depends on agriculture.} Agricultural can describe anything related to farming: {agricultural policy}, {agricultural land}.

People say Aha! when they discover something or learn something, often something that they suspected was true. This has given rise to the expression aha moment, a moment when someone gains a sudden insight or suddenly understands what is happening.

Ahead means in front or in advance of a position. You walk ahead of someone, plan ahead for the future, or get ahead in your career. It suggests forward motion or progress: {The road ahead looks clear}, {She's ahead of schedule}. In competitions, being ahead means winning: {We're ahead by three points}. To go ahead is to proceed: {Go ahead and start without me}.
Ahem is meant to imitate the sound of someone clearing their throat, as when they are about to speak. It nearly always has a negative connotation.
Ahoy is historically associated with sailors but it works on land too. After a noun it indicates that the thing named is within view or on its way: ship ahoy!

Aid is help or assistance, especially of a practical or material kind. Countries send foreign aid—money, food, supplies—to those in need. A hearing aid assists with sound; a visual aid helps explain something. First aid is emergency medical care. To aid someone is to help them: {She aided the investigation}. An aide, spelled differently, is a person who assists.

An ailment is a minor illness or chronic condition—something that bothers you but isn't immediately life-threatening: {She suffers from various ailments}, {an ailment of the liver}. The word suggests ongoing discomfort rather than acute crisis. It sounds slightly old-fashioned, often appearing in contexts of persistent health complaints.

Ailments are minor illnesses or chronic conditions that cause discomfort without being immediately serious: {the usual ailments of old age}, {digestive ailments}, {He complained of various ailments}. The word suggests persistent but manageable troubles rather than acute disease. It often appears in the plural, implying a collection of health problems.

Aim is direction toward a target—either the act of pointing or the skill of doing it well: {Her aim was perfect; she hit the bullseye}. To aim is to direct something toward a goal, whether a weapon, a camera, or an effort: {He aimed the flashlight at the corner}, {The program aims to reduce poverty}. An aim is also a purpose or intention: {What's your aim here?}

Aimless describes movement or activity without purpose or direction. An aimless {walk} has no destination; an aimless {life} lacks goals. The word suggests drifting rather than choosing: {He spent his twenties in aimless wandering}. It can be gently critical or neutrally descriptive, depending on context.

Aims are goals or purposes—what someone intends to accomplish. The aims of an organization state what it hopes to achieve: {The committee outlined its aims for the coming year}. To aim is to point toward a target, literally with a weapon or figuratively with effort: {She aimed for the top of her class}. To {take aim} is to prepare to shoot or criticize.

Air has meanings that may seem unrelated, but that come together under the original meaning of breath. There is the air that we breathe and an air that someone sings (a tune or melody that requires breath). An air of mystery may surround someone, just like air surrounds us all. To air something is to expose it to fresh air; to air grievances or opinions is to expose them to others.

An airbag is a safety device in vehicles that inflates rapidly during a collision to cushion occupants and prevent them from striking hard surfaces. Airbags deploy from the steering wheel, dashboard, doors, or seats when sensors detect sudden deceleration. {The airbag saved her life in the crash.}

Airbags are safety devices in vehicles that inflate rapidly during a collision to cushion occupants. They deploy from the steering wheel, dashboard, or side panels when sensors detect sudden deceleration: {The airbags saved her life in the crash}. The term sometimes appears figuratively for any protective buffer against impact.

An airboat is a flat-bottomed boat propelled by an aircraft-type propeller and powered by an engine mounted above the waterline. The design allows navigation through shallow waters, swamps, and marshes where conventional propellers would snag on vegetation or bottom out. Airboats are common in the Florida Everglades for transportation, tours, and wildlife management: {We took an airboat through the swamp to see alligators}.

Airborne means carried through or suspended in the air. Diseases spread by {airborne transmission} travel on droplets or particles. {Airborne particles} float in atmosphere. The word also describes troops or operations involving aircraft deployment: {airborne divisions} parachute into combat zones. Once a plane leaves the ground, it's airborne: {We'll be airborne in ten minutes}.

An airbrush is a small, pen-shaped tool that sprays paint or ink using compressed air, producing fine, smooth gradients impossible with conventional brushes. Artists use airbrushes for illustration, photo retouching, and detailing. The verb means to alter an image—originally with the tool, now often digitally—to remove flaws or enhance appearance: {The magazine airbrushed her skin to perfection}. Figuratively, to airbrush is to sanitize or erase inconvenient facts: {The regime airbrushed dissidents from official photographs}.

Airbrushed describes something altered or enhanced using an airbrush—a tool that sprays fine mist of paint or ink. The technique smooths imperfections in photographs or artwork: {The magazine cover was heavily airbrushed}. Figuratively, airbrushed means sanitized or made artificially flawless: {an airbrushed version of history}, {Her social media presence feels airbrushed}.

Aircraft is a broad term for any vehicle designed to travel through the air, encompassing airplanes, helicopters, gliders, and drones. The word functions as both singular and plural: {one aircraft}, {several aircraft}. Military and aviation contexts favor this term over more specific words, giving it a somewhat formal or technical register. Commercial planes carrying passengers are aircraft, but so is a hot air balloon or a hang glider.

An airdrop is a delivery made by dropping supplies, equipment, or personnel from an aircraft, typically by parachute: {Humanitarian airdrops brought food to the besieged city}. In cryptocurrency and tech contexts, an airdrop is a distribution of free tokens or digital assets to wallet holders, often as a promotional tactic: {I got some free coins in the airdrop}. As a verb, to airdrop is to deliver by either method. On Apple devices, AirDrop is a feature for wirelessly transferring files between nearby devices: {Just AirDrop me those photos}. (Capitalized AirDrop is Apple's file-sharing feature.)

An airfield is an area of ground equipped for aircraft takeoffs and landings. The term encompasses everything from grass strips to major airports, though it often suggests a smaller or military facility: {The troops secured the airfield before dawn}. Unlike airport, airfield emphasizes the physical landing area rather than passenger terminals or commercial operations.

An airhead is a stupid or scatterbrained person, someone whose head seems filled with air rather than brains: {Don't be such an airhead—read the instructions}. The term is mildly insulting and often applied to women, though it can describe anyone perceived as ditzy or oblivious. In military contexts, an airhead is a secured area for receiving troops and supplies by air, analogous to a beachhead.

An airlift is the large-scale transport of people or supplies by aircraft, especially in emergencies or when ground routes are blocked: {the Berlin airlift}, {an airlift of refugees}. As a verb, to airlift is to transport by such means: {Helicopters airlifted survivors from the flood zone}.

An airline is a company that operates passenger or cargo flights on established routes. The term also refers to the route itself or the business of air transportation generally. {Which airline are you flying?} An airline can also be a tube supplying air, as to a diver or a pneumatic tool.

Airlines are companies that operate passenger and cargo flights. The word typically refers to commercial carriers rather than military aviation: {Which airlines fly direct to Tokyo?} An airline's identity encompasses its routes, fleet, and service reputation. The singular airline can also describe the industry collectively: {She's worked in airline for twenty years}.

An airlock is a chamber with two airtight doors that allows passage between environments at different pressures—typically between a pressurized spacecraft or submarine and the vacuum or water outside. Only one door opens at a time, preserving the pressure differential. The term extends to any trapped air bubble that blocks flow through a pipe or tube: {There's an airlock in the fuel line}.

Airlocks are chambers with two airtight doors that allow passage between environments with different pressures or atmospheres—as on spacecraft or submarines—without exposing either environment to the other. Only one door opens at a time. The term extends to any trapped air bubble that blocks flow in a pipe or system: {There's an airlock in the fuel line}.

An airplane is a powered flying vehicle with fixed wings that generate lift as it moves through air. Airplanes range from single-engine propeller craft to massive jets carrying hundreds of passengers. The word is standard in American English; British English prefers aeroplane. {Their airplane landed two hours late.}

Airplanes are powered aircraft with fixed wings that generate lift as they move through air. The word is American English; British English uses aeroplanes. Airplane covers everything from single-engine propeller craft to commercial jets: {We watched airplanes take off from the runway}. Paper airplanes are folded sheets thrown for amusement.

An airport is a facility where aircraft take off and land, equipped with runways, terminals, and services for passengers and cargo. Major airports function as transportation hubs connecting cities and countries: {We arrived at the airport three hours early}. Airport also works as a modifier: {airport security}, {airport lounge}, {airport novel}—the last being light reading bought for flights.

Airports are facilities where aircraft take off and land, equipped with runways, terminals, and services for passengers and cargo. The word typically refers to commercial aviation hubs: {We arrived at the airport two hours early}. Airport also functions as an adjective for things found there: {airport security}, {airport lounge}, {airport novel}—the last being light reading for travel.

An airship is a large aircraft that stays aloft through buoyancy rather than aerodynamic lift—essentially a steerable balloon. Unlike unpowered balloons, airships have engines and can be directed: {The airship floated over the stadium}. The rigid type with an internal frame was called a zeppelin. Airships dominated early aviation but largely disappeared after the Hindenburg disaster in 1937.

Airships are lighter-than-air aircraft that use gas—historically hydrogen, now helium—for buoyancy and engines for propulsion and steering. Unlike balloons, airships can be directed rather than merely drifting with the wind. The term covers rigid designs with internal frameworks (like the Hindenburg), semi-rigid types, and non-rigid blimps. {The airship drifted silently over the city.}

An airshow is a public event where aircraft perform aerial demonstrations and maneuvers. Military jets fly in formation, stunt pilots do acrobatics, and vintage planes make appearances. Airshows draw crowds who watch from the ground as pilots showcase speed, precision, and daring: {We took the kids to the airshow at the naval base}.

An airstrike is a military attack delivered by aircraft—bombers, fighter jets, helicopters, or drones dropping bombs or firing missiles at ground targets. The term appears frequently in news coverage of armed conflicts: {Coalition airstrikes targeted the weapons depot}. Also spelled air strike.

An airstrip is a runway for aircraft, typically a simple paved or cleared surface without the full facilities of an airport. Airstrips serve remote areas, small planes, or military operations: {The bush pilot landed on a dirt airstrip in the jungle}. Also called a landing strip.

Airtight describes something sealed so completely that air cannot pass through: {an airtight container}. The figurative sense dominates: an airtight argument or alibi has no gaps or weaknesses that opponents could exploit. {The prosecution's case was airtight.} The word implies invulnerability to challenge or escape.

Airtime is time allocated for broadcasting on radio or television: {The candidate bought airtime for campaign ads}. In telecommunications, airtime refers to minutes of mobile phone usage. More broadly, airtime means opportunity to speak or be heard: {The proposal didn't get much airtime in the meeting}. In action sports, airtime is time spent in the air during a jump.

The airwaves are radio frequencies used for broadcasting. The term treats the electromagnetic spectrum as a shared medium through which signals travel: {The song dominated the airwaves all summer}. Though technically imprecise—radio waves aren't "air"—the word evokes public broadcast space: {politicians flooding the airwaves with attack ads}.

Airy describes something characterized by air or its qualities: light, open, spacious, well-ventilated. An airy {room} has good airflow and feels bright and unconfined. The word extends to manner and attitude, where it suggests a casual, breezy, or even dismissive quality: {She gave an airy wave and walked off}. Airy can also mean lacking substance or practicality—an airy {promise} is one unlikely to be kept, and airy {speculation} floats untethered to facts.

An aisle is a passage between rows of seats or shelves—in theaters, airplanes, churches, supermarkets. The phrase {walk down the aisle} means to get married, from the church aisle a bride traditionally walks. In legislatures, {across the aisle} refers to cooperation between opposing parties, who sit on opposite sides: {reaching across the aisle}.

Aisles are the passageways between rows of seats or shelves—in theaters, airplanes, supermarkets, and churches. The church aisle leads to the altar, so to {walk down the aisle} is to get married. Someone who has you {rolling in the aisles} makes you laugh uncontrollably. In politics, {across the aisle} means between opposing parties, from the traditional seating arrangement in legislatures.

Ajar describes a door or other hinged barrier that is slightly open—not closed, but not wide open either: {She left the door ajar so the cat could come in}. The word almost exclusively modifies doors, gates, and similar openings.

Alabaster is a soft, fine-grained stone, typically white or translucent, used for carving ornamental objects and sculptures. The word often describes smooth, pale skin: {her alabaster complexion}. As an adjective, it suggests something white, smooth, and luminous: {alabaster columns}, {alabaster shoulders}.

Alakazam is a magic word spoken when performing a trick or conjuring something, like abracadabra or presto: {Alakazam! The rabbit appeared from the hat}. It evokes stage magic and theatrical flourish, often used playfully to suggest something has appeared or transformed as if by magic: {She waved her hand and—alakazam—dinner was ready}.

Alarm is a warning signal or the fear it provokes. An alarm alerts you to danger—a fire alarm, a burglar alarm, a alarm clock rousing you from sleep. The emotional response is also alarm: {The news caused widespread alarm}. To alarm someone is to frighten or disturb them: {I don't want to alarm you, but there's smoke coming from the kitchen}. False alarms trigger the warning without real danger.

Alarmed describes being suddenly worried or frightened by a perceived threat or danger: {I was alarmed by the strange noise downstairs}. It can range from mild concern to genuine fear. An alarmed {expression} shows visible worry. To become alarmed is to shift from calm to anxious: {Don't be alarmed—it's just a routine check}.

Alarming describes something that causes worry or fear—a warning sign that something may be wrong or dangerous. An alarming {rate of decline} suggests urgent concern. Alarming {news} makes you sit up and take notice. The word implies not just surprise but the sense that action may be needed: {The patient's symptoms were alarming}.

An albatross is a large seabird with exceptionally long wings, capable of gliding vast distances over open ocean. Figuratively, an albatross is a burden that weighs on someone, from the Coleridge poem where a sailor must wear a dead albatross around his neck as punishment: {Student debt has become an albatross for an entire generation}. In golf, an albatross is three strokes under par on a hole—rarer than an eagle.

Albatrosses is the plural of albatross, a large seabird with the longest wingspan of any living bird, capable of gliding vast distances over open ocean. In figurative use from Coleridge's poem, an albatross is a burden of guilt or responsibility that weighs on someone: {The failed project became an albatross around his neck}. In golf, an albatross is three under par on a single hole.

Albitization is a geological process in which existing minerals, especially feldspars, are replaced by albite—a sodium-rich mineral. The process typically occurs when hot, sodium-bearing fluids circulate through rocks, altering their composition. Albitization is significant in the study of ore deposits and rock metamorphism: {The granite showed extensive albitization along fracture zones}.

An album is a collection of items gathered in one place. Originally a blank book for photographs, stamps, or autographs: {a photo album}, {a stamp album}. In music, an album is a collection of songs released together, whether on vinyl, CD, or streaming platforms: {Their new album drops Friday}. The term persists even as physical formats fade.

Albums is the plural of album. An album is a collection of recordings released as a unit—originally vinyl records, now any format: {Their debut album went platinum}. The word also refers to a book with blank pages for collecting photographs, stamps, or other items: {a wedding album}, {a stamp album}. Digital photo albums organize images in folders or apps.

An alchemist is a practitioner of alchemy—the medieval pursuit of transforming base metals into gold and discovering an elixir of immortality. The term now applies figuratively to anyone who transforms ordinary materials into something valuable or magical: {He was an alchemist in the kitchen, turning simple ingredients into extraordinary dishes}.

Alchemists were medieval and early modern practitioners who sought to transform base metals into gold, discover the elixir of life, and unlock the secrets of matter. The term now applies to anyone who transforms things mysteriously or magically: {The chef is an alchemist, turning simple ingredients into something extraordinary}. In fantasy settings, alchemists brew potions and craft magical substances.

Alchemy was a medieval forerunner of chemistry, concerned with transforming base metals into gold and discovering an elixir of immortality. The practice blended proto-scientific experimentation with mystical and philosophical elements. Figuratively, alchemy describes any seemingly magical transformation: {the alchemy of turning a screenplay into a film}, {the strange alchemy between performer and audience}.

Alcohol is a class of organic compounds, but in everyday speech means ethanol—the intoxicating substance in beer, wine, and spirits. {She doesn't drink alcohol.} The word covers both the chemical and beverages containing it: {rubbing alcohol} versus {We need to buy alcohol for the party}. Someone {under the influence of alcohol} is intoxicated. Alcohol-free means containing none.

Alcoholic describes something containing or relating to alcohol: {alcoholic beverages}, {alcoholic content}. As a noun, an alcoholic is a person addicted to alcohol—someone whose drinking has become compulsive and damaging. The term carries clinical weight but also stigma; some prefer "person with alcohol use disorder." {His father was an alcoholic who couldn't hold a job.}

Alcoholics are people addicted to alcohol—those who drink compulsively despite harmful consequences to their health, relationships, or livelihood. The term implies a recognized condition rather than casual heavy drinking: {Alcoholics Anonymous}, {recovering alcoholics}. As an adjective, alcoholic describes drinks containing alcohol or things relating to alcoholism: {alcoholic beverages}, {an alcoholic parent}.

Alcoholism is addiction to alcohol—a chronic condition marked by compulsive drinking despite harmful consequences. The term covers both physical dependence, where the body requires alcohol to function normally, and psychological compulsion. {His alcoholism cost him his marriage and his job.} Medical contexts increasingly favor "alcohol use disorder" as a less stigmatizing alternative.

An alcove is a recessed section of a room, set back from the main space. It might hold a bed, a reading nook, or a small dining area. The word extends to any sheltered recess: {an alcove in a rock face}, {a shady alcove in the garden}. Alcoves offer intimacy within larger spaces.

Alcoves are recessed areas or small spaces set back from a larger room. An alcove might hold a bed, a reading nook, or a statue. The word suggests intimacy and partial enclosure without full separation: {The restaurant had private alcoves for couples}. Architectural alcoves are built into walls; natural alcoves form in cliff faces or caves.

Ale is a type of beer brewed with top-fermenting yeast at warmer temperatures, producing a fuller-bodied, often fruitier flavor than lager. The term covers a wide range of styles: pale ale, brown ale, India pale ale. In casual use, ale and beer overlap, though ale technically names a brewing method: {a pint of ale}, {craft ales on tap}.

Alert describes a state of watchful readiness or keen attention. An alert {guard} stays vigilant; an alert {mind} catches details others miss. As a noun, an alert is a warning signal or notification: {a weather alert}, {phone alerts}. To alert someone is to warn them or bring something to their attention: {She alerted the authorities}.

Alfredo is a rich pasta sauce made from butter, cream, and Parmesan cheese, or a dish prepared with this sauce: {fettuccine alfredo}, {chicken alfredo}. The sauce originated in early 20th-century Rome but became an Italian-American staple, often richer and heavier than its Roman ancestor.

Algebra is the branch of mathematics that uses letters and symbols to represent numbers and quantities in equations and formulas. It moves beyond arithmetic's focus on specific numbers to explore general relationships and patterns. Elementary algebra, taught in middle and high school, covers solving equations and working with variables; abstract algebra, a university subject, studies mathematical structures like groups and rings. {I struggled with algebra until I understood that x was just a placeholder for an unknown number.}

An algorithm is an ordered series of steps that can be carried out to achieve a result. The term arose in the field of mathematics and is used today overwhelmingly in relation to computers, but any fixed sequence of actions can be described as an algorithm (such as the cooking instructions on a box of pasta).

An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure for solving a problem or completing a task. The term comes from mathematics and computing, where algorithms are precise sequences of instructions: {The algorithm sorted the data in milliseconds}. Usage has broadened to describe the automated systems that curate online content—what social media shows you, what ads follow you around: {The algorithm keeps recommending cat videos}. This sense often carries a note of suspicion or resignation about opaque systems controlling what we see.

Alias means otherwise called or otherwise known as, introducing an alternative name: {the hacker, alias "Zero Cool"}. As a noun, an alias is a false or assumed name: {He checked into the hotel under an alias}. In computing, an alias is a shortcut or alternate name for a file, command, or email address.

An alibi is evidence or a claim that a person was somewhere else when a crime or other event occurred, making their involvement impossible. {His alibi checked out—he was in Chicago when the robbery happened.} More loosely, alibi serves as an excuse or justification for any failure or wrongdoing: {She always has an alibi for why she's late.} As a verb, to alibi is to provide such an excuse, often with a suggestion of evasiveness.

A good way to corral all the meanings of alien is to remember that it comes from a word that means other in the sense of not you. Anything strange and unfamiliar can be called alien, especially if you also want to imply a dislike for it. As a noun, an alien is someone different from you because of their origin – in another country or on another planet.

To alienate is to make someone feel isolated or estranged. You might alienate friends by ignoring them, or alienate voters with unpopular policies. The word suggests pushing away people who were once close or sympathetic: {His arrogance alienated his colleagues}. In law, to alienate property is to transfer ownership to another party.

Alienated describes feeling isolated, estranged, or cut off from others, from society, or from something one was once connected to. An alienated {worker} feels disconnected from their labor or workplace; alienated {youth} feel they don't belong in mainstream society. The word carries connotations of emotional distance and disaffection. In legal contexts, alienated property has been transferred to another owner. {She felt increasingly alienated from her old friends after moving abroad.}

Alienating describes something that creates distance, hostility, or estrangement. An alienating {environment} makes people feel unwelcome or excluded. Alienating {behavior} pushes others away. The word often appears in criticism of institutions or attitudes that fail to connect with people: {The company's alienating policies drove away customers}. Something alienating leaves you feeling like an outsider.

Alienation is the state of being estranged or disconnected. You might feel alienation from family after a falling out, or alienation from society when its values don't match yours. In Marxist theory, alienation describes workers' disconnection from the products of their labor and from meaningful work itself. Legal alienation is the transfer of property to another owner.

Aliens are beings from somewhere else—either foreign nationals or, more vividly, extraterrestrial creatures. In legal contexts, an alien is someone who isn't a citizen: {resident alien}, {illegal alien}. In science fiction and popular imagination, aliens are life forms from other planets: {Do you believe in aliens?} The verb alien, rarely used, means to alienate or transfer property. To feel {alienated} is to feel like an outsider—alien to your surroundings.

Align means to arrange in a straight line or bring into proper position: {Align the text to the left margin}, {The chiropractor aligned my spine}. Extended meanings involve bringing things into agreement or coordination: {We need to align our goals with the company's mission}. Wheels are aligned when adjusted to the correct angle. People align themselves with causes or factions they support: {She aligned herself with the reformers}.

Aligned means arranged in a line or brought into proper position. Wheels are aligned when they point straight. Text can be left-aligned, right-aligned, or centered. The word extends to agreement or cooperation: {Their goals are aligned with ours}. In contemporary usage, aligned often describes shared values or worldview: {We're not politically aligned}. To be aligned with something is to support or identify with it.

Alignment is the arrangement of things in a straight line or proper position relative to each other: {Check the alignment of your tires}. Extended meanings involve being in agreement or accord: {political alignment}, {alignment with company values}. In fantasy games and fiction, alignment describes a character's moral orientation—good, evil, neutral, lawful, chaotic. In machine learning, alignment refers to ensuring AI systems behave according to human intentions and values.

Alike means similar or in the same way. Two things that look alike resemble each other: {The twins dress alike}. It often follows a pair: {young and old alike}, {critics and fans alike}—meaning both groups equally. As an adjective, alike is predicative only: you can say {they are alike} but not "alike people."

Alimony is money paid by one former spouse to support the other after divorce or separation. Courts typically award alimony when one spouse sacrificed career opportunities during the marriage or lacks earning capacity: {She's paying alimony to her ex-husband}. The amount and duration depend on factors like marriage length and financial disparity. Distinguished from child support, which covers children's expenses.

Alive is a predicate adjective (only used after a verb) that gets its meaning from the associated noun life. The literal meaning, having life, is extended to other things that exhibit characteristics of life, such as those that are active, energetic, aware, and healthy: Keep hope alive. Most of the figurative meanings of alive carry over to the more versatile adjective lively: The park was alive with butterflies.

Literally a catchall, this frequently used word can fill several grammatical slots: noun, pronoun, adjective, and adverb. The core idea of totality, wholeness, or completeness is expressed: All plants need sunlight. I was left all alone. Above all you must stay aware of the time. He ate all of the cake. All snags its place in dozens of idioms, though its meaning is diluted: With the weather and all, we just decided to stay home. He walked up to me all friendly and asked me to dance. Arguably, all is most diluted in the common expression at all, which conveys in the slightest degree, for any reason, in any way.

An allegation is a claim that someone has done something wrong or illegal, typically made without proof. The word carries an undertone of accusation—allegations are serious, often public, and imply wrongdoing that remains unverified: {The senator denied the allegations of corruption}. In legal contexts, allegations are formal claims in a complaint or indictment that must be proven at trial.

Allegations are claims or accusations, typically of wrongdoing, that have not been proven. The word implies uncertainty—an allegation may be true or false, substantiated or baseless. Legal and journalistic contexts favor the term precisely because it withholds judgment: {The senator denied the allegations of corruption}. {Multiple allegations of misconduct surfaced during the investigation}.

Alleged describes something claimed but not yet proven: an alleged {crime}, an alleged {victim}. The word signals that accusations exist without confirming their truth—a careful hedge in legal and journalistic contexts. {The alleged perpetrator was taken into custody}. Allegedly works the same way as an adverb: {He allegedly stole the money}.

Allegedly marks a claim as unproven—something asserted but not established as fact. The word appears constantly in news reporting to avoid libel: {The senator allegedly accepted bribes}. It signals that the speaker isn't vouching for truth. In casual speech, allegedly often carries skepticism or sarcasm: {He's allegedly working from home today}.

Allegiance is loyalty or commitment to a person, group, cause, or nation. The word often appears in formal contexts: citizens pledge {allegiance} to their country, vassals swore {allegiance} to their lords. Someone's allegiance can shift: {Her allegiance moved from the party to the movement}. Unlike loyalty, allegiance suggests a public or binding commitment rather than personal affection.

Allegiances are loyalties or commitments to a person, group, cause, or nation. The word typically appears in plural because people hold multiple loyalties that may conflict: {Her allegiances were divided between family and career}. To pledge allegiance is to formally declare loyalty, as in the American oath to the flag. Shifting or questioning allegiances often signals political or personal upheaval: {The scandal tested party allegiances}.

An allegory is an extended metaphor. While a metaphor represents one thing in terms of another, an allegory is a narrative in which abstract ideas (often relating to human existence) are represented with concrete or physical entities. A statue of Justice, depicted as a blindfolded woman holding scales, is an allegory. Most people think of an allegory as being narrative (as in a fable or fairytale) but an allegory can also be visual or musical.

Allergic describes a physiological sensitivity to a substance that causes an immune reaction: {allergic to peanuts}, {an allergic reaction to bee stings}. The condition is an allergy. Figuratively, allergic expresses strong aversion: {He's allergic to hard work}, {I'm allergic to meetings that could have been emails}.

Allergies is the plural of allergy—an immune system reaction to substances that are harmless to most people. Common triggers include pollen, dust, pet dander, and certain foods. Someone with allergies may sneeze, itch, swell, or in severe cases experience anaphylaxis. {My allergies are terrible this time of year.} {She has allergies to nuts and shellfish.}

An allergy is an immune system reaction to a substance that's harmless to most people—pollen, peanuts, pet dander, bee stings. The body treats the substance as a threat, producing symptoms from mild (sneezing, hives) to severe (anaphylaxis). Figuratively, having an allergy to something means strong aversion: {He seems to have an allergy to hard work}.

An alley is a narrow passage between or behind buildings, typically in urban areas. Alleys provide service access, shortcuts, or space for garbage collection: {We cut through the alley to save time}. In bowling, the alley is the lane down which the ball rolls. Something {right up your alley} suits your interests or expertise perfectly.

Alleys is the plural of alley—narrow passages between or behind buildings, or lanes for bowling. Back alleys suggest hidden urban spaces, often seedy: {drug deals in back alleys}. A bowling alley contains multiple alleys. {Right up my alley} means suited to one's interests or abilities.

An alliance is a formal agreement between parties—typically nations, organizations, or individuals—to cooperate for mutual benefit or protection. Countries form military alliances; businesses form strategic alliances. The word extends to any close association based on shared interests: {an unlikely alliance between environmentalists and hunters}. Alliance implies commitment stronger than mere cooperation but allows partners to retain independence.

Alliances are formal agreements between nations, groups, or individuals to cooperate for mutual benefit, especially in war or politics: {NATO is a military alliance}, {The company formed strategic alliances with local distributors}. The word can describe any close association based on shared interests: {an unlikely alliance between environmentalists and hunters}. Alliance also names the relationship itself—the state of being allied.

Allies are people, groups, or nations joined together for a common purpose, especially in war or politics. The word implies mutual support and shared interests: {The two countries became allies against their common enemy}. In social contexts, an ally is someone who supports a marginalized group they don't belong to: {She considers herself an ally to the LGBTQ community}. (Capitalized Allies refers specifically to the Allied Powers of World War I or II.)

An alligator is a large reptile native to the Americas and China, distinguished from crocodiles by its broader, U-shaped snout. Alligators inhabit freshwater swamps, marshes, and rivers. {See you later, alligator} is a playful farewell expecting the response {After a while, crocodile}. In jazz and swing culture, an alligator was an enthusiastic fan of the music.

Alligators is the plural of alligator, a large reptile with a broad snout found in freshwater habitats of the southeastern United States and China. Distinguished from crocodiles by their wider, U-shaped snouts. {The swamp was full of alligators}. Alligator also names the leather made from their hides: {alligator boots}, {alligator handbag}.

An allnighter is a session of work, study, or activity that continues through the entire night: {I pulled an allnighter to finish the paper}. The term is especially common among students cramming for exams. Also spelled all-nighter.

An allochthon is rock or geological material that has been transported from its place of origin to its current location, typically by tectonic forces or large-scale earth movements. The term contrasts with autochthon, material that formed where it now rests. In ecology, the word sometimes describes organisms or organic matter originating elsewhere: {Allochthonous nutrients washed into the lake from surrounding hillsides}.

Allow means to permit or give permission for something to happen. You might allow a child to stay up late, or a rule might allow exceptions. Allow also means to provide or set aside: {Allow an hour for traffic}. To {allow for} something is to take it into account: {The budget allows for unexpected costs}. When something allows of a possibility, it admits or leaves room for it: {The evidence allows of no other interpretation}.

An allowance is a sum of money given regularly for a specific purpose: a child's weekly allowance, a travel allowance, a clothing allowance. The word extends to permitted amounts more broadly—a baggage allowance, a daily calorie allowance. To {make allowance for} something is to take it into account: {We should make allowance for his inexperience}. An allowance can also be a discount or reduction: {a trade-in allowance on a new car}.

Allowed is the past tense of allow, meaning permitted or given permission. {Smoking is not allowed indoors.} {We were allowed to leave early.} It can also mean conceded or acknowledged: {She allowed that he might have a point.} Not to be confused with aloud, meaning spoken audibly.

An alloy is a metal made by combining two or more metallic elements, typically to achieve properties superior to the pure metals alone: {Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin}. Steel alloys iron with carbon. By extension, alloy can mean any mixture that dilutes purity: {pleasure without alloy}. To alloy is to mix metals or, figuratively, to diminish something by addition: {Joy alloyed with sorrow}.

Allspice is a spice made from the dried berries of a Caribbean tree, named because its flavor suggests a blend of cinnamon, nutmeg, and cloves. It appears in both sweet and savory cooking—pies, cakes, jerk seasoning, pickling spices: {The recipe calls for a teaspoon of allspice}. Despite the name, it's a single spice, not a mixture.

Allure is magnetic appeal—the quality that draws people toward something desirable. A city has allure, a career has allure, a mysterious stranger has allure. The word suggests attraction that's hard to resist but also hard to explain: {the allure of fame}, {the allure of the forbidden}. As a verb, to allure is to entice or attract powerfully.

Alluring describes something powerfully attractive or tempting, drawing you in with a promise of pleasure or fascination. The word suggests seduction rather than simple appeal—an alluring {smile}, an alluring {offer}, an alluring {mystery}. What's alluring beckons; it doesn't just please.

An ally is someone who joins with another for mutual benefit, especially in conflict or competition: {The two nations became allies during the war}. The verb means to unite or form such a partnership: {She allied herself with the reformers}. More recently, ally describes someone from a majority group who actively supports a marginalized group: {He considers himself an ally to the LGBTQ community}.

An almanac is a yearly publication containing a calendar along with astronomical data, weather predictions, and practical information like tide tables, planting guides, or sunrise times. The most familiar examples are agricultural almanacs that have guided farmers for centuries. More broadly, almanac can refer to any annual compendium of facts and statistics on a particular subject: {The World Almanac is useful for settling bar arguments}. {Farmers still consult the almanac for planting dates}.

Almighty means having unlimited power or authority. The word most commonly appears as a title for God: {the Almighty}, {Almighty God}. In casual speech, almighty intensifies what follows: {an almighty mess}, {an almighty crash}. The exclamation {almighty!} expresses shock or emphasis, often in combination: {God almighty!}

An almond is the edible seed of a tree related to peaches and plums, enclosed in a hard shell within a leathery hull. Almonds are eaten whole, ground into flour, or pressed for oil and milk. The pale tan color of blanched almonds gives its name to the shade: {almond walls}, {almond-shaped eyes}. Bitter almonds contain compounds that yield cyanide and are used only for flavoring extracts.

Almonds are edible nuts from a tree native to the Mediterranean and Middle East. They're eaten raw, roasted, or processed into almond milk, almond butter, and almond flour. The flavor profile—slightly sweet, mildly bitter—appears in marzipan and amaretto. {She sprinkled slivered almonds over the salad.}

Almost means nearly but not quite—falling just short of some mark. It modifies verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs to indicate that something came close to happening or being true: {I almost forgot}, {almost ready}, {We're almost there}. Almost can soften assertions: {almost never}, {almost always}. It suggests proximity without completion—the gap may be tiny or significant, but something remains unfulfilled.

Aloe is a genus of succulent plants with thick, fleshy leaves, native to Africa and the Arabian Peninsula.
