Antivenom is a medicine used to treat venomous bites and stings, typically from snakes, spiders, or scorpions. It contains antibodies that neutralize the specific toxins in venom. Antivenom is produced by injecting small amounts of venom into animals (usually horses) and harvesting the resulting antibodies. {The hospital administered antivenom within an hour of the snakebite.} Also called antivenin.

An antler is a branching bony growth on the head of deer and related animals. Unlike horns, which are permanent, antlers are shed and regrown annually. The branches are called points or tines: {a twelve-point buck}. Antlers appear in hunting trophies, rustic décor, and folk medicine.

Antlers are the branching bony growths on the heads of deer, elk, moose, and related animals. Unlike horns, which are permanent, antlers are shed and regrown annually. The size and number of branches typically increase with age. {The buck's antlers got tangled in the fence}. Antlers appear decoratively on walls, chandeliers, and furniture.

Ants are small social insects that live in colonies, often underground or in mounds. A colony contains workers, soldiers, and queens, each with distinct roles. Ant colonies can number in the millions. The insects are known for organized labor and collective strength: {The picnic was ruined by ants}. To have {ants in your pants} is to be restless or fidgety.

Antsy means restless, fidgety, or impatient—unable to sit still or wait calmly. The word evokes the sensation of having ants crawling on you: {The kids were getting antsy after two hours in the car}. It can also suggest nervous anxiety: {I'm antsy about the test results}.

An anvil is a heavy iron or steel block with a flat top on which metal is hammered and shaped. Blacksmiths place hot metal on the anvil and strike it with a hammer to forge tools, horseshoes, and other objects. The characteristic shape—flat working surface with a pointed horn at one end—has remained largely unchanged for centuries. Figuratively, something caught {between the hammer and the anvil} faces pressure from two sides.

Anvils is the plural of anvil, a heavy iron or steel block with a flat top and pointed horn, used by blacksmiths as a surface for shaping heated metal with hammer blows. The anvil's weight and solidity make it a symbol of immovability: {The decision dropped like an anvil}. In cartoons, falling anvils became a staple of slapstick violence.

Anxiety is a state of unease, worry, or fear about uncertain outcomes. It ranges from mild nervousness to overwhelming dread: {Her anxiety about the interview kept her up all night}. Clinical anxiety disorders involve persistent, excessive worry that interferes with daily life. The word also describes eager anticipation tinged with worry: {He waited with anxiety for the test results}.

Someone who is feeling anxious is experiencing fear, nervousness, or uncertainty about the present or the future. The related noun is anxiety. Occasionally people use anxious with less intensity, where the meaning is closer to enthusiastic or excited: I’m anxious to see what happens to his character in the sequel.

Anything is the sum of its parts: any thing. It is a pronoun or a noun that can stand in place of any noun, except a noun that designates a person (in which case you use anyone or anybody). Anything can stand for both concrete and abstract nouns: Do you need anything from the supermarket? There wasn’t anything wrong with him when I saw him. Anything is typically used in questions and in negations instead of something. Anything has a minor role as an intensifying adverb in the phrase anything like: The hotel wasn’t anything like the one we stayed in last year.

Anytime means at any time or whenever convenient: {Call me anytime}. It also serves as a casual response to thanks, equivalent to "you're welcome": {Thanks for the ride. Anytime.} The single word anytime is an adverb; the two-word phrase any time works as a noun: {Do you have any time to help?}
Anywhere is a compound of any and where and is used to mean to any place or in any place: You can go anywhere you like for your vacation. Is there anywhere I can get a snack around here?

Apart means separated by distance or not together. Things taken apart are disassembled; people who drift apart grow distant. {They live apart now.} Apart from means except for or in addition to: {Apart from the cost, it's perfect.} To set something apart is to distinguish it: {Her voice sets her apart from other singers.} To tell things apart is to distinguish between them.

Apartheid was the system of racial segregation enforced in South Africa from 1948 to 1991, under which the white minority government denied political rights and restricted movement, residence, and economic opportunity for Black South Africans and other non-white groups. The word is Afrikaans for "separateness." Extended to describe any system of rigid racial or ethnic separation: {gender apartheid}, {economic apartheid}.

An apartment is a self-contained living unit within a larger building, typically rented rather than owned. The word is standard in American English; British English prefers flat. An {apartment building} or {apartment complex} contains multiple units. {Studio apartment} denotes a single room serving as both bedroom and living space. {She's looking for a two-bedroom apartment downtown.}

Apartments is the plural of apartment—a self-contained living unit within a larger building, typically rented rather than owned. The word often appears in compound forms: {apartment building}, {apartment complex}, {apartment hunting}. In British English, the equivalent is usually flat.

Apathy is a lack of interest, enthusiasm, or concern. Where passion or engagement would be expected, apathy offers indifference: {voter apathy}, {public apathy toward the crisis}. The apathetic person doesn't care enough to act—or even to object. {His apathy about his own health worried his family.}

An ape is a large tailless primate—gorillas, chimpanzees, orangutans, and gibbons. Humans are technically apes but rarely called so. To ape is to mimic clumsily: {He aped his teacher's mannerisms}. To {go ape} is to become wildly excited or angry. {Apeshit} intensifies this: {The crowd went apeshit when the band took the stage}.

Apes are large primates without tails—gorillas, chimpanzees, orangutans, and gibbons, along with humans. In casual use, ape often means any monkey-like creature. To ape someone is to imitate them clumsily or mockingly: {He aped his teacher's mannerisms}. To {go ape} is to become wildly excited or angry.

Apeshit means wildly out of control, usually in the phrase {go apeshit}: {The crowd went apeshit when she walked onstage}. The image evokes primates in chaotic frenzy. It can express excitement, anger, or general mayhem.

The apex is the highest point, peak, or tip of something—literally the top of a triangle, mountain, or structure. Figuratively, it means the culmination or pinnacle: {She reached the apex of her career}. In anatomy, apex refers to the pointed end of organs like the heart or lung. As an adjective, apex describes something at the top of a hierarchy: an {apex predator} sits atop the food chain.

Aphidophagous means feeding on aphids. The term describes insects and other creatures that eat these small plant-sucking pests: {Ladybugs are aphidophagous and valued by gardeners for natural pest control}. The word appears mainly in entomology and agriculture.

An aphrodisiac is a substance believed to arouse sexual desire—foods like oysters and chocolate, drugs, or herbs. Named for Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love. The adjective describes anything that stimulates desire: {the aphrodisiac effect of power}. Most alleged aphrodisiacs lack scientific support, but the belief persists across cultures.

Apicomplexa is a phylum of parasitic single-celled organisms, nearly all of which live inside the cells of animals. The group includes the parasites responsible for malaria, toxoplasmosis, and cryptosporidiosis. The name refers to a complex of structures at one end of the cell used to penetrate host cells. {Apicomplexa are among the most medically significant parasites worldwide.} (Capitalized Apicomplexa is the standard scientific form.)

Apocalypse originally meant a revelation or unveiling of hidden knowledge, particularly divine truth. The word now primarily refers to a catastrophic destruction of the world or civilization: {zombie apocalypse}, {nuclear apocalypse}, {climate apocalypse}. Capitalized, the Apocalypse refers specifically to the biblical Book of Revelation and its prophecy of end times. The adjective apocalyptic describes catastrophic events or visions of total destruction: {apocalyptic imagery}, {an apocalyptic landscape}.

Apocalyptic describes total destruction or catastrophic upheaval: {apocalyptic scenes of devastation}, {an apocalyptic wildfire}. The word derives from religious prophecies about the end of the world, particularly the biblical Book of Revelation. Something apocalyptic suggests not just disaster but finality—the collapse of civilization or existence itself. The tone is often dramatic or hyperbolic: {My inbox is apocalyptic right now}.

Apologetic describes someone who is expressing regret or making excuses for a fault or failure: {She was apologetic about arriving late}. The word can also describe a tone or manner that conveys this sense of regret: {an apologetic smile}, {an apologetic shrug}. Someone who is unapologetic shows no regret or remorse. Separately, apologetics refers to the formal defense of a position, especially religious doctrine—not about saying sorry but about making a case.

Apologies is a plural of apology, but it often functions as a standalone expression of regret: {My apologies for the delay}. This usage is slightly more formal than "sorry" and slightly less formal than "I apologize." The phrase {apologies all around} suggests everyone involved owes or receives an apology.

Apologise is the British spelling of apologize—to express regret for a fault or offense: {I apologise for the delay}. The word can range from genuine contrition to mere social lubricant. To apologise for something can also mean to defend it formally, though this sense is rare outside academic contexts.

The verb apologize reduces the three words, say you’re sorry, to one, and also makes the expression slightly more formal: The company publicly apologized for the inappropriate content that appeared briefly on its website. Apologize is weakly used in some formulas and recordings to acknowledge awareness that there is a problem: We apologize for any inconvenience that the closure will cause for our customers.

Apologizing is expressing regret or asking forgiveness for a wrong or offense. The act ranges from casual acknowledgment {I'm just apologizing for being late} to formal admission of fault. Someone who is always apologizing may be genuinely contrite or merely performing social ritual. To apologize for something can also mean to defend it, though this older sense is rare: {He spent his career apologizing for the regime's excesses}.

An apology is an expression of regret for having done something wrong: {I owe you an apology for what I said}. The word can also mean a defense or justification of a position, though this sense is now rare outside formal contexts. A weak or inadequate example of something is {an apology for}: {The meal was an apology for fine dining}.

An apostle is someone sent on a mission, originally one of the twelve disciples Jesus chose to spread his teachings. The term extends to any early Christian missionary, especially Paul. More broadly, an apostle is a leading advocate of any cause or movement: {an apostle of free-market economics}, {an apostle of nonviolence}. The word implies passionate, pioneering commitment.

Apostles are the twelve disciples chosen by Jesus to spread his teachings, or more broadly, early Christian missionaries like Paul. The word extends to any pioneering advocates of a cause or movement: {an apostle of free-market economics}, {apostles of the new artistic movement}. The singular apostle follows the same pattern—original disciple or fervent proponent.

An apostrophe is the punctuation mark (') used to indicate possession {the dog's tail}, contractions {don't}, or omitted letters {rock 'n' roll}. Separately, apostrophe is a rhetorical device in which a speaker addresses an absent person or abstract concept as if present: {O Death, where is thy sting?}

An apothecary is a person who prepares and sells medicines—the historical predecessor of the modern pharmacist. The term also refers to the shop where such preparations were made and sold: {The village apothecary stocked herbs and tinctures}. The word now appears mainly in historical contexts or to evoke old-fashioned charm, as in boutique shops styled as apothecaries selling soaps, candles, or remedies.

App is short for application, specifically software designed for a particular purpose. The word became ubiquitous with smartphones: {I downloaded an app for tracking my runs}. Apps range from games to banking to social media. The term now extends beyond phones to any focused piece of software: {a desktop app}, {a web app}.

Appalled describes a state of shock mixed with horror or disgust at something morally offensive or deeply disturbing. To be appalled is stronger than surprised or disappointed—it suggests visceral revulsion: {I was appalled by the conditions in the factory}. The verb appall produces this state: {The violence appalled everyone who witnessed it}.

Appalling describes something that causes shock, dismay, or horror. The word carries moral weight—appalling conditions suggest not just unpleasantness but wrongness: {The report revealed appalling treatment of prisoners}. It can also express strong disapproval of quality or taste: {Her spelling is appalling}. The participle comes from appall, meaning to dismay or horrify.

Apparent describes something that seems to be true or real based on available evidence. An {apparent} contradiction may dissolve upon closer examination. The {heir apparent} is the one who will inherit unless circumstances change. Apparent also means clearly visible or obvious: {It was apparent she hadn't slept}. The word carries a hint of uncertainty—what's apparent may not be actual.

Apparently signals that something seems to be the case based on available evidence or what others say, though the speaker may not have verified it firsthand: {Apparently they're getting divorced}. It can express mild surprise at learning something: {She's apparently been doing this for years}. Sometimes apparently carries a note of skepticism or irony, suggesting doubt about a claim: {Apparently I'm supposed to just accept this}.

An apparition is something that appears, especially something ghostly or supernatural—a specter, phantom, or vision: {The apparition of a woman in white haunted the old manor}. The word can also describe any sudden or unexpected appearance of a person or thing: {He made a brief apparition at the party before vanishing again}.

Apparitions are ghostly figures or supernatural appearances—spirits of the dead made visible to the living. The word suggests something that appears suddenly and mysteriously: {The apparition vanished as quickly as it came}. More broadly, an apparition can be any strange or unexpected sight: {A lone figure emerged from the fog like an apparition}.

Appeal’s many meanings as both noun and verb fall into the categories of general and legal. A legal appeal is a request for a decision, verdict, or order to be reviewed by a higher court: The plaintiff filed an appeal. An appeal can also be a request for money or help, as well as the quality that makes something attractive: The movie will have appeal for dating teenagers, but few others will be interested. The related verb meaning is followed by for: Police appealed for help from people who may have witnessed the accident.

Appealing describes something that attracts interest or desire, that you find attractive or tempting: {The job offer was appealing, but the location gave me pause}. It also functions as the present participle of appeal, describing the act of making a formal request or legal challenge: {The defendant is appealing the verdict}. An appealing look or gesture is one designed to elicit sympathy or assistance from someone.

Appeals are requests for help, sympathy, or a decision to be reconsidered. A charity makes an appeal for donations. A defendant files an appeal to have a conviction overturned by a higher court. Something that appeals to you attracts or interests you: {The job didn't appeal to me}. Appeal as a noun can mean attractiveness: {The old house had a certain appeal}.

Appear means to come into view or become visible: {A figure appeared in the doorway}. It also means to seem: {She appears tired}, {It appears we were wrong}. To appear somewhere is to show up, whether at an event, in court, or on stage. Published or broadcast material appears when it becomes available: {The article appeared in yesterday's paper}.

Appearance is how something looks or seems to others—the outward aspect rather than the inner reality. {Appearances can be deceiving.} An appearance is also an instance of showing up: a court appearance, a guest appearance on a talk show, a celebrity's public appearances. To {keep up appearances} is to maintain an outward show of prosperity or respectability despite private troubles. To {make an appearance} is to show up, often briefly or as a formality.

Appearances is the plural of appearance, covering looks, acts of showing up, and instances of seeming. {She made several public appearances}. {Appearances can be deceiving} warns that how things look may not reflect reality. To {keep up appearances} is to maintain an outward show of normality or prosperity despite private troubles. {By all appearances} means judging from what can be seen.

Appeasement is the act of calming or pacifying someone, especially by giving in to their demands. The word carries a strong negative connotation from its association with British and French efforts to satisfy Hitler's territorial ambitions in the late 1930s, a policy now widely regarded as having enabled rather than prevented war. Today, accusing someone of appeasement suggests they are making dangerous concessions to an aggressor: {Critics called the treaty appeasement rather than diplomacy}.

An appendix is supplementary material at the end of a book or document—charts, data, or detailed information that supports but isn't essential to the main text: {The full interview transcripts appear in the appendix}. In anatomy, the appendix is a small tube-shaped pouch attached to the large intestine, vestigial in humans and prone to painful inflammation requiring surgical removal. Plural: appendices or appendixes.

Appetite is a desire for food, or the capacity to eat: {I worked up an appetite hiking}. The word extends to any strong desire or inclination: {an appetite for risk}, {an appetite for adventure}. Someone with no appetite for something lacks interest in pursuing it. A healthy appetite suggests robust enthusiasm, whether for meals or for life generally.

Appetites is the plural of appetite—a desire or craving, especially for food. The word extends beyond hunger to any strong wanting: sexual appetites, an appetite for risk, an appetite for power. {His appetites got him into trouble}. Someone with large appetites wants much from life; someone who has lost their appetite—literal or figurative—no longer desires what once drew them.

An appetizer is a small portion of food served before the main course of a meal, intended to stimulate the appetite: {We ordered bruschetta and calamari as appetizers}. The term extends to anything that whets interest in what follows: {The trailer was just an appetizer for the film}. British English prefers starter.

Appetizers are small dishes served before a main course to stimulate the appetite. They range from simple fare like cheese and crackers to elaborate preparations: {We ordered appetizers while we waited for our entrees}. At parties, appetizers may constitute the entire spread. The British equivalent is starters. Figuratively, an appetizer is anything that whets interest in what follows: {The trailer was an appetizer for the film}.

Appetizing describes food or drink that looks, smells, or sounds appealing enough to stimulate hunger: {The appetizing aroma of fresh bread filled the kitchen}. By extension, anything attractive or enticing can be appetizing: {The job offer wasn't particularly appetizing}. The negative form unappetizing is equally common, describing things that fail to appeal or actively repel.

To applaud is to clap your hands together to show approval or appreciation, typically at a performance or speech: {The audience applauded enthusiastically}. Extended uses cover any expression of approval: {Critics applauded the decision}. You can applaud someone's courage or applaud their efforts without making a sound.

Applause is the sound of people clapping their hands together to show approval, appreciation, or enthusiasm, typically after a performance, speech, or achievement. It can range from polite and scattered to thunderous and sustained. Figuratively, applause extends to any expression of praise or approval: {The proposal met with applause from environmental groups}. To do something {to applause} is to receive recognition for it.

Apple, the noun for a tree and the fruit that it bears, is among the oldest words in English, with roots dating from before 900 CE and having relatives in many other Indo-European languages. Apple as the name of a technology company is a phenomenon that arose in the 20th century, but Apple computer is nearly twice as frequent as apple pie in modern text. The ancient history of the apple is evident from its mention in the book of Genesis and in other religious and mythological texts.

Apples are the round fruit of trees in the genus Malus, typically red, green, or yellow with crisp flesh. Among the most familiar fruits in temperate climates, apples appear in countless varieties and uses—eaten raw, baked into pies, pressed into cider. Figuratively, something is {apples to oranges} when comparisons are invalid. The {apple of your eye} is someone you cherish. {How do you like them apples?} expresses triumph or challenge.

Applesauce is a soft, sweet preparation of cooked apples, typically eaten as a side dish or snack: {The pork chops came with applesauce}. In dated American slang, applesauce means nonsense or insincere flattery: {That's a lot of applesauce}.

An appliance is a device designed for a specific practical task, especially a household machine like a refrigerator, washing machine, or toaster: {The kitchen came with new appliances}. Small appliances sit on countertops; major appliances are large and often built in. The word sometimes extends to other equipment: {dental appliances}, {orthopedic appliances}.

Appliances are devices designed for specific practical tasks, especially household machines like refrigerators, washing machines, and toasters. The term usually implies electrical or mechanical operation: {The kitchen came with all new appliances}. Small appliances sit on countertops; major appliances are large fixtures. In technical contexts, appliance can mean any apparatus serving a particular function.

An applicant is someone who applies for something—a job, admission to a school, a loan, a permit. The word emphasizes the formal act of requesting consideration: {We received three hundred applicants for the position}. Until accepted, one remains an applicant rather than an employee, student, or member.

Application centers on putting something to use. An application of force achieves a purpose; an application of paint covers a surface. The word extends to focused effort: {She showed great application to her studies}. A job application or college application is a formal request for consideration. In computing, an application (or app) is software designed for a specific task: {a word processing application}.

Applications are formal requests, typically submitted in writing: a job application, a college application, a loan application. The word also names software programs designed for specific tasks—apps on your phone, word processors on your computer. In technical contexts, application refers to putting something to practical use: {the application of scientific principles to engineering problems}. To apply ointment is an application of ointment.

The central meaning of the verb apply always involves contact. When tangible things are involved, the contact is physical; when abstract things are involved, the contact is figurative. When you apply a substance to a surface you put down a layer of it: Apply adhesive to both edges and press them together. When you apply a skill to a problem, you use that skill to try to solve the problem. Applying for something such as a job, a benefit, or a license, you formally request to obtain or be considered for it. If a rule or law applies, it has relevance or force.

An appointment is a scheduled meeting or engagement: {I have a doctor's appointment at three}. It also means the act of assigning someone to a position: {Her appointment to the Supreme Court surprised many}. The position itself may be called an appointment. In the plural, appointments refers to furnishings or equipment: {The hotel's appointments were luxurious}.

The predominant meanings of the verb appreciate have to do with value and divide roughly along the lines of whether there is an object present or not. When you appreciate someone or something, you value them because they provide some benefit for you. When something appreciates it grows in value, usually slowly and in a predictable way. The first meaning, usually with a personal subject and an object, is far more frequent.

Appreciation is the recognition of something's value, quality, or significance. When you have an appreciation for art or music, you understand and enjoy it; when you show appreciation to someone, you express gratitude for what they've done. {I have a deeper appreciation for her work now that I understand the process.} The word also has a financial sense: appreciation is an increase in value over time, as when real estate or investments appreciate. This contrasts with depreciation, which describes a decrease in value.

Apprehension has two main meanings that seem unrelated but share an underlying sense of grasping or seizing. The more common meaning is anxious unease about something that might happen: {She felt growing apprehension as the interview approached}. The other meaning involves the act of arresting or capturing someone: {The suspect's apprehension followed a three-day manhunt}. A third, more formal sense refers to understanding or perception: {His apprehension of the situation proved accurate}.

Apprehensive describes a state of worry or unease about something that might happen: {She was apprehensive about the interview}. The word suggests anticipatory anxiety rather than immediate fear—you're apprehensive before the results come in, not while the building is on fire. {He gave an apprehensive glance toward the door}.

An apprentice is a person, usually young, in a program that enables him or her to learn a trade. Before another noun, apprentice indicates a tradesperson who is still in training (apprentice electrician). To apprentice someone (or yourself) is to enter a program of such training. When capitalized as The Apprentice, the phrase refers to a global reality TV franchise in which contestants are eliminated one by one as they fail to impress a boss.

Apprentices are people learning a trade or craft under the guidance of a skilled practitioner. The arrangement typically involves hands-on training in exchange for labor: {The master craftsman took on two apprentices}. Figuratively, anyone new to a field learning from experienced practitioners: {We were all apprentices once}.

An apprenticeship is a period of training under a skilled practitioner, combining hands-on work with formal instruction. Traditionally associated with trades like plumbing, carpentry, and electrical work, apprenticeships have expanded into technology, healthcare, and other fields. The term also applies figuratively to any formative period of learning: {His years as a junior reporter were an apprenticeship in hard news}.

Whether used as a noun or verb, approach always involves two people or things and some notion of decreasing distance between them. An airplane will approach the runway when it has permission from air traffic control. The approach of the army alarmed the villagers. Outside the physical world, approach has more leeway in its meanings. We say that a holiday approaches when its time is near on the calendar. Your approach to a problem is a particular manner of trying to arrive at a solution.

As an adjective, by far the most common use, appropriate is a near synonym of suitable, to which it adds the idea of correct or best: The most appropriate time to prune this tree is in the fall. It’s not appropriate for you to take this problem over your supervisor’s head. As a verb, appropriate has a long vowel in the last syllable and a meaning not closely related to the adjective. To appropriate something (typically money or property) means to seize it for a particular use: The government has sought to appropriate the land for a nature preserve.

Appropriation is the act of taking something for one's own use. Governments appropriate funds by setting aside money for specific purposes: {The appropriation for defense exceeded last year's budget}. In broader use, appropriation suggests taking without permission or right. Cultural appropriation refers to adopting elements of another culture, especially when a dominant group borrows from a marginalized one: {Critics called the headdress cultural appropriation}. In art, appropriation means incorporating existing images or objects into new work.

Approval is favorable acceptance or agreement. To give approval is to sanction or endorse: {The board gave its approval to the merger}. Official approval often implies formal permission: {The drug received FDA approval}. Seeking approval suggests wanting validation or acceptance from others: {She craved her father's approval}.

To approve is to regard favorably or give formal consent. You might approve of someone's choices, or a committee approves a proposal. {The board approved the budget unanimously.} Approval often implies authority—a manager approves expenses, a parent approves a request. {I don't approve of his methods} expresses moral or personal disapproval without formal power.

Approved describes something that has received official acceptance or authorization: {an approved vendor}, {FDA-approved medications}. It signals that something has passed scrutiny or met required standards. In casual use, approved can simply mean sanctioned or endorsed by someone whose opinion matters: {mother-approved boyfriend}.

Apps is the plural of app, short for application—software designed to perform specific tasks. The term became ubiquitous with smartphones: {I have too many apps on my phone}. Apps range from games and social media to productivity tools and utilities. The word has largely displaced "program" in casual speech about consumer software.

An apricot is a small, soft fruit with fuzzy yellowish-orange skin, sweet flesh, and a large pit. The color apricot—a pale orange with peachy undertones—takes its name from the fruit: {apricot walls}, {an apricot dress}. Apricots are eaten fresh, dried, or preserved.

Apricots are small, soft stone fruits with fuzzy orange-yellow skin and sweet flesh. Related to peaches but smaller and slightly tart. Fresh apricots bruise easily and don't travel well, so many people know them mainly dried or in jam. {We picked apricots from the tree in the backyard.}

An apron is a protective garment worn over the front of the body, tied at the waist and sometimes the neck, to shield clothing from spills and stains while cooking or working. The word extends to any protective or covering surface: the paved area where aircraft park, the strip of stage extending toward the audience, or the skirt around machinery. To be tied to someone's {apron strings} is to be overly dependent on them, especially a mother.

Aprons are protective garments worn over clothing, typically tied at the waist and covering the front of the body. Cooks wear aprons to shield against spills and stains; craftspeople wear them for protection from tools and materials. The word extends to protective or covering surfaces: the apron of a stage is the area in front of the curtain, and an airport apron is the paved area where aircraft park and load.

Apt means appropriate or fitting: {an apt comparison}, {an apt reply}. It also means having a tendency toward something: {He's apt to forget appointments}. A person who is apt at something learns or performs it readily: {She proved apt at languages}. The word suggests a natural suitability or quickness. (Capitalized APT is an acronym.)

Aqua is a blue-green color, the shade of tropical seawater or swimming pools. As a prefix or combining form, it relates to water: {aquarium}, {aquatic}, {aqueduct}. In chemistry and pharmacy, aqua simply means water, appearing in terms like aqua regia (a mixture of acids that dissolves gold).

Aquamarine is a pale blue-green color, named for the gemstone that resembles seawater. The gem itself is a variety of beryl, prized in jewelry for its clear, watery hue. As a color term, aquamarine describes things with that distinctive blue-green tint: {aquamarine eyes}, {an aquamarine swimming pool}.

An aquarium is a glass or plastic tank for keeping fish and other aquatic creatures. The word also applies to buildings housing such exhibits: {We took the kids to the aquarium}. Home aquariums range from simple fishbowls to elaborate setups with filters, heaters, and live plants.

An aqueduct is a channel or conduit built to carry water over long distances, typically from a source to a city or agricultural area. The term often evokes the arched stone bridges the Romans built to maintain water flow across valleys: {The ancient aqueduct still stands outside the city}. Any artificial channel for water transport qualifies, including modern pipelines and canals.

Aqueducts are channels or conduits built to carry water over long distances, typically from a source to a city or agricultural area. The word often evokes the arched stone structures of ancient Rome, though aqueducts may also run underground or at ground level. Modern aqueducts supply water to cities like Los Angeles and Phoenix: {The California Aqueduct stretches over 400 miles}.

An arabesque is an ornate decorative design of intertwining flowing lines, typically featuring stylized leaves, flowers, and geometric patterns. The style originated in Islamic art, where religious prohibitions discouraged figurative representation. In ballet, an arabesque is a pose where the dancer stands on one leg with the other extended straight behind and arms outstretched: {She held the arabesque for several counts}. The term extends to any elaborate, intricately patterned design or flourish.

Aragoto is a style of kabuki theater characterized by bold, exaggerated performance—dramatic poses, stylized movements, vivid makeup, and larger-than-life characters. The word translates roughly as "rough business" or "wild style," contrasting with the softer, more realistic wagoto style. Aragoto roles typically feature superhuman heroes, warriors, or demons: {The actor's aragoto technique brought the vengeful spirit to terrifying life}.

Arbitrary has a meaning similar to random but it is often used with a negative connotation. An arbitrary decision is one made because of personal preference or prejudice. An arbitrary system is one that probably treats someone unfairly. Someone held in arbitrary detention by authorities is being held for reasons that others may consider unjustified; in other words, for arbitrary reasons. In math, arbitrary characterizes an undetermined or unassigned value.

The meanings of arc can be collected under the more general idea of a line, usually a curved line: The novel’s story arc reached its apex in the sixth chapter. Any segment of a circle is an arc, as is the apparent path of a heavenly body or some other projectile across the sky. An electric arc is the bright, visible bridge discharge of light between two electrodes. To arc is either to form an electric arc or to follow a curved path, especially through the sky: The baseball arced into the outfield.

An arcade is a covered passageway, often lined with shops, or a series of arches supported by columns. The architectural sense extends to any arched or vaulted space. In modern usage, arcade most often means a place with coin-operated games: {We spent hours at the arcade after school}. Video games played in such venues are arcade games, distinguished from home console or computer games by their quarter-eating design.

Arcades are covered passageways, typically lined with shops or stalls, often featuring arched roofs or colonnades. The term also refers to establishments filled with coin-operated games—video games, pinball machines, and the like: {We spent hours at the arcade after school}. In architecture, an arcade is a series of arches supported by columns or piers.

Arcane describes knowledge that is mysterious, obscure, or understood by only a few: {arcane rituals}, {arcane legal procedures}, {the arcane world of derivatives trading}. The word suggests specialized or esoteric information—not necessarily secret, but requiring particular study to understand. What seems arcane to outsiders may be routine to experts.

An arch is a curved structure spanning an opening, typically supporting weight above it—doorways, bridges, windows. The shape appears throughout nature and anatomy: the arch of the foot, an eyebrow's arch. As a verb, to arch is to form this curve: {The cat arched its back}. Separately, arch as an adjective means playfully mischievous or knowingly teasing: {an arch smile}, {an arch tone}. This second word derives from the prefix arch- (chief, principal), suggesting someone who acts as though they know more than they're saying.

An archaeocyte is a type of cell found in sponges—amoeba-like cells that move freely through the sponge's body and perform multiple functions. Archaeocytes can transform into other cell types, digest food, transport nutrients, and produce reproductive cells. They're essential to sponge regeneration: a sponge broken apart can reassemble largely through archaeocyte activity.

An archaeologist is a person who studies human history through excavation and analysis of physical remains—artifacts, structures, and other traces left behind by past cultures. The work combines fieldwork (digging, surveying) with laboratory analysis and interpretation: {The archaeologists uncovered pottery shards dating to 3000 BCE}. {She's an archaeologist specializing in Bronze Age settlements}.

Archaeology is the study of human history through excavation and analysis of physical remains—artifacts, structures, bones, and other material evidence. The British spelling is archaeology; Americans often write archeology. An archaeologist digs at sites to uncover how people lived: {The archaeology of the region reveals extensive trade networks}.

An archangel is a chief angel, ranking above ordinary angels in celestial hierarchy. In Jewish, Christian, and Islamic traditions, archangels serve as God's principal messengers and agents: Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael are the most commonly named. {The archangel Gabriel appeared to Mary}. The term extends figuratively to anyone seen as a divine protector or messenger. (Capitalized Archangel is a Russian port city.)

Archangels are angels of high rank in religious hierarchies, particularly in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Michael and Gabriel are the most widely recognized; others include Raphael and Uriel. The prefix arch- indicates chief or principal status, placing archangels above ordinary angels in celestial order: {The archangel Michael is often depicted with a sword}.

An archbishop is a bishop of the highest rank, overseeing a province of dioceses in Christian churches that maintain episcopal hierarchy—Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, and some Lutheran denominations. The archbishop's territory is called an archdiocese: {the Archbishop of Canterbury}, {the Archbishop of New York}. The title carries administrative authority over other bishops in the province.

Archenemies is the plural of archenemy—a principal enemy or greatest rival. The prefix arch- means chief or most extreme, elevating an ordinary enemy to supreme status. Comic book heroes have archenemies: Batman has the Joker, Superman has Lex Luthor. The term applies beyond fiction: {The two nations were archenemies for centuries}. {She considered her former business partner her archenemy}.

An archenemy is someone's principal or most formidable enemy—the one who stands out above all other adversaries. The prefix arch- here means chief or preeminent, as in archbishop or archrival. While the term can describe real-world antagonists, it appears most often in fiction, especially comics and superhero stories, where heroes typically have one signature villain who defines their ongoing struggle: {The Joker is Batman's archenemy}.

An archeologist is a person who studies human history and prehistory through the excavation and analysis of artifacts, structures, and other physical remains. The spelling with an e (archeologist) is more common in American English, while British English typically uses archaeologist. {The archeologist carefully brushed away centuries of dirt from the pottery shard.}

Archeology is the study of human history through excavation and analysis of physical remains—artifacts, structures, bones, and other material evidence. Archeologists dig at sites to reconstruct how ancient peoples lived, worked, and died. The field spans from prehistoric cave dwellings to nineteenth-century settlements. Also spelled archaeology, especially in British English.

An archer is a person who shoots with a bow and arrow, whether in combat, hunting, or sport. The word evokes medieval warfare and Olympic competition alike. {She trained as an archer from age twelve.} In the zodiac, Archer refers to Sagittarius.

Archers are people who shoot with bows and arrows. The term covers those who practice archery as sport, those who hunt with a bow, and historical or fantasy warriors armed with longbows or crossbows: {The archers released a volley of arrows}. In astrology, Archer refers to Sagittarius.

Archery is the skill or sport of shooting arrows with a bow. It encompasses both target shooting and hunting. Someone who practices archery is an archer. {She took up archery after trying it at summer camp.}

An archetype is an original model or prototype from which copies are made, or a perfect example of a type: {She's the archetype of the self-made entrepreneur}. In Jungian psychology, archetypes are universal symbols or patterns residing in the collective unconscious—the hero, the trickster, the wise old man. Literary criticism uses the term for recurring character types, plot patterns, or symbols across cultures and eras: {the archetype of the quest narrative}.

Archetypes are original patterns or models from which copies are made—the prototypical example of a type. In Jungian psychology, archetypes are universal symbols and themes residing in the collective unconscious: the hero, the trickster, the wise old man, the shadow. Literary and cultural analysis uses the term similarly for recurring character types and narrative patterns: {The mentor is one of the oldest archetypes in storytelling}. More loosely, archetype describes any quintessential example: {She's the archetype of the struggling artist}.

An architect designs buildings and oversees their construction, balancing aesthetics, function, and structural requirements. The term extends to anyone who designs complex systems: {the architect of the new tax policy}, {a software architect}. As a verb, to architect is to design or plan comprehensively: {She architected the company's expansion strategy}.

Architects design buildings and oversee their construction, balancing aesthetics, function, and safety. The term extends to anyone who designs complex systems: {the architect of the peace agreement}, {a software architect}. To architect something is to plan or design it at a high level: {She architected the company's expansion into Asia}.

Architecture is the art and practice of designing buildings and other structures. More broadly, it refers to any systematic design or underlying structure: {the architecture of a software system}, {the architecture of the federal government}. As a mass noun, architecture means buildings collectively or a particular style of building: {Victorian architecture}, {the architecture of ancient Rome}.

An archive is a collection of historical documents or records, or the place where such materials are stored: {the National Archives}, {She found the letters in the family archives}. In computing, an archive is a file containing compressed data or a backup copy. To archive something is to store it for long-term preservation, whether physical documents or digital files. The word implies organized storage for future reference rather than active use.

Archives are collections of historical records, documents, or other materials preserved for reference and research. The word also refers to the place where such collections are kept: {The letter was discovered in the university archives}. In computing, an archive is a file containing compressed data or a backup copy. To archive is to store systematically for long-term preservation: {archived emails}, {archived footage}.

An archrival is your chief rival—the one opponent who stands above all others in intensity or importance. The prefix arch- means principal or most extreme: {Batman's archrival is the Joker}. Sports teams, businesses, and nations all have archrivals. The relationship implies ongoing competition, often with personal animosity: {The two senators had been archrivals for decades}.

Archrivals are opponents locked in intense, long-standing competition. The prefix arch- signals supremacy—these aren't just rivals but the foremost ones, defined by their mutual opposition: {The two schools have been archrivals for decades}. The singular archrival names a specific nemesis: {He finally defeated his archrival in the championship}.

Arcs is the plural of arc—a curved line or portion of a circle. In geometry, an arc is part of a circle's circumference. Electric arcs are luminous discharges between electrodes. In storytelling, a character arc traces development over time: {Her arc from villain to hero spans three seasons}. The verb arcs describes curved motion: {The ball arcs toward the basket}.

Arctic means extremely cold, like the polar region: {arctic temperatures}, {arctic winds}. The word describes frigid conditions or things designed for them: {arctic gear}, {arctic survival training}. It can also suggest emotional coldness: {She gave him an arctic stare}. (Capitalized Arctic refers to the polar region itself.)

Area is the extent of a surface, measured in square units: {The area of the room is 200 square feet}. More loosely, an area is any defined space or region: {a residential area}, {the area around the wound}. Area extends to abstract domains: {areas of expertise}, {area of concern}. In telecommunications, an area code identifies a geographic region for phone numbers.

When designating a physical space, an arena harkens back to the area of a Roman amphitheater where gladiators fought. Modern arenas are typically used for mass-audience spectator sports or other events: I’m heading to the arena early for tonight’s basketball game. Figuratively, an arena is any notional space dedicated to a particular activity or competition, such as the political arena or the healthcare arena.

To argue is to give reasons for or against something, or to contend in verbal conflict. You argue a position by presenting evidence; you argue with someone when you disagree: {They argued about money for hours}. Lawyers argue cases before courts. To argue someone into or out of something is to persuade them through reasoning. The tone ranges from civil debate to heated dispute.

Arguing is engaging in verbal conflict or debate. You argue with someone when you disagree and exchange opposing views, often heatedly: {They were arguing about money again}. You argue for or against a position when making a case: {She argued convincingly for reform}. Arguing can range from reasoned discourse to shouting matches.

An argument doesn’t necessarily involve conflict. An argument between two people is a disagreement: The neighbors were having a noisy argument. When you present an argument, you present a sequence of statements that lead to a certain conclusion: It was hard to follow her argument for changing the law. The argument of a book, thesis, paper, or report is the main point it makes, or the course of action that it advocates: He makes a strong argument for dating these artifacts to 1000 B.C. In technical contexts such as math, logic, or computer science, an argument is a variable: The debugger says you have a missing argument at line 97.

Arguments are reasons or evidence offered to support a position: {Her arguments for the policy were persuasive}. An argument is also a dispute or quarrel: {They got into an argument about money}. The word can mean a summary of a work's content, as in the argument preceding each book of *Paradise Lost*. In computing and mathematics, an argument is a value passed to a function.

Argyle is a pattern of diamonds in contrasting colors, typically with thin diagonal lines crossing through them. The design is most associated with socks and sweaters: {argyle socks}, {an argyle vest}. As an adjective, it describes anything featuring this pattern: {an argyle print}.

An aria is a self-contained song for solo voice with instrumental accompaniment, typically in an opera, oratorio, or cantata. Arias showcase a singer's vocal abilities and express a character's emotions at a dramatic moment: {The soprano's aria brought the audience to tears}. The term distinguishes these elaborate pieces from recitative, the speech-like passages that advance the plot.

Aristocracy is a class of people holding hereditary titles and privileges—nobility, in other words. The term also denotes government by such a class: {France was an aristocracy before the Revolution}. More loosely, aristocracy refers to any elite group considered superior within a domain: {the aristocracy of Silicon Valley}, {baseball's aristocracy}. The adjective is aristocratic.

An aristocrat is a member of the nobility or ruling class, someone belonging to a society's hereditary elite. The term implies not just high social rank but the manners, bearing, and privileges associated with it: {She carried herself like an aristocrat}. Used figuratively for anyone at the top of their field: {an aristocrat among chefs}.

Aristocrats are members of the highest social class, typically holding hereditary titles and historically wielding political power through land ownership and lineage. The term can describe actual nobility—{dukes, earls, and other aristocrats attended the coronation}—or anyone perceived as elite or privileged: {the aristocrats of Silicon Valley}. The word often carries connotations of wealth, refinement, and social distance from ordinary people.

Arithmetic is the branch of mathematics dealing with basic operations on numbers—addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. It's the math most people learn first and use daily: balancing a checkbook, splitting a bill, calculating a tip. {Do the arithmetic and you'll see we can't afford it.} By extension, arithmetic can mean any practical calculation of costs and benefits: {the arithmetic of electoral politics}.

An ark is a vessel of refuge or salvation, most familiar from the biblical story of Noah's ark, the boat that preserved animals during the great flood. By extension, any container that protects something precious may be called an ark. The Ark of the Covenant was the chest holding the Ten Commandments. In Jewish tradition, an ark is also the cabinet in a synagogue where Torah scrolls are kept. {The old barn served as an ark for the stray animals she collected.} (Capitalized Ark may refer to the biblical vessel specifically or appear in proper names.)

The appendage that begins at your shoulder and ends at your hand inspires the many uses of the word arm. Animals whose uppermost or foremost limbs are distinct also have arms. A limb that does not typically touch with the ground is also an arm, which may be why invertebrates such as squid and octopi have arms but spiders and insects have legs. Figuratively speaking, an arm is one of multiple divisions of an organization: the retail arm of the corporation. Arm is commonly a shortened version of firearm, and so arms can refer to weapons. When someone is armed, they are carrying a weapon.

An armada is a large fleet of warships, or by extension any impressive assembly of vehicles or vessels: {an armada of fishing boats}, {an armada of trucks heading north}. The word carries connotations of power and coordinated force, often with a hint of menace or overwhelming scale. (Capitalized Armada typically refers to the Spanish Armada.)

An armadillo is a burrowing mammal native to the Americas, distinctive for its armor of bony plates covering its back and sides. The nine-banded armadillo is the only species found in the United States, known for its habit of jumping when startled—unfortunately often into the undercarriage of passing vehicles. Some species can roll into a ball when threatened.

Armadillos are mammals native to the Americas, distinguished by their armor-like shell of bony plates covering their back, head, legs, and tail. These nocturnal burrowers range from the small pink fairy armadillo to the giant armadillo, with the nine-banded armadillo being the most common and the only species found in the United States. When threatened, some species can roll into a ball for protection. {Armadillos have been digging up my lawn looking for grubs.}

An armband is a band worn around the upper arm, typically to signal something—mourning (black), team membership, or official status like a captain's armband in soccer. Armbands may also be inflatable devices worn by children learning to swim: {She put the armbands on her daughter before they got in the pool}.

An armchair is a chair with supports for the arms. The term also works as an adjective for someone who engages in an activity only from the comfort of home, without real experience or risk: an armchair {quarterback}, an armchair {traveler}, an armchair {detective}. The implication is of theorizing from safety rather than doing.

Armed means carrying weapons or equipped for combat: {armed guards}, {armed robbery}, {the armed forces}. The word extends to anything equipped with a particular feature: {armed with the facts}, {armed with a good lawyer}. Something with arms in the anatomical sense can also be armed: {a chair with armed rests}. The opposite is unarmed.

Armies is the plural of army—organized military land forces of nations or factions. The word extends to any large mobilized group: {armies of volunteers}, {armies of the night}. When multiple nations field forces, each has its army: {The allied armies converged on Berlin}.

An armistice is an agreement between warring parties to stop fighting, typically while negotiating peace terms. Unlike a surrender or peace treaty, an armistice is often temporary and doesn't resolve underlying conflicts—it simply halts combat: {The armistice ended the fighting but left the border disputed}. Armistice Day commemorates the end of World War I on November 11, 1918.

Armor is protective covering, originally metal suits worn in combat: {a knight in armor}. Modern armor includes bulletproof vests and reinforced vehicle plating. Figuratively, armor is emotional defense: {Her sarcasm was armor against vulnerability}. To armor something is to equip it with protective covering: {armored vehicles}, {armored guards}. The spelling armour is British.

Armored means protected by armor—a hard covering that shields against weapons or impact. Armored {vehicles} carry soldiers through combat zones. An armored {car} transports cash and valuables. Armored {divisions} form the tank units of modern armies. Figuratively, someone emotionally armored has built defenses against hurt or vulnerability.

An armory is a place where weapons and military equipment are stored. In the United States, armories also serve as headquarters and training facilities for National Guard units, often doubling as civic buildings for public events: {The craft fair was held at the old armory}. The word extends to any collection of resources: {a whole armory of legal tactics}.

Armour is the British spelling of armor—protective covering worn in battle or fitted to vehicles and ships. Medieval knights wore suits of armour; modern tanks have armoured plating. The word extends to natural protection: {the armour of a turtle's shell}. Figuratively, armour is emotional defense: {Her sarcasm was armour against vulnerability}.

Armoury is the British spelling of armory—a place where weapons and military equipment are stored, or a collection of such equipment. By extension, an armoury is any stock of resources or techniques available for use: {She deployed her full armoury of rhetorical tricks}. In North America, an armory may also be a building used by military reserve units for training and drill.

The armpit is the hollow beneath the arm where it joins the shoulder. It's warm, often sweaty, and contains lymph nodes and scent glands. Figuratively, the armpit of something is its least desirable part: {That town is the armpit of America}.

Armpits are the hollow areas beneath the arms where they join the shoulders. These warm, often sweaty recesses contain lymph nodes and hair follicles, making them both medically significant and a site of grooming attention. Because armpits can develop strong odors, they're associated with poor hygiene or exertion: {The subway car reeked of armpits}. The armpit of a place is its least desirable area: {They called the neighborhood the armpit of the city}.

Arms has two distinct meanings. Most commonly, arms are weapons: {They took up arms against the invaders}, {the right to bear arms}. A coat of arms is a heraldic emblem. Arms also names the upper limbs of the human body, from shoulder to hand: {She held the baby in her arms}. The verb means to supply with weapons: {The rebels armed themselves with rifles}.

An army is a large organized force of soldiers trained for war on land, or a nation's entire military ground forces: {The army was deployed to the border}. By extension, army describes any large group mobilized for a purpose: {an army of volunteers}, {an army of ants}. The word suggests numbers, organization, and collective effort toward a goal.

Aroma is a distinctive, usually pleasant smell. The word suggests something more complex and appealing than odor: the aroma of {fresh coffee}, {baking bread}, {wine}. In wine tasting, aroma technically refers to scents from the grape itself, distinct from bouquet (scents from fermentation and aging), though casual use ignores this distinction.

Around‘s main idea can be found in the word’s origin, which is the word round: it refers to the area forming a circle or perimeter around a point. From here it soon came to mean on all sides and then throughout. If you have to go around something, it presents a physical or notional obstacle that is in your way. When abstract nouns and verbs are used with around the suggestion is of a basis or center for something: the meetings tend to center around financial matters; she has some issues around her popularity.

Arousal is the state of being stirred up or awakened. Sexual arousal is physical and mental readiness for sex: {the physiological signs of arousal}. But arousal applies to any heightened state—emotional arousal, arousal from sleep, the arousal of suspicion or curiosity. To arouse is to trigger such a state: {The speech aroused the crowd}.

Arouse means to stir up or awaken. You can arouse someone from sleep, arouse their curiosity, or arouse suspicion. Without an object, arouse typically means to become sexually excited: {The film's love scene aroused him}. The noun form is arousal. Arouse carries more intensity than simply wake or interest—it suggests something has been activated that was dormant.

Aroused means stirred up or awakened—brought from a dormant state to an active one. Curiosity can be aroused, as can suspicion, anger, or interest: {The strange noise aroused her curiosity}. Without further context, aroused often implies sexual excitement: {He was visibly aroused}. The past participle works as both verb and adjective.

To arrange is to put things in a particular order or position: {She arranged the flowers in a vase}, {The books were arranged alphabetically}. The word extends to making plans or preparations: {We arranged to meet at noon}, {He arranged for a car to pick us up}. In music, to arrange is to adapt a composition for different instruments or voices than originally written. An arrangement is the result of any of these activities—a spatial configuration, a plan, or a musical adaptation.

An arrangement is how things are organized or positioned relative to each other: {a seating arrangement}, {a floral arrangement}. It extends to plans or agreements: {We made arrangements to meet at noon}, {a financial arrangement}. In music, an arrangement adapts a composition for different instruments or voices than originally intended. The word implies deliberate ordering rather than randomness.

Arrangements are things put in order or organized for a purpose. You make arrangements for a trip, for childcare, for a funeral. A flower arrangement is blooms organized artfully. A musical arrangement adapts a composition for different instruments or voices: {a jazz arrangement of a classical piece}. The word implies deliberate organization rather than happenstance.

An array is an orderly arrangement or impressive display: {an array of options}, {a dazzling array of colors}. The word suggests both quantity and organization. In computing, an array is a data structure holding multiple values accessible by index. To array is to arrange or dress impressively: {troops arrayed for battle}, {arrayed in silk}.

Arrest means to stop or seize. Police arrest suspects, taking them into custody. A judge may issue an arrest {warrant}. Beyond law enforcement, arrest describes any sudden halt: {cardiac arrest} is when the heart stops. Something that arrests your {attention} captures it completely. {Under arrest} means in legal custody. An arresting {image} or {performance} is one that stops you in your tracks.

Arrested is the past tense of arrest, meaning stopped or taken into custody. Police arrest suspects; cardiac arrest stops the heart. Arrested also describes development that has halted prematurely: {arrested development} suggests someone whose emotional or psychological growth stalled at an earlier stage. {He was arrested for shoplifting.}

Arrests is the plural of arrest—instances of being taken into custody by legal authority: {The police made several arrests during the protest}. It also works as a verb meaning to seize or stop: {The photograph arrests your attention}. A cardiac arrest is when the heart stops beating. Something that arrests development halts its progress.

Arrival is the act of reaching a destination or the moment when someone or something appears: {We awaited their arrival at the airport}. It extends to abstract appearances—the arrival of {spring}, the arrival of a {new era}. A new arrival is someone who has just shown up or, commonly, a newborn baby.

To arrive is to reach a destination or endpoint: {We arrived at the hotel around midnight}. Extended to abstract goals, arriving means achieving success or recognition: {After years of struggle, she had finally arrived}. Things also arrive—packages, moments, conclusions: {The day of reckoning has arrived}. A newborn {arrives} when born.

Arrogance is an attitude of superiority—the belief that you're better, smarter, or more important than others, often displayed through dismissive or condescending behavior. Where confidence stays grounded, arrogance overreaches: {His arrogance made him impossible to work with}. The word carries strong disapproval; no one describes their own arrogance approvingly.

Arrogant describes someone who has an inflated sense of their own importance or abilities, often combined with dismissiveness toward others. An arrogant person assumes they deserve special treatment or that their opinions matter more than anyone else's: {He was too arrogant to ask for directions}. The word implies not just confidence but an offensive excess of it.

An arrow is a slender projectile shot from a bow, with a pointed tip at one end and stabilizing feathers at the other. The shape gives rise to arrow symbols (→, ↑) used to indicate direction: {Follow the arrows to the exit}. To {arrow} somewhere is to move swiftly and directly. {Straight as an arrow} means perfectly aligned or honest.

An arrowhead is the pointed tip of an arrow, traditionally made of stone, bone, or metal, designed to pierce a target. Archaeological arrowheads, particularly those chipped from flint or obsidian by indigenous peoples, are prized finds for collectors and historians. The term also names a common aquatic plant with arrow-shaped leaves that grows in marshes and shallow water. {We found a Native American arrowhead while hiking along the creek.}

Arrowheads are the pointed tips attached to arrow shafts, designed to penetrate targets. Historically made of stone, bone, or metal, they're now commonly found as archaeological artifacts: {We found Native American arrowheads in the field}. The term extends to anything arrow-tip-shaped, including a plant genus with triangular leaves and the typographic symbol (‹ or ›) used in interfaces and notation.

Arrows are projectiles shot from bows—a shaft with a pointed tip and stabilizing fletching. The shape gives us arrows as directional symbols: arrows on signs, arrows in diagrams, the cursor arrow on a screen. To {arrow} through something is to move swiftly and directly. {Straight as an arrow} means perfectly aligned. {The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune} are life's misfortunes.

Arse is the British spelling and pronunciation of ass, meaning buttocks. Unlike American ass, which has merged with the donkey meaning, arse remains purely anatomical. The word appears in many expressions: {arse over tit} (falling head over heels), {can't be arsed} (can't be bothered), {pain in the arse} (annoying person or thing), {arse about face} (backwards). To arse about means to fool around: {Stop arsing about}. Arse is vulgar but common in British speech, carrying roughly the same weight as American ass.

Arsehole is the British spelling of asshole—the anus, or a contemptible person: {Don't be such an arsehole}. The word carries the same force as its American counterpart: a strong insult for someone selfish, cruel, or obnoxious. {Tight as an arsehole} means extremely stingy.

Arseholes is the plural of arsehole, referring to contemptible people: {The arseholes in charge don't know what they're doing}. Like asshole, the word is a versatile insult for anyone behaving selfishly or cruelly.

An arsenal is a collection of weapons, or a place where weapons are stored and manufactured. By extension, it refers to any impressive collection of resources or tools: {She has an arsenal of techniques for dealing with difficult customers}. The word often appears in discussions of military capability: {nuclear arsenal}, {the country's growing arsenal}.

Arsenic is a chemical element, a metalloid notorious as a poison. Arsenic compounds have been used for centuries in murder and suicide because they're tasteless and produce symptoms resembling natural illness. In smaller doses, arsenic appears in pesticides, wood preservatives, and some semiconductor applications. {The Victorian wallpaper contained arsenic pigments.}

Arson is the crime of deliberately setting fire to property. The act requires intent—accidental fires don't qualify. Insurance fraud motivates some arson; revenge or vandalism motivates other cases. {The fire marshal determined the blaze was arson}. {He was convicted of arson after burning down the warehouse}.

An arsonist is someone who deliberately sets fire to property. The term applies whether the motive is insurance fraud, revenge, thrill-seeking, or pyromania: {Police arrested an arsonist who had set fires across three counties}. The word carries criminal connotation—accidentally starting a fire doesn't make someone an arsonist.

Art is a uniquely human product, based on the feature of perceived beauty and created for human enjoyment. Art is a very general word and encompasses many things that are examples of it, including painting, sculpture, film, music, literature, and architecture. When art is used to talk about tangible objects, it is likely to mean paintings or sculpture: She left her huge collection of art to the local museum. State of the art is a common phrase that is not about art per se, but about an accepted and current way of doing something. As a completely different word, art is the archaic second person singular indicative form of the verb be, now seen only in older text: Art thou the King of the Jews?

An artefact is an object made or modified by humans, especially one of historical or archaeological interest: {The museum displayed artefacts from the Bronze Age}. In technical contexts, an artefact is an unintended byproduct of a process—a flaw in an image, a glitch in data, or an anomaly in an experiment that doesn't reflect reality. This is the British spelling; Americans write artifact.

Artefacts is the British spelling of artifacts—objects made or modified by humans, especially those of historical or archaeological significance. The word also describes unintended byproducts in technical processes: visual artefacts in compressed images, artefacts in audio recordings. {The museum's collection includes artefacts from Roman Britain.}

Arteries are blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart to the rest of the body. Most carry oxygen-rich blood; the pulmonary arteries are the exception, delivering blood to the lungs for oxygenation. Figuratively, arteries are major routes of transport or communication: {The interstate highways are the arteries of American commerce}. A main artery carries heavy traffic; clogged arteries slow movement.

An artery is a blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart to the body's tissues—the counterpart to veins, which return blood to the heart. The word extends to major routes of transportation or communication: {The highway is a vital artery connecting the two cities}. Arterial describes roads that carry heavy traffic between smaller routes.

A form of creative expression recognized as having aesthetic value: painting, sculpture, music, dance, literature, film. The term validates something as worthy of serious attention: {She treats cooking as an artform}. Often spelled as two words (art form). Calling something an artform elevates it above mere craft or entertainment.

Arthouse describes films, theaters, or other media that prioritize artistic vision over commercial appeal. An arthouse {film} typically features unconventional narrative structure, ambiguous themes, or experimental techniques. An arthouse {cinema} screens such films, often foreign or independent productions unlikely to reach mainstream multiplexes. The term can suggest pretension: {too arthouse for general audiences}.

Arthritis is inflammation of the joints, causing pain, stiffness, and swelling. The term covers many conditions—osteoarthritis from wear on cartilage, rheumatoid arthritis from autoimmune attack, gout from crystal deposits. {Her arthritis flares up in cold weather.} Severity ranges from mild discomfort to disabling chronic pain.

An artichoke is a thistle-like plant cultivated for its large, edible flower bud. The overlapping leaves surround a fuzzy center called the choke, which is scraped away to reveal the prized heart: {artichoke hearts in olive oil}, {stuffed artichokes}. The unrelated Jerusalem artichoke is a tuber.

Artichokes is the plural of artichoke, a thistle-like plant cultivated for its large edible flower bud. The globe artichoke has tough outer leaves surrounding a tender heart; eating one involves peeling away layers to reach the prized center. {We had steamed artichokes with butter}. Jerusalem artichokes are unrelated—a type of sunflower grown for its knobby tuber.

An article is an individual item or thing, often one of several: {an article of clothing}, {articles of furniture}. In publishing, an article is a piece of nonfiction writing in a newspaper, magazine, or website. In grammar, articles are the words *a*, *an*, and *the*. Legal documents have numbered articles setting out terms: {Article I of the Constitution}. To article is to bind someone through a formal agreement, as in apprenticeship.

Articulate describes speech or expression that is clear, fluent, and well-organized: {an articulate defense of her position}, {He's surprisingly articulate for a five-year-old}. The verb means to express thoughts clearly or to pronounce distinctly: {She articulated her concerns to management}. In anatomy, articulate means to connect at a joint—bones articulate with each other, allowing movement. The adjective form for jointed structures is articulated: {an articulated bus}, {articulated skeleton}.

An artifact (artefact in British English) is a product of human effort. In most uses of the word, the product is intentional: The archaeologists discovered artifacts from an ancient civilization. A more limited technical meaning is for something resulting from human effort that was not the thing sought or intended, but instead a side effect: Wastage is an artifact of the dilapidated distribution system.

Artifacts are objects made or modified by humans, especially ones of historical or archaeological interest: {The museum displays artifacts from ancient Egypt}. In technical contexts, an artifact is an unintended byproduct of a process—a flaw in an image, a glitch in data, or an anomaly in a scientific measurement that results from the method rather than the phenomenon being studied. British spelling: artefacts.

Artificial describes things made by humans rather than occurring naturally: {artificial sweeteners}, {artificial intelligence}, {artificial turf}. The word often implies imitation of something natural—artificial flowers look like real ones but aren't. Applied to behavior, artificial suggests fakeness or affectation: {Her cheerfulness seemed artificial}. The connotation can be neutral (artificial light) or negative (artificial smile), depending on context.

Artillery refers to large-caliber military weapons—cannons, howitzers, missile launchers—too heavy to carry and typically operated by crews. The term also designates the branch of an army that operates such weapons: {He served in the artillery}. Figuratively, artillery can mean any heavy firepower or powerful resources brought to bear: {They brought out the legal artillery}.

An artisan is a skilled worker who makes things by hand, typically in a traditional craft: an artisan {baker}, an artisan {cheesemaker}, an artisan {woodworker}. The word emphasizes manual skill and quality over mass production. Marketing has stretched artisan to cover anything positioned as handcrafted or small-batch: {artisan bread}, {artisan pizza}. The overuse has diluted its meaning.

Artisans are skilled workers who make things by hand, typically in traditional crafts like woodworking, pottery, metalwork, or textiles. The word emphasizes craftsmanship and manual skill over industrial production: {artisan bread}, {artisan cheese}. An artisan bakery suggests care and quality that mass production lacks. The term has become a marketing buzzword, sometimes applied loosely to anything positioned as handmade or small-batch.

An artist creates works of art—paintings, sculptures, drawings, or other visual pieces. The term extends to practitioners of any creative discipline: a recording {artist}, a {con artist}, a {martial artist}. Someone called an artist at their craft has achieved mastery: {She's an artist with a needle and thread}. The word carries connotations of creativity, skill, and dedication to craft.

Artistic describes things related to art or showing creative skill and aesthetic sensibility. An artistic {temperament} suggests sensitivity and imagination. Someone artistic has talent for creating or appreciating visual art, music, or other creative work: {She's always been the artistic one in the family}. Artistic can also mean aesthetically pleasing or done with flair: {an artistic arrangement of flowers}.

Artistry is exceptional skill in creative work, especially in the arts. It suggests not just technical competence but imagination, taste, and expressive power: {The artistry of her brushwork}, {He brought real artistry to the role}. The word extends beyond traditional arts to any endeavor performed with unusual grace or creativity: {the artistry of a master chef}, {There's artistry in how she negotiates}.

Arts encompasses creative and imaginative pursuits—painting, sculpture, music, literature, theater, dance. The term often appears in contrast to sciences: a {college of arts and sciences}. The {liberal arts} are academic subjects valued for general knowledge rather than technical training. {The arts} collectively refers to creative disciplines and the cultural sector that supports them: {government funding for the arts}. Someone skilled in {the arts of persuasion} has mastered techniques requiring finesse.

Artsy describes something or someone that aspires to artistic sophistication, often with a hint of pretension or superficiality. An artsy {film} favors style over accessibility. An artsy {neighborhood} has galleries and coffee shops. The word can be affectionate or dismissive depending on tone: {She's gotten really artsy since art school}. Artsy-fartsy is the mocking intensification.

Artwork is any creative visual product—paintings, sculptures, illustrations, photographs. In publishing and design, artwork refers specifically to images prepared for reproduction: {The artwork for the album cover isn't finished yet}. A single piece may be called an artwork, though "work of art" is more traditional for fine art contexts.

Asbestos is a fibrous mineral once widely used for insulation and fireproofing because it resists heat and doesn't burn. When disturbed, asbestos releases microscopic fibers that cause serious lung diseases and cancers when inhaled. Its use is now banned or heavily restricted in most countries: {The old building had to be tested for asbestos before renovation}.

To ascend is to move upward—climbing stairs, rising through air, or scaling a mountain. The word carries formality that *go up* lacks: {The balloon ascended into the clouds}.
