Figuratively, one ascends to higher status or power: {She ascended to the throne}, {He ascended the corporate ladder}. In music, notes ascend when they move from lower to higher pitch.

Ascension is the act or process of rising or moving upward. It often describes advancement to a higher position or rank: {her ascension to the throne}, {his ascension through the corporate ranks}. The word carries a sense of elevation—physical, social, or spiritual—that distinguishes it from simple movement. In astronomy, right ascension is a coordinate measuring position along the celestial equator. (Capitalized Ascension refers to Christ's bodily rising into heaven.)

Ascent is the act of going up—climbing a mountain, rising through the air, or advancing in status or rank. The word emphasizes upward movement: {the ascent of the balloon}, {her ascent to the presidency}. An ascent is also an upward slope or path: {The final ascent to the summit took three hours}.

Ascomycota is a major division of fungi characterized by spores produced in sac-like structures called asci. This phylum includes yeasts, morels, truffles, and many plant pathogens. Most fungi that form lichens belong to this group. The term appears primarily in scientific and taxonomic contexts: {Ascomycota represents the largest phylum of fungi}.

Asexual describes organisms that reproduce without sexual union—a single parent producing offspring genetically identical to itself: {Bacteria reproduce asexually}. In human sexuality, asexual describes someone who experiences little or no sexual attraction to others. Such people may identify as ace: {She came out as asexual in college}. The term encompasses a spectrum of experiences, from complete absence of sexual interest to occasional or conditional attraction.

The spelling a-s-h represents two words in English. The more frequent meaning, often used in the plural, is for the residue of burning a solid substance, like the ashes you find in a fireplace. Someone’s ashes are what remain of their corpse after cremation. The other meaning of ash is for a genus of trees and other plants found across the Northern hemisphere, occurring in forests and also planted ornamentally.

Ashamed describes the feeling of guilt, embarrassment, or disgrace that comes from recognizing you've done something wrong or fallen short of standards—your own or others'. {I'm ashamed of how I treated her}. You can be ashamed of yourself, of your actions, or of someone else whose behavior reflects on you. The feeling implies self-awareness and often a desire to hide: {too ashamed to show his face}.

Ashes are the powdery residue left after something burns completely. Wood fires leave ashes in the fireplace; cigarettes leave ashes in the tray. Human remains after cremation are called ashes: {We scattered her ashes at sea}. Figuratively, ashes suggest destruction or ruin: {The city lay in ashes}. To {rise from the ashes} is to recover from devastation. {Ashes to ashes, dust to dust} comes from funeral rites, emphasizing mortality.

Ashore means onto or on the shore, from the water to land: {The sailors went ashore for supplies}, {The waves washed debris ashore}. It contrasts with being aboard a vessel or out at sea. Someone who comes ashore arrives on land after a voyage.

An ashtray is a small receptacle for cigarette and cigar ash and butts. Ashtrays were once standard fixtures in homes, restaurants, and offices; their disappearance from public spaces tracks the decline of indoor smoking. {She stubbed out her cigarette in the ashtray}.

Aside means to one side or out of the way: {She stepped aside to let him pass}. To set or put something aside is to reserve it for later or dismiss it from consideration: {Let's set aside our differences}. An aside is a remark not meant for everyone present, or in theater, words spoken to the audience that other characters supposedly can't hear. {Aside from} means except for or in addition to: {Aside from the weather, the trip was perfect}.

Ask is the most common verb to indicate that an answer is sought or that a question has been put forward. There are several subsidiary meanings that have to do with a request or demand for something to happen or be provided. Ask is one of the oldest and most frequently used verbs. It is most typically transitive and takes a person as an object (Ask her if she wants to come) but it participates in many other patterns with little change in meaning.

Asleep describes the state of sleeping: {The baby is finally asleep}. To {fall asleep} is to transition into sleep. Body parts that are asleep have gone numb from restricted blood flow: {My foot fell asleep}. Figuratively, someone asleep is inattentive or unaware: {The regulators were asleep at the switch}.

Asparagus is a vegetable with long green stalks and a distinctive, slightly bitter flavor. The edible shoots are harvested in spring before the tips open into feathery fronds. Asparagus is typically steamed, roasted, or grilled: {grilled asparagus with lemon}, {a side of buttered asparagus}. It notoriously makes urine smell pungent.

Aspect is a particular part, feature, or angle of something: {We need to consider every aspect of the proposal}. The word emphasizes one element among many that together make up a whole. In astrology, aspect refers to the angular relationship between celestial bodies. In grammar, aspect describes how a verb expresses the flow of time—whether an action is completed, ongoing, or repeated.

Aspen is a tree of the poplar family, known for leaves that tremble in the slightest breeze—the source of phrases like {quaking aspen} and {trembling like an aspen leaf}. The pale bark and golden fall foliage make aspens distinctive in mountain landscapes. Aspen groves spread through connected root systems, forming vast clonal colonies.

Aspens are deciduous trees of the poplar family, known for leaves that tremble in the slightest breeze—a feature that gives the quaking aspen its name. The trees often grow in large stands connected by a single root system, their white bark and golden autumn foliage making them iconic in mountain landscapes: {The aspens were turning gold along the ridge}.

Asphalt is a dark, sticky petroleum-based substance used for paving roads and waterproofing. Mixed with gravel, it forms the black surface of most streets and parking lots: {fresh asphalt steaming in the summer heat}. To asphalt is to pave with this material. The word is sometimes pronounced with a long A in the second syllable.

Aspiration is a strong desire to achieve something significant: {She had aspirations of becoming a surgeon}. The word suggests ambition directed toward a worthy goal. In medicine, aspiration is the drawing of fluid or foreign matter into the lungs, or the removal of fluid from the body by suction. To aspirate a sound is to pronounce it with an audible breath.

Aspirations are hopes or ambitions for achieving something, typically something significant: {She had aspirations of becoming a doctor}, {His political aspirations were well known}. The word implies reaching upward—toward goals not yet attained. Aspiration in the singular can also refer to the medical act of drawing fluid from the body, or in phonetics, the puff of air accompanying certain consonants.

To aspire is to reach toward something higher—a goal, achievement, or state of being. The word carries ambition and longing: {She aspires to be a doctor}, {He aspired to greatness}. You can aspire to concrete positions or abstract qualities. What you aspire to is your aspiration. The word suggests earnest striving rather than idle wishing.

Aspirin is a common pain reliever and anti-inflammatory drug, also used to reduce fever and prevent blood clots. The word began as a trademark but became generic through widespread use. People take aspirin for headaches, muscle aches, and heart health: {Take two aspirin and call me in the morning}.

Aspiring describes someone who hopes or strives to become something they aren't yet: an aspiring {actor}, an aspiring {novelist}, an aspiring {chef}. The word carries earnestness and ambition but also implies the goal remains unachieved. {She's an aspiring singer working as a waitress.} Unlike would-be, aspiring suggests active effort rather than mere wishing.

Ass has two origins that have merged in American English. One is the donkey, a beast of burden known for stubbornness, which gives us {make an ass of yourself}. The other is the buttocks. Ass spawns countless expressions: {kick ass}, {haul ass}, {kiss my ass}, {bust your ass} (work hard), {piece of ass} (crude for a sexual partner). Someone described as a {dumb ass} or {smart ass} is characterized by that quality in an unflattering way.

An assassin is someone who murders a prominent person, typically for political or ideological reasons. The word implies premeditation and often a hired killer: {The president's assassin was captured fleeing the scene}. Unlike ordinary murderers, assassins target figures of importance—leaders, activists, rivals. The verb is assassinate; character assassination destroys reputation rather than life.

To assassinate is to murder a prominent person, typically for political or ideological reasons. The word implies premeditation and often public significance—presidents, civil rights leaders, and religious figures are assassinated; ordinary citizens are simply murdered. {Lincoln was assassinated in 1865.} {They plotted to assassinate the ambassador.} The noun is assassination; the killer is an assassin.

Assassinated is the past tense of assassinate—to murder a prominent person, typically for political or ideological reasons. The victim is usually a political leader, activist, or public figure: {President Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas}. The word implies deliberate targeting rather than random violence. Unlike ordinary murder, assassination carries historical weight and suggests the killing was meant to change the course of events.

Assassination is the killing of a prominent person, typically for political or ideological reasons. The targets are usually political leaders, activists, or public figures: {the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.}, {an assassination attempt on the president}. The verb is assassinate. Character assassination destroys someone's reputation rather than their life.

Assassinations are killings of prominent figures—political leaders, public officials, activists—typically carried out for ideological or political motives. The plural often refers to a pattern or series: {political assassinations destabilized the region}, {the assassinations of the 1960s shaped American politics}. Distinguished from ordinary murder by the target's significance and the killer's calculated intent.

Assassins is the plural of assassin—a person who murders someone, usually a public figure, typically for political or ideological reasons or for payment. The word implies premeditation and often stealth: {The assassins waited in the crowd}. Extended uses include paid killers in fiction and gaming, where assassin is a character class specializing in stealth kills.

Assault is a physical attack or the threat of one. In law, assault often means the threat alone, while battery is the actual contact—but common usage treats assault as the attack itself: {He was charged with assault}. Sexual assault covers a range of unwanted sexual contact. The verb means to attack: {The troops assaulted the fortress}. Figuratively, loud noises or bad smells assault the senses.

Assemble means to gather people or things into one place, or to fit parts together into a whole. A crowd assembles in a square; workers assemble cars on a factory line. {Some assembly required} warns that a product arrives in pieces. In computing, to assemble is to convert code into machine language. {The team assembled for the briefing.}

Assembly is the act of bringing parts or people together into a unified whole. Workers on an assembly line fit components together to manufacture products. A kit requires assembly. Assembly also means a gathering of people for a common purpose—a school assembly, a legislative assembly. In computing, assembly language is low-level code that communicates more directly with hardware than high-level languages. The right of assembly, protected in many constitutions, allows people to gather peacefully. (Capitalized Assembly often names a specific legislative body.)

Assert means to state something confidently and forcefully, often without offering proof: {She asserted her innocence despite the evidence}. The word implies conviction—you don't assert things you're uncertain about. To assert yourself is to behave confidently and claim your rights or position. To assert a claim or right is to insist on its recognition: {He asserted his authority over the department}. In computing, an assertion is a statement that checks whether a condition is true, halting execution if it fails.

Assertive describes someone who states opinions and defends positions confidently, without being passive or apologetic. An assertive person speaks up for themselves: {She was assertive in salary negotiations}. The word carries positive connotations of healthy self-advocacy, distinct from aggressive, which implies hostility or pushiness.

Assessment is the act of evaluating or measuring something—its value, quality, condition, or significance. A tax assessment determines property value. A risk assessment weighs potential dangers. In education, assessments test student knowledge: {The final assessment counts for half the grade}. The word often implies systematic judgment rather than casual opinion.

An asset is something that has value. The broad meaning of asset can be divided for practical purposes between assets that are exchangeable for money or some other compensation, and those that can’t, such as the qualities of a person or place. In law, assets are all the property and valuable things that a person owns. In accounting, assets appear on a balance sheet in contrast with liabilities. Some assets arise situationally, where they can be thought of as an advantage: On-the-job experience is one of the assets we’re looking for in our next general manager.

Assets are things of value that a person, company, or organization owns. In accounting and finance, assets include cash, property, equipment, investments, and money owed by others. Personal assets might include savings, real estate, and vehicles. The singular asset often means any useful quality or advantage: {Her language skills are a real asset to the team}. In espionage, an asset is a person who provides intelligence.
Asshole is a vulgar term for the anus, but it's primarily used as an insult for a contemptible, selfish, or obnoxious person: {My neighbor is a complete asshole}. The British spelling is arsehole.
Assholes is the plural of asshole, a vulgar insult for contemptible people: {The meeting was full of assholes trying to take credit for my work}.

Assign means to designate or allocate something for a particular purpose or person. A teacher assigns homework; a manager assigns tasks to employees. You can assign blame, assign a value to a variable, or be assigned to a project. In law, to assign is to transfer rights or property to another: {She assigned the lease to her business partner}. The noun assignment covers both the act and the thing assigned.

An assignment is a task given to someone as part of their job or studies: {The reporter got the assignment to cover the trial}, {I have three assignments due this week}. Assignment also means the act of assigning—allocating resources, designating roles, or transferring rights: {the assignment of seats}, {the assignment of a patent}. In military and diplomatic contexts, an assignment is a posting: {His first assignment was in Germany}.

Assimilate means to absorb and integrate. Food is assimilated into the body. Information is assimilated into understanding. Immigrants assimilate into a new culture by adopting its language, customs, and values—though the word can carry undertones of pressure to abandon one's original identity. In science fiction, assimilate often describes forced absorption into a collective: {Resistance is futile; you will be assimilated}.

Assimilation is the process of absorbing something into a larger whole. In sociology, it describes how minority groups adopt the customs and attitudes of a dominant culture: {The pressure for assimilation was strong among immigrant families}. In biology, it's how organisms convert food into living tissue. The word often carries tension—assimilation can mean belonging or erasure, depending on who's describing it.

To assist is to help or support someone in completing a task. The word often implies a secondary role—you assist the lead surgeon, assist with dinner preparations. In sports, an assist is a pass or play that directly leads to a score: {She had twelve assists in the game}. As a noun outside sports, assist appears mainly in phrases like {an assist from} meaning help received.

An assistant is someone who helps or supports another person, typically in a professional or organizational role: {a research assistant}, {the assistant manager}. The word implies subordination—assistants work under someone else's direction. As an adjective, it describes a secondary position: {assistant coach}, {assistant professor}. In computing, an assistant is software designed to help users accomplish tasks.

Asskissing is excessive flattery or servile behavior toward someone in power, motivated by self-interest rather than genuine admiration. The term is vulgar but common: {His promotion was pure asskissing, not merit}. An asskisser engages in such behavior. Also spelled ass-kissing. The verb is kiss ass or kiss someone's ass.

Variable pronunciation of the last syllable distinguishes the verb associate from the noun and adjective with the same spelling. Verbal meanings are all connected with the idea of joining two or more things; you can associate ideas, and you can associate with people in your peer group. The noun and adjective partly share this meaning – of one who associates with another – but there is also a connotation of being subordinate (associate professor, meet with his associate).

Associates are people connected by work, business, or shared activity—colleagues rather than close friends. The word suggests professional distance: {business associates}, {known associates of the suspect}. As a verb, to associate is to connect mentally or socially: {I associate that smell with my grandmother's kitchen}. To associate with someone is to spend time with them, often with implications about character: {You shouldn't associate with those people}. Associate as an adjective indicates a junior or partial status: {associate professor}, {associate member}.

Association is the act of connecting things mentally or the connection itself: {The smell had strong associations with childhood}. It also means a group organized around shared interests: {a trade association}, {a homeowners association}. To be {in association with} someone is to work alongside them. Free association is saying whatever comes to mind without filtering.

When you assume that something is true or that something is the case, you take it to be that way without having proof: Students in the course are assumed to have good mathematical knowledge and programming experience. It’s reasonable to assume that the package was delivered yesterday. If you assume a responsibility, role, or position, you take it on yourself: She won’t assume responsibility of the department till next month. The government has decided to assume control of all the ports.

An assumption is something taken for granted or accepted as true without proof: {The plan rests on the assumption that costs will stay stable}. In logic and argument, assumptions are the unstated premises underlying a conclusion. The assumption of a role or responsibility is the act of taking it on: {her assumption of the presidency}. In Catholic doctrine, the Assumption refers to the Virgin Mary's bodily elevation to heaven, but lowercase assumption can describe any such taking up. {That's a big assumption to make.}

Assumptions are things accepted as true without proof, serving as starting points for reasoning or action. When you make an assumption, you take something for granted—sometimes reasonably, sometimes not. {The budget was based on the assumption that sales would increase.} In logic and mathematics, assumptions are premises from which conclusions follow. The word often carries a note of caution: unchecked assumptions can lead to faulty conclusions or embarrassing mistakes. {Don't make assumptions about what people want—just ask them.}

Assurance is confident certainty, either felt or conveyed to others: {She spoke with quiet assurance}. To give assurance is to promise or guarantee: {He gave assurances that the project would be completed on time}. In British usage, assurance is insurance, particularly life insurance. Self-assurance is confidence in one's own abilities.

An asterisk is the star-shaped symbol (*) used in writing and printing. It typically marks a footnote or draws attention to something requiring explanation. In informal writing, asterisks may indicate emphasis or surround a word to convey action or tone: {*sigh*}, {*chef's kiss*}. In computing, the asterisk serves as a wildcard character matching any string of characters.

An asteroid is a rocky object orbiting the sun, smaller than a planet but larger than a meteoroid. Most asteroids occupy the belt between Mars and Jupiter. The term sometimes applies loosely to any small celestial body: {The spacecraft was destroyed by an asteroid}. In figurative use, something can hit like an asteroid—sudden, devastating, world-changing.

Asteroids are rocky objects orbiting the sun, smaller than planets but larger than meteoroids. Most occupy the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. The term also names the classic arcade game where players destroy space rocks: {I spent hours playing Asteroids at the arcade}.

Asthma is a chronic respiratory condition in which the airways narrow and swell, making breathing difficult. Symptoms include wheezing, coughing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. Attacks can be triggered by allergens, exercise, cold air, or stress: {Her asthma acts up in the spring}. Most people manage asthma with inhalers containing bronchodilators or steroids.

To astonish is to strike with sudden wonder or amazement. Unlike mere surprise, astonishment suggests being momentarily overwhelmed: {The magician's finale astonished the crowd}. Something astonishing defies expectation so completely that it stops you short: {It astonishes me that anyone still believes that}.

Astonished describes a state of intense surprise or amazement, typically at something unexpected or hard to believe. It conveys stronger shock than merely surprised—someone astonished is momentarily stunned or overwhelmed by what they've witnessed or learned. {I was astonished to find her waiting at my door after all these years.} The word often appears with at or by to indicate the cause: {astonished at his nerve}, {astonished by the results}.

Astonishing describes something that causes great surprise or wonder—remarkable enough to momentarily stun: {The magician performed an astonishing trick}. It implies more intensity than surprising but less than shocking. Something astonishing defies expectation in a way that demands attention: {an astonishing recovery}, {astonishing speed}.

Astray means off the right path or course. Something that goes astray gets lost or misdirected: {The package went astray in the mail}. The word often carries moral weight—to lead someone astray is to tempt them toward wrongdoing or error: {Bad company led him astray}. Astray usually functions as an adverb or predicate adjective, rarely appearing before a noun.

An astrologer is someone who practices astrology—the study of celestial bodies to interpret their supposed influence on human affairs. Astrologers cast horoscopes and make predictions based on planetary positions and zodiac signs: {The astrologer said Mercury in retrograde explained my communication problems}. The term implies belief in a system most scientists reject.

Astrology is the study of celestial bodies—stars, planets, the moon—as influences on human affairs and earthly events. Practitioners interpret birth charts and planetary alignments to describe personality traits or predict outcomes: {What's your sign?} Though once intertwined with astronomy, astrology now lacks scientific standing and is typically regarded as pseudoscience or entertainment.

An astronaut is a person trained to travel and work in space. The term typically applies to crew members of spacecraft, whether military pilots or civilian scientists. Americans use astronaut; Russians use cosmonaut; the Chinese use taikonaut—but all describe the same role. {She dreamed of becoming an astronaut since watching the moon landing.}

Astronauts are people trained to travel and work in space, typically as crew members aboard spacecraft or space stations. The term comes from Greek words meaning "star sailor," though most astronauts operate in Earth orbit rather than among the stars. Russians use the equivalent term cosmonaut, and the Chinese use taikonaut. {Two astronauts conducted a spacewalk to repair the solar panels.} The word often appears in contexts of childhood aspiration and human achievement.

An astronomer is a scientist who studies celestial objects and phenomena—stars, planets, galaxies, and the universe at large. The work ranges from observational astronomy, using telescopes to gather data, to theoretical modeling of cosmic processes. {Astronomers confirmed the existence of a ninth planet}. Unlike astrologers, astronomers practice science, not divination.

Astronomical describes what relates to astronomy—the scientific study of celestial bodies: {astronomical observations}, {astronomical data}. More commonly, it characterizes numbers or quantities so large they evoke cosmic scales: {astronomical costs}, {astronomical odds}. Medical bills, executive salaries, and national debts are frequently called astronomical. The word implies not just bigness but excess bordering on absurdity.

Astronomy is the scientific study of celestial objects and phenomena—stars, planets, galaxies, and the universe as a whole. It examines everything from nearby moons to distant quasars, addressing questions about the origin, structure, and fate of the cosmos. {She studied astronomy in college}. Distinguished from astrology, which claims celestial positions influence human affairs.

Astroturf in its generic sense refers to any artificial grass surface, or metaphorically to fake grassroots movements—political campaigns or advocacy that appear to arise spontaneously from ordinary citizens but are actually orchestrated and funded by corporations, political groups, or wealthy interests. The verb means to create such deceptive campaigns: {The pharmaceutical company astroturfed opposition to the bill}. (Capitalized AstroTurf is the brand name.)

Astroturfing is the practice of creating fake grassroots support—manufacturing the appearance of organic public enthusiasm for a product, cause, or political position. The term plays on AstroTurf, the artificial grass: astroturfing is artificial grass roots. It typically involves paid operatives, fake social media accounts, or coordinated campaigns designed to seem spontaneous: {The company was caught astroturfing positive reviews}.

As a physical space and in its original meaning, asylum suggests a place that is protected from invasion or violation. Today the word sees more usage as a state of being in which someone vulnerable is protected. If you seek asylum, the presumption is that you are currently in danger. If you grant asylum, you are offering protection. Asylum as a designation for a residential psychiatric facility is now dated and considered offensive.

Asylums are institutions offering refuge or protection. Historically, an asylum was a place where those seeking sanctuary could not be seized—a concept surviving in political asylum, protection granted to refugees from persecution. In the 19th and early 20th centuries, asylum became synonymous with institutions for the mentally ill: {the state asylum}, {locked away in an asylum}. That usage now sounds dated and carries connotations of grim, warehouse-like facilities. Modern terminology favors psychiatric hospital or mental health facility.

An atarah is a decorative collar or neckband sewn onto a Jewish prayer shawl (tallit), typically made of silver thread, embroidery, or ornate fabric. The atarah often bears a Hebrew blessing and marks which side faces up when worn: {The rabbi's tallit had a beautifully embroidered atarah}.

Ate is the past tense of eat. {I ate breakfast at seven}. {She ate the whole thing}. The word appears in idioms: {What ate you?} asks what's bothering someone. To have {eaten one's words} is to retract a statement. In slang, especially online, ate means performed excellently: {She ate that performance}.

Atheism is the absence of belief in gods, or the active belief that no gods exist. The two senses differ: one is simply lacking theistic belief, the other is a positive claim. Atheism contrasts with agnosticism, which holds that the existence of gods is unknown or unknowable. {Her atheism developed gradually after years of questioning her faith.}

An atheist is someone who doesn't believe in God or gods. The term ranges from active denial that deities exist to simple absence of belief. {She was raised Catholic but became an atheist in college.} Atheist can be self-identified or applied by others, sometimes pejoratively. The adjective atheistic describes views or arguments: {an atheistic worldview}.

Atheists are people who don't believe in any god or gods. The term ranges from those who actively reject theism to those who simply lack religious belief. Some atheists identify strongly with the label; others prefer "nonreligious" or "secular." {The atheists in our philosophy club had lively debates with the believers.}

An athlete is someone who competes in sports or engages in physical exercise requiring strength, speed, or endurance. Professional athletes make their living from competition; amateur athletes compete for other rewards. The term implies training and physical conditioning: {She's a natural athlete}. Student-athlete refers to someone balancing academics with varsity sports.

Athletes are people who train and compete in sports or physical activities requiring strength, speed, agility, or endurance. The term covers professionals and amateurs alike—from Olympic sprinters to weekend marathon runners. {She's a natural athlete.} Student athletes balance academics with competitive sports. The word implies physical conditioning and dedication to performance.

Athletic describes physical strength, agility, and fitness—the qualities associated with sports and exercise. An athletic {build} is muscular and well-proportioned. An athletic {person} excels at or enjoys physical activity. Athletic {shoes} and {wear} are designed for sports or exercise, though often worn casually. {She's always been athletic, lettering in three sports in high school.}

Athleticism is physical prowess—the combination of strength, speed, agility, and coordination that makes someone good at sports. The word emphasizes natural gifts and trained abilities together: {Her athleticism was evident in every move}. Someone can have athleticism without being an athlete, and vice versa, though the terms overlap.

Athletics refers to sports and physical activities requiring strength, speed, or endurance. In American usage, athletics covers organized sports generally: {the athletics department}, {college athletics}. In British usage, athletics specifically means track and field events—running, jumping, throwing. The word often implies competitive sport rather than casual exercise: {She excelled at athletics in high school}.

The Greek Titan who supported the heavens on his shoulders is the eponym for all other things called atlas, especially a bound volume of maps. Following the tradition of naming things in the sky after the Greek gods, some heavenly bodies (such as a moon of Saturn) also bear the name Atlas. The theme of support extends to architecture, where a column sculptured in the figure of a man is called an atlas.

Atmosphere is the layer of gases surrounding a planet—Earth's atmosphere is the air we breathe. By extension, atmosphere describes the pervading mood or tone of a place: {The restaurant had a romantic atmosphere}. A room with atmosphere has character or ambiance. In physics, one atmosphere is a unit of pressure equal to the weight of air at sea level.

Atmospheric describes things relating to the atmosphere—the layer of gases surrounding a planet: {atmospheric pressure}, {atmospheric carbon dioxide}. More commonly, atmospheric describes something that creates a distinctive mood or ambiance: {The restaurant had atmospheric lighting}. An atmospheric film or novel evokes a strong sense of place or feeling, often through visual or sensory detail rather than plot.

An atom is the smallest unit of a chemical element, consisting of a nucleus surrounded by electrons. For most of history, atoms were thought indivisible—the word comes from Greek for "uncuttable"—but physicists split them in the 20th century. Figuratively, an atom is any tiny amount: {not an atom of truth in it}.

Atomic relates to atoms—the smallest units of matter that retain chemical properties. In physics, atomic describes phenomena at this scale: atomic {structure}, atomic {mass}. Atomic {energy} and atomic {bombs} harness power released by splitting atoms. Figuratively, atomic means indivisible or fundamental: in computing, an atomic {operation} completes entirely or not at all, with no partial states.

Atoms are the smallest units of matter that retain the properties of a chemical element. Everything physical is made of atoms—your body, the air, the ground beneath you. An atom consists of a nucleus surrounded by electrons. The word often signals fundamental particles or tiny amounts: {There isn't an atom of truth in what he said}. To {split the atom} is to release nuclear energy, or figuratively, to accomplish something requiring extreme precision.

To atone is to make amends for wrongdoing or sin. The word carries a sense of compensating through action or sacrifice: {He tried to atone for years of neglect by caring for her in her final days}. Religious contexts speak of atonement as reconciliation with God, while secular use focuses on repairing harm done to others.

Atonement is the act of making amends for wrongdoing or sin. The word carries religious weight—in Christian theology, Christ's atonement reconciles humanity with God through sacrifice. More broadly, atonement is any effort to repair a wrong: {He spent years in atonement for his betrayal}. The Jewish Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur) is devoted to repentance and reconciliation.

An atrium is a central open space in a building, typically rising through multiple stories and often topped with a skylight or glass roof: {The hotel's atrium was filled with tropical plants}. In anatomy, an atrium is one of the two upper chambers of the heart that receive blood from the veins. The word originally meant the central hall of a Roman house, open to the sky.

Atrocious describes something shockingly bad or cruel. An atrocious crime is brutal and horrifying. But the word often appears in lighter contexts for emphasis: {The service was atrocious}, {Her spelling is atrocious}. This casual use has diluted the word's original force—truly atrocious acts involve cruelty or violence, not just incompetence.

Atrocities are acts of extreme cruelty or violence, typically committed during war or by those in power: {atrocities committed against civilians}, {documenting the regime's atrocities}. The word implies actions so brutal they shock the conscience—mass killings, torture, systematic abuse. An atrocity can also be something shockingly bad or tasteless, though this lighter use risks trivializing the word's core meaning.

An atrocity is an act of extreme cruelty or brutality, especially one committed during war or conflict: {The massacre was among the worst atrocities of the civil war}. The word implies not just violence but moral horror—acts that shock the conscience. In looser use, atrocity describes anything appallingly bad: {That haircut is an atrocity}.
Attaboy is a sound spelling of an informal pronunciation of that’s a boy. It is used to give encouragement or to convey approval to males.

To attach is to fasten or connect one thing to another: {Attach the document to your email}, {The handle attaches with two screws}. The connection can be physical or abstract—you attach conditions to an agreement, or become emotionally attached to a person or place. In legal contexts, to attach property is to seize it by court order. Something attached comes along with something else: {The job comes with certain responsibilities attached}.

Attached means connected or fastened to something else: {The receipt is attached to the email}. Beyond physical connection, attached describes emotional bonds—to be attached to someone or something is to feel fondness or loyalty: {She's very attached to that old sweater}. In relationships, attached means not single: {Sorry, I'm attached}. An attaché is a specialist assigned to a diplomatic mission.

Attachment is the state of being connected to something, whether physically or emotionally. A document or file sent along with an email is an attachment. In law, attachment is the seizure of property by legal process. The word often describes emotional bonds: {her attachment to her childhood home}, {forming attachments too quickly}. An attachment can also be a device that connects to something larger to extend its function: {a vacuum cleaner attachment}.

Attachments are things fastened to something else. An email attachment is a file sent along with a message. A vacuum cleaner's attachments are its interchangeable parts. The word also names emotional bonds: {She formed a strong attachment to her mentor}. In psychology, attachment theory describes how early bonds shape later relationships. Legal attachments are court orders seizing property.

A dependable feature of any attack, whether it’s used as a noun or verb, is that it’s typically intended to hurt (attack on a city, attack someone’s character). When applied to disease, it refers to a sudden and acute episode: She had a sports-induced asthma attack. A variety of attack that doesn’t hurt can be musical (she attacked Beethoven’s Fifth) or intellectual (attack a problem).

An attacker is someone who attacks—physically assaulting another person, launching a military offensive, or attempting to breach a computer system. In sports, an attacker is an offensive player whose role is to score: {The attacker broke through the defense}. The word implies aggression and initiative, positioning someone as the one who starts the conflict or action.
Attagirl is a sound spelling of an informal pronunciation of that’s a girl. It is used to give encouragement or to convey approval to females.

An attempt is an effort to do something, especially something difficult or uncertain: {Her attempt to climb Everest ended at base camp}. The verb means to try: {He attempted to explain but gave up}. An attempt on someone's life is an effort to kill them. Unlike try, attempt suggests formality or seriousness—you try a new restaurant but attempt a summit.

Attend means to be present at something: {She attended the conference}, {Will you attend the wedding?} It also means to pay attention to or take care of: {Attend to your studies}, {A nurse attended the patient}. To attend to a matter is to deal with it. An attendant is someone who assists or accompanies.

Attendance is the act of being present somewhere, or the number of people present: {Attendance at the rally exceeded expectations}. To {take attendance} is to record who has shown up. School attendance may be mandatory; church attendance voluntary. The word often implies obligation or expectation—you attend classes, meetings, court dates. Poor attendance suggests chronic absence from somewhere you should be.

An attendant is someone whose job involves waiting on, serving, or assisting others in a particular setting: flight {attendant}, parking lot {attendant}, {pool attendant}. The word also works as an adjective meaning accompanying or connected with something else: {the responsibilities attendant upon parenthood}. Attendant circumstances or conditions are those that exist alongside a main event or situation. The noun can also refer simply to someone who attends or is present at an event.

Attention is the mental focus you direct toward something. To {pay attention} is to concentrate; to {call attention to} something is to make others notice it. {Attention!} commands soldiers to stand alert and ready. In the plural, attentions are acts of courtesy or romantic interest: {unwanted attentions}. Something that {comes to your attention} enters your awareness.

Attentive means paying close attention or being alert and watchful: {an attentive audience}, {attentive to every detail}. It also describes someone who is considerate and responsive to others' needs: {an attentive host}, {He was attentive to her throughout the evening}. The word suggests focused awareness, whether directed at information or at people.

An attic is the space directly under a roof, typically used for storage. Unlike a finished upper floor, an attic is usually unheated and accessed by a ladder or narrow stairs. Attics accumulate forgotten belongings: {We found old photographs in the attic}. The word also describes anything relating to this space: {attic insulation}, {attic fan}. (Capitalized Attic relates to ancient Athens.)

Your attitude toward or about something is the way you feel about it, as reflected in your behavior. Attitudes can be positive, negative, or neutral, but often when people talk about attitude without characterizing it, they mean a bad attitude: He had such an attitude when he came in this morning that no one wanted to talk to him. This usage may explain why one of the most frequent verbs that precedes attitude is change: The community has slowly changed its attitude and now seems very welcoming to newcomers. You can also use attitude to talk about posture or physical position: Several statues of the Buddha show him in a reclining attitude.

Attitudes are settled ways of thinking or feeling about something, often reflected in behavior: {Her attitude toward work changed after the promotion}. The word commonly implies a negative disposition: {Don't give me attitude}. In physical contexts, attitude describes body position or posture, especially in dance, gymnastics, or aviation where aircraft orientation matters.

An attorney is a person legally appointed to act on another's behalf, particularly a lawyer authorized to represent clients in legal matters. In American usage, attorney and lawyer are nearly interchangeable, though attorney often sounds more formal: {The defendant's attorney filed a motion to dismiss}. An attorney-in-fact holds power of attorney to handle someone's affairs without necessarily being a lawyer.

To attract is to draw something toward oneself. A magnet attracts iron filings. A person may attract attention, criticism, or romantic interest. Attractive places or opportunities draw people to them. The word suggests a pull rather than a push—something about the object creates the drawing force: {The smell of coffee attracted me to the kitchen}. {She attracts controversy wherever she goes}.

Attraction is a force that draws things together—whether physical objects, people, or interest. Gravity is an attraction between masses; magnetism attracts iron. Between people, attraction usually means romantic or sexual interest: {I felt an immediate attraction to her}. A tourist attraction draws visitors. The word covers anything that pulls attention or desire toward itself.

Attractions are things that draw interest or visitors. Tourist attractions are places people travel to see: {The Grand Canyon is one of Arizona's main attractions}. The attractions of a job or lifestyle are its appealing qualities. An attraction between people is a pull toward each other, often romantic or sexual: {There was an obvious attraction between them}. In entertainment, attractions are featured performances or exhibits.

Attractive describes something that draws interest or attention. An attractive person is pleasing to look at; an attractive offer appeals to your interests. The word implies a pull toward something: {She found the idea of moving abroad attractive}. What's attractive exerts a kind of magnetism—whether physical beauty, favorable terms, or appealing qualities.

Attribute can be a noun (first syllable stressed) or a verb (second syllable stressed). When you attribute something you name the person or thing that is responsible for it or the cause of it: The plague of insects is being attributed to an unusually mild winter. When text or a work of art is attributed to someone, that person is identified as its author or creator. An attribute is one among a number of qualities of something. For me the most important attributes in a partner are fidelity, intelligence, and humor. In a computing environment, an attribute is a variable that provides additional information about something.

Attrition is gradual reduction through sustained pressure or loss. In warfare, a war of attrition wears down the enemy through continuous losses rather than decisive victory. In business, attrition refers to workforce reduction through resignation or retirement rather than layoffs: {We'll reduce headcount through natural attrition}. The word implies slow erosion—of numbers, strength, or resolve—rather than sudden elimination.

Auburn is a reddish-brown color, typically describing hair. The shade falls between brown and red, often with copper or chestnut tones: {She had long auburn hair that caught the light}. The word appears almost exclusively in descriptions of hair color, though it can technically describe anything with that warm, brownish-red hue. (Capitalized Auburn refers to cities or universities.)

An auction is a public sale where items go to the highest bidder. Bidders compete by offering progressively higher amounts until no one will bid more: {The painting sold at auction for three million dollars}. To auction something is to sell it this way: {They auctioned off the estate's contents}. Auction extends to any competitive bidding process: {The government auctioned wireless spectrum licenses}.

An auctioneer is a person who conducts auctions, calling out bids and managing the sale of goods to the highest bidder. The role requires a distinctive rapid-fire speaking style: {The auctioneer's chant rattled off numbers too fast to follow}. To auctioneer is to work in this capacity or to sell something at auction.

Auctions are sales where goods go to the highest bidder. Participants compete by offering progressively higher prices until no one will bid more. The verb auction means to sell this way: {They auctioned off the estate's contents}. Auctions range from livestock sales to fine art at Sotheby's to eBay listings. To {auction off} suggests disposing of items, often to settle debts or clear inventory.

Audacious describes bold willingness to take risks or defy convention. An audacious plan might seem reckless to cautious minds: {an audacious heist}, {an audacious debut novel}. The word can carry admiration for daring or disapproval of presumption, depending on context. {She made the audacious decision to quit her job and sail around the world.}

Audacity is bold daring, often with a hint of recklessness or disregard for normal limits. It can be admirable—the audacity to challenge authority, to attempt what others won't. But it frequently carries disapproval, suggesting presumption or impudence: {He had the audacity to ask for a raise after missing three deadlines}. The word implies that someone has crossed a line others would respect.

Audible means capable of being heard. An audible {sigh} is loud enough to reach nearby ears. {The music was barely audible over the noise of the crowd.} In American football, an audible is a play called at the line of scrimmage, changing the planned play—the quarterback literally makes it audible to teammates. To {call an audible} has spread to general use for any last-minute change of plan.

An audience is the group of people who watch, listen to, or read something. A performer has an audience, as does a book or podcast. The word also means a formal meeting with an important person: {She was granted an audience with the Pope}. In marketing and media, audience refers to a target demographic: {The show skews toward a younger audience}.

Audiences is the plural of audience—groups of people who watch, listen to, or receive some form of performance, presentation, or communication. A play draws audiences, a podcast builds audiences, a politician addresses audiences. The word emphasizes the collective nature of reception: {The film found audiences worldwide}. In marketing, audiences are demographic segments targeted for messaging: {We're trying to reach younger audiences}.

Audio refers to sound, especially as recorded, transmitted, or reproduced electronically. It covers the range of frequencies humans can hear. Audio works as both noun and adjective: {The audio was terrible on that call}, {audio equipment}, {audio file}. In video contexts, audio is the sound component as distinct from the visual: {We have picture but no audio}.

An audiobook is a recording of someone reading a book aloud. Once distributed on cassette tapes and CDs, audiobooks now stream or download digitally. They range from single-narrator readings to full productions with voice actors and sound effects: {I listened to the audiobook on my commute}.

Audiobooks are books read aloud and recorded for listening rather than reading. Once distributed on cassette tapes and CDs, they now come primarily as digital files. Audiobooks allow consuming literature while commuting, exercising, or doing chores: {I listened to the audiobook on my drive to work}. Professional narrators or sometimes the authors themselves perform the readings.

An audiophile is someone passionate about high-fidelity sound reproduction. Audiophiles invest in quality speakers, amplifiers, and headphones, often spending considerable sums pursuing sonic perfection: {He's such an audiophile he can hear the difference between cable types}. The term can carry mild mockery when applied to those obsessed with imperceptible improvements.

An audit is a formal examination of records, accounts, or practices to verify accuracy or compliance. Auditors review financial statements, tax returns, or organizational procedures: {The IRS audited her returns for the past three years}. To audit a college course is to attend without receiving credit. The verb and noun share the same form.

An audition is a trial performance where an actor, musician, or other performer demonstrates their abilities for a role or position: {She auditioned for the lead in the school play}. The verb works both ways—performers audition for parts, and directors audition performers. The process typically involves prepared pieces or cold readings from a script.

Auditioning is the process of trying out for a role or position by performing for those making the selection. Actors audition for parts, musicians audition for orchestras, dancers audition for companies. The word works as both a present participle and a gerund: {She's auditioning for the lead} or {Auditioning is nerve-wracking}.

Auditions are tryouts where performers demonstrate their abilities for a role or position. Actors audition for parts in plays and films, musicians audition for orchestras, dancers for companies. The word works as both noun and verb: {She auditioned for the lead} or {The auditions lasted all day}. A {callback} is a second audition for those who passed the first.

An auditorium is a large room or building designed to seat an audience for performances, lectures, or public gatherings. The term emphasizes the space where listeners sit rather than the stage: {The auditorium filled quickly before the concert}. Schools, theaters, and convention centers all have auditoriums.

An aunt is the sister of one's parent, or the wife of one's parent's brother (an uncle). The term extends to women who fill aunt-like roles without biological connection, such as close family friends. {My aunt always sends a card on my birthday.} In some communities, aunt is used as a respectful address for older women generally. The informal auntie or aunty conveys affection or familiarity.

Auntie is an informal or affectionate form of aunt, used especially by children or when addressing one's aunt directly: {Can I have another cookie, Auntie?} The term extends beyond blood relatives to familiar older women in a child's life, such as close family friends. In some cultures, particularly South Asian and African communities, auntie is a respectful form of address for any older woman, regardless of relation.

Aunts is the plural of aunt—the sisters of one's parents, or the wives of one's uncles. The word appears in contexts involving family gatherings or inheritance: {My aunts always brought the best dishes to Thanksgiving}. An aunt by marriage may be distinguished from a blood aunt, though both are simply aunts in everyday use.

Aunty is an informal spelling of aunt, used especially in British English and Commonwealth countries. It often carries a warmer, more familiar tone than the standard spelling: {Aunty came over for tea}. In some cultures, aunty extends beyond blood relations to address older women with affection or respect. Also spelled auntie.

An aura is an atmosphere or quality that seems to surround a person or thing: {an aura of mystery}, {an aura of calm}. The word suggests something intangible yet perceptible—a presence you sense rather than see. In New Age contexts, auras are supposedly visible energy fields around living beings. In medicine, an aura is a sensory warning that precedes a migraine or seizure.

Auras is the plural of aura—a distinctive atmosphere or quality surrounding a person, place, or thing: {The old library had an aura of quiet scholarship}. In New Age and spiritual contexts, auras are fields of colored light said to emanate from living beings, visible to some: {She claimed to see auras around people}. In medicine, an aura is a sensory warning before a migraine or seizure.

Aurora refers to the natural light displays in polar skies—the aurora borealis (northern lights) and aurora australis (southern lights)—caused by charged particles from the sun interacting with Earth's atmosphere. The term extends to any similar atmospheric glow. In literary or poetic use, aurora means dawn itself: {The aurora crept over the eastern hills}. (Capitalized Aurora is the Roman goddess of dawn or a given name.)

Auroras are luminous displays in the night sky caused by charged particles from the sun interacting with Earth's atmosphere, producing curtains and ribbons of colored light. They appear near the poles—aurora borealis in the north, aurora australis in the south. The singular aurora can also mean dawn or the Roman goddess of dawn, from whom the phenomenon takes its name.

Austerity is primarily used in the context of an economy and scarcity of something: money, goods, or jobs. It is a term that governments and economists like to use to characterize difficult times. Governments may impose austerity measures, policies, programs, or packages in order to reduce spending. The underlying adjective, austere, is closely related and characterizes severity, strictness, and abstinence.

Authentic means genuine or real, not counterfeit or copied: {an authentic Picasso}, {authentic Mexican cuisine}. Something authentic is true to its origins or claims. A person described as authentic is sincere and unpretentious—their behavior matches their true self rather than being performed for others: {She appreciated his authentic personality}. The word often signals approval, implying integrity and trustworthiness.

Authenticity is the quality of being genuine or real rather than fake or imitation. A document's authenticity determines whether it's original or forged. A person's authenticity means they act according to their true self rather than performing for others: {I admire her authenticity—she never pretends to be someone she's not}. In philosophy and psychology, authenticity often describes living in accordance with one's values despite social pressure.

An author is someone who writes—especially books, articles, or other substantial works. The term carries more weight than "writer," suggesting completed, published work: {the author of three novels}, {a best-selling author}. Author also extends to anyone who creates or originates something: {the author of the plan}. As a verb, to author is to write or create: {She authored the report}.

Authoritarian describes a system or person demanding strict obedience to authority at the expense of personal freedom. An authoritarian {government} concentrates power and limits dissent. An authoritarian {parent} enforces rigid rules without explanation. As a noun, an authoritarian is someone who favors or exercises such control: {The new CEO governed like an authoritarian}.

Authoritarianism is a political system or philosophy in which a central authority holds power and limits individual freedoms, often suppressing opposition and controlling many aspects of public and private life. Unlike totalitarianism, authoritarianism may tolerate some social institutions operating independently, provided they don't challenge state power. The term also describes attitudes or behaviors that demand strict obedience to authority at the expense of personal freedom: {The company's authoritarianism drove away talented employees who valued autonomy}.

Authoritarians are people who favor or enforce strict obedience to authority at the expense of personal freedom. The term describes both leaders who concentrate power and suppress dissent, and followers who prefer strong hierarchical control: {The regime was run by authoritarians who tolerated no opposition}. As an adjective, authoritarian describes systems, tendencies, or personalities marked by this preference for unquestioning compliance.

Authorities are people or institutions with official power to make decisions, enforce rules, or control others. Police, government agencies, and regulatory bodies are {the authorities}: {He was questioned by authorities}. The word often implies legitimate power that demands compliance. An authority on a subject is an expert whose knowledge commands respect: {She's an authority on medieval history}. In the singular, authority is the power itself: {Who has authority here?}

Authority is the power to determine or judge things, or the right to control or command: In our house, only our father had absolute authority. A person or institution who has this power or right can also be called an authority: Authorities have issued a warning of very severe weather tonight. Almost any government department or organization can be called an authority in a particular area. If you are an authority about a subject, you know a lot about it and others may come to you for advice or information: The book has made her an international authority on mineral nutrition.

Authorization is official permission or approval to do something: {You'll need authorization from the department head}. In computing and security, authorization determines what actions a user is permitted to perform after their identity has been verified. The verb authorize and the act of granting permission share this sense of sanctioned access or action.

Autism is a neurological condition characterized by differences in social communication, sensory processing, and patterns of behavior or interests. It exists on a spectrum, meaning autistic people vary widely in how the condition affects them—some need significant daily support while others live independently with few accommodations. The clinical term is autism spectrum disorder (ASD), though many in the autistic community reject framing it as a disorder. {My son was diagnosed with autism at age three.} {She's autistic and advocates for neurodiversity acceptance.}

Autistic describes someone with autism, a neurological condition affecting social interaction, communication, and sensory processing. The condition exists on a spectrum—some autistic people need significant support while others live independently. The word also appears as informal slang for obsessive focus or social awkwardness: {I went full autistic on spreadsheets this weekend}. This casual use is controversial.

Auto is a prefix meaning self or automatic: {autocorrect}, {autopilot}, {autobiography}. As a standalone word, auto is a somewhat dated informal term for automobile: {auto insurance}, {auto mechanic}, {the auto industry}. In photography and electronics, auto refers to automatic settings: {Switch the camera to auto}.

An autobiography is a person's account of their own life, written by themselves. The term distinguishes such works from biographies, which are written by others. Autobiographies typically cover significant portions of a life and reflect on formative experiences: {She published her autobiography at seventy}. A memoir is similar but usually focuses on specific periods or themes rather than a full life story.

Autocorrect is software that automatically fixes typing errors or suggests corrections as you type. It catches misspellings and typos but sometimes "corrects" words you meant to type, producing unintended—often embarrassing—substitutions: {Autocorrect changed "coming" to "cumming" in my text to grandma}. The term also works as a verb: {My phone autocorrected it}.

Autocracy is government by a single person with unlimited power. The autocrat's authority faces no constitutional checks—no legislature, judiciary, or electorate constrains their decisions. The term often carries negative connotations, implying tyranny or oppression: {The country slid from democracy into autocracy}. Autocracy can also describe any organization where one person holds absolute control: {He runs the company as an autocracy}.

An autocrat is a ruler with absolute power, unchecked by laws or other governing bodies. The term extends to anyone who wields authority in a domineering, unilateral way: {My boss is a complete autocrat—she never consults anyone}. Autocratic describes this style of rule or behavior.

An autograph is a person's signature, especially a famous person's, sought as a memento: {She waited outside the stadium to get autographs from the players}. The word also means any document written in the author's own hand—the original manuscript rather than a copy. As a verb, to autograph is to sign something: {He autographed my baseball}.

Autographs are signatures, especially those of famous people collected as keepsakes or sold as memorabilia: {She got autographs from the entire cast}. The verb means to sign something for a fan or collector: {He autographed baseballs for an hour after the game}. An autograph can also mean any document in the author's own handwriting.

Automatic describes actions or processes that happen without conscious effort or human intervention. An automatic {door} opens by sensor. An automatic {transmission} shifts gears without driver input. Automatic {breathing} continues without thought. The word also suggests inevitability: {Membership comes with automatic renewal}. As a noun, an automatic is a self-loading firearm or a car with automatic transmission.

Automation is the use of machines, computers, or technology to perform tasks with minimal human involvement. What once required hands now requires only switches, sensors, or software. Factory automation replaced assembly-line workers; home automation lets you control lights and thermostats from your phone. The word often surfaces in debates about jobs: {Automation threatens to eliminate millions of positions in the service sector.} To automate a process is to convert it from manual to automatic operation.

An automaton is a machine that operates by itself, especially one designed to imitate human or animal actions. The word often suggests mechanical, unthinking movement—a robot following its programming. Figuratively, someone who acts like an automaton behaves without emotion or independent thought: {He moved through his workday like an automaton}. Plural: automata or automatons.

Automatons is a plural of automaton—a self-operating machine, especially one designed to imitate human or animal actions. Early automatons were mechanical marvels: clockwork figures that wrote, played music, or performed tricks. The word extends to people who act mechanically, without thought or feeling: {The workers moved like automatons on the assembly line}. The alternate plural automata appears in technical and academic contexts.

Autonomy is the capacity to govern oneself—to make decisions and act according to one's own judgment rather than external control. Nations seek political autonomy from colonial powers. Individuals value personal autonomy in medical decisions: {The patient has autonomy over her treatment}. In philosophy, autonomy is central to moral agency—the ability to choose freely makes ethical responsibility possible. Autonomous vehicles and systems operate without human intervention.

Autopilot is a system that controls a vehicle—originally aircraft, now also cars and ships—without continuous human input. The pilot or driver can disengage to let the machine maintain course, altitude, or speed. Figuratively, to be {on autopilot} is to act mechanically, without conscious thought: {I was so tired I drove home on autopilot}.

An autopsy is an examination of a dead body to determine the cause of death. A medical examiner or pathologist performs it by dissecting the corpse and examining organs, tissues, and fluids. Autopsies may be required by law in cases of suspicious or unexplained death: {The autopsy revealed traces of poison}. Figuratively, an autopsy is any after-the-fact analysis of a failure: {The team conducted an autopsy of the failed product launch}.

Autumn is the season between summer and winter, when temperatures cool and deciduous trees shed their leaves. In North America, *fall* is the more common term; *autumn* sounds slightly more formal or literary. The word extends to periods of decline or maturity: {the autumn of her career}, {an autumn romance}. As an adjective: {autumn leaves}, {autumn colors}.

Availability is the state of being accessible or obtainable. A product's availability determines whether you can buy it; a person's availability determines whether they can meet. The word often implies readiness for use or action: {Check the doctor's availability for next week}. In dating contexts, availability suggests being single or open to romantic interest.

Available describes something ready for use or accessible when needed. A product is available if it's in stock; a person is available if free to meet or, in dating contexts, not in a relationship: {Is she available?} {The report will be available next week.} {No rooms were available.} Something that {avails} itself to you presents itself for your use.

An avalanche is a mass of snow, ice, and debris sliding rapidly down a mountainside. The word extends to any overwhelming quantity arriving suddenly: {an avalanche of mail}, {an avalanche of criticism}. As a verb, to avalanche is to descend or accumulate like an avalanche: {Letters avalanched into the office}.

Avalanches is the plural of avalanche—a mass of snow, ice, and debris sliding rapidly down a mountainside. The term extends to any sudden overwhelming quantity: {an avalanche of emails}, {an avalanche of criticism}. As a verb form, avalanches describes the action: {Snow avalanches down the slope when conditions are right}.

An avatar is a digital representation of a person in virtual spaces—video games, chat rooms, social media. Users customize avatars to represent themselves or create alternate identities: {My avatar has purple hair and wings}. The word comes from Hindu mythology, where an avatar is the earthly incarnation of a deity, particularly Vishnu descending to earth in human or animal form. This religious sense persists in discussions of Hinduism and occasionally in figurative use for someone who perfectly embodies a quality: {He was the avatar of cool}.

Avatars is the plural of avatar, which has meanings that connect through the idea of embodiment or manifestation. In Hindu tradition, an avatar is a deity descended to earth in physical form—Vishnu's avatars include Krishna and Rama. The word extends to any embodiment of a concept or quality: {She was the avatar of elegance}. In computing, an avatar is a digital representation of a user—a character, icon, or image that stands in for you in games, forums, or virtual worlds: {Players customize their avatars before entering the game}.

To avenge is to inflict harm or punishment in return for a wrong done to oneself or another: {She vowed to avenge her brother's murder}. Unlike revenge, which centers on personal satisfaction, avenge carries a sense of justice or righting a wrong. The person avenged is typically the victim, not the one acting: {He avenged his fallen comrades}.

Avenged is the past tense of avenge, meaning to inflict punishment or harm in retaliation for a wrong done to oneself or another: {She avenged her father's murder}. Unlike revenge, which often implies personal spite, avenge carries a sense of justice or righteous retribution. {The defeat was avenged in the rematch}.

An avenger is someone who inflicts harm or punishment in return for a wrong done to themselves or others. The word carries overtones of righteous retribution: {He styled himself an avenger of the oppressed}. In superhero contexts, avengers are heroes who fight injustice, though the original sense implies retaliation rather than prevention.

Avengers are people who inflict punishment or harm in return for a wrong done to themselves or others. The word carries a sense of righteous retaliation rather than mere revenge: {The avengers tracked down the men who had killed their father}. An avenger acts on behalf of justice, often outside legal channels. (Capitalized Avengers refers to the Marvel superhero team.)

Avenging describes the act of taking revenge or inflicting punishment on behalf of oneself or another. An avenging {angel} brings divine retribution. An avenging {hero} seeks justice for wrongs done. The word carries connotations of righteous payback rather than mere retaliation: {She returned as an avenging force against those who had betrayed her family}.

Avenue is a broad street, often tree-lined or otherwise distinguished from ordinary roads. In city grids, avenues typically run perpendicular to streets: {Fifth Avenue}, {Park Avenue}. Figuratively, an avenue is a means of approach or access: {We've explored every avenue}. The word suggests a path toward something—whether physical or abstract.

Common elements of meaning can be found in uses of average, whether as noun, verb, or adjective. The core meaning is a single value that represents a summary of a range of unequal values: The average of 4, 6, and 20 is 10. When derived mathematically, that number is technically called the mean, but colloquially, it’s known as the average. To average a set of values is to find their mean. Anything designated as average is intermediate in value or quality: The movie was just average; the baby’s length is average for his age.

Aversion is a strong dislike or disinclination toward something: {She has an aversion to public speaking}. The word suggests turning away—you avoid what you find distasteful or repellent. An aversion can be mild preference or visceral disgust: {His aversion to needles made blood draws difficult}. Risk-averse investors avoid uncertainty; the averse person steers clear of what bothers them.

Aviation encompasses the design, development, operation, and use of aircraft, particularly heavier-than-air machines like airplanes and helicopters. The term covers both the technical aspects of flight and the broader industry surrounding it, including commercial airlines, military air forces, and private flying. Someone who works in aviation might be a pilot, engineer, air traffic controller, or flight attendant. {She pursued a career in aviation after getting her pilot's license.}

An aviator is a person who flies aircraft—a pilot. The term carries a slightly formal or historical tone, often evoking early aviation pioneers or military flyers: {Amelia Earhart was a celebrated aviator}. Aviator sunglasses, with their teardrop shape and thin metal frames, were designed for pilots and remain a popular style.

Aviators are sunglasses with large teardrop-shaped lenses and thin metal frames, originally designed for pilots to reduce glare. The style remains popular for its classic look: {He pushed his aviators up on his head}. Aviator can also simply mean a pilot, though this use sounds dated or formal.

Avocado is a fruit with buttery green flesh and a large pit. The word comes from Nahuatl, the Aztec language, where {ahuacatl} meant both the fruit and, because of its shape, testicle. People eat avocados mashed into guacamole, sliced on toast, or blended into smoothies. {I'll have the avocado toast.}

Avocados is the plural of avocado, the pear-shaped fruit with green or blackish skin, creamy pale-green flesh, and a large pit. Native to Mexico and Central America, avocados are eaten raw—in guacamole, on toast, in salads, or sliced into sandwiches. {The avocados at the market were finally ripe.}

To avoid something is to stay away from it or prevent it from happening: {Avoid the freeway during rush hour}, {She avoided eye contact}. The word suggests deliberate effort to not encounter or experience something unwanted. You can avoid a person, a topic, a collision, or a mistake. To avoid doing something is to refrain from it: {He avoided answering the question directly}.

Avoidance is the act of staying away from something or preventing it from happening. You might practice {avoidance of conflict} or {tax avoidance}—legal strategies to minimize what you owe. The word often carries a slight judgment: {His avoidance of the topic was obvious}. In psychology, avoidance behavior means steering clear of situations that trigger anxiety.

Awake means not asleep, or to stop sleeping. You can lie awake at night, be wide awake at dawn, or stay awake through a boring lecture. To awaken is to wake up or to rouse: {The noise awoke him}. Figuratively, awake suggests alertness or awareness: {awake to the dangers}, {a rude awakening}. The adjective pairs with to: {I'm awake to the possibilities}.

Awaken means to wake up or rouse from sleep: {A noise awakened me at three in the morning}. It extends to stirring any dormant state—awakening memories, suspicions, or desires. The word carries a slightly more literary or dramatic tone than wake: {The experience awakened something in her}. A spiritual or political awakening marks a profound shift in consciousness or understanding.

Awakening is the act of waking up or becoming aware. The literal sense involves rousing from sleep: {The baby's awakening came earlier than usual}. More often it describes a new awareness or realization: {a spiritual awakening}, {a political awakening}. An awakening can be pleasant—discovering a passion—or harsh: {a rude awakening} is an unpleasant confrontation with reality.

An award is something given in recognition of achievement or merit—a prize, medal, or honor: {She won the award for best director}. Awards are also sums granted by official decision: {The jury's award exceeded what the plaintiff sought}. To award is to grant or bestow: {The committee awarded her the scholarship}. {The contract was awarded to the lowest bidder}.

Awards are honors or prizes given in recognition of achievement, merit, or victory: {She won three awards at the ceremony}, {The film swept the awards season}. To award is to grant such recognition, or more broadly, to give officially: {The jury awarded damages to the plaintiff}. Award can also mean something granted by decision rather than negotiation: an arbitration award, a contract award.

Aware means having knowledge or consciousness of something: {I wasn't aware you were coming}. It implies perception or realization: {She became aware of footsteps behind her}. Someone who is aware of current events or social issues stays informed. The word often pairs with prepositions: aware {of} dangers, aware {that} time is short.

Awareness is the state of knowing or perceiving something. You can have awareness of your surroundings, of a problem, or of your own thoughts and feelings. The word often implies conscious attention: {She had no awareness that anyone was watching}. Awareness campaigns aim to inform the public about issues: {breast cancer awareness}, {climate awareness}. Self-awareness is understanding your own character and motivations.

Away indicates distance or separation from a reference point—usually here, now, or the speaker. Someone who is away is not present: {She's away on business}. To move away is to increase distance: {He walked away without looking back}. Away can mean into storage or safekeeping: {Put the dishes away}. It also suggests continuous action: {They talked away the afternoon}. In sports, an away game is played at the opponent's venue. {Right away} and {straight away} mean immediately.

Awe is a feeling of reverential wonder mixed with fear or admiration, inspired by something vast, powerful, or sublime: {We stood in awe of the mountain}. The word suggests being overwhelmed—rendered small or speechless by what you're witnessing. To be in awe of someone is to regard them with profound respect. Awesome originally meant inspiring awe; now it's casual praise for anything good. Awful once meant the same but shifted to mean very bad. Awe-inspiring retains the original force.

Until the late 20th century, awesome was used mainly for things that genuinely inspired awe and it was often used in a religious context. It is a frequent word in Bible translations: Before our own eyes, the Lord performed great and awesome deeds of power against Egypt, Pharaoh, and his entire dynasty. Today, awesome has much wider and weaker use and is synonymous with such words as great, remarkable, or fantastic: You get Friday off? Awesome!

Awestruck describes being filled with awe—a mix of wonder, reverence, and sometimes fear in the presence of something vast or powerful. Someone might stand awestruck before the Grand Canyon, a great work of art, or a display of extraordinary talent: {The audience sat awestruck as she played}. Also spelled awe-struck.

Awful describes something extremely bad, unpleasant, or of poor quality: {The weather was awful all week}. It intensifies negative states—you might feel awful when sick or guilty. Informally, awful works as an intensifier meaning "very" or "a great deal of": {an awful lot of people showed up}.
