The word originally meant "inspiring awe," a sense now largely obsolete except in the related adverb awfully, which can mean either terribly or very: {I'm awfully sorry}.

Awkward describes something clumsy, ungainly, or lacking grace. An awkward {movement} is physically ungraceful. An awkward {silence} is socially uncomfortable—people don't know what to say. An awkward {situation} puts someone in a difficult position: {It was awkward running into my ex at the party}. The word often captures that cringe-inducing feeling when something doesn't flow naturally. An awkward {angle} or awkward {shape} is hard to manage or maneuver around.

Awkwardness is the quality of being uncomfortable, clumsy, or socially uneasy. Physical awkwardness shows in ungainly movement: {the awkwardness of a newborn foal}. Social awkwardness involves discomfort in interactions: {There was an awkwardness between them after the breakup}. A situation's awkwardness comes from tension or embarrassment that no one quite knows how to dispel.

Awoke is the past tense of awake. Someone who awoke at dawn woke up then. The word extends to figurative awakening: {She awoke to the dangers of complacency}. Awoken is the past participle: {I had awoken before sunrise}.

Awry means turned or twisted to one side, not straight: {His tie was slightly awry}. More commonly, it describes plans or situations that have gone wrong: {Something went awry with the delivery}. The word carries a sense of deviation from what was intended or expected—not catastrophic failure, just things not quite right.

Aww is an exclamation of sympathetic or sentimental response, typically to something endearing, cute, or touching: {Aww, look at the puppy!} It can also express mild disappointment or sympathy: {Aww, that's too bad}. The spelling stretches to match the sound—more w's for more feeling.

An axe is a tool with a heavy metal blade on a wooden handle, used for chopping wood or felling trees. The figurative axe is a cutting instrument of a different sort—to {get the axe} is to be fired or eliminated, and to {have an axe to grind} is to have a personal agenda. In music slang, an axe is a guitar. Also spelled ax.

Axed is the past tense of axe. To axe something is to cut it with an axe, but the word more often means to eliminate or cancel abruptly: {The network axed the show after one season}. People get axed when they're fired: {Half the department got axed in the layoffs}. The word suggests swift, decisive removal.

Axes is the plural of two different words. An axe is a tool with a heavy blade on a handle, used for chopping wood or, historically, as a weapon. To axe something is to eliminate it: {The network axed three shows}. An axis is a line around which something rotates or a reference line on a graph: {the x and y axes}. Someone with {an axe to grind} has a grievance or selfish motive.

An axis is an imaginary straight line around which something rotates or is symmetrically arranged. The Earth spins on its axis once every twenty-four hours. In geometry and graphs, axes are reference lines used to locate points in space: {the x-axis and y-axis of a coordinate plane}. The word extends to any central line or organizing principle: {the axis of a debate}. In World War II, the Axis referred to Germany, Italy, Japan, and their allies.

An axle is a rod or shaft on which wheels rotate. In vehicles, axles connect opposite wheels and transmit power from the engine to the road: {The rear axle needs replacing}. The word extends to any central shaft around which something turns. To {wrap around the axle} is to become excessively tangled in a problem.

An axolotl is a salamander native to Mexico that remains in its aquatic larval form throughout life, retaining external gills and a finned tail. Unlike most amphibians, it never undergoes metamorphosis to become land-dwelling. Axolotls are studied for their remarkable ability to regenerate limbs and organs, and are kept as aquarium pets.

Aye means yes, used in parliamentary voting {all in favor say aye}, nautical contexts {aye aye, captain}, and some British and Scottish dialects. The ayes are the affirmative votes or those who cast them: {The ayes have it}. A separate word aye, pronounced differently, means always or forever, now archaic except in {for aye}.

Babble is rapid, incoherent speech—the sounds a baby makes before learning words, or what adults produce when excited, confused, or delirious: {The fever had him babbling nonsense}. A brook babbles when it makes continuous murmuring sounds over stones. Babble can also mean idle chatter or gossip: {office babble}, {the babble of the crowd}.

Babbling describes continuous, rapid talk that's hard to follow—either because it lacks sense or because too much comes at once: {The witness was babbling incoherently}. Babies babble before they can speak, producing streams of meaningless but speech-like sounds. A brook babbles when water tumbles over stones, making a continuous murmuring sound.

Babe is an affectionate term for a baby or small child, now somewhat old-fashioned in that sense. More commonly, babe is a term of endearment for a romantic partner: {Hey babe, how was your day?} It also refers to an attractive person, especially a woman: {She's a total babe}. The phrase {babe in the woods} describes someone naive or inexperienced. (Capitalized Babe is a given name or nickname.)

A babel is a confused mixture of sounds, especially many voices speaking at once so that nothing is intelligible: {The meeting dissolved into a babel of competing opinions}. The word comes from the biblical Tower of Babel, where God confounded human speech into mutually incomprehensible languages. Any scene of noise and confusion qualifies. (Capitalized Babel refers to the biblical story.)

Babies is the plural of baby—human infants or the very young of other species. The word extends to anyone treated as immature or helpless: {Don't be such babies about it}. Projects or creations someone feels protective of become their babies: {This startup is my baby}. As a term of endearment, babies addresses multiple loved ones: {Hey babies, I'm home}.

A baboon is a large, ground-dwelling monkey native to Africa and Arabia, known for its dog-like snout, prominent canine teeth, and often brightly colored rear. Baboons live in hierarchical social groups and have a reputation for aggression. As an insult, baboon suggests someone crude, stupid, or brutish: {Don't be such a baboon}.

Baboons are large, ground-dwelling monkeys native to Africa and Arabia, recognizable by their dog-like snouts, powerful jaws, and prominent canine teeth. They live in hierarchical social groups and have a reputation for aggressive, opportunistic behavior. As an insult, calling someone a baboon suggests they're crude, loud, or stupid: {Those baboons in the back row won't stop talking}.

Baby is the standard and most frequent term for a newborn human. That core meaning informs all other uses, which partake of some qualities of real babies. Any newborn or very young animal can be called a baby, and it is also a term of endearment, typically used between people who are intimate with each other. Less frequently, baby is used appreciatively to designate inanimate things in small sizes (baby carrots). To baby someone is to either nurture them or treat them inappropriately, as if they were a baby.

To babysit is to look after someone else's children, typically for a few hours while the parents are out: {Can you babysit on Saturday night?} The term extends to watching over anything requiring supervision: {I spent the afternoon babysitting the printer}. A babysitter is usually a teenager or young adult earning pocket money, though the verb applies regardless of who's doing it.

A babysitter is someone hired to look after children while parents are away, typically for a few hours at a time. The term usually implies a teenager or young adult rather than a professional caregiver: {We need to find a babysitter for Saturday night}. By extension, anyone tasked with watching over something that shouldn't need supervision: {I'm not here to babysit the new hires}.

Babysitting is watching over children while their parents are away, typically for a few hours. A babysitter handles basic care—feeding, entertainment, bedtime—without the deeper responsibilities of parenting. The term extends to temporary oversight of anything: {I'm babysitting my neighbor's plants while she's on vacation}. To babysit someone can imply they need excessive supervision: {I shouldn't have to babysit you through every step}.

A bachelor is an unmarried man, particularly one who has never married. The word often implies someone living independently and perhaps enjoying single life: {He's a confirmed bachelor}. A bachelor's degree is the first level of university degree, and a bachelor apartment (or bachelor pad) is a small dwelling suited for one person. In older usage, a bachelor was also a young knight serving under another's banner.

A bachelorette is an unmarried woman, formed as a feminine counterpart to bachelor. The word appears most often in {bachelorette party}—a celebration for a woman about to be married, typically involving her female friends. Outside this context, bachelorette sounds dated or playful; unmarried women are more often called single.

Bachi are the wooden sticks used to play taiko drums in Japanese drumming. They resemble thick drumsticks, typically made from oak, maple, or other hardwoods. The word comes from Japanese and appears in English mainly in contexts involving taiko performance: {She gripped the bachi and struck the drum}.

Back, as adverb, adjective, noun, and verb, is the opposite of front and roughly synonymous with rear. When time is involved, back refers to the past: I wrote the letter back in 2010. When space is involved, back is the direction behind you, or behind the speaker or subject at hand: She walked back three steps. Your back is the rear side of your torso, where your spine is: I strained my back when I bent over. The back of a building or physical object is the side opposite the front: They left through the house’s back door. In some sports, a back plays behind the front line of players: The running back scored a touchdown. To back is to move backwards: Please back the car out of the garage.

A backbend is a gymnastic or yoga position in which the body arches backward, typically with hands and feet on the ground and the torso curved upward: {She held a perfect backbend for ten seconds}. The move requires flexibility in the spine and shoulders.

Backbiting is speaking maliciously about someone who isn't present to defend themselves. The word emphasizes the cowardly or treacherous nature of the criticism—attacking from behind rather than face to face: {Office backbiting poisoned the whole team's morale}. The verb is backbite; the agent noun is backbiter.

A backboard is a flat vertical surface, typically rectangular, that supports and frames a basketball hoop. Shots that bank off the backboard and into the basket use the {glass} or {board} strategically. In medical contexts, a backboard is a rigid board used to immobilize and transport patients with suspected spinal injuries.

Backbone is the spine—the column of vertebrae running down the center of the back in humans and other vertebrates. Figuratively, backbone means courage, determination, or moral strength: {She showed real backbone standing up to them}. It also means the central supporting structure of something larger: {Small businesses are the backbone of the economy}. In computing, a backbone is the main high-capacity network line that smaller networks connect to.

Backbones is the plural of backbone—the spine, the column of vertebrae running down the center of the back. Figuratively, backbone means courage or resolve: {Those senators lack the backbones to stand up to their party}. Backbone also refers to the main supporting structure of something: {Small businesses are the backbones of local economies}.

Backbreaker refers to any task or burden so demanding it could figuratively break your back—exhausting physical labor, an overwhelming workload, or a crushing financial obligation: {Moving all that furniture was a real backbreaker}. In wrestling, a backbreaker is a move where one wrestler drops an opponent's spine across their knee.

Backbreaking describes work so physically demanding it could break your back—heavy labor requiring intense exertion: {backbreaking work in the coal mines}, {the backbreaking task of hauling stones}. The term emphasizes grueling effort, though it extends to any exhausting undertaking: {the backbreaking process of editing a manuscript}.

Backburner, usually appearing as two words or hyphenated, refers to a state of reduced priority or temporary neglect. The metaphor comes from cooking: pots on the back burners of a stove receive less attention than those in front. To put something {on the backburner} means to postpone dealing with it while attending to more urgent matters. As a verb, to backburner a project or issue is to deprioritize it: {We had to backburner the expansion plans until funding came through}.

A backdoor is a rear or secondary entrance, but the word usually carries connotations of secrecy or circumvention. A backdoor {deal} happens through unofficial channels. In computing, a backdoor is a hidden method of bypassing normal authentication—sometimes built in by developers, sometimes installed by hackers. As an adjective: {backdoor access}, {backdoor negotiations}. Also spelled back door or back-door.

Backdoors names hidden methods of bypassing normal security or authentication in a computer system. Programmers sometimes build them in deliberately for maintenance access; hackers install them to maintain secret entry after a breach. The term extends to any covert way around official channels: {The lobbyist found a backdoor into the senator's office}. As a verb, to backdoor is to gain access through such means. In basketball, a backdoor play sends a player cutting behind the defense toward the basket.

A backdraft is an explosive surge of fire that occurs when oxygen suddenly enters a confined space where flames have depleted the air supply. The superheated gases ignite violently when a door or window opens. Firefighters are trained to recognize warning signs—bowing windows, smoke-stained glass, pulsing smoke—before entering burning buildings.

A backdrop is a painted cloth or screen hung at the back of a stage, creating the visual setting for a performance. The term extends to any background: {The mountains provided a stunning backdrop for the ceremony}. Figuratively, backdrop describes the circumstances or context surrounding events: {The negotiations took place against a backdrop of rising tensions}.

Backfire originally describes an engine's premature combustion, producing a loud bang when fuel ignites in the exhaust or intake rather than the cylinder. The figurative use now dominates: when a plan backfires, it produces the opposite of the intended result. {Her attempt to make him jealous backfired spectacularly.} A backfire is also a controlled burn set to stop an advancing wildfire by depriving it of fuel.

Backfired is the past tense of backfire. An engine backfires when fuel ignites in the wrong place, producing a loud bang. A plan backfires when it produces the opposite of its intended result: {The smear campaign backfired spectacularly—it only made her more popular}. The metaphor captures how something meant to propel you forward instead explodes in your face.

Backfires is the third-person singular of backfire. An engine backfires when combustion occurs in the wrong place or at the wrong time, producing a loud bang: {The old truck backfired as it pulled away}. More commonly now, a plan or action backfires when it produces the opposite of its intended result: {Her attempt to make him jealous backfired spectacularly}.

Backfiring is when something produces the opposite of its intended effect. A plan backfires when it fails in a way that harms the person who made it: {Her attempt to make him jealous backfired spectacularly}. The term comes from engines—a backfire is a loud bang caused by fuel igniting at the wrong time, either in the intake or exhaust system.

A backflip is an acrobatic move where you leap and rotate backward, landing on your feet. Gymnasts, divers, and cheerleaders perform backflips; so do skateboarders and parkour practitioners, often off obstacles. Figuratively, to do a backflip is to reverse position dramatically: {The senator did a backflip on the tax bill}.

Backflips are acrobatic maneuvers in which someone rotates backward through the air, typically landing on their feet. Gymnasts, divers, and cheerleaders perform backflips as technical elements. Figuratively, to do backflips is to go to extreme lengths or express excessive enthusiasm: {The company did backflips to accommodate the client}. Also spelled as two words.

Backgammon is a board game for two players, each moving fifteen pieces according to dice rolls along a track of twenty-four triangular points. The goal is to move all your pieces around the board and off before your opponent does. One of the oldest known board games, it combines luck and strategy: {We played backgammon on the beach}.

Background is what lies behind something more prominent. A painting has figures in the foreground and scenery in the background. A person's background is their history—education, experience, family origins: {She has a background in finance}. Background music or noise exists without being the focus of attention. To background something is to make it less prominent. {In the background} means present but not central: {He prefers to stay in the background}.

A backhand is a stroke in tennis and similar sports made with the back of the hand facing the direction of movement—the opposite of a forehand. The term extends to any swing or blow delivered this way: {a backhand slap across the face}. As a verb, to backhand is to strike with this motion. Backhanded can mean indirect or ambiguous: a backhanded {compliment} carries an insult within apparent praise.

Backhanded describes something done with the back of the hand facing forward—a backhanded {stroke} in tennis, a backhanded {slap}. The figurative sense dominates: a backhanded {compliment} seems positive but contains an insult or criticism: {Saying she's "pretty smart for a blonde" is backhanded}. Backhanded can also mean indirect or underhanded: {backhanded methods}.

Backing is support or assistance, whether financial, political, or moral: {The project has backing from several major investors}. It also refers to material placed behind something for reinforcement or support—the backing on a mirror, the backing on carpet. In music, backing refers to the instrumental or vocal accompaniment behind a lead performer: {backing vocals}, {backing track}.

Backlash is a strong negative reaction against a change or trend, typically from people who feel threatened by it: {The policy provoked immediate backlash}, {backlash against feminism}. The word comes from machinery—the jarring backward motion when gears or chains have too much play. The social sense captures that same sudden, forceful recoil.

A backlog is an accumulation of unfinished work or unfilled orders: {We have a six-month backlog of customer requests}. The word implies tasks waiting in queue, often more than can be handled promptly. In software development, a backlog is a prioritized list of features or fixes to be addressed. The original meaning—a large log placed at the back of a fire to burn slowly—is now rare.

Backlogs are accumulations of unfinished work or unfilled orders. A company with more orders than it can immediately fulfill has a backlog—often a positive sign of demand. But backlogs of paperwork, emails, or maintenance suggest falling behind: {The court system has a massive backlog of cases}. In software development, a backlog is a prioritized list of features or tasks awaiting implementation.

A backpack is a bag with shoulder straps designed to be carried on the back, leaving hands free. Students carry books in them; hikers carry gear. As a verb, to backpack is to travel or hike while carrying one's belongings this way: {We backpacked through Europe after graduation}. Also called a rucksack or knapsack.

A backpacker is someone who travels with their belongings in a backpack, typically on a budget and for extended periods. The term suggests youth hostels, trains, and flexible itineraries rather than package tours: {We met some backpackers from Australia at the hostel}. Backpacker also describes anyone hiking with a loaded pack: {The backpackers set up camp near the ridge}.

Backpackers are travelers who carry their belongings in a backpack, typically associated with budget-conscious, independent travel. The term suggests hostels over hotels, flexibility over fixed itineraries: {The hostel was full of backpackers from all over Europe}. Backpackers also refers to hikers on extended wilderness trips, carrying everything needed for multiday treks.

Backpacking is traveling with belongings carried in a backpack, typically on a budget and for extended periods. It suggests independence and mobility—staying in hostels, using public transit, moving frequently: {We spent six months backpacking through Southeast Asia}. Backpacking also means hiking with overnight camping gear: {a backpacking trip in the Sierra Nevada}.

Backpacks are bags carried on the back, supported by shoulder straps and often a waist belt. Designed to distribute weight comfortably, they range from small daypacks to large frames for hiking and camping. Students carry books in backpacks; travelers live out of them. As a verb, to backpack is to travel with one's belongings on one's back: {We backpacked through Europe after college}.

To backpedal is to pedal a bicycle backward or, in sports like boxing, to move backward quickly while facing an opponent. The figurative sense dominates: to retreat from a previous position or statement. Politicians backpedal when their remarks prove unpopular; companies backpedal on controversial policies. {After the backlash, she backpedaled on her earlier comments.}

Backpedaling is moving backward while facing forward, literally by pedaling a bicycle in reverse or by taking steps backward. The word is far more common in its figurative sense: retreating from a position, commitment, or statement one has previously made. Politicians backpedal when their remarks prove unpopular; companies backpedal on policies that generate backlash. {After the public outcry, the mayor started backpedaling on her proposed budget cuts.} The spelling backpedalling is preferred in British English.

Backpedalling is reversing course—literally pedalling backward on a bicycle, or figuratively retreating from a position or statement. Politicians backpedal when their remarks prove unpopular: {After the backlash, she started backpedalling on her earlier comments}. The spelling with double L is British; American English prefers backpedaling.

A backroad is a minor road, typically rural, that winds through countryside away from main highways. Backroads suggest slower travel, scenic routes, and places off the beaten path: {We took the backroads to avoid traffic}. The term evokes a kind of unhurried exploration—{backroad driving through small towns}.

Backroads are secondary roads through rural or less-traveled areas, away from highways and main routes. The term evokes countryside driving, scenic detours, and places off the beaten path: {We took the backroads to avoid traffic}. Figuratively, backroads suggests the overlooked or hidden parts of something: {the backroads of American music history}.

A backroom is a private space away from public view, typically behind a main area where business is conducted. As an adjective, it describes activities done secretly or unofficially: {backroom deals}, {backroom politics}. The implication is often of decisions made by insiders without public scrutiny or accountability.

Backs is the plural of back—the rear surface of the human body from shoulders to waist, or the corresponding part of animals, chairs, books, or buildings. In sports, backs are players positioned behind the front line: {The backs carried the ball on most plays}. To back someone is to support them; backs as a verb means supports: {She backs her team no matter what}. Something that backs onto a place faces it from the rear: {The house backs onto a park}.

The backseat is the rear seat in a vehicle, behind the driver. By extension, a backseat position is one of lesser importance or authority. To {take a backseat} is to assume a secondary role: {Career took a backseat once the baby arrived}. A {backseat driver} offers unwanted advice from a position of no responsibility.

The backside is the rear surface of something, or the side opposite the front: {the backside of the building}, {flip it over to see the backside}. Most commonly, backside is a mild or polite term for the buttocks: {She fell right on her backside}. In surfing and snowboarding, backside describes maneuvers where the rider faces away from the wave or slope.

To backslide is to slip back into bad habits, sinful behavior, or a less desirable state after making progress. The term originated in religious contexts—a backslider has fallen away from faith—but now applies broadly: {He backslid into drinking after six months sober}. The past tense is backslid or backslided.

Backsliding is reverting to bad habits, sinful behavior, or a worse condition after a period of improvement. The term originates in religious contexts, where it describes someone who has fallen away from faith or moral discipline, but it applies broadly to any regression: {After six months sober, one bad weekend sent him backsliding}. A backslider is someone prone to such lapses. The word carries a tone of moral judgment—it implies not just failure but a kind of weakness or betrayal of progress already made.

Backspace is the key on a keyboard that deletes the character to the left of the cursor, moving the insertion point backward. The verb means to use this key: {I backspaced over the typo}. On typewriters, backspace moved the carriage back without erasing, allowing overtyping for corrections or accents.

To backstab is to betray someone who trusts you, especially by attacking their reputation or undermining them secretly: {She backstabbed her best friend to get the promotion}. The image is of a literal knife in the back—harm delivered when the victim can't see it coming. As a noun, a backstab is such an act of betrayal.

Backstabbed is the past tense of backstab—to betray someone who trusted you, especially by attacking their reputation or undermining them secretly: {I can't believe she backstabbed me after everything I did for her}. The image is of stabbing someone in the back while they face away, unaware of the threat.

A backstabber is someone who pretends friendship while working against you—the image is of attacking someone from behind while embracing them. The word implies betrayal by a trusted person: {I thought she was my ally, but she turned out to be a backstabber}. The verb is backstab; the act is backstabbing.

Backstabbers are people who betray others while pretending to be friendly or loyal. The image is of someone attacking from behind—striking when the victim can't see it coming. The word implies deceit and cowardice: {Watch out for backstabbers in that office}. A backstabber smiles to your face while undermining you to others.

Backstabbing is betraying someone who trusts you, especially by criticizing or undermining them when they're not present. The image is of attacking from behind—a cowardly strike against someone who considers you an ally. {The office was full of backstabbing and petty rivalries.} As an adjective: {a backstabbing colleague}. One who does this is a backstabber.

Backstage is the area of a theater hidden from the audience—dressing rooms, wings, and work spaces where performers prepare and crew operates. As an adverb or adjective, it describes what happens in these spaces: {She went backstage to meet the actors}. Figuratively, backstage refers to any behind-the-scenes activity concealed from public view: {backstage negotiations}, {backstage maneuvering}.

Backstories are the histories behind characters, situations, or events—the background that explains how things came to be. In fiction, a character's backstory includes formative experiences that shaped their personality: {The villain's tragic backstory made him almost sympathetic}. The term extends beyond fiction to anything with a hidden history worth knowing: {Every antique in her shop has a backstory}.

A backstory is the history behind a character, situation, or narrative—events that occurred before the main story begins. In fiction, backstory explains motivations and relationships: {The villain's backstory reveals childhood trauma}. The term extends beyond fiction to any context where understanding the past illuminates the present: {What's the backstory on this merger?}

A backstreet is a minor road away from main thoroughfares, often in older or less prosperous parts of town. As an adjective, backstreet suggests something hidden, unofficial, or illicit: a backstreet {abortion}, a backstreet {deal}. The connotation is of activities conducted away from public scrutiny.

Backstroke is a swimming stroke performed while lying face-up, arms alternating in backward circular motions while legs kick. It's one of the four competitive swimming strokes: {She won the 100-meter backstroke}. The term can also mean any backward stroke or movement, as in rowing or tennis.

Backtalk is impudent or argumentative response to someone in authority—a child answering back to a parent, a soldier to an officer. The word implies disrespect through the very act of responding: {Don't give me any backtalk}. To backtalk is to respond this way: {She backtalked the teacher and got detention}.

To backtrack is to retrace your steps—returning along the path you came. Hikers backtrack when they've gone the wrong way: {We had to backtrack half a mile to find the trail}. Figuratively, backtrack means to reverse position on a statement or commitment: {The senator backtracked on her promise to oppose the bill}. The noun backtrack is the path itself.

Backtracking is reversing course to return the way you came, whether literally on a trail or figuratively in conversation: {We had to backtrack two miles to find the turnoff}. In argument or negotiation, to backtrack is to retreat from a position: {The senator backtracked on her earlier comments}. In computing, backtracking is an algorithmic method that abandons partial solutions when they prove unworkable, returning to try alternative paths.

Backtracks means to reverse course, either literally by retracing one's steps or figuratively by withdrawing from a position or statement. Politicians backtrack on campaign promises; hikers backtrack when they realize they've taken a wrong turn. {After the public outcry, the company backtracked on its new pricing policy.} The word implies going back over ground already covered, often reluctantly or under pressure.

Backup is a copy kept in case the original is lost or damaged: {Make sure you have a backup of your files}. The word extends to anything held in reserve as a substitute: a backup {plan}, a backup {generator}, backup {singers}. As a verb (usually two words: back up), it means to create such a copy or to provide support. A backup can also be an accumulation causing delay: {a backup on the freeway}.

Backups are copies of data stored separately from the original, kept as protection against loss or corruption: {Make sure you have backups before updating the system}. The term extends to anything held in reserve—backup {plans}, backup {generators}, backup {singers}. In traffic, a backup is congestion or blockage: {There's a backup on the highway}.

In its most frequent use as an adverb, backward refers to movement in the direction opposite to forward and it is found most frequently in the company of action verbs (step backward, bend backward, slide backward, stumble backward). This meaning extends to adjectival use (backward glance, backward motion). Figurative use of backward is pejorative, suggesting lack of sophistication, development, or intelligence. In expressions of time, backward refers to the past.

Backwards means in the reverse direction—opposite to usual forward motion or sequence. You can walk backwards, count backwards from ten, or play a video backwards. It also describes something oriented the wrong way: {You've got your shirt on backwards}. Figuratively, backwards suggests being behind the times or underdeveloped: {a backwards town}. The adverb form backward is interchangeable, though backwards is more common in British English.

A backwater is a part of a river where the water is stagnant or flows backward, cut off from the main current. The figurative sense dominates: a backwater is an isolated place untouched by progress or new ideas. {The town remained a cultural backwater}. The word usually carries a dismissive tone—suggesting somewhere dull and behind the times.

Backwaters are bodies of water cut off from the main current—stagnant pools fed by a river but lying aside from its flow. The term extends to any place or condition characterized by stagnation and isolation from progress: {a cultural backwater}, {an economic backwater}. The singular backwater works the same way: {The town remained a backwater until the highway came through}.

Backwoods refers to remote, heavily forested, or sparsely settled rural areas far from cities and towns: {a cabin in the backwoods of Maine}. The term often carries connotations of isolation, lack of sophistication, or resistance to modern ways: {backwoods culture}, {a backwoods accent}. As an adjective, it describes things characteristic of such regions: {backwoods hospitality}, {backwoods ignorance}.

A backyard is the outdoor area behind a house, typically private and enclosed. Americans hold barbecues, let children play, and keep dogs in their backyards. Figuratively, something {in your own backyard} is close to home or within your sphere: {They opposed the landfill—not in my backyard}. As an adjective, backyard suggests informal or amateur: {backyard mechanic}, {backyard wrestling}.

Backyards are the areas behind houses, typically enclosed or bounded by fences. In American English, the backyard is where children play, families gather for barbecues, and dogs run. Figuratively, something {in your own backyard} is close to home or within your sphere of concern: {The scandal was happening in their own backyard}.

Bacon is cured meat from a pig, typically from the belly or back, sliced thin and fried until crisp. It's a breakfast staple in American and British cuisine, prized for its salty, smoky flavor and satisfying crunch. Bacon has become something of a cultural phenomenon, appearing in everything from desserts to novelty items: {bacon-wrapped dates}, {maple bacon donuts}. To {bring home the bacon} is to earn a living or achieve success. To {save someone's bacon} is to rescue them from trouble. (Capitalized Bacon is a surname.)

Bacteria are microscopic single-celled organisms found virtually everywhere—in soil, water, air, and living bodies. Some cause disease; others are essential for digestion, decomposition, and ecological balance. The word is technically plural (singular: bacterium), though {the bacteria is spreading} appears in casual speech. {Good bacteria in yogurt aid digestion.}

Though less frequent than its usual opposite good, bad has a wide range of meanings that grow out of its core function of characterizing something or someone as lacking good or desirable qualities. The large number of adjectives that may be considered as synonyms of bad in various contexts are all words with a negative connotation. To the consternation of many, bad developed a slang meaning in the late 20th century that is its opposite; in some limited contexts, bad means good.
A badass is someone tough, intimidating, or impressively skilled: {She's a total badass on the guitar}. As an adjective, badass describes something formidable or cool: {That was a badass move}.

Badassery is the quality or display of being a badass—tough, fearless, impressively skilled, or defiantly cool. The word celebrates audacious competence or swagger: {That stunt was pure badassery}. It often carries admiration for someone who breaks rules or defies expectations while looking good doing it.
Badasses is the plural of badass, describing tough or impressively skilled people: {The squad was full of badasses}.

A baddie is a villain or antagonist, especially in movies, TV shows, or stories. The term is informal and often playful, used when the villain isn't particularly menacing: {The kids cheered when the superhero defeated the baddie}. In recent slang, baddie has taken on a second meaning: an attractive, confident person, usually a woman, who projects a bold or fierce persona on social media. {She posted her vacation pics looking like a total baddie}.

A baddy is a villain or antagonist, especially in fiction: {The movie's baddy gets defeated in the final scene}. The word is informal and slightly playful, often used when discussing entertainment or when speaking to children. Also spelled baddie.

A badge is a small object worn or displayed to indicate membership, authority, or achievement: a police badge, a scout badge, a name badge. The word extends to any visible marker of identity or status: {Carrying a tote bag became a badge of the educated class}. To badge in or out is to use an identification card for access.

A badger is a stocky burrowing mammal with distinctive black and white facial markings, known for its powerful digging claws and fierce temperament when cornered. To badger someone is to pester or harass them persistently: {She badgered him until he agreed to help}. The verb captures the animal's reputation for tenacity.

Badgers are stocky burrowing mammals with distinctive black and white striped faces, known for their powerful digging claws and nocturnal habits. They live in elaborate underground dens called setts. To badger someone is to pester or harass them persistently: {Stop badgering me about it}. The verb likely comes from the cruel practice of badger-baiting.

Badges are small emblems worn to indicate membership, rank, achievement, or authority. A police officer wears a badge; a scout earns merit badges. The word extends to any marker of status or identity: {Owning a hybrid became a badge of environmental consciousness}. In digital contexts, badges are icons showing notifications or accomplishments: {The app icon showed three badges}.

Badlands are barren, heavily eroded terrain characterized by steep gullies, ravines, and sparse vegetation. The soil is typically too poor for farming and the landscape too rugged for easy travel. The term describes any such desolate region: {The drought turned the overworked farmland into badlands}. (Capitalized Badlands refers to the specific region in South Dakota.)

Badminton is a racket sport in which players hit a feathered shuttlecock back and forth over a high net. Unlike tennis, the shuttlecock must not touch the ground—points are won when one side fails to return it. The game can be played as singles or doubles, indoors or out: {We set up a badminton net in the backyard}.

To badmouth someone is to speak critically or disparagingly about them, usually behind their back: {She's always badmouthing her coworkers to the boss}. The word implies unfair or malicious criticism rather than legitimate complaint. Also spelled as two words: bad-mouth.

Badmouthed means spoke negatively or disparagingly about someone or something: {She badmouthed her ex to anyone who would listen}. The word implies criticism delivered behind the subject's back rather than to their face. Also spelled bad-mouthed.

Badmouthing is speaking disparagingly about someone or something, usually behind their back: {She's always badmouthing her ex}. The term implies criticism that's unfair, excessive, or motivated by personal grievance rather than honest assessment. Also spelled as two words or hyphenated: bad-mouthing, bad mouthing.

Baffle means to confuse or perplex completely: {The instructions baffled me}. Something baffling defies understanding or explanation. A baffle is also a device that controls flow—of air, sound, or liquid—by blocking or redirecting it: {acoustic baffles in the ceiling}, {a baffle in the exhaust system}. The connection is obstruction: one blocks comprehension, the other blocks passage.

Baffled describes a state of complete confusion or bewilderment—unable to understand or explain something despite effort. {I'm baffled by her decision to quit}. {The detective was baffled by the lack of evidence}. To be baffled is stronger than merely puzzled; it suggests hitting a wall where comprehension fails entirely.

Baffling describes something that confuses or puzzles completely, resisting explanation or understanding: {The detective faced a baffling series of clues that led nowhere}. What's baffling isn't merely unclear—it actively defies comprehension, leaving you stumped.

Most meanings of bag have some reference to the core meaning, a non-rigid and often portable container. To bag something may mean to put it in a bag (bag groceries) or it may mean to acquire or obtain it (bag a bargain). Bag is also a disparaging term for an unattractive woman, and more recently it has gained traction as a combining form for a range of insulting epithets (douchebag, scumbag).

A bagel is a dense, ring-shaped bread roll with a chewy texture, made by boiling the dough before baking. Originally associated with Jewish cuisine, bagels have become a mainstream breakfast food, typically sliced and topped with cream cheese, lox, or other spreads: {I grabbed a bagel on my way to work}.

Bagels are ring-shaped bread rolls with a dense, chewy texture, made by boiling the dough before baking. A staple of Jewish-American cuisine, they're typically split and eaten with cream cheese, lox, or other toppings: {I'll grab bagels on my way over}. The hole in the center ensures even cooking and creates the characteristic crust.

Baggage is the suitcases, bags, and containers a traveler carries. The word emphasizes the burden of transport more than the contents: {We had too much baggage for one taxi}. Figuratively, baggage means accumulated emotional burdens or past experiences that complicate present situations: {He comes with a lot of baggage from his previous marriage}. A {baggage claim} is the airport area where checked luggage arrives.

Baggy describes clothing or material that hangs loosely, not fitting close to the body: {baggy jeans}, {baggy sweater}. The word suggests excess fabric that sags or billows rather than conforming to shape. Baggy can also describe puffy flesh: {baggy eyes} from lack of sleep. The noun baggies refers to loose-fitting shorts or small plastic bags.

A bagman is someone who collects or distributes money, especially illicit payments. The term typically refers to an intermediary in bribery, extortion, or political corruption—the person who physically handles the cash so principals can maintain distance: {The senator's bagman picked up the envelope}. In British usage, a bagman can simply be a traveling salesman.

A bagpipe is a wind instrument with a bag that serves as an air reservoir, feeding multiple pipes—typically a melody pipe (chanter) and one or more drones that produce continuous tones. The player inflates the bag by blowing through a tube or pumping bellows. Most associated with Scottish Highland culture, bagpipes exist in many regional varieties across Europe and beyond: {The sound of bagpipes filled the glen}.

Bagpipes are a wind instrument in which air from a bag is forced through pipes to produce sound. The player inflates the bag by blowing into a tube or pumping a bellows, then squeezes it to maintain continuous drone notes while fingering a melody pipe called the chanter. Most associated with Scottish Highland tradition, bagpipes exist in many cultures: {The bagpipes led the funeral procession}.

Bags is the plural of bag—containers made of flexible material. Beyond the literal, bags refers to loose pouches of skin, especially under tired eyes: {She had bags under her eyes from the all-nighter}. In British slang, {bags of} means plenty: {bags of time}. To call {bags} on something is to claim it, like calling dibs: {Bags the front seat!}

A baguette is a long, narrow loaf of French bread with a crisp crust and soft interior. The shape is distinctive—typically about two feet long and only a few inches wide. Baguettes are meant to be eaten fresh, ideally the same day they're baked, as they go stale quickly. In jewelry, a baguette is a gemstone cut into a long rectangular shape, resembling the bread in silhouette.

Baguettes is the plural of baguette, a long, thin loaf of French bread with a crisp crust and soft interior. The shape extends to other elongated forms: in jewelry, a baguette is a gemstone cut into a narrow rectangle. {She picked up two baguettes from the bakery}. {The ring featured diamond baguettes flanking a central stone}.

The spelling b-a-i-l represents four different words in English with diverse meanings and parts of speech. The most common bail is the one associated with the criminal justice system, whereby money is bonded to ensure an arrestee’s later court appearance: He’s going to post bail. Bail is also a verb for removing water from a boat, which you can do with a pail that features a bail (a semicircular handle). The meaning associated with removing water leads to the sense of abandoning something: My buddy bailed on me when I needed his help. Less frequent meanings have to do with metal hoops, cricket, and keeping animals separated from each other.

Bailed is the past tense of bail, which has several distinct meanings. To bail someone out of jail is to pay for their temporary release. To bail water is to scoop it out of a boat. To bail on someone or something is to abandon them: {He bailed on us at the last minute}. To bail out of a plane is to parachute from it. {She bailed me out when I couldn't make rent.}

Bailing is the present participle of bail in its various senses. Most commonly, bailing means removing water from a boat: {We spent an hour bailing out the canoe}. It also means securing someone's release from jail by posting bail, or abandoning a situation: {I'm bailing on the party tonight}. In skydiving or aviation, bailing out means jumping from an aircraft.

A bailout is financial rescue of a failing entity—typically when governments inject funds into banks, corporations, or industries to prevent collapse. The term carries connotations of controversy: critics see bailouts as rewarding irresponsibility with taxpayer money, while defenders argue they prevent broader economic catastrophe. {The 2008 bank bailouts sparked protests across the country.} More generally, any rescue from difficulty: {My parents gave me a bailout when I couldn't make rent.}

Bailouts are financial rescues—injections of money or credit to save a failing business, bank, or economy from collapse. The term gained prominence during the 2008 financial crisis when governments used taxpayer funds to stabilize major banks and automakers: {The bailouts were controversial but prevented a deeper recession}. A bailout implies the recipient couldn't survive on its own and often carries negative connotations of rewarding failure or moral hazard.

Bait is something used to lure prey—worms on a fishhook, cheese in a mousetrap. The verb means to set such a lure or to entice: {They baited the trap with peanut butter}. To bait someone is to provoke or tease them, trying to get a reaction: {He kept baiting her until she lost her temper}. Online, bait describes content designed to trigger engagement: {rage bait}, {clickbait}. To {take the bait} is to fall for a provocation or trick.

Baited describes something fitted with bait to attract prey: a baited {hook}, a baited {trap}. By extension, baited can mean lured or enticed: {He walked right into the baited question}. The phrase {with baited breath} is a common misspelling of "bated breath," where bated (from abate) means held or restrained.

Baiting is the act of luring or provoking. You bait a hook to catch fish, bait a trap to catch animals. Extended to people, baiting means deliberately provoking a reaction—often anger: {He kept baiting her until she snapped}. Online, baiting describes posts designed to provoke outrage or argument: {rage baiting}, {engagement baiting}. Historically, bear-baiting and bull-baiting were blood sports using dogs to torment chained animals.

To bake is to cook food in an oven using dry heat, typically bread, pastries, or casseroles: {I baked a cake for her birthday}. Extended uses describe anything subjected to prolonged heat: {The pavement baked in the summer sun}. A bake is a social gathering featuring baked goods: {church bake}, {clam bake}. In slang, to bake or get baked means to become intoxicated from marijuana.

Baked means cooked in an oven using dry heat: {freshly baked bread}. {She baked a cake for his birthday}. Baked also describes something hardened by heat: {baked clay}, {baked earth}. In slang, baked means very high on marijuana: {We got baked and ate everything in the fridge}. The connection may be from feeling slow and warm, or from the heat of smoking.

A baker is a person who bakes bread, pastries, and other goods, either professionally or as a serious pursuit. The term extends to the business: {The baker on Main Street opens at six}. A {baker's dozen} is thirteen—traditionally an extra item added to avoid accusations of shortchanging customers. (Capitalized Baker is a surname.)

A bakery is a place where bread, pastries, cakes, and other baked goods are made or sold. The word covers everything from small neighborhood shops to large commercial operations: {I stopped by the bakery for a fresh loaf}. Someone who works in or owns a bakery is a baker.

Baking is cooking food in an oven using dry heat, as opposed to frying, boiling, or grilling. The term applies especially to bread, pastries, and cakes: {The kitchen smelled of fresh baking}. As an adjective, baking describes intense heat: {We sat in the baking sun}. Something {baking hot} is extremely hot.

Baklava is a rich Middle Eastern and Mediterranean pastry made of layers of thin phyllo dough filled with chopped nuts and soaked in honey or syrup. The result is intensely sweet and flaky: {We ordered baklava for dessert}. Regional variations use pistachios, walnuts, or almonds, with different spices and syrups.

The core meaning of balance, an instrument for weighing things, informs all of its senses. Abstractly, a balance is equilibrium between opposing states; something in balance is in equilibrium. To balance something is either to place it on a balance, or to try to achieve a state in which opposing forces cancel each other: He balanced the ball on the tip of his finger. In meanings related to accounting, balance refers to a positive amount: Her checking account had a balance of $500. The verb denotes the activity of reconciling accounts: She reviewed her bank statement to balance her checkbook.

Balanced describes something in equilibrium—neither tilting nor favoring one side over another. A balanced {diet} includes appropriate proportions of nutrients. A balanced {account} has debits equaling credits. Balanced {reporting} presents multiple perspectives fairly. A balanced person maintains emotional stability: {She stayed balanced despite the chaos}. The word implies moderation and proportion rather than excess.

Balances is the plural of balance, covering both its noun and verb senses. A balance is a state of equilibrium—physical, financial, or emotional: {She checked her account balances}. To balance is to keep steady or make equal: {He balances work and family well}. The verb form appears in continuous constructions: {She's balancing the budget}.

A balcony is a platform projecting from the wall of a building, enclosed by a railing or balustrade: {We had coffee on the balcony overlooking the garden}. In theaters and auditoriums, the balcony is an upper level of seating that projects over the main floor: {We got cheap seats in the balcony}.

Bald means lacking hair, especially on the head. The word extends to anything stripped of its usual covering: a bald {tire} has worn treads, a bald {eagle} has a white-feathered head that looks bare from a distance. Figuratively, bald describes something plain and unadorned: a bald {lie}, a bald {statement of fact}—direct, with nothing to soften it.

Balding describes the process of losing hair, typically from the scalp. It's the present participle of bald used as an adjective: {a balding man in his forties}, {He's balding at the temples}. The word captures hair loss in progress rather than completion—someone balding still has some hair left.

A bale is a large bundle of material—hay, cotton, wool, paper—compressed and bound for storage or transport. The verb bale means to form such bundles: {We spent the afternoon baling hay}. In a different sense, to bale (or bail) out means to remove water from a boat or to escape from an aircraft by parachute. A bale can also be great suffering or sorrow, though this literary usage is rare outside poetry.

Bales is the plural of bale, a large bundle of material compressed and bound for storage or transport: {bales of hay}, {bales of cotton}, {bales of recycled cardboard}. As a verb, bales means to form such bundles: {The farmer bales the alfalfa in late summer}. To {bale out} is a British spelling variant of bail out.

A ball is a round object used in games, or any spherical thing: {tennis ball}, {ball of yarn}. A ball is also a formal dance: {Cinderella went to the ball}. To have a ball is to have a great time. Someone on the ball is alert and competent. The verb means to form into a ball: {He balled up the paper and threw it}. In vulgar slang, ball can mean to have sex: {They were balling in the back seat}. And in the plural, balls refers to testicles, with its own extensive set of meanings.

A ballad is a narrative song or poem, typically telling a dramatic story in short stanzas. Traditional ballads recount tales of love, tragedy, or adventure: {the ballad of John Henry}. In popular music, ballad has come to mean any slow, emotional song, especially about love: {power ballad}, {The album closes with a ballad}.

Ballads are narrative songs or poems that tell a story, typically in simple stanzas with a repeated refrain. Traditional ballads recount tales of love, tragedy, or adventure: {old Scottish ballads}, {murder ballads}. In popular music, a ballad is a slow, emotional song, usually about love or heartbreak: {a power ballad}, {The album closes with a tender ballad}.

Baller originally meant a basketball player, especially a skilled one. The meaning expanded to anyone who lives large—spending freely, dressing well, succeeding conspicuously: {He pulled up in a new Mercedes, total baller move}. As an adjective, baller means impressive or excellent: {That was a baller presentation}. The term carries admiration for someone who's made it and isn't shy about showing it.

A ballerina is a female ballet dancer, especially one who performs principal roles in a company. The term carries connotations of grace, discipline, and physical precision: {She trained for years to become a ballerina}. Male ballet dancers are not called ballerinos in English—they're simply ballet dancers or danseurs.

Ballet is a highly formalized style of dance characterized by precise, graceful movements, pointed feet, and often performed on the tips of the toes. It originated in European courts and developed into theatrical performances with elaborate costumes and orchestral accompaniment: {She studied ballet for twelve years}, {the Bolshoi Ballet}. A ballet is also a specific work in this form: {Swan Lake is a famous ballet}. The word extends to any carefully choreographed sequence: {a ballet of synchronized movements on the factory floor}.

A ballgame is any game played with a ball—baseball, football, basketball, soccer. In American usage, ballgame without qualification usually means a baseball game: {Let's go to the ballgame}. The phrase {a whole new ballgame} means a completely changed situation: {Once they got a lawyer involved, it was a whole new ballgame}.

A ballgown is a formal dress worn to balls, galas, and other elegant evening events. Ballgowns are typically full-length with voluminous skirts, distinguished from other formal dresses by their grandeur and often elaborate construction: {She spent months searching for the perfect ballgown for the charity gala}. The term evokes fairy-tale imagery—Cinderella's transformation centers on her ballgown.

Ballistic describes the motion of projectiles—objects propelled through space, subject to gravity and air resistance: {ballistic missile}, {ballistic trajectory}. The science of ballistics studies how bullets, bombs, and rockets travel. To {go ballistic} is to become explosively angry, like a missile launched beyond control: {She went ballistic when she saw the credit card bill}.

A balloon is an inflatable bag, typically rubber or plastic, often used as a decoration or toy. Larger balloons filled with hot air or gas can carry passengers or cargo. The shape suggests expansion: costs balloon, a person balloons in weight. In comics, a balloon is the outlined space containing a character's speech or thoughts. As a modifier: {balloon payment}, {balloon animal}.

Ballooning is the sport or activity of flying in a hot-air balloon: {We went ballooning over the wine country}. The word also describes rapid expansion or swelling: {ballooning costs}, {ballooning debt}. In medicine, ballooning refers to a procedure using an inflatable catheter to widen blocked vessels.

Balloons are inflatable bags, typically rubber or plastic, filled with air or gas. Children's party balloons hold air; helium balloons float. Hot-air balloons carry passengers in baskets beneath enormous fabric envelopes. A speech balloon in comics contains dialogue. As a verb, to balloon is to swell or expand rapidly: {Costs ballooned out of control}.

A ballot is a method of voting, or the paper or device used to cast a vote: {She marked her ballot and dropped it in the box}. By extension, ballot refers to the total votes cast or the list of candidates: {He barely made it onto the ballot}. As a verb, to ballot is to vote or draw lots: {The committee balloted on the proposal}.

Ballots are the papers, cards, or electronic records used to cast votes in an election: {The ballots were counted by hand}. The term extends to the voting process itself: {The measure will be on the ballot in November}. To ballot is to vote or to draw lots. A ballot box holds completed ballots and symbolizes democratic elections generally.

A ballpark is a stadium where baseball is played. The word extends to rough estimates and approximations: {Give me a ballpark figure}. Something {in the ballpark} is close enough to be reasonable: {Your guess was in the ballpark}. As a verb, to ballpark is to estimate roughly: {I'd ballpark the cost at fifty thousand}.

Ballparks are enclosed grounds where ball games—especially baseball—are played. The word extends to rough estimates or ranges: {Give me a ballpark figure}. Something {in the ballpark} is approximately correct or within acceptable limits: {Your guess wasn't exact, but it was in the ballpark}.

A ballplayer is someone who plays a ball sport professionally or seriously, almost always baseball in American usage: {He was a ballplayer in the minor leagues for six years}. The term can apply to other sports but rarely does without context making it clear.

A ballroom is a large room designed for formal dancing and social events. Grand houses, hotels, and public buildings have ballrooms for galas, weddings, and other occasions requiring space for many guests: {The hotel's ballroom accommodates three hundred}. Ballroom dancing refers to partnered social dances like the waltz, foxtrot, and tango.

Balls are round objects or formal dances in the plural. In vulgar slang, balls means testicles and, by extension, courage: {It takes balls to say that to his face}. Balls can also mean nonsense: {That's balls and you know it}. Common expressions include {bust your balls} (work hard or mock mercilessly), {balls to the wall} (full throttle), and {have the balls} (have the courage): {He didn't have the balls to ask for a raise}. To ball something up is to ruin it.

Balm is a soothing or healing substance, typically an aromatic ointment or oil applied to skin: {lip balm}, {tiger balm}. The word extends to anything that soothes or comforts: {The music was a balm for her grief}. Balm also names fragrant plants of the mint family, especially lemon balm.

Baloney is nonsense or foolishness—talk that shouldn't be taken seriously: {That's a load of baloney}. The word derives from bologna, the processed meat, perhaps suggesting something cheap or of dubious composition. The spelling baloney distinguishes the slang sense from the cold cut, though both spellings appear for both meanings.

Bam is an exclamation representing a sudden impact or dramatic moment: {Bam! The door flew open}. It emphasizes quickness or force—something happening all at once. Emeril Lagasse popularized it as a catchphrase when adding spices. As a verb, to bam is to strike forcefully. In slang, bam can mean to inject drugs intravenously.

Bamboo is a tall grass with hollow, woody stems that grows in tropical and subtropical regions. The stems are used for construction, furniture, flooring, and countless other purposes—prized for being lightweight yet remarkably strong. Bamboo shoots are edible and common in Asian cuisines. Some species grow extraordinarily fast, several feet per day under ideal conditions.

Bamboozle means to trick or deceive, often through elaborate confusion or misdirection. The word suggests a con rather than a simple lie—someone bamboozled has been led astray by cleverness: {The salesman bamboozled her into buying the extended warranty}. It carries a slightly playful tone, more suited to swindles than serious betrayals.

Bamboozled means tricked or deceived, usually through confusion or misdirection rather than outright lies. Someone bamboozled has been made a fool of: {I got completely bamboozled by that sales pitch}. The word carries a lighter, almost comical tone—you might be bamboozled by a con artist or a cunning child, but the word suggests bewilderment as much as betrayal.

Bamboozling is deceiving or tricking someone, usually through cunning or elaborate confusion: {The con artist was bamboozling tourists with fake jewelry}. The word carries a playful tone—more mischievous than sinister. Someone bamboozling you might use fast talk, misdirection, or sheer audacity rather than outright lies.

The main uses of ban are as a noun and verb about forbidding an activity: if you ban smoking you have instituted a smoking ban. This meaning is related to banish. A less frequent ban is a noun, hardly used in American English, denoting a public proclamation. Less frequent still is the ban that is a unit of Romanian currency, and the ban that is a defunct title in some eastern European nations.

A banana is a long curved fruit with a soft, sweet interior and yellow skin when ripe. Bananas grow in bunches on tropical plants and are among the world's most popular fruits. The phrase {go bananas} means to become wildly excited or crazy. {Banana republic} describes a small, unstable country dependent on a single export, often with a corrupt government. Something described as {bananas} is absurd or insane: {The prices at that restaurant are bananas}.

Bananas functions as a slang adjective meaning crazy, wild, or intensely enthusiastic: {The crowd went bananas when she walked onstage}. The word suggests excitement or absurdity rather than genuine mental instability. It likely derives from the earlier expression {go ape}, with bananas adding comic reinforcement. (Lowercase banana is the fruit.)

The spelling b-a-n-d is two words. The more frequent noun denotes a group with a common interest, by default a group that makes music together (rock band, jazz band). A band can also be any ring-shaped strip that binds or encircles (wedding band, cigar band, elastic band). This band can also be a verb meaning to gather or encircle with a band: The birds have been banded for later identification.

A bandage is a strip of material wrapped around a wound or injury—to protect it, apply pressure, or hold a dressing in place. To bandage is to apply such a strip: {She bandaged his sprained ankle}. Figuratively, to bandage something is to cover or patch it hastily: {They bandaged over the real problems}.

Bandages are strips of material used to cover and protect wounds or hold dressings in place. The word works as both noun and verb: {The nurse applied fresh bandages to the burn}, {She bandaged his sprained ankle}. Figuratively, to bandage something is to cover it up temporarily without addressing the underlying problem.

A bandaid is a small adhesive strip with a gauze pad, used to cover minor cuts and scrapes. The word comes from Band-Aid, the brand name that became generic. Figuratively, a bandaid is a superficial fix that doesn't address underlying problems: {Tax rebates are just a bandaid on a broken economy}. Also spelled band-aid.

A bandana is a square piece of cloth, typically cotton with a printed pattern, folded into a triangle and worn around the head or neck. Cowboys wore them to keep dust out; gang members use colored bandanas to signal affiliation. The paisley pattern is most traditional: {She tied a red bandana around her hair}.

Bandanas are large, usually square pieces of cloth worn as head coverings, face masks, or neck accessories. Traditionally printed with paisley or geometric patterns, they serve practical purposes—absorbing sweat, filtering dust, or holding back hair—and cultural ones, signaling gang affiliation, political solidarity, or personal style. {She tied a red bandana around her head.}

A bandanna is a large square of cotton fabric, typically brightly colored or printed with a pattern, worn around the head or neck or carried as a handkerchief. The classic paisley bandanna comes in red or blue: {She tied a bandanna over her hair}. Gang members sometimes use bandanna colors to signal affiliation.

A bandit is an outlaw who robs travelers or raids settlements, typically operating in remote areas beyond the reach of law enforcement. The word evokes horseback robbers, mountain hideouts, and lawless frontiers. Extended uses describe anyone who takes unfairly: {Those insurance companies are bandits}. A {one-armed bandit} is a slot machine.

Bandits are outlaws who rob travelers or conduct raids, typically operating in groups in remote areas. The word evokes Wild West stagecoach robbers or mountain brigands. By extension, bandit describes anyone who takes unfairly: {insurance bandits}, {one-armed bandit} for a slot machine. {The bandits ambushed the convoy at dawn.}

Bands is the plural of band, covering all its senses. Musical bands are groups that play together: {rock bands}, {marching bands}, {jazz bands}. Bands can be strips or loops of material: {rubber bands}, {wedding bands}, {wristbands}. Bands also means ranges or divisions: {tax bands}, {frequency bands}. As a verb, bands means to form groups or encircle: {The neighbors banded together}.

A bandstand is a raised platform or open-sided structure where musicians perform outdoors, typically found in parks or public squares. The classic design features a roof supported by pillars, allowing sound to carry while sheltering performers from weather: {The brass band played waltzes from the Victorian bandstand}.

A bandwagon was originally a wagon carrying a band in a parade—something people literally jumped onto. Now it's almost always figurative: to {jump on the bandwagon} or {climb aboard the bandwagon} is to join a popular movement or trend, often opportunistically. The bandwagon effect describes how popularity breeds more popularity, as people follow what others are doing.

Bandwidth is the capacity of a channel to transmit data, originally referring to the range of frequencies a signal can occupy. In computing and telecommunications, higher bandwidth means faster data transfer: {We need more bandwidth to stream video}. Figuratively, bandwidth describes mental or organizational capacity to handle tasks: {I don't have the bandwidth to take on another project right now}.

Bane is something that causes ruin, death, or persistent misery. Poisons were once called banes—wolfsbane, henbane, ratsbane. The word now appears mostly in the phrase {bane of my existence}, meaning a constant source of annoyance or frustration: {Spreadsheets are the bane of my existence}. As an adjective, baneful means harmful or destructive.

A bang is a loud, sudden noise: {The door closed with a bang}. {I heard a bang from the basement}. To bang is to strike loudly or move violently: {He banged his fist on the table}. {She banged into the doorframe}. A bang is also a fringe of hair cut straight across the forehead, usually plural in American English: {She got bangs}. In vulgar slang, to bang is to have sex with: {They banged in the back seat}. Related expressions: {bang up} (damage or do excellently), {bang for your buck} (value), {bang on} (British for exactly right).

A banger is something that bangs—a firecracker, an old noisy car, or anything that makes a loud noise: {The car was a rusty old banger}. {Kids set off bangers in the street}. In British English, bangers are sausages: {bangers and mash}. The name may come from sausages bursting with a bang when cooked. In music slang, a banger is an excellent, energetic song: {That track is a banger}. {The DJ played nothing but bangers}.

Bangers is the plural of banger—firecrackers, old cars, British sausages, or excellent songs: {We had bangers and mash for dinner}. {The DJ played bangers all night}. {Those old bangers shouldn't be on the road}.

Banging is the present participle of bang—making loud noises, striking: {Someone is banging on the door}. {Stop banging those pots together}. As a slang adjective, banging means excellent or attractive: {That song is banging}. {She's banging}. In vulgar slang: {They were banging all night}.

A bangle is a rigid bracelet, typically a solid ring that slips over the hand onto the wrist. Unlike flexible chain bracelets, bangles hold their shape. They're often worn in multiples, clinking together as the arm moves: {Her bangles jangled as she gestured}. The word can also describe a small ornamental pendant or charm.

Bangles are rigid bracelets, typically circular and slipped over the hand onto the wrist. They're often worn in multiples, creating a jingling sound when they knock together: {Her bangles clinked as she gestured}. Bangles can be made of metal, glass, plastic, or wood, and are traditional adornments in South Asian cultures.

Bangs are hair cut in a fringe across the forehead: {She wore her bangs straight across}. {I'm thinking of getting bangs}. Bangs is also the third-person verb—strikes loudly or produces a loud noise: {He bangs the drums too hard}. {The shutter bangs in the wind}. In slang: {He bangs a different girl every weekend}.

To banish is to send someone away, typically as punishment or by official decree: {The king banished the traitor from the realm}. The word implies forced departure with prohibition against return. Figuratively, to banish something is to drive it out or dismiss it entirely: {She tried to banish the thought from her mind}, {banish all doubt}.

Banished is the past tense of banish, meaning to expel someone from a place or group, typically as punishment: {The king banished the traitor from the realm}. It extends to driving away unwanted things: {She banished all doubt from her mind}. The word carries a formal, sometimes literary tone suggesting permanent or official removal.

Banishment is the act of being sent away from a place, typically as punishment. A king might order the banishment of a traitor from the realm. The word carries a formal, often historical tone: {His banishment from court lasted seven years}. Figuratively, banishment can describe any forced exclusion: {the banishment of doubt from her mind}.

A banjo is a stringed instrument with a round body, a membrane stretched over a frame like a drumhead, and a long neck with frets. It produces a bright, twangy sound associated with American folk, bluegrass, and country music. The five-string banjo is most common, though four-string versions exist for jazz and Irish music. {He picked out a tune on the banjo.}

At least two – and maybe three – separate words have entered English with the spelling bank, and the original nouns have spawned verbs, so you might say there is a whole bank (that is, series of objects in a row) of meanings associated with bank. The bank of a river or lake is the part where land and water meet. This meaning gives rise to the banks which are the edges of a pool table; when you bank a shot, you drive a ball to one of these banks. The institution called a bank stores and lends money. When you bank money, you put it in a bank. When you bank on something, you depend on it: I’m banking on getting a raise.

A banker is someone who works in banking, especially in an executive or management role at a bank. The term suggests someone involved in high-level financial decisions rather than a teller handling routine transactions: {Investment bankers on Wall Street}. In British slang, a banker is a sure thing—a bet considered certain to win.

Banking is the business of operating a bank—accepting deposits, making loans, and managing money. The term covers both the industry {a career in banking} and the act of conducting bank transactions {I do my banking online}. In other contexts, banking refers to tilting sideways, as when an aircraft or cyclist leans into a turn.

A bankroll is a supply of money, especially cash on hand for a specific purpose: {He blew his entire bankroll at the casino}. The word evokes a physical roll of bills. As a verb, to bankroll is to finance or fund something: {Her parents bankrolled her startup}. The term often implies backing a venture or enterprise rather than routine expenses.

Bankrolled is the past tense of bankroll, meaning to finance or fund something, especially a venture, project, or person's activities. The word suggests substantial financial backing: {The film was bankrolled by a tech billionaire}. It often implies a single wealthy source rather than collective funding: {Her father bankrolled her startup}.

Bankrolls functions as both noun and verb around the idea of funding. A bankroll is a roll of paper money or, more broadly, available funds: {He flashed his bankroll at the casino}. To bankroll someone or something is to finance it: {Her parents bankrolled her startup}. The verb often implies substantial or ongoing financial backing rather than a one-time payment.

Bankrupt describes a person or entity legally declared unable to pay their debts. A bankruptcy court may liquidate assets to satisfy creditors or approve a repayment plan. The word extends to any kind of exhaustion or emptiness: {morally bankrupt}, {bankrupt of ideas}. As a verb, to bankrupt someone is to cause their financial ruin: {The lawsuit bankrupted the company}.

Bankruptcy is a legal status declaring that a person or organization cannot pay their debts. The process, initiated either by the debtor or creditors, typically involves a court overseeing the orderly settlement of financial obligations—through liquidation of assets, restructuring of payments, or discharge of certain debts entirely. Someone who has declared bankruptcy is called a bankrupt. Figuratively, bankruptcy can describe any state of utter failure or depletion: {moral bankruptcy}, {the intellectual bankruptcy of the movement}.

Banks are financial institutions that hold deposits, make loans, and facilitate transactions. The term also refers to raised ground along rivers or other waterways: {the banks of the Mississippi}. A bank can be any stored supply: a blood bank, a data bank. To bank is to deposit money, to tilt an aircraft, or to rely on something: {Don't bank on good weather}.

Banned means officially prohibited or forbidden. A banned substance is one that authorities have declared illegal to use or possess. A banned book has been removed from libraries or schools. Someone who is banned from a place or activity has been formally excluded: {He was banned from the stadium for fighting}. The word implies an official prohibition rather than informal disapproval.

A banner is a long piece of cloth bearing a design or message, typically hung or carried in processions and protests: {Protesters unfurled banners outside city hall}. The word extends to any prominent display strip—website banners, banner headlines that stretch across a newspaper's front page. As an adjective, banner means outstanding or notably successful: {a banner year for sales}.

Banners are large pieces of cloth or other material bearing a symbol, logo, slogan, or message. They hang from buildings, stretch across streets, or wave at demonstrations. In digital contexts, a banner is a graphic element spanning the top of a webpage or an advertisement strip: {banner ads}. Something done {under the banner of} a cause is done in its name. A banner year or banner day is an exceptionally good one.

A banquet is a formal, elaborate meal for many guests, typically marking a special occasion: {the wedding banquet}, {an awards banquet}. The word suggests ceremony and abundance—multiple courses, speeches, toasts. To banquet is to feast lavishly: {They banqueted late into the night}.

Banquets are elaborate formal meals, typically for many guests and often marking a special occasion: {The wedding banquet fed three hundred guests}. The word suggests ceremony and abundance—multiple courses, speeches, toasts. Organizations hold banquets to honor achievements or raise funds. To banquet is to feast lavishly, though the verb is less common than the noun.

Bans is the plural of ban, a prohibition or official restriction: {The city enacted bans on plastic bags and smoking in parks}. As a verb form, bans means prohibits or forbids: {The school bans cell phones during class}. What gets banned typically involves public health, safety, or moral concerns—though the wisdom of specific bans is often contested.

A banshee is a wailing female spirit in Irish and Scottish folklore whose shriek supposedly foretells a death in the family. The word now commonly describes any loud, high-pitched screaming: {The wind howled like a banshee}, {She let out a banshee scream when she saw the spider}.

Banshees is the plural of banshee, a female spirit in Irish and Scottish folklore whose wailing warns of an approaching death in a family. The shriek itself is sometimes called a banshee: {The wind made a banshee sound through the trees}. Figuratively, anything that screams or wails may be compared to a banshee: {She came at him screaming like a banshee}.

Banter is playful, teasing conversation between people who enjoy verbal sparring.
