The concept extends to any situation involving strategic deception: {She's bluffing about having another job offer}.

Bluffs works across two unrelated words. From one: a bluff is a steep cliff or riverbank with a broad face, and the plural names such features: {the bluffs overlooking the Missouri River}. From the other: to bluff is to deceive by false confidence, especially in poker, and bluffs are instances of this—attempts to mislead about what you hold or intend: {He called her bluffs and won the pot}.

A blunder is a careless or stupid mistake, typically one with consequences: {a tactical blunder}, {a diplomatic blunder}. The word suggests the error was avoidable—someone should have known better. To blunder is to make such a mistake, or to move clumsily and uncertainly: {He blundered through the dark room}, {She blundered into the wrong meeting}.

Blunders are serious mistakes, typically caused by carelessness or poor judgment rather than ignorance. The word suggests clumsiness—stumbling into error rather than being misled: {a series of diplomatic blunders}, {The company's marketing blunders cost them millions}. To blunder is to make such mistakes, or to move clumsily: {He blundered through the dark room}.

Blunt describes something with a dull edge or point—the opposite of sharp. A blunt {knife} cuts poorly. Figuratively, blunt speech is direct and unsparing of feelings: {She was blunt about his chances}. A blunt {instrument} in detective fiction is any heavy object used to bludgeon. To blunt something is to dull it: {The setback blunted his enthusiasm}. A blunt is also slang for a marijuana cigar, typically rolled in tobacco leaf.

Blur is indistinctness—the loss of sharp edges or clear boundaries. A photograph can be blurry, and so can vision or memory: {The details have blurred over time}. To blur is to make something indistinct or to become so: {Tears blurred her vision}, {The line between work and life has blurred}. A blur of motion suggests speed that defeats perception: {The days passed in a blur}.

A blurb is a short promotional description, typically found on book jackets, movie posters, or product packaging. Blurbs praise the work in breathless terms: {Critics are calling it a masterpiece}. The word was coined by humorist Gelett Burgess in 1907, mocking the extravagant endorsements that adorned book covers.

Blurred describes something with unclear edges or outlines, as if seen through fog or tears: {The photo came out blurred}. Vision blurs when eyes lose focus. Distinctions blur when boundaries become indistinct: {The line between work and life has blurred}. A blurred memory is one whose details have faded or merged together.

Blurry describes something indistinct or out of focus, lacking sharp edges or clear definition. A blurry {photograph} failed to capture a crisp image. Blurry {vision} may indicate you need glasses. The word extends to anything vague or unclear: {My memory of that night is blurry}.

Blurt means to say something suddenly and impulsively, usually without thinking first. The word almost always appears with out: {She blurted out the secret before she could stop herself}. What gets blurted is typically something that should have been kept private or at least delivered more carefully—a confession, an insult, an awkward truth. The spontaneity implied by blurt suggests the speaker immediately regrets the utterance or at least didn't intend to make it.

Blush is the reddening of the face from embarrassment, shame, or modesty: {She felt a blush creep up her cheeks}. The verb means to redden this way: {He blushed when she caught him staring}. By extension, blush describes any rosy tint—a blush {wine} is pale pink, and blush as a cosmetic adds color to cheeks. {At first blush} means on initial impression: {At first blush, the plan seemed reasonable}.

Blushed is the past tense of blush—to redden in the face from embarrassment, shame, or modesty. {She blushed when he complimented her}. The word extends to anything taking on a rosy tint: {The sky blushed pink at dawn}. A blushing bride is traditionally modest; to make someone blush is to embarrass or flatter them.

Blushing is the involuntary reddening of the face from embarrassment, shame, or self-consciousness. The word works as both verb and adjective: {She was blushing furiously} or {the blushing bride}. A blushing person is modest or easily embarrassed. By extension, things tinged pink or red may be described as blushing: {blushing peaches}, {a blushing sky at dawn}.

Bluster is loud, aggressive talk that lacks substance—empty threats or boastful claims meant to intimidate or impress: {His bluster couldn't hide his inexperience}. As a verb, to bluster is to speak or behave this way. Wind also blusters when it blows in strong, noisy gusts. The noun and verb share the sense of forceful noise without follow-through.

Blustery describes weather marked by strong, gusty winds, often with rain or snow: {a blustery November afternoon}. The word suggests unpredictable gusts rather than steady gales. Extended to people, blustery means loudly aggressive or boastful but without real substance—all bluster: {His blustery threats didn't intimidate anyone}.

A boa is a large snake that kills prey by coiling around it and squeezing—a constrictor. The term covers various species, most famously the boa constrictor of Central and South America. A boa is also a long, fluffy scarf made of feathers or fur, worn draped around the neck and shoulders: {She wore a pink feather boa to the party}. The garment takes its name from its snake-like shape and the way it wraps around the wearer.

A boar is a male pig, especially an uncastrated one kept for breeding. Wild boar refers to the tusked ancestor of domestic pigs, native to Eurasia and hunted as game: {Wild boar have returned to parts of Britain}. The word often evokes something fierce or brutish.

The many meanings of the noun board can be roughly divided in three: a rigid piece of wood, longer than it is wide (2’ x 4’ board); a group of persons with a particular authoritative function (board of directors); and daily meals, provided for pay (room and board). Things like a circuit board grow out of the first meaning. The verb board is related to the first and third meanings. You can board up a building (cover it with boards), or you can board at a hotel (get your meals there).

A boardgame is a game played on a marked surface—a board—with pieces, cards, dice, or other components. Chess, Monopoly, and Scrabble are classic examples. The term distinguishes tabletop games from card games, video games, or sports. Also spelled as two words: {board game}.

Boarding is the act of getting onto a vehicle for travel—a plane, ship, train, or bus. Airlines announce boarding by zones; cruise passengers await boarding times. Boarding also means covering with boards: {They boarded up the windows before the hurricane}. In hockey, boarding is the penalty for violently checking an opponent into the boards. A boarding school provides room and board for students who live on campus.

A boardroom is a room where the board of directors of a company meets to conduct business, make decisions, and set policy. By extension, boardroom often refers to corporate leadership itself or the culture of high-level business decision-making: {The deal was hammered out in the boardroom}. Boardroom politics suggests the maneuvering and power dynamics among executives, while boardroom diversity addresses representation at the highest levels of corporate governance.

Boards are flat, rigid pieces of material—typically wood cut into planks for construction or other purposes: {The floor boards creaked underfoot}. Board extends to any flat surface serving a function: a cutting board, a circuit board, a board game's playing surface. A board is also a group that governs or advises: {board of directors}, {school board}. To tread the boards is to perform on stage, from the wooden planks of theater floors. In hockey, the boards are the walls surrounding the rink.

A boardwalk is a walkway made of wooden planks, typically found along beaches or through marshy areas where the ground is unstable or prone to flooding. The term especially evokes the famous promenades at seaside resorts—Atlantic City's boardwalk being the most iconic—lined with shops, amusements, and carnival attractions: {We strolled the boardwalk eating saltwater taffy}. The boardwalk in Monopoly references Atlantic City's.

Boardwalks is the plural of boardwalk—a walkway made of wooden planks, typically found along beaches or through marshy areas. Seaside boardwalks often feature shops, games, and amusements: {the Atlantic City boardwalk}, {We strolled the boardwalk eating cotton candy}. Nature boardwalks protect fragile ecosystems while allowing foot traffic through wetlands or forests.

Boars are male pigs, especially uncastrated ones raised for breeding. The word also refers to wild pigs—the tusked ancestors of domestic swine that still roam forests in Europe, Asia, and parts of the Americas: {Wild boars have been spotted in the hills outside town}. A boar is larger and more aggressive than a castrated male, which is called a barrow.

To boast is to speak with excessive pride about one's accomplishments, possessions, or abilities: {He boasted about his promotion to anyone who would listen}. The word carries a whiff of disapproval—boasting suggests self-praise that crosses into bragging. A boast is also the thing claimed: {His boast that he could beat anyone proved hollow}. A place or thing can boast a feature, meaning it possesses something noteworthy: {The hotel boasts a rooftop pool}.

Boasting is talking with excessive pride about oneself or one's achievements. The word carries a negative connotation—someone who boasts isn't just sharing good news but doing so in a way that feels self-aggrandizing or tiresome to others: {His constant boasting about his salary alienated his coworkers}. A boast can sometimes prove hollow: {All that boasting, and he came in last}.

A boat is a watercraft—a vessel for traveling on water. Boats are generally smaller than ships, though the line is imprecise. You can boat across a lake or down a river. To {be in the same boat} is to share circumstances with others. To {rock the boat} is to disturb a stable situation. To {miss the boat} is to lose an opportunity.

Boating is the activity of traveling on water in a boat for recreation or sport. The term covers everything from casual rowing on a pond to sailing, motorboating, and yachting. {We spent the afternoon boating on the lake.} Someone who enjoys boating regularly might be called a boating enthusiast, and areas with marinas and waterways often develop boating communities around the pastime.

A boatload is the amount a boat can carry—passengers, cargo, or fish. By extension, a boatload means a large quantity of anything: {We made a boatload of money on that deal}. The figurative sense is informal and emphatic, suggesting abundance without specifying an exact amount.

Boats are watercraft—vessels that float and move across water. The word typically suggests smaller craft: rowboats, sailboats, motorboats. Larger vessels are usually called ships, though the line blurs. To boat is to travel by boat or to transport something in one: {We boated across the lake}. {In the same boat} means sharing circumstances, usually unfortunate ones.

Several words have settled on the spelling b-o-b in English. The most common is the verb, indicating a quick up-and-down movement: Let’s bob for apples. The noun bob indicates an instance of this. A bob is also a kind of short women’s haircut; it is the result when you bob your hair. In British slang, a bob is shilling, and still notes a quantity of money even though the shilling is obsolete: I lent him a few bob. When capitalized, Bob is a standard nickname for Robert.

Boba is a tea-based drink featuring chewy tapioca pearls, originating in Taiwan. The pearls settle at the bottom and are sucked up through an oversized straw. Boba can refer to the drink itself or just the pearls: {Let's get boba}, {I love the boba in this}. Also called bubble tea. The drink comes in countless flavors, from classic milk tea to fruit blends.

Bobbing is repeated quick up-and-down or side-to-side movement. A cork bobs on the water. A head bobs in agreement or to music. {She kept bobbing her head to the beat.} Bobbing for apples is the Halloween game of catching floating apples with your teeth. The word suggests light, buoyant motion rather than deliberate action.

A bobble is a small, soft ball of material, often decorative—the kind found on winter hats or curtain trim. In British usage, a bobble is also a hair tie. As a verb, to bobble is to fumble or handle clumsily: {He bobbled the catch and the ball rolled away}. A bobblehead is a figurine with an oversized head on a spring that wobbles when touched.

A bobblehead is a collectible figurine with an oversized head attached by a spring, causing it to wobble when touched or jostled. Most depict athletes, celebrities, or fictional characters, often given away at sporting events: {I got a free bobblehead at the baseball game}. The nodding motion can suggest mindless agreement: {Don't be a bobblehead—think for yourself}.

Bobbleheads are figurines with oversized heads attached by springs, causing them to wobble when touched or jostled. They typically depict athletes, celebrities, or cartoon characters and are popular as collectibles and promotional giveaways at sporting events: {I have a whole shelf of baseball bobbleheads}. The term sometimes describes people who nod along agreeably without independent thought.

A bobcat is a wild cat native to North America, named for its short, stubby tail. About twice the size of a house cat, bobcats have tufted ears and spotted coats. They're solitary, nocturnal hunters found from southern Canada through Mexico: {We spotted a bobcat crossing the trail at dusk}.

Bobcats are wild cats native to North America, named for their short, bobbed tails. Smaller than lynxes but larger than housecats, they're adaptable predators found from Canadian forests to Mexican deserts. {A bobcat was spotted near the hiking trail}. The term also refers to a brand of compact construction equipment: {We rented a Bobcat to grade the driveway}.

A bobsled is a racing sled with runners, a steering mechanism, and brakes, used to hurtle down an ice-covered track. Teams of two or four push the sled at the start, then jump in and navigate banked curves at high speeds. The sport features in the Winter Olympics. Also called bobsleigh, especially in British English.

A bobsleigh is a racing sled used on ice tracks, typically crewed by two or four people who steer and shift their weight through banked curves at high speeds. The sport originated in Switzerland in the late 19th century. Also spelled bobsled, which is more common in American English: {The Jamaican bobsleigh team became unlikely Olympic heroes}.

A bodega is a small neighborhood grocery store, especially in Hispanic communities in the United States. The word is Spanish for "warehouse" or "wine cellar." In urban areas like New York City, bodegas typically sell everyday essentials—snacks, drinks, cigarettes, lottery tickets—and often stay open late: {I ran to the bodega for milk}. The term carries cultural weight, evoking corner-store convenience and neighborhood character.

Bodegas are small grocery or convenience stores, especially in Latino neighborhoods of American cities. The word is Spanish for storeroom or wine cellar. In urban areas like New York, a bodega typically stocks basics—milk, bread, beer, cigarettes, lottery tickets—and stays open late: {I'm running to the bodega for some eggs}. The term carries neighborhood familiarity; your bodega is the one on your corner.

Bodies is the plural of body—physical forms of humans, animals, or objects. The word often implies corpses: {They found three bodies in the wreckage}. Bodies can be collective groups: governing bodies, bodies of water, bodies of work. In casual speech, body positivity movements have made {bodies} a term for celebrating physical diversity: {All bodies are beautiful}.

The core meaning of body is the physical part of living things—the part that decays when life ends. In a narrower sense, body may refer to the torso. By extension, body often refers to the main or surrounding part of something that has ancillary or interior parts. The body of a car is the exterior, exclusive of its mechanical parts. The body of a document or book is the main part, exclusive of indices, appendices, or front matter. In expressions where body is followed by an of prepositional phrase, the thing designated is a physically separate or separately conceived entity: a body of water, a body of knowledge.

A bodybag is a zippered bag, usually made of heavy plastic or rubber, used to transport human corpses. They are standard equipment for military personnel, emergency responders, and morgue workers. The term sometimes appears in aggressive contexts to suggest killing someone: {They'll be leaving in bodybags}. Bodybag can also function as a slang verb meaning to defeat someone decisively, especially in gaming or sports: {Our team got bodybbagged in the finals}.

A bodybuilder is someone who develops their muscles through weight training and diet, typically for competition or aesthetic display. The sport emphasizes symmetry, definition, and size, with competitors posing to showcase their physiques: {Professional bodybuilders follow strict training regimens}. The term also applies to serious recreational lifters pursuing muscular development.

Bodybuilders are people who develop their muscles through weight training and diet, typically for competition or aesthetic goals. The sport emphasizes muscular size, symmetry, and definition, with competitors posing to display their physiques: {The bodybuilders backstage were applying oil before going onstage}. The term can also describe anyone serious about building muscle mass.

Bodybuilding is the practice of developing muscle size and definition through weight training, diet, and exercise. Competitive bodybuilders display their physiques in poses before judges who evaluate symmetry, proportion, and muscular development. The activity exists on a spectrum from casual gym-goers seeking to {build muscle} to professionals using rigorous regimens and sometimes performance-enhancing drugs.

A bodycheck is a defensive move in ice hockey and lacrosse where a player uses their body to block or knock an opponent off the puck or ball. The contact must target the torso rather than the head or legs to be legal: {He delivered a hard bodycheck at center ice}. As a verb, to bodycheck is to execute such a hit.

A bodyguard is a person hired to protect someone from physical harm. Bodyguards accompany their clients in public, watch for threats, and intervene if danger arises. The term applies to individual protectors and to security details: {The celebrity traveled with two bodyguards}. By extension, anything that shields or defends can serve as a bodyguard: {The lawyer acted as a bodyguard against legal threats}.

Bodyguards are people employed to protect someone from physical harm or unwanted contact. The term typically suggests close personal protection rather than general security work: {The celebrity traveled with two bodyguards}. A single protector is a bodyguard; the plural often refers to a protective detail or team.

Bodysnatching is the practice of stealing corpses from graves, historically to sell them for medical dissection when legal cadavers were scarce. The term extends to any unauthorized removal of a body. Figuratively, it describes taking someone away from a group or organization: {Corporate bodysnatching of university researchers has become common}.

A bog is wet, spongy ground, a kind of wetland. If you get bogged down, it’s possible that you are stuck in a bog, but more likely that you have stopped making progress because of obstacles or impediments. Bog is a slang term for toilet in British English.

A bogey in golf is a score of one stroke over par on a hole. Beyond the links, bogey names something undesirable or troublesome—a persistent problem or source of worry. In military contexts, a bogey is an unidentified aircraft, presumed hostile until proven otherwise. British English also uses bogey for the dried nasal mucus that children (and some adults) pick from their noses. As a verb, to bogey a hole means to complete it one over par.

A bogeyman is a frightening imaginary creature used to scare children into obedience: {The bogeyman will get you if you don't behave}. By extension, any object of dread or fear, often one exaggerated or fabricated: {Communism was the bogeyman of Cold War politics}. Also spelled boogeyman or bogyman.

To boggle is to hesitate or waver, usually from astonishment or alarm: {The mind boggles at the scale of the universe}. Something that boggles the mind overwhelms comprehension. The word suggests a moment of mental stumbling—you encounter something so strange or vast that thought itself falters. Boggle is also a word game where players find words in a grid of lettered dice.

Bogs are wetlands characterized by soft, waterlogged ground composed largely of decomposing plant matter, especially sphagnum moss. The verb bog, nearly always followed by down, means to become stuck or mired, whether literally in mud or figuratively in complications: {The project got bogged down in committee}. In British slang, bog is a crude term for a toilet, giving rise to expressions like {bog roll} for toilet paper.

Bogus means fake, counterfeit, or not genuine. Originally applied to counterfeit money, it now describes anything fraudulent or without merit: {a bogus insurance claim}, {bogus credentials}. In casual speech, bogus can simply mean bad or disappointing: {That's totally bogus}.

A bohemian is someone who lives an unconventional, artistic life, rejecting bourgeois values in favor of creative freedom and casual attitudes toward money and social norms. The term evokes artists, writers, and musicians living cheaply in garrets, prioritizing art over respectability: {She fell in with a bohemian crowd in the Village}. As an adjective, bohemian describes this lifestyle or aesthetic: {a bohemian apartment full of mismatched furniture and half-finished canvases}. (Capitalized Bohemian refers to the Czech region or its people.)

To boil is to heat liquid until it bubbles and turns to vapor, or to cook something in boiling water: {Boil the pasta for eight minutes}. Water boils at 212°F at sea level. Emotions boil when they reach an intense state: {His anger boiled over}. To {boil down} is to reduce to essentials. A boil is also a painful, pus-filled skin infection—unrelated to the cooking sense.

Boiled describes something cooked in boiling water or other liquid: {boiled eggs}, {boiled potatoes}. The past tense of boil, it extends to anything subjected to intense heat or agitation. Figuratively, boiled can mean extremely angry: {I was boiled when I found out}. In older slang, boiled means drunk: {He came home boiled at 3 a.m.}

A boiler is a large tank or vessel in which water is heated, typically to produce steam for heating buildings or powering engines. Industrial boilers generate steam for manufacturing processes or electricity generation. In domestic settings, a boiler heats water for radiators or household use. The term also applies informally to a chicken too old and tough for roasting, suitable only for long, slow cooking in liquid—hence {boiler} as opposed to {broiler}.

Boilerplate is standardized text used repeatedly without change—contract clauses, legal disclaimers, or form letters. The term comes from the metal plates newspapers once used for syndicated content, which arrived ready to print. In computing, boilerplate is template code that appears in many programs with little modification. The word often carries a dismissive tone: {Skip the boilerplate and get to the actual terms}.

Boiling describes liquid heated to the point where it churns with bubbles and produces steam—water boils at 212°F at sea level. The word extends to intense heat generally: {It's boiling outside}. Figuratively, boiling describes barely contained anger: {She was boiling with rage}. As an intensifier, boiling hot emphasizes extreme temperature.

Boils covers both the verb and the noun. Water boils when heated to the point where it bubbles and turns to vapor. To boil something is to cook it in boiling water: {boil the pasta for ten minutes}. Figuratively, emotions boil when they reach an intense point: {His anger boiled over}. To {boil down} is to reduce to essentials. A boil is also a painful, pus-filled skin infection—an inflamed swelling that eventually ruptures.

Boing represents the sound of something springy bouncing or rebounding—a diving board, a coiled spring, a trampoline. The word is onomatopoeic, imitating the twangy vibration of elastic recoil: {The ball hit the rim and—boing—bounced away}. It often appears in cartoon contexts or playful speech.

Boisterous describes noisy, energetic, and slightly unruly behavior—the kind that comes from high spirits rather than malice. A boisterous {crowd} cheers loudly; boisterous {children} run and shout; a boisterous {party} keeps the neighbors awake. The word suggests exuberance that's barely contained, energetic but not quite out of control. Weather can also be boisterous: {boisterous winds}, {boisterous seas}.

Bold describes willingness to take risks or face challenges without fear: {a bold move}, {a bold strategy}. It can shade toward audacious or presumptuous: {That was bold of you to ask}. In design and typography, bold means visually prominent—heavy strokes that stand out: {Set the title in bold}. Bold flavors are strong and distinct. To be {bold as brass} is to act with shameless confidence.

Boldness is the quality of being willing to take risks or act with confidence despite potential consequences. It suggests courage that borders on audacity: {Her boldness in challenging the CEO surprised everyone}. Boldness can be admirable or reckless depending on context—a bold move might be praised as visionary or criticized as foolhardy.

Bollocks is vulgar British slang for testicles. More commonly, bollocks means nonsense or rubbish: {That's complete bollocks}. As an exclamation, it expresses frustration or disbelief: {Oh bollocks, I left my wallet at home}. {Bollocks to that} is dismissive refusal. Confusingly, {the dog's bollocks} means something excellent—the best of its kind: {That curry is the dog's bollocks}. The word is versatile, vulgar, and quintessentially British.

Bologna is a seasoned smoked sausage made from finely ground meat, typically beef and pork. In American usage, it's the familiar pink lunch meat sliced for sandwiches: {a bologna and cheese sandwich}. The word is often spelled and pronounced "baloney." Separately, bologna is slang for nonsense or lies: {That's a load of bologna}—though "baloney" is the more common spelling for this sense. (Capitalized Bologna is the Italian city.)

Bolognaise is a meat sauce for pasta, originating from Bologna, Italy. The authentic version (ragù alla bolognese) is a slow-cooked mixture of ground meat, tomatoes, wine, and aromatics, traditionally served with tagliatelle. Outside Italy, bolognaise typically means any tomato-meat sauce served over spaghetti: {spaghetti bolognaise}. Also spelled bolognese.

Bolognese is a meat sauce originating from Bologna, Italy, typically made with ground beef, tomatoes, onions, and wine, simmered slowly. It's the traditional sauce for tagliatelle and lasagna: {spaghetti bolognese}, {I made a bolognese from scratch}. The term also describes anything in the style of Bologna's cuisine.

A bolster is a long cylindrical pillow or cushion, typically placed under other pillows or used for back support. The word extends to any structural support—a bolster beneath a beam, a bolster in a saddle. The verb dominates modern usage: to bolster is to strengthen, support, or prop up: {The new evidence bolstered her case}. You bolster confidence, bolster defenses, bolster an argument. The physical prop becomes metaphorical reinforcement.

A bolt may be a threaded fastener (nuts and bolts), an arrow (shoot a bolt), a flash of lightening, or a sliding mechanism: Pull on the bolt to unlock the door. One sense of the verb bolt is related to these meanings: to bolt is to move or depart rapidly: He bolted from the scene of the crime. If a plant bolts, it produces seed earlier than is desired. A different verb bolt is used only of flour; if you bolt flour, you sift it through a cloth or sieve.

Boltcutters are heavy-duty hand tools with long handles and short, powerful jaws designed to cut through padlocks, chains, bolts, and wire fencing. The long handles provide leverage to shear metal that ordinary pliers can't touch. Associated with both legitimate work and breaking into places: {Someone had taken boltcutters to the chain-link fence}.

Bolted describes something secured with a bolt—a metal fastener or sliding bar: {a bolted door}, {bolted to the floor}. More commonly, bolted means having fled suddenly: {The horse bolted when the gun fired}, {She bolted from the room}. To bolt food is to eat it hastily, so bolted can describe food gulped down without chewing. In plant terminology, bolted describes vegetables that have prematurely gone to seed: {The lettuce bolted in the heat}.

Bolting covers several actions united by sudden movement or securing. A horse bolts when it runs off unexpectedly; a person bolts from a room in alarm or haste. To bolt food is to swallow it quickly without chewing: {He bolted his lunch and ran}. Bolting also means fastening with a bolt—a metal pin or bar: {bolting the door shut}. In gardening, bolting describes plants that shoot up prematurely to produce seeds, usually ruining the crop: {The lettuce is bolting in this heat}.

Bolts are threaded metal fasteners used with nuts to hold things together, or sliding bars that secure doors and windows. A bolt of lightning is a sudden discharge of electricity. A bolt of fabric is a roll. To bolt is to secure with a bolt, to run suddenly {The horse bolted}, or to eat quickly {He bolted his dinner}. Someone who {bolts upright} snaps suddenly to attention. To {make a bolt for} something is to dash toward it.

A bomb is primarily an explosive device, usually used as a weapon. The bomb is the atomic bomb, specifically in contexts of whether a country has one or not. As a verb, bomb means drop bombs on. All extended meanings of bomb reference the destructive nature of the core meaning and the inevitable negative result. A work of art or performance is a bomb when it fails spectacularly. By contrast, the slang expression da bomb characterizes something that is wildly successful or appealing: Her newest movie is really da bomb.

To bombard is to attack with artillery fire or bombs—a sustained assault: {Allied forces bombarded the fortifications for three days}. The word extends to any overwhelming barrage: bombarded with {questions}, bombarded with {emails}, bombarded with {information}. In physics, to bombard is to direct a stream of particles at a target.

Bombarded is the past tense of bombard, meaning to attack with artillery fire or explosives: {The city was bombarded for three days}. More commonly now, it describes being overwhelmed with a barrage of something—questions, requests, information, criticism: {She was bombarded with emails after the announcement}. The figurative sense suggests relentless, exhausting volume.

Bombardment is a sustained attack with artillery, bombs, or other projectiles: {The city endured weeks of bombardment}. By extension, any overwhelming barrage—of questions, criticism, information, or stimuli: {a bombardment of emails}, {the constant bombardment of advertising}. In physics, bombardment refers to directing particles at a target to study atomic structure.

Bombed means drunk or intoxicated: {We got completely bombed at the wedding reception}. The image suggests being hit hard, as if by explosives. In American slang, bombed also means failed spectacularly: {The movie bombed at the box office}. In British usage, bombed can mean moved very fast: {He bombed down the motorway}.

A bomber is a military aircraft designed to drop bombs on targets. The term extends to people: one who plants or detonates bombs {The bomber was caught on security footage}, or in American football, a quarterback known for long passes. A bomber jacket is a short, waist-length jacket originally worn by flight crews. In slang, bomber can mean a large marijuana cigarette or, in British usage, a strong beer or pill.

Bombers is the plural of bomber—an aircraft designed to drop bombs on targets, or a person who plants or delivers explosives. A bomber jacket is a short, waist-length jacket originally worn by military pilots. In American football slang, a bomber is a long pass: {He threw a few bombers in the fourth quarter}.

Bombing is an attack using explosive devices, whether from aircraft, planted charges, or suicide bombers: {The bombing killed dozens of civilians}. To bomb a place is to attack it this way. In informal speech, bombing means failing spectacularly—a comedian bombs when jokes don't land, a movie bombs at the box office. Conversely, in British slang, bombing can mean moving very fast: {He went bombing down the motorway}.

Bombs are explosive devices designed to detonate and cause destruction. The word extends to any spectacular failure: {The movie bombed at the box office}. In American slang, something that's {the bomb} is excellent—the opposite of bombing. To bomb is to attack with explosives, to fail badly, or to move very fast: {We bombed down the highway}. A bomb can also be a long forward pass in football.

A bombshell is a bomb dropped from an aircraft, though this literal sense has faded. The word now primarily means shocking or sensational news: {The resignation was a bombshell}, {drop a bombshell}. Since the mid-20th century, bombshell also describes a strikingly attractive woman, especially a blonde: {a blonde bombshell}, {She was a bombshell in that dress}.

Bombshells are bombs, especially large ones dropped from aircraft. The figurative sense dominates: a bombshell is shocking, unexpected news—a revelation that explodes into a situation: {The article dropped several bombshells about the mayor's finances}. A bombshell can also be a strikingly attractive woman, usually blonde: {a blonde bombshell}. This sense is dated but still understood.

A bonanza is a source of sudden wealth or good fortune—originally a rich vein of ore in mining: {They struck a bonanza in the hills}. The word now applies to any windfall or abundance: {The merger proved a bonanza for shareholders}, {a bonanza of new customers}. A bonanza episode in television is a special extended installment.

Bonbons are small candies, typically chocolates with soft centers—cream, fruit, or liqueur fillings coated in a chocolate shell. The word comes from French, where *bon* means good, so bonbons are doubly good. The term can extend to any fancy confection: {a box of bonbons}, {sitting around eating bonbons}. The latter phrase often carries a dismissive tone, implying idle indulgence.

Nearly all meanings of bond involve the idea of a binding connection between things. People can form bonds, and you can bond one object to another using glue. A bond is also a document recording a debt, and therefore one usually having some value for the bearer. An atomic or chemical bond is the force that stably binds atoms and molecules. If an arrestee bonds out, they are temporarily free through the purchase of a bail bond.

Bondage is the state of being bound—physically, legally, or figuratively. Historically it meant slavery or serfdom: {generations held in bondage}. The word now commonly refers to sexual practices involving restraint with ropes, chains, or other devices: {bondage and discipline}. Figuratively, anything that constrains freedom: {bondage to debt}, {bondage to addiction}.

Bonded describes things joined or secured together. Materials are bonded with adhesive; atoms bond chemically. People who are bonded share a close emotional connection: {The team bonded over shared hardship}. In commerce, bonded goods are held in a customs warehouse until duties are paid. A bonded employee is covered by insurance against dishonesty or failure to perform: {bonded contractors}, {bonded warehouse}.

Bonding is the process of forming a close connection—between people, animals, or materials. Parent-child bonding happens in early infancy. {Team-building exercises are supposed to encourage bonding}. In chemistry, bonding describes how atoms link to form molecules. In construction, bonding joins materials: {dental bonding}, {adhesive bonding}. The common thread is attachment that holds things together.

Bonds are things that tie, fasten, or unite. A bond can be a physical restraint {(the prisoner's bonds)}, a chemical connection between atoms, or an emotional tie {(the bond between mother and child)}. In finance, bonds are debt securities—loans to governments or corporations that pay interest over time: {She invested in municipal bonds}. To bond is to form a close connection: {The teammates bonded during training camp}. (Capitalized Bonds typically refers to the baseball player or the fictional spy.)

A bone is the hard tissue forming the skeleton: {He broke a bone in his arm}. {The dog chewed on a bone}. Bone extends to material made from bone ({bone china}), the essence of something ({bone of contention}, {bone to pick}), and to dice (originally made of bone). As a verb, to bone means to remove bones from meat or fish: {Bone the chicken before roasting}. In slang, to bone is to have sex: {They boned in the guest room}. To bone up means to study intensively: {I need to bone up on my French}.

A bonehead is a stupid person—someone whose skull seems solid bone with no room for brains. The word functions as mild insult or affectionate ribbing: {Don't be such a bonehead}. As an adjective, bonehead describes foolish actions: {a bonehead mistake}, {a bonehead play}. The tone is usually more exasperated than vicious.

Boneheaded means stupid or foolish, suggesting someone whose skull is solid bone with no room for brains. It describes decisions or actions that lack basic common sense: {a boneheaded mistake}, {That was a boneheaded thing to say}. The word carries exasperation more than malice—you call someone boneheaded when they should have known better.

Boneheads is the plural of bonehead—a stupid person, someone whose skull seems filled with bone rather than brain. The word is mildly insulting but rarely taken as fighting words: {Those boneheads left the gate open and the dog got out}. A bonehead play or bonehead move is a foolish mistake.

Boneless describes meat or fish with bones removed: {boneless chicken thighs}, {boneless salmon fillet}. The word extends to anything lacking structural support or firmness—a boneless handshake feels limp and weak. In internet slang, boneless became an absurdist modifier meaning "without," spawning jokes like "boneless pizza" (no crust) or "boneless water" (nothing removed, just surreal).

Bones is the plural of bone—skeletal parts, dice, or the body generally: {I feel it in my bones}. {Roll them bones}. {The archaeologists found bones in the cave}. As a verb, bones means removes bones from meat: {She bones the fish before grilling}.

A boneyard is a place where bones accumulate—originally a cemetery, now more often a storage area for discarded vehicles, machinery, or aircraft: {rows of decommissioned planes baking in the desert boneyard}. In dominoes, the boneyard is the pile of undrawn tiles. The word carries a sense of abandonment and decay.

A bonfire is a large outdoor fire, typically built for celebration, warmth, or burning waste. Bonfires mark occasions like Guy Fawkes Night, beach parties, and homecoming rallies. The word originally meant a fire for burning bones. {We gathered around the bonfire to roast marshmallows.}

Bonfires is the plural of bonfire—a large outdoor fire built for celebration, warmth, or disposal. Bonfires mark occasions like Guy Fawkes Night, beach parties, or autumn gatherings: {We roasted marshmallows over the bonfire}. They also serve practical purposes, burning yard waste or brush. The word evokes communal gathering around open flames.

A bong is a water pipe used for smoking cannabis or tobacco. Smoke passes through water before inhalation, cooling it and filtering some particulates. The word imitates the bubbling sound the device makes. As a verb, to bong is to smoke from one: {We bonged a few bowls before the movie}. Separately, bong is the deep resonant sound of a large bell.

Bongos are a pair of small drums of different sizes, joined together and played with the hands. They originated in Cuba and became standard in Latin jazz and popular music. The drums are held between the knees or mounted on a stand: {She tapped out a rhythm on the bongos}. Separately, a bongo is a large African antelope with white stripes.

Bongos are a pair of small drums of different sizes, joined together and played with the hands. They originated in Cuba and appear prominently in Latin music, jazz, and percussion ensembles. The player typically holds them between the knees: {She kept rhythm on the bongos while he played guitar}.

Bonk is a verb and noun representing the sound of a solid impact—something hitting something else with a dull thud. You might bonk your head on a low doorframe or bonk someone playfully with a pillow. In British slang, bonk is a mildly vulgar term for sexual intercourse: {They had a bonk in the back seat}. Cyclists and runners use bonk to describe hitting a wall of exhaustion when glycogen stores are depleted: {I bonked at mile twenty}.

Bonkers means crazy or mad, used informally and usually without serious clinical implications: {The whole plan sounds bonkers}, {She went bonkers when she found out}. British in origin but widely used. The tone is typically playful rather than harsh—you might call a friend's idea bonkers without real insult.

A bonnet is a hat that ties under the chin, traditionally worn by women and children. The style varies from close-fitting caps to wide-brimmed sun bonnets: {a baby's bonnet}, {pioneer women in calico bonnets}. In British English, the bonnet is the hood of a car—the hinged cover over the engine compartment. To have a {bee in your bonnet} is to be preoccupied with an idea, often obsessively.

Bonsai is the Japanese art of growing miniature trees in shallow containers, using careful pruning and training to create aesthetically pleasing shapes that mimic full-sized trees in nature. The word also refers to trees cultivated this way: {a bonsai juniper}, {Her collection includes several bonsai}. The practice requires years of patient attention to produce gnarled, ancient-looking specimens only inches tall.

A bonus is something extra beyond what's expected or required. In employment, it's additional pay beyond regular salary, often tied to performance or holidays: {year-end bonus}, {signing bonus}. The word extends to any pleasant extra: {The view from the room was a bonus}. As an adjective, bonus describes something additional or unexpectedly good: {bonus points}, {bonus feature}.

Bony describes something characterized by prominent bones or a skeletal quality. A bony person or animal is thin enough that their bones are visible or easily felt beneath the skin. The word also applies to things made of or resembling bone, or to meat that has many bones in it: {The fish was too bony to enjoy}. A bony {finger} or bony {hand} suggests gauntness, age, or a skeletal appearance that can seem eerie or frail.

Boo has two main uses, often distinguishable by pronunciation. When uttered loudly and quickly, it is used to frighten or startle someone. When pronounced with a prolonged vowel it’s a sign of disapproval or rejection.

A boob has two meanings that occasionally collide. A boob is a foolish person or a stupid mistake: {Don't be such a boob}. {I made a real boob of myself}. This sense is somewhat dated. More commonly now, boob is informal slang for a breast: {Her boob popped out of her dress}. The plural boobs refers to breasts generally. The foolish-person sense came first; the breast sense emerged mid-20th century, possibly from booby (a stupid person, also a seabird).

Boobies is the plural of booby—seabirds, stupid people, or childish slang for breasts: {Look at the blue-footed boobies}. {She flashed her boobies at the camera}. The breast sense is playful and relatively mild.

A booboo is a minor injury, especially a child's scrape or bruise: {Let me kiss your booboo and make it better}. By extension, a booboo is a small mistake or blunder: {I made a booboo on the report}. The word belongs to baby talk and casual speech. Also spelled boo-boo.

Boobs is informal slang for breasts: {Nice boobs}. The word is vulgar but less crude than tits—casual and common in everyday speech. Boobs can also mean stupid mistakes or foolish people, though this usage is fading: {Those boobs in accounting lost the paperwork}.

A booby is a tropical seabird known for its clumsy appearance and trusting nature—easy to catch, hence the name from Spanish bobo (stupid). Booby also means a stupid person: {You booby, you fell for it}. A booby prize is given mockingly to the last-place finisher. A booby trap is a hidden trap for unsuspecting victims. In slang, booby is a childish term for a breast, usually plural: {baby sucking on mommy's booby}.

A boobytrap is a hidden device designed to harm or surprise someone who triggers it unknowingly—a grenade rigged to a door, a bucket balanced to fall on whoever enters. The word extends to any concealed hazard or trick: {The contract was boobytrapped with hidden fees}. As a verb, to boobytrap is to set such a device: {They boobytrapped the abandoned building}.

Booger is nasal mucus, especially a dried piece picked from the nose. The word is mildly vulgar and associated with childhood: {Don't wipe your boogers on the couch}. Booger can also be an affectionate term for a child or pet: {Come here, you little booger}.

Boogers are dried or semi-dried nasal mucus, the crusty bits you pick from your nose. The word is mildly crude but standard among children and in casual speech: {Stop picking your boogers}. Booger can also be an affectionate term for a small child, especially a mischievous one: {Come here, you little booger}.

A boogeyman is an imaginary monster used to frighten children into good behavior: {The boogeyman will get you if you don't go to sleep}. More broadly, it refers to any object of irrational fear or a scapegoat blamed for problems: {Inflation has become the boogeyman of economic policy}. Also spelled bogeyman.

Boogie began as a style of blues piano playing with a driving, repetitive bass pattern—boogie-woogie. From there it became a verb meaning to dance, especially to rock or disco music: {Let's boogie}. In casual speech, to boogie also means to leave or move quickly: {We'd better boogie if we want to make the movie}. A boogie can be a piece of nasal mucus, though that's usually spelled booger.

A boogieman is a frightening creature invoked to scare children into good behavior—a monster in the closet, under the bed, or lurking in the dark. The word extends to any feared person or thing used as a threat: {The tax man has become the boogieman of small business owners}. Also spelled bogeyman or boogeyman.

Boohoo imitates the sound of loud, exaggerated crying—sobbing with theatrical tears. It often carries a mocking or dismissive tone, suggesting the crying is overdone or unwarranted: {Oh, boohoo, you didn't get your way}. As a verb, to boohoo is to cry noisily: {She boohooed for an hour after the breakup}.

Booing is the act of making a prolonged "boo" sound to express disapproval or contempt, typically directed at performers, speakers, or athletes: {The booing started as soon as he took the stage}. Crowds boo to signal displeasure collectively, making it a public form of rejection that's hard to ignore.

A book is a collection of text designed for human hands. Whether books are printed on paper or read on a tablet, their intended use provides practical limits on their dimensions. Even if books printed on paper become rare one day, the high frequency of the word book is unlikely to change because it represents a very successful, time-tested method of gathering together information on a topic and collecting it in one place for ease of access. The noun book is much older than the thing it designates today but the verb book did not come into use until much later. All of its meanings preserve the idea of recording or registering the name of a person or thing in a book for a purpose: Have you booked accommodations for your vacation yet?

A bookcase is a piece of furniture with shelves for storing books. Bookcases range from small freestanding units to built-in floor-to-ceiling installations. The word applies whether the case has doors or not: {The lawyer's office had glass-fronted bookcases along every wall}.

Booked means reserved or scheduled in advance: {The restaurant is fully booked}, {I'm booked solid all week}. In law enforcement, to book someone is to formally record their arrest at a police station: {He was booked on assault charges}. In British slang, a player who gets booked receives a yellow card from the referee.

Bookends are supports placed at either end of a row of books to keep them upright on a shelf. They come in pairs, which gives rise to the figurative use: things that bookend something frame it at beginning and end: {Two anthems bookended the ceremony}. Events or items that match or mirror each other may be called bookends: {The twins were bookends—one on each side of their mother}.

Bookends are L-shaped supports placed at either end of a row of books to keep them upright on a shelf. By extension, bookends refers to a matching pair of things that frame something between them: {The two home runs were bookends to an otherwise forgettable game}. As a verb, to bookend is to bracket or frame: {Two guitar solos bookend the album}.

A bookie is someone who takes bets on events, especially horse races and sporting contests, and pays out winnings. The term is informal shorthand for bookmaker. Bookies set odds, accept wagers, and manage the risk of paying out more than they collect. While legal sportsbooks now operate openly in many places, bookie still carries associations with illegal gambling operations. {My uncle's bookie got arrested last week.}

Bookies is the plural of bookie, an informal term for a bookmaker—someone who takes bets on races, games, or other events and pays out winnings. The word carries a slightly shady connotation, evoking backroom gambling operations: {He owed money to bookies all over town}. In places where sports betting is legal, bookies operate openly.

A booking is a reservation or arrangement made in advance—for a hotel room, flight, restaurant table, or performance: {I made a booking for two nights}. In entertainment, a booking is a scheduled engagement: {The band has three bookings this weekend}. In law enforcement, booking is the process of formally recording an arrest at a police station, including fingerprints and photographs.

Bookish describes someone devoted to reading and study, often with a suggestion of being more comfortable with books than with people or practical matters. A bookish {child} prefers the library to the playground. The word can be affectionate or slightly dismissive, depending on context: {She was bookish and shy}, {His bookish manner seemed out of place at the construction site}. Bookish language or style is overly literary or formal for the situation.

A bookkeeper is a person who records financial transactions and maintains accounts for a business. The work involves tracking income, expenses, payroll, and invoices—the day-to-day monetary activity that accountants later analyze or audit. {She hired a bookkeeper to handle the shop's finances.} The word is notable for having three consecutive pairs of double letters.

Bookkeeping is the systematic recording of financial transactions—tracking money coming in and going out of a business or organization. A bookkeeper maintains ledgers, reconciles accounts, and ensures records are accurate and current. Bookkeeping provides the raw data that accountants later analyze. {She handles the bookkeeping for three small businesses.}

A bookmaker is a person or business that sets odds and accepts bets on sporting events, elections, and other outcomes. The bookmaker profits by setting odds that ensure a margin regardless of results. In Britain, bookmakers operate legally in betting shops; in the US, the term often implies illegal gambling operations. Also called a bookie.

Bookmakers are people or businesses that set odds and accept bets on sporting events, elections, and other outcomes. They profit by adjusting odds to ensure a margin regardless of results. In British English, {the bookmakers} or {the bookies} refers to betting shops: {I'm popping down to the bookmakers to put a fiver on the match}. In publishing, a bookmaker is simply someone who makes books—a printer or publisher—though this sense is now rare.

Bookmaking is the business of accepting and paying out bets, especially on horse races and sporting events. A bookmaker (or bookie) sets odds and takes wagers, profiting from the margin between payouts. {He ran an illegal bookmaking operation out of the back room.} Separately, bookmaking can mean the craft of physically producing books—binding, printing, and design—though this sense is less common.

A bookmark is a strip of paper, ribbon, or other material placed between pages to mark one's place in a book. The word extends to saved links in web browsers—digital markers for returning to specific pages: {I bookmarked that article to read later}. To bookmark something is to save its location for future reference.

Bookmarking is the act of saving a location for easy return—originally by placing a physical marker in a book, now most commonly by saving a webpage or digital content for later access. In browsers, bookmarking a site adds it to a personal list so you don't have to remember or retype the URL. {I've been bookmarking recipes all week.} The term extends to any system that lets users flag content for future reference, from social media posts to streaming queues.

Bookmarks are markers placed in a book to save your spot—a ribbon, slip of paper, or dedicated strip. The term extends to saved links in a web browser, letting you return to pages without retyping addresses. To bookmark something is to mark it for later: {I bookmarked that article to read on the train}.

Books are bound collections of written or printed pages, the primary vessel for storing and transmitting knowledge, stories, and ideas across time. A book may be a novel, a manual, a religious text, or a record of accounts. To book something is to reserve it: {I booked a table for eight}. The books are financial records: {cooking the books}, {on the books}. To {throw the book at} someone is to prosecute or punish them severely. {By the book} means following rules exactly.

A bookshelf is a piece of furniture with horizontal surfaces for storing books. The term applies whether freestanding or mounted on a wall, and whether holding books or other items: {The bookshelf was cluttered with photos and knickknacks}. A bookshelf may have one shelf or many.

A bookshop is a retail store that sells books. The term is more common in British English, where Americans typically say bookstore. Both words describe the same thing—from small independent shops to large chains: {I found a first edition at a bookshop in London}.

A bookstore is a retail shop that sells books. The word distinguishes such establishments from libraries, which lend rather than sell. Large chain bookstores often include cafés and sell gifts, stationery, and music alongside books. An independent bookstore is locally owned rather than part of a chain: {I found it at a used bookstore downtown}.

A bookworm is someone who reads constantly and voraciously, often preferring books to social activities: {She's such a bookworm—always has her nose in a novel}. The term comes from larvae that bore through book bindings and pages, though it's now used almost exclusively for devoted readers. The connotation is gentle teasing rather than criticism.

Bookworms are people who read voraciously and enthusiastically, often preferring books to social activities: {She's a real bookworm—always has her nose in a novel}. The term comes from the larvae of various insects that bore through and damage books, though calling someone a bookworm is affectionate rather than critical.

The commonest use of boom is a noun denoting something sudden and massive – either a sound (we heard a loud boom and saw smoke) or very rapid growth (housing boom, stock boom). If something booms, it increases very rapidly or makes a loud sound. A different boom is a horizontal bar with various functions in shipping, construction, or audio engineering. To lower the boom is to initiate some form of punishment.

A boombox is a large portable stereo with built-in speakers, popular in the 1980s for playing cassette tapes and radio at high volume. The name suggests both the bass-heavy sound and the box-like shape. Boomboxes became icons of hip-hop culture, carried on shoulders through city streets: {He walked down the block with a boombox blasting}.

Boomer is informal for baby boomer—someone born during the post-World War II birth surge, roughly 1946 to 1964. The term often carries generational tension: younger speakers use it dismissively to characterize attitudes seen as outdated or self-satisfied. {OK boomer} became a viral retort to patronizing advice. Separately, a boomer is a large male kangaroo.

A boomerang is a curved throwing stick, originally an Aboriginal Australian weapon and tool. Some boomerangs are designed to return to the thrower when thrown correctly—these became popular as toys and sporting equipment. Figuratively, something boomerangs when it comes back to harm the person who initiated it: {His attack ads boomeranged when voters turned against the negativity}.

Boomerangs are curved throwing sticks, originally Aboriginal Australian weapons. Some are designed to return to the thrower when they miss their target—the feature that defines the word's figurative use. When something boomerangs, it comes back to affect its originator: {His criticism boomeranged when voters turned against him}. A boomerang effect is an unintended consequence that harms the person who caused it.

Boomers is informal shorthand for baby boomers—the generation born roughly 1946–1964, during the post-World War II population surge. The term often carries generational tension, especially when younger speakers use it dismissively: {OK boomer} became a catchphrase for brushing off attitudes perceived as out of touch. In Australian slang, a boomer is also a large male kangaroo.

Booming describes deep, resonant, loud sounds—thunder, cannons, a booming voice. The word extends to rapid, vigorous growth: a booming economy, booming sales, a booming population. A boom town grows explosively, usually around a resource discovery. {Business is booming.} The two senses connect through the idea of forceful expansion.

A boomtown is a town or city experiencing rapid growth, typically due to sudden economic opportunity—a gold strike, oil discovery, or new industry. The term captures both explosive expansion and its precariousness: {The mining boomtown doubled in population every six months}. Many boomtowns become ghost towns when the resource depletes or the industry moves on.

A boon is a benefit or blessing, something helpful or welcome: {The new highway was a boon to local businesses}. The word carries a slightly formal or literary tone. A boon companion is a close friend you enjoy spending time with, especially in convivial pursuits—though this phrase is now old-fashioned.

Boondocks refers to remote, rural, or undeveloped areas far from urban centers—the middle of nowhere. The word comes from Tagalog *bundok* (mountain), brought back by American soldiers from the Philippines. It often carries connotations of isolation or backwardness: {They live way out in the boondocks}. Usually shortened to {the boonies} in casual speech.

A boondoggle is a project that wastes time and money, especially one funded by taxpayers: {The new stadium was dismissed as a billion-dollar boondoggle}. Originally American slang for trivial handcraft work, it now typically describes government programs or infrastructure projects critics consider pointless or corrupt. The verb means to waste resources on such projects.

The boonies are remote, rural areas far from cities or civilization—short for boondocks. The term carries connotations of isolation and lack of amenities: {We had to drive out to the boonies to find the cabin}. Originally U.S. military slang from the Philippines, it now appears in casual American speech whenever someone means the middle of nowhere.

Boop is a playful sound made when lightly touching someone's nose, or the gentle tap itself: {She booped the cat on the nose}. The word is onomatopoeic and affectionate, common in interactions with pets, babies, or loved ones. Online, boop often accompanies images of animals being touched on the snout.

Boost means to lift, raise, or increase. You might boost someone over a fence, boost sales figures, or boost morale. A boost is the lift itself—a helping push upward or forward: {The good reviews gave the film a boost}. In informal use, to boost something is to steal it, especially by shoplifting. A booster amplifies or supports: a rocket booster, a signal booster, a booster shot.

Boosted is the past tense of boost, meaning lifted, increased, or enhanced: {Sales were boosted by the holiday season}, {The coach's speech boosted morale}. In contemporary slang, boosted means stolen, especially shoplifted: {He got caught with boosted merchandise}. In gaming and online contexts, boosted describes an account or player whose rank was artificially inflated, often by paying someone else to play: {That guy's definitely boosted—he can't even aim}.

A booster is something that increases or amplifies. A booster {shot} reinforces immunity from an earlier vaccination. A booster {seat} raises a child to proper height. A booster {rocket} provides extra thrust at launch. A booster can also be an enthusiastic supporter: {community boosters}, {team boosters}. In slang, a booster is a shoplifter, especially one who steals for resale.

Boosters are things or people that increase, support, or amplify something. A {booster shot} reinforces immunity from an earlier vaccination. {Booster seats} raise children to proper height. Campaign boosters are enthusiastic supporters who promote a cause or candidate. Rocket boosters provide extra thrust during launch. The word suggests augmentation—adding power, height, protection, or enthusiasm to what already exists.

The foot covering that extends up the leg gives rise to nearly all common meanings of boot. To kick forcefully or to eject (whether you’re wearing boots or not) is to boot. When you do this, you have given someone or something the boot. To start up a computer is to boot it. If you boot a car, however, you have immobilized it using a Denver boot. In British English, the rear storage area in a car is called the boot.

A bootcamp is an intensive, short-term training program. The term comes from military basic training camps known for rigorous physical conditioning and strict discipline. Now bootcamp commonly describes accelerated programs in coding, fitness, or other skills: {She learned Python at a twelve-week bootcamp}. The format emphasizes immersion and rapid results over traditional pacing. Also spelled boot camp.

Bootcamps are intensive, short-term training programs designed to teach specific skills quickly. Originally military basic training—grueling physical and mental conditioning for new recruits—the term now most commonly refers to accelerated courses in coding, data science, or other technical fields: {She enrolled in a twelve-week coding bootcamp}. Fitness bootcamps apply the same philosophy to exercise: high-intensity, structured workouts with drill-sergeant energy.

A booth is a small enclosed or semi-enclosed space for a specific purpose: a phone booth, a voting booth, a ticket booth, a photo booth. At restaurants, a booth is a seating arrangement with high-backed benches facing each other across a table: {We asked for a booth instead of a table}. At fairs and conventions, vendors and exhibitors set up booths to display their goods.

Bootleg refers to goods that are made, distributed, or sold illegally—typically alcohol during Prohibition, but now more commonly recordings, software, or other media produced without authorization. As a verb, to bootleg is to make or traffic in such goods: {He bootlegged concert recordings in the '90s}. The adjective describes anything unauthorized or illicit: {bootleg whiskey}, {bootleg copies of the album}. In American football, a bootleg is a deceptive play where the quarterback fakes a handoff and runs with the ball hidden against his leg.

Bootlegged describes something produced, distributed, or sold illegally—originally liquor during Prohibition, now most often recordings, software, or other copyrighted material: {bootlegged concert recordings}, {a bootlegged copy of the album}. The word suggests unauthorized reproduction rather than outright theft, often with a hint of underground appeal.

A bootlegger is someone who makes, transports, or sells illegal goods—originally liquor during Prohibition, when smugglers supposedly hid flasks in their boot legs. The term now applies to anyone dealing in contraband or unauthorized copies: {bootlegger whiskey}, {a bootlegger selling pirated DVDs}. The verb is bootleg; the activity is bootlegging.

Bootleggers are people who make, transport, or sell illegal goods—originally and especially liquor during Prohibition. The term comes from smugglers hiding flasks in their boot legs. The meaning extends to anyone trafficking in contraband or unauthorized copies: {bootleggers selling pirated DVDs}. The verb is bootleg; the adjective describes illicit goods: {bootleg whiskey}, {bootleg recordings}.

Bootlegging is the illegal production, distribution, or sale of goods—originally and especially liquor. The term became prominent during Prohibition in the United States, when smugglers concealed flasks in their boot legs. Today it extends to unauthorized recordings, pirated software, or any contraband trade: {bootlegging concert footage}, {a bootlegging operation for knockoff handbags}.

Bootlegs are unauthorized copies or recordings, especially of music, film, or other media. The term comes from the practice of hiding contraband in tall boots. A bootleg concert recording captures a live performance without official permission, while bootleg merchandise copies trademarked designs. As a verb, to bootleg means to produce or distribute such unauthorized goods. {I found some rare bootlegs from their 1975 tour.} The word also appears in American football, where a bootleg play involves the quarterback faking a handoff and running with the ball hidden against his hip.

To bootlick is to behave obsequiously toward someone in power, flattering and fawning to gain favor. A bootlicker is someone who does this habitually—the image is of someone so servile they'd lick another person's boots clean. {He bootlicked his way to a promotion.} The term is always contemptuous.

A bootlicker is someone who flatters or fawns over people in power to gain favor—the image being someone so servile they'd literally lick another's boots. The term is always contemptuous: {He's nothing but a bootlicker for management}. The verb bootlick and noun bootlicking share this meaning of obsequious behavior toward authority.

Bootlickers are people who behave obsequiously toward those in power, seeking favor through excessive flattery and compliance. The term is contemptuous—it suggests someone so eager to please authority that they would literally lick boots clean: {The boss surrounded himself with bootlickers who never challenged his ideas}. The singular bootlicker and verb bootlick follow the same pattern.

Bootlicking is excessive flattery or subservience toward someone in power, motivated by self-interest. A bootlicker debases themselves to curry favor: {The promotion went to the biggest bootlicker in the department}. The image is of someone so eager to please that they'd literally lick another's boots. The verb bootlick and noun bootlicker follow naturally.

Boots are footwear that covers the foot and extends up the leg, typically to the ankle or higher. Work boots protect; fashion boots adorn; cowboy boots signal a style. To boot up a computer is to start it—from bootstrap, the loop used to pull boots on. {Too big for your boots} means arrogant. To get the boot is to be fired or rejected. {Boots on the ground} means deployed military personnel.

Bootstrap originally meant the loop at the back of a boot used to pull it on. The phrase {pull yourself up by your bootstraps} described an impossible feat—lifting yourself off the ground by tugging your own boots—making it useful for ironic commentary on self-reliance rhetoric. In computing, to bootstrap or boot is to start up a system using a small program that loads larger programs. More broadly, bootstrapping means starting something with minimal resources: {She bootstrapped the company from her garage}. The adjective describes self-starting processes or self-funded ventures: {a bootstrap startup}.

Bootstrapping is starting something using only existing resources, without external help. The image comes from the impossible task of pulling yourself up by your own bootstraps. In computing, bootstrapping (or booting) is a system starting itself by loading progressively more complex programs. In business, bootstrapping means building a company without outside investment: {We bootstrapped the startup from our garage}. In statistics, bootstrapping generates data by resampling from an existing dataset.

Bootstraps are the loops or tabs attached to the sides of boots, used to pull them on. The phrase {pull yourself up by your bootstraps} originally described an impossible act—you can't lift yourself off the ground by tugging your own footwear. The meaning has shifted: now it typically means to succeed through one's own effort without outside help, often with political overtones about self-reliance versus systemic support. In computing, to bootstrap (or boot) is to start up a system, the machine metaphorically pulling itself into operation.

Booty is plunder taken in war or by pirates—treasure seized by force. The word extends to any valuable haul: {They made off with the booty}. In slang, booty means buttocks, especially an attractive one: {She's got a nice booty}. This sense dominates contemporary usage, appearing in music, dance, and casual speech. A {booty call} is a late-night summons for casual sex.

Booze is alcoholic drink, or the act of drinking it. The word is casual and often implies excess: {We bought some booze for the party}, {He's been boozing all night}. A boozer is a heavy drinker or, in British slang, a pub. Boozy describes something characterized by alcohol: {a boozy brunch}, {boozy breath}.

A boozehound is someone who drinks alcohol excessively—a habitual heavy drinker. The term is informal and mildly humorous, suggesting someone who pursues alcohol with a dog's single-minded determination: {My uncle was a real boozehound back in his younger days}. Less harsh than alcoholic but more pointed than social drinker.

Boozing is drinking alcohol, usually to excess. The word implies sustained or heavy consumption rather than a single drink: {We spent the weekend boozing with old friends}. A boozer is someone who drinks heavily, or in British English, a pub.

Boozy describes something characterized by alcohol or drunkenness. A boozy {brunch} features plenty of drinks. A boozy {night out} involves heavy drinking. The word is casual and often affectionate rather than disapproving—it suggests cheerful indulgence more than problem drinking. A person who is boozy has had a few too many.

Bop works as both verb and noun for a quick, light hit: {She bopped him on the head with a rolled-up newspaper}. To bop somewhere is to go casually or aimlessly: {We bopped around town all afternoon}. Bop is also short for bebop, the improvisational jazz style that emerged in the 1940s. A bop, in recent slang, is a song that really hits—an undeniable jam: {This track is a bop}.

A border is a line or edge marking where one thing ends and another begins. Countries share borders; a garden has a border of flowers. Border can describe the area near such a line: {border town}, {border patrol}. To border something is to share an edge with it or to come close: {His comments bordered on insult}. To border something is also to put an edge around it: {bordered by hedges}.

Borderline marks the boundary between two conditions or categories, often implying uncertainty about which side something falls on. A borderline {case} could go either way. Borderline {acceptable} means barely acceptable, hovering at the threshold. In psychiatry, borderline personality disorder is a specific diagnosis involving emotional instability and impulsive behavior—but casual use of borderline simply means on the edge: {His behavior was borderline obsessive}.

Borders are boundary lines separating territories—countries, states, or regions: {The river forms the border between the two nations}. The verb means to share such a boundary: {Mexico borders the United States}. Something that borders on a quality approaches it: {His confidence borders on arrogance}. A border can also be a decorative edge or frame: {a floral border on the tablecloth}.

The busy word b-o-r-e has three main jobs. One noun and verb are about making holes: When the beetle bored into the wood, the bore was small. If you bore someone, you are a bore, and it’s because you fail at being engaging or interesting. Finally, bore is the past tense of the verb bear: She bore her last child at the age of 41.

Bored describes a state of restless dissatisfaction from lack of interest or stimulation. You might be bored with a tedious lecture, bored by small talk, or simply bored because nothing is happening: {I'm so bored I could scream}. The adverb stiff intensifies it: {bored stiff}. Boredom often prompts seeking distraction or mischief.

Boredom is the restless, dissatisfied state of having nothing interesting to do or engage with. It implies a mismatch between desire for stimulation and available activity: {The lecture filled me with boredom}. Boredom can be temporary or chronic, and is often treated as something to escape: {I took up knitting out of sheer boredom}.

Boring describes something that fails to hold attention or interest. A boring lecture drags on without engaging the audience. A boring person has nothing interesting to say. The word comes from bore, to weary by dullness—unrelated to bore meaning to drill a hole, though being bored feels like having your patience slowly worn away. {The movie was so boring I fell asleep.}

Born is the past participle of bear in its sense of giving birth: {She was born in 1985}. It describes coming into existence or originating: {born of necessity}, {a star is born}. As an adjective, born indicates natural aptitude: {a born leader}, {a born musician}. The spelling borne applies to other senses of bear—carried, endured, produced: {airborne}, {mosquito-borne diseases}.

A borough is an administrative division of a city or town, or in some cases, an incorporated municipality. New York City's five boroughs—Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island—are the most familiar American example. In Alaska, boroughs function like counties elsewhere. British boroughs are towns with special charters or parliamentary representation.

To borrow is to take something with the understanding you'll return it: {Can I borrow your car?} You borrow money from a bank, books from a library, ideas from other thinkers. The borrower receives; the lender gives. Languages borrow words from each other, adopting foreign terms into native use. In arithmetic, borrowing moves value from one column to another during subtraction. {Living on borrowed time} means surviving beyond what was expected.

Borrowed describes something taken temporarily with the intention to return it: {a borrowed car}, {borrowed money}. The word extends to things adopted from elsewhere—borrowed words enter English from other languages, borrowed ideas come from other thinkers. {Living on borrowed time} means surviving beyond when death seemed likely. The past tense of borrow.

A borrower is someone who receives something with the understanding they'll return it or pay it back. Most often the word appears in financial contexts: a borrower takes out a loan and owes repayment to a lender. {The bank requires borrowers to provide proof of income.} More casually, a borrower is anyone who temporarily takes something belonging to another: {She's a chronic borrower of other people's phone chargers.}

Borrowing is taking something with the expectation of returning it: {Can I get a borrowing of your ladder?} More commonly, borrowing refers to the act itself rather than the thing borrowed. In linguistics, a borrowing is a word adopted from another language—*café* from French, *kindergarten* from German. Financial borrowing means taking on debt: {The company's borrowing has increased significantly}.

Borscht is a beet soup from Eastern Europe, particularly associated with Ukrainian and Russian cuisine. The deep red broth typically contains cabbage, potatoes, and meat, served hot or cold with a dollop of sour cream. {We had borscht and black bread for lunch.} The Borscht Belt was a region of Jewish resort hotels in New York's Catskill Mountains, named for the soup commonly served there.

Borsht is a beetroot soup from Eastern Europe, especially associated with Russian and Ukrainian cuisines. The soup typically has a deep red color from the beets and is often served with sour cream. Spelling varies: borscht, borsch, and borsht all appear in English. The {Borscht Belt} was a cluster of Catskills resorts popular with Jewish vacationers from the 1920s through the 1960s.

Bosom is the human chest, especially a woman's breasts or the area between them. It suggests warmth and intimacy—to hold someone {to your bosom} is to embrace them closely. A {bosom friend} is an intimate companion, close to your heart. The bosom of something is its innermost part: {the bosom of the family}, {the bosom of the church}. As an adjective, it means cherished or intimate: {bosom buddy}.

The commonest use of boss is as a noun to denote a person in charge. That person bosses others around, though you can do that without actually being a boss – and thereby make yourself unpopular and bossy. A different word boss is related to the verb emboss and denotes various things that stick out from their surroundings. Boss is also a dated slang adjective used appreciatively: Last night’s concert was totally boss.
