Bosses is the plural of boss—people in charge of workers or organizations: {She's had three bosses in two years}. The verb form means to give orders, often with around: {Stop bossing me around}. In architecture and design, bosses are decorative raised knobs or studs on surfaces like ceilings or shields.

Bossy describes someone who gives orders in a domineering way, often without the authority to do so: {Stop being so bossy}. The word typically characterizes children or, controversially, women—critics note that assertive men are rarely called bossy. A bossy person wants to control others rather than collaborate with them.

A bot is a software program that performs automated tasks, especially on the internet. Bots index websites for search engines, moderate chat rooms, or execute rapid trades. In gaming and social media, bot often carries a negative connotation—either a fake account spreading spam or propaganda, or an insult suggesting someone plays with mechanical incompetence: {You're such a bot}. The word comes from robot.

A botanist is a scientist who studies plants, including their structure, growth, classification, and ecological relationships. The field encompasses everything from microscopic cellular processes to large-scale forest ecosystems. {The botanist spent years cataloging rare orchid species in the Amazon.} Botanists work in settings ranging from university laboratories to botanical gardens to remote wilderness areas.

To botch is to bungle or spoil through poor work or clumsiness: {He botched the repair job}. A botch is the ruined result itself—a mess made of something that should have been done properly. The word often implies carelessness rather than incompetence: {The surgery was botched}. A botch job is shoddy work.

Botched describes something badly done or bungled, especially a task requiring skill: {a botched surgery}, {a botched robbery}. The word implies failure through incompetence rather than bad luck—someone attempted something and made a mess of it. As a verb, to botch is to ruin through poor execution: {They botched the repair job}.

Botching is doing something badly or clumsily, ruining it through poor workmanship or careless mistakes. A botched {surgery} goes wrong. A botched {robbery} fails due to incompetence. The word implies the job could have been done right but wasn't: {They're botching the renovation—nothing is level}.

Though it is unrelated to the word two, both, whether used as a pronoun, conjunction, or adjective, always has the idea of two behind it. It means, essentially, one and the other. The things designated can be concrete (We need both cars tonight) or abstract (I found the lecture both provocative and entertaining). When not followed by the things it designates, both can refer back to recent nouns to group them together: I told Mom and Dad and both were really excited.

Bother covers a range of mild irritation and inconvenience. To bother someone is to annoy or disturb them: {Sorry to bother you, but do you have a minute?} Something that bothers you causes low-grade distress: {It bothers me that he never apologized}. As a noun, a bother is a nuisance or hassle: {Parallel parking is such a bother}. To not bother doing something is to skip the effort: {Don't bother calling—I'll be asleep}. The British exclamation {Bother!} expresses mild frustration.

Bothered describes being troubled, annoyed, or put to inconvenience. If you're bothered by something, it disturbs your peace of mind: {The noise really bothered me}. To say you {can't be bothered} means you lack the motivation or willingness to make the effort: {I can't be bothered to cook tonight}. In British slang, {I'm not bothered} expresses indifference.

Botox is a brand name for botulinum toxin, a neurotoxic protein used in cosmetic procedures to reduce wrinkles by temporarily paralyzing facial muscles. The term has become genericized to refer to any such injection: {She gets botox every few months}. Beyond cosmetics, it treats medical conditions like migraines, muscle spasms, and excessive sweating. As a verb, to botox means to inject with the substance: {Her forehead looks botoxed}. (Capitalized Botox is the trademark.)

Bots are automated software programs that perform tasks without human intervention. Internet bots crawl websites, answer customer queries, or post spam. In gaming, bots are computer-controlled opponents: {I practiced against bots before playing online}. Bot also refers to the larva of a botfly, a parasitic insect whose larvae develop inside animal hosts.

A bottle is a container, typically glass or plastic, with a narrow neck for holding liquids: {a bottle of wine}, {a water bottle}. To bottle something is to put it in bottles: {They bottle their own beer}. To {bottle up} emotions is to suppress them. In British slang, bottle means courage or nerve: {He lost his bottle at the last minute}. To bottle it is to lose nerve and back out.

Bottled describes something stored or sold in a bottle: {bottled water}, {bottled beer}. The term extends to emotions that are suppressed or contained rather than expressed: {bottled-up rage}, {She kept her feelings bottled inside}. In British slang, to bottle it means to lose courage at the last moment: {He was going to ask her out but bottled it}.

A bottleneck is a narrow section of a bottle where the neck meets the body—and by extension, any point where flow is restricted. Traffic bottlenecks occur where lanes merge. In business or computing, a bottleneck is whatever slows the whole process: {The approval stage is our biggest bottleneck}. A bottleneck can also be a glass or metal tube slid over a guitarist's finger to produce a sliding sound on the strings.

Bottlenecks are points of congestion where flow is restricted—named for the narrow neck of a bottle that slows pouring. Traffic bottlenecks form where lanes merge; production bottlenecks occur when one slow process holds up an entire operation. The term applies anywhere capacity constraints create delays: {The approval process is the bottleneck}. To bottleneck is to constrict or impede flow.

Bottles is the plural of bottle—a container, typically glass or plastic, with a narrow neck for holding liquids: {wine bottles}, {baby bottles}, {plastic water bottles}. To bottle something is to put it in bottles: {They bottle their own beer}. To {bottle up} emotions is to suppress them. In British slang, to bottle it means to lose your nerve: {He was going to ask her out but bottled it}.

In most of its meanings, bottom is the opposite of top and refers to a lower or lowest part of something. In figurative use, the bottom of something is the cause or explanation for it: The detective vowed to get to the bottom of the murder. Bottom is also, figuratively, the worst point or phase of something before an improvement begins: He had to hit rock bottom before seeking treatment for his addiction. Informally, your bottom is your buttock. In baseball, the bottom of an inning is the second half. If something bottoms out, it reaches its lowest point.

Bottomless describes something without a bottom or with no apparent limit. A bottomless pit has no floor; a bottomless appetite never seems satisfied. {The coffee is bottomless—free refills all day}. Bottomless also means naked from the waist down, often paired with topless: {a bottomless waiter}, {bottomless brunch} (which playfully combines both senses—unlimited mimosas and sometimes undressed servers).

Bottoms is the plural of bottom—the lowest parts, the undersides, the bases. Pajama bottoms or bikini bottoms are garments covering the lower body. To drink to the bottoms of your glasses is to drain them completely. In sexual slang, bottoms are the receptive partners in anal intercourse, opposite of tops. {Bottoms up!} is a toast inviting everyone to finish their drinks.

Bought is the past tense and past participle of buy. It indicates completed acquisition: {I bought groceries}, {She had bought the house years ago}. In informal speech, {bought} sometimes emphasizes authenticity versus homemade: {store-bought cookies}. To say someone {bought it} can mean they believed something dubious, or slang for died: {He bought it in the war}.

Bougie is slang for aspiring to or affecting an upper-middle-class lifestyle, often with a hint of pretension. Short for bourgeois, it describes tastes, habits, or people perceived as upscale or status-conscious: {She's too bougie for fast food}, {That's a bougie coffee shop}. The term can be affectionate, self-aware, or mocking depending on context.

A boulder is a large rock, typically rounded by erosion or glacial action—big enough that you couldn't easily move it yourself. Boulders dot landscapes from riverbeds to mountainsides. In climbing, bouldering is scaling short rock formations without ropes. {We sat on a boulder overlooking the valley.} (Capitalized Boulder is a city in Colorado.)

Bouldering is rock climbing done on low formations or artificial walls without ropes, relying on crash pads and spotters for safety. Routes are short but technically demanding, emphasizing strength and problem-solving over endurance. The sport can be practiced outdoors on natural rock or indoors at climbing gyms: {I've been bouldering at the new gym downtown}.

Boulders are large rocks, typically rounded by weathering or water erosion. The term implies rocks too big to move easily by hand—bigger than stones or cobbles. {Massive boulders lined the riverbed.} {We scrambled over boulders to reach the summit.}

A boulevard is a broad, often tree-lined urban street, typically with a planted median or decorative landscaping. The word suggests a grand thoroughfare meant for leisurely travel rather than pure efficiency: {They strolled down the boulevard past sidewalk cafés}. In American city planning, boulevard often appears in street names regardless of the road's actual character.

Boulevards is the plural of boulevard, a broad urban street, often tree-lined or landscaped. The word suggests a grand, well-maintained thoroughfare: {We strolled along the boulevards of Paris}. In American usage, boulevard often appears in street names without implying grandeur: {Sunset Boulevard}, {Santa Monica Boulevard}.

Bounce, as both noun and verb, suggests a return to or away from the direction of origin, often rapid and sometimes complete. If an email bounces, it cannot be delivered and is returned to the sender. If a ball bounces, it is reflected off a hard surface and either back to the direction of original force or in a different direction: The player chased the ball after it bounced in the infield. A bounce is an instance of return or upward movement, especially after a fall: After failing the test, the student bounced back and received a good grade in the class. A check that bounces is refused by a bank because there is no money to cover it.

Bounced is the past tense of bounce. A ball bounced off the wall; a check bounced when the account lacked funds to cover it. Someone who was bounced got thrown out: {He was bounced from the club for fighting}. In computing, an email bounces when it fails to deliver and returns to sender. {The idea bounced around for weeks before anyone acted on it.}

A bouncer is a person employed to maintain order at a bar, club, or event—typically by checking IDs at the door and ejecting troublemakers. The term comes from their authority to bounce unwanted patrons out. Bouncers are often large and intimidating by design. In cricket, a bouncer is a ball bowled short so it bounces high toward the batter's head.

Bouncers are security personnel stationed at bars, clubs, or other venues to control entry and maintain order. They check IDs, enforce dress codes, and remove disruptive patrons—often physically, hence the name. {The bouncers wouldn't let us in without ID.} In cricket, a bouncer is a short-pitched ball that rises sharply toward the batsman's head.

Bouncing describes vigorous, energetic movement—the kind associated with a ball rebounding or a child jumping excitedly. A bouncing baby is healthy and lively, full of vitality: {She gave birth to a bouncing baby boy}. As a present participle of bounce, it covers literal rebounding: {The bouncing ball rolled into the street}.

Bouncy describes something that springs back when pressed or struck—a bouncy ball, a bouncy mattress. By extension, bouncy characterizes lively, energetic movement or personality: {bouncy pop music}, {She arrived in a bouncy mood}. Hair that's bouncy has springy volume rather than lying flat.

Bound is closely related to bind and bond in some of its meanings, and it serves as the past tense and past participle of bind. If something is bound, it is tied up or connected with a bond. The infinitive bound means to leap: The deer bounded over the fence. In the plural, bounds refers to a limit or boundary: Play stopped when the ball went out of bounds. If you’re bound to do something, it’s likely or inevitable that you will. If a vehicle or traveler is bound for a place, they are headed there.

Boundaries are lines that mark where one thing ends and another begins. A fence marks a property boundary; a river may form a boundary between countries. The word extends to limits on behavior or interaction: {She set clear boundaries with her coworkers}. In this psychological sense, boundaries define what someone will and won't accept from others—a usage that has become central to discussions of relationships and mental health.

A boundary is a line or limit that separates one area from another—between countries, properties, or zones. The word extends to abstract limits: {personal boundaries}, {the boundaries of acceptable behavior}. To push or test boundaries is to challenge established limits. In cricket, a boundary is a hit that reaches the edge of the field, scoring four or six runs.

Boundless means without limits or boundaries—extending indefinitely in space, quantity, or degree. It typically describes abstract qualities: boundless {energy}, boundless {enthusiasm}, boundless {optimism}. The word carries a positive connotation, suggesting abundance rather than mere absence of constraint: {Her boundless generosity touched everyone who knew her}.

Bounds are limits or boundaries—the edges of what is permitted or possible. To stay {within bounds} is to remain acceptable; to go {out of bounds} is to exceed limits or enter forbidden territory. In sports, bounds mark the playing area: {The ball went out of bounds}. As a verb, bounds means leaps: {The dog bounds across the yard}. Something that {knows no bounds} is limitless: {Her generosity knows no bounds}.

Bounties is the plural of bounty, which has two main threads: generous gifts and rewards for capture. A region's natural bounties are its abundant resources. A bounty on someone's head is money offered for catching them—originally criminals or enemies, now extended to bugs in software or invasive species: {The state pays bounties on wild boar}. {Bounty hunters} pursue fugitives for the reward.

Bounty is generous abundance: {the bounty of the harvest}, {nature's bounty}. It also means a reward offered for capturing someone or something—a fugitive, a predator, an invasive species: {There's a bounty on his head}. A bounty hunter pursues people for such rewards. The word carries a sense of largeness, whether in giving or in payment.

A bouquet is a bunch of flowers arranged for display or presentation: {The bride carried a bouquet of white roses}. By extension, bouquet refers to the characteristic scent of wine, encompassing its complex aromas: {This Burgundy has an earthy bouquet with hints of cherry}. The word can also describe any pleasant arrangement or collection: {a bouquet of compliments}.

Bouquets is the plural of bouquet—an arrangement of flowers, typically cut and gathered for display or presentation: {The bride carried a bouquet of white roses}, {He sent bouquets to the dressing room after opening night}. Figuratively, bouquets are compliments or praise: {The critics had only bouquets for her performance}. In wine terminology, bouquet refers to the complex aroma of an aged wine.

Bourbon is American whiskey distilled primarily from corn and aged in charred oak barrels. The name comes from Bourbon County, Kentucky, though bourbon can legally be made anywhere in the United States. It has a distinctive sweet, caramel-like flavor: {He ordered bourbon neat}, {a bourbon and Coke}. (Capitalized Bourbon refers to the European royal dynasty.)

Bourgeois describes the middle class, especially its conventional values and materialistic concerns. The term carries a whiff of Marxist critique—the bourgeoisie as the property-owning class opposed to workers. In casual use, bourgeois suggests comfortable conformity, prioritizing respectability and possessions over creativity or authenticity: {Their bourgeois taste in furniture}, {too bourgeois to take risks}. As a noun, a bourgeois is a member of this class.

The bourgeoisie is the middle class, particularly as a social and economic category. In Marxist theory, the bourgeoisie are the capitalist class who own the means of production, distinguished from the proletariat (workers) and the aristocracy. Outside strict Marxist usage, the term often carries connotations of conventional, materialistic values and concern with respectability: {the comfortable bourgeoisie of the suburbs}. The adjective is bourgeois.

Bourgie is slang for bourgeois—exhibiting or aspiring to middle-class tastes, materialism, or pretension. It can be affectionate or cutting depending on context: {She's gotten all bourgie since she moved to the suburbs}. Sometimes spelled bougie. The term often carries ironic self-awareness when used among friends: {I know it's bourgie, but I love a good brunch}.

A bout is a period of intense activity or experience, often unpleasant: {a bout of flu}, {a drinking bout}, {a bout of insomnia}. The word suggests something that comes and goes rather than persisting. In combat sports, a bout is a single match or fight: {a boxing bout}, {a wrestling bout}.

A boutique is a small shop selling fashionable clothing, accessories, or specialty goods, often with a curated or upscale feel: {a bridal boutique}, {a vintage boutique on the corner}. As an adjective, boutique describes something small-scale, specialized, or exclusive: {a boutique hotel}, {a boutique law firm}, {boutique wines}. The term suggests personalized service or niche appeal rather than mass-market offerings.

Boutiques are small shops selling fashionable clothing, accessories, or specialty goods, typically with a curated selection and personalized service. The word suggests exclusivity and style over mass-market retail: {She found the perfect dress at a little boutique downtown}. By extension, boutique describes anything small-scale and specialized: a boutique {hotel}, a boutique {law firm}, a boutique {winery}.

Three words with two pronunciations share the spelling b-o-w. The bow that rhymes with now means to bend forward, often in submission or respect: He bowed in prayer. Bow is an instance of this: His bow was heartfelt. Another bow, same pronunciation, is the forward part of a ship. The bow that rhymes with no is mainly a noun for something with a curved shape (bow and arrow, violin bow), or the configuration of ribbon used as an adornment in the hair or on a gift: The package was festooned with a beautiful yellow bow. If something is bowed (rhymes with node), it is bent in the middle.

Bowels are the intestines—the long tube in the abdomen where digestion completes and waste forms. The word typically appears in plural: {bowel movement} is the exception. Figuratively, bowels means the innermost depths of something: {the bowels of the earth}, {the bowels of the ship}. This sense draws on the old association of intestines with the seat of emotions, as in the archaic {bowels of compassion}.

Bowing is the act of bending at the waist as a gesture of respect, greeting, or acknowledgment: {The performer's bowing went on for several curtain calls}. In music, bowing refers to the technique of drawing a bow across stringed instruments, or the specific pattern of up and down strokes marked in a score: {The conductor insisted on uniform bowing throughout the string section}.

The bowl that you eat out of inspires other noun meanings of bowl that share this shape, such as a crater or a sports stadium. When you bowl, you play a game in which the object is to knock down pins with a ball that you roll towards them. This word, converted to a noun and pluralized, designates a version of this game: bowls, also called lawn bowling. If something bowls you over it has an overwhelming effect.

A bowler is a hard felt hat with a rounded crown and narrow brim, also called a derby in American English. The style was once standard business attire in Britain: {He wore a dark suit and bowler}. Separately, a bowler is someone who bowls—whether in cricket, where the bowler delivers the ball to the batsman, or in bowling, where the bowler rolls a ball at pins.

Bowling is a game where players roll a heavy ball down a lane to knock over pins arranged in a triangle. The most common form uses ten pins, though variations exist like candlepin and duckpin bowling. The term also covers lawn bowling (bowls), where players roll balls toward a target on grass. {We went bowling on Friday night.}

Bowls is a lawn game in which players roll biased balls toward a smaller target ball called the jack. The balls curve as they slow, requiring skill to anticipate their path. British in origin and still popular in Commonwealth countries, bowls is played on manicured grass or indoor surfaces. {They play bowls at the club every Sunday.}

Bows names several things that share a curved shape. A bow is a weapon for shooting arrows, or a decorative knot with loops: {She tied the ribbon in a bow}. Musicians draw a bow across violin strings. The bow of a ship is its curved front. To bow is to bend forward at the waist in greeting or deference: {He bowed to the queen}. A bow can also acknowledge applause: {The cast took their bows}.

A bowstring is the taut cord connecting the two ends of an archer's bow, drawn back and released to propel an arrow. The term extends to any similar taut cord or the structural element in a bowstring truss or bridge. As a verb, to bowstring someone is to strangle them with a cord—a historical method of execution in Ottoman Turkey.

A bowtie is a necktie that fastens in a bow at the collar rather than hanging down the chest. Bowties suggest formality ({black-tie dress code}) or a certain professorial eccentricity. In other contexts, bowtie describes the shape—a bowtie {pasta}, a bowtie {antenna}. Also spelled bow tie.

Three words in English have the spelling box, but the main one—a cubicle container—far outnumbers the other two in usage. This main meaning is extended to other hollow spaces with the capacity to contain something: post office box, in-box. The verb from this meaning conveys confining to a container: Box the cookies and send them off. The verb is more frequent for another meaning of box: to fight with the fists, usually in the competitive sport of boxing. The third box is a noun only, one that designates a family of slow-growing, evergreen shrubs with small leaves.

A boxcar is a fully enclosed railroad freight car with sliding doors on the sides, used for transporting goods that need protection from weather. The rectangular shape lends itself to figurative use: boxcar numbers or boxcar figures are very large amounts, from the image of freight cars lined up in a long train. In dice games, boxcars means double sixes.

Boxed describes something enclosed in a box or shaped like one. Boxed {wine} comes in a cardboard container rather than a bottle. A boxed {set} packages related items together. In typography, boxed {text} appears inside a bordered rectangle. To feel boxed {in} is to feel trapped or constrained, with limited options: {I felt boxed in by their demands}.

A boxer is a person who fights with their fists as a sport, following rules that govern rounds, weight classes, and legal punches. The word also names a breed of medium-sized dog with a short muzzle and muscular build, known for playful energy and standing on hind legs to "box" with front paws. In the plural, boxers are loose-fitting men's undershorts: {He prefers boxers to briefs}. (Capitalized Boxer refers to the Chinese rebellion.)

Boxers are loose-fitting undershorts for men, characterized by an elastic waistband and legs that extend partway down the thigh. They contrast with briefs, which fit more snugly. The name references the shorts worn by boxing athletes. Boxers also refers to people who engage in the sport of boxing, and to a breed of medium-sized, muscular dog with a square muzzle and short coat, known for its energetic and playful temperament.

Boxes is the plural of box—containers, typically rectangular, used for storage or transport: {cardboard boxes}, {a box of chocolates}. To box something is to put it in a box or to confine: {We boxed up the old photos}. To {box someone in} is to trap or limit their options. Boxes also refers to fighting with fists: {He boxes at the local gym}.

Boxing is a combat sport where two opponents fight using only their fists, typically wearing padded gloves. Matches take place in a ring and are divided into rounds. The sport emphasizes footwork, defense, and punching technique: {He took up boxing to get in shape}. Boxing also refers to the act of putting things in boxes: {I spent the weekend boxing up old books}.

The core meaning of boy is the least problematic meaning: a male human who is not yet fully mature. There is no sharp division between boy and man, but usage suggests that the shift occurs at age 18 or 19 for most speakers. Designating a male over 19 as boy is either an insult or part of a compound (old boy, good old boy, local boy, golden boy) that has a specific, not necessarily disparaging meaning. In other compounds, boy maintains its core meaning to denote a role or function normally filled by younger males: bat boy, rent boy, altar boy. Boy is also a general-purpose exclamation to express surprise, admiration, or some other intense feeling.

A boyband is a pop music group of young male singers, typically assembled by producers rather than formed organically. The members are usually chosen for looks and choreographed appeal as much as vocal ability. Boybands target teenage audiences, especially girls: {My daughter is obsessed with whatever boyband is popular now}. The term often carries a dismissive edge, implying manufactured rather than authentic artistry.

A boyband is a pop music group composed of young male singers, typically assembled by producers rather than formed organically. The members usually don't play instruments, focusing instead on vocals, choreographed dancing, and cultivated personas designed to appeal to teenage girls: {My sister's walls were covered with boyband posters}. The term emerged in the 1990s with groups like Backstreet Boys and *NSYNC, though the formula dates earlier.

Boycott is a refusal to buy, use, or participate in something as a form of protest or pressure. Consumers boycott companies over labor practices; nations boycott another country's exports. The word comes from Charles Boycott, an Irish land agent so shunned by tenants in 1880 that his name became the act itself. {They called for a boycott of the Olympics.}

Boycotting is refusing to buy from, work with, or otherwise engage with a company, country, or organization as a form of protest or pressure. The term comes from Charles Boycott, an Irish land agent shunned by his community in 1880. People boycott businesses over labor practices, governments over human rights abuses, or products over environmental concerns: {They're boycotting the company until it changes its policies}.

Boycotts are organized refusals to buy from, sell to, or otherwise engage with a company, country, or entity as a form of protest or pressure. The tactic aims to cause economic harm until demands are met: {Consumer boycotts forced the company to change its labor practices}. To boycott is to participate in such a campaign or simply to avoid something on principle: {She boycotts fast fashion}.

A boyfriend is a male romantic partner, typically in a relationship that isn't marriage. The term implies some ongoing commitment beyond casual dating: {She's been with her boyfriend for two years}. Adults sometimes find the word inadequate for serious long-term partners, preferring "partner" or "significant other." With a possessive, boyfriend usually means current romantic interest, though context matters: {my daughter's boyfriend}.

Boyfriends is the plural of boyfriend—a male romantic partner, typically in a relationship that isn't yet marriage. The word implies ongoing involvement rather than casual dating: {She's had three boyfriends since college}. Someone's boyfriend is usually exclusive, though the term can describe non-monogamous arrangements too.

Boyhood is the period of life when a male is a boy—roughly from early childhood until the late teens. It often carries nostalgic connotations of innocence, adventure, or formative experiences: {He spent his boyhood on a farm in Iowa}. The word emphasizes the quality or state of being a boy rather than a specific age range.

Boyish describes qualities associated with boys—youthful energy, playfulness, or a certain innocent mischief. A boyish {grin} suggests unguarded charm. Boyish {looks} or a boyish {figure} implies a youthful, slender appearance. The word usually carries positive connotations of freshness and vitality, though it can suggest immaturity when applied to adult men.

Boys is the plural of boy—male children or young men. The word often extends to adult males in casual contexts: {a night out with the boys}, {the boys in the band}. It can signal camaraderie or informality among men of any age. Applied to grown men in professional settings, it may sound dismissive or condescending.

A bozo is a stupid or foolish person—someone who bumbles through situations or makes obvious mistakes. The word carries mild contempt but is rarely harsh: {Some bozo cut me off in traffic}. It suggests incompetence more than malice, often applied to strangers whose names you don't know or care to learn.

A bra is an undergarment that supports a woman's breasts, typically consisting of two cups held in place by shoulder straps and a band around the torso. The word is shortened from brassiere, which sounds dated. Bras come in many styles—sports bras, push-up bras, strapless bras—each serving different purposes: {I need a strapless bra for that dress}.

Most meanings of brace have to do with the idea of strengthening or reinforcing, or various objects that accomplish this. A knee brace supports the injured joint. To brace something is to secure it with a brace, unless the thing you’re bracing is yourself, in which case you prepare yourself for a shock. Curly marks of punctuation that come in pairs, and wires placed on crooked teeth to straighten them, are also called braces.

A bracelet is an ornamental band worn around the wrist. Bracelets may be rigid (bangles) or flexible (chains, beads, links). They serve as jewelry, fashion accessories, or markers of identity: {friendship bracelets}, {medical alert bracelets}, {charm bracelets}. In slang, bracelets sometimes means handcuffs: {The cop slapped the bracelets on him}.

Bracelets are decorative bands worn around the wrist, made from materials ranging from precious metals and gemstones to leather, beads, or woven thread. They serve as jewelry, fashion accessories, or symbols of friendship, identity, or commemoration. Some bracelets have functional purposes, like medical alert bracelets that display health information. In slang, bracelets sometimes refers to handcuffs: {The cops slapped bracelets on him before he could run.}

Braces are devices that hold, support, or strengthen. Orthodontic braces are wire-and-bracket systems that straighten teeth. A back brace supports the spine. Carpenters use braces to reinforce structures. In British English, braces are suspenders—straps holding up trousers. The punctuation marks { } are also called braces, though Americans more often say curly brackets. To brace is to prepare for impact: {Brace yourself}.

Bracing describes something invigorating or refreshing, often with a sharp quality: {a bracing walk in the cold morning air}, {bracing sea winds}. The word suggests stimulation that wakes you up or strengthens you—challenging but beneficial. Bracing can also mean serving as structural support: {bracing beams held up the roof}.

The original bracket, a kind of support projecting from a surface, has spawned all other meanings. Bracket sometimes denotes a grouping of people (age bracket, income bracket). Some pairs of punctuation marks are called brackets (square brackets, wavy brackets); they bracket the information that comes between them. In sports, a bracket is a diagram depicting the teams in a tournament.

Brackets are punctuation marks that come in pairs to enclose words or figures. Square brackets [ ] set off editorial insertions or clarifications within quoted material. Round brackets, usually called parentheses, enclose supplementary information. Curly brackets { } appear mainly in mathematics and programming. Angle brackets < > mark HTML tags. In British usage, bracket alone often means parenthesis. Beyond punctuation, a bracket is a support projecting from a wall, or a category grouping similar items: {tax bracket}, {age bracket}. In sports tournaments, a bracket diagrams the matchups leading to a final.

Brag is to boast or speak with excessive pride about oneself or one's accomplishments: {He bragged about his promotion all week}. The word carries a negative connotation—bragging implies self-importance that annoys listeners. As a noun, a brag is an instance of boasting or the thing boasted about. Brag is also a card game similar to poker.

Bragging is boastful talk about one's achievements, possessions, or abilities. The word carries a negative connotation—someone who brags seeks admiration but often produces annoyance: {All his bragging about his new car got old fast}. As an adjective, bragging describes the boastful tone itself: {bragging rights} are the privilege of boasting after a victory.

A braid is a length of hair or cord formed by weaving three or more strands over and under one another: {She wore her hair in a long braid down her back}. The verb means to create such a pattern: {My mother used to braid my hair every morning}. Braid also refers to decorative woven trim on uniforms or upholstery.

Braided describes something woven by intertwining three or more strands: {braided hair}, {a braided rug}, {braided leather}. The pattern creates texture and strength. Rivers and streams that split into multiple channels and rejoin are also called braided: {The braided river spread across the valley floor}.

Braiding is the act of weaving three or more strands together in an overlapping pattern. Hair braiding ranges from simple three-strand plaits to elaborate cornrows and box braids. The technique applies to rope, leather, bread dough, and decorative trim. {She spent an hour braiding her daughter's hair.}

Braids are lengths of hair or other flexible material woven together by interlacing three or more strands. The technique creates a rope-like pattern that holds without ties until unraveled. As a verb, to braid is to form such an interlaced structure: {She braids her daughter's hair every morning}. Braids appear in hairstyling across cultures, from cornrows to French braids, and the same weaving principle applies to rope, leather, and decorative trim.

The brain is the organ inside the skull that controls thought, memory, emotion, and bodily functions. By extension, brain means intelligence or mental capacity: {She has the brains to solve this}. To brain someone is to strike them on the head. A brain or {the brains} behind something is its mastermind: {He was the brains of the operation}. To {pick someone's brain} is to extract their knowledge through questioning.

A brainchild is something a person has originated or invented—an idea, plan, or creation they're proud of. The word emphasizes personal ownership and creative investment: {The festival was her brainchild}. Like a biological child, a brainchild is something you've brought into existence and feel responsible for.

Braindead describes a state of no brain activity, the medical criterion for death even when machines maintain heartbeat and breathing. Extended to mean utterly stupid or incapable of thought: {I'm completely braindead after that exam}. Also describes ideas or entertainment lacking any intellectual content: {braindead television}. Sometimes hyphenated or two words.

A braindump is an unstructured outpouring of everything you know or remember about a topic, typically written quickly without organizing or editing: {Before the meeting, I did a braindump of all my concerns}. The term comes from computing, where dumping means transferring data wholesale. Braindumps prioritize completeness over coherence—get it all out, then sort through it.

Brainiac is informal for an exceptionally intelligent person, often with a hint of teasing or affection: {My sister's the brainiac of the family}. The term can be admiring or gently mocking, depending on tone—sometimes implying bookishness or social awkwardness alongside intellectual prowess.

Brainless means lacking intelligence or common sense—stupid, foolish. The word is hyperbolic; those described as brainless do have brains, just not ones they're using well: {a brainless decision}, {some brainless bureaucrat lost my paperwork}. Brainless entertainment requires no mental effort to enjoy.

Brainpower is mental capacity or intelligence—the ability to think, reason, and solve problems. It can refer to an individual's cognitive abilities {She has the brainpower to figure this out} or collectively to the intellectual resources of a group {The company's brainpower is concentrated in its research division}. Often used to emphasize that a task requires serious thinking.

Brains is the plural of brain—the organ of thought, or intelligence itself. But brains often functions as a singular noun meaning mental ability: {She's the brains of the operation}. To have brains is to be smart. As food, brains are the cooked cerebral tissue of animals, served scrambled or in dishes like tacos de sesos. To beat someone's brains out is to kill them violently; to rack your brains is to think very hard.

Brainstorm has two distinct meanings. One is a sudden clever idea or mental inspiration: {I had a brainstorm and solved the problem}. The other, more common in American usage, is to generate ideas freely in a group setting, withholding criticism until later: {Let's brainstorm some solutions}. The noun brainstorm can refer to either the flash of insight or the collaborative session itself.

Brainstorming is generating ideas freely and spontaneously, usually in a group, without immediately judging their merit. The goal is quantity over quality—criticism comes later. {We spent an hour brainstorming solutions to the budget problem.} The term applies both to the activity and the session itself: {Let's schedule a brainstorming for Tuesday}.

A brainteaser is a puzzle or problem designed to challenge thinking, often requiring lateral reasoning or clever insight rather than straightforward knowledge: {The interviewer asked a brainteaser about how many golf balls fit in a school bus}. Brainteasers appear in job interviews, games, and casual conversation as entertainment or tests of mental agility.

Brainwash means to pressure someone into adopting beliefs or behaviors through prolonged psychological manipulation—isolation, repetition, emotional coercion. The term emerged from Cold War fears about communist indoctrination techniques. It now applies broadly to any systematic attempt to override independent thinking: {cult leaders brainwashing followers}, {He accused the media of brainwashing the public}. Often used hyperbolically for any strong persuasion.

Brainwashed describes someone whose beliefs or thinking have been fundamentally altered through intense psychological pressure or propaganda. The term suggests a person has been manipulated into accepting ideas they wouldn't have chosen freely: {He emerged from the cult completely brainwashed}. It's often used loosely to dismiss anyone with views the speaker finds inexplicably wrong: {You've been brainwashed by the media}.

Brainwashing is the systematic effort to change someone's beliefs or loyalties through psychological pressure, often involving isolation, repetition, and coercion. The term emerged from Cold War accounts of prisoners subjected to intense indoctrination: {POWs were accused of being brainwashed by their captors}. It now applies more loosely to any perceived manipulation of thought: {He accused the cult of brainwashing its members}. The verb is brainwash.

A brainwave is a fluctuation in electrical activity in the brain, measurable by electroencephalogram. In casual British usage, a brainwave is a sudden clever idea or inspiration: {I had a brainwave—we could take the back roads instead}. Americans more often say brainstorm for this sense.

Brainwaves are the electrical impulses produced by brain activity, measurable by electroencephalography. Different frequencies correspond to different mental states—delta waves during deep sleep, beta waves during alert concentration. In casual use, a brainwave is a sudden clever idea: {I had a brainwave about how to fix the problem}.

Brainy means intelligent or intellectually sharp: {She's the brainy one in the family}. The word is informal and often affectionate, suggesting someone who excels at academic or analytical thinking. It can carry a hint of nerdiness—brains over brawn: {the brainy kid who always aced the tests}.

The commonest use of brake is as a noun for a device that stops movement; it can be singular (emergency break) or plural: Put on the brakes! Figuratively, a brake may be anything that impedes progress or activity: We must put a brake on new hiring. The spelling brake is also used for some archaic and infrequent words in English, the commonest of which is a kind of fern.

Brakes are devices that slow or stop motion, typically by applying friction to wheels or axles. A car's brakes press pads against rotating discs; a bicycle's brakes squeeze the wheel rim. To brake is to apply brakes: {She braked hard at the yellow light}. Figuratively, to {put the brakes on} something is to slow or halt it: {The recession put the brakes on expansion plans}.

Bramble refers to prickly shrubs of the rose family, especially blackberries and raspberries, or the tangled thickets they form. The thorny, scrambling growth makes brambles difficult to navigate: {We pushed through the brambles at the edge of the field}. Figuratively, a bramble suggests something thorny or entangled: {a bramble of legal complications}.

Brambles are thorny, sprawling shrubs—especially blackberries and raspberries—or the prickly thickets they form. The word evokes wild, tangled growth that catches at skin and clothing: {We pushed through the brambles at the edge of the field}. Bramble can refer to a single plant or to the whole mass of intertwined growth.

A branch is a limb extending from a tree's trunk, or any similar division from a main body. Rivers have branches, as do roads, families, and organizations: {The company opened a new branch in Denver}. Fields of study branch into specializations. To branch out is to expand into new areas: {She branched out from acting into directing}.

Branches are limbs extending from a tree trunk or main stem. The word extends to anything that divides from a main body: a river branch, a branch of government, a bank branch, a branch of study. To branch is to divide or spread outward: {The road branches ahead}. To {branch out} is to expand into new areas: {The company branched out into software}.

Various meanings of brand can be summarized under the idea of distinguishing mark. A brand on an animal is an enduring mark made by its owner: The brand on this cow means it’s from the Lazy Z Ranch. Such an animal has been branded. A brand is also a distinct product or line of products that share a name and other distinctive marks, such as a logo: I’m loyal to the General Motors brand. A product or service that has been branded has been distinguished in this way by its maker. When brand is attributed to a person, it refers to their reputation, character, and style.

Branded describes something marked with a brand—a distinctive symbol burned or stamped to show ownership or origin. Cattle are branded to identify their owner. Branded products carry a company's name or logo, distinguishing them from generic alternatives: {branded merchandise}, {branded content}. In marketing, branded emphasizes association with a recognizable identity. Historically, criminals and enslaved people were branded on the skin as permanent marks of status or punishment.

Branding is the practice of creating a distinctive identity for a product, company, or organization through names, logos, design, and messaging. Originally literal—burning a mark into cattle or goods to show ownership—branding now refers to shaping public perception: {The company invested heavily in branding}. A brand is both the identity itself and the reputation it carries.

Brands are distinctive names, symbols, or designs that identify products or services and distinguish them from competitors. A brand encompasses not just visual identity but also reputation and the emotional associations consumers have with it—{brand loyalty}, {brand recognition}. Companies invest heavily in building and protecting their brands. As a verb, brand means to mark with an identifying symbol, originally by burning a mark onto livestock or, punitively, onto human skin. To be branded a {traitor} or {liar} is to be publicly labeled as one.

Brandy is a spirit distilled from wine or fermented fruit juice. Grape brandy is the standard; fruit brandies specify their source: {apple brandy}, {cherry brandy}. The drink is traditionally sipped after dinner or used in cooking. {She warmed the brandy in her hands before drinking.} (Capitalized Brandy is a given name.)

Bras is the plural of bra, the undergarment that supports a woman's breasts. {She tried on several bras before finding one that fit}. The word is a shortened form of brassiere, now the standard term in everyday speech.

The metal alloy (made of copper and zinc) called brass is present, literally or figuratively, in most of its meanings. Wind instruments made of metal are collectively called brass. The top officials of a military or other organization are called the brass, a metonym for the decorations they wear. Aside from this, brass does not share any of the prestigious associations that gold and silver have. Informally, brass is a brazen attitude, or another term for money.

Brassinosteroids are plant hormones that regulate growth and development. They influence cell elongation, division, and differentiation throughout a plant's life cycle—from seed germination to flowering. First isolated from pollen of the mustard family, brassinosteroids are now known to occur in nearly all plant tissues and to help plants respond to environmental stress.

A brat is a child who behaves badly—whiny, demanding, or spoiled: {Their kids are such brats}. The word carries affectionate exasperation as often as genuine criticism. In adult contexts, brat describes someone acting childishly entitled. A brat is also a type of sausage, short for bratwurst. In BDSM, a brat is a submissive who playfully defies their dominant. (Capitalized Brat refers to the 2024 Charli XCX album and cultural phenomenon.)

Brats is the plural of brat—a child who behaves badly or gets whatever they want: {Those brats broke my window}. The word carries affection when parents use it about their own children. A military brat is someone who grew up in a military family, moving frequently between bases. Brats is also short for bratwurst, the German sausage: {We grilled brats for the cookout}.

Bratty describes behavior typical of a brat—spoiled, demanding, or petulant. A bratty child whines when denied candy; a bratty adult sulks when they don't get their way. The word often carries affectionate exasperation rather than genuine condemnation: {She's being bratty because she's tired}. In kink contexts, bratty describes a submissive who playfully defies or provokes their dominant.

Bratwurst is a German sausage made from pork, beef, or veal, typically seasoned with spices like nutmeg, ginger, and caraway. The sausage is usually grilled or pan-fried and served in a bun with mustard and sauerkraut: {We grilled bratwursts for the cookout}. Often shortened to brat.

Bravado is a bold or swaggering display of confidence, often masking fear or uncertainty. It suggests performance rather than genuine courage—the loud boasting before a fight, the defiant pose when cornered: {His bravado crumbled when they called his bluff}. The word carries a note of skepticism about whether the boldness is real.

Brave describes a willingness to face danger, pain, or difficulty without giving way to fear. A brave {soldier} charges into battle; a brave {decision} risks consequences for the sake of principle. The word suggests courage that's active rather than passive—not just enduring hardship but confronting it. To brave something is to face it boldly: {She braved the storm to reach the hospital}. The noun brave, now dated, referred to a Native American warrior.

Bravery is the quality of facing danger, pain, or difficulty without giving way to fear. It suggests deliberate courage rather than mere recklessness: {The firefighters showed remarkable bravery}. Bravery can be physical or moral—standing up for principles requires bravery too: {It took bravery to speak out against her own party}.

Bravo is an exclamation of approval and admiration, shouted especially after a performance: {The audience cried bravo as the soprano finished her aria}. It comes from Italian and retains associations with opera and classical music, though it can be used for any impressive feat. The NATO phonetic alphabet uses bravo for the letter B. (Capitalized Bravo is a cable television network.)

A brawl is a noisy, chaotic fight involving multiple people—the kind that breaks out in bars or at sporting events: {A brawl erupted in the stands after the game}. Unlike a duel or boxing match, a brawl is disorderly and unregulated. To brawl is to engage in such fighting. The word can extend to heated verbal disputes.

A brawler is someone who fights, especially in rough, disorderly scuffles rather than formal combat. The word suggests a person prone to or skilled at physical altercations: {He was a barroom brawler in his younger days}. In video games, a brawler is a fighting game or a character class built for close-quarters combat.

Brawlers is the plural of brawler—someone who engages in rough, physical fights, typically spontaneous and unrefined rather than organized combat. The word suggests scrappy aggression: {The bar was full of brawlers looking for trouble}. In gaming, brawlers often refers to fighting games or characters built for close-range combat.

Brawls are noisy, disorderly fights, typically involving multiple people in a public place: {A brawl broke out in the parking lot after the game}. The word suggests chaotic physical conflict rather than organized combat—bar brawls, street brawls, bench-clearing brawls in sports. To brawl is to engage in such fighting.

Brawn refers to muscular strength and power, especially of the kind developed through physical labor or training. It often appears in contrast with brain, suggesting a distinction between physical and intellectual capability: {The job requires more brawn than brains}. In British usage, brawn is also a cold cut made from the meat of a pig's head set in gelatin—what Americans call head cheese. Someone described as brawny has well-developed muscles and appears physically powerful.

Brazen describes behavior that is bold and shameless, showing no attempt to hide wrongdoing or impropriety. A brazen {lie} is one told without apparent guilt; a brazen {thief} operates openly rather than covertly. The word originally meant "made of brass," and this metallic sense survives in phrases like brazen {trumpets}. To brazen something out is to face a difficult situation with defiant confidence rather than backing down: {She decided to brazen it out despite the accusations}.

A breach is a break or gap in something—a wall, a barrier, a defense. The word extends to violations of agreements or duties: a breach of {contract}, a breach of {trust}, a breach of {etiquette}. To breach is to break through or violate: {Whales breached the surface}; {The company breached its agreement}. A security breach means unauthorized access. To {step into the breach} is to fill a gap left by someone's absence.

Breaches is the plural of breach, a gap or break in something that should be continuous or intact. A breach in a wall, a breach in security, or a breach of protocol all suggest something has been broken through or violated. {The storm caused several breaches in the levee.} As a verb form, breaches means to break through or violate: {The company routinely breaches its own privacy policy.} A whale that breaches leaps dramatically out of the water.

Breaching is the act of breaking through or violating something. Security forces breach walls or doors to gain entry. Whales breach when they leap from the water. A contract is breached when its terms are violated: {The company was sued for breaching the agreement}. A breach in a dam or defensive wall is a dangerous opening.

Bread is a staple food made from flour and water, typically leavened with yeast and baked. It comes in countless varieties—sliced sandwich bread, crusty loaves, flatbreads, rolls. {Breaking bread} with someone means sharing a meal. Bread is also slang for money: {I need to make some bread}. The verb means to coat food with breadcrumbs before cooking: {breaded chicken cutlets}.

A breadcrumb is a small fragment of bread, the kind that falls from a loaf when sliced or accumulates at the bottom of a toaster. In the plural, breadcrumbs are used for coating foods before frying: {chicken coated in breadcrumbs}. Figuratively, breadcrumbs are small hints or pieces of information left as a trail—from the fairy tale where children mark their path through the forest. In web design, breadcrumbs are navigational links showing your location within a site's hierarchy. To breadcrumb someone is to string them along with sporadic, minimal attention: {He kept breadcrumbing her with occasional texts}.

Breadcrumbs are small pieces of dried or toasted bread, used as coating for fried foods or as a topping: {chicken cutlets dredged in breadcrumbs}. In computing and web design, breadcrumbs are a navigation trail showing your path through a site's hierarchy, letting you retrace your steps. The term alludes to the trail Hansel and Gretel left in the forest. To {leave breadcrumbs} is to drop hints or clues leading somewhere.

A breadline is a queue of people waiting to receive free food, typically bread, from a charity or government agency during times of economic hardship. The image of breadlines became iconic during the Great Depression. The phrase {on the breadline} means living in poverty, barely able to afford basic necessities: {Many families are just one paycheck away from the breadline}.

Breadlines are queues of people waiting to receive free food, typically bread or basic provisions, distributed by charities or government agencies during times of economic hardship. The term evokes images of the Great Depression, when unemployed workers lined up for handouts. Today breadlines appear both literally, at food banks and soup kitchens, and figuratively to suggest widespread poverty or economic collapse: {If this policy continues, we'll all be standing in breadlines}.

A breadwinner is the person whose income supports a household. The term evokes traditional family structures where one spouse—historically the husband—earned money while the other managed the home: {She became the family's breadwinner after her husband's injury}. The word remains common even as dual-income households have become the norm.

Breadwinners are the members of a household who earn money to support the family. The term evokes the image of bringing home bread—basic sustenance. Traditionally applied to fathers in single-income households, it now describes anyone whose earnings are primary: {Both parents are breadwinners in most families today}. A sole breadwinner carries the full financial burden.

Break is highly varied in its noun and verb meanings and it also forms the foundation of several frequent phrasal verbs, such as break down, break in, and break off. The ideas common to all meanings of break are discontinuity or separation. You might think that the things most often broken are tangible, like windows or vases, but the words that most often follow the verb break are abstract, such as law, record, rule, and heart. The most popular meaning of break as a noun is not about things being broken; it’s about discontinuity in time or activity: Take a break to think about it.

Breakaway describes something that separates or breaks off from a larger group. A breakaway faction splits from a political party; a breakaway republic declares independence. In sports, a breakaway is a sudden rush toward the goal, having broken free from defenders: {She scored on a breakaway}. As an adjective, breakaway also describes objects designed to break apart on impact for safety: {breakaway glass}, {breakaway bases}.

Breakdance is a style of street dance that emerged from hip-hop culture, characterized by acrobatic moves performed close to the ground—spins, freezes, and power moves like headspins and windmills. As a verb, to breakdance is to perform this style: {He learned to breakdance in the '80s}. Also spelled break-dance or written as two words.

A breakdancer is someone who performs breakdancing—an acrobatic street dance style originating in 1970s New York hip-hop culture. Breakdancers execute spins, freezes, and floor work, often in competitive battles or ciphers: {The breakdancers took turns in the center of the circle}.

Breakdancing is an acrobatic style of street dance that emerged from hip-hop culture, featuring athletic moves performed close to the ground—spins, freezes, and fluid footwork. Dancers (b-boys and b-girls) often compete in battles, taking turns showing off increasingly difficult combinations: {He learned to breakdance in the park}. Also called breaking.

Breakdown is a failure or collapse—of machinery, negotiations, relationships, or mental health. A car has a breakdown when it stops working; a person has a breakdown when stress overwhelms them. Breakdown also means analysis by components: {a breakdown of costs}, {a breakdown of the vote by demographic}. In compounds, it becomes break down: {Let me break down the numbers for you}.

Breakdowns are failures or collapses. A mechanical breakdown stops a machine from working. A breakdown in communication means people aren't understanding each other. A nervous breakdown is a period of severe mental distress. The word also means an analysis that separates something into parts: {Give me a breakdown of the costs}. In some contexts, breakdowns are energetic dance moves or musical passages.

A breaker is something that breaks, in any of that verb's many senses. A wave that breaks on the shore is a breaker. A circuit breaker interrupts electrical flow when current exceeds safe levels. In CB radio culture, "breaker" announces someone wanting to join a conversation: {Breaker, breaker, anyone got eyes on traffic ahead?} Compound forms like lawbreaker, dealbreaker, and icebreaker specify what's being broken or disrupted.

Breakers are waves that crash onto shore, their crests collapsing into foam as they meet shallow water or obstacles. The term extends to anything that breaks: a circuit breaker interrupts electrical flow; a breaker at a salvage yard dismantles ships. In CB radio slang, {breaker, breaker} announces someone seeking to join a conversation.

Breakfast is the first meal of the day, typically eaten in the morning. The word reflects the idea of breaking the overnight fast. Breakfast foods vary by culture but often include eggs, bread, cereal, or pastries: {We grabbed a quick breakfast before work}. As a verb, to breakfast is to eat this meal: {They breakfasted on the terrace}.

Breaking is the act of causing something to separate into pieces, or the moment when something gives way. It extends to violations ({breaking the law}), interruptions ({breaking news}), and transitions ({breaking free}, {day is breaking}). In hip-hop culture, breaking is a style of acrobatic street dance, also called breakdancing.

Breakneck describes a dangerously fast pace or speed, suggesting recklessness that could result in a broken neck. It appears almost exclusively before the noun it modifies: {The project proceeded at breakneck speed}. Despite the violent imagery, breakneck is often used with a hint of admiration for ambitious velocity rather than genuine warning.

A breakout is an escape, especially from confinement: {a prison breakout}. The word extends to any sudden emergence from constraint—a disease breakout spreads rapidly, a breakout {session} at a conference splits from the main group. In entertainment and sports, a breakout {role} or breakout {season} marks someone's transition from obscurity to prominence. As an adjective, breakout describes unexpected success: {a breakout hit}, {a breakout star}.

Breakouts are instances of breaking out—escaping confinement, emerging suddenly, or erupting. A prisoner might attempt a breakout from jail. In skin care, a breakout is an outbreak of acne or blemishes: {I always get breakouts when I'm stressed}. In business and finance, a breakout occurs when a stock price moves beyond an established trading range, signaling potential momentum. The term also describes separating into smaller groups for focused discussion: {We'll do breakouts after the main presentation}.

Breaks is the plural of break—pauses, interruptions, or fractures: {We took several breaks during the hike}, {breaks in the clouds}. In music and dance, breaks are rhythmic passages where instruments drop out, leaving drums or bass exposed—the foundation of breakdancing and hip-hop sampling. {Give me a break} asks for leniency or expresses disbelief. {That's the breaks} accepts misfortune philosophically.

A breakthrough is a sudden advance or important discovery that overcomes an obstacle or barrier. The word suggests a decisive moment when progress that was blocked finally occurs: {a breakthrough in cancer research}, {a major diplomatic breakthrough}. Scientists, negotiators, and researchers all pursue breakthroughs. The term can describe anything from solving a stubborn problem to a personal moment of clarity.

Breakthroughs are significant advances or discoveries that overcome obstacles previously blocking progress. The term implies a barrier that has been penetrated—whether in science, medicine, technology, or personal development. {Researchers announced a breakthrough in cancer treatment.} A breakthrough can also describe a sudden moment of understanding or success after prolonged effort: {After months of therapy, she finally had a breakthrough.} The word carries connotations of hard-won achievement rather than gradual improvement.

A breakup is the ending of a romantic relationship: {The breakup was hard on both of them}. The term extends to any dissolution or separation—the breakup of a {company}, of the {Soviet Union}, of {ice} on a frozen river in spring. To break up is to end such a relationship or to separate into pieces.

Breakups are endings of romantic relationships. The term implies emotional weight—a clean split rather than a gradual fade. A breakup can be mutual or one-sided, amicable or bitter: {She's still not over the breakup}. The word extends to any dissolution: {the breakup of the Soviet Union}, {the breakup of a business partnership}.

A breakwater is a barrier built to protect a harbor or shoreline from the force of waves. Breakwaters are typically made of stone, concrete, or timber, extending into the water to create calmer conditions for boats and prevent erosion: {The fishing boats sheltered behind the breakwater during the storm}.

A few words have an uncomfortable edge because they combine ordinary meanings with others that are taboo in certain contexts. Breast is certainly one of these words. The core meaning is to denote either of the pair of lactating glands in mature female primates (including humans). Discussion of women’s breasts in a non-medical context is associated with sexuality and arousal. No such issue arises in talk about chicken breasts, where the word denotes the mound of flesh on the front of a game bird.

To breastfeed is to feed an infant milk directly from the breast. The mother breastfeeds the baby; the baby breastfeeds from the mother—both constructions are standard. {She breastfed her daughter for eighteen months.} The practice is also called nursing. Breastfeeding in public remains socially contested in some places despite legal protections.

Breastfeeding is the practice of nursing an infant at the breast, providing milk directly from mother to child. The term covers both the act and the broader experience: {She's still breastfeeding}, {breastfeeding in public}, {the challenges of breastfeeding}. It can modify other nouns: {breastfeeding mother}, {breastfeeding support group}. The hyphenated form breast-feeding also appears.

A breastplate is a piece of armor covering the chest, worn historically by soldiers and knights for protection in battle. The term extends to similar protective gear worn by modern police or military personnel, and to the decorative chest piece worn by horses in ceremonial contexts. In Jewish tradition, a breastplate refers to the jeweled vestment worn by the high priest, set with twelve stones representing the tribes of Israel.

Breasts are the pair of soft, rounded organs on the front of a woman's chest that contain mammary glands for producing milk to feed infants. The word applies to the corresponding area on men as well, though male breasts lack the same development. Breast also refers to the chest area more generally, especially in older or literary usage: {He clutched the letter to his breast}. In poultry, the breast is the cut of meat from this part of the bird. To breast something is to face or push against it: {breast the waves}.

Breaststroke is a swimming stroke performed face-down, with the arms pushing forward together then sweeping outward while the legs execute a frog-like kick. It's the slowest of the competitive strokes but often the first taught to beginners: {She prefers breaststroke because she can keep her head above water}.

Breath is the air taken into and expelled from the lungs. A single instance is also a breath: {Take a deep breath}. By extension, breath suggests life itself—to draw breath is to be alive, and a dying breath is a final one. Breath can mean a slight movement of air: {not a breath of wind}. To {hold your breath} is to wait anxiously. Something {under your breath} is spoken very quietly. {In the same breath} means almost simultaneously, often of contradictory statements.

A breathalyser is a device that measures blood alcohol content from a breath sample. Police use breathalysers during traffic stops to determine whether drivers are legally impaired: {He failed the breathalyser and was arrested for drunk driving}. Also spelled breathalyzer, especially in American English.

A breathalyzer is a device that measures blood alcohol content from a breath sample. Police use breathalyzers during traffic stops to determine if drivers are legally intoxicated: {He failed the breathalyzer and was arrested for DUI}. The word comes from breath plus analyzer, originally a trademark now used generically.

To breathe is to draw air into the lungs and expel it—the fundamental act of respiration. Extended uses preserve the sense of air moving: fabrics that breathe allow air to pass through, wine breathes when exposed to air. To breathe a word is to speak very softly or not at all: {Don't breathe a word of this}. To {breathe down someone's neck} is to monitor them oppressively. {Breathe easy} means relax.

A breather is a brief pause or rest from activity: {Let's take a breather before we start the next section}. The word suggests catching one's breath—a short recovery period rather than an extended break. Someone who breathes is also a breather, though this use is uncommon outside phrases like {mouth breather}, which can be literal or insulting slang for someone dim or socially oblivious.

Breathing is the process of drawing air into and expelling it from the lungs. As an adjective, it means alive: {Every breathing creature on earth}. A breathing {space} or breathing {room} is a pause or margin that allows relief from pressure. {Heavy breathing} suggests exertion, fear, or sexual arousal. {Fire-breathing} describes dragons and aggressive people alike.

Breathless describes being out of breath, as after exertion: {She arrived breathless from running up the stairs}. It extends to states of intense emotion—excitement, anticipation, or awe—that feel like they stop your breath: {breathless with anticipation}, {The view left us breathless}. Breathless prose or narration moves rapidly without pause, creating urgency. Something breathless can also be airless or still: {the breathless summer heat}.

Breathtaking describes something so striking it seems to momentarily stop your breath—stunning beauty, unexpected news, or overwhelming experience: {The view from the summit was breathtaking}. The word implies sudden impact rather than gradual appreciation. A breathtaking performance astonishes; a breathtaking fall terrifies. The intensity has softened through overuse, sometimes meaning merely impressive.

Bred is the past tense and past participle of breed. Something bred has been raised or produced through controlled reproduction: {a horse bred for racing}, {born and bred in Texas}. It extends to upbringing and training: {well-bred} suggests good manners, {ill-bred} the opposite. In combinations, bred indicates origin or development: {purebred}, {crossbred}, {inbred}.

Breed refers to a distinct variety within a species, especially domestic animals developed through selective breeding: {a rare breed of cattle}, {What breed is your dog?} The verb means to produce offspring or raise animals for particular traits. Extended uses cover anything that generates or fosters: {Familiarity breeds contempt}. A breed of person shares distinctive characteristics: {a new breed of politician}. Well-bred and ill-bred describe manners and upbringing.

Breeding is the process of mating animals or plants to produce offspring, especially to develop desired traits: {selective breeding}, {a breeding program for endangered species}. The breeding season is when animals mate. Breeding also means upbringing and manners—someone of good breeding behaves with refinement and social grace. A breeding ground is where animals reproduce, or figuratively, where something develops: {a breeding ground for crime}.

Breeds functions as both noun and verb around the idea of producing offspring or types. A breed is a distinct variety within a species, developed through selective reproduction: {dog breeds}, {cattle breeds}. To breed is to produce offspring or to raise animals for particular traits. Figuratively, familiarity breeds contempt, and certain conditions breed problems. A person's breeding refers to their upbringing and manners: {good breeding}, {ill-bred}.

A breeze is a light, gentle wind—stronger than still air but not forceful enough to be called wind proper: {A cool breeze came off the lake}. Figuratively, a breeze is something effortless: {The exam was a breeze}. To breeze through is to accomplish something with casual ease. To breeze in or out is to arrive or leave in a carefree manner: {She breezed into the meeting ten minutes late}.

Breezy describes weather with a light, pleasant wind—stronger than calm but gentler than windy. The word extends to manner and tone: a breezy {attitude} is casual, carefree, cheerful. Breezy {conversation} flows easily without heaviness. The connotation is usually positive, though it can suggest someone is too casual for the situation: {Her breezy dismissal of the complaint annoyed him}.

Brew originally means to make beer—steeping grain, fermenting, producing alcohol. The process extends to tea and coffee: {Let the tea brew for five minutes}. A storm brews when it gathers force; trouble brews when it develops. As a noun, a brew is any beverage made by brewing, or informally any drink: {a cold brew}, {What's your favorite brew?}

Brewed is the past tense of brew, which means to make beer or other fermented drinks, or to prepare tea or coffee by steeping or boiling. {She brewed a fresh pot of coffee}. Figuratively, something brewed has been developing or forming gradually: {Trouble had been brewing for months}. {A storm brewed on the horizon}.

A brewer is someone who brews beer or ale, either professionally or as a hobbyist. The term applies to individuals and by extension to companies: {Anheuser-Busch is one of the world's largest brewers}. A brewer's yeast is the strain used in fermentation, also sold as a nutritional supplement.

Brewers are people or companies that brew beer or other fermented beverages. The term covers everything from craft brewery owners to industrial beverage manufacturers: {Local brewers have transformed the city's warehouse district}. Brewer's yeast is the strain used in fermentation, also sold as a nutritional supplement. (Capitalized Brewers refers to the Milwaukee baseball team.)

A brewery is a facility where beer is made. The term covers operations of all sizes, from industrial plants producing millions of barrels to small craft breweries and brewpubs that serve their beer on-site. {We toured a local brewery and sampled their seasonal ales.}

Brewing is the process of making beer or ale by steeping, boiling, and fermenting grain and hops. The term extends to making tea or coffee by steeping: {The coffee is brewing}. Figuratively, something brewing is developing or gathering force, usually something ominous: {There's trouble brewing}, {A storm is brewing on the horizon}.

Brews is the plural of brew and the third-person singular verb form. A brew is a batch of beer or other fermented drink, or any concoction that has steeped: {local craft brews}, {a witch's brew}. To brew is to make such drinks, or more broadly to develop or gather strength: {A storm is brewing}, {Trouble brews when those two get together}.

A bribe is money or something else of value given to influence someone's actions, especially to make an official act corruptly: {The judge accepted bribes from defendants}. The verb bribe means to offer such inducements: {They tried to bribe the inspector}. Lighter uses describe small rewards for cooperation: {I bribed the kids with ice cream to behave}.

Bribed is the past tense of bribe—to offer money or favors to influence someone's actions, especially to get them to act dishonestly or against their duties: {The official was bribed to approve the permit}. Someone who has been bribed has accepted such an inducement: {The jury was bribed}.

Bribery is the act of offering, giving, or accepting something of value to influence someone's actions—especially an official's decisions. The bribe might be money, gifts, or favors: {The senator was convicted of bribery}. Bribery corrupts institutions by substituting private incentives for public duty. The word covers both sides of the transaction: giving and receiving.

Bribes are payments or favors offered to influence someone's actions, typically to get them to act dishonestly or against their duties: {The official accepted bribes from contractors}. The singular bribe works as both noun and verb—to bribe someone is to offer such inducement. Bribes range from cash to gifts to promises of future benefit. The word carries inherent disapproval; people rarely describe their own payments as bribes.

Bribing is offering money, gifts, or favors to influence someone's actions, especially to get them to act improperly or illegally. The word implies corruption—inducing someone to betray a duty or trust: {He was caught bribing a judge}. Bribing can be playful when the stakes are low: {I'm bribing the kids with ice cream to behave}.

A brick is a rectangular block of fired clay used for building walls, paths, and other structures. Bricks are laid in rows and bonded with mortar, and the term extends to anything brick-shaped: a brick of cheese, a brick of cash. As slang, brick describes a failed shot in basketball that clangs off the rim, or an electronic device so broken it's useful only as a paperweight. To brick a phone is to render it unusable. Calling someone a brick means they're dependable and solid.

Bricked describes an electronic device rendered completely unusable—as functional as a brick. A phone, game console, or computer becomes bricked when a failed software update, botched modification, or corrupted firmware leaves it unable to start: {I tried to jailbreak my phone and bricked it}. The term emerged from tech communities where tinkering sometimes produced expensive paperweights.

Bricks are rectangular blocks of fired clay used for building walls, paths, and structures. The standard shape makes them stackable and easy to handle. Figuratively, to {shit bricks} is to be terrified. A {brick} can be a dependable person, or a phone or device rendered useless: {I updated the firmware and bricked my phone}.

Bridal means relating to a bride or wedding: {bridal gown}, {bridal shower}, {bridal party}. The word functions almost exclusively as an adjective, though it occasionally appears as a noun for wedding festivities. Despite sounding identical to bridle (the horse equipment), the words have different origins and meanings.

A bride is a woman on her wedding day or in the period just before and after marriage. The term applies from engagement through the ceremony and briefly beyond: {The bride wore her grandmother's veil}. Bridal relates to brides and weddings: {bridal shower}, {bridal party}. A bride-to-be is an engaged woman.

Brides is the plural of bride, a woman about to be married or recently married. The word appears frequently in contexts involving wedding planning, ceremonies, and the wedding industry. A bridal party typically includes bridesmaids who attend to the bride. {The brides were all smiles as they posed for photos after the ceremony.} In same-sex weddings, both partners may be referred to as brides if they are women.

A bridesmaid is a woman who attends the bride at a wedding, typically helping with preparations and standing alongside her during the ceremony. Bridesmaids traditionally wear matching dresses chosen by the bride. The phrase {always a bridesmaid, never a bride} describes someone who helps others succeed but never achieves success themselves.
