Bridesmaids are women who attend a bride at her wedding, typically friends or relatives who participate in the ceremony and help with preparations. They traditionally wear matching dresses and stand beside the bride during the vows: {She asked her college roommate to be one of her bridesmaids}. The singular bridesmaid refers to one such attendant.

A bridezilla is a bride-to-be who becomes obsessively demanding or difficult while planning her wedding. The blend of bride and Godzilla suggests someone who has transformed into a monster, terrorizing vendors, bridesmaids, and family members with unreasonable expectations: {My sister turned into a total bridezilla—she screamed at the florist for twenty minutes}. The term is usually disparaging but sometimes used self-deprecatingly.

A bridge is a structure that carries a road or path over water or some other obstacle or depression. This connecting feature in the meaning of bridge gives rise to many other meanings that share an element of joining or spanning two things that would otherwise be separate: The halfway house serves a bridge between addiction and the return to society. Bridge can also denote an anatomical feature, a dental appliance, or a passage in music, all of which form important connections. As a verb, bridge means to connect: a grant that will bridge the gap in funding. The name of the card game bridge is separately derived.

Bridges is the plural of bridge—structures spanning gaps to allow passage across rivers, valleys, or other obstacles. Beyond physical crossings, bridges metaphorically connect disparate things: {building bridges between communities}, {bridges between disciplines}. In dentistry, a bridge is a false tooth anchored to adjacent teeth. In music, a bridge is a passage connecting two sections of a song.

A bridle is the headgear used to control a horse, consisting of straps, bit, and reins. The rider uses it to direct the animal's movement. To bridle a horse is to put this gear on. Figuratively, to bridle something is to restrain or control it: {She bridled her temper}. To bridle at something is to react with indignation, like a horse jerking its head back: {He bridled at the suggestion that he'd cheated}.

Brie is a soft French cheese with a white edible rind and creamy interior. It ripens from the outside in, becoming increasingly runny as it ages. Brie is typically served at room temperature, often with crackers or fruit: {We brought a wheel of brie to the party}.

All meanings of brief contain the underlying idea of shortness, either in length or duration. A brief report is short. When you brief someone, you convey necessary information. The information may be called a brief, especially if it is in written form. In law, a brief is a statement of a case. Briefs are a kind of underwear that fit closer to the body than boxers and do not cover the leg.

A briefcase is a flat, rectangular case with a handle, used for carrying documents, papers, and other work-related materials. The term evokes professional or business contexts, and briefcases are associated with lawyers, executives, and office workers. Modern briefcases may include compartments for laptops and other electronics. {He grabbed his briefcase and headed to the meeting.}

A briefing is a meeting or document in which essential information is conveyed, typically to prepare someone for an action or decision. The term suggests efficiency and purpose—briefings are meant to be brief. Government officials hold press briefings to update journalists, military commanders conduct mission briefings before operations, and executives receive briefings before important meetings. {The intelligence briefing lasted twenty minutes.} To brief someone is to give them such information.

Briefs are short, close-fitting underpants without leg extensions—the classic underwear style as opposed to boxers. The word also refers to short written summaries, especially legal documents outlining arguments for a case: {The lawyer filed a brief with the court}. To brief someone is to give them essential information before an event or task: {The general briefed the troops on the mission}.

A brig is a two-masted sailing vessel with square sails on both masts. In naval and military usage, a brig is a jail or detention facility, especially one aboard a ship or at a military installation: {They threw him in the brig for insubordination}. The prison sense likely derives from the practice of confining offenders on such vessels.

A brigade is a military unit, typically comprising several battalions and forming part of a division. The term extends to organized groups working toward a common purpose: {fire brigade}, {bucket brigade}. It can describe any coordinated team effort: {The cleanup brigade tackled the mess after the party}. To brigade is to form into a brigade or group together.

Bright describes something that gives off or reflects strong light: {a bright sun}, {bright colors}, {a bright smile}. The word extends to intelligence—a bright student is quick and clever. Bright can mean cheerful or promising: {a bright future}, {looking on the bright side}. To arrive {bright and early} is to show up promptly, alert and ready.

Brighten means to make or become lighter, more luminous, or more vivid. The sun brightens a room when clouds part; a fresh coat of paint brightens dull walls. The word extends naturally to mood and demeanor: {Her face brightened when she heard the news.} To brighten up a space is to add light, color, or cheerful touches. Things that brighten your day lift your spirits or improve your outlook.

Brightness is the quality of emitting or reflecting light. A room has brightness when sunlight floods it; a screen's brightness can be adjusted. The word extends to vividness of color and to mental quickness: {the brightness of her smile}, {a student of unusual brightness}. Brightness also describes cheerfulness or optimism: {Despite everything, she maintained her brightness}.

Brilliance is exceptional brightness or radiance: {the brilliance of the summer sun}, {diamonds prized for their brilliance}. Extended to mental qualities, it means outstanding intelligence or talent: {Her brilliance in mathematics was evident early}. A brilliant performance or idea displays remarkable skill or insight. The word carries connotations of dazzling effect—something that impresses or even overwhelms.

Brilliant describes intense light or exceptional quality. A brilliant sun blazes; brilliant diamonds catch and scatter light. Extended to intellect, brilliant means exceptionally clever or talented: {a brilliant scientist}, {a brilliant idea}. British speakers use it as an enthusiastic term of approval: {That's brilliant!} The noun brilliance covers both radiance and mental sharpness.

The brim is the projecting edge of a hat, the part that shades your face. More generally, a brim is the upper edge of a container: {The cup was filled to the brim}. To brim is to be full to the point of overflowing: {Her eyes brimmed with tears}. {He was brimming with enthusiasm}.

Brimstone is an old name for sulfur—the yellow mineral that burns with a choking smell. The word survives mainly in the phrase {fire and brimstone}, evoking hellfire and divine punishment in religious rhetoric: {The preacher delivered a fire-and-brimstone sermon}. A brimstone butterfly is bright yellow, like the element.

Brine is water saturated with salt—the liquid in which pickles sit, the ocean itself. To brine meat is to soak it in salted water, tenderizing and flavoring it before cooking: {I brined the turkey overnight}. Brine also describes any strong saline solution used in food preservation or industrial processes.

Bring is a simple and frequent verb that packs a lot into a few letters. Most uses of bring involve the idea of motion toward the speaker or some other point of reference, as well as accompaniment. Did you bring your guitar with you? When a phrasal particle is added to bring, the core meaning stretches considerably: What brought about their decision to leave? Please don’t bring up that subject again. The verb most closely opposite to bring is take.

Brink is the edge of a steep place—the brink of a cliff, the brink of a precipice. The word almost always appears figuratively: {on the brink of war}, {on the brink of disaster}, {on the brink of a breakthrough}. It suggests the moment just before something significant happens, often something dangerous or transformative.

Brinkmanship is the practice of pushing a dangerous situation to the edge of disaster to achieve an advantage, especially in politics or diplomacy. The term evokes standing at the brink of a cliff—going as far as possible without falling. During the Cold War, nuclear brinkmanship meant threatening catastrophic war to force concessions: {The Cuban Missile Crisis was brinkmanship at its most terrifying}. The word implies calculated risk, though critics suggest the calculation is often reckless.

Brinksmanship is the practice of pushing a dangerous situation to the edge of disaster to achieve an advantage. The term emerged during Cold War nuclear diplomacy, where nations threatened catastrophic action to extract concessions: {The Cuban Missile Crisis was brinksmanship at its most terrifying}. Now applied to any high-stakes negotiation where one party risks mutual destruction to win: {The debt ceiling debate devolved into fiscal brinksmanship}. Also spelled brinkmanship.

Brisk describes something quick, energetic, and efficient. A brisk {walk} is faster than a stroll. Brisk {business} means trade is lively. Brisk {weather} is cool and invigorating, not bitter. A brisk {manner} suggests someone efficient but perhaps curt—getting things done without lingering on pleasantries.

Brisket is a cut of beef from the breast or lower chest of the animal. The meat is tough with significant connective tissue, making it ideal for slow cooking methods—braising, smoking, or pot roasting. In American barbecue, smoked brisket is a centerpiece: {We waited three hours for brisket at that Austin joint}. In Jewish cuisine, braised brisket is traditional for holidays.

Bristle is a short, stiff hair or fiber—the kind found on a pig's back, a toothbrush, or a man's unshaven chin. To bristle is to raise these hairs, as an animal does when threatened, which extends to any display of defensiveness or hostility: {She bristled at the suggestion that she'd been careless}. Something bristling with objects has many of them projecting outward: {a rooftop bristling with antennas}.

Bristles are short, stiff hairs or fibers—the kind found on a brush, a pig's back, or an unshaved chin. The verb means to stand up stiffly, like hackles raised in alarm: {The dog bristled at the stranger}. More often figurative: to bristle is to react with visible irritation or defensiveness: {She bristled at the suggestion that she was unqualified}.

Bristling describes something standing stiffly upright, like the raised hairs on an angry animal's back. A bristling {beard} is thick and coarse. Bristling with something means densely packed or armed: {a fortress bristling with cannons}, {a contract bristling with legal traps}. Someone bristling is visibly offended or defensive, their hackles metaphorically raised: {She bristled at the suggestion}.

Brittle describes something hard but easily broken—it snaps or shatters rather than bending: {brittle bones}, {brittle fingernails}, {The pages had grown brittle with age}. Figuratively, brittle applies to things that seem stable but lack resilience: a brittle {economy}, a brittle {alliance}. A brittle {laugh} or brittle {smile} sounds forced, masking tension or fragility underneath. Peanut brittle is a hard candy that breaks into shards.

Bro is informal for brother, used both for actual siblings and as casual address between men: {What's up, bro?} The term signals male friendship or solidarity. In contemporary use, bro often characterizes a type of young man associated with sports culture, fraternity life, and boisterous behavior: {total bro energy}, {bro culture}. The related adjective bro-y describes anything exhibiting these qualities.

Broad means wide or expansive: a broad {river}, broad {shoulders}, a broad {smile}. Extended uses suggest range or inclusiveness: broad {appeal}, a broad {spectrum} of opinions. In broad {daylight} means openly visible. Broad can also mean general rather than detailed: a broad {outline}. As a noun, broad is dated slang for a woman, now considered dismissive or offensive.

Broadcast originally meant to scatter seed widely by hand, and the sense of wide distribution persists in all its uses. To broadcast is to transmit radio or television signals to a large audience, or more generally to spread information widely: {The network will broadcast the game live}, {Don't broadcast my personal business}. As a noun, a broadcast is a radio or television program. The past tense is broadcast or broadcasted, with broadcast preferred.

A broadcaster is a person or organization that transmits programs by radio or television. The term covers both the on-air talent—news anchors, commentators, hosts—and the companies that own and operate stations or networks. {She worked as a broadcaster for thirty years before retiring.} In a more general sense, broadcaster can describe anyone who disseminates information widely, though this usage is less common than the media-specific meaning.

Broadcasting is the transmission of audio or video content to a wide audience through radio, television, or the internet. The term comes from agricultural scattering of seeds—casting broadly rather than in rows—and retains that sense of dispersal to many recipients at once. A broadcaster sends; viewers or listeners receive. The word also applies to spreading information widely: {He was broadcasting our business to everyone who would listen}.

Broadcasts are transmissions sent out over radio, television, or the internet—programs intended for wide reception rather than a specific recipient. The word also serves as a verb: a station broadcasts news, a network broadcasts a game. To broadcast information more generally is to spread it widely: {She broadcast the news to everyone she knew}. The agricultural sense—scattering seed broadly rather than in rows—came first.

A broadside is the side of a ship above the waterline, and by extension, a simultaneous firing of all guns on that side: {The frigate unleashed a broadside}. This sense of overwhelming force extends to verbal attacks—a broadside is a harsh, comprehensive criticism: {The senator delivered a broadside against the proposed legislation}. The word also names a large sheet of paper printed on one side, used historically for announcements or proclamations. As an adverb, broadside means sideways: {The truck hit the car broadside}.

Broadsides are verbal attacks or criticisms delivered forcefully and all at once, like a naval ship firing all its cannons from one side simultaneously: {The senator launched broadsides against the proposed legislation}. The original broadside was a ship's flank or a volley fired from it. A broadside is also a large sheet printed on one side only, used historically for announcements, ballads, or propaganda. To hit something broadside is to strike it squarely on the side: {The truck hit the car broadside}.

Broccoli is a green vegetable with dense clusters of flower buds on thick stalks. It belongs to the cabbage family and is typically eaten cooked, though raw broccoli appears in salads and with dips. The florets—the bushy tops—are the most prized part, though the stems are edible: {Eat your broccoli}. George H.W. Bush famously declared his hatred of it.

A brochure is a small booklet or pamphlet containing information or advertising about a product, service, place, or organization. Brochures are typically folded sheets of paper with text and images, designed to be handed out or displayed in racks. {Pick up a brochure at the visitor center.} Travel agencies, real estate offices, and college admissions departments rely heavily on brochures to present information in an accessible, portable format.

Broiling is cooking with intense direct heat from above, as in an oven's broiler setting. The word also describes oppressively hot weather: {We sat through a broiling afternoon without air conditioning}. As the present participle of broil, it functions as both verb form and adjective.

Broke is the past tense of break, but it has developed its own life as an adjective meaning without money: {I'm broke until payday}, {flat broke}, {dead broke}. To {go broke} is to lose all your money or go bankrupt. To {go for broke} is to risk everything on a single attempt. {If it ain't broke, don't fix it} advises against unnecessary changes to something that works.

Broken describes something that has been damaged, separated into pieces, or no longer functions: {a broken window}, {a broken leg}, {a broken phone}. The word extends to non-physical damage—a broken {promise} has been violated, a broken {home} split by divorce or conflict. Someone who is broken has been emotionally devastated or defeated: {He was a broken man after the scandal}. Broken speech or English is halting or imperfect. A broken {record} repeats endlessly.

Brokenhearted describes the state of overwhelming grief or sorrow, typically from romantic loss or rejection. Someone whose heart has been broken feels deep emotional pain, as if the organ of feeling itself has been damaged. The term applies most naturally to romantic disappointment—being dumped, betrayed, or losing a loved one—but extends to any profound loss: {She was brokenhearted when her dog died}. The spelling varies between one word and hyphenated broken-hearted.

A broker is a person or firm that arranges transactions between buyers and sellers, typically earning a commission for the service. Real estate brokers help people buy and sell property; stockbrokers execute trades in financial markets; insurance brokers find policies for clients. The term extends to anyone who negotiates or mediates deals: {She brokered a peace agreement between the factions}. To broker something is to arrange or negotiate it, often involving parties who might not otherwise connect directly.

A bromance is a close, affectionate friendship between men that doesn't involve sex or romance. The word blends "brother" and "romance" to capture emotional intimacy that goes beyond casual buddies: {Those two have a serious bromance going—they text constantly and finish each other's sentences}. The term emerged in the early 2000s as cultural attitudes toward male friendship loosened.

A bronco is an untrained or half-wild horse, especially one prone to bucking. The word comes from Spanish and is associated with the American West, where breaking broncos was essential ranch work. Bronco busting—riding an unbroken horse until it accepts a rider—became a staple of rodeo competition. The term occasionally applies to any spirited, unruly horse.

Broncos is the plural of bronco, an untamed or half-tamed horse, especially one used in rodeos for bucking competitions: {He rode broncos on the circuit for years}. The word comes from Spanish for "rough" or "wild." Broncos also names professional sports teams, most notably the NFL's Denver Broncos.

Brontosaurus is a large, long-necked dinosaur that lived during the Jurassic period—one of the iconic plant-eating giants with a massive body, pillar-like legs, and whip-like tail. The name was once considered invalid by scientists who classified it under Apatosaurus, but recent research has restored it as a distinct genus. In popular culture, brontosaurus remains the quintessential gentle giant of prehistory: {The museum's brontosaurus skeleton towered over the visitors}.

Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin with a dark gold color, frequently used in statuary. In rankings in which metals represent values, it is usually third, behind gold and silver: The Olympian was awarded the bronze medal in figure skating. Bronze is also popular as a verb and adjective to describe fair people’s skin that is agreeably tanned. The Bronze Age was a period of antiquity (~4000 to 3000 BCE) when people used bronze widely. To bronze something is to give it the color or appearance of bronze.

A brooch is an ornamental pin worn on clothing, typically at the collar, lapel, or chest. Unlike functional pins, brooches are decorative jewelry, often featuring gemstones, enamel, or intricate metalwork: {She wore her grandmother's cameo brooch}. The word rhymes with "coach," not "pooch."

Brood works both as noun and verb around the idea of offspring and dwelling on them. A brood is a group of young hatched or born together: {a brood of chicks}, {a brood of puppies}. Extended humorously to human children: {She arrived with her whole brood}. To brood is to sit on eggs to hatch them, or more commonly, to dwell moodily on something troubling: {He brooded over the insult for days}. A brooding person is darkly thoughtful, often attractively so: {his brooding intensity}.

Brooding as an adjective describes a dark, moody quality—either in atmosphere or temperament. A brooding sky threatens storms; a brooding person seems lost in troubled or melancholic thought. The verb brood means to dwell on dark thoughts or to sit on eggs to hatch them, and the noun brood refers to a group of offspring, especially chicks. {He sat brooding over his failed marriage.} {The hen brooded her eggs in the corner of the barn.}

Broods serves as both noun and verb around the idea of offspring and anxious dwelling. A brood is a group of young animals, especially birds hatched together: {a brood of chicks}. By extension, it can refer humorously to someone's children: {She arrived with her whole brood}. To brood is to sit on eggs to hatch them, or figuratively, to think anxiously about something for a long time: {He brooded over the insult for days}. A brooding person dwells on dark thoughts; a brooding sky threatens storms.

Broody describes a hen ready to sit on eggs and hatch them—she stops laying and becomes protective of her nest. Extended to people, broody means wanting to have a baby: {She's been feeling broody since her sister had twins}. A separate sense means moody and withdrawn, given to silent contemplation or sulking: {He sat in the corner looking broody}.

A brook is a small stream, typically one that flows through woods or countryside. The word appears often in pastoral or literary contexts and in place names. As a verb, brook means to tolerate or accept, almost always in negative constructions: {She would brook no interference in her affairs}. This sense suggests a refusal to endure something objectionable.

A broom is a long-handled brush used for sweeping floors and outdoor surfaces. The sweeping end traditionally consists of stiff plant fibers or straw bundled together, though modern brooms often use synthetic bristles. In folklore and fantasy, witches ride broomsticks through the sky. To {make a clean sweep} of something is to broom it figuratively—clearing everything away.

Brooms are long-handled cleaning tools with stiff bristles or fibers at one end, used for sweeping floors and other surfaces. The verb broom means to sweep with a broom. In curling, players broom the ice in front of a sliding stone to control its speed and direction. Broom also names a shrub with yellow flowers and slender branches that were traditionally used to make brooms.

A broomstick is the long wooden handle of a broom. In folklore and fantasy, witches fly on broomsticks, making them standard Halloween imagery: {The decoration showed a witch cackling on her broomstick}. Something described as thin as a broomstick is extremely slender.

Broomsticks are the long wooden handles of brooms. In folklore and fantasy, witches fly on broomsticks, straddling them like horses: {The witch mounted her broomstick and disappeared into the night}. In the Harry Potter universe, broomsticks are the standard vehicle for the sport of Quidditch.

Bros is the plural of bro, informal for brother or a male friend. The term evokes casual male bonding and friendship: {I'm hanging out with the bros tonight}. Bros often suggests a certain type of young man—athletic, sociable, perhaps fraternity-affiliated: {a bunch of bros at the sports bar}. The singular bro functions as a greeting or form of address between men.

Broth is a savory liquid made by simmering meat, fish, or vegetables in water. It serves as the base for soups, stews, and sauces, or is consumed on its own: {chicken broth}, {beef broth}. Broth differs from stock mainly in that stock relies more heavily on bones for body and gelatin. {She sipped warm broth while recovering from the flu.}

A brothel is a building where people pay to have sex with prostitutes. The word is slightly formal; in casual speech, whorehouse is more common. Brothels may be legal or illegal depending on jurisdiction: {The police raided an illegal brothel downtown}. {Nevada is the only U.S. state with legal brothels.}

Brothels are establishments where people pay for sexual services. The word carries a seedy, old-world connotation—you're more likely to encounter it in historical contexts or fiction than in contemporary news, where terms like massage parlor or sex work operate as euphemisms or reframings. {The police raided a brothel on the outskirts of town.}

A brother is a male who shares at least one parent with another person. The term extends to men bound by shared membership or commitment: fraternity brothers, brothers in arms, fellow monks. Black Americans use brother (often shortened to bro) as a term of solidarity among men. To brother someone is to treat them as kin. {He's been like a brother to me.}

Brotherhood is the bond between brothers, extended to any close fellowship among men who share a purpose, profession, or identity: {the brotherhood of firefighters}, {a brotherhood of artists}. It can name an organization built on such bonds—fraternities, labor unions, religious orders. More abstractly, brotherhood suggests universal human kinship: {the brotherhood of man}.

Brotherly describes behavior or feelings characteristic of a brother toward a sibling—affectionate, protective, supportive. {He gave her some brotherly advice}. The word often distinguishes familial warmth from romantic interest: {Their relationship was strictly brotherly}. Brotherly love is deep caring without sexual dimension, famously associated with Philadelphia, "the city of brotherly love."

Brothers are males who share at least one parent. The term extends to men bound by close friendship, shared experience, or common cause: {brothers in arms}, {fraternity brothers}. In religious contexts, brothers are male members of a monastic order or fellow congregants. African American usage of {brother} as a term of solidarity among Black men gives the plural special cultural weight: {The brothers were looking out for each other}.

A brouhaha is a noisy commotion or uproar, typically over something trivial: {The new policy caused quite a brouhaha at the meeting}. The word suggests excited fuss that exceeds the importance of whatever sparked it—a tempest in a teapot.

The brow is the forehead or the ridge above the eye where the eyebrow grows. By extension, it describes the top edge of a slope or hill: {We crested the brow of the hill}. A furrowed brow suggests worry or concentration. Brow appears in compounds describing intellectual pretension: highbrow, lowbrow, middlebrow.

Brown is a color produced by mixing red, yellow, and black—the color of earth, wood, chocolate, and coffee. As an adjective, brown describes this color or things having it: {brown eyes}, {brown sugar}. To brown something is to cook it until it turns brown: {Brown the meat before adding vegetables}. Brown can also describe skin tone, either from sun exposure or natural complexion. In compounds: {brownstone}, {brownie}, {brown-bag}. (Capitalized Brown is a surname.)

A brownie is a small, rich, chocolate cake, typically dense and chewy, cut into squares or rectangles. Brownies are also junior members of the Girl Scouts or Girl Guides, typically ages six to eight, who wear brown uniforms. In folklore, a brownie is a helpful household spirit that performs chores at night. To earn brownie points is to gain favor through good deeds or flattery, often with slightly cynical overtones: {He's just trying to score brownie points with the boss}.

Brownies are dense, fudgy chocolate squares—a classic American dessert somewhere between cake and cookie: {She brought a pan of brownies to the potluck}. In folklore, brownies are helpful household spirits who do chores at night. Brownie is also a junior level of Girl Scouts or Girl Guides, for girls roughly ages six to eight. The plural sometimes refers to brown fat cells in biology.

Brownnose means to curry favor through excessive flattery or obsequious attention—the image being of having one's nose up someone's backside. The term is mildly vulgar but widely used: {He brownosed his way to a promotion}. As a noun, a brownnose is someone who engages in such behavior. Also spelled brown-nose.

A brownnoser is someone who flatters or fawns over authority figures to gain favor—a sycophant or toady. The term is mildly vulgar, evoking the image of having one's nose up someone's rear end: {The other employees resented the brownnoser who always agreed with the boss}. The verb is brownnose; the practice is brownnosing.

Brownnosing is currying favor through excessive flattery or obsequious attention to someone in authority. The image is crude but vivid—putting one's nose so far up someone's backside that it comes away brown. A brownnoser is someone who habitually does this: {He got promoted by brownnosing the boss}. The term is mildly vulgar but widely used.

A brownshirt is a member of a fascist organization, originally referring to the Sturmabteilung (SA), the paramilitary wing of the Nazi Party in Germany whose members wore brown uniforms. The term now serves as a general label for any thuggish enforcer of authoritarian politics or someone who uses intimidation and violence for political ends. {The protesters called the security forces brownshirts.} The word is always pejorative when applied to contemporary figures.

A brownstone is a row house built of or faced with brown sandstone, particularly the distinctive reddish-brown variety quarried in the northeastern United States. The term evokes urban neighborhoods in New York City and other Eastern cities where these buildings line entire blocks: {They bought a brownstone in Brooklyn}. The word often suggests genteel city living, whether preserved historic elegance or gentrified renovation.

Brows are eyebrows—the arched lines of hair above the eyes. The word appears in expressions about facial movement conveying emotion: {She raised her brows in surprise}, {His brows furrowed in concentration}. A brow is also a forehead, or the projecting upper edge of a steep place: {the brow of the hill}.

Browse means to look through things casually, without a specific goal—scanning shelves in a bookstore, flipping through a magazine, or wandering a market: {I browsed the antique shops all afternoon}. In computing, to browse is to navigate websites or files: {browsing the internet}. Animals browse when they feed on leaves and shoots rather than grass. A browser is software for viewing web pages, or an animal that browses.

A browser is software for accessing and navigating the internet—Chrome, Safari, Firefox. The word comes from browse, meaning to look through things casually, as animals browse on vegetation or shoppers browse in stores. A browser in a shop looks without necessarily buying: {The store was full of browsers but few buyers}.

Browsers are programs for accessing the internet—web browsers like Chrome, Safari, or Firefox that let you view websites and navigate between pages. The term comes from the verb browse, suggesting casual exploration rather than focused searching. Outside computing, a browser is simply someone who browses: {The shop was full of browsers, not buyers}.

Browsing is looking through things casually without a specific goal—flipping through a magazine, wandering a bookstore, or scanning websites. Animals browse when they feed on leaves and shoots rather than grass. The word suggests leisurely, uncommitted attention: {I'm just browsing} signals no intent to buy. Internet browsing has become the dominant sense, describing navigation through web pages.

A bruise is a discolored area where blood has pooled under the skin after an impact, typically progressing through purple, blue, and yellow as it heals. Fruit bruises similarly—soft spots from mishandling. The verb means to cause such damage: {I bruised my knee on the coffee table}. Figuratively, a bruised ego or bruised feelings have been hurt by criticism or rejection.

Bruised describes something that has suffered a bruise—discolored and tender from impact without breaking the skin. Fruit becomes bruised when bumped or dropped, showing soft dark spots. The word extends naturally to feelings: a bruised {ego}, bruised {pride}. {She came away from the interview feeling bruised but not defeated.}

A bruiser is a big, tough person—someone who looks like they could handle themselves in a fight. The word suggests physical intimidation without necessarily implying violence: {The bouncer was a real bruiser}. It can be used affectionately for a rough-and-tumble child or admiringly for an imposing athlete.

Bruises are discolored marks on the skin caused by blood pooling under the surface after an impact. The plural often appears where singular would work: {She had bruises on her arms}. As a verb, bruises means causes such marks or handles roughly: {That kind of talk bruises his ego}. Fruit bruises easily, showing dark spots where damaged.

Bruising describes something harsh, damaging, or physically punishing: a bruising {defeat}, a bruising {schedule}, a bruising {tackle}. The word suggests impact that leaves marks—literal or figurative. A bruising {battle} may be won, but not without cost. As a noun, bruising refers to the discoloration from damaged tissue: {There was significant bruising around the eye}.

Brunch is a meal eaten late in the morning that combines breakfast and lunch, typically on weekends. It often features eggs, pastries, and alcoholic drinks like mimosas or Bloody Marys: {We're meeting for brunch at eleven}. The word blends breakfast and lunch. To brunch is to eat this meal: {Let's brunch on Sunday}.

A brunette is a person, usually a woman, with brown or dark hair. The word carries a feminine association—a dark-haired man is more often called simply dark-haired than a brunet. {She's a natural brunette who dyes her hair blonde}. As an adjective: {brunette hair}, {a brunette actress}.

Bruschetta is an Italian appetizer of grilled bread rubbed with garlic and drizzled with olive oil, typically topped with diced tomatoes, basil, and seasonings. The bread is toasted until crisp, then loaded with fresh toppings: {We ordered bruschetta to start}. The word is Italian, properly pronounced with a hard K sound, though the soft CH pronunciation is common in English.

Brush, a noun and verb, has three distinct meanings. The implement with bristles comes in many different types (toothbrush, paintbrush, hairbrush) and when you use one of these, you brush. Vegetation that is close to the ground is called brush. Finally, a brief encounter or conflict with someone or something is a brush; or you can say that you brush up against such a thing or person.

Brushes is the plural of brush—tools with bristles used for cleaning, painting, or grooming: {She keeps her brushes in a jar by the easel}. In music, brushes are wire implements drummers use for a softer, swishing sound on cymbals and snare drums. The verb form means to sweep lightly or make brief contact: {He brushes past her in the hallway}. To give someone the brush-off is to dismiss them curtly.

Brutal describes actions, conditions, or qualities marked by extreme harshness, cruelty, or violence. A brutal {attack} is savage and merciless; brutal {honesty} is blunt to the point of being hurtful. Weather or physical conditions can be brutal when they're punishingly severe: {The brutal heat made outdoor work impossible}. In casual speech, brutal often emphasizes how difficult or unpleasant something is: {That exam was brutal}. The word suggests a roughness that disregards comfort or feeling.

Brutality is savage cruelty or violence, especially when inflicted by those with power over others: {police brutality}, {the brutality of the regime}. The word emphasizes not just harm but callousness—a disregard for suffering. Brutalities, in the plural, names specific acts: {the brutalities of war}.

To brutalize is to treat with cruelty or violence, often repeatedly: {Years of war had brutalized the population}. The word can mean to make brutal—hardening someone through exposure to violence—or simply to subject them to it. {Prison conditions brutalized inmates rather than rehabilitating them.} The British spelling is brutalise.

Brutalized is the past tense of brutalize, which means to subject someone to cruel, violent, or degrading treatment. A person who has been brutalized has suffered physical abuse or psychological trauma at the hands of others: {The prisoners were brutalized by their captors}. The word can also describe being made brutal or insensitive through exposure to violence: {soldiers brutalized by years of combat}. In British English, the spelling is typically brutalised.

A brute is a savage, violent creature—an animal or a person who behaves like one. The word emphasizes raw physical force without reason or compassion: {The brute attacked without warning}. As an adjective, brute describes strength or force that is purely physical and unrefined: {brute strength}, {brute force}. A brute fact is simply and undeniably there, requiring no explanation.

Brutes is the plural of brute—creatures lacking reason or refinement. Animals are brutes in contrast to humans; violent or cruel people are brutes in contrast to civilized ones. The word emphasizes raw physical force without intelligence or moral restraint: {Those brutes destroyed everything in their path}. As an adjective, brute modifies nouns to suggest sheer, unthinking power: {brute strength}, {brute force}.

A bubble is a thin sphere of liquid enclosing air or gas—soap bubbles, bubbles in boiling water. The verb means to form bubbles or rise in them: {The soup bubbled on the stove}. Figuratively, a bubble is something fragile or inflated beyond sustainable value: {the housing bubble}, {the tech bubble}. To {burst someone's bubble} is to disillusion them. A bubble can also be an isolated environment: {living in a bubble}, {the NBA bubble}.

Bubblegum is a soft, chewy candy designed to be blown into bubbles. The flavor—sweet, fruity, synthetic pink—has become its own category: {bubblegum-flavored lip gloss}. As an adjective, bubblegum describes things that are bright, saccharine, and aimed at children or teens: {bubblegum pop}, {bubblegum pink}. The connotation is lightweight, unchallenging, maybe disposable.

Bubbles are thin spheres of liquid enclosing air or gas, as in soap bubbles or the bubbles in champagne. The word extends to anything similarly round and hollow, or to any situation that swells impressively before bursting: {the housing bubble}, {the tech bubble}. To bubble is to form bubbles or rise in them: {Water bubbled up from the spring}. Something that bubbles over exceeds its container, literally or figuratively: {She was bubbling over with enthusiasm}.

Bubblewrap is plastic sheeting with air-filled pockets, used as protective packaging for fragile items. The bubbles cushion against shock during shipping. Popping the bubbles is a common idle pastime, satisfying enough that apps simulate the experience: {I spent ten minutes popping bubblewrap instead of unpacking}. Also spelled bubble wrap.

Bubbling describes the formation or movement of bubbles—small pockets of gas rising through liquid or emerging from a surface: {bubbling water}, {a bubbling stream}. The word extends to sounds that resemble this: {bubbling laughter}. Figuratively, bubbling suggests something barely contained and ready to emerge: {bubbling enthusiasm}, {anger bubbling beneath the surface}.

Bubbly describes something full of bubbles, especially sparkling wine or champagne: {Let's open a bottle of bubbly to celebrate}. Applied to personality, bubbly means cheerful, animated, and effervescent—someone whose energy seems to rise and fizz like carbonation: {She has a bubbly personality that lights up the room}.

A buccaneer is a pirate, specifically one of the sea raiders who preyed on Spanish ships and settlements in the Caribbean during the 17th century. The term now applies broadly to any pirate or, figuratively, to someone who operates with bold disregard for rules: {corporate buccaneers}, {a buccaneering approach to business}. The verb buccaneer means to act as a pirate or to pursue something aggressively and unscrupulously.

Buccaneers were pirates who operated in the Caribbean during the 17th century, raiding Spanish ships and settlements. The term now applies broadly to any pirates or, figuratively, to bold adventurers who operate outside conventional rules: {corporate buccaneers}, {financial buccaneers}. The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are an NFL team. A buccaneer buccaneers.

Buck has many jobs as noun, verb, adjective, and adverb. The male of various mammals is called a buck: The buck had eight-point antlers. So is a U.S. dollar: Lend me ten bucks. If a horse jumps with an arched back (sometimes throwing off a rider), it bucks. Something that bucks a trend runs counter to it. In the buck stops here, buck means responsibility. In fixed phrases like buck naked, buck means completely. Finally, buck may characterize the lowest rank or quality, as in a buck sergeant.

Buckaroo is a cowboy, especially one working in the Great Basin region of the western United States. The word comes from Spanish *vaquero* (cow herder) filtered through the ears of English speakers. It carries a rougher, more working-class connotation than cowboy: {The buckaroos rounded up strays at dawn}. In casual use, buckaroo is playful or affectionate, often directed at children: {Hey there, buckaroo}.

The handled container we call a bucket informs the other meanings of the word. A bucket is also the amount such a container can hold, or any appreciable amount: a bucket of water. It’s a notional storage space in computing, as well as a machine part that resembles a bucket: The front loader’s bucket scooped the dirt. The verb bucket is typically used only in reference to heavy rain, which is said to bucket down, but to bucket can also mean to move or drive very fast, or to transport in buckets.

Buckets is the plural of bucket—containers with handles for carrying liquids or materials. The word appears in phrases like {kick the buckets} (a confused plural of the idiom) and {buckets of rain}. In casual speech, buckets means a large quantity: {It's raining buckets}, {She cried buckets}. In basketball, buckets are successful shots: {He was getting buckets all night}.

Bucking is the action of a horse or similar animal jumping with an arched back and stiff legs, trying to throw off a rider: {The bronco was bucking wildly}. Extended to machinery, bucking describes jerky, uncontrolled movement: {The engine kept bucking}. To be bucking something is to resist or oppose it: {bucking the system}, {bucking the trend}. In forestry, bucking means cutting felled trees into logs.

A buckle is a clasp with a frame and prong, used to fasten straps or belts: {He tightened his belt buckle}. To buckle is to fasten with such a device: {Buckle your seatbelt}. The other buckle means to bend or collapse under pressure—knees buckle, metal buckles in heat, a bridge buckles. To {buckle down} is to apply oneself seriously to work. To {buckle under} is to yield to pressure.

Buckled describes something fastened with a buckle—a clasp with a frame and prong: {She buckled her seatbelt}. It also means bent, warped, or collapsed under pressure: {The metal buckled in the heat}, {His knees buckled}. Figuratively, to buckle is to yield or give way: {He finally buckled under the stress}. To {buckle down} is to apply oneself seriously to a task.

Buckles are clasps with frames and prongs used to fasten straps or belts: {She adjusted the buckles on her sandals}. To buckle is to fasten with such a device, or to bend or collapse under pressure: {The bridge buckled in the heat}, {His knees buckled}. To {buckle down} is to apply oneself seriously to a task. To {buckle under} is to yield to pressure.

Bucks is the plural of buck in its main senses: male deer, dollars, and the act of resisting. A hunter might bag several bucks in a season. {That'll cost you fifty bucks.} A horse that bucks repeatedly is said to be bucking, but the animal {bucks} when it does it once. To pass the buck is to shift responsibility; {The buck stops here} means someone accepts it. (Capitalized Bucks may refer to the Milwaukee basketball team.)

Buckskin is soft, pliable leather made from the hide of a deer or similar animal, traditionally used for clothing, gloves, and moccasins. The yellowish-tan color of this leather gives its name to a horse coat color—a buckskin horse has a tan body with black mane, tail, and lower legs. In the plural, buckskins are garments made from this leather: {a frontiersman in buckskins}.

A bud is a small growth on a plant that develops into a leaf, flower, or shoot. The word extends to anything in an early stage of development: {nipped in the bud} means stopped before it can grow. To bud is to produce buds or begin developing. Bud is also informal address between men, short for buddy: {Hey bud, how's it going?}

A rare lowercase spelling sometimes used when referring to the concept of an enlightened being in Buddhist tradition, rather than to Siddhartha Gautama specifically. In Buddhist thought, a buddha is any person who has achieved complete awakening: {The tradition holds that many buddhas have appeared throughout history}. The lowercase form emphasizes the category rather than the historical founder. (Capitalized Buddha refers to the founder of Buddhism.)

Buddies is the plural of buddy, a casual term for a friend or companion. The word carries warmth without formality, suggesting easygoing camaraderie rather than deep intimacy. People often use it to address a group of friends: {Hey buddies, want to grab lunch?} It can also describe people paired together for a shared activity or mutual support, as in {swim buddies} or {study buddies}.

Budding describes something in an early stage of development, showing promise but not yet mature. A budding {artist} or budding {romance} is just beginning to emerge. The word comes from the botanical sense—buds are the small growths on plants that will become leaves or flowers. To bud is to produce such growths, or figuratively, to begin developing: {Her interest in astronomy budded early}.

Buddy is an informal word for a friend or companion, suggesting easy camaraderie: {We've been buddies since high school}. It also serves as a casual form of address, sometimes friendly {(Hey buddy, good to see you!)}, sometimes condescending or confrontational {(Listen, buddy, I was here first)}. To buddy up is to pair off or become friendly with someone. The buddy system pairs people for safety or mutual support.

To budge is to move, usually slightly and often reluctantly. The word almost always appears in negative constructions: {The door wouldn't budge}, {She refused to budge on the price}. When something or someone won't budge, they remain stubbornly fixed in place or position. To budge someone is to get them to move or change their stance: {Nothing could budge him from his opinion}.

A budget is a plan for spending money over a period of time, allocating funds across categories like rent, food, and entertainment. Governments pass budgets; households keep them. As an adjective, budget means inexpensive or economy-class: {budget airline}, {budget hotel}. To budget is to plan expenditures or set aside money: {We budgeted for a new car}.
A budgie is a small Australian parakeet, popular as a pet for its bright plumage and ability to mimic speech. Short for budgerigar. {The budgie chirped from its cage.}

Budgies are small parakeets native to Australia, popular as household pets for their bright colors and ability to mimic speech. The word is a clipped form of budgerigar. {We had a pair of budgies growing up—one blue, one green.}

Buds is the plural of bud—the small swelling on a plant that develops into a leaf, flower, or shoot: {The trees are covered in buds}. Taste buds are sensory organs on the tongue. As slang, buds means friends or companions, from buddy: {Me and my buds are going to the game}. Buds also refers informally to cannabis flower: {He picked up some buds from the dispensary}.

Buff was originally a kind of buffalo leather. Other meanings, some quite divergent, can be traced back to that. Buff is a tannish color. If you’re in the buff, you have no clothes on. When you buff something, you polish it (perhaps using buff to do the job!). Finally, a fan or collector of something may also be a buff: My brother is a film buff. As a verb, buff is sometimes used like buffer and means to deaden or mitigate the force of something.

A buffalo is a large bovine mammal—either the Asian water buffalo, domesticated for agriculture, or the African Cape buffalo, a wild and dangerous animal. Americans often call the American bison a buffalo, though this is technically imprecise. The verb means to intimidate or bewilder: {Don't let them buffalo you into signing}. The famous sentence {Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo} uses all three parts of speech—noun, verb, and proper adjective—to demonstrate English syntax. (Capitalized Buffalo is the city in New York.)

The principle meanings of buffer share a common element of imposing a barrier or layer of protection, often temporary. Chemical buffers reduce the acidity of a substance. A buffer in computer memory sets aside data that may be used later. A physical buffer reduces the impact of a collision. The action of doing any of these things is to buffer. A buffer may also simply be something that buffs (polishes).

Buffering is the process of preloading data to ensure smooth playback or transmission. When streaming video or audio, buffering builds a reserve so interruptions in the data flow don't cause stuttering: {The video keeps buffering—my connection must be slow}. The familiar spinning circle has made buffering shorthand for any digital delay or loading state.

A buffet is a meal where food is set out on a table for guests to serve themselves, or the piece of furniture on which such food is displayed—typically a sideboard in a dining room. The word also names restaurants featuring self-service food stations: {an all-you-can-eat buffet}. Separately, to buffet is to strike repeatedly or be struck by forces: {Waves buffeted the ship}, {buffeted by criticism}. This verb, pronounced with stress on the second syllable, suggests being knocked about by circumstances beyond one's control.

Buffets has two pronunciations for two meanings. With stress on the second syllable, it's the verb form of buffet meaning to strike repeatedly or batter: {The wind buffets the shutters}; {She was buffeted by criticism}. With stress on the first syllable, it's the plural of buffet—a self-service meal or the furniture displaying it: {The hotel offers breakfast buffets}; {We hit several buffets in Vegas}.

A buffoon is a person who amuses others through crude, clownish behavior—pratfalls, exaggerated gestures, loud foolishness. The word carries contempt: calling someone a buffoon suggests they're undignified or ridiculous, whether intentionally or not. {He made a buffoon of himself at the party.} {The president surrounded himself with buffoons.}

Buffoonery is foolish or clownish behavior, the kind of antics that make others laugh or cringe. The word suggests exaggerated silliness rather than genuine wit: {His buffoonery at the party embarrassed his wife}. It often implies the behavior is inappropriate for the setting or beneath the person's dignity.

Buffoons are people who act foolishly or clownishly, often for comic effect. The word carries more contempt than *clown*—buffoons may not intend to be ridiculous: {The meeting devolved into chaos, run by buffoons who had no idea what they were doing}. A buffoon entertains others at the cost of dignity, whether knowingly or not.

Buffs are enthusiasts or devoted fans of a particular subject: {film buffs}, {history buffs}, {wine buffs}. The term suggests amateur expertise—someone who knows a lot about something without being a professional. Separately, buffs are the plural of buff in its other senses: a yellowish-tan color, a soft polishing cloth, or the verb meaning to polish to a shine. In gaming slang, buffs are temporary enhancements to a character's abilities: {The healer cast buffs on the whole party}.

Small creatures whose company we do not enjoy (insects, viruses, bacteria) are all called bugs. A figurative bug is one that prevents a computer program from executing properly. A bug can also be a hidden microphone; if you place one of these in a room, you bug the room. You can also bug a person by annoying them. If something bugs or bugs out, it protrudes or sticks out from its surroundings – either literally or metaphorically: Her eyes bugged out in disbelief.

Bugbears are sources of persistent annoyance, dread, or irritation—problems that loom larger than they perhaps should: {Late fees are a bugbear for library patrons}, {Grammar mistakes are his particular bugbear}. The word originally referred to a goblin or imaginary creature invoked to frighten children, and retains a sense of something feared out of proportion to its actual threat.

Bugged has two main senses. Something bugged is fitted with a hidden listening device: {The room was bugged}. More commonly, bugged describes being annoyed or bothered: {I'm still bugged by what she said}. The adjective comes from the verb bug, meaning to pester or to plant surveillance equipment.

Bugger is a British and Commonwealth term with a range from serious to almost affectionate. Originally it meant someone who practices buggery (anal sex), from medieval accusations against Bulgarian heretics. As a noun, bugger now usually means a person in a neutral or sympathetic way: {The poor bugger lost his job}. {You lucky bugger}. As an exclamation, it expresses frustration: {Oh bugger, I've missed the train}. As a verb, it can mean to ruin: {That's buggered the whole plan}. Common phrases include {bugger off} (go away), {bugger all} (nothing whatsoever), and {I'll be buggered} (expression of surprise). The word is mild enough for casual speech but still vulgar.

Bugging is the act of secretly installing listening devices to record conversations: {The FBI was bugging his office}. More commonly, bugging means persistently annoying someone: {Stop bugging me about it}. The informal sense dominates everyday speech—a person or thing that bugs you gets under your skin until you can't ignore it.

Buggy describes something infested with bugs—insects or software errors. Code that's buggy has glitches: {The app is too buggy to release}. A buggy summer night swarms with mosquitoes. As a noun, a buggy is a light horse-drawn carriage, still used by Amish communities, or a small wheeled vehicle: {shopping buggy}, {baby buggy}, {golf buggy}.

A bugle is a brass instrument without valves, used primarily for military signals and ceremonies: {A bugle sounded reveille at dawn}. The limited notes a bugle can play give its calls—taps, charge, retreat—their distinctive character. To bugle is to play this instrument or, of elk, to make a similar high-pitched call during mating season.

Bugs are insects and similar small creatures—beetles, ants, spiders, and the like. In computing, a bug is a flaw in software that causes errors or unexpected behavior: {We found a bug in the code}. A bug can also be a hidden microphone for surveillance: {The room was bugged}. To bug someone is to annoy them persistently: {Stop bugging me}. Something that bugs you gets under your skin. (Capitalized Bugs refers to the cartoon rabbit.)

Build means to construct or assemble something from parts or materials: {build a house}, {build a fire}, {build a website}. The meaning extends to gradual development: {build a career}, {build trust}, {build momentum}. As a noun, build describes someone's physical frame: {a stocky build}, {an athletic build}. A build is also a particular version of software under development. To {build on} something is to use it as a foundation for further progress.

A builder is someone who constructs things—houses, bridges, relationships, empires. The term applies literally to construction workers and contractors: {We hired a builder to renovate the kitchen}. It extends to anyone who creates or develops something over time: {a builder of coalitions}, {a community builder}. In compounds, builder specifies what's being constructed: {bodybuilder}, {shipbuilder}, {team-builder}.

A building is a structure with walls and a roof—houses, offices, factories, schools. The word emphasizes the structure itself rather than its purpose: {The building was condemned}. Building also names the act or process of construction: {The building of the dam took three years}. It extends to any gradual creation: {team building}, {nation building}.

Buildup is a gradual increase or accumulation. Traffic buildup clogs highways during rush hour. Military buildup precedes conflict. The buildup of plaque damages teeth. Buildup also means the period of promotion or preparation before an event: {After all that buildup, the movie was disappointing}. The verb form is two words: {Pressure continued to build up}.

Built is the past tense and past participle of build—to construct or assemble: {They built a house}, {Rome wasn't built in a day}. As an adjective, built describes how something is constructed: {a solidly built bridge}, {a well-built argument}. Applied to bodies, built means muscular or physically impressive: {That guy is built}. In slang, built can describe a woman's figure, often with sexual overtones.

A bulb is a rounded underground structure from which certain plants grow, consisting of fleshy leaves or scales surrounding a bud—tulips, onions, and garlic all grow from bulbs. The shape gives rise to other meanings: a light bulb is the glass enclosure containing the filament or LED that produces light, and any rounded swelling at the end of something may be called a bulb, like the bulb of a thermometer or a nasal bulb syringe. {Plant the bulbs in fall for spring blooms.} {The bulb in the hallway burned out.}

Bulbs are rounded underground storage organs from which certain plants grow—tulips, onions, garlic. The shape extends to any bulb-like object, especially the glass enclosure of an incandescent light: {The bulb burned out}. A camera's bulb setting holds the shutter open as long as the button is pressed. In anatomy, the bulb is any rounded enlargement, as in {olfactory bulb}.

A bulge is a rounded swelling or protrusion where a surface curves outward: {a bulge in his pocket}, {the bulge of her pregnant belly}. To bulge is to swell or stick out: {His eyes bulged with surprise}. The Battle of the Bulge was a WWII German offensive that created a bulge in Allied lines. In slang, bulge refers to the visible outline of male genitals through clothing.

Bulimia is an eating disorder characterized by cycles of binge eating followed by purging—typically self-induced vomiting, but also laxative abuse or excessive exercise. The full clinical term is bulimia nervosa. Unlike anorexia, people with bulimia often maintain normal weight, making the condition less visible: {She hid her bulimia for years}.

Bulk is large size or mass: {the sheer bulk of the cargo ship}. In bulk means in large quantities, usually at lower per-unit cost: {We buy paper towels in bulk}. The bulk of something is the main or largest part: {The bulk of the work is done}. To bulk up is to gain mass, especially muscle. Bulk as an adjective describes large-quantity goods: {bulk purchases}, {bulk shipping}. Something that bulks large looms importantly.

Bulky describes something large and difficult to handle because of its size or shape rather than its weight. A bulky {package} is awkward to carry. Bulky {clothing} adds volume to the body. The word often implies inconvenience—something that takes up more space than you'd like: {The bulky equipment barely fit in the trunk}.

Bull refers to an uncastrated male bovine and some other large male mammals (bull elephant). A different kind of bull entirely is a papal edict; it may help to remember that this bull is related to bulletin. If someone is talking a load of bull they are talking nonsense. In securities trading, bull refers to various scenarios in which values are rising or expected to rise: We’re in the midst of a bull market.

A bulldog is a stocky, muscular dog breed with a wrinkled face, pushed-in nose, and distinctive underbite. Originally bred for bull-baiting, modern bulldogs are companion animals known for their stubborn but gentle temperament. The word extends to anything tenacious or determined: {bulldog determination}, {bulldog grip}. As a verb, to bulldog is to wrestle a steer to the ground by grabbing its horns—a rodeo event. British and French bulldogs are distinct breeds, the latter smaller with bat-like ears.

Bulldogs are a breed of dog with a muscular, stocky build, broad head, and wrinkled face with an undershot jaw. Originally bred for bull-baiting, they're now companion animals known for their gentle temperament despite their fierce appearance. The term extends to anyone tenacious or stubbornly determined: {She pursued the story with bulldog persistence}. Bulldog is also a mascot for schools and sports teams.

To bulldoze is to clear or level ground with a bulldozer—a powerful tractor with a broad blade at the front. The figurative sense dominates casual use: to bulldoze is to force through by sheer power, disregarding opposition or obstacles: {They bulldozed the proposal through committee}. To bulldoze someone is to intimidate or coerce them into compliance.

Bulldozed means flattened or cleared by force, literally with a bulldozer or figuratively through overwhelming pressure. A developer bulldozed the old neighborhood to make way for condos. Politicians get bulldozed by well-funded opponents. {She bulldozed her way through the crowd}. The word implies something swept aside without regard for what stood there.

A bulldozer is a powerful tracked vehicle with a broad metal blade at the front, used to push earth, debris, or other heavy materials. Construction and demolition sites rely on bulldozers to clear and level ground. Figuratively, to bulldoze is to force something through by sheer power or intimidation: {He bulldozed the proposal through committee}. A person who acts this way may be called a bulldozer.

Bulldozers are heavy machines with a broad metal blade at the front, used to push earth, debris, or other material. They clear land, grade surfaces, and demolish structures. Figuratively, a bulldozer is someone who pushes through obstacles or opposition with force and little regard for others: {He bulldozed his way through the meeting}.

Bulldozing is using a bulldozer—a powerful tractor with a broad blade—to push earth, debris, or structures. The word extends to any forceful clearing or flattening: {They bulldozed the old neighborhood for a shopping center}. Figuratively, to bulldoze is to push through opposition by sheer force or intimidation: {She bulldozed the proposal through committee}.

The projectile that leaves a fired gun or rifle is the bullet. This core meaning inspires other uses, such as the black dots that abut a bulleted list. To bullet an item is to put one of these dots next to it. A bullet train is one that travels at very high speeds. A magic bullet or silver bullet is an unrealistic, quick solution to a problem.

A bulletin is an official announcement or news update, typically brief and timely: {a news bulletin}, {a weather bulletin}. The word extends to regular publications from organizations: {a church bulletin}, {a company bulletin}. A bulletin board is a surface for posting notices, or its digital equivalent—an online forum where users post messages.

Bulletproof describes something that can stop bullets from penetrating: {a bulletproof vest}, {bulletproof glass}. Figuratively, bulletproof means invulnerable to criticism or failure: {a bulletproof alibi}, {a bulletproof legal strategy}. In tech contexts, bulletproof code or systems are robust against errors or attacks. {Their plan seemed bulletproof until the market crashed.}

Bullets are projectiles fired from guns, typically small metal cylinders with pointed tips. The word extends to any small, filled circle used as a typographical marker to set off items in a list: {The memo had three bullet points}. To {bite the bullet} is to endure something painful or difficult. To {dodge a bullet} is to narrowly avoid disaster.

A bullfight is a public spectacle, traditional in Spain and Latin America, in which a matador confronts and ultimately kills a bull in an arena. The event follows ritualized stages, with the matador using a cape to provoke charges before delivering a final sword thrust. Supporters consider it art and cultural heritage; opponents condemn it as animal cruelty. {We watched a bullfight in Madrid.}

A bullfighter is a person who engages bulls in an arena as public spectacle, particularly in the Spanish tradition of corrida. The matador is the principal bullfighter who confronts and kills the bull; other bullfighters assist with capes and lances. {Hemingway romanticized the bullfighter as a figure facing death with grace.}

Bullfighters are people who face bulls in the ritualized combat of bullfighting, traditionally in Spain, Portugal, and Latin America. The matador is the principal bullfighter who kills the bull; others on foot (banderilleros) and horseback (picadors) assist. The term extends to anyone who confronts danger with theatrical flair: {He fancied himself a bullfighter in the boardroom}.

Bullfighting is a spectacle in which a matador confronts and kills a bull in an arena, following elaborate ritual traditions. The practice is most associated with Spain but also occurs in Portugal, southern France, and parts of Latin America. Supporters consider it an art form; opponents call it animal cruelty. The related adjective is taurine.

Bullfights are spectacles in which a matador confronts and kills a bull in an arena, traditional in Spain, Portugal, and parts of Latin America. The event follows a ritualized sequence—the bull is weakened by mounted lancers and barbed sticks before the matador delivers the fatal sword thrust. Supporters consider it art and cultural heritage; opponents call it animal cruelty. {We attended a bullfight in Madrid.}

Bullheaded means stubbornly unwilling to change course or consider other viewpoints. Unlike merely persistent, bullheaded carries negative connotations—suggesting someone who charges ahead without thinking, like a bull: {He was too bullheaded to admit he was wrong}. The word implies that flexibility or compromise would be wiser.

A bullhorn is a portable loudspeaker with a built-in microphone and amplifier, shaped like a cone and held by a handle. Police use them to address crowds, protesters to lead chants, coaches to bark instructions across a field: {She grabbed the bullhorn and called for order}. Also called a megaphone.

Bullish means optimistic or confident, especially about rising prices. In finance, a bullish investor expects markets to go up and buys accordingly—the opposite of bearish. The term extends beyond markets: {I'm bullish on the new hire}. The underlying image is of a bull charging forward aggressively. Bullish can also simply mean stubborn or forceful.

A bullpen is the area in a baseball stadium where relief pitchers warm up before entering the game, and by extension, the relief pitchers themselves as a group: {Their bullpen blew another save}. The term comes from an enclosure for bulls. In offices, a bullpen is an open workspace where multiple employees sit together without private offices. In police stations, a bullpen is a holding area for detainees awaiting processing.

Bullpens is the plural of bullpen. In baseball, a bullpen is the area where relief pitchers warm up during a game, and by extension, the relief pitchers themselves: {The team's bullpen has been unreliable this season}. Outside baseball, a bullpen is any large, open workspace where people work together without private offices: {The interns shared a bullpen on the third floor}.

Bulls is the plural of bull—the intact adult male of cattle and certain other large mammals like elephants, moose, and whales. In finance, bulls are investors who expect prices to rise, buying in anticipation of gains: {The bulls are betting on a market rebound}. Bull markets rise; bear markets fall. Bulls can also mean papal decrees or official documents sealed with a bulla. As slang, bulls means nonsense or lies: {That's complete bulls}. (Capitalized Bulls refers to sports teams, especially the Chicago Bulls.)

A bullseye is the center of a target, typically marked with concentric circles, and hitting it earns the highest score in archery, darts, or shooting. By extension, bullseye describes any precisely accurate hit or achievement: {That guess was a bullseye}. The exclamation {Bullseye!} celebrates getting something exactly right. Bullseye also names a round peppermint candy and a type of circular window or thick glass lens used in ships and buildings.

Bullshit is talk, writing, or behavior that presents itself as meaningful but is hollow underneath. Unlike a lie, which conceals a known truth, bullshit is often indifferent to truth altogether—the bullshitter cares only whether it sounds convincing. Corporate jargon, pseudo-profound platitudes, and empty promises all qualify: {That mission statement is pure bullshit}. Bullshit also describes things that are unfair or violate expected norms: {Getting towed for that is bullshit}. And it can mean pointless burden: {I spent all day on bullshit paperwork}. As a verb, to bullshit is to deceive with empty talk: {Don't bullshit me}.

Bullshitting can mean deceiving someone with empty talk: {He's bullshitting you about the deadline}. It also means faking competence: {I was bullshitting my way through the presentation}. In a friendlier sense, bullshitting is casual, low-stakes chat: {We were just bullshitting on the porch}. Context distinguishes deceit from camaraderie.

A bully is someone who habitually intimidates, threatens, or mistreats those weaker or less powerful: {The playground bully took his lunch money}. To bully is to behave this way: {She was bullied throughout middle school}. Bullying can be physical, verbal, or social—spreading rumors, excluding someone, or now, harassing online (cyberbullying). As an adjective, bully once meant excellent or first-rate: {Bully for you!} This sense survives mainly in ironic or mocking use.

Bullying is the repeated use of power—physical, social, or psychological—to intimidate, harm, or dominate someone weaker or more vulnerable. It includes threats, insults, exclusion, and physical aggression. School bullying has received particular attention, but workplace bullying and cyberbullying are recognized as serious problems: {The company finally addressed the bullying in her department}. As an adjective, bullying describes intimidating behavior: {his bullying tone}.

Bum has an informal tone in all of its meanings, which are not related but share a somewhat negative connotation. A bum is a vagrant, lazy, or incompetent person. To bum something, such as a cigarette, is to ask for it to be given to you. If you bum around, you spend time relaxing, doing little. Something of poor quality or reliability can be characterized as bum: I have a bum ankle. If you’re bummed out, you’re disappointed or depressed.

Bumble means to move, act, or speak in a clumsy or confused way. Someone who bumbles through a presentation stumbles over words or loses their place. To bumble around is to proceed awkwardly without clear direction: {We bumbled around the unfamiliar city looking for the restaurant}. The word also describes the low droning sound bees make, giving us bumblebee. A bumbler is someone prone to making mistakes through ineptitude rather than malice.

A bumblebee is a large, fuzzy bee that flies with a distinctive loud buzz. Bumblebees are rounder and hairier than honeybees, often with yellow and black stripes. They live in small colonies and are important pollinators, visiting flowers in gardens and meadows. {A bumblebee landed on the lavender.}

Bumblebees are large, fuzzy, flying insects known for their round bodies and distinctive black-and-yellow striped coloring. They are important pollinators, visiting flowers to collect nectar and pollen, and unlike honeybees, most bumblebee species live in small underground colonies. The word often evokes a sense of gentle clumsiness, as these heavy-bodied insects seem to defy aerodynamic expectations. {The garden was alive with bumblebees humming among the lavender.}

Bumbling describes clumsy, incompetent action—someone who fumbles through tasks with awkward inefficiency. A bumbling {assistant} makes mistakes; a bumbling {attempt} lacks coordination or skill. The word suggests well-meaning ineptitude rather than malice: {The bumbling detective stumbled onto the solution by accident}. To bumble is to act this way.

Bummed means disappointed, let down, or mildly depressed: {I was really bummed when the concert got canceled}. The feeling is genuine but not devastating—more dejected than despairing. Often appears as {bummed out}. To bum someone out is to disappoint or depress them: {Don't bum me out with bad news}.

Bummer expresses disappointment about an unfortunate situation: {What a bummer that the concert got canceled}. The word is casual and relatively mild—appropriate for minor setbacks rather than serious misfortune. A bummer can also be the disappointing thing itself: {The rain was a real bummer}. In older slang, a bummer was a bad drug experience, especially on hallucinogens.

Bump, a noun and verb, sounds like what it is: an abrupt collision, or a swelling that results from this. If you bump something, you hit it strongly enough to note the impact and perhaps to suffer from it. In figurative use, if something gets bumped it is displaced or removed from its location or position. You might be bumped up (promoted) or you might be bumped from an overbooked flight.

Bumped is the past tense of bump, meaning to collide with something or someone, usually with minor force: {I bumped into the table in the dark}. To bump into someone can also mean to encounter them unexpectedly: {I bumped her at the grocery store}. In travel, to be bumped is to lose a reserved seat due to overbooking: {We got bumped from the flight}.

A bumper is a protective bar at the front or rear of a vehicle, designed to absorb impact in minor collisions. The word extends to anything that buffers or protects: {bumper cars}, crib bumpers. As an adjective, bumper means unusually large or abundant: a bumper {crop}, a bumper {year}. Bumper-to-bumper describes traffic so dense that cars nearly touch, or warranty coverage that's comprehensive.

Bumpers are the protective bars at the front and rear of vehicles, designed to absorb impact in minor collisions. The word extends to anything that cushions: bumpers on a pool table keep balls in play, bumper pads line a baby's crib. Bumper crops and bumper years are unusually large or successful. As an adjective, bumper suggests abundance: {a bumper harvest}. In British usage, a bumper is also a brimming glass, especially for toasts.

A bumpkin is an unsophisticated person from a rural area—someone whose manners or knowledge mark them as provincial. The word is mildly contemptuous: {Some country bumpkin who's never seen a subway}. It implies not just rural origin but social awkwardness in more cosmopolitan settings.

Bumps are small raised areas on a surface—skin bumps, bumps in the road, goose bumps. To bump is to knock against something: {I bumped my head on the cabinet}. To bump into someone is to encounter them unexpectedly. A bump can be a slight increase: {a bump in salary}. To bump someone from a flight is to deny them their seat due to overbooking. {Bump} alone, especially online, revives a discussion thread by adding a comment.

Bumpy describes a surface with irregularities—lumps, ridges, or uneven spots: {a bumpy road}, {bumpy skin}. A bumpy ride or flight involves jolts and shaking. Figuratively, bumpy describes experiences with difficulties or setbacks: {a bumpy relationship}, {The project got off to a bumpy start}.

Bums are buttocks, especially in British English: {Get off your bum}. In American English, a bum is a vagrant or homeless person, or more broadly anyone seen as lazy or worthless: {a beach bum}, {the guy's a total bum}. To bum something is to obtain it by begging or mooching: {Can I bum a cigarette?} To bum around is to idle or wander aimlessly. As an adjective, bum means defective or worthless: {a bum knee}, {a bum deal}.

A bun is a small rounded bread roll, often soft and slightly sweet: {hamburger bun}, {hot dog bun}. Bun also refers to a tight coil of hair gathered at the back or top of the head: {She wore her hair in a bun}. In informal usage, buns are buttocks: {Get off your buns and help me}. A {bun in the oven} is slang for pregnancy.

A bunch is an appreciable but indeterminate number of something: A bunch of people showed up for the auction. A number of like things gathered in a characteristic way is also a bunch (bunch of parsley, bunch of bananas). When you bunch items, you gather them in one place, or treat them as like, even though they may be different: Bunch up the flowers and place them in a vase. Someone’s bunch is the people that they ordinarily hang around with.

Bundle, a noun and verb, is related to the verb bind and that helps to organize its meanings. A bundle of things is fastened or tied together: I bought a bundle of firewood. A bundle after many verbs is about a large amount of money: That must have cost a bundle. To bundle physical items is to wrap, fasten, or tie them together. You can also bundle services, as companies are fond of doing with your internet, phone, and TV.

A bungalow is a small house, typically one story, often with a low-pitched roof and a front porch. The style became popular in early 20th-century American suburbs. In British usage, bungalow specifically means a single-story dwelling, often associated with retirement homes: {They downsized to a bungalow when the kids moved out}.

A bungee is an elastic cord, typically with hooks at each end, used to secure cargo or for recreational jumping. Bungee cords stretch under load and snap back, making them useful for strapping items to bike racks or truck beds. In bungee jumping, a long elastic cord attached to the ankles allows a person to plunge from a height and bounce back before hitting the ground.
