To bungle is to carry out a task clumsily or incompetently, ruining the result through ineptitude: {The contractor bungled the renovation so badly we had to start over}. A bungle is an instance of such failure. A bungled {robbery} goes wrong; a bungled {surgery} harms the patient. The word emphasizes not just failure but awkward, avoidable failure.

Bungled means badly botched or mishandled. A bungled {robbery} fails through incompetence. A bungled {surgery} goes wrong due to error. The word emphasizes clumsy execution rather than bad luck—someone bungled it, and the mess was avoidable: {The whole operation was bungled from the start}.

Bunk has two unrelated origins. One gives us the narrow bed built into a wall or stacked in tiers: {bunk beds}, ship's bunks, summer camp bunks. To bunk is to sleep, especially in makeshift quarters: {We bunked in the barn}. The other bunk means nonsense or empty talk, shortened from bunkum (itself from Buncombe County, North Carolina, whose congressman notoriously spoke just to impress constituents): {That's a load of bunk}. To debunk is to expose such nonsense.

A bunker is a reinforced shelter, typically underground or partially buried, designed to protect occupants from bombs, artillery, or other attacks. Military bunkers house troops or equipment; civilian bunkers provide protection during air raids or nuclear threats. In golf, a bunker is a sand-filled hazard on the course, also called a sand trap. To bunker down means to take refuge or prepare to withstand difficulty. {The family bunkered in the basement during the tornado warning.}

Bunkers are fortified shelters, typically underground or reinforced, designed to protect against attack or bombardment: {The troops retreated to their bunkers}. In golf, a bunker is a sand trap—a hazard filled with sand. Bunkers on a ship or at a port store fuel, and to bunker is to refuel a vessel. To {bunker down} (more often {hunker down}) is to shelter in place or prepare for difficulty.

A bunkhouse is a simple building with sleeping quarters for workers, typically on a ranch, farm, or work camp. The bunks are usually arranged in rows, housing multiple laborers in shared space: {The ranch hands slept in the bunkhouse behind the main barn}.

Bunnies is the plural of bunny, an informal and affectionate word for rabbit. The term suggests something soft and cute: {Look at the bunnies in the yard}. Bunny appears in compounds like {bunny slope} (a beginner ski run) and {dust bunny} (a ball of fluff under furniture). A Playboy bunny is a waitress at the defunct Playboy Club, wearing rabbit ears and a tail.

A bunny is a rabbit, especially a young one or in children's speech. The word carries connotations of softness and cuteness: {the Easter bunny}, {a bunny rabbit}. Bunny extends to other soft, appealing things—a ski bunny frequents slopes more for socializing than sport, and bunny ears are the V-shaped hand gesture behind someone's head in photos.

Buns are small rounded bread rolls, often soft and slightly sweet: {hamburger buns}, {hot dog buns}. A hair bun is hair gathered and coiled at the back of the head. In informal speech, buns refers to the buttocks: {She does squats to tone her buns}. A {bun in the oven} is a pregnancy.

Bunting has two distinct sources. One is a group of small seed-eating birds related to finches and sparrows, including the indigo bunting and snow bunting. The other is decorative fabric or flags, typically in national colors, hung as festive decoration: {The stadium was draped in red, white, and blue bunting}. A bunting is also a soft sleeping bag for infants.

A buoy is a floating marker anchored in water to guide navigation, mark hazards, or indicate swimming boundaries: {The channel buoys kept us clear of the shoals}. To buoy something is to keep it afloat or support it. Figuratively, to buoy spirits or confidence is to lift them: {The good news buoyed her mood}. Buoyant describes things that float easily or people with cheerful, resilient temperaments.

Buoys are floating markers anchored in water to guide navigation, mark channels, or warn of hazards: {The red buoys marked the harbor entrance}. A life buoy is a flotation device thrown to someone in the water. To buoy something is to keep it afloat or, figuratively, to lift spirits or sustain hope: {The good news buoyed her confidence}. What buoys you up keeps you from sinking.

Bupkis means nothing at all, zero, zilch. From Yiddish, literally meaning goat droppings. The word emphasizes emptiness or worthlessness: {After all that work, we got bupkis}. {The investigation turned up bupkis}. Often spelled bubkes or bupkes.

A burden is something heavy that must be carried—literally a load, figuratively a responsibility or hardship. {The tax burden falls disproportionately on the middle class.} {She didn't want to be a burden to her children.} To burden someone is to load them down physically or emotionally. The burden of proof is the obligation to demonstrate a claim.

A bureau is a chest of drawers, typically for storing clothes, or a writing desk with drawers. The word extends to offices and agencies that handle administrative work: the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Census Bureau, a travel bureau. In government contexts, bureau often suggests a subdivision within a larger department: {She works for the bureau that handles immigration cases}.

Bureaucracy is a system of administration through departments, rules, and hierarchical authority—typically in government or large organizations. The term often carries negative connotations of excessive procedures, paperwork, and inefficiency: {We got lost in the bureaucracy trying to get a simple permit}. A bureaucracy can also mean the officials who run such systems collectively: {The federal bureaucracy employs millions}.

A bureaucrat is a government official, especially one who follows rules and procedures rigidly. The term often carries negative connotations—suggesting someone more concerned with paperwork and protocol than with actually helping people: {I spent three hours dealing with bureaucrats at the DMV}. In neutral usage, bureaucrats are simply administrators who keep large organizations functioning.

Bureaucratic describes anything characteristic of bureaucracies—large organizations with rigid hierarchies, formal procedures, and extensive paperwork. The word almost always carries negative connotations: {bureaucratic red tape}, {bureaucratic delays}, {bureaucratic nightmare}. A bureaucratic process is slow, impersonal, and frustrating, requiring forms and approvals that seem excessive relative to the task at hand.

Bureaucrats are government officials or administrators who work within large organizational systems, typically following established rules and procedures. The term often carries a negative connotation, suggesting people more concerned with paperwork and protocol than with solving problems: {The bureaucrats keep sending me back to fill out more forms}. A bureaucrat may work in any large institution, not just government.

A burger is a sandwich consisting of a cooked patty—typically ground beef—served in a split round bun with various toppings: {I'll have a burger with everything}. The word derives from hamburger, which got shortened. Non-beef versions specify their protein: turkey burger, veggie burger, chicken burger. In compounds, burger often just means the patty itself.

Burgers is the plural of burger, a shortened form of hamburger—a ground beef patty served in a sliced bun, typically with toppings like lettuce, tomato, cheese, and condiments. The word extends to patties made from other ingredients: {turkey burgers}, {veggie burgers}, {salmon burgers}. {We grilled burgers for the Fourth of July}.

A burglar is someone who breaks into a building to steal. The word specifically implies unlawful entry—a thief who snatches your bag on the street isn't a burglar, but one who climbs through your window at night is. {The burglars made off with jewelry and electronics.} To burglarize is to commit such a crime.

Burglars are people who break into buildings to steal. The term specifically implies unlawful entry—through a window, a picked lock, a forced door—rather than theft by other means. {The burglars took jewelry and electronics but left the television}. A burglar differs from a robber, who confronts victims directly.

Burglary is the crime of unlawfully entering a building with intent to commit a crime inside, typically theft. The legal definition varies by jurisdiction but generally requires breaking and entering or remaining unlawfully. Unlike robbery, burglary doesn't require confronting a victim—it's about the intrusion itself: {The house showed signs of burglary}. A serial burglar might commit dozens of burglaries before being caught.

To burgle is to commit burglary—to break into a building to steal. The word is a back-formation from burglar, more common in British English than American, where burglarize dominates: {Someone burgled our flat while we were on holiday}. The tone can be slightly humorous to American ears.

Burgundy is a dark purplish-red color, named for the wine from the French region. The color appears in fashion, home décor, and team uniforms: {a burgundy sweater}, {burgundy lipstick}. As a wine term, burgundy once referred broadly to any red wine, though this usage has faded as wine vocabulary has become more precise. (Capitalized Burgundy is the French region.)

Burial is the act of placing a dead body in the ground or a tomb. The word extends to anything interred or hidden away: {the burial of toxic waste}, {the burial of old memories}. A burial can also be the ceremony surrounding interment: {We attended his burial at the family plot}.

Burials is the plural of burial—the act of placing a dead body in the ground, a tomb, or the sea. The word covers both the physical act and the ceremony surrounding it: {The cemetery has conducted thousands of burials}. Burial extends to anything interred or hidden away: {the burial of old grievances}, {the burial of evidence}.

Buried means placed in the ground and covered, most often referring to the dead: {They buried her next to her husband}. The word extends to anything hidden beneath a surface or concealed within something larger: {buried treasure}, {buried in paperwork}, {The admission was buried in the footnotes}. To bury the hatchet is to make peace. To bury your head in the sand is to ignore unpleasant realities.

Burlap is a coarse, heavy fabric woven from jute or hemp fibers, used for sacks, upholstery, and craft projects. Its rough texture makes it durable but uncomfortable against skin. Burlap sacks traditionally hold agricultural goods like potatoes or coffee beans: {The warehouse was stacked with burlap bags of grain}.

Burlesque is exaggerated imitation for comic effect—a send-up that mocks by overdoing it. A burlesque of Shakespeare might give Hamlet a Brooklyn accent and a therapy appointment. The word also names a theatrical tradition featuring bawdy comedy, striptease, and variety acts: {She performs at a burlesque club downtown}. As a verb, to burlesque something is to parody it broadly.

Burly describes a person who is large and strongly built, with an emphasis on muscular bulk rather than fat: {a burly construction worker}, {burly security guards}. The word suggests physical power and a certain roughness—you might call a lumberjack or bouncer burly, but not a ballet dancer or accountant.

Meanings of burn have mostly to do with fire and heat, and the results of these. To burn something is to expose it to flame or extreme heat. Marks and evidence of this process are called burns. When something is consumed by fire, it is burned up or burnt up. Figuratively, this also applies to other exhausted resources: We’ve already burned through our budget. If you get burned by someone, you get cheated or badly treated.

Burned is the past tense and past participle of burn. Something burned has been damaged or destroyed by fire or heat: {The building burned to the ground}. Burned also describes the sensation of heat or irritation: {My eyes burned from the smoke}. To get burned is to suffer a loss or betrayal: {I got burned on that deal}. In slang, burned means insulted or humiliated: {You just got burned}. Interchangeable with burnt, though burned is more common in American English.

A burner is the part of a stove or furnace that produces flame: {Turn the soup down to a low burner}. A burner phone is a cheap prepaid mobile phone, easily discarded to avoid being traced—the phone itself is often called simply a burner: {He used a burner to make the call}. To put something on the back burner is to deprioritize it; the front burner gets immediate attention.

Burners are parts of stoves or furnaces where fuel combustion occurs and flames emerge. The term extends to any device designed to produce a controlled flame, from Bunsen burners in labs to the massive burners that heat hot air balloons. In slang, a burner is a prepaid cell phone used temporarily to avoid being traced—{I picked up a burner so they couldn't track my calls}. Someone described as a burner in sports or gaming is exceptionally fast or dominant.

Burning describes something on fire or something that feels intensely hot, like a burning sensation from a wound or spicy food. The word extends to intense emotions and desires: a burning {ambition}, burning {curiosity}, a burning {need to know}. A burning question or issue is one that demands urgent attention. As a noun, burning refers to the act of setting fire to something or the process of combustion itself.

Burnout is a state of physical and emotional exhaustion from prolonged stress, especially at work. The term implies having used up all your fuel—nothing left to give. {After three years of eighteen-hour days, she hit complete burnout}. Burnout also describes mechanical failure from overheating, or the moment a rocket engine depletes its fuel.

Burns are injuries caused by heat, fire, chemicals, electricity, or radiation: {She treated the burns on her arm}. As a verb form, burns describes the process of combustion or destruction by fire: {The candle burns slowly}, {That comment really burns me}. To say something burns is to say it stings or smarts. In fitness, {feel the burn} refers to muscle fatigue during exercise. (Capitalized Burns is a Scottish surname, notably the poet Robert Burns.)

Burnt is the past tense and past participle of burn, used interchangeably with burned in most contexts. British English tends toward burnt, American toward burned, but both are correct everywhere. As an adjective, burnt often describes color or flavor: {burnt orange}, {burnt sienna}, {burnt sugar}. Something with a burnt taste has been overcooked or charred.

A burp is an audible release of gas from the stomach through the mouth. To burp is to produce this sound, or to help a baby release swallowed air by patting its back: {Don't forget to burp the baby after feeding}. The word is mildly impolite but not vulgar—the clinical term is eructation.

A burpee is a calisthenics exercise combining a squat, plank, and jump in rapid sequence. From standing, you drop into a squat, kick your legs back into a plank position, return to the squat, then jump upward with arms overhead. Burpees are notorious for their intensity and appear frequently in CrossFit and military fitness training: {We had to do fifty burpees as punishment}.

Burping is releasing gas from the stomach through the mouth, producing a characteristic sound. The verb burp covers both the involuntary act and the deliberate inducement: {The baby needs to be burped after feeding}. A burp is the sound or instance itself. Belching is the more formal term for the same thing.

Burps are releases of gas from the stomach through the mouth, often with a characteristic sound. The verb means to expel such gas: {The baby burped after feeding}. To burp a baby is to pat or rub its back to help release trapped air. Informally, any short emission may be called a burp: {The engine gave a burp and died}.

A burr is the rough, prickly seed case of certain plants that clings to fur or clothing. By extension, burr describes anything that sticks or irritates—a burr under your saddle is a persistent annoyance. In metalworking, a burr is the rough edge left on cut metal. A burr is also a rolled or trilled *r* sound, characteristic of certain regional accents: {He spoke with a Scottish burr}. To burr is to speak with such a sound, or to form rough edges on metal.

A burrito is a Mexican dish consisting of a flour tortilla wrapped around a filling—typically beans, rice, meat, cheese, and various toppings. The tortilla is folded to enclose the contents completely, distinguishing it from tacos. {I grabbed a burrito for lunch.} Burritos vary widely, from simple bean-and-cheese versions to elaborate creations loaded with guacamole, sour cream, and salsa.

Burritos is the plural of burrito, a Mexican dish consisting of a flour tortilla wrapped around a filling—typically beans, rice, meat, cheese, and salsa. American versions tend to be larger and more stuffed than traditional Mexican burritos: {We grabbed burritos for lunch}. A breakfast burrito contains eggs and morning fare.

A burrow is a hole or tunnel dug by a small animal for shelter—rabbits, foxes, and groundhogs live in burrows. To burrow is to dig such a passage, or to move by digging: {The mole burrowed under the garden}. Extended uses describe any nestling or tunneling motion: {She burrowed under the covers}. To burrow into something is to investigate it deeply: {He burrowed into the archives looking for evidence}.

Burrows are tunnels or holes dug in the ground by animals for shelter: {The rabbit disappeared into its burrow}. Creatures burrow to create homes, escape predators, or find food. Extended uses describe digging into anything: {She burrowed under the covers}, {He burrowed through the archives}. To burrow into something is to nestle or press closely: {The child burrowed into her mother's side}.

Burst means to break open or apart suddenly, usually from internal pressure: {The pipe burst in the cold}. Things burst when they can no longer contain what's inside—balloons, dams, bubbles. The word extends to sudden releases of any kind: a burst of {laughter}, a burst of {energy}, a burst of {gunfire}. To burst into a room is to enter suddenly; to burst into tears is to begin crying abruptly. {I'm bursting} means urgently needing to urinate. The past tense is also burst, not bursted.

Bursting describes something breaking open suddenly from internal pressure, or the state of being extremely full. A pipe bursts when water pressure exceeds what it can contain; a balloon bursts when overinflated. The word extends to emotional and figurative fullness: someone {bursting with pride} can barely contain their feelings, while a room {bursting at the seams} has too many people. {I'm bursting} often signals an urgent need to urinate.

To bury is to put something in the ground and cover it. The dead are buried in graves; dogs bury bones; pirates bury treasure. Extended uses keep the sense of concealment or submersion: {She buried her face in her hands}, {He buried himself in work}. To bury the hatchet is to make peace. To bury the lede is to delay the main point of a story.

Burying is the act of putting something in the ground and covering it. Bodies are buried in graves, dogs bury bones, and treasure gets buried for safekeeping. The word extends to hiding or concealing: {She buried herself in work}, {He buried the evidence}. To bury the hatchet is to make peace. {They're burying their grandmother tomorrow}.

A bus is a large motor vehicle designed to carry many passengers along a fixed route: {I take the bus to work}. School buses transport students; city buses run urban routes; tour buses carry travelers. In computing, a bus is a system that transfers data between components. To bus dishes is to clear them from tables in a restaurant—the busboy's job.

A busboy is a restaurant worker who clears tables, refills water glasses, and assists servers—handling tasks that keep the dining room running without taking orders or serving food. The term is American and somewhat dated; *busser* is now more common as a gender-neutral alternative. {The busboy swooped in to clear our plates before we'd even finished.}

Buses is the plural of bus, a large vehicle for public transportation carrying multiple passengers along a set route: {The buses run every fifteen minutes}. In computing, buses are pathways that transfer data between components: {The motherboard has several buses connecting the CPU to memory}. The verb form works the same way: {She buses tables at a restaurant downtown}.

As a noun and in its core use, bush is synonymous with shrub. A place where bushes are the main form of vegetation can also be called bush. Things that resemble a bush also get the name, like a thick growth of hair. Something that bushes or bushes out begins to look like a bush. If you beat around the bush, you avoid talking about a subject, but if you beat the bushes, you’re looking for something that is scarce.

Bushes is the plural of bush—woody plants smaller than trees, with multiple stems rising from the ground. A yard may have ornamental bushes; a field may have wild ones. To {beat around the bushes} is to avoid getting to the point. The bushes can mean rough terrain or a hiding spot: {He ducked into the bushes}.

A bushfire is an uncontrolled fire burning through vegetation in wild or rural areas, particularly in Australia where the term is standard. Elsewhere the same phenomenon is called a wildfire or brush fire. Bushfires can spread rapidly through grassland, scrub, and forest, especially during hot, dry, windy conditions: {The bushfires destroyed thousands of hectares}. Bushfire season in Australia typically peaks in summer.

Bushfires are wildfires that burn through scrubland, grassland, or forest—the term used primarily in Australia, where such fires are a recurring and often catastrophic natural hazard. The Australian bushfire season brings intense heat, strong winds, and drought conditions that can turn small blazes into devastating infernos: {The 2019-2020 bushfires burned across millions of hectares}.

Bushwhack has two main meanings united by the idea of rough, wild terrain. To bushwhack is to cut through dense brush or vegetation where no trail exists: {We bushwhacked through the jungle for three hours}. It also means to ambush someone, attacking from concealment in wild country: {Guerrillas bushwhacked the convoy}. The ambush sense is especially associated with irregular warfare in the American Civil War, where bushwhackers operated as partisan raiders.

The idea of purposeful, goal-oriented activity is central to business. It’s easy to lose sight of the fact that business is formed from busy + ness; partly because of the shortened pronunciation of business, and partly because busyness does the work of busy + ness. Business usually connotes the involvement of money, except in the case of personal business. You can own a business, you can do business overseas, or you may have to attend to some business with your in-laws. In a more general way, business can designate a matter or affair (the whole business was embarrassing), or someone’s personal concern (I don’t think this is any of your business).

A businessman is a man who works in commerce or industry, typically in a managerial or executive role. The term suggests someone involved in deals, negotiations, or running a company rather than performing technical or manual work. {He's a successful businessman with interests in real estate and manufacturing.} Businessperson is the gender-neutral alternative.

A busker is a street performer who entertains passersby for tips—playing music, juggling, doing magic tricks, or other acts in public spaces. The practice is busking: {She spent a summer busking in the subway}. The term is more common in British than American English, where street performer predominates.

Buskers are street performers who entertain in public places for tips—musicians, magicians, jugglers, mimes, or other entertainers working sidewalks, subway stations, and plazas. The term is more common in British than American English, where "street performer" predominates. To busk is to perform this way: {She busked in the London Underground for years before getting her record deal}.

Busking is performing music, magic, or other entertainment in public spaces for tips from passersby. A busker might play guitar in a subway station, juggle on a street corner, or sing outside a café. The practice is common in cities worldwide, though regulations vary: {She made enough busking to cover her rent}. The performer is a busker; the activity is busking.

Bust gathers meanings around the idea of breaking or the human chest. A bust is a sculpture of a person's head, shoulders, and upper chest, or informally, a woman's breasts. To bust something is to break it: {I busted my phone screen}. A bust can be a failure {(The party was a bust)} or a police raid {(a drug bust)}. To go bust is to go bankrupt. Bust also works as an adjective meaning broken: {The TV's bust}. To bust someone is to arrest them or catch them misbehaving: {busted for speeding}, {Mom busted me sneaking out}.

Busted means broken or no longer working: {The TV's busted}. It also means caught in the act of wrongdoing: {You're busted!} Police bust people for crimes; parents bust kids for sneaking out. In poker, going bust means exceeding twenty-one or losing everything. Busted can describe someone who's broke: {I'm busted until payday}. As an adjective, busted sometimes means ugly or unappealing in slang.

Buster is an informal term of address for a man or boy, often carrying a note of mild confrontation or condescension: {Listen here, buster, I'm not going to tell you again}. It also forms compounds for things that break or destroy: {crime-buster}, {blockbuster}, {ghostbuster}. A buster can be someone who breaks up something undesirable: a {union buster}, a {trust buster}. In Australian slang, a buster is a strong wind or a spectacular fall.

Busting is the present participle of bust, carrying all its meanings: breaking {busting down doors}, arresting {cops busting drug dealers}, or going bankrupt {the company is busting}. It also works as an intensifier meaning extremely: {busting proud of you}. To be busting to do something is to be eager or desperate: {I'm busting to tell you the news}. {Busting a gut} means laughing hard or working strenuously.

Bustle is energetic, often noisy activity—the kind that accompanies preparation or crowded movement: {the bustle of the kitchen before dinner}, {the bustle of the city streets}. To bustle is to move with purposeful hurry: {She bustled around the office}. A bustle is also a pad or frame worn under a skirt to puff out the back, fashionable in the late 1800s—a different word that happens to share the spelling.

Bustling describes a place full of energetic activity and movement: {a bustling marketplace}, {the bustling streets of Manhattan}. The word suggests productive commotion rather than chaos—people going about their business with purpose. A person who bustles moves quickly and busily: {She bustled around the kitchen preparing dinner}.

Busts is the plural of bust in its noun senses: sculpted heads and shoulders {a gallery of Roman busts}, a woman's breasts and chest {dress styles for different bust sizes}, and police raids or arrests {drug busts}. As a verb form, busts means breaks {He busts the lock}, arrests {The cop busts him for possession}, or in poker, exceeds twenty-one and loses.

Busy describes being engaged in activity, with attention or effort occupied: {I'm busy right now, can I call you back?} A busy schedule is full of commitments. A busy street has heavy traffic. A busy pattern has many competing visual elements—often too many. The verb means to occupy oneself: {She busied herself with preparations}. A busybody is someone who meddles in others' affairs.

Busybodies are people who pry into others' affairs or offer unwanted opinions about how others should live. The term is always negative, suggesting someone who meddles where they have no business: {The neighborhood busybodies noticed every visitor to her house}. A busybody acts from nosiness rather than genuine concern.

A busybody is someone who pries into or meddles in other people's affairs. The word carries disapproval—busybodies offer unsolicited advice, spread gossip, and insert themselves where they don't belong: {The neighborhood busybody always knows who's visiting whom}. The busy- prefix suggests misplaced energy, someone occupied with everyone's business but their own.

Busywork is activity that keeps someone occupied without accomplishing anything meaningful. It fills time rather than serves a purpose: {The teacher assigned busywork while she graded papers}. The term is always dismissive—work that matters is never called busywork.

Busy as a bee, this word can act as a noun, a preposition, an adverb, and even a pronoun, but its main job is as a conjunction. But introduces a clause that contrasts with what came before it. The distinction can be weak or can amount to an exception or concession. As a preposition but expresses contrast in a single noun phrase rather than a clause: There’s no one home but me. As an adverb, but often means only or merely: These obstacles are but trifles in the overall plan.

Butch describes a masculine appearance or manner, especially in a woman or gay man. A butch woman might have short hair, wear men's clothing, and carry herself with traditionally male body language. The term originated in lesbian communities as a counterpart to femme. It can be affectionate or disparaging depending on context: {She's pretty butch}. As a noun, a butch is a person who presents this way.

A butcher slaughters animals and prepares their meat for sale. The work requires skill with knives, so butcher extends to anyone who cuts flesh—including surgeons, in older or humorous usage. To butcher is to slaughter or cut up, but also to ruin through clumsy execution: {He butchered the pronunciation of her name}. A butcher of people kills brutally or in large numbers.

Butchered is the past tense of butcher—to slaughter and prepare an animal for meat. Extended uses describe killing brutally or violently: {The villagers were butchered by invading soldiers}. Figuratively, to butcher is to ruin through incompetence: {He butchered the pronunciation of her name}, {The editor butchered my article}.

Butchering is the work of slaughtering animals and preparing their meat for sale or consumption—cutting, cleaning, and portioning carcasses. The word extends to any brutal killing: {the butchering of civilians}. Figuratively, to butcher something is to ruin it through clumsy execution: {He's butchering that song}, {They butchered the translation}.

A butler is the chief male servant in a wealthy household, responsible for managing other staff, overseeing the wine cellar, and attending to the household's formal needs. The role suggests dignified service and discretion: {The butler answered the door}. {Jeeves is literature's most famous butler}. In modern usage, butler sometimes describes premium concierge services: {hotel butler}, {virtual butler}. (Capitalized Butler is a surname.)

Butlers is the plural of butler, the chief male servant in a wealthy household. A butler traditionally manages other domestic staff and oversees formal service—answering doors, serving meals, maintaining the wine cellar. The role evokes old-money elegance: {The butlers stood at attention as guests arrived}. Butler has become shorthand for any attendant service: {The hotel offers a ski butler to help with equipment}.

A butt is the thicker or blunt end of something: {the butt of a rifle}, {a cigarette butt}. A butt is also a target for shooting practice or ridicule: {the butt of the joke}. In archery and shooting, butts are the mounds or targets. A butt is also a large barrel for wine or ale, typically holding about 126 gallons. To butt is to strike with the head or horns: {The goat butted him}. In informal usage, butt means buttocks—milder than ass: {Get off your butt}. {A pain in the butt}. Butt is acceptable in most company where ass might offend. {Butt in} means to intrude; {butt out} means mind your own business.

Butter is a solid yellow fat made by churning cream, used for cooking and spreading on bread. As a verb, to butter is to spread butter on something: {buttered toast}. To {butter someone up} is to flatter them, usually to gain favor. Butter appears in compounds describing rich or smooth textures: {buttercream}, {butterscotch}, {buttery leather}.

Buttercream is a rich, creamy frosting made by beating butter with powdered sugar, often flavored with vanilla or other extracts. It's the standard American cake frosting—spreadable, pipeable, and sweeter than European varieties that incorporate egg whites or yolks. {She piped buttercream roses onto the wedding cake.}

Buttercup is a common wildflower with bright yellow, glossy petals, found in meadows and fields. Children hold buttercups under each other's chins—a yellow reflection supposedly proves you like butter. As a term of endearment, buttercup suggests someone sweet and delicate: {Come on, buttercup, let's go}.

Buttercups are wildflowers with bright yellow, glossy petals, common in meadows and fields. Children hold them under chins to see if the reflected yellow glow proves you "like butter." The plant is mildly toxic to grazing animals. As a term of endearment, buttercup suggests someone sweet or delicate: {Come on, buttercup, you can do it}.

Someone who drops things is a butterfinger—their hands are so slippery they can't hold on to what they're carrying: {Nice catch, butterfinger}. The word is usually playful teasing rather than harsh criticism. More common in the plural: {I've got butterfingers today}.

Butterfingers is a playful insult for someone who drops things or fails to catch them, as if their fingers were slippery with butter: {Nice catch, butterfingers}. The word treats clumsiness as a defining trait rather than a momentary lapse. Despite the plural form, it takes a singular verb: {He's such a butterfingers}.

Butterflies are insects with large, often colorful wings, known for their transformation from caterpillar through chrysalis to winged adult. The word also names a swimming stroke performed face-down with simultaneous arm movements and a dolphin kick. As a verb, to butterfly is to split and spread flat: {butterfly a chicken breast}. The plural commonly describes nervous fluttering in one's stomach: {I get butterflies before every performance}.

A butterfly is a flying insect with large, often colorful wings that undergoes metamorphosis from caterpillar to winged adult. The word extends to things resembling this creature's shape or movement: the butterfly stroke in swimming involves simultaneous arm movements that arc outward, and a butterfly knife has a split handle that folds around the blade. Butterflies in your stomach describes the fluttery sensation of nervousness or excitement. To butterfly something, especially meat or shrimp, is to cut it nearly through and spread it flat.

Buttermilk is the liquid left after churning butter from cream. Traditional buttermilk is thin and slightly sour. Modern buttermilk is cultured—milk fermented with bacteria to produce a thick, tangy liquid used in baking and cooking: {buttermilk pancakes}, {buttermilk biscuits}. The acidity reacts with baking soda to create lift.

Butterscotch is a confection made by heating butter and brown sugar together, resulting in a rich, golden-brown candy with a distinctive sweet, buttery flavor. The term extends to anything flavored or colored to resemble this candy: butterscotch {pudding}, butterscotch {chips}, butterscotch {sauce}. As a color, butterscotch describes a warm golden-tan shade. {The butterscotch cookies were gone within minutes.}

Buttery describes something containing, resembling, or spread with butter: {buttery croissants}, {a buttery sauce}. The word extends to textures and flavors that evoke butter's richness and smoothness: {a buttery chardonnay}, {buttery soft leather}. As a noun, a buttery is a room for storing provisions, especially in British colleges and universities.

Buttheads is a casual, mildly insulting term for stupid or annoying people. The word carries playground-level vulgarity—rude but not seriously offensive: {Those buttheads left the gate open again}. Often used affectionately among friends or dismissively about minor irritants rather than genuine enemies.

The anus. Butthole is the most common casual term for this body part in American English—cruder than *bottom* or *rear end* but milder than *asshole*. It appears in childish insults: {You're such a butthole}. The word combines the directness of anatomical reference with the mild absurdity of *butt*, making it less harsh than alternatives.

The buttocks are the two fleshy mounds forming the rear of the human body, where the back meets the thighs. The word is plural—a single cheek is a buttock, though this singular form sounds clinical and rare. Buttocks serves as the neutral anatomical term, sitting between formal medical language and the many slang alternatives: {The injection goes in the buttocks}.

A button is a small disk with a function, such as to fasten a shirt, to activate or stop a process, or to summon an elevator. Most buttons are pushed to put them into use, but the buttons on a shirt are buttoned. Things that are small and round may attract this word, like belly button or button mushrooms. Something that’s buttoned up is securely closed; similarly, a buttoned up person is reserved or doesn’t say much.

Buttons is the plural of button—small fasteners on clothing, or knobs you press to operate machines and devices. The word often appears in phrases: {push someone's buttons} means to provoke them deliberately, while {cute as a button} describes something small and appealing. A buttons or Buttons is also a nickname for a hotel bellhop, from the rows of brass buttons on the traditional uniform.

Butts is the plural of butt—thick ends, cigarette remains, targets, barrels, or buttocks: {The ashtray was full of cigarette butts}. {Get your butts in gear}. {The soldiers practiced at the rifle butts}. As a verb: {The rams butted heads}.

Buy means to obtain something by paying money for it, the everyday verb for acquiring goods and services through purchase. {I need to buy groceries} or {She bought a new car}. Extended uses include gaining something through effort or sacrifice: {His apology bought him some time}. If you buy an idea or explanation, you accept or believe it: {I don't buy that excuse}. A buy is a purchase, especially a good one: {That coat was a real buy at half price}.

A buyer is someone who purchases something. The word often implies a role rather than a single transaction: a buyer for a department store selects merchandise professionally, while {first-time home buyers} represent a category in real estate markets. In business contexts, buyers negotiate with sellers: {We need to find a buyer for the company}.

Buying is the act of obtaining something in exchange for money. It covers everything from routine purchases to major acquisitions: {buying groceries}, {buying a house}. The word extends to accepting or believing: {I'm not buying that excuse}. To {buy time} is to delay something to gain an advantage.

A buyout is the purchase of a controlling share in a company or business. In a leveraged buyout, the buyer uses borrowed money, often secured against the target company's assets. Buyout also applies to paying someone to relinquish a position or contract: {The team negotiated a buyout with their underperforming coach}.

Buzz is the continuous humming sound made by bees, electric currents, or vibrating machinery. Extended uses describe any low, persistent noise or activity: {The room buzzed with conversation}. A buzz is also a phone call {Give me a buzz} or a mild thrill from alcohol or excitement: {I got a buzz from that first drink}. To buzz somewhere is to move quickly: {She buzzed around the kitchen}. Buzz can mean rumors or excited talk: {The buzz around town is that they're engaged}. As slang, a buzzcut is a very short haircut; a buzzkill ruins the fun.

A buzzard is a large bird of prey. In North America, the term usually means a vulture—particularly the turkey vulture, which circles high and feeds on carrion. In Britain and elsewhere, buzzard refers to hawks of the genus Buteo. Figuratively, a buzzard is a greedy, ruthless, or contemptible person: {The old buzzard finally sold the property}.

Buzzards are large birds of prey. In British usage, buzzard refers to hawks of the genus Buteo—broad-winged, soaring raptors. In American usage, buzzard typically means a vulture, especially the turkey vulture that circles over carrion. The word often carries connotations of scavenging or circling ominously: {The buzzards were already gathering overhead}.

A buzzcut is a very short hairstyle where the hair is clipped uniformly close to the scalp, typically with electric clippers. The name comes from the buzzing sound of the clippers. Associated with military grooming standards, buzzcuts are low-maintenance and practical: {He got a buzzcut before basic training}. The style has moved in and out of fashion among civilians.

A buzzcut is a very short hairstyle cut uniformly close to the scalp with electric clippers. The style is associated with military recruits and athletes, though it's worn by anyone wanting low-maintenance hair: {He got a buzzcut before basic training}. The name comes from the buzzing sound of the clippers.

Buzzed describes a state of mild intoxication from alcohol or drugs—not drunk, but noticeably affected: {I'm just a little buzzed}. The word captures the pleasant, energized feeling of early intoxication, from the humming sensation it produces. Buzzed also describes hair cut very short with electric clippers: {a buzzed head}. A phone that buzzed has vibrated.

A buzzer is a device that makes a buzzing sound as a signal or alarm—a doorbell, a timer, an intercom. In sports, the buzzer signals the end of a period: {They scored at the buzzer}. A {buzzer beater} is a shot made just before time expires. To buzz someone in is to unlock a door remotely after they ring.

Buzzing is the continuous, low humming sound made by bees, electrical equipment, or vibrating objects: {The buzzing of flies kept me awake}. A place buzzing with activity is full of excited movement and noise. If your head is buzzing, your thoughts are racing. As slang, buzzing means mildly intoxicated or pleasantly excited: {I'm buzzing after that coffee}.

A buzzkill is a person or thing that spoils others' enjoyment or excitement: {Don't be such a buzzkill—we're just having fun}. The term comes from killing someone's buzz—their pleasant state of mild intoxication or general good mood. Anything dampening enthusiasm qualifies: bad news, a rule-enforcer, an unwelcome reminder of responsibilities.

Buzzkills are people or things that spoil excitement or dampen enthusiasm. The term combines buzz—the pleasant feeling from alcohol or stimulants—with kill: {Don't be such a buzzkill}. A buzzkill might be a person who points out problems, an unwelcome piece of news, or anything that deflates a good mood: {The rain was a total buzzkill for the party}.

A buzzword is a word or phrase that gains currency in a particular field or context, often through overuse rather than precision. Buzzwords sound impressive but may obscure more than they clarify: {synergy}, {disruption}, {pivot}, {leverage}. They proliferate in business, politics, and tech, where they signal insider status or dress up ordinary ideas. {His presentation was nothing but buzzwords.}

Buzzwords are fashionable terms that circulate heavily in business, politics, or media—often more impressive-sounding than substantive. They signal familiarity with current trends: {The presentation was full of buzzwords like "synergy" and "disruption"}. Buzzwords frequently lose meaning through overuse, becoming vague or empty. What counts as a buzzword shifts as language evolves—yesterday's fresh insight becomes today's tired cliché.
Bye and bye-bye are both informal versions of good-bye, used to express farewell.

Bygone means belonging to an earlier time, now past: {bygone days}, {a bygone era}. As a noun, bygones are past events or grievances. The phrase {let bygones be bygones} means to forgive past wrongs and move on rather than dwelling on old conflicts.

Bygones are things from the past, especially past grievances or conflicts. The word appears almost exclusively in the phrase {let bygones be bygones}—agreeing to forget past offenses and move forward without resentment. Occasionally used as an adjective meaning former or past: {bygone era}, {bygone days}.

Byliny are traditional Russian oral epic poems, typically recounting the deeds of heroic warriors called bogatyrs. These narrative songs date from medieval times and were passed down through generations of performers before being collected by folklorists in the 19th century. The singular is bylina.

Bypass means to go around rather than through. A bypass road routes traffic around a congested area rather than through it. In medicine, a bypass is a surgical procedure that creates an alternative passage for blood flow: {coronary bypass surgery}. To bypass something is to circumvent or avoid it entirely: {She bypassed the usual channels and went straight to the director}. The word implies finding a way around an obstacle, whether physical, procedural, or technological: {bypass the security system}.

A bystander is someone present at an event without participating in it—a witness or onlooker. The word often appears in contexts of accidents, crimes, or emergencies: {Several bystanders called 911}. An {innocent bystander} is harmed by events they had nothing to do with. The {bystander effect} describes the tendency for people to avoid intervening when others are present, each assuming someone else will act.

Bystanders are people who happen to be present at an event without participating in it. The word often implies witnessing something dramatic or violent: {Several bystanders were injured in the explosion}. A {bystander effect} describes the phenomenon where individuals are less likely to help someone in distress when others are present.

A byte is a unit of digital information, typically consisting of eight bits. Bytes measure computer memory and file sizes: {The document is only a few kilobytes}. Prefixes scale up: kilobyte, megabyte, gigabyte, terabyte. The byte became standard because eight bits can represent 256 values—enough for all characters in basic text encoding.

Byzantine describes something excessively complicated, with many interconnected parts that are difficult to navigate or understand: {byzantine bureaucracy}, {byzantine tax regulations}, {the byzantine rules of academic publishing}. The word suggests not just complexity but labyrinthine intricacy—systems so convoluted they seem designed to confuse. (Capitalized Byzantine relates to the Byzantine Empire.)

A cab is a taxi—a vehicle for hire with a driver. The word comes from cabriolet, a horse-drawn carriage, and persists in {cab driver}, {cab fare}, and {hail a cab}. Cab also refers to the enclosed compartment where a driver sits in a truck, locomotive, or piece of heavy equipment: {The trucker climbed into the cab}.

A cabal is a small group of people secretly plotting together, usually to gain power or influence. The word carries sinister overtones—cabals scheme behind closed doors, advance hidden agendas, and manipulate events: {a cabal of generals plotting a coup}, {The decision was made by a cabal of insiders}. Cabal can also mean the plot itself.

Cabals are small groups of people who scheme together in secret, usually to gain power or influence through underhanded means. The word carries strong connotations of conspiracy and self-serving manipulation: {a cabal of wealthy donors pulling strings behind the scenes}. While any tight-knit group working toward shared goals might technically qualify, cabal almost always implies something sinister or at least suspicious about the group's methods or intentions.

A cabana is a small shelter or changing room, typically at a beach, pool, or resort. Cabanas range from simple roofed structures to furnished private spaces with seating and curtains: {We rented a cabana by the pool}. The word comes from Spanish for cabin or hut.

A cabaret is a nightclub or restaurant offering live entertainment—typically singing, dancing, or comedy—while patrons eat and drink. The term also refers to the style of entertainment itself, often featuring intimate performances with a master of ceremonies: {She got her start performing cabaret in small clubs}. The genre evokes a particular atmosphere of sophistication, irreverence, and theatrical intimacy.

Cabarets are nightclubs or restaurants offering live entertainment—typically singing, dancing, comedy, or burlesque—while patrons eat and drink. The format flourished in early 20th-century Paris and Berlin, associated with bohemian culture and risqué performances. Today cabaret describes both the venue and the entertainment style: {a cabaret singer}, {dinner and a cabaret show}.

Cabbage is a leafy vegetable with dense, layered leaves forming a compact head. Green cabbage is most common, though red and savoy varieties exist. It appears in coleslaw, sauerkraut, and countless cuisines worldwide. In slang, cabbage means money, especially paper bills: {He's got serious cabbage}. To cabbage is British slang for pilfering, especially scraps of cloth by tailors.
A cabbie is a taxi driver. The word is informal and affectionate, suggesting the working-class character of the job: {The cabbie knew every shortcut in the city}. Also spelled cabby.

A cabby is someone who drives a taxi for a living. The word is informal and slightly dated, largely replaced by *cab driver* or *taxi driver* in contemporary usage: {The cabby knew every shortcut in the city}.

Cabernet is a grape variety used to make red wine, or the wine itself. Cabernet sauvignon is the most widely planted, producing full-bodied wines with dark fruit flavors and firm tannins. Cabernet franc, one of its parent grapes, yields lighter, more herbaceous wines. {We ordered a bottle of cabernet with dinner.}

A cabin is a small, simple dwelling, typically in a rural or wilderness setting: {a log cabin in the woods}, {a lakeside cabin}. On ships and aircraft, a cabin is an enclosed compartment—either a private room for passengers or the main interior space: {first-class cabin}, {the pilot emerged from the cabin}. The word suggests modest, functional shelter rather than luxury.

A cabinet is a piece of furniture with shelves or drawers, typically enclosed by doors, used for storage or display: {a kitchen cabinet}, {a medicine cabinet}, {a filing cabinet}. The word extends to any box-like enclosure housing equipment: {a speaker cabinet}. Cabinet also refers to a body of senior government advisors, typically department heads who meet with a chief executive: {The president met with her cabinet}. This governmental sense derives from the private room where such meetings historically occurred. (Capitalized Cabinet emphasizes the formal governmental body.)

A cable is a member of a class of things like string, rope, cord, or wire. Cable is distinguished typically by being thick, multi-stranded, and usually metallic. Cables may carry current, so even smaller ones get this name if they have this function, like the one that connects you cable TV. In the old days, to cable something was to send it by telegraph; such messages were also called cables. Today, cabling something is more likely to mean connecting it with cables.

Cables are thick ropes or bundles of wires, typically used for support or transmission. Steel cables hold up suspension bridges; electrical cables carry power or data. To cable is to send a message by telegraph or undersea line—a usage fading as the technology becomes obsolete. {The crew secured the ship with heavy cables.} In knitting, a cable is a twisted pattern resembling braided rope.

A caboose is the car at the end of a freight train, traditionally housing crew members and serving as a rolling office and shelter. Cabooses have largely disappeared from modern railroads, replaced by electronic monitoring devices. In informal American English, caboose is a playful term for the buttocks: {Get your caboose off the couch}.

Cacao is the tropical tree whose seeds are processed into chocolate and cocoa. The seeds themselves, found in large pods, are also called cacao—or cocoa beans after fermentation and drying. Cacao often appears in marketing to suggest less-processed chocolate products: {raw cacao nibs}, {cacao powder}. The spelling cocoa emerged as a variant and now typically refers to the processed powder or drink.

A cache is a hidden storage place, or the items stored there. Originally referring to provisions concealed by explorers or trappers, it now commonly means a stockpile: {a cache of weapons}, {a cache of documents}. In computing, a cache stores frequently accessed data for faster retrieval: {Clear your browser cache}. The verb means to store in such a place.

A cackle is the sharp, clucking cry a hen makes, especially after laying an egg. Extended to human laughter, a cackle is a shrill, harsh laugh—often suggesting wickedness, mockery, or uncontrolled amusement: {The witch's cackle echoed through the forest}. To cackle is to make such a sound, or to chatter noisily. {The old friends cackled over their wine.}

Cackles is the harsh, clucking laugh associated with witches, villains, and genuine amusement that's gotten out of control. A hen cackles after laying an egg; a person cackles when something strikes them as wickedly funny: {She cackled at her own joke}. The word suggests sharp, staccato bursts of laughter rather than warm chuckling.

Cackling is the sharp, broken sound a hen makes after laying an egg, or more broadly, any similar harsh, staccato laughter. The word often suggests something unpleasant or sinister about the laugh: {The witch's cackling echoed through the forest}. A group might be described as cackling over gossip or jokes, implying loud, somewhat raucous amusement.

Cacophony is harsh, jarring sound—a discordant mixture of noises that grates on the ear: {the cacophony of car horns and jackhammers}. The word extends to any chaotic jumble: {a cacophony of competing voices}, {a cacophony of architectural styles}. The opposite is euphony.

Cacti is the Latin plural of cactus, referring to multiple plants of the spiny, water-storing family native to the Americas. Both cacti and cactuses are acceptable plurals, though cacti appears more often in scientific and formal contexts: {The desert was dotted with cacti of every shape and size}.

A cactus is a spiny succulent plant native to arid regions of the Americas, though now found worldwide. Cacti store water in their thick stems and have adapted to survive extreme drought, making them popular as low-maintenance houseplants. The plural may be either cacti or cactuses. {She forgot to water the cactus for three months and it was fine.} Figuratively, someone prickly or difficult to approach might be compared to a cactus.

A cadaver is a dead human body, especially one used for medical study or scientific examination. The word is clinical and formal—doctors and medical students work on cadavers in anatomy labs, forensic investigators examine cadavers. Outside technical contexts, corpse or body are more common: {The medical school needs cadaver donations for its anatomy program}.

A caddy is a small container for storing tea, or more broadly, any compact storage box or organizer: {a silverware caddy}, {a shower caddy}. In golf, a caddy is the person who carries a player's clubs and offers advice on the course. The verb means to serve as a golf caddy: {He caddied at the country club all summer}.

Cadence is the rhythmic flow or pattern of sounds, especially in speech or music. A speaker's cadence combines pace, pitch, and pause: {the measured cadence of a funeral march}, {her voice rising and falling in familiar cadence}. In music, cadence also means a sequence of chords that brings a phrase to rest. Military cadence is the rhythm of marching, or the chants that keep soldiers in step. Extended to any rhythmic pattern: {the cadence of waves}, {the cadence of daily routines}.

A cadet is a young person training for military service or law enforcement, typically at an academy: {West Point cadets}, {police cadets}. The word originally meant a younger son, especially one entering military service because he wouldn't inherit the family estate. In some contexts, cadet refers to any trainee in a structured program: {a space cadet} (though that phrase now usually means someone who seems spacey or out of touch).

Cadets are young people training for military service or police work, typically at a specialized academy. The term extends to junior members of other organizations: {sea cadets}, {space cadets}. In some contexts, cadet indicates a younger son or junior branch of a family. {The cadets stood at attention during inspection.}

A cafeteria is a restaurant where customers serve themselves or are served at a counter, then carry their food to tables. The format is common in schools, hospitals, workplaces, and other institutional settings where large numbers of people need to eat efficiently. Unlike traditional restaurants, cafeterias typically display prepared food along a serving line, allowing diners to see and select items before paying. {The hospital cafeteria stays open around the clock.}

Caffeinated describes something containing caffeine, the stimulant found in coffee, tea, and many soft drinks: {I need something caffeinated to get through this meeting}. The term distinguishes from decaffeinated options. Figuratively, caffeinated can suggest energized or hyperactive: {Her caffeinated enthusiasm was exhausting}.

Caffeine is a stimulant compound found naturally in coffee, tea, and cacao, and added to soft drinks and energy drinks. It works by blocking adenosine receptors in the brain, reducing drowsiness and increasing alertness. Most adults consume caffeine daily, making it the world's most widely used psychoactive drug: {I can't function without my morning caffeine}. Caffeine withdrawal can cause headaches and irritability.

A cage is a framework enclosure for animals. Several things that look like this also get the name, like the wire mask that a baseball catcher wears, or the enclosure for the goal in hockey. Cage is also an informal term for prison, because of its confining associations. To cage is to confine in a cage or otherwise restrict activity or movement. If you rattle someone’s cage, you annoy them, typically in a pestering and effective way.

Caged describes something confined in a cage or enclosure: {caged birds}, {caged animals at the zoo}. The word extends to any feeling of confinement or entrapment: {She felt caged in her small apartment}, {a caged rage ready to explode}. Caged suggests not just physical containment but the frustration or restlessness that comes with it.

Cages are enclosures of bars or wire mesh used to confine animals or birds: {The parrot rattled the bars of its cage}. The word extends to any confining structure—a batting cage, a shark cage, a rib cage. To cage something is to put it in one, literally or figuratively: {She felt caged by the relationship}. In sports, the cage is slang for the goal or net.

Cahoots appears almost exclusively in the phrase {in cahoots}, meaning in secret partnership or conspiracy: {The mayor was in cahoots with the developers}. The word carries a whiff of shady dealing—people in cahoots are usually up to something underhanded. It's informal and slightly old-fashioned, with a hint of playfulness even when describing genuine corruption.

A cairn is a mound of rough stones built as a memorial or landmark. Hikers stack cairns to mark trails across barren terrain where paths aren't obvious: {We followed the cairns across the rocky summit}. Ancient cairns often cover burial sites. The cairn terrier, a small Scottish breed, was developed to hunt among such rock piles.

Cake is a sweet baked dessert, typically made from flour, sugar, eggs, and butter, often layered and frosted for celebrations: {birthday cake}, {wedding cake}. The word extends to other flat, shaped masses: {crab cake}, {rice cake}, {cake of soap}. As a verb, to cake is to form a hardened layer: {Mud caked on his boots}. Something easy is {a piece of cake}. To {have your cake and eat it too} is to want incompatible benefits.

Cakes are sweet baked goods made from flour, sugar, eggs, and fat—typically layered, frosted, or decorated for celebrations: {birthday cake}, {wedding cake}. A cake can also be a flat, compact mass: {cake of soap}, {crab cake}, {rice cake}. As a verb, to cake is to form a crusty layer: {Mud caked on his boots}. Something easy is {a piece of cake}. {Cakewalk} similarly suggests effortlessness.

A cakewalk is something easily accomplished: {Getting the permit was a cakewalk}. The term comes from a 19th-century dance competition where enslaved Black Americans performed an exaggerated, high-stepping promenade; the best couple won a cake. The dance spawned a musical genre and eventually the figurative sense of an effortless task.

Calamities is the plural of calamity—disasters or events causing great damage, distress, or misfortune. The word typically describes large-scale catastrophes rather than personal setbacks: {The region has suffered floods, earthquakes, and other calamities}. A series of calamities suggests compounding misfortune: {Calamities befell the expedition one after another}.

Calamity is a disaster or grave misfortune—an event causing widespread suffering or destruction: {The earthquake was a calamity for the region}. The word suggests scale and severity beyond ordinary troubles. A personal calamity might be financial ruin or devastating loss. {One calamity after another befell the expedition.}

Calcium is a chemical element, a soft silver-white metal that is the fifth most abundant element in Earth's crust. The body requires calcium for bones, teeth, and nerve function: {The doctor recommended calcium supplements}. Calcium appears in compounds like calcium carbonate (chalk, limestone) and calcium chloride (road salt). Symbol: Ca.

To calculate is to determine a number or outcome through mathematical or logical reasoning: {Calculate the total cost before checking out}. The word extends to any careful estimation or planning: {She calculated the risks before investing}. Calculated can suggest cold deliberation: {a calculated move}, {calculated cruelty}. A calculating person schemes strategically, usually with self-interest in mind.

Calculated describes something done with careful forethought and deliberate intention. A calculated {risk} is one taken after weighing the odds. A calculated {move} in business or politics is strategic, not impulsive. The word often carries a cold or manipulative edge: a calculated {insult} is delivered with precision, and a calculated {smile} masks true feelings. Someone described as calculating is shrewd and self-interested, always weighing advantages.

Calculating describes someone who plans carefully to advance their own interests, often at others' expense. The word implies cold, strategic thinking—weighing outcomes rather than acting on emotion or principle: {a calculating politician}, {There was something calculating in the way she befriended him}. The negative connotation distinguishes it from merely being thoughtful or deliberate. In its neutral sense, calculating simply means performing mathematical operations: {a calculating machine}.

Calculation is the process of using mathematics to determine an amount or result: {My calculations show we'll need twice the budget}. Beyond pure math, calculation suggests careful reasoning or planning: {a political calculation}, {cold calculation}. A calculated move is deliberate and strategic, sometimes implying self-interest or manipulation: {Her generosity was pure calculation}.

A calculator is an electronic device that performs mathematical operations—addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and often more complex functions. Before pocket calculators became ubiquitous in the 1970s, the word referred to a person who calculates: {The bank employed several calculators}. Now it's almost exclusively the device: {I need a calculator for this math class}. Calculator apps on phones have largely replaced physical ones for everyday use.

Calculus is the branch of mathematics dealing with rates of change and accumulation—differential calculus handles instantaneous rates, integral calculus handles accumulated quantities. {I failed calculus twice in college.} In medicine, a calculus is a hard mass formed in the body, such as a kidney stone or dental tarite. The plural for math is usually calculus; for stones, calculi.

A calendar is a system for organizing time into days, months, and years. The familiar grid showing a month's days is also a calendar, as is any schedule of events: {The band's touring calendar is packed through September}. To calendar something is to schedule it: {Let's calendar a meeting for next week}.

Calendars is the plural of calendar—systems for organizing time into days, weeks, months, and years. Different cultures have developed their own: the Gregorian calendar dominates international use, while Jewish, Islamic, and Chinese calendars serve religious and cultural purposes. Calendars are also the physical or digital objects displaying these systems: {wall calendars}, {desk calendars}, {I'll check my calendar}. As a verb, to calendar something is to schedule it: {The hearing has been calendared for June}.

A calf is a young cow or bull, or the young of certain other large mammals: elephant calves, whale calves. The word also names the fleshy back portion of the leg between the knee and ankle. The plural for both senses is calves. Calfskin is soft leather made from young cattle hides.

Caliber is the internal diameter of a gun barrel, or the diameter of a bullet or shell. A .22 caliber rifle fires smaller rounds than a .45. Extended from this, caliber means quality or level of ability: {a musician of the highest caliber}, {We need employees of that caliber}. The British spelling is calibre.

Calico is cotton fabric printed with a colorful pattern, typically small flowers or geometric shapes on a light background. In American usage, calico especially describes cats with patches of orange, black, and white fur: {a calico cat}. The word comes from Calicut, an Indian port city where such fabrics were traded. As an adjective, calico suggests patchwork coloring or cheap, printed material.

Call is a multi-faceted verb and noun. Its many meanings have grown from its 12th century origins: a verb that meant “speak loudly so as to be heard at a distance.” The verb call retains this meaning, even though today we may think of it first in connection with the telephone. The noun meanings of call all arise naturally from its verb definitions.

A callback is a return phone call, or an invitation to return for a second audition or interview: {She got a callback for the lead role}. In computing, a callback is a function passed to another function to be executed later. In comedy, a callback references an earlier joke: {The callback to his opening bit killed}.

Callbacks are references to earlier material, especially jokes or moments that return later for comic effect. A comedian sets up a bit, then calls back to it later in the set: {The callback to the airport joke killed}. In programming, a callback is a function passed as an argument to be executed later, often when an operation completes. In entertainment, a callback is an invitation for a second audition: {She got a callback for the lead role}.

A caller is someone who calls. In its oldest sense, a caller shouts or cries out—a square dance caller announces the moves. A caller may be someone who visits: {We had callers this afternoon}. Most commonly now, a caller is someone on the telephone: {We have a caller on line two}. In computing, a caller is code that invokes a function or subroutine.

Calligraphy is the art of beautiful handwriting, practiced with specialized pens, brushes, or other implements. The term covers both Western traditions—elegant scripts for diplomas, invitations, and manuscripts—and East Asian brush arts, where the aesthetic quality of characters carries cultural and spiritual significance. {She took up calligraphy to address her wedding invitations.}

A calling is work or a way of life that feels like more than just a job—a sense of purpose or vocation, often with spiritual overtones: {She felt a calling to medicine}. Originally the word referred to a divine summons to religious service, but now extends to any pursuit that feels deeply meant for you. Calling also simply means the act of making phone calls or shouting to someone.

Callous describes a hardened lack of feeling or sympathy toward others. Someone callous is emotionally tough in a way that makes them indifferent to suffering: {The callous remarks about the victims shocked everyone}. In its physical sense, callous refers to skin that has become thick and hardened, usually from repeated friction or pressure. The verb callous means to make or become hardened in either sense. The related noun is callus, the thickened skin itself.

Calls is the plural of call and the third-person singular verb form. A call is a vocal summons, a telephone conversation, or a decision: {The ref made a bad call}. To call is to shout, phone, or name: {They call him Skip}. Someone who calls the shots makes decisions. A close call is a narrow escape. {She calls her mother every Sunday}.

A callsign is an identifier assigned to a radio transmitter or its operator, used in aviation, military, and amateur radio to establish identity during communications: {What's your callsign, pilot?} Military units and personnel often use callsigns as tactical names. The term extends to usernames or handles in online communities, especially gaming: {My callsign on the server is Ghost}.

Calm describes a state without agitation or disturbance. Calm weather has no wind; calm water has no waves. A calm person remains composed under pressure: {She stayed calm during the crisis}. As a noun, calm is that peaceful state itself: {the calm before the storm}. To calm is to bring about such a state: {He tried to calm the crying child}. {Calm down} is the common imperative for reducing someone's agitation—or your own.

A calorie is a unit of energy, specifically the amount needed to raise one gram of water by one degree Celsius. In nutrition, calorie actually means kilocalorie—a thousand times larger—though the distinction is rarely observed in everyday speech. People count calories to manage weight: {I'm trying to cut calories}. Low-calorie foods provide less energy; high-calorie foods more.

Calories are units measuring the energy content of food and drink. Counting calories is central to weight management—consume more than you burn and you gain weight, less and you lose it. The term appears constantly in nutrition labels, diet talk, and fitness culture: {How many calories are in that?} {I'm trying to cut calories}. Technically, food labels show kilocalories, but in everyday usage, calorie means the same thing.

Calves is the irregular plural of calf, with two distinct meanings. Young cattle and certain other large mammals (elephants, whales) are called calves in their first year or so of life. The fleshy back part of the lower leg, between the knee and ankle, is also called a calf; athletes often speak of tight or sore calves after intense exercise. {The calves were weaned at eight weeks.} {My calves are killing me after that hike.}

Calzones are folded pizzas—dough wrapped around fillings like ricotta, mozzarella, and meat, then baked or fried. The Italian word means "trouser legs," presumably from the shape. Unlike pizza, the toppings are sealed inside: {I ordered a calzone stuffed with sausage and peppers}. Singular: calzone.

The resemblance of camaraderie to comrade is not accidental; the words and their meanings are related. Camaraderie is the spirit of friendliness and goodwill that you find among comrades or companions. A comrade was originally a roommate, someone with whom you would surely enjoy a sense of camaraderie.

A camcorder is a portable video camera with a built-in recorder, combining camera and recorder in one handheld device. The word emerged in the 1980s when home video recording became widely accessible. Though smartphones have largely displaced camcorders for casual recording, dedicated camcorders remain common for professional and semi-professional video work.

A camel is a large humped mammal used for transport and riding in desert regions. The two species—one-humped dromedary and two-humped Bactrian—are adapted to arid climates, capable of going long periods without water. Camel appears in compounds: {camel hair}, {camel toe}. The color camel is a yellowish-brown resembling the animal's coat.

Camels are large, humped mammals adapted to arid environments. The one-humped dromedary dominates the Middle East and North Africa; the two-humped Bactrian camel inhabits Central Asia. Their humps store fat, not water, though camels can go long periods without drinking. Known for endurance and ill temper, they've served as pack animals for millennia. {The caravan's camels carried spices across the desert.}

A cameo is a small carved relief, typically a profile portrait cut from layered stone so the figure stands out against a contrasting background. By extension, cameo describes any brief but memorable appearance—especially an actor's short role in a film: {The director made a cameo as a taxi driver}. The word also works as a verb: {She cameoed in the sequel}.

Cameos are brief appearances by notable people in performances where they wouldn't normally be expected—a famous director in a walk-on role, a celebrity playing themselves for a few seconds. The word comes from cameo, originally a carved gemstone with a raised figure against a contrasting background. That sense of a small, distinct image set against a larger field carries into the theatrical meaning: {The film featured cameos from several rock legends}.

A camera is a device for capturing images—photographs or video. The essential mechanism involves light passing through a lens onto a recording surface, whether film or digital sensor. Cameras range from smartphone cameras to professional cinema equipment. {She brought her camera to the wedding.} In the phrase {on camera}, it means being filmed or recorded; {off camera} is the opposite.

Cameras is the plural of camera, a device that captures images—photographs or video. The word covers everything from smartphone cameras to professional film equipment. {Security cameras recorded the break-in.} {She packed three cameras for the trip.} In the phrase {all eyes and cameras}, it emphasizes media attention on an event or person.

Camo is short for camouflage—the patterns designed to blend into natural surroundings. Originally military, camo has become a fashion statement: {He wore camo pants and combat boots}. The word works as noun or adjective: {a camo jacket}, {dressed in camo}. Hunters wear it for concealment; others wear it for style.

Camouflage is coloring or covering that makes something blend into its surroundings. Animals have natural camouflage; soldiers wear camouflage fatigues. The word extends to any disguise or concealment: {His friendliness was camouflage for his true intentions}. As a verb, to camouflage is to disguise or hide: {She camouflaged her disappointment with a smile}.

The most frequent meaning of camp is a place of temporary and somewhat primitive accommodation, such as that created by a traveling army, a group of mountain climbers, or a band of refugees. When you stay at such a place voluntarily, you camp. Sometimes, a group of people sharing values or ideas are called a camp: She’s in the pro-globalization camp. The unrelated word camp is an abstract concept for a kind of humor that satirizes by extreme exaggeration.

A campaign is a connected series of operations or activities designed to achieve a particular goal. Military campaigns involve coordinated battles and maneuvers across a theater of war. Political campaigns aim to win elections through rallies, advertisements, and voter outreach. Marketing campaigns promote products or causes. The verb campaign means to engage in such organized efforts: {She campaigned tirelessly for prison reform}. The unifying thread is sustained, strategic action toward a defined objective.

Campaigning is the activity of working toward a goal through organized, sustained effort—especially seeking political office or promoting a cause. Politicians spend months campaigning before elections: {She's been campaigning in swing states since June}. The term extends beyond politics to any coordinated push: {environmental groups campaigning against plastic waste}.

A camper is a person who camps—staying temporarily in a tent, cabin, or vehicle, usually outdoors for recreation: {The campers gathered around the fire}. A camper is also a vehicle equipped for sleeping and basic living, from small trailers to large motorhomes. In gaming slang, a camper is a player who stays in one spot to ambush others, often considered unsportsmanlike: {Stop camping and actually play}.

Campers are people who camp—staying overnight outdoors in tents, RVs, or similar temporary shelter, usually for recreation: {The campers gathered around the fire}. A camper is also a vehicle equipped for camping, or a child attending summer camp. In gaming slang, a camper is a player who stays in one strategic spot rather than moving around the map, often considered unsporting: {That camper has been hiding in the same corner all game}.

A campfire is a fire built outdoors, typically at a campsite, for warmth, cooking, or gathering around. Campfires are central to the camping experience—roasting marshmallows, telling stories, singing songs. The word evokes rustic sociability: {We sat around the campfire until midnight}. A campfire can also be a group event organized by scouts or similar organizations.

Campfires is the plural of campfire—an outdoor fire built for warmth, cooking, or gathering, typically at a campsite. The word evokes wood smoke, marshmallows, and stories told under stars. {We sat around the campfire until midnight.} {The smell of campfires drifted through the valley.}

A campground is a place where people can set up tents or park recreational vehicles for overnight stays, typically outdoors and often in a natural setting. Campgrounds range from primitive sites with no amenities to developed facilities with electricity, showers, and fire pits: {We reserved a campground near the lake for the weekend}. Also called a campsite, though campsite more often refers to a single spot within a larger campground.

Camping is the activity of staying outdoors overnight, typically in a tent or recreational vehicle, as a form of recreation.
