People go camping to enjoy nature, escape routine, or pursue outdoor activities like hiking and fishing. {We went camping in the mountains last summer.} The word also describes the act of setting up such temporary shelter: {The campground charges twenty dollars per night for camping.}

Camps is the plural of camp—temporary outdoor settlements, often with tents: {refugee camps}, {summer camps}, {military camps}. The verb camps means to set up or stay in such a place: {She camps by the river every August}. In cultural contexts, camps can mean opposing factions or schools of thought: {The debate divided critics into two camps}.

A campsite is a place where people set up tents or park campers for overnight stays outdoors. It may be a designated spot within a larger campground, with amenities like fire rings and picnic tables, or simply a patch of ground in the wilderness: {We found a campsite near the river}. Also called a campground when referring to the larger area.

A campus is the grounds of a university, college, or school, including its buildings, lawns, and walkways: {I spent four years on that campus}. The term extends to any unified cluster of buildings belonging to a single institution—a corporate campus, hospital campus, or tech campus. {Campus police} patrol these grounds. As an adjective, campus describes things located there: {campus housing}, {campus life}.

Campy describes entertainment or behavior that's exaggerated, theatrical, and often intentionally tacky in a way that's amusing rather than embarrassing. Camp revels in artifice, melodrama, and over-the-top aesthetics—think drag queens, old horror films, or kitschy décor. Something campy isn't trying to be taken seriously; it winks at its own absurdity. {The movie's campy dialogue and dramatic deaths made it a cult classic.} The related noun camp refers to this aesthetic sensibility itself.

Modal verbs slightly alter the meaning of a main verb, and among modals can is critical. Its effect on meaning is always related to ability (I can type 70 words a minute), capacity (This barrel can hold 60 gallons), or possibility (Weird stuff can happen late at night.). When combined with a sensory verb, can indicates perception that is happening now, or happens under given circumstances: I can hear something scratching at the window. From our roof we can see the fireworks. The past tense of can is could. In meanings connected with possibility, can is used interchangeably with may: Can I have a cookie? May I have a cookie?

A canal is an artificial waterway constructed for navigation, irrigation, or drainage. Unlike rivers, canals are human-made channels that connect bodies of water or carry water where nature didn't provide it: {The Panama Canal links the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans}. The word also applies to tubular passages in the body, such as the ear canal or alimentary canal. To canalize something is to channel it, literally or figuratively, into a particular direction or course.

Canals are artificial waterways constructed for navigation, irrigation, or drainage. The Panama and Suez canals connect major bodies of water, shortening shipping routes. Smaller canals irrigate farmland or drain wetlands. In anatomy, a canal is any tubular passage: the ear canal, the spinal canal. {The city's canals froze over in winter.}

A canary is a small yellow songbird, originally from the Canary Islands, popular as a cage bird for its melodious singing. The bright yellow color gives rise to canary as a color term. A canary in a coal mine—historically used to detect toxic gases—now means any early warning indicator: {The housing market is the canary in the coal mine for the broader economy}. In slang, a canary is an informant who sings to authorities. (Capitalized Canary refers to the Canary Islands.)

Cancel means to call off or revoke something previously arranged or agreed upon: {cancel a reservation}, {cancel a subscription}, {cancel the meeting}. To cancel a debt is to void it. In math, terms cancel when they offset each other. The contemporary slang sense means to publicly reject a person—usually a celebrity—for objectionable behavior, withdrawing support and attention: {They tried to cancel him after the tweets surfaced}.

Canceled is the past tense of cancel—to call off, revoke, or end something: {The flight was canceled due to weather}. In contemporary slang, canceled describes someone publicly rejected for offensive behavior or statements: {He got canceled after those tweets surfaced}. This sense emerged from social media call-out culture in the late 2010s. Also spelled cancelled.

Cancellation is the act of calling something off or voiding it. You can cancel an appointment, a subscription, a flight, or a contract. In contemporary usage, cancellation also refers to the public rejection of a person—typically a celebrity or public figure—for offensive behavior or statements: {The comedian faced cancellation after old tweets resurfaced}. A cancellation may also be the mark showing a stamp has been used.

Cancelled is the past tense and past participle of cancel, meaning to call off, revoke, or annul something previously planned or agreed upon: {The flight was cancelled due to weather}. British English strongly prefers this double-l spelling, while American English typically uses canceled, though both are acceptable in either dialect. In contemporary slang, cancelled describes someone who has been publicly rejected or boycotted, usually for offensive behavior: {He got cancelled after those tweets surfaced}.

Cancelling is the British spelling of canceling, the present participle of cancel. Both forms mean calling off, revoking, or nullifying: {She's cancelling the appointment}. In recent usage, cancelling someone means publicly withdrawing support due to objectionable behavior: {They're cancelling him over old tweets}.

Cancer refers to a group of diseases in which abnormal cells grow uncontrollably and can spread to other parts of the body. The word extends to anything that spreads destructively: {Corruption is a cancer eating away at the institution}. Someone's cancer is their particular case of the disease: {Her cancer went into remission}. (Capitalized Cancer is the zodiac sign.)

A candelabra is a branched candleholder, typically ornamental, designed to hold multiple candles. The classic form has a central stem with arms extending outward, each ending in a socket for a candle. Candelabras range from modest tabletop pieces to elaborate fixtures and are associated with formal dining, religious ceremonies, and decorative grandeur. The word is technically a Latin plural, but in English it functions as a singular noun, with candelabras as its plural.

Candid means honest and direct, especially about something others might avoid saying: {Let me be candid with you—this isn't working}. A candid assessment holds nothing back. Candid also describes unposed photographs that capture people naturally, without their awareness or preparation: {candid shots from the party}. The connection is authenticity—saying what's true, showing what's real.

A candidate is someone being considered for a position, award, or selection. Political candidates seek office; job candidates compete for employment. The word extends to things under consideration: {The building is a candidate for demolition}. A doctoral candidate has completed coursework and is writing a dissertation. Anything that seems likely to meet some fate can be called a candidate for it: {That old car is a candidate for the junkyard}.

Candidates is the plural of candidate—people being considered for a position, award, or selection. Job candidates interview for positions. Political candidates run for office. Candidates for an award are nominees. The word extends to things under consideration: {Several candidates for the bug fix have been proposed}. A doctoral candidate has completed coursework and is working on a dissertation.

Candied describes food that has been cooked or coated in sugar, giving it a sweet, often glossy appearance. Fruits, nuts, and citrus peels are commonly candied for use in baking or as confections. The word also applies to anything preserved in sugar syrup. Figuratively, candied can describe something excessively sweet or flattering: {candied words of praise}.

A candle is a cylinder of wax or tallow with a wick running through its center, burned to produce light. Before electric lighting, candles were essential household items. The phrase {can't hold a candle to} means to be far inferior: {Her cooking can't hold a candle to my grandmother's}. To {burn the candle at both ends} is to exhaust yourself through overwork or excess.

Candlelight is the soft, flickering illumination produced by a candle flame. The word evokes intimacy, romance, or old-fashioned simplicity: {a candlelight dinner}, {reading by candlelight}. Before electric lighting, candlelight was simply how people saw at night. Now it suggests atmosphere rather than necessity.

Candles are sticks of wax with a wick running through the center, burned to produce light. Before electric lighting, candles were essential for illumination—hence {candlelight dinner} evokes old-fashioned romance. Birthday candles are blown out while making a wish. To {burn the candle at both ends} is to exhaust yourself through overwork. {She can't hold a candle to her sister} means she doesn't compare favorably.

A candlestick is a holder for a candle, typically with a base for stability and a cup or spike to secure the candle upright. Candlesticks range from simple functional objects to ornate decorative pieces. In financial charts, a candlestick is a bar showing price movement over time, its shape resembling the household object.

Candlesticks are holders designed to support candles, typically with a base, stem, and cup or spike to secure the candle upright. They range from simple functional objects to ornate decorative pieces: {silver candlesticks on the mantelpiece}. In financial charts, candlesticks are bar-shaped indicators showing price movements over time, with the body representing opening and closing prices and thin lines (wicks) showing highs and lows.

Candor is openness and honesty, especially when discussing difficult or uncomfortable subjects. Someone speaking with candor holds nothing back: {I appreciated her candor about the company's problems}. The word suggests a willingness to say what others might avoid—not brutal honesty, but forthright sincerity without evasion or sugarcoating.

Candour is the British spelling of candor—the quality of being open, honest, and direct in expression. Someone speaking with candour tells you what they really think without evasion or sugarcoating: {I appreciate your candour, even if I don't like what you're saying}. The word implies both honesty and a willingness to address uncomfortable truths.

Candy is sweet food made primarily from sugar, often combined with flavorings, colorings, chocolate, or nuts. Americans say candy where the British say sweets. {The kids filled their bags with Halloween candy.} As a verb, to candy fruit or nuts is to coat or cook them in sugar syrup. Figuratively, candy describes something appealing but lacking substance: {eye candy}, {arm candy}.

Candyfloss is the British term for cotton candy—spun sugar wound around a stick into a fluffy mass, sold at fairs and amusement parks. Figuratively, candyfloss describes anything insubstantial or lacking depth: {The film was pure candyfloss—enjoyable but forgettable}.

A candyman is a drug dealer, especially one selling cocaine or heroin—candy being slang for drugs. The term carries a sinister undertone, suggesting someone who makes dangerous things seem sweet or appealing. In older or more innocent usage, a candyman is simply someone who sells candy: {The candyman comes around every afternoon}.

A cane is a stick used as a walking aid or a weapon for striking. Walking canes are usually slender with a curved handle; disciplinary canes are used to beat someone: {The headmaster gave him six strokes of the cane}. Cane also refers to the woody stems of certain plants—sugarcane, bamboo, rattan—and products made from them: {a cane chair}, {cane sugar}. To cane someone is to strike them with a cane as punishment.

Canines are the pointed teeth situated between incisors and premolars, designed for tearing food. Humans have four; in predators like dogs and wolves, they're more prominent fangs. The word also refers to dogs and their relatives—wolves, foxes, coyotes—members of the dog family. As an adjective, canine means relating to dogs: {canine behavior}, {canine companions}.

Cannabis is a plant genus whose dried flowers and leaves are used as a psychoactive drug, producing relaxation, altered perception, and euphoria. The term often appears in legal, medical, or scientific contexts: {medical cannabis}, {cannabis dispensary}. More casual synonyms include marijuana, weed, and pot. Cannabis also yields hemp fiber and CBD products.

Canned describes food preserved in sealed metal containers: {canned tomatoes}, {canned tuna}. The meaning extends to anything pre-prepared or recorded rather than fresh or live: {canned laughter}, {canned music}, {a canned speech}. These uses often carry a dismissive tone—something lacking spontaneity or authenticity. In slang, canned means drunk or fired from a job.

A cannibal is a person who eats human flesh. The term extends to animals that eat their own species: {Some spiders are cannibals}. Cannibalize means to take parts from one thing to repair another: {They cannibalized the old car for parts}. The word carries connotations of savagery and taboo violation.

Cannibalism is the practice of eating the flesh of one's own species. Among humans, it carries extreme taboo in most cultures, though it has occurred in ritual contexts, survival situations, and serial killings. The term extends to animals: {Some spider species are known for sexual cannibalism}. Figuratively, corporate cannibalism describes a company's new product eating into sales of its existing ones.

Cannibalize originally meant to eat the flesh of one's own kind, but the word now more often describes taking parts from one thing to repair or build another: {We cannibalized the old truck for spare parts}. In business, a new product cannibalizes sales when it draws customers away from the company's existing products rather than from competitors: {The cheaper model cannibalized their premium line}.

Cannibals are people who eat human flesh. The term extends to animals that consume their own species. Cannibalism appears in survival narratives, anthropological accounts, and horror fiction. Figuratively, a company that cannibalizes itself takes sales from its own products: {The new model cannibalized their bestseller}.

Canning is the process of preserving food by sealing it in airtight containers and heating to destroy microorganisms: {She spent the weekend canning tomatoes from the garden}. Home canning uses glass jars with metal lids; commercial canning uses tin-plated steel cans. The term extends to any large-scale firing or dismissal: {The new CEO started canning employees on day one}.

Cannoli are Italian pastries consisting of tube-shaped fried dough shells filled with sweet ricotta cream, often studded with chocolate chips or candied fruit. The singular is cannolo, though cannoli commonly serves for both: {I'll have a cannoli}. Associated especially with Sicilian cuisine and Italian-American bakeries.

A cannon is a large mounted gun that fires heavy projectiles—historically the principal artillery weapon in warfare and naval combat. The word extends to any similar tube-based launcher: a water cannon, a snow cannon at ski resorts. In billiards, a cannon (British) is a shot where the cue ball strikes two other balls in succession. To cannon into something is to collide with force: {He came around the corner and cannoned into me}.

A cannonball is a round metal projectile fired from a cannon—the original ammunition before explosive shells. The word now more commonly refers to a diving technique where you tuck your knees to your chest and hit the water in a ball shape, maximizing the splash: {He did a cannonball off the high dive}. As a verb, to cannonball is to dive this way or to move with similar compact force.

Cannonballs are heavy metal spheres fired from cannons—the original artillery ammunition before modern shells. The word extends to a style of jumping into water with knees tucked to the chest, creating maximum splash: {He did a cannonball off the diving board}. As a verb, to cannonball is to move rapidly and forcefully: {The car cannonballed down the highway}.

Cannons is the plural of cannon, large mounted guns that fire heavy projectiles. The word covers historical artillery pieces and modern military weapons alike. In sports, a cannon is a powerful arm: {He has a cannon for an arm}. In billiards, a cannon is a shot where the cue ball strikes two other balls successively.

A canoe is a narrow, lightweight boat pointed at both ends, propelled by paddling. Traditional canoes were made from bark, wood, or animal skins; modern ones are typically fiberglass or aluminum. Unlike kayaks, canoes are open-topped and paddled with a single-bladed paddle while kneeling or sitting on a raised seat. {We paddled the canoe across the lake.} To canoe is to travel by canoe: {They canoed down the river}.

Canoeing is the activity of paddling or traveling in a canoe—a narrow, lightweight boat propelled by single-bladed paddles. It ranges from leisurely recreation on calm lakes to demanding whitewater navigation: {We went canoeing on the river last summer}. The word also serves as the present participle of canoe: {She was canoeing upstream when the storm hit}.

Canoes are narrow, lightweight boats pointed at both ends, propelled by paddles. Traditional canoes were made from bark, wood, or animal skins; modern ones are typically fiberglass, aluminum, or plastic. Canoeing usually means recreational paddling on lakes and rivers: {We rented canoes and spent the afternoon on the lake}. To canoe is to travel by canoe.

Canon is an authoritative collection of works or principles accepted as genuine or foundational. The biblical canon is the set of books recognized as scripture. Literary canons are bodies of work considered essential: {the Western canon}, {the canon of English literature}. In fiction, canon refers to events officially part of a story's universe, as opposed to fan-created content: {That spinoff isn't canon}. Canon law is the body of rules governing a church. A canon is also a member of the clergy attached to a cathedral or collegiate church. In music, a canon is a composition where voices enter successively, each imitating the melody—{Pachelbel's Canon} being the famous example. (Capitalized Canon is the camera and electronics company.)

Canoodle is to kiss, cuddle, or fondle amorously—light physical affection between romantic partners: {a couple canoodling on a park bench}. The word has a playful, slightly old-fashioned quality, suggesting public displays of affection that are affectionate rather than overtly sexual.

Canoodling is affectionate physical intimacy—kissing, cuddling, caressing—especially in a playful or semi-public way. The word has a slightly old-fashioned, teasing quality, often used to describe couples caught in the act: {The paparazzi spotted them canoodling at a café}. It suggests behavior more flirtatious than serious, more endearing than scandalous.

A canopy is a covering suspended overhead. The term applies to fabric stretched above a bed, throne, or outdoor area for shade or ceremony, to the transparent enclosure over an aircraft cockpit, and to the uppermost layer of a forest where treetops form a continuous cover: {Monkeys swung through the canopy}. By extension, anything that spreads overhead like a roof: {a canopy of stars}.

Cans is the plural of can—metal containers for food, beverages, or other goods: {a six-pack of cans}, {recycling the cans}. In slang, cans refers to headphones (from their shape over the ears), breasts, or buttocks: {nice cans}. To {get canned} is to be fired from a job.

A canteen is a portable container for carrying water or other drinks, typically used by soldiers, hikers, or campers: {He unscrewed the cap of his canteen and took a long drink}. In British English and some institutional settings, a canteen is a cafeteria or dining hall, especially in a workplace, school, or military base. A canteen may also be a set of cutlery stored in a fitted case: {a canteen of silver}.

Canvas is a heavy, tightly woven fabric used for sails, tents, and bags—anything requiring durability. Because painters stretch canvas over frames to paint on, canvas extends to paintings themselves: {The museum acquired three canvases by Monet}. A boxing or wrestling ring has a canvas floor. To canvas (also spelled canvass) is to solicit opinions or votes door-to-door.

A canyon is a deep, narrow valley with steep sides, typically carved by a river over geological time. The Grand Canyon is the iconic example. Canyon appears in compounds describing similar formations: {slot canyon}, {box canyon}. Figuratively, urban canyons are streets flanked by tall buildings that channel wind and shadow.

Canyons is the plural of canyon—a deep, narrow valley with steep sides, typically carved by a river over geological time. The Grand Canyon is the most famous example. The word extends to similar formations: {urban canyons} describes city streets flanked by tall buildings. {We hiked through slot canyons in Utah.}

A cap is a close-fitting hat without an encircling brim. This meaning informs many others. The top or protective covers of a number of things are called caps (mushroom cap, mountain cap). An upper limit placed on something is also a cap: He’s hit the salary cap for his pay grade. Two longer words are often shortened to cap: capital, when it refers to a capital letter (type in all caps), and capsule when it refers to a dose of medicine in pill form. To cap something is to put a cap or an upper limit on it, or to print it with a capital letter.

Capable means having the ability or qualities needed to do something: {a capable administrator}, {capable of great kindness}. It suggests competence and reliability without implying excellence—a capable person gets the job done. When followed by "of," it can take on darker tones: {capable of murder}, {capable of anything}. The word often damns with faint praise; calling someone merely capable suggests they lack brilliance.

Capacity is the amount something can hold or contain: the {capacity} of a fuel tank, a stadium's seating {capacity}. Extended, it means ability or potential: {She has the capacity for great kindness}. In a {professional capacity}, someone acts in their official role. At {full capacity}, a system operates at maximum capability. {Capacity} crowds fill every available space.

A cape is a sleeveless outer garment that hangs from the shoulders, fastened at the neck and flowing loosely over the back—think superheroes or Victorian opera-goers. Capes suggest drama and flair: {She swept into the room in a red velvet cape}. A cape is also a point of land jutting into water: {We sailed around the cape at sunset}. The geographic sense appears in many place names. (Capitalized Cape often refers to specific locations like Cape Cod or the Cape of Good Hope.)

A caper is a playful leap or skip, or more broadly, a prank or escapade: {The kids were cutting capers in the yard}. In crime fiction and heist movies, a caper is a robbery or scheme, often with a lighthearted tone: {The movie follows a diamond caper gone wrong}. Separately, capers are the pickled flower buds of a Mediterranean shrub, used as a tangy garnish in cooking: {Chicken piccata calls for lemon and capers}.

Capers are the pickled flower buds of a Mediterranean shrub, used as a pungent seasoning in cooking: {Capers give the sauce its briny kick}. The word also names the plant itself. Separately, a caper is a playful leap or skip, or an adventurous escapade—often a crime: {a jewel heist caper}. To caper is to frolic or prance about.

Capes are sleeveless outer garments that fasten at the neck and hang over the shoulders, flowing freely rather than fitting the arms. Shorter than cloaks, they range from practical rain gear to dramatic costume pieces. Capes are iconic in superhero imagery: {No capes!} Geographically, a cape is a point of land extending into water: {Cape Cod}, {the Cape of Good Hope}.

Capital has two unrelated main meanings. One is money that is used for investment or development: The company attracted $1.5 million of venture capital. The other is connected with a seat of government (capital city, the capital of Utah). In architecture, the capital is the top of a column. Capital may also be short for capital letter. As an adjective, capital conveys prime importance. Capital punishment is punishment by death.

Capitalism is an economic system in which private individuals or businesses own the means of production and operate them for profit. Markets determine prices, wages, and the distribution of goods. The term often carries political weight—praised as the engine of prosperity and innovation, or criticized as a source of inequality and exploitation. {Under capitalism, competition drives efficiency.} {Critics argue capitalism prioritizes profit over people.}

A capitalist is someone who owns capital—wealth used to generate more wealth through investment or business ownership. The term describes both individual investors and advocates of capitalism as an economic system. As an adjective, capitalist describes economies or policies favoring private ownership and free markets: {capitalist countries}, {capitalist ideology}. Critics use it pejoratively: {capitalist exploitation}, {late-stage capitalism}.

Capitalists are people who own capital—money, property, or other assets used to generate wealth. In economic discussion, capitalists are those who own the means of production and employ workers: {The capitalists closed the factory and moved operations overseas}. The term can be neutral or pejorative depending on the speaker's politics. More loosely, a capitalist is anyone who supports or participates in a capitalist economic system.

Capitalize has two main threads. One involves letters: to capitalize is to write with an uppercase letter, or to begin a word that way. The other involves money and advantage: to capitalize a business is to fund it with capital; to capitalize on an opportunity is to exploit it for gain. {She capitalized on her early success to build a media empire.}

Capitals has several distinct meanings united by the idea of primary importance or position. Most commonly, capitals are the uppercase letters of an alphabet, distinguished from their lowercase counterparts. A capital is also the city serving as a government's seat of power: {Paris is the capital of France}. In architecture, a capital is the decorated top of a column. Capital as wealth or assets—especially money used for investment—yields the plural in financial contexts: {They raised capitals from multiple investors}.

A capitol is a building where a state legislature meets. In the United States, each state has a capitol housing its legislative chambers: {The protesters gathered on the capitol steps}. The word comes from the Capitoline Hill in ancient Rome, where the temple of Jupiter stood. (Capitalized Capitol refers specifically to the U.S. Congress building in Washington, D.C.)

Cappuccino is an espresso drink topped with steamed milk foam, traditionally served in a small cup. The foam layer is thick enough to hold its shape, distinguishing it from a latte's thinner milk. Named for the brown robes of Capuchin friars, the color resembling the drink. {I'll have a cappuccino with an extra shot.}

Caps are hats, particularly ones with a visor or brim at the front: {baseball caps}, {trucker caps}. The word also refers to any covering that fits over the top of something—a bottle cap, a lens cap, a cap on a tooth. To cap something is to put a limit on it: {The city capped property tax increases}. To cap off an event is to conclude it fittingly: {We capped off the evening with champagne}. In online communication, caps means capital letters, with typing in all caps understood as shouting: {Why are you yelling at me in caps?} (All-caps CAPS may refer to the television network.)

To capsize is to overturn in the water. Boats capsize when they flip upside down or roll onto their side: {A sudden gust capsized the sailboat}. The word applies almost exclusively to watercraft, though occasionally extends to other vehicles or situations that tip over dramatically.

Capsized describes a boat or ship that has overturned in the water. The term applies whether the vessel flips completely upside down or simply rolls onto its side: {The capsized ferry trapped passengers below deck}. Figuratively, capsized can describe any sudden, disastrous upset: {Their capsized plans left them scrambling}.

Capsizing is the overturning of a boat or ship, when the vessel rolls onto its side or flips completely upside down. Small boats capsize from shifting weight or rough water; larger vessels from taking on water or cargo imbalance. The word extends to any sudden overturning: {The canoe capsized in the rapids}.

A capsule is a small container, typically one that encloses medicine in a dissolvable shell for swallowing. The shape—a cylinder with rounded ends—extends to spacecraft designed to carry astronauts: {the Apollo capsule}. Capsule also describes something compact or condensed: a {capsule wardrobe} contains only essential pieces, a {capsule history} covers key points briefly. In anatomy, a capsule is a membrane enclosing an organ or joint.

Capsules are small containers, typically cylindrical with rounded ends. A medicine capsule is a gelatin shell holding a dose of medication: {Take two capsules daily with food}. The term extends to any compact, self-contained unit—a space capsule carries astronauts, a time capsule preserves artifacts. To capsule or encapsulate is to enclose something in condensed form: {The article capsules the main arguments}.

A captain is the person in command—of a ship, aircraft, or sports team. In the military, captain is a specific rank: mid-level for army officers, senior for naval ones. The verb means to lead or serve as captain: {She captained the volleyball team to three championships}. By extension, any leader or prominent figure in a field: {captains of industry}. (Capitalized Captain is used as a title before a name.)

Captains is the plural of captain—a person in command of a ship, aircraft, or military unit, or the leader of a sports team. The word also verbs: {She captains the volleyball team}. In restaurants, a captain oversees a section of servers. {The captains met before the coin toss.}

A caption is text accompanying an image, explaining or describing what appears in it: {The caption identified everyone in the photograph}. Captions also refer to the text at the bottom of a screen translating or transcribing dialogue, especially for deaf viewers or foreign films. The verb means to provide such text: {She captioned the video for accessibility}.

Captions are text accompanying images or video. A caption under a photograph identifies what's shown or adds context. In film and television, captions display dialogue and sound descriptions for deaf or hard-of-hearing viewers, or translate foreign languages. To caption something is to provide such text: {She captioned the photo before posting it}.

Captivated means completely absorbed or charmed by something or someone. The word carries a sense of being held spellbound, unable to look away: {The audience sat captivated through the entire performance}. You can be captivated by a story, a view, or a person's presence. The root suggests capture—your attention has been seized and held.

Captivating describes something that holds attention completely, as if by a spell. A captivating {story}, {performance}, or {smile} draws you in and won't let go. The word suggests enchantment rather than mere interest—you're not just paying attention, you're held there: {She gave a captivating account of her travels}.

Captive describes someone or something held in confinement or under another's control. A captive {animal} is kept in a cage or enclosure. A captive {audience} cannot easily leave. A captive {market} has no alternative suppliers. As a noun, a captive is a prisoner: {The captives were held for ransom}. To be held captive is to be detained against one's will. Figuratively, something holds you captive when it commands your attention completely: {The story held me captive until the final page}.

Captivity is the state of being confined or held against one's will. Animals live in captivity in zoos and aquariums, as opposed to the wild. Prisoners of war are held in captivity. The word often carries connotations of powerlessness: {She felt trapped in the captivity of a bad marriage}. A captive audience can't easily leave.

A captor is someone who takes and holds a person or animal against their will. The word typically appears in contexts involving kidnapping, hostage situations, or warfare, where the relationship between captor and captive is defined by force or coercion. {The hostages eventually developed sympathy for their captors.} Captor can also describe anyone or anything that traps or confines, though this figurative use is less common.

Captors are people who hold others prisoner or in confinement. The word implies an ongoing relationship of control—someone who has captured and continues to detain: {The hostages described their captors as nervous but not cruel}. A captor may be a kidnapper, a prison guard, or an enemy combatant holding prisoners of war.

Capture means to take possession of something, typically by force or skill. Soldiers capture prisoners; photographers capture images; words capture feelings. The emphasis is on seizing and holding: {The photo captured her smile perfectly}. A capture is an instance of capturing, or the thing captured. In games, to capture a piece is to remove it from play.

Captured is the past tense of capture—to take possession of something by force, skill, or effort. A soldier is captured in battle, a criminal captured by police, a chess piece captured by an opponent. The word extends to less physical takings: a photograph captures a moment, a painting captures a likeness, a book captures the spirit of an era. {The film captured the chaos of the period perfectly.} Data or footage that has been captured has been recorded or collected: {The security camera captured the whole incident.}

A capybara is a large South American rodent—the world's largest, reaching about 130 pounds. These semiaquatic animals live near water in groups and have become internet favorites for their calm, friendly demeanor. They're often photographed lounging with other animals: {The capybara sat unbothered as birds perched on its back}.

Capybaras is the plural of capybara, a large semiaquatic rodent native to South America—the world's largest living rodent, weighing up to 140 pounds. They're social animals that live in groups near water. Online, capybaras have become beloved for their placid demeanor and apparent friendliness with other animals: {The capybaras just sat there while the ducks climbed on them}.

A car is a four-wheeled motor vehicle designed to carry passengers on roads. The word applies most commonly to automobiles: {We took the car to the grocery store}. Car also designates compartments in larger conveyances—a railroad car, a cable car, the car of an elevator. A {car crash} may be literal or figurative: {That interview was a car crash}.

A carabiner is a metal loop with a spring-loaded gate, used to quickly connect ropes, harnesses, and other equipment. Essential in rock climbing, mountaineering, and industrial rigging, carabiners come in locking and non-locking varieties: {Clip the carabiner to your harness before ascending}. Also spelled karabiner.

Caramel is sugar heated until it browns, producing a rich, sweet flavor used in candies, sauces, and desserts. The word names both the process and its products: caramel {apples}, caramel {sauce}, {salted caramel}. As a color, caramel is a warm golden-brown: {caramel highlights in her hair}. Pronunciation varies—some say three syllables, others two.

To caramelize is to heat sugar until it browns and develops a rich, complex flavor. The process transforms white sugar into amber liquid with notes of butter and toffee. By extension, caramelize describes cooking any food until its natural sugars brown: {caramelized onions}, {caramelized bananas}. The result is deeper color and sweeter, more complex taste.

A caravan is a group traveling together, especially across a desert or hostile territory—merchants with camels, refugees in vehicles. The word extends to any procession: {a caravan of SUVs heading to the beach house}. In British English, a caravan is also a trailer pulled behind a vehicle for camping or temporary housing.

Caravans is the plural of caravan. A caravan is a group traveling together, especially across desert or hostile territory: {a caravan of merchants crossing the Sahara}. The word extends to a line of vehicles moving together. In British English, a caravan is a travel trailer—a wheeled dwelling towed behind a vehicle for camping holidays: {They spent summers in their caravan}.

Carb is short for carbohydrate—sugars, starches, and fibers found in foods like bread, pasta, and fruit. The term appears constantly in diet talk: {I'm cutting carbs}, {low-carb recipes}. In automotive contexts, carb is short for carburetor, the engine component that mixes fuel with air: {The carb needs adjusting}.

Carbon is a chemical element fundamental to life on Earth—the backbone of organic chemistry. All known living things are carbon-based. Carbon atoms bond readily with other elements, forming millions of compounds. Pure carbon appears as diamond, graphite, and other forms. A {carbon footprint} measures greenhouse gas emissions. {Carbon dating} determines the age of organic materials.

Carbonara is an Italian pasta sauce made from egg yolks, hard cheese (usually Pecorino Romano), cured pork (guanciale or pancetta), and black pepper. The eggs are tempered by the hot pasta to create a creamy coating without scrambling: {I'll have the spaghetti carbonara}. The dish originated in Rome and remains associated with Roman cuisine.

Carbs is the casual shorthand for carbohydrates—sugars, starches, and fibers found in foods like bread, pasta, fruit, and vegetables. The term dominates diet talk, where carbs are often cast as the enemy: {I'm cutting carbs}, {low-carb diet}. Athletes may {load up on carbs} before competition for energy.

A carcass is the dead body of an animal, especially one slaughtered for meat or left after predators have fed: {Vultures circled the carcass}. The word extends to the framework or shell of something stripped or abandoned: {the burned-out carcass of a car}. Applied to a living human body, it's humorous or self-deprecating: {I need to drag my carcass out of bed}.

Carcasses is the plural of carcass—the dead body of an animal, especially one slaughtered for meat or found after death. Butchers work with beef carcasses; vultures circle animal carcasses in the wild. The word extends to anything lifeless or abandoned: {Rusting carcasses of old cars lined the yard}. Applied to humans, it's either humorous or deliberately dehumanizing.

Most things called card are made of stiff paper or plastic and come in specialized forms (credit card, playing card, greeting card, membership card, business card). Integrated circuits are printed on graphics cards and memory cards. If you card someone, you ask to see their driver’s license as proof of their age. A different and less frequent word card is a verb that means to disentangle fibers, using a device that does this: She was busy carding wool.

Cardboard is stiff, thick paper made from layers of pulp pressed together, used for boxes, packaging, and craft projects. The material suggests cheapness or flimsiness: a {cardboard cutout}, {cardboard furniture}. Figuratively, cardboard describes something lacking depth or authenticity: {cardboard characters}, {a cardboard villain}.

A cardigan is a knitted sweater that opens at the front, typically fastened with buttons or a zipper. Unlike pullovers, cardigans don't go over the head: {She threw on a cardigan when the office got cold}. The style ranges from casual to dressy, lightweight to chunky.

Cardinal is a noun and adjective with several meanings that are related in less than obvious ways. The original meaning was “of great importance.” This meaning was transferred to the senior ecclesiastical official. Since these fellows wear red vestments and red pointy hats, the bird we call a cardinal got its name by association. Finally a cardinal number is one that expresses amount, such as four, twenty, or thousand. Cardinal numbers are distinguished from ordinal numbers, which express order.

Cardinals are high-ranking officials in the Roman Catholic Church, second only to the pope and responsible for electing new popes. The word also refers to bright red songbirds native to the Americas, named for their color resembling the red robes worn by church cardinals. In mathematics, cardinal numbers indicate quantity—one, two, three—as opposed to ordinal numbers indicating position. {The cardinals gathered in Rome for the conclave.} (Capitalized Cardinals refers to sports teams.)

Cardio is exercise that elevates heart rate—running, cycling, swimming, aerobics. Short for cardiovascular, it emphasizes the heart and circulatory system rather than strength or flexibility: {I need to do more cardio}. At gyms, cardio often refers to the machines: treadmills, ellipticals, stationary bikes. {She spent forty minutes on cardio before lifting weights}.

Cards are small flat pieces of stiff paper or plastic used for countless purposes. Playing cards come in decks and are used for games and magic tricks. Credit cards and debit cards facilitate purchases. Business cards identify people professionally. Greeting cards convey messages for occasions. ID cards verify identity. To be {in the cards} means something is likely to happen. If you {play your cards right}, you handle a situation skillfully to your advantage.

A cardshark is someone highly skilled at card games, especially one who uses that skill to win money from less experienced players. The term carries a hint of sharp dealing or hustling—a cardshark may not cheat outright but plays with predatory cunning: {He lost three hundred dollars to some cardshark at the casino}. Also spelled card shark.

A cardsharp is someone who cheats at card games, especially for profit. The word implies skill and cunning rather than crude deception—a cardsharp manipulates cards or exploits opponents through sleight of hand, marked decks, or psychological tactics: {The riverboat was notorious for cardsharps fleecing naive travelers}. Also spelled cardsharper.

Care centers on attention and concern. To care about something is to regard it as important; to care for someone is to look after them. A caregiver provides care. {I don't care} dismisses something as unimportant. {Take care} means be careful or, as a farewell, stay well. {Handle with care} warns of fragility. Cares are worries or burdens: {the cares of the world}. {Couldn't care less} expresses total indifference—though {could care less}, logically backward, means the same thing.

Careening describes wild, uncontrolled movement—lurching from side to side while moving fast: {The car came careening around the corner}, {He careened through the crowd}. The word suggests both speed and instability. Originally a nautical term for tilting a ship on its side for cleaning or repair, that sense survives mainly in historical contexts.

Career is the arc of one's working life, especially in a particular field: {a career in medicine}, {a career politician}. It implies progression and commitment rather than just a job. The older sense—rapid movement or rushing—survives in the verb: {The car careered off the road}. To career through something is to move fast and somewhat out of control.

Careers is the plural of career, referring to long-term professional paths or occupations: {She counseled students on their careers}. The verb careers means to move swiftly and erratically: {The car careered down the hillside}. This sense is more common in British English; Americans typically use careen for uncontrolled motion.

Carefree means without worry or responsibility. A carefree attitude takes things lightly; a carefree summer lacks obligations. The word suggests pleasant lightness rather than recklessness: {She had a carefree childhood}, {those carefree days before the diagnosis}. Someone carefree isn't necessarily careless—just unburdened.

Careful means taking care to avoid mistakes, damage, or harm. A careful driver watches the road attentively. A careful reader notices details others miss. {Be careful with that vase—it's fragile.} The word can also mean thorough and deliberate: {careful analysis}, {careful planning}. To be careful about something is to give it proper attention and consideration.

A caregiver is someone who looks after another person who cannot fully care for themselves—typically a child, elderly person, or someone with illness or disability. The term covers both paid professionals and unpaid family members: {Her daughter became her primary caregiver after the stroke}. Caregiving often involves physical assistance, emotional support, and managing medical needs.

Caregivers is the plural of caregiver—a person who provides care for someone unable to fully care for themselves. The term typically refers to those who tend to children, the elderly, or people with disabilities or chronic illness. Caregivers may be family members providing unpaid care or professionals: {Her mother's caregivers rotate in twelve-hour shifts}. The word emphasizes the ongoing, often demanding nature of the work.

Caregiving is the work of looking after someone who cannot fully care for themselves—typically the elderly, chronically ill, or disabled. The term encompasses both professional care and the unpaid labor of family members: {She left her job to focus on caregiving for her mother}. Caregiving often implies sustained, demanding responsibility rather than occasional help.

Careless means lacking attention or concern. A careless driver fails to notice hazards. A careless remark is made without thinking of consequences. Careless can also suggest ease and freedom from worry: {a careless summer afternoon}. The word implies negligence when stakes are high but relaxed indifference when they're not.

A carer is someone who looks after a person unable to care for themselves fully—typically an elderly, disabled, or chronically ill family member. The term is primarily British; Americans more often say caregiver. {She became her mother's carer after the stroke.} Professional carers provide similar support for pay.

A caress is a gentle, affectionate touch—stroking someone's hair, brushing fingers along a cheek. The verb means to touch in this tender way: {He caressed her face}. Caress extends to anything that touches lightly and pleasantly: {A warm breeze caressed the curtains}. The word implies intimacy, tenderness, or sensuality rather than mere contact.

A caretaker looks after something in the owner's absence or incapacity—a property, an estate, a person. In British English, a caretaker maintains a building; Americans would say janitor or custodian. As an adjective, caretaker describes someone holding a position temporarily until a permanent replacement is found: {a caretaker government}, {a caretaker manager}.

Cargo is goods transported by ship, plane, truck, or train—freight in bulk rather than individual packages. The word emphasizes commercial transport: {cargo ship}, {cargo hold}, {cargo plane}. Cargo pants have large pockets on the thighs, originally for carrying tools or supplies. {The ship arrived with a cargo of grain}.

Caribou is a large deer native to Arctic and subarctic regions of North America, known for its broad hooves and large antlers carried by both sexes. The same animal is called reindeer in Europe and Asia. Caribou migrate in vast herds across tundra and boreal forest: {The caribou crossed the frozen river by the thousands}.

A caricature is a portrait that exaggerates distinctive features for comic or satirical effect—a politician's prominent nose made enormous, a celebrity's quirk amplified. The term extends beyond visual art: any depiction that distorts through oversimplification becomes a caricature. {The villain was a caricature of corporate greed.} To caricature someone is to portray them this way.

Caricatures are exaggerated representations that distort distinctive features for comic or satirical effect. A caricature artist at a fair might enlarge a subject's nose or ears. The term extends beyond visual art: {His portrayal of the CEO was a caricature, reducing her to a handful of quirks}. To caricature someone is to depict them this way, emphasizing traits to the point of absurdity.

Caring describes genuine concern for someone's wellbeing and the willingness to act on it. A caring {parent} attends to a child's needs; a caring {friend} checks in during hard times. The word implies warmth and attentiveness rather than mere obligation. As a noun, caring refers to the work of looking after someone: {the challenges of caring for elderly relatives}.

To carjack is to steal a vehicle by force or threat while the driver is present—distinguished from ordinary auto theft by the element of confrontation. The carjacker typically approaches at a stoplight or parking lot and demands the keys at gunpoint: {She was carjacked outside the grocery store}. The noun carjacking names the crime.

Carjacked means having had one's vehicle stolen by force or threat while present. The term combines car with hijacked: {She was carjacked at a stoplight}. Someone who carjacks is a carjacker, and the crime is carjacking. Unlike ordinary auto theft, carjacking involves confronting the driver or occupants directly.

A carjacker is someone who steals a vehicle by force or threat while the driver is present—distinguishing carjacking from ordinary auto theft, which typically targets unoccupied cars. {The carjacker pulled a gun and ordered her out of the vehicle.}

Carjacking is stealing a vehicle by force or threat while the driver is present—distinguished from ordinary auto theft by the element of confrontation. The term emerged in the early 1990s as such crimes increased in American cities: {He was convicted of carjacking after pulling a gun on a woman at a gas station}. The verb is carjack.

Carnage is the killing of many people, especially in war or violence. The word emphasizes brutal, bloody destruction—bodies and devastation left behind: {The battlefield was a scene of carnage}. Extended to any severe destruction: {The stock market crash left financial carnage in its wake}.

A carnation is a flowering plant with fringed petals in white, pink, red, or yellow, widely cultivated for bouquets and boutonnieres. Carnations are traditional for Mother's Day and proms. The flowers have a spicy-sweet fragrance. The color carnation is a light pinkish-red, like the most common variety of the flower.

Carnations are flowering plants prized for their ruffled, fragrant blooms that come in white, pink, red, yellow, and purple varieties. They are among the most popular cut flowers for bouquets, corsages, and boutonnieres, often appearing at weddings, funerals, and on Mother's Day. Different colors carry traditional meanings: red for love, white for luck, pink for gratitude. {She pinned a carnation to his lapel before the dance.}

A carnie is someone who works at a carnival, especially traveling fairs with rides, games, and sideshows. The term often carries connotations of rough living, transience, and insider knowledge of rigged games: {The carnie running the ring toss made it look easy}. Also spelled carny.

Carnies are the workers who operate carnival rides, games, and attractions. The term carries connotations of transience and seediness—carnies travel from town to town, live in trailers, and have a reputation (fair or not) for running rigged games and living rough: {The carnies were setting up the Ferris wheel when we arrived}. Sometimes used dismissively for anyone who seems shabby or untrustworthy.

A carnival is a traveling amusement show with rides, games, and sideshows, typically set up temporarily in towns and fairgrounds. The word also refers to a period of public festivity before Lent, especially the elaborate celebrations in places like Rio de Janeiro and New Orleans: {Carnival season brings parades and costumes}. By extension, any wild, chaotic scene can be called a carnival: {The press conference turned into a carnival}.

Carnivals is the plural of carnival, a traveling amusement show with rides, games, and sideshows, or a festival of public celebration, often before Lent. The word carries connotations of bright lights, noise, and slightly seedy entertainment: {State fairs and carnivals came through every summer}. Figuratively, any chaotic or colorful spectacle: {The trial became a media carnival}.

A carnivore is an animal that eats meat—lions, wolves, sharks. The term also applies to meat-eating plants like the Venus flytrap. In casual use, carnivore describes a person who loves meat or eats it enthusiastically: {I'm a carnivore—I need steak at least twice a week}. The opposite is herbivore.

Carnivores are animals that eat meat—predators like lions, wolves, and sharks, or scavengers like vultures and hyenas. The term also applies to carnivorous plants that trap insects. In taxonomy, Carnivora is an order of mammals including cats, dogs, bears, and seals. Informally, carnivore describes any enthusiastic meat-eater: {I'm a carnivore—I need steak at least once a week}.

A carny is a person who works at a carnival, typically operating rides or running games on the midway. The word carries connotations of seediness—carnies are stereotyped as drifters, con artists, or rough characters: {The carny running the ring toss looked like he hadn't slept in days}. Also spelled carnie. The word can also refer to carnival culture or lifestyle generally.

A carol is a joyful song, especially one sung at Christmas: {We went caroling through the neighborhood}. The word applies to any celebratory hymn, though Christmas carols dominate modern usage. To carol is to sing such songs, typically in a group moving from house to house. {The choir caroled late into the evening.} (Capitalized Carol is a given name.)

Carolers are people who sing carols, especially groups who go door to door singing Christmas songs during the holiday season: {Carolers came by last night with "Silent Night"}. The tradition involves neighbors or church groups spreading seasonal cheer, often collecting donations for charity. Also spelled carollers.

Caroling is the act of singing carols, especially Christmas songs, often in a group going door to door: {We went caroling through the neighborhood}. The tradition involves visiting homes or public spaces to spread holiday cheer through song. Also spelled carolling.

Carols are joyful songs, especially those sung at Christmas: {We went caroling through the neighborhood}, {The choir sang traditional carols}. The word once applied to any celebratory song accompanied by dancing, but now Christmas carols dominate usage. To carol is to sing such songs, typically going door to door during the holiday season.

A carousel is a rotating amusement ride with seats, often shaped like horses or other animals, that move up and down as the platform spins: {The children begged for another ride on the carousel}. The term extends to any rotating mechanism—a luggage carousel at an airport, a slide carousel for projectors. In digital interfaces, a carousel is a display element that cycles through images or content horizontally.

Carousels are rotating platforms, most commonly the amusement park ride with decorated horses and other animals that move up and down as the platform spins. The term extends to any rotating mechanism: a luggage carousel at an airport, a slide carousel for a projector. In digital interfaces, a carousel is a display element that cycles through images or content: {Swipe through the carousel to see more photos}.

Carp is a large freshwater fish, often bottom-feeding, found in ponds and slow rivers. Common carp are farmed for food in many parts of the world; koi are ornamental carp bred for their colors. Separately, to carp is to complain or find fault in a petty, nagging way: {He carped about every little thing}.

A carpenter is a skilled worker who builds and repairs wooden structures—framing houses, installing cabinets, constructing furniture. The trade divides into rough carpentry (structural framing) and finish carpentry (trim, moldings, fine detail work). {We hired a carpenter to build the deck.} As a verb, to carpenter is to do such work, though the noun dominates.

Carpentry is the craft of cutting, shaping, and joining wood to build or repair structures and objects. A carpenter builds houses, frames walls, installs doors and cabinets. The term covers rough work like framing and finish work like trim and molding. {He learned carpentry from his father.}

Carpet is a thick floor covering of woven or felted fabric, typically extending wall-to-wall rather than as a smaller rug. To carpet a room is to install this covering. Carpet extends to anything resembling such a covering: {a carpet of wildflowers}. To carpet someone (British) is to reprimand them severely, from being called to stand on the boss's carpet. To {sweep under the carpet} is to hide something inconvenient.

A carpetbagger is an outsider who moves to a new area seeking political or economic advantage. The term originated after the American Civil War for Northerners who went South during Reconstruction, supposedly carrying all their belongings in a carpetbag. Now it applies broadly to any opportunist exploiting a place where they have no roots: {The candidate was dismissed as a carpetbagger who'd only moved to the district six months before the election}.

Carpetbaggers were Northerners who went to the South after the American Civil War, supposedly carrying all their belongings in a bag made of carpet fabric—implying they were opportunists with no real stake in the region. The term now describes any outsider who moves somewhere to exploit local opportunities, especially political ones: {The candidate was dismissed as a carpetbagger who'd only lived in the district for six months}.

Carpetbagging is exploiting a place or situation where one has no genuine roots or stake. The term comes from Northerners who moved to the South after the Civil War, carrying their belongings in carpet bags, to profit from Reconstruction. Now it often describes politicians who run for office in districts where they don't truly live: {She accused her opponent of carpetbagging into the district just to win a seat}. The word implies opportunism and lack of authentic connection.

A carpool is an arrangement where people share rides to a common destination, typically work or school, rotating drivers or splitting costs: {We started a carpool to save on gas}. The verb means to participate in such an arrangement: {I carpool with three coworkers}. A carpool lane on highways is reserved for vehicles carrying multiple passengers.

Carpooling is sharing a car ride with others traveling the same route, typically to work or school: {We started carpooling to split the cost of gas}. The arrangement reduces expenses, traffic, and environmental impact. A carpool lane on highways is reserved for vehicles carrying multiple passengers. Also spelled car-pooling or car pooling.

A carposporophyte is the spore-producing phase that develops on a red alga after fertilization. It remains attached to the parent plant and generates carpospores, which disperse to continue the organism's complex life cycle. The term appears almost exclusively in phycology—the study of algae.

A carriage is a wheeled vehicle, especially one drawn by horses for transporting people. The word extends to anything that carries or conveys: a baby carriage, the carriage of a typewriter (the part that moves), or a railway carriage (British for a passenger car). Carriage also means bearing or posture—how someone carries themselves: {She has the carriage of a dancer}. The carriage of goods is their transport, and carriage charges are shipping fees.

A carrier is someone or something that transports goods or people—a mail carrier, an aircraft carrier, a common carrier like a trucking company. In medicine and genetics, a carrier harbors a disease or gene without showing symptoms: {She's a carrier of the sickle cell trait}. Telecommunications carriers provide phone or internet service. In physics and electronics, a carrier wave transmits a signal.

Carrion is the decaying flesh of dead animals. Vultures, crows, and other scavengers feed on carrion. The word often carries connotations of rot and disgust: {The battlefield reeked of carrion}. As an adjective, it describes creatures that eat the dead: {carrion birds circled overhead}.

A carrot is an orange root vegetable, long and tapered, eaten raw or cooked. Carrots appear in the phrase {carrot and stick}—reward paired with punishment—from the image of luring a donkey forward with a dangled carrot while threatening it from behind. A carrot alone is any promised incentive: {They dangled a promotion as a carrot}.

Carrots are orange root vegetables, long and tapered, eaten raw or cooked. They're a common side dish and salad ingredient, often associated with good eyesight. A carrot dangled before someone is an incentive or reward: {The promotion was the carrot that kept her working late}. The phrase {carrot and stick} pairs reward with punishment as motivational tools.

Carry shares core ideas with another frequent verb, bring. When used literally, the subject of carry is a person or thing that is capable of holding or transporting an object, and the object so held would probably not be moving on its own: Ask the porter to carry your bags to the car. When used figuratively, carry includes the idea of accompaniment that may also be present with bring: a crime that carries the death penalty. Without a direct object, carry may include the idea of succeed or pass: the motion carried on a vote of 23-7.

Carrying is the present participle of carry—moving something while supporting its weight. You can be carrying groceries, carrying a child, or carrying a weapon. Extended uses include bearing responsibility {carrying the team}, maintaining something {carrying insurance}, or being pregnant {She's carrying twins}. In sports, carrying often means advancing the ball: {He's averaging four yards per carry}.

Cars are motor vehicles designed to carry passengers on roads—the dominant form of personal transportation in developed countries. The word is the standard informal term for automobiles: {We took two cars to the airport}. Cars also refers to railroad vehicles: {freight cars}, {passenger cars}. In an elevator, the car is the enclosure that moves.

Carsick describes the nausea and discomfort some people feel while riding in a car, caused by the disconnect between what the eyes see and what the inner ear senses. Reading or looking at screens often makes it worse. {I get carsick if I sit in the back seat.} Similar terms exist for other vehicles: seasick, airsick.

A cart is a vehicle for hauling goods, typically with two wheels and pulled by an animal or pushed by hand. Shopping carts and golf carts extend the sense to wheeled conveyances in retail and recreation. To cart something is to transport it, often with effort or complaint: {I carted all those boxes up three flights of stairs}. To {put the cart before the horse} is to do things in the wrong order.

A cartel is a group of independent businesses or nations that coordinate to control prices, limit competition, or dominate a market. OPEC is perhaps the most famous cartel, controlling oil production. The term also refers to criminal organizations, particularly Latin American drug trafficking syndicates: {The Sinaloa cartel controls much of the border region}. More loosely, cartel suggests any powerful coalition acting in concert against outside interests.

Cartels are groups of independent entities—typically businesses or nations—that collude to control prices, limit competition, or divide markets. Oil-producing nations form cartels to regulate supply. Companies form illegal cartels to fix prices: {The Justice Department broke up the cartel}. Drug cartels are criminal organizations that control narcotics trafficking, often wielding military-level power: {Mexican cartels fighting for territory}.

A cartographer is a person who makes maps. The work combines geographic knowledge with design skills to represent spatial information visually. Modern cartographers often use satellite imagery and digital tools, though the term covers mapmakers across all eras and methods: {The cartographer spent years surveying the coastline}.

Cartography is the science and art of making maps. The term covers everything from ancient hand-drawn charts to modern satellite-based mapping systems. A cartographer studies geography, surveys terrain, and represents spatial relationships on paper or screen. {The cartography of the region was unreliable until aerial photography became available.}

A carton is a lightweight container, typically made of cardboard or paperboard: a {carton of eggs}, a {carton of milk}, a {carton of cigarettes}. The word suggests something boxlike and disposable, distinct from heavier containers like crates or permanent packaging like bottles.

A cartoon is a drawing, typically humorous or satirical, often with captions or speech bubbles. Editorial cartoons comment on politics; comic strips are cartoon sequences. The word extended to animated films—motion pictures made from drawings—and now covers any animation: {Saturday morning cartoons}, {a Pixar cartoon}. Cartoon also means a simplified or exaggerated version of something: {He's a cartoon villain}.

A cartoonist is someone who draws cartoons—whether single-panel comics, comic strips, editorial illustrations, or animated sequences. The term covers a range from newspaper cartoonists producing daily strips to political cartoonists commenting on current events: {The cartoonist captured the senator's arrogance in a few lines}.

Cartoons are drawings, typically humorous or satirical, often published in newspapers and magazines. Political cartoons comment on current events through caricature and visual metaphor. The word also refers to animated films or television shows: {Saturday morning cartoons}, {cartoon characters}. A cartoon can be a preliminary sketch for a painting or fresco, though this sense is now rare outside art history.

A cartridge is a container holding material ready to be fed into a device. A gun cartridge contains propellant and usually a bullet, designed to be loaded and fired as a unit. Ink cartridges slot into printers; game cartridges into consoles. The word implies a standardized, replaceable unit: {I need to buy new toner cartridges for the copier}.

Cartridges is the plural of cartridge, a self-contained unit designed to be loaded into a device. The oldest sense is ammunition—a casing holding a bullet, powder, and primer: {The rifle holds five cartridges}. The concept extends to replaceable containers for ink, toner, or video games: {I need to buy new printer cartridges}. A cartridge simplifies reloading by packaging components together.

Carts is the plural of cart—a wheeled vehicle for transporting goods, typically pushed or pulled by hand or drawn by animals. Shopping carts hold groceries; golf carts ferry players across courses. In computing, a cart (short for cartridge) holds game software: {old Nintendo carts}. Online, carts hold items selected for purchase: {I have three things in my cart}.

A cartwheel is a sideways flip where hands and feet touch the ground alternately, arms and legs extended like spokes of a wheel. Children turn cartwheels on lawns; gymnasts perform them in routines. The word extends to any wheel-like rotation: {The plane cartwheeled across the runway}. A cartwheel is also slang for a large coin, especially the old silver dollar.

Cartwheeling is performing cartwheels—the acrobatic move where you turn sideways with arms and legs extended like wheel spokes. The term extends to any spinning or tumbling motion: {The car went cartwheeling off the cliff}. Figuratively, something cartwheeling moves wildly or dramatically: {Stock prices went cartwheeling after the announcement}.

Cartwheels are acrobatic movements where the body rotates sideways with arms and legs extended like wheel spokes, hands and feet touching the ground in sequence. Children do cartwheels on lawns; gymnasts perform them in routines. Figuratively, to do cartwheels is to express exuberant joy: {When she got the acceptance letter, her heart did cartwheels}.

Carve is to cut into a solid material with a blade or sharp tool. You carve wood, stone, or ice to create shapes or designs: {She carved a figure from a block of oak}. At the dinner table, to carve is to slice meat from a larger piece: {Who's going to carve the turkey?} To carve out something—a career, a niche, a territory—is to establish it through sustained effort. To carve up is to divide: {The victors carved up the defeated empire among themselves}.

Carved describes something that has been shaped by cutting away material—typically wood, stone, or ice. A carved {statue} shows the marks of deliberate shaping. Carved {initials} in a tree trunk are cut into the bark. Figuratively, features can look carved: {Her face was carved from granite}. Something deeply carved feels permanent, etched, established.

Carving is the act of cutting into a solid material to shape it—wood, stone, meat. A carving is the result: a decorative object cut from wood or stone, or a slice of meat from a roast. The carving knife is the large blade used at the table: {Who's doing the carving this Thanksgiving?}

A carwash is a facility where vehicles are cleaned, either by automated machinery or by hand. Drive-through carwashes pull cars along a track through sprayers, brushes, and dryers. A carwash can also mean the act of washing a car: {The team held a carwash to raise money for new uniforms}.

A cascade is a waterfall, especially one of several falling in stages down a rocky slope. The word extends to anything that flows or falls in a similar pattern: {a cascade of auburn hair}, {a cascade of events}. In technical contexts, cascade describes processes that trigger subsequent processes in sequence—a cascade of failures, a cascade effect in electronics. As a verb, things cascade when they pour or tumble downward in stages: {Water cascaded over the rocks}. (Capitalized Cascade refers to the mountain range.)

Cascades are waterfalls, especially a series of small falls or water flowing over rocks in stages. The word extends to anything that falls or flows in succession: {a cascade of curls}, {a cascade of events}. In computing, cascading describes how styles or effects pass down through hierarchies. As a verb, to cascade is to fall or flow in this tumbling, sequential way: {Errors cascaded through the system}.

Cascading describes something falling or flowing in stages, like water over a series of rocks. Each level triggers the next: {cascading waterfalls}, {cascading failures in the power grid}. In computing, cascading style sheets (CSS) apply formatting rules that flow down through nested elements. The word emphasizes succession and accumulation—effects that multiply as they descend.

Case is really two words with a single spelling, a fact that partly explains its high frequency. One kind of case is a physical object that encloses or contains something; the other case is abstract and stands for a set of circumstances, a situation requiring action, or a matter in a court of law. The relatively infrequent verb case is derived from the first meaning. The second kind of case is frequently used idiomatically in the phrase in case.

Cases is the plural of case, covering all its senses. A case can be a container {a glasses case}, an instance or example {a case of mistaken identity}, a legal matter {the case goes to trial}, or a medical situation {confirmed cases of flu}. In grammar, case refers to the form a noun or pronoun takes based on its function in a sentence.

A caseworker is a professional who manages individual cases in social services, healthcare, or similar fields. They assess needs, coordinate resources, and advocate for clients—whether helping families access benefits, monitoring child welfare, or guiding patients through treatment programs. {The caseworker visited the home twice a month to check on the children.}

Cash is money in physical form—coins and paper currency rather than checks, cards, or digital transfers: {Do you have cash or should I put it on the card?} To cash a check is to exchange it for currency. To {cash in} on something is to profit from it. To {cash out} is to convert assets to money, often when leaving a game or investment.

A cashew is an edible kidney-shaped nut that grows attached to the bottom of a fleshy fruit called the cashew apple. The nut is sold roasted and often salted: {a bowl of cashews}, {cashew butter}. Cashews are native to Brazil but now cultivated widely in tropical regions. The shell contains a caustic oil that must be removed before eating.

Cashews are kidney-shaped nuts that grow from the bottom of cashew apples, native to Brazil but now cultivated across the tropics. They're always sold shelled because the shell contains a caustic oil. Cashews appear in stir-fries, curries, and trail mixes, and are processed into dairy substitutes: {cashew milk}, {cashew cheese}.

A cashier is a person who handles payments at a store, bank, or other business, receiving money and making change. The word also functions as a verb meaning to dismiss someone from a position, especially in disgrace: {The officer was cashiered for misconduct}. This sense carries connotations of formal discharge with dishonor, used particularly in military contexts.

Cashmere is a luxuriously soft, lightweight wool made from the undercoat of cashmere goats, originally from the Kashmir region. The fiber is prized for warmth without bulk: {a cashmere sweater}, {cashmere scarf}. Because genuine cashmere is expensive, the word connotes quality and refinement. Fabrics blended with cashmere or imitating it may also be called cashmere.

A casino is an establishment where people gamble, typically featuring games like blackjack, poker, roulette, and slot machines. Casinos range from massive resort complexes in Las Vegas and Macau to modest riverboat operations. The word extends to card games played at home: {We're having a casino night}. Casino is also a specific card game involving capturing cards that match or sum to cards on the table.

Casinos are establishments where gambling takes place—typically offering games like blackjack, poker, roulette, and slot machines. The word evokes places like Las Vegas or Monte Carlo, where gambling is the main attraction surrounded by hotels, restaurants, and entertainment. {The casino floor was packed on Saturday night.} Online casinos have expanded gambling beyond physical venues.

A cask is a barrel-shaped container, typically wooden, used for storing and aging liquids—especially wine, whiskey, and beer. The word suggests craftsmanship and tradition: {aged twelve years in oak casks}. Cask-strength spirits are bottled directly from the barrel without dilution. A casket was originally a small cask.

A casket is a box for storing or displaying valued objects, or more commonly in American English, a coffin—the box in which a dead body is buried or cremated. The burial sense dominates modern usage, though the older meaning of a small ornamental box for jewelry or keepsakes persists in some contexts. {The family chose a mahogany casket for the funeral.} Casket tends to sound more euphemistic and genteel than coffin, which may explain its preference in American funeral industry language.

Caskets are containers for burial—coffins, typically rectangular with a hinged lid. The word sounds gentler than coffin, which is why American funeral homes prefer it. Originally, a casket was a small ornamental box for jewelry or keepsakes, and this sense survives: {a casket of love letters}. The burial meaning arose in 19th-century America.

Casks are barrel-shaped containers, typically made of wooden staves bound by metal hoops, used for storing and aging liquids—especially wine, whiskey, and beer. The wood imparts flavor during aging: {The bourbon aged twelve years in charred oak casks}. Cask can also refer to the quantity a cask holds, or any barrel-like container.

A casserole is a deep dish used for slow-cooking in an oven, and by extension, the food cooked in it—typically a one-pot meal combining meat or vegetables with a starchy binder like rice, pasta, or potatoes: {tuna casserole}, {green bean casserole}. The dish is associated with home cooking and potlucks. To casserole something is to cook it this way.

Casseroles is the plural of casserole—a deep dish used for slow-cooking in an oven, or the food prepared in such a dish. A casserole typically combines meat, vegetables, and starch in a sauce, baked until the flavors meld: {She brought three casseroles to the potluck}. The dish is associated with home cooking and communal meals, often appearing at funerals and family gatherings.

A cassette is a small plastic case containing magnetic tape for audio or video recording and playback. Audio cassettes dominated music distribution from the 1970s through the 1990s before CDs displaced them: {I found my old cassette collection in the attic}. Cassette tapes could be recorded at home, enabling mixtapes and bootlegs. The format survives mainly in nostalgia and lo-fi aesthetics.

Cassettes are small plastic cartridges containing magnetic tape, used for recording and playing audio or video. Audio cassettes dominated music distribution from the 1970s through the 1990s before CDs displaced them: {I found a box of old cassettes in the attic}. Videocassettes (VHS, Betamax) served the same function for film. The format has nostalgic appeal and a small revival among audiophiles and indie musicians.

Cast, a busy and complex word, is most frequent as a verb literally meaning throw (cast a fishing line) and figuratively, cause to be felt or present (cast doubt, cast a shadow, cast a spell). Noun meanings are also extremely varied and many of them have an associated, specific verb meaning. The cast of a play or movie consists of the actors in it. When you cast a film, you choose these people. A cast is also something formed by molding (a copper cast of the statue), and to cast something is to mold it: The company cast a bell for city hall. A protective covering for a broken limb is also called a cast; the medical professional casts the limb.
