The word also works as an adjective: a climbing {wall}, climbing {gear}, a climbing {rose} that grows upward by attaching to surfaces.

To clinch is to secure something decisively—a deal, a victory, a playoff spot: {The home run clinched the championship}. In boxing and wrestling, to clinch is to hold an opponent close, limiting their movement. A clinch is also an embrace, especially a passionate one: {The lovers were locked in a clinch}. As hardware, a clinch is a fastening made by bending over a nail or bolt after it passes through material.

Clinched is the past tense of clinch, meaning to secure or settle decisively. A boxer clinches by holding an opponent close to prevent punches. You clinch a deal, a victory, or a playoff spot by making the outcome certain: {The home run clinched the championship}. A clinched fist is tightly closed, though clenched is more common for that sense.

A clincher is the decisive fact, argument, or event that settles a matter: {The DNA evidence was the clincher}. In cycling, a clincher is a tire that hooks onto the rim with a bead, the standard type for most bikes. In construction, a clincher is a nail or bolt bent over after driving to secure it.

Cling means to hold on tightly, resisting separation. A child clings to a parent's leg. Wet clothes cling to the body. The verb extends to emotional attachment: {She clings to the hope that he'll return}. Someone clingy is excessively dependent or needy. Cling wrap adheres to surfaces. {The smell of smoke clung to his jacket for days.}

Clingy describes something or someone that clings—holds on tightly and won't let go. Clingy fabric sticks to the body. A clingy child won't leave a parent's side. Most often the word describes emotionally dependent behavior in relationships: {My ex was way too clingy}. The connotation is usually negative, suggesting excessive neediness or lack of independence.

A clinic is a medical facility smaller than a hospital, typically focused on outpatient care or specialized treatment: {a dental clinic}, {an urgent care clinic}, {a fertility clinic}. The word extends to instructional sessions where experts demonstrate techniques: {a basketball clinic}, {a writing clinic}. When someone dominates a competition so thoroughly it becomes educational, they're said to have {put on a clinic}.

Clinical describes what happens in direct contact with patients—a clinical {examination}, clinical {trials}, clinical {experience}. The word extends to anything resembling a medical setting: clean, efficient, emotionally detached. A {clinical} approach to a problem is coolly analytical, stripped of sentiment. In sports, a {clinical} finish is precise and ruthless—no wasted motion, no drama, just results.

Clink is the short, sharp sound of hard objects striking together—glasses touching in a toast, coins dropping, keys jingling: {They clinked their champagne flutes}. The word imitates the sound it describes. Separately, the clink is slang for jail or prison, from a famous London prison called the Clink: {He spent six months in the clink}.

Clinking describes the sharp, light metallic sound made when hard objects strike together—glasses touching in a toast, coins jangling in a pocket, keys rattling on a ring. The word captures that bright, high-pitched quality: {the clinking of ice cubes in a glass}, {clinking champagne flutes}. As British slang, clinking means excellent or first-rate, though this use is dated.

Clip represents two verbs and their derivative nouns. If you clip one thing to another, you attach it, as you might do with a paper clip. If you clip something using a sharp instrument, you cut it, usually with the result of leaving it shorter: It’s time to clip your toenails. This clip can also refer to a hit or blow, especially an unintentional one: I clipped a light pole when I was backing out. Something happening at a good clip is happening agreeably fast.

A clipboard is a rigid board with a spring clip at the top for holding papers in place while writing. The design lets you write without a desk. In computing, a clipboard is temporary storage for cut or copied data—text, images, files—waiting to be pasted elsewhere: {Copy the link to your clipboard}. {She walked through the store with a clipboard, taking inventory}.

Clipped describes something cut short or trimmed. A clipped hedge has been shaped by shears. Clipped speech is brief and curt, with words or syllables cut off: {She answered in clipped tones}. A clipped accent—especially British—sounds precise and abbreviated. In linguistics, a clipped word is shortened from a longer form: phone from telephone, flu from influenza.

A clipper is a tool for cutting or trimming—nail clippers, hair clippers, hedge clippers. The word usually appears in plural even for a single implement. A clipper was also a fast sailing ship of the 19th century, designed for speed with tall masts and sharp lines: {the great tea clippers racing from China}. In basketball, the Clippers are the Los Angeles team.

Clippers are cutting tools with two blades that meet, used for trimming hair, nails, or hedges: {nail clippers}, {hair clippers}, {hedge clippers}. Electric clippers buzz through hair quickly. Historically, clippers were fast sailing ships with sharp bows designed to "clip" through waves: {The tea clippers raced from China to London}.

Clips are small fastening devices that grip or hold things together—paper clips, hair clips, binder clips. A clip is also a container holding ammunition for quick loading into a firearm. In media, a clip is a short segment extracted from longer footage: {Did you see that clip from the interview?} To clip is to cut or trim: {clip the hedges}, {clip coupons}. A clip can also be a sharp blow: {a clip on the ear}. At a good clip means at a brisk pace.

A clique is a small, exclusive group of people who associate closely and tend to exclude outsiders. The word carries negative connotations of snobbishness and insularity: {the popular clique in high school}, {Washington's political cliques}. Members of a clique may not see themselves as exclusionary, but those left out usually do.

Cliques are small, exclusive groups whose members share common interests and tend to exclude outsiders. The word carries a negative connotation—it suggests the group is insular and perhaps snobbish: {High school cliques can be brutal to anyone who doesn't fit in}. A clique differs from a circle of friends mainly in its perceived exclusivity and unwelcoming attitude toward newcomers.

The clitoris is a small, sensitive organ at the front of the vulva, above the vaginal opening. Though only a small portion is externally visible, most of its erectile tissue extends internally. Its sole function is sexual pleasure—the clitoris has more nerve endings than any other part of the human body. {clitoral stimulation}, {clitoral orgasm}.

A cloak is a loose outer garment without sleeves, fastened at the neck and hanging from the shoulders—the kind worn in medieval times or fantasy settings. The word extends to anything that conceals or covers: {a cloak of secrecy}, {under the cloak of darkness}. To cloak something is to hide or disguise it: {The organization cloaked its true purpose in charitable language}.

Cloaked means covered or concealed, as if hidden beneath a cloak. The word usually appears figuratively: a town {cloaked in fog}, motives {cloaked in secrecy}, an operation {cloaked in mystery}. In fantasy and science fiction, cloaked often describes invisibility technology: {The ship remained cloaked until it was too late}.

Cloaking is the act of concealing or disguising something. In science fiction, a cloaking device renders spacecraft invisible. In computing, cloaking is a deceptive technique where a website shows different content to search engines than to human visitors—typically to manipulate search rankings. The word suggests technological or deliberate concealment rather than simple hiding.

Cloaks are loose outer garments that hang from the shoulders, typically without sleeves—the kind of dramatic wrap you see in period films or fantasy settings. The word extends to anything that conceals: {a cloak of secrecy}, {under the cloak of darkness}. To cloak something is to cover or hide it: {The project was cloaked in mystery}. A {cloaking device} renders something invisible.

Clobber means to strike hard or defeat decisively: {The team got clobbered in the semifinals}. It suggests overwhelming force—you don't clobber someone in a close match. In computing, to clobber a file is to overwrite it, destroying the original contents. British slang uses clobber as a noun meaning clothing or personal belongings: {Get your clobber and let's go}.

Clobbered is the past tense of clobber, meaning to hit hard or defeat decisively. Someone gets clobbered in a fight, a team gets clobbered in a game, or stocks get clobbered in a market crash: {We got clobbered by the competition}. In computing, to clobber a file is to overwrite it, destroying its previous contents.

Clobbering is the act of hitting or defeating someone or something decisively and often violently. In physical contexts, it suggests a heavy, forceful blow: {He took a clobbering in the ring}. The word extends readily to competitive situations where one side dominates: {Our team took a clobbering in the playoffs}. In computing, clobbering refers to accidentally overwriting data or files.

The timekeeping device that we call a clock is the source of most other meanings of the word. If you clock something, you time it. Something or someone that clocks achieves a certain timing or level: The website has clocked six million hits this month. If your job requires you to clock in, you use a time clock that records your arrival. If you’re on the clock, you’re at work. Unrelatedly, if you clock someone, you hit them hard.

Clocks are devices that measure and display time—from grandfather clocks to alarm clocks to the clock on your phone. To clock something is to time it or to notice it: {I clocked his lap at under a minute}, {Did you clock her new haircut?} To clock in or out is to record arrival or departure from work. In slang, to clock someone can mean to hit them hard or to recognize something they're trying to hide: {She got clocked immediately}.

Clockwatching is the habit of repeatedly checking the time, especially when waiting for work to end or an event to arrive. The term implies impatience, boredom, or lack of engagement: {The meeting dragged on and everyone started clockwatching}. A clockwatcher is someone who does this habitually—often used disparagingly for employees who care more about quitting time than their work.

Clockwise describes rotation in the direction a clock's hands move—rightward at the top, leftward at the bottom. {Turn the dial clockwise to increase the volume.} The opposite is counterclockwise (or anticlockwise in British English). The term extends to any circular or spiral motion: {The dancers moved clockwise around the floor.}

Clockwork is the internal mechanism of a clock—gears, springs, and wheels working in precise coordination. The term extends to any intricate mechanical system operating with similar regularity. {Like clockwork} describes anything happening with perfect predictability and timing: {The trains run like clockwork}. Clockwork as an adjective describes mechanical devices powered by wound springs rather than electricity: {a clockwork toy}, {a clockwork orange}.

A clog is a shoe with a thick wooden sole, traditionally worn in the Netherlands and other parts of Europe. The word extends to anything that blocks or obstructs: a clog in a drain, a clog in the system. To clog is to block or become blocked: {Hair clogged the drain}. Arteries clog with plaque. Bureaucracy clogs progress.

Clogged describes something blocked or obstructed, preventing normal flow. A clogged drain won't empty; clogged arteries restrict blood flow; clogged pores lead to acne. The word suggests accumulated matter—hair, grease, debris—that has built up over time: {The sink is clogged with food scraps}. Figuratively, a clogged system or process has become sluggish from overload.

Clogging is a form of folk dance characterized by rhythmic footwork that strikes the floor to create percussive sounds. The dancer wears hard-soled shoes, often with metal taps. Clogging has roots in Appalachian and Irish traditions and remains popular at folk festivals and competitions: {She's been clogging since she was six}. Separately, clogging is the process of becoming blocked or obstructed: {Hair clogging the drain caused the backup}.

Clogs are shoes with thick wooden soles, traditionally worn for protection or warmth. The rigid base elevates the foot above wet or dirty ground. Dutch wooden shoes are the iconic example, though clogs appear across cultures. As a verb, to clog means to block or obstruct: {Hair clogged the drain}. Something that clogs up becomes jammed or congested: {Traffic clogged the highway}.

A cloister is a covered walkway around a courtyard, especially in a monastery or convent, with arched openings on one side. By extension, cloister refers to any place of religious seclusion or monastic life itself: {She entered the cloister at nineteen}. To cloister is to seclude or shelter from the outside world: {He cloistered himself in his study}. A cloistered life suggests withdrawal from worldly concerns, whether literal or figurative.

A clone is a genetically identical copy of an organism, produced either naturally (as with identical twins) or artificially through laboratory techniques. The term extends to any exact duplicate: {a clone of the original software}, {cheap clones of designer handbags}. In computing, to clone a hard drive is to copy its entire contents. Informally, someone who closely imitates another may be called a clone: {He's basically a clone of his father}.

Clones are genetically identical copies of a living thing—produced naturally (as with identical twins) or artificially through laboratory techniques. The word extends to any close copy: {The company released a series of iPhone clones}. In science fiction, clones are often artificially grown duplicates of humans. To clone is to create such copies: {Scientists cloned the sheep from adult cells}.

Cloning is creating a genetically identical copy of an organism or cell. In biotechnology, cloning produces organisms with the same DNA as a parent—Dolly the sheep was cloned from an adult cell. The term extends to exact duplication generally: cloning a hard drive, cloning a credit card. To clone is to make such a copy; a clone is the copy itself.

Close, when pronounced with an “s” sound, is an adjective, noun, or adverb, representing one group of meanings relating to proximity and confinement. Close with a “z” sound is a noun or a verb with other meanings relating to termination and obstruction. Anything that can be thought of as open in some sense is a typical object of close: close the door/window/gap. A close friend or relative is one who may be geographically distant but intimately connected. As a noun, close is similar to end: He spoke at the close of the service. #

Closed describes something not open—a door, a store, a case. A closed shop requires union membership for employment. A closed meeting excludes outsiders. A closed mind won't consider new ideas. When something is closed to discussion, the matter is settled: {The subject is closed}. A closed system has no outside input. In math, a set is closed under an operation if applying it yields another member of the set.

Closeness is the state of being near—physically, emotionally, or in degree. Physical closeness is proximity: {the closeness of the houses made privacy impossible}. Emotional closeness is intimacy: {I value the closeness I have with my sister}. Closeness can also describe similarity: {the closeness of their test scores surprised the teacher}. A close race or close call has closeness—a narrow margin.

Closer describes something nearer in distance, time, or relationship—the comparative form of close. As a noun, a closer is someone who finishes things: a relief pitcher who closes out games, a salesperson who seals deals, or the final act at a concert. In real estate and law, a closer handles the final steps of transactions. A closer can also be the concluding element itself: {That song was the perfect closer for the album}.

Closers are people who finalize deals or bring things to completion. In sales, the closer is the person who gets customers to sign—the one who seals the transaction: {Send in the closers}. In baseball, a closer is the relief pitcher who finishes games, typically entering in the ninth inning to preserve a lead. The word carries connotations of skill under pressure and the ability to finish what others started.

A closet is a small room or enclosed space for storage, especially for clothes. In American English, closets are built into bedrooms; in British English, the term more often refers to a wardrobe or small storage room. Closet also describes something private or secret: a {closet smoker} hides the habit; to {come out of the closet} is to reveal one's homosexuality publicly. To closet yourself is to withdraw into privacy: {She closeted herself in her study}. A {skeleton in the closet} is a shameful secret.

Closeted describes someone who keeps a significant aspect of their identity hidden, especially being gay or otherwise LGBTQ+: {He was closeted for years before coming out to his family}. The metaphor is of hiding in a closet—concealed from public view. Extended to other secrets: {a closeted conservative in a liberal workplace}. The opposite is out or openly: {She's been out since college}.

Closets are small enclosed spaces used for storage, most often for clothing and household items. In American homes, a closet typically refers to a built-in storage area with a door, while British English more often uses wardrobe or cupboard. The phrase {in the closet} or {closeted} describes someone hiding an aspect of their identity, especially their sexuality, from others. To closet oneself is to withdraw into privacy, often for private conversation or work. {They closeted themselves in the study to discuss the matter.}

A closeup is a photograph, film shot, or view taken at close range, showing detail: {The director called for a closeup of the actor's face}. By extension, any detailed or intimate examination: {a closeup of life in rural America}. Also spelled close-up.

Closing is the act of shutting, ending, or concluding something. A closing {door}, a closing {argument}, the closing {minutes} of a game. In real estate, the closing is the final meeting where property transfers and documents are signed: {We're scheduled for closing on Friday}. Closing can also describe something that comes at the end: {closing remarks}, {closing credits}.

Closure is the act of closing something or the state of being closed. A road closure blocks traffic; a factory closure ends operations. Emotionally, closure means resolution after a difficult experience—the sense that a painful chapter has ended: {She needed closure after the breakup}. In legislation, closure (or cloture) is a procedure to end debate and force a vote.

A clot is a thickened mass formed when liquid—especially blood—coagulates: {a blood clot in his leg}, {clots formed in the wound}. The verb means to form such a mass: {The blood clotted quickly}. In British slang, a clot is a stupid person: {Don't be such a clot}.

Cloth is fabric—material made by weaving, knitting, or felting fibers together. A cloth is a piece of such material used for a specific purpose: a {tablecloth}, a {washcloth}, a {dish cloth}. {The cloth} refers collectively to the clergy, from their distinctive garments. {Cut from the same cloth} means made alike, sharing essential qualities.

Clothes are garments worn on the body—shirts, pants, dresses, and the like. The word covers everything from underwear to outerwear: {Put on some clothes before you answer the door}. Clothes often appears with modifiers indicating purpose or quality: {work clothes}, {dress clothes}, {designer clothes}. To change clothes is to put on different garments.

A clothesline is a rope or wire strung between two points for hanging laundry to dry: {She hung the sheets on the clothesline}. In sports, especially football and hockey, to clothesline someone is to strike them across the neck or chest with an extended arm, knocking them down—the motion resembling running into a taut line.

Clotheslined describes being struck across the neck or upper chest by an outstretched arm, knocking you backward off your feet—as if you'd run into a taut clothesline at full speed. The move is common in wrestling and football, often illegal in the latter: {The defender clotheslined the receiver and drew a flag}. Figuratively, anything that stops you abruptly: {I was clotheslined by the news}.

Clothing is the collective term for garments worn on the body—shirts, pants, dresses, coats, and the like. Unlike clothes, which tends toward the concrete and countable, clothing functions as a mass noun and often appears in more formal or commercial contexts: {a clothing store}, {protective clothing}, {winter clothing}. The word emphasizes the category or type rather than specific items. {She packed enough clothing for a week.}

The clouds you see in the sky inspire the many other meanings of this word, all of which relate to a quality associated with the airborne water vapor. Today’s commonest uses are inspired by the cloud associated with the Internet, where data storage and processing takes place far from people’s own devices but immediately available to them. The verbal meanings of cloud mostly draw on the ability of clouds to block the sun: anything that darkens, obscures, or occludes can be said to cloud: A look of distress clouded his features.

Clouds are visible masses of water droplets or ice crystals suspended in the atmosphere. They form when moist air cools and condenses around tiny particles. Beyond weather, clouds describe anything that obscures or darkens: {a cloud of dust}, {a cloud of suspicion}. To cloud is to make unclear: {Emotions clouded her judgment}. In computing, {the cloud} refers to remote servers accessed via the internet for storage and processing.

Cloudy describes a sky covered or partly covered with clouds: {a cloudy afternoon}, {cloudy with a chance of rain}. The word extends to anything lacking clarity or transparency—cloudy water is murky, cloudy thinking is confused, and a cloudy future is uncertain. Cloudy emotions suggest sadness or gloom: {Her expression turned cloudy when she heard the news}.

Clout is influence or power, especially in political or social contexts: {She has clout with the mayor}, {His endorsement carries real clout}. The word suggests the ability to make things happen through connections or reputation rather than formal authority. In its older sense, a clout is a heavy blow: {He gave him a clout on the ear}. To clout is to hit hard. Among younger speakers, clout increasingly refers to social media fame or cultural cachet: {chasing clout}, {clout chaser}.

Clove has two unrelated meanings. The spice clove is the dried flower bud of a tropical tree, pungent and aromatic, used in cooking and baking: {ham studded with cloves}, {a pinch of ground clove}. Separately, a clove of garlic is one of the segments that make up a garlic bulb: {Mince three cloves of garlic}.

Clover is a low-growing plant with distinctive three-lobed leaves, common in lawns and pastures. Finding a four-leaf clover is considered lucky because the mutation is rare. To be {in clover} is to live in comfort or prosperity, from the plant's value as rich fodder for livestock.

Clovers is the plural of clover, the low-growing plant with three-lobed leaves common in lawns and fields. Finding a four-leaf clover is considered lucky, making it a symbol of good fortune. {The yard was covered in clovers and dandelions.} To be {in clover} is to live in comfort or prosperity.

Cloves are the dried flower buds of a tropical tree, used as a pungent spice in cooking and baking. Their intense, warm flavor appears in spiced drinks, ham glazes, and pumpkin pie. Whole cloves look like small dark nails—the name comes from the Latin word for nail. Clove oil, extracted from the buds, has traditional uses as a dental analgesic. A clove of garlic is an unrelated sense: one of the segments that make up a garlic bulb.

A clown is a comic performer, traditionally in colorful costume and exaggerated makeup, who entertains through slapstick, jokes, and physical comedy—originally in circuses, now at children's parties and other venues. Clown extends to anyone who acts foolishly or seeks attention through buffoonery: {Stop clowning around}. To clown on someone is to mock or ridicule them. In slang, calling someone a clown dismisses them as incompetent or unserious: {That guy's a complete clown}.

Clownfish are small, brightly colored tropical fish known for their orange bodies with distinctive white bands outlined in black. They live among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones in a mutually beneficial relationship—the fish gains protection while helping clean and defend the anemone. The animated film *Finding Nemo* made them widely recognizable. Also called anemonefish.

Clowning is acting in a silly, playful, or attention-seeking way. Children clown around in class; adults clown at parties. The word carries a mild note of disapproval—clowning implies the behavior is excessive or inappropriate to the situation: {Stop clowning and pay attention}. It can also refer to the art of performing as a clown.

Clowns are comic performers, typically in exaggerated makeup and costumes, who entertain through slapstick, physical comedy, and buffoonery. The circus clown is the archetype, but clowns appear at children's parties, in theater, and in horror films that play on their unsettling appearance. Informally, a clown is someone who acts foolishly: {Stop clowning around}. To clown is to joke or behave playfully: {We were just clowning}.

A club is a heavy stick used as a weapon, thick at one end for striking. From this come specialized clubs—the golf club, the billy club. Playing cards have a suit marked with a three-lobed symbol called clubs. A club is also a group organized around shared interests: {a book club}, {a chess club}. The place where such groups meet is also a club, which extends to venues for drinking, dancing, or entertainment: {nightclub}, {strip club}, {comedy club}. To club is to strike with a club, or to combine resources: {We clubbed together to buy her a gift}.

Clubbing is going to nightclubs, typically for dancing and drinking: {We went clubbing every weekend that summer}. The activity implies loud music, late hours, and often a scene built around fashion or social display. Separately, clubbing can mean beating with a club or heavy object: {the clubbing of baby seals}.

A clubhouse is a building where members of a club gather for meetings, socializing, and activities. Sports teams have clubhouses where players change, shower, and relax before and after games—these are also called locker rooms. Golf courses typically have clubhouses serving as social hubs for members. In children's usage, a clubhouse might be a backyard fort or treehouse where kids hold secret meetings. {The team celebrated their victory in the clubhouse.}

Clubs is a suit in playing cards, marked by a black three-lobed symbol resembling a clover. In the standard deck, clubs rank alongside spades, hearts, and diamonds. The word also refers to the cards themselves: {I'm out of clubs}. Separately, clubs are the plural of club—organizations, venues, or blunt implements used as weapons.

Cluck is the short, throaty sound a chicken makes, especially a hen calling her chicks. The verb means to make this sound, or by extension, to express fussy disapproval: {She clucked her tongue at the mess}. A cluck or dumb cluck is a stupid person—someone with a chicken's brain.

A clue is a piece of evidence or information that helps solve a mystery, puzzle, or problem: {The detective found a clue at the crime scene}. In crosswords and games, clues are hints that point toward answers. To clue someone in is to inform them: {Can you clue me in on what happened?} Someone clueless lacks awareness or understanding.

Clueless means lacking understanding or awareness about something. Someone clueless about fashion doesn't know what looks good. The word often implies obliviousness that others find obvious or frustrating: {He's completely clueless about how his comments affect people}. It can shade toward innocent naïveté or willful ignorance depending on context.

Clues is the plural of clue—pieces of evidence or information that help solve a puzzle, mystery, or problem. Detectives follow clues to catch criminals; crossword solvers work from clues to fill in answers. {The detective gathered clues at the crime scene}. To be {clueless} is to lack understanding entirely.

A clump is a compact mass or cluster of things grouped together: a clump of {trees}, a clump of {dirt}, a clump of {hair} in the drain. The word suggests irregular, natural grouping rather than deliberate arrangement. To clump is to gather into such masses, or to walk with heavy, thudding steps: {He clumped up the stairs in his boots}.

Clumsiness is a tendency to move awkwardly or handle things without grace, often resulting in dropped objects, stumbles, or minor accidents. The word implies a lack of coordination rather than intent: {His clumsiness around the house meant broken dishes were routine}. Extended to speech or social behavior, clumsiness suggests tactlessness or inelegance: {the clumsiness of his apology made things worse}.

Clumsy describes someone who moves awkwardly and tends to knock things over or drop them: {a clumsy waiter spilling drinks}. It extends to anything lacking grace or skill—a clumsy {attempt} at humor, a clumsy {apology}. The word suggests unintentional awkwardness rather than incompetence: {My clumsy fingers couldn't manage the tiny buttons}.

Clunk is a dull, heavy sound—the noise of metal hitting metal or something solid dropping: {The car door shut with a clunk}, {I heard a clunk from the engine}. As a verb, to clunk is to make or move with such a sound: {He clunked the wrench down on the workbench}. A clunker is an old, unreliable car prone to making such noises.

A clunker is an old, unreliable machine—typically a car in poor condition: {He drove that clunker until the engine finally gave out}. The term extends to anything that fails or performs badly: a joke that doesn't land, a movie that bombs, a line of dialogue that thuds. The word suggests something heavy, graceless, and past its usefulness.

Clunky describes something awkward, heavy, or lacking grace. Clunky shoes are bulky and inelegant. Clunky prose reads clumsily. Clunky software has an unintuitive interface: {The app works, but the navigation is clunky}. The word suggests something functional but unrefined—it gets the job done without finesse.

A cluster is a group of similar things gathered or growing close together: a cluster of {grapes}, a cluster of {stars}, a cluster of {buildings}. The word emphasizes natural or loose grouping rather than rigid arrangement. Things cluster when they bunch together: {Fans clustered around the entrance}. In computing, a cluster is a group of connected computers or storage units working as a single system.

A clusterfuck is a situation gone chaotically wrong through a combination of incompetence, poor planning, or cascading failures. The military slang origin suggests multiple people fucking up simultaneously, creating a mess worse than any single mistake could produce: {The evacuation was a complete clusterfuck}. The word is vulgar but widely used when ordinary terms like "disaster" or "fiasco" feel inadequate.

Clusters are groups of similar things positioned close together. Grapes grow in clusters. Stars form clusters in the night sky. Data analysts look for clusters in their datasets—natural groupings that emerge from proximity or similarity. The verb means to gather or form such groups: {Fans clustered around the stage}. A {cluster bomb} disperses smaller munitions over a wide area. A {clusterfuck} (vulgar) is a situation gone chaotically wrong.

A clutch is a tight grip or grasp: {She held the railing in a desperate clutch}. To clutch is to grab or hold tightly: {He clutched the steering wheel}. In machinery, a clutch connects and disconnects rotating shafts—notably in manual-transmission vehicles, where the clutch pedal disengages the engine from the drivetrain. A clutch of eggs is a batch laid together; a clutch of anything is a small group. In sports slang, clutch describes performance under pressure: {He hit a clutch three-pointer with seconds left}. A clutch bag is a small handbag without straps, held in the hand.

Clutches is the plural of clutch, most often appearing in the figurative phrase {in the clutches of}, meaning under someone's control or power: {She fell into the clutches of a cult leader}. The image derives from clutching hands or claws gripping tightly. A clutch is also a group of eggs or chicks, and the pedal that engages a vehicle's transmission.

Clutter is a disordered accumulation of things, typically in a space where they shouldn't be: {The desk was buried under clutter}. The word suggests mess without purpose—stuff that crowds out what matters. To clutter is to fill a space this way: {Magazines cluttered the coffee table}. Figuratively, clutter can crowd the mind: {too much clutter to think straight}.

Cluttered describes a space filled with too many things in a disorganized way: {a cluttered desk}, {a cluttered apartment}. The meaning extends to anything overwhelmed by excess—a cluttered {mind} has too many competing thoughts, a cluttered {schedule} has too many commitments. To clutter is to fill a space this way: {Don't clutter up the counter with appliances}.

A coach is a person who trains athletes or teams: {a basketball coach}, {a life coach}. The word extends to anyone who guides development—vocal coaches, executive coaches. As a verb, to coach is to instruct or prepare someone: {She coached him through the interview}. Coach also means the economy section of an airplane or train, or a large enclosed carriage. A coach bag or purse refers to the luxury brand.

Coaches is the plural of coach. A coach is someone who trains athletes or teams: {The coaches met to discuss strategy}. In education, coaches guide improvement in specific skills: {literacy coaches}, {executive coaches}. Coach also means a bus for long-distance travel, a train car, or economy-class seating on an airplane. The verb means to train or instruct: {She coaches the debate team}.

Coaching is the work of guiding someone toward improvement in a skill, sport, or area of life. A coach provides instruction, feedback, and encouragement: {She's been coaching youth soccer for ten years}, {He hired a life coach to help with career decisions}. The term covers everything from athletic training to executive development to personal growth work.

Coal is a black or brownish-black solid fuel formed from ancient plant matter compressed over millions of years. It burns to produce heat and has powered industrial economies since the 1800s. To {rake someone over the coals} is to criticize them harshly. {Coals to Newcastle} describes something pointlessly redundant—Newcastle was England's coal-mining center.

A coalition is a temporary alliance of distinct groups or parties pursuing a common goal. Political coalitions form when no single party holds a majority: {The coalition government collapsed after six months}. The term applies beyond politics to any strategic partnership where separate entities join forces while retaining their identities: {a coalition of environmental groups}.

Coals are pieces of coal or, more commonly, glowing fragments of burned wood or fuel. A fire burns down to coals when flames subside but heat remains: {We roasted marshmallows over the coals}. To {rake someone over the coals} is to criticize them harshly. To {carry coals to Newcastle} is to bring something where it's already abundant—Newcastle being a historic coal-mining center. {Hot coals} appear in expressions about walking on fire or enduring discomfort.

Coarse describes texture that is rough, unrefined, or composed of large particles: {coarse sand}, {coarse fabric}, {coarse salt}. The word extends to manner and speech—coarse language is crude or vulgar, and a coarse person lacks refinement or delicacy. {His coarse jokes made everyone uncomfortable.} The opposite is fine in matters of texture, refined in matters of behavior.

A coast is the land along the edge of a sea or ocean: {the California coast}, {a drive down the coast}. To coast is to move without applying power—a bicycle coasting downhill, a car coasting to a stop. By extension, coasting means getting by with minimal effort: {He coasted through his senior year}. {The coast is clear} means no one is watching and it's safe to proceed.

A coaster is a small mat placed under a glass or cup to protect the surface beneath from moisture or heat. The word extends to things that coast: a roller coaster, a ship engaged in coastal trade, or a sled for coasting downhill. In casual use, someone coasting through life—expending minimal effort—might be called a coaster.

Coasters are small mats placed under drinking glasses to protect surfaces from moisture, heat, or scratches. They come in countless materials and designs—cork, cardboard, ceramic, novelty shapes. Separately, coasters are amusement park rides: roller coasters. A coaster can also be a ship that travels along coastlines rather than across oceans.

A coastguard is a maritime organization that patrols coastal waters, performing search and rescue, enforcing maritime law, and protecting borders. In the US, the Coast Guard is a branch of the armed forces. The term also refers to an individual member of such a service: {The coastguard spotted the capsized vessel}. Also spelled as two words: coast guard.

Coasting is moving without applying power—a car coasting downhill, a bicycle coasting after you stop pedaling. The word extends to any situation where momentum carries you forward without effort: {He's been coasting on his early success}. This figurative use often implies criticism—that someone capable of more is settling for the minimum: {She coasted through the semester}.

A coastline is the boundary where land meets the sea—the outline of a coast as seen on a map or from above. The term often emphasizes shape and extent: {California's rugged coastline}, {the coastline stretches for hundreds of miles}. Coastlines shift with tides and erosion, making precise measurement famously difficult.

Coasts is the plural of coast—the land along the sea. The coasts of a country are its shorelines: {The hurricane threatened both coasts}. As a verb form, coasts means to move without effort or propulsion: {She coasts downhill on her bicycle}, {He coasts through life on charm}. To coast is to rely on momentum rather than active exertion.

A coat is an outer garment with sleeves, typically worn for warmth or protection: {She grabbed her coat before heading out}. The word extends to any covering layer—a coat of {paint}, a coat of {fur} on an animal, a coat of {dust}. To coat something is to cover it with a layer: {Coat the pan with butter}.

Coats is the plural of coat—outer garments worn for warmth or protection, or layers covering a surface. A closet holds winter coats; a painter applies multiple coats. The verb form means to cover with a layer: {The chef coats the chicken in breadcrumbs}. {Sugar coats the pills to make them easier to swallow}.

A coattail is the back flap of a formal coat, extending below the waist. The plural coattails appears most often in the phrase {ride someone's coattails}, meaning to benefit from another's success or influence without earning it independently. In politics, a popular candidate's coattails can carry lesser-known running mates to victory: {She won on the governor's coattails}.

Coattails are the two flaps at the back of a formal coat, hanging below the waist. The word appears most often in the figurative phrase {on someone's coattails}, meaning benefiting from another's success or popularity: {She rode into office on the president's coattails}. The image is of someone literally clinging to a more powerful person's coat as they advance.

To coax is to persuade gently through patience, flattery, or persistent encouragement: {She coaxed the cat out from under the bed}. You coax a reluctant child into eating vegetables, coax information from someone hesitant to share. The word implies gradual success through soft persistence rather than force or demand. Things can also be coaxed into working: {He coaxed the old engine back to life}.

Cobalt is a hard, silvery-blue metallic element used in alloys, batteries, and blue pigments. The distinctive deep blue color it produces in glass and ceramics has made cobalt blue a standard color name: {a cobalt sky}, {cobalt eyes}. As an adjective, cobalt describes this vivid blue shade.

A cobbler is a person who repairs shoes, or formerly, one who makes them. The word also names a type of deep-dish fruit dessert with a thick biscuit or cake topping: {peach cobbler}, {blackberry cobbler}. In British English, a load of cobblers means nonsense—from rhyming slang (cobbler's awls = balls).

A cobblestone is a naturally rounded stone used for paving roads and walkways, common in European cities before modern asphalt. The stones fit together to create durable but uneven surfaces: {The carriage rattled over the cobblestones}. Cobblestoned streets evoke historic charm or, for cyclists and pedestrians, an ankle-twisting nuisance.

Cobblestones are rounded stones used to pave streets and walkways, fitted together to create a durable surface. The term evokes old European city centers and historic districts: {We walked along the cobblestone streets of Prague}. Cobblestone roads are charming but notoriously rough on feet, wheels, and suspensions.

A cobla is a traditional Catalan instrumental ensemble, typically comprising eleven or twelve musicians playing wind and percussion instruments. The cobla accompanies the sardana, Catalonia's national folk dance, performed in circles at festivals and public gatherings. {The cobla played in the town square while dancers joined hands.}

A cobra is a venomous snake native to Africa and Asia, known for spreading its neck ribs into a hood when threatened. Cobras are iconic in snake charming, though the snake responds to movement rather than music. The king cobra is the world's longest venomous snake. Figuratively, cobra may describe something dangerous or poised to strike.

A cobweb is a spider's web, especially an old or dusty one found in neglected corners: {She brushed the cobwebs from the attic rafters}. Figuratively, cobwebs suggest mental dullness or confusion from disuse: {A morning walk helps clear the cobwebs}. Something cobwebby is thin, delicate, or gauzy.

Cobwebs are the dusty, abandoned webs of spiders, typically found in neglected corners and unused spaces. The word evokes disuse and neglect: {The attic was thick with cobwebs}. Figuratively, to {blow away the cobwebs} is to clear one's mind or refresh oneself after stagnation: {A morning walk blows away the cobwebs}.

Cocaine is a powerful stimulant drug extracted from coca leaves. It produces intense euphoria and energy, followed by a sharp crash. Cocaine is typically snorted as a white powder, though it can be injected or smoked in crystalline form (crack). The drug is highly addictive and illegal in most countries. {He had a cocaine habit that cost him his job}.

A cock is a rooster—the adult male of domestic fowl. The word appears in compounds like {cockfight}, {cockcrow}, and {cockerel} (a young rooster). Cock also means a device for controlling liquid flow (a stopcock), or a slight tilt: {the cock of his hat}. The verb cock means to tilt or prepare: cock a {gun}, cock an {eyebrow}. If you cock up (British), you make a serious mistake. Cock is also vulgar slang for a penis, which makes the word ripe for double entendre and has gradually displaced its innocent uses in American speech.

A cockatiel is a small Australian parrot with a distinctive crest and orange cheek patches, popular as a pet. Cockatiels are known for their whistling ability and can learn to mimic tunes and simple words. They're smaller and generally easier to care for than their cockatoo relatives: {The cockatiel bobbed its head when I walked in}.

A cockatoo is a large parrot native to Australia and nearby islands, typically white or pale-colored with a distinctive crest of feathers that rises when the bird is excited or alarmed. Cockatoos are popular as pets, known for their intelligence, loud calls, and long lifespans: {The cockatoo shrieked whenever someone entered the room}.

Cockatoos are large parrots native to Australia and nearby islands, distinguished by their curved bills and prominent head crests that rise when the bird is alarmed or excited. Most species are white, though some are black or pink. They're popular as pets but notoriously loud and demanding. {The cockatoo shrieked whenever anyone entered the room.}

A cockfight is a blood sport in which roosters fight each other, typically to the death, while spectators bet on the outcome. The birds are often fitted with metal spurs to inflict maximum damage. Cockfighting is illegal in most Western countries but persists in parts of Latin America, Southeast Asia, and elsewhere. {They raided an illegal cockfight in the warehouse district.}

Cockfighting is a blood sport in which roosters, often fitted with metal spurs, fight each other until one is killed or incapacitated. The practice has ancient roots and continues in parts of Latin America, Southeast Asia, and elsewhere, though it is illegal in most Western countries. Spectators typically gamble on the outcome.

Cockfights are organized contests in which roosters, often fitted with metal spurs, fight each other until one is killed or incapacitated. Once widespread entertainment, cockfighting is now illegal in most countries due to animal cruelty concerns, though it persists underground and in some cultures where it holds traditional significance: {Police raided an illegal cockfight in a rural barn}.

A cockney is a working-class Londoner, traditionally one born within earshot of the bells of St Mary-le-Bow church in the East End. The term also refers to their distinctive accent and dialect, marked by dropped H's, glottal stops, and rhyming slang where {apples and pears} means stairs and {dog and bone} means phone. {He spoke in broad cockney.} (Capitalized Cockney is interchangeable.)

A cockpit is the compartment where a pilot sits to control an aircraft, or where the driver sits in a racing car. On boats, the cockpit is a recessed area in the deck where the helmsman steers. The word originally meant a pit for cockfighting—a small enclosed space where combat takes place—which extended to any cramped area of intense activity: {the cockpit of Europe}, meaning a region of frequent warfare.

Cockpits is the plural of cockpit, which originally meant an arena for cockfighting. The enclosed, confined sense carried over to the pilot's compartment in an aircraft, the driver's area in a racing car, or the helmsman's station on a boat. A cockpit may also be any scene of intense conflict: {the cockpit of war}.

A cockroach is a flat-bodied insect with long antennae, known for infesting buildings and scavenging on food scraps. Cockroaches are notoriously hard to kill and associated with filth, though they thrive in clean environments too. Their survival skills make them symbols of resilience and disgust in equal measure: {The apartment had cockroaches}. To call someone a cockroach is to suggest they're repulsive or unkillable.

Cockroaches are insects of the order Blattodea, known for their flat, oval bodies, long antennae, and remarkable resilience. They thrive in warm, dark environments and are commonly associated with unsanitary conditions, though most species live outdoors and pose no threat to humans. A few species have adapted to human dwellings and are notoriously difficult to eliminate, giving rise to their reputation as survivors of nearly anything. {The apartment had a cockroach problem that no exterminator could solve.}

A cocktail is a mixed alcoholic drink, typically combining spirits with other ingredients like juice, soda, or bitters: {She ordered a cocktail before dinner}. The word extends to other mixtures: a {shrimp cocktail} is an appetizer, a {cocktail of drugs} combines multiple medications. As an adjective, cocktail describes things associated with semiformal drinking occasions: {cocktail dress}, {cocktail party}, {cocktail hour}.

Cocktails are mixed alcoholic drinks combining spirits with other ingredients—juices, syrups, bitters, liqueurs. The term covers everything from a simple gin and tonic to elaborate creations requiring specialized equipment. A cocktail party is a social gathering where such drinks are served with light appetizers. Figuratively, cocktail describes any mixture: {a cocktail of medications}, {a toxic cocktail of stress and exhaustion}.

Cocky describes someone arrogant and overly self-confident, strutting like a rooster: {He's gotten cocky since his promotion}. The word implies swagger and bravado, often unearned. A cocky attitude might be charming in small doses but grating in excess.

Cocoa is the powder made from roasted cacao beans, used to make chocolate drinks and baked goods: {a cup of hot cocoa}, {cocoa powder}. The word also refers to the drink itself, typically served hot with milk: {The children warmed up with cocoa after sledding}. Cocoa and cacao refer to the same plant, though cacao often designates the raw form.

Coconut is the large seed of a tropical palm, with a hard brown shell, white flesh, and liquid center. The flesh is eaten fresh or dried (as copra), and coconut milk and oil are cooking staples. The fibrous outer husk yields coir for rope and matting. As a slur, coconut describes someone seen as betraying their ethnic identity—brown outside, white inside: {accused of being a coconut for assimilating}.

Coconuts are the large, hard-shelled fruits of the coconut palm, containing white flesh and a liquid called coconut water or coconut milk. The outer husk is fibrous, the inner shell woody, and the meat inside can be eaten fresh, dried, or processed into oil, cream, and flour. Coconut is a staple ingredient across tropical cuisines. In vulgar slang, coconuts refers to a woman's breasts or, offensively, to a person of color perceived as culturally assimilated to whiteness—brown on the outside, white on the inside.

A cocoon is the silky protective case spun by certain insect larvae, especially silkworms, as they transform into adults. The word extends to anything that wraps or shelters: {She cocooned herself in blankets}. To cocoon is to wrap protectively or to withdraw into comfortable isolation: {We spent the weekend cocooning at home}.

Cocoons are the protective silk casings that caterpillars spin around themselves during metamorphosis into moths or butterflies. The word extends to any snug, protective wrapping: {She cocoons herself in blankets}. To cocoon is to wrap protectively or to withdraw into sheltered domesticity: {We spent the winter cocooning at home}.

Cod is a large cold-water fish prized for its mild white flesh, historically one of the most important commercial fish in the Atlantic. Cod fishing shaped economies and diets across northern Europe and North America for centuries. The word also appears in British slang: a cod accent or cod philosophy is fake or mocking, a parody of the real thing. {The cod was so plentiful they said you could walk across the sea on their backs.}

Coddled describes someone treated with excessive care or protection, shielded from difficulty or discomfort: {coddled children who can't handle criticism}, {the coddled rich}. The word carries disapproval—coddling produces weakness. A coddled egg is gently cooked in water just below boiling, the culinary sense from which the metaphor extends.

Coddling is treating someone with excessive care or protection, shielding them from difficulty or discomfort. The word carries a note of criticism—coddling implies the care is unwarranted or weakening: {Stop coddling him; he needs to learn responsibility}. Parents coddle children, institutions coddle students, critics accuse governments of coddling criminals. Separately, coddling is a gentle cooking method—eggs coddled in barely simmering water.

Code suggests a medium of communication that is at least one step removed from ordinary language, such as the instructions a computer uses to execute a program. When you code, you convert some message or information into a code. The related verb codify is helpful for remembering some other meanings of code, such as a systematic body of laws. A code may also be a short sequence of letters that has a particular function, like a coupon code.

A codebreaker is someone who deciphers encrypted messages or cracks secret codes. The term evokes wartime cryptanalysts like those at Bletchley Park who broke the Enigma cipher. More broadly, codebreaker applies to anyone who solves puzzles or figures out hidden patterns: {She's a natural codebreaker—solved the riddle in seconds}.

Codebreakers are people who decipher encrypted messages or crack secret codes. The term evokes wartime cryptanalysts—those who broke enemy ciphers at places like Bletchley Park. More broadly, codebreaker applies to anyone who solves puzzles or unravels hidden patterns: {The codebreakers worked around the clock to decrypt the intercepted transmissions}.

Codebreaking is the work of deciphering encrypted messages or solving secret codes, typically without having the key that was used to create them. The term evokes wartime cryptanalysis, particularly the famous efforts at Bletchley Park during World War II, but it applies equally to modern cybersecurity and puzzle-solving. Someone engaged in codebreaking is a codebreaker. {The codebreaking team worked around the clock to intercept enemy communications.}

Coded means converted into a system of symbols or signals: {coded messages}, {coded data}. More commonly now, coded describes language that conveys meaning indirectly or to a particular audience while maintaining plausible deniability: {coded racism}, {coded appeals to voters}. A {coded message} might be encrypted, or it might simply mean one thing on the surface and another underneath.

A codename is a word or phrase used to conceal the true identity of a person, project, or operation. Military operations receive codenames to maintain secrecy: {Operation Overlord} for the D-Day invasion. Software companies use codenames during development before official product names are announced. Intelligence agencies assign codenames to agents and sources. The verb is to codename: {The project was codenamed Phoenix}.

Codependence is a pattern in relationships where one person's sense of identity and worth becomes excessively tied to caring for or controlling another—often someone with an addiction or other dysfunction. The codependent person enables harmful behavior while neglecting their own needs: {Her codependence kept her in the marriage long after it became destructive}. Originally from addiction psychology, the term now applies broadly to any relationship marked by unhealthy emotional reliance.

Codependency is an unhealthy reliance on another person, especially one with addiction or behavioral problems. The codependent person's self-worth becomes tied to caring for, rescuing, or controlling the other: {Her codependency kept her in the marriage long after it turned abusive}. Originally from addiction recovery contexts, the term now applies broadly to any relationship where one person enables another's dysfunction while neglecting their own needs.

Codependent describes a relationship dynamic where one person's sense of identity or emotional wellbeing depends excessively on another, often someone with an addiction or dysfunction. The codependent partner enables harmful behavior while neglecting their own needs: {She realized she'd been codependent, making excuses for his drinking for years}. As a noun, a codependent is someone caught in this pattern. The term emerged from addiction recovery circles but now applies broadly to any relationship marked by unhealthy emotional reliance.

Codes are systems of symbols, words, or rules that convey meaning. A building code establishes construction standards; a dress code sets clothing expectations; a moral code guides behavior. In computing, code is the instructions that make software run—programmers write code, debug code, break code. To code is to write such instructions or to encode information: {The message was coded to prevent interception}. A code can also be a secret system for communication: {They spoke in code so no one would understand}.

A codeword is a word or phrase with a secret or prearranged meaning, used to communicate without others understanding: {The codeword for the operation was "Neptune"}. In espionage or military contexts, codewords classify sensitive information. More loosely, codeword describes any term that signals membership or shared understanding: {"States' rights" became a codeword for racial segregation}.

Coding is the activity of writing computer programs—translating instructions into a language machines can execute. The term emphasizes the practical, hands-on work of programming: {She spent the weekend coding a new app}. In medical contexts, coding refers to a patient going into cardiac arrest: {The patient is coding}.

A codpiece is a pouch or flap covering the crotch in men's clothing, prominent in 15th- and 16th-century European fashion. Originally functional—allowing men to urinate without removing tight hose—codpieces evolved into elaborate, padded displays meant to emphasize the genitals. The term now appears mostly in historical contexts or costume design, though it sometimes surfaces as a joke about masculine vanity.

Coed (also co-ed) describes something involving both sexes together, especially in education: {a coed dormitory}, {the school went coed in 1975}. As a noun, coed is a dated term for a female college student, from when women were the newcomers to previously all-male institutions. The noun now sounds quaint or condescending.

Coerced is the past tense of coerce, meaning forced or compelled through pressure, threats, or intimidation. Someone coerced into signing a contract did so unwillingly: {She claimed she was coerced into confessing}. A coerced confession is legally suspect because it wasn't given freely. The word implies the absence of genuine choice.

Coercion is the use of force, threats, or pressure to compel someone to act against their will. It implies a lack of free choice—the coerced person complies because the alternative is worse: {The confession was obtained through coercion}. Legal and political contexts distinguish coercion from persuasion or consent. To coerce is the verb.

Coexist means to exist at the same time or in the same place, especially when the parties involved might otherwise be in conflict. Nations with different ideologies may coexist peacefully. Species coexist in an ecosystem. The word often implies tolerance despite differences: {Art and commerce can coexist}, {She learned to coexist with her chronic pain}.

Coexistence is the state of existing together, especially when the parties involved might otherwise be in conflict or competition. The term gained prominence during the Cold War as peaceful coexistence, describing the uneasy but nonviolent relationship between capitalist and communist nations. More broadly, it applies to any situation where different groups, species, or ideas occupy the same space without one eliminating the other: {The coexistence of wolves and livestock remains controversial in ranching communities.}

Coffee is the roasted and ground seeds of a tropical shrub, brewed into a bitter, caffeinated drink. The beverage is so central to daily life that coffee can mean a cup of it: {I need my morning coffee}. Coffee also names the social occasion: {Let's get coffee sometime}. As a modifier, coffee describes a medium brown color. A {coffee table} sits low before a sofa.

A coffeehouse is an establishment serving coffee and other beverages, often with light food. Coffeehouses have historically been gathering places for conversation, reading, and intellectual exchange—17th-century London coffeehouses functioned as early social clubs and business centers. Modern coffeehouses range from independent cafés to chains like Starbucks: {We met at a coffeehouse to discuss the project}.

Coffers are chests or strongboxes for storing valuables, especially money. The word almost always appears in the plural, referring to financial reserves or treasury funds: {The scandal drained the party's coffers}, {The tax cut would add billions to corporate coffers}. A coffer is also a recessed panel in a ceiling or dome, used decoratively in architecture.

A coffin is a box in which a dead body is buried or cremated. The word traditionally refers to the six-sided, shoulder-tapered shape, while casket describes the rectangular style common in American funerals—though the terms are often used interchangeably. To coffin is to place in a coffin. {The final nail in the coffin} is the last in a series of problems that ensures failure.

Coffins are boxes designed to hold a dead body for burial or cremation. The word evokes the traditional elongated hexagonal shape—wider at the shoulders, tapering toward the head and feet—though rectangular caskets are now more common in American funeral practice. Coffin also works as a verb: to coffin a body is to place it in one. The phrase {nail in the coffin} refers to something that contributes to an eventual failure or downfall.

A cog is one of the teeth or projections on the rim of a gear or wheel that meshes with another gear to transmit motion. By extension, cog refers to a person who is just one small part of a large organization or system, usually with the implication that they are unimportant or replaceable: {I'm just a cog in the machine}. The phrase captures the feeling of being a minor, interchangeable component in something much bigger than oneself.

Cognac is brandy distilled from wine in the Cognac region of France. The name is protected—only brandy from this area can legally be called cognac. It's aged in oak barrels and graded by age: VS, VSOP, XO. Cognac has become associated with luxury and celebration: {He poured two glasses of cognac after dinner}. The word sometimes appears generically for any fine brandy, though purists object.

Cogs are the teeth on a gear wheel that mesh with other teeth to transmit motion. By extension, a cog is a small but necessary part of a larger system: {just a cog in the machine}. The phrase suggests being replaceable and insignificant within a vast mechanism—useful but interchangeable.

Coherence is the quality of fitting together logically and consistently. An argument has coherence when its parts connect and support each other. A story lacks coherence when events seem random or contradictory. The word applies to writing, thought, speech, or any system where unity matters: {The essay lacked coherence—ideas jumped around without transitions}. In physics, coherent light waves maintain a fixed phase relationship, as in lasers.

A coil is something wound in a spiral or series of loops—a coil of rope, a coil of wire, the coils of a snake. To coil is to wind into such a shape: {The snake coiled around the branch}. Coils appear in electrical and mechanical devices: the coils of a motor, a heating coil. An IUD is sometimes called a coil. {Mortal coil}, from Hamlet, refers to the troubles of earthly life—a different word meaning turmoil.

Coiled describes something wound in loops or spirals—a snake coiled to strike, a rope coiled on a deck, a spring coiled tight. The shape suggests stored energy or compact arrangement: {Her hair was coiled at the nape of her neck}. To coil is to wind into such a shape: {He coiled the hose after watering}.

The basic meaning of coin, a metallic disk used as money, gives rise to many common expressions. Two sides of the same coin are two perspectives or aspects of the same thing. A coin toss is a way of deciding something, based on which side of a coin is facing up after tossing it into the air. If you coin a word or expression, you invent it to suit some occasion.

A coincidence is the occurrence of events that seem meaningfully connected but happen by chance. Two old friends booking the same flight without coordinating is a coincidence. The word often carries a sense of improbability or wonder: {What a coincidence that we both wore the same dress!} In more neutral usage, coincidence simply means things happening at the same time or place: {a coincidence of interests}.

Coincidences are events that occur together in a way that seems meaningful but lacks any apparent causal connection. The plural often emphasizes accumulation—one coincidence is unremarkable, but multiple coincidences invite suspicion or wonder: {Too many coincidences for my taste}. {The coincidences kept piling up until she couldn't ignore them}.

Coined means newly created or invented, especially of words and phrases: {Who coined the term "robot"?} The metaphor comes from minting coins—stamping new money into existence. A {newly coined expression} has just entered the language. Something {freshly coined} suggests recent invention, while a {well-coined phrase} implies successful creation that caught on.

Coins are small flat pieces of metal used as money, typically round and stamped with official designs. The word covers both the objects and the act of making them—governments coin currency, and by extension, to coin a phrase is to invent new language. {She flipped a coin to decide}. {The term was coined in the 1990s}. The other side of the coin refers to an alternative perspective on a situation.

Coke is the solid carbon residue left after coal is heated to drive off gases and tar. It burns hotter than coal and is essential in steelmaking for smelting iron ore in blast furnaces. To coke coal is to convert it through this heating process. Coke also serves as informal shorthand for cocaine: {He was caught with coke in his pocket}. (Capitalized Coke is the soft drink.)

Cola is a carbonated soft drink flavored with kola nuts, citrus, vanilla, and spices—though the exact recipes of major brands remain proprietary secrets. Coca-Cola and Pepsi dominate the category, making cola nearly synonymous with soda in some regions: {Want a cola?} The word also refers to the kola nut itself, a caffeine-rich seed from African trees.

A colander is a bowl-shaped kitchen utensil with holes or perforations, used for draining liquid from food—typically pasta, vegetables, or washed produce. The holes allow water to escape while retaining the solids: {She dumped the spaghetti into the colander in the sink}.

Cold is the go-to adjective when for the opposite of hot. Humans provide the conventional reference point for what is cold, namely a temperature that is too low for comfort. The common viral infection called a cold has no causal connection with things that are cold, other than people stay indoors when it’s cold outside and infect each other more easily. As an adverb, cold carries an idea of absoluteness or completeness: he was knocked out cold in the third round.

Coldblooded describes animals whose body temperature varies with their environment—reptiles, fish, amphibians. The figurative sense dominates: a coldblooded act is calculated and merciless, done without emotion or hesitation: {a coldblooded killer}, {coldblooded murder}. The spelling varies: cold-blooded, coldblooded, cold blooded.

Coldhearted describes someone who lacks warmth, sympathy, or compassion toward others. A coldhearted person remains unmoved by suffering or appeals for help: {It was coldhearted of him to evict the family right before Christmas}. The word implies deliberate emotional distance rather than mere indifference.

Coleslaw is a salad made from shredded raw cabbage, typically dressed with mayonnaise or a vinegar-based dressing. It often includes other ingredients like carrots, onions, or celery seed. Coleslaw is a staple side dish in American cuisine, appearing alongside barbecue, fried chicken, and sandwiches. {The pulled pork came with a generous helping of coleslaw.} The word comes from Dutch *koolsla*, meaning cabbage salad.

A coliseum is a large stadium or arena for sports, concerts, or other public events. The word derives from the Colosseum in Rome, the ancient amphitheater where gladiatorial contests were held. Modern coliseums host everything from basketball games to rock concerts: {The band sold out the coliseum three nights in a row}.

Collaborate means to work together toward a shared goal. Scientists collaborate on research, musicians collaborate on albums, writers collaborate on screenplays. The word carries positive connotations of pooling talents and resources: {We collaborated on the project for months}. During wartime, however, to collaborate is to cooperate treasonously with an enemy occupier—a collaborator aids the opposition.

Collaboration is working together toward a shared goal. The word emphasizes joint effort and contribution: {The project was a collaboration between three universities}. In creative fields, a collaboration typically means a work produced by two or more artists: {Their collaboration resulted in a Grammy-winning album}. During wartime, collaboration takes on a darker sense—cooperating with enemy occupiers: {accused of collaboration with the Nazis}.

A collaborator is someone who works jointly with others on a project or enterprise: {She was my collaborator on the research paper}. The word carries a second, darker meaning: one who cooperates with an enemy, especially an occupying force. A French collaborator during World War II aided the Nazis. Context usually makes clear which sense applies—creative partnership or treasonous cooperation.

Collaborators are people who work together on a shared project or goal. Scientists, artists, and writers often have collaborators: {She and her collaborators published the findings together}. The word carries a darker sense when applied to those who cooperate with an enemy or occupying force: {Nazi collaborators faced prosecution after the war}. Context usually makes clear which meaning applies.

A collage is an artwork made by gluing various materials—paper, photographs, fabric, found objects—onto a surface. The technique emphasizes juxtaposition and layering. By extension, any composite of disparate elements: {The film is a collage of interviews, archival footage, and animation}. The verb means to create such a composition.

Collages are works of art made by assembling diverse materials—paper, photographs, fabric, found objects—onto a surface. The technique emphasizes juxtaposition and layering: {She made collages from old magazines and ticket stubs}. Figuratively, anything assembled from disparate elements may be called a collage: {The film was a collage of documentary footage and interviews}.

Collapse is a sudden loss of structure or support. Buildings collapse when they give way; people collapse when they fall or faint. Systems, governments, and negotiations collapse when they fail completely. A collapsed lung has lost its ability to inflate. To collapse into something—a chair, tears, laughter—is to surrender to it suddenly: {She collapsed onto the sofa after work}. Figuratively, things collapse when distinctions between them disappear: {The two categories collapse into one}.

Collapsed is the past tense of collapse—to fall down or inward suddenly, to fail or break down. A building collapses under structural failure. A person collapses from exhaustion or illness. An argument collapses when its logic fails. {She collapsed into the chair after the long shift.} {The talks collapsed over disagreements about funding.}

Collapsing is the present participle of collapse—falling in on itself, giving way, or failing suddenly. A building may be collapsing under its own weight. A person collapsing is falling down, often from exhaustion or illness. Markets, negotiations, and governments can be collapsing when they fail rapidly: {The economy was collapsing around them}.

A collar is the part of a garment that encircles the neck. Other things that do this also get the name, like jewelry worn around the neck, or a bird’s differently colored neck feathers. Dogs wear collars around their necks for identification, or as a point of attachment for a leash. When police collar someone, they arrest them, sometimes by restraining them at the neck. If you collar someone, you compel them to address a topic that they may have been avoiding.

The collarbone is the bone that runs horizontally from the shoulder to the base of the neck, connecting the shoulder blade to the breastbone. Anatomists call it the clavicle. It's one of the most commonly broken bones in the body, typically from falls or impacts: {She fractured her collarbone in the cycling accident}.

Collars are bands that encircle the neck. A shirt collar frames the face; a dog collar holds tags and a leash. The word extends to anything ring-shaped that encircles: a pipe collar, a bearing collar. To collar someone is to grab them by the collar or, more broadly, to apprehend: {Police collared the suspect outside the bank}. A collar can also mean an arrest itself. Blue-collar and white-collar distinguish manual laborers from office workers, based on traditional work attire.

Collateral is something pledged as security for a loan—if you default, the lender takes it: {The house serves as collateral for the mortgage}. The adjective means accompanying or secondary: {collateral damage} refers to unintended harm, especially civilian casualties in military operations. Collateral also means parallel or side-by-side: a {collateral branch} of a family descends from the same ancestor but through a different line.

A colleague is someone with whom you work, either in the same physical location or profession. Occasionally, colleague is used to describe people who simply belong to the same organization, such as a political party. Colleague is typically used by those who work at universities, making its relationship with college obvious—you just have to remember where the two extra vowels go.

Colleagues are people you work with professionally. The term implies a peer relationship—shared occupation, organization, or field—without suggesting close friendship: {I'm meeting some colleagues for drinks after work}. Unlike coworkers, which emphasizes shared workplace, colleagues can extend to others in your profession generally: {Her colleagues in academia respected her research}.

Collect means to gather or bring together. You collect stamps, debts, or your thoughts. A collector gathers items systematically; a collection is what's gathered. To collect someone is to pick them up: {I'll collect you at eight}. To collect yourself is to regain composure. A collect call charges the recipient rather than the caller. As an adverb, collect means with charges paid by the receiver: {Call collect}.

Collectable, also spelled collectible, describes items considered worth collecting, typically because of rarity, age, craftsmanship, or nostalgic appeal. As a noun, a collectable is such an item: {vintage toys and other collectables}. The term spans everything from stamps and coins to sports memorabilia and limited-edition figurines. What qualifies as collectable often depends on market trends and collector communities rather than inherent worth.

Collected describes a state of calm composure, especially under pressure: {She remained collected during the crisis}. Someone collected has gathered their thoughts and emotions rather than letting them scatter. The word also means brought together: {his collected works}, {the collected essays of James Baldwin}. To collect oneself is to regain composure after being rattled.

Collectible describes items valued and sought by collectors: {collectible coins}, {collectible cards}, {vintage collectible toys}. As a noun, a collectible is such an item—anything people accumulate as a hobby or investment, from stamps to sneakers to Star Wars memorabilia. The appeal often lies in rarity, nostalgia, or condition. Also spelled collectable.

Collectibles are items valued and sought by collectors—often for rarity, nostalgia, or potential appreciation rather than practical use. The category spans sports cards, coins, stamps, vintage toys, and limited editions. The term often suggests mass-produced items marketed to collectors, as opposed to antiques or fine art: {The shop sells comics and other collectibles}. Also spelled collectables.

Collecting is the activity of gathering objects of a particular type, typically as a hobby: {stamp collecting}, {She's been collecting vintage postcards for years}. The word emphasizes the ongoing practice rather than a single act of acquisition. What you accumulate becomes a collection.

Collection is the verbal noun of collect and denotes the activity, instance, or result of collecting. In some contexts, collection refers to the activity of trying to satisfy overdue debts, which is the work of collection agencies that send out collection letters. A group of objects that someone has collected is a collection and the holdings of a museum, a published anthology, and a recording or set of recordings may all be called this.

Collective describes things done by or belonging to a group acting together: {collective bargaining}, {collective responsibility}, {collective memory}. A collective is a cooperative enterprise owned and operated by its members. In grammar, collective nouns name groups—*team*, *flock*, *committee*—that can take singular or plural verbs depending on whether the group acts as a unit.

A collector is someone who gathers objects of a particular type, typically for study, display, or personal satisfaction: {a stamp collector}, {an art collector}, {a collector of rare books}. The term extends to anyone or anything that collects: a {bill collector} pursues unpaid debts, a {tax collector} gathers revenue, and a {dust collector} is either a device or something that sits unused. In electronics, a collector is a terminal in a transistor.

College has different meanings in different English-speaking countries, but its commonest meaning designates an institution of learning, usually one for post-secondary education: He’ll attend college in the fall. Occasionally, college designates people who come together for a specific, and usually specified purpose, as the Electoral College, which elects the U.S. president and vice president.

Collide means to strike against something with force, typically while both objects are in motion: {The two cars collided at the intersection}. The word extends to any forceful coming together—schedules collide when they conflict, ideas collide when they clash. Particles collide in physics experiments; cultures collide when they meet with friction.
