A collie is a breed of herding dog with a long, pointed snout and thick coat, originally from Scotland. The rough collie has a luxuriant mane; the smooth collie has shorter fur. Collies are known for intelligence and trainability: {The collie rounded up the sheep with minimal commands}. The breed gained fame through Lassie, the fictional dog of film and television.

A collision is an impact between moving objects—two cars, two particles, two people rounding a corner. The word emphasizes forceful contact: {The collision totaled both vehicles}. Extended uses describe conflicts between incompatible things: a collision of {ideas}, a collision of {cultures}, {scheduling collisions}. In computing, a collision occurs when two pieces of data compete for the same space or identifier.

Colluding is cooperating secretly for fraudulent or deceptive purposes. The word implies conspiracy—working together while hiding the collaboration from those who would object: {The companies were colluding to fix prices}. Unlike legitimate cooperation, colluding carries inherent disapproval, suggesting the parties are cheating someone or subverting fair dealing.

Collusion is secret cooperation between parties for a deceptive or fraudulent purpose. The word implies wrongdoing—you don't collude to plan a surprise party. Legal contexts often involve collusion to fix prices, rig bids, or manipulate markets. Political collusion suggests covert coordination with foreign powers or adversaries: {The investigation found no evidence of collusion with Russia}.

Cologne is a type of scented liquid worn on the body, lighter and less concentrated than perfume. Originally associated with men's fragrances, though the distinction has blurred: {He splashed on some cologne before the date}. The word comes from the German city where it was first made. (Capitalized Cologne is the city.)

A colonel is a military officer rank, typically below general and above lieutenant colonel. The word's spelling preserves its Italian origin while the pronunciation (/KER-nuhl/) reflects a different historical form. In American usage, colonel appears as an honorary title in some Southern states, and {Colonel Sanders} made it familiar as a corporate mascot. {The colonel addressed the troops at dawn.}

Colonial relates to colonies—territories under the political control of a distant nation. Colonial {architecture}, colonial {rule}, colonial {history}. The word often carries critical weight, implying exploitation or cultural imposition: {a colonial mindset}. In American usage, colonial describes the period before independence or its distinctive style: {colonial furniture}, {a colonial-era farmhouse}. A colonial is a person living in a colony, especially a settler from the ruling nation.

Colonialism is the practice of acquiring and maintaining control over foreign territories, typically exploiting their resources and people for the benefit of the colonizing power. European colonialism from the 15th through 20th centuries reshaped much of the world, leaving lasting effects on borders, economies, and cultures. The adjective colonial describes this era or its remnants: {colonial architecture}, {colonial attitudes}. In extended use, colonialism describes any relationship of domination and exploitation: {cultural colonialism}, {digital colonialism}.

A colonialist supports or participates in colonialism—the policy of acquiring and maintaining control over foreign territories and their peoples. The term carries strong negative connotations, implying exploitation and cultural domination: {colonialist attitudes}, {colonialist powers}. As a noun, it describes someone who advocates or benefits from colonial rule: {The colonialists extracted resources while suppressing local traditions}.

Colonies is the plural of colony. A colony is a territory controlled by a distant power, or a group of people who settle in such a territory: {the thirteen colonies that became the United States}. Colonies also refers to groups of organisms living together: {ant colonies}, {colonies of bacteria}. In casual use, colonies of anything cluster in one place: {colonies of artists in Greenwich Village}.

Colonisation is the British spelling of colonization—the act of establishing control over a territory and its people. A nation colonises by sending settlers, extracting resources, and imposing its laws and culture on indigenous populations. The term now carries heavy connotations of exploitation and cultural destruction: {the colonisation of Africa by European powers}. Extended uses describe any takeover or spread: {the colonisation of the gut by bacteria}, {corporate colonisation of public space}.

Colonise is the British spelling of colonize. To colonise is to establish control over a territory and its people, typically by settling there and imposing outside governance: {Britain colonised much of Africa in the 19th century}. The word extends to any takeover or spreading occupation: {Weeds colonised the abandoned lot}. In biology, organisms colonise new habitats when populations establish themselves there.

A coloniser is a person or nation that establishes control over a foreign territory, typically exploiting its resources and imposing authority over indigenous populations. The term carries strongly negative connotations in contemporary usage, emphasising the harm done to colonised peoples through displacement, cultural destruction, and extraction of wealth. In modern discourse, coloniser often appears as a pointed accusation: {The protesters called the developers colonisers for displacing longtime residents}. This is the British spelling; American English uses colonizer.

Colonisers is the British spelling of colonizers—people who establish control over foreign territory and its inhabitants. The term carries strong negative connotations, evoking exploitation, displacement of indigenous peoples, and cultural destruction: {The colonisers imposed their language and religion on the native population}. In contemporary discourse, coloniser often appears as an accusation or insult.

A colonist is a person who settles in a colony—a territory claimed and controlled by a distant power. The term applies both to early settlers who establish colonies and to later inhabitants who maintain them: {The colonists struggled through their first winter}. Unlike immigrant, colonist emphasizes the extension of one nation's authority over another land, often displacing indigenous peoples.

Colonists are people who settle in a new territory while maintaining ties to their country of origin. The term applies both to those who establish colonies and to their descendants who continue living there: {The colonists declared independence from Britain}. The word carries different weight depending on perspective—colonists saw themselves as settlers and pioneers; indigenous peoples experienced them as invaders.

Colonization is the process of establishing control over a foreign territory and its people. A nation sends settlers to occupy land, extract resources, and impose its political and cultural systems. European colonization of Africa and the Americas reshaped global demographics and power structures. The term extends to any takeover of space: bacterial colonization of a wound, colonization of Mars. In postcolonial discourse, colonization often emphasizes exploitation and displacement of indigenous peoples.

Colonize means to establish a colony—a settlement of people from one country in foreign territory. European powers colonized much of Africa and the Americas, displacing indigenous populations. The word extends to any takeover of space: {Weeds colonized the abandoned lot}. Bacteria colonize surfaces. In contemporary discourse, colonize often carries critical weight, implying exploitation or cultural imposition: {Tech companies colonizing public spaces with advertising}.

Colonized describes a place or people that have been brought under the control of a foreign power. A colonized {territory} is settled and governed by outsiders. Colonized {peoples} have had their land, resources, or governance taken over. The term extends to cultural domination: {colonized minds} have internalized the values of their colonizers. In biology, a surface colonized by bacteria has been populated by them.

A colonizer is someone who establishes control over a foreign territory and its people, typically through settlement, exploitation, or displacement of indigenous populations. The term carries strong negative connotations, emphasizing the harm done to colonized peoples: {The colonizers seized land that had been inhabited for centuries}. In contemporary discourse, colonizer often appears as a pointed critique of historical injustice and its ongoing effects: {You're on colonizer land}. It may be used loosely to describe anyone perceived as appropriating or dominating spaces where they don't belong.

Colonizers are people who establish control over foreign territories and their populations. The term carries strong negative connotations, emphasizing exploitation and displacement of indigenous peoples: {The colonizers imposed their language and religion on the native population}. In contemporary usage, colonizer often appears as a pointed criticism of historical and ongoing power imbalances: {You can't just show up and take over—don't be a colonizer}.

Colonizing is the act of establishing control over a territory and its people, typically by a foreign power. Settlers colonize lands by displacing or subjugating indigenous populations: {European powers spent centuries colonizing Africa and the Americas}. The term extends to any takeover of space: bacteria colonizing a wound, invasive species colonizing an ecosystem. In contemporary discourse, colonizing often carries critical weight, implying exploitation or cultural erasure.

A colony is a territory controlled by a distant country, with settlers or administrators sent to govern it: {Britain's American colonies declared independence in 1776}. The word extends to groups of organisms living together—a colony of ants, a colony of bacteria, a leper colony. Artists or writers may form colonies, gathering in a shared location to work.

Color (colour in British English) is a visual quality of objects, owing to distinctions our eyes perceive in various wavelengths of light. Put more simply, a color is any of the many named variations of this light that we distinguish, such as red, gold, orange, or blue. When you color something, you add one or more colors to it. Color may also describe emotional qualities. Prejudice colored his account means that his account was influenced by prejudice.

Colorblind describes inability to distinguish certain colors, most commonly red from green. The condition is usually inherited and more common in men. Figuratively, colorblind means deliberately ignoring distinctions of race or ethnicity: {a colorblind society}, {colorblind hiring policies}. Critics argue such approaches can overlook systemic inequalities. Also spelled colour-blind.

Colorblindness is the inability to distinguish certain colors, most commonly red and green. The condition is usually inherited and far more prevalent in men. Figuratively, colorblindness means disregarding racial or ethnic distinctions: {The company claims colorblindness in its hiring practices}. Critics argue such colorblindness can ignore real inequities rather than transcending them.

Colorful describes something with many colors, especially bright or vivid ones: {a colorful garden}, {colorful illustrations}. By extension, colorful applies to anything lively or striking: a colorful {personality}, a colorful {past}. Colorful {language} is profane or obscene—the expression is often euphemistic: {The coach was known for his colorful vocabulary}.

Coloring is the application of color to something, or the colors themselves: {the coloring of autumn leaves}, {artificial coloring in food}. A person's coloring is their skin tone, hair, and eye color considered together: {She has her mother's coloring}. A coloring book contains outline drawings for children to fill in with crayons or markers. Figuratively, coloring suggests influence or bias: {His account was colored by resentment}.

Colors are the visual qualities we perceive through differences in light wavelength—red, blue, green, yellow, and so on. The word extends to any distinguishing visual element: {The team wore their colors proudly}. To color is to apply pigment or, figuratively, to influence: {His past colored his judgment}. A {person of color} is non-white. To {show your true colors} is to reveal your real character. {With flying colors} means with complete success.

Colossal means extremely large—beyond ordinary bigness into the realm of the monumental. The word evokes ancient statues of impossible scale: {a colossal statue}, {colossal columns}. It extends readily to abstractions: {a colossal mistake}, {colossal arrogance}, {colossal waste of time}. The emphasis is on impressiveness or excess, not mere measurement.

A colossus is something enormous in size, power, or importance. The word originally referred to a giant statue, especially the Colossus of Rhodes—a bronze figure of the sun god that stood at the harbor entrance in ancient Greece. Now it describes anything of overwhelming scale: {a colossus of industry}, {an intellectual colossus}. The plural is colossi or colossuses. (Capitalized Colossus may refer to specific statues, machines, or fictional characters.)

Colour (color in American English) is a visual quality of objects, owing to distinctions our eyes perceive in various wavelengths of light. Put more simply, a colour is any of the many named variations of this light that we distinguish, such as red, gold, orange, or blue. When you color something, you add one or more colors to it. Colour may also describe emotional qualities. Prejudice coloured his account means that his account was influenced by prejudice.

Colourblind describes the inability to distinguish certain colours, most commonly red and green. The condition is usually inherited and more prevalent in men. Figuratively, colourblind means deliberately ignoring differences, especially racial ones: {a colourblind society}, {colourblind hiring practices}. This figurative use is sometimes criticized for implying that noticing race is itself problematic. British spelling of colorblind.

Colourful describes things with many colours or vivid hues: {a colourful garden}, {colourful fabrics}. Figuratively, it means lively, interesting, or distinctive: {a colourful character}, {colourful language}. The latter phrase often euphemizes profanity or vulgarity. British spelling of colorful.

Colouring is the British spelling of coloring. It refers to the process of adding colour to something, or to the colours themselves: {the bird's distinctive colouring}. Colouring also means complexion or skin tone. A colouring book contains outlined drawings for children to fill in. Food colouring is dye added to alter appearance.

Colours is the British spelling of colors—the visual qualities of objects produced by different wavelengths of light. The word covers the same range of meanings: literal hues {the colours of the rainbow}, figurative associations {show your true colours}, and military flags {trooping the colours}. In British usage, colours appears in {colour film}, {colour scheme}, and {colourful language}.

A colt is a young male horse, typically under four years of age. The term extends to young males of related animals like donkeys and zebras. Figuratively, colt describes an inexperienced young man or a rookie athlete: {The team's colts showed promise in preseason}. A colt may also be a young, spirited person of either sex. (Capitalized Colt is the firearms manufacturer.)

Colts is the plural of colt, a young male horse typically under four years old. The term extends to young or inexperienced people, especially in sports: {The colts on the junior varsity showed promise}. A colt revolver is a firearm made by the Colt company. {Three colts grazed in the pasture.} (Capitalized Colts usually refers to the Indianapolis NFL team.)

A column is a vertical structural pillar that supports weight in buildings, or any similarly shaped upright object. The word extends to vertical arrangements of text, numbers, or data on a page or screen: {newspaper columns}, {spreadsheet columns}. A column of soldiers or vehicles is a formation moving in a line. In journalism, a column is a regular feature by a particular writer expressing opinions or covering a specific topic: {She writes a weekly advice column}. The person who writes such a feature is a columnist.

Columns are vertical structural supports—pillars holding up a building or monument. The term extends to anything arranged vertically: a column of {soldiers} marching in formation, a column of {numbers} in a spreadsheet, or a column of {text} on a page. In newspapers and magazines, a column is also a regular feature by a particular writer: {She writes a weekly advice column}.

A coma is a state of deep unconsciousness from which a person cannot be awakened. It results from severe injury, illness, or poisoning affecting the brain: {He remained in a coma for three weeks after the accident}. Separately, coma is an astronomy term for the hazy envelope surrounding a comet's nucleus.

A comb is a toothed implement for untangling and styling hair. To use this implement is to comb. To comb a place is to examine it very carefully, usually because you are looking for something. One thing that slightly resembles a comb also gets the name: the fleshy growth on the heads of some birds and reptiles. A comb that doesn’t resemble any others is the mass of hexagonal cells built by honeybees – that is, the honeycomb.

Combat is fighting, especially organized armed conflict between military forces. The word carries more formality than fight: {hand-to-hand combat}, {combat troops}, {combat zone}. As a verb, to combat something is to fight against it: {measures to combat inflation}, {combating misinformation}. A combat can also be a struggle or contest between opposing forces or ideas.

Combination is what you get when you join separate things together. A combination of {factors} led to the crisis. In reference to a lock, the combination is the specific sequence of numbers that opens it. Combination underwear is a single garment covering both torso and legs. To work {in combination} is to work together: {Diet and exercise work in combination}.

Combinations is the plural of combination—things joined or mixed together. A combination of factors produced the result. Combinations are also one-piece undergarments covering the torso and legs, now old-fashioned: {He stripped down to his combinations}. In mathematics, combinations are selections of items where order doesn't matter, unlike permutations.

To combine is to bring things together into a unified whole: {Combine the ingredients in a bowl}, {The two companies combined to form a conglomerate}. Things that combine merge or join forces. A combine is also a large farm machine that harvests grain—so called because it combines the operations of cutting, threshing, and cleaning in one pass.

Combo is short for combination, typically referring to a grouped set offered together. In restaurants, a combo meal bundles items at a reduced price: {I'll have the burger combo}. In music, a combo is a small jazz or dance band. In video games, a combo is a rapid sequence of attacks chained together for extra damage. The word keeps its casual, clipped feel across all uses.

Combos is the plural of combo, an informal clipping of combination. A combo meal bundles a main dish with sides and a drink. In music, a combo is a small jazz or dance band. In video games, a combo is a rapid sequence of moves executed together for amplified effect: {I finally landed that 12-hit combo}. The word appears wherever things are bundled or chained together.

A combover is a hairstyle that attempts to cover a bald spot by growing hair long on one side and combing it across the scalp. The style rarely fools anyone and often invites ridicule: {His combover flapped in the wind}. Also spelled comb-over.

Come is among the most common verbs in English, indicating movement toward the speaker or a destination: {Come here}. {She came to the party}. Come conveys arrival, occurrence, or result: {Spring has come}. {It came as a surprise}. {Come what may}. The word appears in countless expressions: {come and go}, {come to terms}, {come of age}, {come clean}. In vulgar slang, come means to have an orgasm: {She came twice}. As a noun (often spelled cum), it means semen or orgasm: {There was come on the sheets}.

A comeback is a return to prominence after a period of absence or decline: {The singer staged a remarkable comeback after years out of the spotlight}. In conversation, a comeback is a quick, clever reply to criticism or an insult—the retort you wish you'd thought of in the moment. To {make a comeback} or {mount a comeback} is to recover from a losing position, especially in sports.

Comebacks are returns to prominence after a period of decline or absence. An aging athlete stages a comeback; a politician mounts one after scandal. The word also means quick, clever replies to criticism or insult: {I couldn't think of a good comeback until hours later}. Both senses share the idea of answering something—adversity or an opponent.

A comedian is someone who performs comedy—telling jokes, doing impressions, or otherwise trying to make audiences laugh. Stand-up comedians work alone on stage with a microphone. The word also applies more broadly to anyone who habitually cracks jokes: {He's the comedian of the family}. In older usage, comedian meant any comic actor, especially in theater.

Comedy is entertainment designed to amuse—plays, films, or performances meant to provoke laughter. The term contrasts with tragedy and drama: {I'm in the mood for a comedy tonight}. A comedy of errors involves absurd mishaps. Beyond entertainment, comedy describes any ludicrous situation: {The meeting devolved into comedy}. Stand-up comedy features a solo performer delivering jokes to a live audience.

A comet is a celestial body that orbits the sun, distinguished by a glowing tail of gas and dust that streams behind it when near the sun. Comets appear periodically—Halley's comet returns roughly every 76 years. Figuratively, someone who rises to sudden prominence and fades quickly might be called a comet: {She blazed through Hollywood like a comet}.

Comets are icy bodies that orbit the sun, developing glowing tails of gas and dust as they approach it. Ancient observers saw them as omens. Unlike planets, which follow predictable paths, comets appear irregularly—some returning on cycles of decades or centuries, others passing through the solar system only once. {Halley's Comet won't return until 2061.}

Comeuppance is a deserved punishment or misfortune that befalls someone who has behaved badly. The word carries a sense of poetic justice—the idea that wrongdoers eventually face consequences for their actions. {After years of cheating investors, the CEO finally got his comeuppance when he was arrested.} It's almost always used with "get" or "have" and appears most often when the speaker takes satisfaction in someone's downfall.

Comfort is a state of ease and contentment, free from pain or anxiety. Physical comfort comes from soft chairs, warm blankets, adequate food. Emotional comfort comes from reassurance and support: {She found comfort in her friend's words}. To comfort someone is to console them. A comfort is something that provides ease: {the comforts of home}. Cold comfort is consolation so slight it hardly helps.

Comfortable describes a state of physical or mental ease. A comfortable chair supports the body well. A comfortable room has pleasant temperature and furnishings. Comfortable extends to psychological states: {I'm not comfortable with that decision}. Someone who is comfortable financially has enough money to live without worry. The word implies adequacy rather than luxury—comfortable is less than lavish but more than merely tolerable.

A comforter is a thick, quilted bedcover filled with down or synthetic material, used for warmth. In British usage, the same item is often called a duvet. Comforter also means one who provides comfort: {She was a comforter to the grieving family}. In religious contexts, the Comforter refers to the Holy Spirit.

Comforting describes something that provides solace or eases distress: {a comforting thought}, {comforting words from a friend}. Food or activities can be comforting when they restore a sense of security or well-being: {There's something comforting about a bowl of soup on a cold day}. The word often carries warmth and reassurance rather than mere relief.

Comforts are things that provide physical ease or emotional solace. The word often appears with modifiers: {creature comforts} are material pleasures like good food and soft beds; {cold comfort} is consolation that fails to console. {Home comforts} are the familiar amenities of domestic life. To take comfort in something is to find reassurance there: {She took comfort in the routine}.

Comfy is informal for comfortable, almost always referring to physical ease—a comfy {chair}, comfy {clothes}, a comfy {bed}. The word has a cozy, casual quality that formal *comfortable* lacks. {I'm getting comfy on the couch}. It rarely describes emotional comfort or financial security the way *comfortable* can.

Comic describes something intended to provoke laughter or amusement: a comic {novel}, a comic {performance}. A comic is a person who performs comedy, or a publication featuring sequential illustrated panels—what longer form becomes a comic {book}. The plural comics refers to the newspaper section containing comic strips: {I always read the comics first}. Comic overlaps with comical, though comical more often describes things unintentionally funny.

Comical describes something that provokes laughter or amusement, often through absurdity or incongruity: {The dog's comical expression made everyone laugh}. It differs slightly from comic—comical emphasizes the effect of being funny, while comic can describe intent or genre. Something comical is often unintentionally amusing: {His comical attempts at dancing}.

Comics are sequential images, usually with text, that tell a story or convey humor—from newspaper strips to graphic novels to superhero serials. The form ranges from single-panel gags to elaborate narratives. Comic also works as an adjective meaning funny or related to comedy, and as a noun for a comedian: {She's a stand-up comic}. The phrase {the comics} typically refers to the comics section of a newspaper.

Coming is the present participle of come. It describes approaching, arriving, or imminent occurrence: {The train is coming}. {The coming year looks promising}. In vulgar usage, coming means approaching orgasm: {I'm coming!}

A comma is a punctuation mark (,) indicating a pause or separation between elements in a sentence. Commas set off clauses, separate items in lists, and clarify meaning: {Let's eat, Grandma} versus {Let's eat Grandma}. In numbers, commas mark groups of three digits: {1,000,000}. A comma can also be a brief pause or interval in music or speech.

All meanings of command suggest power, authority, or advantage. Command is the right or authority to order, and if you have it, you can issue commands. Computers respond to commands, that is, instructions it receives from a program or user. Command of a skill is mastery of it. When you command someone or something, your expectation is that your wish will be satisfied. If a place commands a view, it is situated so as to provide one.

Commandeer means to seize something for official or military use, typically without permission: {The army commandeered civilian vehicles during the evacuation}. More loosely, it means to take control of something for your own purposes: {My sister commandeered the TV remote}. The word carries a sense of authority or forcefulness, whether legitimate or playfully asserted.

A commander is a person in charge—especially one who leads military forces. In naval ranks, commander falls between lieutenant commander and captain. The word extends to anyone exercising authority: {the commander of the rescue operation}, {commander in chief}. To command is to direct with authority, and a commander is one who does so.

Commanding describes someone or something that demands attention and respect through authority or presence. A commanding {voice} carries power; a commanding {lead} in a race is dominant and secure. A commanding {view} overlooks a wide area from an advantageous position. To have a commanding {presence} is to naturally draw focus and inspire deference without effort.

A commandment is an authoritative order or rule that must be obeyed. The word carries religious weight from the Ten Commandments of Judeo-Christian tradition: {Thou shalt not kill}. Outside scripture, commandment suggests rules treated as sacred or absolute: {The first commandment of good writing is clarity}.

Commandments are orders or rules that must be obeyed, carrying moral or divine authority. The term most often refers to the Ten Commandments—biblical laws given to Moses, including prohibitions against murder, theft, and adultery. More broadly, any authoritative directive can be called a commandment: {The first commandment of good writing is clarity}.

A commando is a soldier trained for quick, aggressive raids into enemy territory—operations requiring stealth, speed, and self-sufficiency. The term extends to the units themselves: {a commando of elite troops}. In casual use, {going commando} means wearing no underwear, the image being of unencumbered readiness for action.

Commandos are soldiers trained for quick, dangerous raids into enemy territory. Commando units operate with speed and stealth, often behind enemy lines: {The commandos slipped ashore under cover of darkness}. The term extends to anyone undertaking a bold or stealthy operation. To {go commando} is slang for wearing no underwear.

Commands are orders or instructions given with authority, expecting obedience or execution. A military officer issues commands to troops; software accepts commands from users. The word functions as both noun and verb: you can {command attention} or {take command} of a situation. Someone who commands respect earns it through presence or achievement. In computing, commands are specific instructions entered to perform operations: {Type the command and press enter}.

Commencement is a beginning or start: {the commencement of hostilities}, {from the commencement of the trial}. The word is formal and appears often in legal and official contexts. In American English, commencement also means a graduation ceremony—the beginning of life after school: {She delivered the commencement address}.

A comment is a remark or observation, usually brief: {Any comments on the proposal?} In writing, comments are explanatory or critical notes. In programming, a comment is text ignored by the computer, meant only for human readers. To comment is to make such remarks. {No comment} is a standard refusal to respond to questions, especially from journalists.

Commentary is spoken or written explanation accompanying something else—a text, broadcast, or event. Sports commentary describes action as it unfolds. Biblical commentary interprets scripture. DVD commentary features filmmakers discussing their work. More broadly, commentary is observation or opinion on any subject: {The film serves as commentary on modern capitalism}. To provide commentary is to comment.

A commentator is someone who provides commentary—analysis, explanation, or opinion on events as they unfold. Sports commentators describe the action during broadcasts. Political commentators offer perspectives on news and policy. The term implies ongoing engagement with a subject rather than one-time reporting: {She's a regular commentator on cable news}.

Comments are remarks or observations about something, often expressing an opinion or reaction: {The article received hundreds of comments}. In computing, comments are notes within code that explain functionality but don't execute—meant for human readers, not machines. To comment is to offer such remarks. {No comment} is a stock refusal to respond, especially to journalists.

Commerce is the buying and selling of goods and services, especially on a large scale between businesses or nations: {international commerce}, {the commerce clause of the Constitution}. The word suggests trade as a system or activity rather than individual transactions. Extended uses cover any exchange or interaction: {the commerce of ideas}, {social commerce}.

Commercial connects to commerce—buying and selling. As an adjective, it describes things intended for profit or wide distribution: {commercial real estate}, {commercial fishing}, {a commercial flight}. Something too commercial has sacrificed quality or integrity for mass appeal. As a noun, a commercial is an advertisement on television or radio: {We'll be right back after these commercials}.

Commercials are advertisements broadcast on television or radio, interrupting programming to promote products, services, or causes. The word usually refers to video spots: {We'll be right back after these commercials}. Someone's commercial is their paid promotional appearance: {She landed a commercial for a car company}. The singular often means advertising work generally: {He does commercial and film}.

Commie is informal and usually disparaging slang for a communist—someone who supports communist political ideology or belongs to a communist party. The term peaked during Cold War anti-communist sentiment in the United States, when {commie} carried strong negative connotations of disloyalty or subversion. Today it's often used loosely or humorously to label anyone perceived as far-left or anti-capitalist: {My uncle calls anyone who supports universal healthcare a commie}.

The most basic meaning of commission is carrying out or engaging in (as in the commission of a crime) and from this meaning, many others have developed. A commission may be a group assembled for a particular purpose (an electoral commission) or it may be the order that causes such a group to form. People or companies may get or be given commissions to do particular work: We commissioned an article from the freelance writer. A military commission is the authority given to officers to carry out their responsibilities.

A commissioner is an official, usually appointed, with a specific duty or authority: The police commissioner announced that an investigation was underway. In British English, a commissioner is the head of a government department, or the representative of the government in a region. In business, a commissioner is someone who receives commission from a sale.

Commit means to carry out or perform, usually something consequential: {commit a crime}, {commit an act of violence}. To commit to something is to pledge yourself to it: {She committed to the project}. To commit someone is to place them in confinement, especially psychiatric care. In computing, to commit is to save changes permanently to a database or repository. A committed person is dedicated or obligated: {a committed relationship}, {committed to the cause}.

Commitment is one of two nouns derived from the verb commit; the other is commission. When you make a commitment, you give assurance that you will be responsible for something. Someone’s commitment is their dedication to a responsibility: Her commitment in leading the scout troop was admirable. If you honor a commitment, you fulfill an obligation. Sometimes commitment refers to financial matters: The club’s other commitments make it impossible to carry out the improvements this year.

Committed describes dedication or obligation. Someone committed to a cause devotes themselves to it fully: {a committed environmentalist}. In relationships, committed means pledged to exclusivity: {They've been in a committed relationship for years}. The word also describes being bound by decision or circumstance: {Once you sign, you're committed}. A committed person may be one confined to an institution: {He was committed after the breakdown}.

A committee is a group of people appointed or elected to perform a specific function, typically within a larger organization. Committees investigate, deliberate, or oversee: {a hiring committee}, {the ethics committee}, {a committee meeting}. {The bill died in committee} means it never reached a full legislative vote. To {design by committee} suggests the awkward compromises of group decision-making.

Commodities are raw materials or basic goods that can be bought and sold—grain, oil, copper, coffee. The term implies interchangeability: one barrel of crude oil is essentially equivalent to another, unlike manufactured products with brand differences. {Commodity prices fell sharply}. Financial markets trade commodity futures, betting on future prices. Figuratively, anything treated as interchangeable becomes a commodity: {Time is a precious commodity}. When something is commodified, it has been reduced to a tradeable good, often with negative connotations: {Health care shouldn't be treated as a commodity}.

A commodity is a raw material or primary product that can be bought and sold: oil, wheat, copper, coffee. Because commodities are interchangeable—one barrel of crude is much like another—they're traded on exchanges where price matters more than source. The word extends to anything treated as fungible or generic: {Labor became just another commodity}. When something is {commodified}, it's reduced to its exchange value.

A good mnemonic for the many meanings of common is the related word community. Things that are common are available to or shared by all: common interests, common water source. This meaning inspires another frequent sense of common, namely that with is ordinary: The robin is our most common bird. Carried to an extreme, this idea gives rise to common as coarse or vulgar. As a noun, common denotes a piece of land for use by everyone. The plural commons has several specialized senses, all of which relate to the idea of community.

A commoner is a person without noble rank or title—an ordinary member of society rather than aristocracy. The term belongs mostly to historical or British contexts, where the distinction between nobility and common people retains some currency: {As a commoner, she couldn't expect an invitation to court}. In casual use, commoner can mean anyone of average or unremarkable status.

Commons refers to shared resources or spaces available to all members of a community. Land held in common allows anyone to graze livestock or gather wood. The concept extends to shared cultural or natural resources: {the creative commons}, {the commons of the internet}. In universities, a commons is a dining hall or gathering space. The House of Commons is the elected lower chamber of the British Parliament. {Tragedy of the commons} describes how shared resources get depleted when individuals act in self-interest.

Commonwealth is a political community founded for the common good, or the body of citizens constituting such a community. The term appears in the official names of four U.S. states—Kentucky, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, and Virginia—though it carries no legal distinction from "state." More broadly, commonwealth describes any organized political unit or republic: {The commonwealth prospered under democratic rule}. (Capitalized Commonwealth often refers specifically to the Commonwealth of Nations.)

Commotion is noisy disturbance or agitation—a state of confused, turbulent activity: {The announcement caused quite a commotion}. It suggests disruption of normal calm, whether from crowds, arguments, or sudden events: {What's all the commotion about?} The word implies disorder rather than violence.

Communal describes what belongs to or is shared by a community or group rather than individuals. A communal {kitchen} serves all residents of a building. Communal {land} is owned collectively. The word often implies cooperative living arrangements or shared resources: {The farm operated on communal principles}. Communal can also relate to relations between ethnic or religious communities, especially in contexts of conflict: {communal violence}.

Commune captures ideas of sharing and communication. To commune is to connect intimately, often spiritually: {commune with nature}, {commune with God}. A commune is a group living together and sharing resources, property, or responsibilities—from 1960s hippie communes to agricultural collectives. In some countries, a commune is also an administrative district, the smallest unit of local government.

To communicate is to convey information, ideas, or feelings to others. The word covers every mode of exchange—speaking, writing, gesturing, or simply making eye contact. {We communicate mostly by text now.} Animals communicate through calls and body language. A room may communicate with another by sharing a doorway or passage. Good communication requires not just sending but being understood.

Communication is used to describe the act of conveying information (good communication is vital for successful relationships) or an instance or result of it (have you received any communications from Warsaw?) It can also refer to vehicles for conveying information: Radio, television, telephone, and the Internet are forms of mass communication. There is also a technical meaning of “physical connection”: A secret passageway provided communication between the isolated buildings.

Communion is intimate sharing or exchange, especially of thoughts or feelings. It suggests deep connection: {a moment of communion with nature}, {communion between old friends}. In Christianity, Communion (often capitalized) is the sacrament commemorating the Last Supper, in which bread and wine are consumed—also called the Eucharist or the Lord's Supper. A communion of people is a group united by shared beliefs.

Communism is a political and economic ideology advocating collective ownership of property and the means of production, with goods distributed according to need rather than market forces. In theory, communism aims for a classless society without a state. In practice, 20th-century communist regimes—the Soviet Union, Maoist China, Cuba—featured authoritarian one-party rule and centralized planning. {The Cold War pitted communism against capitalism.} In American political discourse, communism often functions as a loose epithet for any left-wing policy the speaker dislikes.

A communist is someone who advocates for communism—a political and economic system where property and production are collectively owned rather than privately held. The word ranges from precise ideological identification {a committed communist who joined the Party} to loose political accusation {Republicans called the policy communist}. During the Cold War, communist often meant specifically Soviet-aligned. Capitalized Communist typically refers to party membership or official state ideology: {the Communist Party}, {Communist China}.

Communists are people who support or advocate for communism—a political and economic ideology favoring collective ownership of property and the means of production. The term applies broadly to anyone holding such views, from casual sympathizers to active revolutionaries: {The communists organized a demonstration downtown}. During the Cold War, {communists} became a catch-all accusation for political enemies, sometimes applied loosely to anyone with leftist views. (Capitalized Communists typically refers to party members.)

Communities is the plural of community—groups of people sharing something in common. That shared element might be geography {the communities along the river}, identity {LGBTQ communities}, interest {the gaming community}, or circumstance {the intelligence community}. The word often implies connection and mutual support, though communities can also be defined by shared problems: {communities affected by the hurricane}.

You could think of community as a word to describe a place where people commune, though the noun is much more frequent that the verb. A community may exist in one place (small farming communities are scattered all over the county), or it may characterize a group of people separated in space but sharing particular common interests (the intelligence community was surprised by the attacks). Community nearly always has positive connotations, reflecting the idea that common interests and pursuits are good for people.

Commute has two main branches. The familiar one is traveling regularly between home and work: {My commute takes forty minutes each way}. The noun and verb share this sense. The other branch involves substitution or exchange—to commute a prison sentence is to replace it with a lighter one: {The governor commuted her death sentence to life imprisonment}. In electronics, to commute is to reverse current direction.

A commuter is someone who travels regularly between home and work, typically covering a significant distance. The word implies routine—daily or near-daily trips, usually by car, train, or bus. {The train was packed with morning commuters}. Commuter appears as a modifier for things serving this population: commuter {rail}, commuter {traffic}, commuter {town}.

Commuting is regular travel between home and work, typically daily. The word implies routine—the same route, the same crowds, the same delays: {My commute takes forty-five minutes each way}. Someone who commutes is a commuter. The verb commute also means to reduce a sentence or convert one form of payment to another, but the travel sense dominates modern usage.

Compact describes something pressed together, dense, or occupying little space: {a compact car}, {compact soil}. The verb means to compress or pack tightly: {compact the trash}. A compact is a small case for cosmetics, especially face powder with a mirror. It's also a formal agreement: {The Mayflower Compact established governance for the Plymouth colonists}. The adjective stresses on the second syllable; the nouns stress on the first.

Companies is the plural of company—a business enterprise or firm: {Several tech companies announced layoffs}. Company also means companions or guests: {We're expecting company tonight}. To keep someone company is to stay with them so they're not alone. A company of soldiers is a military unit. {Two's company, three's a crowd.}

A companion is someone who accompanies or spends time with another—a friend, partner, or associate: {a traveling companion}, {a constant companion}. The word suggests ongoing presence rather than a single encounter. Companion extends to things that go together: {a companion volume}, {a companion piece}. In caregiving, a companion is someone hired to provide company and assistance to an elderly or ill person.

Companions are people or animals who accompany someone, sharing time and experience. The word suggests ongoing association rather than momentary encounter: {traveling companions}, {a faithful companion}. A companion can be a paid caregiver who provides company to someone elderly or ill. The term extends to things that go together: {a companion volume}, {companion plants}. As a verb, to companion someone is to keep them company.

Companionship is the state of having a companion—the comfort and warmth that comes from not being alone. It emphasizes the emotional quality of the relationship rather than its practical aspects: {She got a dog for companionship}. People seek companionship in marriage, friendship, or even from pets. The word often appears when someone lacks it or fears its absence.

Company is closely related to companion, and that explains the earliest and still common meaning of this word: association with others. From this core idea developed the many other meanings that company enjoys, including the one that probably springs first to mind: a commercial business.

Compare is to examine things side by side to find similarities or differences: {Let's compare prices before we buy}. To compare something to another is to liken them: {She compared his singing to a cat in heat}. Beyond compare means unmatched: {Her beauty is beyond compare}. The noun comparison appears in phrases like {by comparison} and {no comparison}.

Comparison is the act of examining things to see how they're similar or different: {a comparison of the two candidates' tax plans}. Something that holds up well {by comparison} looks good relative to alternatives. {There's no comparison} means one thing clearly outclasses another. In grammar, comparison refers to adjective and adverb forms showing degree: positive, comparative, superlative.

A compartment is a separate section within a larger enclosed space. Train cars have compartments for passengers. A toolbox has compartments for different tools. {She kept her work life and personal life in separate compartments.} The verb compartmentalize extends this to mental separation—keeping thoughts or feelings isolated from one another.

A compass is an instrument with a magnetized needle that points north, used for navigation and orientation. More broadly, compass means range or scope: {beyond the compass of human understanding}, {within the compass of the law}. To compass something is to achieve or encompass it. A pair of compasses (or simply a compass) is the hinged drafting tool for drawing circles—the two arms pivot around a central point, which connects to the directional compass through the idea of circumscribing or encircling.

Compassion is sympathetic concern for the suffering of others, coupled with a desire to help. It goes beyond mere pity—compassion implies emotional engagement and often motivates action: {She showed compassion for the homeless man by buying him a meal}. The word carries warmth without condescension, suggesting genuine fellow-feeling rather than looking down from a position of comfort.

Compassionate describes someone who feels genuine concern for others' suffering and wants to help relieve it. The word suggests both emotional sensitivity and active kindness: {a compassionate nurse}, {compassionate toward the homeless}. Compassionate leave is time off work granted for family emergencies or bereavement. To act compassionately is to respond with empathy rather than indifference.

Compatibility is the quality of being able to exist or work together without conflict. People assess romantic compatibility on dating apps. Computer hardware and software must be compatible with each other to function. {The two medications have compatibility issues.} Compatible things share characteristics that allow harmonious coexistence: {We tested the compatibility of the new system with our existing infrastructure.}

Compatible describes things that work well together or can coexist without conflict. Compatible {software} runs on a particular system; compatible {personalities} get along easily. Blood types must be compatible for transfusions. The word often implies meeting requirements: {Is this charger compatible with my phone?} Romantically, compatible people share enough values or temperament to sustain a relationship.

To compel is to force or drive someone to action. External pressures compel: {The evidence compelled a guilty verdict}. Internal forces also compel: {She felt compelled to speak up}. What compels has an irresistible quality—you don't merely want to act, you must. A compelling argument or story is one that grips and convinces.

Compelled describes being driven to act by force, obligation, or inner necessity. External compulsion is explicit: {The court compelled him to testify}. Internal compulsion is felt as irresistible: {I felt compelled to speak up}. The word suggests the person wouldn't have acted otherwise—something overcame their resistance or inertia.

Compelling describes something that demands attention or agreement through sheer force of quality. A compelling {argument} is so well-constructed you can't dismiss it. A compelling {story} grips you—you have to keep reading. The word suggests irresistibility: you feel compelled, as if you have no choice but to engage. {The evidence was compelling enough to change my mind.}

Compensation is what you receive in exchange for something—typically money for work: {The job offers competitive compensation}. It also means making up for a loss or deficiency: {He received compensation for his injuries}; {She compensated for her shyness with humor}. In psychology, compensation is unconsciously counterbalancing a weakness by emphasizing a strength.

To compete is to strive against others for something not everyone can have—a prize, a position, a victory. Athletes compete in tournaments, businesses compete for customers, siblings compete for attention. The word implies rivalry without necessarily implying hostility: {We competed fiercely but stayed friends}. Someone who competes well is competitive; a price that competes well is also competitive.

Competence means adequate ability, and is somewhat related to the idea of skill: By passing the exam, she demonstrated competence in math. Competence in a language suggests an ability to understand or speak it, but without the suggestion of outstanding ability. If you question the competence of an authority or expert, you are suggesting that they may not have the necessary knowledge, skill, or ability to perform adequately.

Competent describes someone who has sufficient ability or skill to do something adequately. A competent {employee} performs their job without major problems. A competent {witness} is legally qualified to testify. The word implies adequacy rather than excellence—calling someone competent is faint praise, suggesting they meet the minimum standard but don't exceed it: {The work was competent but uninspired}.

Competition is the act of striving against others for something—a prize, victory, customers, resources, or recognition. The word covers both the activity and any particular contest: {The competition starts at noon}. It also refers collectively to one's rivals: {We need to see what the competition is doing}. Competition can be friendly or fierce, and extends from sports and business to evolution, where organisms compete for survival.

Competitive describes the drive to win or outperform others. A competitive {person} wants to come out on top; a competitive {market} has many rivals vying for customers. Something competitively {priced} matches or beats what others charge. The word can suggest healthy ambition or excessive fixation on winning: {She's too competitive to let anyone beat her at anything}.

A competitor is someone who competes—a rival seeking the same goal, prize, or market share. In business, competitors are companies offering similar products or services: {Our main competitor just lowered their prices}. In sports or contests, competitors are the participants: {Twelve competitors entered the race}. The word implies active opposition, not mere presence in the same field.

Competitors are rivals vying for the same goal—a prize, a market, a customer, a mate. The word applies equally to individuals and organizations: {Our competitors just launched a similar product}. In business, competitors offer alternatives that could win your customers away. In sports or games, they're whoever you're trying to beat. Competition can be direct or indirect, friendly or cutthroat.

Complacency is self-satisfied contentment that blinds you to problems or dangers. It suggests being so comfortable with the current state that you stop paying attention or making effort: {Success bred complacency, and the company failed to innovate}. The word nearly always carries criticism—complacency is what you accuse others of, or warn against in yourself.

Complacent describes someone smugly satisfied with themselves or their situation, often without awareness of potential dangers or deficiencies. A complacent {attitude} suggests contentment that has curdled into laziness or overconfidence: {The team grew complacent after their early lead and lost the game}. Not to be confused with complaisant, which means eager to please.

To complain is to express dissatisfaction or annoyance: {She complained about the noise}, {He's always complaining}. You can complain to someone or about something. A complaint may be informal grumbling or a formal grievance: {file a complaint with HR}. The word often carries a whiny connotation—chronic complainers are tiresome. In medical contexts, to complain of something is to report a symptom: {The patient complained of chest pain}.

A complainer is someone who expresses dissatisfaction habitually or excessively. The word carries mild criticism—everyone complains sometimes, but a complainer does it enough to be tiresome: {He's such a complainer—nothing is ever good enough for him}. The term suggests the complaints may be petty or unproductive rather than legitimate grievances.

Complaining is expressing dissatisfaction or annoyance, often repeatedly or habitually. The word carries a mildly negative tone—someone who is {always complaining} tends to focus on grievances rather than solutions. {She's been complaining about the noise for weeks.} A complaining tone suggests whiny or aggrieved delivery.

A complaint is an expression of dissatisfaction or grievance: {I filed a complaint with the manager}, {Her main complaint was the noise}. In legal contexts, a complaint is the formal document initiating a lawsuit. Medical complaints are symptoms a patient reports: {The patient's chief complaint was chest pain}. The word implies something is wrong and someone wants it addressed.

Complaints are expressions of dissatisfaction or grievance. You file a complaint with a company, lodge one with authorities, or simply voice one to whoever will listen: {The main complaint was slow service}. In medicine, a complaint is the symptom or condition that brings a patient to the doctor: {Her chief complaint was persistent headaches}. The singular complaint can also name the act itself: {a letter of complaint}.

Complement is easy to confuse with its homonym compliment, but their meanings don’t overlap. A complement is a part or addition to something that makes it complete. A full complement is the whole number or amount that is needed. In grammar, complement is a word that completes a grammatical construction. In ready to go, “to go” is the infinitive complement of “ready.”

Complete means whole, with all parts present and nothing missing. A complete {set} lacks no pieces; a complete {sentence} has all required grammatical elements. When something is complete, it has reached its finished state—a task is complete when done, a building is complete when construction ends. The verb complete means to finish or to supply what is lacking: {Complete the form before submitting}. Completely, the adverb, intensifies adjectives: {completely satisfied}, {completely wrong}.

Completion is the state of being finished or the act of finishing something. A project reaches completion when all its parts are done. {The bridge is nearing completion.} In real estate, completion is the final stage when ownership transfers and the transaction closes. {We're scheduled for completion next month.}

Complex describes something with many interconnected parts that make it difficult to understand or analyze: {a complex system}, {complex emotions}, {the complex relationship between diet and health}. The word suggests intricacy rather than mere difficulty—a complex problem has layers that interweave. As a noun, a complex is a group of related buildings or facilities ({apartment complex}, {shopping complex}), or in psychology, a cluster of repressed feelings that influence behavior: {inferiority complex}, {Oedipus complex}. In chemistry, a complex is a compound of linked molecules.

Complexes is the plural of complex in its noun senses. A complex is a group of interconnected buildings or facilities: {apartment complexes}, {shopping complexes}. In psychology, a complex is a group of repressed feelings that influence behavior: {inferiority complex}, {Oedipus complex}. The psychological sense has spawned casual usage for any preoccupation or hang-up: {She has a complex about her weight}.

Complexion is the natural color, texture, and appearance of the skin, especially on the face: {a fair complexion}, {a ruddy complexion}, {Her complexion cleared up after she changed her diet}. The word extends to the general character or aspect of something: {The election changed the complexion of the Senate}. Both senses concern outward appearance rather than underlying substance.

Complexity is the quality of having many interconnected parts or layers that make something difficult to understand or analyze. A complex system resists simple explanation: {The complexity of the tax code frustrates even accountants}. The word often signals that oversimplification would miss something important: {We need to appreciate the complexity of the situation before proposing solutions}.

Compliance is the act of following rules, orders, or requests. A company in compliance with regulations meets legal requirements. The word often implies yielding to authority or pressure rather than acting from conviction: {She agreed out of compliance, not enthusiasm}. In medicine, patient compliance means following prescribed treatment. The adjective compliant describes someone who readily goes along with what's asked of them.

To complicate is to make something more difficult or involved than it needs to be: {Let's not complicate things}. Adding variables, conditions, or obstacles complicates a situation. A complicating factor introduces new difficulty. Medical conditions that worsen or trigger other problems are complications. The adjective complicated describes anything intricate or hard to understand: {It's complicated}.

Complicated describes something with many interconnected parts that make it difficult to understand or deal with. A complicated {situation} has multiple factors at play. Complicated {instructions} require careful attention. The word often implies that difficulty arises from intricacy rather than simple confusion: {It's complicated} suggests layers of nuance that resist easy explanation, especially regarding relationships.

A complication is something that makes a situation more difficult or complex than it would otherwise be. Medical complications are problems arising during treatment or recovery: {Pneumonia is a common complication of the flu}. In storytelling, a complication introduces conflict or obstacles. The plural often signals a messy situation: {There were complications with the divorce}.

Complications are factors that make something more difficult or complex. A medical complication is a secondary condition arising from an existing illness or its treatment: {Pneumonia developed as a complication of the flu}. More broadly, complications are entanglements or obstacles that emerge in any situation: {There were complications with the paperwork}. The word implies that what seemed straightforward has become messy.

Complicit means involved in wrongdoing, typically by knowing about it and failing to prevent or report it. The word implies shared guilt without necessarily being the primary actor: {The bank was complicit in the money laundering scheme}. Someone complicit may have actively participated or simply looked the other way: {Her silence made her complicit}.

Complicity is involvement in wrongdoing, typically as a partner or accomplice rather than the principal actor. The word implies shared guilt: {Her silence made her complicit in the cover-up}. Complicity can be active or passive—you can be complicit by helping, by knowing and not acting, or simply by benefiting from harm done to others.

Compliment is easy to confuse with its homonym complement but their meanings are distinct. A compliment is a favorable remark about another person: the mayor went through the crowd, shaking hands and paying compliments. If you return a compliment, you compliment someone who has just done the same for you. When you compliment someone, you say something nice about them: He complimented the astronomer for her insightful research.

Compliments are expressions of praise, admiration, or approval: {She received compliments on her presentation}. To compliment someone is to offer such praise. The phrase {with compliments} or {compliments of} indicates something given free as a courtesy: {Drinks are compliments of the house}. Often confused with complements, which are things that complete or go well together.

Compose means to create by arranging parts into a whole. You compose music, poetry, or a letter by putting elements together thoughtfully. To compose yourself is to calm down and regain control: {She took a moment to compose herself before speaking}. What composes something makes it up: {The committee is composed of five members}. In printing and typesetting, to compose is to arrange type for printing.

Composed describes a state of calm self-possession, especially under pressure. Someone who remains composed during a crisis keeps their emotions in check and thinks clearly: {She stayed composed throughout the interview}. The word implies deliberate control rather than natural ease—composure that might require effort to maintain. Separately, composed means made up of constituent parts: {The committee is composed of seven members}.

A composer is someone who writes music, especially classical or orchestral works: {Beethoven was deaf when he composed his Ninth Symphony}. The term applies broadly to anyone who creates original musical pieces, from film scores to operas. In computing, a composer is software that manages code dependencies.

Composers are people who write music. The term typically implies original creation rather than arrangement or performance, and suggests formal musical training: {Bach and Beethoven are among history's greatest composers}. Classical music uses the term most, though it applies to anyone who creates musical works: {film composers}, {jingle composers}.

Composition is the verbal noun from compose and reflects that verb’s many meanings. A musical composition is the product of composing music; composition generally is the art or craft of doing this. If you teach composition, it may be this subject, or it may be English composition (writing). The composition of a substance or any other compound thing is its components and their proportions.

Compost is decayed organic matter used to enrich soil. Kitchen scraps, leaves, and grass clippings break down into dark, crumbly material that gardeners mix into beds or spread as mulch. The verb means to convert waste into compost or to add compost to soil: {We compost our vegetable scraps}. A compost heap or bin is where this decomposition happens.

Composting is the process of breaking down organic waste—food scraps, leaves, grass clippings—into nutrient-rich soil amendment. Bacteria, fungi, and invertebrates do the work; you provide the raw material and conditions. The verb compost means to add material to a compost pile or to undergo this decomposition: {We compost our kitchen scraps}. {The leaves will compost over winter}.

Composure is a state of calm self-possession, especially under stress or provocation. Someone who maintains composure doesn't visibly panic, cry, or lash out: {She kept her composure throughout the cross-examination}. To lose composure is to let emotion show; to regain it is to collect yourself. The word suggests dignified restraint rather than mere stillness.

A compound is something that results from compounding, that is, putting together unlike things to form something new. In usage, a compound is typically a drug or chemical substance. Putting together two words results in a compound (sawhorse, snowball, mailbox). When you compound a problem, you add something to it that makes it worse. An enclosed group of buildings that share some features or functions is also called a compound.

Comprehension is the ability to understand something: Children with good language comprehension learn to read earlier than others do. The word is used in the same way as a countable noun to describe a test of comprehension: The reading comprehension was very difficult. Comprehension has a second meaning with a different emphasis: the ability to appreciate the full range of something. In this sense it is typically used in the phrase beyond comprehension: The damage that was done was beyond comprehension.

Compression is the act of pressing or squeezing something into a smaller space. In physics, compression is the opposite of tension—force that pushes inward rather than pulling apart. Digital compression reduces file sizes by eliminating redundant data: {audio compression}, {video compression}. In medicine, compression applies pressure to an injury or body part: {compression bandage}, {compression socks}. Engine compression refers to the squeezing of fuel and air before ignition.

Compromise is an agreement reached when each side gives up something it wanted. To compromise is to settle by mutual concession: {They compromised on the price}. Compromise also means to expose to risk or suspicion: {The leak compromised national security}. A compromised {immune system} is weakened. To find oneself in a {compromising position} is to be caught in circumstances that suggest misconduct.

Compromised describes something whose integrity, security, or effectiveness has been damaged or undermined. A compromised {immune system} can't fight infections properly. A compromised {password} has been exposed to unauthorized parties. A compromised {position} is one weakened by revelation or circumstance: {His authority was compromised when the emails leaked}. The word often implies vulnerability that wasn't immediately apparent—the breach may have happened before anyone noticed.

Compromising describes something that exposes a person to suspicion, disgrace, or damage to reputation. A compromising {position} suggests sexual impropriety—being caught in circumstances that look bad. Compromising {evidence} or {photos} could be used against someone. The word implies vulnerability to blackmail or scandal: {The leaked emails contained compromising information about several executives}.

Compulsion is an irresistible urge to do something, often against one's better judgment. The word carries a sense of being driven by forces beyond conscious control: {She felt a compulsion to check the locks again}. In psychology, compulsions are repetitive behaviors performed to relieve anxiety, as in obsessive-compulsive disorder. Compulsion also means the act of compelling—forcing someone to do something: {They acted under compulsion, not by choice}.

Compulsions are urges to perform certain actions, especially repetitive behaviors driven by anxiety or obsessive thoughts. In clinical contexts, compulsions pair with obsessions in OCD—the obsessive fear of contamination produces compulsive handwashing, for instance. More loosely, a compulsion is any strong, hard-to-resist impulse: {She felt a compulsion to check her phone every few minutes}.

Compulsive describes behavior driven by an irresistible urge rather than rational choice. A compulsive {liar} lies even when truth would serve better. A compulsive {gambler} can't stop despite mounting losses. The word suggests psychological compulsion—the person feels unable to control the behavior. As a noun, a compulsive is someone who acts this way: {He's a compulsive when it comes to cleaning}.

A computer is a machine that processes information according to programmed instructions. Originally the word meant a person who performs calculations—a sense now obsolete. Modern computers range from pocket-sized smartphones to warehouse-scale data centers. {My computer crashed and I lost an hour of work.} {She's good with computers.}

Computers are electronic machines that process information according to instructions. The term once meant people who performed calculations—human computers—but now refers almost exclusively to the devices. Desktop computers, laptop computers, and the computers in smartphones all share the essential function: taking input, processing it, and producing output. {My computer crashed during the update.}

Computing is the use of computers to process information, solve problems, or perform calculations. The term covers both the activity and the field: {She works in computing}, {cloud computing has transformed how businesses store data}. Computing power refers to a machine's capacity for processing: {The simulation required massive computing power}.

A comrade is a companion or fellow member of a group, especially one sharing a common purpose or hardship. Soldiers call their fellow soldiers comrades; activists address each other the same way. The word carries a socialist or communist connotation from its use as a form of address in leftist movements: {Comrade Lenin}, {Hello, comrade}.

Con has two distinct origins. One means against: the pros and cons of a decision. The other comes from confidence—a con is a swindle that exploits trust, and to con someone is to deceive them: {He conned her out of her savings}. A con artist runs such schemes. Con is also short for convict: {an ex-con}. As a prefix, con- means with or together: connect, congregate.

To conceal is to hide something or keep it from being seen or known. You might conceal a weapon under a coat, conceal evidence of wrongdoing, or conceal your true feelings. The word often implies deliberate secrecy: {She couldn't conceal her disappointment}. Concealed suggests hidden from view; {concealed carry} refers to carrying a weapon out of sight.

Concealer is a cosmetic product used to hide blemishes, dark circles, or other skin imperfections. Thicker than foundation, it provides targeted coverage for specific areas: {She dabbed concealer under her eyes before the interview}. The term extends to anything that hides or masks: {The shrubs acted as a concealer for the ugly fence}.

To concede is to admit something reluctantly or under pressure: {I concede that you have a point}. In competitions, to concede is to acknowledge defeat before the final result is official: {The candidate conceded the election}. Concede also means to yield or grant something: {The company conceded several demands to the union}. A goal conceded is one allowed by the defending team.

Conceit is an excessively high opinion of oneself—vanity or self-importance: {His conceit was insufferable}. In literary criticism, a conceit is an elaborate or unusual metaphor, especially one that draws surprising comparisons: {The poem's central conceit compares the lovers to a compass}. The two senses connect through the idea of something conceived in the mind—whether flattering self-regard or imaginative invention.

Conceited describes someone who has an excessively high opinion of themselves, their abilities, or their appearance. A conceited person assumes others share their self-admiration and may talk about themselves constantly or dismiss others' accomplishments. {He's so conceited he checks his reflection in every window.} The word carries strong disapproval—unlike confident or self-assured, conceited implies the self-regard is unwarranted or obnoxious.

Conceive means to form something in the mind—an idea, a plan, an image. {I can't conceive of a reason to refuse.} The word also means to become pregnant: {They conceived their first child that summer.} The connection is generative: whether mental or physical, conceive is about bringing something new into being.

Conceived most often means formed in the mind—an idea, plan, or belief that someone thought up: {The project was conceived as a way to reduce waste}. It also means to become pregnant: {She conceived after years of trying}. The passive construction {conceived in} describes origins: {a nation conceived in liberty}. Something {poorly conceived} was badly planned from the start.

Concentrate means to focus attention or effort on a single point: {I can't concentrate with all this noise}. It also means to gather or collect in one place: {Power concentrated in the capital}. As a verb in chemistry and cooking, concentrate removes water or diluting substances, making something stronger or more intense. The noun concentrate is the resulting product—orange juice concentrate, protein concentrate. To concentrate troops is to mass them in one location.

Concentrated describes something made stronger or denser by removing diluting elements. Concentrated orange juice has had water removed. A concentrated solution holds more solute per volume. The word extends to mental focus: {concentrated effort}, {concentrated attention}. Concentrated also describes things gathered into a small area: {concentrated fire}, {concentrated population}.

Concentrating is giving full attention to something, gathering mental focus on a single task or subject: {I can't think with all this noise—I'm trying to concentrate}. The word also describes making something more dense or potent by removing diluting elements: {concentrating the sauce by simmering}. Both senses share the idea of drawing scattered things toward a center.

Concentration is the focusing of attention or effort on a single thing: {The job requires intense concentration}. It also means a gathering or accumulation in one place: {a concentration of troops near the border}, {high concentrations of lead in the water}. In chemistry, concentration measures how much of a substance is dissolved in a solution. A concentration camp is a facility for mass detention, most notoriously the Nazi death camps of World War II.

A concept is an idea, especially one that arises by generalizing from many instances or characteristics: Democratic concepts arose in reaction to the despotic rule of kings and tyrants. The concept of a concrete thing is an idea that includes all of its particular characteristics: The concept of a creator God is present, with some variation, in many different cultures. When used as an adjective, concept designates something that is built around a single idea or is intended to illustrate a concept, such as a concept car or a concept building.

Conception is the moment when a new life begins—the fertilization of an egg by sperm. From this biological sense comes the broader meaning of bringing something into existence: the conception of an {idea}, the conception of a {plan}. A conception is also an understanding or mental picture of something: {Her conception of justice differs from mine}. The word bridges physical creation and mental formation.

When one thing concerns another, it is related to it in an important way. A matter that concerns you is one to which you must attend or pay attention. A movie that concerns three orphans is about them. If something does not concern you, you are not involved or interested in it. A concern is a matter that is important to someone: Those attending the meeting were able to air their concerns. If something causes concern, it makes people worry that something bad may happen if action is not taken.

Concerned means worried or troubled about something: {I'm concerned about your health}. It also means interested or involved: {All concerned parties should attend the meeting}. The phrase {as far as I'm concerned} introduces a personal opinion or perspective: {As far as I'm concerned, the matter is closed}.
