To be concerned with something is to deal with or relate to it: {The book is concerned with climate change}.

Concerns, as a noun, are matters that engage someone's attention, interest, or care, often because they involve worry or responsibility. A business or organization may also be called a concern. The verb concern means to relate to or affect someone: {This matter doesn't concern you}. If something concerns you, it causes worry or unease. To concern yourself with something is to take an active interest in it. Concerned can mean worried {I'm concerned about her health} or involved {all concerned parties were notified}.

A concert is a live musical performance, typically by one or more musicians or groups playing for an audience. Concerts range from intimate acoustic sets to massive stadium events, and the word applies across genres from classical to rock to hip-hop. {We got tickets to the concert downtown.} The phrase {in concert} means working together in coordination: {The agencies acted in concert to address the crisis.}

A concerto is a musical composition for orchestra featuring one or more solo instruments. The soloist and orchestra engage in dialogue—sometimes the soloist takes the spotlight while the orchestra accompanies, sometimes they play in conversation: {a piano concerto}, {a violin concerto}. The form emerged in the Baroque period and remains central to classical repertoire. Plural: concertos or concerti.

Concerts are live performances of music before an audience, typically featuring one or more musicians or groups playing for an extended period. The word covers everything from symphony orchestras in formal halls to rock bands in arenas to jazz combos in clubs. {We got tickets to the concert downtown.} As a verb, concert means to arrange or plan together, and appears most often in the adjective concerted, meaning coordinated or done in combination: {a concerted effort to raise funds.}

A concession is something yielded or granted, often reluctantly. In an argument, you make a concession by acknowledging a point for the other side: {I'll make one concession—the data isn't perfect}. A concession can be a right or privilege granted by an authority: {mining concessions}, {logging concessions}. In American English, a concession is also a vendor's right to sell goods at a venue—hence {concession stand} at stadiums and theaters. To {concede} is the verb.

Concessions are things yielded or granted, often reluctantly. In negotiation, making concessions means giving ground: {Both sides made concessions to reach a deal}. At stadiums and theaters, concessions are the snacks and drinks sold to patrons, or the stands selling them: {The concessions at the arena are overpriced}. A concession can also be a right granted to operate a business within a larger property.

A conch is a large spiral-shelled sea snail, or the shell itself. The shells have been used as trumpets, decorative objects, and symbols of the ocean. In *Lord of the Flies*, the conch represents order and authority. Conch meat is eaten in Caribbean cuisine: {conch fritters}, {conch salad}. Pronounced with a hard k or as "konch."

A concierge is a staff member at a hotel or apartment building who assists guests or residents with services—making reservations, arranging transportation, securing tickets, recommending restaurants. The role combines doorman, information desk, and personal assistant. In healthcare, a concierge practice offers enhanced access to a physician for an annual fee: {concierge medicine}.

A conclave is a private meeting, especially one where participants deliberate in secret. The word is most associated with the gathering of Catholic cardinals to elect a new pope—historically locked in isolation until they reach a decision. More broadly, any closed-door meeting of insiders qualifies: {The party leaders met in conclave to choose their candidate}.

A conclusion is the end or final part of something—a speech, an essay, a negotiation. It also means a judgment reached through reasoning: {The detective arrived at a startling conclusion}. To {jump to conclusions} is to decide without sufficient evidence. A {foregone conclusion} is an outcome that seems inevitable. In formal contexts, to {bring something to a conclusion} is simply to finish it.

Conclusions are judgments or decisions reached through reasoning. After weighing evidence, you {draw a conclusion} or {reach a conclusion}. A conclusion is also the end or final part of something—the conclusion of a speech, a novel's conclusion. To {jump to conclusions} is to decide without sufficient evidence. {In conclusion} signals a summary or final remarks.

A concoction is something made by mixing various ingredients together, often with a suggestion of improvisation or dubious results: {She whipped up some concoction of leftover vegetables and rice}. The word can describe drinks, potions, remedies, or dishes, and extends to elaborate schemes or fabricated stories: {His alibi was an obvious concoction}.

Concrete in its oldest sense means solid and real, as opposed to abstract: {concrete evidence}, {concrete proposals}. The word extends to the building material—a mixture of cement, sand, gravel, and water that hardens into stone-like mass. Concrete dominates modern construction: sidewalks, foundations, highways. To concrete something is to cover or set it in this material. The jungle metaphor describes urban environments dominated by concrete structures.

A concubine is a woman who lives with a man in a sexual relationship without being his wife, typically in cultures or historical periods where such arrangements had recognized social status. Unlike a mistress, whose relationship is usually secret, a concubine often held an acknowledged position in the household, though inferior to that of a wife. The term appears frequently in historical and biblical contexts, where men of wealth or power maintained multiple concubines alongside their legal wives.

A concussion is a brain injury caused by a blow to the head, typically producing temporary symptoms like confusion, headache, or memory problems. The word also means a violent shaking or jarring impact: {the concussion from the blast rattled windows}. In sports medicine, concussion protocols now govern when athletes can return to play after head trauma.

Concussions is the plural of concussion, a brain injury caused by a blow to the head. The impact causes the brain to move within the skull, resulting in temporary impairment: {He suffered two concussions playing football}. Symptoms include headache, confusion, and memory problems. The term has gained prominence as awareness of sports-related brain injuries has grown. Concussion can also mean violent shaking from an impact: {the concussion of the blast}.

Condemn means to express strong disapproval or to declare something wrong or evil: {The senator condemned the attack}. Courts condemn prisoners to punishment—especially death. Buildings are condemned when declared unsafe for use. To condemn someone to a fate is to doom them to it: {His injury condemned him to a life of chronic pain}. The word carries weight and finality.

Condemnation is strong disapproval or censure: {The policy drew condemnation from human rights groups}. It also refers to official judgment that something is unfit—a building condemned as unsafe, meat condemned as diseased. In legal contexts, condemnation is the formal seizure of private property for public use. A condemnation can also be a sentence of punishment: {The judge's condemnation was swift}.

Condemned describes something officially declared unfit, guilty, or destined for destruction. A condemned building is too dangerous for occupation. A condemned prisoner awaits execution. The word carries finality—what is condemned has been judged and found wanting: {The condemned man ate his last meal}. To feel condemned is to feel doomed or beyond redemption.

Condescending describes behavior that implies superiority over the person being addressed—a patronizing tone that suggests the other person is less intelligent, capable, or worthy of respect: {Don't be so condescending; I understand the basics}. The word carries strong negative judgment; calling someone condescending is never a compliment. A condescending {smile}, condescending {explanation}, or condescending {attitude} all suggest the person thinks they're doing you a favor by engaging at your level.

Condescension is an attitude of superiority that shows in how someone speaks or behaves toward others. A condescending person talks down to people, often while appearing gracious: {His condescension was obvious in the way he explained basic concepts to the expert}. The word usually implies the superiority is unearned or the manner offensive, though historically it could mean a gracious willingness to lower oneself to others' level.

A condiment is a substance added to food to enhance its flavor—ketchup, mustard, mayonnaise, relish, hot sauce. Condiments are typically applied at the table rather than during cooking, distinguishing them from spices and seasonings. {Pass the condiments, please.} The word can extend to pickles, chutneys, and similar accompaniments.

Condiments are flavorings added to food at the table or during preparation—mustard, ketchup, mayonnaise, relish, hot sauce. The term covers a wide range from simple salt and pepper to elaborate sauces. Unlike spices used in cooking, condiments are typically applied by the eater to suit personal taste: {Pass the condiments, please}.

A condition is the state something is in (weather condition, market condition). An illness that lingers or requires attention is euphemistically called a condition. If conditions are attached to an agreement, they stipulate what you must do or accept. If you condition someone to something, you get them used to it. If you condition yourself, you get in shape. If you condition your hair or some other physical thing, you treat it with a substance that improves it.

Conditioned describes something that has been trained, treated, or modified to respond in a particular way. A conditioned {response} is learned through repeated association—Pavlov's dogs salivating at a bell. Hair or leather can be conditioned by applying substances that soften or protect. Air is conditioned when mechanically cooled or heated. More broadly, we are all conditioned by our upbringing and culture: {Years of poverty had conditioned her to hoard food}.

Conditioner is a product that improves the condition of something. Hair conditioner softens and detangles after shampooing. Fabric conditioner (or softener) makes laundry feel less stiff. Leather conditioner keeps hides supple. Air conditioners don't condition air in this sense—they cool it—but the name stuck from early claims about improving air quality. {My hair is dry without conditioner.}

Conditioning is preparation or training that shapes behavior, skills, or physical capacity. Athletes undergo conditioning to build strength and endurance. In psychology, conditioning refers to learned associations between stimuli and responses—Pavlov's dogs salivating at a bell being the classic example. Hair conditioner and air conditioning share the root sense of bringing something into proper condition. {Years of conditioning made her flinch at raised voices.}

Conditions are the circumstances or factors that affect a situation: {working conditions}, {weather conditions}, {living conditions}. A condition can also be a requirement that must be met: {The loan came with strict conditions}. As a verb, to condition is to train or accustom someone to respond in a particular way, or to treat something to improve its state: {condition your hair}, {condition your muscles}. A medical condition is an ailment or health problem. {On condition that} means only if: {I'll go on condition that you come with me}.

A condo is a housing unit in a building or complex where each unit is individually owned, while common areas are shared. Short for condominium. The term emphasizes the ownership structure rather than the physical building: {They bought a condo downtown}. Condos typically come with association fees and rules governing the property.

Condolence is an expression of sympathy for someone experiencing grief or misfortune, especially after a death. The word appears most often in the plural: {Please accept my condolences}. To {offer condolences} or {pay condolences} is to express sympathy formally, whether in person, by card, or at a funeral.

Condolences are expressions of sympathy offered to someone grieving a loss, especially a death: {Please accept my condolences}, {We sent our condolences to the family}. The word appears almost exclusively in this plural form and in formal contexts—cards, funeral visits, official statements. To {offer condolences} or {extend condolences} is to express sorrow for another's misfortune.

A condom is a thin sheath worn over the penis during sex to prevent pregnancy and reduce transmission of sexually transmitted infections. Most are made of latex, though polyurethane and lambskin versions exist. The female condom is inserted into the vagina. {Do you have a condom?}

Condoms are thin sheaths worn over the penis during sex to prevent pregnancy and reduce transmission of sexually transmitted infections. They're typically made of latex, though polyurethane and lambskin versions exist. {Do you have a condom?} The word also appears in safer-sex campaigns: {No condom, no sex}.

A condor is a very large vulture of the Americas, among the largest flying birds in the world. The Andean condor inhabits South American mountain ranges; the California condor, once nearly extinct, survives through conservation efforts. Condor sometimes appears figuratively for something that circles or looms: {Creditors hovered like condors over the failing business}.

Condors are very large New World vultures with wingspans exceeding ten feet—among the largest flying birds. The Andean condor inhabits South American mountains; the California condor, nearly extinct by the 1980s, has been slowly recovering through captive breeding programs. Both species are scavengers, feeding on carrion.

Conduct as a noun (first syllable stressed) is a near synonym of behavior and usually includes the idea of propriety: The teachers received compliments on the conduct of the schoolchildren. When used as a verb (second syllable stressed), conduct has meanings that all involve the idea of leadership. If you conduct an orchestra or choir you lead it when it rehearses or performs. If you conduct an investigation, you carry it out, either alone or in a leadership role. When no agent is identified, conduct just means carry out: a study was conducted to determine how many trees were infected.

Conducting is directing or leading, especially an orchestra or other musical ensemble. A conductor uses gestures to guide tempo, dynamics, and expression. Beyond music, conducting means carrying out or managing: {conducting research}, {conducting business}, {conducting a survey}. Materials that are conducting allow electricity or heat to pass through them.

A conductor leads an orchestra or chorus, directing performers through gesture and expression. The word extends to anyone who guides or directs: a tour conductor, a train conductor who manages passengers and tickets. In physics, a conductor is a material that allows heat or electricity to pass through it—copper is an excellent conductor, rubber a poor one. The underlying sense is something that leads or carries forward.

Conductors is the plural of conductor, which centers on leading or conveying. An orchestra conductor directs musicians, interpreting the score and coordinating performance. A train conductor manages passengers and operations aboard the cars. In physics, a conductor is a material that transmits heat or electricity: {Copper and silver are excellent conductors}. The word implies something that channels flow—whether of music, passengers, or electrons.

A conduit is a channel or pipe through which something flows or is conveyed, typically water, electrical wires, or other utilities. The word extends naturally to figurative uses: a person or organization can serve as a conduit for information, money, or influence, channeling it from one place to another. {The nonprofit acted as a conduit for donations to reach disaster victims.} The emphasis is always on transmission—something passes through a conduit rather than originating there.

Conduplicatio is a rhetorical device in which a word or phrase from the end of one clause or sentence is repeated at the beginning of the next: {Fear leads to anger. Anger leads to hate.} The repetition creates emphasis and links ideas in a chain. The technique appears in oratory, poetry, and persuasive writing to build momentum or hammer a point home.

A cone is a three-dimensional shape that tapers smoothly from a flat circular base to a point called the apex. This geometric form appears throughout daily life: ice cream cones, traffic cones, pine cones, and the cones in your eyes that detect color. The verb cone means to shape something into a cone or to mark off an area with traffic cones: {Police coned off the accident scene}. In casual use, to cone can mean to eat ice cream from a cone.

Cones are three-dimensional shapes with a circular base tapering to a point: {traffic cones}, {ice cream cones}, {pine cones}. The shape extends to anything cone-like—a volcano's peak, a megaphone, the paper holder for soft serve. In anatomy, cones are photoreceptor cells in the retina responsible for color vision, distinguished from rods that detect light and dark. To {cone off} an area is to mark it with traffic cones.

A confederacy is an alliance or league, especially of states or groups united for a common purpose. The term implies a looser bond than a federation—members retain more independence. {The confederacy of tribes controlled trade routes throughout the region.} Any group joined in common cause, even informally, may be called a confederacy: {a confederacy of dunces}. (Capitalized Confederacy refers to the Confederate States of America.)

A confederate is an ally or accomplice—someone joined with others in a common purpose, often with overtones of conspiracy or secrecy: {The detective suspected the witness was a confederate of the accused}. To confederate is to unite in a league or alliance. As an adjective, confederate describes things joined together or relating to a confederation. (Capitalized Confederate relates to the American Civil War.)

A conference is a formal meeting where people gather to discuss a shared subject—typically a professional, academic, or political one. Business conferences bring together industry members; academic conferences present research papers. Conference also names a grouping of sports teams that compete against each other: {the Western Conference}. To conference is to meet and discuss, often by phone: {Let's conference in the marketing team}.

To confess is to admit something you've concealed—typically a wrongdoing, secret, or uncomfortable truth: {He confessed to the crime}, {I have to confess I never liked her}. In religious contexts, to confess is to acknowledge sins to a priest or to God. A confession may be coerced or voluntary, formal or casual. {I confess} often introduces reluctant admissions: {I confess I haven't read the book}.

Confessing is admitting to something, usually something wrong or hidden. A suspect confesses to a crime; a person confesses sins to a priest; someone confesses feelings they've kept secret: {I have to confess, I never liked him}. The word implies reluctance overcome—you confess what you'd rather not reveal.

A confession is an admission of something concealed—typically wrongdoing, guilt, or an uncomfortable truth. In religious contexts, confession is the formal acknowledgment of sins to a priest: {She went to confession every Saturday}. Police seek confessions from suspects. More casually, confession introduces personal revelations: {I have a confession—I've never seen that movie}. The word implies disclosure of something the speaker might prefer to hide.

A confessional is a small enclosed booth in a Catholic church where a priest hears confessions—typically a wooden structure with a partition separating priest from penitent. As an adjective, confessional describes writing or speech that reveals intimate personal details: {confessional poetry}, {a confessional memoir}. The tone suggests unburdening private thoughts or admitting uncomfortable truths.

Confessions are admissions of wrongdoing, guilt, or secret information. In legal contexts, a confession is a statement acknowledging criminal responsibility: {The police obtained a confession after hours of interrogation}. In religious practice, confession is the ritual acknowledgment of sins to a priest. The word also applies to intimate revelations generally: {late-night confessions about past relationships}. A confession can be a public declaration of faith or belief. As a literary genre, confessions are autobiographical works revealing private thoughts and experiences, after Augustine's *Confessions*.

Confetti is small pieces of colored paper thrown during celebrations—weddings, parades, New Year's Eve. The pieces flutter down over the honorees or revelers. Confetti was originally small candies thrown at Italian carnivals; the paper version is cheaper and less painful. {The newlyweds emerged from the church amid a shower of confetti.}

A confidant is someone you trust with private matters—a person to whom you confide secrets, fears, or sensitive information. The relationship implies intimacy and discretion: {She had been his confidant for years}. The feminine form confidante exists but is increasingly rare; confidant now serves for any gender.

A confidante is a person, especially a woman, to whom secrets are entrusted. The word implies deep trust and intimacy—a confidante knows what others don't: {She had been my confidante since college}. The masculine form is confidant, though confidante now often applies regardless of gender.

Confidants are people to whom one tells secrets or private matters. The word implies deep trust—a confidant receives information you wouldn't share widely. {She had been his confidant for years, knowing things even his wife didn't}. The feminine form confidante exists but confidant now serves for any gender.

To confide is to share something private or secret with someone you trust: {She confided her fears to her sister}, {He confided that he was thinking of leaving}. The word implies both intimacy and discretion—you confide in someone, expecting them to keep your confidence. To confide something to someone's care is to entrust it to them.

Confidence is trust or faith in something—a person, an outcome, or especially oneself. {She spoke with confidence}. A confident person believes in their own abilities; overconfidence tips into arrogance. To confide is to share secrets, so a confidence is something told in trust: {He took me into his confidence}. A confidence game or con exploits misplaced trust. A vote of confidence affirms faith in leadership; a vote of no confidence withdraws it.

Confident describes assurance in oneself or certainty about something. A confident person believes in their own abilities: {She gave a confident presentation}. You can be confident about outcomes: {I'm confident we'll win}. The word suggests composure without arrogance, though overconfidence tips into hubris. A confidant (different spelling) is someone you trust with secrets.

Confidential describes information meant to be kept private or shared only with authorized people. A confidential {document} contains sensitive material. A confidential {source} provides information on condition of anonymity. {This is strictly confidential.} The word implies trust—breaking confidentiality means betraying someone who shared something in confidence.

Confined means restricted to a limited space or area. A confined {space} is enclosed and cramped—basements, tanks, crawlspaces. Someone confined to {bed} or confined to a {wheelchair} cannot move beyond it. Prisoners are confined to cells. The word suggests enclosure that restricts movement: {She felt confined in the small apartment}. In older usage, a woman who was confined was in the late stages of pregnancy or childbirth—restricted to home or bed.

Confinement is the state of being restricted to a place or enclosed space. A prisoner serves time in confinement. Someone ill or injured may be confined to bed: {The doctor ordered strict confinement for two weeks}. In an older sense, confinement referred specifically to the period surrounding childbirth, when women were expected to remain indoors. Solitary confinement isolates a prisoner from all human contact.

Confines are boundaries or limits that restrict movement or activity. The word usually appears in phrases like {within the confines of} or {beyond the confines of}: {within the confines of the law}, {beyond the confines of the classroom}. Physical confines are enclosing walls or borders; abstract confines are constraints on thought or behavior. The stress falls on the first syllable, distinguishing the noun from the verb confine.

Confirm means to establish something as true, valid, or definite. You confirm a suspicion by finding evidence, confirm a reservation by calling ahead, confirm an appointment by showing up. In religious contexts, confirmation is a rite affirming one's faith or membership: {She was confirmed in the Catholic Church at fourteen}. To confirm someone in a position is to formally approve their appointment.

Confirmation is verification that something is true, accurate, or settled: {We're waiting for confirmation of the booking}, {The blood test was confirmation of what we already suspected}. In Christianity, confirmation is a rite admitting a baptized person to full church membership, typically in adolescence. The ritual confirms the faith commitment made at baptism. In government, confirmation is the formal approval of an appointment: {Senate confirmation of the nominee}.

Confirmed means verified or established as true: {The airline confirmed my reservation}. It also describes something firmly settled or habitual: a confirmed {bachelor}, a confirmed {skeptic}. In religious contexts, confirmed refers to someone who has undergone confirmation, the rite admitting them to full church membership. {We're still waiting for confirmed reports from the scene.}

To confiscate is to take possession of something by authority, typically as a penalty or for security reasons. Teachers confiscate phones, customs agents confiscate contraband, governments confiscate assets. The word implies official power—a thief steals, but a principal confiscates: {The guard confiscated my water bottle at the gate}.

Confiscated describes something seized by authority—typically by government, police, or officials acting under legal power. Contraband gets confiscated at borders; a teacher confiscates a student's phone. The past tense of confiscate: {Police confiscated the weapons}. As an adjective: {the confiscated goods were destroyed}.

Conflict as a noun (first syllable stressed) denotes a state of antagonism, incompatibility, or opposition between two things or parties: He is wracked by internal conflict. The conflict arose over an argument about borders. When used as a verb (second syllable stressed), conflict is frequently followed by with and means to show antagonism, opposition, or incompatibility: The report conflicts with statements made by the police last month. The concert date conflicts with the religious holiday and will probably be moved.

Conflicted describes the state of having incompatible feelings, desires, or loyalties pulling in different directions. Someone conflicted about a decision sees merit on both sides: {I'm conflicted about taking the job—the money is great but I'd have to relocate}. The word implies genuine internal struggle rather than simple indecision.

Conflicts are clashes between opposing forces, interests, or ideas. A conflict may be armed warfare, a dispute between people, or an internal struggle: {conflicts in the Middle East}, {a conflict with my landlord}, {the conflict between ambition and family}. To conflict is to be incompatible: {The meetings conflict with each other}. A conflict of interest arises when competing obligations compromise impartiality.

To conform is to act in accordance with prevailing standards, expectations, or rules: {Students are expected to conform to the dress code}. The word often carries a whiff of pressure or loss of individuality—someone who conforms goes along with the group rather than standing apart. Things that conform match or fit a pattern: {The building conforms to safety regulations}. To conform can also mean to make similar or bring into harmony: {She conformed her behavior to local customs}.

A conformist is someone who follows prevailing standards, attitudes, or practices rather than thinking or acting independently. The word often carries a negative connotation, suggesting a lack of originality or courage: {He dismissed them as conformists who never questioned authority}. As an adjective, conformist describes behavior or attitudes that align with social expectations: {conformist tendencies}, {a conformist culture}.

Conformity is the state of acting in accordance with prevailing standards, attitudes, or practices. It often carries a slightly negative connotation, suggesting someone has abandoned their individuality to match what others do or expect: {The suburbs were criticized for their stifling conformity}. In a neutral sense, conformity simply means compliance with rules or specifications: {The building was inspected for conformity with safety codes}. To be in conformity with something is to match or agree with it.

To confront is to face directly, especially something difficult or threatening. You confront a problem by addressing it head-on rather than avoiding it. You confront a person by challenging them or forcing an encounter: {She confronted him about the missing money}. To be confronted with something is to have it placed unavoidably before you: {Detectives confronted him with the evidence}.

A confrontation is a face-to-face meeting between opposing parties, typically hostile or tense in nature. The word emphasizes direct engagement rather than avoidance: {The confrontation between protesters and police turned violent}. It can describe anything from a diplomatic standoff between nations to a personal dispute between neighbors. To have a confrontation with someone is to challenge or oppose them directly, though the encounter need not be physical—verbal confrontations are equally common.

Confrontations are face-to-face encounters marked by conflict or opposition. The word implies direct engagement rather than avoidance: {The meeting devolved into confrontations between union leaders and management}. Confrontations can be verbal or physical, ranging from tense arguments to violent clashes. Someone who seeks out such encounters is confrontational.

To confuse is to make unclear or difficult to understand: {The instructions only confused me further}. You can confuse a person by bewildering them, or confuse a situation by muddling it. To confuse one thing with another is to mistake them for each other: {People always confuse the twins}. Confused describes both the mental state and the thing causing it: {a confused old man}, {a confused explanation}.

Confused describes a state of mental disorientation or uncertainty—unable to think clearly or understand what's happening. A confused {expression} shows bewilderment. You might feel confused by contradictory instructions or wake up confused about where you are. Things can also be confused, meaning mixed up or disordered: {a confused jumble of papers}, {confused memories of the accident}.

Confusing describes something that creates uncertainty or makes understanding difficult. A confusing {explanation} leaves you unsure what was meant. Confusing {instructions} are hard to follow. The word applies to situations, statements, or anything that muddles clarity: {The signs were confusing, so we took the wrong exit}.

Confusion is the state of being unclear or bewildered—unable to think clearly or understand what's happening. A confusing explanation creates confusion in the listener. Confusion can also mean disorder or mixing things up: {There was some confusion about which room to use}. In the confusion of a crowd, things get lost. To {throw into confusion} is to disrupt or disorient.

A conga is a tall, narrow drum of Cuban origin, played with the hands and typically used in Latin music. It also names the dance performed to such drums—a line dance where participants form a chain, hands on the hips of the person ahead, stepping in unison with periodic kicks: {The wedding reception ended with everyone doing the conga around the dance floor}.

Congas are tall, narrow drums of Cuban origin, played with the hands. They typically come in sets of two or three with different pitches and are essential to Latin music, salsa, and jazz. The conga is also a line dance where participants form a chain, hands on the hips of the person ahead, moving to a syncopated beat: {The whole party joined the conga line}.

Congested means overcrowded or blocked, impeding normal flow. Traffic becomes congested when too many vehicles clog the roads. Airways become congested when mucus accumulates during illness: {My sinuses are completely congested}. A congested city center has more people or cars than it can comfortably handle. The noun is congestion.

Congestion is overcrowding that impedes flow. Traffic congestion slows vehicles to a crawl. Nasal congestion blocks breathing passages with swollen tissue and mucus. Network congestion occurs when data traffic exceeds capacity. The word always implies too much of something in too little space: {The congestion downtown was unbearable during rush hour}.

Congrats is an informal shortening of congratulations, used to express pleasure at someone's achievement or good fortune: {Congrats on the promotion!} The clipped form suits casual speech and text messages, while the full word remains standard in formal contexts.

To congratulate is to express pleasure at someone's success, achievement, or good fortune: {Let me congratulate you on your promotion}. The word implies shared happiness—you acknowledge that something good has happened to them. People congratulate newlyweds, new parents, graduates, and winners. To {congratulate yourself} is to feel self-satisfied, sometimes smugly: {He congratulated himself on his foresight}.

Congratulations is an expression of praise or good wishes for someone's achievement, success, or happy occasion: {Congratulations on your promotion!} The word acknowledges that something worth celebrating has happened. It works equally for major milestones like graduations and weddings and for smaller wins: {Congratulations, you finally beat that level}.

A congregation is a group of people gathered together, especially for religious worship. The word emphasizes collective assembly—a congregation fills a church, listens to a sermon, sings hymns together. {The congregation rose for the blessing.} Beyond religion, congregation can describe any gathering: {a congregation of protesters}, {a congregation of birds at the feeder}.

A congressman is a member of a congress, especially the United States Congress. The term applies to members of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, though in practice it usually refers to representatives: {My congressman voted against the bill}. The gender-neutral congressperson exists but sees limited use; congresswoman is the standard feminine form.

To conjure is to summon or produce as if by magic: {The magician conjured a rabbit from his hat}. The word extends to any impressive act of bringing forth: {She conjured a meal from nearly empty cupboards}. To {conjure up} is to evoke or call to mind: {The smell conjured up memories of childhood}. A name {to conjure with} belongs to someone powerful or influential.

Conjured is the past tense of conjure, which means to summon or produce as if by magic: {The wizard conjured a fireball}. More commonly, conjure means to evoke or call to mind: {The smell conjured memories of childhood summers}. To {conjure up} an image or feeling is to create it vividly in the imagination. {She conjured a solution out of nothing} suggests resourceful creation from limited materials.

A conjurer performs magic—either the stage variety involving sleight of hand and illusion, or the supernatural kind involving summoning spirits or casting spells. The word carries a slightly old-fashioned flavor, evoking traveling performers and medieval sorcerers alike: {The conjurer produced a rabbit from his hat}. Also spelled conjuror.

Conjuring is the performance of magic tricks—sleight of hand, illusions, making things appear or disappear. A conjurer pulls rabbits from hats and coins from behind ears. The word extends to any act of summoning or producing as if by magic: {conjuring spirits}, {conjuring memories of childhood}. To conjure up is to evoke or bring vividly to mind: {The smell conjured up my grandmother's kitchen}.

A conman is a person who swindles others through deception, gaining their trust before exploiting it for money or advantage. The term is short for confidence man—one who wins confidence to abuse it: {The conman posed as a financial advisor and bilked retirees of their savings}. Con artist is a near-synonym.

Connect means to join or link things together. Wires connect to terminals, roads connect cities, flights connect through hubs. People connect when they form relationships or find common ground: {We really connected at the conference}. To connect the dots is to perceive relationships between separate facts. A connecting flight gets you from one leg of a journey to another.

Connected describes things that are joined or linked. Physical connections attach objects: {connected rooms}, {connected cables}. Abstract connections link ideas, people, or events: {The two crimes are connected}. A well-connected person has influential relationships or contacts. To feel connected is to experience belonging or emotional closeness: {I've never felt so connected to another person}. In technology, connected means online or networked: {Make sure you're connected to Wi-Fi}.

Connection is a link or relationship between things. Physical connections join objects: {The connection between the pipe and the faucet was leaking}. Abstract connections link ideas, people, or events: {I see no connection between the two crimes}. A connection can be a person who provides access or advantage: {She has connections in the industry}. In travel, a connection is a transfer between vehicles: {We missed our connection in Chicago}. To {make a connection} with someone is to establish rapport or understanding.

Connections are relationships or links between people, things, or ideas. A connection may be physical: {The plumber checked the pipe connections}. Social connections are people you know who might help you: {She got the job through connections}. Mental connections link ideas: {I'm not seeing the connection between those two points}. A travel connection is a transfer between routes: {We missed our connection in Chicago}.

Conned is the past tense of con, meaning to deceive or swindle someone through a confidence trick—a scheme that exploits trust: {He conned her out of her life savings}, {I got conned into buying a worthless timeshare}. The victim believes they're dealing with someone trustworthy, which is what makes the deception work.

Conniving describes someone who schemes or plots, typically through dishonest means. A conniving person manipulates situations for personal advantage, often by secretly cooperating with others in wrongdoing: {a conniving business partner}, {She's conniving to get the inheritance}. The word carries strong negative connotations of sneakiness and moral untrustworthiness.

A connoisseur is someone with expert knowledge and refined taste in a particular field, especially the arts, food, or wine. The word implies not just expertise but discriminating judgment—the ability to distinguish quality from mediocrity: {a connoisseur of fine whiskey}, {a connoisseur of Renaissance painting}. It can be used seriously or with light irony: {He fancies himself a connoisseur of cheap beer}.

To conquer is to defeat and take control of, typically through military force: {Alexander conquered most of the known world}. The word extends to overcoming obstacles or fears: {She conquered her addiction}, {He finally conquered his fear of heights}. A conquering personality or smile wins people over through charm or force of will.

Conquered is the past tense of conquer, meaning to defeat and take control of by force. Armies conquer territories; nations conquer other nations: {The Romans conquered Gaul}. Extended uses describe overcoming challenges or obstacles: {She conquered her fear of heights}. To be conquered is to be subdued or won over: {He was conquered by her charm}.

Conquering is the act of defeating and taking control—of enemies, territories, or challenges. A conquering army seizes land; a conquering hero returns victorious. The word extends to overcoming obstacles: {conquering your fears}, {conquering a mountain}. Someone conquering hearts wins them over through charm or appeal.

A conqueror is someone who defeats and takes control of people, territory, or obstacles. The word carries overtones of military victory and domination: {William the Conqueror invaded England in 1066}. Extended uses describe anyone who overcomes challenges or achieves mastery: {a conqueror of fears}, {conquerors of Everest}.

Conquerors are those who defeat and take control through force—of territories, peoples, or rivals. The word carries historical weight: {Spanish conquerors brought disease to the New World}. It extends to anyone who overcomes great obstacles: {conquerors of Everest}, {conquerors of their own fears}. William the Conqueror established the template.

Conquest is the act of taking control of a place or people through military force, or the territory so acquired. The Norman Conquest of England in 1066 is the most famous example in English-speaking history. Beyond warfare, conquest extends to any decisive victory or successful effort to overcome: {the conquest of disease}, {the conquest of space}. In romantic contexts, a conquest is someone whose affections have been won, often implying pursuit and triumph rather than mutual attraction.

Conquests are acts of conquering—taking control of territory, people, or resources through force or sustained effort. Military conquests expand empires; romantic conquests are people seduced or won over: {He boasted of his conquests}. The word can describe any hard-won achievement: {her conquest of the literary establishment}. See also conquest.

A conquistador is a Spanish or Portuguese conqueror, specifically the soldiers and explorers who invaded and colonized the Americas in the sixteenth century. Cortés, Pizarro, and their contemporaries subjugated the Aztec and Inca empires, often with brutal efficiency. The term now applies figuratively to anyone who conquers aggressively: {corporate conquistadors expanding into new markets}.

Conquistadors were the Spanish soldiers and explorers who conquered much of the Americas in the 16th century, toppling the Aztec and Inca empires and claiming vast territories for Spain. The word is Spanish for "conquerors." Figuratively, conquistador suggests aggressive conquest or domination: {Silicon Valley conquistadors reshaping entire industries}.

Cons are disadvantages or arguments against something, typically weighed against pros: {Let's consider the pros and cons before deciding}. A con is also a swindle or confidence trick, and to con someone is to deceive them for gain: {He conned her out of her savings}. A con is also informal for a convict: {an ex-con}. In programming, cons is a function that constructs data structures.

Conscience is the inner sense of right and wrong that guides behavior and produces guilt when violated. It functions as a moral compass: {My conscience wouldn't let me keep the money}. A {guilty conscience} troubles someone who has done wrong. To do something {in good conscience} is to act without moral conflict. {Conscience} can also mean conscientiousness: {a conscience about returning calls}.

Conscious means awake and aware—able to perceive and respond to surroundings. An unconscious person lacks this awareness; a conscious one has it. The word extends to deliberate attention: a {conscious effort}, a {conscious decision}. To be {conscious of} something is to notice or consider it: {She was conscious of being watched}. {Self-conscious} describes heightened awareness of oneself, often uncomfortably so.

Consciousness is the state of being aware—of yourself, your surroundings, your thoughts. At its most basic, it distinguishes waking from sleep or coma: {The patient regained consciousness after surgery}. More abstractly, consciousness is subjective experience itself—what philosophers call the "hard problem" of explaining why physical processes produce inner awareness at all. A consciousness can also mean a particular mindset or awareness: {class consciousness}, {environmental consciousness}. To {raise consciousness} is to increase awareness of social or political issues.

Conscription is compulsory military service—the government's power to require citizens to serve in the armed forces. Countries institute conscription during wartime or maintain it permanently. The term often carries negative connotations that voluntary enlistment doesn't: {He fled to Canada to avoid conscription}. Also called the draft.

Conscripts are people compelled by law to serve in the military, as opposed to volunteers. The term carries connotations of unwillingness or inexperience: {an army of poorly trained conscripts}. To conscript is to draft someone into service. The word extends beyond military contexts to forced participation generally: {conscripted into helping with the move}.

Consensus means general agreement or agreement among all. When people reach a consensus, they come to agree about something, even if the agreement is a small part of a larger issue: After much debate, a consensus emerged to allocate funds for the initial phase of the project. When there is no consensus, members of a group cannot come to even a modicum of agreement. Since consensus is about opinion, it is redundant to say consensus of opinion, and since consensus is by definition general, it is redundant to say general consensus. Despite that, both phrases are very common.

When you consent to something, you agree to do it: More than 500 volunteers consented to participate in the study. You can give your consent about an action that doesn’t involve you directly: Students are required to get their parents’ consent in writing before using the facilities. The participle consenting is used to talk about activities, usually involving two people, in which both of them consent to what they are doing—that is, neither is acting by compulsion: consenting partners.

A consequence is what follows from an action or condition—the result, outcome, or effect. {The scandal had consequences for his career.} To face the consequences is to accept responsibility for outcomes, usually negative ones. A person of consequence has importance or distinction; something of no consequence doesn't matter. In consequence means as a result.

Consequences are the results or effects that follow from an action, condition, or decision. The word often carries a negative weight—{actions have consequences} typically warns of unpleasant outcomes rather than rewards. {Face the consequences} means accepting responsibility for what follows. Something {of consequence} matters; something {of no consequence} doesn't. The phrase {truth or consequences} names a game where refusing to answer honestly results in a penalty.

Conservation is the act of preserving, protecting, or carefully managing something to prevent its loss, waste, or destruction. The term applies most often to natural resources and wildlife—{conservation efforts helped the bald eagle recover}—but extends to energy, water, and cultural heritage like historic buildings or artworks. In physics, conservation refers to principles stating that certain quantities (energy, momentum, mass) remain constant in a closed system. A conservation area is land set aside for environmental protection. The word emphasizes thoughtful stewardship rather than mere non-use.

Conservatism is a political philosophy favoring tradition, established institutions, and gradual rather than radical change. Conservatives typically emphasize individual liberty, limited government, free markets, and traditional social values. The word also describes any disposition toward preserving existing conditions: {His conservatism about investing meant he avoided risky stocks}. What counts as conservative shifts with time and place—today's mainstream was often yesterday's radical reform.

Conservative describes a disposition toward preserving existing conditions and institutions, or being cautious about change. In politics, conservatives generally favor traditional values, limited government, and free markets. A conservative {estimate} is deliberately low to avoid overstatement. Conservative {dress} is modest and conventional. A conservative {approach} avoids unnecessary risk. {She's conservative with her money.} (Capitalized Conservative refers to specific political parties.)

Conservatives are people who favor traditional values and institutions, resist rapid change, and prefer gradual reform over sweeping transformation. In politics, conservatives typically support limited government, free markets, and established social norms: {Conservatives opposed the new spending bill}. The term is relative—what counts as conservative shifts across eras and cultures. American conservatives often emphasize individual liberty and religious values; British Conservatives (capitalized) belong to the specific political party.

A conservatory is a glass-enclosed room attached to a house, used for growing plants or as a sunlit living space. The term also refers to a school devoted to training in music or other performing arts: {She studied violin at the conservatory}. The botanical and musical meanings both suggest cultivation—of plants or of talent.

Conserve means to protect from loss, waste, or decay. You conserve energy by using less of it, conserve water during a drought, or conserve natural resources for future generations. Conservation efforts protect endangered species and wild habitats. As a noun, conserve is a fruit preserve, typically with whole or large pieces of fruit: {a jar of strawberry conserve}.

When you consider an abstract issue or option, you think about it or agree to think about it. When you consider a person for something, you regard them as a candidate: Only applicants with industry experience were considered for the job. Consider can also convey your opinion about someone or something: I considered the case closed after I received the check. We consider him to be the most valuable member of this community.

Considerate is an adjective that characterizes someone who is thoughtful in a way that shows concern for others. Though the word is always a compliment, it may be used sarcastically when someone’s behavior is inconsiderate, that is, they fail to show concern for others: It was very considerate of you to park in front of the driveway! Considerate is used predicatively (she is considerate) but also attributively with some nouns: considerate, parents, considerate behavior.

Consideration is careful thought before deciding or acting: {After much consideration, she accepted the job}. It also means regard for others' feelings or circumstances—thoughtfulness: {Show some consideration for your neighbors}. In law, consideration is something of value exchanged between parties to make a contract binding. To {take into consideration} is to factor something in. {Under consideration} means being thought about but not yet decided.

Considered describes something arrived at through careful thought: a {considered opinion}, a {considered response}. It implies deliberation rather than impulse—you've weighed the matter before speaking or acting. {After much debate, she gave her considered judgment}. To be {well-considered} is to be thoughtfully planned; {ill-considered} suggests the opposite.

Consistency is the quality of staying the same or holding together. A substance has consistency—thick, thin, smooth, lumpy: {Beat the batter to a smooth consistency}. Behavior has consistency when it doesn't vary: {Her consistency in meeting deadlines made her invaluable}. Arguments have consistency when their parts don't contradict each other. The word implies reliability, though critics might call the same quality rigidity.

Consistent means staying the same over time or across instances. A consistent performer delivers reliable results; consistent behavior follows the same pattern. Something consistent with something else aligns or agrees with it: {The evidence is consistent with her account}. Inconsistency is the failure to maintain this steadiness—changing standards, contradicting oneself, or producing uneven results.

Consociationalism is a political arrangement for governing deeply divided societies—those split along ethnic, religious, or linguistic lines. Power is shared among group leaders through coalition governments, mutual vetoes, and proportional representation, rather than simple majority rule. Belgium and Lebanon have consociational systems. The approach prioritizes stability over efficiency, critics say, by entrenching divisions it claims to manage.

Consolation is comfort received after a loss or disappointment. A {consolation prize} goes to a loser—something, but not what they wanted. The word often carries a sense of inadequacy: {It was small consolation that others had failed too}. To console someone is to offer such comfort, though the comfort may fall short of actually helping.

Console unites several meanings around the idea of comfort and support. To console someone is to offer comfort during distress or grief: {Nothing could console her after the loss}. A console is a cabinet or panel housing controls—for a stereo system, a car's dashboard, or a video game system. In computing and gaming, console refers both to the physical hardware and to a text-based interface for entering commands. The word also names a decorative bracket or a narrow table designed to stand against a wall.

Consoles is the verb form of console, meaning to comfort someone in distress or grief: {She consoles him after the loss}. As a plural noun, consoles are control panels or cabinets housing electronic equipment—particularly video game systems: {The kids were glued to their gaming consoles}. A console table is a narrow decorative table against a wall.

Conspiracies is the plural of conspiracy—a secret plan by multiple people to do something harmful or illegal, or the act of planning together in secret. The word often appears in {conspiracy theories}, explanations attributing events to hidden plots rather than official accounts: {She doesn't believe the conspiracies about the moon landing}. A conspiracy can also be a legal charge: {conspiracy to commit fraud}.

A conspiracy is a secret plan by two or more people to do something harmful or illegal: {a conspiracy to overthrow the government}, {conspiracy to commit fraud}. The word also describes the group doing the planning or the act of planning itself. A {conspiracy theory} alleges that powerful hidden forces orchestrate events—often without solid evidence: {conspiracy theories about the moon landing}. To {conspire} is to participate in such plotting, or more loosely, for circumstances to combine toward some end: {Everything conspired against us}.

A conspirator is someone involved in a conspiracy—a secret plan with others to do something harmful or illegal. The word emphasizes active participation in plotting: {The conspirators met in secret to plan the assassination}. Unlike mere accomplices, conspirators are in from the beginning, helping devise the scheme rather than just carrying it out.

Conspirators are people who secretly plan together to do something harmful or illegal. The word carries connotations of treachery and hidden schemes—political conspirators plot coups, criminal conspirators plan heists. {The conspirators met in secret to finalize their plan.} Unlike mere accomplices, conspirators implies active participation in the plotting itself.

To conspire is to plan something secretly with others, usually something harmful or illegal: {They conspired to overthrow the government}. The word carries connotations of scheming and hidden motives. Events or circumstances can also conspire when they seem to combine against someone: {Everything conspired to ruin the picnic}. A conspiracy is the noun form.

Conspired is the past tense of conspire, meaning to plan secretly with others toward some end, often unlawful or harmful: {They conspired to overthrow the government}. The word carries undertones of shadowy coordination. Figuratively, circumstances can conspire when multiple factors align to produce an outcome: {Everything conspired against us that day}.

Conspiring is plotting secretly with others, typically to do something harmful or illegal: {They were conspiring to overthrow the government}. The word carries implications of secrecy and shared intent. More loosely, circumstances or events can conspire against someone when multiple factors combine unfavorably: {Everything seemed to be conspiring against us that day}.

Constant describes something that doesn't change or stop. A constant {temperature} stays the same. Constant {interruptions} keep coming. In science, a constant is a value that remains fixed—the speed of light is a physical constant. The word can suggest reliability {(a constant companion)} or relentlessness {(constant pain)}. Constantly means continuously or repeatedly.

A constellation is a group of stars that form a recognizable pattern in the night sky, typically named after mythological figures, animals, or objects. Ancient cultures identified these patterns to navigate and mark seasons, and astronomers still use 88 officially recognized constellations to map the celestial sphere. The word extends figuratively to any cluster of related things, especially notable people or qualities: {a constellation of Hollywood talent gathered for the premiere}.

Constellations are groups of stars that form recognizable patterns in the night sky, named after mythological figures, animals, or objects: {Orion}, {the Big Dipper}, {Scorpius}. Astronomers have formally designated 88 constellations that divide the celestial sphere into regions. Figuratively, a constellation is any cluster of related things: {a constellation of symptoms}, {a constellation of talent}.

Constipated describes difficulty emptying the bowels—infrequent or painful defecation. The word extends to anything blocked or sluggish: {constipated prose} is stilted and unflowing, a {constipated bureaucracy} moves nothing through. Someone emotionally constipated has trouble expressing feelings: {He's too constipated to say he loves her}.

Constipation is difficulty emptying the bowels, typically from hard, dry stool. The condition ranges from occasional discomfort to chronic problems requiring medical attention. Figuratively, constipation describes any state of being blocked or stuck: {emotional constipation}, {creative constipation}. The adjective constipated works similarly: {The bureaucracy was constipated with paperwork}.

Constitution refers to the fundamental makeup of something—its essential character and composition. A person's constitution is their physical or mental nature: {She has a strong constitution}, {His nervous constitution couldn't handle the stress}. The word also means the act of establishing or forming something: {the constitution of a new committee}. More commonly, it refers to the basic principles and laws governing an organization or nation, typically written in a founding document: {The club's constitution requires annual elections}. (Capitalized Constitution refers to a specific national founding document, especially the U.S. Constitution.)

Constitutional describes what relates to or is established by a constitution—the fundamental principles governing a nation or organization: {constitutional rights}, {constitutional law}, {a constitutional amendment}. A constitutional monarchy limits royal power through founding documents. Something constitutional to a person belongs to their physical or mental makeup: {a constitutional weakness}. As a noun, a constitutional is an old-fashioned word for a health-promoting walk: {taking one's morning constitutional}.

Constitutions are the fundamental principles and laws that establish a government's structure and powers. Most nations have a written constitution as their supreme legal document: {The U.S. Constitution established three branches of government}. Constitution also means a person's physical or mental makeup: {She has a strong constitution}, {His delicate constitution couldn't handle the stress}. The plural often refers to the founding documents of organizations or the varying health and temperaments of different individuals.

A constraint is a limitation or restriction on what is possible. Physical constraints like gravity or material strength determine what can be built. Budget constraints limit what can be purchased. Time constraints restrict how much can be accomplished. In technical contexts, constraints are conditions that a solution must satisfy: {The design had to work within tight constraints}. To act {under constraint} is to act without free choice, compelled by circumstances or force.

Constraints are limitations or restrictions that bound what's possible. Physical constraints govern what materials can do; budget constraints limit spending; time constraints restrict how long you have. The word implies external forces rather than personal choices: {We're working under tight constraints}. In technical fields, constraints are conditions a solution must satisfy.

To construct is to build or put together from parts: {construct a building}, {construct an argument}. The noun construct (stress on first syllable) refers to something built, especially an abstract idea or theoretical framework: {Gender is a social construct}. In grammar, a construct is a phrase or clause arrangement. The word emphasizes deliberate assembly rather than organic development.

As the verbal noun from construct, construction has numerous meanings related to the action of putting something together or forming a whole. Construction is commonly associated with the industry whose job is to build houses, buildings, and the infrastructure that supports them. In a more abstract way, construction can represent something put together in the mind, or with words. A grammatical construction is a group of words that derives its meaning partly from the order in which words are put together.

Constructive describes actions, attitudes, or criticism that aim to improve or build something rather than tear it down. Constructive {feedback} helps someone get better; constructive {dialogue} moves toward resolution. The word implies usefulness and positive intent, even when addressing problems. In legal contexts, constructive has a technical sense meaning "implied by law rather than explicit": constructive {dismissal} occurs when an employer makes conditions intolerable enough that an employee feels forced to quit.

A consulate is the office or residence of a consul—a government official stationed in a foreign city to assist citizens and promote commercial interests. Unlike an embassy, which handles diplomatic relations at the national level, consulates serve regional functions: issuing visas, helping stranded travelers, registering births abroad. {The nearest consulate is in Chicago.} Major cities often host consulates from dozens of countries.

To consult is to seek information or advice from a source—a person, book, or reference: {I consulted a lawyer before signing}. Professionals who consult offer expert guidance, often as outside advisors rather than employees: {She consults for several tech firms}. A consultation is such an exchange. To consult with someone suggests a more mutual discussion: {The president consulted with his cabinet}.

A consultant is someone hired to provide expert advice in a particular field. Companies bring in consultants for specialized knowledge they lack internally—management consultants, IT consultants, legal consultants. The term can suggest expensive outside help: {They paid consultants millions to tell them what employees already knew}. In some contexts, consultant is a euphemism for someone between jobs or working freelance.

Consultants are people hired to give expert advice in a particular field. Companies bring in consultants for specialized knowledge they lack internally: {management consultants}, {IT consultants}, {political consultants}. The term can carry a whiff of skepticism—consultants are sometimes seen as expensive outsiders who state the obvious or avoid accountability for their recommendations. {We hired a consultant to streamline operations.}

Consultation is the act of seeking advice or information from someone with expertise: {a consultation with a lawyer}, {a medical consultation}. It also means a meeting where parties discuss options before making decisions: {The policy was developed in consultation with stakeholders}. The word implies deliberation rather than action—you consult, then decide.

Consume means to use up or take in completely. You consume food and drink by eating and drinking them. A fire consumes what it burns. Time, energy, and resources are consumed by activities that deplete them: {The project consumed most of our budget}. To be consumed by an emotion is to be overwhelmed by it: {consumed with jealousy}. In economics, consumers are those who purchase and use goods and services.

Consumed is the past tense of consume, meaning to use up, eat, drink, or destroy completely. Fire consumes fuel; people consume food and beverages; industries consume resources. The word extends powerfully into emotional territory: to be consumed by grief, rage, or jealousy suggests being overwhelmed to the point where the feeling dominates everything else. {She was consumed with worry about the test results.} In economics, consumed goods are those purchased and used by end consumers rather than businesses.

A consumer is someone who buys or uses goods and services. The term emphasizes the end user rather than the producer or seller, making it central to economics and marketing: {Consumer spending drives the economy}. Consumer protection laws shield buyers from fraud and unsafe products. In ecology, consumers are organisms that obtain energy by eating other organisms rather than producing their own food through photosynthesis. The word often appears in compounds like {consumer goods}, {consumer confidence}, and {consumer debt}.

Consumerism is the preoccupation with acquiring goods and services, or the belief that personal happiness comes through consumption. The term often carries critical weight, implying excessive materialism: {Holiday consumerism starts earlier every year}. In a neutral sense, consumerism can mean advocacy for consumer rights and protections against deceptive business practices.

Consumers are people who buy and use goods or services. The term frames people through their economic activity—what they purchase rather than what they produce or create. {Consumer confidence drives the economy}. In ecology, consumers are organisms that eat other organisms rather than producing their own food. {Consumer protection laws} shield buyers from unfair practices.

Consuming describes something that dominates attention or energy so completely that little remains for anything else. A consuming {passion} or consuming {interest} absorbs a person fully. Consuming {flames} devour everything in their path. The word emphasizes totality—whatever consumes leaves nothing untouched: {Her consuming ambition left no room for relationships}.

Consumption is the act of consuming—using up resources, eating or drinking, or purchasing goods. In economics, consumption drives demand: {Consumer spending accounts for most of the economy}. The word once commonly referred to tuberculosis, from how the disease seemed to consume the body: {She died of consumption at twenty-three}. This medical sense is now archaic.

When two things touch or make a connection, they contact. Eye contact happens when people’s eyes meet. Physical contact happens when their bodies touch. If you’re in contact with someone, you are able to communicate with them. All such people collectively can be called your contacts. When you contact someone, you establish a channel of communication with them. Contacts may also be short for contact lenses, which rest in direct contact with your eyeballs.

Contacts are people you know, especially those useful for business or information: {She has contacts in the industry}. The word also refers to contact lenses—thin corrective discs worn directly on the eye: {I need to put my contacts in}. As a verb, to contact someone is to get in touch with them: {Contact me if you have questions}.

Contagion is the transmission of disease through direct or indirect contact. By extension, it describes anything that spreads from person to person like an infection—fear, panic, laughter, or financial instability: {The contagion of enthusiasm swept through the crowd}. In epidemiology, contagion specifically means spread requiring physical contact, distinguished from airborne transmission.

Contagious describes diseases that spread from person to person through direct or close contact: {Measles is highly contagious}. The word extends to anything that spreads readily from one person to another—laughter, enthusiasm, fear, yawning: {Her excitement was contagious}. Contagious emphasizes transmission between individuals, while infectious (often used interchangeably) technically refers to diseases caused by pathogens.

To contain is to hold something within limits or boundaries. A jar contains pickles; a building contains offices; a report contains findings. The word extends to restraint: {She could barely contain her excitement}. To contain a threat, disease, or fire is to prevent it from spreading. In math, a set contains its elements.

A container is anything that holds something else—a box, jar, bottle, can, bag, or similar receptacle: {Store leftovers in airtight containers}. In shipping, a container is a large standardized metal box for transporting goods by truck, train, or ship. In computing, a container is a lightweight package that bundles software with everything needed to run it.

Containment is the act of keeping something within limits—preventing it from spreading or escaping. The word applies to physical substances {containment of the oil spill}, diseases {containment measures slowed transmission}, and abstract threats. In Cold War policy, containment was the U.S. strategy of preventing the spread of Soviet communism without direct military confrontation. Nuclear containment structures house reactors to prevent radiation leaks.

To contaminate something is to make it impure or unsuitable by introducing a harmful or unwanted substance. Water supplies can be contaminated by industrial runoff, food by bacteria, and crime scenes by careless handling of evidence. The word extends beyond physical pollution to abstract corruption: {His judgment was contaminated by personal bias}. Contaminated materials require decontamination before they're safe to use or consume again.

Contaminated describes something made impure or unsafe by the introduction of unwanted substances. Water becomes contaminated when pollutants enter it; food becomes contaminated with bacteria. The word extends beyond physical impurity: {contaminated evidence} has been compromised by mishandling, and {contaminated data} contains errors that undermine its reliability. The past participle of contaminate, it functions as both verb form and adjective.

Contamination is the presence of something unwanted that makes a substance impure or unsafe. Water contamination renders it undrinkable; radioactive contamination makes an area uninhabitable. The term extends beyond physical substances: {cross-contamination of evidence} compromises a crime scene, and ideas can suffer contamination from bias. In scientific contexts, contamination invalidates experiments by introducing foreign variables.

To contemplate is to look at or think about something carefully and at length. You might contemplate a painting, contemplate your options, or contemplate the meaning of life. The word suggests unhurried, serious reflection: {She sat contemplating the view}. To contemplate doing something is to consider it as a possibility: {He's contemplating a move to Portland}.

Contemplation is deep, focused thought—the act of considering something carefully and at length. It suggests a calmer, more reflective mode than mere thinking: {She sat in quiet contemplation of the mountains}. The word often carries spiritual connotations, describing meditative attention to the divine or transcendent. In religious traditions, contemplation is distinguished from prayer or study as a more passive receptivity to insight.

Contemporary is primarily used as an adjective to characterize one thing that exists at the same time as another: Analysis determined that the two manuscripts were contemporary with each other. A secondary meaning is belonging to the present time: Contemporary art leaves me cold. As a noun, contemporary designates a person who lives at the same time as another: At six feet, the skeleton found in the cave would have been much taller than his contemporaries.

Contempt is a negative feeling or attitude towards something that is considered worthless, low, and offensive. It may be combined with feelings of hatred, ridicule, or anger. Various prepositions can follow contempt but the most common is for: The locals consider themselves descendants of saints and often show contempt for outsiders. Contempt has a special meaning in law: Contempt of court is willful disobedience or open disrespect for the rules of a court.

A contender is someone competing for something—a title, prize, or position. The word implies genuine possibility of winning: a contender for the {championship}, a contender for the {nomination}. Someone who isn't a serious contender is {not in contention}. A {pretender to the throne} claims it; a contender actually has a shot.

Contenders is the plural of contender—those competing for a position, title, or prize. The word implies serious candidacy: not everyone in a race is a contender, only those with a realistic chance of winning. {The two leading contenders for the nomination squared off in tonight's debate.} A {pretender to the throne} claims legitimacy; a contender actually fights for it.

Stress on the first syllable of content means it’s a noun; on the second syllable, it’s an adjective or verb, or possibly a noun with different meaning. These days, content (noun, first syllable stress) is the most frequently encountered form because it designates what we see and listen to on web pages. A distant second in terms of frequency is the adjective content (second syllable stress), which characterizes a feeling of comfort and satisfaction. The verb content is related to this meaning: I’m contented with my marriage and my job.

Contention is disagreement or dispute: {The main point of contention was who would pay}. It also means a position argued for: {Her contention is that the policy causes more harm than good}. In competition, to be {in contention} is to have a realistic chance of winning. {Out of contention} means eliminated from consideration.

Contentment is a state of peaceful satisfaction with one's circumstances. Unlike happiness, which may spike with joy, contentment suggests a quieter, more settled feeling—not wanting more than you have: {She found contentment in her small garden and simple routines}. The adjective content describes someone in this state: {I'm content to stay home tonight}.

Contents refers to what is inside something—the contents of a box, a stomach, a document. For written works, contents specifically means the list of chapters or sections at the front of a book: {Check the table of contents}. The word always appears plural in these senses, though the singular content refers to substance or meaning: {the content of his speech}.

A contest is a competition in which participants vie against each other to win a prize or determine superiority: {a beauty contest}, {a writing contest}. The word works as both noun and verb, with stress shifting accordingly—CONtest for the noun, conTEST for the verb. To contest something is to challenge or dispute it: {She plans to contest the will}. A contested election is one where the outcome is disputed or closely fought. Something uncontested faces no opposition or challenge.

A contestant is someone who competes in a contest—a game show, a beauty pageant, an athletic competition. The word emphasizes participation rather than skill level; both frontrunners and longshots are contestants. {Three contestants remain in the final round.} {She was a contestant on Jeopardy.}

Contested describes something disputed or challenged. A contested election has results that one side refuses to accept. A contested divorce involves disagreement over terms. In sports, a contested shot faces defensive pressure. The word implies active opposition rather than mere doubt: {The will was contested by the disinherited nephew}. Uncontested is the opposite.

Contests are competitions where participants vie for a prize, title, or recognition: {a beauty contest}, {a writing contest}. The word also covers disputes or challenges: {a contest over the will}, {no contest} in legal pleas. To contest something is to compete for it or to challenge its validity: {She contested the election results}. {The divorce was uncontested.}

Context is a noun whose parts reveal its meaning: con- is “together” and text refers to words. Context is the neighboring text of a word or expression that can shed light on its meaning. A natural extension of this sense of context is the conditions in which something exists, occurs, or is considered: The context of their very formal relationship meant that feelings were rarely expressed openly. The author introduces the characters without any historical context, so their actions seem strange.

A continent is one of the large continuous landmasses that make up most of Earth's dry land—traditionally counted as seven: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America. The boundaries between continents are somewhat arbitrary, following convention rather than strict geological criteria. As an adjective, continent means exercising self-restraint, particularly regarding bodily functions or sexual urges: {The patient was continent and ambulatory}. The opposite, incontinent, is more commonly encountered.
