Continents are the large landmasses of Earth—Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America. The count varies by convention; some combine Europe and Asia into Eurasia, others count the Americas as one. Continental describes things pertaining to a continent: {continental drift}, {continental breakfast}. Continent as an adjective, a different word, means exercising self-restraint, especially regarding bodily functions or sexual urges.

Continue means to keep doing something without stopping, or to resume after an interruption: {The rain continued through the night}, {We'll continue this discussion tomorrow}. Something that continues extends in space or time: {The path continues beyond the ridge}. In legal contexts, to continue a case is to postpone it to a later date.

Continuity is unbroken connection or consistency over time. A story has continuity when its details remain consistent across scenes; a business maintains continuity when operations persist despite changes in leadership. In film and television, continuity refers to consistency in props, costumes, and settings between shots: {The continuity error showed her glass full in one frame, empty in the next}. More abstractly, continuity suggests smooth persistence rather than abrupt change: {There's remarkable continuity between her early and late work}.

Continuous describes something that goes on without interruption or breaks. A continuous {line} has no gaps. Continuous {rain} falls steadily. Continuous {improvement} happens gradually over time. The word emphasizes unbroken duration or connection, distinguishing it from continual, which suggests repeated occurrence with pauses between.

Contortion is the act of twisting or bending something, especially the body, into an unusual or unnatural shape. The word often describes the extreme flexibility of circus performers: {The contortionist's contortions amazed the audience}. Faces contort in pain or disgust. Arguments can be contorted—twisted to mean something they don't: {His contortions of logic convinced no one}.

A contortionist is a performer who twists their body into extreme positions—bending backward until their head touches their feet, folding into impossibly small spaces. The word extends to anyone who achieves difficult flexibility, literal or figurative: {The administration's contortionist explanations grew less convincing by the day}.

Contortions are twisting movements that distort the body or face into unnatural positions. A circus contortionist performs extreme bends and stretches. The word extends to strained efforts: {the verbal contortions of a politician avoiding a direct answer}, {mental contortions to justify a bad decision}. The singular contortion works the same way but emphasizes a single instance.

Contour is the outline or shape of something, especially as defined by its edges or curves: {the contour of the coastline}, {the contours of her face}. Contour lines on a map connect points of equal elevation, revealing terrain. As a verb, to contour is to shape something to follow curves: {seats contoured to the body}. Contour farming follows the natural slopes of land to prevent erosion.

Contours are the lines that define a shape's outline or the curves of a surface. The word often describes terrain: {the contours of the hillside}, {a contour map showing elevation}. It extends to bodies: {the contours of her face}. Figuratively, contours are the general shape or character of something: {the contours of the argument}, {the contours of foreign policy}. To contour is to shape along natural lines, as in contouring makeup to emphasize facial structure.

Contraband is goods that are illegal to import, export, or possess—smuggled items that cross borders or prison walls in violation of law. The word often appears in legal and military contexts: {The border agents seized contraband worth millions}. Contraband can also function as an adjective: {contraband weapons}, {contraband cigarettes}. Anything forbidden by regulation might be called contraband, even informally: {The camp counselor confiscated contraband candy from the cabin}.

Contraceptives are devices, drugs, or methods used to prevent pregnancy. The category includes condoms, intrauterine devices, birth control pills, and spermicides, among others. {She keeps her contraceptives in the bathroom cabinet.} The adjective contraceptive describes anything serving this purpose: {contraceptive methods}, {contraceptive effectiveness}.

Contract follows the sound pattern of many Latinate words in distinguishing the noun (stress on first syllable) from the verb (stress on second syllable) for some meanings. As a noun, contract represents a formal, enforceable, binding agreement between parties. Verb uses of contract related to this meaning have the same pronunciation: We contracted with a roofer for the job. When used as a verb with any other meaning, the stress is on the second syllable: contract tuberculosis (to shrink or incur), contracting “it is” gives us “it’s” (to shorten).

A contraction is a shortening—of words, muscles, or time intervals. In grammar, contractions combine words by omitting letters: {can't}, {won't}, {I'm}. Muscles contract when they tighten or shorten. The contractions of childbirth are periodic tightenings of the uterus. An economic contraction is a period of decline. All senses share the idea of drawing inward or becoming smaller.

Contractions are shortened forms created by combining words and omitting letters, marked by an apostrophe: {can't}, {won't}, {I'm}, {they're}. In physiology, contractions are the tightening of muscles—particularly the rhythmic uterine contractions of labor: {Her contractions were five minutes apart}. Any shortening or shrinking can be called a contraction: {economic contraction}, {the contraction of a cooling metal}.

A contractor is a person or company hired to perform work under contract—typically construction, renovation, or other services requiring specialized skills. General contractors oversee entire projects and hire subcontractors for specific tasks: {We're meeting with contractors to get bids on the kitchen remodel}. The term extends to independent workers in any field who work on contract rather than as employees, and to private firms providing services to government: {defense contractors}, {military contractors}.

Contractors are people or companies hired to perform work under contract, typically for a specific project or period rather than as permanent employees. A building contractor manages construction projects; an independent contractor works freelance rather than on staff. Government contractors provide goods or services to federal agencies. {We hired contractors to renovate the kitchen.} The term often implies skilled trades—plumbing, electrical, roofing—but extends to any contracted work.

Contracts covers both the verb and noun forms built on the idea of drawing together. A contract is a binding agreement between parties—legal documents {sign a contract}, but also informal ones {We had a contract: I cook, you clean}. To contract is to enter such an agreement, or to shrink and tighten: muscles contract, pupils contract in bright light. You can also contract a disease, drawing it into yourself. The opposite motion appears in expand and relax.

To contradict is to assert the opposite of what someone has said, or to deny the truth of a statement: {She contradicted his account of events}. Evidence or facts can contradict claims: {The data contradicts the theory}. To contradict oneself is to say something inconsistent with what you said before. The word implies direct opposition, not mere disagreement.

Contradiction is a statement or situation in which elements conflict or cancel each other out. Two claims contradict when both cannot be true: {His alibi was full of contradictions}. A contradiction in terms is a phrase whose parts oppose each other, like "deafening silence." To say something is {a contradiction} suggests internal inconsistency or logical impossibility.

Contradictions are statements or facts that conflict with each other, making both impossible to accept simultaneously. Logic treats contradiction as fatal—if a claim contradicts itself, it cannot be true. In everyday use, contradictions often reveal complexity rather than error: {She was a contradiction—fiercely independent yet desperate for approval}. To {speak in contradictions} is to say incompatible things. A {contradiction in terms} is a phrase that defeats itself, like "deafening silence."

Contradictory describes things that cannot both be true at the same time. Two statements are contradictory when affirming one means denying the other: {His testimony was contradictory—he said he was home, then said he was at the bar}. People can be contradictory when their words or actions don't align: {She's so contradictory, telling me to relax while piling on more work}. As a noun, a contradictory is a proposition that negates another.

Contrails are the white streaks that form behind aircraft at high altitudes, created when hot exhaust meets cold air and water vapor condenses into ice crystals. Short for condensation trails. They dissipate quickly or linger depending on atmospheric conditions: {The sky was crisscrossed with contrails}.

A contraption is a machine or device that appears awkward, complicated, or improvised. The word carries a tone of skepticism or bemusement about whether the thing will actually work: {He built some kind of contraption to keep squirrels off the bird feeder}. Contraptions are often homemade or jury-rigged, assembled from whatever parts were available rather than professionally engineered.

Contraptions are mechanical devices, usually makeshift, improvised, or unnecessarily complicated. The word carries a slightly dismissive tone—suggesting something cobbled together or overly elaborate for its purpose: {What's this contraption supposed to do?} {He built some contraption out of spare parts to open the gate automatically}. Often used when the speaker doesn't know or care what something is properly called.

A contrarian takes positions opposed to prevailing opinion, often deliberately. The term applies especially in investing, where contrarians buy when others sell and vice versa, betting that the crowd is wrong. More broadly, someone contrarian habitually argues the opposite side: {He's such a contrarian—if you say it's hot, he'll insist it's cold}.

Contrary describes opposition or reversal. A contrary wind blows against you; a contrary opinion opposes yours. {Contrary to what you might expect, the experiment succeeded.} Someone described as contrary is stubbornly disagreeable, inclined to oppose whatever others say. {On the contrary} introduces a statement that reverses what came before. The noun contrary refers to the opposite: {I believe the contrary}.

Contrast is about difference—specifically, the kind that becomes visible or meaningful when things are placed side by side. You might contrast two candidates' positions, or notice the contrast between someone's public persona and private behavior. In visual contexts, contrast refers to the degree of difference between light and dark areas: {Turn up the contrast on your monitor}. The word works as both noun and verb, with stress on the first syllable for the noun (CONtrast) and often on the second for the verb (conTRAST), though this distinction is fading.

To contribute is to give something—money, effort, ideas—toward a shared purpose or collection: {She contributed fifty dollars to the fund}, {Everyone contributed to the discussion}. The word implies adding to something larger than oneself. One can contribute to a cause, a publication, or a problem: {Stress contributes to heart disease}. A contributor gives; a contribution is what's given.

A contribution is something given or done to help achieve a goal or support a cause. The word covers both material gifts—money, goods, time—and less tangible offerings like ideas or effort. {Her contribution to the discussion changed the direction of the project.} In financial contexts, contributions often refer to payments into retirement accounts, insurance plans, or charitable organizations. The word can also acknowledge someone's role in a larger outcome: {His contributions to the field earned him lasting recognition.}

Control is the power to direct or restrain something. You control a car by steering it, control your temper by holding it in check, control a meeting by deciding who speaks. Controls are the buttons, levers, or switches that operate a machine: {the controls of an aircraft}. A control group in an experiment receives no treatment, providing a baseline for comparison. To be {in control} is to have command of a situation; to be {out of control} is to have lost it. {Everything is under control.}

Controlled describes something kept in check, regulated, or restrained. A controlled {substance} is legally restricted. A controlled {experiment} holds variables constant. A controlled {burn} is deliberately set and managed. Someone who remains controlled stays calm under pressure: {Her voice was controlled despite her anger}. The word often implies discipline or deliberate limitation rather than natural freedom.

A controller is a person or device that controls something. In organizations, a controller (also comptroller) is an executive who oversees financial operations and accounting. In gaming and computing, a controller is a handheld device for giving input: {She grabbed the controller and started a new game}. In engineering, controllers are components that regulate systems—a temperature controller maintains desired heat levels.

Controllers are people or devices that direct, regulate, or manage something. An air traffic controller guides aircraft. A game controller is a handheld device for input. In business, a controller (also comptroller) is the chief accounting officer who oversees financial operations. {The controllers approved the budget revision.}

Controlling describes the exercise of power or influence over something or someone. A controlling {interest} in a company is enough ownership to direct decisions. A controlling {personality} dominates others, often to an unhealthy degree—managing their choices, monitoring their behavior, demanding compliance. The word carries negative connotations when applied to people: {Her ex was controlling and jealous}.

Controls are mechanisms for operating or regulating something—the controls of an aircraft, the controls on a stereo. The word extends to any means of restraint or direction: {parental controls}, {price controls}, {border controls}. In experiments, controls are comparison groups left untreated to measure the effect of intervention. A control freak insists on managing everything.

Controversial describes something that provokes strong disagreement or public debate. A controversial {decision}, {figure}, or {topic} divides opinion and invites argument. The word often signals that reasonable people hold opposing views: {The film proved controversial for its graphic violence}. Something can be controversial without being wrong—it simply means people fight about it.

Controversy is public disagreement or debate over a matter that provokes strong opposing views. A controversy surrounds something when people argue about whether it's right, true, or acceptable: {The film sparked controversy for its graphic violence}. Controversial topics invite dispute; controversial figures attract criticism. The word can describe anything from political scandals to disputes over pineapple on pizza.

A conundrum is a problem that does not have a solution, or whose apparent solution only creates another problem: Workers faced the conundrum of being unable to live on their wages while knowing that a raise would bankrupt the company. An older meaning of conundrum is a riddle whose answer involves a pun or a play on words, but this meaning is rarely employed today.

Conundrums is the plural of conundrum—a puzzling question or problem, especially one without a clear answer. A conundrum often involves a dilemma where every option has drawbacks: {The committee faced several conundrums about how to allocate the budget}. The word can also mean a riddle whose answer involves a pun.

Convenience is ease of access or use—whatever makes something simpler or more comfortable. A {convenience store} stays open late for easy access. Modern {conveniences} are amenities that reduce effort: running water, electricity, appliances. Something done {at your convenience} happens when it suits you. A {marriage of convenience} serves practical purposes rather than love. As an adjective, convenience describes ready-made products: {convenience foods}, {convenience meals}.

Convenient describes what suits your needs or saves effort. A convenient {location} is easy to reach. A convenient {time} works well with your schedule. Something convenient is ready at hand when you need it: {I keep a flashlight in a convenient spot}. The word can carry a faint suggestion of being too easy or suspiciously well-timed: {a convenient excuse}, {a convenient memory lapse}.

A convent is a community of nuns living under religious vows, or the building where they reside. The term sometimes extends to communities of monks or friars, though monastery is more common for men. {She entered a convent at nineteen.} Convent schools are educational institutions run by nuns.

Convention centers on agreement and gathering. A convention is a large formal assembly—political parties hold conventions to nominate candidates, and industries hold conventions to network and exhibit: {the annual comic book convention}. Convention also means an established practice or custom accepted by general consent: {social conventions}, {the conventions of the genre}. What's conventional follows these norms; to flout convention is to defy them. In contracts, a convention is a formal agreement between parties, especially nations.

Conventional describes what follows established customs, standards, or accepted practices. A conventional {approach} does things the expected way. Conventional {weapons} are non-nuclear. Conventional {wisdom} is what most people believe, whether true or not. The word often carries a faint dismissiveness—conventional implies safe, unimaginative, or conformist: {Her taste in art is utterly conventional}.

Conventions are established practices or customs that groups follow without formal rules requiring them. Writing has its conventions (spelling, punctuation), as do social situations (shaking hands, saying "bless you"). A convention is also a large gathering of people with shared interests: {the annual comic book convention}, {the Democratic National Convention}. In art, conventions are accepted techniques or devices: {the conventions of the detective genre}.

Convents are communities of religious women living under vows, or the buildings housing them. Nuns in convents follow a rule of life—prayer, work, and communal living. The word sometimes extends to communities of friars or monks, though monastery is more common for men. {She entered a convent at nineteen.}

Conversation is spoken exchange between people. The word emphasizes back-and-forth interaction rather than one-way speech: {We had a long conversation about her future}. A {conversation starter} is something that prompts discussion. To {make conversation} is to chat politely, often to fill silence. In computing, conversational interfaces respond to natural language.

Conversations is the plural of conversation—verbal exchanges between two or more people. A conversation involves back-and-forth dialogue, distinguishing it from speeches or monologues. {We had several conversations about the project}. The word extends to any ongoing exchange of ideas: {national conversations about race}, {the conversation around climate change}.

Converse means to talk with someone, to engage in conversation: {We conversed for hours over coffee}. The word is slightly formal—people more often say "talk" or "chat." As an adjective and noun, converse describes something reversed or opposite: {the converse is also true}, {the converse of a proposition}. In logic, a converse swaps the subject and predicate of a statement. (Capitalized Converse is the sneaker brand.)

Conversion is turning one thing into another. A religious conversion changes a person's faith or commitment. In football, a conversion adds points after a touchdown. Converting a file changes its format; converting currency exchanges one for another. A conversion van has been modified from a standard vehicle. The word implies transformation—something becomes what it wasn't before.

When convert is stressed on the last syllable, it’s a verb that conveys changing from one thing to another (convert dollars into euros, convert the old church into apartments). Less commonly, when the stress is on the first syllable, convert is a noun and designates a person who has adopted a new religion (Catholic convert). This is the usual meaning if a person converts.

Converted describes something that has been changed from one form, function, or state to another. A converted {warehouse} is now apartments; a converted {atheist} now believes. The word often implies the change is complete and the original purpose abandoned. In religion, a convert has adopted a new faith. As a football term, a converted {try} or {field goal} successfully scored after a touchdown or penalty.

Convertible describes something that can be changed from one form or state to another. A convertible {sofa} becomes a bed. A convertible {currency} can be exchanged for other currencies. Most commonly, a convertible is a car with a roof that folds down or detaches: {We drove along the coast with the top down in her convertible}. In finance, convertible {bonds} or convertible {notes} can be exchanged for company stock.

Convertibles are things that can be transformed from one state to another. Most commonly, a convertible is a car with a roof that folds down or detaches: {We drove along the coast in a convertible}. In finance, convertible bonds or securities can be exchanged for stock. A convertible sofa becomes a bed. The singular convertible usually means the car.

Converts functions as both verb and noun around the idea of change or transformation. To convert is to change something from one form, function, or belief to another: {They converted the garage into a studio}, {She converted to Islam}. In sports, to convert is to score after an opportunity: {He converted the penalty kick}. A convert is someone who has adopted a new religion, belief, or cause—often with the zeal associated with fresh conviction: {a recent convert to veganism}.

A convict is a person found guilty of a crime and serving a prison sentence. The word carries a harsher edge than "prisoner" or "inmate," often implying serious offenses: {escaped convicts}, {a gang of convicts breaking rocks}. As a verb (stress on second syllable), to convict is to find guilty in court: {The jury convicted him of murder}. A conviction is the resulting judgment.

Convicted describes someone found guilty of a crime by a court: {a convicted felon}, {convicted of murder}. The word carries the weight of official judgment—not merely accused or suspected, but determined guilty through legal process. As a verb, to convict is to deliver that guilty verdict: {The jury convicted him on all counts}.

Conviction carries two distinct meanings united by the idea of firmness. In law, a conviction is a formal declaration that someone is guilty of a crime: {His conviction on fraud charges ended his political career}. The other sense refers to a strong, unwavering belief: {She spoke with conviction about the need for reform}. Someone with deep convictions holds firm principles they're unlikely to abandon. To carry conviction means to be persuasive or believable.

Convictions are firmly held beliefs or opinions: {a woman of strong convictions}, {Nothing could shake his political convictions}. A conviction is also a formal declaration of guilt in court—the outcome when someone is found guilty of a crime: {His prior convictions made bail unlikely}. To speak {with conviction} is to speak with certainty and confidence.

Convicts functions as both noun and verb. A convict is a person found guilty of a crime, especially one serving a prison sentence: {The convicts worked on a chain gang}. To convict someone is to find them guilty in court: {The jury convicted him of fraud}. The noun stresses the first syllable, the verb the second.

To convince someone is to bring them to belief or agreement through argument, evidence, or persuasion: {She convinced me that the project was worth pursuing}. You can also convince someone to do something: {They convinced him to stay}. A convinced person holds firm belief: {a convinced vegetarian}. Convincing evidence or arguments are persuasive enough to produce belief.

Convinced means firmly believing something to be true or right. When you're convinced of a fact, you feel certain: {I'm convinced she's lying}. Someone who is a convinced {atheist} or convinced {socialist} holds their position as settled belief, not tentative opinion. To become convinced is to move from doubt to certainty.

Convincing describes something that produces belief or agreement. A convincing argument persuades you; a convincing performance makes you believe the character. The word often implies overcoming initial doubt: {The evidence was convincing enough to change my mind}. A convincing victory is decisive, leaving no question about the outcome.

Convoluted means intricately folded or twisted, like the convolutions of the brain. The word usually describes something unnecessarily complex or hard to follow: a convoluted {plot}, convoluted {reasoning}, convoluted {bureaucratic procedures}. {The tax code is so convoluted that even experts disagree on its interpretation.}

A convoy is a group of vehicles or ships traveling together, typically for protection or mutual support. Military convoys move troops and supplies under armed escort. Civilian convoys form for safety or solidarity: {a convoy of aid trucks}, {a convoy of truckers protesting fuel prices}. To convoy is to travel in or escort such a group.

Convoys is the plural of convoy—a group traveling together for protection or efficiency. Military convoys move troops and supplies under armed escort. Truck convoys coordinate long-haul journeys. Ship convoys were crucial in wartime, crossing dangerous waters in formation: {Allied convoys crossed the Atlantic despite U-boat attacks}. The verb convoys means accompanies protectively.

A convulsion is a violent, involuntary contraction of the muscles—the body seizing and shaking uncontrollably. Medical convulsions occur with epilepsy, high fevers, or other conditions. The word extends to any violent upheaval: political convulsions, convulsions of laughter. {The country was racked by convulsions following the coup.} {She went into convulsions of giggles.}

Convulsions are violent, involuntary muscle contractions that shake the body uncontrollably. The word most often describes seizures: {The child went into convulsions from the high fever}. It extends to any violent shaking—convulsions of laughter, convulsions of grief, political convulsions that shake a nation. {The economy went through convulsions after the crash.}

Cooing is the soft, murmuring sound doves and pigeons make—a gentle, repetitive vocalization. By extension, cooing describes any soft, affectionate talk: {The couple sat cooing at each other}. Parents coo at babies; lovers coo endearments. The word suggests tenderness bordering on saccharine excess: {Stop your cooing and get to work}.

Cook is the most common verb for the activity of preparing food using heat. A person who does this is a cook, especially if it’s a job or profession. If food is cooking, it has been prepared and is being heated. The verb has several informal uses. What’s cooking? is a way of asking what is happening. If you cook up something, you fabricate it to deal with the situation at hand. Someone who cooks the books does dishonest and illegal bookkeeping.

A cookbook is a book containing recipes and instructions for preparing food. The term extends to any collection of procedures: {a cookbook for laboratory protocols}, {a cookbook approach to software development}. The adjective cookbook suggests following instructions mechanically rather than understanding underlying principles: {cookbook chemistry}.

Cooked describes food that has been heated to prepare it for eating: {a cooked breakfast}, {cooked vegetables}. Beyond the kitchen, cooked means ruined or doomed—if you're cooked, your situation is hopeless: {Once the evidence came out, he was cooked}. In Australian slang, cooked describes someone exhausted, intoxicated, or mentally fried: {I'm absolutely cooked after that shift}.

A cookie is a small, sweet baked treat, typically flat and round: {chocolate chip cookies}, {sugar cookies}. In computing, a cookie is a small file stored by a website on your device to track preferences or activity. To {toss one's cookies} is slang for vomiting. Someone described as a {tough cookie} or {smart cookie} is resilient or clever.

Cookies are sweet baked treats, typically small, flat, and crisp or chewy: {chocolate chip cookies}, {oatmeal raisin cookies}. In British English, these are called biscuits. In computing, a cookie is a small file stored by a website on your device to track preferences or activity: {Accept cookies?} The phrase {that's the way the cookie crumbles} expresses resignation about how things turn out.

Cooking is the practice of preparing food by applying heat—boiling, frying, baking, roasting, grilling. The term extends to the whole process of meal preparation: {I do most of the cooking in our house}. Someone's cooking is their characteristic style or skill: {Her cooking reminds me of my grandmother's}. Figuratively, if something is cooking, it's developing or happening: {What's cooking?} To cook the books is to falsify financial records.

A cookout is an outdoor meal where food is grilled or barbecued, typically in a backyard or park. The word emphasizes the social gathering as much as the cooking: {We're having a cookout for the Fourth of July}. Cookout is more common in American English, where it overlaps with but is more casual than barbecue.

Cookouts are outdoor gatherings where food is grilled or barbecued, typically in a backyard or park. The term emphasizes the social occasion as much as the cooking method—friends and family assembling for burgers, hot dogs, and conversation. Cookouts are associated with warm weather and American holidays like the Fourth of July and Labor Day: {We're having a cookout this weekend}.

Cooks is the plural of cook, a person who prepares food: {Too many cooks spoil the broth}. As a verb, cooks means prepares food by heating: {She cooks dinner every night}. Extended uses include falsifying records {(cooks the books)} and progressing well {(Now we're cooking)}. Something that cooks is also being planned or developed: {What's cooking?}

Cool is mainly a designation of a usually comfortable place between warm and cold. Cool relations or a cool reception, however, are uncomfortable because they are better when they’re warm. To cool something is to reduce its temperature. This is especially positive when it applies figuratively to tempers or emotions. The adjective cool is a frequent, informal way to express approval or appreciation: He’s a cool dude.

A cooldown is a period of reduced activity after exertion—light stretching after a workout, easy jogging after a sprint. In gaming, cooldown is the waiting period before a skill or ability can be used again: {The spell has a thirty-second cooldown}. More broadly, any enforced pause before something can happen again: {There's a cooldown between login attempts}.

A cooler is an insulated container for keeping food and drinks cold, typically portable: {We packed the cooler with ice and beer for the picnic}. Cooler also refers to any device that lowers temperature: an {air cooler}, a {wine cooler}. In slang, the cooler is jail or a solitary confinement cell: {They threw him in the cooler for the night}. As an adjective, cooler is the comparative form of cool.

Coolers are insulated containers that keep food and beverages cold, typically portable boxes used for picnics, camping, or tailgating: {Pack the coolers with ice and beer}. A cooler can also be a cold drink, especially wine mixed with fruit juice or soda: {wine cooler}. In slang, the cooler is a jail or solitary confinement cell.

Cooling is the process of becoming or making something less warm. It describes temperature reduction {Leave the pie out for cooling} or systems that manage heat {the cooling system in a car}. Figuratively, cooling applies to diminishing intensity—a cooling economy slows down, cooling enthusiasm wanes, and a cooling-off period lets tempers settle before resuming negotiations.

Coolness is the quality of being cool—either in temperature or in manner. A room's coolness provides relief from summer heat. Personal coolness can mean calm composure {She handled the crisis with admirable coolness} or emotional distance {There was a coolness between them after the argument}. In casual use, coolness describes social appeal or stylishness: {His effortless coolness made everyone want to be around him}.

A coop is a small enclosure for poultry, especially chickens: {We built a chicken coop in the backyard}. The word extends to any cramped or confining space: {Their apartment felt like a coop}. To coop someone up is to confine them in a small space: {The kids were cooped up inside all winter}. Separately, coop is short for cooperative—a jointly owned enterprise: {a food coop}, {a housing coop}.

To cooperate is to work together toward a shared goal or to comply with a request. Nations cooperate on trade agreements; witnesses cooperate with investigators. The word implies willingness—cooperation under duress is coercion. {The children refused to cooperate}. {If everyone cooperates, this will go smoothly}.

Cooperation is working together toward a shared goal. The word emphasizes willing participation rather than coerced effort: {The project succeeded through cooperation between departments}. Cooperation can also mean compliance or assistance: {We need your cooperation to complete the investigation}. The adjective cooperative describes both the attitude and organizations owned jointly by members.

Cooperative describes willingness to work with others toward a shared goal: {The witness was cooperative with investigators}. A cooperative venture involves collaboration rather than competition. As a noun, a cooperative (or co-op) is an organization owned and operated by its members for mutual benefit—housing cooperatives, food cooperatives, worker cooperatives. Members share costs, decisions, and profits.

Coordinate means to arrange elements so they work together harmoniously. You coordinate {schedules}, {outfits}, or {efforts} between teams. The verb implies bringing multiple parts into proper relation. As an adjective, coordinate describes things of equal rank or importance: {coordinate clauses} in grammar. As a noun, coordinates are numbers that specify a position—map coordinates locate a point on Earth, and in fashion, coordinates are matching separates designed to go together.

Coordinates are numbers that identify a position in space—on a map, a graph, or the earth's surface. GPS coordinates pinpoint locations using latitude and longitude: {I'll send you the coordinates}. In math, coordinates specify points on axes. The word also names matching separates in clothing: {a set of coordinates in navy and cream}.

Coordination is the organization of different elements to work together effectively. In physical movement, coordination means controlling body parts smoothly: {She has excellent hand-eye coordination}. In planning, it means arranging activities so they don't conflict: {The project required coordination between three departments}. The word implies bringing separate things into harmonious operation—whether muscles, schedules, or people.

Cooties are imaginary germs or parasites that children attribute to members of the opposite sex—or anyone deemed undesirable—to justify avoiding contact: {Don't touch him, he has cooties!} The word originated as World War I slang for body lice. The childhood sense treats contamination as a game, with elaborate rituals like "cootie shots" providing immunity.

Cooties are imaginary germs or parasites that children claim someone has—usually to justify avoiding them: {Don't touch him, he has cooties!} The concept functions as playground currency for social exclusion, with elaborate rituals like "cootie shots" to protect against contamination. Originally, cooties was World War I slang for body lice.

A cop is a police officer, from an old slang verb meaning to catch or seize—cops catch criminals. The word is informal but not disrespectful: {The cops showed up within minutes}. To cop something is to get or take it, sometimes illicitly: {cop a feel}, {cop a plea}. To {cop out} is to avoid responsibility or commitment. To {cop to} something is to admit it: {He copped to stealing the car}.

A coparent is someone who shares parenting responsibilities with another person, typically after divorce or separation. The term emphasizes cooperation between parents who are no longer romantically involved: {We coparent pretty well despite everything}. Coparenting can also describe arrangements between friends or others who choose to raise a child together without being a couple.

Coparenting is the shared raising of a child by two or more adults, typically parents who are divorced or separated. The term emphasizes cooperation and coordination between caregivers who don't live together: {We've worked out a coparenting arrangement that gives the kids stability}. It can also describe arrangements between unmarried parents or non-romantic partners who choose to raise a child together.

Cope is mainly a verb that means deal with effectively, and is used of people in relation to challenging situations: How does she cope with four kids and a full-time job? Other words spelled c-o-p-e are infrequent and only likely to be encountered in older or specialized literature. One kind of cope is an ecclesiastical garment. In woodworking, to cope is to fit two pieces of wood together by cutting a miter joint.

A copier is a machine that makes copies of documents, short for photocopier. The word also means someone who copies—either neutrally {a fast copier of notes} or negatively, implying imitation without originality: {He's just a copier, not a real artist}.

Copies are reproductions or duplicates of an original, whether physical objects like documents and artworks or digital files. A copy of a book or magazine is one of many identical items produced for distribution. To copy something is to make a reproduction of it, or to imitate someone's behavior or style: {She copied his homework} or {He copies everything his older brother does}. In computing, copy places data on a clipboard for pasting elsewhere.

Coping is the cap or covering on top of a wall, designed to shed water and protect the masonry beneath. The term extends to any protective top edge. Separately, coping refers to the psychological strategies people use to manage stress, difficulty, or trauma: {Her coping mechanisms include exercise and journaling}. The verb cope means to deal with challenges: {He's coping with the loss}.

A copout is an evasion of responsibility or commitment, typically one that disappoints others who were counting on you. Someone who backs out of a difficult situation or avoids taking a stand when one is expected may be accused of copping out. {Blaming the weather was such a copout.} The term carries connotations of weakness or dishonesty—taking the easy way out rather than facing consequences or honoring obligations.

Copper is a reddish-brown metallic element, valued since ancient times for conducting heat and electricity. Copper wire runs through buildings; copper pipes carry water. The color copper describes that distinctive brownish-red. Coppers are copper coins or British slang for police officers—from the verb cop, to catch. {The old pennies were solid copper.}

A copperhead is a venomous pit viper native to eastern North America, named for its copper-colored head. The snake is responsible for more snakebites than any other North American species, though bites are rarely fatal. {Watch where you step—copperheads blend right into the leaf litter.} (Capitalized Copperhead is a historical term for a Northern Democrat who opposed the Civil War.)

Copperheads are venomous pit vipers native to eastern North America, named for their copper-colored heads. The term also refers to Northern Democrats who opposed the Civil War and advocated peace with the Confederacy—their enemies compared them to the snake that strikes without warning. {The copperhead was coiled under the woodpile.}

Coproporphyrin is a porphyrin compound found in feces and urine, formed during the biosynthesis of heme. Elevated levels in urine or stool can indicate certain metabolic disorders, liver disease, or lead poisoning. The term appears primarily in clinical laboratory contexts: {The lab tested for coproporphyrin levels to assess porphyria}.

Cops is the common informal term for police officers. The word carries no inherent disrespect—it's simply casual: {The cops showed up within minutes}. To cop is to get or take: {cop a plea}, {cop an attitude}, {cop a feel}. A cop-out is an evasion of responsibility.

The idea uniting all meanings of copy is duplication. A copy of a letter, software program, or painting is a duplicate that can fill some or all functions of the original. When you copy something tangible, you make a copy of it. If you copy someone’s behavior, you imitate some or all aspects of what they did. In publishing, journalism, and increasingly in the world of online content, copy refers to text that is being prepared for or is ready for publication or broadcast: Their press release came to us as camera-ready copy.

A copycat imitates someone else's actions, style, or work—often with the suggestion of lacking originality. The term appears frequently as an attributive noun: a copycat {crime} mimics an earlier one, copycat {products} knock off successful brands. Children use it as a taunt: {Copycat, copycat!} The verb means to imitate: {She's just copycatting what the cool kids do}.

Copycats is the plural of copycat—someone who imitates another's behavior, work, or style, often without originality. The term carries mild disapproval, suggesting the imitation lacks creativity: {The success spawned dozens of copycats}. Copycat also works as an adjective: a copycat {crime} replicates methods from an earlier offense.

Copyright is the legal right to control reproduction and distribution of creative work—books, music, films, software, images. The creator or rights holder can authorize or prohibit copying: {The photograph is protected by copyright}. To copyright something is to secure this protection: {She copyrighted her designs}. Copyright infringement is unauthorized use of protected material.

Coral refers to marine invertebrates that build hard calcium carbonate skeletons, forming reefs in warm shallow seas. A coral reef is an ecosystem of extraordinary biodiversity. The word also names the pinkish-orange color of certain coral species: {coral lipstick}, {a coral sunset}. As a modifier, coral describes this distinctive hue or things made from coral: {coral jewelry}, {coral beads}.

Corals are marine invertebrates that build hard skeletons, forming reefs in tropical waters. A single coral is one such organism or a piece of its skeleton, often used decoratively. Coral also names the pinkish-orange color of these skeletons: {coral lipstick}, {a coral dress}. Coral reefs support extraordinary biodiversity and face threats from warming oceans.

A cord is a length of flexible material—thicker than string, thinner than rope—used for tying, binding, or connecting: {Pull the cord to close the blinds}. Electrical cords carry power to devices. Anatomically, the spinal cord runs through the vertebrae, and the umbilical cord connects fetus to placenta. To {cut the cord} is to sever a dependent relationship. A cord is also a unit of firewood measuring 128 cubic feet, typically a stack four feet by four feet by eight feet.

Cordial describes warmth and friendliness, especially the polite kind shown to guests or acquaintances: {a cordial greeting}, {cordial relations between the two countries}. The warmth is genuine but measured—cordial suggests civility more than deep affection. As a noun, a cordial is a sweet liqueur or, in British usage, a concentrated fruit drink diluted with water.

Corduroy is a durable cotton fabric with distinctive raised parallel ridges called wales. The texture comes from cut pile woven in lengthwise rows. Corduroy pants were once standard schoolboy wear; now the fabric suggests casual or vintage style: {a corduroy jacket with elbow patches}. As an adjective, corduroy describes roads made of logs laid crosswise over swampy ground—the ridges resembling the fabric's texture.

The core of something is its innermost part. The cores of some things – like apples – are dispensable. When you core an apple, you remove its core. The core of something abstract is usually taken to be the most important, essential part: What is the core of your argument? In computing, a core is an element of hardware used in memory.

A corgi is a small herding dog with a long body, short legs, and large upright ears. The breed originated in Wales, where two varieties developed: the Pembroke and the Cardigan. Corgis gained wider recognition as the favored dogs of Queen Elizabeth II. Despite their size, they're energetic working dogs bred to herd cattle by nipping at their heels.

Coriander is an herb whose leaves and seeds are used in cooking. The plant is also called cilantro, though in American usage coriander typically refers to the dried seeds while cilantro means the fresh leaves. The seeds have a warm, citrusy flavor used in curries, pickling, and baking: {toast the coriander before grinding}. The leaves are pungent and polarizing—some people taste soap.

Cork is the buoyant, spongy bark of a Mediterranean oak tree, used to make bottle stoppers, flooring, bulletin boards, and other products. A cork is specifically the stopper itself: {Pull the cork on that wine}. To cork is to seal with a cork. Corked wine has been contaminated by a faulty cork, giving it a musty taste. In baseball, a corked bat has been illegally hollowed and filled with cork to make it lighter. (Capitalized Cork is a city in Ireland.)

Corks is the plural of cork—the lightweight, buoyant bark of the cork oak tree, or stoppers made from it. Wine bottles are sealed with corks; to cork a bottle is to close it this way. Cork also describes anything made from the material: cork {flooring}, cork {board}. As an exclamation, corks is a mild, old-fashioned oath: {Oh corks, I've forgotten my wallet!}

A corkscrew is a tool for removing corks from wine bottles, typically featuring a pointed metal spiral that twists into the cork and a mechanism for pulling it out. The spiral shape gives the word its extended uses: corkscrew {curls}, a corkscrew {staircase}. As a verb, to corkscrew is to move in a twisting spiral: {The plane corkscrewed toward the ground}.

Cormorants is the plural of cormorant, a large dark waterbird with a long neck and hooked bill. Cormorants dive underwater to catch fish and are often seen perched with wings spread to dry. In some Asian fishing traditions, trained cormorants catch fish for their handlers. {Cormorants lined the rocky shore, drying their wings in the sun.}

Corn is a tall grain plant with kernels growing in rows on a cob, a staple crop in the Americas. In British English, corn means grain generally—wheat, barley, oats. Corny jokes or sentiments are trite and unsophisticated, evoking rural simplicity. A corn is also a painful hardening of skin on the foot, unrelated to the grain.

Cornbread is a quick bread made from cornmeal, a staple of Southern American cooking. It's typically baked in a cast-iron skillet and served alongside beans, greens, or barbecue. Regional variations abound—Southern cornbread is usually unsweetened and crusty, while Northern versions tend sweeter and cakier: {She crumbled cornbread into her bowl of chili}.

A corndog is a hot dog coated in cornmeal batter and deep-fried on a stick. It's classic American fair and carnival food, though widely available frozen. The stick makes it portable finger food: {We grabbed corndogs at the state fair}. Also spelled corn dog.

A corner is where two lines, edges, or surfaces meet at an angle. Rooms have corners, pages have corners, streets have corners. To corner someone is to trap them where escape is difficult: {The reporter cornered the senator after the hearing}. To corner a market is to gain control of a commodity's supply. Something done {on the corner} happens at a street intersection. To {cut corners} is to take shortcuts, often sacrificing quality. {Around the corner} means nearby or imminent: {Spring is just around the corner}.

Cornered describes being trapped or forced into a position with no escape. A cornered {animal} is most dangerous because it has nowhere to flee. Someone cornered in an argument has no good response left. To have something cornered—or to {corner the market}—is to control it completely, leaving others no access.

Corners is the plural of corner—the points where edges meet, or the angles they form. Streets have corners where they intersect; rooms have corners where walls join. To corner someone is to trap them where escape is difficult. To cut corners is to take shortcuts, often by skimping on quality or effort: {They cut corners on safety to save money}. In commerce, to corner a market is to gain controlling influence over it.

A cornerstone is literally a stone at the corner of a building's foundation, often ceremonially laid to mark construction's beginning. Figuratively, it means the fundamental element on which something depends: {Trust is the cornerstone of any relationship}. The word implies both foundational importance and structural necessity—remove it and everything built upon it weakens.

A cornfield is a field where corn is grown. In American English, this means maize; in British English, it typically means wheat or other cereal grains. The word evokes rural agricultural landscapes: {We drove past miles of cornfields}. A cornfield can serve as a setting for hide-and-seek, horror movies, or getting lost.

Fields where corn is grown. In American English, cornfields are planted with maize—the tall stalks with yellow ears. In British English, they may contain wheat or other cereal grains. Cornfields evoke rural farmland and agricultural heartland: {We drove past miles of cornfields in Iowa}. {Children of the Corn} made them briefly sinister.

Cornflakes are a breakfast cereal made from toasted flakes of corn, typically eaten with milk: {a bowl of cornflakes}. The word often appears generically for any similar flaked cereal, regardless of brand. Cornflakes have become emblematic of plain, wholesome breakfast fare—something reliable but unremarkable.

Cornhole is a lawn game where players toss beanbags at a slanted wooden board with a hole in it, scoring points when bags land on the board or pass through the hole. Popular at tailgates and backyard gatherings: {We set up cornhole at the cookout}. Separately, cornhole is vulgar slang for anal sex or the anus itself.

Cornrows are a hairstyle in which the hair is braided flat against the scalp in narrow, raised rows, typically running from front to back. The style originated in Africa and remains culturally significant in Black communities. As a verb, to cornrow is to braid hair this way: {She cornrowed her daughter's hair for the first day of school}.

Cornrows are a hairstyle in which the hair is braided flat against the scalp in narrow, raised rows, typically running from front to back. The style has deep roots in African cultures and remains popular in Black communities worldwide. Creating cornrows requires sectioning hair and weaving it tightly in continuous, attached braids: {She sat for hours getting her cornrows done}. The name comes from the rows' resemblance to planted corn.

A cornucopia is a horn-shaped container overflowing with fruits, vegetables, and flowers—a symbol of abundance associated with harvest festivals and Thanksgiving decorations. The image extends to any overflowing plenty: {a cornucopia of options}, {a cornucopia of delights}. The word comes from Latin for "horn of plenty."

Corny describes something so sentimental, outdated, or obvious that it feels trite or embarrassing—a corny {joke}, a corny {pickup line}, a corny {movie}. The word suggests excessive sweetness or predictability: {I know it sounds corny, but I really do believe in true love}. Something corny isn't necessarily bad—it can be endearing in its earnestness—but it lacks sophistication or originality.

Corona is Latin for crown, and its English senses branch from that image. In anatomy, a corona is a crown-like structure—most often the rounded rim of the glans penis. In astronomy, the corona is the luminous halo visible around the sun during an eclipse. Corona became shorthand for coronavirus during the COVID-19 pandemic: {I had corona twice in 2021}. Corona is also a brand of Mexican beer.

A coronation is the ceremony of crowning a monarch. The ritual typically involves religious rites, the placing of a crown on the sovereign's head, and formal investiture with symbols of power: {The coronation drew millions of television viewers}. Figuratively, coronation describes any formal elevation to a position of dominance or acclaim: {The tournament was supposed to be his coronation as the sport's next superstar}.

A coronavirus is any of a family of viruses named for the crown-like spikes on their surface. Coronaviruses cause respiratory infections ranging from common colds to severe diseases. The word became ubiquitous during the COVID-19 pandemic, often used interchangeably with COVID-19 itself: {The coronavirus shut down schools worldwide}, {coronavirus restrictions}, {Did you get coronavirus?} Scientists distinguish specific coronaviruses like SARS-CoV-2, but in everyday speech, {the coronavirus} means the one responsible for the pandemic.

A coroner is a public official who investigates deaths, particularly those that are sudden, violent, or unexplained. The coroner determines cause of death and whether an inquest or autopsy is needed. In some jurisdictions, the role requires medical training; in others, it's an elected position that may not. {The coroner ruled the death a homicide.}

Corporate relates to corporations—business entities legally distinct from their owners. As an adjective, it describes things belonging to or characteristic of such organizations: {corporate headquarters}, {corporate culture}, {corporate responsibility}. The word often carries connotations of impersonal bureaucracy or profit-driven priorities: {The decision felt very corporate}. Used disparagingly, corporate suggests bland conformity or soulless efficiency: {The neighborhood lost its character after all the corporate chains moved in}.

A corporation is a business entity legally separate from its owners, who hold shares of ownership. This structure shields shareholders from personal liability—if the corporation fails, they lose only their investment. Corporations can own property, enter contracts, and sue or be sued in their own name. {She works for a large corporation.} The word often carries connotations of impersonal bigness: {faceless corporations}, {corporate greed}.

Corporations are businesses organized as legal entities separate from their owners. This structure limits owners' liability—shareholders can lose their investment but not personal assets if the corporation fails. Corporations can own property, enter contracts, and sue or be sued in their own name. The word often carries connotations of faceless bureaucracy or profit-driven indifference: {You can't fight the corporations}.

A corpse is a dead body, especially a human one. The word carries a clinical or literary tone—news reports prefer {body}, while {corpse} appears in crime fiction, horror, and formal contexts. In theater slang, to corpse is to break character by laughing uncontrollably during a performance.

Corpses is the plural of corpse—dead bodies, especially of humans. The word appears in contexts ranging from crime scenes to battlefields to horror fiction: {Corpses littered the field after the battle}. Unlike "bodies," which can refer to living people, corpses are unambiguously dead.

A corral is an enclosure for confining livestock—horses, cattle, sheep. The word comes from Spanish and remains common in the American West and Southwest. To corral animals is to drive them into such an enclosure. Figuratively, to corral is to gather or round up: {She corralled the kids for dinner}. {He corralled enough votes to pass the bill}.

Correct means free from error or conforming to fact, standard, or convention: {the correct answer}, {correct spelling}, {politically correct}. As a verb, to correct is to fix what's wrong—correcting a mistake, correcting a child's behavior, correcting course. A correction in financial markets is a decline that adjusts inflated prices. To {stand corrected} is to acknowledge you were wrong.

Correction is the act of making something right or accurate. A teacher's corrections mark errors on student work. A correction to a news story fixes a mistake. In finance, a market correction is a significant decline after prices have risen too high. Corrections can also mean punishment intended to reform: {a house of correction}, {the department of corrections}.

Corrections refers to changes made to fix errors or improve accuracy: {The editor marked corrections in red}. In institutional contexts, corrections is the system of prisons, jails, and supervision programs that handle convicted offenders: {He worked in corrections for twenty years}, {the Department of Corrections}. A corrections officer is a prison guard.

Correspond has two main senses. First, to match or be equivalent: {The punishment should correspond to the crime}. Second, to exchange letters or messages: {They corresponded for years before meeting}. Things that correspond are in agreement or harmony; people who correspond communicate in writing. A correspondent is someone who corresponds—or a journalist reporting from a particular location.

A correspondent is someone who exchanges letters or messages with another: {pen pals are correspondents}. More commonly, a correspondent is a journalist who reports from a particular location or on a specific subject: {a war correspondent}, {a White House correspondent}. As an adjective, correspondent means matching or analogous, though corresponding is more common in this sense.

A corridor is a long, narrow passage in a building, typically with rooms opening off it on both sides: {The hotel corridor stretched endlessly ahead}. The word extends to any narrow strip of land, especially one providing access: an {air corridor}, a {wildlife corridor}, a {corridor of power}. The plural {corridors of power} refers to the inner circles where political decisions are made.

Corrosion is the gradual destruction of material, especially metal, through chemical reaction with its environment. Rust is the most familiar form—iron corroding through exposure to oxygen and moisture. The word extends to any slow wearing away: {the corrosion of trust}, {the corrosion of democratic institutions}. What corrodes doesn't shatter; it degrades incrementally.

Corrosive describes substances that chemically destroy or eat away at materials they contact. Strong acids and bases are corrosive to metals, skin, and eyes: {corrosive chemicals require special handling}. Figuratively, corrosive describes things that gradually damage or undermine: {corrosive cynicism}, {a corrosive influence on public trust}. The noun names the substance itself.

Corrupt describes something tainted, dishonest, or morally degraded. A corrupt official abuses power for personal gain. Corrupt {data} has been damaged and is unreliable. Corrupt {practices} involve bribery or fraud. To corrupt is to make something impure or to pervert its original state: {Power corrupts}. A corrupting {influence} leads others toward wrongdoing. The word implies decay from a better original condition.

Corrupted describes something altered from its original, proper, or pure state—usually for the worse. Data becomes corrupted when errors make files unreadable: {The hard drive crashed and corrupted my photos}. Text is corrupted when copying errors distort it over time. A corrupted official has been morally compromised, typically through bribery. The word implies decay from something once sound or whole.

Corruption is the decay of integrity or proper functioning. In its most common use, corruption involves abuse of entrusted power for private gain—bribery, embezzlement, or exploiting public office: {The mayor was convicted of corruption}. Data corruption means files have been damaged or altered. Moral corruption suggests a degraded character. The word implies something once sound has been spoiled or perverted from its original state.

Corrupts is the verb form of corrupt, meaning to degrade, spoil, or make dishonest. Power corrupts those who wield it unchecked. Money corrupts political systems. In computing, data corrupts when files become damaged or unreadable: {The virus corrupted my hard drive}. A corrupting influence leads others toward moral decay or wrongdoing.

A corsage is a small bouquet of flowers worn on the body, typically pinned to a dress or worn on the wrist. Corsages are traditional accessories for formal occasions like proms and weddings: {He picked up her corsage from the florist before the dance}. The word originally referred to the bodice of a dress, where such flowers were pinned.

Corsages is the plural of corsage, a small arrangement of flowers worn on a woman's dress or wrist for formal occasions. Corsages are most associated with American high school dances—proms and homecomings—where a date traditionally presents one: {He picked up the corsage from the florist before the dance}. They also appear at weddings, usually worn by mothers of the bride and groom.

A corsair is a pirate, especially one operating in the Mediterranean. The term also applies to a pirate ship itself. Corsair carries a slightly romantic or swashbuckling connotation compared to the blunter pirate: {The corsairs of the Barbary Coast terrorized European shipping for centuries}.

Corsairs are pirates or privateers, especially those who operated in the Mediterranean. The word carries a slightly romantic or historical flavor compared to plain pirate: {Barbary corsairs raided European coastal towns for slaves}. Corsair can also refer to the fast ships these raiders sailed.

A corset is a close-fitting undergarment stiffened with boning and tightened with laces, designed to shape the torso—typically narrowing the waist and supporting the bust. Once standard women's wear, corsets fell from everyday use in the early twentieth century but persist in fashion, costume, and fetish contexts: {She laced her corset tight for the period drama}. To corset is to confine or restrict: {corset-like regulations}.

Corsets are close-fitting undergarments stiffened with boning to shape the torso, traditionally worn by women to narrow the waist and support the bust. Once standard foundation garments, they fell from everyday use in the early twentieth century but persist in fashion, costume, and fetish contexts. The verb corset means to confine tightly: {a bureaucracy corseted by regulations}.

Cosmetic refers to products or procedures meant to beautify the face and body: {cosmetic surgery}, {the cosmetics industry}. The word extends to anything superficial or surface-level—changes that improve appearance without addressing underlying substance: {The renovations were purely cosmetic}. A cosmetic fix makes something look better without solving the real problem.

Cosmetics are substances applied to the body, especially the face, to enhance appearance or alter skin condition. The category includes makeup like lipstick and foundation, as well as skincare products, lotions, and perfumes. As an adjective, cosmetic describes something superficial or intended only to improve appearance without addressing underlying issues: {The renovations were purely cosmetic.} A cosmetic procedure in medicine improves looks rather than treating disease or injury.

Cosmic relates to the cosmos—the universe as an ordered whole. It describes things pertaining to outer space: {cosmic rays}, {cosmic dust}. More often, cosmic conveys vastness or profound significance: {cosmic questions about existence}, {a discovery of cosmic importance}. Something can be cosmically {insignificant} or a {cosmic coincidence}. The word suggests scale beyond ordinary human concerns.

A cosmonaut is a Russian astronaut—a person trained to travel and work in space as part of the Russian (formerly Soviet) space program. The distinction is purely national: Americans are astronauts, Russians are cosmonauts, though both do the same work. {Yuri Gagarin became the first cosmonaut to orbit Earth in 1961.}

Cosmonauts is the plural of cosmonaut, a Russian space traveler—the equivalent of an American astronaut. The term comes from Russian and reflects the Soviet space program's parallel development during the Cold War space race: {Yuri Gagarin was the first cosmonaut to orbit Earth}. The distinction persists today, with cosmonauts typically referring to those in the Russian space program.

Cosmopolitan describes someone or something at home in many countries and cultures, free from local prejudices or national limitations. A cosmopolitan city like New York draws people from everywhere. A cosmopolitan person has broad international experience and outlook: {She's thoroughly cosmopolitan—educated in Paris, working in Tokyo}. The noun means such a person, or the vodka-and-cranberry cocktail popular since the 1990s.

Cosmos refers to the universe as an ordered, harmonious whole—the opposite of chaos. Ancient Greek philosophers used the term to describe a reality governed by natural laws rather than arbitrary forces. {The cosmos stretches beyond what we can observe.} More modestly, cosmos can mean any complete, self-contained system: {the cosmos of medieval thought}. Cosmos is also a garden flower with delicate, daisy-like petals.

Cosplay is dressing up as a character from fiction, video games, anime, or other media—the word blends "costume" and "play." What distinguishes cosplay from ordinary costume-wearing is the culture around it: cosplayers often make elaborate outfits, attend conventions, and pose for photos in character. The verb means to engage in this practice: {She cosplays as Sailor Moon}.

A cosplayer is someone who dresses up as a character from fiction, gaming, or popular culture—the word blends "costume" and "player." Cosplayers create elaborate outfits to wear at conventions, competitions, or photo shoots: {The cosplayers at Comic-Con were incredible this year}. The practice ranges from casual fan tribute to intricate craftsmanship requiring months of work.

Cosplayers are people who dress in costumes to portray specific characters, typically from anime, video games, comics, or films. The practice—cosplay—blends costume and roleplay, ranging from casual fan appreciation to elaborate craftsmanship competitions. Cosplayers gather at conventions, photo shoots, and online communities: {The cosplayers at Comic-Con spent months on their outfits}.

Cosplaying is the activity of dressing up as a character from fiction, video games, anime, or other media, often with elaborate costumes and accessories crafted by the wearer. The term blends "costume" and "play," and practitioners take pride in accuracy and craftsmanship. Cosplaying is most visible at fan conventions, where participants pose for photos and compete in costume contests. {She spent months cosplaying as her favorite anime character.}

Cosplays is the plural of cosplay, the practice of dressing as characters from fiction, video games, anime, or other media. People cosplay at conventions, Halloween, or for social media content. As a verb, cosplays means engages in this activity: {She cosplays obscure anime characters}. The word blends "costume" and "play."

Cost is what must be given up to obtain something—usually money, but also time, effort, or sacrifice. The cost of a car is its price; the cost of success might be years of work. Costs in business are expenses: {operating costs}, {labor costs}. To cost is to require payment or loss: {The mistake cost him his job}. At all costs means regardless of what must be sacrificed.

A costar is a performer who shares top billing with another in a film, play, or television show. The word implies roughly equal prominence—neither is supporting the other. As a verb, to costar is to appear alongside another lead: {She costars with him in the new thriller}. Also spelled co-star.

Costly means expensive or requiring significant resources: {a costly renovation}, {a costly mistake}. The word emphasizes the burden of the expense rather than just the price—something costly depletes what you have. Costly errors aren't just expensive in money; they may cost time, reputation, or opportunity. {The delay proved costly to the campaign}.

Costs are expenses—the money, effort, or resources required to obtain or accomplish something. In business, costs include materials, labor, and overhead: {We need to cut costs}. Legal costs are fees for litigation. The phrase {at all costs} means regardless of sacrifice required. To cost is to require expenditure: {The renovation cost us fifty thousand}.

A costume is clothing worn to portray a character or disguise identity—for Halloween, theater, or themed events: {She made her own witch costume}. The word also describes the characteristic dress of a particular time, place, or group: {period costume}, {national costume}. As a verb, to costume is to provide with or dress in such clothing. Costume jewelry is decorative but made of inexpensive materials.

Costumes are clothing worn to transform appearance, typically for theatrical performances, Halloween, or costume parties. Actors wear costumes to become their characters; partygoers wear costumes to become pirates, zombies, or celebrities for a night. {The kids picked out their Halloween costumes in September}. A costume drama or costume piece is set in a historical period, with actors dressed accordingly. As a verb, to costume is to provide or dress in such attire: {She costumed the entire production herself}.

Cosy describes warm, comfortable snugness—a quality of sheltered intimacy: {a cosy cottage}, {a cosy evening by the fire}. The word suggests pleasant smallness rather than cramped space. A cosy is also a padded cover that keeps a teapot warm. To cosy up to someone is to ingratiate yourself or become friendly, often with ulterior motives. British spelling; Americans write cozy.

A cot is a small, portable bed with a collapsible frame, typically used for camping or as temporary sleeping arrangements: {We set up cots for the overnight guests}. In British English, cot refers to what Americans call a crib—a baby's bed with raised sides. A cot may also be a simple bed in a military barracks or summer camp.

A cottage is a small, simple house, typically in a rural or semi-rural setting. The word evokes quaintness and charm: {a cottage in the woods}, {a thatched cottage}. Cottages often serve as vacation homes: {We rented a cottage by the lake for the summer}. In some contexts, cottage suggests modest or cozy rather than strictly small.

Cotton is a soft, fluffy fiber that grows around the seeds of cotton plants, harvested and spun into thread for textiles. Cotton fabric is lightweight and breathable: {a cotton shirt}, {cotton sheets}. The plant itself is also called cotton. To {cotton to} something is to take a liking to it: {I never cottoned to his way of doing things}.

A couch is a common piece of furniture, also called a sofa, which accommodates cushioned seating or lying down. Before another word, couch signifies things you do while on a couch in a formal or humorous way, like couch surfing (flipping through TV channels) or couch potato (a person who spends too much time on a couch). To couch an argument is to express it in a particular way or context.

Couchsurfing is staying temporarily at someone's home, typically sleeping on their couch or spare bed, rather than paying for a hotel. The practice gained popularity through online networks connecting travelers with hosts willing to offer free accommodation: {I couchsurfed my way across Europe}. The term implies informal, budget travel and often a spirit of cultural exchange. (Capitalized Couchsurfing is the branded hospitality platform.)

A cougar is a large wild cat native to the Americas, also called mountain lion, puma, or panther. Tawny-colored and solitary, cougars range from Canadian wilderness to South American mountains. In slang, a cougar is an older woman who pursues younger men romantically or sexually: {She's a total cougar—her boyfriend is twenty-three}.

Cougars are large wild cats native to the Americas, also called mountain lions, pumas, or panthers. They're solitary predators ranging from Canadian wilderness to South American mountains. In slang, a cougar is an older woman who pursues younger men romantically or sexually: {She's a cougar—her boyfriend is twenty years younger}. The term can be playful or disparaging depending on context.

Cough is both the verb for the sudden, noisy expulsion of air from the lungs—usually involuntary and often triggered by irritation or illness—and the noun for that sound or the condition causing it. {I couldn't stop coughing during the movie.} An engine or machine that sputters may also be said to cough. To cough up is to expel something by coughing, or informally, to reluctantly produce something owed: {He finally coughed up the money he borrowed.}

Coughing is the act of expelling air from the lungs with a sudden sharp sound, typically to clear the throat or airways. A coughing fit is a prolonged bout that's hard to control. The word also works as a noun for the sound itself: {The coughing from the back row was distracting}.

A council is a group of people assembled to deliberate, advise, or govern. Cities have city councils, churches have church councils, and organizations convene councils to make decisions: {The council voted to approve the budget}. A council of war is a meeting to plan military strategy. The word often appears in official bodies: {the UN Security Council}, {student council}.

Councils is the plural of council, a group of people assembled to deliberate, advise, or govern. City councils make local laws. A council of elders guides a community. Student councils represent their peers. The word often appears in official names: {the UN Security Council}, {the Council of Trent}. Not to be confused with counsel, which means advice or a lawyer.

Counsel is advice, especially of a thoughtful or professional kind: {legal counsel}, {seek counsel from a mentor}. As a verb, to counsel is to advise or guide: {She counseled him to wait}. A counsel is also a lawyer or group of lawyers representing someone in court: {counsel for the defense}. To {keep one's own counsel} is to keep thoughts private.

Counseling is professional guidance for personal, psychological, or vocational problems. A counselor helps clients work through difficulties—marriage troubles, career decisions, grief, addiction. The term covers various approaches: {marriage counseling}, {grief counseling}, {career counseling}. In American English, counseling; in British, counselling. Distinguished from therapy mainly by being shorter-term and more focused on specific issues rather than deep psychological exploration.

Counselling is the British spelling of counseling—professional guidance for personal, psychological, or vocational problems. A counsellor helps clients work through difficulties by listening and offering perspective rather than direct advice: {She started counselling after the divorce}. The term covers everything from marriage counselling to grief counselling to career counselling.

Counsellor is the British spelling of counselor—someone who gives advice or guidance. A counsellor may work professionally in therapy, school guidance, or legal matters, or serve in an advisory role: {She spoke with a grief counsellor}. At summer camps, counsellors supervise young campers. The spelling with double L prevails in British, Canadian, and Australian English.

A counselor is someone who gives guidance or advice. School counselors help students with academic and personal matters. Camp counselors supervise children at summer camp. In therapy contexts, a counselor provides professional support for emotional or psychological issues: {She's been seeing a counselor since the divorce}. In law, counselor (or counsellor) is a formal title for an attorney: {Counselor, you may proceed}.

Counselors are people who give guidance or advice. School counselors help students with academic and personal matters. Camp counselors supervise children at summer camps. In therapy contexts, a counselor provides professional support for mental health or substance abuse issues: {She started seeing a counselor after the divorce}. Legal usage refers to attorneys: {counselor at law}. Also spelled counsellors in British English.

The noun and verb count is about numbers. When children learn numbers in sequence, they know how to count. When you count something, you determine how many there are. The number you come up with is the count. When something counts, it matters, has value, or is significant: Make your vote count! If you don’t count something, you do not acknowledge its significance: You treat me like my feelings don’t count. A different count is a title of rank for European nobility, the equivalent of a British earl.

A countdown is a backward count to zero marking the start of an event—most famously a rocket launch: {Ten, nine, eight...} The term extends to any final period before something significant: {the countdown to Christmas}, {the countdown to election day}. As a verb, to count down is to mark this decreasing sequence.

Counter can function as a noun, verb, adjective or adverb, with a number of different meanings, behind many of which lies the idea of counting. In the most basic sense, a counter is something that measures, such as a Geiger counter (which detects levels of radiation) or a bean counter (a slang term for an accountant). Another common meaning of counter is a place where counting may be done (a checkout counter in a store), although kitchen counters don’t typically involve counting. When you counter something, you oppose, contradict, or act in opposition to it.

A counterattack is an attack made in response to an enemy's attack, aimed at regaining lost ground or seizing the initiative: {The army launched a counterattack at dawn}.
