A curmudgeon is a bad-tempered, difficult person, especially an older man who's chronically irritable or stubbornly set in his ways: {The old curmudgeon yelled at kids for cutting across his lawn}. The word often carries a hint of grudging affection—curmudgeons may be cantankerous, but they're frequently seen as characters rather than villains.

Currencies is the plural of currency, which is money in circulation within a country or economic zone: {The euro and dollar are the world's most traded currencies}. Currency also means general acceptance or prevalence: {The idea gained currency in academic circles}. Foreign currencies fluctuate in value against one another, creating exchange rates that matter for trade and travel.

Currency is money in circulation within an economy—coins, bills, or digital equivalents: {foreign currency}, {The local currency is the peso}. More broadly, currency means general acceptance or prevalence: {The idea gained currency among economists}. Something that has currency is in common use or widely acknowledged as valid: {outdated theories that no longer have currency}.

Current describes what flows or what exists now. Water currents and electrical currents move through channels; air currents move through atmosphere. The currency of money flows through economies. What is current is happening in the present moment: {current events}, {the current issue of a magazine}, {my current address}. A currant, spelled differently, is a small dried grape or berry.

Currents is the plural of current—flows of water, air, or electricity moving in a particular direction. Ocean currents carry warm or cold water across vast distances. Electrical currents power devices. The word also covers prevailing trends or movements: {the currents of public opinion}, {political currents sweeping the nation}.

A curriculum is the set of courses and content that make up a program of study. Schools design curricula; teachers implement them. The word often appears in debates about what students should learn: {The district added financial literacy to the curriculum}. A curriculum vitae (CV) is a summary of one's educational and professional history—literally, the course of one's life.

Curry is a dish or sauce seasoned with a blend of spices—turmeric, cumin, coriander, chili—originating in South Asian cuisines but now global. The word also names the spice blend itself: {curry powder}. To curry favor is to seek approval through flattery, from an unrelated word meaning to groom a horse. A currycomb is a grooming tool with metal teeth. {We ordered chicken curry and naan.}

A curse is a spoken wish for harm or misfortune to befall someone, often invoking supernatural power: {She put a curse on the family}. The word extends to the harm itself—an affliction or source of persistent trouble: {Flooding has been the curse of this region}. To curse is to utter such a wish, or more commonly, to swear or use profanity: {He cursed under his breath}. Cursed describes something afflicted by a curse or, informally, something frustrating: {This cursed printer never works}.

Cursed means under a curse—afflicted by supernatural misfortune or divine punishment: {The tomb was said to be cursed}. Extended uses describe anything plagued by persistent bad luck: {a cursed project that kept failing}. In internet slang, cursed describes images or content that feel deeply unsettling or wrong in ways hard to articulate: {That photo of a hairless cat in a sweater is cursed}. As an adjective before a noun, cursed can simply mean damned or detestable: {this cursed weather}.
Curses, simply the plural of curse, is a mild oath used to express surprise or some undesirable emotion. It is often used ironically.

Cursing is the act of uttering curses—swear words, profanity, or wishes of harm. Someone who is cursing may be swearing in anger {Stop your cursing!} or invoking supernatural punishment {The old woman stood cursing the thieves who robbed her}. The word covers both casual profanity and formal malediction.

Cursive is a style of handwriting in which letters connect fluidly within words, allowing the pen to stay on the paper. The style developed for speed and efficiency before typing became dominant. Cursive writing is still taught in schools, though less universally than before: {Her cursive is elegant but hard to read}. The term also applies to typefaces that mimic this connected, flowing style.

A cursor is a movable indicator on a computer screen showing where the next action will occur—where typed text will appear, or where a click will land. The blinking vertical line in a text field is a cursor; so is the arrow you move with a mouse. The word originally meant a sliding part on a measuring instrument, from Latin for "runner."

A curtain is a piece of fabric hung to cover a window, divide a space, or conceal something behind it. Theater curtains separate stage from audience; shower curtains keep water contained. Figuratively, a curtain obscures: {a curtain of fog}, {the iron curtain}. To curtain is to provide or conceal with curtains. {Curtains} as slang means the end, especially death: {If they find us, it's curtains}.

Curtains are pieces of fabric hung to cover windows, block light, or provide privacy. They also hang at the front of a stage, opening and closing to mark acts. From this theatrical use comes the slang meaning: the end, especially death or ruin. {If they find out, it's curtains for us.} To draw the curtains can mean either to open or close them.

A curtsy is a gesture of respect or greeting in which a woman or girl bends her knees while keeping her back straight, often with a slight bow of the head. Traditionally performed before royalty or in formal settings: {She curtsied to the queen}. The male equivalent is a bow. Also spelled curtsey.

A curve is a line that bends smoothly, without angles. Roads curve through mountains, rivers curve across plains. The word extends to anything with such a shape: the curve of a hip, a curve in the road. To curve is to bend or follow such a path. A curveball in baseball breaks unexpectedly; to {throw someone a curve} is to surprise them with something difficult. To {grade on a curve} adjusts scores relative to class performance. {Ahead of the curve} means anticipating trends before others do.

A curveball is a baseball pitch thrown with spin that causes it to curve as it approaches the batter, making it harder to hit. The figurative meaning dominates everyday usage: an unexpected development that catches someone off guard. {Life threw me a curveball when I lost my job}. To {throw someone a curveball} is to surprise them with something difficult or unforeseen.

Curveballs are unexpected difficulties or surprises that disrupt plans or expectations. The term comes from baseball, where a curveball is a pitch that breaks sharply as it approaches the batter, making it hard to hit. Figuratively, life throws curveballs: {Just when I thought everything was settled, the company threw me a curveball with the layoffs}.

Curvy describes something with curves—not straight or angular. A curvy {road} winds through hills. Curvy {handwriting} has flowing loops. Applied to bodies, curvy typically describes women with prominent bust, hips, and waist: {She has a curvy figure}. The term is generally complimentary, suggesting shapeliness rather than thinness.

A cushion is a soft pad used for sitting, kneeling, or resting against—typically a fabric case stuffed with foam, feathers, or other yielding material. Cushion extends to anything that absorbs impact or provides a buffer: {a cushion of air}, {a financial cushion}. To cushion is to soften a blow or protect from harsh effects: {Savings cushioned the loss of her job}.

Cushions are soft pads used for comfort or decoration—on sofas, chairs, or floors. A cushion absorbs impact: {The snow cushioned her fall}. To cushion something is to soften or protect it from shock: {Savings can cushion the blow of job loss}. A cushion can also be a protective margin: {We built in a two-week cushion before the deadline}.

Cushy means comfortable, easy, or involving little effort. A cushy {job} pays well without demanding much work. A cushy {assignment} poses no real challenge. The word often carries a hint of envy or resentment—implying someone has it easier than they deserve: {He landed a cushy position through connections}.

A cusp is a pointed end where two curves meet—the cusps of a crescent moon, the cusps of teeth. In astrology, a cusp is the boundary between zodiac signs. The most common use is figurative: to be {on the cusp} of something is to be at the point just before it begins or changes: {on the cusp of adulthood}, {on the cusp of a breakthrough}.

Cuss is an informal American word for curse in both noun and verb senses. A cuss is a swear word: {He let out a string of cusses}. To cuss is to swear: {She cussed him out good}. Cuss also means a person, usually with an adjective: {He's a stubborn old cuss}. The tone is folksy and rural.

Cussing is the act of using profane or vulgar language, synonymous with cursing or swearing. The term is informal and somewhat folksy, more common in American English and regional dialects. Someone who cusses a lot might be described as having a {cussing habit}, and a parent might scold a child for {cussing in front of grandma}. To cuss someone out is to berate them with profanity.

Custard is a creamy dessert or sauce made from milk or cream thickened with eggs, sugar, and often vanilla. It can be poured over fruit or cake, baked into pies, or served on its own. The texture ranges from pourable to firmly set depending on preparation. {She drizzled custard over the warm apple crumble.}

A custodian is someone responsible for the care and protection of something. In American English, custodian often means a janitor—the person who maintains and cleans a building: {The custodian unlocked the gym for us}. More broadly, a custodian guards assets or records: a {custodian} of financial accounts, a {custodian} of cultural heritage. The role implies stewardship rather than ownership.

Custody is the state of being held or kept somewhere, especially under guard. A suspect is {taken into custody} by police. In legal contexts involving children, custody refers to the right and responsibility to care for a child: {She has full custody of the kids}, {They share joint custody}. A custodian is someone who has custody of something—whether a prisoner, a child, or a building.

Custom is a habitual practice or long-established tradition within a group: {It's our custom to open presents on Christmas Eve}. Customs in the plural refers to duties levied on imported goods, or the government agency that collects them: {We went through customs at the airport}. As an adjective, custom means made to order rather than mass-produced: {custom furniture}, {a custom suit}. The adjective often compounds: custom-built, custom-made.

A customer is someone who buys goods or services from a business. The word emphasizes the transaction: a person browsing is a shopper, but once they buy, they become a customer. {The customer is always right} reflects the commercial principle of deferring to buyers. Regular customers may be called regulars. In informal speech, customer can describe any person you're dealing with: {He's a tough customer}.

Customers is the plural of customer—people who buy goods or services from a business. The word emphasizes the commercial relationship: {The store opens early to accommodate customers}. Customer also appears in expressions like {tough customer} (someone difficult to deal with) or {ugly customer} (someone dangerous or unpleasant).

Customization is the act of modifying something to suit individual preferences or requirements. A product or service can be customized to meet specific needs: {The software allows extensive customization of the interface}. Mass customization refers to producing goods tailored to individual customers while maintaining efficiency. The British spelling is customisation.

To customize is to modify something to fit particular preferences or requirements. You customize a car with aftermarket parts, customize software settings, or order a customized {birthday cake}. The word implies personal choice—making something yours rather than accepting the default: {You can customize your homepage layout}.

Customs has two main uses. One refers to the practices and traditions of a group or culture: {local customs}, {wedding customs}. The other refers to the government agency that inspects goods and people entering a country, or the place where this happens: {We got held up at customs}. Customs duties are taxes on imported goods.

The verb cut is frequent and has many meanings, all of which spring from its original and core definition: penetrate (and often separate) with a sharp-edged instrument. From this you might expect that the most frequent subject of cut is knife, but figurative meanings have far overtaken the original. Today, cut is most often used to mean reduce, as if by cutting: governments cut programs, companies cut prices. The noun cut simply names an instance of what the verb does: Recent cuts resulted in the area losing its bus service. She fell and got a cut on her leg.

A cutback is a reduction, especially in spending, production, or personnel: {The company announced cutbacks in its workforce}. Budget cutbacks trim expenses; cutbacks in oil production reduce output. In surfing, a cutback is a sharp turn back toward the breaking part of a wave. To cut back is to reduce or prune.

Cutbacks are reductions in something, especially spending, services, or staff levels. Organizations announce cutbacks when they need to reduce costs or scale down operations. {The company's cutbacks meant laying off three hundred workers.} Budget cutbacks often affect programs that serve the public. The word carries negative connotations since cutbacks typically mean people lose jobs or access to services they previously had.

Cute describes something appealing in a delicate or endearing way—a cute baby, a cute puppy, a cute outfit. The word often implies smallness or youthfulness. Applied to adults, cute usually means attractive in a fresh, approachable way rather than strikingly beautiful: {He's cute, but not my type}. Cute can also mean cleverly contrived, sometimes dismissively: {Don't get cute with me}. A cute trick or cute idea may be too clever for its own good.

Cuteness is the quality of being attractive in an endearing, often childlike way. Babies, kittens, and small things with large eyes trigger cuteness responses. The word can be dismissive when applied to attempts at cleverness: {Enough with the cuteness—just give me a straight answer}. Something done {for the cuteness} prioritizes charm over substance.

Cutie is an informal term of endearment for someone or something considered attractive, charming, or appealing in a sweet way. It's applied to people, animals, and occasionally objects: {What a cutie that puppy is!} The word often carries playful or affectionate connotations and is especially common when addressing or describing children, romantic interests, or anything deemed adorable. The diminutive form cutie pie intensifies the sweetness.

A cutlass is a short, broad sword with a slightly curved blade, associated especially with sailors and pirates of the 17th and 18th centuries. The design suited close combat in the cramped quarters of ships. The word now evokes romanticized piracy: {The pirate brandished his cutlass}.

Cutlery refers to eating utensils—knives, forks, and spoons used at the table. In British usage, cutlery covers all these implements; Americans more often say silverware or flatware. The word also extends to cutting instruments generally, especially knives: {a cutlery set}, {a shop selling fine cutlery}.

A cutoff is a point where something stops or is no longer included: {The cutoff for applications is Friday}. A cutoff can be a shortcut that cuts across a longer route, or a device that stops flow. Cutoffs are jeans cut off at the knee or higher. As an adjective, cutoff marks a limit: {cutoff date}, {cutoff score}.

Cutoffs are jeans or other pants that have been cut short to make them into shorts, typically with a raw, frayed edge rather than a finished hem. The term also refers to points or levels at which something stops or is excluded: {The cutoff for applications is Friday at midnight}. A cutoff can be a shortcut or a road that branches from a main route, or a device that stops a flow of liquid or gas.

A cutout is something cut from a larger piece—a shape removed from paper or cardboard, a hole cut in a wall, or a magazine figure snipped for a scrapbook. A cardboard cutout is a life-sized figure of a person, often a celebrity, used for display or photos. In espionage, a cutout is an intermediary who shields communication between agents: {The handler never met the asset directly—everything went through a cutout}. A cutout can also be a device that interrupts an electrical circuit.

Cuts is the plural of cut, covering the noun's many senses: wounds from sharp objects, portions of meat, reductions in amount or size, or versions of a film. In music, cuts are individual tracks: {The album has some great cuts}. Someone's cuts at the gym are their visible muscle definition. To make the cut is to qualify; to not make it is to be eliminated.

A cutter is a person or tool that cuts. The word appears in compounds describing specific functions: {box cutter}, {wire cutters}, {cookie cutter}. A cutter is also a small, fast boat—originally one that cuts through water. In baseball, a cutter is a fastball that breaks sharply. In self-harm contexts, a cutter is someone who cuts their own skin.

Cutthroat describes ruthless competition where participants show no mercy: {cutthroat business practices}, {a cutthroat industry}. The image is of someone willing to slit throats to win. As a noun, a cutthroat is a murderer or assassin. Cutthroat trout, a species native to western North America, has red markings under its jaw resembling a slashed throat.

Cutting describes the act of dividing something with a blade or sharp edge, or the result of such action. A cutting remark is sharply hurtful: {Her cutting words left him speechless}. Cutting-edge technology is at the forefront of innovation. In horticulture, a cutting is a piece of plant removed for propagation. The adjective describes cold that seems to slice through clothing: {a cutting wind}.

A cuttlefish is a marine mollusk related to squid and octopus, with eight arms, two tentacles, and an internal shell called a cuttlebone. Cuttlefish are known for their ability to rapidly change color and texture for camouflage or communication. The cuttlebone, rich in calcium, is often given to pet birds to sharpen their beaks.

Cyanide is a rapidly acting poison that prevents cells from using oxygen. The term covers several compounds containing a carbon-nitrogen group—most notoriously hydrogen cyanide (the gas used in Nazi death chambers) and potassium cyanide (the crystalline salt of spy capsules and murder mysteries). Despite its lethal reputation, cyanide has industrial uses in mining, metallurgy, and chemical synthesis. {The detective suspected cyanide when he smelled bitter almonds.}

Cyber is a prefix or adjective relating to computers, digital technology, and the internet. It appears in compounds: {cybersecurity}, {cybercrime}, {cyberspace}, {cyberattack}. Standing alone, cyber often refers to online threats or warfare: {The Pentagon is investing heavily in cyber}. In casual use, it can sound dated or bureaucratic—a relic of 1990s internet terminology that persists mainly in government and security contexts.

A cyberattack is a malicious attempt to damage, disrupt, or gain unauthorized access to computer systems, networks, or data. Cyberattacks range from individual hackers stealing personal information to state-sponsored operations targeting critical infrastructure: {The cyberattack knocked out the power grid for three days}. Common forms include ransomware, phishing, and denial-of-service attacks.

To cyberbully is to harass, intimidate, or humiliate someone through digital channels—social media, text messages, online forums. Unlike schoolyard bullying, cyberbullying follows victims home and can spread rapidly to wide audiences. As a noun, a cyberbully is someone who engages in this behavior: {The cyberbullies created fake accounts to torment her}.

Cyberbullying is harassment, intimidation, or cruelty conducted through digital channels—social media, text messages, online forums, or gaming platforms. Unlike schoolyard bullying, it follows victims home and can spread rapidly to wide audiences: {The cyberbullying got so bad she deleted all her accounts}. It often involves public shaming, spreading rumors, or sharing embarrassing content without consent.

Cybercrime is illegal activity conducted through computers or the internet. It ranges from hacking and identity theft to online fraud, ransomware attacks, and distribution of illegal content. {The FBI's cybercrime division investigates data breaches affecting millions of users.} The term covers both crimes unique to digital technology and traditional crimes committed through digital means.

Cyberpunk is a science fiction genre set in dystopian futures where advanced technology—especially computing and cybernetics—coexists with social decay. The aesthetic combines high tech with low life: hackers, megacorporations, neon-lit slums, and body modification. {Blade Runner} and {Neuromancer} defined the genre. The term extends to the subculture and visual style it spawned.

Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting computer systems, networks, and data from digital attacks, unauthorized access, and damage. It encompasses everything from password protocols to firewalls to encryption. As more of life moves online, cybersecurity has become a major concern for individuals, corporations, and governments alike: {The company hired a cybersecurity firm after the breach}.

Cybersex is sexual activity conducted through digital communication—exchanging erotic messages, images, or engaging in mutual stimulation while connected online. The term emerged with internet chat rooms in the 1990s and now covers texting, video calls, and virtual reality encounters: {We had cybersex over video chat}. Also called *cyber* for short.

Cyberspace is the notional environment where digital communication and online activity occur—the interconnected realm of computers, networks, and the internet experienced as a place rather than infrastructure. {Kids today spend half their lives in cyberspace.} The term emerged from science fiction but now appears in serious contexts like cybersecurity policy and international law. It implies a space you enter or navigate, distinct from physical reality.

Cyberstalking is the use of digital technology to harass, monitor, or threaten someone—typically through repeated unwanted contact, tracking online activity, or sending threatening messages. Unlike casual online annoyance, cyberstalking implies a pattern of behavior that makes the target fear for their safety: {She filed a police report about the cyberstalking after he created fake accounts to follow her everywhere online}.

A cyborg is a being that combines organic and mechanical parts—a human or other organism enhanced with technological components. The term blends "cybernetic" and "organism." Science fiction imagines cyborgs with robotic limbs or computer-integrated brains, but in a looser sense, anyone with a pacemaker or cochlear implant qualifies: {We're all becoming cyborgs, glued to our devices}.

Cyborgs are beings that combine organic and mechanical parts—humans enhanced with technological implants or machines given biological components. The term blends "cybernetic" and "organism." In science fiction, cyborgs range from humans with prosthetic limbs to figures more machine than flesh: {The villain was a cyborg with a mechanical arm}. The concept extends to anyone deeply integrated with technology: {We're all cyborgs now, dependent on our phones}.

Cycle is closely related to circle. A typical cycle is abstract and has the quality of repetitiveness or ebbing and flowing (business cycle, cycle of seasons). A set of artistic works with separate, related parts is called a cycle (song cycle). Something that cycles repeats: The phases of the moon cycle each month. A person who cycles to work rides a bicycle.

Cycles is the plural of cycle—a series of events that repeats in the same order: {the cycles of the seasons}, {business cycles}, {sleep cycles}. In exercise, cycles often refers to stationary bikes or spinning equipment: {The gym just got new cycles}. As a verb form, cycles means to ride a bicycle or to move through phases: {She cycles to work}, {The thermostat cycles on and off}.

Cycling is the activity of riding a bicycle, whether for transportation, exercise, or sport. As a sport, it encompasses road racing, track racing, mountain biking, and BMX, with events like the Tour de France drawing global attention. The term also describes any process that moves through repeated phases or stages: {the cycling of nutrients through an ecosystem}. In everyday use, someone who cycles commutes or exercises by bike.

A cyclist is a person who rides a bicycle. The term applies to casual riders and competitive racers alike: {Cyclists filled the bike lane during rush hour}. In traffic contexts, cyclist often distinguishes bicycle riders from motorists and pedestrians.

A cyclone is a large-scale rotating storm system, with winds spiraling inward around a low-pressure center. In the Indian Ocean and South Pacific, cyclone names what's called a hurricane in the Atlantic or typhoon in the western Pacific—all the same phenomenon. More loosely, cyclone describes any violent rotating windstorm: {The cyclone tore through the trailer park}. Figuratively, a person or force that moves with destructive energy: {She swept through the office like a cyclone}.

Cyclones are large-scale weather systems characterized by rotating winds around a low-pressure center. In the Northern Hemisphere they spin counterclockwise; in the Southern Hemisphere, clockwise. The term covers tropical storms and hurricanes as well as the broader atmospheric disturbances that bring unsettled weather to temperate regions. Colloquially, cyclone may refer to any violent windstorm, including tornadoes, though meteorologists distinguish between them. {The cyclone made landfall with devastating winds.}

A cyclops is a one-eyed giant from Greek mythology—creatures who forged Zeus's thunderbolts and whom Odysseus famously outwitted. The image extends to anything with a single central eye or lens: a cyclops {camera}, a cyclops {fish}. In biology, Cyclops is a genus of tiny one-eyed crustaceans. Plural: cyclopes or cyclopses.

A cylinder is a three-dimensional shape with straight parallel sides and circular ends of equal size, like a soup can or a drinking glass. The term extends to any object with this form, from engine cylinders where pistons move to the rotating cylinders of a revolver that hold cartridges. {The engine runs on four cylinders.} In casual speech, saying something is {firing on all cylinders} means it's operating at full capacity or performing optimally.

A cymbal is a round metal plate that produces a ringing or crashing sound when struck or clashed against another cymbal. Cymbals come in pairs for hand-clashing or mount singly on stands for drumsticks and brushes. They're essential to drum kits, orchestras, and marching bands: {The drummer hit the cymbal at the song's climax}.

Cymbals are a pair of brass percussion instruments, circular plates that produce a crashing or shimmering sound when struck together or hit with a drumstick. They appear in orchestras, marching bands, and drum kits. The singular cymbal usually refers to one mounted on a stand: {a ride cymbal}, {a crash cymbal}, {hi-hat cymbals}.

A cynic believes people act from self-interest and distrusts claims of altruism or sincerity. The attitude ranges from healthy skepticism to corrosive distrust: {Don't be such a cynic—she might actually want to help}. Cynical describes the outlook; cynicism names it. A cynic sees the price of everything and the value of nothing.

Cynical, an adjective, is used to characterize people who are pessimistic or who are ready to believe the worst about others. Opinions of such people are also characterized with cynical: His cynical view of human nature is evident in all of his films. If you are cynical about someone’s motives or actions, you think they have a self-serving agenda, despite what they may say. If you are cynical about something abstract—politics, for example—you don’t expect good results.

Cynicism is a disposition to distrust others' motives and dismiss claims of sincerity or goodness. A cynic assumes people act from self-interest and that idealistic talk masks baser intentions: {Her cynicism about politics kept her from voting}. The word can describe a general worldview or a reaction to specific disappointments: {Years in corporate law had bred a deep cynicism about justice}.

Cypress is a type of evergreen conifer with dark foliage and a distinctive tall, narrow shape. The trees grow in warm climates and are associated with Mediterranean landscapes and American swamps, where bald cypress trees rise from standing water. Cypress wood is valued for its durability and resistance to rot. The trees have ancient associations with mourning and cemeteries: {A row of cypress lined the path to the grave}.

Czar was the title of Russian emperors until 1917, from a word meaning Caesar. The spelling tsar is closer to the Russian. In American English, czar commonly refers to someone given broad authority over a particular domain: {drug czar}, {energy czar}, {climate czar}. These appointed officials typically coordinate policy across agencies.

Czars is the plural of czar, the title of Russian emperors before the 1917 revolution. The word derives from Caesar. In American politics, czar denotes an official with broad authority over a particular policy area: {drug czar}, {energy czar}, {border czar}. These appointments typically lack formal power but signal political priority. The spelling tsar is preferred in British English.

A dab is a small amount or portion of something: I’ll take a dab of butter. A quick, small motion involving some purpose is also a dab. This dab is frequently encountered as a verb: Dab the sponge gently around the wound. The fixed expression smack dab in the middle (or center) means exactly in the middle. A concentrated form of cannabis is called dab and using this for recreational purposes is called dabbing.

To dabble is to splash or play in water with hands or feet, like a child at the edge of a pool. Ducks dabble when they feed in shallow water, tipping forward to reach below the surface. The word extends to casual or superficial involvement in an activity: {She dabbles in painting but never commits to it}. A dabbler tries things without serious dedication.

A dactylozooid is a specialized defensive or feeding polyp in colonial marine invertebrates like siphonophores and hydroids. Unlike reproductive polyps, dactylozooids are modified for capturing prey or protecting the colony, typically bearing stinging cells. They lack mouths and depend on other colony members for nutrition.

Dad is an informal word for father, used both as a term of address and a general noun: {Dad, can I borrow the car?}, {My dad taught me to fish}. Dad joke refers to corny, pun-based humor stereotypically favored by fathers. The word carries warmth and familiarity compared to the more formal father. (Capitalized Dad is used when addressing one's father directly or as a name substitute.)

Daddy is a child's word for father, often the first form children use before graduating to dad. Adults may use it affectionately or nostalgically: {I still call him Daddy}. In sexual contexts, daddy refers to an older male partner, often implying dominance or a provider role: {Who's your daddy?} A {sugar daddy} is a wealthy older man who lavishes gifts on a younger partner. Informally, daddy can mark someone as the best or most dominant in a field: {He's the daddy of all quarterbacks}.

Dads is the plural of dad, an informal word for father. The term appears in contexts discussing fathers collectively: {Dads today are more involved in childcare than previous generations}. It also labels social groups: {a support group for new dads}, {soccer dads}. In direct address, Dad typically remains singular even with multiple fathers present.

A daemon is a background process in computing that runs without direct user interaction, handling system tasks like printing, email, or network services. The spelling distinguishes these programs from the older sense of daemon (also spelled daimon), a spirit or supernatural being in Greek thought—neither good nor evil, but an intermediary force. The computing sense plays on this: daemons work invisibly, attending to tasks behind the scenes. {The mail daemon processes incoming messages automatically.}

A daf is a large frame drum used in Middle Eastern and Central Asian music, particularly in Persian, Kurdish, and Sufi traditions. It consists of a wooden ring with an animal skin stretched across one side, often decorated with metal rings or chains that jingle when struck. The daf features prominently in devotional music and folk celebrations: {The daf players led the procession}.

A daffodil is a spring-flowering bulb plant with bright yellow or white trumpet-shaped blooms. Native to Europe, daffodils are among the first flowers to appear after winter, making them symbols of renewal and hope: {The daffodils are coming up}. The flower is also called narcissus or jonquil, though these terms have slightly different botanical applications.

Daffodils are spring-flowering plants with trumpet-shaped yellow or white blooms, among the first flowers to appear after winter. They grow from bulbs and are widely cultivated in gardens and naturalized in meadows. The singular is daffodil: {The daffodils are blooming early this year}.

Daffy means silly, eccentric, or slightly crazy in a harmless, endearing way: {She has a daffy sense of humor}, {His daffy antics made everyone laugh}. The word suggests lighthearted foolishness rather than genuine mental instability—more whimsical than unhinged.

Daft means silly, foolish, or not thinking clearly. The word is more common in British than American English: {Don't be daft—of course I'll help}. Someone who is {daft about} something is infatuated with it. A daft idea lacks sense or practicality. The word is mild, often affectionate rather than harsh.

A dagger is a short knife with a pointed blade, designed for stabbing. Unlike swords, daggers are typically held close and used in tight quarters. The word carries associations with treachery and assassination—daggers are concealed, then drawn at close range. To {look daggers} at someone is to glare with hostility. In printing, a dagger (†) is a reference mark, often indicating a footnote or that a person is deceased.

Daggers are short, pointed knives designed for stabbing. The word extends to dagger-shaped symbols (†) used in typography, often to mark footnotes or indicate death dates. To {look daggers} at someone is to glare with hostility. To be {at daggers drawn} is to be in open conflict, ready to fight.

Daily describes something that happens every day or relates to a single day: a daily {routine}, a daily {newspaper}, your daily {commute}. As an adverb, it means once each day: {Take the medication daily}. A daily can be a newspaper published every day, or in British usage, a cleaning person who comes each day. {Daily} emphasizes regularity and routine—the ordinary rhythm of life.

Dainty describes something delicately small, pretty, or refined: {dainty teacups}, {dainty fingers}, {dainty steps}. The word often suggests fastidiousness—someone dainty may be overly particular about food or manners. A dainty is a small, choice morsel of food, now old-fashioned: {The table was spread with dainties}. The word can carry a faintly dismissive edge, implying something too precious or fragile.

A daiquiri is a cocktail made with rum, lime juice, and sugar. The classic version is served straight up, shaken with ice and strained. Frozen daiquiris are blended with ice into a slush, often with added fruit flavors: {strawberry daiquiri}, {banana daiquiri}. The drink originated in Cuba.

Dairy refers to milk and products made from it—cheese, butter, yogurt, cream. A dairy is also a farm that produces milk or a facility that processes it: {The dairy delivers fresh milk every morning}. As an adjective, dairy describes things related to milk production: {dairy cow}, {dairy industry}. People who are lactose intolerant often say they {can't do dairy}.

Daisies is the plural of daisy, a common flowering plant with white petals radiating from a yellow center. The word comes from "day's eye," describing how the flower opens at dawn and closes at dusk. Daisies grow wild in lawns and meadows and are among the first flowers children learn to recognize. The phrase {pushing up daisies} is a darkly humorous way of saying someone is dead and buried.

A daisy is a flower with white petals radiating from a yellow center, common in lawns and meadows. The word extends to similar flowers in the composite family. Something described as daisy suggests freshness or innocence: {fresh as a daisy}. To {push up daisies} is to be dead and buried. As slang, a daisy is something excellent of its kind: {That car's a real daisy}. (Capitalized Daisy is a given name.)

A dalang is the puppeteer and narrator in traditional Indonesian shadow puppet theater (wayang). The dalang manipulates the puppets, voices all characters, directs the gamelan orchestra, and serves as storyteller—often performing epic tales from the Ramayana or Mahabharata through the night. The role carries spiritual significance; the dalang mediates between the human and divine realms. Figuratively, a dalang is a mastermind or puppet master orchestrating events from behind the scenes: {The general was the dalang of the coup}.

A dalmatian is a breed of dog with a white coat covered in black or liver-colored spots. Originally bred as carriage dogs, they became associated with firehouses in the era of horse-drawn fire engines. The breed is known for its distinctive spotted pattern and high energy: {The dalmatian ran alongside the carriage}. (Capitalized Dalmatian refers to the region or its people.)

A dam is a barrier built across a river or stream to hold back water, creating a reservoir: {The Hoover Dam supplies power to three states}. By extension, any obstruction that blocks flow. To dam is to block or hold back: {dam a stream}, {dam up emotions}. A dam is also an animal's mother, used mainly for horses and livestock—the counterpart to sire.

Damage is harm or injury that reduces value, usefulness, or normal function: {The storm caused extensive damage to the roof}. The plural damages refers to money awarded in legal compensation: {The jury awarded two million dollars in damages}. To damage something is to inflict such harm. Colloquially, {what's the damage?} asks for the cost of something.

Damaged describes something that has been harmed, impaired, or made less valuable or effective. Physical objects suffer damage: {The storm damaged the roof}. Reputation, relationships, and credibility can also be damaged. Informally, calling a person damaged suggests they carry psychological wounds from past trauma: {She's too damaged to trust anyone}.

Damages is the legal term for money awarded to compensate someone who has been wronged. A court orders damages after finding liability for injury, breach of contract, or other harm: {The jury awarded her $2 million in damages}. Punitive damages go beyond compensation to punish egregious conduct. Outside legal contexts, damages sometimes means costs or expenses informally: {What's the damages?}

Dammit is a spelling of "damn it" that reflects its pronunciation as a single stressed unit. It expresses frustration, annoyance, or emphasis: {Dammit, I forgot my keys}. The spelling signals casual or emphatic speech rather than the more deliberate "damn it." Mild profanity, acceptable in most informal contexts.

Damn means to condemn to eternal punishment in hell, or to condemn or curse generally: {The priest warned that sinners would be damned}. {The critics damned the play}. As an exclamation, damn expresses anger, frustration, or emphasis: {Damn, I forgot my keys}. As an intensifier, it adds force: {That's a damn good idea}. {I'm damn tired of this}. Damn ranks among the milder profanities—offensive to some, especially in religious contexts, but common enough to appear in polite company. {Damn it} or {dammit} is the exclamation; {not worth a damn} means worthless; {damn with faint praise} means to praise so weakly as to imply criticism.

Damnation is condemnation to eternal punishment in hell, the fate religious traditions promise to the wicked: {The preacher threatened damnation for unrepentant sinners}. As an exclamation, damnation expresses anger or frustration, though it sounds old-fashioned now: {Damnation! I've lost my wallet again}. The word carries religious weight even in secular use.

Damned means condemned to hell, or cursed: {the damned souls in Dante's Inferno}. As an intensifier, damned adds emphasis: {That's a damned shame}. {I'm damned tired of waiting}. {I'll be damned} expresses surprise: {Well, I'll be damned—he actually showed up}. {Damned if you do, damned if you don't} describes a no-win situation. The damned are those condemned to hell, collectively.

Damning as a verb means condemning to hell or cursing. As an adjective, damning describes evidence or testimony so incriminating it virtually guarantees condemnation: {The emails were damning}. {She gave a damning account of his behavior}. Damning implies something so conclusive it leaves no room for defense.

Damp means slightly wet—more than dry but less than soaked: {The basement walls were damp}. A damp cloth has absorbed some moisture. Damp weather feels humid and clammy. As a verb, to damp (or dampen) is to make slightly wet, or to reduce intensity: {damp the fire}, {damp someone's enthusiasm}. In mining, damp refers to dangerous gases like firedamp or blackdamp.

Dams is the plural of dam—a barrier built across a river or stream to hold back water: {Beavers build dams from sticks and mud}. The word also refers to female parents of animals, especially horses and dogs: {The pups' dams were both champions}. As a verb, to dam is to block or obstruct flow: {They dammed the creek to create a swimming hole}.

A damsel is a young unmarried woman—the word is archaic or literary, surviving mainly in the phrase {damsel in distress}, which describes a woman needing rescue. The trope appears throughout fairy tales, romances, and adventure stories, though modern usage often invokes it ironically or critically: {She refused to play the damsel in distress}.

Dance is rhythmic movement of the body, usually to music. People dance socially, ceremonially, or as performance art. A dance is a particular sequence of steps {the waltz is an elegant dance} or a social gathering where dancing occurs {the school dance}. To dance around something is to avoid addressing it directly. Flames dance; light dances on water—anything that moves with lively irregularity.

A dancefloor is the area in a club, ballroom, or venue designated for dancing—typically a smooth, open surface distinct from seating areas. The word evokes nightlife and electronic music culture: {We stayed on the dancefloor until 3 a.m.} A packed dancefloor signals a successful party. Also spelled as two words: dance floor.

Dancehall is a genre of Jamaican popular music that emerged in the late 1970s, characterized by faster rhythms than reggae, digital instrumentation, and often explicit or boastful lyrics delivered in Jamaican patois. The term originally referred to the physical venues where sound systems played music for dancing, but came to name the musical style itself. Dancehall has influenced hip-hop, pop, and electronic music worldwide. {The dancehall riddim got everyone moving.}

A dancer is someone who dances, whether professionally or recreationally. The word usually implies skill or training: {She's been a dancer since age five}, {ballet dancers}, {backup dancers}. Someone moving awkwardly at a wedding isn't typically called a dancer—they're just dancing.

Dances is the plural of dance and the third-person singular verb form. A dance is a series of rhythmic movements to music, or a social gathering for dancing: {She knows all the traditional dances}, {He dances every weekend}. Figuratively, to dance around something is to avoid addressing it directly: {The candidate dances around the question}.

Dancing is moving the body rhythmically, usually to music. It can be social, artistic, or ceremonial—from ballroom to ballet to ritual. As an adjective, dancing describes lively movement: {dancing flames}, {dancing eyes}. The gerund often implies ongoing activity: {She took up dancing}, {They went dancing}.

A dandelion is a common wildflower with bright yellow heads that mature into fluffy white spheres of seeds. Children blow on the seed heads and watch them scatter. The plant is considered a weed in lawns but the leaves are edible as salad greens, and the roots can be roasted as a coffee substitute. {The yard was full of dandelions.}

Dandelions is the plural of dandelion, a common yellow-flowered weed with jagged leaves and a fluffy white seed head that children blow to make wishes. The plant is hardy and persistent, sprouting in lawns despite efforts to eradicate it: {The yard was covered in dandelions}. The leaves are edible and sometimes used in salads or wine.

Dandruff is the flaking of dead skin from the scalp, appearing as small white or grayish particles in the hair and on clothing. The condition is common and usually harmless but cosmetically unwelcome: {He brushed the dandruff off his shoulders before the interview}. Severe cases may indicate seborrheic dermatitis.

A dandy is a man excessively devoted to elegant dress and refined manners. The word carries a whiff of affectation—someone more concerned with appearance than substance: {He fussed over his cravat like a Victorian dandy}. As an adjective, dandy means fine or satisfactory, often with mild irony: {Well, that's just dandy}. The informal {dandy} suggests something is acceptable, though rarely enthusiastic: {Everything's dandy}.

Danger is the possibility of harm, injury, or loss. A situation presents danger when something bad might happen: {The hikers were in danger of hypothermia}. A danger is also a source of risk: {Icy roads are a danger to drivers}. To be {out of danger} is to have passed through a crisis safely. Dangerous is the adjective.

Dangerous describes something that poses a threat of harm, injury, or damage. A dangerous {animal} might attack. A dangerous {intersection} has frequent accidents. A dangerous {idea} threatens established order. The word can suggest excitement alongside risk: {He has a dangerous charm}. To {live dangerously} is to court risk, sometimes admiringly.

Dangle means to hang loosely, swinging or swaying: {Keys dangled from his belt}. Something dangled is suspended without firm attachment. To dangle something before someone is to offer it temptingly: {They dangled a promotion in front of her}. A dangling modifier in grammar attaches to the wrong word, creating confusion or unintended humor.

Danish refers to Denmark—its people, language, or culture: {Danish pastries}, {the Danish government}. A danish (lowercase) is a flaky pastry filled with fruit, cheese, or custard, named for its Scandinavian origins though the style has been thoroughly Americanized: {coffee and a danish}. The pastry sense often appears capitalized even when referring just to breakfast.

Dank describes something unpleasantly damp and cold, usually with a musty smell: {a dank cellar}, {the dank air of the cave}. The word suggests stagnant moisture and decay. In internet slang, dank flipped to mean excellent or high-quality, especially for memes: {dank memes}. This ironic use originated in cannabis culture, where dank described potent, pungent marijuana.

Dare means to have the courage or audacity to do something risky or unconventional: {How dare you speak to me that way}, {She dared to challenge the ruling}. To dare someone is to challenge them to prove their courage: {I dare you to jump}. A dare is such a challenge, especially among children testing each other's nerve. {Don't you dare} is a warning against an action. Daring describes boldness or adventurousness: {a daring rescue}, {a daring new approach}.

A daredevil is someone who takes reckless risks, especially performing dangerous stunts for thrills or spectacle: {motorcycle daredevils jumping over flaming cars}. The word combines admiration for boldness with a suggestion of foolhardiness—courting danger as if daring the devil himself. As an adjective, it describes such behavior: {daredevil stunts}, {daredevil antics}.

Daredevils is the plural of daredevil—a person who takes reckless risks, especially for thrills or spectacle. The word combines dare with devil, suggesting someone bold enough to challenge danger itself. Daredevils perform dangerous stunts: {Evel Knievel and other daredevils drew crowds with motorcycle jumps}. The term can also describe reckless behavior more broadly: {teenage daredevils racing on the highway}.

Daring describes boldness in the face of risk or danger. A daring {rescue} involves brave action; a daring {plan} courts failure. The word often carries admiration—daring suggests courage rather than recklessness. As a noun, daring is the quality itself: {His daring impressed everyone}. Someone who is daring takes chances others wouldn't.

Dark is the absence or near-absence of light: {a dark room}, {dark clouds}. By extension, dark describes deep colors closer to black than white: {dark blue}, {dark hair}. Figuratively, dark suggests gloom, evil, or the unknown: {dark thoughts}, {dark secrets}, {the dark side}. A {dark horse} is an unknown competitor who might surprise. To be {in the dark} is to lack information. To {keep someone in the dark} is to withhold it from them.

To darken is to make or become darker—less bright or more shadowed: {The sky darkened as the storm approached}. Figuratively, darken describes mood or outlook becoming gloomy or troubled: {His expression darkened when he heard the news}. To {darken someone's door} is to visit them, usually in negative constructions: {Don't darken my door again}.

A dark horse is a competitor about whom little is known, making their chances hard to predict. The term comes from horse racing—an unfamiliar horse whose abilities are uncertain. In politics, a dark horse candidate emerges unexpectedly to become a serious contender: {He was a dark horse who won the nomination on the fifth ballot}. More broadly, anyone who surprises others with hidden talents or unexpected success: {She was the dark horse of the competition}.

Darkness is the absence of light. At night, in caves, or in closed rooms, darkness prevails. The word extends to anything hidden or unknown: {the darkness of the human heart}, {kept in darkness about the plan}. Darkness also suggests evil or despair: {the forces of darkness}, {a period of darkness in her life}. To do something {under cover of darkness} is to act at night, often secretly.

A darkroom is a room kept dark or lit only with special red light, used for developing photographs. The red light doesn't expose light-sensitive film and paper, allowing photographers to process images by hand. Before digital photography, darkrooms were essential equipment for serious photographers: {She spent hours in the darkroom perfecting her prints}.

Darling is a term of affection for someone dearly loved, often used between romantic partners or toward children: {Come here, darling}. As an adjective, it means cherished or adorable: {What a darling little cottage}. The word can sound old-fashioned or theatrical, and is sometimes used sarcastically: {Oh, that's just darling}.

To darn is to mend fabric by weaving thread across a hole: {She darned his socks by the fire}. {The sweater needs darning at the elbow}. A darn is a mended place in fabric. Separately, darn is a euphemism for damn, avoiding the mild profanity: {Darn it, I missed the bus}. {Darn tootin'} is folksy American for "certainly." The mending verb and the euphemism are unrelated.

A dart is a small pointed missile thrown by hand, typically at a circular target in the game of darts. The word extends to any quick, darting movement: {The lizard made a dart for cover}. To dart is to move suddenly and rapidly: {Her eyes darted around the room}. A dart in sewing is a tapered fold stitched to shape fabric to the body. (Capitalized Dart refers to the programming language or the Dodge vehicle.)

A dartboard is the circular target used in the game of darts, divided into numbered sections with different point values. The bullseye sits at the center. Figuratively, something that attracts repeated criticism or attack becomes a dartboard: {The proposal became a dartboard for opponents}.

Darts is a throwing game in which players toss small pointed missiles at a circular board divided into numbered sections. The goal is typically to reduce a starting score to exactly zero. A dart is one of these missiles—a slender shaft with a weighted point and stabilizing fins. As a verb, to dart is to move suddenly and swiftly: {The cat darted across the room}. A darting {glance} is quick and furtive.

Three seemingly unrelated nouns meet in dash. A quick, short run or race is a dash. A mark of punctuation longer than a hyphen, and with several specific uses, is a dash. And a dash is short for dashboard, which is a panel in a vehicle holding instruments, or a similar panel on a web page where functions are arranged. Dash is simpler as a verb; it means to run quickly, or to hit violently and forcefully: The storm dashed the ship against the rocks.

A dashboard is the panel in a vehicle facing the driver, containing instruments and controls—speedometer, fuel gauge, warning lights. The term originally named a board at the front of a horse-drawn carriage that prevented mud from being dashed onto passengers. By extension, a dashboard is any display presenting key information at a glance: {The analytics dashboard shows real-time sales data}.

Dashcams are cameras mounted on a vehicle's dashboard or windshield that continuously record the view through the front windscreen, and sometimes the rear or interior. They provide video evidence in case of accidents, insurance disputes, or encounters with police. Originally popular in Russia due to insurance fraud concerns, they've spread worldwide: {The dashcam footage showed the other driver ran the red light}.

Dashing describes someone or something that cuts a striking, stylish figure—typically a man who combines good looks with confident flair. A dashing {hero} or dashing {young officer} suggests romantic appeal and spirited boldness. The word connects to dash in its sense of vigorous movement and showy style; someone who dashes about with energy and panache earns the adjective. It carries a slightly old-fashioned, swashbuckling flavor today.

Data is information consisting of numerous separate items: The data from the study indicated that the city’s population is decreasing by five percent each year. Technically, data is a plural noun, but the singular datum is rarely seen. There is no good argument for insisting that data be treated as plural: The data were collected over a period of weeks. The data in the study confirms what researchers have long believed.

A database is an organized collection of information stored electronically for easy access and retrieval. Databases underlie most modern software—from banking systems to social media platforms. The term often refers specifically to relational databases, which organize data into linked tables. {The customer database crashed and we lost three months of records.}

Two different English words have settled on the spelling date, which explains their very different meanings. One date is the edible fruit of a desert palm, which has countless cultivars. The other date is a point on a calendar corresponding to a day: What happened on this date in 1950? When scientists or researchers date something, they determine the date (or more general time period) in which it arose, flourished, or was used. When two people date, or when one dates the other, they are romantically involved and see each other regularly—on occasions that are called dates.

Dated describes something that shows its age, seeming old-fashioned or out of style: {The special effects look dated now}. A dated document bears a specific date. A dated reference places something in time. In British usage, dated can also mean having a romantic appointment arranged: {Are you dated for Saturday?}

Dates function as both noun and verb around the concept of time marked on a calendar. A date is a specific day: {What's today's date?} It's also a social appointment, especially romantic: {We're going on a date Friday}. The person you meet is also your date. To date someone is to see them romantically. To date something is to determine when it occurred or was made: {Carbon testing dated the artifact to 3000 BCE}. Something dated feels old-fashioned. Separately, dates are the sweet, sticky fruit of the date palm, eaten fresh or dried.

Dating is the practice of going on dates—social outings with romantic or sexual potential. It can describe a single activity {We've been dating for a few months} or a relationship stage between meeting and commitment. Dating someone means seeing them regularly in a romantic context. The dating scene refers to the social world of meeting potential partners. Carbon dating and similar technical senses use dating to mean determining age through scientific analysis.

A daughter is a female child in relation to her parents. The term extends to any female descendant: {a daughter of the American Revolution}. Daughter also describes something that originates from or is closely connected to something else: a {daughter cell}, a {daughter company}. With a possessive, daughter emphasizes the relationship: {my daughter}, {their daughter}.

Daughters is the plural of daughter—a female child in relation to her parents. The word extends to female descendants generally and to women connected by origin or allegiance: {daughters of the American Revolution}, {a daughter of the South}. In scientific contexts, daughter describes something derived from a parent source: {daughter cells}, {daughter isotopes}.

Daunting describes something that seems intimidating or difficult to face—a task, challenge, or prospect that makes you hesitate before tackling it: {The daunting task of clearing out my parents' house took months}. A daunting opponent appears formidable. The word suggests discouragement without implying impossibility.

Dawdling is wasting time by moving or acting slowly, lingering when you should be getting on with things. A child dawdles on the way to school, stopping to examine every interesting rock. {Quit dawdling and get dressed!} The word carries mild disapproval—dawdling suggests laziness or lack of purpose rather than deliberate patience.

The time of day when light begins, usually considered to precede sunrise, is dawn. By extension, the dawn of something is its beginning: It happened during the dawn of civilization. If something dawns on you, it occurs to you, especially suddenly or surprisingly: It dawned on me that he was ill. To say that the day dawns is to say that it comes or begins.

Dawning is the beginning of daylight, when the sun first appears: {We watched the dawning of a new day}. More often it describes the start of something abstract—an era, understanding, or awareness: {the dawning of the computer age}, {the dawning of civilization}. When something {dawns on} you, you gradually realize it: {It finally dawned on me that she wasn't coming back}.

Day designates the smallest unit of time that is a natural phenomenon and not one determined arbitrarily, as second, minute, and hour are. Day technically designates the 24-hour period in which the earth makes a rotation around the sun, from one midnight to the next. In ordinary discourse, however, day often represents some dedicated part of a day when light is present, such as the time that is devoted to work or school. Day may also denote a period with certain characteristics, such as in the day of the steam engine.

Daybreak is the moment when light first appears in the sky, marking the transition from night to day. It's interchangeable with dawn and sunrise in most contexts: {We set out at daybreak}. The word emphasizes the breaking or rupturing of darkness rather than the sun itself.

Daycare is a facility where children are supervised during the day while their parents work. The term covers everything from home-based operations to large centers: {She drops the kids at daycare before her shift}. Also used attributively: {daycare costs}, {daycare center}. Extended to facilities for elderly or disabled adults: {adult daycare}.

A daydream is a pleasant fantasy or series of thoughts that absorbs your attention while you're awake: {She stared out the window, lost in a daydream}. To daydream is to indulge in such reverie, typically when you should be focusing on something else. The word suggests idle, wishful thinking rather than practical planning: {He daydreamed about quitting his job and moving to the coast}.

A daydreamer is someone who drifts into idle fantasy or pleasant reverie, especially when they should be paying attention to something else. The word carries mild criticism—daydreamers aren't getting things done—but also suggests imagination and a rich inner life. {She was always a daydreamer, staring out windows during class.}

Daydreaming is letting the mind wander into pleasant thoughts or fantasies while awake, usually when you should be paying attention to something else. A student daydreams during a lecture; an office worker daydreams about vacation. The activity suggests idle, unfocused reverie rather than deliberate imagination: {I caught myself daydreaming and missed what she said}.

Daydreams are pleasant, idle fantasies indulged while awake—the mind wandering away from present tasks toward imagined scenarios: {She stared out the window, lost in daydreams}. As a verb, to daydream is to engage in such reverie: {He daydreamed through the entire meeting}. The word implies inattention to reality, sometimes with a note of impracticality.

Daylight is the natural light of day, as opposed to darkness or artificial light. It extends to the period when the sun is up: {We need to finish before we lose daylight}. The plural daylight appears in {scare the daylights out of} and {beat the daylights out of}—intensifiers suggesting something essential is expelled. To {see daylight} is to glimpse an end or solution after difficulty.

Days is the plural of day—a period of twenty-four hours or the portion when there's sunlight. Extended uses mark periods in someone's life: {in my younger days}, {back in the days when phones had cords}. Something's days can mean its remaining lifespan: {This old car has seen better days}. {These days} means currently or lately.

Daytime is the hours when the sun is up, roughly from sunrise to sunset. It contrasts with nighttime and carries associations of visibility, activity, and wakefulness: {I work better during the daytime}. As an adjective, it describes things happening in those hours: {daytime television}, {daytime running lights}.

A daytrip is an excursion that departs and returns on the same day, requiring no overnight stay: {We took a daytrip to the coast}. The word emphasizes the brevity and self-contained nature of the outing—a manageable adventure that fits within daylight hours. Also spelled as two words: day trip.

Daze describes a state of stunned confusion or bewilderment, as if the mind can't quite process what's happening. A blow to the head leaves you dazed; shocking news can do the same. {She wandered through the aftermath in a daze}. The word works as both noun and verb—something dazes you, and you're left in a daze.

Dazed describes a state of confused disorientation, as if stunned by a blow or shock. Someone dazed by an accident may stagger or stare blankly. The word extends to mental states: {dazed by grief}, {dazed and confused after the news}. A daze is the condition itself: {She wandered through the day in a daze}.

Dazzle is to overwhelm with brilliant light—a camera flash dazzles the eyes, leaving temporary blindness or disorientation. By extension, to dazzle is to impress or amaze through spectacular display: {She dazzled the audience with her performance}. A dazzle of zebras describes a herd, evoking their visually confusing stripes. Something dazzling combines brightness with beauty or skill.

Dazzled describes being temporarily blinded or overwhelmed by intense light: {I was dazzled by the oncoming headlights}. More often, it means deeply impressed or amazed: {The audience sat dazzled by her performance}. Both senses share the idea of being stunned into a kind of helplessness—unable to see clearly or think straight.

Dazzling describes something so bright it overwhelms the eyes, or so impressive it overwhelms the senses. Sunlight off snow can be dazzling; so can a performer's talent or a series of rapid successes. {She gave a dazzling performance.} {The dazzling light made him squint.} The word suggests brilliance that temporarily stuns or bedazzles.

Dead characterizes something that is not living, inanimate, expired, or all of these. The dead refers to dead people generally. It has an intensifying force in some fixed expressions, like a dead giveaway and dead certain. Similarly, dead of winter and dead of night refer to the darkest, most intense part. Things that were never literally alive may be called dead when they are no longer of use or required: The batteries in my remote control are dead.

Deadass is slang meaning completely serious or genuinely true, used to emphasize that you're not joking or exaggerating: {I'm deadass not going to that party}, {He deadass showed up three hours late}. Originally from New York City speech, it functions as both an adverb and an adjective. The term conveys earnest sincerity in contexts where skepticism might be expected.

A deadbeat is someone who avoids paying debts or obligations, especially financial ones. The word often appears in {deadbeat dad}—a father who fails to pay child support. More broadly, a deadbeat is a lazy person who contributes nothing: {Her ex-husband was a total deadbeat}. As an adjective, deadbeat describes mechanisms that stop without recoil.

Deadbeats are people who fail to pay their debts or meet their obligations, especially those who seem capable but unwilling to do so. The term carries strong moral judgment—a deadbeat isn't just broke but irresponsible: {The landlord finally evicted the deadbeats in 4B}. A {deadbeat dad} neglects child support payments.

A deadbolt is a lock mechanism that extends a solid metal bolt into the door frame, operated by a key or thumb turn rather than a spring. Unlike spring latches, deadbolts can't be pushed back without the key, making them more secure: {Make sure you lock the deadbolt before bed}. Standard on exterior doors.

A deadeye is someone who shoots with exceptional accuracy—a marksman who rarely misses: {She's a deadeye with a rifle}. The term comes from a circular wooden block used in sailing to tension rigging, which has holes resembling eye sockets. In casual use, deadeye describes anyone with precise aim or sharp focus: {He's a deadeye at darts}.

A deadhead is a spent flower head that should be removed to encourage new blooms; the verb means to remove such flowers: {I spent the morning deadheading the roses}. In transportation, deadhead describes traveling empty—a truck returning without cargo, or a crew member riding as a passenger to reposition: {The pilot deadheaded back to Chicago}. As slang, a deadhead is a dull, unproductive person. (Capitalized Deadhead is a fan of the Grateful Dead.)

Deadjectival describes a word formed from an adjective. English routinely creates nouns and verbs from adjectives: {sadness} from sad, {harden} from hard, {the poor} from poor. The term belongs to linguistics and grammar instruction: {The suffix -ness creates deadjectival nouns}.

A deadline is a time or date by which something must be completed: {The deadline for applications is Friday}. Missing a deadline typically brings consequences—a rejected submission, a penalty, lost opportunity. The word originally referred to a line around a military prison that prisoners crossed at risk of being shot, but this origin has faded from modern awareness. Deadlines structure work, school, journalism, and bureaucracy: {I work better under deadline pressure}.

Deadlines are the times or dates by which something must be completed. The term originated in American prisons as a line beyond which inmates would be shot—now it survives only in its figurative sense of a cutoff point. A deadline may be firm or soft, depending on consequences for missing it: {The deadline for applications is Friday}. To {meet a deadline} is to finish in time; to miss one is to fail.

A deadlock is a standstill where opposing forces block each other and neither can move forward: {Contract negotiations reached a deadlock}. In computing, deadlock occurs when two processes each wait for resources the other holds, freezing both. The verb means to bring to such an impasse: {The jury was deadlocked}.

Deadlocked describes a situation where opposing sides are stuck, unable to move forward or reach agreement. A jury is deadlocked when members cannot achieve the required consensus for a verdict. Negotiations become deadlocked when neither party will compromise: {Peace talks remained deadlocked over territorial disputes}. The image is of a lock that won't open—progress completely blocked.

Deadly means capable of causing death: a deadly {weapon}, a deadly {disease}, a deadly {poison}. It extends to anything extremely harmful or dangerous: deadly {serious}, deadly {accurate}. In informal British usage, deadly can mean excellent or thrilling: {That concert was deadly}. The adverb form means in a way suggesting death: deadly {pale}, deadly {quiet}.

Deadpan describes a deliberately expressionless manner, especially when delivering humor. A deadpan face shows no emotion; deadpan comedy relies on the contrast between absurd content and flat delivery: {She told the joke completely deadpan}. The word works as adjective, adverb, noun, and verb: {He deadpanned the punchline}.

Deadwood is wood that is dead—branches or trees no longer living. In forestry, clearing deadwood reduces fire risk. Figuratively, deadwood refers to people or things that are no longer useful or productive: {The new CEO promised to cut the deadwood from upper management}. The word implies dead weight that burdens an organization. (Capitalized Deadwood is a place name.)

Deaf describes the inability to hear, whether total or partial. Someone deaf in one ear has hearing loss on that side. The deaf as a group are those with significant hearing loss. Figuratively, deaf means refusing to listen: {My complaints fell on deaf ears}. To be {deaf to} something is to ignore it willfully. Capitalized Deaf often refers specifically to the cultural community of deaf people who use sign language.

Deafening describes sound so loud it overwhelms hearing—a deafening {roar}, deafening {applause}. The word is nearly always hyperbolic; truly deafening noise would cause hearing damage. Paradoxically, {deafening silence} describes an absence of sound so conspicuous it feels overwhelming.

Deafness is the inability to hear, ranging from partial to complete. It may be present from birth or acquired through age, illness, or injury. The Deaf community—capitalized—refers to those who identify culturally with sign language and deaf institutions. Figuratively, deafness suggests willful refusal to listen: {His deafness to criticism ultimately cost him the job}.

Deal centers on distribution and arrangement. To deal cards is to distribute them; a dealer handles this task. The meaning extends to distribution generally: {Who's dealing?} A deal is an agreement or transaction: {We made a deal}, {What's the deal with parking?} To deal with something is to handle or address it: {I'll deal with this later}. A great deal or good deal means a large amount: {a great deal of trouble}. As an adjective, deal refers to pine or fir wood, especially planks—a separate word from the same spelling.

A dealbreaker is something that causes a negotiation, agreement, or relationship to fail. In business contexts, it's a condition one party cannot accept: {The salary was fine, but no remote work was a dealbreaker}. In dating, dealbreakers are traits or behaviors that make someone unacceptable as a partner: {Smoking is a dealbreaker for me}. Also spelled deal-breaker or deal breaker.

A dealer is someone who buys and sells goods, especially as a business: a car dealer, an antiques dealer, a dealer in rare books. In card games, the dealer distributes cards to players. Without further context, dealer often means a person who sells illegal drugs: {Her son got the stuff from a dealer in the neighborhood}. A dealer may also be a firm that trades securities for its own account rather than as a broker for clients.

A dealership is a business authorized to sell a particular manufacturer's products, especially vehicles: {a Ford dealership}, {a motorcycle dealership}. The term implies an official franchise relationship with the brand, distinguishing it from independent sellers. Dealerships typically also provide service, repairs, and financing.

Deals covers agreements, transactions, and the act of distributing. A deal is an arrangement between parties: {We made a deal}. In commerce, a deal is a bargain or special offer: {I got a great deal on flights}. To deal cards is to distribute them to players. To deal with something is to handle or address it: {I'll deal with this later}. A dealer sells goods, often with connotations of illicit trade: {drug dealer}, {arms dealer}. {What's the deal?} asks what's happening or what the situation is. {Big deal} dismisses something as unimportant.

Dealt is the past tense and past participle of deal. Cards are dealt to players. A blow can be dealt to an opponent, literally or figuratively: {The scandal dealt a serious blow to his campaign}. If you've dealt with something, you've handled it: {I've already dealt with that problem}.

A dean is an administrator in a college or university, typically overseeing a school or division: {the dean of the law school}, {dean of students}. The term extends to the senior or most respected member of any group: {the dean of American sportswriters}. In church contexts, a dean heads a cathedral chapter or group of parishes. {She was appointed dean of the medical school last year.} (Capitalized Dean is a given name.)

Dear and oh dear are mild exclamations used to signal that something is not as it should be or as someone would like it to be. Dear is also used as a term of endearment or affection: Of course, dear. Many consider them old-fashioned expressions.

Dearest is a superlative form of dear, used as both adjective and noun. As an adjective, it means most beloved: {my dearest friend}, {her dearest wish}. As a noun, it's a term of endearment for someone deeply loved: {Come here, dearest}. The word appears often in letter salutations: {Dearest Mother}. Dearest can also mean most expensive, though this use is uncommon.

Death is the end of life—the permanent cessation of biological functions. It extends to the end of anything: {the death of a friendship}, {the death of an era}. To {be the death of} someone is to cause them extreme distress or amusement: {You'll be the death of me with these jokes}. A {death blow} or {death knell} signals the end of something. To {do something to death} is to overuse it until it loses meaning. {At death's door} means near dying. (Capitalized Death is the personification.)

A deathbed is the bed where someone dies or lies dying. The word usually appears in contexts about final moments: a {deathbed confession}, a {deathbed conversion}, {deathbed wishes}. To be {on one's deathbed} is to be dying or very close to death. The term evokes solemnity—last words spoken, final reconciliations attempted, wills amended at the last moment.

A deathblow is a strike or action that kills, or more often, something that destroys or ends something definitively: {The scandal dealt a deathblow to his campaign}. The word usually appears figuratively—the final, decisive blow that finishes off something already weakened.

A deathmatch is a competitive video game mode where players fight to kill each other, typically with the winner being whoever reaches a kill count first or has the most kills when time expires. The format emphasizes individual combat over team objectives: {I spent hours in deathmatch perfecting my aim}. The term extends to any chaotic free-for-all competition: {The meeting devolved into a deathmatch over the budget}.

A deathtrap is a place or structure so dangerous it could kill you—a building with blocked fire exits, a car with failed brakes, a mine with no ventilation. The word implies negligence or disregard for safety: {That old elevator is a deathtrap}. Often used hyperbolically for anything perceived as hazardous: {I'm not getting on that deathtrap of a roller coaster}.

Deathwatch is a compound noun with two meanings. The more common one is a vigil, either private or public, that is maintained as someone dies or is about to be executed. In a related meaning, a deathwatch is a guard that is mounted for someone who is about to die or be executed. This meaning is sometimes used in extended senses to talk about the anticipation of the death of something other than a living thing, like a business or a project: The company’s board is on deathwatch, waiting for the CEO to resign. The other meaning of deathwatch is for a kind of beetle that infests wood and that makes a noise that is considered a harbinger of death.

A deathwish is a conscious or unconscious desire for one's own death, or behavior so reckless it suggests such a desire: {Riding a motorcycle without a helmet? You have a deathwish}. Often used hyperbolically for any foolhardy risk-taking. Also spelled as two words: death wish.

A debacle is a sudden, complete disaster or failure—often one that's embarrassing or humiliating. The word suggests not just defeat but collapse, a situation falling apart spectacularly: {The product launch was a debacle from start to finish}. Unlike mere setbacks, a debacle implies something that went catastrophically wrong in a way that's hard to recover from.

A debate is a formal argument between opposing sides, typically following structured rules: {a presidential debate}, {a debate over immigration policy}.
