Democratization is the process of making something more democratic—either in the political sense of transitioning toward democratic governance, or in the broader sense of making something accessible to ordinary people. A country undergoes democratization when it moves from authoritarian rule toward elections and civil liberties. The democratization of {technology} or {education} means wider access to what was once restricted to elites: {The internet enabled the democratization of information}.

Democrats are members or supporters of the Democratic Party, one of the two major political parties in the United States. The term appears frequently in political discourse: {Democrats control the Senate}, {Many democrats voted against the bill}. Though conventionally capitalized when referring to the party, lowercase usage occurs in casual writing and headlines. (Capitalized Democrats is the standard form.)

Demolish means to tear down or destroy completely. Buildings are demolished to clear land for new construction. The word extends to anything reduced to rubble or ruin: {The team demolished their opponents 42-0}. To demolish an argument is to refute it thoroughly. A hungry person might demolish a plate of food—consume it entirely and quickly.

Demolished means completely destroyed or torn down. Buildings are demolished by wrecking balls or explosives. The word extends to thorough defeats: {Our team got demolished 7-0}. In casual speech, demolished can mean devoured: {We demolished that pizza in ten minutes}. To demolish an argument is to refute it decisively.

Demolition is the act of tearing down or destroying a structure, typically a building. The term applies both to deliberate, controlled destruction—often using explosives or heavy machinery—and to the resulting rubble and chaos. {The old factory was scheduled for demolition.} Extended uses describe any thorough defeat or dismantling: {The team's demolition of their rivals was complete by halftime.} A demolition derby is a competition where drivers intentionally crash cars until only one remains operable.

Demolitions is the plural of demolition, referring to multiple instances of tearing down or destroying structures, typically buildings. The term appears most often in military and construction contexts: demolitions {experts} specialize in controlled destruction using explosives, while demolitions {crews} clear sites for new development. In casual use, demolitions can describe any systematic dismantling: {The demolitions of his arguments left him speechless.}

A demon is an evil spirit or supernatural being, typically one that torments, possesses, or tempts humans. In Christian tradition, demons are fallen angels serving Satan. The word extends to inner struggles: {He battled his demons for years}. Someone called a demon at something excels with fierce intensity: {She's a demon on the tennis court}. A demon can also be a person of unusual energy or cruelty.

Demonic means of or resembling a demon—a malevolent supernatural being. The word describes anything characterized by evil, cruelty, or destructive force: {demonic laughter}, {demonic possession}. Extended uses suggest intense or frenzied energy: {She attacked the piano with demonic fury}. The related demoniac carries similar meaning but sounds more archaic.

To demonize is to portray someone or something as evil, threatening, or worthy of hatred. The word implies exaggeration or unfairness—turning an opponent into a demon rather than engaging with them honestly: {Politicians demonize immigrants to stoke fear}, {The media demonized him before his trial}. Often used critically of propaganda or partisan rhetoric.

Demonized means portrayed as evil or threatening—turned into a demon in the public imagination. Politicians demonize opponents; media demonizes minorities; industries demonize regulations. The word implies the portrayal is exaggerated or unfair: {Nuclear power has been unfairly demonized}. Someone who feels demonized believes they've been cast as a villain without justification.

Demonizing is portraying someone or something as evil, dangerous, or worthy of contempt. The word implies exaggeration or unfairness—turning opponents into monsters rather than engaging their actual positions: {Politicians demonizing immigrants}, {The media has been demonizing the industry for years}. The participle works as both verb and adjective: {a demonizing campaign}.

Demons are malevolent supernatural beings—spirits of evil in religious and mythological traditions. Christianity, Islam, and Judaism all feature demons as tempters or tormentors of humans. In figurative use, a demon is something that torments or drives a person: {He struggled with his demons}. Someone who is a demon at something pursues it with fierce energy: {a demon for work}, {a demon on the tennis court}. The word also describes exceptional skill: {She's a demon behind the wheel}.

Demonstrate means to show clearly or prove by evidence. A scientist demonstrates a hypothesis through experiments; a protester demonstrates against injustice by marching. To demonstrate a product is to show how it works: {Let me demonstrate the new features}. The noun demonstration covers both meanings—a public protest or a practical showing of how something functions.

A demonstration is a display or exhibition that shows how something works or proves a point: {The chef gave a demonstration of proper knife technique}. In politics, a demonstration is a public gathering to protest or support a cause—a march, rally, or sit-in: {Thousands joined the demonstration against the war}. The shortened form demo serves both meanings informally.

Demonstrations are public gatherings where people express support for or opposition to a cause—marches, rallies, protests: {Demonstrations against the war drew thousands}. The word also covers acts showing how something works or is done: a cooking demonstration, a product demonstration. In logic or mathematics, a demonstration proves a proposition through reasoning.

Demoralise is the British spelling of demoralize. To demoralise is to undermine someone's confidence, spirit, or will to continue: {The constant criticism demoralised the team}. A demoralising defeat leaves people discouraged and dispirited. The word suggests wearing down morale rather than a single crushing blow.

Demoralised is the British spelling of demoralized. To be demoralised is to have lost confidence, hope, or spirit—typically after setbacks or discouragement: {The team was completely demoralised after their third straight loss}. The word suggests a psychological deflation that saps motivation and resolve.

Demoralization is the loss of confidence, hope, or will to continue. An army suffers demoralization after repeated defeats; a workforce experiences it under poor leadership. {The team's demoralization was evident after their fifth straight loss.} The word can also mean corruption of morals, though this sense is now rare. To demoralize is to cause this state.

To demoralize is to undermine someone's confidence, spirit, or will to continue. A crushing defeat demoralizes a team; prolonged hardship demoralizes a population. The effect is psychological—not destroying capacity but destroying belief: {The constant criticism demoralized her}. Demoralized troops may still have weapons but lack the will to fight.

Demoralized means having lost confidence, hope, or the will to continue. A demoralized team has suffered defeats that sap their spirit. A demoralized workforce lacks motivation. The word suggests not just discouragement but a deeper collapse of morale—the psychological foundation that sustains effort: {After months of setbacks, the staff was completely demoralized}.

Demoralizing describes something that crushes spirit, confidence, or motivation. A demoralizing defeat leaves a team questioning whether they can compete. Demoralizing work conditions—low pay, no recognition, arbitrary rules—drain enthusiasm until employees stop caring. {The constant criticism was demoralizing.} The effect is psychological: not just disappointing but eroding the will to continue.

Demoted is the past tense of demote—to lower someone in rank, status, or position. The opposite of promoted. A manager might be demoted to a regular employee after poor performance. Sports teams get demoted to lower leagues. {He was demoted from captain to lieutenant.} The demotion is usually a punishment or consequence of failure.

Demotion is a reduction in rank, status, or position—the opposite of promotion. An employee demoted from manager to associate loses authority and often pay. The word applies beyond workplaces: a sports team can face demotion to a lower league, or a planet can suffer demotion to dwarf status. {After the scandal, his demotion was swift.}

A den is the home of a wild and often ferocious animal, like a lion. In a family home, and in somewhat dated use, a den is a comfortable family room for leisure activity. Some dens are places where illegal and immoral things happen (gambling den, den of iniquity). Some English dialects that convert the sound /th/ to /d/ may use den as the eye dialect spelling for then.

Deniability is the ability to deny knowledge of or responsibility for something, especially wrongdoing. The term typically appears as {plausible deniability}—a situation arranged so that a person (usually a leader or official) can credibly claim ignorance if the action is exposed: {The operation was structured to give the president plausible deniability}. The concept originated in intelligence and political contexts but now applies broadly to any situation where someone maintains distance from questionable activities.

Denial is refusing to acknowledge something as true. In everyday use, it's rejecting an accusation or claim: {The senator issued a denial of the allegations}. Psychologically, denial is an unconscious defense mechanism—refusing to accept painful realities: {He's in denial about his drinking}. To be {in denial} has become common shorthand for anyone avoiding uncomfortable truths they should face.

Denied is the past tense of deny. To deny is to declare something untrue, refuse to grant a request, or withhold something from someone. A request can be denied by authorities: {His visa application was denied}. A person can be denied access, entry, or rights. In sports, denied describes a blocked shot or thwarted scoring attempt: {He was denied at the rim}. To feel denied is to feel deprived of something deserved or desired.

Denim is a sturdy cotton twill fabric, typically blue, used primarily for jeans and casual clothing. The diagonal weave creates its characteristic durability. Blue jeans are so dominant that denim often simply means jeans: {She wore denim to the party}. Denim jackets, shirts, and skirts extend the fabric beyond pants. {Canadian tuxedo} is slang for denim worn head to toe.

Dens is the plural of den—a wild animal's lair, a cozy private room, or a place for secret activity. Thieves have dens; so do foxes and suburban fathers with recliners. {The cubs stayed in their dens through winter.} {Gambling dens operated throughout the district.}

Dense describes something packed tightly together, with little space between parts. A dense {forest} has trees growing close together; dense {fog} limits visibility. Dense materials are heavy for their size—lead is denser than aluminum. Dense prose is difficult to penetrate, packed with ideas or jargon. Calling a person dense means they're slow to understand: {He's too dense to get the hint}.

Density is how tightly packed something is—the amount of mass or substance in a given space or volume. In physics, it's calculated as mass divided by volume: lead has high density, styrofoam has low density. The term extends to population density (people per square mile) and to abstract uses: {the density of ideas in the lecture was overwhelming}. Dense can also suggest thickness or impenetrability, and informally, stupidity: {He's too dense to get the joke}.

A dent is a depression in a surface caused by impact or pressure: {The shopping cart left a dent in my car door}. To dent is to create such a mark. Figuratively, to {make a dent} in something is to make noticeable progress: {We barely made a dent in the workload}. To dent someone's confidence or pride is to diminish it.

A dentist is a medical professional who specializes in the care of teeth and gums. Dentists examine, diagnose, and treat problems of the mouth—filling cavities, extracting teeth, performing root canals, and advising on oral hygiene. {I need to schedule a dentist appointment}. The term also applies to the practice: {She's studying to become a dentist}.

Dentures are artificial teeth, a removable prosthetic device replacing some or all natural teeth. A full set replaces all teeth in the upper or lower jaw; partial dentures fill gaps while clasping onto remaining teeth. {My grandmother soaks her dentures overnight.} The singular denture exists but is rarely used outside dental contexts.

Denunciation is a public accusation or condemnation, typically strong and formal: {The senator's denunciation of the policy dominated the news cycle}. To issue a denunciation is to denounce—to declare something or someone wrong, evil, or worthy of punishment. The word carries weight; casual criticism doesn't rise to denunciation.

To deny is to declare something untrue or refuse to acknowledge it: {He denied the accusations}. You can deny a request by refusing to grant it: {The bank denied her loan application}. To deny yourself something is to go without it voluntarily. In law, defendants deny charges; in psychology, people deny painful realities they can't face.

Deodorant is a substance applied to the body—usually the underarms—to prevent or mask the smell of sweat. Most deodorants come as sticks, sprays, or roll-ons. Antiperspirants, which block sweat glands, are often called deodorants, though technically they work differently: {I forgot to put on deodorant this morning}.

Depart means to leave or go away from a place: {The train departs at noon}, {She departed for Paris yesterday}. It's more formal than leave. To depart from something is to deviate from it: {The film departs from the novel in several ways}. The departed refers to those who have died—a euphemism that frames death as a journey.

Departed means gone or left. As an adjective, it describes someone or something that has gone away: {the departed guests}, {our departed glory days}. Most often, departed is a euphemism for dead: {our departed friend}, {prayers for the departed}. The departed refers collectively to those who have died. As a verb form, departed is the past tense of depart: {The train departed at noon}.

A department is a division within a larger organization—a section with its own function or specialty. A company has departments for marketing, finance, and human resources. A university has academic departments. Government has the Department of Defense, the State Department. A department store contains separate retail departments under one roof. In casual speech, something outside your expertise is {not my department}.

Departure is the act of leaving a place: {Our departure is scheduled for 6 a.m.}, {the departure gate at the airport}. The word extends to any significant change from what's expected or established: {a departure from tradition}, {a bold departure from her usual style}. In formal contexts, departure is a euphemism for death.

Departures are acts of leaving or setting out. At airports and train stations, departures are scheduled outbound trips, often displayed on boards opposite arrivals. A departure from standard practice is a deviation or change in direction: {The new policy marked a departure from tradition}. The word can euphemistically mean death—a final leaving.

Depend means to rely on or be contingent upon something else. You depend on your paycheck for rent; the outcome depends on circumstances beyond your control. {It depends} is a common hedge when the answer varies by situation. A dependent is someone who relies on another for support, especially financially. To depend from something is to hang from it, though this sense is rare outside formal or literary contexts.

Dependable describes someone or something you can count on to perform reliably. A dependable {car} starts every morning. A dependable {friend} shows up when needed. The word emphasizes consistency over time—not just capable once, but trustworthy repeatedly: {She's been a dependable employee for fifteen years}.

Dependence is the state of relying on something or someone for support, survival, or functioning. A child's dependence on parents is natural; an addict's dependence on a substance is pathological. Countries may have economic dependence on trade partners. The word often carries connotations of vulnerability or weakness: {She resented her dependence on others}. Also spelled dependency, though that form more often names the condition itself or a dependent territory.

Dependent describes something that relies on or is determined by something else: {The outcome is dependent on several factors}. A dependent is a person who relies on another for support, especially financial—typically children or elderly relatives: {She claimed three dependents on her taxes}. The spelling dependant exists as a British variant, mainly for the noun. To be dependent on a substance is to be addicted to it.

Depends signals that an answer isn't fixed but varies according to circumstances. The full construction is {it depends on}—what happens next depends on what you decide, the price depends on the quantity. Standing alone, {depends} or {it depends} is a common reply meaning the answer could go either way: {Are you coming tonight? Depends.}

To deplatform is to remove someone's access to a platform—usually social media, streaming, or other online venues—as punishment for violating terms of service or community standards. The term emerged alongside debates about free speech online: {Twitter deplatformed several accounts for spreading misinformation}. Critics see deplatforming as censorship; supporters view it as accountability.

Deplatformed describes someone who has been banned or removed from a social media platform or other public forum, typically for violating terms of service or community standards. The term emerged alongside debates about online speech: {After the controversy, he was deplatformed by Twitter and YouTube}. To deplatform someone is to deny them access to a venue where they previously had an audience.

Deploy means to position or arrange for use, especially strategically. Military forces deploy to a region, spreading out for tactical advantage. The meaning extends to any purposeful distribution: {The company deployed resources across three divisions}. In computing, to deploy is to release software into a live environment: {We'll deploy the update tonight}. Something deployed unfolds or spreads open: {The airbag deployed on impact}.

Deployed means positioned or arranged for use, especially in military or strategic contexts. Troops are deployed to a region; resources are deployed where needed. In computing, software is deployed when released to production: {We deployed the update last night}. The word suggests deliberate, organized placement rather than casual distribution.

Deployment is the act of putting something into position or use. Military forces are deployed to a region; equipment is deployed in the field. In computing, deployment means releasing software to a production environment where users can access it: {We're deploying the update tonight}. The word suggests organized, purposeful distribution of resources.

To deport someone is to expel them from a country, typically for violating immigration laws or as a legal punishment: {The government deported thousands of undocumented workers}. The formal, bureaucratic tone of the word often appears in news and policy discussions. Separately, to deport oneself is an old-fashioned way of saying to conduct or behave oneself: {She deported herself with dignity}.

Deportation is the official removal of a person from a country, typically for violating immigration laws or committing serious crimes. Governments deport foreign nationals who have entered illegally, overstayed visas, or been convicted of offenses that trigger expulsion: {She faced deportation after her asylum claim was denied}. The process is administrative rather than criminal, though it often follows criminal proceedings.

Deportations are instances of forcing people to leave a country, typically because they entered or stayed illegally, committed crimes, or are otherwise deemed unwelcome by authorities. The word often appears in political debates about immigration policy: {The administration has ramped up deportations}. Mass deportations have historically been used as tools of ethnic cleansing and political repression.

Deported is the past tense of deport, meaning to expel someone from a country, typically by government authority. A person is deported when they lack legal status to remain or have violated conditions of their stay: {He was deported back to Guatemala after his visa expired}. Deportation often follows arrest, detention, and legal proceedings.

Deposed is the past tense and past participle of depose, meaning to remove from a position of power or authority, especially a ruler or leader. A king may be deposed by revolution, a dictator by coup, or an executive by a board of directors. {The military deposed the elected president in an overnight takeover.} In legal contexts, deposed can also mean gave testimony under oath, as in a deposition: {The witness was deposed before the trial began.}

A deposit is something placed somewhere for safekeeping or as a partial payment. You make a deposit at a bank, putting money into an account. A security deposit on an apartment guarantees against damage. In geology, a deposit is material left behind by natural processes: {mineral deposits}, {sediment deposits}. To deposit is to put down or leave behind: {She deposited her keys on the counter}. {The flood deposited silt across the fields}.

A depot is a storage facility or distribution center—a place where goods or vehicles are kept until needed: {a bus depot}, {a freight depot}. In military usage, it's where supplies and equipment are stockpiled. In American English, depot also means a train station, especially a smaller one: {We waited at the depot for the 5:15}.

Depraved describes moral corruption taken to an extreme—not merely wrong but thoroughly debased. A depraved act suggests cruelty, perversion, or wickedness beyond ordinary wrongdoing: {depraved indifference to human life}, {the depraved crimes of a serial killer}. The word implies someone has fallen far from decent standards, often with connotations of sexual deviance or sadistic pleasure in harm.

Depravity is moral corruption or wickedness carried to an extreme. The word implies not just wrongdoing but a thoroughgoing rottenness of character: {The trial revealed the full depravity of his crimes}. In legal contexts, depravity often describes conduct showing complete indifference to human life. A depraved person has sunk below ordinary standards of decency.

Depress means to push or press down: {Depress the brake pedal}. More commonly, it means to lower someone's spirits or make them feel sad: {The news depressed her for days}. Economic conditions can be depressed—slowed or weakened: {High interest rates depressed housing sales}. A depression is a sunken area, a psychological condition, or an economic downturn.

Depressed describes a state of low spirits or diminished vitality. A depressed person feels persistently sad, hopeless, or empty—the clinical term is depression. The word extends to economies and markets that have declined: {a depressed housing market}, {depressed wages}. A depressed surface or button has been pushed down. {She's been depressed since losing her job}.

Depressing describes something that causes sadness, discouragement, or low spirits. A depressing {movie} leaves you feeling down; depressing {news} weighs on the mind. The word often characterizes environments or situations that drain energy or hope: {The gray weather and empty streets made the town feel depressing}. Something can be depressing without being tragic—mundane bleakness qualifies.

Depression is a sunken area or low point—in terrain, atmospheric pressure, or economic activity. The Great Depression was the severe worldwide economic downturn of the 1930s. In psychology, depression is a mood disorder marked by persistent sadness, hopelessness, and loss of interest in daily life: {She's been struggling with depression since her divorce}. To be {in a depression} can mean either a geographic hollow or an emotional state.

Deprivation is the state of lacking something considered necessary or desirable, or the act of taking such things away. It often appears with modifiers specifying what's missing: {sleep deprivation}, {sensory deprivation}, {material deprivation}. The word carries connotations of hardship and suffering, suggesting not just absence but harmful absence. In legal and social contexts, deprivation may refer to the denial of rights or resources: {The lawsuit alleged deprivation of due process}.

Deprived describes someone or something lacking basic necessities or advantages that others have. A deprived {childhood} lacks adequate care, resources, or opportunities. Deprived {areas} suffer from poverty and limited services. The word implies not just absence but wrongful absence—something that should be present isn't: {Sleep-deprived parents struggled through the early months}.

Depth is how far down or inward something extends—the opposite of height or surface. Water has depth; so do holes, shelves, and feelings. {The pool's depth surprised her.} In figurative use, depth suggests thoroughness or profundity: a person of great depth, an {in-depth analysis}. The depths are the deepest or most remote parts: {the depths of the ocean}, {the depths of despair}. Depth perception is the ability to judge distance. Something {out of your depth} exceeds your understanding or ability.

Depths is the plural of depth, referring to deep places or the deepest parts of something. The ocean has its depths, as does the earth. Figuratively, depths describes extremes of emotion or condition: {the depths of despair}, {the depths of winter}. To plumb the depths is to explore thoroughly or reach the lowest point. {In the depths of the cave, they found ancient paintings.}

Deputies are people appointed or elected to act on behalf of others. A deputy sheriff assists or substitutes for a sheriff; deputies in this sense often carry law enforcement authority. In some governments, elected legislators are called deputies. More generally, a deputy is anyone designated to act as a substitute: {She left her deputy in charge while traveling}.

A deputy is someone authorized to act on behalf of another, especially as a second-in-command: {the deputy director}, {deputy mayor}. In American law enforcement, a deputy is an officer working under a sheriff. The word implies both subordination and delegation of authority—a deputy can exercise power, but that power flows from someone else's position.

To derail is to leave or cause to leave the rails—said of trains and other rail vehicles: {The freight train derailed after hitting debris on the tracks}. Figuratively, to derail is to throw off course or disrupt progress: {The scandal derailed his campaign}. A derailment can be literal or metaphorical: {the derailment of peace talks}.

Derailed means thrown off the rails, literally of a train that has left the track. Figuratively, to be derailed is to be diverted from an intended course: {The scandal derailed his campaign}. A conversation or plan gets derailed when something disrupts its progress: {We got derailed by an argument about the budget}.

Derailing is disrupting or diverting something from its intended course. A train derails when it leaves the tracks; a conversation derails when it veers off topic: {Let's not get derailed by side issues}. Someone who derails a plan causes it to fail: {The scandal derailed his presidential campaign}. In online discussions, derailing often means hijacking a thread toward an unrelated subject.

Derailment is the event of a train leaving its tracks, whether from mechanical failure, obstruction, or collision. The word extends to anything thrown off course: {The scandal caused the derailment of his campaign}. In psychiatry, derailment describes speech that shifts between unrelated topics without logical connection.

Derails means causes to leave the tracks, said of trains: {The freight train derailed after hitting debris on the line}. More often figurative—to throw off course or disrupt progress: {The scandal derailed his campaign}, {Don't let distractions derail your focus}. A person who derails a conversation or meeting diverts it from its intended direction, often unproductively.

Deranged means mentally disturbed or irrational, suggesting a mind thrown into disorder. A deranged person has lost touch with reason: {a deranged gunman}, {deranged ramblings}. The word implies someone whose mental state has become disordered rather than someone born with a condition. It carries dramatic, even sensational overtones—more common in news reports and thrillers than clinical settings.

A derby is a race or competition, especially a horse race or a sporting event between local rivals: {the Kentucky Derby}, {a crosstown derby}. The word also names a stiff felt hat with a rounded crown and narrow brim—called a bowler in British English. A roller derby is a contact sport on roller skates. Derby comes from the Earl of Derby, who founded the famous English horse race.

Derelict describes something abandoned and in disrepair: a derelict {building}, a derelict {ship}. As a noun, a derelict is an abandoned vessel at sea, or a person without home or resources—a vagrant or outcast: {derelicts sleeping under the overpass}. Derelict in one's {duty} means negligent or failing to fulfill responsibilities.

Descend means to move downward, from a higher position to a lower one. You descend a staircase, an airplane descends for landing, and darkness descends as night falls. The word extends to abstract movement: prices descend, and a conversation can descend into chaos. To descend from someone is to be their biological offspring across generations: {She descends from Norwegian immigrants}. If relatives or visitors descend on you, they arrive in large numbers, often unexpectedly.

A descendant is someone related to a person who lived earlier—a child, grandchild, great-grandchild, and so on down the family line. The word extends to anything that derives from an earlier form: {Modern English is a descendant of Anglo-Saxon}. {She's a direct descendant of Thomas Jefferson.} The adjective descendent means moving downward.

Descendants are the people who come after someone in a family line—children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and so on through generations. The word extends beyond biology: {descendants of enslaved people}, {intellectual descendants of Marx}. Anything that derives from an earlier form can be called a descendant: {Spanish is a descendant of Latin}.

Descent is movement downward—a plane's descent, a descent into a valley. The word extends to decline or deterioration: {a descent into madness}, {the company's descent into bankruptcy}. Descent also means lineage or ancestry, tracing one's origins through generations: {She is of Italian descent}. A steep descent is a slope or stairway going down.

To describe is to give an account of something in words—its appearance, nature, or qualities: {She described the suspect to the police}, {He described the process in detail}. Description can be brief or elaborate, objective or impressionistic. To describe someone as something is to characterize them: {Critics described the film as groundbreaking}. In geometry, to describe a shape is to draw or trace it: {The compass describes a circle}.

Description is an account of something's characteristics—what it looks like, how it works, what happened. A police description helps identify a suspect. A job description outlines duties and qualifications. {The brochure's description didn't match reality.} Something that {fits the description} matches the stated criteria. {Of every description} means of all kinds: {tourists of every description}.

To desecrate is to violate the sacred character of something—a church, a grave, a holy text. The word implies not just damage but profanation: {Vandals desecrated the cemetery with spray paint}. Extended uses apply to anything treated as inviolable: {They desecrated his memory with lies}.

Desecrated describes something sacred or highly respected that has been violated, profaned, or treated with contempt. A church is desecrated by vandalism, a grave by robbery, a flag by burning. The word implies deliberate disrespect toward what others hold holy or venerable: {The tomb had been desecrated by looters}. Past tense and past participle of desecrate.

Desecration is the act of treating something sacred or highly revered with violent disrespect or irreverence. Churches, cemeteries, monuments, and religious symbols are common targets of desecration—acts that may include vandalism, destruction, or deliberate defilement. The word extends beyond religious contexts to describe the ruination of anything held in deep esteem: {the desecration of a pristine wilderness by strip mining}. Desecration implies not just damage but a violation of what the thing represents to those who cherish it.

Desegregation is the ending of racial segregation—the forced separation of people by race in schools, housing, public facilities, and other institutions. In American history, desegregation refers specifically to the dismantling of Jim Crow laws and practices, particularly after the 1954 Supreme Court ruling in *Brown v. Board of Education*: {The desegregation of Southern schools proceeded slowly despite federal mandates}. The term implies an active process of integration, not merely the absence of segregation laws.

Desensitized describes a state of reduced sensitivity or responsiveness, whether physical or emotional. In medical contexts, someone may be desensitized to an allergen through gradual exposure. More commonly, the word describes emotional numbing—becoming less shocked or disturbed by something through repeated exposure: {Years of covering violent crime had desensitized her to gruesome details}. The implication is often negative, suggesting a loss of appropriate feeling or reaction that was once present.

Desert has two pronunciations with different meanings. With stress on the first syllable, a desert is a dry, barren region with little rainfall—the Sahara, the Mojave. With stress on the second syllable, to desert is to abandon: {He deserted his family}, {soldiers who desert their posts}. A deserted place is empty of people. Your just deserts (same stress) are what you deserve, good or bad.

Deserted describes a place that has been abandoned or emptied of people: {a deserted village}, {deserted streets at dawn}. It can also describe someone who has been abandoned by others: {She felt deserted by her friends}. The word emphasizes absence where presence is expected—a deserted island isn't just uninhabited but conspicuously empty.

A deserter is someone who abandons a duty or obligation, most often a soldier who leaves military service without permission. The word carries strong moral weight—deserters face court-martial and imprisonment, and historically execution. Beyond military contexts, deserter applies to anyone who abandons a cause or group when loyalty was expected: {The party faithful called him a deserter after he switched sides}.

Deserters are people who abandon a duty, post, or cause—most often soldiers who flee military service without permission. The term carries strong disapproval, implying betrayal of obligations to comrades or country. Beyond military contexts, deserters may abandon political movements, organizations, or relationships: {The party's deserters joined the opposition}. {Army deserters faced execution if caught}.

Deserts has two pronunciations with different meanings. With stress on the first syllable, it's the plural of desert—arid, barren regions. With stress on the second syllable, it means what someone deserves, almost always in the phrase {just deserts}: {The swindler finally got his just deserts}. The spelling trips people up—it's deserts, not "desserts," though both are pronounced the same.

To deserve something is to have earned it through actions or qualities—good or bad. You can deserve praise, punishment, respect, or blame. The word implies a moral calculation: behavior produces fitting consequences. {She deserves credit for her work}. {He got what he deserved}. {They deserve better than this}.

Deserved describes something earned or merited through one's actions: {a well-deserved rest}, {deserved criticism}. The word implies a fitting match between behavior and outcome—good or bad. {She got her deserved recognition after years of hard work}. {He received his deserved punishment}. The adverb deservedly emphasizes that justice was served: {They deservedly lost}.

Deserving means worthy of something, usually something good: {a deserving cause}, {deserving of praise}. The word often implies merit through effort or character rather than luck or circumstance. {She's deserving of the promotion after all those years}. The deserving poor, in older usage, were those considered worthy of charity—as opposed to those blamed for their own misfortune.

When you design something you decide how it will look, how it will work, and what its important features are: Architects designed the building to store the sun’s heat during the day and release it at night. Design is usually regarded as a creative process. The noun design is the result of designing something and may be as simple as a logo or as complex as a weather satellite. It’s common to use designed as an adjective in order to emphasize a feature of something rather than the person who created it: The program is designed to give parents and teachers an opportunity to work together.

A designer is someone who plans the form or structure of something before it's made—a fashion designer, graphic designer, interior designer. The word emphasizes creative conception rather than construction. As an adjective, designer describes expensive branded goods: {designer jeans}, {designer handbags}. By extension, designer can modify anything custom-made or specially engineered: {designer drugs}, {designer babies}.

Designing describes someone who schemes or plots to achieve selfish ends, often through manipulation or deception: {a designing woman}, {designing rivals at court}. The word carries connotations of calculated cunning rather than spontaneous mischief. As a noun, designing is the activity of creating plans or patterns: {She studied graphic designing}.

Designs serves as both noun and verb, unified by the idea of intentional planning. A design is a plan or pattern: {the design of the building}, {a floral design}. To design is to create such plans: {She designs furniture}. The plural {designs} often implies schemes or intentions, sometimes sinister: {He has designs on your job}, {She has designs on him}. By design means intentionally, as opposed to by accident.

Desire is wanting something, especially intensely. The word carries more weight than want—a desire suggests depth of feeling: {a desire for revenge}, {sexual desire}, {her deepest desires}. As a verb, to desire something is to want it strongly: {He desired nothing more than peace}. {Leave much to be desired} means something falls short of expectations.

Desires are strong wishes or longings for something. The word carries more intensity than wants—desires suggest deeper yearning, often with emotional or physical dimensions: {Her desires conflicted with her obligations}. Sexual desires refer specifically to physical attraction and arousal. To desire something is to want it keenly: {He desired nothing more than peace}. A desired outcome is one hoped for.

A desk is a piece of furniture with a flat surface for writing, reading, or working. Desks typically have drawers for storage and are associated with study or office work: {She sat at her desk all morning}. By extension, desk refers to a department or station: {the front desk}, {the news desk}. A {desk job} involves sedentary office work rather than physical labor.

Desks is the plural of desk, a piece of furniture with a flat surface for writing, reading, or working. A desk typically has drawers for storage and may refer to a workstation generally: {She cleared off her desk before leaving}. In organizations, desk can mean a department or function: {the city desk}, {the front desk}.

Desktop refers to the surface of a desk, and by extension, the primary screen of a computer's graphical interface—the virtual workspace where icons, files, and windows appear. A desktop computer is one designed to sit on a desk, as opposed to a laptop or mobile device. {I keep my most-used apps on the desktop.}

Desmoplasia is the growth of fibrous connective tissue, especially around a tumor. The body produces this dense, scar-like tissue in response to cancer cells invading surrounding structures. Desmoplastic tumors feel hard and woody to the touch. The phenomenon can make surgical removal difficult and may affect how tumors respond to treatment.

Desolate describes places that are bleak, empty, and lifeless—a desolate {landscape}, a desolate {stretch of highway}. The word extends to emotional states: someone desolate feels utterly alone and without hope. As a verb, to desolate is to lay waste or devastate: {War desolated the region}. The noun desolation captures both the physical ruin and the feeling of profound loneliness.

Desolation is a state of complete emptiness or devastation—a landscape stripped of life, a building reduced to rubble, a heart hollowed by grief. The word applies to places and feelings alike: the {desolation of a bombed city}, the {desolation of losing a child}. Where loneliness suggests being alone, desolation suggests being utterly forsaken.

Despair is the complete loss of hope—a state where you see no way forward and no possibility of improvement. The noun names this condition: {She fell into despair after losing her job}. The verb means to lose hope entirely: {Don't despair; things will get better}. Despair differs from sadness or discouragement by its finality—it suggests not just difficulty but impossibility.

A desperado is a reckless outlaw or bandit, especially one from the American Old West or the lawless frontiers of the Spanish-speaking world. The word carries a romantic, slightly antiquated flavor—evoking wanted posters, dusty saloons, and men with nothing left to lose: {The sheriff warned that desperados had been spotted near the canyon}. It suggests someone dangerous precisely because they're desperate.

Desperate describes an extreme state driven by urgency or hopelessness. A desperate person has exhausted normal options and will try anything: {desperate measures}, {a desperate attempt to save the company}. The word can describe situations themselves: {desperate poverty}, {a desperate shortage of supplies}. Someone desperate for something craves it intensely: {I'm desperate for a cigarette}. A desperate criminal is dangerous because they have nothing to lose.

Desperation is the state of having lost hope, often driving reckless or extreme action. A desperate person sees no good options and may try anything: {In desperation, she called her estranged father}. The word implies urgency born from circumstances that feel unendurable. An {act of desperation} acknowledges the attempt is unlikely to succeed but feels necessary anyway.

Despicable means deserving to be despised—worthy of contempt or moral disgust. The word carries strong condemnation: a despicable {act}, a despicable {person}. It implies not just wrongdoing but a meanness or cowardice that invites scorn: {It was despicable of him to blame his assistant for his own mistakes}.

To despise is to regard with contempt or deep dislike—stronger than dislike, more visceral than disapprove. You despise things you find beneath you or morally repugnant: {She despised his cowardice}, {He despised everything the regime stood for}. The word implies looking down on someone or something as worthless or vile.

Despised is the past tense and past participle of despise, meaning to regard with intense dislike or contempt. What is despised is looked down upon, held in low esteem, or actively hated: {a despised dictator}, {the most despised man in town}. The word suggests not just dislike but a kind of moral rejection—despised figures are seen as beneath respect.

Despite, like its synonyms in spite of and although, introduces something that must be considered and is in contrast with what is expressed in the main clause of a sentence: We played till the end despite the snow. Despite our repeated requests, we could not get into the building.

A despot is a ruler with absolute power, especially one who wields it oppressively or tyrannically. The word often describes dictators and authoritarian leaders: {The despot crushed all political opposition}. In looser use, despot applies to anyone who exercises control in a domineering way: {My boss is a petty despot who micromanages everything}.

Despots is the plural of despot, a ruler who exercises absolute power, typically oppressively. The term implies tyranny and disregard for the rights of subjects: {The country had been governed by a succession of despots}. In looser usage, anyone who wields authority harshly may be called a despot: {Her father was a despot who controlled every aspect of her life}.

Dessert is the sweet course served at the end of a meal—cake, pie, ice cream, fruit, or similar. The word comes from a French term meaning to clear the table, reflecting when dessert arrives. {We skipped dessert.} {Save room for dessert.} To {get your just deserts} (note the spelling) means to receive deserved consequences, using a different word entirely.

Desserts are sweet foods served at the end of a meal—cakes, pies, ice cream, pastries, puddings. The word can refer to the course itself: {We skipped dessert}. In American dining, dessert follows the main course; in European traditions, it may follow cheese. {Just desserts}, meaning deserved outcomes, uses a different word—an archaic term for what one deserves.

A destination is the place where you're going or where something is being sent. It implies intentional travel toward a specific endpoint: {We reached our destination after three hours}. Tourist destinations are popular places to visit. A destination {wedding} or destination {resort} is one people travel specifically to attend or experience.

Destinations are places where someone or something is going or being sent. The word implies purposeful travel toward a specific endpoint rather than wandering: {We should reach our destination by nightfall}. Tourist destinations are places that attract visitors, while shipping destinations are where packages end up. Figuratively, destination can suggest a goal or final state: {financial independence as a destination}. The phrase {destination wedding} describes a ceremony held somewhere requiring travel for most guests.

Destined means fated or predetermined to reach a particular end. A person destined for greatness seems marked for it from the start. A package destined for Chicago is headed there. The word implies inevitability—whether by fate, circumstance, or design: {They were destined to meet}, {The project was destined to fail from the beginning}.

Destinies is the plural of destiny—the predetermined courses of events in people's lives, or the powers thought to control them. The word often appears when discussing multiple people's fates together: {Their destinies were intertwined from childhood}. It can also refer to different possible outcomes for a single person: {She stood at the crossroads of two very different destinies}.

Destiny is the predetermined course of events, often viewed as controlled by a higher power or fate. It implies that certain outcomes are inevitable regardless of human action: {It was destiny that brought us together}. Destiny can also mean a particular future awaiting someone or something: {She felt her destiny was to become a doctor}. Unlike fate, which often carries negative connotations, destiny tends toward the grand or purposeful.

Destitute means utterly lacking in resources, especially money. A destitute person has nothing—no income, no savings, no means of support: {The flood left hundreds of families destitute}. The word can also describe complete absence of something abstract: {destitute of hope}, {destitute of any real talent}. Destitute is stronger than poor; it suggests desperate, rock-bottom poverty.

Destitution is extreme poverty—the state of lacking basic necessities like food, shelter, and clothing. The word implies not just being poor but being utterly without resources: {The family was reduced to destitution after the factory closed}. Someone in destitution has nothing left to fall back on.

To destroy is to damage something so completely that it no longer exists or functions: {The fire destroyed the building}. Destroy can apply to physical objects, abstract things like reputations or relationships, or living beings—to destroy an army is to defeat it utterly, to destroy an animal is to kill it, usually by euthanasia. Informally, to destroy someone can mean to defeat them decisively: {We destroyed them in the finals}.

Destroyed means ruined, demolished, or completely eliminated. A destroyed building has been reduced to rubble. A destroyed reputation is beyond repair. In casual speech, destroyed often means utterly defeated or humiliated: {We got destroyed in the second half}. It can also describe being extremely drunk or high: {I was completely destroyed last night}.

A destroyer is someone or something that causes destruction—ruins, demolishes, or brings to an end: {a destroyer of dreams}, {the destroyer of worlds}. In naval terminology, a destroyer is a fast, maneuverable warship designed to escort larger vessels and hunt submarines. The military sense dominates modern usage, though the general meaning remains active in literary and dramatic contexts.

Destroyers is the plural of destroyer—someone or something that destroys. A destroyer is also a fast, maneuverable warship designed to escort larger vessels and hunt submarines. The naval sense dates to the late 19th century, when "torpedo boat destroyers" were built to counter small attack craft. {The destroyers patrolled the convoy's perimeter.}

Destruction is the act of destroying something or the state of being destroyed—the complete ruin or annihilation of a thing. Buildings face destruction in war or natural disaster. A scandal can mean the destruction of someone's reputation. The word implies thoroughness: what's destroyed no longer functions or exists in its former state. {The hurricane left a path of destruction across the coast.}

Destructive describes something that causes destruction—damage, ruin, or harm. A destructive {storm} levels buildings. Destructive {criticism} tears down without building up. The word applies to physical damage {(destructive force)} and abstract harm {(destructive behavior in relationships)}. What's destructive undoes, dismantles, or devastates rather than creates or preserves.

Detached describes something separated or disconnected from what it was once part of. A detached {garage} stands apart from the house. A detached {retina} has pulled away from the eye. The figurative sense means emotionally uninvolved or objective: {She maintained a detached perspective on the family drama}. A detached manner can suggest admirable composure or troubling coldness, depending on context.

Detachment is the state of being separate or disconnected from something. Emotional detachment means not being personally invested: {She viewed the situation with cool detachment}. A detachment is also a military unit separated from a larger force for a special assignment: {A detachment of soldiers secured the bridge}. The word can suggest either admirable objectivity or troubling indifference, depending on context.

Detail is a small individual part or feature of something larger: {The painting's details reward close inspection}. In the plural, details are the specifics: {I'll spare you the details}. To detail something is to describe it thoroughly, or to assign someone to a particular duty—a detail being a group assigned to such work: {a security detail}. To detail a car is to clean it meticulously, attending to every small part.

Detailed means marked by attention to particulars and fine points. A detailed {report} covers every aspect thoroughly. Detailed {instructions} leave nothing to guesswork. The word implies completeness and precision—the opposite of sketchy or superficial. As a verb form, detailed means assigned to a specific task: {She was detailed to the investigation}.

Details are the small individual parts or features that make up a larger whole. A plan has details to work out; a story has details that bring it to life. To detail something is to describe it thoroughly: {She detailed her complaints to management}. In military contexts, a detail is a group assigned to a specific task: {cleaning detail}, {guard detail}. To detail a car is to clean it meticulously, inside and out.

Detained means held or kept from proceeding, usually by authority. Police detain suspects for questioning. Immigration officials detain people at borders. The word implies temporary custody rather than formal arrest or imprisonment: {He was detained for several hours before being released}. More casually, detained can mean delayed: {I was detained at the office}.

Detect means to discover or notice something, especially something that is not immediately obvious or is hidden. The word often implies the use of careful observation, specialized equipment, or keen perception: {The test can detect traces of the drug in your system}. Dogs detect scents imperceptible to humans. You might detect a hint of sarcasm in someone's voice or detect early signs of a problem before it becomes serious.

Detection is the act of discovering or noticing something, especially something hidden or not immediately obvious: {early detection of cancer}, {detection of fraud}. The word often appears in contexts involving careful observation, investigation, or technology designed to sense what might otherwise escape notice: {The submarine evaded detection}.

A detective is someone who investigates crimes or gathers information, either as a police officer or a private investigator. The word also works as an adjective: {detective work}, {detective fiction}. Detectives in stories—from Sherlock Holmes to film noir gumshoes—have made the role iconic. {The detective examined the crime scene for evidence.}

Detectives is the plural of detective—a person who investigates crimes or gathers information. Police detectives work within law enforcement: {Homicide detectives arrived at the scene}. Private detectives work independently, often hired for surveillance or locating people. The word also modifies: {detective work}, {detective novel}, {detective agency}.

A detector is a device or instrument that senses the presence of something and signals when it finds it: {smoke detector}, {metal detector}, {lie detector}. The word extends to any mechanism—physical or abstract—that identifies or reveals: {a good detector of sarcasm}. In physics, detectors register particles or radiation.

Detention is the act of holding someone or something back. In schools, detention is a punishment requiring students to stay after hours: {She got detention for talking back to the teacher}. In law, detention means confining someone, often before trial or for immigration violations: {The suspect was held in detention pending arraignment}. To detain is the corresponding verb.

Detergent is a cleaning agent, especially a synthetic soap substitute used for washing clothes or dishes. Unlike traditional soaps made from fats, detergents are manufactured from petroleum-based compounds and work better in hard water. The word can also function as an adjective meaning cleansing: {detergent properties}, {detergent action}.

Deterioration is the process of becoming worse or declining in quality, condition, or value. Physical things deteriorate: {deterioration of the building's foundation}, {deterioration of eyesight with age}. Abstract things do too: {deterioration of relations between the two countries}, {mental deterioration}. The word implies gradual decline rather than sudden collapse.

Determination is firm resolve to achieve something despite obstacles: {Her determination to finish medical school never wavered}. The word suggests sustained commitment rather than momentary enthusiasm. Determination also means the act of settling or deciding something: {the determination of guilt}, {a determination of eligibility}. In technical contexts, it refers to finding out precisely: {the determination of a ship's position}.

Determine means to settle or establish something conclusively. You determine the cause of a problem, determine someone's eligibility, or determine the best course of action. The word often implies reaching a decision after investigation or deliberation: {We need to determine whether the bridge is safe}. Determine also means to be the deciding factor: {Your genes determine your eye color}. A determined person has firm resolve—their mind is settled on a goal.

Determined describes someone who has firmly decided on a course of action and won't be easily discouraged: {She was determined to finish the marathon}. The word suggests resolve and persistence in the face of obstacles. Determined can also mean established or settled: {The cause of death has not yet been determined}. A determined effort is one marked by strong intention and focus.

A deterrent is something that discourages or prevents an action by making the consequences seem worse than the benefit. Nuclear weapons serve as deterrents against attack; harsh sentences are meant to be deterrents to crime. The word works as both noun and adjective: {a deterrent effect}, {the threat acted as a powerful deterrent}. Something that deters creates hesitation through fear of consequences rather than physical barriers.

To dethrone is to remove a monarch from power, and by extension, to displace anyone or anything from a position of dominance. A boxing champion is dethroned by a challenger. A bestseller is dethroned from the top of the charts. {The scandal dethroned the once-beloved CEO.} The word implies not just defeat but loss of an elevated status.

Dethroned means removed from a position of power or supremacy. The literal sense involves deposing a monarch: {The king was dethroned in the revolution}. More commonly, it describes anyone or anything losing a dominant position: {The defending champion was dethroned in the semifinals}. {Streaming has dethroned cable as the primary way people watch TV}.

Dethroning is removing someone from a position of power or supremacy. The literal sense involves deposing a monarch, but the word applies more broadly to anyone displaced from a dominant position: {The upset match dethroned the defending champion}. The term carries connotations of dramatic reversal—the mighty brought low.

To detonate is to explode or cause to explode, typically with sudden violence. Bombs detonate, demolition charges detonate buildings, and triggers detonate explosives. The word implies a rapid, forceful release of energy: {The device detonated on impact}. Figuratively, situations or people can detonate—erupting suddenly: {The scandal detonated his political career}.

Detonation is a violent explosion, specifically one that propagates through a material faster than the speed of sound within it. The word applies to bombs, demolition charges, and other explosive devices: {The detonation was heard miles away}. In engines, detonation refers to premature combustion that causes knocking—fuel igniting from pressure rather than from the spark plug.

A detonator is a device that triggers an explosion in a larger explosive charge. It contains a small amount of sensitive explosive that ignites when struck, heated, or electrically activated, producing a shock wave that sets off the main charge. Detonators are used in mining, demolition, and weapons: {The bomb squad carefully removed the detonator}.

Detonators are devices that trigger explosions in larger charges. A detonator contains a small amount of sensitive explosive that, when activated by heat, shock, or electrical current, sets off the main explosive. Blasting caps are common detonators in mining and demolition. {The bomb squad carefully removed the detonator from the device.}

A detour is a route taken when the usual path is blocked or unavailable: {Construction forced us to take a detour}. The word implies temporary deviation with intent to return to the original course. Figuratively, any digression from a planned path: {Her career took a detour into teaching before she returned to medicine}. As a verb, to detour is to take such an alternate route.

Detours are routes that bypass the usual path, typically because of road construction, accidents, or closures: {Follow the detour signs}. More broadly, a detour is any departure from a planned course: {My career took a few detours before I found my calling}. To detour is to take such an alternate route: {We detoured around the flooded road}.

Detox is short for detoxification—the process of clearing harmful substances from the body. In medical contexts, it refers to supervised withdrawal from drugs or alcohol: {He checked into a detox facility}. More loosely, detox describes regimens meant to purge toxins through special diets or fasting: {a juice detox}, {a digital detox}. The latter uses are often more aspirational than medical.

Detoxing is the process of removing toxins or harmful substances from the body. In medical contexts, it refers to supervised withdrawal from addictive substances: {He spent a week detoxing from alcohol}. In wellness culture, detoxing often means dietary cleanses or juice fasts claimed to purge impurities—though such regimens lack scientific support. Figuratively, people detox from technology or social media: {I'm detoxing from my phone this weekend}.

A deubiquitinase is an enzyme that removes ubiquitin—a small regulatory protein—from other proteins. This reverses the tagging process that marks proteins for degradation or alters their function. Deubiquitinases help regulate protein turnover, cell signaling, and DNA repair: {Mutations in deubiquitinases have been linked to various cancers}.

Deuce connects meanings through the number two. In tennis, deuce is a tied score (40-40) requiring two consecutive points to win. In cards and dice, the deuce is the two. {What the deuce?} is a mild oath, a euphemism for "devil." In casual speech, to deuce out is to leave: {I'm about to deuce}. A deuce can also mean a bowel movement, from "number two."

Devastate means to destroy or ruin completely. A hurricane devastates a coastal town; grief devastates a family. The destruction can be physical or emotional: {The news devastated her}. Devastated often describes overwhelming shock or disappointment: {I was devastated when I didn't get the job}. Devastating can mean extremely effective: {a devastating critique}, {a devastating serve}.

Devastated describes being emotionally crushed or overwhelmed by loss, grief, or terrible news: {She was devastated when her mother died}, {He was devastated by the breakup}. The word carries more weight than merely upset—it suggests being laid waste emotionally, as if nothing remains. Also describes physical destruction: {The earthquake left the city devastated}.

Devastating describes something that causes severe damage, destruction, or emotional distress. A devastating {earthquake} levels buildings; a devastating {loss} leaves someone grief-stricken. The word often emphasizes completeness—a devastating {critique} thoroughly dismantles an argument. In casual use, devastating can mean stunningly impressive: {She looked devastating in that dress}.

Devastation is severe destruction or ruin, especially on a large scale. A hurricane leaves devastation in its wake. The word carries emotional weight—beyond mere damage, devastation suggests something laid waste: {the devastation of war}, {economic devastation}. It can also describe overwhelming grief or shock: {The news left her in complete devastation}.

When something develops it changes, sometimes in a desired way that makes it better, and sometimes without any perceived direction for better or worse: Tadpoles develop from embryos. As the story developed, more and more people began to suspect that information was being withheld. When you develop something you introduce deliberate changes to it in order to bring it to a more advanced state: We’re developing several proposals aimed at winning grants to improve our facilities. Develop can also suggest a process of investigation and experiment leading to invention or discovery: They are developing new drugs for the treatment of lupus.

A developer is someone who builds or creates something, especially in two domains. In real estate, a developer buys land and constructs buildings for sale or lease: {The developer proposed a mixed-use project downtown}. In computing, a developer writes software—a programmer: {She works as a front-end developer}. The verb develop spawns both senses: bringing forth something that wasn't there before.

Developers are people who build or create things, particularly software. A developer writes code, designs applications, or builds digital products: {The developers pushed an update last night}. In real estate, a developer acquires land and constructs buildings for sale or lease. The word implies someone who takes something from concept to completion.

Developing describes something in the process of growth, progress, or coming into being. A developing {story} is still unfolding. A developing {country} is one transitioning toward industrialization and higher living standards. In photography, developing is the chemical process that makes a latent image visible on film or paper. The developing {world} refers collectively to less industrialized nations.

Development is the natural course of things that develop: Development of the vaccine is expected to take several years. Any particular change in a thing that is developing can also be called a development: We go now to our reporter in Istanbul for the latest developments. A development is also an area of land that is built upon for a particular purpose, such as housing, retail, or industry: The area has several developments under construction that are expected to accommodate growth for the next few years.

Deviant describes someone or something that departs from accepted norms or standards, particularly in behavior or beliefs. As a noun, a deviant is a person who differs markedly from what society considers normal or acceptable. The word carries negative connotations, often implying moral disapproval: {The study examined how communities label certain members as deviants}. In technical contexts like statistics, deviant simply means differing from an average or expected value without any judgment attached.

Deviants are people who depart from accepted norms or standards, especially in behavior or beliefs. The word carries judgment—society labels someone a deviant, implying they've strayed from what's proper or normal: {The program aimed to rehabilitate sexual deviants}. In sociology, deviant is more neutral, describing anyone whose behavior differs from group expectations, whether criminal, eccentric, or merely unconventional.

Device belongs to a class of words that generally denote a useful, constructed thing, like a tool, implement, instrument, or machine. In computer technology, device refers to an item of hardware connected to a computer, like a printer or scanner. A figurative device is a stratagem that accomplishes something (plot device, rhetorical device). Bombs are often characterized as devices: The soldier disarmed the improvised explosive device.

Devices are tools, instruments, or machines designed for particular purposes. The word covers everything from simple mechanical gadgets to complex electronics: {medical devices}, {storage devices}, {mobile devices}. A literary device is a technique like metaphor or irony. A rhetorical device persuades through structure rather than argument. To {leave someone to their own devices} is to let them manage without supervision or interference.

The devil, as conceived in Christianity, is Satan, the chief opponent of God and the ruler of hell. A devil, therefore, is never a good thing. A bad child may be called a little devil; a devil of a problem is one difficult to solve. A few fixed phrases characterize people, usually men, as devils (handsome devil, lucky devil, sly devil, poor devil) without neutral or negative connotation. In these instances, the meaning comes primarily from the adjective.

Devilish describes something wicked, mischievous, or suggestive of the devil. A devilish {grin} hints at mischief or cunning. A devilish {plot} is cruel or malicious. The word often carries playful rather than truly sinister connotations—a child might have a devilish {gleam} in her eye. As an intensifier, devilish means extremely: {devilish hard}, {devilish clever}.

Devils is the plural of devil—the supreme evil spirit in Christian theology, or any malevolent supernatural being. The word extends to wicked or mischievous people: {Those little devils got into the cookie jar}. To devil is to prepare food with hot spices: {deviled eggs}, {deviled ham}. A devil's advocate argues an opposing position to test an idea.

Devious describes someone who uses underhanded or indirect methods to achieve their goals, often through deception or trickery: {a devious scheme}, {He's devious—never trust him}. The word suggests cunning combined with dishonesty. A devious route is one that winds or deviates from the direct path, though this older sense is now less common than the moral one.

Devolatilization is the removal of volatile substances from a material, typically through heating. In industrial processes, coal or biomass undergoes devolatilization to drive off gases and leave behind char or coke. The term appears in chemistry, metallurgy, and polymer processing: {Devolatilization occurs rapidly when the material reaches critical temperature}.

To devote is to give time, energy, or resources to something completely: {She devoted her life to medicine}, {He devoted the morning to answering emails}. The word implies sustained commitment rather than casual attention. Devoted as an adjective describes deep loyalty or affection: {a devoted husband}, {devoted fans}. A devotee is someone wholly given over to a pursuit or belief.

Devoted describes deep commitment or loyalty to someone or something. A devoted {parent} gives unwavering care; a devoted {fan} follows faithfully through wins and losses. The word implies emotional attachment beyond mere duty—devotion that shapes how one spends time and energy. {She was devoted to her garden}. {They remained devoted to each other for fifty years}.

A devotee is someone with strong dedication to a person, cause, activity, or belief. The word suggests enthusiasm beyond casual interest: {a devotee of yoga}, {devotees of the band followed them on tour}. In religious contexts, a devotee practices fervent worship or follows a spiritual teacher: {Krishna devotees chanting in the street}.

Devotion is deep commitment or loyalty to something—a person, cause, belief, or practice. Religious devotion involves worship and spiritual dedication; personal devotion means steadfast attachment: {her devotion to her children}, {his devotion to the craft}. Devotions (plural) are prayers or religious observances: {morning devotions}. The word implies emotional investment beyond mere duty.

To devour is to eat hungrily or consume rapidly: {The starving dog devoured its food}. The word suggests eagerness and thoroughness—nothing left behind. By extension, devour applies to anything consumed with intense appetite: {She devoured three novels over the weekend}. Fire devours what it burns. Guilt or jealousy can devour a person from within.

Devoured is the past tense of devour, meaning to eat hungrily or consume completely. Animals devour prey; people devour meals when ravenous: {She devoured the pizza in minutes}. Figuratively, to be devoured is to be consumed by something overwhelming—emotion, curiosity, flames: {He was devoured by jealousy}. To devour a book is to read it eagerly and quickly.

Devouring describes consuming eagerly and completely. The literal sense involves eating ravenously: {The wolves set about devouring the carcass}. Figuratively, it extends to any intense consumption—devouring books, attention, or resources. A devouring {passion} or devouring {ambition} consumes someone entirely, leaving room for little else.

Devout describes deep religious commitment and sincere piety: {a devout Catholic}, {devout prayer}. The word extends to any earnest dedication: {a devout follower of the team}, {a devout believer in free markets}. A devout {wish} or {hope} is heartfelt and fervent. The religious sense remains primary, carrying connotations of genuine faith rather than mere observance.

Dew is moisture that condenses from the air onto cool surfaces, typically overnight. Grass glistens with dew in early morning. The word suggests freshness and purity: {morning dew}, {dewdrops on a spider's web}. Mountain Dew is a soft drink brand. Dew point is the temperature at which condensation begins. (Capitalized Dew is a surname.)

Dexterity is skill and ease in using the hands or body. A surgeon needs dexterity to perform delicate operations; a pianist's dexterity allows rapid passages. The word extends to mental quickness and cleverness: {She handled the awkward question with dexterity}. The adjective is dexterous or dextrous.

Dhrupad is the oldest surviving form of North Indian classical vocal music, characterized by its austere, meditative quality and precise adherence to raga structure. Performances typically begin with an extended improvised section called alap, sung without rhythmic accompaniment, before moving into a composed portion with drum accompaniment. The style emphasizes purity of tone and spiritual depth over ornamentation: {He trained for years in the dhrupad tradition}.

Diabetes is a chronic condition where the body cannot properly regulate blood sugar levels. In Type 1 diabetes, the pancreas produces little or no insulin. In Type 2, the more common form, the body becomes resistant to insulin or doesn't produce enough. Without management, diabetes causes serious complications affecting the heart, kidneys, eyes, and nerves. {She monitors her diabetes with daily glucose checks.}

Diabetic describes something related to diabetes, a condition where the body cannot properly regulate blood sugar: {diabetic complications}, {diabetic neuropathy}. As a noun, a diabetic is a person with diabetes: {She's been a diabetic since childhood}. Diabetic products are formulated with reduced sugar: {diabetic chocolate}, {diabetic-friendly recipes}.

Diabolical means devilish or fiendishly cruel. A diabolical {plot} is wickedly clever; a diabolical {villain} delights in causing suffering. The word can describe genuine evil or be used with theatrical exaggeration: {The parking situation downtown is diabolical}. In British English especially, diabolical serves as an emphatic complaint about anything awful: {The service was diabolical}.

To diagnose is to identify what's wrong—typically a disease or malfunction—by examining symptoms or evidence. A doctor diagnoses an illness; a mechanic diagnoses why the engine won't start. {She was diagnosed with diabetes at forty}. The word implies expert analysis leading to a specific conclusion, distinguishing it from mere guessing.

Diagnosis is the identification of a disease, condition, or problem based on examination of symptoms or evidence. A doctor makes a diagnosis after reviewing test results and patient history: {The diagnosis was diabetes}. The term extends beyond medicine to any systematic identification of what's wrong: {His diagnosis of the company's problems proved accurate}. To receive a diagnosis is often a turning point—clarifying uncertainty but also confirming fears.

Diagonal describes a line or direction that runs at an angle between horizontal and vertical—connecting non-adjacent corners of a square or rectangle, for instance. {She drew a diagonal line across the page.} The noun refers to such a line or to movement in that direction: {The bishop moves on the diagonal in chess.} Fabric cut {on the diagonal} runs at an angle to the weave.

A diagram is a drawing that explains or illustrates something, typically using lines, shapes, and labels rather than realistic depiction: {a diagram of the human heart}, {a wiring diagram}. Diagrams simplify complex information into visual form—flowcharts, floor plans, circuit schematics. To diagram something is to represent it this way; in grammar education, to diagram a sentence is to map its structure.

A dial is a face with markings used to display or control something—the dial of a clock, a radio dial, a telephone dial. The circular design unites these: hands sweep across clock dials, tuners rotate across frequencies, fingers trace rotary phone circles. To dial is to enter a number on a phone, though the verb persists even for phones without physical dials: {I dialed her number but got voicemail}. {Dial it back} means to reduce intensity. In British slang, your dial is your face.

A dialect is a variety of a language spoken by a particular group, usually defined by region or social class. Dialects differ in pronunciation, vocabulary, and grammar: {the Appalachian dialect}, {urban dialects}. Every speaker uses some dialect—standard forms are simply dialects that gained prestige. The line between dialect and separate language is often political rather than linguistic.

Dialects are varieties of a language distinguished by vocabulary, grammar, and pronunciation that are associated with particular regions or social groups. Everyone speaks a dialect, though people often use the term to describe speech patterns different from their own or from a perceived standard. {The Appalachian dialect preserves some features of older English.} Linguists distinguish dialects from accents, which involve only pronunciation differences, though the terms are often used interchangeably in casual speech.

Dialog is an alternative spelling of dialogue, more common in American English and in technical contexts. In computing, a dialog box is a window prompting user input or displaying information. The spelling without the -ue has become standard in software interfaces: {The save dialog appeared on screen}.

Dialogue is conversation between two or more people, or the exchange of ideas between groups: {The two sides agreed to enter into dialogue}.
