In fiction and drama, dialogue refers specifically to the spoken words of characters, as distinct from narration or stage directions: {The script had sharp dialogue but a weak plot}. The verb means to engage in discussion: {Management agreed to dialogue with the union}. Also spelled dialog, especially in American English and computing contexts.

Diamond is a form of pure carbon and the hardest known mineral. A diamond is a piece of this, especially one cut to a symmetrical shape for jewelry or some technical function. A much less rare and valuable diamond is the four-sided shape of a slightly squashed square or rectangle; also, this symbol is one of the suits in playing cards. Baseball is played on a field with roughly this shape that is called a diamond.

Diamondback refers to any of several animals marked with diamond-shaped patterns. The diamondback rattlesnake, found in the American South and Southwest, is among the largest and most dangerous venomous snakes in North America. The diamondback terrapin is an edible turtle of Atlantic coastal marshes. Diamondback also names a species of moth whose larvae damage cabbage crops.

Diamonds is the plural of diamond—the precious gemstone or the playing card suit marked with red diamond shapes. In baseball, diamonds refers to the playing fields: {He spent his youth on the diamonds of the Dominican Republic}. In card games, diamonds is one of four suits: {She led with diamonds}.

A diaper is an absorbent garment worn by infants and others who cannot control their bladder or bowels. In American English, diaper covers both cloth and disposable varieties; British English prefers nappy. To diaper a baby is to put one on: {I need to diaper him before we leave}. The phrase {in diapers} indicates infancy or extreme youth.

Diapers are absorbent garments worn by infants and others who cannot control bladder or bowel functions. They wrap around the lower body and fasten at the waist. Disposable diapers dominate modern use, though cloth diapers persist for environmental or economic reasons. {The baby needs a diaper change.} In British English, the word is nappy.

Diaries is the plural of diary—a book for recording daily events, thoughts, or appointments. People keep diaries as personal journals: {She found her grandmother's diaries in the attic}. A diary can also be a datebook for scheduling: {Let me check my diary for next week}. The intimate nature of diaries makes them symbols of privacy: {reading someone's diary}.

Diarrhea is the condition of having frequent, loose, or watery bowel movements. It's usually a symptom of infection, food poisoning, or digestive upset rather than a disease itself. The word serves as both medical term and everyday vocabulary: {I can't come in today—I have diarrhea}. Figuratively, {diarrhea of the mouth} describes someone who talks excessively without restraint.

Diarrhoea is the British spelling of diarrhea—abnormally frequent and liquid bowel movements, typically caused by infection, food intolerance, or illness. The condition ranges from mild inconvenience to life-threatening dehydration: {The contaminated water caused an outbreak of diarrhoea throughout the village}. Figuratively, diarrhoea describes an excessive outpouring: {verbal diarrhoea}.

A diary is a book for recording daily experiences, thoughts, or observations. The entries are typically personal and private—reading someone's diary is a violation of trust. Diary also refers to the practice itself: {She's kept a diary since childhood}. In British English, diary can mean a calendar or appointment book: {Let me check my diary}.

Diaspora was originally applied to the exile of Jews from Judaea in Biblical times. Today, diaspora refers to Jews living around the world outside of Israel, but it can also be used of any other ethnic or national group that lives outside the place of its origin. Some of the most common uses of diaspora today are in compounds such as African diaspora and Indian diaspora, the latter with reference to Indians who live outside of India, especially in the West.

Dibs is an informal claim on something, typically called out to establish priority: {I call dibs on the front seat}. The word functions as both the claim itself and the act of claiming. Children use it to settle who gets what; adults use it semi-ironically for the same purpose. {Dibs on the last slice of pizza.}

Dice are small cubes marked on each face with one to six dots, used in games of chance. The singular is die, though dice now serves for both. To dice is to cut into small cubes: {Dice the onions}. To {dice with death} is to take dangerous risks. {No dice} means no luck or refusal: {I asked for an extension—no dice}. The adjective dicey means risky or uncertain.

Diced describes something cut into small cubes, typically food: {diced tomatoes}, {diced onions}. The size varies but suggests uniform pieces smaller than chopped. As the past tense of dice, it also means gambled with dice or took a risk: {They diced with death on that mountain road}.

Dicey means risky or uncertain, with outcomes that could go either way—as if determined by a roll of the dice. The word suggests unpredictability rather than outright danger: {The weather looks dicey for the picnic}. A dicey situation might turn out fine but involves real chance of failure. More common in British than American English.

Dick is vulgar slang for a penis. It's also a common insult for a man who is selfish, obnoxious, or contemptible—similar to asshole but perhaps slightly milder: {Don't be such a dick}. As a verb, to dick someone is to mistreat or cheat them: {They really dicked us on that deal}. To dick around is to waste time or behave foolishly: {Stop dicking around and get to work}. Dick appears in many compounds: {dick pic}, {dick move}. It's also a nickname for Richard, which creates endless opportunity for jokes.

Dickhead is a vulgar insult for a stupid or contemptible person—someone whose head might as well be a penis for all the good it does them: {Some dickhead parked across two spaces}. The word is stronger than jerk but roughly equivalent to asshole in force.

Dictating is giving orders or commands authoritatively: {The general was dictating terms of surrender}. It also means speaking aloud for someone else to transcribe: {She spent the morning dictating letters to her assistant}. More broadly, dictating is determining or controlling outcomes: {Market conditions are dictating prices}.

A dictator is a ruler with absolute power, typically one who seized control rather than inheriting or being elected to it. The word carries strongly negative connotations of tyranny and oppression: {The country suffered under the dictator for decades}. Informally, dictator describes anyone who acts with overbearing authority: {My boss is a total dictator about the dress code}.

Dictators is the plural of dictator, a ruler who holds absolute power, typically seized rather than inherited or democratically granted. Dictators govern without meaningful checks on their authority: {The country suffered under a succession of military dictators}. The word extends to anyone who demands unquestioning obedience: {My boss is a dictator about the dress code}.

A dictatorship is a government in which one person or small group holds absolute power, typically maintained through force rather than consent. The term also describes the period of such rule: {under the dictatorship}, {during the military dictatorship}. By extension, any situation where one person exercises unchecked control: {Her kitchen was a dictatorship}.

The core meaning of dictionary is a list of words arranged alphabetically, along with their definitions. This meaning is extended to many other kinds of specialized lists of entries, such as a dictionary of biography (one that contains short biographical sketches about important people) or a rhyming dictionary (one that enables you to find the rhymes of a given word). The computer age expanded the meaning further and today dictionary is used to describe any formatted list of words, such as the list used by a spellchecking program or the list of legal commands in a computer language.

Diddlysquat means nothing at all, zero, not a thing: {He doesn't know diddlysquat about cars}. The word is informal and emphatic, typically appearing after negatives. Also spelled diddly-squat or shortened to diddly. Squat alone carries the same meaning: {You don't know squat}.

A didgeridoo is a wind instrument traditionally made from a hollowed eucalyptus branch, producing a deep, resonant drone. It originated with Aboriginal peoples of northern Australia and remains central to their ceremonial music. Players use continuous circular breathing to maintain the drone while adding rhythmic patterns and overtones.

Didgeridoos is the plural of didgeridoo, an Australian Aboriginal wind instrument—a long wooden tube, traditionally made from eucalyptus hollowed by termites, that produces a deep, droning sound. Players use circular breathing to sustain continuous tones: {The didgeridoos hummed through the night ceremony}.

A didjeridoo is a wind instrument of the Aboriginal peoples of northern Australia—a long wooden tube, traditionally made from a termite-hollowed eucalyptus branch, that produces a deep, droning tone when blown with vibrating lips. Players use circular breathing to sustain continuous sound. Also spelled didgeridoo.

Die is two separate words. The verb die means to pass from life or from active or useful existence (my uncle died, the bill died on the House floor). Figuratively and informally, die is used to communicate intense feelings (die laughing, dying to meet him). The noun die is less frequent and is either the unusual singular of dice, or a noun denoting a device for precise cutting or molding: The die-cut medallion.

Died is the past tense of die—to cease living. A person, animal, or plant that died has stopped being alive: {She died in her sleep}, {The flowers died from frost}. Extended uses follow naturally: a fire dies, a battery dies, an engine dies. To say someone {died laughing} or {nearly died of embarrassment} is hyperbole for extreme reaction.

A diehard is someone who stubbornly refuses to abandon a position, belief, or allegiance even when circumstances have turned against it: {diehard fans stayed until the final out}, {a diehard conservative}. The word suggests admirable loyalty or pigheaded refusal to accept reality, depending on perspective. As an adjective, it describes such people or their commitments: {diehard supporters of the losing candidate}.

Diehards are people who cling stubbornly to a cause, belief, or preference long after others have abandoned it. The term suggests both admirable loyalty and excessive resistance to change: {a few diehards still insist the old system was better}, {diehard fans showed up despite the losing season}. As an adjective, diehard describes this unwavering commitment: {a diehard conservative}, {a diehard Cubs fan}.

Dies has two sources in English. From die meaning to cease living: everything dies eventually, {she dies in the final act}, a phone battery dies when it runs out of power. The plural of die (a stamping tool or a single gaming cube) gives the other dies: {The machinist replaced the worn dies}. A die is also a decorative stamp, so dies can refer to those.

Diesel is a type of fuel for internal combustion engines, heavier and oilier than gasoline, ignited by compression rather than spark plugs. Diesel engines power trucks, buses, trains, ships, and some cars—valued for fuel efficiency and torque. The fuel and engine type take their name from Rudolf Diesel, who invented the engine in the 1890s. As an adjective: {a diesel truck}, {diesel fumes}. The verb means to run on diesel fuel or, informally, to keep running after the ignition is turned off. (Capitalized Diesel is the inventor's surname.)

Diet is the food and drink a person or animal regularly consumes: {a diet rich in vegetables}, {the diet of a hummingbird}. More narrowly, a diet is a restricted eating plan for health or weight loss: {She's on a diet}, {a low-sodium diet}. As a modifier, diet describes reduced-calorie versions: {diet soda}. To diet is to restrict food intake, usually to lose weight. A diet (from a different root) is also a legislative assembly in certain countries, as in the Japanese Diet.

Dieting is the practice of restricting food intake to lose weight or achieve a health goal. The word often implies temporary or cyclical behavior rather than permanent change: {She's been dieting since January}, {yo-yo dieting}. Diet as a verb means the same thing: {I'm dieting for the wedding}.

Difference is what distinguishes one thing from another—the way they're not alike. You can {tell the difference} between twins, {split the difference} in a negotiation, or {make a difference} by having an impact. In math, the difference is what remains after subtraction. A difference of opinion is a disagreement. {What's the difference?} asks why a distinction matters—or dismisses it as irrelevant.

Differences are the ways in which things are unlike each other, or the state of being unlike: {What are the differences between these two models?} A difference can be a disagreement or dispute: {We had our differences, but we worked them out}. To {make a difference} is to have an effect or matter: {Your vote makes a difference}. The difference between two numbers is what remains when one is subtracted from the other.

Different is an important and frequent adjective used to characterize a lack of identity or similarity between things. Using different to talk about anything is an implicit form of comparison. In typical constructions, one thing is named as the subject of a clause or sentence and the other, dissimilar thing appears after different and a preposition that may be from, than (especially in American English), or to (especially in British English).

Difficult describes something that requires effort, skill, or struggle to accomplish. A difficult exam challenges even prepared students; a difficult climb taxes experienced mountaineers. Applied to people, difficult means hard to deal with—stubborn, demanding, or uncooperative: {She can be difficult when she doesn't get her way}. A difficult situation offers no easy solutions.

Difficulty is the quality of being hard to do, understand, or deal with: {the difficulty of learning a new language}, {We underestimated the difficulty of the climb}. A difficulty is a problem or obstacle: {financial difficulties}, {She's having difficulties at work}. The phrase {with difficulty} means laboriously or barely: {He walked with difficulty after the accident}. To be {in difficulty} or {in difficulties} is to be in trouble.

To dig is to break up and move earth, typically with a shovel or hands: {digging a hole}, {digging for buried treasure}. The meaning extends to searching or rummaging: {She dug through her purse for keys}. To dig into something is to investigate it thoroughly. In older slang, to dig something means to understand or appreciate it: {I really dig jazz}. A dig can be a critical remark: {He got in a few digs about her cooking}. In archaeology, a dig is an excavation site.

Digest centers on breaking down and absorbing. The body digests food, extracting nutrients. The mind digests information, processing it into understanding: {Give me time to digest this news}. As a noun, a digest is a condensed summary of longer material—already broken down for easier consumption: {a weekly news digest}, {Reader's Digest}.

Digestion is the body's process of breaking down food into nutrients that can be absorbed and used. The stomach and intestines handle most digestion, converting what you eat into energy and building blocks for cells. The word extends to mental processing: {I need time for digestion of all this new information}. Something's digestibility is how easily it can be digested.

A digger is a person or machine that digs—excavates earth or other material. Gold diggers once dug for gold; now the term usually means someone who pursues relationships for money. In Australian and New Zealand English, digger is an informal term for a soldier, originally from World War I, and extends to a friendly form of address between men: {How ya going, digger?}

Digging is the act of breaking up and moving earth or other material, typically with a shovel or hands. The word extends to any vigorous excavating motion: {digging through old boxes in the attic}. In informal use, digging can mean strongly liking or appreciating something: {I'm really digging this new album}.

A digit is a finger or toe—humans have twenty digits total. Because we count on our fingers, digit also means any numeral from 0 through 9: {a four-digit PIN}, {the last four digits of your phone number}. The digital age takes its name from the discrete digits that encode all computer data.

Digital relates to fingers or to numerical digits. In computing, digital describes information stored as discrete numerical values—typically ones and zeros—as opposed to analog's continuous signals. Digital technology has transformed how we create, store, and share information: {digital photography}, {digital music}, {the digital age}. A digital clock displays numerals rather than hands. In medicine, a digital exam uses fingers: {a digital rectal exam}.

Digits are the fingers and toes—the ten appendages at the ends of hands and feet. In mathematics, digits are the numerals 0 through 9, the basic symbols for writing numbers. The connection is ancient: humans counted on their fingers. In slang, {Can I get your digits?} asks for a phone number.

Dignified describes someone or something showing calm self-respect and seriousness of manner. A dignified {response} to criticism doesn't stoop to pettiness. A dignified {ceremony} maintains appropriate gravity. The word suggests composure and restraint—not flashy or attention-seeking, but quietly commanding respect: {She made a dignified exit despite the chaos}.

Dignity is the quality of being worthy of respect or honor. It suggests composed self-possession and seriousness of manner: {She accepted the award with dignity}. To stand on one's dignity is to insist on being treated respectfully. Dignity also names the inherent worth of human beings: {human dignity}, {die with dignity}. Something beneath your dignity is too lowly for you to do.

Dilapidated describes something fallen into disrepair through age or neglect. Buildings are most often dilapidated—roofs sagging, paint peeling, foundations crumbling: {a dilapidated farmhouse at the edge of town}. The word suggests decay over time rather than sudden damage, and carries a sense of former solidity now compromised.

A dilemma is a situation requiring a choice between two options, both of which are undesirable or mutually exclusive. The classic dilemma forces you to pick the lesser of two evils: {She faced the dilemma of reporting her friend's theft or staying silent and being complicit}. In casual use, dilemma often just means a difficult decision or problem, though purists insist the word should involve exactly two alternatives. The phrase {on the horns of a dilemma} captures the sense of being caught between two equally painful choices.

Dilemmas is the plural of dilemma—a situation requiring a choice between equally undesirable alternatives. A classic dilemma offers two options, both with significant drawbacks: {She faced the dilemma of telling the truth and hurting her friend, or lying to protect her}. The word has loosened to mean any difficult decision: {I'm in a dilemma about which job offer to accept}.

Diligence is careful, persistent effort toward a task or goal. It suggests thoroughness and steady attention rather than bursts of enthusiasm: {She reviewed the contract with diligence}. Due diligence is the reasonable investigation expected before entering a business transaction or making a decision: {The investors conducted due diligence before the acquisition}.

Diligent describes someone who works with careful, persistent effort. A diligent student does assignments thoroughly; a diligent researcher checks every source. The word implies conscientiousness rather than mere speed—steady attention to detail over time: {Through diligent practice, she mastered the piano}. Diligence is the noun.

Dill is an herb with feathery leaves and a distinctive tangy flavor, used fresh or dried in cooking. It pairs especially well with fish, pickles, and potatoes: {dill pickles}, {salmon with dill}. The seeds are also used as a spice. Dill weed refers specifically to the leaves.

To dillydally is to waste time through indecision or aimless dawdling: {Stop dillydallying and make up your mind}. The word suggests puttering about when you should be acting—not quite laziness, but a failure to get on with things. Also spelled dilly-dally.

Dim describes low light—not dark, but poorly illuminated: {a dim hallway}, {the dim glow of a candle}. By extension, dim applies to things hard to perceive or remember: {a dim outline}, {dim memories of childhood}. A dim view is unfavorable: {She takes a dim view of his excuses}. Calling someone dim suggests they're slow-witted. To dim is to reduce brightness: {Dim the lights}.

A dime is a U.S. coin worth ten cents, one-tenth of a dollar. Because it's the smallest U.S. coin in circulation, dime suggests something tiny or insignificant: {a dime a dozen} means common and cheap. To {turn on a dime} is to change direction instantly. To {drop a dime} is to make a phone call, especially to inform on someone—from the days when pay phones cost ten cents.

Dimension is a measurable extent—length, width, height, depth, or time. The dimensions of a room are its measurements. In physics, the fourth dimension is time; in science fiction, alternate dimensions are parallel realities. Figuratively, dimension means an aspect or facet: {The scandal added a new dimension to the campaign}. Something with dimension has depth or substance: {a character with real dimension}.

Dimensions are measurable extents—length, width, height, depth. A box has three dimensions; a line has one. The dimensions of something are its measurements: {What are the dimensions of the room?} Figuratively, dimensions are aspects or facets: {The scandal took on new dimensions}. A fourth dimension typically means time, or in fiction, a parallel realm.

A dimple is a small natural indentation in the flesh, especially the kind that appears in the cheeks or chin when someone smiles. The word extends to any small depression in a surface: {dimples on a golf ball}, {dimples in sheet metal}. As a verb, to dimple is to form such indentations: {Her cheeks dimpled when she laughed}.

Dimples are small natural indentations in the flesh, most often in the cheeks or chin. Cheek dimples appear when smiling and are generally considered attractive: {Her dimples showed when she laughed}. The word extends to any small depression in a surface—golf balls have dimples to improve aerodynamics. As a verb, to dimple is to form such indentations: {The rain dimpled the pond's surface}.

A dimwit is a stupid person—someone whose mental light burns low. The word is insulting but relatively mild, more dismissive than vicious: {Don't be such a dimwit}. The adjective dimwitted describes slow or foolish thinking: {a dimwitted plan}.

Din is a loud, prolonged, and unpleasant noise—the kind that makes conversation difficult or thought impossible. A {din of voices} filled the crowded restaurant. Construction creates a din. Unlike mere loudness, din suggests confusion or chaos in the sound. To din something into someone is to instill it through constant repetition: {My parents dinned good manners into me}.

Dine means to eat a meal, typically dinner, often with connotations of formality or leisure. You dine at a restaurant rather than grab a quick bite; you dine with colleagues rather than eat with them. {We dined at a lovely French bistro.} To dine out is to eat at a restaurant rather than at home. If you dine on something, you eat it as a meal: {We dined on fresh lobster.} The phrase dine and dash describes leaving a restaurant without paying.

A diner is a person who dines, but the word more often names a type of American restaurant—informal, inexpensive, serving simple fare like burgers, eggs, and coffee. The classic diner has a long counter with stools, booths along the windows, and operates long hours: {We stopped at a diner for breakfast at 3 a.m.}

Diners is the plural of diner—a person eating a meal, especially at a restaurant: {The diners complained about the slow service}. A diner is also a small, informal restaurant, typically with counter seating and an extensive menu of American comfort food: {We stopped at a roadside diner for coffee and pie}. The classic American diner often occupies a converted railroad car or imitates that aesthetic.

Ding is the sound of a bell or similar metallic ring—short, clear, and high-pitched: {The elevator gave a ding}. It extends to any brief alert tone: {My phone dinged with a notification}. To ding something is to make a small dent or nick: {I dinged the car door in the parking lot}. A ding can also be a minor negative mark against someone: {That mistake was a ding on his record}.

A dinghy is a small boat, typically used as a tender to ferry passengers and supplies between a larger vessel and shore. The term also covers small recreational sailboats and inflatable rubber boats: {We rowed the dinghy to the beach}. The word comes from Hindi.

A dingo is a wild dog native to Australia, typically tawny-colored with a bushy tail. Dingoes are descended from domestic dogs brought to Australia thousands of years ago but have lived feral ever since. They hunt alone or in packs and are known for preying on livestock, which has made them controversial among ranchers. {A dingo took my baby} became a cultural catchphrase after a famous 1980 case.

Dingoes are wild dogs native to Australia, characterized by their sandy-yellow coat, erect ears, and bushy tail. They are Australia's largest land predator and have lived on the continent for thousands of years, likely introduced by early human migrants. Dingoes hunt both solo and in packs, preying on kangaroos, rabbits, and livestock—which has made them controversial among farmers. {Dingoes howl rather than bark like domestic dogs.}

Dingy describes something that looks dirty, dull, or shabby from neglect or wear. A dingy apartment has grimy walls and faded paint. Dingy clothes have lost their brightness through repeated washing. The word suggests accumulated grime rather than fresh dirt—a gradual descent into drabness: {The once-grand hotel had become dingy and depressing}.

Dining is eating, especially in a formal or social context. You dine at restaurants, not at home over the sink. A dining {room} or dining {table} is where meals are served. To {dine out} is to eat at a restaurant; to {dine on} something is to eat it: {We dined on fresh lobster}. Fine dining implies upscale restaurants with elaborate service.

Dinner is the main meal of the day, typically eaten in the evening. In some regions and older usage, dinner refers to a midday meal, with supper being the evening one. The word also describes formal meals or banquets: {a state dinner}, {a dinner party}. {What's for dinner?} is among the most common household questions.

Dinnertime is the hour when dinner is typically eaten. The actual time varies by culture, region, and household—anywhere from late afternoon to late evening. {Is it dinnertime already?} The word often signals a transition in the day's activities: work stops, family gathers, screens get put away.

Dinosaurs are a group of reptiles that dominated Earth for over 160 million years before going extinct about 66 million years ago. They ranged from chicken-sized to the largest land animals ever. Calling someone a dinosaur suggests they're outdated or unable to adapt: {He's a dinosaur who still refuses to use email}. The word comes from Greek for "terrible lizard."

Dinosaurs is the plural of dinosaur—the group of reptiles that dominated Earth for over 160 million years before going extinct roughly 66 million years ago. The word now applies to anything outdated or unable to adapt: {These mainframe computers are dinosaurs}. Someone called a dinosaur is behind the times: {He's a dinosaur when it comes to social media}.

A diorama is a three-dimensional miniature scene, typically displayed in a box or case with a painted background. Museum dioramas show animals in recreated habitats or historical moments frozen in time. Children build dioramas for school projects: {She made a diorama of the rainforest in a shoebox}. The word sometimes describes any elaborate miniature display.

For a short word, the noun and verb dip has somewhat complex associations. It often suggests downward motion, and there is sometimes liquid involved, as when you take a dip (go for a swim). If you dip a spoon into a pan, you put it in and bring it out again. If a surface dips (dip in the road) it descends suddenly and perhaps unexpectedly. The thick-ish food that you dip chips into is called – what else – dip!

A diploma is an official document certifying that someone has completed a course of study or earned a degree: {She framed her high school diploma}. The word can refer to the physical certificate or to the qualification itself. In American usage, diploma often specifically means a high school credential, while college completion yields a degree—though both come with diplomas.

Diplomacy is the conduct of relations between nations through negotiation rather than force. Diplomats represent their countries in foreign capitals, managing treaties, trade agreements, and conflicts. Extended to personal dealings, diplomacy means tact and skill in handling sensitive situations: {She handled the family dispute with diplomacy}. The adjective is diplomatic.

A diplomat is an official who represents their country in relations with other nations, typically stationed at an embassy or consulate. Diplomats negotiate treaties, manage crises, and maintain communication between governments. By extension, anyone skilled at handling sensitive situations tactfully may be called a diplomat: {She was the family diplomat, smoothing over every argument}.

Diplomatic describes conduct or speech that is tactful and sensitive to others' feelings, especially in delicate situations: {She gave a diplomatic answer that avoided offending anyone}. The word derives from diplomacy—the art of managing international relations—where careful communication prevents conflict. A diplomatic person navigates social tensions skillfully. In its literal sense, diplomatic refers to official relations between nations: {diplomatic immunity}, {diplomatic channels}.

Diplomats are officials who represent their country in foreign nations, conducting negotiations and maintaining international relationships. The work requires tact and careful communication—hence the adjective diplomatic, which describes anyone skilled at handling sensitive situations without giving offense: {She was diplomatic about declining the invitation}. A diplomat navigates competing interests while preserving goodwill.

Dipping is the act of briefly submerging something in liquid: {dipping chips in salsa}, {dipping a brush in paint}. It extends to any quick downward motion—a bird dipping toward water, prices dipping before recovering. In American slang, dipping means using dip tobacco: {He started dipping in high school}. To be dipping into something is to take from it gradually: {dipping into savings}.

Dips is the plural of dip—downward movements, brief immersions, or creamy foods for dunking. {She did fifty dips on the parallel bars}. {We brought chips and dips to the party}. In slang, dips are pickpockets, from their habit of dipping into pockets. In finance, buying the dips means purchasing assets after price drops: {I'm buying the dips on tech stocks}.

Diptera is the taxonomic order comprising flies and mosquitoes—insects with a single pair of functional wings. The name comes from Greek for "two wings." In scientific contexts, diptera appears lowercase when used descriptively rather than as the formal order name: {The region's diptera populations have exploded this summer}. (Capitalized Diptera is the formal taxonomic order.)

Dire means extremely serious, urgent, or dreadful. A dire situation threatens catastrophe: {dire consequences}, {dire warnings}, {dire need}. The word emphasizes gravity and often implies that action is required to prevent disaster. Something in dire straits faces desperate circumstances. Dire can also simply mean terrible: {The movie was dire}.

Direct means straight, without deviation or intermediary. A direct {route} takes you there without detours. A direct {answer} addresses the question without evasion. Direct {sunlight} reaches you unobstructed. To direct is to guide or aim: direct {traffic}, direct a {film}, direct your {attention}. A director oversees; directions tell you how to get somewhere or how to proceed. Someone who is direct speaks plainly, without softening or hedging—a quality that can be refreshing or blunt depending on context.

Directing is guiding something toward a destination or purpose. You direct traffic, direct attention, direct a question to someone. In film and theater, directing means overseeing the creative vision of a production—working with actors, making artistic decisions, shaping the final work: {She's been directing commercials for ten years}. A person directing others exercises authority over their actions.

Direction is the course along which something moves or faces, or the point toward which it is oriented. {Which direction is north from here?} {The wind changed direction.} Direction extends to guidance or instruction: following {directions} to assemble furniture, or working under someone's {direction}. In film and theater, direction is the creative oversight a director provides to shape a production. If something is moving {in the right direction}, it is progressing favorably toward a goal.

Directions are instructions for reaching a destination or accomplishing a task. You ask for directions when lost, or follow directions on a recipe or medicine bottle. The word implies sequential steps: {Read the directions before assembling}. Directions also refers to the ways something can go—north, south, up, down: {The wind shifted directions}. A sense of direction is the ability to orient oneself spatially.

A director is someone who guides, manages, or controls. In film and theater, the director shapes the creative vision—choosing how scenes are staged, how actors perform: {The director called for another take}. In business, a director sits on a board overseeing company policy. A director of an organization heads a department or division: {director of marketing}, {museum director}. The word implies authority over some enterprise or activity.

Directors are people who direct—who guide, manage, or oversee something. A film director shapes a movie's creative vision. A company's board of directors governs corporate decisions. A director of a department or organization leads its operations: {She was named director of the research institute}. The title suggests authority over a defined domain.

Dirt is loose earth or soil: {The kids were playing in the dirt}. Extended to any substance that makes something unclean—dust, grime, mud tracked indoors. Figuratively, dirt is scandalous or damaging information about someone: {They're digging up dirt on the candidate}. To {treat someone like dirt} is to show them no respect. {Dirt cheap} means extremely inexpensive.

A dirtbag is a contemptible or worthless person—someone dishonest, sleazy, or generally lowlife: {Her ex-boyfriend turned out to be a total dirtbag}. The term is mildly vulgar but common. In a separate sense, dirtbag describes a minimalist outdoor lifestyle, especially among climbers who live cheaply to maximize time on the rock: {dirtbag climbing}.

A dirtbike is a lightweight motorcycle designed for off-road riding on rough terrain—dirt trails, mud, hills, and motocross tracks. Dirtbikes have knobby tires for traction, long suspension travel, and minimal bodywork. {He spent weekends racing dirtbikes in the desert.} Also spelled as two words: dirt bike.

In its most literal use, the adjective dirty suggests the presence of dirt, and the less frequent verb dirty means make dirty. There are many figurative uses, mostly with the negative connotations of the literal use. Anything dishonorable, illegal, improper, or immoral can be called dirty. A dirty little secret is one that is probably damaging to someone’s reputation. It can also express a sense of distortion or impurity that may or may not be desirable: a dirty color is less vibrant but dirty guitar playing can be a hallmark of certain music.

Disabilities are physical, mental, or developmental conditions that limit a person's movements, senses, or activities. The word covers a wide spectrum—from mobility impairments requiring wheelchairs to cognitive differences affecting learning. {The building was retrofitted for accessibility to accommodate people with disabilities.} In legal and social contexts, disability often determines eligibility for accommodations, benefits, or protections against discrimination.

Disability is a physical or mental condition that limits a person's movements, senses, or activities. The word covers a vast range—from blindness and paralysis to chronic illness and cognitive differences. Legal definitions matter: a recognized disability may entitle someone to accommodations, benefits, or protections. {She has a learning disability}. {The building lacks disability access}. In disability communities, the term is neutral and preferred over euphemisms like "differently abled."

Disable means to make something unable to function or to deprive someone of ability. You disable a device by turning off its power or removing a component: {Disable notifications in settings}. A person may be disabled by injury or illness, losing physical or mental capacity. The adjective disabled describes people with lasting impairments, though preferences vary on whether to say {disabled people} or {people with disabilities}. To disable a security system is to deactivate it.

Disabled describes someone with a physical, mental, or sensory condition that limits major activities—movement, sight, hearing, cognition. The word functions as both adjective and collective noun: {services for the disabled}, {a disabled veteran}. A disabled vehicle or machine is one that has been rendered inoperable. Some prefer "person with a disability" to emphasize the person before the condition, though many in disability communities embrace disabled as a neutral descriptor rather than a euphemism to avoid.

A disadvantage is an unfavorable condition or circumstance that makes success harder: {Growing up poor is a disadvantage in many ways}. It can also mean a weakness relative to others: {Her lack of experience was a disadvantage in the interview}. To disadvantage someone is to put them in an unfavorable position. At a {disadvantage} means in a weaker position than competitors or opponents.

To disagree is to hold a different opinion or to differ in judgment: {We disagree about politics, but we're still friends}. People disagree with each other or with statements and ideas. Things that disagree fail to match or correspond: {The two accounts disagree on key details}. When food or climate disagrees with you, it causes discomfort or illness: {Spicy food disagrees with me}.

Disagreement is a difference of opinion or failure to agree: {There was some disagreement about how to proceed}. It can range from mild difference to open conflict. A disagreement between accounts or stories means they don't match up. The word often softens what might otherwise be called an argument or dispute: {We had a minor disagreement}.

To disappear is to pass out of sight or cease to exist. A person disappears around a corner, into a crowd, or without a trace. Things disappear when lost, stolen, or consumed: {My keys have disappeared}, {The cake disappeared in minutes}. In sinister contexts, to disappear someone is to abduct or kill them secretly, often by state actors: {The regime disappeared thousands of dissidents}.

Disappearance is the act of vanishing or ceasing to be visible or present. A person's disappearance may be voluntary or mysterious: {Police are investigating her disappearance}. Things undergo disappearance when they're removed or fade away: {the disappearance of small farms}, {the gradual disappearance of cash transactions}. The word often carries undertones of concern or loss.

Disappeared is the past tense of disappear—to vanish or cease to be visible: {The magician's assistant disappeared behind the curtain}. Something can disappear gradually {(The fog disappeared by noon)} or suddenly {(My wallet disappeared from my pocket)}. In political contexts, disappeared often describes people who vanish under state violence—detained, killed, or abducted without official acknowledgment: {Thousands disappeared during the dictatorship}.

Disappearing describes something in the process of vanishing or becoming invisible. A disappearing {act} is a magic trick—or someone's sudden, unexplained departure. Disappearing {ink} fades after writing. Species are disappearing from ecosystems. The word often carries urgency about loss: {a disappearing way of life}, {disappearing glaciers}.

To disappoint is to fail to meet expectations or hopes. A movie disappoints when it doesn't live up to its trailer. A person disappoints by not coming through: {I hate to disappoint you, but I can't make it}. The disappointed person feels let down; the disappointing thing or person caused that feeling. {The team's performance disappointed everyone who'd believed in them}.

Disappointed describes the feeling when expectations or hopes aren't met. You're disappointed in a person who let you down, disappointed with a result that fell short, disappointed by news you didn't want to hear. The emotion ranges from mild letdown to profound deflation: {I was disappointed but not surprised}. A disappointed {sigh} or {look} expresses this feeling nonverbally.

Disappointing describes something that fails to meet expectations or hopes. A disappointing {meal} leaves you unsatisfied; a disappointing {performance} falls short of what you anticipated. The word implies a gap between what was promised or hoped for and what actually arrived: {The sequel was disappointing compared to the original}.

Disappointment is the feeling when expectations or hopes go unmet. You feel disappointment when something turns out worse than anticipated: {The movie was a disappointment after all the hype}. A person or thing that disappoints can itself be called a disappointment: {He felt like a disappointment to his parents}. The word covers a spectrum from mild letdown to crushing defeat.

Disapproval is an unfavorable opinion or judgment of something or someone. It ranges from mild reservation to outright condemnation: {Her parents made no secret of their disapproval}. A {look of disapproval} signals displeasure without words. To disapprove is to hold or express such a view: {He disapproved of her career choice}.

To disapprove is to regard something unfavorably or consider it wrong: {Her parents disapproved of the relationship}. The word often implies moral or social judgment rather than mere preference. You can disapprove silently or express disapproval openly. In formal contexts, to disapprove a request or proposal is to reject it officially: {The board disapproved the budget amendment}.

To disarm is to remove weapons from someone or something: {The police disarmed the suspect}. Nations may disarm by reducing military arsenals. Figuratively, to disarm someone is to defuse their hostility or suspicion, often through charm or unexpected warmth: {Her candor disarmed the critics}. A disarming smile puts people at ease.

Disarmament is the reduction or elimination of military weapons and forces. The term usually applies to nations reducing their arsenals through treaties or agreements: {nuclear disarmament}, {multilateral disarmament talks}. It can also describe the act of taking weapons from individuals or groups: {the disarmament of rebel forces}. The word often appears in contexts of peace negotiations and international security.

Disarmed is the past tense and participle of disarm, which means to remove weapons from someone or to reduce military forces. Beyond the literal sense, disarmed often describes having one's defenses lowered emotionally or socially: {Her candor completely disarmed me}. Someone who is disarmed in this figurative sense has had their suspicion, hostility, or resistance neutralized, often by charm or unexpected kindness.

Disarming describes something that overcomes suspicion or hostility by being unexpectedly charming or sincere. A disarming {smile} puts people at ease. A disarming {honesty} catches you off guard in a pleasant way. The word suggests defenses being lowered—as if emotional weapons were being set aside: {His disarming manner made it hard to stay angry}.

A disaster is a sudden event causing widespread destruction or suffering—floods, earthquakes, plane crashes. The word extends to anything that goes catastrophically wrong: {The dinner party was a complete disaster}. A disaster can also be a person who's hopelessly disorganized or prone to failure: {She's a disaster in the kitchen}.

Disasters are sudden events causing widespread destruction, suffering, or loss of life. Natural disasters include earthquakes, floods, hurricanes, and wildfires. Human-caused disasters include industrial accidents, oil spills, and acts of terrorism. The word extends to any serious failure or fiasco: {The dinner party was a complete disaster}. {Disaster struck when the levee broke}.

Disastrous describes something that causes or constitutes a disaster—a catastrophic failure or calamity. A disastrous {flood} destroys homes; a disastrous {decision} leads to ruin. The word often carries a sense of irreversibility: {The merger proved disastrous for both companies}. In casual use, disastrous can mean merely very bad: {a disastrous haircut}, {a disastrous first date}.

Disbelief is the state of not believing something, often because it seems impossible or shocking: {She stared in disbelief at the wreckage}. To {suspend disbelief} is to temporarily accept the impossible premises of a story or performance. Disbelief can also mean rejection of religious faith, though unbelief is more common for that sense.

Disc is a variant spelling of disk, preferred in British English and in specific technical contexts. Compact disc and disc brake use this spelling by convention. In anatomy, the pads between vertebrae are usually spinal discs. American English generally favors disk for computing contexts: {hard disk}, {floppy disk}. The spellings are often interchangeable, though consistency within a document matters more than which you choose.

Discard means to throw away or get rid of something no longer wanted or useful: {She discarded the worn-out shoes}. In card games, to discard is to remove a card from your hand, placing it in a discard pile. The noun refers to something thrown away or the act itself: {The pile of discards grew}.

Discernment is the ability to perceive differences or judge wisely. Someone with discernment notices subtle distinctions others miss: {She showed real discernment in choosing her advisors}. The word implies careful evaluation rather than snap judgment, often in matters of taste, character, or moral complexity. {His discernment of quality wines impressed even the sommelier}.

Meanings of the noun and verb discharge vary according to whether associated with a person, an abstraction, or an object. To discharge a weapon is to fire it. To discharge a person is to fire them or relieve them of duty. To discharge a debt is to excuse it. The noun discharge represents an instance of any of these, such as an honorable discharge from military service. A discharge from a body orifice is usually something gooey, like nasal discharge.

Discharged means released from an obligation, duty, or confinement. A soldier is discharged from the military when service ends—honorably or dishonorably. A patient is discharged from a hospital when well enough to leave. A debtor is discharged from bankruptcy when obligations are cleared. Discharged also describes the release of energy or matter: {The gun discharged}, {The wound discharged pus}, {The battery discharged overnight}.

A disciple is a follower who accepts and helps spread the teachings of a leader or philosophy. The word most often appears in religious contexts—the twelve disciples of Jesus, or disciples of Buddha. More broadly, anyone devoted to learning from a master qualifies: {She became a disciple of the minimalist architect}. A disciple differs from a mere student in the depth of commitment implied.

Disciples are followers or students of a teacher, leader, or philosophy. The term most often refers to the twelve followers of Jesus in Christian tradition, but extends to devoted adherents of any influential figure or movement: {a disciple of Freud}, {disciples of minimalist design}. A disciple implies committed study and personal allegiance, not casual interest.

Discipline is a noun and a verb with a range of loosely related meanings. Discipline in a classroom is behavior in accordance with rules or order. A field of study can also be called a discipline: disciplines of the humanities. Training undertaken to improve skills can also be called discipline. When you discipline someone, you take steps to bring them under control, either as a part of their training or as a form of punishment: They expect nannies to provide quality care but then do not allow them to discipline the children.

Disciplined describes someone who exercises control and follows a regimen consistently: {a disciplined athlete}, {a disciplined approach to saving money}. It suggests the ability to resist temptation or distraction in pursuit of goals. Disciplined can also mean having received correction or punishment: {The employee was disciplined for repeated tardiness}.

Disciplines are fields of study or practice with their own methods and standards: academic disciplines like physics or philosophy, artistic disciplines like ballet. The word also means controlled behavior and the training that produces it: {Military discipline kept the troops calm under fire}. To discipline someone is to punish or correct them, especially children. Self-discipline is the ability to make yourself do difficult things. As a verb, discipline also means to train systematically: {She disciplined herself to write every morning}.

A disclaimer is a statement that limits responsibility or denies connection to something. Legal disclaimers appear before potentially controversial content or risky activities: {The views expressed are those of the author and do not reflect the opinions of this network}. Product disclaimers warn of dangers: {Results may vary}. To disclaim is to deny or renounce.

Disclosure is the act of revealing information that was previously hidden or unknown. Companies make financial disclosures to investors; individuals disclose conflicts of interest. In legal contexts, disclosure refers to the required sharing of relevant documents between parties: {The defense requested full disclosure of the evidence}. A disclosure can also be the information itself: {The senator's disclosure shocked the committee}.

Disco is a style of dance music that emerged in the 1970s, characterized by a steady four-on-the-floor beat, lush orchestration, and pulsing bass lines. The term also names the nightclubs where people danced to this music: {We're going to the disco tonight}. As a verb, to disco is to dance to such music or frequent such clubs. The disco era peaked in the late 1970s, and the word now carries nostalgic or retro connotations: {disco ball}, {disco fever}.

Discombobulated means confused, flustered, or thrown off balance. The word describes a state of disorientation where someone can't quite collect their thoughts or composure: {I was completely discombobulated after the time zone change}. Despite its playful, invented-sounding quality, discombobulated has been in use since the nineteenth century. The shorter form discombobulate works as a verb: {The contradictory instructions discombobulated everyone}.

Discomfort is mild physical or psychological unease—not quite pain, but not comfort either. A hard chair causes discomfort; so does an awkward silence. The word often appears where stronger terms would overstate: {I felt some discomfort during the procedure}. To discomfort someone is to make them uneasy, though this verb sounds formal or old-fashioned.

To disconnect is to sever a connection—unplugging a cable, ending a phone call, or cutting off a utility: {They'll disconnect your power if you don't pay}. The noun disconnect describes a gap between things that should align: {There's a disconnect between what politicians say and what they do}. To feel disconnected is to feel isolated or out of touch.

Disconnected describes things no longer linked or joined. A disconnected {phone line} has been cut off from service. Disconnected {thoughts} lack logical flow between them—they don't hang together coherently. A person who feels disconnected experiences emotional distance from others or from their surroundings: {I've felt disconnected from my family since the move}. The word implies that a connection once existed or should exist.

Discontent is dissatisfaction with one's circumstances—a restless unhappiness that something isn't as it should be. {The workers' discontent grew as wages stagnated}. As an adjective, discontent means dissatisfied: {She was discontent with the arrangement}. The noun often appears with modifiers suggesting it might lead to action: {simmering discontent}, {growing discontent}, {the winter of our discontent}.

Discontinued describes something that is no longer being made, sold, or provided. Manufacturers discontinue products that aren't selling well or that have been replaced by newer versions; services get discontinued when they're no longer viable. {They discontinued my favorite shampoo, so now I have to find a new one.} The word often appears in retail contexts where customers learn a desired item is simply no longer available.

Discord is lack of harmony or agreement—whether between people, factions, or musical notes. {Discord among the partners doomed the business.} The word suggests ongoing tension rather than a single disagreement. A discordant note clashes with others; discordant opinions clash similarly. To sow discord is to deliberately create conflict. (Capitalized Discord is a communication platform.)

Discos is the plural of disco, the dance music and nightclub culture that dominated the late 1970s. Disco featured synthesizers, steady four-on-the-floor beats, and orchestral flourishes. The venues themselves were also called discos: {We hit three discos that night}. The word survives in compounds like {disco ball} and {disco nap}—a pre-evening rest before going out.

A discotheque is a nightclub where people dance to recorded music rather than live bands. The word, borrowed from French in the 1960s, has largely given way to its shortened form disco, though discotheque retains a retro or European flavor: {The old discotheque had a mirrored ball and flashing lights}.

A discount is a reduction from the usual price: {The store offers a 20% discount on clearance items}. To discount something is to reduce its price, or more broadly, to diminish its importance or credibility: {Don't discount her opinion just because she's young}. A discount {rate} is a reduced price or, in finance, the interest rate central banks charge for loans. Something done {at a discount} comes cheaper than expected, sometimes implying lower quality.

To discourage is to diminish someone's confidence or enthusiasm: {Don't let setbacks discourage you}. It also means to try to prevent something by expressing disapproval or creating obstacles: {The high price discourages impulse buying}, {Her parents discouraged the relationship}. A discouraged person feels disheartened; a discouraging situation dampens hope or motivation.

Discouraged describes a state of having lost confidence, enthusiasm, or hope, typically after setbacks or criticism. Someone who feels discouraged has had their motivation dampened: {After months of rejection letters, she was discouraged but kept applying}. The word can also describe something that has been actively opposed or dissuaded: {Smoking is discouraged on hospital grounds}. This second sense comes from the verb discourage, meaning to persuade someone against a course of action or to make something less likely to happen.

Discouragement is the feeling of having lost confidence or enthusiasm—the deflation that follows setbacks or criticism. It can also mean the act of trying to prevent something: {Despite discouragement from her parents, she pursued acting}. A discouragement is anything that dampens spirits or deters effort: {The long commute was a major discouragement}.

Discover means to find or learn something for the first time. You discover a new restaurant, a hidden talent, or that your keys were in your pocket all along. The word often implies uncovering what already existed but was unknown: {Columbus didn't discover America—people already lived there}. Scientists discover cures; explorers discover lands; you discover the truth. To be discovered is to be found by someone who recognizes your potential: {She was discovered singing in a café}.

Discoveries is the plural of discovery, denoting things that have been found or learned for the first time. The word applies across domains: scientific discoveries advance human knowledge, archaeological discoveries reveal the past, and personal discoveries shape individual understanding. {Recent discoveries in genetics have transformed medicine.} Discovery also has a legal sense referring to the pretrial process where parties exchange relevant information and evidence.

Discovery is the act of finding or learning something for the first time: {the discovery of penicillin}, {a voyage of discovery}. It extends to the thing found: {The cave paintings were an astonishing discovery}. In law, discovery is the pretrial process where opposing parties exchange relevant information and evidence: {The emails emerged during discovery}. A discovery can also be a person whose talent is newly recognized: {The young actress was the director's discovery}.

To discredit something is to damage its credibility or reputation: {The leaked emails discredited the entire investigation}. You can discredit a person, theory, or institution by exposing flaws or casting doubt. As a noun, discredit is the state of diminished trust or respect: {The scandal brought discredit on the department}. To someone's discredit means reflecting poorly on them.

Discredited describes something that has lost credibility or been shown to be unreliable. A discredited {theory} has been disproven or rejected by experts. A discredited {politician} has lost public trust, usually through scandal or exposed dishonesty. The word implies that reputation or authority once existed but has been undermined: {a discredited witness}, {discredited claims}.

The adjective discreet must not be confused with another adjective, discrete, which is a homonym but not related in meaning. Someone who is discreet shows good judgment and tact with regard to privacy or other people’s feelings or reputations: We made discreet inquiries and learned that the family did not have a place to stay. When concrete things are described as discreet it usually means that they are unobtrusive and do their job without calling attention to themselves: The room’s discreet lighting makes for a pleasant dining experience.

Discretion is the freedom to make decisions according to one's own judgment: {The judge has discretion in sentencing}. It also means the quality of being careful about what you say or do, especially to avoid embarrassment or offense: {I trust your discretion with this information}. The phrase {at your discretion} leaves the choice entirely to you. {Discretion is the better part of valor} suggests knowing when to hold back is wiser than rushing in.

To discriminate is to recognize or make distinctions. A wine expert discriminates among vintages; a person of discriminating taste notices fine differences. But discriminate more often carries negative weight—to treat people unfairly based on group membership: {The company was found to have discriminated against women in hiring}. The neutral sense (perceive differences) and the charged sense (act on prejudice) coexist, though the latter now dominates.

Discrimination is the activity or the result of making a judgment about difference: Discrimination improved considerably when subjects were given more time to study the objects. The core meaning of discrimination is neutral but in usage, it often refers to the unfair effects of judgment about differences: The study found that racial discrimination in housing is still widespread in the city. Discrimination is sometimes used positively to talk about someone’s judgment: Her discrimination during interviews gave us a very good field of candidates.

Discs is the plural of disc, the British English spelling of disk. Both forms refer to flat, circular objects or shapes. In British usage, discs commonly describes vinyl records, CDs, DVDs, and similar media: {I found a box of old discs in the attic}. The spelling also appears in anatomical contexts like spinal discs and in disc brakes. American English generally prefers disk, though compact disc uses the British spelling universally.

A discus is a heavy disk thrown as an athletic event, one of the oldest Olympic sports. The thrower spins in a circle to build momentum before releasing. The shape extends to anything disk-like: {a discus fish}, {a discus-shaped UFO}. The event itself is also called the discus: {She competed in the discus}.

Discuss means to talk about something with others, typically to share information, examine different perspectives, or work toward understanding. The word implies more depth and exchange than casual conversation—you discuss {politics}, discuss {options}, or discuss {a problem} when you want to explore it thoroughly. In academic and professional settings, discuss often appears as an instruction: {Discuss the implications of the study's findings}. The noun form is discussion.

Discussion is the exchange of ideas through conversation, often to reach understanding or make decisions: {We need to have a discussion about the budget}. Unlike debate, discussion implies collaborative exploration rather than opposing sides. The word covers everything from casual talks to formal meetings: {The matter is still under discussion}. To table something {for discussion} is to put it on the agenda.

Disdain is a feeling of contempt or scorn toward something considered beneath one's dignity or unworthy of respect: {She regarded his excuses with disdain}. The verb means to look down on or reject as unworthy: {He disdained to answer the accusation}. Disdain carries a note of superiority—not merely disliking something but considering it too low to merit serious attention.

Disease is a condition in which the body or mind functions abnormally, causing discomfort, dysfunction, or distress. Diseases may be caused by infection, genetics, environment, or lifestyle: {heart disease}, {infectious disease}, {Alzheimer's disease}. The word extends to unhealthy conditions in plants, animals, or systems. Figuratively, disease describes corrupting social problems: {Racism is a disease}.

Disenchanted describes someone who has lost faith, enthusiasm, or idealized belief in something—the spell is broken. A disenchanted voter no longer trusts the political process. A disenchanted employee has seen through the company's promises. {After three years of broken promises, she grew disenchanted with the organization.} The word implies previous enchantment: you can only become disenchanted with something you once believed in.

Disenchantment is the loss of illusion or idealism about something once admired or believed in. The word suggests a spell being broken—what once seemed magical or promising now appears ordinary or flawed: {Her disenchantment with corporate life led her to quit}. Political disenchantment describes voter cynicism toward institutions. The feeling often follows enthusiasm: {The disenchantment set in after the first year of marriage}.

Disenfranchised means deprived of rights or privileges, especially the right to vote. Historically, various groups were disenfranchised by law: {Black voters were systematically disenfranchised through poll taxes and literacy tests}. The word now extends to anyone made to feel excluded or powerless within a system: {disenfranchised youth}, {economically disenfranchised communities}. To feel disenfranchised is to feel shut out from participation or belonging.

Disfigured describes something whose appearance has been damaged or marred, especially a face or body that bears visible scars, burns, or deformities: {The acid attack left her permanently disfigured}. The word implies that the original form was altered in a way that makes it less attractive or harder to recognize. It applies beyond bodies—a disfigured landscape has been scarred by mining or development.

Disgrace is a state of shame or dishonor, often public: {He resigned in disgrace}. A disgrace is also something that brings shame: {The condition of these roads is a disgrace}. To disgrace someone is to bring shame upon them: {She disgraced the family name}. To be in someone's disgrace is to have lost their favor.

Disgraced describes someone who has lost respect or reputation through shameful conduct. A disgraced {politician} resigned after the scandal. A disgraced {doctor} lost her license. The word implies a fall from a previous position of honor or trust—you can only be disgraced if you once had grace to lose.

Disgruntled means annoyed, dissatisfied, or resentful, usually because of unfair treatment or unmet expectations. The word often describes workers or customers who feel wronged: {disgruntled employees filed a complaint}, {a disgruntled voter}. Despite appearances, there is no common verb "disgruntle" or opposite "gruntled"—the word exists mainly in this form.

A disguise is an altered appearance meant to conceal identity—a costume, wig, or false beard that makes someone unrecognizable. To disguise yourself is to put on such a covering. The word extends to anything that masks true nature: {a blessing in disguise}, {thinly disguised contempt}. To disguise a voice is to alter it so the speaker can't be identified.

Disguised describes something altered to conceal its true identity or nature. A person in disguise wears different clothes or makeup to avoid recognition: {She arrived at the party disguised as a pirate}. The word extends to anything hidden behind a false appearance: {a blessing disguised as a setback}, {criticism disguised as concern}. Thinly disguised suggests the concealment is unconvincing: {a thinly disguised attempt to take credit}.

Disguises are outward alterations meant to conceal identity—costumes, masks, wigs, or changes in appearance that make someone unrecognizable: {The spy traveled under various disguises}. The word extends to anything that obscures true nature: {His friendliness was a disguise for ambition}. As a verb form, disguises means to conceal or misrepresent: {She disguises her accent when she's nervous}.

Disgust is a strong feeling of revulsion or distaste, often physical in origin—the response to rotting food, bodily fluids, or foul smells. The feeling extends to moral repugnance: {His behavior disgusted everyone}. As a verb, to disgust is to provoke this reaction: {The corruption disgusts me}. {She left in disgust.}

Disgusted describes a strong feeling of revulsion or distaste. The reaction can be physical—triggered by foul smells, rotting food, or bodily fluids—or moral, provoked by behavior that offends one's values: {I'm disgusted by the way they treated her}. The word often implies contempt alongside the revulsion: {He gave a disgusted sigh and walked out}.

Disgusting describes something that provokes revulsion or strong distaste—a visceral reaction of wanting to turn away. The feeling can be physical, as with rotting food or bodily fluids, or moral, as with cruelty or corruption: {The conditions in the factory were disgusting}. The word often expresses emphatic disapproval: {His behavior at the funeral was disgusting}.

Dish is the most generic term for a food container, especially one you eat out of or off of. Dishes are what you wash when all the eating is done. Before the eating, dishes are all the different things that have been prepared to eat. When you dish out food, you remove individual servings from a pot (or dish). In slang use, a dish is someone sexually attractive. To dish the dirt is to gossip.

Dishes are plates, bowls, cups, and other containers used for serving and eating food. The term often refers specifically to dirty tableware needing washing: {Whose turn is it to do the dishes?} A dish is also a prepared food item: {a traditional Mexican dish}. To dish is to serve food or, informally, to gossip: {She's always dishing about her coworkers}.

Disheveled describes hair, clothing, or general appearance that is untidy, rumpled, or in disarray: {She arrived looking disheveled after running for the bus}. The word suggests carelessness or the aftermath of activity rather than deliberate styling—someone who just woke up, came through a storm, or has been too busy to attend to their appearance.

Dishevelled describes a person or their appearance as untidy, unkempt, or in disarray—hair uncombed, clothes rumpled, looking like you've just rolled out of bed or been caught in a windstorm: {He arrived dishevelled and out of breath}. The word suggests disorder that happened to someone rather than deliberate carelessness. Also spelled disheveled.

Dishonest describes someone who lies, cheats, or deceives—or actions characterized by such behavior. A dishonest {person} can't be trusted. A dishonest {answer} conceals or distorts the truth. {It would be dishonest to pretend I didn't know}. The word carries moral weight: dishonesty isn't just inaccuracy but deliberate deception.

Dishonesty is the quality of being untruthful or deceptive—lying, cheating, or misrepresenting facts. It covers everything from small lies to systematic fraud: {intellectual dishonesty}, {financial dishonesty}, {a pattern of dishonesty}. The word often implies a character trait rather than a single act: {His dishonesty finally caught up with him}.

Dishonor is the loss or absence of honor—a state of shame or disgrace. To dishonor someone is to bring shame upon them or treat them disrespectfully: {He dishonored his family's name}. To dishonor a commitment is to fail to fulfill it. A dishonored check is one the bank refuses to pay. The word carries weight in contexts where reputation matters: military conduct, family standing, broken promises.

Dishonored describes someone or something that has lost honor or been disgraced. A dishonored soldier has been stripped of standing through misconduct or failure. A dishonored {check} has been refused by a bank—it bounces. {He returned home dishonored after the scandal}. To be dishonored is to have one's reputation or commitments rejected.

Dishonour is the British spelling of dishonor—loss of reputation or respect, or the act of bringing shame upon someone or something. To dishonour a person is to disgrace them; to dishonour a commitment is to fail to keep it. A bank dishonours a cheque when it refuses payment: {The cheque was dishonoured due to insufficient funds}.

Dishonoured is the British spelling of dishonored—the past tense of dishonour, meaning to bring shame upon or fail to honor. A dishonoured {promise} was broken. A dishonoured {cheque} was rejected by the bank for insufficient funds. A dishonoured {soldier} has lost reputation through misconduct or cowardice.

A dishwasher is a machine that washes dishes, or a person employed to wash dishes in a restaurant kitchen. The machine sense now dominates in everyday speech: {We need to run the dishwasher}. The human sense persists in food service: {He started as a dishwasher and worked his way up to line cook}.

Disillusion is to strip away false beliefs or naive ideals, revealing a harsher reality. The noun names this state of lost innocence: {His disillusion with politics came after years of broken promises}. The related disillusionment is more common as a noun. Someone disillusioned has had their hopeful expectations shattered—not necessarily wiser, but certainly less trusting.

Disillusioned describes the state of having lost faith or belief in something once admired or trusted. The word implies a painful awakening—discovering that a person, institution, or ideal isn't what you thought: {She became disillusioned with politics after the scandal}. Someone disillusioned with their job has lost the enthusiasm or hope they once had. The feeling combines disappointment with a sense of having been naive.

Disillusionment is the disappointment that comes from discovering something isn't as good, noble, or true as you believed. It follows the collapse of an illusion—about a person, institution, or ideal: {Her disillusionment with politics came after years of broken promises}. The feeling often carries a bitter edge, the sense of having been naïve or deceived.

A disinfectant is a substance that kills germs, bacteria, or viruses on surfaces. Unlike antiseptics, which are safe for living tissue, disinfectants are typically too harsh for skin and are used on countertops, floors, and equipment: {Wipe down the handles with disinfectant}. Bleach and alcohol solutions are common disinfectants.

Disinformation is false information deliberately created and spread to deceive. Unlike misinformation, which may be shared innocently, disinformation implies intent—someone knows it's false and spreads it anyway: {Russian disinformation campaigns targeted the election}, {The report was pure disinformation}. The word entered English from Russian dezinformatsiya, a Soviet intelligence term.

To disintegrate is to break apart into smaller pieces or fragments. Physical objects disintegrate through decay, explosion, or erosion: {The old book disintegrated in my hands}. The word extends to abstract things that fall apart: {Their marriage disintegrated over the following year}. In physics, disintegrate describes radioactive decay or particle breakdown.

Disintegrating describes something breaking apart into smaller pieces or losing its structural integrity. A disintegrating building crumbles over time; a disintegrating marriage falls apart through accumulated strain. The word captures the process of coming undone: {The old manuscript was disintegrating in my hands}. Figuratively, anything cohesive can disintegrate—plans, alliances, composure.

Disintegration is the process of breaking apart into smaller pieces or components, often to the point of destruction or collapse. Physical objects disintegrate when their structure fails—a crumbling building, a decaying body, a spacecraft burning up on reentry. The word extends to abstractions: the {disintegration of a marriage}, the {disintegration of social order}. In physics, it refers specifically to radioactive decay, where atomic nuclei break down spontaneously.

A disk is a flat, circular object—or something shaped like one. The sun appears as a bright disk in the sky. In anatomy, spinal disks cushion the vertebrae. In computing, a disk stores data: {hard disk}, {floppy disk}. The spelling disc is British and appears in specific terms like {compact disc} and {disc brake}, while disk dominates American usage and computing contexts.

Dislike is a mild aversion or lack of fondness for something or someone. It falls well short of hate or loathing—more a preference against than active hostility: {I dislike getting up early}, {She took an instant dislike to him}. As a noun, dislike names the feeling itself: {his dislike of crowds}, {likes and dislikes}.

Dislocation is displacement from a proper position. In medicine, a dislocated joint has bones forced out of alignment: {She suffered a shoulder dislocation in the fall}. More broadly, dislocation describes any severe disruption of normal arrangement or function: {the economic dislocation caused by the pandemic}, {the dislocation of communities during wartime}. The word captures both physical displacement and the disorder that follows.

Disloyal describes someone who fails to maintain allegiance or commitment where it's expected—to a person, group, cause, or country. A disloyal {friend} betrays confidences. A disloyal {employee} undermines the company. The word implies a relationship that should command faithfulness: {She felt disloyal for even considering the competitor's offer}.

Disloyalty is the failure to remain faithful to a person, group, or cause that has a claim on your allegiance. It implies betrayal or abandonment of a bond—to a spouse, employer, country, or team: {The general was executed for disloyalty to the crown}. Disloyalty suggests not just distance but active breach of trust.

Dismal describes something dreary, gloomy, or depressingly inadequate. A dismal day is gray and cheerless. A dismal performance falls far short of expectations. Dismal prospects offer little hope. The word carries emotional weight beyond mere badness—it suggests something that dampens the spirit: {The team's dismal record left fans despairing}.

To dismantle something is to take it apart piece by piece: {They dismantled the scaffolding after the project finished}. The word implies methodical deconstruction rather than destruction—you dismantle a machine to repair it or a tent to pack it away. Figuratively, to dismantle is to systematically undo: {The new administration dismantled environmental regulations}.

Dismantling is taking something apart piece by piece, whether a machine, a structure, or a system. You might dismantle scaffolding after construction or dismantle a corrupt institution through reform. The word implies methodical deconstruction rather than destruction: {The crew began dismantling the stage after the concert}. Dismantling suggests the parts may remain intact even as the whole ceases to function.

Dismay is a feeling of distress or discouragement when facing something unexpected or daunting. It suggests being thrown off balance: {To her dismay, the files had been deleted}. The verb means to cause this feeling: {The test results dismayed the doctors}. Dismay implies a sudden loss of confidence or hope rather than simple disappointment.

Dismayed describes feeling sudden discouragement or distress when confronted with something daunting or disappointing. It suggests being thrown off balance by unwelcome news or circumstances: {She was dismayed to learn the project had been canceled}, {He looked dismayed when he saw the bill}. The feeling combines shock with a sinking sense that things have gone wrong.
