To dismember is to cut or tear the limbs from a body, or more broadly, to divide something into pieces: {The killer dismembered the corpse}. The word extends to separating parts from any whole: {The empire was dismembered after the war}. The violence of the literal sense colors figurative uses.

Dismembered describes a body that has had its limbs or other parts cut off or torn away. The word applies to corpses—victims of violence, accidents, or deliberate mutilation: {Police found the dismembered remains in a shallow grave}. Figuratively, dismembered can describe anything broken into pieces: {the dismembered empire}, {a dismembered organization}.

Dismiss means to send away or allow to leave: {Class dismissed}. It extends to ending employment: {She was dismissed after three warnings}. More commonly, dismiss means to reject something as unworthy of consideration: {He dismissed her concerns as paranoia}. To dismiss a legal case is to end it without a verdict. A dismissive attitude treats others or their ideas as unimportant.

Dismissal is the act of sending someone away or ending their employment. A worker receives dismissal when fired; a case receives dismissal when a judge terminates proceedings. The word carries finality—something has been judged unworthy of further attention or continuation: {Her dismissal of his concerns hurt him deeply}. A dismissive attitude treats something as beneath consideration.

Dismissed is the past tense of dismiss, meaning sent away or released from duty, attention, or consideration. A class is dismissed when the teacher ends it; an employee is dismissed when fired. {The judge dismissed the case} means it was thrown out, not allowed to proceed. To feel dismissed is to feel brushed off—your concerns treated as unworthy of serious attention.

Dismissive describes treating something or someone as unworthy of serious attention. A dismissive {wave of the hand} brushes aside an idea. A dismissive {tone} signals that what's being said doesn't matter. The attitude ranges from casual disregard to contemptuous rejection: {She was dismissive of his concerns about the project}.

To dismount is to get off something you're riding—a horse, bicycle, or motorcycle. The word suggests a deliberate, controlled descent rather than falling. In gymnastics, the dismount is the final move off an apparatus: {She stuck the dismount}. In computing, to dismount a drive is to disconnect it from the operating system before removal.

Disobedience is the act of refusing to obey rules, commands, or authority. A child's disobedience might mean ignoring a parent's instructions; civil disobedience is the deliberate, nonviolent breaking of laws to protest injustice: {Thoreau's essay on civil disobedience influenced Gandhi and King}. The word implies willful defiance rather than mere failure to comply.

Disobedient describes someone who refuses to follow rules or obey authority: {a disobedient child}, {disobedient to his commanding officer}. The word implies willful defiance rather than mere failure—you can't be disobedient by accident. It applies mostly to children, soldiers, pets, and others expected to submit to direction.

To disobey is to fail or refuse to follow a rule, order, or authority. Children disobey parents, soldiers disobey commanders, citizens disobey laws: {She disobeyed her doctor's orders and went back to work}. The word implies willful defiance rather than mere failure—you can't accidentally disobey.

Disorder is a lack of order—things out of place, systems not functioning properly, or conditions deviating from normal. A room in disorder is messy; civil disorder is public unrest. In medicine, disorder names conditions that disrupt normal function: {anxiety disorder}, {eating disorder}, {sleep disorder}. The verb means to disturb arrangement or health: {The news disordered his thoughts}.

Disoriented means confused about where you are, what time it is, or what's happening around you. The word suggests losing your bearings—literally or figuratively. A head injury can leave someone disoriented. Jet lag disorients travelers. {She woke up disoriented, unsure what city she was in.} In British English, the spelling is usually disorientated.

To disown someone is to reject any connection with them, especially to renounce a family member: {His parents disowned him when he came out}. The word suggests a formal, often permanent severing of ties. You can also disown actions, statements, or beliefs—refusing to acknowledge them as yours: {She disowned her earlier comments}.

Disowned is the past tense of disown, meaning to reject or sever ties with someone or something previously acknowledged as one's own. Parents who disown children cut them off emotionally and often financially: {His father disowned him when he dropped out of law school}. One can also disown beliefs, actions, or statements: {She disowned her earlier remarks}.

As a verb (second syllable stressed), dispatch has a meaning similar to send in the sense of send someone to do something: An elite SWAT team was dispatched to intervene in the standoff. As a noun (first syllable stressed), dispatch designates a message or an update about a situation. Dispatch can also mean the act of sending something (Dispatch of the documents was delayed), or it can stand for promptness and efficiency (She handled the difficult project with dispatch).

A dispatcher is a person who coordinates and directs the movement of vehicles, personnel, or resources. Emergency dispatchers receive 911 calls and send police, fire, or ambulance services. Trucking dispatchers assign drivers to routes. The role involves rapid decision-making and communication: {The dispatcher radioed all available units to the scene}.

A dispensary is a place where medicines or medical supplies are given out. In older usage, it referred to charitable clinics providing free care to the poor. Today the term most commonly describes a retail shop licensed to sell cannabis: {There are three dispensaries within walking distance of my apartment}.

Displaced describes something moved from its proper or usual position. A displaced {vertebra} has shifted out of alignment. More commonly, it refers to people forced from their homes by war, disaster, or persecution: {millions of displaced refugees}, {displaced families seeking shelter}. To feel displaced is to feel out of place or unsettled: {She felt displaced after moving to the new city}.

Displacement is the act of moving something from its usual place or position. People experience displacement when forced from their homes by war, disaster, or development: {The flooding caused mass displacement of residents}. In physics, displacement measures the volume of fluid pushed aside by an object—a ship's displacement is the weight of water it displaces. In psychology, displacement is redirecting emotions toward a safer target: anger at your boss becomes snapping at your spouse. The word captures both physical removal and the sense of something being where it doesn't belong.

Display centers on showing something visibly for others to see. A museum displays artifacts, a store displays merchandise, a peacock displays its feathers. The word suggests deliberate presentation—you display confidence, display affection, display ignorance. As a noun, it's both the act of showing and the thing shown: {a fireworks display}, {a display of strength}. In computing, a display is a screen: {The display went dark}. Display often implies performance or ostentation: {His generosity was just for display}.

Disposable describes something designed to be used once or briefly, then discarded: {disposable razors}, {disposable diapers}, {disposable income}. The last phrase means money available after necessities are paid—income you can "throw away" on wants rather than needs. Applied to people, disposable suggests they're treated as expendable or easily replaced: {The company views its workers as disposable}.

Disposal is the act of getting rid of something: {waste disposal}, {the disposal of hazardous materials}. A garbage disposal is a device in a kitchen sink that grinds food scraps. At your disposal means available for your use: {I'm at your disposal if you need anything}. Disposal can also mean the arrangement or settlement of a matter: {the disposal of the estate}.

Disposition has two jobs, corresponding to the primary meanings of its underlying verb dispose. Someone’s disposition is the way they tend to be, or the way they are habitually: Sheila has such a sunny disposition. Your disposition toward something is your attitude toward it. Disposition can also mean the disposing of something—that is, the getting rid of it or the dealing with it: An official will oversee the disposition of the company’s assets.

A dispute is a disagreement or argument, often one that persists: {a property dispute}, {a labor dispute}, {The facts are not in dispute}. To dispute something is to challenge or contest it: {She disputed the charges on her bill}. To dispute with someone is to argue with them. {Beyond dispute} means undeniable.

Disputes are disagreements or arguments, typically formal or prolonged: {labor disputes}, {territorial disputes}, {disputes over property lines}. The verb means to argue against or call into question: {She disputed the charges on her bill}. To dispute a claim is to challenge its validity. {The matter remains in dispute} means it's unresolved.

Disqualified means ruled ineligible or removed from consideration. An athlete may be disqualified for breaking rules, a candidate disqualified for lacking credentials. {She was disqualified from the race for a false start}. To be disqualified from something is to lack the necessary qualifications or to have them revoked: {His criminal record disqualified him from the position}.

To disqualify is to declare someone ineligible or unfit for something—a competition, a position, a benefit. A runner may be disqualified for a false start, a candidate disqualified by lack of credentials. The word often implies that requirements existed and weren't met: {His criminal record disqualified him from serving on the jury}. To disqualify yourself is to remove yourself from consideration, often due to conflict of interest.

Disregard means to ignore or pay no attention to something: {She disregarded the warning signs}. It often implies deliberate dismissal rather than mere oversight—you disregard advice, instructions, or evidence when you choose not to let it influence your actions. As a noun, disregard is the state of ignoring: {His disregard for safety regulations was well known}.

Disrespect is a lack of regard or esteem for someone or something. To disrespect is to show that lack of regard through words or actions: {Don't disrespect your mother}. The noun often appears with a possessive: {I meant no disrespect}. In casual speech, the clipped form *diss* serves as both noun and verb.

Disrespectful describes behavior or speech that shows a lack of respect or courtesy toward someone or something: {Don't take that disrespectful tone with me}. It can range from mild rudeness to serious insult, depending on context and cultural norms. Children are called disrespectful for talking back; adults for ignoring social hierarchies or sacred traditions.

To disrupt is to interrupt the normal course or operation of something: {The protest disrupted traffic for hours}. A disruptive child breaks the flow of a classroom. In business jargon, to disrupt an industry is to radically transform it through innovation—a sense that has become so overused it often sounds hollow: {Every startup claims to be disrupting something}.

Disruption is the act of interrupting or throwing into disorder. A disruption breaks the normal flow of things: {The power outage caused major disruption to the conference}. In business jargon, disruption describes innovation that upends established industries—Uber disrupted taxis, streaming disrupted cable television. This sense carries positive connotations of progress, though critics note it often just means displacement.

Disruptions is the plural of disruption—interruptions that disturb normal functioning or flow. Traffic disruptions delay commutes. Supply chain disruptions affect availability of goods. The word often appears in business contexts where disruption has been recast as positive: {tech disruptions that reshape industries}. But the core sense remains something that breaks continuity: {The protests caused major disruptions to city services}.

Disruptive describes something that causes disorder or interruption to normal functioning. A disruptive {student} interferes with classroom learning. Disruptive {technology} upends established industries—streaming was disruptive to cable television. The word can be negative {(disruptive behavior)} or positive {(disruptive innovation)}, depending on whether the disruption is seen as chaos or progress.

Diss is slang for disrespect—to insult, belittle, or show contempt for someone: {Why you gotta diss me like that?} The word emerged from hip-hop culture in the 1980s and spread into mainstream usage. As a noun, a diss is the insult itself: {That song was a diss aimed at his rival}. Also spelled dis.

To dissect is to cut apart systematically for examination. The word applies literally to biological specimens in labs and morgues: {We dissected a frog in biology class}. Figuratively, to dissect is to analyze something in detail, separating its parts to understand the whole: {Critics dissected the president's speech}. The noun is dissection.

Dissection is the act of cutting something apart to examine its structure. In biology, students dissect frogs or cadavers to study anatomy. The word extends to any methodical analysis: {a dissection of the company's financial problems}, {Her dissection of his argument was merciless}. The literal cutting apart becomes figurative taking apart.

Dissed is the past tense of diss, slang for showing disrespect or speaking contemptuously about someone: {He dissed her in front of everyone}. The word emerged from hip-hop culture in the 1980s and has since become mainstream. To get dissed is to be insulted or snubbed: {I can't believe you dissed me like that}.

Dissent is disagreement, especially with an official position or majority view. A Supreme Court justice writes a dissent when disagreeing with the court's ruling. Religious dissenters refuse to conform to established doctrine. The verb means to hold or express such disagreement: {Three members dissented from the committee's recommendation}. Dissent carries a sense of principled opposition rather than mere difference of opinion.

A dissenter is someone who disagrees with or refuses to accept prevailing opinion, especially official doctrine. The word often appears in religious contexts—Protestant dissenters broke from the Church of England. More broadly, any person who voices opposition qualifies: {Political dissenters faced imprisonment}. The term carries a note of principled resistance rather than mere disagreement.

A dissertation is a lengthy formal document presenting original research, typically required for a doctoral degree. The candidate conducts independent investigation, then defends the dissertation before a committee. In American usage, dissertation usually refers to doctoral work, while thesis covers master's-level projects—British usage sometimes reverses this. {She spent four years writing her dissertation on medieval trade routes.}

A dissident is someone who publicly disagrees with and criticizes their government or ruling authority, especially in countries where such opposition is dangerous. The term carries connotations of courage and principle—dissidents risk imprisonment or worse for their beliefs. {Soviet dissidents were often sent to labor camps.} As an adjective, dissident describes opposing views or groups: {dissident factions within the party}.

Dissidents are people who openly oppose official policy, especially in authoritarian states where such opposition carries serious risk. The term implies principled resistance rather than mere disagreement: {Soviet dissidents faced imprisonment or exile}. A dissident voice within any organization challenges prevailing orthodoxy. As an adjective, dissident describes such opposition: {dissident factions within the party}.

Dissing is showing disrespect or contempt, typically through dismissive comments or insults. From hip-hop slang of the 1980s, clipped from "disrespecting." {Why are you always dissing my friends?} The word has moved well beyond its origins into general informal usage.

Dissolve means to cause a solid to disperse into a liquid until it disappears: {Sugar dissolves in water}. The word extends to anything that gradually disappears or breaks apart: {The crowd dissolved}, {Their marriage dissolved}. A legislature can be dissolved, ending its session. In film and video, a dissolve is a transition where one image fades as another emerges.

Dissolved describes something that has been broken down and absorbed into a liquid, disappearing into solution: {The sugar dissolved in the hot coffee}. By extension, dissolved applies to things that have ended or dispersed: a dissolved {marriage}, a dissolved {partnership}, a dissolved {parliament}. When something dissolves, it loses its distinct form and ceases to exist as a separate entity.

Dissonance is a lack of harmony or agreement. In music, dissonance is the harsh, unstable sound of notes that clash rather than blend: {The composer used dissonance to create tension before the resolution}. More broadly, dissonance describes any jarring inconsistency—between ideas, actions, or expectations: {There was dissonance between his words and his behavior}. Cognitive dissonance is the mental discomfort of holding contradictory beliefs.

Distance is primarily a noun and is based on the adjective distant, whose core meaning is far away or not near. Distance is used to note any separation: of things in space, of events in time, or of people in relationships. If you keep your distance from someone, you avoid close involvement with them. Distance learning is used to describe online courses where the instructor is remote from the student. If you distance yourself from someone or something, you make a point of being less involved with them.

Distant means far away in space or time: {a distant galaxy}, {distant memories of childhood}. It also describes relationships with little closeness—a distant {relative} shares ancestry but not intimacy, while someone acting distant is emotionally removed or aloof: {She seemed distant after the argument}. A distant {resemblance} is faint or slight.

To distill is to purify a liquid by heating it until it vaporizes, then cooling the vapor back into liquid form—separating alcohol from water, for instance, or extracting essential oils. The process removes impurities and concentrates what matters. Figuratively, to distill is to extract the essence from something complex: {Let me distill the main points}. A distillery produces distilled spirits.

Distillation is a process of separating components from a liquid mixture by selective evaporation and condensation. The technique exploits differences in boiling points: heat a mixture, capture the vapor, cool it back to liquid, and you've isolated the more volatile component. This is how spirits like whiskey and vodka are made, and how crude oil becomes gasoline, diesel, and other fuels. Figuratively, distillation refers to extracting the essence or purest form of something: {The essay is a distillation of years of research}.

Distilled describes something purified by heating a liquid until it vaporizes, then collecting the condensed vapor. Distilled {water} has had impurities removed this way. Distilled {spirits}—whiskey, vodka, gin—are concentrated through distillation. Figuratively, distilled means reduced to its essence: {The book distills thirty years of research into three hundred pages}.

A distillery is a facility where alcoholic spirits are produced through distillation—the process of heating fermented liquid to separate and concentrate the alcohol. Whiskey, vodka, gin, and rum each come from distilleries. The word also refers to the company operating such a facility: {The distillery has been family-owned for five generations}.

Distilling is the process of purifying a liquid by heating it until it vaporizes, then cooling the vapor back to liquid form. The technique separates alcohol from fermented mixtures to make spirits, or removes impurities from water. Figuratively, distilling means reducing something to its essence: {The report distills years of research into key findings}. The spelling distilling (double L) is standard in both American and British English.

Distinct means clearly separate or different from something else. Two distinct {categories} don't overlap. A distinct {possibility} is real and recognizable, not vague. Something distinct stands out clearly: {Her voice was distinct even in a crowded room}. Distinctly is the adverb: {I distinctly remember locking the door}.

Distinction refers to a difference or contrast that sets things apart: {The law makes no distinction between violent and nonviolent offenders}. It also means excellence or eminence that elevates someone above others: {She graduated with distinction}. A person of distinction has achieved notable recognition in their field. The phrase {a distinction without a difference} describes a supposed contrast that is meaningless in practice. To draw or make a distinction is to identify and articulate what separates one thing from another.

Distinguish means to recognize or perceive a difference between things, or to identify something as separate from others. {I can barely distinguish the twins apart.} It also means to make something special or notable: {Her wit distinguishes her from other comedians.} If you distinguish yourself, you do something worthy of notice or praise. The adjective distinguished describes someone respected and admired, often for accomplishments or dignified bearing.

Distinguished describes someone or something marked by excellence, dignity, or eminence. A distinguished {career} or distinguished {service} is one worthy of recognition and respect. When applied to appearance, distinguished suggests an air of refinement and authority, often associated with maturity: {He cut a distinguished figure with his silver hair and tailored suit}. To be distinguished from something else is to be recognized as different or set apart from it.

To distort something is to change it in a way that makes it less true. Distort suggests that the change is deliberate and that the motive is to deceive: The newspaper distorted the facts in its coverage of the event. Distort is sometimes used in a neutral way to mean to change in a way that is undesirable: Sound waves are distorted in the open air by wind and temperature. Distort can also mean to change the shape of something.

Distorted means twisted out of true shape or form. A distorted {image} appears warped or misshapen. Sound becomes distorted when equipment can't handle it cleanly—the crackle of an overdriven speaker. The word extends to information: a distorted {account} misrepresents what actually happened, whether through bias, exaggeration, or selective omission. {The mirror gave a distorted reflection of her face.}

Distortion is a change that makes something different from its original or true form, usually in a way that misrepresents or degrades it. Physical distortion alters shape or appearance: {The funhouse mirror created a distortion of my reflection}. In audio and electronics, distortion refers to unwanted changes in a signal that affect sound quality, though guitarists often use it deliberately for effect. Figuratively, distortion applies to facts, truth, or meaning that have been twisted or misrepresented: {His account was a distortion of what actually happened}.

Distortions are alterations that twist something from its true, original, or intended form. Physical distortions warp shape or sound: {The funhouse mirrors created wild distortions of our bodies}. Distortions of truth misrepresent facts: {His account was full of distortions}. In audio or visual media, distortion degrades signal quality—though guitar distortion is often deliberately sought.

To distract is to pull attention away from something. A loud noise distracts you from reading; you distract a crying child with a toy. The word often implies unwanted interruption: {I keep getting distracted by my phone}. But distraction can be welcome—entertainment distracts from worry, a friend distracts you from grief. To be distracted is to have your focus divided or scattered.

Distracted means unable to focus because attention has been pulled elsewhere. A distracted {driver} isn't watching the road. A distracted {student} misses what the teacher says. The word suggests attention divided or scattered rather than deliberately redirected: {Sorry, I'm distracted—what did you say?} Someone distracted by worry or grief may seem absent even while physically present.

Distracting describes something that pulls attention away from what you're trying to focus on. A distracting {noise} makes it hard to concentrate. A distracting {thought} interrupts your train of reasoning. The word can be neutral or negative depending on context—a distracting conversation might be welcome or unwelcome: {I find her habit of humming incredibly distracting}.

Distraction is something that diverts attention from what you're trying to focus on: {My phone is a constant distraction}. It can also mean the state of being diverted: {I worked to the point of distraction}. The phrase {driven to distraction} suggests being pushed toward mental agitation or madness by persistent annoyance.

Distractions are things that pull attention away from what someone is trying to focus on. A ringing phone, a wandering thought, a coworker stopping by—all are distractions from the task at hand. The word often carries mild disapproval, suggesting the interruption is unwelcome or frivolous: {I need to work without distractions}. But distractions can be welcome escapes: {The movie was a good distraction from my worries}.

Distraught describes extreme emotional distress—upset to the point of being unable to think clearly or function normally. The word suggests visible agitation: {She was distraught when she heard about the accident}. Someone distraught with grief or worry may be tearful, frantic, or barely coherent. It's stronger than upset or troubled, implying emotions have overwhelmed composure.

Distress is suffering or anxiety caused by pain, trouble, or misfortune: {The news caused her great distress}. A ship or plane in distress faces danger and needs help. Financial distress means serious money trouble. Distressed furniture has been deliberately aged or weathered. To distress someone is to cause them worry or anguish.

Distressed describes a state of suffering, anxiety, or pain. A distressed {person} is upset or troubled; a distressed {company} faces financial difficulty. In furniture and fashion, distressed means intentionally aged or worn: {distressed leather}, {distressed jeans}. The deliberate wear mimics authentic weathering. A distress {signal} calls for help; a damsel {in distress} needs rescue.

The verb distribute, to deal out shares of something, gives rise to the noun distribution, which can characterize the act of or result of giving out, or something that is given out. In a more abstract way, anything that can be observed in multiple places while having the same characteristics can be called a distribution: the distribution of squirrels across Wyoming. In commerce, distribution refers to the business of ensuring that products reach consumers. In computing, a distribution is a particular release of a version of software.

A district is a defined area within a larger region, typically established for administrative, electoral, or functional purposes: {the financial district}, {a school district}, {congressional districts}. Cities divide into districts by character or use—theater districts, historic districts, red-light districts. To district is to divide an area into such zones, though the noun dominates.

Distrust is a lack of trust or confidence in someone or something: {She regarded his promises with distrust}. The verb means to doubt the reliability or honesty of: {I distrust anyone who won't look me in the eye}. Distrust suggests watchful suspicion—not outright accusation, but unwillingness to extend faith.

To disturb is to interrupt or interfere with something settled or at rest. You might disturb someone's sleep, disturb papers on a desk, or disturb the peace. The word carries a sense of unwelcome intrusion: {Sorry to disturb you, but there's a call}. Disturb also means to trouble emotionally—disturbing news unsettles the mind. Something disturbed has been thrown out of its natural state.

Disturbance is an interruption of peace, order, or stability. A {disturbance in the neighborhood} might be a loud argument; a {sleep disturbance} disrupts rest. The word covers everything from minor annoyances to serious disruptions—emotional disturbances, atmospheric disturbances, civil disturbances. In legal contexts, creating a disturbance means conduct that disturbs public peace: {He was arrested for causing a disturbance}.

Disturbed describes a state of being unsettled or disrupted. Sleep can be disturbed by noise; water is disturbed when something breaks its surface. Applied to people, disturbed often suggests emotional or psychological instability: {a deeply disturbed individual}, {disturbed by what she witnessed}. The word ranges from mild unease to serious mental illness depending on context.

Disturbing describes something that causes unease, anxiety, or emotional discomfort. A disturbing {news report} or disturbing {images} provoke feelings of alarm or distress in those who encounter them. The word suggests something that interrupts mental peace or challenges one's sense of normalcy: {The documentary contained some disturbing footage of animal cruelty}. What counts as disturbing varies by person and context, but the term typically signals content that may upset sensitive viewers.

A ditch is a long narrow trench dug in the ground, typically for drainage or irrigation: {a drainage ditch along the roadside}. To ditch something is to get rid of it or abandon it: {I ditched the old couch}, {She ditched her date at the party}. To ditch class is to skip it. A pilot who ditches lands an aircraft in water in an emergency.

Ditched is the past tense of ditch, meaning to abandon or get rid of something. You can ditch a plan, ditch class, or ditch a person: {She ditched her boyfriend after prom}. The word carries a casual, slightly callous tone—ditching suggests leaving without much ceremony or regret. Originally from literally throwing something into a ditch.

Ditches are long narrow channels dug in the ground, typically for drainage or irrigation. A roadside ditch catches runoff; a drainage ditch carries water away from fields. To ditch something is to abandon or discard it: {We ditched the car and ran}, {She ditched class}, {He ditched his girlfriend}. In aviation, to ditch is to make an emergency landing on water.

Ditching is abandoning or getting rid of something—or someone. You ditch class by skipping it, ditch a plan by dropping it, ditch a boyfriend by breaking up. {I'm ditching this old laptop.} The word carries casual disregard: what's ditched wasn't worth keeping. In aviation, ditching is an emergency water landing: {The pilot ditched in the Hudson River.}

Ditto means the same as what was just said or written. It originated as a mark (〃 or ") used in lists to avoid repeating the item above. In speech, ditto expresses agreement: {I'm exhausted. —Ditto.} The word can also function as a verb meaning to duplicate or repeat: {Just ditto what I did}.

A diva is a celebrated female opera singer, from the Italian word for goddess. The term extends to any distinguished woman in entertainment—a pop diva, a diva of Broadway. In contemporary use, diva often describes someone dramatic, demanding, or temperamental: {She's being a total diva about the seating arrangements}. The negative sense has largely overtaken the complimentary one.

Divas is the plural of diva—a celebrated female singer, especially in opera. The term extends to any woman with exceptional talent who commands attention. It often carries connotations of demanding, temperamental behavior: {The divas on set refused to share a dressing room}. Men who act similarly may be called divas mockingly.

The noun and verb dive suggests downward movement, often rapid, and perhaps with water waiting at the bottom. To dive into a pool is to jump in, head first. If prices or ratings dive, they decrease rapidly. A dive is an instance of either of these but also a more complicated scenario where people and equipment spend some time underwater (scuba dive, cave dive, wreck dive). In slang use, a dive is a cheap and dirty club or bar.

To divebomb is to plunge steeply downward toward a target, like a military aircraft attacking from above. The term extends to any sudden swooping descent: {A seagull divebombed my sandwich}. Figuratively, it describes rapid decline: {The stock divebombed after the earnings report}. As a noun, a divebomb is such an attack or descent.

A diver is someone who dives—into water from a height, or beneath the surface with breathing equipment. Competitive divers perform acrobatic maneuvers from springboards or platforms. Scuba divers and deep-sea divers explore underwater. By extension, diver describes birds that plunge or swim underwater for food: {The loons are expert divers}.

Diverse means varied or composed of different kinds. A diverse {group} includes people of different backgrounds, perspectives, or identities. A diverse {portfolio} spreads investments across different assets. The word often appears in discussions of representation: {The company is working to build a more diverse workforce}. Diverse sometimes serves as a euphemism for including racial minorities or other underrepresented groups.

Diversion is the act of turning something aside from its course. A river diversion redirects water flow; a traffic diversion routes vehicles around an obstruction. The word extends to anything that draws attention away: {The fire was a diversion while accomplices robbed the vault}. In gentler use, a diversion is a pleasant distraction or amusement: {Golf was his favorite diversion from work pressures}.

The core meaning of diversity is closely related to its underlying adjective, diverse: having many distinct or unlike elements or qualities: The organization tries to preserve the genetic diversity of cattle. In modern use, diversity is often applied to the condition of having, allowing, or welcoming people of many different backgrounds or beliefs: Parents were concerned that the textbooks in use did not reflect the cultural diversity of the students.

Divide, noun and verb, suggests division: either the strictly arithmetic kind (divide 32 by 4), or a split into sides or factions: The town was divided along racial lines. When cells divide, they make copies of themselves by meiosis or mitosis. A geographic divide is a higher border between separate watersheds (the Continental Divide). A divide of people or opinions is the fact of their disagreeing and taking different sides on an issue: The marriage equality movement created a cultural divide.

Divided describes something separated into parts or sections: {a divided highway}, {a house divided against itself}. When people are divided, they disagree or hold opposing views: {The jury was divided on the verdict}. A divided {attention} is split between multiple things. In arithmetic, a number divided by another yields a quotient. Something that divides opinion provokes strong disagreement: {a deeply divided electorate}.

A dividend is a sum of money paid regularly by a company to its shareholders from profits: {The stock pays a quarterly dividend}. In arithmetic, a dividend is the number being divided by another. Figuratively, a dividend is a benefit or bonus: {Regular exercise pays dividends in energy and mood}.

Dividends are payments a company makes to its shareholders from profits. The word also applies to any returns or benefits from an investment of effort: {Her patience paid dividends when the promotion came through}. In arithmetic, the dividend is the number being divided.

Divination is the practice of seeking knowledge of the future or hidden things through supernatural means. Methods include reading tarot cards, casting runes, examining entrails, interpreting dreams, or consulting oracles. The word covers both the general practice and specific acts: {She studied various forms of divination}; {His divination predicted a harsh winter}. Whether treated as genuine insight or mere superstition depends on the believer.

Divine means of, from, or relating to a god or the sacred: {divine intervention}, {divine right of kings}. Something divine is supremely good or beautiful: {The dessert was divine}. To divine is to discover through intuition or supernatural insight, or to locate underground water with a divining rod. A divine is a member of the clergy or a theologian.

Diving is the activity of plunging into water, typically headfirst. Competitive diving involves acrobatic maneuvers from platforms or springboards: {She won gold in the 10-meter platform diving}. Scuba diving and skin diving refer to swimming underwater, often to explore reefs or wrecks. In sports like soccer, diving means faking a foul by falling dramatically: {The referee ignored his obvious diving}.

Divinity is the quality or state of being divine—godlike nature or essence. It refers to a god or goddess: {the divinities of ancient Greece}. The study of religion and theology is also called divinity: {a divinity school}, {a doctor of divinity}. In American English, divinity is also a soft, creamy candy made with sugar, corn syrup, and egg whites.

Division is the act of separating something into parts, or the state of being so separated. In arithmetic, division determines how many times one number contains another: {twelve divided by four}. A division can be a distinct section of an organization—a military unit, a corporate department, a sports league grouping. Division also names disagreement that splits a group: {The issue caused deep division within the party}.

Divisive describes something that causes disagreement or conflict among people, splitting them into opposing camps: {a divisive issue}, {divisive rhetoric}. The word often appears in political contexts where opinions polarize sharply: {The policy proved deeply divisive}. A divisive figure provokes strong reactions—admired by some, despised by others.

Divorce is the legal dissolution of a marriage. The term extends to any decisive separation: {a divorce between theory and practice}, {She divorced herself from the controversy}. As a verb, to divorce is to end a marriage or to separate completely: {They divorced after twenty years}, {You can't divorce the art from the artist}.

Divorced describes the state of having legally ended a marriage: {She's been divorced for three years}. As a verb form, it marks the action: {They divorced in 2019}. Figuratively, divorced from means separated or disconnected: {His theories are divorced from reality}. The word carries less stigma than it once did.

A divorcee is a person, typically a woman, whose marriage has ended in divorce. The word carries a slightly dated or formal tone: {The apartment building was popular with young divorcees}. The masculine form divorcé exists but is rarely used; divorcee now serves for any gender, or people simply say divorced person.

Divorces is the plural of divorce, which is the legal dissolution of a marriage. As a verb, divorces means formally ends a marriage or, more broadly, separates one thing from another: {She divorces emotion from logic when making decisions}. The noun form refers to multiple instances of marital dissolution: {The county recorded three hundred divorces last year}. Someone who has gone through this process is a divorcee or divorcé.

Diy is a nonstandard or casual spelling of DIY, the acronym for "do it yourself." It appears in informal contexts like social media hashtags or text messages: {just finished my diy bookshelf}. The lowercase form lacks the visual punch of the standard acronym but carries the same meaning of making, building, or repairing things yourself rather than hiring professionals. (Standard form is uppercase DIY.)

Dizziness is a sensation of unsteadiness, lightheadedness, or feeling that one's surroundings are spinning. It can result from inner ear problems, low blood pressure, dehydration, or simply standing up too quickly: {A wave of dizziness hit her when she stood}. Figuratively, dizziness describes mental confusion or disorientation from overwhelming circumstances: {the dizziness of sudden fame}.

Dizzy describes a sensation of spinning or unsteadiness, as if you might fall: {I felt dizzy after the roller coaster}. The feeling can come from illness, spinning, heights, or standing up too fast. Extended uses suggest confusion or being overwhelmed: {The pace of change left everyone dizzy}. Calling someone a dizzy blonde or just dizzy means they're scatterbrained or frivolous.

A djinn is a supernatural being in Islamic and Arabian mythology—a spirit created from smokeless fire, capable of appearing in human or animal form. Djinn (also spelled jinn or genie) can be benevolent, malevolent, or neutral, and feature prominently in folklore and the Quran. The anglicized "genie" derives from this word, though Western genies—wish-granting lamp-dwellers—represent a simplified version of the richer Islamic tradition.

A Doberman is a large, muscular dog breed with a sleek coat, typically black or brown with rust markings. Developed in Germany as a guard dog, Dobermans are known for their alertness, loyalty, and intelligence. The breed's cropped ears and docked tail give it a distinctive sharp-angled silhouette. Also called Doberman pinscher. {Their Doberman barked at every stranger who approached the gate.}

Doc is an informal title or form of address for a doctor, especially a physician: {What's the diagnosis, doc?} It can also refer affectionately to anyone with expertise: {He's the doc when it comes to fixing cars}. In computing, doc is short for document, appearing in filenames and as slang for documentation: {Read the docs before asking questions}. (Capitalized Doc is a name or nickname.)

Dock represents four words with different meanings. In descending order of frequency, a dock is a place where a ship or other vehicle or device parks for loading, unloading, or charging. When something docks, it settles at a dock. To dock something is to cut it shorter. When wages are docked, money is withdrawn from them. A docked tail is one that has been trimmed. In a courtroom, the dock is where the accused stands during trial. Finally, dock is a genus of weedy plants in the buckwheat family.

Docked describes something that has been cut short, reduced, or connected to a station. A dog with a docked tail has had it surgically shortened. Docked pay has been reduced as a penalty: {They docked her wages for being late}. A ship that has docked has moored at a dock. A laptop that's docked is connected to a docking station for additional functionality.

Docking is the act of bringing two things together to connect. A ship docks at a pier; a spacecraft docks with a station. In computing, docking a laptop means connecting it to a docking station that provides additional ports and peripherals. To dock wages or points is to deduct from them: {They docked his pay for being late}. Docking also refers to cutting short an animal's tail or ears—a controversial practice in dog breeding. In sexual slang, docking describes a specific act involving two penises, one uncircumcised.

Docks are structures extending into water where boats moor for loading, unloading, or repairs. A dock may also be an enclosed basin for ship maintenance. In a courtroom, the dock is the enclosure where a defendant stands during trial. To dock is to bring a vessel into port, or to join spacecraft in orbit: {The shuttle docked with the space station}. Separately, to dock means to cut short—docking a dog's tail, or docking someone's pay by deducting from it.

A dockyard is a shipyard—a facility where ships are built, repaired, and maintained. The term is more common in British English and often refers specifically to naval installations: {the Royal Dockyard at Portsmouth}. Dockyards include dry docks, warehouses, and workshops for outfitting vessels.

A doctor is a person qualified to practice medicine—diagnosing illness, prescribing treatment, and caring for patients. The title extends to holders of doctoral degrees in any field: {She's a doctor of philosophy}. To doctor something is to alter or tamper with it: {Someone doctored the photos}, {He doctored his coffee with whiskey}. A doctored document has been falsified.

A doctorate is the highest academic degree awarded by universities, requiring years of advanced study and original research beyond the master's level. The most common is the PhD (Doctor of Philosophy), but doctorates exist across fields: medicine (MD), law (JD), education (EdD). {She spent six years earning her doctorate in biochemistry.}

Doctored describes something that has been altered, tampered with, or adulterated—often to deceive. A doctored {photograph} has been manipulated; doctored {evidence} has been falsified; a doctored {drink} has had something added without the drinker's knowledge. The word implies the original has been changed in ways that aren't immediately apparent: {The document had clearly been doctored}.

Doctoring is tampering with something to alter its nature or appearance, often deceptively: {The accountant was accused of doctoring the books}. You can doctor a drink by adding something to it, doctor a photo to change what it shows, or doctor evidence to mislead. The word implies manipulation rather than improvement—making something appear other than it is.

Doctors is the plural of doctor—physicians who diagnose and treat illness, or holders of doctoral degrees. As a verb, doctors means to tamper with or alter something: {Someone doctored the evidence}. It can also mean to provide medical treatment: {She doctored her own wounds}. To doctor a drink is to add something to it, often secretly.

Doctrine is a set of beliefs or principles taught and held by a group—religious, political, or institutional. Church doctrine defines what adherents believe. Military doctrine establishes standard procedures for operations. Legal doctrine refers to established principles that guide court decisions: {the doctrine of precedent}. The word implies official teaching that followers are expected to accept.

A document is a piece of written or printed matter containing information or evidence: {legal documents}, {historical documents}, {government documents}. The word emphasizes official or formal status—a scribbled note isn't usually called a document, but a signed contract is. In computing, document extends to any file: word processing documents, PDFs, spreadsheets. To document something is to record it systematically: {She documented every step of the process}. Documentation means supporting records or, in technical contexts, instructional materials for software.

Documentaries are nonfiction films or television programs that document real events, people, or subjects. The genre ranges from observational footage to heavily narrated investigations, from nature films to true crime. A documentary typically presents factual material, though the filmmaker's perspective shapes what's shown: {The documentary exposed corruption in the industry}. {We watched a documentary about deep-sea creatures}.

A documentary is a nonfiction film or program that presents factual material about real events, people, or subjects. Unlike fictional narratives, documentaries aim to inform, persuade, or explore actual phenomena: {a documentary about climate change}, {a true-crime documentary}. As an adjective, documentary means consisting of or based on documents or factual records: {documentary evidence}, {documentary proof}.

Documents are written or printed records that provide information or evidence: birth certificates, contracts, legal filings, identification papers. To document something is to record it systematically: {She documented every expense}. In computing, a document is any file containing text or data that a user creates or edits. {Do you have the documents I need to sign?}

To dodge is to move quickly to avoid something—a blow, a ball, or a person. By extension, dodge means to evade or escape through cleverness or trickery: {dodge taxes}, {dodge the draft}, {dodge a question}. A dodge can also be a scheme or trick: {It's just a dodge to avoid responsibility}. The word suggests nimble evasion, whether physical or figurative. (Capitalized Dodge is the automobile brand.)

Dodgeball is a game where players throw balls at opponents while trying to avoid being hit themselves. Getting struck eliminates you; catching a thrown ball may eliminate the thrower or revive a teammate. The game is associated with school gymnasiums and playground culture: {We played dodgeball in P.E.} To dodge is to evade—the sport's essential skill.

Dodgy is British slang for something questionable, unreliable, or potentially dangerous. A dodgy {character} seems untrustworthy. A dodgy {deal} might be fraudulent. A dodgy {knee} gives trouble. The word suggests something not quite right without specifying exactly what's wrong: {The whole situation felt a bit dodgy}.

A dodo was a large flightless bird native to Mauritius, hunted to extinction by the late 17th century. The dodo's inability to fly or flee made it easy prey, and it has become a symbol of obsolescence and extinction. To call someone a dodo is to call them stupid or hopelessly out of touch: {Don't be a dodo}. The phrase {dead as a dodo} means completely extinct or defunct.

Dodos are flightless birds that became extinct in the late 17th century, native to Mauritius. Unable to fly and unafraid of humans, they were easily hunted to extinction—making the dodo a symbol of obsolescence and vulnerability. To call someone a dodo is to call them stupid or hopelessly out of touch: {Those old dodos in management don't understand the internet}.

Dog is a native English word that denotes the domesticated form of canine that is descended from the gray wolf. Dog combines with many other words to form compounds such as bulldog and sheepdog. It is also frequently modified by adjectives, since there are so many kinds of dogs and they serve so many different purposes: police dog, attack dog, and stray dog. As a slang word, dog can mean feet (my dogs are tired) or it can designate a person, as in You lucky dog!

Dogeared describes pages with corners folded down to mark a place, and by extension, anything worn from heavy use. A dogeared {paperback} shows signs of being read and reread. Dogeared {notes} have been consulted many times. The term suggests something well-loved rather than merely damaged: {Her dogeared copy of the cookbook was full of marginal notes}.

A dogfight is aerial combat between fighter aircraft at close range, characterized by rapid maneuvering as pilots try to get behind their opponents. The term evokes the chaotic, snarling quality of dogs fighting. By extension, dogfight describes any fierce, close-quarters struggle or intensely competitive situation: {The election turned into a real dogfight in the final weeks}. As a verb, to dogfight is to engage in such combat.

Dogfighting is the blood sport of pitting dogs against each other in fights, typically to the death or serious injury. It's illegal in most countries but persists underground, with gambling on outcomes. Separately, dogfighting refers to close-range aerial combat between military aircraft: {The pilots engaged in a dogfight over the channel}.

Dogfights are aerial battles between fighter aircraft at close range, involving tight maneuvers as pilots try to gain position on opponents: {The skies over Britain were filled with dogfights during the Blitz}. The term comes from the chaotic, swirling nature of fighting dogs. Dogfights also names the cruel practice of setting dogs against each other for sport, now illegal in most places.

Dogged means stubbornly persistent, continuing despite difficulty or discouragement: {dogged determination}, {a dogged pursuit of the truth}. The word suggests tenacity that borders on obstinacy—someone who won't give up even when others might. {She showed dogged resistance to the proposed changes.} Pronounced with two syllables: DOG-id.

Doggy is a childish or affectionate word for a dog: {Look at the cute little doggy!} As an adjective, it means resembling or relating to dogs: {a doggy smell}, {doggy treats}. Doggy style (or doggie style) refers to a sexual position where one partner enters from behind while the other is on hands and knees.

A doghouse is a small outdoor shelter for a dog. The phrase {in the doghouse} means in disfavor or trouble with someone, as if banished from the comfort of home: {He forgot their anniversary and ended up in the doghouse}.

Dogma is a set of principles laid down by an authority as incontrovertibly true. Religious dogma comprises official doctrines that believers must accept: {the dogma of papal infallibility}. Outside religion, dogma often carries a negative connotation—rigid beliefs held without evidence or openness to question: {economic dogma}, {political dogma}. Someone who clings to dogma is dogmatic.

Dogmatic describes someone who asserts opinions as unquestionable truth, refusing to consider alternatives: {He was dogmatic about his political views}. The word implies rigidity and closed-mindedness—a dogmatic person states beliefs as if they were established facts. In theology, dogmatic refers to official church doctrine, but the everyday sense carries negative connotations of arrogance and inflexibility.

Dognapping is the theft of a dog, formed on the model of kidnapping. The crime has increased with the rising value of certain breeds: {The French bulldog was recovered three days after the dognapping}. Dognapper is the agent noun.

A dogpile is a heap of people piling on top of one person, often in celebration or roughhousing: {The team formed a dogpile on the pitcher after the final out}. Figuratively, to dogpile is to join others in attacking or criticizing someone: {Everyone dogpiled on him after his controversial tweet}. The image comes from dogs piling together.

Dogpiled means overwhelmed by a sudden rush of people or responses, from the literal image of multiple people jumping onto someone in a heap. Online, it describes being flooded with criticism, replies, or attacks: {She made one unpopular tweet and got dogpiled}. In sports or play, it's the physical pile-on after a big moment: {The team dogpiled the pitcher after the final out}.
A dogpile is either a literal or figurative heap of people or things. If you dogpile, you take part in the activity of piling up on someone or something.

Dogpiling is ganging up on someone, especially online—when multiple people attack, criticize, or mock a single target in rapid succession. The image is of dogs piling onto prey or each other. {She posted one controversial opinion and got dogpiled by hundreds of strangers}. The noun dogpile refers to the heap itself or the act of joining one.

Dogs are domesticated canines kept as pets, working animals, or companions. The word extends to related animals (prairie dog, wild dog) and mechanical gripping devices. Informally, dogs are feet: {My dogs are killing me}. To dog someone is to follow persistently: {Bad luck dogged him for years}. Something that {goes to the dogs} falls into ruin.

A dogsled is a sled pulled by a team of dogs, used for transportation across snow and ice. Dogsleds were essential to Arctic and subarctic peoples and later to polar explorers. The verb means to travel by dogsled: {We dogsledded across the frozen lake}. Also spelled dog sled.

A dogtag is a metal identification tag worn by military personnel, typically on a chain around the neck. The tags bear essential information—name, service number, blood type—for identifying casualties. The name comes from their resemblance to pet identification tags. In extended use, dogtag applies to any similar identification tag: {The gym requires members to scan their dogtags at entry}.

Dogtags are metal identification tags worn around the neck by military personnel, stamped with name, serial number, blood type, and other vital information. The tags help identify soldiers who are wounded or killed in combat. The term extends to any similar identification tag: {The gym requires members to scan their dogtags at the entrance}. Also spelled dog tags.

A dogwhistle is a signal that is intended to be heard or understood by a particular audience. In politics, this may be a reference to an earlier statement or event that is understood by those familiar with the earlier context. The idea behind the term is that only dogs can hear dogwhistles; similarly, only those for whom a dogwhistle is intended can understand it.

Dogwhistles are coded messages that appear innocent to general audiences but carry specific meaning to a targeted group. The term comes from ultrasonic whistles only dogs can hear. In politics, a dogwhistle signals alignment with particular views—often controversial or prejudiced—without stating them explicitly: {Critics accused the candidate of using racial dogwhistles}. The verb is to dogwhistle.
Doh and duh are used ironically to signal that you, or someone else, have been very slow to understand something obvious.

A doily is a small decorative mat, typically made of lace, paper, or linen, placed under dishes, vases, or other objects to protect surfaces or add ornamentation. Doilies evoke Victorian domesticity and grandmother's parlors—either charming or fussy depending on your taste: {The cake sat on a paper doily}.

A dojo is a training hall for martial arts—judo, karate, aikido, and similar disciplines. The Japanese word literally means "place of the way," suggesting a space for learning and practice. In figurative use, dojo extends to any space dedicated to intensive skill development: {a coding dojo}, {a writer's dojo}.

The doldrums are a state of stagnation or listlessness: {The economy has been in the doldrums for months}, {She's been in the doldrums since the breakup}. The word comes from a region near the equator where sailing ships could be becalmed for weeks in still air—the original doldrums were geographical before becoming psychological.

A doll is a small figure of a human, typically a toy for children. Dolls range from simple cloth figures to elaborate collectibles. The word extends to attractive people, especially women: {She's a real doll}. To {doll up} is to dress elaborately or apply heavy makeup. Calling someone a doll can be affectionate or condescending depending on context.

A dollar is the basic unit of currency in the United States, Canada, Australia, and several other countries. The word often stands for money generally: {I don't have a dollar to my name}. A {dollar store} sells cheap goods. To {look like a million dollars} is to look fantastic. {The sixty-four-thousand-dollar question} is the crucial one everyone wants answered.

Dollars is the plural of dollar, the basic unit of currency in the United States and several other countries. Beyond counting money, dollars appears in expressions about value and cost: {That painting is worth big dollars}. To {look like a million dollars} is to look fantastic. {Dollars to donuts} expresses high confidence in a bet.

A dollhouse is a miniature model of a house, typically furnished with tiny furniture and figures, used as a child's toy or adult collectible. The scale and detail vary from simple play sets to elaborate replicas. Figuratively, dollhouse describes anything diminutive or precious: {The cottage was a perfect little dollhouse}. Also spelled doll's house, especially in British English.

Dollhouses are miniature model houses, typically furnished with small-scale furniture and accessories, used as children's toys or adult collectibles. The appeal lies in creating and controlling a complete domestic world in miniature: {She spent hours arranging the tiny furniture in her dollhouse}. Elaborate dollhouses with handcrafted details can be serious hobbies for adults. Also spelled as two words: doll houses.

A dollop is a small, soft lump or blob of something, typically food: {a dollop of whipped cream}, {a dollop of sour cream on the baked potato}. The word suggests an imprecise, casually applied portion rather than a measured amount. Figuratively, a dollop of something is a small quantity: {The story needs a dollop of humor}.

Dolls are figures resembling humans or animals, typically used as children's toys. A doll can be simple or elaborate—from rag dolls to porcelain collectibles to action figures. To {doll up} is to dress elaborately or apply heavy makeup. Calling someone a doll is dated slang for an attractive person or a term of endearment: {Thanks, you're a doll}.

A dolly is a small platform on wheels used for moving heavy objects: {We loaded the refrigerator onto a dolly}. In film and television, a dolly is a wheeled platform that carries a camera for smooth tracking shots—to dolly is to move the camera this way: {The director wanted to dolly in slowly on the actor's face}. Dolly is also a child's word for a doll. (Capitalized Dolly is a given name.)

Dolphins are marine mammals known for their intelligence, playfulness, and streamlined bodies adapted for swift swimming. They breathe air through a blowhole, live in social groups called pods, and communicate through clicks and whistles. Dolphins appear frequently in human culture as symbols of friendliness and grace, and some species are trained for entertainment or research. In nautical contexts, a dolphin is also a mooring post or buoy cluster used to secure boats.

Dolphins are marine mammals known for their intelligence, playfulness, and streamlined bodies. They breathe air through a blowhole, travel in social groups called pods, and communicate through clicks and whistles. Dolphins appear frequently in mythology and popular culture as friendly, even mystical creatures. The Miami Dolphins are an NFL team. {We watched dolphins leaping alongside the boat.}

A domain is an area, either physical or abstract, that is separate from others because of unique qualities. The public domain includes everything freely available to or concerning the public. A domain expert is someone who is an authority on a particular topic. Historically, a domain was all the territory governed by a particular ruler. Today, we encounter domain most frequently in connection with the internet: The company has purchased a group of domain names in preparation for its launch.

Domains are areas of territory, knowledge, or activity over which someone or something has control or influence: {the king's domain}, {the domain of physics}, {that's outside my domain of expertise}. In computing, a domain is a distinct subset of the internet identified by a common address suffix: {.com}, {.org}, {.edu}. The word often implies ownership or sovereignty—a domain is yours to govern.

A dome is a rounded vault forming a roof or ceiling, typically hemispherical: {the dome of the Capitol building}. The shape extends to anything dome-like—a bald head, the sky, or a stadium roof. To dome in gaming slang is to shoot someone in the head: {He domed me from across the map}.

Domes is the plural of dome—a rounded vault forming a roof or ceiling, typically hemispherical: {The domes of the cathedral gleamed in the sunlight}. Dome extends to anything dome-shaped: the dome of the skull, a sports stadium with a domed roof. In slang, domes means heads: {Use your domes, people}.

Domestic relates to the home, household, or family life: {domestic chores}, {domestic bliss}. It also means within one's own country rather than foreign: {domestic flights}, {domestic policy}. A domestic is a household servant. Domestic animals are tamed species that live alongside humans. In law enforcement, a domestic is a call involving household members in conflict—often a {domestic dispute} or {domestic violence} situation.

Domesticated describes animals or plants that have been bred over generations to live alongside humans and serve human purposes. Dogs, cats, and cattle are domesticated; wolves, wildcats, and bison are wild. The word extends to people who have settled into conventional home life: {Marriage has domesticated him—he does dishes now}. A domesticated person has traded wilder ways for comfortable routines.

Domestication is the process of taming wild animals or plants for human use over generations. Dogs emerged through domestication of wolves; wheat through domestication of wild grasses. The term extends to cultural adaptation: {the domestication of foreign customs}. To speak of someone's domestication is to suggest they've been trained for household life: {Marriage completed his domestication}.

Dominance is control or power over others, or the state of being dominant. In animal behavior, dominance describes hierarchical relationships where some individuals have priority access to resources: {The alpha wolf maintained dominance over the pack}. The word applies to competitive situations—market dominance, military dominance—and to personality traits: {Her dominance in meetings intimidated colleagues}. In genetics, dominance describes how one allele masks another.

Dominant describes what prevails, controls, or stands above others. A dominant {trait} in genetics masks recessive ones. A dominant {player} overpowers competitors. The dominant {theme} of a novel is its most prominent. In music, the dominant is the fifth note of a scale. In BDSM, a dominant (or dom) is the partner who takes control.

To dominate is to exert control or power over something or someone. A dominant team dominates its opponents. A dominant personality dominates conversations. {The cathedral dominates the skyline}—it towers over everything else, commanding attention. Market domination means controlling a large share: {Three companies dominate the industry}. To be dominated by a fear or obsession is to be ruled by it.

Dominated is the past tense of dominate, meaning to have control, power, or commanding influence over something or someone. A team that dominated a game won decisively; a figure who dominated a field shaped it more than anyone else. {The empire dominated the region for centuries.} {She dominated the conversation.} In sexual contexts, particularly BDSM, dominated describes being under the control of a dominant partner.

Domination is control or power over others. A country achieves domination over a region through military conquest or economic leverage. A team's domination of a sport means consistent, overwhelming superiority. In BDSM, domination refers to the role of exercising control over a submissive partner: {She's into domination}. To seek {world domination} is to aim for global control—often used hyperbolically or in fiction.

A dominatrix is a woman who takes the dominant role in BDSM activities, typically as a professional service. She controls and sometimes humiliates submissive partners, often using restraints, commands, or corporal punishment. The term evokes a specific aesthetic—leather, latex, high heels, whips: {She worked as a dominatrix in a Manhattan dungeon}. Plural: dominatrices or dominatrixes.

Domineering describes someone who asserts control over others in an overbearing way. A domineering {boss} micromanages every decision. A domineering {parent} dictates rather than guides. The word emphasizes not just authority but its aggressive, suffocating exercise—the kind that leaves little room for others to act or think independently.

Dominion is supreme authority or control over something: {The king held dominion over the realm}. It can also mean the territory subject to such rule: {the vast dominions of the empire}. In theology, dominion often refers to God's sovereignty over creation, or humanity's granted authority over the natural world. The word carries a formal, sometimes archaic tone, appearing in legal and religious contexts more than everyday speech.

A domino is a small rectangular tile marked with dots on one face, used in games where players match ends with equal values. A set of these tiles is called dominoes, as is the game itself. The domino effect describes a chain reaction where one event triggers the next: {Defaults spread through the banking system like dominoes falling}. Separately, a domino is a loose hooded cloak worn at masquerades, or the mask that accompanies it.

Dominoes is a game played with rectangular tiles divided into two squares, each marked with dots (pips) indicating value. Players match ends with equal pip counts, building chains across a table. The tiles themselves are also called dominoes. A single tile is a domino. The {domino effect} describes a chain reaction where one event triggers others in sequence—like toppling dominoes stood on end.

Dominos is the plural of domino, referring to the rectangular game pieces marked with dots, or to the game played with them. The word also names a loose hooded cloak with a half-mask, worn at masquerades—though this sense is now rare. {We played dominos until midnight.} (Capitalized Domino's is the pizza chain.)

To don something is to put it on—usually clothing or equipment: {He donned his coat and hat}. The word is literary and somewhat old-fashioned, the opposite of doff. Don also appears as a title of respect in Spanish-speaking contexts, placed before a man's first name: {Don Miguel}. In British university slang, a don is a senior member of a college, especially at Oxford or Cambridge. (Capitalized Don is a given name.)

To donate is to give something—usually money, blood, or goods—to a cause, organization, or person in need. Unlike ordinary giving, donate implies generosity without expectation of return: {She donated her old clothes to charity}, {He donates blood regularly}. The word often appears in formal or institutional contexts: {Please donate to our campaign}.

A donation is something given to a cause, charity, or person in need—typically money, but also goods, blood, or organs. The word implies voluntary giving without expectation of return: {Please consider making a donation to the food bank}. To donate is to give in this way. A donor is one who donates.

Donations are things given to a cause, charity, or person in need—typically money, but also goods, blood, or organs. The word emphasizes voluntary giving without expectation of return: {The shelter relies on donations from the community}. A donation to a political campaign may be called a contribution instead, perhaps to downplay the one-sidedness of giving.

Done indicates completion or finish. When something is done, it has reached its end state—a task is done when completed, food is done when fully cooked, and a person is done when they've had enough: {I'm done with this conversation}. The expression {done and dusted} emphasizes finality. In informal speech, done often replaces finished: {Are you done with the bathroom?} When someone says {I'm done}, context determines whether they mean finished with a task or exhausted by a situation.

A donkey is a domesticated animal related to the horse but smaller, with longer ears and a bray instead of a neigh. Donkeys are known for stubbornness and surefootedness, making them useful as pack animals in rough terrain. Calling someone a donkey suggests they're foolish or stubborn: {Don't be a donkey about this}.

Donkeys are domesticated members of the horse family, smaller and with longer ears than horses. They're known for stubbornness and sure-footedness, traditionally used as pack animals. A donkey can also mean a stupid person. {Donkey's years} means a very long time. In British slang, {donkey work} is tedious labor.

A donor is someone who gives something—typically blood, organs, money, or time—without receiving payment. Blood donors supply hospitals. Organ donors provide kidneys or hearts for transplant. Donors to charities or political campaigns give money: {The museum's largest donor got a wing named after him}. A sperm donor or egg donor contributes genetic material for reproduction.

Donors are people who give something—typically money, blood, or organs—to help others or support a cause. A blood {donor} gives blood for transfusions; an organ {donor} provides organs for transplant. In charitable contexts, donors contribute money: {The museum honored its major donors at a gala}. A sperm or egg donor provides genetic material for reproduction.

Donut is a variant spelling of doughnut—a small, sweet fried cake, typically ring-shaped with a hole in the center or filled with jam or cream. The simplified spelling dominates in American commercial contexts: {Dunkin' Donuts}, {a dozen donuts}. In driving, to do donuts is to spin a vehicle in tight circles, leaving circular tire marks.

Donuts is the spelling preferred by the food industry for doughnuts—ring-shaped fried dough, typically glazed or frosted. The simplified spelling gained traction through chains like Dunkin' Donuts. {I grabbed a dozen donuts for the office}. In automotive slang, doing donuts means spinning a car in tight circles, leaving circular tire marks.

A doodle is an aimless drawing made while the mind is elsewhere—during a phone call, a boring meeting, a lecture. The verb means to make such drawings: {She doodled in the margins of her notebook}. By extension, to doodle can mean to waste time or putter around without purpose.

Doodles are casual, absentminded drawings made while attention is elsewhere—during phone calls, lectures, or meetings. The verb doodle means to make such sketches: {She doodled in the margins of her notebook}. Doodles range from geometric patterns to rough figures, typically unplanned and idle rather than deliberate artwork.

Doodling is drawing idly, usually while attention is elsewhere—during a phone call, a lecture, a meeting. The drawings themselves are doodles: absent-minded sketches, shapes, or patterns in the margins of notebooks. {She filled the page with doodling while waiting on hold.} Despite its association with distraction, doodling may actually aid concentration and memory.

A doofus is a fool or idiot—someone who acts stupidly or clumsily. The word is mildly insulting but usually affectionate, suggesting bumbling incompetence rather than malice: {Don't be such a doofus}. {He locked his keys in the car again—what a doofus}.

A doohickey is a thing whose name you don't know or can't recall—a gadget, device, or small mechanical part: {Hand me that doohickey over there}. The word belongs to a family of informal placeholder terms including thingamajig, whatchamacallit, and gizmo, used when the proper name escapes you or when the object seems too minor to name precisely.

Doom is fate or destiny, especially when terrible or unavoidable. The word carries weight—not just misfortune but inescapable ruin: {a sense of impending doom}, {the doom of civilization}. To doom someone is to condemn them to a grim fate: {The expedition was doomed from the start}. Doomsday is the day of final judgment or catastrophic destruction. In gaming, Doom became iconic as a pioneering first-person shooter, lending the word associations with demonic combat and heavy metal aesthetics.

Doomed means fated to fail, die, or meet disaster. Something doomed cannot be saved: {The ship was doomed from the moment it left port}. A doomed relationship has no future. The doom in question is usually death or destruction, though it can mean any inevitable bad outcome: {Their plan was doomed to fail}. To doom is to condemn to such a fate.

A doomsayer is someone who predicts disaster, catastrophe, or the end of the world. The term typically carries a dismissive tone, suggesting the person's warnings are exaggerated or unwarranted. {Climate doomsayers have been predicting imminent collapse for decades.} Doomsayers may turn out to be right, but the label usually implies skepticism about their dire forecasts.

Doomscrolling is compulsively consuming negative news or social media content, typically on a phone, despite the anxiety it causes. The term emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic when people found themselves unable to stop scrolling through upsetting headlines: {I stayed up until 3 a.m. doomscrolling}. The noun doomscroll refers to such a session.

Doomscrolling is the habit of compulsively scrolling through bad news online, especially on social media, despite the emotional toll. The term emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic when people found themselves unable to stop consuming distressing content: {I stayed up until 3 a.m. doomscrolling through Twitter}. Also spelled doom-scrolling or doom scrolling.

Doomsday is the end of the world—the day of final judgment or catastrophic destruction. Religious traditions speak of a literal day when God judges humanity; secular usage extends to any civilization-ending catastrophe: nuclear doomsday, a {doomsday scenario}. A {doomsday clock} measures how close humanity stands to annihilation. A {doomsday prepper} stockpiles supplies for societal collapse.

A door is a movable barrier that opens and closes an entrance—to a room, building, vehicle, or cabinet. Doors provide privacy, security, and climate control. By extension, a door is any means of access: {The internship opened doors for her}. To {show someone the door} is to dismiss them. {Behind closed doors} means in private. To {darken someone's door} is to visit, usually unwelcome.

A doorbell is a button near an entrance that rings a bell or chime inside, alerting occupants to a visitor: {Ring the doorbell}. Modern doorbells often include cameras and speakers for remote communication. The word also names the sound itself: {I heard the doorbell}.

A doorman is an attendant stationed at the entrance of a building—typically an upscale apartment building, hotel, or club—who opens doors, greets visitors, monitors access, and assists with packages or taxis. The position suggests a certain level of service and security: {The doorman hailed a cab for us}. {He slipped the doorman a twenty}.

A doormat is a mat placed at a doorway for wiping shoes before entering. Figuratively, a doormat is a person who lets others walk all over them—someone too passive or submissive to stand up for themselves: {Don't be a doormat; tell him what you really think}.

Doormats are mats placed at doorways for wiping shoes before entering. The plural also refers to people who let others walk all over them—those too passive to resist mistreatment: {She's tired of being a doormat in that relationship}. The metaphor connects literally to the object's function and placement.

Doors is the plural of door—a hinged or sliding barrier that closes an opening in a wall, vehicle, or piece of furniture. The word often appears in phrases about access or opportunity: {behind closed doors} means in private, {open doors} suggests new possibilities. {Doors open at seven} announces when a venue admits the public.
