To {show someone the door} is to dismiss them.

A doorstep is the step or platform at a building's entrance, just outside the door. By extension, something {on your doorstep} is very close or immediately accessible: {The beach is right on our doorstep}. As a verb, chiefly British, to doorstep is to approach someone at their home uninvited, typically for journalism or canvassing: {Reporters doorstepped her for days after the scandal broke}.

Doorsteps are the steps leading up to a door, especially the single step or threshold directly outside an entrance. Something {on your doorstep} is very close by or easily accessible. To doorstep someone (British) is to approach them uninvited at their home, typically as a journalist or canvasser seeking comment: {Reporters doorstepped the minister all morning}.

A doorway is the opening or passage that a door closes off, or the space immediately around and including a door. People stand in doorways, pause in doorways, and block doorways. {She appeared in the doorway holding a cup of coffee.} Figuratively, doorway suggests an entry point or threshold to something new: {College was a doorway to opportunities she'd never imagined.}

Doo-wop is a style of vocal rhythm and blues that emerged in the 1950s, characterized by close harmonies, nonsense syllables, and a cappella or lightly accompanied arrangements. The name itself mimics the backing vocals typical of the genre. Groups like the Platters and the Drifters exemplified the sound, which influenced later pop and rock music. {My grandmother still listens to her old doo-wop records.}

Dopamine is a neurotransmitter—a chemical messenger in the brain associated with pleasure, reward, and motivation. It plays a role in how we experience satisfaction and pursue goals. In popular usage, dopamine often serves as shorthand for the brain's reward system: {Social media is designed to trigger dopamine hits}. The term appears frequently in discussions of addiction, habit formation, and what makes activities feel rewarding.

Dope began as a thick liquid or paste—a lubricant, a preparation, or a drug in viscous form. From there it branched. Dope means a narcotic drug, especially heroin or marijuana: {They found dope in his car}. A dope is a stupid person: {What a dope I was}. As an adjective, dope is slang for excellent or cool: {That's a dope jacket}. The verb means to administer drugs: {The horse had been doped}. To {dope out} something is to figure it out. The {dope} on a subject is inside information: {What's the dope on the new boss?}

Dopey describes someone sluggish, drowsy, or mentally slow—as if sedated or half-asleep: {I was still dopey from the anesthesia}. It also means foolish or dim-witted: {a dopey grin}, {What a dopey thing to say}. The word connects to dope in its sense of a stupefying drug, though the association has faded. Also spelled dopy.

Doping is the practice of administering performance-enhancing drugs to athletes or animals, especially in competitive sports where such substances are banned: {The cyclist was stripped of his title after doping allegations}. The term also applies in electronics, where doping means introducing impurities into a semiconductor to alter its electrical properties. To dope something is to add a substance to it—whether drugs to a person, additives to fuel, or impurities to silicon.

A doppelganger is a person who looks strikingly like someone else—an uncanny double or lookalike. The German word literally means "double-goer." In folklore, seeing one's own doppelganger was an omen of death. Today the word usually describes any remarkable resemblance: {I saw your doppelganger at the grocery store}. Also spelled doppelgänger.

Doppelgangers are look-alikes—people who closely resemble each other despite being unrelated. The word comes from German meaning "double-goer." In folklore, a doppelganger is a ghostly double of a living person, often an omen of misfortune. Modern usage is usually lighter: {Everyone says my doppelganger works at the coffee shop downtown}. Also spelled doppelgängers.
A doppelganger is a ghostly double of a living person. The word is borrowed from German. A less common use of doppelganger refers to a double, counterpart, or alter ego.

A dork is a socially awkward or unfashionable person, someone out of step with what's cool: {He was such a dork in high school}. The word is mildly insulting but often affectionate—you might call a friend a dork for an embarrassing enthusiasm or clueless moment. Dork is also slang for penis, though this sense has faded as the social-misfit meaning took over.

Dorks are people perceived as socially awkward, unfashionable, or obsessively interested in niche subjects. The word carries less sting than similar terms—a dork is more endearingly clueless than genuinely contemptible: {We were such dorks in high school}. Many wear the label proudly now, especially fans of comics, gaming, or tech. Dork originally meant penis, but that sense has faded almost entirely.

Dorky describes someone or something socially awkward, unfashionable, or enthusiastically uncool—often in an endearing way. A dorky {laugh}, dorky {glasses}, or dorky {dance moves} suggest harmless awkwardness rather than genuine offense. The word is gentler than its cousins nerdy and geeky, implying lovable clumsiness: {He made a dorky joke that somehow worked}.

A dorm is a dormitory—a building with rooms for sleeping, typically at a college or university. The word implies shared living spaces for students: {I lived in the dorms my freshman year}. Dorm can also modify related nouns: {dorm room}, {dorm life}, {dorm mate}.

Dormant describes something inactive but capable of becoming active again. A dormant volcano hasn't erupted in recorded history but isn't extinct. Seeds lie dormant until conditions favor germination. A dormant bank account sees no transactions. Animals enter dormancy to survive harsh seasons. {The disease can remain dormant for years before symptoms appear.}

A dormitory is a building providing sleeping quarters for many people, especially at a school or university. Students live in dormitories during the academic year, often sharing rooms: {My freshman dormitory had communal bathrooms}. Informally shortened to dorm. A dormitory can also be a large room with multiple beds, as in a hostel. In British usage, a dormitory town or suburb is a residential area whose inhabitants commute elsewhere to work.

A dormouse is a small European rodent resembling a mouse but with a furry tail, known for hibernating through winter. The name likely comes from a word meaning "sleep"—dormice can hibernate for six months or more. {The Dormouse kept falling asleep} at the Mad Hatter's tea party. Plural: dormice.

Dorms is the informal plural of dormitory, referring to residential buildings where students live at colleges and universities. Each student typically has a small room, often shared with a roommate, with communal bathrooms and common areas on each floor. {Freshman are usually required to live in the dorms.} The word extends to any institutional group housing, such as for workers or athletes during training camps.

Dosage is the amount of a medicine, drug, or other substance to be taken at one time or over a period: {The recommended dosage is two tablets daily}. It can also refer to the administration schedule: {Dosage varies by age and weight}. In broader use, dosage applies to any measured quantity of something administered or experienced: {a healthy dosage of skepticism}.

A dose is a measured quantity of something, especially medicine or a drug, meant to be taken at one time: {The doctor prescribed a higher dose of the antibiotic}. By extension, dose applies to any portion of experience, particularly unpleasant ones: {a healthy dose of reality}, {a dose of his own medicine}. As a verb, to dose someone is to administer medicine to them, or to add a substance to something in measured amounts.

Doses is the plural of dose—measured quantities of medicine, radiation, or other substances administered at one time: {The doctor prescribed smaller doses for children}. By extension, doses can be portions of any experience: {healthy doses of skepticism}, {daily doses of exercise}. As a verb form, doses means to administer medicine: {She doses the cat with antibiotics twice daily}.

A dossier is a collection of documents about a particular person, subject, or case. The word suggests thoroughness—intelligence agencies compile dossiers on persons of interest, lawyers assemble dossiers of evidence, journalists build dossiers on investigative subjects. {The FBI maintained a dossier on the civil rights leader.} A dossier implies organized information gathered over time, often with an element of surveillance or scrutiny.

A dot is a small round mark or spot. It appears in punctuation (the period), in digital displays (the dot-matrix printer), and in web addresses where {dot-com} became synonymous with internet business. To dot is to mark with dots or to scatter: {Farms dotted the landscape}. To {dot the i's and cross the t's} is to attend to every detail. {On the dot} means exactly at the specified time: {She arrived at noon on the dot}. (Capitalized DOT is the Department of Transportation.)

Doting describes excessive, uncritical affection—the kind that overlooks faults and indulges every whim. A doting {grandmother} spoils her grandchildren. Doting {parents} can't see their child's flaws. The word carries a gentle criticism: the love is real but perhaps blinds the doting person to reality.

Dots are small round marks or points. A dot marks the end of a sentence (period) or sits above the letter i. Polka dots are a pattern of evenly spaced circles on fabric. To dot is to mark with dots or to scatter across a surface: {Cottages dotted the hillside}. {On the dot} means exactly on time. (Capitalized DOTS refers to braille software.)

Double implies two, sometimes for things with a counterpart that is called single. If you double a number, you add it to itself. Double digits means some number from 10 to 99. A double standard is two expectations that apply separately and unfairly. A competition of doubles involves teams of two. In baseball, hitting a double will get you to second base. A double bed or a double room has space for two. Double the expense means twice as much.

To doublecross someone is to betray them after gaining their trust, especially by secretly working against an agreement or alliance. The noun doublecross is the act itself: {The heist fell apart because of a doublecross}. The word implies deliberate deception—not merely backing out, but actively undermining someone who believed you were on their side.

Doublecrossed means betrayed by someone you trusted, especially a partner in crime or scheme who turned against you: {We had a deal, but he doublecrossed me and took the money}. The double suggests a cross within a cross—pretending loyalty while planning treachery. Also spelled double-crossed.

A doubledecker is something with two levels stacked vertically. The term most commonly describes buses with an upper and lower passenger deck, iconic in London: {We rode the doubledecker through the city}. It extends to sandwiches made with three slices of bread creating two layers of filling, and to any two-tiered structure: {a doubledecker bunk bed}.

A doubleheader is two games played consecutively between the same teams on the same day, originally and still most commonly in baseball: {The Yankees swept the doubleheader}. The term extends to any two events scheduled back-to-back: {a doubleheader of horror films}. Also spelled double-header.

Doubles is a plural that takes several directions from double. In sports, doubles is a format with two players per side: {mixed doubles in tennis}. A doubles match contrasts with singles. In darts or dominoes, doubles are tiles or throws with matching numbers. The bartender meaning—a second pour of the same drink—also pluralizes: {He ordered two doubles}.

Doublespeak is language designed to obscure, disguise, or reverse meaning—making the unpleasant sound acceptable or the simple sound profound. It encompasses euphemisms, jargon, and deliberately ambiguous phrasing: {The company announced a "workforce reduction" of 2,000 employees}. Unlike straightforward lies, doublespeak technically says something while meaning another. The term derives from George Orwell's concepts of "doublethink" and "newspeak" in *1984*.

A doubletake is a delayed reaction where someone looks at something, looks away, then looks back sharply upon realizing what they saw. The word captures that moment of belated recognition: {I did a doubletake when I saw my ex at the party}. Often spelled as two words: double take.

Doubletalk is deliberately evasive or ambiguous language designed to confuse or mislead. Politicians engage in doubletalk when they want to seem responsive without committing to anything: {His answer was pure doubletalk—ten minutes of talking without saying a thing}. The word can also mean rapid nonsense speech mixing real words with gibberish, performed for comic effect.

Doublethink is the mental capacity to hold two contradictory beliefs simultaneously and accept both as true. George Orwell coined the term in *1984* to describe how totalitarian regimes condition citizens to embrace logical impossibilities: war is peace, freedom is slavery. The word now applies broadly to any willful self-deception or cognitive dissonance that allows someone to ignore contradictions in their own thinking: {The company's doublethink lets them claim environmental leadership while expanding oil drilling}.

A doubloon is a Spanish gold coin that circulated from the sixteenth through nineteenth centuries, worth about two escudos. The word appears most often in pirate stories and treasure-hunting contexts: {a chest full of doubloons}, {buried doubloon}. Outside historical or fictional settings, doubloon sometimes means any gold coin or, loosely, money.

Doubloons were Spanish gold coins that circulated widely from the 16th through 19th centuries, particularly in the Americas and Caribbean. The word now evokes pirate treasure and adventure fiction more than actual currency: {a chest full of doubloons}, {pieces of eight and doubloons}. Informally, doubloons can mean money generally, usually with a playful or ironic tone: {I don't have the doubloons for that}.

Doubt is uncertainty about whether something is true, will happen, or is the right choice. To doubt is to question or disbelieve: {I doubt he's telling the truth}. A doubt is an instance of such uncertainty: {I have my doubts about this plan}. {Beyond a reasonable doubt} is the legal standard for criminal conviction. {No doubt} concedes a point or expresses near-certainty: {No doubt you're right}. To give someone {the benefit of the doubt} is to trust them despite uncertainty.

Doubtful describes uncertainty or skepticism. A doubtful outcome is uncertain; a doubtful claim invites skepticism. Someone who is doubtful has reservations: {I'm doubtful we'll finish on time}. The word can also mean unlikely to be true or genuine: {evidence of doubtful authenticity}. A doubtful look conveys visible skepticism.

Doubts are feelings of uncertainty or lack of conviction. When you have doubts about something, you're not sure it's true, wise, or likely to succeed: {I have my doubts about this plan}. To doubt is to question or feel uncertain: {I doubt he'll show up}. {Beyond a reasonable doubt} is the legal standard for criminal conviction—near certainty. {No doubt} means certainly or very probably: {No doubt she's already heard the news}.

A douchebag is literally the bag component of a douche used for vaginal irrigation. As an insult, douchebag describes an arrogant, pretentious, or obnoxious person—almost always a man: {What a douchebag, parking his BMW across two spaces}. The insult implies someone aggressively unpleasant and unaware of it, often with overtones of privilege and entitlement. Frequently shortened to douche.

Dough is a thick mixture of flour and liquid, worked into a mass for baking bread, pastries, or other foods. {She kneaded the dough until it was smooth.} The texture—soft, pliable, substantial—makes dough natural slang for money: {He's got plenty of dough}.

A doughnut is a small fried cake of sweetened dough, typically ring-shaped with a hole in the center, though filled varieties are solid. The ring shape comes from how the dough cooks—centers would remain raw without the hole. In driving, a doughnut is a tight circular skid performed intentionally: {He did doughnuts in the parking lot}. Also spelled donut.

Doughnuts are sweet fried cakes, typically ring-shaped with a hole in the center, though filled varieties are solid. The hole allows even cooking and has become iconic—{doughnut hole} names both the missing center and the small round pastries made from that dough. In automotive slang, to {do doughnuts} is to spin a car in tight circles, leaving circular tire marks. Also spelled donut.

Doused is the past tense of douse, meaning to drench with liquid or to extinguish. You douse a fire with water, or douse yourself in cologne. {The protesters were doused with pepper spray}. {She doused the flames before they could spread}. The word suggests thorough soaking or complete extinguishing.

Dove is the past tense of dive in American English: {She dove into the pool}. British English prefers dived. As a noun, a dove is a bird in the pigeon family, typically smaller and more delicate than what we call pigeons. Doves symbolize peace and gentleness—a political dove favors negotiation over military action, opposite of a hawk. {The administration's doves urged diplomatic solutions.} (Capitalized Dove is a brand name.)

Doves are birds of the pigeon family, typically smaller species with pointed tails. The word carries connotations of gentleness, peace, and purity—a dove with an olive branch symbolizes peace, and white doves appear at weddings and memorials. In politics, doves favor diplomacy over military action, contrasted with hawks: {The administration was split between doves and hawks on intervention}.

Dovetail names a joint where wedge-shaped projections on one piece interlock with matching notches on another, creating a strong connection without nails—common in fine woodworking and cabinetry. The verb means to fit together neatly: {Her skills dovetail with his}. Plans or schedules that dovetail align conveniently: {The meetings dovetailed perfectly with my travel}.

Down is much less frequently used than its opposite up, mainly from having fewer extended and figurative uses. Its core meaning, lower, is present in most of its uses having to do with space, but not all: down the street doesn’t mean to a lower place on the street. Down is far more frequent as an adverb and adjective than as a preposition, where it has many extended meanings that are usually the opposite of the figurative meanings of up.

Downbeat has two distinct meanings. In music, the downbeat is the first beat of a measure—the strong beat where a conductor's hand moves downward. More commonly, downbeat describes a gloomy or pessimistic mood or tone: {The report struck a downbeat note about the economy}. The musical and emotional senses share a quality of heaviness or descent.

Downcast describes eyes or a gaze directed toward the ground, often signaling sadness, shame, or dejection: {She sat with downcast eyes, unwilling to meet anyone's gaze}. By extension, downcast describes a person's mood—dejected or dispirited: {He seemed downcast after the rejection}. The word pairs physical posture with emotional state.

A downer is something that dampens spirits or causes sadness or disappointment: {The news about layoffs was a real downer}. The word also refers to a depressant drug, such as a barbiturate or tranquilizer, that slows bodily functions and produces sedation—the opposite of an upper. Someone described as a downer is persistently negative or gloomy, the kind of person who brings down the mood of a gathering.

Downers are drugs that depress the central nervous system, producing sedation, relaxation, and reduced anxiety—the opposite of uppers or stimulants. Barbiturates, benzodiazepines, and opioids all qualify as downers. Outside pharmacology, a downer is anything that dampens mood or spirits: {The news about layoffs was a real downer}. A person who habitually kills the mood might be called a downer as well.

Downfall is a sudden loss of power, status, or success—the collapse of someone or something that was once high. A politician's downfall may come from scandal, a company's from mismanagement. The word often implies that the fall was caused by a specific weakness or error: {Pride was his downfall}. It can also mean heavy rain or snow, though this sense is rare.

To downgrade is to reduce in rank, status, or quality. A storm may be downgraded from hurricane to tropical storm. Software gets downgraded when you install an older version. Airlines downgrade passengers from business to economy. As a noun, a downgrade is a descent or decline: {The stock was on a downgrade}. A literal downgrade is a downward slope in a road or track.

Downhill describes movement toward lower ground, following a slope's descent: {The trail runs downhill for two miles}. As an adjective, it modifies things oriented toward the bottom: a downhill {ski run}, a downhill {race}. Figuratively, downhill suggests decline or deterioration: {Everything went downhill after she left}. But {it's all downhill from here} can mean either easier going or worsening conditions, depending on context.

To download is to transfer data from a remote system to your own device—the opposite of upload. You download files, apps, music, movies: {The download took forever on this connection}. As a noun, a download is the file itself or the act of transferring it. Figuratively, to download information to someone is to brief them thoroughly: {Let me download you on what happened at the meeting}.

Downloading is the transfer of data from a remote computer or server to your own device. You download files, apps, movies, music. The opposite is uploading. Figuratively, downloading means absorbing information rapidly: {Let me download everything that happened at the meeting}. As a noun, a download is either the act or the thing transferred: {The download took forever}.

Downloads are files transferred from a remote server to a local device, or the act of transferring them: {My downloads folder is full of PDFs}. The term covers music, software, documents, videos—anything pulled from the internet or network. As a verb form, downloads describes this retrieval: {The app downloads updates automatically}. Download speed measures how fast data arrives.

A downpayment is an initial partial payment toward a larger purchase, with the remainder to be paid later. Most commonly used for real estate and vehicles: {They saved for years to make a downpayment on a house}. The downpayment reduces the amount financed and demonstrates buyer commitment. Also spelled as two words: down payment.

To downplay something is to minimize its significance or importance: {The company downplayed the security breach}. It suggests deliberately making something seem less serious, dramatic, or noteworthy than it actually is—often to avoid alarm, criticism, or unwanted attention: {He downplayed his role in the project}.

A downpour is a sudden, heavy rain—the kind that soaks you in seconds: {We got caught in a downpour on the way home}. The word emphasizes intensity and volume, as if rain were being poured from above rather than falling in drops.

Downpours is the plural of downpour—a sudden, heavy rainfall. The word emphasizes intensity and volume: rain coming down in sheets rather than drops. {We got caught in one of those summer downpours}. Figuratively, a downpour can describe any sudden deluge: {a downpour of criticism}, {a downpour of emails}.

Downshift means to shift to a lower gear in a vehicle, typically to slow down or gain power for climbing: {She downshifted as she approached the curve}. Figuratively, to downshift is to reduce pace or intensity, especially in work or lifestyle: {After the heart attack, he downshifted to part-time consulting}. The noun describes such a shift: {a downshift in consumer spending}.

The downside is the negative aspect or disadvantage of something: {The upside is more money, but the downside is longer hours}. It pairs naturally with upside in weighing pros and cons. In finance, downside refers to potential losses or declining value: {downside risk}, {limit your downside}.

Downsize means to make smaller, especially to reduce a company's workforce or to move to a smaller residence. Corporations downsize by laying off employees: {The company downsized and eliminated three hundred positions}. People downsize their living situations, typically after children leave or in retirement: {After the kids moved out, we downsized to a condo}. The word emerged as corporate euphemism for firing but has lost some of that evasive quality.

Downsizing is reducing something's size or scale, especially a company's workforce through layoffs: {The merger led to significant downsizing}. The term emerged as corporate euphemism—firing people sounds harsh, downsizing sounds strategic. It also applies to individuals choosing smaller living spaces, often in retirement: {After the kids left, we started downsizing}.

Downstairs refers to the lower floor or floors of a building, or the direction toward them: {I left my phone downstairs}, {She ran downstairs to answer the door}. As a noun, it names that area: {The downstairs needs painting}. In British period contexts, the downstairs was where servants worked, distinct from the family's upstairs quarters.

Downstream describes the direction water flows in a river or stream—toward the mouth, away from the source: {The canoe drifted downstream}. By extension, it means later in a sequence or process: {downstream effects of the policy}, {downstream in the supply chain}. In oil and gas, downstream refers to refining and distribution rather than extraction. The opposite is upstream.

Downtime is time when something isn't operating or productive. Machines have downtime for maintenance; websites have downtime during outages. For people, downtime means leisure or rest between activities: {I need some downtime after this project}. The word implies a pause in normal function—whether scheduled, forced, or welcomed.

Downtown is the central business district of a city—where offices, shops, and commercial activity concentrate. As an adverb or adjective, it indicates direction toward or location in this area: {I'm heading downtown}, {a downtown apartment}. In American usage, downtown often implies urban energy and density, contrasting with residential neighborhoods and suburbs.

Downtrodden describes people who have been oppressed or treated harshly by those with power over them: {the downtrodden masses}, {giving voice to the downtrodden}. The image is of being trampled underfoot. The word appears almost exclusively as an adjective, though it began as a past participle of the now-rare verb downtread.

A downturn is a decline in economic or business activity. The word typically describes periods when growth slows, profits fall, or markets contract: {The company laid off workers during the downturn}. It implies a temporary dip rather than permanent collapse—downturns eventually reverse. The term applies beyond economics to any measurable decline: {a downturn in her health}.

A downvote is a negative vote on social media or online forums, used to express disapproval or disagreement with a post or comment. The opposite of an upvote. As a verb, to downvote is to cast such a vote: {I downvoted the comment because it was misleading}. On platforms like Reddit, accumulated downvotes push content lower in visibility.

A dowry is money, property, or goods that a bride's family gives to her husband or his family upon marriage. The practice, ancient and widespread across cultures, ranges from symbolic gifts to substantial wealth transfers. In societies where dowries persist, they can create financial pressure on the bride's family and have been linked to domestic abuse when payments are deemed insufficient. The reverse arrangement—payment from the groom's family—is called a bride price.

Doxed means having had one's private information—real name, home address, phone number, workplace—publicly exposed online without consent, typically with malicious intent. The spelling varies: doxed, doxxed. The practice weaponizes personal data, often to enable harassment or threats: {She was doxed after posting a controversial opinion}. From "docs" (documents).

Doxing is publicly revealing someone's private information online—real name, home address, workplace, phone number—typically with malicious intent. The practice weaponizes personal data, often to enable harassment or intimidation: {After she criticized the game, trolls doxed her and she had to leave her apartment}. Also spelled doxxing.

To doxx someone is to publicly reveal their private information online—real name, home address, phone number, workplace—typically with malicious intent. The word comes from "docs" (documents). Doxxing is a form of harassment, often used to intimidate, enable stalking, or incite others to target the victim: {She was doxxed after her tweet went viral}. Also spelled dox.

Doxxing is publicly revealing someone's private information online—real name, home address, phone number, workplace—typically with malicious intent. The term comes from "dropping docs" (documents). Someone might be doxxed as punishment, harassment, or to enable others to threaten them: {She was doxxed after her tweet went viral, and strangers started showing up at her house}.

Doze is a light, intermittent sleep—the kind you drift into without meaning to. You doze in a chair, doze through a lecture, doze off during a movie. A doze is briefer and shallower than proper sleep: {I caught a quick doze on the train}. To doze is to hover at the edge of consciousness, not fully asleep but not alert.

A dozen is twelve of something: {a dozen eggs}, {a dozen roses}. The word functions as a convenient unit for counting, especially in commerce. In the plural, dozens indicates a large but indefinite number: {I've told you dozens of times}. A {baker's dozen} is thirteen—traditionally an extra item to avoid accusations of shortchanging customers.

Dozens means an indefinitely large number, roughly in the range of twenty-four to perhaps a hundred: {Dozens of people showed up}. The literal meaning—multiples of twelve—rarely applies; the word simply conveys "many" with a sense of scattered abundance. {Playing the dozens} is a form of ritualized insult exchange, especially in Black American culture, where participants trade escalating put-downs about each other's mothers.

Dozing is light, intermittent sleep—the kind where you drift in and out of awareness. Unlike deep sleep, someone dozing can be easily roused: {He was dozing in front of the television when the phone rang}. To doze off is to fall into this state unintentionally: {I dozed off during the lecture}.

Draconian describes laws, measures, or punishments that are excessively harsh or severe: {draconian budget cuts}, {draconian sentencing guidelines}. The word comes from Draco, an ancient Athenian lawgiver whose legal code prescribed death for even minor offenses. The sense has broadened to any rules or actions considered unreasonably strict or cruel.

Draft, noun, verb, and adjective, has seemingly unrelated meanings, most of which are spelled draught in British English. The most frequent meaning concerns writing: a draft is a non-final version of a document, subject to revision: The author submitted her draft manuscript to the publisher. When you draft a text, you write a version of it that will probably be modified later. Draft legislation is a preliminary version of it. A draft is also many other things: an unwelcome gust of air (draft through an open window); a process by which a selection is made (first-round draft pick); and an instance of drinking (take a long, cool draft of beer). If a team drafts a player, it selects them for the team. If you get drafted, you are conscripted for military service.

Drafted is the past tense of draft, covering its various senses. Someone drafted into military service was conscripted: {He was drafted during the Vietnam War}. A document that's been drafted has been written in preliminary form: {The contract was drafted by our lawyers}. In sports, a player drafted was selected by a team: {She was drafted third overall}. In racing or cycling, someone drafted used another's slipstream to reduce wind resistance.

Drafting is the act of creating preliminary versions of documents, plans, or designs. A lawyer drafts contracts; an architect drafts blueprints. The word implies work subject to revision: {I'm still drafting the proposal}. In racing and cycling, drafting means following closely behind another vehicle or rider to reduce wind resistance. The draft in professional sports—selecting new players—makes drafting the verb for that selection process.

Drafts are preliminary versions of written work, meant to be revised before reaching final form. The term extends to other kinds of rough plans or sketches. A draft is also a current of air moving through an enclosed space, or the act of drawing liquid from a container—hence draft beer, drawn directly from a keg. In American English, the draft refers to compulsory military service, and to draft someone is to select them for duty or, in sports, for a team. {I'm still working on early drafts of the manuscript.}

Drag implies movement, often along the ground, and often somewhat slowed by friction. When you drag something, you pull on it, unless you drag and drop with your mouse on a computer screen. Drag is the force that resists movement through air or water: The drag of the current prevented the swimmer from reaching shore. In slang use, drag is dressing in clothes associated with a gender not assigned at birth. A boring person or activity is a drag. The main drag of a town is its principal street. If you take a drag of a cigarette, you inhale from it.

Dragging is the present participle of drag, carrying all its senses—pulling something along a surface, moving slowly, or extending tediously: {The meeting kept dragging on}. In internet slang, dragging someone means publicly criticizing or mocking them, often at length: {Twitter was dragging him for that take}. Drag-and-drop computing uses dragging to move files or objects across a screen.

A dragnet is a net dragged along the bottom of a body of water to catch fish. The word extends to any systematic search or coordinated effort to catch criminals or gather suspects: {Police set up a dragnet across the city}. The figurative sense suggests sweeping up everything in a wide area, sometimes indiscriminately.

A dragon is a mythical creature typically depicted as a giant, fire-breathing reptile with wings, scales, and claws. Western dragons are usually fearsome beasts to be slain by heroes; Eastern dragons tend to be benevolent symbols of power and wisdom. Figuratively, a dragon is a fierce or formidable person, especially a stern older woman: {Her grandmother was a real dragon}. In computing, {dragon} sometimes refers to speech recognition software.

Dragonflies is the plural of dragonfly, a large flying insect with an elongated body, two pairs of transparent wings, and prominent eyes. Dragonflies hunt mosquitoes and other small insects in flight, often hovering near water where they breed. {Dragonflies darted over the pond.}

A dragonfly is a large flying insect with a long slender body, two pairs of transparent wings, and enormous multifaceted eyes. Dragonflies are often seen near ponds and streams, where they hunt mosquitoes and other small insects in flight with remarkable speed and agility. They hover, dart, and change direction instantly—capabilities that have inspired drone and helicopter designs. Despite their fierce appearance and name, dragonflies are harmless to humans.

Dragons are mythical creatures typically depicted as large, reptilian beasts capable of flight and breathing fire. They appear across cultures—menacing villains in European folklore, benevolent symbols of power in East Asian tradition. In fantasy fiction and gaming, dragons are often the ultimate adversary or a source of ancient wisdom. To {chase dragons} is to pursue something elusive; in drug slang, {chasing the dragon} refers to inhaling heroin vapor.

A dragster is a vehicle built or modified for drag racing—short, straight-line acceleration contests. Purpose-built dragsters are long, narrow machines with oversized rear tires and powerful engines, designed purely for speed off the line: {The dragster covered the quarter mile in under four seconds}. The term also applies to street cars modified for racing.

A dragstrip is a straight, paved track designed for drag racing—typically a quarter-mile long with timing equipment at both ends. Cars launch side by side and race in a straight line to the finish. The term extends to any stretch of road used informally for the same purpose: {They turned the abandoned airfield into a makeshift dragstrip}.

A drain is a pipe or channel that carries away water or waste. To drain is to draw liquid off or out: {drain the pasta}, {drain the swamp}. What drains away gradually disappears: energy drains, resources drain. A drain on something depletes it: {Commuting is a drain on my time}. If something goes {down the drain}, it's wasted or lost.

Drained describes something emptied of liquid or resources. A drained pool has no water; a drained battery has no charge. When applied to people, drained means exhausted—depleted of energy or emotion: {I felt completely drained after the meeting}. The word implies something has been drawn out, leaving emptiness behind.

Draining describes something that depletes energy, resources, or emotional reserves: {Taking care of my mother is draining}, {a draining commute}. The word captures gradual exhaustion rather than sudden collapse—the slow emptying of a sink rather than pulling a plug. Physically draining tasks tire the body; emotionally draining ones wear on the spirit.

A drake is an adult male duck. The word is less common than the female counterpart "duck," which serves for both sexes in casual speech, but appears in nature writing and among hunters: {The drake's iridescent head distinguished it from the drab hen}. Drake is also an archaic or poetic term for a dragon. (Capitalized Drake is a surname or given name.)

Drama is a form of storytelling performed by actors, typically on stage—plays, theater, the dramatic arts. By extension, drama describes intense emotional situations or conflict: {There was so much drama at the office today}. The informal sense often carries dismissiveness—unnecessary emotional excess or attention-seeking behavior: {I don't need this drama in my life}, {She's always stirring up drama}.

Dramatic describes what relates to drama or theater: a dramatic {performance}, dramatic {arts}. More commonly, it means striking, vivid, or emotionally intense—the qualities that make good theater: a dramatic {entrance}, dramatic {improvement}, dramatic {scenery}. Someone who is dramatic tends toward heightened emotion or exaggerated expression: {She's so dramatic about everything}.

Drape means to hang or arrange fabric loosely: {She draped a shawl over her shoulders}, {Curtains draped the windows}. The word suggests graceful, flowing folds rather than tight arrangement. To drape yourself over something is to sprawl or lean languidly: {He draped himself across the couch}. As a noun, drape refers to the way fabric hangs, or in the plural, to curtains themselves.

Drapes are heavy curtains, typically hanging in folds from a rod over a window. The word is more common in American English, where it often suggests something more substantial or formal than simple curtains: {She pulled the drapes closed against the afternoon sun}. Drapes can also refer to the way fabric hangs: {the drapes of a toga}.

Drastic describes actions or measures that are severe, extreme, or far-reaching in effect. A drastic change is sudden and dramatic; drastic measures are aggressive responses to serious problems: {The company took drastic steps to cut costs}. The word often implies necessity—drastic action suggests the situation demanded nothing less.
Drat is a little-used and old-fashioned exclamation that expresses a sudden, negative emotion.

Draw, a verb and noun, is very frequent and highly varied in its meanings. When you draw a picture you create a likeness. If you draw a load, you pull it. If you draw a liquid, you cause it to come out of a container. If you draw something from your pocket, you take it out. In sports, a draw is a game that ends without a winner. More generally, a draw is an instance of most of the verbal meanings of the word; for example you can draw a card (pick it up) in a card game, and that act is called a draw.

A drawback is a disadvantage or negative aspect of something that is otherwise appealing or beneficial. It often appears in evaluations where pros and cons are weighed: {The main drawback of the apartment is its distance from public transit}. Unlike a flaw, which suggests something inherently wrong, a drawback implies a trade-off—an acceptable downside to an otherwise desirable thing.

Drawbacks are disadvantages or negative aspects that offset something's benefits. Every option has its drawbacks: {The apartment is perfect except for one drawback—no parking}. The word implies weighing pros and cons, acknowledging that even good things come with downsides. A drawback doesn't disqualify something entirely but deserves consideration.

A drawbridge is a bridge that can be raised, lowered, or drawn aside to allow passage beneath or to prevent crossing. Medieval castles had drawbridges over moats, raised to keep invaders out. Modern drawbridges span waterways and lift to let boats pass: {Traffic backed up waiting for the drawbridge to lower}.

Drawbridges is the plural of drawbridge, a bridge designed to be raised, lowered, or drawn aside to allow or prevent passage. Medieval castles used drawbridges over moats for defense—raised to keep enemies out, lowered for friendly entry. Modern drawbridges span waterways, lifting to let boats pass: {Traffic backed up while the drawbridge was raised for a sailboat}.

A drawer is a sliding compartment in a piece of furniture—a desk, dresser, or cabinet—that pulls out for access and pushes back in for storage: {She rummaged through the junk drawer}. Drawers (plural) is an old-fashioned or humorous term for underpants. A drawer is also one who draws—an artist who sketches, or the person who writes a check or draft.

Drawers are undergarments covering the lower body—what Americans now usually call underwear or underpants. The term sounds old-fashioned or humorous today: {He stood there in his drawers}. Drawers is also simply the plural of drawer, the sliding compartment in furniture: {She rummaged through the desk drawers}.

Drawing is the act of making marks on a surface to create images, or the image itself: {a pencil drawing}, {a child's drawing of a house}. The word extends to any pulling or extracting motion—drawing water from a well, drawing a weapon, drawing conclusions. A drawing is also a selection by chance: {The raffle drawing is tonight}.

Drawings are pictures or diagrams made with a pen, pencil, or other marking instrument, typically without paint. A drawing can be a rough sketch or a finished work of art. The word also refers to selections made by chance: a lottery drawing, a drawing of names from a hat. {The architect presented her drawings to the committee.}

A drawl is a way of speaking in which vowels are stretched and words come out slowly, giving speech a lazy or relaxed quality. The term often describes Southern American accents: {He spoke with a Texas drawl}. As a verb, to drawl is to speak this way: {She drawled her greeting}.

Drawn is the past participle of draw, covering all that verb's meanings: a picture drawn in charcoal, curtains drawn shut, a bath drawn, a gun drawn, a conclusion drawn. As an adjective, drawn describes a face showing strain or exhaustion—features tight and haggard, as if pulled taut by worry or fatigue: {She looked pale and drawn after the ordeal}.

Dread is intense fear or apprehension, especially about something anticipated: {She felt a growing dread as the court date approached}. To dread something is to fear or be reluctant to face it: {I dread going to the dentist}. As an adjective, dread means feared or fearsome—mostly literary now: {the dread pirate}, {dread disease}. Dreaded serves the same function in everyday speech: {the dreaded Monday meeting}.

Dreaded describes something regarded with great fear or apprehension: {the dreaded phone call finally came}, {my dreaded in-laws are visiting}. The word often carries a touch of hyperbole or dark humor, dramatizing ordinary unpleasantness: {the dreaded Monday morning meeting}, {the dreaded blank page}.

Dreadful means causing dread or fear, though it now more commonly expresses strong disapproval or poor quality: {a dreadful mistake}, {dreadful weather}, {The food was absolutely dreadful}. The word has softened from its literal sense—something truly dread-inducing—to general intensified negativity. British speakers use it more freely as an emphatic: {I'm dreadfully sorry}.

A dreadlock is a ropelike strand of hair formed by matting or braiding and not combing out. The style has roots in Rastafarian culture and various African traditions, though it has spread widely. Usually plural: {She's been growing her dreads for years}. The shortened form dreads is common in casual speech.

Dreadlocks are a hairstyle in which the hair is allowed to mat and twist into long, ropelike strands. The style has roots in various cultures but is most associated with Rastafarian culture and reggae music. Often shortened to dreads: {She's been growing her dreads for three years}. The style can form naturally or be cultivated through various techniques.

Dreads is short for dreadlocks—rope-like strands of matted or braided hair. The style has roots in Rastafarian culture but has spread widely: {She's been growing her dreads for three years}. Dreads also serves as the plural of dread, meaning fears or anxieties: {Sunday night dreads kicked in before the work week}.

A dream is a series of thoughts and images experienced by sleepers, sometimes recalled in narrative form on awakening. When you dream you have this experience. By extension, and building on the sometimes-hopeful aspect of this, a dream is a vague plan or wish for the future. Figuratively, when you dream of something, you long to do it, even though it might be unrealistic. A person or situation characterized as a dream is extremely attractive.

A dreamboat is someone extremely attractive or romantically ideal—the kind of person you might dream about. The term emerged in mid-20th-century American slang and retains a slightly dated, playful quality: {She thought the new teacher was an absolute dreamboat}. It can also describe anything considered ideal or wonderful, though this use is less common.

A dreamcatcher is a handcraft of Native American origin, traditionally a willow hoop with a woven net and hanging feathers. In Ojibwe tradition, dreamcatchers hung above sleeping children filter dreams—good ones pass through while nightmares catch in the web. Now widely commercialized as decorative objects: {She hung a dreamcatcher from her rearview mirror}.

Dreamcatchers are handmade objects traditionally crafted by some Native American peoples, consisting of a woven web inside a hoop, often decorated with feathers and beads. According to tradition, they filter dreams—letting good ones pass through while trapping nightmares. Mass-produced versions have become popular decorations, hung in bedrooms, cars, and dorm rooms: {She bought a dreamcatcher at the craft fair}.

A dreamer is someone who dreams—either literally during sleep or figuratively through imagination and aspiration. The word often carries a gentle criticism: dreamers indulge in fantasy rather than practical action. {He's a dreamer who never follows through}. But it can also suggest visionary qualities: {Every great invention started with a dreamer}. The tension between impractical and idealistic runs through most uses.

Dreamers are people who dream—whether in sleep or in imagination. The word often carries a gentle criticism: dreamers have impractical hopes, heads in the clouds rather than feet on the ground. {He's a dreamer who never follows through.} But dreamers also envision what others can't: {Every great invention started with a dreamer.} In American political discourse, Dreamers (often capitalized) refers to undocumented immigrants brought to the U.S. as children, from the proposed DREAM Act legislation.

Dreaming is the experience of images, sensations, and narratives during sleep. As an adjective, it describes someone lost in thought or fantasy: {a dreaming child gazing out the window}. The word carries connotations of imagination and aspiration—someone dreaming of success envisions a desired future. {I must have been dreaming} dismisses an unrealistic expectation.

Dreamland is the imaginary realm of sleep and dreams, or any place of fantasy and unreality. It often describes a state of pleasant obliviousness: {She was off in dreamland during the meeting}. The word can refer to an idealized place: {a dreamland of endless summer}. Parents use it when coaxing children to sleep: {Time to head off to dreamland}.

Dreams are the images, sensations, and narratives that unfold in the mind during sleep—often vivid, sometimes bizarre, rarely remembered in full. The word extends to waking life for hopes and aspirations: {She had dreams of becoming a doctor}. To dream is to experience these visions or to imagine possibilities: {I never dreamed it would actually happen}. Something dreamlike has the quality of dreams—hazy, surreal, detached from ordinary reality.

A dreamscape is an imaginary landscape resembling a dream—surreal, fluid, distorted. The word appears most often in art criticism and literary description: {The painter's dreamscapes blend melting clocks with impossible architecture}. It can describe actual dream imagery or any scene with dreamlike qualities: {The fog turned the harbor into a dreamscape}.

Dreamsicle is a frozen treat consisting of vanilla ice cream or ice milk coated with flavored ice, typically orange—a creamy core inside a fruity shell. The word often appears as a flavor descriptor for anything evoking that orange-vanilla combination: {dreamsicle cake}, {dreamsicle smoothie}. Sometimes spelled Creamsicle, which is a trademark.

Dreamy describes a soft, hazy quality suggestive of dreams. A dreamy expression suggests someone lost in thought or reverie: {She had a dreamy look in her eyes}. Dreamy music or lighting is gentle and ethereal. In casual speech, dreamy means attractively appealing: {He's so dreamy}. A dreamy person tends toward fantasy and impracticality.

Dreary describes something depressingly dull, bleak, or cheerless. A dreary day is gray and dispiriting. A dreary landscape offers nothing to lift the spirits. The word applies equally to weather, places, tasks, or moods: {a dreary commute}, {dreary office walls}, {the dreary routine of daily chores}. Dreary suggests not just unpleasantness but a wearing monotony.

Dredge has two distinct meanings. One is to scoop up material from the bottom of a body of water, either to deepen it or to search for something: {They dredged the river for the missing weapon}. To {dredge up} old memories or grievances is to bring them back to the surface. The other dredge is a cooking term—to coat food lightly in flour, breadcrumbs, or sugar before cooking: {Dredge the chicken in seasoned flour before frying}.

Dregs are the sediment that settles at the bottom of a liquid—the bits of grounds left in a coffee cup, the residue in a wine bottle. By extension, dregs means the least valuable remnants of anything: {the dregs of society}, {drinking the dregs of his savings}. The word almost always appears in plural form.

A dreidel is a four-sided spinning top used in a Hanukkah game. Each side bears a Hebrew letter, and players spin to determine whether they win or lose tokens from a central pot. The game is especially popular among children during the Jewish holiday season. {The kids played dreidel for chocolate coins.}

Dreidels is the plural of dreidel, a four-sided spinning top used in a traditional Jewish game played during Hanukkah. Each side bears a Hebrew letter, and players spin to determine whether they win or lose tokens from a central pot. {The children played with dreidels after lighting the menorah.}

A dreidl is a four-sided spinning top used in a traditional Hanukkah game. Each face bears a Hebrew letter, and players spin to determine whether they win or lose tokens from a shared pot. Children play for coins, nuts, or chocolate gelt. Also spelled dreidel.

To drench is to soak thoroughly with liquid, usually water: {The sudden downpour drenched us}. Something drenched is completely saturated—not merely damp but soaked through. The word often suggests being caught unprepared by rain or waves. Figuratively, light or sound can drench a space by filling it completely: {Sunlight drenched the room}.

Drenched means thoroughly soaked, completely saturated with liquid. The word almost always describes wetness from water or rain: {We got drenched in the downpour}, {Her clothes were drenched with sweat}. Figuratively, something can be drenched in light, color, or atmosphere: {a room drenched in afternoon sun}. The past participle of drench, it functions primarily as an adjective.

Drenching is a thorough soaking—the kind that leaves something completely wet. Rain can give you a drenching, or you can give plants a drenching with the hose. The word implies saturation, not just dampness: {We got a drenching walking back from the car}. In veterinary contexts, a drenching is the forced administration of liquid medicine to an animal.

Verbal uses of dress are about putting one thing on another, such as clothes on a person, medicine on a wound, or condiments on a salad. If you simply dress, you put clothes on yourself, which results in the state of being dressed. As a noun, dress divides its meanings between countable and uncountable uses. Dress, generally, characterizes the clothes that people wear: ceremonial dress, casual dress. A dress, on the other hand, is a one-piece garment for women.

Dressed means wearing clothes, especially with care or formality: {She was dressed for the occasion}. To get dressed is to put on clothes. Dressed can specify the type of attire: {dressed in black}, {dressed as a clown}. A dressed wound has been cleaned and bandaged. Dressed meat has been prepared for cooking—cleaned, trimmed, and readied. A dressed stone or board has been smoothed or finished.

A dresser is a piece of bedroom furniture with drawers for storing clothes, typically with a mirror attached. In British English, dresser refers to a kitchen sideboard with shelves for displaying dishes. A dresser is also someone who dresses in a particular way: {a stylish dresser}, {a sloppy dresser}. In theater, a dresser helps performers with costumes and quick changes.

Dresses is the plural of dress—a one-piece garment with a bodice and skirt, typically worn by women and girls: {She tried on several dresses before finding the right one}. The verb dresses means puts on clothing or prepares something: {He dresses quickly in the morning}, {She dresses the salad with vinaigrette}. To dress a wound is to clean and bandage it.

Dressing covers things applied to other things. Salad dressing coats greens. A wound dressing covers an injury. Dressing on a turkey is stuffing—seasoned bread mixture applied inside the bird. Window dressing makes storefronts attractive, and figuratively means superficial embellishment: {The policy changes were just window dressing}. A dressing-down is a severe scolding.

A dressmaker is a person who makes women's clothing, especially dresses, typically as a trade or profession. The term suggests custom work—measuring, cutting, fitting, and sewing garments for individual clients—rather than factory production. {She apprenticed with a dressmaker in Paris before opening her own shop.}

Drew is the past tense of draw, covering all that verb's meanings. You drew a picture, drew a bath, drew a crowd, drew a conclusion, drew a weapon, or drew the short straw. {She drew the curtains and sat down}. {The game drew thousands of fans}. (Capitalized Drew is a given name.)

Dribble describes liquid falling or flowing in small drops or a thin stream: {Water dribbled from the faucet}. A person dribbles when saliva escapes the mouth uncontrolled—common in infants and the infirm. In basketball, to dribble is to bounce the ball repeatedly while moving; in soccer, to advance the ball with short kicks. The noun covers any of these: {a dribble of sauce}, {a dribble down the court}.

Dribbles is the third-person singular of dribble. Liquid dribbles when it flows in a thin, irregular stream: {Water dribbled from the faucet}. A person dribbles when saliva escapes their mouth uncontrollably. In basketball and soccer, to dribble is to advance the ball with short, controlled bounces or kicks. As a noun, dribbles are small amounts trickling out: {dribbles of information}, {dribbles of funding}.

Dribbling is the present participle of dribble—letting liquid fall in drops or a thin stream, or moving a ball with repeated short touches. In basketball, dribbling means bouncing the ball while moving; in soccer, it means advancing with light kicks. A baby dribbling has saliva trickling from its mouth. {He was dribbling the ball up the court.}

When something drifts, it moves somewhat slowly and not always in a consistent direction. When a conversation drifts, it moves gradually from one topic to another. Drift is an instance of such movement (continental drift). If you get the drift of what someone is saying, you understand their underlying message. Genetic drift is the process by which the genomes of a population change through gain and loss of genes.

A drifter is someone who moves from place to place without a fixed home, job, or purpose—a person who drifts through life rather than putting down roots. The term carries connotations of rootlessness and sometimes aimlessness, though it can also suggest freedom from conventional obligations. {A drifter came through town looking for odd jobs.} In fishing, a drifter is a boat that uses drift nets.

Drifters are people who move from place to place without fixed purpose or destination. The word carries connotations of rootlessness and lack of ambition—someone who drifts through life rather than directing it: {The town attracted drifters looking for seasonal work}. In older crime narratives, drifters often appear as suspects precisely because they have no ties to the community.

Drifting is moving slowly without direction or purpose, carried by currents of water, air, or circumstance. Snow drifts into piles; a boat drifts downstream; a conversation drifts to other topics. Someone who drifts through life lacks clear goals: {He spent his twenties drifting from job to job}. In driving, drifting is a technique of intentionally oversteering to slide through turns while maintaining control—a motorsport style that emerged in Japan.

Drifts are accumulations of snow, sand, or other material piled up by wind: {The drifts blocked the road}. The word also names the plural of drift in its other senses—a gradual movement or shift {(the drifts of public opinion)}, the general meaning of speech {(I catch your drift)}, or a state of aimless wandering {(He fell into one of his drifts)}. As a verb form, drifts describes slow, undirected movement: {The boat drifts downstream}, {Her attention drifts during meetings}.

Driftwood is wood that has been washed ashore by waves, tides, or currents. It typically comes from fallen trees, broken branches, or shipwrecks, weathered smooth and bleached pale by sun and salt water. Driftwood is collected for decoration, furniture, or fuel: {The beach was littered with driftwood after the storm}. Figuratively, driftwood suggests someone adrift or rootless: {He felt like driftwood, carried wherever life took him}.

The main meanings of drill, noun and verb, fall into two categories. First, a drill is a tool with a cutting attachment that makes holes. When you drill, you use one of these. By extension, when you figuratively drill into or drill down on something, you get past the surface of it to look at it in greater detail. Second, drill is an activity that is repeated for mastery or reinforcement (fire drill). When you drill, you take part in such an activity (drill Spanish verbs, drill multiplication tables).

Drilled is the past tense of drill. To drill is to bore a hole using a rotating tool, or to train through repetitive practice: {The sergeant drilled the recruits until they moved as one}. Students are drilled on multiplication tables; dentists drill teeth. In slang, to drill someone is to shoot them or, vulgarly, to have sex with them.

Drilling is the act of making holes with a rotating tool, or the repetitive practice of skills through exercises: {The coach had the team drilling plays all afternoon}. Military drilling involves marching and maneuvers in formation. In textiles, drilling is a sturdy twilled cotton fabric used for workwear and uniforms.

Drills are exercises repeated for mastery—military drills, fire drills, spelling drills. The repetition builds automatic response. A drill is also a tool that bores holes by rotating, or the act of boring: {Drill through the wall carefully}. To drill someone is to train them through repetition or to question them intensely: {The lawyer drilled the witness}. A drill is also a sturdy cotton fabric used for workwear.

Drink is to take liquid into the mouth and swallow it. Without specification, drink often implies alcohol: {Do you drink?} {She doesn't drink anymore}. A drink is a serving of liquid, especially an alcoholic beverage: {Let me buy you a drink}. To drink to someone is to toast them. To {drink in} a sight is to absorb it eagerly. {Drink the Kool-Aid} means to accept something uncritically.

Drinking is the act of consuming liquids, but used alone it almost always means consuming alcohol: {She doesn't approve of drinking}. A drinking {problem} is alcoholism. Drinking {water} is water safe to consume. A drinking {buddy} is someone you regularly drink alcohol with. {We stayed out drinking until two in the morning.}

Drinks are beverages—liquids meant for consumption. The word often implies alcoholic beverages specifically: {Let's grab some drinks after work}, {The drinks are on me}. A drinks menu at a restaurant lists what you can order to sip. As a verb, drinks is the third-person singular: {She drinks too much coffee}.

When a liquid, body part, or a device drips, drops fall (from it). A drip is an instance, or the sound of this. In a hospital, a drip is a device for introducing a liquid slowly into a patient’s bloodstream. Drip coffee is coffee made by letting hot water slowly drip through ground coffee beans. In slang use, a drip is an annoyingly stupid person. If someone is dripping in something, they have a needless excess of it: He was dripping with money.

Dripping describes liquid falling in drops: {a dripping faucet}, {dripping wet from the rain}. Something dripping with a quality has it in excess: {dripping with sarcasm}, {dripping with jewels}. As a noun, dripping is the fat rendered from roasting meat, used in British cooking for frying or spreading on bread.

Drive, noun and verb, is about directional and usually intentional movement (drive a car). A drive may be an instance of driving a vehicle, or it could be a directed movement of animals (a cattle drive). A fundraising drive is an activity aimed at raising money. Drive is also a motivational force: This job requires a lot of drive. If you drive someone to do something, you compel them: Her love of mathematics drives her to succeed. In computers, a drive is a device that stores data.

A driveby is a shooting from a moving vehicle, typically gang-related: {Two teenagers were killed in a driveby last night}. The term extends to any quick, passing action—especially a brief, dismissive comment online: {He left a driveby insult and never responded to replies}. As an adjective, driveby describes something done hastily or superficially: {driveby journalism}, {driveby diagnosis}.

Driven describes someone powerfully motivated to achieve, often to an unusual degree: {She's incredibly driven—works eighteen-hour days}. The word suggests ambition that comes from within, sometimes obsessively. As a past participle of drive, driven also describes things propelled or operated by a force: {wind-driven turbines}, {a character-driven story}, {snow driven sideways by the wind}.

A driver is someone who operates a vehicle: a taxi driver, a truck driver, a getaway driver. The word extends to golf clubs designed to hit the ball far off the tee. In computing, a driver is software that enables hardware to communicate with an operating system. Figuratively, a driver is anything that propels or motivates: {Consumer spending is a key driver of economic growth}. A backseat driver offers unwanted advice.

Drivers is the plural of driver—people who operate vehicles or other things that drive. A driver is someone behind the wheel: {taxi drivers}, {drunk drivers}. In golf, a driver is the club for long-distance shots off the tee. In computing, drivers are software programs that allow hardware to communicate with an operating system: {You need to update your graphics drivers}. A driver can also be a motivating factor: {Cost was the main driver of the decision}.

Drives is the plural of drive and the third-person singular verb form. A drive is a journey by car, a paved path to a house, or inner motivation: {She has incredible drives—ambition, curiosity, hunger for success}. Computer drives store data. In sports, a drive is a powerful shot or sustained offensive push. To drive is to operate a vehicle, propel forward, or compel: {What drives you?} {Ambition drives her}. {He drives me crazy.}

A driveway is a private road leading from a street to a house, garage, or other building. Unlike public roads, driveways belong to the property: {The kids were playing basketball in the driveway}. In American suburbs, the driveway often serves as overflow parking, workspace, or gathering spot.

Driveways is the plural of driveway, a private road or paved surface connecting a house or building to a public street. Driveways provide access for vehicles to garages, carports, or parking areas: {The neighborhood driveways were lined with basketball hoops}. They range from short suburban strips to long rural lanes.

Driving is operating a vehicle, especially a car: {I learned driving at sixteen}. As an adjective, driving describes forceful, propelling motion: {driving rain}, {driving rhythm}. A driving force is what pushes something forward—the main cause or motivation: {She was the driving force behind the project's success}.

Drizzle is light rain falling in fine, scattered drops—heavier than mist but gentler than a steady rain: {We walked through the drizzle without umbrellas}. As a verb, to drizzle is to rain lightly, or to pour a thin stream of liquid over food: {Drizzle olive oil over the salad}. The cooking sense suggests a slow, controlled pour rather than a splash.

Drizzling describes light rain falling in fine, scattered drops—more than mist but less than a steady rain. Weather reports distinguish drizzling from heavier precipitation: {It's just drizzling; you won't need an umbrella}. In cooking, drizzling means pouring a thin stream of liquid over food: {drizzling olive oil over the salad}, {drizzling chocolate over the cake}.

Droid is science fiction slang for a robot or android—a mechanical being, often humanoid, with artificial intelligence. The term was popularized by Star Wars, where droids serve various functions from protocol to astromech. Outside fiction, droid sometimes describes any automated system or person who acts mechanically: {He's a total droid—just follows orders without thinking}.

Droids are robots, especially humanoid ones. The term comes from android and was popularized by the Star Wars films, where droids serve as servants, translators, and companions. Outside that franchise, droid often carries a playful or science-fiction flavor: {These aren't the droids you're looking for}. It can describe anyone acting mechanically or without independent thought.

A drone is an unmanned aircraft, typically remote-controlled or autonomous: {Drones delivered packages to rural areas}. The word comes from the male honeybee, which makes no honey and exists only to mate with the queen—hence drone for a person who does tedious work or lives off others' labor. The bee's deep humming sound gives us the verb drone, meaning to make a low continuous sound or to speak monotonously: {He droned on about quarterly projections}. A drone is also a sustained bass note in music, especially from bagpipes.

Drones are unmanned aircraft, typically controlled remotely or by onboard computers. Military drones conduct surveillance and airstrikes; consumer drones take aerial photos or race. The word comes from the male honeybee, which doesn't work—so a drone is also a person who does tedious labor or lives off others. A drone can be a monotonous humming sound, or to speak in such a tone: {He droned on about quarterly projections}.

Droning describes a continuous, low, monotonous sound—the hum of bees, the buzz of machinery, or a voice that never varies in pitch or intensity. A droning {engine} produces steady background noise. A droning {speaker} puts listeners to sleep. The word suggests tedium: something that goes on and on without relief or variation.

Drool is saliva that flows uncontrollably from the mouth. Babies drool; so do sleeping adults and people who've had dental work. The verb means to let saliva escape: {The dog drooled on the carpet}. Figuratively, to drool over something is to desire it intensely: {He was drooling over the sports car}.

Drooling is letting saliva flow from the mouth, whether involuntarily (as babies and some elderly or ill people do) or from eager anticipation: {The dog was drooling over the steak}. Figuratively, to drool over something is to desire it openly and perhaps excessively: {He was drooling over the new sports car}.

Droop describes a downward sag or hang, typically from weakness, fatigue, or lack of support. Flowers droop when they need water; eyelids droop when someone is tired; shoulders droop in defeat or exhaustion. The word works as both verb and noun: {The droop of his head suggested he'd fallen asleep}. Things that droop lack the stiffness or energy to remain upright, giving the word connotations of wilting, flagging spirits, or physical decline.

Drop is mainly a verb, with the noun meanings derived from the verb meaning of descending to a lower place. The thing dropping can be an object (Helicopters dropped relief supplies) or an abstraction (The price of gas dropped five cents today). If you drop an activity, you stop doing it: I dropped physics because it was too hard. A drop is a sudden descent: The first drop over the ridge made the skiing treacherous. A tiny quantity of liquid that falls as a round mass is also called a drop.

A dropkick is a kick executed by dropping a ball and kicking it just as it bounces off the ground—still legal but rare in American football and rugby. In wrestling and martial arts, a dropkick is an aerial attack where you jump, kick with both feet, and land on your back: {He dropkicked his opponent into the ropes}. Informally, to dropkick something is to punt it decisively: {I'd dropkick that idea right now}.

Dropkicking is delivering a kick where the ball is dropped and struck just as it bounces, or in wrestling and fighting, jumping to kick an opponent with both feet. The term extends to forceful rejection or removal: {I'm dropkicking that idea from the proposal}. The gerund form of dropkick, used as verb or noun.

A droplet is a very small drop of liquid: {droplets of rain on the window}, {respiratory droplets spread the virus}. The diminutive suffix emphasizes tininess—droplets are smaller than ordinary drops, often fine enough to hang suspended in air or mist.

A dropout is someone who quits school before completing their degree or program: {a high school dropout}, {college dropout}. The term carries connotations of failure or giving up, though some famous dropouts have succeeded spectacularly. Dropout also describes the act of leaving: {the dropout rate}. In electronics and audio, a dropout is a brief loss of signal.

Dropouts are people who leave school, a program, or an activity before completing it. The term most often refers to those who quit high school or college without graduating: {High school dropouts face limited job prospects}. It extends to anyone who withdraws from conventional society or mainstream expectations, carrying connotations of failure or nonconformity depending on context. In technical contexts, a dropout can also mean a brief loss of signal or data.

Dropped is the past tense of drop. Something dropped has fallen or been released: {She dropped her keys}. A dropped call disconnects unexpectedly. A dropped charge is no longer being pursued. In music, dropped tuning lowers one or more guitar strings. To get dropped is to be removed from a team, label, or roster: {He got dropped from the squad}.

Drops is the plural of drop—small amounts of liquid that fall or hang in rounded masses: {A few drops of rain hit the windshield}. Eye drops and ear drops are medicinal liquids applied in small quantities. In theater and film, drops are large painted backdrops. To {do drops} in certain contexts means to deliver packages, often drugs, to multiple locations.

A drought is an extended period of abnormally low rainfall, causing water shortages and crop failure. The word extends to any prolonged absence or scarcity: {a drought of new ideas}, {The team's scoring drought lasted three games}. In some regions, drought also means thirst or dryness generally.

Droughts is the plural of drought—prolonged periods of abnormally low rainfall causing water shortages and crop failure. The word extends to any sustained scarcity: {a drought of new ideas}, {The team's scoring drought lasted three games}. Droughts can last months or years and may trigger famine, migration, and economic crisis.

Drove is the past tense of drive, but it also stands alone as a noun meaning a group of animals being driven together: {a drove of cattle}. By extension, drove describes any large moving group: {Droves of tourists descended on the city}. The phrase {in droves} emphasizes large numbers arriving or departing together.

Droves is the plural of drove, which originally meant a herd of animals being driven somewhere—cattle, sheep, pigs moving along a road. Now droves almost always appears in the phrase {in droves}, meaning in large numbers: {Fans left in droves after the third quarter}. The word emphasizes mass movement, usually of people arriving or departing together.

To drown is to die by submersion in water, unable to breathe. The verb works both ways: a person drowns, or water drowns them. Figuratively, to drown is to be overwhelmed: {drowning in debt}, {drowning in paperwork}. To {drown out} is to overpower with louder sound: {The music drowned out our conversation}. To {drown your sorrows} is to drink alcohol to forget troubles.

Drowned is the past tense of drown—to die by submersion in water, unable to breathe: {Three swimmers drowned in the flood}. Extended uses describe overwhelming quantities: {drowned in debt}, {drowned out by noise}. A drowned landscape is submerged or waterlogged. {Her voice was drowned by the crowd's roar.}

Drowning is death by suffocation in water or other liquid. The lungs fill with fluid, preventing oxygen from reaching the body. Someone who is drowning struggles at the surface before going under. Figuratively, to be drowning is to be overwhelmed: {I'm drowning in paperwork}. {She was drowning in debt}.

Drowsy means sleepy or inclined toward sleep: {The warm afternoon made me drowsy}. It suggests a pleasant, heavy-lidded state rather than exhaustion. Drowsy extends to things that induce sleepiness: {a drowsy summer afternoon}, {the drowsy hum of bees}. Warning labels caution that medications may cause drowsiness.

Drudgery is hard, tedious, unpleasant work—the kind that feels endless and offers no satisfaction beyond its completion. The word emphasizes monotony and lack of reward: {the drudgery of data entry}, {household drudgery}. Unlike labor, which can be fulfilling, drudgery suggests work that dulls the spirit.

A drug is a substance that alters body function, whether for medical treatment or intoxication. Prescription drugs treat illness; recreational drugs produce altered states. The line between medicine and drug depends on context and legality—the same substance might be either. To drug someone is to administer a substance without consent: {Someone drugged my drink}. To {drug up} is to take medications or intoxicants heavily.

Drugged describes a state of being under the influence of drugs, especially when administered without consent or for incapacitation: {She felt drugged and couldn't keep her eyes open}. It also describes something that has had drugs added to it: {a drugged drink}, {drugged food}. The word often implies impairment, sedation, or vulnerability.

Drugging is the act of administering drugs to someone, typically without their knowledge or consent. The term most often appears in contexts of crime or assault: {She suspected someone had been drugging her drinks}. It can also refer to the ongoing use of sedatives on patients or animals: {The constant drugging left him groggy and disoriented}.

A druglord is a high-ranking leader of a drug trafficking organization, typically controlling production, distribution, and territory through a combination of wealth, corruption, and violence. The term evokes powerful figures in the illegal narcotics trade: {Colombian druglords of the 1980s}, {Mexican druglords who control border smuggling routes}. Also spelled as two words: drug lord.

Drugs are substances that alter the body's chemistry—whether to treat illness, relieve pain, or produce intoxicating effects. The word covers everything from prescription medications to illegal narcotics, though in casual speech {drugs} usually means the illicit kind: {He got into drugs in high school}. To drug someone is to administer a substance without their knowledge or consent: {Someone drugged her drink}.

A drugstore is a retail store where medicines and prescriptions are dispensed, typically alongside everyday household items, toiletries, and convenience goods. The term is primarily American; British English prefers chemist or pharmacy.
