Unlike a pure pharmacy, a drugstore usually sells snacks, magazines, cosmetics, and sundries. {I picked up my prescription and some toothpaste at the drugstore.}

A druid was a member of the learned priestly class among ancient Celtic peoples, serving as religious leaders, judges, and keepers of oral tradition. Modern druids practice nature-based spirituality loosely inspired by these ancient figures: {The druids gathered at Stonehenge for the summer solstice}. In fantasy games and fiction, a druid is typically a magic user with powers over nature and shapeshifting abilities.

Druids are members of the priestly class of ancient Celtic peoples, associated with nature worship, oak groves, and sacred rituals. Modern druids belong to neo-pagan movements that revive or reimagine these traditions: {The druids gathered at Stonehenge for the summer solstice}. In fantasy games and fiction, druids are magic users with power over nature and animals. (Capitalized Druids emphasizes the historical priesthood.)

A drum is a percussion instrument—a hollow body with a membrane stretched over one or both ends, struck with hands or sticks to produce sound. Drums extend to cylindrical containers: an oil {drum}, an {eardrum}. To drum is to play drums or tap rhythmically: {She drummed her fingers on the table}. To {drum up} support or business is to generate it through effort. To {drum something into} someone is to teach it through repetition.

A drumbeat is the sound made by striking a drum, or the rhythmic pattern produced by repeated strikes. In figurative use, drumbeat often describes a persistent, repetitive message or campaign pushing toward a particular outcome: {the drumbeat of criticism}, {a drumbeat for war}. The word emphasizes relentlessness—like an actual drum, the message keeps pounding until it can't be ignored.

A drummer is a person who plays drums, whether in a band, orchestra, or solo: {The drummer kept perfect time throughout the set}. Historically, drummers signaled commands in military units. A drummer can also be a traveling salesperson—one who "drums up" business—though this sense is now dated. To {march to the beat of a different drummer} is to follow one's own path.

Drumming is the act of playing drums or making rhythmic percussive sounds. It extends to any repeated beating or tapping: {the drumming of rain on the roof}, {He drummed his fingers on the table}. In nature, drumming describes the rapid bill-beating of woodpeckers or the wing-beating displays of grouse. To drum something into someone is to instill it through repetition: {They drummed the rules into us}.

A drumroll is a sustained sound produced by rapid, continuous beats on a drum, creating a rolling effect. Drumrolls traditionally precede announcements, dramatic revelations, or climactic moments: {And the winner is—drumroll please—Sarah Chen!} The word often appears figuratively to signal that something significant is about to be revealed, sometimes ironically for trivial announcements.

Drums are percussion instruments—hollow cylinders with membranes stretched over one or both ends, played by striking with sticks or hands. The term covers everything from a child's toy to a concert timpani. A drum kit or drum set is also called drums: {She plays drums in a band}. To drum is to beat rhythmically, whether on an instrument or impatiently on a table. To {drum up} support or business is to generate it through effort. To {drum something into} someone is to teach through repetition.

A drumstick is a stick used to strike a drum, typically wooden with a padded or rounded tip. Drumsticks also refers to the lower leg of a chicken or turkey, resembling a drum mallet in shape: {I saved the drumsticks for the kids}. The dual meaning comes from the shared silhouette—a knob at one end tapering to a handle.

Drumsticks are sticks used to strike drums and cymbals, typically wooden with a rounded tip. The word also refers to the lower leg of a chicken or turkey, shaped like a club—the dark meat portion often eaten by hand: {The kids always fight over the drumsticks at Thanksgiving}.

Drunk describes the state of impairment from alcohol—coordination falters, speech slurs, judgment wavers. The word works as adjective {(He was too drunk to drive)} and noun {(The drunk stumbled home)}. A drunk is also someone who habitually drinks to excess. Drunk doubles as the past participle of drink: {I've drunk three cups of coffee}. To be drunk on something besides alcohol is to be intoxicated by it: {drunk on power}, {drunk with success}.

Drunken describes the state of intoxication or things associated with it: {a drunken sailor}, {drunken revelry}, {a drunken stupor}. The word functions only as an adjective before a noun—you say someone is drunk, not drunken, but a drunken {brawl} or drunken {driving}. Drunken often carries connotations of disorder or excess.

Drunkenness is the state of being drunk—impaired by alcohol to the point where coordination, judgment, and speech are affected. The word covers everything from mild intoxication to complete incapacitation: {arrested for public drunkenness}, {His drunkenness cost him his marriage}. It can describe a pattern of behavior as much as a single episode.

Drunks is the plural of drunk, a person who is intoxicated or who habitually drinks to excess. The noun carries more judgment than the adjective—calling someone {a drunk} suggests a pattern, not just a state: {The bar was full of drunks by closing time}. {Staggering drunks spilled onto the sidewalk}.

Dry means without moisture or liquid. A dry {towel} absorbs water; a dry {climate} receives little rain. Dry {wine} lacks sweetness. Dry {humor} is deadpan and understated. A dry {cough} produces no phlegm. To go dry or be {dry} can mean abstaining from alcohol, or a place where alcohol sales are prohibited. To dry is to remove moisture: {Dry your hands}. If inspiration or supply runs out, it {dries up}.

A dryer is a machine or device that removes moisture. The clothes dryer tumbles wet laundry in heated air. A hair dryer blows hot air. Dryer also works as the comparative form of dry: {The climate here is dryer than back east}. The spelling drier is equally valid for both uses.

Drywall is the standard interior wall material in modern construction, consisting of gypsum plite pressed between paper sheets. It replaced plaster-and-lath construction because it's faster and cheaper to install—you screw or nail the panels to studs, tape the seams, and apply joint compound. As a verb, to drywall means to install this material: {We spent the weekend drywalling the basement}. Also called wallboard, gypsum board, or by the brand name Sheetrock.

Dual means consisting of two parts or having a twofold nature. A dual {citizenship} grants belonging to two countries. A dual {purpose} serves two functions. Dual {carriageways} have lanes running in both directions. The word emphasizes pairing or doubling: {She led a dual life as teacher and spy}. In grammar, some languages have a dual number for exactly two of something, distinct from singular and plural.

Duality is the state or quality of having two parts, aspects, or natures, often ones that contrast or complement each other. Philosophers speak of mind-body duality, the idea that mental and physical existence are fundamentally different. In physics, wave-particle duality describes how light behaves as both wave and particle depending on how it's observed. More loosely, duality refers to any pairing of opposing forces or ideas: {the duality of good and evil}, {the duality of public persona and private self}.

Despite low frequency, dub has several meanings that don’t overlap. Most frequent is the verb that is about giving names and titles to people and things: He dubbed the pastry chef “Bakemaster.” Another dub verb means to add or replace the audio part of a video presentation: The film was dubbed in English. The most frequent noun use of dub today is for a genre of music with irregular and unexpected sounds: Dubstep is the epitome of electronic dance music.

Dubbed means named or given a title, often informal or descriptive: {The media dubbed him "the king of pop"}. The word carries a sense of bestowing identity through declaration rather than formal process. Separately, dubbed describes audio that has been replaced or added—a dubbed {film} has dialogue recorded in a different language from the original, or dubbed {music} has vocals layered over a track.

Dubbing is the process of adding or replacing sound in a film or recording. Most often this means replacing dialogue in one language with another: {The movie was dubbed into Spanish}. Dubbing also covers adding sound effects, music, or voiceover to video. The related sense of copying recordings—{dubbing a tape}—comes from the same studio practice of layering audio tracks.

Dubious expresses doubt or uncertainty. A dubious claim is one you're not sure you believe; a dubious expression shows skepticism: {She gave him a dubious look when he explained his whereabouts}. Something of dubious quality or value is questionable, probably not good: {a dubious honor}, {dubious accounting practices}. The word often implies something is suspect or shady rather than merely uncertain.

A duchess is a woman who holds the highest hereditary rank below princess in British and European nobility, either in her own right or as the wife of a duke. The title carries significant social prestige and traditionally comes with ceremonial duties and estates. {The Duchess of Cambridge attended the charity gala.} In informal usage, duchess can be an affectionate or ironic term of address for a woman perceived as acting grand or imperious.

There are three English words spelled d-u-c-k. Most frequent is a noun for a family of swimming birds that are often hunted and sometimes eaten (mallard duck). As a verb, duck is the motion of lowering your head or body, especially quickly in order to avoid an obstacle or projectile: He ducked through the doorway. A related meaning is push underwater: I ducked my head into the river to cool off. Figuratively, it is to evade (duck out of the party, duck responsibility for the project). Duck is also a noun for a heavy cotton fabric used for clothing and especially pants.

A duckling is a young duck, typically one still covered in down rather than adult feathers. The word often evokes images of fluffy yellow hatchlings following their mother. In the fairy tale "The Ugly Duckling," a bird thought homely becomes a swan—making {ugly duckling} a term for someone whose potential isn't yet apparent.

Ducklings are young ducks, typically covered in soft downy feathers before developing adult plumage. The word evokes images of fluffy, vulnerable creatures following their mother in a line—a behavior so iconic it appears in children's stories and wildlife documentaries alike. {The ducklings waddled behind their mother toward the pond.} Figuratively, someone's ducklings might be the people they guide or mentor, especially in a group setting.

Ducks are waterfowl with broad flat bills, webbed feet, and waterproof feathers. They float, dive, and waddle—the archetypal pond bird. To duck is to lower your head or body quickly to avoid something: {She ducked under the branch}. By extension, to duck a question or responsibility is to evade it. As a term of endearment, duck is British: {Thanks, duck}. A duck in cricket is a score of zero.

A dud is something that fails to work as expected. Originally a bomb or shell that doesn't explode, the term now applies broadly to anything disappointing: a movie that flops, a product that malfunctions, a firework that fizzles. {The new phone was a complete dud.} As an adjective, dud means defective or worthless: {a dud battery}.

Dude is an informal term for a man or guy, used especially as a casual form of address: {Dude, you're not going to believe this}. Originally 19th-century slang for a fastidious man overly concerned with dress, it evolved through surfer and skater culture into a general exclamation of surprise, enthusiasm, or emphasis. The word now transcends gender in casual speech—women address other women as dude. A dude ranch is a Western-style vacation resort where guests can play cowboy.

Dudes is the plural of dude, a casual term for a man or guy. Originally 19th-century slang for a dandy or city slicker unfamiliar with rural life, dude evolved into a general-purpose word for any male person: {The dudes at the gym were hogging the weights}. In relaxed speech, dudes can address or refer to a mixed-gender group: {What's up, dudes?} The word carries an informal, friendly tone and appears frequently in youth and surf culture.

Duds has two distinct meanings. The original sense is clothing, especially casual or work clothes: {I threw on some old duds}. The other meaning is things that fail to work as intended—fireworks that don't explode, products that disappoint: {Half the batch turned out to be duds}. A single dud is a failure or disappointment.

The small but important word due can be a noun or an adjective. All of its meanings are related to the idea of debt, obligation, or the timing of an event. When a bill is due, it is time to pay it. When a baby is due, it is time for it to be born. When a library book is due, it is time to return it. If you give someone their due, you give them what they are owed or what they deserve. Before a noun, due carries the idea of something that is required, expected, or necessary, as in due diligence.

A duel is a prearranged combat between two people, traditionally fought with matched weapons to settle a point of honor. The practice is now largely historical, though some cultures retain ritualized forms. Figuratively, any intense one-on-one contest is a duel: {The debate became a duel of wits}. To duel is to engage in such combat: {They dueled at dawn}.

Dueling is the act of fighting a formal combat between two people, traditionally with matched weapons like swords or pistols, often to settle a point of honor. The practice was once common among aristocrats and military officers but is now illegal virtually everywhere. The word extends to any intense one-on-one contest: {dueling guitarists}, {dueling op-eds}. Politicians or lawyers with competing agendas may have {dueling press conferences}. The spelling duel**l**ing is standard in British English.

A duelist is someone who fights duels—formal combats between two people, traditionally to settle disputes of honor. The term evokes an earlier era of swords at dawn and pistols at ten paces: {He fancied himself a duelist, though he'd never held a rapier}. In gaming contexts, a duelist is a player who specializes in one-on-one combat.

Duelling is the British spelling of dueling—fighting a formal combat between two people, typically with weapons, to settle a point of honor. The practice was once common among aristocrats and military officers: {He was killed in a duelling accident}. The word extends to any intense one-on-one contest: {duelling pianos}, {duelling headlines}.

Duels are formal, prearranged fights between two people, historically conducted with swords or pistols to settle a matter of honor or resolve a dispute. The practice was once a socially accepted way for gentlemen to defend their reputations, though it was often illegal and frequently fatal. Today the word extends to any intense one-on-one contest: {The two candidates engaged in a verbal duel during the debate}. As a verb, to duel is to fight or compete in this manner.

Dues are regular payments required for membership in an organization: {union dues}, {club dues}, {membership dues}. The word is almost always plural. To {pay your dues} is to earn your place through hard work or difficult experience before enjoying success: {She paid her dues playing small clubs before hitting it big}.

A duet is a performance by two musicians or singers, or a piece of music composed for two performers: {They sang a duet at the wedding}. The term extends to any collaborative effort between two people: {The comedy duo's verbal duets were legendary}. In dance, a duet is a pas de deux.

Duets is the plural of duet, a musical performance by two people—singers or instrumentalists—or the composition written for such a performance. The term extends to any collaborative effort between two: {The film featured several duets between the lead actors}. A duet implies coordination and harmony between partners.

Dug is the past tense and past participle of dig. You dug a hole yesterday; you have dug many holes in your life. Separately, a dug is an udder or teat, especially of a domestic animal—now archaic or dialectal: {The calf nuzzled at the cow's dug}.

A dugout is a shelter or space created by digging into the ground or a hillside, or by hollowing out a log. The term most commonly refers to two things: a canoe made from a hollowed tree trunk, and the covered bench area in baseball where players and coaches sit when not on the field. {The team watched nervously from the dugout as the final inning began.} Dugouts also historically served as primitive shelters or military positions dug into embankments.

Dugouts are shelters dug into the ground or a hillside, often used for military protection or basic habitation. In baseball, a dugout is the sunken bench area where players and coaches sit when not on the field: {The manager paced the dugout}. A dugout canoe is a boat carved from a single log, hollowed out to form the hull.
Duh and doh are used ironically to signal that you, or someone else, have been very slow to understand something obvious.

A duke is the highest rank of nobility below royalty in European aristocracies, ruling over a duchy. The title appears in fairy tales and period dramas: {The duke summoned his advisors}. In American slang, dukes means fists: {Put up your dukes}. To duke it out is to fight or compete intensely: {The two candidates duked it out in the debate}. (Capitalized Duke is a name or university.)

Dull describes something lacking sharpness, brightness, or intensity. A dull knife doesn't cut well; a dull color lacks vibrancy; a dull ache persists without being acute. Applied to people or things, dull means boring or uninteresting: {The lecture was so dull I nearly fell asleep}. A dull mind is slow to understand. Weather can be dull—gray and overcast. To dull something is to make it less sharp or intense: {Time dulls the pain}.

Dumb originally meant unable to speak—a meaning that persists in {deaf and dumb} and {struck dumb with amazement}. The sense shift to stupid now dominates casual usage: {That was a dumb idea}, {Don't be dumb}. This evolution has made the original meaning problematic, as calling a mute person dumb now risks implying stupidity. To {dumb down} is to simplify for a less sophisticated audience.
Dumbass is a vulgar insult for a stupid person: {I felt like a dumbass for locking my keys in the car}. It can be affectionate among friends.
Dumbasses is the plural of dumbass, a vulgar term for stupid people: {Those dumbasses forgot to book the venue}.

A dumbbell is a short bar with weights at each end, held in one hand for exercise: {She grabbed a pair of dumbbells for bicep curls}. The word also means a stupid person—someone whose head is as useful as a bell that makes no sound: {Don't be such a dumbbell}.

Dumbbells are handheld weights used for exercise, consisting of a short bar with a weight at each end. They're lifted repeatedly to build strength and muscle: {She grabbed the dumbbells for her arm workout}. The name comes from an older device for practicing bell-ringing that made no sound—a "dumb" (silent) bell. By extension, a dumbbell is a stupid person.

Dumbfounded means utterly astonished—so shocked or surprised that you're momentarily speechless. The word combines dumb (unable to speak) with confounded (bewildered): {She stood dumbfounded when they announced her name}. Unlike mere surprise, dumbfounded suggests being rendered temporarily incapable of response.

Dumbstruck means so shocked or astonished that you're rendered speechless. The dumb here is the old sense meaning mute, not stupid—you're literally struck silent by surprise, disbelief, or overwhelming emotion: {She stood dumbstruck when she saw the damage}. Also spelled dumfounded or dumbfounded.

Dummies is the plural of dummy—a figure representing a human body, as in a ventriloquist's dummy or a crash-test dummy. A dummy is also a stupid person: {Those dummies left the door unlocked}. The "For Dummies" book series popularized the self-deprecating phrase: {I need a guide for dummies}. In card games, the dummy is the exposed hand played by the declarer's partner.

A dummy is a model or replica that substitutes for the real thing—a ventriloquist's dummy, a crash-test dummy, a dressmaker's dummy. The word extends to anything serving as a placeholder: a dummy {corporation} exists only on paper, a dummy {variable} holds a position in code. Informally, dummy means a stupid person: {Don't be such a dummy}. As a verb, to dummy up is to remain silent or to create a mock-up: {We dummied up a prototype}.

Dump is most frequently a verb about getting rid of things, often in a way that shows no affection for them. If you dump a boyfriend or girlfriend, you end the relationship summarily. If you dump your possessions somewhere, you drop them carelessly. Someone may dump a lot of trash by the side of the road. It would be more desirable, however, if they took it to the dump, informal for a landfill. To take a dump is an informal and somewhat vulgar expression for emptying your bowels.

Dumped is the past tense of dump—to drop or unload something, often unceremoniously: {She dumped the laundry on the bed}. To dump someone is to end a romantic relationship abruptly: {He got dumped right before prom}. Data gets dumped when transferred in bulk or output for analysis. Dumped goods are sold cheaply abroad, often below cost.

Dumping is getting rid of something, often carelessly or in large quantities: {They were caught dumping waste in the river}. In commerce, dumping means selling goods in a foreign market below cost to undercut competitors—a practice often subject to trade penalties. To dump someone is to abruptly end a romantic relationship: {She dumped him right before prom}.

A dumpling is a small mass of dough, often filled with meat or vegetables, cooked by boiling, steaming, or frying. Dumplings appear across cuisines—Chinese jiaozi, Polish pierogi, Southern American chicken and dumplings. The word extends affectionately to a chubby or endearing person: {Come here, my little dumpling}.

Dumplings are pieces of dough cooked by boiling, steaming, or frying. The simplest are balls of flour and water dropped into soups or stews. Many cuisines wrap dough around savory or sweet fillings: {We ordered pork dumplings}, {apple dumplings for dessert}. The term covers a vast range—from pierogi to potstickers to gnocchi—united by the dough-based structure.

Dumps is a state of low spirits or depression, appearing almost exclusively in the phrase {down in the dumps}: {He's been down in the dumps since he lost his job}. The word has no singular form in this sense—you're never in just one dump. Separately, dumps is the plural of dump (a place for discarding waste, or an act of dumping).

A dumpster is a large metal container for trash, typically with a hinged lid, designed to be lifted and emptied by a garbage truck. The word comes from Dempster, the brand name of the company that patented the design. To {dumpster dive} is to scavenge discarded items from such containers—for food, furniture, or other usable goods.

A dumptruck is a heavy vehicle with a hinged bed that tilts to unload loose materials—sand, gravel, dirt, debris. The bed dumps its contents out the back or side. In slang, dumptruck describes a person with a notably large rear end: {She's got a dumptruck}.

A dunce is a person regarded as slow-witted or stupid, especially someone who struggles to learn. The word often implies repeated failure despite instruction: {He felt like a dunce in math class}. A dunce cap—the tall conical hat once used to humiliate slow students—survives as an image of public shaming for stupidity.

A dune is a hill or ridge of sand shaped by wind. Dunes form along coastlines and in deserts, constantly shifting as wind moves grains from one side to the other. Beach dunes protect inland areas from storm surges. {The children ran up and down the dunes.} Sand dunes can grow to hundreds of feet tall in places like the Sahara. (Capitalized Dune is the science fiction novel and franchise.)

Dunes are hills or ridges of sand shaped by wind. They form along coastlines and in deserts, where wind piles loose sand into characteristic slopes—gentle on the windward side, steeper where sand cascades down. Dunes migrate slowly as wind moves sand from one face to the other. {We climbed the dunes to watch the sunset over the beach.}

Dung is animal excrement, especially from large herbivores like cattle, horses, and elephants. The word sounds more rural and agricultural than *shit* or *feces*: {dung beetle}, {cow dung}, {dung heap}. Dung has been used for millennia as fertilizer and, when dried, as fuel. The verb means to spread dung on fields.

A dungeon is an underground prison cell, especially in a medieval castle—dark, damp, and often used for torture or indefinite confinement. The word evokes historical cruelty: {The prisoner was thrown into the dungeon and forgotten}. In fantasy games and fiction, dungeons are underground labyrinths filled with monsters and treasure to be conquered: {We spent the weekend crawling through dungeons in the new RPG}.

Dungeons are dark underground prison cells, typically in castles or fortresses. The word evokes medieval settings—damp stone chambers where prisoners were confined and sometimes tortured. In fantasy games and literature, dungeons are underground complexes filled with monsters, traps, and treasure to be explored: {We spent the weekend playing Dungeons & Dragons}. A dungeon may also be a BDSM space equipped for bondage activities.

To dunk is to dip something briefly into liquid—a doughnut into coffee, a cookie into milk. In basketball, a dunk is a shot where a player thrusts the ball directly through the hoop from above, and to dunk is to score this way: {He dunked on three defenders}. Internet slang extends this to verbal takedowns: {She dunked on him with one tweet}.

Dunking is the act of dipping something into liquid—a donut into coffee, a cookie into milk. In basketball, dunking means slamming the ball downward through the hoop: {He's famous for his powerful dunks}. The slang sense of dunking on someone means humiliating them, especially online, derived from the dominance a basketball dunk displays over a defender.

Dunks is the plural of dunk—a forceful basketball shot where a player thrusts the ball down through the hoop. Highlight-reel dunks showcase athleticism and power: {He had three dunks in the first quarter}. Outside basketball, dunks are acts of dipping something briefly into liquid: {a few dunks of the cookie into milk}.

A duo is a pair, especially two people who perform or work together: {a comedy duo}, {a musical duo}. The word emphasizes partnership or collaboration more than simply counting two of something. It can also describe any twosome: {The duo spent the afternoon plotting their next move}.

Duodji is the traditional handicraft of the Sámi people of northern Scandinavia and Russia. It encompasses functional objects made from materials like reindeer hide, bone, antler, and wood—knives, clothing, drums, jewelry. The practice carries cultural and spiritual significance beyond mere craft: {She learned duodji from her grandmother}. The term distinguishes indigenous Sámi artisanship from generic Nordic folk craft.

A dupe is someone who has been deceived or tricked, often implying they were gullible or naive enough to fall for it: {The investors were dupes in an elaborate Ponzi scheme}. As a verb, to dupe someone is to deceive them, usually for personal gain. In casual usage, dupe also functions as a shortened form of duplicate, referring to a copy or knockoff: {This lipstick is a dupe for the high-end brand}.

Duped means deceived or tricked into believing something false. Someone who has been duped was taken in by a lie, scam, or manipulation: {Investors were duped by promises of guaranteed returns}. The word implies the victim was made to look foolish—you feel duped when you realize you've been had.

Dupes are people who have been deceived or tricked—victims of a con, scam, or manipulation: {The fraudster's dupes lost their life savings}. The word carries a note of foolishness; dupes are seen as gullible, not just unlucky. As a verb, to dupe is to deceive: {They duped him into signing the contract}. In casual usage, dupes also means duplicates, especially cheaper alternatives to expensive products: {These lipsticks are dupes for high-end brands}.

Duplicate means to make an exact copy of something, or the copy itself: {duplicate the file}, {a duplicate key}. As an adjective, it describes things that are identical copies: {duplicate receipts}. Something done {in duplicate} exists in two identical versions. The word can also mean to repeat unnecessarily: {We don't want to duplicate effort}.

Duplicity is deliberate deception—saying one thing while meaning or doing another. Unlike simple lying, duplicity implies a sustained pattern of two-facedness: {His duplicity was revealed when the emails surfaced}. The word suggests calculated betrayal of trust rather than momentary dishonesty. A person acting with duplicity maintains one appearance while secretly pursuing contrary ends.

Durability is the ability to withstand wear, pressure, or damage over time. A product's durability determines how long it lasts under normal use: {The durability of this fabric makes it ideal for outdoor furniture}. The quality extends beyond physical objects—a relationship's durability, an idea's durability. Durable goods are items expected to last years rather than be quickly consumed.

A durag is a close-fitting cloth head covering, typically made of silky material, tied at the back. Worn primarily by Black men and women, durags compress and protect hairstyles—especially waves and braids—while sleeping or between styling sessions. They've become a fashion statement and cultural symbol beyond their practical function: {He never leaves the house without his durag}.

Duration is how long something lasts—the span of time from beginning to end. A movie has a duration; so does a war, a battery charge, or a headache. {The duration of the flight was three hours.} The phrase {for the duration} means for as long as something continues, often implying an indefinite or extended period: {We're stuck here for the duration.}

Durian is a large tropical fruit native to Southeast Asia, notorious for its powerful odor—often described as sewage-like or rotten—that gets it banned from hotels and public transit in the region. Those who tolerate the smell find the custard-like flesh rich and complex. The spiky husk can weigh several pounds. {Durian is an acquired taste.}

Unusual among prepositions ending in –ing, during has no use in modern English other than as a preposition. Its meaning is always connected with time and its object is typically a divisible period of time: practices that began during the Middle Ages, a disturbance during the night.

Dusk is the time just after sunset when daylight fades but darkness hasn't fully arrived—the transitional period between day and night. It's dimmer than twilight's beginning but not yet night: {We walked home at dusk}. The word can also describe the dim light itself or, figuratively, a period of decline: {the dusk of an empire}.

Dust is fine particles of matter that are ubiquitous in the human environment. Before another noun, dust means either consisting of it (dust storm, dust cloud) or for protection from it (dust jacket, dust mask). As a verb, dust means remove dust from surfaces where it settles. Dust can also mean sprinkle with a fine powder: Dust the cake with powdered sugar.

Dusty describes something covered with or full of fine dry particles—the kind that accumulate on surfaces left undisturbed: {a dusty shelf}, {dusty old books in the attic}. By extension, dusty suggests neglect, staleness, or being out of date: {dusty ideas}, {a dusty corner of the archive}. A dusty color is muted or grayish, as if seen through a film of dust: {dusty rose}, {dusty blue}.

Duties are obligations or responsibilities—things you're expected or required to do. A soldier's duties include following orders; a parent's duties include caring for children. Duty also refers to taxes on imports: {customs duties}, {duty-free shops}. The phrase {on duty} means actively working, while {off duty} means not: {The officer was off duty when the accident occurred}.

Duty is an obligation—something you must do because of your role, position, or moral code. A soldier has duties, as does a nurse, a citizen, or a child. {Jury duty} is compulsory service. To be {on duty} is to be working; {off duty} means free from responsibilities. Duty also refers to a tax on imports: {customs duty}, {duty-free}. The phrase {do one's duty} can mean anything from fulfilling basic responsibilities to a euphemism for using the toilet.

A duvet is a soft, thick bed covering filled with down, feathers, or synthetic material, used in place of blankets and a top sheet. Common in European bedding traditions, duvets typically have removable covers for washing: {I need to change the duvet cover}. Americans sometimes call them comforters, though duvets are usually fluffier and designed with covers.

Dvija is a Sanskrit term meaning "twice-born," referring in Hindu tradition to members of the three upper castes—Brahmin, Kshatriya, and Vaishya—who undergo a spiritual rebirth through initiation rites. The first birth is physical; the second is the religious ceremony (upanayana) that marks entry into spiritual study. The term appears in discussions of caste, Hindu scripture, and Indian history.

A dwarf is a person of unusually small stature, or in folklore, a small humanoid creature often associated with mining, metalwork, and underground realms. The word extends to anything notably smaller than typical: a dwarf {planet}, dwarf {varieties} of fruit trees. As a verb, to dwarf something is to make it seem small by comparison: {The skyscraper dwarfs the surrounding buildings}. The plural is dwarfs or dwarves, the latter popularized by Tolkien's fantasy novels.

Dwarves is a plural of dwarf, used especially for the mythological beings—short, bearded, skilled in mining and metalwork—found in Norse legend and modern fantasy: {The dwarves forged magical weapons in their mountain halls}. Tolkien popularized this spelling over the older dwarfs. For people of short stature, dwarfs remains standard; dwarves may seem to equate real people with fantasy creatures.

A dweeb is a socially awkward, unfashionable person—someone perceived as boring, studious, or out of touch with what's cool. The term emerged in 1980s American slang alongside nerd and geek, though dweeb carries more contempt and less suggestion of technical competence: {Don't be such a dweeb}. The insult has softened over time but remains mildly derogatory.

Dwell means to live or reside somewhere, though the word sounds literary or old-fashioned for everyday use: {They dwelt in a cottage by the sea}. More commonly, dwell appears with "on" or "upon" to mean lingering mentally on something, usually unpleasantly: {Don't dwell on the past}. {She dwelt on every mistake she'd made}.

Dwindle means to shrink or diminish gradually over time. Supplies dwindle, populations dwindle, hopes dwindle. The word emphasizes slow decline rather than sudden loss: {Her savings dwindled to nothing}. Unlike decrease, dwindle carries a sense of fading away toward insignificance or exhaustion.

Dwindling describes something gradually shrinking, diminishing, or becoming less. Resources dwindle, populations dwindle, hopes dwindle: {Their dwindling savings forced them to sell the house}. The word emphasizes slow decline rather than sudden loss—a candle burns down, a crowd thins out, enthusiasm fades. {She watched her dwindling options with growing alarm}.

Dye is a substance used to color materials—fabric, hair, food, or other things that absorb it. Unlike paint, which coats a surface, dye penetrates and bonds chemically: {She dyed her hair purple}. The verb and noun share spelling with die, but the continuous forms disambiguate: dying versus dyeing. {A dye job} is a hair coloring, sometimes implying it's obvious or poorly done.

Dyes are substances used to color materials—fabrics, hair, food, or other surfaces. Unlike paints, dyes penetrate and bond with the material rather than coating it. The verb means to apply such coloring: {She dyed her hair purple}. The past tense dyed distinguishes it from died.

Dying is the process of ceasing to live, the transition toward death. Someone dying of cancer is in their final decline. The word extends to things fading or ending: {a dying art}, {dying embers}, {her dying wish}. To be {dying to} do something is to want it intensely: {I'm dying to know what happened}. To be {dying for} something is to crave it: {I'm dying for a cup of coffee}.
Dyke is the British spelling of dike and represents all meanings of that word that represent structures, natural or built. Dyke is also a slang and sometimes disparaging word for a lesbian.

Dynamic describes things characterized by energy, motion, or change. A dynamic {personality} is forceful and engaging. A dynamic {economy} grows and evolves. In physics, dynamics is the study of forces and motion, as opposed to statics. Dynamic contrasts with static—what's dynamic moves, shifts, or develops rather than staying fixed. In computing, dynamic content changes based on user input or conditions.

Dynamics refers to forces that produce motion or change. In physics, it's the branch of mechanics dealing with motion and the forces causing it. More broadly, dynamics describes the interacting forces within any system: {group dynamics}, {family dynamics}, {market dynamics}. In music, dynamics means the variation in loudness—the contrast between soft and loud passages. The word nearly always appears in plural form.

Dynamite is a powerful explosive made from nitroglycerin absorbed into a stabilizing material. Invented by Alfred Nobel, it revolutionized mining, construction, and demolition—and warfare. Figuratively, dynamite describes anything explosive or sensational: {That story is dynamite}. As slang, dynamite means excellent or exciting: {The band was dynamite last night}. To dynamite is to blow something up.

Dynasties is the plural of dynasty, a sequence of rulers from the same family line who maintain power across generations. The term appears most often in historical contexts—the Ming dynasty, the Romanov dynasty—but extends to any family that dominates a field over time: {political dynasties like the Kennedys} or {sports dynasties like the Manning family}. In casual use, dynasty can describe any team or organization that sustains dominance: {The Patriots built a dynasty in the 2000s}.

A dynasty is a sequence of rulers from the same family line, each inheriting power from predecessors: {the Ming dynasty}, {the Habsburg dynasty}. The word extends to any family that maintains prominence across generations in business, politics, or entertainment: {a banking dynasty}, {a Hollywood dynasty}. In sports, dynasty describes teams that dominate their league over multiple seasons.

Dysfunction is impaired or abnormal functioning. A bodily dysfunction affects an organ or system: {erectile dysfunction}, {kidney dysfunction}. Family dysfunction describes unhealthy relationship patterns. Organizational dysfunction means a workplace or institution operates poorly. The adjective dysfunctional appears more often than the noun: {a dysfunctional family}, {dysfunctional communication}.

Dysfunctional describes something that fails to function properly or healthily. Most often applied to families or relationships marked by poor communication, conflict, or harmful patterns: {She grew up in a dysfunctional household}. The word extends to organizations, systems, or governments that don't work as they should: {a dysfunctional Congress}, {dysfunctional management}. Sometimes used loosely for anything messy or problematic.

Dyslexia is a learning disorder that affects reading, writing, and spelling despite normal intelligence. The brain processes written language differently, making it difficult to connect letters with sounds or recognize words fluently. Someone with dyslexia might reverse letters, read slowly, or struggle with spelling: {Her dyslexia wasn't diagnosed until college}. The condition is lifelong but manageable with specialized instruction.

Dystopia is an imagined society characterized by oppression, suffering, or injustice—the opposite of utopia. The word typically describes fictional worlds where authoritarian control, environmental ruin, or technological excess has created nightmarish conditions: {Orwell's 1984 remains the quintessential dystopia}. Dystopian as an adjective extends beyond fiction to describe real conditions that feel oppressively bleak: {The abandoned factory district had a dystopian quality}.

Dystopian describes an imagined society characterized by oppression, suffering, or degradation—the opposite of utopian. Dystopian fiction depicts futures gone wrong: totalitarian control, environmental collapse, technological enslavement. {The novel paints a dystopian vision of surveillance capitalism.} The word also describes real situations that feel ominously like such fiction: {The abandoned factory district looked dystopian.}

Dystopias are imagined societies characterized by oppression, suffering, and dehumanization—the opposite of utopias. In fiction, dystopias typically feature authoritarian governments, environmental catastrophe, technological control, or social collapse. The word gained currency through twentieth-century novels like *1984* and *Brave New World*. People also use dystopia loosely to describe real-world conditions they find oppressive or nightmarish: {This airport feels like a dystopia.}

Eager describes strong enthusiasm or impatient desire for something anticipated: {eager to please}, {eager for news}, {an eager student}. The word suggests positive energy and readiness rather than passive waiting. An {eager beaver} is someone who shows excessive enthusiasm, sometimes annoyingly so.

An eagle is a large bird of prey with powerful wings, keen eyesight, and a hooked beak—apex predators that hunt fish, small mammals, and other birds. The bald eagle serves as the national symbol of the United States, appearing on currency and official seals. In golf, an eagle is a score of two under par on a hole: {She made eagle on the par five}. As a verb, to eagle a hole is to achieve this score. {Eagle-eyed} means having sharp vision or keen attention to detail.

Eagles are large birds of prey known for their keen eyesight, powerful talons, and soaring flight. The word typically appears as the plural of eagle, referring to multiple birds: {Bald eagles have rebounded since DDT was banned}. In golf, eagles are scores of two under par on a hole. The term also applies to various coins bearing an eagle image, particularly the American gold eagle. (Capitalized Eagles refers to sports teams or the rock band.)

Any part of the organ of hearing, from the innermost to the outermost part, can be called the ear; context usually reveals which particular part or parts is meant. When an adjective that characterizes shape or size precedes ear (pointy/floppy/rounded/huge), the reference is to the visible parts of the ear, as opposed to the “hearing” parts. Ear has figurative use with reference to hearing, listening, and understanding: He has the ear of the President, lend me your ears, in one ear and out the other.

An earbud is a small speaker designed to fit inside or just outside the ear canal, typically used in pairs for listening to audio from phones, computers, or music players. Unlike over-ear headphones, earbuds are compact and portable: {I lost one of my earbuds on the subway}. Wireless earbuds have largely replaced wired versions.

Earbuds are small headphones that fit inside or just outside the ear canal, typically connected by a cord or wirelessly via Bluetooth. They're compact and portable, favored for listening to music or taking calls while commuting, exercising, or working: {I can't find my earbuds anywhere}. Also called earphones or in-ears.

The eardrum is the thin membrane inside the ear that vibrates in response to sound waves, transmitting them to the inner ear. Loud noises or sudden pressure changes can rupture it: {The explosion burst his eardrum}. Also called the tympanic membrane.

Eardrums are the thin membranes inside the ear that vibrate in response to sound waves—the mechanism that makes hearing possible. Loud noises, pressure changes, or infection can damage or rupture an eardrum: {My eardrums were ringing after the concert}. Also called the tympanic membrane.

An earful is a large amount of talk, usually unwelcome—a scolding, complaint, or lengthy lecture: {I got an earful from my mother about coming home late}. Less commonly, it can mean as much as one can absorb: {That concert was quite an earful}.

Earl is a British noble rank, falling between marquess and viscount in the peerage hierarchy. The title corresponds to count in other European systems—a countess is an earl's wife. Earls were originally royal officials governing shires, though the title became hereditary. {The Earl of Sandwich}, {the Earl of Essex}.

Early can function as an adjective or adverb with a range of related meanings, most of which are the opposite of late. Early is typically associated with concepts such as before, soon, and beginning, just as late is connected with after and end. In anything that develops over time, early suggests a form or stage that is relatively primitive, immature, or undeveloped.

Earmuffs are a pair of soft coverings worn over the ears, connected by a band that passes over the head. They provide warmth in cold weather or muffle loud sounds in noisy environments: {She pulled on her earmuffs before heading out into the snow}. Protective earmuffs for noise reduction are bulkier than the fuzzy kind worn for warmth.

To earn is to receive something in exchange for work or effort: {She earns a good salary}, {He earned his degree after years of night classes}. The word implies deserving what you get—earned income differs from inherited wealth, and an earned victory differs from a lucky one. Earn extends to intangibles: {earn someone's trust}, {earn a reputation}. Interest or investments earn returns.

Earned is the past tense of earn—to receive something through effort, work, or merit. Money is earned through labor: {She earned sixty thousand last year}. Respect, trust, and reputation are earned over time. {Earned} often emphasizes that something was deserved rather than given freely: {He earned every bit of that promotion}. In sports, an earned run scores without fielding errors.

Earnest describes serious intent and sincere conviction. An earnest {student} applies genuine effort. An earnest {plea} comes from the heart. To begin {in earnest} is to start with full commitment after preliminary steps: {After months of planning, construction began in earnest}. The word suggests authenticity but can imply a lack of humor or lightness—calling someone earnest isn't always a compliment.

Earning is the act of gaining something through effort, work, or merit. Most often it refers to money received for labor: {She's earning good money at her new job}. But earning extends to non-monetary rewards—you earn respect, trust, or a reputation through your actions. The plural earnings refers to income or profits: {quarterly earnings}, {lifetime earnings}.

Earnings are money received for work or from investments. In personal finance, earnings usually means wages or salary: {Her earnings increased after the promotion}. In business contexts, earnings refers to profits—revenue minus expenses: {The company reported strong quarterly earnings}. The word nearly always appears in plural form.

Earphones are small speakers designed to be worn in or over the ears, connected to an audio device by wire or wirelessly. The term covers both earbuds that sit in the ear canal and larger headphones that cover the entire ear, though some reserve *headphones* for the latter: {I forgot my earphones on the train}.

An earring is a piece of jewelry worn on the ear, typically attached through a pierced hole in the earlobe or clipped to the edge. Earrings come in countless styles—studs, hoops, dangles, cuffs. They may be worn singly or in pairs, and multiple piercings allow for several at once: {She wore three earrings in each ear}.

Earrings are jewelry worn on the ears, typically attached through pierced holes in the earlobes or clipped onto them. They range from simple studs to elaborate dangles: {She wore diamond earrings to the gala}. Earrings appear across cultures and genders, though Western conventions have historically associated them more with women.

Ears are the organs of hearing, located on either side of the head. The visible outer part catches sound waves; the inner structures convert them to signals the brain interprets. Ears also govern balance. Figuratively, an ear is attention or receptiveness: {lend an ear}, {have someone's ear}. A good ear for music or language means natural aptitude for hearing distinctions. To {play it by ear} is to improvise rather than follow a plan.

Earshot is the distance within which sounds can be heard. If you are within earshot of something, you are close enough to hear it; if you are out of earshot, you are too far away. The word appears almost exclusively in these two phrases: {Let's wait until we're out of earshot before we talk about the surprise party.}

Earth is the name for the planet we inhabit; this is nearly always the meaning if the word is capitalized. Earth can also mean land (in contrast to air or sea) or soil: I planted seeds in the loamy earth. Some fixed expressions using earth are not to be taken literally, like cost the earth (cost a lot) or I felt the earth move (I was deeply impressed). In British English, earth (noun and verb) has the same meaning as ground in American English as it applies to electrical connections.

An earthquake is a sudden, violent shaking of the ground caused by movement of rock beneath the earth's surface. Earthquakes range from imperceptible tremors to catastrophic events that destroy cities. The scale of destruction depends on magnitude, depth, and proximity to populated areas. {The earthquake leveled most of the downtown.} Figuratively, an earthquake is any event that fundamentally disrupts the status quo: {a political earthquake}.

Earthquakes is the plural of earthquake—a sudden shaking of the ground caused by shifting tectonic plates or volcanic activity. The term extends to any major upheaval: {political earthquakes}, {earthquakes in the financial markets}. {California experiences frequent earthquakes along the San Andreas Fault.}

Earthshattering describes events or revelations of enormous significance—momentous enough to shake the foundations of what came before. The word is often used hyperbolically: {It's not exactly earthshattering news that teenagers like to sleep late}. Genuinely earthshattering developments change how we understand something fundamental. Also spelled earth-shattering.

An earthworm is a long, segmented worm that burrows through soil, aerating it and breaking down organic matter. Earthworms are familiar to gardeners and children alike—pinkish-brown, soft-bodied, emerging after rain. They lack eyes and limbs but can regenerate lost segments. {We dug up earthworms for fishing bait.}

Earthworms are segmented worms that live in soil, aerating it as they burrow and enriching it with their castings. They're the familiar wriggling creatures that surface after rain and get threaded onto fishhooks as bait. Gardeners prize them as indicators of healthy soil: {The compost bin was full of earthworms}.

Earthy describes qualities associated with soil or the ground—an earthy {smell} after rain, an earthy {color} palette of browns and ochres. Extended to people and art, earthy means unrefined, direct, and unpretentious: {Her earthy humor made everyone feel at ease}. Earthy jokes or language tend toward the crude or sexual without being genuinely vulgar—more robust than delicate, more peasant than aristocrat.

An earwig is a slender insect with pincers at its tail end. The name comes from an old superstition that they crawl into people's ears—they don't, though they do favor dark, tight spaces. To earwig is to eavesdrop or whisper insinuatingly: {He earwigged their conversation from the next booth}.

Earwigs are slender insects with pincers at the rear of their abdomen, commonly found in gardens and damp places. Despite folklore that they crawl into human ears, they pose no such threat. The pincers look menacing but are mostly harmless to humans. As a verb, to earwig is British slang for eavesdropping: {She was earwigging on their conversation}.

An earworm is a catchy piece of music that gets stuck in your head, repeating involuntarily: {I've had that jingle stuck as an earworm all day}. The term captures how these melodic fragments seem to burrow into consciousness and resist dislodging. Earworm also refers to various moth larvae that damage corn and other crops by boring into the ears.

An earworm is a catchy piece of music that is easy to remember and that people like to sing or hum. When people use the word earworm they are usually talking about a song that they themselves have stuck in their head that they can’t get rid of.

The various noun and verb uses of ease do not travel far from the related adjective easy. When you ease an unpleasant condition (congestion, tension, pressure, strain), you diminish its force and make it more bearable. When something eases, such as wind or rain, it diminishes in strength. As a noun, ease is a condition or state in which little or no effort is required and there is freedom from discomfort: Retirement led to a life of ease.

An easel is a freestanding frame, typically with three legs, used to hold a canvas or board upright while an artist paints. Easels range from small tabletop versions to large studio models, and some fold flat for portability. The word extends to any similar stand used to display artwork, posters, or presentation boards. {She set up her easel in the park to paint the landscape.}

Easels are upright frames for supporting an artist's canvas, a display board, or a flip chart. The typical easel is a tripod of wooden or metal legs that holds a surface at a convenient angle for painting or viewing. {She set up her easel in the garden to paint the roses.}

East is the direction where the sun rises, one of the four cardinal points of the compass, opposite to west. As a noun or adjective, it describes this direction or regions lying in that direction: {The sun comes up in the east}; {the east side of town}. When capitalized, East often refers to specific regions—the Eastern Hemisphere, East Asia, or the eastern United States—and carries cultural weight in phrases like {East meets West}. The adverb form describes movement toward that direction: {We drove east for hours}.

Eastern describes location or direction toward the east—where the sun rises. An eastern {exposure} faces that direction; the eastern {states} lie on the Atlantic coast. Capitalized, Eastern often refers to Asia or Asian culture ({Eastern philosophy}, {Eastern medicine}) or to the Orthodox churches of Christianity. During the Cold War, {Eastern bloc} meant Soviet-aligned nations.

Easy describes something requiring little effort, presenting few difficulties, or causing no discomfort. An easy {test} doesn't challenge much. An easy {chair} is comfortable. Easy can suggest relaxed or unhurried: {Take it easy}. Someone {easy to talk to} is approachable. In older slang, an easy woman was sexually available—a usage now recognized as sexist. {Easy come, easy go} dismisses losses that arrived without effort.

Easygoing describes someone relaxed and tolerant, not easily upset or bothered by difficulties. An easygoing person doesn't sweat the small stuff: {He's pretty easygoing about deadlines}. The word can also describe atmospheres or situations that feel casual and unstressed: {an easygoing workplace}, {an easygoing pace of life}.

Eat is to take food into the body through the mouth, chew, and swallow. The word extends to gradual consumption or destruction: rust eats metal, guilt eats at you. To eat something is also to absorb or accept it: {I'll eat the cost}. If something is {eating you}, it's bothering you persistently. {Eat your words} means to retract a statement, usually with embarrassment. In vulgar slang, to eat someone out is to perform oral sex.

Eaten is the past participle of eat, used with helping verbs to form perfect tenses: {I have eaten}, {The leftovers had been eaten}. It also works as an adjective: {half-eaten sandwich}, {moth-eaten sweater}. To be {eaten up} by something is to be consumed by it: {She was eaten up with guilt}.

Eating is the act of consuming food—taking it into the mouth, chewing, and swallowing. The word covers everything from basic sustenance to pleasure: {We were eating dinner when she called}. Eating often implies the manner or context: {clean eating}, {emotional eating}, {eating out}. To {eat someone alive} is to overwhelm or destroy them. Something that's {eating at you} is troubling you persistently.

To eavesdrop is to listen secretly to a private conversation. The word comes from the practice of standing under the eaves of a building—where rainwater drips—to overhear what's said inside. {I couldn't help eavesdropping on their argument}. The noun eavesdropper describes someone who habitually listens in.

An eavesdropper is someone who secretly listens to private conversations. The word comes from the practice of standing under the eaves of a building—where rainwater drips—to overhear what's happening inside. {The eavesdropper pressed her ear to the wall}. The verb is eavesdrop; the activity is eavesdropping.

Eavesdropping is secretly listening to private conversations. The word comes from the practice of standing under the eaves of a house to hear what's said inside. Now it applies to any covert listening—through walls, on phone calls, or via electronic surveillance: {The NSA's eavesdropping programs sparked controversy}. To eavesdrop is to engage in such listening: {I couldn't help eavesdropping on their argument}.

Ebb is the receding of the tide as water flows back out to sea, opposite of flow. The tide ebbs twice daily. By extension, anything that diminishes or declines ebbs: {Her enthusiasm began to ebb}. The phrase {ebb and flow} describes natural cycles of increase and decrease. At a low ebb means at a weakened or depleted state: {Morale was at a low ebb}.

Ebony is a dense, dark hardwood prized for its deep black color and fine grain. It's used for piano keys, chess pieces, and decorative objects. The word extends to anything sharing that distinctive black color: {ebony hair}, {ebony skin}. As an adjective, ebony describes this rich, lustrous black: {an ebony finish on the cabinet}. (Capitalized Ebony is a name or the magazine.)

Eccentric describes something or someone deviating from the norm, especially in behavior or personality. An eccentric person has unusual habits or unconventional ways: {My eccentric aunt collects vintage typewriters and talks to her plants}. The word carries affection more than criticism—eccentricity suggests harmless oddity rather than troubling deviance. In technical contexts, eccentric means off-center: an eccentric wheel doesn't rotate around its middle. As a noun, an eccentric is a person known for peculiar behavior: {The neighborhood eccentric fed pigeons at exactly 3 PM daily}.

Eccentricity is deviation from conventional or expected behavior—the quality of being odd or unconventional: {His eccentricity charmed some colleagues and alienated others}. The word carries a gentler connotation than similar terms; an eccentric person is quirky rather than disturbed. In geometry and astronomy, eccentricity measures how much an ellipse deviates from a perfect circle: {The comet's high eccentricity gives it an elongated orbit}.

Eccentrics are people who behave in unconventional or peculiar ways—those who deviate from social norms in dress, habits, or thought. The term carries affection or admiration more often than criticism: {The neighborhood had its share of harmless eccentrics}. In mechanical contexts, an eccentric is a disk or wheel mounted off-center, used to convert rotary motion to reciprocating motion.

A literal echo is the reflection of sound off a surface after some delay; when sound does this, it is said to echo. The most frequent use of echo is figurative, to characterize things that repeat. If you echo a sentiment or opinion, you express the same one as someone else. Some sounds that are said to echo, such as footsteps, merely repeat. If you hear or find an echo of some idea, you come across another instance of it.

Echoes is the plural of echo—sound waves that bounce back from a surface and return to the listener. The word extends to any repetition or reverberation: {echoes of the past}, {Her words found echoes in his own experience}. As a verb, echoes means repeats or reflects: {The canyon echoes with birdsong}, {His speech echoed the president's remarks}.

Echolocation is a biological sonar system used by certain animals—bats, dolphins, some whales—to navigate and locate prey in darkness or murky water. The animal emits sounds and interprets the returning echoes to map its surroundings. {Bats use echolocation to catch insects in flight.} The term also applies to similar technology in submarines and robotics.

An eclair is an oblong pastry made from choux dough, filled with cream or custard, and topped with chocolate icing. The shape distinguishes it from round cream puffs, which use the same light, airy dough. {She ordered a chocolate eclair with the coffee.}

Eclectic is an adjective used to characterize something that contains elements drawn from many different sources. It is similar in meaning to diverse and heterogeneous. Groups of objects can be characterized as eclectic, such as an eclectic collection of modern art or an eclectic group of actors. If someone has eclectic tastes, they like a number of different but related things equally, such as different kinds of music or food.

The relatively rare celestial event called an eclipse, in which one astronomical object is obscured by another, inspires more frequent use of the word. If one thing eclipses another, the first thing diminishes the importance or prominence of the second. If a celestial body is in eclipse, it is obscured by another; but if your hopes are in eclipse, they don’t have much chance of success. Eclipse plumage is exhibited by birds after the mating season, when they shed their bright features.

Eclipsed means overshadowed or surpassed, from the astronomical event where one celestial body blocks light from another. A star's performance can be eclipsed by a newcomer's brilliance. A company's achievements may be eclipsed by scandal. {Her early work was eclipsed by her later masterpieces.} The literal sense describes a sun or moon during an eclipse: {The moon eclipsed the sun.}

Eclipses is the plural of eclipse—an astronomical event where one celestial body passes into the shadow of another, as when the moon blocks the sun or enters Earth's shadow. The word extends to any overshadowing: {Her later work eclipses her early novels}. To eclipse someone is to surpass them so completely they seem diminished by comparison.

Ecology is the study of how living things relate to each other and their environment—the web of interactions between organisms and the systems they inhabit. The term extends to any complex of such relationships: {the ecology of a coral reef}, {the ecology of the human gut}. Figuratively, ecology describes interconnected systems more broadly: {the ecology of social media}, {the media ecology}. The related adjective ecological appears in phrases like {ecological balance} and {ecological disaster}.

Ecommerce, also written e-commerce, is the buying and selling of goods and services over the internet. The term covers everything from massive online marketplaces to small businesses selling handmade items through their websites. {Most of our ecommerce sales come from mobile users.} The rise of ecommerce has transformed retail, enabling consumers to shop from anywhere while forcing traditional brick-and-mortar stores to adapt or close.

Economic relates to the economy—the system of producing, distributing, and consuming goods and services. Economic {policy}, economic {growth}, economic {crisis}. The word also means financially practical or efficient: {It wasn't economic to repair the old car}. This second sense overlaps with economical, though economical more often describes thrifty behavior while economic connects to larger systems.

Economics is the study of how societies allocate scarce resources—how goods and services are produced, distributed, and consumed. The field divides into microeconomics (individual choices, markets, firms) and macroeconomics (national output, unemployment, inflation). As a modifier, economic describes things relating to the economy: {economic growth}, {economic policy}. The plural form economics takes a singular verb when referring to the discipline: {Economics is called the dismal science}.

Economies is the plural of economy. A country's economy is its system of producing and distributing goods and services: {emerging economies}, {the world's largest economies}. Economies also means instances of saving money or resources: {We found economies in the production process}. {Economies of scale} are cost reductions achieved by producing in larger quantities.

An economist is a person who studies or specializes in economics—the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services. Economists analyze data, develop theories, and advise governments and businesses on policy: {The economist predicted a recession}. The term can carry skepticism about the gap between economic models and real-world outcomes: {Economists disagreed, as usual}.

Economy centers on the management of resources—money, goods, labor, time. A country's economy is its system of production, distribution, and consumption: {The economy grew by three percent}. To practice economy is to avoid waste: {She ran the household with strict economy}. An economy {car} or economy {class} offers basic service at lower cost. The adjective economical means thrifty or efficient: {an economical use of space}. In writing, economy of language means expressing ideas with minimal words.

An ecosystem is a community of living organisms together with their physical environment, functioning as an interconnected system: {the marine ecosystem}, {a forest ecosystem}. The term extends to any complex network of interdependent elements: {the startup ecosystem}, {the Apple ecosystem of devices and services}. Disrupting one part affects the whole.

Ecosystems are communities of living organisms interacting with their physical environment—the plants, animals, microbes, soil, water, and climate of a particular place functioning as a unit. A pond is an ecosystem; so is a rainforest. The term extends to any complex system of interdependent elements: {the startup ecosystem}, {the media ecosystem}. Damage to one part affects the whole.

Ecoterrorism is the use of violence, sabotage, or intimidation in the name of environmental causes. Acts range from spiking trees to injure loggers, to burning construction sites, to attacks on research facilities: {The FBI classified the arson as ecoterrorism}. The term is contested—activists may call it direct action while opponents and law enforcement call it terrorism.

Ecstasy is intense joy or rapture—a state of being overwhelmed by emotion, often to the point of losing ordinary self-awareness. Religious mystics describe ecstatic visions; lovers speak of ecstasy in intimate moments. The word implies being transported beyond normal experience: {She listened in ecstasy as the orchestra reached its climax}. Ecstasy (or E) is also slang for MDMA, a drug that induces euphoria and emotional openness.

Ecstatic describes overwhelming joy or delight—emotion so intense it seems to transport you beyond ordinary experience. {She was ecstatic when she got the job offer.} The word implies more than happiness; it suggests being carried away by feeling. Ecstasy is the noun form.

Ectoplasm is a supernatural substance supposedly exuded by mediums during séances—a luminous, gelatinous material through which spirits manifest. The concept flourished in 19th-century spiritualism, though "ectoplasm" proved consistently to be cheesecloth or other fakery when examined. In biology, ectoplasm is the outer layer of a cell's cytoplasm. The ghostly slime in *Ghostbusters* popularized the word beyond its spiritualist origins.

An eddy is a circular movement of water or air that runs counter to the main current, forming a small whirlpool or vortex: {Leaves spun in the eddy near the riverbank}. The verb means to move in such a pattern: {Smoke eddied around the chimney}. By extension, anything that swirls or circles back on itself eddies: {Rumors eddied through the office}. (Capitalized Eddy is a given name.)

Present in many of the uses of edge are the ideas of a boundary and a linear feature (house on the edge of town, feathers edged in red). The edge of a blade is the sharp part. Figuratively, an edge may be an advantage (height is an edge in basketball) or a state of nervousness or agitation: Traffic puts me on edge. When you edge or edge an object, you move (yourself) or move the object slowly closer in a specified direction: She edged closer to him on the bench.

Edgelords are people who deliberately say shocking, offensive, or provocative things online to get attention or seem darkly sophisticated. The term is dismissive—it mocks those who mistake being transgressive for being interesting: {The comments section was full of edgelords posting racist jokes}. The singular edgelord describes an individual practitioner of this posturing.

Edges are the outermost boundaries or sharp borders of things—where a surface ends or two surfaces meet at an angle. A knife's edge is its cutting line; a cliff's edge is where land drops away. To edge is to move gradually: {She edged toward the door}. Figuratively, edge suggests sharpness or advantage: a competitive edge, an edge in your voice. On edge means tense or irritable. To be on the edge of something is to be close to it: {on the edge of bankruptcy}. Edgy describes something nervously tense or provocatively unconventional.

Edging is the process of creating or trimming a border or boundary—the edge of a lawn, a garden bed, a garment. As a noun, edging is material used for such borders: decorative edging, brick edging. In sexual slang, edging is the practice of bringing oneself or a partner close to orgasm repeatedly without completion, prolonging arousal: {He's been edging for an hour}.

Edgy describes someone or something tense, nervous, or irritable—on edge: {She's been edgy since the layoffs were announced}. The word also means daringly unconventional or provocatively avant-garde: {an edgy film}, {edgy humor}. Online, edgy often carries ironic dismissal of content that tries too hard to shock or seem cool: {Wow, so edgy}.

Edible means safe or suitable to eat. The word distinguishes what can be consumed from what cannot: {The berries looked tempting but weren't edible}. Edible doesn't imply appetizing—something can be technically edible but unpleasant. As a noun, edibles often refers to cannabis-infused foods: {She prefers edibles to smoking}.

Edibles are things fit to be eaten—food, broadly. The word often distinguishes what's safe to consume from what isn't: {foraging for edibles in the forest}, {Are these berries edible?} In contemporary usage, edibles frequently refers specifically to food products containing cannabis: {She brought edibles to the party}, {I prefer edibles to smoking}.

To edit is to prepare written or recorded material for publication or presentation—correcting, revising, selecting, or arranging content. An editor edits manuscripts, films, or broadcasts. The word extends to any modification: {I edited my comment before posting}, {She edited him out of the photo}. An edit is an instance of such revision. In computing, edit mode allows changes to a document or file.

Editing is the process of revising and refining written, visual, or audio material. An editor cuts, rearranges, corrects, and polishes: {She spent the weekend editing her manuscript}. In film and video, editing means assembling footage into a coherent sequence. The word covers everything from fixing typos to reshaping a work's entire structure.

An edition is a particular version of something published or produced. A book's first edition is its original printing; later editions may be revised or expanded. Newspapers have morning and evening editions. A limited edition restricts the number of copies: {a limited edition print}. Special editions of products feature added content or packaging: {the collector's edition of the game}.

An editor is someone who prepares written material for publication—selecting, revising, correcting, and arranging content. A newspaper editor decides what stories run; a book editor shapes manuscripts. In film and video, an editor assembles footage into a coherent whole. Editor also names software for creating or modifying files: {a text editor}, {a photo editor}. To edit is to perform this work.

Editorial describes material expressing opinion rather than reporting facts. An editorial is a newspaper or magazine article stating the publication's official position: {The Times ran an editorial opposing the bill}. As an adjective, editorial distinguishes opinion from news: {editorial content}, {editorial page}. It also relates to the editing process: {editorial decisions}, {editorial staff}.

Editors are people who prepare written material for publication. A book editor shapes a manuscript, suggesting revisions and corrections. A newspaper or magazine editor selects and organizes content, or oversees a section: {the sports editor}. A film or video editor assembles footage into a finished product. In computing, an editor is software for creating or modifying files: {a text editor}, {a photo editor}.

To educate is to develop someone's knowledge, skills, or character through instruction or experience. Schools educate children in academic subjects; parents educate them in values. The word implies systematic development rather than casual learning: {She was educated at Oxford}. To educate yourself is to pursue knowledge independently. An educated guess draws on relevant knowledge rather than pure speculation.

Educated describes someone who has received formal schooling or training, especially at advanced levels: {an educated woman}, {a Harvard-educated lawyer}. More broadly, it suggests knowledge, refinement, or good judgment—an educated {guess} is informed rather than random. To educate is to teach or develop understanding: {The campaign educated voters about climate change}.

In its most common meaning, education is the action or process of instructing learners in the knowledge, skills, or information that they need. Education encompasses formal learning experiences for people from childhood to adulthood; the various stages are designated with compound terms such as primary education, secondary education, and higher education. When someone talks about their education, they may mean the entire process or the last part of it. But education can be used outside of a formal instructional setting. If you say that an experience was an education, you mean that you learned something important.
Eek!, often used ironically, is mainly an expression of sudden fear or alarm.

An eel is a long, slender fish with a snakelike body, typically lacking scales and covered in slippery mucus. Eels live in both fresh and salt water, with some species migrating between the two. The slipperiness makes them hard to grasp, giving rise to {slippery as an eel} for someone evasive or hard to pin down.

Eels are long, snakelike fish found in both fresh and salt water. Most species have smooth, scaleless skin and lack pelvic fins. Some, like the moray eel, are marine; others migrate between rivers and oceans to spawn. Eels are notoriously slippery—hence {slippery as an eel} for someone evasive or hard to pin down.

Eerie describes something strange and unsettling, suggesting supernatural or inexplicable forces. An eerie {silence} feels unnatural. An eerie {glow} seems otherworldly. The word captures that specific unease when something feels wrong in ways you can't quite name: {The abandoned hospital had an eerie atmosphere}. Eerie differs from merely scary—it emphasizes the uncanny rather than outright fear.

Like the word it is often confused with (affect), effect can be both a noun and a verb. Unlike affect, effect is usually a noun. An effect is a noticeable change or result from some action or condition: What effect will the disease have on the child’s development? When something takes effect it becomes active or operational: The new law will take effect January 1st. Effect is used infrequently as a verb to mean bring about: Organizers felt that the campaign had effected positive changes.

Effective means producing the intended result. An effective {treatment} works; an effective {leader} gets things done. Something effective has the power to accomplish its purpose: {The new policy proved effective at reducing wait times}. Effective also marks when something takes force: {The changes become effective January 1}. The distinction from efficient is that effective concerns results while efficient concerns resources—a method can be effective but wasteful.

Effects are belongings or possessions, especially personal items: {She gathered her effects and left}. The word often appears in legal or formal contexts—someone's {personal effects} are collected after death or hospital stays. Effects also names the technical elements that create illusions in film and theater: {special effects}, {sound effects}, {practical effects}.

Efficiency is accomplishing something with minimal waste of time, effort, or resources. An efficient {engine} extracts more work from its fuel; an efficient {worker} produces more in less time. The word implies optimization—getting the maximum output from given inputs. {We need to improve efficiency in the warehouse.} In physics, efficiency is the ratio of useful work performed to total energy expended.

Efficient describes achieving results with minimal waste of time, effort, or resources. An efficient {engine} extracts more power from less fuel. An efficient {worker} completes tasks quickly without unnecessary steps. The word implies optimization—getting the most output from the least input. {She found a more efficient route to work.}
