An effigy is a sculpture or model of a person, typically made to be destroyed as an act of protest or contempt: {Protesters burned the dictator in effigy}. The phrase {in effigy} distinguishes symbolic destruction from actual harm to a person. Effigies also appear in neutral contexts—carved stone figures on medieval tombs, or stuffed dummies burned on Guy Fawkes Night.

Effort is the energy or exertion applied toward accomplishing something. Physical effort involves bodily strain; mental effort involves concentration and will. An effort is also a particular attempt: {Her effort to quit smoking lasted three weeks}. Something that requires {no effort} comes easily. To {make an effort} is to try, often implying the attempt matters more than the outcome.

Effortless describes something done with apparent ease, without visible struggle or strain: {Her effortless grace on the dance floor}. The word often implies skill so refined that difficulty becomes invisible—what looks effortless usually required considerable effort to master. {He made the complicated maneuver look effortless}.

An egg is the reproductive body produced by female birds, reptiles, fish, and insects—a rounded structure containing an embryo and nutrients enclosed in a shell or membrane. Most commonly, egg refers to a chicken egg used as food: {scrambled eggs}, {egg salad}. To egg someone on is to urge or provoke them. Egg also appears in compounds describing shapes: {egghead} (an intellectual), {egg-shaped}. To have {egg on your face} is to be embarrassed by a mistake.

An eggbeater is a handheld kitchen tool with rotating blades used to beat eggs, whip cream, or mix batters. The classic design has two interlocking beaters turned by a hand crank. Electric versions are now more common. In slang, eggbeater refers to a helicopter, from the resemblance of its rotor blades: {The eggbeater touched down on the hospital roof}.

Eggnog is a rich, creamy drink made from eggs, milk or cream, sugar, and usually alcohol—traditionally rum, brandy, or bourbon. It's associated with winter holidays, particularly Christmas and New Year's: {We spiked the eggnog with bourbon}. The nonalcoholic version is popular with children. Store-bought eggnog appears seasonally alongside other holiday foods.

Eggplant is a large, egg-shaped vegetable with glossy purple skin and spongy white flesh. It's a staple in Mediterranean and Asian cuisines—baba ghanoush, ratatouille, eggplant parmesan. The flesh absorbs oil readily and turns creamy when cooked. In British English, the vegetable is called aubergine. As slang, the eggplant emoji suggests a penis.

An eggroll is a fried appetizer in American Chinese cuisine—a wheat wrapper encasing shredded cabbage, pork, and other fillings, rolled into a cylinder and deep-fried until crispy. The wrapper blisters during frying, giving it a bubbly texture. Eggrolls are served with duck sauce or hot mustard: {We ordered eggrolls to start}.

Eggs are the reproductive cells produced by female animals, enclosed in protective shells or membranes. Most commonly, eggs refers to chicken eggs used as food—scrambled, fried, boiled, or in baking. To {egg someone on} is to encourage them, usually toward mischief. To {put all your eggs in one basket} is to risk everything on a single venture. {Walking on eggshells} means being extremely careful not to upset someone. In slang, eggs can mean testicles.

Eggshell is the hard outer covering of an egg, thin and brittle. The word extends to things sharing these qualities: eggshell {paint} has a slight sheen between flat and satin; an eggshell {finish} is delicate and easily damaged. To {walk on eggshells} is to act with extreme caution to avoid upsetting someone. As a color, eggshell is off-white with a faint yellow or cream tint.

Eggshells are the hard outer covering of eggs, thin and brittle once dried. They break easily and leave sharp fragments—hence {walking on eggshells}, meaning to act with extreme caution around someone easily upset or offended. The image is of tiptoeing through a kitchen floor covered in broken shells.

Ego is one's sense of self—personal identity, self-image, and self-importance. In everyday use, ego often implies excessive self-regard: {His ego won't let him admit he was wrong}. A {big ego} suggests arrogance; a {bruised ego} means wounded pride. In Freudian psychology, the ego mediates between primitive drives and moral constraints. {Check your ego at the door.}

Egomania is obsessive preoccupation with oneself—an extreme, pathological form of self-centeredness. Unlike ordinary egotism, egomania suggests a compulsive quality, an inability to see beyond one's own importance: {His egomania made collaboration impossible}. The term is used loosely for anyone excessively self-absorbed, though psychiatry reserves it for more severe conditions.

An egomaniac is a person with an obsessive preoccupation with their own importance, abilities, or desires. The term implies not just ordinary self-centeredness but a pathological inability to consider others: {He's such an egomaniac he can't even ask how your day was}. Unlike clinical narcissism, egomaniac is informal—an insult rather than a diagnosis.

Egos is the plural of ego, a person's sense of self-importance or self-esteem. When egos clash, competing personalities create conflict: {Too many egos in the room made collaboration impossible}. A bruised ego has suffered a blow to pride. Someone with a big ego thinks highly of themselves, often excessively.

Egotism is excessive preoccupation with oneself—talking about yourself too much, steering conversations back to your own experiences, assuming others share your interest in your affairs. An egotist believes they're the main character. The word overlaps with egoism, though egoism more often refers to a philosophical position that self-interest is the basis of morality. {His egotism made every dinner party exhausting.}

An egret is a wading bird with white plumage and long decorative feathers, typically found near water. Egrets are herons, distinguished mainly by their breeding plumage—the elegant, wispy feathers once prized for hat decorations: {A snowy egret stalked the shallows}.

Eight is the number between seven and nine, represented as 8. It appears throughout measurement and culture: eight ounces in a cup, eight bits in a byte, a figure eight, behind the eight ball. To be {behind the eight ball} is to be in a difficult position, from the pool ball that blocks clean shots.

An eightball is the black ball numbered 8 in pool, pocketed last to win—or first to lose, if sunk prematurely. To be {behind the eightball} is to be in a difficult position, from the disadvantage of having the eightball between cue ball and target. In drug slang, an eightball is an eighth of an ounce of cocaine or methamphetamine.

Eighteen is the number between seventeen and nineteen, written 18. It marks legal adulthood in many countries—the age when one can vote, sign contracts, or buy cigarettes: {She turned eighteen last month}. An eighteen-wheeler is a large truck with that many wheels.

The eighties refers to the decade from 1980 to 1989, or to the numbers 80 through 89. Someone in their eighties is between 80 and 89 years old. When the temperature is in the eighties, it falls within that range. {The music of the eighties is making a comeback.} {My grandmother is in her eighties but still plays tennis.}

Eighty is the cardinal number between seventy-nine and eighty-one, equal to eight tens. {She lived to be eighty years old.} The eighties refers to the decade from 1980 to 1989, or to temperatures or ages in that range: {The heat wave kept us in the eighties all week.}

Eject means to force or throw out. A pilot ejects from a crashing plane; a bouncer ejects a rowdy patron; a machine ejects a disc. The word suggests sudden, forceful removal: {He was ejected from the game for fighting}. To eject can also mean to push out mechanically: {Press the button to eject the cartridge}.

Ejected is the past tense of eject, meaning forcibly expelled or thrown out. A pilot who ejected launched from a crashing aircraft. A fan who was ejected got removed from a venue for bad behavior. A disc that ejected popped out of its slot. {Security ejected the heckler from the concert}. {The cartridge ejected smoothly after each shot}.

When pronounced with an unstressed final vowel, elaborate is an adjective that means richly detailed or complex: The tribal elders wore elaborate headgear. They unveiled an elaborate plan for taking over the department. The verb elaborate has a long final vowel and means to expand something in detail: An audience member asked the mayor to elaborate on the implications of the new zoning rules.

Elastic describes materials that stretch under force and return to their original shape—rubber bands, waistbands, bungee cords. The noun elastic refers to such material, especially fabric woven with rubber threads: {The elastic in these socks has lost its stretch}. Figuratively, elastic means flexible or adaptable: {elastic interpretation of the rules}, {elastic demand} in economics. The opposite is rigid or inelastic.

Elated means extremely happy, often with a sense of triumph or relief. The feeling typically comes from good news or achievement: {She was elated when she got the job offer}. Elated suggests a buoyant, soaring quality—happiness that lifts you up rather than simply pleases.

Elation is a feeling of intense happiness and excitement, often following success or good news. It suggests being lifted up emotionally—a buoyant, energized joy rather than quiet contentment: {She felt a surge of elation when she got the acceptance letter}. The feeling is typically intense but temporary.

The elbow is the joint connecting the upper and lower arm, where the arm bends. By extension, elbow refers to anything shaped like a bent arm, such as a pipe fitting or a sharp turn in a road. To elbow someone is to push or nudge them with your elbow, often to get past: {She elbowed her way through the crowd}. Elbow grease is vigorous physical effort, especially scrubbing or polishing. If you rub elbows with someone, you associate with them socially.

Elbows are the joints connecting the upper and lower arm, where the arm bends. The word extends to angular bends in pipes or corridors. To elbow is to push or nudge with one's elbow: {She elbowed her way through the crowd}. {Elbow grease} means vigorous physical effort. To {rub elbows} with someone is to mingle with them socially.

Elder means older, used when comparing ages within a family or group: {my elder brother}, {the elder of the two sisters}. As a noun, an elder is someone older and often wiser—elders command respect in many cultures and hold formal authority in some churches and tribal communities. The elder tree or elderberry is unrelated, named for a different root entirely.

Elderberry is the small, dark purple berry of the elder tree, used in wines, jams, syrups, and folk medicine. The berries grow in clusters and have long been valued for supposed immune-boosting properties: {elderberry syrup for cold season}. Raw elderberries are mildly toxic and must be cooked before consumption.

Elderly means old, especially referring to people past middle age. The word is somewhat formal and often appears in institutional contexts: {elderly care}, {the elderly population}. Some consider it more respectful than "old," though others find it euphemistic or patronizing. {My elderly neighbor needs help with yard work.} As a noun, {the elderly} refers to old people collectively.

Elders are people who are older, especially those deserving respect or holding authority by virtue of their age and experience. In many cultures and religious traditions, elders serve as leaders, advisors, or custodians of wisdom: {The tribal elders gathered to settle the dispute.} The term implies not just advanced age but earned standing within a community. Elder can also refer to certain shrubs or small trees of the genus Sambucus, whose berries are used in wines and preserves.

Eldest means oldest among a group, typically siblings: {the eldest of four children}, {my eldest daughter}. Unlike older, which compares two, eldest usually implies three or more. The word is somewhat formal; oldest serves the same function in casual speech. Eldest can also describe the senior member of any group: {the eldest statesman in the room}.

Elect means to choose, especially by voting: {We elected a new mayor}. To elect to do something is to decide on that course: {She elected to stay home}. As an adjective, elect follows a title to indicate someone chosen but not yet serving: {the president-elect}. The elect, as a noun, refers to a select group—in religious contexts, those chosen by God for salvation.

An election is a formal process by which people vote to choose a person or decide an issue: {presidential election}, {local election}, {election day}. The word also means the act of choosing more broadly: {her election to stay home surprised everyone}. In theology, election refers to God's selection of individuals for salvation.

Elections are formal processes by which people vote to choose leaders or decide issues. The word typically appears in plural because voting happens across multiple offices, districts, or cycles: {midterm elections}, {local elections}, {presidential elections}. An election can also refer to a single contest: {She won the election by twelve points}. The verb elect means to choose by voting, and by extension, to choose generally: {He elected to stay home}.

Electric describes phenomena involving electricity—the flow of charged particles that powers modern life. An electric {current} moves through wires; an electric {car} runs on batteries rather than gasoline. Figuratively, electric describes an atmosphere charged with excitement or tension: {The crowd was electric}. Electric also distinguishes powered instruments from acoustic ones: an electric {guitar}, an electric {piano}.

An electrician is a tradesperson who installs, maintains, and repairs electrical wiring and equipment. Electricians work in residential, commercial, and industrial settings, handling everything from household outlets to complex building systems. The trade typically requires apprenticeship and licensing: {We called an electrician to rewire the basement}.

Electricity is a form of energy resulting from charged particles, harnessed to power lights, machines, and devices. It flows through wires as current and can be generated from various sources: coal, nuclear reactions, wind, sunlight. The word also describes the scientific study of electrical phenomena. Figuratively, electricity means excited tension or energy: {There was electricity in the air before the concert}.

Electrified describes something supplied with or affected by electricity. An electrified {fence} delivers a shock to deter animals or intruders. A railroad may be electrified when it converts from steam or diesel to electric power. Figuratively, electrified means thrilled or galvanized: {The crowd was electrified by her speech}. The word suggests sudden, intense energy—whether literal current or emotional charge.

To electrify is to charge with electricity or convert to electric power: {The railroad was electrified in the 1930s}. More commonly, electrify means to thrill or excite intensely: {Her performance electrified the audience}. The metaphor captures how strong emotion seems to jolt through a person like current through a wire.

Electrifying describes something that generates intense excitement or sudden energy, as if delivering an electric shock to the senses. An electrifying {performance} thrills an audience; electrifying {news} jolts people to attention. The word captures that quality of being powerfully stimulating: {The atmosphere in the stadium was electrifying}.

To electrocute is to kill or seriously injure by electric shock. The word blends "electric" and "execute," originally referring to death by electric chair, but now covers any fatal or severe electrical injury: {He was electrocuted while repairing the power line}. Loosely, people use it for any electric shock, even minor ones: {I electrocuted myself on the outlet}.

Electrocuted means killed or severely injured by electric shock. The word blends electric and executed, originally referring specifically to death by electric chair. Usage has loosened—people now say {I almost got electrocuted} to mean any significant shock, though purists insist the word requires death or near-death. {The worker was electrocuted when he touched a live wire.}

Electrocution is death or serious injury caused by electric shock. The word blends electric and execution, reflecting its origin in the electric chair. Usage has loosened—people now say they were {electrocuted} when they received a painful shock but survived, though purists insist electrocution requires death. {The faulty wiring nearly electrocuted him.}

An electron is a subatomic particle carrying a negative electric charge. Electrons orbit the nucleus of an atom and are fundamental to chemical bonding, electricity, and magnetism. In everyday contexts, electron appears in compounds: {electron microscope}, {electronics}, {free electron}. The flow of electrons through a conductor is electric current.

Electronic describes devices or systems that use circuits and components to control electrical current—transistors, microchips, semiconductors. An electronic {keyboard} differs from an electric {guitar} in complexity of circuitry. Electronic also describes communication or transactions conducted through such devices: electronic {mail}, electronic {payments}. The plural electronics refers both to the technology as a field and to consumer devices: {the electronics section of the store}.

Electronics is the branch of physics and engineering dealing with the flow of electrons through circuits—the technology behind computers, televisions, radios, and countless devices. The term also refers collectively to such devices: {the electronics aisle at the store}, {consumer electronics}. Electronic as an adjective describes anything operating on these principles: {electronic music}, {electronic funds transfer}.

Elegance is refined grace and tasteful simplicity—the quality of being pleasingly ingenious yet understated. An elegant solution to a problem achieves much with little: {The proof was elegant in its simplicity}. Elegant dress, manners, or surroundings suggest sophistication without excess: {She moved through the room with quiet elegance}. The word implies that beauty and effectiveness arise from restraint rather than elaboration.

Elegant describes something refined, graceful, and tastefully understated. An elegant {solution} achieves its goal with surprising simplicity. An elegant {dress} or elegant {room} shows sophistication without excess. The word suggests quality achieved through restraint rather than elaboration—nothing wasted, nothing lacking: {The proof was elegant in its brevity}.

An elegy is a mournful poem or song, typically one written to honor someone who has died. The form has ancient roots and traditionally features reflective, sorrowful meditation on loss, mortality, or the passage of time. While elegies most often commemorate the dead, the term extends to any literary work with a tone of grief or lamentation: {Gray's "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" remains a classic of the form}. The adjective elegiac describes anything expressing sorrow or nostalgia.

Element denotes one constituent of a thing composed of many, or an irreducible constituent, such as a chemical element. In its original use, element comprised only four things—earth, air, fire, and water. Science has now determined that these are not irreducible, and has transferred the meaning of element to things that are (such as silicon, lead, or krypton). More generally, element refers to something that can be isolated or abstracted from its context and identified: elements of a good play, the game has an element of luck.

Elemental means relating to the basic forces or components of something. The elemental {power of the storm} suggests nature's raw, fundamental energy. In chemistry, elemental refers to a substance in its pure, uncombined form: {elemental carbon}, {elemental iron}. The word often carries overtones of primal force—something stripped to its essence, unrefined and powerful: {an elemental struggle for survival}.

Elementary means basic, fundamental, or introductory—concerned with first principles rather than advanced concepts: {elementary arithmetic}, {elementary school}, {an elementary course in physics}. Something elementary is simple or rudimentary: {The mistake was elementary}. In chemistry, elementary refers to a single element: {elementary particles}, {elementary substances}.

Elements are the basic parts or components that make up something larger. Chemical elements are pure substances that cannot be broken down further—hydrogen, oxygen, carbon. The elements of a skill or subject are its fundamentals: {She's learning the elements of music theory}. The elements also refers to weather, especially harsh conditions: {exposed to the elements}. To be {in your element} is to be in circumstances where you thrive.

An elephant is a massive land mammal with thick gray skin, a long trunk, and large ears, native to Africa and Asia. Elephants are the largest living land animals. The phrase {elephant in the room} describes an obvious problem everyone ignores. A {white elephant} is a burdensome possession or an expensive gift of little use. To {have a memory like an elephant} is to remember everything.

Elephants is the plural of elephant, the largest living land animal—a massive mammal with a long trunk, tusks, and large ears. African and Asian elephants are the surviving species. The phrase {the elephant in the room} describes an obvious problem everyone avoids discussing. {Pink elephants} are hallucinations associated with drunkenness. {White elephants} are burdensome possessions or gifts.

Elevate means to raise something higher—physically or figuratively. A platform elevates speakers above the crowd. To elevate someone is to promote them: {She was elevated to partner}. Elevated language or style is formal and refined. An elevated heart rate is higher than normal. The word often suggests improvement or enhancement: {Good design elevates the ordinary}.

Elevated means raised above a normal level. An elevated {platform} sits higher than the ground; elevated {blood pressure} exceeds healthy ranges. The word often suggests improvement or refinement: elevated {discourse}, elevated {taste}. In American cities, {the elevated} or {the el} is a railway built on an overhead structure. Someone in an elevated {mood} feels unusually happy or excited.

Elevation is height above a reference point, usually sea level: {The city sits at an elevation of 5,000 feet}. It also means the act of raising something or someone to a higher position—physical or metaphorical: {his elevation to the Supreme Court}. In architecture, an elevation is a flat drawing showing one face of a building. An elevated mood or style has a lofty, dignified quality.

An elevator is a platform or compartment that moves vertically to transport people or goods between floors of a building. The British term is lift. Elevator also names various mechanical devices that raise things: a grain elevator stores and moves grain; a small flap on an airplane's tail controls pitch. To give someone an {elevator pitch} is to deliver a brief persuasive summary—short enough for an elevator ride.

Elevators are enclosed platforms or compartments that move vertically to transport people or goods between floors of a building. The term is American; British English prefers lift. An elevator can also be a hinged surface on an aircraft's tail that controls pitch. In agriculture, a grain elevator is a tall structure for storing and moving grain. Elevator shoes have thick soles to make the wearer appear taller.

Eleven is the number after ten, written 11. It's the first number that English doesn't construct from smaller parts—unlike thirteen (three + ten) or twenty-one. In sports, eleven often names a team's starting lineup, especially in soccer and cricket: {the starting eleven}. {Eleven o'clock} marks late morning or late night. The adjective eleventh indicates position in sequence: {the eleventh hour} means the last possible moment.

An elf is a small supernatural being from Germanic folklore, typically depicted with pointed ears and magical powers. In traditional tales, elves could be mischievous or malevolent; modern fantasy has largely reimagined them as noble, immortal beings skilled in archery and magic. Santa's elves are cheerful workshop helpers. {She dressed as an elf for the Renaissance faire.}

Eligible means qualified or entitled to be chosen. Someone eligible for a position meets the requirements: {All citizens over eighteen are eligible to vote}. An eligible bachelor is unmarried and considered a desirable match—available and worth pursuing. The word implies both meeting criteria and being available for selection.

Eliminate means to remove or get rid of something completely. You eliminate {errors} from a document, eliminate {candidates} from consideration, or eliminate {foods} from your diet. In sports, a team eliminated from a tournament can no longer advance. The euphemistic sense—to kill—appears in crime and espionage contexts: {The target was eliminated}.

Eliminated is the past tense of eliminate, meaning to remove, get rid of, or rule out. A suspect is eliminated from an investigation when evidence clears them. A team eliminated from a tournament can no longer advance. In clinical language, to eliminate is to expel waste from the body. {We've eliminated several possibilities.}

Elimination is the act of removing or getting rid of something. In competitions, elimination means being knocked out—unable to continue: {single-elimination tournament}, {process of elimination}. The word applies to bodily waste functions in medical or polite contexts: {bowel elimination}. To work through possibilities by elimination is to rule them out one by one until only the answer remains.

Elite refers to a select group regarded as superior—the best, most powerful, or most privileged within a larger population. The elite may be defined by wealth, talent, education, or social standing: {political elite}, {academic elite}, {elite athletes}. As an adjective, elite describes things associated with or reserved for such groups: {an elite private school}, {elite military units}. The word can carry either admiration or resentment, depending on whether excellence or exclusivity is emphasized.

Elites are the people at the top of a hierarchy—those with the most power, wealth, influence, or skill in a given domain. Political elites shape policy; cultural elites set taste; athletic elites dominate their sports. The word often carries suspicion: {The elites don't understand ordinary people}. Elite as an adjective means top-tier or exclusive: {elite universities}, {an elite fighting force}.

Elitism is the belief that society should be led by a select group of superior individuals, or the sense of entitlement that comes from belonging to such a group. The word is almost always pejorative—accusing someone of elitism suggests they look down on ordinary people or favor the privileged few: {The candidate was accused of coastal elitism}. Elitist works as both noun and adjective: {an elitist attitude}, {Silicon Valley elitists}.

Elitist describes someone who believes certain people deserve more power, influence, or resources based on superior ability, education, or status. The word is almost always pejorative, accusing someone of looking down on ordinary people: {His elitist attitude alienated voters}. As a noun, an elitist is a person who holds such views. The related noun elite refers to a select group at the top of a hierarchy—elitist suggests excessive devotion to that group or contempt for those outside it.

An elixir is a magical or medicinal potion, especially one believed to cure all ailments or grant immortality: {the elixir of life}. Medieval alchemists sought an elixir to turn base metals into gold. More broadly, any solution or remedy that seems to work wonders: {Exercise became her elixir}. In pharmacy, an elixir is a sweetened liquid used to deliver medication.

Elixirs is the plural of elixir, a magical or medicinal potion. In medieval alchemy, the elixir of life promised immortality. Modern use is often figurative or playful: {coffee is my morning elixir}. Pharmaceutical elixirs are sweetened liquid medicines: {cough elixirs}. The word suggests something with transformative or restorative powers.

Elk is a large deer native to North America, known for its impressive antlers on males and its bugling call during mating season. In British English, elk refers to what Americans call a moose. The animal is prized by hunters and figures prominently in the iconography of the American West. The Elks, formally the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks, is a fraternal organization whose lodges are found throughout the United States.

An elm is a large deciduous tree with serrated leaves and rough bark, common in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. Elms were once a defining feature of American streets and parks until Dutch elm disease devastated populations in the mid-20th century. The wood is valued for its strength and resistance to splitting.

To elope is to run away secretly, typically to get married without parental consent or public ceremony. The word suggests romantic urgency and often disapproval from family: {They eloped to Vegas over the weekend}. More broadly, elope can mean to slip away or abscond: {The couple eloped with the company funds}, though the marriage sense dominates modern usage.

Eloped is the past tense of elope, meaning to run away secretly to get married, typically without parental consent or an elaborate ceremony: {They eloped to Vegas last weekend}. The word often implies spontaneity or avoiding family disapproval. More broadly, to elope can mean to run off with a lover, married or not.

Elopement is the act of running away secretly, typically to get married without parental consent or public ceremony: {Their elopement shocked both families}. The word implies haste and secrecy, often romantic urgency. In healthcare settings, elopement refers to a patient—especially one with dementia—leaving a facility without authorization: {The nursing home installed alarms to prevent elopement}.

Eloping is running away secretly to get married, typically without parental consent or a formal wedding: {They eloped to Las Vegas}. The word once meant any secret escape, especially a wife leaving her husband for a lover, but now almost exclusively refers to impromptu marriages. By extension, eloping can mean slipping away from any expected situation: {We eloped from the party early}.

Eloquence is the power to speak or write in a way that moves, persuades, or delights. It combines fluency with force—not just smooth delivery but language that lands: {His eloquence swayed the jury}. The word implies a natural gift, though eloquence can be cultivated. Someone eloquent makes complex ideas clear and ordinary ideas memorable.

Else is an important function word that also carries the idea of other or alternative. As an adjective it is placed after a word beginning with some- or any-: Does anyone else want to go with us? I would really like to live somewhere else. The combinations anything else and nothing else are used talk about any or no additional thing: Is there anything else you need from the store? Or else introduces a necessary alternative if what comes before it does not work: Hurry up or else we’ll go without you.

Elsewhere means in or to another place: {The book you want isn't here—try looking elsewhere}. It suggests an unspecified alternative location: {If you're not happy with our service, take your business elsewhere}. The word often implies that something exists or is happening, just not in the current context: {Elsewhere in the building, a meeting was underway}.

Elusive describes something difficult to catch, find, or pin down. An elusive {criminal} evades capture. An elusive {answer} stays just out of reach. The word often suggests something that seems almost within grasp but slips away: {Sleep proved elusive that night}. Elusive memories, meanings, or qualities resist clear definition or recall.

Elves are mythical beings of folklore and fantasy, typically depicted as human-like but with pointed ears, magical powers, and exceptional longevity. In older traditions, elves ranged from mischievous household spirits to dangerous supernatural creatures. Modern fantasy, shaped by Tolkien, usually portrays them as tall, graceful, and wise. {Santa's elves} are the industrious toymakers of Christmas lore—a quite different image. Elf is the singular.

Email is electronic mail—messages sent and received through computer networks, primarily the internet. As a noun, it refers both to the system itself and to individual messages: {I'll send you an email} or {Check your email}. As a verb, it means to send such a message: {Email me when you get a chance}. Though the hyphenated e-mail was once standard, the solid form now dominates in everyday use.

Emancipation is the act of freeing someone from bondage, oppression, or legal restriction. The word is most associated with the abolition of slavery—Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation declared enslaved people in Confederate states to be free. More broadly, emancipation applies to liberation from any constraining authority: {the emancipation of women}, {emancipation from parental control}. In law, an emancipated minor gains adult rights before reaching the age of majority.

An embalmer is a person who preserves corpses for burial or display, typically by draining blood and replacing it with preservative fluids. Embalmers work in funeral homes, preparing bodies for viewing and slowing decomposition. The work requires technical skill and comfort with the dead: {The embalmer made her grandmother look peaceful}.

Embalming is the process of preserving a dead body from decay, typically by replacing blood with chemical solutions like formaldehyde. Funeral homes embalm corpses to allow viewing before burial: {The embalming took several hours}. The practice dates to ancient Egypt, where it was essential to mummification. As a participle, embalming also describes anything that preserves: {the embalming cold of the arctic}.

A misspelling of embarrassed—note the double r and double s. The word means feeling self-conscious, awkward, or ashamed, typically from social discomfort: {I was embarrassed when I tripped on stage}. The spelling trips people up because the double letters fall in unexpected places.

An embargo is an official ban on trade or commerce with a particular country, or a government order prohibiting ships from entering or leaving ports. More broadly, it means any prohibition or restriction: {The court placed an embargo on publishing the documents}. To embargo something is to impose such a ban: {The administration embargoed all Cuban imports}.

To embark is to board a ship, aircraft, or other vessel for a journey: {We embarked at dawn}. The word extends naturally to beginning any significant undertaking: {She embarked on a new career}, {They embarked on a journey of self-discovery}. The sense of setting out on something consequential—with its mix of anticipation and uncertainty—carries through both literal and figurative uses.

To embarrass is to make someone feel self-conscious, awkward, or ashamed, usually in front of others: {Don't embarrass me in front of my friends}. The feeling can range from mild discomfort to acute mortification. You can also embarrass yourself through your own actions. Extended uses describe situations that create difficulty or inconvenience: {The leak embarrassed the administration}. Financial embarrassment means being short of money.

Embarrassed describes the self-conscious discomfort of being exposed to others' judgment—whether from a mistake, awkward situation, or unwanted attention. The feeling ranges from mild sheepishness to acute shame: {I was embarrassed when I forgot her name}, {He felt embarrassed about asking for help}. Someone can also be embarrassed on another's behalf, cringing at their missteps.

Embarrassing describes something that causes self-consciousness, awkwardness, or shame—typically by exposing a flaw, mistake, or private matter to others. An embarrassing {moment} might involve tripping in public or forgetting someone's name. The word can also characterize situations that reflect poorly on someone: {The leaked emails were embarrassing for the company}. What counts as embarrassing varies by person and culture, though bodily functions, social blunders, and being caught in lies are near-universal triggers.

Embarrassment is the uncomfortable self-consciousness that comes from being exposed to others' judgment—whether from a social blunder, public mistake, or unwanted attention. {I could die of embarrassment.} An embarrassment can also be something that causes this feeling: {His drunk uncle was an embarrassment at the wedding}. An {embarrassment of riches} is an overabundance, so much of a good thing that it becomes awkward to manage.

Embassies is the plural of embassy—the official headquarters of an ambassador in a foreign country, or the diplomatic staff working there. Embassies handle relations between governments, issue visas, and assist citizens abroad. {The embassies were evacuated when fighting broke out.} By extension, any formal delegation sent to negotiate may be called an embassy.

An embassy is the official residence and offices of an ambassador in a foreign country, or the diplomatic mission itself: {The protesters gathered outside the American embassy}. By extension, embassy can mean the ambassador's staff collectively. To seek refuge at an embassy is to request diplomatic protection on what is technically foreign soil.

Embedded means fixed firmly within a surrounding mass or context. A splinter is embedded in skin; a journalist is embedded with military troops, living and traveling with them. In computing, embedded code or media sits within a larger document or system: {an embedded video in a webpage}, {an embedded chip in a device}. The word suggests something so integrated it can't easily be separated from its context.

Embellishment is decoration or ornamentation added to make something more attractive or interesting: {The dress featured embellishments along the neckline}. The word extends to stories and accounts—an embellishment is an added detail that enhances the narrative but may stretch the truth: {His version of events contained a few embellishments}. To embellish is to add such flourishes.

Embellishments are decorative additions that enhance or beautify something. A dress might have embellishments of lace or beading. In music, embellishments are ornamental notes added to a melody. The word often implies excess or falsification: {His story contained a few embellishments}. To embellish a tale is to add details that may not be strictly true.

An ember is a glowing piece of wood or coal in a dying fire. Embers retain heat long after flames have gone out, capable of reigniting fuel or causing burns. Figuratively, embers represent what remains of something once intense: {the embers of a former passion}, {stirring the embers of an old rivalry}. The plural embers often describes the final stage of a fire: {We sat watching the embers}.

Embers are the glowing remains of a fire after flames have died down—small pieces of wood or coal that stay hot and faintly luminous. You can {stir the embers} to rekindle a fire or {watch the embers fade}. Figuratively, embers suggest something nearly extinguished but not quite dead: {the embers of their romance}, {embers of hope}.

Embezzled describes money or property that has been stolen by someone entrusted with it. An accountant embezzles company funds; a treasurer embezzles from the organization. The word implies betrayal of trust rather than theft by an outsider: {He embezzled thousands before anyone noticed the discrepancies}.

Embezzlement is the theft of money or property by someone entrusted with it—an employee skimming from the register, an accountant diverting company funds, a trustee misappropriating assets. The crime requires a breach of trust: the embezzler had legitimate access before stealing. {She was convicted of embezzling three million dollars from the nonprofit.}

An embezzler is someone who steals money or property entrusted to their care, typically from an employer or organization. The crime involves betrayal of trust—a bookkeeper skimming funds, a treasurer diverting donations: {The embezzler had siphoned off millions before anyone noticed}.

Embezzling is the act of stealing money or property entrusted to your care, typically from an employer or organization. The crime involves breach of trust rather than breaking and entering—an accountant embezzling company funds, a treasurer embezzling from a charity: {She was caught embezzling from the nonprofit where she'd worked for years}.

An emblem is a symbol or design representing an idea, organization, or identity: {The eagle is the emblem of the United States}. Unlike a logo, which may be abstract, an emblem typically depicts something recognizable—an animal, object, or figure. Emblems appear on flags, shields, uniforms, and official documents. Figuratively, anything serving as a symbol qualifies: {She became an emblem of resistance}.

Embodiment is a physical form given to something abstract. A person can be the embodiment of a quality: {She was the embodiment of grace}. A document or system can be the embodiment of principles: {The Constitution is the embodiment of democratic ideals}. The word suggests that an abstraction has become concrete and visible—incarnated in a particular person, object, or form.

Embody means to give a body to something abstract or intangible, making it concrete or visible. A person can embody a quality like grace or courage by expressing it so fully that they seem to be its physical form: {She embodies everything I admire about the profession}. Ideas, principles, or values can be embodied in documents, institutions, or works of art: {The Constitution embodies the founders' vision of democracy}. To embody also means simply to include or contain: {The report embodies all our findings from the past year}.

To embrace is to hold someone in your arms, typically as a greeting or expression of affection: {They embraced at the airport}. The noun is the act itself: {a warm embrace}. Figuratively, to embrace something is to accept or adopt it willingly: {embrace change}, {embrace a new philosophy}. An embrace can also mean inclusion: {a theory that embraces multiple disciplines}.

Embroider is to decorate fabric with needlework, creating patterns or images by stitching thread into cloth. The craft ranges from simple monograms to elaborate tapestries. The figurative sense extends naturally: to embroider a story is to add decorative details that weren't originally there, enhancing it beyond plain truth. {She tends to embroider her childhood memories.} The noun embroidery covers both the craft and its products.

Embroidering is the act of decorating fabric with needle and thread, creating patterns or images through stitching. The figurative sense means adding invented details to a story or account: {He couldn't help embroidering the tale with each retelling}. Both senses share the idea of adding ornamental flourishes to something that exists.

Embroidery is decorative needlework—patterns or pictures stitched onto fabric with thread. The craft ranges from simple monograms on handkerchiefs to elaborate tapestries. Figuratively, embroidery means adding fanciful details to a story: {His account of the fishing trip included considerable embroidery}.

Embroiled means deeply involved in a conflict, dispute, or difficult situation. The word suggests being caught up in something messy and hard to escape: {The company became embroiled in a legal battle}. You don't choose to be embroiled—you find yourself that way, often through circumstances beyond your control.

An embryo is an organism in its earliest stage of development, before it has taken recognizable form. In humans, the term applies from fertilization through about eight weeks, after which it becomes a fetus. The word extends to anything in an undeveloped state: {The plan was still in embryo}. Embryonic means rudimentary or just beginning: {an embryonic democracy}.

An emcee is the host or master of ceremonies at an event—someone who introduces performers, makes announcements, and keeps things moving: {The emcee warmed up the crowd before the main act}. In hip-hop, emcee (also MC) specifically means a rapper. The spelling reflects the pronunciation of the initials M.C. As a verb, to emcee is to serve in this role.

Emerald is a precious green gemstone, a variety of beryl colored by trace amounts of chromium. The color itself—a vivid, slightly bluish green—is called emerald: {emerald waters}, {emerald eyes}. Ireland is the Emerald Isle for its lush green landscape. In printing, emerald was a size of type between minion and nonpareil.

Emeralds is the plural of emerald, a green precious gemstone prized since antiquity. The color emerald green takes its name from the stone. Figuratively, emeralds can describe anything of that distinctive deep green: {The emeralds of the Irish countryside stretched before us}.

To emerge means to appear as a new phenomenon, or to become obvious or prominent: Problems emerged when we tried to start the engine. When emerge is followed by an adjective it works as a linking verb to show a result or outcome: The Greeks emerged victorious from the battle. Today, the participle emerging is often used in economic contexts to characterize growing financial systems: The fund is invested entirely in Asian emerging markets.

Emergence is the act or process of coming into view, existence, or notice. A celebrity makes a public emergence after years of seclusion. A butterfly's emergence from its cocoon marks its transformation. In philosophy and science, emergence describes how complex properties arise from simpler components—consciousness emerging from neural activity, or traffic patterns from individual drivers. {The emergence of social media changed political discourse.}

Emergencies is the plural of emergency—urgent situations requiring immediate action. The word appears in contexts where multiple crises exist or might occur: {emergency room staff see all kinds of emergencies}, {the kit contains supplies for emergencies}. An emergency {fund} or emergency {plan} prepares for such situations generally.

An emergency is a serious, unexpected situation requiring immediate action. Medical emergencies threaten life or health. A {state of emergency} grants governments special powers during crises. Emergency serves as an adjective for things used in urgent situations: emergency {exit}, emergency {room}, emergency {fund}. {In case of emergency, break glass.}

Emigrants are people who leave their home country to settle elsewhere. The word emphasizes departure rather than arrival—the same person is an emigrant from one country and an immigrant to another. {The emigrants boarded ships bound for America.} {Many emigrants never saw their homeland again.}

An emissary is a person sent on a mission to represent or advance the interests of another—typically a government, organization, or leader. The role suggests diplomacy and negotiation: {The president dispatched an emissary to negotiate the ceasefire}. Unlike an ambassador with permanent posting, an emissary usually handles a specific task or message.

Emissions are substances released into the environment, especially gases discharged into the atmosphere. The word appears most often in environmental contexts: {carbon emissions}, {greenhouse gas emissions}, {vehicle emissions}. Emissions standards regulate what factories and cars can release. The singular emission refers to any act of sending something out—light, sound, radiation, or bodily fluids.

Emo is a style of rock music characterized by emotional, confessional lyrics and a melodic punk sound that emerged in the 1980s and peaked in mainstream popularity in the 2000s. The term extends to the associated subculture—dark clothing, side-swept hair, eyeliner, and an aesthetic embracing melancholy and sensitivity: {She went through an emo phase in high school}. Often used dismissively for anything perceived as overly emotional or dramatic: {Stop being so emo about it}.

An emoji is a small digital image used in electronic communication to convey emotion, tone, or meaning—a smiley face, a thumbs up, a heart. The term comes from Japanese for "picture character." Unlike emoticons made from punctuation :), emojis are standardized graphics built into keyboards and platforms. They range from facial expressions to animals, foods, flags, and abstract symbols: {She responded with three crying-laughing emojis}. Plural: emoji or emojis.

Emojis is the plural of emoji—the small pictographic characters used in digital communication to convey emotion, tone, or meaning: {She replied with a string of emojis}. Hearts, faces, and hand gestures are among the most common. Emojis help signal intent where text alone might seem flat or ambiguous: {Added some emojis so she'd know I was joking}.

An emoticon is a small picture made from keyboard characters to express emotion in text, such as :-) for a smile or :-( for sadness. The term blends "emotion" and "icon." Emoticons emerged in early internet communication when text lacked tone cues. They've been largely supplanted by emoji—actual images rather than character combinations—though the terms are often confused.

Emoticons are combinations of keyboard characters used to convey emotion or tone in text, typically read sideways: :-) for a smile, :-( for a frown, ;-) for a wink. The term blends *emotion* and *icon*. Emoticons emerged in early internet communication to clarify intent where tone of voice was absent. They've been largely supplanted by emoji—actual pictographic images—though the terms are often confused.

Emotion is a mental state arising in response to circumstances—joy, anger, fear, sadness, love, disgust. Emotions are distinguished from thoughts (which are cognitive) and sensations (which are physical), though all three intertwine. Someone {full of emotion} is visibly moved. An {emotional person} feels things strongly or expresses feelings readily. To {show emotion} is to let inner states become visible; to {hide emotion} is to suppress that display.

Emotional describes something relating to or arising from feelings rather than reason: {an emotional response}, {emotional support}. A person who is emotional experiences feelings intensely or expresses them readily—sometimes admirably ({She gave an emotional speech}), sometimes dismissively ({Don't get so emotional}). The word can suggest someone is being irrational, particularly when applied to women, where it often carries sexist undertones.

Emotions are feelings that arise in response to experiences, thoughts, or situations—joy, anger, fear, sadness, love, disgust. The word often distinguishes feeling from thinking: {Don't let your emotions cloud your judgment}. Someone {in touch with their emotions} acknowledges and understands their feelings. To {show emotion} is to display feeling outwardly, especially in contexts where restraint is expected.

An empanada is a pastry turnover with a savory or sweet filling, folded and sealed before baking or frying. Fillings vary by region—beef, chicken, cheese, vegetables, or fruit. The dish is ubiquitous across Latin America and Spain, with each country claiming distinctive versions: {We grabbed empanadas from the food truck}.

Empanadas are pastries made by folding dough around a filling and baking or frying. The filling varies by region—beef, chicken, cheese, vegetables, or fruit. Common throughout Latin America and Spain, each country has distinctive styles: Argentine empanadas differ from Chilean, which differ from Colombian. {We ordered a dozen empanadas for the party.}

An empath is someone who feels others' emotions intensely, as if absorbing them. The term gained currency in science fiction and New Age spirituality, describing people who claim heightened sensitivity to others' mental states: {As an empath, crowded rooms exhaust me}. Often used loosely for anyone highly attuned to others' feelings.

Empathetic describes someone who feels or understands what another person is experiencing—who can put themselves in someone else's position: {She's an empathetic listener}. The word overlaps almost entirely with empathic, though empathetic is more common in everyday speech. {He gave me an empathetic nod when I described my frustration}.

To empathize is to understand and share another person's feelings—to imaginatively enter their emotional experience. Unlike sympathy, which observes suffering from outside, empathy attempts to feel it from within: {I could empathize with her frustration after going through something similar}. The ability to empathize is considered fundamental to human connection and moral behavior.

Empathy is a noun describing the ability to imagine another person’s feelings or attitudes, based on your experience of your own feelings. It is thought to be a key component of being human and people who are unable to feel empathy are usually regarded as pathological or developmentally disabled. The most common preposition after empathy is for, but with and toward are also seen: Her empathy for her subjects makes her photographs compelling. The nearest synonym of empathy is compassion.

An emperor is the male ruler of an empire—a sovereign who reigns over multiple territories or peoples. The title historically ranked above king, suggesting broader dominion: {the Roman emperor}, {the Emperor of Japan}. Emperor can describe anyone exercising supreme power in a domain: {He was emperor of his own little kingdom}. The emperor penguin is the largest penguin species.

Emperors is the plural of emperor, a male sovereign who rules an empire—a domain larger or more powerful than a kingdom. Historically, emperors held supreme authority over vast territories: {the emperors of Rome}, {Chinese emperors}. The emperor penguin, the largest penguin species, takes its name from this sense of supremacy.

Emphasis is special stress or importance given to something. In speech, emphasis falls on particular words or syllables to highlight meaning: {She put emphasis on the word "never"}. In writing, emphasis comes through italics, repetition, or structure. More broadly, emphasis indicates where attention or priority lies: {The company's emphasis on customer service}, {with emphasis on practical skills}.

An empire is most strictly the domain under the rule of an emperor. In common usage, an empire is any extensive territory under single rule that is not geographically continuous, such as the one-time British Empire. When empire is capitalized, it is typically preceded or contextualized by a specifying adjective (the Roman Empire). Figuratively, an empire is any vast entity that exerts great influence: Amazon has a global business empire. Empire is also a women’s fashion style featuring a waistline under the bust.

Empires is the plural of empire—a group of nations or territories under a single authority, typically an emperor or empress. The word evokes vast scale and central control: {the Roman Empire}, {the British Empire}. Empire extends to dominant commercial entities: {a real estate empire}, {a media empire}. {Empires rise and fall.}

To employ is to put something to use or to hire someone for work. You employ {strategies}, {methods}, or {tools} to accomplish tasks. An employer employs workers; those workers are employees in that employer's employ. {The factory employs three hundred people.} {She employed every trick she knew to win him over.}

An employee is a person who works for another person or organization in exchange for wages or salary. The term implies a formal arrangement: employees typically have set hours, receive benefits, and work under supervision, distinguishing them from contractors or freelancers. {The company has over five hundred employees.} {She's been an employee here for ten years.}

An employer is a person or organization that hires workers and pays them for their labor. The term emphasizes the relationship from the hiring side: {Her employer offers good benefits}. Employer appears frequently in legal and HR contexts—employer contributions, employer liability, employer of record. The relationship implies ongoing work arrangements rather than one-time transactions.

Employment is the state of having paid work, or the work itself: {She found employment at a law firm}. It also refers to the act of using something: {the employment of new teaching methods}. The term often appears in economic and policy contexts: {employment rate}, {full employment}, {employment opportunities}.

Empower means to give someone authority or power to do something: {The new law empowers regulators to impose fines}. More commonly, it describes building confidence or capability in people who lack it: {The program empowers young women to pursue careers in science}. This second sense became prominent in self-help and social justice contexts during the late twentieth century, sometimes attracting criticism for overuse.

Empowered describes having been given power, authority, or confidence. Someone empowered to act has official authorization: {The board empowered her to negotiate on their behalf}. More often, empowered suggests a psychological state—feeling capable and in control: {The workshop left participants feeling empowered}. This softer sense dominates contemporary usage, appearing in self-help, marketing, and corporate contexts until the word risks meaning little more than "good about oneself."

Empowerment is the process of gaining power, authority, or confidence—or of granting these to others. The word appears frequently in discussions of social justice, workplace dynamics, and self-help: {women's empowerment}, {employee empowerment}, {personal empowerment}. Critics sometimes dismiss the term as corporate or political jargon, but it remains widely used to describe giving people control over their own circumstances.

An empress is a female sovereign ruling an empire, or the wife or widow of an emperor. The title historically carried immense power and prestige: {Catherine the Great was empress of Russia}. Figuratively, empress describes a woman who dominates her sphere: {She was the empress of Broadway during its golden age}.

Emptiness is the state of containing nothing or being devoid of content. A room's emptiness strikes you when the furniture is gone. The word extends to emotional hollowness—the emptiness after a loss, the emptiness of a meaningless routine. {She felt a profound emptiness after her children left home.} Emptiness can also describe futility: {the emptiness of his promises}.

Empty describes something with nothing inside. An empty {container}, {room}, or {stomach} lacks contents. Empty {streets} have no people. Empty {words} or {promises} lack substance or sincerity. To empty is to remove contents: {She emptied her pockets}. Figuratively, to {feel empty} is to experience emotional hollowness or absence of meaning.

Emptyhanded means without bringing or taking anything. You arrive emptyhanded at a party when you forget to bring a gift. You leave emptyhanded when a search or negotiation yields nothing: {The police searched the house but came away emptyhanded}. Also spelled empty-handed.

An emu is a large flightless bird native to Australia, second only to the ostrich in size. Emus have shaggy gray-brown plumage, long necks, and powerful legs built for running. They're farmed for meat, oil, and leather: {Emu oil is marketed as a skin treatment}. (Uppercase EMU is the European monetary union.)

Emus are large flightless birds native to Australia, second only to ostriches in size. They have shaggy gray-brown feathers, long necks, and powerful legs built for running. The plural follows standard English rules: {We spotted several emus in the outback}. Singular: emu.

Enable means to make something possible or give someone the ability to do something: {The scholarship enabled her to attend college}. It often appears in technical contexts—enabling a feature turns it on. In psychology, to enable someone is to facilitate their harmful behavior, especially addiction, by removing consequences or providing resources that allow the behavior to continue.

An enabler is someone who makes something possible, often with the connotation of facilitating harmful behavior. In psychology and addiction contexts, an enabler shields someone from the consequences of destructive actions—covering for an alcoholic spouse, lending money to a gambler: {His mother was his chief enabler, bailing him out every time}. The term can also be neutral, describing anyone who helps others accomplish goals: {a great enabler of young talent}.

Enamel is a hard, glossy coating. The outermost layer of teeth is enamel—the hardest substance in the human body. Enamel is also a glassy coating fused onto metal, pottery, or glass by heat, used decoratively or for protection: {enamel jewelry}, {enamel cookware}. Enamel paint dries to a similar hard, shiny finish. To enamel is to coat with enamel.

Enamored means filled with love or deep admiration. You can be enamored of a person, idea, or thing: {She was enamored of the old house from the moment she saw it}. The word suggests strong attraction that may cloud judgment—being enamored doesn't guarantee the feeling is warranted. Often used with "of" or "with": {He's not enamored with the idea of moving}.

An encampment is a place where a group of people have set up tents or temporary shelters, whether for military purposes, protest, or because they lack permanent housing. Military encampments are temporary bases established during operations or training. The term increasingly describes gatherings of unhoused people in urban areas or protest camps like those on college campuses. {The encampment grew to over a hundred tents within a week.}

Enchant originally meant to cast a spell on someone, from the Latin for singing or chanting magical words. The literal sense persists in fantasy contexts: {The witch enchanted the prince}. More commonly now, enchant means to delight or captivate thoroughly: {The children were enchanted by the puppet show}. Someone enchanting possesses irresistible charm.

Enchanted describes something magical or under a spell: an enchanted {forest}, an enchanted {castle}. More commonly, it means delighted or captivated: {I was enchanted by the old town's narrow streets}. The formal phrase {enchanted to meet you} expresses pleasure at an introduction, though it sounds old-fashioned or affected in casual settings.

An enchanter is someone who casts spells or charms, typically in fantasy and folklore contexts: {The enchanter transformed the prince into a frog}. The word carries connotations of mysterious power and seduction rather than malevolence—enchanters beguile and captivate. Figuratively, anyone who charms or fascinates might be called an enchanter: {He was an enchanter on the piano}.

Enchanting describes something that captivates or delights as if by magic: {an enchanting smile}, {an enchanting melody}. The word suggests charm that holds attention and stirs wonder. A place, person, or performance can be enchanting when it produces a spell-like effect on the observer. The related verb enchant means to cast such a spell, literally or figuratively.

Enchantment is the state of being under a magical spell, or the act of casting one. Fairy tales feature enchantments that transform princes into frogs or put princesses to sleep. Extended to ordinary life, enchantment means captivated delight: {The garden held a certain enchantment at dusk}. To fall under someone's enchantment is to be utterly charmed by them.

Enchantments are magic spells or the states they produce—being under a spell, bewitched, charmed. The word extends to anything that captivates completely: {the enchantments of Paris}, {the enchantment of first love}. Something possessing enchantment holds you spellbound, whether through actual magic or metaphorical allure. In gaming, enchantments are magical properties applied to weapons or items.

An enchantress is a woman who casts spells or practices magic—a sorceress or witch. The word extends to any woman with an almost magical power to captivate: {She was an enchantress who held the whole room spellbound}. The suggestion is of irresistible allure or charm rather than literal sorcery.

An enchilada is a Mexican dish consisting of a tortilla rolled around a filling—typically meat, cheese, or beans—and covered with chili sauce. The phrase {the whole enchilada} means everything, the entire matter: {They wanted the whole enchilada, not just a partial settlement}. A {big enchilada} is an important person.

Enchiladas are a Mexican dish of tortillas rolled around a filling—typically meat, cheese, or beans—and covered with chili sauce. The dish is baked until the sauce soaks into the tortillas. {We ordered chicken enchiladas with green sauce.} The {whole enchilada} means the entirety of something: {They wanted the whole enchilada—house, furniture, everything}.

An enclave is a territory entirely surrounded by another territory—a pocket of one country within another's borders, or a distinct area within a larger region. The word extends to any group or space set apart from its surroundings: {an ethnic enclave in the city}, {an enclave of wealth in a poor neighborhood}. The defining feature is isolation or distinctiveness within a surrounding whole.

An enclosure is a space that has been fenced or walled off: {The animals were kept in a large enclosure}. The word also refers to something included with a letter or package: {Please find the enclosure with your policy documents}. To enclose is to surround, contain, or include something within.

The interjection Encore! is a request for continuation of a performance. When it succeeds, the audience gets an encore. By extension, encore is used to characterize actions that are viewed as a repetition or continuation of what has gone before: Fans are hoping for an encore of the previous score when the team plays next week. As a verb, encore usually means perform an encore: The band encored with new material.

Encores are additional performances given after the scheduled program ends, demanded by enthusiastic applause. The word comes from French for "again." At concerts, the encore is often anticipated—artists leave the stage knowing they'll return for one or two more songs. {The crowd cheered until the band came back for an encore.} Figuratively, an encore is any repeat performance: {Her second novel was an encore to her debut success.}

Encounter means to meet or come upon, often unexpectedly or in the course of doing something else. You might encounter an old friend at the grocery store or encounter difficulties while renovating your house. The noun encounter denotes such a meeting or experience: {a chance encounter with a celebrity}, {a close encounter with a bear}. In gaming and fantasy contexts, an encounter is a specific confrontation or battle that players must face.

Encourage means to give someone confidence, hope, or support to do something: {Her teacher encouraged her to apply to medical school}. It can also mean to foster or promote: {Warm weather encourages plant growth}. The word suggests helping something along rather than forcing it—a gentle push rather than a shove.

Encouragement is support or confidence given to someone, boosting their resolve or spirits: {A few words of encouragement helped her get through the interview}. It can also mean something that promotes or fosters an activity: {Tax breaks served as encouragement for small businesses}. To give encouragement is to hearten; to offer it is often simply to approve.

Encouraging means giving hope, confidence, or support. An encouraging {word} lifts spirits; encouraging {news} suggests things may turn out well. To be encouraging is to foster someone's efforts: {Her teacher was encouraging about her writing}. Encouraging results or signs point toward a positive outcome: {The early data is encouraging}.

Encryption is the process of encoding information so only authorized parties can read it. Data is transformed using an algorithm and key, rendering it unintelligible to anyone who intercepts it without the corresponding decryption key. Encryption protects everything from text messages to financial transactions: {The app uses end-to-end encryption}. {Make sure the website has encryption before entering your credit card}.

An encyclopedia is a comprehensive reference work containing articles on a wide range of subjects or covering one field in depth. Traditional encyclopedias arranged entries alphabetically across multiple volumes; digital versions now dominate. The word suggests authoritative, systematically organized knowledge: {She's a walking encyclopedia of baseball statistics}. {I looked it up in the encyclopedia}.

Encyclopedias are reference works containing articles on a wide range of subjects or on many aspects of a single field, typically arranged alphabetically. Before the internet, a set of encyclopedias—often sold door-to-door—was a household's primary research resource: {We looked it up in the encyclopedia}. Wikipedia has largely displaced print encyclopedias for general reference.

End is a very frequent noun and verb with several meanings corresponding to ideas of stop, last, and boundary: I was dead tired at the end of the day. Tie one end of the rope to a tree. She ended the service with a prayer. If you put or make an end to something, you cause it to stop: Peacekeeping troops were unable to put an end to the rioting. When you reach the end of something in time or space, you come to the point where there is no more.

Endangered describes something at serious risk of extinction or disappearance. The term applies most often to species whose populations have declined to critical levels: {The giant panda is no longer classified as endangered}. Conservation laws protect endangered animals and plants. The meaning extends to anything threatened with loss: {endangered languages}, {an endangered way of life}.

Endearing describes qualities that inspire affection or fondness in others. An endearing {smile}, an endearing {habit}, an endearing {awkwardness}—something that makes you like a person more, not less. The word often applies to minor flaws or quirks that charm rather than annoy: {His tendency to mispronounce words was oddly endearing}.

An endearment is a word or phrase expressing affection: {honey}, {sweetheart}, {my love}. The word also refers to the feeling itself or acts that inspire it: {small endearments that sustained their marriage}. Terms of endearment range from the universal to the private—couples often develop their own.

Endeavor is a formal word that is roughly synonymous with attempt and try. Like those two words, endeavor can act as a noun or a verb: Didn’t you endeavor to contact her again? We will take better equipment on our next endeavor to reach the summit. In referring to a project, endeavor can mean the equivalent of undertaking: They have a lot of venture capital supporting their latest endeavor. The British spelling of endeavor is endeavour.

Endeavour is the British spelling of endeavor—to try earnestly or make a serious effort toward a goal: {We shall endeavour to finish by Friday}. As a noun, it refers to a purposeful undertaking or field of activity: {scientific endeavour}, {a worthy endeavour}. The word carries a slightly formal or literary tone, suggesting sustained effort rather than casual attempt.

Endgame is the final stage of a chess game, when few pieces remain and victory depends on precise maneuvering. The word extends to any concluding phase of a process, especially one involving strategy: {What's your endgame here?} {The negotiations entered their endgame}. It implies that earlier moves have shaped what's now possible.

An ending is the final part of something—a story, a relationship, a journey. It marks termination or conclusion: {The movie had a satisfying ending}, {the ending of an era}. In grammar, an ending is a suffix attached to a word: the -ing ending, the -ed ending. The ending of a word can signal tense, number, or part of speech.

Endings are the concluding portions of stories, events, or periods of time: {The movie's ending surprised everyone}. In grammar, an ending is a suffix that changes a word's form—the -ed that marks past tense, the -s that marks plural. Nerve endings are the terminal points where sensory nerves detect stimuli. Happy endings resolve satisfyingly; unhappy ones don't.

Endless means having no end—continuing indefinitely or seemingly forever. An endless {road} stretches beyond sight. Endless {possibilities} are unlimited. Often the word conveys weariness or frustration: {endless meetings}, {endless paperwork}, {the endless wait}. Something can be literally endless (a loop) or just feel that way.

Endoreduplication is a cellular process in which DNA replicates without subsequent cell division, resulting in cells with multiple copies of the genome. This occurs naturally in certain tissues—plant cells, insect salivary glands, and mammalian liver cells use endoreduplication to increase cell size or metabolic capacity without proliferation. {Endoreduplication produces the giant chromosomes visible in fruit fly larvae.}

Endorphins are chemicals produced by the body that reduce pain and create feelings of pleasure or euphoria. The brain releases them during exercise, excitement, pain, or orgasm. The term comes from "endogenous morphine"—morphine made within. {Runner's high comes from endorphins.} {The massage triggered a rush of endorphins.}

Endorphins are chemicals produced naturally in the brain that reduce pain and create feelings of pleasure or euphoria. The body releases them during exercise, laughter, sex, and other activities—hence the term {runner's high}. They function similarly to opioid drugs but are manufactured internally: {My endorphins kicked in around mile three}.

To endorse is to give public approval or support: {The union endorsed the Democratic candidate}. Originally, to endorse meant to sign the back of a check or document, transferring rights or confirming receipt—a meaning that persists in banking. The extended sense of backing or recommending now dominates: {She endorsed the new policy}, {celebrity endorsements}. An endorsed product carries someone's public approval, often for payment.

Endorsement is approval or support, especially public backing of a person, product, or idea. A politician seeks endorsements from unions; a celebrity gives an endorsement to a brand. In business, endorsement also means signing the back of a check to transfer or deposit it: {She wrote her account number below her endorsement}. An insurance endorsement is an amendment to a policy.

Endorsements are statements of approval or support. A political endorsement is a public declaration backing a candidate: {The senator's endorsement boosted the campaign}. Product endorsements involve celebrities promoting brands for pay. On documents like checks, an endorsement is a signature authorizing transfer. In insurance, an endorsement modifies a policy's terms or coverage.

An endowment is something given to provide ongoing support—typically a fund whose principal remains intact while its interest or returns fund an institution: {The university's endowment exceeds two billion dollars}. More broadly, endowment refers to natural gifts or qualities someone possesses: {Her musical endowment was evident from childhood}. In insurance, an endowment policy pays out after a set term or upon death. Informally, endowment is a euphemism for the size of a man's penis: {He's not lacking in the endowment department}.

Ends are the points where something terminates—the physical extremities of an object or the conclusion of an event: {the end of the road}, {the end of the movie}. Ends also means purposes or goals: {a means to an end}, {to what end?} To make ends meet is to earn enough to cover expenses. In football, ends are players positioned at the edge of the offensive or defensive line.

The endtimes are the final days of the world, particularly in religious traditions that prophesy apocalyptic events preceding divine judgment. Christian usage draws heavily on Revelation: {Many believe we're living in the endtimes}. The term appears in both sincere eschatological discourse and ironic commentary on current events: {This news cycle feels very endtimes}. Also spelled end times or end-times.

Endurance is the capacity to withstand hardship, strain, or prolonged effort without giving way. Physical endurance lets athletes complete marathons; mental endurance gets people through grief or tedious work. {Her endurance impressed everyone on the team.} Endurance events test how long participants can last rather than how fast they can go. The word implies not just surviving difficulty but maintaining function throughout it.

Endure means to bear something difficult or painful without giving way: {She endured years of chronic pain}. It also means to last or continue existing: {Their friendship endured for decades}. The two senses connect—what endures has withstood time or hardship. An enduring legacy persists; an enduring marriage survives its trials.

Enduring means lasting through time or hardship. An enduring {friendship} survives years and difficulties. An enduring {legacy} remains influential long after its origin. The word suggests not just duration but resilience—something that endures has withstood challenges: {Her enduring optimism surprised everyone who knew what she'd been through}.

The endzone is the area at each end of an American football field where touchdowns are scored. A player must carry or catch the ball in the opponent's endzone to score. The term extends to similar scoring areas in other sports like rugby and ultimate frisbee. Usually spelled as two words: {end zone}.

Enemies is the plural of enemy—those who oppose, threaten, or wish harm. The word covers personal antagonists {She made enemies at work}, military adversaries {The enemies surrounded the city}, and abstract forces {Stress and poor sleep are enemies of good health}. Unlike rivals, who compete for the same goal, enemies actively work against each other's interests.

An enemy is someone who opposes, threatens, or seeks to harm you. The term applies to personal adversaries, military opponents, or hostile nations: {They were childhood friends who became bitter enemies}. Enemy extends to abstract threats: {Sugar is the enemy of good health}. As an adjective, enemy describes hostile forces: {enemy territory}, {enemy fire}. The enemy can refer collectively to opposing forces in conflict.

Energetic describes someone or something full of energy, vigor, or enthusiasm. An energetic {person} tackles tasks with vitality; an energetic {performance} crackles with intensity.
