The word applies to activities requiring sustained effort: {an energetic workout}, {an energetic campaign}. In physics, energetic refers to high energy levels: {energetic particles}, {energetic radiation}.

Energize means to give energy or vitality to something. Coffee energizes the tired, a speech energizes a crowd, and solar panels energize electrical systems. The word works for both physical and figurative invigoration: {The good news energized the team}. In technical contexts, to energize a circuit or device is to supply it with electrical power.

Energy is the capacity for doing work or producing change—the fundamental currency of physics. In everyday use, energy describes vitality and vigor: {I don't have the energy to argue}. A person with energy is lively and active. Energy also refers to power sources: {renewable energy}, {nuclear energy}. To {put energy into} something is to apply sustained effort.

To enforce is to compel compliance with a rule, law, or obligation—to make sure it's actually followed rather than merely stated. Police enforce laws, referees enforce rules, parents enforce bedtimes. The word implies authority backed by consequences: {The contract is unenforceable without penalties}. Enforce can also mean to impose by force: {enforce one's will on others}.

Enforcement is the act of compelling compliance with a law, rule, or obligation. Police handle law enforcement; agencies pursue enforcement of regulations. The word implies authority and consequences: {Enforcement of the new policy begins Monday}. Without enforcement, rules have no teeth. An enforcer is someone who ensures compliance, sometimes through intimidation.

An enforcer is someone who compels compliance with rules or demands, often through intimidation or force. The term appears in sports for players who protect teammates through physical aggression, and in organized crime for those who collect debts or punish disloyalty: {The mob sent their enforcer to deliver a message}. More broadly, any person or mechanism that ensures rules are followed: {The IRS acts as the chief enforcer of tax law}.

Enforcers are people who ensure rules or laws are followed, often through intimidation or force. In organized crime, an enforcer threatens or commits violence on behalf of a boss: {The mob sent their enforcer to collect the debt}. In hockey, an enforcer is a player whose role is to fight and physically intimidate opponents. More broadly, anyone who compels compliance—a strict teacher, a regulatory agent—might be called an enforcer.

Engage means to occupy attention or involve actively. You engage someone in conversation, engage with difficult material, or engage the services of a lawyer. Gears engage when their teeth interlock; a clutch engages when it connects. To be engaged is to be busy, already committed, or pledged to marry: {They got engaged last summer}. In military use, to engage the enemy is to enter combat.

Engaged describes being occupied or committed. Someone engaged in conversation is absorbed in it. An engaged employee is invested in their work. The word often signals a formal commitment to marry: {They got engaged last spring}. A busy signal means a phone line is engaged. Gears engage when they mesh and transfer power.

Engagement centers on the idea of involvement or commitment. To have an engagement is to have an appointment or obligation that demands your presence: {I have a prior engagement}. A couple's engagement is their promise to marry, usually formalized with a ring. In military contexts, an engagement is an armed encounter or battle. The broader sense describes active participation or connection: {student engagement in the classroom}, {social media engagement}. To engage is to participate, attract attention, or interlock, as gears do.

Engaging describes something that captures and holds attention—a quality of being interesting, charming, or absorbing. An engaging {speaker} draws you in; an engaging {smile} invites connection. The word suggests active involvement rather than passive observation: {The documentary was engaging from start to finish}. To engage is to occupy attention or involve oneself, and engaging is its natural adjective.

An engine converts one kind of energy into another, like the engine in a car that converts fossil fuel to motion. Until the late 20th century, engines were mostly thought of as heavy metal things with moving parts. Thanks to search engines, that idea is changing. In even more figurative use, engine can refer to a person or group who supply the energy or force to make something happen: She was the engine behind the suffragist movement in the Northeast.

An engineer designs, builds, or maintains structures, machines, or systems—from bridges to software. The word covers a vast range of specializations: civil, mechanical, electrical, chemical, software. An engineer also operates engines or technical equipment: a railroad engineer drives trains, a sound engineer manages audio. To engineer something is to skillfully arrange or bring about: {She engineered his downfall}.

Engineered describes something deliberately designed or constructed, typically with technical skill: {an engineered solution}, {genetically engineered crops}. The word often implies careful planning or manipulation—sometimes with negative connotations suggesting artificiality or contrivance: {The whole controversy felt engineered to distract from the real issues}. {A beautifully engineered bridge.}

Engineering is the application of scientific and mathematical principles to design, build, and maintain structures, machines, systems, and processes. Civil engineering deals with infrastructure; mechanical with machines; electrical with circuits and power; software with computer systems. The verb engineer means to design or construct, or more broadly to bring something about through skillful planning: {She engineered a meeting between the two rivals}. An engineer is a practitioner of the field, or someone who operates an engine—particularly a locomotive.

Engineers design, build, and maintain complex systems—bridges, software, engines, electrical grids. The word covers many specialties: civil, mechanical, electrical, chemical, software. To engineer something is to design or bring it about through skillful planning: {She engineered the merger}. The verb often implies cleverness or manipulation: {He engineered his rival's downfall}.

Engines are machines that convert energy into motion. The term originally meant any mechanical device (as in {siege engines} or {engines of war}), but now usually refers to motors that power vehicles or equipment: {car engine}, {jet engine}, {search engine}. A steam engine converts heat to mechanical force. A fire engine is the truck, not just its motor. Figuratively, something can be an engine of change or growth—a driving force.

English in lowercase is rare in edited prose but appears in certain contexts. In billiards, english refers to spin imparted to a ball to control its path after striking: {He put english on the cue ball}. The term likely derives from a technique associated with English players. To put english on something can also mean to add spin or a particular slant to a story or presentation. (Capitalized English is the language or nationality.)

To engrave is to cut or carve a design into a hard surface—metal, glass, stone, wood. The technique produces decorative items, printing plates, and personalized objects: {a watch engraved with his initials}, {an engraved invitation}. Figuratively, something engraved on your memory or heart is permanently fixed there: {That moment is engraved in my mind}.

Engraved describes something with designs or letters cut into its surface: {an engraved silver bracelet}, {engraved wedding invitations}. The image of cutting into material extends to memory and emotion—something engraved {on your heart} or {in your mind} is permanently fixed there, impossible to forget.

Engraving is the art or process of cutting designs into a hard surface—metal, wood, glass, or stone—using sharp tools or acid. The term also refers to the product: a print made from an engraved plate, or the incised design itself. {The museum displayed Renaissance engravings}. {The engraving on the watch read "To my beloved."}

Engravings are images or designs cut into a hard surface, or prints made from such surfaces. The term covers both the carved original and the reproductions pulled from it: {The museum displayed Renaissance engravings}. An engraving may also be decorative work incised into metal objects like jewelry or trophies: {The watch had a personal engraving on the back}.

Engrossed means completely absorbed in something, with attention so fully captured that other things fade from awareness: {She was engrossed in her book and didn't hear me come in}. The word suggests deep, willing concentration rather than mere distraction. You become engrossed in novels, conversations, or work that genuinely holds your interest.

Engulfed describes being completely surrounded or swallowed up by something overwhelming. Flames engulf a building; floodwaters engulf a town. The word works for abstract forces too: {She was engulfed by grief}. {The scandal engulfed the administration}. Something engulfed has been overtaken entirely, often suddenly.

Enhancement is the act of improving or intensifying something, or the improvement itself. Software receives security enhancements. Photos undergo digital enhancement to sharpen details or adjust colors. {The new lighting was a real enhancement to the room}. Performance-enhancing drugs boost athletic ability. Enhancement suggests augmentation of existing qualities rather than fundamental transformation.

An enigma is something puzzling or mysterious—a riddle that resists easy explanation. The word often describes people whose motives or character remain opaque: {He was an enigma to everyone who knew him}. It extends to any baffling situation or phenomenon: {The disappearance remains an enigma}. Something enigmatic invites interpretation but withholds clear answers.

Enjoy means to take pleasure in something: {I really enjoyed the concert}, {Enjoy your meal}. It can also mean to have the benefit of: {She enjoys good health}, {They enjoy certain privileges}. The imperative {enjoy!} has become a standalone wish, especially from servers delivering food. To {enjoy yourself} is to have a good time.

Enjoyment is the pleasure or satisfaction derived from something: {She took great enjoyment from her garden}. The word emphasizes the experience itself rather than the source—you find enjoyment in activities, not just from them. Legal usage refers to the use and benefit of property or rights: {quiet enjoyment of the premises}.

To enlighten is to give someone knowledge or understanding they lacked: {The documentary enlightened me about the history of redlining}. The word suggests illumination—bringing light to darkness, clarity to confusion. In spiritual contexts, enlightenment is a state of profound wisdom or awakening: {The Buddha became enlightened under the Bodhi tree}. To enlighten can also mean simply to inform: {Would you care to enlighten us about your plans?}

Enlightened describes someone who has gained wisdom, understanding, or freedom from ignorance. An enlightened {ruler} governs with reason and compassion. The term often implies progressive thinking: {enlightened views on education}. In spiritual contexts, particularly Buddhism, enlightenment is a state of awakening or liberation from suffering—one who has achieved this is enlightened. The word can also be used ironically for those who consider themselves superior: {our enlightened critics}.

Enlightening describes something that provides insight, clarity, or understanding—illuminating what was previously unclear or unknown. The word implies genuine learning or revelation: {The documentary was enlightening}. An enlightening conversation leaves you knowing more than before. The term carries positive connotations, suggesting valuable knowledge gained rather than mere information received.

Enlightenment is the state of gaining deep understanding or insight, often after confusion or ignorance: {Reading that book was a moment of enlightenment for me}. The word suggests clarity breaking through—a light turning on in the mind. In Buddhism, enlightenment is the ultimate spiritual awakening, liberation from the cycle of suffering and rebirth. More casually, enlightenment is simply being informed: {I'd appreciate some enlightenment on what happened at the meeting}. (Capitalized Enlightenment is the 18th-century intellectual movement.)

To enlist is to join the armed forces voluntarily, as opposed to being drafted: {He enlisted in the Marines right after high school}. Extended uses apply the same idea of signing up for a cause or effort. To enlist someone's help is to recruit their support: {She enlisted her neighbors to search for the missing dog}. An enlisted soldier holds a rank below officer.

Enlisted describes military personnel who are not officers—the ranks that form the bulk of armed forces. Someone enlisted holds a position entered through enlistment rather than commission: {enlisted men}, {enlisted ranks}. The past tense of enlist, it also means joined or recruited: {She enlisted in the Navy}, {He enlisted his friends to help move}.

Ennui is a listless weariness born of boredom or dissatisfaction—not mere boredom, but a deeper spiritual fatigue when nothing seems worth doing. The word retains its French flavor and tends toward the literary or dramatic: {Summer ennui had set in by July}. It suggests privileged dissatisfaction, the malaise of those with too much leisure and too little purpose.

Enormous means extremely large in size, extent, or degree. The word carries more weight than big or large but less than colossal or gargantuan: {an enormous house}, {enormous pressure}, {an enormous mistake}. Enormous often suggests something impressively or problematically oversized rather than merely big.

Enough can operate as an adjective, adverb, or pronoun to convey the idea of sufficiency: Make sure there’s enough food for everyone. Do you need more time or is that enough? Enough is also one of a handful of frequent words in English in which the letters gh are pronounced as /f/.

Enraged means filled with rage—intensely, visibly angry. The word suggests anger that has built to a peak: {The enraged crowd stormed the gates}. Unlike merely angry or upset, enraged implies a loss of composure, someone pushed past the point of restraint.

To enrich something is to make it richer—more valuable, more nutritious, more interesting. You can enrich soil with compost, enrich a curriculum with new courses, or enrich someone's life with friendship. Enriched flour has nutrients added back after processing. Enriched uranium has a higher concentration of fissile isotopes, used in nuclear reactors or weapons.

Enrichment is the process of making something richer or more valuable. Soil enrichment adds nutrients. Cultural enrichment expands knowledge or experience: {The museum offers enrichment programs for children}. In nuclear contexts, uranium enrichment increases the concentration of fissile isotopes. Animal enrichment provides stimulation to captive creatures: {The zookeepers designed enrichment activities for the primates}.

To enroll is to sign up officially—for a class, a program, or an institution: {She enrolled in the nursing program}, {The school enrolled 500 new students this fall}. Enrollment implies formal registration and often a commitment. In British English, spelled enrol.

Enrollment is the act of registering or being registered for something—a school, a program, an insurance plan. It also refers to the total number of people registered: {Enrollment at the university increased by twelve percent}. The enrollment period is when registration is open. British spelling: enrolment.

An ensemble is a group of things considered as a whole, especially performers who work together: a jazz ensemble, a theater ensemble. In fashion, an ensemble is a coordinated outfit—pieces selected to complement each other: {She wore a stunning ensemble to the gala}. The word emphasizes unity and harmony among parts, whether musicians, actors, or garments.

To enslave is to make someone a slave—to strip them of freedom and hold them in bondage. The word applies literally to the historical practice of slavery and figuratively to anything that dominates or controls: {enslaved by addiction}, {enslaved to debt}. The figurative use can seem tone-deaf given slavery's brutal reality.

Enslaved describes people held in bondage—forced to work without freedom or compensation. The term has largely replaced "slave" as a noun in historical writing, emphasizing that slavery was a condition imposed on people rather than an identity: {enslaved Africans}, {enslaved workers}. This framing recognizes humanity first, captivity second.

Enslavement is the act of making someone a slave—reducing a person to property that can be bought, sold, and forced to labor. The word covers both the historical institution and individual acts of subjugation: {the enslavement of captured peoples}, {her enslavement to an abusive employer}. Figuratively, enslavement describes being controlled by something: {enslavement to debt}, {enslavement to addiction}.

Enslaving is the act of making someone a slave—depriving them of freedom and forcing them into servitude. The word extends to anything that dominates or controls completely: {enslaving debt}, {an enslaving addiction}. Work that consumes all your time and energy can feel enslaving: {The job was enslaving—I had no life outside it}.

Entangled describes things twisted together in a way that's difficult to separate. Hair becomes entangled, fishing line becomes entangled, and so do people in complicated relationships or situations: {She got entangled with the wrong crowd}. In physics, entangled particles remain connected across distance, their states linked regardless of separation. To be entangled in something is to be caught up in it, often unwillingly: {entangled in a legal dispute}.

Entanglement is the state of being tangled up in something—caught, ensnared, or complicated by involvement. A physical entanglement might be fishing line wrapped around a propeller. More often the word describes messy involvements: {a romantic entanglement}, {legal entanglements that delayed the project}. In physics, quantum entanglement describes particles whose states remain correlated regardless of distance—a phenomenon Einstein called "spooky action at a distance."

Enter is to go or come into a place: {She entered the room without knocking}. The word extends to beginning participation: enter a {competition}, enter a {profession}, enter into {negotiations}. To enter data is to input it into a system. The enter key on a keyboard submits commands or creates line breaks. {It never entered my mind} means something never occurred to you.

Enterocoely is the formation of a body cavity (coelom) from pouches that bud off the embryonic gut. This developmental process characterizes deuterostomes—animals like sea urchins, starfish, and vertebrates—distinguishing them from protostomes, where the body cavity forms differently. {In enterocoely, the mesoderm originates as outpocketings of the archenteron.}

Enterprise is a project or undertaking, especially one requiring effort or boldness: {a risky enterprise}, {a commercial enterprise}. The word also names the quality itself—initiative and resourcefulness: {She showed real enterprise in building her business}. An enterprise is often a business venture or company: {a state-owned enterprise}, {free enterprise}. The word carries connotations of ambition and scale.

Entertain covers a range of activities that share the idea of holding attention or holding in mind. To entertain guests is to receive and accommodate them, keeping them engaged and comfortable. To entertain an audience is to provide them with amusement or diversion: {The comedian entertained the crowd for two hours}. More abstractly, to entertain an idea or proposal is to consider it, holding it in your mind without necessarily accepting it: {I won't even entertain that suggestion}.

An entertainer is someone who performs for an audience—singers, comedians, magicians, dancers, actors. The term is broad enough to cover anyone whose job is to amuse or engage others professionally. {She was a natural entertainer, commanding the room effortlessly.} The word often implies versatility or showmanship rather than mastery of a single art form.

Entertaining describes something that holds attention and provides enjoyment or amusement. An entertaining {movie} or entertaining {speaker} keeps you engaged rather than bored. The word also functions as a noun for the activity of hosting guests: {She does a lot of entertaining during the holidays}. What counts as entertaining varies wildly by person—one viewer's entertaining documentary is another's tedious lecture.

Entertainment is anything that holds attention in an enjoyable way—a movie, a concert, a party trick. The word covers both the activity and the industry that produces it: {the entertainment business}, {That's entertainment!} To entertain guests is to host them; entertainment in this sense means hospitality, including food and drink provided.

Enthralled means captivated or spellbound, completely absorbed by something fascinating. The word suggests being held in place by wonder or interest: {The children sat enthralled by the magician's tricks}. Someone enthralled by a book or performance can't look away. The older sense—literally enslaved—survives mainly in fantasy literature.

Enthusiasm is eager interest or excitement about something: {Her enthusiasm for the project was contagious}, {He spoke with great enthusiasm about his travels}. The word implies energy and wholehearted engagement rather than passive approval. Someone who lacks enthusiasm is indifferent or going through the motions. An enthusiast is a person with strong interest in a particular subject: {a car enthusiast}, {a wine enthusiast}.

An enthusiast is someone with intense interest or passion for a particular subject or activity: {a car enthusiast}, {wine enthusiasts gathered for the tasting}. The word implies deep engagement beyond casual interest—enthusiasts collect, study, discuss, and advocate for their chosen pursuit. It's often used attributively: {enthusiast forums}, {enthusiast-grade equipment}.

Enthusiastic describes someone showing eager interest or intense enjoyment. An enthusiastic {supporter} backs a cause wholeheartedly. An enthusiastic {response} signals genuine excitement. The word suggests energy and positivity rather than mere approval—you can be supportive without being enthusiastic, but enthusiasm implies active engagement: {She wasn't just willing to help; she was enthusiastic about it}.

To entice is to attract or lure someone toward something, usually by making it seem appealing or desirable: {The smell of fresh bread enticed customers into the bakery}. The word often implies temptation—drawing someone toward pleasure, opportunity, or sometimes trouble. You entice with promises, rewards, or charm: {They enticed him away from his old job with a bigger salary}.

Enticing means tempting or alluring, drawing someone toward something desirable: {The smell of fresh bread was enticing}. What entices appeals to appetite or interest, promising pleasure or reward. An enticing {offer} is hard to refuse. An enticing {glimpse} makes you want to see more.

Entitled means having a right or claim to something: {She's entitled to half the estate}. A book or article entitled something has that as its title: {a memoir entitled "My Life in Paris"}. The word has developed a strongly negative sense describing someone who believes they deserve special treatment without earning it: {entitled customers demanding refunds}, {an entitled attitude}. This pejorative use now dominates casual speech.

Entitlement is a right to something—benefits, privileges, or treatment. Government entitlements are programs like Social Security or Medicare that qualifying citizens receive by law. The word often carries negative connotations: someone with {a sense of entitlement} expects special treatment without earning it. {The entitlement of that generation is astounding.} The adjective entitled works the same way: an entitled person believes they deserve more than others.

Entitlements are benefits or rights one is owed, especially government programs like Social Security or Medicare that citizens qualify for automatically: {Entitlement spending dominates the federal budget}. The word often carries negative connotations of undeserved expectation: {Kids these days have such a sense of entitlement}. In computing, entitlements are permissions granted to software.

Entombed means placed in a tomb or buried, often with connotations of permanence or finality: {The pharaohs were entombed with their treasures}. Figuratively, it describes being trapped or sealed within something: {The miners remained entombed for days before rescue}. The word suggests enclosure that is complete and difficult to escape.

An entourage is a group of attendants or associates who accompany an important person: {The celebrity arrived with her entourage of stylists, assistants, and bodyguards}. The word carries connotations of status and sometimes excess—having an entourage signals that someone is important enough to require a supporting cast.

Entrails are the internal organs of an animal, especially when removed during butchering or sacrifice. The word typically refers to intestines and other abdominal organs: {The hunter cleaned the deer and left the entrails for scavengers}. Figuratively, entrails can mean the innermost parts of anything: {the entrails of the ship}, {the entrails of the bureaucracy}.

Entrance has two distinct meanings depending on pronunciation. With stress on the first syllable, an entrance is a way in—a door, gate, or opening that allows access: {the entrance to the building}, {the main entrance}. It also means the act of entering: {She made a grand entrance}. With stress on the second syllable, to entrance is to fill with wonder or delight, to captivate completely: {The magician entranced the audience}. Someone entranced is spellbound, as if in a trance.

Entranced means captivated or spellbound, as if under a magical influence. Someone entranced by a performance is so absorbed they forget their surroundings: {She stood entranced before the painting}. The word suggests being held in a kind of pleasant paralysis, unable or unwilling to look away.

Entrances serves two words. The noun entrance (stress on the first syllable) is a way in or the act of entering: {The building has two entrances}; {She made a dramatic entrance}. The verb entrance (stress on the second syllable) means to fill with wonder or delight: {The magician entranced the children}. The plural entrances belongs to the noun; the verb form appears in {The music entrances anyone who hears it}.

Entrapment is the act of luring someone into a compromising situation, especially when law enforcement induces a person to commit a crime they wouldn't otherwise have committed. It serves as a legal defense: {The defendant claimed entrapment, arguing the undercover officer pressured him into the sale}. More broadly, entrapment describes any situation where someone is tricked or manipulated into a trap.

An entree is a dish served as the main course of a meal in American usage: {The entrees include steak, salmon, and a vegetarian option}. In formal dining and much of the world outside the United States, an entree is a course served before the main dish—closer to an appetizer. The spelling entrée, with the accent, is also common.

An entrepreneur is someone who takes a financial risk and launches a new business. In market economies, entrepreneur usually has positive connotations. Someone who simply owns or runs a business is not usually called an entrepreneur, unless they also started the business.

Entrepreneurs are people who start and run their own businesses, typically taking on financial risk in pursuit of profit. The term implies initiative and innovation—entrepreneurs don't just manage existing operations but create new ventures: {Tech entrepreneurs flocked to Silicon Valley}. The word carries connotations of ambition and self-reliance, though it's sometimes used loosely for anyone self-employed.

Entropy is a measure of disorder or randomness in a system. In thermodynamics, it quantifies the energy unavailable for useful work—systems tend toward higher entropy over time, which is why heat flows from hot to cold and not the reverse. In information theory, entropy measures uncertainty or unpredictability in data. Figuratively, entropy suggests inevitable decline into chaos or disorganization: {The project descended into entropy once the manager quit}.

Entry is the act of going in or the place where you go in: {The entry to the building was blocked}. It extends to items entered somewhere—an entry in a ledger, a dictionary entry, an entry in a competition. Entry also names the right or ability to enter: {She was denied entry to the country}. In law, unlawful entry is entering property without permission.

An envelope is a flat paper container for a letter or document, typically with a flap that folds over and seals. The word extends to any wrapper or covering: the {envelope of gas surrounding a star}. To {push the envelope} is to test limits or boundaries—originally aviation slang for exceeding a plane's performance parameters.

Envelopes are flat paper containers for letters or documents, with a flap that folds over and seals. The word extends to any enclosing layer: {the envelope of atmosphere surrounding Earth}. To {push the envelope} is to test limits—from aviation, where the flight envelope defines a plane's safe operating range. The verb envelope (no s) means to surround completely: {Fog enveloped the city}.

Envious describes wanting what someone else has—their possessions, qualities, or advantages. {She was envious of her sister's natural talent.} The feeling ranges from mild longing to bitter resentment. Envious often implies awareness that the desire is somewhat shameful, distinguishing it from the more neutral admiring or the harsher covetous.

Environment is a multipurpose word, but its meaning always relates to surroundings or conditions. Without qualification, environment often refers to the complex factors that make life possible on earth, including living things themselves. A specific environment means the surroundings and factors that have an influence on a person or place: The environment in my office gets increasingly stressful toward the end of the week.

Environmental relates to the surroundings or conditions in which people, animals, or plants live. It often concerns the natural world and human impact on it: {environmental protection}, {environmental damage}, {an environmental activist}. The word also applies to any setting or context: {environmental factors in child development}. An {environmental impact assessment} evaluates how a project might affect its surroundings.

Environmentalism is advocacy for protecting the natural world from pollution, resource depletion, and human destruction. The term covers a spectrum from mainstream conservation efforts to radical activism. An environmentalist might support recycling programs, oppose offshore drilling, or chain themselves to trees. {Her environmentalism began with childhood hikes and grew into a career in climate policy.}

An environmentalist is someone who advocates for protecting the natural world from pollution, habitat destruction, and climate change. The term can describe casual supporters of conservation or dedicated activists: {Environmentalists protested the pipeline}. It sometimes carries political connotations, used admiringly by allies or dismissively by opponents: {Those environmentalists want to shut down the whole industry}.

An envoy is a messenger or representative sent on a mission, especially a diplomatic one. The term typically refers to someone dispatched by a government to conduct negotiations or deliver communications: {The president sent a special envoy to broker peace talks}. An envoy ranks below an ambassador but carries similar authority for specific assignments.

Envy is resentful longing for what someone else has—their possessions, qualities, or good fortune. Unlike jealousy, which fears losing what you have, envy wants what belongs to another: {I envy her ability to speak five languages}. The feeling can be mild admiration or bitter covetousness. As a verb, to envy is to feel this way: {Don't envy the rich; they have their own troubles}. One of the seven deadly sins in Christian tradition.

An eon is an immensely long period of time. In geology, it's the largest division of Earth's history, spanning hundreds of millions of years. In everyday use, eon is hyperbolic: {I haven't seen you in eons}. The word suggests time so vast it becomes almost abstract. Also spelled aeon, especially in British English.

Eons is a vast stretch of time, typically spanning millions or billions of years. In geology, an eon is the largest division of Earth's history. More loosely, eons describes any period that feels immeasurably long: {I haven't seen her in eons}, {It took eons for the food to arrive}. Also spelled aeons.

Genuine epics, that is, long poems about legendary heroes, such as The Iliad and The Odyssey, are not common. Things characterized as epic are a dime a dozen and include any enjoyable or out of the ordinary phenomenon or experience: That sunset was epic! Something of epic proportions is impressively large or grand. Novels of great length with a historical setting are frequently called epics, especially by their publishers.

The epicenter is the point on Earth's surface directly above where an earthquake originates: {The epicenter was located twelve miles offshore}. By extension, epicenter means the focal point or center of any activity or phenomenon: {Silicon Valley remains the epicenter of tech innovation}. The figurative use sometimes draws criticism when center would suffice, but it emphasizes intensity or impact.

Epicentre is the point on the earth's surface directly above the origin of an earthquake. The seismic waves radiate outward from this location, making it the area of greatest intensity. Figuratively, epicentre describes the central point of any activity or phenomenon: {Paris was the epicentre of the art world}, {The tech company found itself at the epicentre of the scandal}. Also spelled epicenter.

Epics are long narrative works centered on heroic deeds and grand events—the *Iliad*, *Beowulf*, *Paradise Lost*. The term extends to any ambitious, sweeping story: an epic film, an epic novel. Informally, epic describes anything impressively large or memorable: {That party was epic}. {We're planning an epic road trip across the country}.

An epidemic is a widespread occurrence of disease in a community or region during a particular period, affecting many people at once. When diseases spread across multiple countries or continents, they become pandemics rather than epidemics. The word extends beyond medicine to describe any rapid spread or sudden increase: {an epidemic of violence}, {the opioid epidemic}. As an adjective, epidemic describes something spreading rapidly and extensively: {Fear had reached epidemic proportions}.

Epidemics are outbreaks of disease that spread rapidly through a population, affecting many people at once: {The flu epidemic swept through the school}. The term extends to any widespread occurrence of something undesirable: {an epidemic of gun violence}, {an epidemic of misinformation}. As an adjective, epidemic describes such rapid spread: {Violence had reached epidemic proportions}.

Epilepsy is a neurological condition characterized by recurring seizures—episodes of abnormal electrical activity in the brain. Seizures range from brief lapses in awareness to full-body convulsions. The condition is chronic but often manageable with medication. Someone with epilepsy is epileptic, though many prefer "person with epilepsy."

An epilogue is a concluding section that comes after the main action of a story ends. In novels and films, it often shows what happened to characters years later: {The epilogue revealed they'd stayed married for fifty years}. In plays, an actor may deliver an epilogue directly to the audience, commenting on the story's meaning. More broadly, any concluding event or period can be called an epilogue: {The treaty was an epilogue to decades of conflict}.

A sudden realization is often called an epiphany when it is sparked by an event or when it is especially helpful or important. The most common epiphanies are personal, religious, or spiritual; that which is realized is of interest only to the person himself: After years in therapy, he experienced an epiphany about his motivations. Epiphany, when capitalized, is a day in the Christian calendar relating to the birth of Jesus.

An episode is a distinct event or period within a larger series. Television shows are divided into episodes—individual installments of a continuing narrative. In life, an episode is a notable incident or stretch of time: {a brief episode of happiness}, {an embarrassing episode from my youth}. Medical episodes are occurrences of illness or symptoms: {a psychotic episode}, {an episode of chest pain}. The word suggests something bounded—with a beginning and end—set against a longer backdrop.

Episodes are individual installments of a serialized work—distinct segments of a television series, podcast, or other ongoing narrative: {I've only watched the first three episodes}. More broadly, an episode is any distinct event or period within a larger experience: {a brief episode of unemployment}, {an episode of chest pain}. The word suggests bounded incidents within a continuing story.

An epitaph is an inscription on a tomb or gravestone commemorating the person buried there. By extension, it can be any brief statement honoring the dead, or a fitting final summation of someone's life or work: {His last failed venture was a fitting epitaph for his career}. The related word epithet is sometimes confused with epitaph.

The epitome of something is the perfect example or embodiment of it: {She was the epitome of grace}. The word implies that the person or thing fully represents a quality or type. Less commonly, epitome refers to a summary or condensed version of a longer work—a meaning now mostly found in academic contexts.

An epoch is a distinct period of time, especially one marked by notable events or characteristics: {the epoch of industrialization}, {the Victorian epoch}. In geology and astronomy, epoch has precise technical meanings for divisions of time. The word suggests a significant era rather than just any stretch of time—epochs are memorable, defining periods that shape what follows.

Equal describes things that match in quantity, degree, or status. Two halves are equal portions. {All men are created equal} asserts equivalent moral standing. To equal something is to match it: {Nothing equals a home-cooked meal}. An equal is a peer: {She treats her employees as equals}. Equal also means capable of meeting a challenge: {Are you equal to the task?}

Equality is the condition of being equal—having the same status, rights, opportunities, or value as others. In social and political contexts, equality typically refers to the principle that all people deserve the same treatment regardless of characteristics like race, gender, or wealth: {The movement fought for equality under the law.} Mathematical equality means two expressions have the same value. The word often appears in debates about whether formal equality (same rules for everyone) achieves genuine fairness.

An equalizer is something that levels a playing field or neutralizes an advantage. A gun is sometimes called {the great equalizer}—it lets a smaller person match a larger one. In audio, an equalizer adjusts frequency levels to balance sound: {She boosted the bass on the equalizer}. In sports, an equalizer is a goal or score that ties the game.

Equals functions as verb and noun around the idea of sameness or equivalence. Two plus two equals four. To equal something is to match it: {Nothing equals the thrill of a live performance}. As a noun, an equal is someone of the same rank or ability: {She treats everyone as equals}. The phrase {first among equals} describes nominal leadership within a group of peers.

An equation is a mathematical statement that two expressions are equal, connected by an equals sign: {2 + 2 = 4}. Solving an equation means finding values that make it true. Outside mathematics, equation describes a complex situation where multiple factors must balance: {the political equation}, {factoring climate change into the equation}. To say something is {part of the equation} acknowledges it as one element among several that matter.

Equations are mathematical statements asserting that two expressions are equal, connected by an equals sign: {The equation x + 2 = 5 has the solution x = 3}. Beyond math, equation can mean any complex situation with multiple factors to balance: {the political equation}, {factoring childcare into the equation}. To equate things is to treat them as equivalent.

The equator is an imaginary line circling Earth at its widest point, equidistant from the North and South Poles. It divides the planet into Northern and Southern Hemispheres and marks zero degrees latitude. Countries {on the equator} experience roughly equal day and night year-round. The term extends to similar lines on other celestial bodies or any central dividing line: {the celestial equator}.

Equilibrium is a state of balance between opposing forces or influences. In physics, a body is in equilibrium when forces acting on it cancel out, producing no net change. In chemistry, equilibrium occurs when a reaction proceeds equally in both directions. The word extends to mental or emotional steadiness: {She recovered her equilibrium after the shock}. Economic equilibrium describes markets where supply meets demand. {The ecosystem remained in delicate equilibrium until the invasive species arrived.}

An equinox is either of two moments each year when the sun crosses the celestial equator, making day and night approximately equal in length worldwide. The vernal equinox occurs around March 20, marking spring in the Northern Hemisphere; the autumnal equinox falls around September 22, marking fall. {The equinox signals the changing of seasons.}

To equip is to supply with what's needed for a particular purpose—tools, gear, knowledge, or skills. You equip a soldier with weapons, a kitchen with appliances, a student with critical thinking. {The expedition was fully equipped for arctic conditions}. To be {well-equipped} for something is to have adequate resources or preparation. Equipment is the noun.

Equipment is the set of tools, gear, or supplies needed for a particular purpose: {camping equipment}, {medical equipment}, {gym equipment}. The word is uncountable—you don't have "an equipment" or "equipments," but rather a piece of equipment. Equipment can also refer to mental or emotional resources: {He lacks the emotional equipment to handle criticism}.

Equity is fairness or justice in how people are treated. In finance, equity is ownership value—what remains after debts are subtracted: {home equity}, {shareholder equity}. Equity in a company means ownership shares, distinct from debt. In recent usage, equity often appears alongside diversity and inclusion, emphasizing fair outcomes rather than merely equal treatment: {The policy aims for equity, not just equality}.

An era is a distinct period of time marked by particular characteristics, events, or developments. Eras are defined by what makes them different from what came before: {the Victorian era}, {the digital era}, {the end of an era}. In geology, an era is a major division of time containing multiple periods. The word often signals historical or cultural turning points: {We're entering a new era in medicine}.

Eradication is complete elimination or destruction—wiping something out entirely. The word applies most often to diseases, pests, or social problems: {the eradication of smallpox}, {efforts toward poverty eradication}. Unlike control or reduction, eradication implies total removal with no trace remaining.

Eras are distinct periods of time marked by particular characteristics, events, or figures. History divides into eras: the Victorian era, the Cold War era, the digital era. The word works at any scale—geological eras span millions of years, while someone might speak of {the Jordan era} in basketball or {the end of an era} when a favorite restaurant closes.

Erase means to remove something, typically marks from a surface. You erase pencil with a rubber eraser, chalk from a blackboard, files from a hard drive. The word extends to removing anything as if by rubbing out: {erase the memory}, {erase all doubt}. To erase someone from history is to eliminate their record or legacy entirely.

Erased means rubbed out or removed. Pencil marks are erased with an eraser; digital files are erased with a keystroke. The word extends to anything eliminated or made to disappear: {The scandal erased years of goodwill}. To feel erased is to feel ignored or rendered invisible, as though your presence or identity doesn't register.

An eraser is a piece of rubber or similar material used to remove pencil marks from paper. In British English, the same object is called a rubber. Erasers also appear on digital devices as tools that remove pixels or strokes: {Use the eraser to clean up the edges of your drawing}.

Erasers is the plural of eraser—a tool for removing marks, typically pencil marks from paper. The most familiar is the rubber or vinyl block found at the end of pencils or sold separately. Erasers also remove chalk from blackboards and dry-erase marker from whiteboards. {I keep a pack of erasers in my desk drawer.}

Erasure is the act of erasing or the state of being erased—the removal of marks, records, or traces. You might correct an erasure on a form or notice erasures in a ledger. The word extends to figurative removal: the erasure of someone's {contributions from history}, the erasure of {cultural identity}. In critical theory, erasure describes the systematic omission or marginalization of groups from discourse or representation.

Erect means upright or standing straight up. An erect {posture} is tall and rigid. A structure that has been erected has been built or raised into position: {They erected a monument in the town square}. Erect also describes body parts that have stiffened and risen—most often the penis during arousal, but also nipples or ears: {The dog's ears were erect}.

An erection is the state of being erect—stiff, upright, or raised. Most commonly, the word refers to the engorgement of the penis with blood, causing it to become rigid: {He woke up with an erection}. The word also applies to the act of constructing something: {the erection of a monument}, {the erection of trade barriers}. A structure itself may be called an erection, though this use sounds dated.

Ermine is a stoat in its white winter coat, or the fur from such animals. The white fur with black tail tips became associated with royalty and high office—judges' robes and monarchs' capes traditionally feature ermine trim. By extension, ermine can refer to the office or dignity itself: {the ermine of a peer}. The animal is also called a short-tailed weasel.

Erode means to wear away gradually through natural forces—water erodes rock, wind erodes soil. The word extends to any slow deterioration: {Inflation erodes purchasing power}, {Trust between them had eroded over the years}. What erodes doesn't collapse suddenly but diminishes bit by bit until significantly reduced or gone.

Eroded describes something that has been gradually worn away or diminished. Water erodes rock; wind erodes soil. The past participle works as an adjective for the result: {eroded cliffs}, {eroded coastline}. Figuratively, trust, support, or rights can be eroded—weakened slowly over time: {Public confidence in the institution has eroded}.

Eroding is the present participle of erode, describing the gradual wearing away of something. Physically, wind and water erode rock and soil: {The coastline is eroding at an alarming rate}. Figuratively, things erode when they diminish slowly over time: {Public trust in institutions is eroding}, {eroding profit margins}. The word emphasizes process rather than result—something actively being worn down.

Erosion is the gradual wearing away of material by natural forces—wind, water, ice, or gravity. Rivers erode canyons, waves erode coastlines, glaciers erode valleys. The word extends to any slow deterioration: {the erosion of civil liberties}, {erosion of trust}, {erosion of purchasing power}. Soil erosion from poor farming practices remains a global concern.

Erotic describes what arouses sexual desire or relates to sexual love. Erotic {literature}, erotic {art}, erotic {dreams}. The word carries more refinement than sexual or sexy—it suggests aestheticized or elevated sensuality rather than crude arousal. {The film's erotic tension built slowly}. Erotica refers to sexually stimulating creative works, distinguished from pornography by artistic intent.

Erotica is literature, art, or other media depicting sexual desire and activity, intended to arouse. Unlike pornography, erotica suggests artistic merit or emotional depth beyond mere titillation: {She writes erotica exploring female desire}. The distinction is subjective—one person's erotica is another's porn.

Eroticism is sexual desire or the quality of arousing it. The term applies to art, literature, and imagery that depicts or evokes sensuality: {The film's eroticism made censors nervous}. Unlike pornography, eroticism often implies aesthetic intent or subtlety—suggestion rather than explicitness. The word can also describe a general atmosphere or quality: {an air of eroticism}.

An errand is a short trip to accomplish a specific task, usually routine: picking up dry cleaning, mailing a package, buying groceries. {I have to run a few errands this afternoon.} The word implies going somewhere and returning, often on behalf of someone else or a household. A {fool's errand} is a pointless or hopeless task.

Errands are short trips to accomplish specific tasks, usually routine ones like picking up groceries, dropping off dry cleaning, or mailing a package. The word implies minor obligations that take you out of the house: {I have to run some errands this afternoon}. Errands are distinguished from more significant outings by their mundane, practical nature.

Erratic describes movement or behavior that is irregular, unpredictable, or inconsistent: {erratic driving}, {erratic mood swings}, {The stock has been erratic all week}. The word implies deviation from a steady or expected pattern—not merely unusual, but varying without apparent logic. In geology, an erratic is a boulder transported by glacial ice and deposited far from its origin.

Error is a mistake—a deviation from what is correct, accurate, or intended. An error in {judgment} is a bad decision. An error in {calculation} produces a wrong result. In baseball, an error is a fielder's misplay that allows a batter or runner to advance. In computing, error messages indicate something has gone wrong. {Trial and error} is learning by making mistakes and correcting them. To {err} is the verb form.

Erupt means to burst forth suddenly and violently. Volcanoes erupt, sending lava and ash into the air. The word extends to any sudden outbreak: violence erupts, applause erupts, a crowd erupts in cheers. Skin erupts in a rash. Teeth erupt when they break through the gums. {Fighting erupted in the streets}. {She erupted in anger when she heard the news}.

An eruption is a sudden, violent release—typically of lava and ash from a volcano, but also of emotion, conflict, or physical symptoms. Crowds erupt in anger, violence erupts in a region, rashes erupt on skin. The word emphasizes the abruptness and force of the outbreak: {The eruption sent ash clouds miles into the atmosphere}. {An eruption of applause followed the finale}.

Erusin is the Jewish betrothal ceremony, the first stage of traditional marriage. Unlike modern engagement, erusin creates a legally binding state—the couple is considered married for purposes of Jewish law, though they don't yet live together. The second stage, nissuin, completes the marriage. Today both ceremonies typically occur together under the wedding canopy.

Esca is a destructive fungal disease of grapevines, causing leaf discoloration, wood decay, and sometimes sudden vine death. The disease has plagued vineyards since ancient times and remains a significant problem for wine producers: {Several vines in the old block showed classic esca symptoms}. Also called black measles for the dark spotting it produces on grape berries.

Escalate means to increase in intensity, scope, or severity. A disagreement escalates into a fight. Costs escalate beyond projections. {The conflict escalated when both sides brought in reinforcements.} The word often implies a progression through stages—each step raising the stakes. To escalate something can also mean to refer it to a higher authority: {I'd like to escalate this complaint to your supervisor.}

Escalation is an increase in intensity, scope, or severity—typically of conflict, tension, or costs. What begins as a minor disagreement may undergo escalation into something serious: {The border skirmish threatened escalation into full-scale war}. The term implies a step-by-step progression upward, each move prompting a larger response. De-escalation is its opposite.

An escalator is a moving staircase—a mechanized set of steps that carries people between floors in buildings. Escalators loop continuously, with steps flattening at top and bottom for easy boarding. The word began as a trademark but became generic. To escalate is to increase or intensify, often gradually: {The argument escalated into a shouting match}.

Escalators are moving staircases—continuously circulating steps that carry people between floors in buildings. They're standard in shopping malls, airports, and subway stations. The singular escalator also works as a general term for anything that increases or intensifies: {an escalator clause} in a contract automatically raises prices or wages under certain conditions.

An escapade is a reckless adventure or wild prank—something exciting that flirts with trouble or breaks from routine: {youthful escapades}, {a drunken escapade that landed him in jail}. The word often carries a tone of amused indulgence, as if the misbehavior were forgivable or even charming in retrospect.

Escapades are daring, reckless, or unconventional adventures, often with a hint of mischief or rule-breaking. The word suggests excitement and perhaps a touch of irresponsibility—the kind of exploits that make good stories later. {Their college escapades became legendary among younger students.} Escapades can range from harmless pranks to genuinely risky behavior, but the word typically carries a tone of affectionate indulgence rather than serious condemnation. A romantic escapade usually implies an affair or fling.

Escape, noun and verb, is about getting away from an undesirable person, place, or thing – sometimes in order to avoid hardship or danger. If a prisoner escapes, he gets free of detention or prison. This might enable him to escape punishment. Something that escapes detection goes unnoticed. An escape is an instance of escaping. An escape clause is a feature of a contract that allows for avoiding an obligation. In computers, escape is a character generated by a keystroke that has various functions.

Escaped is the past tense of escape—having gotten away from confinement, danger, or an undesirable situation. An escaped {prisoner} has broken free from custody. Escaped also describes things that have gotten loose: {an escaped zoo animal}, {escaped gas from a pipeline}. What has escaped your notice went undetected: {The error escaped everyone's attention}.

Escapes is the plural of escape—instances of getting away from confinement, danger, or unpleasant situations: {The prison had three escapes last year}. It also refers to diversions from routine or stress: {weekend escapes to the country}. As a verb, escapes is the third-person singular: {Nothing escapes her notice}.

Escapism is the tendency to seek distraction from unpleasant realities through entertainment, fantasy, or other absorbing activities. The term usually carries mild disapproval, suggesting avoidance rather than engagement: {Video games are pure escapism for him}. But escapism can also be defended as necessary mental relief: {Sometimes you need a little escapism}.

Escapist describes something designed to distract from reality or unpleasant circumstances, or a person who seeks such distraction. Escapist {fiction}, escapist {fantasy}, and escapist {entertainment} offer temporary refuge from everyday concerns. As a noun, an escapist is someone who habitually avoids facing problems: {He's an escapist who buries himself in video games}.

An escort accompanies someone for protection, guidance, or courtesy. A dignitary travels with a police escort; a guest is escorted to their table. The term extends to paid companions—sometimes implying sexual services, sometimes not. Escort services often use the word as a euphemism for prostitution, though many escorts provide only companionship: {She worked as an escort for wealthy businessmen}.

Escorts are people who accompany others, whether for protection, guidance, or companionship. A military escort guards a convoy; a funeral escort leads a procession. The verb means to accompany: {Security escorted him from the building}. Escort also refers to a paid companion for social events, and euphemistically to a prostitute—hence {escort service}, which may offer either.

Espionage is the practice of spying—gathering secret information about a government, organization, or competitor through covert means. The word usually implies state-level intelligence operations: {Cold War espionage}, {industrial espionage}. An espionage {agent} works undercover; an espionage {ring} is a network of spies. {He was convicted of espionage and sentenced to life in prison.}

Esport is competitive video gaming at a professional or organized level, typically with spectators and prize money: {League of Legends is the biggest esport in Asia}. The term is modeled on sport, treating gaming as athletic competition. Also spelled e-sport or eSport. The plural esports often refers to the industry as a whole: {She works in esports}.

Esports refers to competitive video gaming at a professional or semi-professional level, with organized tournaments, teams, and spectators. Players compete in games like League of Legends, Counter-Strike, or Fortnite for prize money and sponsorships. The industry has grown to include leagues, arenas, and broadcast coverage rivaling traditional sports: {She made a career in esports commentary}.

Espresso is coffee brewed by forcing hot water through finely ground beans under pressure, producing a concentrated shot with a layer of crema on top. It serves as the base for drinks like lattes, cappuccinos, and Americanos. The word comes from Italian, suggesting coffee made expressly for the customer. The common misspelling "expresso" appears frequently enough that some dictionaries acknowledge it, though purists consider it an error.

An essay is a short piece of writing on a particular subject, typically expressing the author's perspective or argument: {a five-paragraph essay}, {an essay on climate change}. The form ranges from academic assignments to personal reflections. As a verb, to essay something is to attempt it—a formal or literary usage: {She essayed a smile}.

Essays are short pieces of prose writing on a particular subject, typically presenting the author's own perspective or argument. The word carries a sense of attempt or exploration—an essay tries out ideas rather than settling them definitively. As a verb, to essay something is to attempt it: {She essayed a smile despite her grief}. The noun also appears in phrases like {photo essay}, where images rather than words explore a theme.

Essence is the fundamental nature of something—what makes it what it is. The essence of a {contract} is agreement between parties. In cooking and perfumery, an essence is a concentrated extract: {vanilla essence}, {essence of rose}. The phrase {in essence} means fundamentally or at its core: {In essence, we agree}. Something {of the essence} is critically important: {Time is of the essence}.

Essential describes what is absolutely necessary or fundamental to something's nature. An essential {ingredient} cannot be left out. Essential {oils} contain the concentrated essence of plants. The essentials are basics you can't do without: {We packed only the essentials}. Something's essential {character} is its core identity stripped of incidentals.

Establish means to set up or bring into being on a firm, lasting basis. You establish a business, a rule, a precedent, or a reputation. To establish something as true is to demonstrate it beyond doubt: {The investigation established that no crime had occurred}. Once established, something is accepted, settled, or entrenched: {an established tradition}, {the established order}. To {establish yourself} somewhere is to settle in securely.

Established describes something that has been set up and made permanent or stable. An established {business} has operated long enough to prove its viability. An established {fact} is accepted as true. The established {order} refers to existing social or political structures that have become entrenched. To become established is to gain recognition or secure footing: {She established herself as an authority on the subject}.

An establishment is a place of business or an institution: {a dining establishment}, {an educational establishment}. The word often implies permanence and formality. With the definite article, the establishment refers to the dominant group controlling politics, business, and cultural institutions—those invested in maintaining existing power structures. To be {anti-establishment} is to oppose these entrenched interests. Establishment also names the act of establishing: {the establishment of diplomatic relations}.

Estate centers on property and standing. In its primary sense, an estate is a large piece of landed property, often with a substantial house: {The family estate has been in our hands for generations}. Estate also means the total property someone owns, especially at death: {His estate was divided among three heirs}. In British usage, an estate (or housing estate) is a residential development. The word extends to social rank—the three estates of medieval society were clergy, nobility, and commoners. A {real estate} agent deals in property; an {estate sale} liquidates a deceased person's belongings.

Esteem is respect and admiration for someone or something: {She held her mentor in high esteem}. The verb means to regard favorably or value highly: {His colleagues esteem him for his integrity}. Self-esteem is one's sense of personal worth. To esteem something can also mean to consider or judge it: {I esteem it an honor to be asked}.

An estimate is a rough calculation or judgment about quantity, size, cost, or value when exact figures aren't available: {The contractor gave us an estimate of twelve thousand dollars}. To estimate is to form such a judgment: {I estimate we'll arrive around noon}. Estimates acknowledge uncertainty—they're informed guesses, not guarantees. An {estimated} crowd size or {estimated} time of arrival signals approximation.

Estranged describes a relationship that has become distant or hostile, typically between family members or spouses who were once close: {her estranged husband}, {estranged from his father for years}. The word implies a breach that may or may not be permanent—more serious than distant, less final than divorced or disowned.

Estrangement is the condition of being alienated or cut off from someone or something once close. Family estrangement describes relatives who no longer speak: {His estrangement from his father lasted decades}. The word implies a relationship that existed before distance grew—you can't be estranged from a stranger. Estrangement can also describe disconnection from institutions, beliefs, or one's own feelings.

Eta is the seventh letter of the Greek alphabet (Η, η), used in mathematics, physics, and engineering to represent various quantities like efficiency or viscosity. Outside technical contexts, eta appears mainly in fraternity and sorority names. (Capitalized ETA is the acronym for estimated time of arrival.)

To etch is to cut into a surface using acid or a sharp tool, creating lines or designs. The technique is central to printmaking, where acid eats into metal plates to hold ink. By extension, etch describes any sharp, precise rendering: {The skyline was etched against the sunset}. Something deeply memorable is {etched in memory}.

Etched describes something cut or engraved into a surface, originally through acid on metal or glass. The word usually appears as a past participle: an etched {design}, etched {glass}. Figuratively, something etched in memory or etched on the mind is vividly and permanently fixed there: {The image of her face was etched in his memory forever}.

Etching is a printmaking technique where an image is incised into a metal plate using acid, then inked and pressed onto paper. The resulting print is also called an etching. The verb etch means to create such marks, or more broadly, to engrave or impress deeply: {The scene was etched in her memory}. {His face was etched with worry}.

Eternal means lasting forever, without beginning or end. Religious and philosophical contexts speak of eternal {life}, eternal {damnation}, the eternal {soul}. More loosely, eternal describes anything that seems to go on indefinitely: {the eternal wait at the DMV}, {eternal optimism}. The Eternal City is Rome. Eternally is the adverb: {I'm eternally grateful}.

Eternity is time without end—infinite duration extending forever into the future, the past, or both. In religious contexts, eternity is the timeless realm where God exists or where souls go after death: {eternal life}, {spending eternity in heaven}. Colloquially, an eternity is any period that feels interminably long: {We waited an eternity for the results}. {It seemed like an eternity before she answered}.

Ether names something rarefied or intangible. In old physics, the ether was a hypothetical substance filling all space, through which light waves traveled. In chemistry, ethers are volatile organic compounds; the most familiar is diethyl ether, once used as an anesthetic: {The patient was put under with ether}. Figuratively, voices or signals travel {through the ether}—the airwaves, the atmosphere, the vague medium of transmission. {The announcement vanished into the ether.}

Underlying the adjective ethereal is the noun ether, which provides an important clue to its meaning. Ether was once thought to be the substance or element that filled the heavens, and ethereal conveys intangibility or lacking material substance. It may also have a connotation of delicacy or exquisiteness, especially in writing about the arts. People use ethereal today when they can’t pinpoint specifics: The ethereal beauty of her voice filled the concert hall. Ethereal is usually complimentary.

Ethernet spelled with a lowercase e is occasionally seen in casual or technical writing, though the capitalized form is standard. The technology is a system for connecting computers in a local area network using cables and standardized protocols. It remains the dominant wired networking technology in offices and homes: {The ethernet port on my laptop stopped working}. (Capitalized Ethernet is the standard spelling.)

Ethical means conforming to accepted standards of right and wrong conduct: {an ethical business practice}, {ethical treatment of animals}. It also describes things relating to ethics as a field of study: {ethical philosophy}, {ethical dilemmas}. Someone who is ethical acts with integrity and moral principle. The word often implies careful consideration of consequences and fairness, not just following rules.

Ethics are a set of values that guides a particular endeavor, or when no context is specified, the general values held by a group or society that help people decide what is right and wrong: The committee is tasked with developing research ethics that will serve the institution in the 21st century. Anthropologists struggle to recreate the code of ethics of societies that left no written records. An ethics committee in a legislature or other institution is one that develops rules of conduct or examines breaches of conduct.

Ethnicity refers to shared cultural identity—common ancestry, language, traditions, or national origin that bind a group: {Her ethnicity is Korean}, {a neighborhood with diverse ethnicities}. Unlike race, which categorizes by physical features, ethnicity emphasizes cultural heritage and group affiliation. Someone may identify with multiple ethnicities or none at all. Forms and surveys often ask about ethnicity alongside race, treating them as distinct categories.

Ethos is the characteristic spirit or guiding beliefs of a community, culture, or movement: {the Protestant work ethic}, {the ethos of Silicon Valley startups}. It captures the underlying values and attitudes that shape how a group thinks and acts. In rhetoric, ethos refers specifically to a speaker's credibility or moral character as a persuasive tool—distinct from logos (logic) and pathos (emotion).

Etiquette is the set of unwritten rules governing polite behavior in social or professional settings. It covers everything from table manners to email conventions to how you address royalty. Etiquette varies by culture and era—what's proper in one context may be rude in another. {Business etiquette requires a prompt reply.} {The etiquette of formal dining can be intimidating.}

Eucalyptus is a genus of trees native to Australia, known for aromatic leaves that produce a pungent oil used in medicines and cleaning products. The trees grow tall with distinctive peeling bark. Koalas feed almost exclusively on eucalyptus leaves. The oil clears congestion: {eucalyptus cough drops}, {a few drops of eucalyptus in the humidifier}.

Eugenics is the idea of improving human populations through selective breeding—encouraging reproduction among people deemed genetically "fit" while discouraging or preventing it among those deemed "unfit." The term now carries heavy stigma due to its association with forced sterilization programs and Nazi racial policies. {Eugenics was taught as legitimate science in American universities into the 1930s.} The adjective is eugenic.

Euhedral describes a crystal that has developed its full, characteristic geometric shape with well-formed faces and sharp edges. The term appears in geology and mineralogy when crystals grow without interference from neighboring minerals: {The rock contained euhedral quartz crystals}. The opposite is anhedral, describing crystals with no defined faces.

A eulogy is a speech honoring someone who has died, typically delivered at a funeral or memorial service. The speaker recounts the deceased's life, character, and impact on others: {She gave a moving eulogy for her father}. More broadly, eulogy can mean high praise for anyone or anything: {The book is a eulogy to small-town life}.

Euphemisms are mild or indirect expressions substituted for ones considered too harsh, blunt, or offensive. Death becomes {passing away}, firing becomes {letting go}, and lies become {misinformation}. The impulse to euphemize touches nearly every sensitive domain—bodily functions, sex, death, money, and politics. Euphemisms can soften difficult conversations or obscure uncomfortable truths.

Euphoria is a state of intense happiness, elation, or well-being that goes beyond ordinary good feelings. It can arise from positive life events, success, or love, but also from drugs, mental health conditions, or physical exertion like runner's high. The feeling is characteristically powerful but often temporary. {The team was in a state of euphoria after winning the championship.} Something that produces this feeling is euphoric.

Euphoric describes a state of intense happiness, elation, or well-being—often beyond what circumstances might warrant. The feeling may come from achievement, drugs, or brain chemistry: {The runners described a euphoric high after the marathon}. Something that produces this state is euphoric or euphoriant. The noun is euphoria.

In ancient Greek eureka means “I have found.” It was reportedly uttered by Archimedes on making a great discovery, and has been used since then for the same purpose. It is often associated with an exclamation by miners who found a vein of gold.

The euro is the official currency of most European Union countries, introduced in 1999 and symbolized by €. It replaced national currencies like the German mark and French franc. The word functions as both singular and plural in financial contexts: {The euro fell against the dollar}, {That costs fifty euro}. Outside the eurozone, euros is the standard plural. (Capitalized Euro- appears in compounds relating to Europe.)

Euthanasia is the practice of painlessly bringing about the death of people or animals who are so ill or injured that they have no possibility of a useful or enjoyable life. Euthanasia is widely practiced with domestic animals but is illegal in relation to humans. Euthanasia law is a misnomer for a law permitting physician assisted suicide for people who are terminally ill.

Evacuate means to leave or empty a place, especially in response to danger. Authorities evacuate buildings during fires, cities before hurricanes, civilians from war zones. The word implies urgency and organized departure: {We had to evacuate when the gas leak was detected}. In medical contexts, evacuate means to empty the bowels or bladder. Figuratively, to evacuate is to remove or withdraw: {The army evacuated its troops from the region}.

Evacuation is the act of leaving or removing people from a dangerous place. During fires, floods, or other emergencies, authorities order evacuations to move populations to safety: {The hurricane prompted a mandatory evacuation of coastal areas}. In medical contexts, evacuation refers to emptying the bowels or bladder. Military evacuations remove troops or civilians from combat zones.

Evacuations are instances of emptying out or withdrawing. The word most often refers to organized removals of people from dangerous areas: {Evacuations began as the wildfire approached}. In medical contexts, evacuation means emptying the bowels or bladder. The military uses evacuation for withdrawing troops or removing casualties from combat zones.

Evacuees are people who have been evacuated—removed from a dangerous place to somewhere safer. The term appears most often during wars, natural disasters, and other emergencies: {Evacuees from the hurricane filled the shelters}. The word carries a sense of displacement and vulnerability, emphasizing the people rather than the process.

To evade is to avoid or escape, especially through cleverness or deception. You can evade capture, evade detection, or evade a question by steering around it. To evade taxes is to illegally avoid paying them—distinct from tax avoidance, which uses legal means. {He evaded her questions about where he'd been.}

Evaluation is the process of judging the quality, value, or condition of something. Teachers write evaluations of students; employees receive performance evaluations from supervisors. The word often implies systematic assessment against criteria: {The evaluation found the program effective but underfunded}. To evaluate is to make such a judgment.

Evangelical describes Christians who emphasize personal conversion, biblical authority, and spreading the faith. An evangelical {church} prioritizes these commitments. The word often appears in political contexts, where evangelicals form a significant voting bloc in the United States: {Evangelical voters supported the candidate}. More broadly, evangelical describes zealous advocacy for any cause: {She's evangelical about veganism}.

Evangelicals are Christians who emphasize personal conversion, the authority of the Bible, and actively sharing their faith with others. The term comes from a Greek word meaning "good news" or "gospel." In American usage, evangelicals often refers specifically to Protestant Christians associated with conservative social and political positions, though the movement is theologically diverse. {Evangelicals turned out in large numbers for the election.} The singular evangelical works as both noun and adjective.

Evangelism is zealous preaching or advocacy, originally and still primarily associated with spreading the Christian gospel. The word implies active persuasion rather than passive belief: {street evangelism}, {door-to-door evangelism}. The meaning has expanded to enthusiastic promotion of any cause or product: {brand evangelism}, {tech evangelism}. {His evangelism for the new framework converted several skeptical developers.}

An evangelist is someone who spreads a message with missionary zeal. Originally and still commonly, the term refers to Christian preachers who seek converts, especially through revivals or public campaigns: {a televangelist}, {Billy Graham was America's most famous evangelist}. The four Evangelists—Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John—wrote the Gospels. In secular use, an evangelist champions any cause or product with fervent advocacy: {a technology evangelist}, {an evangelist for clean energy}.

Evangelists are people who spread a message with fervent conviction. The word comes from Greek for "bringer of good news," and its oldest sense refers to those who preach the Christian gospel—particularly the authors of the four Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. More broadly, an evangelist promotes any cause or product with missionary zeal: {a tech evangelist}, {an evangelist for clean energy}. The term implies not just belief but active persuasion.

Evaporate describes liquid turning to vapor and dispersing into air. Water evaporates from puddles, sweat evaporates from skin. The meaning extends to anything that disappears gradually or suddenly: {My enthusiasm evaporated when I saw the price}. Evaporated milk has had water removed through heating.

Evaporated describes something that has turned from liquid to vapor and dispersed. Water evaporates from a puddle; enthusiasm evaporates from a crowd. {Her patience had evaporated by the third delay.} Evaporated milk is milk with most of its water removed through heating, resulting in a thick, shelf-stable liquid used in cooking and baking.

Evaporation is the process by which a liquid turns into vapor, typically at the surface rather than throughout. Water evaporates from puddles, sweat evaporates from skin.
