The word extends to gradual disappearance: {the evaporation of public support}, {the evaporation of their savings}. In science, evaporation rate depends on temperature, humidity, and air movement.

Evasion is the act of avoiding something—capture, responsibility, or direct confrontation. Tax evasion is the illegal nonpayment of taxes. A politician's evasion of questions frustrates reporters. The word implies deliberate maneuvering: {His evasion of the topic made her suspicious}. Evasive answers dodge rather than address what's asked.

Evasive describes behavior that avoids directness or commitment. An evasive {answer} sidesteps the question rather than addressing it. Evasive {maneuvers} help a vehicle or aircraft avoid detection or attack. Someone being evasive is deliberately vague, withholding information or dodging confrontation: {She grew evasive when asked about her whereabouts}.

Eve is the evening or day before a notable event: {Christmas Eve}, {New Year's Eve}, {the eve of battle}. It suggests anticipation—the moment just before something significant begins. More broadly, {on the eve of} means shortly before: {on the eve of the election}. The word is literary or formal in most uses. (Capitalized Eve is the biblical first woman.)

Even functions mainly as an adjective and adverb. Its adjectival meanings are varied but all of them center around the idea of equality and uniformity, as in an even surface or an even exchange. As an adverb, even is often an intensive whose purpose is to emphasize any of several features of meaning. In these usages even is usually required, there being no other word in English that does the same work: You didn’t even apologize to her, this pie is even better than the one we had yesterday.

Evening is the later part of the day, after afternoon and before night—roughly from sunset until bedtime. The word often suggests a period of leisure or social activity: {We spent the evening playing cards}, {an evening out}. As an adjective, it describes things associated with this time: evening {news}, evening {gown}, evening {classes}. Good evening is a greeting used during these hours.

An event is something that happens, especially something notable or significant: {The discovery was a major event in scientific history}. Events can be planned occasions—social gatherings, ceremonies, sporting competitions: {a fundraising event}, {track and field events}. In physics, an event is a point in spacetime. The phrase {in the event of} means if something happens: {In the event of fire, use the stairs}.

Events are things that happen, especially ones of significance or note. The word spans from the grand to the mundane: a {historic event}, a {sporting event}, a {fundraising event}. In casual use, events often implies organized occasions with attendees and schedules. The phrase {in the event of} means if something happens: {In the event of rain, the concert moves indoors}. At any event or in any event means regardless of what happens.

Eventually means at some unspecified future time, after a period of waiting or a series of events. It implies that something will happen, though not immediately: {Eventually the rain stopped}, {I'll get around to it eventually}. The word carries a sense of inevitability—the outcome is expected, just delayed.

Ever is an adverb that usually has a time-related meaning. In its strictest and original sense it means always: we are ever looking to expand our customer base. It can also mean at any time or in any way; from these meanings, it has found a home in compound words that have a generalizing effect, such as whatever, whenever, however, and many others.

Evergreen describes trees and shrubs that retain green foliage year-round, shedding leaves gradually rather than all at once: pines, spruces, hollies. The word extends to anything that stays fresh or relevant indefinitely: an evergreen {song}, evergreen {content}. In finance, an evergreen {fund} or {contract} renews automatically. {Holiday evergreens decorated the mantel.}

Evergreens are trees and shrubs that retain their foliage year-round, unlike deciduous plants that shed leaves seasonally. Pines, spruces, firs, and hollies are common examples. The term extends figuratively to things that remain perpetually fresh or relevant: {evergreen content}, {evergreen songs}. In finance, an evergreen contract renews automatically.

Everlasting means lasting forever or for an indefinitely long time: {everlasting love}, {everlasting life}. Religious contexts promise everlasting salvation or damnation. The word can express weariness with something that seems never to end: {I'm tired of his everlasting complaints}. Everlasting flowers are varieties that retain their form when dried.

The adjective every is a very old marriage of two other function words—ever and each—but unlike ever, every is necessarily related to time. The function of every is to convey that each member of a group of things shares some characteristic and in this respect it is similar to each. Every also plays a role in a few idioms in which its meaning is not precise, such as every bit and every now and then.

Everybody and it synonym everyone are both pronouns that mean every person. Even though their designation is plural, they are used with singular verbs: Everybody knows that the election was rigged. The people designated by everybody is contextual rather than literal: Everybody who works at the factory punches a time clock.

Everyday means ordinary, routine, or encountered regularly: {everyday tasks}, {everyday life}, {an everyday occurrence}. It describes things that are commonplace rather than special or exceptional. Do not confuse with the two-word phrase every day, which means each day: {I exercise every day}.

An everyman is a common or typical person, someone who represents ordinary humanity rather than exceptional individuals. The term often describes characters in fiction deliberately designed to be relatable and unremarkable: {The protagonist is an everyman caught up in extraordinary circumstances}. In broader use, it suggests the average person's perspective or experience: {an everyman's guide to investing}. (Capitalized Everyman is the medieval morality play.)

Everyone and it synonym everybody are both pronouns that mean every person. Even though their designation is plural, they are used with singular verbs: Everyone is born with a unique set of chromosomes. The people designated by everyone is contextual rather than literal: Everyone who came really enjoyed the lecture.

The most literal meaning of everything is every thing—that is, every thing that exists in the universe. People rarely use everything in this way, and instead use surrounding words to limit what it refers to: Write down everything he says. I’ve done everything I can to make sure she is comfortable. When no context is provided, meaning can be inferred: Everything changed for the children after their parents’ divorce. The expression everything from _____ to ______ suggests a wide range; I play everything from Bach to the Beatles.

Everywhere means in or to all places: {I've looked everywhere for my keys}. It can suggest ubiquity or omnipresence: {Coffee shops are everywhere now}. The word often intensifies statements about thoroughness or extent: {There was confetti everywhere}. In casual speech, everywhere sometimes exaggerates: {I can't go anywhere without running into him—he's everywhere}.

To evict is to legally force someone out of a property they occupy—typically a tenant who hasn't paid rent or has violated lease terms. A landlord evicts; a court orders eviction. The word extends to any forcible removal: {Police evicted protesters from the park}. {They were evicted for keeping unauthorized pets}.

Evicted is the past tense of evict—to force someone to leave a property, typically through legal process. Landlords evict tenants for unpaid rent or lease violations. The word extends to any forcible removal: {The protesters were evicted from the building}. Being evicted carries connotations of displacement and loss of home.

Eviction is the legal process of forcing someone to leave a property, typically for nonpayment of rent or violation of lease terms. Landlords evict tenants; banks evict homeowners who default on mortgages. The word implies formal removal through legal channels rather than informal pressure: {They received an eviction notice giving them thirty days to vacate}.

Evidence is something that proves or disproves another thing: What evidence do you have that no one had visited the property? The two areas where evidence is most important are in law and in scientific research. In law, evidence is the basis on which a court or jury decides the outcome of a trial. In science, evidence is used to support or disprove a theory or hypothesis: The evidence that came out of the study provided the basis for new guidelines.

Evil is profound immorality or wickedness—the opposite of good in its deepest moral sense. Evil describes acts, people, or forces that cause serious harm or suffering: {an evil dictator}, {the evil of slavery}. In religious contexts, evil is a cosmic force opposed to God or goodness. Informally, evil can describe something unpleasant or harmful: {an evil smell}, {an evil hangover}. As a noun, evil is wrongdoing or harm itself: {the struggle between good and evil}, {a necessary evil}.

Evolution is the verbal noun of evolve, which means to develop or change gradually. Without further context, it typically refers to biological evolution, the process by which organisms adapt to their environments through natural selection. Outside of the biological sphere, evolution is used to describe anything that develops or changes gradually, from psychological evolution to the evolution of views on marriage equality.

Evolutionary describes something related to evolution—the gradual development of species through natural selection, or more broadly, any process of gradual change and development. {Evolutionary biology}, {evolutionary theory}. The word often contrasts with revolutionary: evolutionary change happens incrementally rather than through sudden transformation. {The company took an evolutionary approach to product development.}

Evolve means to develop gradually over time. In biology, species evolve through natural selection across generations: {Humans evolved from earlier primates}. More broadly, anything that changes incrementally evolves: {Her style evolved over the years}, {The plan evolved as we learned more}. The word implies organic, unforced development rather than sudden transformation.

Evolved is the past tense of evolve, meaning to develop gradually or change over time. In biology, species evolve through natural selection: {Humans evolved from earlier primates}. More loosely, evolved describes someone or something that has progressed beyond a previous state: {She's really evolved since college}. Calling oneself evolved often implies spiritual or emotional growth, sometimes with a whiff of self-congratulation.

Eww is an exclamation of disgust or revulsion, reacting to something unpleasant—a bad smell, a gross image, or an unsettling idea: {Eww, what is that on your shoe?} The spelling varies (ew, ewww) with more letters suggesting stronger disgust. Common in casual speech and text, especially among younger speakers.

Exact means precise, with no variation or error: the exact {time}, the exact {amount}, the exact {words} someone used. Something exact corresponds perfectly to a standard or requirement. As a verb, to exact is to demand and obtain, often by force or authority: {The hurricane exacted a heavy toll}. Exacting describes standards or people that demand precision.

To exaggerate is to represent something as larger, better, worse, or more significant than it actually is. The impulse ranges from innocent embellishment to outright distortion: {He exaggerated his accomplishments on the résumé}. Someone who exaggerates habitually may be called an exaggerator. Physical features can be exaggerated too—enlarged or emphasized beyond normal proportions: {The cartoon exaggerated the politician's ears}.

Exaggerated describes something that has been made to seem larger, more important, or more extreme than it actually is. An exaggerated {claim} stretches the truth; exaggerated {movements} are theatrical and overdone; exaggerated {fears} blow a threat out of proportion. The word often carries a note of skepticism or criticism, implying that someone has gone beyond what the facts support. {Reports of his incompetence were greatly exaggerated.}

Exaggerating is making something seem bigger, better, worse, or more important than it really is. People exaggerate for emphasis, humor, or to make a story more compelling: {I'm not exaggerating when I say it was the worst meal of my life}. The word often carries a hint of accusation—if you say someone is exaggerating, you're suggesting they're stretching the truth or being dramatic.

Exaggeration is overstatement—representing something as greater, better, worse, or more extreme than it actually is. A fish story grows with each telling; a minor inconvenience becomes {the worst day of my life}. Exaggeration can be deliberate rhetorical effect, unconscious distortion, or outright lie. The line between emphatic expression and exaggeration often depends on the listener's tolerance: {That's not an exaggeration—it really was a hundred degrees}.

Exaggerations are statements that stretch the truth beyond what's accurate, making something seem bigger, better, worse, or more extreme than it actually is. The word covers everything from harmless hyperbole to deliberate distortion: {His fishing stories are full of exaggerations}. To say something is {not an exaggeration} emphasizes that a surprising claim is literally true.

An exam is a test of knowledge or ability, short for examination. Students take exams in school; professionals pass licensing exams to practice medicine or law. {I have three exams next week.} The word implies a formal assessment with stakes attached, distinguishing it from casual quizzes or self-checks.

Examination is a close, careful inspection or investigation: {a medical examination}, {examination of the evidence}. In academic settings, an examination (often shortened to exam) is a formal test of knowledge or ability. In law, examination refers to the formal questioning of a witness: {direct examination}, {cross-examination}. The word suggests methodical scrutiny rather than casual looking.

To examine is to inspect closely or investigate: {The doctor examined my knee}. The word suggests careful, systematic attention—you examine evidence, examine a patient, examine your conscience. In academic settings, to examine someone is to test their knowledge: {Students will be examined on the material next week}. An examiner administers tests; an examinee takes them.

Example is a specific instance chosen to represent a larger category or illustrate a principle. When you give an example, you offer something concrete to clarify something abstract: {Can you give me an example of what you mean?} Examples may be typical ({a classic example of Art Deco architecture}) or cautionary ({Let that be an example to you}). To set an example is to behave in a way others should imitate. If you lead by example, your actions demonstrate what you expect from others.

Exams are formal tests of knowledge or ability, typically in academic settings. The word is a clipped form of examinations, now more common than the full word in everyday speech: {I have three exams next week}, {final exams}. Medical exams assess physical health rather than knowledge.

Exasperated describes intense frustration or irritation, often after repeated annoyances or failed attempts: {She was exasperated by his constant excuses}. The feeling suggests patience worn thin—you've had enough. Someone exasperated sighs, throws up their hands, or snaps. {After the third delay, even the calmest passengers looked exasperated}.

Exasperation is intense frustration or annoyance, typically after repeated provocations or failed attempts. It implies patience worn thin: {She sighed in exasperation when he asked the same question for the fifth time}. The feeling suggests you've reached a limit—not quite anger, but close.

Excavating is digging out and removing earth, rock, or other material from the ground. The word applies to construction sites, archaeological digs, and mining operations: {They've been excavating the foundation for weeks}. Figuratively, to excavate is to uncover something buried or hidden: {excavating the truth from old records}.

Excavation is the act of digging out and removing earth or rock, or the hole or cavity created by such digging. The term applies both to construction projects {excavation for the foundation} and archaeological work {excavation of a Roman villa}. An excavation site is where systematic digging uncovers buried remains or prepares ground for building.

An excavator is a large machine used for digging, typically featuring a rotating cab, a long articulated arm, and a bucket at the end. Excavators are essential equipment on construction sites for trenching, demolition, and moving earth: {The excavator dug out the foundation in a single day}. The word can also mean simply a person who excavates, especially in archaeological contexts.

To excel is to be exceptionally good at something or to surpass others: {She excels at mathematics}, {He excelled in every sport he tried}. The word implies standing out from the crowd through superior performance or ability. Someone who excels doesn't just succeed—they distinguish themselves. (Capitalized Excel is the Microsoft spreadsheet software.)

Excellence is the quality of being exceptionally good—superiority that stands out from the ordinary. It implies sustained high performance rather than a single achievement: {a reputation for excellence}, {academic excellence}, {centers of excellence}. The word often appears in institutional language: mission statements, awards, and aspirational slogans. {Excellence is not a destination but a continuous journey.}

Excellent describes something of exceptionally high quality or merit—better than merely good. An excellent {meal}, an excellent {student}, an excellent {decision}. The word carries genuine praise without the inflation of words like amazing or incredible. {Excellent!} alone expresses strong approval or satisfaction.

An exception is something that doesn't follow the general rule or pattern. If most students failed but one passed, that student is the exception. The phrase {with the exception of} means excluding or apart from: {Everyone attended with the exception of Tom}. To {take exception to} something is to object to it or be offended by it. In computing and law, exception has technical meanings: a runtime error that disrupts normal program flow, or a formal objection to a court ruling.

Exceptional means standing out from the ordinary, usually in a positive way: {an exceptional student}, {exceptional talent}. The word can also mean unusually difficult or challenging: {exceptional circumstances}. In educational contexts, exceptional often refers to students with special needs—a euphemism covering both disabilities and giftedness. {She showed exceptional skill under pressure.}

Exceptions are cases that don't follow the general rule. Grammar has exceptions; so do laws and policies. To {take exception} to something is to object or be offended: {She took exception to his remarks}. {With the exception of} means excluding: {Everyone came, with the exception of Tom}. In computing, an exception is an error condition that disrupts normal program flow.

Exceptious means inclined to take exception or make objections; quarrelsome or captious. The word is rare and archaic, largely replaced by *exceptionable* (open to objection) or simply *quarrelsome*. {He was an exceptious man, finding fault with every proposal.}

An excerpt is a passage or segment taken from a longer work—a book, speech, film, or musical composition. To excerpt something is to select and reproduce such a portion: {The magazine excerpted three chapters from her memoir.} Excerpts serve to give readers or listeners a taste of the whole, often appearing in reviews, anthologies, or promotional materials.

Excess is more than what is needed, wanted, or appropriate. An excess of anything suggests too much: {an excess of caution}, {an excess of enthusiasm}. As an adjective, excess describes the surplus portion: {excess baggage}, {excess inventory}. To do something {to excess} is to overdo it. {In excess of} means more than: {Damages were in excess of two million dollars}. The plural excesses usually implies indulgent or immoral behavior: {the excesses of the wealthy}.

Excessive means more than necessary, normal, or desirable—beyond what the situation warrants. Excessive {force} goes past what's needed. Excessive {drinking} crosses into harmful territory. The word carries implicit judgment: what one person considers excessive another might find reasonable. {The fees seemed excessive for such a simple service.}

Exchange is giving something and receiving something else in return. The core image is reciprocal transfer: you exchange currency at the airport, exchange vows at a wedding, exchange words in conversation. An exchange is both the act and what's traded: {a heated exchange}, {an exchange of gunfire}. It also names institutions where trading happens: stock exchange, commodity exchange. To exchange something is to swap it: {I exchanged the shirt for a larger size}.

Excite means to stir up strong feeling or activity. News can excite interest, a discovery can excite the scientific community, and a lover can excite desire. To be excited is to feel eager anticipation: {I'm so excited for the concert}. In technical contexts, to excite is to energize—light excites electrons, current excites a motor. An excitable person is easily stirred up.

Excited describes a state of heightened energy or anticipation. You might be excited about an upcoming trip, excited to see someone, or sexually excited. The word can also describe physical states—excited electrons have absorbed energy and moved to higher orbits. {The kids were too excited to sleep.} {Don't get excited} asks someone to calm down.

Excitement is a state of heightened energy and anticipation, the feeling of being stirred up by something interesting or thrilling: {The excitement in the stadium was palpable}. It can describe the emotion itself or what causes it: {the excitement of opening night}, {We need some excitement around here}. To create excitement is to generate buzz or enthusiasm. Sexual excitement refers to arousal.

Exciting describes something that stirs strong feelings of enthusiasm, anticipation, or exhilaration. An exciting {movie} keeps you on edge; exciting {news} makes your heart race. The word suggests heightened energy and engagement: {It's an exciting time to be in tech}. What counts as exciting varies widely—a quiet discovery can be as exciting as a roller coaster.

Exclamation is the verbal noun from exclaim, which means cry out in emotion, surprise, or pain. Exclamation can also designate a word or expression that people use when they call out in this fashion. Some people also use exclamation interchangeably with interjection to designate the part of speech that consists of expressive utterances that do not usually participate in grammatical or syntactic relationships with other sentence elements.

To exclude is to keep out or leave out. A club may exclude certain people from membership. A diet may exclude sugar. To exclude a possibility is to rule it out: {The evidence excludes any other explanation}. When you focus on one thing to the exclusion of others, you give those others no attention. Tax-excluded income isn't counted toward what you owe.

Exclusion is the act of keeping someone or something out, or the state of being kept out. A club practices exclusion when it bars certain people from membership. {Her exclusion from the meeting felt deliberate.} The word often implies unfairness or discrimination: {social exclusion}, {exclusion based on race}. In legal and insurance contexts, an exclusion is a specific condition or circumstance not covered: {The policy has an exclusion for flood damage}.

Exclusive means shutting out others or being limited to a particular person, group, or thing. An exclusive {club} restricts membership. An exclusive {interview} goes to only one outlet. Exclusive {rights} belong to one party alone. Mutually exclusive options cannot both be true: {The two explanations are mutually exclusive}. As a noun, an exclusive is a story or product available from only one source.

Exclusivity is the quality of being exclusive—limited to a particular person, group, or circumstance. A contract may grant exclusivity to one distributor. {The club prided itself on exclusivity}. The word often carries connotations of privilege or prestige, suggesting that restriction itself adds value: {The resort's exclusivity justified its prices}.

Excommunicated describes someone who has been formally expelled from membership in a religious community, most commonly the Roman Catholic Church. The punishment bars the person from participating in sacraments and other rites of the faith. {Henry VIII was excommunicated after breaking with Rome.} The term extends figuratively to anyone cast out of a group or organization: {After the scandal, he was effectively excommunicated from Hollywood.} The root communicate originally meant to share in common, so excommunication literally means being cut off from shared participation.

Excommunication is formal exclusion from a religious community, especially the Catholic Church. The excommunicated person is cut off from sacraments and fellowship with other believers. The term extends to any formal expulsion from a group or organization: {His excommunication from the party was swift and total}. The verb is excommunicate.

Excruciating describes pain so intense it feels unbearable—the word comes from crucifixion, suggesting agony worthy of the cross. Physical pain is excruciating: {an excruciating migraine}, {excruciating back spasms}. The word extends to emotional torment or extreme discomfort: {the excruciating wait for test results}, {an excruciating silence}. Sometimes used hyperbolically for anything tedious or awkward: {The movie was excruciatingly boring}.

An excuse is a reason offered to justify or obtain forgiveness for a fault or failure: {His excuse was that traffic made him late}. To excuse someone is to forgive a minor offense or release them from an obligation: {Please excuse my interruption}. {Excuse me} serves as a polite apology or request to pass. As a verb, excuse can mean to make allowances for: {Nothing excuses that behavior}. A weak or dishonest explanation is {just an excuse}.

Excuses are explanations offered to justify or deflect blame for a failure or wrongdoing: {He always has excuses for being late}. The word often implies the explanation is weak or insincere—a real reason needs no excuse. To excuse someone is to forgive or release them from obligation: {Please excuse me}. {Excuse me} serves as an apology for minor intrusions or a polite way to get attention.

Execute means to carry out or put into effect. You execute a plan, a command, a will, or a legal document. In law, to execute someone is to put them to death as legal punishment: {The state executed the prisoner at dawn}. In computing, to execute a program is to run it. A sports commentator might praise how well a team {executed} on offense. The word implies completing something according to a design or instruction.

Executed is the past tense of execute, which centers on carrying something through to completion. A plan is executed when it's put into action. A legal document is executed when it's signed and made official. A computer executes commands by running them. Most grimly, a person is executed when they're put to death as punishment: {The state executed the prisoner at dawn}. Something {well-executed} is done skillfully.

Execution is carrying something out—completing an act or plan. A soldier's execution of orders, an artist's execution of a vision. In law, execution means putting a condemned person to death: {The execution is scheduled for midnight}. It also means signing a document to make it legally valid: {execution of the contract}. In computing, execution is running a program or command. Quality of execution distinguishes competent performance from poor: {The idea was good but the execution was terrible}.

An executioner is a person who carries out death sentences—historically by hanging, beheading, or other methods prescribed by law. The role extends figuratively to anyone who delivers a decisive end: {The closer served as the team's executioner in the ninth inning}. An executioner acts on authority, distinguishing the role from murderer or assassin.

Executioners are people who carry out death sentences. The term extends to anyone who kills in an official capacity or with cold efficiency. Figuratively, an executioner is someone who destroys or ends something decisively: {He became the executioner of his own career}.

Executions is the plural of execution, which primarily means carrying something out or putting something into effect. A business execution is the implementation of a plan: {The strategy was sound, but the execution was flawed}. In law, execution is the carrying out of a death sentence—the act of killing someone as legal punishment. Execution also refers to how skillfully something is performed: {a flawless execution of the dive}. In computing, execution is running a program or process.

Executive relates to carrying out plans, decisions, or laws. An executive is a senior manager who runs an organization or division: {She's a marketing executive at a Fortune 500 company}. In government, the executive branch enforces laws that the legislative branch creates. As an adjective, executive describes things relating to management or administration: {executive decision}, {executive suite}, {executive privilege}. An {executive summary} condenses a longer document for decision-makers.

Exempt means excused from a requirement or obligation that applies to others. Someone exempt from jury duty doesn't have to serve. Tax-exempt income isn't taxed. To exempt is to grant such freedom: {The policy exempts small businesses from the regulation}. An exemption is the state of being exempt or the provision that creates it.

Exercise is physical activity undertaken to maintain or improve health and fitness: {I need to get more exercise}. The word extends to any practice meant to develop a skill: {piano exercises}, {military exercises}. An exercise can also be a task with a specific purpose: {The meeting was an exercise in frustration}. To exercise is to engage in physical activity, to use something {(exercise caution, exercise your rights)}, or to trouble someone's mind: {The question exercised philosophers for centuries}.

Exercises are activities designed to develop or maintain physical fitness, skill, or knowledge. Physical exercises strengthen the body: {morning exercises}, {breathing exercises}. Mental exercises sharpen the mind. An exercise can also be a task assigned for practice: {grammar exercises}, {piano exercises}. Military exercises are training maneuvers. To exercise is to perform such activities, or more broadly, to put something into practice: {exercise caution}, {exercise your rights}. {The whole meeting felt like an exercise in futility.}

Exertion is vigorous effort or the act of applying force: {The climb required considerable physical exertion}. It implies strain or expenditure of energy beyond the casual—you don't speak of exertion when reaching for the remote. {He collapsed from the exertion of running up six flights of stairs}. The word often appears with physical, but mental exertion works too.

Exes is the plural of ex, meaning former romantic partners—ex-girlfriends, ex-boyfriends, ex-spouses: {I'm still friends with some of my exes}. The term can also refer to former versions of anything marked by ex-: ex-presidents, ex-employees. In another sense entirely, exes are expenses: {I'll submit my exes for reimbursement}.

To exhale is to breathe out, releasing air from the lungs: {She exhaled slowly to calm her nerves}. The word extends to anything that gives off vapor or gas: {The swamp exhaled a foul mist}. Figuratively, exhale suggests release or relief after tension: {The whole office exhaled when the deadline passed}.

Exhaust covers the idea of draining completely. You exhaust your savings, your patience, or yourself. To exhaust a topic is to treat it so thoroughly that nothing remains to say. The noun exhaust is the waste gases expelled from an engine, or the system that expels them: {The car's exhaust was billowing black smoke}. Exhausted means depleted of energy or resources: {I'm completely exhausted}.

Exhausted means completely drained of energy or resources. A person who is exhausted has no strength left: {I was exhausted after the marathon}. Supplies can be exhausted when entirely used up: {We've exhausted our options}. A topic is exhausted when there's nothing more to say about it. The word implies not just tiredness but depletion—having given everything until nothing remains.

Exhausting describes something that drains energy or resources completely. An exhausting day leaves you spent. Exhausting work taxes physical or mental reserves: {The exhausting climb took six hours}. The word can apply to processes that are thorough rather than tiring: an exhausting {search}, an exhausting {analysis}—one that leaves nothing unexamined.

Exhaustion is the state of being completely drained of energy or resources. Physical exhaustion follows intense exertion; mental exhaustion follows prolonged concentration or stress. The word implies depletion beyond ordinary tiredness: {She collapsed from exhaustion after the marathon}. Exhaustion also describes using something up entirely: {the exhaustion of our natural resources}.

Exhibit connects display with formal presentation. To exhibit something is to show it publicly: {The museum exhibits ancient artifacts}. An exhibit is something displayed, or a collection of displayed items: {the dinosaur exhibit}. In legal contexts, an exhibit is a document or object presented as evidence: {Exhibit A}. To exhibit behavior or qualities is to display them: {She exhibited no signs of distress}.

Exhibition is a public display of art, objects, or achievements: {The museum's new exhibition runs through March}. It can also mean a demonstration of skill or quality: {an exhibition of strength}. In sports, an exhibition game or match is played for practice or entertainment rather than as part of official competition. To {make an exhibition of yourself} is to behave embarrassingly in public.

Exhibitionism is the compulsion to expose one's body, especially the genitals, to others without their consent—a recognized psychiatric disorder and criminal offense. More broadly, it describes any attention-seeking behavior designed to attract notice: {His constant interruptions were pure exhibitionism}. The term applies equally to flashers in raincoats and performers who crave the spotlight.

An exhibitionist is someone who craves attention and behaves in ways calculated to attract it: {He's such an exhibitionist—always the loudest person in the room}. In psychology, the term specifically describes someone with a compulsion to expose their genitals to strangers. The broader sense dominates casual usage, while the clinical sense appears in legal and psychiatric contexts.

Exhibitions are public displays of art, products, or other items for viewing. A museum mounts an exhibition of paintings; a trade show features exhibitions of new technology. The word also describes showy displays of behavior or skill: {His outburst was an exhibition of poor judgment}. In sports, an exhibition game is played for practice or entertainment rather than competition.

Exhilarated describes a state of intense excitement, elation, or energized joy. The feeling is physical as much as emotional—a rush of vitality: {I felt exhilarated after the jump}. Something exhilarating produces this effect: {an exhilarating ride}, {exhilarating news}. The related noun is exhilaration.

Exhilarating describes something that produces a rush of excitement, energy, or joy. An exhilarating {rollercoaster ride}, an exhilarating {victory}, an exhilarating {first kiss}. The word suggests an intensity that's almost physical—a quickening of breath or pulse. {The view from the summit was exhilarating.}

Exhilaration is a feeling of intense excitement, happiness, or elation—the kind of rush you get from a thrilling experience or unexpected good news. It suggests a heightened state beyond ordinary pleasure, often with physical sensations like a racing heart or lightness. {The exhilaration of skydiving is hard to describe.} {She felt a wave of exhilaration when she crossed the finish line.} The feeling is typically short-lived but memorable.

Exhumed is the past tense and past participle of exhume, meaning to dig up something that has been buried, especially a corpse. Bodies are typically exhumed for legal investigations, reburial in a different location, or forensic examination: {The remains were exhumed after new evidence emerged in the case}. Figuratively, exhumed describes bringing forgotten things back to attention: {The journalist exhumed a scandal from the politician's past}.

Exile is forced separation from one's home or country, usually as punishment or for political reasons. A person in this state is also called an exile: {The poet spent years as an exile in Paris}. To exile someone is to banish them. The word extends to any prolonged, unwilling absence: {a self-imposed exile from social media}. Exile carries connotations of loss and longing that mere absence does not.

Exiled describes someone who has been banished or forced to leave their homeland, typically for political reasons: {the exiled king}, {exiled dissidents}. It can also describe voluntary departure under pressure: {She lived exiled from her family for years}. The word carries connotations of loss and longing for home.

Exiles are people forced to leave their homeland, typically for political reasons. The term covers both the banished and those who flee to avoid persecution. Exile can also be self-imposed: writers and artists sometimes live as exiles by choice, finding creative freedom abroad. {The exiles gathered in Paris, plotting their return.}

To exist is to be real, to have actual presence in the world: {Does life exist on other planets?} The word often marks the difference between reality and imagination, possibility and actuality. Something that exists is there whether or not anyone notices it. To exist can also mean merely to survive or persist in minimal fashion: {We existed on rice and beans for a month}. Existing conditions or laws are those currently in effect.

Existence is the state of being real or present in the world. Whatever exists has existence; whatever doesn't, lacks it. The word often appears in philosophical contexts about what kinds of things truly exist, but everyday use is simpler: {The company went out of existence in 2019}. An existence is also a way of living: {They eked out a meager existence on the farm}.

Existential relates to existence itself—the fact or experience of being alive. In philosophy, existential questions concern meaning, purpose, freedom, and mortality: {an existential crisis}, {existential dread}. More broadly, existential describes threats to continued existence: {Climate change poses an existential risk}. The word carries weight, suggesting fundamental rather than superficial concerns.

Existentialism is a philosophical movement emphasizing individual existence, freedom, and choice. It holds that humans define their own meaning in an indifferent or absurd universe, rather than having purpose assigned by God, nature, or society. Associated with Sartre, Camus, and Kierkegaard, existentialism influenced literature, psychology, and popular culture throughout the twentieth century. The term now sometimes appears loosely to describe any brooding reflection on life's meaning: {He's going through an existentialist phase}.

Exit is a way out—a door, gate, or passage through which you leave: {The emergency exits are at the rear of the plane}. On highways, an exit is a ramp leading off the main road. To exit is to leave a place, situation, or stage: {She exited the meeting early}. In computing, to exit is to close a program or end a session.

Exits are ways out—doors, gates, passages that let you leave a place. Highway exits are ramps leading off the main road. In theater, an exit is a departure from the stage: {Exit, pursued by a bear}. To exit is to leave: {She exited the building}, {He exited the conversation gracefully}. The exit from any situation is how you get out of it.

When capitalized, Exodus is the title of the second book of the Old Testament, which documents the legendary departure of the Jews from Egypt in ancient times. As a common noun, exodus refers to any situation in which a lot of people leave at the same time. An exodus might be from a war-ravaged region, or it might be from a crowded football stadium at the end of a game.

Exonerated means cleared of blame, accusation, or responsibility. Someone exonerated of a crime has been officially declared not guilty, often after new evidence emerges: {DNA evidence exonerated him after twenty years in prison}. The word carries weight—it suggests not just acquittal but vindication, the lifting of a burden that shouldn't have been there.

Exoneration is the clearing of blame, guilt, or responsibility. A prisoner may receive exoneration when new evidence proves innocence. The word implies formal vindication—not just doubt about guilt, but confirmation that the accused did nothing wrong: {After twenty years, DNA evidence led to his exoneration}. To exonerate is to grant such clearance.

To exorcise is to drive out an evil spirit through ritual or prayer: {The priest exorcised the demon from the possessed girl}. By extension, exorcise means to rid oneself of troubling thoughts, memories, or influences: {She wrote the memoir to exorcise her childhood trauma}. The spelling exorcize is also standard.

Exorcism is the practice of expelling evil spirits or demons from a person, place, or object, typically through religious rituals, prayers, or incantations. The concept appears across many cultures and religions, though it's most associated in the West with Catholic rites performed by priests. {The film depicted a harrowing exorcism that lasted for days.} By extension, exorcism can describe any dramatic attempt to rid oneself of unwanted influences or painful memories.

An exorcist is a person who performs exorcisms—rituals to expel evil spirits or demons from possessed people or places. The role exists across many religious traditions, though in popular culture it's most associated with Catholic priests: {The family called in an exorcist after other interventions failed}. The term also applies more loosely to anyone who banishes unwanted influences.

Exorcists are people who perform exorcisms—rituals intended to expel demons or evil spirits from possessed persons, places, or objects. The role exists across many religious traditions, though Catholic exorcists are perhaps most familiar from popular culture. {The priest trained as an exorcist for years before his first case.} Figuratively, anyone who helps purge unwanted influences might be called an exorcist.

An exoskeleton is a hard external covering that supports and protects an animal's body—the shell of a crab, the carapace of a beetle. Unlike vertebrates with internal skeletons, insects, crustaceans, and arachnids wear their skeletons on the outside. The term also applies to wearable mechanical frameworks that enhance human strength or mobility: {The factory workers use exoskeletons to lift heavy parts without injury}.

Exotic describes something strikingly unusual because it originates from a distant place or unfamiliar culture: {exotic spices}, {exotic birds}, {an exotic accent}. The word carries connotations of allure and fascination—the appeal of the foreign and rare. It can shade into fetishizing difference: calling a person exotic often reduces them to their otherness. An exotic dancer is a stripper, the adjective serving as euphemism.

Expand means to make or become larger, wider, or more extensive. A business expands by opening new locations. Lungs expand when filling with air. To expand on an idea is to develop it further, adding detail or explanation: {Could you expand on that point?} The opposite is contract or shrink.

An expanse is a wide, open area stretching out before you—typically of land, water, or sky: {a vast expanse of desert}, {the blue expanse of the Pacific}. The word emphasizes unbroken continuity and scale. It can extend to abstract domains: {an expanse of time}, {the expanse of human knowledge}.

Expansion is the act of becoming larger or more extensive, or the state that results. A company undergoes expansion when it opens new locations. The expansion of a gas fills available space. Urban expansion pushes city boundaries outward. An expansion can also be an extended version of something: {The director's cut is a two-hour expansion of the original film}. In gaming, an expansion adds new content to an existing game.

An expat is someone living outside their native country, typically for work or lifestyle reasons rather than as a refugee or immigrant. The term carries connotations of choice and often privilege—retirees in Costa Rica, executives in Singapore, writers in Paris. {She's been an expat in Barcelona for fifteen years.} Short for expatriate.

Expats is the plural of expat, a clipped form of expatriate—someone living outside their native country. The term usually implies a voluntary, often privileged relocation: {a community of American expats in Paris}, {British expats retiring to Spain}. Unlike immigrant or refugee, expat suggests choice and often temporary residence, though many stay permanently.

To expect is to consider something likely or certain to happen: {I expect it'll rain tomorrow}. Expect also means to anticipate or await: {We're expecting guests}. When you expect something of someone, you believe they should deliver it: {They expect too much from their employees}. A woman who is expecting is pregnant.

Expectation is what you anticipate will happen or what you believe should happen. You can have expectations about outcomes {(The movie didn't live up to expectations)} or about behavior {(There are certain expectations that come with the job)}. Expectations may be realistic or unrealistic, and they shape how we experience what actually occurs—met expectations satisfy, exceeded ones delight, and unmet ones disappoint.

Expectations are what you anticipate or believe will happen. The word often implies a sense of entitlement or standard: {She had high expectations for the project}. Expectations can be hopes {(against all expectations, he survived)} or demands {(The job didn't meet my expectations)}. To {manage expectations} is to temper what others believe they'll receive. Social expectations are unwritten rules about behavior: {There were certain expectations about how a lady should dress}.

Expected describes what is anticipated or considered likely to happen. An expected {guest} is one whose arrival is planned. Expected {results} are those predicted beforehand. The word often implies a standard or norm: {expected behavior}, {expected performance}. When something falls short of expectations, it's {less than expected}; when it exceeds them, {better than expected}. To be expecting usually means to be pregnant.

Expecting means anticipating or looking forward to something: {I'm expecting a package today}, {We're expecting rain this afternoon}. When used without an object, expecting is a euphemism for pregnant: {She's expecting}, {They're expecting their first child in June}. The pregnant sense has become so common that {expecting} alone usually implies pregnancy rather than general anticipation.

An expedition is a journey undertaken for a specific purpose, especially exploration, research, or military action: {a polar expedition}, {a scientific expedition to the Amazon}. The word also refers to the group making such a journey: {The expedition set out at dawn}. By extension, expedition can describe any organized outing: {a shopping expedition}. The formal noun expedience shares a root but has diverged in meaning.

Expeditions are journeys undertaken for a specific purpose, typically exploration, research, or military action. The word suggests organized effort and planning: {a polar expedition}, {a scientific expedition to the Amazon}. By extension, any purposeful outing can be called an expedition, often with mild humor about its ambition: {a shopping expedition}, {an expedition to the grocery store}.

Expelled is the past tense of expel, meaning to force out or eject. A student expelled from school is permanently removed for misconduct. A country may expel diplomats during political disputes. The word also applies to physical ejection: {The volcano expelled ash and lava}. Being expelled carries a sense of formal, often punitive removal rather than casual departure.

Expendable describes something or someone considered acceptable to sacrifice or use up for a larger goal. Supplies are expendable when they're meant to be consumed. More starkly, soldiers or workers are called expendable when those in charge view their loss as tolerable: {In war, infantry are often treated as expendable}. The word carries a cold, utilitarian edge.

An expense is money spent or cost incurred. Business expenses include rent, salaries, and supplies. Personal expenses cover daily living costs. The plural often appears in set phrases: {travel expenses}, {medical expenses}, {at the company's expense}. To expense something is to charge it to an account or claim reimbursement: {I expensed the client dinner}. Figuratively, {at someone's expense} means to their detriment or as the butt of a joke: {They laughed at his expense}.

Expenses are costs incurred in doing something—running a business, completing a project, or traveling for work. The term often appears in phrases like {business expenses}, {operating expenses}, or {travel expenses}. To expense something is to record it as a cost or submit it for reimbursement: {I'll expense the hotel}. An {expense account} covers work-related costs.

Expensive means costing a lot of money: {an expensive restaurant}, {an expensive mistake}. The word implies a price high enough to give pause or strain a budget. What counts as expensive varies by context—expensive for a meal differs from expensive for a house. Something can be expensive in a good way (worth the cost) or bad (overpriced): {It's expensive, but you get what you pay for}.

As a noun, experience has two related meanings. One is the internal residue of events in your life: Her experience as a lawyer makes her question people’s motives. The other is an event in which you take part and which has an effect on you: I once had a harrowing experience on the New York subway. The verb experience simply means to have an encounter of some kind: People who have never experienced hunger cannot imagine its long-term effects on the mind.

Experienced describes someone who has gained knowledge or skill through practice and exposure over time. An experienced {surgeon} has performed many operations; an experienced {traveler} knows how to navigate airports and foreign cities. The word implies competence earned through doing, not just studying. It can also describe events that have been felt or undergone: {the worst pain I've ever experienced}.

Experiences is the plural of experience, referring to events or occurrences that leave an impression on someone or contribute to their knowledge. The word often emphasizes the subjective or personal nature of what happens: {Her experiences abroad shaped her worldview}. As a verb form, experiences indicates someone undergoing or encountering something: {She experiences anxiety before public speaking}. The noun frequently appears in marketing contexts to describe curated activities or encounters: {The resort offers unique dining experiences}.

An experiment is a test designed to discover something unknown or verify a hypothesis. Scientists conduct experiments by controlling variables and observing outcomes: {The experiment confirmed that the drug reduced symptoms}. The word extends to any deliberate trial of something new: {an experiment in open marriage}, {The restaurant is experimenting with a new menu}. To experiment is to try things out, often with an implication of risk or novelty.

Experimental describes something done as an experiment—testing an idea, method, or product that isn't yet established. An experimental {drug} is still being evaluated. Experimental {music} or {film} breaks from convention to try new forms. The word often signals that results are uncertain or that something exists as a trial rather than a finished product: {The program is still experimental}.

Experimenting is trying things out to see what happens. Scientists experiment with controlled variables; cooks experiment with ingredients; teenagers experiment with identity, drugs, or sexuality. The word suggests openness to outcomes rather than commitment: {We're just experimenting with the relationship}. To experiment is to test possibilities without knowing where they'll lead.

Experiments are tests or trials designed to discover something unknown, demonstrate something known, or examine a hypothesis. Scientists conduct experiments to gather empirical evidence, but the word extends beyond labs: {I've been experimenting with different recipes}. The verb experiment means to carry out such tests, often implying a willingness to try new approaches. {The band experimented with electronic sounds on their latest album.} An experimental treatment or method is one still being tested rather than established.

An expert possesses deep knowledge or skill in a particular field, acquired through study or experience. The word works as both noun and adjective: {She consulted a tax expert}; {expert advice}. Expertise implies mastery beyond ordinary competence—experts are who you call when the problem exceeds normal ability. {He's no expert, but he knows enough to get by}.

Expertise is specialized knowledge or skill in a particular field, typically gained through training and experience. An expert has expertise; a novice lacks it. The word often appears in professional contexts: {legal expertise}, {technical expertise}, {We brought in a consultant for her expertise in cybersecurity}. Unlike mere familiarity, expertise implies depth sufficient to make authoritative judgments.

Expiration is the act of coming to an end or the moment when something ceases to be valid. A driver's license has an expiration {date}. A contract reaches expiration. Food past its expiration may be unsafe. In physiology, expiration is the act of breathing out—exhaling air from the lungs. The related verb is expire.

Expire means to come to an end or cease to be valid. A driver's license expires after a set period. A deadline expires when the time runs out. The word also means to die—to breathe one's last breath: {He expired peacefully in his sleep}. Food and medications expire when they pass their safe-use date. {My membership expired last month.}

Expired means no longer valid, usable, or alive. Food past its expiration date has expired. A passport or license that's no longer current has expired. {My membership expired last month.} When someone dies, especially in formal or euphemistic contexts, they expire: {The patient expired at 3:47 AM.} A lease expires when its term ends. Expired breath is air breathed out.

Expires means reaches the end of validity or usefulness. A passport expires after ten years. A coupon expires on a certain date. Food past its expiration date has expired. The verb also means to breathe out, and by extension, to die—though this sense now sounds literary or clinical: {He expired peacefully in his sleep}.

To explain is to make something clear or understandable by describing it in detail or revealing relevant facts: {Let me explain how this works}, {She explained the procedure step by step}. You explain concepts, reasons, or circumstances. To explain away is to minimize or dismiss with justification: {He tried to explain away his absence}. An explanation that accounts for behavior may excuse it: {That explains everything}.

An explanation is a statement or account that makes something clear or understandable. You might offer an explanation for being late, or seek an explanation of how something works. The word covers both justifications {(What's your explanation for this mess?)} and clarifications {(The teacher's explanation helped)}. To explain is to provide one.

Explicit is an adjective meaning clearly or directly stated: The report contains no explicit statement of what the authors believe. Explicit can also be used to mean “containing direct references to sex”: Parents are concerned that the explicit material on the website will be damaging to children. The opposite of explicit is implicit.

Explode means to burst violently outward with sudden release of energy: {The bomb exploded}. Things that expand rapidly or dramatically also explode: {The population exploded after the war}. A person explodes when anger or laughter erupts uncontrollably: {She exploded at him}. To explode a theory or myth is to disprove it decisively—to blow it apart.

Exploded describes something that has burst apart violently or suddenly: {The bomb exploded}. Beyond physical blasts, it applies to rapid expansion or increase: {The population exploded}. A person who explodes loses their temper suddenly: {She exploded when she heard the news}. An exploded diagram shows components separated but arranged to reveal how they fit together.

Exploding describes something in the act of bursting violently apart, or figuratively, undergoing rapid expansion or intense expression. An {exploding bomb} detonates; an {exploding population} grows dramatically; someone {exploding with rage} releases sudden, forceful emotion. The word captures the moment of rupture or release: {The exploding fireworks lit up the sky}.

To exploit something is to make use of it, often skillfully or to maximum advantage: {exploit natural resources}, {exploit a market opportunity}. The word carries a double edge—it can mean smart utilization or selfish manipulation. To exploit workers is to take unfair advantage of them. An exploit as a noun is a notable deed or feat, especially a bold or daring one: {tales of military exploits}, {the exploits of legendary heroes}. In computing, an exploit is code that takes advantage of a security vulnerability.

Exploitation is the act of using something or someone for benefit—often with connotations of unfairness or extraction. Natural resources are exploited for profit; workers may be exploited through low wages and poor conditions. The word can be neutral {exploitation of new technology} but more often suggests taking advantage: {corporate exploitation of cheap labor}. In film, exploitation refers to low-budget movies emphasizing sensational content: {blaxploitation}, {sexploitation}.

Exploited describes something or someone that has been used, often unfairly or selfishly. An exploited {worker} is taken advantage of—underpaid or overworked for someone else's gain. Exploited {resources} have been extracted or depleted: {The region's oil reserves were heavily exploited}. The word carries connotations of imbalance: one party benefits while another bears the cost.

Exploits works in two directions. As a noun (with stress on the first syllable), exploits are bold or daring deeds—adventures worthy of recounting: {His wartime exploits became legendary}. As a verb (stress on the second syllable), to exploit is to make use of something, often unfairly or selfishly: {The company exploits cheap labor overseas}. In computing, an exploit is code that takes advantage of a software vulnerability.

Exploration is the act of traveling through unfamiliar territory to learn what's there. Early European exploration mapped coastlines and trade routes. The word extends to any systematic investigation of the unknown: {space exploration}, {exploration of new ideas}, {oil exploration}. To explore a topic is to examine it thoroughly. Exploratory describes preliminary investigation: {exploratory surgery}, {exploratory talks}.

To explore is to travel through unfamiliar territory to learn about it: {We spent a week exploring the Scottish Highlands}. The word extends to any systematic examination of the unknown—exploring options, exploring ideas, exploring feelings. In medicine, exploratory surgery investigates what's happening inside the body. Children explore their surroundings; adults explore possibilities. {Let's explore that further.}

An explorer is a person who travels to unfamiliar regions to discover what's there—historically mapping unknown territories, now often investigating remote or extreme environments: {Arctic explorers}, {cave explorers}. The word extends to anyone who investigates the unfamiliar: {an explorer of ideas}, {urban explorers} who document abandoned buildings. Explorer can also name vehicles or tools designed for investigation. (Capitalized Explorer is a Microsoft web browser or a Ford SUV model.)

Explorers is the plural of explorer—people who travel to unfamiliar places to discover or investigate. The word applies both to historical figures who mapped unknown territories {the Spanish explorers of the Americas} and to anyone venturing into uncharted areas, whether physical, intellectual, or creative: {explorers of the deep sea}, {explorers of consciousness}.

Exploring is the activity of investigating unfamiliar territory or subjects. You might spend an afternoon exploring a new city, or years exploring the limits of human knowledge. The word suggests curiosity and openness to discovery: {We're still exploring our options}. Children explore their surroundings; scientists explore hypotheses; couples explore each other's bodies.

An explosion is a sudden, violent release of energy—a bomb detonating, a gas tank rupturing, a chemical reaction going wrong. The word extends to any rapid, dramatic increase: {an explosion of interest in AI}, {a population explosion}. Something explosive can literally blow up or figuratively erupt: an explosive {temper}, explosive {growth}.

Explosions is the plural of explosion—a sudden, violent release of energy, typically with a loud noise and rapid expansion of gases. Bombs cause explosions; so do chemical reactions and pressure buildups. The word extends to any sudden outburst: {an explosion of laughter}, {a population explosion}, {an explosion of color across the canvas}.

Explosive describes something capable of exploding—detonating with sudden, violent force. An explosive device contains materials that combust rapidly. As a noun, an explosive is such a material: dynamite, C-4, gunpowder. The meaning extends to anything that erupts suddenly or intensely: an explosive {temper}, explosive {growth}, an explosive {situation}. In sports, explosive describes powerful, sudden movement: {explosive speed off the line}.

Explosives are substances or devices that undergo rapid chemical reactions releasing large amounts of gas and energy, producing violent expansion. The term covers everything from dynamite and TNT to plastic explosives and improvised bombs. {The building was demolished with explosives}. Explosive can also function as an adjective: {explosive materials}, {an explosive temper}.

Expo is short for exposition, meaning a large public exhibition or trade show: {the world expo}, {a home and garden expo}. The informal clipping has largely replaced the fuller form in everyday speech. Expos showcase products, industries, or innovations, typically running for several days and drawing crowds from various regions.

Export means to send goods or services to another country for sale or trade: {Coffee is Brazil's major export}. The word extends to sending data out of one program or format into another: {Export the file as a PDF}. As a noun, an export is a product sent abroad, or the act of sending it. To export an idea or practice is to spread it elsewhere: {Hollywood exports American culture worldwide}.

Exports are goods or services sent to another country for sale. A nation's exports represent what it sells abroad, as opposed to imports, which come in: {Oil is their primary export}. The verb export means to send products out of a country or, more broadly, to spread something outward: {Hollywood exports American culture worldwide}. In computing, to export is to convert data for use in another program.

Expose means to uncover or make visible something that was hidden or protected. You expose skin by removing clothing, expose film by letting in light, expose a lie by revealing truth. To expose someone to something is to subject them to it: {children exposed to violence}, {patients exposed to the virus}. An exposé (with the accent) is a journalistic revelation of wrongdoing. To expose oneself is to display one's genitals publicly—a criminal act in most jurisdictions.

Exposed means uncovered or unprotected—open to view, harm, or the elements. An exposed {wire} lacks insulation. An exposed {hillside} has no shelter from wind. To feel exposed is to feel vulnerable, whether physically or emotionally: {Standing at the podium, she felt completely exposed}. In photography, exposed film has been subjected to light. A scandal exposes wrongdoing; the wrongdoer is then exposed.

Exposition is the act of explaining or setting forth ideas clearly. In writing and drama, exposition provides background information—character histories, settings, prior events—that audiences need to understand what follows: {The first chapter is mostly exposition}. An exposition is also a large public exhibition showcasing products, industries, or achievements: {the World's Fair exposition of 1893}.

Exposure is the state of being unprotected or uncovered. You can die of exposure to cold, or suffer exposure to harmful substances. Public exposure means being seen or known: {The scandal brought unwanted exposure}. Media exposure can build a career. In photography, exposure is the amount of light reaching the film or sensor, or a single frame: {I have a few exposures left on this roll}. To expose oneself is to display one's genitals publicly—indecent exposure.

The noun and adjective express have to do with rapid movement; the verb express means to manifest in some communicable or understandable form (express an opinion, express anger). Things are characterized with the adjective express to distinguish them from slower things: The restaurant offered express delivery. As a noun, express may designate a mode of fast service, or a vessel: Take the 5 o’clock express.

Expression is the act of conveying thought, feeling, or meaning outward—through words, art, gestures, or facial movements. A {pained expression} crosses someone's face. Freedom of {expression} protects speech and creative work. In mathematics, an expression is a combination of symbols representing a value: {algebraic expression}. To do something {as an expression of} gratitude or love is to communicate that feeling through action.

A broad approach in art, literature, music, and drama that emphasizes subjective emotional experience over realistic representation. The artist distorts or exaggerates reality to express inner feelings rather than depict outward appearances. The term applies loosely to any work prioritizing emotional intensity: {The painting had a raw expressionism that unsettled viewers}. (Capitalized Expressionism refers to the specific early 20th-century movement.)

Expressions are outward manifestations of inner states. A facial expression reveals emotion—joy, disgust, surprise. An expression is also a word or phrase: {That's an odd expression}. In mathematics, an expression is a combination of symbols representing a value. To express is to convey meaning outward, and expressions are what results. {Her expression said everything her words didn't}.

Expressive describes something that effectively conveys meaning, feeling, or character. An expressive {face} reveals emotion readily. Expressive {language} communicates vividly. An expressive {performance} moves the audience. The word often implies emotional transparency or artistic power: {Her eyes were remarkably expressive}. In linguistics, expressive language is the ability to produce speech, contrasted with receptive language (comprehension).

Expulsion is the act of forcing someone or something out. A student faces expulsion from school for serious misconduct. A country may order the expulsion of foreign diplomats. The word applies to physical ejection too: {the expulsion of air from the lungs}, {the expulsion of waste from the body}. Where dismissal might be voluntary, expulsion implies forcible removal.

Exquisite describes something of exceptional beauty, craftsmanship, or refinement—the kind that rewards close attention: {exquisite embroidery}, {an exquisite wine}. The word often implies delicacy or intricacy: {exquisite detail}. Exquisite can also intensify sensations, pleasant or not: {exquisite pleasure}, {exquisite pain}. The underlying sense is something so finely wrought it stands apart from the ordinary.

Extend means to stretch out or make longer. You extend an {arm}, extend a {deadline}, extend a {road}. The meaning broadens to offering: extend an {invitation}, extend {credit}, extend {sympathy}. Something that extends covers a certain distance or duration: {The forest extends for miles}. Extended means lengthened or prolonged: an extended {warranty}, an extended {stay}.

Extension is the act of stretching something out or the state of being stretched. A limb held straight is in extension. An extension cord lengthens an electrical connection. A deadline extension grants more time. A phone extension connects to the main line. A building extension adds space. In computing, a file extension (like .pdf or .jpg) indicates format. Hair extensions add length. The word covers anything that extends—literally or figuratively—the reach of something else.

Exterior refers to the outer surface or appearance of something, as opposed to its interior: {the exterior of the building}, {exterior walls}. It extends to outward manner or behavior that may not reflect inner reality: {His calm exterior hid considerable anxiety}. As an adjective, exterior describes what is outside or outward-facing: {exterior paint}, {exterior lighting}.

To exterminate is to destroy completely, especially to kill off an entire population of pests or people. Exterminators eliminate rats and roaches; genocides exterminate ethnic groups. The word implies thoroughness—not just killing some, but wiping out all: {The regime sought to exterminate its political opponents}. Extermination carries clinical coldness, suggesting systematic rather than passionate violence.

Exterminated means completely destroyed or killed off. The word applies to deliberate, thorough elimination—of pests, populations, or groups: {The invasive species was exterminated from the island}. When applied to people, exterminated carries the cold efficiency of genocide or mass killing: {Millions were exterminated in the camps}.

Extermination is the complete destruction or elimination of something, especially a population. The word typically describes killing on a mass scale: the extermination of pests, the extermination of indigenous peoples, the extermination of Jews in Nazi death camps. {The landlord called for extermination of the roaches}. The clinical tone can mask horror when applied to humans.

An exterminator is a person or company that kills pests—insects, rodents, or other unwanted creatures in homes and buildings. The work involves traps, poisons, and pesticides: {We called the exterminator about the roaches}. The term also applies more broadly to anyone who destroys or eliminates something completely.

Exterminators are people or companies hired to eliminate pests—insects, rodents, or other unwanted creatures—from buildings or properties. The term emphasizes killing rather than removal: {We called the exterminators about the termites}. Figuratively, an exterminator destroys or eliminates anything systematically: {an exterminator of hope}.

Extinct describes something that no longer exists. A species becomes extinct when its last member dies: {Dinosaurs went extinct millions of years ago}. The word extends to anything that has disappeared entirely—extinct languages, extinct volcanoes (no longer active), extinct customs. To be extinct is to be gone permanently, beyond recovery.

Extinction is the state of no longer existing—when every member of a species has died, leaving none alive: {The dodo was hunted to extinction}. The word extends beyond biology: extinction of a debt means paying it off completely, and behavioral extinction occurs when a response disappears after reinforcement stops. To face extinction is to face complete elimination: {Without intervention, the language faces extinction within a generation}.

Extinctions is the plural of extinction, which denotes the complete dying out of a species or the end of something's existence. Scientists track mass extinctions in Earth's history, such as the one that killed the dinosaurs. The term extends beyond biology to describe the disappearance of languages, cultures, or practices. {Human activity has accelerated the rate of extinctions worldwide.} In psychology, extinction refers to the gradual weakening of a conditioned response when reinforcement stops.

To extinguish is to put out a fire or light: {Extinguish all campfires before leaving}. The word extends to ending or eliminating anything: extinguish a {debt}, extinguish {hope}, extinguish a {species}. To extinguish a right is to terminate it legally. The formal tone makes extinguish more common in official contexts than everyday speech—you put out a cigarette but extinguish a blaze.

To extort is to obtain something—usually money—through force, threats, or abuse of power. The threat may be physical harm, exposure of secrets, or misuse of official authority: {The gang extorted protection money from local businesses}. Extortion differs from robbery in relying on intimidation rather than direct taking. Someone who extorts is an extortionist.

Extorted is the past tense of extort—to obtain something, typically money, through force, threats, or intimidation. The word implies coercion rather than voluntary exchange: {He extorted thousands from local businesses by threatening violence}. What's extorted is usually money or favors, and the extorter typically exploits a position of power or knowledge of damaging secrets.

Extorting is obtaining something—usually money—through threats, intimidation, or abuse of power. The threat might be physical harm, exposure of damaging information, or misuse of official authority: {The gang was extorting local businesses for protection money}. Extorting differs from robbery in relying on coercion rather than direct force.

Extortion is obtaining money, property, or cooperation through threats or coercion. The threat might be violence, exposure of damaging information, or abuse of official power. Unlike robbery, which takes by force, extortion compels the victim to hand something over: {The gang ran an extortion racket on local businesses}. Blackmail is extortion through threatened exposure.

Extra means beyond what is usual, expected, or necessary. An extra blanket provides additional warmth; extra credit offers bonus points. As a noun, an extra is something added—a car with all the extras—or a person hired to appear in the background of a film. As an adverb, extra intensifies: {extra large}, {extra careful}. In recent slang, extra describes someone being excessive or dramatic: {She's being so extra right now}.

Extract centers on the idea of pulling something out from a larger whole. You extract a tooth from a jaw, a confession from a suspect, data from a database. The noun extract is the concentrated substance drawn from something—vanilla extract, plant extract. A literary extract is a passage pulled from a longer work. The process often implies effort or force: {extracting information from reluctant witnesses}, {extracting meaning from a difficult text}.

Extraction is the act of removing or pulling something out—often with effort or specialized methods. A dentist performs a tooth extraction. In chemistry, extraction separates a substance from a mixture. Military forces conduct extractions to retrieve personnel from dangerous areas. Extraction also refers to ancestry or origin: {a family of Italian extraction}.

Extradition is the legal process of surrendering a person from one jurisdiction to another to face criminal charges or serve a sentence. Countries negotiate extradition treaties specifying which offenses qualify and what protections apply. {The U.S. sought his extradition from Mexico on drug trafficking charges.} A person who flees to a country without an extradition treaty may avoid prosecution.

Extraordinary means beyond the ordinary—exceptional, remarkable, or surpassing what is usual. An extraordinary {talent} stands out from the crowd. Extraordinary {measures} go beyond normal procedures. The word can intensify almost any noun: extraordinary {beauty}, extraordinary {circumstances}, extraordinary {luck}. In formal contexts, extraordinary may indicate something outside regular arrangements: an {ambassador extraordinary}, an {extraordinary session} of Congress.

Extras are additional items beyond what's standard or expected. A movie's extras are the unnamed performers who populate background scenes. In cricket, extras are runs scored without the batsman hitting the ball. On a bill, extras are charges beyond the base price. The word often implies optional additions: {The car comes with leather seats and other extras}. In film production, to work as an extra is entry-level acting work requiring no lines.

Extraterrestrial means originating or existing outside Earth or its atmosphere. As an adjective, it describes phenomena beyond our planet: {extraterrestrial life}, {extraterrestrial intelligence}. As a noun, an extraterrestrial is a being from another world—the alien of science fiction. The word is often shortened to ET: {The search for ET continues}.

Extravagance is spending or behavior that exceeds what's reasonable or necessary. The word carries a sense of excess—too much money, too much flair, too much of anything: {The wedding was an extravagance they couldn't afford}. An extravagance can be a specific indulgent purchase: {The sports car was his one extravagance}. The term sometimes suggests admirable boldness rather than wastefulness: {the extravagance of her imagination}.

Extravagant means exceeding reasonable limits, especially in spending money: {an extravagant lifestyle}, {extravagant gifts}. The word suggests excess beyond what's necessary or prudent.
