Extravagant praise or claims are exaggerated or overblown. An extravagant production is elaborate and costly. The noun extravagance covers both the quality and specific instances: {such extravagance!}, {We can't afford these extravagances}.

An extravaganza is a spectacular, elaborate production—typically entertainment on a grand scale with lavish sets, costumes, and effects: {The halftime show was a musical extravaganza}. The word implies excess and showiness, sometimes with a hint of overindulgence: {a shopping extravaganza}, {a fireworks extravaganza}. Any event designed to impress through sheer scale or abundance qualifies.

Extreme marks the farthest possible point on a scale or spectrum. An extreme {temperature} is very hot or very cold. Extreme {measures} go beyond what's normal or moderate. An {extreme sport} involves exceptional risk. As a noun, extremes are the outermost limits: {the extremes of wealth and poverty}. To {go to extremes} is to act excessively. {In the extreme} means to the highest degree: {The situation was dangerous in the extreme}.

Extremes are the farthest points on a spectrum or the most intense versions of something. In temperature, the extremes are scorching heat and bitter cold. In politics, the extremes are radical positions at opposite ends. To {go to extremes} is to take excessive action: {She went to extremes to prove her point}. The phrase {in the extreme} means to the highest degree: {The situation was dangerous in the extreme}.

Extremism is holding political, religious, or ideological views far outside the mainstream, especially views that advocate radical action or reject compromise. The term is almost always applied by outsiders—few call themselves extremists: {The government cracked down on religious extremism}. What counts as extreme shifts with time and context; yesterday's extremism sometimes becomes tomorrow's orthodoxy.

An extremist holds views far outside the mainstream, typically in politics or religion, and often advocates radical action to advance them. The term is almost always applied by opponents rather than claimed by the people it describes: {The government labeled the protesters extremists}. As an adjective, it describes such views or groups: {extremist ideology}, {extremist factions}.

Extremists are people who hold radical political, religious, or ideological views far outside the mainstream. The term implies not just strong beliefs but willingness to pursue them through uncompromising or violent means: {The group was infiltrated by extremists}. Whether someone counts as an extremist depends heavily on the speaker's own position—one person's extremist is another's freedom fighter.

Extroversion is a personality trait marked by outward focus—drawing energy from social interaction, external stimulation, and engagement with the world. An extrovert thrives in company and may feel drained by too much solitude. The term comes from psychology, where it pairs with introversion as opposite ends of a spectrum: {Her extroversion makes her a natural networker}. Also spelled extraversion, especially in technical contexts.

An extrovert is a person who draws energy from social interaction and external stimulation, typically outgoing and talkative. The term comes from psychology but now appears in everyday speech: {She's a total extrovert—parties energize her}. The spelling extravert appears in technical contexts. The opposite is introvert.

Extroverted describes someone who draws energy from social interaction and external stimulation. An extroverted person tends to be outgoing, talkative, and comfortable in groups: {She's too extroverted to enjoy working from home}. The opposite is introverted. Also spelled extraverted, especially in psychology.

Extroverts are people who gain energy from social interaction and external stimulation. The term comes from psychology, contrasting with introverts. Extroverts tend to be outgoing, talkative, and energized by being around others: {The extroverts at the party were still going strong at midnight}. The spelling extravert appears in clinical contexts but extrovert dominates in everyday use.

Exuberance is lively, unrestrained enthusiasm or energy: {youthful exuberance}, {the exuberance of the crowd}. It suggests abundance spilling over—too much vitality to contain. The word extends to luxuriant growth: {the exuberance of tropical vegetation}. Alan Greenspan famously warned of {irrational exuberance} in financial markets—enthusiasm untethered from reality.

Eye denotes the light-sensitive organ with which humans and other organisms process visual stimuli. From this meaning a number of other meanings have developed that are connected with sight or vision. Other physical structures that bear a resemblance to the eye are also called eye, such as the eye of a storm or the eye of a needle. Eye occurs as often in the plural as the singular, reflecting the fact that most organisms have two.

An eyeball is the spherical organ of sight, housed in the eye socket. The term often emphasizes the physical globe itself: {His eyeballs darted back and forth}. To eyeball something is to look at it directly or estimate by sight rather than measurement: {She eyeballed the distance at about ten feet}. To be {up to your eyeballs} in something is to be overwhelmed by it.

Eyeballed is the past tense of eyeball, meaning to look at something closely or to estimate by sight rather than measurement: {She eyeballed the distance and figured it was about thirty feet}. To eyeball someone is to stare at them, often with suspicion or hostility: {The bouncer eyeballed us as we walked in}.

Eyeballing is estimating or measuring something by sight alone, without instruments or precise calculation: {I was just eyeballing the distance—maybe fifty feet?} The term suggests rough approximation rather than accuracy. Eyeballing can also mean looking at someone or something intently, often with suspicion or interest: {He kept eyeballing me from across the room}.

Eyeballs are the spherical organs of sight that sit in the eye sockets. The word emphasizes the physical, globular nature of the eye rather than the sense of vision itself. In informal usage, eyeballs often means attention or views: {We need more eyeballs on this website}. To eyeball something is to look at it carefully or to estimate by sight rather than measurement: {I eyeballed the distance at about fifty feet}.

The eyebrow is the arch of hair above each eye. Eyebrows protect the eyes from sweat and debris, but their expressive function dominates: raised eyebrows signal surprise or skepticism, furrowed brows suggest concentration or anger. To {raise an eyebrow} is to express doubt or disapproval. Something that {raises eyebrows} causes surprise or mild shock.

Eyebrows are the strips of hair growing above each eye, following the curve of the brow bone. They help keep sweat and debris from the eyes and play a major role in facial expression—raised eyebrows signal surprise, furrowed ones concentration or anger. To {raise eyebrows} is to cause surprise or mild shock: {Her comments raised a few eyebrows at the meeting}.

An eyelash is one of the short hairs that grow along the edge of the eyelid. Eyelashes help protect the eye from dust and debris. They figure in expressions of narrow margins: {She won by an eyelash}. To {bat one's eyelashes} is to flutter them flirtatiously or in feigned innocence.

Eyelashes are the short hairs that grow along the edge of the eyelids, curving outward from the eye. They help protect the eye from dust and debris. Long or thick eyelashes are considered attractive, prompting various enhancement methods: {She wore false eyelashes to the gala}. To {bat one's eyelashes} is to flutter them flirtatiously.

An eyelid is the fold of skin that covers and protects the eye when closed. Humans have upper and lower eyelids, though the upper does most of the work in blinking and sleeping. To {not bat an eyelid} is to show no reaction to something surprising or disturbing.

Eyelids are the folds of skin that close over the eyes. They protect the eye and spread moisture across its surface with each blink. Heavy eyelids signal drowsiness: {I could barely keep my eyelids open}. Drooping eyelids may indicate fatigue, aging, or medical conditions. Cosmetics and surgery often focus on the eyelids as expressive features of the face.

Eyeliner is a cosmetic applied along the edges of the eyelids to define or accentuate the eyes. It comes in pencil, liquid, gel, and felt-tip forms, each producing different effects from soft and smudged to sharp and dramatic: {She applied a thin line of eyeliner to her upper lid}. Winged eyeliner extends past the outer corner of the eye.

An eyepatch is a covering worn over one eye, held in place by a strap or cord around the head. Eyepatches protect injured eyes or conceal missing ones. The black eyepatch is iconic pirate imagery: {He dressed as a pirate with an eyepatch and hook hand}. Medical eyepatches treat conditions like amblyopia by forcing the weaker eye to work.

An eyeroll is a gesture of exasperation, disbelief, or contempt—rotating the eyes upward or to the side to signal that something is ridiculous or tiresome. The gesture and the word appear as both noun and verb: {She gave an eyeroll when he started mansplaining}; {I couldn't help but eyeroll at that excuse}. Also spelled eye-roll or eye roll.

Eyerolls are upward rotations of the eyes expressing exasperation, disbelief, or dismissive contempt. The gesture signals that something is too stupid or tedious to deserve a proper response: {Her suggestion was met with eyerolls from the entire team}. Often spelled as two words: eye rolls.

Eyes are the organs of sight, set in sockets on either side of the nose. The word extends to anything resembling an eye: the eye of a needle, the eye of a storm, the eye of a potato. To eye something is to look at it with interest or suspicion: {She eyed the contract warily}. Eyes often stand for attention or judgment: {all eyes were on her}, {in the eyes of the law}. To {see eye to eye} is to agree.

Eyeshadow is cosmetic powder or cream applied to the eyelids to add color and depth around the eyes. It comes in countless shades and finishes—matte, shimmer, glitter—and can be subtle or dramatic: {She blended three shades of eyeshadow for a smoky eye}. Also spelled as two words: eye shadow.

An eyesore is something unpleasant to look at, especially a building or structure that mars its surroundings: {The abandoned factory is an eyesore on Main Street}. The word suggests visual offense in an otherwise acceptable setting—not just ugliness, but ugliness that stands out and bothers people.

An eyewitness is someone who personally saw an event happen, especially a crime or accident: {Police are looking for eyewitnesses to the shooting}. Eyewitness testimony carries weight in court because the person observed directly rather than hearing about it secondhand. As a verb, to eyewitness something is to see it happen: {She eyewitnessed the whole thing}.

A fable is a short story that teaches a moral lesson, typically featuring animals who speak and act like humans. Aesop's fables—the tortoise and the hare, the fox and the grapes—established the form. By extension, fable can mean any fictitious tale or falsehood: {His account of that night was pure fable}. The adjective fabled means legendary or famous: {the fabled city of El Dorado}.

Fabled describes something famous from legend or story—creatures, places, or treasures that exist primarily in myth: {the fabled city of Atlantis}, {a fabled dragon}. By extension, it applies to real things so celebrated they seem legendary: {the fabled wealth of the Rockefellers}, {her fabled generosity}. The word carries an air of wonder and renown.

Fables are short stories, typically featuring animals or mythical creatures as characters, that convey a moral lesson. Aesop's fables are the most famous examples in Western tradition, teaching practical wisdom through tales of foxes, tortoises, and ants. The term extends to any fictitious narrative or falsehood: {His account of that night was pure fable}. As a verb, to fable means to tell or invent such stories, though this use is now rare and literary.

Fabric is cloth or textile material, woven or knitted from fibers: {cotton fabric}, {a fabric store}. The word extends to any underlying structure or framework: {the fabric of society}, {the social fabric}. In construction, fabric refers to the basic structure of a building. The metaphorical uses emphasize interconnection—threads woven together to form something larger.

Fabricated describes something invented or constructed, often with an implication of falseness. A fabricated story is made up rather than true: {The witness fabricated her testimony}. Fabricated evidence is manufactured to deceive. In manufacturing, fabricated refers to something built from components: {fabricated metal parts}. The word carries suspicion—what's fabricated usually shouldn't have been.

Fabricating is making or building something, especially by assembling parts: {The company fabricates steel components for bridges}. The word also means inventing or making up, particularly falsehoods: {He was caught fabricating evidence}, {She accused him of fabricating the whole story}. Both senses share the idea of constructing something that didn't exist before—whether a physical object or a lie.

Fabrication is something made up—an invention or lie presented as truth: {His alibi turned out to be a complete fabrication}. The word also means the act of constructing or manufacturing something, especially from components: {metal fabrication}, {the fabrication of circuit boards}. Both senses share the idea of making something that didn't exist before.

Fabulous originally meant like something from a fable—mythical, legendary, extraordinary beyond belief. That sense of amazement survives when something is {fabulous} enough to seem unreal: {fabulous wealth}, {fabulous success}. In casual use, fabulous has softened to enthusiastic praise for anything impressive or delightful: {The party was fabulous}. The word carries a particular association with gay culture and camp aesthetics.

A facade is the front or face of a building, especially an architecturally significant one. The word extends to any outward appearance that conceals something different behind it: {His confidence was just a facade}. A facade suggests deliberate presentation—what you show the world versus what lies beneath. Also spelled façade.

Facades is the plural of facade, the front face of a building, especially an ornamental one: {The facades along Main Street date to the 1890s}. The figurative sense—an outward appearance concealing something different—extends naturally: {Behind their cheerful facades, both families were struggling}. Also spelled façades, retaining the French cedilla.

The front of the head, where sense organs are concentrated, is the face, and this meaning inspires all other uses of the word. The expression you are wearing is your face: Put on a happy face. Face distinguishes the front or visible part of objects: (clock face, cliff face). The main uses of the verb face are spatial (a building that faces the square) or psychological: They do not seem ready to face their problems.

Faceless describes someone or something without a distinct identity or individual character. A faceless {bureaucrat} is an anonymous figure in a larger system. Faceless {corporations} lack human personality. The word often carries negative connotations of impersonality or menace: {faceless attackers}, {a faceless crowd}. Literally, it means lacking a face or having features obscured.

A facelift is a cosmetic surgical procedure that tightens facial skin to reduce signs of aging such as wrinkles and sagging. The term extends to any renovation or update that refreshes the appearance of something without fundamentally changing it: {The old theater got a facelift last year.} {The website's facelift made it look more modern.} Whether applied to faces or buildings, the word suggests cosmetic improvement rather than structural overhaul.

Facelifts is the plural of facelift, a cosmetic surgical procedure that tightens facial skin to reduce signs of aging. The term extends to any renovation that refreshes appearance without fundamental change: {The old theater got a facelift last year}. As a verb, to facelift is to give such treatment: {They facelifted the entire downtown strip}.

A facemask is a covering worn over the nose and mouth. Medical facemasks protect against airborne particles and pathogens: {Wear a facemask in the hospital}. In football, the facemask is the protective metal cage attached to a helmet, and grabbing an opponent's facemask draws a penalty. Beauty facemasks are treatments applied to cleanse or moisturize the skin.

A faceoff is a direct confrontation between opposing sides. In hockey, it's the method of starting play—two players face each other while an official drops the puck between them. The term extends to any showdown or competitive clash: {Tonight's debate is a faceoff between the two frontrunners}. Also spelled face-off.

Facepalm is the gesture of covering your face with your palm, expressing exasperation, embarrassment, or disbelief at something foolish—usually someone else's stupidity, but sometimes your own. The word emerged from internet culture, where it often appears as a reaction: {When he asked if Africa was a country, I facepalmed}. As a noun: {That comment deserves a facepalm}.

Facepalming is the act of slapping or covering one's face with the palm of the hand, expressing frustration, embarrassment, or disbelief—typically at someone else's stupidity or one's own mistake. The gesture became a popular internet meme, often captioned or referenced in text: {I'm facepalming so hard right now}. The noun facepalm and verb facepalm are more common than this participial form.

A faceplant is a fall in which someone lands face-first on the ground, typically with sudden, ungraceful impact. Common in skateboarding, cycling, and other activities where forward momentum meets an abrupt stop: {He hit a crack in the sidewalk and did a total faceplant}. As a verb: {She faceplanted on the ice}. The term extends to spectacular public failures: {The product launch was a complete faceplant}.

Faceplanted is the past tense of faceplant—to fall forward and hit the ground face-first: {She tripped on the curb and faceplanted right in front of everyone}. The term often describes spectacular or embarrassing falls, especially in skateboarding, snowboarding, or other action sports. Figuratively, to faceplant is to fail dramatically: {The product launch completely faceplanted}.

Faceplants is the plural of faceplant—a fall in which someone lands face-first on the ground. The term comes from skateboarding and snowboarding but applies to any such tumble: {The compilation video was nothing but faceplants}. As a verb, to faceplant is to fall this way: {She faceplanted on the ice}.

Faces is the plural of face—the front of the head, or any surface presented outward. A building has faces; a cliff face looms over hikers; a die has six faces. The verb faces means to confront or orient toward something: {The house faces the ocean}. To make faces is to contort your expression, usually for humor or mockery.

A facet is one side or aspect of something with multiple parts. The term comes from the flat polished surfaces of a cut gemstone, each angled to catch light differently. By extension, any complex subject has facets: {We need to consider every facet of the problem}. The facets of a compound eye are its individual visual units.

Facetime is in-person interaction, as distinguished from communication by phone, email, or text. The word gained currency alongside digital communication—when so much contact became virtual, a term emerged for the real thing: {I need some facetime with the boss before the decision gets made}. In workplace contexts, facetime often implies visible presence for its own sake: {He's not productive, just putting in facetime}. (Capitalized FaceTime is Apple's video-calling application.)

Facets are the flat polished surfaces cut into a gemstone to reflect light. By extension, facets are any of the many sides or aspects of something complex: {The story explores different facets of grief}. A multifaceted problem has many dimensions requiring consideration. The word suggests that what you see depends on which angle you're viewing from.

Facial relates to the face: facial {hair}, facial {expressions}, facial {features}. A facial is a skincare treatment involving cleansing, exfoliating, and moisturizing the face. In pornography, a facial is ejaculation onto someone's face.

Facility is a place or building designed for a particular purpose: a manufacturing {facility}, a medical {facility}, a research {facility}. The word often appears in bureaucratic or institutional contexts where it sounds more formal than "building" or "place." Facility also means ease or skill in doing something: {She speaks French with great facility}. The plural facilities commonly refers to restrooms: {Where are the facilities?}

Facing is the direction something points or looks toward: {The house has a southern facing}. In construction, facing is material applied to the exterior of a building for appearance or protection: {brick facing}, {stone facing}. In sewing, facing is fabric sewn inside a garment's edge to finish it neatly. To be facing something is to confront it: {facing a difficult decision}, {facing the consequences}.

A fact is something that actually exists, or a statement that is true. Since the number of things conceivable or presentable as facts is infinite, fact turns out to be a very frequent word. In law, fact has a more specific and limited meaning: it denotes an actual event or circumstance, as distinct from an effect or consequence.

To factcheck is to verify the accuracy of claims, statements, or published information. The practice became prominent with political journalism: {The newspaper factchecks candidates' debate claims}. A factcheck (noun) is the verification itself or a published assessment of accuracy: {The factcheck revealed several misleading statistics}. Also spelled fact-check.

A faction is a group within a larger organization that has distinct interests or goals, often in conflict with other groups: {The party split into rival factions}. The word carries connotations of division and internal struggle—factions form when unity breaks down. In gaming and fiction, factions are competing groups players can join or oppose: {Which faction did you choose?}

Factions are groups within a larger organization that hold distinct positions or pursue separate interests, often in opposition to other groups or the whole: {Warring factions within the party threatened to derail the nomination}. The word implies internal division—a country doesn't have factions, but its government might. In gaming, factions are competing teams or allegiances players can join.

In one sense, factor is a near synonym of element, designating a thing that can be analyzed in a context and identified: factors that contribute to juvenile delinquency. Factor also has several specialized meanings in mathematics, law, and accounting. If you factor something in, you take into account its influence or effects. If you factor a number, you identify its factors (that is, the numbers that when multiplied are equal to it).

Factories is the plural of factory—buildings or complexes where goods are manufactured, typically using machinery and assembly-line production. The word evokes industrial-scale operations: {Factories churned out munitions during the war}. Figuratively, any place producing things in volume: {a diploma factory}, {a hit factory}.

Factors are elements that contribute to a result or outcome: {Several factors influenced her decision}. In mathematics, factors are numbers that multiply together to produce another number—2 and 3 are factors of 6. To factor is to break something into its component parts, or to include it in consideration: {You need to factor in the cost of shipping}. To {factor out} is to exclude from consideration or, in math, to extract a common element from an expression.

A factory is a building or complex where goods are manufactured, typically using machinery and assembly lines: {The factory produces car parts}. The word extends to any site of mass production: {a puppy factory}, {a diploma factory}. Factory farming raises livestock in high-density, industrial conditions. A factory {worker} or factory {job} suggests manual labor in manufacturing.

Facts are things known to be true or to have happened, as opposed to opinions, beliefs, or interpretations. A fact can be verified: {The fact that she was there is undisputed}. To say something is {a fact} emphasizes its truth. {In fact} and {as a matter of fact} introduce corrections or clarifications. {The fact of the matter} is the real situation beneath appearances.

Faculty has two main clusters of meaning. One refers to an inherent ability or power: the faculty of {speech}, mental {faculties}, the faculty of {reason}. The other refers to the teaching staff of a school or university, or a division within one: {the faculty voted to change the curriculum}, {the Faculty of Arts and Sciences}. A person might join the faculty or attend a faculty meeting.

A fad is something that becomes wildly popular for a short time, then fades away—a fashion, activity, or craze that burns bright but doesn't last. Pet rocks, fidget spinners, and dance crazes are classic fads. The word carries a slightly dismissive tone, implying the enthusiasm is shallow: {Is this a fad or a real trend?} A fad diet promises quick results but rarely delivers lasting change.

Fade describes gradual disappearance or loss of intensity. Colors fade in sunlight, sounds fade into silence, memories fade with time. A person who fades grows weaker or withdraws: {She faded after the diagnosis}. In film and audio, a fade is a gradual transition to or from black or silence. In golf, a fade curves gently left to right (for right-handers). To fade someone in slang is to ignore or dismiss them.

Faded describes something that has lost its original brightness, intensity, or strength. Colors fade in sunlight; jeans fade with washing. Memories fade over time. A faded photograph has dulled with age. In slang, faded means intoxicated—high or drunk: {I got so faded last night}. The term suggests being diminished from a normal state, whether cloth, recollection, or sobriety.

Fading describes something growing dimmer, weaker, or less distinct over time. Light fades at dusk. Colors fade in sunlight. Memories fade with age. A fading star loses brightness or fame. In audio and film, fading is the gradual decrease in volume or visibility: {The scene ended with the music fading to silence}. What's fading is in the process of disappearing but hasn't gone yet.

Fads are passing enthusiasms—trends that catch on quickly and fade just as fast. Pet rocks, fidget spinners, dance crazes: each dominated briefly, then vanished. The word carries a dismissive edge, implying the interest is shallow or fleeting: {Is this a genuine movement or just another fad?} Fad diets promise quick results but rarely last.

The verb fail is the opposite of succeed. You can fail an exam, a year in school, or an inspection. If a business fails it goes bankrupt. If you fail to do something, you do not do it. Without fail is used as a stronger version of always, to suggest that failure must be avoided. Failure is the normal verbal noun of fail but in recent use, fail is a count noun in its own right: Her attempt at the pole vault was a huge fail.

Failed describes something that did not succeed or has ceased to function properly. A failed {attempt} didn't achieve its goal. A failed {state} can no longer perform basic governmental functions. A failed {marriage} ended in divorce. The word often marks someone who didn't succeed at their intended role: a failed {actor}, a failed {businessman}. Failed can also describe mechanical breakdown: a failed {engine}, a failed {kidney}.
Failing is a participle that can be used as a preposition, where it means in the absence of.

Fails is the verb fail in its third-person singular form: {The engine fails}, {She never fails to impress}. As a plural noun, fails are instances of failure, especially humorous or embarrassing ones shared online: {epic fails}, {compilation of cooking fails}. This noun usage emerged from internet culture, where fail became a standalone exclamation of mockery.

A failsafe is a mechanism designed to prevent harm if something goes wrong—a backup that activates automatically when the primary system fails. A nuclear reactor's failsafe shuts it down if cooling fails. As an adjective, failsafe describes systems built with such protections: {failsafe brakes}, {failsafe procedures}. The word implies that failure defaults to safety rather than catastrophe.

Failure is the lack of success or the state of not achieving a desired outcome: {The experiment ended in failure}. A failure is also a person or thing that fails: {He felt like a failure}. The word extends to mechanical or systemic breakdowns: {heart failure}, {power failure}, {crop failure}. Failure can be partial or complete, temporary or permanent. {Failure to appear} in legal contexts means not showing up as required.

Failures is the plural of failure—instances of not succeeding, or people or things that have not succeeded. The word covers everything from mechanical breakdowns {(equipment failures)} to personal shortcomings {(I've had my share of failures)}. Unlike the singular, which often names an abstract state, failures typically points to specific, countable instances: {a string of failures}, {learning from past failures}.

Faint describes something weak or barely perceptible: a faint {sound}, a faint {smell}, a faint {hope}. A faint {resemblance} is slight. To feel faint is to feel lightheaded, on the verge of losing consciousness—and to faint is to do so, briefly blacking out. {She fainted from the heat}. The fainthearted lack courage or conviction.

Fainted is the past tense and past participle of faint, meaning to temporarily lose consciousness, typically from physical causes like heat, hunger, or shock. Someone who has fainted has briefly blacked out and usually collapsed. {She fainted at the sight of blood.} The word can also appear in humorous exaggeration: {I nearly fainted when I saw the price.}

Fainting is losing consciousness briefly, typically from insufficient blood flow to the brain. The sensation often includes lightheadedness, tunnel vision, and weakness before everything goes dark: {She felt herself fainting and grabbed the railing}. Someone prone to fainting at the sight of blood has a common vasovagal response. A fainting spell or fainting fit is an episode of such unconsciousness.

Two words in English have the spelling fair: the noun that designates a kind of festival or event (a county/recruitment/craft fair), and the adjective with multiple meanings that has also spawned an adverb. This fair carries several meanings, nearly all of which have a positive connotation. A fair day or fair weather is pleasant and enjoyable, without storms. A fair outcome is one that is just. Fair hair or a fair complexion is light, relative to others. If you play fair, you play honestly and according to the rules.

A fairground is an outdoor area where fairs, carnivals, and amusement events are held, typically featuring rides, games, food vendors, and exhibition spaces. The term often evokes images of Ferris wheels, cotton candy, and midway attractions. In British usage especially, fairground may refer to the permanent or semi-permanent site where traveling fairs set up seasonally. {The old fairground sat empty except during the county fair each August.}

Fairgrounds are the outdoor grounds where a fair is held, typically featuring exhibition halls, arenas, and open spaces for rides, livestock shows, and vendor booths. Most counties and states have permanent fairgrounds that host annual agricultural fairs and other events throughout the year: {We parked near the fairgrounds and walked to the midway}.

Fairies are small supernatural beings of folklore, typically depicted with wings and magical powers. They inhabit an enchanted realm parallel to ours, appearing in countless stories as mischievous, helpful, or dangerous creatures: {fairy tales}, {fairy godmother}, {tooth fairy}. Fairy is also a derogatory term for a gay man, now largely dated but still offensive when used by outsiders.

Fairness is the quality of being just, impartial, or reasonable. It implies treating people equally and making decisions without favoritism or bias: {The fairness of the trial was questioned}. In games and competitions, fairness means following rules that give everyone an equal chance. The word carries moral weight—unfairness provokes strong reactions because people expect equitable treatment. {In all fairness} introduces a point that balances or tempers what came before.

A fairway is the closely mowed strip of grass between the tee and the green on a golf hole, where players aim to land their shots for the easiest approach. Fairways contrast with the rough—the longer grass flanking them—and with hazards like bunkers and water. In nautical contexts, a fairway is a navigable channel in a river, harbor, or coastal waters, marked for safe passage of vessels. {Her drive landed perfectly in the center of the fairway.}

A fairy is a small magical being from folklore, typically depicted with wings and supernatural powers. Fairies inhabit enchanted realms in children's stories and fantasy literature: {fairy tales}, {fairy godmother}, {tooth fairy}. The word is also a derogatory term for a gay man, though less common than it once was.

A fairytale is a story featuring magical elements—enchanted forests, talking animals, witches, princes, and happy endings. The genre includes classics like Cinderella and Snow White. As an adjective, fairytale describes something idyllic or improbably perfect: {a fairytale wedding}, {a fairytale ending}. The implication can cut both ways—either wonderfully romantic or naively unrealistic. Also spelled fairy tale.

Fairytales are traditional stories featuring magical elements—enchanted forests, talking animals, witches, princes, and happy endings. The term extends to any fanciful or implausible narrative: {Don't give me fairytales, tell me what really happened}. A fairytale ending is improbably perfect. Also spelled as two words: fairy tales.

One of the oldest and best definitions of faith is from the Bible: “the substance of things hoped for and the evidence of things not seen.” Most people have strong beliefs about things that cannot be proved scientifically, often relating to religious belief. Faith has strong connotations with religion, and a particular religion can even be called a faith: She married a man of a different faith, against her family’s wishes. If you have faith in a person, you believe that they are capable of doing something that they have not yet done.

Faithful means loyal and steadfast in allegiance or affection: {a faithful friend}, {faithful to her husband}. It also means accurate or true to an original: {a faithful reproduction}, {a faithful translation}. The faithful are devoted believers or supporters, often religious: {The faithful gathered for mass}. Faithfully closes formal letters: {Yours faithfully}.

Fajita is a Tex-Mex dish of grilled meat—originally skirt steak—sliced into strips and served with tortillas, onions, and peppers: {The sizzling fajita platter arrived at the table}. The dish has expanded to include chicken, shrimp, and vegetarian versions. Usually plural: {We ordered fajitas for the table}.

Fajitas are a Tex-Mex dish of grilled meat—originally skirt steak—served sizzling on a hot plate with sautéed peppers and onions. Diners assemble their own by wrapping the ingredients in warm flour tortillas with toppings like sour cream, guacamole, and salsa: {The waiter brought out chicken fajitas still hissing from the grill}.

Fake describes something made to look genuine but isn't—a fake {ID}, fake {fur}, fake {news}. As a noun, it's either the counterfeit object itself or a person who pretends to be something they're not: {He's a total fake}. The verb means to falsify or counterfeit, but also simply to pretend: {She faked enthusiasm for the gift}. To fake {it till you make it} means projecting confidence until genuine competence develops. To fake {someone out} is to deceive them with a feint or misdirection.

A fakeout is a deceptive move or feint designed to mislead—common in sports, games, and trading. A basketball player fakes left before driving right; a stock appears to break out before reversing. The term emphasizes the victim's perspective: someone got faked out. {He fell for the fakeout and went the wrong way.}

Fakes are things that aren't what they appear or claim to be—counterfeits, forgeries, or imitations passed off as genuine: {The paintings turned out to be fakes}. A fake can also be a person who pretends to have skills or qualities they lack: {He's a total fake}. In sports, a fake is a deceptive move intended to mislead an opponent.

Faking is pretending or counterfeiting—making something appear to be what it isn't. You might be faking an illness to skip work, faking enthusiasm for a gift you don't want, or faking a signature on a document. {She suspected he was faking his limp}. The word implies deliberate deception, though the stakes range from harmless to criminal.

Falafel is a Middle Eastern food consisting of spiced, ground chickpeas or fava beans formed into balls or patties and deep-fried until crispy. Typically served in pita bread with tahini sauce, vegetables, and pickles, falafel has become a popular vegetarian street food worldwide. {We grabbed falafel from the cart on the corner.} The word comes from Arabic.

A falcon is a bird of prey with long pointed wings and a hooked beak, built for speed and aerial hunting. Falcons dive on prey from above, sometimes reaching extraordinary velocities—the peregrine falcon is the fastest animal on Earth. Falconry is the ancient practice of training these birds to hunt. The word extends to various related raptors and appears in sports team names.

Falconry is the practice of hunting with trained birds of prey—typically falcons, hawks, or eagles. The falconer trains the bird to pursue game and return to the glove. Once a practical hunting method, falconry is now primarily a sport and cultural tradition: {He took up falconry after retiring}. The related adjective is falconic.

Falcons are birds of prey known for their speed, hooked beaks, and tapered wings. They hunt by diving at tremendous velocity to strike prey in flight. Falconry is the ancient practice of training falcons to hunt. The word extends to sports teams and military equipment: {the Atlanta Falcons}, {the F-16 Fighting Falcon}.

As a verb, fall has a meaning similar to that of drop, but with an important difference: fall is always intransitive and does not take a human subject. When you drop something it falls, but you can’t fall it. When an event falls on a certain day, it happens on that day. All of the noun meanings of fall are derived from the verb meanings: a fall is a change from a higher to a lower place, whether actual or figurative: The sudden fall in temperatures surprised everyone. In North American English, the noun fall means the same as autumn.

A fallacy is a mistaken belief or a flaw in reasoning. In logic, fallacies are specific types of defective arguments—the straw man, the slippery slope, the appeal to authority. More loosely, any widespread but erroneous idea qualifies: {the fallacy that money buys happiness}. Fallacious reasoning may sound convincing while being fundamentally unsound.

A fallback is something you turn to when the first choice fails or isn't available: a fallback {plan}, a fallback {position}. In negotiations, your fallback is your acceptable alternative if you can't get what you want. As an adjective, it describes backup options: {We need a fallback strategy}. To fall back on something is to resort to it when needed.

Fallen is the past participle of fall, used as an adjective to describe something or someone that has dropped, collapsed, or declined from a former state. A fallen {tree} has toppled; fallen {leaves} have dropped from branches. The word carries strong moral and religious connotations: a fallen {angel} has been cast out of heaven, and a fallen {woman} is an old-fashioned term for one who has lost her virtue. The fallen, as a noun phrase, refers collectively to soldiers killed in battle.

Falling is the present participle of fall, used as adjective, noun, and verb form. As an adjective, it describes something moving downward or decreasing: {falling leaves}, {falling prices}, {falling temperatures}. The noun falling appears in compounds like {falling-out} (a quarrel that damages a relationship) and {falling star} (a meteor). {Falling in love} describes the often sudden, uncontrolled experience of becoming romantically attached to someone—the metaphor suggesting one doesn't choose it so much as succumb to it.

Fallout is radioactive particles scattered into the atmosphere by a nuclear explosion, eventually settling back to earth. By extension, fallout describes any adverse consequences or aftermath of an event: {The political fallout from the scandal cost him the election}. The verb phrase fall out means to happen or result, or to quarrel and become estranged: {They fell out over money}.

Falls is the plural of fall—instances of dropping or tumbling: {The gymnast had three falls during her routine}. It also refers to the season in some contexts: {We've had several beautiful falls in a row}. Most distinctively, falls denotes a waterfall or series of cascades, often used with singular agreement: {Niagara Falls is spectacular}, {The falls was roaring after the spring rains}. (Capitalized Falls appears in place names.)

False means not true or not genuine. A false {statement} contradicts fact. A false {friend} pretends loyalty. False {teeth} replace real ones. False can indicate something designed to deceive: a false {bottom} in a suitcase, a false {name}. To {play someone false} is to betray them. A {false start} is a premature beginning that must be restarted.

Falsetto is a method of singing that produces a high, light voice by vibrating only the edges of the vocal cords rather than their full mass. Male singers use falsetto to reach notes above their normal range: {He hit the high note in falsetto}. The technique creates a breathy, ethereal quality distinct from the fuller sound of a trained countertenor. The word also describes speaking in an artificially high voice, often for comic effect.

Falter means to lose strength, momentum, or resolve. If your steps falter, you stumble or walk unsteadily; if your voice falters, it wavers or breaks. More often the word applies to abstract things: confidence falters, economies falter, negotiations falter. {Her determination never faltered despite the setbacks.} To falter is not necessarily to fail completely—it suggests a wobble, a moment of uncertainty or weakness that may or may not be overcome.

Faltering describes movement, speech, or effort that is unsteady, hesitant, or losing momentum. A faltering step suggests physical weakness or uncertainty; a faltering voice breaks with emotion or doubt. The word implies something once steady now struggling to continue: {The economy showed faltering growth}. {Her faltering confidence made the presentation difficult}.

Fame is widespread recognition or renown—being known by many people: {Her fame spread after the viral video}. Fame often implies admiration but can be neutral or negative: {He achieved fame as a serial killer}. The adjective famous and verb {famed for} derive from the same root. To {claim to fame} is a notable accomplishment or distinction, however minor: {His only claim to fame was a walk-on role in a soap opera}.

Familiar describes what you know well through repeated exposure or experience: {a familiar face}, {familiar surroundings}, {a familiar tune}. To be familiar with something is to have knowledge of it. The word also describes behavior that's overly casual or presumptuous: {He got a bit too familiar with me}. A familiar is also a spirit or animal companion to a witch, supposedly aiding in magic.

Familiarity is the state of knowing something well through repeated exposure or experience: {Her familiarity with the neighborhood made her an excellent guide}. It also describes informal closeness between people, which can be comfortable or presumptuous—hence {Familiarity breeds contempt}. To {take familiarities} with someone is to behave too intimately for the relationship.

Families is the plural of family—groups of people related by blood, marriage, or adoption, or who share a household. The word appears in discussions of social structure: {Many families struggle with childcare costs}. It extends to any close-knit group: {crime families}, {military families}. In biology, families are taxonomic ranks grouping related genera.

The core meaning of family is a group of first-degree relatives (parents, siblings, children) living together. In relation to people and sometimes other animals, this meaning is expanded to include more distant relatives or people who are related by law rather than genetics (step relations, adoptees, and the like). The concept of family is conveniently applied to many other things that appear to share relations in the same hierarchical structure as human families: This stage of development is governed by a family of proteins unique to reptiles. What family do cottonwood trees belong to?

Famine is extreme scarcity of food affecting a large population, typically causing widespread starvation and death. Famines result from drought, crop failure, war, or political decisions. The word extends to severe shortages of other necessities: {a famine of ideas}, {an energy famine}. The Irish Potato Famine of the 1840s killed a million people and drove mass emigration.

Famines is the plural of famine—periods of extreme food scarcity causing widespread hunger, malnutrition, and death. Famines result from crop failure, drought, war, or economic collapse, often compounded by political failures: {The famines of the twentieth century killed tens of millions}. Historically, famines have reshaped populations and toppled governments.

Famous describes someone or something widely known and talked about: {a famous actor}, {a famous battle}, {a famous recipe}. Fame usually implies positive recognition, though {famous last words} refers ironically to confident statements proven wrong. The word can intensify: {We had a famous time}. To be famous for something is to be particularly associated with it: {France is famous for its wine}.

A fan is a device that moves air, either handheld and waved or mechanical with rotating blades. To fan is to direct air toward something: {She fanned herself with a magazine}. Things spread out in a fan shape: {The search party fanned out across the field}. Separately, a fan is an enthusiastic follower of a team, performer, or activity—short for fanatic: {a baseball fan}, {a fan of her work}.

Fana is an Arabic term used in Sufi Islamic mysticism to describe the annihilation or dissolution of the self in the divine presence. It represents a spiritual state where the ego dissolves and the individual consciousness merges with God, similar to concepts of ego death in other mystical traditions. The term appears in discussions of Islamic spirituality and comparative religion. {The mystic sought fana through years of devoted practice.}

Fanart is artwork created by fans depicting characters, settings, or scenes from existing media—movies, video games, anime, books. It ranges from casual sketches to polished digital paintings, shared primarily online in fan communities. {She posts her fanart on Tumblr}. The term acknowledges both tribute and transformation: fans reimagining beloved properties through their own creative lens.

A fanatic is someone with extreme, obsessive devotion to a cause, belief, or activity. The word implies zeal that goes beyond reasonable bounds—{a religious fanatic}, {a political fanatic}. In casual use, fanatic softens to mean merely an enthusiast: {a fitness fanatic}, {a fanatic about cleanliness}. The shortened form fan derives from this word.

Fanaticism is excessive, uncritical devotion to a cause, belief, or pursuit. The fanatic tolerates no dissent and sees compromise as betrayal. Religious and political fanaticism drive people to extreme acts: {His fanaticism made him impossible to reason with}. The word implies zeal that has crossed into dangerous territory—passion without proportion or restraint.

Fanatics are people with extreme, uncritical devotion to a cause, belief, or activity. The word implies zealotry that goes beyond reasonable enthusiasm—a fanatic won't hear opposing views: {religious fanatics}, {political fanatics}. In casual use, fanatic softens to mean simply an enthusiast: {a fitness fanatic}, {a football fanatic}. The clipped form fan comes from this word.

A fanbase is the collective body of devoted followers of a performer, team, franchise, or cultural property. The term treats fans as a measurable asset: {The show has built a loyal fanbase}, {Their fanbase skews young}. A strong fanbase suggests reliable support—people who buy tickets, stream content, and defend their favorites online.

A fanboy is a male devotee of some entertainment property—a video game franchise, comic book universe, film series, or tech brand—whose enthusiasm others find excessive or uncritical. The term carries dismissive connotations, suggesting someone who defends their obsession against all criticism: {The fanboys are already attacking anyone who gave the movie a bad review}. Fangirl is the female equivalent, though fanboy sometimes applies regardless of gender.

Fanboys is a mnemonic for the coordinating conjunctions in English: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so. These seven words join grammatically equal elements—words, phrases, or clauses: {I wanted to go, but I was too tired}. The term is taught in grammar classes as a memory aid. Separately, fanboys (singular fanboy) are obsessive male enthusiasts of media franchises, games, or technology.

A fanclub is an organized group of enthusiasts devoted to a celebrity, band, sports team, or other public figure. Members share news, attend events, and connect with fellow admirers. The term extends loosely to any group united by shared enthusiasm: {She has a whole fanclub at work}. Also spelled fan club.

The adjective fancy typically distinguishes a costlier or more elaborate variety of a thing that also has a plain version. Fancy may also suggest, slightly pejoratively, opulence or expense: He only eats in fancy restaurants. The verb fancy is more common in British than American English and means to consider, imagine, or take a liking to: I fancy that dress. The noun fancy may denote the imagination, something imagined, or something desired: He went on a flight of fancy.

Fandom is the collective community of fans devoted to something—a TV series, book, celebrity, sports team, or other cultural phenomenon. The word covers both the people and their shared culture: fan fiction, fan art, conventions, online forums. {She's deep in the Taylor Swift fandom.} {The Star Trek fandom has been active since the 1960s.} Fandom can also mean the state of being a fan: {His fandom borders on obsession.}

Fandoms are communities of devoted fans who share enthusiasm for a particular work of fiction, celebrity, or cultural phenomenon. The term emerged from science fiction and fantasy circles but now covers any passionate fan community—from {Harry Potter fandom} to {K-pop fandoms}. These communities create fan art, fiction, and elaborate online discussions. Fandom culture involves shared vocabulary, in-jokes, and sometimes intense rivalries between competing groups.

Fanfare is a short, dramatic flourish of brass instruments, typically trumpets, used to announce arrivals or ceremonial moments: {A fanfare greeted the queen}. By extension, fanfare means showy public attention or celebration: {The product launched with great fanfare}. {They slipped away without fanfare.}

Fanfic is fiction written by fans using characters, settings, or worlds from existing media—TV shows, movies, books, video games. Short for fan fiction. The practice ranges from short stories to novel-length works, often exploring scenarios the original creators never addressed: {She's been writing Harry Potter fanfic since middle school}. Fanfic communities have their own terminology for pairings, ratings, and tropes.

Fanfiction is fiction written by fans using characters, settings, or worlds from existing stories—novels, films, TV shows, video games. It ranges from short scenarios to novel-length works, often exploring relationships or plotlines the original didn't pursue: {She writes Harry Potter fanfiction where Draco is the hero}. The genre thrives online in dedicated communities. Also spelled fan fiction or shortened to fanfic.

A fang is a long, pointed tooth. Venomous snakes have hollow fangs that inject poison; dogs and wolves have fangs for tearing meat. The word extends to fang-like things: the prongs of a fork, the root of a tooth. Vampires sink their fangs into victims' necks. {The dog bared its fangs and growled.}

A fangirl is a female fan whose enthusiasm borders on obsession—typically for a band, actor, fictional character, or media franchise. The term suggests intense emotional investment, from collecting merchandise to defending the object of devotion online: {She's been fangirling over that K-pop group for years}. As a verb, to fangirl is to express such enthusiasm: {I fangirled so hard when I met him}. Originally dismissive, the word has been reclaimed by many who embrace passionate fandom. The male equivalent is fanboy.

Fangirling is expressing enthusiastic, often excessive admiration for a celebrity, fictional character, band, or other object of devotion. The term captures the intense, gushing quality of fan behavior—squealing, obsessing, collecting merchandise, attending events: {I was fangirling so hard when I met the cast}. Though derived from girl, the verb applies regardless of gender. The noun fangirl denotes someone who engages in such behavior.

Fangirls are female fans who express intense, often obsessive enthusiasm for a celebrity, fictional character, band, TV show, or other cultural phenomenon. The term captures both devoted appreciation and the stereotype of emotional excess—screaming at concerts, collecting memorabilia, writing fan fiction, and defending their favorite against criticism. {The fangirls lined up overnight for concert tickets.} Though sometimes dismissive, fangirl has been reclaimed by many who embrace passionate fan culture. It also works as a verb: {She fangirls over every post he makes.}

Fangs are the long, pointed teeth that certain animals use to bite, grip, or inject venom. Snakes have hollow fangs that deliver poison; dogs and wolves have fangs for tearing flesh. In vampire lore, fangs are the signature feature that allows blood-drinking. Figuratively, if someone {bares their fangs}, they show aggressive intent. The word occasionally describes any prominent or sharp tooth: {The kid's fangs came in crooked}.

Fanny means different things depending on where you are. In American English, fanny is a mild, almost childish term for the buttocks: {She fell on her fanny}. In British English, fanny is vulgar slang for the female genitals—not a word to use casually. This regional split makes fanny a minefield for travelers: a {fanny pack} in America is a {bum bag} in Britain for good reason.

Fans are devices that move air for cooling or ventilation, from handheld folding fans to electric ceiling fans. The blades spread out from a central point, which gives us the verb: to fan out is to spread in a widening pattern. To fan flames—literal or figurative—is to intensify them by directing air. Separately, a fan is an enthusiastic devotee: sports fans, music fans, {I'm a big fan of her work}. This sense is short for fanatic.

Fantasies are imagined scenarios, especially pleasurable or wishful ones. The word covers daydreams about success or romance, sexual imaginings, and elaborate fictional worlds. A fantasy can be harmless escapism or a worrying detachment from reality: {He had fantasies of quitting his job and sailing around the world}. In the plural, fantasies often suggests recurring or indulgent imaginings: {She kept her fantasies to herself}.

Fantasize means to imagine something desirable, often something unlikely or impossible. The word frequently implies sexual daydreaming: {He fantasized about his coworker}. But fantasizing can be about any wish: {She fantasized about quitting her job and moving to Paris}. The tone often suggests the vision is impractical or self-indulgent.

Fantasizing is imagining things you desire or find pleasurable—scenarios that may be unlikely, impossible, or simply not present. The word often carries sexual connotations: {She caught him fantasizing about his coworker}. But fantasizing applies broadly to any wishful imagining: {He spent the meeting fantasizing about quitting}. Unlike daydreaming, fantasizing usually involves specific desires rather than idle mental wandering.

Fantastic originally meant existing only in fantasy—imaginary or unreal: {fantastic creatures}, {fantastic tales}. The word shifted to mean extraordinarily good or impressive: {The concert was fantastic}. This positive sense now dominates casual speech, though the older meaning persists in contexts emphasizing imagination or implausibility: {fantastic claims}, {fantastic voyage}. Something fantastic may also be bizarre or grotesque: {fantastic rock formations}.

Fantasy is imagination unrestrained by reality. A fantasy can be a daydream, a wishful scenario, or an elaborate imagined world: {She indulged in fantasies of early retirement}. Sexual fantasies are erotic scenarios that arouse. As a genre, fantasy fiction features magic, mythical creatures, and invented worlds—distinct from science fiction's technological basis. Fantasy sports leagues let participants build imaginary teams from real players. To fantasize is to indulge in such imaginings: {He fantasized about quitting his job}.

A fanzine is an amateur magazine produced by and for enthusiasts of a particular interest—originally science fiction, later punk rock, sports teams, or any niche passion. The word blends "fan" and "magazine." Fanzines are typically photocopied or cheaply printed, distributed informally, and valued for their grassroots authenticity: {She discovered the band through a local punk fanzine}.

Far indicates great distance in space, time, or degree. A far {country} is remote; the far {future} is distant in time. Far often appears with comparatives: {far better}, {far worse}, {far more likely}. As an adjective, it typically means the more distant of two: the far {end} of the room, the far {side} of the moon. {So far} means until now; {by far} emphasizes degree; {far and away} means by a great margin.

Faraway means distant in space or time: {a faraway land}, {faraway memories of childhood}. A faraway look or expression suggests someone lost in thought, mentally distant from their surroundings: {She had a faraway look in her eyes}. The word carries a slightly dreamy or romantic quality that distant lacks.

A farce is a comedy built on absurd situations, improbable coincidences, and physical humor—mistaken identities, doors slamming, people hiding in closets. The genre values chaos over wit. Extended to any situation that's absurdly inadequate or a mockery of what it should be: {The trial was a farce}. To farce, rarely used, is to stuff—the original meaning, surviving in "forcemeat."

Fare is the price of transportation—what you pay to ride a bus, taxi, train, or plane: {The fare to the airport is thirty dollars}. A fare is also the passenger who pays it, especially in taxi driving: {The cabbie picked up a fare downtown}. Fare extends to food, particularly what's offered or served: {pub fare}, {simple fare}. As a verb, fare means to get along or manage: {How did you fare on the exam?} To fare well or poorly is to experience good or bad fortune.

Farewell is a formal or literary way of saying goodbye, often implying a final or long-term parting: {They bade farewell to their homeland}. As a noun, it's the act of leaving or the occasion of departure: {a farewell party}, {a fond farewell}. The word carries more weight than casual goodbyes—you don't say farewell when leaving for lunch.

Farfetched describes something unlikely or hard to believe—an explanation, theory, or story that seems too improbable to accept: {His alibi was farfetched at best}. The word suggests someone has reached too far for a connection or conclusion. Also spelled far-fetched.

The most frequent use of farm is an area of land, bigger than a garden, that is set aside for agricultural use. The archetypal farm includes a barn and a house, the farmhouse, where the farmer and his family live. Farms are sometimes characterized by their product, which may or may not be related to agriculture: pig farm, wind farm. Someone who farms makes a living in agriculture. Something that is farmed out is assigned to another: the company farms out its hiring efforts to an agency.

A farmer is someone who works the land, raising crops or livestock. The term covers everything from small family operations to industrial agriculture. Farmer often implies ownership or management rather than hired labor: {My grandfather was a dairy farmer in Wisconsin}. The word extends metaphorically to anyone who cultivates something systematically: {a fish farmer}, {a server farmer}.

Farmers are people who work the land, raising crops or livestock for food, fiber, or other products. The term covers a wide range—from small family operations to managers of industrial agricultural enterprises. {Local farmers sell produce at the weekend market.} {Farmers in the region shifted from tobacco to soybeans.} Figuratively, farmer suggests rural simplicity or lack of sophistication.

Farmhands are workers hired to do manual labor on a farm—tending livestock, operating equipment, harvesting crops. The term suggests physical, often seasonal work rather than farm ownership or management: {The ranch employed a dozen farmhands during harvest season}.

A farmhouse is the main dwelling on a farm, typically where the farmer and family live. The word evokes rural architecture—sturdy, practical houses often with large kitchens and wraparound porches. As a modifier, farmhouse describes a rustic aesthetic popular in interior design: {farmhouse style}, {farmhouse sink}, {farmhouse table}. The look emphasizes natural materials, distressed wood, and vintage touches.

Farming is the practice of cultivating land and raising animals for food, fiber, or other products. The word covers everything from small family operations to industrial agriculture. Beyond agriculture, farming describes any systematic harvesting: {wind farming}, {fish farming}, {click farming}. To farm out work is to delegate it to others.

Farms are areas of land used for growing crops or raising animals. A farm typically includes cultivated fields, pastures, or facilities for livestock. The word extends to specialized operations: fish farms, wind farms, server farms. To farm is to work the land or raise animals. To farm something out is to delegate it to others: {They farmed out the design work to contractors}.

A farmyard is the area immediately surrounding farm buildings—the barn, stables, and outbuildings—typically enclosed or partially enclosed. It's where daily farm activity concentrates: animals fed, equipment stored, vehicles parked. {Chickens scratched in the farmyard.} The word evokes rural life and its characteristic sounds and smells.

Farsighted describes a condition in which distant objects are seen more clearly than nearby ones, the opposite of nearsighted. This literal meaning extends to people who plan wisely for the future: {Her farsighted investments paid off decades later}. A farsighted leader anticipates problems before they arise. The word can also be spelled far-sighted, and the condition itself is called farsightedness.

A fart is an expulsion of intestinal gas through the anus, or the sound or smell it produces. The verb means to release such gas: {Who farted?} The word is mildly vulgar but common in casual speech. To {fart around} is to waste time or act aimlessly. An {old fart} is a boring or out-of-touch older person.

Farted is the past tense of fart—to expel gas from the anus. The word is mildly vulgar but common in casual speech: {Who farted?} {The dog farted and cleared the room}. Figuratively, to {fart around} is to waste time on trivial things.

Farthest is the superlative of far, indicating the greatest distance: {the farthest reaches of the galaxy}, {Who can throw the ball farthest?} It works for both physical and figurative distance: {the farthest thing from my mind}. Furthest is interchangeable in most contexts, though farthest tends toward literal distance while furthest leans abstract.

Farting is the act of expelling gas from the digestive system through the anus. The word is mildly vulgar but universal—everyone farts, and the term appears freely in casual speech: {The dog kept farting during dinner}. Farting around means wasting time or goofing off.

Farts are expulsions of intestinal gas through the anus, typically with an audible sound. The word is mildly vulgar but common in casual speech. To fart is to release such gas: {Who farted?} Figuratively, to {fart around} is to waste time on trivial activities. An {old fart} is a boring or out-of-touch older person.

To fascinate is to capture and hold someone's attention completely, often with an element of wonder or compelling interest. A speaker fascinates an audience; a mystery fascinates investigators. The word carries a hint of its original meaning—to bewitch or cast a spell—though modern usage is almost always positive: {I'm fascinated by how languages evolve}. Something fascinating draws you in and holds you there.

Fascinated describes being intensely captivated or absorbed by something. The word suggests more than casual interest—a fascinated person is held almost spellbound: {She was fascinated by the magician's sleight of hand}, {He sat fascinated as the documentary unfolded}. Originally tied to bewitchment, the modern sense retains that quality of being unable to look away.

Fascinating describes something that captures and holds attention through strong interest or curiosity. A fascinating {book} engrosses the reader; a fascinating {person} commands attention. The word implies more than mere interest—something fascinating exerts a kind of pull, drawing you in and making it hard to look away. {I find the history of medicine fascinating.}

Fascination is intense interest or attraction—the state of being captivated by something. A subject holds fascination when it commands attention almost involuntarily: {She developed a fascination with deep-sea creatures}. The word suggests something compelling, even slightly obsessive: {His fascination with true crime worried his mother}. What fascinates often combines curiosity with a hint of the mysterious or forbidden.

Fascism, especially when capitalized, refers to a 20th century political movement in Italy and Germany that valued the country and a particular ethnic group above the individual. When used today, and not capitalized, fascism is used loosely and pejoratively to characterize any political movement, idea, or action that is seen as concentrating power in a single individual or group in ways that are detrimental to ordinary people: The militia’s seizure of power is being criticized as a huge step towards fascism.

In the mid-20th century, a Fascist was someone who was a member of or supported the autocratic governments of Hitler in Germany or Mussolini in Italy. Today, fascist is used loosely as an insulting way to characterize the ideas or behavior of anyone who is perceived as trying to exercise strict control over people using undemocratic and sometimes violent or terroristic means: The state media now appears to be under the control of religious fascists.

Fascists are adherents of fascism—an authoritarian political ideology emphasizing nationalism, dictatorial power, and suppression of opposition. The term originated with Mussolini's movement in 1920s Italy. In strict usage, fascists support specific far-right ideologies: {The fascists marched through the streets}. More loosely, fascist is an epithet for anyone perceived as authoritarian or intolerant: {Don't be such a fascist about the dress code}.

Fashion is the prevailing style in dress, behavior, or way of life at a given time. What's in fashion changes constantly—{last year's fashion is this year's embarrassment}. The word extends beyond clothing to any domain with trends: {the fashion for open floor plans}. As a verb, to fashion something is to make or shape it: {She fashioned a crown from wildflowers}. {After a fashion} means in a rough or imperfect way.

Fashionable means in accordance with current style or popular taste. Fashionable {clothes}, fashionable {neighborhoods}, fashionable {ideas}—all suggest what's currently in vogue among those who set trends. The word carries slight connotations of superficiality or transience: what's fashionable today may not be tomorrow. {It became fashionable to dismiss his early work.}

A fashionista is someone intensely devoted to fashion—following trends, curating their wardrobe, and often working in the fashion industry. The term can be admiring or gently mocking, depending on context: {She's a total fashionista who never wears the same outfit twice}. It suggests enthusiasm bordering on obsession.

The adjective and adverb fast are distinct from the noun and verb. The main meanings of the adjective and adverb are firmly fixed (held fast in a trap) and quick or quickly (a fast train, how fast can you get here?). Less frequent meanings are unlikely to fade (color fast) and very loyal (hold fast to your faith). The verb fast means go without food. A fast is a period of conscious abstention from eating: The monk undertook a seven-day fast.

A fastball is a pitch in baseball thrown at maximum velocity with minimal spin variation, relying on speed rather than movement to challenge the batter. It's the most basic and common pitch type, typically clocked between 90 and 100 miles per hour at the professional level. Figuratively, to {throw someone a fastball} is to give them something straightforward rather than tricky.

Fasten means to attach, secure, or close something firmly. You fasten a seatbelt, fasten a button, fasten a lock. The word implies making something fixed or immovable: {Fasten the boards together with screws}. To fasten onto something is to grip it tightly or focus on it intently: {The detective fastened onto a single detail in the testimony}.

Fasting is the practice of abstaining from food, drink, or both for a period of time. Religious fasting appears across traditions—Muslims fast during Ramadan, Jews on Yom Kippur, Christians during Lent. Medical fasting prepares patients for procedures or blood tests. Intermittent fasting has gained popularity as a health practice: {I've been fasting sixteen hours a day}. The adjective fasting describes the state: {fasting blood sugar}.

Fat is first an adjective, secondly a noun, with closely related meanings. A fat person has a relatively high percentage of body fat. Fat is the general term for two things: a greasy substance that is insoluble in water, and animal tissue that contains a lot of this substance. Fat can have positive associations: a fat paycheck, a fat contract.

Fatal means causing death or destruction: a fatal {accident}, a fatal {disease}, a fatal {blow}. The word extends to anything that causes ruin or failure: a fatal {flaw}, a fatal {error}, a fatal {mistake}. Something fatal is decisive in a way that can't be undone—the consequences are final and irreversible.

Fatalism is the belief that events are fixed in advance and human effort cannot change them. A fatalist accepts outcomes as inevitable: {With a fatalist's shrug, she said whatever happens, happens}. The term often carries connotations of passive resignation or refusal to struggle against circumstances. Fatalistic describes this attitude: {His fatalistic outlook kept him from even trying}.

A fatalist believes that events are predetermined and human effort cannot change outcomes. The term carries connotations of passive resignation—a fatalist accepts whatever happens rather than fighting against it: {He was a fatalist about his health, refusing to see doctors}. Fatalism can be philosophical conviction or simply a temperament that shrugs at circumstance.

Fatalities is the plural of fatality—deaths resulting from accidents, disasters, violence, or war. News reports tally fatalities from earthquakes, car crashes, and military operations: {The storm caused twelve fatalities}. The word carries clinical distance, preferred in official contexts over more direct terms like deaths or people killed.

A fatality is a death, particularly one resulting from an accident, disaster, or violent incident. The word emphasizes the fatal outcome rather than the circumstances: {The crash caused three fatalities.} Traffic reports, military briefings, and emergency services favor this clinical term over more emotionally charged alternatives like deaths or casualties. Fatality can also refer to the quality of being destined or inevitable, though this philosophical sense is now rare outside academic contexts.

Fate is the force or power believed to determine what happens—the idea that events are fixed in advance and beyond human control. Your fate is your destiny, the outcome awaiting you: {He accepted his fate}. The fates, in Greek mythology, were three goddesses who spun, measured, and cut the thread of each life. To be fated is to be destined: {They were fated to meet}. A fateful decision has momentous consequences. To fate something is rare; the passive dominates: {It was fated from the start}.

Fated describes something destined to happen, as if determined by fate: {They were fated to meet}. It often carries a sense of inevitability, whether fortunate or tragic: {a fated encounter}, {fated to fail}. An ill-fated venture is doomed from the start. Fated suggests forces beyond human control have already decided the outcome.

Fateful describes something that determines or reveals fate—a turning point with significant consequences. A fateful {decision} shapes everything that follows. A fateful {day} is one when destiny unfolds. The word carries a sense of inevitability, as if larger forces are at work. Fateful moments are usually serious, often ominous: {That fateful meeting changed the course of history}.

Fates is the plural of fate, referring to destinies or outcomes beyond human control. People speak of the fates of individuals, nations, or enterprises: {The fates of the two brothers diverged wildly}. To leave something to the fates is to abandon it to chance or providence. (Capitalized Fates refers to the mythological goddesses.)

Father means male parent—the man whose genetic material or parental role produced a child. The term extends to founding figures: {the Founding Fathers}, {the father of modern physics}. To father a child is to sire one, though the word increasingly implies active parenting rather than mere biological contribution. {My father taught me to fish.} (Capitalized Father is a religious or clerical title.)

Fatherhood is the state of being a father—having a child for whom you are responsible. The word encompasses both the biological fact and the social role: {He wasn't ready for fatherhood}. Fatherhood often carries connotations of duty, provision, and guidance that go beyond mere procreation: {Fatherhood changed him completely}.

Fatherland is one's native country, especially when viewed with patriotic attachment. The term emphasizes ancestral connection to the land—where one's fathers lived and are buried. {He returned to the fatherland after decades abroad.} Though neutral in most languages, fatherland in English carries associations with Nazi Germany, where *Vaterland* featured prominently in nationalist rhetoric. Motherland and homeland are often preferred.

Fatherless describes someone whose father is absent, dead, or unknown. The term emphasizes lack rather than mere absence—a fatherless child lacks paternal guidance, support, or connection: {He grew up fatherless in rural Tennessee}. The word carries emotional weight, suggesting vulnerability or deprivation in ways that "without a father" does not.

Fatherly describes qualities associated with a good father—protective, caring, wise, and gently authoritative. A fatherly {smile} conveys warmth and approval. Fatherly {advice} comes from experience and genuine concern for someone's wellbeing. The word typically carries positive connotations, suggesting benevolent guidance rather than stern control: {He took a fatherly interest in the young apprentice}.

Fathers is the plural of father—male parents. Beyond biology, fathers extends to founders or originators: {the founding fathers}, {the fathers of the church}. The verb fathers means to sire offspring or to create something: {He fathered three children}. {Einstein fathered modern physics}.

Fathom is a unit of water depth equal to six feet, used in nautical contexts: {The harbor was only three fathoms deep}. More commonly, fathom means to understand or comprehend something difficult or mysterious: {I can't fathom why she would do that}. The connection is probing depths—whether of water or meaning. The negative is especially common: {unfathomable}, {I couldn't fathom it}.

Fathoms is the plural of fathom, a unit of measurement equal to six feet, used primarily for measuring water depth. Sailors and maritime charts still use fathoms: {The wreck lies at twelve fathoms}. The verb fathom means to measure depth, but its figurative sense—to understand or comprehend something difficult—is now more common: {I can't fathom why she quit}. If something is unfathomable, it's too deep or complex to grasp.

Fatigue is weariness from exertion—physical, mental, or emotional. {The fatigue of a long day set in}. Materials also fatigue: metal fatigue is weakening from repeated stress. In the military, fatigues are work uniforms, and fatigue duty is menial labor. The verb means to tire: {The climb fatigued us all}.

Fattening describes food or habits that tend to cause weight gain: {Avoid fattening snacks if you're watching your weight}. The word implies high calories, often from fats or sugars. Something fattening isn't necessarily unhealthy, but the connotation leans toward indulgence: {The pasta was delicious but fattening}.

A faucet is a valve with a handle or knob that controls the flow of water from a pipe, typically at a sink or bathtub: {Turn off the faucet}. Americans say faucet; the British say tap. The word extends to any similar spigot controlling liquid flow.
