The plural findings also refers to small parts and tools used in jewelry-making or crafts—clasps, settings, and the like.

Fine is two words, representing multiple parts of speech. Most frequent is the adjective meaning of good quality or free from impurity (fine wines), thin or small in gauge, texture, or scale (fine sand) or satisfactory or pleasing (fine day). Fine also works as an adverb (I feel fine). As a noun and verb, fine is associated with money arising from penalty or punishment: He was fined for failing to pay income tax.

Fines are monetary penalties imposed for violations—parking fines, library fines, court-ordered fines. To fine someone is to impose such a penalty: {The company was fined for environmental violations}. Separately, fines are very small particles—the powdery residue left after processing ore, grain, or coffee grounds.

Finesse is delicate skill in handling difficult situations—the ability to navigate tricky circumstances with subtlety and tact: {She handled the awkward question with finesse}. In card games, a finesse is an attempt to win a trick with a lower card by playing it when an opponent is unlikely to hold the higher one. As a verb, to finesse something is to achieve it through clever maneuvering rather than direct force: {He finessed his way past the objections}.

The fingers are the terminal appendages of the primate hand. The finger of a glove is the part the encloses your finger. If you give someone the finger you make a vulgar gesture with your middle finger. To finger someone is to accuse or blame them: Police fingered the boy’s uncle for the robbery. If you work your fingers to the bone, you make the greatest possible effort, often in a thankless way.

Fingering refers to the technique of placing and moving fingers, especially on a musical instrument. A pianist's fingering determines which fingers play which notes; sheet music often includes fingering notations. In sexual contexts, fingering means manually stimulating the genitals: {They were fingering each other in the back seat}. The word also describes pointing out or identifying someone: {The witness's fingering of the suspect led to his arrest}.

A fingernail is the hard, flat plate of keratin covering the upper tip of each finger. Fingernails protect the fingertips and aid in fine manipulation—scratching, peeling, prying. They grow continuously and require trimming. {She tapped her fingernails on the table}. To do something {by one's fingernails} is to barely manage it, as if clinging to a ledge.

Fingernails are the hard, flat coverings at the tips of human fingers, made of keratin. They protect the fingertips and help with fine manipulation—scratching, peeling, picking at small objects. Long fingernails can be decorative; bitten fingernails suggest anxiety. To fight {tooth and nail} is to fight with everything you have. {She tapped her fingernails on the table impatiently.}

Fingerpainting is a technique of applying paint directly with the hands rather than brushes, typically done by young children as an early art activity. The method emphasizes tactile experience over precision: {The preschoolers spent the morning fingerpainting}. As a verb, to fingerpaint is to create art this way. The results—often messy, colorful abstractions—are valued more for the process than the product.

A fingerprint is the pattern of ridges on the tip of a finger, unique to each person and used for identification. Police lift fingerprints from crime scenes; phones and laptops use fingerprint scanners for security. Figuratively, a fingerprint is any distinctive identifying mark: {The attack bore the fingerprint of state-sponsored hackers}. To fingerprint someone is to record their prints.

Fingerprinting is the practice of recording someone's fingerprints for identification, typically by pressing inked fingers onto paper or scanning them digitally. Police fingerprint suspects; employers fingerprint new hires. The term extends to any method of identifying something by its unique characteristics: {browser fingerprinting tracks users online}, {DNA fingerprinting revolutionized forensics}.

Fingerprints are the unique patterns of ridges on the tips of human fingers. Because no two people share identical patterns, fingerprints serve as reliable identifiers—detectives dust for fingerprints at crime scenes, and smartphones use fingerprint scanners for security. Figuratively, anything distinctive left behind: {The architect's fingerprints are all over the design}. To fingerprint someone is to record their prints.

Fingers are the five slender digits extending from the human hand—or four, if the thumb is counted separately. They grasp, point, type, and gesture. To finger something is to touch or handle it: {She fingered the fabric}. In music, fingering refers to which digits play which notes. To {point the finger} at someone is to blame them. To {keep your fingers crossed} is to hope for luck.

The fingertip is the fleshy pad at the end of a finger, dense with nerve endings and highly sensitive to touch. To have something {at your fingertips} means it's immediately accessible—whether physical objects within reach or knowledge you can recall instantly. {Fingertip control} suggests precise, delicate handling.

The fingertips are the ends of the fingers, where touch sensitivity is highest. To have something {at your fingertips} is to have it readily accessible—information, skills, or resources available for immediate use. {To your fingertips} means completely or thoroughly: {She's a professional to her fingertips}.

Finicky describes someone excessively particular or hard to please, especially about small details. A finicky eater refuses most foods. A finicky cat won't touch certain brands. The word suggests fussiness that others find unreasonable or tiresome: {She's finicky about how her coffee is made}. Finicky machinery or processes are temperamental and require careful handling.

Finish means to bring something to completion or its end: {I need to finish this report by Friday}. A finish is the final stage or surface quality—wood has a matte or glossy finish, a race has a photo finish. To finish someone off is to kill or defeat them decisively. If you're finished with something, you're done using it or done tolerating it: {I'm finished with his excuses}.

Finished means completed or at an end. A finished {project} is done; a finished {product} is ready for sale. When someone is finished, they've completed a task: {Are you finished with the bathroom?} But finished also means ruined or defeated beyond recovery: {If this gets out, I'm finished}. A finished {performance} shows polish and refinement—the work of completion evident in its quality.

Finishing is bringing something to completion or adding final touches. A finishing {coat} of paint is the last one applied. The finishing {line} marks where a race ends. To have a finishing {school} education is to have been trained in social graces and etiquette—the polish that "finishes" a young person for society. In manufacturing, finishing refers to surface treatments that complete a product.

Finite means having limits or bounds—an end point, a countable quantity, a defined scope. A finite {number} of options can be exhausted. Finite {resources} will eventually run out. The word often appears in contrast to infinite: {Human life is finite}. In grammar, a finite verb is one marked for tense and person, as opposed to infinitives or participles.

A fink is an informer—someone who reports others' misdeeds to authorities. The word carries strong disapproval, suggesting betrayal: {He finked on his friends to the cops}. In labor contexts, a fink is a strikebreaker or company spy. To fink out is to back out of a commitment through cowardice: {Don't fink out on me now}.

Fins are the flat appendages fish use for swimming—steering, stabilizing, and propelling through water. The concept extends to similar structures on other animals (dolphin fins, shark fins) and to fin-shaped equipment: the rubber fins swimmers wear on their feet, or the stabilizing surfaces on rockets and surfboards. In slang, fins can mean hands or, in old American usage, five-dollar bills.

A fir is an evergreen conifer with flat needles and upright cones, common in northern forests and mountainous regions. Firs are popular as Christmas trees and valued for timber. The wood itself is also called fir: {a cabin built of fir}. Douglas fir, despite its name, belongs to a different genus.

Although fire has been demoted from its ancient status as an element, it still denotes many things that share some quality with the destructive chemical reaction involving flame and heat. Fire designates attack by weapons (troops under fire), and an extremely strong emotion (the fire of love). As a verb, fire usually signifies bad news for whoever is on the receiving end: to fire a person is to end their employment. To fire a weapon is to discharge it.

A firearm is a weapon that uses explosive propellant to launch projectiles—pistols, rifles, shotguns, and similar devices. The term appears frequently in legal and regulatory contexts: {firearm registration}, {licensed to carry a firearm}. It's more formal than gun, which covers the same range of weapons in everyday speech.

Firearms are weapons that use explosive propellant to launch projectiles at high velocity through a barrel. The category includes handguns, rifles, shotguns, and automatic weapons. Firearms may be distinguished from other guns by their portability and their use of gunpowder or similar chemical propellants. {The debate over firearms regulation intensifies after each mass shooting.} Laws governing the sale, possession, and use of firearms vary widely by jurisdiction.

A fireball is a bright, blazing mass of fire—either a ball of flame or something resembling one. Large meteors that flare brilliantly as they enter Earth's atmosphere are fireballs. Nuclear explosions produce characteristic fireballs. Informally, a fireball is a person of intense energy or passion: {She's a real fireball on the sales floor}.

A firebird is a mythical bird associated with fire, appearing in various folklores—most famously the Russian tale where a glowing golden bird sets heroes on impossible quests. The phoenix is sometimes called a firebird. In nature, firebird names several species with flame-colored plumage, including orioles and tanagers. {The firebird's single feather lit up the dark forest.} (Capitalized Firebird is the Pontiac model or the ballet.)

Firebombing is attacking a target with incendiary weapons designed to start fires. The term applies to military operations—the firebombing of Dresden and Tokyo in World War II—and to smaller-scale attacks: {Someone firebombed the clinic overnight}. The weapon is often a Molotov cocktail or similar improvised device.

A firebrand is a piece of burning wood—a stick pulled from a fire. The figurative sense dominates: a firebrand is someone who stirs up trouble or passions, especially in politics or social causes. The word implies provocation and intensity: {She was a firebrand who refused to compromise}. The connotation can be admiring or dismissive depending on the speaker's sympathies.

A firecracker is a small explosive wrapped in paper that produces a loud bang when ignited, used for celebrations and holidays: {Kids set off firecrackers on the Fourth of July}. Figuratively, a firecracker is someone lively and spirited: {She's a real firecracker}.

Firecrackers are small explosive devices designed to produce a loud bang, typically wrapped in paper with a fuse. They're associated with celebrations—Fourth of July in America, Chinese New Year, Diwali. A string of firecrackers goes off in rapid succession. Figuratively, a firecracker is someone with explosive energy or a sharp temper: {She's a real firecracker}.

Fired means dismissed from a job, terminated by an employer: {She got fired for showing up late too many times}. The word comes from the image of being shot out—expelled forcefully. Fired also means ignited or heated: a {wood-fired} oven, {fired} ceramics. To be {fired up} is to be enthusiastic or angry: {The team was fired up for the championship}.

A firefight is an exchange of gunfire between opposing forces, typically brief and intense: {The patrol got into a firefight with insurgents}. The term implies active combat rather than a one-sided attack—both sides are shooting. It's military in origin but extends to police actions and any armed confrontation involving sustained gunfire.

A firefighter is a person trained to extinguish fires and rescue people from burning buildings or other emergencies. The term has largely replaced fireman in official and neutral contexts: {Firefighters responded within minutes}. Firefighters also handle hazardous material spills, medical emergencies, and car accidents.

Firefighters is the plural of firefighter—a person trained to extinguish fires and respond to emergencies. The term has largely replaced fireman as the gender-neutral standard: {Firefighters arrived within minutes of the call}. Beyond fighting fires, firefighters perform rescues, provide medical assistance, and respond to hazardous material incidents.

Firefighting is the work of extinguishing fires and rescuing people from burning buildings. It extends to any effort to contain or suppress urgent problems: {The IT team spent the week firefighting server crashes}. The metaphor captures the reactive, emergency nature of the work—putting out fires rather than preventing them.

Fireflies are beetles that produce light through bioluminescence, typically flashing in patterns to attract mates on summer evenings. Also called lightning bugs, depending on region. The glow comes from their abdomens. Children often catch them in jars: {We spent the evening chasing fireflies in the backyard}.

A firefly is a beetle that produces light through bioluminescence, flashing patterns in the dark to attract mates. Also called lightning bugs, they're familiar summer sights in many regions, their soft glow appearing at dusk: {The children chased fireflies across the lawn}. The light comes from their abdomen, not actual fire.

A firehose is a large-diameter hose designed to deliver water at high pressure for firefighting. Figuratively, a firehose describes any overwhelming flood of information or activity: {Drinking from the firehose} suggests being overwhelmed by more input than you can process. {The firehose of social media} never stops. To firehose is to blast someone with rapid, continuous output.
A firehouse is a building where fire engines are kept and firefighters are stationed, ready to respond to emergencies. Also called a fire station. {The old firehouse was converted into a restaurant.}

Firelight is the warm, flickering glow cast by a burning fire, especially from a fireplace or campfire. The word evokes intimacy and atmosphere: {Their faces glowed in the firelight}. It suggests a softer, more romantic quality than electric light—reading by firelight, shadows dancing in the firelight.

A fireman is a person who fights fires as an occupation—a member of a fire department who responds to emergencies, operates equipment, and rescues people from burning buildings. The term also applies to someone who tends a furnace or boiler, especially on steam locomotives. Firefighter is now preferred as a gender-neutral alternative, though fireman remains common in informal speech: {The firemen arrived within minutes}.

A fireplace is a recessed opening in a wall designed to contain a fire for heating or ambiance, typically with a chimney to draw smoke outside. The fireplace traditionally served as a home's primary heat source and cooking area; now it's mostly decorative or supplemental: {We gathered around the fireplace on Christmas Eve}. The word also refers to the entire surrounding structure including mantel and hearth.

Firepower is the destructive capacity of weapons or military units—the amount of ammunition a force can deliver on target. A battalion with more firepower has greater offensive capability. The term extends to any concentrated force or resources: {The company brought serious firepower to the negotiation with its team of lawyers}. In sports, firepower means scoring ability: {Their offense lacks firepower}.

Fires is the plural of fire—combustion producing flames, heat, and light. A fire burns in a fireplace; wildfires burn across landscapes. To set fires is to start them, whether literally or figuratively: {The article set fires across social media}. The verb fires means to discharge a weapon {(He fires three shots)}, to dismiss from employment {(The company fires underperformers)}, or to ignite enthusiasm {(The speech fires up the crowd)}.

A firestarter is anything used to ignite a fire, from commercial cubes and kindling to newspaper twisted into knots. The term extends to people who spark conflict or controversy, whether deliberately provocative figures or those who simply can't help stirring things up. {She's a firestarter—every meeting ends in an argument.} In British slang, particularly after the Prodigy song, firestarter can describe someone intense, chaotic, or dangerously exciting.

A firestorm is a massive, intense fire that generates its own wind system, creating a self-sustaining vortex that draws in surrounding air. The term applies literally to conflagrations in forests or bombed cities, but more often appears figuratively: a firestorm of {criticism}, a firestorm of {controversy}. In this sense, it describes an intense, rapidly spreading public reaction: {The CEO's remarks sparked a firestorm on social media}.

A firetrap is a building that would be especially dangerous in a fire—lacking adequate exits, built of flammable materials, or otherwise unsafe. The word implies neglect or code violations: {The old theater was a firetrap waiting to happen}. Sometimes used loosely for any cramped, cluttered, or poorly maintained space.

A firetruck is a large vehicle equipped for fighting fires, carrying hoses, ladders, water tanks, and firefighting personnel. Also called a fire engine, though some distinguish between the two based on equipment—engines pump water, trucks carry ladders. The bright red color is iconic: {red as a firetruck}.

Firetrucks are large vehicles equipped to fight fires, carrying hoses, ladders, pumps, and firefighters to emergencies. They're typically painted bright red with flashing lights and sirens. The phrase {holy firetrucks!} serves as a minced oath, substituting for profanity: {What the firetrucks is going on?}

Firewalking is the practice of walking barefoot over hot coals or embers, typically as a religious ritual, spiritual test, or demonstration of mind-over-matter principles. The activity appears in various cultures and has been adopted by motivational seminars as a confidence-building exercise: {The retreat culminated in a firewalking ceremony}.

A firewall is a barrier designed to prevent the spread of fire—originally a physical wall in buildings or vehicles. In computing, a firewall is software or hardware that monitors network traffic and blocks unauthorized access: {The company's firewall detected the intrusion attempt}. Figuratively, any protective barrier between things: {a firewall between church and state}.

Firewalls are barriers designed to prevent fire from spreading—walls of fire-resistant material built into structures. The term now dominates in computing, where a firewall is software or hardware that monitors network traffic and blocks unauthorized access: {The company's firewall prevented the intrusion}. To firewall something is to isolate it protectively: {We need to firewall this project from the budget cuts}.

Firewood is wood cut and prepared for burning, typically in a fireplace or stove. It may be sold in bundles or by the cord—a stack measuring four by four by eight feet. {We need to chop more firewood before winter}. Firewood that's been properly dried is called seasoned.

A firework is a device that produces a spectacular display of light, color, and sound through controlled combustion or explosion. Fireworks are traditionally set off during celebrations—New Year's Eve, Independence Day, Chinese New Year. In the plural, fireworks can mean dramatic confrontation: {There were fireworks at the meeting when the budget cuts were announced}.

Fireworks are explosive devices designed to produce spectacular effects of light, color, and sound, typically launched into the sky for entertainment. They're most associated with celebrations like Independence Day, New Year's Eve, and major sporting events. The singular firework exists but is less common; people usually refer to the display collectively. Figuratively, fireworks describes any dramatic confrontation or exciting display: {There were fireworks at the board meeting when the merger was announced}.

Firing is the act of discharging a weapon or setting something ablaze. In employment, firing means terminating someone's job: {She was fired for repeated absences}. In ceramics, firing hardens clay by heating it in a kiln. An engine's firing refers to its ignition cycle. The firing of neurons describes their electrical activation. {The firing squad took their positions.}

Firm describes something solid, stable, or resistant to pressure. A firm handshake is strong and confident. A firm mattress doesn't sink much. Firm ground supports weight reliably. Figuratively, firm conveys resolve or certainty: {a firm decision}, {firm in her beliefs}, {a firm no}. A firm is also a business enterprise, especially a professional partnership: {a law firm}, {an accounting firm}. To firm something is to make it more solid or stable: {Exercise firms the muscles}. Prices or markets firm when they stabilize after decline.

Unlike most ordinal numbers, first has no etymological connection with its cardinal number one; it came to be associated with one through usage. In all of its uses, first carries the idea of “before all others,” just as one comes before all the other whole numbers. First can apply to things in time, space, or any other logical or ordered sequence: I shifted into first gear. We got there first. Theirs is the first house on the left.

Firstborn describes or refers to the first child born to a parent or couple: {Their firstborn arrived in May}. The term carries weight in contexts of inheritance, birth order psychology, and biblical tradition, where firstborn sons held special status and rights. As an adjective: {firstborn son}, {firstborn daughter}.

Firsthand means obtained directly from the original source, without intermediaries: {firsthand knowledge}, {firsthand experience}, {a firsthand account}. If you witness an event yourself rather than hearing about it from others, your information is firsthand. The word works as both adjective and adverb: {I learned firsthand how difficult it is}.

Whether swimming in a river or served up on a dinner plate, fish is the term for vertebrate creatures that have gills, are cold-blooded, and live in water. Informal and slang meanings of fish a person born under the sign of Pisces and a card game. As a verb, fish denotes the activity of trying to catch fish. By extension, fish is applied to activities in which bait or lure is offered in the hope of attracting something sought after: fishing for compliments. A fish out of water is someone in a situation where they feel alienated and without bearings.

A fishbone is one of the thin, sharp bones found in fish flesh, notorious for getting stuck in throats when fish is eaten carelessly. The word also names a pattern of short diagonal lines meeting at a central spine, used in textiles, brickwork, and diagrams. A fishbone diagram, also called an Ishikawa diagram, is a problem-solving tool that maps causes branching off from an effect, resembling a fish skeleton. {I spent ten minutes picking fishbones out of the fillet.}

A fishbowl is a round glass container for keeping pet fish, typically goldfish. The transparent, exposed nature of the bowl makes it a metaphor for lack of privacy: {Living in a small town is like living in a fishbowl}. A fishbowl can also be any glass-walled space where people are visible to observers: {The conference room felt like a fishbowl}.

A fisherman is a person who catches fish, whether commercially or for sport. The term applies to professionals working on boats and to hobbyists casting lines from docks or riverbanks. {The fishermen hauled in their nets at dawn.} Though fisherman remains common, fisher has gained ground as a gender-neutral alternative.

Fishermen is the plural of fisherman—people who catch fish, whether commercially or for sport. The term traditionally covers both professionals who make their living from the sea and recreational anglers: {The fishermen hauled in their nets at dawn}. Though fishers has gained currency as a gender-neutral alternative, fishermen remains standard and is often used generically regardless of sex.

A fisheye is an ultra-wide-angle lens that produces a distinctive curved distortion, making straight lines bow outward toward the edges of the frame: {The fisheye shot made the skatepark look like a bowl}. The name comes from how a fish might see the world from underwater—everything visible in nearly 180 degrees. A fisheye is also a suspicious or hostile look: {She gave him the fisheye when he walked in late}.

A fishhook is a curved metal hook, typically barbed, used to catch fish. The hook is baited and attached to a line; when a fish bites, the barb prevents escape. Fishhook extends to anything with that distinctive curved-and-pointed shape: {a fishhook cactus}, {a fishhook in the road}.

Fishing is the activity of trying to catch fish, whether for food, sport, or livelihood. Commercial fishing supplies seafood markets; recreational fishing is a popular pastime: {We went fishing at the lake}. Figuratively, fishing means seeking something indirectly: {fishing for compliments}, {a fishing expedition} to uncover information without knowing what you'll find.

Fishnet is a loose, open-weave mesh fabric with large holes, resembling the netting used to catch fish. It most often describes stockings or tights: {She wore fishnets with her miniskirt}. The material appears in other garments too—shirts, dresses, sleeves—typically suggesting edgy or provocative style. As a modifier: {fishnet stockings}, {fishnet top}.

Fishnets are stockings or tights made with an open, diamond-shaped mesh pattern resembling a fishing net. The term usually refers to the hosiery itself rather than actual nets for catching fish: {She wore fishnets with her punk outfit}. The style suggests boldness or edge, common in rock, goth, and burlesque fashion.

Fishtailing is the side-to-side swinging motion of a vehicle's rear end, typically when traction is lost on slippery roads or during hard acceleration: {The truck started fishtailing on the icy highway}. The image is of a fish's tail sweeping back and forth. The term extends to anything that sways similarly: {The trailer was fishtailing behind us}.

Fishy describes what resembles or smells like fish. The figurative sense dominates: something fishy arouses suspicion or seems dishonest. {There's something fishy about this deal}. {The whole situation seemed fishy to me}. The connection is to the unpleasant smell of fish gone bad—if something smells off, it probably is.

Fission is the splitting of something into parts. In physics, nuclear fission is the splitting of an atomic nucleus, releasing enormous energy—the principle behind nuclear reactors and atomic bombs. In biology, fission is reproduction by dividing into two or more parts, as when a single-celled organism splits in half. Figuratively, any group splitting apart might undergo fission: {The party's fission into rival factions weakened its influence}.

A fist is a hand with the fingers curled tightly into the palm, typically formed for striking or gripping. To fist is to clench the hand this way: {She fisted her hands in frustration}. In sexual slang, fisting refers to inserting a fist into a body cavity. A fist bump is a greeting where two people touch closed fists together.

A fistbump is a greeting or gesture of approval where two people tap their closed fists together. Less formal than a handshake, it signals camaraderie, agreement, or celebration: {They exchanged a fistbump after closing the deal}. The verb is to fistbump or fist-bump: {He fistbumped his teammate}. Also spelled fist bump.

A fistfight is a physical fight using bare fists rather than weapons. The term emphasizes the unarmed, hand-to-hand nature of the combat: {The argument escalated into a fistfight}. As a verb, to fistfight is to engage in such a brawl.

Fistfights is the plural of fistfight—a physical fight using the fists rather than weapons. The word emphasizes bare-knuckle combat: {Fistfights broke out in the stands after the game}. It can describe spontaneous brawls or more deliberate confrontations: {He'd been in plenty of fistfights growing up}.

A fistful is the amount that can be held in a closed hand: {a fistful of coins}, {a fistful of hair}. By extension, it suggests a small but substantial quantity of anything: {a fistful of documents}, {a fistful of complaints}. The word implies grabbing—taking hold of something with force or urgency.

Fisticuffs is a humorous or old-fashioned word for fighting with fists—a brawl or boxing match. The word sounds quaint and slightly absurd to modern ears, which makes it useful for comic effect: {The debate devolved into fisticuffs}. It typically describes unrefined fighting rather than formal boxing.

Fists is the plural of fist—hands with fingers curled tightly into the palm. Fists appear in contexts of fighting, anger, or determination: {He clenched his fists}, {She pounded her fists on the table}. To make money {hand over fist} is to accumulate it rapidly. {Fistfuls} emphasizes grabbing large quantities.

F-i-t is two words in English. The most frequent one is a noun, verb, or adjective. If clothing fits, it is the right size. If a description fits someone, it describes them well. The fit of a piece of clothing is how it conforms to your body. If you are fit, you’re physically conditioned. A fit subject for humor is suitable to make jokes about. The other fit, a noun, is an informal word for an episode of anger or a seizure.

Fitness describes a state of physical health and conditioning, particularly the body's capacity for exercise and exertion: {She improved her fitness by running every morning}. The word extends to general suitability or appropriateness for a purpose: {They questioned his fitness for office}. In biology, fitness refers specifically to an organism's ability to survive and reproduce in its environment—a central concept in evolutionary theory. A fitness center or fitness class focuses on exercise and physical training.

Fits is the plural of fit in its noun senses and the third-person singular of the verb. A fit is a sudden episode—a seizure, a coughing fit, an outburst of emotion: {She had a fit when she saw the mess}. Something that fits conforms to a space or requirement: {This key fits the lock}, {The description fits him perfectly}. Fits and starts describes irregular, intermittent progress: {The project advanced in fits and starts}. (Capitalized FITS is an astronomy data format.)

Fitting describes something appropriate or suitable for a particular situation: {It seemed fitting to end the evening with a toast}. A fitting is a small standardized part—a plumbing fitting, an electrical fitting. In tailoring, a fitting is a session where garments are tried on and adjusted for proper fit: {She has a fitting for her wedding dress tomorrow}.

Five is the number between four and six, represented by the numeral 5. It's the number of fingers on a human hand, which is why a high five involves slapping palms. {Give me five} requests either that gesture or five dollars. In basketball, a team's starting five are its first-string players. {Take five} means take a short break—originally five minutes.

Fix works mainly as a verb with multiple meanings; it can be synonymous with repair (fix a computer), prepare (fix dinner), decide (fix a date for the wedding), or secure (fix the hook to the wall). Something described as fixed might be ready, repaired, decided, or secured in place. The dialectal modal verb fix means getting ready: We’re fixing to leave. A fix can be a difficult situation (lying to his parents put him in a fix) or something illegal or unethical: The fix was in for the horserace. In slang usage, a fix is a dose of a drug for an addict.

Fixated describes an obsessive focus on something, often unhealthily so. Someone fixated on an ex-partner can't stop thinking about them. A person fixated on weight checks the scale constantly. The word implies a preoccupation that crowds out other concerns: {He's fixated on revenge}. In psychology, fixation refers to arrested development at an early stage—hence {oral fixation}, {anal fixation}.

Fixation is an intense, often obsessive focus on something. In psychology, it describes an unhealthy attachment to a person, object, or idea: {She developed a fixation on her ex-boyfriend}. The word implies preoccupation beyond what's reasonable or healthy. In technical contexts, fixation refers to making something stable or stationary—chemical fixation preserves biological specimens, and visual fixation is holding the eyes steady on a point.

Fixed means secured in place, not moving or changeable: {a fixed address}, {fixed costs}, {fixed income}. A fixed gaze is steady and unmoving. Fixed ideas or opinions are rigid, unlikely to change. Something fixed has been repaired: {Is the car fixed yet?} In informal use, fixed can mean rigged or prearranged dishonestly: {The fight was fixed}. To be {fixed for} something is to be supplied with it: {How are you fixed for cash?}

A fixer is someone who solves problems, often through unofficial channels or connections. In journalism, a fixer is a local contact who arranges interviews, translates, and navigates logistics for foreign correspondents: {Our fixer in Kabul got us access to the village}. In politics or crime, a fixer handles sensitive matters discreetly—paying off accusers, silencing witnesses, making problems disappear. In photography, fixer is a chemical solution that stabilizes developed images.

Fixing is preparing or repairing something: {I'm fixing dinner}, {He's fixing the fence}. In the American South, {fixing to} means about to: {I'm fixing to leave}. A fix can be a solution, a dose of an addictive drug, or a rigged outcome—fixing a race or election means predetermining the result dishonestly. Fixings are accompaniments: {a turkey with all the fixings}.

A fixture is something fixed in place—a permanent attachment to a building or property. Light fixtures, plumbing fixtures, and built-in shelving are fixtures because they're installed rather than freestanding. The term extends to anything or anyone that seems permanently established: {He's been a fixture at the bar for twenty years}. In British sports, a fixture is a scheduled match or event: {Saturday's fixture against Arsenal}.

Fizz is the hissing, bubbling sound of gas escaping from liquid—the noise a freshly opened soda makes, or champagne in a glass. The word extends to the bubbles themselves and to effervescent drinks: {a gin fizz}. As a verb, to fizz is to produce this sound and action: {The tablet fizzed in the water}. Fizz can suggest energy or excitement: {The team played with real fizz}.

Fizzing describes something producing small bubbles and a hissing sound, like carbonated drinks or effervescent tablets dissolving in water: {The soda was still fizzing when she handed it to me}. Figuratively, fizzing can mean buzzing with energy or excitement: {The crowd was fizzing with anticipation}. In British slang, fizzing sometimes means furious: {He was absolutely fizzing}.

Fizzle is to sputter weakly and die out. A firework fizzles when it fails to explode properly. More often the word describes endeavors that start promisingly but end in disappointment: {The romance fizzled after a few weeks}. To {fizzle out} emphasizes the gradual decline: {The protest movement fizzled out by summer}. A fizzle is such a failure.

Fizzled is the past tense of fizzle—to fail or peter out after a promising start. A romance fizzles, a campaign fizzles, enthusiasm fizzles. The word suggests gradual deflation rather than dramatic collapse: {The protest fizzled when rain started}. {Their plans fizzled out over the summer}. The original sense was to make a hissing sound, like a damp firework that sputters but never explodes.

Fizzles is the plural noun and third-person singular verb form of fizzle. A fizzle is a weak, sputtering sound or a disappointing failure after a promising start. When something fizzles, it makes a hissing noise while losing energy, like a damp firework. More commonly, fizzles describes efforts or events that fail to deliver: {The rally fizzled when only a dozen people showed up.} The phrase {fizzle out} emphasizes gradual decline into nothing.

Fizzy describes drinks or liquids that contain dissolved carbon dioxide, which produces bubbles and a slight effervescence on the tongue. Sodas, sparkling water, and champagne are all fizzy. The word can extend to anything with similar bubbly qualities: {The bath bomb made the water fizzy}. In British English, fizzy drinks is the standard term for what Americans call soda or pop.

Flabbergast means to astonish or astound someone completely: {I was flabbergasted when she announced her resignation}. The word suggests being struck speechless by surprise. It carries a slightly theatrical, almost comic quality—you might be flabbergasted by unexpected news, but devastated by tragedy.

Flabbergasted means utterly astonished or overwhelmed with surprise. The word carries a theatrical quality, suggesting shock so complete it leaves someone momentarily speechless: {I was flabbergasted when they announced my name}. It's stronger than surprised but playful rather than grave—you might be flabbergasted by unexpected news, not by tragedy.

Flabby describes flesh that is soft and loose rather than firm—the opposite of toned or muscular: {flabby arms}, {a flabby belly}. The word extends to anything lacking firmness or vigor: a flabby {handshake}, flabby {prose}, a flabby {argument}. The connotation is always unflattering, suggesting weakness or insufficient effort.

Three different words are spelled f-l-a-g. The most frequent by far is the usually rectangular piece of cloth that symbolizes a state, a country, a ship, and the like. The derived verb literally means mark with a flag but more often the idea of calling attention to something. Another flag is a verb that signifies lessening intensity: Interest flagged when she started preaching. Finally, flag can be short for flagstone. If you flag a pathway, you line it with these.

Flags are pieces of cloth, often rectangular, displaying distinctive colors or designs to represent nations, organizations, or signals. Ships fly flags to indicate nationality; referees throw flags to mark penalties. To flag is to mark something for attention {flag this email for follow-up} or to lose energy and slow down {The runners flagged in the final mile}. In computing, a flag is a variable that signals a condition or triggers an action.

A flagship is the ship carrying the commander of a fleet, flying that officer's flag. By extension, flagship describes the leading or most important item in a group: a company's flagship {product}, a flagship {store}, a network's flagship {program}. The word implies prominence and the standard by which others in the group are measured.

Flagships are the leading or most important items in a group. The word comes from naval usage—the flagship carried the fleet commander's flag. Now it typically describes a company's premier products or locations: {the flagship store in Manhattan}, {their flagship smartphone}. A flagship represents the best a brand has to offer, setting the standard for everything else in the line.

A flail is a farm tool for threshing grain, consisting of a wooden handle with a shorter stick swinging from it. This image of uncontrolled swinging informs the verb: to flail is to wave or swing wildly, often suggesting panic or lack of coordination. {She flailed her arms trying to keep her balance.} When someone is flailing, they may be struggling physically or metaphorically—thrashing about without making progress. {The campaign has been flailing since the scandal broke.}

Flailing describes wild, uncontrolled movement—arms and legs thrashing without coordination or purpose. A drowning swimmer flails in the water. Beyond physical motion, flailing suggests desperate ineffectiveness: {The campaign was flailing in the polls}, {He flailed for an answer}. The present participle of flail, it emphasizes ongoing struggle rather than momentary action.

Flair is a distinctive talent or aptitude, especially one that comes naturally: {She has a real flair for languages}. It also suggests stylishness or panache—a certain confident elegance in how someone does things: {He dresses with flair}. The word carries connotations of effortlessness; having flair implies the skill or style appears innate rather than laboriously acquired.

Flak is anti-aircraft fire—shells exploding around planes to bring them down. From this comes the figurative sense: heavy criticism or opposition directed at someone. {The mayor took flak for the proposal.} {She's catching flak from all sides.} A flak jacket protects against shrapnel. A flak (also flack) is a publicist or press agent.

An archetypal flake is something small, thin or flat, and light that exists in large numbers (pepper flakes, bran flakes). When you flake something, you reduce it to flakes or remove flakes from it. If something flakes, flakes come off it, often in an undesirable way: The paint flaked off the side of the barn. In slang use, a flake is an undependable person with a flighty disposition and unreliable mind.

Flakes are small, flat, thin pieces that break or peel off a larger surface: {flakes of rust}, {flakes of paint}, {snowflakes}. Breakfast cereals come in flake form. To flake is to break into such pieces or to peel away in layers. A flake is also slang for an unreliable person—one who cancels plans or doesn't follow through: {Don't count on him; he's a total flake}.

Flakey is an alternate spelling of flaky. Something flaky breaks into thin, flat pieces: {flakey pastry}, {flakey skin}. A flaky person is unreliable or eccentric—prone to forgetting commitments or acting unpredictably: {He's too flakey to trust with anything important}.

Flaky describes things that break or come off in thin, light pieces: {flaky pastry}, {flaky skin}, {flaky paint peeling from the wall}. The texture suggests layers that separate easily. Informally, flaky describes someone unreliable or unpredictable—prone to canceling plans, forgetting commitments, or behaving erratically: {She's too flaky to count on for anything important}.

Flamboyance is showy, dramatic style—behavior, dress, or manner designed to attract attention. The word suggests boldness and confidence rather than quiet taste: {His flamboyance made him impossible to ignore at parties}. It can carry admiration or disapproval depending on context, praising someone's flair or criticizing excess.

Flamboyant describes someone or something dramatically colorful, ornate, or attention-grabbing. A flamboyant person dresses boldly, gestures expansively, and generally refuses to blend in: {He made a flamboyant entrance in a velvet cape}. The word can be admiring or faintly critical, suggesting excess. In architecture, Flamboyant refers to a late Gothic style featuring flame-like curves in the tracery.

A flame is the visible, glowing part of a fire—the hot gases that produce light as fuel burns. Flames can be small {(a candle flame)} or engulfing {(flames spread through the building)}. Figuratively, flame suggests passion: an old {flame} is a former lover. To flame out is to fail spectacularly. Online, to flame someone is to attack them with hostile, often personal messages: {He got flamed for his comment}.

Flamenco is a style of Spanish music and dance originating in Andalusia, characterized by passionate vocals, intricate guitar work, rhythmic handclapping, and percussive footwork. The dance features proud posture, dramatic arm movements, and emotional intensity: {She studied flamenco in Seville}. The term also describes the music, guitar style, and cultural tradition surrounding the art form.

Flames are the visible, glowing part of a fire—tongues of burning gas that rise from combustible material. The word extends to anything resembling fire's appearance or intensity: {flames of orange and red in the autumn leaves}. To go down {in flames} is to fail spectacularly. An old flame is a former romantic partner. Online, to flame someone is to attack them with hostile messages: {He got flamed for his controversial take}.

A flamethrower is a weapon that projects a stream of burning fuel at targets. Military flamethrowers were used extensively in World War II and Vietnam to clear bunkers and fortifications. Smaller versions exist for controlled agricultural burns. The word sometimes describes anything that produces dramatic flames: {The chef's flambé technique turned his pan into a flamethrower}.

Flamethrowers are weapons that project streams of burning fuel, used militarily to clear fortifications and vegetation. The device typically consists of a fuel tank, pressurized gas, and an ignition system. Figuratively, a flamethrower is anyone or anything that attacks with fierce intensity: {The senator was a flamethrower in the debate}.

Flaming describes something on fire or resembling fire: {flaming torches}, {flaming red hair}. As an intensifier, it expresses anger or emphasis: {a flaming idiot}, {What a flaming mess}. In internet culture, flaming is attacking someone with hostile, abusive messages: {The comment section devolved into flaming}. Flaming is also a slur for ostentatiously effeminate gay men.

A flamingo is a tall wading bird with pink or reddish plumage, long legs, and a distinctively curved bill. Flamingos get their color from pigments in the crustaceans and algae they eat. They're known for standing on one leg and are often seen in large flocks in shallow lakes and lagoons. Plastic flamingos are a famously kitschy lawn ornament.

Flamingos is the plural of flamingo, the tall wading bird with pink plumage, long legs, and a curved bill. The pink color comes from pigments in their diet of shrimp and algae. They're known for standing on one leg and for their large, noisy colonies: {We saw flamingos at the lake}. Plastic flamingos are a kitschy lawn ornament.

Flammable means capable of catching fire easily: {flammable materials}, {highly flammable gas}. The word arose as a clearer alternative to inflammable, which some people misread as meaning "not flammable" due to the in- prefix. Both words mean the same thing—able to burn. For safety labels and warnings, flammable is now standard.

Flan is a baked custard dessert with a caramel topping, the caramel forming a sauce when the dish is inverted onto a plate. The word comes from Spanish and is especially associated with Latin American and Spanish cuisines. In British usage, flan refers to an open tart with a sweet or savory filling: {a fruit flan}, {a cheese and onion flan}.

Flank refers to the side of something—originally the fleshy part between ribs and hip on an animal or person. A flank {steak} comes from this cut. In military contexts, the flank is the vulnerable side of a formation: {The cavalry attacked the enemy's left flank}. To flank is to be positioned at the side: {Mountains flanked the valley}, {bodyguards flanking the president}. To outflank is to maneuver around an opponent's side, literally or strategically.

Flanking is positioning at or moving along the side of something. In military contexts, to flank is to attack from the side rather than head-on: {Enemy forces flanked our position}. The tactic extends to any strategic positioning: {Mountains flanked the valley}. In gaming and sports, flanking means outmaneuvering opponents by approaching from an unexpected angle.

Flannel is a soft, loosely woven fabric, typically wool or cotton, with a slightly napped surface. It's associated with warmth and comfort: flannel {shirts}, flannel {pajamas}, flannel {sheets}. A flannel or face flannel is British for a washcloth. In British slang, flannel means evasive or flattering talk meant to deceive: {Don't give me that flannel}.

Flap captures the motion of something broad and flexible moving up and down or back and forth: a bird's wings flap, a flag flaps in the wind, a loose shutter flaps against the house. A flap is a hinged or attached piece that covers an opening—the flap of an envelope, a tent flap, a cat flap. On aircraft, flaps are movable surfaces that increase lift during takeoff and landing. Informally, a flap is a state of agitation or a minor controversy: {Don't get in a flap over it}, {The memo caused quite a flap}.

A flapjack is a pancake in American English—a flat cake of batter cooked on a griddle: {We had flapjacks with maple syrup}. In British English, a flapjack is something different: a dense, chewy bar made from oats, butter, and golden syrup, baked until golden.

Flapjacks are pancakes in American English—flat, round cakes made from batter and cooked on a griddle: {We had flapjacks with maple syrup}. In British English, flapjacks are something entirely different: chewy oat bars baked with butter and golden syrup. The American sense evokes diners and lumberjack breakfasts; the British sense suggests teatime treats.

A flapper was a young woman of the 1920s who flouted conventional expectations—wearing short skirts, bobbing her hair, smoking, drinking, and embracing jazz culture. The term captured both the fashion and the attitude: bold, modern, sexually liberated. {She dressed like a flapper for the costume party.} The word has faded into historical reference, evoking the Jazz Age and Prohibition-era rebellion.

Flappers were young women of the 1920s who defied conventional expectations—wearing short skirts and bobbed hair, drinking and smoking in public, dancing to jazz. The term captured both their style and their spirit of rebellion against Victorian morality. A flapper is also anything that flaps: a hinged part, a broad fin, or a young bird learning to fly.

Flare combines brightness with spreading outward. A flare is a burst of light or flame—a distress signal, a solar eruption, or the brief blaze of a match. To flare is to burn or shine suddenly: {Tempers flared}. Flare also means to spread gradually wider: jeans that flare at the bottom, nostrils that flare in anger. A flare-up is a sudden recurrence of trouble, whether conflict or chronic illness.

Flares are devices that produce a bright light or flame, used for signaling, illumination, or as a distress signal: {The stranded hikers set off flares to alert rescuers}. In fashion, flares are pants that widen below the knee, popular in the 1970s and periodically revived. Solar flares are sudden eruptions of radiation from the sun's surface. As a verb form, flares describes something bursting into light or spreading outward: {Her temper flares when she's tired}. A medical condition may flare or flare up when symptoms suddenly worsen.

Meanings of flash are divergent but often convey the idea of suddenness, short duration, light, and significance. A flash of light is bright and appears suddenly, as does a flash of lightning. A hot flash is a sudden surge of heat felt in the body. Something that is flash fried or flash frozen is fried or frozen quickly. If you flash a smile at someone, you smile suddenly, and perhaps briefly. Flash also describes solid-state computer memory.

A flashback is a scene in a film, novel, or other narrative that interrupts the present action to show earlier events. The technique fills in backstory or explains motivation. In psychology, a flashback is an involuntary vivid memory, often traumatic, that intrudes on present consciousness: {Veterans may experience flashbacks to combat}. The verb is flash back: {The story flashes back to her childhood}.

Flashbacks are vivid, often involuntary memories of past events that intrude on the present moment. The term originated in film, where a flashback is a scene depicting earlier events: {The movie uses flashbacks to reveal the character's childhood}. In psychology, flashbacks are a symptom of trauma, particularly PTSD, where someone relives a distressing experience as if it were happening again. The word also describes the recurrence of drug effects long after taking a hallucinogen.

A flashbang is a grenade designed to disorient rather than kill, producing a blinding flash and deafening bang without lethal shrapnel. Used by military and police in hostage rescues and room-clearing operations: {SWAT tossed a flashbang through the window before entering}. Also called a stun grenade.

A flashcard is a card used for memorization and study, typically with a question, term, or prompt on one side and the answer or definition on the other. Students flip through flashcards to test themselves, and the format has migrated from physical index cards to digital apps. {I made flashcards to study for my biology exam.} The spaced repetition method, which schedules review of flashcards at optimal intervals, has made them central to language learning.

Flashcards are cards used for memorization, typically with a question or prompt on one side and the answer on the other. Students flip through them repeatedly, testing recall: {She made flashcards for her vocabulary quiz}. The format has migrated to apps and software, where algorithms optimize review timing.

Flashes is the plural of flash—brief, sudden bursts of light or insight. Lightning flashes illuminate the sky; flashes of brilliance interrupt ordinary thinking. Camera flashes fire in rapid succession. {Flashes of memory came back to her}. News flashes interrupt regular programming. Hot flashes are sudden feelings of heat, especially during menopause.

Flashing serves as a present participle of flash, covering its range of meanings—light appearing suddenly, something happening quickly, or brief exposure. The noun flashing refers to sheet metal strips used to weatherproof joints in roofing and construction: {The flashing around the chimney needs replacing}. It also names the act of briefly exposing one's body, especially genitals, in public: {He was arrested for flashing}.

A flashlight is a portable, battery-powered light source, typically cylindrical and held in the hand. The British term is torch. Flashlights range from tiny keychain models to heavy-duty versions used by police and rescue workers. The verb flashlight means to illuminate with one: {He flashlighted the path ahead}.

Flashlights are portable, battery-powered devices that produce a beam of light, typically from an LED or incandescent bulb. The term is primarily American; British English prefers torch. Flashlights range from tiny keychain models to heavy-duty tactical lights used by police and military. {I keep a flashlight in the glove compartment for emergencies.} The verb form, to flashlight, occasionally appears meaning to illuminate with one.

Flashpoint has both a technical and a figurative sense, connected by the idea of ignition. In chemistry and physics, the flashpoint of a substance is the lowest temperature at which its vapors will ignite when exposed to a flame or spark. Figuratively, a flashpoint is a place, moment, or issue where tension or conflict suddenly erupts into violence or crisis: {The disputed border region has become a flashpoint between the two nations}. The word emphasizes how quickly situations can escalate from stable to volatile.

Flashy describes things that are showy, eye-catching, and designed to impress—often in a way that suggests more style than substance. A flashy {car} or flashy {jewelry} grabs attention through bright colors, elaborate design, or obvious expense. When applied to people or their behavior, flashy often carries a hint of disapproval, implying that someone is trying too hard to be noticed or is prioritizing appearance over quality. {He showed up in a flashy suit that screamed new money.}

A flask is a container for liquids, typically with a narrow neck. A hip flask is a small, flat bottle designed to fit in a pocket for carrying alcohol. In chemistry, flasks are glass vessels of various shapes—round-bottomed, flat-bottomed, Erlenmeyer—used for mixing, heating, or storing substances. A vacuum flask (thermos) keeps beverages hot or cold.

The adjective and adverb flat describes a condition of being smooth, level, horizontal, or possibly all of these. A flat roof lies in a single plane. Flat feet do not have much of an arch. A flat fee does not change based on some other variable. If you do something in ten seconds flat you do not exceed that time. As a noun, flat may denote a shoe without an elevated heel, and in British English, a condominium or apartment.

A flatbed is a truck or trailer with a flat, open cargo area—no sides or roof—used for hauling large or awkwardly shaped loads: {The lumber arrived on a flatbed}. The term also describes a type of scanner or printer where documents lie flat on a glass surface: {a flatbed scanner}. As an adjective: {flatbed truck}, {flatbed trailer}.

A flatearther believes the Earth is flat rather than spherical, rejecting established science in favor of conspiracy theories about government cover-ups and faked space exploration. The term is often used dismissively for anyone who denies overwhelming scientific consensus: {Arguing with him about vaccines is pointless—he's basically a flatearther}.

Flatline refers to the straight horizontal line on a monitor that indicates the absence of electrical activity, particularly in a heart monitor showing cardiac arrest. As a verb, to flatline means to die or to show no vital signs: {The patient flatlined twice during surgery but was resuscitated}. The term extends figuratively to anything that shows no activity, growth, or variation: {Sales have flatlined since the new competitor entered the market}. Something that flatlines goes completely still or ceases to function.

Flatlined comes from the flat line on a heart monitor when cardiac activity stops. Literally, to flatline is to die or experience cardiac arrest: {The patient flatlined twice during surgery}. Figuratively, it describes anything that has stopped progressing or gone completely inactive: {Sales flatlined after the initial buzz}, {The project flatlined when funding dried up}.

Flatlining originally describes the flat line on a heart monitor when cardiac activity stops—the patient is dying or dead. The term extends to anything showing no activity or movement: {Sales have been flatlining for months}, {The project is flatlining}. To flatline is to show this pattern, whether literally in a medical crisis or figuratively for stagnant performance.

Flatpack describes furniture or other items sold disassembled in a flat box, designed for home assembly: {We spent the afternoon wrestling with flatpack bookshelves}. The term is strongly associated with IKEA and similar retailers. As a noun, it refers to the item itself or its packaging: {The flatpack arrived with missing screws}.

Flats are shoes without elevated heels, worn for comfort or practicality: {She changed from heels into flats for the walk home}. The word also refers to level expanses of land, especially wetlands: {salt flats}, {mud flats}, {tidal flats}. In theater, flats are lightweight framed panels used as scenery. In music, flats are notes lowered by a half step, or the symbol indicating this. In British English, flats are apartments.

Flatten means to make flat or flatter—to compress, level, or smooth something out. You flatten dough with a rolling pin, flatten a box for recycling, or flatten your hair against your head. Extended uses follow naturally: a storm flattens crops, an army flattens a city, bad news flattens your mood. To flatten someone can mean to knock them down or defeat them decisively: {He flattened his opponent in the third round}.

To flatter is to praise someone, often insincerely or excessively, usually to win favor or manipulate: {He flattered her to get the promotion}. Flattery may also be genuine admiration: {I'm flattered you asked}. To say something flatters a person means it makes them look good: {That dress flatters your figure}. To {flatter yourself} is to hold an inflated self-opinion.

Flattered describes the pleased feeling when someone's attention or praise suggests you matter to them. To feel flattered is to be gratified by a compliment or honor: {I'm flattered you remembered my birthday}. It can also acknowledge praise while deflecting it: {I'm flattered, but I really don't deserve the credit}. Sometimes it signals suspicious pleasure—flattery implies possible insincerity.

Flattering describes something that makes a person look or feel more attractive, capable, or admirable than they might otherwise appear. A flattering {photograph} captures someone at their best; a flattering {dress} accentuates favorable features while minimizing less desired ones. Flattering remarks or attention may be sincere compliments or may be exaggerated praise designed to win favor. When someone is described as flattering, it often carries a hint of insincerity or ulterior motive.

Flattery is excessive or insincere praise, usually offered to gain favor or manipulate. Unlike genuine compliments, flattery has an agenda—the flatterer wants something. {She saw through his flattery immediately.} The line between flattery and sincere admiration depends on motive and proportion: {A little flattery never hurts, but don't overdo it.}

Flaunt means to display something ostentatiously, usually to provoke admiration or envy: {She flaunted her new diamond ring}, {He likes to flaunt his wealth}. The word implies showing off deliberately rather than simply being visible. Flaunt is often confused with flout (to openly disregard), but they're distinct: you flaunt possessions, you flout rules.

Flaunting is showing something off ostentatiously, displaying it to attract attention or admiration: {flaunting her new diamond ring}, {flaunting his wealth}. The word carries a note of disapproval—flaunting suggests excess or poor taste. Often confused with flouting, which means openly defying rules or conventions.

Flavor is the distinctive taste of something, the sensation produced when food or drink meets the tongue and nose: {The soup had a rich, savory flavor}. Extended, flavor means a characteristic quality or style: {The neighborhood has an old-world flavor}. In physics, flavor distinguishes types of quarks and leptons. To flavor something is to add taste to it. Flavors can be literal (vanilla, chocolate) or figurative (flavors of political conservatism).

Flavors are the distinctive tastes that characterize foods, drinks, and other substances we put in our mouths. The word extends beyond literal taste to describe varieties or versions of things: {The software comes in several flavors}. In physics, flavor distinguishes types of quarks and leptons. As a verb, to flavor something is to add taste to it, and figuratively, experiences can flavor our perceptions: {His time in the military flavored his approach to management}.

Flavour is the British spelling of flavor. The taste of something, or more precisely the combination of taste and smell that makes food distinctive: {The soup had a rich, earthy flavour}. Extended to any distinctive quality or character: {The town retains its medieval flavour}. In physics, flavour distinguishes types of quarks and leptons. To flavour food is to add seasoning or enhance its taste.

A flaw is an imperfection that diminishes quality or value. A diamond has a flaw if it contains a visible inclusion. A flaw in an argument is a weakness in its logic. A character flaw is a personal failing: {His temper was his fatal flaw}. To flaw something is to mar it, though flawed as an adjective is more common: {a deeply flawed study}.

Flawed means having a flaw—an imperfection, defect, or weakness. A flawed {diamond} has visible impurities. A flawed {argument} contains logical errors. A flawed {character} has moral shortcomings. The word often acknowledges imperfection without total condemnation: {He was flawed but fundamentally decent}. Deeply flawed or fatally flawed signal more serious problems.

Flawless means without any imperfection or defect. A flawless {diamond} has no visible inclusions. A flawless {performance} contains no errors. The word often carries hyperbolic force—praising something as ideal or beyond criticism: {Her logic was flawless}. In casual use, flawless has become enthusiastic approval: {That outfit is flawless}.

Flaws are imperfections or defects—features that mar something otherwise sound. A diamond has flaws if it contains visible inclusions. A plan has flaws if it contains weaknesses that could cause failure. Character flaws are personal shortcomings: {His fatal flaw was pride}. The verb means to introduce such defects: {A single error flawed the experiment}.

Flayed means stripped of skin. Literally, to flay is to remove the skin from a body, whether as butchery, torture, or punishment—an image of extreme pain and exposure. Figuratively, to be flayed is to be harshly criticized or verbally attacked: {The critics flayed her performance}. {He felt flayed by her words}.

A flea is a tiny wingless insect that feeds on blood, jumping between hosts with powerful hind legs. Fleas infest dogs, cats, and other mammals, causing itching and sometimes transmitting disease. A {flea market} is an outdoor bazaar selling secondhand goods—the name suggesting items might carry fleas. A {flea bag} or {fleabag} is a shabby hotel.

A fleabag is a shabby, run-down place—typically a cheap hotel or rooming house: {We spent the night in some fleabag motel off the highway}. The word suggests a place so dirty it might harbor fleas. It can also refer to a mangy animal, especially a dog or cat, or more loosely to any decrepit thing or disreputable person.

Fleas are tiny wingless insects that feed on the blood of mammals and birds. They're infamous for infesting pets and homes, jumping remarkable distances relative to their size. A flea market sells secondhand goods—the name suggests you might find items that have been around long enough to harbor parasites. To {put a flea in someone's ear} is to give them a sharp rebuke or unwelcome hint.

Fled is the past tense and past participle of flee. To flee is to run away from danger or pursuit: {They fled the burning building}, {The suspect fled on foot}. Fled also applies to leaving a place urgently due to threat or hardship: {Refugees fled the war zone}, {She fled an abusive marriage}.

A fledgling is a young bird that has recently grown its flight feathers and is learning to fly. From this concrete image comes the more common figurative use: anything new and inexperienced, especially a person or organization just starting out. {The fledgling company struggled to find investors.} As an adjective, fledgling characterizes things that are new, immature, or just beginning to develop: {a fledgling democracy}, {fledgling efforts at reform}.

Fledglings are young birds that have developed enough feathers to leave the nest but are still learning to fly and fend for themselves. The term extends to any inexperienced person or thing just starting out: {The company hired several fledglings fresh out of college}. A fledgling business or fledgling democracy is one in its early stages of development, not yet fully established or proven.

To flee is to run away from danger or unpleasantness. You flee a burning building, a war zone, or an uncomfortable conversation. The past tense is fled: {They fled the country when the regime changed}. Flee suggests urgency—you don't flee casually. Things can also flee figuratively: {All hope fled when we saw the damage}.

Fleece is the woolly coat of a sheep, or the wool sheared from one: {The shepherd sold the fleece at market}. By extension, fleece names soft fabric that mimics wool's warmth: {a fleece jacket}. To fleece someone is to swindle them—shearing them of their money as a sheep is shorn of wool: {The con artist fleeced tourists out of thousands}.

Fleeced means swindled or overcharged—stripped of money the way a sheep is stripped of wool. Someone who paid three hundred dollars for a counterfeit watch got fleeced. The word implies the victim was naive or the swindler particularly skilled: {Tourists get fleeced at that market}. Less commonly, fleeced describes fabric with a soft napped surface.

Fleecing is cheating or swindling someone, typically by charging excessive prices or extracting money through deception: {tourists getting fleeced by street vendors}, {The casino fleeced him for everything he had}. The image comes from shearing a sheep—stripping away what covers someone, leaving them exposed and poorer.

Fleeing is the act of running away from danger, threat, or an undesirable situation. The word captures active escape in progress: {Residents were photographed fleeing the wildfire}, {refugees fleeing persecution}. It emphasizes urgency and often fear—you flee what threatens you, not merely what inconveniences you.

Fleet describes a group of vehicles or vessels with a common purpose or mission. All of the vehicles owned by a company for their own use may be called a fleet, just as all the ships of a nation are. As an adjective, fleet is seen mainly in literary use meaning fast, in the expressions fleet of foot and a fleet horse.

Fleeting describes something that passes quickly or lasts only a moment: a fleeting {glimpse}, a fleeting {thought}, fleeting {happiness}. The word emphasizes how briefly something exists before vanishing. What's fleeting may be precious precisely because it doesn't last: {Their time together was fleeting but unforgettable}.

Fleets is the plural of fleet—groups of ships, vehicles, or aircraft operating together under common ownership or command: {The company operates fleets of delivery trucks across three states}. A nation's naval fleet is its warships collectively. Fleet also works as an adjective meaning swift, and as a verb meaning to pass quickly, though these uses are literary and uncommon.

Flesh refers to skin (typically of humans) or other soft tissue (typically of animals). Flesh is also a common metaphor for humankind and its vulnerabilities. Flesh and blood may designate your blood relatives, the human body, or human nature. If you flesh out an idea, you add more detail or information about it. Things appreciatively described as fleshed out have all needed information or features available.

Flew is the past tense of fly. A bird flew overhead. Time flew by. She flew into a rage. He flew to Chicago. The ball flew over the fence. In each case, flew describes movement through air or rapid motion that has already occurred.

Flex means to bend or contract a muscle, showing its shape and strength: {He flexed his biceps in the mirror}. By extension, to flex is to demonstrate power or capability: {The company flexed its market dominance}. In slang, flex means to show off or boast, especially about wealth or status: {She's always flexing on Instagram}. As a noun, a flex is an act of showing off: {Buying that car was a flex}.

Flexibility is the ability to bend without breaking, whether physical or figurative. A gymnast has flexibility; so does a schedule that accommodates changes. Flexible arrangements adapt to circumstances: {We need some flexibility on the deadline}. The word implies willingness to adjust rather than rigid adherence to fixed plans or positions.

Flexible means able to bend without breaking: {flexible plastic}, {a flexible wire}. The word extends naturally to anything that can adapt or adjust. A flexible schedule accommodates changes. A flexible person is open to new ideas or willing to compromise. Flexible thinking allows for creative problem-solving. The opposite is rigid, whether describing materials or mindsets.

Flexing is contracting a muscle to make it bulge, the way bodybuilders do to display their physiques. The meaning extends to any show of strength or capability: {Russia is flexing its military power}. In slang, flexing is showing off wealth, status, or possessions: {He's always flexing his new watch on Instagram}. The slang usage often carries a note of disapproval—suggesting the display is excessive or insecure.

A flick is a quick, light motion—a snap of the fingers, a flip of a switch, a brush of the wrist: {She flicked a crumb off the table}. To flick through something is to browse it rapidly: {flicking through channels}, {flicking through a magazine}. In casual speech, a flick is a movie: {We caught a flick last night}. A chick flick targets female audiences.

Flicker describes unsteady, wavering light or movement—a candle flame disturbed by a draft, a dying lightbulb, an old film projection. The noun names such movement or a brief instance of something: {a flicker of hope}, {a flicker of recognition crossed her face}. To flicker is to move or shine in this unstable way. A flicker is also a North American woodpecker with a distinctive undulating flight.

Flickering describes light or flame that wavers unsteadily, alternating rapidly between brightness and dimness: {flickering candles}, {the flickering glow of the television}. The word suggests instability or impermanence. A flickering hope or interest is one that appears and fades, uncertain whether it will sustain itself or die out entirely.

Flicks is informal for movies or the cinema: {Let's catch a flick}, {going to the flicks}. The term comes from the flickering of early film projectors. Flicks is also the plural of flick—a quick, light motion or strike: {flicks of the wrist}, {flicks of a light switch}. To flick is to move something with such a motion: {She flicked a crumb off the table}.

Flies is the plural of fly in its noun senses—the common insect, the zipper flap on trousers {your flies are undone}, or the space above a theater stage. As a verb, flies is the third-person singular: {She flies to Boston every week}, {Time flies}. In baseball, a player flies out by hitting a ball caught in the air.

Flight is a noun closely related to the verb fly, which explains most of its meanings. It denotes the ability to fly, or an act or instance of flying. Flight can also mean escape: fight or flight, flight of the Israelites out of Egypt. A flight of steps is the group of stairs from one level to another: I didn’t know she lived five flights up! Today, the most frequent use of flight is to designate the journeys of aircraft. This is also true when flight comes before another noun: flight attendant, flight path, flight recorder.

Flights is the plural of flight, covering all its senses. A bird takes flight; you book flights to distant cities; flights of stairs connect floors. A flight can be a group moving together: {a flight of geese}, {a flight of arrows}. Flights of fancy are imaginative excursions, sometimes impractical ones. In drinking, a flight is a sampler of several varieties: {a flight of wines}, {a beer flight}.

Flimflam is nonsense or deceptive talk, especially when used to swindle someone. A flimflam is a confidence trick or petty fraud: {The whole investment scheme was a flimflam}. To flimflam is to cheat through fast talk or misdirection: {He flimflammed tourists out of their cash}. The word has an old-fashioned, almost playful ring despite describing dishonesty.

Flimsy describes something weak, thin, or insubstantial—easily torn, broken, or seen through. A flimsy {excuse} won't hold up to scrutiny. Flimsy {curtains} let light through. Flimsy {construction} suggests poor quality that won't last. The word carries connotations of cheapness or inadequacy: {The evidence against him was flimsy at best}.

Flinch is a quick, involuntary movement away from something painful or startling—a wince, a recoil: {She flinched when the nurse inserted the needle}. Figuratively, to flinch is to shrink from difficulty or unpleasantness: {He didn't flinch from telling her the truth}. The noun names the movement itself: {a visible flinch}.

Fling emphasizes force and carelessness in throwing: {She flung the door open}, {He flung his coat on the chair}. The word extends to any abrupt, energetic action: {fling yourself into work}, {fling accusations}. A fling is also a brief romantic or sexual affair, implying something casual and temporary: {a summer fling}. To {have a fling} at something is to give it a try.

Flings is the plural of fling and the third-person singular verb form. A fling is a brief, carefree episode—especially a short romantic or sexual relationship: {We had a fling one summer}. To fling is to throw with force or abandon: {She flung open the door}. A {final fling} or {last fling} is one more indulgence before settling down or giving something up.

Flint is a hard, fine-grained stone that produces sparks when struck against steel. This property made flint essential for starting fires and firing early guns—a flintlock rifle uses a piece of flint to ignite gunpowder. The word extends to anything that sparks or ignites: the flint in a lighter, or figuratively, a person with a {heart of flint}—cold and unyielding.

A flintlock is an old firing mechanism that uses a flint striking steel to create sparks, igniting gunpowder to discharge the weapon. By extension, flintlock refers to any gun using this mechanism—muskets, pistols, and rifles from roughly the 17th through mid-19th centuries: {a pair of dueling flintlocks}, {The militia carried flintlock muskets}.

Flintlocks are firearms that use a flint striking steel to create sparks that ignite gunpowder. The mechanism dominated from the 17th through early 19th centuries before percussion caps replaced it. A flintlock is also the firing mechanism itself. The term evokes colonial America, pirates, and Revolutionary War muskets: {The militia shouldered their flintlocks}.

Flip captures a quick, snapping motion—turning something over with a flick: flip a {coin}, flip a {pancake}, flip through {pages}. A flip is also a backward somersault. To flip out is to lose control emotionally: {She flipped when she saw the mess}. To flip someone off is to extend the middle finger as an insult. Flip as an adjective means casually disrespectful: {a flip remark}. In real estate, to flip a property is to buy and quickly resell it for profit.

A flipbook is a small book with a series of images that, when pages are rapidly flipped with the thumb, create the illusion of animation. Each page shows a slightly different position, so the sequence appears to move: {She made a flipbook of a stick figure doing a backflip}. The format demonstrates the basic principle behind film and animation. Also spelled flip book.

A flipbook is a small book with a series of images that, when pages are rapidly thumbed, create the illusion of motion—a primitive form of animation. The technique exploits persistence of vision: {She made a flipbook of a stick figure doing a backflip}. Digital flipbooks are electronic documents designed to simulate page-turning.
