It can be a deliberate decision or a gradual emotional release: {She asked for his forgiveness}, {Forgiveness doesn't mean forgetting}. Religious and therapeutic contexts treat forgiveness as spiritually or psychologically beneficial. To forgive a debt is to cancel the obligation to repay it.

Forgiving describes someone willing to pardon offenses or let go of resentment: {She's remarkably forgiving of his faults}. The word can also describe things that tolerate error or imperfection: a forgiving {golf club} compensates for bad swings, a forgiving {recipe} works even if measurements are off. The opposite is unforgiving—demanding precision or holding grudges.

Forgot is the past tense of forget—to fail to remember or to leave behind unintentionally: {I forgot her name}, {He forgot his wallet}. It also expresses neglect of duty or consideration: {You forgot to call}, {She forgot about the meeting}. In casual speech, forgot sometimes substitutes for forgotten as the past participle: {I had forgot all about it}.

Forgotten is the past participle of forget, describing something no longer remembered or attended to: {a forgotten anniversary}, {forgotten dreams}. What's forgotten has slipped from memory or been neglected over time. A {forgotten man} is someone society has overlooked. {Long-forgotten} emphasizes how much time has passed since something was last recalled.

Meanings of fork suggest a branching into two (or more) from a single source. Implements with multiples tines attached to a single handle include the pitch fork, the tuning fork, and of course the fork that you eat with. A fork in a river or stream is a place where a single stream splits in two, the converse of a confluence. Something that forks or is forked has a point of division where one becomes two. When you fork over something, especially money, you transfer it, perhaps unwillingly.

Forked describes something that divides into branches or prongs. A forked {road} splits in two directions. A forked {tongue} is literally split at the tip, as in snakes, but figuratively suggests deceptive speech: {He speaks with a forked tongue}. Lightning that branches across the sky is forked {lightning}. In software development, a forked {project} has split from the original to pursue a different direction.

A forklift is a small industrial vehicle with two horizontal prongs at the front that slide under pallets or heavy loads to lift and move them. Forklifts are essential equipment in warehouses, shipping yards, and construction sites where materials need to be stacked or transported short distances. The operator typically sits in a cab and controls both the vehicle's movement and the raising and lowering of the fork mechanism. {We need a forklift to unload this shipment.}

Forks is the plural of fork—utensils with prongs for spearing food, or any pronged tool. Forks also names places where roads or rivers divide: {We reached a forks in the trail}. In computing, forks are copies of software projects that develop independently from the original: {Several forks of the open-source code emerged after the dispute}.

Forlorn describes something pitifully sad, lonely, or abandoned. A forlorn figure sits alone on a park bench. A forlorn house stands empty and neglected. The word carries a sense of desolation and hopelessness: {She cast a forlorn glance at the departing train}. A {forlorn hope} is a faint, desperate one—almost certainly doomed to fail.

Form is a very general noun that for a tangible thing denotes its shape and structure, and for an intangible thing, denotes an essential feature or identifying characteristic: What form did the protest take? One of the commonest uses of form is for a piece of paper, or a web page, that contains blanks to be filled in by a person: Have you filled out the application form? In some countries, form is also the name given to levels in school: the sixth form. As a verb, form means to take shape, or to give shape to: The insect forms a nest out of leaves. When something abstract forms or is formed, it comes into being: We formed a partnership with our former rivals.

Formal describes what follows established rules, conventions, or ceremonies. A formal {dinner} has set courses and dress codes. Formal {attire} means suits and gowns. A formal {complaint} goes through official channels. Formal {education} happens in institutions with curricula, as opposed to learning on your own. The word often contrasts with casual or informal: formal {English} avoids contractions and slang. As a noun, a formal is a dance requiring dressy clothes: {the winter formal}.

Formalities are the conventional procedures or requirements that must be observed in official or ceremonial contexts: {We completed the legal formalities and signed the papers}. The word often carries a dismissive tone, suggesting mere ritual rather than substance: {Let's skip the formalities and get down to business}. Social formalities are polite customs like introductions or thank-you notes.

Formality is adherence to established rules, conventions, or ceremonies—the opposite of casualness. A formality is a required procedure that may feel perfunctory: {Signing the paperwork was just a formality}. The formality of an event determines dress codes and behavior. Formalities are conventional courtesies: {Let's skip the formalities and get to business}.

The format of something is the specification that defines its form (magazine format, television format). A file format describes the conventions for a computer file that determine how it can be used (MP3 format, HTML format). When you format something, you add the features that will make it conform to a particular format. When you format a disk or hard drive, you erase all of the data on it.

Formation is the process of something coming into being or taking shape, or the result of that process. Rocks have formations; so do military units, marching bands, and football offenses—any group arranged in a deliberate pattern. {The band practiced their halftime formation for weeks.} The word often implies structure emerging from less organized elements: the formation of {a government}, the formation of {an opinion}, the formation of {ice crystals} on a window.

Former identifies something or someone from an earlier time, no longer holding that position or status: {a former president}, {my former husband}, {a former factory now converted to lofts}. When distinguishing between two items already mentioned, former refers to the first one, contrasting with latter for the second: {Between tea and coffee, I prefer the former}.

Formidable describes something that inspires fear, respect, or dread through its power, size, or difficulty. A formidable opponent is one you'd rather not face. A formidable challenge tests your limits. A formidable intellect commands respect. The word carries admiration alongside apprehension—what's formidable is impressive precisely because it's daunting: {She built a formidable reputation in the courtroom}.

Forms are the shapes, structures, or configurations things take. A form can be physical {the human form} or abstract {a form of government}. Form also means a document with blank spaces to fill in: {tax forms}, {application forms}. In education, form is British for grade level. To form something is to create or shape it: {form an opinion}, {form a committee}. Ice forms when water freezes. Athletes and musicians work on their form—their technique or manner of execution.

A formula is a fixed form of words used for a specific purpose—a ritual phrase, a legal statement, a mathematical expression. In math and science, formulas express relationships between quantities: {the formula for calculating velocity}. A formula can also be a recipe or method: {a formula for success}, {baby formula}. The word often implies something mechanical or unoriginal: {The movie follows a predictable formula}. Plural: formulas or formulae.

Formulas is the standard plural of formula. A formula is a set form of words or symbols expressing something precisely—a mathematical formula, a chemical formula, a formula for success. Baby formula is manufactured milk substitute. In racing, Formula One designates a class of vehicle specifications. The alternative plural formulae appears in scientific contexts. {The formulas in this textbook are well explained.}

Forsaken means abandoned or deserted, left behind by those who should have stayed. A forsaken {village} has no remaining inhabitants. A forsaken {lover} has been left by their partner. The word carries emotional weight—being forsaken suggests not just absence but betrayal or neglect. {God-forsaken} describes places so desolate they seem beyond divine care. Forsaken is the past participle of forsake.

A fort is a fortified military structure built for defense, typically with thick walls, strategic positioning, and provisions for withstanding attack. The word extends to any stronghold or refuge: {The kids built a fort out of couch cushions}. To {hold down the fort} is to maintain operations while others are away.

Forth means forward or onward, especially in expressions of movement or progress: {go forth}, {set forth}, {from this day forth}. The word appears mainly in fixed phrases and formal contexts. {Back and forth} describes repeated movement in opposite directions. {And so forth} means "and more of the same." Forth sounds archaic in everyday speech but survives in these common expressions.

Forthcoming describes something about to appear or happen: {Her forthcoming novel releases in March}. Applied to people, it means willing to share information openly: {He wasn't very forthcoming about his past}. The two senses connect through the idea of things coming forward—whether events approaching in time or information offered freely.

Fortification is the act of strengthening something against attack, or the structure built for that purpose—walls, ramparts, trenches, bunkers. Medieval castles were elaborate fortifications; modern ones are often concrete and steel. The word extends to other kinds of strengthening: the fortification of flour with vitamins, or the fortification of wine with added alcohol. {The old fortifications still line the harbor}.

Fortified means strengthened or reinforced. A fortified position has defensive structures—walls, barriers, or weapons emplacements: {The troops retreated to a fortified compound}. Fortified wine has added alcohol, typically brandy, raising its strength: port, sherry, and Madeira are fortified wines. Fortified foods have added nutrients: {fortified milk}, {fortified cereal}. To feel fortified is to feel strengthened for a challenge ahead.

Fortitude is strength of mind that enables someone to endure pain, adversity, or danger with courage. The word implies quiet, steady resolve rather than dramatic heroism—the capacity to bear hardship without complaint: {She faced her illness with remarkable fortitude}. {It takes fortitude to rebuild after losing everything}.

A fortress is a large, heavily fortified structure built to withstand attack—typically a military stronghold with thick walls, towers, and defensive positions. Unlike a castle, which implies residence, fortress emphasizes military function. Figuratively, anything impregnable or secure: {The company's market share made it a fortress against competitors}. To {fortress up} is to make something defensively secure.

Forts is the plural of fort—a fortified military installation designed to defend against attack. Forts have walls, sometimes moats, and positions for weapons. Children build forts from blankets or snow. To {hold down the fort} is to maintain operations while others are away: {I'll hold down the fort while you're on vacation}.

Fortunate means favored by luck or circumstance. A fortunate person has good things happen to them, often without having earned them: {She was fortunate to survive the crash}. Fortunate can also describe the advantageous thing itself: {a fortunate turn of events}. The word often implies gratitude or awareness of one's advantages: {We're fortunate to live in such a safe neighborhood}.

Fortune is luck or chance, especially as a force shaping events: {Fortune smiled on us that day}. A fortune is also a large amount of money or wealth: {She inherited a fortune}, {He made a fortune in real estate}. To tell someone's fortune is to predict their future, as with cards or palm reading. Good fortune and bad fortune are luck of either kind. {Fortune favors the bold.}

Fortunes are the things that happen to a person, especially over time—the ups and downs of fate. Someone's fortunes may rise or fall: {The company's fortunes improved after the merger}. A fortune is also great wealth: {She inherited a fortune}. Fortune-tellers predict fortunes, and fortune cookies contain fortunes—slips of paper with predictions or advice.

A fortuneteller is someone who claims to predict the future, typically for payment. Fortunetellers use various methods—palm reading, tarot cards, crystal balls, astrology—to divine what lies ahead for their clients. The term often carries skeptical connotations, suggesting charlatanry rather than genuine insight: {The fortuneteller at the carnival said I'd meet a tall stranger}.

Forty is the cardinal number between thirty-nine and forty-one, written as 40. Note the spelling—forty drops the u from four. {She turned forty last month.} {Forty winks} means a brief nap. The forties refers to the decade from 40 to 49, whether in age, temperature, or century: {He's in his forties.}

A forum is a place for public discussion. In ancient Rome, it was the central marketplace where citizens gathered to debate. The word now applies to any setting where ideas are exchanged: a {public forum}, a {forum on climate policy}. Online forums are websites where users post messages and reply to each other in threaded discussions. A forum may also be a court or tribunal with jurisdiction over certain matters: {the proper forum for this dispute}.

Forums are places for public discussion. Originally physical spaces where people gathered to debate civic matters, the word now most commonly refers to online message boards where users post and reply to topics: {I found the answer on a tech support forum}. A forum can also be any opportunity for open discussion: {The town hall served as a forum for community concerns}.

Forward is mainly an adverb that means toward the front (lean forward). As an adjective it conveys movement toward the front (forward momentum). Figurative meanings arising from this include progressive (forward thinking) and socially assertive: He was forward in asking the woman he just met for a date. In some team games, a forward is a player whose position is near the opponents’ goal. If you forward an email or letter, you send it on to another address. Don’t confuse forward with the noun foreword, which has the same pronunciation.

A fossil is the preserved remains or traces of ancient life—bones, shells, footprints, or plant impressions—typically found embedded in rock and dating back thousands or millions of years. Fossils provide crucial evidence for understanding evolution and the history of life on Earth. Figuratively, fossil describes something outdated or someone who seems stuck in the past: {Don't be such a fossil—try the new software}. Fossil fuels like coal and oil formed from decomposed prehistoric organisms.

Fossils are the preserved remains or traces of ancient organisms found in rock or sediment. Bones, shells, and plant imprints become fossils through mineralization over millions of years. Paleontologists study fossils to understand prehistoric life. Figuratively, a fossil is someone or something outdated or resistant to change: {He's a fossil who still uses a flip phone}. Fossil fuels—coal, oil, natural gas—formed from decomposed organisms over geological time.

To foster is to encourage or promote the development of something: {foster cooperation}, {foster good relations}. With children, fostering means caring for them temporarily without legal adoption—a foster {parent}, foster {home}, or foster {child} provides or receives such care. The word implies nurturing something that isn't originally your own. (Capitalized Foster is a surname.)

Fought is the past tense and past participle of fight. It describes combat, struggle, or vigorous effort that has already occurred: {They fought in the war}, {She fought her way to the top}, {We fought over the last piece of cake}. The word covers physical confrontation, legal battles, emotional struggles, and metaphorical conflicts alike.

Foul is a noun, verb, and adjective, nearly always designating something undesirable. A foul odor or smell is unpleasant. Foul play is a breach of rules in a game – perhaps in the form of a foul, or illegal action. When one player fouls another, the first commits an illegal action that hampers the second. To foul something inanimate is to damage it and detract from its beneficial use: The chemical plant fouled the waterways.

Fouled is the past tense of foul, meaning something became dirty, tangled, or obstructed. A rope fouls when it tangles; machinery fouls when debris clogs it. In sports, a player who fouled committed an illegal action: {He fouled out in the fourth quarter}. Something fouled up has gone wrong through error or malfunction: {The whole system got fouled up}.

Foulmouthed describes someone who habitually uses profanity, obscenity, or vulgar language: {a foulmouthed drunk}, {foulmouthed tirades}. The word implies not just occasional cursing but a pattern—someone whose speech is regularly coarse or offensive. Also spelled foul-mouthed.

Fouls is the plural of foul—violations of rules in sports or games. In basketball, accumulating fouls leads to free throws for opponents; in baseball, foul balls land outside the baselines. The verb form means to commit such violations or to make something dirty or tangled: {The propeller fouls on kelp}, {Pollution fouls the air}. To foul up is to bungle: {He fouls up everything he touches}.

Found means to establish or create something meant to be permanent—an institution, organization, or settlement: {The college was founded in 1847}, {They founded a new colony on the coast}. A founder is the person who establishes something. Found also means to base or ground: {a theory founded on observation}. Separately, found is the past tense of find: {I found my keys}. In metalworking, to found is to melt and pour metal into a mold—the work done at a foundry.

Foundation is the base on which something rests or is built. A building's foundation is the concrete or stone structure supporting it from below. A foundation can also be an underlying principle or basis: {the foundation of democracy}, {shaking the foundations of society}. Organizations established to fund charitable or research activities are called foundations: {the Gates Foundation}. In cosmetics, foundation is a skin-toned base applied before other makeup.

Foundations are the underlying bases on which structures rest—literally the concrete or stone footings of buildings, figuratively the fundamental principles supporting ideas or institutions: {the foundations of democracy}, {a course covering the foundations of computer science}. A foundation is also an organization established to fund charitable or research activities, typically with an endowment: {the Gates Foundation}, {a private foundation}. In cosmetics, foundation is the base layer applied before other makeup.

Founded is the past tense of found, meaning to establish or set up something intended to last—an institution, organization, or settlement: {The university was founded in 1636}, {They founded a new colony}. Founded also serves as the past tense of the other found, meaning to melt and pour metal into a mold, though this use is rare. To be {well-founded} or {founded on} something is to have a solid basis: {Her suspicions were well-founded}.

Founder has two distinct clusters of meaning. One relates to founding—establishing something. A founder creates an institution, company, or movement: {Steve Jobs was a founder of Apple}. The other meaning is to fail or sink. A ship founders when it takes on water and goes down. A plan or enterprise founders when it collapses: {The negotiations foundered over territorial disputes}. Horses founder when they develop a painful hoof condition called laminitis.

Founders is the plural of founder, someone who establishes an institution, organization, or movement: {the founders of the company}, {the Founding Fathers}. As a verb, to founder is to fail or collapse—a business founders, a plan founders. Ships founder when they fill with water and sink. Horses founder when their hooves become painfully inflamed. The verb is often confused with flounder, which means to struggle awkwardly.

Founding refers to the act of establishing or creating something meant to endure—an institution, organization, city, or nation. The founding of a company marks its official beginning; the {founding fathers} were those who established the United States. As an adjective, founding describes original participants: a {founding member}, a {founding partner}. The word carries weight and formality, suggesting deliberate creation rather than casual beginnings.

A foundry is a facility where metal is melted and cast into shapes—producing everything from engine blocks to church bells. The word extends to any place where things are created or shaped: {a type foundry} designs and produces fonts. {The startup became a foundry for new ideas in renewable energy.}

A fountain is a structure that sends water upward in a stream or spray, typically decorative: {The children played in the fountain at the park's center}. The word extends to any source that flows upward or outward: a drinking fountain, a soda fountain. Figuratively, a fountain is an abundant source: {a fountain of knowledge}, {a fountain of youth}. A fountain pen contains an internal ink reservoir that feeds the nib.

Fountains is the plural of fountain—structures that send water into the air, either naturally as springs or artificially as decorative features in parks and plazas. Drinking fountains dispense water for public use. Figuratively, a fountain is any abundant source: {a fountain of knowledge}, {a fountain of youth}. The verb form means to flow upward like a fountain: {Blood fountained from the wound}.

Four is the number between three and five, written as 4. It appears constantly in everyday contexts: {a table for four}, {four corners of the earth}, {four-leaf clover}. On all fours means on hands and knees. Four-letter word refers to short vulgar terms, most of which have four letters.

A foursome is a group of four people doing something together. The word appears most often in golf, where four players make up a standard group: {We had a foursome for Saturday's round}. In sexual contexts, a foursome is group sex involving four participants.

Fourteen is the cardinal number between thirteen and fifteen, represented as 14 in Arabic numerals and XIV in Roman numerals. It appears frequently in everyday contexts like ages, dates, and quantities: {She just turned fourteen}; {We need fourteen chairs for the dinner party}. In some traditions, fourteen marks an important threshold—Jewish boys celebrate becoming a bar mitzvah at thirteen, while fourteen often signals the start of high school eligibility.

Fourth indicates position number four in a sequence: {She finished fourth in the race}, {the fourth of July}. As a noun, a fourth is one of four equal parts—a quarter: {Cut the apple into fourths}. In music, a fourth is an interval spanning four notes of a scale.

A fox is a smallish mammal in the dog family known for its cleverness. The qualities of the fox inspire other uses of the word. To fox someone is to trick or confuse them. Crazy like a fox infers that someone is cunning. When pages in old books develop yellowish-brown spots, they are said to be foxed. As slang, fox is a demeaning term for an attractive woman.

Foxes is the plural of fox—small, bushy-tailed canids known for cunning and adaptability. The word extends to people: foxes can be shrewd individuals or, informally, attractive ones. As a verb form, foxes means to baffle or trick: {The riddle foxes everyone who tries it}.

Foxglove is a tall flowering plant with tubular blossoms arranged along a spike, typically purple or white with spotted throats. The plant is highly toxic but medicinally important—digitalis, a heart medication, derives from its leaves. Foxgloves are common in cottage gardens and woodland edges: {The foxgloves along the fence were in full bloom}.

Foxgloves is the plural of foxglove, a tall flowering plant with tubular blossoms that cluster along a spike. The flowers, typically purple or white with spotted interiors, bloom in early summer. Foxglove contains digitalis, a compound used in heart medication but toxic if ingested directly: {The foxgloves along the fence were beautiful but kept away from the children}.

A foxhole is a small pit dug by a soldier for protection from enemy fire—just large enough for one or two people. The word appears in the expression {there are no atheists in foxholes}, suggesting that extreme danger prompts even nonbelievers to pray. Figuratively, any defensive position held under pressure: {The CEO retreated to his foxhole as the scandal broke}.

Foxholes are small pits dug by soldiers for individual protection during combat. The term comes from the resemblance to burrows dug by foxes. The expression {there are no atheists in foxholes} suggests that extreme danger prompts even skeptics to pray. Foxhole has become shorthand for any position of immediate peril: {We were in the foxholes together during the merger}.

Foxtrot is a ballroom dance in 4/4 time characterized by smooth, gliding steps: {They learned the foxtrot for their wedding}. The dance emerged in the early twentieth century and remains a staple of formal dance instruction. In military and aviation communication, foxtrot is the NATO phonetic alphabet word for the letter F.

Foxy describes someone cunning or sly, like a fox: {a foxy negotiator who always gets the better deal}. In informal use, foxy means sexually attractive, usually describing a woman: {She looked foxy in that dress}. The word carries a playful, slightly dated charm—more seventies disco than contemporary slang.

Fracking is hydraulic fracturing—a method of extracting oil or natural gas by injecting high-pressure fluid into rock formations to create cracks. The technique has dramatically increased fossil fuel production but draws environmental criticism over water contamination, earthquakes, and methane emissions: {The company wants to frack on protected land}. Often used pejoratively by opponents.

A fraction is a part of a whole, expressed mathematically as one number divided by another: {three-quarters}, {one-half}. More loosely, a fraction is any small portion: {Only a fraction of applicants get accepted}. To fraction something is to separate it into parts, though the verb fractionate is more common in technical contexts.

Fractions are parts of a whole, expressed as one number divided by another: {three-quarters}, {one-half}, {two-fifths}. In math, the top number (numerator) sits over the bottom (denominator), separated by a line. Fraction extends to any small portion: {Only a fraction of applicants get accepted}. {She moved a fraction of an inch}.

A fracture is a break or crack, most often in a bone but also in rock, glass, or other rigid materials. Doctors distinguish between simple fractures, where the bone breaks cleanly, and compound fractures, where bone pierces the skin. The word extends to abstractions: a fractured {relationship} or fractured {trust} suggests something once whole that has been damaged or broken apart. As a verb, fracture means to break or cause to break: {She fractured her wrist in the fall}.

Fractured describes something broken or cracked, typically bone: {a fractured rib}, {a fractured skull}. The word extends to anything disrupted or divided: {fractured relationships}, {a fractured political party}. Fractured speech or English is broken and imperfect. The past tense of fracture works the same way: {She fractured her wrist in the fall}.

Fractures are breaks or cracks, most often in bones: {She suffered multiple fractures in the accident}. The term extends to any breaking apart—fractures in rock formations, fractures in political alliances. To fracture something is to cause it to break: {The fall fractured his wrist}. Figuratively, relationships or communities fracture when unity breaks down: {The scandal fractured the party}.

Fragile describes things easily broken, damaged, or destroyed. A fragile vase shatters if dropped. Fragile extends to anything delicate or vulnerable: a fragile {ecosystem}, a fragile {peace}, a fragile {ego}. Someone in fragile {health} is weak and susceptible to decline. {Handle with care—it's fragile.}

Fragility is the quality of being easily broken, damaged, or destroyed. Glass has physical fragility; a ceasefire has political fragility. The word often extends beyond the material to describe vulnerability in relationships, mental states, or systems: {the fragility of trust}, {emotional fragility}. When applied to people, it can suggest delicacy requiring careful handling, though it sometimes carries a dismissive edge, implying excessive sensitivity.

A fragment is a piece broken off from something larger—a shard, remnant, or incomplete portion: {fragments of pottery}, {a fragment of conversation overheard}. The word emphasizes incompleteness; you have part but not the whole. To fragment is to break into pieces or scatter: {The empire fragmented into rival states}. In grammar, a sentence fragment lacks a subject or verb.

Fragmentation is breaking into pieces or the state of being broken into pieces. Glass shatters into fragments; a grenade scatters fragmentation. The word applies to anything that becomes disjointed or scattered: {the fragmentation of the empire into warring states}, {habitat fragmentation threatens wildlife}. In computing, fragmentation occurs when files are stored in noncontiguous blocks across a disk, slowing access.

Fragmented means broken into pieces or disconnected parts. Something fragmented lacks wholeness or continuity: {a fragmented narrative}, {fragmented memories of childhood}. The word often suggests incompleteness or disorganization rather than clean division: {The fragmented opposition couldn't mount an effective challenge}. Data or files become fragmented when scattered across non-contiguous storage locations.

Fragments are pieces broken off from something larger. A fragment of glass, a fragment of bone, a fragment of a conversation overheard. The word suggests incompleteness—you have part but not the whole: {Only fragments of the ancient text survive}. To fragment is to break apart: {The empire fragmented into warring states}. Fragmented information or memories come in disconnected pieces, lacking coherent structure.

Fragrance is a pleasant smell, typically one that's delicate or subtle: {the fragrance of jasmine}, {a light floral fragrance}. The word carries connotations of refinement—you wouldn't describe garbage as having a fragrance. Fragrance also refers to perfume or cologne products: {She picked up a new fragrance at the department store}.

Frail describes something or someone weak and easily broken or damaged. A frail {elderly woman} lacks physical strength and resilience. Frail {health} is precarious. A frail {structure} might collapse under stress. The word suggests delicacy and vulnerability—something requiring careful handling. Figuratively, frail {hopes} or frail {arguments} lack robustness and may not withstand pressure.

Frailty is the quality of being frail—weak, delicate, or easily broken. Physical frailty comes with age or illness: {the frailty of her ninety-year-old grandmother}. Moral frailty is susceptibility to temptation or error: {human frailty}. The word often carries a note of sympathy rather than judgment, acknowledging weakness as part of the human condition.

Frame is originally a verb that communicates form or constructing by fitting parts, but today the noun is more common. A frame is usually the structural part of a physical thing (frame of a building), but it can also be a surrounding or supporting part: picture frame, window frame. When someone frames a house, they build the supporting structure, to which other parts will be added. When someone frames a question, they provide the context in which the question is relevant or should be considered. If someone is framed, they are made to look guilty of something they did not do.

Framed describes something set within a frame—a picture mounted and bordered, a view bounded by a window, a face framed by hair. In construction, a framed house has a wooden skeleton. The past tense of frame covers these and more: {She framed the photo}, {He framed his argument carefully}. But framed alone most often means falsely incriminated—evidence planted or manipulated to make an innocent person appear guilty: {He swore he'd been framed}.

Frames are rigid structures that support or enclose something: a picture {frame}, a window {frame}, the {frame} of a house or bicycle. A person's frame is their body's skeletal structure: {a large frame}, {a small frame}. To frame something is to put it in a frame, or to construct or formulate: {frame an argument}, {frame a question}. To frame someone is to make them appear guilty through false evidence. In film and video, frames are individual still images that create motion when played in sequence.

A framework is a basic structure that supports or contains something else. In construction, it's the skeletal structure—beams and joints—before walls go up. The word extends to conceptual structures: a {legal framework}, a {theoretical framework}, a {framework for understanding}. In software, a framework is a platform providing reusable code and conventions that developers build applications on top of: {a web development framework}. The core idea is always scaffolding that shapes what's built within it.

Framing is the act of constructing a frame—the skeletal structure of a house, the border around a picture. More abstractly, framing is how something gets presented or contextualized: {The framing of the question influenced the responses}. In rhetoric and media, framing shapes perception by emphasizing certain aspects over others. To frame someone is to falsely make them appear guilty: {He claimed the evidence was planted and he'd been framed}.

The main related meanings of franchise have to do with rights or with businesses. Generally, the franchise is the right to vote in public elections. An owner of intellectual property may grant a franchise to a group or company that licenses that property for a particular purpose: J.K. Rowling granted LEGO the franchise for Harry Potter mini-figures. Businesses in multiple locations that share a name but operate under a variety of owners are called franchises (hotel franchise, restaurant franchise). To franchise is to operate using such a business model.

Franchises is the plural of franchise, a word with meanings tied to rights and privileges. A franchise can be a license to operate a business using an established brand: {McDonald's franchises dot every major highway}. In sports, a franchise is a team and its entire organization: {The franchise hasn't won a championship in decades}. Franchise also means the right to vote, though this sense appears mainly in formal contexts. The verb franchise means to grant such rights: {The company franchises its restaurants rather than operating them directly}.

Frank means honest and direct, especially about uncomfortable topics: {Let me be frank with you—this isn't working}. A frank {discussion} holds nothing back. The word suggests candor that might be blunt but is meant helpfully. As a noun, a frank is a frankfurter or hot dog. To frank mail is to mark it for free delivery, a privilege of certain officials. (Capitalized Frank is a given name or historical people.)

Frankalmoin is a medieval English legal term for land held by a religious institution in exchange for prayers and religious services rather than secular obligations. A church or monastery held property in frankalmoin free from military service or rent, owing only spiritual duties to the grantor. The term combines "frank" (free) with "almoin" (alms).

Frankincense is an aromatic resin obtained from trees of the genus Boswellia, native to the Arabian Peninsula and northeastern Africa. It has been prized for millennia as incense in religious ceremonies and is one of the gifts the Magi brought to the infant Jesus according to Christian tradition. When burned, frankincense produces a distinctive sweet, woody smoke used in worship across many faiths. It also appears in perfumes and traditional medicine.

Frantic describes urgent, desperate activity driven by anxiety or fear. A frantic {search} for missing keys suggests panicked haste. Frantic {calls} to emergency services convey desperation. The word implies loss of composure—someone frantic has abandoned calm deliberation for wild, sometimes chaotic action: {She was frantic when her child went missing}.

Frat is short for fraternity—a Greek-letter social organization at American colleges. The word carries connotations of party culture, hazing rituals, and privileged young men: {frat boy}, {frat house}, {frat party}. As an adjective, frat describes the stereotypical culture: {That bar has a real frat vibe}.

A fratboy is a member of a college fraternity, or more broadly, any young man who embodies the stereotypical fraternity culture: heavy drinking, casual hookups, sports obsession, and aggressive masculinity. The term is usually dismissive or mocking: {The bar was full of fratboys in backwards caps}. Also spelled as two words.

Fraternity captures the sense of brotherhood—a bond among people who share something in common. A fraternity is a group united by shared interests, profession, or purpose: {the medical fraternity}, {the fraternity of jazz musicians}. In American colleges, a fraternity is a social organization for male students, typically identified by Greek letters: {He pledged a fraternity his freshman year}. The broader sense extends to any community of like-minded people, often with overtones of mutual loyalty and insider knowledge.

Fraud is deliberate deception for unfair or unlawful gain—lying to get money, property, or advantage. Insurance fraud, tax fraud, wire fraud. A fraud is also a person who pretends to be something they're not: {He claimed to be a doctor but was a complete fraud}. The adjective fraudulent describes deceptive acts or the people who commit them.

A fraudster is a person who commits fraud—someone who deceives others for financial or personal gain. The term is slightly more casual than "fraud" used as a noun for a person, and emphasizes habitual or professional deception: {The fraudster bilked retirees out of their life savings}. More common in British than American English.

Fraudulent describes something involving deliberate deception for unfair or unlawful gain. A fraudulent {scheme} tricks people out of money. Fraudulent {documents} are forged or falsified. The word applies to acts, claims, or people: {fraudulent transactions}, {fraudulent insurance claims}, {a fraudulent contractor}. It carries legal weight—fraudulent conduct can be criminal.

Fray has two distinct sources. One means to unravel at the edges—threads come loose from fabric through wear or friction: {The cuffs of his jacket were starting to fray}. Nerves and tempers also fray under stress. The other fray is a fight or heated contest: {She entered the fray}, {the competitive fray of election season}.

Frayed describes something worn or unraveled at the edges, typically fabric or rope whose fibers have come loose through wear: {frayed cuffs}, {a frayed electrical cord}. The word extends to anything showing strain or deterioration: {frayed nerves}, {frayed tempers}, {Their relationship had become frayed after years of conflict}.

Fraying is the process of becoming worn at the edges, with threads loosening and separating. Fabric frays where it's been cut or rubbed repeatedly. The word extends to anything gradually coming apart: {fraying nerves}, {a fraying coalition}, {the fraying of civil discourse}. What's fraying hasn't broken yet, but the unraveling has begun.

Frazzle suggests wearing down to the point of exhaustion or disintegration. To frazzle is to fray, exhaust, or reduce to tatters—literally or figuratively. The noun appears almost exclusively in the phrase {worn to a frazzle}, meaning completely exhausted: {By the end of the semester, I was worn to a frazzle}. Frazzled describes someone stressed and depleted: {frazzled parents}, {frazzled nerves}.

Frazzled describes a state of exhaustion and nervous strain, as if worn to threads. Someone frazzled has been stretched past their limits by stress, overwork, or chaos: {By the end of the holiday season, the retail workers were completely frazzled}. The word suggests being both tired and rattled—not just weary but undone.

The common element to all meanings of freak is out of the ordinary, usually in an undesirable way: The freak snowstorm dumped seven inches on the town in 24 hours. Applied to a person, freak denotes someone strange and perhaps disturbing. A freak of nature is a living thing with an abnormality: The six-toed cat was a freak of nature. If you freak someone or freak them out, you frighten and upset them. A person who overdoes something may be called a freak: He was a control freak.

Freaked means disturbed, upset, or overwhelmed—usually by something strange or unexpected. {I was completely freaked when I saw the spider}. To freak out is to lose composure or have a strong emotional reaction: {Don't freak out, but I crashed your car}. Someone can also freak others out by unsettling them: {That movie really freaked me out}.

A freakout is a sudden loss of composure—an episode of panic, rage, or overwhelming emotion: {She had a total freakout when she saw the spider}. The term emerged from 1960s drug culture, where it described bad trips or drug-induced episodes, but now applies to any intense emotional reaction. As a verb phrase, to freak out is either to lose control or to alarm someone: {Don't freak out, but I crashed your car}.

Freaks is the plural of freak—originally someone with an unusual physical condition, often displayed in sideshows. The word extends to anyone obsessive or eccentric about something: {fitness freaks}, {control freaks}. As slang, freaks can mean people who are sexually uninhibited. To freak or freak out is to panic or lose composure: {She freaked when she saw the bill}.

A freakshow, sometimes spelled as two words, was historically a carnival or circus exhibition displaying people with unusual physical characteristics or abilities, often exploiting those with disabilities or rare medical conditions for entertainment. The term now functions mainly as an insult or dismissive label for any person, group, or situation perceived as bizarre, chaotic, or disturbingly abnormal. {That press conference was a complete freakshow.} The word carries strong connotations of spectacle and mockery.

Freaky describes something strange, unusual, or unsettling—often with a hint of the uncanny or bizarre: {That was a freaky coincidence}. It can mean sexually unconventional or kinky: {She's into some freaky stuff}. In casual speech, freaky sometimes just means exciting or intense: {The roller coaster was freaky}. The word carries playful energy rather than serious alarm.

A freckle is a small brownish spot on the skin, typically appearing in clusters on fair-skinned people exposed to sun. Freckles concentrate on the face, arms, and shoulders. As a verb, to freckle is to develop or mark with such spots: {Her nose freckles in summer}. The word extends to any small scattered markings: {freckles of light through the leaves}.

Freckles are small, flat spots of concentrated pigment on the skin, typically tan or light brown. They appear most often on fair-skinned people, especially on areas exposed to sun—the face, arms, and shoulders. Freckles tend to multiply and darken in summer, fade in winter. {Her nose was dusted with freckles.} The word can describe similar markings on animals or speckled patterns generally.

The adjective free has branched out considerably from its original meaning of enjoying liberty. This idea pervades many things that free frequently characterizes: free will, free speech, free trade, free agent. Another common use of free is a thing that is available without cost: free kick, free download, free parking, free meal. When a physical, inanimate thing is free, it is not secured: Take the free end and loop it through the hook. When you free something or someone, you cause them to be free, releasing them from a state of security, control, or bondage.

A freebie is something given away at no cost—a promotional item, complimentary sample, or bonus: {The conference booth was handing out freebies}. The word suggests something small or incidental rather than a major gift, often with a slightly dismissive tone: {Don't expect any freebies around here}.

Freebies are things given away for free, typically as promotional items or perks: {The conference table was covered with freebies—pens, tote bags, water bottles}. The word carries a slightly informal, enthusiastic tone, often implying pleasant surprise at getting something for nothing: {One of the freebies was actually useful}.

Freed is the past tense and past participle of free. Someone who has been freed was released from confinement, bondage, or restriction: {The hostages were freed after three days}. Things can also be freed—resources, time, space: {Canceling the meeting freed up my afternoon}.

Freedom is the state of being unfettered. An individual freedom (freedom of assembly) expresses lack of government oversight or control. The idea of freedom figures centrally in many political debates over the role of government in people’s lives. The freedoms that concern people most, judging by usage statistics, are freedom of speech, freedom of the press, academic freedom (the right of teachers and professors to speak freely without censorship from their institutions), and religious freedom.

Freefall is the state of falling under gravity alone, without resistance or support. Skydivers experience freefall before opening their parachutes. In physics, even orbiting astronauts are technically in freefall—falling continuously around the Earth. The word extends to any rapid, uncontrolled decline: {The stock market went into freefall}. Also spelled free fall or free-fall.

Freefalling is falling through air without resistance or support—the state of a skydiver before the parachute opens, or an object dropped from height. The word extends to any uncontrolled plunge: {The stock market is freefalling}, {Her grades went into freefall}. The sense is of rapid, unchecked descent with nothing to slow the drop.

Freelance describes work done independently rather than as an employee—hired for specific projects without long-term commitment to one employer. A freelance writer pitches articles to various publications; a freelance designer takes clients as they come. The word works as adjective, noun, verb, and adverb: {She works freelance}, {hired a freelance}, {freelancing for tech companies}. The term originated with medieval mercenary knights—lances for hire.

A freelancer is someone who works independently rather than as an employee, typically taking on projects for multiple clients. The term originated with medieval mercenary soldiers—lances for hire—but now applies to writers, designers, programmers, and other professionals who sell their services without long-term commitment to one employer: {She works as a freelance photographer}. The word functions as noun, verb, and adjective: {freelance work}, {to freelance for magazines}.

To freeload is to take advantage of others' generosity without contributing or reciprocating—getting free meals, lodging, or other benefits while giving nothing back. A freeloader exploits hospitality or shared resources: {He's been freeloading off his parents since graduation}. The word carries clear disapproval, implying laziness or shamelessness.

A freeloader is someone who takes advantage of others' generosity without contributing or reciprocating—accepting free food, lodging, or favors while giving nothing back. The term carries clear disapproval: {Her brother's been freeloading off her for months}. To freeload is to live or benefit this way.

Freeloaders are people who take advantage of others' generosity without contributing their fair share. The term carries strong disapproval, suggesting someone who habitually gets free food, lodging, money, or other benefits while giving nothing in return. {The freeloaders showed up right at dinnertime, as usual.} Unlike guests, who are invited, freeloaders impose themselves and exploit hospitality or resources meant for others.

Freeloading is taking advantage of others' generosity without contributing or paying one's share. A freeloader habitually mooches off friends, crashes on couches indefinitely, or eats food they didn't buy: {He's been freeloading off his parents since he dropped out}. The term carries clear disapproval—freeloaders exploit hospitality rather than reciprocate it.

Freestyle describes performance done spontaneously without predetermined structure or rules. In rap, freestyle means improvised lyrics delivered on the spot: {He dropped a freestyle over the beat}. In swimming, freestyle is the fastest stroke category where competitors choose their technique. In wrestling, freestyle allows leg attacks forbidden in Greco-Roman style. The word suggests creative freedom within a general framework—skiing freestyle, freestyle dance, or any activity where improvisation replaces choreography.

Freestyling is improvising, especially in hip-hop—rapping without prepared lyrics, creating verses spontaneously: {He was freestyling over the beat}. The term extends to any unscripted, off-the-cuff performance or approach: {We're just freestyling this presentation}. In dance, freestyling means moving without choreography, responding to the music in the moment.

A freethinker forms opinions independently, rejecting authority and tradition—especially religious doctrine—in favor of reason and evidence. The term emerged from Enlightenment debates and still carries a secular, skeptical connotation: {He considered himself a freethinker who questioned everything}. It's often self-applied with pride, though critics may use it dismissively.

A freeway is a high-speed highway with controlled access—no traffic lights, no intersections, entry and exit only through ramps. The term is most common in the western United States; elsewhere the same roads are called expressways, motorways, or interstates. {Traffic on the freeway was backed up for miles.}

To freewheel is to coast without pedaling on a bicycle, or more broadly, to move forward without active propulsion—a car freewheeling downhill in neutral. Figuratively, freewheeling describes acting without constraints or planning: {a freewheeling discussion}, {his freewheeling lifestyle}. The noun freewheel is the bicycle mechanism that allows coasting. A freewheeler moves through life casually, unconcerned with rules or structure.

The core idea of freeze is solidification by cold, as water freezes to become ice. The idea of immobilization or stoppage is present in some meanings: if you freeze prices, you effectively initiate a price freeze. If you report that you are freezing, it’s unlikely that you’ll turn to ice, but likely that you feel very cold. A freeze happens overnight when temperatures fall below freezing and some plants may be damaged or die.

A freezer is a refrigerated compartment or appliance that keeps food frozen, typically at temperatures below 0°F (−18°C). Most household refrigerators include a freezer section; standalone units called chest freezers or deep freezers offer more storage. {We stocked the freezer with meat for winter.}

Freezing is the temperature at which water turns to ice—32°F or 0°C—and by extension, any temperature cold enough to feel painfully cold: {It's freezing in here}. As an adjective, it describes extreme cold: {freezing rain}, {freezing winds}. The verb freeze covers the process of becoming solid through cold, or becoming motionless: {She froze when she heard the noise}.

Freight is goods transported in bulk, typically by truck, train, ship, or plane: {The freight arrived damaged}. It also means the cost of such transport or the transport system itself: {We'll ship it by freight}. As a verb, to freight is to load or transport cargo. A freight {train} carries goods rather than passengers. Figuratively, something freighted with meaning carries heavy significance.

A freighter is a ship or aircraft designed primarily to carry cargo rather than passengers. The term most often refers to oceangoing cargo ships: {The freighter carried grain across the Atlantic}. Air freighters transport goods by plane, typically converted passenger aircraft or purpose-built cargo planes.

Freighters are ships or aircraft designed primarily to carry cargo rather than passengers. The term usually refers to cargo ships: {Freighters loaded with grain crossed the Atlantic}. Air freighters transport goods by plane, often converted passenger aircraft or purpose-built cargo jets. The word emphasizes the vessel's commercial hauling function.

Frenemies is the plural of frenemy—a person who acts as a friend but is actually a rival or enemy. The blend of friend and enemy captures relationships marked by underlying competition, jealousy, or hostility beneath a veneer of friendliness: {We were frenemies in high school—always competing for the same things}. The term often describes social dynamics where people maintain cordial appearances despite mutual dislike.

A frenemy is someone who acts like a friend but is actually a rival or enemy—or someone whose relationship with you oscillates between friendship and antagonism. The term blends "friend" and "enemy" and captures relationships marked by competitive undercurrents, passive aggression, or alternating warmth and hostility: {She's my frenemy from work—we grab lunch together but she'd steal my promotion in a heartbeat}.

Frenzied describes wild, uncontrolled activity driven by intense emotion or urgency. A frenzied {crowd} surges chaotically. Frenzied {trading} on the stock market suggests panicked buying and selling. The word implies something beyond merely busy or energetic—there's an element of desperation or loss of control: {a frenzied search for survivors}.

Frenzy is a state of wild, uncontrolled excitement or activity. A crowd can work itself into a frenzy; so can a single person in the grip of strong emotion. The word suggests temporary madness—behavior that would seem irrational in calmer moments: {a feeding frenzy}, {a media frenzy}, {She cleaned the house in a frenzy before the guests arrived}.

Frequencies is the plural of frequency, referring to rates of occurrence or repetition. In physics, frequencies measure how often waves cycle per second: {radio frequencies}, {sound frequencies}. In statistics, frequencies count how often values appear in a dataset. More generally, frequencies describe how often events happen: {the frequencies of various side effects}.

Frequency is how often something happens or appears. A radio station's frequency is the specific wavelength it broadcasts on—you tune to that number on the dial. In physics, frequency measures cycles per second: {sound waves of different frequencies}. High frequency means happening often; low frequency means rarely: {the frequency of her visits has dropped off}.

Frequent means happening often or at short intervals: {frequent flyer}, {frequent visitor}, {a frequent cause of death}. The verb, stressed on the second syllable, means to visit regularly or habitually: {He frequents the same coffee shop every morning}. Frequently is among the most common adverbs in English.

Fresco is a technique of painting on freshly applied wet plaster, so that the pigments bond with the wall as it dries. The word comes from Italian for "fresh." Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling is the most famous example. By extension, fresco refers to any painting made this way: {The church contains several Renaissance frescos}. Plural: frescos or frescoes.

Fresh describes something recently made, obtained, or experienced—not stale, spoiled, or worn. Fresh {bread} just came from the oven. Fresh {air} is clean and invigorating. Fresh {water} is not salty. A fresh {start} begins anew, unburdened by the past. Fresh can mean impudent or forward: {Don't get fresh with me}. In slang, fresh means cool or stylish: {Those sneakers are fresh}.

A freshman is a first-year student at a high school or college: {She's a freshman at UCLA}. The term extends to anyone new to a role or organization: a freshman {congressman}, a freshman {employee}. As an adjective, it describes inexperience or newness: {freshman year}, {freshman mistakes}. The gender-neutral alternative first-year has gained ground in academic settings.

Freshmen is the plural of freshman, designating students in their first year of high school or college. The term combines fresh (new) with men, though it applies to students of any gender. Some institutions now prefer first-year students to avoid the gendered suffix. {The freshmen orientation runs all week.} {She remembers how lost she felt as one of hundreds of freshmen on campus.}

Freshwater is water that isn't salty—rivers, lakes, ponds, and streams as opposed to oceans and seas. As an adjective, it describes organisms or environments associated with such water: {freshwater fish}, {freshwater ecosystems}. Figuratively, freshwater can suggest inexperience or provincialism, as someone from inland waters rather than the open sea.

F-r-e-t is three words in one. Most frequent is a verb conveying irritation or worry: She’s fretting about her grades. On guitars and other stringed instruments, the frets are the ridges along the fingerboard that enable the sounding of different notes from the same string. Finally, a fret or fretwork is a design with lines intersecting at various angles.

Frets are the raised metal strips across a guitar or similar instrument's neck that divide it into segments for producing different notes. To fret is to press strings against these strips. Separately, to fret is to worry or be anxious: {Don't fret about it}. As a noun, a fret can mean a state of vexation: {She was in a fret over the delay}.

A friar is a member of certain Roman Catholic religious orders—Franciscans, Dominicans, Carmelites, and Augustinians. Unlike monks, who live in monasteries, friars move through the world, preaching and serving communities while taking vows of poverty. The word shares roots with fraternal, reflecting the brotherhood of these orders: {Friar Tuck}, {a wandering friar}.

Friction is resistance between surfaces in contact. Physical friction slows or stops motion: {The friction of brakes against wheels}. Figuratively, friction is tension or conflict between people or groups: {There's been friction between the departments lately}. Something frictionless moves smoothly or, in social contexts, proceeds without resistance or disagreement.

A fridge is a refrigerator—an appliance that keeps food cold to prevent spoiling. The word is informal but standard: {Is there any milk in the fridge?} Fridge preserves the soft g sound of refrigerator, which explains the unusual spelling with d.

Fried describes food cooked in hot oil or fat: {fried chicken}, {fried eggs}. The past tense of fry works the same way. Extended uses capture the idea of being subjected to intense heat or energy—electronics get fried by power surges, skin gets fried by the sun. In slang, fried means mentally exhausted or impaired: {I'm completely fried after that exam}. It can also mean intoxicated on drugs, especially after heavy use.

A friend is someone you know, like, and trust—distinct from family and romantic partners. Friendship implies mutual affection and shared experiences: {We've been friends since college}. The word extends to allies, supporters, or anyone not hostile: {Are you friend or foe?} On social media, to friend someone is to add them to your network. {A friend in need is a friend indeed.}

Friendly describes someone or something warm, welcoming, and well-disposed toward others: {a friendly smile}, {a friendly neighborhood}. It can mean informal or casual: {a friendly reminder}, {a friendly game of cards}. In military contexts, friendly distinguishes allied forces from enemies: {friendly fire} is accidental shooting of one's own troops. As a noun, friendlies are allies. The adverb form is also friendly: {She waved friendly at the neighbors}.

Friends are people you share a bond of mutual affection with—not family, not romantic partners, but people you genuinely like and who like you back. The word covers a spectrum from casual acquaintances to lifelong intimates: {We're just friends}, {She's one of my closest friends}. To be friends with someone is to have this relationship: {Are you two friends?} In social media, friends often means people in your network regardless of actual closeness. {Friends with benefits} describes a sexual relationship without romantic commitment. (Capitalized Friends is the television series.)

Friendship is a relationship of mutual affection and trust between people who aren't family or romantic partners. Unlike kinship, friendship is chosen. Close friendships involve emotional intimacy, loyalty, and shared experiences: {Their friendship goes back twenty years}. The word also describes the state of being friends: {The two nations developed a friendship based on trade}.

Friendzoned describes being relegated to friendship status by someone you're romantically interested in—they like you, but not *that* way. The term implies a one-sided situation where romantic pursuit has been gently but firmly declined: {He asked her out but got friendzoned}. Often carries a note of resigned disappointment, sometimes resentment.

Fries are strips of potato deep-fried until crisp, typically served hot with salt. The full term is French fries, though the shortened form dominates casual speech: {I'll have a burger and fries}. The word also serves as the third-person singular of fry: {She fries an egg every morning}.

A frigate is a warship, historically a fast sailing vessel with guns on a single deck, now a modern naval escort ship smaller than a destroyer. Frigates typically handle convoy protection, patrol, and anti-submarine warfare. The word also names a type of seabird, the frigatebird, known for its speed and piratical habit of stealing food from other birds.

Fright is a sudden, intense fear—the kind that makes you jump or gasp. A fright is an instance of this: {You gave me a fright!} The word often appears in set phrases: {stage fright}, {take fright}, {frightened to death}. Something frightful inspires fear or, more loosely, is simply awful: {frightful weather}. To look a fright is to look disheveled or ridiculous.

Frighten means to cause fear or alarm. A sudden noise frightens you; a horror movie frightens audiences deliberately. The passive form is common: {I was frightened by the sound}. Frightened of and frightened by both work, with subtle difference—you're frightened of spiders generally, frightened by the one that just dropped on your arm. To frighten someone off or away is to scare them into leaving or abandoning something: {The price tag frightened off potential buyers}.

Frightened means afraid or alarmed, typically in response to a perceived threat or danger. It describes a state of fear that may be sudden or sustained: {The frightened child hid under the bed}, {I was frightened by the noise}. Frightened carries less intensity than terrified but more than nervous or uneasy.

Frightening describes something that causes fear or alarm. A frightening {movie} makes you jump; a frightening {diagnosis} fills you with dread. The word covers a wide range of intensity—from mildly unsettling to genuinely terrifying. {The speed of the car was frightening.} {It's frightening how quickly things can change.}

Frigid means extremely cold: {frigid Arctic temperatures}, {a frigid winter morning}. The word extends to emotional coldness—someone frigid is unfriendly, distant, or unresponsive: {a frigid reception}. Applied to women, frigid describes an inability or unwillingness to experience sexual arousal, a usage that has fallen out of favor as sexist and clinical.

Frills are decorative ruffles or gathered fabric edging, as on clothing or curtains. By extension, frills are any unnecessary extras or embellishments: {a no-frills airline}, {We just want the basic model without all the frills}. The phrase suggests ornamentation that adds cost or complexity without improving core function.

Frilly describes something with frills—ruffled or gathered strips of fabric used as decoration. A frilly {blouse} or frilly {curtains} have these ornamental edges. The word often carries connotations of excessive femininity or fussiness: {The bedroom was too frilly for his taste}. Figuratively, frilly can describe anything elaborately decorative or unnecessarily ornate.

Fringe is the decorative border of hanging threads or tassels on fabric, curtains, or clothing. By extension, fringe describes the outer edge of anything: the {fringe of the forest}, the {fringe of a crowd}. Figuratively, fringe means marginal or unconventional: {fringe groups}, {fringe benefits} (perks beyond regular salary), {fringe theater}. To fringe is to border or edge something.

A frisbee is a plastic disc designed to be thrown and caught, gliding on air currents when spun with a flick of the wrist. The name comes from the Frisbee brand, now used generically for any flying disc. Frisbees are tossed casually at parks and beaches, or used in organized sports like ultimate frisbee and disc golf: {We threw the frisbee around until it got dark}.

Frisk means to move about playfully and energetically, the way a puppy or lamb might: {The dog frisked around the yard}. More commonly now, frisk means to pat down someone's body and clothing searching for concealed weapons or contraband: {The officer frisked the suspect}. The noun frisk refers to such a search.

Frisky describes a state of playful, lively energy—the kind of spirited behavior you'd see in a puppy or a child who's had too much sugar. {The kittens were frisky after their nap.} When applied to adults, frisky often carries sexual undertones, suggesting flirtatious or amorous energy: {A couple glasses of wine made her frisky.} The word implies harmless, good-natured liveliness rather than anything aggressive or threatening.

Fritter has two unrelated meanings. A fritter is a small fried cake, often containing fruit or vegetables: {apple fritters}, {corn fritters}. Separately, to fritter is to waste something gradually, almost always with "away": {He frittered away his inheritance on gambling}. The sense is of dissipating resources bit by bit until nothing remains.

Fritters are pieces of food coated in batter and deep-fried until golden—apple fritters, corn fritters, clam fritters. The batter puffs and crisps around whatever's inside. Separately, to fritter something away is to waste it gradually on trivial things: {He frittered away his inheritance on gambling and bad investments}.

Frivolity is lighthearted behavior that lacks seriousness or substance. The word carries mild disapproval—someone indulging in frivolity is wasting time on trivial amusements when weightier matters await: {There's no room for frivolity in a courtroom}. In the plural, frivolities are the specific silly things people occupy themselves with: {youthful frivolities}.

Frizz describes hair that has become a mass of tight, unruly curls or flyaway strands, typically from humidity or damage: {The rain turned her hair to frizz}. As a verb, to frizz is to form or cause such texture: {My hair frizzes in humid weather}. Frizzy is the common adjective form.

A frog is a small amphibian with smooth skin, long hind legs for jumping, and webbed feet for swimming. Frogs begin life as aquatic tadpoles before metamorphosing into air-breathing adults. The word extends to things resembling frogs: a decorative fastener on clothing, a holder for flowers in a vase, or the triangular pad on a horse's hoof. {The pond was full of frogs in spring.}

Frogs are small amphibians with smooth skin, long hind legs for jumping, and webbed feet for swimming. They begin life as aquatic tadpoles before metamorphosing into their adult form. Frogs appear widely in folklore and children's stories. A frog in someone's throat is hoarseness that makes speaking difficult. As a slur, frog is a derogatory term for a French person.

Frolic suggests playful, carefree activity—romping, gamboling, or cavorting with lighthearted energy. Children frolic in the snow; lambs frolic in spring meadows. The word carries an old-fashioned, innocent quality: {a frolic in the park}, {beach frolics}. As a noun, a frolic is an episode of such play. To describe adult activity as a frolic often adds a note of whimsy or gentle euphemism.

Frolicking is playful, carefree activity—running, jumping, or moving about in a lively, happy way. The word suggests lighthearted abandon, often outdoors: {children frolicking in the sprinklers}, {lambs frolicking in the meadow}. It carries a wholesome, innocent quality that makes it sound slightly old-fashioned or deliberately whimsical when applied to adults. Frolicking is the present participle of frolic, used as a verb or gerund.

The primary meaning of front, a noun, is the part of something that is foremost, facing outward, or facing forward. Front occurs before other nouns so often that it can be regarded as a full-fledged adjective, denoting the location of something: front door, front wheel, front tooth, front row. In military contexts, a front is an area where conflict is occurring. A weather front is where two air masses collide. Front may also designate a deceptive appearance: The agency was a front for espionage. If a building fronts something, its front faces that direction: The hotel fronts a busy highway.

A frontier is the edge of settled or explored territory—where civilization meets wilderness. Historically, {the American frontier} shaped national mythology about expansion and opportunity. By extension, frontier describes any boundary between the known and unknown: {the frontiers of science}, {the final frontier} of space. A frontier can also be a border between countries, especially in British usage.

Frontiers are the outer edges of settled or explored territory—the boundaries between the known and unknown. The American frontier was the advancing edge of westward expansion. The word extends to any field's outer limits: {the frontiers of science}, {new frontiers in medicine}. Frontier suggests possibility and challenge, places where established rules give way to discovery.

A frontiersman is a man who lives on the frontier—the edge of settled territory, where civilization meets wilderness. The term evokes American expansion westward in the 18th and 19th centuries: {Daniel Boone was the archetypal frontiersman}. Frontiersmen were hunters, trappers, and settlers who carved out existence in unsettled land. The word carries connotations of self-reliance, ruggedness, and adventure.

Frontline refers to the forward edge of a military position—where opposing forces meet in combat. By extension, frontline describes anyone working directly with a problem or population: frontline {workers}, frontline {responders}. During the pandemic, frontline became near-synonymous with essential workers in healthcare, retail, and delivery. As an adjective: {frontline communities bear the brunt of pollution}. Also spelled front line or front-line.

The frontlines are where opposing forces meet in conflict—originally military, now often figurative. Soldiers fight on the frontlines of battle; healthcare workers serve on the frontlines of a pandemic. The term emphasizes direct engagement with danger or difficulty: {Nurses were on the frontlines during the crisis}. Also spelled as two words: front lines.

A frontman is the lead performer of a band or musical group, typically the vocalist who stands at the front of the stage and serves as the public face of the act. The term extends beyond music to describe anyone who serves as the visible representative of an organization or operation, sometimes implying that the real power lies elsewhere: {He was just a frontman for the cartel}. In this sense, a frontman may provide legitimacy or distraction while others make the actual decisions.

A frontrunner is the person or thing leading in a competition or race. In politics, the frontrunner is the candidate polling ahead of rivals: {She's been the frontrunner since the primaries began}. The term implies the lead could change—frontrunners can stumble, and underdogs can catch up. Also spelled front-runner or front runner.

Frost is the thin layer of ice crystals that forms on cold surfaces when water vapor freezes: {frost on the windshield}, {frost on the grass}. Frost also refers to freezing temperatures: {an early frost killed the tomatoes}. To frost is to cover with frosting (icing on a cake) or to make glass opaque. Figuratively, frosty behavior is cold and unfriendly. (Capitalized Frost is a surname, notably the poet Robert Frost.)

Frostbite is tissue damage caused by exposure to extreme cold. Ice crystals form in the skin and underlying tissue, typically affecting extremities like fingers, toes, ears, and nose. Mild frostbite causes numbness and pale skin; severe cases can lead to permanent damage or require amputation. {We got frostbite waiting for the bus in subzero temperatures.}

Frostbitten describes tissue that has been damaged by extreme cold. When skin and underlying flesh are exposed to freezing temperatures for too long, ice crystals form in the cells, causing injury that ranges from superficial numbness to deep tissue destruction requiring amputation. Fingers, toes, ears, and noses are most vulnerable. {The climbers returned from the summit with frostbitten hands.} The word also appears figuratively to describe anything harmed or withered by cold conditions.

Frosted describes something covered with frost or made to resemble frost. Frosted {glass} is translucent, its surface roughened to obscure what lies behind. Frosted {cake} is covered with icing. Frosted {hair} has highlights that lighten it. In American slang, to be frosted is to be angry or annoyed: {She was frosted when they canceled at the last minute}.

Frosting is the sweet, creamy coating spread on cakes and other baked goods—typically made from sugar, butter, and flavorings. Americans use frosting and icing interchangeably, though some distinguish frosting as thicker and fluffier. {She licked the frosting off the cupcake}. Figuratively, frosting is the attractive finishing touch: {The promotion was frosting on an already good year}.

Frosts is the plural of frost, the thin layer of ice crystals that forms on surfaces when temperatures drop below freezing. It also serves as the verb form meaning to cover with frost or frosting: {She frosts the cake while it's still warm}. In informal use, to frost someone means to anger or irritate them. The word appears in compounds like {killing frosts}, which are cold snaps severe enough to damage crops.

Frosty describes things covered with frost or cold enough to produce it: {a frosty morning}, {frosty windows}. The word extends to anything suggesting cold—frosty colors are pale blues and whites, and a frosty manner is unfriendly or unwelcoming: {She gave him a frosty reception}. A frosty beverage is ice-cold, which advertisers love: {a frosty mug of beer}. (Capitalized Frosty is a name, notably the snowman.)

Froth is the mass of small bubbles that forms on the surface of liquids, whether from agitation, fermentation, or chemical reaction. Beer develops a frothy head when poured; ocean waves leave froth on the shore. The verb froth means to produce such bubbles: {The cappuccino machine frothed the milk perfectly}. Figuratively, froth suggests something insubstantial or trivial beneath an appealing surface—the frothy plot of a romantic comedy, or {media froth} that distracts from serious news.

Frothy describes something covered with or consisting of foam—small bubbles formed in liquid: {a frothy cappuccino}, {frothy waves}. The word extends to anything light and insubstantial: frothy {entertainment}, frothy {conversation}. Such things may be pleasant but lack depth or seriousness. A frothy {market} shows excessive, possibly unsustainable enthusiasm.

A frottola is a type of Italian secular song popular in the late 15th and early 16th centuries, typically featuring a simple melody with chordal accompaniment. The form preceded and influenced the madrigal. Frottole (the Italian plural) were often lighthearted, dealing with love themes in a direct, sometimes bawdy manner.

A frown is a facial expression of displeasure, disapproval, or concentration, made by drawing the eyebrows together and wrinkling the forehead. To frown is to make this expression: {She frowned at the mess}. To frown on or upon something is to disapprove of it: {The committee frowns on late submissions}.

Frowns are facial expressions of displeasure, disapproval, or concentration—the furrowing of the brow and downturning of the mouth. As a verb, to frown is to make this expression: {She frowns whenever I mention his name}. To frown on something is to disapprove of it: {The committee frowns on late submissions}.

Froze is the past tense of freeze. Water froze in the pipes. A deer froze in the headlights. {I froze when I saw her}. The word applies to literal cold, to sudden stillness from fear or surprise, and to halting activity: {The company froze hiring during the recession}.

Frozen is the past participle of freeze, describing something subjected to cold temperatures until solid or immobilized. Water becomes frozen ice; frozen food is preserved by freezing. Extended meanings follow naturally: a frozen expression shows no emotion, frozen assets cannot be accessed, and someone frozen with fear is unable to move. {I stood frozen in place.} The adverb stiff intensifies: {frozen stiff}.

Frugal describes careful, sparing use of resources—especially money. A frugal person avoids waste and unnecessary expense: {frugal habits}, {a frugal lifestyle}. A frugal meal is simple and inexpensive. The word carries approval rather than criticism, suggesting wisdom rather than stinginess: {My grandmother's frugal ways got the family through hard times}.

Fruit is the fleshy, seed-bearing part of a plant, typically sweet and eaten as food: apples, oranges, berries. Botanically, fruits include tomatoes, peppers, and cucumbers—anything that develops from a flower's ovary. Figuratively, fruit is the product of effort: {the fruits of our labor}. As offensive slang, fruit is a derogatory term for a gay man. To fruit is to produce fruit: {The trees fruited early this year}.

Fruitcake is a dense cake containing candied fruits, nuts, and spices, often soaked in brandy or rum.
