It's traditionally associated with Christmas and has a reputation for being heavy and long-lasting—jokes abound about regifting the same fruitcake for years. In slang, fruitcake means an eccentric or crazy person: {He's a total fruitcake}. The insult may also carry a homophobic edge, from the slang sense of fruit meaning gay man.

Fruitful means producing abundantly. Originally about plants bearing fruit, it extends to anything yielding good results: {a fruitful collaboration}, {fruitful negotiations}. A fruitful mind generates ideas; a fruitful discussion produces insights. The opposite, fruitless, describes efforts that yield nothing.

Fruitless means producing no fruit—literally for a barren tree, figuratively for efforts that yield nothing useful. A fruitless {search} finds nothing. A fruitless {endeavor} accomplishes nothing. The word emphasizes wasted effort more than simple failure: {After hours of fruitless negotiation, both sides gave up}.

Fruits are the seed-bearing parts of flowering plants, often sweet and edible: apples, oranges, berries. In broader use, fruits means results or rewards: {the fruits of your labor}, {fruits of the spirit}. As a verb, fruit means to produce fruit: {The tree fruits in late summer}. Fruit is also derogatory slang for a gay man.

Fruity describes something with the taste, smell, or quality of fruit: {a fruity wine}, {fruity notes in the perfume}. Extended to mean rich or resonant: {a fruity voice}. In British slang, fruity means slightly risqué or suggestive: {fruity jokes}. In American slang, fruity is a mildly offensive term for effeminate or gay, derived from fruit as slang for a gay man.

To frustrate is to prevent someone from achieving what they want, or to thwart a plan or effort: {Weather frustrated our attempts to reach the summit}. The feeling that results is also frustration—the state of being blocked or stymied: {I'm frustrated by the lack of progress}. Things that cause this feeling are frustrating: {a frustrating day}, {frustrating bureaucracy}. The word implies repeated or ongoing obstruction rather than a single defeat.

Frustrated describes the feeling of being blocked from achieving something—plans thwarted, efforts stymied, desires unfulfilled. {I'm so frustrated with this software}. The word covers a range from mild annoyance to deep exasperation. Sexually frustrated means unable to satisfy sexual urges. To frustrate is to cause this feeling: {The delays frustrated everyone involved}.

Frustrating describes something that causes feelings of annoyance, disappointment, or defeat, typically because efforts to achieve a goal are being blocked or thwarted. A frustrating experience is one where progress feels impossible despite continued attempts: {The most frustrating part was watching my edits disappear every time the page refreshed}. The word applies equally to minor daily irritations and to deeply discouraging situations that test one's patience over time.

Frustration is the feeling of being blocked or thwarted—when effort meets obstacle and progress stalls. You feel frustration when stuck in traffic, when technology fails, when someone won't listen. The word also names the cause: {The delays were a constant frustration}. To express frustration is common; to hide it takes effort. Frustration builds when repeated attempts yield no result.

Frustrations is the plural of frustration—the feeling of being blocked or thwarted when you can't achieve what you want. The word covers both the emotional state and its causes: {He vented his frustrations about the project}. Someone's frustrations accumulate over time, building from repeated obstacles or disappointments: {After years of frustrations with the system, she quit}.

Fry means to cook in hot fat or oil. You can fry an egg, fry bacon, or deep-fry chicken. The noun fry refers to food cooked this way, especially french fries: {Do you want fries with that?} Separately, fry is a collective term for young fish or recently hatched creatures: {salmon fry}. To {have bigger fish to fry} is to have more important matters to attend to.

Frying is cooking food in hot fat or oil. The term covers several techniques: deep frying submerges food completely, pan frying uses a shallow layer, and stir frying tosses ingredients quickly over high heat. {The smell of frying bacon filled the kitchen.} When something is frying, it's being cooked this way—or metaphorically, suffering intense heat or pressure.

Fubar is military slang meaning utterly ruined or hopelessly bungled: {The whole operation went fubar}. It originated as an acronym for "fucked up beyond all recognition" (or "repair"), joining a family of World War II–era military abbreviations like snafu. The term has spread to civilian use, especially in computing and business, where it describes situations past the point of salvage.

Fuchsia is a vivid purplish-red color, named after the flowering plant whose drooping blossoms display this distinctive hue. The plant itself, with its teardrop-shaped flowers, is popular in hanging baskets and shaded gardens. The word is frequently misspelled because the silent *ch* defies expectation: {Is it spelled f-u-s-c-h-i-a or f-u-c-h-s-i-a?}

Fuck is among the most versatile vulgar words in English, serving as verb, noun, adjective, adverb, and exclamation. The core meaning is to have sexual intercourse: {They fucked in the back seat}. But fuck extends far beyond sex—it expresses anger, surprise, emphasis, or dismissal. It appears in countless expressions: {fuck off}, {fuck up}, {fuck around}, {what the fuck}, {I don't give a fuck}, {fuck it}, {fuck around and find out}. As an intensifier, fucking amplifies nearly any word: {That's fucking brilliant}.

A fuckbuddy is a person with whom one has sex regularly without romantic commitment or emotional attachment. The arrangement is purely physical—friends or acquaintances who sleep together but aren't dating: {We're not in a relationship; he's just my fuckbuddy}. Also spelled as two words or hyphenated.

Fucked is the past tense of fuck, meaning had sex with. But its adjectival use dominates: something fucked is broken, ruined, or hopeless: {The engine is fucked}. To be fucked is to be in serious trouble: {If they find out, we're fucked}. To get fucked over is to be cheated or treated unfairly. {Fucked if I know} expresses emphatic ignorance.

Fucker is a vulgar term for a person, ranging from contemptuous insult to rough affection depending on context: {That fucker stole my parking spot}. {You lucky fucker.} It can also describe something difficult: {This jar lid is a fucker to open}.

Fuckery is nonsense, bullshit, or outrageous behavior—actions that are absurd, deceptive, or infuriatingly wrong: {I'm tired of all this corporate fuckery}. The word implies not just wrongdoing but a brazenness about it, often with systemic overtones: {political fuckery}, {bureaucratic fuckery}. Sometimes used more loosely for general chaos or foolishness: {What fuckery is this?}

Fucking is the present participle of fuck, but its power is as an intensifier—an all-purpose amplifier that can modify almost anything: {That's fucking amazing}. {I'm fucking tired of this}. It can even be inserted into words for emphasis: {abso-fucking-lutely}. Linguists call this tmesis.

Fucks is both the plural noun and third-person verb form of fuck. As a noun, fucks are acts of sex or, more commonly, units of caring: {I have no fucks left to give}. As a verb: {He fucks up everything he touches}.
A fuckup is either a serious mistake or a person who habitually makes them: {The launch was a total fuckup}. {He's a lovable fuckup.}
Fuckups is the plural of fuckup—either serious mistakes or people who habitually make them: {We've had too many fuckups this quarter}. {Those fuckups in accounting lost the invoice.}

Fudge is a soft, rich candy made from sugar, butter, and milk, often with chocolate or other flavorings. The verb fudge means to present something in a vague or misleading way, especially to avoid commitment or hide the truth: {The candidate fudged on the details of his tax plan}. To fudge numbers or facts is to manipulate them dishonestly. As an exclamation, fudge is a mild substitute for fuck, expressing frustration or annoyance.

Fudging is adjusting facts, figures, or rules in small, often dishonest ways: {She was fudging the numbers on her expense report}. The word suggests minor deception rather than outright fraud—hedging, rounding, or conveniently omitting details. To fudge an answer is to give something vague when you don't really know: {He fudged when asked about his qualifications}.

Fuel is any substance burned or consumed to produce energy—wood, coal, oil, gasoline. The meaning extends to anything that powers or sustains: {Coffee is my fuel}. To fuel is to supply with fuel or to intensify: {The scandal fueled public outrage}. {Fuel the car before the trip}. To {add fuel to the fire} is to worsen a situation.

Fuels is the plural of fuel—substances burned to produce energy or power: {fossil fuels}, {alternative fuels}. The verb fuels means to supply with fuel or to stimulate growth: {Coffee fuels my mornings}, {Resentment fuels the conflict}. What fuels something keeps it going, whether a car, a fire, or a grudge.

A fugitive is someone who has fled, especially from law enforcement or legal custody: {The fugitive was captured after three weeks on the run}. The word extends to anything fleeting or hard to capture—a fugitive {thought}, a fugitive {glimpse}. As an adjective, fugitive describes what escapes or evades: fugitive {emissions} are gases that leak unintentionally from industrial equipment.

Fugitives are people fleeing or in hiding, typically to escape law enforcement or legal authority: {Police are searching for the fugitives}. The term extends to anyone evading capture or pursuit. As an adjective, fugitive describes things that are fleeting or elusive: {fugitive thoughts}, {fugitive pleasures}. A {fugitive from justice} is someone who has fled to avoid prosecution or imprisonment.

A fugue is a musical composition built on a theme that enters successively in different voices, each imitating the others in a complex interwoven pattern. Bach's fugues remain the form's highest achievements. In psychiatry, a fugue state is a period of amnesia during which a person may travel or assume a new identity, then return to normal awareness with no memory of the episode: {He wandered the city in a fugue for three days}.

Fulfill (spelled fulfil in British English) means generally to meet a requirement or to achieve a goal or a desirable result. When you fulfill a promise, you do what you said you would do. If you fulfill the requirements of a position, you have or have done everything necessary to get the position. A person who feels fulfilled is content because everything needed or desired is present. An activity that you find fulfilling is one that is rewarding and that makes you happy.

Fulfilled describes the state of having achieved satisfaction or completion. A fulfilled promise has been kept; a fulfilled order has been delivered. More personally, someone who feels fulfilled has found meaning or purpose: {She felt fulfilled in her work as a teacher}. The word suggests not just accomplishment but deep contentment—needs met, potential realized.

Fulfilling describes something that brings deep satisfaction or a sense of purpose. A fulfilling {career} or {relationship} makes you feel your time and effort matter. The word implies more than pleasure—it suggests completion, as though something essential in you has been met: {She found volunteer work more fulfilling than her corporate job}.

Fulfillment is the satisfaction that comes from achieving something or having needs met: {She found fulfillment in her work}. The word also names the process of carrying out or completing something—fulfillment of a {promise}, fulfillment of a {prophecy}. In commerce, fulfillment refers to processing and shipping orders: {The company handles its own fulfillment}. Also spelled fulfilment in British English.

Fulfilment is the British spelling of fulfillment—the satisfaction that comes from achieving something or having needs met: {She found fulfilment in her work}. It also means the completion or carrying out of something: {the fulfilment of a promise}, {order fulfilment}. The word connects inner satisfaction with external completion.

The adjective and adverb full is related to the verb fill and has associated meanings. Full characterizes things that are filled up, large and rounded rather than thin or narrow, or having a replete and robust quality: The hotel offers a full range of accommodations. If you know something full well there is no question that you know it. Something that’s full blown has all the qualities of that thing: His HIV morphed into full-blown AIDS. Someone who’s full of something expresses or shows a great deal of it: She’s full of mirth.

To fumble is to handle something clumsily or grope about uncertainly: {She fumbled for the light switch in the dark}. You fumble with keys, buttons, or words when coordination fails you. In American football, to fumble is to drop the ball while in play—a costly error. The noun fumble names such an instance: {The fumble cost them the game}. Figuratively, fumbling suggests ineptitude: {He fumbled his way through the presentation}.

Fumbled is the past tense of fumble, meaning to handle something clumsily or fail to hold onto it securely. A receiver fumbles when the ball slips from their grasp; you fumble for your keys in the dark. Figuratively, to fumble is to bungle or mishandle: {He fumbled the announcement and confused everyone}.

Fumbling describes clumsy, awkward handling or searching, typically with the hands: {She went fumbling through her purse for the keys}. It suggests groping without clear direction or skill, whether physical or metaphorical. A fumbling {attempt} at explanation lacks confidence or competence. In American football, fumbling refers to losing control of the ball. The word carries connotations of nervousness, inexperience, or uncertainty—someone fumbling with a lock is having trouble getting it open.

Fume refers to smoke, vapor, or gas—especially when irritating or toxic: {exhaust fumes}, {paint fumes}. The verb means to emit such vapors, or figuratively, to seethe with anger: {She fumed at the delay}. Someone who is fuming is visibly agitated, anger rising off them like smoke.

Fumes are gases or vapors, especially unpleasant or harmful ones: {exhaust fumes}, {paint fumes}, {toxic fumes}. The word almost always appears in the plural and carries negative connotations—you breathe fresh air but inhale fumes. To fume is to emit fumes or, more commonly, to seethe with anger: {She was fuming after the meeting}.

Fuming means giving off fumes or smoke, but the word appears most often in its figurative sense: extremely angry, seething with barely contained rage. Someone who is fuming may not be shouting but is visibly upset: {She was still fuming about the insult hours later}. {He sat fuming in the waiting room}.

Fun is enjoyment, amusement, or lighthearted pleasure: {We had fun at the beach}. Something done {for fun} has no serious purpose. A fun person or activity is enjoyable: {She's really fun to be around}. To {make fun of} someone is to mock them. To {poke fun at} is gentler teasing. {Fun and games} can be genuine play or ironic understatement for something difficult.

The noun and verb function has considerable overlap in meaning with the more common words purpose and work. The function of something is one of the ways it works (brain function, kidney function). A function is also an event with a purpose: The dinner was a work function. Such an event might happen in a function room in a hotel. When something functions, it works or does what it is expected to do: The machine will not function properly with the hood open. Function also expresses something dependent on another factor: Her privileged position was a function of her advanced education.

Functional means working or operative—a functional {appliance} does what it's supposed to do. It can also mean practical rather than decorative: functional {design} prioritizes utility over aesthetics. In specialized contexts, functional describes things organized around purpose or function: functional {programming}, functional {medicine}. Someone described as functional is managing adequately despite difficulties: {She's barely functional before her morning coffee}.

A fund is a sum of money set aside for a specific purpose: a retirement fund, an emergency fund, a scholarship fund. Organizations that manage such money are also called funds: hedge funds, mutual funds. To fund something is to provide money for it: {The project was funded by private donors}. In the plural, funds simply means available money: {I'm low on funds right now}.

Fundamental describes what lies at the foundation or base of something—the essential elements without which the whole structure fails. Fundamental {rights}, fundamental {principles}, fundamental {skills}. A fundamental {flaw} undermines everything built upon it. In music, the fundamental is the lowest frequency of a harmonic series. As a noun, fundamentals are basics: {master the fundamentals before advancing}. Fundamentally means at the deepest level: {We fundamentally disagree}.

Fundamentalism is strict adherence to the basic principles of a religion or ideology, especially when resisting modern reinterpretation. The term originated with early 20th-century American Protestants who insisted on literal biblical truth. It now applies broadly to rigid, uncompromising belief systems: {Islamic fundamentalism}, {market fundamentalism}. A fundamentalist holds such views.

A fundamentalist holds strictly to the basic tenets of a religion or ideology, rejecting modern reinterpretations or compromises. The term emerged from early 20th-century American Protestantism but now applies broadly: {Islamic fundamentalists}, {free-market fundamentalists}. The word often carries pejorative weight, suggesting rigidity or extremism: {He's a fundamentalist about grammar}.

Fundamentalists are people who adhere strictly to the basic principles of a religion, ideology, or movement, often interpreting foundational texts literally and resisting modern reinterpretations. The term originated with early 20th-century American Protestants who insisted on biblical inerrancy, but now applies broadly: {Islamic fundamentalists}, {free-market fundamentalists}. The word often carries negative connotations, suggesting inflexibility or extremism, though some embrace it as commitment to core truths.

Fundamentals are the essential principles or elements that form the foundation of a subject or skill. You learn the fundamentals before advancing: {She drilled the fundamentals of piano technique}. In finance, fundamentals are the core metrics—earnings, assets, debt—that determine a company's underlying value: {The stock price collapsed despite strong fundamentals}.

Funding is money provided for a particular purpose, especially by an organization or government: {The project lost its funding}, {We're seeking funding for the research}. The word emphasizes the source and allocation of financial support rather than the money itself. To fund something is to provide the money for it.

A fundraiser is an event or campaign organized to collect money for a cause, organization, or individual: {The school held a fundraiser for new library books}. The word also refers to a person whose job involves soliciting donations: {She works as a fundraiser for the nonprofit}. Political fundraisers are events where candidates court donors.

Fundraisers are events or campaigns organized to collect money for a cause, organization, or individual. A charity dinner, a bake sale, and an online crowdfunding drive are all fundraisers. The word also refers to people who organize such efforts or solicit donations professionally: {She works as a fundraiser for the university}. {The gala was their biggest fundraiser of the year.}

Fundraising is the organized effort to collect money for a cause, organization, or project. Schools hold fundraisers, charities run fundraising campaigns, and political candidates spend much of their time fundraising. The word covers everything from bake sales to billion-dollar capital campaigns: {She's in charge of fundraising for the new hospital wing}.

Funds are money available for a particular purpose. Organizations maintain funds for operations, emergencies, or specific projects: {The charity's funds were running low}. To fund something is to provide money for it: {The grant funded her research}. Someone who is well-funded has ample financial resources. In the plural, funds often simply means available money: {I don't have the funds right now}.

A funeral is a ceremony held after someone dies, typically involving rituals of mourning and disposal of the body through burial or cremation. The word extends to the procession accompanying the deceased: {The funeral passed slowly through town}. {It's your funeral} means the consequences are yours to bear—a warning that someone's choice will end badly for them.

Funerals is the plural of funeral—ceremonies honoring the dead, typically involving a viewing of the body, religious rites, and burial or cremation. The word extends to anything resembling such a gathering in solemnity: {The meeting felt like a funeral}. To say {it's your funeral} warns someone they'll bear the consequences of their choice.

Fungi is the plural of fungus—organisms like mushrooms, molds, yeasts, and mildews that form their own biological kingdom, distinct from plants and animals. They lack chlorophyll and obtain nutrients by decomposing organic matter or living as parasites. {The fungi growing on the fallen log included several species of bracket mushroom.} The singular fungus works as an adjective: {fungus infection}.

Fungus refers to a kingdom of organisms that includes mushrooms, molds, yeasts, and mildews. Unlike plants, fungi don't photosynthesize—they absorb nutrients from organic matter, often decomposing dead material or parasitizing living hosts. A fungus can be microscopic or produce large fruiting bodies like the mushrooms we eat. {The fungus spread across the fallen log}. Fungal infections affect skin, nails, and internal organs. Plural: fungi or funguses.

A funhouse is an attraction at amusement parks and carnivals featuring disorienting or surprising elements—distorting mirrors, moving floors, dark passages, air jets. The appeal lies in mild fright and loss of control in a safe environment. Figuratively, any chaotic or bewildering situation: {The interview felt like a funhouse of weird questions}.

Funk has two distinct meanings. One is a state of fear or panic, or a dejected mood: {He's been in a funk since losing his job}. The other is a style of rhythmic, bass-heavy Black American music that emerged in the 1960s, emphasizing groove over melody. The musical sense comes from funky, originally meaning earthy or smelling of sex—the music had that raw, sweaty quality. Something funky can be stylishly unconventional or simply smelly, depending on context.

Funky has two main meanings that rarely overlap. In music, funky describes a style with heavy rhythmic bass and a raw, earthy feel—originating in African American soul and R&B: {a funky groove}, {funky bass line}. By extension, anything unconventional or stylishly offbeat can be funky: {a funky little café}, {funky vintage clothes}. The older meaning describes something smelling bad or musty—the funk of body odor or damp basements. Context usually makes clear which sense applies.

A funnel is a cone-shaped device with a tube at the narrow end, used to channel liquids or powders into containers with small openings: {She used a funnel to pour oil into the engine}. The shape extends to anything that narrows: a funnel {cloud} tapers toward the ground. To funnel is to move through a constricting passage or to direct flow: {Traffic funneled through the single open lane}, {They funneled money into offshore accounts}. In marketing, a funnel tracks potential customers through stages from awareness to purchase.

Funny describes what provokes laughter or amusement: {a funny joke}, {She's the funniest person I know}. It also means strange or peculiar: {There's something funny going on here}, {The milk tastes funny}. These senses occasionally blur—{That's funny} can mean either "that's hilarious" or "that's odd." Funny can also describe physical discomfort: {a funny feeling in my stomach}. As a noun, funnies are comic strips in newspapers.

Fur is the soft, thick hair covering an animal's body, or the pelt with hair attached used for clothing and decoration: {a fur coat}, {synthetic fur}. The word extends to similar coatings—fur on a tongue indicates illness, fur in pipes is mineral buildup. As a verb, to fur up is to become coated. In internet culture, a furry is someone interested in anthropomorphic animal characters; fur sometimes appears in that context.

Furious means extremely angry—rage at full intensity: {She was furious when she found out he'd lied}. The word also describes violent force or frantic speed: {a furious storm}, {working at a furious pace}. Something done {fast and furious} happens with reckless, intense energy.

Furlough is a temporary leave from work or military duty. Employees may be placed on furlough during budget cuts or slow periods—they remain employed but don't work or get paid: {Government workers faced furloughs during the shutdown}. In military contexts, soldiers on furlough have authorized time away from their post. The verb means to grant or impose such leave: {The company furloughed two hundred workers}.

A furnace is an enclosed structure for generating intense heat. Industrial furnaces smelt metal ore or fire ceramics. Residential furnaces burn fuel to heat buildings: {The furnace kicked on when the temperature dropped}. Figuratively, a furnace is any intensely hot place: {The kitchen was a furnace in summer}. A {blast furnace} produces iron from ore using forced air.

Furnaces is the plural of furnace, an enclosed structure for generating intense heat. Furnaces burn fuel to heat buildings, smelt ore, or fire ceramics. Industrial furnaces reach temperatures that melt steel. Figuratively, any place of intense heat or trial: {The summer city was a furnace}, {the furnace of war}.

Furnish means to supply or provide. You furnish a room by equipping it with furniture and other necessities: {a sparsely furnished apartment}. More broadly, to furnish is to give what's needed: {The report furnished evidence of wrongdoing}. Furnishings are the furniture and accessories in a space.

Furniture is the movable objects that make a space usable—chairs, tables, beds, desks, sofas. The word covers both functional items and decorative pieces: {We need to buy furniture for the new apartment}. To be {part of the furniture} is to be so familiar or longstanding as to go unnoticed: {He's been here so long he's part of the furniture}.

Furries are people who have strong interest in anthropomorphic animals—fictional creatures with human characteristics like walking upright, speaking, and wearing clothes. The furry fandom encompasses art, costumes, online communities, and conventions. Some furries create animal personas called fursonas and wear elaborate fursuits. The subculture is often mischaracterized as primarily sexual, though for most participants the appeal centers on creativity, identity expression, and community: {My daughter got into furries through DeviantArt}.

A furrow is a long, narrow trench cut into the earth, especially one made by a plow for planting seeds. The word extends to any groove or channel resembling this: the furrows of a plowed field, the furrows in tree bark. Furrows on the face are wrinkles, particularly the deep lines on a furrowed brow—which suggests concentration, worry, or age. To furrow is to make such grooves: {She furrowed her brow in thought}.

Furrows are long, narrow trenches cut into the earth, especially by a plow preparing soil for planting: {The farmer drove the tractor in straight furrows across the field}. The word extends to any similar groove or channel—the furrows on a vinyl record, or the deep lines that form on a worried brow. To furrow is to make such grooves: {She furrowed her brow in concentration}.

Furry describes something covered with fur or resembling fur: {a furry cat}, {furry slippers}. The noun furry refers to a member of a subculture interested in anthropomorphic animal characters—often creating art, costumes, or personas around them. The community ranges from casual fans to those who adopt "fursonas" as alternate identities: {The convention attracted thousands of furries}.

Further means to a greater extent or degree, or in addition to what has been said: {I have nothing further to add}. It also means more distant in space or time, though farther is preferred for physical distance in American English. As a verb, to further something is to advance or promote it: {She took classes to further her career}. Further can introduce an additional point: {Further, the evidence suggests fraud}.

Fury is intense, often violent anger—rage that overwhelms restraint. A person in a fury may lash out destructively: {He smashed the dishes in a fury}. Fury also describes violent force in nature: {the fury of the storm}. The phrase {hell hath no fury like a woman scorned} warns of the wrath of rejected love. (Capitalized Fury refers to mythological figures or proper names.)

A fuse is a safety device containing a strip of metal that melts when too much current flows through it, breaking the circuit: {The microwave blew a fuse}. To fuse is to join by melting together, or more broadly, to merge: {The two styles fused into something new}. A fuse is also a cord or mechanism that ignites an explosive—if someone has a {short fuse}, they anger quickly. The spellings fuse and fuze are both used for the explosive device, though fuze is preferred in military contexts.

Fused describes things that have been joined together by melting or heating, or more broadly, merged into a single unit. A fused {spine} has vertebrae grown together. Fused {glass} is melted and bonded. Figuratively, elements can be fused without heat: {The album fused jazz and hip-hop into something new}. In British English, a fused appliance has blown its fuse and stopped working.

Fuses names devices that protect electrical circuits by melting when current exceeds safe levels, breaking the connection before damage occurs. The verb fuse means to join things together, typically through heat: {The blast fused the metal fragments into a single mass}. By extension, fuse describes any thorough blending or merging: {The chef fuses Asian and Latin flavors}. When someone blows a fuse, they lose their temper suddenly, like an overloaded circuit.

Fusion is the joining of separate things into a unified whole. In physics, nuclear fusion occurs when atomic nuclei combine, releasing enormous energy—the process that powers the sun. In cooking, fusion blends culinary traditions: {Thai-Mexican fusion}. Fusion jazz merges jazz with rock or funk. The word emphasizes that distinct elements have merged rather than merely mixed.

Fuss is agitated activity or commotion, often disproportionate to the cause: {What's all the fuss about?} To fuss is to worry or busy oneself with small matters: {She fussed over the table settings}. A fussy person is hard to please or overly attentive to details. To {make a fuss} can mean to complain or to lavish attention: {They made a fuss over the new baby}.

Fussing is showing excessive concern or agitation over small matters. A parent fusses over a child's appearance before a photo. Someone fusses with their hair, making tiny adjustments. A baby fusses when uncomfortable—whimpering and squirming without full-blown crying. {Stop fussing and just submit the application.} {The cat was fussing at the door to be let out.}

Fussy describes someone excessively concerned with small details or hard to please: {a fussy eater}, {Don't be so fussy about the font}. A fussy baby is irritable and difficult to soothe. Fussy also describes things overly elaborate or ornate: {fussy Victorian decor}, {a fussy arrangement of doilies and figurines}.

Futile describes efforts or actions that have no chance of success—pointless, useless, doomed to fail. A futile {attempt} produces no result. A futile {gesture} accomplishes nothing. The word often carries a sense of wasted energy against impossible odds: {Resistance was futile}. Futility is the noun form.

Futility is the quality of being pointless or incapable of producing any useful result. An action has futility when it cannot possibly succeed or when any effort invested in it will be wasted: {He recognized the futility of arguing with someone so stubborn}. The word often carries a tone of resignation or despair, acknowledging that further attempts would be meaningless. Futile is the corresponding adjective.

A futon is a low bed or couch that converts between seating and sleeping surfaces. The Western futon typically has a foldable frame with a thick cotton mattress that serves as cushion when upright and bed when flat: {The guest room just has a futon}. The Japanese original is a floor mattress rolled up and stored during the day.

Future is the time that hasn't happened yet—what lies ahead. As an adjective, it describes things yet to come: {future generations}, {future plans}, {my future self}. A person's future is their prospects or destiny: {She has a bright future}. In grammar, future tense indicates actions that will occur. In finance, futures are contracts to buy or sell commodities at a predetermined price on a specified date.

Futures are financial contracts obligating the buyer to purchase, or the seller to sell, an asset at a predetermined future date and price. Traders use futures to speculate on commodities like oil, wheat, or gold, or to hedge against price changes: {Oil futures dropped on news of increased production}. The futures market allows betting on where prices will go without owning the underlying asset.

Futurism is a general orientation toward or emphasis on the future rather than the past or present. It can describe artistic or design sensibilities that evoke advanced technology or speculative futures: {The building's futurism feels dated now}. In broader use, futurism means the study of or speculation about future developments: {corporate futurism}, {technological futurism}. (Capitalized Futurism is the early 20th-century art movement.)

A futurist is someone who studies, predicts, or speculates about future developments in society, technology, or culture. The term applies both to professional forecasters who advise businesses and governments and to enthusiasts who engage with speculative possibilities. Futurist also refers to an adherent of Futurism, the early 20th-century avant-garde movement in art and literature that celebrated speed, machinery, and modernity. {The company hired a futurist to predict consumer trends over the next decade.}

Futuristic describes something that seems to belong to or evoke the future—typically through sleek design, advanced technology, or unconventional aesthetics: {a futuristic skyscraper}, {futuristic spacecraft in the film}. The word often carries optimistic connotations of progress and innovation, though it can also suggest cold sterility or impracticality: {The concept car looked futuristic but would never see production}.

Fuzz is a soft, fluffy mass of fine fibers or hair—the fuzz on a peach, the fuzz accumulating in a dryer vent. Fuzzy things have this texture: a fuzzy sweater, a fuzzy caterpillar. Figuratively, fuzz suggests indistinctness: a fuzzy {memory}, a fuzzy {picture}. In slang, {the fuzz} means the police—dated but still recognized. In music, fuzz is a distorted guitar effect: {a fuzz pedal}.

Fuzzy describes something covered with soft, fine fibers or hair: {a fuzzy sweater}, {fuzzy peach skin}. By extension, fuzzy means indistinct or blurred: {a fuzzy photograph}, {fuzzy memories}. Thinking can be fuzzy when unclear or imprecise. In computing and logic, fuzzy refers to systems that handle degrees of truth rather than strict binary values: {fuzzy logic}.

A gadget is a small mechanical or electronic device, typically one that's clever or novel: {kitchen gadgets}, {the latest tech gadgets}. The word often implies something useful but not essential—a tool for a specific task that you could probably manage without. Gadget carries a hint of novelty or gimmickry, distinguishing it from more serious equipment.

Gadgets are small mechanical or electronic devices, often clever or novel in design. The word suggests something useful but not essential—a kitchen gadget, a tech gadget. Gadgets tend toward the gimmicky: {He loves his gadgets but rarely uses them}. The term often carries slight dismissiveness, implying the device is more toy than tool.

A gaffe is an embarrassing blunder, especially a social mistake or tactless remark: {The senator's gaffe about the economy dominated the news cycle}. Unlike a simple error, a gaffe implies awkwardness or loss of face—saying the wrong thing at the wrong time, often publicly.

Gaffes is the plural of gaffe, a blunder or faux pas—an embarrassing mistake, especially one made in public or social situations. Politicians are particularly prone to gaffes: {His campaign never recovered from his gaffes about women voters}. A gaffe often reveals something the speaker didn't intend to expose.

A gag is something placed in or over the mouth to prevent speech or screaming—a cloth, ball, or restraint. To gag someone is to silence them this way, or figuratively to suppress their expression: {The court order gagged the press}. Gag also means to retch or choke: {The smell made me gag}. As comedy slang, a gag is a joke or prank: {a running gag}, {a sight gag}. A gag order prohibits public discussion of legal proceedings.

Gagaku is the ancient court music of Japan, dating back over a thousand thousand years. It encompasses orchestral music, dance, and song performed at imperial ceremonies, Shinto rituals, and state occasions. The ensemble typically includes wind instruments like the shō (mouth organ), string instruments, and percussion. Gagaku remains one of the oldest continuously performed musical traditions in the world.

Gagged means having something placed in or over the mouth to prevent speaking or crying out: {The kidnappers gagged their victim}. By extension, to gag someone is to silence or censor them: {The court order gagged the press}. Gagged also serves as the past tense of gag in its other senses—to choke or retch, or to tell jokes: {He gagged on the bitter medicine}; {The comedian gagged his way through the set}.

Gagging is the reflexive throat spasm that precedes vomiting, or the choking sensation when something triggers that reflex: {The smell had me gagging}. To be gagging for something (British slang) is to want it desperately: {I'm gagging for a cup of tea}. Gagging also refers to silencing someone, from the noun gag meaning a device or order that prevents speech: {a gagging order from the court}.

A gaggle is a flock of geese, especially when on the ground rather than in flight. The word extends to any noisy, disorderly group: {a gaggle of reporters}, {a gaggle of schoolchildren}. The informal use emphasizes chaos or chattiness rather than mere quantity.

Gags are jokes, pranks, or comic bits—anything meant to provoke laughter. A gag can be a visual stunt, a one-liner, or an elaborate practical joke: {The movie is packed with sight gags}. A running gag recurs throughout a performance. Separately, gags are devices placed in the mouth to prevent speech or screaming, and to gag is to retch or choke: {The smell made me gag}.

The idea of the verb gain is closely related to get and obtain: when you gain something, it comes into your possession or becomes associated with you. Gain is typically used for immaterial things (gain experience, gain access, gain insight), but you can also gain weight, which is not immaterial. A gain is anything obtained or acquired and usually has positive connotations: an investment strategy intended to maximize gains. A gain in a quality or attribute is an increase: The new procedure gave us a significant gain in efficiency.

Gains refers to increases, profits, or improvements obtained through effort. In finance, gains are returns on investments: {The stock showed modest gains}. In fitness culture, gains specifically means muscle growth from training: {No pain, no gain}, {Check out these gains}. The plural emphasizes accumulated progress rather than a single instance of gaining.

A gala is a festive celebration or special event, typically formal and elaborate: {the museum's annual fundraising gala}, {a gala dinner honoring the award recipients}. As an adjective, gala describes something festive or celebratory: {gala occasion}, {gala performance}. The word suggests glamour, dressing up, and occasions worth commemorating.

Galactic means relating to a galaxy—a vast system of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity. Most often it refers to our own Milky Way: {the galactic center}, {galactic coordinates}. Figuratively, galactic suggests enormous scale: {galactic ambitions}, {a galactic waste of money}. The adjective appears frequently in science fiction: {galactic empire}, {intergalactic travel}.

Galaxies is the plural of galaxy, a massive system of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter bound together by gravity. The Milky Way is our home galaxy; billions more exist across the observable universe. Galaxy comes from a Greek word meaning milk, referring to the milky appearance of stars across the night sky. Figuratively, a galaxy of something means a brilliant gathering: {a galaxy of Hollywood stars}.

A galaxy is a vast system of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity—like the Milky Way, which contains our solar system. By extension, galaxy describes any brilliant assemblage: {a galaxy of Hollywood stars}, {a galaxy of talent}. The Samsung Galaxy line of devices borrows the cosmic grandeur. (Capitalized Galaxy often refers to the Milky Way specifically or to branded products.)

A gale is a very strong wind, stronger than a breeze but typically not as destructive as a hurricane or tornado. Meteorologists define it precisely on the Beaufort scale, but in general use it simply means powerful, sustained wind: {The ship struggled through the gale}. Figuratively, a gale of laughter is a sudden burst of loud, uncontrolled laughing. (Capitalized Gale is a given name or surname.)

Gales is the plural of gale—a very strong wind, typically between 32 and 63 miles per hour on the Beaufort scale. Storms at sea produce gales that threaten ships: {The fishing boats returned to harbor ahead of the gales}. Figuratively, gales describes sudden bursts of emotion or sound: {gales of laughter}, {gales of applause}.

Some meanings of gall arise from the gall bladder, the organ that stores bile (which is also called gall). This extremely bitter substance is the inspiration for the meaning brazen impudence: She had the gall to ask me to lend her money after she didn’t pay back the last loan! To gall someone is to irritate or vex them, perhaps unreasonably. Another gall is a growth that appears on some plants as a result of insect infestation (oak gall). Finally, a gall is a sore, especially on an animal, that emerges from chronic irritation or friction.

A galleon is a large sailing ship used from the 15th to 18th centuries, especially by Spanish and Portuguese fleets. Galleons were built for warfare and cargo transport, with multiple decks and distinctive high forecastles and sterncastles. They carried treasure from the Americas and became iconic targets for pirates: {The Spanish galleon was laden with gold}.

Galleons were large, multi-decked sailing ships used from the 16th to 18th centuries, primarily by European powers for trade and warfare. Spanish galleons famously transported treasure from the Americas. The word now evokes the age of exploration and piracy: {The galleon was laden with gold}. In the Harry Potter series, a galleon is a gold wizard currency.

Galleries is the plural of gallery. A gallery is a room or building for displaying art: {The museum's galleries house works spanning five centuries}. It also means a balcony or upper level in a theater or church where spectators sit—hence {playing to the gallery}, performing for the cheap seats rather than discerning critics. An underground passage in a mine is also a gallery. A gallery can be any long, narrow space: a shooting gallery, a corridor lined with windows.

A gallery is a room or building for displaying art: {The museum's new gallery opens next month}. The word extends to any long, narrow space—a corridor, a covered walkway, or a balcony in a theater where cheaper seats are located. To {play to the gallery} is to seek approval from the least sophisticated audience. A gallery can also be a collection: {a rogues' gallery}, {a gallery of photographs}. In mining, a gallery is a horizontal underground passage.

A galley is a large ship propelled mainly by oars, used in ancient and medieval times for warfare and trade in the Mediterranean. Rowers sat in long rows below deck—often slaves or prisoners. The word extends to the kitchen on a ship or aircraft, typically a narrow space with equipment along the walls. In publishing, a galley is a preliminary printed version of text used for proofreading before final production: {The editor marked up the galleys}.

Gallivanting is going about in search of pleasure or entertainment, often with a hint of aimlessness or irresponsibility. The word carries mild disapproval—someone gallivanting isn't attending to duties: {While you were gallivanting around Europe, I was here paying the bills}. It suggests carefree wandering, socializing, or adventure-seeking when perhaps one should be doing something more productive.

A gallon is a unit of liquid volume. In the United States, a gallon equals 128 fluid ounces or about 3.8 liters. The British imperial gallon is larger—about 4.5 liters. Milk, gasoline, and paint are commonly sold by the gallon. {The car gets thirty miles to the gallon.} {We bought a gallon of milk.}

Gallons is the plural of gallon, a unit of liquid volume. In the United States, a gallon equals 128 fluid ounces; the British imperial gallon is slightly larger. The word appears constantly in discussions of fuel economy, milk purchases, and water usage: {The car gets thirty miles to the gallon}. Informally, gallons means a large quantity: {We have gallons of time}.

Gallop is the fastest gait of a horse, a bounding run where all four hooves leave the ground simultaneously. The word extends to any rapid pace: {We galloped through the presentation}. A gallop is also an instance of this gait: {We took the horses for a gallop across the field}. At full gallop means at top speed.

Galloping describes the fastest gait of a horse, with all four hooves leaving the ground in each stride. Extended to any rapid, bounding movement: {The children came galloping down the stairs}. Figuratively, galloping means advancing at an alarming pace: {galloping inflation}, {galloping consumption} (an old term for rapidly progressing tuberculosis).

A gallows is a wooden frame, typically consisting of two upright posts and a crossbeam, used for execution by hanging. The structure allows a noose to be suspended at a height, with the condemned person dropped through a trapdoor or pushed from a platform. Though executions by hanging have largely disappeared in Western countries, gallows remains common in figurative use: {gallows humor} is joking about grim or morbid subjects, especially one's own misfortune or impending doom.

Galvanize means to shock into action, as if by electric current. A scandal galvanizes public opinion; a coach galvanizes a team at halftime. {The assassination galvanized the protest movement.} The word comes from Luigi Galvani, who famously made dead frogs' legs twitch with electricity. In metalworking, to galvanize is to coat iron or steel with zinc to prevent rust.

Galvanized describes metal coated with zinc to prevent rust, or figuratively, someone shocked into action. Steel is galvanized by dipping it in molten zinc. A person is galvanized by sudden motivation: {The tragedy galvanized the community into demanding reform}. Both senses share the idea of protective or energizing transformation through an external force.

Galvanizing means stimulating into sudden action or awareness, as if by electric shock: {a galvanizing speech}, {The news had a galvanizing effect on the team}. The word comes from galvanize, originally meaning to apply electric current to muscles, causing them to twitch. The metaphor captures that jolt—something galvanizing overcomes inertia and compels movement or response.

A gambit is an opening move that sacrifices something to gain a later advantage. The term comes from chess, where a gambit offers a pawn or piece to improve position. More broadly, any calculated maneuver or strategic ploy: {Her opening gambit was to question his credentials}. A {conversational gambit} is a remark intended to start or steer discussion.

Gambits are opening moves, originally in chess where a player sacrifices a piece to gain positional advantage. The term extends to any calculated opening maneuver in negotiation, conversation, or strategy: {Her opening gambit was to feign disinterest}. A gambit implies some risk taken for potential gain—not just any first move, but one with tactical intent.

To gamble is to bet money or something of value on an uncertain outcome—cards, dice, horses, sports. The word extends to any risky action taken in hope of a favorable result: {She gambled on the new job paying off}. A gamble is such a bet or risk: {Starting the business was a gamble}. {He gambled away his inheritance}.

A gambler is someone who bets money on uncertain outcomes—cards, dice, horses, sports, or financial markets. The term can be neutral or carry connotations of recklessness: {He's a compulsive gambler}. Extended uses describe anyone who takes significant risks: {She's a gambler in business, always making bold moves}.

Gamblers are people who gamble—who bet money or valuables on uncertain outcomes. The term covers casual players at casinos and professional poker players alike. It often carries connotations of compulsion or recklessness: {He's a gambler who's lost everything twice}. More broadly, gamblers are risk-takers: {Entrepreneurs are gamblers by nature}.

Gambling is risking money or valuables on an uncertain outcome—cards, dice, sports, horse races, slot machines. The appeal lies in the possibility of winning more than you wager, though the odds typically favor the house. Extended uses apply to any risky venture: {Starting a business is always a gamble}. Gambling can become compulsive, leading to addiction.

The earliest meaning of game is still the most frequent: an activity undertaken for amusement. The verbs most frequently occurring before game are play, win, and lose, and they say a lot about why people play games. When associated with hunting for food, game encompasses animals collectively (fish, birds, mammals). If you game something, such as a system, you rig it to operate unfairly. Game is also used as a mainly predicate adjective to characterize an attitude of eager readiness: they wanted to go to Niagara Falls and we were game.

A gamechanger is something that fundamentally alters how a situation develops or how people approach a problem. The term comes from sports, where a single play or player can shift momentum decisively, but now applies broadly to innovations, discoveries, or events that transform expectations: {Electric vehicles were a gamechanger for the auto industry}. Often hyphenated or two words: game-changer, game changer.

A gamekeeper is a person employed to manage and protect game animals and birds on a private estate, ensuring healthy populations for hunting while preventing poaching. The role involves habitat management, predator control, and enforcing hunting regulations on the property. {The gamekeeper caught two men setting snares on the estate.}

A gamemaster is the person who runs a tabletop roleplaying game, controlling the story, setting, and non-player characters while the other players control their individual characters. The gamemaster creates scenarios, adjudicates rules, and responds to player choices: {Our gamemaster spent weeks preparing the campaign}. Different game systems use different terms—dungeon master in Dungeons & Dragons, storyteller in World of Darkness—but gamemaster serves as the generic term across the hobby.

A gameplan is a strategy for achieving a goal, originally from sports—a coach's plan for winning a specific game. The term has spread to any situation requiring coordinated effort: {What's our gameplan for the product launch?} Unlike a general strategy, a gameplan implies a concrete, near-term objective with specific steps. Also spelled as two words: game plan.

A gamer is someone who plays video games, typically as a regular hobby rather than casually. The term carries connotations of enthusiasm and identity—gamers often invest significant time mastering games, following gaming culture, and identifying with gaming communities. {He's been a gamer since the Nintendo days.} The word can describe anyone from casual mobile players to competitive esports professionals, though hardcore gamers sometimes gatekeep the label.

Gamers are people who play video games, especially as a regular hobby or lifestyle. The term implies more than casual play—gamers typically invest significant time in gaming, follow gaming culture, and may identify with the community. {He's been a gamer since childhood.} The word can carry both pride and stereotype, evoking images ranging from dedicated enthusiasts to basement-dwelling shut-ins.

Games are structured activities with rules, played for enjoyment or competition. Board games, card games, video games, and sports all qualify. The singular game extends to contests, matches, and rounds within larger competitions. To {play games} with someone is to manipulate or deceive them. Someone's {game} is their strategy or skill level: {Her tennis game has really improved}. {Game on} signals readiness to compete.

A gameshow is a television program where contestants compete for prizes by answering questions, solving puzzles, or performing tasks. The format typically involves a host, rules governing play, and escalating stakes: {She won a car on a gameshow}. Also spelled as two words: game show.

Gamesmanship is the art of winning games or gaining advantage through psychological tactics, borderline rule-bending, or unsporting behavior that stops just short of outright cheating. A tennis player who takes excessive time between points or a negotiator who schedules meetings to inconvenience opponents practices gamesmanship. The term often carries a mildly disapproving tone: {His constant trash-talking was pure gamesmanship}.

Gaming is playing games, especially video games or gambling. The word now leans heavily toward video games: {gaming PC}, {gaming console}, {the gaming industry}. Someone deep into video games is a gamer. In casinos, gaming is the preferred euphemism for gambling: {gaming tables}, {gaming commission}. To game a system is to exploit its rules for advantage.

Gang usually refers to a group of people (gang of friends, gang of thieves). Before another noun, gang references criminal gang activity (gang warfare, gang violence). If you gang up on someone, you join with others to exert pressure, oppose, or criticize. To gang together is positive, as animals might do to protect each other.

Gangland refers to the world of organized crime and criminal gangs, or the territory they control. The word appears most often as an adjective: a gangland {slaying}, a gangland {boss}, gangland {violence}. It evokes a shadowy underworld with its own rules, hierarchies, and brutal methods of settling disputes.

A gangplank is a movable board or ramp used to bridge the gap between a ship and a dock, allowing people to board or disembark. The term evokes the age of sailing ships and pirate lore—prisoners forced to {walk the plank} were sent off a similar board into the sea. Modern equivalents are usually called gangways.

Gangrene is the death and decay of body tissue, usually caused by loss of blood supply or bacterial infection. The affected flesh turns black and may spread if untreated, often requiring amputation: {The wound became gangrenous and they had to take the leg}. Figuratively, gangrene describes corruption spreading through an institution or system.

Gangs is the plural of gang—a group united by common purpose or identity. The word ranges from innocent to sinister: a {gang of kids} playing together, a work {gang} on a construction site, or a criminal organization controlling territory through violence. {Street gangs} and {biker gangs} carry connotations of lawlessness. As a verb, to gang up on someone is to unite against them: {They ganged up on the new kid}.

Gangsta is a hip-hop spelling of gangster, reflecting African American pronunciation. It emerged with West Coast rap in the late 1980s and 1990s, particularly in the subgenre {gangsta rap}, which depicted street life, crime, and gang culture. The spelling marks authentic connection to that musical and cultural moment: {He's got that gangsta swagger}. Outside hip-hop contexts, it often signals ironic or playful toughness.

A gangster is a member of an organized criminal group. The term evokes images of prohibition-era mobsters in pinstripe suits, but applies to any era's organized crime figures: {The gangsters ran numbers rackets throughout the neighborhood}. In hip-hop culture, gangster (often spelled gangsta) describes a street-tough persona or lifestyle. As an adjective, gangster can mean impressively bold or ruthless: {That was a gangster move}.

Gangsters are members of criminal organizations, typically involved in activities like racketeering, drug trafficking, or extortion. The term evokes organized crime figures of the Prohibition era—suited men with tommy guns—but applies broadly to anyone operating in a criminal gang: {The neighborhood was controlled by local gangsters}. Gangster also works as an adjective: {gangster rap}, {gangster movies}.

A gangway is a passageway, especially a temporary or movable one that allows people to board or leave a ship, aircraft, or other vessel. The term extends to any narrow walkway or aisle, particularly in British English where it refers to the passage between sections of seats in a theater or the House of Commons. As an exclamation, gangway! is a command to clear the way, demanding that people step aside to let someone through. {Gangway! Coming through!}

Ganja is marijuana, especially in forms associated with Rastafarian culture or Caribbean origin. The word comes from Hindi and entered English through Jamaican usage: {He was smoking ganja on the porch}. It appears in reggae lyrics and cannabis culture generally, carrying a slightly more exotic or countercultural flavor than plain *marijuana* or *weed*.

A gap is an opening, difference or separation; the word is related to the much less frequent verb gape. The gender gap refers to differences in attitudes by and about, and opportunities for, males and females: By voting in large numbers, women created a gender gap that elected the progressive candidate. A budget gap is the difference between how much is available and how much is needed or wanted. To bridge a gap is to supply whatever missing thing resulted in there being a gap. Physical gaps might include one between a person’s front teeth, or between two mountains.

Gaping describes something wide open, especially a mouth or wound: {a gaping hole in the wall}, {He stared with gaping mouth}. The word emphasizes the size or conspicuousness of an opening. A gaping {chasm} yawns before you. Figuratively, a gaping {flaw} in an argument is one impossible to miss.

Gaps is the plural of gap—empty spaces or intervals where something is missing or incomplete. Physical gaps are openings or breaks: {gaps in the fence}, {gaps between teeth}. Abstract gaps are deficiencies or disconnects: {gaps in knowledge}, {gaps in the fossil record}, {the gap between rich and poor}. To fill or close gaps is to address what's lacking.

A garage is a building or enclosed structure for housing vehicles, typically attached to or near a home. It often doubles as storage space or a workshop. In British usage, a garage is also a gas station or auto repair shop. To garage a vehicle is to put it in a garage: {We garage the car in winter}. A garage sale offers household items for sale, typically in the driveway.

Garbage is waste material, especially household refuse: {Take out the garbage}. The word extends to anything worthless or of poor quality: {That movie was garbage}, {garbage in, garbage out}. In computing, garbage refers to corrupted or meaningless data. To garbage something is to discard it, though this use is less common than simply throwing it away.

Garbled describes communication that has become confused, distorted, or incomprehensible—whether through poor transmission, faulty memory, or deliberate scrambling. A garbled {message} arrives with words missing or jumbled. Garbled {instructions} are impossible to follow. {The recording was so garbled I couldn't make out what she said.} Information can become garbled as it passes from person to person.

A garden is a plot of land where plants are cultivated—flowers, vegetables, herbs, or ornamental shrubs. British English uses garden where Americans say yard: {The children played in the garden}. To garden is to tend such a space. {Garden-variety} means ordinary or unremarkable. To {lead someone down the garden path} is to deceive them gradually.

A gardener is someone who tends a garden—planting, weeding, watering, and cultivating plants. The term covers both hobbyists who maintain home gardens and professionals hired to care for others' landscapes: {We hired a gardener to handle the yard work}. A {master gardener} has completed horticultural training, often through extension programs.

A gardenia is a fragrant flowering shrub with glossy dark leaves and waxy white or cream-colored blooms. Native to tropical and subtropical regions, gardenias are prized for their intensely sweet scent and are popular in gardens, corsages, and perfumery: {The gardenia's perfume filled the room}.

Gardenias are flowering shrubs prized for their creamy white blooms and intensely sweet fragrance. Native to tropical and subtropical regions, they're cultivated as ornamentals and used in perfumery. The flowers are associated with romance and formal occasions—often worn as corsages or boutonnieres: {She pinned a gardenia to her dress}.

Gardening is the activity of cultivating plants—flowers, vegetables, herbs, or ornamental shrubs—typically in a yard or designated plot. It encompasses planting, watering, weeding, pruning, and tending soil. The word covers everything from casual weekend puttering to serious horticultural pursuit: {She took up gardening after retirement}. Someone with {a green thumb} has a knack for it.

A gargoyle is a carved stone figure, typically grotesque or monstrous, projecting from a building's roofline to channel rainwater away from the walls. The term extends to any grotesque carved figure on a building, even decorative ones without drainage function. By extension, gargoyle describes an ugly person: {He sat in the corner like a gargoyle}.

Gargoyles is the plural of gargoyle, a carved stone figure projecting from a building's roofline. True gargoyles are waterspouts—the grotesque faces channel rainwater away from walls. Similar decorative figures without drainage function are technically called grotesques, though gargoyle covers both in casual use. The creatures are usually monstrous or demonic: {Stone gargoyles leered down from the cathedral}.

A garland is a wreath or decorative chain of flowers, leaves, or other materials, typically hung as decoration or worn on the head: {garlands of holly}, {a garland of roses}. To garland something is to adorn it with such decoration: {The victors were garlanded with laurels}. The word suggests festivity, honor, or celebration. (Capitalized Garland is a proper name.)

Garlands are decorative wreaths or chains of flowers, leaves, or other materials, typically hung as festive ornaments or draped around something: {The hall was hung with garlands for the wedding}. To garland is to adorn with such decorations: {They garlanded the winner with flowers}. Figuratively, garlands can mean honors or praise: {the garlands of literary fame}.

Garlic is a pungent bulb used as seasoning in cooking worldwide. The bulb divides into segments called cloves, which are peeled, minced, or crushed to release their sharp, aromatic flavor. Raw garlic is more intense than cooked. Garlic appears in countless dishes and is said to ward off vampires—and, less fancifully, to repel people with its lingering smell on the breath.

Garnet is a group of hard silicate minerals occurring in various colors, most commonly deep red. Prized as gemstones and used industrially as abrasives, garnets appear in jewelry and sandpaper alike: {a garnet ring}, {garnet paper for finishing wood}. The deep reddish-brown color itself is called garnet. (Capitalized Garnet is a given name.)

Garnets are a group of hard, glassy minerals occurring in many colors, most commonly deep red. Prized as semiprecious gemstones, they appear in jewelry and also serve industrial purposes as abrasives: {a garnet ring}, {garnet sandpaper}. The deep reddish-brown color itself is called garnet.

Garnish means to decorate or embellish, most commonly food: {The chef garnished the plate with parsley and a lemon wedge}. A garnish is such a decoration—something added for visual appeal rather than substance. In legal contexts, to garnish wages is to withhold money from someone's paycheck to satisfy a debt, typically by court order: {The IRS garnished his wages until the back taxes were paid}.

A garrison is a body of troops stationed at a military post, or the post itself: {The garrison held out for three weeks}. To garrison a place is to station troops there for defense. The word suggests permanent or semi-permanent military presence rather than troops passing through. A {garrison town} is one where soldiers are regularly stationed.

A garter is a band worn around the leg to hold up a stocking. Before elastic waistbands, garters were essential undergarments; now they appear mainly in formal or erotic contexts. A {garter belt} is a piece of lingerie with straps that attach to stocking tops. The Order of the Garter is Britain's highest order of chivalry. A garter snake is a harmless North American snake with lengthwise stripes.

Garters are bands worn around the leg to hold up stockings or socks. Before elastic waistbands, garters were essential undergarments—either simple bands below the knee or straps attached to a belt or corset. Modern garters are mostly decorative, associated with lingerie or wedding traditions: {The groom removed the bride's garter and tossed it to the groomsmen}.

The most general use of gas is to designate one of the primary states of matter: one in which molecules move about randomly and would expand infinitely in the absence of containment or pressure. Gas is also used as shorthand for some common fossil fuels—some of which actually are gasses, such as natural gas. In American English, the petroleum distillate that is used to power internal combustion engines (petrol in British English) is gas. If a person has gas, they are experiencing indigestion that is accompanied by the release of gas through belching or flatulence. As a verb, gas may mean to fuel a vehicle (gas up the car) or to subject a person or animal to a harmful or lethal gas: The shelter was reportedly gassing surplus animals.

A gasbag is a bag that holds gas, such as the inflatable compartment of a balloon or airship. The figurative sense dominates: a gasbag is a person who talks excessively without saying much of substance. {Uncle Frank is a gasbag—he'll corner you for an hour about nothing.}

Gases is the plural of gas—substances like air, helium, or methane that expand to fill any container. The word covers both natural phenomena {(greenhouse gases)} and practical applications {(anesthetic gases)}. In informal use, gases can mean instances of flatulence. The verb form gases means supplies with gas or, informally, talks idly: {He gases on about nothing}.

A gash is a long, deep cut or wound, typically jagged or ragged rather than clean: {The fall left a nasty gash on his forehead}. The word extends to similar cuts in materials: {a gash in the leather seat}. As a verb, to gash is to make such a cut: {He gashed his knee on the rocks}. In British slang, gash is vulgar for female genitalia, and by extension, a crude term for women generally.

To gaslight someone is to manipulate them into doubting their own perceptions, memory, or sanity. The term comes from a 1938 play in which a husband dims the gas lights while denying any change, making his wife question her grip on reality. Gaslighting is a form of psychological abuse: {He gaslit her for years, insisting her concerns were imaginary}. The word has broadened to describe any attempt to make someone distrust their own judgment: {The company tried to gaslight customers about the defective product}.

Gaslighted is the past tense of gaslight, meaning to manipulate someone psychologically so they question their own memory, perception, or sanity. The term comes from a 1944 film in which a husband dims the gas lights while denying any change, making his wife doubt her reality. Someone who has been gaslighted has experienced sustained psychological manipulation designed to make them distrust themselves: {She realized she'd been gaslighted for years when friends confirmed what she'd always suspected}. The alternate past tense gaslighted competes with gaslit.

A gaslighter is someone who manipulates another person into doubting their own perceptions, memories, or sanity. The term comes from a 1938 play in which a husband dims the gaslights while denying any change, making his wife question her grip on reality. Gaslighters deny events that happened, dismiss concerns as overreactions, or insist their victims are imagining things: {My ex was a gaslighter—he'd say cruel things and then swear I'd misheard him}.

Gaslighting is a form of psychological manipulation where someone makes another person question their own memory, perception, or sanity. The manipulator denies events that happened, dismisses the victim's feelings, or insists their recollections are wrong: {He kept gaslighting her about the argument until she wondered if it had even occurred}. The term comes from the 1944 film *Gaslight*, where a husband dims the gas lights while insisting his wife is imagining it. Now widely applied to any sustained attempt to undermine someone's grip on reality.

Gaslights can be lamps that burn gas for illumination, the kind that lit streets and homes before electricity. More commonly now, gaslights is the verb form of gaslight—to manipulate someone into questioning their own perception or sanity: {He gaslights her by denying conversations that happened}. The psychological sense comes from the 1944 film *Gaslight*, where a husband dims the gas lamps while telling his wife she's imagining it.

Gaslit describes someone who has been manipulated into doubting their own perceptions, memories, or sanity. The term comes from a 1944 film in which a husband dims the gas lights while denying any change, making his wife question her reality. To be gaslit is to have experienced this psychological manipulation: {I thought I was going crazy, but I was being gaslit}. The verb gaslight and noun gaslighting are now common in discussions of abusive relationships and political rhetoric.

A gasmask is a device worn over the face to protect against poisonous gases, smoke, or airborne contaminants. It typically covers the nose and mouth with a filter or connects to an air supply. Gasmasks became iconic in World War I when chemical warfare made them essential for soldiers. Also spelled gas mask.

Gasoline is a flammable liquid fuel refined from petroleum, used primarily to power internal combustion engines in cars and other vehicles. Americans say gasoline or gas; the British say petrol. {Gas prices are up again}. The shortened form gas dominates casual speech, though it invites confusion with gaseous substances.

A gasp is a sudden, sharp intake of breath, typically triggered by surprise, shock, pain, or exertion. To gasp is to take such a breath or to struggle for air: {She gasped when she saw the price tag}. Someone at their last gasp is near death or exhaustion. If you gasp for something, you desperately need or want it: {I'm gasping for a coffee}. Gasp also functions as an interjection conveying mock surprise or drama in informal writing.

Gasping is breathing in short, labored bursts, usually from exertion, shock, or lack of air: {She came up gasping for breath}. It suggests desperate or involuntary inhalation. Figuratively, to be gasping for something is to crave it urgently: {I'm gasping for a cup of tea}. This figurative use is more common in British English.

Gassed has several distinct meanings. To be gassed is to be exposed to poison gas or anesthetic—soldiers were gassed in the trenches, patients gassed before surgery. In slang, gassed means intoxicated or, more recently, excited and energized: {I'm so gassed for this concert}. To get gassed up is to be hyped or flattered: {Don't get too gassed—stay humble}.

A gate is a passage through a fence or wall that can be opened and closed. This meaning is extended to computing, where a gate is a logical pathway that has two settings, on or off. A place that is gated is accessible only through a gate. The combining form -gate arises from Watergate, the name of a Washington, DC, hotel that was the kernel of the Nixon political scandal in the 1970s. From this, -gate is appended to other words to designate official wrongdoing, like “Irangate” or “Travelgate.”

To gatecrash is to enter a party or event without an invitation or ticket. The term evokes pushing past the gate of a private gathering. A gatecrasher is someone who does this habitually or on a particular occasion: {Three gatecashers showed up at the wedding reception}. The word can extend to any uninvited intrusion into exclusive spaces or situations.

A gatecrasher is someone who enters a party, event, or venue without an invitation or ticket. The term implies deliberate intrusion rather than innocent mistake: {Security removed several gatecrashers from the reception}. The verb is gatecrash: {We gatecrashed the after-party}.

Gatecrashing is entering an event without an invitation or ticket—showing up at a party you weren't asked to, slipping into a concert without paying. The term evokes literally crashing through a gate. Someone who does this is a gatecrasher: {Security caught three gatecrashers at the wedding reception}. The verb is gatecrash: {We gatecrashed the afterparty}.

Gatekeep means to control access to something—resources, communities, or cultural spaces. The term often carries negative connotations, suggesting someone is arbitrarily deciding who belongs or what counts as authentic: {Stop gatekeeping—let people enjoy things}. A gatekeeper traditionally guards an entrance, but gatekeeping now frequently describes policing the boundaries of fandoms, identities, or hobbies: {He was gatekeeping the music scene, dismissing anyone who discovered the band after 2010}.

A gatekeeper controls access to something—originally the person who guards a gate, now usually figurative. Gatekeepers decide who gets in: editors gatekeep publication, administrators gatekeep resources, fans gatekeep fandoms by challenging newcomers' credentials. {The interview is just the first gatekeeper}. To gatekeep is to restrict access, often with connotations of elitism or excessive control: {Stop gatekeeping—let people enjoy things}.

Gatekeepers are people who control access to something—originally literal gates, now usually figurative. A gatekeeper decides who gets in: {The editor served as gatekeeper for what got published}. The term often carries skepticism about whether such control is legitimate: {Self-appointed gatekeepers of the art world}. In medicine, a gatekeeper is a primary care physician who must approve referrals to specialists.

Gatekeeping is controlling access to something—resources, communities, or information. A gatekeeper decides who gets in and who doesn't. The term often carries negative connotations, especially online, where it describes excluding people from fandoms or identities based on arbitrary standards: {Stop gatekeeping—let people enjoy things}. But gatekeeping can be neutral or positive when it means maintaining quality or protecting boundaries: {Editors do necessary gatekeeping}.

Gates are movable barriers controlling passage through walls, fences, or other boundaries. A gate swings open; a door slides or lifts. Gates also control flow in other systems: a gate at an airport terminal, a logic gate in electronics, a gate controlling water in a dam. To gate is to restrict access: {The community is gated}. In skiing, gates are pairs of poles marking a course. (Capitalized Gates often refers to Bill Gates.)

A gateway is an entrance or passage through a barrier—a gate in a wall, fence, or hedge, or the structure framing it. By extension, gateway means a point of entry or access to something larger: {St. Louis was the gateway to the West}. A gateway {drug} is one thought to lead users toward harder substances. In computing, a gateway is a device or software that connects different networks, translating between protocols.

Gateways are openings or passages that allow entry—literal or figurative. A gateway is an entrance through a wall or fence, or the structure framing it. More often, gateway describes something that provides access to a larger domain: {a gateway to success}, {a gateway drug}. In computing, a gateway connects different networks, translating between protocols. The plural emphasizes multiple points of access: {international gateways}, {payment gateways}.

Gather means to bring together into one place or group. You gather firewood, gather your thoughts, gather people for a meeting. Cloth gathers when it's drawn into folds or puckers: {The skirt gathered at the waist}. To gather something is also to conclude or infer: {I gather you're not coming}. A gathering is an assembly of people. Things gather gradually—dust gathers, clouds gather, momentum gathers.

Gathered is the past tense of gather, meaning to bring together or collect. People gather berries, information, or courage. Fabric that is gathered has been drawn into folds or pleats: {a gathered skirt}. If you've gathered correctly, you've understood through inference: {I gathered from her tone that she was upset}.

A gathering is a group of people who have come together in one place: {a family gathering}, {a gathering of world leaders}. The word can emphasize either the assembly itself or the act of assembling.
