The term often carries political charge, with "globalist" sometimes used as a slur suggesting shadowy international elites.

A globalist is someone who advocates for or supports globalism—the idea that international cooperation, free trade, and interconnected economies benefit humanity more than nationalist or isolationist policies. In neutral contexts, it describes politicians, economists, or business leaders who favor multinational institutions and open borders for commerce. However, globalist has become a pejorative in populist and nationalist discourse, often implying that elites prioritize international interests over their own country's citizens. {The candidate accused globalists of selling out American workers.}

Globalization refers to any phenomenon that was formerly localized (confined to a region, country, continent, or the like) and is now “global,” that is, effective or observable around the world. Electronic communication and improved transportation are the main drivers of globalization. In an economic context, globalization often is associated with the availability of markets or labor in places where a company does not have a physical presence: Globalization of industrial production is blamed for high rates of unemployment in many developed countries.

A globe is a sphere, especially one representing the Earth with its continents and oceans mapped onto the surface. Classrooms and offices display globes as reference objects and décor. The globe means the Earth itself: {travelers who've circled the globe}, {known around the globe}. Globe extends to any spherical object: a snow globe, a glass globe covering a light bulb. To globe is to form into a sphere, though this use is rare. (Capitalized Globe refers to the famous Shakespearean theater.)

Globes is the plural of globe, a spherical object or representation. Most commonly, globes are spherical maps of the Earth used for education or decoration: {The library had antique globes from the 18th century}. The word extends to any sphere-shaped object—light fixtures, glass ornaments, or anatomical structures like eyeballs. In vulgar slang, globes refers to breasts.

A globetrotter is someone who travels widely and frequently around the world, often for pleasure or adventure rather than necessity. The word suggests enthusiasm for exploration and a cosmopolitan spirit: {She's a real globetrotter—she's been to forty countries}. The term gained additional fame as the name of the Harlem Globetrotters basketball team.

Globetrotting is traveling widely around the world, especially for pleasure or adventure. The term suggests frequent, far-flung journeys rather than a single trip: {She spent her twenties globetrotting through Asia and South America}. A globetrotter is someone who travels this way. The word carries connotations of leisure, curiosity, and perhaps privilege.

Gloom is darkness or dimness—the absence of adequate light: {the gloom of a winter afternoon}, {eyes adjusting to the gloom}. The word extends naturally to emotional darkness: a mood of sadness, pessimism, or despair. {Gloom settled over the household after the news}. To gloom is to look or feel sullen, though the verb is rare. The adjective gloomy covers both senses: a gloomy basement, a gloomy outlook.

Gloomy describes darkness or dimness that feels oppressive: {a gloomy forest}, {gloomy winter afternoons}. The word extends naturally to mood—someone gloomy is melancholy or dejected, and a gloomy outlook expects the worst: {He gave a gloomy assessment of our chances}. Gloomy suggests heaviness rather than simple sadness.

Glorified describes something given a grander name or status than it deserves. A glorified {secretary} has a fancy title but does the same work. A glorified {shed} is called a cottage. The word deflates pretension by revealing what something really is beneath its elevated label: {The new office is just a glorified closet}.

Glorify means to praise, honor, or elevate something to a position of great importance. Religious use centers on praising God: {glorify the Lord}. More broadly, to glorify is to make something seem more impressive or admirable than it really is: {The film glorifies violence}. A glorified thing is given a grander name than it deserves: {The "executive suite" was just a glorified closet}.

Glorious means magnificent, splendid, or worthy of great praise. A glorious {victory} is complete and impressive. A glorious {sunset} is strikingly beautiful. The word often carries a sense of triumph or radiance: {the glorious revolution}, {a glorious career}. Informally, glorious can simply mean wonderful or delightful: {We had a glorious time at the beach}.

Glory is great honor, praise, or distinction achieved through remarkable deeds or qualities: {He won glory on the battlefield}, {the glory days of Hollywood}. Religious glory refers to the magnificence and splendor of God or heaven: {angels singing glory}. To glory in something is to take great pride or delight in it: {She gloried in her children's success}. The expression {glory be} is a mild exclamation of surprise or wonder.

Gloss is a shine or luster on a surface: {lip gloss}, {high-gloss paint}. By extension, gloss can mean an attractive appearance that hides something less appealing: {The report put a gloss on the company's failures}. To gloss over something is to treat it superficially or minimize its importance. Separately, a gloss is an explanatory note or translation, especially in the margin of a text—to gloss a word is to explain or interpret it.

Glossy describes surfaces that are smooth and shiny, reflecting light with a polished appearance: {glossy hair}, {glossy paint}, {glossy photographs}. The noun glossy typically refers to a magazine printed on high-quality paper with a shiny finish, often featuring fashion, celebrities, or lifestyle content: {She flipped through the glossies at the salon}. Something glossy may also suggest superficial attractiveness that conceals a lack of substance beneath the polished exterior.

A glove is a covering for the hand with separate sheaths for each finger. Gloves protect against cold, dirt, or injury: {winter gloves}, {surgical gloves}, {boxing gloves}. To {fit like a glove} is to fit perfectly. To {handle with kid gloves} is to treat delicately. In baseball, a glove is the leather mitt used to catch the ball.

Gloves are coverings for the hands with separate sections for each finger, distinguishing them from mittens. They protect against cold, dirt, chemicals, or injury: {rubber gloves}, {boxing gloves}, {surgical gloves}. To {handle with kid gloves} is to treat delicately. When gloves {come off}, restraint ends and conflict intensifies. To {fit like a glove} is to fit perfectly.

Glow is the soft, steady light something emits without flame—the glow of embers, of a screen in a dark room, of city lights on the horizon. Skin can glow with health or exertion. A pregnant woman is said to glow. To glow with pride or happiness is to radiate visible contentment: {She was glowing after the promotion}. As a noun, glow names both the light itself and the warm feeling: {the glow of satisfaction}.

Glowing describes something that emits light or warmth, especially with a soft, steady radiance: {glowing embers}, {a glowing screen in the dark}. Extended to people, it suggests health, happiness, or inner warmth: {She was glowing after the workout}, {a glowing bride}. Figuratively, glowing describes enthusiastic praise: {The film received glowing reviews}.

A glowstick is a small plastic tube containing chemicals that produce light when mixed, typically activated by bending the tube to break an internal glass vial. Glowsticks glow for several hours and come in various colors, making them popular at concerts, raves, and Halloween. They're also practical for emergency kits and nighttime activities since they require no batteries or external power source. {The kids waved glowsticks during the fireworks show.}

Glue is a sticky substance used to bond surfaces together. The word extends to anything that holds things in place or creates cohesion: {She's the glue that holds the team together}. To glue is to attach with adhesive, or to fix attention intently: {His eyes were glued to the screen}. Glued to a spot means unable or unwilling to move.

Glued is the past tense of glue—to attach with adhesive. Beyond literal bonding, glued describes intense focus or fixation: {She was glued to her phone}, {His eyes were glued to the screen}. Something glued in place is stuck fast, whether physically or figuratively: {I stood there, glued to the spot}.

Glug is the sound of liquid pouring from a bottle or container in intermittent bursts: {The wine glugged into the glass}. As a noun, it's both the sound itself and an informal measure—a splash or pour of liquid: {Add a glug of olive oil}. The word imitates what it describes.

Glum describes a mood of quiet dejection or sullen discontent—not dramatic grief, but a low-grade unhappiness that shows in the face. Someone glum sits silently, unenthusiastic about everything: {He looked glum after hearing the news}. A glum expression suggests disappointment or worry without tears or outbursts.

Gluten is a protein found in wheat and related grains like barley and rye. It gives dough its elasticity and helps bread rise and hold its shape. People with celiac disease cannot tolerate gluten; it damages their intestines. {Gluten-free} products have become widely available, though some who avoid gluten have no medical need to do so.

Glutes is the casual term for gluteal muscles—the three muscles forming each buttock. The word appears constantly in fitness contexts: {My glutes are sore from yesterday's squats}, {This exercise really targets your glutes}. The singular glute refers to one buttock or one side's muscles: {I pulled my left glute}.

A glutton is someone who eats excessively or greedily. The word extends to anyone with an insatiable appetite for something: {a glutton for punishment}, {a glutton for work}. A glutton for punishment is someone who keeps subjecting themselves to unpleasant experiences. The wolverine is also called a glutton, from its reputation for voracious feeding.

Gluttony is excessive eating or drinking—indulgence beyond what the body needs or can reasonably enjoy. One of the seven deadly sins in Christian tradition, it represents lack of self-control around physical appetites. The word extends to overconsumption generally: {His gluttony for power knew no bounds}. A glutton is someone who eats to excess, or figuratively, someone insatiable: {a glutton for punishment}.

Glycosyltransferases are enzymes that transfer sugar molecules from one compound to another, building the complex carbohydrate structures found throughout living organisms. They play essential roles in assembling cell surface markers, creating the sugary coatings on proteins, and synthesizing polysaccharides like starch and glycogen. These enzymes are critical in biology and medicine, influencing everything from blood type determination to how cells communicate and recognize each other.

A glyph is a carved or inscribed symbol—a character or figure cut into stone, wood, or other material. The term appears most often in discussions of ancient writing systems: Egyptian hieroglyphs, Mayan glyphs. In typography and computing, a glyph is any distinct visual representation of a character: the letter A in different fonts produces different glyphs. {The archaeologists documented each glyph on the temple wall.}

Gnarled describes something twisted, knotted, and rough—most often applied to old trees with thick, contorted branches or to weathered hands marked by age and hard work. The word evokes decades of growth or labor that have left their visible mark: {a gnarled oak at the edge of the property}, {her gnarled fingers still moved nimbly over the piano keys}. Gnarled carries connotations of toughness and endurance rather than decay.

Gnarly began as surfer slang for waves that are dangerously large or difficult—knotted and twisted like the gnarls on an old tree. From there it split two ways. In admiring use, gnarly means impressively extreme or hardcore: {That skateboard trick was gnarly}. In negative use, it describes something unpleasant, ugly, or gross: {a gnarly wound}, {gnarly traffic}. Context usually makes the intent clear.

A gnat is any of various tiny flying insects, especially those that bite or swarm around the face. The word covers midges, fungus gnats, and similar pests. To {strain at a gnat} is to fuss over trivial matters while ignoring larger ones—from the biblical image of filtering gnats from wine. Something negligible may be dismissed as not worth a gnat's attention: {I don't give a gnat's ass what they think}.

The gnathosoma is the front section of a mite or tick's body, consisting of the mouthparts and their supporting structures. Distinguished from the idiosoma (the main body), the gnathosoma contains the chelicerae and pedipalps used for feeding. The term appears primarily in acarology—the study of mites and ticks.

Gnats are tiny flying insects, often seen in swarms near water, plants, or rotting matter. The word covers various small flies including fungus gnats and fruit flies. Something insignificant may be compared to a gnat: {Don't sweat the gnats}. To {strain at a gnat} is to fuss over trivial matters while ignoring larger problems.

To gnaw is to bite or chew persistently, usually with small, repeated motions: {The dog gnawed on a bone}, {Mice had gnawed through the wires}. Figuratively, something that gnaws at you causes persistent distress or unease: {Guilt gnawed at her conscience}, {a gnawing sense of dread}. The physical and psychological senses share the idea of slow, relentless wearing away.

Gnawing describes persistent biting or chewing, the way a rodent works at something with its teeth: {a dog gnawing on a bone}. More often the word is figurative—a gnawing {doubt}, a gnawing {hunger}, a gnawing {sense of guilt}. The image is of something that won't stop wearing at you.

Gnocchi are small Italian dumplings, typically made from potato, flour, and egg, then boiled and served with sauce. The singular is gnocco, though English speakers rarely use it—gnocchi functions as both singular and plural: {The gnocchi was excellent}, {These gnocchi are homemade}. Variations substitute ricotta, semolina, or other bases for potato.

A gnome is a small, bearded creature from European folklore, said to live underground and guard treasures. Garden gnomes are the painted ceramic statues that populate suburban lawns—a kitschy decorative tradition. In finance, the gnomes of Zurich are Swiss bankers, suggesting secretive figures hoarding wealth. {A ceramic gnome stood by the birdbath.}

Gnomes are small mythical beings that live underground and guard treasures, typically depicted as bearded old men. In garden statuary, gnomes appear as cheerful figures with pointed hats: {My neighbor's yard is full of garden gnomes}. In fantasy gaming and fiction, gnomes are often tinkers or inventors. On the internet, gnome refers to a bait-and-switch image or video prank featuring a dancing gnome.

Goading is the act of provoking or urging someone toward action, typically through persistent irritation or challenge. A goad was originally a pointed stick for driving cattle, and the verb retains that sense of prodding: {His goading finally pushed her to respond}. The word suggests deliberate provocation rather than encouragement—you goad someone into losing their temper, not into doing their best.

A goal is an aim or desired outcome—something you're working toward: {My goal is to finish by June}. In sports, a goal is both the target area where points are scored and the act of scoring: {She kicked the ball into the goal}, {That's his third goal this season}. Goals give direction to effort, whether in personal ambition, team strategy, or organizational planning.

A goalie is the player who guards the goal in sports like hockey, soccer, and lacrosse—the last line of defense against scoring. Short for goalkeeper or goaltender. {Their goalie made an incredible save in the final seconds.}

Goalies is the plural of goalie, the player who guards the goal in hockey, soccer, lacrosse, and similar sports. The position requires quick reflexes and specialized equipment: {Both goalies played exceptionally well}. Goalie is informal; the formal term is goalkeeper or goaltender.

A goalkeeper is the player positioned in front of the goal in sports like soccer, hockey, or lacrosse, tasked with preventing the opposing team from scoring. Often shortened to goalie or keeper. The goalkeeper typically wears distinctive gear and operates under special rules—in soccer, the only player allowed to handle the ball within the penalty area.

A goalpost is one of the vertical posts (usually a pair) that form the goal in sports like football, soccer, and hockey. The crossbar connects them; a ball must pass between or above them to score. Figuratively, to {move the goalposts} is to change the rules or criteria after someone has already begun trying to meet them—a common accusation in arguments and negotiations.

Goalposts are the vertical posts that define the scoring area in sports like football, soccer, and hockey, typically connected by a crossbar. The phrase {move the goalposts} describes changing the rules or criteria after someone has already begun working toward a goal, making success harder to achieve. This figurative use suggests unfairness—like literally relocating the posts mid-game so a player can't score.

Goals are aims or objectives—outcomes you want to achieve. A goal can be concrete {(score a goal)} or abstract {(my goal is to be more patient)}. In sports, a goal is both the target area and the act of sending the ball or puck into it. Goals imply intention and effort: you set them, work toward them, reach them or fall short.

A goat is a hoofed mammal related to sheep, domesticated for milk, meat, and fiber. Goats are known for eating almost anything and for their ability to climb steep terrain. A goat can also be someone blamed for a failure—the {scapegoat} who cost the team the game. In recent slang, calling someone {the goat} means they're highly skilled or admirable, from the acronym for "greatest of all time." {They made him the goat for the project's failure.} (All-caps GOAT is the acronym.)

A goatee is a small pointed beard on the chin, without a mustache or sideburns—resembling the tuft on a goat's chin. The term now loosely includes any beard confined to the chin area, sometimes connected to a mustache: {He trimmed his goatee in the mirror}.

Goats are hooved mammals related to sheep, domesticated for milk, meat, and fiber. They're known for climbing ability and willingness to eat almost anything. A goat can be a lecherous man or a scapegoat—someone blamed for others' failures. In sports slang, GOAT means "greatest of all time": {Jordan is the GOAT}. To {get someone's goat} is to annoy them.

To gobble is to eat greedily and quickly, swallowing food in large chunks: {He gobbled down his lunch in five minutes}. Gobble also describes the throaty, rapid call of a turkey. To gobble something up is to consume it eagerly or completely—food, resources, or attention: {The project gobbled up our entire budget}.

Gobbled is the past tense of gobble, meaning to eat quickly and greedily: {He gobbled his dinner and ran outside}. It also describes the sound a turkey makes. To gobble up is to consume eagerly or completely: {The company gobbled up its competitors}.

Gobbledegook is language so full of jargon, technical terms, or convoluted phrasing that it's meaningless or incomprehensible to ordinary readers: {The contract was twenty pages of legal gobbledegook}. The word often criticizes bureaucratic or official writing that obscures rather than communicates. Also spelled gobbledygook.

Gobbledygook is language so full of jargon, technical terms, or convoluted phrasing that it's practically meaningless to ordinary readers. Government documents, legal contracts, and corporate memos are frequent offenders: {The memo was pure gobbledygook—nobody understood what we were supposed to do}. The word itself mimics the sound of a turkey's gobble, suggesting noise without sense.

Gobbling is eating rapidly and greedily, often noisily: {He was gobbling his food like he hadn't eaten in days}. The word suggests consumption without restraint or manners. Gobbling is also the throaty, bubbling call made by a male turkey, especially during mating season.

A goblet is a drinking vessel with a stem and base, typically used for wine. The word suggests something more formal or ceremonial than an ordinary glass—medieval banquets, communion services, ornate metalwork: {He raised the silver goblet in a toast}. In fantasy contexts, goblets often appear as magical or cursed objects.

Goblets are drinking vessels with a foot and stem supporting a bowl, typically used for wine or other beverages at formal occasions. The form suggests elegance and ceremony, distinguishing goblets from ordinary cups or glasses. Medieval imagery often features goblets made of metal or jeweled materials, while modern goblets are usually glass or crystal. {The wedding guests raised their goblets in a toast.}

A goblin is a small, ugly creature from folklore, typically depicted as mischievous or malevolent. Goblins appear throughout European mythology and fantasy literature, often living underground or in dark places, hoarding treasure, and causing trouble for humans. In modern usage, goblin has taken on informal meanings: someone might call a messy or antisocial person a goblin, or describe emerging from isolation looking disheveled as {full goblin mode}.

Goblins is the plural of goblin, a small, mischievous, and often malevolent creature from European folklore. Goblins appear throughout fantasy literature and games as troublemaking creatures—greedy, ugly, and cunning. {The goblins guarded their treasure jealously.} In figurative use, goblins are nagging fears or problems: {the goblins of self-doubt}.

Gobsmacked means utterly astonished, as if struck speechless. The word is British slang that suggests being so surprised your mouth falls open—gob being slang for mouth: {I was absolutely gobsmacked when they announced my name}. It conveys shocked amazement rather than mild surprise.

A gobstopper is a large, hard, spherical candy designed to be sucked rather than chewed, lasting a long time in the mouth. The British term references "gob," slang for mouth—it literally stops the mouth. Americans typically call these jawbreakers. {The gobstopper changed colors as each layer dissolved.}

A godchild is a child for whom an adult serves as godparent—a person who sponsors the child at baptism and traditionally assumes responsibility for their religious upbringing. The relationship is spiritual rather than biological: {My godchild turns five next month}. The term implies an ongoing bond, though the actual closeness varies widely.

Goddammit is a profane exclamation expressing anger, frustration, or exasperation—a contraction of "God damn it": {Goddammit, I told you to be careful}. The word is blasphemous to religious believers and vulgar generally, though common in casual speech. Also spelled goddamn it or god damn it.

Goddamn is a profane intensifier invoking God's damnation for emphasis: {That's a goddamn lie}. {I'm so goddamn tired}. The word is offensive to religious believers who consider it blasphemous—taking the Lord's name in vain. Also spelled goddamned, god damn, or god-damn. Despite its profanity, goddamn is common in casual American speech, expressing frustration, anger, or mere emphasis.

Goddamnit is a profane exclamation expressing frustration, anger, or exasperation. It combines "God" and "damn it" into a single emphatic outburst, making it more offensive than milder alternatives like "dammit" or "darn it." The word appears in various spellings—goddammit, god damn it, goddamn it—all representing the same exclamation. {Goddamnit, I just missed the train.} It is considered vulgar and offensive to many, particularly those with religious sensibilities.

A goddaughter is a female godchild—a girl or woman for whom someone has assumed spiritual responsibility, traditionally at baptism. The godparent pledges to support the child's religious upbringing and moral development: {My goddaughter just turned sixteen}. The relationship often carries affectionate obligation beyond the religious context.

A goddess is a female deity in polytheistic religions—Athena, Isis, Lakshmi. The word extends to women of extraordinary beauty or grace: {She looked like a goddess in that dress}. Someone might also call a woman they adore or worship their goddess. The male equivalent is god.

Goddesses is the plural of goddess, a female deity in polytheistic religions or mythologies. Greek goddesses like Athena and Aphrodite remain culturally prominent through literature and art. In figurative use, goddess describes a woman who is greatly admired or adored, often for her beauty or grace: {She was a goddess of the silver screen}. The term carries connotations of worship, reverence, or exceptional feminine power.

A godfather is a man who sponsors a child at baptism, traditionally pledging to oversee their religious upbringing. The role extends figuratively to any powerful patron or mentor. {The Godfather} popularized its use for a mafia boss, and the term now often implies someone who originated or dominates a field: {the godfather of soul}, {the godfather of punk}. To godfather something is to sponsor or shepherd it.

Godfathers are men who sponsor children at baptism, traditionally assuming responsibility for their religious education. The term extends to influential patrons or founders: {the godfathers of rock and roll}. Through *The Godfather* films, the word became synonymous with Mafia bosses, lending it connotations of power, loyalty, and organized crime: {He was the godfather of the Chicago underworld}.

Godless describes someone or something without belief in or reverence for God: {a godless atheist}, {godless communism}. The word carries moral judgment—implying not just absence of faith but wickedness or depravity: {godless heathens}. A godless place or time lacks religious influence: {the godless modern age}.

Godlike describes qualities befitting a deity—supreme power, transcendent beauty, or seemingly infinite capability. The word suggests awe at something beyond ordinary human limits: {Her godlike patience with the children}, {godlike reflexes on the basketball court}. In gaming, godlike often describes an unbeatable player or overwhelming performance. The term can be sincere or hyperbolic.

A godmother is a woman who sponsors a child at baptism, traditionally promising to help with the child's religious upbringing. The role often extends beyond religious duties to general mentorship and gift-giving: {My godmother always remembered my birthday}. A fairy godmother is a magical helper in folklore, and by extension anyone who provides unexpected aid or generosity.

A godparent is a person who sponsors a child at baptism, traditionally accepting responsibility for the child's religious upbringing. The role often extends beyond its religious origins to mean a trusted adult who takes special interest in a child's welfare: {She asked her best friend to be the baby's godmother}. The corresponding child is a godson, goddaughter, or godchild.

Godparents are the adults who sponsor a child at baptism, traditionally promising to help with the child's religious upbringing. In Christian tradition, a godfather and godmother take on a special relationship with the godchild, sometimes expected to serve as guardians if the parents die. The role has become largely ceremonial in secular contexts, where godparents are simply trusted friends or family members given honorary status in a child's life. {We asked my college roommate and her husband to be godparents.}

Gods are supernatural beings with power over aspects of nature or human life, worshipped in polytheistic religions: {the gods of ancient Greece}, {the Norse gods}. In monotheistic contexts, the singular God (capitalized) denotes the supreme being. Figuratively, gods are objects of excessive devotion: {Money is his god}. The exclamation {oh my god} or {gods} expresses surprise or dismay.

A godsend is something unexpectedly helpful that arrives at just the right moment, as if sent by divine providence. The word implies relief or rescue from difficulty: {The extra funding was a godsend for the struggling nonprofit}. {Finding a cheap apartment in the city felt like a godsend}.

Godspeed is a wish for success and safe travel, typically offered to someone embarking on a journey or new venture: {She wished him godspeed as he left for the expedition}. The word combines God and speed in its old sense of prosperity or good fortune—literally asking for divine favor. It sounds formal or old-fashioned today, often used at moments of significance or finality: {Godspeed, and may we meet again}.

Goggles are protective eyewear that fit snugly against the face, shielding eyes from water, wind, debris, or bright light. Unlike glasses, goggles form a seal around the eye socket: {swimming goggles}, {ski goggles}, {safety goggles}. The word is always plural, like glasses or spectacles. To goggle is to stare with wide eyes.

Going is the present participle of go, but it functions independently in many contexts. As an adjective, it describes current rates or conditions: the {going price}, a {going concern}. {Get out while the going is good} means leave before conditions worsen. Goings-on are activities or events, often suspicious ones. {Going on} followed by a number means approaching that age: {She's going on sixteen}.

The chemical element gold has been highly valued since ancient times and most non-literal uses of the word have direct reference to its qualities. Gold is the commonest name for a dark yellow, especially metallic, color. Anything considered very valuable can be called gold informally: Her response was pure gold. In competition awards, gold typically indicates the first-place winner: The Olympian is going for gold.

A golddigger is someone who pursues romantic relationships primarily to extract money or material benefits from wealthy partners. The term is almost always applied to women, though the behavior isn't exclusive to them: {She's just a golddigger after his inheritance}. The word carries strong disapproval, implying manipulation and insincerity. Also spelled gold digger. The original sense—a person who mines for gold—is now rarely encountered.

Golddiggers is the plural of golddigger, a person who pursues romantic relationships primarily for financial gain. The term usually describes women seeking wealthy men, though it applies to anyone using intimacy as a path to money: {He's convinced all his dates are golddiggers after his inheritance}. The spelling varies—one word, two words, or hyphenated.

Golddigging is pursuing romantic relationships primarily for financial gain—dating or marrying someone for their money rather than affection. The term derives from the literal extraction of gold, applied metaphorically to extracting wealth from a wealthy partner. A golddigger is the person doing it: {She's just a golddigger after his inheritance}. The accusation falls disproportionately on women, though the practice isn't gender-specific.

Golden means made of gold or having gold's color—a rich, warm yellow: {golden hair}, {golden sunlight}. The word extends to things precious or ideal: a golden {opportunity}, the golden {age} of Hollywood, golden {years} of retirement. Golden can mean highly favored: a golden {boy} or golden {child} is someone who seems to succeed effortlessly. In cooking, golden describes food browned to an appetizing color: {Fry until golden}.

A goldfinch is a small songbird with bright yellow and black markings, common across North America and Europe. The American goldfinch, sometimes called the wild canary, is known for its vibrant yellow breeding plumage and undulating flight pattern. These birds frequent backyard feeders, showing particular fondness for thistle and sunflower seeds. {A pair of goldfinches has been visiting our feeder all summer.}

A goldfish is a small orange or yellow freshwater fish, commonly kept as a pet in bowls or aquariums. Native to East Asia, goldfish were among the first fish domesticated for ornamental purposes. A goldfish's supposed three-second memory is a myth, but the idea persists: {He has the memory of a goldfish}.

A goldmine is literally a mine where gold is extracted, but more often the word appears figuratively for any source of great wealth or valuable resources: {The database turned out to be a goldmine of information}. A business or investment that generates substantial profits is a goldmine: {That little food truck became a goldmine}. Also spelled as two words: gold mine.

A golem is a creature from Jewish folklore—an animated figure made of clay or mud, brought to life through ritual and Hebrew inscriptions. The most famous is the Golem of Prague, said to protect the Jewish community. In broader use, golem describes any artificial humanoid or automaton, or a person who acts mechanically without independent thought: {He moved through his duties like a golem}.

Golems are creatures from Jewish folklore—clay figures brought to life through mystical means, typically by inscribing sacred words on their bodies. The most famous is the Golem of Prague, said to protect the Jewish community. In fantasy games and fiction, golems are any magically animated construct: {The wizard summoned a stone golem to guard the chamber}. Figuratively, a golem suggests something powerful but mindless, following orders without independent thought.

Golf is a sport where players use clubs to hit a ball into a series of holes across a landscaped course, aiming to complete each hole in as few strokes as possible. A round typically covers eighteen holes. The verb means to play the game: {He golfs every weekend}. Golf appears in compounds like {golf course}, {golf cart}, and {golf club}—the last referring to both the equipment and the organization.

A golfer is someone who plays golf. The term applies equally to weekend amateurs and touring professionals: {Tiger Woods was the dominant golfer of his generation}. Golfer carries no judgment about skill level—anyone who plays is a golfer.

A goliath is a giant or a person or thing of enormous size and power. The word comes from the biblical Philistine warrior slain by young David with a sling and stone, making it a byword for imposing but potentially vulnerable opponents. In modern use, goliath often appears in David-and-Goliath contexts describing an underdog facing a powerful adversary: {The startup is taking on the goliaths of the tech industry}. (Capitalized Goliath is the biblical figure.)

A gondola is a long, narrow boat with a high prow, propelled by a single oar and associated with the canals of Venice. The meaning extends to enclosed cabins suspended from cables—a ski gondola carries passengers up a mountain, and a gondola on a hot air balloon or airship holds the crew. In American retail, a gondola is a freestanding shelving unit in the middle of a store aisle.

Gondolas are the long, narrow boats propelled by a single oar that navigate Venice's canals, or the enclosed cabins suspended from cables in ski lifts and aerial tramways. The word extends to similar hanging compartments: the basket beneath a hot-air balloon, or a car attached to an airship. In retail, a gondola is a freestanding shelving unit in a store aisle.

A gondolier is a person who propels and steers a gondola—the traditional flat-bottomed boat used on the canals of Venice. Gondoliers stand at the stern, rowing with a single oar in a distinctive sweeping motion. The occupation is iconic to Venice, often associated with striped shirts and straw hats: {The gondolier serenaded tourists as they glided under the bridge}.

Gone is the past participle of go, used with auxiliary verbs: {She has gone home}. It also functions as an adjective meaning departed, used up, or no longer present: {The milk is gone}, {My headache is gone}. Someone far gone is in an advanced state—of illness, drunkenness, or obsession. Gone can mark time elapsed: {It was gone midnight when we left}. In slang, to be gone on someone is to be infatuated with them.

A goner is someone or something doomed or beyond saving. The word implies that death, failure, or destruction is inevitable: {When the engine caught fire, I knew the plane was a goner}. It often appears in first-person declarations of imminent doom: {If my wife finds out, I'm a goner}.

Goners is the plural of goner—someone or something doomed, ruined, or beyond saving. The word implies certainty about a bad outcome: {When the engine caught fire, we knew we were goners}. It appears in casual speech about anything past the point of rescue: {Those plants are goners if you don't water them}.

A gong is a large metal disc that produces a resonant tone when struck, used as a musical instrument or signal. Gongs appear in orchestras, ceremonies, and as dinner bells. In British slang, a gong is a medal or award: {He collected gongs throughout his military career}. To gong someone, from the television show, is to cut them off mid-performance.

Gongs are large metal discs that produce a resonant tone when struck, used in orchestras, ceremonies, and as signals. The gong that ends a boxing round or summons diners differs from the suspended orchestral gong, but both share the characteristic reverberating sound. In British slang, gongs are medals or decorations: {He came back from the war covered in gongs}.

Goo is any thick, soft, sticky substance—the kind that clings to fingers and stretches when pulled: {There's some kind of goo on the bottom of my shoe}. The word often carries mild disgust, describing mystery substances or excessive amounts of something viscous. Gooey is the adjective: {gooey caramel}, {gooey sentimentality}.

A goober is a peanut, chiefly in Southern American dialect. More commonly now, goober means a goofy, silly, or endearingly awkward person: {He's such a goober}. The tone is affectionate rather than cutting—you'd call a friend a goober, not an enemy. {Stop being a goober and just ask her out.}

Good vs. bad: in frequency of use, good wins by a ratio of about four to one. With myriad meanings, good is a catchall adjective. Beyond the core favorable or beneficial meaning (good news, a good investment), we use good to characterize things that we like and enjoy (good food, good books), things that are valid (a good excuse, a good driver’s license) and things that are usable (see if that milk is still good). When followed by a preposition, good takes on nuances: she’s good at tennis, he’s good about keeping promises, aspirin is good for a fever.

Goodbye is a parting word, said when leaving or ending a conversation: {Goodbye, see you tomorrow}. It can be permanent or casual depending on context. The noun refers to an act of parting: {We said our goodbyes at the airport}. To {kiss something goodbye} is to accept its loss: {You can kiss that deposit goodbye}.

Goodbyes are parting words or gestures exchanged when people separate. The word carries emotional weight—goodbyes can be casual {(quick goodbyes at the office)} or laden with feeling {(tearful goodbyes at the airport)}. To {say your goodbyes} is to take leave of people or places, sometimes permanently: {She said her goodbyes and walked out the door}.

A goodie is something pleasant or desirable, especially a treat or small gift. Children receive goodies at birthday parties; gift bags contain goodies. The plural often refers to desirable features: {a laptop loaded with goodies}. In stories, the goodies are the heroes, opposed to the baddies. Also spelled goody.

Goodies are desirable things, especially treats or small pleasures: {She brought goodies from the bakery}, {The gift bag was full of goodies}. The word often applies to food—sweets, snacks, special dishes—but extends to any appealing items: software features, promotional freebies, or perks. Goodies carries a childlike enthusiasm, suggesting eager anticipation or delight.
Goodness! and My goodness! are old-fashioned and mild interjections that express a passing emotion.

Goodnight is a parting expression used when leaving someone in the evening or before sleep: {Goodnight, sleep well}. It functions as both farewell and well-wishing. As an attributive, it modifies words like kiss or hug: {a goodnight kiss}. Sometimes written as two words: good night.

Goods are physical items that can be bought, sold, or traded, as distinguished from services, which are actions performed for others. The term appears frequently in commerce and economics: {The store sells dry goods and hardware.} Goods may be further classified by type—consumer goods, durable goods, capital goods. In the phrase {the goods}, it means evidence or proof of wrongdoing: {They caught him with the goods.} If someone {delivers the goods}, they fulfill expectations or promises.

Goodwill is friendly, helpful, or cooperative feelings toward others. It often appears in contexts of diplomacy or public relations: {a goodwill tour}, {a gesture of goodwill}. In business, goodwill is an intangible asset representing a company's reputation, customer relationships, and brand value—the premium a buyer pays beyond the value of physical assets: {The acquisition price included $2 million in goodwill}. (Capitalized Goodwill is the thrift store chain.)

Gooey describes something soft, sticky, and wet—the consistency of melted cheese, caramel, or mud that clings to your shoes. The word often carries warmth: {gooey chocolate chip cookies}, {gooey cinnamon rolls}. Figuratively, gooey means excessively sentimental: {a gooey love song}, {She gets all gooey around babies}.

A goof is a silly mistake or a foolish person. To goof is to make such a mistake: {I goofed and sent the email to the wrong person}. To {goof off} is to waste time or avoid work. To {goof around} is to act playfully or without seriousness. The tone is light—goofs are blunders, not disasters.

A goofball is a silly, playful, or eccentric person—someone who acts foolish in an endearing rather than annoying way: {My brother's a total goofball}. The term is affectionate, suggesting harmless clowning. In older slang, goofball referred to barbiturate pills, from their stupefying effects.

Goofy means silly, foolish, or amusingly eccentric—not in a harmful way, but in a way that invites affection or eye-rolling. A goofy {smile} is lopsided and unselfconscious. Goofy {humor} relies on absurdity rather than wit. Someone acting goofy is being playfully ridiculous: {Stop being so goofy and focus}. In skateboarding and snowboarding, goofy refers to riding with the right foot forward rather than the left—the less common stance. (Capitalized Goofy is the Disney character.)

Google is a trademark of the California-based Internet search and advertising company. Because of the dominance of Google in Internet searching, popular usage has turned google into a lower-case-g verb: I googled his name and learned that he had been sued for malpractice several times. As a verb, google borrows syntactic patterns from search, being used as a regular transitive verb or followed by a prepositional phrase with for: I was googling for cookie recipes to find one that uses cream cheese. When someone says the are looking for something on Google they are using Google as a search engine.

Googled is the past tense of google, meaning to search for information online using the Google search engine. The verb has become generic for any internet search regardless of which search engine is used: {I googled her before our date}, {Have you googled the symptoms?} The word exemplifies how dominant brands become verbs—like xerox for photocopying.

Googling is using the Google search engine to look something up on the internet. Though Google is a trademark, the verb has become so common that it often refers to any internet search, regardless of which search engine is used: {I googled her name and found her LinkedIn profile}. The gerund form appears frequently as a noun: {A little googling turned up the answer}. (Capitalized Google is the company and search engine.)

A goon is a thug or enforcer, especially one hired to intimidate or rough people up: {The boss sent his goons to collect the debt}. In hockey, a goon is a player whose main role is fighting rather than scoring. The word can also mean a foolish or clumsy person: {Stop being such a goon}. Online slang uses goon as a verb meaning to masturbate obsessively, often to pornography.

Goons are thugs or enforcers, typically hired to intimidate or rough people up: {The boss sent his goons to collect the debt}. The word suggests menacing but not particularly bright muscle. In hockey, a goon is a player whose main role is fighting rather than skill. Goon can also mean any foolish or clumsy person, though the hired-muscle sense dominates.

A goose is a large waterfowl with a long neck, related to ducks and swans but typically bigger than ducks and smaller than swans. Geese fly in V-formations and are known for their honking calls. A goose can also be a silly person. To goose someone is to poke or pinch their buttocks, or to prod them into action: {The manager goosed the sales team with a new bonus structure}. To {cook someone's goose} is to ruin their plans.

A gooseberry is a small, round, tart berry that grows on a thorny shrub, typically green or reddish and used in jams, pies, and preserves. In British slang, a gooseberry is an unwanted third person intruding on a couple: {I felt like a gooseberry on their date}. To {play gooseberry} is to be that awkward extra presence.

A goosebump is a small raised bump on the skin caused by cold, fear, or strong emotion. The tiny muscles around hair follicles contract, creating a pebbled texture—the same reaction that makes fur stand up in other mammals. Usually plural: {I got goosebumps when she hit that high note}. Also called goose pimples or gooseflesh, from the resemblance to plucked goose skin.

Goosebumps are the tiny bumps that form on skin when cold or strong emotion causes small muscles to contract, making body hairs stand erect. The skin resembles that of a plucked goose. The effect is involuntary: {The music gave me goosebumps}. Fear, awe, nostalgia, and cold all trigger the response. Also goose bumps, goose pimples, or gooseflesh.

Goosestep is a military marching style in which the legs swing stiffly forward without bending at the knee. Most associated with Nazi Germany and other authoritarian regimes, making it a symbol of militarism and blind obedience: {The soldiers goosestepped past the reviewing stand}. The name comes from the rigid, mechanical gait resembling a goose's walk.

A gopher is a burrowing rodent native to North America, known for digging extensive tunnel systems and pushing soil to the surface in mounds. The word extends to the gopher tortoise and gopher snake, which share habitats or burrowing habits. In computing, Gopher was an early internet protocol for organizing and retrieving documents, largely superseded by the World Wide Web. As a verb, to gopher (or gofer) is to run errands—fetching things for others: {She started as a gopher at the production company}.

Gophers are burrowing rodents native to North America, known for tunneling through lawns and gardens. The word extends to various animals with similar habits, including ground squirrels and a burrowing tortoise. In computing, Gopher was an early internet protocol for organizing and retrieving documents, predating the World Wide Web. A gopher is also someone who runs errands—a gofer: {The intern worked as a gopher for the production team}.

Gore is blood that has been shed, especially when clotted or dried—the stuff of violence and horror films. As a verb, to gore is to pierce with a horn or tusk: {The bull gored the matador}. A gore is also a triangular piece of fabric used in making skirts, sails, or umbrellas to add fullness. (Capitalized Gore is a surname.)

A gorge is a deep, narrow valley with steep rocky walls, typically carved by a river over time: {We hiked along the rim of the gorge}. The word also names the throat or gullet. To gorge is to eat greedily until stuffed: {We gorged ourselves on Thanksgiving dinner}. Something gorgeous was originally throat-adorning—a necklace or ruff—before it came to mean beautiful generally.

Gorgeous means strikingly beautiful or magnificent. The word carries warmth and enthusiasm beyond merely attractive—it suggests something that delights the senses: {a gorgeous sunset}, {She looked absolutely gorgeous}. Gorgeous applies freely to people, places, weather, or anything visually stunning. In casual speech, it extends to non-visual pleasures: {The cake was gorgeous}.

Gorges is the third-person singular of gorge, meaning to eat greedily or to excess: {He gorges himself on pizza every Friday}. As a plural noun, gorges are deep, narrow ravines with steep rocky walls, typically carved by rivers: {The Colorado River carved spectacular gorges through the plateau}.

A gorgon is a repulsive or terrifying woman, especially one with a fierce, petrifying stare. The word draws on the Greek mythological creatures whose gaze turned onlookers to stone: {His mother-in-law was an absolute gorgon}. The term is always unflattering, suggesting someone monstrous in appearance or temperament. (Capitalized Gorgon refers to the mythological creature.)

Gorgons are monstrous female creatures from Greek mythology with snakes for hair and faces so hideous that looking at them turned onlookers to stone. Medusa is the most famous, slain by Perseus. The word extends to any terrifyingly ugly or repulsive woman: {His mother-in-law was a gorgon}.

A gorilla is the largest of the great apes, native to the forests of central Africa. The word extends to anything massive or powerful: a {gorilla of a man}, an {800-pound gorilla} (a dominant force that cannot be ignored). In slang, gorilla sometimes describes a thug or enforcer: {The loan shark sent his gorillas to collect}.

Gorillas are the largest living primates, native to the forests of central Africa. They live in family groups led by a dominant male called a silverback, named for the gray hair that develops on mature males' backs. Figuratively, gorilla describes someone large and powerful, often brutishly so: {a gorilla of a man}, {corporate gorillas}. In finance, an {800-pound gorilla} is a dominant force that can't be ignored.

Gory describes something covered in blood or involving graphic bloodshed: {a gory crime scene}, {the gory details of the accident}. The word often appears in discussions of violent films or literature: {The movie was too gory for my taste}. Figuratively, gory can describe anything unpleasantly detailed or explicit: {She spared us the gory details of her divorce}.

A gosling is a young goose, typically still covered in soft down feathers. The word follows the same pattern as duckling and other names for young birds. {The goslings followed their mother across the pond.}

Gospel has two connected meanings rooted in "good news." In Christianity, the gospel is the message of salvation through Jesus Christ, and the Gospels are the four New Testament books (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) that narrate his life and teachings. Extended, gospel means absolute truth: {Her word is gospel around here}. Gospel music is a genre of passionate Christian song rooted in African American church traditions, blending spirituals with blues and jazz influences.

Gospels are the four New Testament books—Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John—that narrate the life and teachings of Jesus Christ. More broadly, a gospel is any doctrine or set of principles held as absolutely true: {the gospel of free markets}. Gospel music is a genre of religious song rooted in African American church traditions. To take something as gospel is to accept it without question.

Gossip is casual talk about other people's private affairs, often speculative or judgmental: {Have you heard the latest gossip?} The word covers both the activity and the person who engages in it: {She's such a gossip}. To gossip is to share such talk: {They gossiped about the neighbors for hours}. Gossip can be harmless social bonding or malicious rumor-spreading, depending on intent and content.

Got is the past tense of get, and for some uses, also the past participle of get. Speakers of British English always use got as the past participle. Americans use got as the past participle in meanings of get related to obligation and possession: Have you got a quarter? You’ve got to be more careful. For other meanings of get, Americans use gotten: I’ve gotten used to her accent. I should have gotten a haircut when I was in town.
Gotcha!, a pronunciation spelling of the expression “(I) got you!”, can represent two distinct senses of get: understanding or seizure. Context makes clear which one is expressed.

Gotchas are hidden problems or unexpected catches that trip people up. In programming, a gotcha is a counterintuitive feature or quirk that causes bugs: {Python's mutable default arguments are a classic gotcha}. More broadly, any surprise complication qualifies: {The contract looked good, but the fine print was full of gotchas}. Also an exclamation when catching someone out: {Gotcha!}

Goth describes a subculture emerging from 1980s post-punk music, characterized by dark clothing, pale makeup, and an aesthetic embracing the macabre and melancholic. As a noun, a goth is someone who identifies with this style: {She's been a goth since high school}. The music tends toward atmospheric, brooding rock with introspective lyrics. Goth fashion favors black clothing, silver jewelry, and dramatic eye makeup. The adjective describes anything associated with this aesthetic: {goth clubs}, {goth bands}. (Capitalized Goth refers to the ancient Germanic people.)

Gothic describes things dark, mysterious, and dramatic. Gothic architecture features pointed arches, ribbed vaults, and flying buttresses—the soaring medieval cathedrals of Europe. Gothic fiction traffics in haunted castles, brooding atmospheres, and supernatural dread: {a gothic novel}, {gothic horror}. The gothic subculture embraces black clothing, pale makeup, and darkly romantic aesthetics: {She went through a gothic phase in high school}. As a typography term, gothic refers to heavy, angular typefaces without serifs. (Capitalized Gothic refers specifically to the ancient Germanic people or their language.)

Goths are people who embrace a dark aesthetic in fashion, music, and lifestyle—black clothing, pale makeup, moody music descended from post-punk bands like Bauhaus and Siouxsie and the Banshees. The subculture emerged in the early 1980s and persists today: {The goths gathered at the club every Friday night}. The term can be used dismissively by outsiders or embraced as identity. (Capitalized Goths are the ancient Germanic people.)

A gouge is a chisel with a curved blade for cutting grooves or hollows in wood. To gouge is to cut or scoop out, often roughly or violently: {The accident gouged a chunk from the door}. To {gouge someone's eyes out} is to dig them from the sockets. In American usage, to gouge is to overcharge or swindle: {Hotels gouge tourists during peak season}.

Gouging is digging or scooping out material, typically with a pointed tool or fingers: {He gouged a hole in the wood}, {She nearly gouged his eyes out}. Extended to pricing, gouging means charging excessively, especially when customers have no alternative: {price gouging during the hurricane}. The noun gouge is the tool or the groove it makes.

Goulash is a hearty Hungarian stew of meat and vegetables seasoned with paprika, giving it a distinctive reddish color. The dish varies widely—some versions are soupy, others thick; some use beef, others pork or a mix. Outside Hungary, goulash often refers loosely to any paprika-spiced meat dish: {We made a quick goulash with what was in the fridge}. Figuratively, goulash can mean a jumbled mixture of things.

A gourd is the hard-shelled fruit of certain vines in the cucumber family, typically dried and hollowed out for use as a container, decoration, or musical instrument. The term also refers to the plant itself. Gourds come in a wide variety of shapes—from round to bottle-shaped to bizarrely lumpy—and are often displayed as autumn decorations alongside pumpkins. Informally, gourd means head: {Use your gourd!} If someone is {out of their gourd}, they're crazy or intoxicated.

Gourds are hard-shelled fruits of the cucumber family, typically inedible but valued for their shapes. Dried gourds serve as containers, birdhouses, musical instruments, and decorations—pumpkins and squash at harvest festivals, carved jack-o'-lanterns at Halloween. In slang, {out of one's gourd} means crazy or intoxicated, gourd standing in for head.

Gourmet describes food, cooking, or dining of especially high quality and refinement: {a gourmet restaurant}, {gourmet coffee}. As a noun, a gourmet is someone with cultivated taste in food and drink—a connoisseur who appreciates fine cuisine. The word can shade into pretension: {He's such a gourmet he won't eat at chain restaurants}. Marketing has diluted the term; "gourmet" now appears on everything from frozen pizzas to dog food.

To govern is to exercise authority over a political unit—a country, state, or city. A governing body makes and enforces rules: {The council governs the township}. Beyond politics, govern means to control or regulate: {Supply and demand govern prices}. What governs your decisions influences or determines them. A governor controls speed in machinery, preventing runaway acceleration.

A governess is a woman employed to educate and care for children in a private household. Unlike a nanny, who focuses primarily on childcare, a governess provides formal instruction—teaching reading, languages, music, and deportment. The role was common among middle- and upper-class families in the 18th and 19th centuries, often filled by educated women of reduced circumstances. {Jane Eyre worked as a governess at Thornfield Hall.} The word now sounds historical or British.

Government is the system or group that holds authority over a territory and its people—making laws, enforcing them, and managing public affairs. It can refer to a specific administration {the current government}, the abstract institution {government exists to serve the people}, or the act of governing {democratic government}. Forms range from democracies to dictatorships, federal systems to city councils.

Governments is the plural of government—the systems or bodies that exercise authority over states, nations, or organizations. It often emphasizes variety or comparison: {Governments around the world responded differently to the pandemic}. The word also refers to successive administrations: {Three governments have fallen since the crisis began}.

Most uses of governor are for an elected or appointed official. In the U.S., the elected head of every state is the governor. In British English, governor is more likely to refer to someone in charge of a prison or other large institution: Write to the governors of the BBC. On some kinds of motors, the governor maintains a constant speed with variable loads by regulating the supply of fuel.

Governors is the plural of governor—those who govern. Most often these are elected chief executives of states or provinces: {The governors met to discuss the new federal policy}. A governor can also be a device that regulates speed or flow, as in an engine governor that prevents overspeeding. In institutional contexts, a board of governors oversees an organization: {The Federal Reserve's board of governors sets monetary policy}.

A gown is a long, flowing garment. For women, a gown is a formal dress: {evening gown}, {ball gown}, {wedding gown}. For professionals, it's a loose outer robe indicating status or function: a judge's gown, a graduation gown, a hospital gown. The verb means to dress in a gown: {gowned and ready for surgery}.

Gowns are loose, flowing garments. A gown may be a woman's formal dress {an evening gown}, a robe worn for official ceremonies {academic gowns at graduation}, or a simple covering worn in medical settings {a hospital gown}. The word carries associations of formality, elegance, or institutional function depending on context.

Grab means to take hold of something quickly or forcefully: {He grabbed her arm}. It suggests urgency or lack of ceremony—you grab a snack, not a formal dinner. To grab attention is to seize it suddenly. Something {up for grabs} is available to anyone who wants it. As a noun, a grab is a quick snatch: {She made a grab for the phone}.

Grace in a secular sense denotes elegance combined with beauty, movement, or form: The dancer leapt across the stage with grace. The sacred sense of grace is the loving generosity of God towards humans. If you say grace before a meal, you say a short prayer for the occasion. A grace period is a time after a particular deadline when no penalty will be assessed for failure to meet the deadline. When capitalized, Grace may be an old-fashioned female name, or a title for various nobility or church officials.

Graceful describes movement or form that is smooth, elegant, and pleasing to watch—suggesting effortless control and coordination: {a graceful dancer}, {the graceful arc of a diving bird}. The word extends to behavior and expression: a graceful {apology} handles an awkward situation with tact and dignity. To make a graceful {exit} is to leave without causing disruption or embarrassment.

Gracious describes someone who is kind, courteous, and generous in manner—particularly toward those of lower status or in difficult situations: {a gracious host}, {She was gracious in defeat}. The word often implies elegance or refined charm: {gracious living}. As an exclamation, {goodness gracious} expresses mild surprise or dismay—a euphemistic oath avoiding "God."

Grade, in all of its uses, implies a range or continuum of values or degrees of quality. In the U.S., grade denotes any of the 12 years of compulsory education (first grade, eighth grade), and also the evaluative marks received by students for their work: My math grade is an A. Many commodities and foods are distinguished in quality by grade (Grade A sheepskin). When you grade something, you assign it a degree of quality on a scale; in other words, a grade. The grade of a road is the degree to which it slopes.

Grades are levels or ranks on a scale. In education, grades are marks indicating quality of work—letter grades run from A to F, with A being excellent. Grade also means a year of schooling: {My son is in fourth grade}. The grade of a road is its slope or incline. To grade is to assign a rank or to level ground: {Workers graded the site for construction}. To {make the grade} is to meet a standard.

Grading is the act of assigning grades or ratings to evaluate quality, performance, or rank. Teachers grade student work; inspectors grade meat or produce. Grading also means leveling or smoothing a surface: {The crew finished grading the lot before construction began}. In construction and landscaping, grading ensures proper drainage and foundation stability.

Gradual means happening slowly, by degrees rather than all at once. A gradual {increase} in temperature differs from a sudden spike. Gradual {change} accumulates over time, often imperceptibly in the moment but noticeable in retrospect. The word implies steady progression without abrupt shifts: {a gradual slope}, {gradual improvement}.

Graduate centers on completion and advancement. To graduate is to complete a course of study and receive a degree or diploma: {She graduated from medical school last spring}. The noun is someone who has done so: {a Harvard graduate}. As an adjective, graduate describes advanced academic work beyond a bachelor's degree: {graduate school}, {graduate students}. Graduate also means to mark with degrees or divisions—a graduated cylinder has measurement lines. More broadly, to graduate is to progress through stages: {The program graduates participants from basic to advanced levels}.

Graduated describes something marked with units of measurement: a graduated {cylinder}, a graduated {measuring cup}. It also means arranged in stages or degrees: graduated {tax rates} increase as income rises. Most commonly, graduated is the past tense of graduate—to complete a course of study and receive a degree: {She graduated from college last spring}.

Graduates are people who have completed a course of study, especially at a school or university: {This year's graduates faced a tough job market}. The verb graduate means to complete such a course and receive a diploma or degree: {She graduated from medical school in May}. Graduate also works as an adjective for advanced academic work: {graduate studies}, {graduate student}. To graduate something like a measuring cup is to mark it with degrees or increments.

Graduating is the process of completing a course of study and receiving a degree or diploma: {She's graduating from medical school in June}. It also means progressing through stages or levels: {The program uses graduating levels of difficulty}. To graduate something is to mark it with incremental measurements, as on a thermometer or measuring cup.

Graduation is the completion of an academic program and the ceremony marking it: {Her graduation from medical school took six years}. The word extends to any movement through stages or levels—graduation from training wheels to a real bike, or the gradual progression of colors in a sunset. Graduations are also the marks on a measuring instrument indicating units or degrees.

Graffiti is writing or drawings scrawled on public surfaces—walls, subway cars, buildings, bridges. The word is Italian and technically plural, though English treats it as a mass noun: {The graffiti was removed overnight}. Graffiti ranges from crude tags and obscenities to elaborate murals. Whether it constitutes art or vandalism depends on who you ask and who owns the wall.

Graft has two distinct origins yielding different meanings. One graft is a shoot or bud inserted into another plant to grow there, or tissue transplanted surgically: {a skin graft}, {a bone graft}. The verb means to attach in this way: {graft a branch onto the rootstock}. The other graft is corrupt use of a position for personal gain, especially in politics: {The mayor's administration was riddled with graft}. In British slang, graft also means hard work: {It took years of graft to build the business}.

Grafting is joining plant tissue from one specimen to another so they grow as one—typically attaching a cutting (the scion) to an established root system (the rootstock). Orchardists graft to propagate fruit varieties that won't breed true from seed. The technique extends metaphorically: {grafting new ideas onto old traditions}. In medicine, grafting transfers tissue—skin grafts cover burns. In British slang, grafting means working hard, especially at seduction: {He's been grafting on her all night}.

Grafts covers two unrelated words. One involves attachment: a graft is tissue transplanted from one site to another, or a shoot inserted into a plant to grow there. Surgeons perform skin grafts; gardeners graft branches onto rootstock. The other graft means corrupt acquisition of money through political position—bribery, kickbacks, backroom deals. {The mayor's administration was riddled with graft.}

A grail is an object of prolonged quest or ultimate aspiration—something pursued with devotion despite difficulty: {For decades, room-temperature superconductivity has been the grail of physics}. The word comes from the Holy Grail of medieval legend, the cup Christ used at the Last Supper, sought by knights as the supreme spiritual prize. The lowercase form emphasizes the secular sense of any ardently pursued goal.

Two main meanings of grain inspire nearly all uses of the word. One is to designate a small, hard seed that might be used as food (grain of rice) or something resembling that (grain of sand). The other denotes the pattern in a surface, especially of wood, where the grain means the general direction in which fibers are oriented. Something that goes against the grain is contrary to what is wanted or expected. A grain of truth or some other thing is a very small but meaningful quantity of it.

Grains are the edible seeds of cereal plants like wheat, rice, corn, and oats—staple foods that form the foundation of diets worldwide. The word extends to any small, hard particle resembling these seeds: grains of {sand}, grains of {salt}. A grain is also a tiny amount: {There's a grain of truth in what she says}. In woodworking and textiles, grain refers to the directional pattern of fibers: {Sand with the grain, not against it}. To go {against the grain} is to act contrary to one's nature or prevailing expectations.

Grainy describes a texture of small particles or granules, like sand or coarse salt. A grainy photograph or video has visible specks or pixels that reduce sharpness—sometimes an unwanted flaw, sometimes a deliberate aesthetic: {The old footage had that grainy look}. Grainy can also describe food texture: {The sauce turned out grainy instead of smooth}.

A gram is a unit of mass in the metric system, equal to one thousandth of a kilogram—roughly the weight of a paperclip. In drug slang, a gram typically refers to that quantity of an illegal substance: {He bought a gram of coke}. The abbreviation is g or gm.

Grammar is the system of rules governing how words combine into sentences—how they inflect, agree, and arrange themselves. Native speakers internalize grammar without formal study; what schools teach as "grammar" is largely style and usage conventions. {Her grammar is impeccable.} Grammar also refers to a book describing such rules: {a Latin grammar}.

A gramophone is an early device for playing recorded sound, using a needle that traces grooves in a rotating disc. The word is largely historical now, replaced by record player and turntable, though it survives in the Grammy Awards (short for Gramophone Awards) and in British English as an old-fashioned term for any phonograph.

Grand means large, impressive, or magnificent in scale or ambition: a {grand staircase}, {grand plans}, a {grand gesture}. It can describe something ambitious or elevated: {the grand scheme of things}. In informal use, grand is a noun meaning a thousand dollars or pounds: {The car cost twenty grand}. A grand {total} is the final sum. A grand {jury} investigates potential crimes. Family terms with grand— {grandmother}, {grandson}—indicate a generation removed.

Grandad is an informal spelling of granddad—one's grandfather. The spelling with one *n* is common in British English: {My grandad fought in the war}. Like granddad, it can address or refer to any elderly man, though this risks condescension.

A grandchild is the child of one's son or daughter. The term encompasses both grandsons and granddaughters: {She has four grandchildren}. The relationship extends through any number of generations with the prefix great-: a great-grandchild is the child of one's grandchild.

Grandchildren are the children of one's children—the generation two steps down from oneself. The word combines the familial relationships: your son's daughter is your granddaughter, your daughter's son is your grandson, and collectively they are your grandchildren. {She has six grandchildren, ages three to fifteen.}

Granddad is an informal word for grandfather—your parent's father. The spelling granddad is more common than grandad, though both appear. Like other grandparent terms, it often drops the first syllable in speech and casual writing: {My grandad taught me to fish}.

Granddaddy is an informal term for grandfather, used especially by children or in Southern American speech: {My granddaddy taught me to fish}. Extended, it means the earliest, largest, or most respected example of something: {the granddaddy of all rock festivals}, {the granddaddy of horror films}. Also spelled grandaddy.

A granddaughter is the daughter of one's son or daughter. The relationship spans two generations: {My granddaughter just started kindergarten}. Like other family terms, it can be modified to show further remove: great-granddaughter, great-great-granddaughter.

Grandeur is impressive greatness in scale, appearance, or character. The word applies to physical things—the grandeur of the {Grand Canyon}, of {Versailles}—and to abstract qualities: grandeur of {vision}, of {ambition}. {Delusions of grandeur} are fantasies of one's own importance or power. The word carries a note of nobility or magnificence that mere bigness lacks.

A grandfather is your parent's father. The word extends to any male ancestor further back: {My grandfather immigrated from Poland; his grandfather fought in the Napoleonic Wars}. Grandfather also works as a verb meaning to exempt from new rules based on prior status: {Existing tenants were grandfathered in under the old rent policy}. A grandfather clock is a tall freestanding pendulum clock.

Grandma is an informal word for grandmother—the mother of one's parent. It's among the most common terms children use for this relationship, along with grandpa for grandfather. {Grandma's coming for Thanksgiving}. The spelling grandma reflects casual pronunciation; the more formal grandmother preserves both syllables.

A grandmaster is a chess player who has achieved the highest title awarded by the World Chess Federation, requiring exceptional tournament performance against other top players. The term extends to masters of other pursuits—martial arts, competitive gaming, or any domain where hierarchical ranks exist: {He's a grandmaster of Go}. Sometimes used loosely for anyone with supreme skill: {a grandmaster of negotiation}.

Grandmasters is the plural of grandmaster, a title for those who have achieved the highest level of skill in a field. In chess, grandmaster is the supreme title awarded by FIDE to elite players: {Three grandmasters competed in the final round}. The term extends to martial arts, where grandmasters head schools or styles, and to any domain where mastery is formally recognized.

A grandmother is the mother of one's parent—either father's mother or mother's mother. The word often carries associations of nurturing, wisdom, and family tradition: {My grandmother taught me to bake}. Informal variants include grandma, granny, nana, and nanna. To {teach your grandmother to suck eggs} is to presumptuously offer advice to someone more experienced.

Grandpa is an informal term for grandfather—a father's or mother's father. It's a child's word that persists into adulthood as an affectionate form of address or reference: {Grandpa taught me to fish}. The variant grandpapa is old-fashioned. Grandpa can also refer to any elderly man, sometimes dismissively: {Some grandpa was holding up traffic}.

A grandparent is the parent of one's parent—a grandmother or grandfather. The term encompasses both maternal and paternal sides: {My grandparents on my mother's side lived in Ohio}. Grandparents often occupy a special role in family life, associated with spoiling children and passing down traditions. The verb grandparent means to act in that capacity: {She grandparents three kids}.

Grandparents are the parents of one's parents—maternal grandparents on the mother's side, paternal on the father's. The term often carries associations of wisdom, indulgence, and family history: {My grandparents spoiled me rotten}. Grandparents may serve as primary caregivers when parents are absent or unable.

A grandson is a son of one's son or daughter—the male child one generation removed. {My grandson is starting kindergarten this fall.} The relationship implies the perspective of grandparents looking down the family tree.

A grandstand is a large, often covered seating structure for spectators at stadiums, racetracks, and fairgrounds, typically with tiered rows facing the action. To grandstand is to perform or speak in a way calculated to impress an audience rather than achieve substance: {The senator was grandstanding for the cameras}. The adjective grandstand describes showy plays or catches made with flair: {a grandstand catch in center field}.

Grandstanding is behaving in a way designed to attract attention or impress others rather than to accomplish anything substantive. Politicians grandstand when they make speeches aimed at voters rather than colleagues. The term comes from the grandstand—the main seating area at a stadium—where spectators sit watching. To grandstand is to play to that crowd: {He accused the senator of grandstanding during the hearing}.

Grandstands are tiered seating structures for spectators at sporting events, races, or parades—typically large, open-air, and facing the action. The verb grandstand means to perform showily to impress an audience rather than accomplish something substantive: {He's just grandstanding for the cameras}. A grandstander seeks attention over results.

Granite is a coarse-grained igneous rock, typically gray or pink, composed mainly of quartz and feldspar. It forms deep underground as magma cools slowly, creating the visible crystalline texture. Granite is prized for its hardness and durability in construction—countertops, monuments, building facades. Figuratively, something {set in granite} is unchangeable, and a {granite jaw} suggests stern determination.

Grannies is the plural of granny, an informal word for grandmother. The term extends to any elderly woman, sometimes affectionately, sometimes dismissively. Granny glasses are small, round spectacles. A granny flat is a small secondary dwelling, often for an aging parent. A granny knot is a square knot tied incorrectly. {The grannies sat knitting on the porch.}

Granny is an informal word for grandmother, suggesting warmth and familiarity. It extends to any elderly woman: {a little granny in a rocking chair}. A granny knot is tied incorrectly, the way a grandmother supposedly might. Granny Smith is a variety of green apple. A granny flat is a small dwelling for an aging relative, typically on adult children's property.

Granola is a breakfast food or snack made from oats, nuts, honey, and other ingredients, baked until crunchy. It's eaten as cereal with milk or yogurt, or formed into bars. As slang, granola describes someone with earthy, health-conscious, environmentally aware sensibilities—the kind of person who might eat granola: {She's pretty granola—composting, hiking, the whole thing}.

To grant is to give something formally—permission, a request, a wish, money. Governments grant rights, foundations grant scholarships, genies grant wishes. A grant is something given this way, especially funding for research or projects: {She received a grant to study climate change}. To {take for granted} is to assume something without question or fail to appreciate what you have. {Granted} concedes a point: {Granted, he's difficult, but he's also brilliant}. (Capitalized Grant is a surname or given name.)

Granted functions mainly in two expressions. To {take something for granted} is to assume it without question, or to fail to appreciate what you have: {We take clean water for granted}.
