As a sentence opener, granted concedes a point before pivoting: {Granted, it's expensive, but it's worth it}. The past tense of grant appears in phrases like {granted permission} or {wish granted}.

A grape is a small, round fruit that grows in clusters on vines, eaten fresh or dried as raisins and crushed to make wine and juice. Grapes come in varieties from deep purple to pale green. {Sour grapes} describes disparaging something you can't have, from Aesop's fable of the fox who couldn't reach the grapes.

Grapefruit is a large citrus fruit with a thick yellow or pinkish rind and tart, slightly bitter flesh that ranges from pale yellow to deep pink or red. It grows in clusters on the tree, which may explain the name—though the fruit itself resembles an oversized orange more than a grape. Grapefruit is eaten fresh, juiced, or used in salads and desserts. {I have half a grapefruit for breakfast most mornings.} The fruit is known for interacting with certain medications, affecting how drugs are metabolized.

Grapes are small, round fruits that grow in clusters on woody vines. They come in green, red, purple, and black varieties, eaten fresh or dried into raisins. Grapes are the source of wine—the fermented juice of the fruit. {Sour grapes} describes dismissing something you can't have, from the Aesop fable about a fox who couldn't reach the grapes.

A grapevine is a climbing plant that produces grapes. More commonly, the grapevine is an informal network through which rumors and information spread: {I heard through the grapevine that they're getting divorced}. The metaphor suggests news traveling along interconnected pathways, passing from person to person like tendrils linking one vine to the next.

Grapevines are the climbing plants that produce grapes, trained on trellises or arbors for wine production and table fruit. The singular grapevine also names an informal channel for rumors and gossip: {I heard through the grapevine that they're getting divorced}. The image is of information traveling along interconnected social paths, like tendrils spreading vine to vine.

A graph is a diagram showing the relationship between variables, typically with values plotted along horizontal and vertical axes: {The graph showed sales declining over time}. In mathematics, graph theory studies networks of points connected by lines. To graph something is to represent it in such a diagram. Graph also appears as a suffix meaning something written or recorded: {photograph}, {telegraph}, {seismograph}.

Graphic describes something visual or vividly detailed. A graphic {designer} works with images and layout. A graphic {novel} tells its story through sequential art. When describing violence, sex, or disturbing content, graphic means explicit and detailed—nothing left to imagination: {The documentary contained graphic footage of the aftermath}. As a noun, a graphic is an image or visual element: {The presentation needs better graphics}.

Graphics refers to visual images, designs, or representations—especially those produced by computers. The term covers everything from simple charts and diagrams to elaborate digital artwork and video game visuals. A graphics {card} processes visual data; graphics {design} arranges visual elements for communication. The singular graphic works as both noun and adjective: {a graphic showing population trends}, {graphic violence}.

Graphs are visual representations of data or mathematical relationships. A line graph tracks change over time; a bar graph compares quantities. In mathematics, a graph plots points and lines on coordinate axes to show how variables relate: {The graph of y = x² forms a parabola}. To graph something is to represent it this way. In technical contexts, a graph is also a network of nodes connected by edges.

Grapple means to seize and struggle with something at close quarters. Wrestlers grapple, as do people fighting for control of an object: {They grappled for the gun}. The word extends to mental struggle: {grappling with a difficult decision}, {grappling with grief}. A grapple or grappling hook is a multi-pronged device for catching and holding.

Grappling is close-quarters fighting that involves grabbing, holding, and wrestling rather than striking. Wrestlers and martial artists grapple for position and control. Figuratively, to grapple with something is to struggle with it mentally: {She's been grappling with the decision for weeks}. Grappling hooks catch and hold surfaces for climbing.

Grasp means to seize and hold firmly with the hand: {She grasped the railing to steady herself}. The word extends naturally to mental holding—to grasp an idea is to understand it: {I finally grasped what she was trying to say}. A grasp is both a grip and the capacity to comprehend: {a good grasp of the fundamentals}. Something {within your grasp} is attainable; something {beyond your grasp} exceeds your reach or understanding.

Grasping describes someone excessively eager to acquire money or possessions—greedy, avaricious. A grasping {landlord} squeezes every penny from tenants. The word carries strong disapproval, suggesting someone who clutches at wealth without generosity or scruple: {His grasping nature alienated everyone who tried to help him}.

The general, nonspecific use of grass is to denote any member of the plant family Poaceae: plants with single seed leaves that are usually called blades. Types of grass that are planted for ornamental purposes in lawns are also simply called grass: Keep your dog off the grass. When are you going to mow the grass? A pasture for grazing, or a field that will be harvested for hay might also be said to contain grass, and grass is also a dated slang term for marijuana. In British slang, to grass on someone is to inform the police of their illegal activity.

A grasshopper is a jumping insect with long hind legs, known for leaping through grass and fields. Grasshoppers chirp by rubbing their legs against their wings. In large numbers they become locusts, devouring crops. Figuratively, a grasshopper is someone who lives for the moment without planning ahead, from Aesop's fable of the improvident grasshopper and the industrious ant.

Grasshoppers are jumping insects with powerful hind legs, found in fields and meadows worldwide. They're known for their chirping sounds and occasional swarming as locusts. Figuratively, a grasshopper is someone who lives for the moment without planning ahead—from Aesop's fable contrasting the carefree grasshopper with the industrious ant: {Don't be a grasshopper; save for retirement}.

Grassroots describes activity originating from ordinary people rather than leaders or institutions. A grassroots {movement} or {campaign} builds support from the ground up—local volunteers, small donors, community organizing—rather than from established power structures. {The candidate relied on grassroots fundraising}. The word evokes organic growth, like grass spreading across a field. As a noun, the grassroots are the common people, especially as a political base: {The party has lost touch with its grassroots}.

A grate is a framework of metal bars—in a fireplace to hold burning fuel, or over a drain or window as a cover. To grate is to reduce something to small pieces by rubbing against a rough surface: {grate some cheese}. Grating also produces harsh scraping sounds, and by extension, harsh effects on the nerves: {Her voice grates on me}.

Grateful describes feeling or expressing thanks for something received or experienced: {I'm grateful for your help}, {She gave him a grateful smile}. The word implies recognition that something good has come from outside oneself—a gift, a kindness, an outcome. To be grateful to someone is to feel indebted to them; to be grateful for something is to appreciate having it.

A grater is a kitchen tool with a surface of sharp-edged holes or slits, used to shred food into small pieces by rubbing it against the surface: {a cheese grater}, {Grate the carrots with a box grater}. Different hole sizes produce different textures, from fine zest to coarse shreds.

Gratification is the pleasure that comes from having a desire fulfilled or a need satisfied. The word often appears in discussions of delayed versus immediate gratification—whether to take a smaller reward now or wait for a larger one later: {She chose instant gratification over long-term savings}. Sexual gratification refers specifically to sexual pleasure or release.

Grating describes sounds or sensations that are harsh, irritating, or abrasive: {Her grating voice made it hard to concentrate}, {the grating screech of metal on metal}. A grating personality wears on you through repeated annoyance. As a noun, a grating is a framework of parallel or crossed bars—a drain cover, a ventilation screen, or a barrier over a window.

Gratitude is the feeling of appreciation for something received or experienced—a gift, a kindness, an unexpected good turn. It implies recognition that the benefit came from outside oneself: {She expressed her gratitude to the doctors who saved her life}. Gratitude can be fleeting or cultivated as a disposition: {He kept a gratitude journal}.

Grave covers both noun and adjective territory with quite different meanings. The noun grave is a burial site, typically a hole dug in the earth to receive a corpse, or the mound or marker above it. {She visits her father's grave every year.} The adjective grave means serious or solemn, suggesting weighty concern: {The doctor's expression was grave.} A grave situation or grave danger is one requiring urgent attention. As a verb, grave is an archaic term meaning to carve or engrave.

A gravedigger is someone who digs graves for burial. The work is manual labor, traditionally done with a shovel, though modern cemeteries often use machinery. Gravedigger carries associations with death and darkness—the figure appears in folklore and literature as someone comfortable among corpses, most famously in the scene from *Hamlet*. {The gravediggers had the plot ready by morning.}

Gravel is a loose collection of small stones and rock fragments, coarser than sand but smaller than cobbles. It forms naturally in riverbeds and is manufactured for construction—driveways, paths, roadbeds. A gravel {road} or {driveway} is surfaced with it. To gravel someone is to irritate or perplex them, though this use is old-fashioned. A gravelly {voice} is rough and low-pitched, as if full of small stones.

Graverobbing is the act of stealing from graves—whether taking valuables buried with the dead or the corpses themselves. Historically, bodies were stolen to supply medical schools with cadavers for dissection. The term extends to any distasteful exploitation of the deceased or their legacy: {Critics called the posthumous album release pure graverobbing}.

Graves are holes dug in the earth for burying the dead, or the mounds marking such burial sites. The word extends to any final resting place: {a watery grave}, {mass graves}. To dig your own grave is to cause your own downfall. Something carries weight {from beyond the grave} when it influences events after the person's death. To work yourself {into an early grave} is to harm your health through overwork. (Capitalized Graves is a surname.)

A gravestone is a stone marker placed at a burial site, inscribed with the deceased person's name, dates, and sometimes an epitaph. The terms gravestone, headstone, and tombstone overlap considerably, though headstone specifically marks the head of a grave and tombstone may refer to a larger monument. {We found our ancestor's gravestone in the old cemetery.}

Gravestones are stone markers placed at graves, typically inscribed with the deceased's name, dates of birth and death, and sometimes an epitaph or decorative carving. The terms gravestone, tombstone, and headstone are largely interchangeable, though headstone specifically marks the head of a grave. {We walked through the old cemetery reading the gravestones.}

A graveyard is a burial ground for the dead, typically adjacent to a church. The term is largely interchangeable with cemetery, though cemetery often implies a larger, independent burial ground. Figuratively, a graveyard is where things go to die or be forgotten: {a graveyard of abandoned projects}, {the elephants' graveyard}. The graveyard shift is the late-night work shift, roughly midnight to 8 a.m.

Graveyards are burial grounds, places where the dead are interred. The term originally referred specifically to churchyards—land surrounding a church used for burials—while cemetery denoted any burial ground. This distinction has largely faded: {The old graveyard behind the church dates to the 1700s}. Figuratively, a graveyard is where things go to die or be forgotten: {a graveyard for failed startups}. The graveyard shift is the overnight work shift, roughly midnight to 8 a.m.

Gravitas is dignified seriousness of manner or bearing. The word suggests weight and substance—the quality that makes people take someone seriously. A leader with gravitas commands respect through presence rather than force: {She brought gravitas to the role}. The term often appears in discussions of politicians or executives who either possess or conspicuously lack it.

Gravity is the force, not completely understood by science, which causes objects with mass to attract each other. That is the most frequent use of the word, but gravity is also the verbal noun of the adjective grave (meaning extremely serious), so gravity also means that state or condition of being. This use typically occurs in phrases such as the gravity of the situation.

Gravy is a sauce made from meat juices, typically thickened with flour and served over meat, potatoes, or biscuits. Beyond the kitchen, gravy means easy money or unexpected profit—something extra beyond what's needed or earned: {The base salary covers expenses; bonuses are gravy}. A {gravy train} is a situation providing effortless income or benefits.

Gray is the color between black and white, the color of ash, overcast skies, and aged hair. It suggests neutrality, ambiguity, or dullness: {a gray area}, {gray weather}. To gray is to become gray, especially of hair with age. Gray matter is brain tissue, and by extension, intelligence. Also spelled grey, especially in British English.

Graybeards are old men, especially those viewed as wise or venerable elders: {The graybeards on the committee favored caution}. The term can be respectful, suggesting accumulated wisdom, or dismissive, implying outdated thinking: {The graybeards in management don't understand the new technology}. In some contexts, graybeard refers specifically to senior experts or veterans in a field.

Graze has two distinct meanings. One involves feeding: cattle graze on grass, moving across a field eating as they go. By extension, people graze when they eat small amounts throughout the day rather than sitting down to meals: {I grazed on snacks all afternoon}. The other graze means to scrape lightly in passing—a bullet grazes an arm, a car grazes a fence. A graze is also the resulting scrape or abrasion: {She cleaned the graze on her knee}.

Grazing is the act of animals feeding on growing grass or other vegetation in a field or pasture: {cattle grazing on the hillside}. The word extends to human eating habits—nibbling small amounts throughout the day rather than eating full meals: {She spent the afternoon grazing on snacks}. A grazing wound or impact barely touches the surface, passing by with only light contact.

Grease is thick, oily substance used for lubrication or produced by cooking fatty foods. Mechanics apply grease to moving parts; bacon leaves grease in the pan. To grease something is to apply this substance: {grease the axle}, {grease the baking pan}. To {grease someone's palm} is to bribe them. Grease also refers to oily buildup in hair or on skin. As slang, grease can mean to kill: {The hitman greased him outside the restaurant}.

Greasers were members of a 1950s-60s youth subculture characterized by slicked-back hair (hence the name), leather jackets, and working-class swagger. The look was associated with rock and roll, motorcycles, and a rebellious attitude: {The greasers hung out by the gas station}. The term is now mostly historical or nostalgic. Separately, greaser is an old ethnic slur for Mexicans or other Latin Americans.

Greasy describes something coated or saturated with grease or oil: {greasy fingers from the fried chicken}, {greasy hair}. Food that's greasy has excessive fat: {a greasy spoon} is a cheap diner serving such fare. Figuratively, greasy suggests something slick and untrustworthy: {a greasy salesman}, {greasy charm}. The word carries connotations of uncleanliness or moral slipperiness.
Great is mainly an approving adjective and as an interjection it also expresses a positive response or feeling—except when used ironically.

Greatest is the superlative of great—the most great among a group. It describes whatever surpasses all others in size, extent, or importance: {the greatest threat to democracy}, {the greatest basketball player of all time}. In casual speech, greatest often expresses enthusiastic approval: {This is the greatest!} The phrase {greatest of all time} has spawned the acronym GOAT.

Greatness is the quality of being great—exceptional, distinguished, or remarkably superior in some domain. It applies to achievements, abilities, or character that rise well above the ordinary: {She never doubted his greatness as a composer}. Greatness can describe historical significance, moral stature, or sheer excellence in a field. The word often carries weight and formality, invoked when ordinary praise falls short: {Some are born to greatness, others achieve it}.

Greats is the plural of great used as a noun—the outstanding figures in a field: {one of the all-time greats}, {She studied the greats of jazz piano}. At Oxford University, Greats refers to the classics curriculum covering ancient Greek and Roman literature, history, and philosophy, or the final examinations in that program.

Greed is excessive desire for more than one needs or deserves, especially money or possessions. The word carries moral weight—greed isn't just wanting things but wanting them beyond reasonable measure, often at others' expense. {Corporate greed}, {greed for power}. The greedy hoard what they have while craving what they don't.

Greedy describes an excessive desire for more than one needs or deserves—typically food, money, or possessions. A greedy {child} wants all the candy; a greedy {corporation} maximizes profits at others' expense. The word carries moral judgment: greed is one of the seven deadly sins. In computing, a greedy {algorithm} takes the largest available option at each step without considering long-term consequences.

The color adjective green designates things that are the usual color of living leaves and grass. Its many figurative meanings differ greatly across languages, but in English, green can stand for inexperience, envy, jealousy, youth, vigor, and nausea. In politics, green indicates an agenda of environmental issues, and in fact many countries have a Green Party that puts the environment first. Green occurs frequently in food names (green onion, green salad, green bean, green pepper) and characterizes places dominated by plant life, such as a green belt. In golf, a green is the area immediately around the pin and cup.

Greenery means the green parts of plants, used to describe the pleasant effect plants have on a space. It's less formal than foliage and suggests comfort or life: {The office added some greenery to brighten the room}. Anything green could theoretically be greenery, but in practice the word applies only to plants.

A greenhorn is someone new and inexperienced, especially a naive newcomer to a job, place, or activity. The word originally referred to a young animal with immature horns, then extended to inexperienced people—particularly immigrants or newcomers to the American frontier: {Every greenhorn thinks he can survive in the wilderness}. The term carries condescension, implying the person is easily fooled or unprepared for what lies ahead.

A greenhouse is a structure with glass or transparent walls and roof, designed to trap heat and grow plants in controlled conditions. The trapped warmth creates a warmer interior than the outside air—the basis of the {greenhouse effect} in climate science, where atmospheric gases trap heat around Earth. As an adjective, greenhouse describes gases or emissions that contribute to global warming: {greenhouse gas emissions}.

Greenhouses are structures with glass or transparent walls and roof, designed to trap heat and grow plants in controlled conditions. The greenhouse effect describes how gases in Earth's atmosphere trap solar heat similarly—a natural process that becomes problematic when intensified by carbon emissions. {The tomatoes in the greenhouse ripened weeks early.}

To greenlight something is to authorize it to proceed, especially a creative project: {The studio greenlit the sequel}. The metaphor comes from traffic signals—green means go. A green light is such authorization: {We got the green light to start hiring}. Common in entertainment, business, and government contexts where projects require approval.

A greenroom is a room in a theater, television studio, or concert venue where performers wait before and after going on stage. The term extends to similar spaces at talk shows, conferences, or any event with a backstage area: {We chatted in the greenroom before the interview}. Despite the name, greenrooms are rarely green.

Greens are leafy vegetables, especially dark ones like spinach, kale, and collard greens: {She cooked a pot of greens with ham hocks}. In golf, greens are the closely mown areas around each hole. Greens can also mean money, from the color of U.S. currency. As a political term, greens are environmentalists or members of a Green Party: {The greens pushed for stronger climate legislation}. (Capitalized Greens typically refers to the political party.)

A greenscreen is a bright green backdrop used in film and video production, allowing editors to replace the green area with other imagery through digital compositing. The technique works because the saturated green contrasts sharply with human skin tones: {The weather forecaster stands in front of a greenscreen}. As a verb, to greenscreen is to film using this method. Blue screens serve the same purpose but green has become standard in digital workflows.

Greenwash is the practice of making a company or product appear more environmentally friendly than it actually is. The term blends green (as in eco-friendly) with whitewash (to cover up wrongdoing). A company greenwashes when it emphasizes minor environmental efforts while ignoring larger harmful practices: {Critics accused the oil company of greenwashing with its solar panel ads}. Also used as a noun for the deceptive messaging itself.

Greenwashed describes something made to appear more environmentally friendly than it actually is. Companies greenwash products through misleading labels, vague claims, or token gestures that distract from larger environmental harms: {The "eco-friendly" packaging was greenwashed—the product inside was still full of toxic chemicals}. The term suggests deliberate deception rather than genuine sustainability efforts.

Greenwashing is the practice of making misleading claims about environmental benefits to appear more eco-friendly than reality warrants. Companies greenwash when they emphasize minor green initiatives while ignoring larger harmful practices, or use vague terms like "natural" or "eco-friendly" without substance: {Critics accused the oil company of greenwashing with its solar panel ads}. The term blends "green" with "whitewashing."

To greet is to acknowledge someone's arrival or presence, typically with words, gestures, or both: {She greeted him with a warm smile}. A greeting can be formal or casual—a handshake, a wave, a simple hello. Things that greet you are the first things you encounter: {The smell of coffee greeted us as we entered}.

A greeting is a word, phrase, or gesture acknowledging someone's presence or beginning communication: {She waved in greeting}. Common greetings include hello, hi, good morning, and handshakes. The plural often appears on cards: {Season's greetings}. A greeting can be warm or perfunctory depending on the relationship and context.

Greetings is a salutation—a word spoken or written when meeting someone or opening correspondence. It works as a standalone hello: {Greetings, traveler}. The singular greeting refers to any such expression: {a friendly greeting}, {a greeting card}. To send greetings is to convey good wishes: {She sent her greetings to the family}.

A gremlin is a mischievous imaginary creature blamed for mechanical failures, especially in aircraft. The term originated among British pilots in the early twentieth century to explain mysterious malfunctions. By extension, any unexplained glitch or malfunction may be attributed to gremlins: {There must be a gremlin in the system}. In the 1984 film *Gremlins*, the creatures became iconic movie monsters.

Gremlins are imaginary mischievous creatures blamed for unexplained mechanical failures or technical glitches. The term emerged among British pilots in World War II to explain mysterious aircraft malfunctions: {There must be gremlins in the system}. Now applied broadly to any frustrating technical problem with no obvious cause: {Software gremlins kept crashing the app}. (Capitalized Gremlins is the 1984 film.)

A grenade is a small explosive device thrown by hand or launched from a rifle. The standard military grenade detonates after a few seconds, scattering shrapnel. Other grenades deliver smoke, tear gas, or flash-bang effects. The word extends to any small container designed to burst: a fire extinguisher grenade, a glass grenade of perfume.

Grenades are small explosive devices thrown by hand or launched from a rifle. The classic grenade has a pin that, once pulled, starts a timer before detonation: {He pulled the pin and lobbed the grenade into the bunker}. Figuratively, to {throw a grenade} into a situation is to introduce something disruptive or controversial. Smoke grenades and flashbang grenades produce non-lethal effects. The word comes from the French for pomegranate, which the early bombs resembled.

Grew is the past tense of grow. Something that grew increased in size, developed, or became: {The company grew rapidly}, {She grew tired of waiting}. Plants grew from seeds, children grew into adults, feelings grew stronger. {He grew up in Ohio} means that's where he spent his childhood.

Grey is the color between black and white, the color of ash, overcast skies, and shadows. This is the standard British spelling; Americans prefer gray. Both forms work as noun, adjective, and verb: {grey skies}, {hair turning grey}, {the greys of winter}. Grey suggests neutrality, ambiguity, or dullness—{a grey area} is one without clear boundaries. (See also gray.)

A greyhound is a tall, slender breed of dog built for speed, with a narrow head, long legs, and deep chest. Greyhounds are the fastest of all dog breeds, historically bred for coursing game and now often associated with racing: {We adopted a retired greyhound from the track}. The word also refers to a cocktail of grapefruit juice and vodka or gin. (Capitalized Greyhound is the bus company.)

Greyhounds are a breed of tall, slender dogs built for speed, with long legs, a narrow head, and a deep chest. They're among the fastest land animals, bred historically for coursing game and later for racing. The greyhound's distinctive silhouette—lean and aerodynamic—has made it an emblem of swiftness: {The bus line's greyhound logo suggests speed and efficiency}.

A grid is a network of lines crossing at regular intervals, forming a pattern of squares or rectangles. City streets may follow a grid. An electrical grid distributes power across a region. A grid can be any systematic framework: {The search party divided the area into a grid}. In computing and gaming, grids organize space into discrete cells for navigation or display.

A griddle is a flat cooking surface, typically made of cast iron or steel, used for frying foods like pancakes, eggs, and bacon. Unlike a pan, a griddle has no sides or very shallow ones, allowing easy flipping. The verb means to cook on such a surface: {griddled onions}. A griddle cake is a pancake.

Gridlock is a traffic jam so severe that vehicles cannot move in any direction—the grid of streets locked in mutual obstruction. The term extends to any situation where opposing forces create complete paralysis: {Congressional gridlock prevented any legislation from passing}. Political gridlock has become the dominant use, describing government unable to act because factions block each other.

Gridlocked describes traffic so congested that vehicles cannot move in any direction—the image is of cars blocking each intersection in a grid pattern, paralyzing the entire system. The term extends to any situation where competing forces create total stalemate: {Congress remains gridlocked on the budget}. A gridlocked negotiation has reached impasse, with no side able to advance.

Grief is deep sorrow, especially from loss or death. The emotion is heavy and prolonged, unlike momentary sadness: {She was overcome with grief when her mother died}. Grief extends to other painful losses—a relationship, a homeland, a way of life. To {come to grief} is to fail or meet disaster. {Good grief} is a mild exclamation of surprise or frustration.

Griefing is deliberately harassing or annoying other players in online games—destroying their creations, blocking their progress, or otherwise ruining their experience for one's own amusement. The term comes from causing grief. Someone who does this is a griefer: {He spent the whole match griefing instead of playing the objective}.

A grievance is a complaint about unfair treatment or a wrong that has been suffered. The word implies the complaint has legitimacy—a grievance is not mere whining but a genuine cause for resentment: {The workers aired their grievances at the meeting}. In formal contexts, a grievance is a complaint filed through official channels, especially in labor disputes: {She filed a grievance with HR}.

Grievances are complaints about unfair treatment or wrongdoing. The word implies legitimate grounds for protest—not mere gripes but substantive injuries deserving redress: {The workers filed grievances with the union}. In formal contexts, grievance often appears in legal or institutional settings where complaints follow established procedures. To {air grievances} is to voice them openly: {Festivus includes the airing of grievances}.

Grieve means to feel deep sorrow, especially over a death: {She grieved for months after losing her father}. The grief may be private or expressed openly. You can grieve a person, a loss, or an abstraction: {grieving the end of a relationship}, {grieving what might have been}. To grieve someone is to cause them distress, though this use is now rare outside formal contexts like labor disputes, where filing a grievance is called grieving.

Grieving is the process of experiencing grief—the emotional response to loss, especially the death of someone close. The word captures ongoing sorrow rather than a single moment: {She's still grieving}. Someone who is grieving may feel sadness, anger, numbness, or all of these. The grieving {process} or grieving {period} acknowledges that mourning takes time.

A griffin is a mythical creature with the body of a lion and the head and wings of an eagle. Griffins appear in ancient Greek art and medieval heraldry, typically as symbols of strength and vigilance. The creature combines the king of beasts with the king of birds: {A golden griffin adorned the family crest}. Also spelled gryphon.

Griffins is the plural of griffin, a mythical creature with the body of a lion and the head and wings of an eagle. Griffins appear throughout ancient and medieval mythology as fierce guardians of treasure and symbols of strength: {Stone griffins flanked the entrance to the palace}. The spelling varies—griffin, griffon, and gryphon all refer to the same creature.

Grift is petty swindling or fraud, typically involving clever manipulation rather than outright theft. A grift is a particular scheme or con, and a grifter is someone who makes a living this way. The verb grift means to obtain money through such dishonest means. {He ran a small grift selling fake concert tickets.} In contemporary usage, grift often describes any hustle that exploits people's trust or gullibility for profit, from televangelism to dubious online courses.

A grifter is a swindler or con artist—someone who obtains money through deception, typically through small-scale schemes rather than elaborate heists. The word carries connotations of charm and manipulation: {He was a grifter who preyed on lonely widows}. The related verb grift means to engage in such swindles, and the noun grift refers to the practice itself.

Grifters are people who obtain money through swindles, fraud, or petty cons. The term suggests small-scale operators rather than criminal masterminds—someone running a shell game, selling fake investment opportunities, or exploiting trust for quick profit. {The town attracted grifters looking for easy marks.} Politicians and salespeople sometimes get called grifters when their promises seem designed to enrich themselves at others' expense.

Grifting is swindling or running small-scale scams—obtaining money through deception, trickery, or exploitation of trust. A grifter works confidence games, petty frauds, or schemes that separate marks from their money: {He spent years grifting tourists with fake charity collections}. The term has expanded to describe any manipulative hustle, from dubious influencer promotions to political fundraising that enriches the fundraiser more than the cause.

Grifts are petty swindles or confidence schemes—small-scale frauds that rely on deception rather than force. The word covers both the schemes themselves and the act of running them: {He's been running grifts since he was a teenager}. Someone who grifts is a grifter. The term has expanded to describe any hustle or dubious money-making venture: {influencer grifts}, {political grifts}.

A grill is a framework of metal bars used for cooking food over an open flame or heat source: {burgers on the grill}. The word extends to the cooking device itself and to restaurants specializing in grilled food: {a neighborhood bar and grill}. To grill is to cook this way, or figuratively, to interrogate intensely: {The detective grilled the suspect for hours}. Grill also refers to a metal grating—on a car's front end, over a window, or as decorative dental jewelry in hip-hop culture.

Grilled describes food cooked on a grill—over direct heat, typically from flames or hot coals: {grilled chicken}, {grilled vegetables}. The method produces characteristic char marks and smoky flavor. Separately, to be grilled is to be questioned intensely: {The suspect was grilled for hours}. The interrogation sense evokes being subjected to heat.

Grilling is cooking food over direct heat, typically on a grate above flames or coals: {We're grilling burgers tonight}. The method produces charred marks and smoky flavor. Grilling also means subjecting someone to intense, persistent questioning: {The detective gave him a real grilling}. Both senses share the idea of applying heat.

Grills are metal grates used for cooking food over an open flame or heat source, or the appliances containing them: {We fired up the grill for burgers}. To grill is to cook this way, or to interrogate someone intensely: {The detective grilled the suspect for hours}. In slang, grills are decorative metal dental covers, often gold or diamond-studded, worn as jewelry: {He flashed his grills}. Someone's grill is also their face: {Get out of my grill}.

Grim describes something harsh, forbidding, or relentlessly serious. A grim {expression} shows no warmth or humor. Grim {news} is bad news delivered without softening. A grim {reality} is an unpleasant truth that must be faced. The word often suggests bleakness or severity: {The outlook is grim}. A grim {determination} is fierce and unyielding—someone who persists despite hardship. {The Grim Reaper} personifies death as a skeletal figure with a scythe.

A grimace is a facial expression of pain, disgust, or disapproval—the face twisting or contorting involuntarily or deliberately. To grimace is to make such a face: {She grimaced at the bitter taste}. Unlike a smile or frown, a grimace involves multiple features working together to signal discomfort or distaste.

Grime is ingrained dirt—the kind that accumulates in layers and resists easy cleaning: {years of grime on the kitchen walls}, {factory grime}. Unlike dust or mud, grime suggests stubborn, greasy buildup. To grime something is to make it dirty. Grimy is the common adjective. In British music, grime is a genre blending electronic beats with rapid-fire rap, originating in early 2000s London.

A grimoire is a book of magic—spells, rituals, invocations, and instructions for summoning spirits or crafting talismans. The term evokes medieval and Renaissance occult texts, leather-bound and handwritten. In fantasy fiction and games, grimoires are standard equipment for wizards and witches: {She found an ancient grimoire in the attic}. The word retains an air of forbidden knowledge.

Grimy means covered with grime—ingrained dirt or soot that's hard to remove. A grimy {window} obscures the view. Grimy {hands} need serious scrubbing. The word suggests accumulated filth rather than fresh mud: {a grimy factory}, {grimy streets}. Figuratively, grimy can mean morally sordid: {the grimy details of the scandal}.

A grin is a broad smile that typically shows the teeth, often expressing amusement, satisfaction, or mischief. Unlike a polite smile, a grin tends to be wider and less restrained: {She couldn't suppress a grin when she heard the news}. To grin is to produce such an expression. If you {grin and bear it}, you accept an unpleasant situation without complaining. A grin can also suggest something slightly sinister or knowing, as in a {Cheshire cat grin}.

A grinch is a spoilsport or killjoy, especially someone who dampens holiday cheer or ruins others' fun: {Don't be such a grinch about the office party}. The word derives from the Dr. Seuss character but has become a common noun for any curmudgeonly person who resents festivity or generosity. (Capitalized Grinch is the original fictional character.)

Grind, a noun and verb, carries the idea of crushing force resulting in disintegration. When you grind a substance you reduce it to powder (grind wheat into flour). The noun grind may indicate the relative size in the particles of something ground: I bought espresso grind coffee. If you grind your teeth, you press them together when your mouth is empty. The grind or the daily grind is the crushing monotonous work routine that some people experience.

A grinder is something that grinds—a machine, tool, or person that crushes, sharpens, or pulverizes: {coffee grinder}, {meat grinder}, {knife grinder}. Grinder also names a long sandwich on a crusty roll, regional to parts of the American Northeast. In slang, a grinder is someone who works relentlessly at a task, especially in sports or gaming: {He's not talented, just a grinder}. To be {on the grind} is to hustle persistently.

Grinders are teeth, especially the molars used for chewing: {My back grinders are killing me}. A grinder is also a tool or machine that grinds—a meat grinder, coffee grinder, or angle grinder. In parts of the northeastern United States, a grinder is a submarine sandwich. In skateboarding and video games, grinders are those who repeat tasks to build skill or accumulate rewards through persistent effort rather than talent.

Grinding is the act of crushing, wearing down, or reducing something through friction or pressure. Coffee beans are ground; gears grind against each other; you grind your teeth in frustration or sleep. The adjective describes something relentlessly wearing: {the grinding poverty of the slums}, {the grinding pace of bureaucracy}. In gaming and work contexts, grinding means repetitive effort to achieve incremental progress: {I spent hours grinding to level up my character}.

Grinds is the third-person singular of grind—to crush, wear down, or work steadily at something tedious: {She grinds coffee every morning}, {The machine grinds to a halt}. As a noun, grinds are acts of grinding or, in Irish and British slang, private tutoring sessions, especially for exam preparation: {He's taking grinds in maths}.

Grinning is smiling broadly, typically showing teeth. A grin usually signals amusement, pleasure, or self-satisfaction, though it can also suggest nervousness or discomfort: {He stood there grinning like an idiot}. {She couldn't stop grinning after hearing the news}. To be {grinning from ear to ear} is to smile as widely as possible.

Grins is the plural noun and third-person singular verb form of grin. A grin is a broad smile, often one that shows teeth and suggests amusement, mischief, or self-satisfaction. To grin is to smile in this way. The expression {grin and bear it} means to endure something unpleasant without complaining. Someone described as {all grins} is visibly happy or pleased about something.

The noun and verb grip relate mainly to the grasping of something by the human hand; this core idea inspires other uses. When you grip something, you hold it tightly with your hand. The grip of an object, such as a gun or a suitcase, is the handle, the part where your hand goes. The grip of a person may refer to their handshake: He has an iron grip. Grip also indicates your level of mastery or control in expressions like get a grip, lose your grip, and tighten your grip.

Gripe means to complain, especially persistently about minor matters: {He's always griping about the weather}. A gripe is such a complaint: {My only gripe is the slow service}. The word suggests petty or habitual grievances rather than serious objections. An older sense refers to sharp intestinal pain—gripes or griping—now largely displaced by the complaining meaning.

Gripes are complaints, usually minor and persistent: {I'm tired of hearing your gripes about the commute}. The verb gripe means to complain in this nagging way. Gripes can also refer to sharp intestinal pains—griping in the gut. {Gripe water} is a traditional remedy for colicky babies. To have a gripe with someone is to have a grievance against them.

Gripping describes something that seizes and holds your attention completely. A gripping {thriller} or gripping {documentary} keeps you engaged from start to finish, unwilling to look away. The word derives from the physical sense of grip—to hold tightly—and applies that sensation to mental engagement. Something gripping has you in its clutches, whether it's a novel, a courtroom drama, or a news story you can't stop following.

Grisly describes something causing horror or disgust, especially through violence or death: {grisly murder scene}, {grisly discovery}. The word suggests gruesome physical details—blood, wounds, decay. Often confused with grizzly (the bear) and grizzled (gray-haired), but grisly is strictly about the horrifying.

Grit refers to small, coarse particles of stone or sand—the kind that gets in your shoes or between your teeth. By extension, grit describes mental toughness and perseverance: {She had the grit to finish the marathon on a sprained ankle}. To grit your teeth is to clench them, either physically or in determination. In the plural, grits are coarsely ground corn, a staple of Southern American cuisine.

Grits are coarsely ground dried corn, boiled into a porridge-like consistency. A staple of Southern American cuisine, grits are served as a breakfast side dish or as a base for shrimp and other toppings: {She ordered eggs with a side of grits}. The word is plural but refers to a single dish: {Grits is my favorite breakfast}.

Gritty describes something containing or covered with grit—small, hard particles like sand or dirt: {a gritty texture}, {gritty residue on the windowsill}. Extended to character, gritty means showing courage and resolve: {a gritty performance}, {gritty determination}. In describing stories, films, or settings, gritty signals harsh realism—unpolished, unglamorous, often depicting urban decay or difficult circumstances: {a gritty crime drama}, {the gritty streets of Baltimore}.

Grizzled describes hair that is gray or streaked with gray, and by extension, a person whose hair has grayed: {a grizzled old sailor}, {his grizzled beard}. The word carries connotations of age and weathered experience—grizzled characters in fiction tend to be tough, world-weary veterans rather than merely elderly.

Grizzlies is the plural of grizzly, referring to the large North American brown bear known for its silver-tipped fur and formidable size. The term also names sports teams, most notably the NBA's Memphis Grizzlies: {The Grizzlies won in overtime}. In plural form, it often appears in discussions of wildlife conservation or encounters in bear country.

A grizzly is a large North American brown bear, distinguished by the grizzled (gray-tipped) fur that gives it its name. Grizzlies are powerful and potentially dangerous, making them icons of wilderness and subjects of both fear and conservation efforts: {We hung our food to keep it away from grizzlies}. As an adjective, grizzly means gray or partly gray, though grizzled is more common in that sense.

A groan is a deep, inarticulate sound expressing pain, despair, or displeasure: {He let out a groan when he saw the bill}. People groan at bad jokes, groan under heavy burdens, and groan with effort. Things can groan too—floorboards groan under weight, economies groan under debt. The word captures both the sound and the weariness behind it.

Groaned is the past tense of groan, a deep sound made in the throat that typically expresses pain, displeasure, or weariness. {He groaned when he saw the pile of paperwork on his desk.} People groan at bad jokes, from physical exertion, or when confronted with unwelcome news. Objects can also be said to have groaned when they make similar low, creaking sounds under strain: {The old floorboards groaned beneath our feet.}

A grocer is a person who sells food and household supplies, or a store that sells such goods. The word now usually appears in compound forms: {grocery store}, {grocery shopping}, {groceries}. A standalone grocer typically means a small neighborhood shop rather than a supermarket chain.

Groceries are food and household supplies purchased from a store. The word almost always appears in plural—you buy groceries, not a grocery. {I need to pick up groceries on the way home.} A grocery or grocery store is where you buy them. To {do the groceries} is to shop for them.

A grocery is a store selling food and household supplies: {I need to run to the grocery}. In the plural, groceries are the items purchased there: {Help me carry in the groceries}. The older sense—a grocer's shop or the trade itself—survives mainly in the full phrase {grocery store}.

Grog is alcoholic drink, especially rum diluted with water—originally a British naval ration. The term now applies loosely to any liquor or alcoholic beverage: {After a long day, he poured himself some grog}. Groggy, meaning dazed or unsteady, comes from the effects of drinking too much of it.

Groggy describes a state of sluggish confusion, typically from incomplete sleep, illness, or intoxication. Someone groggy has trouble thinking clearly and may be unsteady: {I was still groggy from the anesthesia}. The word originally described sailors drunk on grog, a diluted rum ration.

The groin is the area where the inner thigh meets the lower abdomen—the crease on either side of the body where the leg joins the torso. It's a vulnerable region in combat and sports: {He took a knee to the groin}. In architecture, a groin is the curved edge formed where two vaulted ceilings intersect.

A groom is a man on his wedding day or about to be married. The word also means a person who cares for horses—brushing, feeding, and maintaining them. To groom is to clean and tend to appearance: {She groomed herself in the mirror}, {a well-groomed lawn}. Extended uses include preparing someone for a role: {He was groomed for leadership}. More darkly, to groom is to cultivate a victim's trust for exploitation, especially a child for sexual abuse.

Groomed is the past tense and participle of groom, carrying meanings related to careful preparation and maintenance. When applied to appearance, it describes someone whose hair, clothing, and overall presentation have been deliberately tended to: {He arrived impeccably groomed for the interview}. Animals, especially horses and dogs, are groomed by brushing and cleaning their coats. In a darker sense, groomed describes someone, typically a child, who has been psychologically manipulated over time by a predator to gain trust before abuse. One can also be groomed for a position or role, meaning prepared and cultivated for future responsibilities.

A groomer is someone who grooms—prepares or tends to something's appearance. Dog groomers wash and trim pets. A groomer can also be a vehicle that maintains ski slopes. In its darker sense, a groomer is someone who cultivates a relationship with a child or vulnerable person to exploit them, typically sexually: {He was convicted as a groomer who targeted teenagers online}. This sense has expanded in political rhetoric to accuse opponents of corrupting children ideologically.

Grooming is the care of appearance—brushing hair, trimming nails, cleaning fur. Animals groom themselves and each other; humans groom for job interviews and dates. A well-groomed person looks neat and put-together. Extended, grooming means preparing someone for a role: {He's being groomed for partner}. More darkly, grooming describes how predators cultivate trust with potential victims, especially children, before abuse: {The coach's grooming went undetected for years}.

Grooms is the plural of groom—men about to be married or recently married, or people who care for horses. As a verb, grooms means to clean and maintain: a cat grooms itself, a person grooms their appearance. To groom someone for a position is to prepare them through training and mentorship. In a darker sense, predators groom victims by building trust before exploitation.

A groomsman is a male friend or relative chosen by a groom to assist and stand beside him during a wedding ceremony. Groomsmen typically help with pre-wedding tasks, attend the rehearsal dinner, and wear matching attire. The groom's principal attendant is distinguished as the best man. {He asked his college roommate to be a groomsman.}

Groomsmen is the plural of groomsman—men who attend the groom at a wedding, typically standing beside him during the ceremony and participating in related events. The groomsmen often include close friends, brothers, or relatives. One among them is usually designated the best man. {He asked his college roommates to be his groomsmen.}

A groove is a long, narrow channel cut or worn into a surface: the grooves on a vinyl record, grooves in wood for joining pieces. Figuratively, a groove is a settled routine: {stuck in a groove}. In music, groove means a compelling rhythmic feel that makes you want to move: {The band found their groove}. To groove is to enjoy something thoroughly or move rhythmically: {We were grooving to the music}.

Groovy means fashionable, exciting, or excellent. The word emerged from jazz slang—a musician {in the groove} was playing with effortless rhythm. Groovy became emblematic of 1960s counterculture: {groovy music}, {groovy vibes}. Today it sounds dated or ironic, though some use it earnestly: {That's groovy with me} means that's fine.

Groping is touching someone's body in a sexual way without consent, typically grabbing at breasts, buttocks, or genitals. The term implies fumbling, unwanted contact rather than a single deliberate act: {She reported him for groping her on the subway}. More innocently, groping means feeling about blindly: {groping for the light switch}, {groping for words}.

Gross means large, obvious, or offensive in degree. A gross {injustice} or gross {negligence} is flagrant and inexcusable. Gross {income} is the total before deductions—the whole amount before anything is taken away. In informal speech, gross means disgusting: {That's so gross}. A gross is also a quantity of 144 (twelve dozen), from an old word for "large" that survives mainly in wholesale contexts.

Grotesque describes something distorted, ugly, or bizarrely unnatural—often combining the disturbing with the absurd. A grotesque {figure} might have exaggerated or misshapen features. Grotesque {behavior} is shockingly inappropriate. The word carries a sense of fascinated repulsion: {The trial revealed grotesque details of the crime}. As a noun, a grotesque is a fantastical carved figure, like those on medieval cathedrals, or a style of ornamental design featuring strange hybrid creatures and tangled forms.

A grotto is a small cave, especially one that's picturesque or has been artificially created for ornamental purposes. Natural grottos often feature in coastal landscapes, while artificial ones appear in gardens and parks as decorative retreats: {The garden path led to a shaded grotto with a fountain}. Grottos also serve as religious shrines, particularly Catholic ones dedicated to the Virgin Mary.

A grouch is a habitually irritable or complaining person: {Don't be such a grouch}. The word also names the mood itself—a state of grumpy dissatisfaction: {He's been in a grouch all morning}. To grouch is to grumble or complain: {She grouched about the weather for an hour}.

Grouchy describes someone who is irritable, bad-tempered, and prone to complaining. A grouchy person tends to be easily annoyed and quick to express displeasure, often over minor things. {Don't talk to Dad before his coffee—he's always grouchy in the morning.} The word suggests a sour disposition that may be temporary rather than a permanent character trait.

The ground is the most natural place for us to stand—the surface of the Earth—and from that core meaning, most others arise. Senses of ground often have to do with support and basis: the DA found there were no grounds for prosecution. A preceding noun or adjective indicates a particular place: breeding ground, test ground. When you ground something, you provide a foundation or basis for it: the book is solidly grounded in primary research. Ground also serves as the past tense and past participle of the verb grind, and is frequent as an adjective: ground pepper.

Groundbreaking describes something innovative or pioneering—the first of its kind to break new ground: {groundbreaking research}, {a groundbreaking court decision}. The word derives from the literal ceremony of breaking ground to begin construction. As with many superlatives, overuse has dulled its edge; not every new product or study deserves the label.

Grounded describes something firmly established or connected to a foundation. A grounded person is stable, sensible, and emotionally secure—not easily swayed by circumstances: {Despite her fame, she remains remarkably grounded}. In electricity, grounded means connected to the earth for safety. A grounded airplane or teenager has been prevented from flying or going out: {You're grounded for a week}. To be grounded in something is to have solid knowledge of it: {well grounded in the classics}.

A groundhog is a stocky North American rodent that burrows in the ground, also called a woodchuck. Groundhogs hibernate through winter, emerging in early spring. In American folklore, Groundhog Day (February 2) holds that if a groundhog sees its shadow upon emerging, six more weeks of winter follow.

Groundhogs are large North American rodents, a type of marmot. They dig extensive burrows and hibernate through winter. Groundhog Day on February 2nd follows folklore that if a groundhog emerges and sees its shadow, six more weeks of winter follow. {We saw a groundhog waddle across the backyard}.

Grounding is the foundation or basis for something: {a solid grounding in mathematics}. In electricity, grounding connects a circuit to the earth for safety. As punishment, grounding confines someone—usually a teenager—to their home: {She's grounded for a month}. An aircraft that's grounded cannot fly, whether for mechanical reasons or weather. In psychology, grounding techniques anchor attention to the present moment.

Grounds are the basis or foundation for something—reasons that justify a belief, action, or legal claim: {grounds for divorce}, {on what grounds?}, {reasonable grounds for suspicion}. Grounds also means an area of land surrounding or belonging to a building: {the hospital grounds}, {palace grounds}. Coffee grounds are the sediment left after brewing. To be grounded is to be prohibited from flying or, for teenagers, from leaving the house as punishment.

A groundswell is a broad, deep movement of ocean waves, often generated by distant storms and felt as a powerful undulation rather than breaking surf. The word is now primarily figurative: a groundswell of {support}, {opposition}, or {enthusiasm} describes widespread sentiment rising from ordinary people rather than from leadership or institutions. {There's a groundswell of demand for reform.}

Groundwork is the preliminary work that makes later progress possible. You {lay the groundwork} for a project by doing the essential preparation—research, planning, establishing relationships. The term comes from construction, where groundwork means the foundation or base on which a structure rests. {Her early experiments laid the groundwork for modern genetics.}

Group is a useful noun for designating three or more of anything that share features: a group of houses, arrange the students in groups, a methyl group at one end of the molecule. The verb group developed within a century of the noun and has several meanings related to formation and membership of groups.

A groupchat is a text conversation among three or more people, typically in a messaging app. Groupchats range from casual friend circles to family coordination to workplace teams: {The groupchat has been blowing up all morning}. They often develop their own culture—inside jokes, recurring topics, unwritten rules about who responds to what.

A groupie is a devoted fan who follows a band, celebrity, or public figure, often seeking personal contact or sexual encounters. The term emerged from rock music culture but extends to anyone who avidly pursues proximity to the famous or powerful: {political groupies}, {tech-industry groupies}. The word usually carries a dismissive or slightly contemptuous edge, implying obsessive or undignified devotion.

Groupies are devoted fans who follow a band, celebrity, or public figure, often seeking personal access or sexual encounters. The term emerged from rock music culture in the 1960s and typically refers to young women pursuing musicians: {Groupies hung around the tour bus after every show}. Extended to any enthusiastic follower: {policy groupies}, {tech groupies}.

Groups are collections of people or things considered together. People form groups around shared interests, identities, or purposes: {a support group}, {a focus group}, {an ethnic group}. In music, a group is a band: {a rock group}. The verb means to arrange into categories or clusters: {Students grouped themselves by major}. To group something with another is to classify them together.

Groupthink is the tendency of cohesive groups to reach consensus without critically examining alternatives or dissenting views. The desire for harmony overrides realistic appraisal of options: {The board's groupthink led them to ignore obvious warning signs}. The term emerged from studies of foreign policy disasters where advisers suppressed doubts to maintain unity.

Grouse names several species of plump game birds found in northern regions, known for their feathered legs and elaborate mating displays: {We flushed a grouse from the underbrush}. As a verb, grouse means to complain or grumble persistently: {He's always grousing about the weather}. The complaining sense is unrelated to the bird—it emerged from British military slang.

A grove is a small group of trees, often of the same kind, standing together without dense underbrush: {an olive grove}, {a grove of aspens}. Groves suggest orderliness or cultivation more than wild forest—orchards are groves, as are deliberate plantings in parks or on estates. The word carries a slightly poetic or pastoral quality.

To grovel is to lie or crawl face down, typically in a posture of submission or humility. The word now appears almost exclusively in its figurative sense—to behave obsequiously or debase oneself before someone: {He refused to grovel for forgiveness}. Someone who grovels abases themselves, often to gain favor or avoid punishment: {Stop groveling and stand up for yourself}.

Groveling is crawling or lying face down in a posture of submission or abasement. The word usually appears figuratively: to grovel is to humble oneself excessively, often in hopes of gaining favor or forgiveness: {He spent the weekend groveling after forgetting their anniversary}. Groveling suggests a loss of dignity—the supplicant debases themselves before someone with power over them.

Grovelling is lying face down or crawling on the ground, typically in submission or humiliation. The word now mostly describes servile, self-abasing behavior toward someone in power: {He spent the meeting grovelling to the CEO}. The British spelling doubles the l; Americans write groveling.

Groves is the plural of grove—a small group of trees, typically without dense underbrush: {olive groves}, {orange groves}, {a grove of aspens}. Groves are often cultivated or have a park-like quality, distinguishing them from wild forest. The word appears in place names and carries pastoral, sometimes sacred connotations: {the sacred groves of ancient Greece}.

Grow means to increase in size, number, or degree. Plants grow from seeds; children grow into adults; cities grow as populations expand. The word covers both natural development {The tree grew tall} and deliberate cultivation {She grows tomatoes}. Hair and nails grow continuously. Figuratively, feelings and relationships grow: {Their friendship grew over the years}. To grow can also mean to become: {grow old}, {grow tired}, {grow accustomed to something}. In business, companies grow revenue or grow their customer base—a usage some find grating but now standard.

Growing is the present participle of grow, used as an adjective or verb form to describe something that is increasing, developing, or becoming larger over time. A growing {child} is getting bigger; a growing {concern} is becoming more serious or widespread; a growing {business} is expanding. The word emphasizes ongoing change rather than a completed state. {There's a growing sense that something needs to change.}

A growl is a low, rumbling sound of hostility or warning, typically from an animal: {The dog's growl deepened as the stranger approached}. Humans growl too—in anger, frustration, or to speak in a rough, threatening voice: {He growled his displeasure}. Machinery and stomachs also growl, producing similar low, rumbling sounds.

Growling is the low, rumbling sound made in the throat, typically by dogs or other animals as a warning or sign of aggression. Humans growl too, usually to express anger, frustration, or impatience: {My stomach was growling through the whole meeting}. The word also describes rough, gravelly vocal qualities in speech or singing—a bluesman's growling voice, or someone growling a threat through clenched teeth.

Grown is the past participle of grow, used to describe something that has developed or matured: {a fully grown adult}, {home-grown tomatoes}. A grown man or grown woman emphasizes adulthood, often with slight reproach: {You're a grown man—act like it}. Grown-up functions as both noun and adjective for adults or adult behavior.

A grownup is an adult, especially from a child's perspective: {The grownups are talking}. The word carries a hint of childhood vocabulary—adults speaking formally say adult. As an adjective, grownup describes mature or adult behavior: {That's a very grownup decision}. Also spelled grown-up.

Grownups are adults, especially from a child's perspective. The word carries a childlike quality even when used by adults: {The grownups sat at the big table while the kids had their own}. It can be gently ironic when adults feel they're not measuring up to some standard of maturity: {I guess the grownups will have to figure this out}. Also spelled grown-ups.

Grows is the present-tense form of grow, covering its range of meanings. Plants grow from seeds; children grow into adults; businesses grow or fail. Hair grows back after cutting. A feeling can grow stronger or weaker: {My frustration grows with each delay}. To grow something is to cultivate it: {She grows tomatoes in the backyard}. {It grows on you} means something becomes more appealing over time.

Growth is the process of increasing in size, number, or degree. Plants and children grow; so do economies and populations. A growth is also something that has grown—often a tumor or abnormal mass: {The doctor found a growth on her lung}. Personal growth suggests psychological or spiritual development: {The experience led to tremendous growth}.

Grub is an informal word for food, especially plain or hearty fare: {Let's grab some grub before the movie}. The older and more literal meaning is a soft, thick larva of certain insects, particularly beetles, that lives in soil or decaying matter. As a verb, grub means to dig or root around in the ground, often to extract something: {grubbing for potatoes}. By extension, to grub around can mean to search laboriously or rummage through things.

Grubs are the larvae of beetles and certain other insects—pale, soft-bodied, often C-shaped creatures found in soil or decaying wood. Gardeners dig them up; fish and birds eat them. In casual speech, grubs means food: {Let's get some grubs}. To grub is to dig or root around, often for something buried or hidden: {grubbing for potatoes}.

A grudge is resentment held against someone for a past wrong, real or perceived. To hold or bear a grudge is to nurse that resentment rather than let it go: {She's still holding a grudge about what happened at the wedding}. The verb grudge means to give or allow reluctantly: {I don't grudge him his success, but I wish he'd stop bragging}.

Grudges are persistent feelings of resentment toward someone for a past offense. To hold a grudge is to nurse that resentment rather than let it go: {She's still holding a grudge about what happened at the wedding}. Some people {bear grudges} for years. A grudge match is a contest between longtime rivals with scores to settle.

Gruel is a thin, watery porridge made by boiling grain—usually oats—in water or milk. It was historically fed to the sick, the poor, and prisoners, making it a symbol of deprivation and punishment: {Oliver Twist famously asked for more gruel}. The adjective grueling, meaning exhausting or punishing, derives from the idea of being reduced to gruel.

Grueling describes something extremely demanding and exhausting, typically requiring sustained effort over time: {a grueling marathon}, {a grueling work schedule}, {grueling negotiations that lasted through the night}. The word suggests not just difficulty but the wearing down of physical or mental reserves. Also spelled gruelling in British English.

Gruelling describes something extremely demanding and exhausting, testing the limits of endurance: {a gruelling marathon}, {a gruelling schedule}, {gruelling negotiations that lasted through the night}. The word implies sustained effort over time rather than a single burst of difficulty. Also spelled grueling in American English.

Gruesome describes something causing horror or disgust, especially through graphic violence or death: {gruesome crime scene photos}, {the gruesome details of the murder}. The word suggests visceral revulsion—not just frightening but stomach-turning. Something can be gruesomely fascinating, drawing attention even as it repels: {We couldn't look away from the gruesome footage}.

Gruff describes a rough, low-pitched voice or brusque manner. A gruff voice sounds harsh or hoarse: {He answered in a gruff whisper}. A gruff person is abrupt and unfriendly in speech, though often the gruffness conceals underlying warmth: {Behind his gruff exterior, he was kind}.

Grumble is to complain in a low, muttering voice, expressing dissatisfaction without full confrontation: {He grumbled about the long wait}. The word also describes low rumbling sounds—thunder grumbles, stomachs grumble. As a noun, a grumble is the complaint itself or the sound: {We heard grumbles from the back of the room}.

Grumpy describes a persistently irritable mood—not quite angry, but easily annoyed and quick to complain. A grumpy person is unpleasant company, prone to short answers and minor grievances: {Don't talk to me before coffee—I'm grumpy in the morning}. The word suggests temporary bad temper rather than a permanent disposition, though some people seem grumpy by nature.

Grunge is dirt or grime, especially the kind that accumulates in grimy, neglected spaces. The word gained prominence as a music genre emerging from Seattle in the late 1980s and early 1990s—characterized by distorted guitars, angst-laden lyrics, and bands like Nirvana and Pearl Jam. The associated fashion embraced a deliberately unkempt aesthetic: flannel shirts, ripped jeans, unwashed hair. As an adjective, grungy means dirty or run-down: {a grungy apartment}, {grungy sneakers}.

Grungy means dirty, grimy, or run-down: {a grungy apartment}, {grungy clothes}. The word suggests accumulated grime or general seediness rather than fresh mess. It can describe places, objects, or people who look unwashed or unkempt. The related noun grunge names the 1990s rock genre associated with Seattle bands and their deliberately unpolished aesthetic.

A grunt is a short, low sound made in the throat—the noise of physical effort, displeasure, or minimal acknowledgment: {He answered with a grunt}. Pigs grunt characteristically. The verb means to make such a sound or to speak in grunts. In military slang, a grunt is an infantry soldier, especially one doing unglamorous ground work—the term captures the hard labor and low status.

Grunts are short, low sounds made with effort or minimal communication—the noise of physical exertion, acknowledgment without words, or animal vocalizations. Pigs grunt. So do people lifting heavy objects or responding noncommittally: {He answered with a grunt}. In military slang, a grunt is an infantry soldier—someone doing the hard, unglamorous work on the ground. The term extends to any low-level worker: {corporate grunts}.

Gruntwork is tedious, unglamorous labor that requires effort but little skill or creativity. It's the necessary but mind-numbing tasks that support more interesting work: data entry, filing, cleaning up code, stuffing envelopes. {I spent all weekend doing the gruntwork so the presentation would be ready Monday.} The term evokes the grunt of exertion and the low status of the work—it's what interns and new hires get stuck with. The word sometimes appears as two words or hyphenated.

Guacamole is a Mexican dip or spread made from mashed avocado, typically mixed with lime juice, salt, cilantro, onion, and often tomato or jalapeño. It's served with tortilla chips, tacos, or as a topping. The word comes from Nahuatl, combining words for avocado and sauce. {Extra guac costs two dollars.}

A guarantee is a formal promise or assurance that something will happen or that a product will perform as expected. Manufacturers offer guarantees against defects; banks guarantee loans. The verb means to make such a promise: {I guarantee you'll love it}. More loosely, guarantee expresses strong confidence: {Nothing in life is guaranteed}. A guarantor is someone who backs another's obligation.

Guaranteed means assured or certain, backed by a promise or warranty. A guaranteed {refund} comes without conditions. {Guaranteed delivery by Friday} means the seller commits to that deadline. The word often emphasizes certainty: {That's guaranteed to cause problems}. Something guaranteed has a guarantee behind it—formal or implied.

Guarantees are promises or assurances that something will happen or be done. A product {guarantee} pledges repair or replacement if it fails. To guarantee something is to make such a promise: {I guarantee you'll love it}. The word implies certainty or confidence, though guarantees are sometimes broken. A guarantor is someone who guarantees another's debt or obligation.

A guard is someone who provides protection; when something is guarded, it is protected, usually against a specific threat or danger: new measures to guard the city’s water supply. A body of guards with the same job can also be called a guard, collectively, and some devices that have a protective function can be called guards: Wipe down the sneeze guard at the salad bar. In sports, the noun and verb uses of guard have to do with defensive play. Someone who stands guard acts as a guard. If you are on your guard, you are taking precautions against possible threats.

Guarded describes careful restraint, especially in speech or manner. A guarded {response} reveals little, protecting the speaker from commitment or vulnerability. Someone guarded about their past keeps details private. The word suggests wariness—not hostile, but unwilling to be fully open. A guarded {prognosis} from a doctor signals uncertainty and caution about predicting outcomes.

A guardian is someone who watches over and protects another person or thing. In legal terms, a guardian has formal responsibility for someone who cannot care for themselves—typically a child whose parents have died or an incapacitated adult: {The court appointed her as guardian of her nephew}. More broadly, guardians protect places, traditions, or values: {guardians of democracy}, {a guardian of the gate}. The word implies ongoing vigilance and protective authority rather than momentary defense.

Guardians are people who protect, watch over, or have legal responsibility for someone or something. A legal guardian has court-appointed authority over a child or incapacitated adult: {The court named her grandmother as guardian}. Guardian extends to protectors generally—guardians of democracy, guardians of tradition. {Guardian angel} refers to a spiritual protector or someone who helps in times of need.

Guardianship is the legal responsibility for caring for someone who cannot care for themselves—typically a minor child or an incapacitated adult. A court grants guardianship when parents die, become unfit, or when adults lose capacity through illness or injury. The guardian makes decisions about the ward's welfare, finances, or both: {She was awarded guardianship of her nephew after the accident}. The term extends figuratively to any protective oversight: {guardianship of democratic values}.

A guardrail is a protective barrier along roads, bridges, or elevated areas to prevent vehicles or people from going over the edge. Highway guardrails absorb impact and redirect vehicles back onto the road. Figuratively, guardrails are limits that keep things on track: {The company needs guardrails on AI development}. In tech contexts, guardrails are constraints built into systems to prevent misuse or harmful outputs.

Guardrails are barriers along roads, bridges, or elevated areas to prevent vehicles or people from going over an edge. Metal guardrails line highways; wooden ones border mountain trails. Figuratively, guardrails are safeguards that keep processes or behavior within acceptable limits: {We need guardrails on AI development}, {The company put guardrails around employee spending}.

Guards are people who watch over something to protect or control it—prison guards, security guards, bodyguards. The term extends to protective devices: a mouth guard, a shin guard, a guard rail. To guard is to protect or watch over: {Guard the door while I'm gone}. To be on guard is to be watchful; to let your guard down is to become vulnerable. In basketball, guards are the smaller players who handle the ball.

Guava is a tropical fruit with green or yellow skin and pink or white flesh, typically eaten fresh or made into juice, paste, or jelly. The fruit is fragrant and sweet, studded with small edible seeds. Guava trees are cultivated throughout tropical regions: {The guava trees in the backyard produced more fruit than we could eat}.

Guerrilla is the standard spelling, but guerilla appears frequently enough to be considered a variant. A guerrilla is a member of an irregular armed force that uses tactics like ambushes, sabotage, and hit-and-run attacks rather than conventional warfare: {guerrilla fighters}, {guerrilla warfare}. Extended to any unconventional, scrappy approach: {guerrilla marketing}, {guerrilla gardening}.

Guerillas (also spelled guerrillas) are irregular fighters who use hit-and-run tactics, ambushes, and sabotage rather than conventional warfare. The term typically describes small armed groups fighting against larger government or occupying forces: {The guerillas operated from mountain hideouts}. Guerilla as an adjective describes this style of unconventional combat: {guerilla warfare}, {guerilla tactics}. The word extends to any underdog strategy using surprise and agility: {guerilla marketing}, {guerilla gardening}.

A guerrilla is a member of an irregular fighting force that uses tactics like ambushes, sabotage, and hit-and-run attacks rather than conventional warfare. Guerrillas typically operate in small bands against larger, established armies: {guerrilla fighters}, {guerrilla warfare}. The word extends to unconventional tactics in other domains: {guerrilla marketing}, {guerrilla gardening}. Also spelled guerilla.

Guerrillas are irregular fighters who use hit-and-run tactics, ambushes, and sabotage rather than conventional warfare. The term typically describes small, mobile groups fighting larger government or occupying forces: {The guerrillas operated from jungle hideouts}. Guerrilla as an adjective describes this style of unconventional combat: {guerrilla warfare}, {guerrilla tactics}. The word extends to unconventional approaches in other domains: {guerrilla marketing}, {guerrilla gardening}.

To guess is to offer an answer without being certain it's correct. A guess may be based on incomplete information, intuition, or pure chance: {Guess how old I am}, {If you don't know the answer, just guess}. To guess can also mean to suppose or think: {I guess we should get going}. A guess is the noun form—the answer itself: {That's a good guess}, {Your guess is as good as mine}. An educated guess draws on relevant knowledge rather than random speculation.

Guessing is forming an answer or judgment without sufficient information to be certain. It can be wild speculation or educated estimation: {I'm just guessing, but I'd say she's about forty}.
