The continuous form often signals tentativeness: {I'm guessing you didn't read the email}. To {keep someone guessing} is to deliberately withhold information.

Guesswork is the process of forming conclusions or making decisions based on incomplete information rather than certainty or careful analysis. When you rely on guesswork, you're essentially making educated guesses—sometimes informed by experience or intuition, sometimes not. {Without proper documentation, troubleshooting the system was pure guesswork.} The word often carries a slightly negative connotation, suggesting that more rigorous methods would be preferable.

A guest is someone received and entertained at another's home, or someone paying for lodging at a hotel or similar establishment. The word implies a temporary presence and often an expectation of hospitality: {We're having guests for dinner}, {The hotel guest complained about the noise}. Guest extends to anyone invited to participate: a guest {speaker}, a guest {star} on a television show. As a verb, to guest is to appear as a guest performer: {She guested on several podcasts}.

Guests are people who have been invited somewhere or who are receiving hospitality. A guest at a party or wedding attends by invitation; a guest at a hotel pays to stay there temporarily. The word suggests a relationship where someone is welcomed into another's space or event. Guest also works as an adjective for things associated with visitors: a guest {bedroom}, a guest {list}. To guest somewhere, especially on a show or podcast, is to appear as an invited participant rather than a regular.

Guidance is direction or advice intended to help someone make decisions or navigate situations: {career guidance}, {parental guidance}. The word implies ongoing counsel rather than a single instruction. Guidance also refers to the system that steers missiles or spacecraft to their targets: {a guidance system}. To seek guidance is to ask for help finding the right path.

A guide is something that directs or shows the way. It may be a person, a device, or text: We hired a guide to show us the old city. All new students are directed to a downloadable guide to dormitory life. As a verb, guide serves a similar function: subheadings guide the reader through the complicated process. As an adjective, guided typically communicates step-by-step direction: guided tour, guided meditation.

A guideline is a recommendation or principle intended to guide decisions or actions without being strictly mandatory. Guidelines suggest how something should be done while allowing flexibility: {The company issued guidelines for remote work}. Unlike rules, guidelines can be adapted to circumstances. Often plural: {Follow the safety guidelines}.

Guidelines are recommendations or instructions that direct behavior or decision-making without being strict rules. Unlike laws or regulations, guidelines suggest rather than mandate: {The CDC issued new guidelines for indoor masking}. They establish standards while allowing flexibility: {editorial guidelines}, {dietary guidelines}, {community guidelines}. To {follow guidelines} is to adhere to suggested best practices.

Guides are people or things that lead or direct. A tour guide shows visitors around; a trail guide leads hikers through wilderness. Extended to objects: a user guide explains how something works, a style guide sets standards. To guide is to lead, direct, or influence: {She guided him through the process}. {Let your conscience be your guide.}

A guild is an organized group of people who share a common trade, craft, or pursuit. Historically, guilds were associations of craftsmen or merchants who set standards, regulated training through apprenticeships, and protected their members' economic interests. Medieval Europe had powerful guilds of weavers, blacksmiths, and other tradespeople. The term now applies more broadly to any professional association or, in gaming, to groups of players who band together for cooperative play: {Our guild raids every Thursday night}.

Guilds are associations of craftspeople or merchants formed to protect shared interests. Medieval guilds controlled who could practice a trade, set quality standards, and trained apprentices. The term extends to any organized group with common pursuits: {a writers' guild}, {the Screen Actors Guild}. In video games, guilds are player-formed groups who collaborate on quests or raids.

A guillotine is a device for beheading, consisting of a heavy blade that slides down between vertical guides to sever the head from the body. Associated with the French Revolution, when it became the standard method of execution. The word extends to paper cutters with similar blade-drop mechanisms. As a verb, to guillotine is to execute by this method or, in British parliamentary procedure, to cut off debate by imposing a time limit.

Guillotines is the plural of guillotine, a device for beheading by dropping a heavy blade between two posts. Named for the French physician who advocated it as a humane execution method during the Revolution. The word extends to any device with a similar dropping-blade mechanism: a paper guillotine cuts stacks of sheets. As a verb, to guillotine is to execute by this method, or in British parliamentary procedure, to impose a time limit that cuts off debate: {The government guillotined the bill through committee}.

Guilt is the state of having committed a wrong or offense—a jury determines guilt or innocence. More commonly, guilt names the uncomfortable feeling that accompanies having done something wrong: {The guilt was eating at him}. Guilt can linger even without clear wrongdoing, as in survivor's guilt. To guilt someone is to make them feel guilty, often as manipulation: {She guilted me into going}.

Guilty describes someone who has committed an offense or wrong. In legal contexts, it's the formal verdict: {The jury found him guilty}. Beyond courtrooms, guilty captures the feeling of having done something wrong: {I felt guilty about lying to her}. A guilty {pleasure} is something enjoyed despite knowing it's lowbrow or embarrassing. A guilty {conscience} is an awareness of one's own wrongdoing. To {plead guilty} is to admit responsibility.

A guitar is a stringed musical instrument with a fretted neck and a hollow or solid body, played by plucking or strumming. The acoustic guitar has a resonating chamber; the electric guitar uses pickups to amplify sound electronically. Guitar appears in countless compound forms: {bass guitar}, {guitar solo}, {lead guitar}, {rhythm guitar}. {She's been taking guitar lessons since she was twelve.}

A guitarist is a person who plays the guitar. The term applies across styles and skill levels—from bedroom strummers to concert virtuosos. {The lead guitarist launched into a solo.} {She's been a guitarist in local bands for years.}

Guitars is the plural of guitar, a stringed musical instrument with a fretted neck and a flat or slightly curved body. The standard guitar has six strings, though bass guitars typically have four and twelve-string guitars double the usual complement. {She collects vintage guitars}. Electric guitars require amplification; acoustic guitars project sound through a hollow body.

A gulag is a prison camp where political prisoners are held under brutal conditions, or any oppressive, inescapable situation: {This office is a gulag}. The word comes from the Soviet system of forced labor camps that imprisoned millions. It now applies broadly to any place of harsh confinement or grinding misery: {summer school gulag}, {corporate gulag}.

Gulags were the Soviet system of forced labor camps where political prisoners and criminals were sent, often to remote Siberian regions. Conditions were brutal—prisoners faced starvation, exhaustion, and extreme cold. Millions died. The word now applies loosely to any oppressive prison or detention system: {The detention centers were described as modern-day gulags}.

A gulf is a large body of water partially enclosed by land—bigger than a bay: {the Gulf of Mexico}, {the Persian Gulf}. Extended, gulf means any wide separation or difference: {the gulf between rich and poor}, {a gulf of misunderstanding}. The word emphasizes vastness and difficulty of crossing, whether geographic or metaphorical. (Capitalized Gulf often refers specifically to the Persian Gulf or Gulf of Mexico region.)

A gull is a seabird with long wings, webbed feet, and typically gray and white plumage—the birds that wheel and cry over harbors, beaches, and parking lots. Seagull is the common name, though gulls range far inland. To gull someone is to deceive or trick them, treating them as credulous: {He was gulled into signing away his inheritance}. A gull in this sense is a dupe.

Gullibility is the tendency to be easily deceived or manipulated—a readiness to believe things without sufficient evidence. It suggests naivety or poor judgment: {His gullibility made him an easy mark for scammers}. The word carries mild contempt, implying the person should know better. Someone with gullibility lacks healthy skepticism.

Gullible describes someone easily deceived or quick to believe things without sufficient evidence. A gullible person falls for scams, accepts implausible stories, and takes things at face value: {He was gullible enough to wire money to a stranger}. The word carries a note of criticism—being gullible suggests naivety or poor judgment rather than innocent trust.

Gulp is to swallow hastily or greedily, often in large mouthfuls: {He gulped down his coffee and ran out the door}. It also describes the involuntary swallowing motion caused by fear or nervousness: {She gulped when she saw the exam questions}. As a noun, a gulp is a single act of swallowing or the amount swallowed: {He drained the glass in one gulp}. In British slang, a gulp can be a gullible person.

Gum is a sticky substance that comes from certain trees and plants, used in adhesives and food. Chewing gum is a rubbery confection meant to be chewed but not swallowed: {She popped a piece of gum in her mouth}. The gums are the firm pink tissue surrounding the teeth. To gum something is to stick it with adhesive, or to chew without teeth: {The baby gummed the cracker}. To {gum up the works} is to cause something to malfunction or slow down.

A gumball is a small, round piece of chewing gum with a hard candy shell, typically brightly colored and sold from coin-operated dispensers. The machines themselves are often called gumball machines: {She put a quarter in the gumball machine}. Gumballs are associated with childhood and often appear in nostalgic contexts.

Gumballs are small, round pieces of chewing gum with a hard candy shell, typically brightly colored and dispensed from coin-operated machines: {The kid put a quarter in and got three gumballs}. A gumball machine is a glass globe on a stand, iconic in American diners and arcades.

Gumbo is a thick, hearty stew that originated in Louisiana, typically containing meat or shellfish, vegetables, and a roux-based broth, often served over rice. The dish reflects the region's cultural fusion, drawing from African, French, and Native American culinary traditions. Okra or filé powder (ground sassafras leaves) traditionally serves as a thickener. By extension, gumbo can describe any mixture of diverse elements: {The city's music scene is a gumbo of jazz, blues, and zydeco}.

Gummies are chewy, gelatin-based candies with a soft, elastic texture—gummy bears being the most iconic. The term now commonly refers to edible cannabis products in this form: {I took a couple of gummies before the concert}. Gummy vitamins have also become popular, especially for children and adults who dislike swallowing pills.

Gummy describes something sticky, soft, and chewy—like gum. Gummy {bears} and gummy {worms} are gelatin candies with that characteristic texture. A gummy {smile} shows the gums above the teeth. Something can become gummy when wet or old: {The adhesive turned gummy in the heat}. Eyes may be gummy with sleep or discharge.

Gumption is spirited initiative and resourcefulness—the combination of courage and common sense that gets things done. Someone with gumption doesn't wait for permission or instructions: {She had the gumption to start her own business at nineteen}. The word carries admiration for practical boldness rather than reckless daring.

Gums are the firm pink tissue surrounding the base of the teeth. Healthy gums hold teeth securely; diseased gums recede or bleed. To gum something is to chew it without teeth: {The baby gummed the cracker}. {By the numbers} means to obstruct progress through excessive procedure—to gum up the works.

A gumshoe is a detective, especially a private investigator. The term comes from soft-soled rubber shoes that allowed quiet movement—ideal for tailing suspects without being heard. The word evokes noir fiction and old Hollywood: {The gumshoe lit a cigarette and watched the building from across the street}. As a verb, to gumshoe is to investigate or snoop around.

Gumshoes are soft-soled shoes, originally made with rubber (gum) soles that allow quiet movement. From this stealthy quality, gumshoe became slang for a detective or private investigator—someone who sneaks around gathering information: {The gumshoe tailed the suspect through back alleys}. The term has an old-fashioned, noir flavor.

Guns that are weapons range in size from hand-held—a handgun—to jumbo sized, such as a cannon. The essential features of a gun are a tube through which a high-speed projectile is fired, and a mechanism for making this happen. Guns that aren’t weapons retain some of their features: usually the trigger, barrel, or projectile: glue gun, laser gun. If you jump the gun, you start too soon; the expression references the harmless starting pistol fired to begin a race. When you gun someone down, you shoot them with a real gun. If you are gunning for something, you actively support it: the hardliners are gunning for execution.

A gunfight is a battle or confrontation in which the participants shoot guns at each other. The word evokes the Old West—two men facing off in a dusty street—but applies to any exchange of gunfire: {The robbery turned into a gunfight with police}. A gunfighter is someone skilled in such confrontations.

A gunfighter is someone skilled in armed combat with pistols, especially in the context of the American Old West. The term evokes frontier lawmen, outlaws, and duelists of the late 1800s: {Wyatt Earp was a legendary gunfighter}. In modern use, gunfighter often appears in westerns and video games, carrying romantic or mythologized connotations of quick draws and showdowns at high noon.

Gunfights is the plural of gunfight—a battle or duel between people with guns. The word evokes the Old West, where lawmen and outlaws supposedly settled disputes in the street: {The movie climaxed with a gunfight at high noon}. Modern usage extends to any armed exchange of fire: {The robbery ended in a gunfight with police}.

Gunfire is the repeated discharge of firearms—the sound and action of guns being shot: {We heard gunfire in the distance}. The term typically suggests multiple shots or sustained shooting rather than a single report. Gunfire appears in contexts ranging from combat to crime scenes to celebratory shooting.

Gunk is thick, sticky, unidentifiable residue—the greasy buildup in an engine, the mysterious substance clogging a drain, the crud accumulating in corners. The word suggests something unpleasant that needs cleaning: {There's gunk all over the stovetop}. To gunk up is to clog or foul with such residue: {Hair and soap had gunked up the pipes}.

A gunman is a person armed with a gun, especially one who uses it to commit violence or crime. News reports describe bank robbers, assassins, and mass shooters as gunmen: {A gunman opened fire in the shopping mall}. The term sometimes applies to hired killers or armed enforcers. Despite the -man suffix, gunman occasionally describes women in news coverage, though {shooter} increasingly serves as a neutral alternative.

Gunmen is the plural of gunman—a person armed with a gun, especially one who uses it to commit crimes or acts of violence. News reports describe {gunmen opening fire} or {masked gunmen robbing a bank}. The term typically implies threat or aggression rather than lawful gun ownership.

Gunmetal is a dark bluish-gray color resembling the metal alloy traditionally used in gun barrels and other hardware. The color suggests industrial toughness and understated sophistication: {a gunmetal sky before the storm}, {gunmetal finish on the watch}. The alloy itself is a bronze containing copper, tin, and zinc.

A gunner is someone who operates a gun, especially a military crew member who fires artillery, machine guns, or aircraft weapons. In sports, particularly basketball, a gunner is a player who shoots frequently, sometimes to a fault: {He's a talented gunner but needs to pass more}. In British English, a gunner is a private in the Royal Artillery.

Gunning is the present participle of gun, used in several distinct ways. If you're gunning for something or someone, you're aggressively pursuing it: {She's gunning for the promotion}. When gunning for a person, it often implies seeking to harm or defeat them. Gunning also describes the act of shooting or hunting with firearms, or revving an engine hard: {He was gunning the motor at the stoplight}.

Gunplay is the shooting of guns, especially in a confrontation or fight. The word appears most often in descriptions of action movies, crime scenes, or violent encounters: {The film features extended gunplay in the final act}. It treats shooting as spectacle or activity rather than emphasizing its consequences.

Gunpoint appears almost exclusively in the phrase {at gunpoint}, describing a situation where someone is threatened or coerced by a person holding a gun: {They were robbed at gunpoint}. The word emphasizes the threat of the weapon rather than its discharge—compliance is demanded under implied violence.

Gunpowder is an explosive mixture of saltpeter, charcoal, and sulfur—the original propellant for firearms and the first chemical explosive in widespread use. It remains important in fireworks, blasting, and ammunition primers. {The smell of gunpowder hung in the air}. Green gunpowder is a type of Chinese tea, its leaves rolled into pellet shapes.

A gunrunner is someone who smuggles or illegally traffics firearms, typically across borders or to prohibited buyers. The term suggests organized criminal activity rather than casual lawbreaking: {The gunrunner supplied weapons to rebel forces}. Also gun-runner or gun runner.

Gunrunning is the illegal smuggling of firearms, typically across borders or into conflict zones. The term emphasizes the clandestine, often dangerous nature of the trade: {He was arrested for gunrunning to rebel militias}. A person engaged in this activity is a gunrunner.

Guns is the plural of gun—weapons that fire projectiles, or devices shaped like them. As a verb, guns means to shoot or pursue aggressively: {She guns the engine}, {He's gunning for a promotion}. In slang, guns are muscular arms, especially biceps: {Check out the guns on that guy}.

A gunship is a heavily armed military aircraft designed to provide close air support, typically a helicopter or fixed-wing plane fitted with powerful weapons systems. Attack helicopters and converted cargo planes serve as gunships, delivering sustained firepower against ground targets: {The gunship circled overhead, providing cover for the troops below}.

A gunshot is the firing of a gun or the sound it produces: {We heard gunshots in the distance}. Gunshot also describes the range a gun can reach: {within gunshot of the cabin}. A gunshot wound is an injury caused by a bullet or other projectile fired from a gun.

Gunshots are the sounds or discharges produced when guns are fired. The word can refer to the explosive noise itself {I heard gunshots in the distance}, the act of firing {multiple gunshots rang out}, or the projectiles and their impact {gunshot wounds}. A gunshot is also the range a gun can shoot: {within gunshot of the village}.

Gunshy describes someone who flinches or hesitates because of a past bad experience—like a hunting dog that cowers at gunfire after being startled by it. The word applies to any learned wariness: {After the divorce, she was gunshy about relationships}. Also spelled gun-shy.

A gunslinger is someone skilled and quick with a handgun, especially in the context of the American Old West. The term evokes frontier outlaws, lawmen, and duels: {The gunslinger pushed through the saloon doors}. Figuratively, a gunslinger is someone bold and aggressive in their field—a corporate gunslinger, a legal gunslinger—suggesting someone who shoots first and asks questions later.

Gunslingers are people skilled with handguns, especially in the context of the American Old West. The term evokes frontier lawmen, outlaws, and hired guns who settled disputes with six-shooters: {The movie featured a showdown between two gunslingers}. Figuratively, a gunslinger is anyone bold and aggressive in their field—a corporate gunslinger, a legal gunslinger.

A guppy is a small, brightly colored freshwater fish popular in home aquariums, native to South America and the Caribbean. Guppies are hardy, breed prolifically, and are often a beginner's first pet fish. The word sometimes describes someone perceived as small, weak, or insignificant: {He's just a guppy in a tank full of sharks}.

Gurgle is the bubbling, throaty sound of liquid moving through a narrow passage—water draining, a brook flowing over stones, a baby's contented vocalization. The word imitates the sound it describes: {The drain gurgled}. {The baby gurgled happily}. As a noun, it's an instance of that sound: {the gurgle of the coffee pot}.

Gurgles is the sound of liquid flowing irregularly, with bubbles and interruptions—water down a drain, a stream over rocks, a baby's throat. The word imitates the sound itself. Babies gurgle contentedly; stomachs gurgle with hunger or digestion. A brook gurgles through a meadow. As a noun: {the gurgle of wine being poured}.

Gurgling is the sound of liquid moving irregularly through a narrow passage—water draining, a brook flowing over stones, a baby's throat producing bubbly noises. The word imitates what it describes: {The coffee maker gurgled to life}. A gurgling {stomach} signals hunger or digestion. {The baby gurgled happily in her crib.}

A gurney is a wheeled stretcher used to transport patients in hospitals and ambulances. The patient lies flat while medical staff roll the gurney through hallways or into emergency vehicles: {They rushed him through the ER on a gurney}. The term is primarily American; British English favors trolley.

A guru is a spiritual teacher or guide, originally in Hinduism and Buddhism, where the relationship between guru and disciple is central to religious practice. The word has spread to mean any authoritative expert or influential leader in a field: {a fitness guru}, {a tech guru}, {a self-help guru}. In casual use, guru often carries a whiff of skepticism about whether the expertise is genuine.

Gurus is the plural of guru, a spiritual teacher or guide in Hindu and Buddhist traditions. The word has expanded to mean any expert or authority figure with devoted followers: {fitness gurus}, {tech gurus}, {self-help gurus}. The term often carries slight skepticism about whether the expertise or wisdom is genuine.

Gush describes liquid flowing out rapidly and forcefully: {Water gushed from the broken pipe}. The word extends to any sudden outpouring—emotions, words, praise. To gush over something is to express effusive, often excessive enthusiasm: {She gushed about the new restaurant}. The noun works similarly: {a gush of water}, {a gush of sentiment}. Gushing praise often implies insincerity or lack of restraint.

A gusher is an oil well that produces a powerful, uncontrolled flow—oil shooting into the air from underground pressure. The term extends to anything that pours forth abundantly: a gusher of tears, a gusher of praise. A person who gushes effusively may also be called a gusher: {She's such a gusher about her grandchildren}.

Gushes is the third-person singular of gush. To gush is to flow out rapidly and abundantly: {Water gushed from the broken pipe}. Figuratively, to gush is to express enthusiasm effusively, often to an excessive or cloying degree: {She gushes over every new restaurant like it's the best thing she's ever tasted}. As a noun, a gush is a sudden outpouring.

Gushing describes liquid flowing out rapidly and abundantly: {Water came gushing from the broken pipe}. More often, gushing refers to excessive or effusive expression of emotion or praise: {gushing compliments}, {She was gushing about the wedding}. The word implies lack of restraint—enthusiasm that may seem overdone or insincere.

A gust is a sudden, brief rush of wind: {A gust nearly knocked her off balance}. The word extends to any similar burst—a gust of {rain}, a gust of {laughter}, a gust of {emotion}. To gust is to blow in such bursts: {Winds gusted to forty miles per hour}.

Gusto is enthusiastic enjoyment or vigor in doing something: {She tackled the project with gusto}, {He ate with gusto}. The word implies wholehearted, energetic engagement rather than mere participation. Someone who does something with gusto throws themselves into it completely.

Gusts are sudden, brief rushes of wind stronger than the prevailing breeze: {Gusts of up to fifty miles per hour knocked down power lines}. The word extends to any sudden outburst: a gust of {laughter}, a gust of {emotion}. As a verb, wind gusts when it blows in bursts rather than steadily.

Gut refers to the digestive tract, especially the intestines. A {gut feeling} or {gut reaction} comes from instinct rather than deliberation—the belly as seat of intuition. Guts means courage: {It takes guts to stand up to a bully}. To gut something is to remove its internal organs, or to strip out the interior: {They gutted the building}. A gut punch is a blow to the stomach, or figuratively, devastating news.

Gutless means lacking courage or determination—cowardly. The gut has long been associated with bravery and resolve, so to be gutless is to lack that inner fortitude: {a gutless decision}, {too gutless to speak up}. The word carries contempt, implying not just fear but a fundamental weakness of character.

Guts are the intestines and other internal organs of the body, especially the stomach and bowels: {I felt it in my guts}. The word extends to the inner workings of anything: {the guts of a computer}. Figuratively, guts means courage or determination: {It takes guts to stand up to a bully}. To gut something is to remove its insides or strip it bare: {gut a fish}, {fire gutted the building}. To {hate someone's guts} is to despise them utterly.

Gutshot describes being shot in the abdomen, a wound that in the era before modern medicine was typically fatal and notoriously painful. The term extends to poker, where a gutshot straight draw means you need one specific card in the middle of a sequence to complete your hand—like needing a 7 to fill 5-6-8-9. Both uses share the sense of something hitting you in the vulnerable middle. {He was gutshot in the firefight and barely survived.}

Gutsy means showing courage, boldness, or nerve—especially in circumstances where caution might be expected. A gutsy {decision} involves risk. A gutsy {performance} displays fearless commitment. The word carries admiration for someone willing to take chances: {It was gutsy of her to confront the board directly}. More casual than courageous, with a hint of scrappy determination.

Gutted describes having the internal organs removed: {a gutted fish}. By extension, it means stripped of contents or destroyed inside: {The fire left the building gutted}. In British slang, gutted means devastated or bitterly disappointed: {I was absolutely gutted when we lost}.

A gutter is a depressed area in which water or other liquid collects. Gutters are installed around the edges of roofs to carry rain to a downspout, and they run along the sides of roads for proper drainage. If someone is in the gutter they are in a low, poor condition – as if by the side of the road. As an adjective, gutter means low and vulgar (gutter talk). When a candle gutters, liquid wax runs down its side.

Gutters are channels that collect and direct water, especially the troughs along the edges of roofs that carry rainwater away from buildings: {The gutters are clogged with leaves}. Streets have gutters at the curb for drainage. The gutter suggests degradation or squalor: {born in the gutter}, {gutter language}. In bowling, the gutters are the troughs flanking the lane. In printing and bookbinding, the gutter is the blank space where facing pages meet at the spine.

Gutting is the act of removing the internal organs from a fish or animal, or figuratively, stripping the essential contents from something: {gutting a house before renovation}. Most commonly, gutting describes an emotionally devastating experience: {The loss was absolutely gutting}. Something gutting leaves you feeling hollowed out, as if your insides have been removed.

A guy is a man or fellow: {Some guy called for you}. In the plural, guys has become a casual address for any group regardless of gender: {Hey guys, what's going on?} To guy something is to secure it with ropes or wires—guy wires stabilize tents, towers, and masts. The word also means to mock or ridicule, though this sense is rare outside British English. (Capitalized Guy is a given name.)

Guys is the plural of guy, a man or fellow. In casual speech, guys has become a general address for groups regardless of gender: {Hey guys, what's up?} Some object to this usage as excluding women, though many speakers consider it gender-neutral in the plural. {Those guys over there} can mean any group of people.

Guzzle means to drink greedily or in large quantities: {He guzzled three beers before anyone else finished one}. The word suggests rapid, unrefined consumption—gulping rather than sipping. It extends to fuel consumption: {That old truck guzzles gas}. A guzzler is someone or something that consumes excessively.

Guzzling is drinking greedily or in large quantities, often with enthusiasm and little restraint. The word suggests rapid, noisy consumption—someone guzzling beer at a party isn't sipping delicately. By extension, guzzling applies to anything that consumes resources voraciously: a {gas-guzzling SUV} burns through fuel the way a thirsty person downs a cold drink. {He spent the afternoon guzzling sodas by the pool.}

A gym is a place for physical exercise and fitness training, typically equipped with weights, machines, and space for activities. Short for gymnasium, gym is now the dominant form in everyday speech: {I'm heading to the gym}. School gyms double as spaces for basketball, assemblies, and dances. The adjective form appears in compounds: {gym clothes}, {gym bag}, {gym rat}.

A gymnasium is a large room or building equipped for indoor sports, physical education, and exercise. In American schools, it's where students take gym class and where basketball games and assemblies are held. The word is often shortened to gym. In German-speaking countries and some others, a Gymnasium is a secondary school that prepares students for university.

A gymnast is an athlete who performs gymnastics—exercises requiring strength, flexibility, balance, and coordination on apparatus like bars, beams, rings, and floor mats. Gymnasts train intensively from childhood, and the sport is known for producing competitors who peak in their teens: {She was a gymnast before becoming a stunt double}.

Gymnastics is a sport involving physical exercises that demonstrate strength, flexibility, balance, and coordination—typically on apparatus like bars, beams, and rings, or on floor mats. The word extends to any display of agility or elaborate maneuvering: {mental gymnastics}, {rhetorical gymnastics}. These figurative uses often carry a note of skepticism, suggesting someone is working too hard to justify something.

Gymnasts are athletes who perform gymnastics—a sport involving strength, flexibility, balance, and acrobatic skill. They compete on apparatus like bars, beams, and rings, or perform floor routines. The word applies across competitive levels, from Olympic gymnasts to children in recreational classes: {The gymnasts warmed up on the mats before practice}.

Gyoza are Japanese dumplings, typically crescent-shaped with thin wheat wrappers crimped along one edge, filled with seasoned ground pork and cabbage. They're usually pan-fried to create a crispy bottom while the top steams tender: {We ordered gyoza as an appetizer}. The word comes from Chinese, where similar dumplings are called jiaozi.

A gyro is a Greek sandwich of sliced meat (usually lamb or beef) roasted on a vertical spit, served in pita bread with tomatoes, onions, and tzatziki sauce. The name comes from the Greek word for "turn," referring to the rotating spit. Pronounced with a soft g (YEE-roh), though "JY-roh" is common in American English. Separately, gyro is short for gyroscope—a spinning device that maintains orientation—used in aviation, navigation, and smartphones.

Gyros is the standard plural of gyro, the Greek sandwich of sliced meat cooked on a vertical rotisserie, served in pita with tomatoes, onions, and tzatziki sauce. The word comes from Greek for "turn," referring to the rotating spit. Pronounced with either a hard or soft g: {I ordered two gyros for lunch}.

A gyroscope is a spinning wheel or disc mounted so it can rotate freely in any direction. Once spinning, it resists changes to its orientation, maintaining a stable axis regardless of how its frame moves. This property makes gyroscopes essential for navigation systems, aircraft instruments, and smartphone motion sensors. {The ship's gyroscope kept the compass steady through rough seas.}

A habanero is a small, lantern-shaped chile pepper known for intense heat. Among the hottest peppers in common culinary use, habaneros have a fruity, citrusy flavor beneath the fire. They're central to Caribbean and Yucatecan cuisine: {habanero salsa}, {habanero hot sauce}. The name comes from Havana, though the pepper likely originated in South America.

A habit is a behavior repeated so often it becomes automatic: {I'm trying to break my habit of checking my phone first thing in the morning}. The word can suggest something hard to stop, especially with addictive substances: {a cocaine habit}. A habit is also the distinctive garment worn by members of religious orders: {a nun's habit}. To be {in the habit of} doing something is to do it regularly.

A habitat is the natural environment where a plant or animal lives and finds what it needs to survive. Each species has its preferred habitat—fish need water, cacti need arid ground. A natural habitat is one found in nature; an artificial habitat is one humans create, as in a zoo. {Deforestation is destroying the habitat of countless species.} Habitat destruction and conservation are ongoing concerns as humans encroach on wild places.

Habitats is the plural of habitat, the natural environment where a species lives and thrives. Conservation efforts focus on protecting habitats: {The wetlands provide critical habitats for migratory birds}. The word extends to any environment suited to particular needs: {The city's coffee shops became habitats for remote workers}.

Habits are behaviors repeated so regularly they become automatic. A habit can be personal routine {(her habit of reading before bed)}, an addiction {(a drug habit)}, or a characteristic pattern {(force of habit)}. The word also names the distinctive garment worn by members of a religious order: {a nun's habit}.

A hacienda is a large estate or plantation, especially in Spanish-speaking regions of the Americas. The term evokes colonial-era agricultural operations with sprawling lands, often including a substantial main house. In contemporary use, hacienda may describe any large rural property with Spanish architectural influence: {They converted the old hacienda into a boutique hotel}.

In modern use, the commonest meaning of hack, noun and verb, has to do with invasive access to computer data: They hacked the email account and forwarded the contents to WikiLeaks. This meaning arose from the earlier core meaning of hack, to chop or cut crudely, as with a hatchet or machete. If someone is hacking without computers or sharp instruments, they are coughing loudly. A person referred to as a hack is being disparaged as a poor writer who turns out words for money. A life hack is a clever shortcut for an ordinary task.

A hackathon is an event where programmers, designers, and others collaborate intensively over a short period—typically 24 to 48 hours—to build software projects or solve technical problems. The name combines "hack" (in its creative coding sense) with "marathon." Originally common in tech companies and universities, hackathons have spread to other fields: {The city hosted a hackathon to develop civic apps}.

Hacked has two main clusters of meaning. From hack as rough cutting: something crudely chopped or shortened, or a person who is exhausted or fed up: {I'm completely hacked after that shift}. From hack as unauthorized computer access: a system that has been broken into or compromised: {My account got hacked}. In gaming and tech culture, hacked can mean cleverly modified or repurposed: {a hacked router running custom firmware}.

A hacker is someone who gains unauthorized access to computer systems, often to steal data or cause disruption: {Hackers breached the company's servers}. In its original and still-current sense among programmers, a hacker is simply someone skilled at creative problem-solving with technology—an enthusiast who enjoys exploring systems deeply. The negative sense now dominates popular usage, though insiders distinguish between hackers (curious explorers) and crackers (malicious intruders). More loosely, a hack or life hack is any clever shortcut, and someone who finds such solutions hacks their way through problems.

Hackers are people who gain unauthorized access to computer systems, whether for mischief, theft, or exposing vulnerabilities. The word originally meant skilled programmers who could solve problems creatively—{life hackers} and {growth hackers} retain this positive sense of clever improvisation. But the dominant meaning now involves breaking into networks: {Hackers stole millions of credit card numbers}. White-hat hackers test security legally; black-hat hackers exploit it criminally.

Hacking is working with computer systems in ways that probe their limits or bypass their security. The word covers a spectrum: a hacker might be a skilled programmer solving problems creatively, or someone breaking into systems without authorization. {She spent the weekend hacking together a prototype.} {The breach resulted from hacking by a foreign group.} Context usually clarifies whether the sense is admiring or criminal. Outside computing, hacking means chopping roughly: {hacking through underbrush}.

Hackles are the erectile hairs or feathers along an animal's neck and back that rise when the creature feels threatened or aggressive—a dog's hackles stand up when confronting an intruder. The word appears most often in the figurative phrase {raise someone's hackles}, meaning to provoke anger or defensiveness: {His condescending tone raised her hackles}. In fly fishing, hackles are feathers wound around a hook to create artificial flies.

Hacks connects to cutting or chopping—rough, forceful strokes rather than precise ones. A hack is a crude cut, or the tool that makes it. To hack through something is to chop your way: {We hacked through the underbrush}. A hacking cough is harsh and repetitive. In computing, to hack is to break into systems or to code cleverly; a hack is either an intrusion or an ingenious shortcut: {life hacks}, {productivity hacks}. A hack writer produces work quickly without artistry. A hack is also a taxi or a worn-out horse—something for hire, used hard.

A hacksaw is a fine-toothed saw with a blade held in a rigid frame, designed for cutting metal and other hard materials. The blade is thin and replaceable, mounted under tension. To hacksaw something is to cut it with this tool: {He hacksawed through the padlock}.

A hag is an ugly old woman, especially one perceived as frightening or malevolent. In folklore, hags are witches or evil spirits: {The old hag cursed the village}. The word is insulting when applied to real women, implying both age and unpleasantness: {Some hag yelled at me for parking in her spot}.

Haggard describes someone looking exhausted, gaunt, or worn down—typically from prolonged stress, illness, lack of sleep, or suffering. The word suggests visible deterioration: sunken cheeks, dark circles, a drawn face. {She looked haggard after weeks of caring for her dying mother.} In falconry, haggard refers to a hawk caught as an adult, already wild—a sense that may have influenced the word's connotations of being weathered by hard experience.

Haggis is a Scottish dish made from sheep's organs—heart, liver, and lungs—minced with oatmeal, suet, and spices, traditionally encased in the animal's stomach and boiled. It has a savory, nutty flavor and crumbly texture. Haggis is the centerpiece of Burns Night suppers, where it's ceremonially addressed before serving: {We had haggis with neeps and tatties}.

To haggle is to negotiate persistently over price or terms, typically in a back-and-forth exchange where each party tries to get a better deal: {We haggled over the rug for twenty minutes}. Haggling is expected in bazaars and flea markets, less so in department stores. The word suggests minor commerce and mild contention rather than formal negotiation.

Haggling is negotiating over price or terms, typically in a back-and-forth exchange where each party pushes for better conditions. The practice is expected in some markets and cultures, awkward in others: {We spent twenty minutes haggling over the rug}. To haggle is to engage in such negotiation, often with a sense of persistent or petty bargaining.

Hags is the plural of hag, an ugly old woman, especially one perceived as malicious or frightening. The word carries strong negative connotations—calling someone a hag suggests they are not just aged but withered, bitter, or cruel. In folklore, hags are often witches or supernatural beings who torment the living: {The three hags stirred their cauldron}. The singular appears in compounds like {old hag} and {haggard}.

A haiden is the worship hall of a Shinto shrine, the building where visitors pray and make offerings. It stands in front of the honden, the inner sanctuary where the deity resides. Most shrine visitors interact only with the haiden, approaching to clap, bow, and offer coins: {We rang the bell and prayed at the haiden}.

A haiku is a form of Japanese poetry consisting of three lines with a fixed syllable pattern: five syllables, then seven, then five. Traditional haiku evoke nature or seasons through brief, vivid imagery. The form has been widely adopted in English, though some argue the syllable count matters less than the spirit of compression and observation: {An old silent pond / A frog jumps into the pond / Splash! Silence again.}

Haikus is the plural of haiku, a form of Japanese poetry consisting of three lines with five, seven, and five syllables respectively. Traditional haikus capture a moment in nature or evoke a season, though contemporary ones range widely: {She writes haikus on her commute}. The plural haiku is equally correct.

Hail is mainly a verb with meanings connected with greeting, welcoming, and getting attention. The interjection hail has mainly archaic and formal uses, but is used in expressions such as Hail to the chief.

A hailstorm is a storm that produces hail—pellets of ice that form in thunderclouds and fall to the ground. Hailstorms can damage crops, vehicles, and rooftops. Figuratively, a hailstorm describes any intense barrage: {a hailstorm of criticism}, {a hailstorm of bullets}.

Hair is the fine threadlike strands that grow from the skin of mammals. Human hair grows most densely on the head, where it serves as protection and decoration. A single strand is also a hair: {There's a hair in my soup}. Hair suggests extreme fineness—a {hair's breadth} is the narrowest possible margin, and to {split hairs} is to make overly fine distinctions. {Let your hair down} means relax; {hair of the dog} is a drink to cure a hangover.

A hairball is a compact mass of fur that accumulates in an animal's digestive tract, typically from grooming, and is eventually regurgitated. Cats are especially prone to them: {The cat hacked up a hairball on the rug}. In computing, hairball describes tangled, unmanageable code—a mess that's hard to untangle: {The legacy system was a complete hairball}.

A haircut is the act of cutting someone's hair, or the style that results: {I need a haircut}, {That's a nice haircut}. In finance, a haircut is a reduction in an asset's value for accounting or lending purposes, or a loss taken on an investment: {Bondholders took a 50% haircut in the restructuring}.

Haircuts are acts of cutting someone's hair, or the styles that result. You get a haircut at a barbershop or salon. A {buzz cut} or {pixie cut} names the style; {I need a haircut} refers to the service. In finance, a haircut is a percentage reduction from an asset's value—what a lender discounts when accepting collateral: {The bank applied a 20% haircut to the bonds}.

A hairdo is a hairstyle—the way someone's hair is cut, arranged, or worn. The word often implies deliberate styling or a particular look: {She spent an hour on her hairdo before the party}. It can sound slightly dated or playful compared to the neutral "hairstyle."

A hairdresser is a person who cuts, styles, and colors hair professionally. The term is interchangeable with hair stylist, though hairdresser sounds slightly more traditional. A hairdresser's workplace is a salon or hairdresser's: {I have an appointment at the hairdresser's}.

The hairline is where hair meets forehead—the boundary of scalp hair growth. A receding hairline moves backward with age or baldness. As an adjective, hairline means extremely thin or fine: a hairline {crack}, a hairline {fracture}. Such flaws are barely visible but potentially serious.

A hairpin is a U-shaped pin used to hold hair in place, typically made of metal or plastic. The shape gives rise to figurative uses: a hairpin turn or hairpin curve is an extremely sharp bend in a road that doubles back on itself. As an adjective, hairpin describes anything with that characteristic tight, looping shape: {The mountain road had three hairpin turns before the summit}.

Hairpins are U-shaped pins used to hold hair in place, typically made of wire or plastic. The shape gives rise to figurative uses: a hairpin turn or hairpin curve is a road bend so sharp it doubles back on itself. As a verb, to hairpin is to make such a sharp reversal: {The trail hairpins up the mountain}.

Hairsplitting is making distinctions so fine they seem pointless or pedantic. The image is of someone attempting to split a single hair—an exercise in excessive precision: {The debate devolved into hairsplitting over word choices}. A hairsplitter is someone prone to such distinctions. The adjective hairsplitting describes arguments or people: {hairsplitting objections}.

Hairspray is an aerosol or pump product sprayed onto hair to hold a style in place. It works by coating strands with a fine layer of stiffening polymer. Hairspray ranges from flexible hold to extra-firm: {She used so much hairspray her hair felt like a helmet}. The product became iconic in mid-20th-century bouffant styles.

A hairstyle is the way hair is cut, arranged, or worn. The term covers everything from basic cuts to elaborate arrangements: {She changed her hairstyle after the breakup}. A particular hairstyle may signal cultural identity, professional context, or personal expression. Hair styled for a specific occasion—a wedding, prom—is also a hairstyle.

Hairy means covered with hair or having abundant hair: {a hairy chest}, {hairy legs}. Things resembling hair can make something hairy: {hairy roots}, {hairy caterpillars}. Informally, hairy describes situations that are dangerous, difficult, or anxiety-inducing: {The drive through the mountains got pretty hairy in the fog}.

Hajj is the annual Islamic pilgrimage to Mecca, Saudi Arabia, one of the Five Pillars of Islam. Every Muslim who is physically and financially able is required to make the hajj at least once in their lifetime. The pilgrimage occurs during the Islamic month of Dhu al-Hijjah and involves specific rituals over several days: {After completing the hajj, he added the honorific "Hajji" to his name}. Also spelled hadj.

Halal is an Arabic term meaning permissible under Islamic law, most commonly applied to food prepared according to Muslim dietary requirements. Meat must come from animals slaughtered in a specific ritual manner, and pork and alcohol are forbidden entirely. {Is this restaurant halal?} The term extends beyond food to describe anything permissible in Islam, including financial practices, clothing, and conduct. Halal certification has become a significant consideration in global food production and marketing.

Half is one of two equal parts of something: {Cut the apple in half}. It functions as noun, adjective, and adverb: {the first half}, {half price}, {half asleep}. Half often suggests incompleteness or insufficiency: {half measures}, {half-baked ideas}, {He only half listened}. In time expressions, half past means thirty minutes after: {half past three}. {Half the battle} is a significant portion of the difficulty; {my other half} is a spouse or partner.

Halfassed describes something done with minimal effort or care—sloppy, incomplete, or barely adequate: {a halfassed attempt at an apology}, {Don't give me some halfassed excuse}. The image suggests using only half of one's rear end, implying insufficient commitment. Also spelled half-assed. The word is mildly vulgar but common in casual speech.

Halfhearted describes effort or enthusiasm that falls short of full commitment. A halfhearted {apology} lacks sincerity; a halfhearted {attempt} suggests going through the motions without real investment. The word implies the person could try harder but doesn't: {He made a halfhearted effort to find his keys before giving up}.

A halfling is a small humanoid creature in fantasy fiction, typically standing about half the height of a human. The term was popularized by J.R.R. Tolkien as an alternative name for hobbits, and later adopted by Dungeons & Dragons and other fantasy games to describe similar diminutive folk—cheerful, nimble, and often underestimated: {The halfling rogue slipped past the guards unnoticed}.

Halflings are a fictional race of small humanoid creatures, most famously appearing in J.R.R. Tolkien's Middle-earth stories, where they are also called hobbits. Standing roughly half human height, they are typically depicted as peaceful, fond of comfort, and possessing unexpected courage when circumstances demand it. The term has been adopted by fantasy role-playing games and fiction as a generic name for hobbit-like peoples, often to avoid trademark issues.

Halfmast describes a flag positioned partway down its pole as a sign of mourning or respect for the dead: {Flags flew at halfmast after the president's death}. The term extends to anything lowered or drooping: {His pants were at halfmast}. Also spelled half-mast. On land, half-staff is the more formal term in American English.

A halfpipe is a U-shaped ramp or channel used in skateboarding, snowboarding, and skiing, where athletes ride up the curved walls to perform aerial tricks. The name describes the shape—like a pipe cut lengthwise in half. {She landed a 1080 in the halfpipe}. A superpipe is an oversized version used in professional competitions.

Halfpipes are U-shaped ramps or channels used in skateboarding, snowboarding, and skiing. The structure resembles a pipe cut lengthwise—riders descend one wall, cross the flat bottom, and ascend the opposite wall to perform aerial tricks before dropping back in. {She landed a 1080 in the halfpipe}. Olympic halfpipe events feature walls over twenty feet high.

Halftime is the interval between the two halves of a game, especially in football or basketball. Teams retreat to locker rooms, bands perform, and viewers raid the refrigerator. The halftime {show} at major events like the Super Bowl has become a spectacle rivaling the game itself. As an adjective, halftime describes something occurring at or lasting half the standard time: {a halftime job}, {the halftime score}.

Halfway describes a point or position equidistant between two others, whether in space, time, or degree. If you meet someone halfway, you compromise by each giving up something. A halfway house provides transitional housing for people leaving institutions like prisons or rehabilitation centers. Something done halfway is incomplete or lacking full commitment: {Don't do the job halfway}. The word functions as both adjective and adverb: {We're halfway through the project} or {a halfway decent attempt}.

Halibut is a large flatfish prized for its firm, mild white flesh. Among the biggest of the flatfish, halibut can weigh several hundred pounds. The name comes from "holy" and "butt" (flatfish)—it was eaten on holy days. {Grilled halibut with lemon butter.}

A hall is a corridor or passageway inside a building: {The bathroom is down the hall on the left}. Hall also means a large room for gatherings—a concert hall, lecture hall, or dance hall. In older or grander buildings, the hall is the main entrance room. University buildings are often called halls: {residence hall}, {dining hall}. A hall of fame honors distinguished people in a field. (Capitalized Hall is a surname.)

Halleluiah is an alternate spelling of hallelujah—an exclamation of praise or thanksgiving to God, used especially in religious worship and hymns. The word appears in scripture and sacred music: {Handel's "Hallelujah Chorus"}. Outside worship, it expresses relief or joy: {Halleluiah, the rain finally stopped!}

Hallelujah is the same word as alleluia; the H- spelling is always used when the word is an interjection. Hallelujah literally means (in Hebrew) “praise God” and it is typically used as an enthusiastic and positive expression of joy or success.

A hallmark is a distinguishing feature or characteristic that identifies something as genuine or of high quality: {Attention to detail is the hallmark of her work}. The term comes from the official marks stamped on gold and silver in Britain to certify purity, and this original sense persists in jewelry and metalwork. More broadly, hallmark describes any defining trait: {The hallmark of a good teacher is patience}. As a verb, to hallmark is to stamp with such a mark or to characterize distinctively. (Capitalized Hallmark is the greeting card company.)

Hallmarks are distinctive features that identify or characterize something: {Attention to detail is the hallmark of her work}, {The hallmarks of a good teacher}. The term comes from official marks stamped on precious metals to certify purity—a practice still used in Britain. By extension, anything that serves as a reliable indicator of quality or authenticity becomes a hallmark.

Hallowed means made holy or sacred, set apart for religious veneration. A hallowed {ground} or hallowed {tradition} commands deep respect. The word appears in the Lord's Prayer: {Hallowed be thy name}. By extension, hallowed describes anything revered through time or association: the hallowed {halls} of a university, hallowed {memories} of the past.

Halls is the plural of hall—large rooms or passageways. The word often appears in institutional contexts: {the halls of Congress}, {the halls of academia}, {walking the halls of the hospital}. School hallways are simply {the halls}: {No running in the halls}. {Deck the halls} invokes festive decoration of grand interior spaces.

To hallucinate is to perceive something that isn't there—seeing, hearing, or sensing things without external stimulus. Hallucinations can result from mental illness, drugs, fever, or sleep deprivation: {She hallucinated spiders crawling on the walls}. In AI contexts, hallucinate describes when a system generates false information presented as fact: {The chatbot hallucinated a citation that doesn't exist}.

Hallucinated is the past tense of hallucinate—to perceive something that isn't there, whether through mental illness, drugs, sensory deprivation, or fever: {She hallucinated spiders crawling on the walls}. In contemporary usage, hallucinated describes AI systems generating false information presented as fact: {The chatbot hallucinated a citation that doesn't exist}.

Hallucinating is perceiving things that aren't there—seeing, hearing, or sensing what others cannot detect. The cause may be drugs, fever, mental illness, or exhaustion: {I was so sleep-deprived I started hallucinating}. More loosely, it means being wildly mistaken: {If you think I'm paying that much, you're hallucinating}. In AI contexts, hallucinating describes when a system generates plausible-sounding but false information.

A hallucination is a perception of something that isn't there—seeing, hearing, or feeling things that have no external source. Hallucinations can result from mental illness, fever, drugs, or sensory deprivation: {The patient reported auditory hallucinations}. In artificial intelligence, a hallucination is when a system generates false information presented as fact: {The chatbot's hallucination cited a study that doesn't exist}.

Hallucinations are sensory experiences of things that aren't there—seeing, hearing, or feeling something with no external cause. They occur in psychosis, drug use, sleep deprivation, and certain neurological conditions: {The fever gave him hallucinations}. In artificial intelligence, hallucinations are confident assertions of false information: {The chatbot's hallucinations included citations to nonexistent papers}.

A hallway is a corridor or passageway in a building, typically connecting rooms or leading to an entrance: {The bedrooms are down the hallway on the left}. In American English, hallway and hall are often interchangeable for interior passages, though hall can also mean a large room for gatherings.

A halo is a circle of light, originally the luminous ring sometimes seen around the sun or moon due to ice crystals in the atmosphere. In religious art, a halo is the golden disk or ring depicted around the heads of saints and holy figures, symbolizing divine radiance. By extension, anything that surrounds something like a glowing ring can be called a halo: {a halo of frizzy hair}, {a halo of smoke}. To halo something is to encircle it with light or glory. (Capitalized Halo is the video game franchise.)

Halt means to stop or come to a stop. A marching column halts on command. Production halts during a strike. Traffic grinds to a halt. As a noun, halt names the stoppage itself: {The project came to a halt when funding ran out}. The command {Halt!} demands immediate cessation of movement. To halt something is to cause it to stop: {Officials halted construction pending review}.

Ham is the meat from a pig's hind leg, typically cured, smoked, or both. A ham is also the thigh and buttock region itself—in humans or animals. In theater and film, a ham is an actor who overacts, mugging and emoting excessively; to ham it up is to perform this way. In radio, a ham is an amateur operator: {ham radio}.

A hamburger is a cooked patty of ground beef served in a sliced round bun, typically with condiments and toppings like lettuce, tomato, onion, and pickles. The word often refers to the complete sandwich: {Let's grab a hamburger for lunch}. Ground beef itself may be called hamburger: {a pound of hamburger}. Shortened to burger, the term extends to patties made from other ingredients: turkey burger, veggie burger.

Hamburgers is the plural of hamburger—a cooked patty of ground beef, typically served in a sliced bun with various toppings. The name comes from Hamburg, Germany, though the sandwich itself is American. Hamburgers anchor backyard cookouts, fast-food menus, and diners: {We grilled hamburgers for the Fourth of July}. The word often shortens to burgers, which has spawned countless variations: turkey burgers, veggie burgers, salmon burgers.

Hamfisted describes clumsy, heavy-handed action lacking finesse or delicacy. A hamfisted {attempt at diplomacy} blunders where subtlety was needed. The image is of hands too thick and awkward for precise work—fists where fingers should be. Also spelled ham-fisted. The variant hamhanded means the same thing.

A hamlet is a small village, typically smaller than a village proper and lacking a church or other central institutions. The word suggests rural isolation and modest population—a cluster of houses in the countryside rather than any organized settlement. {We drove through several hamlets before reaching the town.} (Capitalized Hamlet is Shakespeare's play.)

A hammer is a tool for driving nails into wood or doing other work that requires repetitive blows. To hammer something is to pound it with a hammer. If you hammer a person, you defeat them decisively. When you hammer home a point, theme, or message, you express it repeatedly until it is understood. If you hammer away at something, you work at it vigorously. If you come home hammered, you’re drunk.

Hammered means struck repeatedly with a hammer, or shaped or driven by hammering: {He hammered the nail into the wall}. {The metal was hammered into sheets}. Hammered can also mean attacked relentlessly: {The defense was hammered by the prosecutor}. In slang, hammered means extremely drunk: {I got hammered at the wedding}. The image is of being beaten into a state of incoherence.

A hammerhead is a shark with a distinctively flattened, T-shaped head, the eyes positioned at the outer edges. The shape extends to anything resembling it: a hammerhead crane has a horizontal beam atop its tower. As slang, a hammerhead is a stupid or stubborn person—someone whose head seems as dense as a hammer's striking surface.

Hammering is the act of striking repeatedly with a hammer or similar force. The word extends to any sustained pounding: {The rain kept hammering the roof}. In informal use, a hammering is a severe defeat or criticism: {The team took a hammering in the playoffs}. To give something a hammering is to use it heavily or treat it roughly.

A hammock is a hanging bed made of canvas, netting, or other fabric, suspended between two points—typically trees or posts. Originally used on ships where space was limited, hammocks now appear mainly in backyards and campsites as places to relax: {She spent the afternoon reading in the hammock}.

Hammocks are hanging beds made of fabric or netting, suspended between two points—typically trees or posts. They originated in the Caribbean and became standard sleeping equipment on sailing ships, where swinging with the vessel's motion proved more comfortable than fixed bunks. Today hammocks serve mostly for outdoor leisure: {We spent the afternoon reading in hammocks on the porch}.

A hamper is a large basket, typically with a lid, used for storage or transport. A laundry hamper holds dirty clothes; a picnic hamper carries food and supplies. In British usage, a hamper often refers specifically to a gift basket of food and drink: {We sent them a Christmas hamper}. Separately, to hamper is to hinder or impede progress: {Bad weather hampered rescue efforts}.

Hams is the plural of ham—cured pork from the upper hind leg of a pig. The word extends to the back of the human thigh: {My hams are sore from squatting}. Hams also refers to amateur radio operators, shortened from ham radio. In theater, hams are actors who overact with exaggerated gestures and expressions: {Those hams couldn't deliver a line without mugging}.

A hamster is a small rodent with a stout body, short tail, and large cheek pouches for storing food. Hamsters are popular pets, especially for children, typically kept in cages with exercise wheels. {The hamster stuffed its cheeks with sunflower seeds.} Wild hamsters burrow underground and are native to Europe and Asia.

Hamsters are small rodents kept as pets, known for their plump bodies, short tails, and cheek pouches that store food. They run on exercise wheels and burrow in bedding. Wild hamsters are native to parts of Europe and Asia. The singular hamster appears in compounds: {hamster wheel}, describing any repetitive, seemingly pointless activity.

The hamstrings are the three muscles running along the back of the thigh, connecting the hip to the knee. Athletes commonly strain or tear them: {She pulled her hamstring in the second quarter}. To hamstring someone or something is to cripple or severely hinder effectiveness: {Budget cuts hamstrung the investigation}. The verb comes from the old practice of disabling animals or enemies by cutting these tendons.

Hamstrung means crippled or rendered ineffective. The literal sense refers to cutting the hamstring tendons to disable a person or animal. The figurative sense dominates modern usage: {The investigation was hamstrung by lack of funding}. To be hamstrung is to have your capacity for action severely limited, usually by external constraints rather than personal failings.

Your hand is the terminal body part of your arm that anchors your fingers. A hand can also be a person who works using the hands (farmhand). The playing cards you hold are your hand. Firsthand, secondhand, and thirdhand refer to the successive distance from an original source: I only heard it secondhand. When hand comes before another noun, it denotes something for the hands, done with the hands, or otherwise concerning the hands (handbag, hand sanitizer, hand grenade). To hand something to someone is to deliver it – usually with your hands.

A handbag is a bag carried by hand or over the shoulder, typically used by women to hold personal items—wallet, keys, phone, cosmetics. The term is more common in British English; Americans often say purse. Handbags range from practical everyday carriers to luxury fashion accessories: {She spent a month's salary on that designer handbag}.

Handbags are bags carried by hand or on the arm, typically by women, for personal items like wallets, keys, and cosmetics. The word also appears in British slang for a weak, ineffectual fight or confrontation—from the image of two people flailing at each other with purses: {The players squared off but it was just handbags}.

Handball refers to several ball games played by hitting a ball with the hand. In one version, players strike a small rubber ball against a wall, popular in urban playgrounds and fitness clubs. In another, teams pass and throw a ball trying to score in a goal—an Olympic sport. In soccer, handball is a foul: touching the ball with the hand or arm. {The referee called handball in the penalty area.}

A handbook is a concise reference book covering the essentials of a particular subject: {an employee handbook}, {a student handbook}, {a handbook of English grammar}. Unlike comprehensive textbooks, handbooks aim for quick consultation—practical guidance you can hold in one hand.

Handcrafted describes something made by hand rather than by machine, implying care, skill, and individual attention: {handcrafted furniture}, {handcrafted jewelry}. The term suggests quality and uniqueness, often commanding higher prices. Marketing has stretched the word—a "handcrafted" sandwich may just mean someone assembled it. {Each piece is handcrafted by local artisans.}

Handcuffs are metal restraints that lock around the wrists, used by police to secure arrested persons. The verb means to apply such restraints: {The officer handcuffed the suspect}. Figuratively, to be handcuffed is to have one's options severely limited: {The new regulations have handcuffed small businesses}.

Handcuffed describes someone whose wrists have been bound together by handcuffs, the hinged metal restraints used by police and other authorities. Beyond the literal sense, handcuffed often appears figuratively to describe being severely restricted or unable to act freely: {The new regulations left small businesses handcuffed}. Someone who is handcuffed in this sense faces constraints that prevent them from doing what they want or need to do.

Handcuffing is restraining someone with handcuffs—metal rings that lock around the wrists. Police handcuff suspects during arrests: {The officer was handcuffing the man when his partner arrived}. Figuratively, handcuffing means severely restricting someone's ability to act: {Budget cuts are handcuffing the department's efforts}.

Handcuffs are metal restraints that lock around a person's wrists, typically connected by a short chain. Police use them to secure suspects during arrest: {The officer put him in handcuffs}. As a verb, to handcuff someone is to restrain them this way, or figuratively to limit their options: {Budget cuts handcuffed the department}.

A handful is the amount that fits in one hand, but the word is almost always used loosely to mean a small quantity or number: {Only a handful of people showed up}. When someone, especially a child, is described as a handful, they are difficult to manage or control—more than one can handle, as it were. {The twins are a real handful.}

A handgun is a firearm designed to be held and fired with one hand—pistols and revolvers. The term distinguishes these from long guns like rifles and shotguns. {The suspect was carrying a handgun.} Handguns are the most common weapons in civilian self-defense and urban crime alike.

Handheld describes something small enough to hold and operate in one hand: a handheld {device}, a handheld {vacuum}, a handheld {game console}. As a noun, a handheld is such a device—typically a portable electronic gadget like a GPS unit or gaming system: {She played her handheld on the bus}.

Handholding is the act of holding someone's hand, typically as a gesture of affection or reassurance. More commonly, it refers to giving someone excessive guidance or support through a process they could manage independently: {The software requires too much handholding}, {I don't have time to do all this handholding with new hires}. The figurative sense often carries mild criticism—implying the person being helped should be more self-sufficient.

Handicap is a disadvantage that makes success more difficult. In sports, a handicap is an adjustment that levels competition—giving weaker players an advantage or stronger ones a burden: {a golf handicap}, {handicap racing}. The word was once standard for physical or mental disability but is now considered offensive in that context; disability or specific terms are preferred. To handicap is to place at a disadvantage: {The team was handicapped by injuries}.

A handkerchief is a small square of cloth carried for wiping the nose, face, or eyes. Traditionally cotton or linen, it folds into a pocket or purse. A decorative handkerchief worn in a jacket's breast pocket is a pocket square. {She dabbed her eyes with a handkerchief.} The word is often shortened to hanky.

Most meanings of handle are related to or inspired by the underlying word hand. A handle is the part of something that can be grasped with the hand, or figuratively, with the mind: I have a handle on the math assignment. When you handle something physical, you manipulate or control it with your hands. Figuratively, to handle something is to deal with it effectively: The situation is under control; I handled it. To get a handle on something is to deal with it. Informally, a handle is someone’s name or nickname: The trucker’s handle was Bobcat.

A handlebar is a steering bar on a bicycle, motorcycle, or similar vehicle, typically curved and gripped at both ends. Usually plural: {She gripped the handlebars and pedaled hard}. A handlebar mustache curves upward at the ends, resembling the shape of bicycle handlebars.

Handlebars are the steering mechanism on a bicycle, motorcycle, or similar vehicle—a bar with grips at each end that the rider holds and turns to control direction. A handlebar mustache curves upward at the ends, resembling the shape. The singular handlebar appears mainly in compounds: {handlebar grips}, {handlebar bag}.

A handler is someone who manages, trains, or controls—especially animals or people who need guidance. Dog handlers work with police or show dogs; boxing handlers manage fighters between rounds. In espionage, a handler runs agents in the field. In computing, a handler is code that responds to specific events or inputs: {The error handler caught the exception}. Political handlers manage candidates' public images and messaging.

Handles is the plural of handle—the part of an object you grip to move or operate it: door handles, knife handles, shovel handles. A handle is also a name or nickname, especially online: {What's your handle on Twitter?} To handle something is to manage or deal with it: {She handles customer complaints}. If you {fly off the handle}, you lose your temper suddenly. {Love handles} are informal for the fat around someone's waist.

Handling is how something is managed, treated, or dealt with. The handling of a {crisis}, a {complaint}, or {sensitive materials} refers to the approach taken. In shipping, handling means the physical moving and processing of goods: {shipping and handling}. A vehicle's handling describes how it responds to steering and road conditions. To get a handle on something is to understand or control it.

Handmade describes something made by hand rather than by machine. The term implies craftsmanship, individual attention, and often higher quality: {handmade jewelry}, {handmade furniture}, {handmade pasta}. In an era of mass production, handmade carries connotations of authenticity and care that justify premium prices.

A handmaid is a female servant or attendant, now archaic or literary in most contexts. The term suggests personal service to someone of higher status, often a lady or noblewoman. Margaret Atwood's 1985 novel *The Handmaid's Tale* revived the word, depicting women forced into reproductive servitude. The related phrase {handmaiden to} describes something that serves or supports another: {Technology should be the handmaiden to human flourishing, not its master}.

A handmaiden is a female servant or attendant, especially one who serves a person of high rank. The word is archaic in its literal sense but persists in figurative use to describe something that serves or supports another: {Technology became the handmaiden of commerce}. The implication is subordination—useful but secondary to a greater purpose.

A handoff is the transfer of responsibility or control from one person or system to another. In football, a handoff is when the quarterback places the ball directly into a running back's hands. The term extends to any transition of duties: {The handoff between shifts went smoothly}. In telecommunications, a handoff occurs when a mobile call transfers between cell towers.

A handout is something given free to those in need—food, clothing, money. The word often carries a dismissive tone, implying the recipient hasn't earned it: {He's not looking for a handout, just a fair chance}. In educational settings, a handout is printed material distributed to students or attendees: {The professor passed out a handout summarizing the key points}.

Handouts are things given away free, especially printed materials distributed at meetings, lectures, or events: {The professor's handouts summarized each chapter}. The word also refers to money or goods given to those in need, often with a dismissive or critical edge suggesting the recipient hasn't earned them: {He refused to accept government handouts}. Politicians accuse opponents of giving handouts to constituents they want to disparage.

Handpicked means individually selected with care, as if choosing fruit by hand rather than harvesting mechanically. The term implies deliberate, personal selection based on quality or suitability: {a handpicked team of experts}, {handpicked candidates for the position}. The suggestion is that someone took time to evaluate each choice rather than accepting whatever was available.

A handprint is the impression left by a hand pressed against a surface—in paint, ink, mud, or other substances. Children make handprints in art projects; prehistoric humans left handprints on cave walls. Forensically, handprints can identify individuals like fingerprints. {The toddler left handprints all over the window.}

Hands is the plural of hand, so most often refers to the pair at the ends of your arms. To have your hands full is to be occupied. Hands can mean workers or helpers: {All hands on deck}. To be in good hands is to be well cared for. Hands also means possession or control: {The documents fell into the wrong hands}.

A handshake is a greeting or gesture of agreement in which two people clasp right hands and move them briefly up and down. Handshakes seal deals, conclude introductions, and mark reconciliation: {They shook hands on it}. A firm handshake is traditionally valued; a limp one suggests weakness. In computing, a handshake is an automated exchange of signals establishing a connection between devices or systems.

Handshakes is the plural of handshake—the gesture of grasping and briefly shaking another person's right hand as greeting, agreement, or farewell. The ritual varies by culture and context: {firm handshakes}, {limp handshakes}, {secret handshakes} used by fraternal organizations. In computing, a handshake is an automated exchange of signals establishing a connection between devices or systems.

Handsome describes physical attractiveness, typically applied to men where beautiful applies to women—though a handsome woman suggests striking, dignified features rather than delicate prettiness. The word extends to things that are well-proportioned or impressive: {a handsome building}, {a handsome profit}. A handsome sum or reward is notably generous. The underlying sense is something pleasing through its substance and proportion rather than mere prettiness.

A handspring is an acrobatic move where you launch forward or backward, land briefly on your hands, and push off to land on your feet. A front handspring goes forward; a back handspring (or backflip) goes backward. It's a fundamental gymnastics and cheerleading skill: {She did a handspring across the mat}.

A handstand is an acrobatic position in which you balance upside down on your hands with your body and legs extended vertically above you: {She held a handstand for thirty seconds}. Handstands are fundamental in gymnastics and yoga, and a common playground feat for children showing off.

A handstand is a position where the body is held upright balanced on the hands, legs extended in the air. It's a fundamental gymnastics skill and yoga pose requiring strength and balance: {She can hold a handstand for thirty seconds}. To {do a handstand} is the usual phrasing.

Handsy describes someone who touches others too freely, especially in ways that feel intrusive or sexually forward: {He gets handsy after a few drinks}.
