The word implies unwanted physical contact—hands that won't stay to themselves. It's mildly critical, suggesting the behavior is inappropriate but stopping short of assault.

Handwaving is the act of glossing over details, gaps, or difficulties rather than addressing them properly. In academic or technical contexts, it describes arguments that gesture vaguely toward conclusions without rigorous support: {The proof relies on a lot of handwaving about boundary conditions}. The term suggests intellectual laziness or deliberate evasion—waving one's hands as if to distract from what's missing.

Handwriting is writing done by hand with a pen or pencil, as opposed to typing or printing. The word also refers to the distinctive style of someone's script: {I recognized her handwriting on the envelope}. Handwriting can be neat or illegible, and like a fingerprint, varies enough between individuals to serve as identification. {The handwriting on the wall} means an ominous sign of things to come.

Handwritten describes text produced by hand rather than typed or printed: {a handwritten note}, {handwritten letters from the war}. The word often implies personal touch or authenticity—handwritten thank-you cards feel more sincere than printed ones. In legal contexts, a handwritten will may have different requirements than a typed one.

Handy means conveniently within reach or useful for a task. A handy {tool} is close at hand when you need it. A handy {person} is skilled at practical tasks, especially home repairs: {She's handy with a wrench}. Something that {comes in handy} proves useful when the occasion arises. {Keep this number handy in case of emergency}.

A handyman is someone who does small repairs and maintenance tasks, typically around homes or buildings. The work ranges from fixing leaky faucets to patching drywall to assembling furniture. A handyman handles jobs too minor to call a specialist for: {We hired a handyman to fix the fence and install some shelves}. The term implies competence across many trades without mastery of any particular one.

The many meanings of hang all arise from the core meaning of the verb: to suspend or be suspended from a fixed point. Hang has regular inflections (hanged) that are used only in the context of capital punishment: He was hanged for treason. Other meanings arise from hung: I’ve never hung wallpaper before. As a noun the most common meaning of hang is in the expression get the hang of it, which means to develop the skill of doing something.

A hangar is a large building for housing aircraft. The word applies to structures ranging from small private shelters to massive industrial facilities capable of holding jumbo jets: {The plane was wheeled into the hangar for maintenance}. Hangars typically feature wide doors and high ceilings to accommodate wingspan and tail height.

Hanged is the past tense of hang when referring to execution or suicide by suspension from the neck: {The murderer was hanged at dawn}. For all other meanings of hang, the past tense is hung: pictures are hung, coats are hung, juries are hung. The distinction is fading in casual speech, but {hanged} remains standard in legal and formal contexts when death is involved.

A hanger is a shaped frame for holding clothes, typically with a hook for hanging in a closet: {wire hangers}, {wooden hangers}. The word extends to anything that hangs or supports hanging: a {plant hanger}, a {stocking hanger}. A hanger is also a covered structure for housing aircraft. Someone who hangs around is a {hanger-on}—a persistent, often unwelcome follower.

Hanging refers to suspension from above, with nothing supporting from below. A hanging plant dangles from a hook; hanging fog clings to the air. As a method of execution or suicide, hanging means death by suspension from a rope around the neck: {Public hangings drew crowds in the Old West}. A hanging is also a decorative fabric mounted on a wall: {medieval tapestry hangings}. A hanging question or matter remains unresolved: {Several issues were left hanging}.

Hangman is a word-guessing game where one player thinks of a word and another tries to guess it letter by letter. Wrong guesses add body parts to a stick figure being hanged; too many mistakes and the figure is complete—you lose. {We played hangman on the back of the menu while waiting for our food.} A hangman is also a person who executes condemned prisoners by hanging.

A hangout is a place where someone spends leisure time regularly: {The coffee shop became our hangout after school}. It suggests casual, repeated visits rather than formal occasions. As a verb phrase, to hang out means to spend time idly or socially: {We just hung out at her place all weekend}.

Hangouts are places where people regularly spend time in a casual, relaxed way: {The coffee shop became our usual hangout}. The word suggests informality and familiarity—a neighborhood bar, a friend's basement, a park bench. To hang out is to spend time without particular purpose: {We just hung out and watched TV}.

A hangover is the unpleasant physical state following heavy drinking—headache, nausea, fatigue, dehydration. {I woke up with a terrible hangover}. By extension, a hangover is anything left over from a previous period: {These regulations are a hangover from the Cold War}. The adjective hungover describes someone experiencing one: {She was too hungover to function}.

Hangovers are the unpleasant physical effects that follow a bout of heavy drinking—headache, nausea, fatigue, and general misery. The word also applies to anything that lingers unpleasantly from a previous time or situation: {outdated policies that are hangovers from the colonial era}. A hangover suggests something you're stuck dealing with because of earlier excess or poor judgment.

Hangry describes irritability or bad temper caused by hunger. The word blends hungry and angry, capturing how low blood sugar can shorten your fuse: {Don't talk to me until I've eaten—I'm hangry}. The term moved from slang to mainstream use in the 2010s, now appearing in clinical discussions of mood and appetite.

Hangtime is the duration something stays airborne. In basketball, a player with good hangtime seems to float while shooting or dunking: {Jordan's hangtime was legendary}. In football, a punter wants maximum hangtime to let coverage reach the returner. The term extends to any suspended moment: {The joke had perfect hangtime before the punchline landed}.

A hangup is a psychological block or emotional preoccupation that interferes with normal functioning: {She has a hangup about public speaking}, {He's got hangups about commitment}. The term suggests something irrational or neurotic—a personal issue that shouldn't be as big a deal as it is. Often plural: {We all have our hangups}.

Hangups are psychological obstacles or inhibitions that prevent someone from acting freely or comfortably: {She has hangups about her body}, {He's got hangups about commitment}. The term suggests issues rooted in past experiences or anxieties that interfere with present behavior. Often used dismissively: {Get over your hangups}. Also spelled hang-ups.

A hankering is a persistent desire or craving for something: {I've had a hankering for barbecue all week}. The word suggests a longing that won't quite go away, often for something specific and attainable—comfort food, a place you miss, an activity you haven't done in a while. To hanker is to feel such a craving: {She's been hankering to visit her hometown}.

Haphazard describes something done without plan or order, governed by chance rather than design. A haphazard arrangement looks thrown together. A haphazard approach lacks method: {Books were shelved haphazardly, with no system anyone could discern}. The word suggests carelessness or randomness, though not necessarily with negative results—sometimes haphazard efforts stumble onto success.

Happen means to occur or take place, often with a sense of chance or unexpectedness: {It happened so fast}. When something happens to someone, it befalls them: {What happened to your arm?} To {happen to} do something suggests coincidence: {I happened to be in the neighborhood}. {As it happens} introduces a relevant fact: {As it happens, I know her sister}. To {happen upon} something is to encounter it by chance.

Happening describes something that is occurring right now or is current and exciting: {There's a lot happening downtown tonight}. As a noun, a happening is an event or occurrence, especially one that's notable: {The festival was quite a happening}. In the 1960s, happenings were avant-garde performance art events with audience participation. The adjective means fashionable or trendy: {a happening nightclub}, though this use now sounds dated.

Happiness is the state of feeling pleasure, contentment, or joy. It ranges from momentary delight to deep, lasting satisfaction with life: {Money can't buy happiness}. The word covers everything from {the happiness of a child with a new toy} to philosophical discussions about what constitutes a good life. To wish someone happiness is to hope for their well-being.

Happy describes a state of pleasure, contentment, or joy. You can be happy about something specific {I'm happy you came} or happy in general {She's a happy person}. Happy also means willing or pleased to do something: {I'd be happy to help}. In set phrases, happy marks occasions: {happy birthday}, {happy anniversary}. A happy accident or coincidence is fortunate rather than joyful.

Harakiri is ritual suicide by disembowelment, practiced by Japanese samurai to preserve honor or avoid capture. The blade is thrust into the abdomen and drawn across. The word is used figuratively for self-destructive acts: {The candidate's gaffe was political harakiri}. Also spelled hara-kiri. Seppuku is the more formal Japanese term.

To harass is to subject someone to persistent, unwanted attention or pressure. The word covers a spectrum from minor annoyance to serious misconduct: a salesman who won't take no for an answer, a bully who targets the same kid daily, a boss who makes repeated sexual advances. {She was harassed by debt collectors}. {He filed a harassment complaint against his supervisor}.

Harassed describes someone subjected to persistent unwanted attention, pressure, or hostility. A harassed {parent} juggles too many demands. A harassed {employee} endures repeated mistreatment. The word captures both the external pressure and the resulting frazzled, worn-down state: {She looked harassed after fielding calls all morning}.

Harassment is persistent, unwanted behavior that disturbs, threatens, or demeans someone. It can be verbal, physical, or digital—{workplace harassment}, {sexual harassment}, {online harassment}. The word implies a pattern rather than a single incident, though severe single acts may qualify. Legal definitions vary, but the core sense is conduct that creates a hostile or intimidating environment for the target.

A harbinger is something that signals or foreshadows what is to come, typically something significant. The word often carries a sense of foreboding: {Dark clouds were a harbinger of the storm ahead}. Harbingers can be positive too, as when crocuses are called harbingers of spring. Originally a harbinger was a person sent ahead to arrange lodgings for travelers, which explains the modern sense of something that precedes and announces an arrival.

A harbor is a sheltered body of water where ships can anchor safely—either a natural inlet or one improved with breakwaters and docks. By extension, harbor means any place of refuge or shelter: {a harbor from the storm}. To harbor is to shelter or conceal: {harbor a fugitive}. Figuratively, to harbor feelings or thoughts is to hold them privately: {She harbored doubts about the plan}. {He still harbors resentment toward his brother.}

Harboring means sheltering or giving refuge to someone or something, often with implications of concealment or protection from authorities: {accused of harboring a fugitive}, {harboring illegal immigrants}. The word extends to holding thoughts or feelings privately, especially negative ones: {harboring resentment}, {harboring suspicions}. Both senses suggest keeping something hidden that others might want exposed.

Harbors are sheltered bodies of water where ships can anchor safely, protected from open sea conditions. As a verb, harbor means to give shelter or refuge—you might harbor a fugitive, but you can also harbor feelings, suspicions, or grudges, keeping them safely tucked away inside. {The city's harbor bustled with cargo ships.} {She harbored doubts about his story for years.}

Harbour is the British spelling of harbor—a sheltered body of water where ships anchor and dock. {The fishing boats returned to harbour at dusk.} Beyond the nautical, to harbour is to give shelter or hold onto something, often with a sense of concealment: harbour a {fugitive}, harbour {resentment}, harbour {doubts}. The figurative uses suggest keeping something hidden or protected within oneself.

Harbours is the British spelling of harbors. A harbour is a sheltered body of water where ships dock and find protection from open seas: {The fishing boats returned to harbour before the storm}. To harbour is to shelter or conceal—often someone or something unwanted: {harbouring a fugitive}, {harbouring resentment}. The noun extends to any place of refuge or safety.

The adjective hard has two related but distinct core senses: those that are the opposite of “soft” and those that are the opposite of “easy.” Together, they communicate the idea of requiring effort. A hard problem is one that is difficult to solve. A hard rock is one that is difficult to penetrate. Hard often expresses intensity: hard labor, hard frost. As an adverb, hard communicates great effort: work hard, fight hard.
A hardass is someone strict, uncompromising, and tough: {The new coach is a real hardass}. As an adjective: {She has a hardass approach to management}.

Hardball is baseball, as distinguished from softball. The figurative sense dominates: to {play hardball} is to use aggressive, uncompromising tactics, especially in politics or business negotiations. {The union decided to play hardball with management}. Someone who plays hardball prioritizes winning over diplomacy or fairness.

Hardboiled describes an egg cooked until both white and yolk are solid, as opposed to softboiled. The figurative sense—tough, cynical, unsentimental—dominates: {a hardboiled detective}, {hardboiled prose}. The style emerged in American crime fiction of the 1920s and 30s, featuring world-weary protagonists who've seen too much to be shocked. Also spelled hard-boiled.

Hardcore intensifies whatever it modifies, suggesting extreme commitment or uncompromising nature. A hardcore {fan} is deeply devoted. Hardcore {punk} strips rock to aggressive essentials. In exercise, hardcore means grueling: {a hardcore workout}. Hardcore pornography shows explicit sexual acts without softening or simulation, as opposed to softcore material that suggests rather than depicts.

A hardcover is a book bound with rigid boards covered in cloth, paper, or leather, as opposed to a flexible paperback binding. Publishers typically release hardcovers first at higher prices, with paperback editions following: {I'll wait for the paperback—I can't afford the hardcover}. The term works as both noun and adjective: {a hardcover edition}.

Harden means to make or become hard, firm, or solid. Water hardens into ice; steel is hardened by tempering. The word extends naturally to abstract toughening: a person may harden after repeated disappointments, becoming less emotionally vulnerable. {Years of rejection hardened her resolve.} If someone hardens their position, they become less willing to compromise. Markets harden when prices firm up after a decline.

Hardened describes something that has become hard or harder, literally or figuratively. Steel is hardened through heat treatment. A hardened criminal has become callous through repeated offenses—no longer affected by consequences or moral appeals. Hardened arteries have stiffened with plaque. Someone hardened by experience has grown tough or unsympathetic: {Years of rejection had hardened her}.

A hardhat is a rigid protective helmet worn on construction sites and in industrial settings to guard against falling debris and head injuries. By extension, hardhat refers to a construction worker: {The hardhats broke for lunch}. In the 1970s, hardhat became associated with blue-collar political conservatism after New York construction workers clashed with antiwar protesters.

Hardline describes an uncompromising, inflexible stance on political or ideological matters. A hardline {position} refuses to negotiate or moderate. Hardline {conservatives} or hardline {communists} represent the most rigid factions of their movements. The word often implies severity: hardline {immigration policies}, hardline {tactics}. Also spelled hard-line. A hardliner is someone who holds such views.

A hardliner is someone who takes an uncompromising position, especially in politics. Hardliners resist negotiation or moderation, holding firm to ideology or principle regardless of opposition: {Hardliners in the party blocked the compromise}. The term often implies inflexibility that others find unreasonable, though hardliners themselves see it as principled consistency.

Hardly means barely, scarcely, or almost not at all: {I could hardly hear her over the noise}. It emphasizes how little or how narrowly something occurs: {We hardly know each other}, {I can hardly wait}. Despite containing "hard," hardly doesn't mean "in a hard manner"—that sense is archaic. {Hardly anyone showed up} means almost no one did.

Hardship is difficulty, suffering, or privation—conditions that make life harder than it should be. The word often appears in contexts of endurance: {economic hardship}, {years of hardship}, {endure hardship}. A hardship can also be a specific burden or deprivation: {The long commute was a real hardship for her}.

Hardships are conditions that cause suffering or difficulty—poverty, illness, deprivation, persecution. The word implies sustained adversity rather than momentary setbacks: {The settlers endured many hardships during their first winter}. Hardship often appears in contexts of resilience or complaint: {economic hardship}, {undue hardship}, {a life of hardship}.

There are two main meanings of hardware. The older one concerns durable parts and equipment used in making and repairing things: I bought hardware for the cupboards at the hardware store. The newer meaning expresses the fixed parts of computers that are physical and not modifiable by programming.

Hardwired originally describes electrical circuits with fixed, permanent connections—not programmable or changeable. The term extends to anything built-in or innate: {Humans are hardwired to seek connection}. In computing, hardwired refers to functions implemented in hardware rather than software. The figurative sense dominates casual use, suggesting traits so fundamental they feel unchangeable: {Fear of snakes seems hardwired into us}.

Hardworking describes someone who puts sustained effort into their work or pursuits: {a hardworking student}, {hardworking immigrants building new lives}. The term implies diligence and conscientiousness rather than mere long hours. Also spelled hard-working.

A hare is a long-eared mammal resembling a rabbit but typically larger, with longer legs built for speed. Unlike rabbits, hares live above ground and their young are born fully furred with open eyes. To hare is to run fast: {We hared off down the street}. In the fable, the hare loses to the tortoise through overconfidence.

Harebrained means reckless, foolish, or poorly thought out: {a harebrained scheme}, {some harebrained idea about getting rich quick}. The word suggests impulsive stupidity rather than mere ignorance—acting without thinking, like a hare darting erratically. Sometimes spelled hairbrained, though hare is the original form.

A harem is the part of a household reserved for women in some Muslim and South Asian cultures, or the women who live there—wives, concubines, and female relatives. The term extends to any group of women associated with one man: {He arrived with his harem of admirers}. In biology, a harem is a group of females controlled by a single dominant male, as in elephant seals or gorillas.

Hares are long-eared mammals related to rabbits but typically larger, with longer legs built for speed. Unlike rabbits, hares live above ground and their young are born fully furred with open eyes. To hare is to run fast: {We hared off across the field}. A harebrained scheme is reckless or foolish.

A harlequin is a clown or buffoon, especially one dressed in a colorful diamond-patterned costume. The word often describes anything with that distinctive multicolored diamond pattern: {harlequin floors}, {harlequin print}. In zoology, harlequin appears in species names for creatures with bold, contrasting markings: harlequin duck, harlequin beetle. The word suggests playful theatricality or eye-catching patchwork color. (Capitalized Harlequin is the theatrical character or the romance publisher.)

Harm is damage or injury—physical, emotional, or otherwise. To harm someone is to hurt them or make them worse off: {The scandal harmed his reputation}. Harm can be intentional or accidental, serious or minor. {No harm done} dismisses a mistake as inconsequential. {Out of harm's way} means safe from danger.

Harmless means causing no harm or injury. A harmless {prank} is playful, not damaging. A harmless {snake} poses no danger. The word often minimizes: {It was just a bit of harmless fun}. Something rendered harmless has been neutralized as a threat. Harmless can also suggest ineffectual or insignificant—a harmless {old fool} is too weak to matter.

A harmonica is a small rectangular wind instrument played by blowing and drawing breath through a row of metal reeds. Each reed produces a different note, allowing melodies and chords. The harmonica is central to blues music and common in folk and rock: {He pulled out a harmonica and played a mournful tune}. Also called a mouth organ.

Harmonize means to bring into agreement or make compatible. Musical voices harmonize when they blend pleasingly, each singing different notes that work together. Beyond music, people harmonize conflicting opinions, regulations harmonize across jurisdictions, and colors harmonize in a design. {We need to harmonize our schedules}. The underlying idea is creating unity from diversity.

Harmony is the pleasing combination of different musical notes played or sung together, creating chords rather than single melodic lines. This sense extends to any agreeable arrangement of parts into a unified whole: {The room's colors were in perfect harmony}. When people live or work in harmony, they do so without conflict or disagreement. To be {in harmony with} something means to be consistent or compatible with it: {His actions were not in harmony with his stated beliefs}.

A harness is a set of straps fitted around an animal or person to control movement or distribute force. Horses wear harnesses to pull carts; climbers wear harnesses attached to ropes. To harness something is to put it to work: {harness the wind}, {harness your creativity}. The phrase {in harness} means at work, especially routine work: {He died in harness at seventy-two}.

Harnessed is the past tense of harness. A horse or other draft animal is harnessed when fitted with straps and gear for pulling a load: {The team was harnessed and ready to plow}. Figuratively, to harness something is to bring it under control for productive use: {They harnessed solar energy to power the village}. Things harnessed are captured and directed toward a purpose.

Harnesses is the plural of harness—the system of straps that secures a horse to a cart or a person to safety equipment: {The stable had a dozen harnesses hanging on the wall}. As a verb form, harnesses means to put a harness on, or more often, to channel something for productive use: {The dam harnesses the river's power}, {She harnesses her anxiety into creative energy}.

A harp is a stringed instrument with a triangular frame, played by plucking with the fingers. The strings run at an angle from a curved neck to a soundboard. Harps range from small folk instruments to the large concert pedal harp of orchestras. To harp on something is to dwell on it tediously: {She keeps harping on my mistakes}.

Harpies are creatures from Greek mythology—winged female monsters with women's faces and birds' bodies who snatched food and carried off souls. The singular harpy has become a common insult for a shrewish, grasping woman: {His ex-wife was a harpy who took everything in the divorce}. The word implies someone predatory, nagging, or relentlessly unpleasant.

A harpoon is a barbed spear designed to be thrown or fired at large marine animals—whales, seals, large fish. The barbs prevent the weapon from pulling free once lodged. To harpoon is to strike with one: {The crew harpooned the whale from the bow}. Figuratively, to harpoon something is to attack or destroy it decisively.

Harpoons are barbed spears designed to pierce and hold fast, used historically for hunting whales and large fish. The barb prevents the prey from escaping once struck. A rope typically attaches the harpoon to the boat or a float. As a verb, to harpoon is to strike with one: {The whalers harpooned the beast from their small boat}. Figuratively, to harpoon something is to attack or undermine it decisively.

Harps is the plural of harp, a large stringed instrument played by plucking with the fingers. The harp's distinctive triangular frame and ethereal sound make it iconic in classical music and Celtic traditions. To harp on something means to dwell on it tediously, repeating the same point: {She keeps harping on about my mistakes}. This figurative use suggests the monotonous quality of playing the same notes repeatedly.

A harpsichord is a keyboard instrument in which pressing a key causes a mechanism to pluck a string, producing a bright, percussive tone. Unlike the piano, which strikes strings with hammers, the harpsichord cannot vary volume through touch. It was the dominant keyboard instrument in European music from the Renaissance through the Baroque era: {Bach composed most of his keyboard works for harpsichord}.

A harpy is a grasping, unpleasant woman—shrewish, predatory, or relentlessly nagging. The word comes from Greek mythology, where Harpies were winged creatures with women's faces who snatched food and souls. The mythological sense survives in fantasy literature, but the insult is the common use: {His ex-wife was a harpy who never let him see the kids}.

Harrowing describes experiences that are intensely distressing or traumatic—events that wound the psyche: {a harrowing account of survival}, {the harrowing final days of the war}. The word suggests something that tears at you, leaving you shaken. A harrow is a farm implement with metal teeth that breaks up soil; harrowing experiences break up your composure the same way.

Harsh describes something unpleasantly intense or severe. Harsh {light} is too bright; harsh {words} are unkind or critical; a harsh {climate} is difficult to endure. The word often suggests something grating or abrasive—a harsh {sound}, a harsh {texture}. Harsh {treatment} or a harsh {sentence} implies excessive severity: {The punishment seemed harsh for such a minor offense}.

Harvest is the gathering of mature crops from fields. The word extends to the season when this happens and to what's collected: {a bountiful harvest}, {the wheat harvest}. Figuratively, harvest applies to gathering anything accumulated over time: {harvest the rewards of hard work}, {organ harvest}. To harvest is to collect or reap: {They harvested the grapes in October}.

A harvester is a person or machine that gathers crops from fields. The term applies broadly to anyone engaged in harvest work, but more commonly refers to agricultural machinery designed to cut and collect grain, corn, or other crops. A combine harvester performs multiple operations—cutting, threshing, and cleaning grain—in a single pass through the field. Harvester extends metaphorically to anything that systematically collects: {data harvesters}, {organ harvesters}.

Harvesting is the act of gathering crops or other products when they're ready. Farmers harvest wheat, fishermen harvest oysters, beekeepers harvest honey. The term extends to collecting anything accumulated: {harvesting data}, {harvesting organs for transplant}. In computing, harvesting often describes extracting information from systems, sometimes illicitly: {The malware was harvesting email addresses}.

Harvests is the plural of harvest—the gathering of ripe crops, or the crops themselves. A region may have multiple harvests per year, or harvests of different crops: {The wheat and corn harvests came in strong this season}. Figuratively, harvests can refer to accumulated results of effort: {reaping the harvests of years of research}.

Hash has several distinct meanings. As a dish, it's chopped meat and potatoes fried together: {corned beef hash}. Hash is also short for hashish, the cannabis derivative. To hash something out is to discuss it thoroughly until resolved: {Let's hash out the details}. A hash mark (#) is the pound sign or number symbol. In computing, a hash is a fixed-length value generated from data, used for verification and indexing: {The password is stored as a hash}. To make a hash of something is to bungle it badly.

A hashbrown is a breakfast food made from shredded or diced potatoes, pressed flat and fried until crispy and golden brown: {I'll have eggs, bacon, and hashbrowns}. The dish is a staple of American diners and fast-food breakfasts. Also spelled hash brown or hash browns.

Hashbrowns are shredded or diced potatoes fried until crispy and golden brown, typically served at breakfast alongside eggs. The texture varies from loose shreds to compressed patties. Also spelled as two words: {hash browns}. {I'll have the eggs with hashbrowns instead of toast}.

A hashtag is a word or phrase preceded by the # symbol, used on social media to categorize content and make it searchable: {The post went viral after someone added #MeToo}. Clicking a hashtag shows other posts using the same tag. Hashtags can mark topics, movements, or jokes. The word also refers to the # symbol itself, though that symbol is more precisely called a pound sign or number sign.

Hashtags is the plural of hashtag—a word or phrase preceded by the # symbol, used on social media to tag content by topic: {I added hashtags to make the post more discoverable}. People speak of hashtags as a category: {Hashtags help organize conversations online}. The term can refer to the symbols themselves or to trending topics they create.

Hassle is trouble, bother, or annoying difficulty: {Parking downtown is such a hassle}. It can also mean an argument or confrontation: {I got into a hassle with my neighbor about the fence}. As a verb, to hassle someone is to pester or harass them: {Stop hassling me about it}.

Haste is urgency or speed, especially when rushing: {In her haste to leave, she forgot her keys}. The word often carries a note of excessive hurry—acting too quickly invites mistakes. {Haste makes waste.} To {make haste} is to hurry. Hasty is the adjective form.

Hasty describes something done too quickly, with insufficient thought or care. A hasty {decision} is one you might regret; a hasty {retreat} suggests panic rather than strategy. The word implies recklessness or impatience: {Don't be hasty—let's think this through}. Hasty can also simply mean quick or speedy, though this neutral sense is less common now.

A hat is a shaped covering for the head, typically with a crown and brim, worn for warmth, sun protection, fashion, or to signal role or status. Hats range from casual baseball caps to formal top hats to functional hard hats. To {wear many hats} means to hold multiple roles or responsibilities. If you {keep something under your hat}, you keep it secret. To {pass the hat} is to collect money, usually for a cause. {Hat in hand} suggests humble supplication.

Hatch has two main clusters of meaning. One involves emerging from an egg—birds hatch, eggs hatch, schemes hatch when they finally come together: {They hatched a plan to escape}. The other involves an opening or covering: a ship's hatch, an escape hatch, a hatchback car. To hatch in drawing is to shade with fine parallel lines; crosshatching uses intersecting lines.

A hatchback is a car with a rear door that swings upward, providing access to a cargo area that shares space with the passenger compartment. The design offers more flexible storage than a traditional sedan trunk: {She folded down the back seats of her hatchback to fit the furniture}. Hatchbacks are typically compact and fuel-efficient.

Hatched describes something that has emerged from an egg, or a plan that has been devised: {The chicks hatched overnight}, {a newly hatched scheme}. In art and drafting, hatched means marked with parallel lines for shading or texture: {The map showed hills with hatched contours}. Cross-hatched uses intersecting lines for deeper shading.

A hatchery is a facility where eggs are incubated and hatched under controlled conditions, typically for fish, poultry, or other animals raised commercially. Fish hatcheries stock rivers and lakes; chicken hatcheries supply farms: {The salmon hatchery releases thousands of fingerlings each spring}.

Hatches is the plural of hatch, with meanings that cluster around openings and emergence. A hatch is a door or opening in a floor, ceiling, deck, or aircraft: {battening down the hatches}, {escape hatch}. To hatch is to emerge from an egg, or for an egg to produce young: {The chicks hatched this morning}. Figuratively, to hatch a plan or scheme is to devise it secretly: {They hatched a plot to overthrow the government}. In art, hatching means drawing fine parallel lines to create shading.

A hatchet is a small axe designed for one-handed use, with a short handle and a single blade. It's suited for light chopping, splitting kindling, or rough carpentry. To {bury the hatchet} is to make peace after a conflict. A {hatchet job} is a harsh, damaging attack—usually verbal or written. A {hatchet man} does someone's dirty work.

Hatching is the emergence of a young animal from an egg, or the act of incubating eggs until they hatch: {We watched the hatching of the chicks}. In drawing and engraving, hatching is the technique of shading with closely spaced parallel lines; cross-hatching uses intersecting sets of lines for darker tones. To hatch a plan is to devise it secretly: {They were hatching a scheme to steal the documents}.

A hatchling is a young animal that has recently emerged from an egg. The term applies most often to birds, reptiles, and fish: {The sea turtle hatchlings made their way toward the ocean}. Hatchling emphasizes the creature's newness and vulnerability—freshly hatched and not yet developed.

Hatchlings are young animals that have recently emerged from eggs. The term applies to birds, reptiles, fish, and insects alike: {The sea turtle hatchlings made their way toward the ocean}. Hatchling emphasizes the newness—once an animal has grown past its earliest stage, it's no longer a hatchling but a chick, fry, or juvenile.

Hate is intense hostility or aversion toward someone or something. You can hate a person, an idea, or broccoli—the word spans murderous loathing and mild dislike: {I hate getting up early}. As a noun, hate names the emotion itself: {eyes full of hate}. Hate crimes and hate speech target people based on identity. To {hate on} someone is to criticize or disparage them, often unfairly.

Hateful describes something that inspires or expresses hatred. A hateful {person} harbors intense ill will toward others. Hateful {remarks} are malicious and cruel. The word can also mean deserving hatred—a hateful {crime} is one that provokes disgust. {She gave him a hateful look.} The distinction between feeling hatred and provoking it often blurs in use.

A hater is someone who habitually criticizes, disparages, or resents others—often those who are successful or popular. The word gained currency in hip-hop and internet culture, where it describes people whose negativity seems motivated by jealousy rather than legitimate grievance: {Don't listen to the haters}. To hate on someone is to express such resentment: {Why you gotta hate on my success?}

Haters are people who express intense dislike or criticism, especially toward someone's success or popularity. The term emerged from hip-hop culture and spread into general slang, typically implying that the criticism stems from jealousy rather than legitimate grievance: {Don't let the haters get you down}. To dismiss critics as haters can deflect valid feedback.

Hatred is intense, persistent hostility toward someone or something. Unlike anger, which flares and fades, hatred settles in and stays: {Her hatred of injustice drove her activism}, {a hatred that festered for years}. Hatred can target individuals, groups, or abstractions. Self-hatred turns this hostility inward. The word carries moral weight—to accuse someone of hatred is serious.

Hats are head coverings, the plural of hat. Beyond literal headwear, hats represent roles or capacities: {She wears many hats at work} means she handles multiple responsibilities. To {take your hat off} to someone is to express admiration. {Old hat} means outdated or no longer novel: {That technology is old hat now}.

Haughty describes someone who acts superior to others, displaying arrogant pride and disdain for those they consider beneath them. The word suggests not just confidence but contemptuous dismissiveness: {She gave him a haughty look and turned away}. A haughty manner often masks insecurity, though the word focuses on outward behavior rather than inner state.

Haul means to pull or drag something heavy, usually with sustained effort: {They hauled the boat onto shore}. Extended uses keep the sense of effortful transport: {hauling groceries up three flights of stairs}. As a noun, a haul is what you've collected or acquired—a fisherman's haul, a thief's haul, or the loot from a shopping trip. A {long haul} is a considerable distance or extended effort: {We're in this for the long haul}.

Hauling is the act of pulling, dragging, or transporting something heavy or bulky, often over a distance. The word emphasizes effort and weight: {We spent the weekend hauling furniture up three flights of stairs}. In trucking, hauling refers to the commercial transport of goods by vehicle. Informally, if you're hauling, you're moving fast: {That truck was really hauling down the highway}. To haul someone in means to bring them before an authority, often unwillingly.

Haunt means to visit repeatedly, especially as a ghost or spirit: {The old mansion is said to be haunted}. A place someone haunts is one they frequent: {This café was Hemingway's haunt}. Memories or worries that haunt you keep returning unbidden: {The decision haunted her for years}. A haunting melody or image lingers in the mind.

Haunted describes a place supposedly inhabited by ghosts: {a haunted house}, {a haunted cemetery}. More broadly, haunted means troubled or preoccupied by persistent memories or feelings: {haunted by regret}, {a haunted look in her eyes}. The word suggests something that won't leave you alone—whether supernatural presence or psychological weight.

Haunting describes something that lingers in the mind, refusing to fade—often beautiful but touched with sadness or unease. A haunting {melody} stays with you. A haunting {image} keeps returning unbidden. The word suggests emotional resonance that won't let go: {Her haunting eyes followed him for days}. As a noun, a haunting is a supernatural visitation by ghosts or spirits.

Haunts are places someone frequents—their regular spots, familiar territory: {We visited his old haunts from college}, {the usual haunts of artists and writers}. The word carries a sense of belonging or habitual return. As a verb, to haunt is to visit repeatedly, whether as a ghost lingering in a place or a memory that won't leave: {The melody haunted her for days}.

Have is the most second most frequently used verb (after be). There are two reasons for this: its very important primary meanings as a main verb (indicating ownership, experience, acquisition, and relationship) and its use as an auxiliary verb to form all of the perfect tenses and some constructions that express obligation, necessity, and compulsion. Add to that the many idiomatic expressions in which a form of have is the verb (had better, have at someone or something, have something coming) and have ends up with at least one spot in nearly every paragraph of English writing. As a noun, have is a latecomer to English and very limited in meaning. You only hear about the haves when the have-nots are also mentioned.

A haven is a place of safety or refuge—somewhere you go to escape danger, stress, or the outside world. Originally a harbor where ships found shelter from storms, the word now applies broadly: a {tax haven} shields money from taxation, a {safe haven} offers protection from threats. {The cabin became our haven from city life.}

Havens is the plural of haven, a place of shelter or safety. Harbors are havens for ships; sanctuaries are havens for refugees. The word often appears figuratively: {The library was a haven from the chaos of home}. A tax haven is a jurisdiction with low or no taxes where money can be sheltered.

Havoc is widespread destruction or chaos. The word appears most often in set phrases: to {wreak havoc} is to cause extensive damage or disorder; to {play havoc with} something is to disrupt it severely. {The storm wreaked havoc on coastal towns.} {Inflation played havoc with their retirement plans.}

A hawk is a bird of prey with sharp talons, a hooked beak, and keen eyesight—smaller than eagles, larger than falcons. Hawks hunt by day, swooping on rodents, rabbits, and smaller birds. To hawk is to hunt with trained hawks. Separately, to hawk is to sell aggressively, especially by calling out in public: {street vendors hawking their wares}. A hawk also describes someone who favors aggressive or militaristic policies, opposed to a dove: {The hawks in Congress pushed for intervention}.

Hawks are birds of prey with sharp talons, hooked beaks, and keen eyesight—smaller than eagles but equally predatory. The word extends to people who favor aggressive or military action, especially in politics, opposed to doves who prefer diplomacy: {Defense hawks pushed for intervention}. To hawk is to sell aggressively, often by calling out in public: {vendors hawking their wares}. A different hawk means to clear the throat noisily.

Hay is grass or other plants that have been cut and dried for use as animal feed, especially for horses and cattle. A hay bale is a compressed bundle for storage and transport. To {make hay while the sun shines} is to take advantage of favorable conditions. {Hit the hay} means go to bed. To hay is to cut and dry grass for this purpose.

Hay fever is an allergic reaction to pollen, causing sneezing, itchy eyes, and a runny nose. Despite the name, it involves neither hay nor fever—the term dates from a time when symptoms peaked during hay-harvesting season. Also spelled as two words: {hay fever}.

A hayloft is the upper level of a barn where hay is stored. Hay is lighter than grain and benefits from air circulation, so farmers traditionally hoisted it to lofts above livestock stalls. The hayloft appears in rural fiction as a site for children's play, secret meetings, or romantic encounters: {They climbed up to the hayloft to talk in private}.

A haymaker is a powerful, sweeping punch thrown with full force, typically arcing wide rather than jabbing straight: {He threw a haymaker that connected with the guy's jaw}. The term comes from the swinging motion used to toss hay with a pitchfork. Haymakers are dramatic but leave the thrower off-balance and exposed. The word also refers to a person or machine that cuts and dries hay.

A hayride is a recreational outing where people ride in a wagon or truck bed filled with hay or straw, typically pulled by a tractor or horses. Hayrides are associated with autumn activities—pumpkin patches, corn mazes, Halloween festivities: {The farm offers hayrides every October}. The rustic, nostalgic quality makes them popular for group outings and family entertainment.

A haystack is a large pile of hay, typically conical or rounded, stored outdoors after harvest. The phrase {needle in a haystack} describes something nearly impossible to find—a small item lost in an overwhelming mass of similar material. {We searched for hours but it was like looking for a needle in a haystack.}

Haystacks are large mounds of hay piled for storage and drying, traditionally cone-shaped or dome-shaped to shed rain. The singular haystack appears in the idiom {needle in a haystack}—something nearly impossible to find among vast quantities of similar material. Haystacks also names a no-bake candy of chocolate or butterscotch mixed with chow mein noodles, shaped into small mounds.

Haywire means erratic, out of control, or malfunctioning. The word comes from the thin wire used to bale hay, which tangles easily when cut. Something that {goes haywire} stops working properly: {The computer went haywire and deleted everything}. A person who goes haywire becomes irrational or crazy. Haywire can also describe something improvised or shoddy—held together with the proverbial baling wire.

A hazard is a source of danger or risk: {health hazard}, {fire hazard}, {occupational hazards}. In golf, a hazard is a bunker or water obstacle. To hazard something is to risk it or venture an uncertain attempt: {I'll hazard a guess}. The word carries a sense of chance—something that might cause harm but hasn't yet.

Hazardous means dangerous or risky, typically describing things that pose threats to health, safety, or well-being. The word appears frequently in official and technical contexts: {hazardous waste}, {hazardous materials}, {hazardous conditions}. Something hazardous isn't just unpleasant—it carries real potential for harm. {Smoking is hazardous to your health.}

Hazards are dangers or sources of potential harm. A hazard is something that poses risk: {fire hazards}, {health hazards}, {occupational hazards}. In golf, hazards are obstacles like sand traps and water. To hazard something is to risk it or venture it tentatively: {I'd hazard a guess that she's not coming back}.

Haze is a thin atmospheric obscuration—dust, smoke, or moisture suspended in air that dims visibility without blocking it entirely. A haze of something suggests a diffuse, enveloping quality: {a haze of cigarette smoke}. Figuratively, haze describes mental fogginess: {I've been in a haze all morning}. To haze someone is to subject them to humiliating initiation rituals, especially in fraternities or military units.

Hazel is a shrub or small tree that produces edible nuts, and the light brown color of those nuts—a warm shade tinged with green or gold. Hazel eyes are notable for shifting between brown and green depending on lighting. The wood was traditionally used for divining rods and woven fencing. {She has beautiful hazel eyes.} (Capitalized Hazel is a given name.)

A hazelnut is the edible nut of the hazel tree, round with a hard brown shell and a sweet, mild flavor. Hazelnuts appear in confections, baked goods, and spreads like Nutella: {The cake was topped with crushed hazelnuts}. Also called filbert or cobnut in some regions.

Hazing is the practice of subjecting newcomers to humiliating, degrading, or dangerous rituals as a condition of acceptance into a group—most commonly fraternities, sports teams, or military units. Activities range from forced drinking and sleep deprivation to physical abuse: {The fraternity was suspended after a hazing incident sent a pledge to the hospital}. Though often defended as tradition or team-building, hazing has caused deaths and is illegal in many jurisdictions.

Hazmat is short for hazardous materials—substances that pose risks to health, safety, or the environment, such as chemicals, radioactive materials, or biological agents. The term usually appears as a modifier: hazmat {suit}, hazmat {team}, hazmat {training}. {A hazmat crew responded to the chemical spill.}

Hazy describes reduced clarity or visibility. A hazy sky is dimmed by dust, smoke, or moisture—not quite foggy, but not clear. The word extends naturally to mental states: hazy memories are indistinct, and someone hazy on the details doesn't remember them sharply. {The mountains were hazy in the distance.} {I'm a little hazy about what happened that night.}

The head is the upper part of the body containing the brain, face, and sensory organs: {She turned her head}. {He hit his head on the door}. Head extends to tops of things ({head of a pin}, {head of lettuce}), leaders ({head of state}, {head of the department}), foam on beer, the front of a line, and the source of a river. A head is also a toilet on a ship. To head means to lead, direct, or move toward: {She heads the committee}. {We're heading home}. In vulgar slang, head means oral sex: {She gave him head}. This sense likely comes from the position of the giver's head relative to the recipient's body.

A headache is pain in the head, ranging from mild discomfort to debilitating agony. Headaches have many causes—tension, dehydration, illness, hangovers. Figuratively, a headache is any source of trouble or annoyance: {Parking downtown is such a headache}. {This project has been one headache after another}.

A headband is a strip of fabric, elastic, or other material worn around the head. It may hold hair back from the face, absorb sweat during exercise, or serve as decoration. {She wore a headband to keep her hair out of her eyes while running.}

To headbang is to shake the head rhythmically and violently to heavy music, typically metal or hard rock. The motion ranges from nodding vigorously to whipping the head in full circles. As a noun, a headbang is an instance of this: {The song's breakdown triggered a massive headbang from the crowd}. Headbanging emerged from 1970s metal culture and remains a signature expression of intense musical engagement.

A headbanger is someone who bangs their head rhythmically to heavy metal or hard rock music—the motion itself is headbanging. The term extends to mean any devoted fan of heavy metal: {The concert was packed with headbangers}. The word can also describe someone reckless or crazy, though this use is less common.

Headbangers are fans of heavy metal music, named for the vigorous head-shaking that accompanies the genre's aggressive rhythms: {The front row was packed with headbangers}. The term can extend to the musicians themselves or anyone who enjoys loud, intense rock music. A headbanger is also someone who bangs their head against things, whether from frustration or as a symptom of certain conditions.

Headbanging is the vigorous shaking of one's head in time with loud, driving music, especially heavy metal or hard rock. The motion typically involves whipping the head up and down or in circles, often with long hair flying dramatically. It emerged from metal concert culture as a way for fans to physically express the music's intensity. {The crowd was headbanging so hard the floor shook.} Someone who does this is a headbanger, a term that also refers more broadly to fans of heavy metal music.

A headbutt is a blow delivered with the forehead, typically to an opponent's face or body. It's a fighting move—sometimes deliberate in combat sports, often a foul in others like soccer. To headbutt someone is to strike them this way: {He headbutted the defender and got a red card}. The term also applies to the affectionate bumping cats do with their heads.

Headbutting is striking someone or something with your forehead, whether as an attack, a show of aggression, or rough affection. In sports like soccer, it's a legitimate technique for directing the ball. As interpersonal violence, a headbutt is sudden and close-range: {He was ejected for headbutting the referee}.

Headbutts is the plural of headbutt—a blow delivered with the forehead, typically to an opponent's face or body. Common in combat sports and street fights, it's often illegal in formal competition: {The referee warned him after two headbutts}. As a verb, headbutts means strikes with the head: {The goat headbutts anyone who gets too close}.

A headdress is an ornamental covering or decoration worn on the head, typically more elaborate than a hat. The term often refers to ceremonial or traditional headwear: Native American feathered headdresses, bridal headdresses, or the headdresses worn by showgirls. {The chief wore an elaborate headdress of eagle feathers.}

The noun header designates various things whose name is inspired by the underlying word head: things that are at the top or first. In a computer file, a header is the first sequential information in the file that contains metadata. In print, a header is repeating text at the top of a page. In soccer, a header is an instance of hitting the ball with the head. A brick in a wall with its short end showing is also called a header.

Headfirst means with the head leading, diving or plunging forward: {She dove headfirst into the pool}. Figuratively, it describes rushing into something without caution or preparation: {He jumped headfirst into the new project without reading the contract}. Also spelled head-first or as two words.

To headhunt is to recruit skilled professionals, typically executives or specialists, away from their current employers. Headhunters actively pursue candidates rather than waiting for applications: {She was headhunted by a rival firm}. The term derives from the literal practice of taking enemies' heads as trophies, now applied to corporate talent acquisition.

Headhunted describes being recruited for a job, typically by a specialized recruiter who sought you out rather than you applying: {She was headhunted by a tech startup}. The term implies being poached—targeted for your skills or reputation rather than discovered through ordinary hiring channels. Being headhunted often suggests flattering professional recognition.

A headhunter is a recruiter who seeks out candidates for high-level or specialized positions, often approaching people who aren't actively job-hunting: {A headhunter contacted me about a VP role}. The term comes from the original meaning—a member of a society that takes and preserves enemies' heads as trophies, a practice documented in various cultures historically.

Headhunters are recruiters who seek out candidates for executive or specialized positions, often approaching people who aren't actively job-hunting: {The headhunters called about a VP position in Chicago}. The term comes from the original meaning—members of certain tribal cultures who took enemies' heads as trophies. That sense now appears mainly in historical or anthropological contexts.

Headhunting is the practice of recruiting executives or highly skilled professionals for organizations, typically by specialized agencies that actively pursue candidates rather than waiting for applicants: {The firm was headhunted for a VP position at a rival company}. The term evokes the older, literal meaning—taking enemies' heads as trophies—suggesting aggressive pursuit of valuable talent.

A heading is a title or caption at the top of a page, section, or document that indicates what follows: {chapter headings}, {section headings}. In navigation, a heading is the direction in which a vehicle is pointed, expressed in compass degrees: {The pilot adjusted the heading to 270}. More broadly, heading can mean a direction or course of action: {What heading are we on with this project?}

Headless describes something without a head. A headless statue has lost or never had one. A headless corpse is missing its head. Figuratively, headless means without a leader: {The organization was headless after the CEO resigned}. In computing, headless refers to systems running without a monitor or graphical interface: {a headless server}.

A headlight is a powerful lamp mounted on the front of a vehicle to illuminate the road ahead. Cars typically have two headlights, with settings for low beam and high beam. The term extends to lights on trains, motorcycles, and bicycles. {She flashed her headlights to warn oncoming traffic.}

Headlights are the forward-facing lamps on a vehicle, used to illuminate the road ahead at night or in poor visibility. Cars have high beams and low beams; you dim your headlights for oncoming traffic. {She flashed her headlights to warn of a speed trap.} In slang, headlights refers to a woman's breasts, especially when visibly prominent through clothing.

A headline is the title of a newspaper article or story, set in large type to capture attention: {The scandal made headlines}. Headlines compress information into punchy phrases, often dropping articles and auxiliary verbs. By extension, headlines are the main stories themselves: {Let's go to the headlines}. To headline is to be the featured performer: {She headlines at the comedy club tonight}. Something that {grabs headlines} attracts significant media attention.

A headliner is the main attraction at an event, especially a concert or festival—the act that appears last and draws the largest crowd: {The band headlined at Coachella}. In automotive contexts, a headliner is the fabric lining the interior of a car's roof. The entertainment sense dominates contemporary usage.

Headliners are the main attractions at a performance or event—the acts that appear last and largest on promotional materials. A music festival might have several headliners across different nights: {Taylor Swift and Kendrick Lamar are this year's headliners}. The term extends beyond entertainment to anyone given top billing or prominent attention. Separately, a headliner is the fabric covering the interior ceiling of a car.

Headlines are the titles of news articles, printed in large type above the story: {The scandal dominated headlines for weeks}. To make headlines is to become newsworthy. Headlines also refers to the main act at a concert or show—the performer whose name appears largest on promotional materials. The verb means to serve as that main attraction: {She headlined the festival}.

Headlining means serving as the main attraction, especially in entertainment. A band headlining a festival plays the prime slot; a comedian headlining a club is the featured act. The term extends beyond performance: {The scandal was headlining the news all week}. From headline—the story or act that gets top billing.

A headlock is a wrestling hold in which one person wraps an arm around another's head and neck, trapping it against their body. It's used in competitive wrestling, martial arts, and playground scuffles alike: {He got me in a headlock and wouldn't let go}. Figuratively, to have someone in a headlock is to have them trapped or at a disadvantage.

Headlong means with the head leading—diving or falling face-first: {She tumbled headlong down the stairs}. By extension, it describes rushing forward without caution or deliberation: {They plunged headlong into marriage}, {a headlong rush to judgment}. The word works as both adverb and adjective: {a headlong dive}, {running headlong into danger}.

A headmaster is the principal of a private school, particularly in British usage. The term suggests traditional authority—a male administrator who runs the institution. {The headmaster called an assembly to address the incident.} Female counterparts are headmistresses, though the gender-neutral head or head teacher has largely replaced both in contemporary usage.

A headphone is a small speaker worn on or in the ear to listen to audio privately. Usually plural: {I left my headphones on the bus}. Headphones range from earbuds to large over-ear models. The singular form typically appears as a modifier: {headphone jack}, {headphone amp}.

Headphones are a pair of small speakers worn on or over the ears, connected by a band across the head. They deliver audio directly to the listener without disturbing others nearby: {She put on her headphones and tuned out the world}. The term covers everything from bulky over-ear models to compact on-ear designs. Earbuds that sit inside the ear canal are sometimes called headphones loosely, though they lack the headband.

Headquarters is the central location from which an organization operates—where leadership resides and major decisions are made: {The company moved its headquarters to Austin}. Military headquarters coordinate operations. The word takes a singular or plural verb: {Headquarters is downtown} or {Headquarters are aware of the situation}. Often shortened to HQ.

Heads is the side of a coin bearing a face or portrait, opposite tails. A coin flip that lands {heads} shows this side up. Heads also refers to multiple individual people: {Let's do a head count—how many heads?} To {put heads together} is to collaborate on thinking through a problem.

A headscarf is a piece of fabric worn over the head, typically tied under the chin or at the back. Women wear headscarves for warmth, fashion, or religious observance: {She adjusted her headscarf before entering the mosque}. The term often appears in discussions of Muslim women's dress, though headscarves cross many cultures and faiths.

A headscratcher is something puzzling or confusing—a problem that makes you figuratively scratch your head in bewilderment. The term applies to riddles, unexpected outcomes, or baffling decisions: {The ending of that movie was a real headscratcher}. {Why they traded their best player remains a headscratcher}.

A headset is a pair of headphones, often with a microphone attached. The term emphasizes hands-free communication: {She put on her headset before joining the video call}. Headsets range from lightweight earbuds with built-in mics to padded over-ear models favored by gamers and call center workers. Virtual reality headsets are wearable displays that cover the eyes.

A headshot is a photograph focused on someone's face and shoulders, typically used for professional purposes like acting portfolios, corporate websites, or social media profiles: {She updated her LinkedIn headshot}. In video games and action contexts, a headshot is a shot that strikes the head, usually causing maximum damage or instant death: {He got the kill with a clean headshot}.

Headshots are photographs focused on a person's face and shoulders, typically used for professional purposes like acting portfolios, corporate profiles, or social media. Actors get headshots to submit for auditions; executives use them for company websites. In video games and action movies, a headshot is a shot to the head—usually lethal: {That was a clean headshot}.

Headspace is the mental or emotional state a person is in at a given moment, often with implications about their capacity to handle situations or think clearly. Someone in a {good headspace} feels mentally prepared and balanced, while a {bad headspace} suggests anxiety, distraction, or emotional turmoil. The term also has technical meanings: in firearms, it's the distance between the bolt face and the chamber; in food preservation, it's the air gap left at the top of a jar or container.

A headstone is a stone marker placed at the head of a grave, typically inscribed with the deceased person's name, birth and death dates, and sometimes an epitaph: {We visited the cemetery to clean my grandfather's headstone}. The terms headstone, gravestone, and tombstone are largely interchangeable in modern usage.

Headstones are stone markers placed at the head of graves, typically inscribed with the deceased's name, birth and death dates, and sometimes an epitaph. The term applies to markers of various sizes, from modest tablets to elaborate monuments: {We walked through the old cemetery reading the headstones}. Also called gravestones or tombstones.

Headstrong describes someone determined to do things their own way, resistant to advice or direction. The word carries a note of disapproval—a headstrong person may be admirably independent but is more often recklessly willful: {Her headstrong daughter refused to listen to reason}. The image is of someone who leads with their head, charging forward regardless of obstacles or warnings.

A headwind is a wind blowing directly against the direction of travel, slowing progress. Pilots and cyclists factor headwinds into their calculations: {We lost twenty minutes flying into a headwind}. Figuratively, headwind describes any force working against success or momentum: {The company faced regulatory headwinds}. The opposite is tailwind.

To heal is to restore to health or wholeness. Wounds heal, sometimes leaving scars. Doctors heal patients, though time heals most injuries on its own. The word extends naturally to emotional and social repair: {Time heals all wounds}, {healing a rift between friends}. A healer is one who heals, whether physician, shaman, or supportive presence.

Healed describes something that has been restored to health or wholeness. A healed wound has closed and mended. A healed relationship has recovered from damage. The word implies a process that's complete—you're healed when the healing is finished: {Her broken arm has fully healed}, {Time healed old grievances between them}.

A healer is someone who heals—restores health or wholeness. The term applies broadly: a physician is a healer, but so is a spiritual practitioner who works through prayer, energy, or ritual. In fantasy games and fiction, healers are characters whose abilities restore health points to allies. {The village healer treated wounds with herbs and poultices.}

Healers are people who heal—whether through conventional medicine, alternative practices, or spiritual means. The term often implies something beyond standard medical treatment: {She visited healers when doctors couldn't help}. In gaming and fantasy contexts, a healer is a character class specializing in restoring health to allies: {Every raid group needs a good healer}.

Healing is the process of becoming whole or healthy again. A wound heals as tissue repairs itself; a relationship heals when trust is restored. The adjective describes things that promote recovery: {healing waters}, {a healing touch}. In spiritual contexts, healing often implies restoration beyond the physical—emotional, relational, or communal. {Time is healing, but slowly.}

Heals is the verb form of heal, meaning to make or become whole again. Wounds heal, relationships heal, time heals. A healer heals the sick. The word applies to physical recovery {The cut healed without scarring} and emotional or spiritual restoration {She's still healing from the divorce}. What heals may also simply improve: {a good night's sleep heals most frustrations}.

Health is the condition of a living thing's body and mind—whether good or bad, though the word alone often implies wellness: {in good health}, {health problems}, {mental health}. Health extends to the condition of systems and organizations: {the health of the economy}, {ecosystem health}. A toast {to your health} wishes someone well-being.

Healthcare is the organized provision of medical services—prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and recovery. It encompasses hospitals, clinics, insurance systems, and public health programs. The word often appears in policy debates: {healthcare reform}, {universal healthcare}, {healthcare costs}. Also spelled as two words: health care.

Healthy describes a state of physical well-being—free from illness, functioning as it should. A healthy person isn't sick; a healthy heart pumps blood efficiently. The meaning extends to things that promote well-being: a healthy diet, healthy habits. Healthy also means robust or substantial: {a healthy profit}, {a healthy skepticism}. A healthy attitude or relationship functions well without dysfunction. {She has a healthy respect for the ocean's power.}

A heap is a pile of things thrown or lying together without order: {a heap of dirty laundry}, {a heap of rubble}. The word extends to large quantities: {heaps of money}, {a heap of trouble}. To heap is to pile up or load abundantly: {She heaped food on his plate}. In computing, the heap is a region of memory for dynamic allocation. A heap can also be an old, barely functioning car.

To hear is to perceive sound through the ears. You hear music, voices, thunder. Extended meanings involve receiving information: {I hear you're moving to Boston}, {Have you heard the news?} To hear someone out is to listen to their full explanation. {Hear, hear!} expresses agreement in formal settings. A court hears a case by receiving testimony and arguments. {I won't hear of it} means you refuse to consider something.

Heard is the past tense and past participle of hear. Where hear covers receiving sound or information, heard places that reception in the past: {I heard a noise}, {She heard the news yesterday}. To feel heard is to feel that others have genuinely listened and understood: {I just want to be heard}.

Hearing is the sense by which sound is perceived—one of the five traditional senses. It also names the act of listening: {Give me a hearing before you decide}. A hearing is a formal proceeding where testimony is taken: {a congressional hearing}, {a custody hearing}. Within hearing means close enough to hear: {Don't say that within hearing of the children}. Hard of hearing describes partial deafness.

Hearings is the plural of hearing, which beyond the sense of perceiving sound refers to formal proceedings where evidence and arguments are presented. A congressional hearing investigates matters of public concern. A court hearing addresses legal questions before trial. An administrative hearing reviews government decisions: {The zoning board scheduled hearings on the proposed development}. The word implies an opportunity to be heard—to present one's case before decision-makers.

Hearsay is information received secondhand—something you heard someone else say rather than witnessed yourself. In everyday use, hearsay suggests unreliable gossip or rumor: {That's just hearsay}. In law, hearsay is an out-of-court statement offered as evidence, generally inadmissible because the original speaker isn't available for cross-examination.

A hearse is a vehicle for transporting a coffin to a funeral or burial site. Modern hearses are typically long, black automobiles with a rear compartment visible through side windows: {The hearse led the procession to the cemetery}. The word sometimes extends metaphorically to anything associated with death or funerals.

Heart designates the blood-pumping vital organ in vertebrates, but it is used to talk about emotional or moral feelings (as distinct from intellect). Two frequent collocations are win someone’s heart (succeed in attracting their love), and break someone’s heart (withdraw your love or affection from them when they don’t want this). The expression at heart means essentially or in essence: She’s a country girl at heart. The heart of something is the most central or vital part of it.

Heartache is emotional anguish, especially from grief or disappointed love. The word locates suffering in the chest, where strong emotions register physically: {the heartache of losing a child}, {all the heartache she'd been through}. It suggests deep, lingering pain rather than sudden shock.

A heartbeat is one complete cycle of the heart's contraction and relaxation, pumping blood through the body. The word often refers to the rhythmic sound or sensation: {I could feel my heartbeat racing}. Figuratively, someone or something can be the heartbeat of a place or movement—its vital center: {Small businesses are the heartbeat of the local economy}. In a heartbeat means instantly or without hesitation: {I'd do it again in a heartbeat}.

Heartbreak is the crushing emotional pain that follows loss—especially the end of a romantic relationship or the death of someone loved. The word captures how grief can feel physical, as if the heart itself has been damaged. A heartbreak can also be any devastating disappointment: {It was a heartbreak to see the old theater torn down}.

A heartbreaker is someone who causes romantic disappointment or emotional pain, typically by ending a relationship or failing to return affection: {She's a heartbreaker—left a trail of broken hearts across three states}. The word can also describe a devastating loss or near-miss: {That last-second field goal was a real heartbreaker for the home crowd}.

Heartbreaking describes something that causes intense emotional pain or grief. A heartbreaking {story} moves you to tears; heartbreaking {news} delivers devastating information. The word applies to situations that evoke deep sympathy or sorrow: {It was heartbreaking to watch her say goodbye}. Unlike merely sad, heartbreaking suggests something that pierces you emotionally.

Heartbroken describes the devastation of profound emotional loss—the end of a relationship, the death of someone loved, the collapse of a cherished hope. The heart is imagined as literally broken, unable to function normally: {She was heartbroken when he left}. The noun is heartbreak; the adjective heartbreaking describes what causes such pain.

Heartburn is a burning sensation in the chest caused by stomach acid rising into the esophagus. Despite the name, it has nothing to do with the heart—the discomfort just occurs in that general area. Spicy food, overeating, and lying down after meals commonly trigger it. {I shouldn't have had that second helping—now I've got heartburn.}

Heartfelt describes emotions or expressions that are deeply sincere and genuine: {a heartfelt apology}, {heartfelt thanks}, {heartfelt condolences}. The word implies that feeling comes from somewhere essential rather than being performed or obligatory. Something heartfelt may be simple or inarticulate but carries authentic emotional weight.

A hearth is the floor of a fireplace, typically made of stone or brick, extending into the room. By extension, hearth represents home and domestic life: {hearth and home}, {defending hearth and family}. The word evokes warmth, safety, and the traditional center of household gathering.

Hearths is the plural of hearth, the floor of a fireplace or the area immediately surrounding it. The hearth was traditionally the center of home life—where families gathered for warmth and cooking. This makes it a symbol of domesticity: {hearths and homes}, {defending their hearths}. The word extends to the floor of furnaces and forges in metalworking.

Heartland refers to the central or most important part of a country or region, especially one considered essential to its character or identity. In American usage, the heartland typically means the rural Midwest, evoking images of farms, small towns, and traditional values distinct from coastal urban centers. {Politicians love to campaign in the heartland.} The term can apply to any nation's core territory, or metaphorically to the essential center of anything: {the heartland of conservative thought}.

Heartless means lacking compassion or feeling—cruel, unfeeling, indifferent to others' suffering. A heartless {decision} disregards human cost. A heartless {person} shows no sympathy. The word implies coldness rather than active malice: {It was heartless to fire her on Christmas Eve}. Something heartless treats people as if they don't matter.

Hearts are the plural of heart—the organ, the shape, or the seat of emotion. In cards, hearts is one of the four suits, marked by red heart symbols. Hearts is also a trick-taking card game where players try to avoid winning hearts and especially the queen of spades: {Let's play hearts after dinner}. (Capitalized Hearts may refer to the Scottish football club.)

Heartsick describes deep emotional distress—the ache of grief, disappointment, or longing. Someone heartsick over a breakup or a death feels the pain almost physically, as if the heart itself were afflicted: {She was heartsick when she learned he had married someone else}. The word is slightly literary but still current.

A heartstopper is something so surprising, thrilling, or beautiful that it figuratively stops the heart—a moment of breathless shock or awe. The word often describes dramatic moments in sports or entertainment: {The last-second goal was a real heartstopper}. It can also refer to a person of stunning attractiveness: {She's an absolute heartstopper}.

Heartstrings are the deepest feelings of love or compassion. The word appears almost exclusively in the plural and with a possessive: {The documentary tugged at my heartstrings}. To tug, pull, or pluck at someone's heartstrings is to evoke strong emotion, especially sympathy or tender sentiment. The image suggests invisible cords connecting the heart to what it loves.

Heartstrings are the deep emotions, especially love, sympathy, or sentimental attachment. The word appears almost exclusively in the phrase {tug at the heartstrings} or {pull at the heartstrings}, describing something that evokes tender feelings: {The documentary about orphaned animals really tugged at my heartstrings}. The image is of emotions as strings that can be plucked or pulled.

A heartthrob is a celebrity or public figure who inspires romantic admiration, especially among young fans: {He was a teen heartthrob in the nineties}. The term evokes the quickened pulse of infatuation. It typically describes actors, musicians, or other performers known for their physical appeal.

Heartthrobs is the plural of heartthrob—a celebrity or public figure who inspires romantic infatuation, especially among young fans: {teen heartthrobs of the 1990s}, {The actor was a heartthrob before becoming a serious dramatic performer}. The word evokes the quickened pulse of adolescent crushes.

Heartwarming describes something that evokes tender, positive emotions—a feeling of warmth in the chest associated with affection, gratitude, or restored faith in human goodness. The word typically applies to stories, gestures, or moments: {a heartwarming reunion}, {a heartwarming tale of kindness}. It suggests emotional uplift without sentimentality tipping into saccharine.

Hearty describes something robust, vigorous, or wholehearted. A hearty {meal} is substantial and satisfying. A hearty {laugh} comes from deep within. Hearty {congratulations} are warm and sincere. A hearty {welcome} is enthusiastic. The word often suggests physical vigor or abundance: {hearty appetite}, {hale and hearty}. In nautical tradition, {me hearties} addresses fellow sailors.

Heat, a verb and noun, is related to the adjective hot. When you heat something, you make it warmer. Heat has the same figurative meanings as hot that are associated with anger and passion. If a discussion heats up, it becomes more intense. When a female animal is in heat, it is receptive to pregnancy. If someone is applying heat, they are bringing pressure in order to achieve a result.

Heated describes something with elevated temperature: {heated seats}, {a heated pool}. More often, heated refers to emotional intensity, especially anger or passionate disagreement: {a heated argument}, {The discussion grew heated}.
