Verbs associated with horse typically reveal the human connection, such as ride, race, and breed. Various figurative and slang uses of horse don’t always have an obvious connection with the animal, although a sawhorse, sometimes just called a horse, stands on four feet and has a flat back.

Horseback refers to the back of a horse, used almost exclusively in the phrase {on horseback}, meaning mounted on a horse: {They traveled on horseback through the mountains}. As an adverb, it describes doing something while riding: {The soldiers arrived horseback}. Horseback riding is the common American term for the activity the British call horse riding.

A horsefly is a large biting fly that feeds on the blood of horses, cattle, and other mammals, including humans. The bite is painful—horseflies slice skin rather than pierce it. They're persistent pests around livestock and near water in summer months: {The horses swished their tails at the horseflies}.

A horseman is a man who rides horses, especially one skilled in horsemanship. The term suggests expertise rather than casual riding: {an accomplished horseman}. Horseman also refers to a man who breeds or raises horses. In apocalyptic imagery, the Four Horsemen are harbingers of catastrophe—conquest, war, famine, and death.

Horsemen is the plural of horseman—a person who rides horses, especially one skilled in horsemanship. The term applies to cavalry soldiers, equestrians, and mounted herders. The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse are biblical figures representing conquest, war, famine, and death, often invoked figuratively for any group bringing catastrophe: {The four horsemen of the financial collapse}.

Horseplay is rough, boisterous play or fooling around—the kind of rowdy physical antics that might knock things over or get someone hurt: {The lifeguard told us to cut out the horseplay}. The word typically describes behavior that's energetic and careless rather than malicious, though it often precedes trouble.

Horsepower is a unit measuring the rate at which work is done—the power output of engines, motors, and machines. One horsepower equals the force needed to lift 550 pounds one foot in one second, roughly the sustained output of a draft horse. Engine specifications always include horsepower: {a 300-horsepower engine}. Figuratively, horsepower suggests raw capability or force: {We need more horsepower on this project}.

A horserace is a competitive event in which horses run against each other, typically with jockeys riding them. The term extends to any close, dramatic competition: {The election turned into a horserace in the final weeks}. Horserace journalism focuses on who's winning rather than substantive issues. Also spelled as two words: horse race.

Horseradish is a pungent root vegetable used as a condiment, prized for its sharp, sinus-clearing heat that dissipates quickly unlike the lingering burn of chile peppers. The grated root, often mixed with vinegar or cream, accompanies roast beef, gefilte fish, and cocktail sauce. Prepared horseradish loses potency over time, so fresh-grated delivers the strongest kick. The plant itself, with its large leaves and white taproot, grows aggressively and can become invasive in gardens.

Horses is the plural of horse, the large hoofed mammal domesticated for riding, draft work, and racing. The word appears in countless expressions: {hold your horses} means wait or slow down, {wild horses couldn't drag me} expresses firm resolve, and {straight from the horse's mouth} means from a reliable source. To {beat a dead horse} is to belabor a settled matter. {Horses for courses} suggests different approaches suit different situations.

A horseshoe is a U-shaped metal plate nailed to a horse's hoof for protection. The shape has become a symbol of good luck, often hung above doorways with ends pointing up to "hold" the luck. Horseshoes is a game where players toss horseshoes at a stake, scoring points for getting close or ringing it: {We played horseshoes at the picnic}. As a verb, to horseshoe is to fit a horse with shoes.

Horseshoes is a lawn game in which players toss U-shaped metal pieces at stakes set in the ground, scoring points for landing close or ringing the stake. A {ringer} circles the stake completely. The expression {close only counts in horseshoes} (sometimes adding {and hand grenades}) means that near-misses usually don't matter—except in games where proximity earns points.

Hose is a flexible tube for conveying water or other fluids: {garden hose}, {fire hose}. To hose something is to spray it with water: {He hosed down the driveway}. In slang, to hose someone is to cheat or defeat them badly: {We got hosed on that deal}. Hose also means stockings or tights, from the old sense of a leg covering—still seen in {pantyhose} and in period costumes where men wear hose.

Hosed is informal slang meaning defeated, ruined, or put in a hopeless situation. If you get hosed, you've been cheated or treated unfairly: {We got totally hosed on that deal}. The word also describes being drunk or, in computing, a system that's completely broken and unrecoverable. {The server is hosed—we'll have to reinstall everything.} The underlying image is of being blasted with a fire hose, overwhelmed by force you can't resist.

Hospice is a facility or program providing care for terminally ill patients, focusing on comfort rather than cure. The emphasis is on managing pain and maintaining quality of life in final weeks or months: {She entered hospice care after stopping chemotherapy}. Hospice philosophy extends to home care, where medical teams visit patients who prefer to die at home surrounded by family.

A hospital is a facility where sick or injured people receive medical treatment, often staying overnight or longer. Hospitals range from small community buildings to vast medical centers with specialized departments: {She was rushed to the hospital after the accident}. In British English, you go {to hospital} without the article; Americans go {to the hospital}.

Hospitality is the friendly and generous reception of guests or strangers. It encompasses welcoming people, offering food and drink, and making visitors comfortable: {Southern hospitality}, {We were overwhelmed by their hospitality}. The hospitality industry includes hotels, restaurants, and other businesses serving travelers and diners. To {extend hospitality} is to offer someone your welcome.

Hospitalized means admitted to a hospital for medical care. The term implies staying overnight or longer, not just an emergency room visit: {She was hospitalized for three days after the accident}. In British English, the spelling is hospitalised.

Hospitals are medical facilities where sick or injured people receive treatment, often staying overnight or longer. The word covers everything from small rural clinics to sprawling urban medical centers with specialized departments. {She was rushed to the hospital after the accident.} In British English, the article is often dropped: {He's in hospital.}

Most meanings of host suggest an unequal relationship between parties. A host is the counterpart of a guest – that is, one who provides or manages facilities and services that guests enjoy. To host an event or person is to act in the role of host. In biology, a host is an organism that harbors another, often a parasite. In computing, a host is the server on which particular files or sites reside. An older meaning of host is a great number: He gave a host of excuses.

A hostage is a person held captive as security for the fulfillment of demands—typically the payment of ransom or compliance with political conditions. Kidnappers take hostages; governments negotiate for their release. The term extends to situations of powerlessness: {I was held hostage by my own fears}. A {hostage to fortune} is something that makes you vulnerable to future misfortune.

Hostages are people held captive to compel others to meet demands—typically for ransom, political concessions, or safe passage. Governments negotiate for hostages; terrorists take them. The word extends to situations of dependency: {We're hostages to the weather}. A hostage {situation} or hostage {crisis} involves active negotiations for release.

A hostel is inexpensive lodging, typically with shared rooms and communal facilities, catering mainly to young travelers and backpackers: {We stayed at hostels across Europe to save money}. Youth hostels specifically serve younger guests. The word also applies to supervised residences for homeless people or those in transitional housing.

Hostels are budget accommodations offering dormitory-style rooms with shared facilities. Travelers, especially young backpackers, use hostels for cheap lodging: {We stayed in hostels across Europe}. Unlike hotels, hostels emphasize communal spaces and socializing over privacy. Some hostels offer private rooms at higher rates. Youth hostels traditionally served young travelers but now welcome all ages.

A hostess is a woman who receives and entertains guests, whether at home or professionally. In restaurants, a hostess greets diners and manages seating. On aircraft, the term *stewardess* or *flight attendant* has largely replaced *air hostess*. A hostess may also be a woman who works at a bar or club, paid to converse with and entertain male customers—a role that can shade into prostitution depending on context. {She worked as a hostess at the new Italian place downtown.}

Hostile describes opposition or antagonism—an attitude of unfriendliness or active resistance. A hostile {witness} works against the side that called them. A hostile {takeover} acquires a company against management's wishes. Hostile {territory} belongs to the enemy. The environment itself can be hostile: {conditions hostile to life}. As a noun, a hostile is an enemy combatant.

Hostilities are acts of warfare or armed conflict between opposing forces. The word typically appears in formal or diplomatic contexts: {Hostilities broke out along the border}, {a cessation of hostilities}. Unlike the singular hostility, which describes unfriendly feelings, hostilities almost always refers to actual fighting rather than mere antagonism.

Hostility is unfriendliness, antagonism, or opposition directed toward someone or something. It ranges from cold disapproval to active aggression: {I sensed hostility in the way she refused to look at me}. In the plural, hostilities refers to acts of warfare or armed conflict: {Hostilities broke out along the border}. A hostile environment is one marked by tension or threat, whether in a workplace, a combat zone, or nature itself.

Hosting is providing space, resources, or services for something to operate or occur. A person hosts a party or guests; a server hosts a website; a city hosts the Olympics. In computing, hosting typically refers to storing and serving websites or applications: {We pay fifty dollars a month for web hosting}. A host organism hosts a parasite.

Hosts is the plural of host—people who receive guests, organisms harboring parasites, or servers providing network services. Someone who hosts entertains or provides a platform: {She hosts a podcast}, {The city hosts the Olympics}. The communion wafer is also a host, from a different origin meaning sacrifice. {Several hosts competed to throw the best party.}

Hot is the opposite of cold and significantly beyond warm on the temperature scale in nearly all its meanings. In frequent figurative use, hot may mean exciting (hot imagination), carrying current (hot wires), quick to anger (hot tempered), or erotically intense (hot sex scene). Opaque idioms in which hot features include hot water (trouble), hot spot (place of conflict), and hot air (empty talk). The more common related verb is heat but, informally, to hot up means to become hotter or more intense.

A hotbed is a place or situation where something flourishes intensely, usually something undesirable: {a hotbed of corruption}, {a hotbed of radical politics}. The term comes from gardening, where a hotbed is a glass-covered bed of soil heated by fermenting manure to force early plant growth. The figurative sense dominates modern usage.

A hotdog is a cooked sausage, typically beef or pork, served in a sliced bun with condiments like mustard, ketchup, or relish. It's iconic American stadium and street food. As a verb, to hotdog is to show off with flashy, risky moves: {He was hotdogging on the ski slopes}. A hotdogger seeks attention through stunts. Also spelled hot dog.

A hotel is a commercial establishment that provides lodging for travelers, typically offering private rooms with beds, bathrooms, and various amenities. Hotels range from budget accommodations to luxury resorts and are distinguished from motels by their interior hallways and fuller services. {We booked a hotel near the airport for our layover.} In the NATO phonetic alphabet, hotel represents the letter H.

Hotels are establishments providing lodging and usually meals for travelers and guests. The term covers everything from budget roadside motels to luxury resorts. A hotel room is the basic unit of accommodation. To {hotel} somewhere is to stay in hotels: {We hoteled our way across Europe}. The hotel industry encompasses hospitality, tourism, and real estate.

A hothead is someone quick to anger or rash action—a person who flies off the handle easily. The term is mildly critical, suggesting impulsiveness rather than thoughtful response: {Don't be such a hothead; think before you react}. As an adjective, hotheaded describes the temperament: {his hotheaded approach to negotiations}.

Hotheaded means quick to anger or act impulsively, without thinking through consequences. A hotheaded person flares up easily and may make rash decisions: {His hotheaded response cost him the negotiation}. The word suggests a temperament prone to emotional outbursts rather than cool deliberation.

Hotheads are people who lose their temper easily or act impulsively without thinking. The term suggests someone quick to anger or rash action: {The hotheads in the group wanted to confront management immediately}. A hothead lets emotion override judgment.

A hothouse is a heated greenhouse for growing plants that need warmth year-round. The word extends to any environment of artificial intensity: a hothouse {atmosphere}, a hothouse {of creativity}. As an adjective, hothouse describes something cultivated under protected conditions, often suggesting fragility or overprotection: {a hothouse flower who wilted at the first challenge}.

A hotline is a direct telephone line for rapid communication, especially during emergencies or crises. The term emerged from Cold War diplomacy—the hotline between Washington and Moscow—but now applies broadly to any dedicated line for urgent contact: a suicide {hotline}, a consumer {hotline}, a tip {hotline}. The "hot" suggests immediacy and constant readiness.

Hotlines are telephone lines providing direct, immediate access to information or assistance. A crisis hotline connects callers to counselors; a customer hotline handles complaints. The term originated with the direct communication link between Washington and Moscow during the Cold War—a line kept perpetually ready for urgent contact. {Call the hotline if you need help.}

Hotpot is a communal cooking method where diners simmer raw ingredients—thinly sliced meat, vegetables, tofu, noodles—in a shared pot of simmering broth at the table. The dish originated in East Asia and varies by region: Sichuan hotpot features a fiery, numbing broth, while Cantonese versions are milder. In British English, hotpot (or hot pot) refers to a different dish entirely—a slow-cooked casserole of meat and vegetables topped with sliced potatoes, associated with Lancashire: {a lamb hotpot}.

A hotrod is a car—typically an older American model—modified for speed and performance, with souped-up engines, lowered suspensions, and flashy paint jobs. Hotrods emerged from 1940s and 1950s youth culture, when young men stripped down and rebuilt cars to race on dry lake beds and drag strips. The term extends to anyone who drives fast or recklessly: {Some hotrod nearly sideswiped me on the freeway}. Also spelled hot rod.

Hotrods are automobiles—typically older American cars from the 1930s through 1960s—modified for speed and style. The modifications usually involve souped-up engines, lowered suspensions, and custom paint jobs. Hotrod culture emerged in postwar America and remains associated with drag racing and car shows: {He spent weekends working on hotrods with his dad}.

A hotshot is someone who is conspicuously skilled or successful, often with an edge of arrogance or showiness: {Some hotshot lawyer from New York took over the case}. The term can be admiring or dismissive depending on tone—acknowledging talent while suggesting the person knows it a little too well. As an adjective: {a hotshot pilot}, {hotshot developers}.

Hotshots are people who are exceptionally skilled or successful, often with an implication of cockiness: {Some hotshot lawyer from New York took the case}. The word carries a whiff of resentment—calling someone a hotshot acknowledges their talent while suggesting they know it too well. In wildfire fighting, hotshots are elite firefighters trained for the most dangerous conditions.

A hotspot is a place of concentrated activity or intensity. In technology, it's a location offering wireless internet access, or a device that creates one: {I used my phone as a hotspot}. Geographic hotspots are areas of unusual concentration—crime hotspots, biodiversity hotspots, volcanic hotspots. The word suggests somewhere things are happening, often with urgency or risk.

Hotspots are areas of concentrated activity, intensity, or interest. A crime hotspot sees unusually high criminal activity. A WiFi hotspot provides wireless internet access—either a public location or a device that shares a cellular connection. In geology, hotspots are volcanic regions where magma rises through the earth's crust. The word implies a focal point worth attention: {The bar district is a hotspot for nightlife}. Also spelled as two words.

Hottie is informal for a sexually attractive person: {Did you see that hottie at the bar?} The word is playful and casual, more complimentary than objectifying in most contexts. It applies to any gender. Also spelled hotty.

To hotwire a vehicle is to start it without a key by bypassing the ignition system—typically by connecting wires directly. The term evokes theft or emergency: {He hotwired the car and drove off before anyone noticed}. Figuratively, to hotwire something is to bypass normal procedures to get quick results: {We hotwired the approval process to meet the deadline}.

Hotwiring is starting a vehicle without a key by bypassing the ignition system—typically by exposing wires under the dashboard and connecting them directly. The technique is associated with car theft: {He learned hotwiring from older kids in the neighborhood}. Figuratively, to hotwire something is to bypass normal procedures to get quick results.

A hound is a dog bred for hunting, typically one that tracks by scent or sight: {bloodhound}, {greyhound}, {foxhound}. The word extends to any persistent pursuer. To hound someone is to chase or harass them relentlessly: {Creditors hounded him for months}. A {news hound} or {publicity hound} pursues something obsessively.

Hounded is the past tense of hound, meaning to pursue or harass someone relentlessly. The word draws on the image of hunting dogs chasing prey without letting up. Someone who is hounded feels constantly pressured or followed, whether by creditors, reporters, or their own guilt. {She was hounded by the press after the scandal broke.} {He felt hounded by his past mistakes.}

An hour is a unit of time equal to sixty minutes, one twenty-fourth of a day. Hours structure daily life: business hours, office hours, visiting hours. The hour can mean the present moment: {the man of the hour}, {the question of the hour}. To do something {on the hour} is to do it when the clock strikes exactly. An {eleventh-hour} decision comes at the last possible moment. In the plural, hours often indicates a long stretch of time: {We talked for hours}.

An hourglass is a device for measuring time, consisting of two glass bulbs connected by a narrow neck through which sand flows from the upper chamber to the lower. The process takes a fixed duration—historically one hour, though modern versions vary. Hourglass describes the shape: narrow in the middle, wider at top and bottom. An {hourglass figure} has a slim waist with fuller bust and hips.

Hours is the plural of hour, a unit of time equal to sixty minutes. Hours often refers to the time during which something operates or someone works: {business hours}, {office hours}, {after hours}. To {keep late hours} is to stay up late regularly. The {wee hours} are the early morning hours after midnight. {It took hours} suggests a long, tedious wait.

A house is a building that people live in. Though it is closely associated in meaning with home and is interchangeable with it in many contexts, it is not a related word. Without modification, house typically refers to single family dwelling, but there are many variants, such as an apartment house (a building consisting of several or many residential units), or a guest house, which may be a large structure for many paying visitors, or a small house for one. When you house someone, you provide accommodations for them. When one thing houses another, it provides a protected and enduring place for it: The new museum will house the painter’s entire collection.

A houseboat is a boat designed or modified for use as a dwelling. Some houseboats have motors and can navigate waterways; others remain moored permanently in place. Houseboats range from modest floating cabins to luxurious vessels with full amenities: {They spent the summer on a houseboat in the Florida Keys}.

Housebound means confined to one's home, typically due to illness, disability, or age. Someone who is housebound cannot easily leave their residence: {My grandmother became housebound after her hip surgery}. The term sometimes extends to temporary situations: {The blizzard left us housebound for three days}.

Housecleaning is the work of cleaning a house—dusting, vacuuming, scrubbing, and tidying. The term extends to any thorough removal of unwanted things: {The new CEO promised a housecleaning of corrupt executives}. Such figurative housecleaning suggests sweeping out problems that have accumulated through neglect.

A household is the people who live together in one dwelling—a family or other domestic unit sharing a home. The word also works as an adjective meaning domestic or relating to running a home: {household chores}, {household expenses}, {household appliances}. A {household name} is someone or something widely recognized: {The app became a household name overnight}.

A househusband is a married man whose primary role is managing the household and caring for children while his spouse works outside the home. The term mirrors housewife, applying the same domestic arrangement with reversed gender roles: {He's been a househusband since their second child was born}.

A housekeeper is someone employed to manage domestic tasks—cleaning, laundry, cooking, and general upkeep of a home or hotel rooms. The role ranges from occasional cleaning help to live-in staff who run an entire household: {The housekeeper comes on Tuesdays}. In hotels, housekeepers clean and prepare guest rooms between stays.

Housekeeping is the work of maintaining a home or living space—cleaning, tidying, laundry, and related tasks. In hotels, housekeeping is the department responsible for cleaning rooms. The word extends to routine maintenance in any domain: {Let's take care of some housekeeping before we begin the meeting}. Such administrative housekeeping covers minor but necessary details like announcements, scheduling, or procedural matters.

A houseplant is a plant grown indoors, typically for decoration. Most houseplants are tropical species that thrive in the stable temperatures and indirect light of interior spaces: {The fiddle-leaf fig has become a trendy houseplant}. Houseplants range from low-maintenance succulents to finicky orchids requiring careful attention.

Houseplants are plants grown indoors, typically in pots, for decoration or to bring greenery into living spaces. Common houseplants include ferns, succulents, and philodendrons. The term implies plants suited to indoor conditions—tolerating lower light and requiring only occasional watering: {She filled her apartment with houseplants}. Some people credit houseplants with improving air quality or mood.

Houses is the plural of house—buildings where people live. It extends to any sense of house: {The village had a dozen houses}, {both houses of Congress}, {fashion houses}. As a verb, houses means provides shelter or contains: {The museum houses a remarkable collection}, {The building houses three hundred apartments}.

A housewarming is a party celebrating someone's move into a new home. Guests typically bring gifts for the house—wine, plants, kitchen items. The word also works as a modifier: {a housewarming gift}, {a housewarming party}. The underlying metaphor suggests making a cold, empty space warm and lived-in.

A housewife is a married woman whose primary occupation is managing the household—cooking, cleaning, childcare—rather than working for pay outside the home. The term carries mid-twentieth-century associations when single-income families were the norm: {a 1950s housewife}, {housewife and mother of three}. Some find it dated or diminishing; alternatives include homemaker or stay-at-home mom.

Housewives is the plural of housewife—a woman who manages a household as her primary occupation rather than working outside the home. The term carries traditional gender-role connotations that some find dated or limiting: {a 1950s sitcom about housewives}. Despite this, it remains common in phrases like {desperate housewives} and {real housewives}, often with ironic or dramatic overtones.

Housework is the routine tasks required to maintain a home—cleaning, laundry, cooking, tidying. The term typically excludes major repairs or outdoor maintenance, focusing on recurring indoor chores: {I spent Saturday catching up on housework}. Housework has historically fallen disproportionately on women, making it a frequent subject of domestic and feminist discussion.

Housing is the buildings or structures where people live, considered collectively: {affordable housing}, {public housing}, {the housing shortage}. It extends to shelter for animals or protective enclosures for machinery: {a motor housing}. As a verb form, housing means providing accommodation: {The facility is capable of housing five hundred refugees}.

A hovel is a small, crude, or wretched dwelling—the sort of place characterized by poverty and squalor. The word appears in descriptions of desperate living conditions: {peasants crowded into hovels}, {a one-room hovel with a dirt floor}. Used loosely, hovel disparages any shabby or cramped space: {His apartment was a hovel}.

To hover is to remain suspended in air or stay in one place without moving far. A helicopter hovers; a hummingbird hovers at a flower. The word extends to lingering nearby: {She hovered by the door, waiting for news}. In computing, to hover is to position a cursor over an element without clicking: {Hover over the icon to see the tooltip}. Someone who hovers pays excessive attention, often unwanted: {Stop hovering—I can handle this myself}.

A hoverboard is a self-balancing electric scooter with two wheels side by side, ridden standing up. The name comes from the fictional levitating boards in *Back to the Future*, though real hoverboards don't actually hover—they roll. {She got a hoverboard for Christmas but wiped out on the first day.}

Hoverboards come in two varieties. The original is a fictional levitating skateboard, popularized by the *Back to the Future* films—a board that floats above the ground. The real-world hoverboard, appearing in the 2010s, doesn't hover at all but rolls on two self-balancing wheels: {She rides her hoverboard to school}. The name stuck despite the lack of actual hovering.

Hovering is staying in one place in the air, suspended without landing or moving away. A hummingbird hovers at a flower; a helicopter hovers over a building. The word extends to lingering nearby without committing to action: {She hovered by the door, unsure whether to enter}. A hovering presence suggests watchfulness that may feel protective or intrusive: {helicopter parents hovering over their children}.

How, though it is not technically a wh- word—like when, where, why, and what—behaves like them grammatically and is a frequent and important function word. When it is followed immediately by a verb or subject it is about the method or means that something happens: How did you get here? Uncle Ed showed me how to make jam. When it is followed by an adjective it is about the degree or extent to which the adjective applies: You won’t believe how nasty she was to us. How can also be used to inquire or tell about condition (How the heck are you?) or reason (How can you believe such rubbish?).
Howdy is a shortening of the now obsolete phrase how do ye? It is an informal greeting.

A howl is a long, loud, mournful cry—the sound wolves and dogs make, or the wail of wind through trees. People howl in pain, grief, or rage. To howl is also to laugh uncontrollably: {We howled at his impression}. A howl of protest is a loud objection. {The wind howled all night}. Something that's {a howl} is hilarious.

A howler is a glaring, obvious mistake—the kind that makes people wince or laugh: {That typo in the headline was a real howler}. The word suggests an error so bad it practically screams. Howler also refers to things that howl: howler monkeys, or something hilariously funny: {The comedian's set was full of howlers}.

Howling describes the long, mournful cry of wolves or dogs, or any similar wailing sound: {the howling of the wind}. It extends to loud, unrestrained expression: {howling with laughter}, {a howling baby}. As an intensifier, howling means extreme or glaring: {a howling success}, {a howling error}. The word suggests something impossible to ignore.

A hub is the central part of a wheel, where the spokes converge and the axle passes through. This core meaning extends to any central point of activity or connection: a transportation {hub}, a tech {hub}, a {hub of commerce}. In networking, a hub is a device connecting multiple computers. To be the hub of something is to be its focal point: {She was the hub of the organization}.

Hubbub is a loud, confused noise produced by many voices or activities at once—the din of a crowded room, a busy marketplace, or excited chatter. It can extend to any commotion or uproar: {The announcement caused quite a hubbub}. The word suggests chaotic sound rather than orderly noise.

Hubris is a noun that characterizes excessive pride or arrogance: It is sheer hubris to think that because you’re at the top, you can’t fail. Usually, those who are accused of showing hubris are in a position of power or authority. Journalists use the word more than anyone else, though hubris is also common in writing about the arts because it’s frequently displayed in plays and films.

A hub is a central point where things connect, converge, or are distributed outward. The word originally described the central part of a wheel from which spokes radiate, and this image carries into modern usage: an airport hub routes passengers through a central location, a tech hub concentrates companies and talent in one area, and a USB hub connects multiple devices to a single port. {Atlanta is a major hub for domestic flights.} The common thread is centrality and connection.

A huckleberry is a small, round berry native to North America, similar to a blueberry but typically smaller and with a more intense flavor. The shrubs that produce them grow wild in forests and mountains. In older American slang, {I'm your huckleberry} means I'm the right person for the job—the exact one you need.

A huckster is an aggressive seller of cheap goods, originally one who hawks wares in the street or door-to-door. The word carries connotations of pushiness and questionable ethics. In modern use, huckster often describes anyone who promotes something through exaggerated claims or manipulative tactics: {political hucksters}, {a huckster peddling miracle cures}. The verb means to sell or promote aggressively.

Hucksters are aggressive sellers or promoters, originally peddlers hawking goods in the street but now more often people who use pushy or questionable tactics to sell products or ideas. The term carries strong negative connotations of shameless self-promotion and dubious authenticity. {The candidates surrounded themselves with hucksters and spin doctors.} Politicians, advertisers, and media personalities are frequent targets of the label, suggesting they prioritize persuasion over substance.

To huddle is to crowd together, typically for warmth, protection, or private discussion: {The players huddled on the sideline}. A huddle is such a gathering—in American football, the brief formation where players receive the next play. To huddle with someone is to confer closely: {Let me huddle with my team and get back to you}. Huddled suggests vulnerability: {huddled masses}, {huddled in a doorway}.

Huddled describes people or things crowded closely together, usually for warmth, protection, or conference. Bodies huddle against cold; conspirators huddle to whisper. The word suggests both physical closeness and shared vulnerability or purpose: {huddled masses yearning to breathe free}, {The team huddled before the final play}.

Huddles is the plural of huddle—a tight cluster of people or things pressed close together. Football players form a huddle between plays to discuss strategy. People huddle for warmth or to confer privately: {The executives went into huddles throughout the afternoon}. The word suggests intimacy, secrecy, or shelter from something outside the group.

Hue is a color or shade of color: {autumn leaves in hues of red and gold}. More precisely, hue is the quality that distinguishes one color from another—what makes blue blue rather than green. The word appears in {hue and cry}, an old phrase for a public outcry or clamor, though this hue derives from a different source meaning a shouting or hooting.

Hues are colors, especially when distinguished by their position on the spectrum—red, orange, yellow, and so on. The word often emphasizes variety or gradation: {autumn leaves in every hue}, {the subtle hues of a sunset}. Hue can also mean character or aspect: {political opinions of every hue}.

Huff captures the idea of a sharp, forceful breath—blown out in annoyance or exertion. Someone {in a huff} is sulking or offended: {She left in a huff when no one agreed with her}. To huff is to breathe heavily or to sniff substances for intoxication: {huffing paint fumes}. The phrase {huff and puff} means to breathe laboriously or to bluster without effect.

Huffing is inhaling chemical vapors to get high—typically from aerosol sprays, paint, glue, or solvents. The practice is dangerous and can cause sudden death even on first use: {Three teenagers were caught huffing paint behind the school}. Separately, huffing describes breathing heavily or expressing annoyance through audible breath: {She stood there huffing after climbing the stairs}; {He was huffing about the long wait}.

A hug is an embrace—wrapping your arms around someone to express affection, comfort, or greeting. The gesture can be brief and casual or long and intimate. To hug is to hold someone or something close: {She hugged her knees to her chest}. Things that fit tightly may hug: {The road hugs the coastline}. A bear hug is an especially tight embrace.

Huge means very large in size, extent, or degree. A huge building towers over its surroundings; a huge mistake has serious consequences. The word carries more emphasis than big or large but less than enormous or colossal. Informally, huge can mean significant or successful: {That album was huge in the nineties}.

Hugging is the act of wrapping one's arms around someone or something, typically to express affection, comfort, or greeting. People hug loved ones, friends, and sometimes strangers in moments of joy or consolation. The word extends to holding things close: {She sat hugging her knees}. To hug a curve or coastline is to stay close to it: {The road hugs the cliff}.

Hugs are embraces—wrapping your arms around someone as a gesture of affection, comfort, or greeting. The word works as both noun and verb: {She gave him a hug}, {They hugged goodbye}. Hugging ranges from brief social gestures to prolonged emotional holds. {Hugs, not drugs} became a slogan promoting wholesome alternatives to substance use.

Hula is a traditional Hawaiian dance characterized by flowing arm movements and swaying hips, performed to chants or music. The dance tells stories through gesture and motion. A hula hoop—the toy twirled around the waist—takes its name from the similar hip rotation: {She can keep a hula hoop going for ten minutes}.

A hulk is something massive and unwieldy—originally the body of an old ship, stripped of masts and rigging, often used for storage or as a prison. By extension, hulk describes any large, heavy object or person: {The abandoned factory was a rusting hulk}. To hulk is to loom or move ponderously: {He hulked in the doorway}. A hulking figure is big and clumsy. (Capitalized Hulk refers to the Marvel Comics character.)

Hulking describes something large and heavy, often with a suggestion of clumsiness or menace. A hulking figure looms in a doorway. A hulking SUV dominates a parking space. The word evokes bulk without grace—something imposingly massive rather than impressively large: {A hulking bodyguard stood by the door}.

Hulks is the plural of hulk, referring to large, heavy, often clumsy things or people. Old ships stripped of their fittings and used for storage or as prisons were called hulks: {convicts sentenced to the hulks}. A person who hulks moves heavily or looms threateningly: {He hulks around the gym intimidating everyone}. The Hulk, Marvel's green-skinned strongman, has made the word nearly synonymous with massive muscularity: {He really hulked out after six months of training}.

A hull is the outer covering of a seed or fruit, especially the leafy cap on a strawberry or the husk of a grain. To hull strawberries is to remove those caps. Hull also names the main body of a ship—the watertight shell that sits in the water, distinct from masts, rigging, or superstructure: {The hull was breached below the waterline}. By extension, aircraft fuselages and tank bodies are sometimes called hulls. (Capitalized Hull is a city in England.)

Hulls are outer coverings removed to get at what's inside. The hull of a seed or grain is its husk or shell: {hull strawberries}, {sunflower seed hulls}. The hull of a ship or aircraft is its main body or frame—the shell that holds everything else. To hull is to remove the hull from seeds or fruit.

The imitative word hum characterizes a sound like that produced when the vocal cords vibrate but the mouth is closed. If you hum a tune, you produce the notes of the melody but do not sing them. Other things that hum include insects, electrical appliances, and machinery. A hum is an instance of humming: The droning hum of cars on the freeway is annoying. If a place hums with activity, it is busy and active. Hum is sometimes used like hmm to indicate a sound people make between words to indicate thought or doubt.

A human is a member of the species Homo sapiens—the bipedal primates distinguished by language, complex tool use, and abstract reasoning. Human works as both noun and adjective: {human trafficking}, {human trafficking victims}, {the human condition}. To be human is to be fallible: {I'm only human}. Human often contrasts with animal, divine, or machine: {a human-readable format}, {human-computer interaction}.

Humane means showing compassion and benevolence toward others, especially by minimizing suffering. Humane treatment of animals avoids cruelty; humane policies consider human dignity. The word shares roots with human but has diverged in meaning—human describes what we are, humane describes what we aspire to be: {a humane approach to criminal justice}, {humane methods of slaughter}.

Humanism is a philosophical stance that emphasizes human values, reason, and dignity over supernatural or divine authority. The term covers various movements that place humanity at the center of ethical and intellectual life: {secular humanism rejects religious frameworks}, {literary humanism values classical education}. In art criticism, humanism refers to focus on human subjects and concerns rather than abstract or spiritual themes. (Capitalized Humanism often refers specifically to Renaissance intellectual movement.)

A humanist emphasizes human values, potential, and dignity over supernatural or divine authority. The term applies to Renaissance scholars who revived classical learning, to secular thinkers who ground ethics in human welfare rather than religion, and more loosely to anyone with compassionate concern for humanity: {a humanist approach to education}, {secular humanist philosophy}.

Humanitarian describes concern for human welfare and the relief of suffering. A humanitarian crisis involves widespread harm—famine, war, natural disaster. Humanitarian aid addresses such emergencies. As a noun, a humanitarian is someone devoted to promoting human welfare: {She spent decades as a humanitarian in refugee camps}. The word emphasizes practical help over abstract philosophy.

The humanities are academic disciplines that study human culture, thought, and expression—including literature, philosophy, history, languages, art, and religion. Unlike the sciences, which seek empirical truths about the natural world, the humanities explore meaning, values, and the human experience through interpretation and analysis. {She majored in the humanities before going to law school.} The term often appears in discussions about liberal arts education and its value in developing critical thinking.

Humanity is humankind collectively—all human beings as a group: {crimes against humanity}, {the future of humanity}. It also names the quality of being human, especially the compassionate aspects: showing {humanity} to prisoners, appeals to someone's {humanity}. The humanities are academic disciplines studying human culture—literature, philosophy, history, languages—as distinct from sciences.

To humanize is to make something more human or relatable. You might humanize a public figure by showing their personal struggles, or humanize statistics by telling individual stories: {The documentary humanized the refugees by following three families}. In another sense, to humanize conditions is to make them more humane or bearable: {Prison reform efforts sought to humanize the facilities}.

Humanoid describes something having human form or characteristics. The word appears most often in science fiction for robots, aliens, or creatures that walk upright on two legs with a head, torso, and arms arranged like a human: {The humanoid aliens communicated through gestures}. As a noun, a humanoid is such a being: {The ship's crew encountered several humanoids on the planet's surface}.

Humans is the plural of human—members of the species Homo sapiens. The word often appears when discussing people as a category distinct from animals, machines, or supernatural beings: {Humans are the only species that uses language}, {The AI was designed to assist humans}. It can sound clinical or detached compared to "people": {How do humans cope with loss?}

Humble, an adjective, has two core meanings. Someone who comes from humble origins was underprivileged in some way. The other sense of humble is closely related to the noun humility and is a positive characterization of people or actions that show an attitude of respectful modesty, in which pride is absent: The mayor made a convincing and humble apology for the lack of facilities at the festival. Eating humble pie is a metaphor for a forced apology or a humiliating failure.

A humblebrag is a boast disguised as self-deprecation or complaint: {So exhausted from my book tour—five cities in three days!} The speaker feigns modesty while drawing attention to something impressive. The term captures a specific form of social media posturing where false humility barely conceals genuine self-promotion. As a verb, to humblebrag is to make such statements.

Humblebragging is boasting disguised as self-deprecation or complaint: {So exhausted from all these job offers}, {Ugh, my new car is too fast}. The humblebrag lets someone showcase achievements while appearing modest. The maneuver often backfires—listeners tend to find humblebragging more annoying than straightforward boasting.

Humbled describes someone whose pride or self-importance has been reduced, often through defeat, failure, or encountering something greater than themselves. Athletes say they're {humbled} by awards or fan support—though this fashionable use inverts the original meaning, expressing gratitude rather than diminishment. Genuinely humbled implies being brought low: {He was humbled by the crushing loss}.

Humbling describes an experience that diminishes pride or self-importance, often by revealing one's limitations or smallness in a larger context. A humbling {defeat} exposes weakness. A humbling {honor} makes you feel unworthy of the recognition. Standing before vast mountains can be a humbling experience—reminding you how little you are.

Humbug is deceptive or dishonest talk, behavior, or practices—especially pretentious nonsense meant to impress or mislead: {The whole ceremony was pure humbug}. A humbug is also a person who deceives through false claims or pretenses. As an exclamation, it dismisses something as fraudulent or absurd—famously Scrooge's {Bah, humbug!} in response to Christmas cheer. In British usage, a humbug is also a hard striped peppermint candy.

Humdrum describes what is dull, monotonous, and lacking variety—the tedious routine of everyday life. {The humdrum of office work wore him down.} As an adjective: {a humdrum existence}, {humdrum tasks}. The word itself mimics the droning quality it describes.

Humid describes air that contains a lot of water vapor. Humid weather feels heavy and often uncomfortable because perspiration doesn't evaporate easily: {The humid summer made everything feel sticky}. Tropical climates are typically humid, while deserts are arid. A {humid} greenhouse keeps plants moist.

Humidity is the amount of moisture in the air. High humidity makes hot weather feel more oppressive because sweat evaporates slowly; low humidity dries out skin and nasal passages. {The humidity today is unbearable.} Relative humidity expresses moisture as a percentage of what the air could hold at that temperature.

To humiliate someone is to make them feel ashamed or foolish, often publicly. The act attacks their dignity or self-respect: {He humiliated her in front of the whole office}. Humiliation can be deliberate cruelty or an unintended consequence: {Losing so badly humiliated the team}. The feeling lingers—humiliation cuts deeper than mere embarrassment.

Humiliated describes the state of having one's dignity or pride stripped away, often publicly. To be humiliated is to feel diminished, shamed, or made to look foolish: {He was humiliated when his lies were exposed in front of everyone}. The feeling lingers—humiliation cuts deeper than mere embarrassment.

Humiliates is the third-person singular of humiliate—to make someone feel ashamed, foolish, or stripped of dignity, often publicly. The act implies a power imbalance: a boss humiliates an employee, a bully humiliates a victim. {He humiliates her in front of their friends.} Unlike embarrassment, humiliation suggests deliberate cruelty or deep degradation.

Humiliating describes something that causes a painful loss of dignity or self-respect. A humiliating {defeat} is one that exposes weakness publicly. A humiliating {experience} leaves you feeling diminished or shamed: {It was humiliating to be corrected in front of everyone}. The word emphasizes the social dimension—humiliation typically involves witnesses or an audience, real or imagined.

Humiliation is the experience of being made to feel ashamed, foolish, or stripped of dignity—usually publicly. It differs from embarrassment in intensity and from shame in its external source: someone or something humiliates you. {The humiliation of being fired in front of coworkers stayed with him for years.} To humiliate is to inflict this feeling; humiliating describes what causes it.

Humiliations are experiences of being made to feel ashamed, foolish, or stripped of dignity. The word emphasizes the depth of embarrassment—not minor awkwardness but genuine degradation: {the daily humiliations of poverty}, {She never forgot the humiliations of her first job}. Public humiliations carry special weight because they involve witnesses to one's diminishment.

Humility is the quality of being modest about one's abilities or importance—the opposite of arrogance or pride. It implies an accurate, unpretentious assessment of oneself: {She accepted the award with humility}. Humility can be genuine self-awareness or a strategic posture: {His humility seemed calculated to disarm critics}.

Humming is producing a continuous low sound with closed lips, often while breathing out a tune: {She was humming to herself in the kitchen}. A place that's humming is full of activity and energy: {The restaurant was humming on Saturday night}. Things that hum mechanically produce a steady drone: {the humming of the refrigerator}.

A hummingbird is a tiny, brightly colored bird native to the Americas, named for the humming sound its rapidly beating wings produce. Hummingbirds hover in place while feeding on flower nectar, their wings beating up to eighty times per second. They are the only birds capable of sustained backward flight.

Hummingbirds are tiny, brightly colored birds of the Americas known for their ability to hover in place by beating their wings rapidly—fast enough to produce the humming sound that gives them their name. They feed on flower nectar, their long bills adapted to reach deep into blossoms. {The hummingbirds returned to the feeder in early spring.}

Hummus is a thick Middle Eastern spread or dip made from mashed chickpeas blended with tahini, lemon juice, garlic, and olive oil. It's typically eaten with pita bread or vegetables: {We ordered hummus and falafel}. The word comes from Arabic for "chickpeas." Also spelled houmous or hommos.

Humongous means extremely large—bigger than huge, enormous, or gigantic would suggest: {a humongous portion of fries}, {The project turned into a humongous mess}. The word is informal and emphatic, often chosen for comic effect or childlike exaggeration. Also spelled humungous.

Humor is the quality that makes something funny or amusing, or the ability to perceive and enjoy what's funny: {She has a great sense of humor}. It also means a mood or state of mind: {He was in good humor after the promotion}. To humor someone is to indulge them, going along with what they want even if you disagree: {Just humor me and try it}. In older medical theory, the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile—were bodily fluids thought to determine temperament, which is why humor came to mean mood.

Humour is the British spelling of humor, covering all the same meanings: the quality of being amusing or comic, a person's mood or temperament, and the ability to appreciate what's funny. {She has a wicked sense of humour.} The word traces to medieval medicine's four bodily humours—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—whose balance supposedly determined temperament. To humour someone is to indulge their wishes or go along with their whims, even if you disagree.

A hump is a rounded protuberance—the hump on a camel's back, a speed bump in the road, a mound of earth: {The camel stores fat in its hump}. {Slow down for the humps}. To hump is to carry something heavy on one's back, bending under the load: {They humped their packs through the jungle}. Wednesday is hump day—the middle of the workweek, after which you're "over the hump." In vulgar slang, to hump is to have sex, especially with thrusting motions: {They humped on the couch}. The sex sense is crude but common.

A humpback is a rounded deformity of the back, or a person with such a condition—now considered offensive when applied to people. The word more commonly refers to the humpback whale, a large baleen whale known for its acrobatic breaching and complex songs: {We watched humpbacks feeding off the coast}. As an adjective, humpbacked describes anything with a humped shape: {a humpbacked bridge}.

Hums is the sound of humming—a low, steady, continuous tone made with closed lips: {the hum of bees}, {the hum of machinery}. To hum is to produce this sound, often while singing a melody without words: {She hummed softly while she worked}. A place that hums is busy with activity: {The office was really humming today}.

A hunch is an intuitive feeling or suspicion not based on evidence: {I had a hunch she wasn't telling the truth}. To hunch is to arch or draw up: {He hunched his shoulders against the cold}. A hunch can also be a rounded lump, as in hunchback—someone with a curved spine.

A hunchback is a person with a pronounced curvature of the upper spine, creating a rounded or humped back. The term is old-fashioned and now considered offensive when applied to people—medical language prefers kyphosis for the condition. The word persists mainly through literary references: {The Hunchback of Notre Dame}.

Hunched describes a posture with the shoulders raised and the back curved forward, typically suggesting cold, discomfort, or dejection: {He sat hunched over his desk}. Someone who hunches draws their body inward protectively. A hunched figure appears smaller, contracted: {She walked hunched against the wind}.

Hunches is the plural of hunch in its noun sense—an intuitive feeling or suspicion not based on evidence: {I had a hunch she was lying}. To {play a hunch} is to act on intuition rather than logic. The verb hunch means to bend or curve the body forward: {He hunched over his desk}. Hunched shoulders suggest tension or cold.

Hundred is the number 100, ten times ten. It serves as a basic unit for counting and measuring: {a hundred dollars}, {a hundred years}. In the plural, hundreds indicates a large but indefinite quantity: {Hundreds of people showed up}. {A hundred percent} means completely or totally: {I'm a hundred percent certain}. Historically, a hundred was also an administrative subdivision in English counties.

Hung is the past tense and past participle of hang in most senses: {She hung the picture on the wall}, {The fog hung over the valley}. The exception is execution by hanging, which uses hanged: {The murderer was hanged at dawn}. Separately, hung is slang for having a large penis: {hung like a horse}. A hung jury cannot reach a verdict.

Hunger is the bodily sensation of needing food—the discomfort or weakness that comes from not eating. Extended, it describes severe food scarcity: {Millions face hunger in the region}. Figuratively, hunger is intense desire or craving: {a hunger for success}, {hunger for knowledge}. To hunger for something is to yearn for it deeply.

Hungover describes the unpleasant physical state following heavy alcohol consumption—headache, nausea, fatigue, sensitivity to light. {I was so hungover I couldn't get out of bed until noon.} The noun form is hangover. Someone perpetually hungover might be called a drunk; someone occasionally hungover had a rough night.

Hungry describes the physical sensation of needing food—the body signaling it wants to eat. Beyond literal hunger, it expresses strong desire or eagerness: {hungry for success}, {hungry for attention}. A hungry look suggests intense longing. Athletes described as hungry are driven and ambitious, not yet satisfied with their achievements.

A hunk is a large piece of something, typically torn or cut off roughly: {a hunk of bread}, {a hunk of cheese}. The word suggests irregular shape and substantial size. In informal use, a hunk is an attractive, well-built man: {She thinks the new lifeguard is a real hunk}.

Hunks is the plural of hunk. A hunk is a large, thick piece of something: {hunks of bread}, {hunks of cheese}. Informally, a hunk is an attractive, muscular man: {She thinks the new lifeguard is a total hunk}. The plural often appears in this sense: {a calendar full of hunks}.

Hunt is to pursue and try to capture or kill, especially game animals: {They hunted deer every fall}. The noun is an instance of hunting or a group that hunts together. Hunt extends to any determined search: {hunting for a job}, {hunting for the car keys}. To {hunt down} is to pursue until caught. A {witch hunt} is a campaign against people considered undesirable, often with flimsy evidence.

Hunted describes someone or something being pursued, especially by hunters or those seeking to capture or kill: {the hunted fox}, {a hunted fugitive}. The word carries connotations of fear and desperation—a hunted {look} in someone's eyes suggests they feel watched or threatened, unable to relax: {She had the hunted expression of someone always looking over her shoulder}.

A hunter is a person who hunts—pursuing and killing wild animals for food, sport, or pest control. The term extends to anyone who searches persistently: {a bargain hunter}, {a job hunter}, {a bounty hunter}. Hunter also names a type of horse bred for fox hunting, and a style of tall waterproof boot. {The hunters returned at dusk with two deer.} (Capitalized Hunter is a given name.)

Hunters is the plural of hunter—people who pursue and kill wild animals for food, sport, or wildlife management. The term extends to anyone who seeks something persistently: {job hunters}, {bargain hunters}, {bounty hunters}. In nature, hunters are predatory animals: {Wolves are pack hunters}. {The hunters returned with two deer}.

Hunting is the pursuit and killing of wild animals, typically for food, sport, or population control. The word extends to any determined search: {a job hunt}, {house hunting}, {hunting for my keys}. A hunting dog or hunting rifle is designed for the activity. To go hunting is to engage in the pursuit: {We went hunting every fall}.

Hunts is the third-person singular of hunt. To hunt is to pursue animals for food or sport, or to search persistently for something: {She hunts for bargains every weekend}. A hunt is the activity itself or an organized hunting party. Hunts as a noun refers to multiple such pursuits or groups: {Fox hunts were once common in the English countryside}.

A hurdle is a barrier to be jumped over, especially the lightweight frames used in track-and-field races. By extension, a hurdle is any obstacle or difficulty that must be overcome: {The biggest hurdle was getting funding}. To hurdle is to leap over something while running: {She hurdled the fence and kept going}.

Hurdles are barriers to be jumped over, originally in track-and-field races where runners leap a series of them. The sport itself is called hurdles or the hurdles: {She won gold in the 400-meter hurdles}. By extension, any obstacle or difficulty becomes a hurdle: {We still have a few hurdles to clear before the deal closes}. To hurdle is to jump over something while running.

Hurdling is the track-and-field event of running a course with hurdles—barriers that athletes must leap over at speed. The term covers both the activity and the sport: {She took up hurdling in high school}. By extension, hurdling can describe overcoming any series of obstacles: {hurdling bureaucratic requirements}.

Hurl means to throw with great force: {He hurled the ball across the field}, {She hurled insults at her opponent}. The violence of the motion distinguishes hurling from ordinary throwing—you hurl something when you want it to travel fast or hit hard. Informally, hurl also means to vomit: {I thought I was going to hurl}.

Hurling is an Irish sport played with wooden sticks and a small ball, resembling a fast-paced combination of field hockey and lacrosse. Teams score by hitting the ball into or over the goal. The sport has ancient origins and remains central to Irish athletic culture: {The hurling match drew thousands to Croke Park}. Separately, hurling is the present participle of hurl—to throw forcefully.

Hurls is the third-person singular of hurl, meaning to throw something with great force: {She hurls the ball across the field}. The word often carries a sense of violence or aggression—you hurl insults, accusations, or abuse at someone. To hurl can also mean to vomit: {He hurled after drinking too much}.

A hurricane is a powerful tropical storm with sustained winds of at least 74 miles per hour, forming over warm ocean waters. Hurricanes bring destructive winds, heavy rain, and storm surges to coastal areas. The term applies specifically to such storms in the Atlantic and eastern Pacific; elsewhere they're called typhoons or cyclones. Figuratively, a hurricane of activity or emotion suggests overwhelming intensity: {a hurricane of criticism}.

Hurricanes is the plural of hurricane, a powerful tropical storm with sustained winds of at least 74 miles per hour, rotating around a calm central eye. Hurricanes form over warm ocean waters and can cause catastrophic damage through wind, rain, and storm surge: {Three hurricanes hit the Gulf Coast that season}. The term applies specifically to such storms in the Atlantic and eastern Pacific; equivalent storms elsewhere are called typhoons or cyclones.

Hurried describes something done quickly, often with a sense of urgency or insufficient time. A hurried {breakfast} is eaten in haste. A hurried {glance} is brief and cursory. The word often implies carelessness or lack of thoroughness: {Her hurried response contained several errors}. Someone who looks hurried appears rushed or pressed for time.

Hurry is urgent haste—moving or acting faster than comfortable pace allows. You hurry to catch a train, hurry through a meal, hurry someone along. {What's the hurry?} asks why speed is necessary. {No hurry} signals patience. To be {in a hurry} is to feel pressed for time. {I won't do that again in a hurry} means not anytime soon.

Hurt covers physical pain and emotional distress. Something hurts when it causes pain: {My back hurts}, {That hurts!} To hurt someone is to injure or wound them, literally or figuratively: {I didn't mean to hurt your feelings}. As an adjective, hurt describes the injured state: {a hurt expression}, {deeply hurt by the betrayal}. The noun is the pain itself: {the hurt in her eyes}. Things that {wouldn't hurt} are advisable: {It wouldn't hurt to ask}.

Hurtful describes words, actions, or behavior that cause emotional pain or distress to someone. A hurtful {remark} wounds feelings; a hurtful {decision} may damage a relationship. The word implies intent or at least carelessness—something hurtful could have been avoided. It tends to describe interpersonal slights rather than physical harm: {What you said about her weight was really hurtful.}

Hurting describes being in pain, whether physical or emotional: {My back is hurting}, {She's still hurting from the breakup}. As an adjective, it characterizes someone or something in a bad state: {a hurting team}, {hurting for cash}. To be {hurting for} something is to need it badly. The word carries more immediacy than simply saying something hurts—it emphasizes ongoing distress.

Hurts is the third-person singular and plural form of hurt, covering both physical pain and emotional distress. Something hurts when it causes or feels pain: {My back hurts} or {It hurts to watch him struggle}. As a noun, hurts are injuries or sources of pain, though this usage is less common than the verb. The word applies equally to stubbed toes and wounded feelings, making no sharp distinction between bodily sensation and emotional anguish.

A husband is a man in a marriage—the male counterpart to a wife. The word carries connotations of commitment, partnership, and domestic responsibility: {her husband of thirty years}, {a devoted husband and father}. As a verb, to husband means to manage resources carefully and economically: {They husbanded their supplies through the winter}.

Husbands is the plural of husband, a man to whom someone is married. The word can also function as a verb meaning to manage resources carefully and economically: {She husbanded her savings through the lean years}. This sense connects to the older meaning of husband as one who manages a household, though that usage is now archaic outside of compounds like animal husbandry.

Hush calls for silence or quiet. As an interjection, it's a gentle command: {Hush, the baby's sleeping}. The verb means to make or become quiet: {She hushed the children}. A hush is a period of silence: {A hush fell over the crowd}. To hush something up is to suppress it, keeping it from becoming known: {They tried to hush up the scandal}. Hushed describes quiet, subdued tones: {They spoke in hushed voices}.

Hushed means quiet, silent, or subdued. A hushed {voice} is lowered to avoid being overheard. A hushed {room} has fallen silent, often in anticipation or reverence. The word suggests deliberate quieting rather than mere absence of sound: {The crowd fell hushed as the ceremony began}. Hushed {tones} implies secrecy or solemnity.

Hushpuppies are small, deep-fried balls of cornmeal batter, a staple of Southern American cooking typically served alongside fried fish or barbecue. The name supposedly comes from cooks tossing scraps to quiet barking dogs: {Hush, puppies}. {The catfish platter came with coleslaw and hushpuppies.} (Capitalized Hush Puppies is a shoe brand.)

A husk is the dry outer covering of a seed or fruit—corn husks, coconut husks. To husk corn is to strip away this covering. Figuratively, a husk is an empty shell of what once held life: {After the divorce, he was just a husk of his former self}. The adjective husky, meaning dry-throated or rough-voiced, derives from the same image.

Huskies is the plural of husky, a breed of sled dog developed in Arctic regions. These dogs are known for their thick coats, endurance, and wolf-like appearance: {The huskies pulled the sled across the frozen tundra}. Husky also means a person or thing that is big and sturdy, so huskies can refer to multiple such individuals. (Capitalized Huskies refers to sports teams.)

Husks are the dry outer coverings of seeds, grains, or fruits—the papery sheaths around corn kernels, the rough casings of wheat. To husk corn is to strip away these layers. Figuratively, a husk is what remains when substance is gone: {He was a husk of his former self}. The word suggests emptiness, something hollowed out.

Husky has two unrelated origins. One comes from husk—husky corn has its husk on, and a husky voice is rough and dry like a husk. This extends to sturdy or burly: {a husky farmhand}. The other husky is a sled dog bred for Arctic conditions, probably from a shortening of Eskimo. {A team of huskies pulled the sled across the ice.}

Hustle centers on energetic, often aggressive activity. To hustle is to move quickly or push someone along: {The guards hustled him out of the building}. It means to work hard and fast, especially to make money: {She's been hustling to pay rent}. In American English, hustle often implies swindling—a hustle is a scam, and a hustler is someone who deceives for profit, whether at pool or on the street. The noun also names a disco-era line dance. {Side hustle} is a secondary job or income source.

A hustler is someone who pursues money or success aggressively, often through dubious means. The word carries a spectrum of meanings from admiring to criminal. A street hustler might sell stolen goods or run scams. A pool hustler pretends to play poorly, then wins big bets. In sex work, a hustler is typically a male prostitute. More positively, calling someone a hustler can praise their tireless drive and resourcefulness: {She's a real hustler—started three businesses before she was thirty}. (Capitalized Hustler is the magazine.)

Hustlers is the plural of hustler—someone who pursues money or success aggressively, often through questionable means. A hustler might be a swindler running scams, a pool shark feigning incompetence, or simply someone with relentless drive: {She admires hustlers who built empires from nothing}. In some contexts, hustler means prostitute, especially a male sex worker.

Hustles covers energetic effort and deceptive schemes. To hustle is to move quickly or push aggressively: {She hustled the kids out the door}. In sports, hustle means relentless effort: {He's not the most talented, but he hustles}. The shadier sense involves swindling or aggressive selling: {street hustlers}, {hustling pool for money}. As a noun, a hustle is a scheme or scam, or the daily grind of making money: {the side hustle}.

Hustling is energetic, aggressive activity toward a goal. In sports and work, it means giving maximum effort: {I admire his hustling on defense}. Hustling also means pursuing money through aggressive salesmanship, schemes, or fraud: {He's been hustling tourists on the boardwalk}. It can specifically mean working as a prostitute or soliciting customers for sex.
Hut and hup, along with hep, are used to set the pace for people, especially soldiers, who are marching. It is also a small, simple house or shelter.

A hyacinth is a bulb flower known for its dense clusters of fragrant, bell-shaped blooms in purple, pink, white, or blue. Native to the eastern Mediterranean, hyacinths are spring garden staples: {The hyacinths are finally blooming}. The word also names a reddish-orange gemstone, a variant of zircon. (Capitalized Hyacinth is a given name from Greek mythology.)

A hybrid combines elements from different sources. In biology, a hybrid is offspring from two different species or varieties: a mule is a hybrid of horse and donkey. The term extends to anything of mixed origin: hybrid {cars} use both gasoline and electric power, hybrid {work} splits time between office and home. {The film is a hybrid of comedy and horror.}

A hydra is a many-headed serpent from Greek mythology that grew two heads for each one cut off—making it nearly impossible to kill. The word now describes any problem that multiplies when you try to solve it: {Every time we fix one bug, two more appear—it's a hydra}. In biology, hydra refers to tiny freshwater organisms with remarkable regenerative abilities, named for the mythical creature. (Capitalized Hydra is the specific mythological monster or a constellation.)

A hydrant is a connection point for drawing water from a main supply, typically a short post with valves and outlets found along streets for firefighters to attach hoses: {The truck pulled up next to the hydrant}. Fire hydrant is the full term, though hydrant alone usually means the same thing. {Don't park in front of a hydrant.}

Hydration is the process of absorbing or supplying water. The body needs hydration to function—{Drink plenty of fluids to stay hydrated}. Athletes and health-conscious people track their hydration levels. In chemistry, hydration refers to water molecules bonding with other substances. Skincare products promise to improve skin hydration.

Hydrogen is the lightest and most abundant element in the universe, a colorless, odorless gas that combines with oxygen to form water. Its name means "water-former." Hydrogen appears in countless compounds and serves as a fuel source: {hydrogen fuel cells}, {the hydrogen bomb}. In chemistry, hydrogen has atomic number 1.

A hyena is a carnivorous mammal native to Africa and Asia, known for its sloping back, powerful jaws, and distinctive vocalizations—the spotted hyena's call sounds like laughter, giving rise to {laughing hyena}. Hyenas are scavengers and hunters, often traveling in packs. Figuratively, a hyena is someone who profits from others' misfortune or laughs cruelly.

Hyenas are carnivorous mammals native to Africa and Asia, known for their powerful jaws, sloping backs, and distinctive vocalizations—the spotted hyena's call sounds like cackling laughter. Despite their doglike appearance, they're more closely related to cats. Figuratively, a hyena is someone who laughs cruelly or preys on others' misfortune: {The paparazzi descended like hyenas}.

Hygiene is the practice of keeping oneself and one's surroundings clean to maintain health and prevent disease. Personal hygiene includes bathing, handwashing, and dental care. The word extends to anything kept clean or uncontaminated: {code hygiene}, {sleep hygiene}. {Good hygiene habits start in childhood.}

A hymn is a song of praise or worship, especially one sung in religious services: {The congregation sang a hymn}. By extension, any expression of devoted praise can be called a hymn: {The film is a hymn to small-town America}. To hymn something is to praise it effusively, though this use is literary and uncommon.

Hymns are religious songs, typically sung in worship by a congregation. The word usually implies traditional compositions with multiple verses, as opposed to contemporary praise music. A hymnal or hymnbook collects these songs. Figuratively, anything that praises effusively might be called a hymn: {His speech was a hymn to free enterprise}.

Hype is extravagant publicity or promotion, often exceeding what the thing deserves: {The movie couldn't live up to the hype}. To hype something is to promote it aggressively: {They've been hyping the new product for months}. Hyped or hyped up can mean excited or agitated: {The kids were all hyped up on sugar}. Something overhyped has been promoted beyond its merits.

Hyped means excited or full of anticipation, often with the suggestion of being worked up beyond what's warranted: {I'm so hyped for this concert}. Something hyped has been heavily promoted or publicized: {The movie was hyped for months before release}. The word carries a hint of inflation—hype often exceeds reality. {Don't believe the hype.}

Hyper describes a state of being overly energetic, excitable, or wound up. It's often applied to children or pets who can't seem to settle down: {The kids got hyper after eating all that candy}. As a prefix, hyper- means excessive or above normal, appearing in words like hyperactive, hypersensitive, and hyperlink. The standalone adjective hyper is informal and typically carries a mildly negative connotation, suggesting someone is too amped up for the situation.

Hyperactive describes excessive activity or restlessness beyond normal levels. A hyperactive child can't sit still in class. The term has clinical weight—attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is characterized by hyperactive behavior—but casual use is common: {My brain gets hyperactive at night}. An overactive immune system or imagination might also be called hyperactive.

Hyperbole describes exaggeration for obvious (I’ve told you a million times) or subtle (the dawn of a new era) effect. Not meant to be taken literally, hyperbole is an impactful literary device in poetry and speechwriting.

Hyperdrive is a fictional faster-than-light propulsion system that allows spacecraft to travel across vast interstellar distances almost instantaneously. Popularized by science fiction franchises like Star Wars, it typically works by propelling a ship into an alternate dimension or "hyperspace" where normal physics don't apply. Outside of fiction, hyperdrive describes any state of extreme speed, intensity, or productivity: {The whole team went into hyperdrive to meet the deadline}.

Hyperfixation is intense, consuming focus on a single interest, activity, or topic—often to the exclusion of other responsibilities or needs. The term originated in discussions of ADHD and autism, where such episodes are common: {I've been in hyperfixation mode on this video game for three days}. Unlike casual enthusiasm, hyperfixation implies difficulty disengaging even when you want or need to.

Hyperfocus is intense, sustained concentration on a single task or subject, often to the exclusion of everything else. The term appears frequently in discussions of ADHD, where it describes the paradoxical ability to focus deeply on engaging activities while struggling with routine tasks: {I was in hyperfocus mode and didn't notice three hours had passed}. The verb hyperfocus follows naturally: {She hyperfocuses on puzzles but can't sit through a meeting}.

Hyperspace is a theoretical higher-dimensional space through which spacecraft can travel faster than light, a staple of science fiction: {The ship jumped into hyperspace}. The concept sidesteps relativity by having ships exit normal space rather than exceed light speed within it. In mathematics, hyperspace refers to any space of more than three dimensions.

Hyperventilating is breathing abnormally fast and shallow, often triggered by panic, anxiety, or physical exertion. The rapid breathing expels too much carbon dioxide, causing dizziness, tingling, or lightheadedness. Figuratively, hyperventilating describes any overwrought reaction: {The internet is hyperventilating over the casting announcement}. The noun is hyperventilation.

Hyping is building excitement or enthusiasm for something, often through exaggerated promotion or publicity. Someone hyping a product, event, or person is generating buzz and anticipation: {The studio has been hyping the film for months}. Self-hyping is boastful self-promotion. The word often implies the reality won't match the buildup.

Hypnosis is a trance-like state of focused attention and heightened suggestibility, typically induced by another person's verbal guidance. A subject under hypnosis may follow suggestions, recover buried memories, or experience altered perceptions. The state has therapeutic uses—treating phobias, managing pain, breaking habits—though claims about its power vary widely. {She quit smoking through hypnosis.}

Hypnotic describes something that induces or relates to hypnosis—a trance-like state of heightened suggestibility. A hypnotic {suggestion} is planted during such a trance. More loosely, hypnotic describes anything that captures attention so completely it seems to entrance: {the hypnotic rhythm of the drums}, {her hypnotic gaze}. As a noun, a hypnotic is a drug that induces sleep.

Hypnotise is the British spelling of hypnotize, meaning to induce a trancelike state in someone, typically through focused attention and suggestion. A hypnotist may hypnotise a subject for therapeutic purposes, entertainment, or to access buried memories. The word extends figuratively to describe anything that captivates or fascinates completely: {The flickering flames hypnotised us into silence}. Someone hypnotised by an idea or person is utterly absorbed by them.

Hypnotised is the British spelling of hypnotized—put into a trance-like state of focused attention and heightened suggestibility. A hypnotist hypnotises subjects for therapy or entertainment.
