An innovation is a new product, method, or approach that results from that process: Technological innovations have enabled the school to accommodate students with special needs.

Innovations are new methods, ideas, or products that change how things are done. The word emphasizes novelty and improvement over existing approaches: {The company's innovations in battery technology extended range by fifty percent}. Innovation as a mass noun refers to the process itself: {The department rewards innovation}. In business contexts, innovation has become somewhat buzzword-ish, applied loosely to minor updates.

Innovative describes something that introduces new ideas, methods, or technologies. An innovative approach breaks from convention; an innovative product offers features not seen before. The word carries positive connotations of creativity and forward-thinking: {The company's innovative design changed the industry}. Overuse in marketing has diluted its impact—not everything labeled innovative actually is.

An innovator is someone who introduces new ideas, methods, or products. The word carries connotations of creativity and forward thinking—innovators don't just improve existing things but bring genuinely novel approaches: {Steve Jobs was an innovator in personal computing}. In business contexts, innovator often describes first movers who create markets rather than follow them.

Inns are small hotels or lodging establishments, typically offering food and drink alongside overnight accommodation. The word evokes a traditional, intimate atmosphere—{a country inn}, {a roadside inn}—often suggesting cozier quarters than a modern hotel chain. Historically, inns provided rest stops for travelers, and some old establishments still trade on that heritage.

Innuendo is an indirect suggestion or hint, usually about something negative or scandalous. Rather than stating something outright, innuendo implies it through tone, context, or carefully chosen words: {The article was full of innuendo about the senator's personal life}. Sexual innuendo suggests something risqué without explicit statement. The plural is innuendos or innuendoes.

Input is what goes into a system, process, or device—data entered into a computer, raw materials fed into a machine, contributions to a discussion: {We need your input on this decision}. The verb means to enter such information: {She inputted the figures into the spreadsheet}. Input contrasts with output, what comes out the other end.

All of the meanings of inquiry relate to asking questions: the underlying verb is inquire. Inquiry is a formal word for a question or a request for information: A man came in today with an inquiry about membership. An inquiry can also be an official, systematic investigation about the details of an event such as a crime, a disaster, or a scandal. In American English, inquiry is usually pronounced with stress on the first syllable. In British English, the stress falls on the second.

An inquisition is a prolonged, rigorous investigation or questioning, often with implications of harshness or hostility: {The job interview felt more like an inquisition}. The word suggests relentless probing that makes the subject uncomfortable. Any formal inquiry might be called an inquisition, though the term usually carries negative overtones of excessive scrutiny or intimidation. (Capitalized Inquisition refers to the historical Catholic tribunal.)

An inquisitor is someone who conducts an inquisition—a formal, often aggressive investigation or interrogation. The word carries overtones of relentless, probing questioning: {My mother-in-law turned into an inquisitor the moment we walked in}. Historically, inquisitors were officials of the Catholic Inquisition who investigated heresy, lending the word associations of severity and zealous persecution.

Inquisitors are people who conduct rigorous questioning or investigation. The word carries connotations of aggressive, relentless interrogation—often with the implication that the questioner has already decided on guilt. Historically, inquisitors were officials of the Catholic Inquisition who examined suspected heretics: {The inquisitors extracted confessions through torture}. In modern use, the term often appears critically or sarcastically for anyone who questions with excessive zeal: {Congressional inquisitors grilled the witness for hours}.

Inroads are advances into territory or progress against something resistant. The word almost always appears in the plural with "make": {The company has made inroads into the Asian market}. Originally military—troops making inroads into enemy territory—the term now describes any gradual encroachment or successful penetration of a difficult space: {Disease made inroads on her health}.

Insane means severely mentally ill, unable to think or behave rationally. Legal and medical usage has largely abandoned the term, but it persists in everyday speech to mean wildly unreasonable or extreme: {The traffic was insane}, {an insane schedule}. Something insane might be impressively bold: {That skateboard trick was insane}. The adverb insanely intensifies: {insanely talented}, {insanely expensive}.

Insanity is severe mental illness that impairs a person's grasp on reality. In legal contexts, insanity is a defense claiming the accused couldn't understand their actions or distinguish right from wrong: {The jury rejected the insanity plea}. Loosely, insanity describes any wild irrationality: {It was insanity to attempt the climb in that weather}. The popular quotation attributing insanity to repeating the same action while expecting different results has no clear origin.

Insatiable describes a desire or appetite that cannot be satisfied, no matter how much is consumed or obtained. Someone with an insatiable {curiosity} keeps asking questions; an insatiable {hunger} for power drives people to seek ever more control. The word carries connotations of excess or obsession, suggesting something bottomless or unquenchable. {Her insatiable need for approval exhausted everyone around her.}

An inscription is text carved, engraved, or written on a surface—stone monuments, metal plaques, the flyleaf of a book. The word emphasizes permanence: {The inscription on the tombstone had weathered but remained legible}. A personal inscription in a gift book is a handwritten dedication: {She wrote a brief inscription to her nephew on the title page}.

Inscriptions are words carved, engraved, or written on a surface—typically stone, metal, or the opening pages of a book. Ancient inscriptions on monuments and tombs provide historical records. A book inscription is a handwritten message from the giver: {The inscription read "To my daughter on her graduation"}. The word covers both the act of inscribing and what results from it.

An insect is a small invertebrate animal with six legs, a three-part body, and typically wings—ants, beetles, flies, bees, butterflies. The term is often loosely applied to any small crawling creature: {There's an insect in the bathtub} might describe a spider or centipede. Calling someone an insect suggests they're insignificant or contemptible.

Insects are small animals with six legs, a body divided into three segments, and typically one or two pairs of wings. They include flies, beetles, ants, bees, and butterflies—the most diverse group of animals on Earth. Informally, insect extends to any small crawling creature: {The porch light attracts insects}. Figuratively, calling someone an insect suggests they're insignificant or contemptible.

Insecure describes something not firmly fixed or stable: {an insecure railing}, {an insecure internet connection}. More commonly, it describes a person lacking confidence or certainty about themselves: {She felt insecure about her appearance}. The emotional sense dominates contemporary usage—someone insecure doubts their worth or worries about others' opinions. An insecure situation is unsafe or uncertain: {an insecure job market}.

Insecurities are doubts about oneself—anxieties about one's worth, abilities, or how others perceive you: {Her insecurities about her appearance started in middle school}. The word names the specific vulnerabilities rather than a general state: {He played on her insecurities}. Also refers to multiple unsafe conditions or unstable situations: {the insecurities of life in a war zone}.

Insecurity is the state of feeling unsafe or uncertain. Physical insecurity means vulnerability to harm: {food insecurity}, {job insecurity}. Emotional insecurity is self-doubt or anxiety about one's worth or standing: {His constant bragging masked deep insecurity}. The plural insecurities refers to specific anxieties: {We all have our insecurities}.

Insensitive describes a lack of awareness or responsiveness. Someone insensitive to others' feelings fails to notice or care about them: {That was an insensitive thing to say}. The word extends to physical responses—skin insensitive to touch, equipment insensitive to small changes. An insensitive remark is one that disregards how it might affect others, whether through carelessness or indifference.

Inseparable describes things so closely connected they cannot be divided or considered apart. Two concepts may be inseparable: {For her, art and politics were inseparable}. Most often applied to people whose bond is exceptionally close: {The twins were inseparable from birth}. {She and her dog are inseparable}.

To insert is to put something into something else—a key into a lock, a clause into a contract, a comment into a conversation. The noun insert refers to something placed inside: a magazine insert, an insert in a shoe. In film and video, an insert is a brief shot cut into the main action, typically showing a detail: {The director wanted an insert of the ticking clock}.

Inside shares many of the meanings of in that apply to space and time and can be used to give a slightly more emphatic or definite meaning. It is also interchangeable with within in most of its meanings but is less formal than within.

An insider is someone within a group, organization, or system who has access to information or influence that outsiders lack. The term often implies privileged knowledge: {insider information}, {insider trading}. Political insiders know how power actually works. Industry insiders hear news before the public. The word can suggest either legitimate expertise or unfair advantage, depending on context.

Insiders are people with access to information or influence that outsiders lack. The term often appears in contexts of exclusive knowledge: {Insiders say the deal will close by Friday}. In finance, insider trading refers to illegal buying or selling based on confidential information. More broadly, insiders belong to a group's inner circle—those who know how things really work: {Only insiders understood the company's true financial state}.

The insides of something are its interior parts or contents—what you find when you open it up or look within. A person's insides are their internal organs, especially the stomach and intestines: {My insides were churning with anxiety}. The word often appears in contexts of gutting or revealing: {The mechanic spread the engine's insides across the garage floor}.

Insidious is an adjective that negatively characterizes something that is designed to trap someone with enticement: Recreational drugs have an insidious appeal. Insidious also describes detrimental effects that develop gradually: the insidious onset of clinical depression. Threats, diseases, and plots are typically characterized as insidious.

Insight is understanding that penetrates beneath the surface—seeing into the nature of something. An insight is a specific instance of such understanding: {Her insight about the company's culture proved accurate}. To gain insight is to reach deeper comprehension: {The interview gave me insight into how he thinks}. Someone with insight perceives what others miss.

Insights are moments of clear understanding, especially ones that penetrate beneath surface appearances to reveal something essential. The word implies sudden clarity rather than gradual learning: {The research yielded valuable insights into consumer behavior}. In business contexts, insights often refers to data-driven discoveries about customers or markets, sometimes inflated to mean any observation at all.

Insignia are badges, emblems, or symbols that indicate rank, membership, or affiliation. Military uniforms display insignia showing unit and rank. Organizations use insignia to identify members: {The scout's sash was covered with insignia}. The word is Latin plural but often treated as singular in English, with insignias as an alternative plural.

Insignificant means too small or unimportant to matter: {an insignificant detail}, {an insignificant amount of money}. It often carries a dismissive tone—calling someone insignificant suggests they have no power or consequence worth considering. The word can express genuine smallness or deliberate belittlement: {He made her feel insignificant}.

Insincere describes words or behavior that don't reflect genuine feeling—saying something you don't mean, or acting in ways calculated to deceive. An insincere {apology} lacks real remorse. Insincere {flattery} aims to manipulate rather than express admiration. The word suggests a gap between outward expression and inner truth: {His smile seemed insincere}.

An insinuation is an indirect suggestion, typically of something negative or discrediting. Rather than stating outright, you hint: {His question carried an insinuation that she hadn't earned her promotion}. The word often implies slyness or manipulation—the insinuator plants doubt while maintaining deniability. To make an insinuation is to insinuate.

Insist means to demand firmly or maintain a position despite resistance. You insist on something you consider essential: {She insisted on paying for dinner}. You insist that something is true when others doubt it: {He insisted he was innocent}. The word carries determination—insisting is more forceful than asking or suggesting. Someone insistent won't let the matter drop.

Insistence is firm or persistent demand or assertion. Someone's insistence that something happen means they won't let it drop: {At her insistence, we stayed for dinner}. The word can also describe a quality of pressing urgency: {the insistence of the drumbeat}, {the insistence of his questioning}. To do something with insistence is to do it emphatically and repeatedly.

Insomnia is the inability to fall asleep or stay asleep. The condition ranges from occasional restless nights to chronic sleeplessness requiring medical treatment. {Stress-induced insomnia kept her awake for weeks.} Someone suffering from insomnia is an insomniac.

An insomniac is someone who suffers from insomnia—chronic difficulty falling or staying asleep. The word works as both noun and adjective: {an insomniac friend}, {insomniac nights}. {I've been an insomniac since college.}

Insomniacs are people who suffer from insomnia—chronic difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep. The term often carries a sense of shared identity among those who know the frustration of lying awake at 3 a.m.: {Fellow insomniacs will understand the appeal of late-night television}. It can also describe someone temporarily sleepless: {The coffee made insomniacs of us all}.

To inspect is to examine something carefully, looking for flaws, verifying condition, or ensuring compliance: {The health department inspects restaurants annually}. Officials inspect buildings, troops, documents. You might inspect a used car before buying or inspect your work before submitting it. The word suggests methodical, often official scrutiny rather than casual looking.

Inspection is the act of looking at something carefully to assess its condition, quality, or compliance with standards. Officials conduct inspections of buildings, vehicles, or facilities: {The restaurant failed its health inspection}. You might give something a quick inspection before buying it. The word implies systematic examination rather than casual observation.

An inspector is someone who examines things officially to ensure they meet standards or regulations: a building inspector, a health inspector, a school inspector. In police forces, inspector is a rank—in Britain, a mid-level officer; in the U.S., typically higher. {The inspector found three code violations.} Inspector also appears in fiction as a title for detectives: Inspector Clouseau, Inspector Gadget.

Inspiration is a sudden spark of creative or motivating energy—an idea that seems to arrive from outside yourself. Artists wait for inspiration; leaders provide it. The word comes from breath, and the oldest sense is literally breathing in. To inspire someone is to fill them with enthusiasm or purpose: {Her courage inspired the whole team}. Inspiration can also mean the source itself: {She was the inspiration for his novel}.

Inspirational describes something that arouses motivation, creativity, or elevated feeling: {an inspirational speech}, {an inspirational teacher}. The word often appears in contexts of self-improvement and religious encouragement. It can carry a whiff of the saccharine—{inspirational quotes} printed on posters or coffee mugs suggest earnest uplift rather than genuine profundity.

Inspirations is the plural of inspiration—moments, ideas, or sources that spark creativity or motivation. A painter might cite nature and old masters as her inspirations. The word can also refer to sudden brilliant ideas: {Several inspirations came to her while showering}. In its older sense, inspirations were divine influences or breathings-in of the spirit.

Inspire originally meant to breathe life into, which illuminates its modern senses. To inspire someone is to fill them with creative energy or motivation: {Her courage inspired me to speak up}. A person, work, or event can inspire feelings: {The landscape inspired awe}. To inspire also means to draw breath into the lungs—the technical term in medicine for inhaling.

Inspired describes someone or something moved by a force beyond ordinary motivation—as if breathed into by a higher power. An inspired {performance} transcends the routine. An inspired {choice} shows unexpected brilliance. The word suggests creativity, enthusiasm, or insight that seems to come from outside oneself: {She felt inspired after visiting the museum}. To be inspired by something is to draw creative energy from it.

Inspiring describes something that fills you with motivation, creativity, or elevated feeling. An inspiring {speech} moves people to action. An inspiring {teacher} awakens potential in students. The word suggests a transfer of energy or vision from source to recipient: {Her courage was inspiring to everyone who knew her}. Something inspiring makes you want to do, create, or become more.

Instability is the condition of being unstable—liable to change, collapse, or give way. Physical structures have instability when they might topple or fail. Political instability suggests a government vulnerable to upheaval. Emotional instability describes someone whose moods shift unpredictably. Financial instability signals precarious economic conditions: {The instability in the markets spooked investors}.

Install means to set something in place for use. You install software on a computer, appliances in a kitchen, or a new president in office. The word implies both placement and preparation—an installed dishwasher is connected and ready to run. {We're having solar panels installed next week.} To install yourself somewhere is to settle in comfortably: {She installed herself in the corner booth with a book}.

Installation is the act of putting something in place and making it ready for use: {The installation took three hours}. Software gets installed on computers, appliances in kitchens, art in galleries. An installation can also be the thing installed—a military installation is a base or facility, and an art installation is a work designed for a specific space, often immersive or interactive. To install someone in office is to formally establish them in a position; that ceremony is also an installation.

An installment is one part of something delivered or paid in portions over time. A novel published in installments appears chapter by chapter. {We're paying for the car in monthly installments.} An installment can also be one episode in a series: {the latest installment of the franchise}. Also spelled instalment in British English.

Installments are parts of something delivered or paid over time rather than all at once. A novel published in weekly installments appears chapter by chapter. Paying in installments spreads a purchase across multiple payments: {We bought the furniture on an installment plan}. The British spelling is instalments.

An instance is a single example or occurrence of something: {In this instance, the rule doesn't apply}. It often appears with {for instance}, meaning "for example." In computing, an instance is a specific realization of something general—a running copy of a program, or an object created from a class. To instance something is to cite it as an example, though this verb use is formal and uncommon.

An instant is a very brief moment in time—so brief it seems to have no duration: {It was over in an instant}, {I'll be there in an instant}. As an adjective, instant describes things that happen immediately or require minimal preparation: instant {gratification}, instant {coffee}, instant {messaging}. The instant can function as a conjunction meaning "as soon as": {The instant I saw her, I knew something was wrong}.

Instead means in place of something else or as an alternative: {I skipped the meeting and went for a walk instead}. It often follows a rejected option: {She didn't want coffee; she asked for tea instead}. With "of," it introduces what's being replaced: {Instead of complaining, do something about it}.

An instigator is someone who starts or provokes something, usually trouble. The word carries negative connotations—instigators stir up conflict, incite others to act, or set events in motion that wouldn't have happened otherwise: {He was the instigator of the bar fight}. In legal contexts, an instigator may bear responsibility for crimes they encouraged others to commit.

Instinct is an inborn tendency to behave in a certain way without learning or conscious thought. Animals act on instinct when they migrate, build nests, or flee predators. In humans, instinct often means a natural aptitude or intuitive response: {My instinct told me something was wrong}, {She has good instincts for business}. To do something {on instinct} is to act without deliberation.

Instincts are inborn patterns of behavior, impulses that arise without learning or conscious thought. Animals act on instinct when they migrate, nest, or flee predators. In humans, instinct often means intuitive knowledge or gut feeling: {Trust your instincts}. Someone with {good instincts} makes sound judgments without deliberation. A {survival instinct} or {maternal instinct} suggests behavior rooted in biology rather than reason.

An institute is an organization dedicated to a particular purpose—usually educational, scientific, or professional: {the Massachusetts Institute of Technology}, {a research institute}. The word suggests formality and specialized focus. As a verb, to institute is to establish or set in motion: {institute new policies}, {institute legal proceedings}. The related noun institution covers a broader range of established organizations and practices.

An institution is an established organization or practice, especially one serving a public purpose: {financial institutions}, {the institution of marriage}. Universities, hospitals, and governments are institutions. The word can suggest permanence and authority, sometimes critically—institutional implies impersonal or rigid. A person or thing that has become a fixture may be called an institution: {He's an institution around here}. Institution also names the act of instituting something: {the institution of new policies}.

Institutions are established organizations or systems that structure society—governments, courts, schools, banks, churches. The word often implies permanence and authority: {democratic institutions}, {financial institutions}. An institution can also be a long-standing custom or fixture: {Sunday dinner was an institution in our family}. Someone who has become an institution is a deeply familiar presence: {She's an institution around here}. To institutionalize is to place someone in a facility for care or confinement, or to establish something as standard practice.

Instruction is direction or teaching given to guide action or build knowledge. A {set of instructions} explains how to assemble furniture or operate a device. In education, instruction is the act of teaching: {reading instruction}, {classroom instruction}. Computing uses instruction for a single operation a processor executes. The plural often appears in commands: {Follow the instructions carefully}.

Instructions are directions that tell you how to do something. They come with products you need to assemble, recipes you want to follow, or tasks you need to complete: {Read the instructions before you start}. Instructions can be written, spoken, or demonstrated. To follow instructions is to do as directed; to ignore them often leads to trouble.

An instrument is a tool designed for precise work—surgical instruments, measuring instruments, musical instruments. The word emphasizes careful design for a specific function. A person used by another to accomplish something is also an instrument: {She became an instrument of his revenge}. Legal documents formalizing agreements are called instruments: {a debt instrument}, {a negotiable instrument}. As a verb, to instrument means to equip with measuring devices or to arrange music for instruments.

Instrumental describes something that serves as a means to an end—a tool or agent in achieving a result: {She was instrumental in getting the legislation passed}. In music, instrumental refers to compositions performed without vocals: {an instrumental track}, {instrumental jazz}. As a noun, an instrumental is such a piece. In grammar, the instrumental case marks nouns used as instruments of action.

Instrumentals are musical pieces performed without vocals—the instruments alone carry the composition. The term appears most often in hip-hop and electronic music, where producers release instrumentals as standalone tracks or for other artists to rap over: {I've been looking for beats—do you have any instrumentals?} In other contexts, instrumental serves as the adjective: {an instrumental version of the song}.

Instruments are tools or devices used to accomplish specific tasks. Musical instruments produce sound: {She plays three instruments}. Scientific instruments measure or observe: {surgical instruments}, {instruments of navigation}. Legal instruments are formal documents like contracts or deeds. The verb instrument means to equip with measuring devices or to arrange music for particular instruments. Figuratively, a person can be an instrument of change or destruction—a means through which something is accomplished.

Insufferable describes someone or something so irritating, arrogant, or obnoxious that they're impossible to tolerate: {He became insufferable after his promotion}, {the insufferable heat of August}. The word suggests you must suffer through their presence—and can barely manage it. An insufferable bore, an insufferable know-it-all, insufferable smugness.

Insulated means protected from outside influences by a barrier or separation. Electrical wires are insulated with rubber or plastic to prevent shock. An insulated container keeps contents hot or cold. Figuratively, someone insulated from hardship has been sheltered from it: {Growing up wealthy, she was insulated from financial worry}. The verb insulate and noun insulation follow the same pattern.

Insulation is material that prevents or slows the transfer of heat, electricity, or sound. Homes use insulation in walls and attics to maintain temperature: {We added insulation to cut heating costs}. Electrical wires have insulation to prevent shocks. Figuratively, insulation is protection from unpleasant realities: {His wealth provided insulation from everyday concerns}.

Insulin is a hormone produced by the pancreas that regulates blood sugar by enabling cells to absorb glucose. Without sufficient insulin, glucose accumulates in the bloodstream—the core problem in diabetes. Diabetics may inject synthetic insulin to manage their condition: {She takes insulin twice a day}. The word extends to the medication itself: {the rising cost of insulin}.

An insult is a remark or action intended to offend or demean: {She hurled insults at him}. To insult someone is to treat them with such disrespect. The word carries a sense of deliberate affront—accidents aren't insults. {Adding insult to injury} means compounding harm with humiliation. In medicine, an insult is damage to tissue: {a cardiac insult}.

Insulting describes words or actions that offend someone's dignity or self-respect. An insulting remark demeans or belittles: {He made insulting comments about her intelligence}. Something can be insulting even without intent—an insulting job offer is one so low it feels like a slap: {They offered me an insulting salary}.

Insults are words or actions meant to offend, demean, or show disrespect toward someone. The term covers everything from mild teasing to deeply hurtful verbal attacks. {She traded insults with her rival.} As a verb, to insult someone is to say or do something offensive to them. An insult can also describe something inadequate or contemptuous: {The low offer was an insult to his years of service.}

Insurance is protection against potential loss, typically through a contract where one party pays premiums and the other promises compensation if specified misfortunes occur: {health insurance}, {car insurance}, {life insurance}. The term extends to any safeguard against unwanted outcomes: {I brought an umbrella as insurance against rain}. To {take out insurance} is to purchase a policy.

To insure is to secure financial protection against potential loss or damage by purchasing an insurance policy: {We insured the house for its full value}. The word extends to any act of making something certain or safe: {Double-check the address to insure delivery}. In this broader sense, insure overlaps with ensure, though careful writers often reserve insure for matters involving actual insurance.

Insurgency is armed rebellion against an established authority, typically a government. Unlike conventional warfare between armies, insurgency relies on guerrilla tactics, local support, and gradual destabilization: {The military struggled to contain the insurgency in the northern provinces}. The term often appears in discussions of counterinsurgency—efforts to suppress such movements.

Insurgents are people who rebel against an established authority, typically through armed resistance. The term usually describes fighters opposing a government or occupying force rather than a formal military: {Coalition forces clashed with insurgents outside the city}. Unlike revolutionaries, insurgents may lack a unified political program—the word emphasizes the act of rising up rather than the ideology behind it.

An insurrection is an organized uprising against established authority, typically a government. It falls between a riot and a full-scale revolution—more sustained and purposeful than spontaneous unrest, but not necessarily aiming to overthrow the entire system. {The insurrection was quickly suppressed by federal troops.} The word gained renewed currency in American political discourse after the January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol.

Intact means whole, complete, and undamaged—nothing missing or broken off. A package arrives intact when it survives shipping unharmed. A reputation remains intact when scandal fails to tarnish it. {The ancient temple was found remarkably intact.} The word often implies survival through threat or time: {Her sense of humor remained intact despite everything}.

Intake is what is taken in, or the act of taking in. A nutritionist monitors your {caloric intake}. An engine's {air intake} is where air enters. The word also names a point of entry—the intake for a water system, or a hospital's intake desk where new patients are processed. {The program limits intake to twenty students per year.}

Integrate means to bring parts together into a unified whole. You might integrate new employees into a team, integrate data from multiple sources, or integrate ideas from different disciplines. In mathematics, to integrate is to find the integral of a function—essentially summing infinitely small quantities. The word also carries important social meaning: to integrate a school or neighborhood is to end racial segregation by bringing together people of different races. {The district was ordered to integrate its schools.}

Integration is the act of combining parts into a unified whole. Racial integration brings previously separated groups together in schools, neighborhoods, or institutions: {The integration of public schools began in the 1950s}. In mathematics, integration is the process of finding integrals—the reverse of differentiation. Software integration connects different systems to work together. To integrate is to unify or incorporate: {We need to integrate these databases}.

Integrity is a quality ascribed to both people and abstract things. Someone with integrity is viewed favorably as being moral, consistent, honest, and steadfast in beliefs and action. The integrity of a system, process, or object refers to its reliability, completeness, and soundness: In such a volatile housing market, some fear that the integrity of the appraisal process may be compromised.

Intel is informal shorthand for intelligence in the espionage or military sense—information gathered about enemies, competitors, or situations: {We need more intel before we make a move}, {The intel suggests they're planning something big}. The word has spread from spy thrillers and military contexts into casual use for any useful information: {What's the intel on the new boss?} (Capitalized Intel is the semiconductor company.)

Intellect is the capacity for thinking, reasoning, and understanding—the mind's ability to process ideas and acquire knowledge. It often implies high mental ability: {a person of great intellect}. The word can also refer to intelligent people collectively: {the nation's leading intellects gathered for the symposium}. Intellect emphasizes rational thought over emotion or intuition.

Intellectual describes matters of the mind, especially those requiring serious thought, analysis, or reasoning. An intellectual pursuit or activity engages the higher faculties rather than emotions or physical skills. As a noun, an intellectual is someone who spends considerable time thinking about ideas, often in academic, artistic, or philosophical domains. The term can carry either respect or mild derision depending on context: {She's a real intellectual} might praise someone's depth of thought, while {Don't be so intellectual about it} suggests overthinking. {The café attracted intellectuals and artists from across the city.}

Intellectuals are people who engage seriously with ideas, analysis, and critical thought—scholars, writers, philosophers, and commentators who shape discourse on culture, politics, and society. The term can be neutral or admiring, but it often carries a skeptical edge, implying people more comfortable with abstract theory than practical reality: {The intellectuals debated while ordinary people struggled}. Public intellectuals participate in broader conversations beyond academia.

Intelligence is the capacity to learn, reason, and apply knowledge. It encompasses understanding, problem-solving, and adapting to new situations: {a child of remarkable intelligence}, {artificial intelligence}. Intelligence also means information gathered about an enemy or competitor, especially by governments: {military intelligence}, {the intelligence community}. An intelligence is a sentient being or mind: {extraterrestrial intelligences}.

Intelligent describes the capacity to learn, reason, and apply knowledge effectively. An intelligent person grasps concepts quickly and thinks through problems: {She's one of the most intelligent people I've ever met}. The word extends to actions and designs that show good judgment: an intelligent {decision}, an intelligent {question}. In technology, intelligent systems adapt or respond to input: {intelligent design}, {smart} and {intelligent} devices. Intelligent life refers to beings capable of complex thought—often in speculation about extraterrestrial existence.

Intend means to have something in mind as a purpose or plan: {I intend to finish by Friday}, {The gift was intended for you}. What someone intends is their aim or design—distinct from what actually happens. An intended consequence is deliberate; an unintended one wasn't part of the plan. The intended, now old-fashioned, is a person's fiancé or fiancée.

Intense describes extreme strength or degree. Intense heat, intense pain, intense concentration—all suggest something pushed to its limits. An intense person is deeply serious or emotionally forceful, sometimes uncomfortably so: {He was so intense it made people nervous}. Intense experiences are vivid and consuming: {an intense love affair}, {intense grief}.

Intensity is the degree of strength, force, or concentration of something. Physical intensity can be measured: the intensity of {light}, {heat}, or {sound}. Emotional intensity is felt: {the intensity of her gaze}, {the intensity of first love}. Intense experiences are vivid and consuming. High intensity suggests something demanding or extreme: {a high-intensity workout}, {the intensity of combat}.

Intent is purpose or aim—what someone means to do or accomplish. In law, intent distinguishes accidental acts from deliberate ones: {The prosecution must prove criminal intent}. As an adjective, intent means focused with determination: {She was intent on finishing before dark}. An {intent gaze} is fixed and unwavering.

Intention is what you mean to do—a purpose or aim held in mind before acting. {Her intention was to apologize}. Intentions often contrast with outcomes: {I had good intentions, but it went badly}. The phrase {with intention} suggests deliberateness rather than accident. In legal contexts, intention distinguishes premeditated acts from negligent or accidental ones.

Intentional means done on purpose, not by accident or coincidence. An intentional {foul} in basketball is committed deliberately, usually for strategic reasons. {The omission was intentional.} The word emphasizes that the actor chose the action and its consequences—distinguishing deliberate acts from mistakes, reflexes, or oversights.

Intentions are what you mean to do—your aims or purposes. The word often implies doubt about whether actions will follow: {She had good intentions but never followed through}. To {declare your intentions} is to state your plans formally. When someone asks about your intentions toward a person, they're asking whether your motives are honorable, especially romantically.

To interact is to act upon or communicate with something or someone else, implying mutual influence or exchange: {The characters barely interact in the first act}, {Users interact with the software through a touchscreen}. The word emphasizes back-and-forth engagement rather than one-way action. Interaction is the noun form; interactive describes things designed for two-way participation.

Interaction is the action or influence that occurs between two or more things. People have interactions—conversations, exchanges, encounters: {My interactions with her have always been pleasant}. In science, interaction describes how forces, particles, or substances affect each other. In computing, it refers to communication between user and system. The adjective interactive describes things designed for two-way engagement.

Interactive describes things that respond to user input, creating a two-way exchange rather than passive reception. An interactive {exhibit} lets visitors touch and manipulate displays. Interactive {software} adjusts based on what you do. The word applies to any medium where the audience participates rather than just observes: {interactive storytelling}, {interactive maps}. In education, interactive methods engage students actively rather than having them sit and listen.

To intercept is to stop or catch something in transit before it reaches its destination. You can intercept a pass in football, intercept enemy communications, or intercept someone on their way out the door. {The defense intercepted three passes}. In mathematics, an intercept is a point where a line or curve crosses an axis. As a noun in sports, an interception is often shortened to intercept: {He had two intercepts in the fourth quarter}.

Interception is the act of catching or seizing something in transit before it reaches its destination. A defender makes an interception by catching a pass intended for the opponent: {He threw three interceptions in the first half}. Intelligence agencies intercept communications. To intercept someone is to stop them en route: {She intercepted him in the hallway before the meeting}.

Intercepts functions as both verb and noun around the core idea of stopping or catching something before it reaches its intended destination. You intercept a pass in football by catching it before the receiver does; agencies intercept communications by capturing them in transit. {The defender intercepted the ball at the goal line.} In mathematics, an intercept is the point where a line or curve crosses an axis. The noun also refers to the act of interception itself or the thing intercepted: {The intelligence team analyzed the intercepts.}

Intercourse is interaction or communication between people or groups: {diplomatic intercourse between nations}, {social intercourse at the party}. The word now most commonly means sexual intercourse—the physical act of sex, especially penetration: {They had intercourse}. The sexual sense has largely overtaken the older meaning of general exchange or dealings.

Interest connects to what engages attention or provides advantage. An interest in something is curiosity or concern about it: {She developed an interest in astronomy}. To interest someone is to engage their attention. Something interesting holds that attention. Interest also means a stake or share: {business interests}, {a controlling interest in the company}. Financial interest is money paid for borrowing money, calculated as a percentage: {The loan carries 8% interest}. {In the interest of} means for the benefit of. To act in someone's {best interests} is to do what helps them, whether they recognize it or not.

Interested means having your attention engaged or curiosity aroused: {I'm interested in learning more about that}. It also describes wanting to participate or pursue something: {Let me know if you're interested}. An interested party has a stake in an outcome—financial, personal, or otherwise—which may compromise their objectivity: {All interested parties should recuse themselves from the vote}.

Interesting describes something that captures attention or curiosity. An interesting {book}, {idea}, or {person} engages the mind and invites further exploration. The word is common but vague—it can express genuine fascination or serve as polite filler when stronger opinions go unstated: {That's an interesting theory} may mean remarkable or merely strange. {Interesting times} suggests upheaval rather than boredom.

Interests are the things that engage someone's attention or curiosity—hobbies, subjects, activities they care about: {Her interests include photography and hiking}. An interest in something can also mean a stake or share: {He has a financial interest in the company}. In the plural, interests often refers to what benefits a person or group: {acting in the best interests of the child}. Interest on money—the cost of borrowing or the return on saving—becomes interests mainly in legal or financial contexts involving multiple parties or rates.

An interface is where two systems or entities meet and interact. In computing, it's the point of contact between user and machine—a graphical interface presents visual elements to click; a command-line interface accepts typed commands. More broadly, interface describes any boundary where different things connect: {the interface between science and policy}. As a verb, to interface is to interact or connect: {We need to interface with the marketing team}. The verb sounds corporate and is often mocked as jargon.

To interfere is to get involved in something in a way that hinders or disrupts it. A meddling neighbor interferes in your affairs. Static interferes with radio signals. The word implies unwanted involvement: {Don't interfere with my plans}. In sports, interference is illegal obstruction of an opponent. In physics, waves interfere when they overlap, either reinforcing or canceling each other.

Interference is the act of getting involved in something that isn't your concern, usually unwelcomely: {I resent your interference in my personal life}. In sports, interference is illegal obstruction of an opponent. In physics, interference occurs when waves meet and combine, either reinforcing or canceling each other. Radio interference is static or disruption from competing signals. To {run interference} is to clear obstacles for someone else—from football blocking.

Intergalactic means between or among galaxies—the vast spaces separating these cosmic structures: {intergalactic travel}, {intergalactic dust}. In science fiction and casual use, it often just means outer space or extraterrestrial: {an intergalactic adventure}, {intergalactic beings}. The word suggests immense distances and cosmic scale.

Interior refers to the inside part of something, contrasted with its exterior or surface. A car's interior includes seats and dashboard; a building's interior is the space within its walls. Interior can describe what lies inland: {the interior of the continent}. It also means inner or private: {interior thoughts}, {interior life}. In government, interior departments handle domestic rather than foreign affairs.

An interloper is someone who intrudes where they don't belong or weren't invited. The word suggests trespass into a space, situation, or group where the person has no right to be: {The cat eyed the new puppy as an interloper in her domain}. It can describe romantic rivals, business competitors encroaching on established territory, or anyone perceived as an unwelcome outsider.

Interlopers are people who intrude where they don't belong or aren't wanted. The word suggests unauthorized presence—someone inserting themselves into a situation, place, or group without invitation: {The old-timers viewed the newcomers as interlopers}. In business, an interloper may be a competitor encroaching on established territory.

An interlude is a period of time between two events or activities—a pause or interval that interrupts the main flow: {a brief interlude of peace between the wars}, {a musical interlude between acts of the play}. The word often suggests something lighter or different in character from what surrounds it: {Their romance was a pleasant interlude in an otherwise difficult year}. In music and drama, an interlude is a short performance filling a gap between longer pieces.

An intermission is a pause or break in the middle of something, especially a scheduled break during a performance: {We got drinks during the intermission}. The word appears most often in theatrical contexts—plays, concerts, operas—where audiences need time to stretch or use the restroom. Outside entertainment, intermission suggests any temporary cessation: {a brief intermission in the rain}.

An intern is someone gaining supervised practical experience, typically a student or recent graduate working temporarily in a profession: {She's doing a summer intern at the law firm}. Medical interns are newly graduated doctors in their first year of hospital training. To intern someone is to confine them, especially during wartime: {Japanese Americans were interned in camps during World War II}. The confinement sense comes from a different root than the trainee sense.

Internal means situated within or occurring inside something. Internal {organs} are inside the body. Internal {affairs} concern matters within an organization or country rather than external relations. Internal can also describe mental or emotional states—what happens in someone's mind rather than what they express outwardly: {He kept his doubts internal}. The internal workings of a machine or system are its inner mechanisms.

International describes things involving two or more nations: {international trade}, {international law}, {an international airport}. It can also mean spanning or transcending national boundaries: {an international reputation}, {international waters}. As a noun, an international is a person who has represented their country in sport, especially in British usage: {She's a former England international}.

An internet is any network of interconnected computer networks—multiple separate networks linked together to communicate. Before the global network dominated, the term described various interconnected systems: {The company built an internet linking its regional offices}. The word is now rarely used in this generic sense. (Capitalized Internet is the global network.)

Internment is the confinement of people, typically during wartime or political crisis. Unlike imprisonment for crimes, internment detains groups based on nationality, ethnicity, or perceived threat: {the internment of Japanese Americans during World War II}. The term carries connotations of injustice—detention without trial or individual evidence of wrongdoing.

An internship is a temporary position offering practical experience in a field, typically for students or recent graduates. Internships may be paid or unpaid, lasting weeks to months: {She landed a summer internship at a law firm}. The term increasingly describes any entry-level arrangement where experience substitutes for full compensation.

Internships are temporary positions that give students or recent graduates practical experience in a field. They may be paid or unpaid, and often serve as a bridge between education and employment. Companies use internships to evaluate potential hires; interns use them to build skills and connections: {She landed a job through her summer internship}.

Interplay is the way two or more things affect or respond to each other—a back-and-forth dynamic where each element influences the others. The word emphasizes mutual action rather than one-sided effect: {the interplay between genetics and environment}, {the interplay of light and shadow}. It appears often in discussions of complex systems where multiple factors work together.

To interpret is to explain or make sense of something not immediately clear. You interpret a dream, a poem, a legal statute, or someone's silence. An interpreter translates spoken language in real time: {She interpreted for the ambassador}. Musicians and actors interpret works by bringing their own understanding to a performance: {His interpretation of Hamlet was brooding and restless}. Data requires interpretation—the numbers don't speak for themselves.

Interpretation is the act of explaining or making sense of something. A translator offers an interpretation of a foreign text; a musician offers an interpretation of a sonata. In law, interpretation determines what statutes or contracts mean: {The court's interpretation of the amendment proved controversial}. An interpretation can be one of several possible readings—your interpretation of events may differ from mine.

An interpreter translates speech between languages in real time, allowing conversation across a language barrier—distinguished from a translator, who works with written text. In computing, an interpreter is a program that executes code line by line rather than compiling it first: {Python uses an interpreter}. More broadly, anyone who explains or renders meaning: {an interpreter of dreams}, {an interpreter of the law}.

To interrogate is to question someone formally and intensively, typically to extract information. Police interrogate suspects; intelligence officers interrogate prisoners. The word implies pressure and persistence beyond casual questioning: {They interrogated him for hours about his whereabouts}. More loosely, to interrogate an idea or assumption is to examine it critically: {The essay interrogates conventional notions of gender}.

Interrogation is intensive, often aggressive questioning, typically by police or military authorities seeking information from a suspect or prisoner. The word implies pressure and persistence beyond ordinary inquiry: {The suspect broke down after hours of interrogation}. More loosely, any pointed or probing line of questioning: {My mother's interrogation about where I'd been lasted twenty minutes}.

Interrogations is the plural of interrogation, the act of questioning someone intensely and systematically. Police conduct interrogations of suspects. Military and intelligence agencies interrogate prisoners. The word implies persistent, often aggressive questioning aimed at extracting information: {The interrogations lasted for hours}. Extended uses cover any thorough examination: {Her constant interrogations about my personal life were exhausting}.

An interrogator is a person who questions someone intensively, especially in official or adversarial contexts. Police interrogators extract confessions; military interrogators seek intelligence from prisoners. The word carries overtones of pressure, persistence, and power imbalance: {The interrogator leaned in, asking the same question for the fifth time}.

To interrupt is to break into something continuous—a conversation, a process, a flow. You interrupt someone speaking by cutting in before they finish: {Sorry to interrupt, but your car is being towed}. A power outage interrupts service. In computing, an interrupt is a signal that stops normal processing to handle something urgent. The noun interruption is more common than the verb for describing the break itself: {constant interruptions}, {without interruption}.

Interrupting is breaking into someone's speech or activity before they've finished. The word carries a note of rudeness—to interrupt is to cut someone off, to insert yourself where you weren't invited: {Stop interrupting me}. Beyond conversation, interrupting applies to any disruption of continuity: {An emergency broadcast kept interrupting the program}.

An interruption is something that stops a process or activity, or the act of stopping it. A phone call interrupts a conversation; a power outage interrupts work. {Sorry for the interruption.} To speak while someone else is speaking is to interrupt them: {His constant interruptions made discussion impossible}. An interruption in service means a temporary stoppage.

An intersection is where two or more things cross or meet. Most commonly, it's the place where roads meet: {Turn left at the next intersection}. In geometry, an intersection is where lines or shapes overlap. The word extends to any point of overlap or connection: {the intersection of art and technology}, {the intersection of race and class}. What falls within the intersection shares characteristics of both crossing elements.

Intersex describes people born with reproductive or sexual anatomy that doesn't fit typical definitions of male or female. This may involve chromosomes, hormones, genitals, or internal organs. Some intersex traits are apparent at birth; others emerge at puberty or are discovered incidentally. The term replaces older medical language like "hermaphrodite," now considered outdated and offensive. {Many intersex advocates oppose unnecessary surgeries on infants.}

Interstate means between or among states, particularly the states of the United States. An interstate {highway} crosses state boundaries; the Interstate Highway System is the network of such roads. Interstate {commerce} involves trade across state lines. As a noun, an interstate is one of these highways: {We took the interstate to avoid traffic}.

Interstellar means between or among stars: {interstellar space}, {interstellar travel}. The word describes the vast regions of a galaxy outside individual star systems, or objects and phenomena that cross those distances. {Interstellar dust clouds eventually coalesce into new stars.} The term gained wider cultural currency from the 2014 science fiction film of the same name.

To intertwine is to twist or weave together, with each element winding around the others: {Their fingers intertwined}. The word often describes abstract connections—intertwined {fates}, intertwined {histories}, intertwined {economies}. Things that intertwine become difficult to separate, suggesting deep or complicated involvement: {Her personal and professional lives had become hopelessly intertwined}.

Intertwined describes things twisted or woven together, whether literally or figuratively. Vines become intertwined as they grow. Lives, fates, or histories that are intertwined are closely connected and hard to separate: {Their financial interests were deeply intertwined}. The word suggests mutual entanglement rather than one thing wrapped around another.

An interval is a space between things—in time, distance, or sequence. Musical intervals measure the gap between pitches. In mathematics, an interval is a range of values between two points. Events happen {at regular intervals} or {at intervals of ten minutes}. The word suggests measured separation: {She paused at intervals to catch her breath}.

To intervene is to come between—stepping into a situation to alter its course. Someone might intervene in a dispute to restore peace, or a government might intervene in markets to stabilize prices. Medical intervention means treatment that changes what would otherwise happen naturally. {She intervened before the argument turned physical}. The word implies purposeful action to change an outcome, usually by an outside party.

An intervention is an act of stepping in to change the course of events, typically to prevent harm or improve a situation. Medical interventions range from surgery to medication; political interventions may involve diplomacy or military action. The word has a specific informal meaning for a planned confrontation where friends and family urge someone to address destructive behavior, especially addiction: {Her family staged an intervention after she lost her job}. To intervene is the corresponding verb.

An interview is a formal meeting where one party questions another—typically for a job, news story, or research. The interviewer asks questions; the interviewee answers. Job interviews assess candidates: {She nailed the interview and got the offer}. Journalists interview sources for information. As a verb, to interview is to conduct or undergo such a meeting: {We interviewed six applicants}. Police interview suspects and witnesses.

Interviews are formal meetings where one party questions another—typically to assess qualifications for a job, gather information for a story, or investigate a matter. The word covers both the event and its product: {She gave a great interview} means she performed well; {I read the interview} refers to the published exchange. To interview is to conduct such a meeting or to be its subject: {We're interviewing candidates tomorrow}, {He interviewed with three companies}.

The intestines are the long, coiled tube in the abdomen where digestion is completed and nutrients absorbed. The small intestine handles most nutrient absorption; the large intestine (colon) absorbs water and forms waste. Intestinal fortitude is a polite way of saying guts—courage or resolve: {She had the intestinal fortitude to finish the race}.

Intimacy is closeness between people—emotional, physical, or both. Emotional intimacy involves sharing thoughts and vulnerabilities: {Their late-night conversations created a real intimacy}. Physical intimacy ranges from affectionate touch to sex; {intimacy} alone often euphemizes sexual contact: {The relationship became physical, but she wasn't ready for intimacy}. The plural intimacies usually means private acts or exchanges: {the intimacies of marriage}.

Intimate describes what is closest and most personal. An intimate friend shares your deepest confidences. Intimate knowledge of a subject runs deep. An intimate setting is small and private: {an intimate dinner for two}. Intimate relations is a euphemism for sex; an intimate is a close friend or lover. To intimate something is to hint at it indirectly: {She intimated that changes were coming}.

To intimidate is to frighten or threaten someone into compliance or submission. The effect may be intentional—{The lawyer tried to intimidate the witness}—or simply a byproduct of presence or reputation: {His size alone intimidated opponents}. Someone intimidating inspires fear or unease, often through implied power rather than direct threat.

Intimidated means made to feel fearful, timid, or inadequate—often by someone or something perceived as more powerful or impressive. You might feel intimidated by a demanding boss, a complex task, or an unfamiliar social setting: {She was intimidated by the crowd of experts}. The feeling can arise from deliberate threat or simply from being outmatched: {He felt intimidated by her confidence}.

Intimidating describes something or someone that makes others feel fear, nervousness, or inadequacy. An intimidating {person} projects power or hostility. An intimidating {task} seems daunting before you begin. The word often describes situations where confidence falters: {Walking into the interview felt intimidating}. Something intimidating may be genuinely threatening or merely impressive enough to unsettle: {The sheer size of the library was intimidating}.

Intimidation is the act of frightening or threatening someone to influence their behavior. It suggests using fear rather than persuasion: {The witness refused to testify after intimidation from the defendant's associates}. Intimidation can be overt—threats, aggression—or subtle, as when someone's presence or reputation alone creates unease. The word often appears in legal contexts describing witness tampering or workplace harassment.

Two prepositions, in and to, spent so much time together that a union seemed the only respectable thing. In nearly all of its uses, the fusion into suggests movement toward the center or inside, and its most usual position is after a verb of motion: Don’t drive the car into the ditch. She rushed into the room screaming. In literal meanings, into typically denotes entry, introduction, insertion, superposition, or inclusion. Figuratively it is used to talk about resultant states, activities, or conditions: How did you get into stamp collecting? It’s also the preposition used to indicate arithmetic division: How many times will 7 go into 58?

Intolerable describes something so unpleasant, painful, or offensive that it cannot be endured: {The heat became intolerable by midday}. The word implies reaching a threshold—what might be merely unpleasant crosses into what cannot be borne: {intolerable cruelty}, {intolerable working conditions}. Something intolerable demands action or escape.

Intolerance is the unwillingness to accept views, beliefs, or behaviors that differ from one's own. It often manifests as hostility toward particular groups based on race, religion, or other characteristics: {The rally was a response to rising intolerance in the community}. In medicine, intolerance describes the body's inability to process certain substances without adverse effects, as in lactose intolerance or gluten intolerance.

Intolerant describes unwillingness to accept views, beliefs, or behaviors different from one's own: {intolerant of dissent}, {religiously intolerant}. The word often carries moral judgment—calling someone intolerant implies narrow-mindedness. In medicine, intolerant means unable to tolerate a substance without adverse effects: {lactose intolerant}, {intolerant of certain medications}.

Intoxicated means drunk or under the influence of alcohol or drugs. The word appears frequently in legal and medical contexts where {drunk} might seem too informal: {The driver was visibly intoxicated}. Figuratively, intoxicated describes being overwhelmed by strong emotion or excitement: {intoxicated by success}, {intoxicated with love}.

Intoxicating means capable of causing intoxication—literally through alcohol or drugs, figuratively through intense pleasure or excitement. An intoxicating {perfume} overwhelms the senses. Intoxicating {power} corrupts judgment like drink. {The intoxicating rush of victory}. The word implies something so potent it impairs clear thinking.

Intoxication is the state of being affected by alcohol or drugs—impaired judgment, altered perception, diminished coordination. The word extends to any overwhelming sensation: {the intoxication of first love}, {drunk with power}. Legal contexts specify blood alcohol levels for intoxication: {public intoxication}, {driving under the influence}. The root meaning involves poison (toxic), suggesting substances that alter normal function.

Intricate describes something with many interconnected parts or fine details that make it complex and difficult to follow or understand. An intricate {pattern} has elaborate ornamentation. An intricate {plot} has many interwoven threads. The word suggests complexity that rewards careful attention rather than confusion that frustrates: {the intricate workings of a watch}, {an intricate web of relationships}.

Intrigue has two main threads. As a noun, it means secret scheming or a clandestine plot: {palace intrigue}, {political intrigue}. It can also mean a secret romantic affair. As a verb, to intrigue someone is to arouse their curiosity or fascination: {The mystery intrigued her}. The noun sense emphasizes hidden machinations; the verb sense emphasizes captivated interest.

Intrigued describes a state of curiosity mixed with fascination—your interest has been piqued by something mysterious or unusual. {I'm intrigued by her theory}. The word implies more than casual interest; something has captured your attention and you want to know more. From the verb intrigue, which can mean to fascinate or to scheme secretly.

Intrigues are secret schemes or plots, often political: {palace intrigues}, {the intrigues of rival factions}. The word suggests covert maneuvering and hidden agendas. As a verb, intrigue means to arouse curiosity or fascination: {The mystery intrigued her}. It can also mean to scheme: {They intrigued against the king}. The noun carries darker connotations than the verb, which usually just means to interest.

Intriguing describes something that arouses curiosity or fascination, usually because it's mysterious, complex, or not immediately understood: {an intriguing possibility}, {The detective found the case intriguing}. Unlike merely interesting, intriguing suggests something that draws you in and makes you want to know more.

Intro is short for introduction—an opening segment that precedes the main content. Music tracks have intros before verses begin, television shows have intros with theme music and credits, and presentations have intros that set context: {Skip the intro and get to the point}. The word works as both noun and verb: {Let me intro you to my colleague}.

Introduce means to bring something or someone into a situation for the first time. You introduce a friend to your parents, a speaker to an audience, or a new policy to an organization. To introduce yourself is to tell someone your name upon first meeting. Introduce also means to present something new: {The company introduced a redesigned model}. In formal contexts, bills are introduced in legislatures. To introduce someone to a subject or activity is to give them their first experience of it: {My uncle introduced me to jazz}.

Introduction is the act of bringing something into use or notice for the first time: {the introduction of vaccines transformed public health}. It also means presenting one person to another: {After a brief introduction, they shook hands}. An introduction to a book or speech sets up what follows. A course titled "Introduction to Philosophy" covers basic principles for beginners.

Introductions are the opening portions of books, speeches, or presentations—the part that comes before the main content and prepares you for it. Introductions are also the acts of presenting people to each other: {We skipped the introductions and got right to business}. An introduction to a subject is a basic or beginner-level treatment: {Introduction to Biology}.

Introspection is the examination of one's own thoughts, feelings, and mental states. The practice involves turning attention inward rather than outward: {A period of introspection followed his divorce}. Psychology distinguishes introspection from observation—you can observe someone's behavior but only introspect your own mind. The adjective is introspective: {an introspective person}, {introspective lyrics}.

Introversion is a personality orientation toward one's inner world rather than external stimulation. Introverts typically recharge through solitude and find extended social interaction draining, though this doesn't necessarily mean shyness or social anxiety. {After the party, I needed a day of introversion to recover}. The concept gained wide currency through the Myers-Briggs personality framework, where it contrasts with extroversion.

An introvert is a person who tends toward inner thoughts and feelings rather than external stimulation. Introverts often prefer solitary activities or small groups to large social gatherings, and may feel drained by extensive interaction: {As an introvert, she needed quiet time to recharge after parties}. The term comes from psychology but now describes personality more broadly. The verb introvert means to turn inward.

Introverted describes a temperament oriented toward inner experience rather than external stimulation. Introverted people tend to feel drained by extensive social interaction and recharged by solitude: {She's too introverted for sales work}. The trait exists on a spectrum with extroverted, and most people fall somewhere between the extremes.

To intrude is to enter where you're not welcome or wanted. A stranger intrudes on a private conversation; unwanted thoughts intrude on concentration. The word implies violation of boundaries—physical, social, or psychological: {I hope I'm not intruding}. Someone who intrudes is an intruder; the act is intrusion. {Reality has a way of intruding on our fantasies.}

An intruder is someone who enters a place without permission or welcome. The word typically implies unwanted presence—a burglar in a home, a hacker in a computer system, or simply someone who shows up uninvited: {The security system detected an intruder}. Intruder suggests violation of boundaries, whether physical, digital, or social.

Intruders are people who enter where they don't belong—typically a building, property, or space where they have no right to be. The word usually implies unwelcome presence and possible threat: {The alarm system detected intruders}. Security systems, guard dogs, and warning signs all address potential intruders. The term extends to anything that encroaches where it shouldn't: {Invasive species are intruders in native ecosystems}.

Intrusion is the act of entering where you're not wanted or welcome. A physical intrusion violates space: {The security system detected an intrusion}. Social intrusions violate privacy or solitude: {Forgive the intrusion, but I need to speak with you}. In geology, an intrusion is magma that forces its way into existing rock formations. The word carries connotations of unwelcome presence—something that pushes in where it doesn't belong.

Intuition is knowledge or understanding that arrives without conscious reasoning—a sense of something that bypasses deliberate thought. You might have an intuition that something is wrong, or trust your intuition when making decisions: {My intuition told me not to take the job}. The word often implies a kind of direct perception, as if truth were felt rather than figured out. Some treat intuition as mystical; others see it as pattern recognition operating below awareness.

Intuitive describes knowledge or understanding that comes without conscious reasoning—you grasp it directly rather than working it out step by step. An intuitive {person} relies on gut feelings. An intuitive {interface} feels natural to use without instruction. {She had an intuitive sense that something was wrong}. The word suggests immediate comprehension rather than learned skill, though what feels intuitive often reflects deep familiarity.

To invade is to enter territory with hostile intent, typically with military force: {Germany invaded Poland in 1939}. The word extends to any unwelcome intrusion—invading someone's privacy, invasive species invading ecosystems, or thoughts invading your mind. Cancer invades surrounding tissue by spreading into it. The noun is invasion.

Invaded is the past tense of invade—to enter a place by force, typically with hostile intent. Armies invade countries; pests invade homes. The word extends to unwelcome intrusion: {Tourists invaded the quiet village}. Privacy can be invaded, and so can personal space. {Cancer had invaded the surrounding tissue.}

An invader is someone or something that enters by force or without permission—typically a military force crossing into another country's territory: {The invaders swept through the countryside}. The term extends to anything unwelcome that intrudes: invasive species are ecological invaders, and viruses are invaders of the body. In video games, Space Invaders established a genre.

Invaders are people or forces that enter a place by force, typically with hostile intent. Armies invade countries, pests invade gardens, and unwanted thoughts invade the mind. The word carries connotations of violation and unwelcome intrusion: {The invaders burned the village}. In science fiction, invaders often means aliens attacking Earth.

Invading is the present participle of invade—entering a place by force, typically with hostile intent. Armies invade countries; pests invade homes. The word extends to unwelcome intrusions generally: {You're invading my personal space}. An invading {army}, invading {species}, or invading {force} represents something entering where it doesn't belong.

Invalid has two distinct pronunciations with different meanings. With stress on the first syllable, an invalid is a person weakened by illness or disability: {She spent years caring for her invalid mother}. With stress on the second syllable, invalid means not valid—legally void, logically unsound, or technically rejected: {an invalid passport}, {an invalid argument}, {invalid data}. The verb invalidate means to render something void or ineffective.

Invaluable means extremely valuable—so precious that its worth cannot be measured: {Her advice proved invaluable during the crisis}. Despite the negative prefix, invaluable doesn't mean "not valuable" but rather "beyond valuation." The word applies to things whose worth exceeds any price: invaluable {experience}, invaluable {contributions}, an invaluable {resource}.

An invasion is the entry of a military force into territory to conquer or occupy it: {the invasion of Normandy}. The word extends to any unwelcome intrusion in large numbers: an invasion of {tourists}, an invasion of {privacy}. Invasive species spread aggressively into new ecosystems. Medical procedures are invasive when they enter the body.

Invasions is the plural of invasion—acts of entering by force, typically military forces crossing into hostile territory: {The invasions of Poland marked the beginning of World War II}. The word extends to unwelcome intrusions of any kind: {invasions of privacy}, {invasions of pests}. In medicine, invasion describes how disease spreads into tissue: {The tumor showed signs of vascular invasion}.

Invasive describes something that intrudes where it doesn't belong or spreads aggressively. An invasive {species} colonizes new territory and displaces native life. An invasive {procedure} enters the body surgically. Invasive {questions} probe into private matters. The word carries connotations of unwelcome encroachment—whether biological, medical, or personal.

Invected is a heraldic term describing a line or edge decorated with small curved scallops pointing inward, toward the field. It's the opposite of engrailed, where the points face outward. The term appears almost exclusively in descriptions of coats of arms and heraldic designs: {a chief invected}, {an invected bordure}.

To invent is to create something that didn't exist before—a device, method, or concept: {Edison invented the phonograph}. The word implies originality rather than discovery of something already present. Invent also means to fabricate or make up: {She invented an excuse for being late}. An invention can be a useful creation or a lie.

Invention is the act of creating something new, especially a device or method that didn't exist before: {The invention of the printing press transformed society}. An invention is also the thing created: {The telephone was Bell's most famous invention}. The word extends to fabricated stories or lies: {His alibi was pure invention}. In rhetoric and music, invention refers to the creative faculty or a compositional exercise.

Inventions are things created or devised for the first time—new devices, processes, or ideas that didn't exist before. The telephone was an invention; so was democracy. Invention also names the act of creating: {Necessity is the mother of invention}. Extended to stories, invention means fabrication: {The whole tale was pure invention}.

An inventor is a person who creates something new—a device, method, or process that didn't exist before. The term typically applies to practical or technical innovations: {the inventor of the telephone}, {a prolific inventor with dozens of patents}. Unlike a discoverer, who finds what already exists, an inventor brings something into being.

Inventory is a complete list of items, especially goods held by a business for sale or use. A store's inventory includes everything on its shelves and in its warehouse. To inventory something is to count and catalog it: {We inventory the stockroom every quarter}. The word extends to any systematic accounting: {a personal inventory of strengths and weaknesses}. When inventory runs low, supplies are nearly depleted.

To invest is to commit money or resources expecting future returns: {She invested in real estate}, {They invested heavily in tech stocks}. The word extends to non-financial commitments—you invest time, energy, or emotion in relationships, projects, or causes. To be {invested in} something is to care about its outcome.
