Figuratively, journey describes any extended process of development or change: {a spiritual journey}, {the journey to recovery}. As a verb, to journey is to travel: {They journeyed across the desert}.

A journeyman is a worker who has completed an apprenticeship and is qualified to practice a trade, though not yet a master. The term comes from the French word for day—a journeyman was paid by the day rather than bound to a single employer. Extended to sports and other fields, journeyman describes a competent professional who moves between teams or positions without achieving star status: {He spent fifteen years as a journeyman pitcher, reliable but never spectacular}.

Journeys is the plural of journey—a trip from one place to another, especially one covering considerable distance or time. The word carries connotations of significance beyond mere travel: {life's journeys}, {spiritual journeys}. As a verb form, journeys means travels: {She journeys across Europe every summer}.

A joust is a combat between two mounted knights charging at each other with lances, a staple of medieval tournaments. The verb means to engage in such combat. Figuratively, to joust is to compete or spar: {The candidates jousted over immigration policy}. A verbal joust is a sharp exchange of wit or arguments.

Jousting is a medieval combat sport in which two armored riders on horseback charge at each other with lances, each trying to unseat the other. The word now appears mostly in figurative contexts—political jousting, verbal jousting—describing competitive back-and-forth exchanges: {The candidates spent the debate jousting over tax policy}.

Jousts are medieval combat contests between mounted knights charging at each other with lances, typically as tournament entertainment. The singular joust names either the event or an individual encounter within it. Figuratively, any competitive clash between rivals: {The debate became a joust between two opposing philosophies}. To joust is to engage in such combat, literal or metaphorical.

Jowls are the fleshy, often sagging parts of the lower cheeks and jaw. The word typically appears in plural form and carries connotations of heaviness or looseness: {His jowls quivered when he laughed}. Jowly describes someone with prominent jowls. The word also applies to similar folds of flesh on animals, particularly dogs like bulldogs and bloodhounds.

Joy is a feeling of great happiness, typically one of short duration that is occasioned by some event. To characterize someone or something as a joy is a way of saying that they evoke very pleasant feelings: His singing is a joy to experience. People sometimes say no joy to signal that they have not been successful in finding or doing something. When capitalized, Joy is a somewhat old-fashioned female given name.

Joyful describes a state of great happiness or delight. Someone joyful radiates pleasure: {a joyful reunion}, {joyful tears}. The word often appears in celebratory or religious contexts: {joyful noise}, {joyful tidings}. Unlike mere happiness, joyful suggests emotion that overflows—too full to contain.

A joyride is a reckless drive taken purely for pleasure, often in a stolen vehicle: {Teenagers took the car for a joyride and crashed it}. The term extends to any thrilling but irresponsible adventure, especially one at others' expense: {The CEO's joyride with company funds ended in bankruptcy}. To joyride is to take such a trip.

Joyriding is driving recklessly for thrills, typically in a stolen vehicle. The term emphasizes the driver's pursuit of excitement rather than transportation: {Three teenagers were arrested for joyriding in a stolen SUV}. The word can extend to any unauthorized or irresponsible use of equipment: {He got fired for joyriding on the company forklift}.

A joystick is a control lever that moves in multiple directions, used to steer aircraft, operate machinery, or play video games. The stick translates hand movements into corresponding motion on screen or in mechanical systems: {She grabbed the joystick and banked hard left}. In slang, joystick is a playful term for penis.

Joysticks are control devices with a lever that pivots in multiple directions, translating hand movements into input. Originally designed for aircraft control, they became iconic through video games—the lever letting players steer, aim, or navigate: {I wore out the joystick on my old Atari}. Industrial machinery and accessibility devices also use joysticks for precise directional control.

Jubilant means feeling or expressing great joy and triumph: {The jubilant crowd flooded the streets after the championship victory}. The word suggests celebratory exuberance, often shared collectively—fans jubilant after a win, a nation jubilant at war's end. It implies not quiet satisfaction but visible, often boisterous elation.

Jubilation is a state of extreme joy and celebration, the kind that bursts out when something wonderful happens. It suggests not just private happiness but expressive, often public rejoicing—cheering crowds, triumphant shouts, people literally jumping for joy. {There was jubilation in the streets when the war ended.} The word carries a sense of release, as if happiness has been building and finally spills over into visible celebration.

A jubilee is a special anniversary celebration, especially one marking 25, 50, or 75 years: {The queen's golden jubilee drew millions to the streets}. The word carries connotations of festivity, commemoration, and collective rejoicing. In biblical tradition, a jubilee was a year of emancipation and restoration occurring every fifty years, when slaves were freed and debts forgiven. This sense of release and renewal underlies modern usage: {The campaign called for a debt jubilee for developing nations}.

A judas is a traitor, especially one who betrays under the guise of friendship. The term derives from Judas Iscariot, the apostle who betrayed Jesus for thirty pieces of silver. A judas hole or judas window is a small peephole in a door, allowing someone to observe without being seen—watching others as Judas watched for his opportunity. {He turned judas on his own crew.} (Capitalized Judas is the biblical figure or a given name.)

A judge is a public official who presides over legal proceedings, hearing evidence and ruling on matters of law. Judges interpret statutes, instruct juries, and issue sentences. The word extends to anyone who evaluates or decides: {a judge at a baking competition}, {a good judge of character}. To judge is to form an opinion or make a determination: {Don't judge me}. The verb often carries connotations of criticism or disapproval: {She felt judged by her in-laws}. {Who are you to judge?}

Judged is the past tense of judge—to form an opinion, make a decision, or evaluate something. A court case is judged by a jury. A competition is judged by experts. {She judged the distance carefully before jumping}. In casual speech, to feel judged is to sense others disapproving of you: {I felt so judged when I ordered dessert}.

Judgement is a British spelling of judgment—the act of judging or the conclusion reached. A court delivers a judgement. You exercise judgement when making decisions. Someone with good judgement consistently makes sound choices; poor judgement leads to mistakes. {I'll trust your judgement on this.} The spelling without the e is standard in American English and legal contexts.

Judgemental means inclined to make harsh or critical evaluations of others, often based on limited information or rigid standards: {She's so judgemental about how other people raise their kids}. The word typically carries negative connotations—being judgemental suggests unfair criticism rather than thoughtful assessment. Also spelled judgmental.

Judges are people who make official decisions. In courts, judges preside over trials and render verdicts. In competitions, judges evaluate performances and award scores. The verb means to form an opinion or assessment: {Don't judge me}, {She judged the distance carefully}. To judge someone is often to evaluate them critically: {I'm not here to judge}. {Who are you to judge?}

A judgment is the conclusion reached after weighing information. When an authority issues a judgment, it offers an opinion about its merits, viability, truth, or other characteristic: The tribunal is expected to issue a judgment in the matter soon. Judgment in general is the capacity to draw sound conclusions and can be viewed as good or bad: Her judgment about boyfriends seems to be pretty dicey these days. I thought you showed good judgment in declining their offer. Judgement is an alternative spelling.

Judgmental describes someone inclined to make harsh or critical evaluations of others, often based on personal standards of right and wrong: {Don't be so judgmental—you don't know what she's been through}. The word implies excessive or unfair criticism rather than reasoned assessment. Less commonly, judgmental relates neutrally to judgment or the capacity for it: {judgmental errors}, {judgmental skills}.

Judo is a Japanese martial art and Olympic sport focused on throws and grappling rather than strikes. Developed in the late nineteenth century, it emphasizes using an opponent's force against them. A practitioner is a judoka. The word means "gentle way" in Japanese, reflecting its philosophy of maximum efficiency with minimum effort: {She earned her black belt in judo}.

A jug is a container for liquids, typically with a handle and a lip or spout for pouring: {a jug of water}, {a milk jug}. In British usage, a jug is what Americans call a pitcher. Jugs is vulgar slang for breasts. In slang, the jug is jail: {He spent six months in the jug}.

A juggernaut is an overwhelming, unstoppable force that crushes whatever stands in its path. The word comes from a Hindu festival where a massive cart carrying an image of the god Jagannath was pulled through streets—Western observers mythologized devotees throwing themselves beneath its wheels. Now juggernaut describes any massive, relentless entity: {The team became a juggernaut in the second half of the season}, {a corporate juggernaut}, {a juggernaut of public opinion}.

To juggle is to keep multiple objects in the air by tossing and catching them in continuous motion: {She can juggle five balls at once}. The word extends naturally to managing multiple demands simultaneously: {juggling work and family}, {juggling three projects at once}. To juggle figures or accounts is to manipulate them deceptively. A person who juggles is a juggler.

A juggler is someone who tosses and catches multiple objects in a continuous pattern, keeping several items airborne at once: {The street juggler kept five balls in the air}. By extension, anyone managing multiple demands simultaneously juggles them: {She's a juggler of career, kids, and grad school}. The verb is juggle.

Jugglers are performers who keep multiple objects in continuous motion, tossing and catching them in patterns. The term extends to anyone managing several things simultaneously: {She's a juggler of work, kids, and grad school}. A juggler may also be someone who manipulates facts or accounts deceptively—juggling the books to hide losses.

Juggling is the skill of keeping multiple objects in the air by continuously throwing and catching them in sequence. The word extends to managing several tasks or responsibilities simultaneously: {She's juggling work, school, and childcare}. The implication is precarious balance—drop your attention and something falls.

Jugs are containers with handles, typically used for holding and pouring liquids: {a jug of water}, {a milk jug}. In British English, a jug often has a lip for pouring; in American English, it may be a large bottle with a handle. Jugs is also vulgar slang for a woman's breasts, emphasizing size.

The jugular veins are the large blood vessels in the neck that return blood from the head to the heart. Because they're vital and exposed, {go for the jugular} means to attack someone's most vulnerable point—to fight ruthlessly for the kill. As an adjective, jugular describes anything relating to the throat or neck.

Juice is the liquid component of a fruit or vegetable, extracted by crushing, squeezing, or some other means. Liquid components of other foods may also be called juice, like the drippings from meat. If you juice apples, for example, you extract the juice from them. Informal and slang meanings of juice include electricity (the motor isn’t getting any juice), an agreeable quality of energy and enthusiasm, or power or influence: Ask Tom to introduce you; he’s got juice with the boss.

A juicebox is a small cardboard container of fruit juice or fruit-flavored drink, fitted with a straw for drinking. Marketed primarily to children, juiceboxes are a staple of packed lunches and snack time: {She tucked a juicebox into his lunchbox}. The attached straw punctures a foil-covered hole in the top.

Juicing is extracting liquid from fruits and vegetables, typically with a dedicated appliance. The practice became associated with health fads promising detoxification or weight loss: {She's doing a three-day juicing cleanse}. In sports, juicing means using anabolic steroids or other performance-enhancing drugs: {He was juicing during his record-breaking season}.

Juicy describes something full of juice—the liquid from fruits, meat, or other sources: {a juicy peach}, {a juicy steak}. By extension, juicy means enticingly interesting, especially when involving scandal or gossip: {juicy details}, {a juicy story}. Something juicy promises rich rewards: {a juicy contract}, {a juicy role}.

Jujitsu is a Japanese martial art emphasizing throws, joint locks, and holds rather than strikes. Developed by samurai for unarmed combat, it focuses on using an opponent's force against them. Jujitsu spawned modern derivatives including judo and Brazilian jiu-jitsu. Also spelled jiujitsu or jiu-jitsu.

Juju is a West African term for magical power or the objects that embody it—charms, amulets, or fetishes believed to hold supernatural force. In broader use, juju refers to luck or mystical influence, good or bad: {That place has bad juju}. The word suggests folk magic or superstition rather than formal religion.

Juke has two main threads. One involves evasive movement—to juke is to make a quick, deceptive move to avoid a tackler or opponent: {He juked left and sprinted past the defender}. The other involves music: a jukebox plays recorded songs, and a juke joint is a roadhouse or informal bar, especially in the American South, where people drink, dance, and listen to music. Both senses carry energy and spontaneity.

A jukebox is a coin-operated machine that plays music selections. Traditional jukeboxes held records and let patrons choose songs by pressing buttons; the term now applies to any device offering music on demand: {The bar had an old Wurlitzer jukebox in the corner}. Digital jukeboxes and streaming services have largely replaced the mechanical originals.

A jumble is a confused mixture or disordered mass of things: {a jumble of papers on the desk}, {a jumble of thoughts}. To jumble is to mix up or throw together without order: {The movers jumbled everything into boxes}. In British English, a jumble sale is what Americans call a rummage sale—a charity event selling donated secondhand goods.

Jumbled means mixed up in a disordered or confused way. Jumbled objects are thrown together without arrangement: {a jumbled pile of clothes}, {jumbled papers on the desk}. Jumbled thoughts or words lack coherent order: {His explanation came out jumbled}. The word suggests randomness rather than deliberate disorder.

Jumbo means unusually large: {jumbo shrimp}, {jumbo jets}, {a jumbo-sized portion}. The word comes from the name of a famous circus elephant in the 1880s, whose name became synonymous with enormous size. Jumbo often modifies products to indicate the largest available option: {jumbo eggs}, {jumbo roll of paper towels}.

A jumbotron is a large video screen used at sports stadiums, concert venues, and public events to display live action, replays, and announcements to crowds: {The kiss cam caught them on the jumbotron}. Originally a brand name, it now refers generically to any giant LED display screen at a venue.

Jump characterizes quick movement, usually self-propelled, vertically or horizontally. You can jump overboard or jump ahead. A jump is an instance of jumping. Figurative use extends to quick movement in time or thought (jump back to ten years ago, jump from one topic to another) or on a scale (jump in prices). Phrasal verbs with jump usually suggest suddenness: jump at an opportunity means respond to it with enthusiasm; to jump on someone is to criticize them sharply, perhaps unexpectedly.

The prosaic and predictable meaning of jumper is the one who jumps. Beyond that, jumper represents two different pieces of clothing. In British English, a jumper is a sweater – a knitted upper body garment. In American English, a jumper is a sleeveless dress worn over a blouse or shirt. Sometimes, jumper is short for jumper cable, an apparatus for starting a car using the battery power from another car. On a circuit board, a jumper is a pin that forms a removable connection.

Jumpers are people or things that jump. A jumper can be someone who leaps from heights—a parachutist, a bungee jumper, or tragically, someone attempting suicide from a bridge or building. In basketball, a jumper is a jump shot. In British English, a jumper is a pullover sweater. Jumper cables connect a dead car battery to a live one. {She's one of the best high jumpers in the country.}

Jumping is the present participle of jump—propelling oneself off the ground or a surface. It describes the action in progress: {The kids were jumping on the bed}. Jumping appears in compounds: {jumping jacks}, {jumping-off point}, {jumping the gun}. As an adjective, it can mean lively or thriving: {The club was jumping last night}.

Jumps is the third-person singular of jump—to propel oneself off a surface, typically upward or forward: {She jumps rope every morning}. As a plural noun, jumps refers to multiple instances of jumping: {The horse cleared all the jumps}. The jumps can also mean a state of nervous agitation: {Loud noises give me the jumps}.

A jumpscare is a sudden, startling moment in a horror film, video game, or haunted attraction—a face appearing without warning, a loud noise breaking silence. The technique relies on shock rather than sustained dread: {The movie was mostly boring, but the jumpscares got me}. As a verb, to jumpscare someone is to frighten them this way.

Jumpstart means to start a car with a dead battery by connecting it to another power source—typically another vehicle's battery via cables. The term extends to reviving anything stalled or sluggish: {The tax cuts were meant to jumpstart the economy}. As a noun, a jumpstart is the act itself or any boost that gets something going: {Her career got a jumpstart when she won the award}. Also spelled jump-start.

A jumpsuit is a one-piece garment combining top and bottom, originally designed for parachutists who needed clothing that wouldn't catch or separate during a jump. The practical design spread to mechanics, pilots, and other workers, then to fashion. Modern jumpsuits range from utilitarian coveralls to elegant evening wear: {She wore a black jumpsuit to the party}.

A jumpsuit is a one-piece garment combining top and bottom, typically with a front zipper or buttons. Originally designed for parachutists—who literally jump—the term now covers everything from mechanics' coveralls to fashionable evening wear: {She wore a sleek black jumpsuit to the party}. The singular jumpsuit appears far more often than the plural.

Jumpy describes a state of nervous agitation where someone startles easily or can't sit still. A jumpy person might flinch at sudden noises or seem unable to relax, often because they're anxious, overcaffeinated, or expecting something bad to happen. {I've been jumpy ever since I heard footsteps outside my window last night.} The word can also describe erratic movement, like a jumpy video feed that skips and stutters.

Junction is a point where things meet, connect, or cross—especially roads, railway lines, or rivers: {Take the highway to the next junction}. In anatomy, it's where tissues or structures join: {the neuromuscular junction}. The word emphasizes the meeting point itself rather than the paths that converge there.

A jungle is dense, tangled tropical vegetation—the kind of forest where trees, vines, and undergrowth grow so thickly that passage is difficult. Jungle often appears interchangeably with rainforest, though technically jungle refers to the impenetrable undergrowth rather than the canopy. Figuratively, jungle describes any environment of fierce competition or confusion: {the corporate jungle}, {the urban jungle}, {It's a jungle out there}. Jungle law suggests survival of the fittest, where ruthlessness prevails over civilization.

Jungles is the plural of jungle—dense tropical forests with tangled vegetation. The word extends to any wild, overgrown area and metaphorically to chaotic, competitive environments: {the urban jungle}, {the corporate jungle}. {It's a jungle out there} suggests a hostile world where survival requires vigilance.

Junior describes someone younger or lower in rank. A junior {employee} has less seniority. A junior {partner} holds a subordinate position. In American schools, a junior is a third-year student in high school or college. Junior can also mean the younger of two, especially a son named after his father: {John Smith Junior}. As a noun, it addresses a young boy: {Come here, junior}. (Capitalized Junior appears after names as a suffix.)

Juniper is an evergreen shrub or small tree with needle-like leaves and aromatic berry-like cones. The bluish berries give gin its distinctive flavor—the word gin derives from the Dutch for juniper. Juniper grows widely in temperate regions and appears in landscaping, traditional medicine, and cooking: {juniper-rubbed venison}, {the scent of juniper in the mountain air}.

Junk is discarded or worthless stuff, rubbish: {Clean out that junk from the garage}. A junk is also a Chinese sailing vessel with distinctive sails. Junk food is unhealthy food with little nutritional value. Junk mail is unsolicited advertising. In slang, junk means heroin: {He was strung out on junk}. And junk is slang for male genitals: {He took a ball to the junk}. {Check out the junk on that guy}. The genital sense is vulgar but common, especially in sports contexts involving groin injuries.

A junkie is slang for a drug addict, originally a heroin user (from junk meaning heroin): {He's been a junkie for years}. The word extends to anyone obsessive about something: {a news junkie}, {a coffee junkie}. The addiction sense remains primary and carries negative connotations.

A junkyard is a place where discarded items—especially old vehicles—are stored, dismantled, or sold for parts and scrap. The word often implies disorder and accumulation: {The garage had become a junkyard of broken appliances}. A {junkyard dog} is fierce and territorial, from the guard dogs kept at such places.

A junta is a group that seizes political power, typically military officers who have overthrown a civilian government: {The junta suspended the constitution and imposed martial law}. The word comes from Spanish, where it simply means a committee or council, but in English it almost always carries connotations of illegitimate rule and authoritarian control.

Juries is the plural of jury—a group of citizens sworn to hear evidence and deliver a verdict in legal proceedings. Trial juries decide guilt or liability; grand juries determine whether charges should be brought. The phrase {the jury is still out} means a matter remains undecided: {The jury is still out on whether remote work improves productivity}.

Jurisdiction is the authority to make legal decisions or the territory where that authority applies. A court has jurisdiction over certain cases; a police department has jurisdiction within city limits. {The crime occurred outside their jurisdiction.} The word extends to any sphere of control: {That falls under the marketing department's jurisdiction.}

A juror is a member of a jury, the group of citizens who hear evidence in a court trial and deliver a verdict. Jurors are typically selected from voter registration or driver's license records and must meet certain qualifications, such as being of legal age and having no felony convictions. {The jurors deliberated for three days before reaching a unanimous verdict.} In the U.S., criminal trials usually require twelve jurors, while civil cases may use fewer.

A jury is a group of citizens who hear evidence in a legal case and deliver a verdict. In criminal trials, the jury decides guilt or innocence; in civil cases, liability and damages. {The jury deliberated for three days before reaching a verdict.} To jury-rig something is to improvise a temporary fix—a different word, from nautical use. As a verb, to jury means to serve on or select for a jury, or to judge entries in a competition: {a juried art exhibition}.

From its humble beginnings as an adjective meaning reasonable or fair, just has become an adverb with a wide range of precise applications. It is the go-to word for relating degree and precision. It can mean exactly (just right), recently (I just got here), barely (We just made it), directly (a ranch just south of town), only (just yesterday you thought differently), or very (just fantastic). Just nearly always comes before a main verb but after an auxiliary verb.

Justice is a righteous word that conveys the quality of being fair. It frequently arises when someone has been wronged or injured; justice is sought to right the wrong. For this reason, justice is closely tied to law; laws are designed to ensure that justice will prevail. In some courts, especially the highest court within a jurisdiction, the judges are called justices. The criminal justice system is the whole network of police, courts, prisons and the like.

Justification is the act of showing something to be right, reasonable, or warranted: {There's no justification for that kind of behavior}. In law, justification is a defense showing conduct was lawful despite causing harm. In typography and word processing, justification is the alignment of text—left-justified, right-justified, or fully justified with even margins on both sides.

Justified means shown to be right, reasonable, or warranted. An action is justified when sufficient grounds support it: {Her anger was completely justified}. A person feels justified in doing something when they believe they have good reason: {He felt justified in leaving early}. In typesetting, justified text has even margins on both sides, with spacing adjusted so lines align flush left and right.

Justify means to show or prove something is right, reasonable, or warranted: {How can you justify spending that much on a handbag?} The word often implies defending against criticism or doubt—you justify your actions, your decisions, your existence. In typesetting and word processing, to justify text is to align it evenly along both margins. A justified belief in philosophy is one supported by adequate evidence or reasoning.

Juvenile means young or relating to young people: {juvenile offenders}, {juvenile court}. The word often carries negative connotations when applied to behavior—juvenile actions are immature or childish: {His jokes were juvenile}. In biology and law, juvenile refers specifically to individuals not yet adult. As a noun, a juvenile is a young person, especially one who has committed a crime.

Juvie is informal for juvenile detention—a facility where minors are held for criminal offenses: {He spent six months in juvie for stealing cars}. It can also refer to a young person held there: {The juvies were separated from adult inmates}. The word carries a casual, streetwise tone.

Kabob is meat and often vegetables threaded onto a skewer and grilled or roasted: {chicken kabobs with peppers and onions}. The dish appears across Middle Eastern, Mediterranean, and South Asian cuisines in countless variations. Also spelled kebab, kebob, or kabab. A {shish kabob} specifically features cubed meat on a skewer.

Kaboom represents the sound of a loud explosion or impact—a comic-book onomatopoeia for bombs, crashes, and dramatic destruction: {And then—kaboom!—the whole building came down}. It often emphasizes sudden, dramatic events, not always literal explosions: {The stock market went kaboom}.

Kabuki is a traditional form of Japanese theater characterized by elaborate costumes, stylized movements, and dramatic makeup. In American political usage, kabuki (or kabuki theater) describes an elaborate performance where the outcome is predetermined—going through the motions for show while real decisions happen elsewhere: {The congressional hearing was pure kabuki}. (Capitalized Kabuki emphasizes the Japanese theatrical tradition.)

Kafkaesque describes situations that are nightmarishly complex, illogical, or oppressively bureaucratic—evoking the fiction of Franz Kafka, whose characters face absurd systems they cannot understand or escape. A kafkaesque experience involves helpless confusion before impersonal authority: {Trying to get my passport renewed was kafkaesque—I was sent to five different offices, each claiming the others were responsible}. The lowercase form is less common than capitalized. (Capitalized Kafkaesque is standard.)

Kaiju is a Japanese word for giant monsters, especially those from Japanese films and media. Godzilla is the archetypal kaiju, but the term covers any colossal creature that threatens cities or battles other monsters: {Pacific Rim is basically a kaiju movie with American production values}. The genre emphasizes spectacle—massive scale, urban destruction, and creatures with distinctive silhouettes and powers.

A kaleidoscope is a tube containing mirrors and loose colored fragments that form symmetrical patterns when rotated and viewed through one end. The shifting, colorful designs give rise to figurative use: any constantly changing pattern or mixture is a kaleidoscope: {a kaleidoscope of emotions}, {the kaleidoscope of city life}.

Kalokagathia is an ancient Greek ideal combining physical beauty and moral virtue—the notion that external grace reflects inner goodness. The word literally joins "beautiful" and "good." In classical thought, a person of kalokagathia possessed both an admirable body and an admirable character, the two inseparable: {The gymnasium trained young men toward kalokagathia, cultivating body and soul together}.

Kamikaze comes from Japanese words meaning "divine wind." In World War II, kamikaze pilots flew suicide missions, deliberately crashing explosive-laden aircraft into enemy targets. The term now describes any recklessly self-destructive action: {a kamikaze mission}, {kamikaze tactics}. A kamikaze is also a cocktail of vodka, triple sec, and lime juice.

A kangaroo is a large marsupial native to Australia, known for its powerful hind legs, long tail, and distinctive hopping locomotion. Females carry their young, called joeys, in a pouch on their belly. The word extends to informal contexts: a kangaroo court is an unauthorized or irregular tribunal that ignores proper legal procedure, suggesting the jumping, unpredictable nature of such proceedings. {The kangaroo bounded across the outback.}

Kangaroos is the plural of kangaroo, the large marsupial native to Australia known for powerful hind legs, a long tail, and a pouch for carrying young. The animals move by hopping and can cover great distances at speed. {Kangaroos bounded across the road at dusk.} Kangaroo appears in compounds like {kangaroo court}, an unofficial tribunal that ignores proper procedure.

Kapow is an exclamation representing the sound of an explosion, gunshot, or forceful impact—the comic book equivalent of a punch landing or a bomb going off. It appears in action sequences and emphatic speech to convey sudden, dramatic force: {Kapow! The superhero's fist connected with the villain's jaw}. Like similar words (bam, pow, wham), it adds cartoonish energy to descriptions of violence or sudden events.

Kaput means broken, ruined, or no longer functioning. From German, it entered English as informal slang for something that has failed completely or ceased to work: {The engine is kaput}, {My phone went kaput}. It can also describe plans or relationships that have fallen apart: {After that argument, their friendship was kaput}.

Karaoke is a form of entertainment where people sing along to recorded music with the vocals removed, following lyrics displayed on a screen. The activity originated in Japan and became popular worldwide in bars, private rooms, and at home. {We're going out for karaoke tonight}. The word combines Japanese terms for "empty" and "orchestra."

Karate is a martial art developed in Japan, emphasizing strikes, kicks, and blocks rather than grappling or weapons. Practitioners train in forms called kata and may spar or break boards to demonstrate technique and power. {She's been taking karate since she was eight.} A karate chop is a sharp blow with the edge of the hand.

At its core, karma means “the result of past action.” It is usually misconstrued to mean moral causation: bad things happen (bad karma) as a result of wrong, harmful, or immoral action; good things happen (good karma) as a result of virtuous action. This concept has a corollary in Christianity’s “as you sow, so shall you reap.” In religions that place an emphasis on karma, such as Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism, the belief in the cycle of rebirth means that karma may play out over many lifetimes.

Karmic describes something related to karma—the idea that actions generate consequences that return to the actor. A karmic {debt} is owed for past wrongs; karmic {justice} arrives when someone gets what they deserve. The word implies a cosmic or spiritual accounting: {There's something karmic about him losing his fortune to a scam artist}.

A katana is a Japanese sword with a curved, single-edged blade and long grip for two-handed use. Traditionally carried by samurai, katanas are associated with Japanese martial culture and craftsmanship. The word appears frequently in martial arts, anime, and video game contexts: {He collected replica katanas}.

A kayak is a small, narrow boat propelled by a double-bladed paddle. The paddler sits low in a cockpit, legs extended forward. Originally an Inuit hunting vessel made of sealskin stretched over a wooden frame, modern kayaks are typically plastic or fiberglass and used for recreation: {We rented kayaks and explored the coastline}. To kayak is to travel by kayak.

Kayaking is the activity or sport of paddling a kayak—a narrow, low boat propelled by a double-bladed paddle. It ranges from leisurely lake paddling to whitewater rapids and ocean expeditions: {We went kayaking on the river}. Sea kayaking and whitewater kayaking are distinct disciplines with specialized equipment.

Kayaks is the plural of kayak, a small narrow boat propelled by a double-bladed paddle. Originally an Inuit vessel made of sealskin stretched over a frame, modern kayaks are typically plastic or fiberglass and used for recreation: {We rented kayaks and paddled around the lake}. As a verb, kayaks means travels by kayak: {She kayaks every weekend}.

A kazoo is a small tube-shaped musical instrument that produces a buzzing sound when you hum into it. A membrane inside vibrates against the player's voice, creating a nasal, reedy tone that sounds vaguely like a brass instrument. Kazoos require no musical training and are popular at parties, parades, and anywhere people want to make joyful noise without much skill. {The kids formed a kazoo band and marched around the backyard.}

Kazoos are small, simple musical instruments that produce a buzzing sound when you hum into them. A membrane inside vibrates against the voice, creating the characteristic nasal tone. Kazoos require no musical training—anyone who can hum can play one, making them popular with children and in novelty performances: {The birthday guests played "Happy Birthday" on kazoos}.

Kebab is meat—and often vegetables—cooked on a skewer over an open flame. The word comes from Turkish and Arabic, covering various grilled meat dishes across Middle Eastern, Mediterranean, and South Asian cuisines. In British English, kebab often means specifically the döner kebab: spiced meat sliced from a rotating vertical spit, typically served in pita bread as late-night takeaway: {We grabbed kebabs after the pub}.

Kebabs are pieces of meat, fish, or vegetables cooked on a skewer, typically grilled or roasted. The word comes from Middle Eastern cuisine, where variations abound: chunks threaded on sticks, ground meat molded around skewers, or meat carved from a rotating spit. {We ordered chicken kebabs from the Turkish place.} In British slang, a late-night kebab is the classic post-drinking food.

A keel is the central structural beam running along the bottom of a boat or ship, from bow to stern—the spine that everything else attaches to. To keel over is to capsize or, for a person, to collapse suddenly: {He keeled over from heat exhaustion}. On an even keel means steady and balanced, whether describing a vessel or someone's emotional state.

Keelhauling was a brutal naval punishment in which a sailor was tied to a rope, thrown overboard, and dragged under the ship's keel from one side to the other. The barnacles encrusting the hull would shred flesh, and many didn't survive. Now used figuratively for any severe reprimand or punishment: {The boss gave him a real keelhauling for losing the account}.

Keen is most common as an adjective, and commoner in British English than in American English to characterize a feeling of eagerness, excitement, and enthusiasm: I have a keen interest in scrapbooking. A keen gardener is an enthusiastic and probably very skilled one. A keen desire is a strong desire. A keen edge on a knife is very sharp. Keen is also a dated one-word reaction similar in meaning to groovy or cool. The verb keen, a different word, conveys wailing in lamentation: She keened in response to the news that her daughter had died.

Keep is one of the most frequent verbs in English, with meanings centered around the idea of preservation, storage, and conservation. If you keep a record of something, you maintain and update it as needed. If you keep animals or pets, they live on the same property as you do. Food that keeps for a week remains unspoiled for that long. When keep is followed by a participle, it means do continuously: How can I explain if you keep interrupting? Keep is also used in many fixed expressions, such as keep an eye out (watch for something), keep track of (maintain or monitor something’s condition), and keep pace with (stay current or move at the same speed).

A keeper is someone who keeps—a person who maintains, guards, or has charge of something: a {zookeeper}, a {beekeeper}, a {goalkeeper}, the {keeper of records}. In sports, a keeper is a goalkeeper. Informally, a keeper is something worth keeping—a fish large enough to keep rather than throw back, or a person worth holding onto: {He's a keeper}.

Keepers is the plural of keeper—those who keep, guard, or maintain something: {zookeepers}, {beekeepers}, {gatekeepers}. In casual speech, keepers are things worth keeping: {Most of the photos were duds, but a few were keepers}. The phrase {finders keepers} asserts that whoever finds something gets to keep it.

Keeping is the act of holding, maintaining, or preserving something. It often implies ongoing care or custody: {The documents are in my keeping}. In the phrase {in keeping with}, it means consistent or harmonious: {The décor was in keeping with the building's Victorian architecture}. Something out of keeping clashes or seems inappropriate.

A keepsake is a small object kept because it reminds you of a person, place, or occasion: {She saved the ticket stub as a keepsake from their first date}. The word emphasizes sentimental rather than monetary value—a lock of hair, a photograph, a dried flower. Keepsakes are typically given or preserved, not purchased for oneself.

Keepsakes are small objects kept because they evoke memories of a person, place, or occasion rather than for their practical value. A lock of hair, a ticket stub, a photograph—things that might seem worthless to others but carry personal significance: {She kept her grandmother's ring as a keepsake}. The word emphasizes sentiment over utility.

A keg is a small barrel, typically used for storing and transporting beer or other beverages. The standard beer keg holds about fifteen gallons and connects to a tap for dispensing: {We ordered a keg for the party}. A keg party centers on one or more such containers. Keg also appears in compounds for barrel-shaped things: {powder keg}, {keg stand}.

Kelp is large brown seaweed that grows in dense underwater forests in cold coastal waters. It can reach lengths of over a hundred feet, anchored to the seafloor by root-like structures called holdfasts. Kelp is harvested for food, fertilizer, and as a source of iodine and other compounds. {The divers swam through towering kelp forests.}

A kennel is a shelter for a dog, typically a small outdoor structure. In the plural, kennels refers to an establishment where dogs are bred, trained, or boarded: {We left the dogs at a kennel while we were on vacation}. The word extends to where foxes and other animals den. To kennel a dog is to put or keep it in a kennel.

Kennels is a facility where dogs are housed, either temporarily while owners are away or as a breeding or training operation: {We boarded the dog at the kennels while we were on vacation}. The plural form often refers to a single establishment. As a verb, to kennel is to place a dog in such a facility. A kennel can also be a doghouse.

Kept is the past tense and past participle of keep, carrying all its meanings into past contexts: {She kept the secret for years}; {He kept his promise}. A kept person, usually a kept woman or kept man, is one maintained financially by a lover, often with connotations of being a mistress or dependent in a transactional relationship. Something well-kept is maintained in good condition; a well-kept secret is one successfully hidden.

A kerfuffle is a commotion or fuss, typically over something minor: {There was a kerfuffle about the seating arrangements}. The word is informal and often carries a note of bemusement—suggesting the disturbance is somewhat overblown or unnecessary. British in origin but common in American English.

Kerfuffles is the plural of kerfuffle, a commotion or fuss over something relatively minor. The word suggests agitation that's somewhat overblown—disputes, controversies, or disturbances that generate more noise than they warrant: {The policy change caused several kerfuffles before everyone settled down}. British in origin but common in American English.

A kernel is the inner, softer part of a seed, nut, or grain—the part you eat after removing the shell or husk: {popcorn kernels}, {a kernel of wheat}. By extension, a kernel is the essential core of something: {a kernel of truth in every rumor}. In computing, the kernel is the central component of an operating system that manages communication between hardware and software.

Kernels are the inner, essential parts of seeds or nuts—the edible portion inside the shell. By extension, a kernel is the core or most important part of anything: {There's a kernel of truth in what she says}. In computing, the kernel is the central component of an operating system that manages hardware and software interactions. Popcorn kernels are the whole dried seeds that burst when heated.

Kerosene is a thin, flammable oil distilled from petroleum, used as fuel for lamps, heaters, and jet engines. Before electricity became widespread, kerosene lamps were the standard for indoor lighting. The fuel still powers portable heaters and camping stoves: {The cabin smelled of kerosene}. Also spelled kerosine; called paraffin in British English.

Kerplunk is an exclamation or adverb representing the sound of something falling or dropping into water or onto a surface with a heavy, resonant thud. The *ker-* prefix intensifies the basic *plunk*, suggesting a more dramatic or emphatic impact. {The phone slipped from her hand and landed kerplunk in the toilet.} Kerplunk is also a children's game involving marbles that drop through a tube when supporting sticks are removed.

Ketchup is a thick, sweet-tangy condiment made primarily from tomatoes, vinegar, sugar, and spices. It's the default accompaniment to French fries, burgers, and hot dogs in American cuisine: {Do you want ketchup with that?} The spelling catsup is an older variant now rarely seen. Ketchup originated as a fermented fish sauce in Southeast Asia before evolving into its modern tomato-based form.

Keto is short for ketogenic, describing a high-fat, very-low-carbohydrate diet that forces the body to burn fat for fuel instead of glucose. The diet aims to induce ketosis, a metabolic state where the liver converts fat into ketones for energy. {I've been doing keto for three months}. Keto appears as a modifier for compliant foods: {keto bread}, {keto snacks}.

A kettle is a container for boiling water, typically with a handle and spout. Electric kettles are common in Britain; stovetop kettles remain popular elsewhere. The word extends to large cooking pots and industrial vats. A {kettle of fish} is a problematic situation: {That's a different kettle of fish entirely}. In geology, a kettle is a depression left by melting glacial ice.

Kevlar is a synthetic fiber known for exceptional strength and heat resistance, used in bulletproof vests, helmets, and other protective gear. The material is five times stronger than steel by weight. Though technically a brand name, kevlar often appears lowercase in general usage: {The vest was lined with kevlar}. (Capitalized Kevlar is the trademark.)

The commonest and oldest use of key is for an object that opens a lock: car key, card key. The implicit idea of a thing that is essential for the use of something else has imbued key with an important adjectival role: the candidates avoided many of the key issues. If one thing is keyed to another, one either depends on, or provides, a reference to the other: she keyed her sermon to the congregation’s need for comfort. The small island called a key is separately derived.

A keyboard is a panel of keys for typing or playing music. Computer keyboards descended from typewriter keyboards; both arrange letters in the QWERTY layout. Musical keyboards—pianos, organs, synthesizers—have keys that produce notes when pressed. To keyboard is to type: {She keyboarded the data into the system}. As an adjective: {keyboard shortcuts}, {keyboard warrior}.

Keyboards is the plural of keyboard—a panel of keys for typing or playing music. Computer keyboards input text and commands. Musical keyboards include pianos, organs, and synthesizers; a band's keyboardist often plays {keyboards} to mean any of these instruments. The verb keyboards means to type: {She keyboards faster than anyone in the office}.

A keychain is a small ring or chain for holding keys together, often attached to a decorative fob or practical item like a flashlight or bottle opener. Keychains frequently serve as souvenirs or promotional items: {I brought back keychains from every city I visited}. Also spelled key chain.

A keyhole is the opening in a lock through which a key is inserted. The shape—a circle atop a vertical slot—has become iconic, appearing in decorative and symbolic contexts. Keyhole suggests privacy and secrets: to peek through a keyhole is to spy. As an adjective, keyhole describes things shaped like or sized for that opening: {keyhole surgery} uses tiny incisions.

Keyholes are the openings in locks through which keys are inserted. The shape—narrow slot widening to a circle—has become iconic, appearing in designs and logos. A keyhole offers a restricted view: to look {through the keyhole} is to spy or glimpse something private. Keyhole surgery uses tiny incisions. A {keyhole neckline} is a small opening in a garment.

A keynote is the central or defining element of something—the main idea around which everything else is organized. In music, it's the tonic note of a scale. A keynote speech or keynote address opens a conference and sets its theme; the person delivering it is the keynote speaker, often shortened to just {the keynote}: {She's the keynote at this year's summit}. As a verb, to keynote is to deliver such an address or to emphasize a central theme.

Keys are small metal devices cut to fit specific locks, allowing them to be opened. The plural covers literal keys and figurative ones: {I can't find my car keys}, {the keys to success}. Keys also refers to buttons pressed on keyboards and pianos: {Her fingers flew across the keys}. In music, keys are tonal systems: {The piece modulates through several keys}. To key something is to enter data or to scratch a car's paint maliciously. (Capitalized Keys refers to the Florida island chain.)

A keystone is the wedge-shaped stone at the top of an arch that locks all the other stones in place. Without it, the arch collapses. This architectural reality makes keystone a natural metaphor for anything essential that holds a system together: {Tourism is the keystone of the local economy}. A keystone {species} is one whose presence is critical to an ecosystem's survival. (Capitalized Keystone appears in various proper names.)

A keytar is a portable keyboard instrument worn with a strap like a guitar, allowing musicians to move freely on stage rather than stand behind a stationary keyboard. Popular in 1980s rock and pop, the keytar became associated with that era's aesthetic: {He strapped on a keytar for the synth solo}. The instrument retains nostalgic and sometimes ironic appeal.

A keyword is a word that unlocks something—access, meaning, or search results. In computing, keywords are reserved terms with special functions in programming languages, or the terms you type into search engines to find information: {Try different keywords if you're not getting good results}. More broadly, a keyword is a significant word that captures the essence of a topic: {Innovation is a keyword in the company's strategy}.

Khaki is a dull yellowish-brown color, like dusty earth. The word names both the color and fabric dyed that shade, originally for military uniforms in colonial India. Khakis are casual cotton trousers in this color: {He wore khakis and a polo shirt}. Khaki suggests practicality over style—workwear, uniforms, weekend clothes.

Khakis are casual pants made from a durable cotton twill fabric, typically in a tan or beige color. The term comes from the fabric's original dusty brown shade, which made it practical for military uniforms in hot climates. In American English, khakis has become nearly synonymous with chinos and refers to the style of pants regardless of exact color. {Business casual usually means khakis and a button-down.} The singular khaki describes the fabric or color itself.

Khan is a title of authority used historically across Central Asia, Mongolia, and parts of the Middle East. It designated rulers of various ranks—from local chieftains to supreme sovereigns like Genghis Khan. The title persists as a common surname in South Asian Muslim communities: {Mr. Khan will see you now}. In American usage, khan sometimes appears in fantasy or science fiction contexts evoking exotic tyranny.

Kibble is dry pet food formed into small, crunchy pellets or chunks: {The dog gets two cups of kibble twice a day}. The word almost always refers to commercially processed food for dogs or cats. As a verb, to kibble means to grind coarsely, which is how the noun acquired its meaning.

Kick characterizes forceful motion with the foot or leg. You can kick a ball (send it flying with your foot) or kick a door (strike it forcefully with your foot). A kick is an instance of kicking. If you kick a habit or drug, you rid yourself of the habituation or addiction. Movement in time can be characterized with kick, as in kick the meeting to next week. The plural kicks is informal for a feeling or source of extreme pleasure: How do you get your kicks?

Kickass is a vulgar adjective meaning excellent, powerful, or impressive: {That was a kickass concert}. As a verb phrase, to kick ass means to defeat decisively or perform impressively: {Our team is going to kick ass this season}.

A kickback is an illicit payment—money returned to someone who facilitated a deal or contract, typically in exchange for favorable treatment: {The contractor paid kickbacks to the official who awarded the bid}. The term implies corruption or bribery. Separately, kickback describes physical recoil, as when a power tool or firearm jerks backward upon use.

Kickbacks are illicit payments made in return for favorable treatment, typically in business or politics. A contractor might pay kickbacks to an official who steered a lucrative contract their way: {The senator resigned after revelations of kickbacks from defense contractors}. The term implies corruption—money flowing back to someone who helped make a deal happen.

Kickboxing is a combat sport combining boxing punches with kicks from martial arts traditions. Fighters strike with fists, feet, shins, and knees, unlike boxing which permits only punches. The sport developed in the mid-20th century, blending Western boxing with Asian fighting styles like karate and Muay Thai. {She takes kickboxing classes at the gym.}

Kicked is the past tense and past participle of kick, meaning to strike with the foot. Beyond the physical action, kicked extends to forceful removal or rejection: {She got kicked out of the bar} or {He was kicked off the team}. If something kicked in, it became active or took effect: {The painkillers finally kicked in}. To say you kicked yourself means you felt regret over a mistake. If you kicked the bucket, you died—though that one's informal and a bit callous.

A kicker is someone or something that kicks. In American football, the kicker is the specialist who kicks field goals and extra points. In journalism, a kicker is a surprising final element—the twist at the end of a story or the punchline that lands: {The kicker is that he never actually read the book}. A kicker can also be a hidden drawback or catch: {The salary sounds great, but here's the kicker—no benefits}.

Kicking is the act of striking with the foot, or the motion involved. It often appears as an adjective meaning active or lively: {The party was really kicking last night}. In the phrase {alive and kicking}, it emphasizes continued vitality. A kicking can also be a beating delivered with feet: {The gang gave him a kicking}.

Kickoff is the start of something—originally the kick that begins a football game, now extended to any launch or commencement. A {kickoff meeting} initiates a project. {What time is kickoff?} asks when the game starts. The verb phrase is two words: {We kick off the campaign next week}.

Kicks are shoes, especially stylish or collectible sneakers: {Nice kicks—are those the new Jordans?} The term reflects sneaker culture, where footwear is fashion statement and status symbol. Separately, kicks means thrills or enjoyment: {I get my kicks from live music}. To do something {for kicks} is to do it purely for fun.

Kickstart originally means to start a motorcycle by pushing down on a lever with your foot. The figurative meaning now dominates: to give something the initial push it needs to get going. {The grant kickstarted her research.} {We need something to kickstart the economy.} As a noun, it's that initiating boost: {The project needs a kickstart.}

The noun kid is used least often in its narrowest sense: to designate the young of goats or leather fashioned from them. Kid is more typically and frequently used an informal term for child. Kid can be used interchangeably with child in many contexts and appears in the compound forms, such grandkid. Before brother or sister, kid means younger. As a verb, you kid someone by teasing them or tricking them in a lighthearted way. The common question, Are you kidding me?, can be used incredulously or sincerely to question the truth of what has been said.

Kiddie is an affectionate or casual term for a small child: {The kiddies are asleep}. As an adjective, it describes things designed for or appealing to young children: {kiddie pool}, {kiddie rides}, {kiddie menu}. The diminutive form gives it a warmer, more playful tone than simply saying "kid" or "child."

Kidding is joking or teasing—saying something not meant to be taken seriously. {I'm just kidding} reassures someone that a remark was playful. {Are you kidding me?} expresses disbelief. {No kidding} can confirm something surprising is true, or sarcastically note the obvious. Kidding also means giving birth to young goats, though this use is rare outside farming contexts.

Kiddo is an informal, affectionate term for addressing a child or younger person, though it extends to anyone the speaker feels warmly toward or slightly senior to. {Hey kiddo, how was school?} It carries a casual, friendly tone rather than condescension, often used by parents, older relatives, or mentors. Adults sometimes use it with peers in a teasing or encouraging way: {You've got this, kiddo.}

To kidnap is to seize and hold someone against their will, typically for ransom, political leverage, or other criminal purposes. The victim is usually taken to a hidden location: {The rebels kidnapped three aid workers}. Kidnapping can also describe taking someone through deception rather than force. The word applies whether the victim is a child or adult, though child abduction by a parent in custody disputes occupies a legal gray area.

Kidnapped is the past tense of kidnap—to seize and hold someone against their will, typically for ransom or other criminal purpose. The spelling with double p (kidnapped) is standard in British English; American English accepts both kidnapped and kidnaped, though the double p predominates. {She was kidnapped from her home and held for three days.}

A kidnapper is someone who seizes and holds a person against their will, typically for ransom, political leverage, or criminal purposes. The term applies whether the victim is a child or adult: {The kidnappers demanded two million for her release}. Also spelled kidnaper.

Kidnapping is the crime of seizing and holding someone against their will, typically for ransom, political leverage, or other criminal purposes. The victim may be moved to another location or simply confined. {The kidnapping made national news}. A kidnapper takes people; a kidnapping is the act itself. Also spelled kidnaping.

Kidnappings is the plural of kidnapping—instances of seizing and holding people against their will, typically for ransom, political leverage, or other criminal purposes. {A wave of kidnappings terrorized the region}. {The kidnappings were linked to a single cartel}.

A kidney is one of two bean-shaped organs in the lower back that filter blood and produce urine. The word extends to this organ as food: {steak and kidney pie}. Kidney also appears in {kidney bean}, named for its shape. To describe something as being of the same kidney is to say it's of the same type or temperament—an old-fashioned usage.

Kidneys are the pair of organs that filter blood and produce urine, located in the back of the abdominal cavity. In cooking, kidneys from animals like lamb or beef are prepared as offal: {steak and kidney pie}. Figuratively, kidneys once referred to temperament or character, surviving mainly in phrases like {of that kidney}, meaning of that type or disposition.

Kids are children or young people. The word is informal but extremely common, often preferred over the more formal "children" in everyday speech: {I have three kids}, {the kids are at school}. Kid also means a young goat, which is the original sense. As a verb, to kid is to joke or tease: {I'm just kidding}, {Don't kid yourself}.

The verb kill is usually transitive and requires an agent, the killer, and a victim, who ends up dead. A kill is an instance of killing: I shot the buck in a clean kill. Figurative use extends to the sudden or definitive end of other things. When legislators kill a bill, it does not progress towards passage. If you kill the lights, you turn them off. If something really kills you, you were highly entertained. Someone who kills it does something extremely effectively: The singer aimed for the high note and killed it.

Killed is the past tense of kill—to cause death or end life. Beyond literal death, killed extends to stopping or defeating something: {The committee killed the proposal}. In casual speech, killed means exhausted {My feet are killing me} or impressed greatly {She killed it at the audition}. To {kill time} is to occupy yourself while waiting.

Killer is someone or something that kills. A serial killer murders multiple victims. A killer whale is the orca. The word extends to anything destructive or exhausting: {That exam was a killer}. In slang, killer means excellent or impressive: {That guitar solo was killer}. A killer app is software so essential it drives adoption of a platform.

Killers is the plural of killer—those who kill, whether people, animals, or abstract forces. A serial killer murders repeatedly. A killer {whale} is the orca. Killer also means something outstandingly impressive or difficult: {That exam was a killer}. {These shoes are killers} means they're either striking or painfully uncomfortable.

Killing is the act of causing death. A killing can be a murder, an accident, or a justified act—the word itself carries no judgment about legitimacy. To {make a killing} is to profit enormously, especially in business or gambling: {She made a killing in real estate}. As an adjective, killing means exhausting: {a killing pace}, {killing hours}.

A killjoy is someone who spoils others' fun or dampens enthusiasm. The word captures exactly what it describes—a person who kills joy: {Don't be such a killjoy, it's a party}. A killjoy might object to harmless pleasures, enforce rules at the wrong moment, or simply radiate disapproval that makes enjoyment feel guilty.

Killjoys are people who spoil others' enjoyment, typically by disapproving of fun or enforcing rules when no one asked. The word combines killing with joy—a killjoy extinguishes pleasure: {Don't be such a killjoy, it's just a party}. The term often targets those who impose their seriousness on others' good times.

Kills is the plural of kill, referring to instances of causing death—especially in hunting, combat, or games. A hunter might have {three kills this season}. In video games, players track their kills. To {move in for the kill} is to deliver the final blow. The expression {dressed to kill} means strikingly attractive. In the Hudson Valley, a kill is a creek or stream—a Dutch legacy appearing in place names like Catskill and Peekskill.

A killshot is a shot intended to kill, especially a final or decisive one that ends a hunt or fight. The term extends to any decisive blow that finishes off an opponent or settles a contest: {The debate was close until her killshot in the final round}. In gaming, it's the shot that eliminates a player or enemy.

A kiln is an oven or furnace for processing materials at high temperatures. Kilns fire pottery and ceramics, dry lumber, cure tobacco, and produce lime or charite fromite. Unlike ordinary ovens, kilns reach temperatures that transform materials chemically—turning soft clay into hard ceramic, orite intoiteite. {The potter loaded her pieces into the kiln for their first firing.}

Kilns are ovens or furnaces for firing, drying, or hardening materials at high temperatures. Pottery is fired in kilns to harden clay and set glazes. Lumber is dried in kilns to reduce moisture. Cement and lime are produced in industrial kilns. {The ceramics studio has three kilns running constantly.}

Kilo is short for kilogram, a unit of mass equal to about 2.2 pounds: {I've lost three kilos since January}. In drug contexts, kilo typically means a kilogram of narcotics: {They seized twenty kilos of cocaine}. Kilo also represents the letter K in the NATO phonetic alphabet.

A kilogram is the base unit of mass in the metric system, equal to 1,000 grams or approximately 2.2 pounds. Originally defined by a physical platinum-iridium cylinder kept in France, the kilogram is now defined by fundamental physical constants. Often shortened to kilo: {I've lost three kilos since January}.

A kilometer is a unit of length equal to 1,000 meters, or about 0.62 miles. It's the standard measure for road distances in most countries outside the United States: {The village is twelve kilometers from here}. Americans pronounce it with stress on the second syllable; British speakers stress the first.

A kilt is a knee-length pleated skirt traditionally worn by Scottish men, made of tartan wool and wrapped around the waist. The pattern typically indicates clan affiliation. Kilts appear at formal occasions, highland games, and military ceremonies. The garment has no underwear by tradition, prompting jokes about what's worn underneath: {Nothing—it's all in perfect working order}.

Kilts are knee-length skirts with pleated backs, traditionally worn by men in Scotland and Ireland. The Scottish kilt is made of tartan wool, with the pattern identifying clan affiliation. Outside the Highlands, kilts appear mainly at weddings, formal events, and cultural celebrations: {He wore the family tartan kilt to his sister's wedding}.

Kimchi is a Korean dish of fermented vegetables, typically napa cabbage seasoned with chili pepper, garlic, ginger, and fish sauce. It's served as a side dish or used as an ingredient in soups, stews, and fried rice. The fermentation gives it a tangy, pungent flavor that ranges from mild to fiery: {The kimchi was too spicy for me}.

A kimono is a traditional Japanese garment—a long, T-shaped robe with wide sleeves, wrapped left over right and secured with a sash called an obi. Kimonos are worn for formal occasions, ceremonies, and festivals in Japan. In Western usage, kimono often refers loosely to any robe-style garment with wide sleeves: {She threw on a silk kimono over her pajamas}.

Kin are your relatives—people connected to you by blood, marriage, or adoption. The word often appears in phrases: {next of kin} (your closest living relative), {kith and kin} (friends and family). Kin can be singular or plural: {She's no kin of mine}. As an adjective, kin means related: {We're kin on my mother's side}.

The very common noun kind is used to categorize and characterize things. When you ask about the kind of something (What kind of fruit is it?), you are asking someone to categorize the thing in question. Kind of is an informal adverb to indicate an indefinite but appreciable degree: She seemed kind of upset. The adjective kind denotes a quality of friendliness motivated by caring and concern: He has always been kind to stray animals.

Kindergarten is the year of schooling before first grade, typically for children around age five. The word comes from German meaning "children's garden," reflecting its origin as a nurturing environment for early learning through play. In American usage, kindergarten is part of the formal school system: {Is your daughter in kindergarten yet?} British English uses reception or reception year for the equivalent stage.

To kindle is to start a fire or cause something to catch flame: {She kindled the campfire with dry leaves}. The word extends naturally to emotions and ideas—kindling interest, curiosity, or passion means sparking them into life: {The lecture kindled her enthusiasm for astronomy}. Kindle suggests a gentle beginning that may grow into something larger. (Capitalized Kindle is Amazon's e-reader device.)

Kindling is small, dry material used to start a fire—twigs, wood shavings, crumpled paper. It catches flame easily and burns hot enough to ignite larger fuel: {She gathered kindling for the campfire}. Figuratively, kindling is anything that sparks or feeds a growing force: {His words were kindling for the unrest}.

Kindness is the quality of being friendly, generous, and considerate toward others. It implies warmth and a genuine concern for someone's wellbeing: {She showed great kindness to the new employee}. A kindness is a kind act: {He never forgot her many kindnesses}. The word suggests gentleness without expectation of reward.

Kindred refers to relatives or family members collectively: {All her kindred gathered for the funeral}. As an adjective, it means related by blood or sharing similar qualities and interests. A {kindred spirit} is someone whose temperament or outlook closely matches your own—you feel an immediate connection despite being strangers. The word carries a warm, slightly literary tone.

A king is a hereditary male monarch, counterpart of the female queen. A king in playing cards is the highest or second-highest ranking card, with a stylized king on it face. The king in chess is the piece on which winning and losing hinges. By extension, someone characterized as the king of something is viewed as being the most accomplished: Louis Armstrong was the king of jazz. King before a noun designating a product indicates the largest size (king prawns, king-size bed).

A kingdom is a territory ruled by a king or queen. The word extends to any realm or domain: {the kingdom of heaven}, {the animal kingdom}. In biology, kingdom is the highest taxonomic rank, grouping organisms by fundamental characteristics—plants, animals, fungi. Figuratively, someone's kingdom is their sphere of control or expertise: {the kitchen was her kingdom}.

Kingdoms is the plural of kingdom—a territory ruled by a king or queen, or a realm of any kind. The word often appears in historical or fantasy contexts: {the kingdoms of medieval Europe}, {warring kingdoms}. In biology, kingdoms are the highest taxonomic ranks: the animal kingdom, plant kingdom, fungal kingdom. Figuratively, any domain of influence or expertise: {the kingdom of fashion}.

A kingfisher is a brightly colored bird with a large head, long sharp bill, and short tail, typically found near water where it dives to catch fish. Most species display vivid blues and oranges. Despite the name, many kingfishers eat insects, lizards, and other small prey rather than fish. {A kingfisher perched on the branch, watching the stream.}

A kingmaker is someone who influences the selection of a leader without seeking the position themselves. The term originated with the Earl of Warwick, who controlled English succession during the Wars of the Roses. Now it applies broadly to power brokers in politics, business, or any realm where one person determines who rises to the top: {The party chairman became a kingmaker, deciding which candidates received funding}.

Kingmakers are people with enough influence to determine who gains power, especially in politics. The term evokes medieval nobles who could install rulers of their choosing. Today it describes party bosses, major donors, or power brokers who shape elections and appointments behind the scenes: {The kingmakers in the party had already decided on their candidate}.

A kingpin is the most important person in an organization, especially a criminal one: {a drug kingpin}, {a mafia kingpin}. The term implies someone who controls operations from the top. Originally, a kingpin was the front pin in bowling or the central bolt in a vehicle's steering mechanism—the one everything else depends on.

Kingpins is the plural of kingpin, the central pin in a bowling arrangement or the bolt around which a vehicle's wheels pivot. The dominant meaning is figurative: a kingpin is the most important person in an organization, especially a criminal one: {drug kingpins}, {cartel kingpins}. The term suggests someone at the top of an illicit hierarchy.

Kings is the plural of king—monarchs who rule kingdoms. Chess players capture kings, card games rank them high, and checkers crown pieces that reach the back row. In casual speech, kings can mean dominant figures in any domain: {the kings of Wall Street}, {the kings of comedy}. (Capitalized Kings refers to biblical books or sports teams.)

A kink is a tight curl or twist in something normally straight—a kink in a hose, a kink in your neck. Figuratively, a kink is a flaw or difficulty: {We need to work out the kinks in the plan}. The word also refers to unconventional sexual practices or preferences, often involving bondage, role-play, or power dynamics: {Everyone has their kinks}. Someone's kink is whatever arouses them outside the mainstream. As a verb, to kink is to form a twist: {The cable kinked when I coiled it too tight}.

Kinks are bends, twists, or tight curls in something normally straight or smooth: {a kink in the hose}, {kinks in her hair}. A kink in your neck is a painful muscle cramp. To {work out the kinks} is to solve problems in a plan or system. Kink also refers to unconventional sexual preferences or practices—bondage, role-play, fetishes: {They're open about their kinks}. Someone kinky enjoys such things.

Kinky describes tight curls or twists—kinky {hair} coils tightly rather than flowing in waves. The word extends to anything bent, twisted, or unconventional. Most commonly now, kinky refers to sexual practices outside the mainstream: bondage, role-play, fetishes. {They're pretty kinky in the bedroom.} The noun kink follows the same pattern—a twist in a hose, or an unusual sexual preference.

Kinship is the state of being related by blood, marriage, or adoption—the network of family relationships. More broadly, kinship describes any sense of connection or shared nature between people or things: {She felt an immediate kinship with the other volunteers}. The word suggests bonds deeper than mere acquaintance, implying common ground or mutual understanding.

A kiss is a touch of the lips to another person's mouth, face, or body, usually expressing affection or greeting. When two people kiss, it's typically mouth-to-mouth. Figuratively, kiss means to touch lightly: {The cue ball kissed the six ball}. Common expressions include kiss {off} (dismiss abruptly), kiss {and make up} (reconcile), and kiss it {good-bye} (accept that something is lost). (Capitalized Kiss is the rock band; KISS is the design principle.)

A kissass is someone who flatters or fawns over people in authority to gain favor—a sycophant. The term is vulgar and dismissive: {He's such a kissass around the boss}. As a verb, to kiss ass (or kiss someone's ass) is to behave obsequiously: {She's been kissing ass ever since the promotion opened up}. The adjective kissass describes such behavior: {his kissass attitude}.

Kissed is the past tense of kiss, meaning to touch with the lips as a sign of affection, greeting, or reverence: {She kissed him goodbye}, {He kissed the ring}. Figuratively, things that barely touch have kissed: {The ball kissed the rim and bounced away}. Sun-kissed describes skin or landscapes touched by warm light.

Kisser is slang for the mouth or face, especially as a target for hitting: {a punch right in the kisser}. The word sounds slightly dated or jocular. In its literal sense, a kisser is someone who kisses: {She's a good kisser}.

Kisses is the plural of kiss, which is a sweet or affectionate gesture made with the lips. If you kiss someone, you press your lips against theirs or against some part of their body in a gesture of affection. If you kiss something, you touch your lips to it. A kiss can also be a small quantity of something: She added a kiss of lemon to the sauce. A kiss is also a small piece of candy in the shape of a teardrop.

Kissing is the act of pressing lips against someone or something, typically as a sign of affection, greeting, or desire. A kissing cousin is a relative close enough to kiss in greeting—or loosely, anything closely related: {The two languages are kissing cousins}. Kissing up to someone means flattering them for advantage.

The handy word kit characterizes a set of two or more objects with a common use or purpose (first aid kit, toolkit). An object to be assembled from parts may be sold as a kit (model airplane kit). The idiom the whole kit and caboodle means everything. In British English to kit someone out means to supply them with the equipment needed for some purpose.

A kitchen is a room equipped for preparing and cooking food. Most homes have one; restaurants have commercial kitchens with industrial equipment. The word extends to the staff who work there: {The kitchen is backed up tonight}. A {kitchen sink} drama depicts gritty domestic realism. If something includes {everything but the kitchen sink}, it's excessively comprehensive.

A kitchenette is a small cooking area, typically a compact corner or alcove with minimal appliances—often just a sink, small refrigerator, and microwave or hotplate. Hotels, studio apartments, and efficiency units commonly feature kitchenettes instead of full kitchens: {The room came with a kitchenette, so we could make our own breakfast}.

A kite is a framework covered in paper or plastic that is suspended in windy air as a recreational activity. Before that meaning developed, kite was (and still is) the name for various small hawks with forked tails. Some sports that use a sail have kite in their names (kite surfing, kite boarding). If you kite a check, you write it for an amount that exceeds your balance in the hope that you will be able to supply the shortfall before the check is cashed.

Kites are light frames covered with paper or fabric, flown in the wind at the end of a long string. Children fly kites; adults fly them too, sometimes competitively. The word extends to a bird of prey known for soaring flight. To kite is to move swiftly and lightly, or in finance, to write bad checks exploiting the delay before they clear: {kiting checks between accounts}. In gaming, kiting means leading enemies while staying out of their attack range.

Kits is the plural of kit—a collection of items assembled for a specific purpose: {first-aid kits}, {tool kits}, {model airplane kits}. A kit can also be the gear itself: {drum kit}, {camera kit}. Young animals of certain species are kits: fox kits, rabbit kits. To {kit out} is to equip fully: {The expedition was kitted out with the latest gear}.

Kitsch is art, décor, or design considered tacky, garish, or in poor taste—often mass-produced, sentimental, or appealing to lowbrow sensibilities: {lawn flamingos and other kitsch}, {the kitsch of velvet Elvis paintings}. What counts as kitsch shifts with time and taste; yesterday's kitsch becomes today's ironic collectible. As an adjective, kitschy: {a kitschy souvenir shop}.

Kitschy describes something tastelessly gaudy or sentimental, often with a certain charm despite—or because of—its cheapness or vulgarity. Velvet Elvis paintings, plastic flamingos, and souvenir snow globes are kitschy. The word can be dismissive or affectionate: {The diner had a kitschy 1950s theme}. What's kitschy to one person may be ironic décor to another.

A kitten is a young cat, typically under one year old. The word extends to the young of some other animals: rabbit kittens, beaver kittens.
