Laurels are the leaves of the bay laurel tree, which in ancient Greece and Rome were woven into wreaths to crown victors and poets. The word now means honors or achievements: {She earned her laurels through years of dedicated research}. To {rest on one's laurels} is to coast on past accomplishments rather than pursuing new ones.

Lava is molten rock that flows from a volcano during an eruption. Once it cools and solidifies, it becomes volcanic rock but may still be called lava: {The hikers crossed an ancient lava field}. Lava extends to similar flowing substances: {a lava lamp}, {lava cake} with its oozing chocolate center.

Lavender is a fragrant plant with pale purple flowers, grown for its scent and used in sachets, soaps, and essential oils. The color lavender is a soft purple with a grayish or bluish tint: {lavender walls}, {a lavender dress}. Lavender has long associations with femininity and, since at least the early twentieth century, with male homosexuality—sometimes used dismissively: {the lavender set}.

Lavish means abundant to the point of excess. A lavish {banquet} features more food than anyone could eat. Lavish {praise} may be effusive. The word can suggest generosity or extravagance depending on context. As a verb, to lavish is to give freely and abundantly: {She lavished attention on her grandchildren}.

A law is a rule that has some official sanction or truth. Statutory law is enacted by legislatures. Common law is not necessarily enacted but is enforced by custom and precedent. A law of nature is something that experience or experiment has proven to be true. A mathematical law is a characteristic of numbers that can be proven or demonstrated as always being true. As an uncountable noun, law (often the law) refers to the entire set of laws that regulate a society or those who enforce them: Under the law he could serve ten years in prison; She got in trouble with the law last month.

Lawful means permitted or recognized by law: {a lawful search}, {lawful permanent resident}. It implies conformity with legal requirements rather than violation of them. Lawful often appears in formal or official contexts where legal status matters. In role-playing games and fantasy settings, lawful describes characters who follow codes and rules, contrasted with chaotic.

Lawless describes a state without law or regard for it. A lawless {frontier town} has no functioning legal authority. A lawless {mob} ignores the law entirely. The word can describe places, people, or actions: {lawless regions}, {lawless behavior}. It suggests chaos, disorder, or defiance of established rules.

Lawlessness is the state of being without law or order—either the absence of laws altogether or widespread disregard for them. It describes chaos where rules don't apply or aren't enforced: {The region descended into lawlessness after the government collapsed}. The word can characterize places, periods, or behavior: {frontier lawlessness}, {the lawlessness of the mob}.

A lawman is a law enforcement officer, especially in the American West or in contexts evoking that era: {The lawman rode into town at sunset}. The term appears most often in westerns and historical accounts, carrying a nostalgic or romanticized tone. In contemporary usage, it sounds old-fashioned or deliberately evocative compared to neutral terms like police officer.

A lawn is an area of grass kept mowed and maintained, typically surrounding a house or in a park. The ideal lawn is uniform, green, and weed-free—a suburban standard that requires considerable water and care. {The kids played on the lawn.} Lawn also names a fine, sheer fabric used in clothing, from the French city Laon where it was made.

A lawnmower is a machine with rotating blades that cuts grass to an even height. Most are either push mowers powered by the user or self-propelled models with gasoline or electric motors. Riding mowers handle larger areas. {I need to get the lawnmower serviced before summer}. Also spelled lawn mower.

Lawnmowers are machines that cut grass to a uniform height. The most common type is the push mower, either manual or powered by a gasoline engine or electric motor. Riding mowers handle larger areas. {I need to get the lawnmower serviced before spring}. The singular lawnmower is more common.

Lawns are areas of grass kept short by regular mowing, typically surrounding houses or covering parks and recreational spaces. The lawn emerged as a status symbol—land devoted to appearance rather than agriculture. Maintaining one requires watering, fertilizing, and cutting: {He spends every Saturday on lawn care}. Lawn also modifies related items: lawn {mower}, lawn {chair}, lawn {party}.

Laws are rules established by authority—typically governments—that members of a society must follow or face penalties. The term extends beyond legislation to include natural regularities: the laws of {physics}, the laws of {thermodynamics}. {Murphy's Law} and similar formulations name observed patterns presented as inevitable truths. {The law} collectively means the legal system or police: {He's in trouble with the law}. To {lay down the law} is to state rules emphatically.

A lawsuit is a legal action brought before a court, in which one party claims to have been harmed or wronged by another and seeks a remedy, typically monetary compensation or a court order. Filing a lawsuit initiates formal litigation, distinct from informal dispute resolution. {She threatened to file a lawsuit after the accident.} {The company settled the lawsuit out of court to avoid a lengthy trial.}

Lawsuits are formal legal actions brought before a court, where one party seeks a remedy from another. Someone files a lawsuit claiming they've been wronged—through breach of contract, negligence, discrimination, or other grievances. {The company faces multiple lawsuits over the defective product.} Lawsuits may seek monetary damages, injunctions, or other relief. The threat of a lawsuit often motivates settlement before trial.

A lawyer is someone licensed to practice law—advising clients on legal matters, drafting documents, and representing people in court. The term covers attorneys, solicitors, and barristers depending on jurisdiction. {You should talk to a lawyer before signing anything}. To lawyer is to parse language with excessive precision: {Stop lawyering the contract and just tell me what it means}.

Lawyers are people licensed to practice law—advising clients, drafting legal documents, and representing them in court. The term covers a range of specializations: criminal defense lawyers, corporate lawyers, divorce lawyers. In American usage, lawyer and attorney are interchangeable, though attorney often sounds more formal. {She hired a lawyer to handle the estate}. Lawyers are frequent targets of jokes and cultural suspicion, cast as mercenary manipulators of language and loopholes.

A laxative is a substance that promotes bowel movements, used to relieve constipation. The word works as both noun and adjective: {The doctor recommended a mild laxative}; {Prunes have a laxative effect}. Laxatives range from gentle fiber supplements to powerful purgatives.

Laxatives are substances that promote bowel movements, used to relieve constipation. They work through various mechanisms—some soften stool, others stimulate intestinal contractions. Available over the counter or by prescription: {The doctor recommended a mild laxative}. Overuse can cause dependency, so they're meant for occasional rather than regular use.

Lay is a verb meaning to put down or place: {Lay the book on the table}. {The hen lays eggs}. {Lay the foundation before building}. Lay is also the past tense of lie (to recline): {She lay on the bed for hours}. This distinction confuses many speakers. A lay is something's position or arrangement: {the lay of the land}. A lay is also a song or poem, especially a medieval narrative. In slang, a lay is a sexual partner or act of sex: {She was an easy lay}. To lay someone is to have sex with them: {He laid her after dinner}.

A layer is a single thickness of something spread over or under another surface: {a layer of dust}, {layers of paint}. Things arranged in layers stack horizontally—geological strata, cake tiers, clothing worn for warmth. To layer is to arrange in this fashion. In computing and design, layers are stacked planes that can be edited independently. A layer is also a hen that produces eggs.

Layered describes something arranged in layers—distinct horizontal levels or strata stacked upon each other. Layered rock formations reveal geological history. A layered cake has multiple tiers with filling between. Layered clothing allows adjustment for temperature. Figuratively, layered suggests depth and complexity: {a layered performance}, {a layered narrative with multiple meanings}.

Layering is arranging things in layers—stacked horizontal levels or coatings applied one over another. In fashion, layering means wearing multiple garments for warmth or style: {She's mastered the art of layering for unpredictable weather}. In horticulture, layering propagates plants by burying a stem until it roots. Hair layering cuts strands at different lengths to add texture and movement.

Layers are distinct levels or thicknesses stacked on top of one another. Clothing has layers for warmth; cakes have layers separated by frosting; rock formations reveal geological layers. The concept extends to abstraction: layers of {meaning}, layers of {bureaucracy}, layers of {security}. To layer is to arrange in such strata: {She layered the lasagna with cheese and sauce}. A layered approach tackles complexity in stages.

Laying is the present participle of lay—putting down or producing eggs: {She was laying tiles}. {The hens are laying well this spring}. {He's been laying plans for months}. In slang: {He's been laying everything that moves}.

A layman is someone without specialized knowledge or professional training in a particular field. Doctors explain conditions {in layman's terms}—language non-experts can understand. The word originally distinguished ordinary church members from clergy, and this religious sense persists in some contexts. The female form is laywoman, with laypeople or laypersons as gender-neutral plurals.

A layoff is the termination of employees, typically for economic reasons rather than individual performance: {The company announced layoffs affecting 200 workers}. Unlike firing, layoffs often come with severance packages and the possibility of rehiring when conditions improve. The verb phrase is two words: {They had to lay off half the staff}.

Layoffs are terminations of employment, typically when a company eliminates positions due to economic conditions, restructuring, or declining business rather than employee misconduct. Unlike firings, layoffs carry no implication of fault: {The tech sector announced massive layoffs after the market downturn}. A layoff may be temporary, with workers recalled when conditions improve, or permanent. The singular layoff can describe the event or the period of unemployment that follows.

Layout is the arrangement of elements in a space—text and images on a page, furniture in a room, components on a circuit board. The term emphasizes deliberate positioning: {The layout of the magazine was clean and modern}, {We changed the kitchen layout}. In journalism and design, layout often refers specifically to the visual arrangement before final production.

A layover is a scheduled stop during a journey, especially a wait between connecting flights: {We have a three-hour layover in Chicago}. The term implies a pause rather than a destination—time spent in transit before continuing. Long layovers sometimes allow travelers to leave the airport and explore the stopover city briefly.

A layover is a scheduled stop during a journey, especially a wait between connecting flights at an intermediate airport. The term emphasizes the waiting period rather than the stop itself—passengers endure layovers rather than enjoy them. {We had a four-hour layover in Chicago before the flight to Seattle.} Long layovers sometimes allow travelers to leave the airport and briefly explore the city.

A layup is a basketball shot made from close range, typically by driving to the basket and banking the ball off the backboard: {She scored on an easy layup}. By extension, a layup is anything easy or requiring minimal effort: {That test was a layup}. In manufacturing, layup refers to the process of arranging composite materials in a mold before curing.

Layups are shots in basketball made from close range, typically by driving to the basket and banking the ball off the backboard. The layup is considered the most basic and highest-percentage shot in the game. Figuratively, a layup is any easy opportunity or sure thing: {That question was a layup}, {The interview should be a layup for someone with her experience}.

Laziness is the quality of being unwilling to work or use energy. The word carries moral weight—laziness implies a character flaw rather than simple rest or recuperation. What looks like laziness may be exhaustion, depression, or rational avoidance of pointless effort: {His boss called it laziness, but he was working two jobs}. The lazy person avoids exertion even when effort would benefit them.

Lazing is passing time in idle relaxation, doing little or nothing: {We spent the afternoon lazing by the pool}. The word suggests pleasant, unhurried leisure rather than guilty procrastination. To {laze about} or {laze around} is to move through a space without purpose or urgency.

Lazy describes a reluctance to work or exert effort: {a lazy afternoon}, {too lazy to cook}. The word carries mild disapproval—laziness is a character flaw, though often a forgivable one. Things that move slowly or hang loosely can be lazy: {a lazy river}, {a lazy eye}. To be lazy about something is to neglect it through lack of effort rather than lack of time.

Lead is double the trouble. It’s two different words with two different pronunciations. Plus, both pronunciations are used for one set of its meanings. The lead that rhymes with bed is a heavy metal and a chemical element. The lead that rhymes with bead is a verb meaning to go before others, to be ahead, or to show the way. The past tense and past participle of lead is lead (rhymes with bed). Lead (rhymes with bead) as a noun means the position at the front, the interval between the leader and the next contender, or the main news story, among other things.

The leader is the one that others follow, typically those in business, government, and sports. Leader can be used to denote anyone or anything that commands or is in first place: The company is a leader in finance and accounting software. Leaders of the Church were not prepared for the reaction to their decision. Another kind of leader is the row of dots that leads the eyes from an entry in a table of contents to its page number.

A leaderboard is a display ranking participants by score or performance, typically in games, competitions, or sales contexts. Video games popularized the term—arcade machines showed high scores, and online games track global rankings. The concept extends to business: {The sales leaderboard updates weekly}. Leaderboards gamify competition, motivating participants to climb higher.

Leaderboards are ranked lists showing top performers in games, competitions, or other scored activities. Originally from arcade games displaying high scores, the term now applies to any public ranking system: {She climbed the leaderboard after her winning streak}, {The sales team checks the leaderboard every Monday}. The singular leaderboard refers to one such ranking.

Leadership is the position or role of leading others, or the qualities that make someone effective in that role: {She showed real leadership during the crisis}. It can refer to a group of leaders collectively: {The party leadership voted to proceed}. Good leadership implies vision, decisiveness, and the ability to inspire others toward common goals.

Leading describes what's out front or most important. A leading {candidate} tops the polls. A leading {role} is the main part. A leading {question} steers toward a particular answer. In printing, leading (pronounced "ledding") is the vertical space between lines of type—from the lead strips once used to create that gap.

Leads connects to the idea of being in front or guiding. A person leads a group by going first or directing: {She leads the team}. A lead is a position of advantage: {We have a three-point lead}. Leads are also clues or promising contacts: {The detective followed several leads}, {sales leads}. A lead is a leash for a dog, or a wire conducting electricity. In journalism, the lead (sometimes spelled lede) is the opening paragraph. The verb's past tense is led—not to be confused with the metal lead, a different word entirely.

The characteristics of a leaf on a plant or tree give rise to the many other meanings of the word. Most figurative extensions of leaf pick up on a leaf’s characteristics: flat, thin, and tend to come in multiples rather than singles. The leaves of a book are its pages. When you leaf through a book, you turn its pages. Gold leaf is gold in the form of extremely thin sheets. When a tree leafs out, it produces leaves, typically in the spring.

A leaflet is a small, printed sheet of paper distributed for information or advertising—often folded but unbound: {Someone handed me a leaflet about the rally}. In botany, a leaflet is one of the smaller blade-like divisions of a compound leaf. The verb means to distribute leaflets: {Volunteers leafleted the neighborhood}.

A league is an alliance or association of people, nations, or groups united for mutual benefit or a common purpose: {the League of Nations}, {the Arab League}. In sports, a league organizes teams that compete against each other: {the National Football League}, {a bowling league}. The phrase {in league with} suggests collaboration, often secretive or sinister: {They suspected he was in league with the enemy}. To be {out of someone's league} is to be beyond their level of ability or social standing. Separately, a league is an old unit of distance, roughly three miles—still used figuratively: {twenty thousand leagues under the sea}.

Leagues is the plural of league, a word with two distinct origins. One league is a unit of distance, roughly three miles, now archaic except in literary contexts: {Twenty thousand leagues under the sea}. The other league is an alliance or association—sports teams form leagues, nations join leagues, people {in league with} each other are collaborating, often secretly. To be {out of someone's league} is to be beyond their reach, whether in dating, competition, or ability: {She's way out of my league}.

A leak is an unwanted escape of fluid, gas, or light through a hole or crack: {The roof has a leak}. The hole itself is also a leak. To leak is to escape or allow escape this way: {The pipe is leaking}. Extended to information, a leak is unauthorized disclosure to the press or public: {Someone leaked the memo}. The person who discloses is also called a leak. To {take a leak} is slang for urinating.

Leaked describes information that was released without authorization, or something that escaped through an unintended opening. A leaked {document} was disclosed by an insider. A leaked {pipe} allowed water to seep out. News organizations report on leaked {emails}, leaked {memos}, leaked {footage}. The word implies both the act of disclosure and the resulting public exposure: {The video was leaked to the press}.

Leaks are unwanted escapes of liquid, gas, or information through gaps or breaches. A pipe leaks water; a tire leaks air; a source leaks classified documents to reporters. The noun names both the escape and the opening that allows it: {We found the leak in the roof}. To spring a leak is to develop one suddenly. A leak can also mean urination: {I need to take a leak}.

Leaky describes something that lets liquid, gas, or other contents escape through holes or gaps: {a leaky faucet}, {a leaky roof}. Extended uses cover anything that fails to contain what it should. A leaky organization lets confidential information slip out. A leaky gut allows substances through the intestinal lining that shouldn't pass. {The administration has been plagued by leaky sources.}

Lean describes something with little fat or excess. Lean meat has minimal fat. A lean person is thin, especially in a fit or sinewy way. A lean budget or operation has been stripped to essentials: {We're running a lean startup}. Lean times are periods of scarcity. To lean is to incline from vertical—against a wall, toward a person, or figuratively toward an opinion: {I'm leaning toward accepting the offer}. A lean-to is a simple shelter that leans against another structure.

Leaning is an inclination or tendency toward something—a preference that falls short of full commitment. Someone with {liberal leanings} tends toward liberal views without necessarily identifying as liberal. The word suggests direction without arrival: {She has leanings toward vegetarianism but still eats fish}. As a present participle, leaning describes the physical act of tilting or resting against something: {He was leaning against the wall}.

Leap, noun and verb, is like jump on steroids: it suggests quick and forceful movement, often upward, usually self-propelled, and often figurative. Quantum leap characterizes sudden and great progress or change. A daring leap is a bold and unexpected move. Things that are said to leap as a characteristic movement include flames, lightning, and of course, frogs. If you leap to a conclusion, you decide or infer something too hastily.

Leapfrog is a children's game where players vault over each other's stooped backs, hands pressing down as they spring past. The image extends to any bypassing maneuver—skipping intermediate steps to advance quickly: {The company leapfrogged its competitors by adopting new technology}. As a verb, to leapfrog is to vault over or surpass: {Startups can leapfrog established firms}.

Leaps is the plural of leap and its third-person singular verb form. A leap is a jump or bound, typically one covering significant distance or height: {The gazelle cleared the fence in two leaps}. To leap is to spring through the air or advance suddenly: {She leaps at every opportunity}. Figuratively, a leap is a dramatic change or progression: {a leap of faith}, {leaps and bounds}.

Learn is a verb whose meaning is complementary to teach: Teachers teach students in order that students will learn. Many things we learn directly from our experience, as is the case when someone learns a lesson. If you learn a poem or the dialogue of a play, you memorize it. If you learn a dance or a piece of music, you are able to perform it. If you say that someone will never learn, you believe that they won’t benefit from their experience.

Learned functions as both adjective and verb. As an adjective (usually two syllables: LEARN-ed), it describes someone with extensive knowledge, especially scholarly or academic: {a learned professor}, {learned treatises}. As the past tense of learn (one syllable), it simply indicates acquisition of knowledge: {She learned to swim last summer}. A learned behavior is acquired through experience rather than instinct.

Learning is the process of gaining knowledge or skill through study, experience, or instruction. What you've learned is also your learning: {a person of great learning}. The word often appears in compounds describing how acquisition happens: {distance learning}, {machine learning}, {learning curve}. As an adjective, it describes difficulty with academic skills: {learning disability}, {learning difficulties}.

A lease is a contract for the use of an asset or property, especially real estate and housing, in return for rent. The verb lease can characterize the relationship described in a lease from either party’s point of view. The owner leases property to someone. The rent payer leases the property from the owner. A new lease on something, especially a new lease on life, is an opportunity to regain a former favorable state.

A leash is a strap or cord for restraining an animal, attached to a collar and held by a person: {She walked the dog on a leash}. Figuratively, to keep someone {on a short leash} is to limit their freedom. To {strain at the leash} is to be eager for release from constraint. The verb means to attach a leash or, more broadly, to restrain.

Least is the superlative of little—the smallest amount, degree, or importance: {the least expensive option}, {That's the least of my worries}. As an adverb, it indicates minimum extent: {the least likely outcome}. {At least} sets a floor or offers consolation: {At least no one got hurt}. {Not in the least} means not at all. {Last but not least} introduces a final item while affirming its importance.

Leather is animal hide that has been treated to make it durable and flexible. It's used for shoes, belts, bags, jackets, and furniture upholstery. As an adjective, leather describes things made from or resembling the material: {leather boots}, {a leather-bound book}. In gay slang, leather refers to a subculture associated with BDSM and distinctive clothing: {the leather scene}, {a leather bar}.

Leave is actually two distinct words: the noun and verb are derived from different sources. Leave the verb is a synonym of depart in its core meaning but also has transitive uses that convey the idea of separation of the subject from something else: Did you leave your bike at school? The verb leave is also interchangeable with let in a few expressions. The noun leave has multiple meanings, including permission, parting, and permitted absence.

Leaves is the plural of leaf—the flat green structures on plants that photosynthesize. {The leaves are changing color.} Leaves also serves as the verb for departing: {She leaves tomorrow}. What remains after someone leaves are the things they {leaves behind}. {Two weeks of paid leave} becomes {two leaves of absence} in the plural, though this usage is uncommon.

Leaving is the act of departing or going away from a place, person, or situation: {I'm leaving in ten minutes}. It also refers to what remains after something is taken away—usually in the plural as leavings, meaning remnants or scraps: {The dog ate the leavings from dinner}. To leave someone or something is to abandon, bequeath, or allow to remain: {She's leaving her husband}, {He's leaving everything to charity}.

Lechatelierite is natural silica glass formed when lightning strikes sand or when meteorites impact quartz-rich soil. The intense heat fuses the silica into an amorphous glassy substance. When formed by lightning, the resulting tubes or crusts are called fulgurites: {The geologist found lechatelierite fragments at the impact crater}.

A lecture is a formal talk given to an audience, typically for instruction: {The professor's lecture on quantum mechanics lasted two hours}. The word carries connotations of one-way communication—someone speaks, others listen. This spawns the disapproving sense: to lecture someone is to scold or admonish them at length, often condescendingly: {Don't lecture me about responsibility}. A lecture hall is a room designed for such presentations.

Led is the past tense and past participle of lead, meaning to guide, direct, or be in front. Someone led a group, led a meeting, or led the way. A path led somewhere. An investigation led to conclusions. Events led up to an outcome: {One thing led to another}. (All-caps LED is an acronym for light-emitting diode.)

Lederhosen are traditional leather shorts with suspenders, associated with Bavaria and Alpine regions. The garment features a front flap and decorative embroidery, worn historically by workers and now primarily at folk festivals and Oktoberfest celebrations: {He bought lederhosen for the beer festival}. The word is German, literally "leather trousers."

A ledge is a narrow horizontal surface projecting from a vertical face. Mountain climbers rest on rock ledges. Window ledges hold potted plants. The word suggests something you could stand or place things on, but just barely: {He inched along the ledge twenty stories up}. Figuratively, someone on a ledge is in a precarious situation.

A ledger is a book or digital record where financial transactions are systematically recorded and organized. In traditional bookkeeping, the ledger contains accounts showing debits and credits, serving as the authoritative record of a business's finances. The term extends to any formal registry of important information: {The blockchain functions as a distributed public ledger}. In construction, a ledger is a horizontal board attached to a wall to support joists or scaffolding.

A leech is a blood-sucking worm found in fresh water, historically used in medicine to draw blood from patients. The word extends to anyone who clings to others and drains their resources: {He's a leech who lives off his parents}. To leech is to exploit someone parasitically, or in computing, to download without contributing: {She leeched the entire album without seeding}.

Leeches are bloodsucking aquatic worms, historically used in medicine to draw blood from patients. Modern medicine still uses them selectively to reduce swelling or restore circulation after surgery. Figuratively, a leech is someone who drains others of money, energy, or resources: {He's been leeching off his parents for years}. To leech is to cling parasitically or to extract something gradually.

Leeching is the practice of taking from others without contributing—draining resources, bandwidth, or effort while giving nothing back. In file-sharing networks, a leecher downloads without uploading: {He's just leeching off the torrent without seeding}. More broadly, it describes parasitic behavior: {She's been leeching off her parents for years}. The older sense refers to applying leeches medicinally to draw blood.

A leek is a vegetable in the onion family with a mild, sweet flavor and a distinctive form: a long white cylindrical bulb that transitions into flat, dark green leaves. Unlike onions, leeks don't form a round bulb but grow in overlapping layers that trap dirt, requiring thorough cleaning before cooking. They're essential to dishes like vichyssoise and cock-a-leekie soup, and serve as a national symbol of Wales.

Leeks are vegetables related to onions and garlic, with a milder, sweeter flavor. They have flat green leaves and a white cylindrical stalk, which is the part most commonly eaten. Leeks require thorough washing, as dirt collects between their layers. They appear in soups, stews, and the Welsh national emblem: {potato leek soup}, {braised leeks}.

A leer is a sly, knowing, or lustful sideways glance—the kind that makes the recipient uncomfortable: {He gave her a leer from across the bar}. To leer is to look this way, suggesting sexual interest or malicious amusement. The word carries strongly negative connotations; no one wants to be caught leering.

Leering describes looking at someone in a way that suggests sexual interest or malicious intent—a gaze that lingers too long and makes the recipient uncomfortable. A leer combines a sideways glance with a suggestive or unpleasant expression: {He was leering at her from across the bar}. The word almost always carries negative connotations of predatory or unwelcome attention.

Leeway is room to maneuver—the margin between where you are and where limits begin. A deadline with leeway allows some lateness. A budget with leeway can absorb overruns. {Give yourself some leeway on the estimate.} The word comes from sailing, where it originally meant a ship's sideways drift from its intended course.

Left is the side opposite to right—the direction of the hand most people don't write with. It also names what remains after something is taken: {There's nothing left}. In politics, the left refers to progressive or socialist positions, from the seating arrangement in the French Revolutionary assembly where radicals sat to the speaker's left. As a verb form, left is the past tense of leave: {She left early}.

Lefthanded describes someone who uses their left hand as their dominant hand, or something designed for such use: {a lefthanded pitcher}, {lefthanded scissors}. A lefthanded compliment is one that contains an insult within apparent praise—backhanded. The spelling varies: left-handed and left handed are equally common.

Lefties is the informal plural of lefty—people who are left-handed or, in political contexts, those with left-wing views. The meaning depends on context: {Half the pitchers on the roster are lefties} refers to handedness, while {The lefties in Congress opposed the bill} refers to political orientation. Both uses are casual and sometimes mildly dismissive.

A leftist is someone whose political views fall on the left side of the spectrum—favoring social equality, government intervention in the economy, and progressive reform. The term ranges from mild (center-left liberals) to strong (socialists, communists). As an adjective, it describes such politics: {leftist policies}, {a leftist newspaper}. Often used dismissively by opponents: {the leftist media}.

Leftists are people who hold left-wing political views—broadly, those favoring greater social and economic equality, government intervention in the economy, and progressive social policies. The term ranges from neutral description to dismissive epithet depending on who's using it: {Leftists staged a protest outside city hall}. Critics often use it to paint opponents as radical or extreme, while some on the political left embrace it.

Leftover describes what remains after the main use or event has passed. Leftover {food} is what wasn't eaten at a meal. Leftover {funds} are what remains in a budget. As a noun, usually in the plural: {We had leftovers for dinner}. The word can suggest something diminished or secondary—a leftover from an earlier era, a policy that's a leftover from the previous administration.

Leftovers are food remaining after a meal, saved for later eating: {We had leftover turkey for three days after Thanksgiving}. The term extends to anything remaining from a previous use or time: {The policy is a leftover from the Cold War}. Leftovers often carry a slight sense of being secondary or less desirable than the original.

Leftwing describes political positions favoring progressive reform, greater economic equality, and expanded government role in social welfare. The term comes from the seating arrangement in the French revolutionary assembly, where radicals sat to the president's left. Leftwing policies typically support labor unions, environmental regulation, and social safety nets: {leftwing activists}, {a leftwing newspaper}. Often hyphenated as left-wing, especially as an adjective before a noun.

Lefty is an informal term for a left-handed person, or for someone whose political views lean left—that is, toward liberal or progressive positions. In sports, a lefty pitcher or batter uses their left hand dominantly. The political sense carries mild dismissiveness when used by opponents: {The talk show host blamed lefties for the policy change}. Context usually makes clear whether handedness or politics is meant.

The leg that begins at your hip and ends at your foot inspires the many other uses of the word. Limbs or supports that typically touch the ground are called legs, so most mammals and tables have four, bugs and spiders have six or eight, and squid and octopi don’t have any (they have arms instead). In parts of clothing that cover the lower part of the body, legs are the parts that surround your legs. Figuratively speaking, a leg is one of multiple segments of a journey: We missed a flight on the first leg of our trip. If something abstract has legs, it shows the ability to become quickly known by many people: The story quickly got legs when the president tweeted it.

The narrower legal meaning of legacy is a bequest – money or property left to someone in a will. This meaning spawns the more general use of an often-intangible thing that is passed from one generation to the next: By signing the legislation into law, the president is trying to cement his legacy. Legacy is used to describe a college student whose admission to an elite university is due to the attendance of relatives in previous generations: He was a Princeton legacy. Placed before another noun, legacy refers to systems, methods, or companies that have failed to modernize: The computer was running legacy software.

Legal means permitted or recognized by law: {Is it legal to turn right on red here?} The term also describes anything relating to the law or lawyers: {legal advice}, {legal proceedings}, {legal fees}. A legal pad is a lined yellow notepad associated with lawyers' notes. Legal size paper is longer than standard letter size. To {go legal} is to make something official or legitimate.

Legalese is the specialized, often convoluted language of legal documents—dense with jargon, passive constructions, and archaic phrases like *heretofore* and *party of the first part*. The term is mildly pejorative, implying that lawyers make simple concepts unnecessarily complex: {The contract was buried in legalese}. Plain-language movements push against it.

Legalization is the process of making something legal that was previously prohibited or restricted. The term appears most often in debates about drugs, gambling, prostitution, and immigration: {the legalization of marijuana}, {legalization of same-sex marriage}. To legalize is the verb form.

To legalize something is to make it lawful—to remove legal prohibitions against it. The word appears most often in debates about drugs, gambling, prostitution, and other activities that some jurisdictions ban: {Several states have legalized marijuana}. Legalization implies the activity was previously forbidden, distinguishing it from activities that were never illegal.

Legalizing is the process of making something lawful that was previously prohibited. Governments legalize activities, substances, or practices by changing laws or regulations: {Several states are legalizing recreational marijuana}. The word often appears in debates about drugs, gambling, or same-sex marriage. To legalize removes criminal penalties and typically establishes a regulatory framework.

A legend is a story, typically an old one, which may not be true and is often assumed to be false: The legend told of a vampire living in the castle. An urban legend is a more modern tale of something shocking and probably untrue alleged to have happened. A smaller scale meaning of legend is the explanatory text on a map or illustration that helps you to interpret it. A person can be described as a legend when they have extraordinary accomplishments: Tina Turner is a living legend of music.

Legendary describes something or someone celebrated in legend—stories passed down through time that may blend fact with myth: {the legendary King Arthur}, {legendary creatures like dragons}. By extension, it means extraordinarily famous or remarkable: {her legendary generosity}, {a legendary performance}. In casual use, legendary is hyperbolic praise for anything impressive: {That party was legendary}.

Legends are traditional stories passed down through generations, often featuring heroic figures and supernatural elements: {the legend of King Arthur}, {Greek legends}. A legend is also a person of extraordinary fame: {a basketball legend}, {She's a legend in the industry}. In British slang, legend is high praise for someone impressive or admirable: {Thanks mate, you're a legend}. A legend also refers to explanatory text on a map or chart, or a caption beneath an image.

Leggings are close-fitting garments covering the legs, typically stretchy and worn by women as pants or under other clothing. Originally athletic wear, leggings became mainstream casual dress: {She wore leggings and an oversized sweater}. The term also applies to protective leg coverings worn over trousers, as by soldiers or hikers.

A legion was originally a large unit of the Roman army, numbering several thousand soldiers. The word now means any large group or multitude: {legions of fans}, {their problems are legion}. When something is legion, it exists in great numbers: {The difficulties facing the project are legion}. The word carries a sense of overwhelming quantity or force. (Capitalized Legion often refers to veterans' organizations like the American Legion or French Foreign Legion.)

A legionnaire is a member of a legion—historically a soldier in the Roman army, now typically a member of the French Foreign Legion or the American Legion. The word carries associations of professional soldiering and military discipline: {The legionnaires marched through the desert heat}. Legionnaires' disease, a severe form of pneumonia, was named after an outbreak at an American Legion convention in 1976.

Legionnaires are members of a legion—historically Roman soldiers, now typically members of military veteran organizations like the American Legion or French Foreign Legion. The word appears in {Legionnaires' disease}, a severe pneumonia first identified after an outbreak at an American Legion convention in 1976.

Legions is the plural of legion, a large military unit in ancient Rome comprising several thousand soldiers. The word now typically means vast numbers: {Legions of fans waited outside the stadium}. Someone's admirers, critics, or supporters come in legions when they're impressively numerous. {Her legions of followers hung on every word}.

A legislature is a governmental body with the power to make, change, and repeal laws. In the United States, Congress is the national legislature, while each state has its own. Legislatures typically deliberate and vote on proposed legislation: {The legislature passed the bill after months of debate}. Most democracies have legislatures, though their structure and power vary widely.

Legit is informal for legitimate—real, genuine, or lawful. Something legit meets expected standards or isn't fake: {Is this website legit?} {That's a legit complaint}. The word often expresses approval or authenticity: {Their tacos are legit}. Originally slang, legit has become mainstream in casual speech and writing.

Legitimacy is the quality of being legitimate—lawful, valid, or accepted as proper. A government's legitimacy rests on whether citizens recognize its authority. A claim gains legitimacy through evidence or endorsement. {The scandal undermined the legitimacy of the election.} In older usage, legitimacy specifically meant being born to married parents, as opposed to illegitimacy.

Legitimate means lawful, sanctioned, or conforming to rules and standards. A legitimate {claim} has legal validity. A legitimate {business} operates within the law. The word extends to anything genuine or reasonable: a legitimate {concern}, a legitimate {question}. A legitimate {child} is born to married parents—the opposite of illegitimate. In casual speech, legitimate often shortens to legit: {That's totally legit}. To legitimize something is to make it acceptable or lawful.

Lego is informal shorthand for Lego bricks or the Lego brand of interlocking plastic building toys. Though the company insists on "Lego bricks" rather than "Legos" or "lego," casual usage ignores this: {The kids were playing with lego all afternoon}. The word sometimes appears as a modifier: {lego set}, {lego movie}. (Capitalized Lego is the trademark.)

Legroom is the space available for one's legs while seated. It's a practical concern in cars, airplanes, and theaters: {The budget airline offers minimal legroom}. Legroom can also describe freedom to maneuver or flexibility in negotiations: {The contract gives us some legroom on the deadline}.

Legs are the limbs used for standing and walking—in humans, the lower limbs from hip to foot. The word extends to supports that hold things up: table legs, chair legs, tripod legs. A leg of a journey is one segment of a longer trip. In sports, the {first leg} of a tournament is an early round. If something {has legs}, it has staying power or momentum: {That idea has legs}. To {stretch your legs} is to walk after sitting.

Legwork is the practical, often tedious groundwork required to accomplish something—gathering information, making contacts, running errands. The term evokes physically going from place to place: {Reporters do the legwork while editors stay at their desks}. It implies effort that's necessary but unglamorous: {The detective had done the legwork, interviewing dozens of witnesses}.

Leisure is free time—time not occupied by work or duties. It suggests unhurried ease: {a life of leisure}, {at your leisure}. The leisure {class} has enough wealth to avoid labor. Leisure {activities} are hobbies and recreation. The word appears in {leisurely}, meaning without haste: {a leisurely stroll through the park}.

Leisurely describes something done without hurry, at a relaxed pace. A leisurely {stroll} takes its time; a leisurely {breakfast} isn't rushed. The word works as both adjective and adverb: {We walked leisurely through the park}. Leisurely implies having time to spare and choosing not to rush—unhurried by choice rather than slowness by nature.

A lemming is a small Arctic rodent related to voles. Lemmings are famous for a myth that they commit mass suicide by jumping off cliffs during migration—actually a misconception popularized by a 1958 Disney documentary that staged the footage. The myth persists as metaphor: a lemming is someone who follows the crowd blindly, especially toward disaster: {Don't be a lemming—think for yourself}.

Lemmings are small Arctic rodents known for dramatic population cycles. The plural appears far more often than the singular because lemmings are famous for supposed mass migrations ending in suicidal cliff dives—a myth popularized by a 1958 Disney documentary that staged the footage. The word now typically describes people who follow others blindly toward destruction: {Don't be lemmings—think for yourselves}.

A lemon is a yellow citrus fruit with sour juice, used in cooking, drinks, and cleaning products. The color lemon is a bright, pale yellow. Figuratively, a lemon is something defective—especially a car that turns out to have problems: {I bought a lemon}. {Lemon laws} protect consumers who purchase faulty vehicles.

Lemonade is a sweet drink made from lemon juice, water, and sugar. In the United States, lemonade is typically still; in Britain, it usually refers to a carbonated lemon-flavored soft drink. {Fresh-squeezed lemonade} suggests homemade quality. A lemonade stand is a classic symbol of childhood entrepreneurship. To {make lemonade out of lemons} is to turn a bad situation into something good.

Lemongrass is a tropical grass with a strong citrus flavor and fragrance, widely used in Southeast Asian cooking. The pale lower stalks flavor soups, curries, and teas: {The recipe calls for two stalks of lemongrass}. Lemongrass oil appears in perfumes, candles, and insect repellents.

Lemons are yellow citrus fruits known for their sour taste and high acidity. The juice flavors food and drink; the zest adds fragrance. When life gives you lemons, you're supposed to make lemonade—turn misfortune into opportunity. A lemon is also something defective, especially a car that breaks down repeatedly: {I bought a lemon}.

Lemurs are primates native to Madagascar, characterized by large reflective eyes, long tails, and fox-like faces. They range from the tiny mouse lemur to the cat-sized ring-tailed lemur, and most are arboreal and nocturnal. The name comes from Latin for "spirits of the dead," referring to their ghostly nighttime calls and glowing eyes. {Ring-tailed lemurs are the most recognizable species.}

Lemurs are primates native to Madagascar, distinguished by their large eyes, long tails, and fox-like faces. They range from the tiny mouse lemur to the cat-sized ring-tailed lemur. Unlike monkeys and apes, lemurs have wet noses and rely heavily on scent. The name comes from Latin for "ghost," reflecting their nocturnal habits and eerie calls.

Lend means to give something to someone temporarily, with the expectation of its return. You lend money, books, or tools to friends; banks lend money to borrowers who pay interest. The past tense is lent. Lend extends to non-physical things: lending your name to a cause means associating yourself with it, and something that {lends itself to} a purpose is well-suited for it. {Can you lend me a hand?} asks for temporary help.

Length is the measurement of something from end to end—its extent in space or time. A rope has length; so does a movie. Length often implies the longer dimension: the length of a rectangle versus its width. At length means eventually or in detail: {She spoke at length about her travels}. To go to great lengths is to make extraordinary effort. In swimming and horse racing, a length is a standard unit based on body size: {He won by two lengths}.

A lens is a curved piece of transparent material—typically glass or plastic—that bends light to focus or disperse it. Lenses are essential to eyeglasses, cameras, microscopes, and telescopes. The eye's own lens focuses images on the retina. Figuratively, a lens is any framework through which something is viewed or interpreted: {examining history through a feminist lens}, {the lens of personal experience}. Contact lenses sit directly on the eye.

Lenses is the plural of lens—a curved piece of glass or other transparent material that bends light to focus or disperse it. Eyeglasses have lenses, as do cameras, telescopes, and microscopes. The lens in your eye focuses images on the retina. Figuratively, a lens is a perspective or framework: {She views history through a feminist lens}. Contact lenses sit directly on the eye.

Lent is the past tense and past participle of lend. To lend is to give something temporarily with the expectation of return, or to provide money at interest: {I lent him my car for the weekend}, {The bank lent us the money for the house}. Lend also means to contribute a quality: {Her presence lent credibility to the project}. (Capitalized Lent is the Christian season before Easter.)

A lentil is a small, lens-shaped legume grown for food. Lentils come in varieties—brown, green, red, black—and are a protein staple in cuisines worldwide, especially South Asian: {dal is made from red lentils}. They cook faster than most dried beans and don't require soaking.

Lentils is the plural of lentil, a small lens-shaped legume. Lentils come in several varieties—brown, green, red, black—and are a protein staple in cuisines from India to the Mediterranean: {She made a pot of lentils with cumin and garlic}. They cook faster than most dried beans and don't require soaking.

A leopard is a large wild cat native to Africa and Asia, distinguished by its tawny coat marked with dark rosette-shaped spots. Leopards are solitary, agile hunters known for dragging prey into trees. The phrase {a leopard can't change its spots} means fundamental nature doesn't change. {Snow leopard} is a related but distinct species found in Central Asian mountains.

Leopards is the plural of leopard, a large wild cat native to Africa and Asia, known for its spotted coat and solitary, stealthy nature. Leopards are powerful climbers that often drag prey into trees. The word appears in the idiom {a leopard can't change its spots}, meaning people don't fundamentally change their nature.

A leotard is a stretchy, form-fitting one-piece garment covering the torso, typically sleeveless with leg openings at the hip. Dancers, gymnasts, and acrobats wear leotards for freedom of movement. The garment takes its name from Jules Léotard, a 19th-century French trapeze artist. {She pulled on her leotard before ballet class.}

A leper is a person afflicted with leprosy, a bacterial disease that damages skin and nerves. Because lepers were historically isolated from society, the word extends to anyone treated as an outcast: {After the scandal, he became a leper in Washington circles}. The figurative use is now more common than the literal, as medical terminology has shifted to "person with leprosy."

Lepers is the plural of leper, a person afflicted with leprosy—a disfiguring bacterial disease that historically caused sufferers to be shunned and isolated. The word now primarily appears in figurative use: a social leper is someone treated as an outcast, avoided by others: {After the scandal, he became a leper in Washington circles}. The term is considered offensive when applied to people with the actual disease; "person with leprosy" is preferred.

A leprechaun is a small, mischievous fairy in Irish folklore, typically depicted as an old man in green clothes who guards a pot of gold. According to legend, catching one forces him to reveal his treasure's location, though he'll try to trick his way free. The figure has become a symbol of Ireland and St. Patrick's Day, often reduced to a cartoonish mascot: {leprechaun decorations}, {leprechaun costume}.

Leprechauns are small, bearded fairy creatures from Irish folklore, typically depicted as old men in green coats who guard pots of gold. In popular culture, they've become mascots of Irishness, appearing on St. Patrick's Day decorations and as the logo for Notre Dame athletics. The singular is leprechaun: {She dressed her kid as a leprechaun for Halloween}.

Leprosy is a chronic bacterial infection that attacks the skin, nerves, and mucous membranes, causing disfiguring lesions and, if untreated, progressive disability. The disease has been stigmatized for millennia—biblical references to lepers as unclean persist in the figurative sense of treating someone as a social outcast: {He was shunned like a leper}. The clinical term is now Hansen's disease.

Leptosporangiate describes ferns whose spore-producing structures (sporangia) develop from a single cell and have thin walls, typically only one cell thick. This distinguishes most familiar ferns from the more primitive eusporangiate ferns, whose sporangia develop from multiple cells and have thicker walls. {Leptosporangiate ferns include the vast majority of living fern species.}

A lesbian is a woman sexually attracted to other women. The term comes from the Greek island Lesbos, home of the ancient poet Sappho, whose verses celebrated love between women. Lesbian functions as both noun and adjective: {a lesbian couple}, {She came out as a lesbian in college}. The word is neutral and standard, preferred by most women it describes.

Lesbians are women who are sexually and romantically attracted to other women. The term derives from Lesbos, the Greek island home of the ancient poet Sappho, whose verses celebrated love between women. {The bar was popular with lesbians and bisexual women.} While some women prefer other terms like "gay women," lesbian remains the primary word for female homosexuality. (Capitalized Lesbians refers to people from the island of Lesbos.)
Less is mainly an adverb (the solution was less than ideal), can be used as a preposition meaning minus or without. My profit was twenty dollars, less the sales tax.

Lesser is the comparative form of little, used when comparing two things to indicate the one that is smaller, less important, or lower in degree. Unlike smaller, which focuses on physical size, lesser typically applies to abstract qualities: a lesser {evil}, a lesser {offense}, the lesser {of two options}. It often appears in fixed phrases like {to a lesser extent} or {lesser-known artists}. Lesser can also function as an adjective on its own to mean inferior or subordinate: {a lesser god}, {lesser mortals}.

A lesson is a period of instruction: {piano lessons}, {driving lessons}, {a history lesson}. By extension, it's anything that teaches through experience: {Let that be a lesson to you}. To {learn your lesson} is to be changed by a painful experience. To {teach someone a lesson} is to punish them in a way meant to correct behavior.

Lessons are sessions of instruction, typically scheduled and repeating: {piano lessons}, {driving lessons}. A lesson is also something learned from experience, especially a difficult one: {That failure taught me a lesson}. To {teach someone a lesson} is to punish them in a way meant to change their behavior. In religious contexts, a lesson is a passage read aloud during a service.

Let is a common verb in English that gets its high frequency statistics from its place in fixed expressions and phrasal verbs such as let go, let alone, let be, and let down. It is also the main verb we use for indicating permission or making a suggestion: Don’t let him play with my things. Let‘s get ice cream after dinner.

A letdown is a disappointment—something that fails to meet expectations after anticipation: {The sequel was a real letdown}. The word captures the deflating feeling when reality underperforms hope. To let someone down is to disappoint them: {I trusted you, and you let me down}. In breastfeeding, letdown is the reflex that releases milk.

Letdowns are disappointments—things that fail to meet expectations. A movie sequel can be a letdown after the original. A friend who cancels plans is a letdown. The word implies anticipation followed by deflation: {After all the hype, the concert was a real letdown}. In breastfeeding, letdown refers to the milk ejection reflex, a different and neutral sense.

Lethal means capable of causing death: a lethal {dose}, a lethal {weapon}, a lethal {injection}. The word emphasizes deadliness rather than mere danger. Figuratively, lethal describes anything devastatingly effective: {a lethal combination of charm and ambition}, {Her crosscourt backhand is lethal}.

Lethargic describes a state of sluggishness, drowsiness, or lack of energy. Someone who feels lethargic has little motivation to move or act, as if weighed down by fatigue. {I felt lethargic all afternoon after that heavy lunch.} The word can describe both physical tiredness and mental dullness, and often suggests an abnormal or concerning level of inactivity rather than ordinary tiredness.

Lethargy is a state of sluggishness, drowsiness, or lack of energy. Someone in a lethargy feels too tired or apathetic to act: {The heat left us in a state of lethargy}. The word suggests more than ordinary tiredness—a heaviness that makes even small efforts feel burdensome. Lethargic is the adjective: {I felt lethargic all afternoon}.

The two main meanings of letter are closely connected with written language: there are the letters that compose an alphabet, and these can be combined into words and sentences to compose a letter—a written communication from one party to another. Letters fashioned from cloth are sometimes awarded for athletic achievement in U.S. schools, which accounts for usages like “award a letter” and the verb letter: She lettered in both basketball and soccer. When something is lettered, it is written as individual letters: “Happy Birthday, Joan” was lettered on the cake.

Letters are the symbols of an alphabet—the basic written units that combine to form words. In the plural, letters often means written correspondence: {She kept all his letters from the war}. A {man of letters} is a literary scholar or author. To {letter} in a sport is to earn a varsity award, typically displayed as a fabric letter on a jacket. {To the letter} means exactly as specified: {Follow the instructions to the letter}.

Lettuce is a leafy green vegetable eaten mainly in salads. The leaves grow in loose or tight heads depending on variety—iceberg forms a dense ball, romaine grows tall and narrow, butter lettuce has soft loose leaves. {A head of lettuce}, {lettuce and tomato on a sandwich}. In slang, lettuce means paper money, from the green color of U.S. bills.

Leukemia is a cancer of blood-forming tissues, particularly bone marrow, characterized by the uncontrolled production of abnormal white blood cells. These malignant cells crowd out healthy blood cells, leading to anemia, infection susceptibility, and bleeding problems. There are several types classified by how quickly they progress (acute or chronic) and which blood cells are affected. {She was diagnosed with leukemia at age twelve.} Treatment typically involves chemotherapy, radiation, or bone marrow transplantation.

A levee is an embankment built along a river to prevent flooding. Levees may be natural formations from sediment deposits or engineered structures of earth, concrete, or other materials: {The levees failed during the hurricane}. In American English, levee also means a landing place or pier along a river. Separately, a levee is a formal reception, originally one held by a monarch upon rising—from the French word for getting up.

Levees are embankments built along rivers or coastlines to prevent flooding. They may be natural ridges formed by sediment deposits or artificial structures of earth, concrete, or other materials: {The levees failed during the hurricane, flooding the lower wards}. In the American South, a levee can also be a landing place on a river. The verb means to provide with levees: {The Army Corps of Engineers leveed the Mississippi}.

The level of some measurable quality is its location on a scale (blood sugar level). The various meanings of level, verb and adjective, usually contain the notion of being either equal or horizontal. If something is level, it is roughly horizontal and probably stable: The table is level. If two things are level with each other, they are in the same horizontal plane, or equal in some respect. When you level something, you make it flat, even, or equal. When you level with someone, you tell them the unvarnished truth.

Levelheaded means calm and sensible, especially under pressure. A levelheaded person doesn't panic or act rashly when things go wrong: {We need someone levelheaded to handle the crisis}. The word suggests steady judgment and emotional balance—the opposite of impulsive or excitable.

Leveling is the process of making something flat, even, or equal. You level ground before building, level a playing field to ensure fairness, or level criticism at someone by directing it straight at them. In gaming, leveling means advancing a character through experience points: {I spent the weekend leveling my mage}. The word also describes destruction—to level a building is to flatten it completely.

Levels are positions on a vertical scale—literal or figurative. A building has levels, a video game has levels to complete, a conversation can operate on multiple levels. To level something is to make it flat or even: {level the ground}, {level the playing field}. To level with someone is to speak honestly: {Let me level with you}. As an adjective, level means flat or steady: {a level surface}, {a level gaze}.

A lever is a rigid bar that pivots on a fixed point to move or lift something with less effort—one of the simplest machines. The concept extends to any handle that operates a mechanism: {Pull the lever to release the brake}. Figuratively, a lever is anything that provides advantage or influence: {They used public opinion as a lever to force change}. To lever something is to move it with such force: {She levered the lid off the crate}.

Leverage is a noun that denotes the action of or the advantage gained by using a lever. By extension, it can mean power or effectiveness, as in political leverage. In the mid-20th century, speakers started using leverage as a verb meaning use for gain or exploit: The company is acting aggressively to leverage this new technology for better customer service. Many people consider this usage to be business jargon.

Levers is the plural of lever—a rigid bar that pivots on a fulcrum to transmit force, one of the simple machines. The term extends to any handle or switch that operates a mechanism: {She pulled the levers to start the machine}. Figuratively, levers are means of exerting influence or pressure: {They used every lever at their disposal to close the deal}.

A leviathan is something enormous and powerful, especially a sea creature or ship. The word evokes massive scale and often menace: {The oil tanker was a leviathan of the seas}. By extension, any vast, formidable entity qualifies—a corporation, a government bureaucracy, a whale: {The company had become an unwieldy leviathan}. (Capitalized Leviathan is the biblical sea monster or Hobbes's political treatise.)

To levitate is to rise or float in the air, defying gravity. The word typically implies something supernatural or mysterious—a meditating yogi levitates, a magician makes an assistant levitate. It can describe any hovering effect: {The maglev train levitates above the track}. Figuratively, extreme joy or excitement might make someone feel they're levitating.

Levitating is rising or hovering in the air without visible support, defying gravity. The word appears in accounts of magic tricks, spiritual phenomena, and science fiction: {The magician appeared to be levitating above the stage}. It extends to anything that seems to float mysteriously: {dust motes levitating in a shaft of light}.

Levitation is the act of rising or floating in the air without visible support, defying gravity. The word most often appears in contexts of magic, illusion, or supernatural phenomena—a magician levitates an assistant, or a meditating monk reportedly achieves levitation through spiritual practice. In physics, levitation refers to suspending objects using magnetic fields, acoustic waves, or other forces: {The superconductor achieved stable levitation above the magnet}. The verb form is levitate.

Lewd describes sexual behavior or content that is crude, lustful, or offensive. A lewd {gesture} or lewd {remark} is sexually suggestive in a way that violates social norms. The word often appears in legal contexts: {lewd and lascivious conduct}, {lewd acts with a minor}. Something merely sexy isn't lewd—the word implies vulgarity or impropriety.

A liability is something you're responsible for or obligated to pay—debts, damages, legal obligations. In business and law, liabilities are what an entity owes: {The company's liabilities exceeded its assets}. More casually, a liability is a person or thing that creates disadvantage or risk: {His temper is a liability}. The opposite of an asset in both senses.

Liable means legally responsible or obligated: {The company was held liable for damages}. More loosely, it means likely or apt to do something, usually something undesirable: {He's liable to forget if you don't remind him}. The word carries a sense of exposure to risk or consequence—you're liable for debts, liable to catch cold, liable to get in trouble.

Liaison is a connection or communication between groups or people, often in an official capacity: {She served as liaison between the departments}. A liaison officer coordinates such communication. The word also means a secret romantic or sexual relationship, especially an extramarital affair: {Their liaison lasted several months}. In French cooking, a liaison is a thickening agent like egg yolk or cream.

A liar is someone who tells lies—who says things they know to be untrue. The word carries moral weight; calling someone a liar is a serious accusation, not just noting a single falsehood but suggesting a pattern or character flaw: {He's a compulsive liar}. {Liar!} works as a direct challenge to someone's honesty.

Liars is the plural of liar—people who tell lies, who say things they know to be untrue. The word carries moral weight; calling someone a liar is a serious accusation: {Politicians are liars}. A single false statement makes someone wrong; a pattern of deliberate falsehood makes them a liar.

Libel is a false published statement that damages someone's reputation. In law, it's distinguished from slander, which is spoken defamation—libel is written or otherwise fixed in permanent form: {The newspaper faced a libel suit after printing the allegations}. Loosely, libel describes any unfair public attack on someone's character: {That review was pure libel}.

Liberal describes openness to new ideas, tolerance of different views, and willingness to change or reform. A liberal education exposes students to broad knowledge rather than narrow training. Liberal also means generous or abundant: {a liberal helping of mashed potatoes}. In politics, liberal typically means favoring individual rights, social equality, and government intervention in the economy—the opposite of conservative. {She holds liberal views on social issues.} (Capitalized Liberal refers to political parties bearing that name.)

Liberalism is a political philosophy emphasizing individual liberty, constitutional government, and protection of civil rights. In American usage, liberal typically means left-of-center—favoring government intervention in the economy and progressive social policies. In classical or European usage, liberalism stresses free markets and limited government. {Her liberalism showed in her support for universal healthcare.} The term's meaning shifts with context and country.

Liberals are people who hold liberal political views—generally favoring individual rights, social reform, and government action to address inequality. In American usage, liberal typically means left-of-center: {Liberals tend to support universal healthcare}. The term is often used pejoratively by conservatives: {Those bleeding-heart liberals}. In other countries, liberal may indicate free-market economic views rather than progressive social positions.

Liberate means to set free from confinement, oppression, or control. Prisoners are liberated from captivity, countries from occupation, people from restrictive social norms. {Allied forces liberated the concentration camps in 1945.} The word carries positive connotations of freedom and relief, though it's sometimes used ironically for minor acts of taking: {I liberated a few cookies from the break room.} In chemistry, to liberate a gas or substance is to release it through a reaction.

Liberated describes someone or something set free from confinement, oppression, or restriction. A liberated {prisoner} has been released; a liberated {country} has thrown off occupation. The word often describes freedom from social conventions: a liberated {woman} rejects traditional gender roles, and liberated {attitudes} toward sex suggest openness rather than repression. {She felt liberated after quitting her job}.

Liberating describes something that sets free or provides a sense of freedom. A liberating experience releases you from constraints—physical, emotional, or psychological: {Quitting that job was liberating}. The word often describes moments of relief or empowerment: {She found it liberating to finally speak her mind}. What feels liberating typically involves shedding burdens, expectations, or restrictions.

Liberation is the act of setting free or the state of being freed. Prisoners experience liberation when released; occupied territories achieve liberation when foreign forces withdraw. The word often carries political weight: {women's liberation}, {liberation theology}, {national liberation movements}. Liberation can also mean release from constraining attitudes or circumstances: {the liberation of finally speaking the truth}.

A liberator is someone who sets others free from captivity, oppression, or foreign rule. The term often carries heroic connotations: {Simón Bolívar is called the Liberator of South America}. It can apply to anyone who frees another from any form of constraint: {She saw her therapist as a liberator from old patterns of thinking}.

Liberators are people who free others from captivity, oppression, or foreign control. The term carries heroic connotations, suggesting those who bring freedom to the enslaved or conquered: {The statue honors the liberators who defeated the occupying army}. Historical figures like Simón Bolívar earned the title for leading independence movements. The word can also apply more loosely to anyone who releases others from constraints, whether physical or metaphorical: {She saw her therapist as a liberator from old patterns of thinking}.

A libertarian advocates for individual liberty and minimal government intervention in personal and economic affairs. The political philosophy emphasizes free markets, private property rights, and skepticism of state power. American libertarians often align with neither major party, opposing both conservative social restrictions and liberal economic regulations: {She considers herself libertarian on most issues}. The word also describes anyone who prioritizes personal freedom over collective control. (Capitalized Libertarian refers to the political party.)

Libertarianism is a political philosophy that emphasizes individual liberty and minimal government intervention. Libertarians typically favor free markets, civil liberties, and personal autonomy while opposing taxation, regulation, and state control over private life. The philosophy spans a spectrum from those who want drastically reduced government to anarcho-capitalists who reject the state entirely. {His libertarianism made him skeptical of both conservative social policies and liberal economic ones.}

Liberties is the plural of liberty, referring to freedoms or rights: {civil liberties}, {personal liberties}. The phrase {take liberties} means to act with inappropriate familiarity or to treat something too freely: {He took liberties with the original text}. {At liberty} means free or unoccupied: {I'm not at liberty to discuss that}.

Liberty is freedom from constraint, oppression, or captivity. Political liberty means citizens can act without undue government interference: {civil liberties}, {religious liberty}. To be {at liberty} is to be free, especially from confinement, or to be permitted: {I'm not at liberty to discuss that}. To {take liberties} is to act too freely or familiarly, sometimes with sexual overtones. A liberty can also be a specific right or privilege granted by authority. (Capitalized Liberty often refers to the Statue of Liberty or appears as a proper name.)

Libido is sexual desire or drive. Freud introduced the term to psychology, where it refers broadly to psychic energy or life force, but common usage focuses on the sexual: {The medication lowered his libido}. Someone with a high libido wants sex frequently; a low libido means diminished interest.

A librarian is a person who works in a library, managing collections and helping patrons find information. The role has evolved from organizing physical books to navigating digital databases, archives, and research tools. Librarians often specialize: {a reference librarian}, {a children's librarian}, {a law librarian}. The stereotype of the shushing librarian persists despite the profession's broader scope.

Librarians are professionals who manage libraries and help people find information. They organize collections, assist with research, recommend reading, and increasingly guide users through digital resources. The role has evolved from guardians of books to information specialists: {Ask a librarian—they can help you navigate the database}. The stereotype of the shushing librarian persists, though modern librarians often emphasize community engagement over quiet.

Libraries are institutions that collect and lend books, periodicals, and other materials for public or institutional use. The word also denotes the collections themselves or the rooms housing them: {a personal library}, {the library wing of the mansion}. In computing, a library is a collection of prewritten code that programmers can use in their applications. The singular library covers all these senses.

A library is a place where books and other materials are kept for reading, reference, or borrowing. Public libraries lend books freely; academic libraries serve schools and universities. The word extends to any organized collection: a music {library}, a software {library}, a {library of photographs}. In computing, a library is a collection of prewritten code that programs can use.

Lice is the plural of louse—small wingless insects that live as parasites on mammals and birds, feeding on blood or skin. Head lice infest human scalps, especially among schoolchildren: {The nurse sent home a note about lice in the classroom}. Body lice and pubic lice (crabs) are other varieties. Figuratively, a louse is a contemptible person.
Licence is the British spelling of license when it is a noun.

License is a verb and, in American English, a noun. In British English, the spelling licence is used for the noun. When an authority licenses something, it gives permission for it to operate, be sold, or be used. A license is typically used in a legal sense, and is almost always part of a compound term, as in marriage license, liquor license, and driver’s license. More generally, license means freedom: The witness has taken considerable license in her version of the sequence of events.

The verb lick characterizes the tongue passing over a surface for a variety of purposes: tasting, cleaning, stimulating. Things that move in a similar way may be said to lick, like flames. If you lick a problem or an opponent, however, you overcome them. A lick is an instance of licking, an object or places where animals gather to lick (salt lick), or a hit: His father gave the boy several licks for lying. Lick also refers to a small quantity: It doesn’t make a lick of difference.

Licking is the present participle of lick, used as a verb form, noun, or adjective. As a noun, a licking is a thorough defeat or a physical beating: {Our team took a real licking in the playoffs}. The adjective describes flames or waves that move with tonguelike motion: {licking flames consumed the building}. The gerund covers the act itself: {The dog's constant licking of his paws worried us}.

Licks is the plural of lick—instances of passing the tongue over something: {The dog gave her face several licks}. In music, licks are short melodic phrases or riffs: {He practiced his guitar licks for hours}. To {get your licks in} is to land blows or make your point before an opportunity passes.

Licorice is a plant whose root yields a distinctively sweet, slightly medicinal flavor used in candy and herbal remedies. The word usually refers to the candy itself—black, chewy, and polarizing: {I can't stand black licorice}. Red licorice is fruit-flavored candy in the same rope or twist shape, containing no actual licorice. Also spelled liquorice in British English.

A lid is a removable cover for a container—a pot lid, a jar lid, a trash can lid. The eyelid covers the eye, sometimes shortened to lid in informal speech. To {put a lid on} something is to suppress or contain it: {Let's put a lid on this before it gets out of hand}. In slang, lid can mean a hat.

Lids are covers that close containers—pots, jars, boxes, trash cans. The word extends to anything that functions similarly: eyelids cover eyes, and {lids} alone often means eyelids: {Her lids grew heavy}. In slang, lids are hats. To {put a lid on} something is to suppress or contain it: {Let's put a lid on the rumors}. To {flip your lid} is to lose your temper or sanity.

Two important, mainly intransitive verbs are spelled lie. To lie (past tense lay; usually said of a living thing, but also used of other physical things) is to assume a horizontal position: she was lying on a beach towel.
