The field lay on the other side of the river. To lie (past tense lied; mainly said of persons) is to say something that is untrue: I lied when I said I hadn’t been here before. A lie is the product of lying: His campaign promises have all proven to be lies. Lie is also used to characterize something whose main element is untruth or dishonesty, even if it is not expressed in words: She has been living a lie as a dispossessed princess. #

A lied is a German art song for voice and piano, typically setting poetry to music. The form flourished in the nineteenth century with composers like Schubert, Schumann, and Brahms: {Schubert's lieder include over six hundred songs}. Plural: lieder. The word is unrelated to the English verb "lied."

Lies are false statements made with intent to deceive. The word covers everything from small social fibs to serious fraud. To lie is to make such statements: {She lied about her age}. Lie also means to recline or be situated: {The book lies on the table}, {The valley lies between two mountains}. These are two different verbs—the deception verb has past tense lied; the reclining verb has past tense lay.

Lieutenant is a military rank below captain, typically the most junior commissioned officer grade. In police and fire departments, lieutenant ranks below captain but above sergeant. The word also means a deputy or chief assistant: {The crime boss sent his lieutenant to handle negotiations}. British pronunciation places the stress on the second syllable with a "lef-" sound; American pronunciation uses "loo-."

Verbs that have a v in them are often related to nouns that have an f, and live/life are one such pair. We use life to talk about the quality that separates organisms from inanimate things, about the qualities of being alive, or about the experience of living of some individual. Life can also mean a biography of an individual, or a sentence of punishment that lasts till death.

Lifeblood is the blood necessary for life, but the word almost always appears figuratively. The lifeblood of something is what sustains it or makes it vital: {Small businesses are the lifeblood of the local economy}. {Tourism is the lifeblood of the island}. The metaphor emphasizes essential circulation—without it, the thing dies.

A lifeboat is a small boat kept on a ship for emergency evacuation if the vessel sinks or catches fire. Shore-based lifeboats are deployed by rescue services to save people in distress at sea. Figuratively, a lifeboat is any last-resort means of escape or survival: {The emergency fund was our financial lifeboat}.

Lifeboats are small boats kept on larger vessels for emergency evacuation. When a ship sinks, passengers board lifeboats to await rescue. The word extends to any emergency provision or backup plan: {The severance package was a lifeboat for laid-off workers}. Lifeboat also describes rescue craft launched from shore to reach vessels in distress.

A lifeguard is a person trained to rescue swimmers in distress and prevent drowning, typically stationed at pools or beaches. Lifeguards watch the water, enforce safety rules, and respond to emergencies: {The lifeguard blew her whistle at the kids running on the pool deck}. The job is associated with summer work and, in popular culture, with tanned athleticism.

Lifeguards are people employed to watch over swimmers at pools or beaches, ready to rescue anyone in distress. They typically sit in elevated chairs for better visibility and are trained in water rescue and CPR. {The lifeguard blew her whistle at the kids running on the deck.}

A lifehack is a clever shortcut or unconventional solution that makes everyday tasks easier or more efficient. The term emerged from tech culture in the early 2000s and spread to cover any trick for optimizing daily life: {This lifehack will change how you fold fitted sheets}. Often used for minor productivity tips that may or may not deliver on their promise.

Lifeless means without life. A lifeless body is dead. A lifeless planet has no living organisms. Extended uses describe things lacking vitality or animation: a lifeless {performance}, a lifeless {economy}, {lifeless hair}. The word suggests not just absence but disappointment—something that should have life but doesn't.

Lifelike describes something that closely resembles a living thing in appearance or behavior: {a lifelike portrait}, {lifelike robots}. The word applies to art, mannequins, prosthetics, digital animations, and anything artificial that successfully mimics life. A lifelike quality can be admirable in a sculpture or unsettling in a wax figure.

A lifeline is a rope or line used for safety or rescue—thrown to someone drowning, or securing a person working at heights. By extension, a lifeline is anything essential for survival or continued existence: {The monthly check was her lifeline}. In palm reading, the lifeline is the crease supposedly indicating longevity. On game shows, a lifeline is a form of help available to contestants: {He used his phone-a-friend lifeline}.

Lifelines are things essential to survival or success. A rope thrown to a drowning person is a lifeline. So is an aid package to a struggling nation, a phone call to someone in crisis, or funding that keeps a business alive. The palm reader's lifeline is the crease crossing the palm, supposedly indicating longevity. In quiz shows, lifelines are helps a contestant can use when stuck: {I'll use my lifeline and phone a friend}.

Lifelong describes something lasting or continuing throughout a person's entire life: {a lifelong friendship}, {a lifelong commitment to public service}, {She was a lifelong resident of Philadelphia}. The word emphasizes duration and permanence rather than intensity.

A lifer is someone committed to something for life. In prison slang, a lifer serves a life sentence: {The lifers kept to themselves in the yard}. More broadly, it describes someone devoted to a career or institution for the long haul: {a military lifer}, {a lifer at the company}. The term can carry admiration for dedication or mild derision for lack of ambition.

Lifers is the plural of lifer, someone serving a life sentence in prison: {The lifers had their own section of the yard}. Extended to anyone committed to something for the long haul—career military, devoted employees, lifelong members of an organization: {She's a lifer at the company, been there thirty years}. The term suggests permanence, whether imposed or chosen.

A lifesaver is someone or something that rescues from danger—originally a person who saves drowning swimmers, now often figurative for anything that provides crucial help in a difficult moment: {That extra battery was a lifesaver}. Lifesaver is also a ring-shaped hard candy, named for its resemblance to a life preserver.

Lifesavers are people or things that rescue someone from danger or a difficult situation. A lifeguard is literally a lifesaver; a friend who lends you money when you're broke is figuratively one: {You brought coffee? You're a lifesaver!} The word often appears as hyperbole for anything helpful or convenient. Lifesavers is also a brand of ring-shaped hard candy.

Lifesaving refers to the rescue of people from drowning or other life-threatening situations, or to techniques and equipment used for this purpose: {lifesaving training}, {lifesaving equipment}. As an adjective, it describes anything that preserves life: {lifesaving surgery}, {a lifesaving donation}. The word often appears hyperbolically: {That coffee was lifesaving}.

Lifespan is the length of time something lives or exists. For organisms, it's the duration from birth to death: {The average human lifespan has increased dramatically over the past century}. The word extends to objects and abstractions: the lifespan of a battery, the lifespan of a trend. Also spelled life span.

Lifestyle is the way a person lives—their habits, choices, and daily patterns. It often implies a coherent set of preferences: {a healthy lifestyle}, {an active lifestyle}, {a lavish lifestyle}. The term sometimes carries judgment, suggesting choices are deliberate rather than circumstantial. In marketing, lifestyle frequently modifies products meant to signal identity: {lifestyle brand}, {lifestyle magazine}.

Lifestyles is the plural of lifestyle, referring to the ways different people or groups live—their habits, attitudes, tastes, and values. The word often appears in marketing contexts: {products designed for active lifestyles}. It can also carry moral or political undertones, as when {alternative lifestyles} serves as a euphemism for non-heterosexual orientations or unconventional living arrangements.

A lifetime is the duration of a person's existence from birth to death: {He devoted his lifetime to scientific research}. By extension, it applies to the useful duration of anything—a product's lifetime, a star's lifetime. The phrase {once in a lifetime} describes rare opportunities: {a once-in-a-lifetime chance}. As a modifier, lifetime indicates something lasting for life: a lifetime {membership}, a lifetime {warranty}, a lifetime {achievement award}. Informally, a very long wait feels like a lifetime: {It took a lifetime to get through security}.

Meanings of lift have to do with change or movement, often upwards. When you lift something, you raise it from a lower to a higher level. If something lifts your spirits, it makes you feel better. If authorities lift a ban, rule, or restriction, it no longer applies. If a fog lifts, it abates. A lift is an instance of lifting; a ride provided for someone, usually in a car; and in British English, an elevator.

Lifted is the past tense of lift, meaning raised or elevated. A lifted {ban} has been removed. In slang, lifted means high on drugs or alcohol: {We got lifted at the party}. Lifted also describes vehicles modified with suspension kits to increase ground clearance: {a lifted truck}. To feel lifted is to feel emotionally buoyed: {Her words lifted my spirits}.

Lifting is the act of raising something from a lower to a higher position. Weight lifting or simply lifting refers to strength training with barbells, dumbbells, or machines: {I've been lifting for three years}. To lift something can also mean to steal it or to plagiarize: {He lifted whole passages from Wikipedia}. A lifting of restrictions or sanctions is their removal. In meteorology, lifting describes air rising—a key mechanism in cloud formation.

Liftoff is the moment a rocket or spacecraft leaves the ground, transitioning from stationary to airborne: {We have liftoff}. The term extends to any launch or beginning of upward movement. Figuratively, liftoff marks when something gets underway after preparation: {The startup finally achieved liftoff after years of development}.

Lifts is the third-person singular of lift, meaning to raise something up: {She lifts the box onto the shelf}. A lift is an act of raising, something that elevates (a ski lift, an elevator in British English), or a ride given to someone: {Can I give you a lift?} Lifts also names the thickened insoles placed in shoes to add height.

Light is a form of energy that we detect with our eyes, and in whose absence we experience darkness. Light can also be used to name any particular form, source, or amount of light: Please turn off the lights when you leave. I don’t like to get up until it’s light outside. As a verb, light means ignite or illuminate, as in light the candles. As an adjective, light is the opposite of dark: We bought curtains because the room was too light. A separately derived word with the same spelling, the adjective light, is the opposite of heavy in most of its senses.

A lightbulb is a glass enclosure containing a filament or gas that produces light when electricity passes through it. The term extends to any similar device: LED bulbs, fluorescent tubes. A lightbulb appearing above someone's head in cartoons represents sudden inspiration—hence {lightbulb moment} for a flash of insight or realization.

Lightbulbs are glass enclosures containing a filament or other element that produces light when electrically powered. The plural appears in practical contexts—{I need to pick up some lightbulbs}—and in the figurative sense of sudden inspiration: {Lightbulbs went off in my head}. The cartoon image of a lightbulb appearing above someone's head represents a new idea.

Lighten means to make or become lighter. This splits into two senses: reducing weight or burden {lighten the load}, and increasing brightness {The sky lightened at dawn}. The figurative uses follow both paths—you can lighten someone's mood or lighten up by becoming less serious. {Lighten up, it was just a joke.}

A lighter is a small handheld device that produces a flame, typically used to light cigarettes, candles, or fires. Lighters may use butane gas or liquid fuel with a wick. As an adjective or adverb, lighter is the comparative form of light in all its senses: {a lighter shade of blue}, {traveling lighter this time}, {a lighter workload}. A lighter is also a flat-bottomed barge used to transfer cargo between ships and shore.

Lighters is the plural of lighter. A lighter is a small handheld device that produces a flame, typically for lighting cigarettes, candles, or campfires: {She flicked the lighter twice before it caught}. Lighters are also flat-bottomed barges used to transfer cargo between ships and shore: {The lighters ferried goods from the freighter to the dock}.

Lightheaded describes a sensation of faintness or dizziness, as if you might pass out: {I felt lightheaded after standing up too fast}. The feeling often comes from low blood sugar, dehydration, or sudden position changes. Figuratively, lightheaded can mean giddy or slightly euphoric: {The good news left her lightheaded with relief}.

Lighthearted describes a mood or manner that is cheerful, carefree, and unburdened by worry: {a lighthearted comedy}, {lighthearted banter}. Someone in a lighthearted mood doesn't take things too seriously. The word suggests buoyancy—a spirit not weighed down: {Despite the deadline, she remained lighthearted about the whole project}.

A lighthouse is a tower with a powerful light at its top, built on coasts or islands to guide ships and warn them of dangerous waters. The beam rotates or flashes in distinctive patterns that help sailors identify their location. Lighthouses have largely been replaced by electronic navigation but remain as landmarks and tourist attractions: {We climbed the old lighthouse for the view}.

Lighthouses are towers with powerful lights at the top, built along coastlines to guide ships and warn them of dangerous rocks or shallow water. The lighthouse beam sweeps across the water at night, visible for miles. Figuratively, anything that provides guidance or warning in uncertain situations: {She was a lighthouse for students navigating their first year}.

Lighting is the arrangement or effect of light in a space, photograph, or scene. Stage lighting shapes mood and directs attention; {the lighting in that restaurant is too dim to read the menu}. The term covers both the fixtures themselves and the quality of illumination they produce. Good lighting can transform a room; bad lighting makes everyone look exhausted.

Lightness has two distinct clusters of meaning. One concerns weight: the lightness of a feather, the lightness of a dancer's step. The other concerns brightness or paleness: the lightness of a room, the lightness of her complexion. Both extend to mood and manner—a lightness of spirit suggests either unburdened ease or cheerful brightness, the senses blurring together.

Lightning is the visible electrical discharge during a thunderstorm—a sudden flash of light caused by atmospheric electricity jumping between clouds or from cloud to ground. The word also works as an adjective meaning extremely fast or sudden: a lightning {strike}, lightning {reflexes}, {lightning-fast}. {Lightning never strikes twice} suggests unlikely events won't repeat. To {catch lightning in a bottle} is to capture something elusive or reproduce a rare success.

Lights are the lungs of an animal, especially a pig, sheep, or cow, used as food or pet food. The name comes from their light weight compared to other organs. Lights appear in traditional dishes like haggis and in older cookbooks: {Boil the lights until tender}. The word is now uncommon outside butchery and historical recipes.

A lightsaber is a fictional weapon from the Star Wars universe—a sword with a blade made of concentrated energy or plasma, typically wielded by Jedi and Sith. The blade extends from a metal hilt and can cut through almost anything. Lightsabers have become iconic in popular culture, referenced whenever futuristic or elegant weaponry is discussed: {They were swinging toy lightsabers in the backyard}.

A lightsabre is a fictional weapon from the Star Wars universe—a sword with a blade made of concentrated energy or plasma, typically wielded by Jedi and Sith. The blade extends from a metal hilt and can cut through nearly anything. Spelled lightsaber in American English. {He ignited his lightsabre and deflected the blaster fire.}

A lightshow is a display of moving colored lights, often synchronized to music. The term emerged from 1960s psychedelic culture, where projected lights accompanied rock concerts to enhance the sensory experience. Today lightshows range from concert productions with lasers and strobes to software visualizations: {The DJ's lightshow pulsed with the bass}. Also spelled as two words.

Lightspeed is the speed at which light travels in a vacuum—about 186,000 miles per second, the fastest speed possible according to physics. The term appears in science fiction for faster-than-light travel: {The ship jumped to lightspeed}. Figuratively, lightspeed describes anything extremely fast: {Technology is advancing at lightspeed}. Also written as two words.

Lightweight describes something that weighs relatively little: a lightweight {jacket}, lightweight {materials}. In boxing and other combat sports, lightweight is a weight class for smaller competitors. Figuratively, a lightweight is someone lacking substance, seriousness, or influence: {He's a political lightweight}. The word can dismiss intellectual depth: {lightweight entertainment}, {a lightweight analysis of the problem}.

A lightyear is the distance light travels in one year—about 5.88 trillion miles or 9.46 trillion kilometers. It's the standard unit for measuring astronomical distances: {The nearest star is about four lightyears away}. Informally, lightyears suggests an enormous gap: {Her skills are lightyears ahead of the competition}. Also spelled light-year and light year.

Likable describes someone or something that inspires fondness or approval. A likable person is easy to get along with, pleasant without necessarily being remarkable: {She's perfectly likable, just not very interesting}. The word suggests an accessible, unchallenging appeal—warmth without intensity. Also spelled likeable.

Like is actually two different words, which explains how it manages to occupy seven different parts of speech. The primary verb like (I like dogs) differs in meaning from the like relating to resemblance and comparison. In this meaning like can be a preposition (a smile like a sunny day), an adjective (group like things together), a noun (I’ve never seen the like of it), an adverb (It’s worth like ten bucks), and a conjunction (She looks like she’s seen a ghost).

Likeability is the quality of being easy to like—pleasant, approachable, agreeable. It's often discussed as a trait that can be cultivated: {Politicians obsess over their likeability ratings}. The word sometimes carries a whiff of superficiality, suggesting charm without depth. Also spelled likability.

Likeable describes someone easy to like—pleasant, friendly, agreeable. A likeable person puts others at ease and leaves a good impression: {She's talented, but more importantly, she's likeable}. The word often appears in contexts where charm matters: likeable {candidates}, likeable {protagonists}. Also spelled likable.

Likelihood is the chance or probability of something happening. It sits between possibility and certainty: {There's a strong likelihood of rain tomorrow}. The word often appears with modifiers indicating degree: {in all likelihood} means very probably, while {little likelihood} suggests something is improbable. Unlike probability, likelihood rarely takes numerical values—it deals in qualitative assessment rather than calculation.

Likely means probable or expected to happen: {Rain is likely this afternoon}, {She's likely to win}. As an adverb, it means probably: {They'll likely arrive late}. A likely {candidate} or likely {suspect} is a plausible one. {A likely story} is sarcastic—expressing disbelief. Likely also suggests suitability: {a likely spot for a picnic}.

Likeness is resemblance or similarity in appearance: {The portrait captured her likeness perfectly}. A likeness is also a representation of someone—a portrait, photograph, or statue: {His likeness hangs in the boardroom}. The word implies visual correspondence: {a family likeness}, {a striking likeness to her mother}.

Likes functions as both verb and noun. As a verb, it's the third-person singular of like: {She likes coffee}, {He likes to run}. As a noun, likes are preferences or things one enjoys: {We have similar likes and dislikes}. On social media, likes are approvals users give to posts—a tap indicating appreciation or agreement: {The photo got thousands of likes}. The phrase {the likes of} means people or things of a particular type: {I've never seen the likes of this before}.

Lilac is a shrub with clusters of fragrant purple or white flowers that bloom in spring. The word also names the pale purple color of the common variety: {a lilac dress}, {lilac walls}. The scent is distinctive enough that lilac appears in perfumes and candles. {The lilacs are in bloom.}

Lilacs are flowering shrubs with clusters of small, fragrant blossoms, typically purple but also white or pink. The flowers bloom in spring and carry a distinctive sweet scent that evokes nostalgia and renewal: {The lilacs are in bloom}. Lilac also names the pale purple color of the most common variety.

Lilies are flowering plants of the genus Lilium, known for their large, showy blooms and strong fragrance. They grow from bulbs and produce trumpet-shaped or recurved flowers in colors ranging from white to pink, yellow, orange, and red. Lilies carry heavy symbolic weight in art and religion, representing purity, renewal, or mourning depending on context. {Easter lilies decorated the church altar.} The term extends loosely to similar flowers like water lilies and calla lilies, which belong to different plant families.

A lily is a flowering plant with large, showy blooms, typically trumpet-shaped and often fragrant. Lilies are associated with purity and are common in religious imagery, weddings, and funerals: {Easter lilies}, {tiger lilies}, {lily of the valley}. To {gild the lily} is to add unnecessary ornamentation to something already beautiful. Lily-white means pure white, or figuratively, beyond reproach—sometimes used sarcastically. (Capitalized Lily is a given name.)

A lilypad is the broad, flat, floating leaf of a water lily. The round or heart-shaped leaves rest on the surface of ponds and still water, providing platforms for frogs and insects. In video games, lilypads are often stepping stones the player must hop across: {Jump from lilypad to lilypad to cross the swamp}.

A limb is an arm or leg—any of the major appendages extending from the body. The word extends to the main branches of a tree: {The storm brought down several limbs}. To go {out on a limb} is to take a risk by committing to an uncertain position, like venturing onto a branch that might break. {Limb from limb} describes violent dismemberment.

Limbo has two distinct origins. One is a region on the edge of hell in Catholic theology, where unbaptized souls dwell—neither damned nor saved. This gives rise to the figurative sense of an uncertain in-between state: {The project is in limbo until we get funding}. The other limbo is a West Indian dance where participants bend backward to pass under a progressively lowered bar: {How low can you go?}

Limbs are the major appendages that extend from the body—arms and legs in humans, or the analogous parts in other animals used for locomotion, grasping, or manipulation. The word extends naturally to the large branches of a tree that extend from the trunk. To go out on a limb is to take a risk or adopt a position without support from others, like venturing onto a tree branch that might not hold your weight. {She went out on a limb to defend her colleague.}

Lime names several unrelated things. The lime most people encounter is a small, green citrus fruit, more sour than a lemon, essential to countless cocktails and dishes: {a wedge of lime}, {key lime pie}. Lime is also calcium oxide, a white powder used in construction and agriculture to treat soil. A lime or linden is a deciduous tree with heart-shaped leaves. Lime green is a vivid yellowish-green color.

Limelight was an intense white light produced by heating lime, used in theaters before electric lighting to illuminate performers on stage. The term now means prominent public attention: {She's been in the limelight since her debut album}. To {steal the limelight} is to draw attention away from others.

A limerick is a humorous five-line poem with a distinctive bouncing rhythm and an AABBA rhyme scheme. The form is strongly associated with bawdy or nonsensical content: {There once was a man from Nantucket...} The name comes from the Irish city, though the connection is obscure.

Limericks are short humorous poems with a distinctive bouncing rhythm and an AABBA rhyme scheme—the first, second, and fifth lines rhyme with each other, and the third and fourth lines form a shorter rhyming couplet. The form traditionally opens by naming a person from a place: {There once was a man from Nantucket}. Many limericks are bawdy or obscene, though the form also serves innocent wordplay and nonsense verse.

Limes are small green citrus fruits, more sour than lemons and essential to many cuisines—key lime pie, ceviche, gin and tonic. The juice brightens dishes and drinks: {Squeeze some lime over the tacos}. Like lemons, limes suggest tartness and freshness. A lime is also the linden tree, and lime or quickite is calcium oxide used in cement and agriculture.

Limestone is a sedite sedimentary rock composed mainly of calcium carbonate, formed from the accumulated remains of marine organisms like shells and coral. It's widely used in construction, as a building stone, and in manufacturing cement and lime. Limestone regions often develop distinctive features like caves and sinkholes where water dissolves the rock: {The cliffs were white limestone}.

An implicit idea in the various meanings of limit is the existence of a point or place that marks a difference between two things, as in that fence is the limit of our property or what’s the speed limit here? When limit is used as a verb, it means to create or impose a limit: The government limited its citizens’ access to the Internet. Limits nearly always apply to things that are measurable, with numbers, time, and space being the favorites. Something characterized informally as the limit is exasperating, not to be tolerated, or extremely amusing: I reached my limit with her insubordination.

A limitation is a restriction or constraint that sets boundaries on what's possible. Physical limitations prevent certain movements; legal limitations restrict what's permissible. The word often implies something falling short: {The study has several limitations}. A limitation can also be a personal shortcoming: {He was aware of his own limitations}. In law, a statute of limitations sets a deadline for bringing legal action.

Limited describes something with boundaries or restrictions—the opposite of unlimited or boundless. A limited {edition} has a fixed number of copies. Limited {resources} are scarce. A limited {understanding} is incomplete. In business, a limited company (Ltd.) restricts owners' liability to their investment. Limited can also suggest modest or underwhelming: {The results were limited at best}.

Limits are boundaries or points beyond which something cannot or should not go. Physical limits mark the edge of territories: {city limits}, {within the limits of the park}. Abstract limits constrain what's possible or permitted: {the limits of human endurance}, {spending limits}. To limit is to restrict or cap: {We limited attendance to fifty people}. {Off-limits} means forbidden. {The sky's the limit} means no restriction applies.

A limo is a limousine—a long, luxurious automobile, often with a partition between driver and passengers. Limos are associated with wealth, celebrity, and special occasions: {They rented a limo for prom}. Stretch limos, extended to seat more passengers, became iconic symbols of ostentatious luxury.

Limos is the plural of limo, the clipped form of limousine—a long, luxurious automobile often associated with wealth, celebrity, or special occasions. {A fleet of limos waited outside the hotel}. Stretch limos, extended versions with extra seating, are common for proms, weddings, and bachelor parties.

A limousine is a large, luxurious automobile, typically with a lengthened body and a partition separating the driver from passengers. Originally chauffeur-driven cars for the wealthy, limousines now appear at proms, weddings, and airport pickups. Stretch limos, extended versions seating many passengers, are associated with celebrity excess. Often shortened to limo: {We rented a limo for prom night}.

Limousines is the plural of limousine, a large luxury automobile, typically with a lengthened body and a partition separating the driver from passengers. Limousines are associated with wealth, celebrity, and formal occasions—proms, weddings, airport transfers: {A fleet of limousines waited outside the hotel}. Stretch limousines are extended versions accommodating larger groups.

Meanings of limp often suggest an undesirable quality arising from lack of strength, vigor, or normal function. To limp is to walk slowly and unevenly because of injury or handicap, or to be inadequate or far behind others: He limped behind his classmates in math. A limp is the condition of being unable to walk in a typical fashion. The adjective limp characterizes things that lack needed vigor and stiffness (limp carrots). A limp excuse is unconvincing.

Limping describes movement impaired by injury or disability, typically an uneven gait favoring one leg: {He came limping off the field after the tackle}. Extended to things that function poorly or incompletely: {The project limped along without adequate funding}. A limping economy or campaign barely sustains forward motion.

A linchpin is a pin passed through an axle to keep a wheel in place. Without it, the wheel falls off and the vehicle fails. This gives rise to the figurative sense: a linchpin is whatever holds a system together or makes it work. {She was the linchpin of the organization.} {The treaty served as a linchpin of the peace process.}

The most basic notion of line—a mark that is long in relation to its width and a mark that connects two points—informs the word’s other meanings. Both physical and abstract objects possessing these qualities are characterized as lines: railway lines, dotted lines, picket lines, pickup lines. If you are in line, you are waiting for your turn. Down the line refers to the future. As a verb, line typically makes reference to the formation of a line: mourners lined the streets. When you line a garment, you sew a different material on the inside of it.

Lineage is a line of descent from an ancestor—the chain of people connecting you to those who came before. It emphasizes direct succession: {She traced her lineage back to the Mayflower}. The word often carries weight, suggesting heritage worth claiming: royal lineage, noble lineage. Extended uses apply to anything with traceable origins: {the lineage of an idea}, {the lineage of a musical genre}.

Linear describes something arranged in or relating to a line—straight, sequential, or progressing in one direction. A linear {path} goes from point A to point B without branching. Linear {thinking} proceeds step by step in logical order. In mathematics, linear equations graph as straight lines and involve variables only to the first power. Linear can contrast with nonlinear storytelling, which jumps around in time: {The film's linear structure made it easy to follow}.

A linebacker is a defensive football player positioned behind the line of scrimmage, typically responsible for stopping runs and covering short passes. Linebackers are often a team's leading tacklers and most versatile defenders: {The linebacker read the play perfectly and stuffed the runner at the line}. The position divides into inside and outside linebackers depending on alignment.

Linen is fabric woven from flax fibers, prized for its coolness and durability. By extension, linen refers to household items traditionally made from it—sheets, tablecloths, napkins: {She stored the table linens in the sideboard}. The phrase {wash your dirty linen in public} means to air private matters openly. Linen also describes the fabric's characteristic pale beige color.

Linens are household textiles—sheets, pillowcases, tablecloths, towels, napkins. The term persists from when these items were made of linen fabric, though today they're usually cotton or synthetic. {She kept her linens in the hall closet.} {The hotel changes linens daily.} A linen closet stores such items regardless of material.

A liner is something that lines—that is, covers the inside of something else. Liners provide a protective or functional layer: a trash bag is a bin liner, makeup applied along the edge of an eyelid is eyeliner, and ships or aircraft that travel regular routes are ocean liners or airliners, following established lines of travel. {I need to replace the liner in the slow cooker.} A liner in baseball is a ball hit in a nearly straight line, also called a line drive.

Lines are marks that extend in length without significant width, forming the basis for writing, drawing, and boundaries. A line of text is a horizontal row of words; lines of a play or poem are the words an actor speaks or a poet writes. People wait in lines (queues), and lines form on faces as wrinkles. {She memorized her lines for the audition.} {The lines at the DMV were brutal.} To line something is to mark it with lines or to cover an inner surface: {line a coat with silk}.

A lineup is an arrangement of people or things in a row or sequence. In law enforcement, a lineup presents suspects for witness identification: {She picked him out of a police lineup}. In sports, it's the roster of players for a game. More broadly, any scheduled sequence: {Tonight's lineup of shows}, {the product lineup for next year}.

Lineups is the plural of lineup. A lineup is a group of people or things arranged in a row or sequence. In law enforcement, a lineup presents suspects for identification by witnesses: {The victim picked him out of a police lineup}. In sports, a lineup is the roster of players starting a game. The term extends to any scheduled sequence: {Tonight's lineup includes three new shows}.

Linger means to stay longer than expected or necessary, often reluctantly or with a sense of delay. A guest lingers after a party; a smell lingers in a room. The word suggests something fading slowly rather than ending abruptly: {The taste lingered on my tongue}. To linger over something is to take unhurried time with it: {We lingered over coffee}. A lingering doubt or illness persists when you wish it wouldn't.

Lingered is the past tense of linger, meaning to stay somewhere longer than necessary or expected, often with reluctance to leave: {We lingered over coffee for hours}. It can describe something that persists or fades slowly: {The smell of smoke lingered in her hair}. {His words lingered in my mind long after he'd gone}.

Lingerie is women's underwear and sleepwear, especially when delicate, decorative, or designed to be alluring. The word carries connotations of intimacy and sensuality that plain "underwear" lacks: {She bought lingerie for her honeymoon}. Lingerie departments and shops sell bras, panties, nightgowns, and similar items.

Lingering describes something that persists longer than expected or desired, often with a sense of reluctance to end. A lingering {illness} drags on; a lingering {doubt} refuses to fade; a lingering {look} holds just a beat too long. The word carries connotations of slowness and gradual fading rather than abrupt cessation. When someone lingers, they stay behind or delay leaving: {We lingered over coffee until the café closed}.

Lingo is the specialized vocabulary or way of speaking associated with a particular group, profession, or activity: {I don't understand all the medical lingo}, {tech lingo}. The word carries a slightly dismissive tone—suggesting jargon that's hard for outsiders to penetrate. It can also refer informally to any foreign language: {I picked up some of the local lingo}.

Linguine is a pasta shape—long, flat, and narrow, like flattened spaghetti. The name means "little tongues" in Italian. Linguine pairs traditionally with seafood sauces, especially clam sauce: {linguine alle vongole}. It holds lighter sauces better than round pasta shapes.

Linguini is a type of pasta shaped like flattened spaghetti—long, thin ribbons with an elliptical cross-section. The name comes from Italian for "little tongues." Linguini pairs traditionally with seafood sauces, pesto, or light olive oil preparations: {linguini with clam sauce}, {linguini alle vongole}. Also spelled linguine.

A linguist is someone who studies language scientifically—analyzing structure, sound systems, meaning, and how languages change over time. The word also refers to a person skilled in multiple languages: {She's a talented linguist who speaks five languages fluently}. The scholarly and polyglot senses often overlap but aren't identical; a theoretical linguist may study language without speaking many.

Lining is material attached to the inside surface of something—typically fabric sewn into garments, curtains, or bags to strengthen, insulate, or conceal seams: {a silk lining}, {a coat with a wool lining}. The term extends to any inner layer: the stomach lining, brake linings. {Every cloud has a silver lining} suggests hidden benefits in misfortune.

A link is a connection: a rail link connects two places by rail; a download link connects you with a file that you can download; and link sausages are joined end to end. When two things are linked, they share a connection. When you link two things, you either establish or point out the connection between them. If evidence links you to a crime, watch out for the police! A cufflink is a small piece of jewelry that joins the cuff on a long-sleeved shirt.

Links is the plural of link—connections or things that join. In computing, links are clickable references that navigate between web pages or documents: {Click the links below for more information}. A links is also a golf course, originally one built on sandy coastal terrain: {The Scottish links were windswept and treacherous}.

Lint is the fine, fluffy fibers that accumulate on fabric surfaces or collect in clothes dryer traps. It comes from loose threads shedding during wear or washing. In computing, lint refers to tools that analyze code for errors, style problems, or suspicious constructs: {Run the linter before committing your changes}. A {lint roller} removes fibers from clothing.

A lion is a large wild cat native to Africa and parts of Asia, known for the male's distinctive mane. Lions live in social groups called prides, unusual among cats. The lion appears widely in heraldry, literature, and idiom as a symbol of courage, strength, and royalty: {the lion's share}, {lion-hearted}. A lion may also be a celebrity or person of great interest: {a literary lion}.

A lioness is a female lion. Lionesses are the primary hunters in a pride, working cooperatively to take down prey while male lions typically defend territory. The term appears in figurative use to describe a fierce, powerful, or protective woman, particularly a mother defending her children. {She fought like a lioness to protect her family.}

A lionheart is a person of exceptional courage and bravery—someone whose spirit is as fierce and bold as a lion's. The term evokes medieval ideals of valor, most famously attached to Richard I of England, known as Richard the Lionheart. As an adjective, lionhearted describes this quality: {a lionhearted defender of the weak}.

Lionhearted means exceptionally brave or courageous, with the fierce determination associated with lions. The word evokes medieval valor—Richard I of England was called Richard the Lionheart. Someone lionhearted faces danger or adversity without flinching: {a lionhearted defender of civil rights}, {She gave a lionhearted performance despite her illness}.

Lions are large wild cats native to Africa and a small population in India, or any group of these animals. The word also refers to people of exceptional courage or prominence—a literary lion, a lion of industry. Someone who gets {the lion's share} takes the largest portion. {The lions lazed in the afternoon heat.} (Capitalized Lions refers to sports teams, notably the Detroit Lions.)

A lip is either of the two fleshy folds forming the edges of the mouth. By extension, lip refers to any edge or rim: the {lip of a cup}, the {lip of a crater}. To lip something is to touch it with the lips. Lip also means insolent talk: {Don't give me any lip}. To {read lips} is to understand speech by watching mouth movements. To pay {lip service} is to express support without action.

To lipread is to understand speech by watching the movements of a speaker's lips and face rather than hearing the words. People who are deaf or hard of hearing often develop this skill: {She lipreads well enough to follow most conversations}. Also spelled as two words: lip-read.

Lips are the fleshy edges of the mouth, used for speaking, eating, and kissing. The word extends to any rim or edge resembling them: the lip of a {cup}, the lip of a {cliff}. To {read lips} is to understand speech by watching mouth movements. Giving someone {lip} is talking back disrespectfully. {My lips are sealed} promises secrecy. To {pay lip service} is to express support without backing it with action.

Lipstick is a cosmetic applied to color and define the lips, typically a waxy stick in a retractable tube. The color ranges from subtle nudes to bold reds. {She reapplied her lipstick in the rearview mirror.} Figuratively, {lipstick on a pig} describes superficial improvements to something fundamentally flawed.

Lipsync is moving your lips in synchronization with recorded audio—singing along to a track in performance, or matching dubbed dialogue in film. Performers lipsync when the actual audio comes from elsewhere: {She lipsynced the entire concert}. The practice is common in music videos, live shows with complex choreography, and drag performances. Also spelled lip-sync or lip sync.

Lipsynching is mouthing words to a prerecorded vocal track, matching lip movements to the audio without actually singing or speaking. Performers lipsync on stage when vocal demands are too taxing, or in music videos where live recording isn't practical. The spelling varies: lip-syncing, lip-synching, lipsyncing. {She was caught lipsynching when her backing track skipped.}

Lipsyncing is mouthing words to a prerecorded audio track, matching lip movements to vocals someone else sang or you sang earlier. Performers lipsync at concerts when live singing isn't practical; actors lipsync to dubbed dialogue. On social media, lipsyncing to popular songs or audio clips has become its own art form. Also spelled lip-syncing or lip syncing.

A liqueur is a sweet, flavored alcoholic spirit, typically served after dinner or used in cocktails and cooking. Liqueurs are made by infusing a base spirit with fruits, herbs, spices, nuts, or cream: {coffee liqueur}, {orange liqueur}, {cherry liqueur}. They tend to be lower in alcohol and higher in sugar than straight spirits. Common examples include Kahlúa, Grand Marnier, and Amaretto.

Liquid describes matter that flows freely—water, oil, blood. Unlike solids, liquids take the shape of their container; unlike gases, they maintain constant volume. Liquid {assets} can be quickly converted to cash. A liquid {market} has enough trading activity that buying and selling happen easily. Liquid {eyes} are clear and bright, suggesting moisture.

Liquidation is the process of converting assets into cash, typically to pay off debts when a business closes. A company {in liquidation} sells everything to settle with creditors. The term extends to eliminating or killing: {The regime ordered the liquidation of political opponents}. A {liquidation sale} offers deep discounts as a store closes permanently.

Liquids are substances that flow freely and take the shape of their container—water, oil, blood, milk. The term distinguishes this state of matter from solids and gases. In phonetics, liquids are consonant sounds like *l* and *r* that flow smoothly without friction. {The doctor told him to drink plenty of liquids.}

Liquor is alcoholic drink, especially distilled spirits like whiskey, vodka, or rum—as distinct from beer or wine. A liquor store sells such beverages. In cooking and technical contexts, liquor refers to any liquid in which something has been cooked or dissolved: {pot liquor}, {the liquor from steamed mussels}. To liquor up is to get drunk or get someone drunk.

Liquorice is the British spelling of licorice—a plant whose root yields a distinctively sweet, slightly medicinal flavour used in candy and herbal remedies. The black, chewy confection made from it divides opinion sharply: {I can't stand liquorice, but my grandmother loved it}. Liquorice root is also brewed into tea and used in traditional medicine.

A lisp is a speech pattern where s and z sounds come out as th sounds, so "sing" becomes "thing." The term can describe a genuine speech impediment or an affected, childish way of talking. To lisp is to speak this way: {She lisped her way through the presentation}. The word sometimes carries mocking or effeminate connotations when applied to adults. (Capitalized Lisp is the programming language.)

Several different words spelled list made their way into English, but only two get much contemporary use. The commonest one is a noun denoting a series of like items, typically in written form: passenger list, shopping list. When you list something, you either add it to a list, or make a list: List the names of students who passed the exam. The verbal meaning of list communicates a physical object leaning or deviating from vertical: The building began to list after severe floods.

To listen is to pay attention to sound—someone speaking, music playing, a noise in the distance. Unlike hearing, which happens automatically, listening implies active attention: {I heard the words but wasn't really listening}. To listen to advice or warnings is to heed them. {Listen} by itself can introduce something important: {Listen, I need to tell you something}. A good listener gives others their full attention.

A listener is someone who listens—to music, to a speaker, to a podcast. The word often implies attentiveness or receptivity: {She's a good listener}. In broadcasting, listeners are the audience for radio or audio content. In computing, a listener is a process that waits for incoming connections or events.

Listening is the act of paying attention to sound, especially speech. It implies more than just hearing—listening suggests active engagement and effort to understand: {Are you even listening to me?} Good listening involves focus and response. {Listening to music} means attending to it with appreciation. In surveillance contexts, a listening {device} or listening {post} captures communications covertly.

A listing is an entry in a list or directory—a real estate listing, a job listing, a TV listing. The word emphasizes the item's inclusion in some organized collection: {Check the listings to see what's playing}. In computing, a listing is a printout or display of code. The plural listings often refers to classified advertisements or program schedules as a category.

Lists is an old word for a combat arena—the enclosed field where knights jousted at tournaments. To {enter the lists} is to join a competition or conflict, from the image of a challenger riding into that space. The expression survives mainly in formal or literary contexts: {She entered the lists as a candidate for mayor}.

Lit is the past tense of light—illuminated, ignited, or set on fire: {She lit the candle}. {The room was beautifully lit}. {His cigarette was already lit}. A well-lit space has good lighting; a lit fuse is burning. In slang, lit means drunk, high, or extremely exciting and fun: {The party was lit}. {I got lit last night}. This sense exploded in popularity in the 2010s and can describe both intoxication and general excitement.

A litany is a lengthy, repetitive recitation—originally a form of prayer with a series of invocations and responses. The word now usually describes any tedious enumeration: {a litany of complaints}, {the usual litany of excuses}. The negative connotation suggests weariness with hearing the same grievances or items repeated.

Literacy is the ability to read and write. Basic literacy means functional competence; full literacy suggests fluency. The term extends to competence in other domains: {computer literacy}, {financial literacy}, {media literacy}. These compound forms imply not just familiarity but practical understanding—knowing enough to navigate effectively.

Literal describes something that adheres to the exact, primary meaning of words without metaphor or exaggeration. A literal {translation} renders text word for word rather than capturing its spirit. If you take something literally, you interpret it according to its surface meaning: {I said I was starving, but I didn't mean it literally}. In casual speech, literal and literally have become intensifiers that often contradict their original sense: {I literally died laughing}. This usage irritates purists but is now widespread.

The adverb literally indicates a factual meaning as opposed to a figurative interpretation: They were literally chased out of town by an angry mob. Literally is not successful as an intensifier: Their new album will literally turn the world upside down. If someone translates a work literally, they give a version in the target language that may be truer to the words than to the meaning of the original.

Literate means able to read and write: {a literate population}, {barely literate}. The word extends to competence in any domain: {computer literate}, {financially literate}. A literate person may also be well-read or culturally educated: {a literate and thoughtful critic}. As a noun, a literate is someone who can read, often in contexts discussing literacy rates.

Literature is written work, especially of artistic merit—novels, poetry, drama, essays. The term often implies enduring value: {the literature of the Romantic period}, {American literature}. More broadly, literature means the body of writing on a subject: {medical literature}, {campaign literature}. The adjective literary describes qualities associated with serious writing, sometimes disparagingly: {a literary style that felt overwrought}.

Lithium is a soft, silver-white metal, the lightest of all solid elements. It appears in rechargeable batteries for phones, laptops, and electric vehicles. In medicine, lithium compounds treat bipolar disorder by stabilizing mood: {She's been on lithium for years}. The element's lightness and reactivity make it valuable across industries.

Litmus is a dye derived from lichen that turns red in acid and blue in base, used to test acidity. The figurative {litmus test} has become far more common than the laboratory one—any single criterion that decisively reveals someone's position or character: {Abortion has become a litmus test for Supreme Court nominees}.

Litter gathers around the idea of scattered things. Litter is trash strewn in public places: {The park was covered in litter}. A litter of puppies or kittens is a group born together, scattered from the mother. Litter is also material spread on the ground—straw for animal bedding, or absorbent granules in a cat's litter box. To litter is to scatter carelessly: {Empty bottles littered the floor}.

A litterbug is someone who carelessly discards trash in public places rather than disposing of it properly. The word carries mild disapproval and sounds somewhat dated or childish—the kind of term used in anti-pollution campaigns aimed at schoolchildren: {Don't be a litterbug}.

Littering is the act of discarding trash or waste in public places rather than proper receptacles. Signs warn against it; fines punish it. The word carries moral weight—littering marks someone as inconsiderate or careless about shared spaces. {The beach was ruined by tourists littering.} Littering also refers to animals giving birth to a litter of offspring.

Litters is the plural of litter in its noun senses—scattered trash, a group of animals born together, material spread for animal bedding, or a carried platform. As a verb, litters means to scatter carelessly or to give birth to multiple offspring at once: {She never litters}, {The cat litters twice a year}. {Broken glass litters the street.}

Little, though not as common as its synonym small, is a frequently used word to characterize things as being not big. Usage favors little in a number of common collocations, including little bit, little doubt, little choice, little boy and little girl. In modifier pairs we also commonly say precious little, cute little, and nice little. Little works as an adverb in expressions such as care little and little known.

The verb live (pronounced with a short vowel) has two main meanings: reside (live in Idaho) and have life (lived to the age of 100). If you live off something, it supports you: Carol lived off her pension. The adjective and adverb live (pronounced with a long vowel) characterizes things that are experienced or captured in real time (live performance, recorded live). Live is similar to alive in some phrases (live birth, live wire). The noun life has the plural form lives.

A livelihood is the way someone earns money to support themselves—their occupation or source of income: {Fishing is the livelihood of most villagers here}. The word often appears when that income is threatened: {The factory closing destroyed their livelihoods}. It carries a sense of basic sustenance rather than wealth.

Livelihoods are means of earning a living—the ways people support themselves and their families. The word emphasizes ongoing sustenance rather than wealth: {Fishing provides livelihoods for coastal communities}. Threats to livelihoods—economic shifts, environmental changes, political upheaval—threaten survival itself: {The factory closure destroyed the livelihoods of hundreds of workers}.

Lively means full of energy, spirit, or activity. A lively {conversation} moves quickly with engaged participants. A lively {neighborhood} bustles with people and activity. A lively {debate} features vigorous exchange. The word suggests animation and vitality rather than mere speed: {The band played a lively tune}. Something can be lively without being loud—a lively {mind} is quick and engaged.

The liver is the large organ in the abdomen that filters blood, produces bile, and processes nutrients. It's essential to metabolism and detoxification. Liver also refers to this organ from animals prepared as food: {liver and onions}, {chicken liver pâté}. As an adjective, liver describes a dark reddish-brown color. A liver is also one who lives: {a clean liver}, {a fast liver}.

Lives is the plural of life and the third-person singular of live. As a noun, lives are the spans of existence people or creatures have: {The accident claimed three lives}. The verb means to be alive or to dwell: {She lives in Boston}, {He lives for the weekend}. {Nine lives} is the legendary resilience of cats.

Livestock are animals raised on farms or ranches for food or labor—horses, cattle, sheep, pigs, goats. Chickens, turkeys, and ducks are sometimes included but more often called poultry, with livestock reserved for four-legged animals. The word implies groups; a single horse wouldn't count as livestock. {The rancher moved his livestock to higher ground before the flood.}

A livestream is video or audio broadcast in real time over the internet, allowing viewers to watch events as they happen: {I caught the concert on livestream}. The verb means to broadcast this way: {They're livestreaming the press conference}. Unlike recorded video, livestreams offer immediacy—viewers experience events simultaneously with participants, often interacting through chat.

Livestreaming is broadcasting video content over the internet in real time, as opposed to uploading pre-recorded material. Viewers watch events as they unfold—gaming sessions, concerts, news coverage, product launches: {She's livestreaming on Twitch right now}. The verb livestream works both ways: you can livestream your content or livestream someone else's broadcast by watching it live.

Livestreams are video broadcasts transmitted in real time over the internet, allowing viewers to watch events as they happen. The term covers everything from professional news coverage to casual gaming sessions on Twitch or YouTube. To livestream is to broadcast this way: {She livestreams her workouts every morning}. Also spelled as two words: live streams.

Livid originally describes the bluish-gray color of a bruise, and extends to skin discolored by cold, illness, or death: {His face went livid from the blow}. The more common modern sense is furiously angry: {She was livid when she found out he'd lied}. The connection may be through the pale or flushed appearance of someone in a rage.

Living describes being alive—having life, not dead. As a noun, living means one's livelihood or way of earning money: {She makes a living as a freelance writer}, {It's hard to earn a living in this economy}. The living are those who are alive, as opposed to the dead. A living {language} is still in active use. A living {room} is the main common space in a home. Something can be a {living hell} or a {living nightmare}—intensifiers suggesting ongoing, felt experience rather than mere metaphor.

A lizard is a reptile with a long body, four legs, and a tail—geckos, iguanas, chameleons, and their kin. Unlike snakes, most lizards have visible legs and external ear openings. Informally, lizard describes someone cold-blooded or untrustworthy: {That lizard cheated me out of my savings}. A {lounge lizard} is a man who frequents bars seeking women.

Lizards is the plural of lizard, a typically four-legged reptile with scaly skin and a long tail. Most lizards are small—geckos, skinks, iguanas—though monitor lizards grow quite large. Unlike snakes, most lizards have legs and external ear openings. {The lizards sunned themselves on the rocks.} In slang, a lounge lizard is a man who frequents bars hoping to meet women.

A llama is a South American mammal related to the camel but smaller and without a hump, domesticated for centuries as a pack animal and for its wool. Llamas are known for their calm temperament, though they famously spit when annoyed. In internet culture, llama has become a minor meme, appearing in absurdist humor and as mascots for various platforms. The word also refers to Llama, Meta's family of large language models.

Llamas are large domesticated South American mammals related to camels but without humps. They serve as pack animals in the Andes and are raised elsewhere for their soft wool. Llamas are known for spitting when annoyed. {The farm down the road keeps llamas and alpacas.}

A load is a burden, often a physical one but sometimes abstract. Whatever a cargo or freight vehicle carries is called its load: A semi overturned and dropped its load on the Interstate. In computing and cognitive contexts, load can refer to the amount of information being processed, sometimes with reference to a limit. Load also has many slang meanings. As a verb, load means to add to or create a load: Load the crates into the truck. When something is loaded with a substance of quality, it has a large quantity of it: The new game is loaded with special effects. To say that someone is loaded is an informal way of saying that they are drunk, or rich.

Loaded means carrying a load or full of something: a loaded {truck}, a loaded {gun}. Extended meanings cluster around excess or advantage. A loaded person is drunk or wealthy. Loaded {dice} are weighted to cheat. A loaded {question} contains hidden assumptions that trap the answerer. In computing, a program that has loaded is ready to run. {The question was loaded—any answer would make him look guilty.}

Loading is the process of putting cargo, data, or material into something that will carry or process it: {loading the truck}, {loading the dishwasher}, {the game is still loading}. A loading dock or loading zone is where vehicles receive cargo. In computing, loading refers to transferring data into memory or displaying content: {page loading}. Loading can also mean adding weight or bias to something: {dice loading}, {front-loading a contract with fees}.

A loadout is the specific combination of weapons, equipment, and gear a player selects before entering a game or mission, especially in shooters and tactical games: {I'm still tweaking my loadout for ranked matches}. The term has spread from gaming to military and tactical contexts, referring to how someone has configured their kit for a particular purpose.

Loads means a large amount or many: {There were loads of people at the concert}, {I've got loads of work to do}. The word is informal, common in British English, and functions like lots. It derives from the noun load—a heavy burden or quantity carried—extended to suggest abundance. {Thanks loads} expresses emphatic gratitude.

A loaf is bread baked in a single shaped mass, typically oblong: {a loaf of bread}, {a sandwich loaf}. The shape extends to other foods molded similarly: {meatloaf}, {a loaf of cheese}. To loaf is to idle or waste time: {He spent the afternoon loafing around the house}. A loafer is someone who loafs, or a slip-on leather shoe.

A loafer is a slip-on leather shoe without laces, typically with a low heel and a moccasin-style upper: {She wore penny loafers with her khakis}. Separately, a loafer is someone who idles or avoids work—one who loafs around: {He spent the summer as a loafer, doing nothing productive}.

Loafers are slip-on shoes without laces, typically leather with a low heel and a flat front. The style suggests casual comfort—easy to slip on and off. {He wore penny loafers with no socks}. Separately, loafers are people who idle or avoid work, from the verb loaf: {a bunch of loafers hanging around the pool hall}.

A loan is something lent, typically money given with the expectation of repayment: {She took out a loan to buy the house}. Banks make loans; friends loan each other books and tools. The verb loan is interchangeable with lend in American English, though some consider lend more formal. {On loan} means temporarily borrowed: {The painting is on loan from a private collection}.

Loans are sums of money lent to a borrower, typically with the expectation of repayment plus interest. Banks issue loans for homes, cars, and education. The word works as both noun and verb: {She took out a loan for tuition}; {He loaned me fifty bucks}. In American English, loan and lend are often interchangeable as verbs, though some prefer lend for the action and loan for the thing itself.

A loanshark is someone who lends money at exorbitant interest rates, typically operating outside legal banking systems and often using threats or violence to ensure repayment. The term combines the predatory connotations of shark with the lending business. Loansharking has historically been associated with organized crime, though the word now applies to any exploitative lender. {He borrowed five thousand from a loanshark and ended up owing triple that.}

Loansharking is the practice of lending money at exorbitant interest rates, often with threats of violence for non-payment. The term evokes organized crime—loan sharks operating outside legal lending systems, preying on desperate borrowers who can't access conventional credit. The rates compound so aggressively that victims often can never escape the debt: {He got mixed up with loansharking and ended up owing triple what he borrowed}.

Loathe means to feel intense disgust or hatred toward something: {I loathe getting up early}, {She loathes her ex-husband}. The feeling is stronger than dislike—closer to revulsion. Not to be confused with loath (without the e), which is an adjective meaning reluctant: {He was loath to admit his mistake}.

Loathing is intense disgust or hatred—stronger than dislike, carrying visceral revulsion. You might feel loathing for a person, an idea, or yourself: {She looked at him with undisguised loathing}. Self-loathing is particularly common, describing deep shame or contempt directed inward.

To lob is to throw or hit something in a high, gentle arc—the opposite of a hard, direct throw. In tennis, a lob sends the ball high over an opponent's head. You might lob a ball to a child or lob a crumpled paper toward a trash can. The noun lob describes such a throw or shot: {She hit a perfect lob over the net}. Figuratively, to lob a question or criticism is to deliver it casually or provocatively: {The reporter lobbed a softball question at the candidate}.

Lobbies is the plural of lobby—entrance halls or waiting areas in buildings like hotels, theaters, and office buildings: {The hotel lobbies were packed with convention guests}. Lobbies also names groups that try to influence legislators or officials: {pharmaceutical lobbies}, {gun lobbies}. As a verb form, lobbies means to attempt such influence: {She lobbies Congress on behalf of environmental groups}.

A lobby is an entrance hall or waiting area, especially in hotels, theaters, or office buildings: {We'll meet in the hotel lobby}. The term extends to groups that try to influence legislators or officials—from the practice of approaching politicians in legislative lobbies. To lobby is to attempt such influence: {Environmental groups lobbied Congress for stricter emissions standards}. A lobbyist does this professionally.

Lobbying is attempting to influence legislators or other public officials on behalf of a particular interest. Lobbyists work to shape policy by meeting with lawmakers, providing information, and advocating positions: {The pharmaceutical industry spends millions on lobbying each year}. The term extends to any organized effort to sway decision-makers: {lobbying the school board for longer recess}.

A lobbyist is someone paid to influence legislators or government officials on behalf of a particular interest—a corporation, industry, union, or cause. Lobbyists work to shape policy through meetings, research, and persuasion: {The pharmaceutical lobbyists pushed hard against price controls}. The term derives from the practice of approaching politicians in the lobbies of legislative buildings.

Lobbyists are people who attempt to influence legislators or other public officials on behalf of specific interests. They work for corporations, trade associations, advocacy groups, or foreign governments, meeting with politicians, providing information, and often contributing to campaigns. The term comes from the practice of waiting in legislative lobbies to catch officials. {Lobbyists for the pharmaceutical industry opposed the bill.}

Lobotomized describes someone who has undergone a lobotomy—a surgical procedure that severs connections in the brain's prefrontal lobe, once used to treat mental illness. The procedure often left patients passive and emotionally flattened, which gives the figurative sense: rendered unable to think clearly or respond normally. {I felt lobotomized after that meeting}. {The lobotomized protagonist shuffled through the ward}.

Lobotomy is a surgical procedure that severs connections in the brain's prefrontal lobe, formerly used to treat mental illness. Developed in the 1930s and performed widely through the 1950s, lobotomies often left patients docile but cognitively impaired. The practice is now discredited. Figuratively, lobotomy suggests having one's capacity for thought or feeling removed: {Watching that show is like getting a lobotomy}.

A lobster is a large marine crustacean with a hard shell, stalked eyes, and large front claws, prized as a luxury seafood. Lobsters are typically bluish-green when alive but turn bright red when cooked. The meat is rich and sweet: {We ordered lobster tails with drawn butter}. In informal use, a lobster is someone with badly sunburned skin: {I forgot sunscreen and came home looking like a lobster}.

Lobsters are large marine crustaceans with hard shells, stalked eyes, and large front claws, prized as seafood. They turn red when cooked. The plural often refers to the creatures as food: {We had lobsters for dinner}. A lobster is also someone with badly sunburned skin, from the color: {I forgot sunscreen and turned into a lobster}.

Local means nearby or belonging to a particular place. A local {restaurant} is in your neighborhood; a local {custom} belongs to a specific region. The noun refers to a person from the area: {The locals know the best beaches}. Local can also mean a nearby branch of something larger—a union local, a local anesthetic that numbs only one area. {All politics is local.}

Locals are the people who live in a particular place, especially as distinguished from visitors or outsiders: {The locals know the best restaurants}. In computing, locals are variables accessible only within a specific function or block of code. At a bar, locals are the regular patrons: {He's one of the locals}.

Location is a place or position—where something is or where something happens. A store's location affects its success. You can share your location with an app. {We're still looking for a location for the wedding}. In film and television, shooting on location means filming at real sites rather than on studio sets.

Most meanings of lock convey the idea of a barrier (door lock, caps lock, headlock). When you lock something, you prevent access or movement. When two animals’ horns lock, they become intertwined and not easily separable. Locks on a canal control variable water levels using gates. A different lock is about hair: Her golden locks shone in the sun.

A lockdown is a security protocol confining people to a location during a threat—schools lock down during active shooter situations, prisons during disturbances. The term gained broader currency during the COVID-19 pandemic for restrictions keeping people home: {The city went into lockdown for three months}. Extended, it describes any enforced period of restriction: {My parents put me on lockdown after I crashed the car}.

Lockdowns are emergency measures that restrict movement and activity, typically imposed by authorities during crises. The term gained widespread use during the COVID-19 pandemic to describe orders requiring people to stay home and businesses to close. Schools and other facilities also go into lockdown during security threats, sealing entrances and confining occupants to secure areas. {The city imposed strict lockdowns to slow the spread of the virus.}

Locked means secured or fastened, typically with a lock: {The door was locked}. Something locked is fixed in position or unable to move: {locked in place}, {locked and loaded}. Figuratively, people become locked in conflict, debate, or embrace—held together tightly. To be {locked in} to something is to be committed without easy exit: {We're locked in at that price}. In slang, locked or {locked in} means intensely focused: {He's been locked in all season}.

A locker is a small compartment with a lock, typically in a row of similar compartments, used to store personal belongings in schools, gyms, workplaces, or transit stations. {She kept her gym clothes in her locker}. The term extends to storage compartments on boats and in freezers: {a meat locker}, {Davy Jones's locker} (the ocean floor, where drowned sailors rest).

Lockers are storage compartments, typically in a row of similar units, secured with locks. Schools, gyms, and workplaces provide lockers for personal belongings: {I forgot my combination and couldn't get into my locker}. A locker room is where people change clothes, often near athletic facilities—locker room talk refers to crude conversation, especially among men.

A locket is a small ornamental case, typically worn on a chain around the neck, that opens to reveal a photograph or memento inside. Lockets traditionally hold pictures of loved ones or locks of hair: {She wore a gold locket with her mother's picture in it}. The word suggests sentimental value—lockets are keepsakes, not just jewelry.

Lockjaw is a common name for tetanus, the bacterial infection that causes severe muscle spasms—particularly in the jaw, making it difficult or impossible to open the mouth. The term is also used loosely for any condition causing jaw stiffness: {I woke up with lockjaw after sleeping wrong}.

A lockout is a situation where someone is prevented from entering or accessing something. In labor disputes, a lockout is when management shuts out workers to pressure them during negotiations—the employer's counterpart to a strike. In sports, a lockout suspends play when owners and players can't agree on contracts: {The NHL lockout canceled the entire season}. More generally, a lockout occurs when you're shut out of your car, house, or account: {I had to call a locksmith after a lockout}.

A lockpick is a tool designed to open locks without the original key, typically a thin metal implement inserted into the keyhole to manipulate the internal mechanism. Lockpicking is associated with burglars, but locksmiths and hobbyists also practice it legitimately. The verb lockpick means to open a lock this way: {She lockpicked the filing cabinet in under a minute}.

Lockpicking is the skill or act of opening a lock without its key, using specialized tools to manipulate the internal mechanism. It's practiced legitimately by locksmiths and security professionals, and illegally by burglars. As a hobby, it has enthusiast communities who practice on locks they own: {I got into lockpicking during quarantine}.

Locks are devices that secure doors, containers, or mechanisms, typically opened with a key or combination. A lock of hair is a strand or curl: {a lock of her hair kept in a locket}. Locks also refers to a system of gates controlling water levels in canals, allowing boats to pass between different elevations. As a verb, to lock is to fasten securely or to become fixed: {Their eyes locked across the room}. To be {locked in} is to be committed or trapped. In wrestling, a lock is a hold that immobilizes an opponent.

A locksmith is a person who makes, repairs, and opens locks. The trade involves cutting keys, installing security hardware, and helping people who have locked themselves out: {We called a locksmith when we lost the house keys}. The word combines lock with smith, the old term for a metalworker.

Lockstep is a way of marching in very close formation, each person's feet moving in unison with the person ahead. The term extends to rigid conformity or synchronized action: {The party voted in lockstep with its leadership}. The implication is usually negative—mindless uniformity rather than coordinated teamwork: {They moved in lockstep, never questioning orders}.

A locomotive is the engine that pulls a train—the self-propelled vehicle that provides motive power for railroad cars. The word can also function as an adjective meaning relating to movement or capable of moving: {locomotive power}, {locomotive ability}. In older usage, any self-moving machine might be called a locomotive.

Locomotives are self-propelled railway engines that pull trains. The word comes from Latin roots meaning "moving from place to place." A locomotive hauls freight cars or passenger coaches along tracks: {The steam locomotive pulled into the station}. Figuratively, locomotive can describe anything that drives forward motion or serves as a powerful force.

A locust is a grasshopper that periodically swarms in vast numbers, devouring crops and vegetation across wide areas. The word extends to various large grasshoppers and cicadas. Locust trees—the black locust and honey locust—bear pods resembling the insect. Figuratively, locusts are any devouring horde: {Tourists descended like locusts on the small town}.

Locusts is the plural of locust, a type of grasshopper that periodically swarms in vast numbers, devastating crops and vegetation. Biblical plagues featured locusts as divine punishment. Figuratively, locusts describes any devouring horde: {Locusts of tourists descended on the small town}. The locust tree, with its clustered seed pods, takes its name from the insect.

A lodge is a place to stay temporarily, especially while on vacation and near or in a wild place. Some other kinds of buildings are also called lodges (Masonic lodge, Elks lodge). When you lodge someone, you provide them a place to stay. When you lodge something abstract, like a complaint, protest, appeal, or claim, you put it before an authority that can act on it. If something is lodged in a place, it may be stuck there.

Lodges serves as both noun and verb. A lodge is a small house or cabin, often in a rustic or wilderness setting: {a ski lodge}, {a hunting lodge}. It also names the meeting place of fraternal organizations like the Freemasons, or the local chapter itself. As a verb, to lodge is to stay temporarily {(We lodged at a bed and breakfast)} or to become stuck {(A bone lodged in his throat)}. To lodge a complaint is to formally register it.

Lodging is a place to stay, especially temporarily. The word often appears in the plural: {The university provides lodgings for visiting scholars}. A rooming house or inn might advertise lodging available. To find lodging is to secure somewhere to sleep. The word carries a slightly old-fashioned or formal tone compared to alternatives like accommodation or housing.

Lofi (also lo-fi, short for low fidelity) describes audio with deliberately rough, imperfect sound quality—the opposite of polished studio production. Vinyl crackle, tape hiss, and muffled frequencies become aesthetic choices rather than flaws. The term now primarily evokes {lofi hip-hop}, a genre of mellow instrumental beats often used as background music for studying or relaxing: {I put on some lofi while I work}.

A loft is a space directly under a roof, typically used for storage or converted into living quarters. In buildings, a loft often means an upper floor of a warehouse or factory converted to residential or studio use: {a SoHo loft}.
