A maestro is a master musician, especially a conductor or composer of classical music: {The maestro raised his baton}. The Italian word for master has been borrowed into English for distinguished artists generally, often with a hint of playful reverence: {He's the maestro of horror films}. The plural is maestros or maestri.

A mafia is any organized criminal network, especially one based on family ties, ethnic solidarity, or regional loyalty. The term extends to any tight-knit group that controls access to power or resources: {the literary mafia}, {Hollywood mafia}. The word suggests secrecy, mutual protection, and ruthless enforcement of loyalty. (Capitalized Mafia refers specifically to the Sicilian or Italian-American crime syndicate.)

Mafiosi is the Italian plural of mafioso—members of the Mafia or similar organized crime groups. The term applies to those involved in the hierarchical criminal organizations originating in Sicily and later established in America: {The FBI surveilled known mafiosi in New York}. It sometimes extends figuratively to any tight-knit group operating by its own rules.

A mafioso is a member of the Mafia—the organized crime syndicates originating in Sicily and Italy, or their American counterparts. The term can apply to any participant in such organizations, from foot soldiers to bosses. More loosely, mafioso describes anyone who behaves like a gangster or operates through intimidation and backroom deals: {He ran the union like a mafioso}. Plural: mafiosi.

A magazine is a periodical publication containing articles, photographs, and advertisements, typically on a specific subject or for a general audience: {fashion magazines}, {I read about it in a magazine}. Magazine also means a storage chamber—the part of a gun holding ammunition before it feeds into the chamber, or a room where explosives or weapons are kept. The storage sense came first: a place where goods are deposited.

Magazines are periodical publications containing articles, photographs, and advertisements, typically printed on glossy paper and issued weekly or monthly: {fashion magazines}, {news magazines}. The word also names the ammunition storage component of a firearm—the detachable container holding cartridges that feed into the chamber. Both senses share the idea of a storehouse: the Arabic root meant warehouse.

A mage is a magician or wizard—someone who practices magic. The word appears almost exclusively in fantasy fiction and gaming, where it typically denotes a character class specializing in spells rather than physical combat: {The mage cast a fireball at the approaching orcs}. Outside these contexts, mage sounds archaic or affected.

Magenta is a vivid purplish-red color, sitting between red and blue on the spectrum. The color was named after the 1859 Battle of Magenta in Italy, where a newly synthesized dye gained fame around the same time. In color printing and digital displays, magenta is a primary color alongside cyan and yellow: {The printer is low on magenta ink}.

A maggot is the soft-bodied, legless larva of a fly, typically found in decaying organic matter where adult flies have laid their eggs. Maggots are pale, wormlike creatures that feed voraciously before pupating into adult flies. The word is used as a strong insult to call someone disgusting or contemptible: {You filthy maggot}. In fishing, maggots serve as popular bait.

Maggots are the larval form of flies—soft, legless, wormlike creatures that hatch from eggs laid in decaying organic matter. They feed voraciously on rotting flesh, garbage, or other decomposing material. In medicine, sterile maggots are sometimes used to clean wounds by consuming dead tissue. The word often carries connotations of filth and disgust: {The garbage was crawling with maggots}.

Magic is a power or force that is credited to explain (usually good) things that happen when no logical explanation suffices. If you work magic, the suggestion is that you make something happen that would have seemed impossible. Before another noun, magic usually denotes an imaginary thing that has extraordinary powers (magic wand, magic bullet). Sometimes, magic is used to characterize highly creative and enjoyable works of art or experiences of these: The play was magic; it completed entranced us.

Magical describes things connected to magic—supernatural forces or practices that defy natural laws: {a magical incantation}, {magical powers}. More loosely, magical means enchanting or wonderfully delightful: {a magical evening}, {The light on the water was magical}. This second sense suggests something so special it feels touched by forces beyond the ordinary.

A magician is a person who performs magic. In entertainment, magicians do tricks—card tricks, sleight of hand, making things appear or disappear: {The magician pulled a rabbit from his hat}. In fantasy and folklore, a magician wields supernatural power, casting spells or summoning forces. Figuratively, someone with exceptional skill may be called a magician: {She's a magician with numbers}.

Magicians are people who perform magic. The word covers both entertainers who create illusions—card tricks, disappearing acts, sawing assistants in half—and figures in fantasy and folklore who wield supernatural powers: {Merlin was the most famous magician in Arthurian legend}. Someone exceptionally skilled at something may be called a magician: {She's a magician with numbers}.

Magma is molten rock beneath the earth's surface, held under pressure in the crust or mantle. When it reaches the surface through volcanic eruption, it becomes lava. The word extends metaphorically to any seething, formless source: {a magma of creative energy}, {the magma of political unrest}.

A magnet is an object that attracts iron and certain other metals through an invisible force field. Magnets have two poles—north and south—and opposite poles attract while like poles repel. The word extends to anything that draws people or things powerfully: {The beach is a magnet for tourists}. A person with magnetic charm attracts others effortlessly.

Magnetic describes things that attract iron and certain other metals, or that relate to magnetism as a physical force: a magnetic {field}, magnetic {poles}. The word extends naturally to people or qualities that draw others in: a magnetic {personality}, magnetic {charm}. Someone magnetic commands attention and inspires fascination, as if exerting an invisible pull.

Magnetism is the force by which certain materials attract or repel each other—the invisible pull between a magnet and iron, or between two magnets. The term extends to personal charm or charisma: {Her magnetism drew people to her}. Someone with magnetism commands attention without obvious effort. In physics, magnetism is one of the fundamental forces, closely linked to electricity.

Magnets is the plural of magnet—objects that produce magnetic fields and attract iron, steel, and certain other metals. Magnets can be natural (lodestone) or manufactured. Figuratively, anything that draws people or things acts as a magnet: {The beach is a magnet for tourists}. Fridge magnets hold notes and photos to refrigerator doors.

Magnificent describes something grand, impressive, or exceptionally beautiful—worthy of admiration. A magnificent palace awes with its scale and splendor. A magnificent performance exceeds expectations. The word carries a sense of grandeur that elevates its subject above the ordinary: {The view from the summit was magnificent}. Something magnificent inspires wonder rather than mere approval.

Magnitude measures size, extent, or importance. Stars are classified by magnitude—their brightness as seen from Earth. An earthquake's magnitude quantifies its energy release. In mathematics, magnitude is the absolute value of a number or the length of a vector. More loosely, magnitude describes scale or significance: {a problem of some magnitude}, {the sheer magnitude of the task}.

Magnolia is a tree or shrub known for its large, fragrant flowers—typically white, pink, or purple—that bloom in early spring, often before leaves appear. Native to Asia and the Americas, magnolias are widely planted as ornamentals: {The magnolia in the front yard is spectacular in April}. The word also names the pale cream color of magnolia blossoms, used especially for interior paint. (Capitalized Magnolia is a given name.)

Magnolias are flowering trees and shrubs known for their large, fragrant blossoms—typically white, pink, or purple. Native to Asia and the Americas, they're among the oldest flowering plants. The magnolia is closely associated with the American South, where it symbolizes hospitality and gentility: {The magnolia trees were in full bloom}. {She planted magnolias along the driveway}.

A magpie is a black-and-white bird with a long tail, known for its loud chattering call and attraction to shiny objects. The bird's reputation for collecting bright trinkets gives rise to the figurative sense: a magpie is someone who gathers miscellaneous items, or the adjective describes eclectic accumulation: {her magpie collection of vintage jewelry}, {magpie tendencies}.

Magpies are medium-sized birds in the crow family, known for their striking black-and-white plumage and long tails. They have a reputation for collecting shiny objects, which gives rise to the figurative use: a magpie is someone who compulsively gathers or hoards things, especially trinkets or bits of information. {She's a magpie for vintage jewelry.} The birds are also known for their noisy chattering, so calling someone a magpie can mean they talk too much.

Mahjong is a tile-based game that originated in China, typically played by four players who draw and discard tiles to form winning combinations of sets and runs. The 144 tiles are engraved with Chinese characters and symbols representing suits, honors, and bonus tiles. Players build a hand much like in rummy, aiming to complete specific patterns before opponents do. The game combines skill, strategy, and luck, with regional variations in rules found throughout Asia and the West.

Mahogany is a tropical hardwood prized for its rich reddish-brown color, durability, and fine grain. It has long been the wood of choice for quality furniture, boat building, and musical instruments. The color mahogany—a deep brownish red—derives from the wood: {mahogany hair}, {mahogany skin}.

A maid is a female domestic servant who cleans, cooks, or performs other household duties. The word is a shortened form of maiden and retains some of that word's connotations of youth and unmarried status, though modern usage focuses on the occupation rather than marital state. A {maid of honor} is the principal bridesmaid at a wedding. In hotels, maids clean guest rooms; in private homes, a {live-in maid} may reside with the family she serves.

Maiden is a literary or old-fashioned term for a girl, unmarried woman, or virgin. It may also designate a servant, much like the related maid. As an adjective, maiden either characterizes something about maidens (maiden virtues) or conveys that the thing modified is happening for the first time (a ship’s maiden voyage, maiden victory). A maiden aunt is one who has never married. A woman’s maiden name is her family surname, the one she used before she took her husband’s family name.

Maidens is the plural of maiden—a literary or old-fashioned term for girls, unmarried women, or virgins. The word appears in fairy tales and historical contexts: {The dragon demanded maidens as tribute}. In cricket, maidens are overs in which no runs are scored.

Maids is the plural of maid—women employed in domestic service, particularly for cleaning and household tasks: {The hotel maids clean the rooms daily}. In older or literary usage, maids are young unmarried women or virgins: {fair maids and gallant knights}. The compound {old maid} refers to an unmarried woman past typical marrying age, now considered offensive.

In American English, as both a noun and a verb, mail relates to the postal system (similar to the word post in British English): Has the mail come yet? Put this letter in the mail. I need to mail a letter. Some newspapers include mail in their name (the Daily Mail, the Toronto Globe and Mail) because of their regular delivery, like the mail. Mail occasionally serves as shorthand for email, in terms like mail server, and traditional mail may be called snail mail to make this distinction clear. Another use of mail, separately derived, is to denote a kind of armor made from interlocking metal rings.

A mailbox is a container for receiving or sending mail. In American usage, it's either the box at your residence where postal carriers leave letters, or the blue collection boxes on street corners. In computing, a mailbox is an email inbox: {My mailbox is overflowing with unread messages}. British English prefers letterbox for the physical container.

A mailman is a person who delivers mail to homes and businesses, typically walking a regular route. The term assumes male gender; letter carrier and mail carrier are neutral alternatives. {The mailman comes around noon.} In American English, mailman remains common in casual speech despite official preference for carrier.

To maim is to inflict severe physical injury that results in permanent damage or loss of function—typically the loss of a limb or sense: {The explosion maimed three soldiers}. Unlike wound or injure, maim implies lasting disfigurement or disability. The word appears in legal contexts distinguishing degrees of bodily harm.

Maimed means severely injured, especially with permanent damage to a limb or body part. The word emphasizes disfigurement or loss of function rather than pain: {soldiers maimed by landmines}, {The accident left him maimed for life}. Maimed carries more gravity than injured—it suggests lasting physical impairment that cannot be fully healed.

Maiming is the act of inflicting serious bodily harm, especially damage that permanently disables or disfigures: {The landmine was responsible for the maiming of dozens of civilians}. The word emphasizes lasting injury—loss of limbs, sight, or function—rather than temporary wounds. Legal contexts distinguish maiming from lesser assault charges.

The adjective main characterizes something that is most important, central, or prominent. If there are a number of reasons, the main reason is the really important one. The main character in a book, play, or movie is the one around whom the story revolves. A main road between places carries the most traffic. The noun main has a similar meaning in the expression in the main. A main or mains can also be a pipe or system of pipes for gas, water, or electricity.

A mainframe is a large, powerful computer capable of processing vast amounts of data and supporting many simultaneous users—the workhorses of banks, airlines, and government agencies. Before personal computers, mainframes dominated computing; users accessed them through terminals. The term now often distinguishes centralized institutional computing from distributed systems: {The company still runs its payroll on a mainframe}.

The mainland is the principal landmass of a country or continent, as distinct from its islands or peninsulas. Hawaiians speak of traveling to {the mainland}, meaning the contiguous United States. The term implies centrality—politically, economically, or geographically: {mainland China} versus Taiwan, {mainland Europe} versus Britain.

Mainlining is injecting a drug directly into a vein for immediate effect: {He'd been mainlining heroin for years}. The term comes from the "main line"—a major vein. Figuratively, mainlining means consuming something intensely or in large quantities: {She spent the weekend mainlining true crime podcasts}.

A mainstay is a principal support—the thing or person that holds something together or keeps it going. A business might be the mainstay of a local economy; a reliable employee might be the mainstay of a department: {Coffee has been the mainstay of the Colombian export economy}. The word comes from sailing, where the mainstay is the rope supporting the mainmast.

Mainstream refers to the dominant current of thought, taste, or activity in a culture—what most people accept, consume, or practice. Something mainstream has broad appeal and wide acceptance: {mainstream media}, {mainstream politics}. The term often carries a hint of conventionality, contrasted with alternative, underground, or niche movements: {The band went mainstream after their third album}. To mainstream something is to bring it into general acceptance: {The internet mainstreamed behaviors that were once fringe}.

Maintain means to keep something in its existing state or condition. You maintain a car by servicing it regularly, maintain a friendship by staying in touch, maintain your composure by not losing it. To maintain a position is to hold it against challenge: {She maintained her innocence throughout the trial}. Maintain also means to provide for: {He maintains his family on a modest salary}. A maintained thing continues without deterioration; an unmaintained one falls apart.

Maintenance is the work of keeping something in proper condition. Building maintenance includes repairs, cleaning, and upkeep. Car maintenance means oil changes and tune-ups. The word extends to preserving any state: {maintenance of law and order}, {maintenance of good health}. In legal contexts, maintenance refers to financial support paid to a former spouse—what's also called alimony. {The divorce settlement included monthly maintenance payments.}

Majestic describes something that inspires awe through grandeur, dignity, or nobility. Mountains, cathedrals, and ancient trees are majestic. A majestic {view} commands attention. Majestic bearing suggests regal composure: {She entered with majestic calm}. The word implies both scale and grace—power that doesn't need to assert itself.

Majesty is grandeur or dignity that inspires awe—the quality of being impressively great: {the majesty of the mountains}, {the majesty of the law}. With a capital M and a possessive, Majesty is a title for royalty: {Her Majesty the Queen}, {Your Majesty}. The word carries connotations of power, nobility, and commanding presence.

Major has two main jobs as an adjective: one conveys importance or something on a large scale (major renovation), and the other complements minor. The noun major designates a number of things, most often a high military rank, and an area of concentration at an American university or a student who has declared such an area (chemistry major). To major in a subject is to make it your main field of study. In music, major denotes the most common scale that melodies are based on (C major).

Majority means the greater part or more than half of a total: {The majority of voters supported the measure}. In elections, a majority is more than 50 percent, distinguished from a plurality (the largest share when no one reaches half). Majority also marks the age of legal adulthood: {She reached her majority at eighteen}. As an adjective, it modifies nouns to indicate dominance: {majority opinion}, {majority rule}.

Creation – either tangible or intangible – is at the core of make. You make a cake or make trouble. Make is usually transitive, with the object being the thing created, but it has some intransitive uses typically relating to behavior: She made as if to let me pass. He made like he knew me. Make is also used idiomatically, such as make friends, make a difference, or make a gesture; although it would be more accurate to use verbs like do or get, it’s just the way we talk. As a noun, make is used as a synonym for brand: The make and model of the car.

Makeout functions as an adjective or noun describing romantic or sexual kissing and touching, typically prolonged and passionate: {a makeout session}, {the car was a popular makeout spot}. The two-word verb phrase {make out} is far more common: {They made out in the back seat}.

A makeover is a transformation of appearance, typically involving changes to hair, makeup, clothing, or style. The term extends to renovations of spaces {kitchen makeover} or overhauls of organizations {corporate makeover}. Reality television popularized the dramatic reveal format: {She got a complete makeover on the show}. The verb phrase is make over.

A maker is someone who makes something. In compounds, it specifies what: {a filmmaker}, {a dressmaker}, {a troublemaker}. The maker movement celebrates hands-on creation of physical objects, often with tools like 3D printers: {a maker space}, {a maker faire}. To {meet your maker} is to die—maker here meaning God as creator. (Capitalized Maker refers to God.)

Makers are people who create or produce things. The term often implies hands-on craftsmanship: {The makers of fine furniture take pride in their work}. In recent use, maker culture celebrates DIY electronics, 3D printing, and artisanal production. A product's maker is its manufacturer. Your Maker, capitalized, is God—meeting your Maker means dying.

Makeshift describes something improvised or assembled from whatever is available when the proper materials or equipment are lacking. A makeshift shelter might be constructed from tarps and branches; a makeshift bandage from a torn shirt. The word carries connotations of temporary, rough-and-ready solutions—functional but not ideal. {They set up a makeshift stage in the parking lot.} As a noun, a makeshift is the improvised thing itself: {The cardboard box served as a makeshift for a proper desk.}

Makeup is cosmetics applied to the face—foundation, lipstick, eyeshadow, mascara: {She put on her makeup before leaving}. The word also means composition or constitution: {the genetic makeup of a species}, {the makeup of a committee}. A makeup exam or assignment is one taken after missing the original. To make up is to reconcile after a quarrel, to invent {(make up a story)}, or to compensate {(make up for lost time)}.

Making is the act of creating or producing something: {the making of a film}, {bread making}. The phrase {in the making} describes something being formed or developed: {a disaster in the making}, {history in the making}. If an experience is {the making of} someone, it shapes them into who they become. The makings are the necessary qualities or ingredients: {She has the makings of a great leader}.

Makuuchi is the top division in professional sumo wrestling, comprising the sport's elite wrestlers. The division includes roughly 42 wrestlers, ranked from yokozuna (grand champion) at the top through various grades down to maegashira at the bottom. Tournaments feature makuuchi bouts as the main event: {He was finally promoted to makuuchi after years in the lower divisions}.

Malaria is an infectious disease transmitted by mosquitoes, causing recurring fever, chills, and flu-like symptoms. The disease remains a major killer in tropical regions, particularly sub-Saharan Africa. {She contracted malaria while working in the Congo}. Antimalarial drugs can prevent or treat infection. The word comes from Italian for "bad air," reflecting the old belief that swamp vapors caused the illness.

Malarkey is nonsense, foolishness, or insincere talk—the kind of stuff someone says when they're trying to sound convincing but aren't making any real sense. It's an informal word, often used to dismiss something as ridiculous or untrue: {Don't give me that malarkey about the dog eating your homework}. The word has a slightly old-fashioned, playful quality, sometimes appearing as malarky.

Male designates the sex that produces sperm rather than eggs—the reproductive role that fertilizes rather than gestates. In humans, a male is a man or boy. The word works as both noun and adjective: {the male of the species}, {male pattern baldness}, {male privilege}. Male connectors in electronics have projecting parts that insert into female receptacles. Beyond biology, male often signals masculinity or maleness as social categories: {male-dominated industries}, {male gaze}.

Malevolence is the quality of wishing harm or evil upon others—active ill will rather than mere indifference. The word suggests a deliberate, almost gleeful hostility: {There was pure malevolence in his eyes}. Where malice might be petty or personal, malevolence implies something darker and more sustained.

A malfunction is a failure to work correctly. Equipment malfunctions when it stops operating as designed: {The engine malfunctioned mid-flight}. The word applies to mechanical, electronic, or biological systems—a wardrobe malfunction exposes what clothing should cover, and a brain malfunction suggests cognitive failure. Unlike breakdown, malfunction implies partial or intermittent failure rather than complete stoppage.

Malice is the intention to harm others or see them suffer. It implies deliberate cruelty rather than carelessness or indifference: {There was no malice in her teasing—she was just playing}. In law, malice aforethought is the mental state required for murder charges, indicating premeditation. {He acted without malice} often serves as a defense or excuse.

Malicious describes intent to cause harm or distress. A malicious {rumor} is spread deliberately to damage someone's reputation. Malicious {software} (malware) is designed to harm computer systems. The word implies not just harmful action but pleasure or satisfaction in causing injury: {a malicious grin}. Where harmful might be accidental, malicious never is.

Malignant describes something harmful and spreading—evil that actively works against wellbeing. A malignant tumor is cancerous, growing invasively and threatening life, unlike a benign one. Outside medicine, malignant characterizes intense ill will: {a malignant influence}, {malignant gossip}. The word suggests not just harm but something that worsens over time if unchecked.

A mall is a large enclosed shopping center with multiple stores, restaurants, and common areas under one roof. The term comes from a shaded walkway or promenade—originally a place for playing pall-mall, a croquet-like game. That older sense survives in some place names and in the grassy expanse called the National Mall in Washington, D.C. In everyday American usage, mall almost always means a shopping complex: {Let's meet at the food court in the mall}.

A mallet is a hammer with a large head, typically made of wood, rubber, or rawhide, used for striking without damaging the surface: {She tapped the chisel with a wooden mallet}. Mallets are used in croquet and polo to hit balls, and in music to strike percussion instruments like xylophones and timpani.

Mallets are hammers with large heads, typically made of wood, rubber, or soft material. A carpenter uses a wooden mallet to strike chisels without damaging them. A croquet mallet drives balls through wickets. Percussionists strike xylophones and timpani with mallets. The soft head delivers force without marring surfaces or producing harsh sounds.

Malls are large retail complexes housing multiple stores, restaurants, and services under one roof. The American shopping mall became a symbol of suburban consumer culture in the late twentieth century: {We spent Saturday afternoons wandering the mall}. Many malls have declined as shopping shifted online, leaving dead malls and repurposed spaces. A mall can also be a shaded public promenade.

Malpractice is improper, negligent, or unethical conduct by a professional—especially a doctor or lawyer—that causes harm to a client or patient. A {malpractice suit} seeks damages for such harm: {The surgeon faces malpractice charges after operating on the wrong knee}. The term implies violation of professional standards rather than ordinary negligence.

Malt is grain, usually barley, that has been allowed to sprout and then dried, a process that converts starches to sugars. This malted grain is essential for brewing beer and distilling whiskey, giving these beverages their characteristic flavor. A malt or malted is also short for a milkshake made with malt powder. As a verb, to malt grain is to put it through the malting process. {The brewery sources its malt from local farms.}

Malware is software designed to damage, disrupt, or gain unauthorized access to computer systems. The term covers viruses, worms, trojans, ransomware, spyware, and other malicious programs: {The IT department detected malware on several company laptops}. Short for "malicious software."

Mama is a child's word for mother, one of the earliest sounds babies produce. It appears across many languages because the sounds are among the first humans learn to make. Adults use mama affectionately or informally: {I'm going to visit my mama}. In some contexts, mama addresses or refers to any woman, sometimes flirtatiously: {Hey mama, what's your name?}

Mamaloshen is Yiddish for "mother tongue," referring to Yiddish itself—the language spoken at home, learned from one's mother rather than from formal education. The term carries warmth and nostalgia, evoking Jewish domestic life and cultural continuity: {She still dreams in mamaloshen}. Sometimes used more broadly for any native language with deep emotional resonance.

Mambo is a Cuban dance and musical style characterized by syncopated rhythms and dramatic movements. The dance emerged in Havana in the 1940s and became a ballroom sensation internationally. As a verb, to mambo is to perform this dance: {We mamboed until the band packed up}. The music features brass, percussion, and call-and-response vocals.

A mammal is a warm-blooded vertebrate animal distinguished by having hair or fur, giving birth to live young (with few exceptions), and nursing offspring with milk produced by mammary glands—the feature from which the class gets its name. Mammals range from tiny shrews to blue whales and include humans. The term appears frequently in scientific and educational contexts: {Dolphins are mammals, not fish}. {The exhibit featured mammals native to North America}.

Mammals are warm-blooded vertebrates that nurse their young with milk produced by mammary glands—the feature that gives the class its name. Most mammals give birth to live young, though a few like the platypus lay eggs. Humans, whales, bats, and mice are all mammals. The word works as both scientific classification and casual grouping: {Mammals dominated after the dinosaurs disappeared}.

A mammoth was a large, hairy elephant that lived during the Ice Age, now extinct. The word survives mainly as an adjective meaning enormous or colossal: {a mammoth undertaking}, {a project of mammoth proportions}. The adjective carries connotations of impressive scale rather than mere size.

Mammoths were large, hairy elephants that roamed cold regions during the Ice Age, now extinct for thousands of years. The word commonly appears figuratively to describe anything enormous or unwieldy: {a mammoth undertaking}, {a mammoth corporation}. As an adjective, mammoth means huge: {The project required mammoth effort}.
Man designates a male human, and more problematically, humans in general. When people use man as an interjection it usually indicates a feeling of surprise that may be negative or positive.

Manage means to handle, direct, or control something successfully. You manage a business, a team, or your finances. To manage is also to cope or get by: {We'll manage somehow}. If you {manage to} do something, you succeed despite difficulty: {She managed to finish before the deadline}. A more dismissive sense implies barely tolerating: {I can't manage another bite}.

Management is the activity of controlling or dealing with something. People who do this can also be called management: The management is considering several vendors for the cleaning contract. Anything that is conceived as being controllable in some way can be a target for management, such as risk, waste, resources, projects, and assets. In a medical context, management usually refers to the ways that health professionals deal with medical conditions: The management of advanced-stage patients is not well developed.

A manager is a person who directs or supervises others, especially in a workplace: {She's the manager of the sales department}. The term extends to anyone who handles affairs for another—a band's manager, a boxer's manager. In sports, a manager oversees a team's strategy and personnel. To manage is to handle or cope: {I can manage on my own}.

A manatee is a large, slow-moving aquatic mammal found in warm coastal waters, rivers, and estuaries. Manatees are herbivorous, grazing on sea grasses and other aquatic plants. Their rounded bodies, paddle-like tails, and gentle disposition have earned them the nickname "sea cow." {We spotted a manatee surfacing near the boat.}

Manatees is the plural of manatee, a large aquatic mammal found in warm coastal waters and rivers. These slow-moving herbivores have paddle-shaped tails and flipper-like forelimbs. Sometimes called sea cows for their grazing habits and docile nature: {We spotted manatees in the Florida springs}.

Mancala is a family of board games involving the transfer of seeds, stones, or other small pieces between rows of pits or hollows. Players capture pieces by strategic distribution—picking up all pieces from one pit and dropping them one by one into subsequent pits. The games originated in Africa and the Middle East and remain popular worldwide: {We played mancala on the beach}.

A manchild is an adult male who displays the emotional maturity, responsibility, or self-sufficiency of a child. The term is almost always pejorative, suggesting someone who expects others to handle adult tasks while he plays video games, avoids commitment, or throws tantrums: {Her ex was a total manchild—couldn't even do his own laundry}. Sometimes hyphenated or written as two words.

A mandala is a geometric design, typically circular, used in Hindu and Buddhist traditions as an aid to meditation. The intricate patterns radiate from a center point, representing the universe or wholeness. The term has broadened to include any circular design meant to focus attention or represent cosmic unity: {She colored mandalas to relax}, {The arrangement of stones formed a natural mandala}.

A mandarin is a small, sweet citrus fruit with loose skin that peels easily—a variety of orange popular for snacking. The word also means a powerful bureaucrat or influential figure, especially one seen as out of touch: {The policy was crafted by Washington mandarins with no understanding of rural life}. This sense comes from the Chinese imperial officials who administered the empire for centuries. (Capitalized Mandarin is the Chinese language.)

Mandarins are the small, sweet citrus fruits with loose, easily peeled skin—clementines and tangerines are varieties. The word also names powerful bureaucrats or officials, especially in imperial China, where mandarins administered the empire through examinations and hierarchy. By extension, any elite insider wielding quiet influence: {the mandarins of Wall Street}, {media mandarins}. Mandarin Chinese is the dominant dialect of Chinese, spoken by over a billion people.

A mandate is an authoritative order or command, often from a government or institution: {The state issued a mask mandate}. It also means the authority granted by voters to elected officials: {The landslide victory gave her a clear mandate for reform}. To mandate something is to require it officially. The word carries weight—mandates aren't requests.

A mandolin is a stringed musical instrument with a rounded or flat back and a fretted neck, played by plucking paired strings with a pick. It belongs to the lute family and features prominently in bluegrass, folk, and Italian music: {He played mandolin in a bluegrass band}. Separately, a mandolin or mandoline is a kitchen tool with adjustable blades for slicing vegetables into uniform pieces.

A mane is the long hair growing on the neck of certain animals, especially horses and male lions. The word extends to thick, flowing human hair: {She tossed her mane of red curls}. A lion's mane suggests majesty and power, which carries into figurative uses describing abundant hair.

A maneater is an animal that preys on humans—typically a tiger, lion, shark, or crocodile that has developed a taste for human flesh: {The village lived in fear of the maneater}. Extended to people, maneater describes a woman who aggressively pursues men or uses them callously: {She's a real maneater}. Also spelled man-eater.

Maneuver is a planned movement requiring skill or strategy. Military maneuvers are tactical troop movements; a car maneuver might be a three-point turn. The word extends to any clever action meant to gain advantage: {a political maneuver}, {legal maneuvers to delay the trial}. To maneuver is to guide something skillfully through obstacles or to manipulate a situation: {She maneuvered him into agreeing}. Also spelled manoeuvre in British English.

Maneuvering is the act of moving skillfully or strategically—physically navigating a space or figuratively working toward an advantage. A driver maneuvering through traffic makes careful adjustments; a politician maneuvering for position calculates each move. The word often implies cleverness or cunning: {There was considerable maneuvering behind the scenes before the vote}. Also spelled manoeuvring in British English.

Maneuvers are planned movements requiring skill and coordination. Military maneuvers are large-scale training exercises simulating combat conditions: {The troops conducted maneuvers in the desert}. A driver maneuvers through traffic; a politician maneuvers for advantage. The word implies calculated, often clever positioning—physical or strategic: {Her maneuvers to secure the promotion were subtle but effective}.

Manga is Japanese comic books and graphic novels, characterized by distinctive visual styles, black-and-white artwork, and right-to-left reading format. The term covers all genres—from action and romance to horror and slice-of-life. In Japan, manga is mainstream entertainment for all ages; in the West, it anchors a devoted subculture: {She spent the weekend reading manga}. The plural is manga.

A manger is a trough or open box in a stable or barn from which horses and cattle eat. The word is most familiar from Christmas imagery, where the infant Jesus was laid in a manger because there was no room at the inn. Outside of nativity scenes, manger appears mainly in rural or agricultural contexts. {The horses gathered around the manger at feeding time.}

Mangle has two unrelated meanings. One is to damage severely by cutting, crushing, or tearing: {The machinery mangled his arm}. Text or music can be mangled through poor handling: {The translation mangled the author's intent}. The other mangle is a device with rollers for pressing water from laundry or smoothing fabric—now largely obsolete. To mangle laundry is to run it through such a machine.

Mangled describes something badly damaged, mutilated, or disfigured—typically by crushing, tearing, or violent force. A body can be mangled in a car wreck; machinery can mangle a hand. The word extends to non-physical destruction: a mangled {pronunciation}, a mangled {translation}, a singer mangling a {song}. Whatever is mangled has been twisted beyond its proper form.

Mango is a tropical fruit with sweet, juicy orange flesh surrounding a large flat pit, covered by skin that ranges from green to yellow to red. Native to South Asia, mangoes are now cultivated throughout tropical regions and rank among the world's most popular fruits. The flesh can be eaten fresh, blended into smoothies, or used in chutneys and desserts. {Fresh mango with lime and chili is a perfect summer snack.}

Mangoes is the plural of mango, a tropical fruit with sweet, aromatic orange flesh surrounding a large flat seed. The fruit has smooth skin that ripens from green to yellow, orange, or red. Mangoes are eaten fresh, blended into smoothies, or used in chutneys and desserts: {The mangoes at the market were perfectly ripe}.

Mangos is a plural of mango, the sweet tropical fruit with yellow-orange flesh and a large flat pit. The fruit grows on trees native to South Asia but cultivated throughout warm climates. Both mangos and mangoes are standard plurals: {She bought three mangos at the market}.

A mangrove is a tropical tree or shrub that grows in coastal swamps and tidal waters, with distinctive tangled roots that rise above the waterline. Mangroves form dense thickets called mangrove swamps or mangrove forests, which protect shorelines from erosion and serve as nurseries for fish and other marine life: {The mangroves were teeming with crabs}.

Mangroves are trees and shrubs that grow in coastal tropical and subtropical waters, adapted to survive in salty, oxygen-poor soil. Their tangled root systems rise above the waterline, stabilizing shorelines and creating nursery habitat for fish and crustaceans. Mangrove forests—also called mangroves—buffer coasts against storms and erosion: {The mangroves protected the village from the worst of the hurricane}.

To manhandle is to move something by brute physical force rather than machinery or finesse: {We manhandled the piano up three flights of stairs}. It also means to handle someone roughly or aggressively: {Security guards manhandled the protester out of the building}. The word implies more muscle than care.

Manhandled means physically handled in a rough or forceful way: {The bouncer manhandled him out of the club}. It implies being shoved, grabbed, or moved without gentleness or consent. Figuratively, to be manhandled is to be treated harshly or dominated: {Our team got manhandled in the second half}.

Manhandling is rough physical handling of a person—grabbing, pushing, dragging, or moving them without care or consent: {Security guards were caught manhandling protesters}. The word implies force that's excessive or undignified. It extends to objects treated roughly: {They were manhandling the furniture down the stairs}.

Manhood is the state of being an adult male, or the qualities traditionally associated with men—courage, strength, self-reliance: {He proved his manhood on the battlefield}. It also refers to men collectively: {the manhood of the nation}. Manhood can be a euphemism for male genitals: {a blow to his manhood}. The word often carries cultural weight about what it means to be a "real man."

A manhunt is an organized search for a person, typically a fugitive or criminal suspect. Police conduct manhunts after prison escapes or violent crimes: {The manhunt for the escaped convict entered its third day}. Despite the word, manhunts pursue people of any gender.

Mania is intense enthusiasm or obsession, often excessive: {Beatlemania swept the country}, {a mania for collecting vintage watches}. In psychiatry, mania is a mental state marked by abnormally elevated mood, energy, and activity—the "up" phase in bipolar disorder. Someone in a manic episode may feel invincible, sleep little, and make reckless decisions. The suffix -mania forms words for obsessive interests or conditions: pyromania, kleptomania, megalomania.

A maniac is a person who behaves wildly or dangerously, especially one gripped by violent madness. The word now appears most often in casual exaggeration: {He drives like a maniac}, {She's a maniac about keeping the house clean}. In these uses, maniac suggests excessive intensity rather than actual insanity.

Maniacs is the plural of maniac—people who behave wildly, recklessly, or with dangerous obsession. The word originally meant someone suffering from mania, a mental state of extreme agitation, but now it's mostly informal: {These maniacs were driving ninety on the highway}. It can also describe intense enthusiasm: {fitness maniacs}, {sports maniacs}.

Manic describes a state of intense energy, excitement, or agitation. In psychiatry, it refers to the elevated phase of bipolar disorder—marked by racing thoughts, decreased need for sleep, and impulsive behavior. More loosely, manic describes anyone in a frenzied or hyperactive state: {She cleaned the entire house in a manic burst of energy}. The word carries connotations of being slightly out of control.

A manicure is cosmetic treatment of the fingernails and hands—trimming, shaping, buffing, and often applying polish. The verb means to perform such treatment: {She manicured her nails before the interview}. Extended uses describe anything carefully groomed or meticulously maintained: {a manicured lawn}, {manicured hedges}.

Manicures are cosmetic treatments for the fingernails and hands—trimming, shaping, buffing, and often polishing the nails, along with softening the cuticles and skin. As a verb, to manicure is to perform such grooming: {She manicures her nails every Sunday}. The term extends to any careful tending: {a manicured lawn}, {manicured hedges}.

Manifest means clearly apparent or obvious to perception or understanding: {Her disappointment was manifest}. As a verb, to manifest is to show or display: {The disease manifests as a rash}, {He manifested no interest in the project}. A manifest is also a document listing a ship's or aircraft's cargo and passengers. To manifest something can mean to bring it into reality through intention or belief—a sense popularized by self-help culture: {She's trying to manifest her dream job}.

Manifestation is something that makes an abstract quality visible or concrete: {The riots were a manifestation of widespread discontent}. A disease's manifestations are its symptoms. In spiritual and self-help contexts, manifestation is the practice of bringing desires into reality through focused thought or intention: {She credits manifestation for her career success}. The word can also mean a ghost or apparition.

Manifesting is the practice of visualizing or affirming desired outcomes in the belief that positive thinking can attract them into reality. The term comes from New Age and self-help contexts, where one might manifest wealth, love, or success through focused intention: {I've been manifesting a promotion}. Often used skeptically or ironically: {Maybe if I keep manifesting, my rent will pay itself}.

A manifesto is a public declaration of intentions, beliefs, or principles, typically issued by a political party, movement, or individual. Manifestos announce what someone stands for and what they plan to do: {The Communist Manifesto}, {an artist's manifesto}. The word suggests boldness—manifestos don't hedge or equivocate; they proclaim.

Manipulate means to handle or control something with skill, whether physical objects or abstract situations. A scientist manipulates {variables in an experiment}, while a skilled negotiator manipulates {the conversation toward a favorable outcome}. The word often carries negative connotations of deception or exploitation: {He manipulated her into signing the contract}. This darker sense suggests controlling people through unfair or devious means, exploiting their emotions or vulnerabilities for personal gain.

Manipulating is handling or controlling something with skill, whether physical objects or abstract situations. You might be manipulating controls, manipulating data, or manipulating public opinion. The word often carries negative connotations—manipulating people means influencing them through cunning or deception rather than honest persuasion: {She's manipulating you into feeling guilty}.

Manipulation is the act of handling or controlling something with skill—manipulating objects, data, or machinery. The word extends to influencing people or situations through indirect, deceptive, or underhanded means: {He accused her of manipulation to get what she wanted}. The negative connotation dominates in interpersonal contexts, suggesting exploitation of others' emotions or vulnerabilities. In technical settings—genetic manipulation, image manipulation—the word stays neutral, meaning simply to alter or adjust.

Manipulations are acts of handling, controlling, or influencing something—often with skill or cunning. Physical manipulations involve working with objects: {spinal manipulations}, {manipulations of the controls}. More often the word suggests calculated influence over people or situations: {His manipulations eventually came to light}. Data manipulations may be legitimate analysis or deceptive tampering, depending on context.

Manipulative describes behavior that influences others through indirect, deceptive, or exploitative means rather than honest communication. A manipulative person uses guilt, flattery, or emotional pressure to get what they want: {She recognized his apology as manipulative—designed to make her feel guilty}. The word carries strong negative connotations, implying calculated self-interest. Separately, manipulative can simply mean involving physical manipulation: {manipulative skills in surgery}.

A manipulator is someone who influences others through indirect, deceptive, or underhanded means—working people like levers to get what they want. The term implies skillful but unethical control: {He's a master manipulator who makes you think everything was your idea}. In mechanical contexts, a manipulator is a device for handling objects remotely or precisely, as in robotics or laboratory equipment.

Manipulators are people or things that manipulate. A person who manipulates others—through deception, emotional pressure, or exploitation—is a manipulator: {He's a manipulator who preys on people's insecurities}. The word also refers to mechanical devices for handling objects, especially in contexts where direct human contact is impractical: {robotic manipulators in a nuclear facility}.

Mankind is the human race collectively—all people past, present, and future. The word emphasizes humanity as a whole rather than individuals: {one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind}. Some avoid it as gendered, preferring humankind or humanity, though mankind has historically been understood as gender-neutral.

Manliness is the quality of possessing traits traditionally associated with men—strength, courage, decisiveness, stoicism. The word carries approval: {He showed real manliness in standing up for his beliefs}. What counts as manliness varies by era and culture; Victorian manliness emphasized moral character, while modern usage often stresses physical toughness or emotional resilience.

Manly describes qualities traditionally associated with men—strength, courage, fortitude, decisiveness. A manly {handshake} is firm. A manly {voice} is deep. The word carries approval: to be manly is to embody these traits admirably. The concept is culturally constructed and shifts over time, but the word retains its association with masculine ideals rather than mere maleness.

Manna is the miraculous food that, according to the Bible, God provided to the Israelites wandering in the desert. By extension, manna is any unexpected sustenance or blessing that arrives providentially: {The grant was manna from heaven for the struggling nonprofit}. The phrase {manna from heaven} has become the standard form, emphasizing divine or fortunate origin.

A mannequin is a life-sized model of a human body, typically used to display clothing in stores. The word can also mean a person who models clothes—though this sense has largely given way to *model*. Mannequins are usually made of plastic or fiberglass, posed in lifelike positions: {The mannequin in the window wore a summer dress}. Figuratively, calling someone a mannequin suggests they're stiff, expressionless, or merely decorative.

Mannequins are life-sized human figures used to display clothing in stores. They're typically made of fiberglass or plastic, posed in lifelike positions, and may have realistic features or be stylized and featureless. The word extends to people who seem stiff or expressionless: {She stood there like a mannequin}. In medical and emergency training, mannequins are practice dummies for CPR or other procedures.

Manner is the way something happens or is done: {She spoke in a calm manner}. Someone's manner is their characteristic behavior or bearing: {His brusque manner put people off}. In the plural, manners are social conduct and etiquette—good manners show politeness, bad manners show rudeness. {All manner of} means all kinds of: {all manner of strange creatures}. {In a manner of speaking} qualifies a statement as roughly but not precisely true.

Mannerisms are distinctive habits of speech, gesture, or behavior that characterize a particular person. They are often unconscious quirks—a way of clearing the throat, a repeated phrase, a characteristic hand movement—that others notice and may find endearing, annoying, or useful for identification. Actors study mannerisms to portray real people convincingly. {His mannerisms reminded me of my father.} The word sometimes carries a slightly negative connotation, suggesting affectation or excessive peculiarity.

Manners are the social behaviors that govern polite interaction—saying please and thank you, chewing with your mouth closed, not interrupting. Someone with good manners follows these conventions; someone with bad manners violates them. {Mind your manners.} The word also refers to customs more broadly: a novel of manners depicts the social codes of a particular time and place.
Manoeuvre is the British spelling of the noun and verb maneuver.

A manor is a large country house with surrounding land, historically the estate of a feudal lord. The term evokes old wealth and aristocratic life: {the lord of the manor}, {a Victorian manor house}. In British slang, {manor} means one's home territory or neighborhood: {This is my manor}.

Manors is the plural of manor, a large country house with surrounding land, historically the estate of a feudal lord. The term evokes aristocratic wealth and rural grandeur: {stately manors dotting the English countryside}. In British slang, manor means one's home turf or neighborhood: {Stay off my manor}.

A mansabdar was a military or civil officer in the Mughal Empire, holding a rank (mansab) that determined their status, pay, and the number of cavalry they were obligated to maintain. The system, established by Emperor Akbar in the 16th century, organized imperial administration through numbered ranks: {He rose from a low mansabdar to command thousands of horsemen}.

A mansion is a large, impressive house, typically one that conveys wealth and status through its size, architecture, and grounds. The term suggests grandeur beyond mere spaciousness—mansions often feature multiple stories, numerous rooms, and elaborate design elements. {The old mansion had fallen into disrepair after decades of neglect.} In religious contexts, mansion can refer to a dwelling place in heaven, as in the biblical phrase "many mansions."

Mansions are large, stately houses, grander than ordinary residences. The word implies wealth and status: {They toured the historic mansions of Newport}. Real estate marketing has stretched the term to cover any oversized suburban home. In older religious usage, mansions can mean dwelling places in heaven: {In my Father's house are many mansions}.

Manslaughter is the unlawful killing of a person without premeditation or malice—the element that distinguishes it from murder. Voluntary manslaughter occurs in the heat of passion or under extreme provocation. Involuntary manslaughter results from criminal negligence or recklessness: {The drunk driver was charged with manslaughter}. The distinction determines severity of punishment.

Mansplain means to explain something to a woman in a condescending way that assumes she doesn't already know it—typically when she knows as much or more than the man explaining. The term captures a gendered pattern where men presume incompetence in women: {He mansplained her own research to her at the conference}. The noun is mansplaining.

Mansplaining is when a man explains something to a woman in a condescending way that assumes she lacks knowledge she actually possesses. The term captures a specific dynamic: a man holding forth on a topic while ignoring signals that his listener already understands it, often better than he does. {He started mansplaining her own research to her.} The verb is mansplain.

A mantel is the shelf above a fireplace, often part of a decorative frame surrounding the opening. Family photos, clocks, and seasonal decorations commonly occupy this space: {She arranged the Christmas stockings along the mantel}. The full surround structure is sometimes called a mantelpiece.

A mantelpiece is the shelf above a fireplace, often part of a decorative frame surrounding the opening. It serves as a display surface for photographs, clocks, candles, or ornaments: {Family photos lined the mantelpiece}. The mantelpiece traditionally anchors a room's focal point, especially in older homes where the fireplace was central to daily life.

A manticore is a mythical creature from Persian legend, typically depicted with a human head, a lion's body, and a tail of venomous spines or scorpion stinger. The creature appears in bestiaries and fantasy literature as a fearsome predator: {The manticore stalked the hero through the labyrinth}.

A mantis is a predatory insect with an elongated body, triangular head, and distinctive forelegs held in a raised position as if in prayer—hence the common name praying mantis. Mantises are known for their stillness before striking prey and for the female's occasional habit of eating the male during or after mating. {A mantis sat motionless on the branch, waiting.}

Mantle is mainly a noun and should not be confused with its homonym mantel, even though both spellings are confusingly used for the latter. A mantle is a cloak. In figurative use, mantle is used to characterize something that covers or applies widely (mantle of secrecy). Mantle represents authority or responsibility in expression like don the mantle of director. In geology, the earth’s mantle is the middle layer between the top crust and the core.

A mantra is a word, phrase, or sound repeated during meditation or prayer, originally in Hindu and Buddhist traditions where Sanskrit syllables like {om} are believed to have spiritual power. The term has broadened to mean any statement or slogan repeated frequently to reinforce a belief or goal: {Her mantra is "progress, not perfection"}. In casual use, someone's mantra is simply their guiding principle or favorite saying.

Mantras are words or phrases repeated in meditation or prayer, originating in Hindu and Buddhist traditions. The term extends to any statement repeated for focus or motivation: {Her mantra is "one day at a time"}. In casual use, a mantra is simply a guiding principle someone returns to often: {The company's mantra of "move fast and break things" shaped its culture}.

Manual means done by hand rather than machine or automation: {a manual transmission}, {manual labor}. A manual is also a handbook—a book of instructions for operating something or learning a skill: {the car's owner's manual}, {a training manual}. The connection is that manuals were originally handwritten, and manual tasks require hands-on involvement.

Manufacture is to make things, especially in large quantities using machinery: {The company manufactures auto parts}. The word implies industrial production rather than handcraft. Manufactured goods are mass-produced products. To manufacture something can also mean to fabricate or invent it—manufactured {evidence}, a manufactured {crisis}. A manufacture is an instance of manufacturing or the thing produced.

Manufactured describes something produced by industrial processes, typically in a factory: {manufactured goods}, {manufactured housing}. The word often contrasts with handmade, natural, or organic. Figuratively, manufactured suggests something artificial or contrived rather than genuine: {manufactured outrage}, {a manufactured controversy}. The implication is that someone engineered the thing deliberately, often for manipulative purposes.

Manufacturing is the process of making goods from raw materials, typically on a large scale using machinery: {The region's economy depends on manufacturing}. The term covers everything from automobile plants to food processing. As an adjective, it describes this sector: {manufacturing jobs}, {manufacturing output}. The word often appears in discussions of economic policy and industrial decline.

Manure is animal dung used as fertilizer. Farmers spread manure on fields to enrich the soil with nutrients. The word can also function as a verb: {They manured the garden beds before planting}. Manure occasionally appears as a mild substitute for shit or bullshit: {That's a load of manure}.

A manuscript is a document written by hand, or in modern usage, an author's text before it becomes a published book: {The publisher rejected her manuscript}. Scholars study medieval manuscripts—handwritten books from before the printing press. In music, a manuscript is a composer's handwritten score. The adjective describes anything handwritten: {manuscript letters}.

Manuscripts are documents written by hand, particularly those created before the invention of printing. The term now extends to any author's original text before publication: {She submitted her manuscript to three publishers}. In academic contexts, a manuscript is a paper under review: {The manuscript was rejected by peer reviewers}. Manuscript can also function as an adjective describing handwritten items: {manuscript letters}, {manuscript maps}.

Many indicates a large number—the opposite of few. It modifies countable nouns: {many people}, {many reasons}, {many times}. As a pronoun, many stands alone: {Many were called, but few were chosen}. {A good many} and {a great many} intensify the quantity. {Many a} takes a singular noun but plural sense: {Many a soldier has fallen here}.

A map is a visual representation of an area showing features like roads, terrain, or boundaries. Maps can be literal {a map of Europe} or figurative {a map of the human genome}. To map is to create such a representation or to plan systematically: {We mapped out our strategy}. In math and computing, to map means to establish correspondences between sets or data structures.

Maple is a deciduous tree known for its lobed leaves and winged seeds that spiral as they fall. Many species produce sweet sap that can be boiled into maple syrup. The wood is prized for furniture, flooring, and musical instruments. Maple leaves turn brilliant colors in autumn; the leaf appears on Canada's flag.

A mapping is a correspondence between elements in one set and elements in another—each input matched to an output. The term appears in mathematics, computing, and genetics: {a mapping of genes on a chromosome}, {keyboard mappings}. More loosely, mapping means charting or surveying: {a mapping of the ocean floor}. To do a mapping is to map.

Maps are visual representations of geographic areas, showing features like roads, borders, and terrain. The word extends to any diagram showing relationships or structure: a {gene map}, a {site map}. To map something is to chart it or establish correspondences: {Scientists mapped the human genome}. To {map out} a plan is to plot it in detail.

A maraca is a percussion instrument consisting of a dried gourd or gourd-shaped container filled with seeds, beans, or pebbles, shaken to produce a rattling sound. Maracas are typically played in pairs and feature prominently in Latin American and Caribbean music: {The band's rhythm section included congas, bongos, and maracas}.

Maracas are handheld percussion instruments—hollow gourds or gourd-shaped containers filled with seeds, beads, or pebbles that rattle when shaken. They come in pairs and are associated especially with Latin American and Caribbean music: {The band's rhythm section featured congas and maracas}. Children's toy versions are common.

Maracatu is an Afro-Brazilian musical tradition and processional dance from northeastern Brazil, particularly Pernambuco. It features heavy percussion—especially the alfaia drums—call-and-response singing, and elaborately costumed performers representing African royalty. The term refers both to the musical genre and to the carnival groups that perform it: {The maracatu bloc paraded through Recife}.

A marathon is a long-distance footrace of 26.2 miles, the signature event of major road races worldwide: {She's training for the Boston Marathon}. The word extends to any prolonged, exhausting effort: a {marathon} session, {marathon} negotiations. As a verb, to marathon is to consume media in extended sessions: {We marathoned the entire series over the weekend}. (Capitalized Marathon is the ancient Greek battlefield.)

Marathons is the plural of marathon, a footrace of 26.2 miles (42.195 kilometers). The distance commemorates the legendary run from Marathon to Athens. Beyond running, marathon describes any prolonged, exhausting effort: {a marathon session of negotiations}, {a movie marathon}. The word emphasizes endurance over speed: {We pulled a marathon to finish the project}.

A marauder is someone who roams in search of things to steal or people to attack. The word evokes bands of raiders pillaging villages or countryside: {Marauders swept through the valley, taking livestock and grain}. Unlike a thief who targets specific valuables, a marauder suggests opportunistic violence and plunder.

Marauders are people who roam in search of things to steal or destroy—raiders, looters, pillagers. The word suggests bands rather than individuals, and violence rather than stealth: {Marauders swept through the village, taking whatever they could carry}. Unlike burglars, marauders operate openly and aggressively.

Marauding describes roving in search of things to steal or people to attack. Marauding bands or armies move through territory taking what they want by force. The word often appears with groups—{marauding pirates}, {marauding soldiers}, {marauding gangs}. It can extend to animals: {marauding wolves terrorized the village}.

Marble is a hard, metamorphic stone prized for its smooth texture and often striking veined patterns—used in sculpture, architecture, and flooring. A marble is also a small glass or stone ball used in children's games: {We played marbles at recess}. To {lose one's marbles} is to go crazy. As a verb, to marble is to give something a streaked, veined appearance: {marbled beef}, {marbled paper}.

Marbles are small glass or stone spheres used in children's games, typically played by flicking one marble to hit others: {We played marbles in the schoolyard}. The game itself is also called marbles. Figuratively, to {lose your marbles} is to lose your mind or sanity, while {to have all your marbles} means to remain mentally sharp.

Marbling is the pattern of veins or streaks resembling marble, or the process of creating such patterns. In bookbinding and paper arts, marbling produces swirled decorative designs by floating pigments on liquid. In meat, marbling refers to the white streaks of fat distributed through muscle tissue: {The steak had beautiful marbling}. Well-marbled beef is prized for tenderness and flavor.

March means to walk with regular, measured steps, typically with purposeful rhythm and often in formation. Soldiers march in military parades, protesters march for causes, and bands march while playing. The verb also has figurative uses: time marches on, and you can march someone somewhere by compelling them to go. To {march to the beat of a different drummer} means to act independently of others' expectations. {The troops marched twenty miles that day.} {Thousands marched in protest of the new policy.} (Capitalized March is the month.)

Marches is the plural of march—organized walks with a purpose, often political demonstrations or military movements: {Civil rights marches transformed American politics}. It also serves as the verb form for walking in measured steps: {The band marches at halftime}. Time marches on, and so does progress, whether we like it or not. (Capitalized Marches refers to border regions.)

Marching is walking with regular, measured steps, typically in formation or with purpose. Soldiers do it in parades, protesters in demonstrations. {The marching band led the procession.} Marching orders are instructions to move out, or figuratively, a dismissal: {She gave him his marching orders.}

A mare is an adult female horse, typically four years or older. The term extends to females of related animals: zebras, donkeys, mules. In horse breeding and racing, a mare's lineage matters as much as a stallion's: {The mare produced three Kentucky Derby winners}. Separately, mare appears in nightmare, from an Old English word for an evil spirit thought to suffocate sleepers.

Mares is the plural of mare, an adult female horse. The word appears in contexts involving breeding, racing, and general horsemanship: {The mares were moved to a separate pasture}. A {mare's nest} is a confused or illusory discovery—something that looks significant but turns out to be worthless or nonexistent.

Margarine is a butter substitute made from vegetable oils, water, and emulsifiers. It was developed as a cheaper alternative to butter and later marketed as a healthier option, though nutritional views have shifted over time. Margarine typically comes in tubs or sticks: {I use margarine for baking when I'm out of butter}.

A margarita is a cocktail made with tequila, lime juice, and triple sec or another orange liqueur, typically served in a wide-rimmed glass with salt on the rim. It can be served on the rocks or blended with ice into a frozen drink. Variations include flavored versions like strawberry or mango: {We ordered a pitcher of margaritas for the table}. (Capitalized Margarita is a given name.)

Margaritas is the plural of margarita, a cocktail made with tequila, lime juice, and triple sec or other orange liqueur, typically served in a salt-rimmed glass. The drink comes frozen or on the rocks, and in countless fruit variations: {strawberry margaritas}, {mango margaritas}. {We ordered a round of margaritas.}

A margin is the blank space at the edge of a page or other surface, separating content from the border. This sense of edge or boundary extends to other uses: the margin of a lake, or winning by a narrow margin (a small gap between competitors). In business, margin refers to the difference between cost and selling price—your profit margin. Financial margin also names funds deposited as security for a transaction, as when buying stocks {on margin}. To marginalize someone is to push them to the edges of society or relevance.

Marginalised describes people or groups pushed to the edges of society, excluded from power, opportunity, or mainstream participation. The word implies systemic disadvantage rather than individual misfortune: {marginalised communities}, {economically marginalised populations}. Someone marginalised in a discussion has been sidelined or ignored. Also spelled marginalized.

Marginalized describes people or groups pushed to the edges of society—denied full participation, resources, or influence. The term implies systemic disadvantage rather than individual misfortune: {marginalized communities}, {economically marginalized populations}. Someone marginalized has been relegated to the margins, treated as less important or powerful than the mainstream.

Margins are the blank spaces surrounding text on a page, or more broadly, the edges or borders of any area. In business, margin is the difference between cost and selling price—your profit margin. To buy stock {on margin} is to borrow money from a broker to make the purchase. Figuratively, margins suggest periphery or barely-sufficient amounts: living {on the margins} of society, winning {by a narrow margin}. Something marginal exists at the edge, often implying minimal importance or viability.

Mariachi is a style of Mexican folk music featuring trumpets, violins, and guitars, or a musician who performs it. The music is celebratory and often heard at weddings, quinceañeras, and Mexican restaurants. A mariachi band typically wears matching charro outfits—fitted suits with silver buttons and wide-brimmed sombreros: {The mariachis serenaded the birthday girl}.

Mariachis are traditional Mexican musical groups, or the musicians who perform in them. A mariachi ensemble typically features violins, trumpets, and guitars, with performers in distinctive charro suits—fitted jackets, tight pants, and wide-brimmed sombreros. The music is associated with celebrations, serenades, and Mexican restaurants: {The mariachis played "Cielito Lindo" at the wedding}.

Marigold is a garden flower with dense, ruffled blooms in shades of yellow, orange, and gold. The plants are hardy annuals, popular for borders and companion planting because their pungent scent repels certain pests. {She planted marigolds around the tomatoes.} The name combines Mary (the Virgin) with gold, referring to the flower's color.

Marigolds are flowering plants with round, densely petaled blooms in shades of yellow, orange, and gold. Common in gardens and borders, they're valued for their hardiness and ability to repel certain pests. The flowers have a distinctive pungent smell. Marigolds appear in Day of the Dead celebrations and other cultural traditions honoring the dead.

Marijuana is the dried leaves and flowers of the cannabis plant, used as a psychoactive drug. It's typically smoked or eaten to produce a relaxed, euphoric high. Legal status varies widely—recreational use is permitted in some U.S. states and countries while remaining illegal elsewhere. {She bought marijuana at the dispensary}. Also called weed, pot, grass, and many other slang terms.

A marina is a harbor with moorings and facilities for pleasure boats and yachts: {We docked at the marina for the night}. Marinas typically offer fuel, repairs, and sometimes shops and restaurants. (Capitalized Marina is the given name.)

A marinade is a seasoned liquid in which food soaks before cooking, typically containing acid (vinegar, citrus, wine) and oil along with herbs and spices. The acid tenderizes meat and helps flavors penetrate: {Let the chicken sit in the marinade overnight}. To marinate is to soak food this way.

Marinara is a tomato-based Italian sauce typically made with garlic, olive oil, and herbs like basil and oregano. It's among the simplest pasta sauces—no meat, no cream: {spaghetti with marinara}, {marinara dipping sauce for breadsticks}. The name comes from Italian for "sailor-style," though the connection to seafaring is murky.

To marinate is to soak food in a seasoned liquid before cooking, allowing flavors to penetrate and acids to tenderize: {Marinate the chicken overnight}. The liquid itself is a marinade. Figuratively, to marinate in something is to steep in it over time: {He marinated in resentment for years}. {Let that idea marinate} means to sit with a thought before responding.

Marinated describes food that has been soaked in a seasoned liquid to absorb flavor or become more tender. The marinade typically contains acid (vinegar, citrus, wine), oil, and aromatics. {The marinated chicken was incredibly flavorful.} Figuratively, something marinated has been steeped in an influence over time: {a mind marinated in conspiracy theories}.

Marinating is the process of soaking food in a seasoned liquid to add flavor or tenderize it. Meat, fish, and vegetables can all benefit from marinating. The liquid—a marinade—typically contains acid (vinegar, citrus, wine), oil, and seasonings. {The chicken has been marinating overnight.} By extension, to marinate on something is to let it sit in your mind: {Let me marinate on that idea}.

Marine means relating to the sea: marine {biology}, marine {life}, marine {mammals}. It describes things found in or connected to ocean environments. Marine also refers to seafaring commerce and naval matters: marine {insurance}, merchant marine. As a noun, a marine is a soldier trained for sea-based military operations, though this sense is more commonly capitalized. {The marine ecosystem is under threat from pollution.} (Capitalized Marine refers specifically to members of the U.S. Marine Corps.)

A mariner is a sailor—someone who navigates or works aboard a ship. The term is somewhat formal or literary, appearing in titles like {The Rime of the Ancient Mariner} and in legal or official contexts: {merchant mariner}, {mariner's license}. It suggests professional seafaring rather than casual boating.

Marines are soldiers who serve in a military force specializing in naval operations and amphibious warfare—fighting from ships and establishing beachheads. The term typically refers to members of the U.S. Marine Corps: {Her son joined the marines after high school}. Marines are distinct from regular army or navy personnel, trained for rapid deployment and combat in diverse environments.

A marionette is a puppet controlled by strings or wires attached to its limbs and head, manipulated from above by a puppeteer. The term distinguishes string puppets from hand puppets or rod puppets. Figuratively, a marionette is someone whose actions are controlled by another: {He was just a marionette dancing to the CEO's tune}.

Marionettes are puppets controlled from above by strings or wires attached to their limbs and head. The puppeteer manipulates these strings to make the figure walk, gesture, and move with lifelike fluidity. Figuratively, a marionette is someone controlled by another: {The dictator's cabinet were mere marionettes, dancing to his whims}.

The essential idea of mark is a thing that stands as a visible sign for something else: Leave a mark where you stopped. This general meaning has spawned numerous related senses, both other nouns and verbs. Having or bearing all the marks of something gives a strong impression that it is true: The review had all the marks of being hastily written. When you mark something, you make a visible record, and the thing made is called a mark: What are those marks on your arm? Mark the area where you want the couch to go. Schoolwork-related scores are also called marks, and a teacher marks the work of her students. Mark conveys a target in expressions like beside the mark and wide of the mark.

Marked means bearing a visible mark or sign, but more commonly describes something noticeable or pronounced: {a marked improvement}, {a marked difference in quality}. When applied to people, marked suggests being singled out for attention, often dangerous: {a marked man} is someone targeted for harm. The adverb markedly means noticeably or significantly: {Her mood improved markedly after the news}.

A marker is something that marks—indicates, identifies, or sets apart. The most common meaning is a felt-tipped pen for writing or drawing: {She grabbed a marker and wrote on the whiteboard}. Markers also indicate position or boundaries: a mile marker, a grave marker, a bookmark. In genetics, a marker is a gene or DNA sequence used to identify a chromosome or trait. To {put down a marker} is to stake a position or signal intent.

Markers are things that mark—that indicate, identify, or designate something. The most common concrete sense is a writing instrument with a felt tip, typically with bold, vivid ink: {She labeled the boxes with a black marker}. A marker can also be a physical object that indicates position or location, like a grave marker or a boundary marker. In more abstract uses, markers are indicators or signs of something: {elevated cholesterol is a marker for heart disease}. The word extends to tokens used in games, placeholders in text, or anything that stands as a signal or identifier.
