Milky describes something resembling milk—white, pale, or cloudy. A milky {liquid} is opaque and whitish. Milky {skin} is very pale. A milky {sky} is hazy white. The Milky Way is the pale band of stars across the night sky. Milky can also mean containing or yielding milk: {milky sap}, {milky coconut}.

A mill is a place where raw materials are processed into products using machinery, especially machinery that grinds. Wheat is ground to flour in a mill; a steel mill produces steel from raw materials. By extension, any place that turns out great quantities of something in a mechanical fashion can be a mill (puppy mill, rumor mill, diploma mill). A small device for grinding is also a mill (salt mill, pepper mill, coffee mill). If you mill something, you grind or crush it. If people are milling around, they’re walking around aimlessly.

Millenium is a common misspelling of millennium, which has two n's. A millennium is a period of one thousand years, or specifically the transition from one thousand-year period to the next: {Y2K anxiety peaked as the new millennium approached}. The word also refers to an anticipated age of peace and happiness.

A millennial is a person born roughly between 1981 and 1996, coming of age around the turn of the millennium. The term often carries generational stereotypes—tech-savvy, entitled, avocado-toast-eating—though these vary by who's using it. As an adjective, millennial relates to this generation or to a millennium generally: {millennial attitudes toward work}, {millennial celebrations}.

Millennials are the generation born roughly between 1981 and 1996, reaching adulthood around the turn of the millennium. The term often carries connotations—positive or negative depending on the speaker—of being tech-savvy, entitled, or economically burdened: {Millennials killed the diamond industry}. Also called Generation Y.

A millennium is a period of one thousand years. The word often appears in discussions of calendar transitions: {anxiety about Y2K peaked as the new millennium approached}. In Christian theology, the millennium refers to a prophesied thousand-year reign of Christ on earth. Millennia of human history stretch behind us; the plural can be either millennia or millenniums.

A miller is a person who operates a mill, grinding grain into flour. The occupation was once common enough that it became a surname. Miller also names various moths whose dusty wings resemble flour-covered clothing. In fishing, a miller is an artificial fly imitating these moths. {The old miller ground wheat for the whole village.} (Capitalized Miller is a surname.)

Million is the number equal to one thousand thousands (1,000,000). It serves as a basic unit for large quantities: {a million dollars}, {millions of people}. Casually, million suggests an indefinitely huge number: {I've told you a million times}. A millionaire has wealth of at least a million in some currency. {One in a million} describes something exceptionally rare or special.

A millionaire is someone whose wealth equals or exceeds one million units of currency—typically dollars. The term once suggested extraordinary affluence, but inflation has diluted its impact; today a millionaire may simply be a homeowner with retirement savings. {He became a millionaire before thirty.} Billionaire now carries the weight millionaire once did.

Millionaires is the plural of millionaire—people whose wealth exceeds one million units of currency, typically dollars. The threshold has shifted in significance; a millionaire in 1900 commanded extraordinary wealth, while today the term often describes the merely affluent: {The neighborhood is full of millionaires}. Billionaire has largely replaced it as shorthand for the truly rich.

Millions is the plural of million, denoting multiple quantities of one million each or an indefinitely vast number. {Millions of people watched the broadcast.} The word often emphasizes overwhelming abundance rather than precise count: {I've told you a million times.} As a noun, {the millions} refers to the masses or ordinary people: {entertainment for the millions}.

A millipede is a many-legged arthropod with an elongated, segmented body—each segment bearing two pairs of legs. Despite the name suggesting a thousand feet, most species have between 30 and 400. Millipedes are slow-moving and feed on decaying plant matter, curling into a spiral when threatened. They're often confused with centipedes, which are faster, flatter, and have one pair of legs per segment.

Mills are buildings equipped with machinery for grinding grain into flour, or more broadly, any facility for processing raw materials—sawmills, steel mills, paper mills. The verb means to grind or process: {freshly milled pepper}. To mill about is to move aimlessly in a crowd: {Fans milled around outside the stadium}. A mill is also one-tenth of a cent, used mainly in tax calculations.

A millstone is one of a pair of heavy circular stones used for grinding grain. The weight and relentlessness of the grinding process give rise to the figurative sense: a millstone is a heavy burden that weighs someone down or impedes progress. {Student debt has become a millstone around the necks of young graduates.} The biblical image of a millstone hung around someone's neck before drowning suggests inescapable punishment.

Millstones are the heavy circular stones used in a mill to grind grain into flour. One stone rotates against another, crushing whatever passes between them. The word appears most often in the biblical phrase {a millstone around one's neck}—a burden so heavy it would drown you if thrown into the sea.

A mime is a performer who acts out scenes using only gestures and body movements, without speaking. The art form itself is also called mime. To mime is to perform in this silent, gestural way, or more broadly to move your lips without producing sound: {She mimed along to the song}. In computing, MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) standardizes how email attachments and web content are formatted, but in everyday use this appears lowercase in terms like {mime type}. (All-caps MIME is the technical acronym.)

Mimes are performers who use gesture and movement rather than speech, typically with exaggerated facial expressions and white face paint. The art form descends from ancient theatrical traditions. A mime also refers to the act itself: {She studied mime in Paris}. To mime is to perform silently or mouth words without sound: {He mimed along to the recording}.

To mimic is to imitate closely, especially in speech, gesture, or appearance. A child mimics a parent's mannerisms; a bird mimics human speech; a harmless snake mimics a venomous species to deter predators. As a noun, a mimic is someone skilled at imitation: {He's a talented mimic who can do any politician}. The adjective describes imitative behavior or appearance: {mimic camouflage}.

Mimicry is the act of imitating something else. In biology, it describes how organisms evolve to resemble other species or their environment—a butterfly mimics a toxic species to deter predators, a stick insect mimics a twig. More broadly, mimicry is any close imitation: {His mimicry of the boss was spot-on}. The word suggests copying appearance or behavior rather than substance.

Mimics is the plural of mimic—a person or creature that copies the appearance, sounds, or behavior of another. A mimic might impersonate celebrities or adopt protective coloring like certain insects. The verb mimic means to imitate, often for comic effect or survival: {She mimics her boss perfectly}. Mimics also serves as the third-person singular present tense: {The bird mimics car alarms}.

Miming is communicating through gesture and expression without words—the art of the mime. Someone miming acts out meaning silently: {She was miming drinking from a cup}. The word also covers lip-syncing to recorded music or pretending to play an instrument: {The band was clearly miming during the TV appearance}.

Mimosa names several things united by delicacy or sensitivity. The mimosa plant (also called sensitive plant) has feathery leaves that fold inward when touched. Mimosa trees bear similar foliage with fluffy, fragrant flower clusters. A mimosa is also a brunch cocktail of champagne and orange juice, named for the flower's color: {We ordered mimosas with our eggs Benedict}.

Mimosas are a genus of plants known for their feathery flowers and sensitive leaves that fold when touched—the so-called sensitive plant. More commonly, a mimosa is a brunch cocktail of champagne and orange juice: {We ordered mimosas with our eggs Benedict}. The drink takes its name from the flower's resemblance to the pale yellow-orange beverage.

A minaret is a tall, slender tower attached to a mosque, from which the call to prayer is traditionally announced. Minarets are distinctive features of Islamic architecture, typically cylindrical or polygonal with a balcony near the top: {The city skyline was punctuated by dozens of minarets}.

Minarets are tall, slender towers attached to mosques, from which a muezzin traditionally calls Muslims to prayer. The distinctive silhouette—often with a balcony near the top and a pointed or onion-shaped crown—has become an architectural symbol of Islam: {The minarets of Istanbul punctuate the skyline}.

Mince means to cut or chop into very small pieces: {mince the garlic and add it to the pan}. Minced meat, or simply mince in British English, is finely ground meat. To mince words is to speak evasively or with excessive delicacy—usually negated: {Let me not mince words: you're fired}. To mince is also to walk with short, dainty, affected steps.

Mincemeat is a mixture of chopped dried fruits, spices, sugar, and suet, traditionally used as pie filling—especially in British Christmas mince pies. Despite the name, modern mincemeat rarely contains actual meat, though historical versions did. To {make mincemeat of} someone is to defeat or destroy them utterly: {The defense attorney made mincemeat of the witness's testimony}.

We use mind to talk about consciousness. This meaning is reflected in dozens of common expressions, such as change your mind, keep it in mind, speak your mind, cross your mind, and lose your mind. Mind can be contrasted with heart or body, depending on which aspects of the mind are being emphasized. If you mind something, you pay attention to it. If you don’t mind something, you have no objection to it.

Mindblowing describes something so impressive, surprising, or revelatory that it overwhelms your capacity to process it—as if your mind has been blown apart. The term emerged from 1960s drug culture to describe psychedelic experiences but now applies broadly to anything extraordinary: {The special effects were mindblowing}, {a mindblowing plot twist}. It's often written as two words or hyphenated (mind-blowing) and frequently subject to hyperbole.

Mindboggling describes something so extraordinary, complex, or vast that the mind struggles to comprehend it: {The mindboggling scale of the universe}, {mindboggling amounts of data}. The image is of a mind that boggles—hesitates, recoils—when confronted with something beyond easy grasp. Also spelled mind-boggling.

A mindfuck is an experience that profoundly disorients or destabilizes your sense of reality—a movie twist that makes you rethink everything, a revelation that upends your worldview, or a situation designed to manipulate and confuse: {That ending was a total mindfuck}. To mindfuck someone is to mess with their head, often through psychological manipulation or deception. The term is vulgar but widely used for experiences that leave you questioning what's real.

Mindful means conscious and attentive, usually with an element of care or concern: {Be mindful of the time}, {mindful of her feelings}. In contemporary usage, mindful often connects to meditation practices—being fully present and aware of one's thoughts and surroundings without judgment: {mindful breathing}, {mindful eating}. The noun is mindfulness.

Mindfulness is the practice of maintaining calm, nonjudgmental awareness of the present moment—one's thoughts, feelings, and surroundings. Rooted in Buddhist meditation traditions, it entered mainstream Western psychology as a stress-reduction technique. {Her therapist recommended mindfulness exercises}. To practice mindfulness is to observe experience without reacting: {I'm trying to approach my anxiety with mindfulness rather than panic}.

Mindless describes action or behavior without thought or purpose. A mindless {task} requires no mental engagement. Mindless {violence} is brutal without reason or reflection. To be mindless {of} something is to be heedless of it: {mindless of the consequences}. The word often carries judgment—that someone should have thought but didn't.

A mindreader is someone who claims or appears to know what others are thinking. Stage magicians and mentalists perform as mindreaders, using tricks to simulate telepathy. More commonly, the word appears in denials: {I'm not a mindreader—you have to tell me what you want}. Also spelled as two words.

Mindreading is the supposed ability to perceive another person's thoughts directly, without communication. In everyday use, it often describes intuiting what someone is thinking or feeling: {After twenty years of marriage, she could practically mindread}. The term also appears sarcastically when someone expects you to know something they haven't said: {I'm not mindreading here—you have to tell me what you want}.

Minds is the plural of mind—the faculty of thought, awareness, and reasoning. Multiple minds can collaborate or disagree: {Great minds think alike}. To mind something is to object to it or to look after it: {Do you mind if I sit here?} {Mind the children while I'm out}. To be of two minds is to feel conflicted. {Minds were changed after the debate}.

A mindset is a person's established set of attitudes or way of thinking about something. It shapes how you interpret and respond to situations: {a growth mindset}, {a fixed mindset}. The word often appears in self-help contexts emphasizing that changing your mindset can change your outcomes: {She approached the challenge with a positive mindset}.

Mindsets are habitual attitudes or mental frameworks that shape how someone interprets and responds to situations. A {growth mindset} sees abilities as developable through effort; a {fixed mindset} sees them as innate. The term often appears in self-help and business contexts: {Changing your mindset can transform your approach to challenges}.

Mine combines two jobs in one; to take the place of a noun or noun phrase already named, and to indicate that the thing referred to belongs to or is associated with you: If your car is still in the shop you can use mine. These two jobs give mine and other words in its class the designation “possessive pronoun.”

A minecart is a small wheeled vehicle used to transport ore, coal, or debris through mine tunnels, typically running on narrow-gauge rails. The word appears frequently in video games, especially Minecraft and Donkey Kong Country, where minecarts serve as transport or appear in rail-riding sequences: {We loaded the minecart with iron ore}.

A minefield is an area where explosive mines have been buried, creating deadly hazard for anyone crossing it. The figurative sense dominates contemporary usage: any situation full of hidden dangers or potential problems requiring careful navigation. {The interview was a minefield of controversial topics.} {Navigating office politics can be a minefield.}

Minefields are areas where explosive mines have been planted, whether on land or at sea. Soldiers crossing a minefield risk death with each step. Figuratively, a minefield is any situation full of hidden dangers: {The interview was a minefield of potentially offensive questions}. The singular minefield is more common.

A miner is a person who works in a mine, extracting coal, ore, or other minerals from the earth. The term extends to automated mining equipment: {The company deployed underwater miners to harvest seafloor minerals}. In cryptocurrency, a miner is a computer or person that validates transactions and adds them to the blockchain, receiving coins as reward.

A mineral is a naturally occurring inorganic substance with a specific chemical composition and crystalline structure—quartz, felite, copper. Rocks are made of minerals. The term extends to substances extracted from the earth for human use: {mineral rights}, {mineral deposits}. Mineral water contains dissolved minerals. As an adjective, mineral describes things derived from or relating to such substances: {mineral oil}, {mineral wealth}.

Minerals are naturally occurring inorganic substances with a definite chemical composition. In nutrition, minerals are essential elements like iron, calcium, and zinc that the body needs in small amounts. Informally, minerals often means mineral water: {I'll have a gin and minerals}. In British usage, minerals can mean soft drinks generally.

Miners are workers who extract minerals, coal, or other materials from the earth, typically from underground tunnels or open pits. The term extends to those who dig for precious metals: gold miners, diamond miners. In cryptocurrency, miners are computers or their operators that validate transactions and add them to the blockchain, rewarded with new coins for their computational work.

Mines is the plural of mine—an excavation for extracting minerals or an explosive device buried underground or underwater. Coal mines, gold mines, land mines, naval mines. Figuratively, something that's {a mine of information} is a rich source. The possessive pronoun mine ({That book is mines}) appears in some dialects but is nonstandard.

Minestrone is a thick Italian soup made with vegetables, beans, and pasta or rice. The ingredients vary by region and season, but typically include tomatoes, onions, celery, and carrots in a broth base. {We ordered minestrone and garlic bread.}

A minesweeper is a naval vessel designed to detect and destroy underwater mines, clearing safe passage for other ships. The work is dangerous and methodical, requiring specialized equipment to trigger or disarm explosives before they can damage larger vessels. By extension, minesweeper refers to the classic computer game where players uncover squares on a grid while avoiding hidden mines, using numeric clues to deduce their locations: {I wasted an hour playing minesweeper instead of working}. (Capitalized Minesweeper often refers specifically to the Microsoft Windows game.)

Mingle means to mix or blend together, whether people, substances, or abstract things. At a party, you mingle by moving through the crowd and talking with different people rather than staying in one spot: {She mingled with the guests before dinner}. Things can mingle too—scents mingle in a garden, emotions mingle in a complicated situation. The word suggests combining while still retaining some distinctness, unlike merge or fuse which imply complete blending.

Mingling is mixing or circulating, especially among people at social gatherings. You mingle at a party by moving through the crowd, making small talk with different groups rather than staying in one spot: {She spent the cocktail hour mingling with potential clients}. Things that mingle blend together: {The smell of coffee mingled with cigarette smoke}.

Mini describes something smaller than usual—a miniature version of a standard item. A mini {skirt} or mini {dress} falls well above the knee. A mini {fridge} fits in a dorm room. The word works as noun or adjective: {She drove a mini} or {a mini vacation}. Mini appears in countless compounds: minivan, miniseries, minigolf. (Capitalized Mini is the car brand.)

Miniature describes something much smaller than the standard version: a miniature {poodle}, a miniature {golf course}, a miniature {replica of the Eiffel Tower}. As a noun, a miniature is a small-scale model or a tiny detailed painting, especially a portrait. {In miniature} means on a reduced scale: {The town was Paris in miniature}.

Miniatures are small-scale representations of larger things. A miniature portrait fits in a locket; a miniature golf course shrinks the game to novelty size. In tabletop gaming, miniatures are small figurines representing characters or units: {He spent the weekend painting his miniatures}. The adjective miniature describes anything unusually small for its type: {a miniature poodle}, {a miniature replica of the Eiffel Tower}.

A minibar is a small refrigerator stocked with beverages and snacks, typically found in hotel rooms. Guests help themselves and charges appear on their bill at checkout. The contents are usually overpriced: {I paid eight dollars for a tiny bottle of water from the minibar}. Some minibars have sensors that automatically charge when items are moved.

A minidress is a dress with a hemline well above the knee, typically mid-thigh or higher. The style emerged in the 1960s as part of youth fashion's break from conservative dress codes: {She wore a black minidress to the party}. The mini- prefix has spawned related terms like miniskirt.

Minigolf is a recreational version of golf played on a small course with obstacles, tunnels, ramps, and other novelty features that make each hole a puzzle to navigate. Players use putters to guide a ball through these miniature landscapes, typically completing 18 holes in under an hour. The game requires no special skill or athletic ability, making it a popular activity for families and casual outings. Also called miniature golf or putt-putt.

Minimal means the smallest amount or degree possible, or reduced to the barest essentials. Something minimal is stripped down to only what's necessary: {The recipe requires minimal preparation.} {We experienced minimal delays.} In design and art, minimal describes a style characterized by extreme simplicity and the absence of decoration or ornamentation. The word often carries positive connotations of efficiency or elegance, though it can also suggest insufficiency: {The response was minimal at best.}

Minimalism is a style or approach that emphasizes simplicity and the removal of unnecessary elements. In art and design, it favors clean lines, limited colors, and sparse composition. In lifestyle contexts, it describes deliberately owning fewer possessions and reducing consumption: {Her minimalism means she owns only what she truly needs}. The term can apply to music, architecture, writing, or any domain where stripping away excess reveals essential form.

Minimalist describes a preference for the fewest elements, simplest forms, or least amount necessary. In art and design, minimalism strips away ornamentation to emphasize essential structure: {a minimalist aesthetic}, {minimalist furniture}. As a noun, a minimalist practices this approach: {She's a minimalist who owns only what she needs}. The word applies broadly to lifestyle, music, architecture, or any domain where reduction is the goal.

To minimize is to reduce something to its smallest possible amount or degree: {We took steps to minimize risk}. In computing, to minimize a window is to shrink it to an icon or taskbar. Minimize also means to downplay or represent as less significant than it is: {Don't minimize my concerns}.

Minimum is the smallest amount, degree, or number possible or allowed. A minimum {wage} is the lowest legal pay. {At a minimum}, you should call before showing up. The adjective describes the least acceptable: minimum {requirements}, minimum {effort}. The opposite is maximum. Plural: minimums or minima.

Mining is the extraction of valuable materials from the earth, including metals, coal, gemstones, and other minerals. The process ranges from surface operations like open-pit mines to deep underground excavations. By extension, mining applies to any systematic extraction of resources: {data mining} involves sifting through large datasets for useful patterns, and cryptocurrency mining uses computing power to validate transactions and generate new coins. To mine something is to extract it through such processes: {They've been mining copper in this region for decades}.

A minion is a subordinate who carries out orders, often with excessive eagerness or servility. The word implies someone who exists to do another's bidding: {The CEO surrounded himself with minions who never questioned his decisions}. Minion often carries a mocking or contemptuous tone, suggesting the subordinate lacks independent judgment or dignity. In recent decades, the word has softened through popular culture, sometimes used affectionately for loyal helpers or followers.

Minions are subordinates who carry out someone else's orders, typically with blind loyalty. The word usually carries a negative connotation—suggesting servility or complicity in wrongdoing: {The villain dispatched his minions to do the dirty work}. A minion can also be a favorite or darling, though this older sense is rare. The 2010 animated film *Despicable Me* popularized minions as small yellow cartoon creatures, now ubiquitous in memes and merchandise.

A miniskirt is a very short skirt with a hemline well above the knee, typically mid-thigh or higher. The style emerged in the 1960s as a symbol of youth culture and sexual liberation: {She wore a miniskirt and go-go boots}. Often shortened to mini: {a denim mini}.

A minister is a member of the clergy, especially in Protestant churches: {The minister led the congregation in prayer}. In government, a minister heads a department or ministry: {the Prime Minister}, {the Minister of Finance}. To minister is to attend to someone's needs, especially in a caring or spiritual capacity: {She ministered to the sick}. The word carries a sense of service—ministers serve their congregations, their governments, or those requiring aid.

Ministers are people who serve in positions of authority. In government, ministers head departments or agencies: {the finance minister}, {the defense minister}. In religion, ministers are clergy who lead congregations, especially in Protestant churches: {The minister performed the wedding ceremony}. To minister is to attend to someone's needs: {She ministered to the sick}.

The noun ministry shows an important difference between American and other varieties of English. Parliamentary governments (as in the UK and many other countries) call their major departments of government ministries (Ministry of Justice). In American English, however, these are simply called departments, and ministry refers to the service, job, or activity of a religious minister: The boy felt called to enter the ministry after high school graduation. The ordained ministry refers collectively to religious ministers.

A minivan is a boxy passenger vehicle larger than a station wagon, with sliding side doors and seating for six to eight people. The design prioritizes interior space over style, making minivans practical for families with children: {We piled into the minivan for the road trip}. The word carries suburban-parent connotations that some find unflattering.

Minivans are boxy passenger vehicles designed for families, larger than station wagons but smaller than full-size vans. They typically seat six to eight people, with sliding side doors and fold-flat rear seats for cargo flexibility. The minivan became the suburban family vehicle of choice in the 1980s and 1990s, though SUVs have since claimed much of that market: {We piled the kids into the minivan and headed to soccer practice}.

A mink is a small, semiaquatic mammal prized for its soft, dense fur. Minks are raised on farms specifically for their pelts, which become luxury coats and accessories: {a mink coat}, {a mink stole}. The word often refers to the fur itself or garments made from it: {She wore her grandmother's mink to the opera}.

Minks are small, semiaquatic mammals prized for their soft, dense fur. They belong to the weasel family and are raised commercially on fur farms. The plural also refers to mink fur garments: {She wore her grandmother's minks to the opera}. A mink coat has long signified wealth and glamour, though fur fashion has become controversial.

A minnow is any of various small freshwater fish, often used as bait. The word extends loosely to any tiny fish: {We caught nothing but minnows}. Figuratively, a minnow is a small or insignificant player relative to larger competitors: {a minnow in a sea of corporate giants}.

Minnows are small freshwater fish, typically under a few inches long, belonging to the carp family. The term is used loosely for any tiny fish, especially those used as bait or kept in home aquariums. Figuratively, minnow describes someone or something small and insignificant relative to larger competitors: {In a league of corporate giants, our startup was just a minnow}. Children often try to catch minnows with nets in shallow streams and ponds.

Minor means lesser in size, importance, or seriousness. A minor injury isn't severe. A minor character has a small role. In music, a minor key has a darker, sadder quality than major. A minor is also a person below the age of legal adulthood—typically eighteen in most jurisdictions: {The bar was cited for serving minors}. In education, a minor is a secondary field of study: {She majored in biology with a minor in chemistry}. (Capitalized Minor appears in some proper names.)

Minorities are groups that make up less than half of a larger population. The term typically refers to racial, ethnic, or religious groups that are numerically smaller than the dominant group in a society: {Minorities are underrepresented in corporate leadership}. The word can also describe any smaller faction: {a minority of voters}. Though originally about numbers, minority often implies reduced power or status regardless of actual population size—hence South African blacks were called a minority under apartheid despite being the majority.

Minority refers to the smaller part of a group—less than half: {A minority of voters supported the measure}. In social contexts, a minority is a group distinguished by race, ethnicity, religion, or other characteristics that differs from the dominant population: {racial minorities}, {religious minorities}. The term implies both smaller numbers and often reduced social power. Minority also describes the state of being under legal age: {He inherited the estate during his minority}.

Minors are people who have not yet reached the age of legal adulthood—typically eighteen in most jurisdictions. The term appears constantly in legal contexts: {The sale of alcohol to minors is prohibited}. In education, a minor is a secondary field of study alongside one's major: {She's majoring in biology with a minor in chemistry}. In music, minor keys and chords have a darker, more melancholy quality than major ones.

A minotaur is a mythical creature with a human body and a bull's head. The original Minotaur of Greek mythology was confined to the Labyrinth on Crete and fed human sacrifices until Theseus killed it. In fantasy games and fiction, minotaurs appear as a species of bull-headed humanoids, typically portrayed as fierce warriors or dungeon-dwelling monsters: {The party encountered a minotaur guarding the treasure room}. (Capitalized Minotaur refers to the specific creature of Greek myth.)

A minstrel was a medieval entertainer who performed songs, poetry, and music, often traveling from court to court or town to town. The word evokes romantic images of wandering musicians with lutes. In American history, minstrel specifically refers to performers in minstrel shows—19th and early 20th century entertainment featuring white performers in blackface (and later Black performers) using racist stereotypes. That legacy makes the word fraught when applied to any performer today.

Two words share the spelling m-i-n-t. Mint is the general name for plants in the family Labiatae, many of which are aromatic and used medicinally and for food, such as spearmint or peppermint. Candies with this flavoring are called mints. A mint is also a place where coins or paper money are manufactured. To mint money is to produce the physical tokens of it. If you make a mint, you make a lot of money. Something newly minted has just been produced: The newly minted legislation will take effect on November 1. Something in mint condition is new and unblemished, as if just produced in a mint.

Minted means freshly made or produced, from the original sense of coins being struck at a mint. A {newly minted graduate} has just earned their degree. A {freshly minted phrase} is brand new. In British slang, minted means wealthy—having lots of mint-fresh money: {He's absolutely minted}.

Minting is the process of producing coins by stamping metal, or more broadly, creating something new. The word extends from physical currency to digital assets: {The NFT minting fee was surprisingly high}. Someone minting money is making it rapidly and easily. A freshly minted graduate or executive is newly credentialed: {a freshly minted MBA}.

Mints are candies flavored with mint—the aromatic herb whose oils produce a cooling sensation: {She offered me a mint after dinner}. Breath mints mask odors; after-dinner mints accompany the check at restaurants. Mint also refers to places where coins are manufactured, and things {in mint condition} are pristine, as if freshly minted.

Minus, the word for the arithmetic symbol indicating subtraction, is usually interpreted as a preposition when it occurs in text (twenty-three minus five). The symbol form minus is a slightly elongated hyphen but many people just use the hyphen because it is a single keystroke.

The most frequent use of minute by far is the noun, denoting a 60th of an hour, and by extension, a short amount of time: give me a minute, wait a minute. A minute is also a 60th part of a degree in geometric measurement. The plural minutes frequently denotes the official record of the proceedings of a meeting: He seconded the motion to accept the minutes of the last meeting. The adjective minute (second syllable stressed) expresses the concept of very small: The prices were ridiculous and the portions minute.

A minuteman was an American colonial militiaman ready to fight at a minute's notice during the Revolutionary War era. The term evokes readiness and patriotic defense. Minuteman later became the name of U.S. intercontinental ballistic missiles, and various civilian groups have adopted the name, including anti-immigration activists patrolling the U.S.-Mexico border.

Minutemen were American colonial militia members who pledged to be ready for battle at a minute's notice during the Revolutionary War. The term now applies more broadly to any group claiming readiness for rapid response, often with patriotic overtones: {The governor called the volunteer minutemen to assist with disaster relief}. (Capitalized Minutemen may refer to specific organizations or the punk band.)

Minutes are units of time equal to sixty seconds. A meeting's minutes are the official written record of what was discussed and decided: {Who's taking minutes?} To minute something is to record it officially. Something done {to the minute} happens at exactly the scheduled time. A minute amount is tiny, but that sense belongs to the singular form pronounced with stress on the second syllable.

A miracle is an extraordinary event that seems to defy natural laws, typically attributed to divine intervention: {It would take a miracle for him to survive}. Religious traditions center on miracles—healings, resurrections, parting seas. The word extends to any remarkable or improbable occurrence: {It's a miracle we found parking}. This casual use retains a sense of grateful astonishment at unlikely good fortune.

Miracles are events that seem to defy natural laws, typically attributed to divine intervention. A sick person recovers against all medical odds; believers call it a miracle. The word extends to anything remarkably fortunate or improbable: {It's a miracle we found parking}. To {work miracles} is to achieve extraordinary results. The adjective miraculous describes such events or outcomes.

Miraculous describes something so extraordinary it seems to defy natural explanation—as if produced by divine intervention or supernatural forces. A miraculous recovery happens against all medical expectation. The word often carries religious overtones, referring to genuine miracles: {the miraculous healing at Lourdes}. In casual use, miraculous is hyperbole for anything impressively unlikely or fortunate: {It's miraculous we found parking}.

A mirage is an optical illusion caused by atmospheric conditions, typically heat distorting light to create false images—water on a hot road, distant objects floating above the horizon. The word extends to anything illusory or unattainable: {The oasis turned out to be a mirage}. {His promise of reform was just a mirage}.

Mirages are optical illusions caused by atmospheric conditions, typically heat distorting light to create false images—the shimmering water that appears on hot pavement, or distant objects seeming to float above the horizon. By extension, a mirage is anything deceptively appealing but unattainable: {The oasis turned out to be a mirage}. {His promises of reform were just mirages}.

A mirror is a surface that reflects light, typically glass coated with metal, allowing you to see yourself or what's behind you. Mirrors appear in compounds: {rearview mirror}, {mirror image}, {mirror ball}. To mirror something is to reflect or imitate it: {Her expression mirrored his concern}. {The architecture mirrors classical Greek temples}.

Mirrors are surfaces that reflect images, typically glass coated with reflective metal. A bathroom mirror shows your reflection; a car's mirrors let you see behind. Figuratively, something that mirrors another thing reflects or imitates it: {The child's anxiety mirrored her mother's}. A mirror can be anything that reflects reality: {Art mirrors life}.

Misadventure is an unfortunate incident or unlucky experience—an adventure gone wrong. The word suggests mishap rather than catastrophe: {The camping trip turned into a series of misadventures}. In legal contexts, {death by misadventure} means an accidental death resulting from a lawful but risky act, with no one at fault.

Misadventures are unfortunate or unlucky experiences, typically minor mishaps rather than serious calamities. The word carries a tone of rueful humor—things went wrong, but you can laugh about it later: {She regaled us with tales of her misadventures in online dating}. A misadventure suggests bad luck rather than bad judgment, though the distinction often blurs.

Misbehave means to behave badly or improperly, especially by breaking rules or social norms. Children misbehave when they act out; adults misbehave when they violate expectations of conduct: {The kids misbehaved the entire flight}. The word often carries a tone of mild rebuke rather than serious accusation.

Misbehavior is conduct that violates rules or expectations—typically minor infractions rather than serious offenses. The word appears most often in contexts involving children or institutions: {The teacher sent him to the principal's office for misbehavior}. Adults misbehave too, though the word carries a slightly juvenile or euphemistic tone when applied to them.

Misbehaviour is the British spelling of misbehavior—conduct that violates rules or norms, especially by children. The word implies actions that fall short of serious wrongdoing but warrant correction: {The teacher sent him to the principal's office for misbehaviour}. It can also describe adult conduct that breaches professional or social standards.

A miscalculation is an error in computing or estimating something: {a miscalculation in the budget}, {a miscalculation of the distance}. More often it refers to a mistake in judgment or planning: {The invasion was a strategic miscalculation}. To miscalculate is to make such an error.

Miscarriage is the spontaneous loss of a pregnancy before the fetus can survive outside the womb, typically before twenty weeks. The term carries clinical weight but also deep personal significance: {She had two miscarriages before her son was born}. A miscarriage of justice is a failure of the legal system to reach a fair outcome—an extended sense where something meant to produce good results instead fails catastrophically.

Mischief is playful behavior that causes minor trouble or annoyance without serious harm: {The kids got into mischief while we were out}. It suggests impish troublemaking rather than malice—a child's prank, a pet's antics. {Eyes full of mischief} signals someone is up to something. The phrase {do mischief} or {make mischief} implies stirring up trouble, sometimes deliberately causing discord between people. Legal use retains an older sense of actual harm: {criminal mischief} means property damage or vandalism.

Mischievous describes someone inclined to cause minor trouble or annoyance, usually in a playful rather than harmful way: {a mischievous grin}, {mischievous children}. The word suggests impish behavior—pranks, teasing, rule-bending for fun. Something mischievous may also cause harm without malice: {mischievous rumors}. Often mispronounced with four syllables, but standard pronunciation has three.

Miscommunication is a failure to communicate clearly, resulting in misunderstanding between parties. The prefix *mis-* signals something going wrong—the message sent isn't the message received: {The whole disaster was just a miscommunication about the deadline}. Miscommunication can be minor or consequential, accidental or rooted in deeper failures to listen.

A misconception is a mistaken belief or faulty understanding. Unlike a lie, which involves intent to deceive, a misconception is an honest error—you genuinely think you're right: {There's a common misconception that we only use ten percent of our brains}. The word often appears when correcting widely held but inaccurate ideas.

Misconduct is improper or unacceptable behavior, especially by someone in a position of responsibility or trust. The word usually appears in formal or institutional contexts: {professional misconduct}, {police misconduct}, {sexual misconduct}. A finding of misconduct can lead to discipline, termination, or legal consequences. The verb means to behave improperly or to manage badly: {He misconducted himself at the conference}.

A misdeed is a wrongful or wicked act—something done that shouldn't have been. The word has an old-fashioned, slightly formal quality: {The senator's past misdeeds came back to haunt him}. It suggests moral failing more than legal violation, though the two often overlap.

Misdeeds are wrongful acts—offenses against morality, law, or proper conduct. The word has a slightly formal or literary flavor, often appearing in contexts of accusation or confession: {The politician's misdeeds finally came to light}. Misdeeds tend to be serious but not necessarily criminal; they suggest moral failure as much as legal violation.

A misdemeanor is a criminal offense less serious than a felony, typically punishable by fines, probation, community service, or jail time of less than a year. Common misdemeanors include petty theft, simple assault, trespassing, and minor drug possession. The distinction between misdemeanor and felony varies by jurisdiction, but misdemeanors generally carry lighter sentences and fewer long-term consequences. {He was charged with a misdemeanor for shoplifting.}

Misdirection is the act of drawing attention away from what matters—toward something irrelevant or misleading. Magicians use misdirection to conceal their methods: {While you watch his right hand, his left does the trick}. The word also describes giving wrong directions or guidance: {The witness's misdirection sent police to the wrong address}. More broadly, any deliberate diversion of focus: {The scandal was misdirection from the real policy failures}.

A miser hoards money and refuses to spend it, even on necessities. The word implies not just frugality but obsessive, joyless accumulation—counting coins rather than enjoying what they could buy. {The old miser died alone in a mansion full of rotting furniture}. Scrooge is the archetypal literary miser.

Miserable describes a state of great unhappiness or discomfort: {I felt miserable with the flu}. It can characterize conditions that cause such distress: {miserable weather}, {a miserable apartment}. Applied to quantities, it suggests contemptibly small: {a miserable salary}. A miserable person may also be one who makes others unhappy—unpleasant and ill-tempered: {that miserable old crank next door}.

Misers are people who hoard wealth and hate spending it, even on necessities. The word carries strong negative connotations—misers aren't just frugal, they're obsessively stingy to the point of self-denial: {The old miser died alone in a house full of money he never spent}. Dickens's Scrooge is the archetypal miser.

Misery is intense suffering or unhappiness—physical pain, emotional anguish, or wretched living conditions. {The injury caused her constant misery}. A misery can be a specific source of suffering: {the miseries of poverty}. In British informal use, a misery is a persistently gloomy or complaining person. To {put someone out of their misery} is to end their suffering, literally or figuratively—as when finally giving someone news they've been anxiously awaiting.

A misfire is a failure to fire properly—a gun that doesn't discharge, an engine cylinder that doesn't ignite, a rocket that doesn't launch. Extended to any plan or attempt that fails to achieve its intended effect: {The joke misfired badly}. As a verb, to misfire is to fail in this way: {The engine kept misfiring}.

Misfired describes something that failed to fire or discharge properly. A gun misfires when the trigger is pulled but the cartridge doesn't ignite. An engine misfires when fuel fails to combust correctly in a cylinder. Figuratively, a joke or plan that misfired didn't produce the intended effect: {His attempt at humor misfired badly}.

A misfit is someone who doesn't fit in with their surroundings or social group—awkward, out of place, unsuited to the environment. The word applies to things too: a misfit part doesn't match other components. {She always felt like a misfit in her conservative hometown}. The term can be embraced as identity or used dismissively.

Misfits are people who don't fit in—those who fail to conform to the expectations or norms of a group. The term can be disparaging, suggesting someone awkward or socially inept: {He was always a misfit at school}. But it also carries positive connotations of individuality and creative nonconformity: {Silicon Valley was built by misfits and dropouts}. A misfit can also be something that fits poorly, like an ill-fitting garment.

Misfortune is bad luck or an unfortunate event. It can name the general condition of being unlucky or a specific instance: {a series of misfortunes}, {the misfortune of being born into poverty}. To have {the misfortune to} do something is to be unlucky enough to experience it: {I had the misfortune to witness the whole disaster}.

A misgiving is a feeling of doubt or apprehension about a future action or decision. Unlike outright opposition, misgivings suggest unease rather than certainty: {She had misgivings about the plan but went along with it}. Usually plural: {Despite his misgivings, he signed the contract}.

Misgivings are feelings of doubt, unease, or apprehension about something—typically a decision, plan, or course of action. The word almost always appears in the plural: {I had misgivings about the merger from the start}. Unlike outright opposition, misgivings suggest lingering uncertainty rather than firm conviction: {Despite her misgivings, she signed the contract}.

Misguided describes actions or beliefs based on faulty judgment or wrong assumptions: {a misguided attempt to help}, {misguided policies}. The word implies good intentions gone astray—someone misguided isn't malicious, just mistaken about the right course. It often carries a note of condescension: calling someone misguided suggests you know better.

A mishap is an unlucky accident or minor misfortune—something that goes wrong but typically without serious consequences: {We arrived late due to a mishap with the rental car}. The word suggests bad luck rather than negligence, and usually applies to incidents that are inconvenient rather than catastrophic.

A mishmash is a jumbled mixture of disparate things thrown together without much order or coherence: {The proposal was a mishmash of half-baked ideas}. The word suggests randomness rather than deliberate combination—a hodgepodge. {Her desk was a mishmash of papers, coffee cups, and Post-it notes.}

Misinformation is false or inaccurate information, regardless of intent. Unlike disinformation, which is deliberately deceptive, misinformation may spread through honest error or misunderstanding: {Social media accelerates the spread of misinformation}. The term gained prominence in debates about online content and public health messaging.

To mislead is to cause someone to believe something untrue or to guide them in the wrong direction. The word suggests leading astray rather than outright lying—you can mislead by omission, selective emphasis, or technically true but deceptive statements: {The ad's fine print was designed to mislead consumers}. Unlike deceive, mislead often implies the victim follows willingly, unaware they're being led wrong.

Misleading describes something that creates a false impression or leads toward wrong conclusions. A misleading {statement} isn't necessarily a lie—it may be technically true while omitting crucial context. Misleading {statistics} can distort reality through selective presentation. {The headline was misleading; the article said something quite different.} The verb mislead means to guide someone toward error or false belief.

Misled is the past tense of mislead—to guide someone toward a wrong conclusion or action, whether through deception or honest error. {The witness misled the jury}. {I was misled by the confusing signage}. The word implies the person who was misled bears less fault than whoever or whatever did the misleading.

A mismatch is a pairing of things that don't go well together or aren't suited to each other: {a mismatch between skills and job requirements}, {The game was a mismatch from the start}. To mismatch is to pair things poorly or inappropriately. Mismatched socks don't match; a mismatched couple seems incompatible.

Mismatched describes things that don't go together well or aren't suited to each other. Mismatched {socks} are different colors or patterns. A mismatched {couple} seems incompatible. Mismatched {expectations} between parties lead to conflict. The word implies things were paired or combined when they shouldn't have been: {The teams were badly mismatched—one had professionals, the other amateurs}.

Miso is a thick paste made from fermented soybeans, used as a foundation for Japanese cooking. It flavors soups, marinades, dressings, and glazes: {miso soup}, {miso-glazed salmon}. Varieties range from mild white miso to robust red miso. The fermentation gives it a rich, savory depth—a source of umami.

Misogynist as an adjective characterizes a person, remark, or behavior that demonstrates a prejudice against or a dislike for women: A man in the audience was shouting misogynist insults at the performer. A slightly less intense way of suggesting the same tendency is the term male chauvinist.

Misogyny is hatred or contempt for women. The term covers attitudes ranging from active hostility to subtler forms of prejudice and discrimination. A misogynist holds such views. {The company's misogyny was evident in its promotion patterns}. Misogynistic describes things reflecting or promoting these attitudes: {misogynistic lyrics}, {misogynistic jokes}.

To misplace something is to put it somewhere and then forget where: {I've misplaced my glasses again}. The word implies carelessness rather than loss—the item exists somewhere, you just can't find it. Misplaced can also describe things directed at the wrong target: misplaced {trust}, misplaced {anger}, misplaced {priorities}.

Misplaced describes something put in the wrong location or position, often temporarily lost as a result: {I've misplaced my glasses again}. The word extends to abstract things that are inappropriately directed or applied: misplaced {trust}, misplaced {priorities}, misplaced {anger}. A misplaced modifier in grammar attaches to the wrong word in a sentence. The past participle of misplace, it functions primarily as an adjective.

Miss is two different words, usually easily distinguishable by context. To miss is to fail or fail to experience in some way (miss the target, miss a phone call. If you miss someone, either you weren’t available when a meeting was possible, or you are sad for their absence. A miss is an instance of missing, a failure of some kind. Miss is also a title for a young or unmarried woman (usually capitalized), and by extension designates a young woman, or (in the plural, misses) a clothing size for young women: Miss Johnson will be attending the ceremony with her parents.

Missed is the past tense of miss, covering all its senses. You missed the bus if it left without you, missed the target if you failed to hit it, missed a meeting if you didn't attend. To say you missed someone means you felt their absence: {I missed you while you were away}. A missed {opportunity} is one that passed unexploited. {You missed a spot} points out an oversight.

A missile is an object propelled at a target. In its broadest sense, any thrown or launched object qualifies: {Protesters hurled missiles at police}. More specifically, a missile is a self-propelled weapon carrying explosives—guided missiles can adjust course in flight, while ballistic missiles follow a fixed trajectory. The word often implies military weaponry: {cruise missile}, {nuclear missile}.

Missiles is the plural of missile—objects propelled at a target. The term covers anything thrown or launched as a weapon, from rocks to arrows, but modern usage centers on self-propelled weapons systems: {cruise missiles}, {ballistic missiles}, {surface-to-air missiles}. In military contexts, missiles typically carry explosive warheads and may be guided or unguided: {The strike involved dozens of missiles}.

Missing describes something or someone absent from where they should be. A missing {person} cannot be located. Missing {pages} have been removed or lost from a document. A missing {ingredient} is one you need but don't have. The word implies incompleteness—something that should be present isn't: {What's missing from this picture?} To {go missing} is to disappear, especially under unexplained circumstances.

A mission is a task or assignment given to someone, often with specific goals: {a rescue mission}, {a diplomatic mission}. Religious missions involve sending people to spread faith or do charitable work in distant places. Mission extends to any purposeful undertaking: {His mission was to find the best tacos in the city}. A mission statement declares an organization's core purpose. The phrase {mission accomplished} signals a goal achieved—sometimes used ironically when success is premature or questionable.

Missionaries are people sent to spread religious faith in foreign lands or among non-believers. Christian missionaries have historically combined evangelism with education, healthcare, and humanitarian work. The term extends to anyone zealously promoting a cause: {dietary missionaries}, {democracy missionaries}. The missionary position—face-to-face sexual intercourse with one partner on top—supposedly reflects what missionaries taught as proper.

A missionary is a person sent to spread religious faith, typically in foreign lands. Christian missionaries have historically combined evangelism with education and humanitarian work. The term extends to anyone zealously promoting a cause: {He approached veganism with missionary zeal}. Missionary position—face-to-face sex with one partner on top—supposedly reflects what missionaries taught as proper.

Missions is the plural of mission—tasks or assignments with specific purposes. Military missions are operations with defined objectives. Diplomatic missions are official delegations or their buildings: {the French mission in Geneva}. Religious missions are efforts to spread faith or the establishments where missionaries work: {Spanish missions dot the California coast}. In video games, missions are discrete objectives players must complete.

A misstep is a stumble or awkward step—placing your foot wrong while walking. More often the word is figurative: a mistake or error in judgment, especially one that damages your position or reputation. {One misstep could cost him the election.} {She recovered quickly from her early career missteps.}

Mist is a thin fog—water vapor suspended in air that reduces visibility without obscuring it entirely. {Morning mist hung over the valley}. Mist also describes any fine spray or haze: {a mist of perfume}, {the mist from a waterfall}. Eyes mist over with tears or emotion. To mist plants is to spray them lightly. Something lost {in the mists of time} is obscured by the distant past.

A mistake is an error—something done wrongly or believed incorrectly. You can {make a mistake} in calculation, judgment, or action. To mistake one thing for another is to confuse them: {I mistook her for her sister}. Mistaken as an adjective means wrong: {You're mistaken about that}. {There's no mistaking} something means it's unmistakable.

Mistaken means wrong or in error. A mistaken {belief} or mistaken {impression} is one that doesn't match reality. To be mistaken is to be wrong about something: {If you think I'm paying for this, you're mistaken}. The phrase {mistaken identity} describes confusing one person for another. {Unless I'm mistaken} introduces a tentative claim the speaker believes is correct.

Mistakes are errors or wrong actions, things done incorrectly or poorly judged. A mistake can be minor—a spelling mistake, a mistake in arithmetic—or consequential: {Marrying him was the biggest mistake of my life}. To mistake something is to misidentify it: {I mistook her for her sister}. {Make no mistake} emphasizes certainty about what follows.

Mister is a title of courtesy placed before a man's name, nearly always abbreviated to Mr. It applies to any adult male regardless of status, though it carries slightly more formality than using a first name alone. When used without a name, mister can address a stranger directly: {Hey, mister, you dropped your wallet.} The word also appears in compound titles like {mister chairman} or playfully in {mister know-it-all}.

Mistletoe is a parasitic plant that grows on the branches of trees, drawing water and nutrients from its host. It has leathery evergreen leaves and white berries. In Western tradition, mistletoe is hung as Christmas decoration, and people standing beneath it are supposed to kiss: {They caught each other under the mistletoe}.

A mistress is a woman in a position of authority or control—the mistress of a household manages its affairs. The word parallels master but carries additional meanings master lacks. A mistress is also a woman having an ongoing sexual relationship with a married man: {He kept a mistress in the city}. In some contexts, mistress is an archaic or formal title for a woman, surviving in the abbreviations Mrs. and Ms.

A mistrial is a trial that has been terminated and declared void before a verdict is reached. Common causes include a hung jury that cannot agree, procedural errors, juror misconduct, or prejudicial statements that compromise fairness. When a mistrial is declared, the case may be retried from the beginning: {The judge declared a mistrial after discovering the jury had been tainted}.

Mistrust is doubt about someone's honesty, reliability, or intentions. It implies suspicion without necessarily having proof: {Years of broken promises bred deep mistrust}. As a verb, to mistrust is to regard with suspicion: {She mistrusted his motives from the start}. Mistrust suggests wariness rather than outright accusation—you haven't caught them lying, but you're not convinced they're telling the truth either.

Mists is the plural of mist—light fog or fine water droplets suspended in air. The word often suggests something romantic or mysterious: {The valley was shrouded in morning mists}. Figuratively, mists obscure clarity: {the mists of time}, {the mists of memory}. As a verb, mists means becomes misty or sprays lightly: {The window mists over}, {She mists the plants daily}.

Misty describes something covered with or obscured by mist—a light fog or fine spray: {a misty morning}, {misty mountains}. The word extends to anything hazy or indistinct: {misty memories}, {misty recollections of childhood}. Eyes that are misty are slightly tearful, usually from emotion: {She got a little misty during the wedding vows}. (Capitalized Misty is a given name.)

To misunderstand is to fail to grasp someone's meaning correctly—to interpret words, actions, or intentions in a way the speaker or actor didn't intend. {I think you misunderstood me—I meant next Tuesday, not this one.} The noun misunderstanding can be a simple failure of comprehension or a minor disagreement: {We had a little misunderstanding about the bill.}

A misunderstanding is a failure to interpret something correctly. Two people may have a misunderstanding when each takes the other's words differently than intended: {It was just a misunderstanding—I thought you meant next Tuesday}. The word sometimes euphemizes deeper conflicts: calling a bitter dispute a {misunderstanding} minimizes it.

Misunderstandings are failures to understand correctly—instances where meaning, intention, or information is grasped wrongly. The word often implies no one is fully at fault: {It was just a misunderstanding}. Misunderstandings can be minor confusions or the source of serious conflict: {The war began over a series of diplomatic misunderstandings}.

Misunderstood describes someone or something not properly comprehended or appreciated. A misunderstood {artist} produces work others fail to grasp. A misunderstood {instruction} leads to errors. The word often carries sympathy—the misunderstood teenager isn't difficult, just not seen clearly: {He's not mean, just misunderstood}.

Misuse is improper or harmful use of something. You can misuse a tool by using it for the wrong purpose, misuse power by wielding it unfairly, or misuse a word by applying it incorrectly. The noun follows the same pattern: {the misuse of public funds}, {drug misuse}. Misuse suggests deviation from intended or appropriate function rather than mere overuse.

A mite is a tiny arachnid, often microscopic, that lives on plants, animals, or in soil—dust mites trigger allergies, and mites cause mange in dogs. Mite also means a very small amount or a small creature, especially a child: {The poor mite was exhausted}. A mite as an adverb means slightly: {a mite disappointed}.

Mithril is a fictional metal invented by J.R.R. Tolkien in his Middle-earth novels—silvery, stronger than steel, and lighter than silk. The word has since become standard fantasy vocabulary, appearing in countless games and stories to denote rare, magical metal of exceptional quality: {I finally found a mithril sword}. Sometimes spelled mythril.

A mitt is a type of glove, especially one with a single compartment for the four fingers together: {oven mitt}, {catcher's mitt}. In baseball, the catcher and first baseman wear mitts rather than fingered gloves. Informally, mitts are hands: {Keep your mitts off my stuff}. The word is a shortened form of mitten.

A mitten is a hand covering with a single compartment for all four fingers together and a separate compartment for the thumb. Mittens keep hands warmer than gloves because fingers share heat: {Don't forget your mittens—it's freezing out there}. Oven mitts and boxing mitts extend the concept to protective padding.

Mittens are hand coverings with a single compartment for the four fingers and a separate one for the thumb, distinguishing them from gloves, which have individual finger slots. Mittens keep hands warmer because fingers share heat: {My mother always made us wear mittens in winter}. The word often suggests childhood or cozy warmth.

Mitts are gloves, especially those without separate fingers or with the fingers cut off: {oven mitts}, {baseball mitts}. In informal speech, mitts means hands: {Keep your mitts off my stuff}. A catcher's mitt in baseball is heavily padded for receiving pitches. Mittens, the full form, typically refers to cold-weather handwear with a thumb compartment but no individual fingers.

Mix is about combining things that were separate. You mix ingredients when cooking, mix colors when painting, mix sounds when producing music. A mix is the result—a particular combination: {a mix of styles}, {a trail mix}. To mix with people is to socialize: {She doesn't mix well at parties}. To {mix it up} is to fight or compete aggressively. A mix-up is a confusion or mistake.

Mixed describes things combined or blended together: {mixed nuts}, {mixed feelings}, {mixed company}. A mixed {bag} contains varied elements of uneven quality. Mixed {signals} are contradictory messages. Someone of mixed {race} has parents from different racial backgrounds. A mixed {blessing} brings both advantages and disadvantages. To get mixed {up} is to become confused, or to become involved: {He got mixed up with the wrong crowd}.

A mixer is a device or person that mixes things together. A stand mixer blends ingredients; an audio mixer combines sound signals. A mixer is also a non-alcoholic beverage combined with liquor: {tonic water as a mixer for gin}. Socially, a mixer is an event designed for people to meet and mingle: {a freshman mixer}.

Mixing is combining separate elements into a unified whole. You mix ingredients when cooking, mix paint colors, or mix drinks at a bar. In audio production, mixing balances and blends separate recorded tracks into a final version: {The album took months to mix}. To mix socially is to mingle: {She doesn't mix well with strangers}. A mix-up is a confusion or mistake.

Mixology is the art or skill of preparing mixed drinks, especially cocktails. The term elevates bartending to a craft, suggesting knowledge of ingredients, techniques, and flavor combinations: {The speakeasy prides itself on its mixology}. A mixologist is someone who practices this craft, though many bartenders find the term pretentious.

A mixtape is a compilation of songs recorded onto a single cassette tape, CD, or digital playlist. Originally, mixtapes were personal creations—someone selecting and sequencing tracks for a friend, a crush, or themselves: {He made her a mixtape for Valentine's Day}. In hip-hop, a mixtape is an unofficial release showcasing an artist's work, often with freestyles over borrowed beats, used to build buzz before a commercial album. The term persists even when no tape is involved.

Mixtapes are compilations of songs recorded onto a single cassette tape, CD, or digital file. Originally, people made mixtapes by recording tracks from the radio or copying from other tapes—a personalized selection for a road trip, a party, or a romantic gesture: {He made her a mixtape of love songs}. In hip-hop, a mixtape is an unofficial release showcasing an artist's work, often featuring freestyles over existing beats. The term persists even though the cassette tape has largely disappeared.

A mixture is a combination of different elements or substances: {a mixture of flour and water}, {a mixture of emotions}. Unlike a compound, the components retain their individual properties and can often be separated. The word suggests variety without uniformity—things brought together but not fully blended: {The crowd was a mixture of locals and tourists}.

A mixup is a confusion or misunderstanding, especially one involving mistaken identities or swapped items: {There was a mixup at the hospital and we got the wrong test results}. The word often implies an accident rather than intention—paperwork errors, scheduling conflicts, miscommunication. Also spelled mix-up.

A moan is a low, prolonged sound expressing pain, pleasure, or distress: {She let out a moan as the massage worked the knot from her shoulder}. People moan in grief, during sex, or when sick. The wind moans through empty buildings. To moan is also to complain tediously: {He's always moaning about his job}. British English uses moan for complaint more readily than American.

Moaning is the act of making low, prolonged sounds—whether from pain, pleasure, or complaint. Sexual moaning expresses arousal or climax. Outside the bedroom, moaning often means grumbling or whining: {He's always moaning about his job}. The British use it more readily for habitual complaining: {Stop your moaning and get on with it}.

Moans are low, prolonged sounds expressing pain, pleasure, or dissatisfaction. Someone moans in agony after an injury, moans during sex, or moans about their workload. The verb and noun overlap: {She let out a moan} and {She moaned} describe the same sound. Moaning about something shades into complaining: {He's always moaning about the weather}.

A moat is a deep, wide ditch surrounding a castle or fortified place, typically filled with water to prevent attack. The word extends to any protective barrier: {a moat of lawyers}, {regulatory moats that protect established companies from competition}. In business strategy, a moat is a competitive advantage that shields a company from rivals.

Moats are deep, wide ditches surrounding a castle or fortified place, typically filled with water as a defensive barrier. The word almost always appears in historical or fantasy contexts: {The castle's moat made direct assault nearly impossible}. Figuratively, a moat is any protective barrier that keeps threats at bay—in business, a competitive moat protects market position from rivals.

A mob is a large, disorderly crowd, often with aggressive or violent intent: {An angry mob gathered outside the courthouse}. The word carries connotations of irrationality and herd behavior—a mob mentality. With "the," the mob refers to organized crime, particularly the Mafia: {His uncle had ties to the mob}. In Australian slang, a mob is simply a group or crowd without negative connotations. The verb means to crowd around aggressively or enthusiastically: {Fans mobbed the singer at the airport}.

Mobile describes something capable of moving or being moved. A mobile {phone} travels with you; a mobile {home} can be relocated (though rarely is). Mobile {forces} move quickly across terrain. A {mobile face} is expressive, its features shifting easily. As a noun, a mobile is a hanging sculpture with balanced parts that move with air currents, popularized by Alexander Calder. The word also applies to social movement: {upwardly mobile} means rising in status or wealth. (Capitalized Mobile is a city in Alabama.)

Mobility is the ability to move or be moved. Physical mobility refers to how well a person can get around—someone with limited mobility may use a wheelchair or walker. Social mobility describes movement between economic classes: {upward mobility}, {downward mobility}. The term extends to flexibility in employment or location: {job mobility}, {geographic mobility}. In military contexts, mobility means the capacity to move troops and equipment quickly.

Mobilization is the act of organizing and preparing resources for action, especially assembling military forces for war: {The mobilization of troops along the border signaled escalating tensions}. The term extends to any large-scale organizing effort: {voter mobilization}, {community mobilization}, {the mobilization of public opinion}. To mobilize something is to get it moving and ready for use.

Mobilize means to organize and prepare resources for action, especially military forces: {The country mobilized its troops along the border}. The word extends to any coordinated marshaling of people or assets: {Community organizers mobilized voters}, {The company mobilized its legal team}. To mobilize support is to rally it. In medicine, to mobilize a joint is to restore its movement after injury or surgery.

Mobilizing is organizing people or resources for action, especially urgent or collective action. The word comes from military contexts—mobilizing troops means assembling and preparing them for war—but extends to any coordinated effort: {mobilizing voters}, {mobilizing support for a cause}, {mobilizing emergency response teams}. The emphasis is on moving from static to active, from potential to deployed.

Mobs is the plural of mob—a large, disorderly crowd, often with violent or threatening energy: {Angry mobs surrounded the courthouse}. A mob can also mean any large group: {mobs of tourists}. In organized crime, the Mob refers to the Mafia. In video games, mobs are hostile non-player characters that spawn in groups: {grinding mobs for XP}.

A mobster is a member of an organized crime syndicate, especially the Italian-American Mafia. The term evokes the gangster era of the 1920s and 1930s but applies to contemporary organized crime as well: {The mobster ran gambling operations across three states}. Mobster carries connotations of violence, loyalty codes, and criminal enterprise conducted like business.

Mobsters are members of organized crime groups, particularly the Italian-American Mafia. The term evokes a specific era and style—suited men in smoky rooms, protection rackets, and coded loyalty: {The mobsters ran the neighborhood}. A mobster is a gangster, but with connotations of hierarchy and syndicate membership rather than street-level criminality.

A moccasin is a soft leather shoe, originally made by North American Indigenous peoples, typically constructed from a single piece of hide with the sole turned up and attached to a U-shaped upper. The style has been adapted into casual slip-on shoes. Moccasin also names a venomous North American pit viper, the water moccasin or cottonmouth, which inhabits swamps and waterways of the southeastern United States.

Moccasins are soft leather shoes, originally made by North American Indigenous peoples from a single piece of deerskin with the sole turned up and sewn to a U-shaped upper piece. The style has been widely adopted in casual footwear, often as slip-on loafers: {She kicked off her moccasins by the door}. Water moccasins are venomous snakes, named for their coloring.

Mocha pairs coffee with chocolate. The name comes from Mocha, a port in Yemen that was once the main hub for coffee trade. Today mocha refers to any drink or flavor combining coffee and chocolate: {I'll have a mocha with whipped cream.}

Mochi is a Japanese rice cake made from glutinous rice pounded into a sticky, chewy paste. It appears in many forms—plain, filled with sweet bean paste, wrapped around ice cream, or grilled. The texture is distinctively elastic and slightly stretchy. Mochi is traditional at New Year celebrations but has become popular year-round in various desserts and snacks.

Mock means to ridicule or treat with contempt, often by imitation: {The kids mocked his accent}. It can also mean to mimic derisively or to frustrate expectations: {The locked door mocked our escape plans}. As an adjective, mock describes something simulated or imitation rather than real: a mock {trial}, mock {turtle soup}, a mock {battle}. The noun appears in phrases like {make a mock of}, meaning to make a joke of something serious.

Mockery is ridicule or contemptuous imitation—words or actions that hold someone or something up to scorn: {His apology was pure mockery}. A mockery can also be a ludicrously inadequate or futile attempt: {The trial was a mockery of justice}. To {make a mockery of} something is to render it absurd or worthless through poor execution or disrespect.

Mocking describes speech or behavior that ridicules someone, often by imitation: {She repeated his words in a mocking tone}. A mocking smile or laugh conveys contempt. To mock is to make fun of, sometimes by mimicking: {The children mocked his accent}. In software development, mocking creates simulated objects that stand in for real components during testing.

A mockingbird is a gray North American songbird known for its ability to mimic the calls of other birds and various sounds in its environment. The name comes from this imitative behavior—the bird "mocks" other species. Mockingbirds are territorial and sing persistently, often through the night. {A mockingbird was singing outside my window at 3 a.m.}

Mockingbirds is the plural of mockingbird, a gray North American songbird famous for imitating the calls of other birds and sounds in its environment. The bird gives its name to the novel *To Kill a Mockingbird*, where killing one symbolizes destroying innocence: {There were mockingbirds in the oak tree outside my window}.

Mocks is the third-person singular form of mock, meaning to ridicule or imitate derisively: {She mocks his accent behind his back}. In software development, mocks are simulated objects that stand in for real components during testing: {We wrote mocks for the database calls}. Mock exams or trials are practice versions: {The mocks helped her prepare for finals}.

A mocktail is a mixed drink made without alcohol, designed to resemble a cocktail in presentation and complexity. The word blends *mock* with *cocktail*. Mocktails often feature fruit juices, sodas, herbs, and elaborate garnishes: {The restaurant has an impressive mocktail menu for designated drivers}. Also called a virgin cocktail.

Mocktails are cocktails made without alcohol—mixed drinks that mimic the presentation and complexity of their boozy counterparts using juices, sodas, syrups, and garnishes. The term blends "mock" with "cocktail." Bars and restaurants increasingly offer mocktail menus for designated drivers, pregnant women, or anyone avoiding alcohol: {The mocktail list had a virgin mojito and a sparkling berry spritz}.

A mockup is a model or replica made for demonstration, testing, or planning purposes. Architects show mockups of buildings, designers create website mockups before coding, and manufacturers build mockups of products before production. Unlike a prototype, which functions, a mockup typically shows only appearance or layout: {The mockup looked great but had no working parts}. Also spelled mock-up.

Mod is a shortening that has several applications. A mod is a modification, especially to a video game or software that alters or extends its features: {I installed a graphics mod that makes the game look incredible}. In online communities, a mod is a moderator who enforces rules and manages discussions. As a verb, to mod something is to modify it or to serve as a moderator. The word also refers to a British youth subculture of the 1960s characterized by sharp fashion and motor scooters.

Modding is the practice of modifying video games, software, or hardware—typically by users rather than original creators. Game modding ranges from small tweaks to complete overhauls: {The modding community created hundreds of new quests for Skyrim}. Hardware modding might mean customizing a car or computer case. The term comes from modification, with the doubled consonant following standard spelling conventions for verbs ending in a short vowel plus consonant.
