Mode is a particular way or manner of doing something: {What mode of transportation do you prefer?} In statistics, the mode is the value that appears most frequently in a data set. Mode also describes a state or setting: {The phone is in airplane mode}, {She switched into work mode}. In music, modes are scales with distinct patterns of intervals, like Dorian or Phrygian.

A model is a representation of a thing that is made or used for a particular purpose. A model of a product can be used for testing, in advance of manufacture. A model of climate change can be developed to understand its implications. A fashion model wears clothes for promotional purposes. When you model something, you develop a model of it: Researchers are attempting to model the interactions of these two isomers. As an adjective, model may convey form (a model airplane), or a prototype or ideal (a model legislator).

Modeling is shaping or forming something, especially from a malleable material: {She spent the afternoon modeling clay}. In fashion, modeling is working as a model—displaying clothing or posing for photographers. In science and business, modeling means creating simplified representations of complex systems: {climate modeling}, {financial modeling}. To model behavior is to demonstrate it for others to imitate.

Modelling is the British spelling of modeling. It covers the same range of meanings: working as a model in fashion or art, creating representations of things (such as architectural models or computer simulations), and shaping materials like clay. The word also applies to demonstrating behavior for others to imitate: {The teacher was modelling good listening skills}. In scientific and mathematical contexts, modelling refers to building abstract representations of systems or processes to analyze or predict their behavior.

Models are representations of something else—simplified versions that help us understand, display, or predict. A model {airplane} mimics the real thing at smaller scale. A {computer model} simulates weather or economics. A {business model} describes how a company operates. In fashion and art, a model is a person who poses or displays clothing: {She works as a model}. To model is to create such representations, to pose professionally, or to demonstrate by example: {He models good behavior for his students}. Model as an adjective means exemplary: {a model citizen}, {a model student}.

A modem is a device that converts digital signals to analog and vice versa, allowing computers to communicate over telephone lines or cable systems. The word blends "modulator" and "demodulator." Early modems connected to the internet via dial-up, producing distinctive screeching sounds; modern cable and DSL modems are silent and far faster. {The technician installed a new modem to fix our internet connection.}

Moderate describes something in the middle range—not extreme, not minimal, but somewhere in between. A moderate {climate} is neither too hot nor too cold; moderate {exercise} is neither strenuous nor negligible. As a noun, a moderate is someone whose political views avoid the extremes of left and right. The verb moderate means to preside over a discussion or debate, or to make something less intense: {The medication helped moderate her symptoms}. To do something {in moderation} is to avoid excess.

Moderation is the practice of avoiding extremes or excess, keeping things within reasonable bounds. {Everything in moderation} is common advice about eating, drinking, or any potentially harmful activity. In online contexts, moderation refers to the oversight and management of user-generated content—removing spam, enforcing community guidelines, and keeping discussions civil. A moderator performs this function, whether on a forum, at a debate, or in a panel discussion.

A moderator oversees discussion and enforces rules. In online communities, moderators review content, remove violations, and ban users: {The moderator deleted the post for harassment}. In debates or panels, a moderator guides conversation and keeps participants on topic. In nuclear physics, a moderator is a substance that slows neutrons in a reactor.

Moderators are people who oversee discussions or communities, ensuring rules are followed and civility maintained. Online moderators ({mods}) remove offensive content, ban disruptive users, and shape community culture on forums, social media, and streaming platforms: {The moderators took down the post for violating guidelines}. In debates or panels, a moderator guides conversation and keeps participants on track. In nuclear physics, a moderator is material that slows neutrons in a reactor.

Modern means belonging to the present or recent times rather than the distant past. A modern {building} uses contemporary materials and design; modern {medicine} refers to current scientific practices. Modern can also mean up-to-date or advanced: {modern conveniences}. In historical periodization, the modern era begins roughly with the Renaissance. As a noun, a modern is a person of contemporary times, or someone with progressive views.

Modernism is a broad cultural movement of the late 19th and early 20th centuries that broke with traditional forms in art, literature, architecture, and music. Writers like Joyce and Woolf, painters like Picasso, and architects like Le Corbusier rejected established conventions in favor of experimentation and abstraction. More generally, modernism can mean any embrace of contemporary ideas over traditional ones: {His modernism clashed with the church's conservative teachings}. (Capitalized Modernism often refers specifically to the historical movement.)

Modest describes something moderate or unpretentious. A modest {income} is adequate but not lavish. A modest {proposal} doesn't ask for much. A modest person doesn't boast about accomplishments or draw attention to themselves—sometimes genuinely humble, sometimes falsely so. Modest also means not revealing too much of the body: {modest dress}. {She was modest about her achievements}.

Modesty is the quality of being unassuming about one's abilities or achievements—not boasting or drawing attention to oneself: {She accepted the award with characteristic modesty}. The word also refers to propriety in dress and behavior, particularly regarding sexual matters: {Victorian standards of modesty required covering the ankles}. A modest person avoids excess in self-presentation.

Mods is the plural of mod, with several distinct meanings. In gaming and software, mods are user-created modifications that alter or extend a program: {The mods for this game add hundreds of hours of new content}. Mods also refers to moderators—people who monitor online communities and enforce rules: {The mods banned him for harassment}. Historically, mods were members of a 1960s British youth subculture known for sharp Italian fashion, motor scooters, and soul music, often contrasted with their rivals, the rockers.

A mogul is a powerful or influential person in a particular industry: {a media mogul}, {a real estate mogul}. The word implies wealth and dominance. Separately, moguls are the bumps that form on ski slopes from repeated turns by skiers. (Capitalized Mogul refers to the Mughal dynasty of India.)

Moguls has two unrelated meanings. A mogul is a powerful person, especially in business or entertainment: {a media mogul}, {Hollywood moguls}. Separately, moguls are bumps on a ski slope formed by repeated turns carving out the snow, or the sport of skiing down such terrain: {She competed in freestyle moguls at the Olympics}.

A mohawk is a hairstyle in which the sides of the head are shaved and the remaining center strip of hair stands upright, often spiked. Associated with punk rock culture and rebellion since the 1970s: {She showed up with a bright green mohawk}. In figure skating, a mohawk is a turn from one foot to the other while maintaining the same direction of travel. (Capitalized Mohawk refers to the Indigenous people or their language.)

Mohawks are hairstyles in which the head is shaved on both sides, leaving a strip of hair—often spiked upward—running from forehead to nape. The style became iconic in punk subculture during the 1970s and 1980s: {He showed up with a bright green mohawk}. In figure skating, a mohawk is a turn from one foot to the other while maintaining the same edge and direction of travel. (Capitalized Mohawk refers to the Indigenous people or their language.)

Moist describes something slightly wet—damp but not soaking. A moist {towelette} is wet enough to clean with. Moist {cake} has good texture, not dry. Moist {soil} holds water well for plants. The word has acquired a reputation as unpleasant-sounding, which some people find amusing and others genuinely dislike: {Don't say moist around her}.

Moisture is the presence of water or other liquid in small amounts, especially as dampness in the air, on a surface, or within a material. Soil retains moisture; skin loses it. {The cookies went stale from moisture in the air.} Moisturize means to add moisture, typically to skin or hair.

A moisturizer is a cream or lotion applied to skin to keep it soft and hydrated. Most moisturizers work by trapping water in the outer layer of skin: {She applies moisturizer after every shower}. The term extends to similar products for hair or lips.

A mojito is a cocktail made with white rum, lime juice, sugar, mint, and soda water. The drink originated in Cuba and became popular internationally in the early 2000s. The muddled mint and lime give it a fresh, citrusy character: {We ordered mojitos on the patio}.

Mojo is a person's magic charm, talent, or sexual appeal—an ineffable quality that brings success or power. The word entered mainstream English from African American folk magic traditions, where a mojo was a charm or spell. Now it's usually about personal magnetism or effectiveness: {He's lost his mojo}, {She got her mojo back}. In Austin Powers films, mojo became synonymous with masculine swagger and sex appeal.

A molar is one of the large, flat teeth at the back of the mouth used for grinding food. Humans have twelve molars, including four wisdom teeth. In chemistry and physics, molar means relating to a mole—the standard unit for measuring amounts of a substance: {molar mass}, {molar concentration}.

Molars are the large, flat teeth at the back of the mouth used for grinding food. Humans typically have twelve—three on each side of the upper and lower jaws, including the wisdom teeth. The word sometimes appears figuratively for any crushing mechanism: {The bureaucracy's molars ground through the paperwork}.

Molasses is the thick, dark syrup left over when sugar is refined from sugarcane or sugar beets. It has a bittersweet flavor and is used in baking, especially for gingerbread and brown bread. Blackstrap molasses, from the final extraction, is the darkest and most bitter. Something {slow as molasses} moves very slowly: {Traffic was moving like molasses in January}.

Mold (British spelling mould) is a growth of fungus. When something molds, fungus has begun to grow on or in it. A different mold is a container used to give shape to plastic, plaster, or clay that is poured or pressed into it. When you mold something, you form it using a mold. To mold a person or their character is to have great influence in their development.

Molds are hollow forms that shape liquid or soft material as it hardens: {a candle mold}, {a gelatin mold}. The resulting object is also a mold. To mold is to shape something, literally or figuratively: {She molded the clay}, {experiences that mold character}. Separately, mold is the fuzzy fungal growth on damp or decaying matter: {There's mold on this bread}. To mold in this sense is to become moldy.

Moldy describes something covered with mold—the fuzzy fungal growth that appears on food, walls, or other organic matter left in damp conditions: {The bread had gone moldy}. Extended uses suggest staleness or decay: moldy {ideas}, a moldy {old book}. What's moldy has been neglected or left too long.

Mole gathers several unrelated words. The burrowing mammal digs tunnels underground, lending its name to someone who burrows into an organization to spy from within: {They suspected a mole in the intelligence agency}. A mole is also a small dark spot on skin—a pigmented growth. In chemistry, a mole is a unit measuring amount of substance. A mole can also be a massive stone breakwater protecting a harbor. In Mexican cuisine, mole is a rich sauce made with chiles and often chocolate.

A molecule is the smallest unit of a substance that retains its chemical properties—two or more atoms bonded together. Water molecules consist of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. In casual use, molecule suggests something extremely small: {There's not a molecule of truth in what he said}. The adjective is molecular: {molecular biology}, {molecular structure}.

Molecules are the smallest units of a chemical compound, consisting of two or more atoms bonded together. A water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. The term extends to any small particle or trace amount: {There's not a molecule of truth in what he said}. In scientific contexts, molecular describes things at this scale: molecular {biology}, molecular {structure}.

A molehill is a small mound of earth pushed up by a burrowing mole. The word appears almost exclusively in the idiom {make a mountain out of a molehill}—to treat a minor problem as if it were a major one.

Moles are small burrowing mammals with velvety fur, tiny eyes, and powerful forelimbs adapted for digging. They live underground and are considered pests for the tunnels they create in lawns. A mole is also a dark spot on the skin—a cluster of pigmented cells, usually harmless but sometimes monitored for changes. In espionage, a mole is an undercover agent who infiltrates an organization over a long period: {They discovered a mole in the intelligence agency}. In chemistry, a mole is a unit measuring the amount of a substance, equal to Avogadro's number of particles.

Molt is what animals do when they shed old feathers, fur, skin, or shells to make way for new growth. Birds molt their feathers seasonally; snakes molt their skin; crabs molt their shells as they grow. The noun molt refers to the process or the material shed: {The chicken coop was full of molt}. Also spelled moult in British English.

Molten describes material—usually metal, rock, or glass—that has been liquefied by intense heat: {molten lava}, {molten steel}. The word carries connotations of dangerous heat and fluid movement. Molten is the old past participle of melt, preserved in this specialized sense while melted took over general use.

Mom is an informal word for mother, used especially in American English. It functions both as a term of address {Mom, can I borrow the car?} and as a reference {My mom works nights}. The word carries warmth and familiarity. A {mom and pop} store is a small family-owned business. {Soccer mom} describes a suburban mother devoted to shuttling children to activities.

A moment is a very brief period of time—shorter than a minute, longer than an instant: {Wait here a moment}, {I'll be with you in a moment}. The word also means a particular point in time: {At that moment, everything changed}. A moment can carry weight or significance: {a moment of clarity}, {this is not the moment for jokes}. In physics, moment refers to a turning force around a point.

Moments is the plural of moment, a brief span of time. Moments can signal emotional significance: {One of the happiest moments of my life}. The phrase {has its moments} acknowledges intermittent quality: {The film drags, but it has its moments}. In physics, moment refers to a rotational force—hence {moment of inertia}.

Momentum is the force of movement—what keeps something going once it's started. In physics, it's the product of mass and velocity: a rolling boulder has more momentum than a rolling marble. Figuratively, momentum describes building progress or energy: {The campaign gained momentum after the debate}. To {lose momentum} is to slow or stall. {The momentum of the scandal proved unstoppable}.

Momma is an informal, affectionate term for mother, common in Southern American English and children's speech: {Go ask your momma}. It often carries warmth or nostalgia that the neutral "mother" lacks. In slang, momma can refer to an attractive woman or girlfriend: {She's a fine momma}. Also spelled mama.

Mommy is a child's word for mother, used by young children or when speaking to them: {Go ask Mommy}. Adults may use it affectionately, nostalgically, or ironically. In sexual contexts, mommy appears in phrases like {mommy kink} or {mommy issues}, referring to attraction shaped by maternal dynamics. The standard British equivalent is mummy.

Moms is the plural of mom, an informal word for mother. The term often appears in contexts addressing mothers as a group: {busy moms}, {working moms}, {soccer moms}. In informal direct address, moms can refer to a single mother: {Hey moms, what's for dinner?}

A monarch is a sovereign ruler—a king, queen, emperor, or similar head of state who typically inherits the position and holds it for life. In constitutional monarchies, the monarch's power is largely ceremonial: {The monarch opened Parliament}. The word also names the monarch butterfly, a large orange-and-black species famous for its long migrations.

Monarchs is the plural of monarch, a sovereign ruler such as a king, queen, or emperor who typically inherits the position. The word extends to anyone who dominates a field: {the monarchs of Silicon Valley}. A monarch is also a large orange-and-black butterfly known for migrating thousands of miles: {We watched monarchs pass through on their way to Mexico}.

A monarchy is a system of government in which a single person—king, queen, emperor—holds supreme authority, typically by hereditary succession. The term also refers to a state governed this way: {the British monarchy}, {the fall of the French monarchy}. Modern monarchies range from absolute (the ruler holds real power) to constitutional (the monarch is largely ceremonial while elected officials govern).

Monasteries is the plural of monastery, a building or complex where monks or nuns live in religious community. Monasteries are typically secluded from ordinary society, devoted to prayer, contemplation, and communal religious practice: {Medieval monasteries preserved classical manuscripts through the Dark Ages}. The term applies across religious traditions—Christian, Buddhist, and others.

A monastery is a building or complex where monks live as a religious community, typically following a structured life of prayer, work, and contemplation apart from the wider world. The term applies primarily to Christian and Buddhist traditions, though similar institutions exist in other religions. Monasteries often include a chapel, dormitories, and communal spaces, and historically served as centers of learning and manuscript preservation. {The ancient monastery had been producing wine for centuries.}

Money is a medium for exchange of value, represented concretely by bills and coins (Have you got any money on you?) and abstractly by accounts and credit. The verbs most commonly used with money are raise and make. To raise money is to collect enough of it to do something: They’re trying to raise money for a documentary about hippies. To make money is not to manufacture it, but to receive it in exchange for something, or to realize a profit: Did you make any money when you sold your house? Money is used in common phrases with a related meaning: marry money means marry someone rich. In the money means in a profitable situation.

Moneybags is an informal, slightly mocking term for a wealthy person, emphasizing their abundance of cash. It often carries a tone of envy or mild resentment: {Hey moneybags, you're buying lunch today}. The word can be used as a noun or as a joking form of address. Though sometimes affectionate among friends, it typically implies the person flaunts or is defined by their wealth rather than other qualities.

A moneymaker is something or someone that generates profit or income. A business's moneymaker is its most profitable product or division: {The streaming service became the company's biggest moneymaker}. A person who earns well for themselves or others is also a moneymaker. In slang, moneymaker refers playfully to the body, especially the hips or buttocks: {Shake your moneymaker}.

A mongoose is a small, agile carnivorous mammal native to Africa and Asia, known for its ability to kill venomous snakes. Mongooses are quick and fearless, attacking cobras and other serpents with darting strikes while avoiding fangs. The plural is mongooses, not mongeese: {Mongooses have been introduced to islands to control rats, often with disastrous ecological results}.

A monitor is a device that displays information or tracks conditions. Computer monitors show visual output; heart monitors track vital signs. The word extends to people who watch or supervise: hall monitors in schools, election monitors at polling places. To monitor is to observe systematically: {We're monitoring the situation closely}. A monitor lizard is a large tropical reptile—the name may derive from a belief that they warn of crocodiles nearby.

Monitors are devices that display information—computer screens showing visual output, or medical equipment tracking vital signs. A monitor is also someone who watches or checks on something: a hall monitor supervises students, an election monitor observes voting. To monitor is to observe systematically: {We're monitoring the situation closely}. Monitor lizards are large reptiles, some exceeding ten feet.

A monk is a man who has withdrawn from ordinary life to devote himself to religious practice, typically living in a community under vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience. Christian and Buddhist traditions are best known for monasticism, though the practice exists in other religions. {The monks rose at dawn for prayer.} Monks often live in monasteries, following strict daily routines of worship, work, and contemplation.

A monkey is a primate, typically smaller than apes and usually having a tail. Monkeys divide into Old World species (Africa, Asia) and New World species (Americas). The word extends to playful mischief: {Stop monkeying around}. To {monkey with} something is to tamper with it. {Monkey see, monkey do} describes mindless imitation. A {monkey on your back} is an addiction or persistent problem. In British slang, a monkey is five hundred pounds.

Monkeys are primates, typically smaller than apes and usually possessing tails. The term covers a wide range of species across Africa, Asia, and the Americas. To monkey with something is to tamper or tinker: {Stop monkeying with the thermostat}. To {monkey around} is to behave playfully or mischievously. A {monkey on your back} is a persistent burden or addiction.

Monks is the plural of monk—men who have withdrawn from ordinary society to live under religious vows, typically in a monastery. The term applies across traditions: Christian monks follow rules like those of St. Benedict, while Buddhist monks may beg for alms. {The monks rose before dawn for prayer.} Monks often take vows of poverty, celibacy, and obedience.

Monochrome means using only one color or shades of a single color. A monochrome photograph uses black, white, and grays rather than full color. In design and fashion, monochrome describes an outfit or palette restricted to variations of one hue: {She wore a monochrome look in shades of blue}. The word also works as a noun: {The film was shot in monochrome}.

A monocle is a single lens worn in front of one eye, held in place by the muscles around the eye socket. Once a fashionable accessory among wealthy men in the 19th and early 20th centuries, it now appears mainly as a costume piece or visual shorthand for aristocratic pretension: {He adjusted his monocle and sniffed disapprovingly}.

Monocles is the plural of monocle, a single corrective lens worn in one eye socket, held in place by the brow and cheek. Once a mark of aristocratic refinement, the monocle is now largely a costume piece or visual shorthand for old-money pretension: {The villain adjusted his monocle and sneered}.

Monogamy is the practice of having only one spouse or sexual partner at a time. The term applies both to marriage customs and to mating behavior in animals: {Swans are known for their monogamy}. Serial monogamy describes a pattern of successive exclusive relationships rather than lifelong pairing with one person: {He practices serial monogamy—always faithful, but never for long}.

A monogram is a design made by combining two or more letters, typically someone's initials, into a single symbol: {The towels were embroidered with her monogram}. Monograms appear on stationery, luggage, jewelry, and clothing as marks of ownership or personalization. To monogram something is to add such a design: {a monogrammed shirt}.

A monolith is a single massive block of stone, either natural or shaped into a monument or pillar. The word extends to anything huge, uniform, and imposing: a corporation can be a monolith, as can a government bureaucracy. The adjective monolithic emphasizes uniformity and resistance to change: {a monolithic political system}, {monolithic architecture}. In computing, a monolithic system keeps all components in one unified structure rather than separating them into modules.

Monoliths is the plural of monolith—a large single block of stone, especially one shaped into a pillar or monument. The term extends to anything massive and uniform: a corporate monolith, a monolith of bureaucracy. In science fiction, monoliths often appear as mysterious alien artifacts. The word implies imposing size and undifferentiated wholeness: {The publishing monoliths have swallowed up the independents}.

A monologue is an extended speech by one person. In theater, it's a character speaking alone or at length while others listen—distinguished from dialogue, which involves exchange. The term extends to anyone holding forth without interruption: {He launched into a monologue about his golf game}. A dramatic monologue in poetry is a poem spoken entirely by a single character.

Monologues is the plural of monologue—a long speech by one person. In theater, a monologue is an extended passage spoken by a single character, often revealing inner thoughts: {She nailed the audition monologue}. More loosely, any one-sided conversation where someone talks at length without interruption: {His monologues about work were exhausting}.

Monopolies is the plural of monopoly—exclusive control over a commodity, service, or market. A company with a monopoly faces no competition: {Standard Oil's monopolies were broken up by antitrust action}. The word extends to any exclusive possession: {She has a monopoly on his attention}. Monopolies also names the board game, though that's typically capitalized.

To monopolize is to dominate or control completely. A company monopolizes a market by eliminating competition. A person monopolizes a conversation by not letting others speak. The word implies taking more than one's fair share: {He monopolized her attention all evening}. {Tech giants have monopolized the advertising industry}.

Monopolizing is taking exclusive control of something, leaving none for others. A company monopolizing a market eliminates competition. A person monopolizing a conversation won't let anyone else speak. {Stop monopolizing the bathroom—other people need to get ready}. The word often carries a note of criticism, implying selfishness or excess.

Monopoly refers to exclusive control over something, especially a market or commodity: {The company had a monopoly on telephone service for decades}. A monopoly exists when one entity dominates to the exclusion of competitors. The term extends beyond economics to any situation of singular dominance: {She has a monopoly on his attention}. (Capitalized Monopoly is the board game.)

A monorail is a railway system in which trains run on a single rail, typically elevated above street level. Monorails appear most often at airports, theme parks, and as urban transit in a few cities. The word also refers to the train itself: {We took the monorail from the parking lot to the terminal}.

Monotonous describes something tediously uniform, lacking variety or change. A monotonous voice stays at one pitch. A monotonous job repeats the same tasks endlessly. The word carries a negative connotation—sameness that breeds boredom: {The monotonous hum of the engine put me to sleep}. {Days blurred together in monotonous routine}.

Monotony is tedious sameness or lack of variety. The word suggests weariness from repetition: {the monotony of factory work}, {the monotony of suburban life}. A monotonous voice drones on without variation in pitch or tone. Monotony implies not just uniformity but the boredom it produces—the feeling that nothing changes and nothing will.

A monsoon is a seasonal wind pattern that brings heavy rainfall, especially in South Asia. The word commonly refers to the rainy season itself or the dramatic downpours that accompany it: {The monsoon flooded the streets within minutes}. Informally, any torrential rain might be called a monsoon: {We got caught in a monsoon on the way home}.

A monster is a terrifying and threatening creature, often legendary or imaginary. Other meanings that arise from this are someone badly behaved (their children are monsters), something extremely large (monster truck), and a whimsical cartoon or comic character (Cookie Monster). Someone who is a monster in a particular field is very prominent or dominates it: The master chef was a monster in the kitchen. If you create a monster, you inadvertently bring about a situation that is difficult or unmanageable.

Monsters are creatures that frighten—whether from mythology, fiction, or nightmare. Dragons, vampires, and werewolves are monsters. The word extends to anything unnaturally large or threatening: {a monster truck}, {a monster wave}. A person who commits atrocities is called a monster: {The dictator was a monster}. Informally, monster means impressively large: {a monster hit}, {a monster deal}. Children feared for imaginary {monsters under the bed} grow up to use the word casually for formidable challenges or achievements.

A monstrosity is something shockingly ugly, malformed, or offensive to the senses. The word often describes buildings or other large creations that violate aesthetic norms: {That new shopping center is an absolute monstrosity}. It can also refer to something outrageously wrong or unjust: {The verdict was a monstrosity of the legal system}. Less commonly, monstrosity describes a deformed creature or birth defect, though this usage now sounds dated and callous.

Monstrous describes something unnaturally large, ugly, or horrifying—like a monster. A monstrous {creature} inspires fear; a monstrous {crime} shocks the conscience. The word often emphasizes shocking scale or moral outrage: {a monstrous lie}, {monstrous cruelty}. Informally, monstrous can simply mean enormous: {a monstrous wave}, {monstrous portions}.

A montage is a composite image or sequence made by combining separate elements. In film, a montage compresses time or conveys ideas through rapid succession of shots: {The training montage showed her transformation from novice to champion}. In visual art, montage assembles photographs or other images into a single composition. The technique emphasizes juxtaposition—meaning emerges from how pieces relate to each other.

Montages are composite images or sequences made by combining separate elements. In film, a montage assembles shots to compress time or convey ideas through juxtaposition: {The training montage showed months of preparation in two minutes}. In visual art, a montage combines photographs or other images into a single composition. The technique emphasizes arrangement and contrast over seamless blending.

A month is one of the twelve divisions of the calendar year: January, February, and so on. The word derives from moon—months originally tracked lunar cycles, roughly 29 days each. Modern calendar months range from 28 to 31 days. {I'll be gone for a month}. {She's six months pregnant}. A {month of Sundays} is a very long time.

Months is the plural of month, a unit of time roughly corresponding to one cycle of the moon—about thirty days. The calendar year divides into twelve months of varying lengths. {It took months to finish the project.} In the plural, months often emphasizes duration: {I haven't seen her in months.}

A monument is a structure built to commemorate a person, event, or achievement—statues, obelisks, arches, and memorial buildings. The term extends to anything that stands as lasting evidence of something significant: {His symphonies are monuments to human creativity}. To make a monument of something is to preserve or honor it. A monument can also be a boundary marker or surveying reference point.

Monumental describes something massive in scale or significance. A monumental {achievement} or monumental {effort} is extraordinarily impressive. Monumental {architecture} is built to impress—think pyramids, cathedrals, war memorials. The word can also mean serving as a monument: {a monumental inscription}. Informally, monumental intensifies negatives: {a monumental failure}, {a monumental waste of time}.

Monuments are structures built to commemorate a person, event, or achievement—statues, obelisks, arches, or buildings designed to preserve memory: {The Lincoln Monument draws millions of visitors each year}. By extension, anything that serves as a lasting tribute or evidence can be a monument: {Her body of work stands as a monument to her genius}. Natural landmarks may also be designated monuments for protection: {a national monument}.
Moo is the characteristic low, prolonged sound made by cattle. As a verb, to moo is to make this sound: {The cows mooed at feeding time}. The word is onomatopoeic—it sounds like what it describes.

Mooch means to get something without paying or working for it, usually by exploiting others' generosity: {He's always mooching cigarettes off coworkers}. A mooch is someone who habitually does this—the friend who never reaches for the check, the roommate who empties your fridge. The word carries judgment: mooching implies taking advantage rather than genuine need. To mooch around (British) is to wander aimlessly or loiter.

Mooching is getting things from others without paying or reciprocating—bumming cigarettes, crashing on couches, eating someone else's food. The word carries mild disapproval: {He's always mooching off his parents}. To mooch is to obtain things this way, and a mooch is a person who does it habitually.

Mood is a temporary state of mind or feeling—cheerful, melancholy, irritable. Someone {in a mood} is usually in a bad one. If you're {in the mood} for something, you feel like doing it. The mood of a place or work of art is its atmosphere or emotional tone: {The lighting set a romantic mood}. In grammar, mood indicates whether a verb expresses fact (indicative), command (imperative), or possibility (subjunctive).

Moodiness is the tendency to shift between emotional states, especially toward irritability or sullenness. A moody person's temperament is unpredictable—cheerful one moment, withdrawn the next. {His moodiness made him difficult to work with.} The word usually carries negative connotations, suggesting someone hard to please or be around.

Moods is the plural of mood—emotional states or prevailing feelings. A person experiences different moods throughout the day; a room has moods depending on lighting and atmosphere. In grammar, moods are verb forms indicating whether a statement is factual, conditional, or commanding: indicative, subjunctive, imperative. {Her moods shifted unpredictably.} {The painting captures the moods of the sea.}

Moody describes someone whose emotional state shifts unpredictably, often toward gloom or irritability. A moody teenager might be cheerful one moment and sullen the next. The word suggests emotional volatility rather than a single mood: {He's been moody all week}. Moody weather or moody lighting creates an atmospheric, somber effect. (Capitalized Moody is a surname.)

The moon is Earth's natural satellite, the luminous object that waxes and wanes through its monthly cycle. By extension, any natural satellite of a planet: {Jupiter has dozens of moons}. To moon is to gaze dreamily or listlessly, as if staring at the moon: {He mooned about the house for days}. In slang, to moon someone is to bare your buttocks at them. A moon is also a month, from the lunar cycle: {many moons ago}. (Capitalized Moon refers specifically to Earth's satellite as a proper noun.)

A moonbeam is a ray of light from the moon: {Moonbeams filtered through the curtains}. The word carries a soft, romantic, or whimsical quality—more likely to appear in poetry or fairy tales than scientific contexts. Someone called a moonbeam is dreamy or ethereal, perhaps not quite grounded in reality.

Moonbeams are rays of light from the moon, though the word carries a dreamy, fanciful quality that *moonlight* lacks. The singular appears in poetic or whimsical contexts: {a moonbeam fell across her face}. To call something moonbeams is to dismiss it as insubstantial fantasy: {His business plan was all moonbeams and wishful thinking}.

Moondust is the fine, powdery soil covering the lunar surface, composed of tiny rock fragments, mineral grains, and glass particles created by billions of years of meteorite impacts. It clings to everything and posed unexpected challenges during the Apollo missions: {The moondust got into everything}. Figuratively, moondust suggests something ethereal or magical: {Her voice had moondust in it}.

Mooned is the past tense of moon. To moon someone is to expose your bare buttocks as a prank or insult: {He mooned the passing car}. Separately, to moon over someone is to gaze at them dreamily or pine for them: {She mooned over her crush all semester}. The connection is the moon's pale roundness and its association with romantic longing.

Mooning is the act of baring one's buttocks at someone, typically as a prank or crude gesture of disrespect: {Some kid mooned us from the back of the school bus}. The term derives from moon as slang for buttocks. Separately, mooning can mean gazing dreamily or pining romantically: {She spent the afternoon mooning over old photographs}.

Moonlight is the light of the moon—actually reflected sunlight, but perceived as its own silvery illumination. The word evokes nighttime romance and mystery: {a walk in the moonlight}, {moonlit gardens}. To moonlight is to work a second job, typically at night: {She moonlights as a bartender}. A {moonlight flit} is a hasty departure to avoid paying rent.

A moonlighter is someone who works a second job in addition to their regular employment, typically at night or during off-hours. The term comes from the image of working by moonlight after the day job ends. {She's a moonlighter—teaches during the day and tends bar on weekends.} The practice itself is called moonlighting.

Moonlighting is working a second job, typically in addition to regular full-time employment. The term evokes work done after dark, outside normal hours: {She's been moonlighting as a bartender to pay off her student loans}. The practice may be hidden from the primary employer, though the word doesn't require secrecy.

Moonlit describes something illuminated by the light of the moon. It functions as an adjective to set a scene with soft, silvery natural light, often evoking romance, mystery, or tranquility: {a moonlit walk on the beach}, {the moonlit garden}. The word appears frequently in poetry and literary description, where nighttime settings benefit from this evocative, atmospheric quality.

A moonscape is a barren, desolate landscape resembling the surface of the moon—rocky, cratered, and devoid of vegetation. The word describes actual lunar terrain but more often applies to earthly places with similar stark emptiness: {The volcanic region was a moonscape of black rock and ash}. Bombed cities and strip-mined land become moonscapes.

Moonshine is illegally distilled liquor, especially whiskey made in homemade stills to avoid taxation. The term evokes Appalachian tradition and Prohibition-era bootlegging: {His grandfather used to run moonshine through the mountains}. Moonshine also means foolish talk or nonsense: {That's pure moonshine}. The literal sense—light from the moon—is the oldest but least common today.

A moonshiner is someone who illegally distills liquor, especially in rural areas. The term comes from the practice of working at night to avoid detection: {His grandfather was a moonshiner in the hills of Kentucky}. Moonshine itself is the illicitly produced whiskey, typically unaged and high-proof. The word carries romantic associations with Appalachian independence and defiance of federal authority.

Moonshiners are people who make moonshine—illegally distilled liquor, typically whiskey. The term evokes Appalachian tradition, where homemade spirits were produced in secret stills, often at night to avoid detection: {Revenue agents raided the moonshiners' operation in the hills}. The word can also describe anyone producing alcohol outside legal channels.

Moonshining is the illicit distillation of liquor, especially whiskey, typically done at night to avoid detection—hence the moon. The term evokes rural Appalachian tradition, where homemade corn whiskey was produced to evade taxes or prohibition laws. By extension, moonshining can describe any covert, under-the-table operation: {He's been moonshining auto parts out of his garage}.

A moonshot is an ambitious, groundbreaking project that pushes the boundaries of what seems achievable—originally the Apollo program's mission to land humans on the moon. The term now describes any bold venture with uncertain odds but transformative potential: {The startup's moonshot is to cure Alzheimer's within a decade}. Moonshots accept high risk of failure in pursuit of extraordinary reward.

Moonshots are ambitious, groundbreaking projects that aim for transformative breakthroughs rather than incremental progress. The term derives from the 1960s Apollo missions to land humans on the moon—endeavors that seemed nearly impossible but succeeded through massive investment and coordinated effort. In business and technology, a moonshot is a long-shot venture with potential for enormous impact: {Google's moonshots include self-driving cars and extending human lifespan}. The word implies willingness to risk failure in pursuit of revolutionary change.

Moonstone is a gemstone prized for its adularescence—a soft, glowing light that appears to move across the surface, resembling moonlight. The stone is typically milky white or pale blue and has been used in jewelry for centuries. {She wore a moonstone ring that seemed to glow from within.} In folklore, moonstone is associated with lunar cycles and feminine energy.

Moonstruck means dazed, dreamy, or slightly crazed—traditionally attributed to the influence of the moon. The word most often describes someone romantically besotted: {She was moonstruck from the moment they met}. The older sense of lunar-induced madness survives in literary contexts but has largely given way to the softer romantic meaning.

Moonwalk names two iconic but unrelated movements. The first is walking on the moon's surface, as astronauts did during the Apollo missions: {We watched the moonwalk on a grainy television}. The second is a dance move popularized by Michael Jackson, where the dancer appears to glide backward while mimicking forward steps. Both noun and verb: {He moonwalked across the stage}.

Moonwalking is a dance move where the performer appears to glide backward while their legs mime walking forward. Popularized by Michael Jackson in 1983, it creates an illusion of frictionless sliding: {He moonwalked across the stage}. The term also describes the bouncing gait astronauts use in lunar gravity.

Moonwalks names two famous feats of human locomotion. The first is walking on the moon's surface, as astronauts did during the Apollo missions. The second is the dance move popularized by Michael Jackson—a gliding step that creates the illusion of walking forward while sliding backward. Both capture a sense of defying normal physics. As a verb: {He moonwalks across the stage}.

To moor a boat is to secure it in place, typically by rope or anchor: {We moored at the dock overnight}. A moor is also a tract of open, uncultivated upland, often covered with heather and peat—characteristic of the British Isles: {the Yorkshire moors}, {Wuthering Heights is set on the windswept moors}. (Capitalized Moor is a historical term for North African Muslims.)

A mooring is a place where a boat or ship is secured, or the equipment used to secure it—ropes, chains, anchors, or fixed posts. The plural moorings often refers to the entire arrangement: {The storm tore the yacht from its moorings}. Figuratively, moorings are sources of stability or connection: {She felt cut loose from her moorings after the divorce}.

Moors are broad stretches of open, uncultivated upland, typically covered with heather, coarse grasses, and boggy ground. The term is especially associated with the British Isles: {the Yorkshire moors}, {Wuthering Heights is set on the moors}. Moorland tends to be windswept, treeless, and somewhat desolate—atmospheric territory for Gothic novels and long walks. To moor a boat is a different word, meaning to secure it in place. (Capitalized Moors refers to the Muslim peoples of North Africa.)

A moose is a large deer native to northern forests of North America, Europe, and Asia—the largest living member of the deer family. Males grow massive palmate antlers shed annually. The plural is also moose: {We saw three moose crossing the road}. In British English, the same animal is called an elk.

A mop is a cleaning tool with absorbent material at the end of a handle, used wet for washing floors. To mop is to clean with one, or to wipe as if with one: {She mopped her brow with a handkerchief}. A mop can also be a thick mass of untidy hair: {a mop of curls}. To {mop up} is to finish off remaining resistance or clean up the last of something: {mopping up enemy stragglers}.

To mope is to be listless and dejected, often with an element of sulking or self-pity: {He moped around the house for days after the breakup}. A mope is someone who habitually mopes, or an instance of moping: {Don't be such a mope}. The mopes is a state of low spirits: {She's got the mopes}.

A moped is a low-powered motorized bicycle, typically with pedals and a small engine under 50cc. The word blends "motor" and "pedal." Mopeds occupy a middle ground between bicycles and motorcycles, often requiring less licensing than full motorcycles: {She commutes on a moped to save on gas}. Separately, moped is the past tense of mope.

Mopeds are lightweight motorized two-wheelers with small engines and often pedals, designed for low-speed urban travel. The name blends "motor" and "pedal." They typically require less licensing than motorcycles and are restricted to lower speeds: {She commutes on a moped to avoid parking hassles}. In casual use, moped sometimes loosely includes any small scooter.

Mopey describes someone who is glum, listless, and feeling sorry for themselves. A mopey person sits around looking dejected rather than doing anything about their situation: {He's been mopey ever since she left}. The word carries a hint of impatience with the behavior—moping is passive and unproductive. Also spelled mopy.

Moping is brooding in low spirits, usually with an element of self-pity or sulking. Someone moping wanders aimlessly or sits idle, dwelling on disappointment or sadness: {He spent the weekend moping around the house after the breakup}. The word suggests passivity—not active grieving but listless dejection, often noticed by others who find it tiresome.

Mopping is cleaning a floor with a mop—a long-handled tool with absorbent material at the end, pushed across wet surfaces. The word extends to any wiping or soaking motion: {He was mopping his brow with a handkerchief}. To be {mopping up} is to finish remaining tasks or deal with stragglers after a main effort: {The army spent weeks mopping up resistance}.

Moral is used to talk about subjects, behavior, values, or responsibilities that are rooted in a system of right and wrong. A moral person adheres to principles and behaves in ways judged to be good. Morals, as a plural noun, denotes a set of principles that constitute someone’s ethical principles.

Morale is the spirit, confidence, or enthusiasm of a person or group, especially regarding challenges ahead. Military commanders worry about troop morale. Workplace morale affects productivity. {The team's morale was low after three straight losses.} High morale suggests optimism and willingness to persevere; low morale suggests discouragement or defeat.

Morality is the system of principles governing right and wrong conduct. It can refer to a society's shared standards {Victorian morality}, an individual's ethical code {personal morality}, or the quality of being virtuous {a person of questionable morality}. The morality of an action is whether it's right or wrong: {They debated the morality of capital punishment}. Morality often implies standards beyond mere legality—something can be legal but immoral, or illegal but morally justified.

Morals are principles of right and wrong that guide behavior. They overlap with ethics but tend to be more personal and intuitive—your morals are what you feel is right, while ethics may be codified rules. Someone's morals might forbid lying even when ethics permit it. {She questioned his morals after the affair}. A story's moral is its lesson: {The moral of the fable is that slow and steady wins the race}.

Morbid describes an unhealthy preoccupation with death, disease, or the unpleasant: {a morbid fascination with serial killers}, {morbid curiosity about the accident scene}. The word suggests dwelling on what most people avoid thinking about. In medical contexts, morbid relates to disease or its symptoms: {morbid anatomy} studies diseased tissue. {Morbid obesity} is severe enough to cause health problems.

More is an adjective and adverb used to form comparatives for words that can’t accomplish this with the ending -er; for example, more intelligent. When used alone or followed by a noun, more usually conveys extra, additional, or to a great degree, and is roughly the opposite of less (give me some more, we need more information). The noun mores, meaning moral customs, is construed as plural and does not have a singular form.

A morgue is a place where dead bodies are kept, typically for identification or before autopsy, burial, or cremation. Hospitals, police departments, and medical examiners maintain morgues. The term extends to newspaper archives of clippings and reference materials—a "morgue" of old stories. {The body was taken to the county morgue}.

Morning is the early part of the day, from dawn until noon. It begins when night ends and darkness gives way to light. {Good morning} is a standard greeting. {Morning person} describes someone who functions well early. {The morning after} often refers to consequences following a night of excess—hangovers, regrets, or the realization of what happened.

Moron is a harsh insult for someone perceived as stupid: {What kind of moron leaves their car unlocked in this neighborhood?} The word originated as a clinical term for mild intellectual disability but was abandoned by professionals decades ago. It survives purely as an insult, stronger than *idiot* but less vulgar than profanity-based alternatives.

Moronic means extremely stupid or foolish. The word derives from moron, once a clinical term for mild intellectual disability, now simply an insult for someone acting like an idiot. {That was a moronic thing to say.} {The plan was so moronic it almost worked.}

Morons is the plural of moron—a person of notably low intelligence or poor judgment. The word began as a clinical term for mild intellectual disability but shed that meaning entirely; it now functions as a general-purpose insult for anyone acting stupidly: {The morons in accounting lost the invoice again}. It carries less sting than idiot in most contexts.

Morph means to transform gradually from one form into another. The word comes from computer graphics, where morphing smoothly blends one image into another: {The werewolf's face morphed into human features}. The term has spread to describe any gradual transformation: {The conversation morphed into an argument}. As a noun, a morph is a variant form, especially in biology where it describes different physical types within a species.

Morphine is a powerful painkiller derived from opium, used medically for severe pain relief. It's the standard against which other opioids are measured. Morphine produces euphoria and drowsiness, making it highly addictive: {The doctor prescribed morphine after the surgery}. It remains essential in palliative care despite its potential for abuse.

Mortal means subject to death—the defining condition of human existence, as opposed to gods or immortals: {We are all mortal}. As a noun, a mortal is a human being: {No mortal could survive that fall}. Mortal also intensifies: a mortal {enemy} threatens your very life, mortal {combat} ends in death, mortal {sin} kills the soul. {She lived in mortal fear of being discovered}.

Mortality is the condition of being subject to death—what separates humans from gods in classical thought. It also refers to death on a large scale: {infant mortality rates}, {mortality from heart disease}. A mortality is a death or the number of deaths: {The war caused massive mortalities}. To confront one's mortality is to reckon with the fact that you will die.

Mortals are human beings, especially as distinguished from gods, immortals, or supernatural entities: {The gods looked down upon the mortals below}. The term emphasizes human vulnerability and finite lifespan. In casual use, mortals can humorously contrast ordinary people with those who seem superior: {Unlike us mere mortals, she never seems to need sleep}.

Mortar has two unrelated meanings. One is a bowl in which substances are ground with a pestle—the mortar and pestle of pharmacies and kitchens. The other is a paste of cement, lime, and sand used to bind bricks or stones: {The mortar between the bricks was crumbling}. A mortar is also a short-barreled cannon that fires shells in high arcs, used for lobbing explosives over walls or into trenches.

Mortars are bowl-shaped vessels in which substances are ground or crushed with a pestle—the standard tool for pharmacists, chemists, and cooks preparing spices. The word extends to building materials: mortar is the paste of cement, sand, and water that binds bricks or stones. A mortar is also a short-barreled artillery piece that lobs shells in a high arc: {The position came under mortar fire}. To mortar is to fire such weapons or to apply binding paste between masonry units.

A mortgage is a loan used to buy property, with the property itself serving as collateral. If you fail to make payments, the lender can seize the property through foreclosure. The word also refers to the legal agreement securing such a loan. To mortgage property is to pledge it as security: {They mortgaged the house to pay for her treatment}. Figuratively, to mortgage something is to compromise its future: {mortgaging our children's future}.

A mortician prepares dead bodies for burial or cremation and manages funeral arrangements. The term is more common in American English than British, where undertaker or funeral director prevails. {The mortician applied makeup to give the deceased a peaceful appearance.}

Mortified describes intense embarrassment or shame—the feeling of wanting to disappear after a social blunder or humiliating moment: {I was mortified when I called my teacher "mom" in front of the whole class}. The word suggests embarrassment so acute it feels almost physical. The older sense of mortifying the flesh—subduing bodily desires through discipline—survives mainly in religious contexts.

Mortifying describes something that causes intense embarrassment or humiliation—the kind that makes you want to disappear: {It was mortifying to realize I'd been talking to her with spinach in my teeth}. The word carries more weight than merely embarrassing; mortifying experiences feel like small deaths to one's dignity. The related verb mortify means to humiliate or, in older religious contexts, to subdue bodily desires through discipline.

A mortuary is a place where dead bodies are kept before burial or cremation—either a funeral home or a room within a hospital or similar institution. As an adjective, mortuary relates to death or burial: {mortuary rites}, {mortuary science}. The word is more clinical than funeral home, suggesting cold storage rather than viewing rooms.

A mosaic is a picture or pattern made by arranging small colored pieces of stone, glass, or tile into a surface. The technique dates to antiquity and remains common in decorative arts. By extension, mosaic describes anything composed of diverse elements: {a mosaic of cultures}, {a genetic mosaic}. In biology, a mosaic organism has cells of different genetic makeup. (Capitalized Mosaic relates to Moses.)

Mosaics are decorative artworks made by arranging small pieces of colored glass, stone, or tile into patterns or images. The technique dates to antiquity and appears in floors, walls, and ceilings of churches and public buildings. Figuratively, mosaic describes anything composed of diverse elements: {a mosaic of cultures}, {a mosaic of farmland seen from the air}.

Mosey means to walk in a leisurely, unhurried way, often with no particular destination in mind: {I think I'll mosey on down to the café}. The word has a distinctly casual, folksy tone—you don't mosey anywhere urgent. {We moseyed around the flea market for an hour}.

Mosh is to dance aggressively at rock or punk concerts, typically by shoving and slamming into other dancers in a crowd. The area where this happens is the mosh pit: {We spent the whole show in the mosh pit}. Moshing emerged from hardcore punk culture in the 1980s and remains common at metal and punk shows.

Moshing is a form of aggressive dancing at rock and punk concerts, where participants push, shove, and slam into each other in a crowd—typically in an area called a mosh pit near the stage. Despite its violent appearance, moshing follows unwritten rules: you pick people up when they fall. {The show got intense and we ended up moshing for the whole set.}

A moshpit is an area near the stage at a rock or punk concert where audience members engage in moshing—aggressive, often chaotic physical movement including pushing, shoving, and slamming into one another. The activity is consensual chaos: participants expect contact, and there's an unwritten code to help anyone who falls. {I lost my shoe in the moshpit.} Also spelled as two words: mosh pit.

A mosque is a Muslim place of worship. The building typically features a prayer hall oriented toward Mecca, often with a minaret—a tower from which the call to prayer is announced. Muslims gather at mosques for daily prayers, Friday congregational worship, and religious education: {The new mosque serves the growing Muslim community}.

Mosques are buildings where Muslims gather for worship and prayer. The word comes from Arabic for "place of prostration," reflecting the physical posture of Islamic prayer. A mosque typically features a prayer hall oriented toward Mecca, often with a minaret—a tower from which the call to prayer is announced. {The mosque was filled for Friday prayers.}

A mosquito is a small flying insect, the female of which feeds on blood by piercing skin with a needle-like mouthpart. Mosquitoes are notorious for the itchy welts their bites leave and for transmitting diseases like malaria, dengue, and West Nile virus. The whining sound of a mosquito near your ear is universally dreaded: {I couldn't sleep with that mosquito buzzing around}.

Mosquitoes are small flying insects that feed on blood, leaving itchy bites. The females pierce skin with needle-like mouthparts to draw blood needed for egg production. Mosquitoes breed in standing water and transmit diseases including malaria, dengue, and Zika: {The mosquitoes were relentless at dusk}. They're drawn to body heat, carbon dioxide, and certain scents.

Mosquitos is a plural of mosquito, the small flying insect whose females bite and draw blood from humans and animals. The spelling with -os is less common than mosquitoes but equally correct. {The mosquitos were unbearable near the lake.}

Moss is any of numerous small, soft green plants that grow in dense clumps or mats on rocks, trees, and damp ground. Moss thrives in shade and moisture, making it common in forests and on north-facing surfaces. {The stones were covered in moss.} Figuratively, moss suggests age, stillness, or neglect: {A rolling stone gathers no moss.} (Capitalized Moss is a surname.)

Most functions in several parts of speech to express the idea of the greatest amount, limit, or magnitude. It is the superlative of many, some, or any, and it is used to form the superlative of adjectives that don’t inflect with an –est ending, as in the most advanced or the most ridiculous.

A motel is a roadside hotel designed for motorists, typically featuring rooms that open directly onto a parking area so guests can park near their doors. The word blends "motor" and "hotel." Motels emerged alongside American car culture and highway systems, offering convenient overnight stays for travelers. They range from budget chains to seedy establishments associated with illicit activities. {We pulled off the interstate and found a cheap motel for the night.}

Motels are roadside hotels designed for motorists, with parking directly outside the rooms. The word blends motor and hotel. Unlike traditional hotels with interior hallways and lobbies, motels typically have exterior entrances and single-story or low-rise layouts: {We pulled off the highway and found a motel for the night}. The term often suggests budget accommodations.

A moth is an insect closely related to butterflies but typically distinguished by feathery antennae, nocturnal habits, and a tendency to rest with wings flat rather than upright. Moths range from tiny clothes-eating pests to large, striking species like the luna moth. The phrase {drawn like a moth to a flame} describes an irresistible but potentially dangerous attraction. If clothing is moth-eaten, moths have damaged it by feeding on the fabric.

A mothball is a small ball of pungent chemical—traditionally naphthalene or camphor—placed among stored clothing to repel moths and their larvae. To mothball something is to put it in protective storage or suspend its operation indefinitely: {The Navy mothballed several destroyers after the war}. Something {in mothballs} is inactive but preserved for potential future use.

Mothballed describes something put into long-term storage or suspension, preserved but inactive. The term comes from mothballs—chemical pellets used to protect stored clothing from moths. A mothballed {factory} sits idle but maintained. A mothballed {project} has been shelved indefinitely: {The renovation plans were mothballed when funding fell through}. Military ships are mothballed when decommissioned but kept in reserve.

Mothballs are small balls of pungent chemical—traditionally naphthalene or camphor—placed among stored clothing to repel moths and other fabric-eating insects. The strong odor clings to garments and suggests old closets or grandmother's attic. To put something {in mothballs} is to store it indefinitely or suspend its use: {The project has been in mothballs since the budget cuts}.

A mother is a female parent. It is a formal term of address for one’s own mother, and less frequently used than informal words like mom, mum, ma, and mama. Figurative meanings of mother have to do with the idea of causal generation: Necessity is the mother of invention. Before another noun, mother can be a title of respect or authority: mother superior (a senior nun). Before a nonhuman noun, mother may indicate a source: mother ship, mother lode. Someone who mothers supplies the sort of nurturing care that is associated with mothers.

Motherfucker is a strong vulgar term that can be a contemptuous insult or, paradoxically, express admiration for someone formidable: {He's one bad motherfucker}. It also works as an intensifier: {cold as a motherfucker}, {a motherfucker of a hangover}. Shortened forms include mofo and MF.

Motherhood is the state of being a mother—having borne or adopted children and taken on their care. The word carries strong cultural weight, often idealized: {She embraced motherhood}. It can also refer to mothers collectively: {a victory for motherhood}. The phrase {motherhood and apple pie} describes values so wholesome they're beyond criticism, sometimes used ironically for positions that seem virtuous but lack substance.

Mothering is the act of caring for someone as a mother would—nurturing, protecting, and tending to needs. The term applies regardless of the caregiver's gender or relation: {He did most of the mothering while she worked}. Mothering can carry a negative edge when it suggests excessive or unwanted fussing: {Stop mothering me, I can take care of myself}.

Motherland is one's native country, viewed with emotional attachment as a place of origin and belonging. The term evokes patriotic feeling and cultural identity, often appearing in nationalist rhetoric: {They fought to defend the motherland}. It parallels fatherland, though motherland carries softer, more nurturing connotations—the nation as mother rather than patriarch.

The motherlode is the principal vein or deposit of ore in a mine—the source from which smaller veins branch. Figuratively, it means any rich source or main supply: {We hit the motherlode of vintage records at that estate sale}. Often spelled as two words: mother lode.

Motherly describes qualities associated with a good mother—nurturing, protective, warm, and caring. A motherly person shows gentle concern for others' wellbeing: {She gave him a motherly hug}. The word applies regardless of whether someone is actually a mother: {The motherly nurse checked on her patients throughout the night}.

Mothers is the plural of mother—women who have borne or raised children. The word often appears in compound phrases: {mothers and fathers}, {single mothers}, {working mothers}. To mother someone is to care for them protectively, sometimes excessively: {Stop mothering me, I can handle it}. Mother can also be a verb meaning to give birth to or originate: {She mothered three children}. {Necessity is the mother of invention.}

A mothership is a large vessel—spacecraft, aircraft, or ship—that carries, deploys, or supports smaller craft. Science fiction popularized the term for alien vessels carrying fleets of smaller ships: {The mothership hovered over the city}. By extension, mothership describes any central hub or headquarters from which operations emanate: {The startup's mothership is in Austin, but they have satellite offices everywhere}.

A mothership is a large vessel that carries, deploys, or supports smaller craft—aircraft, boats, or spacecraft. The term appears in science fiction for alien vessels commanding fleets of smaller ships. Figuratively, a mothership is a central hub or headquarters from which operations extend: {The startup operated from a mothership in San Francisco with satellite offices worldwide}.

Moths are insects closely related to butterflies, typically nocturnal with feathery antennae and drab coloring. They're drawn to artificial light—{moths circling a porch lamp}—which has made them symbols of fatal attraction. Some species damage fabric by laying eggs in wool or silk: {mothballs}, {moth-eaten}. Figuratively, {like a moth to a flame} describes irresistible, often dangerous attraction.

A motif is a recurring element that forms a pattern—in art, music, literature, or design. A floral motif might appear throughout wallpaper or fabric. In storytelling, a motif is an image, phrase, or idea that returns to reinforce theme: {the motif of water and drowning runs through the novel}. In music, a motif is a short melodic or rhythmic figure that recurs and develops.

Motifs are recurring elements in art, literature, music, or design—patterns, images, or themes that appear repeatedly to create unity or reinforce meaning. A novel might use water imagery as a motif; a symphony might return to a four-note motif. In decorative arts, motifs are distinctive design elements: {floral motifs}, {geometric motifs}. The word comes from French, sharing roots with motive—both suggest something that drives or shapes a work.

Motion is movement from one place or position to another: {the motion of the planets}, {set the wheels in motion}. A motion is also a formal proposal put to a vote: {She made a motion to adjourn}. To motion is to direct with a gesture: {He motioned me over}. In law, a motion is a request to a court for a ruling. {Go through the motions} means to do something perfunctorily, without real engagement.

To motivate is to provide someone with a reason or incentive to act: {What motivates you to work so hard?} A motivated person has drive and purpose; an unmotivated one lacks initiative. You can motivate yourself or others through rewards, fear, inspiration, or necessity. The noun motivation refers to the underlying reasons or desires that prompt action.

Motivated describes someone who has a reason or drive to act, whether that reason comes from within or from external rewards and pressures. A motivated {student} works hard because they genuinely want to learn or because grades matter to them. The word often carries positive connotations of energy and determination: {She's one of the most motivated employees I've ever managed}. In compound forms like {self-motivated} or {financially motivated}, it specifies the source of that drive.

Motivation is the reason or drive behind action—what makes you do something. It can be internal desire or external pressure: {Her motivation for studying was a genuine love of learning}. In psychology, motivation explains why organisms behave as they do. Someone's motives are their motivations, usually for a specific act: {Police are still trying to determine a motivation for the attack}. To question someone's motivation is to doubt their sincerity or suspect hidden reasons.

A motive is the reason behind an action, especially one that explains why someone did something questionable or criminal: {Police are still trying to establish a motive for the killing}. The word implies purpose driving behavior—detectives seek motives, psychologists analyze them. As an adjective, motive means producing motion: {motive power}, {motive force}.

Motives are the reasons behind actions—the desires, needs, or purposes that drive someone to do something. Police investigate motives for crimes; psychologists explore motives for behavior. The word often implies hidden or questionable intent: {What are his real motives?} {She questioned his motives for helping}. A motive can also be a recurring theme in art or music.

Motocross is a form of motorcycle racing conducted on rough, unpaved courses featuring steep hills, sharp turns, and obstacles like jumps and mud pits. The bikes are lightweight and specially designed for the terrain, with enhanced suspension and knobby tires. Riders compete on closed circuits, and races emphasize both speed and technical skill in handling challenging conditions. {He broke his collarbone in a motocross accident.}

Motor refers to a machine that converts energy into mechanical force and motion, powering everything from cars to appliances. The word comes from Latin for "mover," and this sense of causing movement extends beyond machinery: motor skills involve coordinated physical movement, and to motor somewhere is to travel by car. As an adjective, motor describes things relating to engines or vehicles ({motor oil}, {motor vehicle}) or to muscular movement ({motor neurons}).

A motorbike is a two-wheeled vehicle powered by an engine—synonymous with motorcycle, though motorbike often suggests something smaller or lighter. In British usage, motorbike is the everyday term where Americans might say motorcycle. {She commutes to work on her motorbike.}

A motorcade is a procession of motor vehicles, typically escorting an important person such as a head of state or dignitary: {The presidential motorcade wound through downtown}. The term combines "motor" with the "-cade" ending borrowed from cavalcade. Motorcades often include security vehicles, police escorts, and support cars traveling in formation.

A motorcycle is a two-wheeled vehicle powered by an engine, straddled by the rider like a bicycle but capable of highway speeds. Motorcycles range from small scooters to heavy touring bikes. The word often shortens to {bike} or {cycle}: {He rides his motorcycle to work}. To motorcycle is to travel by one.

Motorcycles is the plural of motorcycle, a two-wheeled motor vehicle with the rider straddling a saddle. Motorcycles range from small scooters to powerful sport bikes and cruisers. The word can also verb: {She motorcycles to work year-round}. Motorcycle culture carries associations with freedom and rebellion—think leather jackets and open roads.

A motormouth is someone who talks excessively and rapidly, often without much regard for whether others want to listen: {My sister's such a motormouth—she barely lets anyone else get a word in}. The term is mildly disparaging. As a verb, to motormouth is to talk this way: {He motormouthed through the entire meeting}.

Motorsport is competitive racing involving motorized vehicles—cars, motorcycles, boats, or aircraft. The term encompasses everything from Formula One and NASCAR to motocross and drag racing. British English favors the singular {motorsport}, while American English often uses the plural {motorsports}: {He's been involved in motorsports his whole life}.

A motto is a short phrase expressing a principle, goal, or ideal—often adopted by a person, family, organization, or nation: {The Boy Scouts' motto is "Be Prepared"}. Mottos appear on coats of arms, school crests, and currency. More loosely, a motto is any guiding principle someone lives by: {Her motto was "Never complain, never explain"}.

Mould is the British spelling of mold in all its senses. A mould is a hollow container that shapes liquid or soft material as it hardens: {a jelly mould}, {a mould for casting bronze}. To mould is to shape something, literally or figuratively: {She moulded the clay with her hands}, {experiences that mould character}. Mould is also the fuzzy fungal growth on damp surfaces or decaying matter: {There's mould on the bread}. The spelling mold predominates in American English.

Moulds is the British spelling of molds, covering all senses of that word. A mould is a hollow container that gives shape to liquid or soft material poured into it, or the growth of fungus that appears on damp surfaces and decaying organic matter. As a verb, to mould something is to shape it, either literally in a container or figuratively through influence: {The program moulds young athletes into disciplined competitors}. If you break the mould, you do something unprecedented.

Mouldy is the British spelling of moldy—covered with mould, the fuzzy fungal growth that appears on decaying food or damp surfaces: {The bread had gone mouldy}. Figuratively, something mouldy is stale, outdated, or musty: {mouldy old ideas}. In British slang, mouldy can mean unpleasant or worthless: {a mouldy deal}.

A mound is a pile or heap, typically of earth: {a burial mound}, {a mound of dirt}. In baseball, the mound is the raised area where the pitcher stands. Mound extends to any rounded mass: {a mound of mashed potatoes}. To mound is to form into a pile: {She mounded the rice on the plate}.

Mounds are raised piles or heaps—of earth, sand, snow, or other material. Some are natural formations; others are deliberately built, like ancient burial mounds or pitcher's mounds in baseball. The word extends to any heap-like accumulation: {mounds of paperwork}, {a mound of mashed potatoes}. To mound is to pile into such a shape.

To mount something smaller than you, such as a picture or a bracket, is to fix it in place – on a wall, for example. To mount something larger than you, such as a horse, is to climb up on its back. Mount is also used to describe the act of a male (animal) engaging with a female in sexual intercourse. A mount is an act of mounting, or if an animal, one that you mount: His mount was a dappled gray horse. A different mount is related to mountain, and occurs as the first term in the official names of many peaks (Mount Rushmore, Mount Sinai, Mount Everest).

A mountain is a large natural elevation of land, typically rising steeply and significantly higher than the surrounding terrain. Mountains are distinguished from hills mainly by height and ruggedness, though no universal threshold exists. The term extends to any massive quantity: {a mountain of debt}, {a mountain of paperwork}. To {move mountains} is to accomplish something seemingly impossible. To {make a mountain out of a molehill} is to exaggerate a minor problem.

A mountaineer is someone who climbs mountains, especially as a sport or profession. The term suggests technical skill and serious alpine pursuits rather than casual hiking: {experienced mountaineers attempting Everest}, {a team of mountaineers roped together on the glacier}. As a verb, to mountaineer is to engage in mountain climbing.

Mountaineering is the sport or activity of climbing mountains, especially those requiring technical skill with ropes, ice axes, and specialized equipment. It combines hiking, rock climbing, and navigation through snow and ice. {She took up mountaineering after years of casual hiking}. The word can also describe the broader culture and community surrounding the pursuit.

Mountains are large natural elevations of land, typically rising steeply and reaching heights far above surrounding terrain. The term often implies rocky peaks, steep slopes, and significant altitude: {We hiked in the mountains all summer}. Figuratively, a mountain is any enormous quantity or obstacle: {a mountain of paperwork}, {make a mountain out of a molehill}. To {move mountains} is to accomplish something seemingly impossible.

A mountaintop is the highest point or summit of a mountain. The word often carries symbolic weight—mountaintops are places of revelation, achievement, or perspective: {a mountaintop experience}, {shouting it from the mountaintops}. Martin Luther King Jr.'s "I've been to the mountaintop" speech drew on this tradition of elevated vision.

Mounted means positioned on or attached to something. A mounted {photograph} is fixed to backing; a mounted {TV} hangs on a wall. Mounted police or soldiers are on horseback. The past tense of mount covers climbing onto ({He mounted the horse}), increasing ({Pressure mounted}), and organizing ({They mounted an expedition}).
