Something that is mounted is secured in place and ready for use or display.

Mounting works as both adjective and noun. As an adjective, it describes something that increases or accumulates over time: {mounting pressure}, {mounting debt}, {mounting evidence}. The word suggests a steady buildup rather than a sudden spike. As a noun, a mounting is a frame, support, or backing on which something is fixed or displayed: {a brass mounting for the telescope}, {the painting's mounting}. The verb mount gives rise to both senses—climbing or increasing, and fixing in place.

To mourn is to grieve, especially for someone who has died. Mourning involves the outward expression of grief—wearing black, observing rituals, withdrawing from normal activities: {The nation mourned the president's death}. You can also mourn losses other than death: {She mourned the end of her marriage}, {He mourned his lost youth}. The period of mourning varies by culture and relationship.

Mourners are people grieving a death, especially those attending a funeral or memorial service. The term emphasizes the collective nature of grief—mourners gather to honor the deceased and support one another: {Mourners filed past the casket}. Professional mourners, hired to weep at funerals, exist in various cultures.

Mournful describes something expressing or suggesting grief or sorrow. A mournful {expression} shows sadness; a mournful {melody} evokes melancholy even without words. The word often describes sounds—a dog's mournful {howl}, the mournful {wail} of a distant train. Something mournful needn't involve actual mourning; it conveys the quality of grief rather than grief itself.

Mourning is the expression of grief, especially after someone's death. It encompasses both the internal experience of sorrow and its outward forms—wearing black, observing periods of withdrawal, holding vigils. {The family is still in mourning.} A mourning {dove} is named for its mournful call. Mourning differs from grief in emphasizing the visible, social dimension of loss.

A mouse is a small rodent with a pointed snout, large ears, and a long tail—the kind that scurries through walls or gets caught in traps. In computing, a mouse is a handheld device that controls a cursor on screen, named for its shape and tail-like cord. To mouse is to hunt mice, said of cats, or to move timidly. Someone {quiet as a mouse} makes little noise or draws no attention. Plural: mice for rodents, mice or mouses for the device.

A mousetrap is a device for catching or killing mice, typically a spring-loaded mechanism that snaps shut when triggered. The word extends to any trap or scheme designed to lure someone into a compromising position: {The police set up a mousetrap for the smugglers}. To mousetrap is to catch someone this way. A mousetrap can also be something basic but effective—the standard against which improvements are measured: {Build a better mousetrap and the world will beat a path to your door}.

Mousetraps are devices designed to catch or kill mice, typically spring-loaded mechanisms baited with food. The word extends to any trap or scheme: {The police set up a mousetrap for the burglars}. To mousetrap is to lure someone into a trap. The phrase {build a better mousetrap} suggests innovation that improves on existing solutions.

Mousse is a light, airy preparation with a foamy texture, held together by whipped cream or beaten egg whites. The word comes from French for foam or froth. Chocolate mousse is the classic dessert version, but savory mousses exist: {salmon mousse}, {chicken liver mousse}. Hair mousse is a styling foam that adds volume and hold.

Moustache is the British spelling of mustache—hair grown on the upper lip. The style ranges from thin pencil lines to thick handlebars. A moustache may be grown alone or as part of a fuller beard: {He twirled the ends of his waxed moustache}. To moustache is to grow one.

The mouth is primarily the opening through which food enters animal bodies. In some contexts, mouth refers to the cavity in which food is chewed. We also use our mouths to form and utter speech, and this function inspires some uses of mouth: You would not believe the things that came out of his mouth. Any opening or terminus that serves an important function may be called a mouth, like the mouth of a cave or river. The verb uses of mouth have to do with speech. Someone who mouths off speaks disrespectfully. If you mouth a word, you silently move your lips as if to pronounce it.

A mouthful is the amount that fills or can fit in a mouth: {She took a mouthful of cereal}. Extended, it means a lot to say—either literally, as when a word or phrase is long and awkward {(Hubert Horatio Humphrey is quite a mouthful)}, or figuratively, when someone says something significant: {That last comment was a mouthful}.

A mouthpiece is the part of an instrument, phone, pipe, or other device that goes in or near the mouth. A mouthpiece is also a spokesperson—someone who speaks on behalf of another person or organization, often with the implication that they lack independent views: {The newspaper became a mouthpiece for the regime}. In boxing, a mouthpiece is a guard protecting the teeth.

Mouths is the plural of mouth—the opening in the face used for eating, breathing, and speaking. Rivers have mouths where they empty into larger bodies of water. A mouth can be any opening: {the mouths of caves dotted the cliff face}. As a verb (rhymes with "clothe"), to mouth is to form words with the lips without sound: {She mouthed "I love you" across the room}. To mouth off is to speak rudely or disrespectfully.

Mouthwash is a liquid used to rinse the mouth, typically to freshen breath or kill bacteria. Most mouthwashes contain alcohol and antiseptic ingredients. The term sometimes extends figuratively to anything that cleanses or purifies speech: {He needed some verbal mouthwash after that outburst}.

Mouthwatering describes food so appealing it triggers salivation in anticipation: {The mouthwatering aroma of fresh bread filled the kitchen}. The word extends to anything temptingly desirable: {a mouthwatering real estate deal}, {mouthwatering profits}. Usually hyphenated as an adjective before a noun, often written as one word after.

Move is the verb most closely associated with motion, and that’s what it’s about. Something that moves goes from one place to another. If someone or something moves you, it could mean a number of things. A song that moves you elicits an emotional response. An authority that moves you puts you in a different place: We were moved to a different classroom because of noise. If you move or if a company moves you, you take up residence in a different place. This sense is move house in British English. A move is the act or result of moving. In a competitive or strategic context, a move is some action undertaken with a goal in view: You made a smart move by declining their invitation.

Moved is the past tense of move, covering physical displacement {We moved to California}, emotional impact {I was deeply moved by her speech}, and taking action {The committee moved to adjourn}. When someone is moved, they've been stirred emotionally: {He was moved to tears}. In formal contexts, to have moved means to have proposed something officially: {She moved that the motion be tabled}.

Movement is motion or the act of moving: {the movement of clouds across the sky}, {a dancer's graceful movements}. It extends to organized efforts toward a goal: the civil rights {movement}, the labor {movement}. In music, a movement is a self-contained section of a larger work. A clock's movement is its internal mechanism. Bowel {movement} is the polite term for defecation.

Movements is the plural of movement, covering all its senses. Physical movements are instances of moving or changing position: {The dancer's movements were fluid and precise}. A movement can also be an organized effort by a group working toward a shared goal: {the civil rights movement}, {the labor movement}. In music, a movement is a self-contained section of a larger composition like a symphony or sonata. The word also refers euphemistically to bowel movements—instances of defecation.

A mover is someone or something that moves. Most commonly, movers are workers who transport furniture and belongings during a relocation: {The movers arrive at eight tomorrow}. A mover can also be someone who proposes a motion in a formal meeting. In figurative use, a {mover and shaker} is an influential person who makes things happen. A {prime mover} is the initial source of motion or action—whether a philosophy concept, an engine, or the driving force behind a project.

Moves is the plural of move—changes of position, actions taken, or strategic decisions: {She made several moves to consolidate power}. In games like chess, moves are individual turns. Someone's moves can be their dancing style or romantic techniques: {He's got no moves}. If you {make moves}, you're taking action toward a goal. {The movers} are people with influence who get things done.

A movie is a motion picture—a story or documentary recorded on film or video for viewing in theaters or at home. The term is American; British English prefers film. {We saw a movie last night.} {She wants to work in movies.} The movies can mean the theater itself: {Let's go to the movies.}

Movies are motion pictures—films produced for entertainment, art, or information. The word often refers to the medium collectively: {I love the movies}. It also means the theater where films are shown: {Let's go to the movies}. A movie is a single film: {We watched a movie last night}. The term is more casual than film or cinema.

Moving describes something in motion or causing motion: {a moving target}, {the moving parts of an engine}. More often, moving means emotionally affecting—stirring feelings of sympathy, sadness, or tenderness: {a moving tribute}, {Her speech was deeply moving}. The act of relocating to a new residence is also moving: {Moving is stressful}, {a moving company}.

To mow is to cut down grass, grain, or other vegetation, typically with a blade or machine: {I need to mow the lawn this weekend}. A mower does the mowing. To {mow down} is to kill or destroy in large numbers, evoking the sweeping motion of a scythe cutting through a field: {The gunner mowed down the advancing troops}. A mow (rhymes with "cow") is also an old word for a stack of hay or grain stored in a barn.

Mowing is cutting grass or grain, typically with a blade or machine. A freshly mowed lawn has that distinctive summer smell. Mowing can also describe cutting down in large numbers: {The machine gun mowed down the advancing soldiers}. A mowing is also a field of grass ready for cutting.

Moxie is spirited courage and determination—the nerve to take on challenges and see them through. Someone with moxie doesn't back down: {She had the moxie to start her own business at nineteen}. The word carries admiration for boldness and resourcefulness, especially when facing long odds.

Mozzarella is a mild, soft Italian cheese with a springy texture, traditionally made from water buffalo milk but now commonly from cow's milk. It melts smoothly and stretches when heated, making it the standard cheese for pizza: {Fresh mozzarella has more moisture than the low-moisture kind used on most pizzas}.

Much indicates a large quantity or degree. It modifies verbs {(I don't sleep much)}, adjectives {(much better)}, and stands alone as a pronoun {(Much remains unknown)}. Much typically appears in negative constructions and questions; in positive statements, *a lot* often sounds more natural. {How much does it cost?} {That's too much.} {Much as I'd like to help, I can't.} As an adjective, much is somewhat formal: {much deliberation}, {much ado}.

Muck is wet, dirty matter—mud, manure, or any foul-smelling filth. Farmers spread muck as fertilizer. To muck out a stable is to clean it. Figuratively, muck is anything degrading or corrupt: {The tabloids love to rake muck}. To muck about (British) is to waste time or fool around. To muck something up is to ruin it through carelessness.

A muckraker is a journalist or writer who investigates and exposes corruption, scandal, or wrongdoing—especially by powerful institutions or public figures. The term emerged in early twentieth-century America for reporters who uncovered corporate abuses and political graft: {The muckrakers revealed unsafe conditions in meatpacking plants}. Though originally dismissive, the label became a badge of honor for investigative journalists.

Muckrakers were early 20th-century American journalists who exposed corruption, scandal, and social injustice in business and government. The term, originally dismissive, became a badge of honor. Their investigative reporting on unsafe food, monopolies, and political machines helped spark Progressive Era reforms. The word now applies to any journalist who digs up institutional wrongdoing: {Modern muckrakers uncovered the company's toxic waste dumping}.

Muckraking is journalism that exposes corruption, scandal, or wrongdoing—especially by powerful institutions or public figures. The term originated in the early 1900s for reporters who investigated corporate abuses and political graft. Though initially disparaging (raking through muck), it became a badge of honor: {Her muckraking brought down the mayor}. The practice continues as investigative journalism.

Mucus is the slippery, viscous secretion produced by membranes lining body passages—the nose, throat, lungs, and digestive tract. It traps dust, bacteria, and other particles, protecting underlying tissues. When you're sick, mucus production increases: {My nose won't stop running}. The adjective is mucous, as in {mucous membrane}.

Mud is wet, soft earth—soil mixed with water to form a thick, sticky substance. Children play in it, vehicles get stuck in it, and it spatters everything. Mud has associations with filth and lowliness: to {drag someone's name through the mud} is to damage their reputation, and {mud-slinging} is making malicious accusations. {Clear as mud} means not clear at all. In cosmetics, a mud mask uses mineral-rich clay for skin treatment.

Muddled means confused, disordered, or mixed up. A muddled {explanation} lacks clarity. Someone with muddled {thinking} can't reason straight. In bartending, muddled describes ingredients crushed together to release flavor: {muddled mint in a mojito}. To be muddled is to be in a state of mental fog: {I was still muddled from sleep}.

Muddy describes something covered with or consisting of mud—wet, soft earth: {muddy boots}, {a muddy field}. The word extends to anything lacking clarity or purity: muddy {water} is clouded with sediment, muddy {colors} are dull and brownish, muddy {thinking} is confused. To muddy something is to make it unclear: {The new evidence only muddied the situation}.

A mudroom is a small room or entryway near a home's exterior door, designed for removing and storing dirty shoes, wet coats, and outdoor gear before entering the main living space. Common in colder climates where tracking in snow, mud, or rain is a concern: {Leave your boots in the mudroom}.

A mudslide is a mass of mud and debris sliding down a slope, typically triggered by heavy rain saturating hillsides. Mudslides can be devastating to communities in their path: {The mudslide buried several homes}. A mudslide is also a cocktail made with vodka, coffee liqueur, and Irish cream—named for its brown, creamy appearance.

Mudslides are flows of mud, rock, and debris down a slope, often triggered by heavy rain or earthquakes. The term also names a cocktail made with vodka, coffee liqueur, and Irish cream—sweet, creamy, and often blended with ice: {We ordered mudslides at the beach bar}.

Mudslinging is the practice of making malicious or scandalous attacks against an opponent, especially in politics. The metaphor suggests throwing dirt to make someone look bad: {The campaign descended into mudslinging}. The word implies the attacks are unfair, exaggerated, or irrelevant to substantive issues. Someone who engages in this is a mudslinger.

A muffin is a small, round baked good, typically sweet and studded with fruit or chocolate chips: {blueberry muffin}, {bran muffin}. American muffins rise into a domed top and are eaten as breakfast or snacks. English muffins are flatter, yeast-leavened, and split for toasting. A {muffin top} is the roll of flesh that spills over tight waistbands—named for its resemblance to the baked good.

Muffins are small, rounded quick breads typically baked in individual cup-shaped molds. American-style muffins are soft and cake-like, often studded with blueberries, chocolate chips, or nuts, and eaten as breakfast items or snacks. English muffins are flatter, denser, and split horizontally for toasting. {I grabbed a blueberry muffin with my coffee.} In British slang, muffin top refers to flesh that spills over tight waistbands.

Muffle means to wrap or cover something to deaden sound, reduce clarity, or provide warmth. A scarf muffles your face against cold; thick walls muffle noise from outside. Muffled sounds are quieter and less distinct: {We heard muffled voices through the door}. Figuratively, to muffle is to suppress or restrain: {The regime muffled dissent}.

Muffled describes sound that has been deadened, dampened, or made indistinct—as if passing through a barrier: {muffled voices through the wall}, {a muffled explosion in the distance}. The word suggests something heard but not clearly, often implying physical obstruction or deliberate suppression. A muffled cry might come through a closed door or a hand pressed over a mouth.

A muffler is a device that reduces noise or provides warmth. On vehicles, the muffler is the part of the exhaust system that dampens engine sound: {The car needs a new muffler—you can hear it coming from a block away}. A muffler is also a warm scarf wrapped around the neck and lower face, now somewhat old-fashioned in this sense.

A mug is a sturdy drinking vessel with a handle, typically used for hot beverages: {a coffee mug}, {a beer mug}. Mug is also slang for face: {What a mug!} To mug is to attack and rob someone on the street, or to make exaggerated facial expressions, especially for a camera: {He mugged for the photos}. A mug shot is a police photograph of someone's face.

Mugged is the past tense of mug, which means to assault someone in a public place with intent to rob them: {She was mugged on her way home from work}. Mugged also describes making exaggerated facial expressions, especially for a camera or audience: {He mugged for the photographers on the red carpet}.

A mugger is someone who attacks and robs people in public places, typically using threats or violence: {The mugger grabbed her purse and ran}. The word implies street crime—an ambush rather than burglary or fraud. Muggers target vulnerable victims in isolated spots. To mug is to commit such a robbery.

Mugging is robbery with violence or threat of violence, typically in a public place: {She was mugged on the subway platform}. The crime implies a sudden attack by strangers rather than planned theft. A mugging is an instance of this crime. Separately, mugging means making exaggerated facial expressions, especially for a camera or audience: {The comedian was mugging for the crowd}.

A muggle is someone outside a particular group or subculture who lacks specialized knowledge. The word originated in the Harry Potter books, where it means a person without magical powers. From there it spread to other communities—geocachers use it for non-players who might stumble upon a cache, and various hobbyist groups apply it to outsiders: {We had to wait for the muggles to leave before we could search for the geocache}. The tone ranges from affectionate to mildly dismissive. (Capitalized Muggle appears in Harry Potter contexts.)

Muggles are people without magical abilities, from the Harry Potter series. The term has spread beyond the books to describe anyone outside a particular group or unfamiliar with specialized knowledge: {The technical jargon went right over the muggles' heads}. In geocaching, muggles are non-players who might stumble upon hidden caches.

Muggy describes weather that is warm and unpleasantly humid—the kind of heavy, damp air that makes you feel sticky and uncomfortable: {a muggy August afternoon}. The word almost always refers to atmospheric conditions rather than other forms of heat or moisture.

Mugs is the plural of mug—a sturdy drinking vessel with a handle, typically for hot beverages: {coffee mugs}, {beer mugs}. Mug is also slang for face: {an ugly mug}. The verb mug means to assault and rob someone, or to make exaggerated facial expressions: {mugging for the camera}. A mug shot is a police photograph of someone's face.

A mugshot is a photograph taken by police when someone is arrested, typically showing the face from the front and in profile. The term combines mug (slang for face) with shot (photograph). Mugshots are official records but often surface publicly, carrying connotations of criminality or disgrace: {His mugshot was all over the news}.

Mugshots are photographs taken by law enforcement when someone is arrested, showing the face from the front and in profile. The term extends to any unflattering identification photo: {My driver's license photo looks like a mugshot}. Mugshot websites controversially publish arrest photos, sometimes demanding payment for removal.

Mulberries is the plural of mulberry, a fruit resembling an elongated blackberry that grows on trees rather than bushes. The berries range from white to deep purple-black depending on variety. They're sweet when ripe but stain readily: {Her fingers were purple from picking mulberries}. Mulberry trees also famously feed silkworms.

Mulberry is a tree of the genus Morus, cultivated for centuries for its sweet, dark berries and its leaves, which are the primary food source for silkworms. The fruit resembles an elongated blackberry and ranges from white to deep purple-red depending on the species. Mulberry also names the fruit itself and the dark reddish-purple color associated with the ripe berries. {The mulberry tree in our backyard produces more fruit than we can possibly eat.}

Mulch is material spread over soil to retain moisture, suppress weeds, and regulate temperature. Common mulches include wood chips, straw, leaves, and bark. As a verb, to mulch is to apply such a covering: {We mulched the flower beds in spring}. Gardeners also use mulch to improve soil as organic materials decompose.

A mule is the offspring of a male donkey and a female horse—a hybrid animal known for strength, endurance, and stubbornness. Because mules are sterile, the word extends to other hybrids or things that bridge categories. A mule is also a backless slipper or shoe. In drug slang, a mule is someone who transports contraband, especially across borders: {She was arrested as a drug mule at the airport}.

Mules are the offspring of a male donkey and a female horse—sterile hybrids prized for their endurance and sure-footedness. The word extends to other hybrids and to stubborn people: {stubborn as a mule}. A mule is also a backless slipper or shoe. In drug slang, a mule is someone who smuggles contraband, especially by carrying it on or inside their body: {The cartel used mules to move cocaine across the border}.

A mullet is a hairstyle cut short on the top and sides but left long in the back—famously described as "business in the front, party in the back." Popular in the 1980s, it became a cultural punchline but never fully disappeared: {He's still rocking the mullet}. Separately, mullet is a type of thick-bodied fish found in coastal waters worldwide.

Mullets are fish prized as food in many cuisines, found in coastal and brackish waters worldwide. The word also names a hairstyle short on the sides and top but long in back—business in front, party in back. The hairstyle became iconic in the 1980s and has cycled between fashion statement and punchline ever since: {He's still rocking a mullet}.

A mulligan is a do-over, especially in golf—a second shot granted informally after a poor first attempt, not counted against the score. The term has spread beyond golf to mean any second chance: {Life doesn't give you mulligans}. Mulligans are understood as friendly accommodations, not official rules. (Capitalized Mulligan is a surname.)

Mulligans are do-overs, especially the informal golf practice of replaying a poor shot without penalty. The term extends beyond golf to any second chance: {Life doesn't give you mulligans}. In casual card games, a mulligan lets you redraw a bad starting hand. The word carries a sense of forgiveness for mistakes—an unofficial grace period that strict rules wouldn't allow.

Multiplayer describes games or activities designed for more than one participant, typically connected through a network: {multiplayer online games}, {multiplayer mode}. The term emerged with video gaming but applies broadly to any shared interactive experience. As a noun, it names the format itself: {I prefer multiplayer to single-player campaigns}.

Multiplication is the mathematical operation of combining quantities by repeated addition: three times four means adding three fours together. The notation uses × or · between numbers, or simple juxtaposition in algebra. Beyond arithmetic, multiplication describes any rapid increase: {the multiplication of cells}, {the multiplication of problems}. The verb is multiply.

To multiply is to increase in number or amount. In arithmetic, multiplying combines quantities: {three multiplied by four equals twelve}. Living things multiply by reproduction: {Bacteria multiply rapidly in warm conditions}. Problems, difficulties, and opportunities also multiply—they grow more numerous: {Our troubles multiplied after the factory closed}. The adverb multiply means in multiple ways: {multiply disadvantaged}.

To multitask is to handle multiple tasks simultaneously or in rapid alternation. Computers multitask by running several programs at once. People multitask by juggling activities—answering emails while on a conference call, cooking dinner while helping with homework. Research suggests human multitasking often reduces efficiency: {I can't multitask like I used to}.

Multitasking is doing multiple things at once, or switching rapidly between tasks. Computers multitask by running several programs simultaneously. People multitask less efficiently than they imagine—studies suggest the brain handles sequential attention rather than true parallel processing: {I was multitasking during the meeting and missed half of what was said}. The word often appears as a verb: {She multitasked her way through the workday}.

A multitude is a large number of people or things: {A multitude of factors contributed to the collapse}. The word often suggests an uncountable mass rather than a specific quantity. {The multitude} can refer to ordinary people as a collective—the masses, the crowd: {Politicians who claim to speak for the multitude}.

Multitudes means large numbers of people or things. A politician addresses {the multitudes}. {Multitudes of birds} darken the sky. The word carries slightly more literary or biblical weight than crowds or masses. The phrase {contain multitudes} (from Whitman) describes someone with contradictory or complex aspects: {I contain multitudes}.

The multiverse is a hypothetical collection of multiple universes, including our own, that together comprise all of physical reality. The concept appears in theoretical physics, where it emerges from quantum mechanics and cosmology, and in fiction, where parallel worlds allow alternate versions of characters and events: {In the multiverse, there's a timeline where you made a different choice}. Comic books and films frequently use multiverse storytelling to explore "what if" scenarios.

Mum means silent or not speaking. To {keep mum} is to say nothing, especially about a secret: {She kept mum about the surprise party}. The phrase {mum's the word} urges secrecy. Separately, mum is British and Australian informal for mother: {I'm visiting my mum this weekend}. A mum is also a chrysanthemum, commonly grown for autumn displays. (Capitalized Mum is a form of address.)

To mumble is to speak indistinctly, with the mouth partially closed or words running together: {He mumbled an apology and left}. Mumbling makes speech hard to understand—the opposite of speaking clearly. As a noun, a mumble is such indistinct speech: {His response was an inaudible mumble}. The word can suggest shyness, reluctance, or simply poor articulation.

Mumbling is speaking in a low, indistinct voice, often with the mouth partially closed so words run together: {Stop mumbling and speak up}. Someone who mumbles may be nervous, embarrassed, or simply not making an effort to be understood. The word can also describe any low, indistinct sound: {the mumbling of distant thunder}.

Mummies is the plural of mummy, which has two distinct meanings. A mummy is a preserved corpse, either through ancient embalming practices like those of Egypt or through natural desiccation. The word also serves as British English for mother, equivalent to American "mommy": {The mummies picked up their children from school}. Context usually makes clear which sense is intended.

Mummified describes a body preserved from decay, either through deliberate embalming (as in ancient Egypt) or natural desiccation. The flesh dries out rather than rotting: {The desert heat had mummified the corpse}. Figuratively, mummified suggests something dried up, shriveled, or frozen in time: {mummified traditions}, {a mummified bureaucracy resistant to change}.

A mummy is a dead body preserved from decay, either through deliberate embalming (as in ancient Egypt) or natural conditions like extreme cold or dryness. The word also means mother in British child speech and informal usage: {I want my mummy}. To mummify is to preserve a body or become dried and shriveled.

Mums is the plural of mum, the informal British term for mother: {The mums waited outside the school gates}. In American English, mums more often refers to chrysanthemums, the flowering plants popular in fall gardens and decorations: {She planted mums along the front walk}.

Munch is to chew steadily and often audibly, usually on something crunchy or substantial: {She munched on carrot sticks while reading}. The word suggests casual, unhurried eating rather than a formal meal. The munchies, in slang, refers to hunger pangs, especially the craving for snacks associated with marijuana use.

The munchies are a craving for snack food, especially the intense hunger that follows marijuana use: {I got the munchies and ate an entire bag of chips}. The word also refers to the snacks themselves: {We need to pick up some munchies for the party}. Both senses are informal.

A munchkin is a small person or child, used affectionately: {The munchkins are ready for bed}. The term comes from the diminutive inhabitants of Munchkinland in *The Wizard of Oz*. It often implies cuteness or insignificance. In fantasy gaming, a munchkin is a player who exploits rules to gain unfair advantages, prioritizing winning over storytelling.

Mundane describes the ordinary, everyday aspects of life—routine tasks, common concerns, earthly matters as opposed to spiritual or transcendent ones. The word often carries a hint of tedium: {I spent the morning on mundane errands like grocery shopping and paying bills}. Something mundane lacks excitement or novelty. In fantasy and science fiction contexts, mundane distinguishes ordinary humans or the non-magical world from those with special abilities.

Munitions are military weapons, ammunition, and equipment—the material of war. The term usually appears in plural form and often in compounds: {munitions factory}, {munitions depot}, {munitions dump}. As a verb, to munition is to supply with weapons, though this use is rare. The word emphasizes the industrial and logistical side of warfare rather than combat itself.

Muppet is a trademark for the puppet characters created by Jim Henson, combining features of marionettes and hand puppets. In British slang, muppet means a foolish or incompetent person: {Don't be such a muppet}. The insult is mild and often affectionate, suggesting someone is clumsy or dim rather than malicious.

A mural is a large painting or artwork applied directly to a wall or ceiling. Unlike framed paintings, murals are integral to the architecture: {The building's exterior features a mural depicting the neighborhood's history}. Murals range from ancient frescoes to modern street art. As an adjective, mural means relating to walls: {mural decoration}.

Murals are large-scale artworks painted or applied directly onto walls, ceilings, or other permanent surfaces. Unlike framed paintings that can be moved, murals become part of the architecture itself. They appear in public spaces like building exteriors, subway stations, and schools, often depicting community themes, historical events, or political messages. {The neighborhood commissioned a mural celebrating local heroes.} Indoor murals in homes or businesses typically serve decorative purposes.

A murder is the malicious killing of one person by another or others. Murder (uncountable) characterizes this crime generally. If you murder someone, you commit a murder. Figurative meanings of murder don’t typically involve death. A task described as murder is difficult and challenging: That chemistry test was murder. If you get away with murder, you escape punishment for wrongdoing. To murder an opponent in a competition is to defeat them soundly.

A murderer is a person who commits murder—the unlawful, deliberate killing of another human being. The term carries moral weight beyond legal designation; calling someone a murderer implies not just that they killed, but that they did so with intent and without justification: {The jury found him guilty, but his family refused to call him a murderer}. Serial murderers kill multiple victims over time. Mass murderers kill many at once.

Murderous describes someone or something capable of or inclined toward murder: {a murderous rage}, {murderous intent}. It extends to anything potentially deadly or extremely dangerous: {murderous heat}, {a murderous climb}. Informally, murderous intensifies difficulty or unpleasantness: {The traffic was murderous}. A murderous look suggests violent hostility, even without actual threat.

Muriculate means covered with small, sharp points or spines—like a surface studded with tiny thorns. The term appears in botanical and zoological descriptions: {muriculate shells}, {muriculate seed pods}. It describes a texture rougher than merely bumpy but finer than prominently spiny.

Murky describes water or air that is dark and cloudy, difficult to see through: {murky pond water}, {the murky depths}. By extension, murky applies to anything obscure or hard to understand: {murky legal language}, {a murky past}. The word often implies something suspicious or concealed: {murky dealings}, {murky motives}.

Murmur is a soft, indistinct sound—voices too low to make out clearly, or continuous background noise like wind or water: {a murmur of conversation from the next room}. To murmur is to speak quietly, often intimately or complainingly. A heart murmur is an abnormal sound detected through a stethoscope, indicating turbulent blood flow. {She murmured her agreement.}

Murmuring is the act of speaking in a low, soft voice, often indistinctly or privately. It can suggest intimacy, secrecy, or discontent depending on context. When people murmur among themselves, there's often an implication of complaint or dissatisfaction: {There was murmuring in the ranks about the new policy}. The word also describes continuous soft sounds, like water or wind: {the murmuring of the brook}. As an adjective, murmuring characterizes something that produces such sounds: {murmuring voices in the next room}.

Murmurs are soft, indistinct sounds—low voices, rustling leaves, flowing water. People murmur when speaking quietly, often intimately or conspiratorially: {She murmured something in his ear}. Murmurs of discontent suggest quiet but spreading dissatisfaction. In medicine, a heart murmur is an abnormal sound detected through a stethoscope, indicating turbulent blood flow.

Muscle is the tissue in animal bodies that contracts to produce movement. It also means physical strength or power: {He's got the muscle to move that furniture}. Figuratively, muscle is force or influence: {political muscle}, {financial muscle}. To muscle your way somewhere is to push through by force. A muscle car is a high-performance American automobile. To {muscle in} is to intrude by force or threat.

Musclebound describes someone whose muscles are so overdeveloped that they've become stiff and clumsy rather than strong and agile. The term carries a mocking edge—implying that excessive bodybuilding has backfired: {He was so musclebound he could barely scratch his own back}. Figuratively, it can describe anything grown rigid through overdevelopment.

Muscles are the fibrous tissues in animal bodies that contract and relax to produce movement. The human body contains hundreds of muscles, from the large ones that move limbs to the tiny ones that focus eyes. Beyond anatomy, muscles often stands for physical strength or power: {Put some muscle into it}. Someone who muscles their way through a crowd uses physical force; to muscle in on something is to intrude aggressively where you're not wanted. A person who provides muscle for an operation supplies intimidation or enforcement rather than brains.

Muscular describes anything relating to muscles or characterized by well-developed muscles. A muscular {physique} or muscular {arms} suggest visible strength and fitness. The word extends to things that display power or force: muscular {prose} is vigorous and direct, a muscular {foreign policy} is assertive and aggressive. Muscular dystrophy is a group of genetic diseases causing progressive weakness and loss of muscle mass.

To muse is to think about something in a leisurely, contemplative way: {She mused on what might have been}. The word suggests reflective pondering rather than urgent problem-solving. As a noun, a muse is a source of inspiration, especially for artists and writers—someone or something that sparks creative work: {His wife was his muse for thirty years}. (Capitalized Muse refers to the Greek goddesses of the arts.)

Muses is the plural of muse—sources of creative inspiration. Artists, writers, and musicians speak of their muses, the people or forces that spark their work: {His muses were the women he loved}. To muse is to ponder or reflect quietly, so muses also means thinks deeply: {She muses on the meaning of life}. (Capitalized Muses are the Greek goddesses of the arts.)

A museum is an institution that collects, preserves, and displays objects of cultural, historical, scientific, or artistic significance. Museums range from vast encyclopedic collections like the Louvre to specialized institutions focused on natural history, modern art, or local heritage. {We spent the afternoon at the museum}. The word can describe any place that feels like a preserved collection: {His office is a museum of 1970s memorabilia}.

Museums are institutions that collect, preserve, and display objects of cultural, historical, scientific, or artistic significance. They range from vast encyclopedic collections like national museums to specialized institutions focused on local history, natural specimens, or single artists. {The city's museums draw millions of visitors annually}. To visit museums is a standard tourist activity; to end up in a museum suggests something is outdated or worthy of preservation.

Mush is soft, thick, shapeless matter—food boiled to a pulp, snow turning to slush, anything reduced to a wet mass: {The vegetables had cooked down to mush}. Figuratively, mush is excessive sentimentality: {The movie's ending was pure mush}. As a command to sled dogs, mush means go or move faster. To mush is to travel by dogsled: {We mushed across the frozen lake}.

Mushroom refers to the fleshy, spore-bearing fruiting body of a fungus, typically with a cap atop a stalk. Some mushrooms are edible delicacies; others are poisonous. The word extends to anything mushroom-shaped: {a mushroom cloud}. As a verb, to mushroom is to spread or grow rapidly: {The small protest mushroomed into a movement}. {Rumors mushroomed after the announcement}.

Mushrooms is the plural of mushroom—the fleshy, spore-bearing fruiting body of a fungus, typically with a cap and stem. Some are edible delicacies; others are deadly. The verb mushroom means to spread or multiply rapidly: {The town mushroomed after the railroad arrived}. A mushroom {cloud} describes the distinctive shape of a nuclear explosion.

Mushy describes something soft and pulpy, lacking firmness—overcooked vegetables, rotting fruit, wet ground that squishes underfoot: {The bananas had gone mushy}. Figuratively, mushy means excessively sentimental or romantic: {a mushy love story}, {Don't get all mushy on me}. The figurative sense carries mild derision, suggesting emotion that's gone soft and shapeless.

Music is organized sound, typically involving melody, harmony, rhythm, or some combination. It ranges from folk songs to symphonies, from jazz improvisation to electronic beats. Music can accompany words {(set a poem to music)} or stand alone. To {face the music} is to accept consequences. {Music to my ears} describes welcome news. Someone who is musical has talent for or sensitivity to music.

Musical describes things related to or characterized by music. As an adjective, it can mean pleasing to the ear {a musical voice}, naturally gifted in music {she's very musical}, or simply pertaining to music {musical instruments}. The noun musical—short for musical comedy or musical theater—denotes a stage or film production where characters express themselves through song and dance alongside spoken dialogue. {We saw a musical on Broadway.} The form emerged in the early twentieth century and remains a popular entertainment genre.

Musicals are theatrical productions that combine spoken dialogue with songs and often dance. The form spans Broadway shows, film adaptations, and school productions: {We're going to see a musical tonight}, {She loves old Hollywood musicals}. The term can also refer to people with musical talent: {The whole family is musical}.

A musician is someone who plays a musical instrument or composes music, whether professionally or as a hobby. The term applies broadly—from orchestral violinists to bedroom guitarists to electronic producers. Professional musicians may perform live, record in studios, or work as session players backing other artists. {She's been a musician since she picked up the piano at age five.} The word carries no implication of skill level; both beginners and virtuosos qualify.

Musing is quiet, reflective thought—the kind of contemplation that wanders without urgency. As a noun, it refers to such thoughts expressed aloud or in writing: {Her musings on mortality filled several journals}. The adjective describes someone absorbed in thought: {He stared out the window with a musing expression}. The verb muse means to ponder or reflect: {She mused about what might have been}.

Musk is a strong, penetrating scent originally obtained from a gland of the male musk deer, used as a base note in perfumery. The smell is earthy and animalistic—some find it alluring, others overpowering. Synthetic musks have largely replaced the natural substance. The adjective musky describes anything with this heavy, pungent quality: {a musky cologne}, {the musky smell of sweat}.

A musket is a long-barreled firearm that preceded the rifle as infantry's standard weapon. Muskets were loaded through the muzzle with powder and ball, fired by various ignition mechanisms, and were notoriously inaccurate beyond short range. They dominated warfare from the 16th through mid-19th centuries before rifled barrels made them obsolete. {The soldiers formed ranks and fired their muskets in volleys.}

A musketeer is a soldier armed with a musket—a muzzle-loaded long gun used from the 16th through 18th centuries. The term evokes romantic notions of swashbuckling adventure, largely thanks to Alexandre Dumas's novel *The Three Musketeers*. By extension, musketeer describes any loyal companion ready to fight alongside others: {The four of us were musketeers back in college}. (Capitalized Musketeer may refer to team mascots or specific characters.)

Musketeers were soldiers armed with muskets—the long-barreled firearms that dominated European warfare from the 16th through 18th centuries. The word now appears almost exclusively in reference to Alexandre Dumas's novel *The Three Musketeers* and its adaptations: {All for one and one for all, as the musketeers say}. The phrase evokes loyal camaraderie and swashbuckling adventure.

Muskets were the dominant infantry firearm from the 16th through 19th centuries—long-barreled, smoothbore guns fired from the shoulder. They required manual loading of powder and ball, making rate of fire slow but deadly in massed volleys. {The muskets crackled across the field.} Musket appears in historical contexts and period pieces; modern firearms aren't called muskets.

A muskrat is a large semiaquatic rodent native to North America, resembling a small beaver with a long, scaly tail. Muskrats live in marshes and wetlands, building lodges from vegetation. The name comes from their musky odor and rat-like appearance, though they're more closely related to voles. Their fur was once prized for coats and hats.

Muskrats are large semi-aquatic rodents native to North America, named for the musky odor they produce. They live in marshes, ponds, and slow-moving waterways, building dome-shaped lodges from vegetation. Despite the name, muskrats are not rats—they're more closely related to voles. Their dense, waterproof fur was historically prized for coats and hats.

A mussel is a bivalve mollusk with a dark, elongated shell, found in both freshwater and marine environments. Mussels attach themselves to rocks, piers, and other surfaces in clusters. They're harvested as seafood, often steamed and served in broth: {moules frites}, {mussels in white wine}. The word is unrelated to muscle, though the spelling confusion is common.

Mussels are edible bivalve mollusks with dark, elongated shells, found in both freshwater and saltwater. They attach to rocks, piers, and other surfaces in dense clusters. Mussels are widely cultivated and eaten steamed, often in wine or garlic sauce: {moules frites}, {mussels marinara}. The shells open when cooked, indicating doneness.

Must expresses necessity or obligation: {You must wear a seatbelt}. It also conveys strong probability or logical certainty: {It must be past midnight}. As a noun, a must is something essential: {This book is a must for anyone interested in the subject}. Separately, must is the freshly pressed grape juice before or during fermentation into wine.

A mustache is hair grown on the upper lip. It may connect to a beard or stand alone. Mustaches range from thin lines to thick handlebars, and styles carry cultural associations—the pencil mustache suggests old Hollywood, the handlebar evokes Victorian gentlemen or hipsters. {He's growing a mustache}. Also spelled moustache, especially in British English.

A mustang is a free-roaming horse of the American West, descended from horses brought by Spanish colonizers. Though often called wild, mustangs are technically feral—domestic animals gone wild rather than a truly wild species. The word evokes rugged independence and untamed spirit: {He had a mustang's temperament, impossible to break}. Mustangs have been both romanticized as symbols of frontier freedom and managed as nuisance animals competing with livestock for rangeland. (Capitalized Mustang is the Ford sports car.)

Mustangs are wild or feral horses of the American West, descended from horses brought to the Americas by Spanish explorers. They roam freely on public lands, particularly in states like Nevada and Wyoming, and have become powerful symbols of freedom and the frontier spirit. The Ford Mustang, a sports car introduced in 1964, borrowed this imagery of speed and untamed energy. In sports, Mustangs is a common team name, most notably for Southern Methodist University athletics.

Mustard is a pungent condiment made from the seeds of the mustard plant, mixed with vinegar or other liquids. The color mustard is a brownish yellow. {Keen as mustard} means very eager. To {cut the mustard} is to meet a standard or perform adequately: {He couldn't cut the mustard anymore}. Mustard gas, despite the name, is an unrelated chemical weapon.

Muster is to gather or assemble, especially troops for inspection or roll call: {The sergeant mustered his platoon at dawn}. The noun refers to such an assembly or the number assembled: {a muster of fifty soldiers}. To {pass muster} is to meet a required standard. {Muster up} means to summon from within: {She mustered up the courage to speak}. To {muster out} is to discharge from military service.

Musty describes a stale, damp smell—the odor of closed spaces, old books, or things left too long in storage: {The attic had a musty smell}. By extension, musty characterizes anything outdated or lacking freshness: {musty ideas}, {musty traditions}. The word suggests neglect and the passage of time without renewal.

A mutant is an organism that differs from its parents due to genetic change—a mutation. In biology, mutations drive evolution; most are neutral or harmful, but some prove advantageous. Science fiction popularized mutant for beings with dramatic alterations: {The X-Men are mutants with superhuman powers}. Informally, mutant can be an insult suggesting someone is abnormal or freakish: {What kind of mutant puts ketchup on eggs?}

Mutants are organisms that have undergone mutation—a change in genetic structure that produces traits different from the parent or original form. In biology, mutations drive evolution and can be neutral, harmful, or beneficial. In popular culture, especially comics and science fiction, mutants are characters with extraordinary abilities resulting from genetic anomaly: {The X-Men are mutants with superhuman powers}. The term can be used loosely or humorously for anyone or anything that seems abnormally different: {These strawberries are mutants—look at the size of them}.

To mutate is to change form or nature, especially through genetic alteration. Cells mutate when their DNA changes, sometimes causing disease. The meaning extends to any significant transformation: {The virus mutated into a more contagious strain}, {The company's mission has mutated beyond recognition}. In fiction, mutants are beings altered by radiation or other forces, typically gaining unusual abilities.

Mutated describes something that has undergone mutation—a change in form, structure, or genetic makeup. In biology, a mutated gene or organism has experienced an alteration in its DNA: {The mutated virus spread more rapidly}. More broadly, mutated suggests transformation, often into something strange or undesirable: {The project mutated into something none of us recognized}.

Mutation is a change or alteration, especially one that produces something noticeably different from the original. In biology, a mutation is a permanent change in genetic material—the mechanism by which evolution introduces variation: {The mutation gave the bacteria resistance to antibiotics}. Outside science, mutation often carries negative connotations of unnatural or unwelcome transformation: {The proposal underwent so many mutations it was unrecognizable}.

Mutations are changes to an organism's genetic material—alterations in DNA that can be inherited or arise spontaneously. Most mutations are neutral or harmful, but occasionally one confers an advantage and spreads through a population. Outside biology, mutation refers to any significant change or transformation: {The company underwent several mutations before finding its current form}. In popular culture, especially comics and science fiction, mutations often grant extraordinary abilities.

Mute means silent or unable to speak. A mute person cannot produce speech; a mute button silences audio. As a noun, a mute is a device that dampens sound from a musical instrument: {The trumpeter inserted a mute}. To mute is to soften or silence: {She muted the TV during commercials}. Muted colors are subdued rather than vibrant. The older use of mute to describe people who cannot speak is now often considered offensive; deaf communities prefer terms like nonverbal or nonspeaking.

Muted describes something softened, subdued, or restrained. A muted {color} is less vivid than usual. Muted {criticism} is tempered or held back. A muted {trumpet} has a device inserted to dampen its sound. On video calls and broadcasts, a muted microphone transmits no audio: {You're on mute}. The verb mute means to soften or silence: {She muted the TV during commercials}.

To mutilate is to inflict severe damage, especially by cutting, tearing, or removing parts. The word most often applies to bodies: {The killer mutilated the corpse}. It extends to objects and abstractions—a mutilated manuscript has passages torn out or destroyed. Self-mutilation refers to intentional injury to one's own body. The damage implied is disfiguring, not merely harmful.

Mutilation is severe damage to a body, typically involving the removal or destruction of a limb or other essential part. The word applies to deliberate acts—{ritual mutilation}, {self-mutilation}—and to violence that leaves someone disfigured: {The victim's body showed signs of mutilation}. Extended uses describe ruinous damage to non-living things: {the mutilation of a manuscript by censors}.

A mutineer is someone who participates in a mutiny—an open rebellion against authority, especially by sailors or soldiers against their commanding officers. The term carries connotations of treachery and danger: {The captain had the mutineers clapped in irons}. Historically, mutineers faced severe punishment, often death.

Mutineers are people who revolt against authority, especially sailors or soldiers who rebel against their commanding officers. The word carries connotations of collective uprising—mutineers act together to refuse orders or seize control: {The mutineers took command of the ship and set the captain adrift}. By extension, anyone who openly defies institutional authority might be called a mutineer.

Mutiny is open rebellion against authority, especially by soldiers or sailors against their commanders. The word implies collective action—a crew mutinies, not a lone dissenter. Famous mutinies include the *Bounty* and the *Potemkin*. Extended uses describe any organized defiance: {The shareholders staged a mutiny against the board}. To mutiny is to participate in such a revolt.

A mutt is a dog of mixed or indeterminate breed—the opposite of a purebred. The term is informal but not derogatory; many people prefer mutts for their hybrid vigor and unique appearance: {We adopted a mutt from the shelter}. Extended to people, mutt means a fool or someone of mixed ancestry, though this use is dated and potentially offensive.

Mutter is to speak in a low, indistinct voice, often as an expression of discontent or complaint: {He muttered something under his breath and walked away}. Unlike whispering, which is quiet by design, muttering suggests words half-swallowed, not meant to be clearly heard. People mutter when annoyed but unwilling to confront directly.

Muttered is the past tense of mutter, meaning to speak in a low, indistinct voice, often with the mouth partly closed. Muttering usually conveys discontent, reluctance, or private commentary not meant to be fully heard: {He muttered something under his breath and walked away}. {She muttered an apology without making eye contact}.

Muttering is speaking in a low, indistinct voice, often to oneself or under one's breath. The tone typically conveys displeasure, complaint, or reluctance: {He walked away muttering about the unfairness of it all}. Muttering suggests words not meant to be fully heard—audible enough to signal discontent but too quiet to invite confrontation.

Mutton is the meat of an adult sheep, distinguished from lamb, which comes from younger animals. The meat is darker, fattier, and stronger in flavor than lamb. Once common in English and American cooking, mutton has become less popular, though it remains a staple in South Asian and Middle Eastern cuisines. {Mutton dressed as lamb} describes someone trying to appear younger than they are.

Mutts is the plural of mutt, a dog of mixed or indeterminate breed—the opposite of a purebred. The word carries affection rather than insult: {I've always preferred mutts to fancy breeds}. Extended to people, mutt suggests mixed heritage, usually self-deprecatingly: {I'm just a mutt—Irish, Italian, who knows what else}.

Mutual describes something shared between two or more parties, going in both directions. A mutual {friend} is a friend to both people discussing them. Mutual {respect} flows both ways. A mutual {fund} pools money from many investors. {The feeling is mutual} confirms that both parties share the same sentiment. Mutual often emphasizes reciprocity: mutual {aid}, mutual {benefit}, mutual {admiration}.
Mutuals is a shortening of mutual friends and is used in the context of social media platforms to refer to people you have a mutual relationship with.

A muzzle is the projecting part of an animal's face—the snout, nose, and jaws together: {The dog pushed its muzzle into my hand}. A muzzle is also a device strapped over an animal's mouth to prevent biting. The front end of a gun barrel is its muzzle. To muzzle someone is to silence or restrain their speech: {The administration tried to muzzle the press}.

Muzzled describes an animal fitted with a muzzle—a device that covers the snout to prevent biting. By extension, muzzled characterizes anyone or anything that has been silenced or prevented from speaking freely: {The press was effectively muzzled by the new regulations}. A muzzled critic or muzzled opposition has been forcibly restrained from expressing views, suggesting suppression rather than voluntary silence.

Muzzles are the projecting nose and mouth of an animal, especially a dog. A muzzle is also a device fitted over an animal's snout to prevent biting: {The aggressive dog wore a muzzle}. The muzzle of a gun is the open end of the barrel where projectiles exit. To muzzle is to put a muzzle on an animal, or figuratively to silence or restrain: {The administration tried to muzzle the press}.

You use myself as the object of a verb or preposition to refer to yourself in a sentence in which I is the subject: I cut myself while peeling potatoes. Myself and other pronouns that end in –self and –selves are called reflexives because they indicate that the action of a verb is reflected back at the subject of the sentence.

Mysteries are things not understood or explained—puzzles waiting to be solved or secrets that may never yield. A mystery novel centers on solving a crime, usually murder. The mysteries of a religion are its sacred truths beyond ordinary comprehension: {the mysteries of the faith}. Something wrapped in mystery remains hidden or unexplained: {Her disappearance remains a mystery}.

Mysterious describes what is difficult to understand, explain, or identify. A mysterious stranger has an unknown background; a mysterious illness defies diagnosis. The word suggests something hidden or beyond ordinary comprehension: {She was being mysterious about her plans}. Mysterious often carries an alluring quality—the unknown invites curiosity rather than mere confusion.

Mystery is something unexplained or difficult to understand: {The disappearance remains a mystery}. It suggests hidden knowledge or secrets beyond ordinary comprehension—the mysteries of the universe, the mystery of consciousness. Mystery also names a genre of fiction centered on solving crimes or puzzles: {She writes mysteries}. A mysterious quality intrigues or unsettles: {an air of mystery}.

A mystic is someone who seeks direct experience of the divine or ultimate reality through contemplation, meditation, or spiritual practices. The word suggests someone attuned to hidden truths beyond ordinary perception: {She consulted the village mystic}. As an adjective, mystic describes things with spiritual or supernatural significance: {mystic visions}, {mystic rites}. The word overlaps with mystical, though mystic as an adjective sounds more poetic or archaic.

Mystical describes experiences or beliefs involving direct communion with ultimate reality, the divine, or hidden truths beyond ordinary understanding. A mystical {vision} transcends rational explanation. Mystical {traditions} exist across religions—Sufism in Islam, Kabbalah in Judaism, contemplative Christianity. The word can also mean simply mysterious or spiritually evocative: {The forest had a mystical quality at dawn}.

Mysticism is the pursuit of direct experience of the divine, ultimate reality, or spiritual truth—typically through contemplation, meditation, or ecstatic states rather than reason or doctrine. Most religious traditions have mystical branches: Sufism in Islam, Kabbalah in Judaism, Christian contemplatives like Meister Eckhart. The mystic seeks union or communion with something beyond ordinary perception. {Her poetry reflected deep mysticism.} More loosely, mysticism describes vague or irrational thinking: {His explanation devolved into mysticism}.

Mystics are people who seek direct experience of the divine or ultimate reality through contemplation, meditation, or spiritual practice. The term suggests someone who pursues knowledge beyond ordinary understanding—through intuition rather than reason. Christian mystics sought union with God; Buddhist mystics pursue enlightenment. The word can carry skepticism: {She dismissed him as one of those mystics}. As an adjective, mystic means the same as mystical: {mystic visions}, {mystic traditions}.

Mystique is an aura of mystery, power, or specialized knowledge that surrounds a person, place, or thing: {the mystique of Hollywood}, {the mystique surrounding the royal family}. It suggests something fascinating yet not fully understood by outsiders—an almost magical quality that enhances appeal or authority. The word often implies this aura is partly cultivated or illusory: {His carefully maintained mystique collapsed when the scandal broke}.

A myth is a traditional story, typically involving gods, heroes, or supernatural beings, that explains natural phenomena, origins, or cultural beliefs: {the Greek myths}, {creation myths}. By extension, myth means a widely held but false belief: {the myth that we only use ten percent of our brains}. Something mythic has legendary or larger-than-life qualities. The mythical can be either legendary or imaginary: {a mythical creature}.

A mythbuster is someone who debunks widely believed falsehoods or misconceptions: {The article's mythbuster section addressed common nutrition claims}. The term gained currency from the television show of the same name, where hosts tested popular beliefs through experiments. Now used broadly for anyone who exposes false assumptions or urban legends.

Mythic describes something belonging to or resembling myth—the stories cultures tell about gods, heroes, and origins. A mythic {hero} appears in ancient tales; a mythic {quality} suggests the grandeur or timelessness of such stories. Mythic often implies larger-than-life status: {His mythic reputation preceded him}. The word overlaps with mythical, though mythic tends toward the elevated while mythical can simply mean imaginary.

Mythical describes things belonging to myths—traditional stories of gods, heroes, and supernatural beings: {mythical creatures}, {mythical heroes}. By extension, mythical can mean imaginary or fictitious: {The town's mythical prosperity existed only in the mayor's speeches}. Something mythical may also have achieved legendary status, suggesting fame beyond ordinary reality: {the mythical Woodstock festival}.

Mythology is a body of myths belonging to a particular culture or religion: Greek mythology, Norse mythology, Celtic mythology. The term also covers the study of myths as a field. Extended uses treat any elaborate belief system as mythology: {the mythology of the American West}, {corporate mythology about innovation}. {Her personal mythology included the idea that she was destined for greatness.}

Mythos is the body of myths belonging to a culture or group—the collected stories that explain origins, beliefs, and values. It can also mean the underlying worldview or symbolic framework of a creative work: {Lovecraft's mythos}, {the mythos of Star Wars}. Where myth is a single story, mythos is the larger pattern those stories form. The word carries more weight than mythology, suggesting something foundational rather than merely collected.

Myths are traditional stories, typically involving supernatural beings or events, that explain natural phenomena, origins, or cultural beliefs. Greek myths explain how the world came to be; creation myths appear across cultures. By extension, a myth is any widely held but false belief: {the myth that we only use ten percent of our brains}. Something mythic has the grandeur or archetypal quality of ancient stories.

Naan is a leavened flatbread from South Asian cuisine, traditionally baked in a tandoor oven. The bread puffs up with charred spots and a soft, chewy interior. It often accompanies curries and other dishes, used to scoop up food: {We ordered garlic naan with our tikka masala}. Also spelled nan.

To nab is to catch or seize, especially quickly or unexpectedly. Police nab suspects; you might nab the last cookie before someone else does. The word suggests swift, opportunistic action: {Security nabbed him at the door}. It can also mean to grab or snatch: {I nabbed a seat in the front row}.

A nacho is a tortilla chip topped with melted cheese, often with additional toppings like jalapeños, beans, or salsa. Usually encountered in the plural: {We ordered nachos for the table}. The dish originated in northern Mexico and became a staple of Tex-Mex cuisine and American bar food.

Nachos are tortilla chips topped with melted cheese and other ingredients—jalapeños, beans, sour cream, guacamole, seasoned meat. The dish originated as a Tex-Mex snack and spread to sports arenas, movie theaters, and casual restaurants. {We ordered nachos for the table.} The cheese-drenched version served at concession stands barely resembles the original.

To nag is to pester someone with persistent criticism or complaints, especially about duties left undone: {She nagged him about fixing the fence}. A nag is someone who does this habitually, or the act itself: {constant nagging}. Separately, a nag is an old or worn-out horse, often used dismissively for any horse of little value.

Nagged is the past tense of nag, meaning to persistently pester or complain at someone: {She nagged him about fixing the fence until he finally did it}. Nagged can also describe a persistent, bothering sensation: {A feeling of unease nagged at her all day}. The word implies repetitive, wearing pressure rather than a single complaint.

Nagging describes persistent, repetitive complaining or urging that wears on the recipient: {Her nagging finally got him to fix the fence}. A nagging person badgers others about tasks or behavior. The word extends to anything that persists annoyingly—a nagging {cough}, a nagging {doubt}, a nagging {pain}. To nag is to engage in this kind of persistent pestering.
Nah is an informal variant of no and may carry slightly less force of finality than no does. It can also express lack of interest.

A nail is a small metal spike with a flat head, hammered in to fasten things together: {He drove a nail into the wall}. {The picture hangs on a nail}. Nails are also the hard keratin plates covering fingertips and toes: {She painted her nails red}. {Trim your nails}. To nail means to fasten with nails, or to catch, secure, or execute perfectly: {The cops nailed him for speeding}. {She nailed the audition}. In vulgar slang, to nail someone is to have sex with them: {He nailed her after the party}.

A nailbiter is something that causes intense suspense or anxiety—a close contest, a tense thriller, a deadline that comes down to the wire: {The election was a nailbiter that wasn't decided until midnight}. The image is of someone nervously chewing their nails while awaiting an outcome. Also spelled nail-biter.

Nailbiting is the nervous habit of chewing one's fingernails, often unconsciously during stress or boredom. As an adjective, nail-biting describes something that creates intense suspense or anxiety: {a nail-biting finish}, {The election results made for nail-biting television}. The image is of someone so tense they gnaw their nails while waiting.

Nailed means fastened with nails, or caught, perfected, or in slang, had sex with: {The boards were nailed securely}. {She nailed the interview}. {He got nailed for tax evasion}. {They nailed each other after the party}. {Nailed it} celebrates perfect execution.

Nailing is the present participle of nail—fastening with nails, catching, or perfecting: {He's nailing boards to the fence}. {She keeps nailing these presentations}. {The prosecutor is nailing witnesses left and right}. In slang: {They were nailing each other all summer}.

Nails is the plural of nail—metal fasteners or the keratin plates on fingers and toes: {I need more nails to finish the fence}. {Her nails were painted blue}. As a verb: {He nails the boards together}. {She nails every performance}. The expression {tough as nails} means extremely hardy or resilient. {Hit the nail on the head} means to be exactly right.

Naive (or naïve) is an adjective that refers to a lack of experience or understanding as the basis for a person’s thinking or conduct: It would be naïve to think that few professional sports have a problem with performance-enhancing drugs. Naïve can be used to label an idea or response as inadequate, while avoiding the suggestion that someone is stupid: The naïve woman didn’t understand the danger involved. Naïve can have a positive connotation when applied to performers and artists, when it suggests natural talent that is uninfluenced by training or technique.

Naivete is a lack of experience, sophistication, or critical judgment—the quality of being naive. It can be innocent and endearing: {There was a charming naivete about her first novel}. Or it can suggest dangerous gullibility: {His naivete about office politics cost him the promotion}. Also spelled naïveté, preserving the French diacritics.

Naivety is the quality of being naive—innocent, unsophisticated, or lacking worldly experience. It can describe charming guilelessness or dangerous credulity: {Her naivety about office politics cost her the promotion}. The word often implies someone should know better. Also spelled naiveté or naïveté, borrowing the French accent.

Naked means without clothing or covering. A naked {body} is unclothed; a naked {tree} has lost its leaves; a naked {sword} is drawn from its sheath. The {naked eye} sees without aid of instruments. Naked can mean exposed or vulnerable: {naked ambition}, {the naked truth}. To the naked eye suggests what's visible without magnification or enhancement.

Namaste is a respectful greeting or farewell from South Asian cultures, literally meaning "I bow to you." In the West, it's strongly associated with yoga classes, where instructors often say it while pressing palms together at the chest: {The teacher closed the session with a gentle namaste}. The gesture and word have become shorthand for spiritual mindfulness, sometimes used ironically to signal forced calm or mock enlightenment.

A name is what something or someone is called—the word or words by which a person, place, or thing is identified and addressed. Your name distinguishes you from others: {What's your name?} Names extend to titles and reputations: {She made a name for herself in journalism}. To name is to give a name or to identify: {They named their daughter after her grandmother}, {Name three state capitals}. In someone's name means on their behalf or in their honor: {a donation in my father's name}. To call someone names is to insult them.

Namecalling is the practice of using insulting or derogatory labels to attack someone: {The debate devolved into namecalling}. It's a common tactic in arguments, playground disputes, and political discourse—substituting insults for substantive engagement. The term itself often appears as a complaint: {Let's stick to the issues and avoid namecalling}. Also spelled name-calling.

To namedrop is to casually mention famous or important people you know (or claim to know) to impress others: {He kept namedropping celebrities he'd met at the party}. The practice carries connotations of insecurity or social climbing. Also spelled as two words: name-drop. The noun is namedropping or name-dropping.

A namedropper is someone who casually mentions famous or important people they know—or claim to know—to impress others. The practice suggests social insecurity or a desire to borrow prestige: {He's such a namedropper, always talking about his celebrity friends}. The verb is namedrop; the noun for the practice is namedropping.

Namedropping is mentioning famous or important people in conversation to impress others, implying personal connection or familiarity: {The interview was mostly namedropping—she worked in every celebrity she'd ever met}. The practice suggests social climbing or insecurity. Also spelled as two words or hyphenated.

Nameless describes what has no name, or whose name is unknown or withheld. A nameless {grave} bears no inscription. A nameless {source} remains anonymous. {Nameless fears} are vague and hard to articulate—horrors too terrible to name. The word can suggest obscurity: {nameless thousands who built the pyramids}. Rarely, nameless means too awful to speak of: {nameless atrocities}.

Names are words that identify specific people, places, or things—distinguishing one from many. To name is to give such an identifier: {They named their daughter after her grandmother}. Names also refers to reputation: {He made a name for himself in finance}. To call someone names is to insult them. In someone's name means on their behalf or authority: {Stop in the name of the law}.

A namesake is someone or something that shares a name with another—specifically, one named after the other. A child named for a grandparent is the grandparent's namesake, and vice versa: {He visited the Florida city that was his namesake}. The term works in both directions, though it most often refers to the one who received the name rather than the original source.

Naming is the act of giving something a name or identifying it by name. Parents spend months naming a baby. In computing, naming conventions establish consistent patterns: {camelCase naming makes code readable}. Naming can also mean publicly identifying someone, often with consequence: {The article stopped short of naming the accused}. To {name and shame} is to expose wrongdoers publicly.

Nana is an informal word for grandmother, used especially by young children or when speaking affectionately: {I'm going to visit my nana this weekend}. The term belongs to a family of child-friendly kinship words like mama, papa, and granny. In British slang, nana can also mean a fool: {Don't be such a nana}.

A nanny is a person, typically a woman, employed to care for children in a private household. Unlike babysitters who work occasionally, nannies usually work regular hours and may live with the family. The term extends to nanny {state}, a disparaging label for a government perceived as overprotective or excessively controlling of citizens' behavior. Nanny is also an affectionate term for grandmother in some families, and can refer to a female goat.

Nanobots are microscopic robots, typically imagined at the scale of molecules or cells. The concept comes from nanotechnology—engineering at the nanometer scale. In science fiction, nanobots swarm through bloodstreams to repair tissue or assemble structures atom by atom. Real-world research pursues similar goals, though practical nanobots remain largely theoretical: {Nanobots could someday deliver drugs directly to cancer cells}.

A nap is a short sleep, usually during the day: {I took a quick nap after lunch}. To nap is to sleep briefly or to be caught off guard: {The announcement caught us napping}. Separately, nap refers to the raised fuzzy surface on fabric like velvet or corduroy—the direction the fibers lie.

Napalm is a highly flammable jellied gasoline used in incendiary bombs and flamethrowers. It clings to surfaces and skin while burning at extreme temperatures, making it devastatingly effective and controversial as a weapon. The term became synonymous with the horrors of the Vietnam War, where it was used extensively: {The village was hit with napalm}. To napalm is to attack with the substance.

A napkin is a piece of cloth or paper used during meals to wipe the mouth and hands and protect clothing from spills: {She unfolded her napkin and placed it on her lap}. In British English, napkin can also mean a diaper, though nappy is more common.

A napoleon is a layered pastry made with puff pastry sheets and pastry cream, typically topped with icing. The dessert is also called mille-feuille. In card games, napoleon (or nap) is a trick-taking game where players bid on how many tricks they'll win. {She ordered a chocolate napoleon for dessert.} (Capitalized Napoleon is the French emperor.)

Napping is sleeping briefly, usually during the day. A nap is a short rest, distinct from a full night's sleep: {I caught her napping on the couch}. To be caught napping is to be found unprepared or off guard: {The announcement caught investors napping}. The fabric sense—raising a soft surface on cloth—is a different word.

Naps are short periods of sleep, typically during the day: {I took a quick nap after lunch}. A nap refreshes without the full commitment of bedtime. The verb means to sleep briefly. To {catch someone napping} is to find them unprepared. Separately, nap refers to the raised fuzzy surface on fabric like velvet or suede.

Naptime is a scheduled period for sleep, especially for young children in the afternoon. Daycare centers and preschools build naptime into daily routines. The word evokes childhood and can be used playfully by adults: {I need a naptime after that meeting}. Also spelled as two words: nap time.

A narc is an informer—someone who reports others' illegal activities to authorities, especially involving drugs. The word comes from narcotics agent, but has broadened: anyone who tattles or snitches can be called a narc. As a verb, to narc is to inform: {Who narced on us?} The word carries strong disapproval—narcs violate codes of loyalty.

Narcissism is excessive self-admiration and preoccupation with one's own importance, appearance, or abilities. In casual use, it describes vanity or selfishness: {His narcissism made him a terrible listener}. In psychology, narcissistic personality disorder involves grandiosity, need for admiration, and lack of empathy.
