A noggin is an informal word for the head: {Use your noggin}. The term is playful rather than crude, often appearing in contexts involving thinking or minor bumps: {I hit my noggin on the cabinet}. Older and now rare meanings include a small cup or a measure of liquor.

Noir refers to a style of crime fiction or film marked by cynicism, moral ambiguity, and bleak atmosphere. The term comes from French for "black," evoking shadowy visuals and dark themes. Classic noir features hard-boiled detectives, femmes fatales, and urban settings drenched in rain and corruption: {a noir thriller}, {film noir from the 1940s}. The aesthetic has extended beyond its origins: {tech noir}, {neo-noir}. As an adjective, noir describes anything with that brooding, fatalistic quality.

Noise is unwanted sound—loud, discordant, or interfering with what you're trying to hear: {The construction noise made it impossible to concentrate}. The meaning extends to any unwanted signal that obscures information: {static noise}, {background noise in data}. To noise something about is to spread it as rumor or gossip. To {make noise} about something is to complain or draw attention to it. In casual speech, noise can mean meaningless talk: {His promises were just noise}.

Noisy means making a lot of sound, or filled with sound. A noisy {crowd}, a noisy {engine}, a noisy {restaurant}. The word carries a negative connotation—loud suggests volume, but noisy suggests unwanted or excessive volume. A noisy {neighbor} disturbs the peace. Data or signals described as noisy contain interference or unwanted variation: {The readings were too noisy to be useful}.

A nomad is a person with no fixed home, moving from place to place—traditionally following herds, seasonal resources, or trade routes. The word extends to anyone who moves frequently: {After five years as a digital nomad, she'd worked from thirty countries}. Nomadic describes this lifestyle or tendency toward restless movement.

Nomadic describes a way of life involving regular movement from place to place rather than permanent settlement. Nomadic peoples traditionally follow seasonal patterns, moving with herds or toward resources: {nomadic tribes of the steppes}. The word extends to anyone who moves frequently: {She lived a nomadic existence, never staying anywhere longer than a year}.

Nomads are people who move from place to place rather than settling permanently in one location. Traditionally, nomadic peoples followed seasonal patterns for grazing livestock or hunting: {The nomads moved their herds to higher pastures in summer}. The word extends to anyone who lives without a fixed home, whether by choice or circumstance: {Digital nomads work remotely while traveling the world}.

To nominate is to formally propose someone for a position, honor, or award: {The president nominated her for the Supreme Court}, {The film was nominated for Best Picture}. A nomination puts a name forward for consideration but doesn't guarantee selection. In politics, to nominate is to select a candidate to represent a party in an election: {The convention nominated him on the first ballot}.

Nomination is the act of formally proposing someone for a position, award, or honor, or the state of being so proposed: {Her nomination for the Supreme Court surprised everyone}, {The film received six Oscar nominations}. A nomination may also refer to the formal selection itself, as when a political party chooses its candidate: {He secured the nomination after a contested primary}.

Nominations are formal proposals of candidates for positions, awards, or honors. The word covers both the act of nominating and the resulting candidacies: {She received three Oscar nominations}. In political contexts, nominations often follow primaries or conventions: {He secured the party's nomination after a long campaign}. The singular nomination works for both the process and its outcome.

A nominee is a person who has been proposed or selected for something—a position, an award, or a role. In elections, nominees are candidates chosen to represent a party: {the Democratic nominee for president}. In awards, nominees are finalists under consideration: {an Oscar nominee}. In legal and financial contexts, a nominee may be someone designated to act on another's behalf or hold assets in their name.

Nonbinary describes a gender identity that doesn't fit neatly into the categories of man or woman. A nonbinary person may identify as both, neither, or somewhere along a spectrum between them. The term emerged in the early 21st century alongside growing recognition of gender as distinct from biological sex. {My coworker is nonbinary and uses they/them pronouns.}

Nonchalance is a cool, casual indifference—the appearance of not caring much about something, especially something others might find stressful or important. The word suggests ease and composure: {She accepted the award with studied nonchalance}. It can be genuine calm or a deliberately cultivated pose: {His nonchalance about the deadline worried his teammates}.

Nonchalant describes a casual, unconcerned manner—cool and unbothered, whether genuinely or as a pose. Someone nonchalant about a crisis either doesn't grasp its severity or wants to appear unfazed: {She gave a nonchalant shrug when asked about the deadline}. The word often carries a hint of admiration for someone's composure under pressure.

A nonconformist refuses to follow established customs, beliefs, or practices. The term can be admiring—suggesting independent thinking and principled resistance to groupthink—or dismissive, implying stubbornness or contrarianism for its own sake. {She was always a nonconformist, dyeing her hair purple before it was fashionable.} As an adjective: {his nonconformist attitude toward corporate culture}. In British history, Nonconformist specifically designated Protestants who separated from the Church of England.

None means not any or no amount of something: {None of the answers were correct}, {I wanted cake but there was none left}. It can refer to people: {None were willing to volunteer}. Despite what some insist, none takes either singular or plural verbs depending on context—both {none of them is ready} and {none of them are ready} are standard. {None other than} emphasizes surprising identity: {The caller was none other than the president}.

Nonfiction is writing that presents factual information rather than imagined stories—biography, history, journalism, essays, and similar works. The term defines itself by what it isn't: not fiction. {I mostly read nonfiction these days.} A nonfiction account may still contain errors or bias, but it claims to represent reality.

A nonprofit is an organization that uses its revenue to pursue a mission rather than distribute profits to owners or shareholders. Charities, foundations, and advocacy groups are typically nonprofits: {She works for a nonprofit that provides legal aid}. As an adjective, it describes this status: {nonprofit organization}, {nonprofit sector}. Also spelled non-profit.
Nonsense, mainly a noun, is used interjectionally to characterize what someone has said as worthless, misleading, untrue, or unacceptable: His premise is nonsense.

A nonstarter is something that has no chance of succeeding or being accepted—an idea, proposal, or plan that fails before it begins. {Raising taxes is a political nonstarter}. The term comes from horse racing, where a nonstarter is an entered horse that doesn't run. In broader use, it dismisses suggestions as not worth considering: {That's a nonstarter for me}.

Nonstop means without stopping or pausing. A nonstop {flight} travels directly to its destination without landing in between. Nonstop {rain} continues without interruption. The word works as adjective or adverb: {The baby cried nonstop for an hour}. Also spelled non-stop.

Nonviolence is the practice or principle of refusing to use physical force, especially as a means of political resistance or social change. Associated with figures like Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr., nonviolence treats peaceful protest—civil disobedience, marches, boycotts—as both morally superior and strategically effective: {The movement was committed to nonviolence even when met with brutality}.

Noob is internet and gaming slang for a newcomer or inexperienced person, especially one who makes obvious mistakes or asks basic questions. The term ranges from affectionate to dismissive depending on context: {Don't be such a noob} implies incompetence, while {We were all noobs once} acknowledges the learning curve. Variant spellings include newb and n00b, the latter using zeros for o's in the style of leetspeak.

Noodle has two main clusters of meaning. The first is a strip or tube of pasta, typically made from wheat flour and eggs, boiled and served in soups or with sauce: {chicken noodle soup}, {rice noodles}. The second is informal for head or brain: {Use your noodle}. To noodle is to improvise casually, especially on a musical instrument: {He noodled on the guitar for a while}. To noodle over something is to think about it in an unhurried way.

Noodles are long, thin strips of pasta or dough, typically boiled and served in soups or with sauces. The word covers both Italian varieties like spaghetti and Asian types like ramen and rice noodles. To noodle is to improvise casually, especially on a musical instrument: {He noodled on the guitar while we talked}. To noodle something over is to think about it idly. As slang, noodle means head: {Use your noodle}.

A noogie is the act of grinding one's knuckles against someone's scalp, typically while holding their head in a headlock. It's a rough but usually playful gesture, common among siblings and schoolyard friends: {He gave his little brother a noogie}. The word emerged in American slang in the 1970s.

Noogies is the plural of noogie, a playful form of minor torment where someone rubs their knuckles against another person's scalp, typically while holding the victim in a headlock. It's associated with roughhousing among children and siblings: {My older brother used to give me noogies until I cried}. The singular also appears as a verb: {He noogied me in front of my friends}.

A nook is a small, secluded space—a corner or recess set apart from a larger area: {a breakfast nook}, {a reading nook}. The word suggests coziness and shelter. In the phrase {every nook and cranny}, it means every small space or hidden corner: {We searched every nook and cranny of the house}.

Nookie is slang for sexual activity, especially intercourse. The word is playful and mildly vulgar rather than crude: {looking to get some nookie}, {a little nookie on the side}. It suggests casual or recreational sex rather than lovemaking.

Noon is twelve o'clock in the daytime, when the sun reaches its highest point. It marks the middle of the day, dividing morning from afternoon. A noon {meeting}, noon {deadline}, or noon {Mass} happens at this hour. {High noon} emphasizes exactness or dramatic confrontation—from Westerns where gunslingers faced off at midday.

A noose is a loop of rope with a slipknot that tightens when pulled, used historically for hanging executions. The image carries heavy associations with lynching and racial terror in America, making noose displays threatening rather than merely morbid. Figuratively, a noose represents a trap or inescapable situation: {The noose was tightening around the corrupt politician}.
Nope is an informal variant of no and may carry slightly less force of finality than no does.

A norm is a standard or pattern, especially of social behavior—what's considered typical or expected within a group: {Tipping twenty percent has become the norm}. In mathematics, a norm is a function that assigns a positive length to vectors. To violate norms is to behave outside accepted boundaries: {Gender norms are shifting}. The word often appears in plural: social norms, cultural norms, community norms. (Capitalized Norm is a given name.)

The adjective normal is far more frequent and varied in meaning than its related noun norm. What is normal is expected, common, usual, unexceptional. The normal time for something is when it usually or customarily happens. Normal practice is what people usually do in a given situation. The frequent phrase perfectly normal is often used to suggest that some phenomenon should not be regarded as unusual: It’s perfectly normal for the president to defend his legacy. Normal is also the place on a scale where most values occur; outside of this range, values are above normal or below normal.

Normalcy is the state of being normal—the condition of things when nothing unusual is happening. The word gained prominence when Warren Harding campaigned on a "return to normalcy" after World War I. Some consider it a less elegant variant of normality, but both are standard: {Life has returned to normalcy}, {We're all craving some normalcy}.

Normalize means to make something standard, typical, or conforming to a norm. In social contexts, to normalize a behavior or condition is to make it seem acceptable or unremarkable: {Society has normalized constant connectivity}. In technical fields, normalizing involves adjusting data or values to a common scale for comparison. The word carries political weight when people argue about whether certain practices should be normalized or whether normalization legitimizes something harmful.

Normalizing is making something standard or acceptable, treating it as normal rather than exceptional or deviant: {Social media is normalizing casual cruelty}. The word often carries disapproval—to accuse someone of normalizing behavior is to say they're making dangerous or harmful things seem ordinary. In metallurgy, normalizing is a heat treatment that refines grain structure in steel.

A normie is someone perceived as boringly conventional—a person with mainstream tastes, typical social habits, and no niche interests or subcultural affiliations. The term originated in online communities where enthusiasts of anime, gaming, or internet culture distinguish themselves from the uninitiated masses: {Normies wouldn't get this meme}. Often mildly disparaging, though sometimes self-aware or ironic.

Norms are standards of behavior or expectation that a group considers typical or acceptable. Social norms govern everything from how close to stand to strangers to whether you tip at a restaurant. To violate norms is to behave in ways that others find inappropriate or offensive. In statistics, a norm is a standard or reference point against which measurements are compared. {Test scores were compared against national norms.}

North is the direction toward the top of a map, toward the pole star, or opposite to south. It serves as both direction and adjective: {north wind}, {north side}, {heading north}. In many countries, the North designates a region—in the United States, the states that opposed the Confederacy. {They drove north for hours.} (Capitalized North may refer specifically to a region or proper name.)

Northeast is the direction midway between north and east, or the region lying in that direction. As an adjective or adverb, it describes movement or position toward that point: {The storm is tracking northeast}, {the northeast corner of the property}. In the United States, the Northeast typically means the states from Maine to Maryland or thereabouts.

Northern means situated in, toward, or coming from the north. A northern {climate} is colder; a northern {wind} blows from that direction. The term often describes the upper portion of a region or country: the northern {states}, the northern {coast}. In American contexts, Northern frequently references the Union states during the Civil War era.

Northwest refers to the direction midway between north and west, or the region lying in that direction. As an adjective or adverb, it describes movement or position toward that compass point: {We drove northwest for three hours}. A northwest wind blows from the northwest. The term often appears in regional names: {the Pacific Northwest}, {Northwest Territories}. (Capitalized Northwest typically refers to a specific region.)

The nose is the part of the face containing the nostrils and the organ of smell. It extends to nose-shaped projections: the nose of an airplane, the nose of a wine (its aroma). To nose around is to pry or investigate. To {nose out} a competitor is to defeat them narrowly. If you {follow your nose}, you go straight ahead or trust your instincts. To {look down your nose} at something is to regard it with contempt. {On the nose} means exactly right.

A nosebleed is bleeding from the nose, usually from dry air, injury, or irritation. As an adjective, nosebleed describes extreme height or elevation: {nosebleed seats} are the cheapest tickets in an arena, so high up the thin air might cause bleeding. Nosebleed prices or valuations are dangerously elevated.

Nosebleeds are episodes of bleeding from the nose, usually from irritated or broken blood vessels inside the nasal passages: {I used to get nosebleeds every winter}. In sports and entertainment venues, the nosebleeds are the cheapest seats—so high up that the altitude might theoretically cause a nosebleed: {We had nosebleed seats but could still see the stage}.

A nosedive is a steep, headfirst plunge—originally of an aircraft dropping with its nose pointed toward the ground. The word extends to any sudden, dramatic decline: {Stock prices took a nosedive}, {His career went into a nosedive after the scandal}. As a verb: {The company's reputation nosedived}.

A nosejob, also spelled as two words, is cosmetic surgery to reshape the nose—technically called rhinoplasty. The term is informal and common in everyday speech: {She's been thinking about getting a nosejob}. People get nosejobs to alter the size, shape, or proportions of the nose, whether for aesthetic reasons or to correct breathing problems.

Noses is the plural of nose—the facial feature used for breathing and smelling. The word extends to nose-shaped projections and the front of things: {the noses of several aircraft}. To say someone {noses around} is to say they pry into others' affairs. {Their noses were pressed against the glass.}

Nosey means overly curious about other people's affairs—prying into business that isn't yours. A nosey neighbor watches your comings and goings; a nosey coworker reads emails over your shoulder. {Don't be so nosey—it's none of your concern.} Also spelled nosy, which is more common.

Nostalgia is a sentimental longing for the past—often for a time, place, or experience that felt happier or simpler. The feeling blends fondness with melancholy, since what's missed cannot return: {The song filled her with nostalgia for her college years}. Nostalgia can be personal or collective, as when generations share {nostalgia for the '90s}. The adjective is nostalgic: {I get nostalgic whenever I visit my hometown}.

Nostalgic describes a sentimental longing for the past, particularly for a period or place associated with happy memories. Someone feeling nostalgic might revisit old photographs, songs, or places that evoke earlier times: {The smell of fresh bread makes me nostalgic for my grandmother's kitchen}. The word can also describe things that evoke such feelings: a nostalgic {film}, nostalgic {décor}. As a noun, a nostalgic is someone prone to dwelling fondly on the past.

A nostril is one of the two external openings of the nose through which air enters and exits. The nostrils filter, warm, and humidify incoming air. Figuratively, something {right under your nose} might as well be in your nostrils—impossible to miss yet somehow overlooked.

Nostrils are the two external openings of the nose, through which air passes for breathing and smelling. The word usually appears in plural since they come in pairs: {Her nostrils flared with anger}. Flaring nostrils signal strong emotion—rage, fear, or arousal. Animals with prominent nostrils may have them described: {The horse's nostrils steamed in the cold air}.

Nosy means prying into other people's affairs, overly curious about things that aren't your business: {Don't be so nosy}, {nosy neighbors}. The word suggests unwelcome intrusion—someone who asks too many questions or snoops where they shouldn't. Also spelled nosey.

English provides a convenient context clue for negative words: the letter n. Not is the most frequently used, even without counting the words in which not is disguised as n’t, such as can’t and won’t. Not gets its impressive usage statistics from being a general purpose negater: it can make clauses, phrases, and words in every part of speech negative by being prefixed to them. Negating a verb means integrating not into the auxiliary verb of a verb phrase, as in hasn’t seen or won’t come. Not is combined with do to make doesn’t or don’t when no auxiliary is present, but in older and formal English, you can negate a verb with not alone: Judge not that you not be judged.

A notch is a V-shaped cut or indentation, typically made in an edge or surface. Notches serve practical purposes like keeping things in place or marking measurements, as on a belt or a tally stick. To notch something is to cut a notch in it, or to achieve or record something: {She notched another win}. A notch can also mean a level or degree: {Turn the volume up a notch}. If something is {a notch above}, it's slightly better than what it's compared to.

Notches are V-shaped cuts or indentations, typically made in an edge or surface. A notch on a belt marks where it buckles; notches on a bedpost supposedly tally sexual conquests. A notch can be a level or degree: {Let's take it down a notch}. Mountain passes are sometimes called notches. To notch something is to cut into it or to achieve it: {She notched another victory}.

The many verb and noun uses of note nearly all have to do with documentation or notice (an obviously related word). If you note something, you either observe it, or both observe it and write down something about it. If you ask someone to note something, you want them to pay particular attention. A note is the product of noting: Did you take notes at the lecture? A note can also be a feature of something with a particular quality: She ended her talk on a positive note. There are notes of garlic and rosemary in the sauce. In music, notes are individual tones. #

A notebook is a book of blank or ruled pages for writing notes. Students carry notebooks to class; writers keep notebooks of ideas. The term extends to portable computers small enough to carry like a book: {She pulled out her notebook and started typing}. A notebook can also be a digital document for organizing notes or code.

Notes are written records of information—observations jotted during a lecture, reminders to oneself, or annotations in a book's margin. Musical notes are symbols representing pitch and duration, or the sounds themselves: {She hit all the notes perfectly}. A note can be a brief written message: {He left a note on the counter}. To note something is to observe or record it. A note of something is a slight quality: {a note of sadness in her voice}.

Nothing is the absence of anything—no thing at all. It functions as both pronoun and noun: {There's nothing in the box}, {Nothing matters anymore}. As a noun, nothing means something of no importance or value: {Don't worry, it was nothing}, {He came from nothing}. In phrases, nothing intensifies: {nothing less than a miracle}, {nothing short of brilliant}. To say someone is {nothing if not} a quality emphasizes that quality above all others. {Sweet nothings} are whispered endearments. As an adverb, nothing means not at all: {She looks nothing like her sister}.

Nothingness is the state or quality of being nothing—complete absence, emptiness, or nonexistence. Philosophy uses it to discuss the void or what lies beyond being: {He contemplated the nothingness that preceded creation}. More loosely, nothingness describes insignificance or worthlessness: {Their achievements faded into nothingness}. The word can evoke existential dread or peaceful emptiness depending on context.

Notice centers on the act of becoming aware of something or bringing something to awareness. As a verb, you notice what catches your attention or what you deliberately observe: {I noticed she was limping}. As a noun, notice is information meant to be observed, often a formal announcement or warning: {The landlord gave thirty days' notice}. To give notice is to inform someone officially, especially about leaving a job. If something escapes your notice, you fail to observe it. A noticeable thing is one that readily draws attention.

A notification is an alert or message informing you of something—an event, update, or required action. The word often appears in digital contexts: phone notifications, app notifications, push notifications. More formally, it can mean official notice: {notification of a lawsuit}, {notification of acceptance}. To receive notification is to be informed.

Notifications are alerts or messages that inform you something has happened or needs attention. In digital contexts, notifications appear on phones, computers, and apps to announce new messages, updates, or activity: {I had to turn off notifications because they were constant}. The singular notification can also mean formal notice of something official: {notification of termination}.

A notion is an idea, belief, or concept, often one that's vague or not fully formed: {I had a notion that something was wrong}. It can suggest whimsy or impulse: {She took a notion to learn piano}. In the plural, notions are small useful items sold in stores—buttons, thread, pins, ribbons—miscellaneous accessories for sewing and crafts.

Notoriety is fame for something negative—a reputation based on scandal, crime, or bad behavior rather than achievement. A criminal gains notoriety; a hero gains fame. The word carries judgment: {The case brought him unwanted notoriety}. Someone notorious is widely known, but not admirably so.

Notorious means widely known for something bad. A notorious criminal has a reputation that precedes them. The word carries negative weight—you wouldn't call someone notorious for their charity work. {The bar was notorious for its rowdy clientele.} {He was a notorious liar.} The noun notoriety follows the same pattern: fame of the unwelcome kind.

Nougat is a chewy confection made from sugar or honey, egg whites, and nuts—typically almonds or pistachios. The texture ranges from soft and pillowy to dense and tooth-sticking, depending on preparation. Nougat appears as a standalone candy or as a layer in chocolate bars: {The candy bar had a nougat center}.

A noun is a name for a person, place, or thing; in fact the words noun and name are related. There are many kinds of nouns that are distinguished by what they designate and by the way they behave in sentences. Nouns can serve as subjects or objects of verbs, and as objects of prepositions. Nouns are by far the most frequent words in most languages, English included.

Nourish means to provide sustenance for growth and health. Food nourishes the body; attention nourishes the mind. The word carries warmth—to nourish is to care for, not merely to feed: {She nourished her garden through the drought}, {Reading nourished his imagination}. What nourishes sustains and strengthens over time.

Nourishing describes food or drink that provides sustenance and promotes health: {a nourishing bowl of soup}, {nourishing meals for growing children}. The word extends to anything that sustains or strengthens: {nourishing conversation}, {a nourishing friendship}. What nourishes feeds something essential—body, mind, or spirit.

Nourishment is food or other substances that sustain life and promote growth. The word carries more warmth than nutrition—it suggests care and sufficiency rather than mere calories. {The soup provided nourishment for the weary travelers.} Figuratively, nourishment extends to anything that sustains or enriches: {intellectual nourishment}, {spiritual nourishment}.

A nova is a star that suddenly increases dramatically in brightness, then fades over weeks or months. Unlike a supernova, the star isn't destroyed—it can flare repeatedly. The term extends to anything that bursts onto the scene with sudden brilliance: {She was a nova in the art world}. In casual use, nova sometimes just means new or innovative. (Capitalized Nova is a proper name.)

Novel is more than a book-length fictional story. Indeed, it’s more than a noun. As an adjective, novel means new, with an emphasis originality, as in a novel approach to ending homelessness. Abstractions, such as ideas, approaches, methods, and concepts are most likely to be characterized as novel.

A novelist is a writer who writes novels—book-length works of fiction. The term distinguishes such writers from those who work primarily in short stories, poetry, journalism, or nonfiction: {She's a novelist, not a poet}. {The novelist spent three years completing her latest work}.

Novelists are writers who compose novels—book-length works of fiction. The term emphasizes the craft and profession: {She ranks among the great American novelists}. Unlike authors, which applies broadly, novelist specifies the form. {He worked as a journalist before becoming a novelist.}

Novels are book-length works of fiction, typically featuring narrative prose and character development. The form emerged in the 18th century and now dominates literary publishing. A novel is distinguished from shorter fiction by length and complexity: {She's working on her first novel}. The adjective novel, a different word, means new or unfamiliar.

Novelty is the quality of being new, fresh, or unusual. A novelty is something that has this quality—an item, experience, or idea that appeals because of its unfamiliarity: {The novelty of working from home wore off after a few months}. Novelty items are cheap, amusing objects sold as curiosities or gags: {novelty t-shirts}, {novelty keychains}. When the novelty wears off, initial excitement fades as something becomes familiar.

Now is a busy function word that typically refers to a time that includes the present – where the present can encompass anything from a second to an eon, depending on context. Leave now means this instant, while there are no dinosaurs now means in the current epoch. In conversation, now may have no reference to time and is used instead to change the subject or to direct focus to something: Now what do you want to talk about? Before a verb, now typically signals that the time reference of the verb introduces new information: We now know that there were witnesses.

Nowhere means not in or to any place: {The keys were nowhere to be found}. It can describe a remote or insignificant location: {a town in the middle of nowhere}. To {get nowhere} or {go nowhere} is to make no progress. {Nowhere near} means not at all close: {We're nowhere near finished}. Something that {comes out of nowhere} arrives unexpectedly.

A nozzle is a spout or tube fitted to the end of a hose, pipe, or container to direct or control the flow of liquid or gas: {Adjust the nozzle to change the spray pattern}. Nozzles appear on garden hoses, fuel pumps, rocket engines, and spray bottles. The word sometimes refers informally to a nose.

Nuance is a subtle distinction or shade of meaning. Where others see black and white, someone attuned to nuance perceives gradations: {Her argument lacked nuance}. A nuanced position acknowledges complexity rather than oversimplifying. The word often appears in criticism of reductive thinking: {That take has zero nuance}. As a verb, to nuance something is to add subtle distinctions to it.

Nuances are subtle distinctions or variations in meaning, tone, or quality—the fine shades that separate things otherwise similar. A translator captures the nuances of the original text. A wine has nuances of oak and cherry. The singular nuance works as both noun and verb: {There's a nuance you're missing}; {She nuanced her argument to address critics}. The adjective nuanced describes something showing or requiring sensitivity to fine distinctions: {a nuanced performance}, {a nuanced understanding of the issue}.

Nuclear relates to the nucleus—the dense core of an atom or a cell. In physics, nuclear energy comes from splitting or fusing atomic nuclei: {nuclear power}, {nuclear weapons}. In biology, nuclear refers to the cell nucleus: {nuclear membrane}. The nuclear family is parents and children only, the core unit without extended relatives. To {go nuclear} is to escalate dramatically or resort to extreme measures.

A nucleus is the central, essential part of something around which other parts gather or from which they develop. In biology, it's the membrane-bound structure in a cell containing genetic material. In physics, it's the dense core of an atom, composed of protons and neutrons. In astronomy, the solid core of a comet. The plural is nuclei or nucleuses. {The old city formed the nucleus of the modern metropolis.}

Nude means naked—without clothing. In art, a nude is a depiction of an unclothed human figure: {She posed for a nude}, {classical nudes in oil}. The word carries associations of artistic or aesthetic nudity rather than mere nakedness. Nude also describes colors matching skin tone: {nude lipstick}, {nude heels}. In the nude means unclothed: {He was caught in the nude}.

Nudes are images depicting naked human bodies, especially photographs or artworks shared digitally. The singular nude refers to a naked figure in art or to a naked state: {The model posed nude}. In contemporary usage, nudes typically means sexually explicit photos exchanged privately: {She asked him to send nudes}. The noun also describes a pale beige color resembling light skin tones: {nude lipstick}, {nude heels}.

A nudge is a gentle push, typically with the elbow, to get someone's attention or signal something: {She gave him a nudge when it was time to leave}. To nudge is to push gently or to encourage someone toward action: {I nudged him to apply for the job}. A nudge can also be a person who persistently pesters—from Yiddish, where it rhymes with "could" rather than "judge."

A nudist is a person who practices social nudity, typically at designated beaches, resorts, or communities. The philosophy holds that nonsexual nakedness is natural and healthy. As an adjective, nudist describes these spaces and practices: {a nudist colony}, {a nudist beach}. The movement is also called naturism.

Nudists are people who practice social nudity, typically at designated beaches, resorts, or camps. The term implies a lifestyle philosophy that views nonsexual nakedness as natural and healthy: {The nudist colony welcomed new members}. Nudist and naturist overlap considerably, though naturist sometimes carries more emphasis on connection with nature.

Nudity is the state of being unclothed—having no clothes on. The word often carries associations with art, sexuality, or vulnerability that *naked* doesn't always share: {The film contains brief nudity}. A nude is a painting or photograph of an unclothed figure: {Modigliani's nudes}. In the nude means naked: {sleeping in the nude}.

A nugget is a small, solid lump of something valuable—originally and especially gold: {They found a nugget in the stream}. The word extends to compact, chunky pieces of food: chicken nuggets, cheese nuggets. Figuratively, a nugget is a small but valuable bit of information or wisdom: {nuggets of advice}, {a nugget of truth buried in his rambling}.

Nuggets are small, solid chunks or lumps of something—most classically gold: {prospectors panning for nuggets}. The word extends to bite-sized pieces of breaded and fried food: chicken nuggets, fish nuggets. Figuratively, a nugget is a compact piece of valuable information or wisdom: {nuggets of advice}, {a nugget of truth}. In sports, the Nuggets are Denver's NBA team.

A nuisance is something or someone that causes annoyance, inconvenience, or minor harm. The word covers a wide range—from a buzzing fly to a neighbor's barking dog to bureaucratic red tape: {What a nuisance to have to fill out all these forms}. In law, a nuisance is an activity or condition that interferes with others' use of property or public spaces.

Nuke is informal for nuclear weapon or nuclear power: {The country is developing nukes}. As a verb, to nuke is to attack with nuclear weapons, or more commonly, to cook in a microwave: {Just nuke the leftovers for two minutes}. The extended sense means to destroy completely: {A virus nuked my hard drive}.

Nuked means destroyed with nuclear weapons, but the word appears far more often in casual contexts. To nuke food is to microwave it: {I'll just nuke some leftovers}. To nuke something in gaming or computing is to wipe it out completely: {I accidentally nuked my save file}. The word captures both the speed and totality of destruction.

Nukes are nuclear weapons—bombs or warheads that derive their destructive force from atomic reactions. The term extends to nuclear power plants and submarines. As a verb, to nuke is to attack with nuclear weapons, or more casually, to microwave something: {Just nuke the leftovers for two minutes}. To nuke also means to destroy utterly: {The update nuked my saved files}.

Nuking is the present participle of nuke. In its literal sense, it means attacking with nuclear weapons: {They're talking about nuking the whole region}. More commonly, it means destroying or eliminating completely: {I'm nuking all my old emails}. In casual speech, nuking often just means microwaving: {I'm nuking some leftovers for lunch}.

Numb describes the loss of sensation or feeling. A numb limb has gone to sleep or been affected by cold or anesthesia: {My fingers were numb from the freezing water}. Emotionally, numb means unable to feel or respond: {She was numb with shock after hearing the news}. The verb means to make numb: {The injection numbed the area}. Extended uses suggest dulled responsiveness: {numb to the violence on the news}.

The word number is used for different concepts and ideas that all involve the symbols that we use to represent quantity: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and the rest. Any one of these symbols, alone or in combination with others, is called a number and the abstract system in which these symbols exist is also sometimes called number. In grammar, number refers the quantity of things being talked about. Many languages distinguish between singular (one thing) and plural numbers. Some languages also have a dual number to represent two things.

Numbers are quantities or amounts—the basic units of counting and measuring. In everyday use, numbers often means statistical data: {The numbers don't look good for the campaign}. To {do a number on} something is to damage or affect it severely. A number is also a musical selection or performance piece: {She sang a few numbers from the show}. To have someone's number is to understand their true character or motives. (Capitalized Numbers is the biblical book.)

Numbing describes something that causes loss of sensation or feeling. Cold water has a numbing effect on skin; a dentist's injection numbs the mouth. Figuratively, numbing applies to experiences so overwhelming or repetitive they dull emotional response: {the numbing boredom of the assembly line}, {numbing grief}. What numbs can be intense or monotonous—either extreme deadens perception.

Numbness is the loss or reduction of sensation in part of the body, typically from nerve compression, cold exposure, or medical conditions. {My fingers went numb from gripping the handlebars.} The word extends to emotional states where feelings are dulled or absent, often as a response to shock or trauma. {A numbness settled over her after hearing the news.} Numbness can also describe mental blankness or inability to think clearly.

Numerology is the belief that numbers have mystical significance and can reveal truths about personality, destiny, or events. Practitioners assign meaning to birth dates, name letters converted to digits, or recurring numbers: {Her numerology reading said she was a life path seven}. The practice has no scientific basis but remains popular in New Age and occult circles.

A nun is a woman who has taken religious vows and lives in a community devoted to prayer, contemplation, and service. Nuns typically reside in convents and follow strict rules of their order—poverty, chastity, and obedience being common requirements. The term applies primarily to Catholic and Orthodox Christian women, though similar roles exist in Buddhism and other faiths. {She became a nun at twenty-two.} (Capitalized Nun is a Hebrew letter.)

Nunation is the addition of a final n-sound to a word, particularly in Semitic languages like Arabic. In Arabic grammar, nunation (called tanwin) marks indefinite nouns with a nasal ending: {kitabun} (a book) versus {al-kitab} (the book). The term appears primarily in linguistic and grammatical discussions of Arabic and related languages.

Nunchucks are a martial arts weapon consisting of two short sticks connected by a chain or cord, swung and spun as striking weapons. Popularized in the West through Bruce Lee films and ninja movies, they became iconic enough that many jurisdictions banned them. The word comes from Okinawan Japanese. Also spelled nunchaku, the original form.

Nunchucks are a martial arts weapon consisting of two short sticks connected by a chain or cord, swung and spun to strike opponents. Popularized in the West through Bruce Lee films and ninja mythology, they became an icon of 1970s martial arts culture: {He practiced with nunchucks in the garage}. Also spelled nunchaku, from Japanese.

Nunchucks are a martial arts weapon consisting of two short sticks connected by a chain or cord, swung and spun for striking. Originating in Okinawa, they became iconic through Bruce Lee films and are now associated with martial arts training and ninja imagery. Also spelled nunchaku. A Wii nunchuk is the motion controller attachment, named for its shape and tethered design.

Nunchuks are a martial arts weapon consisting of two short sticks connected by a chain or cord, swung and spun to strike opponents. Associated with kung fu movies and ninja imagery, they became a pop culture symbol of martial arts prowess in the 1970s and 80s. Also spelled nunchucks or nunchaku, from the Japanese.

Nuns are women who have taken religious vows and live in a community devoted to prayer, contemplation, and service. The term applies across traditions—Catholic, Buddhist, Orthodox—though the specifics of dress, practice, and enclosure vary. {The nuns ran the hospital}. A nun differs technically from a sister, who takes simpler vows and works outside the convent, though the terms blur in casual use.

A nurse is a person trained to care for the sick or injured, typically working under a physician's direction in hospitals, clinics, or homes. The verb nurse means to care for someone during illness: {She nursed him back to health}. To nurse a drink is to consume it slowly. To nurse a grudge is to hold onto it. A nurse also breastfeeds an infant, and a wet nurse does so for another woman's child. Nursery and nursing home extend the caregiving sense to spaces for children and the elderly.

Nurseries is the plural of nursery, a word with meanings connected to nurturing the young. A nursery is a room for babies or small children: {The nurseries were painted in soft colors}. Nurseries also refers to businesses that grow and sell young plants: {We visited three nurseries before finding the right shrubs}. A nursery school is an early childhood educational setting.

A nursery is a room or facility devoted to the care of young children or infants: {The hospital nursery was full of newborns}. The word extends to places where young plants are grown and sold: {We bought tomato seedlings at the nursery}. A nursery rhyme is a traditional children's song or poem. In British usage, nursery school is preschool education.

Nurses are healthcare professionals who care for patients—monitoring conditions, administering medications, and assisting physicians. The term covers various specializations and credentials, from licensed practical nurses to nurse practitioners. To nurse someone is to care for them through illness: {She nursed him back to health}. To nurse a drink is to sip it slowly; to nurse a grievance is to hold onto it. A nurse also breastfeeds: {She nursed the baby until he fell asleep}.

Nursing is the profession of caring for the sick, injured, or infirm, typically in healthcare settings under the direction of physicians. A nurse monitors patients, administers medications, and provides comfort. Nursing also refers to the act of breastfeeding an infant: {She was nursing the baby}. To nurse something is to tend it carefully—a drink, a grudge, an injury back to health.

Nurture is care and support that helps something develop and thrive. Parents nurture children, teachers nurture talent, gardeners nurture plants. The word emphasizes sustained attention over time: {She nurtured his interest in music from an early age}. As a noun, nurture is the environmental side of the nature-versus-nurture debate—what shapes us through upbringing rather than genetics.

Nurturing describes care that supports growth and development. A nurturing {parent} provides emotional warmth and encouragement. A nurturing {environment} fosters learning or creativity. The word emphasizes gentleness and attentiveness—not just providing for needs but actively cultivating wellbeing: {The mentor took a nurturing approach with new employees}. As a noun, nurturing is the act itself: {Children thrive with consistent nurturing}.

A nut is an often-edible fruit with a hard shell that grows on a shrub or tree, like an almond, pecan, or hazelnut. A fastener that is threaded on the inside to fit a bolt or screw is also a nut. A person who is wildly enthusiastic about something is a nut (conspiracy nut, football nut). Such a person with too many such obsessions might be called nuts, and nonsensical ideas are also nuts.

A nutcase is an insane or extremely eccentric person: {Her uncle is a complete nutcase}. The term is informal and often affectionate—calling someone a nutcase suggests they're harmlessly crazy rather than dangerously so.

A nutcracker is a device for cracking open nuts, typically a hinged metal tool that applies leverage to break the shell. The word extends to the nutcracker bird, which wedges nuts into bark crevices and hammers them open. {She set out a bowl of walnuts and a nutcracker.} (Capitalized Nutcracker refers to the ballet.)

Nutcrackers are tools for cracking open hard-shelled nuts, typically hinged levers that apply pressure to the shell. The word also refers to decorative wooden figures with large jaws that mimic this cracking action—a staple of Christmas decoration, immortalized in Tchaikovsky's ballet. In British slang, nutcrackers can mean tight trousers that squeeze uncomfortably.

Nutmeg is a warm, aromatic spice ground from the seed of a tropical tree, used in baking, custards, and eggnog. The flavor is distinctive—sweet and slightly pungent. In large doses, nutmeg has hallucinogenic properties. In soccer, to nutmeg someone is to kick the ball between their legs and collect it on the other side—a humiliating maneuver.

Nutmegs is the plural of nutmeg, the aromatic seed of a tropical tree used as a spice. Ground nutmeg flavors baked goods, eggnog, and savory dishes. In soccer, to nutmeg someone is to kick the ball between their legs—the plural names instances of this move: {He scored after nutmegging two defenders}.

Nutrients are substances that living things need to survive and grow. In nutrition, nutrients include proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins, and minerals—the components of food that nourish the body. Plants absorb nutrients from soil; fertilizers add nutrients back. {The doctor said I wasn't getting enough nutrients.} The adjective form is nutrient: {nutrient-rich soil}.

Nutrition is the process of obtaining and using food for growth, energy, and health. It also refers to the study of how food affects the body, or to the nourishing quality of food itself: {The doctor asked about her nutrition}, {a degree in nutrition}, {This cereal has no nutritional value}. Good nutrition implies a balanced diet; poor nutrition suggests deficiency or excess.

Nuts are hard-shelled fruits with edible kernels—walnuts, almonds, cashews. In mechanical contexts, a nut is the hexagonal piece that screws onto a bolt. To be nuts is to be crazy: {That idea is nuts}. {He's gone completely nuts}. In vulgar slang, nuts means testicles: {He got kicked in the nuts}. {The brass on that guy—he's got nuts}. Nuts expresses frustration as an exclamation: {Ah nuts, I forgot my wallet}. The expression {nuts about} means enthusiastically fond of: {She's nuts about jazz}.

A nutshell is the hard outer covering of a nut. The phrase {in a nutshell} means expressed in the briefest possible form, summarizing something complex in a few words: {In a nutshell, we're broke}. The image is of fitting something large into a tiny space.

Nutty means containing or resembling nuts in taste or appearance: {a nutty flavor}, {a nutty aroma}. {This cheese has a nutty quality}. Nutty also means crazy, eccentric, or foolish: {That's a nutty idea}. {He's nuttier than a fruitcake}. The craziness sense may derive from {nuts} meaning insane, or from {off one's nut} (head). Both senses are common; context clarifies.

Nuzzle is to push or rub gently with the nose or face, typically as a sign of affection: {The horse nuzzled my palm looking for treats}. Animals nuzzle their young; lovers nuzzle each other's necks. The word suggests warmth and closeness. To nuzzle into something is to press against it cozily: {She nuzzled into the blankets}.

Nuzzled is the past tense of nuzzle, meaning to push or rub gently with the nose or face, typically as a sign of affection: {The horse nuzzled my palm looking for a treat}. Animals nuzzle their young; humans nuzzle lovers or children. By extension, to nuzzle is to nestle or snuggle close: {She nuzzled against his shoulder}.

Nuzzling is pressing or rubbing gently with the nose or face, typically as a sign of affection. Animals nuzzle their young; lovers nuzzle each other's necks. The word suggests tender, intimate contact: {The cat was nuzzling against my hand}. To nuzzle can also mean to nestle or snuggle close: {The child nuzzled into her mother's shoulder}.

Nylon is a synthetic polymer used to make fabric, rope, and molded products. Developed in the 1930s, it became famous as the material for women's stockings—so much so that nylons became a word for the stockings themselves: {She put on a fresh pair of nylons}. Nylon is strong, lightweight, and elastic, appearing in everything from parachutes to guitar strings to carpet fibers.

A nymph is a minor nature deity in Greek mythology—a beautiful maiden inhabiting forests, waters, or mountains. The word extends to any attractive young woman, though this use sounds literary or archaic. In entomology, a nymph is an immature insect that resembles the adult form, as in grasshoppers or dragonflies: {The mayfly nymph lives underwater for years before emerging}.

Nymphs are minor female nature spirits in Greek mythology, associated with particular locations or features—streams, trees, mountains, meadows. They appear as beautiful young women, neither fully divine nor mortal. The word extends to any beautiful young woman, and in entomology, to the immature form of certain insects that develops gradually rather than through complete metamorphosis: {The dragonfly nymph lives underwater before emerging}.

An oaf is a clumsy, stupid, or socially awkward person, usually male. The word suggests lumbering physicality combined with dullness—someone who knocks things over and doesn't notice: {The oaf spilled beer all over the table}. Oafish behavior is crude and graceless.

Oak is a hardwood tree known for its strength, durability, and distinctive lobed leaves. Oaks produce acorns and can live for centuries, making them symbols of endurance and steadfastness. The wood is prized for furniture, flooring, barrels, and shipbuilding: {aged in oak barrels}, {a solid oak table}. {Mighty oaks from little acorns grow.}

Oaks are large, long-lived hardwood trees known for their strength and durability. The wood is prized for furniture, flooring, and barrels—wine and whiskey aged in oak take on distinctive flavors. Acorns are the oak's fruit. {The old oak in the churchyard has stood for three hundred years.}

An oar is a long pole with a flat blade at one end, used to row a boat through water. The rower sits facing backward, pulling the oars through the water in a sweeping motion. To {put your oar in} is to offer an unsolicited opinion. Someone who {rests on their oars} stops making effort after achieving something.

Oars are long poles with flat blades at one end, used to propel and steer boats through water. A rower dips the blade beneath the surface and pulls, creating thrust. To {put in one's oar} is to offer an unsolicited opinion. To {rest on one's oars} is to relax after effort.

Oases is the plural of oasis—fertile spots in a desert where water allows vegetation to grow. The word extends to any place of relief amid difficulty or monotony: {The café was an oasis of calm in the hectic city}. The alternative plural oasises exists but sounds awkward to most ears.

An oasis is a water source in a desert, typically surrounded by vegetation. This core meaning gives rise to metaphoric use, in which an oasis is any real or notional place that offers benefits not available in its surroundings. Because of this, oasis is popular in the names of various resorts.

Oat is a cereal grain, typically eaten as oatmeal or rolled oats for breakfast. The plant grows well in cool climates. {Oats} almost always appears in the plural. To {feel one's oats} is to act confidently or frisky. To {sow one's wild oats} is to indulge in youthful excess before settling down.

An oath is a solemn promise, often invoking a higher power as witness: {She took an oath to tell the truth}. Oaths formalize commitments—the oath of office, the Hippocratic oath, wedding vows. An oath is also an exclamation invoking something sacred, often profanely: {He muttered oaths under his breath}. To be {under oath} is to have sworn to tell the truth, with legal consequences for lying.

Oathbreakers are people who violate solemn promises or sworn commitments. The word carries weight because oaths historically bound people to sacred or legal obligations—breaking them meant betraying something fundamental. In fantasy fiction and gaming, oathbreakers are often cursed or dishonored figures: {The oathbreakers were doomed to wander until they fulfilled their pledge}. Outside fiction, the term condemns those who betray trust or duty.

Oaths are solemn promises or declarations, often invoking a deity or something sacred as witness. People take oaths of office, oaths of allegiance, oaths to tell the truth in court. The word also refers to profane exclamations—curses or swear words: {He muttered oaths under his breath}. Both senses share the idea of words spoken with force or gravity.

Oatmeal is a porridge made by boiling oats in water or milk, typically eaten as a hot breakfast cereal. The word also refers to the ground or rolled oats themselves before cooking. As an adjective, oatmeal describes a grayish-beige color resembling cooked oats: {an oatmeal sweater}, {oatmeal walls}.

Oats are a cereal grain, typically eaten as oatmeal or rolled oats for breakfast. The plant grows well in cool climates and serves as livestock feed. To {feel one's oats} is to act energetically or self-importantly. To {sow one's wild oats} is to indulge in youthful excesses, especially sexual ones, before settling down.

Obedience is compliance with authority, rules, or commands. A dog trained to obedience follows its owner's instructions. Children owe obedience to parents; soldiers to officers; monks to religious superiors. The word implies submission to another's will: {blind obedience}, {unquestioning obedience}. In obedience to means in accordance with: {in obedience to the law}.

Obedient describes someone who does what they're told—following commands, rules, or the wishes of an authority. Children are expected to be obedient to parents, soldiers to officers, dogs to owners. The word implies submission to another's will: {an obedient servant}, {obedient to the law}. It can carry negative connotations of excessive compliance or lack of independent thought.

An obelisk is a tall, four-sided stone pillar that tapers to a pyramidal point at the top. Ancient Egyptians carved them as monuments, and the form has been widely imitated: {The Washington Monument is an obelisk}. In typography, obelisk is another name for the dagger symbol (†), used for footnotes or to mark deceased persons.

Obelisks are tall, four-sided stone pillars that taper to a pyramidal point at the top. Ancient Egyptians carved them from single blocks of granite, often inscribed with hieroglyphics. Many now stand in Western cities as trophies of empire: {The obelisk in Central Park was a gift from Egypt}. By extension, any tall, narrow monument of similar shape: {The Washington Monument is technically an obelisk}.

Obese describes a person carrying excessive body fat to the degree that it poses health risks. The clinical definition uses body mass index, but in everyday speech obese simply means very fat—more severe than overweight. {The doctor warned him that he was clinically obese.} The noun is obesity.

Obesity is the condition of having excessive body fat, typically defined medically by a body mass index of 30 or higher. The term carries clinical weight but also social stigma, making it fraught in everyday conversation. Obesity is distinguished from merely being overweight, which suggests a lesser degree of excess. {Childhood obesity rates have tripled since the 1970s.}

To obey is to do what someone tells you to do, or to follow a rule or law. Children obey parents, soldiers obey commanders, citizens obey laws. The word implies submission to authority: {She obeyed without question}. Things that respond predictably also obey: {The car obeyed the slightest touch of the wheel}. To obey your instincts is to act on them.

Obituaries are notices of death, typically published in newspapers or online, that announce someone's passing and summarize their life. A standard obituary includes the person's name, age, date of death, surviving family members, and funeral arrangements, often alongside biographical highlights like career achievements or community involvement. {I check the obituaries every morning to see if anyone I know has died.} The obituary section of a newspaper is sometimes called "the obits" informally.

An obituary is a notice of someone's death, typically published in a newspaper or online, that summarizes their life—birth, family, career, accomplishments, and circumstances of death. Obituaries range from brief announcements to lengthy tributes. The word often shortens to obit: {I read her obit in the Times}. To {write your own obituary} figuratively means to ensure your downfall.

An object is a thing—something you can see or touch, distinct from living beings and abstract ideas. In grammar, the object receives the action: in {She threw the ball}, ball is the object. To object (stress on second syllable) is to express disapproval or opposition: {I object to this plan}. An objection is the noun form. The {object of} something is its target or purpose: {the object of her affection}, {the object of the game}.

Objectification is the act of treating a person as a thing rather than as a human being with thoughts, feelings, and agency. The term appears most often in discussions of how women are reduced to their physical appearance or sexual appeal, particularly in media and advertising. More broadly, objectification can occur whenever someone's humanity is ignored in favor of their usefulness or function: {The objectification of workers as mere productivity units}. The related verb is objectify.

Objectified describes someone or something treated as an object rather than as a full person with agency and dignity. Most often applied to how women are portrayed or regarded—reduced to their physical attributes or sexual appeal: {She felt objectified by the way he stared}. The term also appears in philosophical contexts about treating people as means rather than ends.

To objectify is to treat a person as an object—stripping away their agency, feelings, or individuality. The term appears most often in discussions of how women are reduced to their physical appearance: {Advertisements that objectify women's bodies}. More broadly, objectify can mean to make something abstract concrete or tangible: {The sculpture objectifies grief}.

An objection is a reason or argument offered against something—a statement of disagreement or disapproval: {I have no objection to the plan}. In legal contexts, an objection is a formal protest that evidence or testimony violates court rules: {Objection, your honor—hearsay}. To {raise an objection} is to voice opposition.

Objections are reasons given for disagreeing with or opposing something. A lawyer raises objections in court to challenge evidence or procedure. In sales, objections are concerns a customer voices before buying: {Let me address your objections one by one}. To have {no objection} is to consent or not mind: {I have no objection to your plan}.

An objective is something you wish to accomplish or prove, similar to a goal. As an adjective, objective has myriad meanings. The objective case, in many languages, is the case of nouns or pronouns when they are the object of a verb or of a preposition. If you are objective about something (as opposed to subjective), you evaluate it without distortion from personal prejudices. Objective reality observable by the senses and agreed upon by everyone: The objective reality is that, on sunny days, the sky is blue.

Objectivity is the quality of being based on facts rather than personal feelings or opinions. A journalist strives for objectivity in reporting; a judge maintains objectivity in court. The word implies removing bias and seeing things as they actually are: {The study's objectivity has been questioned}. Complete objectivity may be impossible—everyone brings some perspective—but the ideal shapes how we evaluate evidence, arguments, and decisions.

Objects are things—physical items you can see or touch, or more abstractly, anything that can be perceived or thought about. In grammar, an object receives the action of a verb: {The dog chased the ball}. To object (stress on second syllable) is to express disapproval or opposition: {She objected to the proposal}. An objection is the noun form. The phrase {object of affection} refers to someone who is loved or desired.

An obligation is something you're bound to do—by law, contract, promise, or moral principle. Legal obligations carry penalties for noncompliance; social obligations carry disapproval. {I have an obligation to my family}. Financial obligations are debts or recurring payments. To be {under no obligation} is to be free to decline. The word often implies burden: something you must do whether you want to or not.

Obligations are things you must do—duties, commitments, or responsibilities that bind you. The word carries a sense of external pressure: you may not want to fulfill an obligation, but something compels you. {She felt an obligation to visit her aging parents}. Legal obligations are enforceable; social obligations carry consequences of a different kind. Financial obligations are debts or payments owed: {He couldn't meet his monthly obligations}.

To obliterate is to destroy so completely that nothing remains, or to remove all traces of something: {The bombing obliterated the village}. The word suggests total annihilation rather than mere damage. Extended uses describe overwhelming defeat {(They obliterated the competition)} or erasure from memory or visibility: {Time had obliterated all evidence of the settlement}.

Obliterated is the past tense of obliterate, meaning to destroy completely or wipe out of existence. A bombing obliterates a building; time obliterates memories. The word suggests thoroughness—nothing recognizable remains: {The flood obliterated any trace of the settlement}. In slang, obliterated means extremely drunk or high: {We got obliterated at the party}.

Obliterating is destroying something so completely that no trace remains. A bombing campaign obliterates a city; time obliterates memory. The word implies thoroughness beyond mere destruction—not just breaking but erasing entirely: {The scandal obliterated his reputation}. In sports, obliterating an opponent means defeating them decisively.

Obliteration is complete destruction or erasure—wiping something out so thoroughly that no trace remains. A city faces obliteration in war; a memory undergoes obliteration over time. The word emphasizes totality: not just damage but annihilation. {The bombing brought obliteration to the village}. {Years of neglect led to the obliteration of the old records}.

Oblivion is the state of being completely forgotten or unknown: {His early work faded into oblivion}. It also means the state of being unaware or unconscious of what is happening: {She drank herself into oblivion}. To {consign something to oblivion} is to deliberately forget or discard it. The word suggests total erasure—not mere forgetting, but as if something never existed at all.

Oblivious means unaware or unmindful, typically of something that others notice: {She was oblivious to the stares she was getting}. The word often implies self-absorption or inattention rather than genuine ignorance. Someone oblivious to danger isn't necessarily uninformed—they're just not paying attention to it.

Obnoxious describes behavior or qualities that are highly annoying or objectionable—aggressively unpleasant in a way that's hard to ignore. An obnoxious person forces their presence on others through loudness, rudeness, or general offensiveness: {He was obnoxious at the party, interrupting everyone}. The word suggests more than mere annoyance—something obnoxious actively repels.

An oboe is a woodwind instrument with a double reed and a distinctively plaintive, penetrating tone. It has a conical bore and produces sound when the player blows between two thin reeds bound together. The oboe typically sounds the tuning note for orchestras: {The oboist played an A and the strings adjusted their pitch}.

Obscene describes material or behavior that offends standards of decency, particularly regarding sex. Obscene {language}, obscene {gestures}, obscene {images}. Legal definitions of obscenity focus on sexual content lacking artistic or social value. More loosely, obscene can mean morally outrageous: {obscene wealth}, {obscene profits}. {The CEO's bonus was obscene given the layoffs}.

Obscenities are words or expressions considered indecent or offensive—profanity, vulgar sexual terms, and taboo language generally. The word also covers offensive acts or gestures: {He shouted obscenities at the referee}. What counts as an obscenity varies by culture and era; words once unspeakable now appear routinely in entertainment and casual speech.

Obscenity is language, imagery, or behavior that offends prevailing standards of decency—typically involving sex, bodily functions, or extreme violence. In legal contexts, obscenity refers to material lacking artistic or social value that appeals to prurient interests: {The court ruled the film was not obscenity}. The word also describes individual offensive acts or utterances: {He shouted obscenities at the referee}.

Obscure describes things that are difficult to see, understand, or find. An obscure {passage} in a text is hard to interpret; an obscure {figure} in history is little known. Something hidden in shadow is literally obscure. As a verb, to obscure is to conceal or make unclear: {Fog obscured the road ahead}. {His jargon obscured a simple argument}.

Obscurity is the state of being unknown or unnoticed: {He died in obscurity}. It also means darkness or dimness: {shapes moving in the obscurity}. A third sense is difficulty of understanding—something unclear or hard to interpret: {The poem's obscurity frustrated readers}. The plural obscurities usually refers to unclear passages or meanings: {The contract was full of legal obscurities}.

Observant means quick to notice things: {She's very observant—she spotted the typo immediately}. The word suggests attentiveness and perceptiveness about one's surroundings or details others might miss. Separately, observant describes someone who follows religious rules and practices faithfully: {an observant Jew}, {observant Muslims who pray five times daily}.

Observation is the act of watching or noticing something carefully. Scientific observation involves systematic attention to phenomena: {Her observations of bird behavior filled three notebooks}. An observation can also be a remark or comment based on what one has noticed: {He made a few observations about the state of the economy}. Under observation means being monitored, often medically: {They kept her under observation overnight}.

An observatory is a building or facility designed for observing celestial or atmospheric phenomena, typically equipped with telescopes and other scientific instruments: {The Griffith Observatory offers views of the Los Angeles skyline and the stars above it}. By extension, any elevated structure offering wide views may be called an observatory: {The skyscraper's observation deck functions as an urban observatory}.

Observe means to watch carefully or notice: {I observed a change in her behavior}. Scientists observe phenomena; witnesses observe events. To observe a rule or custom is to follow it: {They observe the Sabbath}. To observe is also to remark or comment: {He observed that the weather had turned}. An observation can be something noticed or something said.

An observer is someone who watches or notices something. In formal settings, an observer attends meetings or events without participating: {The UN sent observers to monitor the election}. Scientific observers record data systematically. In physics, the observer holds special significance—relativity and quantum mechanics both depend on the observer's frame of reference. Someone who is a {keen observer} notices details others miss.

To obsess is to preoccupy the mind excessively and persistently. The word works in two directions: something can obsess you {(The case obsessed her for years)}, or you can obsess over something {(He obsesses over every detail)}. The noun obsession and adjective obsessed are more common than the verb. What obsesses tends to be unwanted or unhealthy—a fixation rather than a passion.

Obsessed describes a state of being consumed by a persistent thought, desire, or fixation. Someone obsessed with a person, idea, or goal can't stop thinking about it: {She's obsessed with true crime podcasts}. The word often implies unhealthy preoccupation, but casual use has softened it to mean simply very enthusiastic: {I'm obsessed with this new restaurant}.

Obsession is a persistent, intrusive preoccupation with something—a thought, person, or desire that dominates the mind. The word implies an unhealthy fixation: {His obsession with her bordered on stalking}. But casual usage softens this: {I have an obsession with true crime podcasts} means strong enthusiasm rather than pathology. In clinical contexts, obsessions are unwanted recurring thoughts that cause distress, often paired with compulsions.

Obsessions are thoughts, ideas, or fixations that occupy the mind persistently and often unwantedly. The word suggests something beyond ordinary interest—an obsession crowds out other concerns: {Her obsession with cleanliness made normal life difficult}. In clinical contexts, obsessions are intrusive thoughts that cause anxiety, often paired with compulsions. More casually, obsession describes intense enthusiasm: {His obsession with vintage cars}, {a cultural obsession with celebrity}.

Obsessive describes a preoccupation that dominates thought or behavior to an excessive degree. An obsessive {fan} fixates on a celebrity; obsessive {thoughts} intrude repeatedly and unwantedly. The word can be clinical—obsessive-compulsive disorder involves intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviors—or casual: {She's obsessive about keeping her kitchen clean}. As a noun, an obsessive is a person prone to such fixations.

An obshchina is a traditional Russian peasant commune that collectively managed village land, redistributing it periodically among member households according to family size. The institution shaped rural Russian life for centuries and figured prominently in debates about Russia's path to modernization. Slavophiles idealized the obshchina as embodying cooperative values distinct from Western individualism.

Obsidian is a dark volcanic glass formed when lava cools rapidly. It has a smooth, glossy surface and breaks into sharp edges, making it useful for ancient tools and weapons. The color is typically jet black but can include bands of gray or brown. {An obsidian blade}, {obsidian arrowheads}. The word often evokes sleekness or darkness: {obsidian eyes}, {an obsidian sky}.

Obsolescence is the process of becoming outdated or falling out of use. Products reach obsolescence when newer versions replace them: {The phone was heading toward obsolescence within two years of its release}. {Planned obsolescence} describes deliberate design choices that shorten a product's useful life, encouraging replacement. The adjective is obsolescent—actively becoming obsolete but not quite there yet.

Something that is obsolete is no longer useful or needed, usually because something newer and better has replaced it: The company is finally getting around to upgrading its obsolete computer system. Abstractions can also be characterized as obsolete: Methods of medical treatment now regarded as obsolete were once viewed as cutting-edge. If a concept is obsolete, the foundation on which it rests has been disproved by new evidence or discovery.

An obstacle is something that blocks progress or stands in the way of achieving a goal. Physical obstacles impede movement: {fallen trees became obstacles on the trail}. Figurative obstacles are difficulties or problems that must be overcome: {lack of funding was the main obstacle to the project}. An obstacle {course} is a training ground with barriers to climb, crawl under, or navigate around.

Obstacles are things that stand in the way of progress or achievement. The word applies to physical barriers—a fallen tree blocking a road, a fence around a property—and to abstract hindrances: {financial obstacles}, {bureaucratic obstacles}, {obstacles to peace}. An obstacle course presents a series of physical challenges to navigate. To overcome obstacles is to find ways past them.

Obstruction is something that blocks passage or progress. A physical obstruction prevents movement: {an obstruction in the airway}, {road obstruction}. The word extends to interference with processes: {obstruction of justice} means hindering legal proceedings. In sports, obstruction is illegally impeding an opponent's movement. To cause an obstruction is to get in the way, literally or figuratively.

Obvious describes something easily perceived or understood, requiring no explanation or special insight. An obvious {answer} is apparent to anyone who looks. An obvious {lie} fools no one. The word can carry slight condescension—stating the obvious means saying what everyone already knows. {Obviously} functions as an intensifier: {Obviously, I'm not happy about this}.

Obviously signals that something is apparent or self-evident: {Obviously, we can't finish by Friday}. It often carries a tone of mild impatience, suggesting the listener should already know this. Sometimes it's ironic—what follows isn't obvious at all. In casual speech, obviously serves as emphatic agreement: {Did you like it? Obviously!}

An occasion is a particular time when something happens, especially something notable: {on this occasion}, {on several occasions}. It also means a special event or ceremony: {a festive occasion}, {dress for the occasion}. To occasion something is to cause or bring it about—formal usage: {The announcement occasioned much debate}. {Rise to the occasion} means to meet a challenge when it matters.

Occasional means happening now and then, not regularly or frequently: {We have the occasional argument, but we get along well}. Something occasional happens when the occasion arises—an occasional table is used only when needed, occasional poetry is written for specific events. An occasional smoker smokes infrequently. The word suggests intermittent but not rare.

Occasions are particular times when something happens, especially significant or noteworthy events: {weddings and other formal occasions}, {I've met her on several occasions}. The word often implies ceremony or importance: {dress for the occasion}, {rise to the occasion}. To occasion something is to cause or bring it about: {The announcement occasioned much debate}.

Occult refers to supernatural beliefs, practices, or phenomena—magic, astrology, alchemy, divination, and communication with spirits. The word carries a sense of secret knowledge hidden from ordinary understanding: {She developed an interest in the occult after her grandmother's death}. As an adjective, occult means hidden or concealed, especially in technical contexts: an occult {fracture} is one not visible on initial X-rays, and occult {blood} is detectable only through testing. To occult something is to hide or eclipse it—one celestial body occults another when passing in front of it.

Occupation is work that occupies your time—a job, profession, or regular employment: {What's your occupation?} The word also means the act of occupying a place. Military occupation is forcible control of territory by foreign troops. Occupation of a building means people are inside using it. An occupying force holds ground; an occupying tenant holds a lease.

Occupied describes something in use or taken up. An occupied seat has someone sitting in it; an occupied bathroom is unavailable. A person who is occupied is busy or engaged: {She was occupied with work all afternoon}. In military and political contexts, occupied territory is controlled by a foreign force: {the occupied West Bank}. To keep children occupied is to give them something to do.

Occupy means to take up space or time. A couch occupies a corner; a meeting occupies an hour. To occupy a place is to live or work there: {The company occupies three floors}. Military forces occupy territory by taking control of it. To occupy yourself is to keep busy: {She occupied herself with gardening}. The 2011 Occupy Wall Street protests gave the word new political resonance—to occupy became a form of protest through physical presence.

An ocean is a vast body of salt water covering most of Earth's surface. The major oceans—Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic, Southern—are distinguished by name but form one continuous system. Ocean suggests immensity: {an ocean of possibilities}, {oceans of time}. {The ocean} often means simply the sea, especially in coastal regions: {Let's go to the ocean this weekend}.
