Oceans are the vast bodies of salt water covering most of Earth's surface—the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic, and Southern. The word often appears in the singular to mean this water collectively: {the ocean}, {ocean currents}. Figuratively, an ocean of something is an immense quantity: {oceans of time}, {an ocean of paperwork}.

Ocelots are medium-sized wild cats native to the Americas, ranging from Texas through Central and South America. They have distinctive spotted coats with chain-like markings, smaller than leopards but larger than house cats. Ocelots are solitary, nocturnal hunters that prey on small mammals, birds, and reptiles. Their striking fur made them targets for the exotic pet trade and fashion industry until protections were established.

Octane is a hydrocarbon found in petroleum, but the word appears most often in discussions of fuel quality. A fuel's octane rating measures its resistance to premature ignition—higher octane prevents engine knock in high-compression engines. {Premium gas has a higher octane than regular.} Figuratively, high-octane describes anything intense or high-energy: {a high-octane thriller}, {high-octane coffee}.

An octave is the interval between one musical pitch and another with double or half its frequency—the distance from one C to the next C, for instance. Notes an octave apart sound like higher or lower versions of the same note. The term extends to any set of eight: in poetry, an octave is an eight-line stanza, particularly the first eight lines of a sonnet.

An octopus is a soft-bodied marine animal with eight arms, a bulbous head, and no skeleton. Octopuses are known for their intelligence, ability to change color and texture, and talent for squeezing through tight spaces. The plural is octopuses or octopi, though octopuses is now more common in scientific and general usage.

Oculocutaneous describes conditions affecting both the eyes and skin. The term appears almost exclusively in medical contexts, particularly {oculocutaneous albinism}, a genetic condition causing reduced pigmentation in the eyes, skin, and hair.

Odd describes something that doesn't fit a pattern or expectation. An odd number can't be divided evenly by two. An odd sock has lost its mate. Odd behavior is strange or unusual: {What an odd thing to say}. Odd also means occasional or miscellaneous: {odd jobs}, {the odd cigarette}. The odds are the probability of something happening, especially in betting.

An oddball is a person who seems strange, eccentric, or unconventional: {He was always the oddball in his family}. The word suggests someone who doesn't quite fit in, though often with mild affection rather than harsh judgment. As an adjective, oddball describes anything quirky or unusual: {an oddball sense of humor}, {oddball theories about the universe}.

Oddballs are people who seem strange, eccentric, or unconventional—those who don't quite fit the norm. The term is affectionate or mildly dismissive rather than harsh: {The drama club attracted oddballs and misfits}. An oddball can also be an adjective: {an oddball sense of humor}, {oddball ideas}.

An oddity is something strange or unusual—a person, thing, or quality that deviates from the expected. The word carries mild curiosity rather than alarm: {The two-headed calf was a local oddity}. Oddity also names the quality of being odd: {the oddity of the situation}. In plural, oddities often appear in collections of curiosities or freak-show contexts.

Odds express the likelihood of something happening, typically as a ratio comparing favorable to unfavorable outcomes. In gambling and sports betting, odds indicate potential payouts: {The odds on the underdog were 5 to 1}. More casually, odds refers to probability in general: {What are the odds we'll finish on time?} If something is {at odds} with something else, they conflict or disagree. When you beat the odds or defy the odds, you succeed despite unfavorable expectations. {Odds and ends} are miscellaneous small items or leftover bits.

An ode is a lyric poem, typically one that praises or celebrates its subject. The classical form follows elaborate structures with stanzas and meter, but modern odes are often freer in form while retaining the tone of elevated address: {Keats's "Ode to a Nightingale"}. Informally, any tribute or enthusiastic appreciation may be called an ode: {His essay was an ode to New York pizza}.

An odor is a smell—a quality perceived through the nose. The word is neutral but often implies unpleasantness: {a foul odor}, {body odor}. Something {in bad odor} has a poor reputation. Odor can suggest a trace or hint: {an odor of corruption surrounded the deal}. British spelling: odour.

An odyssey is a long, eventful journey marked by adventures and hardships: {Her odyssey from refugee camp to medical school took fifteen years}. The word implies not just travel but transformation through experience—obstacles overcome, lessons learned. Any extended quest or wandering qualifies: {his odyssey through the criminal justice system}. (From the Greek epic about Odysseus's ten-year voyage home.)

Off has two core meanings. One is of separation (a restaurant just off the highway, borrow some money off your uncle); the other is of suspension or stoppage (the policeman was off duty at the time). Off is opposite to on in many of its meanings but does not have the same wide range of extended meanings as on has.

Offbeat describes something unconventional or departing from the ordinary: {an offbeat sense of humor}, {an offbeat romantic comedy}. The term comes from music, where the offbeat is the weaker, unaccented part of a measure—the "and" between the main beats. What falls on the offbeat stands apart from the expected rhythm.

Offence is the British spelling of offense. An offence is a violation of rules or law: {a criminal offence}, {a minor offence}. It also means the causing or feeling of hurt or annoyance: {No offence intended}, {She took offence at the remark}. In sports, offence is the attacking side or strategy—the team trying to score.

To offend is to cause displeasure, hurt feelings, or moral outrage: {His remarks offended nearly everyone in the room}. The word covers a spectrum from mild annoyance to deep insult. What offends varies by person and culture—some take offense easily, others rarely. To offend against something is to violate it: {offend against good taste}, {offend against the law}. An offender is someone who commits an offense, especially a crime.

Offended describes the state of feeling hurt, insulted, or resentful after perceiving a slight or disrespect. Someone who is easily offended takes offense at minor provocations. The word can express genuine hurt or signal excessive sensitivity: {She was deeply offended by the accusation}. {Don't be offended—I was only joking}.

An offender is someone who commits an offense—a wrongdoing, crime, or violation. Legal contexts dominate: {first-time offenders}, {repeat offenders}, {sex offenders}. The word implies formal wrongdoing rather than casual error: you're an offender if you break laws or rules, not if you merely annoy someone.

Offense centers on wrongdoing or attack. An offense is a violation of rules or laws: {a criminal offense}, {a minor traffic offense}. To cause offense is to upset or insult someone: {I meant no offense}. In sports, offense refers to the attacking side—the team trying to score, opposite of defense. To {take offense} is to feel insulted or hurt by something said or done. The British spelling is offence.

Offensive describes what attacks or causes displeasure. An offensive military strategy advances rather than defends. Offensive remarks or behavior cause anger or disgust: {His jokes were offensive to nearly everyone}. The noun is the attacking posture itself: {The army launched an offensive}, {on the offensive}. In sports, offense and offensive relate to scoring rather than preventing scores.

When you offer something, you make it available to someone else. If it is something intangible, offer sometimes means you give it without being asked: She’s always offering advice. When you offer to do something, you say that you will do some beneficial thing for someone else. When an institution offers something, that thing is available there: The hotel offers special weekend packages. An offer is the act or result of offering: We had to decline his offer to put us up overnight. An offer can also be associated with an amount of money for buying something: We made a low offer on the house and it was accepted.

An offering is something given or presented, often with a sense of generosity or purpose. The word carries a slightly formal or ceremonial tone: religious offerings to a deity, a company's stock offering, or the offerings at a fundraiser. More casually, it describes what's available: {The restaurant's lunch offerings are limited}. To make an offering is to give something up—sacrifice implied.

Offerings are things presented or made available. The core sense is religious—gifts given to a deity or for sacred purposes: {burnt offerings}, {a collection plate for offerings}. More broadly, offerings are what's on offer: a company's product offerings, a restaurant's seasonal offerings, a university's course offerings. The word suggests items put forward for consideration or acceptance.

Offhand means without preparation or forethought: {I can't give you the figures offhand}. The word suggests casualness—an offhand {remark} is made without much consideration, which can come across as dismissive or rude: {His offhand manner put people off}. As an adverb, offhandedly works the same way.

The most frequent use of office is for designating a place where business or work is done: In some cases, you can get a tax deduction for a home office. Some people say at the office as a way of saying that they’re at their wokplace. A noun or adjective before office typically indicates its function: post office, registry office. An office can also be the position associated with an official job, especially in politics and government: The office of mayor came with many unexpected responsibilities. In some countries, office indicates a large government department, as in Great Britain’s Home Office and Foreign Office.

An officer holds a position of authority or command. In military contexts, officers are commissioned ranks above enlisted personnel: {She was promoted to officer}. Police officers enforce the law. Corporate officers—CEO, CFO, treasurer—hold executive positions. The verb means to staff with officers or to command: {The ship was officered by veterans}. An officer of the court includes judges, lawyers, and court personnel with legal duties.

Official describes what is formally authorized, recognized, or sanctioned by an authority. An official {statement} comes from someone empowered to speak for an organization. Official {records} are the authoritative version. The official {language} of a country is legally recognized for government use. As a noun, an official is a person holding office or authority: {election officials}, {government officials}, sports {officials} who enforce rules. Something becomes official when it receives formal approval: {It's official—we're getting married}.

Officials are people holding positions of authority, typically in government, sports, or organizations. Government officials administer public affairs: {elected officials}, {city officials}. In sports, officials are referees or umpires who enforce rules: {The officials reviewed the play}. The word often implies bureaucratic or formal authority: {Immigration officials detained several passengers}.

Offline means disconnected from a computer network, especially the internet. You can work offline on a document, then sync changes when you reconnect. The word extends to any unavailability: {Let's take this conversation offline} means to discuss privately, away from the current group or meeting. Someone who's offline may simply be unreachable: {I'm going offline for the weekend}.

To offload is to transfer a burden or load elsewhere. Trucks offload cargo at warehouses. Workers offload tasks to subordinates: {I offloaded the paperwork to my assistant}. In computing, processing may be offloaded to specialized hardware. The word carries a slight sense of relief—you're getting rid of something you'd rather not carry: {He offloaded his old furniture before the move}.

Offputting describes something that creates aversion or discomfort—mildly repellent without being outright disgusting. An offputting {manner} makes someone hard to warm to. An offputting {smell} discourages approach. The word suggests a pushing away, a quality that prevents engagement: {His nervous laugh was offputting}. Also spelled off-putting.

An offramp is a road that allows vehicles to exit a highway or freeway: {Take the next offramp for downtown}. Figuratively, an offramp is any way to exit a difficult situation gracefully—politicians speak of giving adversaries an offramp to de-escalate conflict: {The negotiators offered him an offramp to save face}. Also spelled off-ramp.

Offroad describes travel or activity away from paved surfaces—on dirt, gravel, rocks, or rough terrain. An offroad {vehicle} is built for such conditions, with features like high clearance and rugged tires. As a verb, to offroad is to drive in such terrain: {We spent the weekend offroading in the desert}. Also spelled off-road.

Offroading is driving a vehicle over rough, unpaved terrain—dirt trails, mud, rocks, sand, or wilderness. It's both a recreational activity and sometimes a practical necessity in remote areas. Vehicles designed for offroading have features like four-wheel drive, high clearance, and rugged tires: {We spent the weekend offroading in the desert}. Also spelled off-roading.

Offscreen describes what happens outside the visible frame of a film, television show, or video. A character who speaks offscreen is heard but not seen. The term extends to actors' lives away from their roles: {They married offscreen after meeting on set}. In computing, offscreen refers to content rendered outside the visible display area.

The offseason is the time of year when a sport or activity isn't in regular play. Teams make trades, players rest or train, and fans wait: {He bulked up during the offseason}. The term extends to any business with seasonal rhythms—tourism, retail, agriculture. As an adjective: {offseason rates at the beach house}. Also spelled off-season.

Offset centers on the idea of counterbalancing or compensating. Gains offset losses; one factor offsets another. An offset is something that balances or counteracts: {The tax break was an offset against higher costs}. In printing and design, offset refers to a technique where ink transfers to an intermediate surface before paper, or to positioning that's slightly displaced from center: {The text was offset to the left}. As a verb, to offset is to counteract or place at an angle: {Solar panels offset our electricity bill}.

Offshoots are things that branch off from something larger or original. A plant's offshoot is a shoot growing from the main stem. Organizations, movements, or ideas produce offshoots—subsidiary groups or derivative developments: {The splinter party was an offshoot of the original movement}. Family offshoots are descendants or branches of a lineage.

Offshore means away from the shore, in or toward the water: {an offshore breeze}, {offshore drilling platforms}. The term extends to activities conducted in foreign countries, typically for financial advantage: offshore {banking}, offshore {accounts}, offshore {tax havens}. Companies that move operations abroad are said to offshore jobs or manufacturing: {The company offshored its customer service to the Philippines}.

Offside is a violation in sports like soccer and hockey where a player is illegally positioned ahead of the ball or puck relative to opponents. In soccer, you're offside if you're nearer the goal line than both the ball and the second-to-last defender when the ball is played to you. The adjective and adverb describe this position: {The striker was ruled offside}. Figuratively, offside can mean out of line or improper: {His remarks were a bit offside}.

Offspring are a person's or animal's children or young. The word works as both singular and plural: {Their offspring inherited the estate}, {The mare and her offspring grazed together}. It extends to anything produced or generated by something else: {The album was the offspring of their collaboration}. More formal than kids but less clinical than progeny.

Offstage refers to the areas of a theater not visible to the audience—the wings, backstage, dressing rooms. As an adverb or adjective, it describes action or sound occurring out of sight: {The gunshot was heard offstage}. Figuratively, offstage means private or unofficial, away from public scrutiny: {Offstage, the politician was surprisingly vulgar}.

Ogling is looking at someone with obvious sexual interest or desire—an extended, appreciative gaze that lingers on the body. The word carries a slightly leering quality: {He was ogling the women at the pool}. Unlike a glance or admiring look, ogling implies the gaze is noticeable and possibly unwelcome.

An ogre is a man-eating giant in folklore and fairy tales—ugly, brutish, and fearsome. The word extends to any cruel, intimidating person: {My boss is an absolute ogre about deadlines}. In fantasy games and fiction, ogres are typically large humanoid monsters of low intelligence but great strength.

Ogres are large, hideous humanoid monsters in folklore and fantasy, typically portrayed as man-eating brutes. They appear in fairy tales as villains who threaten heroes and devour children. Figuratively, an ogre is someone cruel, frightening, or tyrannical: {My boss is an absolute ogre}.

Oil is a liquid or liquefiable substance that is not soluble in water and is usually combustible. Oils are used as fuel (heating oil), or for nutrition (coconut oil, fish oil, vegetable oil), in which case they may also be classified as fats. In some contexts, oil is understood to be petroleum: oil spill, oil tanker. As a verb, oil means to apply oil, usually for purposes of lubrication: You need to oil that door; it squeaks. If you oil a pot or other cooking container, you add a small amount of oil to prevent sticking.

Oils are greasy liquid substances that don't mix with water. They come from various sources: vegetable oils for cooking, petroleum oils for engines, essential oils for fragrance. As a verb, to oil is to lubricate or apply oil: {He oiled the squeaky hinge}. In art, oils refers to oil paints or paintings made with them: {She works in oils}. To {oil the wheels} is to make a process run smoothly, often through bribery or favor.

Oily describes something covered with, containing, or resembling oil—slick, greasy, or slippery to the touch: {oily skin}, {oily hair}, {oily rags}. Foods can be oily from cooking fat. Extended to behavior, oily describes someone excessively smooth, flattering, or ingratiating in a way that feels insincere: {an oily salesman}, {his oily charm}.

Oink is the sound a pig makes, or a word representing that sound. Children learn it early: {The pig says oink}. As a verb, to oink is to make this sound or to eat greedily like a pig: {He oinked down three helpings}.

Ointment is a thick, greasy substance applied to the skin for healing or protection. Ointments typically contain medication mixed with oil or petroleum bases, distinguishing them from lighter creams and lotions. {Apply the ointment twice daily}. A {fly in the ointment} is a small flaw that spoils something otherwise good.
Okay is a very useful, short utterance that has now traveled far beyond English to indicate assent, agreement, or understanding.

Okra is a tall plant cultivated for its edible green seed pods, which become mucilaginous when cooked. This slippery texture thickens gumbo and other stews, though it puts off some eaters. The pods can also be fried, pickled, or roasted to minimize the sliminess. Okra is common in Southern, Caribbean, African, and South Asian cuisines.

The adjective old is itself quite old, first appearing before 900 C.E. Old is generally the opposite of new and characterizes things that began or existed a long time ago. When something new comes along, the thing that it replaces or supplants immediately becomes old. Old can have either positive or negative connotations, depending on the words it appears with: contrast old friend with old ideas.

An oldie is something old but still valued, especially a song or film from an earlier era that remains popular: {The radio station plays oldies from the sixties and seventies}. The word carries affection rather than dismissal—oldies are classics, not relics. Often appears in the phrase {oldie but goodie}. Can refer fondly to older people: {We oldies remember when phones had cords}.

Oldies are popular songs from an earlier era, typically the 1950s through 1970s rock and roll and pop hits: {The radio station plays nothing but oldies}. The term shifts with time—what counts as oldies keeps getting more recent. More broadly, oldies can refer to old things generally, or affectionately to older people: {a cruise for oldies}.

Oldschool (also old-school or old school) describes attitudes, methods, or styles from an earlier era, often with admiration for their authenticity or proven reliability. Someone oldschool favors traditional approaches over newer trends: {My dad is oldschool—he still balances his checkbook by hand}. In hip-hop, oldschool refers specifically to the genre's foundational era of the late 1970s and early 1980s. The term can signal respect for experience and craftsmanship or gentle teasing about being behind the times.

Oldtimers are people who have been around a long time—veterans of a place, profession, or era. The word suggests experience and longevity: {The oldtimers at the factory remember when everything was done by hand}. It can be affectionate or dismissive depending on context. Oldtimer's disease is a common euphemistic corruption of Alzheimer's disease.

An oligarch is a member of a small group that holds power in a government or organization. The term derives from oligarchy, a form of government where power rests with a few. In contemporary usage, oligarch most often refers to extremely wealthy individuals, especially Russian businessmen who acquired vast fortunes during the privatization of state assets after the Soviet collapse. {Sanctions targeted oligarchs close to the Kremlin.} The word carries connotations of ill-gotten wealth and corrupt political influence.

Oligarchs are members of a small group that holds power in a government or organization. The term often describes Russian billionaires who accumulated vast wealth during the privatization of state assets after the Soviet collapse: {Western sanctions targeted Russian oligarchs}. More broadly, oligarch labels any ultra-wealthy person whose fortune grants outsized political influence: {tech oligarchs}, {media oligarchs}.

Oligarchy is government by a small group, typically the wealthy or powerful. The term implies that power serves the interests of the ruling few rather than the broader population: {The country had become an oligarchy controlled by a handful of billionaires}. By extension, oligarchy can describe any organization where a small elite holds disproportionate control.

Olive is a small oval fruit, green when unripe and black when mature, prized for eating and for the oil pressed from it. The olive tree, native to the Mediterranean, is ancient in cultivation and symbolic of peace—an olive branch signals reconciliation. Olive also names a dull yellowish-green color, common in military clothing: {olive drab}. As an adjective, it describes skin tone: {olive complexion}. (Capitalized Olive is a given name.)

Olives are small oval fruits of a Mediterranean tree, harvested green (unripe) or black (ripe). Too bitter to eat fresh, they're cured in brine, salt, or oil. Olives are pressed to make olive oil, a staple of Mediterranean cooking. The olive branch is a symbol of peace. {Would you like olives on your pizza?}

Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, and by extension means the end or final element of something. The phrase {alpha and omega} encompasses everything from beginning to end. In social hierarchies, an omega is the lowest-ranking individual—opposite of alpha. Omega-3 {fatty acids} are essential nutrients. In physics, omega represents angular velocity. {Every story has its omega.} (Capitalized Omega may refer to watch brands, organizations, or proper names.)

An omelet is eggs beaten and cooked in a pan until set, typically folded around a filling of cheese, vegetables, or meat. The dish is a breakfast staple but appears at any meal. Spelling varies: omelet in American English, omelette in British. {I'll have a mushroom omelet with toast.}

Omelets are eggs beaten and cooked in a pan until set, typically folded around a filling of cheese, vegetables, or meat. The dish is a breakfast staple and a test of technique for cooks—a properly made omelet should be tender inside with no browning. Also spelled omelette.

An omelette is a dish of beaten eggs cooked in a flat round and typically folded around a filling—cheese, vegetables, meat, or herbs. The eggs are stirred briefly in a hot pan, then allowed to set. {She made a mushroom omelette for breakfast.} Also spelled omelet, especially in American English.

An omen is a sign or event believed to foretell the future, especially something momentous or fateful: {The crow at the window seemed like an omen}. Omens can be good or bad, though the word alone often suggests something ominous—a dark portent. To omen is rare; the adjective forms ominous and the verb portend are more common.

Omens are signs believed to foretell future events, especially misfortune. A black cat crossing your path, a broken mirror, an owl's call—these are traditional omens. The word often appears with modifiers: {a bad omen}, {an omen of things to come}. Unlike prophecies, omens are read from ordinary events rather than spoken by seers. Something that omens ill bodes badly for the future.

Omerta is the code of silence associated with the Mafia and other organized crime groups—the rule that members never cooperate with authorities or reveal information about criminal activities. Breaking omerta traditionally carried severe consequences, including death. The term extends to any unwritten rule against informing: {The department's omerta protected corrupt officers for years}.

Ominous describes something that suggests bad things to come—threatening or foreboding. An {ominous sky} portends a storm. An {ominous silence} precedes bad news. {The letter arrived with an ominous warning}. The word carries a sense of dread without specifying the threat, letting imagination fill the gap.

Omission is leaving something out or failing to do something. An omission can be accidental—a name dropped from a list—or deliberate: {The report's omissions were telling}. In law and ethics, an omission may carry the same weight as an action: failing to report abuse, neglecting to disclose a conflict of interest. {Sins of omission} are wrongs committed by not acting.

Omnipotence is unlimited power—the ability to do anything. The word appears most often in religious contexts, where it describes a divine attribute: {the omnipotence of God}. More loosely, omnipotence can describe any seemingly boundless authority or capability: {the omnipotence of the surveillance state}. The adjective is omnipotent.

Onboard means aboard or on a vehicle, vessel, or craft: {onboard navigation systems}, {the onboard computer}. Extended to mean part of a team or project: {We need to get everyone onboard before we proceed}. As a verb, to onboard is to integrate a new employee or customer into an organization's systems and culture: {HR will onboard you next week}. Also spelled as two words: on board.

Onboarding is the process of integrating someone new into an organization or system. In workplace contexts, it covers everything from paperwork to training to cultural orientation: {The company's onboarding takes two weeks}. For software and apps, onboarding refers to the initial steps that familiarize users with features: {The app's onboarding walks you through the basics}. The verb is onboard: {We onboarded three new hires this month}.

Once is a busy function word whose meanings arise mainly from the closely related word one. The adverb conveys one time (I went there once) or formerly: They visited the ruins of the once magnificent castle. At once conveys immediacy or concurrence: I can’t do two things at once. Once is used to join clauses to show one thing immediately follows, and may depend upon, another: Once you light the fuse, get out of there.

One is the written form of the number 1 and works as an adjective in that capacity (one window). One substitutes for a singular noun that has been used already, or when reference is clear from context (buy one, get one free). One is an impersonal and somewhat formal third-person singular pronoun without gender: One should be careful in that situation. Groups of things sharing some characteristic can be designated with an adjective before ones (red ones, lucky ones).

A onesie is a one-piece garment. For infants, it's a bodysuit that snaps at the crotch for easy diaper changes. For adults, it's a loose-fitting jumpsuit worn as loungewear or pajamas, often with a playful or cozy aesthetic: {I spent Sunday in my onesie watching movies}. The plural is onesies.

Onesies is a one-piece garment, either a snap-crotch bodysuit for infants or a full-body jumpsuit for adults, typically casual loungewear with feet: {She bought a dinosaur onesie for the baby shower}. The adult version gained popularity as ironic comfort wear: {We spent New Year's Eve in matching onesies}. Singular: onesie.

Oneupmanship is the practice of gaining or maintaining an advantage over others, especially through subtle competitive tactics. The word suggests a game where each party tries to outdo the other in status, wit, or achievement: {The dinner party descended into oneupmanship as each guest tried to name-drop more impressive connections}. Unlike outright rivalry, oneupmanship often operates through suggestion and implication rather than direct contest.

Ongoing means continuing or in progress, not yet completed: {ongoing negotiations}, {ongoing investigation}, {an ongoing relationship}. The word emphasizes that something started in the past and persists into the present, with no definite end point. {The project is ongoing and expected to take several more months.}

Onion is a bulb vegetable with papery outer layers enclosing concentric rings of pungent flesh. Raw onions have a sharp, eye-watering quality that mellows into sweetness when cooked. The layered structure gives rise to the metaphor of peeling back layers to reveal deeper truths or complexities: {The investigation peeled back the onion on years of corruption}. In internet slang, the onion router (Tor) enables anonymous browsing, and .onion addresses exist on the dark web. If you {know your onions}, you're well-informed about a subject.

Onions are pungent bulb vegetables with papery outer layers and concentric rings inside. They're culinary staples across most cuisines, eaten raw, sautéed, caramelized, or pickled. Cutting onions releases compounds that irritate the eyes, causing tears. To {know your onions} is to be knowledgeable about something.

Online means connected to or available through the internet or a computer network. You can shop online, take classes online, or meet someone online. As an adjective, it describes things accessible digitally: {online banking}, {online dating}. The opposite is offline. Something that {goes online} becomes operational or connected: {The new server goes online tomorrow}.

It’s significant that the closest relative of only is the word one: only always serves to distinguish one thing, group, or quality from others. As an adverb only limits the application of verbs and adjectives: This area is reserved for members only. Before nouns, only suggests singularity: She’s an only child. Is that the only shirt you have to wear? In writing, only precedes the word it modifies; in speech, the word is emphasized, lessening the importance of position. Listeners who hear, “I could only see three people there,” understand that the only goes with “three” and not with “see.”

An onramp is a short road that allows vehicles to enter a highway or freeway, typically curving to merge with faster traffic: {We missed the onramp and had to circle back}. Figuratively, an onramp is any entry point or introductory pathway: {Community college can be an onramp to a four-year degree}. Also spelled on-ramp.

Onslaught is a fierce, overwhelming attack—originally military, now used broadly for any intense assault: {The city couldn't withstand the onslaught}. It suggests force arriving suddenly and in quantity: an onslaught of {criticism}, an onslaught of {emails}, an onslaught of {bad weather}. The word carries a sense of being besieged or overwhelmed.

Onward means forward in space, time, or progress—continuing in a direction already established. {The expedition pressed onward despite the storm.} {From that day onward, everything changed.} It often carries a sense of determination or momentum. As an adjective, it describes forward movement: {the onward march of technology}. Onwards is a British variant.

Onyx is a banded variety of chalcedony, a semiprecious stone typically showing parallel layers of black and white. Pure black onyx is most familiar in jewelry: {an onyx ring}, {onyx cufflinks}. The word extends to anything with that distinctive deep black color or lustrous quality.

Oomph is energy, vigor, or attractive quality—the indefinable something that makes a person or thing stand out. A performer with oomph has charisma and sex appeal. A dish needs more oomph if it lacks punch or excitement. An engine lacks oomph if it doesn't have enough power: {This old truck doesn't have the oomph to make it up the hill}.
People say oops to acknowledge that they—or someone else—have just done something clumsy, made a mistake, or said something awkward or embarrassing.

Ooze is slow, thick movement—liquid seeping gradually through or out of something: {Blood oozed from the wound}, {Water oozed through the cracks}. The word suggests viscosity and unhurried flow. Figuratively, someone can ooze confidence or charm, exuding it so thoroughly it seems to seep from them. As a noun, ooze is soft mud or slime, especially at the bottom of a body of water.

Oozes describes slow, thick movement—liquid seeping gradually through small openings or across surfaces. Mud oozes between toes; sap oozes from tree bark. Figuratively, a person oozes qualities they seem to exude effortlessly: {He oozes confidence}; {The place oozes charm}. The word suggests something emerging steadily, almost involuntarily, rather than flowing freely.

Oozing describes something slowly seeping or leaking out, typically a thick liquid like blood, mud, or pus: {The wound was still oozing}. It can also characterize surfaces that release such substances: {oozing blisters}. Figuratively, oozing suggests an excessive or conspicuous display of a quality: {He was oozing confidence}. The word carries connotations of something uncontrolled and often unpleasant, though the figurative sense can be neutral or even positive.

Opal is a gemstone prized for its iridescent play of colors—flashes of red, blue, green, and yellow that shift as light moves across the surface. This optical effect, called opalescence, comes from the stone's internal structure of silica spheres. Opals range from milky white to black, with black opals being most valuable. {She wore her grandmother's opal ring.} The adjective opalescent describes anything with similar shimmering, shifting colors.

Opals are gemstones prized for their iridescent play of color—flashes of red, blue, green, and orange that shift as the stone moves. Unlike diamonds or rubies, opals display this internal shimmer rather than brilliance from faceting. {Her grandmother's opal ring caught the light}. Australia produces most of the world's gem-quality opals. Superstition once held opals unlucky, though this belief has faded.

The core idea of open is the lack of a closing or confining barrier or limit: open door, open discussions. For many meanings, the nearest antonym of open is closed or shut. When you open something, you cause it to be open, as with a door, window, or gate. For something intangible, open can mean to initiate or create something that becomes usable or available, as when you open an account, or when a situation opens a possibility. To open fire means to start shooting. Open is also used intransitively, in which case the thing opening is the subject: The exhibition opens next week.

An opener is anything that opens something else, whether a tool like a bottle opener or can opener, or a person who initiates an action. In sports, the opener is the first game of a series or season. In conversation, an opener is a remark designed to start a dialogue: {He tried a few openers but she wasn't interested}. The opener in a show or concert is the act that performs first, before the headliner.

Opening is the act of becoming open or making something open, or the gap or space that results: {an opening in the fence}, {the opening of a new store}. An opening is also a beginning—the opening of a book, a chess opening, opening remarks. By extension, an opening is an opportunity or available position: {a job opening}, {an opening in the schedule}. The adjective describes what comes first: {opening night}, {opening statement}.

Openness is the quality of being receptive, accessible, or unrestricted. A person with openness welcomes new ideas and experiences: {Her openness to criticism made her a better writer}. Openness in communication means transparency and candor: {The company promised greater openness about its practices}. Physical openness describes expansiveness or lack of barriers: {the openness of the prairie}. In personality psychology, openness is one of the "Big Five" traits, measuring curiosity and imagination.

Opera is a dramatic art form combining music, singing, and theatrical performance, with the story told primarily through sung dialogue rather than spoken words: {We have tickets to the opera tonight}. The term also refers to a particular work in this genre: {Carmen is my favorite opera}. Opera can mean the opera house or company: {the Sydney Opera}. In computing, Opera is a web browser. (Capitalized OPERA may be an acronym.)

Operate means to function or to cause something to function. Machines operate when they run properly; surgeons operate when they perform medical procedures; businesses operate when they conduct their affairs. {The elevator operates on a pulley system.} {She operates a small bakery downtown.} To operate on someone is to perform surgery. In military and covert contexts, operatives operate in the field, carrying out missions or gathering intelligence.

Anything that operates may be called an operation. Anyone who operates can be said to be performing or conducting an operation. In medicine, an operation is a surgery. A large-scale operation usually involves many people, high-level organization, and a purpose, such as a peacekeeping operation or a rescue operation. The plural is also used suggest multiple things going on: The company began operations in Sudan last year. The operation of a machine is the regular performance of its function. The thread combining all of these meanings is an activity or process that moves toward an end, under the direction of a person or algorithm.

Operations are organized activities directed toward a purpose. In business, operations means the day-to-day functioning that keeps an enterprise running: {She oversees operations for the entire West Coast region}. Military operations are planned campaigns or missions. Medical operations are surgical procedures. The word often implies coordinated, systematic effort: {rescue operations}, {mining operations}, {covert operations}.

An operator is someone who operates something—a machine, a business, a system. A crane operator runs heavy equipment. A tour operator organizes travel. In mathematics, an operator is a symbol indicating an operation: +, −, ×. In computing, operators perform actions on values. The word also describes a person skilled at manipulation or getting what they want: {He's a smooth operator}. To call someone an operator suggests cunning, charm, or shrewd self-interest.

An opiate is a drug derived from opium—morphine, heroin, codeine. The term extends to synthetic drugs with similar effects (opioids). Opiates dull pain and induce euphoria, making them both medically valuable and dangerously addictive. Figuratively, an opiate is anything that soothes or numbs: {Television is the opiate of the masses}, echoing Marx's description of religion.

Opiates are drugs derived from opium, including morphine, heroin, and codeine. They act on the brain's pain receptors, producing relief and euphoria but carrying high addiction potential. The term extends to anything that dulls the senses or induces passivity: {Television is the opiate of the masses}, echoing Marx's famous line about religion.

An opinion is a belief or judgment not necessarily based on proof or certainty. Opinions contrast with facts: {That's just your opinion}. Everyone has opinions on topics from politics to pizza toppings. A professional opinion carries more weight—a doctor's opinion, a lawyer's opinion. To form or hold an opinion is to have one; to express or voice it is to share it.

Opinionated describes someone who holds strong opinions and expresses them readily, often without invitation. The word carries a negative edge—it suggests stubbornness or an unwillingness to consider other views: {He's too opinionated to take advice}. An opinionated piece of writing makes no pretense of neutrality.

Opinions are views or judgments formed about something, not necessarily based on fact or knowledge. Everyone has opinions; the word often appears in contexts distinguishing subjective belief from objective truth: {That's just your opinion}. To {have a high opinion} of someone is to regard them favorably. Professional opinions carry more weight: a doctor's opinion, a legal opinion. {In my opinion} signals that what follows is personal judgment rather than established fact.

Opioid refers to drugs that bind to opioid receptors in the brain to relieve pain—including natural derivatives of opium (morphine, codeine), synthetic compounds (fentanyl, methadone), and semi-synthetics (oxycodone, heroin). Opioids produce euphoria alongside pain relief, making them highly addictive. The opioid epidemic describes widespread addiction and overdose deaths tied to overprescription and illicit supply: {The opioid crisis has devastated rural communities}.

Opioids are drugs that act on the nervous system to relieve pain. The class includes natural derivatives of the opium poppy (morphine, codeine), synthetic compounds (fentanyl, methadone), and semi-synthetic variants (oxycodone, heroin). Opioids are highly effective painkillers but carry significant risk of dependence and overdose: {the opioid epidemic}, {opioid crisis}. Medical contexts distinguish opioids (the broader category) from opiates (strictly poppy-derived).

Opium is a narcotic drug derived from the dried latex of opium poppy seedpods. It contains morphine, codeine, and other alkaloids that produce sedation, euphoria, and pain relief. Historically significant in trade and warfare—the Opium Wars between Britain and China—opium was once widely used medicinally before addiction concerns led to strict controls. {The opium dens of 19th-century San Francisco.} Figuratively, something that dulls awareness or pacifies: Marx called religion {the opium of the people}.

An opossum is a marsupial native to the Americas, most commonly the Virginia opossum found throughout North America. Opossums are nocturnal, omnivorous, and famous for "playing possum"—feigning death when threatened. The shortened form *possum* is standard in casual speech: {There's a possum in the garbage again}.

An opponent is someone who opposes you—in competition, conflict, or argument. In sports and games, your opponent is whoever you're trying to beat: {She studied her opponent's playing style}. In debate or politics, opponents hold contrary positions: {opponents of the legislation}. The word implies active opposition without necessarily suggesting hostility.

Opponents are people or groups who compete against or oppose someone or something. In sports, your opponent is whoever you're playing against: {We face a tough opponent this weekend}. In debate or politics, opponents hold contrary positions: {opponents of the bill}. The word implies active opposition rather than mere difference—opponents engage, they don't just disagree from a distance.

Opportunism is the practice of seizing opportunities for advancement without regard for principles or consequences. The word usually carries negative connotations—an opportunist exploits situations for personal gain rather than acting from conviction: {His sudden support for the policy looked like pure opportunism}. In biology, opportunism describes organisms that thrive by exploiting variable conditions.

An opportunist seizes opportunities as they arise, often without regard for principles or consequences. The word usually carries negative connotations—suggesting someone who exploits situations for personal gain rather than acting from conviction: {He's a political opportunist who changes positions whenever it's convenient}. As an adjective, opportunist describes such behavior: {opportunist tactics}.

Opportunities is the plural of opportunity—favorable circumstances or situations that make something possible. Opportunities can be seized, missed, created, or squandered: {Job opportunities in the region have dried up}. The word often implies potential for advancement or gain: {equal opportunity employer}, {investment opportunities}. {When opportunity knocks, answer the door}.

An opportunity is a chance to do, see, say, or accomplish something. Opportunities are often time-limited, with an implication that if you don’t take advantage of an opportunity, it will not be there later. More generally, opportunity is the availability of choices that enable people to earn a living, have a good life, or fulfill their dreams and ambitions: Young people tend to leave town soon after high school because there are no opportunities here.

To oppose is to stand against something—to resist, obstruct, or compete with it. You can oppose a policy, a candidate, or an idea: {She opposed the merger from the start}. Opposing forces face each other in conflict. As opposed to introduces a contrast: {I prefer tea, as opposed to coffee}. The adjective opposed emphasizes active resistance or fundamental incompatibility: {They hold diametrically opposed views}.

Opposed describes a position of resistance, disagreement, or conflict with something else. If you are opposed to a plan, you disagree with it and may work against it. Opposed forces or ideas stand in contrast or contradiction to each other. The phrase {as opposed to} draws a distinction between two things: {I prefer tea as opposed to coffee}. Diametrically opposed things are completely contrary, like polar opposites.
Opposite is mainly an adjective that can be used as a preposition, especially in British English, with the meaning across from.

Opposites are things that differ from each other as much as possible—hot and cold, up and down, love and hate. The word works as noun or adjective: {They're complete opposites}, {opposite sides of the street}. To be opposite something is to face it directly: {The bank is opposite the post office}. {Opposites attract} suggests that people with contrasting personalities are drawn to each other.

Opposition is the act of resisting, disagreeing with, or standing against something: {The proposal met fierce opposition from local residents}. It also names the people or group doing the opposing—a political opposition party, the opposing team in sports. In astronomy, opposition describes when two celestial bodies appear on opposite sides of the sky, as when Mars is in opposition to the Sun.

To oppress is to keep people down through unjust use of power or authority. Oppression may be violent or subtle—laws that discriminate, systems that exclude, or conditions that deny dignity. The oppressed lack freedom or opportunity that others enjoy. {Colonial powers oppressed indigenous populations for centuries.} {She felt oppressed by her family's expectations.}

Oppressed describes people or groups subjected to harsh, unjust treatment by those with power over them. The oppressed lack freedom or opportunity because of systematic discrimination or exploitation: {The oppressed workers finally organized}. As a past participle, it describes the state of being weighed down: {She felt oppressed by the humid air}, {oppressed by grief}.

Oppression is the cruel or unjust exercise of power over others, keeping them in a state of hardship or subjugation. It implies systematic mistreatment—not a single act but sustained domination: {centuries of oppression}, {liberation from oppression}. The word can also describe a heavy, suffocating feeling: {an oppression in her chest}, {the oppression of the summer heat}.

Oppressive describes something that weighs heavily—whether literally or figuratively. Oppressive heat is stifling and hard to bear. An oppressive regime exercises harsh, unjust control over people: {The oppressive government silenced all dissent}. Oppressive rules or expectations feel burdensome and restrictive. The word carries connotations of cruelty, unfairness, or suffocating pressure that's difficult to escape.

An oppressor is a person, group, or institution that exercises unjust power over others—keeping them down through force, exploitation, or denial of rights. The word carries moral weight, implying the powerful party is wrong: {The colonizers became oppressors of the native population}. Oppressor often appears in political and revolutionary contexts, naming those against whom resistance is justified.

Oppressors are those who exercise cruel or unjust authority over others. The word carries moral weight—it's not neutral like "rulers" but implies abuse of power: {The colonized rose up against their oppressors}. Oppressors may be individuals, governments, or systems that keep people subjugated through force, exploitation, or denial of rights.

Optics is the branch of physics dealing with light and vision. More commonly now, optics refers to how something appears to others—the public perception or political impression it creates: {The optics of the meeting were bad}, {It's not illegal, but the optics are terrible}. This sense treats appearances as something to be managed, distinct from substance.

Optimism is a disposition to expect favorable outcomes—the tendency to anticipate good rather than bad. An optimist believes things will work out, that difficulties are temporary, that the future holds promise: {Her optimism kept the team motivated through setbacks}. The word can carry a hint of naivety when circumstances seem to warrant pessimism: {I admire your optimism, but I don't share it}.

An optimist is someone who tends to expect favorable outcomes and see the positive side of situations. The word implies a general disposition rather than a momentary mood: {She's an optimist who believes things will work out}. Optimist can carry a slight edge, suggesting naïveté or wishful thinking: {Only an optimist would expect this Congress to act}.

Optimistic describes a tendency to expect favorable outcomes or see the bright side of circumstances. An optimistic {forecast} predicts good results; an optimistic {person} believes things will work out. The word can suggest healthy hopefulness or naive overconfidence, depending on context: {She remained optimistic despite the setbacks}. The opposite is pessimistic.

Optimists are people who expect favorable outcomes. Where pessimists anticipate the worst, optimists believe things will work out: {Optimists see the glass as half full}. The disposition can be philosophical—a belief that the world tends toward good—or simply temperamental: {She's one of those natural optimists who bounces back from anything}.

Optimization is the process of making something as effective or functional as possible. In mathematics and computing, it means finding the best solution among many possibilities: {The algorithm uses optimization to minimize load times}. In everyday use, it often describes improving efficiency or performance: {We spent months on supply chain optimization}. The word sometimes carries a clinical tone, as when applied to human behavior or productivity.

To optimize is to make something as effective or functional as possible. In computing, optimizing code means improving its speed or efficiency. In everyday use, you optimize a schedule, a workflow, or a diet: {We optimized the route to avoid traffic}. The word carries connotations of systematic improvement rather than casual tweaking.

An option is a choice among alternatives: {You have three options}. It also means the right but not obligation to do something—in finance, an option is a contract giving the holder the right to buy or sell at a set price within a specified period. As an adjective, optional means not required: {Attendance is optional}. To opt is to choose: {She opted for the cheaper plan}.

Optional describes something you can choose to do or include but aren't required to. An optional {course} isn't mandatory for graduation. Optional {features} cost extra. {Formal attire optional} means you may dress up or not. The word marks a contrast with what's compulsory or expected.

Options are choices available to you—the things you can do or select in a given situation. {We're weighing our options.} {What are my options here?} In finance, options are contracts giving the right (but not obligation) to buy or sell an asset at a set price within a certain time. In computing and software, options are settings you can adjust: {Check the options menu.}

Opulence is great wealth or luxuriousness, especially when displayed lavishly. The word emphasizes visible abundance—gilded furnishings, sumptuous fabrics, extravagant surroundings: {The opulence of the palace overwhelmed visitors}. Unlike mere wealth, opulence suggests richness you can see and touch: {She lived in opulence while her workers barely scraped by}.

An opus is a work of art, especially a musical composition. The plural opera once dominated English but now sounds affected; opuses is standard. Opus often appears with a number identifying a composer's works in sequence: {Beethoven's Piano Sonata No. 14, Opus 27}. A {magnum opus} is someone's greatest work or masterpiece.

An oracle is a source of wisdom or prophecy. In ancient Greece and Rome, an oracle was a priest or priestess through whom gods were believed to speak, or the shrine where such consultations occurred: {The king consulted the oracle at Delphi}. By extension, any person regarded as an infallible authority: {She was the oracle on matters of etiquette}. The word also names the prophecy itself: {The oracle proved true}. (Capitalized Oracle is the software company.)

Oracles are sources of wisdom or prophecy. In ancient Greece and Rome, oracles were sacred sites where priests or priestesses delivered divine messages, or the prophets themselves: {the oracle at Delphi}. The term extends to authoritative pronouncements: {pronouncements from the oracle of Wall Street}. In computing, Oracle is a major database software company.

Oral means relating to the mouth or to spoken language. An oral {exam} is administered verbally rather than in writing. Oral {hygiene} concerns care of the teeth and gums. Oral {traditions} pass knowledge through speech rather than texts. In sexual contexts, oral refers to stimulation using the mouth: {oral sex}.

Orange is a color between red and yellow, named after the fruit. The fruit came first—a citrus with segmented flesh and a thick, peelable rind. The color extends to anything with that hue: {orange sunsets}, {orange traffic cones}. Orange juice is so common that {orange} alone often means the juice: {I'll have an orange with breakfast}. As an adjective, orange describes the color or the flavor. (Capitalized Orange may refer to places or the House of Orange.)

Oranges are the citrus fruit—round, segmented, typically orange-skinned, sweet or tart. The plural appears in contexts involving multiple fruits or varieties: {I bought a bag of oranges}, {blood oranges are sweeter than navels}. To compare {apples and oranges} is to contrast things too different for meaningful comparison.

An orangutan is a large, long-armed ape native to the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra. Orangutans are reddish-brown, highly intelligent, and spend most of their lives in trees. The name comes from Malay words meaning "person of the forest." {The orangutan swung effortlessly between branches.}

Orangutans are large, long-armed apes native to the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra. They have shaggy reddish-brown hair and spend most of their lives in trees. The name comes from Malay words meaning "person of the forest." Orangutans are among the most intelligent primates, known for using tools and problem-solving. {The orangutans at the zoo drew crowds with their antics.}

An orb is a sphere or globe, often one with symbolic significance—a monarch's orb represents earthly power, held alongside the scepter. The word appears in poetic or elevated contexts for celestial bodies: {the pale orb of the moon}. In paranormal circles, orbs are mysterious spherical lights in photographs, claimed as evidence of spirits. Eyes are sometimes called orbs in literary or humorous usage: {She rolled her orbs heavenward}.

An orbit is the curved path one object takes around another in space—Earth's orbit around the sun, the moon's orbit around Earth. By extension, anything that moves in a circular path orbits: {satellites orbiting the planet}, {electrons orbiting a nucleus}. Figuratively, orbit describes a sphere of influence or activity: {She moves in elite social orbits}. To be {in someone's orbit} is to be within their sphere of influence. The eye socket is also called an orbit.

Orbiting is the present participle of orbit—to move in a curved path around something, as planets orbit the sun or satellites orbit Earth. The word extends to figurative circulation: {paparazzi orbiting the celebrity}, {thoughts orbiting an idea}. In dating slang, orbiting means passively monitoring an ex's social media without direct contact—staying in their digital orbit.

Orbits are the curved paths objects follow around other objects in space—a planet orbiting a star, a moon orbiting a planet, a satellite orbiting Earth. The word extends to any regular circuit: {The security guard makes orbits around the building every hour}. Eye sockets are also called orbits—the bony cavities housing the eyeballs. To orbit is to travel such a path: {The spacecraft orbits Mars}. Figuratively, things in someone's orbit fall within their sphere of influence.

An orc is a fictional creature in fantasy literature and games—a brutish, aggressive humanoid typically portrayed as warlike and ugly. J.R.R. Tolkien popularized orcs in his Middle-earth novels, where they serve as foot soldiers of evil. The word has become standard in fantasy gaming: {The party encountered a band of orcs in the mountain pass}. In older usage, orc was a variant spelling of orca, the killer whale.

An orca is a large black-and-white toothed whale found in oceans worldwide, the largest member of the dolphin family. Orcas hunt in coordinated groups called pods, preying on fish, seals, and even other whales—hence the alternative name killer whale. {We watched orcas breaching off the coast.}

Orcas are large black-and-white marine mammals, the largest members of the dolphin family. Also called killer whales, they hunt in coordinated pods and prey on fish, seals, and even other whales. Orcas are found in oceans worldwide, from polar waters to tropical seas: {We spotted a pod of orcas off the coast}.

An orchard is a plot of land planted with fruit or nut trees: {apple orchard}, {peach orchard}, {almond orchard}. The word implies deliberate cultivation rather than wild growth, and usually suggests trees arranged in rows for harvesting. {We picked apples at the orchard last weekend.}

An orchestra is a large group of musicians playing together, typically featuring strings, woodwinds, brass, and percussion under a conductor's direction. The term usually implies a classical ensemble: {the New York Philharmonic Orchestra}. Orchestra also refers to the main floor seating in a theater, nearest the stage—from the ancient Greek performance space where musicians sat.

To orchestrate is to arrange music for an orchestra, assigning parts to different instruments. The figurative sense now dominates: to orchestrate something is to coordinate multiple elements into a unified effort, often with careful planning behind the scenes: {She orchestrated the entire merger}, {a carefully orchestrated campaign}. The word implies both complexity and deliberate control.

Orchestrated means carefully arranged or coordinated, often with multiple moving parts working together toward a planned outcome. The word comes from orchestrating music—arranging a composition for different instruments—but now usually describes deliberate coordination of events or efforts: {an orchestrated campaign}, {an orchestrated attack}. The term often implies behind-the-scenes manipulation: {The whole thing was orchestrated by party insiders}.

Orchestrating is arranging or coordinating multiple elements to achieve a desired outcome. The word comes from the musical sense—adapting a composition for orchestra, assigning parts to different instruments. But the figurative use now dominates: {She was orchestrating the entire campaign from behind the scenes}. It often implies skillful, sometimes covert management of complex moving parts.

Orchestration is the arrangement of music for an orchestra, determining which instruments play which parts. The term extends to any careful coordination of multiple elements: {the orchestration of a political campaign}, {the orchestration of a complex merger}. In computing, orchestration refers to automated coordination of software systems and services. The underlying idea is always bringing many parts into coordinated action.

An orchid is a flowering plant of a vast family known for elaborate, often showy blooms. Orchids range from tropical epiphytes to temperate wildflowers, prized by collectors and hobbyists for their beauty and difficulty to cultivate: {She tends her orchids obsessively}. A pale purple-pink color is also called orchid.

Orchids are a vast family of flowering plants prized for their exotic, often elaborate blooms. They range from tropical species with showy petals to modest wild varieties. Orchids have become popular houseplants and gifts, though they carry a reputation for being finicky: {She finally got her orchid to rebloom}. In Victorian times, orchid collecting became an obsession among wealthy enthusiasts.

Orcs are a fictional race of brutish, warlike humanoids, most famously from J.R.R. Tolkien's Middle-earth legendarium, where they serve as foot soldiers of evil. The concept has spread throughout fantasy literature, films, and games, where orcs typically appear as savage, tribal creatures opposed to elves and humans: {The party encountered a band of orcs in the mountain pass}. In online discourse, orc sometimes serves as dehumanizing slang for enemy combatants or people perceived as mindlessly aggressive.

Ordained describes someone who has been formally invested with religious authority, typically through a ceremony conferring the power to perform sacred rites: {an ordained minister}, {She was ordained as a priest in 1995}. More broadly, ordained means decreed or established by fate, law, or higher authority: {It seemed ordained that they would meet again}. To ordain is to officially order or destine something to happen.

An ordeal is a severe trial or painful experience that tests endurance: {The divorce was a two-year ordeal}. The word originally meant a method of determining guilt by subjecting the accused to physical tests—fire, water, combat—with survival indicating divine judgment of innocence. The modern sense retains that flavor of suffering through something difficult: {Getting through airport security has become an ordeal}.

One group of meanings of the noun and verb order involves the idea of a request for action that carries authority. When you order someone to do something, you request that they do it by virtue of your authority over them. When you order a product, whether a hamburger at a drive-in or a new computer from an online store, you are requesting that it be delivered to you. An order is the process of ordering something, or the content of it: Have you received all of your order? Order also means to put into a systematic arrangement, and order, as an uncountable noun, is the state of being so arranged. Order is also the desirable state of being arranged in an optimal way: law and order, the order of nature.

Orderly describes things arranged in a neat, systematic way or proceeding in a calm, controlled manner: {an orderly room}, {an orderly transition of power}. The opposite of chaotic. As a noun, an orderly is a hospital attendant who performs non-medical tasks—moving patients, changing linens, maintaining order on the ward.

Orders are commands or instructions from someone with authority: {The sergeant gave orders to advance}. In restaurants, an order is what you've requested: {Your order is ready}. To place an order is to request goods or services. Religious orders are communities bound by vows. The order of things is their arrangement or sequence. Something out of order is broken or improper. To order is to command, arrange, or request.

Ordinary means normal, typical, or unremarkable—what you'd expect in the usual course of things. An ordinary {day} has nothing special about it. Ordinary {people} are average citizens, not celebrities or experts. The word can carry slight condescension: calling something ordinary suggests it lacks distinction. {It was just an ordinary Tuesday until the phone rang.}

Ore is rock or mineral from which a valuable substance, especially metal, can be extracted: {iron ore}, {copper ore}. The term implies economic viability—material only counts as ore if it's worth mining. By extension, ore sometimes refers to any raw material awaiting refinement: {The manuscripts were ore waiting to be smelted into prose}.

Ores are rocks or minerals from which metals or other valuable substances can be extracted profitably. Iron ore yields iron, copper ore yields copper. The distinction between ore and ordinary rock depends on economics—a deposit becomes ore when extraction is worthwhile: {The mine closed when the ore ran out}. {They discovered rich gold ore in the hills}.

An organ is a part of a living body that performs a specific function—the heart pumps blood, the liver filters toxins, the brain processes thought. Vital organs are essential for survival. The word extends to musical instruments: a pipe organ produces sound by forcing air through tubes, while an electronic organ simulates this. An organ of government or organization is a body that carries out particular functions: {the official organ of the Communist Party}. Organic relates to living things or, in food, production without synthetic chemicals.

Organic describes something derived from living organisms or their remains. In chemistry, organic compounds contain carbon. Organic food is grown without synthetic pesticides or fertilizers: {We buy organic vegetables at the farmers market}. Organic also means developing naturally rather than being forced or artificial: {The conversation took an organic turn toward deeper topics}. An organic whole has parts that function together as a unified system.

Organisation is the British spelling of organization. It refers to a structured group of people working together for a shared purpose—a business, charity, government body, or similar entity: {She works for an international humanitarian organisation}. It also means the act or manner of arranging things systematically: {The organisation of the conference took months}.

Organised is the British spelling of organized. To be organised is to have things in order—plans made, materials ready, thoughts structured. An organised person manages time and tasks efficiently. An organised event runs smoothly. To get organised is to impose order on chaos: {I need to get organised before the move}. The spelling with s appears throughout British English, while American English uses z.

Organization is the process of putting something in order, or the result of this: The organization of the museum’s fossil collection took several years. His organization of the topic does not include any mention of his mentor’s work. An institution that exists for a purpose—especially a purpose other than moneymaking—is also called an organization: She works for an organization that distributes food and clothing to the poor. Organizations often have members, who may be individuals or other organizations.

When you organize something you put it in a recognizable order. Both concrete and abstract things can be organized: Please organize the clothes you want to take with you on the camping trip. Who’s going to organize the reception for your wedding? When someone organizes workers, or when workers organize, they either form or become members of a labor union. When something is described as organized, it often means conducted by organization, as in organized crime or organized religion.

Organized means arranged in an orderly, systematic way. An organized {desk} has everything in its place. An organized {person} manages tasks and belongings efficiently. Organized also describes collective action with structure and coordination: {organized labor}, {organized crime}, {organized religion}. To {get organized} is to bring order to chaos—whether a closet or a life.

An organizer is a person who arranges or coordinates activities, events, or groups: {The organizers expect thousands at the rally}. In labor contexts, an organizer recruits workers into unions. The word also names containers or systems for keeping things orderly—a desk organizer, a closet organizer, a digital organizer for scheduling. To organize is to bring order to something or to arrange people toward a purpose.

Organizing is the act of arranging things into a coherent structure or system. You might spend a weekend organizing a closet, sorting items and finding proper places for them. Organizing also means coordinating people toward a purpose: {She's been organizing volunteers for the food drive}. In labor contexts, organizing specifically means building union membership: {workers organizing for better wages}.

Organs are parts of a living body that perform specific functions—the heart pumps blood, the lungs exchange gases, the liver filters toxins. By extension, an organ is any instrument serving a particular purpose: {a propaganda organ}, {the official organ of the Communist Party}. A pipe organ or electric organ is a keyboard instrument that produces sound through pipes or electronic circuits. To organize is to arrange parts into a functioning whole, like organs in a body.

An orgasm is the intense physical and emotional climax of sexual arousal, typically accompanied by rhythmic muscular contractions and a release of tension. The verb means to experience this climax: {She orgasmed quickly}. Figuratively, orgasm describes any peak of intense pleasure or excitement, though this usage sounds hyperbolic: {The crowd orgasmed over the announcement}.

Orgasms is the plural of orgasm—the peak of sexual arousal, marked by intense physical pleasure and involuntary muscular contractions. The word also serves as a verb: {She orgasms easily}, {He orgasmed twice}. Figuratively, orgasm describes any intense rush of excitement: {The crowd orgasmed when the band took the stage}.

Orgies is the plural of orgy, which denotes a gathering where multiple people engage in unrestrained sexual activity together. The word carries connotations of excess and abandon. By extension, orgy describes any bout of excessive indulgence: {an orgy of spending}, {an orgy of violence}. The ancient Greek and Roman religious rites honoring Dionysus and Bacchus, which reportedly featured drinking and sexual license, inform the word's historical associations with wild revelry.

An orgy is a gathering where multiple people engage in sexual activity together. The word extends to any excessive indulgence: {an orgy of spending}, {an orgy of violence}. In ancient contexts, orgies were secret rites involving frenzied worship, especially of Dionysus or Bacchus—hence the modern association with uninhibited excess.

To orient is to position or align something in relation to a reference point—originally, toward the east where the sun rises. Maps are oriented with north at the top. You orient yourself by figuring out where you are: {It took me a minute to orient myself in the unfamiliar neighborhood}. To orient someone is to familiarize them with a new situation: {The training program orients new employees}. Orient also means to direct toward a particular interest or goal: {a service-oriented business}, {career-oriented students}. (Capitalized Orient is a dated term for East Asia.)

Orientation is the direction something faces or the position of something relative to its surroundings: {The orientation of the house maximizes morning light}. More abstractly, it's a person's basic attitudes or inclinations—their bearings in the world. Sexual orientation refers to the pattern of romantic and sexual attraction: gay, straight, bisexual. An orientation is also an introductory program for newcomers: {freshman orientation}, {new employee orientation}. To get your orientation is to figure out where you are and which way you're headed.

Origami is the Japanese art of folding paper into decorative shapes—animals, flowers, geometric forms—without cutting or gluing. A single square of paper becomes a crane, a frog, a box. The word comes from Japanese for "folding paper." Beyond craft, origami principles appear in engineering and mathematics, from solar panel deployment to medical stents.

Origin is the point where something begins or comes from—the source of a river, the origin of a species, a word's origin. A person's origins are their background: {a woman of humble origins}. In anatomy, the origin of a muscle is its point of attachment. In mathematics, the origin is the point where coordinate axes intersect, typically designated (0,0).

Original connects to the idea of being first or primary. Something original exists from the beginning: {the original inhabitants}, {the original version}. An original idea or work is new and not derived from something else: {an original composition}, {highly original thinking}. The original of a copy is the first instance from which copies were made. A person described as an original is distinctively unconventional—one of a kind.

Originality is the quality of being new, fresh, or unlike anything that came before. An original idea hasn't been thought of by others; an original artwork doesn't imitate existing work. Originality is prized in creative fields but can be hard to verify—most "original" ideas have antecedents somewhere. {The proposal lacked originality}. {Her originality as a composer set her apart}.

Origins are the points from which things begin or arise—the sources, roots, or starting circumstances of something's existence. A disease may have {origins in contaminated water}. A person's origins are their ancestry, birthplace, or early background: {She never forgot her humble origins}. The word nearly always appears in plural form; the singular origin works for a single source, while origins suggests multiple contributing factors or a broader sense of background and heritage.

An ornament is a decorative object or detail that adds beauty rather than serving a practical function: {Christmas ornaments}, {architectural ornaments}. The word extends to anything that enhances or adorns: {She was an ornament to the profession}. To ornament something is to decorate it, typically with flourishes or embellishments: {The manuscript was ornamented with gold leaf}.

Ornaments are decorative objects that add visual interest without serving a practical function. Christmas tree ornaments hang from branches; architectural ornaments embellish buildings. The word extends to any embellishment: musical ornaments are flourishes like trills. To ornament something is to decorate it: {She ornamented the cake with sugar flowers}.

An orphan is a child whose parents have died. The term sometimes applies when only one parent has died, though this use is less common. Orphan extends metaphorically to anything abandoned or left without support: an orphan {project}, orphan {drugs} (pharmaceuticals for rare diseases that lack commercial backing). In publishing and typesetting, an orphan is a single line of text stranded at the bottom or top of a page.

An orphanage is an institution that houses and cares for children whose parents have died or are otherwise unable to care for them. The term evokes a particular era—orphanages were common through the mid-20th century but have largely been replaced by foster care systems in Western countries: {She grew up in an orphanage during the Depression}. The word still applies to such institutions elsewhere in the world.

Orphaned describes someone, especially a child, who has lost both parents to death. The word extends to anything abandoned or left without its natural support: an orphaned {project} no longer has a sponsor, orphaned {data} exists without connection to its source. In computing, an orphaned {file} or {process} has lost its parent reference. {She was orphaned at six and raised by her grandmother.}

Orphans are children whose parents have died. The word can apply when one parent dies, though it most often suggests both are gone. Extended uses describe anything abandoned or left without support: orphan {drugs} lack commercial interest, orphan {works} have no identifiable copyright holder. In typesetting, an orphan is a lone line stranded at the top or bottom of a page. To orphan is to make someone an orphan: {The war orphaned thousands of children}.

Orthodox means following established, traditional, or conventional beliefs and practices. In religion, it describes strict adherence to accepted doctrine: {orthodox interpretations of scripture}. More broadly, orthodox applies to any conventional or widely accepted approach: {orthodox economic theory}, {orthodox medical treatment}. The opposite is heterodox or unorthodox. (Capitalized Orthodox refers to specific religious traditions.)
