Orthodoxy is adherence to established or traditional beliefs, especially in religion. The orthodox position is the accepted, mainstream one—what most believers or authorities consider correct. The word often appears in contrast to heresy or heterodoxy: {She questioned the orthodoxy of her church}. More broadly, orthodoxy can mean any conventional wisdom or standard view: {economic orthodoxy}, {challenging the orthodoxy of her field}. An orthodoxy is a particular set of such accepted beliefs.

Oryoki is a formal style of meditative eating practiced in Zen Buddhist monasteries, using a nested set of bowls wrapped in cloth. The practice emphasizes mindfulness, gratitude, and minimal waste—practitioners eat in silence, receive only what they will consume, and clean their bowls with water they then drink. {The retreat included instruction in oryoki before meals.}

Ostracised is the British spelling of ostracized—excluded from a group or community, shunned socially. The word comes from ancient Athens, where citizens voted to banish someone by writing names on pottery shards (ostraka). Modern use is usually figurative: {She was ostracised by her former friends after the scandal}. The exclusion may be formal or informal, but the sense of collective rejection remains central.

Ostracism is exclusion from a group or community, whether formal or informal. Ancient Athens practiced literal ostracism—citizens voted to banish someone for ten years. The modern sense is social: {She faced ostracism after the scandal}. To be ostracized is to be shut out, ignored, treated as if you don't exist.

To ostracize someone is to exclude them from a group or from society. The word comes from ancient Athens, where citizens could vote to banish someone by writing their name on a potsherd (ostrakon). Today ostracism is social rather than official: {After the scandal, she was ostracized by her former friends}. The British spelling is ostracise.

Ostracized means excluded from a group or community, deliberately shut out from social participation. The word comes from the ancient Greek practice of voting to exile citizens by writing names on pottery shards. Someone ostracized isn't just ignored but actively rejected: {After the scandal, she was ostracized by her colleagues}. The verb ostracize and noun ostracism share this sense of formal or informal banishment.

An ostrich is a large flightless bird native to Africa—the largest living bird, with long legs built for running rather than wings for flying. The phrase {bury one's head in the sand} comes from the myth that ostriches hide this way when threatened, so {ostrich} or {ostrich-like} behavior means refusing to acknowledge obvious problems: {The committee took an ostrich approach to the budget crisis}.

Ostriches is the plural of ostrich, the large flightless bird native to Africa—the largest living bird species. The phrase {bury one's head in the sand} comes from the mistaken belief that ostriches hide this way when frightened, and means to ignore obvious dangers or unpleasant realities: {The committee buried their heads in the sand about the budget shortfall}.

Left out and leftover. While also a noun or pronoun, other is most often an adjective, where it suggests the idea of “more than one” because other designates the one remaining, not included, not chosen, not mentioned, or not present. It is often followed by a plural noun because singular nouns can be characterized with another. Other has also developed idiomatic meanings, such as every other (meaning alternate, as in every other week), and recent (as in I saw him the other day).

Othering is the act of treating people as fundamentally different or alien, typically to exclude them from a group or deny them equal status. It involves emphasizing distinctions—whether based on race, religion, nationality, or other characteristics—in ways that create an us-versus-them dynamic. {The politician's rhetoric relied heavily on othering immigrant communities.} The term appears frequently in sociology and cultural criticism to describe how dominant groups marginalize those they perceive as outsiders.

Otherwise introduces an alternative or contrast. It often signals what would happen if circumstances were different: {Hurry, otherwise we'll be late}. It can mean in other respects: {The coffee was cold but otherwise fine}. Or it indicates a different way: {She thought otherwise}. {Unless otherwise noted} is a common phrase meaning except where stated differently.

Otherworldly describes something that seems to belong to another realm—strange, ethereal, or supernatural in quality. An otherworldly {glow} suggests something not quite of this earth. The word applies to experiences, appearances, or atmospheres that feel detached from ordinary reality: {Her voice had an otherworldly beauty}. It can also describe someone so spiritually focused or dreamy they seem disconnected from practical concerns.

An otter is a semiaquatic mammal with a streamlined body, webbed feet, and dense waterproof fur, found in freshwater and coastal habitats. Otters are known for floating on their backs and using rocks to crack open shellfish. Sea otters live in kelp forests along Pacific coastlines; river otters inhabit streams and lakes. {We watched the otters playing in the water.}

Otters are semiaquatic mammals with sleek bodies, webbed feet, and dense waterproof fur. They're known for playful behavior—sliding down mudbanks, floating on their backs, using rocks to crack open shellfish. Sea otters live in coastal waters; river otters inhabit freshwater. {We watched the otters chase each other through the kelp.}

An ottoman is a cushioned footstool or low upholstered seat without a back or arms, often used in living rooms for resting feet or as extra seating. The furniture piece typically accompanies an armchair or sofa: {She put her feet up on the ottoman}. Some ottomans have hinged tops for storage. (Capitalized Ottoman refers to the Turkish empire or people.)
Ouch and ow are both ways of spelling the sound that people make to express the feeling of pain. People also sometimes say ouch to show that they understand someone else’s experience as painful.

Ought expresses obligation, duty, or strong expectation: {You ought to apologize}, {That ought to be enough}. It functions like should but carries slightly more moral weight. Ought typically requires "to" before the following verb, unlike most auxiliaries. In negative constructions, {ought not} sounds formal; {shouldn't} is more common in speech.

An ounce is a unit of weight equal to one-sixteenth of a pound, or about 28 grams. In measuring liquids, a fluid ounce is about 30 milliliters. Ounce often appears in figurative expressions emphasizing small quantities: {She doesn't have an ounce of common sense}. If you give something {every ounce} of your strength or energy, you give it everything you have. The ounce is also a rare name for the snow leopard.

Ounces is the plural of ounce, a unit of weight equal to one-sixteenth of a pound, or about 28 grams. A fluid ounce measures volume rather than weight—one-sixteenth of a pint in the US. Figuratively, ounce suggests a small amount: {He doesn't have an ounce of sense}. {She put every ounce of energy into the project}.

An ouroboros is an ancient symbol depicting a serpent or dragon eating its own tail, forming a circle. It represents cyclicality, eternal return, or self-referential systems—things that perpetually consume and regenerate themselves. The image appears across cultures from ancient Egypt to alchemy to modern psychology. Figuratively, anything that feeds on itself or creates an endless loop: {The committee's review process had become an ouroboros, generating more questions than it answered}. Also spelled uroboros.

Ousted is the past tense of oust, meaning forcibly removed from a position or place. Someone ousted from power has been expelled, typically by others acting collectively or through formal process: {The board ousted the CEO after the scandal}. The word implies unwilling departure—you don't oust someone who leaves voluntarily.

Whether as adverb, preposition, or adjective, out is almost always used as the opposite of in. Like in, out has uses in which the core meaning is not present: Look out for potholes in the road, or We were out $50 because of all the extra fees. The connection of out with the idea of outside and public has given rise to the adjective and verb uses of the word: someone who is out makes no secret about their affiliation or identity, and when you out someone, you reveal something formerly concealed about them.

An outage is an instance of something being not available or used up. The most common kind of outage is a power outage, that is, a loss of electrical power. Most other kinds of outage involve the sudden lack of something that is normally provided at all times, such as water, gas, or Internet or GPS service.

Outback refers to remote, sparsely populated rural areas, especially the arid interior regions of Australia. The term evokes vast, dry landscapes far from cities and coastal settlements: {They drove for days through the outback}. By extension, any isolated backcountry can be called outback: {the Nevada outback}. (Capitalized Outback often refers specifically to Australia's interior or the restaurant chain.)

An outbreak is a sudden occurrence or eruption of something undesirable—disease, violence, or conflict. The word implies rapid spread from an origin point: {an outbreak of cholera}, {an outbreak of fighting along the border}. Outbreak emphasizes the initial emergence; what follows might be called an epidemic or a war.

An outburst is a sudden release of strong emotion or energy. Someone prone to angry outbursts explodes with little warning: {His outburst shocked everyone in the meeting}. The word applies to any abrupt expression—an outburst of laughter, of applause, of violence. Natural phenomena can have outbursts too: {an outburst of solar activity}.

Outbursts are sudden, uncontrolled expressions of emotion or activity. An outburst of {anger}, an outburst of {laughter}, an outburst of {applause}. The word usually implies something brief and explosive rather than sustained—a momentary loss of composure or a spontaneous eruption: {His outburst shocked everyone in the meeting}.

An outcast is someone rejected or excluded by a group or society. The word suggests being cast out—expelled from belonging: {He lived as an outcast after the scandal}. As an adjective, it describes this state of rejection: {outcast tribes}, {an outcast existence}. The term often carries sympathy for the excluded rather than judgment.

Outcasts are people who have been rejected or excluded from a group or community. The word suggests both the act of being cast out and the resulting social position—someone living on the margins, denied belonging. It can describe literal exile or metaphorical alienation: {The rebels became outcasts, unwelcome in their homeland}. The term often carries sympathy for those rejected.

An outcome is what results from an action, process, or situation—the end state after events have played out. The word emphasizes finality: {We're still waiting to learn the outcome of the election}. In statistics and probability, an outcome is any possible result of an experiment or event. Unlike consequence, outcome is neutral—it doesn't imply good or bad.

An outcry is a loud shout or cry, especially one of distress, protest, or disapproval. More commonly, it refers to a strong public expression of anger or opposition: {The policy sparked an outcry from civil rights groups}. An outcry suggests widespread and vocal reaction, not just individual complaint.

Outdated means no longer current or useful, superseded by something newer: {outdated technology}, {outdated ideas about gender roles}. The word implies that time has passed something by—what once worked or was acceptable no longer is. {The guidebook was so outdated that half the restaurants had closed.}

To outdo is to surpass or exceed someone else's performance or achievement: {She always tries to outdo her older sister}. The word often implies competitive one-upmanship. To {outdo yourself} is to perform better than you ever have before, sometimes said sarcastically when someone makes an exceptional blunder.

Outdoor describes things situated, done, or used outside rather than inside a building: {outdoor furniture}, {outdoor activities}, {the outdoor life}. It contrasts with indoor. An outdoors person enjoys nature and open-air pursuits. As a noun or adverb, the form is outdoors: {Let's eat outdoors}, {the great outdoors}.

Outdoors refers to the open air, outside of buildings or enclosed spaces: {The kids played outdoors all afternoon}. As a noun with the definite article, {the outdoors} suggests nature or wilderness as a realm of activity: {She loves the outdoors}. The adjective outdoor describes things suited for or occurring outside: {outdoor furniture}, {outdoor concert}.

An outdoorsman is a man who spends considerable time in wilderness or rural settings—hunting, fishing, camping, hiking. The term suggests competence and comfort in nature: {He was a true outdoorsman who could track deer and build shelter from nothing}. The gender-neutral outdoorsperson exists but sounds awkward; outdoors enthusiast serves better.

Outdoorsy describes someone who enjoys outdoor activities—hiking, camping, fishing, and the like. The word is informal and often appears in personal ads or dating profiles: {I'm looking for someone outdoorsy who loves nature}. It can also describe places or things with a rugged, nature-oriented feel: {The cabin had an outdoorsy vibe}.

Outed is the past tense of out, meaning to publicly reveal someone's secret—most commonly their homosexuality. A closeted person who is outed has their sexual orientation disclosed without consent: {He was outed by a tabloid reporter}. The term extends to exposing other concealed identities or affiliations: {She was outed as a former CIA operative}.

Outer describes what is farther from the center or interior: the outer {layer}, the outer {edge}, outer {space}. It contrasts with inner—the outer surface versus the inner core. Outer can suggest what's visible or peripheral rather than essential: {Her outer calm hid inner turmoil}. In compounds: {outerwear}, {outer limits}.

An outfit is a set of clothes worn together, chosen to work as a unit: {I love that outfit}. The word extends to any coordinated set of equipment or supplies: {a camping outfit}, {a first-aid outfit}. An outfit can also be a group of people working together, especially a business or military unit: {She joined a small consulting outfit}. To outfit someone is to equip them with what they need: {We outfitted the expedition with supplies}.

Outfits are sets of clothes worn together, chosen to work as a unit: {She planned her outfits for the trip}. The word also refers to groups organized for a common purpose—a business, military unit, or crew: {He worked for a small publishing outfit in Chicago}. As a verb form, outfits means to equip or supply: {The store outfits hikers for backcountry expeditions}.

Outflanked means maneuvered around or bypassed, originally a military term for attacking an enemy's side or rear rather than meeting them head-on. The word now applies broadly to being strategically circumvented: {The company was outflanked by competitors who anticipated the market shift}. To be outflanked is to find your position undermined by someone who found a way around your defenses.

To outfox is to defeat someone through superior cunning or cleverness—to outsmart them as a fox might evade hunters. The word implies winning not through force or resources but through wit: {She outfoxed her competitors by anticipating their moves}. {He thought he could outfox the IRS, but they caught up with him eventually}.

Outgoing describes movement away from a point of origin: the outgoing {tide}, outgoing {mail}, the outgoing {president} whose term is ending. Applied to personality, outgoing means friendly, sociable, and comfortable initiating conversation with strangers—the opposite of shy or reserved: {She's outgoing enough to talk to anyone at a party}.

To outgrow something is to grow too large or mature for it. Children outgrow their clothes and shoes. People outgrow habits, friendships, or interests that no longer fit who they've become: {She outgrew her teenage insecurities}. One thing can outgrow another by growing faster: {The city's population outgrew its infrastructure}.

Outgrown is the past participle of outgrow. To outgrow something is to grow too large or mature for it. Children outgrow their clothes, their toys, their childhood fears. Adults outgrow relationships, habits, or beliefs that no longer fit: {She had outgrown her hometown}. One plant outgrows another by growing faster or larger.

Outgunned means outmatched in firepower or resources. Literally, it describes having fewer or inferior weapons than an opponent: {The patrol was outgunned by insurgents with heavier artillery}. Figuratively, it extends to any situation where one side lacks the means to compete effectively: {Our legal team was completely outgunned by their army of corporate lawyers}.

An outhouse is a small structure housing a toilet, typically built over a pit and located away from the main dwelling. Before indoor plumbing became standard, outhouses were the primary form of sanitation in rural areas. The term now evokes rustic or primitive conditions: {The cabin had no running water—just an outhouse out back}.

Outhouses are outdoor toilets, typically small wooden structures built over a pit. Before indoor plumbing became standard, the outhouse was a fixture of rural life: {The old farmhouse still had an outhouse out back}. The word can also mean any outbuilding—a shed, barn, or storage structure separate from the main house—though the toilet sense now dominates.

An outing is a short trip or excursion, typically for pleasure: {a family outing to the beach}, {a company outing}. The word also means the public exposure of someone's private identity, especially revealing that someone is gay without their consent: {The magazine was criticized for the outing of several politicians}. To out someone is to expose them this way.

Outings is the plural of outing—a short trip or excursion, typically for pleasure: {family outings to the beach}, {a company outing}. An outing can also mean publicly revealing someone's secret, especially their sexual orientation without consent: {The journalist faced criticism for the outing of several politicians}.

Outlandish describes something strikingly bizarre, unconventional, or far removed from the ordinary. The word suggests excess that goes beyond merely unusual: {outlandish costumes}, {outlandish claims}, {outlandish behavior}. What strikes one person as outlandish may simply be unfamiliar—the word often reveals the speaker's sense of normalcy as much as the thing being described.

To outlast is to endure longer than something else—to remain when others have faded, broken, or given up. {Their marriage outlasted all predictions}. {These boots will outlast anything else in your closet}. The word implies survival through comparison: you outlast competitors, storms, or difficult circumstances by simply persisting beyond them.

An outlaw is someone who operates outside the law—originally a person stripped of legal protection who could be killed without consequence, now simply a criminal or fugitive. The word carries romantic overtones from Western mythology: outlaws like Jesse James became folk heroes. As a verb, to outlaw something is to ban it: {The treaty outlawed chemical weapons}. As an adjective, outlaw describes things operating illegally or unconventionally: an {outlaw country} singer, an {outlaw motorcycle gang}.

Outlawed means banned or prohibited by law or authority. An outlawed {substance} is illegal to possess or sell. Outlawed {practices} have been officially forbidden. Historically, to be outlawed was to be declared outside the protection of the law—an outlaw could be killed or robbed without legal consequence. Now the term usually just means forbidden: {The treaty outlawed chemical weapons}.

Outlaws are people who live outside the law—originally those denied legal protection, now typically criminals or fugitives: {a band of outlaws terrorizing the frontier}. The word evokes romanticized rebels like Robin Hood or Wild West bandits. To outlaw something is to make it illegal: {The city outlawed smoking in parks}. An outlawed practice is banned or prohibited.

An outlet is an opening through which something can escape or be released: {an outlet for water drainage}, {an outlet for creative energy}. In American English, an electrical outlet is a wall socket where you plug things in. An outlet also means a store selling goods at reduced prices, typically from a manufacturer: {outlet mall}, {factory outlet}. A media outlet is a channel for news or information: {The story was picked up by several news outlets}.

Outlets are places where something exits or is released. An electrical outlet provides access to power. A retail outlet sells goods, often at reduced prices: {factory outlet}, {outlet mall}. A media outlet distributes news or entertainment. Figuratively, an outlet is a means of expression or release: {Exercise is my outlet for stress}. Rivers have outlets where they empty into larger bodies of water.

An outlier is something that lies outside the main body or group. In statistics, it's a data point that falls far from the cluster of other values: {The $2 million home was an outlier in a neighborhood of modest houses}. More broadly, an outlier is anyone or anything markedly different from the norm—an exceptional case, an anomaly, a person who doesn't fit the pattern: {She was an outlier among her peers, the only one who hadn't gone to college}.

Outliers are data points or cases that fall far outside the normal range. In statistics, an outlier is a value so distant from others in a dataset that it may skew results or suggest measurement error. The term extends to people or things that don't fit patterns: {She was an outlier among her conservative colleagues}. Malcolm Gladwell's book popularized the word for exceptional achievers whose success defies typical explanations.

An outline is the line marking the outer edge or boundary of something: {the outline of the mountains against the sky}. It also means a general plan or summary showing main points without detail: {an outline of the chapter}, {a rough outline of our strategy}. To outline is to draw such a boundary or to describe something in general terms: {She outlined the proposal in broad strokes}.

Outlines are lines marking the outer edges of something, showing its shape without interior detail: {She drew the outlines of the mountains against the sky}. An outline is also a summary or plan showing main points without elaboration: {an outline of the proposal}, {a course outline}. To outline is to sketch boundaries or summarize key elements: {He outlined his strategy for the board}.

To outlive someone or something is to live longer than they do: {She outlived her husband by twenty years}. The word extends beyond biological life—ideas, institutions, and objects can outlive their usefulness or relevance: {The policy has outlived its purpose}. To outlive something is often to survive it: {He outlived three heart attacks}.

Outlook is a view of what lies ahead—either literally or figuratively. A room with a pleasant outlook overlooks something worth seeing. More often, outlook means a perspective on the future: {The economic outlook remains uncertain}, {She has a positive outlook on life}. Someone's outlook is also their general attitude or way of seeing things: {His outlook changed after the accident}. (Capitalized Outlook is Microsoft's email software.)

To outmaneuver is to gain advantage over an opponent through superior strategy or positioning. The word comes from military contexts—troops outmaneuvering enemy forces—but applies broadly to any competitive situation: {She outmaneuvered her rivals for the promotion}, {The smaller company outmaneuvered the industry giant}. Also spelled outmanoeuvre in British English.

Outmatched means surpassed or defeated by a superior opponent or force. Someone outmatched faces competition they cannot overcome: {The young boxer was clearly outmatched by the veteran champion}. The word implies an imbalance—not just losing, but being overmatched from the start: {Outgunned and outmatched, the rebels retreated}.

To outnumber is to exceed in quantity: {The protesters outnumbered the police three to one}. The word typically appears in contexts of competition or conflict, where numerical advantage matters: {We were badly outnumbered but held our ground}.

Outnumbered describes being faced with superior numbers—having fewer people or forces than the opposing side. A small army can be outnumbered by a larger one; a lone dissenter may feel outnumbered in a room full of agreement. {We were outnumbered three to one}. The word often implies disadvantage but can also set up narratives of heroic resistance against the odds.

Outplayed means defeated through superior skill or strategy. In sports and games, to outplay an opponent is to perform better than them throughout the contest: {We were completely outplayed in the second half}. The term extends to any competitive situation where one side demonstrates clear dominance: {The defense outplayed the prosecution at every turn}.

An outpost is a military position stationed at a distance from the main force, typically for observation or defense: {a remote outpost near the border}. The term extends to any distant branch or settlement far from a center of activity: {a trading outpost}, {an outpost of civilization in the wilderness}. Figuratively, anything representing a presence in unfamiliar territory: {The café was an outpost of hipster culture in the suburbs}.

Outposts are remote stations or settlements at a distance from the main body they serve. A military outpost monitors enemy activity far from headquarters. Frontier outposts marked the edge of settled territory. The word extends to any isolated position: {The cafe was an outpost of civilization in the wilderness}. An outpost of a larger organization operates in distant or unfamiliar territory.

Output is what comes out of a process, system, or effort—the product or result. A factory's output is what it produces; a writer's output is their body of work. In computing, output is data sent from a program or device: {The printer output was garbled}. As a verb, to output is to produce or generate: {The solar panel outputs 300 watts}. Output contrasts with input.

Outrage is intense anger or indignation provoked by something perceived as unjust, offensive, or morally wrong: {The verdict sparked public outrage}. As a verb, to outrage is to provoke such feelings: {His comments outraged the community}. An outrage is also the act itself—a shocking offense or violation: {The massacre was an outrage against humanity}. Outrageous describes things that provoke outrage, though it often softens to mean merely extreme or absurd: {outrageous prices}, {an outrageous outfit}.

Outraged means feeling or expressing intense anger, shock, or indignation—especially at something perceived as unjust or offensive. The word carries moral weight: you're outraged by cruelty, corruption, or violation of standards, not by minor annoyances. {Voters were outraged by the scandal}. {She gave him an outraged look when he suggested she'd lied}.

Outrageous describes something that exceeds acceptable bounds—shocking, offensive, or extreme beyond what's reasonable. An outrageous {insult} crosses lines of decency. Outrageous {prices} are exorbitantly high. The word can also express admiration for bold excess: {Her outfit was absolutely outrageous}. What's outrageous provokes outrage, or at least raised eyebrows.

Outreach is the effort to extend services or assistance beyond usual boundaries, especially to underserved populations: {community outreach}, {voter outreach}. Organizations conduct outreach to connect with people who might not otherwise be reached: {The clinic's outreach program provides care to homeless residents}. As a verb, outreach means to surpass in reaching: {Her influence outreached his}.

An outro is the closing section of a song, broadcast, or video—the opposite of an intro. In music, the outro often features a fade-out or a final instrumental passage that signals the end. In podcasts and YouTube videos, the outro typically includes closing remarks, credits, or calls to action like subscribing. {The outro was just the chorus repeating until it faded out.}

To outrun is to run faster or farther than someone or something else: {She easily outran her pursuers}. The meaning extends beyond literal running to any kind of escape or exceeding: {The company's growth outran its infrastructure}. Demand can outrun supply; expenses can outrun income. If something outruns your ability to handle it, it has surpassed your capacity.

Outs is primarily a baseball term for the number of times batters or runners have been retired: {two outs in the ninth inning}. More broadly, outs are ways of escaping a situation: {He's looking for outs on this contract}. The phrase {on the outs} means estranged or in disfavor: {She's been on the outs with her family since the argument}.

To outshine is to shine brighter than something else, or more commonly, to surpass in excellence or achievement: {Her performance outshone everyone else's}. The word implies comparison—you don't outshine in isolation, but against others. {The younger sister consistently outshone her siblings academically.}

Outside gained use as a preposition after it was already established as a noun, adjective, and adverb; perhaps because of that, it is often followed by of with no change in meaning. Its core sense is movement to or position on the outer side of something. From this it has acquired other meanings, such as beyond the scope of: Those people operate outside the law.

An outsider is someone who doesn't belong to a particular group—whether by circumstance, choice, or exclusion. The term can be neutral {(an outsider's perspective on the dispute)} or carry connotations of rejection {(She always felt like an outsider at school)}. In competitions, an outsider is a contestant considered unlikely to win: {The outsider came from behind to take the race}.

Outsiders are people who don't belong to a particular group, organization, or community. The term implies exclusion—whether by choice or circumstance: {As outsiders, we weren't privy to their internal disputes}. Someone can be an outsider to a profession, a social circle, or an entire culture. The word often carries connotations of fresh perspective or alienation, depending on context: {The company brought in outsiders to shake things up}.

Outskirts refers to the outer edges or peripheral areas of a town, city, or other defined region—the parts farthest from the center. The word appears almost exclusively in the plural and typically follows "on the": {They bought a house on the outskirts of town}. Outskirts suggests a transitional zone where urban development thins out, often carrying connotations of being removed from the action or main activity of a place.

To outsmart someone is to defeat them through cleverness rather than force—finding a way around their defenses or anticipating their moves: {She outsmarted the security system}. The word implies a contest of wits where cunning beats strength or resources: {The smaller company outsmarted its competitors by targeting niche markets}.

Outsmarted is the past tense of outsmart—to defeat someone by being cleverer than they are. The word implies winning through superior thinking rather than force or luck: {She outsmarted the con artist at his own game}. Being outsmarted often carries a sting of humiliation, suggesting you were bested by someone who saw further ahead than you did.

Outsource means to contract work to an external provider rather than handling it internally. A company might outsource its customer service to a call center or outsource manufacturing to overseas factories. The practice became widespread as businesses sought to reduce costs: {We outsource our IT support to a firm in India}. The word often carries connotations of job displacement or declining quality.

Outsourced describes work or services contracted to an external company rather than handled internally. A business might have outsourced its customer service to a call center abroad, or outsourced payroll to a specialist firm. The term often carries connotations of cost-cutting and, when jobs move overseas, displaced workers: {My position was outsourced to India}.

Outsourcing is the practice of hiring outside contractors or foreign companies to perform work that could be done internally. Businesses outsource to reduce costs, access specialized skills, or focus on core operations: {The company outsourced its customer service to a call center in the Philippines}. The term often carries negative connotations when jobs move overseas, becoming shorthand for domestic job loss.

Outspoken describes someone who expresses opinions freely and directly, even when those opinions might be unwelcome or controversial: {She's been outspoken about corruption in the department}. The word implies boldness rather than tactlessness—an outspoken critic speaks up where others stay silent. {He's outspoken but fair.}

Outstanding means exceptionally good or remarkable: {an outstanding performance}, {outstanding academic achievement}. It also means not yet resolved or paid: {outstanding debts}, {outstanding warrants}. These senses diverge—one praises excellence, the other notes incompleteness. Context usually makes clear which is meant: {She received an outstanding evaluation} versus {The balance outstanding is $500}.

An outtake is footage or recorded material that doesn't make it into the final version of a film, television show, or album. Outtakes may result from mistakes, technical problems, or creative decisions. Collections of outtakes—especially bloopers showing actors breaking character or flubbing lines—are often released as bonus material: {The DVD includes twenty minutes of outtakes}.

Outtakes are portions of a recording—film, video, or audio—that don't make it into the final version. They're often mistakes, flubbed lines, or technical failures: {The DVD includes a reel of outtakes}. Outtakes from comedies frequently show actors breaking character or laughing, released as bonus content. The word sometimes extends metaphorically to any discarded material from a creative project.

Outward means directed toward the outside or external surface. An outward {journey} moves away from a starting point. Outward {appearances} are what others can observe, as opposed to inner reality: {He maintained an outward calm despite his panic}. The adverb form—outward or outwards—describes motion away from a center: {The ripples spread outward}.

To outwit someone is to defeat them through cleverness rather than force—to be smarter or more cunning than an opponent. The word implies a contest of minds where quick thinking prevails: {The fox outwitted the hounds}. You can outwit a rival, a security system, or your own bad habits.

Outwitted is the past tense of outwit, meaning to defeat someone through cleverness or cunning rather than force. The word implies a contest of minds where superior strategy prevails: {She outwitted the detective by planting false evidence}. To be outwitted often carries a note of humiliation—you weren't just beaten, you were outsmarted.

Oval describes a shape that is elongated and rounded, like an egg or an ellipse—a circle stretched along one axis. An oval {face}, an oval {mirror}, an oval {track}. As a noun, it names this shape or something having it: {Draw an oval}. The Oval Office is the U.S. president's formal workspace in the White House, often used as shorthand for the presidency itself. (Capitalized Oval typically appears in proper names like Oval Office.)

Ovaries are the pair of reproductive organs in females that produce eggs and hormones. In humans and other mammals, the ovaries release eggs during ovulation and secrete estrogen and progesterone. In flowering plants, the ovary is the part of the pistil containing seeds. {Her ovaries showed multiple follicles on the ultrasound.}

An ovation is enthusiastic applause and cheering from an audience. A standing ovation—when the audience rises to its feet—signals exceptional appreciation: {The performance received a standing ovation}. The word sometimes appears in phrases like {give someone an ovation}, but standing ovation dominates modern usage.

An oven is an enclosed chamber for heating, baking, or drying. Kitchen ovens cook food; industrial ovens cure materials or fire ceramics. A {Dutch oven} is a heavy pot with a lid. Something {oven-ready} requires no preparation before cooking. A room that's unbearably hot is {like an oven}.

As prepositions go, over is busier than most due to its broad range of meanings. When space is the subject, over can mean across or above, or both: a picture over the fireplace, carpets over the floors. In relation to time, over conveys duration: We got to know each other over a period of weeks. Figurative meanings of over also vary widely: We talked about it over dinner. I would take green over pink. They paid over a million dollars for their house. Over can also function as an adverb and an adjective, again with myriad meanings.

An overachiever is someone who accomplishes more than expected, often through exceptional effort or ambition. The term can be admiring—{She's a real overachiever, graduated top of her class while working two jobs}—but frequently carries a hint of criticism, suggesting someone driven by anxiety or unhealthy perfectionism rather than genuine passion: {He's such an overachiever, always staying late to impress the boss}.

Overachievers are people who accomplish more than expected, often exceeding standards that would satisfy most others. The term carries mixed connotations: it can express admiration for exceptional performance or suggest someone who works excessively hard, possibly at the expense of balance or wellbeing. {The overachievers in class always asked for extra credit.} In competitive environments like schools and workplaces, overachievers may be celebrated or resented depending on how their success affects others.

Overachieving means performing beyond what's expected or required—exceeding standards rather than merely meeting them. The term often carries a hint of criticism, suggesting excessive effort or striving: {She's such an overachiever}. Someone called an overachiever may be seen as anxious about success or unable to relax. The word can also describe genuine excellence: {The team has been overachieving all season}.

Overall describes something considered as a whole, taking everything into account: {The overall effect was stunning}, {What's your overall impression?} As an adverb, it means generally or in total: {Overall, I think it went well}. Overalls are loose-fitting work garments with a bib and shoulder straps, worn over other clothes for protection.

Overalls are loose-fitting trousers with a bib front held up by shoulder straps, typically worn as protective workwear over regular clothes. In American usage, overalls are the bib-and-strap garment farmers and mechanics wear: {He wiped his hands on his overalls}. In British usage, overalls often means any protective outer garment, including what Americans call a jumpsuit or coveralls.

To overanalyze is to examine something so thoroughly that you miss the point or create problems that weren't there. Someone who overanalyzes a casual remark reads too much into it. Someone who overanalyzes a decision considers so many factors they can't act: {Stop overanalyzing and just pick a restaurant}. The word implies that analysis, usually valuable, has become counterproductive.

Overanalyzing is thinking about something more than necessary or productive, often to the point of paralysis or anxiety. Where ordinary analysis seeks clarity, overanalyzing finds new complications: {Stop overanalyzing the text message—just reply}. The habit tends toward second-guessing decisions already made or reading meaning into insignificant details.

Overbearing describes someone who dominates others through force of personality—pushy, arrogant, and unwilling to consider other viewpoints. An overbearing {boss} micromanages everything. An overbearing {parent} controls every aspect of a child's life. The word suggests someone whose presence feels oppressive, leaving little room for others to breathe or assert themselves.

Overblown means exaggerated or inflated beyond what's warranted. An overblown {reaction} is disproportionate to its cause. Overblown {rhetoric} uses more force than the subject deserves. {The controversy was overblown}. The word can also describe flowers past their prime, petals blown fully open and beginning to fade.

Overboard means over the side of a boat or ship into the water: {The storm swept three sailors overboard}. Figuratively, to go overboard is to be excessive or extreme—to do too much of something: {She went overboard with the decorations}. To throw something overboard is to abandon or discard it: {They threw caution overboard}.

Overcame is the past tense of overcome. To overcome something is to succeed in dealing with or controlling it, especially a problem, obstacle, or negative feeling. {She overcame her fear of public speaking.} {The team overcame a ten-point deficit to win.} It can also mean to overpower or overwhelm someone, as when a person is overcome by emotion or fumes.

Overcast describes a sky completely covered by clouds, with no blue visible: {The day was gray and overcast}. The word also applies to a type of stitching that wraps thread over a fabric edge to prevent fraying. As a verb in sewing, to overcast is to sew such stitches.

An overcoat is a long, heavy coat worn over other clothing for warmth, typically reaching below the knee. The word emphasizes its function—it goes over everything else: {He buttoned his overcoat against the wind}. Overcoats are associated with formal or professional dress, distinguished from casual outerwear like parkas or jackets.

Overcome means to succeed against opposition or difficulty. You overcome {obstacles}, {fears}, {challenges}, or {adversity}. The word suggests struggle followed by victory: {She overcame her shyness to become a public speaker}. To be overcome by emotion, heat, or fumes is to be overwhelmed or rendered helpless: {He was overcome with grief}. {Overcome} alone often implies prevailing: {We shall overcome}.

Overcoming is the act of prevailing over obstacles, difficulties, or opposition. The word carries connotations of struggle followed by success: {overcoming adversity}, {overcoming fear}, {overcoming addiction}. It implies effort and persistence rather than easy victory. What's overcome is typically something that initially seemed formidable or resistant to change.

Overcompensation is doing too much to make up for a perceived weakness or deficiency. Someone short might overcompensate by acting aggressively dominant. A guilty parent might overcompensate with lavish gifts. The word often carries a critical edge, suggesting the effort is excessive or misdirected: {His sports car feels like overcompensation for something}. In psychology, overcompensation describes exaggerated behaviors masking insecurity.

Overconfidence is excessive or unwarranted belief in one's own abilities, judgment, or chances of success. It often leads to poor decisions, inadequate preparation, or dismissal of genuine risks: {His overconfidence cost him the match}. The term implies a gap between perceived and actual competence—someone displaying overconfidence typically doesn't recognize their own limitations. In psychology and economics, overconfidence is studied as a cognitive bias that affects everything from investment decisions to medical diagnoses.

Overcooked describes food that has been cooked too long, resulting in undesirable texture or taste—dry meat, mushy vegetables, rubbery eggs. Figuratively, something overcooked has been overdone or labored excessively: {The joke was overcooked and fell flat}. {an overcooked metaphor}.

Overcrowded describes a space with too many people or things in it for comfort, safety, or function. An overcrowded {train} has no room to move; overcrowded {prisons} strain resources and breed unrest. The word implies not just fullness but excess—more than a space was designed to hold: {The lifeboat was dangerously overcrowded}.

Overcrowding is the condition of having too many people or things in a space. The term implies strain on resources or comfort: {prison overcrowding}, {overcrowding in schools}. A place can be crowded without being overcrowded—the prefix signals excess beyond acceptable limits.

To overdo something is to do it to excess—too much, too long, or too intensely. You can overdo exercise, overdo the praise, or overdo the garlic. {Don't overdo it at the gym your first week}. Overdone food has been cooked too long: {The steak was overdone}. Overdone acting or decoration is excessive to the point of seeming false or gaudy.

Overdone means taken too far. Food that is overdone has been cooked too long: {The steak was overdone and tough}. Behavior or style that is overdone is excessive or exaggerated: {The apology felt overdone}, {Her makeup was a bit overdone}. The word suggests something has crossed from appropriate to excessive—whether heat applied to meat or effort applied to performance.

An overdose is a dangerous or lethal quantity of a drug or medication—more than the body can safely process. The term usually implies harm: {She was rushed to the hospital after an overdose}. As a verb, to overdose is to take such an amount: {He overdosed on painkillers}. Figuratively, overdose describes excess of anything: {I've overdosed on Christmas music}.

An overdraft is a withdrawal from a bank account that exceeds the available balance, or the amount by which such a withdrawal exceeds the balance. Banks may cover overdrafts as a service, charging fees for the privilege: {I got hit with a $35 overdraft fee}. Overdraft protection links accounts to prevent declined transactions. In British usage, an overdraft can also be a prearranged credit line: {I'm living on my overdraft until payday}.

Overdressed means wearing clothes too formal or elaborate for the occasion. Someone in a tuxedo at a backyard barbecue is overdressed. The word implies a mismatch between attire and setting: {I felt overdressed in my suit when everyone else wore jeans}. The opposite is underdressed.

Overdrive is a gear in a vehicle that allows the engine to run at lower revolutions while maintaining high speed, reducing fuel consumption and engine wear. The term extends to any state of heightened activity or maximum effort: {The campaign went into overdrive in the final weeks}. In audio, overdrive refers to a distortion effect produced when an amplifier is pushed beyond its clean capacity, creating the crunchy tone prized in rock guitar.

Overdue means past the expected or required time. A library book becomes overdue when not returned by its due date. A payment is overdue when it should have been made already. The word extends to anything that should have happened sooner: {This conversation is long overdue}. A pregnant woman past her due date is also overdue.

Overeating is eating more than your body needs or more than is healthy. It can be occasional—{I always overeat at Thanksgiving}—or habitual, potentially leading to weight gain and health problems. The term implies excess rather than simply eating a lot: a marathon runner loading up on carbohydrates isn't overeating, but someone stress-eating a whole pizza might be.

Overexposure is too much exposure to something harmful or unwanted. In photography, overexposure means too much light reached the film or sensor, resulting in a washed-out image. Medically, overexposure to sun causes burns; overexposure to radiation causes illness. In media contexts, overexposure describes excessive public visibility that breeds fatigue or contempt: {The constant coverage led to overexposure, and audiences lost interest}.

Overflow is excess that spills beyond capacity. A river overflows its banks; a bathtub overflows when left running. The noun names both the excess itself and a channel for it: {a drain overflow}. Figuratively, emotions or crowds overflow: {The stadium was overflowing with fans}. In computing, overflow occurs when a calculation exceeds the maximum value a system can store.

Overflowing describes something so full that its contents spill over the edges: {an overflowing bathtub}, {overflowing trash cans}. The word extends readily to abundance of any kind: {overflowing with gratitude}, {a heart overflowing with joy}. An overflowing crowd exceeds the capacity of a space: {The concert hall was overflowing}.

Overgrown describes something that has grown excessively or beyond intended bounds. An overgrown {garden} is choked with weeds; an overgrown {path} has become impassable with vegetation. The word also characterizes someone or something as larger or more developed than expected while retaining immature qualities: {He's just an overgrown child}. {The overgrown lot hadn't been mowed in years.}

Overgrowth is excessive or uncontrolled growth. Vegetation that has overgrown a space is overgrowth: {The path was hidden by overgrowth}. In medicine, overgrowth describes abnormal tissue proliferation: {bacterial overgrowth}, {bone overgrowth}. The word emphasizes growth beyond normal or desired limits.

An overhang is a part that extends or juts out beyond what's below it: {the overhang of the roof}, {a rocky overhang sheltered us from the rain}. In business and finance, an overhang refers to an excess or surplus that weighs on a market—unsold inventory, pending stock options, or accumulated debt that depresses prices or limits future action. To overhang is to extend beyond or loom over: {Branches overhang the path}.

To overhaul something is to examine it thoroughly and make necessary repairs or improvements. Mechanics overhaul engines, taking them apart to fix worn components. The noun refers to this process: {The car needs a complete overhaul}. By extension, overhaul applies to systems and institutions: {an overhaul of the tax code}. In a separate sense, to overhaul is to overtake: {The cruiser overhauled the fleeing vessel}.

Overhauling is thoroughly examining and repairing something—taking it apart to fix what's wrong and restore it to working order: {The mechanic is overhauling the engine}. The word extends to comprehensive revision of systems or processes: {Congress is overhauling the tax code}. In racing or pursuit, overhauling means catching up to and passing: {The lead boat was overhauled in the final stretch}.

Overhead refers to what is above your head or above a reference point: {overhead lights}, {overhead compartments on a plane}. In business, overhead means the ongoing costs of running an operation—rent, utilities, salaries—that aren't tied to producing specific goods: {Our overhead is killing us}. As an adverb: {A plane flew overhead}. An overhead is also a transparency displayed on a projector, or the projector itself.

To overhear is to hear something not intended for you—typically a conversation between others: {I overheard them talking about the layoffs}. The word implies accidental listening rather than deliberate eavesdropping, though the line blurs. What's overheard often shouldn't have been: {She overheard her name and stopped to listen}.

Overheard is the past tense of overhear—to hear something not intended for you, whether by accident or design. You might overhear a conversation through thin walls or overhear your name mentioned at a party: {I overheard them talking about the layoffs}. The word implies the speaker didn't know they were being listened to.

Overhearing is hearing something not meant for you—a conversation, remark, or piece of information you weren't supposed to catch: {I couldn't help overhearing your argument}. Unlike eavesdropping, overhearing is typically accidental rather than intentional. The word often introduces information learned this way: {Overhearing their plans, she decided to act}.

To overheat is to become too hot—hot enough to cause damage or malfunction. Engines overheat when cooling systems fail. People overheat in extreme temperatures. Economies overheat when growth is unsustainably rapid, risking inflation: {The Fed raised rates to cool an overheating economy}. The noun overheating describes the condition itself.

Overheating is becoming too hot, whether literally or figuratively. An engine overheats when its cooling system fails. An economy overheats when rapid growth triggers inflation. A person overheats from exertion or fever. The term often implies crossing from acceptable warmth into dangerous territory: {My laptop keeps overheating during video calls}.

Overhyped describes something that has received more praise, attention, or excitement than it deserves. The term combines "over" (excessive) with "hyped" (promoted or publicized intensely), suggesting that expectations have been inflated beyond what the thing can deliver. {The movie was so overhyped that the actual experience felt disappointing.} It's commonly applied to products, films, restaurants, or trends that fail to live up to their buildup.

Overjoyed means extremely happy—joy taken to an intense degree. The word typically describes reactions to specific good news or events rather than general contentment: {She was overjoyed to learn she'd been accepted}. It suggests happiness so strong it's almost overwhelming.

Overkill is excessive force or effort beyond what's needed to accomplish something. The term originated in nuclear strategy, describing destructive capacity far exceeding what would destroy a target. Now it applies broadly to any disproportionate response: {Bringing three lawyers to a traffic court hearing is overkill}. The word often carries mild criticism—suggesting waste, overreaction, or lack of restraint.

Overlap describes things that extend over and cover part of each other: {The shingles overlap to keep water out}. Schedules overlap when they share common time; interests overlap when they share common ground. As a noun, overlap is the shared portion: {There's considerable overlap between the two job descriptions}. The word captures partial coincidence—not identical, not separate, but sharing territory.

Overload means to burden with too much—more than a system, person, or structure can handle. You can overload a truck, a circuit, or your schedule. As a noun, an overload is the excess itself: {The power grid couldn't handle the overload}. Information overload describes being overwhelmed by too much data. {Don't overload the washing machine}.

Overloaded describes something carrying or handling more than its intended capacity. An overloaded {truck} strains under excessive weight; an overloaded {circuit} trips when too many devices draw power; an overloaded {schedule} leaves no breathing room. The term extends to people who feel overwhelmed by responsibilities or information: {I'm completely overloaded with work this week}. In programming, an overloaded function has multiple definitions that handle different types of input.

To overlook something is to fail to notice or consider it: {I overlooked one important detail}. The word also means to choose not to punish or address: {We'll overlook the violation this time}. A third sense is to have a view over: {The balcony overlooks the harbor}. As a noun, an overlook is a scenic viewpoint, especially along a highway.

Overlooked means missed or failed to notice: {The investigator overlooked a crucial piece of evidence}. It also means ignored or passed over, often unfairly: {She was overlooked for the promotion}. Something overlooked may be undervalued or underappreciated: {one of the most overlooked albums of the decade}. Less commonly, to be overlooked means to have a view over something: {a balcony overlooking the garden}.

Overlooking works in two directions. To overlook something is to fail to notice it or to choose not to address it: {I overlooked the typo}, {We'll overlook your tardiness this once}. But overlooking also means looking down upon from above: {a balcony overlooking the garden}, {rooms overlooking the bay}. Context usually makes the sense clear.

Overlooks has two main senses that point in opposite directions. To overlook something is to have a view over it from above: {The balcony overlooks the harbor}. But to overlook is also to fail to notice or to excuse: {I overlooked the error}, {We can overlook it this once}. The first meaning implies seeing everything; the second implies missing something.

An overlord is a ruler who holds power over other rulers or lords—a supreme authority in a hierarchy of control. The term evokes feudal systems where lesser nobles owed allegiance to a greater one. In modern use, overlord often appears ironically or in fantasy contexts: {Our new robot overlords}, {She appointed herself overlord of the office coffee supply}. The word suggests dominion that is absolute and possibly tyrannical.

Overlords are rulers or masters who hold power over others, especially those who dominate subordinate lords or territories. The term suggests feudal hierarchy or absolute authority: {The Norman overlords imposed their language on England}. In modern use, overlord often carries ironic or sinister overtones—corporate overlords, robot overlords, alien overlords—implying oppressive control: {Our new tech overlords know everything about us}.

Overnight spans the hours of darkness between evening and morning. As an adverb, it describes something happening during the night: {We drove overnight to get there}. As an adjective, it modifies things lasting or occurring through the night: an overnight {stay}, an overnight {bag}. Figuratively, overnight means suddenly or very quickly: {She became famous overnight}. The verb means to stay somewhere for the night: {We overnighted in Chicago}.

An overpass is a bridge that carries a road or railway over another road. The term emphasizes the structure's function of allowing traffic to pass over an obstacle without intersection: {Take the overpass to avoid the traffic light}. In American usage, overpass is more common than flyover, which prevails in British English.

Overplayed describes something repeated so often it has lost its impact or appeal. A song becomes overplayed when radio stations exhaust it: {That track was great until they overplayed it all summer}. The word extends to tactics or arguments used too frequently: {The victim card is overplayed}. To overplay your hand is to overestimate your position and push too hard.

Overpopulation is having more people than an area can sustainably support—exceeding the carrying capacity for resources like food, water, and space. The term applies to regions, countries, or the planet as a whole: {Overpopulation strains infrastructure in rapidly growing cities}. Critics note the concept often masks questions of resource distribution rather than absolute numbers.

To overpower is to defeat or subdue by superior force: {The guards overpowered the prisoner before he could escape}. The word extends to any overwhelming dominance—a smell that overpowers a room, grief that overpowers composure, a flavor that overpowers everything else in the dish. What overpowers doesn't just win; it leaves no contest.

Overpowered means defeated or subdued by superior force: {The guards were overpowered by the mob}. In gaming, overpowered describes a character, weapon, or ability that's too strong relative to others, disrupting balance: {That new hero is totally overpowered—they need to nerf him}. The gaming sense has spread to general slang for anything excessively dominant or effective.

Overpowering describes something so intense it overwhelms resistance or the senses. An overpowering {smell} dominates a room. An overpowering {urge} is nearly impossible to resist. Overpowering {force} defeats opposition completely. The word suggests an intensity that leaves no room for alternatives: {The evidence against him was overpowering}.

Overpriced describes something that costs more than it's worth or more than it should. The judgment is subjective—what seems overpriced to one buyer may seem fair to another: {The drinks at the airport are ridiculously overpriced}. The word implies you're being taken advantage of, not just that something is expensive.

Overprotective describes someone who shields another person—usually a child—from harm or difficulty to an excessive degree. An overprotective parent might not let children play unsupervised or make their own mistakes: {Her overprotective mother still calls her every night}. The word implies the protection does more harm than good, preventing normal development or independence.

Overqualified describes someone whose credentials, experience, or skills exceed what a position requires. Employers sometimes reject overqualified candidates, fearing they'll be bored, demand higher pay, or leave quickly: {They said I was overqualified for the entry-level position}. The term often frustrates job seekers who would happily accept less demanding work.

Overrated describes something that receives more praise, attention, or esteem than it deserves. The term implies a gap between reputation and actual quality: {I think The Beatles are overrated} or {The restaurant is overrated—the food is mediocre at best}. It functions as both an adjective and the past participle of the verb overrate. The judgment is inherently subjective; calling something overrated often says as much about the speaker's contrarian stance as about the thing itself.

Overreach means to extend beyond proper limits, typically by attempting more than one can accomplish or by going too far in pursuit of an advantage. When someone overreaches, they defeat their own purpose through excessive ambition or greed: {The company overreached by expanding into too many markets at once}. In legal and political contexts, overreach often describes an abuse of power or authority: {Critics accused the agency of regulatory overreach}. The noun overreach denotes such an instance of going too far.

Overreaching describes going too far in pursuit of an objective, attempting more than one can accomplish or is entitled to. An overreaching {executive} grabs power beyond their authority. An overreaching {argument} extends logic past its breaking point. The word implies ambition that defeats itself—{The prosecution's overreaching claims alienated the jury}. To overreach is to stretch beyond one's grasp.

To overreact is to respond more intensely than a situation warrants—becoming too angry, too worried, or too excited given the circumstances. {I know I'm probably overreacting, but I can't stop thinking about what she said}. The noun is overreaction: {His resignation was an overreaction to mild criticism}.

Overreacting is responding to something with more intensity than the situation warrants—getting too angry, too worried, or too upset. The word often appears in accusations: {You're overreacting}. Whether someone is actually overreacting or responding appropriately is frequently a matter of perspective.

An overreaction is a response disproportionate to its cause—too strong, too emotional, too hasty. The word implies the speaker's judgment that a calmer response would have been appropriate: {Calling the police was an overreaction; the kids were just being loud}. To overreact is to respond this way. What counts as overreaction often depends on perspective—one person's overreaction is another's justified response.

Override means to use authority to set aside or supersede something—a decision, a rule, or a mechanism. A manager overrides an employee's judgment. Congress can override a presidential veto. In computing, override refers to replacing default behavior with custom instructions. The noun override is the act or means of overriding: {a manual override}, {a congressional override}. To override concerns is to proceed despite them.

Overriding means more important than all other considerations. An overriding concern takes precedence over everything else: {Safety was the overriding priority}. The word suggests something so significant it eclipses competing factors: {Her overriding goal was to finish the project on time}. In computing, overriding replaces inherited behavior with new code.

To overrule is to reject or set aside a decision, objection, or ruling by exercising superior authority. A judge overrules an objection, allowing the questioned testimony or evidence. A parent overrules a child's protest. When a higher court overrules a lower court's decision, it reverses the outcome. The word implies hierarchy—someone with greater power countermanding someone with less: {The CEO overruled the committee's recommendation}.

Overruled is the past tense of overrule—to reject or set aside a decision, objection, or ruling by exercising superior authority. A judge overrules an objection when allowing the challenged testimony or evidence: {Objection! Hearsay. Overruled.} Parents overrule children, executives overrule subordinates, and appellate courts overrule lower court decisions. To be overruled is to have your position rejected by someone with greater power.

To overrun is to spread over and occupy by force or in overwhelming numbers: {Weeds overran the garden}, {Protesters overran the barricades}. The past tense is also overrun. Something that overruns exceeds its boundaries or limits: {The project overran its budget by millions}. As a noun, an overrun is the amount by which something exceeds expectations, especially costs: {a $2 billion overrun on the construction contract}.

Overseas means across or beyond the sea—in or to a foreign country, especially one reached by ocean travel. As an adjective, it describes things foreign or international: {overseas markets}, {overseas travel}, {overseas military bases}. As an adverb, it indicates location or movement abroad: {She lived overseas for ten years}. The word often implies significant distance, not just any border crossing.

To oversee is to supervise or watch over work, a process, or people to ensure things proceed correctly: {She oversees a team of twelve engineers}, {A committee will oversee the election}. The word implies authority and responsibility for outcomes, though not necessarily hands-on involvement in the work itself.

An overseer is someone who supervises work or workers. The term appears most often in historical contexts—particularly describing those who managed enslaved people on plantations: {The overseer drove the field hands from dawn to dusk}. In modern use, overseer sounds formal or archaic, largely replaced by supervisor or manager. It survives in some institutional titles and in figurative use for anyone monitoring others' activities.

To overshadow is to cast a shadow over something, literally or figuratively. A tall building overshadows neighboring structures. More often the word describes something that diminishes another by comparison or draws attention away from it: {Her brother's achievements always overshadowed her own}. Bad news can overshadow good: {The scandal overshadowed the team's victory}.

Overshadowed means cast into shadow by something larger or more prominent. A tall building overshadows nearby houses. More often figurative: a person's achievements may be overshadowed by a sibling's fame, or good news overshadowed by tragedy. The word implies being diminished not through fault but by comparison: {Her early work was overshadowed by her later masterpiece}.

To overshare is to reveal too much personal information, especially in contexts where such disclosure feels inappropriate or uncomfortable for others. The term emerged with social media, where people broadcast intimate details to wide audiences: {She overshared about her divorce on Facebook}. As a noun, an overshare is an instance of such disclosure: {That was a bit of an overshare}.

An oversharer is someone who reveals too much personal information, especially in contexts where such disclosure feels inappropriate or uncomfortable for others. The term implies a lack of social boundaries—sharing intimate details about relationships, health problems, or family drama with acquaintances or strangers: {My coworker is such an oversharer—I know way too much about her divorce}.

Oversharing is revealing too much personal information, especially in contexts where it's unwelcome or inappropriate: {She overshared about her divorce on the first date}. The term emerged with social media, where broadcasting intimate details to wide audiences became easy. What counts as oversharing depends on the relationship and setting—telling a stranger your medical history differs from telling a close friend.

Oversight has two nearly opposite meanings. The first is watchful supervision: {Congressional oversight of intelligence agencies}, {The board has oversight of financial matters}. The second is an error of inattention—something missed or forgotten: {The omission was an oversight, not deliberate}. Context usually makes clear which sense applies.

To oversleep is to sleep longer than intended, typically missing an alarm or appointment: {I overslept and missed my flight}. The word implies sleeping past a point when you should have woken—whether for work, school, or other obligations. Past tense: overslept.

To overstep is to go beyond acceptable limits or boundaries. The word almost always appears with an object indicating what was exceeded: overstep one's {authority}, overstep one's {bounds}, overstep the {mark}. {The manager overstepped by making promises he couldn't keep.} The suggestion is of someone acting presumptuously or exceeding their rightful scope.

Overstepped is the past tense of overstep, meaning to go beyond acceptable limits or boundaries. Someone who overstepped exceeded their authority, violated social norms, or crossed a line: {He overstepped when he criticized her parenting}. The word implies transgression—not just going far, but going too far.

Overstepping is going beyond proper limits or boundaries. The word usually appears with bounds or a similar object: {overstepping his authority}, {overstepping the bounds of decency}. Someone who oversteps has exceeded what's appropriate for their role or position: {The committee felt the director was overstepping by making the decision unilaterally}.

To overtake is to catch up with and pass someone or something moving in the same direction: {The sports car overtook the truck on the highway}. British English uses overtake where American English prefers pass. Figuratively, overtake means to come upon suddenly or unexpectedly: {Exhaustion overtook her}. Events, emotions, or consequences can overtake someone—suggesting being caught by something you can't outrun.

Overtaken is the past participle of overtake, meaning to catch up with and pass someone or something that was ahead. A faster runner overtakes a slower one; a car overtakes another on the highway. The word extends to abstract situations where one thing surpasses another: {Events overtook our careful planning.} When emotions or circumstances are the subject, overtaken suggests being seized or overwhelmed: {She was overtaken by grief.} In this sense, the person affected has no control over what befalls them.

To overthink is to analyze or worry about something excessively, often to the point of paralysis or anxiety. The word implies that less thought would produce better results: {You're overthinking this—just pick one}. Overthinking turns simple decisions into elaborate mental tangles, second-guessing what should be straightforward.

An overthinker is someone who dwells on decisions, problems, or situations far beyond what's useful—analyzing possibilities, imagining outcomes, and second-guessing themselves until paralyzed or anxious. {I'm such an overthinker—I spent an hour deciding what to text back.} The term is often self-applied, acknowledging a tendency to make simple things complicated through excessive mental processing.

Overthinking is dwelling on something longer than useful, analyzing possibilities until the process becomes counterproductive. The word implies that some thinking is appropriate but too much creates anxiety or paralysis: {Stop overthinking it and just ask her out}. {I've been overthinking this decision for weeks}. The noun overthinking and the verb overthink both see heavy use in discussions of anxiety and self-help.

To overthrow is to remove from power by force—a government, ruler, or regime: {The rebels overthrew the monarchy}. The noun is the act itself: {the overthrow of the dictator}. Extended uses suggest defeating or overturning something established: {overthrow conventional wisdom}. In baseball, an overthrow is a wild throw past the intended target.

Overthrown is the past participle of overthrow—to remove from power by force. A government or ruler is overthrown through revolution, coup, or conquest: {The dictator was overthrown by rebel forces}. The word implies sudden, usually violent displacement of authority. Extended uses describe defeating or toppling anything dominant: {Long-held assumptions were overthrown by new evidence}.

Overtime is time worked beyond normal hours, or the extra pay for such work: {I'm pulling overtime this week}. In sports, overtime is an additional period played when the score is tied at the end of regulation: {The game went into overtime}. Figuratively, anything extending past its expected duration is working overtime: {My imagination was running overtime}.

Overtone refers to something implied or suggested beyond what's explicitly stated: {The meeting had overtones of hostility}. The word often appears in the plural to describe secondary qualities or implications layered onto a primary meaning: {political overtones}, {racial overtones}. In music and acoustics, an overtone is a frequency higher than the fundamental tone, contributing to the richness of a sound.

Overtones are subtle or implicit qualities beneath the surface of something: {The meeting had political overtones}. The word suggests additional layers of meaning, feeling, or association beyond what's explicitly stated. In music and acoustics, overtones are higher frequencies that sound alongside a fundamental tone, giving instruments their distinctive character.

An overture is an opening move or proposal, especially one intended to initiate negotiations or a relationship: {diplomatic overtures}, {romantic overtures}, {The company made overtures to potential investors}. In music, an overture is an orchestral piece introducing an opera, ballet, or musical—or a standalone concert work in that style. Both senses share the idea of something that comes before and leads into what follows.

Overtures are preliminary approaches or proposals, often suggesting the beginning of negotiations or a relationship: {diplomatic overtures}, {peace overtures}, {romantic overtures}. The word implies tentative gestures made to gauge receptiveness before committing fully. In music, an overture is an orchestral piece introducing an opera, ballet, or musical—setting the tone for what follows. Both senses share the idea of an opening move.

To overturn is to turn something over—to flip, capsize, or upset it so that what was on top is now on bottom: {The canoe overturned in the rapids}. The word extends to reversing decisions or established states: courts overturn verdicts, revolutions overturn governments. An overturn is such a reversal: {the overturn of the conviction}.

An overview is a broad survey or summary that covers the main points without going into detail. It gives you the general picture before you dive deeper: {Let me give you an overview of the project}. An overview can also be a view from above that takes in a wide area at once.

Overweight means above normal or desirable weight. A person may be clinically overweight based on body mass index, or simply heavier than they'd like. The word extends beyond bodies: an overweight {suitcase} exceeds airline limits, an overweight {portfolio} holds too much of one investment. To be overweight in a stock is to hold more than the benchmark allocation suggests.

To overwhelm is to overpower completely—by force, emotion, or sheer quantity. An army overwhelms defenses. Grief overwhelms the bereaved. Work overwhelms someone who can't keep up. The sense is of being flooded or buried: {I was overwhelmed by the response}. Overwhelmed often describes feeling unable to cope: {She felt overwhelmed by all the decisions}. Something overwhelming is so powerful it's hard to resist: {overwhelming evidence}, {overwhelming support}.

Overwhelmed describes being overcome by something too powerful to manage. The original image is of a wave crashing over and submerging you. Most often the word describes emotional states—flooded by work, grief, or demands that exceed your capacity to cope: {I'm completely overwhelmed with everything going on}. Someone can also be overwhelmed by positive feelings: {overwhelmed with gratitude}. The word implies temporary defeat or paralysis in the face of excess.

Overwhelming describes something so powerful or intense that it's difficult to resist, process, or manage. An overwhelming {majority} is so large it dominates. Overwhelming {evidence} leaves no reasonable doubt. Overwhelming {grief} threatens to consume you. The word suggests being flooded or buried: {The response was overwhelming}. To overwhelm is to overpower completely—by force, emotion, or sheer quantity.

Overwork is excessive labor—working beyond healthy or sustainable limits. As a verb, to overwork is to work too hard or too long, whether yourself or others: {The company overworked its employees during the holiday rush}. The noun names this condition: {She collapsed from overwork}. Things can also be overworked—an overworked {metaphor} has been used too often, and overworked {dough} becomes tough.

Overworked describes someone exhausted from too much work or too many demands: {The overworked nurses barely had time to eat}. It also applies to things used so heavily they've lost effectiveness—an overworked {excuse}, an overworked {metaphor}. The word can modify both people and concepts that have been pushed past their useful limits.

Overworking is working too much or too hard, to the point of exhaustion or diminishing returns. You can overwork yourself, or a boss can overwork employees. The term extends beyond labor: overworking dough makes it tough, overworking a point belabors it. {She's been overworking herself since the promotion.}

To overwrite is to write over existing content, replacing what was there. In computing, overwriting replaces old data with new: {The update overwrote my settings}. In physical writing, it means writing on top of other text, making both hard to read. Figuratively, new experiences can overwrite old memories: {Time had overwritten his recollection of the event}.
