To owe is to be obligated to pay or repay—money, a favor, an explanation: {I owe you twenty dollars}, {She owes me an apology}. The obligation may be abstract: {We owe our success to hard work}. Owing to means because of: {The game was canceled owing to rain}. To owe it to someone is to have an obligation toward them: {You owe it to yourself to take a break}.

Owes is the third-person singular of owe. To owe is to be obligated to pay or repay: {She owes me twenty dollars}. Beyond money, you can owe gratitude, loyalty, or an apology. To owe something to a cause means that cause is responsible: {He owes his success to hard work}. {The team owes him one} suggests a favor is due in return.

An owl is a bird of prey with a flat face, large forward-facing eyes, and the ability to rotate its head nearly full circle. Owls hunt at night and fly silently, giving them associations with wisdom, mystery, and death across many cultures. Someone who stays up late is a {night owl}. (Capitalized Owl may refer to a proper name or mascot.)

Owls are nocturnal birds of prey with large forward-facing eyes, flat faces, and the ability to rotate their heads dramatically. They hunt silently, swooping on rodents and other small animals. Owls appear across mythology as symbols of wisdom or ill omen. A {night owl} is someone who stays up late.

Own functions as an adjective, verb, or pronoun. Its work as a verb is straightforward: it is a synonym of have and possess when the object is a tangible or real thing: We own a cabin in the mountains. When the verb own is followed by a clause it means to admit or believe that the clause is true: He owns that he was never at the site. As an adjective or pronoun, own emphasizes the idea of possession, association, or ownership: Everyone arrived in their own car. Do you have a room of your own at home? She bought it with her own money.

Owned means possessed or held as property: {Who owned the car before you?} In internet and gaming slang, to own someone is to defeat or humiliate them decisively: {We got completely owned in that match}. The past tense owned often appears as a standalone exclamation celebrating someone's embarrassment or defeat. The deliberate misspelling "pwned" carries the same meaning.

An owner is a person or entity that possesses something—property, a business, an animal. Ownership implies legal rights: to use, sell, or dispose of what one owns. {The owner of the restaurant greeted us personally.} {Dog owners are responsible for their pets' behavior.} Owner often appears in compounds: {homeowner}, {landowner}, {business owner}.

Ownership is the state of possessing something—having legal or rightful claim to property, assets, or rights: {home ownership}, {The company changed ownership}. Beyond the legal sense, ownership means taking responsibility: {She took ownership of the mistake}. The word implies not just possession but accountability and control over what one owns.

Oxen is the plural of ox—castrated male cattle used as draft animals. The word preserves an old English plural form, like children or men. Oxen pulled plows and wagons for millennia before mechanized farming: {a team of oxen}, {slow as an ox}. The singular ox can also refer to any bovine generally.

Oxtail is the tail of cattle, sold as a cut of meat. Rich in collagen and gelatin, it becomes tender and flavorful when braised or stewed slowly: {oxtail soup}, {Jamaican oxtail}. The name persists from when oxen were the primary source, though modern oxtail comes from any beef cattle.

Oxygen is the chemical element essential for most life on Earth—the gas we breathe and the component of air that sustains combustion. Water is hydrogen and oxygen combined. In medical contexts, oxygen refers to supplemental breathing support: {The patient was put on oxygen}. Figuratively, oxygen is anything vital to survival or continuation: {Publicity is oxygen for a political campaign}.

An oxymoron is an expression, usually consisting of two words or terms that seem to contradict each other. Awfully good is considered an oxymoron since awful usually means terrible. Many oxymorons that were viewed as clever when first heard eventually become clichés, such as deafening silence or icy hot. New and original oxymorons seem memorable because they require you to combine two ideas that don’t normally go together.

An oyster is a bivalve mollusk with a rough, irregular shell, found in coastal waters worldwide. Oysters are prized as food, often eaten raw on the half shell, and some species produce pearls. {The world is your oyster} suggests unlimited opportunity lies before you. To oyster up is to become silent or uncommunicative, like an oyster clamping shut.

Oysters are bivalve mollusks with rough, irregularly shaped shells, prized as seafood. They're eaten raw on the half shell, fried, or in stews. Oysters produce pearls when irritants become coated with nacre inside their shells. {We ordered a dozen oysters on ice}. The phrase {the world is your oyster} means opportunity lies before you, ready to be seized.

Ozone is a form of oxygen with three atoms per molecule instead of the usual two, giving it a distinctive sharp smell—the fresh scent after a thunderstorm. The ozone layer in the upper atmosphere absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation; holes in this layer caused environmental alarm in the late 20th century. Informally, ozone means fresh air: {Let's get out of the city and breathe some ozone}.
Pace is borrowed from Latin and is rarely used outside of academic writing and discourse. It means with due respect to and is used as a way of introducing some point of disagreement.

A pacemaker is a small electronic device implanted in the chest to regulate heartbeat, sending electrical impulses when the heart's natural rhythm falters. The term extends to anyone or anything that sets the pace for others—a runner who leads the pack, or a company that sets industry standards: {Kenya's pacemaker dropped out at mile twenty}.

Pacemakers are small electronic devices implanted in the chest to regulate heartbeat by sending electrical impulses to the heart muscle. They're used when the heart's natural rhythm is too slow, irregular, or prone to dangerous pauses. Beyond the medical device, pacemaker also refers to someone who sets the pace in a race or competition, or more broadly, anyone who leads the way or establishes a standard that others follow. {She was the pacemaker for innovation in the industry.}

A pacifier is a rubber or silicone nipple given to babies to suck on for comfort. The sucking motion soothes infants without feeding them. Called a dummy in British English. Figuratively, a pacifier is anything that calms or quiets: {The tax cut was a pacifier for angry voters}.

Pacifiers are rubber or silicone nipples given to babies to suck on for comfort. The sucking soothes infants even without feeding—hence the name. British English prefers dummy. Figuratively, a pacifier is anything that calms or appeases: {The tax cut was a pacifier for angry voters}. Someone who pacifies others may also be called a pacifier.

Pacifism is opposition to war and violence as means of settling disputes. A pacifist believes conflicts should be resolved through peaceful means—negotiation, diplomacy, nonviolent resistance. The commitment ranges from personal refusal to bear arms to broader political opposition to military action: {His pacifism led him to register as a conscientious objector}. Some pacifists oppose all violence; others make exceptions for self-defense.

A pacifist is someone who opposes war and violence, often refusing to participate in military action on moral or religious grounds. The term can describe a principled stance {She's a committed pacifist} or be used dismissively to suggest weakness or naivety {Don't be such a pacifist—sometimes you have to fight back}. As an adjective, pacifist describes beliefs or movements: {pacifist ideals}, {pacifist organizations}.

Pacifists are people who oppose war and violence as means of settling disputes, often refusing to participate in military service on moral or religious grounds. The term can be descriptive or dismissive depending on context—pacifists may be praised for principled commitment to peace or criticized as naive about geopolitical realities: {The pacifists staged a protest outside the recruitment center}.

Pacing is the speed or rhythm at which something unfolds. In narrative—film, fiction, theater—pacing determines how quickly events progress and tension builds: {The movie's pacing dragged in the second act}. In performance, pacing governs delivery: a comedian's pacing affects when laughs land. Pacing also means walking back and forth, often from anxiety or restlessness: {He was pacing the hallway, waiting for news}.

As a verb, pack typically conveys the idea of compressing something and fitting it into a smaller place, like the way you pack your bags before traveling. People pack into a crowded place. You can pack down loose soil. An activity that is action packed contains a lot of action in a short time. A pack is a collection of like things gathered in one place (pack of cards, pack of wolves). Some containers that you can pack things into are called packs, like a backpack or a fanny pack.

A package is something wrapped or boxed for transport or delivery: {The package arrived damaged}. In software, a package is a bundle of code distributed as a unit. Package deals combine multiple items at one price. To package something is to wrap it or present it attractively: {They packaged the proposal to appeal to investors}. In vulgar slang, a man's package is his genitals as visible through clothing.

Packaging is the materials and containers used to wrap, protect, and present products—boxes, bottles, bags, and their labels. It extends to how something is presented to make it appealing: {The candidate's packaging was slick, but voters saw through it}. The term covers both the physical wrapping and the marketing strategy behind it.

Packed means tightly filled or crowded. A packed {suitcase} has been filled to capacity. A packed {stadium} is full of people. To be packed for a trip is to have your belongings ready. Packed can also mean carrying a weapon: {He was packing heat}. Food that's packed has been put into containers for preservation or sale.

A packet is a small package or bundle, often containing a specific quantity: a packet of {seeds}, a packet of {sugar}. In computing, a packet is a unit of data transmitted across a network—information broken into manageable chunks for transfer. In British English, packet commonly means a container for cigarettes or crisps where Americans would say pack or bag.

Packing is the process of putting things into containers for transport or storage: {I need to start packing for the trip}. Packing material cushions items for shipping. In manufacturing, packing is material used to seal joints and prevent leaks. To {send someone packing} is to dismiss them abruptly. Packing heat means carrying a gun.

A packrat is a North American rodent that hoards objects in its nest, particularly shiny items. The figurative sense dominates: someone who accumulates and refuses to discard possessions, often useless ones. {My grandmother was a packrat—she kept every newspaper since 1972.} The compulsion ranges from harmless clutter to genuine hoarding disorder.

Packs is the plural of pack—a bundle, group, or container holding things together. A hiker carries packs. Wolves travel in packs. Packs of cigarettes sit behind the counter. The verb means to fill or compress: {She packs her suitcase efficiently}. {The bar packs in crowds on weekends}. Someone who {packs heat} carries a gun.

A pact is a formal agreement between parties, often with serious or binding implications: {The two nations signed a nonaggression pact}. Pact suggests something more solemn than a casual promise—treaties, alliances, or deals sealed with commitment. It can shade toward the sinister: {a pact with the devil}. Informally, friends make pacts too: {We had a pact never to speak of it again}.

Pacts are formal agreements between parties, often carrying a sense of solemnity or binding commitment. The word suggests something weightier than a casual agreement—treaties between nations, deals sealed with ceremony, or promises made with serious intent: {The two countries signed a nonaggression pact}. A pact can also be informal but earnest: {We made a pact never to speak of it again}. The singular is pact.

Pad describes numerous functional items that are relatively flat, perhaps soft, and perhaps situated horizontally (launch pad, mattress pad, heating pad, shoulder pad). Informally, a pad is someone’s comfortable home (bachelor pad). To pad something is to add stuffing (for example) to make it softer. A padded envelope or compartment has a protective layer around it. When money is involved, pad usually means to add extra in a dishonest way.

Padding is soft material used to cushion, protect, or fill out. Athletic gear has padding to absorb impact; a bra may have padding to enhance shape. The word extends to excess material added to inflate something: {The essay was mostly padding—she stretched two good paragraphs into five pages}. In computing, padding is extra space or characters added around content for formatting or alignment.

A paddle is mainly a device with a flat blade for steering and propelling a vessel through water – like an oar. Things that have a similar shape get the name too (ping pong paddle, rice paddle). To paddle is to use a paddle for propulsion or steering. A characteristic way that some animals swim, pumping all limbs, is also described with the verb (dog paddle). To paddle a person is to strike them, perhaps as a punishment, with a paddle.

Paddles are broad, flat implements used to propel or stir. A canoe paddle moves the boat through water with stroking motions. A paddle in table tennis or pickleball strikes the ball. To paddle is to use such an implement, or to wade through shallow water with short steps. Paddles also serve as instruments of corporal punishment: {The principal kept a paddle in his office}. To paddle someone is to spank them with a flat object.

A paddlewheel is a large wheel with boards or paddles around its rim, mounted on the side or stern of a boat. As the wheel rotates, the paddles push against the water to propel the vessel forward. Paddlewheel steamboats were once common on American rivers: {The old paddlewheel churned up the Mississippi}. Also spelled paddle wheel.

Paddling is the act of propelling a boat with a paddle, or the recreational activity itself: {We went paddling on the lake}. It also means wading or splashing in shallow water: {children paddling at the beach}. As discipline, paddling is striking someone with a paddle or flat object, typically on the buttocks: {The school banned paddling in 1985}.

A padlock is a detachable lock with a U-shaped bar that passes through a hasp or chain and clicks shut. Unlike locks built into doors, padlocks are portable—used on gates, lockers, sheds, and storage units. To padlock something is to secure it with one: {The landlord padlocked the gate}.

Padlocks are portable locks with a U-shaped shackle that passes through a hasp or chain and clicks shut. Unlike built-in locks, padlocks can secure gates, lockers, sheds, or storage units—anything with a loop to thread the shackle through. {Someone cut the padlock off the fence}. To padlock something is to secure it this way.

Pads are flat cushioning materials used for comfort, protection, or absorption. You might sit on a seat pad, write on a notepad, or use a heating pad for sore muscles. Menstrual pads absorb blood during periods. In anatomy, pads are the soft fleshy undersides of fingers, toes, or animal paws. To pad something is to add soft material for cushioning, or to walk softly: {She padded barefoot across the kitchen}. Padding out a speech or essay means adding unnecessary material to make it longer.

Paella is a Spanish rice dish cooked in a wide, shallow pan—also called a paella. The rice absorbs flavors from saffron, olive oil, and whatever else goes in: traditionally rabbit, chicken, or seafood, along with vegetables. The prized part is the socarrat, the crispy rice crust at the bottom. {We ordered paella for the whole table.}

A pagan is someone who follows a polytheistic or nature-based religion, or more loosely, anyone outside the major monotheistic faiths. Historically, Christians used the term for non-Christians, often disparagingly. Today pagan often describes modern practitioners of revived pre-Christian traditions like Wicca or Druidry: {She identifies as pagan and celebrates the solstices}. The word can also mean irreligious or hedonistic: {his pagan disregard for conventional morality}. (Capitalized Pagan emphasizes identity with modern religious movements.)

Paganism is religious belief outside the major world religions—especially pre-Christian European traditions involving nature worship, multiple gods, or animistic spirits. The term historically carried Christian disapproval, contrasting "civilized" monotheism with "primitive" folk religion. Modern paganism revives or reimagines these traditions: Wicca, Druidry, Norse heathenry. {She practices a form of Celtic paganism.} The word can still be used dismissively for any non-mainstream spirituality.

Pagans are people who follow polytheistic or nature-based religions outside the major world faiths—or, historically, anyone not Christian, Jewish, or Muslim. The term originally meant rural villagers, who were slower to adopt Christianity than city dwellers. Modern pagans often practice revived or reconstructed pre-Christian traditions: {The pagans gathered for the solstice ritual}. In casual use, pagan can mean irreligious or hedonistic: {a pagan disregard for propriety}.

A page is one side of a leaf in a book, magazine, or document—or the leaf itself. By extension, page refers to a section of a website: {the home page}, {landing page}. To page through something is to turn pages, often casually: {She paged through the magazine while waiting}. A page is also an attendant, originally a youth training for knighthood, now typically someone who runs errands in a legislative body or hotel. To page someone is to summon them, especially over a loudspeaker or electronic device: {The doctor was paged to the emergency room}.

A pageant is a public spectacle or elaborate display, often involving costumes, processions, and ceremonial elements. The word most commonly refers to beauty pageants—competitions judging appearance and poise: {She competed in the Miss America pageant}. Pageants can also be historical reenactments or theatrical presentations depicting scenes from the past: {The town stages an annual Christmas pageant}. The adjective pageantry describes the splendor and ceremony of such events.

Pageantry is elaborate ceremonial display—the costumes, processions, and spectacle of formal occasions. Royal coronations and military parades are rich in pageantry. The word suggests visual splendor with a touch of theater: {the pageantry of the Olympic opening ceremony}. It can imply something impressive but perhaps hollow: {Behind all the pageantry, the organization was in crisis}.

Pageants are elaborate public spectacles or processions, often with costumes, floats, and performances marking historical events or holidays: {the town's annual Christmas pageant}. Beauty pageants are competitions where contestants are judged on appearance, poise, and talent: {She competed in pageants throughout her teens}. The word suggests something showy and ceremonial, sometimes with a hint of artificiality.

A pager is a small wireless device that receives short messages or alerts, typically signaling the wearer to call a specific number. Before cell phones became ubiquitous, pagers were standard equipment for doctors, emergency responders, and drug dealers alike: {The surgeon's pager went off during dinner}. They persist in hospitals where cell signals are unreliable.

Pagers are small wireless devices that receive brief messages, typically numeric codes or short text. Before mobile phones became ubiquitous, pagers were essential for doctors, emergency responders, and anyone who needed to be reachable: {The doctor's pager went off during dinner}. They persist in hospitals where cell signals are unreliable. To page someone is to send them such a message.

Pages are the individual leaves of a book, magazine, or document, or one side of such a leaf. Page numbers help locate information: {Turn to page 47}. The word extends to screens of digital content: {a web page}, {a landing page}. A page is also a young attendant, especially one employed to run errands in a hotel or legislative body. To page someone is to summon them, originally by calling their name aloud, now typically through an electronic device: {The doctor was paged to the emergency room}. To page through something is to flip through its pages.

A pagoda is a tiered tower with multiple eaves, characteristic of East Asian architecture. Pagodas originated as Buddhist temples and still serve religious purposes, though the term now applies to any building in this distinctive style: {The pagoda rose above the garden}. In the West, pagoda-style structures appear in parks and gardens as ornamental features.

Pagodas is the plural of pagoda, a tiered tower found in East and Southeast Asia, typically associated with Buddhist or Hindu temples. The structure features multiple eaves stacking upward, each level slightly smaller than the one below: {The temple complex included several ornate pagodas}. In Western contexts, pagoda-style architecture sometimes appears in gardens or as decorative elements.

Paid is the past tense and past participle of pay. Someone who is paid receives money for work: {a well-paid consultant}, {poorly paid workers}. Paid also describes things you've compensated for: {paid leave}, {paid parking}, {paid subscription}. A paid {advertisement} discloses that someone purchased the placement. {She paid the bill and left.}

Pain is the distress signal of your nervous system caused by intense or damaging inputs. Other states of comfort that do not have a physical component are also called pain (psychic pain, pain of exile). If you describe a person or experience as a pain, you mean that they are hard to endure. To take pains is to be careful in doing something. When something pains you, it causes you (usually emotional) distress.

Pained describes the expression of someone experiencing pain or distress, whether physical or emotional. A pained {look} or pained {expression} suggests discomfort, disappointment, or strained patience: {She gave him a pained smile when he told the same joke again}. The word often implies suppressed frustration rather than acute suffering.

Painful describes what causes or involves pain. Physical pain: {a painful injury}, {painful surgery}. Emotional pain: {a painful memory}, {painful breakup}. The word extends to difficult or laborious experiences: {a painful conversation}, {painfully slow progress}. Something painfully obvious is so clear it almost hurts to acknowledge.

A painkiller is a drug that relieves pain. The term covers everything from aspirin to morphine: {I took a painkiller for my headache}. Painkillers work through various mechanisms—blocking pain signals, reducing inflammation, or altering perception in the brain. The word sometimes appears in discussions of addiction, since many powerful painkillers are opioids.

Painkillers are medications that relieve pain. The term covers everything from over-the-counter drugs like aspirin and ibuprofen to powerful prescription opioids like morphine and oxycodone. {She took a couple of painkillers for her headache}. Alcohol and other numbing substances are sometimes called painkillers figuratively.

Painless means without pain or discomfort. A medical procedure might be painless, or nearly so. The word extends to anything that causes no difficulty or distress: {The software update was painless}. A painless solution avoids hardship or inconvenience. The figurative sense often carries slight surprise—things expected to be unpleasant turning out easy: {The exam was actually painless}.

Pains is the plural of pain, but its most common use is in the phrase {take pains}, meaning to make a careful effort: {She took pains to get every detail right}. The related phrase {painstaking} describes work done with great care. {For your pains} means as a reward for effort, often used ironically when the reward is inadequate or negative: {I helped him move and got a sore back for my pains}.

Painstaking describes work done with extreme care and thoroughness, paying close attention to every detail: {painstaking research}, {a painstaking restoration of the original manuscript}. The word emphasizes the effort invested rather than any suffering—someone who is painstaking takes pains to get things right.

Paint is a liquid substance that is applied to surfaces to protect and to add color. When you paint, you use this substance. House paint is applied to houses. Oil paints or acrylic paints may be used to create works of art. Someone who paints for living may be a painter of houses and buildings, or a creator of the works of art called paintings. If you paint your face, you apply cosmetics. If you paint over some bad thing, you try to disguise it in an amateur way.

Paintball is a competitive game where players shoot capsules of colored dye at opponents using air-powered guns. Getting hit marks you out. The sport combines elements of capture-the-flag with military simulation, played in woods or on specially designed courses: {We're going paintballing this weekend}. The capsules themselves are also called paintballs.

A paintbrush is a brush used to apply paint, consisting of bristles attached to a handle. Brushes vary widely by size, shape, and bristle type—from fine artist's brushes for detail work to broad house-painting brushes for walls. {She cleaned her paintbrushes after finishing the portrait.} Paintbrush also names a wildflower with bright brush-shaped blooms.

A painter is someone who paints—either an artist who creates pictures with paint or a worker who applies paint to surfaces like walls and buildings. The contexts rarely overlap: {She studied the Dutch painters} versus {We hired a painter to do the exterior}. Separately, a painter is a rope at the bow of a boat used for tying up.

Painting is the act of applying paint to a surface, whether for art or utility. A painting is the resulting work—typically pigment on canvas, paper, or wood: {The museum acquired a new painting}. The word covers both the activity {(She took up painting in retirement)} and the art form as a whole {(Dutch painting of the Golden Age)}. House painting and similar practical applications share the word but rarely the prestige.

A pair is two of the same thing that form a natural combination (pair of socks, pair of eyes) or two complementary things in a fixed relationship (a mating pair). Some wearable things that are a single object get called a pair (pair of glasses, pair of pants) because they have identical halves. You pair one thing with another when you put them together in a useful way: The wine pairs nicely with the fish. Electronic devices that pair are able to communicate with each other.

Pairs is the plural of pair—two things that go together or are meant to be used together. Cards or dice showing the same value form pairs. People coupled for dancing, competition, or romance are pairs: {The skating pairs took the ice}. In British slang, pairs can mean stairs, rhyming with "apples and pears."

Paisley is a distinctive teardrop-shaped pattern with a curved, feathery tail, originally from Persia and long associated with decorative textiles. The pattern appears on ties, scarves, bandanas, and fabrics: {a paisley tie}, {paisley print curtains}. The word functions as both noun and adjective. (Capitalized Paisley is a Scottish town.)

Pajama refers to loose, lightweight clothing worn for sleeping, typically consisting of pants and a matching top. The word is almost always plural in American English—{pajamas}—while British English uses {pyjamas}. As a modifier, pajama stays singular: {pajama pants}, {pajama party}. The garment originated in South Asia as loose trousers, adopted by Westerners first as loungewear.

Pajamas are loose-fitting clothes worn for sleeping, typically a matching top and bottom. The word comes from a Persian term for leg garments, adopted by the British in colonial India. In American English, pajamas; in British, pyjamas. {I spent all Sunday in my pajamas}. Informally shortened to PJs.

A pal is a friend, typically casual rather than intimate: {We've been pals since high school}. The word carries an informal, slightly old-fashioned warmth. As a form of address, pal can be friendly or confrontational depending on tone: {Hey pal, good to see you} versus {Listen here, pal}. To pal around is to spend time together as friends.

A palace is a grand, imposing residence, typically one occupied by royalty, a head of state, or other person of high rank and wealth. The word suggests architectural magnificence and often historical significance: {Buckingham Palace}, {the Palace of Versailles}. By extension, palace can describe any lavish or opulent building: {a movie palace}, {an ice palace}. In British usage, the palace often refers metonymically to the royal household or its official positions: {The palace declined to comment}.

A paladin is a heroic champion or noble knight, originally one of Charlemagne's legendary twelve peers. The word now describes any stalwart defender of a cause: {a paladin of free speech}, {paladins of justice}. In fantasy games, a paladin is a holy warrior class combining martial prowess with divine magic—a knight bound by a strict moral code.

Paladins is the plural of paladin, a heroic champion or defender of a noble cause. The word originally referred to the twelve legendary knights of Charlemagne's court. In modern usage, paladin describes someone who fights zealously for a cause: {paladins of justice}, {paladins of free speech}. In fantasy games and fiction, paladins are holy warriors who combine martial prowess with divine magic.

The palate is the roof of the mouth—the hard palate at the front, the soft palate at the back. By extension, palate means one's sense of taste or appreciation for flavors: {a refined palate}, {wines that appeal to the American palate}. A palate cleanser is a neutral food served between courses to refresh the taste buds.

Pale is most often an adjective characterizing things that are faintly or deficiently colored. Pale red, pale yellow, and pale green are all versions of those colors that lack brightness or saturation. If someone turns pale, their skin loses some color, often as a result of shock. The verb pale means to turn pale, but is often used figuratively: if one thing pales in relation to another, the second thing is much worse. An infrequent noun pale denotes a pole or stake, perhaps marking a boundary. Beyond the pale conveys the notion of beyond acceptable limits: His drunken behavior at the party was beyond the pale.

Paleo is short for Paleolithic, the prehistoric era when humans lived as hunter-gatherers. The term usually appears in {paleo diet}, an eating approach that mimics ancestral patterns—meat, fish, vegetables, nuts, and fruit while avoiding grains, dairy, and processed foods. As an adjective, paleo describes this lifestyle: {paleo recipes}, {going paleo}.

Paleontology is the scientific study of ancient life through fossils—the preserved remains or traces of organisms from past geological periods. Paleontologists examine bones, shells, footprints, and other evidence to reconstruct extinct species and understand how life evolved over millions of years. {The museum's paleontology department recently unveiled a new dinosaur skeleton.}

A palette is a board on which an artist mixes paints, traditionally held in one hand while painting with the other. By extension, palette means the range of colors an artist uses or the range of elements available in any creative domain: {The designer works with a muted palette}. A palette can also be a range of flavors in food and wine. In computing, a palette is a set of available colors or tools in graphics software.

Palettes is the plural of palette, a board on which an artist arranges and mixes paints. By extension, a palette is any range of colors or elements available for use: {The designer works with a muted palette}, {The chef's palette includes Asian and Mediterranean flavors}. In computing, a palette is a set of available colors, tools, or options displayed for selection.

A palindrome is a word, phrase, or sequence that reads the same backward as forward. Classic examples include *madam*, *racecar*, and *A man, a plan, a canal: Panama*. Spaces and punctuation are typically ignored when determining whether something qualifies. The concept extends to numbers: 12321 is a numeric palindrome.

A pallbearer is one of several people who carry or escort a coffin at a funeral. The term comes from the pall, a cloth draped over a coffin. Pallbearers are typically chosen from close friends or family members of the deceased: {He was honored to serve as a pallbearer at his uncle's funeral}.

Pallbearers are the people who carry a coffin at a funeral, typically six or eight, walking in formation from hearse to gravesite. The role is usually given to close friends or family members of the deceased as a mark of honor: {His brothers and childhood friends served as pallbearers}. Honorary pallbearers walk alongside without actually bearing weight.

Pallet is most likely to be encountered as a noun designating a platform used for storage and shipment of boxed or wrapped goods. It’s typically made of wood and is moved with a forklift. A different pallet is a small, hard bed, or a hard mattress. A painter’s pallet (also spelled palette) is the colors found in his or her works, or the board that actually holds little blobs of paint while in use.

The palm is the inner surface of the hand between the wrist and fingers. To palm something is to conceal it in your hand, as a magician palms a card or a basketball player illegally palms the ball. To {grease someone's palm} is to bribe them. To {have someone in the palm of your hand} is to have them under your control. Palm also names a family of tropical trees with fan-shaped or feather-shaped leaves and no branches—the coconut palm, date palm, oil palm. Palm fronds have long symbolized victory and peace; {Palm Sunday} commemorates Jesus's entry into Jerusalem, when crowds waved palm branches. (Capitalized Palm appears in product names like Palm Pilot.)

Palmoplantar refers to the palms of the hands and soles of the feet together, used almost exclusively in medical contexts. Palmoplantar {keratoderma} is thickening of skin on these surfaces. Palmoplantar {pustulosis} produces blisters there. The term appears because many conditions affect both areas simultaneously.

Palms are the inner surfaces of the hands, from wrist to fingers. To palm something is to conceal it in the hand: {The magician palmed the coin}. To palm off is to dispose of something deceptively: {He tried to palm off the forgery as genuine}. Palm also refers to tropical trees with fan-shaped or feathery leaves, or a branch carried as a symbol of victory. To win the palm is to triumph.

Palpitations are heartbeats you become uncomfortably aware of—racing, pounding, fluttering, or skipping. The heart may actually beat irregularly, or it may beat normally while feeling abnormal. Causes range from caffeine and anxiety to cardiac arrhythmias. {She felt palpitations after her third cup of coffee.} The singular palpitation exists but rarely appears outside medical contexts.

Pals are friends, typically close ones with an easy, familiar relationship. The word suggests warmth without formality: {We've been pals since college}. As a verb, to pal around is to spend time together casually: {They palled around all summer}. Pal can also be a form of address, sometimes friendly, sometimes confrontational: {Listen here, pal}.

To pamper is to treat with excessive care and attention, indulging someone's desires and shielding them from discomfort: {She pampered herself with a spa day}, {pampered pets}. The word often implies luxury or spoiling—giving more comfort than is strictly necessary. A pampered child may grow up expecting special treatment.

Pampered describes someone who has been treated with excessive care, comfort, or indulgence—often to the point of spoiling. A pampered {child} gets whatever they want. A pampered {pet} eats better than most people. The word can be neutral or slightly disapproving, suggesting someone unaccustomed to hardship: {She lived a pampered life until the money ran out}. To pamper is to indulge in this way.

Pampering is indulgent care or attention—treating someone (or yourself) with unusual comfort and luxury. A spa day, breakfast in bed, or letting a child skip chores might all count as pampering. The word carries a hint of excess: {After the project ended, she spent a week pampering herself}. What qualifies as pampering depends on what's normal—for some, it's a massage; for others, simply sleeping in.

A pamphlet is a small, unbound booklet—typically just a few pages, stapled or folded—covering a single topic. Pamphlets often present information, arguments, or propaganda: {a political pamphlet}, {health pamphlets in the waiting room}. Historically, pamphlets were a key medium for disseminating ideas before mass media.

Pamphlets is the plural of pamphlet, a small unbound booklet or leaflet, typically covering a single topic. Pamphlets have historically served political, religious, and educational purposes—distributed to spread ideas cheaply and widely: {Revolutionary pamphlets circulated through the colonies}. Today the word often suggests informational brochures: {The doctor's office had pamphlets on diabetes}.

A pan is a dish for cooking food in an oven or over heat (frying pan, roasting pan). A pan is usually shallower than a pot. If you pan for gold, you separate rock from gold in a shallow pan. If you pan something such as a movie or proposal, you criticize it severely. A different verb pan is related to panorama, and describes the movement of a camera: The cinematographer panned across the stage. Finally, pan is an adjective or combining form meaning all: The athlete competed in the Pan-American games.

Panache is flamboyant confidence and style—a distinctive flair that makes ordinary actions seem impressive. Someone who dresses with panache has bold, assured taste. To do something with panache is to do it with verve and showmanship: {She handled the crisis with panache}. The word implies not just competence but a certain swagger in the execution.

A panama is a lightweight hat made from plaited leaves of a Central American plant, traditionally worn in warm weather. Despite the name, the hats originated in Ecuador but gained their name from Panama, where they were widely sold to travelers crossing the isthmus. {He wore a cream panama tilted at a rakish angle.} (Capitalized Panama is the country.)

A pancake is a flat, round cake made from batter and cooked on both sides on a griddle or in a pan. Pancakes are typically eaten for breakfast with toppings like syrup or fruit. The flatness gives rise to figurative uses: something {flat as a pancake} is extremely level, and to pancake is to flatten or collapse: {The building pancaked during the earthquake}.

Pancakes are flat, round cakes made from batter and cooked on a griddle or pan. The American version is thick and fluffy, typically served in stacks with butter and maple syrup: {We had pancakes for breakfast}. British pancakes are thinner, closer to French crêpes. The word also works as a verb meaning to flatten or collapse: {The building pancaked during the earthquake}.

A panda is a large black-and-white bear native to China, known for eating bamboo and serving as a symbol of wildlife conservation. The term usually means the giant panda; the red panda is a smaller, unrelated animal with reddish fur and a bushy tail. {We saw the pandas at the zoo.}

Pandas are large bearlike mammals native to central China, with distinctive black and white markings. They eat almost exclusively bamboo. The giant panda is an endangered species and a symbol of wildlife conservation. The lesser-known red panda is a smaller, russet-colored animal more closely related to raccoons. In computing, pandas (often lowercase) is a popular Python library for data analysis and manipulation: {I used pandas to clean the dataset}.

A pandemic is an outbreak of disease that spreads across multiple countries or continents, affecting large populations. Distinguished from an epidemic, which is more geographically contained: {The 1918 flu pandemic killed millions worldwide}. The word gained everyday currency during the COVID-19 pandemic that began in 2020. Figuratively, pandemic describes anything spreading uncontrollably: {a pandemic of misinformation}.

Pandemics is the plural of pandemic, a disease outbreak that spreads across multiple countries or continents, affecting large populations. A pandemic differs from an epidemic mainly in geographic scope: {The 1918 flu and COVID-19 were pandemics; Ebola outbreaks have been epidemics}. The word also works as an adjective: {pandemic influenza}, {pandemic proportions}.

Pandemonium is wild uproar and chaos—noise, confusion, and disorder all at once. The word suggests a scene where control has broken down completely: {Pandemonium erupted when the verdict was announced}. Originally the name of the capital of Hell in Milton's *Paradise Lost*, it now describes any place or situation of tumultuous chaos.

Pandering is catering to base desires or prejudices, especially to gain approval or advantage. A politician panders when they tell audiences whatever they want to hear rather than what's true or responsible: {The speech was pure pandering to the base}. The word carries contempt—pandering suggests cynical manipulation rather than genuine responsiveness. In legal contexts, pandering specifically means procuring customers for prostitutes.

Panel has two main meanings. The first is a broad, flat surface or object with a particular purpose (solar panel, instrument panel). This meaning includes broad, flat boards used in building or to line interior walls. The second is a group of people with a particular task (advisory panel, panel of experts). To panel a room is to line its walls with panels; you may end up with an oak-paneled room.

Panels are distinct sections or pieces that form part of a larger whole. A door may have raised panels; a dress may be cut from panels of fabric; a comic strip tells its story through sequential panels. A panel is also a group assembled for discussion, judgment, or advice: {a panel of experts}, {a jury panel}. Control panels and instrument panels group switches and displays. To panel a room is to cover its walls with wooden panels.

A pang is a sudden, sharp feeling of physical or emotional pain. Physical pangs are typically brief and intense—hunger pangs, pangs of labor. Emotional pangs accompany distressing feelings like guilt, remorse, or longing: {She felt a pang of regret when she saw her old house}. The word nearly always appears with "of" followed by the specific sensation, emphasizing the acute but momentary nature of the discomfort.

Pangs are sudden sharp pains or spasms, physical or emotional. Hunger pangs grip the stomach. Pangs of guilt or remorse strike the conscience. The word almost always appears in the plural and typically with an of-phrase naming the cause: {pangs of jealousy}, {the pangs of unrequited love}.

A panhandle is a narrow strip of territory projecting from a larger region, shaped like the handle of a pan: {the Texas panhandle}, {the Florida panhandle}. The verb panhandle means to beg for money in public places, typically by approaching strangers on the street: {He panhandled outside the subway station}. A panhandler is someone who does this regularly.

A panhandler is someone who begs for money in public places, typically on city streets. The term is American and slightly euphemistic—it sounds more active than "beggar," suggesting someone working a stretch of sidewalk: {Panhandlers approached us outside the subway station}. The verb is panhandle: {He panhandled for bus fare}.

Panhandling is begging for money in public places, typically on streets or sidewalks. The term is American and slightly euphemistic—it sounds more official than "begging," which is why it appears in municipal codes and news reports: {The city passed an ordinance against aggressive panhandling}. A panhandler asks strangers for spare change, often with a sign or cup.

Panic is sudden, overwhelming fear that disrupts rational thought. A crowd may panic during a fire; an investor may panic when markets drop. The adjective panicked describes someone in this state: {a panicked expression}. To panic is to succumb to such fear: {Don't panic}. A panic attack is an episode of intense anxiety with physical symptoms. As slang, panic means to make someone laugh uncontrollably: {That comedian panics me}.

Panicked is the past tense of panic—to suddenly lose composure through fear or anxiety. Someone who panicked acted rashly under pressure: {She panicked and slammed the brakes}. The word can also work as an adjective describing the state itself: {panicked investors sold everything}, {a panicked look in his eyes}.

Panicky describes someone gripped by panic—frantic, overwhelmed by sudden fear or anxiety. It can also describe actions or decisions made in that state: {a panicky phone call}, {panicky selling on the stock market}. The word carries a slightly informal or colloquial tone compared to "panicked."

Panned is the past tense of pan in its critical sense: to disparage or harshly criticize, especially a creative work. {The film was panned by critics but beloved by audiences.} The metaphor comes from panning for gold—sifting through material and finding nothing of value. Separately, panned describes camera movement sweeping horizontally across a scene.

Panning has several meanings united by sweeping horizontal movement. In film and photography, to pan is to rotate the camera sideways, following action or surveying a scene: {The camera panned across the crowd}. In cooking, panning means cooking in a pan. In gold prospecting, panning is swirling water and sediment in a shallow pan to separate gold. To pan something is also to criticize it harshly: {Critics panned the film}. In audio, panning shifts sound between left and right channels.

A panorama is a wide, unobstructed view extending in all directions: {The summit offered a panorama of the valley below}. Originally, panoramas were large circular paintings viewed from inside, creating an illusion of being surrounded by a scene. The word now applies to any sweeping visual or comprehensive survey: {a panorama of 20th-century art}, {panoramic photographs} that capture wider angles than standard shots.

Pans are broad, shallow cooking vessels, typically metal, used on stovetops for frying, sautéing, and simmering. The word extends to similar containers used for other purposes: a {gold pan} for prospecting, a {bedpan} for the bedridden, or the pan of a toilet. To pan is to wash gravel in search of gold, or to criticize harshly: {Critics panned the film}. In filmmaking, to pan is to rotate a camera horizontally across a scene.

Pansies are garden flowers with velvety petals in varied colors, often with dark central markings that suggest a face. They bloom in cool weather and are popular for borders and containers. Pansy is also a derogatory term for an effeminate man or a weak, timid person: {Don't be such a pansy}. This slur, once common, now sounds dated.

A pansy is a garden flower with velvety, multicolored petals, often displaying a distinctive "face" pattern. The word is also a slur for an effeminate man or a gay man, or more broadly, someone considered weak or cowardly: {Don't be such a pansy}. The insult derives from the flower's delicate appearance and its association with effeminacy.

Pant describes rapid, shallow breathing—the kind that follows exertion or comes with strong emotion. Dogs pant to cool themselves; runners pant after sprints. To pant for something is to desire it intensely: {He panted for recognition}. As a noun, a pant is a single labored breath. Pants, the garment, is a separate word—pant as a modifier ({pant leg}, {pant suit}) is a back-formation from it.

A pantheon is the collection of gods belonging to a particular religion or mythology: {the Greek pantheon}, {the Hindu pantheon}. By extension, a pantheon is any group of highly respected or influential figures in a field: {She earned her place in the pantheon of jazz greats}. The word suggests a kind of immortal status within a domain. (Capitalized Pantheon is the ancient Roman temple.)

A panther is a large wild cat, though the term applies differently depending on region. In North America, panther usually means a cougar or mountain lion. In other parts of the world, it refers to leopards, especially black leopards—cats whose dark coloration obscures their spots. The Florida panther is an endangered cougar subspecies native to southern Florida. {A black panther stalked through the jungle undergrowth.} (Capitalized Panther often refers to the Black Panther Party or the Marvel superhero.)

Panthers is the plural of panther, a word that covers several large cats. In the Americas, panther usually means a cougar or mountain lion. Elsewhere it typically refers to a leopard, especially a black one—technically a melanistic leopard, though {black panther} has become the common term. The Florida panther is an endangered cougar subspecies. {Panthers prowled the jungle's edge.}

Panties are women's or girls' underpants, typically lightweight and close-fitting. The word carries a slightly informal or intimate connotation compared to the neutral "underwear." In American English, panties is standard; British English more often uses knickers. {She packed three pairs of panties for the trip.}

Panting is rapid, shallow breathing, typically from exertion or heat. Dogs pant to cool themselves; humans pant after sprinting up stairs. The word extends to eager anticipation: {fans panting for the sequel}. As an adjective, it describes breathlessness: {She arrived at the door, panting and flushed}.

Pantomime is acting without words, using gestures and facial expressions to convey meaning: {The street performer pantomimed being trapped in a box}. As a noun, it refers to this form of expression or a performance using it. In British English, pantomime (often shortened to panto) is a type of comic theatrical production performed during the Christmas season, featuring fairy tales, audience participation, and cross-dressing actors. More broadly, pantomime describes any exaggerated show or empty display: {The trial was a pantomime of justice}.

A pantry is a small room or closet used to store food, dishes, and kitchen supplies. Traditionally located near the kitchen, it keeps dry goods, canned items, and tableware organized and accessible: {The pasta is in the pantry}. A butler's pantry is a service area between kitchen and dining room for storing serving pieces and preparing food for the table.

Pants are a garment covering the body from waist to ankles, with separate sections for each leg. In American English, pants means trousers; in British English, pants means underpants. To pants someone is to yank their pants down as a prank. {She caught him with his pants down} means she found him unprepared or exposed. To {wear the pants} is to be the dominant partner in a relationship.

Pantyhose are sheer nylon stockings fused to panties, worn as a single garment covering the legs and waist. They emerged in the 1960s alongside miniskirts and largely replaced garter-held stockings. The word is usually plural: {She bought three pairs of pantyhose}. British English prefers tights.

Papa is an informal, often affectionate word for father, used especially by young children or in families where it's the traditional term: {Give Papa a kiss}. In some cultures and regions, papa refers specifically to a grandfather. In the NATO phonetic alphabet, Papa represents the letter P.

The papacy is the office and authority of the Pope, the head of the Roman Catholic Church. It also refers to a particular pope's tenure: {The papacy of John Paul II lasted 27 years}. More broadly, the papacy denotes the system of church government centered on papal authority, often discussed in historical or political contexts: {the medieval papacy's influence on European monarchs}.

Paparazzi are freelance photographers who aggressively pursue celebrities to capture candid shots for tabloids and gossip media. The word is Italian, borrowed from a photographer character in Fellini's 1960 film *La Dolce Vita*. A single such photographer is a paparazzo, though paparazzi often serves for both singular and plural: {The paparazzi swarmed the restaurant exit}.

Papaya is a large tropical fruit with orange flesh, black seeds, and a soft, butter-like texture when ripe. The fruit grows on a tall, palm-like tree native to Central America but now cultivated throughout the tropics. Papaya is eaten fresh, added to smoothies, or used in cooking—green papaya appears in Southeast Asian salads. The enzyme papain, extracted from papaya, is used as a meat tenderizer.

The core meaning of paper, a manufactured material for writing and drawing, inspires its many extended meanings. The mass noun refers to the substance generally, and paper (countable) or piece of paper denotes a single sheet of it. Some documents printed on paper, such as a newspaper or an academic report on a particular subject, can be called papers. Someone’s papers may be the documents establishing their identity, such as a passport or travel documents—or they may also be the a loosely defined collection of information on paper associated with a person: We found old love letters among her papers. As a verb, the most frequent meaning of paper pertains to wallpaper.

A paperback is a book with a flexible paper cover, as opposed to a hardcover with rigid boards. Paperbacks are cheaper to produce and lighter to carry. The term works as noun or adjective: {I'll wait for the paperback}, {the paperback edition}. Mass-market paperbacks are the small, inexpensive format sold in drugstores and airports; trade paperbacks are larger and pricier.

A paperboy is a person, traditionally a boy or young man, who delivers newspapers to homes on a regular route. The job was once a common first employment for teenagers, though the role has largely been taken over by adults in cars. {The paperboy tossed the newspaper onto the porch.}

A paperclip is a small bent wire used to hold sheets of paper together. The familiar double-loop design has remained largely unchanged since the late 19th century. To paperclip documents is to fasten them this way: {I paperclipped the receipt to the form}. The word also appears as two words or hyphenated.

A papercut is a small wound made by the edge of a sheet of paper slicing the skin. Despite being minor, papercuts are notoriously painful because they're shallow enough to expose nerve endings without drawing much blood: {I got a papercut opening the envelope}. The word also refers to the art of cutting decorative designs from paper.

Papers are documents, especially official ones establishing identity, status, or authorization: {The officer asked for my papers}. Immigration papers confirm legal residency. Walking papers means dismissal from a job. Divorce papers formalize the end of a marriage. Academic papers are scholarly essays. To paper something is to cover it with wallpaper, or to fill a venue with free tickets: {They papered the house to make the show look popular}.

Paperwork is the documents, forms, and administrative records required for official processes: {I spent the morning doing paperwork}. The term usually carries a tone of tedium—necessary but unexciting clerical tasks. Despite the name, paperwork now includes digital forms and electronic filing: {The paperwork for the loan application was all online}.

Paprika is a spice made from dried, ground peppers—ranging from mild and sweet to smoky or hot, depending on the variety. Hungarian paprika and Spanish pimentón are the most prized. The bright red powder colors and flavors dishes like goulash, deviled eggs, and paella: {She dusted the potatoes with paprika}.

Papyrus is a tall reed that grows in wetlands along the Nile and elsewhere, and also the writing material ancient Egyptians made from it by pressing strips of the plant's pith together. By extension, papyrus refers to any ancient manuscript written on such material: {The museum acquired a papyrus containing fragments of Homer}. Plural: papyri or papyruses.

Par is the standard or expected level—what's normal or acceptable. In golf, par is the number of strokes a skilled player should need for a hole or course: {two under par}, {bogey is one over par}. Something {on par with} another is equal to it. {Below par} or {not up to par} means substandard. {Par for the course} is what you'd typically expect, often said resignedly.

A parable is a short story that illustrates a moral or spiritual lesson. The term is especially associated with the teachings of Jesus—the parables of the Good Samaritan, the Prodigal Son, the Sower. Unlike fables, parables typically involve realistic human situations rather than talking animals. The word sometimes describes any story with an obvious moral: {The film is a parable about greed}.

A parachute is a fabric canopy that opens to slow descent through air. Skydivers and pilots use parachutes to land safely after jumping or ejecting from aircraft. Figuratively, a {golden parachute} is a generous severance package for executives. As a verb, to parachute is to descend by parachute or to insert suddenly: {They parachuted a new CEO into the struggling company}.

Parachutes are fabric canopies that slow descent through air by creating drag. Skydivers and cargo drops use parachutes to land safely. A golden parachute is a generous severance package for executives—a soft landing after being pushed out. To parachute in is to arrive suddenly from outside: {They parachuted in a new CEO from a rival firm}.

Parachuting is the activity of jumping from an aircraft and descending by parachute. The sport version is skydiving, which emphasizes freefall before deploying the chute. Military parachuting delivers troops or supplies behind enemy lines. {She took up parachuting after her sixtieth birthday.}

A parade is a public procession, typically celebratory or ceremonial: {the Thanksgiving Day parade}, {a military parade}. The verb means to march in such a procession, or more broadly, to display something ostentatiously: {He paraded his knowledge at every opportunity}. A parade of things is a series of them: {a parade of witnesses}. To {rain on someone's parade} is to spoil their enjoyment.

Parades is the plural of parade—a public procession celebrating an occasion or displaying military force: {holiday parades}, {victory parades}. The verb means to march in such a procession, or to display something conspicuously: {She parades her wealth}. To parade as something is to pose as it falsely: {He parades as an expert but knows nothing}.

Paradise refers literally to a place believed in some religions to exist or to have existed: that is, the Garden of Eden, heaven, or a sweet spot that the righteous experience before heaven. In this use, Paradise is most likely to be capitalized. Paradise also designates figuratively any earthly place full of enjoyment and delight, and often has a modifier before it (surfers’ paradise, tropical paradise, lovers’ paradise).

A paradox is an idea or fact that seems to contradict itself. A paradox may be true, in which case it has to be explained by unconventional means, or it may be false because of a failure to take a relevant fact into account. People sometimes use the word to talk about the unusual or counterintuitive, rather than the contradictory: The paradox of human life is the existence of an animal body and instincts with a mind that turns toward the heavens.

Paradoxes is the plural of paradox—statements or situations that seem self-contradictory but may contain truth. {The paradoxes of quantum mechanics challenge intuition}. A paradox can be a logical puzzle ({Zeno's paradoxes}), a surprising truth ({the paradox that less is more}), or an apparent contradiction in someone's character: {She was a paradox—generous yet ruthlessly ambitious}.

Paragliding is a recreational sport in which a person glides through the air while suspended from a fabric wing, having launched from a hill or cliff. Unlike hang gliding, the wing has no rigid frame—it's essentially a steerable parachute designed for sustained flight rather than descent. {We went paragliding over the Swiss Alps}.

A paragraph is a distinct section of writing, typically beginning on a new line and containing sentences that develop a single idea or topic. In casual speech, paragraph can mean any chunk of text: {Read me that paragraph}. The paragraph symbol (¶) marks where one begins or should begin. To paragraph is to divide text into such sections.

A parakeet is a small parrot, typically with bright plumage and a long tail. The term covers many species, but in American usage usually means the budgerigar—the common pet bird sold in pet stores: {The parakeet chirped from its cage}. Parakeets can be trained to mimic speech, though less reliably than larger parrots.

Parakeets is the plural of parakeet, a small to medium-sized parrot with a slender build and long tail feathers. The term covers many species kept as pets, most commonly the budgerigar: {The parakeets chattered noisily in their cage}. Parakeets are known for their bright plumage and ability to mimic human speech.

Two lines are parallel if they are aligned in the exact same direction and if extended in one plane would never meet. When cars are parked parallel, they are side by side at the same angle. Events or other abstractions that parallel each other happen at the same time or proceed in the same way. A parallel is something equal to another thing in essential aspects: There were striking parallels in the two accounts.

Parallels are things that correspond or run alongside each other without intersecting. Lines are parallel when they maintain equal distance. Events or situations are parallels when they share notable similarities: {The parallels between the two cases are striking}. To draw parallels is to point out resemblances. As a verb, to parallel something is to match or correspond to it: {Her career paralleled his in many ways}. Parallel bars are gymnastic equipment; parallel parking places a car alongside the curb.

Paralyse is the British spelling of paralyze—to cause loss of movement or sensation, typically through nerve damage or injury: {The accident paralysed him from the waist down}. Figuratively, to paralyse is to render helpless or unable to act: {Fear paralysed her}. Systems can be paralysed too: {The strike paralysed the city's transit network}.

Paralysed is the British spelling of paralyzed. To be paralysed is to lose the ability to move part or all of the body, typically from nerve damage or injury: {He was paralysed from the waist down after the accident}. Figuratively, paralysed describes being unable to act or function: {paralysed by fear}, {paralysed with indecision}. The spelling extends to paralyse and paralysing.

Paralysis is the loss of the ability to move part of the body, typically from nerve damage or disease. The meaning extends to any state of inability to act or function: {The scandal caused paralysis in the administration}. Economic or political paralysis describes systems frozen by indecision or conflict. {Analysis paralysis} is overthinking to the point of inaction.

To paralyze is to cause loss of muscle function, typically through nerve damage or disease: {The accident paralyzed him from the waist down}. The word extends to any inability to move or act: {Fear paralyzed her}. Systems and processes can be paralyzed—a strike paralyzes transportation, indecision paralyzes an organization. Also spelled paralyse in British English.

Paralyzed describes the inability to move or act. In its literal sense, a paralyzed limb or body has lost motor function, often from nerve damage or spinal injury: {She was paralyzed from the waist down}. Figuratively, paralyzed means frozen by overwhelming emotion or indecision: {paralyzed with fear}, {The committee was paralyzed by infighting}. Also the past tense of paralyze.

Paralyzes means to cause paralysis—loss of the ability to move. A spinal injury may paralyze someone from the waist down. The word extends to any kind of immobilization: {Fear paralyzed him}. A government can be paralyzed by gridlock, an economy by uncertainty. {The news paralyzed her; she couldn't speak.}

Paralyzing describes something that causes paralysis—literal inability to move, or figurative inability to act. A paralyzing {injury} damages the spine. Paralyzing {fear} renders someone frozen, unable to respond. Paralyzing {indecision} prevents any choice at all. The word emphasizes completeness: not merely slowing but stopping altogether.

A paramedic is a medical professional trained to provide emergency care outside hospitals—at accident scenes, in ambulances, during transport. Paramedics can administer medications, start IVs, and perform advanced procedures that basic emergency medical technicians cannot. {The paramedics arrived within minutes and stabilized him before the hospital transfer.}

Paramedics are emergency medical professionals who provide care outside hospitals—typically arriving by ambulance to treat injuries, heart attacks, or other acute conditions. They perform procedures like administering medications, inserting IVs, and operating defibrillators. {The paramedics arrived within minutes and stabilized him for transport.} Paramedic training falls between that of EMTs and physicians.

Paramilitary describes groups organized along military lines but operating outside official armed forces. Paramilitary organizations may support or oppose governments—from militia groups to rebel fighters to private security forces. The term often carries sinister overtones, suggesting violence without accountability: {paramilitary death squads}, {paramilitary training camps}. As a noun, a paramilitary is a member of such a group.

Paranoia is excessive, irrational suspicion that others intend harm or are conspiring against you. In clinical contexts, it describes a symptom of mental disorders involving persistent delusions of persecution. More loosely, paranoia is heightened distrust or anxiety about threats: {His paranoia about identity theft made him shred every receipt}. The adjective is paranoid.

Paranoid describes excessive, irrational suspicion—the sense that others are watching, judging, or plotting against you. {I know it sounds paranoid, but I think my coworkers are talking about me}. In clinical contexts, paranoid refers to a mental condition marked by delusions of persecution. Casually, it's often used for ordinary wariness: {Am I being paranoid, or did that car follow us for three blocks?}

Paranormal describes phenomena outside the range of normal experience or scientific explanation—ghosts, telepathy, precognition, and the like. The word implies events that seem to violate natural laws without claiming they actually do: {paranormal activity}, {paranormal investigators}. It occupies territory between skepticism and belief, leaving room for either.

Paraphernalia is the assorted equipment, accessories, or miscellaneous items associated with a particular activity: {fishing paraphernalia}, {camping paraphernalia}. The word often carries a slightly dismissive tone, suggesting clutter or excessive gear. {Drug paraphernalia} refers specifically to items used to consume illegal drugs—pipes, syringes, rolling papers—and appears frequently in legal contexts where possession itself may be criminal.

To paraphrase is to restate something in different words, usually for clarity or brevity: {Let me paraphrase what she said}. A paraphrase is the result—a rewording that preserves meaning while changing expression. Unlike quotation, paraphrase doesn't claim exact wording. Unlike summary, it may be as long as the original. {I'm paraphrasing, but that was the gist.}

A parasail is a parachute-like canopy towed behind a boat, lifting the rider into the air. The activity combines elements of parachuting and sailing—you're harnessed to the chute while a speedboat pulls you aloft over water. To parasail is to ride one: {We parasailed over the bay on vacation}. Also called parasailing.

Parasailing is a recreational activity where a person wearing a parachute-like canopy is towed behind a boat, rising into the air and gliding above the water. It's a common beach resort attraction offering aerial views without requiring skill: {We went parasailing in Cancun}. The participant typically launches and lands on the boat's platform.

A parasite is an organism that lives on or inside another organism, called the host, from which it obtains nutrients while providing no benefit in return and often causing harm. Fleas, tapeworms, and mistletoe are all parasites. The word extends readily to people who exploit others' generosity or resources without contributing anything: {He's been a parasite on his parents for years}. The adjective parasitic describes this relationship in both biological and figurative contexts.

Parasites are organisms that live on or in a host organism, deriving nutrients at the host's expense. Tapeworms, lice, and mistletoe are parasites. Figuratively, a parasite is someone who takes from others without contributing: {He's a parasite living off his parents}. The word carries strong contempt, suggesting both dependency and exploitation.

A parasol is a lightweight umbrella used as a sunshade rather than rain protection. Parasols are typically decorative, with lace or ruffled edges, and associated with women's fashion from earlier eras: {She twirled her parasol as she strolled through the garden}. The word comes from Italian roots meaning "shield from sun."

A paratrooper is a soldier trained to parachute from aircraft into combat zones or tactical positions. Paratroopers typically serve in airborne divisions and specialize in rapid deployment behind enemy lines: {Paratroopers secured the bridge before dawn}.

A parcel is a package wrapped for mailing or delivery: {The parcel arrived damaged}. The word extends to portions of land: {a forty-acre parcel}. To parcel something out is to divide and distribute it: {They parceled out the inheritance among the heirs}. The phrase {part and parcel} means an essential component: {Long hours are part and parcel of the job}.

Parcels are packages or bundles wrapped for shipping or carrying: {The mailroom was stacked with parcels}. A parcel of land is a defined piece of property: {a forty-acre parcel}. To parcel something out is to divide and distribute it: {They parceled out the inheritance among the heirs}. A {parcel of lies} is a collection of them.

Parched means extremely dry, typically from heat or lack of water. Soil becomes parched during drought; lips become parched in winter. The word commonly describes intense thirst: {I'm parched—is there anything to drink?} Parched also describes food dried by roasting: {parched corn}, {parched peanuts}.

Parchment is animal skin—typically sheep, goat, or calf—prepared as a writing surface. Before paper became common, manuscripts and official documents were written on parchment. The material is durable and takes ink well. Modern parchment paper is a treated paper used in baking, designed to be heat-resistant and nonstick: {Line the pan with parchment}.

Pardon functions as both request and grant. To pardon someone is to forgive an offense or excuse a fault: {I beg your pardon}. A pardon is official forgiveness—a government pardon releases someone from punishment for a crime. As an interjection, {pardon} or {pardon me} requests repetition of something not heard clearly, or serves as a polite apology for a minor breach: {Pardon me, I didn't see you there}.

Pardoned means officially forgiven or excused from punishment. A governor may pardon a prisoner, releasing them from further penalty. In everyday use, pardoned extends to social offenses: {Pardon me} or {I beg your pardon} asks forgiveness for a minor intrusion or requests someone repeat themselves. {The turkey was pardoned by the president.}

Pardons is the plural of pardon—official acts releasing someone from punishment for a crime, or more broadly, forgiveness for an offense. A president or governor grants pardons; a friend pardons a thoughtless remark. As a verb, pardons is the third-person singular: {She pardons every slight}. The phrase {pardon me} or {I beg your pardon} excuses minor social breaches or requests repetition.

A parent is a father or mother—someone who has produced or is raising a child. The word extends to any organism that generates offspring, and to things that give rise to others: a parent {company} owns subsidiaries, a parent {directory} contains subdirectories. To parent is to raise children: {She parented three kids on her own}. Parenting as a concept—with theories, styles, and anxieties—is a modern preoccupation.

Parentheses are curved marks ( ) used in pairs to enclose supplementary material—words, phrases, or sentences that clarify or aside from the main text: {The results (see table 3) were unexpected}. In mathematics, parentheses group operations: {(2 + 3) × 4}. Informally, {in parentheses} means as an afterthought or secondary point. The singular is parenthesis.

Parenthood is the state of being a parent—having and raising children. It encompasses the responsibilities, experiences, and identity that come with the role: {The transition to parenthood changed everything}. Parenthood can be biological or adoptive, and the word often appears in discussions of its challenges and rewards: {Nothing prepares you for parenthood}.

Parenting is the work of raising children—feeding, protecting, teaching, and guiding them toward adulthood. The term emerged in the late twentieth century as child-rearing became increasingly discussed as a skill set: {a parenting class}, {parenting styles}. It can describe hands-on care or broader philosophy: {attachment parenting}, {helicopter parenting}. The verb parent follows the same pattern: {How were you parented?}

Parents are a person's mother and father, the two people whose genetic material combined to produce them. The term extends to anyone who raises a child, regardless of biological connection: adoptive parents, foster parents, stepparents. Parent also functions as a verb meaning to raise children: {Parenting is harder than it looks}. In compounds, parent often indicates origin or source: a parent {company} owns subsidiaries, and a parent {directory} contains subfolders.

A parfait is a layered dessert served in a tall glass, typically alternating ice cream, fruit, syrup, and whipped cream. The French original is a frozen custard dessert, but American parfaits are usually unfrozen assemblages—yogurt parfaits layer yogurt with granola and berries: {She grabbed a fruit parfait for breakfast}.

A pariah is someone rejected or avoided by others—a social outcast. The word originally referred to members of a low caste in southern India, but now applies to any person or group shunned by society: {After the scandal, he became a pariah in the industry}. Nations that violate international norms are called pariah states.

Pariahs are people rejected by society or excluded from a group. The word comes from a caste in southern India considered untouchable by higher castes, but now refers to any outcast: {The scandal made him a pariah in his own industry}. Nations can also become pariahs: {a pariah state isolated by sanctions}.

Parikrama is the Hindu and Buddhist practice of walking clockwise around a sacred site, temple, or object as an act of devotion. The circumambulation may circle a shrine, mountain, or holy city, with pilgrims sometimes prostrating at intervals. {Devotees perform parikrama around the temple at dawn}. The practice appears in Jainism and Sikhism as well.

A parish is a district served by a single church or priest, the basic administrative unit of many Christian denominations. The term extends to the congregation itself—the people who belong to that church. In Louisiana, parish replaces county as the primary local government division, a legacy of French and Spanish colonial rule. {The whole parish turned out for the funeral.}

Usage of noun and verb park has resulted in their having fairly different associations. The noun park, in most uses where no modifier is present, conjures up a place with lawn, trees, and perhaps pleasant walkways. Other kinds of parks that are identified with a modifier acquire all of their associations from the modifier, pleasant or otherwise: car park, skate park, trailer park. As a verb, the predominant use of park pertains to putting vehicles in a resting place: You can’t park there. Park your car across the street. When used for something other than a vehicle, park is somewhat informal and means to settle something in a place, often temporarily: Why don’t you park the money in a savings account?

A parka is a heavy hooded jacket designed for cold weather, typically extending to mid-thigh or below. The hood often has a fur or faux-fur trim to protect the face from wind. Originally worn by Arctic peoples, parkas have become standard winter outerwear: {She pulled on her parka before heading out into the snow}.

Parking is the act of leaving a vehicle stationary in a designated spot, or the space where this happens: {Is there parking near the restaurant?} A parking {lot} or parking {garage} provides spaces for multiple vehicles. Parking {meter}, parking {ticket}, parking {permit}. To park is the verb: {I parked on the street}.

Parkour is the athletic discipline of moving through urban environments by running, jumping, climbing, and vaulting over obstacles in the most efficient path possible. Practitioners treat railings, walls, and rooftops as a continuous course: {He did parkour across the rooftops}. The practice originated in French suburbs and spread globally through viral videos. Also called freerunning, though purists distinguish between them.

Parks are public green spaces in urban or suburban areas, set aside for recreation and enjoyment: {We took the kids to the park}. National and state parks preserve natural landscapes on a larger scale. To park is to leave a vehicle stationary: {I parked behind the building}. You can also park yourself somewhere, meaning to sit or settle: {She parked herself on the couch all afternoon}.

Parliament in its general sense is a legislative assembly, typically one with elected representatives who debate and pass laws. The word evokes formal governmental procedure—speeches, votes, motions, and committees.
