Many countries have parliaments as their primary legislative body: {The bill passed parliament after months of debate}. In casual use, parliament can describe any formal deliberative gathering. (Capitalized Parliament refers to a specific national legislature, especially Britain's.)

Parliaments is the plural of parliament, a legislative body that makes laws and oversees government. The word typically refers to multiple such assemblies across different countries or to successive sessions within one nation: {Several European parliaments debated the treaty}. In Britain, each parliament lasts until dissolution and new elections: {Three parliaments have considered the issue}.

A parlor is a room for receiving guests or conducting business, now somewhat old-fashioned for a living room in a home. The word persists in compounds: a funeral {parlor} handles the dead, a beauty {parlor} offers hair and nail services, an ice cream {parlor} serves desserts, a massage {parlor} may or may not be legitimate. {Parlor tricks} are minor entertainments suitable for showing off to guests.

Parmesan is a hard, dry Italian cheese with a sharp, nutty flavor, typically grated over pasta, salads, and soups. True Parmigiano-Reggiano comes from specific Italian regions and ages at least twelve months; generic parmesan varies widely in quality. {Pass the parmesan.} The cheese appears in Caesar salad, chicken parmesan, and countless Italian dishes.

Parmigiana is a style of Italian cooking in which meat or vegetables are breaded, fried, and baked with tomato sauce and melted cheese—typically mozzarella and Parmesan. Eggplant parmigiana and chicken parmigiana are the most common preparations: {I'll have the chicken parm}. The shortened form *parm* is standard in casual American speech.

Parodies are works that imitate others for comic effect or criticism. A parody exaggerates distinctive features of its target—style, mannerisms, conventions—to expose or mock them: {The film is a parody of action movie clichés}. To parody is to create such an imitation. A failed attempt at something serious may be called a parody: {The trial was a parody of justice}.

A parody is a humorous imitation that exaggerates the style or content of something—a work of art, a genre, a person—for comic effect or criticism. Unlike satire, which targets behavior or institutions, parody targets the thing itself: its mannerisms, conventions, clichés. {The film is a parody of action movies}. To parody is to create such an imitation: {He parodies politicians on his podcast}.

Parole is the conditional release of a prisoner before their sentence ends. The parolee must follow rules—regular check-ins, staying employed, avoiding certain people—or risk returning to prison: {He was released on parole after serving eight years}. To parole someone is to grant this release. In linguistics, parole refers to actual speech acts as opposed to the abstract language system.

Paroled means released from prison before serving a full sentence, under conditions that allow authorities to return the person to custody if they violate terms. {He was paroled after serving eight years of a fifteen-year sentence.} The word extends to any conditional release: {The hostages were paroled on condition they leave the country immediately.}

A parrot is a tropical bird with a curved beak and colorful plumage, known for its ability to mimic human speech. Many species are kept as pets: {The parrot repeated everything she said}. As a verb, to parrot is to repeat mechanically without understanding: {He just parrots whatever he reads online}.

Parroting is repeating what someone else has said without understanding or original thought—like a parrot mimicking human speech. The term is usually dismissive: {He's just parroting talking points}. To accuse someone of parroting implies they lack independent thinking or are blindly echoing authority.

Parrots are tropical birds with curved beaks, bright plumage, and the ability to mimic human speech. The word extends to people who repeat others' words without understanding: {He just parrots whatever his boss says}. As a verb, to parrot is to repeat mechanically: {She parroted the talking points}.

To parry is to deflect or ward off a blow or thrust, especially in fencing or combat: {She parried his lunge with a quick flick of her blade}. The word extends to deflecting verbal attacks or awkward questions: {He parried questions about his resignation}, {She deftly parried the criticism}. A parry is such a defensive move. (Capitalized Parry is a surname.)

Parsley is a leafy herb used as a garnish and flavoring in cooking. The flat-leaf variety (Italian parsley) has stronger flavor; the curly variety is milder and often decorative. {Sprinkle fresh parsley over the pasta.} A sprig of parsley on the plate signals a finished dish, though it often goes uneaten.

A parsnip is a root vegetable related to the carrot, with cream-colored flesh and a sweet, earthy flavor that intensifies after frost. Parsnips are typically roasted, mashed, or added to soups and stews: {The roasted parsnips caramelized beautifully}. They were a staple starch in Europe before the potato arrived from the Americas.

Parsnips are root vegetables related to carrots, with cream-colored flesh and a sweet, earthy flavor that intensifies when roasted. They resemble pale, thick carrots and are typically harvested after frost, which converts their starches to sugars: {roasted parsnips with honey glaze}. Common in soups, stews, and as a side dish.

Part is a frequently used word that expresses four different parts of speech. The core meaning is from the noun: a subdivision of a larger thing. All other meanings of part are related to this notion of a whole and its subdivisions. As a verb, part means to divide something that was formerly united. As an adjective, part has the same meaning as partial, an adjective derived from part. The noun party comes from the same source as part.

Partial means incomplete or constituting only a part: {a partial solution}, {partial payment}. It also means biased or favoring one side: {The referee seemed partial to the home team}. To be partial to something is to have a liking for it: {I'm partial to chocolate}. A partial in music is one of the component frequencies that make up a complex tone.

To participate is to take part in something—an activity, event, discussion, or group effort. The word implies active involvement rather than passive observation: {Everyone participated in the cleanup}. Participation can range from minimal {(At least participate in the conversation)} to full engagement {(She participated in every aspect of the campaign)}.

Participation is the act of taking part in something. You can have participation in a contest, a discussion, or a crime. The word often appears in contexts emphasizing inclusion or engagement: {audience participation}, {class participation}, {participation in democracy}. A {participation trophy} is awarded merely for showing up, implying no achievement beyond presence.

A particle is a tiny piece or fragment of something—a speck so small it barely registers: {particles of dust}, {a particle of truth}. In physics, particles are the fundamental units of matter and energy: electrons, protons, photons. In grammar, particles are small functional words like "up" in "give up" or "to" in infinitives—words that don't fit neatly into major categories but do essential work.

Particles are tiny pieces or fragments of matter—specks of dust, grains of sand, droplets in a mist. In physics, particles are the fundamental units of matter and energy: subatomic particles like electrons and quarks. In grammar, particles are small function words that don't fit neatly into major categories—words like *to* in infinitives or *up* in phrasal verbs like {look up}.

The sound pattern of the adjective particular makes it easy to overlook its relation to particle. That’s worthwhile remembering, because particle is about things that are individually identifiable and limited, and ideas are associated with particular. In its core use, particular is the opposite of general, in characterizing something that is single and specific. When used to characterize a person or animal, particular means very selective or attentive to small things: My cats are very particular about their food. As a noun, particulars (nearly always plural) designates specific points or details about something: Let me brief you on the particulars of the case.

Parties is the plural of party in all its senses. A party is a social gathering for celebration or entertainment: {We're throwing a surprise party}. In law and politics, a party is a participant or organized group: {the injured party}, {political parties}. To party is to celebrate, often with drinking: {We partied until dawn}.

Parting is the act of separating or leaving. A parting is a departure, especially a final one: {Such sweet sorrow at our parting}. As an adjective, parting describes something done at the moment of leaving: a parting {glance}, parting {words}, a parting {shot}. In British English, a parting is where hair divides on the head—what Americans call a part.

Partisan describes strong, often uncritical support for a party, cause, or person. A partisan voter supports their party regardless of candidate quality. Partisan politics prioritizes party loyalty over compromise or independent judgment. The word carries connotations of bias: {a partisan account of the conflict}. A partisan is also a member of an armed resistance group operating in enemy-occupied territory—irregular fighters conducting guerrilla warfare. The adjective form describes such fighters: {partisan forces harassed supply lines}.

Partisans are strong supporters of a party, cause, or person—often implying bias or unwillingness to consider opposing views: {partisan politics}, {partisan bickering}. The word works as both noun and adjective. A partisan is also a member of an irregular military force fighting an occupying army, especially in World War II: {Yugoslav partisans harassed German supply lines}.

A partition is a division in something formerly unified. A room partition is a physical barrier that divides a room in two. A partition in a hard drive designates separate storage areas. When you partition something, you introduce a division into it. A partitioned country, like Ireland or Korea, was formerly unified. The act of partitioning is also called partition.

A partner is someone who shares an activity, business, or life with another. Business partners share ownership and responsibility. A partner in a law firm has equity stake. In relationships, partner has become the neutral term for a romantic companion regardless of marital status or gender: {my partner and I are moving in together}. To partner with someone is to join forces: {We partnered with a local nonprofit}.

Partners are people or entities joined in a common purpose. Business partners share ownership and responsibility. Romantic partners share a life: {my partner of twenty years}. Partner has become the neutral term for a significant other regardless of marital status or gender. Dance partners move together. To partner with someone is to join forces: {We partnered with a local nonprofit}.

Partnership is a relationship between people or groups working together toward shared goals. In business, a partnership is a formal arrangement where two or more parties share ownership, profits, and liabilities: {She went into partnership with her college roommate}. The word extends to any cooperative alliance: {a partnership between the university and local hospitals}. In personal contexts, partnership often describes a committed romantic relationship, especially one not formalized by marriage.

A partridge is a plump, ground-dwelling game bird related to pheasants and quail. Several species exist across Europe, Asia, and North America, prized by hunters for sport and meat. The bird appears prominently in the Christmas carol "The Twelve Days of Christmas": {a partridge in a pear tree}.

Parts are pieces or portions of something larger. A machine has parts; so does a story, a country, or a body. To take part is to participate. Parts can mean a region: {She's not from these parts}. In acting, a part is a role: {He landed the lead part}. To part is to separate: {The crowd parted}, {We parted ways}. Someone's parts, now old-fashioned, are their talents or abilities: {a man of many parts}.

The range of meanings of the noun party nearly always involve people. In legal and situational contexts, a party is one person, or a group of people considered as one: None of the parties concerned wished to pursue the matter. A third party is someone not directly involved in a matter between two others (the first and second parties). The party that is an event or activity is a gathering of people united for a purpose, often celebratory: birthday party, wedding party. An institutional party has members who share political beliefs and goals. The verb party is informal and related to the celebratory event: The students partied all night at the end of the semester.

Partying is engaging in social celebration, typically involving drinking, dancing, or other revelry: {We were out partying until 3 a.m.} The word covers everything from casual nights out to extended periods of hedonistic behavior. Someone who's been {partying hard} has been indulging heavily, often with implications of excess.

Pass is a frequent verb and noun with meanings involving the idea of movement. The movement is often of one thing in relation to another: We passed an accident on our way to the concert. The verb pass can imply success: The law is set to pass. He will pass the test. The noun pass can designate any instance of passing: The student asked for a hall pass. He struggled up the mountain pass. There is sometimes confusion between the form passed and the adjective past are sometimes confused because they have the same pronunciation and can have overlapping meanings.

Passage is fundamentally about moving through or across something. A passage is a corridor or narrow way allowing movement: {a secret passage behind the bookcase}. A passage can be a section of text or music: {a difficult passage in the sonata}, {a passage from scripture}. The passage of time is its passing. Passage also means the act of traveling, especially by ship: {We booked passage to England}. In legislation, passage is approval: {passage of the bill}.

Passages are ways through—corridors, channels, or routes that allow movement from one place to another: {a narrow passage between buildings}, {the Northwest Passage}. The word extends to sections of text or music: {a difficult passage in the sonata}, {She highlighted several passages in the book}. Passage also means the act of passing or moving through: {the passage of time}, {the bill's passage through Congress}. A rite of passage marks transition from one stage of life to another.

Passed is the past tense of pass. Something passed through, by, or over: {The parade passed our house}. Time passed: {Years passed before they spoke again}. A bill passed the legislature. You passed an exam or passed on an opportunity. Someone who has passed has died—a gentle euphemism: {Her mother passed last spring}. Not to be confused with past, the adjective and noun referring to earlier time.

A passenger is someone being transported in a vehicle operated by another—in a car, plane, train, bus, or ship. The passenger rides rather than drives or pilots: {The taxi picked up three passengers}. Passenger also modifies: {passenger seat}, {passenger train}, {passenger pigeon}. Figuratively, a passenger is someone who contributes nothing to a group effort: {He's just a passenger on the team}.

Passengers are people being transported in a vehicle, vessel, or aircraft without operating it. A car has a driver and passengers; a plane has pilots and passengers. The word implies passive conveyance—you're along for the ride. A {passenger seat} is the front seat beside the driver. Figuratively, someone who contributes nothing to a group effort may be called a passenger: {He's just a passenger on this project}.

A passerby is someone who happens to be walking past a particular place: {A passerby noticed the smoke and called 911}. The word emphasizes the incidental nature of presence—passersby are witnesses or bystanders, not participants. Plural: passersby.

Passersby is the plural of passerby, a person who happens to be walking past a particular location. The term typically appears in accounts of public incidents where witnesses are needed: {Several passersby stopped to help the injured cyclist}. Though passersby is the standard plural, some speakers use passerby for both singular and plural, and the variant passerbys occasionally appears.

Passes covers movement through or by something, and extensions of that idea. A mountain pass is a route through a range; a pass in sports sends the ball to a teammate; a boarding pass permits you to board. To pass is to go by or beyond: {The truck passed us on the highway}. Time passes. If you pass on an offer, you decline it. A pass at someone is a sexual advance. In plural, passes often refers to attempts or efforts: {He made several passes at fixing the code before giving up}.

Passing describes movement by or through something, or the act of going past. A passing car goes by; passing time moves forward. Something done in passing happens briefly or incidentally: {He mentioned it in passing}. Passing also means the end of something—a passing era, or death itself: {We mourned her passing}. In sports, passing moves the ball to teammates. A passing grade barely meets the standard. To pass as something is to be accepted as that thing, especially when the identity is assumed: a light-skinned Black person passing as white, a transgender woman passing as cisgender.

Passion is a strong feeling of various kinds (sexual passion, passion for gardening). Your passion (it seems everyone is expected to have at least one) is the thing that motivates and interests you most in life. In the context of Christianity, Passion is usually capitalized and designates the suffering of Jesus between the Last Supper and his crucifixion. It may also denote a musical work based on this.

Passionate describes intense emotion or strong feeling. A passionate {kiss} burns with desire. A passionate {advocate} fights fervently for a cause. The word implies heat and fervor—someone passionate about their work throws themselves into it completely. Passion can tip toward excess: a passionate {outburst} may lack restraint. The word often suggests admirable intensity, though it can shade toward the irrational.

Passionfruit is a tropical fruit with a tough outer rind and a soft, seed-filled interior of aromatic, tangy pulp. The flavor is intensely sweet-tart, making it popular in juices, desserts, and cocktails. The name comes from the passion flower vine on which it grows—so called because missionaries saw in its elaborate blooms symbols of Christ's crucifixion. {The pavlova was topped with fresh passionfruit.}

Passions are intense emotions or strong enthusiasms. The word suggests feelings powerful enough to override reason: {crimes of passion}, {a passionate argument}. A passion can be something you care deeply about: {Photography is her passion}. The Passion refers specifically to Christ's suffering and crucifixion. In older usage, passions were any strong emotions—love, hate, anger, grief—that moved the soul.

Passive describes a state of receiving action rather than initiating it. A passive {observer} watches without participating. In grammar, passive voice makes the object of an action into the subject: {The ball was thrown} rather than {He threw the ball}. Passive often carries negative connotations of excessive submission or inaction: {Don't be so passive—stand up for yourself}. Passive {income} requires no active effort. Passive-aggressive behavior expresses hostility indirectly through sulking, stubbornness, or deliberate inefficiency rather than open confrontation.

A passport is a government-issued document certifying the holder's identity and citizenship, required for international travel. Border officials examine passports to control who enters and exits a country. Figuratively, a passport is anything that grants access or acceptance: {A degree from that university is a passport to success}. {She renewed her passport before the trip}.

Passports are official government documents certifying the holder's identity and citizenship, required for international travel. A passport allows entry into foreign countries and re-entry into one's own. The word extends metaphorically to anything granting access or acceptance: {A degree from that university is a passport to success}. {She renewed her passport before the trip.}

A password is a secret word or string of characters used to verify identity and gain access to something protected—an account, a system, a physical space. Passwords authenticate: if you know the password, you're presumed to be authorized. {I forgot my password again.} In casual use, password can mean any key to acceptance: {Knowing the band's early work was the password to his respect.}

Passwords are secret strings of characters used to verify identity and control access to accounts, systems, or secured spaces. Originally spoken phrases that granted entry—{What's the password?}—they now dominate digital security, where users create and manage dozens: {I forgot my password again}. A strong password mixes letters, numbers, and symbols; a weak one invites breach.

The preposition past is related to the verb pass and its meanings are also related. In regard to time, past means after. When talking about space, past is similar to beyond, and it can also be used in figurative meanings of beyond: We’re past the point where we can think about moving.

Pasta is food made from flour and water, formed into shapes and boiled. The word comes from Italian, where it simply means dough or paste. Pasta appears in countless forms—spaghetti, penne, lasagna, ravioli—each suited to different sauces and preparations. {We're having pasta for dinner.} Though associated with Italian cuisine, pasta dishes now appear worldwide.

Paste is a thick, soft, moist substance that can be spread or molded. As a verb, to paste is to attach something using an adhesive paste, or in computing, to insert copied data from a clipboard into a new location: {Just paste the link into your browser}. The copy-and-paste function has become so fundamental that paste now often implies digital insertion rather than physical gluing. A paste can also be a soft food mixture like {tomato paste} or {almond paste}, or an imitation gemstone made from glass.

Pastel describes pale, soft colors—pink, lavender, mint, peach—as if white had been mixed in to mute their intensity. The word comes from the chalky drawing sticks artists use, which produce these gentle hues: {a pastel sketch}, {done in pastels}. Pastel often suggests springtime, nurseries, or deliberate softness: {pastel Easter eggs}, {a room decorated in pastels}.

Pastels are drawing sticks made of powite powdered pigment bound with gum, producing soft, muted colors. The term extends to the colors themselves—pale, delicate shades with low saturation: {The nursery was painted in pastels}. As an adjective, pastel describes these soft hues: {pastel pink}, {pastel blue}. A pastel is also a work of art created with these sticks.

A pastime is an activity done for enjoyment in one's spare time: {Gardening is her favorite pastime}. The word emphasizes pleasant occupation rather than productive work—something that makes time pass agreeably. Reading, fishing, and collecting stamps are classic pastimes.

A pastor is a minister or priest in charge of a Christian church or congregation. The word comes from the Latin for shepherd, and pastors are understood to tend their flocks spiritually—guiding, teaching, and caring for members. {Our pastor gave a moving sermon on forgiveness.} The role varies across denominations, from Catholic priests to Protestant ministers to nondenominational church leaders.

Pastoral relates to the countryside, rural life, and the tending of sheep or cattle. A pastoral scene depicts peaceful farmland or meadows; pastoral duties involve caring for livestock. The word extends to spiritual care: a pastor tends a congregation as a shepherd tends a flock, so pastoral counseling addresses someone's emotional and spiritual needs. In literature and art, the pastoral is a genre idealizing simple rural existence, often contrasting it with urban corruption.

Pastrami is a highly seasoned smoked beef, typically made from brisket or navel cut, cured with a peppery spice rub. It's most associated with Jewish delicatessens and New York City, where a pastrami on rye with mustard is iconic: {I'll have a hot pastrami sandwich}. The meat is sliced thin and served warm.

Pastries are baked goods made from dough, typically rich with butter or other fats. The term covers a range from flaky croissants and puff pastry to filled items like Danish, éclairs, and turnovers. A pastry shop or bakery's pastry case displays these alongside cakes and tarts. {She picked up some pastries for breakfast.}

Pastry is a dough made from flour, fat, and water, used as a base or covering for baked goods like pies, tarts, and croissants. The term also refers to sweet baked items made from such dough: {The bakery sells pastries and bread}. Different types—puff pastry, shortcrust, phyllo—vary in texture and preparation method.

Pasture is land covered with grass or other plants suitable for grazing livestock. Cattle, sheep, and horses feed in pastures. The verb means to put animals out to graze: {We pasture the horses in the lower field}. To {put out to pasture} is to retire someone or something from active service, often implying they've outlived their usefulness.

Pastures are fields of grass or other plants where livestock graze. The word suggests open land maintained for animals rather than crops: {The cattle were moved to fresh pastures}. Figuratively, {greener pastures} means better opportunities elsewhere: {She left for greener pastures in California}. To pasture animals is to put them out to graze. {Put out to pasture} means retired, often dismissively.

Pat is a light touch or tap with the hand, usually to show affection or approval: {She gave the dog a pat on the head}. To pat is to touch this way: {He patted her shoulder reassuringly}. A pat of butter is a small, flat portion. As an adjective, pat means too smooth or rehearsed—suspiciously ready: {a pat answer}, {He had his excuses down pat}. To {stand pat} is to refuse to change position, from poker terminology for keeping one's dealt hand. (Capitalized Pat is a given name.)

Patch, a noun and verb, has multiple meanings, many of them with a common theme of a small area distinct from its surroundings. You grow food in a vegetable patch; a patch on a garment covers a hole. A software patch is new code placed over old code to repair a problem. A nicotine patch placed on the skin delivers nicotine to the bloodstream. When you patch something, you place a patch of some kind on it, usually for repair, but you can also patch up a relationship, that is, take steps to repair it.

Patches is the plural of patch—small pieces of material used to cover holes, wounds, or worn spots: {The jeans had patches on both knees}. Software patches are updates that fix bugs or security flaws. Patches of land or color are distinct areas: {patches of fog}, {patches of sunlight}. To go through a rough patch is to experience a difficult period. Patches is also a common name for spotted dogs and cats.

Patchwork is needlework made by sewing together small pieces of different fabrics to form a larger design, as in a patchwork quilt. The term extends to anything assembled from diverse, often mismatched parts: {a patchwork of fields and forests}, {a patchwork of local regulations}. The implication is usually of improvisation or inconsistency rather than unified design.

Patchy describes something uneven or inconsistent, with gaps or variations across its extent. A patchy lawn has bare spots among the grass. Patchy fog appears in some areas but not others. Patchy knowledge or patchy coverage suggests incomplete or spotty distribution: {My memory of that night is patchy}. {Service in rural areas remains patchy at best}.

A patent is an official grant giving an inventor exclusive rights to make, use, and sell an invention for a limited period—typically twenty years. To patent something is to obtain such protection: {She patented the design before launching the product}. Patent also means obvious or unconcealed: {a patent lie}, {patent nonsense}. As an adjective describing inventions, it means protected by patent: {patent medicine}. Patent leather has a glossy, lacquered finish.

Patents are government-granted exclusive rights to make, use, or sell an invention for a limited period—typically twenty years. The system rewards innovation by protecting inventors from competition while requiring public disclosure of how the invention works. To patent something is to obtain such protection: {She patented the design before seeking investors}. Patent also functions as an adjective meaning obvious or unconcealed: {a patent lie}, {patent nonsense}. Patent leather has a glossy, lacquered finish.

Paternalism is the practice of restricting people's freedom or making decisions for them, ostensibly for their own good. The term evokes a father controlling his children—benevolent intent paired with denial of autonomy. It appears in discussions of government policy, workplace management, and personal relationships: {The new regulations smack of paternalism}. Critics use the word to challenge authority that presumes to know what's best for others.

Paternity is the state of being a father, or the identity of a child's biological father. A paternity {test} determines whether a man fathered a particular child. Paternity {leave} is time off work granted to new fathers. In legal contexts, establishing paternity creates obligations for child support and rights to custody.

A path is a way of reaching a destination or goal. Cyclists travel on a bike path; a spiritual path is your religious or secular practice. A path forward is a way, as yet untried, that may lead to a goal. If something or someone crosses your path, you come across them, perhaps unexpectedly. The path you follow is the particular way you reach a goal, result, or destination.

Pathetic describes something that arouses pity or sadness: {a pathetic sight}, {pathetic cries for help}. More commonly now, it means contemptibly inadequate or weak—deserving scorn rather than sympathy: {That was a pathetic excuse}, {His attempts at flirting were pathetic}. The shift from pitiful to pitiable captures how the word moved from compassion to dismissal.

A pathfinder is someone who goes ahead to find or make a route through unfamiliar territory. The term extends to anyone who pioneers new methods or opens new fields: {She was a pathfinder in women's athletics}. Pathfinder also names various navigation devices and exploration vehicles, including NASA's 1997 Mars mission.

Paths is the plural of path—a track or way for walking, or a course of movement or action. Physical paths are trails through woods or gardens: {The paths through the park were covered in leaves}. Abstract paths are trajectories or approaches: {career paths}, {paths to success}, {We took different paths in life}. In computing, a path specifies a file's location in a directory structure.

Patience is the capacity to wait calmly or endure difficulty without complaint. It implies tolerating delays, frustrations, or suffering with composure rather than anxiety or anger: {Have patience—your turn will come}. To {try someone's patience} is to test the limits of their tolerance. A patient person remains steady; {I don't have the patience for this} signals that limit has been reached.

Patient describes the ability to wait calmly or endure difficulty without complaint. A patient {teacher} explains things repeatedly. {Be patient—your turn will come.} The word implies tolerating delays, annoyances, or suffering with steady composure rather than frustration. As a noun, a patient is someone receiving medical care: {The doctor saw twelve patients today}.

Patients are people receiving medical care or treatment. A doctor's patients are under their professional attention: {The physician sees about thirty patients a day}. The word implies a relationship—you become someone's patient when they take responsibility for your health. In research contexts, patients are human subjects in clinical studies.

Patina is the greenish film that forms on copper and bronze through oxidation over time—the verdigris on old statues and weathered roofs. By extension, patina refers to any surface appearance that develops with age and use: {The leather had acquired a rich patina}. Figuratively, patina suggests a veneer of quality or authenticity that comes from time or experience: {The old hotel had a patina of faded elegance}.

A patio is a paved outdoor area adjoining a house, used for dining, lounging, or entertaining. Unlike a deck, which is raised and made of wood, a patio sits at ground level and is typically made of stone, brick, or concrete: {We grilled burgers on the patio}. In Spanish-speaking regions, patio refers to an interior courtyard.

A patisserie is a bakery specializing in pastries, cakes, and other fine desserts—or the pastries themselves. The word is French and retains its French flavor in English, suggesting elegance and craftsmanship beyond ordinary baked goods: {We stopped at a patisserie for macarons and éclairs}.

A patriarch is the male head of a family, clan, or tribe—the senior figure whose authority extends over generations. In religious contexts, the term designates high-ranking leaders: the biblical patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; or bishops heading major Orthodox Christian churches. More loosely, a patriarch is any venerable old man who seems to embody traditional authority: {He was the patriarch of American jazz}. The word often carries connotations of benevolent but old-fashioned rule.

Patriarchs are male heads of families, clans, or tribes—figures of authority in traditional kinship structures. In biblical usage, the patriarchs are the founding fathers of Israel: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The term extends to venerable old men or senior figures in any hierarchy: {the patriarchs of the civil rights movement}. In Eastern Orthodox and some other Christian churches, a patriarch is a bishop of the highest rank.

Patriarchy is social organization in which men hold primary power—in government, family, property, and cultural authority. Feminist analysis uses the term for systemic male dominance: {Patriarchy shapes everything from workplace hierarchies to domestic expectations}. The word can also mean a society or institution governed by a patriarch, an elder male authority figure.

A patriot is a person who loves and supports their country, often with a willingness to defend it. The word can be straightforwardly admiring or carry undertones of excessive nationalism, depending on context and speaker: {He considered himself a patriot, but his critics called him a nationalist}. Patriots formed the revolutionary faction in the American colonies who opposed British rule. (Capitalized Patriot may refer to the missile system or NFL team.)

Patriotic means showing love and devotion to one's country. A patriotic {song} celebrates national pride; patriotic {duty} appeals to citizens' loyalty. The word carries positive connotations for most speakers, though it can shade into criticism when devotion seems excessive or unquestioning: {He wrapped himself in patriotic fervor}. What counts as patriotic often depends on the speaker's politics.

Patriotism is a feeling of pride in, love of, or devotion to your country. The underlying word, patriot, is distantly related to father and implies achievements over generations. Patriotism is usually viewed positively and celebrated (The country exhibited its patriotism at the Olympics), but extreme patriotism that becomes militaristic or xenophobic is not.

Patriots are people who love and support their country with devoted loyalty. The word can carry positive connotations of civic virtue or negative ones suggesting blind nationalism, depending on the speaker's perspective: {True patriots defend the Constitution}. In American usage, patriots often specifically evokes the Revolutionary War colonists who fought for independence. (Capitalized Patriots usually refers to the New England NFL team.)

Patrol is the activity of moving through an area to monitor, guard, or maintain security. Soldiers patrol borders, police patrol neighborhoods, security guards patrol buildings. A patrol is also the group doing the patrolling: {The night patrol spotted the intruder}. To be {on patrol} is to be actively engaged in this surveillance duty.

Patrolling is moving through an area to monitor, guard, or maintain order. Police officers patrol neighborhoods, soldiers patrol borders, security guards patrol buildings. The word implies repeated, systematic coverage rather than a single pass: {Guards were patrolling the perimeter all night}. Figuratively, someone patrolling a conversation or situation is watching it closely for problems.

A patron is someone who supports or frequents an establishment or cause. Restaurant patrons are customers; patrons of the arts provide financial backing for artists and institutions. The word suggests a relationship beyond mere transaction—ongoing support or regular attendance: {She's been a patron of this gallery for twenty years}. A patron saint is a saint regarded as protector of a particular place, profession, or group.

Patronage is support given by a patron—whether financial backing of the arts, regular business given to a shop, or political favor dispensed by those in power. An artist may depend on wealthy patronage. A restaurant values your patronage. In politics, patronage means distributing jobs or contracts to loyalists: {The mayor's office ran on patronage and backroom deals}.

Patronising is the British spelling of patronizing—treating someone as if they're inferior or less intelligent. A patronising tone suggests condescension, speaking down to someone while pretending kindness: {Don't be so patronising; I know how to use a computer}. The word carries an accusation: the patronising person may think they're being helpful, but they're actually being insulting.

Patronize has two main threads. One is to be a customer or supporter: {She patronizes local businesses}, {a wealthy family that patronized the arts}. The other is to treat someone as inferior while appearing kind or helpful—being condescending: {Don't patronize me}. The first sense is neutral; the second is always negative. Context usually makes clear which is meant, though the condescending sense has become dominant in everyday speech.

Patronizing describes behavior that treats others as inferior while maintaining a veneer of kindness or helpfulness. A patronizing tone or manner conveys condescension—the speaker implies they know better than the person they're addressing. {She found his patronizing explanations insulting.} The word can describe speech, attitudes, or actions that seem supportive but actually belittle: {His patronizing smile made her feel like a child.} The related verb patronize can mean either to condescend to someone or simply to be a customer of a business.

Patrons are people who support or frequent an establishment, institution, or person. A restaurant's patrons are its customers; a library's patrons are its users. The word carries a sense of regular or loyal support: {The bar's patrons knew each other by name}. A patron of the arts financially supports artists or cultural institutions. In historical contexts, a patron was a wealthy supporter who enabled creative work: {Michelangelo's patrons included popes and princes}.

A patsy is someone set up to take blame for others' wrongdoing—a fall guy or scapegoat. The term implies naivety or vulnerability: the patsy doesn't realize they're being used until it's too late. {They needed a patsy, and he was dumb enough to volunteer}. More broadly, a patsy is anyone easily manipulated or deceived.

Patter is rapid, glib speech—the smooth talk of salespeople, magicians, or auctioneers designed to entertain or persuade: {The magician kept up a steady patter while performing the trick}. The word also describes quick, light sounds in succession: {the patter of rain on the roof}, {the patter of little feet}. These are separate words that have converged on the same spelling.

Two general meanings of pattern are closely related. A pattern may be either something created as a model or exemplar for imitation or implementation (dress pattern), or it may be something constituting the common element in observed phenomena (sleep pattern, weather pattern). Things perceived as having a natural order by the mind, sight, or hearing are referred to as patterns: migration pattern, growth pattern). As a verb, pattern means to make according to a pattern, or to mark with a decorative pattern.

Patterns are repeated or recurring forms, designs, or sequences. A wallpaper pattern repeats decorative elements; a speech pattern recurs in someone's pronunciation; a pattern of behavior shows up again and again. A sewing pattern is a template for cutting fabric. To pattern something is to design it after a model: {The building was patterned on Greek temples}. What unifies these uses is regularity—something that can be recognized, followed, or reproduced.

Patties is the plural of patty, a small flat cake of food—typically ground meat shaped for cooking: {hamburger patties}, {chicken patties}. The term extends to other foods pressed into similar shapes: {peppermint patties}, {crab patties}. In Caribbean English, a patty is a spiced meat turnover in flaky pastry.

A patty is a small, flat, round portion of food—most often ground meat shaped for cooking: {burger patty}, {chicken patty}. The shape extends to other foods pressed into discs: {peppermint patty}, {potato patty}. In the Caribbean, a patty is a filled pastry turnover, typically with spiced meat: {Jamaican beef patty}.

Pattycake is a children's clapping game played by two people facing each other, rhythmically clapping their own hands and then each other's while reciting a nursery rhyme. The term also refers to the rhyme itself, which traditionally involves a baker patting cake. By extension, pattycake can describe any interaction perceived as overly gentle, cooperative, or lacking real conflict: {Congress is just playing pattycake with the lobbyists}. Also spelled patty-cake or pat-a-cake.

A pauper is a very poor person, especially one dependent on public assistance or charity. The word carries historical weight from the era of poorhouses and workhouses, where paupers were housed at public expense. Today it sounds old-fashioned or literary: {He died a pauper}. The related adjective is {pauper's grave}—an unmarked burial for the indigent.

Pause is a temporary stop or break in activity, speech, or movement. When you pause, you halt briefly before continuing: {She paused to catch her breath before climbing the next flight}. A pause in conversation might signal hesitation, emphasis, or simply a moment to think. In media playback, the pause button suspends the action without ending it, letting you resume where you left off. The word carries an implication of continuation—unlike a stop, a pause is understood to be temporary.

Pave means to cover a surface with a hard material—stone, brick, asphalt, concrete—to create a road, path, or floor. A paved road is smoother and more durable than a dirt one. Figuratively, to pave the way is to prepare conditions for something: {Her early research paved the way for modern genetics}.

Pavement is a hard surface covering ground, typically made of asphalt or concrete. In American English, pavement usually means a road or parking surface: {The tires squealed against the pavement}. In British English, pavement means sidewalk—the paved path for pedestrians alongside a road. To {pound the pavement} is to walk streets looking for work or business.

A pavilion is a light, open structure used for shelter or display—often in parks, gardens, or fairgrounds: {The band played in the pavilion}. The word extends to any building serving as an annex or wing, especially at exhibitions, hospitals, or sports complexes: {the Olympic swimming pavilion}. In cricket, the pavilion is where players wait when not batting.

A paw is the foot of an animal that has claws or nails—dogs, cats, bears, and the like. The word extends to human hands, usually dismissively: {Get your paws off my stuff}. To paw is to touch or handle clumsily or too eagerly: {He pawed through the drawer looking for his keys}. When animals paw, they scrape or strike with a foot: {The horse pawed the ground}.

A pawn is a chess piece of the lowest rank—each player starts with eight, and they can only move forward one square at a time (two on their first move). By extension, a pawn is a person used or manipulated by others for their own purposes: {He was just a pawn in their political games}. To pawn something is to leave it with a pawnbroker as security for a loan; if you don't repay, the item is sold. To {pawn off} is to pass something unwanted to someone else: {She pawned off the extra work on her assistant}.

A pawnbroker is a person who lends money in exchange for personal property held as security. If the borrower repays the loan plus interest within a set period, they reclaim their item; if not, the pawnbroker sells it. Pawnbrokers operate pawnshops, often recognizable by the traditional symbol of three golden balls: {He took his grandfather's watch to the pawnbroker}.

Pawned describes something left with a pawnbroker as security for a loan. You surrender an item—jewelry, electronics, a guitar—and receive cash; if you repay the loan plus interest, you reclaim your property. If not, the pawnbroker sells it. {He pawned his watch to make rent.} Figuratively, to pawn something off is to pass it to someone else, often deceptively: {She pawned the extra work off on the new guy}.

Pawns are chess pieces of the lowest value, each player starting with eight. They move forward one square at a time but capture diagonally. Because they're expendable and numerous, pawn extends to people used or sacrificed for others' purposes: {The soldiers were pawns in a political game}. To pawn something is to leave it with a pawnbroker as security for a loan—a different word that converged on the same spelling. To {pawn off} is to get rid of something unwanted by passing it to someone else.

A pawnshop is a business where people bring valuables—jewelry, electronics, tools, musical instruments—and receive cash loans using those items as collateral. If the borrower repays the loan plus interest within a set period, they get their item back; if not, the pawnshop sells it. Pawnshops also buy items outright and sell secondhand goods. They serve people who need quick cash without credit checks, though interest rates tend to be high.

Pawnshops are businesses that lend money against personal property left as collateral. You bring in jewelry, electronics, or tools; the pawnbroker appraises them and offers a loan. If you repay the loan plus interest, you get your item back. If not, the shop sells it. Pawnshops also buy items outright and sell unclaimed merchandise: {I found a vintage guitar at a pawnshop}.

A pawprint is the impression left by an animal's paw on a surface—in mud, snow, or sand. The term extends to decorative representations of such marks: {pawprint stickers on a car window}, {a pawprint tattoo}. Also spelled as two words: paw print.

Paws are the feet of four-legged mammals, especially those with claws or soft pads—dogs, cats, bears, rabbits. The word implies something cushioned and furry rather than hooved. To paw is to touch or scrape with a paw, or by extension, to handle clumsily or too intimately: {Stop pawing at me}. {Keep your paws off} means don't touch.

Pay is to give money in exchange for goods, services, or debts: {I'll pay for dinner}. Extended uses involve giving what's owed or deserved: pay {attention}, pay a {compliment}, pay {respects}. Something that pays provides benefit or profit: {Crime doesn't pay}. Pay as a noun is wages or salary. To {pay off} is to succeed or to finish paying a debt. To {pay the price} is to suffer consequences.

Payback is retaliation or revenge—returning harm for harm received: {Losing the election was payback for his arrogance}. It also means repayment of money owed or return on investment: {The payback period on solar panels is about seven years}. As an adjective, it describes something done in retaliation: {a payback killing}.

A paycheck is the regular payment an employee receives for work, or the physical or digital document representing it: {I deposit my paycheck every Friday}. By extension, paycheck often stands for one's job or income generally: {She's just working for a paycheck}, {living paycheck to paycheck}. The latter phrase describes financial precarity—spending each payment before the next arrives.

Paychecks are documents or payments representing wages earned from employment. The term often stands for income generally: {She lives paycheck to paycheck}, meaning earnings are spent before the next arrives. A steady paycheck represents financial security through regular employment. Also spelled as two words: pay checks.

A paycheque is the document or payment received for work performed, typically issued by an employer at regular intervals. The spelling is standard in British and Canadian English. {I deposit my paycheque every Friday.} Beyond the literal payment, paycheque often represents employment itself: {living paycheque to paycheque} means spending each payment before the next arrives.

Payday is the day when workers receive their wages or salary: {I can't afford it until payday}. The word also refers to any significant financial gain or reward: {The lawsuit settlement was a big payday for the plaintiffs}. In boxing and other sports, a payday means a lucrative fight or match: {He's looking for one more payday before retirement}.

Paydirt is earth or ore rich enough in minerals to make mining profitable. The figurative meaning now dominates: to {hit paydirt} or {strike paydirt} is to find something valuable or achieve success after searching. {After months of research, we finally hit paydirt.} Usually written as one word, sometimes two.

Payment is money given in exchange for goods, services, or to settle a debt: {The payment is due on the first of the month}. It extends to non-monetary transfers that satisfy obligations: {payment in kind}. A down payment is an initial partial sum with more to follow. Payment can also mean the act of paying: {Payment can be made by credit card or check}.

A payoff is the return or reward that comes from an action or investment: {The payoff for all that training was a gold medal}. It can be a bribe: {The inspector received a payoff to overlook violations}. In narrative, the payoff is the satisfying resolution that earlier setup promised: {The joke's payoff landed perfectly}. To pay off a debt is to settle it completely; to pay off a bet is to deliver winnings.

Payoffs are returns on an investment or effort—the rewards that justify the work: {The payoffs from learning a second language are enormous}. A payoff can also be a bribe or hush money: {The politician received payoffs from contractors}. In game theory and economics, payoffs are the outcomes assigned to different choices in a strategic situation.

Payola is the secret or illegal payment of money to someone in exchange for promoting a product or service, most famously associated with radio broadcasting, where record labels bribed disc jockeys to play certain songs. The term emerged from scandals in the 1950s and combines "pay" with the ending of "Victrola," an early phonograph brand. By extension, payola describes any undisclosed financial arrangement designed to secure favorable treatment or publicity.

A payout is money paid out, especially a large sum disbursed at once: {The insurance payout covered the rebuilding costs}, {The lottery payout exceeded ten million dollars}. Payouts come from insurance claims, investments, lawsuits, or gambling wins. The word emphasizes the recipient's perspective—money coming to them rather than going from the source.

Payouts are sums of money paid out, especially from a fund or as winnings. Insurance companies make payouts on claims. Casinos advertise their slot machine payouts. The term often appears in business contexts—dividend payouts to shareholders, payouts from settlements. {The lawsuit resulted in a massive payout to the victims.}

A payphone is a public telephone that requires payment—typically coins, though later models accepted cards. Once ubiquitous on street corners, in hotel lobbies, and at gas stations, payphones have largely disappeared with the rise of mobile phones. {I had to find a payphone to call for a ride.}

Payphones are public telephones that require payment—typically coins or a prepaid card—to make calls. Once ubiquitous on street corners, in airports, and outside convenience stores, they've largely disappeared as mobile phones became universal. {I had to find a payphone to call for help.} The singular is payphone.

Payroll is the list of employees a company pays, or the total amount paid to them: {The company has five hundred workers on its payroll}. It also refers to the process of calculating and distributing wages: {She works in payroll}. To {make payroll} is to have enough money to pay employees—a basic measure of business solvency.

A paywall is a barrier on a website or app that restricts access to content unless you pay—typically through a subscription. Some paywalls are hard, blocking everything; others are soft or metered, allowing a few free articles before demanding payment: {I hit the paywall after reading three stories this month}. The word combines pay with wall, evoking a barrier to entry.

Paywalls are digital barriers that restrict access to online content until users pay or subscribe. News sites commonly use paywalls to monetize journalism: {The article is behind a paywall}. A "soft" paywall allows some free articles before requiring payment; a "hard" paywall blocks everything. To paywall content is to put it behind such a barrier.

A pea is a small, round, green seed that grows in pods and is eaten as a vegetable. Peas are among the most common vegetables, eaten fresh, frozen, or canned. The word usually refers to garden peas, though it extends to related plants: {snow peas}, {black-eyed peas}, {chickpeas}. Two things that are alike are {like two peas in a pod}.

A peabrain is a stupid person—someone whose brain is presumably the size of a pea. The word functions as a mild, often playful insult: {Don't be such a peabrain}. As an adjective, peabrained describes foolish ideas or actions: {another peabrained scheme}.

Peace is the absence of war or conflict, a state of calm and security. Nations negotiate peace {treaties}; people seek peace of {mind}. To make peace is to reconcile after a dispute. {Hold your peace} means remain silent. {Rest in peace} wishes tranquility to the dead. To {leave someone in peace} is to stop bothering them. Peace can also express a casual goodbye.

Peaceful describes a state free from disturbance, conflict, or anxiety. A peaceful {afternoon} passes without interruption. A peaceful {resolution} settles a dispute without violence. Peaceful {protesters} demonstrate without aggression. The word can describe temperament—a peaceful {person} remains calm and avoids confrontation—or atmosphere: {The garden felt peaceful at dusk}.

A peacekeeper is someone who maintains or restores peace, especially a soldier deployed as part of an international force to monitor ceasefires or prevent conflict in war-torn regions: {UN peacekeepers were stationed along the border}. More casually, a peacekeeper is anyone who mediates disputes or calms tensions: {She's the peacekeeper in our family}.

Peacekeepers are military or police personnel deployed to maintain peace in conflict zones, typically under international authority such as the United Nations: {UN peacekeepers were stationed along the border}. Their mission usually involves monitoring ceasefires, protecting civilians, or separating hostile factions rather than engaging in combat. The term extends loosely to anyone who mediates disputes or calms tensions: {She's the peacekeeper in our family}.

A peacemaker is someone who works to end conflict or establish harmony between opposing parties. The term applies across scales—from a child who reconciles quarreling siblings to diplomats negotiating treaties between nations. {She acted as peacemaker between the feuding neighbors.} The word carries positive connotations of patience and goodwill, though it can also describe someone who intervenes where they weren't invited. Peacemaker occasionally names weapons, with deliberate irony—most famously the Colt Single Action Army revolver.

Peacemakers are people who work to end conflicts or establish harmony between opposing parties. The term ranges from diplomats negotiating treaties to anyone who calms a dispute: {She was the peacemaker in her family, always smoothing over arguments}. The biblical beatitude "Blessed are the peacemakers" gives the word a moral weight beyond mere conflict resolution.

Peacenik is an informal, often dismissive term for someone who actively opposes war and military intervention. The -nik suffix, borrowed from Russian via beatnik and sputnik, adds a slightly mocking tone, suggesting the person's pacifism is naive or excessive. The word emerged during the Vietnam War era to describe antiwar protesters and remains in use today. {The senator dismissed the peaceniks protesting outside her office.}

A peach is a soft, round fruit with fuzzy skin, sweet flesh, and a large pit. The color peach—a pale pinkish-orange—takes its name from the fruit. Informally, a peach is someone or something wonderful: {She's a real peach}. To peach on someone is to inform against them, though this use is dated: {He peached on his accomplices}.

Peaches is the plural of peach—the fuzzy stone fruit with sweet yellow-orange flesh. Someone who is {peaches and cream} has a smooth, rosy complexion. If everything is {just peaches}, things are going wonderfully. As a term of endearment, peaches addresses someone sweet or dear: {Hey, peaches, how was your day?}

A peacoat is a short, double-breasted wool coat traditionally worn by sailors, characterized by broad lapels, large buttons, and a heavy weight suitable for cold weather. The design originated in European naval uniforms and remains popular as casual outerwear. {He threw on his peacoat before heading out into the wind.} The term is sometimes spelled as two words (pea coat) or hyphenated.

A peacock is the male of a species of large, colorful birds known for the iridescent blue-green plumage and elaborate tail feathers that fan out in spectacular display during courtship. The female is a peahen, and both sexes together are peafowl. The word extends to any vain person who struts or shows off: {He peacocked around the party in his new suit}. To peacock is to display oneself ostentatiously, seeking attention through appearance or behavior.

Peacocks are large, brilliantly colored birds, the males of the peafowl species. The male's iridescent blue-green plumage and spectacular fan-shaped tail display have made the peacock a symbol of pride, vanity, and showiness. To peacock is to strut or display oneself ostentatiously: {He peacocked around the party in his new suit}. Someone who peacocks seeks attention through flashy appearance or behavior.

Peak is the highest point or maximum level of something. A mountain peak is its summit. Peak hours see the heaviest traffic. An athlete at peak performance is at their best. To peak is to reach that high point: {Interest peaked in the early 2000s}. As an adjective, peak describes something at its maximum: {peak efficiency}, {peak season}. In internet slang, peak can mean either excellent or, ironically, terrible: {That's peak} might celebrate or lament depending on context.

Peaks are the pointed tops of mountains, or more broadly, the highest points of anything. A career reaches its peak; demand peaks during holidays. The peak of a cap is the brim that shades the eyes. {Traffic peaks around five o'clock.} {She was at the peak of her powers.} To peak is to reach a maximum: {Interest rates peaked in the eighties}.

A peanut is an edible seed that grows in pods underground, despite being called a nut. Peanuts are eaten roasted, boiled, or ground into peanut butter. The plant is also called a peanut. In the plural, peanuts means a trivially small amount of money: {They're paying peanuts for that job}. As an adjective, peanut suggests small size: {peanut gallery}, {peanut brain}.

Peanuts are legumes that grow underground, eaten roasted, boiled, or ground into peanut butter. Despite the name, they're not true nuts. Peanuts also means a trivially small amount of money: {They're paying her peanuts for that job}. {That's peanuts compared to what he makes}. (Capitalized Peanuts is the comic strip.)

A pear is a sweet, edible fruit with a distinctive shape—rounded at the bottom and tapering toward the stem. Pears grow on trees of the genus Pyrus and are related to apples, though softer and often grainier in texture when ripe. The fruit ranges from green to yellow to reddish-brown depending on variety. {The pears aren't ripe yet—give them a few more days on the counter.}

A pearl is a hard and shiny object produced inside a mollusk that is typically highly valued and is used in jewelry. A figurative meaning arising from this is for something highly valued or resplendent among its peers: Cadaques, the pearl of Costa Brava. Pearls of wisdom, sometimes used ironically, are wise words or statements. To pearl is to dive in order to harvest pearls, or to give something a pear-like shape (pearled barley).

Pearls are lustrous gemstones formed inside oysters and other mollusks when the creature coats an irritant with layers of nacre. Natural pearls are rare and valuable; most sold today are cultivated. The word extends to anything resembling these gems in shape or luster, like dewdrops or teeth. To cast {pearls before swine} is to offer something valuable to those who won't appreciate it. {Pearls of wisdom} are choice insights, though the phrase is often used sarcastically.

Pears are sweet, juicy fruits with soft flesh and a distinctive curved shape—wider at the bottom than the top. They grow on trees related to apples and are eaten fresh, poached, or baked. Unlike most fruits, pears ripen best off the tree. {The pears aren't ripe yet—give them a few days on the counter.}

Peas are small round green seeds that grow in pods, eaten as a vegetable. The word is almost always plural—a single one is {a pea}, but you'd never ask for just one. Peas appear in soups, stir-fries, and as a side dish. {Like two peas in a pod} describes people who are nearly identical. Sweet peas are flowering plants, not edible.

A peasant is a poor agricultural laborer, typically one working land they don't own. The term belongs to historical and foreign contexts—medieval Europe, revolutionary France, rural China: {The peasants worked the lord's fields}. In modern use, peasant is often dismissive or insulting, implying someone crude, uneducated, or of low status: {I'm not eating at that place like some peasant}.

Peasants is the plural of peasant, a poor agricultural laborer of low social status, especially in feudal or pre-industrial societies: {The peasants worked the lord's land}. The term often carries connotations of poverty, lack of education, or rustic simplicity. Used as an insult, it dismisses someone as unsophisticated or beneath consideration: {I don't wait in lines like the peasants}.

A peashooter is a toy weapon—a small tube through which dried peas or other small projectiles are blown at targets. The term extends dismissively to any firearm considered inadequate or underpowered: {That little peashooter won't stop an intruder}. The word captures something child-sized and ineffectual.

Peat is partially decomposed plant material that accumulates in waterlogged areas over thousands of years. It forms in bogs and wetlands where lack of oxygen slows decay. Dried peat has long been used as fuel, and peat smoke gives Scotch whisky its distinctive flavor. Peat moss is used in gardening to improve soil. {The air smelled of burning peat.}

A pebble is a small, smooth stone, typically rounded by the action of water. Pebbles are larger than grains of sand but smaller than cobbles—roughly the size that fits comfortably in a palm. They accumulate on beaches and riverbeds: {The beach was covered in gray pebbles}. Pebbled surfaces have a bumpy texture resembling scattered stones.

Pebbles are small, smooth stones, typically rounded by water action in streams or on beaches. The word usually implies stones small enough to hold several in your hand: {She skipped pebbles across the lake}. Pebble can also describe a texture—pebbled leather has a bumpy, granular surface.

A pecan is an edible nut with a rich, buttery flavor, or the North American tree that produces it. Pecans are native to the southern United States and Mexico, central to regional cuisine: {pecan pie}, {butter pecan ice cream}, {candied pecans}. The shell is smooth and oblong, easier to crack than most nuts.

Pecans are edible nuts from a tree native to North America, with a rich, buttery flavor. The elongated shells crack open to reveal two lobed halves. Pecans feature prominently in Southern American cooking—pecan {pie}, pralines, and butter pecan ice cream. {She candied pecans for the salad.}

When a bird pecks at something, it strikes it repeatedly with its bill or beak. If you peck someone on the cheek, you give them a light kiss. A peck is an instance of either of these kinds of pecking. If you’re sitting at a keyboard, peck is a colorful way of saying slowly type. A different noun peck is a measure of volume (peck of apples) or simply a large quantity (peck of trouble).

Pecks is the plural of peck, a unit of dry volume equal to eight quarts or a quarter of a bushel—now rarely used outside the phrase {a peck of pickled peppers}. More commonly, pecks refers to quick, light kisses: {She gave him a few pecks on the cheek before leaving}. As a verb form, pecks describes the jabbing motion birds make with their beaks: {The hen pecks at scattered grain}.

Pecs is the informal plural of pectoral muscles—the large chest muscles connecting the shoulder to the breastbone. The word appears almost exclusively in fitness contexts: {He's been working on his pecs at the gym}. Well-developed pecs are a standard marker of male physique in bodybuilding and popular culture.

Peculiar means distinctive or belonging exclusively to something: {a flavor peculiar to this region}, {habits peculiar to cats}. More commonly now, peculiar means strange or odd—deviating from what's normal or expected: {a peculiar smell}, {He's a bit peculiar}. The strangeness sense dominates casual speech, while the belonging-to sense persists in formal writing.

A pedal is a lever operated by the foot. Vehicles have gas, brake, and clutch pedals. Pianos have sustain and soft pedals. Bicycles have pedals that drive the chain. To pedal is to operate pedals, especially on a bike: {She pedaled up the hill}. {Soft-pedal} means to downplay: {They soft-pedaled the scandal}. Not to be confused with peddle (to sell).

Pedaling is working the pedals of a bicycle, organ, or other pedal-operated device. The word emphasizes the continuous action: {She was pedaling uphill against the wind}. Figuratively, pedaling can suggest effort to keep something going: {He's been pedaling hard to keep the project alive}. Also spelled pedalling.

Pedals are levers operated by foot. Bicycle pedals transfer leg power to the wheels. Piano pedals modify tone or sustain notes. Car pedals control acceleration, braking, and clutch. To pedal is to operate such a lever: {She pedaled uphill for twenty minutes}. {Pedal to the metal} means pressing the accelerator fully—going all out.

A peddler is someone who travels from place to place selling goods, typically small wares or items carried in a pack or cart: {The peddler sold pots and kitchen tools door to door}. The word now often carries negative connotations—someone who sells questionable things or pushes unwanted ideas: {a peddler of conspiracy theories}, {drug peddler}. Also spelled pedlar in British English.

Peddlers are people who sell goods, typically by traveling from place to place rather than from a fixed shop. The word often carries connotations of small-scale or informal commerce: {peddlers hawking their wares on street corners}. Figuratively, peddlers spread ideas or influence: {peddlers of misinformation}, {influence peddlers}. The spelling pedlars appears in British English.

Peddling is selling goods, especially by going from place to place: {street vendors peddling their wares}. The word often carries a disreputable tinge—you peddle drugs, influence, or lies. Someone peddling an idea is pushing it aggressively, usually with skepticism implied about its worth: {peddling conspiracy theories on social media}.

A pedestal is a base or support that elevates something—typically a statue, column, or decorative object. The word extends to any platform that raises something literally or figuratively. To {put someone on a pedestal} is to idealize them, treating them as worthy of admiration above ordinary people. To {knock someone off their pedestal} is to expose their flaws.

Pedestals are bases or supports on which something stands—a statue on its pedestal, a sink pedestal, a pedestal table. The word appears most often in the figurative expression {put someone on a pedestal}, meaning to admire them excessively or idealize them beyond what's warranted: {She put her father on a pedestal until she learned about his past}. To {knock someone off their pedestal} is to expose their flaws.

A pedestrian is a person traveling on foot, especially in areas shared with vehicles: {Drivers must yield to pedestrians in crosswalks}. The adjective pedestrian means dull, unimaginative, or ordinary—plodding along without flair: {The writing was competent but pedestrian}. Both senses connect to the idea of going by foot rather than soaring.

Pedestrians are people traveling on foot, especially in areas shared with vehicles. Traffic laws, crosswalks, and signals exist to protect pedestrians from cars. The word often appears in contexts of urban planning and road safety: {The city added more pedestrian crossings}. Figuratively, pedestrian as an adjective means dull or uninspired: {The film's pedestrian plot disappointed critics}.

A pedicure is a cosmetic treatment for the feet and toenails—trimming, shaping, and polishing the nails, plus softening and exfoliating the skin. Pedicures are typically performed at nail salons: {I'm getting a pedicure before the wedding}. The word parallels manicure, which is the same treatment for hands.

Pedigree is the recorded ancestry or lineage of a person or animal, especially when that lineage is distinguished or pure. Dog breeders and horse enthusiasts use pedigree to document bloodlines and establish an animal's breeding credentials. By extension, pedigree describes any impressive background or set of qualifications: {Her academic pedigree includes degrees from Oxford and MIT}. Something with pedigree has an established reputation or proven track record: {a wine with real pedigree}.

Pedigrees is the plural of pedigree—a record of ancestry, especially for animals bred for particular traits: {The breeder showed us the puppies' pedigrees}. Extended to people, pedigree suggests distinguished lineage or impressive credentials: {Her academic pedigree includes Harvard and Oxford}. The word can carry both admiration and skepticism about whether background guarantees quality.

Pee is informal for urinate or urine. Children and adults alike use it as a comfortable alternative to clinical terms: {I need to pee}, {There's pee on the toilet seat}. The phrase {pee your pants} means to lose bladder control, sometimes from laughing or fear. Pee-pee is the version for small children.

Peeing is urinating—expelling urine from the body. The word is casual but not vulgar, making it the default term for parents and children: {I need to pee}, {The dog is peeing on the rug}. To pee oneself is to urinate involuntarily, often from fear or laughter.

To peek is to look quickly or furtively, often through a small opening or from a concealed position: {She peeked through the curtains}. A peek is such a glance: {Take a peek at this}. The word suggests brevity and sometimes secrecy—you peek at something you're not supposed to see, or sneak a peek at a surprise. {Peek-a-boo} is the game played with infants. Not to be confused with peak or pique.

Peekaboo is a game played with infants, where an adult hides their face behind their hands or an object, then reveals it while saying "peekaboo!" The game delights babies who are just learning that things continue to exist when out of sight. As an adjective, peekaboo describes clothing or styles with strategic cutouts or see-through elements: {a peekaboo blouse}, {peekaboo bangs}.

Peeking is looking quickly or furtively, often through a small opening or from a concealed position: {I caught him peeking through the blinds}. The word suggests stealing a glance at something you're not supposed to see or looking when you should have your eyes closed: {No peeking until I say so!}

To peel something is to remove its skin or outer layer, as you peel carrots or potatoes. If something peels without your assistance, its outer layer comes off in flakes, as paint or skin peels. A peel is the outer layer or skin of a fruit or vegetable. A potion of chemicals applied to a surface in order to clean it may also be called a peel. A different noun peel is a kitchen implement used to remove flat objects (like pizza) from an oven.

Peeling is the act of removing an outer layer—skin from fruit, bark from a tree, paint from a wall. As a noun, peelings are the removed bits themselves: {potato peelings}, {apple peelings}. Skin can be peeling when it sheds in flakes after sunburn or from dryness. Paint peels when it loses adhesion and curls away from a surface.

Peep captures the idea of something small or brief. A peep is a quick look, often furtive: {I took a peep through the curtains}. To peep is to look quickly or partially: {She peeped around the corner}. A peep is also a short, high-pitched sound made by a young bird or mouse—or by a person who barely speaks: {I didn't hear a peep out of him all night}. Peeps are the people you're close to—your friends or crew: {I'm hanging with my peeps this weekend}.

A peephole is a small hole you look through to see what's on the other side—typically a lens set into a door that lets you see who's there before opening: {She checked the peephole before unlocking the door}. The word extends to any small opening that permits viewing while remaining concealed.

Peeps is informal for people, especially one's friends or social circle: {I'm heading out with my peeps}. The word carries warmth and familiarity. Separately, peeps are quick, high-pitched sounds—the cries of young birds or similar noises. To peep is to make such a sound, or to look quickly and furtively: {She peeped through the curtains}.

A peer is someone of equal standing—in age, rank, or status. Classmates are peers; so are colleagues at the same level. In British usage, a peer is specifically a member of the nobility: {a peer of the realm}. To peer is a different word meaning to look closely or searchingly, often with difficulty: {She peered through the fog}.

Peers are people of equal standing—in age, rank, status, or ability. Students learn from their peers; professionals seek peer review. {She's well respected among her peers.} In British usage, peers are specifically members of the nobility who hold titles. To peer is a different word meaning to look closely or squint: {He peered through the fog}.

A peeve is something that annoys or irritates, usually a minor recurring grievance: {Loud chewing is a pet peeve of mine}. The verb means to irritate: {It peeves me when people don't signal}. Peeved means annoyed. The word is a back-formation from peevish, meaning ill-tempered or easily irritated.

Peeved means annoyed or irritated, typically over something minor. It suggests mild displeasure rather than serious anger: {She was peeved that no one remembered her birthday}. The word carries a slightly old-fashioned, almost quaint quality—being peeved sounds less harsh than being pissed off.

Peeves is the plural of peeve, meaning things that annoy or irritate someone. The word appears most often in the phrase {pet peeves}—minor irritations that bother a particular person disproportionately: {One of my pet peeves is people who chew with their mouths open}. As a verb, to peeve is to annoy: {It really peeves me when they're late}.

Peewee means very small, especially for its kind. A peewee is a small person or thing, often used affectionately for young children: {the peewee football league}. The word likely imitates a small bird's high-pitched call. As an adjective: {a peewee version of the adult game}.

A peg is a device that attaches or binds objects. Tent pegs secure a tent to the ground. Clothes pegs (British English) secure clothes to a line to dry. The pegs of a string instrument hold one end of the strings. When you peg something, you attach it with a peg, but the verb is frequently used to fix one quantity to a certain level: Saudi Arabia’s currency is pegged to the U.S. dollar. To peg someone as something means to identify them as such: I pegged her as a liberal the first time I met her.

A pegasus is a winged horse—a mythical creature capable of flight. The word derives from the Greek mythological horse Pegasus and has become a common noun for any such creature in fantasy literature, games, and art: {The knight rode a pegasus into battle}. Plural: pegasi or pegasuses. (Capitalized Pegasus is the mythological horse or constellation.)

Pegging has several meanings united by the idea of fastening or fixing. To peg something is to fasten it with a peg—a small wooden or metal pin: {peg the tent to the ground}. Prices or currencies can be pegged to a standard: {The dollar was pegged to gold}. To peg someone is to identify or categorize them: {I had him pegged as a lawyer}. A peg leg is a wooden prosthetic. In cribbage, pegging is moving pegs on the scoring board. In sexual slang, pegging refers to a woman penetrating a man anally with a strap-on dildo.

A pegleg is a wooden prosthetic leg, especially the simple post-style replacement traditionally associated with pirates and sailors who lost limbs. The term extends to anyone with such a prosthesis: {The old pegleg hobbled down to the dock}. As an adjective, it describes someone wearing one: {a pegleg pirate}.
