Pegs are small cylindrical or tapered pieces used for fastening, hanging, or marking. A tent peg secures canvas to the ground. A coat peg holds clothing. Cribbage uses pegs for scoring. To peg something is to fasten it with pegs or to fix it at a level: {The currency is pegged to the dollar}. To peg someone is to identify or categorize them: {I had her pegged as a lawyer}. To {take someone down a peg} is to humble them.

A pelican is a large waterbird with a long bill and an expandable throat pouch used for scooping up fish. Pelicans are found near coastlines, lakes, and rivers worldwide. The brown pelican dives from the air to catch prey; white pelicans fish while swimming. {A pelican glided low over the water}.

Pelicans are large waterbirds with long bills and expandable throat pouches used for scooping up fish. They're found near coastlines, lakes, and rivers worldwide, often seen flying in formation or diving for prey. {A squadron of pelicans glided over the bay}. The New Orleans Pelicans are an NBA team. (Capitalized Pelicans typically refers to the basketball team.)

A pellet is a small, rounded mass of compressed material. Animal food often comes in pellets. Guns may fire pellets—small projectiles of metal or plastic. The word extends to any small ball-shaped object: owl pellets (regurgitated indigestible matter), pellets of bread, pellets of ice. To pellet is to form into pellets or to strike with them.

A pelt is an animal skin, especially one with fur still attached: {beaver pelts}, {a stack of fox pelts at the trading post}. The fur trade dealt in pelts. To pelt is to strike repeatedly with thrown objects: {Kids pelted the car with snowballs}. Rain or hail pelts a surface when it hits hard and fast. At {full pelt} means at top speed.

Pelts are animal skins, especially with fur or hair still attached: {beaver pelts}, {fox pelts}. The fur trade dealt in pelts. A pelt is also a beating or bombardment—rain pelts a window, hail pelts a roof. To pelt someone is to throw things at them repeatedly: {The crowd pelted the speaker with tomatoes}. At full pelt means at top speed.

One kind of pen is a writing implement that uses ink. When you pen a letter or some other document, you write it. Another pen is an enclosure that prevents escape, such as one for animals (pig pen). When you pen living things, you enclose them in a pen. Pen is also an informal shortening of penitentiary: Her dad’s in the pen. A female swan is called a pen.

A penalty is a punishment or disadvantage imposed for breaking a rule or law. In sports, penalties give the opposing team an advantage—a free kick, extra shots, or time in the penalty box. In contracts and finance, penalties are fees for violations: {The early withdrawal penalty was steep}. The death penalty is capital punishment. More loosely, a penalty is any unwelcome consequence: {the penalty of fame}.

Penance is an act of self-punishment or devotion performed to show repentance for wrongdoing. In Catholic practice, penance is assigned by a priest after confession—prayers, fasting, or good works to atone for sins. More broadly, any voluntary suffering undertaken to make amends: {He did penance for his neglect by visiting her grave every week}. To {do penance} is the standard phrase.

A pencil is a writing or drawing instrument consisting of a thin rod of graphite or colored material encased in wood or held in a mechanical holder. The word also functions as a verb meaning to write, draw, or mark with a pencil; to pencil something in is to make a tentative arrangement: {Let me pencil you in for Thursday}. Pencil appears in compounds like {pencil skirt}, which is narrow and fitted, and {pencil mustache}, which is thin and precisely shaped.

Pencils is the plural of pencil, a writing instrument with a core of graphite or colored material encased in wood or a mechanical holder. Unlike pens, pencils can be erased. {She sharpened her pencils before the exam.} To pencil something in is to schedule it tentatively: {Let me pencil you in for Thursday}.

A pendant is an ornament that hangs from a chain worn around the neck, or more broadly, anything that hangs or dangles from something else: {a light pendant}, {a pendant earring}. As an adjective, pendant means hanging or suspended, though this use is literary and rare. The spelling *pendent* sometimes appears for the adjective.
Pending is a participle functioning as a preposition with two specific meanings; one similar to during, and one to until. It is frequent in journalism and law.

A pendulum is a weight suspended from a fixed point so it can swing freely back and forth. The regular motion of pendulums made them essential to early clocks. Figuratively, pendulum describes anything that swings between extremes: {The political pendulum has swung back toward conservatism}. The phrase {swing of the pendulum} suggests cyclical reversals.

To penetrate is to pass into or through something—a bullet penetrates flesh, light penetrates darkness, water penetrates soil. The word implies overcoming resistance or crossing a barrier. Extended uses follow naturally: to penetrate a market is to establish presence there; to penetrate a mystery is to understand it deeply; to penetrate an organization is to infiltrate it. A penetrating gaze seems to see through you; a penetrating analysis cuts to the core. {The cold penetrated his thin jacket}. {She couldn't penetrate his reserved exterior}.

Penetration is the act of entering or piercing something. A bullet's penetration depends on its velocity and the material it strikes. Sexual penetration refers specifically to insertion into a body cavity. In military and espionage contexts, penetration means infiltrating enemy territory or organizations: {The agency achieved deep penetration of the terrorist network}. Market penetration measures how much of a potential customer base a product has reached.

Penguin refers to flightless seabirds of the Southern Hemisphere, recognizable by their black-and-white coloring and upright waddle. They swim expertly but cannot fly—their wings have evolved into flippers. Penguins live in colonies, often in Antarctic or subantarctic regions, though some species inhabit temperate coastlines. {We watched the penguins dive for fish.}

Penguins is the plural of penguin, a flightless seabird native to the Southern Hemisphere. Penguins are distinctive for their black-and-white coloring and upright waddle on land, though they're graceful swimmers. They live in colonies and appear frequently in nature documentaries and children's media: {We watched the penguins huddle together against the Antarctic wind}.

Penicillin is an antibiotic derived from mold, the first of its kind to be widely used against bacterial infections. Discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928 and developed for medical use in the 1940s, it revolutionized treatment of wounds, pneumonia, and sexually transmitted diseases. {The doctor prescribed penicillin for strep throat.} Some people are allergic to penicillin, which can cause severe reactions.

A peninsula is a piece of land that projects into a body of water, connected to the mainland by a narrow strip: {the Italian peninsula}, {the Korean Peninsula}. The word captures the idea of being almost an island—surrounded by water on three sides but not quite cut off. Florida and Baja California are peninsulas.

The penis is the male sex organ, used for urination and sexual intercourse. In humans and other mammals, it becomes erect when engorged with blood during arousal. The word appears in clinical, educational, and casual contexts alike: {The doctor examined his penis}. Informally, countless slang terms substitute—cock, dick, dong, johnson, and dozens more.

A penitentiary is a prison, especially a state or federal facility for serious offenders serving long sentences. The word carries a formal, institutional tone—legal documents and news reports use it more than casual speech, where {prison} or {jail} suffice. {He served fifteen years in a federal penitentiary.}

Penmanship is the art or skill of writing by hand. Good penmanship means clear, legible, often elegant handwriting: {Her penmanship was so beautiful that she addressed wedding invitations for extra money}. The word carries an old-fashioned quality now that keyboards have largely replaced handwriting in daily life.

A pennant is a long, narrow flag tapering to a point, typically flown from ships or displayed at sporting events. In American baseball, the pennant is the league championship—winning it means advancing to the World Series: {The Cubs won the pennant}. Triangular pennants also appear as decorative banners at car dealerships and fairgrounds.

Pennies is the plural of penny, referring to individual one-cent coins: {She counted out the pennies from her piggy bank}. When discussing monetary value rather than physical coins, the plural is usually pence (British) or cents (American): {It costs fifty pence}. To {pinch pennies} is to be frugal. {Pennies on the dollar} describes buying something far below its value.

Penniless means having no money at all: {She arrived in the city penniless}. The word emphasizes complete poverty, not just being short on cash. A penniless artist lives in destitution; someone who forgot their wallet is merely without funds at the moment.

A penny is a coin of small value—one cent in the United States, one hundredth of a pound in Britain. The word often stands for trivial amounts: {It won't cost you a penny}. A {penny for your thoughts} invites someone to share what they're thinking. {Penny-wise and pound-foolish} describes saving small amounts while wasting large ones. To {pinch pennies} is to be frugal. {A pretty penny} is actually a large sum: {That car must have cost a pretty penny}.

A penpal is a person with whom you exchange letters, typically someone you've never met in person. The relationship exists primarily through correspondence, often across long distances or between different countries: {I had a penpal in Japan when I was twelve}. The term emerged when letters were written with pens; despite email and messaging largely replacing postal mail, penpal persists for any correspondent-based friendship.

Penpals are people who maintain a friendship through regular correspondence, traditionally by mail. The practice was especially popular before email and social media, often connecting children across countries: {I had a penpal in Japan when I was twelve}. The term still applies to any correspondence-based friendship, including digital ones. Also spelled pen pals.

Pens is the plural of pen—writing instruments that dispense ink: {She keeps a cup of pens on her desk}. Pen also means an enclosure for animals, so pens can be such enclosures: {The pigs were separated into different pens}. As a verb form, pens means writes or composes: {She pens a weekly column for the local paper}.

A pension is a regular payment made to someone who has retired from work, typically funded by contributions during their working years: {She lives on her pension}. Government and employer pensions provide income after age-based retirement. To pension someone off is to retire them with a pension, sometimes implying they've become useless: {They pensioned off the old equipment manager}. In European usage, a pension (pronounced the French way) is a small hotel or boarding house.

A pensioner is someone who receives a pension—regular payments from a retirement fund, government program, or former employer. The term is more common in British English than American, where {retiree} often substitutes: {The pensioners lined up for their monthly checks}. {A bus full of pensioners toured the countryside}.

Pensions are regular payments made to someone who has retired from work, typically funded by contributions during their working years. A pension may come from a former employer, the government, or a private plan. The verb pension appears mainly in {pension off}—to retire someone with a pension, or more broadly, to dismiss as no longer useful: {They pensioned off the old equipment}.

A pentagon is a five-sided polygon. In geometry, a regular pentagon has equal sides and angles, each interior angle measuring 108 degrees. The shape appears in nature, architecture, and design—from starfish to decorative tiles. {Draw a pentagon and connect all its vertices to form a five-pointed star.} (Capitalized Pentagon refers to the U.S. military headquarters.)

A pentagram is a five-pointed star drawn with five straight strokes, forming a continuous line that creates a pentagon at the center. The symbol has ancient associations with mathematics, magic, and mysticism. In modern use, it appears frequently in occult contexts—upright in Wiccan practice, inverted in associations with Satanism: {She wore a pentagram pendant}.

Pentagrams are five-pointed stars drawn with five straight strokes, each line crossing two others. The shape appears in various contexts: mathematical geometry, national flags, and religious symbolism. In occult traditions, a pentagram enclosed in a circle represents magical protection or elemental forces. Inverted pentagrams—with one point downward—are associated with Satanism and the occult: {The album cover featured pentagrams and skulls}.

A pentathlon is an athletic competition comprising five different events. The modern Olympic pentathlon includes fencing, swimming, equestrian show jumping, pistol shooting, and cross-country running. Ancient Greek pentathlons featured discus, javelin, long jump, a foot race, and wrestling. {She trained for years to compete in the pentathlon.}

A penthouse is a luxurious apartment on the top floor of a tall building, typically featuring premium amenities and panoramic views: {They bought a penthouse overlooking Central Park}. The word originally meant a shed or lean-to attached to a larger structure—the modern sense emerged when rooftop additions to apartment buildings became desirable rather than utilitarian.

Penthouses are luxury apartments on the top floor of a building, typically featuring premium amenities, expansive views, and private outdoor space. The term originally meant a shed or lean-to attached to a building's wall—the "top floor apartment" sense emerged in the early twentieth century as urban high-rises became desirable. {The penthouse sold for twelve million.}

A peon is a worker of the lowest rank, especially one doing unskilled or menial labor. The term originally referred to indebted laborers in Latin America bound to work until debts were paid. Now it often describes anyone at the bottom of a hierarchy: {I'm just a peon around here—nobody tells me anything}. The word carries connotations of powerlessness and expendability.

Peonies is the plural of peony, a flowering plant with large, showy blooms in shades of pink, white, red, and yellow. Native to Asia, Europe, and western North America, peonies are prized in gardens and floral arrangements for their lush, fragrant flowers: {The peonies in her garden bloom every May}. They're traditional wedding flowers and symbols of prosperity in Chinese culture.

A peony is a flowering plant prized for its large, showy blooms that appear in late spring and early summer. The flowers, which range from white to pink to deep red, are known for their lush, layered petals and sweet fragrance. Peonies are popular in gardens and floral arrangements, particularly for weddings. {The peonies in her bouquet were gorgeous.} They're perennials that can live for decades with proper care.

The noun people is used as the plural of person in most contexts, even though the words share no history. People is, however, related to popular and population. In addition to denoting any group of two or more humans, people is used to denote groups that share particular characteristics, as in the German people. Even though people is a plural noun, the pluralized form peoples is also used to talk about multiple groups, each of which has a distinct identity.

Pep is lively energy and enthusiasm: {She's full of pep today}. A pep talk is an encouraging speech meant to boost morale or confidence. A pep rally is a gathering, typically at schools, to generate enthusiasm before a sports event. To pep up is to make livelier or more energetic: {A cup of coffee will pep you up}. (Capitalized Pep may be a nickname or brand name.)

Pepper names two unrelated spices. Black pepper comes from dried berries of a tropical vine, ground to season food. Peppers of the capsicum family—bell peppers, jalapeños, cayennes—range from sweet to fiercely hot. To pepper something is to sprinkle it liberally: {The comedian peppered his routine with profanity}. To pepper with gunfire is to riddle with shots.

A peppercorn is the dried berry of a tropical vine, ground to make pepper. Peppercorns come in varieties—black, white, green, pink—depending on processing and ripeness. In legal usage, a peppercorn rent is a nominal payment (historically an actual peppercorn) that satisfies contract requirements without real exchange of value: {They lease the land for a peppercorn}.

Peppermint is a plant in the mint family with a strong, cool flavor from its high menthol content. The flavor itself is also called peppermint, appearing in candies, teas, and toothpaste: {peppermint tea}, {a peppermint candy cane}. The plant yields peppermint oil, used in cooking and medicine for its cooling sensation and ability to soothe digestive issues.

Pepperoni is a spiced, cured sausage made from beef and pork, sliced thin and most familiar as a pizza topping. The word is American, adapted from Italian *peperoni* (bell peppers)—though Italian pepperoni contains no peppers. {A large pepperoni pizza, please.}

Percent means per hundred—a way of expressing a proportion as a fraction of one hundred. {Fifty percent of the class passed}. The word functions as noun, adjective, and adverb: {a ten percent raise}, {sales increased five percent}. In casual speech, percent often emphasizes certainty or completeness: {I'm a hundred percent sure}. Also spelled per cent, especially in British English.

A percentage is a proportion expressed as parts per hundred, indicated by the symbol %: {What percentage of voters support the measure?} The word often appears where portion or share would suffice: {A large percentage of the budget goes to salaries}. In the plural, percentages can mean commission or profit margin: {The salespeople work on percentages}.

Perception is a verbal noun based on the verb perceive. Perception can refer to the faculty of becoming aware through the senses or mind, as in impaired perception. Perception can also be a particular sense impression: The camouflage is so effective that perception of the octopus is nearly impossible. Perception is used appreciatively to describe an ability to discern things quickly, acutely, or intuitively: She is a therapist of very rare and sensitive perception.

A perch is a place where a bird rests, typically a branch or rod, and by extension any elevated seat or vantage point where someone sits or stands: {She watched the parade from her perch on the balcony}. To perch is to sit or rest in such a position, often suggesting something precarious or temporary. Perch is also a common freshwater fish with spiny fins, popular among anglers. In older usage, a perch was a unit of measurement equal to about five and a half yards.

Percussion refers to the striking of one object against another. In music, percussion instruments produce sound through striking, shaking, or scraping: drums, cymbals, xylophones, tambourines. The percussion section of an orchestra or band plays these instruments collectively. In medicine, percussion is a diagnostic technique where a doctor taps the body to assess underlying structures by the resulting sound. {The percussion was thunderous during the finale.}

Perfect describes something without flaw or defect—complete in every way. A perfect {score} has no errors. A perfect {circle} meets exact geometric standards. Perfect also means ideally suited: {She's perfect for the role}. The verb, stressed on the second syllable, means to refine until flawless: {He spent years perfecting his technique}. In grammar, the perfect tenses indicate completed action.

Perfection is the state of being without flaw or defect—complete, accurate, and excellent in every way. The word often describes an ideal that may be unattainable: {Perfection is the enemy of good}. Something done {to perfection} is done exactly right: {The steak was cooked to perfection}. A person who is {perfection} embodies an ideal: {She was absolute perfection in that role}.

Perfectionism is the refusal to accept any standard short of perfection. A perfectionist holds themselves or others to impossibly high standards, often at the cost of completion or satisfaction: {Her perfectionism kept her revising the manuscript for years}. In psychology, perfectionism can be adaptive (driving excellence) or maladaptive (causing paralysis and anxiety). The word sometimes carries a note of criticism—perfectionists may be seen as difficult to work with or unable to finish projects.

A perfectionist is someone who refuses to accept anything less than flawless. The term usually carries a mild criticism—perfectionists may produce excellent work but at the cost of time, flexibility, or their own peace of mind: {She's such a perfectionist that she rewrote the email six times}. Some wear the label proudly; others recognize it as a polite word for obsessive.

Perform means to carry out an action, task, or function—especially one requiring skill or preparation. Musicians perform concerts, surgeons perform operations, and employees perform their duties. The word often implies an audience or evaluation: {How did the new software perform in testing?} When someone performs, they may also be putting on an act, presenting themselves in a calculated way rather than behaving naturally. A performance is an instance of performing, whether a staged show or simply how well something functions.

Performance is the act of carrying out, accomplishing, or executing something—whether a task, function, or duty. It extends naturally to the execution of artistic works before an audience: a musical performance, a theatrical performance. From there it takes on the sense of how well something or someone functions: {The car's performance exceeded expectations}; {Her job performance has been outstanding}. In contemporary usage, performance often implies a degree of deliberate presentation or artifice, as when someone's behavior seems calculated for effect rather than genuine.

A performer is someone who performs—acts, sings, dances, plays music, or otherwise presents entertainment before an audience. The word covers professionals and amateurs alike: {She's been a performer since childhood}. Beyond entertainment, performer can describe anyone executing a task, often with a modifier: {a high performer}, {a consistent performer}.

Performing is doing something in front of an audience—acting, singing, dancing, or playing music. The word extends to any execution of a task: {The car is performing well}. A performing {arts} school teaches theater, music, and dance. To describe someone as performing suggests they may be putting on an act rather than being genuine: {She's always performing for attention}.

Perfume is a fragrant liquid applied to the body for a pleasant scent, typically stronger and longer-lasting than cologne. More broadly, perfume is any sweet or pleasant smell: {the perfume of roses filled the garden}. As a verb, to perfume is to apply fragrance or to fill with scent: {Jasmine perfumed the evening air}.

A pergola is an outdoor structure consisting of vertical posts supporting an open lattice of crossbeams, typically used to create a shaded walkway or sitting area. Climbing plants like vines or roses are often trained to grow over it: {Wisteria draped the pergola in purple}. Unlike a gazebo, a pergola has no solid roof.

Perhaps expresses possibility or uncertainty—something may or may not be true or happen. {Perhaps she's already left}. It can soften statements or requests: {Perhaps you could help me with this}. Perhaps also introduces rough estimates: {Perhaps a dozen people showed up}. The word is slightly more formal than maybe.

Peril is serious danger or risk of harm. The word carries a slightly literary or formal tone: {The climbers faced great peril on the mountain}, {at peril of one's life}. To peril something is to put it at risk, though the verb is rare. {In peril} and {at your peril} are the common phrases—the latter a warning that proceeding means accepting the consequences.

Perils are serious dangers or risks that threaten harm. The word carries a slightly formal or literary tone: {the perils of ocean travel}, {financial perils}. To peril something is to put it at risk, though this verb form is rare. {At your peril} warns of danger: {Ignore the instructions at your peril}.

Perimeter is the outer boundary of an enclosed area, or the total length of that boundary. In geometry, you calculate the perimeter of a shape by adding the lengths of all its sides: {The perimeter of a rectangle is twice the length plus twice the width}. More broadly, perimeter refers to the defended edge of a military position or secured zone: {Guards patrolled the perimeter}. In basketball, the perimeter is the area beyond the lane but inside the three-point line.

An idea implicit in many meanings of period is occurrence in cycles—in other words, periodicity. A period is typically a demarcated length of time with particular characteristics: a mating period, a period of calm. If you wonder why the dot at the end of sentence is called a period (in American English), think of that period as punctuating a cycle of sentences. As an adjective, period typically refers to a period of time in the somewhat distant past that is made more specific by context: a new period drama from the BBC; She’s redone her living room in period furniture.

Periods are intervals of time, whether defined by duration, by historical character, or by recurring events: {the medieval period}, {a period of economic growth}, {class periods}. In punctuation, a period is the dot marking the end of a sentence. In menstruation, a period is the monthly discharge of blood from the uterus. Saying {period} at the end of a statement adds finality: {I'm not going, period}.

A periscope is an optical instrument with mirrors or prisms that lets you see things not in your direct line of sight. The classic periscope is used in submarines to view the surface while submerged: {The captain raised the periscope to scan for enemy ships}. Periscopes also appear in tanks and trench warfare, allowing observation while staying protected.

Periscopes are optical instruments that allow viewing from a concealed or submerged position. A system of mirrors or prisms lets an observer see over or around obstacles—most famously from submarines looking above the water's surface. The term extends to any device using similar principles: {tank periscopes}, {trench periscopes}. As a verb, to periscope is to extend or peer upward like a periscope: {Prairie dogs periscoped from their burrows}.

Perish means to die or be destroyed, often violently or prematurely: {Thousands perished in the earthquake}. The word carries literary or formal weight—news reports say victims perished rather than died. Things that perish may also decay or deteriorate: {The rubber gaskets had perished with age}. To {perish the thought} is to reject an idea as unthinkable.

Periwinkle names two unrelated things. One is a small sea snail with a spiral shell, eaten in coastal cuisines and found clinging to rocks at low tide. The other is a trailing evergreen plant with blue or purple flowers, commonly used as ground cover. The color periwinkle—a pale blue-violet—takes its name from the flower: {a periwinkle cardigan}, {periwinkle bridesmaid dresses}.

Perjury is the crime of lying under oath—deliberately giving false testimony in court or other official proceedings where you've sworn to tell the truth. The charge requires that the falsehood be material to the case, not merely incidental. {He was convicted of perjury after investigators proved he lied to the grand jury.}

Perk is a benefit or advantage that comes with a job or situation beyond the basic compensation: {Free parking is one of the perks}. The word is a shortening of perquisite. As a verb, to perk up is to become more lively or alert: {She perked up when she heard her name}. Coffee perks when it brews in a percolator—the liquid rising and falling through the grounds.

Perks are benefits or advantages that come with a position, membership, or situation—extras beyond the basic compensation or expectation. The word is short for perquisites: {The job doesn't pay much, but the perks are great}. Company cars, free meals, and gym memberships are typical workplace perks. The word has expanded beyond employment: {One of the perks of living downtown is walking to everything}.

Perky describes someone cheerful, lively, and alert—often with a bounce in their step or brightness in their voice: {She was annoyingly perky for 6 a.m.} The word can carry a hint of excess, suggesting enthusiasm that others find tiresome. Perky also describes things that stick up or out jauntily: {a perky ponytail}, {perky breasts}.

A perm is a chemical treatment that gives hair a lasting wave or curl, short for permanent wave. The curls hold their shape through washing until the treated hair grows out. To perm hair is to apply such a treatment: {She permed her hair for the wedding}. Perms were especially popular in the 1980s. In British usage, a perm is also a permutation, especially in football pools.

Permanence is the quality of lasting indefinitely, of remaining unchanged through time. It contrasts with the temporary or fleeting: {the permanence of stone versus the impermanence of ice}. The word often carries philosophical weight—questions about what endures and what passes away: {She doubted the permanence of any human institution}.

Permanent describes something that lasts indefinitely or is intended to remain unchanged. A permanent {job} offers ongoing employment rather than temporary work. Permanent {teeth} replace baby teeth and are meant to last a lifetime. A permanent {marker} creates marks that resist washing or fading. The noun permanent, now somewhat dated, refers to a hair treatment that creates long-lasting curls or waves. Despite its meaning, permanent often admits exceptions: even {permanent} residents can sometimes be deported.

Permission is the act of allowing someone to do something, or the state of being allowed. When you have permission, someone with authority has agreed that you may proceed: {She got permission from her parents to stay out late}. Permission can be granted formally through documents or informally through a nod or verbal okay. To ask permission is to request approval before acting, a convention that acknowledges someone else's authority over the matter.

Permit centers on allowing or authorizing. To permit something is to give consent or make it possible: {The rules don't permit smoking indoors}, {Weather permitting, we'll have the picnic outside}. A permit is an official document granting authorization: a {building permit}, a {parking permit}, a {work permit}. Permit is slightly more formal than let or allow.

Perp is cop slang for perpetrator—the person who committed a crime. Police and crime reporters use it routinely: {The perp fled on foot}. A {perp walk} is the deliberate public display of a suspect being led in handcuffs, often for media cameras.

A perpetrator is someone who commits a crime, harmful act, or other deed—usually something bad. The word appears most often in legal and journalistic contexts: {Police are searching for the perpetrator}. Informally shortened to perp: {The perp fled on foot}. Unlike "suspect," perpetrator implies the person actually did it.

Perpetrators are people who carry out harmful, illegal, or criminal acts. The word appears most often in legal and journalistic contexts: {Police are searching for the perpetrators of the attack}. Unlike neutral terms like "doer," perpetrator implies wrongdoing—you perpetrate crimes, frauds, and atrocities, not kindnesses.

Perpetual describes something that continues indefinitely or never stops: {perpetual motion}, {perpetual winter}. In legal contexts, it means lasting forever without renewal: a {perpetual license}, a {perpetual trust}. The word often carries a sense of weariness—a perpetual {headache} or perpetual {complaints} suggests something that never lets up. {She lived in perpetual fear of being discovered.}

Perplexed describes a state of confusion or bewilderment, typically when faced with something difficult to understand or resolve. Someone perplexed is puzzled, uncertain how to proceed or what to think. {I was perplexed by her sudden change in attitude.} The word suggests more than simple confusion—there's often an element of being troubled or bothered by the inability to make sense of something. A perplexed expression shows visible signs of this mental state: furrowed brow, searching eyes.

Perplexing describes something that confuses or puzzles, leaving you uncertain how to understand or respond: {a perplexing question}, {perplexing behavior}. What's perplexing isn't merely difficult—it's baffling in a way that resists easy explanation: {The results were perplexing; nothing in our data predicted this outcome}.

To persecute is to subject someone to prolonged hostility, mistreatment, or oppression, typically because of their identity, beliefs, or membership in a group. Religious and ethnic minorities have been persecuted throughout history. The word implies systematic cruelty rather than isolated incidents: {They fled the country after being persecuted for their political views}. Persecute is sometimes confused with prosecute, which means to bring legal charges.

Persecuted describes someone subjected to cruel or unjust treatment, especially because of their identity, beliefs, or membership in a group: {persecuted minorities}, {persecuted for their faith}. The word implies systematic mistreatment rather than isolated incidents. A {persecuted complex} (more commonly persecution complex) describes someone who believes others are against them, whether justified or not.

Persecution is the systematic mistreatment of people based on their identity—religion, ethnicity, political beliefs, or similar characteristics. Unlike random cruelty, persecution implies sustained, targeted hostility: {religious persecution}, {political persecution}, {persecution of minorities}. The term often appears in legal contexts, as when refugees claim asylum based on fear of persecution in their home countries. A persecution {complex} is the belief, often unfounded, that others are conspiring against you.

Perseverance is continued effort despite difficulty or delay in achieving success. The word emphasizes steadfastness over time—not a single burst of determination but sustained commitment: {Her perseverance through years of rejection finally paid off}. Unlike stubbornness, perseverance carries positive connotations of admirable resolve.

To persevere is to keep going despite difficulties, obstacles, or discouragement. The word implies sustained effort over time rather than a single burst of determination: {She persevered through years of rejection before publishing her first novel}. Someone who perseveres doesn't necessarily succeed—the word emphasizes the continued trying, not the outcome.

To persist is to continue doing something despite difficulty or opposition: {She persisted with her questions until she got an answer}. It also means to continue existing over time: {The smell persisted for days}. Persistence implies stubbornness or determination—the refusal to give up or fade away. {If symptoms persist, see a doctor.}

Persistence is the quality of continuing steadily despite obstacles, setbacks, or discouragement. Someone with persistence keeps trying even when success seems unlikely or distant: {Her persistence finally paid off when she landed the job after dozens of interviews}. The word also describes the state of continuing to exist over time—a rash that shows persistence doesn't go away quickly. In computing, persistence refers to data that remains available after the program that created it has ended, stored rather than lost when the system shuts down.

Persistent describes something that continues despite obstacles or over extended time. A persistent {cough} won't go away. A persistent {salesman} keeps calling. The word can be neutral or carry judgment depending on context—persistence is admirable when pursuing goals, annoying when someone won't take no for an answer. In computing, persistent {data} remains stored after a program closes or power shuts off.

We often use person and human being synonymously. The origin of person is the Latin persona, which indicates not a person but a person’s role in a play, a situation, or in life. Since actors convincingly portrayed personas, it wasn’t a huge leap for the word’s meaning to morph into the equivalent of an individual human being. Person remains closely related to the idea of role in its is grammatical meaning: the terms first person, second person, and third person are used in virtually all languages to distinguish inflections for verbs and pronouns.

A persona is a character or role someone presents to others, often distinct from their private self. The word suggests deliberate self-presentation: {Her public persona is warm and approachable}. In psychology, particularly Jung's, the persona is the social mask concealing one's inner nature. In marketing and design, a persona is a fictional user profile representing a target audience: {We created three buyer personas for the campaign}.

Personal relates to a particular person rather than to others or the public at large. A personal {opinion} is your own; personal {belongings} are yours alone. Personal matters are private: {Let's not get personal}. A personal {assistant} works for one individual. Personal can also mean directed at someone specifically, often critically: {Don't take it personal}. In grammar, personal {pronouns} refer to specific persons (I, you, she).

Personalities is the plural of personality, referring to the distinctive qualities that make individuals who they are. It often describes the mix of traits in a group: {The team's diverse personalities sometimes clashed}. Personalities also means famous people, especially in entertainment: {TV personalities}, {radio personalities}. The word can emphasize personal dynamics over issues: {Let's focus on policy, not personalities}.

Personality is the combination of qualities, traits, and behaviors that make a person distinctive. Someone with {a lot of personality} is vivid or memorable. In entertainment, a personality is a celebrity or public figure: {a television personality}. The word can describe the character of non-human things too: {The old house had personality}.

Personification is the representation of an abstract idea or thing as a human figure: Justice blindfolded with scales, Death as a hooded skeleton with a scythe. In rhetoric, personification gives human qualities to nonhuman things: {The wind whispered through the trees}, {Fear gripped her heart}. The word also means a perfect embodiment: {She was the personification of grace}.

Perspective refers to a point of view: Each panel member had a different perspective on the problem of increasing violence in schools. Perspective can also refer to a particular opinion: His perspective on reversing environmental degradation make for interesting reading. More narrowly, perspective refers to a way of representing three-dimensional objects in two-dimensional space, as in a drawing.

Perspectives are viewpoints or ways of seeing things. The word works both literally and figuratively: an artist renders a scene {in perspective}, while a historian offers {a fresh perspective on the Civil War}. To {put things in perspective} is to see them in proper relation to other matters. To {gain perspective} is to achieve clearer understanding, often through distance or time.

When you persuade someone, you convince them to do or believe something: They persuaded us to go with them, despite the awful weather. He persuaded us that the other council members were working against us. Persuade usually takes a person or group of people as a subject, but abstract things can also be said to persuade: The fantastic scenery persuaded us to stay an extra week. The related adjective and noun are persuasive and persuasion.

Persuasion is the act of convincing someone to believe or do something through reasoning, argument, or appeal: {After much persuasion, she agreed to come}. The word also refers to a particular belief or set of beliefs: {people of different political persuasions}. Used loosely, persuasion can mean type or kind: {athletes of the professional persuasion}.

Persuasive describes something that effectively convinces or influences. A persuasive {argument} moves people toward agreement; a persuasive {speaker} wins others over. The word implies skill in presenting a case: {She made a persuasive case for expanding the budget}. Something can be persuasive without being true—the word speaks to effectiveness, not accuracy.

Perverse describes behavior or attitudes that are contrary, stubborn, or willfully wrong-headed—doing the opposite of what's expected or reasonable: {He took perverse pleasure in proving everyone wrong}. A perverse outcome defeats the original purpose: {The law had the perverse effect of increasing the problem it was meant to solve}. The word suggests deliberate contrariness rather than simple disagreement.

Perversion is the twisting of something from its proper or natural course. The word often describes sexual behavior considered deviant or abnormal: {His perversion led to criminal charges}. More broadly, it can mean any corruption or distortion: {a perversion of justice}, {a perversion of the truth}. The term carries strong moral judgment—what counts as perversion depends on who's defining normal.

Pervert works as both noun and verb, with the noun carrying more weight in everyday speech. A pervert is someone with deviant sexual desires or behaviors—the word implies something twisted or unnatural: {Some pervert was lurking outside the school}. The verb means to distort from proper purpose or meaning: {pervert the course of justice}, {pervert the truth}. To pervert someone is to corrupt them morally. The adjective perverted and noun perversion share this range from sexual deviance to general corruption.

Perverted describes something twisted away from what is considered normal, natural, or morally correct. Most commonly it refers to sexual desires or behaviors deemed deviant or abnormal: {a perverted old man}, {perverted fantasies}. More broadly, perverted can mean corrupted or distorted from an original purpose: {a perverted sense of justice}. As a noun, a pervert is someone with aberrant sexual interests—the word carries strong negative judgment.

Perverts functions as both verb and noun. To pervert something is to corrupt or distort it from its proper purpose: {pervert the course of justice}, {pervert the truth}. As a noun, a pervert is someone whose sexual desires or behavior deviate from what's considered normal—typically used disparagingly: {Some pervert was lurking in the park}. The noun carries strong negative connotations; calling someone a pervert implies deviance and often danger.

Pesky describes something persistently annoying in a minor way—not dangerous or truly threatening, just irritatingly difficult to get rid of or deal with: {pesky mosquitoes}, {a pesky cough that won't go away}, {those pesky details}. The word is informal and often slightly playful, acknowledging that the nuisance is more exasperating than serious.

Peso is the basic monetary unit of several countries, including Mexico, the Philippines, Argentina, Colombia, and Chile. The word means "weight" in Spanish, reflecting the coin's origin as a measure of precious metal. In American English, peso often refers specifically to Mexican currency: {The exchange rate is twenty pesos to the dollar}.

Pessimism is a tendency to expect the worst outcome or to see the negative aspects of situations. A pessimist anticipates failure, disappointment, or misfortune, even when circumstances don't warrant such gloom. {Her pessimism about the economy kept her from investing.} The word also names a philosophical doctrine holding that this world is fundamentally bad or that evil outweighs good. Pessimism contrasts with optimism, its opposite disposition toward hopefulness.

A pessimist expects unfavorable outcomes—the glass is half empty, the worst is likely to happen. The word often implies a habitual disposition rather than a momentary mood: {He's such a pessimist about everything}. Pessimist can be neutral description or mild criticism, suggesting someone who drains energy or undermines hope. Some self-described pessimists prefer "realist."

Pessimistic describes a tendency to expect bad outcomes or focus on the negative aspects of a situation. A pessimistic person assumes things will go wrong: {I'm pessimistic about our chances}. Pessimistic forecasts or assessments predict unfavorable results. The opposite is optimistic.

Pessimists are people who tend to expect unfavorable outcomes or dwell on the negative aspects of situations. The word often carries mild disapproval: {Don't listen to the pessimists—this plan can work}. Some pessimists wear the label proudly, claiming they're simply realistic: {I'm not a pessimist, I'm a realist}.

A pest is something that causes annoyance or harm. Insects, rodents, and other creatures that damage crops or spread disease are pests: {pest control}, {garden pests}. The word extends to any persistent nuisance, especially a person who won't leave you alone: {Stop being such a pest}. {The kids were pests all afternoon.}

To pester is to annoy someone with repeated requests or interruptions: {Stop pestering me about the car—I said no}. The word suggests persistence rather than intensity—a child pestering for candy, a salesperson pestering with calls. Unlike harass, pester implies minor irritation rather than serious distress.

Pestered is the past tense of pester, meaning to annoy or bother with repeated requests or interruptions: {She pestered him until he agreed to help}. The word suggests persistent, minor harassment rather than serious threat—children pester parents for treats, reporters pester celebrities for comments.

A pesticide is a chemical substance used to kill organisms considered harmful or unwanted—insects, weeds, fungi, rodents. The term covers insecticides, herbicides, fungicides, and similar agents. Pesticides are essential to modern agriculture but controversial for their environmental and health effects: {The farm switched to organic methods to avoid pesticides}.

Pesticides are chemicals used to kill or control organisms considered pests—insects, weeds, fungi, rodents. The term covers insecticides, herbicides, fungicides, and rodenticides. Pesticides protect crops and control disease vectors but raise concerns about environmental contamination, effects on beneficial species, and human health risks from residues in food and water: {organic farms avoid synthetic pesticides}.

Pestilence is a deadly epidemic disease, especially one that spreads rapidly and kills many people. The word is literary and old-fashioned, evoking biblical or medieval catastrophe: {Pestilence swept through the land}. In the Book of Revelation, Pestilence rides as one of the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse. The word sometimes extends to anything destructive or corrupting: {a pestilence of false information}.

A pestle is a club-shaped tool used to crush or grind substances in a mortar—the bowl that holds them. The pair appears in pharmacies, kitchens, and laboratories for pulverizing spices, herbs, or chemicals: {She ground the peppercorns with a mortar and pestle}. As a verb, to pestle is to crush with this tool.

Pesto is an uncooked sauce of crushed basil, garlic, pine nuts, Parmesan cheese, and olive oil, traditionally served with pasta. The name comes from the Italian for "pounded," describing how the ingredients are ground together, traditionally with mortar and pestle. Variations substitute other greens or nuts: {sun-dried tomato pesto}, {arugula pesto}, {walnut pesto}.

Pests are creatures that cause damage or annoyance—insects that destroy crops, rodents that infest buildings, animals that spread disease. The word extends to people who won't leave you alone: {My little brother is such a pest}. Pest control addresses the literal kind; social boundaries address the human variety.

A pet is an animal kept for companionship rather than utility—dogs, cats, hamsters, and the like. The word extends to favorites: a teacher's pet gets special treatment. As an adjective, pet describes personal favorites or preoccupations: a {pet project}, a {pet peeve}. To pet is to stroke affectionately, and by extension, to engage in sexual touching short of intercourse: {petting in the back seat}. As a term of endearment, pet is common in British dialects: {Come here, pet}.

A petal is one of the colored, leaf-like parts that form the outer ring of a flower. Petals attract pollinators and protect the reproductive structures within. The word extends to anything shaped like a flower petal: {petal-shaped earrings}. To {put the pedal to the metal} uses the sound-alike word for an accelerator, not this one.

Petals are the colorful, often delicate parts of a flower that surround its reproductive organs. They attract pollinators and give flowers their distinctive appearance: {rose petals scattered on the bed}, {the petals fell one by one}. Petal is the singular form.

Petite describes a woman who is small and trim in stature. The word comes from French and retains a feminine quality—it's rarely applied to men, who would be called small or short instead. In clothing, petite designates sizes for shorter women: {She shops in the petite section}. The word carries no negative connotation; if anything, it suggests delicacy or elegance.

A petition is a formal written request, typically bearing multiple signatures, addressed to an authority: {They gathered signatures on a petition to save the library}. The word also covers any earnest request or appeal, including prayers. To petition is to make such a request: {Residents petitioned the city council for a traffic light}. In law, a petition initiates certain court proceedings.

Petrified has two meanings united by the image of turning to stone. Organic material becomes petrified when minerals replace its original structure over millennia: {petrified wood}, {a petrified forest}. A person who is petrified is paralyzed by fear, frozen in place as if turned to stone: {I was petrified when I heard footsteps behind me}.

Petrify means to turn to stone. In geology, organic material petrifies when minerals gradually replace its original structure: {petrified wood}. The figurative sense dominates everyday use—to petrify someone is to paralyze them with fear or shock: {The sound of footsteps in the dark petrified her}. Someone petrified is frozen in place, unable to move or react.

Petrifying describes something that causes intense fear—so frightening it seems to turn you to stone, unable to move. A petrifying {scream}, a petrifying {encounter}. The word comes from the same root as petrified, which describes both literal turning to stone and being frozen with terror.

A petroglyph is an image carved or incised into rock, typically by prehistoric peoples. These rock carvings are found worldwide and often depict animals, human figures, geometric patterns, or symbols whose meanings may be lost to time. Unlike pictographs, which are painted onto rock surfaces, petroglyphs are created by removing part of the rock itself through pecking, scratching, or grinding. {The canyon walls were covered with petroglyphs left by ancient inhabitants.}

Petrol is the British term for gasoline—the fuel used in internal combustion engines for cars and other vehicles. Americans say gas or gasoline; Britons say petrol. {The car's nearly out of petrol.} A petrol station is what Americans call a gas station.

Petroleum is crude oil—a dark, thick liquid found underground, formed from ancient organic matter over millions of years. It's refined into fuels like gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel, as well as plastics, lubricants, and countless other products. {The region's economy depends on petroleum exports.} Petroleum jelly is a byproduct used as a skin protectant.

Pets are animals kept for companionship rather than utility—dogs, cats, fish, birds, hamsters. The relationship implies affection and care: {She treats her pets like family}. Pet also means a favorite: {a pet project}, {teacher's pet}. As a verb, to pet is to stroke affectionately, and by extension, to engage in sexual touching short of intercourse: {They were petting in the back seat}. As an adjective, pet describes something cherished or frequently indulged: {my pet peeve}.

Pettiness is excessive concern with trivial matters, or a tendency toward small-minded, spiteful behavior. Someone showing pettiness might hold grudges over minor slights or make mountains out of molehills: {The pettiness of their complaints wore everyone down}. The word suggests a character flaw—caring too much about things that don't deserve attention.

Petting is stroking or caressing, especially of animals: {The dog rolled over, eager for more petting}. Between humans, petting refers to sexual touching short of intercourse—what older generations called "necking" or "making out": {heavy petting in the back seat}. A petting zoo lets children touch and feed docile animals.

Petty describes things that are small, minor, or of little importance, often with a negative connotation suggesting they don't deserve attention. A petty {theft} involves items of low value; petty {cash} is a small fund for minor expenses. When applied to people or behavior, petty implies a smallness of character—someone who is petty fixates on trivial slights or engages in spiteful behavior over inconsequential matters. {She's being petty about who said what at the party.}

A pew is a long wooden bench with a back, typically found in churches for congregants to sit during services: {We slid into the back pew}. The word sometimes appears in the mild exclamation {pew pew}, imitating laser or gun sounds, though this is unrelated—just sound symbolism.

Pews are the long wooden benches with backs found in churches, arranged in rows facing the altar. They're where congregants sit during services. The word appears in phrases like {back pew} for those who sit inconspicuously, or {in the pews} meaning among ordinary churchgoers rather than clergy: {The message resonated in the pews}.

Pewter is a gray metal alloy traditionally made mostly of tin, historically used for tableware, tankards, and decorative objects before cheaper materials replaced it. The word also describes the dull grayish color of the metal. Pewter objects were common in colonial American and European households; antique pewter pieces are now collectibles. {The old tavern displayed pewter mugs behind the bar.} As an adjective, pewter describes things having that characteristic muted gray tone.

Peyote is a small spineless cactus native to Mexico and the southwestern United States, containing mescaline and other psychoactive alkaloids. The plant has been used for centuries in Indigenous spiritual ceremonies. Eating peyote buttons—the rounded tops of the cactus—produces vivid hallucinations and altered states of consciousness. Its religious use is legally protected for members of the Native American Church in the United States.

A phantom is something that appears to exist but doesn't—a ghost, specter, or illusion. The word emphasizes insubstantiality: a phantom {pain} persists after a limb is amputated, felt in tissue that's no longer there. Phantom can modify almost any noun to suggest illusory or nonexistent status: phantom {pregnancy}, phantom {voter}, phantom {limb}. As an adjective, it describes things that seem present but aren't real or detectable: {a phantom menace}, {phantom profits that existed only on paper}.

Phantoms are ghosts or apparitions—things that appear to be present but have no physical reality. The word extends to anything illusory or elusive: {phantom pain} persists after a limb is gone, a {phantom menace} is a threat that may not exist. Phantom also describes things that exist only on paper: {phantom employees} on a payroll, {phantom votes} in an election.

A pharaoh was a ruler of ancient Egypt, considered both king and living god. The title carried divine authority—pharaohs were believed to mediate between gods and people. The word now evokes ancient Egyptian civilization generally: {the pharaohs' tombs}, {treasures of the pharaohs}. Figuratively, pharaoh can describe any absolute ruler or tyrant.

Pharaohs is the plural of pharaoh, the title for ancient Egyptian rulers. The pharaohs were considered divine intermediaries between gods and people, wielding absolute religious and political authority: {The pharaohs built the pyramids as tombs}. The word now evokes ancient Egypt's grandeur and power: {He rules his company like one of the pharaohs}.

Pharma is an informal shortening of pharmaceutical, referring to the drug industry or pharmaceutical companies collectively: {Big pharma lobbies against price controls}. The term often carries a skeptical or critical edge, implying corporate profit motives in healthcare. It also appears as an attributive: {pharma stocks}, {pharma executives}.

A pharmacist is a professional who prepares and dispenses medications. Pharmacists work in drugstores, hospitals, and clinics, filling prescriptions, advising patients on drug interactions and side effects, and recommending over-the-counter treatments. The role has shifted from compounding medicines by hand to primarily verifying and dispensing manufactured drugs: {Ask the pharmacist if this will interact with your other medication}.

A pharmacy is a store or department where medicinal drugs are dispensed, typically by a licensed pharmacist: {Pick up your prescription at the pharmacy}. The term also refers to the profession and science of preparing and dispensing medications. In hospitals, the pharmacy compounds and distributes drugs to patients and departments.

Phase is a distinct stage in a process or cycle of development. The moon has phases as it waxes and wanes. A project moves through phases. A teenager going through {a phase} is experiencing temporary behavior expected to pass. In physics, phase describes the position of a wave at a given moment, which is why things operating in sync are {in phase} and things misaligned are {out of phase}. To phase something in or out is to introduce or discontinue it gradually.

A phaser is a fictional directed-energy weapon from *Star Trek*, capable of stunning or killing targets. The word blends "phase" with the "-er" suffix, echoing "laser." Outside science fiction, a phaser is an electronic audio effect that creates sweeping, swirling sounds by splitting a signal and shifting one copy's phase: {The guitarist ran the solo through a phaser pedal}.

Phases are distinct stages in a process or cycle. The moon has phases as it waxes and wanes. A project moves through phases from planning to completion. To phase something is to introduce or remove it gradually: {The company phased out the old product line}. {It's just a phase} dismisses behavior as temporary, especially in children or teenagers.

A pheasant is a large, long-tailed game bird, the males typically having brilliant plumage. Native to Asia, pheasants were introduced widely for hunting and now inhabit fields and woodland edges across Europe and North America. {We flushed a pheasant from the underbrush.} The meat is considered a delicacy, often roasted: {pheasant under glass}.

Pheasants is the plural of pheasant, a large ground-dwelling bird with a long tail, often brightly colored in males. Pheasants are prized as game birds and hunted for sport: {We flushed three pheasants from the brush}. The ring-necked pheasant, introduced from Asia, is the most common variety in North America.

A phenom is someone who displays exceptional talent or ability, especially at a young age. The word is informal, clipped from phenomenon, and appears most often in sports contexts: {The sixteen-year-old pitching phenom signed with the Yankees}. A phenom attracts attention precisely because their skill seems to exceed what's expected for their experience level.

Phenomena is the plural of phenomenon—observable events, facts, or occurrences. In scientific contexts, phenomena are things that can be studied and explained: {natural phenomena}, {weather phenomena}. The word often carries a sense of something remarkable or unusual: {The northern lights are among nature's most spectacular phenomena}. Using phenomena as a singular ({This phenomena is interesting}) is common in speech but considered nonstandard.

Phenomenal describes something extraordinary or remarkable—noticeably beyond the ordinary: {phenomenal growth}, {phenomenal success}, {a phenomenal athlete}. The word carries emphatic praise, suggesting performance or quality that stands out dramatically. In philosophy, phenomenal refers to things as they appear to consciousness rather than as they exist independently, but everyday usage overwhelmingly means impressively exceptional.

Phenomenon (plural phenomena) is a long word that has about the same meaning as thing or entity, but with emphasis on appearance rather than substance. Phenomenon is typically used to designate something that is perceived but that may not have a full or satisfactory explanation: People in the area hear a low rumbling but no one can explain the phenomenon. A phenomenon is also something that is unique, extremely impressive, or sensational: The teenage pianist is a phenomenon who has the captured the imagination of the classical world.

Phew has a single spelling but distinct meanings that suggest it’s really two words. It may express a feeling of relief, as when a mishap has been averted, or it may be an expression of disgust or repugnance.

Philandering is the behavior of a man who pursues casual sexual relationships with women other than his wife or partner. The word carries connotations of habitual, frivolous unfaithfulness rather than a single affair: {His philandering eventually destroyed the marriage}. A philanderer is a man known for such behavior. The term is somewhat old-fashioned and applies almost exclusively to men.

A philanthropist is a person who donates money, time, or resources to charitable causes, typically on a large scale. The term usually implies substantial wealth and systematic giving rather than casual charity: {The philanthropist funded a new wing of the hospital}. Philanthropists often focus on particular causes—education, medical research, poverty relief—and may establish foundations to direct their giving.

Philanthropy is charitable giving or activity intended to promote human welfare. The term implies generosity on a significant scale—donating to universities, funding medical research, establishing foundations: {The billionaire turned to philanthropy after retiring}. A philanthropist gives money; philanthropy is the practice or philosophy behind such giving. The word carries connotations of wealth and systematic benevolence rather than casual charity.

A philistine is someone indifferent or hostile to art, culture, and intellectual pursuits—a person who values material comfort over aesthetic or spiritual matters. The word carries contempt: {Don't be such a philistine; it's a masterpiece}. A philistine dismisses what they don't understand as pretentious or useless. The adjective describes such attitudes: {philistine tastes}, {philistine disdain for poetry}. (Capitalized Philistine refers to the ancient people.)

Philistines are people who are hostile or indifferent to culture, the arts, and intellectual pursuits—those who value material comfort over aesthetic or spiritual matters: {The philistines on the city council voted to defund the orchestra}. The term carries condescension, implying boorishness or crude taste. (Capitalized Philistines were an ancient people.)

A philosopher is someone who studies fundamental questions about existence, knowledge, ethics, and reality. More loosely, a philosopher is anyone given to deep or abstract thinking: {He fancied himself a philosopher, always pondering life's big questions}. The word can carry a whiff of impracticality—someone more interested in theorizing than acting. To be philosophical about something is to accept it with calm resignation: {She was philosophical about losing the match}.

Philosophers are people who study or practice philosophy—the pursuit of fundamental questions about existence, knowledge, ethics, and meaning. The term covers ancient thinkers like Plato and Aristotle, modern academics, and anyone who engages in deep reflection about life's big questions. {She considered herself a philosopher, always asking why things had to be the way they were.} Informally, calling someone a philosopher can suggest they're prone to abstract thinking or impractical speculation.

Philosophical relates to philosophy—the study of fundamental questions about existence, knowledge, ethics, and meaning. A philosophical {discussion} examines ideas at their roots. The word also describes a calm, detached attitude toward difficulty or misfortune: {She was philosophical about losing the job, seeing it as an opportunity for change}. Someone philosophical tends to reflect deeply rather than react emotionally.

Philosophy is the study of fundamental questions about existence, knowledge, ethics, and reasoning. Philosophers ask what is real, what we can know, what makes actions right or wrong, and how to think logically. The word also names any systematic set of beliefs or guiding principles: {my philosophy of life}, {a coaching philosophy}. Someone who takes bad news calmly is said to be philosophical about it.

Phishing is a type of online fraud where scammers impersonate legitimate organizations to trick people into revealing sensitive information—passwords, credit card numbers, social security numbers. The name plays on "fishing," as criminals cast wide nets hoping victims will bite: {I almost fell for a phishing email that looked exactly like my bank's}. Phishing attempts typically arrive via email, text message, or fake websites designed to mimic trusted sources.

Pho is a Vietnamese soup consisting of broth, rice noodles, herbs, and meat—usually beef or chicken. The broth is typically simmered for hours with spices like star anise and cinnamon. Pho is Vietnam's national dish and has become widely popular internationally: {Let's grab pho for lunch}.

A phobia is an intense, irrational fear of something specific—heights, spiders, enclosed spaces, public speaking. The fear is disproportionate to actual danger and often recognized as unreasonable by the person experiencing it. As a suffix, -phobia forms words for particular fears (claustrophobia, arachnophobia) or, more loosely, aversions and prejudices: {homophobia}, {xenophobia}.

Phobias is the plural of phobia, an intense, irrational fear of a specific thing or situation. The term applies to fears disproportionate to actual danger: {Her phobias included spiders and enclosed spaces}. Phobia combines freely with roots to name specific fears—claustrophobia, arachnophobia, agoraphobia. Loosely, phobia describes strong aversion: {a phobia about public speaking}.

A phoenix is a mythical bird that cyclically burns itself to death and is reborn from its own ashes. The image makes phoenix a powerful metaphor for renewal, resurrection, or dramatic comeback: {The company rose like a phoenix from bankruptcy}. Something described as phoenix-like has emerged transformed from apparent destruction. (Capitalized Phoenix is a city in Arizona.)

Phone is a device for voice communication at a distance. The word began as a shortening of telephone, but now usually means a smartphone—a handheld computer that also makes calls: {I left my phone at home}, {Check your phone}. To phone someone is to call them. Phone appears in compounds: {phone number}, {phone call}, {phone book}.

Phones is the plural of phone, short for telephone—a device for voice communication over distance. In contemporary use, phones almost always means smartphones: {Everyone had their phones out during the concert}. The verb phone means to call someone: {I'll phone you later}. To {phone it in} is to make minimal effort.

Phonies is the plural of phony—people who are fake, insincere, or pretending to be something they're not. The word carries contempt for those perceived as putting on airs or lacking authenticity: {The party was full of phonies trying to impress each other}. Famously central to Holden Caulfield's worldview in *The Catcher in the Rye*, where he sees phonies everywhere among adults.

Phony describes something fake or fraudulent—a person, thing, or quality that pretends to be what it isn't. A phony {smile} masks true feelings. A phony {accent} is put on. As a noun, a phony is an insincere person or an impostor: {He's a complete phony}. The spelling phoney is also used. {That diploma looked phony to me.}

Phosphoenolpyruvate is a high-energy molecule central to cellular metabolism. In glycolysis, it donates a phosphate group to produce ATP and pyruvate. It also serves as a starting point for gluconeogenesis—the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources. Biochemists abbreviate it PEP.

Photo is a clipped form of photograph—an image captured by a camera. The shorter form dominates casual speech and most everyday contexts: {Can I see the photos from your trip?} Photo combines freely: {photo album}, {photo shoot}, {photo op}. As a verb, to photo someone is to photograph them, though this use is less common.

Photobiomodulation is a therapeutic technique using low-level light—typically red or near-infrared wavelengths—to stimulate cellular function and promote healing. The light is absorbed by mitochondria, enhancing energy production and reducing inflammation. Used in medicine and physical therapy for wound healing, pain relief, and tissue repair: {The clinic offers photobiomodulation for chronic joint pain}.

To photobomb is to intrude into someone else's photograph, usually appearing unexpectedly in the background as the picture is taken. The act can be accidental but is often deliberate mischief—a friend making a face behind the couple posing, a stranger wandering into a tourist's shot. {A seagull photobombed our beach selfie.} The noun photobomb refers to the ruined image or the intrusion itself.

Photobombing is the act of inserting yourself into someone else's photograph without their knowledge or consent, typically by appearing in the background just as the picture is taken. The intent is usually humorous or mischievous rather than malicious. {I didn't notice the stranger photobombing us until I looked at the picture later.} The term extends to any unexpected intrusion into a photo, including by animals or objects that disrupt the intended shot.

A photocopy is a duplicate of a document made by a machine that photographs and reproduces the original. To photocopy is to make such a copy: {I need to photocopy my passport}. The word emerged with xerographic technology in the mid-20th century and remains standard despite digital alternatives. A photocopier is the machine that makes them.

Photogenic describes someone or something that looks good in photographs. Some faces photograph better than others—features that seem ordinary in person can appear striking on camera, while conventionally attractive people sometimes photograph poorly. {She's incredibly photogenic; every shot looks professional.} The word occasionally describes anything that produces or relates to light, but the camera-ready sense dominates.

A photograph is an image created by capturing light on a sensitive surface—originally chemical film, now usually a digital sensor. To photograph is to take such an image: {She photographed the wedding}. Unlike paintings or drawings, photographs record what was actually in front of the camera, giving them evidentiary weight: {The photograph proved he was there}.

A photographer is someone who takes photographs, whether as a profession, serious pursuit, or casual hobby. Professional photographers specialize in areas like portraiture, weddings, journalism, fashion, or wildlife. The term applies equally to someone shooting with expensive equipment in a studio and to anyone snapping pictures with a phone. {The photographer asked everyone to smile.}

Photographic describes anything relating to or produced by photography. A photographic {image} or {record} is one captured by a camera. Someone with a photographic {memory} can recall visual details with unusual precision and clarity, as if they had taken a mental photograph. The word also characterizes qualities that resemble photographs: sharp, detailed, realistic. A photographic {likeness} captures someone exactly as they appear.

Photographs are images created by capturing light on a sensitive surface—originally chemical film, now typically digital sensors. The word often shortens to photos. As a verb, to photograph is to take such images: {She photographs weddings for a living}. Someone who {photographs well} looks attractive in pictures. Photographs serve as evidence, art, and memory: {old family photographs}, {crime scene photographs}.

Photography is the art and practice of capturing images using light. A camera records light onto a sensitive surface—historically film, now typically a digital sensor. The word covers both the technical process and the creative discipline: {She studied photography in college}. {Wedding photography} and {nature photography} name specialized fields. {Aerial photography} captures images from above.

Photos is the plural of photo, an informal shortening of photograph. It refers to images captured by a camera: {I took some photos at the wedding}, {She scrolled through old photos on her phone}. The word dominates casual speech and writing, while photograph sounds more formal or technical.

A photoshoot is a planned session where a photographer takes pictures, typically of a model, celebrity, product, or event. The term implies professional or semi-professional work with deliberate staging: {We did a photoshoot for the new catalog}. Also spelled as two words: photo shoot.

Photoshop is image-editing software that became so dominant its name turned into a verb. To photoshop an image is to digitally alter it—removing blemishes, combining elements, or manipulating reality: {That photo is obviously photoshopped}. The verb applies regardless of which software is actually used. A photoshopped image may be subtly retouched or blatantly fabricated.

Photoshopped means digitally altered, from Adobe Photoshop software that became synonymous with image manipulation. A photoshopped image has been edited—retouching blemishes, removing objects, compositing elements, or distorting reality: {That photo is obviously photoshopped}. The term often implies deception or unrealistic beauty standards: {Magazine covers are heavily photoshopped}. Now used generically regardless of which software was actually used.

Photoshopping is digitally altering an image, especially to improve appearance or create deceptive effects. The term comes from Adobe Photoshop software but applies to any image manipulation: {They photoshopped her waist smaller}, {That sunset looks photoshopped}. The practice ranges from minor touch-ups to wholesale fabrication, making photoshopped a synonym for digitally fake.

Photosynthesis is the process by which plants, algae, and some bacteria convert sunlight into chemical energy. Using light, water, and carbon dioxide, they produce sugars for food and release oxygen as a byproduct. Nearly all life on Earth depends on photosynthesis—directly for food or indirectly through the oxygen it generates.

A phrase is a group of words functioning as a unit within a sentence but not containing both a subject and verb—{in the morning}, {running late}, {the old house on the corner}. To phrase something is to express it in particular words: {Let me phrase this carefully}. How you phrase a question affects what answers you get. In music, a phrase is a short melodic passage forming a distinct unit within a longer piece.

Phrases is the plural of phrase—a group of words forming a unit of meaning smaller than a complete sentence. In grammar, phrases function as single parts of speech: a noun phrase, a verb phrase. In music, a phrase is a short melodic passage. The verb phrases means to express in particular words: {Let me phrase this carefully}. To {turn a phrase} is to express something memorably.

Phrasing is the way something is expressed in words—the particular arrangement and choice of language: {The phrasing of the contract left room for interpretation}. In music, phrasing refers to how a performer shapes melodic lines, grouping notes and managing breath or bowing to create musical sentences. A comedian's timing depends on phrasing as much as content.

Phycobiliproteins are water-soluble pigment proteins found in cyanobacteria and certain algae, where they capture light energy for photosynthesis. These proteins—including phycoerythrin (red) and phycocyanin (blue)—give many algae and bacterial mats their vivid colors. Because they fluoresce brightly, phycobiliproteins are widely used as biological markers in laboratory research and medical diagnostics.

Phylactolaemata is a class of freshwater bryozoans—tiny colonial invertebrates that filter-feed through tentacles. Unlike their marine relatives, phylactolaemata have horseshoe-shaped feeding structures and can survive harsh conditions by forming dormant capsules. The term appears almost exclusively in zoological and ecological literature: {The pond's phylactolaemata population indicated good water quality}.

Physical relates to the body and the material world, as opposed to the mind, spirit, or abstract concepts. A physical {exam} assesses bodily health. Physical {labor} requires bodily effort. The physical {sciences} study matter and energy. Physical {contact} involves touching. To {get physical} can mean becoming violent or sexually intimate. A physical is a medical examination: {I need to schedule my annual physical}.

A physician is a doctor—someone licensed to practice medicine and treat illness. The term is slightly formal, often appearing in professional and institutional contexts: {primary care physician}, {attending physician}. In everyday speech, doctor is more common, while physician appears on forms, in hospital settings, and in compounds like {physician assistant}.

A physicist is a scientist who studies physics—the fundamental laws governing matter, energy, motion, and the structure of the universe. Physicists work in fields ranging from quantum mechanics to astrophysics, often splitting between theoretical work {a theoretical physicist} and experimental research {particle physicists at CERN}.
