Physicists are scientists who study physics—the fundamental nature of matter, energy, space, and time. They investigate everything from subatomic particles to the structure of the universe. Some work theoretically, developing mathematical models; others conduct experiments. {The physicists at CERN discovered the Higgs boson.}

Physics is the science of matter, energy, and their interactions—how objects move, how forces act, how the universe behaves at scales from subatomic particles to galaxies. {She majored in physics}. The physics of something refers to its physical properties or behavior: {The physics of a curveball involves spin and air resistance}.

Phytotelmata are small bodies of water held by plants—the pools that collect in tree holes, pitcher plants, bromeliads, or the cups formed by overlapping leaves. These miniature aquatic habitats support specialized ecosystems of insects, amphibians, and microorganisms. The singular is phytotelma, though the plural form appears more often in scientific literature.

A pianist is a person who plays the piano, especially as a profession or serious pursuit. The term typically implies skill or training beyond casual playing: {She's been a concert pianist for twenty years}. {The jazz pianist improvised throughout the set}.

A piano is a large keyboard instrument where hammers strike strings when keys are pressed. The full name, pianoforte, reflects its ability to play soft (piano) and loud (forte)—a revolutionary feature when invented. Grand pianos have horizontal strings; upright pianos stand vertically to save space. Piano also serves as a musical direction meaning softly: {The passage is marked piano}.

The verb pick in many ways combines the ideas of choosing and seizing. Can you pick a winner? If so, you know how to identify one. If you pick a fight, you start it. To pick someone’s brain is to solicit information from them with questions. Someone or something randomly picked is randomly selected. A pick is an instance or the result of picking, but is also the name of a variety of tools (ice pick, hair pick, guitar pick). If you pick at something, you tinker with it to get a desirable result.

A pickax is a hand tool with a heavy metal head mounted on a wooden handle, used for breaking up hard ground, rock, or pavement. One end of the head is pointed, the other typically flattened like a chisel. The tool is associated with mining, construction, and manual labor: {The workers swung pickaxes at the frozen earth}. Also spelled pickaxe.

A pickaxe is a hand tool with a long wooden handle and a head that typically has a pointed end and a chisel end, used for breaking up hard ground or rock. The pointed end loosens material; the chisel end pries it apart. {Workers swung pickaxes to break through the frozen soil.} Also spelled pickax.

A picket is a pointed stake driven into the ground, used for fencing or tethering animals. The meaning extends to a person stationed outside a workplace during a strike to discourage others from entering: {Picketers blocked the factory entrance}. To picket is to protest in this way. A picket fence is a row of pointed wooden slats, an emblem of suburban domesticity. In military use, a picket is a soldier or group posted to watch for the enemy.

Pickets are pointed stakes driven into the ground, typically as part of a fence or to secure something in place. The word extends to people stationed outside a workplace during a strike, standing like human stakes to discourage others from entering: {Union members walked the picket line for three weeks}. As a verb, to picket means to stand guard in this way, or to enclose an area with pointed stakes. A picket fence, with its evenly spaced vertical slats, evokes images of tidy suburban domesticity.

A pickle is a cucumber preserved in brine or vinegar, though other vegetables can be pickled too: {pickled beets}, {pickled onions}. The verb means to preserve food this way. A pickle is also an awkward situation: {We're in a real pickle now}. In baseball, a pickle is a rundown—a baserunner trapped between fielders.

Pickleball is a paddle sport combining elements of tennis, badminton, and ping-pong. Players use solid paddles to hit a perforated plastic ball over a low net on a court smaller than a tennis court. The game has surged in popularity, especially among older adults, for being easier on joints than tennis: {The retirement community added six pickleball courts}.

Pickled describes food preserved in brine or vinegar: pickled {cucumbers}, pickled {herring}, pickled {eggs}. The process gives foods a characteristic sour or tangy flavor. Figuratively, pickled means drunk: {He was thoroughly pickled by midnight}. The connection is immersion—cucumbers soaked in brine, a person soaked in alcohol.

Pickles are cucumbers preserved in brine or vinegar, though the term extends to any vegetable preserved this way: pickled {onions}, pickled {beets}. In British English, pickle (singular) often means a tangy relish or chutney. To be {in a pickle} is to be in a difficult situation. The verb pickle means to preserve in brine: {We pickled the excess cucumbers from the garden}.

Pickling is preserving food in brine or vinegar, creating an acidic environment that prevents spoilage: {pickling cucumbers}, {pickling beets}. The process gives preserved foods their characteristic tangy flavor. In metalworking, pickling means cleaning metal surfaces with acid to remove scale or oxide. To be {in a pickle} is to be in a difficult situation—preserved in trouble, as it were.

A pickpocket is a thief who steals from people's pockets or bags in public places, typically without the victim noticing: {The crowded subway was full of pickpockets}. The verb pickpocket means to steal in this manner: {Someone pickpocketed my wallet at the festival}. The crime requires dexterity and distraction rather than force.

Pickpockets are thieves who steal from people's pockets or bags in public places, typically using stealth and distraction rather than force. The singular pickpocket refers to a person who does this: {The pickpocket worked the crowded subway platform}. The verb pickpocket means to steal in this manner: {Someone pickpocketed my wallet at the concert}.

Picks is the third-person singular of pick, meaning to select or choose: {She picks the ripest tomatoes}. To pick is also to pluck or gather: {picking berries}, {picking flowers}. You pick at something by pulling at it repeatedly. A pick is a pointed tool for breaking hard surfaces, or a thin piece of plastic or bone for plucking guitar strings. Picks can also mean selections or choices: {These are my picks for the playoffs}.

Pickup covers things that are collected or gathered. A pickup is a small truck with an open bed for hauling. In music, a pickup is a device that captures string vibrations for amplification, or the notes before a downbeat. A pickup game is informal and impromptu—players are picked up on the spot. To pick up speed is to accelerate. A pickup line is an opening gambit to attract a stranger: {He tried some cheesy pickup line at the bar}. The adjective describes things assembled ad hoc: {a pickup band}.

Pickups is the plural of pickup, covering all its senses. A pickup is a small truck with an open cargo bed. In music, pickups are the electromagnetic devices on electric guitars that convert string vibrations to electrical signals. A pickup can be casual sex or the person you pursue for it: {He's looking for a pickup at the bar}. A pickup game is informal and impromptu, organized on the spot rather than scheduled.

Picky describes someone who is excessively selective or hard to please, especially about food: {She's a picky eater}. The word suggests fussiness over small details that others might overlook: {He's picky about which brand of coffee he drinks}. Picky carries a mildly critical tone—being picky is pickier than being selective.

A picnic is a meal eaten outdoors, typically in a pleasant setting like a park or beach, with food brought from elsewhere: {We packed sandwiches for a picnic by the lake}. The word extends to the basket or spread itself: {a picnic of cold chicken and lemonade}. Informally, something described as {no picnic} is difficult or unpleasant: {Raising three kids alone is no picnic}.

Picnics is the plural of picnic—an outdoor meal, typically informal and eaten in a pleasant setting like a park or beach. The word also serves as a verb: {She picnics by the river every Sunday}. To say something is {no picnic} means it's difficult or unpleasant: {Raising three kids alone is no picnic}.

A picture is a visual representation—a painting, drawing, photograph, or image on a screen. The word extends to mental images: {I get the picture}, {Picture this}. A picture can be a film: {motion picture}, {picture show}. To picture something is to imagine it: {I can't picture him as a father}. Someone who embodies a quality is {the picture of health} or {the picture of innocence}.

Pictures are visual representations—photographs, paintings, drawings, or images on screens. The word covers an enormous range, from a child's crayon scribbles to museum masterpieces. To picture something is to form a mental image: {I can't picture him with a beard}. A picture can represent a situation: {The picture isn't as grim as the headlines suggest}. The pictures, especially in British usage, means the cinema: {We're going to the pictures tonight}.

Picturesque describes scenes or places that are visually striking in a charming, quaint, or scenic way—the kind of thing that would make a good picture. A picturesque {village} has cobblestone streets and half-timbered houses. A picturesque {coastline} features dramatic cliffs and hidden coves. The word often suggests beauty that feels composed or idealized: {The inn was picturesque but lacked hot water}.

A pie is a baked dish with a filling inside a pastry crust—fruit pies, meat pies, savory pies. The filling is enclosed or topped with more pastry. To describe something as {easy as pie} or {a piece of pie} is to call it effortless. {Pie in the sky} refers to promises unlikely to materialize. To have a {finger in every pie} is to be involved in many activities. {Pie chart} names the circular graph divided into wedges. (Capitalized Pie may refer to the mathematical constant pi spelled out, or to a name.)

Piece is a handy noun to denote any of the parts of component things (piece of an engine) or of things that are typically divided (two pieces of cake). Single examples of general nouns denoting a class of things are called pieces (piece of furniture). Products of creative work (writing, composition, painting) are often called pieces. To piece something out is to divide it into parts, usually equal ones.

Pieces are parts of something that has been divided, broken, or separated: {The vase shattered into pieces}. A piece of something is a portion or segment: {a piece of cake}, {a piece of advice}. Pieces also names the individual units in board games like chess or checkers. To {go to pieces} is to fall apart emotionally. To {pick up the pieces} is to recover after disaster.

A pier is a structure extending from shore into water, typically supported by pillars. Piers serve as landing places for boats, platforms for fishing, or walkways for strolling: {We walked to the end of the pier}. In architecture, a pier is a solid support between windows or other openings, or a pillar supporting an arch or bridge.

To pierce is to penetrate or make a hole through something, typically with a sharp instrument: {The arrow pierced his armor}. Ears and other body parts are pierced to accommodate jewelry. Figuratively, a scream can pierce the silence, cold can pierce to the bone, or a gaze can pierce through pretense. Something piercing is sharp and penetrating—a piercing wind, a piercing cry, piercing eyes. (Capitalized Pierce is a surname or given name.)

Pierced describes something that has been punctured or penetrated, creating a hole or opening. Body parts are pierced for jewelry: {pierced ears}, {a pierced nose}. The word often appears as an adjective describing someone who has such piercings: {She's heavily pierced}. Figuratively, something can pierce the heart or soul—a pierced heart suggests emotional wounding. A piercing sound or gaze is sharp and penetrating.

Piercing describes something that penetrates sharply—a piercing {scream} cuts through noise, a piercing {stare} seems to see through you, piercing {cold} goes right to the bone. As a noun, a piercing is a hole made in the body for jewelry: {She got a nose piercing}. The word always suggests intensity and directness, whether physical or metaphorical.

Piercings are holes made in the body to hold decorative jewelry. Ear piercings are most common, but piercings appear on noses, eyebrows, lips, tongues, navels, nipples, and genitals. The word refers both to the holes themselves and the jewelry worn in them: {She has multiple piercings}, {I need to clean my piercings}. Getting pierced ranges from mall kiosks for earlobes to specialized studios for more intimate locations.

Pierogies are filled dumplings from Eastern European cuisine, particularly Polish and Ukrainian traditions. The dough is unleavened, wrapped around fillings like potato and cheese, sauerkraut, meat, or fruit, then boiled and often pan-fried in butter. They're comfort food, served with sour cream or onions: {We had pierogies at the church festival}. Also spelled pierogi, which is already plural in Polish.

Piers are structures extending from shore into water, used for boarding boats, fishing, or strolling: {We walked to the end of the pier to watch the sunset}. The word also refers to vertical supports in architecture—the solid sections between windows or arches, or pillars supporting a bridge. A buttress pier reinforces a wall. (Capitalized Piers is a given name.)

Pies is the plural of pie—a baked dish with a crust and filling. Savory pies contain meat or vegetables; sweet pies hold fruit or custard. The word appears in idioms: {easy as pie}, {pie in the sky}, {a finger in every pie}. To pie someone is to throw a pie in their face, usually as protest or prank.

Piety is devoted reverence toward God or the sacred—the quality of being deeply religious: {Her piety was evident in daily prayer}. The word extends to dutiful respect for parents, family, or tradition: {filial piety}. Piety can carry a hint of excessive or performative devotion, though the noun for that is usually pietism or the adjective pious.

Pig is the common name for animals in the swine family that are widely raised for food. When used figuratively, pig has more negative associations than its near synonym hog and it is much more frequent. A person called a pig is being called gluttonous, selfish, or offensive. If you pig out, you eat a great quantity of something. Pig is pejorative slang for policeman.

A pigeon is a stout-bodied bird with a small head, common in cities worldwide. Pigeons and doves are the same family—pigeon typically names the larger, urban species. To pigeon someone is to swindle them, and a pigeon is a gullible person easily deceived: {He was a pigeon for every con man in town}. A pigeonhole is a small compartment, and to pigeonhole is to categorize narrowly.

A pigeonhole is one of a set of small open compartments for sorting mail or storing papers—named for the nesting boxes in a dovecote. To pigeonhole something is to assign it to a category, often dismissively or reductively: {Critics pigeonholed her as a romance novelist}. The verb suggests oversimplification—filing something away rather than engaging with its complexity.

Pigeonholed means assigned to a narrow category and kept there. The image comes from the small compartments in a desk or cabinet where papers are sorted and filed away. To pigeonhole someone is to classify them rigidly: {Once you're pigeonholed as a comedy actor, it's hard to get dramatic roles}. The term often carries frustration—being pigeonholed means others refuse to see your full range.

Pigeonholing is categorizing someone or something in a rigid, often dismissive way: {Critics kept pigeonholing her as a pop singer}. The image comes from the small compartments (pigeonholes) in old desks where papers were sorted and filed away. To pigeonhole someone is to assign them a fixed label that ignores their complexity or potential for change.

Pigeons are stout-bodied birds with small heads, found worldwide in cities and wild areas alike. Urban pigeons descend from domesticated rock doves and thrive on human scraps and architecture. The word also means a person easily deceived or swindled—a mark or sucker: {He was a pigeon for every con artist in town}. To pigeon someone is to swindle them. Clay pigeons are targets launched for shooting practice.

Piggy is a child's word for a pig, often used affectionately or playfully. It extends to anything pig-shaped or pig-related: a piggy {bank}, piggy {toes}. As an adjective, piggy describes greedy or gluttonous behavior: {Don't be so piggy with the cookies}. {Piggy eyes} are small and close-set, like a pig's.

Piggyback describes carrying someone or something on one's back or shoulders, with the carried person's legs wrapped around the carrier's waist: {Give me a piggyback ride!} The word extends to anything that rides along on something else, whether physically or figuratively: a piggyback {trailer} rides atop another on a train, and a company might piggyback {on a competitor's success}. As a verb, to piggyback means to attach or add on to something already in motion or existence.

Piggybacking is riding on someone's back with your legs around their waist, the way a child might ride on a parent. The image extends to anything that hitches a ride on something else: a bill piggybacking on popular legislation, a device piggybacking on another's network connection. {She piggybacked on his research to advance her own thesis.} To piggyback is to carry someone this way, or to attach one thing to another for mutual transport.

A piggybank is a small container for saving coins, traditionally shaped like a pig with a slot in the top. Children use piggybanks to accumulate spare change: {She's been dropping quarters into her piggybank for months}. The term extends to any personal savings reserve: {I had to break into my piggybank to cover the repair}. Also spelled piggy bank.

Pigheaded means stubbornly refusing to change one's mind or course of action despite good reasons to do so. The word carries a stronger negative charge than merely stubborn—it suggests willful obstinacy that others find exasperating: {He was too pigheaded to admit he was wrong}. {Don't be so pigheaded about this}.

A piglet is a young pig, typically one still nursing or recently weaned. The word emphasizes smallness and youth: {The sow had a litter of eight piglets}. Piglet also names the timid character in A.A. Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh stories.

Piglets are young pigs, typically those still nursing or recently weaned. The word carries connotations of smallness and cuteness: {The sow had a litter of eight piglets}. Piglet appears as a character name in children's literature, most famously Winnie-the-Pooh's timid companion.

Pigment is a substance that gives color. In biology, pigments are molecules that produce color in living things—melanin in skin, chlorophyll in plants. In art and manufacturing, pigments are finely ground particles mixed into paints, inks, dyes, and cosmetics: {The artist ground her own pigments}. To pigment something is to add color to it.

A pigpen is an enclosure where pigs are kept—a small fenced area or shed on a farm. The word extends to any extremely messy or dirty space: {Your room is a pigpen}. The insult carries the implication of filth and disorder associated with pigs wallowing in mud. Also spelled pig pen or pigsty, which shares the figurative meaning.

Pigs are stout, omnivorous mammals with flat snouts, raised for meat (pork, bacon, ham) or kept as pets. The word extends to people who are greedy, messy, or gluttonous: {He made a pig of himself at the buffet}. Pig is also derogatory slang for police officers. To pig out is to eat excessively.

A pigsty is an enclosure where pigs are kept—typically a small, muddy pen. The word extends to any place that's filthy or chaotic: {Your room is a pigsty}. The figurative use is far more common than the literal one. Also called a pigpen.

A pigtail is a braid or束 of hair hanging from the head. In American usage, pigtails usually means two braids or ponytails, one on each side: {She wore her hair in pigtails}. British usage may refer to a single braid. The word extends to anything twisted or coiled like a braid: a pigtail {connector} in electrical work, or the curly tail of a pig itself.

Pigtails are a hairstyle where the hair is divided and gathered into two bunches, one on each side of the head: {She wore her hair in pigtails}. The style is associated with children, especially girls, though adults wear it too. A single gathering at the back is technically a ponytail, not a pigtail, though usage varies. The name comes from the twisted shape resembling a pig's curly tail.

A pike is a long wooden shaft with a pointed metal head, used as a weapon by infantry before firearms became dominant. The word extends to sharp-pointed things: a pike position in diving tucks the body with legs straight. A pike is also a large predatory freshwater fish with an elongated body and sharp teeth. In American regional use, a pike is a turnpike or toll road: {We took the pike to avoid traffic}. To pike is to thrust or pierce. (Capitalized Pike is a surname.)

Pilates is a system of exercises emphasizing controlled movements, core strength, and flexibility. Developed in the early twentieth century by Joseph Pilates, it focuses on precise, flowing motions coordinated with breathing. Classes typically use mats or specialized equipment like the reformer: {I do Pilates three times a week}. The name is often lowercased when referring to the practice generally.

A pile is an unorganized mass of things in one place (pile of dirty dishes). Pile may also designate a large amount, especially of money. To pile things means to create a pile of them. If people pile in to a place, they get in quickly. If things pile up, they accumulate. Other meanings of pile are a long column driven into the ground as a support; a surface of thick fur or threads (deep pile carpeting); and (usually plural) hemorrhoids.

A piledriver is a machine that hammers heavy posts (piles) into the ground to create foundations for buildings, bridges, and docks. The term extends to anything delivering powerful downward force—a piledriver punch, a piledriver wrestling move where an opponent is driven headfirst into the mat. {He hit him with a piledriver of a right hook.}

Piles has two unrelated meanings. One is the plural of pile—heaps, stacks, or large quantities: {piles of laundry}, {piles of money}. The other is an informal term for hemorrhoids—swollen blood vessels in and around the anus that cause discomfort, itching, and sometimes bleeding: {suffering from piles}.

A pileup is an accumulation of things heaped together, often chaotically. The term most commonly describes a multi-vehicle collision where cars crash into each other in succession: {A pileup on the freeway involved twelve vehicles}. More broadly, any backup or accumulation qualifies: {a pileup of dirty dishes}, {a pileup of unanswered emails}.

A pilgrim is a person who journeys to a sacred place for religious devotion—to a shrine, holy city, or site of spiritual significance: {pilgrims traveling to Mecca}, {pilgrims at Lourdes}. The word extends to any long journey undertaken with purpose or reverence: {a pilgrim in search of meaning}. In figurative use, we are all pilgrims passing through life. (Capitalized Pilgrim refers to the English settlers at Plymouth.)

A pilgrimage is a journey to a sacred place or shrine, undertaken for religious devotion: {Muslims make a pilgrimage to Mecca}, {pilgrimage to the Holy Land}. The word extends to any journey with deep personal significance—visiting a beloved author's home, a musician's grave, or the field where a historic game was played: {an annual pilgrimage to Graceland}. As a verb, to pilgrimage is to make such a journey, though this use is less common than the noun.

Pilgrims are people who journey to a sacred place for religious reasons—to a shrine, holy city, or site of spiritual significance. The word extends to any travelers on a meaningful quest: {pilgrims seeking a new life in California}. More loosely, pilgrims are people new to a place or undertaking. (Capitalized Pilgrims refers to the English colonists who founded Plymouth.)

A pill is a small, smooth tablet containing medicine or food supplements that is typically swallowed. A modifier often specifies what is being treated (birth control pill, sleeping pill, vitamin pill). The pill, in proper context, refers to contraception for women by pill. A bitter pill (to swallow) is something unpleasant that must be done or endured. If you call a person a pill, it means they are tedious or unadventurous.

Pillage is the violent seizure of goods, especially during war or civil unrest—troops pillaging a conquered city, looters pillaging stores during riots. The word works as both verb and noun: {The army pillaged the village} or {The pillage lasted three days}. It implies systematic, often brutal taking rather than opportunistic theft.

A pillager is someone who plunders or loots, taking goods by force during war, raids, or civil unrest. The word carries a sense of violent theft and destruction: {Viking pillagers swept through coastal villages}. In gaming contexts, particularly Minecraft, pillagers are hostile characters that raid settlements.

Pillagers are people who plunder and loot, typically during war, raids, or civil unrest. The word evokes violent seizure of goods and valuables: {Viking pillagers descended on the coastal villages}. It carries a sense of lawless destruction beyond mere theft—pillagers don't just steal, they ransack.

Pillaging is the act of plundering or looting, especially during war or civil unrest. Soldiers pillage conquered cities; rioters pillage shops. The word suggests violent, opportunistic theft on a significant scale: {The invading army spent days pillaging the countryside}. Figuratively, it describes aggressive extraction: {corporate pillaging of natural resources}.

A pillar is a vertical structure that supports something above it—a column holding up a roof or bridge. The word extends to anything that provides essential support: a {pillar of the community} is someone whose presence and contributions are fundamental to it. The {pillars of democracy} are its foundational principles. To go from {pillar to post} is to move frantically from place to place seeking help or resolution.

Pillars are vertical structures that support something above them—columns holding up a roof or bridge. The word extends to anything that provides essential support: {She was a pillar of the community}. The {pillars of democracy} are its foundational principles. A {pillar of strength} is someone others rely on in difficult times. To go from {pillar to post} is to move from place to place without settling.

A pillbox is a small container for pills, often with compartments for organizing daily doses. The shape—squat, cylindrical, flat-topped—gives its name to a pillbox hat, a brimless women's hat fashionable in the mid-20th century. In military usage, a pillbox is a small concrete fortification with gun slits, used as a defensive position.

A pillow is a soft cushion for supporting the head during sleep, typically filled with feathers, foam, or synthetic fibers. Pillows also serve decorative purposes on sofas and beds. To pillow something is to rest it as if on a pillow: {She pillowed her head on her arms}. A {pillow fight} is a playful battle using pillows as weapons.

Pillows are soft cushions for supporting the head during sleep or rest, typically filled with down, foam, or synthetic fibers. Beyond bedding, pillows serve as decorative items on sofas or as support for other body parts: {She propped a pillow under her knees}. To pillow is to rest one's head on something soft: {He pillowed his head on her lap}.

Pills are small solid doses of medicine meant to be swallowed whole. The word extends to anything pill-shaped or pill-like: birth control pills, vitamin pills. To pill is to form into small balls, as when fabric develops those annoying fuzzballs. {A bitter pill to swallow} is something unpleasant you must accept. {On the pill} means using oral contraceptives.

If you pilot an aircraft, you are the pilot. By extension, both the noun and verb are used generally of people who lead or show the way. A different meaning of pilot is a TV program made as a sample for possible future development. From this, a preliminary activity may attract the adjective pilot (pilot project). Sometimes the pilot light that starts a heater or gas appliance is just called a pilot.

Piloting is navigating or controlling the movement of a vessel, aircraft, or vehicle. A pilot does the piloting, whether steering a ship through a harbor or flying a plane. The term extends to guiding anything through difficulty: {She's piloting the legislation through committee}. Piloting also names the skill or practice itself: {He studied piloting before getting his license}.

Pilots are people who operate aircraft, guiding planes through takeoff, flight, and landing. The term extends to those who navigate ships through difficult waters or steer spacecraft. A pilot can also be a trial version of something—a pilot {program}, a pilot {episode}—testing viability before full commitment. To pilot is to guide or steer: {She piloted the company through the merger}.

A pimp is a man who manages prostitutes and takes a share of their earnings. The term carries connotations of exploitation, flashy dress, and street-level crime. To pimp is to act as a pimp, or more broadly, to promote aggressively: {He's always pimping his new book}. To {pimp out} something is to customize it showily: {pimp out a car with chrome rims}. The adjective pimp means stylish or impressive in slang: {That jacket is pimp}.

A pimple is a small inflamed spot on the skin, typically with a raised center that may contain pus. Pimples result from clogged pores and are especially common during adolescence. Figuratively, something insignificant on a larger surface might be called a pimple: {The town was just a pimple on the map}.

A pimple is an irritated spot on the skin, often on the face, caused by a blocked pore. Pimples are usually the result of a condition called acne, which typically affects teenagers. Pimple is not used very often as a verb but if you pimple someone, you inflict pimples on them.

Pimps is the plural of pimp—a person who manages prostitutes and takes a cut of their earnings. The word carries connotations of exploitation and control: {Pimps often use manipulation or violence to keep sex workers dependent}. As a verb, to pimp means to act as a pimp, or more broadly to promote aggressively or customize flashily: {He pimped his ride with chrome rims}.

Pins tend to be cylindrical (cotter pin, bowling pin, rolling pin) and may have a pointed end (safety pin, lapel pin) used for attaching or fixing. If you pin one thing to another, you attach it using a pin. If you pin some bad thing on someone, especially if you pin the blame on them, you hold them responsible. To pin down someone or something is to ascertain details or definitive information.

Pinacolborane is a boron-containing organic compound used in chemical synthesis, particularly for adding boron groups to molecules through hydroboration reactions. It appears as a colorless liquid and serves as a key reagent in pharmaceutical and materials chemistry: {The catalyst enabled efficient hydroboration with pinacolborane}.

A piñata is a decorated container—traditionally of papier-mâché—filled with candy and small toys, hung up to be broken open with a stick by blindfolded participants. Associated with Mexican celebrations and children's birthday parties, the piñata swings from a rope while the blindfolded person swings at it: {The kids lined up to take turns hitting the piñata}.

Piñatas are hollow figures made of papier-mâché or cardboard, filled with candy and small toys, then hung up to be broken open with a stick. Traditional at children's birthday parties and Mexican celebrations, they're often shaped like animals or cartoon characters. Blindfolded participants take turns swinging until the piñata bursts and spills its contents: {The kids lined up to take a crack at the piñata}.

Pinball is an arcade game where players use flippers to keep a metal ball in play on a slanted, obstacle-filled playfield, scoring points by hitting targets and bumpers. The game dominated arcades before video games. Figuratively, to pinball is to bounce erratically between things: {I spent the afternoon pinballing between meetings}.

A pincer is one of a pair of grasping claws on crustaceans and some insects—lobsters, crabs, scorpions. The plural pincers denotes a gripping tool with two pivoting jaws, used to pull nails or grip objects. In military strategy, a pincer movement attacks an enemy from two sides simultaneously, squeezing like the tool: {The army executed a pincer maneuver to surround the retreating forces}.

Pincers are a gripping tool with two pivoting arms that close together, used for grasping, pulling, or cutting: {She used pincers to remove the nail}. The word also describes the claw of a crab or lobster, which works by the same mechanism. A {pincer movement} is a military maneuver attacking from two sides simultaneously.

The verb pinch is for the action of squeezing something, especially between two fingers, and a pinch is an instance of doing this, or a small amount of something (pinch of oregano). Noun uses of pinch mostly carry over the idea of being squeezed or compressed, often uncomfortably. If you’re in a pinch or you feel the pinch, you’re in a stressful situation. If a nerve is pinched, it is compressed and causing pain.

Pinched describes something squeezed, compressed, or constricted. A pinched nerve is painfully compressed. A pinched face looks thin and drawn, suggesting stress or hardship: {Her pinched expression told me the news wasn't good}. In informal use, pinched means stolen: {Someone pinched my bike}. British slang extends this to being arrested: {He got pinched for shoplifting}. To be pinched for money is to have too little of it.

A pincushion is a small padded cushion for holding pins and needles, keeping them organized and accessible during sewing. The shape—typically round or square, stuffed firm—makes it easy to push pins in and pull them out. Figuratively, someone who has been stuck repeatedly by needles or criticism might be called a pincushion: {After all those blood draws, my arm looks like a pincushion}.

Pine is an evergreen conifer with needle-like leaves and woody cones, valued for timber and resin. The wood itself is also pine: {pine furniture}, {pine floors}. To pine is to yearn or waste away from longing: {She pined for her homeland}. Someone pining away suffers visibly from grief or unfulfilled desire.

Pineapple is a tropical fruit with tough, segmented skin and a crown of stiff leaves. The yellow flesh inside is sweet-tart and juicy. The fruit grows from a plant, not a tree, and takes about two years to mature. In slang, pineapple sometimes refers to a hand grenade, from the resemblance of certain designs to the fruit's textured exterior.

Pineapples is the plural of pineapple, the tropical fruit with spiny skin, a crown of stiff leaves, and sweet yellow flesh. Despite the name, pineapples are unrelated to pines or apples—early European explorers named them for their resemblance to pine cones. {Fresh pineapples are cheaper in Hawaii.}

A pinecone is the woody, scaled reproductive structure of a pine tree, roughly oval or conical in shape. The overlapping scales open to release seeds in dry weather and close when wet. Pinecones are common in crafts and holiday decorations: {We gathered pinecones for the wreath}.

Pinecones are the woody, scaled reproductive structures of pine trees and other conifers. They come in male and female forms, though the familiar large ones found on the ground are female cones that have opened to release their seeds. Pinecones are commonly used in autumn and winter decorations, and their scales open and close in response to humidity—a folk method for predicting rain.

Pines are evergreen coniferous trees with needle-like leaves, known for their tall straight trunks and distinctive scent. Pine wood is widely used in construction and furniture. To pine is to yearn or long for something, often with sadness: {She pined for her homeland}. To {pine away} is to waste from grief or longing.

Ping is a short, high-pitched sound—the noise of a small bell, a metal object struck, or a microwave announcing it's finished. In computing, a ping tests whether a server is reachable: {I'll ping the server to check if it's down}. More broadly, to ping someone is to send a quick message or check in: {Ping me when you're free}. The word captures brief, attention-getting contact.

Pinging is sending a brief signal to check if something or someone is reachable and responsive. In computing, pinging tests whether a server or device is online: {I'm pinging the server to see if it's down}. More casually, pinging someone means sending them a quick message to get their attention or check in: {I'll ping you later about dinner}. The word evokes the sharp sound of sonar—a pulse sent out, waiting for a reply.

Pingpong is table tennis—a game where players hit a lightweight ball back and forth across a net on a small table using paddles. The name imitates the sound of play. Figuratively, to pingpong is to go back and forth repeatedly: {The proposal pingponged between committees for months}. Also spelled ping-pong.

A pinhead is the small, rounded end of a pin—something tiny. By extension, pinhead means a stupid person, someone whose brain is supposedly the size of a pin's head: {Don't be such a pinhead}. The insult is mild and somewhat dated. Pinhead also describes anything unusually small: {pinhead-sized dots}.

Pining is yearning or longing, especially with sadness or unfulfilled desire. Someone pines for a lost love, a distant home, or something they can't have: {She spent years pining for him after he left}. The word suggests a wasting away from grief or longing—to pine is to languish, to ache quietly over time.

Pink is a color intermediate between red and white. It has strong associations with femininity and with baby girls, and it’s also common in flowers, of which one family (Dianthus) is called pinks. If you’re in the pink, you’re in good health – this is perhaps with reference to the perception of a white person’s healthy skin color. Pink is sometimes used to disparage political views that are thought to be too left leaning. To pink fabric (a different word) is to add decoration to the edge or border of it, perhaps cut with pinking shears.

Pinkeye is conjunctivitis—inflammation of the membrane lining the eyelid and covering the white of the eye. The condition makes the eye red, itchy, and often crusty with discharge. Highly contagious forms spread rapidly through schools and households: {Half the class came down with pinkeye}. Also spelled pink eye or pink-eye.

The pinkie is the smallest finger, on the outer edge of the hand opposite the thumb. Also called the little finger. A {pinkie promise} or {pinkie swear} is made by linking pinkies with another person—a gesture suggesting childlike sincerity. Also spelled pinky.

Pinkies are the smallest fingers, on the outer edge of each hand. The word is informal and affectionate, often used with children: {Hold up your pinkies}. A {pinkie promise} or {pinkie swear} is a pledge made by linking pinkies with another person—childish but still invoked playfully among adults.

The pinky is the smallest finger, on the outer edge of the hand opposite the thumb. Also called the little finger. A {pinky promise} or {pinky swear} is a childish oath sealed by linking pinky fingers. The spelling pinkie is also common.

A pinnacle is the highest point of something—a mountain peak, a spire atop a building, or the culmination of achievement: {She reached the pinnacle of her career}. The word suggests a sharp, narrow summit rather than a broad plateau, implying that the top is precarious or hard to maintain: {At the pinnacle of his fame, he had nowhere to go but down}.

Pinnacles are the highest points or peaks of something. A mountain pinnacle is its summit; architectural pinnacles are the pointed ornamental tops of towers and buttresses. Figuratively, a pinnacle is the culmination of achievement: {She reached the pinnacle of her career}. The word always implies a sharp, elevated point—literal or metaphorical.

Pinning is the act of holding something or someone in place. You pin fabric before sewing, pin an opponent to the mat in wrestling, or pin a photo to a bulletin board. In computing, pinning keeps an item visible or accessible—pinning a tab in a browser, pinning an app to a taskbar. {She was pinning her hopes on the interview going well.}

Pinpoint describes something extremely precise or exact: {pinpoint accuracy}, {the pinpoint location of the signal}. As a verb, to pinpoint is to identify or locate with precision: {We couldn't pinpoint the source of the noise}. The image is of a pin's point—the smallest possible target. A pinpoint of light is a tiny, concentrated spot.

Pins are thin, pointed pieces of metal or plastic used to fasten things together. A straight pin secures fabric; a safety pin has a clasp that covers the point. Hairpins hold hair in place. Bowling pins stand to be knocked down. In electronics, pins are the metal prongs on a connector. To pin is to hold something in place: {He pinned her arms to her sides}. If you're {on pins and needles}, you're anxiously waiting.

A pinstripe is a very narrow stripe in a fabric. The word is used most frequently in the phrase pinstripe suit, a suit of jacket and trousers that is made from such a fabric. Pinstripe is sometimes used to refer to people who typically wear such suits, as in the pinstripes of Wall Street.

A pint is a unit of liquid measure equal to half a quart—about 473 milliliters in the United States, 568 in Britain. The word commonly refers to a pint of beer: {Let's grab a pint after work}. A pint-sized person or thing is small. In casual British use, {a pint} can mean a drink at the pub generally.

Pints are units of liquid measure, equal to one-eighth of a gallon. In the U.S., a pint is 16 fluid ounces; in Britain, it's 20 fluid ounces, making British pints about 20% larger. The word commonly refers to a pint of beer: {Let's grab a pint after work}. In American contexts, pints often mean containers of ice cream, which hold 16 ounces. {We split a pint of Ben & Jerry's.}

Pintsized means small in stature, especially used affectionately or humorously for children or diminutive adults. The image is of something measured in pints rather than gallons—compact enough to fit in a small container. {The pintsized slugger hit three home runs}. Also spelled pint-sized or pint-size.

A pinup is a photograph or poster of an attractive person, typically displayed on a wall. The term dates from World War II, when soldiers posted pictures of glamorous women in barracks and lockers. A pinup girl is the subject of such an image. The term now applies to any decorative portrait meant for display: {classic pinup style}, {he's got pinup looks}.

Pinups are pictures of attractive people, typically in provocative poses, designed to be displayed on walls. The term emerged from the practice of pinning such images to barracks walls or inside lockers. A pinup can also be the person depicted: {She was a famous pinup during World War II}. The style suggests glamorous, suggestive but not explicit imagery—more tease than reveal.

A pinwheel is a toy consisting of colored vanes attached to a stick, designed to spin when blown or caught by wind. The shape extends to fireworks that spin while emitting sparks, and to things arranged in a radiating pattern: {pinwheel cookies}, {The dancers formed a pinwheel}. As a verb, to pinwheel is to spin or rotate: {His arms pinwheeled as he fell}.

Pinwheels are small wheels with vanes that spin when blown or caught by wind—the kind children hold up while running. The shape extends to fireworks that spin while emitting sparks, and to food arranged in a spiral: {spinach pinwheels}, {ham and cheese pinwheels}. To pinwheel is to spin or rotate: {Her arms pinwheeled as she lost her balance}.

A pioneer is someone who goes first into unsettled territory, blazing trails for others to follow. American history celebrates pioneers who moved westward in the 18th and 19th centuries. The meaning extends to anyone who opens new fields of endeavor: {a pioneer in heart surgery}, {pioneers of early aviation}. As a verb, to pioneer is to be the first to develop or explore: {She pioneered new techniques in gene therapy}. As an adjective, it describes early or groundbreaking efforts: {pioneer research}, {pioneer species} in ecology.

Pioneered is the past tense of pioneer, meaning to be among the first to develop, explore, or settle something. Someone who pioneered a technique or field opened new territory for others to follow: {She pioneered the use of DNA evidence in criminal cases}. The word carries connotations of innovation and courage in venturing into the unknown.

Pioneering describes work that opens new territory—literal or figurative. Pioneer settlers cleared land no one had farmed; pioneering research explores questions no one has asked. The word emphasizes being first: {pioneering work in gene therapy}, {a pioneering spirit}. It carries connotations of courage and innovation, though also sometimes recklessness.

Pioneers are people who venture into new territory before others. Early American pioneers settled the frontier. By extension, pioneers in any field are the first to explore or develop something: {pioneers of aviation}, {pioneers of jazz}. The verb means to be among the first: {She pioneered new surgical techniques}. A pioneer spirit suggests boldness and willingness to face the unknown.

A pip is a small seed, especially from a citrus fruit or apple: {orange pips}, {lemon pips}. It's also one of the small symbols on dice, dominoes, or playing cards that indicate value. In British slang, the pips are the short beeps of a time signal on radio. To pip someone is to narrowly defeat them: {She pipped him at the post}. In computing, pip is a package installer for Python.

Except for the kinds that contain tobacco or that are a musical instrument, a pipe is usually a simple hollow tube. It may channel a fluid (drain pipe) or serve some other purpose, like the pipes on an organ. To pipe something somewhere is to transport it in a pipe, or as if in a pipe (piped-in music, pipe frosting onto a cake). In computing, to pipe data is to transmit it electronically, especially via wires rather than radio signals. The keyboard character | is sometimes called a pipe.

A pipe dream is a hope or plan that is wildly unrealistic or fantastical—the kind of wishful thinking unlikely to survive contact with reality. The term comes from the vivid hallucinations of opium smokers: {Retiring at forty was a pipe dream on his salary}. Also spelled pipedream.

A pipeline is a long tube for transporting liquids or gases over distances: {an oil pipeline}, {a natural gas pipeline}. The word extends to any channel through which things flow in sequence. In business, a pipeline holds deals or products in progress: {We have several contracts in the pipeline}. In computing, a pipeline chains processes so output from one feeds into the next. The verb means to transport through a pipeline or, more broadly, to channel toward a destination: {The program pipelines talented students into engineering careers}.

A pipeline is a system of pipes for transporting liquids or gases over long distances, such as oil or natural gas from extraction sites to refineries or distribution points. The term extends to any channel or process through which something flows in stages: a sales {pipeline} tracks potential customers, a software {pipeline} moves code from development to deployment. In computing, pipelines chain commands or processes so the output of one becomes the input of the next.

A piper is someone who plays a pipe, especially the bagpipes: {The piper led the funeral procession}. The phrase {pay the piper} means to face consequences or settle debts—from the idea that whoever pays the piper calls the tune, controlling what gets played.

Pipes are hollow tubes for conveying liquids or gases: water pipes, gas pipes, drain pipes. A pipe for smoking has a bowl at one end where tobacco burns. Organ pipes and bagpipes produce sound when air passes through tubes. Someone's pipes are their vocal cords or singing voice: {She has great pipes}. To pipe is to convey through pipes or to play a pipe instrument. {Pipe down} means be quiet; {pipe up} means speak up.

Piping is a system of pipes, or the material used to make them: {The old house needed new piping throughout}. In sewing, piping is a narrow cord covered in fabric, used as decorative trim along edges and seams. In cooking, piping is the technique of squeezing soft material through a nozzle to decorate cakes or shape dough. The phrase {piping hot} means very hot—from the hissing sound of steam escaping, like air through a pipe.

Pips are small seeds found in fruits like apples, oranges, and grapes. The word also names the dots on dice and dominoes, or the suit symbols on playing cards. In British military usage, pips are the small insignia indicating officer rank. To pip someone is to narrowly defeat them: {She pipped him at the post}. The pips also refers to the short beeping tones marking the hour on British radio broadcasts.

A pipsqueak is someone small and insignificant, especially a young or inexperienced person who acts bigger than they are: {Some pipsqueak in accounting rejected my expense report}. The word is dismissive but relatively mild—more contemptuous than cruel. It can also describe anything trivially small: {a pipsqueak of a car}.

Piracy is robbery or violence at sea—the hijacking of ships and their cargo by armed attackers. By extension, piracy covers the unauthorized copying or distribution of copyrighted material: software piracy, music piracy, film piracy. {They were charged with piracy for distributing bootleg recordings}. The term carries connotations of theft, though defenders of digital piracy dispute the analogy.

A piranha is a freshwater fish native to South American rivers, known for its sharp teeth and reputation for aggressive feeding. Schools of piranhas can strip flesh from prey with alarming speed, though attacks on humans are rare. The name extends figuratively to people who are ruthlessly aggressive, especially in business or media: {The reporters descended like piranhas}.

Piranhas are freshwater fish native to South American rivers, famous for their sharp teeth and reputation as ferocious predators. While they can strip flesh from bone in feeding frenzies, attacks on humans are rare and usually involve wounded or bleeding swimmers. The word often appears figuratively to describe aggressive people who descend on something vulnerable: {The reporters were like piranhas when the scandal broke}. A single fish is a piranha.

A pirate is someone who robs ships at sea. The term extends to anyone who takes what isn't theirs to take: software pirates copy programs illegally, pirate radio stations broadcast without licenses. To pirate something is to copy or use it without authorization: {They pirated the movie before it hit theaters}. A pirated version is an unauthorized copy.

Pirated describes something that has been copied, distributed, or used without authorization from the copyright holder. The term applies most commonly to software, movies, music, and books that are illegally duplicated and shared. {He downloaded a pirated copy of the game.} Pirated goods are often sold at a fraction of the legitimate price or distributed freely online. The word derives from pirate in its sense of one who takes what doesn't belong to them.

Pirates are people who rob ships at sea, or who attack coastal settlements from the water. The term extends to anyone who takes or uses something without authorization—especially copyrighted material: {software pirates}, {music piracy}. To pirate is to copy or distribute illegally: {The movie was pirated before its theatrical release}. A pirate radio station broadcasts without a license.

Pirating is copying or distributing copyrighted material without authorization—software, movies, music, books. The term borrows from maritime piracy, casting unauthorized copying as theft on the digital seas: {He got caught pirating games}. The practice ranges from casual file-sharing to organized distribution networks. Also used as an adjective: {a pirating website}.

Pirogi are Eastern European dumplings—pockets of unleavened dough filled with potato, cheese, sauerkraut, meat, or fruit, then boiled or fried. They appear in Polish, Ukrainian, and Russian cuisines under various spellings: pierogi, pyrohy, pirozhki. In North America, the potato-and-cheese variety dominates, often served with sour cream and onions: {We ordered a plate of pirogi at the Polish diner}.

A pirouette is a full spin on one foot, especially in ballet, where the dancer rises on pointe or demi-pointe and rotates rapidly. The word extends to any graceful spinning movement: {The figure skater ended with a triple pirouette}. As a verb, to pirouette is to execute such a turn: {She pirouetted across the stage}.

Pirouettes are full-body spins performed on one foot, especially in ballet, where the dancer rises on pointe or demi-pointe and revolves one or more times. The word extends to any graceful spinning movement: {The figure skater executed three pirouettes}. Figuratively, to pirouette is to shift direction with nimble ease: {Politicians pirouette around difficult questions}.

Piss is a vulgar but common term for urine and the act of urinating: {I need to take a piss}. As a verb: {The dog pissed on the rug}. Piss extends into many expressions: {piss away} means to waste (money, opportunity), {piss off} means to anger or to go away (British), and {full of piss and vinegar} describes someone brimming with youthful energy and aggression. Piss can also mean inferior: {piss-poor}, {piss-weak}. The word is cruder than pee but milder than most vulgar terms.

Pissed has a sharp transatlantic split. In American English, pissed means angry: {She was pissed about the parking ticket}. In British English, pissed means drunk: {He got completely pissed at the pub}. Both senses can cause confusion when speakers cross the Atlantic. Pissed off means angry in both dialects: {I'm really pissed off right now}.

Pistachio is a small greenish nut with a hard, partially split shell, prized for its distinctive sweet flavor. The nuts are eaten roasted and salted, used in ice cream and baked goods, or ground into paste. The pale yellow-green color of the nut meat gives its name to a shade: {pistachio walls}, {a pistachio cardigan}.

Pistachios is the plural of pistachio, a small greenish nut with a partially split shell. The shells crack open as the nut matures, making them easy to eat by hand: {a bowl of pistachios}. Pistachio also refers to the pale yellow-green color of the nut's interior: {pistachio ice cream}.

A pistol is a handgun—a firearm small enough to hold and fire with one hand. The term covers revolvers and semi-automatic handguns alike. To pistol-whip someone is to strike them with a pistol's grip. In older slang, a pistol was a lively or mischievous person: {That kid is a real pistol}.

Pistols are small firearms designed to be held and fired with one hand. The term covers both revolvers, which use a rotating cylinder to hold ammunition, and semi-automatic handguns, which feed cartridges from a magazine in the grip. {He kept a pistol in the nightstand.} In figurative use, a pistol can describe someone lively and spirited: {That kid is a real pistol.}

To pistolwhip is to strike someone with a handgun, typically using the grip or barrel as a bludgeon rather than firing: {The robber pistolwhipped the clerk when he didn't open the register fast enough}. The term evokes brutal, close-quarters violence—often associated with crime, interrogation, or police brutality. Also spelled pistol-whip.

A piston is a cylindrical component that moves back and forth inside a tube, transferring force in engines, pumps, and compressors. In internal combustion engines, pistons convert the explosive force of burning fuel into the rotational motion that drives wheels. {The mechanic replaced a cracked piston.} Piston also describes a similar mechanism in brass instruments that changes pitch when depressed.

Pistons are cylindrical components that move back and forth inside a tube, typically to transfer force in an engine or pump. In internal combustion engines, pistons convert the explosive force of burning fuel into the rotating motion that powers a vehicle. Hydraulic systems use pistons to transmit pressure through fluid. The word often appears in discussions of engine performance: {The mechanic said one of the pistons was cracked}. Pistons is also the name of the Detroit NBA basketball team.

A pit is a hole or indentation, often very large and/or serving a particular purpose (gravel pit, barbecue pit), sometimes unpleasant (the pit of hell). A lower area near a stage may be called a pit (orchestra pit, mosh pit). A pit is also the seed of some fruits, and this accounts for some verb use; if you pit cherries, you remove the seed. A pitted surface has many small indentations. To pit one against another is to set them at conflict.

Pita is a round, flat bread that puffs up during baking, creating a hollow pocket inside. Common in Middle Eastern and Mediterranean cuisines, the pocket makes it ideal for stuffing with falafel, shawarma, or other fillings: {I ordered a chicken pita for lunch}. Pita also works as a scoop for hummus or dips.

A pitbull is any of several stocky, muscular dog breeds originally developed for fighting, including the American Pit Bull Terrier and American Staffordshire Terrier. The dogs have a reputation for aggression that advocates dispute, citing owner behavior as the real factor: {Pitbulls are loyal and affectionate when properly trained}. Breed-specific legislation in some jurisdictions restricts or bans ownership. Also spelled pit bull. (Capitalized Pitbull is the stage name of the rapper.)

The noun and verb pitch has many meanings, often unrelated. If you pitch an idea, you solicit interest in it; in other words, you make a pitch for your idea. To pitch a ball is to throw it, especially in baseball; doing this is a pitch. Some games are played on a field called a pitch. Pitch is also a black oily substance, and this inspires the phrases pitch black and pitch darkness. Pitch also indicates a level on a scale (high-pitched voice, fever pitch).

Pitched describes something set at a particular level or angle. A pitched {roof} slopes rather than lying flat. A pitched {battle} is intense and sustained—forces fully committed. The word often appears with modifiers indicating degree: a {high-pitched} voice, a {low-pitched} hum. Something pitched toward a particular audience is aimed or adjusted for them: {The presentation was pitched at beginners}.

A pitcher is a container with a handle and spout for pouring liquids—water, juice, beer. {She filled the pitcher with lemonade.} In baseball, the pitcher is the player who throws the ball to the batter, standing on the mound at the center of the diamond. {The pitcher struck out twelve batters.} The baseball sense has spawned figurative use: in vulgar slang, the pitcher is the insertive partner in anal sex, contrasted with the catcher.

Pitchers is the plural of pitcher, which has two distinct meanings. A pitcher is a container with a handle and spout for pouring liquids: {a pitcher of water}, {a pitcher of beer}. In baseball, the pitcher is the player who throws the ball to the batter: {The pitchers warmed up in the bullpen}. Both uses are common, distinguished by context.

A pitchfork is a long-handled farm tool with two or more widely spaced prongs, used for lifting and tossing hay, straw, or other loose material. The pitchfork's silhouette—a handle topped by pointed tines—has made it an enduring symbol of rural life, angry mobs, and the devil himself. To pitchfork something is to lift or move it with this tool, or figuratively to thrust someone abruptly into a situation: {She was pitchforked into the CEO role after the scandal}.

Pitchforks are long-handled farm tools with two or more prongs, used for lifting and tossing hay or straw. The image of peasants wielding pitchforks represents angry mobs: {The townspeople showed up with pitchforks and torches}. To pitchfork something is to lift it with the tool, or figuratively, to thrust someone abruptly into a situation: {She was pitchforked into the CEO role}.

Pitching covers the act of throwing or the quality of being angled. In baseball, pitching is the art of throwing the ball to the batter: {Her pitching has improved this season}. A ship pitching rocks fore and aft in rough seas. A roof's pitching describes its slope. In business, pitching means making a persuasive presentation: {He spent the afternoon pitching investors}. To be {pitching in} is to help with a shared task.

A pitchman is someone who sells goods or promotes ideas through persuasive, often aggressive talking—originally the hawkers at carnivals and street corners demonstrating products to crowds. The term now applies to anyone doing promotional work: {He became the pitchman for a reverse mortgage company}. Television infomercial hosts are modern pitchmen. The word carries a slight suggestion of slickness or overselling.

A pitfall is a hidden danger or unexpected difficulty—something that catches you off guard: {the pitfalls of online dating}, {common pitfalls for first-time homebuyers}. The word comes from actual pit traps: holes covered with branches or leaves to capture animals or enemies. The figurative sense now dominates completely.

Pitfalls are hidden dangers or unexpected difficulties that can cause failure. The word originally meant a concealed pit for trapping animals, and the figurative sense retains that element of concealment—pitfalls aren't obvious obstacles but lurking hazards: {the pitfalls of online dating}, {pitfalls to avoid when buying a used car}. Nearly always plural.

Pitiful describes something that evokes pity—a pitiful {sight}, a pitiful {cry}. The word often carries contempt alongside sympathy: a pitiful {excuse} is weak and unconvincing, a pitiful {attempt} falls embarrassingly short. Someone in a pitiful {state} deserves compassion, but a pitiful {performance} deserves criticism. The balance between sympathy and scorn depends on context.

A pitmaster is a person skilled in barbecue, particularly one who tends the pit—the smoker or fire where meat cooks low and slow. The term carries connotations of expertise and dedication to craft: {The pitmaster had been smoking brisket since 4 a.m.} Pitmasters are celebrated figures in barbecue culture, often associated with competition circuits and regional styles.

Pits is informal for armpits: {I haven't shaved my pits in weeks}. More broadly, {the pits} means the worst possible situation or quality—an expression of thorough disgust: {This weather is the pits}. {My job is the pits.} The phrase likely derives from the unpleasant associations of armpits or from pit as a dark, undesirable place.

A pitstop is a brief stop during a car race to refuel, change tires, or make repairs. The term extends to any quick break during travel: {Let's make a pitstop at the next exit}. It often implies using a restroom or grabbing food before continuing. Sometimes spelled as two words: pit stop.

Pitstops are brief stops during a journey, originally from auto racing where cars pull into the pit area for refueling, tire changes, and repairs. The term extends to any quick break during travel: {We made a few pitstops on the drive down}. A pitstop often implies using the restroom: {I need to make a pitstop before we hit the highway}.

Pitted describes surfaces marked with small indentations or holes, like pitted {skin} scarred by acne or a pitted {road} damaged by weather. It also describes fruit that has had its pit removed: pitted {olives}, pitted {cherries}. These two meanings come from different senses of pit—one referring to a small cavity or depression, the other to the hard seed inside certain fruits.

Pitterpatter is the light, rapid tapping sound of small feet or raindrops: {the pitterpatter of children running down the hall}, {rain pitterpattered on the roof}. The word imitates the sound it describes. Also spelled pitter-patter.

Pity is sympathetic sorrow for someone's suffering or misfortune: {I felt pity for the homeless man}. It can shade into condescension—pity implies looking down at someone's situation. {What a pity} expresses mild regret about circumstances. To pity someone is to feel sorry for them. {For pity's sake} is an exclamation of exasperation. The plural {pities} is rare; the feeling is usually uncountable.

A pivot is a central point around which something turns or rotates—the pin in a hinge, the foot a basketball player keeps planted while moving the other. Figuratively, a pivot is any crucial person or factor on which outcomes depend: {She was the pivot of the whole operation}. To pivot is to rotate around a fixed point, or to shift strategy abruptly: {The company pivoted from hardware to software}. This business sense has become ubiquitous in startup culture.

Pivoting is turning on a fixed point or axis. In basketball, a player pivots by keeping one foot planted while moving the other. The word extends to any fundamental shift in direction or strategy: {The company is pivoting from hardware to software}. In business contexts, pivoting often describes startups abandoning their original model for something more promising.

Pivots are points around which things turn or rotate. A basketball player plants a pivot foot while moving the other. In data analysis, a pivot table reorganizes information around different variables. The figurative sense dominates: {The story pivots on a single revelation}. A pivot is also a decisive shift in strategy: {The company made a pivot to mobile}.

A pixel is the smallest unit of a digital image—a single point of color on a screen. Images are grids of pixels; higher resolution means more pixels and finer detail. The word blends "picture" and "element." Pixelated describes images where individual pixels are visible, usually unintentionally: {The photo was so pixelated you couldn't make out faces}.

Pixelated describes an image where individual pixels are visible, creating a blocky, low-resolution appearance. This happens when an image is enlarged beyond its native resolution or compressed too aggressively: {The photo was so pixelated you couldn't make out their faces}. Pixelation is sometimes applied deliberately to obscure identity or nudity in video. The word derives from pixel, the smallest unit of a digital image.

Pixels are the tiny individual dots that make up a digital image or display. Each pixel holds color and brightness information; together, millions of pixels form photographs, videos, and everything you see on a screen. Higher pixel counts produce sharper images: {The camera shoots at 12 megapixels}. The word blends "picture" and "element."

A pixie is a small, mischievous fairy-like creature from English folklore, typically depicted with pointed ears and a playful or impish nature. The word often describes someone—especially a woman or child—with a sprightly, elfin quality: {She has a pixie face}. A pixie cut is a short, wispy hairstyle that frames the face.

Pixies are small supernatural creatures from English folklore, typically depicted as mischievous but not malicious. They're associated with southwestern England, particularly Devon and Cornwall. In modern use, pixie often describes someone small and sprightly, especially a woman or child with delicate features. A pixie cut is a short, elfin hairstyle. {She had a pixie face and a mischievous grin.} (Capitalized Pixies is the rock band.)

Pizazz is flair, energy, or exciting stylishness—the quality that makes something eye-catching or impressive: {The presentation lacked pizazz}, {She brought real pizazz to the role}. The word suggests showmanship and vitality, something that commands attention through sheer verve. Also spelled pizzazz.

Pizza is a dish of Italian origin consisting of flat bread topped with tomato sauce, cheese, and various other ingredients, then baked. Toppings range from simple {cheese pizza} to elaborate combinations: pepperoni, sausage, vegetables, anchovies. Pizza comes in regional styles—thin-crust New York, deep-dish Chicago, Neapolitan. {Let's order pizza.} The word extends to the entire experience: {pizza night}, {pizza party}.

Pizzazz is lively energy, flair, or stylish appeal—the quality that makes something exciting or eye-catching. A performance might lack pizzazz, a dress might have pizzazz, a presenter might need more pizzazz: {The show was technically perfect but had no pizzazz}. The word itself has a flashy, attention-grabbing sound that matches its meaning. Also spelled pizazz.

A pizzeria is a restaurant that specializes in pizza. The word comes from Italian and retains its Italian plural, pizzerie, though pizzerias is more common in English: {There's a new pizzeria on Main Street}. The term suggests a casual establishment, often with takeout and delivery options.

Place is primarily a noun that is used to denote a limited physical environment or space. Different kinds of places have different sorts of borders: a city or a country can be described as a place, but so can a small corner on a shelf where you can fit a knickknack. When place is a verb, it has a meaning similar to but usually more specific than put.

A placebo is a treatment or substance with no therapeutic effect, given to patients who believe they are receiving actual medicine. Placebos are essential in clinical trials, where they serve as controls against which real treatments are measured. The placebo effect refers to genuine improvement in symptoms that occurs simply because patients believe they are being treated. More broadly, placebo describes anything meant to placate or satisfy without providing real benefit: {The tax cut was just a placebo for angry voters}.

Placebos is the plural of placebo, an inert treatment given to patients who believe they're receiving real medicine. Doctors once prescribed placebos to satisfy patients demanding unnecessary medication. Now placebos serve mainly as controls in clinical trials—half the subjects get the real drug, half get a placebo, and researchers compare outcomes. The {placebo effect} is genuine improvement from belief in treatment rather than the treatment itself.

Places is the plural of place, covering all its noun senses: locations, positions, roles, and spots where someone or something belongs. It also serves as the third-person singular verb form meaning to put or position something: {She places the book on the shelf}. The phrase {going places} suggests someone is destined for success. In horse racing, a horse that places finishes in a top position, usually second.

A plackart is a piece of plate armor covering the lower front torso, worn over the breastplate for additional protection. It was common in 15th-century European armor, typically hinged or strapped to allow movement while reinforcing the vulnerable midsection against lance strikes and sword thrusts.

To plagiarise is to pass off someone else's work or ideas as your own. The term applies to copying text, stealing concepts, or failing to credit sources: {The student plagiarised entire paragraphs from Wikipedia}. Plagiarism ranges from wholesale theft to careless paraphrasing without attribution. The word is spelled plagiarize in American English.

Plagiarised is the British spelling of plagiarized, the past tense of plagiarise. To plagiarise is to pass off someone else's words, ideas, or work as your own: {The student plagiarised entire paragraphs from Wikipedia}. The accusation carries serious weight in academic and creative contexts, where originality is expected and credited.

Plagiarism is copying someone else’s work without attribution, with the intention of making it appear that you are the author. Plagiarism usually refers to writing but may also encompass research or ideas. While the availability of text on the Internet makes it easier to detect plagiarism, since it is so easy to copy from the Internet, plagiarism is also more common.

To plagiarize means to use someone else’s work, such as their writing, without attribution, so that your audience will think you are the author. The object of plagiarize is usually a created work (The essay was often plagiarized by Addison’s contemporaries), but it may be the name of the original author or creator: You can’t plagiarize Beethoven and get away with it.

Plagiarized describes work that has been passed off as original when it was actually copied from someone else without credit. A plagiarized {essay} contains passages lifted from sources the writer didn't acknowledge. The word implies deception—presenting another's ideas or words as your own: {The professor failed him for submitting a plagiarized paper}.

Plagiarizing is presenting someone else's words, ideas, or work as your own. The term applies whether the copying is deliberate or careless—failing to cite a source counts as plagiarizing even without intent to deceive. {She was expelled for plagiarizing her thesis}. The concept matters most in academic and creative contexts, where originality carries weight.

A plague is a widespread affliction, whether a deadly epidemic disease, an infestation of pests, or any calamity that descends on a population. The word often evokes biblical imagery—the plagues of Egypt included locusts, boils, and death of firstborn. As a verb, plague means to cause persistent trouble or suffering: {Injuries plagued the team all season}. Something plaguing you may be as serious as disease or as minor as a nagging worry that won't go away.

Plagued means afflicted or tormented, especially persistently. Someone plagued by doubts suffers from recurring uncertainty. A project plagued with delays faces repeated setbacks. The word comes from plague—the deadly disease—but now applies to any persistent trouble: {The team has been plagued by injuries all season}. To be plagued is to be beset, hounded, unable to escape the problem.

Plagues is the plural of plague—devastating diseases that spread rapidly through populations, or any widespread afflictions: {Biblical plagues descended upon Egypt}. The verb form means to cause persistent trouble or distress: {Technical problems plagued the launch}, {She was plagued by doubts}. What plagues you torments or harasses relentlessly.

Plaid is a pattern of crisscrossing horizontal and vertical lines forming a checkered design, most famously associated with Scottish tartans where specific color combinations identify particular clans. The word also refers to fabric woven in this pattern or garments made from it: {a plaid flannel shirt}, {wearing plaid to the holiday party}. In American English, plaid and tartan are often used interchangeably, though purists distinguish tartan as the authentic Scottish version with clan significance.

The noun plain has spawned an adjective that surpasses it in frequency, as well as an adverb. The core use of plain is to denote a relatively even and featureless expanse of land. As an adjective, plain picks up the “featureless” and “even” aspects of the noun to characterize things that are simple, undecorated, unmodified. Many foods that have variant forms reserve plain to characterize the simplest one: plain yogurt, a plain hamburger. As an adverb, plain typically conveys absolutely: It was plain rude of you not to answer his question.

Plains are large, flat expanses of land with few trees—the Great Plains of North America, the Russian steppe, African savannahs. The term suggests open country suited to grazing or agriculture. {Buffalo once roamed the plains in vast herds.} Plains can also be the plural of plain, meaning something simple or unadorned.

A plan is a scheme or method worked out beforehand for accomplishing something: {What's the plan for tomorrow?} Plans range from casual intentions to detailed blueprints. To plan is to formulate such a scheme: {We're planning a trip to Mexico}. A floor plan shows the layout of a building. To {plan on} something is to expect or intend it: {I wasn't planning on staying long}.

A plane is a flat surface, especially one extending infinitely in geometry. From this comes the airplane—a craft with flat wings that generate lift—commonly shortened to plane: {We caught the six o'clock plane to Denver}. A plane is also a woodworking tool with a flat bottom that shaves surfaces smooth; to plane is to use one. To plane across water is to skim the surface. On another plane means at a different level of existence or understanding: {The conversation moved to a higher plane}.

Planes are flat surfaces, levels of existence, or aircraft. A geometric plane extends infinitely in two dimensions. A plane of existence suggests a realm or dimension: {on a higher spiritual plane}. The aircraft sense dominates everyday use—a plane flies through the air: {We caught the last plane out}. A woodworking plane shaves surfaces flat. To plane is to smooth with such a tool, or to glide: {The boat planed across the water}.

A planet is a large celestial body that orbits a star, is massive enough for gravity to make it roughly spherical, and has cleared other debris from its orbital path. Our solar system has eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006. In astrology, planets include the sun and moon, believed to influence human affairs: {Mercury is in retrograde}. Informally, {What planet are you on?} questions someone's grip on reality.

A planetarium is a domed building or room where images of stars, planets, and other celestial bodies are projected onto the ceiling, simulating the night sky. The projector itself is also called a planetarium. These facilities typically offer educational shows about astronomy and space: {We took the kids to the planetarium to see a show about the solar system}.

Planets are celestial bodies that orbit a star, are massive enough for gravity to make them roughly spherical, and have cleared their orbital neighborhood of other debris. In our solar system, eight planets orbit the Sun—four rocky inner planets and four outer gas giants. Historically, planet meant "wandering star," since planets appeared to move against the fixed background of stars. Figuratively, {on what planet} questions someone's grasp of reality: {On what planet is that acceptable?}
