Skeptics attribute poltergeist activity to fraud, natural causes, or psychological phenomena.

Polyamory is the practice of having multiple romantic or sexual relationships simultaneously, with the knowledge and consent of everyone involved. Unlike cheating, polyamory operates openly: {They've been polyamorous for years and seem to make it work}. The adjective is polyamorous, often shortened to poly: {a poly relationship}, {Are you poly?}

Polyester is a synthetic fabric made from petroleum-based fibers, widely used in clothing, upholstery, and industrial applications. It's durable, wrinkle-resistant, and holds color well, but breathes poorly compared to natural fibers. The word often carries connotations of cheapness or tackiness: {a polyester leisure suit from the seventies}. Polyester blends combine it with cotton or other materials for improved comfort.

Polygamy is the practice of having multiple spouses simultaneously. The term covers both polygyny (one husband, multiple wives) and polyandry (one wife, multiple husbands), though polygyny is far more common historically and cross-culturally. Polygamy is illegal in most Western countries but practiced in some religious and traditional communities: {The sect permitted polygamy among its elders}.

A polygraph is a device that monitors physiological responses—heart rate, blood pressure, breathing, skin conductivity—while a person answers questions, on the theory that lying produces detectable stress. Commonly called a lie detector, though its reliability is disputed. {He was asked to take a polygraph}. Polygraph also refers to the test itself or, rarely, to a device that produces multiple copies of writing.

A pomegranate is a round fruit with a tough reddish skin containing hundreds of edible seeds, each encased in juicy red flesh. The seeds cluster in compartments separated by bitter white membrane. Native to the Middle East, pomegranates appear in ancient mythology and religious texts. The fruit is eaten fresh, juiced, or used in cooking: {pomegranate molasses}, {pomegranate seeds scattered over a salad}.

Pomp is ceremonial display and grandeur—the elaborate spectacle of formal occasions. Royal coronations have pomp; so do military parades and state funerals. The word often carries a hint of excess or empty show: {all the pomp and circumstance of graduation}. Pompous behavior inflates self-importance with similar theatrical flair.

A pompadour is a hairstyle in which hair is swept upward from the forehead and back from the face, creating height and volume at the front. The style, named after Madame de Pompadour, mistress of Louis XV, has been worn by both men and women. Elvis Presley's signature look revived it in the 1950s: {He spent twenty minutes perfecting his pompadour}.

A pompom is a fluffy decorative ball made of yarn, paper, or similar material. Cheerleaders shake pompoms at sporting events. Smaller versions adorn winter hats, gift wrapping, or craft projects. The word sometimes appears as pom-pom. A pom-pom is also an automatic antiaircraft gun, named for the sound it makes when firing.

Pompoms are fluffy spherical decorations made from gathered strands of material—typically yarn, paper, or plastic strips. Cheerleaders wave large pompoms during routines to add visual flair. Smaller pompoms appear as decorative accents on hats, slippers, or gift wrapping. Also spelled pom-poms or pom pons.

Pompous describes someone who takes themselves too seriously, displaying an inflated sense of importance or dignity. A pompous {speech} is full of grand language meant to impress. A pompous {official} acts as if their position makes them superior. The word suggests self-importance that others find tiresome or ridiculous: {He delivered a pompous lecture on proper etiquette while his fly was down}.

A poncho is a simple outer garment—a single piece of fabric with a hole in the center for the head, worn draped over the shoulders. Traditional ponchos from South America are woven wool or alpaca; modern versions are often waterproof plastic or nylon, used as emergency rain gear: {I keep a poncho in my backpack for hiking}.

A pond is a small body of still water, smaller than a lake though the boundary is imprecise. Ponds are often shallow enough for sunlight to reach the bottom, supporting plant growth throughout. They may be natural or artificial: {a duck pond}, {a garden pond}, {a fish pond}. {The pond} is a humorous term for the Atlantic Ocean, used in phrases like {across the pond}.

To ponder is to think about something carefully and at length, turning it over in your mind: {She pondered whether to accept the job offer}. The word suggests deliberate, unhurried consideration rather than quick judgment. You ponder weighty matters—decisions, mysteries, life's big questions—not what to have for lunch.

Pondering is deep or careful thinking about something, often with no immediate resolution in sight. Where thinking can be quick, pondering suggests sustained consideration: {She sat pondering the decision for hours}. The word carries a meditative quality—you ponder weighty matters, not what to have for lunch.

Pong is a strong, unpleasant smell: {There's a terrible pong coming from the fridge}. Chiefly British. As a verb, to pong is to stink: {Those trainers really pong}. Separately, Pong was an early video game simulating table tennis, released in 1972—one of the first commercially successful arcade games.

Ponies are small horses, typically standing under 14.2 hands at maturity. The word often suggests a child's mount or a gentle riding animal. In British slang, a pony is twenty-five pounds sterling. In American slang, to pony up is to pay what's owed: {Time to pony up for your share of the bill}. A pony is also a small glass for liquor or a crib sheet for cheating on exams.

A pontoon is a flat-bottomed float used to support structures on water. Pontoon bridges rest on a series of these floats. A pontoon boat has two parallel hulls providing stability for leisurely lake cruising: {We spent the afternoon on the pontoon}. In British usage, pontoon is also the card game Americans call blackjack or twenty-one.

A pony is a young horse (pony stallion) or a small horse (Shetland pony). Pony is sometimes used to characterize things that are smaller than the standard size, especially alcoholic drinks. The verb pony up is not related to horses and means to pay or put in money, usually in the context of achieving fairness or settling an account.

A ponytail is a hairstyle in which hair is gathered and fastened at the back of the head, hanging down like a horse's tail. The style keeps hair out of the face and ranges from casual to polished depending on placement and tightness: {She pulled her hair back in a quick ponytail before going for a run}.

Ponytails is the plural of ponytail, a hairstyle in which hair is gathered and fastened at the back of the head, hanging down like a horse's tail. The style is practical for keeping hair out of the face during exercise or work: {She always wears ponytails to volleyball practice}. Pigtails are ponytails worn in pairs, one on each side.

Poo is a childish or euphemistic term for feces, or the act of defecating: {I need to go poo}. Common in households with young children and in casual speech where stronger terms feel inappropriate. Also appears as the verb poop. The word is mild and inoffensive—bathroom humor rather than vulgarity.

Pooch is informal for dog, used affectionately: {I'm taking the pooch for a walk}. The word carries a warm, familiar tone—you'd call your own dog or a friendly neighborhood mutt a pooch, not a show champion or police K-9.

A poodle is a breed of dog known for its curly, dense coat and high intelligence. Poodles come in three sizes—standard, miniature, and toy—and are often associated with elaborate grooming styles, though they were originally bred as water retrievers. The breed's reputation for prissiness makes poodle a mild insult for someone seen as pampered or overly fussy: {He's not cut out for fieldwork—he's a poodle}. As a verb, chiefly British, to poodle means to move in a leisurely, unhurried way: {We poodled around the countryside all afternoon}.

Poodles are a breed of dog known for their curly, dense coat and high intelligence. They come in three sizes—standard, miniature, and toy—and are often associated with elaborate grooming styles, particularly the continental clip with pompoms. Despite a reputation as pampered show dogs, poodles were originally bred as water retrievers: {She trained her poodle for agility competitions}.

Poof is the sound of something vanishing or appearing suddenly, often with a puff of air or smoke: {The magician waved his wand and—poof—the rabbit disappeared}. As an exclamation, it emphasizes how quickly something happened or ceased to exist: {One day the money was just gone, poof}. In British slang, poof is a derogatory term for a gay man, equivalent to American "fag."

Pool has two distinct origins in English. One pool is a body of still water—a pond, a puddle, or an artificial basin for swimming: {The kids splashed in the pool}. Blood or other liquids collect in pools. The other pool is a shared resource or collective stake. A typing pool shares secretarial work; a car pool shares rides; a gene pool contains a population's genetic material. To pool resources is to combine them. Pool is also a billiards game played on a table with pockets, named for the betting pools once associated with it.

Pools is the plural of pool, covering all its senses. A pool is a body of still water, natural or artificial—from a tide pool to a swimming pool. Pool also means a shared resource or collective supply: a car pool, a gene pool, a pool of candidates. The game pool is played on a felt table with cue sticks and numbered balls. To pool resources is to combine them: {We pooled our money for the gift}.

A poolshark is someone highly skilled at billiards who hustles less experienced players for money, often by concealing their ability until bets are placed: {He lost three hundred dollars to a poolshark at the bar}. The term combines the predatory connotation of shark with pool halls' reputation for gambling. Sometimes spelled as two words: pool shark.

Poop is informal for feces, used especially by or around children: {The dog pooped on the carpet}. As a verb, to poop is to defecate. The poop deck is the raised deck at a ship's stern—an unrelated nautical term. To be pooped is to be exhausted: {I'm too pooped to go out tonight}.

Pooped means exhausted or worn out: {I'm completely pooped after that hike}. The word is informal and mild. Separately, pooped is the past tense of poop, the childish or euphemistic verb for defecating: {The dog pooped on the rug}. In nautical use, a ship is pooped when a wave breaks over the stern.

Poor describes a lack of money or resources: {poor families}, {poor countries}. It extends to anything deficient or inadequate: {poor health}, {poor judgment}, {poor visibility}. Poor can express sympathy: {The poor thing looked exhausted}. As a noun with *the*, it refers collectively to people without money: {policies that hurt the poor}. To poor-mouth is to claim poverty, often falsely.

Poorly means in an inadequate or unsatisfactory way: {The team performed poorly}, {a poorly written essay}. In British usage, poorly also works as an adjective meaning unwell or slightly ill: {She's feeling poorly today}. The adverb sense is standard everywhere; the adjective sense sounds distinctly British to American ears.

The many meanings of pop are hard to summarize, but the imitative origin of the word is a good clue. A pop is a sudden, explosive sound. When you pop something, this sound usually results (pop a balloon, pop popcorn). If you pop pills, you swallow them – probably lots of them. If you pop a question, you ask it, perhaps unexpectedly. Pop is one of the names for sweetened, fizzy beverages. Before another noun, pop is often a shortening of popular (pop culture, pop music, pop star).

Popcorn is a variety of corn whose kernels explode when heated, puffing into light, irregular white shapes. It's eaten as a snack, typically with butter and salt, and is strongly associated with movie theaters. {We made popcorn for movie night.} As an adjective, popcorn suggests light entertainment without much substance: a popcorn {movie}, popcorn {fiction}.

The pope is the head of the Roman Catholic Church, considered by Catholics to be the spiritual successor to Saint Peter. The title applies to the Bishop of Rome, who serves as the supreme authority on matters of faith and church governance. Informally, pope can describe anyone treated as the ultimate authority in a field: {the pope of fashion criticism}. The adjective papal relates to the pope or papacy.

Poppies is the plural of poppy, a flowering plant with delicate, papery petals in vivid reds, oranges, and yellows. The opium poppy yields narcotic compounds used in painkillers and heroin. Red poppies are symbols of remembrance for soldiers killed in war, especially in Commonwealth countries on Remembrance Day: {She wore a poppy on her lapel}.

Popping describes the action or sound of small explosions or sharp bursts: {popping corn}, {popping sounds from the engine}. It covers quick movements in and out: {popping into the store}, {popping by for a visit}. Eyes can be popping with surprise or intensity. In dance, popping is a style involving sharp, rhythmic muscle contractions. Something popping is also vibrant or exciting: {The colors are really popping}.

Poppy refers to flowering plants known for their showy, papery blooms and seed pods. The opium poppy yields compounds used in narcotics and painkillers. Red poppies are symbols of remembrance for war dead, worn especially on Veterans Day and Remembrance Day in Commonwealth countries: {She pinned a poppy to her lapel}. Poppy seeds appear in baking. (Capitalized Poppy is a given name.)

Pops is an informal, affectionate term for one's father: {Hey pops, can I borrow the car?} It can also address any older man in a familiar way, sometimes condescendingly: {You okay there, pops?} In music, pops refers to popular orchestral concerts or their repertoire: {the Boston Pops}.

A popsicle is a frozen treat on a stick, typically fruit-flavored ice or frozen juice. The word is used generically for any such frozen confection, though it originated as a trademark: {The kids ran after the popsicle truck}. In American summers, popsicles are childhood staples. (Capitalized Popsicle is the trademark.)

Popsicles is the plural of popsicle, a frozen treat on a stick—flavored ice or ice cream meant to be eaten by hand. The word is a trademark but used generically for any such frozen confection: {The kids ran after the popsicle truck}. {We made popsicles from orange juice}.

A popstar is a famous singer or performer of pop music, typically one with widespread commercial success and public recognition. The term implies celebrity status beyond mere musicianship—popstars attract media attention, fan devotion, and cultural influence: {She dreamed of becoming a popstar}. Also spelled as two words: pop star.

Popular describes what many people like, know, or participate in. A popular {song} gets heavy airplay; a popular {kid} has many friends; a popular {destination} attracts crowds. The word can also mean "of the people" rather than elite or specialized: {popular culture}, {popular vote}, {popular uprising}. Something done {by popular demand} responds to widespread request.

Popularity is the state of being liked, admired, or supported by many people. A politician's popularity rises and falls with public opinion. A song gains popularity through radio play and streaming. The word can also describe how widespread something is: {the popularity of smartphones}, {the growing popularity of remote work}. Popularity often implies broad appeal rather than critical merit—what's popular isn't always what's best.

Population is the total number of people, animals, or organisms living in a particular place: {the population of Tokyo}, {the deer population}. In statistics, a population is the entire group from which samples are drawn for study. The word also describes the act of populating: {the population of the American West}.

Populism is a political approach that frames issues as the common people versus a corrupt elite. It can appear across the ideological spectrum—left-wing populists target wealthy corporations and billionaires, while right-wing populists target cultural elites and established institutions. The term is often used dismissively to suggest demagoguery or oversimplification: {His economic proposals were pure populism}. A populist champions ordinary people's interests, or claims to.

Populist describes political movements or figures claiming to represent ordinary people against a corrupt elite. The term is ideologically flexible—populists appear on both left and right, united by appeals to "the people" versus "the establishment." A populist {candidate} campaigns against Washington insiders; populist {policies} promise to return power to regular citizens. The noun identifies someone who takes this stance: {He ran as a populist}. Critics use the term to suggest demagoguery or oversimplification.

A popup is something that appears suddenly, especially a window or advertisement that opens automatically on a computer screen: {I installed an ad blocker to stop the popups}. Popup books have illustrations that spring into three dimensions when pages are opened. A popup store or restaurant operates temporarily in a space before moving on. Also spelled pop-up.

Porcelain is a hard, white, translucent ceramic made by firing clay at high temperatures. The finest porcelain originated in China, making *china* and *porcelain* near-synonyms for delicate dinnerware. Porcelain appears in decorative objects, dental work, and bathroom fixtures. As an adjective, it suggests smooth paleness: {porcelain skin}. The material's fragility makes it a metaphor for anything delicate or easily damaged.

A porch is a covered structure attached to the entrance of a building, typically with a roof supported by columns or posts. Front porches are traditional gathering spaces in American homes: {We sat on the porch drinking lemonade}. A screened porch keeps out insects while letting in air. Back porches and side porches serve similar functions away from the street.

A porcupine is a large rodent covered in sharp, barbed quills that serve as defense against predators. When threatened, a porcupine raises its quills; contrary to myth, it cannot shoot them, but the quills detach easily on contact and are painful to remove. {The dog learned the hard way to leave porcupines alone.}

Porcupines is the plural of porcupine, a large rodent covered in sharp, defensive quills. When threatened, porcupines raise their quills; contrary to myth, they cannot shoot them, but the barbed spines detach easily on contact. {We spotted porcupines gnawing on the cabin steps.} The animals are nocturnal and found across North America, Africa, and parts of Asia.

A pore is a tiny opening in a surface, especially the minute holes in skin through which sweat passes: {clogged pores}, {open pores}. Plants have pores for gas exchange; rocks and membranes have pores that allow passage of fluids. The verb pore means to study intently: {She pored over the documents for hours}. The verb is almost always followed by "over."

Pores are tiny openings in a surface that allow passage of liquids or gases. Skin pores release sweat and oil; porous materials like sponges absorb water through countless pores. To pore over something is to study it intently: {She pored over the documents for hours}. This verb pore is unrelated to the noun—the spelling pour is a common error.

Pork is the meat of a pig, used as food: {pork chops}, {pulled pork}, {pork belly}. In American politics, pork refers to government spending directed to a particular district primarily to benefit constituents and win votes rather than serve broader public interest: {The bill was loaded with pork}. The verb pork is vulgar slang for having sex.

Porn is short for pornography—sexually explicit material designed to arouse. The word covers everything from magazines to videos to internet content: {He got caught watching porn at work}. As a suffix, -porn describes any content offering visual gratification: {food porn}, {real estate porn}, {disaster porn}. The adjective form is usually porno.

Pornography is material depicting sexual activity, intended to arouse. The term covers everything from explicit photographs and videos to written erotica. Porn is the common shortening. What counts as pornography versus art or erotica depends on who's judging—the line has shifted across eras and cultures. {The internet transformed how pornography is distributed and consumed.} Metaphorically, anything that offers visceral gratification without substance may be called pornography: {poverty porn}, {food porn}, {disaster porn}.

Porphobilinogen is a chemical compound that serves as a building block in the body's production of heme—the iron-containing part of hemoglobin that carries oxygen in blood. Elevated levels in urine indicate certain metabolic disorders, particularly acute intermittent porphyria: {The lab tested for porphobilinogen to rule out porphyria}.

A porphyroblast is a large crystal that grows within metamorphic rock, standing out conspicuously against the finer-grained matrix surrounding it. Garnet porphyroblasts are common in schists. The term distinguishes these crystals from phenocrysts, which form in igneous rocks from cooling magma rather than from metamorphic recrystallization.

A porpoise is a small toothed whale, similar to a dolphin but with a blunter snout and stockier body. Porpoises are found in coastal waters worldwide. The verb porpoise describes the motion of rising and plunging through water—or through air, when an aircraft or vehicle bounces rhythmically: {The plane porpoised down the runway}.

Porridge is a hot cereal made by boiling oats or other grains in water or milk until thick and soft. It's a traditional breakfast food, especially in Britain and Scotland: {a bowl of porridge with honey}. The word appears in the British slang phrase {do porridge}, meaning to serve a prison sentence—from the association of porridge with institutional meals.

The many meanings of the noun port share the idea of an opening or conduit through which something passes, be it cargo, data, or air: What ports do you have on your computer? Chicago is the largest port on the Great Lakes. A separately derived port accounts for the class of sweet wines originally from Portugal. As a verb, port means to carry a weapon, or to send or transmit via a port. In the computer age, the dominant usage for both noun and verb is in relation to the various ports built into hardware devices and the movement of data through or across them.

Portable describes something designed to be carried or moved easily. A portable {radio} or {computer} travels with you. The word implies a tradeoff—portable versions are typically smaller or lighter than stationary ones, sometimes at the cost of power or features. Software is portable when it runs on different systems without modification.

A portal is a doorway or entrance, especially one that's large or imposing: {the cathedral's main portal}. The word suggests a threshold between spaces or states. In fantasy and science fiction, portals are gateways to other worlds or dimensions. In computing, a portal is a website serving as an entry point to other content—a starting place for browsing.

Portals are doorways or gates, especially grand or imposing ones: {the portals of the cathedral}. The word suggests a threshold between realms—hence its adoption for website entry points that aggregate content and services: {Yahoo was once the dominant internet portal}. In fantasy and science fiction, a portal is a magical or technological passage to another place or dimension: {a portal opened in the sky}.

A porter is someone who carries things for others—luggage at hotels and train stations, supplies in hospitals, or goods in markets. The word also names a dark brown beer, supposedly favored by London porters in the 18th century. In buildings, especially British ones, a porter is a doorkeeper or caretaker who manages access and handles deliveries: {The porter signed for the package}. (Capitalized Porter is a surname.)

A porterhouse is a thick cut of beef steak containing both the tenderloin and the strip, separated by a T-shaped bone. It differs from a T-bone only in having a larger portion of tenderloin: {We split a porterhouse for two}. Porterhouse also refers to a pub or chophouse that serves porter and other drinks alongside food, though this sense is now rare.

Porters are workers who carry luggage or goods. At hotels and train stations, porters help travelers with their bags. In hospitals, porters move patients and equipment between departments. The term also applies to workers who carry loads in mountainous regions: {Sherpas work as porters on Himalayan expeditions}. A porter is also a dark beer, supposedly named because London porters favored it.

A portfolio is a case for carrying loose papers, drawings, or documents. From this comes the extended sense of a collection of work samples, especially for artists, designers, or writers seeking employment: {She brought her portfolio to the interview}. In finance, a portfolio is the range of investments held by a person or institution: {a diversified portfolio}. A minister's portfolio is their area of governmental responsibility.

A porthole is a small, usually circular window in the side of a ship or aircraft. Ship portholes are typically fitted with thick glass and a hinged metal cover that can be sealed against water. The shape distinguishes them from ordinary rectangular windows: {light streaming through the porthole}, {She watched the waves through her cabin's porthole}.

Portholes are small, typically circular windows in the side of a ship or aircraft. The round shape and thick glass help withstand pressure and water. On ships, portholes can often be opened for ventilation: {She watched the coastline recede through the porthole}. The term sometimes extends to any small, round window.

A portion is a part of something larger: {a portion of the proceeds}, {a generous portion of mashed potatoes}. It often implies division or allocation—the share that belongs to someone or gets served to them. To portion something is to divide it into shares: {She portioned out the inheritance among her children}. Portion can also mean one's lot or fate, though this use sounds old-fashioned.

A portrait is a painting, drawing, photograph, or other artistic representation of a person, typically focusing on the face and upper body. The goal is usually to capture not just physical likeness but something of the subject's character or mood. Portrait extends to written descriptions that vividly depict someone: {The biography paints an unflattering portrait of the senator}. In photography and design, portrait orientation means the image is taller than it is wide, as opposed to landscape.

Portraits are paintings, photographs, or other artistic representations of a person, typically focusing on the face. The word emphasizes capturing likeness or character: {The gallery featured portraits of former presidents}. A portrait can also be a written or verbal description that reveals someone's nature: {The biography painted a vivid portrait of the artist}. In printing, portrait orientation means the page is taller than it is wide, like a traditional painted portrait.

To portray is to depict or represent someone or something, whether in visual art, writing, or performance. An actor portrays a character; a novelist portrays small-town life; a painting portrays a battle scene. The word implies interpretation—how something is portrayed shapes how it's understood: {The media portrayed him as a hero}. A portrayal can be accurate, sympathetic, or distorted.

A portrayal is a representation or depiction of someone or something, especially in art, film, or writing: {Her portrayal of the queen earned an Oscar nomination}. The word emphasizes interpretation—an actor's portrayal reveals how they understand the character. Portrayals can be accurate or misleading: {The documentary offered a sympathetic portrayal of the controversial figure}.

Ports are openings where things pass through. A port is a harbor town where ships load and unload cargo: {The ship arrived at port}. In computing, a port is a socket where cables connect or a virtual endpoint for network traffic: {USB port}, {port 443}. Port wine is a sweet fortified wine from Portugal. To port software is to adapt it for a different system. In nautical use, port is the left side of a vessel facing forward—opposite starboard.

Pose connects the idea of positioning with the idea of presenting. To pose is to hold a position, especially for a photograph or portrait: {She posed beside the fountain}. A pose is that assumed position. Figuratively, a pose is an affected manner meant to impress: {His cynicism is just a pose}. To pose as someone is to pretend to be them: {He posed as a doctor}. To pose a question or problem is to present it for consideration.

A poser is someone who affects attitudes, behaviors, or styles they don't genuinely hold—pretending expertise or belonging they haven't earned. The word carries contempt: {He's not a real skater, just a poser}. Poser also means a difficult question or problem, though this sense is less common: {The detective faced a real poser}.

Posers is the plural of poser, a person who adopts attitudes, styles, or identities they haven't earned—someone who affects expertise or belonging without the substance: {The regulars dismissed the newcomers as posers}. Common in music and subculture contexts, where authenticity matters: {real punks vs. posers}. The word carries contempt for inauthenticity.

Poses covers both physical positioning and pretense. A pose is a deliberate arrangement of the body—for a photograph, a painting, or in yoga. To pose is to hold such a position: {She posed for the portrait}. But pose also means to present or put forward: {The situation poses a challenge}. When someone poses as something, they pretend to be it: {He posed as a doctor to gain access}. A pose can therefore be an affected manner—behavior meant to impress rather than express: {His cynicism is just a pose}.

A poseur is someone who affects attitudes, behaviors, or styles to impress others without genuine commitment or understanding. The term implies superficiality—a poseur in the punk scene wears the clothes but doesn't grasp the ethos. {He's just a poseur who bought a guitar to look cool.} The word carries contempt for inauthenticity.

Posh means elegantly luxurious or associated with the upper classes. A posh {hotel} is expensively appointed. A posh {accent} suggests privileged British upbringing. The word carries slight mockery—calling something posh often implies it's pretentious or unnecessarily fancy: {We can't afford anywhere that posh}. To posh up is to make something more elegant or refined.

Posing is assuming a position, typically for artistic or photographic purposes: {She spent hours posing for the portrait}. Extended meanings involve pretense—posing as someone you're not, or adopting attitudes for effect rather than sincerity: {He's just posing as an expert}. Something that poses a threat or challenge presents it: {The storm posed serious risks to coastal towns}.

Meanings of the noun position are frequent and familiar, unlike those of its underlying verb posit; but understanding posit tells you most of what you need to know about position. To posit something is to put it in a place, or to put it forward as an assertion. A position is a place or configuration in space with particular characteristics, or abstractly, a condition or situation with reference to a place: The drill will only operate in an upright position. If you take a position on some matter, you announce or declare your attitude or opinion about it: The committee decided against taking a position on the issue. A position in a hierarchy of any kind is a place in it: What position does she occupy at the bank?

Positioning is the act of placing something in a particular location or arrangement: {The positioning of the cameras gave us full coverage of the room}. In marketing, positioning refers to how a brand or product is perceived relative to competitors—its place in consumers' minds: {The company's positioning as a luxury brand justified higher prices}. The word often emphasizes deliberate, strategic placement rather than random location.

Most meanings of positive can be paired with opposites characterized by negative. A positive test result is one finding the presence of something. Positive numbers are those greater than zero. Positive also characterizes what is favorable where negative means unfavorable: The audience gave a very positive reaction to the proposal. These measures will have a positive impact. Finally, positive can convey certainty: I’m positive that I saw her leaving earlier. As a noun, positive most frequently means a positive test result, or a photographic print made from a negative.

Positivity is an optimistic or hopeful outlook—the tendency to focus on what's good rather than what's wrong. The word often appears in self-help contexts: {Try to maintain your positivity during difficult times}. It can also mean simply the quality of being positive: the positivity of a test result, the positivity of an electrical charge.

A posse is a group assembled for a common purpose, originally a body of citizens summoned by a sheriff to help capture a criminal or keep order. The Old West imagery persists: {The sheriff rounded up a posse to track the outlaws}. In casual use, posse means any group of friends or associates: {He showed up with his whole posse}.

To possess something is to have it or own it: {She possesses considerable talent}, {He was arrested for possessing a firearm}. Possess often sounds more formal than have or own, appearing in legal contexts ({possessing stolen property}) and descriptions of qualities ({She possesses an unusual grace}). To be possessed is to be controlled by a spirit or demon, or figuratively by an intense emotion: {What possessed you to do that?}

Possessed describes being controlled or influenced by something external—originally a spirit or demon: {She screamed as if possessed}. The word extends to any overwhelming force: {possessed by jealousy}, {possessed by an idea}. To be possessed of something is to have it: {He was possessed of great wealth}. Self-possessed means composed and in control of oneself.

Possession is having or owning something: {The police found drugs in his possession}. In law, possession may differ from ownership—you can possess what you don't own and own what you don't possess. Possessions are belongings: {She packed her few possessions}. In sports, possession is control of the ball. Spiritual possession means a demon or spirit has taken control of someone's body: {The priest performed an exorcism to end the possession}. In grammar, possession is the relationship shown by apostrophe-s or possessive pronouns.

Possessions are things you own or have with you. The word often appears when belongings are considered as a group: {She gathered her possessions and left}. A possession can also be a territory under another country's control: {The island was a British possession}. In supernatural contexts, possession is the state of being controlled by a spirit or demon: {The priest performed an exorcism to end the possession}.

Possessive describes an excessive desire to own or control something, especially a person: {He's possessive of his girlfriend}. In grammar, possessive refers to forms showing ownership—the 's in {John's book}, or pronouns like my, your, his, her, its, our, their. The possessive can signal either literal ownership or looser relationships: {my doctor}, {her birthday}, {its meaning}.

Possibilities are things that might happen or be true—outcomes not yet determined. The word implies openness rather than certainty: {The possibilities are endless}. Someone with possibilities has potential for development or success. To explore the possibilities is to consider options before committing: {Let's discuss the possibilities over lunch}.

Possibility is something that could happen or be true. It ranges from the barely conceivable to the highly likely: {There's a possibility of rain}. In the plural, possibilities often suggests potential or promise: {The job has real possibilities}. {We need to consider all the possibilities before deciding}.

Possible describes something that can exist, happen, or be done—not blocked by logic, nature, or circumstance. It sits between impossible and certain on the scale of likelihood. {Is it possible to finish by Friday?} The noun form names a person or thing that might succeed or be chosen: {She's a possible for the promotion}. When someone does {everything possible}, they exhaust all available options. The phrase {as soon as possible} is so common it's often abbreviated ASAP.

A possum is any of several marsupials, most commonly the Virginia opossum of North America—a cat-sized creature known for "playing possum," feigning death when threatened. The spelling possum reflects casual pronunciation of opossum, though in Australia and nearby regions, possum refers to distinct species. {A possum got into the garbage again.}

Three different nouns share the spelling post, and all have spun off different parts of speech. Meanings in one group arise from the post that is like a pole or stake: fence post, goalpost. The verb from this post means to display in a public place: He posted it on the Web. The second group of meanings related to the postal service: Did you send the letter by post? What time did you post it? In the third group, post refers to a place where someone is assigned: He has a new post in the State Department. They posted her to a small regional office.

Postage is the cost of sending something through the mail, or the stamps representing that cost. {The postage for international packages has gone up.} {Did you remember to put postage on the envelope?} Postage paid means the sender has already covered the mailing cost.

Postal relates to the mail system—postal {workers}, postal {codes}, the Postal Service. In slang, {go postal} means to suddenly become violently unhinged, especially in a workplace setting. The expression emerged in the 1990s after a series of shootings by U.S. Postal Service employees.

Postapocalyptic describes settings, stories, or scenarios taking place after a catastrophic event has destroyed civilization: {a postapocalyptic wasteland}, {postapocalyptic fiction}. The apocalypse in question is usually nuclear war, pandemic, environmental collapse, or similar global disaster. The genre explores survival, rebuilding, and human nature under extreme conditions. Also spelled post-apocalyptic.

A postcard is a small card for sending a brief message through the mail without an envelope, typically with a picture on one side and space for writing and an address on the other. Postcards are associated with travel—tourists send them from vacation spots: {Wish you were here!} A postcard-perfect scene is one worthy of being photographed for such a card.

Postcards are small cards for mailing without an envelope, typically featuring an image on one side and space for a brief message, address, and stamp on the other. Tourists send postcards from vacation destinations: {Wish you were here!} The format implies brevity and informality—a postcard message is short by design. Figuratively, something {postcard-perfect} is scenic enough to appear on one.

Posted means displayed publicly or sent to a destination. You post a notice on a bulletin board, post a letter in the mail, or post content online. In accounting, to post is to record a transaction: {The payment was posted to your account}. To keep someone posted is to provide ongoing updates. Posted also describes someone stationed somewhere: {guards posted at every entrance}.

A poster is a large printed sheet meant to be displayed on a wall or other vertical surface. Posters announce events, advertise products, or serve as decoration: {a movie poster}, {a concert poster}, {She hung posters of her favorite band}. In online forums, a poster is someone who posts messages: {a frequent poster on Reddit}.

A poster child is someone who perfectly represents or embodies a cause, condition, or quality—originally referring to children featured in charitable campaigns to generate sympathy and donations. The term now applies broadly and often ironically to anyone who exemplifies something, whether positive or negative: {He's the poster child for why you shouldn't skip leg day}. The spelling varies between one word, two words, and hyphenated.

Posters are large printed sheets designed for public display, typically featuring images and text to advertise events, promote causes, or decorate walls. A movie poster promotes a film; a wanted poster seeks a fugitive. The term extends to anyone who posts—someone who contributes messages to online forums or social media: {The poster asked for advice on home repairs}. To be the {poster child} for something is to typify or represent it prominently.

Posting is placing something where others will see it—a notice on a bulletin board, content on social media, a message to an online forum. A posting is also a job assignment, especially to a distant location: {She received a posting to the embassy in Berlin}. In accounting, posting means recording transactions to a ledger.

A postman is a person who delivers mail to homes and businesses. The term is more common in British English; Americans typically say mail carrier or mailman. {The postman comes around ten o'clock.} The female equivalent, postwoman, exists but is rarely used.

A postmark is the official stamp applied by a postal service to a piece of mail, showing the date and location of mailing and canceling the stamp to prevent reuse. The postmark establishes when and where something was sent: {The letter bore a postmark from Chicago dated June 3rd}. As a verb, to postmark is to apply such a stamp: {The package was postmarked yesterday}.

Postmodernism is a broad intellectual and artistic movement that emerged in the mid-twentieth century as a reaction against modernist certainties. It questions grand narratives, objective truth, and fixed meanings, emphasizing instead fragmentation, irony, and the blurring of boundaries between high and low culture. In architecture, postmodernism rejected austere functionalism for playful, eclectic designs. In philosophy and literary theory, it challenged the idea that texts have stable meanings. The term often carries a dismissive edge when critics use it to describe work they find pretentiously obscure or relativistic: {It's just postmodernism—style over substance}. (Capitalized Postmodernism sometimes appears as a proper noun when referring to the movement as a distinct historical period.)

Postmortem means after death. A postmortem examination (or simply a postmortem) is an autopsy—a medical inspection of a corpse to determine cause of death. The word extends to any analysis conducted after something ends: {We held a postmortem on the failed campaign}. In computing and business, postmortems review what went wrong with a project or system failure.

To postpone is to move something to a later time: {The game was postponed due to rain}, {Let's postpone the meeting until next week}. The word implies intention—events are postponed deliberately, not by accident. Postpone suggests rescheduling rather than canceling entirely; the thing still happens, just not when originally planned.

Posts are upright supports—wooden posts hold up fences, metal posts anchor signs. A post is also a position or station: a military post, a trading post, or someone's post within an organization. To post is to station someone: {Guards were posted at the entrance}. In the digital sense, a post is a message published online—to social media, a forum, or a blog—and to post is to publish one: {She posts daily updates}. To post something physically is to display it publicly or send it by mail (chiefly British): {post a notice}, {post a letter}.

A postscript is an addition to a letter or document, written after the main body has been completed and signed. Abbreviated P.S., it typically adds an afterthought: {P.S. I forgot to mention I'll be late Thursday}. By extension, a postscript is any supplementary comment or concluding remark: {The epilogue served as a postscript to the trilogy}.

Postseason refers to the period of competitive play that follows the regular season in sports leagues. Teams that qualify based on their regular-season performance compete in playoff rounds leading to a championship: {The team's postseason hopes ended with last night's loss}. As an adjective, it modifies related terms: {postseason roster}, {postseason stats}.

Posture is how the body is positioned or held. Good posture keeps the spine aligned; poor posture causes slouching. Beyond the physical, posture describes an attitude or stance toward something: {The company adopted a defensive posture toward regulators}. To posture is to assume an attitude for effect, often insincerely: {Politicians posturing for the cameras}.

Posturing is adopting attitudes or positions for effect rather than from genuine conviction. The word suggests performance over substance—striking poses meant to impress or intimidate: {His tough talk was just posturing}. Politicians engage in posturing when they take symbolic stands without intending action. The term is almost always dismissive, implying the behavior is hollow or theatrical.

Postwar means occurring or existing after a war, especially after World War II: {postwar reconstruction}, {the postwar economic boom}. The term typically refers to the period immediately following a conflict, when societies rebuild and adjust: {postwar Germany}, {postwar baby boom}. Without further specification, postwar usually evokes the late 1940s and 1950s.

The frequent noun pot refers to any of various containers: for cooking, for holding plants, for making coffee. Cooking metaphors are at work in expression like melting pot, stir the pot, and sweeten the pot. Less frequent but still prominent is as slang for marijuana (legalize pot, pot smoker). The verb pot usually means put in a pot and is used most often of plants: I need to pot my geraniums.

A potato is a starchy tuber grown underground, one of the world's most important food crops. Potatoes are boiled, baked, fried, or mashed. The word extends to the plant itself and to other tuber-producing plants: {sweet potato}. A {couch potato} is someone who sits around watching television. A {hot potato} is a controversial issue people avoid handling. {Small potatoes} means something trivial or insignificant.

Potatoes is the plural of potato, the starchy tuber that serves as a dietary staple worldwide. The word appears in countless compound forms: {mashed potatoes}, {baked potatoes}, {potato salad}. {Small potatoes} means something trivial or insignificant. {Couch potato} describes someone who spends excessive time watching television.

Potency is strength or power, especially the capacity to produce effects. A drug's potency determines its dosage requirements. {The potency of his argument convinced the jury}. In men, potency refers specifically to the ability to achieve erection and sexual intercourse—the opposite of impotence. Potent is the adjective form.

Potent means having great power, strength, or effect. A potent drug produces strong results; a potent argument persuades forcefully; a potent leader commands influence. The word often implies concentrated effectiveness: {a potent dose}, {a potent symbol}. In older usage, potent specifically meant sexually capable in men—the opposite of impotent.

Potential refers to something possible that could happen or become real now or in the future: She has the potential to become a great conductor. These chemicals have the potential to cause widespread environmental damage. When followed by a noun, potential means not actual but possible: About 200 potential jurors are called to serve every day. He excused himself because of a potential conflict of interest.

A pothead is a person who smokes marijuana regularly, especially to excess. The term is mildly dismissive but not strongly pejorative—potheads themselves may use it self-deprecatingly: {I was such a pothead in college}. The image is of someone whose life revolves around getting high.

Potheads are people who smoke marijuana habitually. The term suggests someone whose identity or lifestyle centers on getting high, often with connotations of laziness or lack of ambition: {a bunch of potheads playing video games all day}. The word is mildly derogatory but sometimes used self-descriptively by marijuana enthusiasts.

A pothole is a hole in a road surface, formed when pavement breaks down from water damage, traffic, and freeze-thaw cycles. Potholes range from minor nuisances to tire-damaging hazards: {I hit a pothole and bent my rim}. In geology, a pothole is a cylindrical hole worn into rock by swirling water and sediment.

Potholes are holes or pits in a road surface, formed when pavement breaks down from water damage, traffic stress, and freeze-thaw cycles. They range from minor nuisances to tire-destroying craters: {I hit a pothole and bent my rim}. Cities with harsh winters are notorious for them. Figuratively, potholes are obstacles or setbacks: {a few potholes on the road to success}.

A potion is a liquid mixture intended to have some special effect when drunk—magical, medicinal, or poisonous. The word carries strong associations with fantasy and folklore: {love potions}, {sleeping potions}, {the witch's potion}. In modern use, potion often appears playfully for any concoction: {What's in this potion you're drinking?}

Potions are liquids with magical, medicinal, or mysterious properties—brewed concoctions meant to produce specific effects when drunk. The word belongs primarily to fantasy and folklore: {love potions}, {healing potions}, {a witch stirring her potion}. In video games, potions restore health or grant abilities. Outside fantasy contexts, potion sounds deliberately archaic or whimsical: {What's in this potion you're brewing?}

Potjiekos is a traditional South African stew cooked slowly in a three-legged cast-iron pot over an open fire. The name comes from Afrikaans, meaning "small pot food." Meat, vegetables, and starches layer in the pot and simmer for hours without stirring, allowing flavors to meld: {We made potjiekos over the coals while camping in the Drakensberg}.

Potluck is a meal where each guest brings a dish to share. The word combines pot (a cooking vessel) with luck (whatever happens to be available). A potluck dinner might feature casseroles, salads, and desserts from different contributors: {We're having a potluck for the office party—I'm bringing my grandmother's mac and cheese}. Extended to mean whatever is available by chance: {take potluck}.

Potlucks are communal meals where each guest brings a dish to share. The format distributes cooking duties and creates variety—you might end up with five casseroles or a perfect spread. {We're having a potluck for the office holiday party.} The singular potluck can also mean whatever happens to be available: {We took potluck at a roadside diner.}

A potpie is a savory pie with a filling of meat and vegetables in a thick gravy, typically topped with a pastry crust. Chicken potpie is the most familiar variety in American cooking, though beef and turkey versions are common. The dish can be baked in a single large pan or in individual portions. Some regional styles, particularly in Pennsylvania Dutch cooking, feature a stew-like version with squares of dough rather than a crust.

Potpourri is a mixture of dried flower petals, herbs, and spices kept in a bowl to scent a room. By extension, potpourri describes any miscellaneous collection or medley: {The album is a potpourri of musical styles}. The word comes from French, literally "rotten pot"—originally a stew of various meats.

Pots is the plural of pot—containers typically round and deep, used for cooking, storing, or growing plants. A pot of coffee, a flower pot, a pot of gold. In poker, the pot is the accumulated stakes. To go to pot is to deteriorate. Pots can also be marijuana: {He smokes a lot of pots} sounds odd because pot as cannabis is usually uncountable.

A potsticker is a Chinese dumpling with a thin wheat wrapper enclosing a filling of ground meat and vegetables, pan-fried until the bottom crisps while the top steams. The name describes the cooking method—the dumplings stick slightly to the pot before being loosened. Also called gyoza (Japanese) or jiaozi (Chinese).

To potter is to occupy oneself in a leisurely, unhurried way with minor tasks—puttering around the garden, pottering about the house. The word is more common in British English; Americans typically say putter. A potter is also a person who makes pottery—ceramic vessels shaped by hand on a wheel or by other methods. {She trained as a potter in Japan.} The potter's wheel is the rotating disk on which clay is shaped. (Capitalized Potter typically refers to Harry Potter or the surname.)

Pottery is objects made from clay that has been shaped and hardened by heat—pots, bowls, vases, and similar vessels. The term covers both the finished products and the craft of making them: {She took up pottery as a hobby}. A pottery is a workshop or factory where such items are produced.

Potty is a child-sized toilet or portable seat for toilet training toddlers: {Time to sit on the potty}. The word itself is childish, used when speaking to or about young children. To {go potty} is to urinate or defecate. Separately, potty means slightly crazy in British informal usage: {She's gone a bit potty}.

A pouch is a small bag or flexible container, often one that closes or fastens: a tobacco pouch, a mail pouch, a pouch for carrying documents. Animals like kangaroos and pelicans have natural pouches—folds of skin that hold young or catch food. Any pocket-like receptacle or bulge qualifies: {She had pouches under her eyes from lack of sleep}. To pouch is to form into or place in a pouch.

Poultry is domestic fowl raised for meat or eggs—chickens, turkeys, ducks, geese. The word covers both the living birds and their flesh as food: {a poultry farm}, {the poultry section of the grocery store}. Unlike beef or pork, the same word serves for animal and meat.

Pounce is to spring or swoop suddenly to seize something, as a cat pounces on a mouse or a hawk on prey. The word extends to any swift, aggressive action: {She pounced on the opportunity}, {Critics pounced on his mistake}. A pounce is an instance of pouncing: {The cat made its pounce}.

Pounced is the past tense of pounce—to spring or swoop suddenly to seize something, as a cat does on prey: {The hawk pounced on the mouse}. Figuratively, to pounce is to act quickly on an opportunity or to attack someone's words: {Critics pounced on the mayor's gaffe}. {She pounced the moment tickets went on sale}.

Pounces is the plural of pounce and the third-person singular verb form. To pounce is to spring suddenly, as a cat on prey: {The kitten pounces on anything that moves}. Figuratively, to pounce is to seize an opportunity or attack a weakness: {Critics pounced on the contradiction in her statement}.

Pouncing is the act of springing or swooping suddenly to seize something. A cat pounces on a mouse; a hawk pounces on prey. Figuratively, to pounce is to seize any opportunity quickly: {She pounced on the job offer}, {Critics pounced on his mistake}. The word suggests predatory quickness—waiting, then striking.

Pound is most frequently a noun denoting a measure of weight in the imperial system equal to just under half a kilo. Another noun meaning is for a unit of currency in the United Kingdom (pound sterling) and in some other countries, notably Egypt. A third meaning of pound is for a place of detention, especially of animals (dog pound). The verb pound is for repetitive, forceful striking. Your heart pounds when you are excited or exerting yourself. You can pound nails with a hammer.

Pounding is heavy, repeated striking—the physical act or its sound. Your heart pounds when racing from fear or exertion. A pounding headache throbs painfully. To give someone a pounding is to beat them badly, whether in a fight or a competition: {Our team took a pounding in the semifinals}. Pounding surf crashes against the shore.

Pounds is the plural of pound, a unit of weight equal to sixteen ounces, or the basic monetary unit of the United Kingdom. Someone pounds on a door by striking it repeatedly and heavily: {He pounded on the table}. Your heart pounds when it beats hard and fast. To pound something out is to produce it with effort: {She pounded out three chapters that night}.

Pour is to cause liquid to flow from a container in a continuous stream: {She poured coffee into mugs}, {Pour the batter into the pan}. Rain pours when it falls heavily. People pour into a space when they arrive in large numbers. To {pour out} feelings is to express them freely and at length. {It never rains but it pours} means troubles come all at once.

Poured is the past tense of pour—to cause liquid to flow from a container: {She poured coffee into mugs}. Rain pours when it falls heavily. People pour into a space when they arrive in large numbers: {Fans poured through the gates}. To pour out feelings is to express them freely: {He poured out his heart to her}.

Pouring describes liquid flowing steadily from a container, or the act of causing it to do so. Rain that comes down heavily is pouring, and we say {it's pouring} when caught in such weather. When people arrive somewhere in large numbers, they pour in: {Fans were pouring into the stadium}. If you pour yourself into something, you give it intense effort and concentration. To pour out emotions or words is to express them freely and abundantly.

A pout is a facial expression of displeasure or sulkiness, with lips pushed forward: {She gave a little pout when he said no}. To pout is to make this expression or to sulk generally: {He's been pouting all day about losing}. Full lips may be described as pouty, sometimes admiringly: {pouty lips}. A pout is also a type of fish with a large head.

Pouted is the past tense of pout—to push out the lips in displeasure, sulkiness, or disappointment. Children pout when they don't get their way; adults pout when feeling slighted: {She pouted when he forgot their anniversary}. Pouted lips can also be deliberately sensual, as in fashion photography or flirtation.

Poutine is a Québécois dish of french fries topped with cheese curds and brown gravy. The heat from the gravy softens the curds without fully melting them. Once regional fast food, poutine has spread across Canada and beyond, with restaurants offering variations that add pulled pork, smoked meat, or other toppings: {We grabbed poutine after the hockey game}.

Pouting is sulking or showing displeasure by pushing out the lips and wearing a discontented expression. Children pout when denied something; adults pout when feeling slighted or ignored: {She spent the evening pouting because he forgot their anniversary}. The gesture can also be deliberately playful or seductive: {pouting for the camera}.

Pouts are expressions of displeasure made by pushing the lips forward, typically signaling sulkiness or mild petulance: {She gave him one of her famous pouts}. The word also refers to the lips themselves when positioned this way, sometimes deliberately for photographs or flirtation: {pursing her lips into a pout for the camera}. As a verb, to pout is to make this expression or sulk silently.

Poverty is the state of having little or no money, goods, or means of support. It ranges from relative deprivation to absolute destitution: {Millions live in poverty}. Extended uses describe any severe lack: {a poverty of imagination}, {intellectual poverty}. The {poverty line} is the minimum income threshold below which a person or family is officially considered poor.

Pow is an exclamation representing a sudden impact, explosion, or punch: {Pow! Right in the kisser}. It appears in comic books and action contexts to convey the sound of a blow landing. Figuratively, pow suggests sudden forceful effect: {The spices hit you—pow—right away}. (Capitalized POW is a prisoner of war.)

Powder is any substance reduced to fine, dry particles. Talcum powder goes on skin, baking powder leavens bread, gunpowder propels bullets. To powder is to apply powder or reduce to powder: {She powdered her nose}. To {take a powder} is to leave hastily, often to avoid trouble. {Powder your nose} is a euphemism for using the restroom. Powder also refers to fresh, dry snow prized by skiers: {The mountain got six inches of powder overnight}.

A powderkeg is literally a barrel for storing gunpowder—highly explosive if ignited. The figurative sense dominates modern usage: a volatile situation that could erupt into violence or chaos at any moment. {The region has been a powderkeg since the disputed election.} {Ethnic tensions turned the province into a powderkeg.} Also spelled powder keg.

Power is mainly a noun used to describe the ability to do something or create an effect: The committee does not have the power to implement these recommendations. There are many specific meanings of power that depend on context, such as electrical power, power of attorney, or an influential country or nation (All the great powers attended the conference). When power is used as a verb, it usually means supply energy to: What powers the aircraft? Before a noun, power typically denotes the availability of mechanical or electrical power, as in power brakes or power steering.

Powerful describes something with great strength, force, or influence. A powerful {engine} generates significant output. A powerful {leader} commands authority. A powerful {argument} persuades effectively. The word scales from physical might {(a powerful blow)} to emotional impact {(a powerful film)} to social dominance {(powerful interests)}. Powerfully is the adverb: {The ending affected me powerfully}.

A powerhouse is a source of great energy or strength. Originally a building where electrical power is generated, the word now most often describes a person, team, organization, or nation with exceptional capability or influence: {an economic powerhouse}, {She's a powerhouse in the courtroom}. A powerhouse performance overwhelms with its force and intensity.

Powerhouses are sources of great energy, influence, or productivity. The term originally meant a building housing machinery that generates electrical power. Now it usually describes people, organizations, or nations with exceptional capability or dominance in their field: {Germany is an economic powerhouse}, {She's a powerhouse in the courtroom}. A powerhouse performance is one of extraordinary force or impact.

Powerless means lacking power, strength, or authority to act or influence outcomes. Someone powerless to stop something cannot prevent it despite wanting to: {She felt powerless to help}. The word often describes a frustrating inability to affect circumstances: {Citizens were powerless against the regime}. It can also mean lacking official authority: {The committee was powerless to enforce its recommendations}.
Powerlessness is the condition or state of being without power. In the abstract, it is the opposite of power, which is the ability to act or influence.

Powerlifting is a strength sport consisting of three lifts: the squat, bench press, and deadlift. Competitors get three attempts at each lift, and their best successful attempts are combined for a total score. Unlike Olympic weightlifting, which emphasizes explosive overhead movements, powerlifting focuses on raw strength through slower, controlled lifts: {She set a state record in powerlifting}.

A powerplay is a strategic maneuver using strength or advantage to pressure others. In hockey and other sports, it's the period when one team has more players on the field due to an opponent's penalty: {They scored twice on the powerplay}. In business or politics, a powerplay is an aggressive move to gain control or force an outcome: {The merger was a classic corporate powerplay}.

Powers is the plural of power in its many senses—abilities, authorities, forces, or influential entities. Nations with global influence are {world powers}. Mathematical powers are numbers multiplied by themselves: {two to the third power}. Someone's powers of observation or persuasion are their capabilities in those areas. {The president's powers are limited by Congress.} (Capitalized Powers is a surname.)

A powerup is an item in video games that temporarily enhances a character's abilities—extra speed, invincibility, stronger attacks: {Grab the powerup before the boss fight}. The term extends to anything that boosts performance or energy: {Coffee is my morning powerup}. Also spelled power-up.

Powwow originally refers to a Native American ceremonial gathering featuring dancing, singing, and spiritual rituals—events that remain culturally significant today. The word has been borrowed into general American English to mean any meeting or conference, often with a casual or planning-oriented tone: {Let's have a quick powwow about the schedule}. This informal use can strike some as disrespectful to Indigenous traditions.

Powwows are gatherings of Native American peoples for ceremonial dancing, singing, and cultural celebration. The word comes from an Algonquian term for a spiritual leader or healing ceremony. In informal use, powwow means any meeting or conference, especially one involving discussion or negotiation: {Let's have a quick powwow about the project}. This casual sense can strike some as trivializing.

Pox refers to diseases that produce skin eruptions or pustules—smallpox, chickenpox, cowpox. The word often appears as a curse: {A pox on both your houses!} In modern usage, pox usually means syphilis when used alone: {He caught the pox}. To call something a pox is to label it a blight or scourge: {Social media is a pox on civil discourse}.

Practical means useful in actual application rather than theoretical. A practical {solution} works in the real world. Practical {skills} have everyday value. A practical person focuses on what can be done rather than abstract ideals. Something impractical may be beautiful or interesting but fails to function effectively. Practical also means virtual or near-complete: {a practical certainty}.

Practicality is the quality of being useful, sensible, or realistic rather than theoretical or idealistic. It emphasizes what works in real conditions: {I admire the design, but I question its practicality}. In the plural, practicalities are the concrete details that must be addressed: {We'll discuss the practicalities of moving overseas}.

Practice is a noun and, in American English, also a verb (the British spelling of the verb is practise). When you practice something do it: Always try to practice kindness. If you practice a skill, you work at it repeatedly in order to learn or master it: She vowed to practice the piano everyday. As a noun, practice usually denotes an instance of training or rehearsing. Practice can also describe a particular professional business, such as a law practice or a dental practice.

Practiced means skilled through repeated experience: {a practiced eye}, {a practiced hand}. Someone practiced at something has done it enough to become proficient. The word suggests competence gained through repetition rather than natural talent. A practiced {smile} or practiced {ease} may imply rehearsed smoothness—polished but possibly insincere.

Pradakshina is the Hindu and Buddhist practice of walking clockwise around a sacred object, shrine, or person as an act of reverence. The circled object—a temple, altar, fire, or holy person—remains on the worshipper's right side throughout. The ritual appears in wedding ceremonies, temple visits, and pilgrimages: {Devotees perform pradakshina around the sanctum three times}.

Pragmatic is a somewhat formal way of saying practical, that is, relating to what is possible or can actually be done, as opposed to what is theoretical or intellectual: Everyone welcomed the new mayor’s pragmatic approach to the city’s long-term problems. More narrowly, pragmatic can refer to the philosophical school called pragmatism, which emphasizes practical application as the main criterion for assessing meaning, truth, or value.

Pragmatism is a practical approach that values results over theory or ideology. A pragmatist asks "Does it work?" rather than "Is it pure?" {Her pragmatism helped the committee reach a compromise}. In philosophy, pragmatism is specifically the American school of thought (James, Dewey, Peirce) holding that the meaning and truth of ideas lie in their practical consequences.

A prairie is a large, flat or gently rolling expanse of grassland, especially in North America. The term typically evokes the Great Plains—treeless terrain once covered in native grasses and wildflowers: {We drove through miles of open prairie}. Prairie can modify related things: {prairie dog}, {prairie schooner}, {prairie fire}.

Prairies are vast, flat grasslands, especially the expansive treeless plains of central North America stretching from Canada through the American Midwest. The word evokes open horizons, tall grasses, and agricultural heartland: {Miles of prairie stretched to the horizon}. Prairie dogs, prairie fires, and prairie schooners all take their names from this landscape.

Praise is expressing approval, admiration, or gratitude—usually toward a person for their actions or qualities. You praise a child for good behavior, an employee for excellent work. Religious praise is directed at God or the divine: {hymns of praise}, {Praise the Lord}. As a noun, praise is what you receive when someone commends you: {The book received widespread praise from critics}. To {damn with faint praise} is to offer such weak approval that it functions as criticism.

Prajnaparamita is a central concept in Mahayana Buddhism, meaning "perfection of wisdom" or "transcendent wisdom." It refers to the highest form of understanding—direct insight into the nature of reality, particularly the emptiness (sunyata) of all phenomena. The term also names a genre of Buddhist sutras exploring this wisdom, including the famous Heart Sutra and Diamond Sutra: {The prajnaparamita literature shaped Zen and Tibetan Buddhist thought}. (Capitalized Prajnaparamita may refer specifically to the personified goddess of wisdom.)

A praline is a confection made from nuts and sugar. In the American South, pralines are creamy, fudge-like candies made with pecans and brown sugar: {New Orleans pralines melt in your mouth}. European pralines typically feature caramelized nuts ground into a paste, used in chocolates and pastries. The pronunciation varies—Americans often say PRAH-leen or PRAY-leen.

A pram is a four-wheeled carriage for a baby, designed so the infant lies flat. The word is primarily British; Americans say stroller or baby carriage. Pram is short for perambulator. Separately, a pram is a small flat-bottomed boat, also spelled prahm.

Prance describes a high-stepping, springy way of moving—horses prance when they lift their legs dramatically, and people prance when they walk with exaggerated, showy energy: {She pranced across the stage in her new heels}. The word often carries a note of vanity or self-display. Children prance when playing; adults who prance may seem affected or overly pleased with themselves.

Prancing is a high-stepping, bouncy way of moving—lifting the knees and placing the feet down with exaggerated flair. Horses prance when spirited or restrained; people prance when showing off or moving with theatrical energy: {She came prancing into the room like she owned the place}. The word often carries a note of mockery, suggesting someone is being overly showy or self-important.

A prank is a playful trick designed to surprise, embarrass, or mildly inconvenience someone: {We pranked him by filling his office with balloons}. Pranks range from harmless jokes among friends to elaborate public stunts. The word can also function as a verb: {They pranked the new employee on her first day}. A prank call is a phone call made as a joke, often to strangers.

Pranks are mischievous tricks played on someone, usually for amusement rather than malice: {The seniors pulled pranks on the freshmen during orientation week}. A prank often involves deception or surprise—hiding someone's belongings, fake spiders, plastic wrap on the toilet. {It started as a harmless prank but got out of hand.} To prank someone is to play such a trick on them.

A prankster is someone who plays pranks—practical jokes or mischievous tricks on others. The word suggests habitual behavior rather than a one-time joker: {He was the class prankster, always hiding the teacher's chalk}. Pranksters range from harmless tricksters to those whose antics cross into cruelty or property damage.

A pratfall is a comedy fall, specifically one landing on the buttocks (prat): {The clown took a spectacular pratfall}. Figuratively, a pratfall is an embarrassing blunder or humiliating failure: {His speech was one pratfall after another}.
Pratfalls is the plural of pratfall—comedy falls or embarrassing blunders: {The slapstick routine was full of pratfalls}.

Pratityasamutpada is the Buddhist doctrine of dependent origination—the principle that all phenomena arise in dependence on causes and conditions, nothing existing independently or permanently. Often illustrated through the twelve links connecting ignorance to suffering, it explains how craving and delusion perpetuate the cycle of rebirth. {Understanding pratityasamutpada is central to liberation from samsara.}

A prawn is a shellfish similar to a shrimp, with a slender body, long antennae, and edible flesh. The distinction between prawns and shrimp is loose—British English favors prawn for larger specimens, American English uses shrimp more broadly. {Grilled prawns with garlic butter.} In Australian slang, to {throw a prawn on the barbie} is quintessential outdoor cooking.

Prawns is the plural of prawn, a shellfish similar to shrimp. In British English and much of the world, prawn is the standard term for what Americans call shrimp, though technically prawns are a distinct species with branching gills. {Prawns on the barbie} is stereotypically Australian. {We ordered garlic prawns.}

To pray is to address a god or spiritual power, typically in petition or thanks: {She prayed for her mother's recovery}. The word extends to earnest requests directed at anyone: {I pray you'll reconsider}. The interjection {pray tell} is an old-fashioned or ironic way of saying "please explain."

Prayed is the past tense of pray—to address words to a deity, ask earnestly, or hope fervently. {She prayed for guidance}. {They prayed the storm would pass}. The word carries religious connotations but extends to any desperate hoping: {I prayed I wouldn't be late}.

Prayer is communication directed toward a deity or spiritual force—expressing gratitude, making requests, seeking guidance, or simply acknowledging the divine. It may be silent or spoken, private or communal, spontaneous or ritualized: {She said a prayer before the meal}. A prayer is also the text of such an address: {the Lord's Prayer}. Figuratively, something that doesn't have {a prayer} has no chance of success.

Prayers are words or thoughts addressed to a deity, often in petition, thanks, or worship: {She said her prayers before bed}. The word extends to any earnest hope or wish: {Our prayers are with the family}. Someone who {doesn't have a prayer} has no chance at all. A prayer can also be the act itself: {a moment of prayer}.

Praying is the act of addressing a god, spirit, or higher power—typically to give thanks, seek guidance, or ask for something. The word extends to any fervent hoping: {I'm praying the rain holds off}. A praying mantis holds its forelegs in a position resembling hands clasped in prayer.

To preach is to deliver a religious sermon or moral instruction: {The pastor preached on forgiveness}. Extended uses suggest unwanted moralizing or repetitive advocacy: {Don't preach to me about my habits}. To {preach to the choir} is to advocate to those already convinced. {Practice what you preach} means live by your own advice.

A preacher is someone who delivers sermons or religious instruction, typically a minister or clergy member. The word often implies passionate, moralizing speech: {He's preaching to the choir}. Outside religious contexts, preacher can describe anyone who lectures others about how they should behave: {Don't be such a preacher about my diet}.

Preachers are people who deliver sermons or religious messages, typically clergy members speaking to congregations. The term extends to anyone who advocates persistently for a cause or moral position: {He's always preaching about the evils of processed food}. To call someone a preacher outside religious contexts often implies unwelcome moralizing.

Preaching is delivering a sermon or religious instruction, typically from a pulpit: {The pastor's preaching drew crowds from across the county}. Extended to any earnest advocacy of beliefs or principles: {preaching the gospel of clean eating}. Often carries a negative sense of lecturing others self-righteously: {Spare me the preaching—I know I shouldn't smoke}.

Preachy describes speech or writing that moralizes excessively, offering unsolicited lessons about right and wrong. A preachy {movie} hammers its message rather than letting viewers draw their own conclusions. A preachy {friend} can't resist turning every conversation into a lecture. The word is always critical—nobody wants to be called preachy.

Precarious describes situations that are unstable, uncertain, or dangerously insecure. A precarious {balance} could tip at any moment. A precarious {living} barely sustains you. Someone in a precarious {position} faces risk from multiple directions. The word often implies that disaster looms if circumstances shift even slightly: {The company's financial situation remains precarious}.

A precaution is something done in advance to prevent harm or prepare for danger: {Take precautions against sunburn}. The word implies foresight—acting before a problem arises rather than reacting afterward. {As a precaution, she backed up all her files}. To take precautions during sex usually means using contraception or protection against disease.

Precautions are measures taken in advance to prevent harm or trouble. You take precautions against risks you anticipate: {safety precautions}, {fire precautions}, {Take precautions against identity theft}. The word often appears with qualifiers indicating degree: {reasonable precautions}, {every precaution}, {extra precautions}. Without modification, {take precautions} commonly refers to contraception or safe sex.

A precedent is an earlier instance that serves as a guide or justification for later ones.
