In law, precedents are past court decisions that establish how similar cases should be decided: {The ruling set a precedent for future discrimination cases}. More broadly, any prior action can set precedent: {There's no precedent for canceling the event}. Something unprecedented has never happened before. As an adjective (pronounced with stress on the second syllable), precedent means coming before: {conditions precedent to the agreement}.

A precinct is a defined district or bounded area, typically for administrative purposes. In American politics, precincts are the smallest voting divisions: {Which precinct do you vote in?} Police precincts are both jurisdictional zones and the station houses within them: {He was taken to the precinct for questioning}. The plural precincts often means the grounds or environs of a place: {the precincts of the cathedral}, {within the precincts of the university}.

Precious describes something of great value or cherished deeply. Precious {metals} like gold and silver have high monetary worth. Precious {memories} are treasured emotionally. A precious {few} means very few indeed—emphasizing scarcity. The word can turn negative when describing affected or overly refined behavior: {Don't be so precious about it}. In direct address, precious is a term of endearment: {Come here, precious}.

A precipice is a very steep or vertical rock face—a cliff edge from which one could fall. The word almost always carries danger or drama: {She stood at the precipice, looking down into the gorge}. Figuratively, a precipice is any point of crisis where disaster looms: {The company teetered on the precipice of bankruptcy}.

Precise means exact, accurate, and free from vagueness. A precise measurement leaves no ambiguity; precise language says exactly what is meant. The word often implies careful attention to detail: {She gave precise instructions}. Someone described as precise may be meticulous to the point of fussiness. {At that precise moment} emphasizes exactness in time.

Precision is exactness or accuracy, the quality of being sharply defined or measured. A precision {instrument} produces reliable, consistent results. Precision differs subtly from accuracy: accuracy means hitting the target, while precision means hitting the same spot repeatedly. {She described the events with surgical precision.} The adjective precise and adverb precisely are more common than the noun.

A predator is an animal that hunts and kills other animals for food: {Lions are apex predators on the African savanna}. The term extends to people who exploit or victimize others, especially in sexual contexts: {a sexual predator}, {online predators targeting children}. In business, a predator is a company that aggressively pursues acquisitions or seeks to destroy competitors. The word carries connotations of stealth, aggression, and the ruthless pursuit of prey—whether literal or figurative.

Predators are animals that hunt and kill other animals for food, occupying a position in the food chain above their prey. The term extends to people who exploit or victimize others, particularly in contexts of financial schemes or sexual violence: {a sexual predator}, {predatory lending}. In sports, especially hockey, Predators refers to the Nashville NHL team. The word carries connotations of aggression, stealth, and ruthlessness whether describing a lion stalking gazelles or a con artist targeting the elderly.

Predatory describes creatures that hunt and kill other animals for food: {predatory birds}, {predatory fish}. The meaning extends to people or practices that exploit others for profit or advantage: {predatory lending}, {predatory pricing}. A predatory person aggressively pursues victims—sexually, financially, or otherwise: {predatory behavior toward young employees}.

A predecessor is someone or something that came before another in a position, sequence, or role. A company's new CEO studies the decisions of her predecessor. A predecessor can also be an earlier version of something: {The smartphone's predecessor was the flip phone}. The word implies replacement or succession—what exists now has taken the predecessor's place.

Predecessors are those who came before in a position, role, or sequence. A new CEO studies her predecessors' decisions. A building replaces its predecessor on the same site. The word applies to people, things, or versions: {This software improves on its predecessor}. The opposite is successor.

Predestination is the theological doctrine that God has already determined all events, including who will be saved and who will be damned. The concept is central to Calvinist Christianity, which holds that salvation cannot be earned through good works but is granted only to those God has chosen in advance. More loosely, predestination suggests that the course of one's life is fixed beforehand by fate or divine will. {She believed predestination meant her choices were already made for her.}

A predicament is a difficult, unpleasant, or embarrassing situation from which escape is not obvious: {How did you get yourself into this predicament?} The word suggests being stuck or trapped by circumstances rather than facing immediate danger. {The company's financial predicament worsened after the scandal.}

Predicaments are difficult, unpleasant, or embarrassing situations from which there is no easy escape. The word implies being stuck—trapped by circumstances rather than facing a simple problem with an obvious solution: {She found herself in quite a predicament when both dates showed up at the same restaurant}. Often used with a touch of wry acknowledgment that one's own choices contributed to the trouble.

To predict is to say what will happen before it happens: {The model predicts rain tomorrow}, {No one predicted the market crash}. Prediction can be based on evidence, intuition, or guesswork. Scientists predict outcomes from data; fortune-tellers predict from tea leaves. The word implies some claim to knowledge about the future, however founded.

Predictable describes something that can be anticipated or foreseen. A predictable {outcome} follows logically from circumstances. Predictable behavior follows established patterns: {Her reaction was entirely predictable}. The word often carries a negative charge—predictable plots bore audiences, predictable people lack spontaneity. But predictability can be reassuring: {I wanted a predictable routine after months of chaos}.

A prediction is a statement about what will happen in the future: {Her prediction about the election proved correct}. Predictions range from scientific forecasts based on data to casual guesses about outcomes. The word implies some basis for the claim, however slight—distinguishing it from mere wishes or random speculation. {The model's predictions were remarkably accurate}.

Predictions are statements about what will happen in the future. The word covers everything from weather forecasts to election polls to psychic readings: {Her predictions about the stock market proved accurate}. In science and statistics, predictions are testable claims derived from theories or models. In casual use, prediction often implies guesswork: {My prediction is they'll be late}.

A preemie is an infant born prematurely—before the normal gestational period is complete. The term is informal and affectionate compared to the clinical "premature infant": {The preemie spent three weeks in the NICU}. Also spelled preemie or premie.

Preen originally describes what birds do—running feathers through the beak to clean and arrange them. By extension, people preen when they groom themselves with obvious self-satisfaction, fussing over appearance in a mirror: {She preened before the party}. Figuratively, to preen is to congratulate oneself smugly: {He preened over his test scores}.

Preening is the act of grooming, especially when birds smooth and arrange their feathers with their beaks. Extended to humans, preening suggests fussy self-admiration—adjusting clothes, fixing hair, or generally primping: {She spent twenty minutes preening in front of the mirror}. The word often carries a note of vanity or self-satisfaction: {He was preening after the compliment}.

Prefab is short for prefabricated—manufactured in sections elsewhere and assembled on site. A prefab house arrives as panels or modules rather than being built from raw materials. The term works as noun or adjective: {They moved into a prefab after the war}; {prefab housing developments}. Prefab sometimes carries connotations of cheapness or uniformity, though modern prefab construction has shed much of that stigma.

A preface is an introductory section at the beginning of a book, typically written by the author to explain the work's purpose, scope, or origins: {In her preface, she describes how the project began}. Unlike a foreword, which is written by someone other than the author, a preface comes from the author's own hand. The verb means to introduce or precede: {He prefaced his remarks with an apology}.

To prefer something is to like it better than alternatives: {I prefer tea to coffee}, {She prefers working from home}. The word implies choice between options rather than absolute judgment. Prefer can soften requests into polite suggestions: {I'd prefer not to discuss it}. The formal construction {prefer that} takes subjunctive: {I prefer that he leave}.

Preference is a greater liking for one thing over another—what you would choose given options: {My preference is to stay home}. Preferences range from trivial {(vanilla over chocolate)} to consequential {(job preferences, sexual preference)}. To give preference to something is to prioritize it: {The company gives preference to internal candidates}. Preferential treatment favors certain people or things.

Preferences are things you like better than alternatives—your favored choices among options. The word often appears in contexts where you're asked to specify what you want: {dietary preferences}, {Update your preferences in the settings menu}. Someone's preferences reveal their tastes and priorities: {Her preference for quiet evenings over parties}. In formal contexts, to give preference to something is to prioritize it: {Preference will be given to local applicants}.

Pregnancy is the condition of carrying developing offspring within the body, in humans lasting about nine months from conception to birth. The term extends to any state of being pregnant with possibility: {a pause pregnant with meaning}, {pregnant with implications}. A pregnancy can be planned, unexpected, or unwanted—each carrying different social weight.

Pregnant describes a female carrying developing offspring in her uterus. The condition lasts about nine months in humans. By extension, pregnant describes anything full of meaning or potential: a pregnant {pause} holds unspoken significance, a pregnant {moment} seems laden with consequence. {She's six months pregnant with twins.}

Prehistoric describes the time before written records began, roughly before 3000 BCE in most regions: {prehistoric cave paintings}, {prehistoric humans}. The word often evokes ancient creatures like dinosaurs, though technically it covers any era lacking documentation. Informally, prehistoric means extremely outdated or primitive: {His views on women are prehistoric}.

Prehistory is the period of human existence before written records—the vast stretch of time known only through archaeology, fossils, and oral traditions. The prefix *pre-* marks what came before: {the prehistory of the internet}, {the prehistory of jazz}. Something belonging to this era is prehistoric, a term often used hyperbolically for anything outdated: {His views on women are prehistoric}.

Prejudice is a judgment or opinion in the absence of reasonable grounds. Prejudice is typically directed against people or groups who are different in a particular way from biased person: As the only African-American children growing up in a white neighborhood, they became familiar with prejudice at an early age. To prejudice someone is to cause them to respond with favorable or unfavorable bias. In a legal context, to prejudice something is to cause damage: The judge decided that admitting the evidence would prejudice the administration of justice.

Prejudiced describes holding preconceived opinions not based on reason or experience—literally, pre-judged. Someone prejudiced against a group has decided their view before encountering individuals: {He was prejudiced against anyone from the city}. The word usually implies unfair bias, especially regarding race, gender, or religion. A prejudiced {jury} has formed opinions before hearing evidence.

Prejudices are preconceived opinions not based on reason or experience—judgments formed before the facts are in. The word usually implies unfavorable attitudes toward groups of people: {racial prejudices}, {prejudices against immigrants}. To have prejudices is human; to act on them causes harm. The verb prejudice means to influence unfairly or to damage: {The publicity prejudiced the jury}, {without prejudice to your rights}.

A prelude is something that comes before and introduces what follows. In music, a prelude is a short piece that precedes a larger work—a fugue, an opera, or a suite—though some stand alone: {Chopin's Preludes}. More broadly, any preliminary event can be a prelude: {The skirmish was a prelude to full-scale war}. To prelude is to serve as such an introduction.

Premature means happening before the proper or expected time. A premature {birth} occurs before full term. A premature {conclusion} is reached without sufficient evidence. {It's premature to celebrate}—the outcome isn't certain yet. The word often carries a note of caution: acting or judging too soon risks being wrong. Premature {ejaculation} is sexual climax occurring sooner than desired.

Premed is short for premedical, describing undergraduate coursework and students preparing for medical school. A premed student—or simply {a premed}—takes the required biology, chemistry, and physics courses needed for admission. The term often carries connotations of intense competition and academic pressure: {The premed track is notoriously cutthroat}.

Premeditated describes actions planned or considered in advance rather than done impulsively. The word appears most often in legal contexts: {premeditated murder} involves deliberate intent, distinguishing it from crimes of passion or accident. Outside law, it emphasizes deliberateness: {a premeditated insult}, {premeditated cruelty}. The planning implied is usually for something harmful or wrong.

Premeditation is planning or thinking about something before doing it, especially a crime. In law, premeditation distinguishes murder from manslaughter—killing with prior intent carries heavier penalties than killing in the heat of passion. {The prosecution argued that buying the gun showed premeditation.} The word implies deliberate calculation rather than spontaneous action.

Premier means first in rank, importance, or time. The premier {scientist in her field} leads all others. As a noun, premier designates a head of government—particularly prime ministers or leaders of Canadian provinces and Australian states: {The premier announced new infrastructure spending}. The verb means to give a first public performance: {The film premiered at Cannes}.

A premiere is the first public performance or showing of a play, film, or other work: {The movie had its world premiere at Cannes}. As a verb, to premiere is to have or give such a first showing: {The series premieres next Thursday}. The adjective use meaning first or chief ({the premiere authority on the subject}) is less common and sometimes criticized, since that sense traditionally belongs to premier.

A premise is a proposition that forms the basis for an argument or conclusion—the starting point from which reasoning proceeds: {The premise of the argument is flawed}. In logic, premises are statements assumed true to derive a conclusion. More loosely, premise means an underlying assumption: {The movie's premise is that time travel is possible}. The plural premises refers to a building and its surrounding land: {Smoking is not allowed on the premises}. To premise something is to base it on a particular assumption.

Premium connects the idea of paying more to get more. A premium product costs extra because it's supposedly superior: {premium gasoline}, {premium seating}. Insurance premiums are regular payments for coverage. Something {at a premium} is scarce and therefore valuable: {Parking spots are at a premium downtown}. As an adjective, premium means high-quality or deluxe: {a premium streaming subscription}.

A premonition is a feeling that something is about to happen, especially something bad. Unlike a prediction based on evidence, a premonition arrives as intuition or unease: {She had a premonition that something was wrong}. The word often appears in stories where the feeling proves justified—a sense of foreboding that precedes disaster.

Premonitions are feelings that something is about to happen, especially something bad. The word implies foreknowledge without rational basis—a sense of impending events that arrives unbidden: {She had a premonition that the flight would crash}. Premonitions may prove accurate or not; the word describes the feeling, not its validity.

A prenup is a prenuptial agreement—a contract signed before marriage specifying how assets will be divided if the marriage ends. Once associated mainly with the wealthy protecting family fortunes, prenups have become more common among ordinary couples: {Her lawyer advised her to get a prenup}. The word can also be used as an adjective: {prenup negotiations}.

Prenups is the informal plural of prenuptial agreement—a contract between partners before marriage specifying how assets and debts will be divided if the marriage ends. Once associated mainly with the wealthy, prenups have become more common: {Their lawyers are still negotiating the prenups}. The singular prenup appears more frequently than the plural.

Preoccupation is the state of being mentally absorbed by something, often to the point of distraction: {His preoccupation with work was affecting his marriage}. The word can also refer to the thing that absorbs attention: {Her main preoccupation these days is the garden}. A preoccupation may be a persistent concern or obsession: {an unhealthy preoccupation with death}.

Preoccupied describes a mind already occupied—absorbed in thought or worry to the point of distraction. Someone preoccupied with work troubles may not hear what you're saying. {She seemed preoccupied and barely touched her food.} The word suggests mental unavailability rather than mere busyness.

Prep means to prepare or make ready. In cooking, prep work involves cutting vegetables, measuring ingredients, and organizing before actual cooking begins: {I spent an hour prepping for dinner}. In medicine, to prep a patient is to ready them for surgery. The noun refers to this preparatory work: {The prep takes longer than the cooking}. Prep can also mean a preparatory school or its culture—the preppy style of dress and manner associated with elite private schools: {He went to prep in New England}. (Capitalized PREP is an HIV prevention medication.)

Preparation is the act of getting ready for something, or the state of being ready: {Preparation for the exam took months}. A preparation can also be a substance made for a specific purpose—a pharmaceutical preparation, a skin preparation. In the plural, preparations are the activities undertaken before an event: {Wedding preparations are underway}. To do something {in preparation for} something else is to ready yourself for what's coming.

Preparations are things done beforehand to get ready for something: {preparations for the wedding}, {emergency preparations}. The word often implies multiple steps or activities: {The preparations took weeks}. A preparation can also be a substance specially made for a purpose—a medicinal preparation, a chemical preparation. In music, a preparation is a note or chord that sets up a dissonance.

To prepare is to make ready for a future purpose or occasion. You prepare a meal by cooking it, prepare for an exam by studying, prepare a room by cleaning it. The word implies anticipation—something is coming and you're getting set: {We prepared for the worst}. To be prepared is to be in a state of readiness. A prepared statement is written in advance rather than improvised.

Prepared means ready for what's coming. You can be prepared for a test, a trip, or an emergency. Food that is prepared has been made ready to eat: {prepared meals}, {prepared mustard}. A prepared statement is written in advance rather than improvised. The Boy Scout motto is "Be Prepared." To come prepared is to have anticipated what you'll need.

Preparing is getting ready for something that hasn't happened yet. You might be preparing {dinner}, preparing {for an exam}, or preparing {to leave}. The word emphasizes the process rather than completion—you're in the midst of making something ready, not yet finished.

A prepper is someone who prepares for emergencies, disasters, or societal collapse by stockpiling supplies, learning survival skills, and developing contingency plans. The term gained currency in the early 21st century, often associated with those anticipating worst-case scenarios: {The prepper had enough canned food to last two years}. Preppers range from practical planners to apocalyptic extremists.

Preppers are people who actively prepare for emergencies, disasters, or societal collapse by stockpiling supplies, learning survival skills, and developing contingency plans. The term ranges from those with modest earthquake kits to those building bunkers against apocalyptic scenarios: {The preppers had enough food and water to last six months}. The practice is prepping.

Preppie describes someone who dresses or acts like a student at an expensive preparatory school—clean-cut, conventional, and upper-middle-class. The style involves polo shirts, khakis, and loafers; the manner suggests privilege and conformity. As a noun, a preppie is such a person: {a bunch of preppies from the suburbs}. Also spelled preppy.

Prepping is preparing—getting ready for something. The word appears in contexts from cooking {prepping vegetables for dinner} to education {prepping for exams}. In its specialized sense, prepping refers to survivalist preparation for disasters or societal collapse: stockpiling food, water, and supplies. A prepper is someone who engages in this practice.

Preppy describes a style associated with expensive private preparatory schools and the social class that attends them—clean-cut, conservative clothing like polo shirts, khakis, and boat shoes, along with a polished, conventional manner. As a noun, a preppy is someone who embodies this aesthetic: {She dressed preppy even in college}. The term can be neutral or slightly mocking, depending on context.

A prequel is a story set before the events of an existing work—a film, novel, or other narrative that depicts what happened earlier in the timeline: {The studio announced a prequel exploring the villain's origin}. The term emerged in the 1970s as the opposite of sequel, which continues a story forward rather than backward.

Prequels are stories set before the events of an existing work. A prequel depicts what happened earlier in a fictional timeline, often showing origins or backstory: {The prequel explains how the villain became evil}. The term emerged in the 1970s, modeled on sequel, and became ubiquitous with film franchises. Unlike sequels, prequels face the challenge of maintaining suspense when audiences know where characters end up.

A prerequisite is something required beforehand—a condition that must be met before proceeding. Courses have prerequisites: {Calculus is a prerequisite for physics}. Jobs list prerequisites in their requirements. The word works as both noun and adjective: {prerequisite knowledge}, {prerequisite skills}. Prerequisites establish that certain foundations must exist before building further.

Preschool is education for children too young for kindergarten, typically ages three to five, or the institution providing it: {She teaches preschool}, {We're touring preschools next week}. As an adjective, it describes this age range or stage: {preschool children}, {preschool education}. The term reflects the view of these programs as preparation for formal schooling.

A prescription is a doctor's written order for medicine or treatment, or the medicine itself: {I need to pick up my prescription from the pharmacy}. The word extends to any authoritative recommendation: {His prescription for success was hard work}. In law, prescription refers to the acquisition of rights through long use or custom. The adjective prescriptive describes rules that dictate how things should be done, as opposed to descriptive approaches that record how things actually are.

Prescriptions are written orders from a doctor authorizing specific medication for a patient: {I need to pick up my prescriptions from the pharmacy}. By extension, a prescription is any authoritative recommendation: {His prescription for success was hard work and patience}. As an adjective, prescription describes medication requiring a doctor's order, as opposed to over-the-counter drugs.

Preseason refers to the period before a sports season officially begins, when teams hold training camps and play exhibition games that don't count in standings: {The team looked sharp in preseason but struggled once real games started}. As an adjective, it modifies related nouns: preseason {training}, preseason {predictions}, preseason {favorite}. The term extends beyond sports to any preparatory period before a main season begins.

Presence is the state of being in a place or existing in something: {Your presence is requested at the meeting}, {the presence of bacteria in the water}. A person with presence commands attention through bearing or charisma: {She has real stage presence}. A military or police presence means personnel stationed somewhere. To be in someone's presence is to be near them physically. A felt presence suggests something unseen but perceived: {a ghostly presence in the room}.

As a noun, present means gift or the current time. As an adjective, present may mean here, there, now, or then, depending on the context: I wasn’t present when the rules were read. Our present opinion is that no changes should be made to the proposal. When present (second syllable stressed) is a verb, it means make known to others: Members of the panel presented information about their organizations and their funding priorities.

Presentation covers the act of presenting and the thing presented. A formal presentation is a prepared talk, often with slides: {Her presentation to the board went well}. The presentation of evidence puts it before a jury. In medicine, presentation describes how a patient's symptoms appear or how a fetus is positioned for delivery: {breech presentation}. The word often emphasizes how something is displayed or arranged: {The food was delicious, but the presentation was lacking}.

Presents works as both noun and verb around the idea of giving or showing. As a noun, presents are gifts: {The children opened their presents}. The verb means to give formally {(present an award)}, to show or display {(present evidence)}, or to introduce {(May I present our guest speaker)}. Something that presents a problem causes one to appear. To present yourself somewhere is to show up.

Preservation is the act of keeping something safe from harm, decay, or destruction. Food preservation extends shelf life through canning, freezing, or drying. Historic preservation protects old buildings from demolition or alteration. {The preservation of wildlife habitats requires careful planning.} Self-preservation is the instinct to protect oneself from danger.

Preservatives are substances added to food, cosmetics, or other products to prevent spoilage, decay, or bacterial growth. Salt and sugar are ancient preservatives; modern ones include chemical compounds like sodium benzoate and potassium sorbate. {Check the label for preservatives.} The term often carries negative connotations in food contexts, where "no preservatives" signals naturalness or health consciousness.

Preserve means to keep something in its existing state, protecting it from decay, damage, or change. You preserve food by canning, salting, or freezing. You preserve a building by maintaining it. You preserve a tradition by continuing to practice it. A preserve is a protected area where wildlife or natural features are safeguarded: {a nature preserve}, {a game preserve}. Preserves are also fruit cooked with sugar to prevent spoiling: {strawberry preserves}. To preserve one's dignity or composure is to maintain it under pressure.

Preserved describes something kept from decay, damage, or loss. Food is preserved through canning, pickling, salting, or freezing: {preserved lemons}, {preserved meats}. Buildings and artifacts are preserved for historical value. A {well-preserved} specimen or person has aged better than expected. To say something is preserved {in amber} suggests it remains frozen in time, unchanged.

Preserves are fruit cooked with sugar to prevent spoilage, typically containing larger pieces of fruit than jam or jelly: {strawberry preserves}, {a jar of homemade preserves}. The word also names protected areas where wildlife or natural resources are maintained: {a nature preserve}, {a hunting preserve}. As a verb, to preserve is to maintain something in its original state or protect it from decay: {preserve the Constitution}, {preserve one's dignity}, {preserve food for winter}.

The presidency is the office or position of president, or the period during which someone holds that office: {during the Obama presidency}, {She announced her candidacy for the presidency}. The term applies to nations, organizations, and institutions alike. A presidency may also refer to the administration or executive branch under a particular president.

A president is the head of a republic or organization—someone who presides over others. In countries without monarchs, the president typically serves as head of state: {The president addressed the nation}. Corporate presidents lead companies; university presidents run institutions. The title implies elected or appointed leadership rather than inherited authority. Presidential describes anything relating to a president or befitting the office: {presidential debates}, {presidential bearing}.

Presidential describes things relating to a president or the office of the presidency: a presidential {election}, presidential {powers}, a presidential {library}. When describing behavior, presidential suggests the dignity and gravitas expected of a head of state: {He looked presidential in his tailored suit}. The opposite implication—that someone's conduct falls short of the office—often lurks nearby: {That outburst was hardly presidential}.

Presidents is the plural of president—a person who presides over an organization, company, or country. In American usage, president most often refers to the head of state: {Four presidents have been assassinated in office}. The word also applies to corporate executives and university leaders: {The presidents of both companies attended the merger announcement}.

Press is a shorthand term for the news media, originally only newspapers but now including all news media in expressions like press conference, press release, and the mainstream press. This is based originally on printing press, a machine used to print words on paper. The underlying verb press means to exert steady, continuous force, the way you press a button or use a steam iron: She pressed the wrinkles out of her blouse. The idea of pressure extends to figurative use, so press also conveys making a demand or forcefulness.

Pressed describes something subjected to pressure—squeezed, flattened, or compacted: {freshly pressed juice}, {pressed flowers}. Pressed clothes have been ironed smooth. To be pressed for time or money is to have too little: {I'm really pressed for time today}. Hard-pressed means struggling or under strain. Pressed can also mean urged or coerced: {He was pressed into service}.

Pressing describes something requiring immediate attention or action: {a pressing need for reform}, {pressing deadlines}. The urgency implied is real but not usually emergency-level—more insistent than casual, less dire than desperate. As a noun, a pressing is an instance of applying pressure, or the quantity of records or CDs manufactured at one time: {the original pressing of the album}.

Pressure is force applied to a surface or object. Atmospheric pressure is the weight of air pressing down. Blood pressure measures force against artery walls. Under pressure, things compress or break—including people: {She cracked under the pressure of the job}. To pressure someone is to push them toward a decision: {They pressured him into signing}. Peer pressure is social influence from one's group. A pressure cooker uses steam pressure to cook food quickly, and figuratively describes any high-stress situation.

Pressured describes feeling pushed or coerced toward some action or outcome. External forces create the pressure—deadlines, expectations, other people's demands: {I felt pressured to accept the job offer}. Someone can be pressured into a decision they wouldn't otherwise make. The word implies the force comes from outside, distinguishing it from internally motivated stress.

Prestige is the respect and admiration that comes from success, achievement, or high status. A prestigious university or job carries weight partly because others recognize its value: {She took a pay cut for the prestige of working at a top firm}. Prestige can attach to institutions, professions, or individuals. The word often implies that reputation matters as much as substance.

Prestigious describes something that commands widespread respect and admiration, usually earned through excellence, success, or high status. A prestigious university attracts top students. A prestigious award confers honor on its recipients. {She landed a position at a prestigious law firm.} The word often signals elite standing within a field or profession.
Presto was traditionally uttered by magicians at the completion of a magic trick. People use it to suggest that something has happened suddenly, as if by magic.

Presumption is an assumption made without proof, or the act of assuming something is true before it's established: {The presumption of innocence protects the accused}. It also means bold or arrogant behavior—taking liberties beyond what's appropriate: {It was sheer presumption to think he could walk in without an appointment}. A presumption in law is something accepted as true until proven otherwise.

A preteen is a child approaching the teenage years, typically between ages nine and twelve. The word functions as both noun and adjective: {preteen girls}, {a magazine for preteens}. The term emphasizes the transitional stage—no longer a young child, not yet a teenager. Also spelled pre-teen.

Pretence is the British spelling of pretense. It covers the act of pretending—making something appear true when it isn't: {She made no pretence of liking him}. A pretence can be a false claim or affectation: {He dropped all pretence of civility}. The word also means a claim to skill or status, often with false implications: {pretences to scholarship}.

To pretend is to act as if something is true when it isn't. Children pretend to be superheroes; adults pretend to be interested in dull conversations. The word can suggest imagination {(Let's pretend we're pirates)} or deception {(He pretended not to notice)}. As an adjective, pretend means imaginary or make-believe: {pretend money}, {a pretend friend}. A pretender is someone who claims something falsely, especially a throne.

A pretender is someone who claims something falsely—typically a title, throne, or status they don't legitimately hold: {the pretender to the Spanish crown}. More broadly, anyone who pretends or feigns: {He's just a pretender who doesn't know what he's doing}. The word carries connotations of fraud or self-delusion, suggesting the gap between claimed and actual merit.

Pretending is acting as if something is true when it isn't. Children pretend when they play: {She's pretending to be a dinosaur}. Adults pretend to hide feelings or deceive: {He pretended not to care}. The word can suggest harmless make-believe or deliberate falseness, depending on context.

Pretense is a false show or claim—presenting something as true when it isn't. To make a pretense of working is to appear busy without accomplishing anything. Under the pretense of friendship, someone might exploit your trust. {He dropped all pretense and admitted he was afraid.} Without pretense describes genuine, unpretentious behavior. Also spelled pretence in British English.

Pretension is a claim to something—merit, importance, or status—that may or may not be justified. A novel with literary pretensions aspires to artistic significance. The word often implies the claim exceeds reality: {His pretensions to expertise were laughable}. Without pretension describes something unpretentious or modest: {a café without pretension}. The plural pretensions emphasizes ambitious self-regard: {She has pretensions above her station}.

Pretensions are claims to importance, merit, or distinction—often implying the claims exceed reality. Someone with {literary pretensions} aspires to be taken seriously as a writer, perhaps without the talent to justify it. {The restaurant has pretensions to fine dining but serves microwaved appetizers.} The word carries skepticism: pretensions are ambitions viewed from outside, usually unfavorably. A place {without pretensions} is unpretentious—comfortable in what it actually is.

The key to all the related meanings of pretentious is the underlying verb pretend. A pretentious person is pretending to be someone other than they are—usually someone more cultured, intelligent, or dignified. Pretentious language is intended to convey importance or some other quality it does not really possess. Pretentious is always used for negative characterizations because it is in many ways the opposite of honest and straightforward.

Pretentiousness is the quality of claiming or projecting importance, sophistication, or artistic merit that isn't warranted. Someone guilty of pretentiousness might use obscure vocabulary to seem intellectual, or affect refined tastes they don't genuinely hold. The word carries strong negative judgment—it suggests not just ambition but dishonesty about one's actual depth or knowledge: {The gallery reeked of pretentiousness}.

A pretext is a false or superficial reason given to disguise the real purpose behind an action: {He used the meeting as a pretext to see her again}. The word implies deliberate deception—the stated reason sounds plausible but masks ulterior motives. {Under the pretext of checking on her health, he searched her apartment}.

Pretty describes something pleasing to look at, usually suggesting delicacy or charm rather than striking beauty: {a pretty face}, {a pretty garden}. As an adverb, pretty means fairly or moderately: {pretty good}, {pretty much done}. The phrase {a pretty penny} means a large sum. {Sitting pretty} means being in a favorable position. To {pretty up} is to make more attractive, often superficially.

A pretzel is a baked bread product twisted into a distinctive knot shape, typically salted on the outside. Soft pretzels are large, chewy, and eaten fresh; hard pretzels are small, crispy snacks. The twisted shape has made pretzel a verb and adjective for contortion: {She pretzel-twisted herself into the yoga pose}, {pretzel logic}.

Pretzels is the plural of pretzel, a baked bread product twisted into a distinctive knot shape. Pretzels come in two main varieties: small, hard, and salted as a crunchy snack, or large, soft, and chewy, often sold at street carts and sporting events. {She grabbed a bag of pretzels from the vending machine.}

Prevail means to prove superior or win out in the end: {Justice will prevail}. It often implies overcoming opposition or difficulty: {Despite the odds, common sense prevailed}. To prevail upon someone is to persuade them, usually after some effort: {She prevailed upon him to stay}. Prevailing conditions or winds are the ones that predominate: {the prevailing winds from the west}.

Prevent means to stop something from happening or someone from doing something. You prevent {accidents}, prevent {disease}, or prevent someone from {entering}. The word implies action taken in advance—you can't prevent what has already occurred. Prevention is the noun: {an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure}.

Prevention is the act of stopping something from happening before it does. The word appears most often in contexts of health and safety: {disease prevention}, {crime prevention}, {fire prevention}. The phrase {an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure} captures the idea that stopping problems early costs less than fixing them later.

A preview is a glimpse of something before its full presentation or release. Movie previews show clips to entice audiences; a preview of a book might be the first chapter. To preview is to see or show in advance: {We previewed the exhibit before it opened to the public}. In computing, preview displays how a document will look when printed or published.

Prey is an animal hunted and killed by another for food: {The owl swooped down on its prey}. By extension, prey includes anyone vulnerable to exploitation or attack: {con artists and their prey}. To prey on something is to hunt it, exploit it, or weigh heavily on it: {The scandal preyed on his mind}. A predator is one who preys; prey is what gets preyed upon.

Price is what you pay to get something—usually money, but it can be any cost or sacrifice. A store sets prices; a buyer pays them. The {price of admission} might be literal or figurative. {At what price?} questions whether something is worth its cost. To price something is to set or determine its cost: {We priced the car too high}. {Everyone has their price} suggests anyone can be bought.

Priceless describes something so valuable it cannot be assigned a price—a priceless {heirloom}, a priceless {work of art}. The word often applies to things whose worth is sentimental or irreplaceable rather than monetary: {priceless memories}, {priceless moments with family}. In casual speech, priceless means hilariously funny or absurd: {The look on his face was priceless}.

Prices is the plural of price—what something costs or what someone asks for it. Prices rise and fall with supply and demand. To price something is to set or determine its cost: {Help me price these items for the garage sale}. If you {price yourself out of the market}, you ask more than buyers will pay.

Pricey means expensive, usually with a note of complaint or hesitation: {The restaurant was good but a bit pricey}. The word suggests something costs more than expected or more than the speaker wants to pay. Also spelled pricy.

To prick is to pierce with a fine point or to cause a sharp localized pain: {She pricked her finger on the needle}. A prick is such a puncture or the sensation it causes. To prick up your ears is to listen attentively, like a dog whose ears rise at a sound. In vulgar slang, prick means penis and serves as a sharp insult for a contemptible man: {Her ex-husband is a real prick}. The insult implies someone mean and penetrating—the puncture sense bleeding into character.

A prickle is a small, sharp point on a plant—finer than a thorn, like those on a raspberry cane. The word extends to any sharp tingling sensation: {a prickle of fear ran down her spine}, {the prickle of wool against skin}. To prickle is to cause or feel such sensations: {Her skin prickled with anticipation}. {The hay prickled his bare arms.}

Prickles are small, sharp points that stick out from a surface—the spines on a cactus, the thorns on a rose stem, or the stiff hairs on a hedgehog. The word also describes the sensation of being pricked: {She felt prickles on her skin as she walked through the tall grass}. Figuratively, prickles of fear or excitement are tingling sensations that seem to pierce the skin from within.

Prickly describes something covered with prickles or sharp points: {a prickly cactus}, {prickly brambles}. A prickly sensation is sharp and stinging, like pins against skin. Figuratively, prickly describes someone easily irritated or quick to take offense: {He gets prickly when you mention his ex}. A prickly subject is sensitive and likely to provoke disagreement.

Pride is a uniquely human emotion of self-importance or accomplishment, sometimes regarded as good (civic pride, hometown pride), and regarded negatively when it is excessive and combined with prejudice (white pride, nationalistic pride). If you pride yourself on something, you experience a feeling of pride for having done or endured it. Your pride and joy is something you are particularly proud of. The collective noun pride is used for a group of lions.

A priest is a person authorized to perform religious rites, serving as an intermediary between worshippers and the divine. In Christianity, priests lead services, administer sacraments, and provide spiritual guidance—the term applies specifically to Catholic, Orthodox, and some Anglican clergy, while Protestants typically use minister or pastor. Other religions have their own priestly traditions: {a Hindu priest}, {a Shinto priest}. Figuratively, someone deeply devoted to an idea or practice may be called its priest: {a high priest of modernism}.

A priestess is a female priest—a woman authorized to perform religious rites and ceremonies. The term appears most often in reference to ancient or non-Christian religions: {a priestess of Apollo}, {a voodoo priestess}. Some modern pagan and Wiccan traditions use priestess as an official title. In contexts where priest applies to women, priestess may sound archaic or deliberately gendered.

Priesthood is the office or status of being a priest, or priests collectively as a group: {He entered the priesthood at twenty-five}, {the Catholic priesthood}. The term can extend to any elite body claiming special authority or access to sacred knowledge: {the priesthood of academic economics}. In some traditions, priesthood refers to specific levels or powers of religious authority.

Priests is the plural of priest, a person authorized to perform religious rites and ceremonies. In Christianity, priests serve as intermediaries between congregations and God, administering sacraments and leading worship. Other religions have priests with varying roles: {The temple priests performed the sacrifice}. Figuratively, priests of any domain are its devoted practitioners: {priests of high fashion}.

Primadonna—from the Italian for "first lady"—originally meant the lead female singer in an opera company. The term now more commonly describes someone who behaves as if they deserve special treatment, is temperamentally difficult, or throws tantrums when things don't go their way: {The director refused to work with her again—total primadonna}. Also spelled prima donna.

Primal means first or original—relating to the earliest stage of something. A primal {instinct} or primal {fear} reaches back to ancient origins, before civilization shaped behavior. The word suggests something raw and fundamental: {a primal scream}, {primal urges}. Primal often implies powerful, elemental forces beneath the surface of modern life.

The adjective primary has two main meanings that often overlap: first in importance and first in order. Primary education is education for young children. A primary reason, goal, or objective is the main one. In this meaning, primary is often contrasted with secondary. A primary election is one that happens before a general election, to choose candidates. Such elections are often just called primaries. The outermost feathers on a bird’s wing are primaries and the three primary colors (red, yellow, blue) may also be called primaries.

A primate is a member of the mammalian order that includes humans, apes, monkeys, and lemurs—animals typically characterized by forward-facing eyes, grasping hands, and large brains relative to body size. In religious contexts, a primate is a high-ranking bishop or archbishop: {the Primate of the Anglican Church}. The biological and ecclesiastical senses share no connection beyond the spelling.

Primates are members of the biological order that includes humans, apes, monkeys, and lemurs—mammals typically characterized by grasping hands, forward-facing eyes, and large brains relative to body size. The word also serves as the plural of primate in its ecclesiastical sense, referring to senior bishops or archbishops: {The primates of the Anglican Communion met in London}.

Like the related adjective primary, prime means main or first in importance (prime minister, prime suspect). A prime number is only divisible by itself and one; the set of such numbers are called primes. To prime something is to prepare it for use or operation (prime a pump). Sometimes prime means to apply primer, which is a substance that prepares a surface for some further treatment or covering.

A primer is an introductory text or course covering the basics of a subject: {a primer on investing}, {a primer on constitutional law}. The word also refers to a substance applied as a preparatory coat—primer on walls before paint, primer on skin before makeup. In ammunition, a primer is the small charge that ignites the main explosive. Pronounced with a short *i* for the coating and ammunition senses, with a long *i* for the introductory text in American English.

Primetime is the evening hours when television viewership peaks, typically 8–11 PM. Networks schedule their most popular shows and charge advertisers premium rates during primetime. The term extends to anything operating at peak capacity or importance: {a primetime player}, {ready for primetime}. Something {not ready for primetime} is amateurish or underprepared.

Primitive describes something basic, early, or undeveloped. A primitive {tool} is simple and unrefined. Primitive {societies} lack modern technology or complexity—though calling people primitive carries condescending overtones. In art, primitive refers to work that appears unsophisticated or childlike, sometimes deliberately. A primitive {instinct} is fundamental and unlearned. In computing, a primitive is a basic building block: {graphics primitives}, {data primitives}.

A primrose is a woodland plant with pale yellow flowers that bloom in early spring, among the first to appear after winter. The {primrose path} is a life of ease and pleasure—attractive but potentially leading to ruin, from Shakespeare's use in Hamlet. Primrose yellow is a pale, delicate shade.

Primroses are flowering plants that bloom in early spring, bearing clusters of pale yellow or other soft-colored flowers. The word evokes innocence and fresh beginnings. The {primrose path} is a pleasant route that leads to ruin—easy choices with bad consequences: {He followed the primrose path of easy credit into bankruptcy}.

A prince is a male member of a royal family, typically a son or grandson of a king or queen. The title extends to rulers of small states (principalities) and is used figuratively for someone preeminent in a field: {a merchant prince}. {The prince will inherit the throne.} (Capitalized Prince may refer to the musician.)

Princes is the plural of prince—male members of a royal family, especially sons of a king or queen. The term extends to rulers of small states and to men of high rank in various hierarchies: {princes of the church}, {merchant princes}. Figuratively, a prince is someone preeminent in a field: {a prince among men}, {princes of industry}.

A princess is a daughter of a king or queen, or the wife of a prince. The term extends to any woman of royal rank. Figuratively, princess describes someone treated with special privilege or who expects such treatment: {She's such a princess—she won't carry her own bags}. The word can be affectionate or disparaging depending on tone. {Daddy's little princess} suggests an indulged daughter.

Princesses is the plural of princess—daughters of monarchs or wives of princes. The word often carries connotations of privilege, delicacy, or entitlement: {She treats her daughters like princesses}. Someone called a princess dismissively is seen as spoiled or demanding: {Don't be such a princess about it}.

As an adjective, principal means most important or first in rank: It’s the principal city in the state, but not the capital. As a noun, principal is typically a person, most frequently the head of a school. However, principal can also represent, for example, the ringleader in a crime or the parties to a contract. Principal is used to designate a sum of money, as in a loan or debt, to which interest is added. Principal is often confused with its homonym principle.

Principle is a noun that designates a rule, law, or doctrine. Unlike its homonym principal, principle does not designate a person. Principle is often used in the plural because where there is one, there are others: The course will acquaint students with the principles of modern physics. The common phrase in principle means fundamentally or in essence: I accept your argument in principle but I have a few questions.

Principles are fundamental truths, rules, or beliefs that guide behavior or reasoning. Scientific principles explain how things work: {the principle of natural selection}. Moral principles shape conduct: {She refused on principle}. A person of principle acts according to ethical standards. {In principle} means theoretically, even if not in practice: {I agree in principle, but the details concern me}. The plural often refers to someone's core values: {He's a man of principles}.

To print is to transfer words and images to a surface, usually using ink on paper. If you print a document, chances are that you are just sending it to your printer to do the work. The noun print refers to anything that results from this process or one like it (print of a Monet painting, print from a photographic negative). To print also means to write in separate letters by hand. Such writing, whether by hand or machine, is also called print: Be sure to read the fine print.

A printer is a machine that produces text or images on paper, typically connected to a computer. Office printers handle documents; industrial printers produce newspapers and books. The older sense—a person who operates a printing press or runs a print shop—persists in publishing contexts: {The manuscript went to the printer last week}.

Printing is the process of reproducing text or images, typically by pressing inked surfaces onto paper. The term covers everything from Gutenberg's movable type to modern laser printers. A printing is also a single production run of a book: {The novel is in its third printing}. Printing as handwriting means forming disconnected letters rather than cursive script: {Please print your name clearly}.

Prior means coming before in time, order, or importance: {a prior engagement}, {prior experience required}. Without prior {notice} means without advance warning. As a noun, a prior is a ranking monk in certain religious orders, below an abbot. In American legal slang, a prior is a previous criminal conviction: {The defendant has two priors}.

Priorities are the things that matter most or demand attention first. To set priorities is to rank tasks or concerns by importance: {We need to get our priorities straight}. When someone says {I have other priorities}, they're explaining why something won't get their attention. The singular priority means the state of being first in importance, or a single item given precedence: {Safety is our top priority}.

Priority is what comes first or matters most. Something given priority receives attention before other things: {Safety is our top priority}. The plural priorities refers to what someone considers most important: {You need to get your priorities straight}. Priority can also mean the right to precede others: {Emergency vehicles have priority at intersections}. To prioritize is to rank things by importance.

A prism is a transparent solid with flat surfaces that refracts light, splitting white light into its spectrum of colors. The classic shape is triangular, but prisms come in various geometries for optical instruments. In geometry, a prism is any solid whose two ends are parallel, congruent polygons. Figuratively, to see something {through the prism of} a particular viewpoint is to have that perspective color your interpretation.

Prisms are transparent objects with flat surfaces that refract light. A triangular glass prism splits white light into a spectrum of colors—the classic rainbow effect. In geometry, a prism is any solid with two identical parallel bases connected by rectangular faces. Figuratively, to see something {through the prism of} a particular viewpoint is to have that perspective shape your understanding.

A prison is a building where people are confined as punishment for crimes. Prisons hold those serving sentences; jails typically hold those awaiting trial or serving short terms, though the words often blur. Prison extends to any confining situation: {Her marriage felt like a prison}. To imprison is to put someone in prison or confine them generally.

A prisoner is someone held in captivity, typically in a jail or prison as punishment for a crime or while awaiting trial. The term extends to anyone confined against their will: a {prisoner of war}, a {prisoner of conscience}. Figuratively, someone trapped by circumstances is a prisoner to them: {a prisoner of his own success}, {held prisoner by chronic pain}.

Prisoners is the plural of prisoner—people held in confinement, typically in a jail or prison. The term extends beyond legal detention: {prisoners of war}, {prisoners of conscience}. Figuratively, anyone trapped by circumstances: {We were prisoners of the weather}, {a prisoner of his own success}.

Prisons are institutions where people convicted of crimes are confined as punishment. The term extends to any place of confinement or captivity: {His own mind became a prison}. To imprison is to confine someone, whether literally in a jail or figuratively in circumstances that trap them: {She felt imprisoned by her marriage}.

Prissy describes someone excessively concerned with propriety, neatness, or appearing proper—often to the point of being fussy or easily shocked. The word carries a dismissive edge, suggesting the person's standards are uptight or prudish: {Don't be so prissy about a little mud}. Prissy behavior prioritizes appearances over substance.

Pristine describes something in its original, unspoiled condition—untouched by damage, decay, or contamination. A pristine {wilderness} shows no human impact. A pristine {1967 Mustang} looks factory-fresh. The word often implies cleanliness or purity: {The kitchen was pristine}. Pristine can also mean ancient or primitive, though this sense is rare outside academic contexts.

Privacy is the state of being free from observation or intrusion by others. It encompasses both physical seclusion and control over personal information: {The fence gave them some privacy}. Privacy concerns have intensified with digital technology—data collection, surveillance, and online tracking prompt debates about {privacy rights} and {privacy settings}. To invade someone's privacy is to intrude on matters they wish to keep to themselves.

The various meanings of the adjective private mostly suggest a separation of information or privilege in contrast to what is public. The private sector is distinct from the public sector, and private property is owned by an entity, not the government. If you want to go somewhere private or do something in private, you mean where others won’t hear or interfere with you. As a noun, private designates a low rank in the military or other institution. Your privates are your genitalia.

A privateer is a privately owned ship authorized by a government to attack enemy vessels during wartime, or the captain or crew of such a ship. The authorization came through a "letter of marque," which distinguished privateers from pirates—though the line often blurred in practice. {British privateers harassed French merchant ships throughout the war.} The term sometimes extends to anyone who profits from conflict while operating in legal gray areas.

Privateering is the practice of privately owned ships attacking enemy vessels under government authorization during wartime. A privateer carried a letter of marque—official permission to raid enemy shipping and keep a share of captured goods. Distinguished from piracy by this legal sanction, privateering was effectively state-sponsored piracy: {American privateers harassed British merchant ships during the Revolutionary War}. The practice was largely abolished by international agreement in the 19th century.

Privateers were private ships or their crews authorized by governments to attack enemy vessels during wartime. A letter of marque made the distinction between privateer and pirate—one operated with official sanction, the other without. The term extends to the sailors themselves: {The privateers captured three merchant ships off the coast}. By extension, privateer can describe anyone who pursues profit through aggressive but technically legal means.

Privates refers to the genitals—the body parts kept covered and private: {The doctor examined his privates}. The term is euphemistic, common when speaking to children or avoiding clinical vocabulary. Separately, privates are soldiers of the lowest rank: {The privates lined up for inspection}.

Privilege is a special right, advantage, or immunity granted to particular people or groups. The wealthy enjoy privileges unavailable to others; {Check your privilege} asks someone to recognize unearned advantages. A privileged {communication} is legally protected from disclosure. To privilege something is to treat it as more important: {The curriculum privileges Western authors}. As an adjective, privileged describes those who benefit from such advantages.

Privileged describes someone who enjoys advantages or special rights not available to everyone. A privileged {upbringing} means access to wealth, education, or social connections. In law, privileged {information} is protected from disclosure: {attorney-client communications are privileged}. The word increasingly appears in discussions of social inequality, where {privilege} denotes unearned advantages from race, class, or gender: {Check your privilege}.

Privileges are special rights, advantages, or immunities granted to particular people or groups. The word often implies unearned benefits: {Check your privilege} asks someone to recognize advantages they take for granted. In computing, privileges are permission levels controlling what users can access: {The admin has root privileges}. To privilege something is to favor it over alternatives.

Prize centers on something of value worth pursuing or possessing. A prize is an award given for achievement or victory: {She won first prize in the competition}. It can be anything captured or seized, especially in war—a prize ship, prize money. As an adjective, prize means outstanding or worthy of a prize: {a prize specimen}, {prize cattle}. To prize something is to value it highly: {I prize these letters from my grandmother}. A prized possession is one you treasure.

A prizefight is a boxing match, especially a professional bout fought for money. The term dates from when boxing operated outside legal sanction, with fighters competing for cash prizes. Modern usage retains a slightly rough or old-fashioned flavor: {The prizefight drew thousands to the arena}. The fighters are prizefighters.

A prizefighter is a professional boxer—someone who fights for prize money. The term carries old-fashioned connotations of bare-knuckle bouts and smoky arenas: {He had the battered face of an aging prizefighter}. Prizefighting is the sport itself, sometimes used to distinguish boxing from amateur competition.

Prizes are awards given for achievement, victory, or luck—trophies, medals, cash, ribbons. A Nobel Prize recognizes exceptional contribution; a lottery prize rewards chance. As a verb, to prize something is to value it highly: {She prized her grandmother's ring above all her possessions}. Prize also works as an adjective: a prize {student}, a prize {pig}. To prize something open is to pry it: {He prized the lid off the crate}.
As a preposition, pro is borrows from Latin and means supporting or in favor of: Are you pro-choice or pro-life?

Proactive means taking initiative rather than waiting to respond to events. A proactive {approach} anticipates problems before they arise. Proactive {measures} prevent rather than react. The word emerged in the mid-20th century as the opposite of reactive, and has become standard in business and self-help contexts: {Be proactive about your career}. Sometimes overused to the point of buzzword status.

Probability measures how likely something is to happen, expressed as a number between zero (impossible) and one (certain). In everyday speech, probability often just means likelihood: {What's the probability he'll show up?} In statistics and mathematics, probability is calculated precisely—the probability of rolling a six on a fair die is one in six. {In all probability} means almost certainly.

Probably expresses likelihood without certainty—more likely than not, but not guaranteed. It hedges predictions and softens assertions: {They're probably stuck in traffic}, {I'll probably regret this}. The word sits between possibly (lower confidence) and certainly (higher): {She's probably right, but I wouldn't bet on it}.

Probation is a period of testing or trial during which someone must prove themselves. In criminal justice, it's a sentence that allows an offender to remain in the community under supervision instead of serving time in prison: {He was given two years' probation for the theft}. In employment and education, probation is a trial period during which performance is monitored and continued participation depends on meeting certain standards: {New hires are on probation for ninety days}.

A probe is something inserted to explore or investigate. Medical probes examine body cavities; space probes travel to distant planets; investigators probe for the truth. The word works as both noun and verb: {The Senate launched a probe into campaign financing}; {Reporters probed the senator's finances}. To probe is to examine thoroughly, often persistently or intrusively.

Problem, a noun, has a handful of related meanings, all of which convey the idea of something that requires effort to solve or put right. The most straightforward kind of problem is one that has a simple mathematical solution. Other kinds of problems are sources of grief, worry, and distress. When problem is used attributively, before another noun, it casts a shadow over the main noun with a suggestion that it is hard to deal with, as in problem child or problem tenant.

Problematic describes something that presents difficulties or raises concerns. A problematic situation is troublesome; a problematic argument has flaws. In contemporary usage, problematic often signals moral or social objection: {His comments about women were problematic}. This newer sense can sound euphemistic—a way of calling something offensive without saying so directly.

Problems are difficulties, obstacles, or situations requiring resolution. A math problem needs solving; a personal problem needs addressing. The word often implies something wrong: {We have a problem with the plumbing}. To say someone {has a problem} with something means they object to it or struggle with it: {Do you have a problem with that?} In slang, {no problem} dismisses thanks or concern.

A procedure is a series of steps followed to accomplish something. Medical procedures, legal procedures, and standard operating procedures all describe established sequences of actions. The word emphasizes method and order: {What's the procedure for filing a complaint?} In computing, a procedure is a set of instructions that performs a specific task.

Process is a series of actions or steps toward an end result: {the hiring process}, {a manufacturing process}. It also names ongoing activity: {Peace is a process, not an event}. In law, process refers to legal proceedings or a summons. In biology, a process is a projection from a body part. To process is to put through a procedure: {process an application}, {process meat}. {Processed foods} have been chemically altered for preservation or flavor.

Processed describes something that has been put through a series of mechanical or chemical operations to alter, preserve, or prepare it. The term appears most often with food: processed {cheese}, processed {meat}, processed {foods}—products that have been modified from their natural state, often with additives for flavor or shelf life. In broader use, processed can apply to anything that has undergone systematic treatment: processed {applications}, processed {data}. The word sometimes carries negative connotations, implying that something natural has been made artificial or less wholesome.

Processing is the act of handling, treating, or transforming something through a series of steps. Food processing converts raw ingredients into packaged products. Data processing organizes information for analysis. When an application is processing, the system is working on it: {Your request is still processing}. To say you're {processing} news or emotions means you're working through them mentally, absorbing their meaning.

A procession is a group of people or vehicles moving forward in an orderly line, often as part of a ceremony or ritual: {a funeral procession}, {a wedding procession}. The word emphasizes formal, deliberate movement rather than a casual crowd. Figuratively, a procession of events or items suggests a continuous sequence: {a procession of witnesses took the stand}.

A processor is something that processes—that is, performs a series of operations on something to change or prepare it. In computing, a processor (or microprocessor) is the chip that executes instructions and performs calculations, the brain of a computer: {My laptop has a fast processor but not much memory}. Food processors chop, blend, and mix ingredients. Word processors are software applications for creating and editing text documents. A person who processes applications, claims, or data may also be called a processor.

A proclamation is a formal public announcement, typically issued by an authority figure or government: {The governor issued a proclamation declaring a state of emergency}. Proclamations carry official weight but often lack the force of law—they announce, commemorate, or urge rather than compel. The verb is proclaim.

To procrastinate is to delay or postpone action, especially habitually or without good reason: {I procrastinated on the essay until the night before it was due}. The word implies knowing you should act but finding excuses not to. Procrastination often involves substituting easier tasks for harder ones, or simply doing nothing at all.

Procrastinating is putting off tasks you should be doing, typically in favor of less important or more pleasant activities. The word carries a note of self-reproach—you know you're delaying: {I spent the whole afternoon procrastinating instead of finishing my report}. Someone who habitually delays is a procrastinator.

Procrastination is the habit or act of putting off tasks, especially ones that should be done promptly. The delay is typically voluntary and often irrational—you know you should do it, but you don't: {My procrastination on the tax return cost me the early refund}. The word implies avoidance rather than legitimate postponement.

A procrastinator is someone who habitually delays or postpones tasks, especially ones that require immediate attention. The word carries a mildly self-deprecating tone when used about oneself: {I'm such a procrastinator—I always wait until the last minute}. Unlike someone who is merely lazy, a procrastinator often intends to act but keeps deferring.

The procuticle is the main structural layer of arthropod exoskeleton, lying beneath the thin outer epicuticle. It consists of chitin fibers embedded in a protein matrix, providing both flexibility and strength. The procuticle typically has two sublayers: a harder outer exocuticle and a softer inner endocuticle. During molting, parts of the procuticle are reabsorbed before the old cuticle is shed.

To prod is to poke or jab, usually with something pointed like a finger or stick: {She prodded the fire with a poker}. Extended, it means to urge or encourage someone toward action: {His parents prodded him to apply for the job}. A prod is both the act and the instrument—a cattle prod delivers an electric shock to move livestock. {She needed a prod to get started.}

Prodding is the act of poking or pushing at something, literally or figuratively. Physical prodding uses a finger, stick, or pointed instrument: {The doctor's prodding revealed tenderness in his abdomen}. More often, prodding means persistent urging or prompting: {After some prodding from his wife, he finally called the doctor}. The word suggests repeated, gentle pressure rather than forceful demand.

Prodigies is the plural of prodigy—a person, especially a child, with exceptional talent or ability: {Mozart was among history's great musical prodigies}. The word can also mean a remarkable thing or event, though this sense is less common now: {prodigies of nature}. A child prodigy shows adult-level mastery in a specific domain at an unusually young age.

A prodigy is a person, especially a young one, with exceptional talent or ability: {a child prodigy}, {a piano prodigy}. The word implies natural gifts that seem to exceed normal human capacity. More broadly, prodigy can mean something extraordinary or marvelous—a wonder or portent—though this older sense is now rare.

Produce centers on bringing something forth. Farmers produce crops; factories produce goods; artists produce work. The verb stresses creation or generation: {The region produces excellent wine}. To produce evidence or documents is to present them. In entertainment, to produce is to oversee and finance a project's creation. As a noun (stress on first syllable), produce means fresh fruits and vegetables: {the produce section of the grocery store}.

A producer is someone who makes or creates something, especially in quantity. In agriculture and economics, producers grow crops or manufacture goods. In entertainment, a producer oversees and finances the creation of films, music, or television—handling logistics while directors handle creative vision. A music producer shapes a recording's sound: {She brought in a new producer for the album}. In ecology, producers are organisms like plants that create energy from sunlight.

The verb produce gives rise to the noun product and the relationship between their meanings is predictable. Anything produced can be called a product: The country has to import most of its food products. He is a product of a very harsh upbringing. An end product is the result of a number of production steps. In chemistry, the product is what results from compounding and chemical reaction of substances. In math, the product is the result of multiplication. Product is usually countable but may be treated as uncountable in business jargon: Our goal is to move more product.

Production is the verbal noun from produce and denotes an instance, the activity, or the result of producing something (gas production, food production). Production is frequent in talk about economics, where it refers to the output of an economy. In the entertainment industry, production is sometimes a count noun and refers to a specific version or presentation of a play, opera, musical, or the like. If you make a production out of something, you give it more importance or complexity than it deserves.

Productive means yielding results, output, or growth. A productive worker accomplishes much; productive land yields abundant crops. The word often implies efficiency: {We had a productive meeting}. In economics, productive activities generate goods or value. Productive can also mean giving rise to something: {a productive cough} brings up mucus; anger may be {productive of} violence.

Productivity is the rate at which work gets done or goods are produced. In economics, it measures output relative to input—labor, time, or resources: {The new machinery doubled our productivity}. In everyday use, productivity describes personal efficiency and the satisfying completion of tasks: {I had a productive morning}. Productivity culture celebrates constant optimization and output, sometimes to unhealthy extremes.

Products are things produced—manufactured goods, agricultural outputs, or the results of any process. A product of one's {environment} or {upbringing} is shaped by those influences. In mathematics, a product is the result of multiplication. In business, products are what companies sell, distinguished from services: {We're launching three new products this quarter}.

Profane describes what lies outside the sacred—the secular, worldly, or irreverent. Profane language is crude or blasphemous: {His profane outburst shocked the congregation}. To profane something sacred is to treat it with irreverence or contempt: {vandals profaned the cemetery}. The word carries judgment—what's profane violates what should be respected.

Profanities are words or expressions considered irreverent, vulgar, or obscene—typically those involving religious blasphemy, bodily functions, or sex. The term covers everything from mild oaths to hardcore obscenity: {The coach let loose a string of profanities}. What counts as profanity shifts with time and culture; words that once shocked may become unremarkable.

Profanity is language considered disrespectful toward sacred things, or more broadly, vulgar or obscene speech. The term covers everything from blasphemy to common swear words: {The movie was full of profanity}. A profanity is a single instance—a curse word or obscene expression: {He muttered a profanity under his breath}.

A profession is an occupation requiring specialized education and training—medicine, law, engineering, accounting. The term carries connotations of expertise, ethical standards, and social status that distinguish professions from ordinary jobs. {She entered the legal profession after law school.} To make a profession of something is to declare it openly: a profession of {faith}, a profession of {love}. The oldest profession is a euphemism for prostitution.

Before a noun, professional imparts the idea that the person, firm, or service designated does work that meets a certain standard: We hired professional landscapers to design the acreage. A professional athlete is one who is skilled enough to earn a living by participating in a sport. A person who is called a professional has a white-collar occupation: The new apartment building is intended to appeal mainly to single professionals who work downtown.
