The word also appears in savory dishes like {black pudding} and {blood pudding}, which are sausages. {The proof is in the pudding} means results matter more than promises.

A puddle is a small, shallow pool of liquid, typically rainwater collected on the ground: {Children splashed through puddles on the sidewalk}. The word extends to any small accumulation of spilled liquid: {a puddle of milk}, {a puddle of blood}. To puddle is to form such pools or to wade through them.

Puddles are small, shallow pools of water, typically formed by rain collecting in depressions on the ground. Children splash in them; drivers avoid them. The verb means to form such pools or to splash about in water: {Rain puddled on the uneven pavement}. To puddle is also to work clay or soil into a watertight mass.

Pudgy describes someone or something that is short and somewhat fat in a soft, rounded way. The word often applies to children or body parts: {pudgy fingers}, {pudgy cheeks}, {a pudgy toddler}. It carries a gentler, more affectionate connotation than words like fat or chubby—suggesting endearing plumpness rather than criticism.

Puff, a noun and verb, suggests inflation and the movement of air. Various kinds of food that consist mostly of air are called puffs (cheese puffs, corn puffs). Puff pastry rises a lot when baked. When you puff on a cigarette or pipe, you inhale smoke from it; you can also take a puff. Difficult breathing is sometimes called puffing, or huffing and puffing. Food or some other object that is puffed is expanded with air. Something that is puffed up is inflated or exaggerated.

A pufferfish is a fish that inflates itself into a spiny ball when threatened, deterring predators. Many species contain tetrodotoxin, a potent poison—yet pufferfish is considered a delicacy in Japan (as fugu), where specially licensed chefs prepare it to avoid the toxic organs. {The pufferfish puffed up the moment I touched the tank.}

A puffin is a stocky seabird with a large, colorful bill, black and white plumage, and bright orange feet. Puffins nest in coastal cliffs and spend most of their lives at sea. Their distinctive appearance—often compared to a clown or parrot—has made them popular symbols of northern coastal regions: {We saw puffins nesting on the cliffs of Iceland}.

Puffins are seabirds of the auk family, recognizable by their stocky bodies, black-and-white plumage, and colorful triangular bills that become brighter during breeding season. They nest in burrows on coastal cliffs and spend most of their lives at sea. The Atlantic puffin is sometimes called the "clown of the sea" for its distinctive face markings.

Puffs are short bursts of air, breath, or smoke: {She took a few puffs on the cigarette}. The word extends to anything light and airy—a cream puff, a powder puff, a puff pastry. A puff piece is promotional writing disguised as journalism. To puff is to breathe heavily or emit short bursts: {He puffed up the stairs}. To puff up is to swell or inflate, literally or with pride.

Puffy describes something swollen, inflated, or puffed up with air. Eyes get puffy from crying or lack of sleep. A puffy jacket is quilted and filled with insulating material. Puffy clouds look soft and rounded. Puffy {sleeves} billow out from the shoulder. The word suggests temporary inflation rather than permanent bulk.

A pug is a small dog breed with a wrinkled face, short muzzle, and curled tail. The breed originated in China and became popular as a companion dog. Pug also refers to clay that has been mixed and kneaded for pottery, or the act of preparing it: {She pugged the clay before throwing}. A pug nose is short and slightly flattened.

Pugs is the plural of pug, a small breed of dog with a flat face, wrinkled brow, and curled tail. The breed originated in China and became popular as a companion dog. {She has two pugs that follow her everywhere.} The compact, sturdy build and expressive face give pugs a distinctive appearance.

Puke is vomit—the noun and the verb. To puke is to throw up: {I think I'm going to puke}. The word is informal but not particularly vulgar, common among children and adults alike. Puke can express disgust figuratively: {This movie makes me want to puke}. A puke is also, informally, a disgusting person.

Puking is vomiting—ejecting stomach contents through the mouth. The word is informal and slightly crude, preferred in casual speech over clinical alternatives: {I was up all night puking}. Someone who looks green or unwell might be described as ready to puke. The sight of something disgusting can make you {want to puke}.

Pull is an important “cause motion” verb, in which the resulting motion is toward the speaker. It is typically the opposite of push: I pulled down a branch and smelled the blossoms. From this, many other meanings arise, such as pulling something behind you so that it moves with you or pulling something out of your pocket toward you. Pull is frequently followed by adverbs of direction, such as pull up in a vehicle or pull off a victory. As a noun, pull represents an act or instance of pulling. Figuratively, it represents influence: She has a lot of pull with the CEO.

A pulley is a wheel with a grooved rim through which a rope or chain runs, used to lift heavy loads or change the direction of force. Multiple pulleys working together form a block and tackle, which multiplies lifting power: {We rigged a pulley system to hoist the engine out of the car}. The word extends to any similar mechanism in machinery.

Pulling is the act of exerting force to move something toward you or in a direction, the opposite of pushing. It extends to drawing or extracting: {pulling weeds}, {pulling a tooth}, {pulling strings} to get favors. In British slang, pulling means successfully attracting a romantic or sexual partner: {He was out pulling last night}. To be {pulling for} someone is to support or root for them.

Pulls is most often the third-person singular of pull—to move something toward oneself or in a specified direction: {She pulls the door open}, {The tractor pulls the trailer}. A pull is an act of pulling, or something you pull: a {drawer pull}, a {pull tab}. Pull extends to attraction or influence: {The city pulls young people from small towns}, {He has pull with the mayor}. To {pull strings} is to use connections; to {pull off} something is to succeed against odds; to {pull out} is to withdraw.

A pullup is an exercise in which you hang from a bar and pull your body upward until your chin clears the bar: {I can do twenty pullups}. The movement builds upper-body strength, particularly in the back and arms. Also spelled pull-up. A pullup diaper is a disposable training pant that a child can pull on and off like underwear.

Pulp is soft, wet, shapeless matter—the fleshy interior of fruit, the fibrous material from which paper is made, or anything reduced to mush: {The banana had turned to pulp}. To pulp something is to crush it into this state. Pulp fiction refers to cheap, sensational magazines printed on rough wood-pulp paper, and by extension any lurid or lowbrow entertainment: {a pulp novel}, {pulp horror}. To {beat someone to a pulp} is to pummel them severely.

A pulpit is an elevated platform or lectern in a church from which a minister delivers sermons. The word extends to preaching generally: {He was a powerful voice from the pulpit}. The {bully pulpit} is a position of authority that gives someone a platform to advocate their views—originally describing the U.S. presidency.

Pulse is two different nouns, plus a verb related to one of them. Your pulse is the rhythmic beat of your heart, as detected in various parts of the body. When your pulse quickens, either it speeds up, or you are a character in a romantic novel getting excited about something. If something pulses (besides your heart), it exhibits rhythmic behavior of some kind. The other noun pulse is a dried legume, such as a lentil or chickpea.

Pulses are the edible seeds of legumes—beans, lentils, chickpeas, and dried peas. The term appears most often in nutrition, agriculture, and international food contexts: {Pulses are a good source of protein}. In everyday American English, people usually say beans or lentils rather than pulses. Separately, pulses is the plural of pulse—rhythmic beats or throbs: {electrical pulses}, {the pulses of light from a strobe}.

A puma is a large wild cat native to the Americas, also called a cougar or mountain lion. It's the largest cat that can purr but cannot roar. The tawny coat and solitary hunting style make it distinctive among American predators: {A puma was spotted near the hiking trail}. (Capitalized Puma is the sportswear brand.)

To pummel is to strike repeatedly with the fists, typically in a sustained assault: {The boxer pummeled his opponent against the ropes}. The word extends to any relentless beating—waves pummel a coastline, critics pummel a film. Also spelled pommel, though that spelling more commonly refers to the front part of a saddle or a sword handle.

Pummeling is the act of striking someone or something repeatedly and forcefully, typically with fists. When a boxer pummels an opponent, she lands blow after blow. The word extends naturally to any sustained assault: {The coastal town took a pummeling from the hurricane}. Sports commentators favor it for lopsided contests where one team thoroughly dominates another. The spelling pummelling is standard in British English.

Pummelled is the past tense of pummel, meaning to strike repeatedly with fists or other blows: {He pummelled the punching bag until his arms ached}. The spelling with double L is standard in British English; Americans typically write pummeled. Figuratively, anything that batters or overwhelms can pummel: {The coast was pummelled by storms all winter}.

Pummelling is the act of striking repeatedly with the fists, or by extension, any sustained beating or battering: {The boxer took a pummelling in the third round}. Figuratively, it describes overwhelming force or criticism: {The stock took a pummelling after earnings}. Also spelled pummeling. The verb is pummel.

A pump is a device that moves fluids using suction, pressure, or a combination of these. Many pumps are natural, like the heart, and many are also made for particular purposes: water pump, gas pump. The verb pump means to use a pump or to move a fluid by means of a pump: Pump the water out of the basement. Pump has taken on figurative meanings. If you move something up and down, as you would the handle of a water pump, the same verb can be used: She said hello and pumped my hand. If you pump someone, you try to elicit information from them.

Pumped describes being filled with energy, excitement, or enthusiasm—like a tire inflated to capacity. Someone who is pumped is ready for action: {I'm so pumped for the concert tonight}. In fitness contexts, pumped describes muscles temporarily enlarged from increased blood flow during exercise: {My arms are totally pumped after that workout}.

A pumpkin is a large, round, orange squash with a thick rind and pulpy interior full of seeds. Native to North America, pumpkins are harvested in autumn and strongly associated with fall traditions, particularly Halloween jack-o'-lanterns and Thanksgiving pie. The word is also used as a term of endearment, especially for children: {Come here, pumpkin}. In informal usage, a pumpkin can describe someone unsophisticated, and {pumpkin spice} has become a ubiquitous autumn flavor profile.

Pumpkins is the plural of pumpkin, the large orange squash harvested in autumn and associated with Halloween and Thanksgiving. Jack-o'-lanterns are carved from pumpkins; pumpkin pie is a holiday staple. {We picked pumpkins at the farm.} Pumpkin also serves as a term of endearment: {How was your day, pumpkin?}

Pumps are devices that move fluids by mechanical action—water pumps, fuel pumps, air pumps. The verb means to operate such a device or move something similarly: {pump water from a well}, {pump iron} at the gym, {pump the brakes}. To pump someone is to question them persistently for information. Pumps are also women's dress shoes with closed toes and low-cut tops, typically with heels.

A pun is a joke that exploits different meanings of a word or similar-sounding words: {Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana}. Puns range from clever wordplay to groan-inducing dad jokes. To pun is to make such jokes. Someone who puns habitually is a punster.

The more frequent of the two words represented by punch is a noun and verb. To punch someone or something is to strike forcefully with the fist or with an instrument that will leave a hole. A punch is an instance of this. A paper punch is a machine for making holes in paper. Punching a time clock doesn’t make a hole; it just leaves a time stamp. The other punch, a noun, designates a drink containing fruit juice and sometimes alcohol, served on festive occasions.

Punching is the act of striking with a closed fist. The word often appears in compounds: {a punching bag}, {punching above your weight}. To be punching above or below your weight is to date or compete with someone perceived as more or less attractive or capable than you: {He's definitely punching above his weight with her}.

A punchline is the final phrase or sentence of a joke that delivers the humor—the part that makes people laugh. The setup creates expectation; the punchline subverts it. By extension, any climactic revelation or key point: {So what's the punchline here?} Also spelled punch line.

Punchlines are the final words of a joke—the part that delivers the humor and makes people laugh. The term comes from the idea of a punch landing: setup creates expectation, punchline subverts it. Extended to any climactic payoff: {The whole speech built to a single punchline}. A weak punchline ruins an otherwise good joke.

Punchy describes something with impact—forceful, vigorous, and to the point. A punchy {headline} grabs attention. A punchy {speech} delivers ideas with energy and economy. The word suggests compression: no wasted words, no soft edges. Separately, punchy can mean dazed or groggy, as if from being punched: {I felt punchy after the red-eye flight}.

Punctual means arriving or happening at the expected or agreed-upon time. A punctual person is reliably on time: {She's always punctual for meetings}. The word implies consistency—not just being on time once, but habitually so. Punctual can also describe things that occur precisely when scheduled: {The train made a punctual departure}.

Punctuality is the quality of being on time—arriving or completing something at the expected moment. It suggests reliability and respect for others' schedules: {Punctuality was never his strong suit}. In professional contexts, punctuality often signals conscientiousness: {The job requires strict punctuality}.

Punctuation is the system of marks used in writing to clarify meaning and structure—periods, commas, question marks, quotation marks, and the rest. These symbols indicate pauses, separate elements, show relationships, and signal tone. {Her punctuation was impeccable.} Figuratively, punctuation can mean any interruption that marks a break: {The silence was punctuated by occasional bursts of laughter.}

A puncture is a small hole made by something sharp, especially in a tire or the skin: {a puncture wound}, {The nail caused a slow puncture}. To puncture is to make such a hole or to deflate something figuratively: {The criticism punctured his confidence}. British English uses puncture as a noun for what Americans call a flat tire.

A pundit is someone who offers expert opinions on a subject, especially in the media. Political pundits analyze elections, sports pundits predict game outcomes. The term often carries a hint of skepticism—pundits confidently pronounce on everything, whether their expertise warrants it or not: {The pundits all said she couldn't win}.

Pundits are commentators who offer opinions and analysis on public affairs, especially in media. The term often carries a slightly dismissive tone, suggesting confident pronouncements without deep expertise: {The pundits predicted she'd lose, but she won decisively}. Political talk shows feature panels of pundits debating the news of the day.

To punish is to impose a penalty for wrongdoing—a parent punishes a child, a court punishes a criminal. The aim may be correction, deterrence, or retribution. Extended uses describe harsh treatment: {The boxer punished his opponent with body shots}. Weather punishes crops; a difficult hike punishes the legs. To {punish} food or drink is to consume large quantities: {We punished that pizza}.

Punished is the past tense of punish—to impose a penalty for wrongdoing or to treat harshly. {He was punished for lying.} In casual use, punished often means subjected to rough treatment or heavy use: {My knees got punished on that hike.} {The defense punished their offense all game.}

Punishing describes something that inflicts severe strain or hardship. A punishing {schedule} exhausts you. A punishing {workout} pushes physical limits. Punishing {heat} or a punishing {pace} tests endurance. The word emphasizes relentlessness—the thing keeps coming at you: {The boxer absorbed punishing blows for twelve rounds}.

Punishment is the infliction of penalty or suffering for wrongdoing. Courts impose punishment on convicted criminals; parents punish misbehaving children. The word extends to any harsh treatment: {My knees took a lot of punishment on that hike}. To punish can also mean to defeat soundly or exploit ruthlessly: {They punished every defensive mistake}.

Punk is a slang word with evolving meanings that may be hard to predict from context. Its older use is pejorative, when a punk was a disrespectful and violent young man. Today, punk is encountered more often in the context of modern youth culture and is associated with various genres of popular music (punk rock), and with the people who make and listen to it. Visual things called punk, like fashion or hairstyles, are often colorful, disorderly, and eclectic.

Punks are rowdy, disrespectful young people—troublemakers or petty criminals: {Some punks vandalized the store}. The word carries contempt, implying someone worthless or insignificant. Punk also names a music genre and subculture emerging in the 1970s, characterized by aggressive sound, DIY ethos, and anti-establishment attitude: {She was into punk before it went mainstream}. Punk rock bands like the Ramones and Sex Pistols defined the style. The adjective punk means of poor quality or in poor health: {I've been feeling punk all week}.

Puns are jokes that exploit words with multiple meanings or similar sounds. A pun on "sole" might involve fish and shoes; one on "time flies" might take the phrase literally. Puns range from clever wordplay to groan-inducing dad jokes. To pun is to make such jokes: {He couldn't resist punning on her name}.

Punt has several distinct meanings. In football, a punt is a kick where the ball is dropped and struck before it hits the ground: {The punter boomed a fifty-yard punt}. In boating, a punt is a flat-bottomed boat propelled by pushing a pole against the riverbed, common on English rivers: {punting on the Thames}. To punt also means to postpone or avoid a decision: {Let's punt on that question until the next meeting}. In gambling, especially British usage, to punt is to bet: {I punted twenty quid on the match}.

Punting is kicking a ball before it hits the ground, especially in American football when a team surrenders possession by kicking downfield: {They were forced to punt on fourth down}. In British English, punting means propelling a flat-bottomed boat with a long pole, popular on rivers in Oxford and Cambridge. To punt also means to defer or avoid a decision: {Let's punt on that question until next week}.

Punts is the plural of punt, a word with several distinct meanings. A punt is a flat-bottomed boat propelled with a pole, common on English rivers: {We hired punts on the Cam}. In American football, a punt is a kick where the ball is dropped and struck before hitting the ground. In gambling, punts are bets; punters are bettors. To punt on something is also to defer or avoid deciding: {We punted on the budget question until next quarter}.

Puny means small and weak, often contemptibly so. A puny opponent poses little threat. A puny effort falls far short of what's needed. The word carries dismissiveness—something puny isn't just small but inadequate: {His puny salary barely covered rent}. {She gave a puny wave from across the room}.

A pup is a young dog, seal, or other mammal. The word is informal and affectionate—you might call your adult dog {pup} the way you'd call a grown child {kid}. To {pup} is to give birth to puppies. A {pup tent} is a small, simple tent.

A pupil is a student, especially a young one receiving instruction from a teacher: {The piano teacher's pupils gave a recital}. The word suggests a closer, more personal teaching relationship than student does. Separately, the pupil is the dark circular opening in the center of the eye's iris that controls how much light enters. The two words share a spelling but have different origins.

Pupils has two meanings from different sources. In education, pupils are students, especially young ones under direct instruction: {The teacher gathered her pupils for the lesson}. In anatomy, pupils are the dark circular openings at the center of the eyes that control how much light enters: {Her pupils dilated in the dim room}.

A puppet is a figure—often resembling a person or animal—manipulated by hand, strings, or rods to create the illusion of independent movement. Hand puppets fit over the hand; marionettes hang from strings. By extension, a puppet is someone controlled by another: {a puppet government}, {He's just a puppet of the regime}. The term implies lack of autonomy or genuine agency.

A puppeteer is someone who manipulates puppets—figures controlled by strings, rods, or hands to create the illusion of independent movement. The term extends to anyone who controls others from behind the scenes: {The CEO was just a figurehead; the real puppeteer was the majority shareholder}. To puppeteer is to control in this way.

Puppeteers are performers who manipulate puppets—figures controlled by strings, rods, hands, or other mechanisms to create the illusion of life. The term extends figuratively to anyone who controls others from behind the scenes: {The CEO was merely a figurehead; the real puppeteers were the board members}. To puppeteer is to control in this manner.

A puppetmaster is someone who controls puppets in a performance. More often, the word appears figuratively for someone who manipulates people or events from behind the scenes: {The campaign manager was the real puppetmaster behind the candidate's rise}. The term implies hidden influence—the puppetmaster pulls strings while others appear to act independently.

Puppetry is the art of manipulating puppets to create performances. It encompasses various traditions—hand puppets, marionettes, shadow puppets—and ranges from children's entertainment to sophisticated theatrical productions. The term extends to figurative manipulation: {The regime's puppetry of the press was an open secret}. A puppeteer practices puppetry.

Puppets are figures—often resembling humans or animals—manipulated by hand, strings, or rods to create the illusion of independent movement. A hand puppet fits over the hand like a glove; a marionette hangs from strings. Figuratively, a puppet is someone controlled by another: {a puppet government}, {He's just a puppet of the regime}. The controller is the puppeteer or puppet master.

Puppies are young dogs, typically under a year old. The word evokes playfulness, clumsiness, and cuteness—qualities that make puppies universally appealing. Figuratively, puppy attaches to inexperience or youthful eagerness: {puppy love}, {eager as a puppy}. {The litter had six puppies, all spoken for before they were weaned.}

A puppy is a young dog, typically under a year old. The word suggests playfulness, clumsiness, and endearing energy: {The puppy chewed through another pair of shoes}. Puppy extends to other young animals, especially seals. {Puppy love} is immature romantic infatuation, usually among adolescents. {Sick as a puppy} means very ill.

Pups is the plural of pup—young dogs, seals, wolves, or other animals. The term extends to inexperienced people: {Those pups don't know what they're doing}. In casual speech, pups often carries affection: {Look at those adorable pups}. The word also appears in compounds like {pup tent} and {puppy love}.

Purchase is mainly a verb with an offshoot noun, just like buy, its more frequent and less formal synonym. The two words are used in similar contexts. When you purchase something, you exchange money for it. A purchase is the act of doing this. Your purchases are the things you bought. The noun purchase has another, less frequent meaning: a firm and dependable grip on something: It was hard to get any purchase on the steep cliff.

Pure means unmixed, unadulterated, or free from contamination. Pure {gold} contains no alloys; pure {water} has no impurities. The word extends to moral and spiritual cleanliness: a pure {heart}, pure {intentions}. Pure can intensify, meaning absolute or sheer: {pure luck}, {pure nonsense}, {pure joy}. In academic contexts, pure {mathematics} or pure {science} pursues knowledge for its own sake rather than practical application.

Purebred describes an animal whose ancestors all belong to the same breed, with no crossbreeding in its lineage: {a purebred German shepherd}, {purebred Arabian horses}. Breeders maintain purebred lines through careful documentation and registry. As a noun, a purebred is such an animal. The term sometimes carries connotations of quality or value, though purebreds may have more health problems than mixed breeds due to limited genetic diversity.

Puree is food that has been blended or mashed to a smooth, uniform consistency: {tomato puree}, {baby food purees}. The verb means to process food this way: {Puree the soup until smooth}. Also spelled purée, retaining the French accent.

Purgatory in Roman Catholic doctrine is an intermediate state after death where souls undergo purification before entering heaven. The term extends to any place or condition of temporary suffering, misery, or expiation: {Waiting at the DMV was absolute purgatory}. Unlike hell, purgatory implies an endpoint—the suffering is finite and purposeful, leading eventually to release or redemption.

Purge means to remove or eliminate something unwanted, often by force or thorough cleansing. You purge toxins from your body, purge files from a hard drive, or purge disloyal members from an organization. Political purges involve systematic removal of opponents, sometimes violently: {Stalin's purges killed millions}. In medicine, a purge empties the bowels. To purge yourself of guilt is to confess or atone. The noun refers to an instance of purging: {a purge of the party leadership}.

Purged is the past tense of purge, meaning to remove or eliminate unwanted elements. Organizations purge disloyal members; governments purge political opponents. You purge files from a hard drive or toxins from your body. The word carries connotations of cleansing, sometimes forcibly: {Stalin purged the party of rivals}. {She purged her closet of everything she hadn't worn in a year}.

Purges is the plural of purge, an act of forcibly removing people or things considered undesirable. Political purges eliminate rivals or dissenters from organizations or governments: {Stalin's purges killed millions}. The word also applies to cleansing the body—a purge empties the bowels, and purging describes the self-induced vomiting of eating disorders. To purge records is to delete them; to purge a system is to flush it clean.

Purging is the act of removing unwanted things—whether physical objects, people, or abstract elements like guilt or impurities. Political purges remove opponents from power, often violently. In eating disorders, purging refers to forced vomiting or laxative use to eliminate consumed food. Technical systems undergo purging when old data or contaminated substances are flushed out: {The technician recommended purging the fuel lines before the repair.} The word carries connotations of cleansing, sometimes ritualistic or extreme.

Purification is the process of removing contaminants or impurities from something. Water undergoes purification to make it safe for drinking. Air purification removes pollutants and allergens. The word extends to ritual or spiritual cleansing: {purification rites}, {purification of the soul}. In chemistry, purification isolates a substance from unwanted compounds.

To purify is to remove impurities or contaminants, making something clean or pure: {purify drinking water}, {purify the air}. The word extends to spiritual or moral cleansing: {purify the soul}, {rituals that purify the body}. In chemistry, to purify a substance is to isolate it from other compounds. {The filter purifies water by removing bacteria and sediment.}

A purist insists on traditional or original forms, rejecting modifications or compromises: {a grammatical purist who objects to split infinitives}, {jazz purists who dismiss fusion}. The term often carries a hint of rigidity—purists may be admired for their standards or dismissed as inflexible. The adjective purist describes this stance: {a purist approach to translation}.

Purists insist on traditional or original forms, rejecting innovations or compromises. A language purist objects to new words or usages; a musical purist prefers acoustic instruments; a culinary purist won't add ketchup to a hot dog. The term often carries a hint of inflexibility: {Purists will hate it, but I like the remix better than the original}.

A puritan is someone who adheres strictly to moral or religious principles, often to the point of being severe or judgmental about pleasure and indulgence. The word usually carries negative connotations—suggesting excessive rigidity or self-denial: {Don't be such a puritan about having a glass of wine}. Puritanical extends this sense to describe attitudes or rules that seem unnecessarily restrictive. (Capitalized Puritan refers to the English Protestant reformers.)

Puritanism is strict moral or religious behavior, especially an excessive concern with avoiding pleasure and enforcing rigid standards. The word carries negative connotations—implying joylessness, repression, or judgmental attitudes toward others' conduct: {Her puritanism about alcohol made her insufferable at parties}. The lowercase form emphasizes the attitude rather than the historical movement. (Capitalized Puritanism refers to the historical Protestant movement.)

Purity is the state of being unmixed, uncontaminated, or free from foreign elements. Gold of high purity contains few impurities. Water purity matters for drinking. The word extends to moral and sexual contexts: {purity of heart}, {purity rings} symbolizing abstinence until marriage. Purity can suggest innocence but also obsessive exclusion—ethnic purity, ideological purity. {The purity of her intentions was never in doubt.}

Purple is a color that sits between red and blue on the spectrum, historically associated with royalty and nobility because the dye was expensive and difficult to produce. The adjective describes anything of this color or, figuratively, prose that is overly ornate or flowery: {His writing tends toward the purple}. Purple also suggests bruising: {Her arm was purple where she'd fallen}. In American politics, purple states are those where neither major party dominates, blending Republican red and Democratic blue.

Purpose shares meaning with other frequent nouns, such as reason, aim, and goal: What is the purpose of your visit? If you do something with a sense of purpose, you do it with determination and a clear goal in mind. If you do something on purpose, you do it with awareness; this is often contrasted with accidentally: I assured him that I hadn’t taken his parking space on purpose. Purpose is often used in the plural: Computers are used for many instructional purposes in the classroom.

Purposeful describes action taken with clear intention and determination. A purposeful stride suggests someone who knows exactly where they're going and why. The word implies both direction and resolve: {She made a purposeful effort to reconnect with old friends}. Purposeful work has meaning behind it, not just routine.

A purr is the soft, vibrating sound a cat makes when content, produced by rapid movement of the laryngeal muscles. Cats purr when stroked, fed, or otherwise comfortable. The sound extends to similar low, continuous hums: {the purr of an engine idling}. To purr is to make this sound, or to speak in a smooth, seductive tone: {She purred her approval}.

Purring is the low, continuous vibrating sound cats make when content, though cats also purr when stressed or injured. The word extends to any similar soft rumble: {the purr of a well-tuned engine}, {She purred her approval}. When someone purrs words, they speak in a low, pleased, or seductive tone.

Purrs is the third-person singular of purr and its plural noun form. A purr is the low, continuous vibrating sound a cat makes when content, or by extension any similar soft rumbling: {the purr of the engine}. To purr is to make this sound, or to speak in a low, pleased, seductive tone: {She purred her approval}.

A purse is a small bag for carrying personal items, especially money. In American English, purse typically means a woman's handbag. In British English and older usage, it's a small pouch for coins. To purse is to pucker or contract, as when pursing one's lips in disapproval. The {public purse} refers to government funds. A purse can also be prize money: {a fight with a million-dollar purse}.

Purses is the plural of purse, a small bag for carrying personal items, especially money. In American English, purse typically means a woman's handbag; in British English, it's a small pouch for coins. The verb purse means to pucker or contract: {She pursed her lips in disapproval}. Purses can also refer to prize money in competitions: {The tournament purses totaled two million dollars}.

When you pursue a person or object, you look for it or follow it in order to accomplish something: Investigators pursued the fugitives across three states. When you pursue an abstraction, such as a career, a policy, or a strategy, you work to make it a success: She pursued a career in aerospace engineering and now she works on satellite launches. If you pursue an inquiry, you do what is required to learn the answer. The verbal noun of pursue is pursuit.

Pursuit is the act of chasing or going after something. A police pursuit involves following a suspect. The pursuit of happiness is seeking it. In the plural, pursuits are activities or interests one engages in regularly: {intellectual pursuits}, {outdoor pursuits}. {He abandoned his pursuit of a medical degree}.

The noun and verb push characterizes applied force that is meant to move something. This works literally (don’t push that button!) and figuratively: He’s pushing the limit of credibility. A push is an instance of pushing. If you give someone or something a push, you expect them to move, or to act. To push forward is to try to make progress in a difficult situation. To push back is to resist something directed at you.

Pushback is resistance or opposition to a proposal, policy, or action. The word suggests active rejection rather than passive disagreement: {The new regulations faced immediate pushback from industry groups}. Someone who gets pushback encounters friction when trying to move forward with something: {I got a lot of pushback when I suggested changing the schedule}.

A pusher is someone who pushes—literally or figuratively. Most commonly, a pusher is a person who sells illegal drugs: {The cops arrested a local pusher}. The term implies persistent, predatory salesmanship rather than passive dealing. In other contexts, a pusher is someone who promotes or pressures: {a pencil pusher} (a bureaucrat), {a paper pusher}. A pusher can also be a device that pushes, like a small utensil helping children scoop food onto a spoon.

Pushing is the present participle of push—applying force to move something away from you. Beyond physical force, pushing extends to urging or pressuring: {She's pushing him to apply for the job}. To be {pushing forty} means approaching that age. A drug pusher pushes drugs. {Don't push your luck} warns against testing limits too far.

A pushover is someone easily persuaded, defeated, or taken advantage of—a person who can't say no or won't put up resistance: {He's such a pushover; the kids get whatever they want}. The word also describes any task that presents no real challenge: {The exam was a pushover}.

Pushovers are people who are easily persuaded, dominated, or defeated. The term implies weakness or excessive compliance: {Don't be such a pushover—stand up for yourself}. A task that's a pushover is easily accomplished: {The exam was a pushover}. The singular pushover works the same way.

A pushup is an exercise performed by lying face down and pushing the body up and down with the arms while keeping the back straight: {I do fifty pushups every morning}. The movement builds chest, shoulder, and arm strength. As an adjective, pushup describes bras designed to lift and enhance cleavage: {a pushup bra}.

Pushups are a bodyweight exercise performed face-down, raising and lowering the body by straightening and bending the arms while keeping the back straight. A staple of physical training, pushups build upper body strength without equipment: {Drop and give me twenty pushups}. Variations include diamond pushups, wide-grip pushups, and one-armed pushups. Also spelled push-ups.

Pushy describes someone who asserts themselves too aggressively, pressing their opinions, requests, or presence on others beyond what's welcome: {a pushy salesman}, {Don't be so pushy}. The word carries disapproval—pushy people don't respect boundaries or take hints. It often describes those pursuing their own interests at others' expense.

A pussycat is a cat, especially in affectionate or childish speech: {Here, pussycat, come get your dinner}. Figuratively, a pussycat is someone gentle or harmless despite appearances: {He looks intimidating, but he's really a pussycat}. The word softens the faintly vulgar associations of pussy when referring to cats.

To pussyfoot is to move cautiously or stealthily, like a cat. More often, it means to avoid committing to a position or speaking directly: {Stop pussyfooting around and tell me what you really think}. A pussyfooter hedges and equivocates rather than stating things plainly.

Put is a “cause motion” verb that is typically followed by an object (the thing moved) and a prepositional phrase with adverbial effect telling where the thing ends up: Put those books on the table over there. Put also participates in many phrasal verbs that are figurative and not about motion, such as put up with (tolerate), put down (insult or criticize), and put out (extinguish, publish, or annoy). In securities terminology, a put is an option to sell an asset at a fixed price within a specified period of time.

A putdown is a remark intended to humiliate or belittle someone: {That wasn't a joke, it was a putdown}. The term captures the downward motion of lowering someone's status or self-esteem. As a verb phrase, to put someone down is to criticize or demean them: {She's always putting him down in front of others}.

A putt is a golf stroke made on or near the green, using a flat-faced club called a putter to roll the ball toward the hole. To putt is to make such a stroke: {She putted from twelve feet and sank it}. Putting is often called the most important part of the game—and the most nerve-wracking.

A putter is a golf club designed for short, precise strokes on the green, rolling the ball toward the hole. To putter is also to occupy oneself with minor tasks in an unhurried way: {He spent the morning puttering around the garage}. This sense, also spelled potter in British English, suggests pleasant aimlessness rather than productive work.

Puttering is occupying oneself with small, unhurried tasks—tidying, fixing, arranging—without urgency or clear purpose. The word suggests pleasant aimlessness rather than productivity: {He spent Saturday puttering around the garage}. British English uses pottering. Someone who putters moves from one minor activity to another, busy but relaxed.

Putting is the act of placing or positioning something somewhere: {She was putting the dishes away when the phone rang}. In golf, putting is specifically the stroke used on the green to roll the ball into the hole, requiring precision rather than power. A putting green is the smooth, closely mown area surrounding each hole. The gerund form also appears in phrases like {putting up with} (tolerating) and {putting off} (postponing).

Putty is a soft, pliable paste used to seal gaps, fill holes, or secure glass in window frames. It hardens after application. The word extends to anything easily shaped or manipulated: {He was putty in her hands} means someone completely yielding to another's influence. As a verb, to putty is to apply this material: {He puttied the cracks in the wall}. (Capitalized PuTTY is software.)

A puzzle is something designed to be figured out—a problem or game that challenges you to find a solution through reasoning, fitting pieces together, or discovering hidden patterns: {jigsaw puzzle}, {crossword puzzle}, {puzzle box}. More broadly, a puzzle is anything confusing or mysterious: {Her behavior was a puzzle to me}. To puzzle over something is to think hard about it. If something puzzles you, it confuses or perplexes you. To {puzzle out} an answer is to arrive at it through effort.

A puzzlebox is a container that can only be opened by solving a mechanical puzzle, typically involving a sequence of hidden movements, sliding panels, or secret compartments. Traditional puzzleboxes originated in Japan and were crafted from wood with intricate inlay patterns. The term extends to video game mechanics where players must manipulate an environment to progress, and metaphorically to any situation requiring clever, methodical problem-solving to unlock: {The estate's inheritance terms were a puzzlebox of legal conditions}.

Puzzled describes the state of being confused or unable to understand something. A puzzled {expression} shows uncertainty; a puzzled {silence} follows something inexplicable. The word suggests active mental effort rather than simple ignorance—you're puzzled when you're trying to figure something out: {I'm puzzled by her sudden change of heart}.

Puzzles is the plural of puzzle—a problem or game designed to test ingenuity or knowledge. Jigsaw puzzles require assembling pieces into a picture. Crossword puzzles fill grids with words from clues. The word extends to anything perplexing: {Her behavior puzzles me}. To puzzle something out is to solve it through effort: {We finally puzzled out what went wrong}.

Puzzling describes something difficult to understand or explain—something that leaves you uncertain or confused. A puzzling {situation} resists easy interpretation. Puzzling {behavior} makes you wonder about motives. The word suggests genuine mental effort: {Her response was puzzling—I couldn't tell if she was joking}.

Pyjama is the British spelling of pajama—loose, lightweight clothing worn for sleeping, typically consisting of a shirt and trousers. The word comes from Persian and Hindi terms for leg garments. In British usage, pyjamas appears almost exclusively in the plural: {I need new pyjamas}. The singular form appears mainly as a modifier: {pyjama bottoms}, {pyjama party}.

Pyjamas is the British spelling of pajamas—loose, comfortable clothing worn for sleeping, typically consisting of a top and trousers. The word comes from Persian and Urdu for loose trousers. {She changed into her pyjamas before bed.} Figuratively, {the cat's pyjamas} means something excellent or impressive.

Pyment is a type of mead made by fermenting honey with grape juice or wine, blending characteristics of both traditional mead and wine. The result is typically sweeter than standard wine but with more complexity than plain mead. Pyment was popular in medieval Europe and has seen modest revival among home brewers and mead enthusiasts. {The meadery's pyment paired surprisingly well with the cheese course.}

A pyramid is a structure with a square or triangular base and sloping sides that meet at a point. The most famous are the ancient Egyptian tombs, massive stone monuments built for pharaohs. The shape extends to any similar form: a pyramid of {oranges}, the food {pyramid}. A pyramid scheme is a fraud where early investors profit from later ones' money until the structure collapses.

Pyramids are massive structures with triangular sides that meet at a point, built on a square or rectangular base. The Egyptian pyramids served as royal tombs and remain among the world's most recognizable monuments. The shape extends to any pyramid-like form: {a pyramid of oranges at the market}. A pyramid scheme is a fraud where early investors profit from money paid by later ones, who inevitably lose out. In anatomy, pyramids are cone-shaped structures in the kidney and brainstem.

A pyre is a pile of wood or other combustible material for burning a corpse as part of a funeral rite. The practice is ancient and continues in some cultures, particularly Hindu tradition. Figuratively, pyre describes anything consumed by flames: {The rioters made a pyre of overturned cars}.

Pyrite is a brass-yellow mineral, iron sulfide, commonly called fool's gold for its resemblance to the precious metal. The similarity has fooled hopeful prospectors, making pyrite a symbol of worthless imitation: {All that glitters is not gold—sometimes it's pyrite}. Despite its nickname, pyrite has industrial uses and appears in jewelry.

A pyromaniac is someone with an irresistible urge to start fires. The term suggests a psychological compulsion rather than arson for profit or revenge: {The pyromaniac had set dozens of brush fires before being caught}. In casual use, pyromaniac loosely describes anyone fascinated by fire or who enjoys setting things ablaze.

Pythia is a name encountered mainly in technical contexts. In machine learning, Pythia refers to a suite of large language models released by EleutherAI for research purposes. In particle physics, PYTHIA (often styled in caps) is a widely used Monte Carlo event generator for simulating high-energy collisions. Both uses derive from the ancient Greek oracle. (Capitalized Pythia is the Oracle of Delphi.)

A python is a large nonvenomous snake that kills prey by constriction, wrapping its muscular body around victims and squeezing until they suffocate. Pythons are found in tropical regions of Africa, Asia, and Australia, with some species reaching over twenty feet in length. {A Burmese python had escaped from someone's exotic pet collection.} The word also describes anything that coils or constricts like the snake. (Capitalized Python is the programming language or the comedy troupe.)

Pythons are large, non-venomous snakes that kill by constriction—coiling around prey and squeezing until it suffocates. Native to Africa, Asia, and Australia, some species grow over twenty feet long. Python is also a widely used programming language known for readable syntax and versatility: {I learned Python in a weekend}. The plural pythons typically refers to the snakes; the language is uncountable.

Quack imitates the harsh cry of a duck. As a noun, it's both that sound and a fraudulent medical practitioner—someone whose credentials are as genuine as a duck's medical degree. The extended sense applies to any pretender to skill: {some quack nutritionist on the internet}. Quackery is the practice of such fraud.

Quackery is the promotion of fraudulent or unproven medical treatments, or the practice of medicine by someone without proper qualifications. The term derives from quack, itself from an old word for someone who "quacks" loudly about the virtues of their remedies. {The internet has become a breeding ground for quackery}. Quackery often exploits desperate patients with false promises of cures.

Quacks is the plural of quack, which has two distinct meanings. A quack is the harsh sound a duck makes, and to quack is to make that sound: {The ducks quacked at us as we approached the pond}. Separately, a quack is a fraudulent or incompetent doctor—someone who quacks like they know medicine but doesn't. The term extends to any charlatan peddling dubious remedies or expertise: {snake oil quacks}, {The internet is full of health quacks}.

Quad has attained word status mostly by being a shortening of several longer words. A quadrangle, especially on a university campus, is a quad, as is the quadriceps muscle: I’m working on my quads today. A quad is one of four children born at once (quadruplet), or a ski lift that accommodates four (quad lift). Quad sound is quadraphonic, that is, coming from four speakers. The verb quad in typography has to do with where white space is concentrated, as in quad left and quad right.

A quagmire is literally an area of unstable ground, like a bog or swamp. People typically use quagmire in the figurative sense, to talk about a precarious situation or predicament: The Internet has made the field of copyright law a quagmire. Journalists use the word frequently to characterize wars and various political situations that have no clear exit strategy.

Quagmires are areas of soft, waterlogged ground that yield underfoot—bogs or marshes where you might sink in and struggle to extract yourself. The figurative sense dominates: a quagmire is any situation that's difficult to escape once entered. {The project became a quagmire of delays and cost overruns.} {Critics called the military intervention a quagmire.}

Quail are small, plump game birds related to partridges, found worldwide and often hunted or raised for food. The word also functions as a verb meaning to shrink back in fear or lose courage: {She quailed at the thought of confronting him}. The bird and the verb are unrelated words that have settled on the same spelling.

Quaint describes something attractively old-fashioned or charmingly unusual. A quaint village has cobblestone streets and thatched roofs. A quaint custom seems pleasantly outdated. The word carries a note of condescension—calling something quaint acknowledges its appeal while marking it as belonging to another era: {How quaint that they still use a rotary phone}.

To quake is to shake or tremble, typically from seismic activity or from fear and cold. The earth quakes during earthquakes; a person quakes with terror: {She stood quaking in the doorway}. As a noun, a quake is an earthquake or any similar tremor: {The quake registered 6.2 on the Richter scale}. (Capitalized Quake is the video game series.)

A quaker is someone or something that quakes—that trembles or shakes. The word sees occasional use for things that cause quaking: {The 1906 San Francisco quaker devastated the city}. More commonly, quaker appears in compounds like {quaker grass}, named for its trembling seed heads. (Capitalized Quaker is a member of the Religious Society of Friends.)

Qualification is what makes someone eligible or suitable for something—the credentials, skills, or requirements that must be met: {She has the qualifications for the job}, {What are the qualifications for this position?} A qualification can also be a limiting condition or reservation that softens a statement: {He praised the proposal, but with qualifications}. To say something {without qualification} is to say it absolutely, holding nothing back.

Qualifications are the credentials, skills, or attributes that make someone suitable for a position or task: {Her qualifications include ten years of experience and an MBA}. The word also refers to conditions or limitations placed on a statement: {He accepted, but with qualifications}. To say something {without qualification} is to state it absolutely, with no reservations or exceptions.

Qualified describes someone who has the necessary skills, credentials, or experience for a task or position: {a qualified surgeon}, {qualified to practice law}. The word also means limited or modified rather than absolute: {qualified approval}, {a qualified success}. A qualified statement comes with reservations or conditions—not a full endorsement but not a rejection either.

Qualify has two directions of meaning. One narrows: to qualify a statement is to limit or modify it, adding conditions that restrict its scope {I should qualify that—it only applies to full-time employees}. The other expands: to qualify for something is to meet requirements that grant access {She qualified for the finals}. To qualify someone is to make them eligible or competent {His experience qualifies him for the role}. A qualified success is partial, not complete.

Quality denotes one of the essential characteristics of something, without which it would not have the same identity: What qualities do you look for in a successful applicant? From this core meaning arises a more frequent use of quality, to denote a degree of excellence, or excellence itself: The quality of the cheeses varied considerably. When I buy a car, money is no object; it’s quality I’m after. When quality comes before another noun it can represent any of these meanings: quality control is the activity of insuring that quality is good and consistent. Quality time is enjoyable time you spend with someone, free from distractions.

Qualms are uneasy feelings of doubt, hesitation, or moral discomfort about an action. Someone who has {no qualms about lying} feels no guilt or reluctance. The word usually appears in negative constructions—people mention their lack of qualms more than their presence: {She had no qualms about asking for a raise}. A qualm can also be a sudden pang of nausea, though this sense is rare.

A quandary is a state of uncertainty or perplexity about what to do—a difficult situation with no clear right answer. The word suggests being genuinely stuck, weighing options that all seem problematic: {I'm in a quandary about whether to take the job or stay where I am}. Unlike a simple choice, a quandary implies real difficulty and often anxiety.

Quantity is the amount or number of something—how much or how many: {What quantity do you need?} The word often appears in contexts of measurement, commerce, or comparison: {bulk quantities}, {a small quantity of salt}. An {unknown quantity} is something unpredictable or not yet understood. Quality and quantity form a natural pair, often in tension: {They chose quantity over quality}.

Quantum refers to the smallest discrete unit of something, especially in physics where energy and matter behave in distinct packets rather than continuous flows. A {quantum leap} in physics is the tiniest possible change—an electron jumping between energy levels—but popular usage has inverted this to mean a dramatic breakthrough: {a quantum leap in technology}. Quantum as an adjective describes phenomena at subatomic scales where classical physics breaks down: {quantum mechanics}, {quantum computing}. Outside science, quantum sometimes appears as an impressive-sounding modifier for anything cutting-edge or transformative.

Quarantine is a period of isolation imposed to prevent the spread of disease. A person exposed to illness may be placed in quarantine until they're confirmed healthy. The term extends to any enforced separation: {The dog spent six months in quarantine before entering the country}. Animals, plants, and digital files can all be quarantined. During the COVID-19 pandemic, quarantine became everyday vocabulary as millions isolated at home. The verb means to place in such isolation: {Officials quarantined the infected passengers}.

Quarantined means isolated to prevent the spread of disease or contamination. A person exposed to illness may be quarantined at home or in a facility: {The passengers were quarantined aboard the ship for two weeks}. The term extends to anything separated for safety—a quarantined computer file has been flagged as potentially harmful and isolated from the system.

Quarantines is the plural of quarantine and also its verb form. A quarantine is a period of isolation imposed to prevent the spread of disease, originally forty days for ships arriving at port. To quarantine someone or something is to place them in such isolation. The term extends beyond medicine: a quarantined file on a computer is isolated to prevent potential malware from spreading. {The infected passengers faced mandatory quarantines before entering the country.}

A quarrel is a heated argument or disagreement, typically between people who know each other: {a quarrel between neighbors}, {a lovers' quarrel}. To quarrel is to argue angrily. You can also quarrel with something abstract—to {quarrel with} a decision or interpretation is to take issue with it. Separately, a quarrel is a short, heavy crossbow bolt.

Quarries is the plural of quarry, which has two distinct meanings. A quarry is an open excavation for extracting stone, slate, or other materials: {The marble came from quarries in Vermont}. Separately, a quarry is prey being hunted—the object of pursuit for a hunter, predator, or investigator: {The detective tracked his quarry through the city}. As a verb, to quarry is to extract from a pit: {They quarried granite for the monument}.

A quarry is an open excavation site where stone, slate, or other materials are extracted from the earth: {The marble came from a quarry in Vermont}. To quarry is to extract such materials. Separately, quarry means the prey being hunted—an animal pursued by a predator or hunter, or figuratively, anyone being chased or sought: {The detective tracked his quarry through the city}.

A quarter is one of four equal parts. In the U.S., a quarter is also a 25-cent coin—one quarter of a dollar. Time divided into quarters gives us fiscal quarters, academic quarters, and the quarters of a football game. A quarter hour is fifteen minutes: {It's a quarter past three}. Quarters as lodging comes from soldiers being assigned to a fourth of a town; now any living space may be called quarters. To quarter is to divide into four parts or to provide lodging. To give no quarter is to show no mercy—from the practice of sparing enemies who surrendered.

A quarterback is the player who leads the offense in American football, calling plays and typically throwing or handing off the ball. The position requires both physical skill and tactical intelligence. Extended to general use, to quarterback something is to direct or coordinate it: {She quarterbacks the whole operation}. A {Monday morning quarterback} criticizes decisions after the fact.

Quarterbacks is the plural of quarterback, the player who directs an American football team's offense—calling plays, throwing passes, and handing off the ball. The position requires both physical skill and strategic thinking. Figuratively, to quarterback is to lead or coordinate any effort: {She quarterbacks our marketing campaigns}. {The team has cycled through three quarterbacks this season.}

The quarterfinals are the round of competition in which eight contestants or teams remain—the stage immediately before the semifinals. Victory advances four competitors; the losers are eliminated. {They lost in the quarterfinals to the eventual champions.} A single match at this stage is a quarterfinal.

A quartermaster is a military officer responsible for supplies, provisions, and logistics—ensuring troops have food, clothing, equipment, and shelter. The term extends to naval use, where a quartermaster handles navigation and steering rather than supplies. In civilian contexts, quartermaster occasionally describes anyone managing inventory or equipment: {She served as quartermaster for the camping expedition}.

Quarters are living accommodations, especially for military personnel or servants: {officers' quarters}, {servants' quarters}. The word implies assigned or provided housing rather than chosen residence. At close quarters means in tight proximity, often implying combat or confrontation. Separately, quarters is the plural of quarter—four of them make a whole, or a dollar.

A quartet is a group of four, especially four musicians performing together or a piece of music written for four voices or instruments: {a string quartet}, {a barbershop quartet}. The term extends to any set of four people or things considered together: {The quartet of candidates debated last night}.

Quartz is a hard, crystalline mineral composed of silicon and oxygen—one of the most abundant minerals in Earth's crust. It occurs in many varieties, from clear rock crystal to colored forms like amethyst and citrine. Quartz is prized in jewelry, used in electronics for its piezoelectric properties, and appears in everyday materials like glass and concrete. A quartz {watch} or {clock} uses a vibrating crystal to keep precise time.

Queasy describes a sensation of nausea—that unsettled feeling in the stomach that suggests vomiting might follow: {The boat's rocking made her queasy}. Extended to emotions, queasy means uneasy or uncomfortable: {I felt queasy about the whole arrangement}. A queasy conscience troubles its owner.

A queen is a hereditary female monarch, counterpart of the male king, or sometimes the wife of one. A queen in playing cards usually ranks below the king and has a stylized drawing of a queen on it face. The queen in chess is the piece with the greatest freedom of movement. The queen in a bee colony lays all the eggs. By extension, a female characterized as the queen of something is someone viewed as being the most accomplished in that field: Aretha Franklin is the Queen of Soul. Queen before a noun designating a product indicates the second largest size (queen bed).

Queens is the plural of queen—female monarchs, the wives of kings, or the most powerful chess pieces. In cards, queens rank below kings. In gay slang, queens are effeminate gay men or drag performers: {The bar was full of queens on Saturday night}. Queen bees and ant queens head their colonies. (Capitalized Queens is the New York City borough.)

Queer originally meant strange, odd, or peculiar: {a queer feeling}, {a queer coincidence}. By the early 20th century, it became a slur for homosexuals—a word shouted from passing cars and wielded to wound. Beginning in the 1980s, activists reclaimed queer as an umbrella term for non-heterosexual and non-cisgender identities, embracing its outsider energy: {queer theory}, {queer studies}, {the queer community}. Today queer is widely used with pride, but not universally—some older LGBTQ people who remember it only as a slur still find it painful. Context and speaker matter.

Queers as a noun was once purely a slur for gay people but has been substantially reclaimed as an umbrella identity term: {Queers have always been part of this neighborhood}. Some still find the word painful. As a verb, queers means ruins or spoils, from the original sense of making something strange or wrong: {That mistake queers the whole deal}.

Quench means to satisfy a thirst or to extinguish something. You quench your thirst by drinking, quench a fire by dousing it with water. The word extends to suppressing or stifling: {The government quenched the rebellion}. In metalworking, to quench is to cool hot metal rapidly by plunging it into liquid, hardening it. {Nothing quenches thirst like cold water}.

A query is a question or request for information. In computing, a query retrieves data from a database or search engine: {The search query returned thousands of results}. To query something is to question it or express doubt: {She queried the accuracy of the report}. {I have a query about the billing}.

A quesadilla is a Mexican dish of a tortilla folded around melted cheese and other fillings, then grilled or toasted. Fillings vary widely—chicken, beef, beans, vegetables—but cheese is essential. {I ordered a chicken quesadilla with guacamole on the side.}

Quesadillas is the plural of quesadilla, a Mexican dish consisting of a tortilla folded around melted cheese and other fillings, then grilled or pan-fried. The fillings vary—chicken, beef, vegetables, beans—but cheese is essential. {We ordered chicken quesadillas and guacamole.} In American restaurants, quesadillas are often served as appetizers or casual fare.

Quest is a search or pursuit, especially one with a noble or difficult goal. Knights went on quests; scientists quest for cures. The word carries a sense of purpose and adventure that distinguishes it from ordinary searching. {Her quest for the perfect apartment lasted months.} {He's on a quest to visit every national park.}

A question is a sentence or utterance seeking information, clarification, or confirmation: {Can I ask you a question?} Questions may be rhetorical, expecting no answer. Beyond speech, question means doubt or uncertainty: {His loyalty is not in question}. To question someone is to interrogate them or express doubt about something: {I question whether that's wise}. {Out of the question} means impossible or not worth considering.

Questionable describes something that invites doubt or suspicion. A questionable {decision} may be unwise; questionable {ethics} may be corrupt; a questionable {claim} lacks solid evidence. The word often serves as polite understatement—calling something questionable frequently means the speaker considers it wrong or false but isn't saying so directly: {His motives are questionable}.

Questioning describes the act of asking questions or expressing doubt. A questioning {look} or questioning {tone} signals skepticism or curiosity. As a noun, questioning refers to formal inquiry: {The suspect was taken in for questioning}. Someone who is questioning may be uncertain about their beliefs, identity, or sexuality—exploring rather than settled.

A questionnaire is a written set of questions used to gather information from respondents, typically for research, surveys, or administrative purposes. Unlike an interview, questionnaires are usually completed independently: {Please fill out this questionnaire before your appointment}. The word retains its French spelling and pronunciation.

Questions are inquiries seeking information, clarification, or confirmation. The word covers everything from simple requests {Any questions?} to profound uncertainties {questions of existence}. To question something is to express doubt about it: {She questioned his motives}. A question can also be a matter under discussion: {The question before us is whether to proceed}. {Without question} means certainly; {out of the question} means impossible.

Quests are journeys or pursuits in search of something, especially in fantasy and gaming contexts where a quest is a mission assigned to a character: {The wizard sent them on a quest for the ancient sword}. More broadly, any determined search qualifies: {her quest for meaning}, {the quest for knowledge}. To quest is to search or seek: {questing after truth}.

A queue is a line of people or things waiting in order: {Join the queue at the back}. More common in British than American English, where line predominates. In computing, a queue is a data structure where items are processed in the order they arrive—first in, first out. The verb means to form or join such a line: {We queued for tickets}, or to add items to a waiting list: {The songs are queued up to play}.

Queues are lines of people or things waiting their turn. The word is more common in British than American English, where *line* dominates: {The queues at the post office were terrible}. In computing, a queue is a data structure where items are processed in the order they arrived—first in, first out. The verb means to wait in line or to add items to such a sequence: {We queued for tickets}.

A quibble is a minor objection or complaint, especially one that seems petty or trivial: {Let's not quibble over details}. To quibble is to raise such objections, often to avoid addressing a larger point: {They quibbled about the wording instead of the substance}. The word carries a dismissive tone—calling something a quibble suggests it's not worth serious consideration.

Quibbles are minor objections or complaints, especially ones that focus on trivial details rather than substance: {I have a few quibbles with the proposal, but overall it's solid}. To quibble is to raise such objections, often in a way that seems evasive or nitpicky: {Let's not quibble over semantics}. The word carries a faint accusation that someone is missing the point.

Quiche is a savory French tart consisting of a pastry crust filled with a custard of eggs and cream, typically combined with cheese, meat, or vegetables. The most famous variety is quiche Lorraine, made with bacon or lardons. Once considered fancy or pretentious in American culture, quiche became so ubiquitous that the 1982 humor book *Real Men Don't Eat Quiche* mocked it as insufficiently masculine. {We're having spinach quiche for brunch.}

Quick is most frequently an adjective and adverb whose meanings overlap largely with fast (quick glance, quick meeting, got there quick). When reactions or thinking are characterized as quick, there is often a connotation of cleverness and skill. If you’re quick to do something, however, it may suggest a lack of forethought: She’s always quick to condemn her critics. In older use, quick means alive, as in the phrase the quick and the dead. A different noun quick refers to a painfully sensitive spot of flesh.

Quickdraw refers to the skill of drawing a weapon—especially a handgun from a holster—and firing it rapidly. The term evokes Old West gunfighters and their legendary speed. Quickdraw competitions test this skill against timers or opponents. In video games, a quickdraw is a fast-aiming mechanic or challenge: {I lost the quickdraw duel}. As an adjective, it describes anything requiring split-second reaction: {quickdraw reflexes}.

A quickie is something done hastily—most often sex, but also a quick drink, a brief meeting, or any rushed activity: {We only have time for a quickie}. The word carries a casual, slightly playful tone. As an adjective, quickie describes something brief or expedient: {a quickie divorce}, {a quickie wedding in Vegas}.

Quicksand is loose, waterlogged sand that yields to pressure and can trap people or animals who step into it. The danger comes from sinking—struggling makes it worse. Figuratively, quicksand describes any situation that's easy to enter but difficult to escape: {The project became a quicksand of budget overruns and delays}.

Quicksilver is an old name for mercury, the liquid metal that flows and shifts unpredictably at room temperature. The word now appears mainly as an adjective meaning mercurial—rapidly changing, elusive, hard to pin down: {her quicksilver moods}, {a quicksilver mind that leaps from topic to topic}.

Quiet means without much noise or activity. A quiet {room} has little sound; a quiet {evening} passes without incident. Quiet can describe personality—someone quiet is reserved and doesn't talk much. To quiet something is to make it less noisy or agitated: {She quieted the baby}. {Keep quiet} means stay silent. {On the quiet} means secretly or discreetly.

A quill is a large feather, especially from the wing or tail of a bird—or more specifically, the hollow shaft of such a feather. Before metal nibs, writers used sharpened quill shafts dipped in ink: {She wrote the letter with a quill}. The word extends to similar pointed structures: a porcupine's quills are its defensive spines. To quill is to pleat fabric into small cylindrical folds resembling quill shafts.

Quills are the hollow, rigid shafts of feathers, especially the large flight feathers whose tips were once sharpened into writing instruments. Before steel nibs, writers dipped quill pens in ink: {He scratched out a letter with his quill}. Quills also refer to the sharp, defensive spines of porcupines and hedgehogs. To quill is to pleat fabric into narrow, rounded folds.

A quilt is a bed covering made of two layers of fabric with padding between them, held together by stitched patterns. The decorative stitching—quilting—creates texture and prevents the filling from shifting. Quilts are often made from patchwork, with pieces of fabric sewn together in geometric or artistic designs: {a handmade quilt passed down through generations}. To quilt is to make such a covering or to stitch layers together in this way.

Quilting is the craft of stitching layers of fabric together, typically a decorative top, padding, and backing. The stitching itself creates patterns—geometric, floral, or freeform—that hold the layers in place while adding texture and visual interest. Quilting can refer to the activity, the technique, or quilted work collectively: {She took up quilting after retirement}, {The quilting on this blanket is exquisite}.

Quilts are bed coverings made of layers—typically a decorative top, padding, and backing—stitched together in patterns. The stitching itself is called quilting, and the craft has deep traditions in many cultures: {a handmade quilt passed down through generations}. To quilt is to make such items or to stitch layers together in this fashion. Figuratively, anything assembled from varied pieces may be called a quilt: {a quilt of small farms across the valley}.

A quinceañera is a celebration marking a girl's fifteenth birthday in Latin American cultures, traditionally signifying her transition from childhood to womanhood. The term refers both to the party itself—typically an elaborate event with formal attire, religious ceremonies, and dancing—and to the birthday girl: {The quinceañera wore a pink ball gown}.

A quintet is a group of five, especially five musicians performing together or a piece of music composed for five performers: {a string quintet}, {a jazz quintet}. The term extends to any set of five people or things working as a unit: {The starting quintet dominated the first half}.

A quip is a witty or clever remark, typically brief and delivered quickly. Quips tend toward the sarcastic or mildly cutting, though they can also be playful observations. The verb quip means to make such remarks: {She quipped that his new haircut made him look like a startled hedgehog}. Someone given to quipping might be called a quipster, though that term sounds a bit dated.

Quips are clever, witty remarks—brief and often sharp. A quip typically comes quickly, as a snappy retort or offhand observation: {She's known for her quips about office politics}. To quip is to make such remarks: {He quipped that the meeting could have been an email}.

A quirk is a peculiar trait or habit—something distinctive but not quite normal: {One of her quirks is alphabetizing everything in her refrigerator}. The word suggests mild oddity rather than serious strangeness. A quirk can also be an unexpected twist or accident: {a quirk of fate}, {a quirk in the system}. By quirk of history, two rivals ended up sharing an office.

Quirks are peculiarities or unexpected behaviors—small oddities that distinguish a person, thing, or system. Someone's quirks might be endearing or annoying: {I've learned to live with his quirks}. A quirk of fate is an unpredictable twist of circumstance. Software has quirks when it behaves unexpectedly: {The app has a few quirks, but it works}.

Quirky describes something or someone characterized by peculiar or unexpected traits—charmingly odd rather than deeply strange. A quirky {sense of humor} finds amusement in unconventional places. Quirky {décor} mixes unexpected elements. The word suggests endearing eccentricity: {She has quirky habits, like naming all her houseplants}. Unlike weird or strange, quirky carries affection.

Quit means to stop doing something or to leave a place or position. You quit a job, quit smoking, quit a program. {I quit!} can be a declaration of resignation or surrender. In computing, quit closes an application. Someone who quits easily gives up without persisting. The past tense is quit or quitted, with quit dominant in American English.

Quite is an intensifier with two nearly opposite uses. In American English, it usually means very or completely: {I'm quite certain}, {quite impressive}. In British English, it often means somewhat or fairly—a softening rather than strengthening: {It's quite good} (meaning decent, not outstanding). Context and intonation distinguish the senses. {Quite right} and {quite so} express agreement.

Quits describes a state where accounts are settled and neither party owes the other anything. Two people are quits when debts or obligations between them have been squared: {After she paid me back, we were quits}. To {call it quits} is to stop an activity or end a relationship: {They called it quits after ten years of marriage}.

A quitter is someone who gives up, especially when things get difficult. The word carries disapproval—quitters lack persistence or resolve: {Don't be a quitter}. In sports and competition, calling someone a quitter questions their mental toughness. The term implies that finishing or persevering was possible but the person chose not to.

Quitting is stopping or giving up an activity, job, or habit. Someone quitting a job is resigning from it: {She's quitting at the end of the month}. Quitting a habit means abandoning it: {He's been trying to quit smoking for years}. The word often carries connotations of surrender or defeat: {Quitting is not an option}. But quitting can also be a healthy choice—leaving something harmful or unfulfilling behind.

A quiver is a case for holding arrows, typically worn on the back or at the hip: {She reached into her quiver and nocked another arrow}. To quiver is to tremble or shake with small, rapid movements—from cold, fear, or strong emotion: {His voice quivered as he spoke}. A quiver of excitement suggests that same trembling anticipation. The noun and verb come from different origins but have converged on the spelling.

Quivering is trembling or shaking with small, rapid movements. Leaves quiver in a breeze, voices quiver with emotion, lips quiver before tears come. The word suggests vulnerability or instability—something barely holding together: {She stood there quivering with rage}. A quivering mass is gelatinous and unstable. The quivering of an arrow suggests vibration after impact.

Quivers names both a container for arrows and the act of trembling. An archer carries a quiver on the back or at the hip. To quiver is to shake with small, rapid movements—from cold, fear, or emotion: {Her lip quivered as she held back tears}. A quiver of excitement runs through a crowd. The noun can also mean a trembling motion itself: {a quiver in his voice}.

A quiz is a short test of knowledge, typically informal or low-stakes: {a pop quiz in history class}, {a personality quiz online}. Quiz also means to question someone closely: {The police quizzed him about his whereabouts}. Quiz nights at pubs test teams on trivia. The word carries a lighter tone than exam or interrogation.

A quota is a fixed share or allotment—the portion assigned to or expected from someone. Sales staff have quotas to meet. Countries impose import quotas to limit foreign goods.
