Hiring quotas set minimum numbers for underrepresented groups, though such policies are often controversial: {Critics argue quotas prioritize numbers over qualifications}. More loosely, quota suggests any expected amount: {I've had my quota of bad news for today}.

Quotas are fixed limits or targets—usually numerical—imposed on quantities. An import quota restricts how much of a good can enter a country. A sales quota sets the minimum a salesperson must achieve. Hiring quotas mandate minimum numbers from underrepresented groups, often controversial as either necessary correction or unfair preference: {The company faced criticism for its diversity quotas}. In computing, a quota caps storage or bandwidth allocation.

A quotation is someone's words repeated by another, usually with attribution: {a quotation from Shakespeare}. The word also names the practice itself: {Quotation without citation is plagiarism}. In commerce, a quotation is a stated price for goods or services: {Get three quotations before hiring a contractor}. Often shortened to quote.

Quote functions as both verb and noun around the idea of repeating or citing words. To quote someone is to repeat their exact words, often to support an argument or add authority: {Let me quote the contract back to you}. A quote is the passage being repeated, or informally, a price estimate: {Get three quotes before hiring a contractor}. Quotation marks, the punctuation that sets off quoted material, are often called quotes. In stock trading, a quote is the current price of a security.

Quotes are quotation marks—the punctuation enclosing direct speech or cited text: {She put quotes around "alleged" to signal skepticism}. Quotes also means passages cited from a source: {The article was full of quotes from unnamed officials}. As a verb, to quote is to repeat someone's exact words or to state a price: {Can you quote me a rate?} In finance, quotes are current prices for stocks or commodities.

A rabbi is a Jewish religious leader and teacher, trained in Jewish law and tradition. Rabbis lead congregations, conduct services, perform weddings and funerals, and offer spiritual guidance. The title comes from a Hebrew word meaning "my master" or "my teacher." {We asked the rabbi to officiate at the ceremony.}

Rabbis is the plural of rabbi, a Jewish religious leader and teacher. Rabbis conduct services, interpret Jewish law, and provide spiritual guidance to their congregations. They officiate at weddings, funerals, and bar mitzvahs. {The rabbis debated the passage's meaning for hours.} Unlike priests, rabbis are not intermediaries—they are scholars and teachers.

A rabbit is a small burrowing mammal with long ears, a short tail, and powerful hind legs for hopping. Wild rabbits live in warrens; domestic rabbits are kept as pets or raised for meat and fur. To {rabbit on} (British) is to talk at length about something trivial. A {rabbit punch} is an illegal blow to the back of the neck. To {pull a rabbit out of a hat} is to produce an unexpected solution.

Rabbits is the plural of rabbit—small, long-eared mammals known for burrowing and rapid breeding. {The rabbits got into the garden again.} To rabbit (British informal) is to talk at length about trivial things: {She rabbited on for hours}. Rabbits also appears in {breed like rabbits}, describing prolific reproduction.

Rabble is a disorderly crowd, especially one viewed with contempt by the speaker. {The guards dispersed the rabble outside the gates.} The term often carries class disdain—{the rabble} suggests common people seen as unruly or beneath consideration. A rabble-rouser stirs up such crowds, inciting agitation or unrest.

Rabid describes an animal infected with rabies, the viral disease transmitted through bites that causes madness and death: {a rabid dog}, {a rabid bat}. Extended to people, rabid means fanatically enthusiastic or extreme: {rabid fans}, {a rabid nationalist}. The figurative sense suggests the foaming, uncontrolled intensity of the disease.

Rabies is a viral disease transmitted through the saliva of infected animals, typically via bites. It attacks the nervous system and is almost always fatal once symptoms appear. The disease causes aggression, confusion, and hydrophobia—an aversion to water due to difficulty swallowing. {The dog was quarantined to rule out rabies.} Vaccination after exposure can prevent the disease from developing.

A raccoon is a medium-sized mammal native to North America, recognizable by its grayish fur, bushy ringed tail, and black mask-like markings across the eyes. Raccoons are nocturnal and notably dexterous, using their front paws to manipulate food and open containers. They thrive in forests and urban areas alike, often raiding garbage cans: {We heard raccoons getting into the trash last night}.

Raccoons is the plural of raccoon, a medium-sized nocturnal mammal native to North America, recognizable by its black facial mask and ringed tail. Raccoons are known for their dexterous front paws and opportunistic diet—they raid garbage cans, campsites, and anywhere else food is accessible: {The raccoons got into the trash again}.

Two words in English share the spelling race. One word, a noun and verb, is related to the ideas of competition and speed: a two-mile horse race. I’ll race you to the field. A channel in which something moves, often swiftly, can be called a race. Some contests that are not about speed are characterized as races: the race to the White House. The other race is a noun that describes a category in which people (and sometimes animals) are divided, based mainly on visual characteristics in people and on breeding in animals: The city is home to people of all races.

A racecar is a car designed or modified for competitive racing, built for speed rather than ordinary road use. The word is a palindrome—spelled the same forward and backward—which makes it a favorite example in wordplay: {Mom, Dad, racecar}. Also spelled as two words: race car.

A racecourse is a track where races are held, especially for horses. The term is more common in British English, where American English prefers racetrack. A racecourse typically includes the oval track itself plus surrounding facilities for spectators and betting: {We spent the afternoon at the racecourse}.

A racehorse is a horse bred and trained for competitive racing. The term usually refers to Thoroughbreds raced on flat tracks or over jumps, though it includes standardbreds for harness racing and quarter horses for sprints. Figuratively, someone who works like a racehorse works hard and fast: {She's been a racehorse all quarter}.

A racer is someone or something that races—a person who competes in speed contests, or a vehicle built for racing: {a stock car racer}, {She's been a racer since her teens}. Racer also names several species of slender, fast-moving snakes. The word emphasizes speed and competition rather than mere participation.

Racers are people, animals, or vehicles that compete in races. The word often names specific things built for speed: a racing bike, a racing car, a fast-moving snake. {The racers lined up at the starting line.} {North American racers are slender, nonvenomous snakes known for their speed.}

Races is the plural of race in its several senses. Races are competitions of speed—foot races, horse races, car races. {She won three races this season.} The races means an event where horse or dog racing takes place: {a day at the races}. Races also refers to categories of humans distinguished by ancestry, physical traits, or cultural identity—a concept now understood as socially constructed rather than biological: {relations between the races}. To say someone {races} is to say they compete in speed contests or move very fast: {He races motorcycles on weekends}.

A racetrack is a course designed for competitive racing—horses, cars, dogs, or other contestants follow a defined path, usually oval or circular. The term also refers to the facility surrounding such a course: {We spent the afternoon at the racetrack}. Figuratively, any fast-paced competitive environment: {The tech industry is a racetrack where companies rise and fall quickly}.

Racing is competitive speed—the act of trying to go faster than others, whether on foot, in vehicles, or on animals. Horse racing, car racing, drag racing. As an adjective, racing describes things designed for or involved in such competition: a racing {yacht}, racing {stripes}, a racing {heart}. That last sense extends to anything beating or moving rapidly, often from excitement or fear.

Racism is a belief that people of different ethnic origins have different characteristics that are superior or inferior in some respects to others. Policies and programs that arise from such a belief can also be called racism: Institutional racism was challenged in Brown v. Board of Education. More generally, racism means hatred of a race other than one’s own, along with the conviction that some races are inferior.

Racist describes attitudes, actions, or systems that discriminate based on race or assume racial superiority. As a noun, a racist is someone who holds such beliefs or engages in such discrimination: {He's a racist who thinks his heritage makes him better than others}. The word can describe overt bigotry or subtler patterns: {racist hiring practices}, {a racist joke}. Calling someone racist is a serious accusation, though people disagree sharply about what qualifies.

A rack is a framework for holding, storing, or displaying things: {a wine rack}, {a luggage rack}, {a coat rack}, {a rack of ribs}. Racks organize and separate items. The rack was also a medieval torture device that stretched the body. As a verb, to rack means to cause suffering, strain, or arrange on a rack: {racked with guilt}, {racked with pain}, {rack the balls} (in pool). In vulgar slang, rack means a woman's breasts, especially large ones: {Nice rack}. To rack up means to accumulate: {rack up points}, {rack up debt}.

Racket has two distinct origins. One is a loud, disturbing noise or commotion: {The neighbors were making quite a racket}. Extended, it means a dishonest scheme or fraudulent business: {a protection racket}, {What a racket—charging that much for parking}. The other racket is the stringed implement for striking a ball in tennis, badminton, or squash. Also spelled racquet for the sporting equipment.

A racketeer is someone who makes money through illegal or fraudulent schemes, especially organized crime operations like extortion, loan sharking, or protection rackets. The term evokes 1920s and 30s gangsters but remains current in legal contexts: {He was convicted under federal racketeering laws}. To racketeer is to engage in such activities.

Racketeering is engaging in organized criminal activity for profit—extortion, fraud, loan sharking, illegal gambling, or other schemes typically run by syndicates. The term gained legal precision through the U.S. RICO Act, which targets patterns of criminal enterprise: {The mobsters were convicted on racketeering charges}. A racket is any such illicit operation, and a racketeer runs one.

Rackets is the plural of racket in all its senses: sports equipment for striking balls, loud disturbing noises, or fraudulent schemes. A separate but related meaning: rackets (also spelled racquets) is a ball game played with rackets in a four-walled court, a precursor to squash. {He learned rackets at boarding school.}

Racks is the plural of rack—frameworks for storage or display, or portions of ribs: {We need more racks for the warehouse}. {We ordered two racks of lamb}. In vulgar slang, racks means breasts. In hip-hop slang, racks also means stacks of money: {He made racks selling cars}.

A raccoon is a nocturnal mammal native to North America, recognizable by its black facial mask and ringed tail. Raccoons are notorious for raiding garbage cans and adapting to urban environments. The spelling raccoon predominates; racoon is a less common variant.

A racquet is a handled frame with a stringed hitting surface, used in tennis, badminton, squash, and similar sports. The strings create a springy surface for striking a ball or shuttlecock. Also spelled racket, though racquet predominates in formal sports contexts: {She gripped the racquet tightly before serving}.

Rad is slang for excellent or impressive, originally surfer and skater vocabulary from the 1980s: {That trick was rad}. The word is a clipping of radical. Rad also serves as a unit measuring absorbed radiation dose, though this technical use has largely given way to the gray. (All-caps RAD may be an acronym.)

Radar is a system that detects objects by bouncing radio waves off them and measuring the reflections—used for tracking aircraft, ships, weather patterns, and vehicle speeds. The word comes from "radio detection and ranging." Figuratively, to be {on someone's radar} is to have their attention; to fly {under the radar} is to go unnoticed.

Radiance is bright, warm light emanating from a source—the radiance of the sun, of a fire, of a lamp. The word extends naturally to people who seem to glow with health, happiness, or inner beauty: {Her face had a radiance I'd never seen before}. A radiant smile, a radiant bride. In physics, radiance is a precise measure of light intensity per unit area.

Radiant describes something that emits light or heat, or seems to: {radiant sunshine}, {radiant heat from the fireplace}. More often, radiant describes a person glowing with joy, health, or beauty: {She looked radiant on her wedding day}. The word suggests light emanating outward—a radiant smile seems to shine from within. In physics, radiant refers to energy transmitted by radiation rather than conduction.

Radiation is energy traveling through space as waves or particles. The term covers everything from visible light and radio waves to the more dangerous X-rays and gamma rays associated with nuclear processes. {Radiation therapy} uses targeted energy to kill cancer cells. Heat radiates from a fire; influence radiates from a center of power. The pattern of spreading outward from a source connects all uses.

A radiator is a device that transfers heat from one medium to another. In buildings, radiators are heating units—typically metal fixtures filled with hot water or steam that warm a room by releasing heat into the air. In vehicles, the radiator is part of the cooling system, dispersing engine heat through a network of fins and tubes: {The car overheated because the radiator was leaking}.

Radical can be a noun or an adjective with a range of meanings, most of which suggest something out of the ordinary. A radical change is a big and fundamental one; radical surgery is extensive, and goes to the root of the problem. Applied to any sort of political thought, radical characterizes the most extreme version of it. A radical is one who embraces radical thinking or actions. Radical in chemistry and math is short for free radical and radical sign, respectively.

Radicalism is the pursuit of fundamental change to political, social, or economic systems—going to the root rather than treating symptoms. The term is relative: what counts as radical depends on the status quo. Radicalism can describe movements across the political spectrum, from revolutionary socialism to libertarian anarchism. {Her radicalism alienated moderate allies.} {The party's radicalism softened as it gained mainstream support.}

Radicalization is the process of adopting extreme political, social, or religious views—typically views that reject mainstream society and may endorse violence. The term usually describes a gradual shift: {His radicalization happened over several years online}. It appears most often in discussions of terrorism and extremism, though the word itself doesn't specify which ideology someone radicalizes toward.

To radicalize is to push someone toward extreme political, social, or religious views—or to undergo that shift yourself. The word implies movement from moderate positions toward the fringes: {He was radicalized online}, {Prison can radicalize inmates}. Radicalization often carries connotations of danger, suggesting views that may lead to violence or terrorism, though the word also applies to any significant ideological shift: {The experience radicalized her politics}.

Radicalized describes someone who has adopted extreme political, social, or religious views, typically through a process of indoctrination or self-directed immersion. The term usually implies a shift toward positions that reject mainstream society or endorse violence: {He was radicalized by online extremist content}. While neutral in structure, radicalized almost always carries negative connotations—you rarely hear it applied to someone who became passionate about recycling.

Radicals are people who advocate for extreme or fundamental change, especially in politics or society. The word comes from a root meaning "root," and this sense of getting to the root of things connects its various uses. In chemistry, a radical is a molecule with an unpaired electron, making it highly reactive. In mathematics, a radical is the symbol for a root, as in square root. {Free radicals in the body can damage cells.} {The radicals called for overthrowing the entire system.}

Radio is the transmission of signals through electromagnetic waves, or a device that receives such transmissions. As a medium, radio once dominated home entertainment before television: {We listened to the radio during dinner}. The word also describes the technology itself: radio {waves}, radio {frequency}. To radio is to communicate by radio transmission: {The pilot radioed the tower}. A two-way radio allows both sending and receiving.

Radioactive describes materials that emit radiation as their atomic nuclei decay. Radioactive {waste}, radioactive {isotopes}, radioactive {contamination}. The word extends figuratively to anything dangerously volatile or best avoided: {That topic is radioactive right now}. A person or issue described as radioactive is toxic to associate with—likely to damage anyone who gets too close.

Radioactivity is the emission of energy from unstable atomic nuclei as they decay into more stable forms. This process releases radiation—alpha particles, beta particles, or gamma rays. Some elements are naturally radioactive; others become so through bombardment. Radioactivity has applications in medicine, energy production, and weapons: {The radioactivity from the reactor leak contaminated the surrounding area}. The adjective is radioactive.

A radish is a pungent root vegetable, typically small and round with red skin and crisp white flesh. Radishes are eaten raw in salads or as garnishes, prized for their peppery bite. The daikon is a larger, milder Asian variety. {She sliced radishes paper-thin for the salad.}

Radishes are small, pungent root vegetables, typically red-skinned with crisp white flesh. They're eaten raw in salads or as a garnish, prized for their sharp, peppery bite. The greens are also edible. Varieties range from mild breakfast radishes to fiery black Spanish types to the large, mild daikon common in Asian cuisines.

Radius is the distance from the center of a circle to its edge, or a line segment representing that distance. By extension, radius describes the area within a certain distance from a point: {There are three good restaurants within a one-mile radius}. In anatomy, the radius is one of the two bones in the forearm, running from the elbow to the thumb side of the wrist.

A raffle is a lottery in which people buy numbered tickets for a chance to win a prize, with winners drawn at random. Raffles are common fundraisers for schools, churches, and charities: {We're raffling off a handmade quilt}. To raffle something is to offer it as a prize in such a drawing.

Raffles is the plural of raffle, a type of lottery where people buy numbered tickets for a chance to win prizes, typically at fundraisers or community events. {We bought ten raffles hoping to win the gift basket.} The verb raffle means to offer something as a prize in such a drawing, usually followed by off: {The school raffled off a new car to raise money for the gym.}

A raft is a flat floating platform, typically made of logs, planks, or inflatable material, used for transportation on water: {We built a raft and floated down the river}. Informally, a raft means a large quantity: {a whole raft of problems}, {a raft of new regulations}. To raft is to travel by raft, especially for recreation: {We went rafting on the Colorado}.

A rafter is one of the sloping beams that form the framework of a roof, running from the ridge to the eaves: {The old barn's rafters were still solid after a hundred years}. Rafters are typically exposed in attics and unfinished spaces. Separately, a rafter is a person who travels by raft: {river rafters}.

Rafters are the sloping beams that form the framework of a roof, extending from the ridge to the eaves. The word often appears in the phrase {packed to the rafters}, meaning completely full—from the image of a space so crowded that people or things reach up to the roof structure. A sports arena with fans {in the rafters} has spectators in the highest seats.

Rafting is the activity of traveling on water using a raft, especially navigating rapids on an inflatable raft as recreation: {We went whitewater rafting in Colorado}. The word also describes the transport of logs by floating them downstream, and in geology, the process by which ice carries rocks or debris.

Rafts is the plural of raft—flat platforms for floating on water, whether improvised from logs or inflatable for whitewater recreation. More commonly, rafts means large quantities: {rafts of data}, {rafts of complaints}, {rafts of new regulations}. This informal sense suggests abundance bordering on excess.

Clothes that are no longer wearable become rags. Some fabrics start their lives as rags (dish rag). Someone dressed in rags has clothes in poor condition. Calling a newspaper a rag disparages its quality. A different kind of rag comes from ragtime music, like the Maple Leaf Rag, or any composition with this syncopated rhythm. The slang verb rag means to scold or tease. If you rag on someone, you make fun of them.

A ragamuffin is a person, especially a child, in ragged, dirty clothes—suggesting poverty or neglect. The word carries affection as often as pity: {The neighborhood ragamuffins played in the vacant lot}. It can describe anyone disheveled or scruffily dressed: {She showed up looking like a ragamuffin after her camping trip}.

A ragdoll is a limp, floppy doll made of cloth and stuffing, the kind a child might drag around by an arm. The term extends to anything that flops limply like such a toy: {His body went ragdoll when he fainted}. In video games and animation, ragdoll physics simulate how a character's body collapses and tumbles when incapacitated—limbs swinging freely rather than following scripted movements. (Capitalized Ragdoll is the cat breed.)

Except in the expression all the rage, which describes something that is wildly popular, rage is extreme and violent anger – and something to be avoided. Certainly avoid anyone in a jealous rage or a murderous rage. Listening to someone vent their rage is rarely enjoyable. To rage is to express violent anger. When the subject is abstract, it describes extremity and violence, and is said of storms, fires, and torrents of water: The raging waters swept the house off of its foundation. When debate rages, people disagree vehemently with no end in sight.

Raged is the past tense of rage. To rage is to feel or express intense, often uncontrollable anger: {He raged at the injustice}. Storms, fires, and battles rage when they continue with violent intensity: {The wildfire raged through the canyon}. In recent slang, to rage means to party hard or go all out: {We raged until dawn}.

Ragequit is to abruptly abandon a video game or online activity out of frustration, usually after losing or failing repeatedly: {He ragequit after dying on the final boss for the tenth time}. The term has spread beyond gaming to describe any angry departure from a frustrating situation: {She ragequit the meeting when her proposal was rejected}.

A rager is a wild, intense party—the kind with loud music, heavy drinking, and chaos that might draw noise complaints: {We threw a rager while my parents were out of town}. The word can also describe someone prone to fits of anger, though this sense is less common than the party meaning.

Rages is the plural of rage—intense, often uncontrollable anger or fury: {His rages frightened the children}. Rages also names events or trends that sweep through a population: {the latest fitness rages}. As a verb form, rages describes something continuing with great intensity: {The fire rages on}, {The debate rages}.

Ragged describes something with rough, torn, or uneven edges—clothes worn to tatters, a coastline of jagged rocks, a ragged wound. By extension, ragged means rough or imperfect in quality: {a ragged performance}, {ragged breathing}. To run someone ragged is to exhaust them through excessive demands. A ragged edge suggests the boundary of control: {living on the ragged edge}.

Raging describes intense, uncontrolled force. A raging fire burns out of control; a raging storm batters the coast. Applied to people, it means furiously angry: {He was raging at the injustice}. Raging can also intensify: a raging headache, a raging success. The word conveys something at full, often destructive, power.

Rags are torn, worn-out pieces of cloth, often used for cleaning or wiping: {He polished the car with an old rag}. Rags also means tattered clothing, suggesting poverty: {dressed in rags}. To go {from rags to riches} is to rise from poverty to wealth. In slang, rags can mean clothes generally: {nice rags}. A rag is also a newspaper, usually one considered low-quality: {that tabloid rag}.

Ragtag describes a group that is disorganized, motley, or thrown together from disparate parts: {a ragtag band of rebels}, {a ragtag collection of secondhand furniture}. The word suggests scrappiness and lack of polish, sometimes affectionately. Often paired with "bunch" or "group." The longer form *ragtag and bobtail* means the rabble or common masses.

Ragtime is a style of American music that flourished from the 1890s through the 1910s, characterized by syncopated or "ragged" rhythms in the melody against a steady bass. Originally piano music, it influenced early jazz and popular song. Scott Joplin's compositions like "The Entertainer" remain the genre's best-known examples. {She learned to play ragtime at the piano}.

A raid is a sudden attack, typically brief and with a specific objective—seizing something, destroying a target, or capturing people. Military forces conduct raids on enemy positions; police raid locations to arrest suspects or seize contraband. Vikings raided coastal villages. The word extends to any sudden incursion: a {raid on the refrigerator}, a corporate raid to acquire a company. In computing, RAID is an acronym for data storage across multiple drives.

Raided is the past tense of raid—to make a sudden attack or incursion, typically to seize something or someone. Police raid hideouts; armies raid enemy positions; kids raid the refrigerator. {The FBI raided the compound at dawn}. {Someone raided my Halloween candy stash}.

A raider is someone who attacks suddenly to steal or destroy—Vikings raiding coastal villages, bandits raiding supply wagons. The term extends to corporate raiders, who acquire companies through aggressive stock purchases, often against management's wishes. In sports, particularly American football, raiders suggests an aggressive, piratical identity: {The Raiders play in Las Vegas}.

Raiders are people who conduct raids—sudden attacks, typically to seize goods or cause damage. The word suggests violence and speed: Viking raiders, corporate raiders who pursue hostile takeovers, or teams that raid opponents' territory in games. {Raiders swept through the village at dawn.} The Oakland Raiders were a professional football team known for their outlaw image.

Raiding is the act of making a raid—a sudden attack or incursion, typically to seize something or cause damage. Police conduct drug raids. Vikings were known for raiding coastal villages. In gaming, raiding means attacking another player's base or joining a group to tackle difficult content: {We spent all night raiding in the new expansion}. In streaming, raiding sends your audience to another channel when you sign off.

Raids is plural of raid—a swift attack meant to surprise, seize, or destroy. Military forces conduct raids on enemy positions. Police raid locations suspected of criminal activity. In gaming, raids are coordinated group assaults on difficult content: {We're organizing raids every Saturday night}. Corporate raiders mount hostile takeover attempts. To raid the refrigerator is to grab food impulsively, often late at night.

By far the most frequent use of rail is as a noun referring to either of two things: something connected with railroads (travel by rail), or a horizontal bar that serves some purpose (hitching rail, fence rail). A different kind of rail is a wading bird with short wings and long toes. The verb rail describes complaining. People who rail bitterly, angrily, or incessantly usually do so because there is no solution to their problem.

A railgun is a weapon that accelerates projectiles using electromagnetic force rather than explosives or propellant. Two parallel rails conduct electrical current through the projectile, generating magnetic fields that propel it at extreme velocities. Railguns appear frequently in science fiction and video games, though military versions remain experimental: {The destroyer's railgun could strike targets hundreds of miles away}.

A railing is a barrier made of rails—horizontal bars supported by vertical posts—installed along stairs, balconies, bridges, or elevated walkways to prevent falls: {She gripped the railing as she descended the icy steps}. Railings also line decks and porches, providing something to lean against. The term can refer to the structure as a whole or to the material used to construct it: {wrought-iron railing}, {wooden railing}.

A railroad is a system of tracks with steel rails on which trains run, or the company that operates such a system: {The railroad runs through three states}. To railroad someone is to pressure them into hasty action without fair consideration: {They railroaded the bill through committee}. To railroad a person can also mean to convict them on false charges or through a rigged process.

Railroaded means forced through hastily or coerced unfairly. To railroad legislation is to push it through without proper deliberation: {The bill was railroaded through committee}. More commonly, to railroad someone is to pressure them into something or convict them unjustly: {He was railroaded into confessing}, {She claimed she'd been railroaded by a corrupt prosecutor}. The image is of being swept along like cargo on a train—no stopping, no choice.

Railroading is the business or activity of operating railroads—building tracks, running trains, managing freight and passengers. The word also names a coercive practice: to railroad someone is to force them into something without fair process or adequate time to respond. A defendant gets railroaded through a sham trial; a bill gets railroaded through committee. In tabletop gaming, railroading describes a game master who forces players along a predetermined plot rather than letting choices matter: {The campaign felt like pure railroading—nothing we did changed anything}.

Railroads are systems of tracks on which trains run, or the companies that operate them. The term is primarily American; British English prefers railways. To railroad someone is to force them into hasty action or push something through without proper consideration: {They railroaded the bill through committee}. To railroad someone also means to convict them on false charges or without fair process.

Rails are the parallel metal bars that form a track for trains and other wheeled vehicles to travel on. By extension, rail refers to train travel generally: {We shipped it by rail}. Rails also serve as horizontal barriers or supports—a handrail, a fence rail, a towel rail. If something goes {off the rails}, it loses direction or control, like a derailed train. To rail against something is to complain bitterly about it, though this verb comes from a different source. {Rails} is also shorthand for Ruby on Rails, a web development framework.

A railway is a track made of parallel steel rails on which trains run, or the entire system of tracks, stations, and trains operated as a transportation network. More common in British English than American English, where railroad predominates: {The railway connected the coastal towns}. Railway also appears in compounds like {railway station} and {railway crossing}.

Railways are systems of tracks, stations, and trains for transporting passengers and freight. The term is more common in British English, where Americans typically say railroads. Railway can refer to the physical infrastructure, the operating company, or the industry as a whole: {She works for the railway}. {The railway runs through the valley}.

The common meanings of noun and verb rain are straightforward: water falling from the sky. Before another noun, rain is also typically literal in usage (rain forest, rain barrel, rain gutter). The verb rain has figurative use to denote things falling in great profusion, like confetti, debris, missiles, or rockets. If boos or chants rain (down) on someone, many people are booing or chanting at once.

Actual rainbows are a rare, colorful, and enjoyable display of a prism in the sky. Figurative use of the word typically borrows one of these qualities. A rainbow flag is a unifying symbol of the LGBTQ community. The expression rainbows and unicorns is used ironically to characterize something that is annoyingly unrealistic or optimistic. A rainbow trout is so called because of a rainbow-like pattern on its sides.

Rainbows are arcs of color that appear in the sky when sunlight refracts through water droplets, displaying the spectrum from red to violet. The phenomenon has become a symbol of hope and promise—from the biblical covenant to modern movements. A rainbow of something means a diverse array: {a rainbow of flavors}. The rainbow flag represents LGBTQ+ pride. To chase rainbows is to pursue unrealistic dreams.

A raincheck is a promise to honor an offer at a later time. The term comes from baseball, where spectators received tickets for a future game if rain cancelled play. Now it applies broadly: stores issue rainchecks when sale items sell out, and {I'll take a raincheck} politely declines an invitation while leaving the door open for next time.

A raincoat is a water-resistant outer garment worn to stay dry in wet weather. Most raincoats are lightweight and designed to be worn over other clothing: {Grab your raincoat—it's supposed to pour this afternoon}. The word sometimes appears as a euphemism for condom.

A raindrop is a single drop of rain. The word appears in descriptions of weather and in figurative contexts suggesting smallness or gentle accumulation: {Raindrops streaked the window}. Children learn the compound early, making it one of the first meteorological terms in a person's vocabulary.

Raindrops are individual drops of water falling as rain. The word emphasizes rain as discrete units rather than a continuous phenomenon: {Raindrops splattered against the window}. Children learn that raindrops aren't actually teardrop-shaped—they're more like tiny hamburger buns, flattened by air resistance as they fall.

A rainforest is a dense forest in a region of heavy rainfall, typically receiving at least 80 inches annually. Tropical rainforests near the equator are known for extraordinary biodiversity—the Amazon rainforest alone contains roughly ten percent of all species on Earth. Temperate rainforests exist in cooler climates like the Pacific Northwest. {Rainforest destruction} and {deforestation} are major environmental concerns.

Rainforests is the plural of rainforest—dense forests found in tropical regions with heavy annual rainfall. These ecosystems contain extraordinary biodiversity, with species found nowhere else on earth. {The Amazon rainforests are often called the lungs of the planet.} Rainforest also appears as two words: rain forest.

Raining describes precipitation falling from the sky in the form of water droplets. It functions as the present participle of rain: {It's been raining all day}. Figuratively, things can rain down in abundance: {Confetti was raining on the parade}. The idiom {raining cats and dogs} means raining heavily.

A rainmaker is someone who generates revenue or brings in business, especially a lawyer or executive who attracts wealthy clients: {She's the firm's top rainmaker}. The term comes from the original sense—a person who claims to produce rain through rituals or technology. Native American ceremonies and 19th-century charlatans both produced rainmakers. The business sense captures the same magic: someone who makes good things happen through mysterious personal power.

Rainmakers are people who bring in money or business. The term originated with those who claimed to produce rain through rituals or technology, but now primarily describes lawyers, executives, or salespeople who attract lucrative clients or deals: {She's the firm's top rainmaker, billing millions annually}. The implication is that their ability seems almost magical—they make prosperity appear.

A rainstorm is a storm characterized by heavy rainfall. The word emphasizes the rain itself rather than accompanying wind, thunder, or lightning—though these may be present. {We got caught in a rainstorm without an umbrella.} A rainstorm can range from a brief downpour to hours of steady, drenching rain.

Rainy describes weather characterized by rain: {a rainy afternoon}, {the rainy season}. To save something for {a rainy day} is to set it aside for future need—the metaphor suggests staying indoors when weather turns bad.

The verb raise is closely related to rise but unlike rise, raise is nearly always transitive. The core meaning is elevate: The builders are raising the ceilings by one foot. Raise is also used to talk about the activity of caring for something while it reaches maturity, as in raising children or raising cotton. In North American English, a raise is an increase in pay; this is called a rise in British English. In poker, a raise is the amount of an increase that a bettor makes.

Raised describes something lifted up or elevated. A raised {platform} sits above ground level. A raised {eyebrow} signals skepticism or surprise. Raised also means brought up or reared: {She was raised in Texas}. In cooking, raised dough has expanded from leavening. A raised {voice} is louder than normal, often in anger.

A raisin is a dried grape, typically dark and wrinkled, used in baking, cereals, and trail mix. Raisins are sweet and chewy, made by sun-drying or mechanically dehydrating grapes. Golden raisins come from green grapes treated to preserve color. {Oatmeal raisin cookies}, {raisin bran}.

Raising is the act of lifting, elevating, or bringing up. You can raise an object physically {raising the flag}, raise children {She's raising three kids on her own}, or raise money for a cause. In card games, a raise increases the bet. Raising also means bringing something into existence or consideration: {raising objections}, {raising awareness}, {raising the alarm}.

Raisins are dried grapes, typically dark and wrinkled, used in baking, cooking, and as a snack. Golden raisins are lighter, often treated with sulfur dioxide. The singular raisin appears less often than the plural: {raisin bread}, {oatmeal raisin cookies}. {She picked the raisins out of her trail mix.}

A rake is an instrument with prongs, used in gardening and to gather leaves. To rake is to use such an instrument. The verb can be used of other things that drag across a surface like a rake: The bear’s claws raked across the tree. A different verb rake means to deviate from vertical, so a steeply raked windshield is one at a low angle. A different noun rake is somewhat old-fashioned or literary and denotes a man who lives for pleasure and disregards others.

Rakes is the plural of rake—the long-handled garden tool with teeth for gathering leaves or smoothing soil. Rake also names a dissolute man devoted to pleasure: {He was one of those charming rakes who left broken hearts everywhere}. As a verb, to rake is to use the tool, or to sweep across: {Machine gun fire raked the hillside}. To {rake in} money is to accumulate it rapidly. To {rake someone over the coals} is to criticize them harshly.

Rallies is the plural of rally and its verb form. A rally is a large gathering for a shared purpose—political rallies, pep rallies, protest rallies. In sports and markets, a rally is a recovery after decline: {The team staged a late rally}; {Tech stocks led the rallies this quarter}. To rally is to come together, recover strength, or rouse others: {She rallied the troops}. In tennis and similar sports, a rally is an extended exchange of shots.

Rally centers on gathering or recovering strength. People rally to a cause, coming together in support; a political rally is such a gathering. In sports and markets, a rally is a comeback after decline: {Stocks rallied in afternoon trading}. In tennis and similar games, a rally is an extended exchange of shots. To rally someone is to rouse them or tease them good-naturedly: {His friends rallied him about the mistake}.

A ram is an adult male sheep, known for its curved horns and aggressive butting behavior. The word extends to any device that batters or forces: a battering ram breaks down doors, a hydraulic ram drives machinery. To ram is to strike or push with force: {The ship rammed the dock}. To ram something through is to force its acceptance despite opposition. To ram something down someone's throat is to force them to accept it. (Capitalized Ram is the zodiac sign; all caps RAM is computer memory.)

To ramble is to walk without a fixed destination, wandering at leisure through countryside or town: {We rambled through the village streets}. The word extends to speech or writing that wanders similarly—moving from topic to topic without clear direction: {He rambled on about his childhood}. A ramble is such a walk or an aimless stretch of talk. Rambling describes both leisurely walking and unfocused discourse: {a rambling old house}, {a rambling speech}.

Rambling describes something that wanders without clear direction or structure. A rambling {speech} meanders from topic to topic. A rambling {house} sprawls irregularly, with rooms added haphazardly over time. A rambling {path} takes an indirect route. The word often carries mild criticism—rambling conversation tends to lose its audience. In British English, rambling is also recreational walking in the countryside: {We went rambling in the Lake District}.

Rambunctious describes boisterous, unruly, and energetically uncontrollable behavior—typically applied to children or animals: {The rambunctious puppies knocked over the lamp}. It suggests high spirits rather than malice, carrying affection alongside exasperation: {After three hours with six rambunctious toddlers, I needed a nap}.

Ramen is a Japanese noodle soup consisting of wheat noodles in a savory broth, typically topped with sliced pork, soft-boiled egg, seaweed, and scallions. The broth varies regionally—miso, soy sauce, pork bone, or salt-based. Instant ramen, sold in packets or cups, is a cheap staple for students and budget-conscious eaters: {I lived on ramen in college}.

Ramifications are the consequences or results that branch out from a decision or event, especially ones that are complex, far-reaching, or unforeseen. The word carries a sense of spreading effects—one action leading to many outcomes: {We hadn't considered the full ramifications of the merger}. Often used in contexts where complications multiply: {The legal ramifications could take years to sort out}.

Ramming is the act of driving something forcefully into or against something else. Ships ram enemy vessels; battering rams breach gates. A car might ram another from behind. The word emphasizes violent, deliberate impact: {He kept ramming his shoulder against the door}. To ram something down someone's throat is to force them to accept it.

A ramp is an inclined surface connecting two levels—a gentler alternative to stairs. Wheelchair ramps provide accessibility; loading ramps let vehicles drive onto platforms. To ramp up is to increase intensity or production: {We're ramping up hiring for the holiday season}. To ramp down is the opposite. In skateboarding, a ramp is a curved structure for launching tricks.

A rampage is a violent, destructive rush—a burst of uncontrolled aggression: {The gunman went on a rampage through the building}. Animals rampage when they charge wildly; crowds rampage during riots. The word extends to any unchecked force: {The virus rampaged through the population}. To be {on the rampage} is to be in such a state.

Rampages is the plural of rampage and also its third-person singular verb form. A rampage is a period of violent, destructive, or uncontrolled behavior, often involving movement through an area while causing damage: {The elephant went on a rampage through the village}. To rampage is to engage in such behavior. The word suggests both physical destruction and a loss of restraint, whether describing animals, angry crowds, or metaphorically, things like wildfires or disease outbreaks.

Rampaging describes violent, uncontrolled movement or behavior—rushing about wildly, often causing destruction. A rampaging {mob} tears through streets; a rampaging {elephant} tramples everything in its path. The word implies both motion and mayhem: {Rampaging wildfires consumed thousands of acres}. Something rampaging doesn't just destroy—it moves aggressively while doing so.

Rampant describes something spreading or growing unchecked, usually something undesirable: {rampant corruption}, {rampant inflation}, {disease running rampant}. The word suggests vigorous, unrestrained proliferation that has gotten out of control. In heraldry, rampant describes an animal depicted standing on its hind legs with forelegs raised, as in a {lion rampant}—the posture suggesting aggressive vitality that connects to the word's broader sense of unbridled force.

Ramparts are the defensive walls or embankments surrounding a fortification, typically broad enough to walk on and often topped with a parapet for protection. The word appears in "The Star-Spangled Banner": {the rockets' red glare, the bombs bursting in air, gave proof through the night that our flag was still there—o'er the ramparts we watched}. Figuratively, ramparts are any protective barriers: {the last ramparts of democracy}.

Ramps are inclined surfaces connecting different levels, allowing gradual ascent or descent: wheelchair ramps, highway on-ramps, loading ramps. To ramp up is to increase intensity or scale: {Production ramped up before the holidays}. Separately, ramps are wild leeks with a pungent garlic-onion flavor, foraged in spring across eastern North America and prized by chefs.

A ramrod is a rod for pushing ammunition down the barrel of a muzzle-loading firearm, or for cleaning gun barrels. The word extends to anything straight and rigid: {ramrod posture}, {sitting ramrod straight}. A ramrod is also someone who pushes things through with force and efficiency—to ramrod a project is to drive it forward relentlessly, overcoming obstacles by sheer will.

Rams is the plural of ram, an uncastrated adult male sheep, known for thick curved horns and aggressive head-butting during mating season. By extension, a ram is any device that batters or forces: a battering ram breaks down doors, a hydraulic ram drives pistons. To ram is to strike forcefully or push something into place: {The ship rammed the dock}. {He rammed his clothes into the suitcase}. (Capitalized Rams refers to sports teams.)

Ramshackle describes something poorly constructed or badly deteriorated—usually a building or vehicle that looks ready to fall apart: {a ramshackle cabin}, {a ramshackle bus held together with wire and prayer}. The word suggests neglect and decay rather than deliberate shoddiness, often with a hint of picturesque charm despite the disrepair.

Ran is the past tense of run. All the meanings of run appear with ran in past contexts: {She ran five miles}, {He ran for office}, {The engine ran smoothly}, {Colors ran in the wash}, {The show ran for three seasons}. The past participle is run, not ran: {I have run} rather than {I have ran}, though the latter appears in casual speech.

A ranch is a large farm for raising livestock, especially cattle or horses, typically in the western United States or similar terrain. The word evokes open rangeland and cowboy culture. Ranch extends to other large-scale agricultural operations: {a chicken ranch}, {a mink ranch}. As a verb, to ranch is to work or manage such a property. Ranch dressing is a creamy salad dressing, and ranch house describes a single-story home style—both named for associations with casual Western living.

A rancher is someone who owns or operates a ranch—a large farm for raising livestock, especially cattle or sheep. The term is most common in the American West and other regions with extensive grazing land: {The rancher rode out to check on the herd}. Rancher can also refer to a ranch-style house, a single-story home with a long, low profile.

Ranchers are people who own or operate ranches—large farms devoted to raising livestock, especially cattle or sheep. The term is most common in the American West and similar regions where extensive grazing land supports large-scale animal husbandry: {The ranchers worried about drought conditions affecting their herds}.

Ranches are large farms, especially in the American West, devoted primarily to raising livestock such as cattle, horses, or sheep on extensive grazing land. The term extends to any large agricultural property: {dude ranches} offer tourists a taste of cowboy life, while {chicken ranches} raise poultry. Ranch also functions as a verb meaning to work on or manage such a property: {Her family has ranched in Montana for four generations}.

Ranching is the business of raising livestock—especially cattle, sheep, or horses—on large tracts of land called ranches. The work involves breeding, grazing, and managing herds for meat, wool, or other products. {His family has been ranching in Montana for four generations.} {Cattle ranching transformed the American West.}

Rancid describes fats or oils that have gone bad, developing a sharp, unpleasant smell and taste through oxidation or bacterial action: {rancid butter}, {The nuts had turned rancid}. The word extends to anything stale and foul-smelling. Figuratively, rancid can describe something morally offensive or disgusting: {rancid politics}, {a rancid sense of humor}.

Random describes something without pattern, order, or predictable cause. A random {selection} gives every option equal chance. Random {events} lack discernible connection: {We kept running into random people from college}. In casual speech, random means arbitrary or unexpected: {That was so random}. As a noun, {at random} means without deliberate choice: {Names were drawn at random}.

Randomness is the quality of lacking pattern, predictability, or purpose. In statistics and computing, randomness describes outcomes determined by chance rather than design: {The randomness of the shuffle ensures fair card distribution}. Colloquially, randomness often means quirky unpredictability or arbitrary variety: {I love the randomness of thrift store finds}. The word can carry positive connotations of spontaneity or negative ones of chaos, depending on context.

The noun and verb range always implies an extent, possibly in space but more often figuratively, in which there are different locations or values. Many ranges are specifically limited: The range of prices was surprisingly low. Values ranged from -7 to 3.5. People often use range when there is no strict relation or scalar quality among items named and they could just as easily use number or a similar word: We have quite a range of dining choices. Physical things designated as ranges are either mountain groups (the Sangre de Cristo range), or an open area for animal grazing. In American English, a kitchen cooking appliance is also called a range.

A ranger is someone who patrols and protects a defined territory. Park rangers manage wildlife areas and enforce regulations: {The ranger warned us about bears in the campground}. Forest rangers monitor woodlands for fires and illegal activity. Army Rangers are elite infantry soldiers trained for special operations. In sports, Rangers appears in team names. The word suggests someone who ranges—moves across wide territory. (Capitalized Ranger often refers to specific organizations or teams.)

Rangers are people who patrol and protect wilderness areas, parks, or forests: {The ranger warned us about bears in the campground}. The term also applies to soldiers trained for raids and reconnaissance, or members of law enforcement units like the Texas Rangers. In sports and games, a ranger is often a skilled archer or scout character. (Capitalized Rangers refers to sports teams.)

To rank something is to assign it a place on a scale or in a hierarchy, the way you might rank your priorities, or how a reviewer might rank universities. The rank of someone or something is their assigned place, like the rank of private in the army, or a page rank algorithm that search engines use. An unrelated adjective rank characterizes excess of various kinds: rank corruption suggests that it’s out of control; rank vegetation may be hard to penetrate. A rank smell is offensive.

Ranked describes things arranged in order of status, ability, or importance. A ranked {list} shows items from highest to lowest. In competitive gaming and sports, ranked {matches} or ranked {play} determines a player's standing relative to others: {I only play ranked when I'm warmed up}. A highly ranked {player} or {team} sits near the top of the standings.

Ranking refers to position in an ordered sequence, usually by merit, importance, or achievement: {Her ranking among tennis players rose to third}. Rankings are the ordered lists themselves: {college rankings}, {search engine rankings}. As an adjective, ranking means highest in position: {the ranking officer present}. To rank is to assign or hold such a position.

Ranks are positions in a hierarchy—military ranks from private to general, academic ranks from instructor to professor. To rank is to assign or hold a position: {She ranks third in her class}. The ranks refers to ordinary members as distinct from leadership: {rising through the ranks}. Rank and file has the same sense. Something rank-and-file comes from ordinary members rather than officials.

To ransack is to search through a place thoroughly, usually in a disorderly or destructive way: {Burglars ransacked the apartment}. The word implies turning things over, opening drawers, leaving a mess. It can also mean to plunder or loot: {Vikings ransacked coastal villages}. The searching and plundering senses often overlap—you ransack looking for valuables, taking what you find.

Ransacked is the past tense of ransack, meaning to search thoroughly and messily, typically while stealing or looking for something valuable. The word implies disorder left behind—drawers pulled out, contents scattered: {The burglars ransacked the apartment}. It can also describe aggressive searching without theft: {She ransacked her purse for the receipt}.

Ransacking is the act of searching through a place thoroughly and often destructively, usually looking for something valuable or specific. When someone ransacks a room, they turn it upside down, leaving chaos behind. {Burglars had ransacked the apartment, emptying every drawer.} The word carries connotations of violation and disorder—a ransacked space has been not just searched but disrupted, with belongings strewn about carelessly.

Ransom is money demanded or paid for the release of a captive. Kidnappers hold victims for ransom; historically, prisoners of war were ransomed back to their families. The verb means to pay such a price or to hold someone for payment: {They ransomed the hostages for two million dollars}. A king's ransom is an enormous sum. In computing, ransomware encrypts files and demands payment for their release.

Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts a victim's files or locks their system, demanding payment for restoration. Attackers typically require cryptocurrency to avoid tracing: {The hospital paid the ransom after ransomware crippled their network}. Some ransomware threatens to publish stolen data if demands aren't met. The term combines ransom with software.

A rant is an extended outburst of complaint or criticism, often loud, emotional, and only loosely organized: {He went on a rant about the government}. To rant is to deliver such a speech: {She ranted for twenty minutes about the parking situation}. The word implies excessive length or intensity—someone ranting has stopped making measured arguments and started venting.

Ranting is speaking or writing at length in an angry, impassioned, or vehement way. The word usually implies someone has gone on too long or too intensely: {He went on a rant about parking tickets}. A rant may be justified outrage or tedious complaint—context determines which. {She was ranting about the new policy for twenty minutes.}

Rants are lengthy, passionate outbursts of complaint or criticism. Someone rants when they speak or write at heated length about something that angers them: {His rants about government waste go on for hours}. The word suggests more emotion than logic, and often implies the speaker has gone on too long. Online, rants are a recognized genre—extended venting that readers may find cathartic or tedious.

Rap connects ideas of striking and speaking quickly. A rap is a sharp knock or blow: {a rap on the door}, {a rap on the knuckles}. To rap is to strike sharply, or to speak rhythmically over a beat—the musical genre where performers deliver rapid, rhyming lyrics. A rap is also an accusation or charge: {a murder rap}, {beat the rap}. To {take the rap} is to accept blame, often for someone else. To rap can also mean to talk or chat: {Let's rap about it}.

Rape is forced sexual intercourse—sex without consent, typically through violence, threats, or incapacitation. The word carries its full gravity in legal and personal contexts: {She reported the rape to police}. Extended uses describe violation or plunder: {the rape of the countryside}. As a verb, to rape is to commit this act. Separately, rape is a plant related to mustard, cultivated for its oil-rich seeds (canola).

Rapid means fast or happening quickly. A rapid {pulse} beats faster than normal. Rapid {growth} occurs over a short time. Rapids (usually plural) are sections of a river where the current moves swiftly over rocks, creating turbulent water: {We shot the rapids in a kayak}. Rapid suggests speed that may feel urgent or accelerated.

Rapidfire describes something delivered in quick, continuous succession—like bullets from an automatic weapon. Rapidfire {questions} come one after another without pause. A rapidfire {wit} produces quick responses. The word emphasizes speed and relentlessness: {The comedian's rapidfire delivery left the audience breathless}. Also spelled rapid-fire or rapid fire.

Rapids are sections of a river where the water flows swiftly over rocks and other obstacles, creating turbulent, choppy surface conditions. The term is almost always plural, treating the stretch of rough water as a collective feature rather than a single point. Rapids are graded by difficulty for whitewater sports, from Class I (easy) to Class VI (extremely dangerous). {We portaged around the rapids rather than risk capsizing.}

A rapier is a slender, sharply pointed sword designed primarily for thrusting rather than cutting, favored in European dueling from the 16th through 18th centuries. The word survives mainly in figurative use: {rapier wit} describes verbal sharpness that cuts with precision and elegance.

Rapiers are slender, sharply pointed swords designed primarily for thrusting rather than cutting. The weapon was favored in European dueling from the 16th to 18th centuries, prized for its precision and reach. {Rapier wit} describes verbal sharpness—quick, pointed, and penetrating.

Rapped is the past tense of rap, which means to strike sharply: {She rapped on the door}. A judge raps a gavel. To rap can also mean to criticize or blame: {The report rapped the agency for poor oversight}. Separately, to rap is to perform rap music—rhythmic spoken verse over beats: {He rapped about growing up in Detroit}.

Rappelling is descending a steep surface by sliding down a rope in a controlled manner, using friction devices or body position to regulate speed. Climbers rappel down cliffs after ascending; rescue teams rappel from helicopters. The British term is abseiling. {We spent the afternoon rappelling down the canyon walls.}

A rapper is a performer who delivers rhythmic, rhyming speech over a beat—the vocal artist in hip-hop music. The style emerged from African American communities in the 1970s. Rapper can also mean one who raps in the older sense: someone who knocks or strikes sharply, as with a door knocker.

Rappers are performers who deliver rhythmic, rhyming vocals over beats—the central figures in hip-hop music. The term covers everyone from underground artists to global superstars. A rapper's skill is measured by flow, wordplay, and delivery: {She's one of the best rappers alive}. The singular rapper denotes the occupation or identity: {He started as a rapper before moving into acting}.

Rapping is performing rhythmic, rhyming speech over a beat—the vocal style central to hip-hop music. A rapper delivers verses with precise timing, wordplay, and flow. Beyond music, rapping can mean knocking sharply {rapping on the door} or criticizing {rapping the administration for its failures}. To {take the rap} is to accept blame.

Raps is the plural of rap—a quick, sharp knock or blow: {raps on the door}, {raps on the knuckles}. It also refers to multiple rap songs or performances: {His early raps showed raw talent}. The verb form means to knock sharply or to perform rap music: {She raps better than most in the game}.

A raptor is a bird of prey—eagles, hawks, falcons, owls, and their kin. These birds hunt with sharp talons and hooked beaks. The word has been revived for the dinosaurs now understood to be ancestral to birds: {The velociraptor scenes in Jurassic Park terrified audiences}. Raptor also names various military vehicles and aircraft.

Raptors are birds of prey—eagles, hawks, falcons, owls, and their kin—characterized by hooked beaks, powerful talons, and keen eyesight adapted for hunting. The term comes from a Latin word meaning to seize, reflecting how these birds capture prey. In popular culture, raptors also refers to the velociraptors of Jurassic Park fame, though actual velociraptors were much smaller than their movie counterparts. {The raptors circled overhead, scanning for rodents.} (Capitalized Raptors is the Toronto NBA team.)

Rapture is a state of intense joy or ecstasy—being so transported by emotion that you're lifted out of ordinary experience: {She listened in rapture}. In Christian theology, the Rapture is the anticipated event when believers will be caught up to meet Christ in the air before or during the end times. The adjective rapturous describes such overwhelming delight: {rapturous applause}.

Rare describes something uncommon or infrequent—a rare {disease}, a rare {opportunity}, a rare {book}. What's rare is often valuable precisely because of its scarcity. Rare also describes meat cooked briefly, leaving the center red and cool: {I'll have my steak rare}. In older usage, rare meant exceptionally fine: {a rare treat}.

Rarity is the quality of being rare—uncommon, scarce, or seldom encountered. A rarity is something that possesses this quality: {A modest politician is a rarity}. The word applies to collectibles, natural phenomena, or human qualities alike: {The stamp's rarity makes it valuable}. In cooking, rarity describes how little meat has been cooked, though this sense is less common than the adjective rare.

A rascal is a mischievous or dishonest person. The word often carries affection rather than real disapproval—parents call children rascals when they're being playfully naughty: {You little rascal, you ate all the cookies}. Applied to adults, it can suggest charming roguishness or, less kindly, untrustworthiness.

Rascals is the plural of rascal—a mischievous or dishonest person. The word often carries affection rather than condemnation, especially for children: {Those little rascals got into the cookie jar again}. Applied to adults, it suggests cunning or roguish behavior: {The rascals in Congress voted themselves another raise}.

Rash describes actions taken too quickly, without enough thought: {a rash decision}, {Don't do anything rash}. The word suggests impulsiveness that may lead to regret. Separately, a rash is an outbreak of red spots or irritation on the skin—from allergies, illness, or contact with irritants. By extension, a rash of something is a sudden cluster of occurrences: {a rash of burglaries}.

Raspberries are small, soft berries composed of tiny clustered drupelets, typically red but also available in black, purple, or golden varieties. They grow on thorny canes and have a distinctive hollow core where the stem detaches. Raspberries are eaten fresh, in jams, or as flavoring. Separately, to blow a raspberry is to make a sputtering sound with the tongue and lips, expressing derision or contempt: {The crowd blew raspberries at the referee}.

A raspberry is a small, soft fruit made of clustered drupelets, typically red but sometimes black or golden. Raspberries grow on thorny canes and are eaten fresh, in jams, or as flavoring. A raspberry is also a rude sound made by sticking out the tongue and blowing—the noise resembles the fruit's bumpy texture. To {blow a raspberry} is to make this sound, expressing mockery or contempt.

Raspy describes a rough, grating quality in sound—typically a voice that's harsh or scratchy: {Her voice was raspy from shouting at the concert}. The texture suggests friction or wear, whether from illness, overuse, or natural timbre. Some singers cultivate a raspy quality for its emotional rawness.

The rodent designated as rat is unwelcome and despised nearly everywhere (exception: the laboratory rat) because of its association with filth and disease. Figurative uses of rat take on these negative characteristics. If you call a person a rat, you imply that they are despicable or disloyal. If you smell a rat, you suspect betrayal or dishonesty. The verb rat is also negative and means to inform on, desert, or to work as a scab. The exception is to rat your hair, that is, make it appear more voluminous.

Ratatouille is a French vegetable stew originating from Nice, made by sautéing or stewing summer vegetables—typically tomatoes, eggplant, zucchini, bell peppers, and onions—with olive oil and herbs like basil and thyme. The dish can be served hot or cold, as a main course or side. {We made ratatouille with vegetables from the garden.} The word gained wider recognition from the 2007 Pixar film featuring a rat who becomes a chef.

A ratchet is a mechanical device with angled teeth that allows movement in one direction only—a wheel or bar clicks forward but can't slip back. The verb ratchet describes incremental, usually irreversible change: {Tensions ratcheted up throughout the negotiations}. In slang, ratchet is an adjective meaning trashy, loud, or lacking class—applied especially to women: {That party was ratchet}. The slang likely derives from a mispronunciation of "wretched."

The noun rate is related to ratio, and that’s a good way to remember its meanings. Rate characterizes a quantity or amount in relation to a unit or standard (rate of speed, currency exchange rate). To rate something is to assign it a place on a scale, in a slightly more informal way than rank does. We rate movies, restaurants, and other things we experience. Something top rated or highly rated enjoys a good reputation.

Rates are measurements of one quantity per unit of another—speed is distance per time, interest is percentage per year. The word often appears in contexts of cost or frequency: {crime rates}, {mortgage rates}, {hourly rates}. To rate something is to assign it a value or rank: {How would you rate the service?} If something {rates}, it deserves consideration: {That barely rates a mention}.

Rather expresses preference or degree. It can mean somewhat: {The movie was rather long}. It can mean instead or preferably: {I'd rather stay home}. It can correct or clarify: {He's not lazy—rather, he's overwhelmed}. British speakers use it as emphatic agreement: {Would you like tea? Rather!} The phrase {would rather} expresses what someone prefers: {She'd rather die than apologize}.

A rating is an evaluation or ranking on a scale. Movies receive ratings indicating age-appropriateness. Credit ratings assess financial reliability. TV ratings measure viewership. A ship's rating historically classified its size and armament; a sailor's rating was their rank. To give something a rating is to assign it a score: {The restaurant has a five-star rating}. Ratings can also refer to harsh criticism: {She gave him a real rating for being late}.

Ratings are evaluations expressed as scores or rankings, typically measuring quality, popularity, or performance. Television ratings measure viewership: {The show was canceled due to low ratings}. Credit ratings assess financial reliability. Movie ratings indicate age-appropriateness. Approval ratings track public opinion of politicians. Online ratings let users score products, restaurants, or services: {The hotel has five-star ratings across the board}.

A ratio is a relationship between two quantities showing how many times one contains or is contained within the other, typically expressed with a colon or as a fraction: {The ratio of teachers to students is 1:15}. Ratios are fundamental to mathematics, cooking, finance, and countless practical applications. In internet slang, to ratio someone means to receive more engagement (likes, retweets) on a reply than the original post received, signaling widespread disagreement: {That take got ratioed hard}.

A ration is a fixed allowance of something, typically food or supplies distributed during scarcity: {war rations}, {emergency rations}. Governments ration goods when demand exceeds supply. The plural rations often means provisions generally: {The soldiers received their daily rations}. To ration is to distribute in controlled amounts or to limit consumption: {We rationed the water carefully}.

Rational describes thinking based on reason rather than emotion or impulse. A rational {decision} follows from logical analysis; a rational {person} weighs evidence before acting. In mathematics, a rational {number} can be expressed as a ratio of two integers. The word often contrasts with emotional or irrational: {Let's be rational about this}. To rationalize is to construct reasons for behavior, often after the fact.

Rationality is the quality of being guided by reason rather than emotion or impulse. It implies logical thinking, sound judgment, and decisions based on evidence: {She admired his rationality in a crisis}. In philosophy and economics, rationality often means acting to maximize one's interests given available information—though what counts as rational varies by context and who's defining it.

Rationalization is the mental process of constructing plausible but often false justifications for behavior or beliefs that might otherwise seem unreasonable. When someone rationalizes, they're not lying outright but rather convincing themselves that questionable choices were actually sensible: {He rationalized the expense as an investment in his career}. In business contexts, rationalization refers to reorganizing operations for greater efficiency, typically involving cuts to workforce or redundant systems.

To rationalize is to devise seemingly logical explanations for behavior or beliefs that are actually driven by emotion, self-interest, or irrational impulse: {He rationalized his affair as saving his marriage}. The word implies self-deception—making excuses that sound reasonable but aren't the real reasons. In British English and technical contexts, rationalize also means to reorganize for greater efficiency: {The company rationalized its supply chain}.

Rationalizing is constructing logical-sounding reasons to justify beliefs, decisions, or behaviors that actually stem from less acceptable motives. The process works backward—starting with the conclusion and finding arguments to support it: {He kept rationalizing his gambling as a form of investment}. In mathematics, rationalizing means eliminating radicals from a denominator.

Rationing is the controlled distribution of scarce resources, limiting how much each person can have. Governments impose rationing during wartime or emergencies: {During the war, sugar and gasoline were subject to rationing}. The verb ration means to distribute in fixed portions or to limit consumption: {We rationed our water supply to make it last the week}.

Rations are fixed portions of food or supplies distributed to people, especially soldiers, prisoners, or those affected by scarcity. During wartime, governments ration essentials like meat, sugar, and fuel. The verb means to distribute in controlled amounts or restrict consumption: {We had to ration our water}. Emergency rations are compact provisions for survival situations.
Rats is a mild expression of disappointment or frustration, similar to nuts.

Rattle is a rapid succession of short, sharp sounds—the clatter of hail on a roof, dice in a cup, or a snake's warning. A rattle is also a baby's toy designed to make this sound when shaken. To rattle someone is to unsettle or fluster them: {The interview questions rattled her}. To {rattle off} a list is to recite it quickly. To {rattle around} a large space is to occupy it loosely, with room to spare.

Rattled means shaken or unnerved, having lost one's composure or confidence: {The heckling rattled the speaker}. Someone who is rattled feels anxious and struggles to think clearly: {She was too rattled to remember her lines}. The word suggests disruption of normal calm—like objects clattering around loose in a container.

Rattles is a rapid series of short, sharp sounds—or the objects that make them. A baby's rattle produces such sounds when shaken. The death rattle is the gurgling breath of someone near death. To rattle someone is to unsettle them: {The question clearly rattled her}. To {rattle off} a list is to recite it quickly. {Rattles} also names a respiratory disease in horses and sheep.

A rattlesnake is a venomous American pit viper with a segmented rattle at the end of its tail that buzzes when the snake feels threatened. The warning sound is distinctive and immediately recognizable: {We froze when we heard the rattlesnake}. Rattlesnakes range from the southwestern deserts to eastern forests, and their bite can be fatal without treatment.

Rattlesnakes is the plural of rattlesnake, a venomous pit viper native to the Americas, named for the segmented rattle at the end of its tail. The rattle produces a distinctive warning buzz when the snake feels threatened: {We heard rattlesnakes before we saw them}. Rattlesnakes range from the timber rattlesnake of eastern forests to the diamondbacks of the desert Southwest.

Raunchy means sexually explicit, crude, or vulgar: {a raunchy joke}, {raunchy lyrics}. The word suggests earthiness rather than elegance—more locker room than boudoir. Something raunchy may also be simply sleazy or run-down: {a raunchy bar on the edge of town}. The tone is mildly disapproving but often affectionate.

Ravage means to cause severe, widespread damage or destruction. Armies ravage cities, storms ravage coastlines, disease ravages populations. The word implies thoroughness—not just harm but devastation: {Years of drought had ravaged the farmland}. As a noun, usually plural: {the ravages of time}, {the ravages of war}. Ravage suggests violent force leaving ruin in its wake.

Ravaged describes something that has been severely damaged or devastated, typically by destructive forces over time. A ravaged {landscape} has been ruined by war, fire, or neglect. A {disease-ravaged body} shows the destructive effects of illness. The word emphasizes visible, lasting damage rather than sudden destruction: {Her face was ravaged by grief}.

Ravages are the destructive effects of something over time—damage that accumulates through sustained force or neglect: {the ravages of war}, {the ravages of time}, {the ravages of addiction}. The word almost always appears in plural and typically follows "the." To ravage is to cause such destruction: {Disease ravaged the population}.

Rave is a noun and verb with contrasting meanings, all of which suggest high enthusiasm and energy. To rave about something is to talk with great enthusiasm – usually in praise, but sometimes in condemnation. If someone is just raving, they are speaking uncontrollably; if they’re also speaking incoherently, they may be raving mad. A rave may be a large party, or it may be short for rave review, that is, a very positive assessment about a place or experience.

A raven is a large black bird of the crow family, known for its intelligence and harsh croaking call. Ravens appear frequently in mythology and literature as symbols of death, prophecy, or ill omen. The word also describes a glossy blue-black color, especially of hair: {raven locks}, {raven-haired}. As a verb, to raven is to devour greedily or prey upon—an older usage now mainly literary. (Capitalized Raven may be a given name or team mascot.)

Ravenous means extremely hungry, suggesting a hunger so intense it feels consuming or predatory: {I skipped lunch and was ravenous by dinner}. The word extends to any fierce, greedy desire: {a ravenous appetite for power}, {ravenous fans buying up tickets}. It implies not just wanting but wanting urgently, almost desperately.

Ravens are large black birds of the crow family, known for their intelligence and harsh croaking calls. They appear throughout mythology and literature as omens or symbols of death. The verb raven (accent on the second syllable) means to devour greedily or to prowl hungrily for prey: {The wolves ravened through the forest}.

A raver is someone who attends raves—all-night dance parties featuring electronic music, often held in warehouses or outdoor venues. The term emerged in the late 1980s with rave culture and carries associations with techno, ecstasy, glow sticks, and marathon dancing: {The ravers didn't leave until sunrise}. More loosely, raver can describe anyone who parties hard or with abandon.
