Something riddled with problems or contradictions is full of them.

Riddled means full of holes or permeated throughout by something undesirable. A body riddled with bullets has been shot many times. A system riddled with corruption is thoroughly compromised. The word suggests damage or infestation so extensive that the thing can hardly hold together: {The old fence was riddled with termites}. Separately, to riddle is to pose riddles or speak enigmatically.

The verb ride suggests accompanied movement through space, where the other party is an animal (ride a horse) or the driver of a vehicle (ride in a car, ride in a train). You can also ride a small vehicle, like an elevator, bicycle, or motorcycle. If one abstract thing rides on another, the first depends on the second: The couple’s offer to buy the house rides on whether or not they qualify for a loan. A ride is an instance of riding. A ride is also a device at an amusement park, such as a roller coaster or carousel.

A rider is someone who rides—a horse, a bicycle, a motorcycle, a bus. The term extends to passengers generally: {The subway had few riders at that hour}. In legal and legislative contexts, a rider is a clause or provision attached to a document, often slipped into a bill to pass something that couldn't succeed on its own: {They added a rider to the spending bill}. A rider to a contract specifies additional terms or conditions.

Riders is the plural of rider—people who ride horses, bicycles, motorcycles, or transit. The word extends to additional clauses attached to legislative bills or contracts: {The bill passed only after they stripped out the controversial riders}. Insurance riders add coverage beyond standard policies. A rider may also list a performer's requirements for a venue: {The band's rider specified no brown M&Ms}.

Rides is the plural of ride—journeys in a vehicle or on an animal, or amusement park attractions: {The rides at the fair were terrifying}. As a verb, rides means to travel on or in something: {She rides the bus to work}, {He rides a motorcycle}. To say someone {rides} another person is to criticize or nag persistently. In sexual slang, to ride is to be on top during intercourse.

Rideshare refers to transportation arranged through a smartphone app, connecting passengers with drivers using personal vehicles. Services like Uber and Lyft have made rideshare the dominant term for this model: {I'll just rideshare to the airport}. The word also covers traditional carpooling—multiple people sharing a vehicle to split costs or reduce traffic. As a verb: {We rideshared to work for years}.

Ridesharing is the practice of sharing car trips with others, either by carpooling with acquaintances or by using app-based services that connect drivers with passengers. The term now primarily refers to services like Uber and Lyft: {I took a rideshare from the airport}. The compound appears as one word, two words, or hyphenated.

A ridge is a long, narrow elevated strip—the top edge where two slopes meet. Mountain ridges form where peaks connect. A roof ridge is where two slanted surfaces join at the top. Ridges appear on smaller scales too: the ridges of corduroy fabric, the ridges on a fingertip. To ridge is to form into ridges: {Wind ridged the sand into parallel lines}.

Ridges are long, narrow elevations—the raised lines on a surface or the crest where two slopes meet. A mountain ridge forms the spine of a range; fingerprint ridges create unique patterns; ridges on a potato chip add crunch. The verb means to form such elevations: {The wind ridged the sand into parallel lines}. Anything with a prominent linear rise can be ridged: {a ridged forehead}, {ridged armor}.

Ridicule is mockery intended to make someone or something appear foolish or contemptible. To ridicule is to subject to such treatment: {The press ridiculed his proposal}. Unlike teasing, which can be affectionate, ridicule carries genuine scorn. Something ridiculous invites ridicule—though the adjective has softened to mean merely absurd or laughable.

Ridiculous describes something so absurd or unreasonable that it invites mockery or disbelief. A ridiculous {price} is outrageously high; a ridiculous {claim} lacks any credible basis. The word carries strong dismissive force—calling something ridiculous signals you find it unworthy of serious consideration. In casual use, ridiculous often gets softened to mean impressively extreme: {That dunk was ridiculous}. The related noun ridiculousness and adverb ridiculously follow the same patterns.

Riding is the act of sitting on and controlling a horse, bicycle, or other vehicle: {She goes riding every weekend}. It extends to being carried as a passenger: {riding in the back seat}. To be {riding high} is to enjoy success or good fortune. In some contexts, riding is vulgar slang for sexual intercourse. In Canada and parts of Britain, a riding is an electoral district.

A riff is a short, repeated musical phrase, especially in rock, jazz, or blues—the memorable instrumental hook that anchors a song: {That guitar riff is iconic}. Extended from music, to riff is to improvise or elaborate freely on a theme: {She riffed on the idea for ten minutes}. The word suggests creative spontaneity built on a foundation.

Riffing is improvising or elaborating freely, originally from jazz where musicians riff by playing variations on a melodic phrase. The term extends to any spontaneous creative elaboration: {She was just riffing on the idea, not proposing anything serious}. Comedians riff when they improvise around a topic. In casual use, riffing suggests playful, loosely structured exploration rather than polished performance.

Riffraff is people considered worthless, disreputable, or of the lowest social class—the undesirable element: {The doorman kept the riffraff out}. The term is dismissive and often snobbish, used by those who consider themselves superior. It can be playfully self-deprecating: {Just us riffraff here tonight}.

Riffs are short, repeated musical phrases, especially the catchy guitar patterns that anchor rock and blues songs: {The opening riff of "Smoke on the Water" is instantly recognizable}. By extension, to riff is to improvise or elaborate on a theme, often playfully: {The comedian riffed on airline travel for twenty minutes}. Someone riffing bounces between related ideas without strict structure.

A rifle is a firearm with a long barrel containing spiral grooves that spin the bullet for accuracy. Rifles are designed for precision at distance, distinguishing them from shotguns and handguns. To rifle through something is to search hastily, rummaging: {She rifled through the drawer looking for her passport}. To rifle also means to steal or plunder.

Rifles are firearms with spiral grooves cut into the barrel, which spin the bullet for greater accuracy over distance. The term distinguishes them from smoothbore weapons like shotguns. Rifles range from hunting and sporting models to military assault weapons. To rifle through something is to search hastily, rummaging: {She rifled through the drawer looking for her keys}. To rifle also means to steal or plunder.

A rift is a crack, split, or gap—especially one caused by breaking apart. Geological rifts are long fractures in the earth's crust where tectonic plates separate. More commonly, rift describes a serious disagreement or estrangement: {a rift between the brothers}, {a growing rift in the party}. The word suggests a relationship once whole, now damaged.

Rifts are breaks or splits in something that was once whole. A rift in rock is a crack or fissure; a rift in a relationship is a serious disagreement that creates distance between people. The word suggests not just separation but tension—something has come apart that perhaps shouldn't have: {A bitter rift developed between the two brothers}. In geology, a rift valley forms where tectonic plates pull apart.

Rig is a general word for various kinds of equipment, or specific equipment when modified or as determined by context. An oil rig is the equipment used for drilling oil. Truckers may refer to a tractor-trailer combination as a rig. In seafaring, the rig is the arrangement of masts and sails on a ship. To rig is to supply something with equipment. To rig also means to manipulate unfairly (rig prices, rig an election).

Rigamarole is a long, complicated, and seemingly pointless procedure or explanation: {You have to go through this whole rigamarole just to get a parking permit}. The word suggests bureaucratic excess or unnecessarily convoluted processes. Also spelled rigmarole.

Rigged describes something manipulated to produce a predetermined outcome. A rigged {election} has been tampered with. A rigged {game} is fixed against fair play. {The whole system is rigged} suggests powerful forces have arranged things to their advantage. In nautical contexts, rigged describes how a ship's sails and masts are configured: {a square-rigged vessel}. To rig something is to set it up, often hastily: {We rigged a shelter from tarps}.

Rigging is the system of ropes, chains, and cables that support and control a ship's masts and sails. By extension, rigging refers to any arrangement of lines and equipment for lifting or supporting: {stage rigging}, {climbing rigging}. To rig something is to set it up, often hastily or improvisingly. Rigging also means fraudulent manipulation: {election rigging}, {price rigging}—the fix is in.

From the original meaning which it still retains—in accordance with what is good and proper—right has developed many meanings in multiple parts of speech to make it a very frequently used word. In addition to its original meaning, right also refers to anything associated with or analogous to the side of the body where the liver is located. In politics, right is associated with conservatism.

Righteous means morally right or justifiable. A righteous person acts according to ethical principles; a righteous cause deserves support. The word carries religious overtones—the righteous shall inherit the earth. Self-righteous describes someone smugly certain of their own virtue. In slang, righteous means excellent or genuine: {That was a righteous guitar solo}. Righteous indignation is anger that feels morally justified.

Righteousness is the quality of being morally right, just, or virtuous. In religious contexts, it often describes alignment with divine will or adherence to moral law: {The prophet spoke of righteousness and justice}. The word carries connotations of moral superiority that can shade into self-righteousness when someone displays their virtue too conspicuously. Righteousness appears frequently in scripture and formal discourse but sounds elevated or archaic in casual speech.

Rights are entitlements—things you're allowed to do, have, or expect. Legal rights are guaranteed by law: {the right to a fair trial}, {voting rights}. Human rights are considered universal: {freedom of speech}, {freedom from torture}. Civil rights concern equal treatment regardless of race, sex, or other characteristics. To {read someone their rights} is to inform an arrested person of their legal protections. Rights also refers to ownership interests: {film rights}, {mineral rights}. To {rights} something is to correct or restore it: {She righted the overturned chair}.

Rightwing describes political positions that emphasize tradition, free markets, limited government, and social hierarchy—the conservative end of the political spectrum. The term comes from seating arrangements in the French Revolutionary assembly, where conservatives sat to the president's right. {Rightwing media}, {rightwing policies}. Often hyphenated as right-wing, especially as an adjective before a noun.

Rigid means stiff and unyielding, not bending or flexing. A rigid structure maintains its shape under pressure: {rigid plastic}, {a rigid frame}. Applied to people or rules, rigid suggests inflexibility to the point of harshness: {rigid discipline}, {rigid adherence to protocol}. Someone rigid in their thinking refuses to adapt or consider alternatives.

Rigmarole is a lengthy, complicated, and often pointless process or set of procedures that seems unnecessarily elaborate. {I had to go through the whole rigmarole of filling out forms just to get a library card.} The word also applies to rambling, incoherent speech or writing that goes on without getting to the point. Both senses carry a tone of exasperation at wasted time and effort.

Rigor is strictness, severity, or exactness in standards or execution: {academic rigor}, {the rigor of scientific method}. The rigors of something are its harsh or demanding conditions: {the rigors of winter}, {the rigors of basic training}. In medicine, rigor describes a sudden chill with shivering, or the stiffening of death (rigor mortis). British spelling: rigour.

Rigs is the plural of rig, which has meanings connected to equipment and setup. Rigs can be large vehicles, especially trucks: {eighteen-wheelers and other big rigs}. Oil rigs are drilling platforms. In computing and gaming, rigs are computer systems, especially custom-built ones: {gaming rigs with high-end graphics cards}. A rig can also be an outfit or costume, or the arrangement of sails and masts on a ship. To rig something is to set it up or, negatively, to manipulate outcomes dishonestly: {They rigged the election}.

Riled means irritated or agitated, worked up into a state of annoyance: {Don't get him riled—he's got a temper}. The word comes from roil, meaning to stir up or disturb. To rile someone is to provoke them: {She knew exactly how to rile her brother}. Riled up intensifies the sense of agitation.

Rim is the outer edge or border of something circular or curved—the rim of a glass, a wheel rim, the rim of a canyon. In basketball, the rim is the metal hoop through which the ball must pass: {The shot bounced off the rim}. To rim is to form or serve as an edge. In sexual slang, to rim is to lick or tongue someone's anus.

Rims are the outer edges or borders of something circular or curved—the rim of a glass, the rim of a canyon, the rim of a basketball hoop. In automotive contexts, rims are the metal wheels on which tires are mounted. Flashy aftermarket rims became a status symbol in car culture: {He put chrome rims on his Escalade}. To rim is to form an edge around something, or in sexual slang, to stimulate the anus with the tongue.

A rimshot is a drumming technique where the stick strikes the drumhead and rim simultaneously, producing a sharp, accented sound. In comedy, a rimshot—or the related sting pattern (ba-dum-tss)—punctuates a punchline, especially a corny joke: {He delivered the pun and waited for the rimshot}. The term now evokes deliberate cheesiness.

Rind is the tough outer layer of certain foods—the skin of citrus fruits, the exterior of cheese, the casing around bacon. Unlike peel, which suggests easy removal, rind implies something thicker and less edible: {Don't eat the rind of that brie}. Watermelon has a rind; apples have skin.

Two words are spelled r-i-n-g and each is both a noun and a verb. First, a ring is a circular band (wedding ring, onion ring). Boxing and wrestling rings are enclosed spaces where those sports happen. When you ring something, you put a ring around it. Second, to ring is to make the characteristic sound of a bell, but if you ring someone, or give them a ring, then you call them on their phone (and make it ring). A ring is an instance of or example of ringing. If something rings true, it sounds like it’s true.

A ringer is someone or something that closely resembles another—often a person brought in as a deceptive substitute: {He's a dead ringer for his father}. In sports, a ringer is a skilled player secretly inserted into a team to gain unfair advantage. Separately, a ringer is someone or something that rings, as in a bell ringer or the ringer on a phone.

Ringing describes a clear, resonant sound that seems to hang in the air—a ringing {bell}, ringing {laughter}, a ringing {endorsement} that leaves no doubt. As a noun, ringing is the sound itself: {the ringing of church bells}, or the persistent tone heard in conditions like tinnitus: {a ringing in my ears}. The adjective can describe anything that resonates with force or conviction: {a ringing declaration of independence}.

A ringleader is the person who leads or organizes a group engaged in some activity—almost always illicit, mischievous, or rebellious. The word suggests someone who instigates trouble and recruits others to join: {Police arrested the ringleader of the smuggling operation}. Among children, the ringleader is whoever hatches the scheme the others follow.

Ringleaders are the people who lead or organize a group engaged in illicit or mischievous activity. The word carries connotations of scheming and influence over others: {Police arrested the ringleaders of the smuggling operation}. A ringleader is often seen as more culpable than followers, the one who instigated trouble others merely joined.

Ringlets are long, spiral curls of hair, typically hanging down: {Her hair fell in perfect ringlets}. The word suggests deliberate styling or naturally bouncy curls, often associated with children or formal hairstyles. A ringlet can also be any small ring or circular shape, though the hair sense dominates.

A ringmaster is the person who announces acts and directs performances in a circus, typically wearing a top hat and tails while commanding the ring. The term extends to anyone who orchestrates or controls a chaotic situation: {She was the ringmaster of our family reunions}. The word often implies theatrical authority and showmanship.

Rings is the plural of ring, which names anything circular and often hollow. Rings include jewelry worn on fingers, the Olympic symbol, circus performance spaces, and the sound a bell makes. To ring is to produce that sound, or to encircle: {The city was ringed by mountains}. Boxing and wrestling happen in rings. Phone calls ring. {That rings a bell} means something sounds familiar. {Rings true} describes what seems genuine.

Ringside is the area immediately surrounding a boxing ring or wrestling ring, where the closest spectators sit. By extension, ringside describes any position offering an unobstructed view of the action: {We had ringside seats for the whole drama}. A {ringside seat} suggests proximity to something exciting or significant, whether literal or figurative.

A ringtone is the sound a mobile phone makes to signal an incoming call or message. Early cell phones offered only simple electronic tones, but modern phones allow customized audio—from preset melodies to snippets of songs: {I set my ringtone to a duck quacking so I'd always know it was my phone}.

Ringtones are the sounds a phone makes to signal an incoming call. Before mobile phones, landlines had mechanical bells; cell phones introduced customizable audio clips. A ringtone might be a simple chime, a snippet of a song, or any sound file: {I set my ringtone to the theme from The Office}. The term extends to notification sounds for texts and apps.

A rink is a smooth surface for skating or a building containing one: an ice rink, a roller rink. The word extends to similar enclosed areas for other sports: a hockey rink, a curling rink. In curling and lawn bowling, a rink also means a team or the lane of play itself. {We reserved the rink for a birthday party.}

Rinse means to wash lightly with water, typically to remove soap, residue, or loose particles: {Rinse the dishes before loading the dishwasher}. A rinse is the act of rinsing or a product used for it—a mouth rinse, a hair rinse that adds temporary color. To {rinse and repeat} follows shampoo instructions but has become shorthand for any mechanical repetition.

A riot is a violent public disturbance by a crowd—people smashing windows, looting, clashing with police. The word extends to anything wild or uncontrolled: {a riot of color}, {Her garden was a riot of wildflowers}. To riot is to participate in such disorder. If something {runs riot}, it spreads unchecked. Informally, a riot is something or someone hilarious: {Your uncle is an absolute riot}.

Rioting is violent public disorder—crowds destroying property, clashing with police, or looting. The term appears in news coverage and legal contexts: {Rioting broke out after the verdict}. Unlike protesting, rioting implies lawlessness and destruction. Someone charged with rioting faces criminal penalties for participating in such disturbances.

Riots are violent public disturbances involving crowds—typically featuring property destruction, clashes with police, or looting. A riot may erupt from protest, celebration, or collective outrage: {The verdict sparked riots across the city}. The verb means to participate in such disorder. Figuratively, something that's {a riot} is extremely funny or entertaining. To {run riot} is to behave without restraint: {Weeds ran riot in the abandoned garden}.

The noun and verb rip imply a ragged separation, one brought about by tearing rather than cutting. If something forceful like a tornado or explosion rips through a place, it leaves damage in its wake. Animals’ claws can rip the flesh from their prey. To rip off means to steal, and this sense is borrowed when you rip a CD or DVD – you copy the content, perhaps without proper permission. A rip is the action or the result of ripping.

A ripcord is a cord that, when pulled, releases a parachute from its pack. The term extends to any cord that activates a mechanism by pulling—inflating a life vest, deploying an emergency brake. Figuratively, to {pull the ripcord} is to bail out of a situation before it gets worse: {She pulled the ripcord on that relationship just in time}.

Ripe describes fruit or grain ready to be picked and eaten—fully developed, at peak flavor. The meaning extends to anything ready for action or use: {ripe for change}, {the time is ripe}. A ripe {old age} is advanced but healthy. Ripe smells are strong and pungent, often unpleasantly so: {The cheese was ripe}.

Ripen means to become ripe—ready for harvest, eating, or use. Fruit ripens on the vine or after picking. The verb extends to anything that develops toward readiness or maturity: {Let the idea ripen before you act on it}. Cheese ripens as it ages. A situation may ripen into crisis. To ripen something is to cause this process: {Ethylene gas ripens bananas}.

Ripening is the process by which fruit or other produce matures and becomes ready to eat. Tomatoes continue ripening after being picked. The word extends to any gradual development toward fullness or completion: {the ripening of their friendship}, {a plan ripening in his mind}.

A ripoff is something that costs too much for what you get—a product, service, or deal that cheats the buyer: {Twenty dollars for a sandwich? What a ripoff!} A ripoff can also be an imitation that steals from an original: {The movie was a ripoff of every heist film ever made}. To rip off is to cheat or steal: {They ripped me off on that car}. Also spelled rip-off.

Ripoffs are instances of being cheated or overcharged, or things that are fraudulent imitations. A {twenty-dollar parking fee is a ripoff}. A cheap knockoff of a designer bag is a ripoff. The word carries indignation—you expected fair value and got exploited instead. Also spelled rip-offs.

Ripped describes something torn or split: {a ripped seam}, {ripped jeans}. The deliberate rips in fashion denim blur the line between damage and style. Ripped also means extremely muscular with visible definition—the body looks like the skin might tear over the muscles: {He got ripped training for the role}. In slang, ripped can mean intoxicated: {We got ripped at the party}.

A ripper is someone or something that rips—tears or cuts forcefully. Jack the Ripper made the word infamous for violent killers. In Australian slang, a ripper is something excellent: {What a ripper of a game!} A seam ripper is a small tool for removing stitches. Software that rips extracts digital content from CDs or DVDs.

Ripple describes small waves or undulations spreading across a surface, like water disturbed by a stone. The word extends to anything that spreads outward in similar fashion: {a ripple of laughter through the crowd}, {ripple effects throughout the economy}. As a verb, to ripple is to form these spreading waves: {Wind rippled the tall grass}. Ripple also names a pattern of wavy lines in fabric or other materials. (Capitalized Ripple is a cryptocurrency platform.)

Ripples are small waves spreading outward from a disturbance—a stone dropped in water creates ripples that expand in concentric circles. The word extends to any similar spreading effect: {The scandal sent ripples through the industry}. As a verb, to ripple is to form such waves or move with a wavelike motion: {Wind rippled the surface of the lake}, {Muscles rippled beneath his skin}.

A riptide is a strong, narrow current flowing outward from shore, capable of pulling swimmers into deeper water. The term is somewhat imprecise—oceanographers prefer "rip current"—but riptide dominates popular usage. Figuratively, a riptide is any powerful force that pulls you in an unwanted direction: {caught in a riptide of debt}, {the emotional riptide of grief}.

Riptides are strong, narrow currents flowing outward from shore, created when water pushed onto beaches by waves funnels back to sea through gaps in sandbars or near jetties. The term is technically a misnomer—they're properly called rip currents, as they're unrelated to tides. They pose a drowning hazard for swimmers who exhaust themselves fighting against the flow: {The lifeguard warned about riptides near the pier}. Figuratively, a riptide suggests being pulled by powerful, dangerous forces: {a riptide of emotions}.

Rise suggests movement upward and has a strong overlap in meaning with increase. The sun rises in the East, usually causing the temperature to rise as well. Wages and prices may rise in a growing economy. A rise is an instance of rising (rise in taxes). When you make bread you let the dough rise, usually more than once; you punch it down after the first rise. To give rise to something is to cause it.

Risen is the past participle of rise. Something that has risen has moved upward or increased: {The sun has risen}, {Prices have risen sharply}. Christ is risen announces the resurrection in Christian tradition. A risen loaf has expanded from yeast. {She had risen through the ranks to become CEO}.

Rising describes upward movement or increase. The rising {sun} comes up over the horizon. Rising {costs} are getting higher. A rising {star} is someone gaining prominence. As a noun, a rising is an uprising or insurrection. The word also indicates approximate age: {a girl of twelve rising thirteen}. In baking, rising refers to dough expanding from yeast or leavening.

Risk is the possibility of loss, damage, or injury that accompanies a course of action. If you take a risk, you act while knowing that the result might be harmful or negative. Risk can also be a verb, where the object is the thing that could be lost or damaged: She risked her life to save her children. The verb risk is also often followed by a gerund phrase: They risked losing their home by taking out the new loan. The common phrase risk factors, is usually just another way of saying risk: Some risk factors will increase, while others will decrease.

Risks are possibilities of loss, harm, or other undesirable outcomes. To take a risk is to act despite uncertainty: {Starting a business involves considerable risk}. As a verb, to risk something is to expose it to potential loss: {She risked her savings on the investment}. You can also risk an action: {I wouldn't risk driving in this weather}. Someone or something {at risk} faces danger or vulnerability. To {risk it} is to proceed despite the odds.

Risky describes something involving the possibility of loss, harm, or failure. A risky {investment} might lose money. A risky {maneuver} could go wrong. The word implies danger without certainty of bad outcome—you might succeed, but the stakes are real: {Starting a business is risky, but the potential rewards are worth it}.

Risotto is an Italian rice dish cooked slowly with broth, stirred continuously until the rice releases its starch and becomes creamy. The base typically includes onion, butter, and white wine, with endless variations: {mushroom risotto}, {seafood risotto}, {risotto Milanese} with saffron. The technique requires patience—the rice absorbs liquid gradually over twenty to thirty minutes.

Risqué describes something slightly indecent or sexually suggestive—provocative enough to raise eyebrows but not explicit enough to shock. A risqué joke pushes boundaries; a risqué outfit reveals more than expected: {Her risqué comments made some guests uncomfortable}. The word implies titillation rather than true offense, suggesting material that's daring but not obscene.

A rite is a formal ceremony or ritual, especially one with religious or cultural significance: {funeral rites}, {rites of passage}, {initiation rites}. The word suggests prescribed actions performed in a traditional manner. A {rite of passage} marks a transition from one stage of life to another—birth, coming of age, marriage, death.

Rites are formal ceremonies or rituals, especially religious or cultural ones marking significant occasions: {funeral rites}, {rites of passage}, {initiation rites}. The word carries solemnity—rites are prescribed actions performed according to tradition or custom, not improvised. {The priest administered the last rites.}

A ritual is a ceremony or series of actions performed according to a prescribed order, often with religious or spiritual significance: {funeral rituals}, {purification rituals}. More loosely, ritual describes any habitual practice that feels meaningful or necessary: {Her morning coffee ritual took exactly fifteen minutes}. As an adjective, ritual describes actions done as part of ceremony or routine: {ritual sacrifice}, {ritual handwashing}. Something done ritually follows established form rather than spontaneous impulse.

Rituals are ceremonies or sequences of actions performed according to a prescribed order, often with religious or cultural significance: {funeral rituals}, {initiation rituals}. The word extends to any habitual practice performed regularly: {morning rituals}, {bedtime rituals}. A ritual can be meaningful tradition or empty formality—the context determines which: {The meeting had become pure ritual, accomplishing nothing}.

Ritzy means fancy, elegant, or ostentatiously luxurious, often with a hint of pretension: {a ritzy hotel}, {a ritzy neighborhood}. The word derives from the Ritz hotels, synonymous with high-end accommodations. Something ritzy impresses with its expense and polish, though the term can carry mild skepticism about whether the elegance is earned or merely showy.

A rival is someone competing for the same goal or position—in sports, business, romance, or any arena where only one can win. The word works as noun, adjective, or verb: {rival teams}, {rival claims}, {Nothing rivals her cooking}. Rivals may be enemies, but the word emphasizes competition more than hostility. {They've been rivals since high school.}

Rivalries are ongoing competitions between people, teams, organizations, or other entities who consistently oppose each other. The word is the plural of rivalry and emphasizes repeated or sustained conflict rather than a single contest. Sports rivalries between traditional opponents often span decades and carry intense emotional weight for fans: {The Yankees-Red Sox rivalry is legendary}. Rivalries can also exist in business, politics, academia, or personal relationships wherever parties compete for the same goals or recognition.

Rivalry is competition between people, teams, or groups striving for the same goal or superiority over each other. The word implies an ongoing relationship—rivals face each other repeatedly: {the rivalry between the two schools goes back decades}. A rivalry can be friendly or bitter, professional or personal. Rivals may push each other to perform better, or their competition may turn hostile.

Rivals are competitors striving for the same objective or superiority in the same domain. The word works as both noun and verb: two athletes can be rivals, and one's skill can rival another's. Rivalry often implies ongoing competition with a specific opponent rather than a general field: {The two schools have been rivals for decades}. Something without rival is unmatched.

A river is a large natural stream of water flowing in a channel toward an ocean, lake, or another river. Rivers drain landscapes, carve valleys, and have shaped human settlement throughout history—cities cluster along them for water, transport, and trade. Figuratively, river describes any flowing mass: {a river of lava}, {rivers of tears}. To {sell someone down the river} is to betray them.

A riverbank is the sloping ground along the edge of a river, where land meets water. Riverbanks may be natural terrain or reinforced with stone or concrete to prevent erosion. The term often evokes pastoral or recreational settings: {We had a picnic on the riverbank.} {Children played along the riverbank while their parents fished.}

A riverboat is a boat designed for navigating rivers, typically with a flat bottom or shallow draft to handle variable water levels and currents. The term often evokes the paddle-wheel steamboats of 19th-century America: {a Mississippi riverboat}, {riverboat gambling}. Modern riverboats range from small craft to large passenger vessels for cruises and casinos.

Rivers is the plural of river, a large natural stream of water flowing in a channel toward the sea, a lake, or another river. Rivers are often named for the lands they traverse or the peoples who lived along them: {the Mississippi}, {the Thames}, {the Nile}. Figuratively, rivers describes abundant flowing quantities: {rivers of tears}, {rivers of blood}, {rivers of money}. (Capitalized Rivers is a surname.)

A rivet is a metal fastener—a pin or bolt with a head on one end, inserted through aligned holes and hammered flat on the other end to join materials permanently. To rivet is to fasten with rivets, but more commonly means to hold attention completely: {The audience sat riveted}. Something riveting is utterly absorbing: {a riveting performance}.

Riveted describes being fastened with rivets—metal pins hammered flat on both ends to join materials permanently. The figurative sense is more common: if you're riveted by something, your attention is completely fixed on it, as if physically fastened in place. {The audience sat riveted throughout the entire performance.} {She was riveted to her seat, unable to look away from the unfolding drama.} Something riveting is intensely absorbing or compelling.

Riveting means completely absorbing attention, so compelling you can't look away: {a riveting performance}, {The documentary was riveting from start to finish}. The metaphor comes from rivets—metal fasteners that hold things firmly in place. Something riveting holds you just as fast. The word often describes narratives, performances, or testimony that grip an audience.

Rivets are metal fasteners—short pins or bolts with a head on one end, inserted through aligned holes and hammered or pressed on the other end to form a second head, permanently joining materials. Before welding became common, rivets held together bridges, ships, and aircraft. As a verb, to rivet is to fasten with rivets, but more often it means to hold someone's attention completely: {The audience sat riveted throughout the performance}. Something riveting is utterly engrossing.

A roach is a cockroach, the flat-bodied insect notorious for infesting homes and surviving almost anything. In drug slang, a roach is the butt end of a marijuana cigarette, held with a roach clip to avoid burning fingers. A roach is also a freshwater fish of Europe. To roach a horse's mane is to trim it short so it stands upright.

Roaches is the plural of roach—a shortened form of cockroach, the hardy household pest notorious for surviving almost anything. In drug slang, a roach is the butt end of a marijuana cigarette, too short to hold without burning your fingers: {He saved the roaches to roll into a new joint}. A roach clip holds these remnants for smoking.

A road is a path or route for travel, typically a prepared surface wide enough for vehicles. Roads connect places: {the road to town}, {a dirt road through the woods}. Figuratively, road suggests a course of action or life direction: {the road to success}, {down that road lies trouble}. On the road means traveling, especially for work: {The band spent months on the road}. A {road trip} is a long-distance journey by car.

A roadblock is a barrier set up to stop or check traffic, typically by police or military: {They set up roadblocks throughout the city looking for the suspect}. Figuratively, a roadblock is any obstacle that halts progress: {Budget cuts proved a major roadblock to the project}. The word emphasizes something that stops movement entirely rather than merely slowing it.

Roadblocks are barriers set up to stop or check traffic, typically by police or military: {They set up roadblocks to catch the escaped prisoner}. Figuratively, a roadblock is any obstacle that prevents progress: {bureaucratic roadblocks}, {We hit a roadblock in the negotiations}. The literal sense often implies authority and control; the figurative sense emphasizes frustration.

A roadie is a member of a rock band's crew who handles equipment during tours—setting up instruments, managing sound systems, loading trucks. The work is physically demanding and largely invisible to audiences. The term derives from being on the road with musicians. By extension, roadie can describe anyone who does behind-the-scenes support work: {I'm basically her roadie for these conferences}.

Roadies are the crew members who travel with musicians or bands to handle the physical labor of live performances—setting up and breaking down equipment, managing sound and lighting rigs, driving trucks, and keeping the show running. The work is grueling and unglamorous: {The roadies had the stage torn down by 2 a.m.} The term derives from being perpetually on the road.

Roadkill is an animal killed by a vehicle on a road: {We saw a deer that had become roadkill}. The word covers both the event and the carcass. Figuratively, roadkill describes someone or something destroyed by larger forces: {Small businesses became roadkill when the chain stores moved in}.

A roadmap is a plan showing how to reach a goal, with stages or milestones marked along the way: {The company released a product roadmap for the next three years}. The metaphor comes from literal road maps—printed guides showing routes between destinations. In tech and business, roadmaps outline planned features, timelines, and priorities. To roadmap something is to create such a plan.

A roadrunner is a ground-dwelling bird of the American Southwest and Mexico, known for running swiftly rather than flying. It preys on lizards, snakes, and insects. The bird's distinctive appearance and speed made it the model for the Looney Tunes character who perpetually eludes Wile E. Coyote.

Roads are paved or unpaved routes for travel, typically by vehicles. A road connects places—cities, neighborhoods, driveways. Roads range from dirt tracks to multilane highways. Figuratively, a road is a path toward something: {the road to success}, {the road to recovery}. {On the road} means traveling, especially for work: {The band spent six months on the road}.

Roadside refers to the edge or border of a road: {We pulled over to the roadside}, {a roadside diner}. As an adjective, it describes things located along roads: roadside {assistance}, roadside {attractions}, roadside {memorials}. The word evokes informal, accessible spots—places you encounter while traveling rather than destinations themselves.

A roadtrip is a long-distance journey by car, typically for pleasure rather than necessity. The appeal lies in the drive itself—scenic routes, spontaneous stops, roadside attractions: {We took a roadtrip down the Pacific Coast Highway}. The word carries associations with freedom and adventure. Also spelled as two words: road trip.

Roam means to move about without a fixed destination or purpose, wandering freely across an area. Animals roam when they range over territory in search of food; people roam when they walk or travel without a particular goal: {We spent the afternoon roaming the city streets}. The word suggests leisurely, unhurried movement rather than aimless confusion. In telecommunications, to roam is to use a mobile device outside one's home network, typically incurring additional charges.

Roaming means wandering without a fixed destination or purpose. Animals roam when they range freely: {Buffalo once roamed the Great Plains}. People roam streets, countryside, or foreign cities. Eyes roam across a scene. In telecommunications, roaming refers to using a mobile phone outside your carrier's home network, often incurring extra charges: {I turned off roaming to avoid fees abroad}.

Roar is a deep, loud, prolonged sound—the cry of a lion, the thunder of an engine, the crash of waves. Animals roar, crowds roar, fires roar. To roar is to make such a sound or to speak very loudly: {The sergeant roared at the recruits}. To roar with laughter is to laugh loudly and freely. Something that roars along moves fast and powerfully: {The economy roared back}.

Roaring describes a deep, loud, continuous sound—the roar of a lion, an engine, a crowd, or flames. A roaring fire burns intensely. Roaring also intensifies: a roaring success, roaring drunk. The Roaring Twenties refers to the 1920s, characterized by economic prosperity, jazz, and cultural exuberance. {Business was roaring along until the crash}.

Roars is the plural of roar—loud, deep, prolonged sounds like those made by lions, crowds, or engines. A stadium roars with cheers; thunder roars across the sky. As a verb, roars describes the act of making such sounds: {The engine roars to life}, {She roars with laughter}. To do something {in roars} suggests waves of loud response: {The audience erupted in roars of approval}.

Roast is a method of cooking with dry heat, typically in an oven: {roast chicken}, {Sunday roast}. A roast is also the cut of meat prepared this way. To roast someone is to mock them harshly, often in a comedic setting where friends take turns insulting the guest of honor: {They roasted him at his retirement party}. Coffee beans are roasted to develop flavor. As an adjective: {roast beef}, {roast potatoes}.

Roasted describes food cooked by dry heat, typically in an oven: {roasted chicken}, {roasted vegetables}. The past tense of roast works the same way—{We roasted marshmallows over the fire}. In slang, roasted means harshly mocked or insulted, often in a comedic setting: {He got roasted by his friends for that haircut}. A celebrity roast features such mockery as entertainment.

Roasting is cooking with dry heat, typically in an oven: {roasting a chicken}, {roasting vegetables}. The method produces browning and concentrated flavors. Roasting also means subjecting someone to intense, often humorous criticism: {His friends gave him a roasting at his birthday party}. As an adjective, roasting describes oppressive heat: {It's roasting in here}.

Roasts are cuts of meat suitable for roasting—cooking with dry heat in an oven or over an open flame. A roast is also the meal or event centered on such a dish: {We're having a roast for Sunday dinner}. In a different sense, a roast is a comedic event where speakers take turns mocking a guest of honor with affectionate insults: {The celebrity roast aired on Comedy Central}. To roast someone informally means to criticize or mock them harshly: {Twitter roasted him for that take}.

To rob is to take property from someone by force or threat: {They robbed the bank}, {He was robbed at gunpoint}. The victim of robbery is a person or place, not the thing taken—you rob a person of their wallet, not rob the wallet itself. Informally, rob describes being cheated or overcharged: {Twenty dollars for parking? What a robbery}. {We was robbed} is the classic protest against an unfair outcome.

Robbed is the past tense of rob—to steal from a person or place, typically by force or threat. You rob a bank, a store, or a person, not the thing taken: {They robbed the convenience store}, {He was robbed at gunpoint}. Informally, robbed describes being cheated or treated unfairly: {We were robbed—that call was terrible}.

A robber is someone who steals through force or threat of force. Unlike a thief, who may steal secretly, a robber confronts victims directly: {The robbers held up the bank}. The term extends to anything that takes unfairly: {These fees are highway robbery}. A robber baron was a ruthless 19th-century industrialist who amassed wealth through exploitative practices.

Robbers is the plural of robber—people who steal, typically through force or threat. The word usually implies direct confrontation: robbers hold up banks, mug pedestrians, or break into occupied homes. {The robbers demanded everyone get on the floor.} Thieves steal; robbers take.

Robbery is theft accomplished through force or threat of force. Unlike burglary, which involves unlawful entry, robbery requires confrontation with a victim: {The robbery occurred at gunpoint}. Armed robbery specifies a weapon was used. Informally, robbery describes any outrageous overcharging: {Twenty dollars for parking? That's robbery}.

Robbing is taking property from someone by force or threat—the act of committing robbery. The word extends to any unfair deprivation: {They're robbing us of our future}. To rob Peter to pay Paul is to solve one problem by creating another. {He was caught robbing a convenience store}.

A robe is a loose, flowing garment that hangs from the shoulders. Bathrobes are worn for warmth or modesty after bathing. Academic robes and judicial robes mark ceremony and office: {The judge entered in her black robe}. To robe is to dress in such a garment, usually for formal occasions. In the plural, robes often suggests ceremonial dress: {robes of state}.

Robes are loose, flowing garments worn for ceremony, authority, or comfort. Judges wear robes in court; graduates wear robes at commencement; monks wear robes as religious dress. At home, a robe is a bathrobe or dressing gown: {She wrapped herself in a robe after her shower}. To robe is to dress in such garments, usually for formal occasions.

A robin is a small songbird with a reddish-orange breast. The American robin is a thrush, larger and different from the European robin, which is a small Old World flycatcher—both named for their distinctive chest coloring. Robins are associated with spring in temperate climates, often the first birds seen after winter: {The robins are back, so spring must be coming}. (Capitalized Robin is a given name.)

A robocall is an automated phone call that delivers a prerecorded message, typically used for telemarketing, political campaigns, or scam operations. The term combines robot with call, reflecting the mechanical, impersonal nature of these mass-dialed communications. Robocalls became a significant nuisance in the early 21st century as technology made them cheap to produce at scale. {I get at least three robocalls a day trying to sell me car warranties.} Laws now restrict robocalls, though enforcement remains challenging.

Robocalls are automated telephone calls that deliver prerecorded messages, typically for telemarketing, political campaigns, or scams. The term carries negative connotations—few people welcome them: {I get five robocalls a day trying to sell me car warranties}. Laws restrict robocalls, but enforcement struggles to keep pace with the volume.

A robot is a machine that performs tasks automatically, often ones that would otherwise require human effort. Robots range from industrial arms assembling cars to humanoid figures in science fiction. The word comes from Czech for forced labor. Figuratively, someone acting mechanically or without independent thought is called a robot: {He moved through his morning routine like a robot}.

Robotic describes something relating to robots or resembling their qualities—mechanical, automatic, lacking human warmth. A robotic {arm} performs factory tasks. Robotic {surgery} uses precision machines. When applied to people, robotic suggests stiff, emotionless behavior: {His delivery was robotic, completely devoid of feeling}. The word can describe anything that feels programmed rather than natural.

Robotics is the field of engineering and science concerned with designing, building, and programming robots—machines that can perform tasks autonomously or semi-autonomously. The discipline draws on mechanical engineering, electronics, and computer science. {She's studying robotics at MIT.} {Advances in robotics have transformed manufacturing.}

Robots are machines that perform tasks automatically, especially ones that would otherwise require human effort. The word comes from a Czech term for forced labor. Robots range from industrial arms assembling cars to humanoid machines in science fiction. Figuratively, someone acting mechanically or without emotion is called a robot: {He moved through his shift like a robot}.

Robust means strong, sturdy, and able to withstand stress or adversity. A robust {economy} resists downturns. A robust {immune system} fights off illness effectively. Robust {debate} is vigorous and energetic. In technical contexts, robust describes systems designed to function reliably under varying conditions: {The software proved robust enough to handle unexpected inputs}. The word often implies not just strength but resilience—the capacity to maintain performance when challenged.

English has three words spelled rock, two of which are frequent today. One is the rock associated with rhythmic movement: rock the cradle, rock and roll. It functions as both noun and verb and is also used figuratively: something that rocks a population or an institution is something that disrupts equilibrium. Something that really rocks is something lively and enjoyable. The other rock, a noun only, denotes a mass of stone. In some contexts it is nearly synonymous with stone in both countable and uncountable uses.

Rockabilly is an early form of rock and roll that emerged in the 1950s, blending country music with rhythm and blues. The style features slap bass, twangy guitars, and energetic vocals: {Elvis Presley's early recordings defined the rockabilly sound}. The term combines rock and hillbilly. A rockabilly revival in the 1980s brought the genre renewed attention.

Rockabye is a soothing word used when lulling a baby to sleep, most familiar from the lullaby "Rock-a-bye Baby." It combines the gentle motion of rocking with the sound of goodbye, suggesting the transition into sleep. The word appears almost exclusively in lullabies or contexts evoking them: {She sang rockabye to the fussy infant}.

Rocked is the past tense of rock. Something that rocked moved back and forth: {The boat rocked gently}. A person who rocked a baby soothed it with rhythmic motion. In slang, something that rocked was excellent or impressive: {That concert rocked}. To be rocked is to be shaken or disturbed: {The scandal rocked the administration}.

A rocker is a curved piece on which something rocks—the arc beneath a rocking chair or cradle. A rocking chair itself is often called a rocker. In music, a rocker is a rock musician or fan: {She's been a rocker since the seventies}. A rocker is also a curved blade on an ice skate. To be {off one's rocker} is to be crazy.

Rockers are curved pieces attached to the bottom of a chair or cradle that allow it to rock back and forth smoothly. The term extends to anyone who rocks: fans and performers of rock music are rockers, as are people who sit in rocking chairs. In British slang, rockers were leather-clad motorcycle enthusiasts in the 1960s who famously clashed with mods. The phrase {off one's rocker} means mentally unstable or crazy.

Modern use of the noun rocket is mostly for spacecraft. This has displaced the older meaning used in the rocket’s red glare, which was about a projectile weapon fueled by gases. The verb rocket is used figuratively for things that fly into space or through the air, or things that rise very quickly: Poverty rates are rocketing upwards. A different noun rocket is the British English name for a plant in the mustard family, also called arugula.

A rocketman is someone who works with rockets—an astronaut, test pilot, or aerospace engineer. The term evokes mid-twentieth-century space-age optimism, when rockets represented humanity's future. It gained cultural resonance through Elton John's 1972 song about an astronaut's lonely isolation: {I'm a rocketman, burning out his fuse up here alone}.

Rockets are projectiles or vehicles propelled by the expulsion of gases from burning fuel. Firework rockets explode in colorful displays; military rockets deliver warheads; space rockets carry payloads into orbit. To rocket is to move with sudden speed: {Prices rocketed after the announcement}. {The band rocketed to fame}. Something that rockets upward rises fast and dramatically.

Rocking describes back-and-forth or side-to-side motion, like a chair or a boat on waves: {She sat rocking on the porch}. To rock a baby is to soothe it with gentle motion. In slang, rocking means wearing something with confidence {(She's rocking that dress)} or performing excellently {(The band was rocking last night)}.

Rocks are solid masses of mineral matter—the hard stuff that forms the earth's crust. A rock can be a stone you skip across water, a boulder too heavy to lift, or the material of mountains. On the rocks describes drinks served over ice cubes, or something falling apart: {Their marriage is on the rocks}. To rock is to sway rhythmically, as in a rocking chair or dancing to rock music. Something that rocks is excellent: {That concert rocked}. As slang, rocks can mean crack cocaine or, vulgarly, testicles.

A rockslide is a mass of rock that breaks loose from a slope and slides or tumbles downward, or the event itself: {The rockslide blocked the mountain highway for days}. Unlike a landslide, which may involve soil, mud, or debris, a rockslide consists primarily of rock. The terms are often used interchangeably when precision doesn't matter.

A rockstar is a famous rock music performer, especially one with celebrity status and a devoted following. The term extends to anyone who excels spectacularly in their field: {She's a rockstar in the marketing world}, {Our new hire is an absolute rockstar}. The figurative use implies someone exceptional, celebrated, or commanding admiration. Also spelled rock star.

Rocky describes something full of rocks or resembling rock. A rocky {shore} is strewn with stones; rocky {terrain} is hard to traverse. Figuratively, rocky means unstable or difficult: a rocky {relationship}, a rocky {start}. The word suggests roughness and uncertainty—things that aren't smooth or easy. {The negotiations got off to a rocky start.} (Capitalized Rocky is a proper name.)

A rod is a straight, thin stick or bar, typically of wood or metal. Fishing rods cast lines into water. Lightning rods conduct electricity safely to ground. A rod can be an instrument of punishment: {Spare the rod, spoil the child}. In anatomy, rods are light-sensitive cells in the retina. Rod is also slang for penis or for a handgun. As a unit of measurement, a rod equals 16.5 feet.

Rode is the past tense of ride. You rode a horse, rode a bike, rode the bus. Extended uses follow: {She rode out the storm}. {He rode his luck as far as it would go}. {They rode him mercilessly about the mistake}. In nautical contexts, a rode is the line or chain connecting an anchor to a boat.

A rodent is a small mammal with continuously growing front teeth adapted for gnawing—mice, rats, squirrels, beavers, and their relatives. The group comprises nearly half of all mammal species. Informally, rodent often implies something unwanted or pestlike: {The building had a rodent problem}. Calling a person a rodent suggests they're sneaky or contemptible.

Rodents are mammals characterized by continuously growing front teeth that require gnawing to keep worn down—mice, rats, squirrels, beavers, and their relatives. They constitute roughly forty percent of all mammal species. The word comes from Latin for "gnawing." Informally, rodent often specifically means rats or mice, especially as pests: {The building has a rodent problem}.

A rodeo is a competitive exhibition of cowboy skills—bronco riding, bull riding, calf roping, steer wrestling. The events originated from the working practices of cattle ranching in the American West. Rodeo extends to any chaotic or competitive scene: {Getting the kids ready for school is a rodeo every morning}. To rodeo is to compete in such events.

Rodeos are competitive events showcasing skills from cattle ranching—bull riding, bronco busting, calf roping, barrel racing. The word comes from Spanish for roundup. A rodeo can also be any chaotic situation requiring wrangling: {Getting the kids ready for school is a daily rodeo}. To rodeo is to compete in such events.

Rods are long, thin, rigid sticks or bars. A fishing rod holds line; a lightning rod attracts electrical discharge; a curtain rod supports drapes. In anatomy, rods are photoreceptor cells in the retina that detect light and motion. Hot rod refers to a modified car built for speed. In slang, rod is an old-fashioned term for a handgun, and vulgar slang for penis.

Roe is fish eggs, especially when still clustered in the ovarian membrane and used as food. Salmon roe and flying fish roe appear in sushi; sturgeon roe becomes caviar. The word also names a small European deer, more fully called roe deer: {A roe bounded across the meadow}.
Roger, a radio code word for the letter R, was used originally in radio communication to indicate that a message had been received. People use it now to indicate understanding or affirmation.

A rogue is someone who operates outside accepted norms—originally a vagrant or dishonest person, now often someone charmingly mischievous: {He's a lovable rogue}. The word extends to things that deviate dangerously from the expected: a rogue {wave}, a rogue {state}, a rogue {cop}. As an adjective, rogue describes something operating independently or out of control: {a rogue elephant}, {rogue AI}. To {go rogue} is to act without authorization or break from one's group.

Rogues is the plural of rogue—a dishonest or unprincipled person, or someone who operates outside accepted norms. The word often carries a hint of charm: {a lovable band of rogues}. In gaming and fantasy, rogues are a character class specializing in stealth and cunning. A rogues' gallery is a collection of unsavory characters or criminal mugshots.

A role is a part played by an actor in a performance, or more broadly, a function someone fills in a situation: {She took on the role of mediator}. The word extends to any expected behavior pattern: gender {roles}, parental {roles}, {the role of government in education}. A role {model} is someone whose behavior others imitate. To {play a role} in something is to contribute to it.

Roleplay is acting out a character or scenario, whether for entertainment, education, or exploration. Children roleplay as doctors and patients. Actors roleplay characters. In therapy or training, people roleplay situations to practice responses: {We'll roleplay a difficult customer interaction}. Online, roleplay often involves collaborative fiction or erotic scenarios between participants. The noun and verb forms are interchangeable: {a roleplay session}, {let's roleplay}.

Roleplaying is acting out a character or scenario, whether for entertainment, training, or exploration. In tabletop games like Dungeons & Dragons, players roleplay fantasy characters. Therapists use roleplaying to rehearse difficult conversations: {Let's roleplay the job interview}. Online, roleplaying ranges from collaborative fiction to erotic scenarios between strangers. The word implies temporary adoption of another identity or perspective.

Roles are parts played or functions assumed. An actor plays a role in a film. In life, people take on roles—parent, employee, mediator—that come with expected behaviors: {She struggled to balance her roles as mother and executive}. Role can also mean function or purpose: {What role does the spleen play in immunity?} A role model is someone whose behavior others imitate.

The wide range of meanings represented by roll often refer to circularity or rotation. To roll is to move while rotating: The ball rolls across the floor. A roll is an instance of this, but also an instance of other meanings of roll (roll the dice, roll your eyes). Various objects that are rolled are called rolls (dinner rolls, roll of film). If you call the roll, you read a list of names: The teacher called the roll to take attendance at the beginning of class. Such a list is called a roll. A drum roll is the sound made by repeated, rapid strokes on a drum.

Rolled is the past tense of roll, covering all that verb's meanings. Something rolled has been turned over repeatedly, shaped by rolling, or moved on wheels: {rolled oats}, {a rolled cigarette}, {The cart rolled down the hill}. In slang, to get rolled is to be robbed, especially while vulnerable—drunk, asleep, or with a prostitute. {We rolled into town around midnight.}

A roller is a cylinder that rotates, used for flattening, spreading, or moving things: a paint roller, a road roller, a hair roller. Rollers under heavy objects allow them to be moved. A roller is also a long, heavy wave that breaks on a shore. In birds, a roller is a brightly colored species known for its tumbling flight displays.

To rollerblade is to skate on inline skates—boots with a single row of wheels along the sole rather than the traditional two-by-two arrangement. The word derives from the brand name but has become the generic verb for this activity: {We used to rollerblade around the park every weekend}. (Capitalized Rollerblade is the trademark.)

Rollerblades are inline skates—boots with wheels arranged in a single row rather than the two-by-two configuration of traditional roller skates. The term comes from the brand name Rollerblade, which popularized inline skating in the 1980s and became genericized: {We used to rollerblade around the neighborhood after school}. The activity is rollerblading.

Rollerblading is skating on inline skates—boots with wheels arranged in a single row rather than side by side. The term comes from Rollerblade, a brand name that became generic. People rollerblade for exercise, transportation, or recreation: {We went rollerblading along the boardwalk}. The activity surged in popularity during the 1990s.

A rollercoaster is an amusement park ride consisting of a train of cars traveling along tracks with steep inclines, sharp curves, and sudden drops. The experience lends itself to metaphor: anything with dramatic ups and downs becomes a rollercoaster—{an emotional rollercoaster}, {a rollercoaster of a season}. Also spelled roller coaster.

Rollercoasters are amusement park rides consisting of small cars traveling along elevated tracks with steep drops, sharp curves, and loops. The plural form appears when discussing multiple rides or comparing them: {The park has three rollercoasters}. Figuratively, a rollercoaster describes any experience with dramatic ups and downs: {The stock market has been a rollercoaster this year}.

A rollerskate is a boot or frame with wheels attached to the sole, allowing the wearer to glide across smooth surfaces. Traditional rollerskates have four wheels in a rectangular arrangement, distinguishing them from inline skates. As a verb, to rollerskate is to move on such devices: {We used to rollerskate at the rink every Saturday}. Also spelled roller skate or roller-skate.

Rollerskates are boots or shoes with wheels attached to the sole, used for gliding across hard surfaces. Traditional rollerskates have four wheels arranged in a rectangle; inline skates (rollerblades) have wheels in a single row. To rollerskate is to move on such devices: {We used to rollerskate at the rink every Saturday}.

Rollerskating is the activity of moving on wheeled boots, typically for recreation or exercise. The wheels are arranged in a two-by-two configuration, distinguishing rollerskates from inline skates. Rollerskating enjoyed peak popularity in the disco era, with rinks serving as social venues: {We went rollerskating every Friday night}. The term covers both the noun (the activity) and the verb form.

Rolling describes continuous circular or back-and-forth motion—a ball rolling downhill, waves rolling onto shore, a ship rolling in heavy seas. Extended uses capture anything ongoing or accumulating: rolling {blackouts}, a rolling {start}, rolling {hills} that rise and fall gently. A rolling {stone} gathers no moss suggests restless movement prevents attachment. In slang, to be rolling means to be flush with money or, separately, experiencing the effects of MDMA.

A rollout is the introduction or launch of something new—a product, service, policy, or program: {The company planned a nationwide rollout of the software}. The term suggests a phased or gradual release rather than an instantaneous debut. In football, a rollout is a play where the quarterback moves laterally behind the line before passing or running.

A rollover is the act of rolling over—turning from one position to another. In finance, a rollover transfers funds from one account or investment to another without tax penalty: {a 401(k) rollover into an IRA}. In accidents, a rollover occurs when a vehicle flips onto its side or roof. Lottery rollovers happen when no one wins and the jackpot carries to the next drawing. In computing, a rollover is a visual change when the cursor passes over an element.

Rolls is the third-person singular and plural of roll. Something rolls when it moves by turning over, like a ball or wheel: {The marble rolls across the floor}. Paper, fabric, or film wound around itself forms a roll. A roll is also a small rounded bread: {dinner rolls}, {cinnamon rolls}. To be {on a roll} is to experience a streak of success. A roll call is a reading of names to check attendance. {Heads will roll} threatens punishment.

Romance is a feeling of excitement and mystery associated with love, or a love affair itself: {a summer romance}, {Is there any romance left in your marriage?} The word extends to idealized or sentimental treatment of a subject: the romance of the Old West. As a verb, to romance someone is to court them or try to win them over. A romance novel centers on a love story, typically with an emotionally satisfying ending. (Capitalized Romance describes languages descended from Latin.)

Romances is the plural of romance, covering love affairs, love stories, and the genre of fiction featuring them. Medieval romances were tales of chivalric adventure. As a verb, romances means to court or woo: {He romances her with flowers and poetry}. It can also mean to idealize or treat fancifully: {The documentary romances the past}.

Romantic describes things connected to love or idealized passion: {a romantic dinner}, {a romantic comedy}. A romantic is someone inclined toward sentiment and idealism in matters of the heart. More broadly, romantic suggests imaginative appeal over practical reality: {romantic notions of adventure}. The word can describe anyone drawn to emotional expression and beauty over reason and restraint. (Capitalized Romantic refers to the artistic movement.)

Romanticise is the British spelling of romanticize—to view or present something in an idealized, appealing way that glosses over flaws or harsh realities. People romanticise the past, poverty, or artistic suffering: {She romanticised her college years, forgetting how anxious she'd been}. The word often carries a note of criticism, suggesting self-deception or naivety.

Romanticism in its general sense is a tendency to see the world through an idealized, emotional lens rather than a practical one. It emphasizes passion, imagination, and feeling over reason: {His romanticism about country life ignored the actual hardships}. The word often implies naivety or impracticality—a preference for how things should be over how they are. (Capitalized Romanticism is the artistic movement.)

To romanticize is to view or present something in an idealized, appealing way that glosses over flaws or harsh realities. People romanticize the past, poverty, mental illness, or war—seeing beauty or nobility where hardship actually dominates. {She romanticized her childhood in the country, forgetting how isolated she'd felt.} The word often carries a note of criticism, suggesting the romantic view is naive or dangerous.

Romanticizing is viewing something through a lens that softens flaws and heightens appeal. You might romanticize a past relationship, remembering only the good times: {She's romanticizing her college years}. The word often carries a note of self-deception—romanticizing poverty or war ignores harsh realities in favor of a pleasing narrative.

A romcom is a romantic comedy—a movie, TV show, or book combining love story with humor. The genre typically follows a couple through misunderstandings and obstacles to a happy ending: {We stayed in and watched romcoms all weekend}. The term blends "romantic" and "comedy" into a casual compound that matches the genre's light tone.

Romp suggests lively, energetic play—children romping in the yard, puppies romping together. The word carries a sense of carefree abandon. A romp can also be an easy victory: {The game turned into a romp}. In informal use, romp describes lighthearted sexual activity: {a romp in the hay}. As a noun, it names the activity itself or something that feels playfully unserious: {The film is a delightful romp}.

A romper is a one-piece garment combining a top with shorts, worn by infants or as casual women's fashion. The children's version typically fastens at the crotch for diaper changes. Adult rompers became popular as summer and beachwear: {She wore a floral romper to the party}. A similar garment with long pants is a jumpsuit.

A ronin was a samurai without a master—whether through the lord's death, disgrace, or dismissal. The word comes from Japanese, literally meaning "wave man," suggesting someone adrift. In modern usage, ronin describes anyone operating independently outside institutional structures: a freelancer, a lone wolf, a professional unattached to any organization. {He left the firm to work as a ronin consultant.}

A roof is the top covering of a building or vehicle, the structure that shelters what's beneath from weather. By extension, roof means any overhead covering or upper limit: {the roof of the mouth}, {a roof of branches}. To {raise the roof} is to make a great commotion. To {hit the roof} is to become suddenly furious. {A roof over your head} means basic shelter.

Roofie is slang for Rohypnol, a powerful sedative. The drug gained notoriety as a "date rape drug" because it can be slipped into drinks to incapacitate victims: {Someone must have roofied her drink}. The verb roofie means to secretly dose someone with such a drug. Any similar sedative used this way may be called a roofie.

Roofies is slang for Rohypnol, a powerful sedative in the benzodiazepine family. The drug became notorious as a date-rape drug because it can be slipped into drinks, causing sedation, memory impairment, and loss of consciousness. To roofie someone is to drug them this way: {Someone must have roofied her drink}.

A rooftop is the outer surface of a roof, especially as a usable space: {We watched the fireworks from the rooftop}. The word emphasizes the top as a location rather than the structure itself. To {shout something from the rooftops} is to proclaim it publicly and loudly.

Rooftops are the outer surfaces of roofs, considered collectively or as a visual element of a landscape: {The city's rooftops stretched to the horizon}. To shout something {from the rooftops} is to proclaim it publicly and emphatically. Rooftop as a singular adjective describes things located on top of buildings: {rooftop garden}, {rooftop bar}.

A rook is a large black crow common in Europe, known for nesting in colonies called rookeries. In chess, a rook is the piece that moves in straight lines across ranks and files—also called a castle. As a verb, to rook someone is to cheat or swindle them: {They rooked him out of his savings}.

A rookie is someone new to a job, profession, or activity—especially in sports and law enforcement, where the term is standard: {a rookie cop}, {rookie of the year}. The word implies inexperience but also potential. As an adjective, it describes beginner-level performance or errors: {a rookie mistake}.

Rookies are people in their first year of a profession or activity—especially in sports, the military, or police work. The term emphasizes inexperience: {The rookies made mistakes the veterans would never make}. A rookie is prone to {rookie mistakes}, errors that betray lack of experience. The word carries no insult; everyone starts as a rookie.

Rooks are large black birds in the crow family, common across Europe and Asia, known for nesting in noisy colonies called rookeries. In chess, a rook is the piece that moves in straight lines along ranks and files—also called a castle. To rook someone is to swindle or cheat them, especially at cards or gambling: {He got rooked out of fifty dollars}.

As a count noun, room designates an enclosed space large enough for human occupation, and typically featuring a floor, walls, and a ceiling. As an uncountable noun, room simply means space adequate for some purpose: There isn’t enough room to work here. This meaning is extended figuratively to mean capacity: I see some room for improvement here. Context sometimes extends the use of room to the people in it: work the room; the whole room exploded in laughter. As a verb, room has a meaning similar to lodge: She rooms with a distant relative in the city.

A roommate is someone you share living space with—typically an apartment or house, though the term originally meant sharing a single room. The relationship is usually practical rather than romantic: roommates split rent and utilities. In American English, roommate covers both sharing a bedroom and sharing a dwelling; British English prefers flatmate for the latter. {My roommate never does the dishes.}

Roommates are people who share a living space—typically an apartment or house, though the term originated with shared bedrooms. The arrangement usually involves splitting rent and utilities. Roommates may be strangers matched through listings, friends who decide to live together, or college students assigned to share a dorm room. {My roommate never does the dishes.}

Rooms is the plural of room—enclosed spaces within buildings. Beyond physical spaces, rooms extends to capacity or opportunity: {There's rooms for improvement}. In lodging contexts, rooms means accommodations: {The hotel has rooms available}. To room is to share living quarters: {We roomed together in college}. Someone who rooms with you is a roommate.

A roost is a place where birds settle to rest or sleep, typically a branch, ledge, or sheltered spot. Chickens return to the roost at nightfall. The verb means to settle in such a place: {Pigeons roosted on the ledge}. When {chickens come home to roost}, past actions return with consequences. To {rule the roost} is to dominate a household or group.

A rooster is an adult male chicken, distinguished by its comb, wattles, and prominent tail feathers. Roosters crow at dawn—and throughout the day—to announce territory. The word emerged as an American euphemism for cock, which had acquired vulgar associations. {The rooster chased me across the yard.}

Roosters is the plural of rooster, the adult male of domestic fowl—distinguished from hens by larger combs, spurs, and the crow that announces dawn. Roosters appear in expressions about confidence and dominance: to {rule the roost} is to be in charge. A {rooster tail} is the spray of water behind a speedboat or vehicle on wet ground.

The core use of root is to designate the part of a plant that is typically underground and that supplies nutrients to it from the soil. Roots that are edible are called root vegetables. Other things that have a securing part not normally visible call it a root, like the root of a tooth or hair. This meaning is extended in ways that maintain the idea of a root being a fundamental part of something, or its source: Money is the root of the problem here. If something takes root, it becomes established. To root something is to fix it in place.

Rooted means firmly established or deeply embedded. A rooted {tradition} has long, stable foundations. A rooted {belief} runs deep and resists change. Plants become rooted when their roots take hold in soil; people become rooted when they feel settled in a place or community: {After twenty years, we're thoroughly rooted here}. To stand rooted is to remain fixed in place, often from shock: {She stood rooted to the spot}. In computing, a rooted device has had its software restrictions removed, granting full administrative access.

Rooting is the process of establishing roots—whether a plant taking hold in soil or a person becoming settled in a place. In computing, rooting means gaining administrative access to a device's operating system, bypassing manufacturer restrictions: {After rooting my phone, I could install custom software}. In American English, rooting for someone means cheering them on: {We're all rooting for you}. In Australian slang, rooting is vulgar for having sex.

Roots are the underground parts of plants that anchor them and absorb water and nutrients. The word extends to origins and foundations: {She returned to her roots in rural Alabama}. To root is to dig with the snout like a pig, or to search by rummaging: {rooting through drawers}. To root for someone is to cheer them on—a different word entirely. To take root is to become established. The root of a problem is its underlying cause. In math, a root is a number that produces a given value when multiplied by itself: the square root of 9 is 3.

Rope is a strong, thick cord made of twisted fibers. Skipping or jumping a rope is a form of exercise. A rope tow is a way of towing an object by attaching it with a rope. To rope something, especially an animal, is to secure it with a rope. If you rope off an area, you separate it by using ropes. When you rope someone in, you cleverly persuade them to do something, often with trickery.

Ropes are lengths of thick, strong cord made from twisted fibers or strands. To rope something is to catch or tie it with a rope: {They roped the calf}. To rope someone in is to persuade or enlist them. To {know the ropes} or {show someone the ropes} refers to understanding how things work—from the rigging on sailing ships. {On the ropes} means nearly defeated, from boxing.

A rosary is a string of beads used in Roman Catholic prayer, with each bead marking a specific prayer in a devotional sequence.
