The term also refers to the prayer cycle itself—a meditation on events in Christ's life while reciting Our Fathers, Hail Marys, and Glorias: {She said the rosary every morning}. Similar prayer beads exist in other traditions.

Rose has two unrelated uses. One is to serve as the irregular past tense of the verb rise: A sadder and a wiser man, he rose the morrow morn. The other is a noun that designates a family of plants (Rosaceae), and especially the genus of this family (Rosa) that comprises the showy and fragrant flowers we call roses. The natural beauty of roses gives rise to figurative use, in which rose designates a beautiful woman or girl. Though roses come in many colors, the color adjective rose is used for a purplish red color that is typical of the flower.

A rosebud is a rose flower before it opens, still tightly wrapped in its petals. By extension, rosebud describes anything small, delicate, and promising—especially a young woman or a child's mouth: {rosebud lips}. The word carries connotations of beauty not yet fully revealed, potential on the verge of blossoming. In the film *Citizen Kane*, "Rosebud" is the famous dying word whose meaning drives the plot.

Rosemary is an aromatic evergreen shrub with needle-like leaves, native to the Mediterranean. The herb flavors lamb, chicken, potatoes, and bread. Its piney, slightly bitter taste intensifies when dried. Rosemary has traditional associations with remembrance: {There's rosemary, that's for remembrance}. (Capitalized Rosemary is a given name.)

Roses is the plural of rose, the thorny flowering shrub prized for fragrant blooms and cultivated in countless varieties. Red roses traditionally symbolize romantic love; other colors carry different meanings. To {come up roses} is for things to turn out well. {Stop and smell the roses} advises slowing down to appreciate life. {A bed of roses} describes easy, comfortable circumstances—often in the negative: {Life isn't always a bed of roses}.

A roster is a list of names, typically of people belonging to a group or scheduled for duty. Sports teams have rosters of players; workplaces post rosters showing who works which shifts. The word implies organized membership or rotation: {She checked the roster to see when she was on call}. To roster someone is to add them to such a list.

Rosy means having a pink or reddish color, like roses or healthy cheeks: {rosy cheeks from the cold}. Extended to outlook and prospects, rosy means optimistic or promising: {a rosy future}, {rosy predictions}. Someone who sees things through {rose-colored glasses} has an unrealistically positive view. The opposite appears in phrases like {not so rosy} or {less than rosy}.

Rot is a noun and verb that is both older and more frequent than its nearest synonym, decay. To rot is to deteriorate in a natural way, as food rots in your fridge, or dead trees rot in the forest. An instance or outbreak of rotting is also called rot, which serves as a general name for various kinds of fungal or bacterial decay. If someone is talking rot, they are speaking nonsense. The phrase stop the rot usually means to stop some undesirable process that is making things worse.

To rotate is to turn around a central point or axis. The Earth rotates on its axis; a wheel rotates around its hub. Rotate also means to take turns in sequence: {Employees rotate through different departments}, {We rotate who brings snacks}. Crops are rotated to preserve soil health. A rotating {president} serves a term before the next takes over.

Rotation is the act of turning around an axis or center point. The Earth completes one rotation every twenty-four hours. The meaning extends to any cyclical sequence: {crop rotation}, {tire rotation}, {The restaurant has a rotating menu}. In sports, a rotation is the order in which players take turns: {He's fifth in the pitching rotation}. To be {in rotation} is to be among items that cycle through use.

Rotgut is cheap, low-quality liquor—the kind that burns going down and leaves you feeling wrecked: {We drank rotgut whiskey in the back of his truck}. The word suggests alcohol so harsh it might rot your insides. It can apply to any poorly made or adulterated spirit.

A rotisserie is a cooking apparatus that rotates meat on a spit before a heat source, ensuring even browning and self-basting: {rotisserie chicken}. The word also names the style of cooking or the prepared food itself. In fantasy sports, rotisserie leagues use cumulative statistics across categories rather than head-to-head matchups—named after the New York restaurant where the format was invented.

Rots is the third-person singular form of the verb rot, meaning to decay or decompose through the action of bacteria and fungi. Organic matter rots when left exposed to moisture and air: {The fallen fruit rots quickly in summer heat}. Figuratively, things rot when they deteriorate through neglect or corruption: {The whole system rots from the inside}. As a plural noun, rots are diseases that cause decay in plants or animals.

Rotten describes organic matter that has decayed and spoiled: {rotten fruit}, {rotten meat}, {rotten teeth}. The smell of rotten eggs is sulfurous and unmistakable. Extended uses convey corruption or poor quality: a rotten {system}, rotten {luck}, a rotten {deal}. Something rotten is thoroughly bad: {I feel rotten about what I said}. To be {rotten to the core} is to be corrupt beyond redemption.

Rotting describes the process of decay—organic matter breaking down through bacterial or fungal action. A rotting {apple} softens and browns. Rotting {wood} crumbles. The word often emphasizes the ongoing, visible nature of decomposition: {the smell of rotting vegetation}, {a rotting corpse}. Figuratively, something rotting is deteriorating or corrupting: {a rotting infrastructure}, {rotting from within}.

Rough is most frequently an adjective, typically opposite to smooth in several senses, and often synonymous with harsh. A rough draft or rough estimate is preliminary and requires further work. Someone going through a rough patch is having difficulties. To rough something is to work with it in a preliminary way. To rough someone up is to hurt them physically. If you are roughing it, you’re living with few comforts.

Roughhouse is boisterous, physical play that stops short of actual fighting—wrestling, tumbling, shoving. Kids roughhouse; siblings roughhouse; puppies roughhouse. The word works as both noun and verb: {The boys were roughhousing in the living room} or {That's enough roughhouse for one afternoon}. The play is rowdy but usually good-natured.

Roughhousing is boisterous physical play—wrestling, tumbling, shoving—that stops short of real fighting. Children roughhouse; so do puppies. The activity walks a line between play and aggression: {The boys were just roughhousing, but someone's going to get hurt}. As a verb, to roughhouse is to engage in such play.

A roughneck is a worker on an oil drilling rig, performing the physically demanding labor of handling pipes and equipment on the drill floor. More broadly, roughneck describes any tough, rowdy, or uncouth person—someone rough around the edges: {He hung around with roughnecks and troublemakers}. The term suggests working-class masculinity and a readiness for hard work or hard living.

Roulette is a casino game where a ball is dropped onto a spinning wheel divided into numbered compartments; players bet on where the ball will land. The wheel has slots numbered 1–36 alternating red and black, plus one or two green zeros. By extension, roulette describes any situation left to pure chance: {Russian roulette} involves spinning a revolver cylinder with one bullet and pulling the trigger—a metaphor for reckless gambles with serious consequences.
Round is used as a preposition in British English in nearly all cases where American English uses around. The meaning is the same.

A roundabout is a circular intersection where traffic flows in one direction around a central island—vehicles yield on entry and exit at their desired road. The design keeps traffic moving without signals. As an adjective, roundabout means indirect or circuitous: {She took a roundabout route to avoid traffic}. A roundabout {way of saying something} avoids directness. In British English, a roundabout is also a merry-go-round.

Roundabouts are circular intersections where traffic flows in one direction around a central island, yielding to vehicles already in the circle. Common in Britain and increasingly in America, they reduce the need for traffic lights. The word also names a British amusement park ride—what Americans call a merry-go-round or carousel.

A roundhouse is a circular building where locomotives are stored and serviced, with tracks radiating from a central turntable. The shape extends to other circular or curved structures. A roundhouse punch or kick swings wide in a sweeping arc rather than traveling straight: {He threw a roundhouse that caught me on the jaw}. In baseball, a roundhouse curve breaks dramatically.

Rounds covers a lot of ground as both noun and verb. A round is something circular or spherical, or a complete cycle or series: {a round of drinks}, {a round of golf}, {rounds of ammunition}. Medical staff make rounds when they visit patients in sequence. The verb means to make round, to go around something, or to complete: {We rounded the corner}. To round up or round down is to adjust a number to a convenient figure. If you round on someone, you turn and confront them sharply.

A roundtable is a discussion among equals, with no one at the head—from the legendary table of King Arthur, where no knight outranked another. The term now describes any meeting or broadcast format where participants share ideas as peers: {a roundtable on climate policy}, {The Sunday morning roundtable debated the election}. Also spelled round table.

A roundup is a gathering of scattered things into one place. Cowboys conduct roundups of cattle. Police conduct roundups of suspects. A news roundup collects related stories: {Here's your weekly tech roundup}. The verb phrase is two words: {We need to round up the usual suspects}.

Roundups collect scattered things into one place. The original sense involves gathering livestock, especially cattle, by riding around them and driving them together. This extends to any systematic gathering of people or things: {a roundup of suspects}, {a news roundup}. The word often appears in journalism to describe compilations of related items or summaries of events: {Here's your weekly roundup of tech news}.

A rout is a disorderly retreat or overwhelming defeat: {The battle ended in a rout}. To rout an opponent is to defeat them decisively, scattering their forces. The word implies not just losing but collapse—an army breaking and fleeing rather than withdrawing in order. By extension, any lopsided victory: {The game was a 42-3 rout}.

Route is a path or course from one place to another: {the shortest route to the airport}, {a bus route}, {a trade route}. It extends to any planned sequence: {a route to success}. In American English, route rhymes with either "root" or "out"—both are standard. To route is to send along a particular path: {Route the cable through the wall}.

A router is a device that directs data traffic between computer networks, connecting your home or office to the internet and managing communication between devices. Pronounced to rhyme with "outer." Separately, a router (rhyming with "hooter") is a power tool that hollows out grooves or shapes edges in wood: {He used a router to cut the decorative molding}.

Routes are paths or courses from one place to another. A bus route connects stops along a fixed path; a trade route links commercial centers. To route something is to send it along a particular path: {They routed the cables through the ceiling}. Route can rhyme with "out" or with "boot"—both are standard. A different word spelled the same, pronounced like "out," means to defeat decisively: {The team was routed in the finals}.

A routine is a regular sequence of actions or a fixed program: {my morning routine}, {a comedy routine}, {a dance routine}. As an adjective, routine means ordinary or standard: {routine maintenance}, {a routine checkup}. What's routine is unremarkable—expected rather than exceptional. In computing, a routine is a set of instructions that performs a specific task.

Routines are regular sequences of actions or established patterns of behavior. A morning routine might include coffee, exercise, and checking email. In computing, a routine is a set of instructions that performs a specific task. In entertainment, a routine is a rehearsed performance: a comedy routine, a dance routine. The word often carries connotations of the mundane or mechanical: {stuck in a routine}, {the same old routines}.

A rover is one who roves—a wanderer or someone who travels without fixed destination. In sports, particularly Australian rules football, a rover is a player with no set position who ranges across the field. The word also names wheeled robotic vehicles designed to explore terrain, especially on other planets: {The Mars rover sent back images of the surface}. In archery, a rover shoots at targets at varying distances. {He spent his twenties as a rover, never settling anywhere long.} (Capitalized Rover is a brand name or proper noun.)

Row has two distinct meanings from different origins. One is a line of things arranged side by side: a row of {houses}, a row of {seats}, {three in a row}. To row is also to propel a boat with oars: {We rowed across the lake}. The other row (rhyming with "cow") is British for a noisy argument or quarrel: {They had a terrible row about money}.

A rowboat is a small boat propelled by oars, typically seating one to four people. The rower sits facing backward, pulling the oars through oarlocks mounted on the gunwales. Rowboats are used for fishing, recreation, or ferrying short distances: {We rented a rowboat and spent the afternoon on the lake}.

Rowdy describes noisy, rough, or disorderly behavior, often involving boisterous energy that disrupts order: {a rowdy crowd}, {rowdy fans}. A rowdy person or rowdy (noun) causes such disturbances. The word carries less menace than violent but more than merely loud—it suggests unruly behavior that might tip into trouble: {Things got rowdy after midnight}.

Rowing is the act of propelling a boat through water using oars, either as transportation, recreation, or competitive sport. In competitive rowing, athletes sit facing backward and pull oars through the water in synchronized strokes, racing in crews of one, two, four, or eight. The sport demands exceptional cardiovascular fitness and technique. {She took up rowing in college and still rows every morning.} Rowing also refers more casually to any oar-powered boating: {We went rowing on the lake.}

Rows are horizontal lines or arrangements of things placed side by side: {rows of corn}, {rows of seats}, {the back row}. To row is to propel a boat with oars. Separately, row (rhyming with "cow") means a noisy quarrel or disturbance: {They had a terrible row about money}.

Royal means of or relating to a king or queen: {the royal family}, {royal decree}, {royal palace}. By extension, royal describes anything magnificent or fit for royalty: {a royal welcome}, {royal treatment}. It also intensifies certain nouns: {a royal mess}, {a royal pain}. In Britain, the Royals are members of the royal family. A royal is also a paper size (20 × 25 inches) and a sail above the topgallant. (Capitalized Royal appears in proper names of institutions and military units.)

Royals are members of a royal family—kings, queens, princes, princesses, and their relatives. The word appears most often in journalism and casual speech: {The royals attended the charity gala}, {tabloid coverage of the royals}. In card games, royals are the face cards: king, queen, jack. The Kansas City Royals are a Major League Baseball team.

Royalties are payments made to owners of intellectual property—authors, musicians, inventors, or patent holders—for each use or sale of their work. A novelist receives royalties on book sales; a songwriter earns royalties when their song is streamed or performed. The term extends to payments for extracting natural resources: {oil royalties}, {mineral royalties}. Royalty in the singular usually means royal status or royal persons collectively.

Royalty refers to people of royal rank—kings, queens, princes, and their families. The word also means the status or power of being royal: {She was born into royalty}. In business, a royalty is a payment to an owner for use of their property, typically a percentage of revenue: authors receive royalties on book sales, musicians on recordings, landowners on mineral extraction. {The patent holder collects royalties from manufacturers.}

An rpg is a rocket-propelled grenade—a shoulder-fired weapon that launches an explosive projectile. The term appears frequently in military and video game contexts: {The soldiers took cover when they spotted the rpg}. In gaming communities, rpg also refers to role-playing games, though that sense is more commonly written in capitals. (Capitalized RPG is the standard form for both meanings.)

RSVP is to respond to an invitation, indicating whether you'll attend: {Have you RSVPed to the wedding yet?} The noun refers to such a response: {We need an RSVP by Friday}. From the French *répondez s'il vous plaît* (please respond), it appears on invitations requesting confirmation. The lowercase form is less common than the all-caps version. (All-caps RSVP is standard.)

Rub is to move something back and forth against a surface with pressure. You rub your eyes when tired, rub lotion into skin, rub a stain to remove it. Things that rub together create friction: {My shoes rub against my heels}. A rub is an act of rubbing or a difficulty: {There's the rub}. To {rub someone the wrong way} is to irritate them. To {rub it in} is to emphasize someone's failure or mistake. A rub is also a spice mixture applied to meat before cooking.

Rubber is an elastic material that stretches and returns to shape, originally derived from tropical tree sap but now often synthetic. It appears in countless products: tires, bands, gloves, erasers. In British usage, a rubber is an eraser. In American slang, a rubber is a condom. To rubber is to gawk or stare: {rubbernecking at an accident}. To {rubber-stamp} something is to approve it automatically, without real scrutiny.

Rubberneck is to crane one's neck to stare at something, especially an accident or spectacle: {Traffic slowed as drivers rubbernecked at the wreck}. The image is of a neck so flexible with curiosity it might be made of rubber. A rubberneck is also a gawking tourist or any nosy onlooker. The word carries mild contempt for idle curiosity.

Rubbernecking is craning your neck to stare at something, especially an accident or disturbance. The image is of a neck so flexible it might be made of rubber, stretching to get a better look. Traffic slows when drivers rubberneck at crashes on the opposite side of the highway. The term can extend to any nosy gawking: {Quit rubbernecking and mind your own business}.

Rubbernecks is the verb form of rubberneck, meaning to crane one's neck to stare at something—typically an accident, celebrity, or spectacle. The image is of a neck so flexible with curiosity it might as well be rubber. Traffic slows when drivers rubberneck at crashes. As a noun, a rubbernecker is a gawker: {Rubbernecks crowded around the crime scene tape}.

Rubberstamping is approving something automatically, without real scrutiny or independent judgment. The image is of an official stamping documents mechanically, not reading them: {The board was accused of rubberstamping the CEO's decisions}. The term implies the approval process is a formality rather than genuine oversight.

Rubbish is waste material or garbage—things thrown away as worthless. British English uses rubbish where American English prefers trash or garbage. Extended to mean nonsense or worthless talk: {That's complete rubbish}. As a verb, to rubbish something is to criticize or dismiss it harshly: {Critics rubbished the proposal}. As an adjective, rubbish means poor quality: {I'm rubbish at tennis}.

Rubble is broken fragments of stone, brick, or concrete—the debris left after a building collapses or is demolished: {Rescuers searched through the rubble for survivors}. The word evokes destruction, whether from earthquakes, bombs, or wrecking crews. Figuratively, rubble can describe anything reduced to ruins: {The scandal left his reputation in rubble}.

Rubies are precious gemstones prized for their deep red color, second only to diamonds in hardness among natural gems. The finest specimens come from Myanmar and command prices rivaling or exceeding diamonds. Ruby is the birthstone for July and traditionally symbolizes passion and vitality. In a figurative sense, ruby describes anything with that characteristic rich red color: {ruby lips}, {ruby wine}. The word also appears in programming as Ruby, a popular scripting language.

Ruby is a deep red precious gemstone, a variety of corundum valued for its color and hardness. The finest rubies rival diamonds in price. Ruby also names the color itself—a rich, vivid red: {ruby lips}, {ruby wine}. In printing, ruby is a small type size (5.5 points). In British slang, a ruby is a curry, from rhyming slang "ruby Murray." (Capitalized Ruby is a given name or programming language.)

A rucksack is a bag carried on the back with shoulder straps—essentially a backpack. The term is more common in British English and among hikers and military personnel: {She packed her rucksack for the trek}. In American English, backpack dominates casual use, while rucksack often suggests rugged or military-style gear.

A ruckus is a noisy disturbance or commotion: {The kids were making a ruckus in the backyard}. It suggests loud, disorderly activity rather than serious conflict—more annoyance than danger. {What's all the ruckus about?}

A rudder is a flat piece hinged to the stern of a boat or ship, used for steering. Moving the rudder redirects water flow, turning the vessel. Aircraft have vertical rudders for the same purpose. Figuratively, a rudder is anything that provides guidance or direction: {Without a clear strategy, the company lacked a rudder}.

Rudderless means lacking direction or guidance. A rudder steers a ship; without one, the vessel drifts wherever currents take it. The word almost always appears figuratively: {The company seemed rudderless after the CEO resigned}. A rudderless person or organization has no clear purpose or leadership.

Rude describes behavior that violates social expectations of politeness or respect: {Don't be rude to the waiter}. A rude {awakening} is an unpleasant surprise that shatters comfortable assumptions. Rude can also mean primitive or roughly made: {a rude shelter}. In older usage, rude meant unrefined or uncultured—this sense survives mainly in literary contexts.

Rudeness is behavior that shows disregard for others' feelings or social conventions—interrupting, ignoring greetings, speaking harshly. What counts as rude varies by culture and context: {His rudeness to the waiter was embarrassing}. The word can describe a single act or a general quality: {I was shocked by the rudeness of her reply}.

Ruffians are violent, lawless people—thugs or hooligans who cause trouble through force or intimidation. The word carries an old-fashioned flavor, often appearing in adventure stories or period pieces: {The travelers were set upon by ruffians}. In modern use, it sometimes has a playful edge when describing rough but harmless mischief: {Those little ruffians tracked mud through the house}.

Ruffle describes a disturbance of smoothness. Wind ruffles water or hair; a bird ruffles its feathers. To ruffle someone is to disturb their composure: {The criticism didn't ruffle her}. A ruffle is also a strip of gathered fabric used as trim on clothing or curtains—the gathering creates deliberate irregularity in what would otherwise lie flat.

Ruffled describes something with its smoothness disturbed—feathers, fabric, hair, or water that has been agitated or displaced: {a ruffled collar}, {ruffled feathers on an angry bird}. Applied to people, ruffled means flustered or annoyed: {She seemed ruffled by the unexpected question}. A ruffled garment has decorative gathered fabric along an edge.

Ruffles are strips of fabric gathered or pleated to create a wavy, decorative edge on clothing or furnishings: {a blouse with ruffles at the collar}, {ruffled curtains}. The word extends to anything similarly textured—wind ruffles water, a bird ruffles its feathers. To ruffle someone is to disturb their composure: {His comment ruffled a few feathers}.

A rug is a floor covering, typically smaller than a carpet and not attached to the floor. Rugs add warmth, define spaces, or protect flooring: {an area rug}, {a bathroom rug}. To {pull the rug out from under} someone is to suddenly remove their support or advantage. To {sweep something under the rug} is to conceal it.

Rugby is a contact sport in which two teams advance an oval ball by carrying, passing, and kicking, scoring by touching it down in the opponent's goal area or kicking it through goalposts. Players may tackle ball carriers but cannot pass forward. Two main codes exist: rugby union (fifteen players) and rugby league (thirteen). {He played rugby at university.} (Capitalized Rugby is the English town where the sport originated.)

Rugged describes something rough, uneven, and wild—typically terrain or landscapes that are difficult to traverse: {rugged mountains}, {rugged coastline}. When applied to people, especially men, rugged suggests a weathered, strong, outdoorsy appearance that implies toughness and self-reliance. Rugged can also characterize something built to withstand harsh conditions: {rugged equipment designed for extreme environments}. The word carries connotations of durability and resilience rather than refinement or smoothness.

Rugs are thick fabric floor coverings, typically smaller than carpets and not wall-to-wall. A rug might cover part of a hardwood floor or define a seating area. Rugs also appear as blankets or wraps: {a lap rug}, {a prayer rug}. In British slang, a rug is a toupee. To {pull the rug out from under} someone is to suddenly withdraw support.

Ruin is destruction or severe damage—the state of being wrecked beyond repair or use. A building falls into ruin; a scandal brings financial ruin. The plural ruins refers to what remains of destroyed structures: {ancient ruins}, {the ruins of the castle}. To ruin something is to destroy or spoil it completely: {The rain ruined the picnic}. A person can be ruined financially, socially, or emotionally. In older usage, a woman's ruin meant loss of virginity or reputation.

Ruined describes something destroyed, spoiled, or reduced to a state beyond repair. A ruined building lies in decay; a ruined reputation cannot recover. The word often carries finality: {The rain ruined the wedding}. In casual speech, ruined can be hyperbolic: {That movie ruined me} means it affected you deeply, not that you're actually destroyed.

Ruins are the remains of something destroyed or decayed—typically buildings, cities, or structures that have collapsed or fallen into disrepair: {ancient ruins}, {the ruins of a bombed cathedral}. The word extends to any state of destruction or collapse: {His gambling left his finances in ruins}. To be {in ruins} is to be devastated. A single ruin is one such remnant, or the state of being ruined: {The scandal brought about his ruin}.

The ideas that pervade the meanings of the noun and verb rule are standard and authority. As a count noun, a rule is a principle that governs conduct, play, or behavior. As an uncountable noun, rule denotes control by government or some other principle: the rule of Queen Christina. As a verb, rule means to govern or control with authority. When a judge rules, she decides the outcome of a case. When a sovereign rules, he holds responsibility for governing his country.

A rulebook is a book or other document that contains rules, especially rules governing a game or sport. When people talk about the rulebook figuratively, they are referring to rules that govern a particular activity: He threw out the rulebook when he made that decision.

A ruler is a strip of rigid material marked with units for measuring length, or a straightedge for drawing straight lines. The other ruler is someone who rules—a monarch, dictator, or other person exercising authority over a territory or people: {The ruler of the kingdom demanded tribute}. Both senses share the idea of imposing order.

Rulers are people who govern or control—monarchs, dictators, heads of state: {The rulers of the ancient world wielded absolute power}. A ruler is also a straight-edged measuring instrument, typically marked in inches or centimeters, used for drawing lines and measuring distances: {She used a ruler to underline the heading}.

Rules are established guidelines governing conduct or procedure. Games have rules; so do institutions, religions, and social settings. To rule is to govern or decide authoritatively: {The court ruled in her favor}. A ruler measures straight lines—and also governs. Something that rules is dominant or excellent: {That song rules}. As a {rule}, something happens generally or usually.

A ruling is an authoritative decision, especially one issued by a judge or official body: {The court's ruling struck down the law}, {We're awaiting a ruling from the committee}. As an adjective, ruling describes whoever holds power: the ruling {party}, the ruling {class}. A ruling {passion} is a dominant interest or obsession that governs someone's life.

The noun rum denotes liquor distilled from cane sugar and its products. It stands for alcoholic drinks generally in the expression demon rum. An unrelated adjective rum, mainly British, characterizes things that are strange and slightly suspect: They’re a rum bunch of people.

Rumba is a ballroom dance of Cuban origin characterized by pronounced hip movements and a slow-quick-quick rhythm. The music accompanying it features syncopated beats and percussion. As a verb, to rumba is to perform this dance: {We rumbad until midnight}. Also spelled rhumba.

Rumble is a deep, continuous, rolling sound—thunder rumbling in the distance, a truck rumbling past, a stomach rumbling with hunger. The word captures low-frequency vibration you can almost feel. As a noun, it's that sound itself: {the rumble of the subway}. In dated slang, a rumble is a street fight between gangs. To rumble someone (British) is to discover their secret: {They rumbled our scheme}.

Rumbles is the third-person singular of rumble and its plural noun. A rumble is a deep, continuous sound like distant thunder or a hungry stomach: {My stomach rumbles when I skip breakfast}. Engines rumble, storms rumble in the distance. To rumble someone (British slang) is to discover their secret or expose their scheme: {The police finally rumbled the gang}. A rumble can also be a street fight between rival groups, now somewhat dated: {The gangs scheduled a rumble for midnight}.

Rumbling describes a low, continuous sound like distant thunder or a heavy truck passing: {We heard the rumbling of the approaching storm}. A rumbling stomach signals hunger. As a noun, rumblings often refers to early signs of discontent or unrest: {There were rumblings of dissatisfaction among the staff}. The word suggests something building or approaching.

Ruminating means chewing over—literally or figuratively. Cows and other ruminants ruminate by rechewing partially digested food brought back up from the stomach. In human contexts, ruminating means turning something over repeatedly in the mind: {She spent the evening ruminating on what went wrong}. The word often carries a negative connotation of unproductive dwelling on problems.

Rummage is to search through something by moving contents around, typically in a disorganized way: {She rummaged through the drawer looking for scissors}. The word suggests hurried, messy searching rather than methodical examination. A rummage sale offers secondhand goods, often donated items sold for charity—things someone has cleared out while rummaging through their belongings.

Rummaging is searching through something by moving items around, typically in a disorderly way. The word suggests pawing through drawers, bags, or cluttered spaces looking for something specific: {She was rummaging through her purse for her keys}. It implies a hands-on, somewhat messy search rather than a methodical one.

Rummy is a family of card games where players draw and discard to form sets and runs—groups of matching cards or sequences in the same suit. Gin rummy and canasta are popular variants. Separately, rummy is dated slang for a drunkard, from rum: {The old rummy sat at the end of the bar}.

A rumor is unverified information passed from person to person, often about someone's private affairs or about events of public interest. Rumors may turn out true or false—the defining feature is that they circulate before confirmation: {Rumors of layoffs spread through the office}. The verb means to circulate such information, usually passive: {It's rumored that they're getting divorced}. British spelling: rumour.

Rumors is the plural of rumor—unverified information passed from person to person. Rumors spread through communities, workplaces, and social media, often gaining or losing details along the way: {Rumors of layoffs circulated through the office}. The word implies uncertainty about truth: {I've heard rumors, but nothing confirmed}.

Rumour is the British spelling of rumor—unverified information passed from person to person: {Rumour has it she's leaving the company}. A rumour may be true, false, or somewhere between. The verb means to spread such information, usually in passive constructions: {He was rumoured to be bankrupt}. Rumours thrive where official information is scarce.

Rumours is the British spelling of rumors—unverified stories or reports passed from person to person: {Rumours of layoffs spread through the office}. Rumours may be true, false, or somewhere between. The word often implies gossip or speculation: {There were rumours about their relationship for months}.

The rump is the hindquarters—the fleshy part of an animal or person where the back meets the legs. In butchery, rump refers to a cut of beef from this area: {rump roast}, {rump steak}. For humans, rump is a slightly humorous or euphemistic term for the buttocks: {She fell flat on her rump}. Figuratively, a rump is what remains of a group after most members have left or been removed: {a rump parliament}, {the rump of the old party}.

A rumpus is a noisy disturbance or commotion, often playful rather than serious: {The kids were making a rumpus upstairs}. A rumpus room is a space—usually in a basement—designated for recreation and rowdy play, where noise won't disturb the rest of the household.

A rumrunner is someone who smuggles alcohol illegally, especially by boat. The term emerged during Prohibition in the United States (1920–1933), when smugglers transported liquor from ships anchored beyond territorial waters or across borders from Canada and the Caribbean. {Rumrunners made fortunes during the dry years.} The word also applies to the boats themselves.

The core meaning of the verb run, meaning to move very fast on foot, is often lost in more frequent uses of the word. If you run a business, a computer program, or a campaign, you are the controller of it. Something that is running (water, a server, an engine) is operating or moving in a normal and useful way. A run is an instance of running; perhaps on foot (morning run), but also an instance of completing a process (trial run) or the things produced in such an activity (print run). In baseball and cricket, a run is the basis for scoring.

A runaway is someone or something that has escaped or fled, especially a child who has left home without permission: {The shelter helps runaways get back on their feet}. As an adjective, runaway describes things out of control—runaway {inflation}, a runaway {train}—or overwhelming victories: a runaway {success}, a runaway {bestseller}. The word emphasizes momentum that can't easily be stopped.

Runaways are people or things that have fled or escaped control. A runaway child has left home without permission; a runaway train has lost its brakes. As an adjective, runaway describes something out of control or overwhelming: {runaway inflation}, {a runaway bestseller}, {a runaway victory}. The word often implies momentum that can't be stopped.

A rundown is a summary or brief overview: {Give me a rundown of what happened at the meeting}. The word also describes something in poor condition from neglect: a rundown {neighborhood}, a rundown {motel}. In baseball, a rundown is when a baserunner gets caught between bases while fielders throw the ball back and forth trying to tag him out.

A rune is a letter from ancient alphabets used by Germanic and Scandinavian peoples, carved into stone, wood, or bone. The angular shapes suited carving. Beyond their literal function, runes carried mystical associations—used for divination, magic, and casting spells. This occult sense persists: fantasy games feature runes as symbols of power, and modern pagans use them for fortune-telling. Any mysterious symbol or inscription might be called a rune: {The document was covered in runes I couldn't decipher}.

Runes are the letters of alphabets used by ancient Germanic peoples, including Vikings and Anglo-Saxons. The angular characters were designed for carving into wood or stone. Because runes appear on amulets and in mystical contexts, the word carries associations with magic and divination: {casting runes}, {reading the runes}. In fantasy games and fiction, runes are symbols of magical power: {The sword was inscribed with ancient runes}.

A runestone is a large stone bearing inscriptions in runic alphabets, typically erected by Norse and other Germanic peoples during the Viking Age and earlier. Most commemorate the dead or mark territorial claims. Runestones are found throughout Scandinavia and in areas of Viking settlement: {The runestone near the church dates from the eleventh century}.

A rung is one of the horizontal bars forming the steps of a ladder. By extension, rung describes any level in a hierarchy or progression: {the bottom rung of the corporate ladder}, {climbing the rungs of success}. Separately, rung is the past participle of ring: {The bells have rung}.

A runner is can describe any number of people or things. A runner is someone who moves very fast on foot or competes in a track event (long-distance runner) or a messenger or carrier of something from one place to another (script runner). In baseball, a runner is a person on base. A runner can also be a strip of wood or metal on a sled, sleigh, or skate, as well as a long, narrow piece of fabric or carpeting. A plant part that grows along the ground and develops new roots is called a runner. A runner is a person who is in charge of something: The TV program’s executive producer is the show runner.

Runners is the plural of runner—people who run, whether for exercise, sport, or errands. The word extends to things that move or enable movement: sled runners glide over snow, drawer runners allow sliding, and table runners are narrow decorative cloths laid lengthwise. In plants, runners are horizontal stems that spread along the ground to propagate: {The strawberry plant sent out runners}. Runner beans climb supports as they grow.

Running is moving rapidly on foot, faster than walking, with both feet briefly leaving the ground between strides. The word extends to anything continuous or ongoing: a running {commentary}, running {water}, a running {total}. A machine that's running is operating. To be {in the running} is to have a chance at winning; {out of the running} means eliminated. Running also describes consecutive occurrences: {three days running}. As a noun, running is the activity itself or the management of something: {the running of a business}.

Runny describes something more liquid than it should be or than expected. A runny {nose} drips mucus. Runny {eggs} have yolks that flow when broken. Runny {paint} is too thin and drips. The word suggests excess moisture or insufficient thickness: {The sauce came out too runny}.

Runs is what a person or animal does when moving fast on foot, and what machines, programs, and organizations do when they're operating: {The dishwasher runs for an hour}, {She runs the department}. A run is an instance of running, a continuous stretch {(a run of bad luck)}, or a score in baseball and cricket. In fabric, a run is a lengthwise tear where stitches have come undone. The runs is informal for diarrhea.

A runt is the smallest or weakest animal in a litter, often struggling to compete with siblings for nourishment: {The runt of the litter survived against the odds}. Extended to people, runt is a disparaging term for someone small or insignificant: {Don't let that little runt push you around}.

Runts is the plural of runt—the smallest or weakest animal in a litter, particularly of pigs: {The runt of the litter rarely survives without special care}. Extended to people, runt is a disparaging term for someone notably small or undersized: {The runts always got picked last for basketball}.

A runway is a paved strip where aircraft take off and land. The term extends to the narrow platform where fashion models walk to display clothing: {She dreamed of walking the runway in Paris}. A runway can also be any defined path or channel—a {runway} for logs floating downstream, or a {runway} worn by animals through brush.

Runways are long strips of paved ground where aircraft take off and land. The term extends to fashion: a runway is the narrow elevated platform models walk down during shows, displaying clothing to seated audiences. {She dreamed of walking the runway in Paris}. Figuratively, runway can mean remaining resources before depletion: {The startup has six months of runway left}.

Rupture is a break or tear, especially one that happens suddenly or violently. A pipe ruptures under pressure; a tendon ruptures during exertion. The word applies to both physical breaks and abstract ones: {a rupture in diplomatic relations}, {the rupture between old friends}. In medicine, a rupture often refers specifically to a hernia or to an organ tearing. To rupture is to break apart or cause to break: {The explosion ruptured the fuel tank}.

Ruptures is the plural of rupture—a break, tear, or burst, especially in tissue or a container. Blood vessels rupture; pipes rupture under pressure. Figuratively, ruptures are breaks in relationships or agreements: {diplomatic ruptures between nations}. In medicine, a rupture often means a hernia. The verb ruptures means causes to break: {The impact ruptures the fuel tank}.

Rural describes areas outside cities and towns—the countryside, farmland, small villages. It contrasts with urban: {rural communities}, {rural roads}, {rural healthcare}. The word suggests lower population density, agricultural land use, and distance from metropolitan centers. {She grew up in rural Montana, hours from the nearest city.}

A ruse is a clever trick or deception designed to mislead someone: {The phone call was just a ruse to get him out of the house}. The word suggests cunning and deliberate misdirection rather than outright lying—a stratagem that exploits someone's assumptions or expectations.

To rush is to move quickly, usually to a destination. To rush in American football is to advance the ball by running. To rush at someone is to move towards them with force. Fast-moving water is said to rush. A rush is an instance of rushing, especially one of many people going to a place (gold rush). A rush is also a feeling of great excitement (adrenaline rush). Before another noun, rush characterizes something done very quickly, often too quickly (rush decision). A different rush is an aquatic plant.

Rushed describes something done hastily, without adequate time or care: {a rushed job}, {a rushed decision}. It also describes the feeling of being pressured by time constraints: {I felt rushed all morning}. The rushed hour before a deadline differs from the leisurely pace of an unhurried afternoon.

Rushes are the unedited footage from a film shoot, reviewed daily by the director and crew to assess what was captured. The term comes from the rush to develop and print film overnight for next-day viewing. Also called dailies. Separately, rushes is the plural of rush—grasslike wetland plants, or instances of rushing: {the morning rushes of commuters}.

Rushing captures the idea of moving or acting with urgent speed, often implying haste that crowds out care or deliberation. You might rush to catch a train or rush through homework to get it done. The noun rushing appears in American football as a technical term for advancing the ball by running rather than passing: {He led the league in rushing yards}. A rush of emotion or sensation comes on suddenly and intensely. If there's no rush, there's no urgency to complete something quickly.

Rust is the reddish-brown coating that forms on iron and steel when exposed to moisture and air—the visible result of oxidation. The color rust names this distinctive brownish-red. Things can rust literally or figuratively: skills rust from disuse, machinery rusts in abandoned factories. {My Spanish has rusted since college.} To rust out is to deteriorate completely from corrosion. (Capitalized Rust is a programming language.)

The Rust Belt is a region of the northeastern and midwestern United States—centered on states like Ohio, Michigan, and Pennsylvania—where heavy manufacturing declined sharply in the late twentieth century. The name evokes abandoned factories rusting in place. The term often carries political connotations, as these areas became pivotal in elections: {Rust Belt voters swung the election}. Also spelled Rust Belt or rust belt.

Rusted describes metal that has developed rust—the reddish-brown corrosion that forms when iron or steel is exposed to moisture and air. A rusted {gate} creaks on its hinges. Rusted {pipes} may need replacement. Figuratively, skills that have rusted have deteriorated from disuse: {My Spanish has rusted since college}.

Rustic describes something rough, simple, or characteristic of country life. A rustic cabin has unfinished wood and lacks modern amenities. Rustic furniture shows natural textures—bark left on, joints visible. The word can be charming {rustic charm} or dismissive {rustic manners}, depending on whether you're romanticizing rural simplicity or contrasting it unfavorably with urban sophistication. As a noun, a rustic is a country person, often implying unsophistication.

Rustle is a soft, whispering sound like dry leaves stirring or fabric brushing against itself: {the rustle of papers}, {wind rustling through the trees}. The word captures light, friction-made sounds. To rustle something up is to gather or prepare quickly: {Let me rustle up some breakfast}. In American English, to rustle cattle or horses is to steal them—a meaning from the Old West that persists in rural areas.

Rustled is the past tense of rustle—to make a soft, crackling sound like dry leaves or paper moving against each other: {The wind rustled the curtains}. Rustled also means stole livestock, especially cattle: {They rustled horses from ranches across the border}. To have {rustled up} something is to have gathered or prepared it quickly: {She rustled up some dinner from leftovers}.

A rustler is someone who steals livestock, especially cattle or horses. The term evokes the American frontier, where cattle rustling was a serious crime often punished by hanging. More broadly, rustler can mean anyone who hustles or scrounges resourcefully: {She's a real rustler when it comes to finding bargains}.

Rustlers are people who steal livestock, especially cattle or horses. The term evokes the American West, where cattle rustling was a serious crime often punished by hanging. {The ranchers formed a posse to track down the rustlers.} More broadly, a rustler is anyone who rustles—makes soft sounds of movement, or rounds things up quickly.

Rustling is the soft, whispery sound of things brushing against each other—leaves in wind, fabric moving, papers being shuffled: {the rustling of her silk dress}. The verb rustle captures this sound or the action producing it. To rustle up something is to gather or prepare it quickly: {Let me rustle up some breakfast}. Rustling also means stealing livestock, especially cattle or horses—a serious crime in ranching country: {He was hanged for cattle rustling}.

Rusty describes metal that has developed rust—the reddish-brown coating that forms when iron corrodes. The color extends to anything with that brownish-red hue: {rusty leaves}, {rusty hair}. Skills or abilities that are rusty have deteriorated from disuse: {My French is a little rusty}. A rusty voice sounds rough or hoarse, as if corroded by time. (Capitalized Rusty is a nickname.)

Rut is two words, each expressed as a noun and a verb. First, a groove worn by repeated passage is a rut. If you’re in a rut, you are bored or frustrated by having to do the same thing all the time. To rut a surface is to make a rut in it. Second, rut is the male counterpart of estrus, the period during which males (especially deer) are sexually aroused. Such animals are in rut or rutting. To rut is also a vulgar way to reference having sexual intercourse.

Ruthless describes someone who pursues goals without mercy or compassion, willing to harm others or ignore their suffering to get what they want. A ruthless {dictator} crushes opposition. A ruthless {negotiator} exploits every weakness. The word implies cold calculation—not hot-blooded cruelty, but deliberate disregard for others when they stand in the way.

Ruts are grooves worn into a surface by repeated passage, especially wheel tracks in soft ground or dirt roads. The word extends to any fixed, monotonous pattern: {I'm stuck in a rut at work}. To be in a rut is to follow the same course so long that deviation becomes difficult. The rut is also the mating season for deer and similar animals, when males compete aggressively for females—a different word entirely.

Rye is a cereal grain related to wheat and barley, used for bread, whiskey, and animal feed. Rye bread has a denser texture and darker color than wheat bread. Rye whiskey, made primarily from rye grain, has a spicier flavor than bourbon. A {rye and ginger} is rye whiskey mixed with ginger ale. {I'll have a corned beef on rye.}

A sabbath is a day of rest, especially a weekly religious observance. The word comes from Hebrew for "to rest" and traditionally refers to the seventh day when God rested after creation. In extended use, any period of rest or cessation from work: {The garden lay in sabbath through the winter months}. A sabbath can also mean a supposed midnight assembly of witches and demons—more fully, a witches' sabbath. (Capitalized Sabbath is the specific Jewish or Christian holy day.)

A sabbatical is an extended leave from work, traditionally granted to academics every seventh year for research, travel, or renewal. The practice has spread to other professions: {She took a sabbatical to write her novel}. Unlike vacation, a sabbatical implies productive purpose—study, creation, or professional development rather than simple rest.

A saber is a curved sword with a single cutting edge, historically used by cavalry. The spelling sabre is British. Saber-rattling is aggressive posturing or threats of military action: {The regime's saber-rattling worried neighboring countries}. In fencing, the saber is one of three weapons, distinguished by rules allowing cuts as well as thrusts.

Sabers are curved, single-edged swords designed for slashing, traditionally used by cavalry. The spelling saber is American; sabre is British. Beyond the weapon, a saber is the modern fencing sword used in one of three Olympic disciplines. To saber champagne is to open a bottle by striking the neck with a blade. {Rattling sabers} means making aggressive threats without yet acting on them.

Sabertooth refers to prehistoric cats with elongated upper canine teeth, most famously the saber-toothed tiger (actually not a tiger but a separate lineage). The teeth could extend several inches, used for piercing prey. The term applies broadly to any animal with similar dentition: {sabertooth salmon}, {sabertooth deer}. Often appears as saber-toothed or sabre-toothed as an adjective.

Sable describes a deep black color, especially in heraldry and fashion: {a sable cloak}, {sable fur}. The word comes from the dark-furred mammal prized for its luxurious pelt—among the most valuable furs in the world. Sable coats and trim have long signified wealth. In poetic or literary use, sable means dark or gloomy: {the sable night}, {sable clouds}. (Capitalized Sable appears in proper names.)

Sabotage is deliberate destruction or disruption of something—equipment, infrastructure, plans, or efforts. The term often implies covert action: workers sabotaging machinery, spies sabotaging military operations, or someone sabotaging a relationship through undermining behavior. {The protesters were accused of sabotaging the pipeline.} To sabotage can also mean to undermine unintentionally: {Don't sabotage your own success by procrastinating.}

Sabotaged is the past tense of sabotage—to deliberately destroy, damage, or obstruct something. The target is usually equipment, a project, or a plan: {Someone sabotaged the factory machinery}. The word extends to undermining efforts or relationships: {He sabotaged his own chances by showing up late}. Self-sabotage describes unconsciously undermining one's own goals.

Sabotages is the verb form of sabotage—to deliberately destroy, damage, or obstruct something. The word often implies undermining from within: {She sabotages every relationship she's in}. One can sabotage equipment, plans, negotiations, or even oneself. Self-sabotage describes unconsciously undermining one's own efforts or success.

A saboteur is someone who commits sabotage—deliberately destroying, damaging, or obstructing something. The term often applies to wartime operatives who disable enemy infrastructure: {Saboteurs blew up the railway bridge}. More broadly, it describes anyone who undermines an effort from within: {Critics called him a saboteur of the peace process}.

Saboteurs are people who commit sabotage—deliberately destroying, damaging, or obstructing something. The term often applies to wartime operatives who disable enemy infrastructure: {Allied saboteurs blew up the railway bridge}. It extends to anyone who undermines an effort from within: {Budget saboteurs in Congress blocked the bill}. The word carries implications of stealth and treachery.

A sabre is a cavalry sword with a curved blade, designed for slashing from horseback. The spelling is British; Americans write saber. By extension, sabre refers to a light fencing weapon with a flexible blade, used for thrusting and cutting. To {rattle sabres} is to make aggressive threats, especially military ones, without actually fighting: {Both nations have been sabre-rattling for months}.

Sabres is the plural of sabre, a curved sword with a single cutting edge, historically used by cavalry. The spelling is British; Americans write sabers. Sabre rattling is aggressive posturing that threatens military action without committing to it: {The general's speech was more sabre rattling than serious threat}.

A sabretooth is any of several extinct cats characterized by elongated upper canine teeth, most famously the sabretooth tiger (Smilodon). The teeth could exceed eight inches in length. The term applies broadly to unrelated mammals that evolved similar dentition: {sabretooth salmon}, {sabretooth marsupials}. Also spelled saber-tooth or sabre-tooth.

Three words are spelled s-a-c-k. The first is a bag without handles (paper sack). If you sack something, you put it in a sack. If you sack a person, you dismiss them from a job. If you sack the quarterback, you tackle him behind the line of scrimmage. If you wear a sack, you’re dressed in something loose fitting or perhaps shabby. If you’re in the sack, you’re in bed, possibly having sex with someone. The second means to plunder or loot: The invaders sacked Rome. A sack is an instance of this. The third is a white wine formerly made in Spain and the Canary Islands, which is called sack.

Sacked means fired from a job, chiefly British: {He got sacked for showing up drunk}. The image is of a worker being handed a sack to collect their belongings on the way out. In American football, sacked describes a quarterback tackled behind the line of scrimmage: {The quarterback was sacked three times in the first half}. Sacked also means plundered or looted, as when an army sacks a conquered city.

Sacking is coarse woven fabric, typically made from jute or hemp, used for bags and wrapping: {The potatoes came in sacking}. In British English, sacking also means dismissal from employment: {He got his sacking notice on Friday}. The word derives from sack in both senses—the bag and the act of firing someone.

Sacks is the plural of sack—a large bag, typically of coarse material: {sacks of grain}, {burlap sacks}. To sack is to put into sacks, to fire someone from a job {(She got the sack)}, or to plunder a conquered place. In American football, a sack is tackling the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage: {He led the league in sacks}. To {hit the sack} is to go to bed.

A sacrament is a religious rite or ceremony considered to convey divine grace. In Christianity, sacraments include baptism, communion, and (in Catholic and Orthodox traditions) confession, confirmation, marriage, ordination, and anointing of the sick. The word extends to anything regarded as sacred or inviolable: {Free speech is a sacrament in American political culture}.

Sacraments are religious rites believed to confer divine grace on participants. In Christianity, the term most often refers to baptism and communion, though Catholic and Orthodox traditions recognize seven sacraments including confession, confirmation, and marriage. The word implies an outward sign of inward spiritual reality: {She received the sacraments before dying}. Extended use covers anything treated as sacred or inviolable: {the sacraments of democracy}.

Sacred means dedicated to religious purposes or connected to the divine: a sacred {text}, sacred {ground}, a sacred {ritual}. What is sacred commands reverence and must not be violated or profaned. The meaning extends to anything held inviolable: {Nothing is sacred to these people}. A sacred {cow} is something exempt from criticism or questioning.

Sacrifice is giving up something valuable for a greater purpose or another's benefit. The oldest sense is religious: an offering to a deity, often an animal killed on an altar. The meaning extends to any significant relinquishment: {She sacrificed her career for her family}. In baseball, a sacrifice is a play where a batter intentionally makes an out to advance a runner. To sacrifice is to make such an offering or to give something up willingly: {He sacrificed his weekends to finish the project}.

Sacrifices is the plural of sacrifice—things given up or destroyed for a purpose beyond themselves. In religious contexts, sacrifices are offerings to a deity, often animals or goods: {The temple required daily sacrifices}. More commonly, sacrifices are personal costs accepted for a larger goal: {She made sacrifices to put her kids through college}. In chess and other games, a sacrifice is a deliberate loss of a piece to gain positional advantage.

Sacrificing is giving up something valuable for a greater purpose or another's benefit. Parents sacrifice sleep for newborns. Athletes sacrifice personal time for training. In chess, sacrificing a piece means deliberately losing it to gain positional advantage: {She's sacrificing the knight to open up the king}. The word carries weight—what's given up should matter.

Sacrilege is violation or disrespect of something sacred—desecrating a holy place, misusing sacred objects, or profaning religious rites. The word extends to any gross disrespect of something held in high regard: {To some fans, trading that player would be sacrilege}. The adjective is sacrilegious, frequently misspelled as "sacreligious."

Sad describes a feeling of unhappiness or sorrow: {I felt sad when she left}. Something sad evokes or expresses that feeling: {a sad song}, {sad news}. Extended uses suggest inadequacy or regret: {a sad state of affairs}, {a sad excuse for a meal}. In internet slang, calling someone or something sad implies they're pathetic or worthy of pity: {Imagine bragging about that—so sad}.

A saddle is a thing to sit on, especially on a horse, but by extension, on a bicycle or motorcycle. Things roughly shaped like a horse saddle also get the name, like a ridge connecting two peaks, a cut of meat that includes some backbone, or the covering of a roof ridge. To saddle a horse is to fit a saddle on it. To saddle someone with a burden is to make it their problem or responsibility. If you’re figuratively in the saddle, you are at work or ready to be in charge.

Saddled means burdened with something unwanted or difficult to manage: {saddled with debt}, {saddled with responsibility for the whole project}. The image comes from placing a saddle on a horse—once it's on, the animal must carry it. In its literal sense, saddled describes a horse fitted with a saddle and ready to ride.

Saddles is the plural of saddle—a seat strapped to the back of a horse or other animal for riding. The shape extends to bicycle saddles and motorcycle seats. A saddle of meat is a cut from the back of an animal, spanning both sides. To saddle someone with something is to burden them: {They saddled him with all the paperwork}. To be {back in the saddle} is to resume control after an absence.

Sadism is deriving pleasure—especially sexual pleasure—from inflicting pain, suffering, or humiliation on others. The term extends beyond the sexual to describe any enjoyment of cruelty: {There was a sadism in how he delivered the bad news}. In clinical contexts, sexual sadism is a paraphilia involving arousal from a partner's physical or psychological distress. Casual use often describes petty cruelties: {The sadism of making employees work Christmas Eve}.

A sadist derives pleasure from inflicting pain, suffering, or humiliation on others. The term originated with the Marquis de Sade, whose novels depicted sexual gratification through cruelty. In clinical contexts, sadism describes a paraphilia involving arousal from another's distress. More loosely, sadist describes anyone who seems to enjoy others' discomfort: {My gym teacher was a sadist who made us run in the rain}.

Sadistic describes deriving pleasure from inflicting pain, suffering, or humiliation on others. The word applies to both sexual gratification from cruelty and the broader enjoyment of others' distress: {a sadistic bully}, {sadistic torture scenes}. A sadistic streak suggests someone who enjoys being cruel even in small ways: {He took sadistic pleasure in pointing out her mistakes}.

Sadness is the emotional state of feeling unhappy or sorrowful. It ranges from mild disappointment to deep grief: {A sadness came over her when she saw the empty house}. Unlike depression, sadness is typically a response to specific circumstances and tends to pass with time. The word can also describe a quality that evokes this feeling: {There was a sadness to the abandoned town}.

A safari is an expedition to observe or hunt wild animals, especially in East Africa. The word comes from Swahili meaning "journey." Modern safaris are typically photographic rather than hunting trips: {We went on safari in Kenya}. The term extends to any expedition-style adventure: {a whale-watching safari}, {an urban architecture safari}. (Capitalized Safari is Apple's web browser.)

Safaris are expeditions to observe or hunt wild animals, especially in East Africa. The word comes from Swahili for "journey." A safari typically involves guided travel through wildlife reserves: {We went on safari in Kenya}. The term extends to any organized excursion with an exploratory feel: {a photo safari}, {a shopping safari}. Safari also names Apple's web browser.

While it has use as a noun and adverb, safe is mainly an adjective whose meanings are related to the idea of security and freedom from distress: We arrived safe and sound. A safe place or route is one that can be used without danger. If it is safe to do something, you can do it without risk of harm: Is it safe to drink the water? If you play it safe, you act in a way that avoids risk. A safe bet is an option that seems likely to have a good outcome. As a noun, safe mainly denotes a sturdy, rigid receptacle for storing valuables: Each room in the hotel has a small safe.

A safecracker is someone who breaks into safes, typically to steal their contents. The term applies both to professional criminals and to legitimate locksmiths called to open safes when combinations are lost. Safecracking may involve drilling, explosives, or manipulating the lock mechanism: {The safecracker worked through the night on the vault}.

Safecracking is the act of breaking into a safe or vault, typically to steal its contents. The term applies whether the method involves drilling, explosives, lock manipulation, or electronic bypass. A safecracker may be a professional thief or a locksmith called to open a safe whose combination has been lost: {The heist film featured an elaborate safecracking sequence}.

Safeguards are measures designed to protect against harm, loss, or unwanted outcomes. The word implies proactive defense—putting something in place before trouble arrives: {constitutional safeguards against tyranny}, {safeguards to prevent data breaches}. To safeguard is to protect or secure: {We must safeguard our children's future}. The term appears frequently in policy, security, and legal contexts.

A safehouse is a secret location used as a refuge or meeting place, typically by people evading authorities or danger. Intelligence agents use safehouses to debrief sources. Criminals hide in safehouses between operations. The term also applies to shelters for abuse victims or witnesses under protection: {The organization operates a safehouse for trafficking survivors}. Sometimes written as two words: safe house.

Safety is the condition of being protected from harm, danger, or risk: {The hikers reached safety before the storm hit}. It extends to devices that prevent accidental discharge or injury—a gun's safety, a safety pin. In American football, a safety is a defensive score worth two points, or the defensive position itself. {Safety first} urges caution as a priority.

A safeword is a prearranged word or signal used during sexual activity, particularly BDSM, that immediately stops the scene when spoken. Because roleplay may involve saying "no" or "stop" without meaning it literally, partners agree on a neutral word—often something unlikely to come up naturally, like {pineapple} or {red}—that clearly communicates a genuine need to pause or end the encounter. The term has extended to any agreed-upon signal for withdrawing from an uncomfortable situation.

Saffron is a spice derived from the dried stigmas of a crocus flower, prized for the intense yellow-orange color and distinctive flavor it imparts to dishes like paella and risotto. Because each flower yields only three stigmas, harvested by hand, saffron is the world's most expensive spice by weight. The color itself is also called saffron—a warm yellow-orange: {saffron robes}.

To sag is to sink, droop, or bend downward under weight or pressure. A mattress sags in the middle after years of use. Spirits sag when hope fades. Stock prices sag during uncertain times. The noun describes the degree or instance of drooping: {There's a noticeable sag in the ceiling}. In fashion, sagging pants hang low, often intentionally. (Capitalized SAG is the actors' union.)

A saga is a long story of heroic deeds, originally the medieval prose narratives of Icelandic and Norse tradition. The word now applies to any extended account of events, especially one spanning generations: {a family saga}, {the saga of westward expansion}. In casual use, saga often describes a drawn-out ordeal: {Let me tell you the saga of trying to get my landlord to fix the heat}.

Sagas are long stories of heroic adventure, originally the medieval Norse prose narratives recounting the deeds of legendary Scandinavian figures. The term extends to any sprawling narrative spanning generations or great events: {a family saga}, {the saga of westward expansion}. In casual use, saga describes any prolonged complicated experience: {Let me tell you the saga of getting my car fixed}.

Sage is an aromatic herb with grayish-green leaves, commonly used in cooking—particularly with poultry and in stuffing. The plant's muted color gives us sage green. Separately, a sage is a person of profound wisdom, and as an adjective, sage means wise: {sage advice}, {a sage observation}. The two words share no origin but have coexisted in English for centuries. (Capitalized Sage is a given name.)

Sagebrush is a shrubby plant with silvery-gray aromatic leaves, native to the arid regions of western North America. It dominates vast stretches of high desert landscape, giving the terrain its characteristic look and smell. The sagebrush steppe is iconic cowboy country: {miles of sagebrush as far as the eye could see}. Despite the name, sagebrush is unrelated to culinary sage.

Sages is the plural of sage, meaning wise people—especially those respected for profound judgment and experience: {The sages of ancient Greece}, {seeking counsel from village sages}. Sages also refers to multiple plants of the aromatic herb used in cooking: {She grows several sages in her garden}.

Said is the irregular past tense and past participle of say and it is by far the most frequent form of say, since it is the verb most often used to report, in the past, what people say. Said has a minor role as an adjective to mean previously mentioned. It is used this way in legal and humorous language.

A sail is a sheet of fabric that catches the wind to propel a boat or other vessel. To sail is to move across the water in a boat; probably a boat with sails, but the verb is also used for people traveling in large ships: They are sailing to Europe. If you sail through something, it’s easy for you and requires little effort for success. To set sail is to begin a sea voyage. Figuratively, to trim your sails is to economize.

A sailboat is a boat propelled primarily by sails catching the wind. Sailboats range from small single-person craft to large ocean-going vessels. The term is American; British English prefers sailing boat. {We rented a sailboat for the afternoon.}

Sailed is the past tense of sail. A boat sails when it moves across water, whether by wind power or engine: {We sailed to the island at dawn}. By extension, anything that moves smoothly and swiftly sails: {The ball sailed over the fence}. To sail through something is to complete it easily: {She sailed through the interview}.

Sailing is the activity of traveling on water using wind power, whether for recreation, sport, or transport. A sailing ship moves by wind in its sails rather than engine power. The word often suggests pleasure or sport: {We went sailing on the lake}. Something that is {smooth sailing} proceeds easily without obstacles.

A sailor is someone who works on a ship or boat, especially as a member of a crew. The term applies to naval personnel and civilian seafarers alike: {He spent twenty years as a merchant sailor}. Sailor also describes anyone who sails recreationally: {She's an experienced sailor who races competitively}. A good or bad sailor refers to susceptibility to seasickness: {I'm a terrible sailor—I get queasy on ferries}.

Sailors are people who work on ships or boats, especially as members of a crew. The term covers everyone from naval personnel to commercial mariners to recreational boaters. A {good sailor} handles rough seas without getting sick. {Hello, sailor} is a flirtatious greeting associated with old port towns. Someone described as {no sailor} gets seasick easily.

Sails are sheets of fabric attached to a ship's mast, catching wind to propel the vessel. By extension, the blades of a windmill are sails. To sail is to travel by boat, especially one with sails: {We sailed to the island}. More broadly, anything that moves smoothly through air or water sails: {The ball sailed over the fence}. To {sail through} something is to accomplish it effortlessly.

A saint is a person formally recognized by a religious authority—especially the Catholic Church—as having lived a holy life worthy of veneration. More loosely, saint describes anyone exceptionally virtuous or patient: {She's a saint for putting up with him}. The verb means to canonize or regard as holy. As a title before names, it's usually capitalized: Saint Patrick, Saint Jude. {He's no saint} acknowledges someone's flaws.

Sainthood is the state or status of being a saint—a person formally recognized by a religious institution, particularly the Catholic Church, as holy and worthy of veneration. Achieving sainthood typically requires evidence of an exceptionally virtuous life and, in Catholic tradition, verified miracles. The term extends figuratively to describe any state of exceptional moral virtue or patience: {After raising five kids alone, she deserves sainthood}.

Saints is the plural of saint—people formally recognized by religious authorities for exceptional holiness, or more loosely, anyone of extraordinary virtue and patience: {She's a saint for putting up with him}. In Christianity, saints are venerated figures who can intercede with God. The word also appears in place names and institutional names: {the streets of New Orleans are named after saints}. (Capitalized Saints often refers to sports teams.)

Sake has two main uses. For the sake of something means for its benefit or purpose: {for the sake of argument}, {for safety's sake}, {art for art's sake}. In exclamations, sake expresses exasperation: {for God's sake}, {for heaven's sake}, {for Pete's sake}. The other sake, pronounced SAH-keh, is Japanese rice wine.

Salad is a dish of raw vegetables, typically leafy greens, served with dressing: {a garden salad}, {Caesar salad}. The term extends to cold dishes mixing chopped ingredients: {potato salad}, {chicken salad}, {fruit salad}. Someone's {salad days} are their youth—a time of inexperience and naïveté. {Word salad} is incoherent, jumbled speech or writing.

A salamander is a small amphibian with a slender body, smooth moist skin, and a long tail—resembling a lizard but lacking scales. Salamanders live in damp environments and breathe through their skin. In mythology and medieval belief, salamanders were thought to live in fire or be immune to flames, which gives the word extended uses: a salamander can be a fire-resistant safe, a heating element, or a broiler used in professional kitchens.

Salamanders are amphibians with slender bodies, moist skin, and long tails that they retain throughout their lives, distinguishing them from frogs and toads. Most live in damp environments near water, though some are fully aquatic and others fully terrestrial. In mythology and folklore, salamanders were believed to be fire spirits capable of living in flames, a notion that arose from the creatures emerging from logs thrown on fires. {We found salamanders under rocks near the creek.}

Salami is a cured sausage of Italian origin, typically made from fermented and air-dried beef or pork. It's seasoned with garlic, salt, and spices, then aged until firm enough to slice thin. Different regions produce distinctive varieties: Genoa salami, hard salami, soppressata. {a salami sandwich}, {salami and cheese on crackers}.

A salary is fixed compensation paid regularly for work, typically expressed as an annual amount and disbursed in portions—monthly, biweekly, or weekly. Unlike wages, which are calculated by hours worked, a salary remains constant regardless of time spent: {She negotiated a starting salary of $85,000}. Salaried employees often don't receive overtime pay.

A sale is the exchange of goods or services for money, or an event where items are sold at reduced prices: {The store is having a sale}. Something {for sale} is available to buy; something {on sale} is discounted. A sale can also be a specific transaction: {We closed the sale yesterday}. Sales as a field refers to the work of selling: {She works in sales}.

Sales refers to the activity of selling goods or services, or the department responsible for it: {She works in sales}. It also means the total amount sold: {Sales are up this quarter}. A sale is a single transaction or a period of discounted prices; sales is both the plural and the broader commercial function. {Sales figures}, {sales tax}, and {sales pitch} all use the attributive form.

A salesman is a man whose job is selling goods or services. The term covers retail workers, door-to-door representatives, and those who negotiate major commercial deals. {The car salesman wouldn't budge on price.} Salesman often implies pushiness or persuasive tactics—someone described as {a natural salesman} has a knack for getting people to buy things, literally or figuratively. The gender-neutral salesperson and sales rep are increasingly preferred in professional contexts.

Saliva is the watery fluid produced by glands in the mouth. It moistens food for swallowing, begins digestion, and protects teeth. Saliva appears in contexts of anticipation {(my mouth watered)}, disgust {(he spat)}, or intimacy {(they exchanged saliva)}. The adjective is salivary; to salivate is to produce saliva, often figuratively: {Investors salivated at the prospect}.

Salivating is producing saliva, the watery fluid in the mouth that aids digestion. Dogs salivate at the smell of food; so do hungry humans. Figuratively, salivating means eagerly anticipating something desirable: {Investors are salivating over the company's IPO}, {She was salivating at the thought of that promotion}.

Salmon are large fish prized for their pink flesh, known for swimming upstream from the ocean to spawn in freshwater rivers where they were born. The fish gives its name to a pinkish-orange color: {salmon walls}, {a salmon dress}. Smoked salmon appears on bagels; canned salmon in salads. The plural is salmon or salmons.

A salon is a room for receiving guests, typically elegant and used for social gatherings or intellectual conversation. The word extends to regular gatherings of artists, writers, or thinkers: {She hosted a literary salon on Thursday evenings}. A salon is also a business establishment for beauty services—hair styling, manicures, facials: {hair salon}, {nail salon}, {beauty salon}. The shortened form appears in compounds: {salon-quality products}.

Salons are establishments where people receive hair styling, beauty treatments, or similar personal services: {hair salon}, {nail salon}, {tanning salon}.
