The word also refers to elegant rooms for receiving guests, or to gatherings of intellectuals and artists hosted by a prominent figure—a usage that evokes 18th-century Parisian culture. {She held a literary salon every Thursday evening.}

A saloon is a place where alcoholic drinks are served, particularly in the American Old West, where saloons were gathering spots for cowboys, miners, and travelers. The term survives today mainly in historical contexts or themed establishments. In British English, saloon has additional meanings: a saloon car is a sedan automobile, and a saloon bar is an upscale section of a pub. A saloon may also refer to a large room for passengers on a ship or a spacious room for receptions.

Saloons are drinking establishments, particularly the rough-and-ready bars of the American Old West with swinging doors and long wooden bars. The word now sounds dated or deliberately evocative of that era. In British usage, a saloon is a large room for gatherings, or the more comfortable section of a pub. A saloon car is a sedan. {The cowboys tied their horses outside the saloon.}

Salsa is a spicy sauce of tomatoes, onions, and chili peppers, central to Mexican and Tex-Mex cuisine. You dip chips in salsa or spoon it over tacos. Salsa is also a style of Latin dance music with Cuban and Puerto Rican roots, and the partner dance performed to it: {We took salsa lessons}. The word is Spanish for sauce.

The naturally occurring chemical compound sodium chloride is the thing usually referred to by the word salt. More specifically, a salt is a compound in which hydrogen has been replaced by another element, thus de-acidifying it. Many figurative expressions draw on some aspect of common salt, such as salt of the earth (a dependable and noble group of people). As a verb, salt means to add the substance to something: The pasta water isn’t salted yet. Before another noun, salt indicates abundant presence of salt or treatment with salt, as in salt marsh, salt cod, saltwater.

Salted means treated or preserved with salt: {salted butter}, {salted cod}, {salted peanuts}. The word also describes something seasoned with salt for flavor. Figuratively, a salted mine or claim has been fraudulently seeded with valuable minerals to deceive buyers. A {salted veteran} is one toughened by experience.

Saltwater is water with a high salt content, especially seawater. As an adjective, it distinguishes ocean-dwelling creatures from their freshwater counterparts: {saltwater fish}, {saltwater crocodile}. A {saltwater taffy} is a chewy candy associated with seaside boardwalks—the name evokes coastal origins rather than actual ingredients.

Salty describes the taste of salt or things containing salt: {salty ocean water}, {salty pretzels}. Extended to mean sharp or pungent: {salty language} is coarse or profane. In contemporary slang, salty means bitter, resentful, or annoyed—especially about a minor slight or loss: {He's still salty about losing that game}.

A salute is a gesture of respect or greeting, most often the military gesture of raising the hand to the forehead. Soldiers salute superior officers; flags and dignitaries receive salutes. The word extends to any formal acknowledgment of honor: a {twenty-one-gun salute}, a {salute to the veterans}. To salute someone is to greet them with such a gesture or to honor their achievement: {Let's salute the workers who made this possible}.

Salutes is the plural of salute, a gesture of respect or greeting. Military salutes involve raising the hand to the forehead; gun salutes fire ceremonial rounds. Beyond the military, a salute is any act of recognition or tribute: {The concert was a salute to jazz legends}. As a verb form: {She salutes the flag every morning}.

Salvage is the rescue of property from destruction or loss—especially ships, cargo, or wreckage from the sea. The word extends to saving anything from ruin: {salvage operations recovered documents from the flooded basement}. To salvage a situation is to preserve what value remains after damage: {She tried to salvage her reputation}. Salvage also names what's been saved—materials recovered for reuse: {The yard sells automotive salvage}.

Salvaged describes something rescued or recovered from loss, damage, or destruction. A salvaged {ship} was raised from the ocean floor. Salvaged {materials} were saved from a demolished building. The word often implies resourcefulness—finding value in what others discarded or wrote off: {The furniture was salvaged from a warehouse fire}. Figuratively, a salvaged {reputation} or salvaged {relationship} has been pulled back from ruin.

Salvation is rescue from danger, destruction, or harm. In religious contexts, particularly Christianity, salvation refers to deliverance from sin and its consequences—the saving of the soul: {He found salvation through faith}. More broadly, salvation is whatever preserves or redeems someone from a difficult situation: {The loan was our salvation}. A person or thing that saves can itself be called a salvation: {That job was my salvation during a hard year}.

A salvo is the simultaneous firing of multiple guns or missiles, or the release of bombs from an aircraft. By extension, a salvo is any burst of forceful action delivered at once: {a salvo of criticism}, {an opening salvo in the debate}. The word suggests coordinated impact—multiple shots landing together for maximum effect.

A samaritan is someone who helps a stranger in distress, from the biblical parable of the Good Samaritan. The word usually appears with "good" attached: {A good samaritan stopped to help change her tire}. Laws called Good Samaritan laws protect people who assist others in emergencies from liability. The lowercase form emphasizes the general sense of charitable helper rather than ethnic or religious identity. (Capitalized Samaritan refers to a person from ancient Samaria or a member of the surviving religious community.)

Samba is a Brazilian dance and music genre characterized by syncopated rhythms and lively movement. It emerged from African and Portuguese influences and remains central to Brazilian culture, especially during Carnival: {The streets filled with samba dancers}. The verb means to dance samba: {They sambaed until dawn}.

Same, mainly an adjective, is an extreme version of like: its core meaning is like in every way. It is often followed by a prepositional phrase with as. Same always references at least two things and implicitly involves the ideas of comparison and equality.

A samosa is a fried or baked pastry with a savory filling, typically triangular and made with a thin, crispy shell. The filling is usually spiced potatoes and peas, though meat versions are common. Samosas originated in South Asia and the Middle East and are now popular street food and appetizers worldwide: {We ordered samosas to start}.

Samosas are fried or baked pastries with savory fillings, triangular in shape and originating in South Asian cuisine. The crisp outer shell typically contains spiced potatoes, peas, onions, or ground meat. They're served as snacks or appetizers, often with chutneys for dipping: {We ordered samosas while we waited for the main course}.

A sample is a small portion taken from something larger—enough to show what the whole is like. You might taste a sample of cheese, analyze a blood sample, or survey a sample of voters. In music, to sample is to extract a snippet from an existing recording for use in a new track. As an adjective, sample indicates something representative: {a sample size of 500}, {sample questions from the exam}.

A sampler is a representative selection or collection of items: {a sampler of local cheeses}, {a sampler platter}. In needlework, a sampler is a piece of cloth embroidered with various stitches, letters, and decorative motifs—traditionally made by young women to demonstrate skill. In music production, a sampler is an electronic instrument that records and plays back snippets of sound, allowing musicians to incorporate and manipulate audio fragments: {He built the beat using a sampler and vintage funk records}.

Samples are small portions taken from a larger whole to represent or test it: a blood sample, a fabric sample, a free sample at the grocery store. In music, a sample is a snippet of recorded sound repurposed in a new composition: {The track samples an old soul record}. To sample is to take or try such a portion: {We sampled the local cuisine}. In statistics, a sample is a subset of a population used to draw conclusions about the whole.

Sampling is taking a small portion to represent a larger whole. In research, you sample a population to draw conclusions without surveying everyone. In music production, sampling means extracting a snippet from an existing recording to incorporate into a new track: {The song samples a 1970s funk bassline}. A sampling of something is a representative selection: {Here's a sampling of what we'll cover today}.

A samurai was a member of the warrior class in feudal Japan, serving a lord and following a strict code of honor called bushido. The word now evokes disciplined martial skill and loyalty: {He approached his work with samurai focus}. In modern usage, samurai often modifies nouns to suggest Japanese warrior tradition: {samurai sword}, {samurai armor}. The plural is also samurai.

Sanction carries opposite meanings that context must resolve. To sanction something is to authorize or approve it: {The board sanctioned the merger}. But sanctions (usually plural) are penalties imposed to punish or coerce: {economic sanctions against the regime}. The shared thread is official action—approval grants permission, punishment enforces compliance. A sanctioned event has backing; a sanctioned country faces restrictions.

Sanctioned carries opposite meanings depending on context. To sanction something is to officially approve or authorize it: {The board sanctioned the new policy}. But sanctions (usually plural) are penalties imposed to punish or coerce, especially in international relations: {economic sanctions against the regime}. A sanctioned country or individual is one facing such penalties. The ambiguity rarely causes confusion—context makes clear whether approval or punishment is meant.

Sanctions can punish or permit. The punitive sense dominates modern usage: economic or political penalties imposed on a nation to pressure behavior change {The UN imposed sanctions on the regime}. But to sanction something is also to authorize or approve it {The committee sanctioned the new policy}. Context usually clarifies which meaning applies—governments impose sanctions but sanction actions.

Sanctity is the quality of being sacred, holy, or inviolable. Religious contexts speak of the sanctity of {life}, {marriage}, or {the Sabbath}. The word extends to anything treated as deserving ultimate respect or protection: the sanctity of {contracts}, the sanctity of {the home}. To violate something's sanctity is to desecrate or profane it.

Sanctuaries are places of refuge or protection. The word originally meant holy places—the inner chamber of a temple, a church where fugitives could claim asylum. Now it extends to any safe haven: {wildlife sanctuaries}, {bird sanctuaries}, {The library was her sanctuary from the chaos at home}. A sanctuary offers shelter from threat or intrusion.

The sanctuary in a church is the room where worship takes place. This idea of a sacred, quiet, and safe place extends to other meanings. A wildlife sanctuary is a protected home for wild animals. A sanctuary city in the U.S. is one that offers undocumented residents protection from federal immigration authorities. When you give someone sanctuary, you offer them protection from some threat. Where no specific place is involved, sanctuary is the state or condition of being protected from harm.

A sanctum is a private space where one is free from intrusion—a personal retreat or inner chamber. The word carries connotations of sacredness, from its origins in temple architecture where the innermost room housed what was most holy. {His study was his sanctum, and no one entered without permission.} An {inner sanctum} is the most private area within an already private space, often where decisions are made by a select few.

Sand is tiny loose grains of rock, typically found on beaches and in deserts. It forms when stone weathers over time. Sand varies in color and texture—from fine white Caribbean sand to coarse volcanic black. To sand is to smooth a surface with sandpaper or a similar abrasive. To {sand down} the rough edges. In the plural, sands often means a beach or desert expanse: {the sands of time}, {the Arabian sands}.

A sandal is an open shoe consisting of a sole held to the foot by straps, leaving much of the foot exposed. Sandals range from simple thong designs to elaborate gladiator styles with multiple straps. They're associated with warm weather, casual wear, and ancient civilizations: {She kicked off her sandals at the beach}. With socks, sandals are a notorious fashion faux pas—or deliberate dad style.

Sandals are open shoes held to the foot by straps, leaving much of the foot exposed. They range from simple flat soles with minimal strapping to elaborate designs with heels and decorative elements. Sandals are ancient footwear, suited to warm climates: {She kicked off her sandals at the beach}. {Sandals with socks} is a fashion choice that draws strong opinions.

Sandalwood is a fragrant wood from trees of the genus *Santalum*, prized for its rich, warm scent. The wood and its extracted oil are used in perfumes, incense, and traditional medicine. Indian sandalwood is considered the finest variety. {The room smelled of sandalwood and jasmine.}

A sandbag is a bag filled with sand, used to build barriers against flooding or as fortification. Sandbags also serve as ballast or improvised weights. To sandbag someone is to hit them with a sandbag, or figuratively, to coerce or bully. In games and competition, sandbagging means deliberately underperforming to gain advantage later—hiding your strength to sandbag opponents who underestimate you.

Sandbagging is deliberately underperforming or concealing strength to gain an advantage later. In poker, it means checking with a strong hand to lure opponents into betting. In business or sports, someone sandbags by lowering expectations so they can exceed them: {He's sandbagging—he'll crush those sales targets}. The term evokes weighted bags slowing someone down on purpose.

Sandbags are bags filled with sand, used primarily to build temporary barriers against flooding or as fortification in military contexts. Stacked together, they form walls that redirect water or stop bullets. The verb sandbag means to reinforce with sandbags, but it has extended meanings: to coerce or bully someone, or to deliberately underperform to gain advantage later. {He sandbagged in the early rounds, then crushed his opponents in the finals.}

A sandbox is a shallow container filled with sand for children to play in. In computing, a sandbox is an isolated environment where programs run without affecting the larger system—safe for testing untrusted code. The verb means to isolate something in such an environment: {We sandboxed the suspicious file before opening it}. Sandbox also appears as an adjective describing open-ended games or modes without fixed objectives: {sandbox gameplay}.

A sandcastle is a structure built on a beach by piling and shaping wet sand, typically made by children as play. The word often appears figuratively for something fragile or impermanent: {Their business plan was a sandcastle waiting for the tide}. To build sandcastles {in the air} is to indulge in unrealistic fantasies.

Sandcastles is the plural of sandcastle—a structure built from wet sand, typically on a beach. Children pile and shape damp sand into towers, walls, and moats, knowing the tide will wash it away. The impermanence makes sandcastle a metaphor for fragile or temporary achievements: {All our careful planning turned out to be sandcastles}.

A sandlot is a vacant lot or open piece of ground, often sandy or unpaved, where children gather to play informal games. The term is most associated with pickup baseball games played without adult supervision or official rules, evoking a nostalgic image of American childhood before organized youth sports. {We played sandlot baseball every summer until dark.} As an adjective, sandlot describes this informal, amateur style of play: {sandlot football}.

The sandman is a mythical figure who brings sleep by sprinkling magical sand in children's eyes. Parents invoke him at bedtime: {The sandman is coming, time for bed}. The "sand" explains the gritty residue sometimes found in the corners of eyes upon waking. The figure appears in folklore, lullabies, and popular culture as a gentle bringer of dreams. (Capitalized Sandman may refer to specific fictional characters.)

Sandpaper is paper or cloth coated with abrasive particles, used for smoothing surfaces or removing material. It comes in grades from coarse to fine, measured by grit number—higher numbers mean finer abrasive. To sandpaper something is to rub it with sandpaper: {I sandpapered the table before staining it}. Figuratively, a sandpaper voice or personality is rough and abrasive.

Sands is the plural of sand, referring to expanses of sandy terrain—beaches, deserts, or dunes: {the white sands of the Caribbean}, {the shifting sands of the Sahara}. Figuratively, {the sands of time} evokes an hourglass, suggesting time passing or running out: {The sands are running low}.

Sandstone is a sedite rock formed from compressed sand grains, typically quartz, ceite together over millions of years. It ranges from soft and crumbly to quite hard, appearing in colors from white to red to brown depending on mineral content. Sandstone is widely used in construction and paving: {The old courthouse was built of local sandstone}. Many famous geological formations—canyon walls, natural arches, desert mesas—are carved from sandstone.

A sandstorm is a strong wind that lifts and carries sand or dust across open terrain, reducing visibility to near zero. Common in deserts and arid regions, sandstorms can last minutes or days: {We waited out the sandstorm in the tent}. Also called a dust storm, though sandstorms typically involve coarser particles.

A sandwich is food between two pieces of bread—meat, cheese, vegetables, or combinations thereof. The format extends to variations: {open-faced sandwich}, {ice cream sandwich}. To sandwich something is to insert it between two other things: {The meeting was sandwiched between two calls}. As an adjective, sandwich describes layered structures: {sandwich panel}, {sandwich construction}. (Capitalized Sandwich refers to the English town or the Earl whose gambling habits supposedly inspired the food.)

Sandwiched means positioned or squeezed between two other things. The image comes from the filling pressed between slices of bread. A person can be sandwiched between two others on a crowded bench, or a meeting can be sandwiched between appointments: {I sandwiched a quick lunch between calls}. The word often suggests being uncomfortably compressed or fitted into limited space.

Sandwiches is the plural of sandwich—food consisting of a filling between slices of bread or in a split roll: {We packed sandwiches for the picnic}. To sandwich something is to squeeze it between two other things: {The meeting was sandwiched between two phone calls}. {She sandwiches her workouts into her lunch break}.

Sandy describes things containing, covered with, or resembling sand. A sandy beach is covered in sand; sandy soil contains a lot of it. Sandy hair is a yellowish-brown color, like light sand. A sandy texture feels gritty. {The path grew sandy as we approached the dunes.} {She had sandy hair and freckles.} (Capitalized Sandy is a given name.)

Sane describes a mind in proper working order—rational, sound, able to perceive reality accurately. The word often appears in legal contexts: a defendant found sane can stand trial. More loosely, sane means reasonable or sensible: {That's the only sane approach to the problem}. To {stay sane} is to maintain composure under stress. {No sane person would accept those terms.}

Sang is the past tense of sing. Someone sang a song, a choir sang hymns, birds sang at dawn. The word appears in expressions like {She sang his praises} (spoke highly of him) and {He sang like a canary} (informed to authorities). The alternative past tense sung is less common in standard usage.

Sangria is a Spanish punch made from red wine, chopped fruit, sweetener, and often brandy or other spirits. The fruit—typically oranges, lemons, and apples—steeps in the wine, which is served chilled over ice. White wine versions exist but are less traditional. {We ordered a pitcher of sangria for the table.}

To sanitize is to make something clean or free of contamination—disinfecting a surface, sterilizing equipment, or purifying water. The word extends to removing objectionable content: sanitizing a document strips sensitive information, sanitizing a story removes offensive elements. This figurative sense often carries negative connotations, suggesting that important truths have been scrubbed away to make something more palatable: {a sanitized version of history}.

Sanitized means cleaned of germs or contaminants, or more commonly, stripped of anything offensive, controversial, or unpleasant. A sanitized version of history omits the ugly parts: {The documentary presented a sanitized account of colonialism}. Sanitized language avoids profanity or harsh truths. The word often carries a critical edge—suggesting something has been made too clean, losing authenticity or important detail in the process.

Sanitizer is a substance that reduces or eliminates germs on surfaces or skin. Hand sanitizer, typically alcohol-based gel or liquid, became ubiquitous during the COVID-19 pandemic: {There's sanitizer by the door}. Surface sanitizers disinfect countertops, equipment, or other objects. Figuratively, sanitizer suggests something that cleans up or makes acceptable: {The PR team acted as sanitizers for the scandal}.

Sanity is soundness of mind—the state of being mentally healthy and able to think rationally. Legal contexts use it narrowly: a defendant's sanity determines whether they understood their actions. More loosely, sanity means reasonableness or good judgment: {Working from home has helped me keep my sanity}. To {question someone's sanity} is to suggest they're acting irrationally.

Sank is the past tense of sink. Something that sank went down—a ship beneath the waves, a stone through water, a person into a chair. The word captures the completed downward motion: {The Titanic sank in 1912}. {My heart sank when I heard the news}. {He sank the eight ball to win}.

Sap is the fluid that circulates through plants, carrying water and nutrients—maple sap becomes syrup. By extension, sap refers to vitality or energy: {The heat sapped my strength}. To sap is to gradually drain or undermine: {Constant criticism sapped her confidence}. A sap is also a fool or dupe, someone easily taken advantage of: {Don't be a sap}. Separately, a sap is a small leather-covered club filled with lead, used to strike someone, and to sap means to hit with one. (All-caps SAP is the software company.)

A sapling is a young tree, typically slender and flexible, past the seedling stage but not yet mature. The word extends to young people, especially lanky adolescents: {The boy had grown into a tall sapling of fifteen}. The term suggests something still developing, not yet fully formed or hardened.

Sapphire is a precious gemstone, typically deep blue, prized in jewelry for its brilliance and hardness—second only to diamond. Sapphires can occur in other colors (pink, yellow, white), but blue dominates the word's associations: {sapphire eyes}, {sapphire waters}. A sapphire anniversary marks 45 or 65 years of marriage, depending on tradition.

Sapphires is the plural of sapphire, a precious gemstone typically deep blue in color. Sapphires are a variety of corundum, the same mineral as rubies but in different hues—sapphires can also be pink, yellow, or colorless. {The ring was set with diamonds and sapphires.} The blue of sapphires serves as a color reference: {sapphire waters}, {sapphire skies}.

Sappy describes something excessively sentimental or emotional in a way that feels cloying or unearned: {a sappy love song}, {The movie got too sappy at the end}. The word suggests sweetness without substance—tears or feelings that come too easily. Literally, sappy means full of sap, the fluid in plants, which is where the figurative sense originates: sticky-sweet like tree sap.

Sarcasm is saying the opposite of what you mean to mock or convey contempt: {Oh, great job} when someone has blundered, {Thanks for the help} when none was given. The tone signals that the literal meaning should be inverted. Sarcasm differs from irony in its hostile edge—it's meant to sting.

Sarcastic describes speech or manner that uses irony to mock or convey contempt—saying the opposite of what you mean to highlight someone's foolishness or failure: {Oh, great job} when someone spills coffee everywhere. A sarcastic person deploys this tone habitually. The delivery often involves exaggerated intonation that signals the words shouldn't be taken at face value.

A sarcophagus is a stone coffin, typically decorated with sculpture or inscriptions. The word evokes ancient burial practices—Egyptian, Greek, Roman—where the elaborate container both preserved and honored the dead: {The museum's Egyptian wing displays a carved granite sarcophagus}. Plural: sarcophagi or sarcophaguses.

A sardine is a small, oily fish typically sold canned in oil or sauce. Several species of small herring and related fish are marketed as sardines. The word appears most often in {packed like sardines}—crammed tightly together, as the fish appear in their tins: {We were packed like sardines on the subway}.

Sardines are small, oily fish typically sold canned in oil or sauce. They're eaten whole, bones and all. The word also names a children's game where one person hides and others join them in the hiding spot until everyone is crammed together—{packed in like sardines}. That phrase describes any crowded space: {We were sardines on that subway car}.

A sari is a garment worn by women in South Asia, consisting of a long piece of cloth wrapped around the body, typically draped over one shoulder. The fabric may be plain cotton or elaborately embroidered silk. {She wore her grandmother's wedding sari.}

A sash is a decorative band of fabric worn around the waist or over one shoulder, often indicating rank, achievement, or ceremonial status: {The beauty queen wore her sash and tiara}. Military officers and dignitaries wear sashes as part of formal dress. Separately, a sash is the frame holding glass panes in a window—a sash window slides up and down within its frame.

Sashay is to walk with exaggerated, swaying movements—a strut that calls attention to itself. The word often implies theatrical confidence or flirtation: {She sashayed across the room}. In square dancing, sashay is a sideways sliding step where partners move past each other. The casual verb sometimes just means to go or proceed: {He sashayed over to the bar}.

Sashimi is a Japanese dish of thinly sliced raw fish or seafood, served without rice. Unlike sushi, which combines raw fish with vinegared rice, sashimi showcases the fish alone, typically arranged on a plate with garnishes like shredded daikon and wasabi: {The sashimi platter had salmon, tuna, and yellowtail}.

Sasquatch is a large, hairy, ape-like creature said to inhabit forests of the Pacific Northwest. The word comes from Salish languages and is interchangeable with Bigfoot, though sasquatch tends toward the regional and folkloric while Bigfoot sounds more tabloid. Despite thousands of reported sightings, no physical evidence has confirmed its existence: {He claims to have seen a sasquatch while hiking in Oregon}.

Sass is impudent or disrespectful talk, especially from someone in a subordinate position: {Don't give me any sass}. The verb means to talk back: {She sassed her teacher and got detention}. Sassy describes someone inclined to sass—bold, spirited, sometimes admirably so: {a sassy comeback}.

Sassy describes someone who is bold, spirited, and slightly impertinent—talking back with confidence and flair rather than deference. The word often carries affection: {I love her sassy attitude}. A sassy remark is cheeky but not truly offensive. The term applies especially to women and children who speak their minds without apology, and to gay men expressing themselves with theatrical confidence.

Sat is the past tense and past participle of sit. You sat in a chair, sat through a lecture, sat for a portrait. A building sits on a foundation; yesterday it sat there too. Food that {sat out overnight} may have spoiled. If something doesn't {sit well} with you, it sat poorly from the start. (Capitalized Sat is the abbreviation for Saturday; all-caps SAT is the standardized test.)

Satanic means relating to or characteristic of Satan, the devil of Christian theology. The word often describes practices or beliefs associated with devil worship: {satanic rituals}, {satanic cults}. More loosely, satanic characterizes anything supremely evil or wicked: {satanic cruelty}. The 1980s saw widespread {satanic panic}—moral alarm about supposed devil worship that proved largely unfounded.

A satchel is a bag with a shoulder strap, typically flat-bottomed with a flap that closes over the top. The word often suggests a bag for carrying books or papers: {She slung her satchel over her shoulder and headed to class}. Satchels are associated with students and messengers, though the style appears in fashion accessories too.

A satellite is an object that orbits a larger celestial body—the moon is Earth's natural satellite. More commonly, satellite refers to artificial objects launched into orbit: communications satellites, weather satellites, spy satellites. By extension, satellite describes anything dependent on or subordinate to something larger: a satellite {state}, satellite {offices}, satellite {campuses}. Satellite television and radio deliver signals via orbiting transmitters: {We get two hundred channels on satellite}.

Satellites are objects that orbit larger bodies. The moon is Earth's natural satellite; artificial satellites are machines launched into orbit for communication, navigation, weather monitoring, or observation. The term extends to anything dependent on or revolving around something more central: {satellite offices}, {satellite states}. A satellite {dish} receives signals from broadcasting satellites. {The company has satellites in twelve countries.}

Satin is a smooth, glossy fabric with a lustrous face and dull back, made from silk, polyester, or other fibers woven in a particular way. The sheen comes from the weave structure rather than the fiber itself. Satin appears in formal wear, lingerie, and bedding: {satin sheets}, {a satin ribbon}. As an adjective, it describes smooth, lustrous surfaces: {satin finish}, {satin skin}.

Satire is a form of humor that accentuates the weaknesses and shortcomings of a person, institution, or enterprise. The phrases political satire and social satire are both frequent because politicians, and people generally, do and say silly things. A particular work such as a play, poem, or story that uses satire can also be called a satire: The movie is a dark satire about political failure in the wake of a natural disaster.

A satirist is someone who uses satire—humor, irony, or exaggeration to criticize and expose foolishness or vice, especially in politics and society. The term typically applies to writers, cartoonists, or performers: {Jonathan Swift was a master satirist}. A satirist's work aims to provoke reflection, not just laughter.

Satisfaction is the feeling of fulfillment when a need, desire, or expectation is met: {She finished the project with a deep sense of satisfaction}. It extends to adequate resolution of a complaint or debt: {The refund was offered to their satisfaction}. To {demand satisfaction} historically meant to challenge someone to a duel to restore wounded honor. In legal and formal contexts, satisfaction is the discharge of an obligation.

Satisfied describes contentment when a need, desire, or expectation has been met. A satisfied {customer} has no complaints. If you're satisfied with an explanation, you accept it as adequate. To be satisfied is to have enough—not necessarily delighted, but no longer wanting: {I'm satisfied with how things turned out}. The word often implies sufficiency rather than excess.

Satisfy means to meet a need, desire, or expectation adequately. If you satisfy your hunger, you eat enough to no longer feel hungry. If you satisfy a requirement, you fulfill what is demanded. {The explanation satisfied her curiosity.} The word carries a sense of sufficiency rather than excess—to be satisfied is to have enough, not necessarily to have everything one might want. Someone who is hard to satisfy has standards that are difficult to meet. In legal contexts, to satisfy a debt or judgment is to pay it in full.

Satisfying describes something that fulfills a need, desire, or expectation. A satisfying {meal} leaves you comfortably full. A satisfying {answer} resolves a question adequately. The word often carries a sense of completeness or closure—there's something satisfying about {finishing a difficult task} or {hearing a door click shut}. What's satisfying varies by person: a satisfying {crunch}, a satisfying {ending}, a satisfying {win}.

Saturated describes something that has absorbed as much as it can hold, whether literally or figuratively. A saturated sponge can't take on more water; a saturated market can't absorb more products. In chemistry, a saturated solution contains the maximum dissolved substance, and saturated fats have no double bonds between carbon atoms. Colors described as saturated are rich and intense, not washed out or pale. {The rain left my clothes completely saturated.}

Saturation is the state of being completely filled or soaked—unable to absorb more. A sponge reaches saturation when it can hold no additional water. Markets reach saturation when demand is fully met: {The smartphone market is approaching saturation}. In color theory, saturation measures intensity or vividness—how pure a hue is versus how washed out or gray. {Turn up the saturation to make the colors pop.}

A satyr is a creature from Greek mythology—part man, part goat, with pointed ears, a tail, and often goat legs. Satyrs were woodland spirits known for drunkenness, lechery, and revelry in the company of Dionysus. The word extends to any man with excessive or uncontrolled sexual appetite: {The old satyr couldn't keep his hands to himself}.

Satyrs are creatures from Greek mythology—half-man, half-goat beings with pointed ears, horse tails, and perpetual erections. They inhabited wild places, chasing nymphs and indulging in wine. The word extends to any man of excessive sexual appetite: {He had a reputation as a satyr}. In entomology, satyrs are a family of brown butterflies.

Sauce is a liquid or semi-liquid accompaniment to food, adding flavor or moisture: {tomato sauce}, {hot sauce}, {cheese sauce}. The word extends to impudent or cheeky behavior: {Don't give me any sauce}. In slang, sauce means alcohol: {He's been on the sauce again}. To sauce something is to add sauce to it, or informally, to speak impudently to someone.

A saucepan is a deep cooking pot with a long handle and usually a lid, used on stovetops for heating liquids, making sauces, boiling eggs, and similar tasks. Unlike a skillet, it has high sides; unlike a stockpot, it's small enough for one hand to manage: {She heated the soup in a saucepan}.

A saucer is a small shallow dish, typically round with a slight depression, designed to hold a cup. The cup sits in the depression, and the saucer catches drips or holds a spoon. By extension, anything saucer-shaped: a {flying saucer}, {saucer-eyed} with surprise. {She set the teacup back on its saucer.}

Saucers are small shallow dishes designed to hold cups, catching drips and providing a resting place for spoons. The shape—round, flat, slightly concave—gives us {flying saucers}, the classic UFO silhouette. Wide eyes are sometimes described as {big as saucers}. A saucer is also the singular form: {She set the teacup back on its saucer}.

Saucy means boldly playful or flirtatious, often with a hint of impudence: {a saucy wink}, {a saucy remark}. It suggests cheekiness without real offense—more teasing than rude. The word can describe someone who talks back with spirit: {Don't get saucy with me}. In older usage, saucy meant impertinent or presumptuous, but modern use leans lighter, even complimentary.

Sauerkraut is finely shredded cabbage fermented in its own juice with salt. The fermentation produces a sour, tangy flavor and extends preservation. A staple of German cuisine, it appears alongside sausages, pork, and in Reuben sandwiches: {I'll have the bratwurst with sauerkraut}.

A sauna is a small room or building designed for dry or steam heat bathing, typically heated to high temperatures. Users sit inside to sweat, believed to promote relaxation and health benefits. The practice originated in Finland, where saunas remain culturally central. The word also refers to a session in such a room: {We had a sauna after swimming}. Informally, any uncomfortably hot space becomes a sauna: {This car is a sauna}.

Sausage is ground meat—usually pork, beef, or a mixture—seasoned and stuffed into a cylindrical casing. Sausages may be fresh, cured, or smoked: {breakfast sausage}, {Italian sausage}, {bratwurst}. The word extends to anything sausage-shaped: {sausage fingers}, {sausage curls}. In British slang, {silly sausage} is an affectionate term for someone being foolish.

Sausages are seasoned ground meat stuffed into casings, typically cylindrical links. The word usually appears as a plural because sausages come in bunches and are eaten multiple at a time: {sausages and eggs for breakfast}. Types vary widely—Italian, breakfast, bratwurst, chorizo. British {bangers and mash} pairs sausages with mashed potatoes.

Sauté is a cooking method where food is fried quickly in a small amount of fat over high heat, typically in a shallow pan. The technique keeps ingredients moving—the word comes from French for "jumped"—to ensure even browning without burning. As an adjective, sautéed describes food cooked this way: {sautéed mushrooms}, {sautéed onions}. A sauté pan has low, sloped sides that make tossing ingredients easier.

Savage means wild, fierce, or untamed. A savage {attack} is brutal and unrestrained. Savage {criticism} is harsh and unsparing. As a noun, savage was historically applied to indigenous peoples by colonizers—a usage now recognized as dehumanizing and offensive. In contemporary slang, savage describes someone admirably bold or ruthless: {That comeback was savage}. To savage is to attack ferociously: {Critics savaged the film}.

Savagery is violent, brutal, or cruel behavior—the conduct of someone acting without restraint or civilization: {The savagery of the attack shocked investigators}. It can describe physical violence or fierce verbal assault. The word implies something primitive or animalistic, though historically it was applied prejudicially to non-European peoples. {The film depicts war in all its savagery}.

A savanna is a flat grassland with scattered trees, found in tropical and subtropical regions where rainfall is seasonal. The landscape supports grazing animals and their predators—the African savanna is famous for lions, elephants, and wildebeest. {Miles of open savanna stretched to the horizon.} Also spelled savannah.

A savannah is a flat grassland with scattered trees, found in tropical and subtropical regions where rainfall is seasonal. The landscape is characteristic of much of Africa, where it supports iconic wildlife like lions and elephants. {The wildebeest migrated across the savannah.} Also spelled savanna. (Capitalized Savannah is a city in Georgia.)

Savannas is the plural of savanna, a tropical or subtropical grassland with scattered trees and seasonal rainfall. Savannas cover much of Africa, where they support iconic wildlife like lions, elephants, and zebras. The ecosystem is characterized by distinct wet and dry seasons: {The savannas of East Africa attract tourists from around the world}.

A savant is a person of profound learning or exceptional skill in a specialized field. The term often appears in {idiot savant}, now usually {savant syndrome}, describing someone with developmental disabilities who demonstrates extraordinary ability in a narrow domain—calculating calendar dates instantly, playing complex music by ear, or drawing cityscapes from memory. Outside clinical contexts, savant suggests deep expertise: {a wine savant}, {a political savant}.

As a verb, save preserves (save a historical landmark), protects (save for a rainy day), and prevents (save from disaster). In imperatives, save can express pointlessness (save your breath) or heroism (save the day). Save also has a minor role as a preposition or conjunction in formal writing, where it means the same thing as except or except for: The dinner was a disaster, save for the delicious dessert.

Saved is the past tense of save, covering all its meanings: rescued from danger {The lifeguard saved him from drowning}, preserved for later {I saved some cake for you}, or stored digitally {Have you saved your work?}. In religious contexts, saved means redeemed from sin or granted salvation: {Are you saved?} {He got saved at a revival meeting}.

Saves is the third person singular form of the verb save and is used when the subject is a single person or thing (other than I or you). The noun saves is the plural of save, which has several meanings. In some sports, a save is a successful effort to stop the other team from scoring. A save is also the action of capturing data on an electronic device.

Saving conveys rescuing (the paramedics are saving the accident victim) and conservation (the principal is saving money by hiring newer teachers). It is also routinely used in sports (the goalie is saving the game) and computing (saving a data backup). The participle saving has a minor role as a preposition or a conjunction in formal writing, where it means the same thing as except.

Savings is money set aside rather than spent, typically accumulated over time for future use: {She dipped into her savings to cover the repairs}. A savings account holds deposited money that earns interest. The singular saving means a reduction in cost or expenditure: {The new system represents a significant saving in labor}.

A savior is someone who rescues or delivers others from danger, harm, or destruction. The word carries strong religious connotations, particularly in Christianity where the Savior refers to Jesus Christ as the redeemer of humanity. In secular use, savior describes anyone who provides crucial help in a desperate situation: {The firefighter was hailed as a savior by the trapped family}. The term can also be used ironically or critically when someone acts with an inflated sense of their own importance in helping others.

Saviors is the plural of savior, one who saves or rescues others from danger, destruction, or difficulty. The word often carries religious weight—Christians call Jesus Christ the Savior. But saviors appear in secular contexts too: {The firefighters were hailed as saviors}. The term can be ironic when someone's help proves unwelcome or self-serving: {He fancied himself the savior of the department}.

A saviour is someone who rescues or delivers others from danger, destruction, or difficulty. The word carries weight—you wouldn't call someone a saviour for minor help. In Christian contexts, the Saviour refers to Jesus Christ as redeemer of humanity. Outside religion, saviour describes anyone who provides crucial rescue: {She was the saviour of the company during the crisis}. The spelling saviour is British; Americans write savior.

Savor means to taste or smell something with pleasure, lingering over the experience: {She savored every bite of the chocolate cake}. The meaning extends to any deliberate enjoyment: {He savored his victory}. As a noun, savor is the distinctive taste or quality of something: {The dish had a smoky savor}. British spelling: savour.

Savory describes food that is flavorful and appetizing, especially in a salty or spicy way rather than sweet: {savory snacks}, {a savory pie}. The word suggests rich, satisfying taste—umami rather than sugar. Figuratively, something savory is morally respectable, usually in the negative: {The neighborhood had some unsavory characters}. Savory is also an herb in the mint family used in cooking.

Savour (or savor in American spelling) means to taste or smell something with pleasure, lingering over it: {She savoured every bite of the chocolate cake}. Extended to any experience, savour means to enjoy fully and deliberately: {He savoured the moment of victory}. As a noun, savour is a distinctive taste, smell, or quality: {The scandal gave the affair an unsavoury savour}. Something that {savours of} a quality suggests or hints at it: {His explanation savoured of dishonesty}.

Savoury is the British spelling of savory, covering both the adjective meaning pleasantly salty or spicy rather than sweet, and the noun referring to aromatic herbs used in cooking. A savoury dish or snack has a rich, full flavor that satisfies without sweetness: {The menu offered both sweet and savoury options}. In British usage, a savoury may also be a small appetizer or final course served at formal dinners.

Savvy is practical understanding or shrewdness—knowing how things actually work: {She has real political savvy}, {He lacks the tech savvy to set it up}. As an adjective, it describes someone with this quality: {a savvy investor}, {media-savvy politicians}. The verb, now dated, means to understand: {You savvy?}

A saw is a tool with a toothed blade for cutting hard materials—wood, metal, bone. The tooth pattern lets the blade bite and remove material on each stroke. Types include handsaw, chainsaw, circular saw, and hacksaw. To saw is to cut with such a tool, or to move back and forth as if sawing: {He sawed at the rope with his knife}. Separately, saw is the past tense of see. A saw is also an old saying or proverb: {the old saw about early birds and worms}.

Sawdust is the fine particles of wood produced when cutting or sanding lumber. It accumulates beneath saws and in woodworking shops. Sawdust has practical uses—as animal bedding, mulch, or fuel for pellet stoves. Figuratively, something described as sawdust is dry and flavorless: {The overcooked chicken tasted like sawdust}.

A sawmill is a facility where logs are cut into lumber using large power-driven saws. Historically powered by water wheels, modern sawmills typically run on electricity. The term can refer to the entire operation or specifically to the machinery that does the cutting. {The old sawmill by the river closed down decades ago.} Sawmills remain central to the timber industry, processing raw logs into boards, beams, and other wood products for construction and manufacturing.

Sawmills is the plural of sawmill, a facility where logs are cut into lumber. The term covers both the building and the machinery inside it—large circular or band saws that slice timber into boards of standard dimensions. {The old sawmills along the river employed half the town.} Sawmill towns often grew around logging operations, declining when forests were depleted.

Sax is informal for saxophone, the curved brass woodwind instrument with keys and a reed mouthpiece: {She plays sax in a jazz quartet}. The word appears in compounds like {alto sax}, {tenor sax}, {sax player}. Less commonly, sax is a tool for cutting roofing slates.

A saxophone is a brass wind instrument with a single reed mouthpiece, curved body, and keys operated by the fingers. Despite being made of brass, it's classified as a woodwind because of its reed. Invented in the 1840s, the saxophone became central to jazz and also appears in classical music, marching bands, and rock: {She plays alto sax in a jazz quartet}.

Saxophones are wind instruments with a single-reed mouthpiece and a curved metal body, invented in the 1840s. The saxophone family spans soprano to bass, with alto and tenor most common. Though made of brass, saxophones are classified as woodwinds because of how they produce sound. They dominate jazz and feature in concert bands, rock, and classical music: {a wailing saxophone solo}.

The three most frequent verbs (be, have, do) earn their status partly because they can be both main and auxiliary verbs. Say is the most frequent verb that doesn’t also have a helping job, probably because we have a predilection for quoting others. Like many frequent verbs, say is irregular, with its inflected form said for the past and past participle. Over the centuries, say has developed figurative uses: The clock says five o’clock. Say can also express a supposition: Let’s say no one responds to your offer; what then?

A saying is a short, familiar expression conveying conventional wisdom or a common observation: {There's an old saying about not counting your chickens before they hatch}. Sayings circulate widely enough that speakers often introduce them with phrases like "as the saying goes" or "you know what they say." The term covers proverbs, adages, and maxims without distinguishing among them.

Sayings are short, well-known expressions that convey wisdom, truth, or advice—often passed down through generations. They overlap with proverbs, maxims, and adages, though sayings is the most general term. {As the old saying goes, you can't teach an old dog new tricks.} People reference sayings to add authority to a point or acknowledge conventional wisdom, sometimes ironically: {You know what they say about assumptions.}

Sayonara is a Japanese word for goodbye, borrowed into English with connotations of finality—a permanent farewell rather than a casual see-you-later. It often signals the definitive end of something: {After that argument, it was sayonara to our friendship}. Sometimes used dismissively: {One more screwup and it's sayonara}.

A scab is the rough crust that forms over a wound as it heals—dried blood and tissue protecting new skin beneath. Picking at scabs delays healing. Extended meanings share the sense of something unwanted or contemptible. A scab is a worker who crosses a picket line or takes a striker's job: {The union called them scabs}. The term is strongly derogatory in labor contexts. As a verb, to scab is to form a crust or to work during a strike.

A scabbard is a sheath for a sword or dagger, typically made of leather or metal and worn at the hip or back. The word appears most often in historical or fantasy contexts: {He drew his blade from its scabbard}. To scabbard a weapon is to return it to its sheath.

Scabs are the crusty formations that develop over wounds as they heal—dried blood and plasma protecting new skin beneath. Picking at a scab delays healing. The word extends to workers who cross picket lines during strikes, replacing union members: {The factory brought in scabs to keep production running}. The term is strongly pejorative in labor contexts.

A scaffold is a temporary framework of poles and planks providing workers access to high surfaces during construction or repair: {Workers erected scaffolding around the building}. Historically, a scaffold was also a raised platform for public executions. Figuratively, to scaffold is to provide supporting structure—in education, scaffolding means giving learners temporary support that's gradually removed as they gain competence.

Scaffolding is the temporary framework of poles and platforms erected around a building under construction or repair, allowing workers to reach high areas. The term extends to any temporary supporting structure: {The scaffolding of assumptions underlying the theory}. In education, scaffolding refers to instructional support that's gradually removed as learners gain competence.

Scaffolds are temporary structures erected alongside buildings during construction or repair, giving workers platforms to stand on at various heights. Figuratively, a scaffold is any temporary framework supporting development: {The teacher provides scaffolds until students can work independently}. Historically, a scaffold was also a raised platform for executions. As a verb, to scaffold is to provide such support.

Scalding describes something hot enough to burn, typically liquid or steam: {scalding water}, {scalding coffee}. The word extends to harsh criticism or rebuke: {a scalding review}, {scalding remarks}. Something scalding inflicts damage—whether physical burns or wounded pride.

Scale has a jumble of uses, owing to its arrival in English from different sources. Meanings fall broadly into three categories: those having to do with the bony plates on fish and some other animals; those connected with the weight-measuring device called a scale or scales; and those referring to a graduated series in which there is usually an understood top and bottom, or upper and lower part. This last group of senses is the most productive as noun and verb. The scale of a drawing or model is its size in relation to the real thing. If you scale something up or down, you make it larger or smaller by adjusting the scale on which it operates.

Scales are the small, overlapping plates covering fish, reptiles, and some other animals—protective armor that flexes with movement. The singular scale extends to similar structures: {scales on a butterfly's wing}, {scales of rust}. A scale is also a device for weighing, or the balance pans themselves. The scales of justice symbolize fair measurement. Musical scales are sequences of notes ascending or descending in pitch. To scale something is to climb it {(scale a wall)} or to adjust proportionally {(scale up production)}. When scales fall from your eyes, you suddenly see clearly.

Scaling is adjusting size or magnitude. In computing and business, scaling means expanding capacity to handle growth: {The startup struggled with scaling its infrastructure}. To scale up is to increase; to scale down is to reduce. Scaling also refers to removing scales from fish, or the buildup of mineral deposits: {scaling on the pipes}. In climbing, scaling means ascending: {scaling the cliff face}.

A scallop is a marine mollusk with a distinctive fan-shaped shell, prized as seafood for its sweet, tender muscle. The shell's radiating ridges give rise to the decorative meaning: a scalloped edge has a series of curved projections, like the edge of a scallop shell. To scallop potatoes is to bake them in cream sauce, typically in layers—the connection to the shell being the traditional baking dish.

Scallops are edible bivalve mollusks prized for their sweet, tender flesh—specifically the round adductor muscle that opens and closes the shell. They're a culinary delicacy, typically seared, grilled, or served raw: {The seared scallops were perfectly caramelized}. Scallops also refers to the decorative wavy edge pattern resembling a scallop shell: {The dress had scallops along the hem}. As a verb, to scallop is to cut such an edge or to bake food in a cream sauce: {scalloped potatoes}.

A scallywag is a mischievous person, especially a child who causes trouble in an endearing way: {You little scallywag, you ate all the cookies}. The word is affectionate rather than harsh—it suggests roguish charm more than genuine wrongdoing. In American history, scallywag (or scalawag) referred disparagingly to white Southerners who supported Reconstruction after the Civil War.

The scalp is the skin covering the top and back of the head, where hair typically grows. Historically, some cultures removed enemies' scalps as trophies—to scalp someone was to cut away this skin. The verb now means to resell tickets at inflated prices: {Scalpers were selling tickets for three times face value outside the stadium}. To scalp can also mean to make small, quick profits through frequent trades.

Scalped is the past tense of scalp, meaning to cut or tear the scalp from someone's head—historically associated with warfare practices among some Native American tribes and American colonists. Extended uses: a ticket scalper has scalped you if they've charged an inflated price. In trading, to scalp is to make quick profits on small price movements: {He scalped the stock for a few cents per share}. To get scalped can also mean to be badly beaten or cheated: {We got scalped in that deal}.

A scalpel is a small, extremely sharp knife used for precise cutting, especially in surgery and dissection. The blade is typically thin and pointed, designed for making clean incisions with minimal tissue damage. Scientists and artists also use scalpels for detailed work requiring fine cuts. Figuratively, scalpel suggests surgical precision: {The editor took a scalpel to the manuscript, excising every unnecessary word}.

Scalpels is the plural of scalpel, a small sharp-bladed knife used for surgery and dissection. The blade is typically thin and pointed, designed for precise incisions. Figuratively, scalpel suggests surgical precision: {The editor took a scalpel to the manuscript}, {budget cuts made with a scalpel rather than an axe}.

A scalper buys tickets or goods at regular prices, then resells them at inflated prices when demand exceeds supply: {Scalpers outside the stadium were asking three hundred dollars for fifty-dollar seats}. The practice thrives around concerts, sporting events, and product launches. In trading, a scalper makes quick transactions to profit from small price movements. The older sense—one who takes scalps—is now rare outside historical contexts.

Scalpers buy tickets or goods at regular prices and resell them at inflated prices when demand exceeds supply. The practice is common with concert tickets, sporting events, and limited-edition products: {Scalpers were asking three times face value outside the stadium}. The term carries negative connotations of opportunistic profiteering. In trading, scalpers make rapid small-margin transactions to profit from tiny price movements.

Scalping is cutting or tearing the scalp from a person's head—historically practiced as a war trophy or proof of killing. The term extends to buying tickets or goods at regular prices and reselling them at inflated rates: {Scalpers were selling concert tickets for triple the face value}. In trading, scalping means making rapid transactions for small profits. To scalp someone figuratively is to exploit or cheat them.

Scalps is the plural of scalp—the skin and hair covering the top of the head. Historically, scalps were cut from enemies as war trophies, particularly associated with conflicts between Native Americans and European settlers: {The raiding party returned with scalps}. In trading and ticketing, scalps are items bought and resold at marked-up prices. The verb scalps means to take a scalp, to resell at inflated prices, or to make quick profits on small price movements: {He scalps concert tickets outside the venue}.

A scam is a fraudulent scheme designed to cheat people out of money or valuables. The word implies deception—victims believe they're getting something legitimate. Scams range from email phishing to elaborate confidence tricks: {That investment opportunity turned out to be a scam}. To scam someone is to defraud them: {He scammed elderly people out of their savings}.

A scammer is someone who deceives others for profit, typically through fraudulent schemes. The term covers everything from email phishers to con artists running elaborate hustles: {The scammer posed as a Nigerian prince}, {Don't give your credit card to phone scammers}. Unlike older words like swindler or grifter, scammer emerged with internet-age fraud and carries a more casual, contemporary tone.

Scammers are people who run scams—fraudulent schemes designed to cheat others out of money, personal information, or valuables. The term covers a wide range of con artists, from email phishers and fake charity operators to romance fraudsters and tech support imposters. {The scammers posed as IRS agents demanding immediate payment.} While scam originally had associations with carnival grifters, scammers now operate predominantly online, making the word ubiquitous in discussions of internet safety and consumer protection.

Scamming is defrauding people through deceptive schemes, typically for money. The word implies deliberate trickery rather than honest misrepresentation: {He's been scamming elderly people out of their savings}, {She got caught scamming insurance companies}. Someone who scams is a scammer; the scheme itself is a scam.

A scamp is a mischievous person, especially a child who gets into minor trouble but remains endearing: {You little scamp, you ate all the cookies}. The word carries affection—a scamp's wrongdoing is playful rather than malicious. Less commonly, to scamp work is to do it carelessly or hastily.

Scamper is to run with quick, light steps, often playfully or in haste. The word suggests small creatures or children darting about: {Squirrels scampered across the lawn}, {The kids scampered off to the playground}. As a noun, a scamper is an instance of such running: {a quick scamper through the rain}.

Scampering is running with quick, light steps, usually playfully or in haste. The word suggests small creatures or children moving rapidly: {Squirrels went scampering up the tree}, {The kids came scampering down the stairs}. There's an innocence to scampering—it's hard to imagine anything menacing doing it.

Scams are fraudulent schemes designed to cheat people out of money or information. The word covers everything from email phishing to elaborate cons: {I keep getting scam calls about my car's warranty}. To scam someone is to swindle them. A scammer runs such schemes. The line between a scam and aggressive marketing can be blurry.

Scan originally meant to analyze verse by examining its meter, but now more often means the opposite—to look over quickly rather than carefully: {She scanned the headlines}. In computing and imaging, to scan is to pass a sensor systematically across something to capture or read data: scanning a barcode, scanning a document. A scan is the act of scanning or its result: {a brain scan}, {a quick scan of the room}.

Scandal is an event or action that causes public outrage or disgrace, typically involving moral wrongdoing or impropriety by someone in a position of trust: {The financial scandal brought down the company}, {a sex scandal}. The word also covers the outrage itself: {The news caused quite a scandal}. Scandals in politics and celebrity culture often end with the suffix -gate, after Watergate. Something scandalous is shocking or disgraceful.

Scandalous describes something that causes public outrage or moral shock: {a scandalous affair}, {scandalous behavior}. It can refer to actions that violate accepted standards of decency or propriety, or to revelations that damage reputations. The word often carries a whiff of the salacious—scandals tend to involve sex, money, or hypocrisy. Something scandalous may also simply be shockingly bad: {The conditions in that nursing home are scandalous}.

Scandals is the plural of scandal—actions or events that cause public outrage or damage reputations. A scandal typically involves behavior that violates moral standards or public trust: {The administration was rocked by a series of scandals}. Political scandals, financial scandals, and sex scandals dominate news cycles, often ending careers. The word implies not just wrongdoing but exposure—a scandal requires an audience to be scandalized.

A scanner is a device that systematically examines something. An optical scanner converts documents or images into digital files: {I need to scan my passport}. A radio scanner monitors multiple frequencies. At airports and hospitals, scanners use X-rays or other technology to see inside bodies or luggage. In computing, a scanner detects malware or vulnerabilities. A person who scans—reading quickly or surveying a crowd—is also a scanner.

Scanning is methodical visual or electronic examination—moving across a surface or through data to detect or extract what matters. Eyes scan a crowd for a familiar face; machines scan documents to digitize them. A medical scan images the body's interior. To scan text is to read it quickly for key points rather than studying every word. In poetry, to scan a line is to analyze its meter: {The verse doesn't scan properly}.

A scapegoat is a person or group blamed for problems they didn't cause, deflecting responsibility from the actual source. The word comes from an ancient Hebrew ritual where a goat was symbolically loaded with the community's sins and driven into the wilderness. Modern use is almost always figurative: {Immigrants became scapegoats for the economic downturn}. To scapegoat someone is to make them bear undeserved blame.

Scapegoated means made to bear blame for others' failures or misdeeds. The scapegoat was originally a goat symbolically burdened with the sins of the community and driven into the wilderness. Now it's anyone unfairly blamed: {He was scapegoated for the team's poor performance}. {Immigrants are often scapegoated during economic downturns}.

Scapegoating is the practice of blaming one person or group for problems caused by others or by circumstances beyond anyone's control. The term comes from an ancient ritual in which a goat was symbolically loaded with the community's sins and driven into the wilderness. Modern scapegoating typically targets vulnerable or marginalized groups: {Immigrants are often scapegoated during economic downturns}. The scapegoat receives punishment or hostility that should be directed elsewhere—or nowhere at all.

Scapegoats are people or groups blamed for problems they didn't cause or bear disproportionate responsibility for. The term comes from an ancient ritual where a goat was symbolically loaded with the community's sins and driven into the wilderness. Modern scapegoats absorb blame that should fall elsewhere: {Immigrants became scapegoats for the economic downturn}. To scapegoat someone is to make them one.

A scar is a mark left on skin or tissue after a wound heals—the body's permanent record of injury. Scars extend to any lasting trace of damage: {The hillside still bears scars from the wildfire}. Emotional scars are psychological marks left by trauma: {The divorce left scars on everyone}. To scar is to leave such a mark: {The accident scarred her face}, {That experience scarred him for life}.

A scarab is a beetle, especially the dung beetle sacred to ancient Egyptians, who saw its ball-rolling as a symbol of the sun's daily journey. The word now usually refers to carved representations of the beetle used as amulets, seals, or jewelry: {a scarab ring}, {an Egyptian scarab pendant}. Scarabs remain popular in decorative arts.

Scarabs are beetles of the family Scarabaeidae, which includes dung beetles and June bugs. The term most often refers to the sacred scarab of ancient Egypt, where the dung-rolling beetle became a powerful symbol of the sun god and regeneration. Ancient Egyptians carved scarab-shaped amulets from stone or faience, often inscribing them with hieroglyphs and placing them with mummies. {The museum's collection includes several carved scarabs from the New Kingdom period.}

Scarce describes something in short supply relative to demand—not absent, but insufficient: {Water is scarce in the desert}, {Jobs were scarce during the recession}. The word implies difficulty obtaining what's needed. To {make yourself scarce} is to leave quickly or stay away, especially to avoid trouble.

Scarcity is the condition of being in short supply relative to demand. Economics treats scarcity as fundamental—resources are finite while wants are unlimited. The word emphasizes insufficiency: {Water scarcity threatens the region}, {a scarcity of affordable housing}. Scarcity often drives up value, as with rare commodities or limited editions.

Scare is sudden fear or alarm, or something that causes it: {a bomb scare}, {quite a scare}. As a verb, to scare is to frighten: {The noise scared me}. To {scare up} something is to find or gather it with effort: {We scared up enough chairs for everyone}. Scary is the adjective. A scarecrow is a decoy figure meant to frighten birds from crops.

A scarecrow is a humanlike figure set up in fields to frighten birds away from crops, typically made of old clothes stuffed with straw and mounted on a pole. The word extends to anyone dressed in ragged clothing or looking disheveled: {He looked like a scarecrow in that old coat}. Scarecrows appear frequently in folklore and fiction as figures that come to life.

Scarecrows is the plural of scarecrow—a human-shaped figure set up in fields to frighten birds away from crops. The typical scarecrow is made of old clothes stuffed with straw, mounted on a wooden frame. By extension, a scarecrow is any person who looks ragged or gaunt: {He was thin as a scarecrow after months in the wilderness}.

Scared means afraid or frightened. It ranges from mild unease to intense fear: {I'm scared of heights}, {The noise scared me}. To be {scared stiff} or {scared to death} is to be extremely frightened. {Running scared} describes acting from fear of failure or defeat. Scared often implies a more immediate or situational fear than afraid, which can describe a general disposition.

A scaremonger is someone who spreads alarming or exaggerated warnings, typically to provoke fear or anxiety in others. The term carries a strongly negative connotation, suggesting that the person's warnings are overblown, manipulative, or self-serving rather than genuinely helpful. {Critics dismissed him as a scaremonger for predicting economic collapse.} The related verb scaremonger and noun scaremongering describe the activity itself: {The tabloids have been scaremongering about immigration for years.}

Scaremongering is the deliberate spreading of alarming or exaggerated claims to provoke public fear, typically for political or commercial advantage. The term is almost always pejorative—accusing someone of scaremongering dismisses their warnings as manipulative rather than legitimate: {Critics called the campaign's ads about crime pure scaremongering}. A scaremonger is one who engages in this practice.

A scarf is a length of fabric worn around the neck or head for warmth, fashion, or modesty. Scarves vary from thin silk to heavy wool. To scarf something down (or scarf it up) is to eat it quickly and greedily: {He scarfed down three slices of pizza}. In woodworking, a scarf joint connects two pieces by overlapping tapered ends.

Scarlet is a brilliant red with a slight orange tinge—bolder and more vivid than crimson. The color has long been associated with royalty, military uniforms, and sin: {a scarlet cloak}, {the Scarlet Letter}. A {scarlet woman} is promiscuous, drawing on biblical imagery of the Whore of Babylon dressed in scarlet. Scarlet fever is a contagious disease marked by a red rash.

Scarred describes something marked by scars—the visible traces left after wounds heal. Skin becomes scarred from cuts, burns, or surgery. The word extends to lasting damage of any kind: {scarred tissue}, {a landscape scarred by wildfires}. Figuratively, scarred suggests emotional or psychological damage from difficult experiences: {She was scarred by the divorce}, {a generation scarred by war}.

Scarring is the formation of scar tissue, either literally on skin or figuratively on the psyche. Physical scarring results from wounds, burns, or surgery: {The accident left permanent scarring on her arms}. Emotional scarring describes lasting psychological damage: {childhood trauma and its scarring effects}. As an adjective, scarring characterizes experiences that leave such marks: {a scarring defeat}, {a scarring memory}.

Scars are marks left on skin or tissue after wounds heal—the body's permanent record of injury. The word extends to any lasting trace of damage: {The landscape still bears the scars of wildfire}. Emotional scars are psychological wounds that persist: {childhood scars}, {the scars of war}. To scar is to leave such marks, literal or figurative: {The accident scarred her for life}.

Scary describes something that causes fear or alarm: {a scary movie}, {a scary noise in the basement}. The word works for genuine threats and mild frights alike—a scary diagnosis versus a scary Halloween costume. Informally, scary can mean impressively extreme: {She has a scary amount of energy}. The related noun is scare; the verb is to scare.

Scat has two unrelated meanings. One is animal droppings, especially from wild animals: {bear scat}, {coyote scat}. Wildlife trackers identify species by their scat. The other scat is a style of jazz singing using improvised nonsense syllables instead of words—{scatting} over instrumental passages. As a command, scat means go away quickly, usually directed at animals: {Scat, cat!}

Scathing describes criticism or remarks that are harshly severe and withering: {a scathing review}, {a scathing rebuke}. The word implies words sharp enough to wound—delivered with contempt or bitter disapproval. {Her scathing assessment of his work left him speechless.}

Scatter means to disperse or spread in various directions. You scatter seeds across soil, or a crowd scatters when startled. Things that scatter end up distributed irregularly rather than grouped: {Papers scattered across the desk}. A scattering of something is a sparse, random distribution: {a scattering of applause}, {a scattering of houses along the road}.

A scatterbrain is someone who has difficulty focusing or organizing their thoughts, frequently forgetting things or jumping erratically from one topic to another. The term is mildly critical but usually affectionate, suggesting disorganization rather than stupidity. {She's such a scatterbrain—she left her phone in the refrigerator again.} The adjective scatterbrained describes this quality: {His scatterbrained approach to planning made the trip chaotic but memorable.}

Scatterbrained describes someone who is disorganized, forgetful, or unable to concentrate on one thing at a time. A scatterbrained person might lose their keys constantly, forget appointments, or jump from topic to topic in conversation. The term suggests a mind that scatters its attention rather than focusing it. {She's too scatterbrained to be trusted with the arrangements.} The related noun scatterbrain refers to such a person.

Scattered describes things spread over an area without pattern or concentration. Scattered {showers} occur here and there, not everywhere. Scattered {papers} lie disorganized across a surface. A scattered {population} lives dispersed rather than clustered. Someone who is scattered lacks focus or seems disorganized: {I've been so scattered lately I keep forgetting appointments}.

Scattershot describes something wide-ranging but unfocused, like pellets spraying from a shotgun rather than a single aimed bullet. A scattershot {approach} tries many things without clear strategy. Scattershot {criticism} hits multiple targets without precision. The word implies inefficiency—covering lots of ground but lacking direction or coherence.

Scavenge means to search through discarded material for something usable. Animals scavenge carrion; people scavenge dumpsters, junkyards, or abandoned buildings: {We scavenged parts from old computers to build a new one}. The word implies resourcefulness in finding value where others see waste. Extended uses cover any opportunistic gathering: {scavenging ideas from competitors}, {scavenging quotes for an essay}.

Scavenged is the past tense of scavenge, meaning to search through discarded material for useful items or to collect food from whatever sources are available. Animals scavenge carrion; people scavenge abandoned buildings or junkyards: {We scavenged parts from old computers to build a new one}. The word suggests resourcefulness amid scarcity.

A scavenger is a person or animal that searches through discarded material for useful items. Vultures and hyenas are scavengers, feeding on carrion. People scavenge at dumps, thrift stores, or curbsides: {He furnished his apartment entirely from scavenging}. The word extends to anything that collects waste or debris—certain cells scavenge dead tissue, and chemical scavengers bind unwanted substances.

Scavengers are creatures that feed on dead or decaying matter rather than hunting live prey. Vultures, hyenas, and certain beetles are classic scavengers. The term extends to people who search through discarded materials for useful items: {Scavengers picked through the dump for recyclables}. In chemistry, a scavenger is a substance that removes impurities or unwanted components from a system.

Scavenging is searching through discarded material for something useful or edible. Animals scavenge carrion; people scavenge dumpsters, junkyards, or abandoned buildings. The word implies picking through what others have left behind: {She spent the afternoon scavenging for spare parts}. In biology, scavengers are organisms that feed on dead matter rather than hunting live prey.

A scenario is a possible sequence of events or an imagined situation. Planners develop scenarios to prepare for various outcomes: {worst-case scenario}, {best-case scenario}. In film and theater, a scenario is an outline of the plot. The word often describes hypothetical situations posed for discussion: {Let's consider a scenario where interest rates rise sharply}.

A scene is a place where something happens: {the scene of the crime}, {the scene of the accident}. In drama and film, a scene is a unit of action in one location—several scenes make an act. To {make a scene} is to create a public disturbance through emotional outburst. A scene is also a sphere of activity or interest: {the music scene}, {the downtown art scene}, {that's not really my scene}. Behind the scenes means out of public view, where the real work or decisions happen.

Scenery is the natural features of a landscape considered in terms of their appearance: {The mountain scenery was breathtaking}. In theater, scenery refers to the painted backdrops and constructed elements that create a stage setting. A {change of scenery} means a shift to new surroundings, often for refreshment or variety.

Scenes is the plural of scene—distinct portions of action in a play, film, or narrative. Extended, scenes are places where particular activities occur: {the music scene}, {the bar scene}. To {make a scene} is to cause a public disturbance. {Behind the scenes} means out of public view. In youth slang, scenes can express enthusiastic agreement or acknowledgment: {Want to grab dinner? —Scenes!}

Scenic describes views or places that are visually striking, especially natural landscapes: {a scenic overlook}, {the scenic route}. Taking the scenic route means choosing a longer path for its beauty—or, figuratively, taking unnecessary time to reach a point. In theater and film, scenic refers to stage sets and backdrops: {scenic design}, {scenic painter}.
