Sew is to join pieces of fabric or other material by passing thread through them with a needle, either by hand or with a sewing machine. The skill extends from basic repairs like {sewing on a button} to elaborate crafts like quilting and tailoring. To sew something up means to close it with stitches, and figuratively to secure or finalize: {They sewed up the deal before competitors could respond}. The past participle sewn is more common than sewed.

Sewage is wastewater and human waste carried through sewer systems. It includes what goes down drains and toilets in homes and businesses, along with industrial discharge. Sewage requires treatment before release into waterways: {The city's sewage treatment plant processes millions of gallons daily}. Figuratively, sewage describes anything foul or worthless: {The internet is full of sewage}.

A sewer is an underground pipe or tunnel that carries wastewater and sewage away from buildings to treatment facilities. The word extends to the whole system: {The city's sewers date back to the 1800s}. Figuratively, a sewer is any place of filth or moral degradation: {a sewer of corruption}. Separately, a sewer is a person who sews.

Sewers are underground systems of pipes and channels that carry wastewater and storm runoff away from populated areas. The word also refers to the pipes themselves: {The city is replacing aging sewers}. Figuratively, a sewer suggests filth or moral degradation: {a sewer of corruption}. Separately, a sewer is a person who sews.

Sewing is the craft of joining fabric or other materials using needle and thread. It encompasses everything from mending a torn seam to constructing garments from scratch. A sewing {machine} automates the stitching process. A sewing {kit} contains needles, thread, and basic supplies. {She took up sewing during the pandemic.}

Sewn is the past participle of sew—to join fabric or other material with needle and thread: {a hand-sewn quilt}, {poorly sewn seams}. It appears after auxiliary verbs: {The button had been sewn on crooked}. Sewed also serves as past participle, though sewn is more common. The phrase {sewn up} means secured or settled: {We've got the contract sewn up}.

Sex has many definitions connected with its core meaning of animal reproduction. When animals have sex, a male and female engage in intercourse. When people have sex, they typically have recreational sex, which can take place between people of any gender and without the implication of reproduction. In many contexts, sex is another term for gender: Have you determined the sex of the kittens yet? People of the same sex can now marry in many states.

Sexes is the plural of sex, referring to the categories of male and female based on reproductive function. The word often appears in phrases emphasizing this division: {the opposite sex}, {the battle of the sexes}, {both sexes were represented}. To say {the sexes} is to invoke men and women as distinct groups: {relations between the sexes}.

Sexism is prejudice or discrimination based on sex, typically against women. It ranges from individual attitudes to systemic patterns in hiring, pay, and opportunity. Sexist assumptions about capabilities or proper roles often operate unconsciously: {The hiring committee didn't realize their questions to female candidates were sexist}. The term emerged from 1960s feminism, modeled on racism.

Sexist describes attitudes, behaviors, or systems that discriminate based on sex, typically against women. A sexist {joke} demeans one sex; a sexist {hiring practice} favors another. The noun identifies someone who holds such views: {He's a sexist}. The word emerged alongside feminism's vocabulary in the 1960s, modeled on racist.

A sextant is a navigational instrument used to measure the angle between a celestial body and the horizon, allowing sailors and aviators to determine their position at sea or in the air. The device uses mirrors and a graduated arc spanning sixty degrees—one sixth of a circle, hence the name. Though largely supplanted by GPS, sextants remain valued as backup instruments and for their elegance: {He took a sextant reading at noon to fix their latitude}.

Sexting is the activity or sending sexually explicit messages or photographs using SMS (on a cell phone, for example). The word is formed from sex and texting. Sexting is usually associated with teenagers and young people, though politicians have occasionally been caught in sexting scandals.

Sexual relates to sex in its two main senses: the biological distinction between male and female, and physical intimacy. Sexual {reproduction} involves combining genetic material from two parents. Sexual {attraction} is desire for physical contact with another person. Sexual {harassment} and sexual {assault} describe unwanted advances or contact. The word covers anatomy, behavior, identity, and orientation: {sexual organs}, {sexual activity}, {sexual identity}.

Sexuality encompasses sexual feelings, attractions, and behaviors. It includes one's orientation—whether attracted to the same sex, opposite sex, both, or neither—as well as broader aspects of identity and expression related to sex. {She's open about her sexuality}. The word also refers simply to capacity for sexual experience: {the sexuality of adolescence}, {a film that explores human sexuality}.

Sexy describes someone or something that arouses sexual interest or desire: {a sexy outfit}, {I find confidence sexy}. The word extends to anything exciting or appealing in a way that captures attention: {a sexy new sports car}, {Spreadsheets aren't exactly sexy, but they get the job done}. This figurative use often describes ideas or products that generate buzz or enthusiasm.

Shabby describes something worn, faded, or in poor condition from use or neglect: {a shabby coat}, {shabby furniture}. It extends to people dressed in worn clothing or to places that look run-down: {a shabby motel on the edge of town}. Figuratively, shabby means mean or unfair: {That was a shabby way to treat a friend}.

Shacharit is the Jewish morning prayer service, the first of the three daily prayers in traditional Jewish practice. It is recited from dawn until midday and includes the Shema, the Amidah, and Torah readings on certain days. {He davened shacharit at the synagogue before work.} Also spelled shaharit or shacharris. (Capitalized Shacharit is the same service.)

A shack is a small, crudely built dwelling—typically rundown or makeshift: {They lived in a shack at the edge of town}. The word suggests poverty or improvisation. To {shack up} is to live together, especially as an unmarried couple: {They've been shacking up for a year now}.

A shackle is a metal restraint, typically a pair of rings connected by a chain, used to bind a prisoner's wrists or ankles. The word extends to any device that fastens or secures, like the U-shaped fitting used in rigging and lifting. Figuratively, shackles are whatever constrains freedom or progress: {the shackles of poverty}, {shackled by outdated regulations}. To shackle someone is to restrain them physically or limit them in some other way.

Shackled means bound with shackles—metal restraints fastened around wrists or ankles: {The prisoners were shackled together}. The word extends to any severe constraint on freedom or movement: {shackled by debt}, {shackled to a job she hated}. The figurative use emphasizes not just limitation but the sense of being trapped against one's will.

Shackles are metal restraints, typically rings connected by a chain, used to bind a prisoner's wrists or ankles. The word almost always appears in plural form, whether referring to literal restraints or figurative ones: {throwing off the shackles of oppression}. To shackle someone is to put them in shackles or, more commonly, to impose severe constraints on their freedom or ability to act. {Budget cuts have shackled the department's ability to respond to emergencies.}

Shacks is the plural of shack, a small, crudely built dwelling or shelter. Shacks suggest poverty, impermanence, or makeshift construction: {fishing shacks along the pier}, {The workers lived in shacks at the edge of the plantation}. To shack up is to live with someone, usually a romantic partner, in informal or temporary arrangements.

Shade is an area out of direct sunlight, like the shade of a tree on the ground around it. By extension, a lampshade is placed over a light bulb to reduce the intensity of its light; informally, shades are sunglasses. A shade of something is a form of it slightly different than another: It was a lighter shade of blue. To shade something is to shelter it from the sun or strong light. This use is usually adjectival (shaded patio, shaded window).

Shades are sunglasses—eyewear with darkened lenses: {She put on her shades and headed to the beach}. The term is casual and cool-sounding. Shades also refers to variations of color: {different shades of blue}. A shade is something that blocks light—a window shade, a lamp shade—or a slight amount: {a shade too bright}. In literary use, shades are ghosts or spirits of the dead.

Shading is the gradual variation of light and dark in a drawing or painting to create the illusion of depth and form. Artists use shading to make flat surfaces appear three-dimensional. The term extends to any subtle gradation: {There are shadings of meaning I hadn't considered}. To give someone shade—public criticism or dismissal—yields a different sense of shading: subtly dissing someone without direct confrontation.

Like the related word shade, shadow is a noun and a verb. A defined space of shade is a shadow, like that of a pole, a person, or a building. Figuratively, a shadow is a faint quality that accompanies something (shadow of doubt). If you are described as someone’s shadow, the suggestion is that you often accompany that person. To shadow someone is to follow them, perhaps in order to learn their job, or perhaps secretly: The detective shadowed the suspect. In parliamentary government, a shadow cabinet minister is a party official in the opposition.

A shadowban is a form of online moderation where a user's posts become invisible to others without notification—the person continues posting, unaware they've been silenced. Platforms use shadowbans to discourage spammers and trolls who might create new accounts if openly banned. As a verb: {I think I've been shadowbanned—none of my comments are getting replies}.

Shadowbanned describes a user whose posts or comments have been secretly hidden from others by a platform, without notifying the user. The person can still post normally, but no one else sees their content—a kind of invisible exile. Platforms use shadowbanning to discourage spammers and trolls without triggering the complaints that explicit bans invite: {I think I've been shadowbanned—my posts aren't getting any engagement}.

Shadowbanning is a moderation technique where a user's posts are hidden from others without notifying the user. The shadowbanned person continues posting normally, unaware their content is invisible to everyone else. Platforms use it to discourage bad actors without provoking them: {I think I've been shadowbanned—my tweets get zero engagement}. Also called a stealth ban or ghost ban.

Shadowboxing is practicing boxing moves against an imaginary opponent, throwing punches at the air to develop technique, footwork, and conditioning. Fighters shadowbox to warm up or train without a sparring partner. Figuratively, shadowboxing describes fighting against something that isn't really there—engaging with phantom threats or rehearsing confrontations that may never happen: {He spent the whole meeting shadowboxing with objections nobody had raised}.

Shadows are dark areas where light is blocked by an object. Every shadow implies both a light source and something standing in its way. Shadows lengthen at dawn and dusk, shrink at midday. Figuratively, a shadow is anything that follows closely or looms ominously: {living in the shadow of her famous mother}, {a shadow of doubt}. To shadow someone is to follow them secretly. The shadows means darkness or obscurity: {lurking in the shadows}.

Shadowy describes something dark, dim, or filled with shadows: {a shadowy corner of the room}, {shadowy figures in the alley}. The word often suggests mystery or obscurity—things not fully visible or knowable. A shadowy organization operates in secret. A shadowy past contains hidden or unclear elements. The connotation is usually ominous or suspicious rather than merely dim.

Shady describes a place sheltered from direct sunlight: {a shady spot under the oak tree}. The figurative sense dominates modern usage—shady means suspicious, dishonest, or of questionable character: {a shady deal}, {That guy seems shady}. The connection runs through darkness and concealment: what happens in the shade is hidden from view.

All shafts have roughly the same shape – long and cylindrical – but vary in composition. A long pole that is part of a weapon or tool is often called a shaft (golf club shaft). A shaft could consist of sunlight. A mineshaft is a deep hole dug in the ground for access to ore. Shaft is also a vulgar synonym for penis. If you shaft someone, you treat them unfairly and meanly.

Shafts is the plural of shaft—long narrow poles or passages. Arrow shafts fly toward targets; mine shafts descend into the earth; elevator shafts run vertically through buildings. Shafts of light pierce darkness. To shaft someone is to treat them unfairly: {He really got shafted on that deal}. The noun the shaft means similar mistreatment: {She gave him the shaft}.

A shag is a type of rough, matted texture—shag carpet has long, thick pile; a shag haircut has layered, textured strands: {The room still had its 1970s shag rug}. {She got a shag cut}. A shag is also a type of cormorant (seabird), and the shag is a dance that originated in the Carolinas. In British slang, to shag is to have sex: {They shagged in the loo}. A shag is an act of sex or a sexual partner: {He's looking for a shag}. The British slang is vulgar but common, popularized in American awareness by the Austin Powers films.

Shaggy means covered with rough, matted hair or fiber: {a shaggy dog}, {a shaggy beard}. A shag-dog story is a long, meandering joke with an anticlimactic or absurd punchline—perhaps from the shagginess suggesting untidiness or lack of direction.

Shake describes a motion, one-time or repeated, of quick, oscillating movement. You can shake your head to indicate no, or you can shake from cold or fear. People shake hands in greeting and to signal agreement. To shake off something is to remove it by shaking, or to rid yourself of something unpleasant: I had to shake off any doubts I had. A shake is an instance of shaking. Or it might be a milkshake. If you have the shakes, you are trembling from fear or some pathological condition.

A shakedown is an act of extortion—demanding money through threats or intimidation: {The protection racket was just a shakedown}. It also means a thorough search, especially of a person or cell by police or guards. As an adjective, shakedown describes a trial run meant to test new equipment or reveal problems: {a shakedown cruise}.

Shakedowns are acts of extortion—demanding money or favors through threats or intimidation. A corrupt cop running shakedowns extracts bribes from business owners. The word also means thorough searches, especially of prisoners or cells: {Guards conducted shakedowns looking for contraband}. A shakedown cruise is a test voyage to identify problems in a new ship or aircraft before regular service.

Shaken is the past participle of shake. Something shaken has been moved rapidly back and forth: {a shaken bottle of champagne}. More often, shaken describes emotional disturbance—being rattled or unsettled by an experience: {She was visibly shaken after the accident}. {Shaken, not stirred} is the famous martini instruction from James Bond.

A shaker is a container designed to be shaken—typically for mixing drinks or dispensing seasonings through perforated holes: {a cocktail shaker}, {a salt shaker}. The word extends to anything that shakes or causes shaking. A {mover and shaker} is someone who gets things done and influences events. (Capitalized Shaker refers to the religious sect.)

A shakeup is a sudden, significant reorganization—usually of personnel or structure within an organization. Companies announce shakeups when they replace executives or restructure departments: {The CEO resigned amid a major shakeup at headquarters}. The term implies disruption and change, often prompted by poor performance or scandal.

Shaking is trembling or vibrating movement, whether from cold, fear, excitement, or external force. A person may be {shaking with rage} or {shaking from the cold}. Buildings shake during earthquakes. {She was shaking her head} indicates disagreement or disbelief. {I can't stop shaking} suggests loss of physical control from emotion or chill.

Shaky describes something that trembles, wobbles, or lacks stability. A shaky hand trembles; a shaky table rocks on uneven legs. The word extends to anything uncertain or unreliable: {shaky evidence}, {a shaky alibi}, {shaky finances}. Someone feeling shaky is unsteady on their feet, often from illness, nerves, or shock: {I felt shaky after the accident}.

Shale is a fine-grained sedimentary rock formed from compressed clay and mud. It splits easily into thin layers along parallel planes. Shale formations often contain oil and natural gas, extracted through hydraulic fracturing: {The company drills for shale oil in North Dakota}. {Shale cliffs crumbled along the shoreline}.

Shallow describes limited depth—the opposite of deep. A shallow pool doesn't reach far below the surface. Shallow breathing doesn't fill the lungs. Shallow understanding doesn't penetrate the subject. Applied to people, shallow is dismissive: concerned only with surfaces, lacking intellectual or emotional depth. {She found him charming but shallow.} The shallows are areas of water near shore.

Shallows refers to a stretch of water that is not deep—the opposite of the depths. The word appears almost exclusively in the plural: {We waded through the shallows}, {fish spawning in the shallows}. Figuratively, shallows suggests superficiality: {content that never ventures beyond the shallows of the topic}.

A sham is something false presented as genuine—a pretense or counterfeit: {The election was a sham}. A person who pretends to be something they're not is also a sham: {He's a sham and a fraud}. As a verb, to sham is to fake: {shamming illness to avoid work}. The adjective describes things meant to deceive: {sham outrage}, {sham marriages}. A pillow sham is a decorative cover—ornamental rather than functional.

A shaman is a person believed to communicate with the spirit world, typically to heal the sick, divine the future, or guide souls. The role appears across many indigenous cultures, from Siberia to the Americas. Shamans often enter trance states through drumming, chanting, or psychoactive substances. The term has been adopted loosely in New Age contexts: {She consulted a shaman for spiritual guidance}.

Shamans are people who act as intermediaries between the natural and spiritual worlds, typically in indigenous or traditional cultures. They enter altered states of consciousness to heal, divine the future, or communicate with spirits. The role combines priest, healer, and mystic: {The shaman performed a ritual to cure the sick child}. In looser usage, shaman describes anyone claiming spiritual powers or practicing alternative healing.

Shambles originally meant a slaughterhouse or meat market, now rarely used that way. The modern sense is a state of complete disorder or destruction: {The kitchen was a shambles after the party}. Unlike mess or disaster, shambles often implies wreckage—things knocked over, scattered, or ruined rather than merely untidy. British speakers may use it with a singular verb: {The economy is a shambles}.

Shame is the painful feeling of having done something wrong, foolish, or disgraceful—or of being exposed as inadequate. It differs from guilt, which focuses on the act; shame focuses on the self. {She couldn't meet their eyes from shame}. To shame someone is to cause this feeling or to publicly disgrace them. A shame is also something regrettable: {It's a shame you couldn't come}. To {put to shame} is to outclass completely: {Her cooking puts mine to shame}. Shameless means without shame, usually as criticism.

Shamed describes someone who has been made to feel shame—the painful emotion of having done something wrong, inadequate, or dishonorable. To be shamed is to have this feeling imposed by others: {He was publicly shamed for his remarks}. The participial form works as both adjective and verb: {a shamed expression}, {They shamed him into apologizing}.

Shameful describes actions, situations, or behaviors that cause or deserve shame—a sense of disgrace or dishonor: {a shameful display of cowardice}, {shameful working conditions}. The word carries moral judgment, suggesting something falls short of accepted standards. What's considered shameful varies by culture and era. Shameful differs from ashamed, which describes the feeling rather than its cause: {He was ashamed of his shameful conduct}.

Shameless describes someone who acts without shame or embarrassment, even when their behavior would normally warrant it. A shameless {liar} lies boldly and without apparent guilt. Shameless {self-promotion} is aggressive and unapologetic. The word carries disapproval—shameless people transgress social norms and don't seem to care: {She made a shameless grab for the inheritance}.

Shaming is the act of causing someone to feel shame—publicly criticizing or humiliating them for perceived wrongdoing. The word often appears with a modifier indicating what's being criticized: {body shaming}, {slut shaming}, {fat shaming}. Online shaming campaigns can destroy reputations: {The internet shaming went viral within hours}.

Shampoo is a liquid soap for washing hair. The verb means to wash with shampoo: {I shampooed twice to get the chlorine out}. Shampoo also cleans carpets and upholstery. A shampoo is an instance of shampooing: {a cut and shampoo}.

A shamrock is a small clover with three leaves, used as a symbol of Ireland. The plant is associated with St. Patrick, who supposedly used its three-part leaf to illustrate the Christian Trinity. People wear shamrocks on St. Patrick's Day: {She pinned a shamrock to her lapel}. The word sometimes extends loosely to any three-leafed clover.

Shamrocks are three-leafed plants, typically clover, serving as the national emblem of Ireland. The plant is associated with St. Patrick, who according to legend used its three leaves to explain the Christian Trinity. Shamrocks appear everywhere on St. Patrick's Day—on decorations, clothing, and greeting cards. A four-leafed clover is not a shamrock but a lucky charm.

To shanghai someone is to coerce or trick them into doing something, originally to kidnap them for service as a sailor. The term comes from the practice of drugging or forcing men aboard ships bound for Shanghai and other distant ports: {They shanghaied him into joining the committee}. The word suggests being pressed into service against one's will. (Capitalized Shanghai is the Chinese city.)

Shank has meanings connected to a long, narrow part. The shank of the leg is the section between knee and ankle. A shank of meat includes this part of an animal: {braised lamb shanks}. Tool shanks are the straight connecting portions—the shaft of a drill bit, the stem of a key, the straight part of a fishhook. In prison slang, a shank is an improvised stabbing weapon, and to shank someone is to stab them with one. In golf, to shank is to mishit the ball with the hosel rather than the clubface: {He shanked it into the rough}.

Shanked is the past tense of shank. In golf, to shank a shot is to mishit the ball with the club's hosel rather than the face, sending it wildly off course: {He shanked it into the rough}. More broadly, to shank something is to botch it badly. In prison slang, to shank someone is to stab them with an improvised blade: {He got shanked in the yard}.

Shanties are small, crudely built dwellings, typically associated with poverty: {a hillside covered with shanties}. The word often appears in compounds like {shantytown}. Separately, shanties (also spelled chanteys) are work songs traditionally sung by sailors to coordinate labor like hauling ropes or raising anchors: {sea shanties}.

A shanty is a crudely built dwelling, typically thrown together from whatever materials are available—scrap wood, corrugated metal, cardboard. Shanties cluster in shantytowns on the outskirts of cities where housing is scarce or unaffordable. A different word spelled the same way is a sea shanty, a rhythmic work song traditionally sung by sailors to coordinate group labor like hauling ropes or raising anchor. {The crew sang a shanty as they hoisted the sails.}

A shantytown is a settlement of makeshift dwellings built from scrap materials—corrugated metal, plywood, tarps. Shantytowns typically arise on the margins of cities where impoverished residents lack access to formal housing: {The hillsides were covered with shantytowns overlooking the city center}. The term emphasizes poverty and improvisation rather than permanence.

Shape is a noun and verb about the outline of a thing that distinguishes it from its background. The shape of a ball is round. Terms such as good shape and bad shape are used to characterize the relative condition of something. When you give shape to something, you define it well enough for others to understand. To shape a thing is to give it a shape. To shape up is to take on a specific form, or to improve bad behavior.

Shapes is the plural of shape—the outline or form of something: circles, squares, triangles. When someone {sees shapes} in darkness or fog, they perceive indistinct forms. To be {in good shape} or {bad shape} describes condition. The verb shapes means to form or influence: {Experience shapes character}. {What shapes up} develops or progresses: {Let's see how this shapes up}.

To shapeshift is to transform one's physical form into another, especially in mythology and fantasy where beings change into animals or other creatures: {The witch shapeshifted into a raven}. Figuratively, it describes fluid transformation of identity, appearance, or approach: {Politicians shapeshift to match their audiences}. A shapeshifter is a being with this ability.

A shapeshifter is a being that can transform its physical form into something else—another creature, another person, an object. The concept appears across mythology and fantasy: werewolves, skin-walkers, gods who take human form. Figuratively, a shapeshifter is someone who adapts their personality or appearance to different situations: {He's a political shapeshifter, changing positions with the polls}.

Shapeshifters are beings capable of changing their physical form, a concept appearing across mythology, folklore, and fantasy fiction. Werewolves, vampires, and trickster gods like Loki are classic examples. The term extends to people who seem to transform their personality or presentation to fit different situations: {Politicians are shapeshifters, adapting their message to each audience}.

Shapeshifting is the ability to transform one's physical form into something else—another creature, person, or object. The concept appears throughout mythology and folklore, from werewolves to trickster gods, and remains a staple of fantasy fiction and superhero stories. As a verb form, it describes the act of transformation: {The witch was shapeshifting into a raven when the hunters arrived}. Figuratively, shapeshifting can characterize someone who readily adapts their personality or position to different situations.

A shard is a broken piece of something brittle—glass, pottery, ceramic: {Shards of the vase littered the floor}. The word implies sharp edges and violent breakage. In computing and gaming, a shard is a partition of a database or game server, where the whole is divided into separate pieces that function independently.

Shards are broken pieces of something brittle—glass, pottery, ceramic, ice. The word implies sharp edges and violent breaking: {Shards of glass covered the floor}. In gaming and fantasy contexts, a shard may be a fragment of a magical object or a separate server instance. The singular shard appears less often than the plural.

Share centers on division into portions. To share something is to divide it among others or to have it in common: {Let's share the pizza}, {They share a love of jazz}. A share is one portion of a divided whole—especially a unit of ownership in a company: {She bought shares in the tech startup}. To share can also mean to tell or reveal: {He shared his concerns with the group}. The adjective shared describes things held or used jointly: {shared custody}, {shared workspace}.

To sharecrop is to farm land belonging to someone else in exchange for a share of the crop produced. The system dominated the American South after the Civil War, often trapping formerly enslaved people and poor whites in cycles of debt to landowners. {His family sharecropped cotton in Mississippi for three generations.}

A sharecropper is a tenant farmer who works land owned by someone else in exchange for a share of the crop produced. The system dominated the American South after the Civil War, often trapping Black farmers in cycles of debt to white landowners: {Three generations of his family had been sharecroppers on that plantation}. The term now evokes poverty and exploitation.

Sharecroppers are tenant farmers who pay rent not in cash but in a share of the crop they produce. The system dominated the American South after the Civil War, often trapping Black farmers in cycles of debt to white landowners. The term now evokes this exploitative history: {Her grandparents were sharecroppers in Mississippi}.

Sharecropping is a farming arrangement where a tenant works land owned by someone else in exchange for a share of the crop produced. The landowner typically provides land, housing, and supplies; the sharecropper provides labor. In the American South after the Civil War, sharecropping replaced slavery but often trapped Black farmers in cycles of debt and dependency: {Three generations of his family had sharecropped that land}.

Shared describes something held, used, or experienced in common by more than one person. A shared {apartment} has multiple occupants splitting costs. Shared {custody} divides parental responsibility. A shared {experience} is one people go through together: {We have a shared love of jazz}. The word implies joint participation rather than sole ownership.

Shares are portions or parts of something divided among multiple people or entities. The word functions as both noun and verb: if you share something, you divide it or allow others access to it; your share is the portion you receive or contribute. In finance, shares are units of ownership in a company—owning shares makes you a shareholder entitled to dividends and voting rights. {She shared her lunch with a coworker.} {He bought 500 shares of the tech company.}

Sharing is the act of giving a portion of something to others or using something jointly. Children learn early that sharing toys builds friendships, while adults share resources, responsibilities, and information. In digital contexts, sharing has become ubiquitous: {I kept sharing that video with everyone I knew}. The word can also describe an emotional openness, as when someone shares their feelings or experiences with others.

A shark is a large predatory fish with cartilage instead of bones, multiple gill slits, and rows of replaceable teeth. Sharks range from small bottom-dwellers to the great white. Figuratively, a shark is someone ruthlessly aggressive in business or skilled at exploiting others—a {loan shark} charges predatory interest, a {card shark} dominates at cards. To shark is to swindle or hustle.

Sharks are large predatory fish with cartilaginous skeletons, typically featuring multiple rows of teeth and a reputation for danger to swimmers—though attacks are rare. The word extends to predatory people, especially those who exploit others financially: {loan sharks}, {card sharks}. To shark is to swindle or cheat. {The lawyers circled like sharks.}

Sharp is most frequently an adjective for characterizing distinctive and sometimes extreme or unpleasant qualities. Sharp surfaces (knives, blades, points) are good for cutting and piercing. Sharp intensifies and accentuates the meaning of many nouns after it (sharp contrast, sharp decline, sharp turn, sharp pain). In music, a sharp is a half step above a tone. If you’re singing or playing sharp you’re higher than the pitch. One o’clock sharp means precisely at one o’clock.

To sharpen is to make something sharp or sharper—giving a blade a finer edge, bringing a point to greater acuteness: {sharpen a knife}, {sharpen a pencil}. The meaning extends to making things more acute or precise: {sharpen your skills}, {sharpen the focus of an argument}. Images sharpen when they become clearer. Conflicts sharpen when they intensify.

Sharpening is the act of making something sharper—giving a blade a finer edge, bringing an image into clearer focus, or intensifying a quality: {The debate is sharpening divisions within the party}. A knife needs sharpening when it dulls. Skills and wits also benefit from sharpening: {She spent years sharpening her craft}.

Sharpness is the quality of having a fine edge or point—a blade's sharpness determines how cleanly it cuts. The word extends to anything precise or acute: sharpness of {vision}, sharpness of {mind}, the sharpness of a {photograph's} focus. Sharpness can also describe harshness or severity: the sharpness of {criticism}, the sharpness of {winter air}, a sharpness in someone's {tone}.

A sharpshooter is someone highly skilled at shooting with precision, typically with a rifle. In military contexts, sharpshooters occupy a tier below snipers but above ordinary marksmen, tasked with accurate fire at greater distances than standard infantry. The term extends figuratively to anyone with exceptional accuracy or skill in a targeted domain: {She's a sharpshooter when it comes to finding errors in contracts}. In basketball, a sharpshooter is a player known for consistently hitting shots, especially three-pointers.

Sharpshooters are marksmen with exceptional accuracy, originally military riflemen who could hit targets at long range. The term extends to anyone with precise aim or, figuratively, to those who strike with accuracy in other domains: {The prosecutor brought in her sharpshooters for cross-examination}. In basketball, a sharpshooter is a player known for accurate shooting, especially from beyond the three-point line.

Shatter means to break suddenly into many pieces, typically with force: {The window shattered on impact}. Glass, ceramics, and other brittle materials shatter. The word extends to abstractions that break apart dramatically: shattered {dreams}, shattered {illusions}, shattered {confidence}. A person who is shattered is emotionally devastated or, in British usage, exhausted.

Shattered describes something broken into many pieces, typically violently: {shattered glass covered the floor}. The word emphasizes completeness of destruction—not cracked or chipped but fragmented beyond repair. Figuratively, shattered applies to emotions or composure utterly destroyed: {shattered by the news}, {shattered dreams}. In British informal use, shattered means exhausted: {I'm absolutely shattered after that shift}.

Shattering describes something that breaks into pieces, literally or figuratively. A shattering {blow} destroys what it strikes. Shattering {news} is devastating, breaking apart one's composure or assumptions: {The diagnosis was shattering}. A shattering {defeat} is overwhelming and complete. The word emphasizes violent fragmentation—not just damage but destruction.

Shave is to cut hair close to the skin with a razor or blade: {He shaves every morning}. The noun is an instance of shaving: {I need a shave}. Extended uses involve cutting thin layers or narrow margins: shave {wood}, shave {costs}, {a close shave} with danger. To shave points in sports is to manipulate the score for gambling purposes.

Shaving is the act of removing hair with a razor or similar blade, typically from the face or legs. A shaving is a thin slice or strip cut from a surface: {wood shavings}, {chocolate shavings}. Shaving also functions as a modifier for related items: shaving {cream}, shaving {brush}, shaving {kit}.

A shawl is a piece of fabric worn draped over the shoulders or wrapped around the upper body for warmth or as a fashion accessory. Shawls are typically square or rectangular, often fringed, and range from everyday wool wraps to ornate ceremonial garments: {She pulled her shawl tighter against the evening chill}.

Shawls are pieces of fabric, typically square or rectangular, worn draped over the shoulders, around the head, or wrapped about the body for warmth or as a fashion accessory. They range from lightweight silk or lace for decorative purposes to heavy wool or cashmere for cold weather. Unlike scarves, which are usually long and narrow, shawls are broader and meant to cover more of the upper body. {She wrapped herself in a warm shawl on the chilly evening.}

You use she to designate a single female baby, girl, or woman, and to designate a female animal when it is important to identify the animal’s gender. Writers today sometimes use she interchangeably with he in texts as a pronoun with general reference, in order to avoid the perceived sexism of always using he. By convention, some inanimate things are sometimes referred to with she, including ships, flags, and countries.

Shears are large scissors, typically with long blades and sturdy handles, used for cutting fabric, hedges, metal, or sheep's wool. The word is almost always plural—you reach for {the shears}, not {a shear}. Specialized types include pinking shears for zigzag fabric edges and pruning shears for garden work. To shear sheep is to cut their wool; the tool doing the cutting is shears.

A sheath is a close-fitting cover, especially one that protects a blade: {He slid the knife back into its sheath}. The word extends to any snug protective covering—the insulating material around a wire, the membrane surrounding a muscle fiber, or a form-fitting dress. To sheathe is to enclose in a sheath; to unsheathe is to draw out.

The verb shed is about separation and getting rid of things. A snake sheds its skin. When you shed weight, blood, or tears, they leave your body. If you shed your inhibitions, you become bold or assertive. When a truck sheds its load, everything falls off it. To shed light on a subject is to bring new information about it. The noun shed designates a small building with some purpose (storage shed, garden shed).

Shedding is the process of losing or casting off something naturally. Animals shed fur or skin, trees shed leaves, people shed tears or pounds. The word often appears in contexts of renewal or unburdening: {The dog is shedding everywhere}, {She's been shedding old habits}. In epidemiology, viral shedding refers to releasing virus particles that can infect others.

Sheen is a soft, lustrous glow on a surface—the quality of reflecting light without being fully shiny: {the sheen of silk}, {Her hair had a healthy sheen}. It suggests smoothness and often quality. A sheen can also be a thin coating that creates this effect: {a sheen of oil on the water}.

Sheep are woolly, domesticated mammals raised for meat, wool, and milk. They're known for flocking behavior and docility, which gives rise to the figurative sense: a sheep is someone who follows others without independent thought. {Don't be a sheep—think for yourself.} To {separate the sheep from the goats} is to distinguish the worthy from the unworthy. The plural is also sheep.

A sheepdog is a dog bred or trained to herd sheep—Border Collies, Australian Shepherds, and similar working breeds. They control flocks by circling, crouching, and responding to whistled commands. The term extends to any dog that guards or manages livestock: {The sheepdog kept the flock together during the storm}. Figuratively, a sheepdog is someone who protects or guides others.

Sheepdogs are dogs bred or trained to herd sheep—border collies, Australian shepherds, and similar breeds. They work by circling, stalking, and occasionally nipping to move flocks where the shepherd directs. The term extends to dogs that guard sheep from predators rather than herd them. Figuratively, a sheepdog is someone who protects others: {He saw himself as a sheepdog watching over his community}.

Sheepish describes the awkward embarrassment of someone caught doing something foolish or mildly wrong. A sheepish {grin} or sheepish {look} acknowledges the awkwardness without deep shame: {He gave a sheepish shrug when I caught him eating cake for breakfast}. The word suggests meekness and self-consciousness, like a sheep that knows it's wandered somewhere it shouldn't.

Sheer emphasizes completeness or purity—nothing mixed in: {sheer luck}, {sheer stupidity}, {the sheer volume of complaints}. Applied to fabric, sheer means thin enough to see through: {sheer curtains}, {sheer stockings}. As a verb or adverb, sheer means to swerve or turn sharply: {The boat sheered away from the rocks}. A sheer cliff face drops straight down, unbroken by ledges.

A sheet is something thin or flat, often rectangular, and often white: especially a sheet of paper or sheets for a bed. Pieces of paper with particular text are called sheets (fact sheet, balance sheet). A cheat sheet supplies answers to questions. Sheet metal is in thin sheets, and can be used to make a baking sheet, a flat, rectangular pan. When rain falls heavily, you can say that it sheets.

Sheets are large rectangular pieces of fabric or other thin material. Bed sheets cover mattresses and sleepers. A sheet of paper, metal, or glass is a flat, thin piece: {a sheet of plywood}, {a sheet of ice}. Rain or fire coming down in sheets falls in broad, continuous expanses. In sailing, a sheet is a rope controlling a sail—hence {three sheets to the wind} for drunk, from a ship lurching out of control.

Sheikh is an Arabic title of respect for a leader, elder, or religious scholar. In Arab societies, it designates tribal chiefs, Islamic clerics, or men of advanced age and wisdom. The term extends to Gulf state royalty and wealthy Arab businessmen: {The sheikh owns half the racehorses in the country}. Also spelled sheik.

Shekels is informal for money or cash: {I don't have the shekels for that}. The word comes from the ancient Hebrew unit of weight and currency. Today the shekel is the official currency of Israel, but the plural shekels in English usually just means money in general, with a slightly humorous or old-fashioned tone.

A shelf is a flat horizontal surface for storing or displaying objects, typically attached to a wall or fitted inside furniture: {books lined the shelf}, {the top shelf of the closet}. To shelve something is to place it on a shelf, or figuratively to set it aside: {We shelved the project indefinitely}. Off the shelf means readily available without customization. On the shelf describes something—or someone—set aside as no longer useful or desirable.

A shell is a natural protective covering, of a sea creature like an oyster or clam, or of an egg or nut. The enclosing aspect of shells inspires other uses, such as a pastry shell (for holding pie contents). A shell company is one that exists merely to own another company. To shell something is to remove the usable part from the shell. When this is already done, the items are shelled: He added the shelled walnuts to the cookie dough. To shell is also to bombard with projectile weapons fired from a cannon, which are shells.

Shellfish is an informal term for aquatic animals that have shells or shell-like exoskeletons, including crustaceans like shrimp, crabs, and lobsters, as well as mollusks like clams, oysters, and mussels. The term is culinary rather than scientific—biologically, these creatures aren't fish at all. Shellfish allergies are among the most common food allergies, and the term often appears in restaurant warnings. {The raw bar had an impressive shellfish selection.}

Shelling is the act of bombarding a place with artillery fire or explosives: {The city endured relentless shelling for weeks}. Separately, shelling means removing the outer covering from nuts, peas, or shellfish: {We spent the afternoon shelling pecans on the porch}. The context—warfare or kitchen—makes the meaning clear.

Shells are the hard outer coverings of mollusks, eggs, nuts, and seeds—anything with a protective casing that must be cracked or removed. By extension, shell describes hollow structures: a building's shell remains after fire guts the interior; an artillery shell is a hollow projectile filled with explosives. To shell peas is to remove them from pods; to shell a city is to bombard it. A shell can be a person's withdrawn exterior: {She retreated into her shell}. In computing, a shell is the interface between user and operating system. To {shell out} is to pay, often reluctantly.

Shellshock is psychological trauma resulting from prolonged exposure to combat, particularly artillery bombardment. The term emerged from World War I, when soldiers developed tremors, nightmares, and emotional numbness after enduring relentless shelling. Now largely replaced by PTSD in clinical use, shellshock persists in figurative contexts for anyone left dazed by overwhelming experience: {After three kids under five, she was shellshocked}. Also spelled shell shock.

Shellshocked originally described soldiers suffering psychological trauma from combat—the term arose from World War I, when artillery bombardment left men dazed, trembling, or mentally broken. Now it more loosely describes anyone left stunned or disoriented by overwhelming events: {I was shellshocked after the accident}. Also spelled shell-shocked.

Shelter is protection from weather, danger, or hardship. A roof provides shelter from rain; a cave shelters hikers from wind. The word extends to any refuge: {a homeless shelter}, {a women's shelter}, {a bomb shelter}. To shelter someone is to provide this protection: {They sheltered refugees in their basement}. To {shelter in place} is to stay indoors during an emergency. Figuratively, a sheltered life is one protected from harsh realities.

Sheltered describes protection from harsh conditions—weather, danger, or unpleasant realities. A sheltered {cove} is shielded from wind and waves. A sheltered {childhood} lacks exposure to life's difficulties, often implying naivety: {She led a sheltered existence and was shocked by the poverty she encountered}. The word can be neutral or gently critical, suggesting someone unprepared for the world.

To shelve something is to place it on a shelf, but the figurative sense dominates: to shelve a plan or project is to set it aside, postponing or abandoning it indefinitely. {The committee shelved the proposal until next year.} {Budget cuts forced them to shelve the expansion.} The word suggests storage rather than destruction—shelved things might be retrieved later.

Shelved describes something placed on a shelf, but the common use is figurative: a plan or project that has been set aside indefinitely. {The proposal was shelved due to budget cuts.} {After poor test screenings, the studio shelved the film.} Like items stored on a shelf, shelved projects aren't destroyed—they're put away, perhaps to be retrieved later, perhaps not.

Shelves is the plural of shelf—horizontal surfaces for storage or display, typically fixed to walls or built into furniture. {The shelves were lined with books.} To shelve something is to place it on a shelf, or figuratively to set it aside indefinitely: {They shelved the project due to budget cuts.} Shelves also serves as the third-person singular of this verb.

Shelving is the act of putting something on a shelf, or more commonly, postponing it indefinitely: {The committee voted to shelve the proposal}. When you shelve a project, you set it aside rather than actively pursue it—the metaphor suggests storage rather than disposal. Shelving also refers collectively to shelves as fixtures: {We need more shelving in the garage}.

Shenanigans are mischievous or deceitful behavior, often with a playful edge: {The kids were up to their usual shenanigans}. The word can suggest harmless pranks or something more underhanded: {financial shenanigans}, {political shenanigans}. Almost always plural. The singular shenanigan occasionally appears but sounds odd to most ears.

A shepherd tends sheep, guiding them to pasture and protecting them from predators. The role extends metaphorically to anyone who guides or watches over others—ministers are shepherds of their congregations, and the word appears throughout religious texts for spiritual guardians. As a verb, to shepherd is to guide or usher: {She shepherded the children through the museum}. German Shepherd is a breed of dog originally used for herding.

Shepherds are people who tend sheep, guiding flocks to pasture and protecting them from predators. The term extends to anyone who guides or watches over others: {The teacher shepherded her students through the museum}. Religious leaders are often called shepherds of their congregations. As a verb, to shepherd is to guide carefully: {She shepherded the project through committee}.

Sherbet is a frozen dessert similar to sorbet but containing a small amount of dairy, giving it a slightly creamier texture while remaining lighter than ice cream. In American usage, it typically refers to this fruit-flavored treat, often served as a palate cleanser or light dessert. British usage extends to a fizzy powder candy that dissolves on the tongue. The word is sometimes mispronounced "sherbert" with an extra r, though this spelling is considered nonstandard.

A sheriff is the chief law enforcement officer of a county in the United States, typically elected rather than appointed. The role varies by state but usually includes running the county jail, serving court papers, and patrolling unincorporated areas. In England, the term is largely ceremonial, referring to a county's chief executive officer. {The sheriff deputized volunteers to search for the missing hiker.}

Sheriffs is the plural of sheriff, a law enforcement officer typically elected to serve a county. In the United States, sheriffs head county police departments, operate jails, and serve court papers. The office carries considerable local authority: {Three sheriffs from neighboring counties coordinated the search}. In England, the role is largely ceremonial.

Sherry is a fortified wine originally from the Jerez region of southern Spain, ranging from dry and pale to sweet and dark. It's typically served as an aperitif or cooking ingredient: {a glass of dry sherry}, {Add a splash of sherry to the soup}. The wine takes its English name from an anglicization of Jerez. (Capitalized Sherry is a given name.)

Shh is a sound used to request silence or quiet, typically a prolonged hissing with a finger raised to the lips: {Shh, the baby's sleeping}. It can be gentle or sharp depending on urgency. Also spelled sh or shhh.

Shhh is a sound made to request silence or quiet, typically a prolonged hissing through pursed lips. It's often directed at someone being too loud: {Shhh, the baby's sleeping}. The spelling varies—sh, shh, shhh—with more h's suggesting greater urgency or duration.

A shield is a piece of armor held in the hand or worn on the arm to deflect blows or projectiles. The shape—broad and protective—extends to anything that guards or screens: a heat shield, a radiation shield, {The mountain range acts as a shield against cold winds}. To shield is to protect: {She shielded her eyes from the sun}, {He tried to shield his children from the news}. A shield is also an emblem or badge, often displayed by police departments or on heraldic crests.

Shields are devices carried or worn to protect the body from blows or projectiles—the classic image is a knight's metal shield deflecting sword strikes. The meaning extends to anything that protects: a heat shield on a spacecraft, a face shield for welders, or a privacy shield on a screen. To shield is to protect: {She shielded her eyes from the sun}. {He tried to shield his family from the scandal}. (Capitalized Shields is a surname.)

The idea underlying most meanings of shift is change, and sometimes the idea of exchange, where one thing takes the place of another. When you shift gears you go from one to the other. Shifting blame means transferring it from one party to another. When people shift their focus they turn it from one thing to another. As a noun, shift indicates change and is typically modified by an adjective (seismic shift, demographic shift) or following an in or of phrase (a shift in emphasis, a shift of position). A work shift is a set continuous number of hours that someone works: night shift.

Shifting describes movement from one position, state, or condition to another. Gears shift in a car, weight shifts from foot to foot, blame shifts to someone else. {The shifting sands made walking difficult.} {Public opinion is shifting on the issue.} The word suggests continuous or repeated change rather than a single transition.

Shifts are changes in position, direction, or state. A shift in the wind, a shift in policy, a shift in someone's mood. To shift is to move something or change its position: {She shifted her weight from one foot to the other}. In driving, you shift gears. A shift is also a scheduled work period: {the night shift}, {I'm working a double shift}. As a garment, a shift is a simple, loose-fitting dress.

Shifty describes someone who seems untrustworthy or evasive—the kind of person whose eyes dart around, who won't give a straight answer. A shifty {look} or shifty {behavior} suggests deception or hidden motives: {He seemed shifty, always glancing toward the exit}. The word implies constant small movements, as if ready to dodge or slip away.

A shill is someone who pretends to be an independent supporter but is secretly working for the person or thing they're promoting. The word originated in carnival and gambling contexts—a shill would pose as a winning player to lure others into a rigged game. Now it applies broadly to covert promotion: {The reviewer turned out to be a shill for the company}. As a verb, to shill is to promote something while hiding your connection to it.

Shills are people who pose as enthusiastic customers or supporters while secretly working for the seller or cause they're promoting. The term comes from carnival and gambling culture, where shills would pretend to win games or place bets to draw in marks. Now it applies broadly to fake endorsers, paid reviewers, or anyone feigning grassroots enthusiasm: {The comment section was full of obvious shills}. To shill is to act as one: {shilling for the pharmaceutical industry}.

Shimmer describes a soft, wavering light—the kind that seems to tremble or ripple rather than shine steadily. Water shimmers in sunlight, heat shimmers off pavement, fabric shimmers when light catches it at changing angles. The word suggests gentle luminosity with movement: {The lake shimmered in the moonlight}. As a noun, a shimmer is this quality of light itself.

Shimmering describes a soft, wavering light—the quality of something that glints or gleams with a trembling radiance: {shimmering water}, {shimmering silk}, {the shimmering heat rising from the pavement}. The effect suggests movement and delicacy, light that shifts rather than holds steady.

Shimmers is the plural of shimmer—a soft, wavering light or gleam: {The shimmers on the lake made it hard to see the far shore}. As a verb, shimmers means to shine with such a light: {Heat shimmers above the pavement}. The word suggests gentle, trembling luminosity rather than steady brightness.

A shimmy is a rapid side-to-side shaking movement. The dance shimmy—popularized in 1920s jazz clubs—involves vibrating the shoulders or hips: {She did a little shimmy on the dance floor}. Mechanical shimmy is unwanted vibration, especially in wheels or steering: {The car developed a shimmy at high speeds}. To shimmy is to move with such motion, or to edge somewhere by wriggling: {He shimmied up the drainpipe}.

Shimmying is moving with a rapid side-to-side vibration or wiggle. The word usually describes a dancer's shoulder-shaking movement or the way someone squeezes through a tight space: {She was shimmying through the crowd}, {shimmying up a drainpipe}. Cars shimmy when wheels vibrate at speed, suggesting mechanical trouble.

The shin is the front of the leg between the knee and ankle, or the bone (tibia) that runs along it. This area is notably sensitive to impact—a kicked shin hurts disproportionately. To shin up something is to climb it using arms and legs: {He shinned up the drainpipe}. A shin of beef is a cut from the lower leg.

A shindig is a lively party or celebration, typically informal and festive: {We're throwing a shindig for her birthday}. The word suggests dancing, music, and general revelry rather than a quiet gathering. It's casual and slightly old-fashioned, often used with affection for a good time.

Shine is what the sun does – emit light. If you shine a light on something, you direct light at it. If someone shines, they perform or act admirably. When a thing shines, it gives off light or has a bright appearance. If you shine an object, you polish it. A shine is an instance of this kind of shining, or the result of it: There was a beautiful shine on the new car. If you take a shine to someone, you begin to like them.

A shiner is a black eye—a bruise around the eye socket from a blow to the face: {He came home from the fight with a shiner}. The word likely comes from the discolored skin's unnatural shine. Shiners are also small silvery freshwater fish, named for their reflective scales.

A shingle is a flat piece of material—wood, slate, or asphalt—used in overlapping rows to cover roofs and walls. The verb means to apply such covering: {We shingled the roof last summer}. A shingle is also a small signboard, especially for a professional practice: {hang out your shingle}. Separately, shingle refers to coarse gravel on a beach: {walking across the shingle to the water}.

Shingles is a painful viral infection causing a blistering rash, typically appearing as a band or strip on one side of the body. It's caused by reactivation of the chickenpox virus, which lies dormant in nerve tissue and can emerge decades later, usually in older adults or those with weakened immune systems: {My father developed shingles at seventy}. The name comes from a Latin word meaning belt or girdle, describing how the rash wraps around the torso.

Shining describes something that gives off or reflects light: {the shining sun}, {shining eyes}. Extended uses suggest brightness of a different kind—excellence or promise: a {shining example}, a {shining moment in her career}. The phrase {shining armor} evokes the knight who rescues someone from difficulty.

Shins are the front parts of the legs between the knees and ankles, where bone lies close beneath the skin. The shinbone (tibia) is vulnerable to painful impact: {She banged her shins on the coffee table}. To shin up something is to climb it by gripping with arms and legs: {He shinned up the drainpipe}.

Shiny describes surfaces that reflect light—polished metal, glossy paint, wet pavement. The word often suggests newness or careful maintenance: {a shiny new car}, {shiny shoes}. In informal use, shiny things attract attention like objects that catch the eye: {I got distracted by something shiny}. The word can be mildly dismissive, implying superficial appeal over substance.

A ship is a large boat that typically carries cargo; many kinds of ships can be characterized by preceding noun: cruise ship, pirate ship. From this meaning, the verb ship arose to denote the carrying of things by ship. The verb meaning is now generalized to characterize the movement of goods by any means: We ship packages via UPS. As an intransitive verb, ship means to be sent: Your order will ship next week. The figurative expression jump ship is inspired by literal abandoning of a ship but refers to any sudden act of leaving an organization: Several middle managers have jumped ship.

A shipmate is a fellow sailor—someone who serves on the same vessel. The term carries connotations of shared hardship and camaraderie forged through close quarters and common purpose: {He stayed in touch with his old shipmates from the Navy}. Used figuratively for any close companion in a difficult endeavor.

Shipmates are fellow crew members aboard the same vessel. The term carries connotations of camaraderie forged through shared work and close quarters at sea: {He stayed in touch with his old shipmates for decades}. Used as a form of address, especially in naval contexts: {Listen up, shipmates}.

A shipment is a quantity of goods sent together from one place to another, typically as part of a commercial transaction. The word covers both the act of shipping and the goods themselves: {We're expecting a shipment of parts next week}. Shipments may travel by truck, rail, ship, or air, and the term applies whether the cargo fills a single box or an entire container. When something is delayed {in shipment}, it hasn't yet arrived at its destination.

Shipped is the past tense of ship, meaning sent or transported: {The package shipped yesterday}. In internet and fan culture, shipped means paired romantically—from "relationship": {I've shipped them since season one}. When something has shipped, it's been released or finalized: {The software shipped with bugs}.

A shipper is a person or company that sends goods from one place to another, or one that arranges such transport: {The shipper is responsible for packaging}. In internet fandom, a shipper is someone who supports a romantic pairing between characters—real or fictional—whether or not that relationship exists in the source material: {Harry Potter shippers debated which couples belonged together}.

Shipping is the transport of goods, especially by sea: {international shipping costs}, {shipping and handling}. The word covers the industry, the process, and the vessels themselves: {enemy shipping}. In internet fandom, shipping means supporting a romantic relationship between characters—real or fictional—whether the pairing exists in canon or only in fans' imagination: {I'm shipping those two so hard}.

Ships are large watercraft designed to carry passengers, cargo, or military forces across bodies of water—distinct from smaller boats by their size and ocean-going capability. To ship goods is to transport them, originally by sea but now by any method: {We ship worldwide}. In informal usage, to ship two people is to enthusiastically support a romantic pairing between them, real or fictional: {I've shipped them since season one}. A relationship may describe a close bond: {their friendship}.

Shipshape means neat, tidy, and in good order—everything properly arranged and ready for use. The standard comes from nautical discipline, where gear must be secured and organized for safety at sea. {Get this place shipshape before your mother arrives.} Often paired with Bristol fashion, referring to the high standards of that English port.

Shipwreck is the destruction or loss of a ship at sea, typically from storms, collisions, or running aground. The wreckage itself is also called a shipwreck: {Divers explored the shipwreck}. Figuratively, shipwreck describes any ruinous failure: {the shipwreck of his marriage}. To shipwreck is to cause or suffer such destruction: {They were shipwrecked on a deserted island}.

Shipwrecked describes being stranded after a ship is destroyed or disabled at sea. Survivors of such disasters are shipwrecked sailors, cast ashore on islands or left adrift: {The shipwrecked crew survived on coconuts for weeks}. Figuratively, shipwrecked can describe any situation of ruin or abandonment: {shipwrecked dreams}, {shipwrecked by circumstance}.

Shipwrecks is the plural of shipwreck—the destruction or sinking of a ship, or the remains of such a vessel. Shipwrecks lie on ocean floors as archaeological sites and diving destinations. Figuratively, any ruined endeavor can be a shipwreck: {the shipwreck of his political career}. The verb means to cause or suffer such destruction: {They were shipwrecked on a remote island}.

A shipyard is a facility where ships are built, repaired, or dismantled. Large shipyards contain drydocks, cranes, and workshops for constructing vessels from keel to launch. The word combines the nautical with the industrial: {The shipyard employed thousands during the war}. Naval shipyards build military vessels; commercial shipyards handle cargo ships and tankers.

Shipyards are facilities where ships are built and repaired. They combine dry docks, cranes, workshops, and storage areas along waterfronts. Major shipyards construct everything from cargo vessels to naval warships, while smaller ones may specialize in repairs or recreational boats: {The old shipyards along the river have been converted to condominiums}.

A shire is a county in England, particularly in traditional or formal usage. The term survives in county names like Yorkshire, Hampshire, and Lincolnshire. In Britain, {the shires} refers to rural hunting country in the Midlands, evoking traditional English countryside. Shire also names an administrative district in some Commonwealth countries. A shire horse is a large draft breed originally from the English shires.

A shirt is a garment covering the torso, typically with sleeves and a front opening or pullover design. The word usually means a button-front dress shirt or a casual top like a T-shirt, distinguished from sweaters, jackets, and underwear. To {lose your shirt} is to lose everything in a failed venture. To {keep your shirt on} is to stay calm.

Shirts is the plural of shirt, a garment covering the upper body, typically with sleeves and a front opening or pullover design. The word appears in compounds describing varieties: {dress shirts}, {T-shirts}, {polo shirts}. To {keep your shirt on} is to stay calm. To {lose your shirt} is to lose everything in a bad investment or gamble. To {give the shirt off your back} is to be extremely generous.

Shishkabob is an alternate spelling of shish kebab—chunks of meat and vegetables threaded on a skewer and grilled. The dish originated in the Middle East but has become standard backyard cookout fare: {We threw some shishkabobs on the grill}. The spelling reflects English speakers' phonetic interpretation of the Turkish.

Shishkebab is meat and vegetables threaded onto skewers and grilled, a dish originating in the Middle East. The chunks are typically marinated before cooking: {We made shishkebabs with lamb, peppers, and onions}. Also spelled shish kebab or shish kabob.

Shit is a vulgar term for excrement. As a noun, shit can also mean stuff ({Get your shit together}), nonsense ({Don't give me that shit}), trouble ({He's in deep shit}), nothing ({I don't know shit}), or quality goods ({This is the shit}). As a verb, it means to defecate, but also to deceive ({Are you shitting me?}). To shit oneself is to be terrified. As an exclamation, it expresses frustration, surprise, or dismay. Common expressions include {no shit}, {tough shit}, {holy shit}, {shit happens}, {up shit creek}, and {when the shit hits the fan}.

A shitbox is a car or other vehicle in terrible condition—rusty, unreliable, barely running: {My first car was a shitbox I bought for five hundred bucks}. The term is vulgar but affectionate; people often speak fondly of the shitboxes they've owned, acknowledging both the vehicle's worthlessness and their attachment to it.

Shitfaced is a vulgar adjective meaning extremely drunk: {We got shitfaced and sang karaoke until 2 a.m.} It belongs to a family of crude intoxication terms that combine an expletive with a body part.
Shithead is a vulgar insult for a stupid or contemptible person—someone whose head is full of excrement rather than brains: {Don't be a shithead about this}.

A shitlist is an informal list of people one dislikes, distrusts, or wants to punish: {After that stunt, you're on my shitlist}. The term implies grudge-keeping and future consequences—being on someone's shitlist means they're watching for opportunities to retaliate or deny favors. Often used humorously or hyperbolically.

A shitpost is low-effort online content posted for amusement rather than substance—often deliberately absurd, nonsensical, or provocative. The term spans everything from meaningless spam to surreal humor that rewards those in on the joke. To shitpost is to produce such content: {He spent the evening shitposting on Discord}. The practice has its own ironic subculture where quality emerges from apparent carelessness.

Shitposts are low-effort online content posted for amusement rather than substance—deliberately absurd, nonsensical, or provocative material meant to entertain or annoy rather than inform. The term emerged from internet culture where users flood forums or social media with intentionally worthless content: {The whole thread devolved into shitposts}. To shitpost is to produce such content, often as a form of ironic humor or trolling.

A shitshow is a situation characterized by chaos, incompetence, or spectacular failure. The term emphasizes not just that something went wrong, but that it descended into visible, often public disorder: {The press conference was a complete shitshow}. Originally military slang, now widespread in casual speech to describe any badly mismanaged event or ongoing disaster.
A shitstorm is a situation of chaos, controversy, or overwhelming trouble: {His comments created a shitstorm on social media}.
Shitty is a vulgar adjective meaning bad, unpleasant, or of poor quality: {I had a shitty day}. {That's a shitty thing to say.}

A shiv is a crude knife or stabbing weapon, typically improvised in prison from available materials—a sharpened toothbrush handle, a filed-down piece of metal. The word carries a strong association with prison violence: {He got shivved in the yard}. Outside prison contexts, shiv appears in crime fiction and slang for any makeshift blade.

Shiver is an involuntary trembling, usually from cold or fear. The body shivers to generate warmth; the mind shivers at what frightens it. {A shiver ran down her spine.} To shiver is to experience this trembling: {She shivered in the cold rain.} The shivers are a bout of shivering, often from illness or dread: {That story gives me the shivers.}

Shivering is the act of trembling or shaking, typically from cold or fear. The body shivers involuntarily to generate warmth through rapid muscle contractions: {She stood shivering in the rain}. Shivering can also accompany fever, shock, or intense emotion: {He was shivering with anticipation}.

Shivers are trembling movements of the body, usually from cold or fear. {A chill ran through her and she felt the shivers}. To shiver is to tremble this way: {He shivered in the doorway, waiting for someone to answer}. The shivers can also be a state of fearful anticipation: {That movie gave me the shivers}. To {shiver your timbers} is nautical slang, now used only in pirate talk.

Shivs are crude knives or stabbing weapons, typically improvised in prisons from available materials—sharpened toothbrushes, filed-down spoons, broken glass bound with tape. The singular shiv can also be a verb: {He got shivved in the yard}. Outside prison contexts, shiv appears in games and fiction for any makeshift blade.

Shlep comes from Yiddish and means to drag or haul something with effort, or to make a tedious journey: {I don't want to shlep all the way downtown for one errand}. As a noun, a shlep is a tiresome trek or a clumsy, slow-moving person. Also spelled schlep.

Shmooze, also spelled schmooze, is a verb meaning to chat in a friendly, often ingratiating way, typically to gain favor or make useful connections. It comes from Yiddish and carries connotations of smooth talk and social maneuvering. {She spent the whole party shmoozing with potential investors.} The noun shmooze refers to such a conversation, and someone skilled at this is a shmoozer.

Shmoozing is engaging in friendly, often self-serving conversation—chatting someone up to build rapport or gain advantage. From Yiddish. The word suggests warmth that may be strategic: {He spent the cocktail hour shmoozing potential investors}. A shmoozer is skilled at this kind of social lubrication. Also spelled schmoozing.

Shock covers a cluster of meanings unified by the idea of sudden, forceful impact. A physical shock is a violent collision or jolt; an electrical shock is current passing through the body. Emotional shock is the stunned state following unexpected news or trauma. In medicine, shock is a dangerous condition where blood pressure drops critically. To shock someone is to disturb or offend them with something unexpected: {The verdict shocked the nation}. A shock of hair is a thick, unruly mass—a different word entirely.

Shocked describes a state of sudden surprise, disbelief, or disturbance. The feeling ranges from mild astonishment to deep emotional distress: {I was shocked to hear about her resignation}, {shocked by the violence in the film}. Someone can be shocked into silence or action. The word often carries moral overtones—{shocked and appalled}—though it's frequently exaggerated for effect: {I'm shocked, shocked to find gambling going on here}.

A shocker is something that shocks—an unexpected event, revelation, or piece of news that startles or disturbs: {The election results were a real shocker}. The word often carries irony, used sarcastically when something is entirely predictable: {He showed up late again—shocker}. In British slang, a shocker is something notably bad or disappointing: {I had an absolute shocker of a day}.

Shocking describes something that causes sudden surprise, dismay, or outrage. A shocking {revelation} upends expectations; shocking {violence} disturbs viewers. The word implies intensity—more than merely surprising, something shocking provokes a visceral reaction. It can also describe things meant to provoke: {shock value}, {shock jock}. Used loosely, shocking expresses mild disapproval: {The prices were shocking}.

Shocks are sudden, jarring impacts—physical or emotional. A car's shocks (short for shock absorbers) cushion against road impact. Electric shocks jolt the body. Emotional shocks arrive as unexpected news: {The diagnosis came as a shock}. To shock is to disturb or offend: {Her language shocked the guests}. Shock can also describe a thick mass of hair: {a shock of white hair}.

A shockwave is a wave of intense pressure that moves through a medium faster than the speed of sound, typically caused by an explosion or supersonic object. The term extends to any sudden, powerful disturbance that spreads outward: {The assassination sent shockwaves through the political establishment}. Also spelled as two words: shock wave.

Shockwaves are intense pressure disturbances that travel through a medium—air, water, or earth—faster than the speed of sound. Explosions and supersonic aircraft produce literal shockwaves. Figuratively, shockwaves describe the spreading impact of dramatic events: {The scandal sent shockwaves through the industry}. Also written as two words: shock waves.

Shoddy describes something poorly made or of inferior quality: {shoddy construction}, {shoddy workmanship}. The word often implies cutting corners or lack of care rather than honest limitation. Shoddy treatment is careless or disrespectful. Originally, shoddy was a noun for cheap fabric made from recycled wool—the material's poor quality gave rise to the adjective.

A shoe is a covering for the foot, typically with a stiff sole and flexible upper. Shoes protect feet from terrain and weather while signaling style, status, or occupation: {running shoes}, {dress shoes}, {work shoes}. To be {in someone's shoes} is to be in their situation. A horseshoe is also called a shoe. To shoe a horse is to fit it with these protective metal plates. {If the shoe fits, wear it} means accept a criticism that applies to you.

A shoebox is a cardboard box designed to hold a pair of shoes. Because shoeboxes are sturdy, uniform, and accumulate in closets, they become storage containers for photographs, letters, receipts, and small keepsakes: {I found the old letters in a shoebox in the attic}. As an adjective, shoebox describes cramped spaces: {a shoebox apartment}.

A shoehorn is a curved implement, typically made of plastic, metal, or horn, that helps you slip your heel into a shoe without crushing the back. The verb shoehorn means to force something into a tight space or situation where it doesn't naturally fit: {They shoehorned three more passengers into the already crowded van}. The figurative use often implies awkwardness or strain: {The director shoehorned a romance subplot into an already bloated script}.

Shoehorning is forcing something into a space or category where it doesn't quite fit. The image comes from the tool used to squeeze a foot into a tight shoe. You might shoehorn a meeting into an already packed schedule, or shoehorn an irrelevant point into an argument: {He kept shoehorning references to his book into every conversation}. The word implies awkwardness or strain—the thing being inserted doesn't belong naturally.

A shoelace is a cord or string threaded through eyelets to fasten a shoe snugly to the foot. Learning to tie shoelaces is a childhood milestone. {Your shoelace is untied.} To do something {on a shoestring} suggests operating with minimal resources—a shoestring being even less substantial than a proper lace.

Shoelaces are the cords threaded through eyelets to secure shoes to feet. They're tied in a bow for easy removal. {Your shoelaces are untied.} Learning to tie shoelaces is a childhood milestone. Velcro and slip-ons have displaced laces on some footwear, but laced shoes remain standard for athletic and formal wear.

A shoemaker is a person who makes or repairs shoes. The trade is ancient, and the term persists even as mass production has largely replaced handcrafting: {The old shoemaker worked from a tiny shop downtown}. A cobbler is similar, though traditionally cobblers only repaired shoes while shoemakers made them.

Shoes are coverings for the feet, typically with a sturdy sole and an upper portion. The word encompasses everything from sneakers to dress shoes to boots. To be {in someone's shoes} is to imagine their situation. {If the shoe fits, wear it} means accept a criticism that applies to you. To {wait for the other shoe to drop} is to anticipate an inevitable consequence.

A shoeshine is the act of polishing shoes, or the polished appearance itself: {He stopped for a shoeshine before the interview}. A shoeshine boy or shoeshine man offers the service, typically from a sidewalk stand. The word can modify other nouns: {shoeshine kit}, {shoeshine stand}.
