Sleepy describes the state of wanting or needing sleep: {I'm getting sleepy}. A sleepy {town} or sleepy {village} is quiet and uneventful, as if drowsing. Sleepy can also mean sluggish or slow-moving: {a sleepy economy}. The word suggests peaceful drowsiness rather than exhaustion.

A sleepyhead is someone who is drowsy or has just woken up, used affectionately rather than critically: {Come on, sleepyhead, breakfast is ready}. The term is typically directed at children or loved ones who are slow to wake or reluctant to get out of bed.

Sleet is precipitation that falls as ice pellets—rain that freezes before hitting the ground, or snow that partially melts and refreezes. It creates a distinctive rattling sound on windows and surfaces: {The forecast calls for sleet turning to snow overnight}. Sleet makes roads treacherous, coating them with ice. As a verb, to sleet means to fall as sleet: {It sleeted all morning}.

A sleeve is the part of a garment that covers the arm, from shoulder to wrist or somewhere in between. Sleeves vary in length and style: {short sleeves}, {long sleeves}, {rolled-up sleeves}. A sleeve is also a protective covering shaped like a tube: a record sleeve, a cable sleeve. To have something {up your sleeve} is to hold it in reserve as a secret advantage. To {wear your heart on your sleeve} is to display emotions openly.

Sleeves are the parts of a garment that cover the arms, from shoulder to wrist or partway. Styles vary widely: long sleeves, short sleeves, cap sleeves, no sleeves at all. To have something {up your sleeve} is to hold it in reserve, hidden from others. To {roll up your sleeves} is to prepare for work. To {wear your heart on your sleeve} is to display emotions openly.

A sleigh is a vehicle on runners designed to travel over snow or ice, typically pulled by horses or reindeer. The word evokes winter scenes—{a one-horse open sleigh}, Santa's flying sleigh. To sleigh is to travel by sleigh, though the verb is rare. {We went sleighing through the countryside.}

Sleighbells are small metal bells attached to a horse's harness, traditionally used on sleighs in winter. They jingle as the horse moves, warning pedestrians and adding festive charm. The sound is strongly associated with Christmas and winter holidays: {Hear those sleighbells jingling}. Also spelled as two words: sleigh bells.

Slender describes something thin relative to its length or height: a slender {waist}, slender {fingers}, a slender {tree}. The word carries a graceful connotation that thin or skinny may lack. Extended uses emphasize smallness or insufficiency: slender {means}, slender {hopes}, a slender {margin of victory}. {The evidence was slender at best.}

Slept is the past tense and past participle of sleep. {I slept poorly last night}. {She had slept through the alarm}. To have {slept with} someone is to have had sex with them. To have {slept on} a decision is to have delayed it overnight: {I slept on it and decided to accept the offer}.

A sleuth is a detective or someone who investigates mysteries. The word carries a slightly playful or literary tone—you're more likely to encounter it in cozy mysteries than police reports: {an amateur sleuth}, {The reporter sleuthed out the truth}. To sleuth is to investigate or track down information.

Sleuthing is detective work—investigating, gathering clues, following leads. The term comes from sleuth, itself shortened from sleuthhound, a tracking dog. Most sleuthing today is amateur or figurative: {After some sleuthing, I found out who had been taking my lunch from the office fridge}.

Sleuths are detectives or investigators, whether professional or amateur. The word carries a slightly literary or playful tone, often evoking fictional investigators: {The amateur sleuths pieced together the clues}. As a verb, to sleuth is to investigate: {She sleuthed around until she found the answer}.

Slew has two distinct origins. One is the past tense of slay: {He slew the dragon}. The other means a large quantity: {a whole slew of problems}, {slews of paperwork}. This informal sense suggests an overwhelming or unmanageable number. As a verb, to slew (or slue) means to turn or swing sideways: {The car slewed across the icy road}.

To slice something is to cut it, with the result that a portion (often small or thin) is removed (slice cake, slice pie, slice salami). A slice is an instance of doing this, or the resulting piece (slice of bacon). In sports such as tennis or golf, to slice suggests a stroke that results in backspin on the ball. A slice in these and other sports is the path of a ball as it curves in the direction of the side from which it was hit.

Slick describes something smooth and glossy, often with a coating that reduces friction: {slick with oil}, {rain-slicked streets}. The word extends to polished performance—a slick presentation is impressively smooth, though perhaps superficially so. A slick operator is clever and persuasive but not entirely trustworthy. As a noun, a slick is a film of oil on water. To slick hair is to smooth it down, often with product: {He slicked his hair back}.

Slid is the past tense and past participle of slide. Something that slid moved smoothly across a surface: {The glass slid off the table}. The word covers both deliberate and accidental motion: {She slid into the booth} describes choosing a seat, while {The car slid on ice} suggests loss of control.

Slide is about smooth movement on a surface with little friction, the way a car slides on ice or a baseball runner slides into a base. By extension, to slide is to move easily through something, to move without others noticing, or to become gradually worse. If you let something slide, you ignore its worsening condition. A slide is an instance of sliding. It is also a piece of playground equipment on which children can slide.

A slider is something that slides. In baseball, it's a pitch that breaks sharply to one side as it reaches the plate. A slider is also a small hamburger, typically two or three inches across, served as an appetizer or in multiples: {We ordered a plate of sliders}. In user interfaces, a slider is a control you drag along a track to adjust a value: {Move the slider to increase brightness}.

Sliders are small hamburgers, typically two to three inches across, served as appetizers or in multiples as a main course. The name suggests they slide down easily. The term originated with White Castle's miniature burgers but now applies to any small sandwich served this way: {We ordered a plate of sliders to share}. In other contexts, a slider is a baseball pitch that breaks laterally, or an interface element—a control you drag along a track to adjust values like volume or brightness.

Slides are smooth, sloped surfaces designed for descending, typically found on playgrounds where children climb up and slide down. The word extends to any controlled descent or lateral movement: a baseball player slides into base, stock prices slide downward, and things slide into place when they fit smoothly. Slides are also individual frames in a presentation, a usage that persists from the era of photographic transparencies projected onto screens. As footwear, slides are backless sandals you slip into without fastening. {She kicked off her slides at the door.}

A slideshow is a sequential presentation of images, text, or other visual content displayed one frame at a time. Originally the term described projected photographic slides shown in order, often accompanied by narration at family gatherings or educational lectures. Now slideshows are almost entirely digital, created with presentation software for business meetings, classrooms, or personal photo collections. {She put together a slideshow of vacation photos for the reunion.}

Sliding describes smooth, continuous movement across a surface. A child goes sliding down a hill; a drawer slides open. The word often implies effortlessness or gradual change: a sliding {scale} adjusts based on variables, sliding {doors} move horizontally rather than swinging. {Prices have been sliding all year} suggests steady decline. To let something slide is to neglect it deliberately.

Slight describes something small in degree or importance: a slight {improvement}, a slight {chance}, a {slight delay}. A slight person has a slender, delicate build. To slight someone is to treat them with disrespect or indifference, often by ignoring them: {She felt slighted when they didn't invite her}. A slight is such an act of disrespect: {He never forgot the slight}.

Slighted describes feeling disrespected or snubbed, typically through being overlooked or treated as unimportant: {She felt slighted when they didn't invite her to the meeting}. The slight needn't be intentional—someone can feel slighted by an innocent oversight. The word suggests wounded pride more than deep offense.

Slights are small acts of disrespect or dismissiveness—being overlooked, snubbed, or treated as unimportant. The word captures offenses that may seem minor but accumulate: {She remembered every slight from her childhood}. As a verb, to slight someone is to treat them with such casual disregard: {He felt slighted when they didn't invite him}.

Slim describes something narrow or slight in width or build: a slim {figure}, a slim {volume}. It extends to things that are barely sufficient or unlikely: slim {chances}, a slim {margin of victory}, slim {pickings}. To slim or slim down is to lose weight or reduce: {She's been slimming down for the wedding}. {The company slimmed its workforce}.

Slime is a viscous, slippery substance that's typically unpleasant—think the trail left by a slug or the gunk coating a neglected drain. The word carries strong connotations of disgust, which is why calling someone a slime or saying they're slimy suggests they're morally repulsive or untrustworthy. As a verb, to slime is to coat with slime or, figuratively, to damage someone's reputation through underhanded tactics. In recent years, slime has also become a popular children's craft material—a stretchy, squeezable goo made from glue and other household ingredients.

A slimeball is a despicable or untrustworthy person, someone whose behavior strikes others as slimy—underhanded, sleazy, or morally repugnant. The term evokes something disgusting to the touch, and that visceral quality carries into its figurative use. {Her ex-boyfriend turned out to be a total slimeball.} It's informal and always derogatory.

Slimy describes something covered with or resembling slime—wet, slippery, and slightly viscous: {slimy seaweed}, {a slimy slug}. The texture provokes disgust, which carries into the figurative sense: a slimy person is repulsively ingratiating or dishonest, someone who makes you feel like you need a shower after dealing with them.

A sling is a device for hurling stones—a pouch on two cords, swung to build momentum. David killed Goliath with one. The word extends to any strap or band that supports, suspends, or carries: a rifle sling, an arm sling for injuries, a baby sling. To sling is to throw casually or carelessly: {She slung her bag over her shoulder}. To {sling hash} is to work as a short-order cook. A sling is also a cocktail of spirits, sugar, and citrus: {a Singapore sling}.

A slingshot is a Y-shaped device with an elastic band stretched between the prongs, used to launch small projectiles like stones. Children's toy and occasional hunting tool. In American English, slingshot also describes the maneuver of using a planet's gravity to accelerate a spacecraft: {The probe used Jupiter for a slingshot toward Saturn}. As a verb, to slingshot is to accelerate rapidly, often by releasing stored energy: {The car slingshoted past the competition}.

Slink means to move quietly and furtively, typically to avoid notice or because of shame or guilt: {The cat slinked through the fence}; {He slinked away after the confrontation}. The word suggests sneaky, stealthy movement—someone who slinks is trying not to be seen. As an adjective, slink describes a prematurely born calf, and by extension, the soft leather made from its hide.

Slinkies is the plural of Slinky, a coiled spring toy that "walks" down stairs through a wave-like motion. The word also describes things with slinky qualities—sinuous, sleek, or seductively smooth: {She tried on several slinkies before settling on a red dress for the party}.

Slinky describes movement that is sinuous, graceful, and suggestively smooth—often with sexual overtones. A slinky {dress} clings to the body and flows with movement. A slinky {walk} suggests seductive confidence. The word evokes sleekness and fluidity: {She made a slinky entrance in black silk}. (Capitalized Slinky is the toy.)

Slip has substantial overlap in meaning with slide, with the added feature that slip often suggests things that are accidental or undesirable. You can slip and fall on ice; time (or people) can slip away quickly without you noticing them. If something slips your mind, you forget it, often regrettably. A slip is an instance of slipping, and several other things, such as a small piece of paper; a mistake in speech or writing; a development for the worse; and a woman’s undergarment, worn like a dress or skirt.

A slipper is a soft, lightweight shoe worn indoors for comfort. Slippers typically slide on easily without laces or buckles: {She padded around the house in her slippers}. The word can also describe a formal shoe for dancing or evening wear, though this usage is old-fashioned.

Slippers are soft, lightweight footwear worn indoors for comfort and warmth. They typically slide on easily and have flexible soles unsuitable for outdoor use. The term covers everything from plush bedroom slippers to ballet slippers worn for dance. {She padded around the house in her slippers.}

Slippery describes surfaces that are smooth, wet, or otherwise difficult to grip or stand on without sliding: {The roads are slippery after the rain}. By extension, slippery characterizes things that are hard to hold onto or pin down—an eel is slippery, but so is a slippery concept that resists clear definition. A slippery person is evasive and untrustworthy, hard to hold accountable. The slippery slope is a rhetorical warning that one step will inevitably lead to worse ones.

Slipping is the present participle of slip, covering movement without firm grip or control. Something slipping is sliding unintentionally: {The glass was slipping from her hands}. Standards or performance that are slipping are declining: {His grades have been slipping lately}. Time slipping away passes quickly or unnoticed. If something is slipping your mind, you're forgetting it.

A slipstream is the area of reduced air pressure behind a moving vehicle or object, where following closely requires less effort. Cyclists and race car drivers draft in a competitor's slipstream to conserve energy before overtaking. The verb means to follow in this zone: {She slipstreamed the lead car until the final lap}. Figuratively, to ride in someone's slipstream is to benefit from their trailblazing effort.

Slither is to move with a smooth, twisting, sliding motion—the way a snake travels across ground. The word suggests something slightly unsettling or sinister: {The snake slithered through the grass}. By extension, people slither when they move in a sneaky or insinuating way: {He slithered out of the room before anyone noticed}.

Slithering describes smooth, gliding movement close to a surface, like a snake's locomotion. The word suggests sinuous, side-to-side motion without legs: {A snake came slithering through the grass}. It can apply to anything moving with similar fluid, slightly unsettling grace: {The rope slithered off the dock into the water}.

Slithers is the verb slither in the third person singular. To slither is to move with a smooth, twisting motion, like a snake sliding across ground: {The python slithers through the grass}. The word suggests something sinuous and often unsettling. People slither when they move sneakily or squeeze through tight spaces: {He slithered out the back door before anyone noticed}.

A sliver is a thin, narrow piece cut or broken from something larger: {a sliver of glass}, {a sliver of cake}. The word suggests sharpness or delicacy—wood slivers can pierce skin, while a sliver of moon is the thinnest visible crescent. To sliver is to cut into such pieces. A sliver of something abstract is a small portion: {a sliver of hope}.

Slivers are thin, narrow pieces cut or broken from something larger. A sliver of wood might lodge painfully under skin; a sliver of glass could cut a finger. The word extends to small portions generally: {a sliver of cake}, {a sliver of hope}. To sliver is to cut into such pieces: {She slivered almonds for the salad}.

A slob is a person who is messy, lazy, or uncouth—someone who neglects personal grooming or keeps their living space in disorder: {He's such a slob, there are pizza boxes everywhere}. The word carries mild contempt, suggesting someone who has let standards slip rather than someone truly offensive.

Slobber is saliva that drips or runs from the mouth. Babies slobber, as do certain dog breeds. To slobber is to drool uncontrollably or to let saliva escape while eating or sleeping: {The baby slobbered all over his bib}. Figuratively, to slobber over something is to show excessive, undignified enthusiasm: {Critics slobbered over the director's latest film}.

Slobs are people who are messy, lazy, or lacking in personal standards. The word suggests someone indifferent to cleanliness or appearance: {The apartment looked like slobs lived there}. A slob may also be slovenly in habits or manners more broadly: {Don't be such a slob—use a napkin}.

Slog is an informal noun or verb that connotes hard, tedious work. Something described as a slog implies that it requires effort, patience, and tolerance: Living in the Arctic is a hard slog for a Southern California boy. If you slog through or slog your way through something, you persist until it is finished, despite the effort: For the last 200 yards we had to slog our way through loose gravel.

A slogan is a short, memorable phrase used to promote a product, cause, or idea. Advertising slogans aim to stick in the mind: {Just Do It}, {I'm Lovin' It}. Political slogans rally support or crystallize a position: {Make America Great Again}, {Yes We Can}. The term can carry a dismissive edge—calling something "just a slogan" suggests empty rhetoric over substance.

Slogans is the plural of slogan—a short, memorable phrase used to promote a product, cause, or idea. Advertising slogans aim to stick in the mind: {Just Do It}, {I'm Lovin' It}. Political slogans rally supporters: {Yes We Can}, {Make America Great Again}. The best slogans compress complex appeals into a few punchy words; the worst become empty clichés.

Slogging is hard, steady, often tedious work or travel. The word suggests persistence through difficulty rather than speed or grace: {After hours of slogging through the mud, we reached camp}. In cricket and boxing, slogging means hitting hard and wildly. The figurative sense dominates: {slogging through paperwork}, {slogging away at a novel}.

Slop is liquid waste or spilled mess—watery food, kitchen scraps fed to pigs, or any unappetizing semi-liquid substance. The verb means to spill carelessly: {Water slopped over the edge of the bucket}. Slop extends to anything carelessly made or of low quality: {The movie was pure slop}. Slops, in the plural, are cheap ready-made clothing or a sailor's loose trousers.

A slope is a surface that lies at an angle rather than flat or level, like the slope of a hill or a roof. The word also denotes the degree of such an incline, measured as a ratio of vertical rise to horizontal run: {The slope of the driveway made it treacherous in winter.} In mathematics, slope describes the steepness of a line on a graph. As a verb, slope means to incline or slant in a particular direction. The plural slopes often refers specifically to ski hills: {We hit the slopes every weekend in January.}

Slopes is an ethnic slur for people of East Asian descent, derived from the perceived shape of their eyes. The term is offensive and dates mainly from American military conflicts in Asia. {The platoon used slurs like slopes and gooks.}

Sloppy describes something messy, careless, or lacking precision. A sloppy room is untidy; sloppy work shows insufficient attention to detail. Sloppy food is wet and unappetizing: {sloppy joe}. Sloppy weather is rainy or muddy. Sloppy clothing is loose and baggy. A sloppy kiss is wet and enthusiastic. {Don't get sloppy with the details.}

Sloshed is informal for drunk, typically quite drunk rather than merely tipsy: {We got absolutely sloshed at the wedding reception}. The word evokes liquid sloshing around, as if the person were a container of alcohol. British English favors it slightly more than American.

A slot is an opening that is probably wider than a slit, though the words are unrelated. When time is involved, a slot is a fixed period of time among others: I’ll fit your appointment into the three o’clock slot. A slot may also be a position or job (among others) in an institution: We have an open slot for a programmer. Slot machines are sometimes called slots. To slot something is to fit it into a slot, or provide a slot for it: I’ll slot you for 4-5 p.m.

Sloth is disinclination to action or labor—laziness elevated to a defining trait. It's one of the seven deadly sins, suggesting spiritual torpor rather than mere idleness: {His sloth kept him from achieving anything meaningful}. A sloth is also a slow-moving arboreal mammal of Central and South America, named for its unhurried movements and long periods of rest.

Sloths, mammals that live in the treetops of Central and South America, sleep a lot and move slowly. They have long arms and claws, and move around upside down. In language, sloth is laziness or a lack of effort.

Slots are narrow openings or positions designed to receive something. A mail slot accepts letters; a time slot accommodates an appointment. Slot machines, often called simply slots, are casino gambling devices: {She lost two hundred dollars playing slots}. To slot something is to place it into position: {They slotted the new player into the lineup}.

Slouch is a drooping, relaxed posture—shoulders rounded, spine curved, head forward. To slouch is to stand, sit, or walk this way: {Don't slouch at the dinner table}. The word carries connotations of laziness or poor discipline. A slouch can also mean someone lacking skill or competence, but almost always in the negative: {She's no slouch at chess}.

Slow means not fast—taking more time than usual or expected. A slow {walk}, a slow {response}, a slow {learner}. Traffic moves slowly; a watch runs slow when it loses time. To slow or slow down is to reduce speed: {Slow down, you're driving too fast}. Figuratively, someone who is slow may be dim-witted, and a slow {day} lacks activity. {Slow burn} describes anger that builds gradually.

A slowdown is a reduction in speed, pace, or activity. Economic slowdowns mean reduced growth or productivity: {The housing market slowdown affected construction jobs}. A work slowdown is a labor action where employees deliberately reduce their pace without striking outright. Traffic slowdowns occur when congestion forces vehicles to crawl.

A slowpoke is a person who moves, works, or acts slowly—usually said with mild impatience or affection: {Hurry up, slowpoke!} The term is informal and often playful, common in American English. British English prefers slowcoach.

Sludge is thick, soft, wet matter—mud, sediment, or industrial waste with a similar consistency. Sewage treatment produces sludge. Oil sludge accumulates in engines. The word suggests something unpleasant and difficult to deal with: {wading through bureaucratic sludge}. As a music genre, sludge (or sludge metal) combines doom metal's slow heaviness with hardcore punk's aggression.

S-l-u-g represents some unrelated words. A slug is a small creature like a snail without a shell that lives in forests and gardens; a piece of metal shaped like a coin that is used deceitfully in machines that accept coins; and a quantity of liquid swallowed at once (slug of orange juice). A slug is a noun and verb for a violent blow with the fist. A boxer might slug his opponent in the jaw or deliver a slug to his jaw.

A slugfest is a fierce, prolonged contest characterized by heavy blows exchanged between opponents. The term originated in boxing to describe fights where both fighters trade punches relentlessly rather than employing defensive strategy, but it extends readily to any brutal competition: {The playoff game turned into a 12-9 slugfest}. Baseball uses it specifically for high-scoring games with lots of hits. The word emphasizes mutual aggression and endurance over finesse.

A slugger is someone who hits hard—originally a boxer known for powerful punches, now most often a baseball player who hits for power rather than average. The term emphasizes brute force over finesse: {He's not fast, but he's a slugger who can clear the fences}. Informally, a slugger is anyone who fights or competes aggressively.

Sluggish means slow-moving or lacking energy. A sluggish economy grows at a disappointing pace. A sluggish stream barely flows. Someone feeling sluggish after a heavy meal moves with reluctance: {I felt sluggish all afternoon}. The word suggests not just slowness but a heaviness or resistance to motion—like a slug dragging itself along.

Slugs are soft-bodied mollusks resembling snails without shells, often found in gardens where they eat plants. A slug is also a bullet or a counterfeit coin used in vending machines. In printing, a slug is a line of type cast as one piece. To slug someone is to punch them hard: {He slugged the guy right in the jaw}. A slug of whiskey is a mouthful swallowed at once.

A slum is a densely populated urban area marked by poverty, substandard housing, and inadequate sanitation. The word often appears in the plural: {the slums of Mumbai}, {growing up in the slums}. To slum or go slumming is to visit places or engage in activities considered beneath one's usual social standing, often with condescending curiosity: {slumming it at a dive bar}.

Slumber is a somewhat literary or gentle word for sleep, often suggesting peaceful, undisturbed rest. It works as both noun and verb: {The baby fell into a deep slumber}; {He slumbered through the afternoon}. Slumber carries a softer connotation than sleep, making it common in children's contexts like slumber parties—overnight gatherings where the actual sleeping is often minimal. Something dormant or inactive can also be said to slumber: {ancient volcanoes that slumber for centuries}.

Slumbering means sleeping, especially peacefully or for a long time. The word carries a gentler, more literary quality than sleeping: {the slumbering child}, {a slumbering village}. Figuratively, something slumbering lies dormant or inactive, waiting to be awakened: {slumbering resentments}, {a slumbering volcano}.

A slumlord is a landlord who owns rundown rental properties, typically in poor urban neighborhoods, and neglects maintenance while extracting maximum rent from tenants who have few housing alternatives. The term is always pejorative, implying exploitation of vulnerable people: {The slumlord hadn't fixed the heating in years}.

Slumlords are landlords who own and rent out substandard housing, typically in poor urban neighborhoods, while neglecting maintenance and repairs. The term is always derogatory, implying someone who profits from desperate tenants while letting properties deteriorate: {The slumlords ignored the broken heating and rat infestations}. The singular is slumlord.

Slumming is visiting places or associating with people considered beneath one's social standing, typically for entertainment or curiosity. The term carries condescension—someone slumming treats lower-status environments as novelty rather than reality: {She's just slumming with us until her trust fund kicks in}. Often used self-deprecatingly: {I'm slumming it at the budget hotel tonight}.

Slump describes a sudden or prolonged drop—in posture, performance, or value. To slump is to sink heavily or collapse: {She slumped into the chair}. A slump in sales or housing prices is a decline. Athletes go through slumps when their performance suffers: {He's been in a batting slump all season}. The word suggests heaviness and defeat.

Slumped describes a posture of collapse or defeat—shoulders dropped, body sagging. A person slumps in a chair from exhaustion or dejection: {He sat slumped over his desk}. Markets or sales that have slumped have fallen sharply. A slumped figure suggests someone overcome by fatigue, disappointment, or despair.

Slumps is the plural noun and third-person singular verb form of slump. A slump is a period of decline or poor performance, whether in economics {the housing slump}, sports {a batting slump}, or personal energy. The verb describes sudden dropping or sagging: {She slumped into the chair after a long day}. Physical slumping involves the body collapsing or slouching; figurative slumping involves declining numbers or diminished output.

Slums is the plural of slum—an overcrowded urban area marked by poverty and deteriorating housing. The word often implies neglect by authorities and lack of basic services. To slum or go slumming is to visit places considered beneath one's social station, often for entertainment or curiosity: {rich kids slumming in dive bars}.

A slur is an insulting word or phrase that disparages a group—racial slurs, ethnic slurs, homophobic slurs. The word also means a damaging insinuation: {a slur on his reputation}. To slur is to speak indistinctly, running sounds together: {She was slurring her words}. In music, a slur is a curved line connecting notes to be played smoothly without separation.

Slurp is both the sound and the act of drinking or eating something noisily, drawing liquid into the mouth with an audible sucking sound. It suggests enthusiasm or lack of table manners, depending on context: {He slurped his soup while reading the paper}. The word imitates the sound it describes. In computing, slurp means to read an entire file into memory at once rather than processing it incrementally.

Slurping is the act of eating or drinking noisily, drawing liquid into the mouth with a sucking sound: {Stop slurping your soup}. The sound itself can also be called a slurp. What's considered rude in Western dining may be acceptable or even complimentary elsewhere—slurping noodles in Japan signals enjoyment.

Slurred describes speech that is indistinct, with sounds running together and words poorly articulated. The most common cause is intoxication: {His slurred words betrayed how much he'd drunk}. Slurred speech also results from fatigue, medication, stroke, or neurological conditions. In music, slurred notes are played smoothly connected, without separation between them.

Slurs are words used to insult or demean people based on group membership—race, ethnicity, sexuality, disability. The singular slur can mean any disparaging remark: {a slur on his character}. In music, a slur is a curved line connecting notes to be played smoothly without separation. To slur is to pronounce indistinctly, running sounds together: {He was slurring his words after a few drinks}.

Slush is partially melted snow or ice, the wet gray mess that accumulates on sidewalks and roads in winter: {My boots were soaked from walking through the slush}. By extension, slush describes anything similarly soft and watery—cheap sentiment in writing, for instance. A slush fund is money set aside for unofficial or illicit purposes, originally sailors' money from selling cooking grease.

A slushee is a frozen drink made from flavored syrup and crushed or shaved ice, sold at convenience stores and movie theaters. The texture falls between a smoothie and shaved ice—cold enough to give you brain freeze. Also spelled slushie or slushy. Brand names like Slurpee and Icee have become nearly generic.

A slushie is a frozen beverage made from flavored ice crystals, served in a semi-solid state that can be drunk through a straw. Sold at convenience stores and movie theaters, slushies come in bright artificial colors and sweet flavors: {We grabbed cherry slushies at the gas station}. Also spelled slushy.

Slushies are frozen drinks made from flavored ice crystals, served at a consistency between liquid and solid. The texture comes from continuously churning flavored syrup and water as it freezes, creating a drinkable slush. Sold at convenience stores and movie theaters, slushies are sweet, brightly colored, and served with a straw-spoon: {We grabbed slushies at 7-Eleven}. Also spelled slushees.

Slushy describes something resembling slush—partially melted snow or ice mixed with water. A slushy {road} is wet and messy with melting snow. The word extends to anything with that semi-frozen, watery consistency: {slushy ice}, {a slushy drink}. Figuratively, slushy means excessively sentimental: {a slushy romance novel}. As a noun, a slushy is a frozen drink made from flavored ice.

Sly describes someone who is clever in a cunning or deceptive way, often pursuing hidden motives while appearing innocent. A sly {smile} or sly {glance} suggests knowing something others don't. The word can be neutral or admiring when it describes shrewd resourcefulness, but more often implies sneakiness or manipulation. {She gave him a sly wink across the room.} On the sly means secretly or covertly: {He was seeing someone on the sly}.

Smack connects several unrelated words. The most common is the sharp sound of a slap or kiss, and the action itself: {She smacked him across the face}, {He smacked his lips}. To smack of something is to suggest or hint at it: {The proposal smacks of corruption}. Smack is also slang for heroin. A smack can be a small fishing boat. {Smack in the middle} means exactly or directly.

A smackdown is a decisive defeat or forceful confrontation—physical or verbal. The term comes from professional wrestling, where it describes a dramatic takedown of an opponent. Now it applies broadly to any situation where someone is thoroughly beaten or put in their place: {The senator delivered a smackdown to her critics}. {It was a legal smackdown of epic proportions}.

Small is the most frequent word in English for characterizing things as being not big. It is often interchangeable with little, though usage favors small in a number of common collocations, including small amount, small print, and extremely small. Small is also commonly used in clothing sizes.

Smallpox was a highly contagious viral disease marked by fever and a progressive skin rash that left severe scarring on survivors. It killed roughly one-third of those infected. Through a global vaccination campaign, smallpox became the first disease eradicated by human effort, with the last natural case occurring in 1977.

Smalltime means minor, insignificant, or operating on a limited scale. A smalltime {crook} commits petty crimes rather than major heists. A smalltime {operation} lacks the resources or ambition of bigger competitors. The word often carries a dismissive tone—calling someone smalltime suggests they'll never amount to much. Also spelled small-time.

Smarmy describes behavior that's excessively flattering or ingratiating in a way that feels false and off-putting. A smarmy person oozes charm but seems insincere—more interested in manipulation than genuine connection: {a smarmy salesman}, {his smarmy compliments made her uncomfortable}. The word implies something slick and slightly repellent.

The adjective smart has a few mostly appreciative meanings. It conveys intelligence or using intelligence (smart phone, smart choice, smart student). This meaning is common today to describe policies that avoid excess (smart growth). Smart also means fashionably attractive (a smart new outfit), and insolent: Don’t get smart with me! The verb smart means to hurt sharply, like a cut, burn, or bite does. Smart can also be used as an adverb, where intelligence is suggested (play smart, work smart, shop smart).

A smartarse is someone who displays knowledge or wit in an irritating, show-off manner—answering questions no one asked, correcting minor errors, or making clever remarks at others' expense. Chiefly British and Australian; the American equivalent is smartass. {Don't be such a smartarse.} The term is mildly vulgar but more dismissive than deeply offensive.

A smartass is someone who makes clever, sarcastic, or irritating remarks, typically showing off at others' expense: {Don't be a smartass}. The word carries an affectionate edge in some contexts—being called a smartass isn't always an insult among friends.

A smartphone is a mobile phone with computing capabilities—internet access, apps, cameras, and touchscreen interface. The term emerged in the 1990s but became ubiquitous after 2007 with devices like the iPhone. Smartphones have largely replaced separate cameras, GPS units, and music players: {I left my smartphone at home and felt completely lost}.

Smartphones are mobile phones with advanced computing capabilities—essentially pocket-sized computers that also make calls. They run apps, connect to the internet, take photos, and handle tasks once requiring separate devices: camera, GPS, music player, calendar. The term emerged in the late 1990s but became ubiquitous after touchscreen models transformed daily life: {I left my smartphone at home and felt lost all day}.

Smarts is informal for intelligence or practical cleverness: {She has the smarts to figure it out}, {street smarts}. The word treats mental ability as something countable and concrete—you either have the smarts for something or you don't. Often appears with modifiers: {book smarts}, {business smarts}.

A smartwatch is a wristwatch that functions as a miniature computer, typically connecting to a smartphone to display notifications, track fitness metrics, and run apps. Beyond telling time, smartwatches monitor heart rate, count steps, and allow quick responses to messages: {I left my phone in the car but saw the text on my smartwatch}.

Smartypants is a mildly teasing term for someone who flaunts their knowledge or cleverness, especially in an annoying way: {Okay, smartypants, if you know so much, you figure it out}. Often used with children or playfully among adults. The tone ranges from affectionate to genuinely irritated depending on context. Also spelled smarty-pants or as two words.

Smash is to break something violently into pieces, or the act of doing so: {The vase smashed against the wall}. Extended uses keep the force: a smash hit is an overwhelming success, and to smash a record is to break it decisively. In tennis, a smash is a powerful overhead shot. As slang, smash means to have sex: {They smashed after the party}.

Smashed means broken violently into pieces: {The plate smashed on the floor}. {He smashed the window to get in}. Smashed also means crushed or hit hard: {smashed potatoes}, {He smashed the ball over the fence}. In slang, smashed means extremely drunk: {He got smashed at the bachelor party}. The image is of being shattered, no longer intact or functional.

Smashing means excellent or wonderful, used enthusiastically to express approval: {What a smashing idea!} The word is characteristically British and sounds old-fashioned or affected to American ears. Separately, smashing describes violent breaking or crushing: {the smashing of windows}, {a smashing blow to the head}.

A smear is a mark made by spreading something sticky or greasy across a surface: {a smear of butter}, {a smear of lipstick on the collar}. The verb means to spread or streak in this way. A smear is also an attempt to damage someone's reputation through false or misleading accusations: {a smear campaign}, {political smears}. In medicine, a smear is a sample of cells spread on a slide for examination: {a Pap smear}.

Smeared is the past tense of smear—to spread a substance messily across a surface: {She smeared sunscreen on her arms}, {The ink smeared before it dried}. Smeared also describes something left in this state: {smeared lipstick}, {smeared windows}. Figuratively, a smeared reputation has been damaged by false or damaging accusations.

Smell is the sense that detects odors through the nose, and also the quality perceived: {What's that smell?} As a verb, to smell is to perceive an odor or to emit one: {I smell smoke}, {The kitchen smells like garlic}. Something that {smells} without qualification usually smells bad. To {smell a rat} is to suspect deception. A smell test checks whether something seems legitimate: {That excuse doesn't pass the smell test}.

Smelly means having a noticeable odor, almost always unpleasant: {smelly feet}, {a smelly garbage can}. The word is informal and mildly childish—adults more often say something stinks or reeks. Smelly rarely describes pleasant scents; you wouldn't call a rose smelly.

Smelting is the process of extracting metal from ore by heating it to high temperatures, typically with a reducing agent like carbon. The heat melts the ore and separates the pure metal from impurities: {Copper smelting has been practiced for thousands of years}. Smelting differs from simply melting metal—it chemically transforms raw ore into usable material.

A smidgen is a tiny amount: {Add just a smidgen of salt}. The word appears most often in cooking and casual speech, suggesting an amount too small to measure precisely. Also spelled smidgeon or smidge.

Smile is a noun and verb used to characterize expressions of the mouth (with the ends turned up) and face. A smile usually signifies happiness, but modifiers may give some other clue: If the smile is wry, faint, crooked, or sly, the suggestion is that its meaning is closer to the emotional sense of the adjective. To smile is to make such an expression with your mouth, face, or eyes.

Smiles is the plural of smile—the facial expression formed by turning up the corners of the mouth, typically indicating pleasure, amusement, or friendliness. Smiles can be genuine, forced, or enigmatic: {Her smiles were rare but radiant}. The word also serves as the third-person singular verb: {She smiles at strangers on the subway}.

Smiley describes someone who smiles frequently or a facial expression showing happiness: {She's always so smiley in photos}. As a noun, a smiley is a simple representation of a smiling face, especially the circular yellow face with two dots for eyes and a curved line for a mouth that became ubiquitous on buttons, stickers, and merchandise from the 1970s onward. In digital communication, smiley refers to emoticons depicting happiness, particularly the original text-based :) and its descendants. (Capitalized Smiley is a surname.)

Smiling describes a facial expression where the corners of the mouth turn upward, typically indicating pleasure, amusement, or friendliness. As an adjective, it modifies faces or people: {a smiling child}, {smiling faces greeted us at the door}. It can also describe things that seem pleasant or welcoming: {smiling fields}, {a smiling future}.

A smirk is a smile that suggests self-satisfaction, smugness, or knowing amusement—often at someone else's expense. Unlike a genuine smile, a smirk carries an edge of superiority or private pleasure: {She couldn't hide her smirk when he failed}. To smirk is to wear such an expression: {He smirked at the suggestion that he might lose}.

Smirking is smiling in a way that suggests smugness, self-satisfaction, or knowing something others don't. A smirk often carries an edge of superiority or mockery: {She stood there smirking while he tried to explain himself}. The present participle of smirk, it functions as both verb and adjective: {a smirking villain}, {Stop smirking at me}.

Smirks is the plural of smirk, a smile expressing smugness, self-satisfaction, or knowing amusement. A smirk often suggests the person knows something others don't, or feels superior: {He couldn't hide his smirks during her presentation}. As a verb, smirks is the third-person singular: {She smirks whenever someone mentions his failed business}.

Smite means to strike with a heavy blow, often with devastating force. The word is biblical and archaic in tone—God smites enemies, plagues smite populations. Modern use is usually playful or ironic: {I shall smite thee}. To be smitten is to be struck, especially by love or infatuation: {He was utterly smitten with her}.

A smith is a person who works metal by heating and hammering it into shape. The word typically appears in compounds specifying the metal: blacksmith (iron), silversmith, goldsmith, coppersmith. By extension, a smith is anyone who crafts or creates: wordsmith, songsmith. The verb means to forge or fashion metal: {The blade was smithed by hand}. (Capitalized Smith is a common surname.)

Smithereens are tiny fragments or pieces, used almost exclusively in the phrase {blown to smithereens} or {smashed to smithereens}. The word emphasizes total destruction—not just broken, but shattered beyond recognition: {The explosion blew the building to smithereens}.

Smitten describes being suddenly and powerfully affected—usually by love or infatuation. Someone smitten with another person is captivated, besotted: {He was completely smitten with her from the moment they met}. The word comes from smite, to strike forcefully, preserving the sense of being struck as if by a blow. Smitten can also describe being charmed by non-romantic things: {smitten with the city}, {smitten by an idea}.

Smog is air pollution that hangs visibly over cities, a hazy mixture of smoke, exhaust, and fog. The word blends *smoke* and *fog*. Heavy smog reduces visibility and aggravates respiratory conditions: {The smog was so thick you could barely see the skyline}. Cities like Los Angeles became notorious for it before emission controls improved air quality.

Smoke is the opaque or translucent mixture of gases given off by things that are burning. It co-occurs with fire more than any other meaningful word, which makes the expression “where there’s smoke, there’s fire” true of both the words and the things they signify. If something smokes, it gives off smoke. If a person smokes, they are a user of cigarettes or some other specified product whose vapors are inhaled. If you smoke a food, you subject it to wood smoke as a way of curing and imparting flavor: smoked salmon, smoked bacon. The phrase smoke someone out can be used figuratively or literally to denote driving them out into the open.

Smoked describes food preserved or flavored by exposure to smoke: smoked {salmon}, smoked {ham}, smoked {cheese}. The process adds distinctive flavor while inhibiting spoilage. Smoked also means past tense of smoke—having inhaled tobacco, cannabis, or other substances: {She smoked a cigarette on the porch}. In slang, to get smoked is to be decisively defeated or killed: {They got smoked in the finals}.

A smokehouse is a building or enclosed structure where meat or fish is cured by exposure to smoke from smoldering wood. The smoke preserves the food and imparts a distinctive flavor. Traditional smokehouses were small outbuildings on farms; modern versions range from backyard sheds to industrial facilities: {The ham had been aged in the smokehouse for months}.

A smoker is a person who smokes tobacco: {He's been a smoker for thirty years}. It also names devices for smoking food—meat, fish, or cheese—by exposing them to wood smoke over hours. In beekeeping, a smoker is a handheld device that puffs smoke to calm bees. A smoker can also be a social gathering, traditionally men-only, where smoking was permitted.

A smokescreen is a cloud of smoke released to conceal military movements or positions. The figurative sense dominates: anything used to obscure, distract, or hide the truth. {The merger talks were just a smokescreen for the real agenda.} Politicians deploy smokescreens to deflect attention from scandals or uncomfortable questions.

A smokestack is a tall chimney, especially one rising from a factory or ship, through which smoke and exhaust gases escape. The word evokes industrial-era manufacturing: {smokestack industries} like steel and coal. A smokestack may also vent from a locomotive or power plant. {The factory's smokestacks blackened the sky.}

Smokestacks are the tall chimneys that release exhaust gases and smoke from industrial facilities, power plants, or ships. The image of belching smokestacks represents heavy industry and, increasingly, environmental pollution. {Smokestack industries} are traditional manufacturing sectors like steel and automobiles, often contrasted with newer technology-based economies.

Smoking is the act of inhaling and exhaling the fumes of burning plant material, most commonly tobacco in cigarettes, cigars, or pipes. {She went outside for a smoking break.} The term extends to other substances: {smoking weed}. As an adjective, smoking describes areas or items related to this activity: {smoking section}, {smoking jacket}. Informally, smoking means extremely hot or fast: {The car was smoking down the highway.} The slang sense attractive or sexy appears in phrases like {smoking hot}.

Smoky describes something filled with, producing, or resembling smoke: {a smoky bar}, {a smoky fire}. The word extends to flavors and aromas that suggest smoke: {smoky whiskey}, {smoky barbecue}. Smoky colors are hazy or grayish: {smoky blue eyes}. A smoky voice is husky or slightly rough. Also spelled smokey.

To smolder is to burn slowly without flame, producing smoke but no visible fire: {The campfire smoldered through the night}. Figuratively, smolder describes suppressed intensity—emotions that burn beneath the surface: {Resentment smoldered in her for years}. A smoldering look conveys barely contained desire or anger. The noun smolder is the state of burning this way.

Smoldered is the past tense of smolder, meaning to burn slowly without flame, producing smoke and heat: {The campfire smoldered through the night}. Figuratively, smoldered describes emotions—especially anger or desire—that remain intense but suppressed: {Resentment smoldered for years before erupting}. A smoldering look conveys barely contained passion.

Smoldering describes burning slowly without flame, producing smoke and heat: {smoldering embers}, {a smoldering cigarette}. The word extends to emotions that burn quietly beneath the surface—suppressed anger, resentment, or desire: {smoldering tension between the two families}. A smoldering look or gaze conveys intense, barely contained sexual attraction: {He gave her a smoldering stare across the room}.

Smooch is an informal, slightly playful word for a kiss, usually implying affection rather than passion: {They shared a quick smooch before parting}. As a verb, to smooch is to kiss in this way, or to engage in kissing and light petting: {The teenagers were smooching in the back row}.

Smooches is the plural of smooch—affectionate kisses, typically playful or casual rather than passionate: {She covered his face in smooches}. The word has a lighthearted, somewhat childish quality. As a verb form, smooches means kisses in this affectionate way: {He smooches his dog every morning}.

Smooching is kissing, especially in an affectionate, leisurely way. The word suggests gentle intimacy rather than passionate making out: {They were smooching on the porch swing}. A smooch is a kiss of this kind. The word has a playful, slightly old-fashioned quality.

Smoosh is to squash or press something soft, flattening or deforming it: {She smooshed the banana into the batter}. The word suggests gentle pressure rather than violent crushing—you smoosh a bug, but you'd crush a can. Smoosh can also mean to press things together affectionately: {They smooshed their faces together for a selfie}. Also spelled smoush or squoosh.

Smooth describes surfaces without roughness, bumps, or irregularities: {smooth skin}, {smooth marble}. Movement can be smooth when free of jolts or interruptions: {a smooth ride}, {a smooth transition}. A smooth talker speaks persuasively, often with implications of slickness or manipulation. Smooth flavors lack harshness: {a smooth whiskey}. To smooth something is to make it even or to ease difficulties: {smooth the wrinkles}, {smooth things over}.

A smoothie is a thick, creamy drink made by blending fruit, ice, and often yogurt, milk, or juice. The name reflects the drink's smooth texture. Smoothies became popular as a health food in the late 20th century and now appear on café menus everywhere, sometimes with added protein powder or greens. {I grab a smoothie on my way to the gym.} The older sense of smoothie—a person who is suave or slick—still appears occasionally but sounds dated.

Smoothies are thick, blended drinks made from fruit, vegetables, or both, often with ice, yogurt, or milk. They're associated with health-conscious eating, though many contain enough sugar to undermine that image: {I grabbed a smoothie after the gym}. The singular smoothie also describes a charming, persuasive person—usually a man whose polish seems calculated: {He's a real smoothie}.

A smore is a campfire treat made by sandwiching toasted marshmallow and chocolate between graham crackers. The name comes from "some more"—what you supposedly ask for after eating one. Making smores is a classic outdoor activity, especially at summer camps: {We roasted marshmallows and made smores around the fire}.

S'mores are a campfire treat made by sandwiching toasted marshmallow and chocolate between graham crackers. The name contracts "some more," reflecting how the gooey, messy snack invites seconds. S'mores are strongly associated with camping, summer camps, and outdoor gatherings: {We made s'mores around the fire pit}. The flavor combination appears in desserts far from any campfire: s'mores ice cream, s'mores cookies.

Smorgasbord comes from Swedish and originally meant a buffet meal featuring a variety of dishes, typically including cold meats, fish, cheeses, and salads. The word has largely been absorbed into its figurative meaning: a wide-ranging mixture or assortment of things. {The festival offered a smorgasbord of musical styles.} {Her reading list was a smorgasbord of genres.} The literal buffet sense persists mainly in Scandinavian restaurants or themed events.

Smother means to suffocate—to kill or nearly kill by cutting off air supply, typically by covering the nose and mouth: {She smothered him with a pillow}. Extended meanings involve covering thickly or overwhelming: {smothered in gravy}, {smothered with kisses}. To smother feelings is to suppress them. To smother a fire is to extinguish it by depriving it of oxygen. A relationship can feel smothering when one person's attention becomes oppressive: {He's sweet but he smothers me}.

Smothered means covered thickly or suffocated. To smother someone is to kill them by cutting off air, often by covering the face. Extended uses involve overwhelming coverage: {smothered in kisses}, {smothered with attention}. In cooking, smothered means covered and cooked slowly under a heavy layer of ingredients: {smothered pork chops}, {chicken smothered in onions and gravy}.

Smothering is covering so completely as to suffocate or extinguish: {She was smothering under the heavy blankets}, {smothering the flames with a wet towel}. The word extends to overwhelming attention or affection that feels oppressive: {His smothering love drove her away}. In cooking, smothering means covering food completely while it cooks: {smothered pork chops}, {chicken smothered in gravy}.

To smoulder is to burn slowly without flame, producing smoke and heat: {The campfire smouldered through the night}. The word extends to emotions held in check but ready to ignite—smouldering resentment, smouldering tension. A smouldering look conveys intense, suppressed desire or anger. Also spelled smolder.

Smouldering is the British spelling of smoldering. It describes fire burning slowly without flame, producing smoke and heat: {smouldering embers}. Figuratively, it suggests suppressed intensity—anger, desire, or resentment that hasn't yet erupted: {a smouldering look}, {smouldering tensions between the two countries}. A smouldering gaze conveys barely contained passion or hostility.

A smudge is a dirty mark or streak, typically made by rubbing: {a smudge of ink on her finger}, {fingerprint smudges on the glass}. To smudge is to make such a mark or to blur something by rubbing: {Don't touch the painting—you'll smudge it}. In spiritual practices, to smudge is to burn herbs like sage for ritual purification, and the noun names this ceremony: {a smudge to cleanse the space}.

Smug describes excessive self-satisfaction, often at others' expense. A smug person radiates complacency about their own superiority, correctness, or good fortune: {He had a smug look after winning the argument}. The word carries strong disapproval—smugness is satisfaction that hasn't been earned or that ignores others' struggles: {She was smug about her promotion while colleagues got laid off}.

To smuggle is to move goods or people illegally across a border or past a checkpoint, evading customs, immigration, or other authorities. The word extends to any secretive conveyance: {She smuggled cookies into the movie theater}. A smuggler deals in contraband—drugs, weapons, endangered species, or people seeking illegal entry.

Smuggled is the past tense of smuggle—to move goods or people illegally across borders or past authorities. The word implies secrecy and evasion: {smuggled drugs}, {smuggled weapons}, {smuggled immigrants}. Things can be smuggled into or out of places: {She smuggled a candy bar into the movie theater}. The term extends to any covert transfer: {He smuggled a note to his friend during class}.

A smuggler is someone who moves goods or people illegally across borders or past authorities, evading customs, taxes, or prohibitions. The term covers those who traffic in contraband—drugs, weapons, stolen goods—as well as those who help people cross borders illegally: {human smugglers}, {The smugglers brought whiskey across the border during Prohibition}. Smuggler can carry romantic connotations from adventure stories, though real smuggling ranges from petty evasion to serious organized crime.

Smugglers are people who move goods or people illegally across borders or past authorities. The term covers those who evade customs duties on merchandise, transport contraband like drugs or weapons, or help migrants cross borders without authorization: {The smugglers charged thousands to cross the desert}. Smuggler can carry romantic associations from literary pirates and rum-runners, but modern usage often centers on criminal networks.

Smuggling is the act of moving goods or people illegally across borders or past checkpoints, typically to avoid taxes, duties, or prohibitions. The term covers everything from drug trafficking to helping refugees cross borders: {a smuggling operation}, {arrested for smuggling contraband}. Smuggling can also mean bringing something in secretly on a smaller scale: {She was caught smuggling snacks into the theater}.

Smugness is excessive satisfaction with oneself, especially when accompanied by a sense of superiority over others. The smug person seems pleased not just with their own position but with the comparative inadequacy of everyone else: {His smugness about getting the promotion was insufferable}. The quality often invites resentment precisely because it feels unearned or exaggerated.

Smurf has two main meanings in contemporary usage. In gaming, a smurf is an experienced player using a secondary account to compete against less skilled opponents: {He's obviously smurfing—no beginner plays like that}. In financial contexts, smurfing is structuring cash transactions to avoid reporting thresholds, using multiple people or accounts to move money without triggering scrutiny. Both senses derive from the small blue cartoon characters, though the connection is obscure.

Smush means to squash or press something into a flattened, compressed, or distorted shape: {The cake got smushed in my bag}, {She smushed her face against the window}. It's informal and suggests softer, messier compression than crush—more playful than violent. Smushing often implies something that was already soft becoming softer or more shapeless.

Smut connects ideas of dirt, blackness, and contamination. Originally soot or black grime, smut extended to the black fungal disease that destroys grain crops. The figurative sense—obscene or sexually explicit material—treats such content as moral contamination: {The book was dismissed as smut}. Smutty describes something mildly dirty or indecent: {smutty jokes}.

A snack is a small amount of food eaten between regular meals, or sometimes instead of a meal. The word can also serve as a verb: {I snacked on chips while watching the game}. In contemporary slang, snack describes an attractive person, suggesting they look good enough to eat: {He's a whole snack}. Snack often implies something quick, casual, and satisfying rather than substantial.

Snacking is eating small amounts between meals. The word carries a casual, often mindless connotation—grabbing chips while watching TV, nibbling at a party. It can suggest unhealthy habits {I've been snacking too much lately} or simply informal eating {We're just snacking, not having dinner}.

Snacks are small portions of food eaten between meals or in place of a full meal. The word covers everything from chips and cookies to fruit and cheese. To snack is to eat this way: {I've been snacking all afternoon}. Snacks can also be the verb's object: {She snacks nuts at her desk}. In slang, a snack is an attractive person: {He's a whole snack}.

A snafu is a mistake, mix-up, or state of confusion—something going wrong due to poor planning or communication: {There was a snafu with the reservations and we lost our table}. The word originated as military slang during World War II. It also works as a verb meaning to bungle: {They snafued the whole operation}. (All-caps SNAFU is the original acronym form.)

A snag is an obstacle on a physical path that may interrupt movement. By extension, any delay, problem, or difficulty in a process can be called a snag: They hit a snag in the negotiations. If you snag a garment on something, it catches and possibly tears. When you snag someone or something, you capture or acquire them quickly, and perhaps unexpectedly: She snagged a lucrative position.

Snagged is the past tense of snag, meaning caught or torn on something projecting: {I snagged my sweater on a nail}. More casually, to snag something is to grab or obtain it, often quickly or opportunistically: {I snagged the last ticket}, {She snagged a good parking spot}. The casual sense implies luck or quick action.

A snaggletooth is a tooth that sticks out awkwardly from the others, usually crooked or broken. The word describes both the tooth itself and, informally, a person who has one: {That snaggletooth kid from down the street}. The adjective snaggletoothed describes the condition: {a snaggletoothed grin}.

A snail is a slow-moving mollusk with a spiral shell it carries on its back. Snails live in gardens, forests, and water. The word commonly describes anything extremely slow: {traffic moving at a snail's pace}, {snail mail} for postal service versus email. Some species are eaten as escargot.

Snails are slow-moving mollusks that carry coiled shells on their backs, found in gardens, freshwater, and the sea. Their sluggish pace makes them symbols of slowness: {Traffic moved at a snail's pace}. Edible land snails, prepared with garlic butter, are the French delicacy escargot. Snail mail is postal service, contrasted with faster electronic communication.

A snake is a legless reptile with an elongated body, moving by slithering. Snakes range from harmless garden varieties to venomous species like cobras and rattlesnakes. Figuratively, a snake is a treacherous person who deceives or betrays: {He's a snake—don't trust him}. To snake is to move in a winding path: {The river snakes through the valley}. {Snakes and ladders} is a children's board game.

A snakebite is a wound inflicted by a snake's fangs, potentially injecting venom: {She was hospitalized after a snakebite while hiking}. The term extends to a British drink mixing lager and cider in equal parts, sometimes with a splash of blackcurrant cordial. In American slang, a snakebite can be a quick, sharp pinch to someone's arm.

A snakepit is literally a pit filled with snakes—a form of execution or torture in legend and film. The figurative sense dominates: any chaotic, hostile, or treacherous environment. An office with vicious politics is a snakepit. A mental institution might be called a snakepit, from the 1948 novel and film depicting asylum conditions. {That workplace is a total snakepit.}

Snakes are legless reptiles with elongated, scaly bodies—pythons, cobras, rattlesnakes, and thousands of other species. Some are venomous. Figuratively, a snake is a treacherous person: {Watch out for him—he's a snake}. The verb means to move in a winding path: {The river snakes through the valley}. {Snakes and ladders} is a children's board game.

A snap is a sudden, sharp sound or movement—a twig snapping, fingers snapping, a dog snapping its jaws. To snap is to break suddenly or speak sharply: {She snapped at him for being late}. A snap is also a fastener that clicks together, a quick photograph (from snapshot), and in football, the pass from center to quarterback. A snap {decision} is made quickly; a cold {snap} is a brief spell of freezing weather. {Oh snap} is an exclamation of surprise. (Capitalized Snap is the tech company; SNAP is the food assistance program.)

Snapdragons are flowering plants with colorful tubular blooms that open and close like a mouth when squeezed—hence the name. They're garden staples, growing in spikes of pink, red, yellow, white, or orange flowers. Children often pinch the blossoms to make them "talk." {The snapdragons along the fence bloomed all summer.}

Snapped is the past tense of snap, covering all its meanings. Something that snapped broke suddenly with a sharp sound: {The branch snapped under the weight}. A person who snapped lost composure abruptly, often speaking sharply or losing their temper: {She finally snapped and told him off}. If you snapped a photo, you took it quickly. Snapped can also describe something that closed or fastened with a clicking sound: {He snapped the case shut}.

Snappy means quick and lively, with a sense of briskness or sharpness. A snappy {comeback} is witty and immediate. Snappy {dialogue} moves fast. {Make it snappy} means hurry up. Snappy can also mean stylish or smart in appearance: {a snappy dresser}, {a snappy suit}. When describing temperament, snappy means irritable or short-tempered: {She gets snappy when she's tired}.

A snapshot is a photograph taken quickly and casually, without elaborate setup or artistic intent—the kind of picture anyone might take with a phone or simple camera. The word emphasizes spontaneity over craft: {vacation snapshots}, {family snapshots}. By extension, a snapshot captures any moment in time: {The poll offers a snapshot of public opinion}. In computing, a snapshot preserves the state of a system at a particular instant for backup or recovery.

Snapshots are photographs, especially ones taken quickly or casually: {vacation snapshots}, {a snapshot of the kids}. The word extends to any brief glimpse or summary capturing a moment in time: {The report offers a snapshot of the economy}. In computing, a snapshot preserves the state of a system at a particular instant, allowing restoration if something goes wrong.

A snare is a trap, typically a loop of wire or cord that tightens around an animal when triggered. The word extends to any entanglement or trap: {caught in a snare of debt}, {the snares of fame}. To snare is to catch or entrap: {She snared the job before anyone else applied}. A snare drum has wires stretched across its bottom head that rattle when struck, giving a sharp, buzzing sound.

Snares are traps for catching animals, typically made of a loop that tightens around prey. The word extends to anything that entraps: {the snares of addiction}, {caught in bureaucratic snares}. To snare is to catch in such a trap, literally or figuratively: {She snared the lead role}. A snare drum has wires stretched across its bottom head that rattle when struck, giving the drum its distinctive buzzing sound.

Snark is snide, mocking criticism delivered with a cutting edge—sharper than sarcasm, less playful than teasing. The word blends snide and remark. Someone full of snark is snarky: {Her reviews are famous for their snark}. The tone implies superiority and often aims to wound rather than amuse. Internet culture has made snark a recognized rhetorical mode.

Snarky describes a tone that's snide, mocking, or rudely critical—often witty but with a sharp edge: {Her snarky comments about the presentation didn't help morale}. The word suggests cleverness deployed unkindly, humor at someone's expense. Snarky remarks may be funny to observers but sting their targets.

Snarl has two distinct meanings. One is an aggressive growl, typically from a dog baring its teeth: {The dog snarled at the intruder}. People snarl when speaking with hostile contempt: {Don't talk to me like that, she snarled}. The other snarl is a tangle or knot—in hair, thread, or traffic: {a snarl of cables behind the desk}. To snarl is to become tangled; to snarl up is to cause confusion or delay: {The accident snarled traffic for hours}.

Snarled describes something tangled or knotted: {snarled fishing line}, {snarled hair}. Traffic snarls when it becomes congested and slow-moving: {Traffic was snarled for miles after the accident}. The word also serves as the past tense of snarl—to growl threateningly or speak angrily: {The dog snarled at the intruder}, {He snarled his response}.

Snarling describes the act of growling with bared teeth, typically of dogs or wolves: {The snarling dog lunged at the fence}. Extended to humans, it means speaking in an angry, hostile tone: {He snarled a reply}. As an adjective, it characterizes something caught in tangles or knots: {snarling traffic}, {snarling cables behind the desk}.

Snarls covers two distinct ideas. A snarl is a tangle or knot—hair snarls, traffic snarls, yarn snarls: {She worked the snarls out of her daughter's hair}. To snarl up is to become entangled or jammed: {An accident snarled traffic for hours}. Separately, to snarl is to growl while baring teeth, or to speak in an angry, hostile tone: {The dog snarled at the mail carrier}; {"Get out," he snarled}.

To snatch is to grab quickly or steal: {He snatched the purse and ran}. {She snatched victory from defeat}. A snatch is a quick grab, a fragment ({snatches of conversation}), or a weightlifting move where the barbell is lifted overhead in one motion. In vulgar slang, snatch means the female genitals: {a kick in the snatch}. The vulgar sense is crude and somewhat dated but still in circulation.

Snatched is the past tense of snatch—grabbed quickly or stolen: {She snatched the phone from his hand}. {He was snatched off the street}. In slang, snatched means looking extremely good, flawless: {Her makeup is snatched}.

Snazzy means stylish, flashy, or impressively attractive in a showy way: {a snazzy new sports car}, {That's a snazzy outfit}. The word is informal and slightly playful, suggesting something eye-catching without being garish. It carries a note of admiration tinged with amusement.

Sneak means to move quietly and furtively, trying to avoid notice: {She sneaked out after curfew}. You can sneak a glance, sneak a cookie, or sneak something past someone. A sneak is a furtive person, or as an adjective, something done without warning: a sneak {attack}, a sneak {preview}. The past tense is sneaked, though snuck has become standard in American speech.

A sneaker is an athletic shoe with a soft rubber sole, designed for sports or casual wear. The name comes from the quiet tread—you can sneak in them. Americans say sneaker; the British prefer trainer. In the plural, sneakers often names the category: {I need new sneakers for the gym}.

A sneakerhead is someone deeply invested in collecting, trading, and knowing about athletic shoes—especially limited-edition releases and vintage styles. The culture centers on brands like Nike and Adidas, with collectors tracking drop dates and resale values: {He's such a sneakerhead, he camps outside stores for new Jordans}.

Sneakerheads are enthusiasts who collect, trade, and obsess over athletic footwear—particularly limited-edition or vintage sneakers. The culture involves tracking release dates, waiting in lines or entering online raffles, and paying premium resale prices for coveted pairs: {Sneakerheads camped outside the store for the new Jordans}. The hobby blends fashion appreciation with investment speculation.

Sneakers are soft-soled athletic shoes, typically with rubber soles and canvas or leather uppers. The name reflects their quiet footfall—you can sneak in them. In American English, sneakers covers everything from running shoes to basketball shoes to casual canvas styles. British English prefers trainers for the same footwear.

Sneaking describes something done secretly or furtively, often with a hint of guilt: {a sneaking suspicion}, {a sneaking admiration for his rival}. A sneaking feeling is one you're reluctant to acknowledge openly. The word also works as the present participle of sneak: {She was sneaking out the back door}.

Sneaky describes someone or something characterized by secrecy and deception—acting in ways meant to avoid notice or detection. A sneaky person operates through stealth rather than openness: {He made a sneaky exit through the back door}. The word carries connotations of dishonesty or untrustworthiness, though it can be playful: {She had a sneaky suspicion he was planning something}.

A sneer is a contemptuous facial expression—lips curled, often with one side raised—that conveys scorn or mockery without words. The verb means to make this expression or to speak with derision: {He sneered at their amateur efforts}. A sneer suggests superiority and dismissal: {She delivered the criticism with a sneer}.

Sneering is showing contempt through facial expression or tone—a curled lip, a mocking voice. A sneer combines superiority with disdain: {He sneered at their modest ambitions}. The word works as adjective, verb, or noun: a sneering {remark}, to sneer at someone, a sneer of contempt. Unlike a smirk, which is private amusement, a sneer is openly hostile.

A sneeze is a sudden, involuntary expulsion of air from the nose and mouth, typically triggered by irritation in the nasal passages. The verb sneeze describes this reflexive action. The phrase {nothing to sneeze at} means something is worthy of respect or consideration—not to be dismissed lightly. If you sneeze, someone nearby might say "bless you" or the German borrowing "gesundheit."

Sneezing is the involuntary expulsion of air through the nose and mouth—a reflex that clears irritants from nasal passages. Beyond the physical act, sneezing appears in expressions: {nothing to sneeze at} means something deserves respect or attention. {I've been sneezing all morning} suggests allergies or a cold coming on.

A snicker is a half-suppressed laugh, often expressing mockery or amusement at something inappropriate: {She couldn't hold back a snicker when he tripped}. The verb means to laugh this way: {The students snickered at the typo on the board}. A snicker suggests less openness than a giggle and more meanness than a chuckle.

A snickerdoodle is a soft, slightly tangy cookie rolled in cinnamon sugar before baking. The tang comes from cream of tartar in the dough. The cookie is American, dating to the late 19th century, and remains a holiday and home-baking staple: {She made snickerdoodles for the bake sale}.

Snickerdoodles are soft, chewy cookies rolled in cinnamon sugar before baking, giving them a crinkled surface and sweet-spicy coating. The dough typically contains cream of tartar, which produces a distinctive slight tang. A classic American cookie, often homemade: {She brought snickerdoodles to the bake sale}.

Snickering is laughing in a half-suppressed way, often with an edge of mockery or knowing amusement. It suggests trying to contain laughter that wants to escape—the sound kids make when someone says something that could be taken the wrong way: {The boys were snickering in the back row}. Snickering usually implies the laughter is at someone's expense.

Snickers are quiet, partly suppressed laughs, often expressing mockery or disrespect: {He heard snickers from the back of the room when he mispronounced the word}. The sound suggests amusement at someone else's expense, though it can also signal nervous or knowing laughter. To snicker is to laugh this way. (Capitalized Snickers is the candy bar.)

Snide describes remarks or attitudes that are subtly mocking or derogatory—criticism delivered with a smirk rather than a shout. A snide comment undermines without direct confrontation: {She made a snide remark about his tie}. The word suggests cowardly hostility, disparagement disguised as wit or offhand observation.

To sniff is to draw air audibly through the nose—either to smell something {She sniffed the milk to check if it was fresh} or as an involuntary response to crying or congestion. A sniff is such an inhalation. To sniff at something is to show disdain: {He sniffed at the suggestion}. Sniffing also describes inhaling substances for their effects: {sniffing glue}, {sniffing cocaine}. To {sniff out} is to discover by investigation: {Reporters sniffed out the scandal}.

Sniffing is drawing air audibly through the nose—to smell something, clear the nasal passages, or express emotion like disdain or sadness. Dogs go sniffing for scents; people sniff suspiciously at unfamiliar food. To be sniffing around is to investigate or pry: {Reporters were sniffing around the mayor's office}. In computing, sniffing is intercepting network traffic to capture data—packet sniffing can monitor or steal information passing through a system.

Sniffle is to breathe noisily through a partially blocked nose, making repeated small sniffing sounds. People sniffle when they have a cold, allergies, or are trying not to cry: {She sniffled through the whole funeral}. The sniffles is a minor cold or nasal congestion: {I've got the sniffles}. A sniffle is also a single instance of the sound.

The sniffles are the runny nose and congestion of a mild cold: {I've got the sniffles}. To sniffle is to breathe audibly through a partially blocked nose, or to make repeated small sniffing sounds while crying. The noun sniffle is a single such sound.

Snip is a quick, sharp cut made with scissors or shears: {She snipped the thread}. The noun is both the action and its sound—that crisp metallic click. A snip can also mean a small piece cut off, or informally, something easily done: {The job was a snip}. In British slang, a snip is a bargain: {At that price, it's an absolute snip}.

A snipe is a wading bird with a long bill, known for erratic flight patterns that make it difficult to shoot. From this comes sniper—someone who shoots from concealment.
