In American usage, spliff and joint are often interchangeable, though purists insist a spliff contains tobacco.

A splint is a rigid support used to immobilize a broken bone or injured joint during healing. Splints can be improvised from boards, sticks, or rolled magazines, or manufactured as medical devices. To splint is to secure with such a support: {The paramedic splinted her arm before transport}. In horses, splints are bony growths on the leg.

A splinter is a thin, sharp fragment broken off from a larger piece of wood, glass, or other material. Small splinters lodge painfully under the skin: {I got a splinter in my thumb from the old railing}. To splinter is to break into such fragments, or figuratively, to fragment into factions: {The party splintered over the issue}. A splinter {group} breaks away from a larger organization.

Splintering is the process of breaking into sharp, thin fragments. Wood splinters when struck or stressed along its grain. The word extends to any fragmentation: {a splintering coalition}, {the splintering of a political party into factions}. Glass, bone, and organizations can all be described as splintering when they break apart into pieces.

Splinters is the plural of splinter—thin, sharp fragments broken off from wood, glass, bone, or other hard materials. A splinter lodged under the skin causes disproportionate pain for its size: {She spent ten minutes extracting splinters from her palm}. Something that splinters breaks into such fragments: {The door splintered under the force of the blow}. Groups splinter when they fracture into factions.

To split something is to divide it in parts, especially two parts. When something splits, it goes from unity to division, as a road may split into two roads. To split wood is to chop it into smaller pieces; to split profits is to share them. A split is an instance or the result of splitting. A split decision is one that has divided opinions: In a 5-4 split decision, The Supreme Court upheld the lower court’s ruling. A split second is a fraction of a second, or informally, a very short amount of time. Split has a variety of related meanings in sports. In gymnastics, split is to move into a position where the legs are at right angles to the torso. In bowling, a split signifies that the 7 and 10 pins remain standing after the first ball is released. In track, it a split represents a fraction of the race: He had a record-setting pace at the 400-meter split.

Splits refers to a position where the legs extend in opposite directions, forming a straight line—a feat of flexibility in gymnastics, dance, and yoga: {She dropped into the splits}. In bowling, a split is when remaining pins stand with a gap between them, making a spare difficult. The splits can also mean a drink made by splitting a standard portion: {banana splits}, {wine splits}. To {do the splits} is to perform the gymnastic position.

A splotch is an irregular spot or stain, typically messy or uneven in shape: {a splotch of ink on his shirt}, {splotches of color across the canvas}. The word suggests something splashed or spread haphazardly rather than neatly placed. Skin conditions often produce splotches—red, discolored patches without defined borders.

To splurge is to spend money freely or extravagantly, especially on something indulgent: {We splurged on a fancy dinner for our anniversary}. The word suggests a departure from normal restraint—treating yourself or others lavishly. As a noun, a splurge is an instance of such spending: {The vacation was a bit of a splurge}.

Splurging is spending money freely or extravagantly, usually on something you don't strictly need: {I'm splurging on a nice dinner for my birthday}. The word suggests indulgence—treating yourself or others without worrying about the cost. A splurge is an instance of such spending: {The vacation was a splurge, but worth it}.

Spoil centers on ruining or damaging something. Food spoils when it goes bad. A surprise spoils when someone reveals it. To spoil a child is to overindulge them, harming their character. A spoiler reveals plot details: {Don't spoil the ending for me}. Spoils (usually plural) are goods taken by force—the victor's rewards: {the spoils of war}. To be {spoiling for a fight} is to be eager for one.

Spoiled describes something that has gone bad or been ruined. Food spoils when it decays: {The milk has spoiled}. A spoiled child has been overindulged to the point of expecting constant gratification: {She's completely spoiled—throws a tantrum if she doesn't get her way}. To be spoiled for choice is to have so many good options that choosing becomes difficult. A spoiler reveals plot points prematurely, ruining the surprise.

A spoiler reveals key plot points of a story before someone has experienced it: {Don't tell me anything—no spoilers!} The term comes from the idea of spoiling the surprise. A spoiler can also be a candidate who draws votes from a frontrunner, affecting election outcomes without winning. On vehicles, a spoiler is an aerodynamic device that disrupts airflow to increase traction or reduce drag.

Spoilers are details that reveal key plot points of a story before someone has experienced it themselves: {Don't tell me—no spoilers!} The term reflects how knowing twists or endings can spoil the pleasure of discovery. On vehicles, a spoiler is an aerodynamic device that disrupts airflow to reduce lift or drag. Someone who spoils something—a third-party candidate who splits votes, a person who ruins plans—may also be called a spoiler.

Spoils are goods seized by force, especially in war or conflict: {the spoils of victory}, {to the victor go the spoils}. The word implies plunder divided among winners. In politics, the spoils system awards government jobs to supporters of the winning party. The singular spoil appears mainly in the verb—food spoils when it goes bad, and to spoil a child is to indulge them excessively.

A spoilsport is someone who ruins others' fun by refusing to participate or by objecting to an activity: {Don't be such a spoilsport—just try it}. The word implies that the person's reluctance or disapproval dampens the mood for everyone else.

Spoke is the past tense of speak: {She spoke softly but carried a big stick}. As a noun, a spoke is one of the rods connecting the hub of a wheel to its rim—on bicycles, wagons, and steering wheels. To {put a spoke in someone's wheel} is to obstruct their plans.

Spoken is the past participle of speak, used to form perfect tenses {I have spoken} and as an adjective describing verbal rather than written communication: {a spoken agreement}, {the spoken word}. With a modifier, it describes manner of speech: {soft-spoken}, {well-spoken}, {plain-spoken}. {Spoken for} means already claimed or reserved: {That last slice of cake is spoken for}.

Spokes are the thin rods or bars radiating from the hub of a wheel to its rim, providing structural support. Bicycle wheels, wagon wheels, and steering wheels all have spokes. Figuratively, spokes can describe anything radiating outward from a center: {The trails spread out like spokes from the visitor center}. Spokes is also the past tense of speak, though this form sounds archaic or dialectal: {He spokes not a word}.

A spokesperson is someone who speaks officially on behalf of a group, organization, or cause. The term emerged as a gender-neutral alternative to spokesman and spokeswoman: {The company spokesperson declined to comment}. Unlike representative or delegate, a spokesperson's role is specifically communicative—conveying positions rather than negotiating them.

A sponge is a piece of lightweight, porous material that quickly absorbs liquid. Originally these were made from the porous skeletons of sea creatures called sponges, but now they are manufactured. If you call someone a sponge, it may be an insult, suggesting that they like to absorb benefits from others while contributing nothing; but if you are a sponge for knowledge, you absorb it quickly. To sponge something is to apply a sponge to it. To sponge off someone is to get some benefit while giving nothing in return.

Sponges are porous marine animals that filter water for food, or the absorbent cleaning tools modeled after them. To sponge is to wipe or clean with a sponge: {She sponged the counter clean}. To sponge off someone is to habitually take from them without giving back: {He's been sponging off his parents for years}.

A sponsor is a person or organization that provides money or support for something, often in exchange for publicity: {The race was funded by corporate sponsors}. To sponsor is to provide such backing: {The company sponsors a Little League team}. A sponsor may also be someone who vouches for another—introducing a candidate for membership, supporting an immigrant's visa application, or guiding someone through a twelve-step program. In legislative contexts, to sponsor a bill is to introduce and champion it.

Sponsored describes something financially supported by a company or organization, usually in exchange for publicity or promotion. A sponsored {post} on social media is paid advertising. A sponsored {athlete} receives money or equipment from brands. Sponsored {content} blurs the line between editorial and advertisement. To be sponsored is to have a backer: {The event was sponsored by local businesses}.

Sponsors are people or organizations that provide financial or other support for an activity, event, or person, typically in exchange for publicity or association: {The race has several corporate sponsors}. A sponsor may also be someone who vouches for another—introducing a candidate for membership, supporting an immigrant's visa application, or guiding a newcomer through a recovery program. To sponsor is to act as such a backer: {She sponsored the bill in Congress}.

Sponsorship is the act of providing financial or other support for an event, organization, or person, typically in exchange for publicity or promotional benefits: {corporate sponsorship of the Olympics}, {The team secured sponsorship from a local car dealership}. A sponsor might fund a charity event, back an athlete, or underwrite a television program. Sponsorship also covers the formal support required for immigration or membership applications: {Her employer provided sponsorship for her work visa}.

Spontaneity is the quality of acting on impulse rather than planning—doing something because the moment feels right. A person with spontaneity suggests they can be playful or unpredictable: {I admire her spontaneity}. The word also describes naturalness, the absence of rehearsal or contrivance: {The interview had a spontaneity that made it compelling}.

Spontaneous describes actions or events that arise naturally, without planning or external cause. A spontaneous {decision} happens on impulse; spontaneous {applause} breaks out without prompting. In science, spontaneous processes occur without outside intervention—spontaneous {combustion}, spontaneous {generation}. The word suggests authenticity and naturalness, free from calculation or rehearsal: {Her laughter was completely spontaneous}.

A spoof is a humorous imitation or parody, typically of a film, book, or genre: {The movie is a spoof of 1950s horror films}. The word also means a hoax or trick. As a verb, to spoof is to parody or to deceive—in computing, to falsify identifying information: {Hackers spoofed the sender's email address}.

Spoofs are humorous imitations that mock their subjects through exaggeration or parody. A spoof of a horror film plays on the genre's conventions for laughs. The term also covers hoaxes or tricks: {The email was a spoof designed to steal passwords}. In computing, spoofing means falsifying data to impersonate a trusted source. To spoof is to create such imitations or deceptions: {They spoofed the president's speech}.

Spook has meanings that cluster around the idea of something hidden or unsettling. A spook is a ghost or specter—something that lurks unseen. The verb means to frighten suddenly: {The noise spooked the horses}. In espionage slang, a spook is a spy, someone who operates in shadows. Spook is also a racial slur for a Black person, now largely confined to historical contexts.

Spooked means startled or frightened, especially in a sudden, skittish way. Horses spook easily at unexpected sounds. The past tense works as an adjective: {The spooked cat bolted under the bed}. In informal use, spooked often describes nervousness or unease rather than outright fear: {Investors got spooked by the earnings report}.

Spooks works across several meanings united by the idea of unseen presences. A spook is a ghost or specter: {The old house is full of spooks}. To spook is to frighten suddenly, especially said of horses: {A car backfiring spooked the mare}. People get spooked too: {Don't sneak up on me—you spooked me}. In slang, spooks are spies or intelligence agents, from their shadowy work. As a racial slur for Black people, spook is offensive and dated.

Spooky means eerie or suggestive of ghosts and the supernatural: {a spooky old house}, {spooky noises in the attic}. The word is lighter than frightening—more playful than genuinely terrifying. Something spooky unsettles without necessarily scaring. Informally, spooky describes uncanny coincidences: {It's spooky how much she looks like her grandmother}.

A spool is a cylinder with flanged ends around which thread, wire, film, or tape is wound for storage: {a spool of thread}, {a spool of fishing line}. The shape keeps material organized and allows controlled unwinding. To spool is to wind onto such a cylinder, or in computing, to queue data for sequential processing—print jobs spool before reaching the printer. {The tape spooled through the machine}.

Spools are cylindrical objects with a rim at each end, used to hold thread, wire, film, or tape wound around a central core. To spool is to wind material onto such a cylinder, or in computing, to queue data for sequential processing: {The document is spooling to the printer}. {She loaded a new spool of thread into the sewing machine.}

A spoon is an implement with a handle at one end and a shallow bowl at the other, used in cooking and eating. To spoon something is to serve it or move it with a spoon. A different verb use of spoon describes affectionate play between two people. To spoon is also a specific posture in which two people lie on their sides, front to back, with their bodies fitting the way that stacked spoons fit.

Spoonfed is the past tense of spoon-feed—to feed someone by putting food into their mouth with a spoon, as with infants or invalids. The figurative sense dominates: to provide information or assistance so thoroughly that no independent effort is required. {Students who are spoonfed facts never learn to think critically.} The word usually carries a negative connotation of excessive hand-holding or intellectual laziness.

A spoonful is the amount a spoon can hold: {a spoonful of sugar}, {two spoonfuls of medicine}. The word usually implies a rough measure rather than a precise one. Plural: spoonfuls or spoonsful, with the former more common.

Spooning is lying closely behind another person with bodies curved together, like nested spoons in a drawer. It's an intimate position associated with cuddling in bed: {We spent the morning spooning}. The term can suggest either affection or sexual intimacy depending on context. As old-fashioned slang, to spoon meant to court or behave amorously.

Spoons are eating utensils with a shallow bowl at the end of a handle, used for liquids and soft foods. The shape extends to measuring spoons, mixing spoons, and tools for scooping. To spoon is to cuddle while lying nested together, bodies curved like stacked spoons. To be born with a silver spoon suggests inherited privilege. {He spooned the soup carefully}.

A spore is a tiny reproductive cell produced by fungi, ferns, mosses, and some bacteria—capable of developing into a new organism without fusing with another cell. Spores are hardy, often surviving extreme conditions that would kill the parent organism. Unlike seeds, they contain no embryo. {Mushrooms release millions of spores into the air.} The verb means to produce or release spores.

Spores are tiny reproductive units produced by fungi, mosses, ferns, and some bacteria—capable of developing into new organisms without fusion with another cell. Unlike seeds, spores are typically single-celled and can survive harsh conditions. The verb means to produce or release spores: {The mushrooms spore in late autumn}. Figuratively, things that spread rapidly may be said to spore across a landscape.

A sport is a particular form of athletic recreation or competition. Together, they are called sport in British English, while American English typically uses the plural sports. The present participle form of the verb sport is used in phrases such as sporting event and sporting dog. A sporting chance is an even or fair opportunity to succeed or win. More often, the verb sport means feature visually: She showed up at the party sporting a new tattoo.

Sporting relates to sports or athletic competition: {sporting goods}, {sporting events}. It also describes someone who shows fairness and generosity, especially in accepting loss or giving others a chance: {It was sporting of him to let the newcomer play}. A {sporting chance} is a reasonable opportunity for success. In British usage, sporting can mean interested in or fond of sports: {He's not very sporting}.

Sports are physical activities involving competition, skill, and rules—from team games like basketball and soccer to individual pursuits like tennis and golf. The word also works as an adjective: a sports {car} is sleek and fast, a sports {coat} is casual. To sport something is to wear or display it: {He was sporting a new haircut}. A good sport accepts outcomes gracefully; a poor sport does not.

Sportsmanship is fair, gracious conduct in competition—respecting opponents, accepting defeat without complaint, and winning without gloating. The concept extends beyond athletics to any competitive situation: {Show some sportsmanship and congratulate the winner}. Good sportsmanship values how you play over whether you win.

Sporty describes someone or something with an athletic quality or style. A sporty person enjoys physical activities or dresses in casual athletic clothing. A sporty car is sleek and fast-looking, built for performance rather than practicality: {She bought a sporty little convertible}. Sporty clothes are casual and comfortable, suited for movement.

In the most general way, a spot is something small, somewhat round, and distinct from its background: What are those spots on your neck? A spot does not have to exist in physical space; it often means something like position: Our team has clinched a spot in the tournament. Spot is often used to characterize an area of something that has distinct qualities from what surrounds it: blind spot, hot spot. As a verb, spot can mean mark (spot your bingo card) or identify (Can you spot the errors?). As an adjective, spot has the idea of immediacy (a spot decision) or intermittency (spot checks for quality).

Spotless means completely clean, without any marks, stains, or blemishes. A spotless {kitchen} has been scrubbed until nothing mars its surfaces. The word extends naturally to reputation and character: someone with a spotless {record} has no history of wrongdoing or failure. {Her apartment was spotless when the landlord came for inspection.} The emphasis is on absolute cleanliness or purity—not just clean, but without a single spot.

A spotlight is a powerful beam of light directed at a particular area or person, typically used in theaters, concerts, and other performances to draw attention to whoever or whatever is illuminated. The term extends naturally to figurative use: if someone is in the spotlight, they are receiving public attention or scrutiny. {The scandal put the mayor in an unwelcome spotlight.} To spotlight something is to direct attention to it or feature it prominently. {The documentary spotlights corruption in local government.}

Spots are small marks or areas that differ from their surroundings—a leopard's spots, spots of paint on a floor, a spot of blood. A spot is also a location: {This is the spot where we first met}. To spot something is to notice it: {I spotted her in the crowd}. To spot someone is to lend them something small: {Can you spot me twenty bucks?} In gymnastics and weightlifting, to spot is to stand ready to catch someone if they fall. {On the spot} means immediately or in a difficult position.

Spotted means marked with spots—patches of color or texture that differ from the background: a spotted {dog}, spotted {leopard}, spotted {owl}. Something spotted has been noticed or identified: {The celebrity was spotted leaving the restaurant}. In British slang, spotted {dick} is a steamed pudding studded with dried fruit.

A spotter is someone who watches and assists. In weightlifting, a spotter stands ready to help if you can't complete a lift: {I need a spotter for bench press}. In gymnastics, spotters prevent falls. Military spotters locate targets or observe enemy positions. Planespotters and trainspotters watch for aircraft or locomotives as a hobby. The term extends to anyone whose job is watching for specific things.

Spotting covers various kinds of seeing or marking with spots. To spot something is to notice it: {I spotted her across the room}. A spotter is someone who watches—a talent scout, a gym partner monitoring a weightlifter, or a military observer locating targets. Spotting also means light, irregular bleeding between menstrual periods. In gymnastics and weightlifting, spotting is standing ready to catch or assist someone during a risky move. The participial form of spot in its staining sense gives us {a spotting of blood on the carpet}.

Spotty describes something marked with spots or patches: {a spotty complexion}, {a spotty dog}. More commonly, spotty means inconsistent or uneven in quality—good in some areas, lacking in others: {The service at that restaurant is spotty}, {Her attendance has been spotty this semester}. British English uses spotty more literally for skin with pimples.

A spouse is someone's husband or wife—their partner in marriage. The term is gender-neutral and appears frequently in legal, administrative, and formal contexts where husband or wife would require specifying sex: {List your spouse's income on line 12.} In casual speech, people more often say husband, wife, or partner, but spouse remains useful when speaking generally about married couples or when the specific gender is unknown or irrelevant.

Spouses is the plural of spouse—a person's husband or wife. The word is gender-neutral and appears often in legal, institutional, and formal contexts: {spouses and dependents}, {employees and their spouses}. It can sound stiff in casual speech, where {husbands and wives} or {partners} might feel more natural.

A spout is a projecting tube or lip through which liquid pours—the spout of a teapot, a waterspout, a drinking fountain's spout. To spout is to discharge liquid forcefully: {Water spouted from the broken pipe}. Whales spout when they exhale through blowholes. Figuratively, to spout is to talk at length, often tediously or pretentiously: {He spouted statistics for twenty minutes}. {Up the spout} (British) means ruined or pregnant.

A sprain is an injury to a ligament—the tissue connecting bones at a joint—caused by sudden twisting or wrenching. Ankles and wrists are most commonly sprained. The verb means to cause such an injury: {I sprained my ankle playing basketball}. Unlike a strain, which affects muscles or tendons, a sprain involves the joint itself.

Sprawl captures the idea of spreading out loosely and irregularly. A person sprawls across a couch, limbs extended carelessly. A city sprawls when it expands outward without plan—{suburban sprawl} describes low-density development consuming land in all directions. As a noun, sprawl is both the posture and the phenomenon: {She collapsed in a sprawl on the bed}; {the sprawl of Los Angeles}.

Sprawled is the past tense and past participle of sprawl, describing a position where limbs are spread out loosely and ungainly. A person sprawled on a couch has collapsed into it with arms and legs extended in various directions. The word can also describe things that spread out irregularly across space: {The city sprawled across the valley}. When used of people, sprawled often suggests relaxation, exhaustion, or having been knocked down: {He lay sprawled on the floor after the tackle}.

Sprawling describes something spread out irregularly over a large area. A sprawling {city} extends outward without compact planning. A sprawling {novel} covers vast territory in plot or theme. The word suggests ungainly expansion, growth without restraint: {The sprawling suburbs consumed farmland for decades}. To sprawl is to sit or lie with limbs spread loosely, or to extend haphazardly.

Spray is liquid dispersed into fine droplets, whether naturally occurring like ocean spray or produced mechanically through a spray bottle or aerosol can. As a verb, to spray means to apply or disperse liquid in this manner: {She sprayed the plants with water}. The word extends to anything scattered in a similar pattern—a spray of bullets, a spray of sparks. A spray can also be a small branch with leaves or flowers arranged along it, typically cut for decoration.

Spraypaint is paint packaged in a pressurized can that releases a fine mist when you press the nozzle, allowing for quick, even coverage without brushes. It's used for everything from car touch-ups and furniture refinishing to graffiti art. As a verb, to spraypaint something is to apply paint this way: {Someone spraypainted obscenities on the overpass}. The term is sometimes written as two words: spray paint.

To spread is to move or grow so as to increase and cover more area: The eagle spread its wings. The suburbs are spreading rapidly. When something abstract spreads, it becomes increasingly established; rumors, diseases, or propaganda can spread. The noun spread arises from the meaning of the verb. Spread in general is an instance of or the phenomenon of spreading: the spread of AIDS. A spread can be something that is spread (low-fat spreads that contain no butter) or a piece of property (a thirty acre spread in the mountains). Other things that spread and are called spreads include large meals (he served quite a spread) and the interval between two extremes (a ten-point spread).

Spread-eagle describes a position with arms and legs stretched wide apart, like an eagle with wings spread. A person lies spread-eagle on a bed or is restrained spread-eagle against a wall. As a verb, to spread-eagle someone is to force them into this position: {The suspect was spread-eagled on the hood of the car}. In skating, a spread eagle is a glide with both feet on the ice, toes pointing outward.

Spreads is the plural of spread—things that extend over surfaces or cover distances. In finance, spreads are differences between prices: the bid-ask spread, yield spreads between bonds. Food spreads are soft substances meant for bread: {cheese spreads}, {fruit spreads}. In publishing, a spread is content spanning two facing pages. Bedding spreads cover mattresses: {bedspreads}, {coverlets}.

A spreadsheet is a document organized as a grid of cells arranged in rows and columns, used for storing, organizing, and calculating data. Each cell can contain text, numbers, or formulas that reference other cells. Spreadsheets are fundamental tools in business, accounting, and data analysis: {I track my budget in a spreadsheet}, {She built a spreadsheet to calculate inventory costs}. The format originated with paper ledger sheets but now refers almost exclusively to digital documents in programs like Excel or Google Sheets.

Spreadsheets are documents organized into a grid of rows and columns, where each cell can hold data or formulas that calculate values from other cells. The format dominates business and personal record-keeping—budgets, inventories, financial projections. {She tracks her expenses in a spreadsheet.} The singular spreadsheet refers to either the document or the software category: {Open a new spreadsheet}, {I learned spreadsheet in college}.

A spree is a bout of unrestrained activity, typically involving excess or abandon. A shopping {spree} means buying freely without usual restraint. A drinking {spree} is a binge. A crime {spree} or killing {spree} is a rapid succession of offenses. The word carries energy and lack of inhibition—whether the activity is harmless fun or deadly serious.

Sprees is the plural of spree, a bout of unrestrained activity. A shopping {spree} involves buying many things impulsively. A killing {spree} is a series of murders in quick succession. A crime {spree} strings together multiple offenses. The word usually implies excess and lack of self-control: {The kids went on a candy spree at the fair}.

A sprig is a small stem or shoot of a plant, typically with leaves or flowers attached: {a sprig of parsley}, {a sprig of holly}. The word suggests something decorative or garnishing rather than substantial. Sprig also refers to small headless nails or tacks used in upholstery and glazing.

The noun spring may describe the season following winter when days lengthen and plants start growing; a natural supply of water from the ground (mineral spring); or a device that returns to its original shape when force is removed. Spring also describes a lively quality, suggestive of the rebounding force of spring. To spring is to move suddenly and quickly, often upwards. An instance of this is also called a spring. Something that springs a leak suddenly starts leaking.

A springboard is a flexible board used for diving or gymnastics, mounted so it bends under weight and propels the user upward. The word extends figuratively to anything that launches further action or advancement: {The internship served as a springboard to a full-time position}. To springboard is to use something as such a launching point.

Springs connects to the idea of sudden movement or emergence. Metal springs store and release energy, bouncing back when compressed. Water springs emerge from underground, giving us spring water and hot springs. The season spring marks when life emerges after winter. To spring is to leap or move suddenly: {The cat sprang from the couch}. To spring something on someone is to surprise them: {She sprang the news at dinner}. To spring for something is to pay for it, usually generously: {I'll spring for lunch}.

Springtime is the season of spring, when winter gives way to warming weather and plants begin to grow. The word often carries poetic or nostalgic overtones that plain "spring" lacks: {in the springtime of youth}, {springtime in Paris}. It suggests renewal, freshness, and new beginnings.

Sprinkle means to scatter in drops or small particles: {sprinkle salt on the popcorn}, {sprinkle water on the plants}. Rain that sprinkles falls lightly. As a noun, a sprinkle is a light scattering or a brief, light rain. Sprinkles are also the tiny candy bits scattered on ice cream or cupcakes. Figuratively, something sprinkled through a text or conversation appears here and there: {The speech was sprinkled with jokes}.

A sprinkler is a device that sprays water in a controlled pattern. Lawn sprinklers distribute water across grass and gardens. Fire sprinklers are ceiling-mounted heads that activate automatically when they detect heat, releasing water to suppress flames. The term also applies to trucks or systems that spray water on roads or crops: {The sprinkler system kept the field irrigated through the drought}.

Sprinklers are devices that spray water in a controlled pattern. Lawn sprinklers distribute water across grass and gardens. Fire sprinklers are ceiling-mounted systems that activate automatically when they detect heat, releasing water to suppress flames: {The sprinklers went off and soaked the entire office}. The term is the plural of sprinkler.

Sprinkles are tiny pieces of candy used to decorate baked goods, especially cupcakes and ice cream cones. They come in various colors and shapes—the elongated kind are also called jimmies. To add sprinkles is to scatter them lightly: {She topped the cake with rainbow sprinkles}. A sprinkle of something is a light scattering: {a sprinkle of rain}, {a sprinkle of cinnamon}.

To sprint is to run at full speed over a short distance. Sprinting prioritizes explosive power over endurance—the opposite of distance running. The word extends beyond foot races: {She sprinted to catch the bus}, {We sprinted through the final chapter}. In business, a sprint is a short, intensive work period focused on completing specific tasks, borrowed from Agile software development: {The team finished the prototype in a two-week sprint}. Sprint can also name the brief burst itself: {a sprint to the finish line}.

A sprinter is someone who runs short distances at maximum speed—typically 100, 200, or 400 meters in track and field. The term extends to anyone or anything built for bursts of speed rather than endurance: {She's more of a sprinter than a marathon runner}. In cycling, sprinters specialize in explosive finishes.

Sprinters are runners who specialize in short, fast races—typically 100, 200, or 400 meters. The term extends to anyone or anything designed for brief bursts of speed rather than endurance: {sprinters in cycling}, {a team of sprinters on the relay}. Sprinters build explosive power; distance runners build stamina.

Sprinting is running at top speed over a short distance. The term applies to both competitive track events—the 100-meter dash, 200-meter—and any burst of all-out running: {She sprinted to catch the bus}. Sprinting emphasizes maximum effort that can't be sustained for long, distinguishing it from jogging or distance running.

Sprints are short bursts of running at maximum speed, or by extension, any intense effort over a brief period. Track events under 400 meters are sprints. In software development, a sprint is a fixed timeframe—typically one to four weeks—during which a team completes a set of tasks: {We'll address that bug in the next sprint}. To sprint is to run or work this way: {She sprinted to catch the bus}.

A sprite is a small supernatural being—an elf, fairy, or similar creature, usually mischievous rather than malevolent: {woodland sprites}, {water sprites}. The word suggests lightness and quickness. In computing and video games, a sprite is a two-dimensional image or animation that moves independently on screen, named for its nimble, hovering quality.

Sprites are mythical beings—small, mischievous spirits of the air, water, or woods. The word suggests lightness and quickness: {sprites dancing in the moonlight}. In computing, a sprite is a two-dimensional image or animation integrated into a larger scene, especially in video games: {The game's character sprites were beautifully designed}. Sprite also names a lemon-lime soft drink.

Spritz means to spray or squirt liquid in short bursts: {She spritzed perfume on her wrists}, {Spritz the plants with water}. As a noun, a spritz is such a burst of liquid. The word comes from German and carries a light, casual feel—you spritz rather than douse. A spritz can also be a cocktail made with prosecco, bitter liqueur, and soda water, especially an Aperol spritz.

A spritzer is a drink made by mixing wine with sparkling water or soda water, producing a lighter, fizzy beverage: {She ordered a white wine spritzer}. The term extends to other carbonated mixed drinks: {an orange juice spritzer}. From German spritzen, to spray or squirt.

A sprocket is a toothed wheel that fits into the links of a chain and transmits rotary motion. It is a key element of the drive train of bicycles and motorcycles, and is sometimes called a chain wheel.

Sprout captures the moment when something begins to grow, whether a seed sending up its first shoot or a potato growing eyes in the pantry. The noun refers to these young growths, especially the edible kind like bean sprouts or Brussels sprouts. As a verb, sprout describes rapid emergence: {New housing developments sprouted along the highway}. Children sprout up, beards sprout on faces, and ideas sprout in fertile minds.

Sprouts are young plant growths that have just emerged from seeds or older plant parts. Brussels sprouts, often shortened to just sprouts, are the small cabbage-like vegetables that grow along a thick stalk. Bean sprouts, commonly used in Asian cooking, are the tender shoots of germinated mung beans or soybeans. As a verb, sprout means to begin growing or to send out new growth: {The potatoes sprouted in the pantry}. Figuratively, things that appear suddenly or proliferate can be said to sprout: {New coffee shops sprouted up all over the neighborhood}.

Spruce is a type of evergreen conifer with short, stiff needles and drooping cones, common in northern forests and often used as Christmas trees. The wood is light and resonant, valued for musical instruments and construction. Separately, spruce means neat and trim in appearance: {He looked spruce in his new suit}. To spruce up is to make something tidier or smarter: {We spruced up the apartment before guests arrived}.

Sprung is the past tense and past participle of spring. A leak has sprung, a trap has sprung, someone has sprung from bed. To have sprung for something is to have paid for it: {He sprung for dinner}. In slang, sprung describes being infatuated or obsessed: {She's sprung on him}. Sprung also works as an adjective for mattresses or seats with springs built in.

A spud is a potato—informal but widespread: {I picked up some spuds at the market}. The word also names a narrow spade-like tool for digging or cutting roots. As a verb, to spud is to dig with such a tool, or in oil drilling, to begin drilling a new well.

Spunk has two main meanings united by the idea of vital essence. The older sense is courage, spirit, or determination: {She showed real spunk standing up to them}. Someone with spunk is plucky and spirited. In British slang, spunk is semen—the vital substance in a more literal sense. The slang use has made the word awkward in American speech, where the innocent meaning still dominates.

A spur is a device worn on the heel that a rider uses to prod a horse. From this meaning, some other things that project from a surface (bone spur), or that are used for encouragement, are called spurs. To spur a horse is to use spurs on it. To spur something abstract is to encourage it with a particular action: The company enacted a program to spur innovation in the tech industry. To earn your spurs in some endeavor is to achieve a level of competency.

Spurned is the past tense of spurn, meaning to reject with contempt or disdain. A spurned lover has been romantically rejected: {He couldn't accept being spurned}. Spurned suggests not just refusal but dismissiveness—the rejection stings: {She spurned his offer of help}, {The spurned candidate withdrew from public life}.

Spurred means urged or driven forward, from the literal act of digging spurs into a horse's sides to make it move faster. The word almost always appears figuratively: {Spurred by rising costs, the company cut staff}. What does the spurring is typically a motive, event, or emotion: {spurred by curiosity}, {spurred into action}. As an adjective, spurred describes something equipped with spurs: {spurred boots}, {spurred heels}.

Spurs are pointed devices worn on a rider's heels to urge a horse forward. The word extends to anything that prods or motivates: {The tax break was a spur to investment}. To spur is to urge on: {She spurred her team to finish}. Spurs also names sharp projections—a rooster's leg spike, a mountain ridge jutting outward, or a short branch line from a main railroad or road.

A spurt is a sudden burst or gush—of liquid, energy, or activity. Water spurts from a broken pipe. A runner spurts ahead in a final burst of speed. Growth spurts are periods of rapid development: {He grew three inches in a spurt}. To spurt is to gush or surge: {Blood spurted from the wound}. Also spelled spirt.

A spy is someone who secretly gathers information, especially for a government or military organization: {Soviet spies infiltrated the agency}. The word extends to anyone who watches covertly: {neighborhood spies peering through curtains}. To spy is to observe secretly or to catch sight of: {I spied him across the room}. To {spy on} someone is to monitor them without their knowledge.

Spycraft is the skills, techniques, and tradecraft used in espionage—surveillance, code-breaking, disguise, dead drops, and similar covert operations. The term covers both the practical methods and the broader art of intelligence work: {She learned spycraft at the agency's training facility}. Often romanticized in fiction, actual spycraft tends toward patience and paperwork.

A spyglass is a small handheld telescope, the kind once used by sailors and explorers to see distant objects: {The captain raised his spyglass to scan the horizon}. The word evokes nautical adventure and pirate stories more than modern optics.

Spying is the act of secretly gathering information, especially about enemies, competitors, or governments. The word covers everything from intelligence operatives working abroad to children peeking at hidden birthday presents. {She caught him spying on the neighbors}. Corporate spying targets trade secrets; espionage is the formal term for state-level spying.

A spymaster is someone who directs espionage operations, typically running a network of agents and coordinating intelligence gathering. The term evokes Cold War intrigue and fiction more than official job titles: {He was the CIA's spymaster in Berlin during the 1960s}. The word combines operational authority with a suggestion of shadowy expertise.

Spyware is software that secretly monitors a user's activity and transmits information without consent. It may track browsing habits, capture keystrokes, or harvest passwords and financial data. Spyware often installs itself covertly, bundled with legitimate downloads or through security exploits: {The computer was infected with spyware that recorded everything she typed}.

A squabble is a noisy argument over something trivial—a petty dispute that generates more heat than the matter deserves. Siblings squabble over toys, neighbors squabble over property lines, politicians squabble over procedural details. The word captures both the pettiness and the noise: {The meeting devolved into squabbling about who said what}.

Squabbles are petty quarrels or minor disputes, typically noisy and undignified: {The siblings' constant squabbles drove their parents crazy}. The word suggests arguments over trivial matters rather than serious conflicts. To squabble is to engage in such quarreling: {They squabbled over who got the window seat}.

Squabbling is engaging in petty, noisy quarreling—bickering over minor matters without real resolution. The word suggests trivial disputes rather than serious conflict: {The children were squabbling over who got the last cookie}. Squabbling often implies ongoing back-and-forth rather than a single outburst: {Congress spent months squabbling while nothing got done}.

A squad is a small group of people working together, originally and still commonly a military unit of soldiers under a single leader. The term extends to police units, sports teams, and any coordinated group: {The bomb squad arrived within minutes.} In casual use, especially among younger speakers, squad refers to one's close friend group: {I'm going out with my squad tonight.} Squad goals describes an achievement or lifestyle that a friend group aspires to.

Squadrismo refers to the organized political violence of the Fascist squads (*squadre d'azione*) in Italy during the early 1920s. These paramilitary groups, known as Blackshirts, attacked socialists, labor organizers, and political opponents through beatings, forced castor oil, and property destruction. The term now describes any systematic political intimidation by organized thugs: {The opposition accused the ruling party of squadrismo tactics}.

A squadron is a unit of military organization, typically a subdivision of a larger force. In air forces, it's a group of aircraft and personnel under one command. In navies, it's a detachment of warships assigned to a particular duty. The term extends to any organized group moving together: {A squadron of motorcycles escorted the procession}.

Squads is the plural of squad—a small organized group working together. Military squads are tactical units of soldiers. Police squads handle specific duties: {bomb squad}, {vice squad}. Sports squads are teams or rosters. In casual use, your squad is your close friend group: {I'm heading out with the squad tonight}.

A squall is a sudden, violent gust of wind, often accompanied by rain or snow. Squalls blow up quickly and pass quickly—sailors watch for them. The word extends to any brief, intense outburst: {a squall of protest}. Separately, to squall is to cry or scream harshly, as an infant does: {The baby squalled through the night}.

Squalor is a state of extreme filth, poverty, and neglect. It describes conditions that are both physically dirty and morally degrading: {They found the children living in squalor}. The word suggests not just mess but accumulated wretchedness—garbage, vermin, broken fixtures, the visible evidence of desperation or abandonment.

To squander is to waste something valuable through carelessness or poor judgment—typically money, time, or opportunity. The word carries moral weight, suggesting the loss was preventable: {He squandered his inheritance on gambling}. You can squander resources, talent, goodwill, or a lead in a game. The noun squander exists but is rare.

Squandered is the past tense of squander, meaning to waste something valuable through careless or foolish use. Money, time, opportunities, and talent are commonly squandered: {He squandered his inheritance on bad investments}. The word carries moral weight—what's squandered could have been put to good use but wasn't.

Squandering is wasting something valuable—money, time, opportunity, talent—through carelessness or foolish spending. The word implies having something worth preserving and letting it slip away: {He's squandering his inheritance on gambling}, {She squandered her early lead in the race}. Unlike merely spending, squandering suggests regrettable loss.

The archetypal square, a rectangle with all sides equal, influences the many other meanings of the word. One of the most common is to designate a public space that is roughly square, bounded by four streets: Hanover Square. Square has frequent use as an adjective, where it usually denotes the quality of having a right angle, or a measurement arising from a space with the same length on each of four sides (a square mile). In math, a square is the result of multiplying a number by itself. When you square a number, you raise it to the power of two to arrive at its square.

Squared describes something multiplied by itself: {three squared is nine}. In geometry, squared refers to right angles or rectangular shapes: {squared corners}, {squared shoulders}. To get squared away is to get organized or settled. If you're squared up with someone, you've settled accounts or are facing them directly, ready to fight or negotiate.

Squares is the plural of square—a four-sided figure with equal sides and right angles, or anything resembling one: city squares, square tiles, the squares on a checkerboard. A square is also someone considered old-fashioned or socially out of touch: {Don't be such a square}. The verb squares means to make even or settle: {That squares our account}. To square with something is to align or agree: {His story doesn't square with the evidence}.

Squash covers two unrelated words. One is a gourd-like vegetable with firm flesh and a thick rind, including varieties like butternut, acorn, and zucchini. The other squash means to crush or compress something flat, or to suppress or silence: {The regime squashed the rebellion before it could spread}. Squash is also a racket sport played in an enclosed court, named for the soft, squashable ball used. As a noun, a squash can be a crowded situation: {It was a tight squash getting everyone into the elevator}.

To squat is to crouch with your feet on the ground and your legs bent all the way. Another way to squat is to occupy a property that does not belong to you, without paying rent. Such a property is sometimes called a squat. A squat can also be an instance of squatting, on your heels; some exercises that incorporate this movement are called squats. The adjective squat means thick and relatively short. In slang, squat can mean anything or nothing: You don’t know squat.

Squats are an exercise in which you lower your body by bending the knees, then rise back up—a fundamental movement for building leg and core strength: {I do fifty squats every morning}. The plural also refers to places where people live without legal claim: {The police cleared the squats along the riverbank}. In weightlifting, squat numbers indicate how much someone can lift in this position: {My squats are finally improving}.

A squatter is someone who occupies land or property without legal title or permission. Squatters may settle on abandoned buildings, unused land, or vacant lots. In some jurisdictions, long-term squatters can eventually claim legal rights through adverse possession. The term also applies to someone who crouches or sits on their heels: {She assumed a squatter's position by the campfire}.

Squatters are people who occupy property—typically land or buildings—without legal right or payment. The term carries connotations of illegitimacy, though squatters may occupy abandoned structures out of necessity: {Squatters had been living in the condemned building for years}. In some legal systems, long-term squatters can eventually claim ownership rights. Squatter also names someone in a squatting position, or historically, a settler on unclaimed land.

Squatting is crouching with knees bent and buttocks near the heels: {She was squatting by the fire}. In property law, squatting means occupying vacant land or buildings without permission or legal right. Squatters may gain certain rights through prolonged occupation in some jurisdictions. In weightlifting, squatting is performing squats—lowering the body while bearing a barbell across the shoulders.

Squawk is the harsh, abrupt cry of a bird—especially a startled or agitated one. By extension, people squawk when they complain loudly or protest: {Customers squawked about the price increase}. The word works as both verb and noun: {The parrot let out a squawk}. In aviation, a squawk is a transponder code assigned to aircraft for identification.

Squawking is the present participle of squawk, which means to make a loud, harsh, abrupt cry like that of a startled bird. People squawk when they complain loudly or protest noisily about something: {The customers were squawking about the price increase}. As a noun, squawking refers to this kind of noise or complaint. In aviation, squawking refers to an aircraft transmitting a specific identification code via its transponder.

A squeak is a short, high-pitched sound—the noise a mouse makes, or a door with rusty hinges, or sneakers on a gym floor. To squeak is to make such a sound, or to barely succeed: {She squeaked through the exam}. A {squeaky wheel gets the grease} means those who complain loudly get attention. A {narrow squeak} is a close call.

Squeal is a high-pitched, prolonged cry or sound—the noise a pig makes, or a child in excitement, or brakes that need replacing. To squeal is to make such a sound: {The tires squealed as the car took the corner}. In slang, to squeal is to inform on someone to authorities: {He squealed to the cops about the whole operation}.

Squealing is making a high-pitched, prolonged sound—the noise of brakes, pigs, or excited children. The word often suggests involuntary or uncontrolled vocalization: {The tires were squealing as the car took the corner}. Informally, squealing means informing on someone to authorities: {He's squealing to the cops}.

Squeamish describes excessive sensitivity to unpleasant sights, smells, or ideas—particularly blood, gore, or bodily functions. A squeamish person might faint at the sight of a needle or turn away during surgery scenes in movies: {I'm too squeamish to watch}. The word extends to moral fastidiousness: {Don't be squeamish about asking for what you're owed}.

To squeeze is to apply pressure from two sides, or all around, like you might squeeze a lemon to extract juice. If you squeeze a person, you apply unwelcome pressure, perhaps as a demand for money. A squeeze is an instance of squeezing something tangible, or the result of being pressured. If you’re in a tight squeeze, you’re in a difficult position. To put the squeeze on someone is to pressure them. They will probably feel the squeeze when you do.

Squeezed is the past tense of squeeze—to press firmly from opposite sides or to extract by pressing: {She squeezed his hand}, {He squeezed juice from the lemon}. Figuratively, squeezed describes pressure or constraint: {squeezed for time}, {squeezed out of the market}. A {squeezed middle} refers to people financially pressured from multiple directions.

Squeezing is applying pressure from opposite sides, typically to compress, extract, or force through a narrow space. You squeeze an orange to get juice, squeeze toothpaste from a tube, or squeeze someone's hand in affection or reassurance. To squeeze into a tight space is to fit with difficulty: {We squeezed into the back seat}. A financial squeeze is pressure from limited resources.

Squelch captures the wet, sucking sound made when walking through mud or soggy ground, and by extension any act of forcefully suppressing or silencing something. If you squelch a rumor or squelch dissent, you crush it decisively. {She squelched through the marsh in her rubber boots.} {The CEO squelched speculation about layoffs.} In electronics, squelch refers to a circuit that suppresses background noise when no signal is present.

A squid is a marine mollusk with a torpedo-shaped body, eight arms, two longer tentacles, and the ability to squirt ink when threatened. Squid are eaten worldwide—fried calamari being the most familiar preparation. In slang, squid describes an inexperienced or reckless motorcyclist, typically one who rides without proper gear: {Some squid in shorts nearly wiped out on the highway}.

Squids are marine mollusks with elongated bodies, large eyes, eight arms, and two longer tentacles. They move by jet propulsion, squirting water through a siphon. Squid is also common seafood, often fried as calamari. In slang, a squid is an inexperienced or reckless motorcyclist: {Some squid in shorts and flip-flops nearly wiped out on the highway}.

A squiggle is a short, wavy or curly line, typically drawn carelessly or playfully: {The toddler's drawing was just a mess of squiggles}. Squiggles appear in doodles, signatures, and informal notation. The word suggests something without precise form—random, wiggly marks rather than deliberate shapes. As a verb, to squiggle is to make such marks or to move in a wriggling way.

Squiggly describes lines or shapes that twist and curve irregularly, like a child's scribble or a worm's path: {squiggly handwriting}, {a squiggly line under the misspelled word}. The word suggests something playful or imprecise rather than geometric. In typography, the tilde (~) is sometimes called a squiggly.

To squint is to partially close the eyes, either to see more clearly in bright light or to focus on something distant or small: {She squinted at the tiny print}. A squint can also be a quick or furtive glance: {He took a squint at the document}. In medical contexts, squint refers to a condition where the eyes don't align properly—one eye turns inward or outward while the other looks straight ahead.

Squinting is partially closing the eyes, either to see more clearly in bright light or to focus on something distant or unclear: {She stood squinting into the sun}. People also squint when suspicious or skeptical, narrowing their eyes as if scrutinizing something: {He squinted at the contract before signing}.

A squire was historically a young nobleman serving a knight, training for knighthood himself. The term later came to mean a country gentleman or landowner, especially in rural England: {the village squire}. As a form of address, squire is informal and slightly old-fashioned, used between men: {What can I get you, squire?} To squire someone is to escort them, especially a woman to a social event.

Squirm is to twist and wriggle the body, especially from discomfort or restlessness: {The child squirmed in her seat}. The word extends to psychological discomfort—feeling uneasy or embarrassed: {He squirmed when asked about his past}. {The question made everyone squirm}.

Squirming is twisting and wriggling the body, typically from discomfort, restlessness, or an attempt to escape restraint. A child squirms in a dentist's chair; a fish squirms on a hook. Figuratively, squirming describes acute embarrassment or unease: {I was squirming through his entire speech}. The image is of someone who can't sit still under pressure.

Squirmy describes restless, wriggling movement—the kind of fidgeting that comes from discomfort, impatience, or an inability to sit still. Children are often squirmy during long car rides or boring events. The word can also characterize situations that make someone feel awkward or uneasy: {The interview got squirmy when they asked about my gap year}. Something squirmy might literally writhe, like a bucket of bait worms, or just make you want to look away.

A squirrel is a small, bushy-tailed rodent that climbs trees and hoards nuts. The verb means to hide or store away for future use: {She squirreled away money for emergencies}. To squirrel around is to move erratically or fidget restlessly. Squirrelly describes someone acting nervous, unpredictable, or slightly crazy.

Squirreling is the act of stashing things away for later, like a squirrel hiding nuts. The word usually implies accumulating small amounts over time: {She's been squirreling away money for years}. It can suggest hoarding or secretive saving. Also spelled squirrelling.

Squirrels is the plural of squirrel—small, bushy-tailed rodents that climb trees and hoard nuts. As a verb, to squirrel something away is to store or hide it for future use, like the animal caching food: {She squirreled away money for emergencies}. To squirrel around is to move in quick, erratic bursts.

Squirt means to force liquid out in a thin stream or jet: {She squirted ketchup on her fries}, {Water squirted from the hose}. The liquid itself can squirt: {Juice squirted everywhere when I bit into the orange}. A squirt is an instance of squirting or the stream produced. Informally, squirt is a dismissive term for a small or insignificant person, especially a child: {Listen here, squirt}.

Squish is to press or squeeze something soft so it deforms or flattens: {She squished the clay between her fingers}, {I accidentally squished a bug}. The word is onomatopoeic—it sounds like what it describes. As a noun, a squish is the act or sound of squishing: {the squish of wet shoes on linoleum}. Something squishy yields easily to pressure.

Squished is the past tense of squish, meaning pressed or crushed so that something flattens, deforms, or oozes: {The tomato got squished at the bottom of the grocery bag}. It suggests soft or yielding material compressed with some force. Squished also describes being packed tightly into a space: {We were all squished together in the back seat}.

Squishy describes something soft and yielding that compresses when squeezed: {a squishy stress ball}, {squishy mud between your toes}. The word suggests pliability and often moisture or give. Figuratively, squishy means vague or lacking rigor: {squishy logic}, {squishy on the details}. In political contexts, squishy describes someone whose positions seem soft or unreliable: {a squishy moderate}.

Stab is a verb and noun centered on the sudden piercing of something with a pointed object, typically a knife or blade. A stabbing is usually a violent attack, but the word extends to any sharp, sudden motion or sensation: a stab of {pain}, a stab of {guilt}. If you take a stab at something, you make an attempt at it without much preparation or confidence. To stab someone in the back is to betray them, especially while pretending friendship.

Stabbing describes a sharp, sudden, piercing sensation or action. As an adjective, it most often modifies pain: {a stabbing pain in my chest} suggests something intense and localized, as if caused by a knife. The noun stabbing refers to an attack in which someone is wounded or killed with a pointed weapon. The word carries violence in both uses—whether literal assault or the figurative assault of acute physical discomfort.

Stability is the quality of being stable—steady, firm, not easily changed or disturbed. Physical stability keeps structures standing and objects balanced: {The table lacks stability on uneven ground}. Emotional or mental stability suggests consistent, reliable temperament. Financial stability means secure resources. Political stability implies enduring governance without upheaval. In science, stability describes systems that resist change or return to equilibrium after disturbance.

Stable describes something firmly established and resistant to change or disruption. A stable {structure} won't collapse; a stable {relationship} endures; a stable {patient} isn't getting worse. The word implies reliability and equilibrium. As a noun, a stable is a building where horses are kept. To stable a horse is to house it there. A stable of something—{athletes}, {writers}, {products}—is a group under common management.

Stables is a building or complex where horses are housed, fed, and cared for. The word often appears as a singular noun despite its plural form: {The stables burned down last night}. A racing stable is a collection of horses under one trainer's management. To stable a horse is to keep it in such a facility.

Staccato describes sounds that are short, sharp, and detached from one another. In music, staccato notes are played crisply, with clear separation between them—the opposite of legato. The term extends to any clipped, abrupt manner of speaking or any rapid succession of distinct sounds: {staccato bursts of gunfire}, {She spoke in staccato sentences}.

A stack is an orderly pile, typically higher than it is wide. A tall chimney can be called a stack or smokestack. In computing, the stack is the part of memory where new things are added on top of the last thing put there. If you blow your stack, you lose your temper. To stack items is to put them in a stack. Stacking chairs are designed to be stacked up when stored. If something is stacked against you, you are at a disadvantage.

Stacked describes things arranged in a pile or layers: {stacked boxes}, {stacked pancakes}. In slang, stacked means having large breasts—the image is of a woman whose chest sticks out in front. To say the deck is stacked or the odds are stacked against you means circumstances have been arranged to favor one side unfairly. In gaming and sports, a stacked team or lineup is loaded with talent.

Stacking is arranging things in a pile, one atop another: {stacking boxes}, {stacking firewood}. The term extends to any layered accumulation—stacking advantages, stacking the odds. In gaming, stacking often means combining multiple bonuses or effects: {The buffs don't stack}. To {stack the deck} is to arrange cards dishonestly, or more broadly, to rig an outcome.

Stacks are things piled one atop another: a stack of {books}, a stack of {pancakes}, a stack of {bills}. A smokestack releases exhaust vertically. Library stacks are shelving areas. In computing, a stack is a data structure where the last item added is the first removed. In slang, stacks means large amounts of money: {He's got stacks}. To be stacked against someone means circumstances favor their opponent.

A stadium is a large outdoor venue for sporting events and concerts, typically oval or horseshoe-shaped with tiered seating surrounding a central field or stage. The word comes from an ancient Greek unit of distance—about 600 feet—which became the name for the track where footraces were held. Modern stadiums seat tens of thousands: {The stadium was packed for the championship game}.

Staff has two core meanings. One is a long stick used as a walking aid, weapon, or symbol of authority—a shepherd's staff, a wizard's staff, the staff of office. The other meaning is the people employed by an organization: {The staff meets every Monday}. As a verb, to staff is to provide workers: {We need to staff the front desk}. In music, a staff is the set of five horizontal lines on which notes are written.

A stag is an adult male deer, especially a red deer. The word extends to men-only gatherings: a stag {party} or stag {night} celebrates a groom before his wedding. To go stag is to attend an event without a date: {He went stag to the prom}. In finance, a stag buys new share offerings hoping to sell quickly at a profit.

A stage is a raised platform where performances occur—theatrical shows, speeches, concerts. By extension, the stage means the theater as a profession: {She's been on the stage for twenty years}. Stage also means a point in a process or development: {the early stages of pregnancy}, {a stage of grief}. To stage something is to produce it for an audience or to arrange it for effect: {stage a play}, {stage a protest}, {stage a photo op}. A stagecoach was a horse-drawn vehicle traveling in stages between stations.

A stagecoach is a large horse-drawn carriage that historically carried passengers and mail along established routes, stopping at stations to change horses. The stage in the name refers to these segments of the journey. {The stagecoach arrived at noon, covered in dust from the trail.} The word evokes the American West and an era before railroads.

Stagecoaches were horse-drawn passenger vehicles that traveled scheduled routes between towns, the primary means of long-distance land travel before railroads. The name refers to traveling in stages—stops where fresh horses replaced tired ones. {The stagecoach arrived twice weekly carrying mail and passengers.} Stagecoach robberies became iconic in Western lore.

Staged describes something arranged or performed rather than occurring naturally or spontaneously. A staged {photograph} is posed rather than candid. A staged {robbery} is faked, meant to deceive. In theater, a staged {production} has been mounted for performance. The word often implies artifice or manipulation: {The whole confrontation looked staged for the cameras}.

A stagedive is the act of jumping from a concert stage into the crowd below, trusting the audience to catch you. Associated with punk and rock shows, it's both a performer's gesture of abandon and a fan's act of participation. To stagedive is to make such a leap: {He stagedived during the encore and the crowd carried him to the back}.

Stagediving is leaping from a concert stage into the crowd below, trusting the audience to catch you and pass you along on raised hands. It's a ritual of punk and metal shows, equal parts performer bravado and audience participation: {The singer went stagediving during the encore}. Security guards generally disapprove.

Stagefright is the nervous anxiety that grips performers before or during an appearance—the racing heart, sweaty palms, and mental blankness that come from facing an audience. The condition affects even experienced performers: {She's done a hundred shows but still gets stagefright}. Also spelled as two words: stage fright.

Stagehands are the workers who handle scenery, props, lighting, and other technical elements during theatrical productions or live events. They move set pieces between scenes, manage curtains, and ensure smooth transitions—essential but typically unseen by the audience. {The stagehands struck the set after closing night.}

Stages are distinct phases in a process or development: the stages of grief, stages of cancer, stages of a rocket. A stage is also a raised platform where performances occur—actors on a stage, a concert stage. To stage something is to arrange or present it: stage a play, stage a protest, stage a comeback. The stage refers to the acting profession: {She's been on the stage for thirty years}. In compounds, stage appears in stagecoach (a horse-drawn vehicle making scheduled stops) and stage fright (nervousness before performing).

Stagestruck describes someone captivated by the theater and eager to become an actor. The condition typically afflicts young people who dream of performing: {She's been stagestruck ever since her first school play}. The word carries a faintly patronizing tone, suggesting naive infatuation rather than serious ambition.

Stagger captures the idea of unsteady, lurching movement—the way someone walks when drunk, injured, or overwhelmed. {He staggered out of the bar at closing time.} By extension, if news or a revelation staggers you, it throws you off balance mentally. The verb also means to arrange things in an alternating or overlapping pattern: {staggered work shifts}, {staggered seating}. As a noun, stagger refers to an unsteady gait or, in the plural staggers, a disease affecting livestock that causes them to walk erratically.

Staggered describes things arranged in alternating positions or times rather than aligned. Staggered seating places each row offset from the one ahead for better sightlines. Staggered work hours spread arrivals across time. As the past tense of stagger, it means walked unsteadily or was shocked: {She staggered under the weight}; {I was staggered by the news}.

Staggering describes something so extreme it makes you figuratively lose your balance. A staggering {sum} or staggering {loss} is hard to comprehend. Staggering {incompetence} leaves you reeling. The word intensifies scale, whether of achievement, failure, or sheer quantity: {The staggering cost of the project forced them to reconsider}.

Staging is the process of preparing or arranging something for presentation or use. In theater, staging is how a production is put on—the blocking, sets, and visual elements that bring a script to life. The word extends to any deliberate arrangement: {the staging of a photo op}, {the staging of troops before an invasion}. In real estate, staging means furnishing a home to make it more appealing to buyers. In medicine and oncology, staging determines how far a disease has progressed: {The cancer staging showed it hadn't spread}. In computing, a staging environment is where software is tested before going live.

Stagnant describes water or air that doesn't flow or circulate, becoming foul or stale: {a stagnant pond}, {stagnant air in the basement}. The meaning extends to anything showing no activity, growth, or development: {stagnant wages}, {a stagnant economy}, {His career had grown stagnant}. The word implies not just stillness but deterioration from lack of movement.

Stagnation is the condition of not moving, growing, or developing. Water that doesn't flow becomes stagnant; economies and careers can similarly stagnate. {The company fell into stagnation after years without innovation.} The word carries negative connotations—stillness where movement is expected or needed.

Stags is the plural of stag—male deer, especially red deer. The word extends to men attending social events without female companions: {a stags-only poker night}. Stag parties (or stag dos in British English) are pre-wedding celebrations for the groom. In finance, stags are speculators who buy new share issues hoping to sell immediately at profit.

A stain is a discoloration left by a substance that has soaked into a surface: {a coffee stain on the carpet}, {grass stains on her jeans}. The verb means to leave such a mark, or to color deliberately with dye or pigment: {stain the deck}. Figuratively, a stain is something that damages reputation or character: {a stain on his honor}. Stainless steel resists corrosion; a stainless record has no blemishes.

Stained describes something marked or discolored by a substance that has penetrated its surface: {a stained tablecloth}, {coffee-stained teeth}. The word extends to reputation or character—a stained {record} or stained {honor} carries the mark of past wrongdoing. Stained {glass} is colored during manufacture, not damaged, though the word is the same.

Stainless means without stains or blemishes. A stainless {reputation} is unblemished. Stainless {steel} is an alloy resistant to rust and corrosion—so common that stainless alone often means stainless steel: {The kitchen has stainless appliances}. The word emphasizes purity or durability: {a stainless record of service}.

Stains are marks or discolorations left on a surface, typically from spilled liquids or contact with substances that penetrate or bond with the material: {coffee stains on the carpet}, {grass stains on jeans}. To stain is to leave such a mark, or to apply coloring deliberately: {stain the deck}. Figuratively, a stain is a blemish on reputation or character: {a stain on his record}.

A stair is one of a series of steps for moving between levels. Stairs usually refers to the whole set: {Take the stairs to the second floor}. A staircase or stairway is the structure containing them. {Stair} alone sometimes means the full flight: {the back stair}, {below stairs}.

A staircase is a set of stairs together with its surrounding structure—the walls, railings, and supporting framework that form a complete unit: {a spiral staircase}, {the grand staircase in the hotel lobby}. Where stairs refers to the steps themselves, staircase emphasizes the architectural whole.

Stairs are a series of steps that allow people to move between different levels of a building or structure. Each individual step is called a stair, though the singular form appears mainly in compounds like {staircase} and {stairwell}. The phrase {up the stairs} or {down the stairs} indicates direction of travel. To {take the stairs} means to walk rather than use an elevator or escalator.

A stairway is a set of stairs providing passage between floors or levels of a building. It includes the steps themselves along with any railings, landings, or enclosing walls. The term is roughly interchangeable with staircase, though stairway more often suggests the passage itself rather than the architectural structure: {The stairway to the basement was dark and narrow}.

A stake is a pointed piece of wood or metal driven into the ground—for support, boundary marking, or tying something to. To stake a plant is to secure it upright. To stake a claim is to assert ownership, from the practice of marking land boundaries. Stakes are also what you wager in a bet or risk in an enterprise: {The stakes are too high}. When the stakes are raised, more is at risk. To have a stake in something is to have an interest in its outcome. To stake someone is to provide them with money or resources: {She staked him to a new set of tools}.

A stakeout is a period of covert surveillance, typically by police watching a location for criminal activity: {We've had a stakeout on the warehouse for three days}. The term comes from the idea of staking out territory—claiming a position and holding it. By extension, any patient waiting and watching: {Her stakeout of the sale rack finally paid off}.

Stakeouts are periods of covert surveillance, typically by law enforcement watching a location for criminal activity or waiting for a suspect to appear: {The detectives spent three nights on stakeout outside the warehouse}. The term evokes long hours in parked cars with coffee and binoculars. Extended to any patient watching and waiting: {Her stakeout of the mailbox finally paid off when the letter arrived}.

Stakes are what you stand to win or lose. In gambling, stakes are the money wagered: {high-stakes poker}, {The stakes are $100 per hand}. More broadly, stakes are what's at risk in any venture or conflict: {The stakes couldn't be higher—if we fail, the company folds}. Stakes also means pointed posts driven into the ground, from which the gambling sense derives—wagers were once placed on or near a stake marking the finish line.

Staking is the act of marking or claiming territory with stakes, or of supporting something—usually a plant—by tying it to a stake: {staking tomatoes}. To stake out a location is to watch it covertly: {The detectives spent weeks staking out the warehouse}. In gambling and investment, staking means putting up money: {She's staking her savings on this venture}. In cryptocurrency, staking refers to locking up coins to support a blockchain network and earn rewards.

A stalactite is a mineral formation that hangs from the ceiling of a cave, created over thousands of years as water drips through rock and deposits dissolved minerals. Stalactites grow downward like icicles: {The cave was filled with stalactites glistening in the lamplight}. The companion formation growing upward from the floor is a stalagmite.

A stalagmite is a cone-shaped mineral deposit that rises from the floor of a cave, formed by the slow dripping of mineral-rich water from above. Stalagmites grow upward, while their counterparts stalactites hang downward from the ceiling. When they meet, they form a column.

Stalagmites are cone-shaped mineral formations that rise from the floor of caves, built up over millennia by dripping water depositing dissolved limestone. They grow upward from the ground, unlike stalactites, which hang from above. When the two meet, they form a column. {The cave tour wound past massive stalagmites taller than a person.}

Stale characterizes negative qualities that arise when something is no longer fresh or new. Stale bread is hard and dry. Stale ideas or news are familiar, known, and offer nothing interesting. Stale things smell or taste unpleasant. The infrequent verb stale means become stale.

Stalemate is a position in chess where the player to move has no legal moves but is not in check—the game ends in a draw. By extension, stalemate describes any deadlock or impasse where neither side can advance: {Contract negotiations reached a stalemate}. The verb means to bring to such a standstill: {The opposing factions stalemated each other}.

Stalemates is the plural of stalemate, a situation where neither side can advance or win. The term comes from chess, where a player not in check has no legal move—the game ends in a draw. More broadly, stalemates are deadlocks or impasses: {The negotiations reached stalemates on several key issues}. As a verb, stalemates means brings to such a standstill.

Stalk names the stem or main axis of a plant, or any slender supporting structure. Eyes may be on stalks, as with crabs.
