Stingy describes someone reluctant to spend money or share resources—unwilling to give more than absolutely necessary. A stingy tipper leaves the minimum. A stingy portion is smaller than expected. The word carries judgment: being stingy isn't prudent or thrifty, it's ungenerous. {Don't be stingy with the butter.}

Stink is about bad smells. As a verb, it means to emit an offensive odor: {The garbage stinks}. As a noun, it denotes the smell itself or a fuss raised about something: {They made a big stink about the new policy}. Figuratively, if something stinks, it's very bad or suspicious: {The whole deal stinks}. To stink at something is to be terrible at it. If you're stinking rich, you have an offensive amount of money.

A stinkbomb is a small device that releases a foul smell when broken or activated, used as a prank. The classic version is a glass vial of hydrogen sulfide or similar compound that shatters when thrown: {Someone set off a stinkbomb in the cafeteria}. Figuratively, anything that creates a noxious situation: {His resignation letter was a stinkbomb}.

A stinker is something or someone that stinks—literally or figuratively. A bad movie is a stinker. A difficult problem is a stinker. The word often carries affection when applied to misbehaving children or pets: {You little stinker, you ate all the cookies}. A {real stinker} of a day is memorably awful.

Stinks is the third-person singular of the verb stink, meaning to emit a foul odor. It's also commonly used as an informal exclamation or assessment meaning something is bad, unfair, or disappointing: {This whole situation stinks}. The phrase {it stinks} often introduces a complaint: {It stinks that we have to work on Saturday}. If something {stinks of} a quality, it reeks of it or strongly suggests it: {The whole deal stinks of corruption}.

Stinky means having an unpleasant smell: {stinky cheese}, {stinky socks}. The word is casual and often playful—parents use it with children, and it can suggest mild disgust rather than genuine offense. Figuratively, something stinky is suspicious or of poor quality: {That deal sounds stinky to me}.

Stir means to move something around, typically a liquid or mixture, using circular motions: {Stir the soup so it doesn't burn}. More broadly, to stir is to cause movement or activity: {The wind stirred the leaves}. To stir emotions is to arouse them: {The speech stirred the crowd}. If you don't stir from a place, you don't move from it. A stir is commotion or excitement: {The announcement caused quite a stir}. In slang, stir means prison: {He did ten years in stir}.

Stir-fry is a cooking technique where ingredients are rapidly fried in a small amount of very hot oil while being continuously stirred: {I'll stir-fry some vegetables for dinner}. The method originated in Chinese cuisine and produces dishes that are crisp and quickly cooked. As a noun, a stir-fry is a dish prepared this way: {We ordered the beef stir-fry}. Also spelled stir fry.

Stirred is the past tense and past participle of stir, which means to move something around in a circular motion, typically with a utensil: {She stirred her coffee}. Beyond physical mixing, stir conveys causing movement or activity where there was none: {The news stirred controversy}. If something stirs you, it provokes an emotional response: {The documentary stirred feelings I'd long forgotten}. To be stirred is to be roused or moved, whether physically awakened or emotionally affected.

Stirring works as both adjective and verb, each tied to the idea of movement or agitation. The verb means to mix by moving something through a substance {stirring the soup}, or to rouse from stillness {nothing stirred in the house}. As an adjective, stirring describes something that moves the emotions—typically in an inspiring or exciting way: {a stirring speech}, {stirring music}. The noun stirring denotes early signs of activity or feeling: {the first stirrings of spring}.

A stirrup is a loop or ring that hangs from a saddle to support a rider's foot. Stirrups come in pairs, one on each side, allowing the rider to mount and maintain balance. The shape extends to similar foot supports: the stirrups on a gynecological examination table, or the small bone in the middle ear (also called the stapes). {She slipped her boots into the stirrups and urged the horse forward.}

Stirrups are the metal loops hanging from a saddle that hold a rider's feet. They provide stability and leverage for mounting, riding, and dismounting a horse: {She put her foot in the stirrup and swung into the saddle}. In medical contexts, stirrups are the supports on an examination table that hold a patient's legs apart and elevated during gynecological procedures.

A stitch is one passage of a needle and thread through fabric, or the fastening that results from this. The term is the same for knitting and crocheting; different kinds of stitches are indicated by modifiers (garter stitch, slip stitch, purl stitch, cross stitch). To stitch fabric is to join it with stitches. If you stitch together abstract things, you put them together in a provisional or haphazard way. A different kind of stitch is a sudden pain, especially in your side.

Stitches is the plural of stitch—a single loop of thread in sewing or a single movement of the needle. In medicine, stitches are sutures closing a wound: {She needed twelve stitches}. A stitch can also be a sharp pain in the side from exertion. To be {in stitches} is to laugh uncontrollably: {His impression of the boss had us in stitches}.

Stitching is the work of making stitches—the loops of thread that hold fabric or other materials together. It refers both to the process and its result: {The stitching on this jacket is coming loose}. Visible stitching may be decorative; invisible stitching hides the seams. In bookbinding, stitching holds pages together. The word extends to any row of punctures resembling sewn thread.

Most of the varied and frequently encountered meanings of stock can be related in some way to the notion of supply and property. The stock in a stock exchange is nominal ownership in companies. The stock of a retail business is the supply of goods it has for sale, and the stock of a rancher is all of her live animals. A stock of housing is the amount of it available for use. The verb meanings of stock mainly have to do with products and retail trade: if you stock the shelves, you fill them with goods. A seller who stocks a particular item offers it for sale and has it on hand. If you stock up on something, you get a supply of it.

A stockade is a defensive barrier made of upright wooden posts or stakes, typically enclosing a fort or settlement: {The colonists built a stockade around the village}. By extension, a stockade is a military prison or detention area, especially for temporary confinement. As a verb, to stockade is to fortify with such a barrier or to confine in a military prison.

A stockbroker is a professional who buys and sells stocks and other securities on behalf of clients, typically working for a brokerage firm. Stockbrokers earn commissions on trades and may also provide investment advice: {My stockbroker recommended diversifying into bonds}. The role has diminished as online trading platforms let individuals manage their own portfolios.

A stocking is a close-fitting covering for the foot and leg, typically made of knit fabric and extending to the knee or thigh. Stockings are often sheer and held up by garters or a garter belt, distinguishing them from pantyhose. In Christmas tradition, a stocking is a decorative sock hung by the fireplace to be filled with small gifts: {The children hung their stockings on Christmas Eve}. To stock is to supply or fill with goods, and stocking as a gerund refers to this activity: {She spent the morning stocking shelves}.

Stockings are close-fitting garments covering the foot and leg, typically reaching the thigh. Before the mid-twentieth century, stockings were standard legwear for both sexes; now they're worn mainly by women, often held up by garters or a garter belt. {She wore silk stockings with seams up the back}. Christmas stockings are decorative socks hung to receive small gifts. Stocking feet means wearing stockings but no shoes: {He padded around in his stocking feet}.

A stockpile is a large accumulated supply of materials or goods held in reserve: {a stockpile of weapons}, {emergency food stockpiles}. The term often appears in military or strategic contexts—nations stockpile ammunition, oil, or medical supplies against future need. As a verb, to stockpile is to accumulate such reserves: {They've been stockpiling canned goods since the pandemic began}.

Stockpiles are accumulated reserves of materials, supplies, or weapons held for future use or emergency. Governments maintain stockpiles of grain, oil, or medical supplies; militaries stockpile ammunition and equipment. The verb means to accumulate such reserves: {Countries began stockpiling vaccines ahead of flu season}. The word implies deliberate buildup against anticipated need or scarcity.

Stockpiling is the act of accumulating large quantities of something for future use, typically in anticipation of scarcity, emergency, or increased need. Governments stockpile weapons, medical supplies, or strategic resources; individuals might stockpile food before a storm or toilet paper during a pandemic. The word carries connotations of deliberate, sometimes anxious preparation. {Countries began stockpiling vaccines as soon as they became available.}

Stocks are shares of ownership in a company, bought and sold as investments: {She put her savings into stocks}. The stock market tracks their collective value. Historically, stocks were a wooden device that locked a person's ankles (or wrists and neck) in place for public punishment and humiliation. In cooking, stock is a flavorful liquid made by simmering bones, meat, or vegetables—the foundation for soups and sauces. Stock also means supply or inventory: {We're low on stock}. To stock shelves is to fill them with goods. Something in stock is available; out of stock means unavailable.

Stocky describes a body type that is broad, solid, and compact—wide through the chest and shoulders but not tall. The word suggests sturdiness rather than fat: {a stocky wrestler}, {He was short and stocky with powerful arms}. Stocky people look built for strength, not speed.

Stoic describes someone who endures pain or hardship without showing emotion or complaining. A stoic response to bad news is calm and controlled. The word suggests dignified self-restraint in the face of suffering: {She remained stoic throughout the funeral}. As a noun, a stoic is a person who displays this quality. (Capitalized Stoic refers to the ancient philosophy.)

Stoicism is calm endurance in the face of pain, hardship, or strong emotion—accepting difficult circumstances without complaint or visible distress. A person who receives devastating news without breaking down displays stoicism. The quality suggests emotional self-control and resignation rather than dramatic reaction: {He bore the diagnosis with remarkable stoicism}. (Capitalized Stoicism is the ancient philosophy.)

Stoics are people who endure pain, hardship, or misfortune without complaint or visible emotion. The term suggests quiet acceptance rather than dramatic suffering: {The stoics in the cancer ward never asked for pity}. The lowercase form emphasizes the character trait rather than philosophical affiliation. (Capitalized Stoics are followers of the ancient philosophy.)

To stoke is to tend a fire by adding fuel or stirring it up: {He stoked the wood stove through the night}. By extension, to stoke something is to encourage or intensify it: {The rumors stoked public outrage}. In slang, stoked means excited or thrilled: {I'm so stoked for the concert}. The adjective use originated in surfer culture and spread into general youth slang. (Capitalized Stoke is a place name.)

Stoked means excited or enthusiastic, often intensely so: {I'm so stoked for the concert}. The word comes from stoking a fire—building it up—and suggests energy that's been fueled or amplified. Originally surfer slang from the 1960s, it remains casual and youthful: {She was stoked to get the job offer}.

Stoking is the act of tending a fire by adding fuel or stirring it to increase heat. A stoker feeds coal into a furnace or boiler. The word extends to anything that intensifies or fuels: {stoking fears}, {stoking controversy}, {stoking demand}. Politicians are often accused of stoking division or resentment among voters.

Stole has two distinct origins. One is the past tense of steal: {Someone stole my bike}. The other is a garment—a long, narrow scarf or shawl worn draped over the shoulders, typically made of fur, silk, or fine fabric: {She wore a mink stole to the opera}. Clergy also wear stoles as liturgical vestments.

Stolen is the past participle of steal, describing something taken without permission or right. Property can be stolen, but so can intangibles: a stolen {glance}, a stolen {kiss}, stolen {moments} together. {The car was reported stolen}. {She felt her childhood had been stolen from her}.

The stomach is the organ where food goes after swallowing, a muscular sac that breaks down what we eat. More loosely, stomach refers to the belly or abdomen: {a punch to the stomach}, {sleeping on your stomach}. To stomach something is to tolerate or endure it: {I can't stomach his arrogance}. A strong stomach means tolerance for unpleasant sights or situations; a weak stomach means the opposite.

A stomachache is pain or discomfort in the abdomen—the general region around the stomach, though the pain may originate from intestines or other organs. The term covers everything from mild indigestion to severe cramping: {I had a stomachache all morning}. Also spelled as two words: stomach ache.

Stomp is to bring your foot down hard, either to crush something underfoot or to express anger or frustration: {She stomped on the spider}; {He stomped out of the room}. A stomp is such a step, or a lively dance featuring heavy footwork. To stomp someone is to beat them decisively: {We stomped them 42–7}.

Stomped is the past tense of stomp—to tread heavily or crush underfoot. You stomp on something to flatten or destroy it: {He stomped the cigarette into the ground}. Stomped also describes emphatic walking: {She stomped out of the room}. In informal use, to get stomped is to be beaten decisively: {We got stomped 42-0}.

Stone is roughly synonymous with rock. A countable stone is likely to be small enough to handle, and may serve some purpose, as in building (house of stone). Gemstones may be called stones in context. Other things that get the name include kidney stones that form naturally in the body, or the large seeds of some fruits. A unit of weight equal to 14 pounds or 6.3 kilograms is a stone. To stone someone is to pelt them with stones. To get stoned is to become intoxicated with cannabis.

Stoned originally means pelted with stones, as in the ancient punishment of stoning: {Blasphemers were stoned to death}. {The mob stoned the building}. The adjective describes something embedded with stones or having a stone removed: {a stoned walkway}, {stoned cherries}. In slang, stoned means intoxicated, especially by marijuana: {We got stoned and watched movies}. The connection may be from feeling heavy or immobilized, like a stone.

Stonefaced describes a face showing no emotion or reaction—impassive, unreadable, giving nothing away. The expression suggests features as fixed and cold as carved stone: {The detective remained stonefaced throughout the confession}. Someone stonefaced might be concealing their feelings, exercising restraint, or simply impossible to read. Also spelled stone-faced.

A stoner is someone who habitually smokes marijuana. The term is informal but not particularly derogatory—stoners often self-identify: {I was a total stoner in college}. Stoner culture has its own aesthetic of laid-back attitudes, munchies, and hazy philosophical musings. {stoner comedies}, {stoner rock}.

Stoners are people who habitually smoke marijuana. The term is mildly pejorative when used by outsiders but often embraced by users themselves: {a bunch of stoners sitting around playing video games}. Stoner culture has its own stereotypes—lethargy, munchies, philosophical rambling, and obsession with weed-related paraphernalia.

Stones is the plural of stone—solid pieces of rock or mineral matter. You skip stones across water, clear stones from a garden, or admire precious stones in jewelry. In British usage, stone is also a unit of weight (14 pounds), though the plural remains stone: {She weighs nine stone}. Stones are also hard masses that form in organs: kidney stones, gallstones. As slang, stones means testicles, and by extension, courage or nerve: {It takes stones to do that}.

To stonewall is to obstruct or delay by refusing to answer questions or cooperate. Politicians stonewall investigations, witnesses stonewall interrogators, bureaucracies stonewall requests: {The committee accused the agency of stonewalling}. The image is of a stone wall—impenetrable, unyielding. As a noun, a stonewall is this kind of obstruction, or literally a wall built of stones without mortar. (Capitalized Stonewall refers to the 1969 uprising or historical figures.)

Stonewalled means blocked, refused, or met with deliberate obstruction. Someone who stonewalls gives no response or refuses to cooperate: {The committee stonewalled every request for documents}. In relationships, stonewalling is shutting down communication entirely—refusing to engage or answer. The image is of a solid stone wall that nothing can penetrate.

Stonewalling is refusing to answer questions or cooperate, especially by being evasive or unresponsive. Politicians stonewall investigations; a spouse stonewalls during arguments by shutting down communication entirely. The term suggests a wall that blocks all progress: {The committee accused the agency of stonewalling their requests for documents}. To stonewall is to engage in this behavior.

Stoning is execution or punishment by throwing stones at the victim until dead. It appears in ancient legal codes and religious texts as punishment for adultery, blasphemy, or other offenses. The practice persists in some countries under religious law. Stoning also refers to removing stones from fruit: {stoning cherries}. In slang, stoning means getting high on drugs.

Stood is the past tense and past participle of stand. Where someone stood is where they were positioned: {She stood by the window}. To have stood for something is to have represented or tolerated it: {The party stood for reform}, {I wouldn't have stood for that behavior}. {It stood to reason} means it was logical or obvious.

A stooge is a person who serves another's purposes, especially as a dupe or pawn. The word often implies someone manipulated or used as a front: {The dictator installed stooges in every ministry}. In comedy, a stooge is a performer who feeds lines to or absorbs abuse from the lead comedian—the Three Stooges being the iconic example. To stooge for someone is to serve as their stooge.

Stooges is the plural of stooge—a person who serves as a pawn or lackey for someone more powerful. The word often implies complicity in dishonest schemes: {The dictator surrounded himself with stooges}. In entertainment, a stooge is a comedian's straight man or fall guy, most famously the Three Stooges. To stooge for someone is to act as their subordinate dupe.

A stool is a seat without a back or arms, typically for one person: {bar stool}, {piano stool}. In medical contexts, stool means feces—the solid waste discharged from the bowels: {a stool sample}. A stool pigeon is an informer, from the practice of tying a pigeon to a stool as a decoy for hunters.

A stoop is a small porch or set of steps at the entrance to a building, especially in urban row houses: {We sat on the stoop and watched the neighborhood go by}. The word is most common in the northeastern United States. Separately, to stoop is to bend forward and downward, or to lower oneself to something undignified: {I won't stoop to that level}. A stoop in posture is a habitual forward bend of the shoulders.

Stoops are small porches or sets of steps at the entrance to a building, especially in urban rowhouses and brownstones. The word is most common in the northeastern United States, where stoop culture—sitting outside on summer evenings, chatting with neighbors—remains a fixture of city life: {Kids played on the stoop while their parents talked}. To stoop is also to bend forward at the waist, and by extension, to lower oneself morally: {I won't stoop to their level}.

Stop, noun and verb, represents a change of state that ends movement, activity, or progress. To stop smoking is to give up the habit. When a wound stops bleeding, blood ceases to flow. To stop up a conduit is to prevent further flow through it. A stop is an instance of stopping, as well as a place where a vehicle stops to pick up and discharge passengers. A place where a journey is interrupted is a stop. Stop occurs frequently before other nouns (stop sign, stop button, stop order, stop watch).

A stoplight is a traffic signal that controls the flow of vehicles at intersections, cycling through red, yellow, and green lights. Red means stop, green means go, yellow means the light is about to change. Also called a traffic light. {Turn left at the next stoplight.}

A stopover is a brief stay at an intermediate point during a journey, especially air travel: {We had a six-hour stopover in Dubai}. Airlines distinguish stopovers from layovers by duration—stopovers typically exceed 24 hours and may require leaving the airport. The term also applies to any planned break in travel: {We made a stopover in Denver to visit my sister}.

A stopper is something that closes an opening—a cork, plug, or cap that seals a bottle or container: {She pulled the stopper from the decanter}. By extension, anything that halts progress or blocks action can be a stopper. In baseball, a stopper is a reliable pitcher who ends losing streaks. To stopper is to seal with a plug: {He stoppered the flask}.

A stopwatch is a handheld timing device used to measure elapsed time with precision, typically featuring buttons to start, stop, and reset the display. Unlike regular watches that tell the time of day, stopwatches measure duration—how long something takes. They're essential equipment for timing races, scientific experiments, and any activity where seconds matter. {The coach clicked his stopwatch as each runner crossed the finish line.}

Storage is keeping things somewhere for later use. Physical storage holds goods in warehouses, closets, or rental units: {We put the furniture in storage during the renovation}. In computing, storage refers to devices or systems that retain data—hard drives, cloud storage, memory cards. Storage also names the cost of storing: {Storage fees add up quickly}.

A store is a place where goods are sold—a retail establishment. Americans say store where Britons say shop: {grocery store}, {department store}, {hardware store}. To store something is to put it away for future use: {Store the wine in a cool place}. A store of something is a supply kept on hand: {a store of canned goods}, {a store of knowledge}. In computing, to store is to save data. The phrase {in store} means awaiting: {You never know what the future has in store}.

A storefront is the front exterior of a retail shop, especially the ground-floor facade facing the street: {The storefront windows displayed the new fall collection}. By extension, storefront describes any business occupying such a space: a storefront {church}, a storefront {law office}. Online, a storefront is a website's shopping interface where customers browse and buy.

Stores serves as both verb and noun. To store something is to put it away for future use; stores is the third-person form: {She stores her winter clothes in the attic}. As a noun, stores are supplies or provisions: {The expedition carried stores for six months}. A store is a retail establishment, and stores can mean multiple such places: {I need to run some errands at a few stores}. In British usage, stores often refers to a large department store or warehouse.

Storied describes something celebrated in history or legend, rich with stories worth telling: {the storied halls of Oxford}, {a storied career}. The word suggests accumulated significance—a storied franchise has decades of memorable moments, a storied rivalry has generated countless tales. It elevates its subject, implying fame that has been earned over time.

Stories are narratives—accounts of events, real or imagined, told to entertain, inform, or persuade. A story can be a novel, a news report, a personal anecdote, or a lie: {What's the story with those two?} {That's my story and I'm sticking to it}. In architecture, a story is one level of a building: {a three-story house}. The British spelling for this sense is storey.

A stork is a large wading bird with long legs, a long neck, and a long bill, found in wetlands across much of the world. Storks are associated in Western folklore with delivering babies—a euphemism for explaining childbirth to children. {The stork brought you} means you were born.

Storks are large wading birds with long legs, long necks, and heavy bills. They stand motionless in shallow water hunting fish and frogs, or nest on rooftops and chimneys in parts of Europe. Western folklore associates storks with delivering babies—a euphemism for explaining childbirth to children: {The stork brought you}.

A storm is an instance of disturbed and often violent weather, typically with wind and precipitation. In figurative use, a storm is a large amount of an undesirable thing: The citizens raised a storm of protest. If the weather is storming, there are storms present. If an army storms a place, they make a forceful attack. If a person storms, they express great anger. To do something by storm is to do it quickly, efficiently, and with great success.

A stormchaser is someone who pursues severe weather—tornadoes, hurricanes, thunderstorms—either professionally for research and forecasting or as a thrill-seeking hobby. Stormchasers track weather systems across open terrain, often driving hundreds of miles to intercept them: {The stormchasers got footage of the tornado touching down}. The term extends figuratively to anyone drawn to chaos or crisis.

Storming describes something done with fierce energy or violent force: {a storming performance}, {a storming finish to the race}. British slang uses it as high praise for something excellent or impressive: {That goal was absolutely storming}. The word also names the second stage of group development, when conflict emerges before cohesion: {The team is still in the storming phase}.

Storms are violent atmospheric disturbances—rain, wind, thunder, snow, or some combination arriving with force. The word extends to any turbulent outburst: {a storm of protest}, {a storm of applause}. To storm is to attack forcefully {(storm the gates)} or to move angrily {(She stormed out of the room)}. A stormy relationship involves frequent conflict.

A stormtrooper was originally a German soldier trained for aggressive assault tactics in World War I, part of specialized units that attacked enemy trenches. The term later applied to Nazi paramilitary forces (the SA or Sturmabteilung) who enforced Hitler's rule through intimidation and violence. More recently, stormtroopers are the white-armored soldiers of the Galactic Empire in Star Wars, depicted as faceless enforcers of authoritarian power: {The stormtroopers missed every shot}. The word now suggests anonymous agents of oppression or, ironically, incompetent minions.

Stormtroopers were members of the SA (Sturmabteilung), the Nazi Party's paramilitary wing in Germany, notorious for political intimidation and violence in the 1920s and 1930s. The term now applies broadly to any brutal enforcers of authoritarian rule: {The regime sent its stormtroopers to silence protesters}. In the Star Wars franchise, stormtroopers are the faceless, white-armored soldiers of the Galactic Empire—a usage now more familiar than the historical one.

Stormy describes weather marked by strong winds, heavy rain, thunder, or other violent atmospheric conditions: {a stormy night}, {stormy seas}. The word extends to turbulent situations or relationships: {a stormy debate}, {their stormy marriage}. A stormy expression suggests visible anger or agitation.

Story is related to history and has some overlap in meaning with it and with narrative. A story may be true (news story), have some particular theme (love story, success story, horror story), or invented (short story). The story of something is a way of characterizing an account that includes causes and effects. In American English, a story is also a level of a building; the British spelling of this word is storey.

A storyboard is a sequence of drawings or images showing the planned shots of a film, animation, or video before production begins. Each panel represents a camera angle or scene, with notes on dialogue, action, and timing. Directors and animators use storyboards to visualize the flow of a project: {We storyboarded the entire chase sequence before shooting}. The verb means to create such a plan.

Storyboards are sequences of drawings or images showing the planned shots of a film, animation, commercial, or video. Each panel represents a scene or camera angle, with notes about action, dialogue, and timing. Directors and production teams use storyboards to visualize a project before filming begins: {We spent weeks on storyboards before shooting a single frame}. The verb storyboard means to create such a sequence.

A storybook is a book containing stories for children, typically illustrated and often featuring fairy tales, fables, or simple narratives. As an adjective, storybook describes something that resembles the idealized world of children's tales—charming, perfect, or too good to be true: {They had a storybook wedding in a castle}. A storybook ending is one where everything works out happily, just as it would in a fairy tale.

Storybooks are books containing stories, especially those written for children with illustrations. The word often evokes tales of fantasy, adventure, or moral lessons: {She read from her favorite storybook before bed}. As an adjective, storybook describes something idealized or fairy-tale perfect: {a storybook ending}, {a storybook romance}.

A storyline is the main sequence of events in a narrative—the plot of a novel, film, television series, or video game. The term often implies a through-line that connects episodes or installments: {The show's romantic storyline dragged on for three seasons}. In soap operas and serialized fiction, multiple storylines may run simultaneously.

A storyteller is someone who tells stories—whether orally, in writing, or through other media. The term can describe professionals (novelists, screenwriters, stand-up comics) or anyone with a gift for narrative: {My grandmother was a natural storyteller}. Calling someone a storyteller often implies skill at holding attention and shaping experience into compelling form.

Storytellers is the plural of storyteller—someone who tells stories, whether orally, in writing, or through other media. The term covers professionals (novelists, screenwriters, comedians) and everyday people sharing anecdotes: {My grandmother was one of the great storytellers in our family}. Good storytellers know how to structure narrative and hold attention.

Storytelling is the act of telling stories—narrating events, whether real or imagined, to an audience. The term covers everything from a parent's bedtime tales to professional narrative craft in film, marketing, or journalism. In contemporary usage, storytelling often emphasizes the skill of shaping information into compelling narrative: {Good storytelling can make data memorable}. The word frequently appears in business contexts where it risks becoming jargon.

Storytime is a period set aside for reading stories aloud, typically to children: {The library hosts storytime every Saturday morning}. In casual use, storytime signals that someone is about to share a personal narrative, often dramatic or entertaining: {Okay everyone, storytime—you won't believe what happened at the airport}.

Stout describes someone heavyset or thickly built, often a polite way to say fat: {a stout woman in her fifties}. It also means sturdy and strong: {stout boots}, {a stout walking stick}. Stout can describe courage or resolve: {stout resistance}, {a stout heart}. As a noun, stout is a dark, heavy beer, richer than porter: {a pint of Guinness stout}.

A stove is an appliance for cooking or heating. Kitchen stoves have burners on top and often an oven below: {She put the kettle on the stove}. Heating stoves burn wood or other fuel to warm a room: {a cast-iron wood stove}. The past tense of stave—to break a hole in something—is staved or stove: {The rocks stove in the hull}.

A stovetop is the flat upper surface of a stove containing the burners for cooking. It functions as both noun and adjective: {stovetop cooking}, {a stovetop espresso maker}. The term distinguishes cooking done on burners from oven cooking below: {This recipe works on the stovetop or in the oven}.

A stowaway is a person who hides aboard a ship, plane, or other vehicle to travel without paying or without permission. The term evokes desperate migrants concealing themselves in cargo holds or wheel wells: {The stowaway was discovered three days into the voyage}. As a verb, to stow away is to hide oneself for such passage.

Stowaways are people who hide aboard ships, planes, or other vehicles to travel without paying or being detected. The term suggests desperation—refugees in cargo holds, runaways in wheel wells. A stowaway risks discovery and the dangers of the journey itself: {Stowaways were found in a shipping container}. Figuratively, anything that sneaks along unnoticed: {The virus was a stowaway in the software update}.

To straddle is to stand or sit with legs on either side of something: {She straddled the motorcycle}, {He straddled the fence}. The fence-straddling image extends to avoiding commitment between two positions: {The candidate straddled the issue}. More broadly, straddle means to span or extend across: {The town straddles the border between two states}. In finance, a straddle is an options strategy involving both a put and a call at the same strike price.

A straggler is someone who falls behind or arrives after the main group. Soldiers who can't keep pace with their unit are stragglers. The word applies to anyone lagging: {A few stragglers wandered in after the meeting started}. It can also describe things that appear scattered or isolated: {a straggler tomato still ripening in October}.

Stragglers are people or things that fall behind or arrive after the main group. Soldiers who can't keep pace with their unit are stragglers. At a party, the stragglers are the last guests to leave: {A few stragglers were still drinking at midnight}. The word implies lateness, slowness, or scattered arrival rather than deliberate separation.

Straight means without curves, bends, or deviations. A straight {line} takes the shortest path between two points. Straight {hair} lacks curl. To go straight {home} is to proceed directly. A straight {answer} is honest and direct. In sequence, five straight {wins} means five consecutive ones. Straight can mean undiluted: {straight whiskey}. To {set something straight} is to correct a misunderstanding. As slang, straight means heterosexual, and in drug culture, someone who's straight is sober or not a user. A straight in poker is five cards in sequence.

To straighten is to make straight—removing curves, bends, or disorder. You straighten a {crooked picture}, straighten your {hair}, straighten {papers} on a desk. To {straighten up} is to tidy a space or correct your posture. To {straighten out} is to resolve confusion or set someone right: {Let me straighten you out on a few things}. Straighten suggests imposing order where things have gone askew.

Straightforward means direct and uncomplicated, without evasion or hidden complexity. A straightforward {answer} addresses the question plainly. A straightforward {process} has clear steps without unexpected difficulties. The word often implies honesty: {She was straightforward about her intentions}. Something straightforward is easy to understand or accomplish: {The instructions were straightforward}.

A straightjacket is a garment with long sleeves that wrap around and fasten behind, used to restrain people who might harm themselves or others—historically in psychiatric institutions. The spelling straitjacket, from strait meaning narrow or confining, is technically more accurate, but straightjacket dominates in everyday use. Figuratively, anything that severely restricts freedom: {bureaucratic straightjackets}, {the straightjacket of tradition}.

Straightlaced describes someone rigidly proper in behavior and morals, often excessively so: {Her straightlaced parents disapproved of the relationship}. The word suggests prudishness or inflexibility about rules and propriety. Also spelled strait-laced, from the original sense of a tightly laced corset—someone bound up, unable to relax.

Strain has two sets of meanings. The noun strain refers to an identifiable group of plants, animals, or characteristics: The infection involved a resistant strain of bacteria. A strain of discontent (for example) is a noticeable recurrence of it in a situation or group. In the second meaning, the noun and verb strain refers to an injury brought about by stress (muscle strain). If you strain a body part, you injure it by overuse or working it too hard. To strain to do something is to put forth great effort.

Strained describes something under tension or pressure. A strained muscle has been overextended. A strained relationship is tense and uncomfortable: {Things have been strained between us since the argument}. A strained smile or laugh looks forced rather than natural. Strained also means filtered through a strainer: {strained tomatoes}, {strained baby food}.

Straining is effort pushed to its limits—muscles, patience, relationships, credulity. Physical straining involves exertion against resistance: {straining to lift the box}, {straining at the oars}. A straining voice or straining eyes show the wear of overuse. Liquids pass through straining when filtered: {straining the pasta}. {That explanation is straining credulity} means it barely holds together.

Strains covers several related ideas of stretching or pulling. Physical strain is force that deforms or damages: {The rope snapped under the strain}. Bodily strain is injury from overexertion: {a muscle strain}. Mental strain is stress or pressure: {the strain of caring for aging parents}. To strain is to stretch, filter through a sieve, or exert great effort: {strain the pasta}, {straining to hear}. A strain is also a distinct variety—of plant, virus, or music: {a new strain of flu}, {strains of Mozart drifting from the window}.

A strait is a narrow passage of water connecting two larger bodies of water: {the Strait of Gibraltar}, {the Bering Strait}. The adjective strait, now archaic except in set phrases, means narrow or restricted. A straitjacket confines the arms. Straitlaced describes someone rigidly proper. In the plural, straits means a difficult situation: {dire straits}, {desperate straits}. The spelling straight refers to something not crooked or bent.

A straitjacket is a garment used to restrain someone, typically in psychiatric settings—a jacket with long sleeves that wrap around the body and tie in back, immobilizing the arms. Figuratively, anything that severely restricts freedom or movement: {Rigid regulations became a straitjacket on innovation}. Also spelled straightjacket, though strait (meaning narrow or confining) is the original element.

Straitjackets are garments used to restrain people, typically in psychiatric settings, with long sleeves that wrap around the body and fasten in back, preventing arm movement. The singular straitjacket extends figuratively to anything that severely restricts freedom: {The regulations were a straitjacket on innovation}. Sometimes misspelled "straightjacket."

Straitlaced describes someone rigidly proper in manners and morals, especially regarding sex. The term suggests excessive primness—a straitlaced person might object to off-color jokes or bare shoulders at dinner. {Her straitlaced parents wouldn't let her date until college.} The spelling straightlaced, treating strait as an error, is now common.

Straits names a narrow passage of water connecting two larger bodies: the Strait of Gibraltar, the Straits of Mackinac. The plural often appears even for a single passage. Figuratively, straits means a difficult situation, almost always modified: {dire straits}, {desperate straits}, {in financial straits}. The singular strait appears mainly in the geographic sense or the adjective meaning narrow or strict, now rare outside {straitjacket} and {straitlaced}.

Strand is two different words with their associated meanings. The first is the strand that is something long and thin, usually one among many such things (strand of hair, strand of DNA). Things that are woven together to make something are called strands, and this meaning is extended figuratively: The strands of work, family, and community in her life were strong. The second strand is the land near water. To strand someone literally is to drive them onto a strand. In more common use, to strand someone is to leave them in a difficult or helpless situation.

Stranded means left without the means to move or escape from a place. A stranded traveler is stuck somewhere—their car broke down, their flight was canceled, they missed the last bus. A stranded ship has run aground. The word implies helplessness and the need for rescue: {We were stranded at the airport for twelve hours}. Figuratively, someone can be stranded in a difficult situation with no clear way out.

Strands are long thin pieces of something—hair, fiber, rope, wire. A rope is made of strands twisted together; a strand of hair falls across someone's face. The word extends to abstract threads: {strands of an argument}, {the different strands of her research}. To strand is to leave someone stuck somewhere, especially by water: {The tide stranded the boat on the sandbar}. A stranded traveler is stuck without transportation or resources.

Strange describes what deviates from the familiar, expected, or ordinary. A strange noise is unfamiliar; a strange coincidence seems improbable; a strange person behaves oddly. {That's strange—I could have sworn I left my keys here.} Strange can also mean unfamiliar without implying weirdness: {I woke up in a strange bed}. To feel strange is to feel unwell or uneasy.

A stranger is someone you don't know. The word emphasizes unfamiliarity rather than foreignness—a stranger might live next door if you've never met. {Don't talk to strangers} warns children about unknown people. {I'm a stranger here myself} means unfamiliar with a place. A stranger to something lacks experience with it: {He was no stranger to hardship}. The comparative adjective stranger means more strange: {Truth is stranger than fiction}.

Strangers are people you don't know. The word often carries a note of wariness—children are taught not to talk to strangers, and {a stranger in town} may attract suspicion. But strangers can also represent possibility: {We were strangers when we met}. To be {no stranger to} something is to have ample experience with it: {She's no stranger to controversy}.

To strangle is to kill or injure by compressing the throat, cutting off air or blood flow. The word extends to anything that suppresses or inhibits: {Regulations are strangling small businesses}. A stranglehold is a grip around the neck, or figuratively, oppressive control: {The corporation had a stranglehold on the market}.

Strangled is the past tense of strangle—to kill or injure by compressing the throat, cutting off air or blood flow. Beyond literal choking, strangled describes sounds that are tight, constricted, or suppressed: {a strangled cry}, {Her voice came out strangled}. Something strangled has been suppressed or stifled: {strangled economic growth}, {strangled by regulations}.

A stranglehold is a choking grip around someone's neck, or more commonly, a position of complete and oppressive control: {The company has a stranglehold on the market}. The word emphasizes that the grip is tight enough to prevent movement or escape—often suggesting the controlled party is being slowly suffocated rather than quickly defeated.

Strangling is the act of killing or attempting to kill by compressing the throat, cutting off air or blood flow to the brain. The word extends to any suppressive force that chokes off vitality or growth: {The regulations are strangling small businesses}. Someone strangling on food or emotion is choking, unable to breathe or speak freely.

A strap is a narrow strip of flexible material—leather, fabric, nylon—used for fastening, holding, or carrying: a watch {strap}, a shoulder {strap}, a guitar {strap}. To strap something is to secure it with straps: {He strapped the luggage to the roof}. To be {strapped for cash} is to be short of money. {Strapped} alone can mean armed with a gun.

Strapped means short of money: {I'm strapped for cash until payday}. The word suggests being tightly constrained, as if bound by financial limitations. In American slang, strapped also means carrying a gun: {He's always strapped when he goes out at night}.

Strapping describes someone tall, strong, and robustly built—the kind of physicality that suggests health and vigor: {a strapping young man}, {strapping farm boys}. The word carries admiration, often applied to youth whose size promises capability. Separately, strapping is the present participle of strap: {She was strapping the luggage to the roof}.

Strategic describes actions, decisions, or thinking designed to achieve a long-term goal or gain advantage. A strategic {plan} maps out how to reach objectives. A strategic {location} offers military or commercial advantage. Strategic thinking weighs future consequences rather than immediate gains. The word often implies careful calculation: {a strategic pause}, {a strategic alliance}. In military contexts, strategic typically refers to large-scale planning as opposed to tactical (immediate, on-the-ground) operations.

A strategist is someone who plans and directs action toward a goal, especially in military, political, or business contexts. The term implies thinking several moves ahead, weighing options, and anticipating obstacles: {She's the campaign's chief strategist}. A strategist focuses on the big picture rather than tactical details.

A strategy is the means used to achieve an objective or an approach to achieving related goals, as in an investment strategy or a strategy for product improvement. Strategy originated as a term for planning military movements and operations in relation to warfare. Strategy is sometimes contrasted with tactics, especially in a military context, where strategy represents the overall plan, while tactics is the deployment of weapons in personnel in a particular place.

The stratosphere is the layer of Earth's atmosphere extending roughly 10 to 50 kilometers above the surface, above the troposphere where weather occurs. It contains the ozone layer that absorbs ultraviolet radiation. Figuratively, the stratosphere suggests extreme heights of achievement or intensity: {Her career rocketed into the stratosphere}, {Prices have reached the stratosphere}.

Straw is the dry stalks of grain plants after harvesting, used for bedding, fodder, or thatching. A straw is also a thin tube for drinking: {She sipped her smoothie through a straw}. Straw describes pale yellow color or something serving as a substitute: a straw {man}, a straw {poll}. The {last straw} is the final burden that breaks tolerance. To {grasp at straws} is to pursue desperate, unlikely solutions.

Strawberries are the red, seed-studded fruits of a low-growing plant, prized for their sweet flavor and fragrance. Unlike most fruits, strawberries wear their seeds on the outside rather than encasing them within. They're eaten fresh, used in desserts, and made into jams and preserves. {Fresh strawberries with cream is a classic summer treat.} The singular strawberry can also describe the distinctive red color or the plant itself.

A strawberry is a small red fruit with tiny seeds on its outer surface, grown on low plants and prized for its sweet flavor. Strawberries are eaten fresh, used in desserts, and made into jams and preserves. A strawberry {blonde} has reddish-blonde hair. A {strawberry mark} is a red birthmark.

A strawman is a misrepresentation of someone's argument, set up to be easily knocked down—like a dummy made of straw rather than a real opponent. {That's a strawman—I never said we should eliminate all regulations}. In business, a strawman is a rough preliminary proposal meant to spark discussion and revision, not to be defended as final. Also spelled straw man.

Straws is the plural of straw—dried stalks of grain, or the hollow tubes used for drinking. The plural appears in expressions: to {draw straws} is to select randomly by pulling hidden sticks of different lengths. A {straw poll} gauges informal opinion. To {grasp at straws} is to pursue desperate, unlikely solutions. {The last straw} is the final small thing that triggers collapse, from the proverb about breaking a camel's back.

Stray describes something that has wandered from where it belongs. A stray {dog} or {cat} has no owner or home. A stray {bullet} hits an unintended target. A stray {thought} wanders into consciousness unbidden. As a noun, a stray is an animal without an owner: {The shelter takes in strays}. To stray is to wander off course or deviate: {The conversation strayed into politics}.

Strays are animals, especially dogs or cats, that have wandered from home or have no owner: {The shelter takes in strays}. The word also functions as a verb—to stray is to wander from a path, group, or proper place: {Don't let your attention stray}. Someone who strays from their marriage commits infidelity. Stray as an adjective describes things separated from the main body: {a stray sock}, {stray hairs}, {a stray bullet}.

A streak is a long, narrow mark or line, often irregular: {a streak of paint}, {streaks of gray in her hair}. Extended meanings keep the sense of something thin cutting through a larger field: a {streak of light}, a {streak of luck}. A streak is also a continuous run: a winning {streak}, a losing {streak}, a {hot streak}. Someone with a rebellious {streak} has that tendency running through their character. To streak is to move very fast, or to run naked through a public place—a prank that had its heyday in the 1970s.

A streaker is a person who runs naked through a public place, typically as a prank or for attention. The practice became a fad in the 1970s, especially at sporting events and college campuses: {A streaker ran across the field during the fourth quarter}. The verb streak and the activity streaking derive from the same impulse—a flash of bare flesh moving quickly past.

Streaking is running naked through a public place, typically as a prank or for thrills: {A streaker ran across the field during the game}. The term emerged in the 1970s when the practice became a fad on college campuses and at sporting events. More generally, streaking describes moving very fast or making streaks: {tears streaking down her face}, {the car went streaking past}.

Streaks are long, narrow lines or marks, often irregular: {streaks of gray in her hair}, {streaks of light through the blinds}. A streak is also a continuous run of something: a winning streak, a losing streak, a streak of bad luck. Someone's personality may have a streak—a tendency or strain: {a mean streak}, {a stubborn streak}. To streak is to mark with lines, move very fast, or run naked through a public place as a prank or protest.

A stream is a body of flowing water smaller than a river. The word extends to any continuous flow: a stream of {traffic}, a stream of {consciousness}, a stream of {income}. Data streams in computing, and to stream video is to transmit or receive it continuously rather than downloading a complete file first. {Tears streamed down her face.}

A streamer is a long, narrow strip of material—paper, ribbon, or fabric—that flows or flutters decoratively: {Party streamers hung from the ceiling}. The word extends to anything ribbon-like that streams: a streamer of smoke, a banner headline. In contemporary use, a streamer is someone who broadcasts live video content online, especially gaming: {She's a popular Twitch streamer}.

Streamers are long, narrow strips of material—paper, ribbon, or plastic—that hang or flutter decoratively, often at parties or celebrations: {The room was covered in streamers and balloons}. A streamer can also be a banner or pennant that streams in the wind. In contemporary usage, streamers are people who broadcast live video content online, especially gaming: {Twitch streamers can earn substantial income from subscribers}.

Streaming is continuous transmission of audio or video data over the internet, played as it arrives rather than downloaded first: {We were streaming the game on my phone}. The term extends to the platforms that deliver such content: {What streaming services do you subscribe to?} More broadly, streaming describes anything flowing steadily in a current: {Sunlight came streaming through the windows}, {tears streaming down her face}.

Streamline originally describes shapes designed to move through air or water with minimal resistance—the tapered forms of fish, aircraft, and racing cars. From this comes the broader sense: to streamline a process is to make it more efficient by removing unnecessary steps or complications. {The company streamlined its approval process from twelve steps to three.} A streamlined organization runs leaner and faster.

Streamlined describes a shape designed to move through air or water with minimal resistance—smooth, tapered, without protrusions that create drag: {a streamlined fuselage}, {the streamlined body of a dolphin}. The figurative sense dominates modern usage: simplified and made more efficient by removing unnecessary steps or complications. {We streamlined the approval process from six weeks to three days.} A streamlined {operation} runs lean and fast.

Streamlining is the process of making something more efficient by removing unnecessary elements or simplifying procedures: {The company is streamlining its operations to cut costs}. The term comes from aerodynamics, where a streamlined shape reduces drag by allowing air or water to flow smoothly around it. The metaphor extends to any effort to make systems faster, leaner, or less cumbersome: {streamlining the approval process}, {streamlining government bureaucracy}.

Streams are bodies of water that flow continuously in a channel, smaller than rivers but following the same principle of moving from higher to lower ground. The word extends naturally to any continuous flow: a stream of {consciousness}, a stream of {data}, a stream of {visitors}. In computing, streaming refers to transmitting or receiving media content continuously rather than downloading it completely before playback. To stream is to flow steadily or to broadcast content this way: {I streamed the game last night}.

A street is a public road in a city or town, typically lined with buildings. Streets are distinguished from highways or rural roads by their urban context and pedestrian accessibility. {Wall Street} and {Main Street} represent financial and ordinary American interests respectively. The street can mean the general public or street-level reality: {word on the street}, {street smarts}. As an adjective, street suggests urban authenticity or grassroots origin: {street fashion}, {street cred}.

A streetcar is a public transit vehicle that runs on rails embedded in city streets, powered by overhead electric cables. Common in American cities from the late 1800s through mid-1900s, most were replaced by buses, though some cities have preserved or restored streetcar lines. Also called a trolley or, in British English, a tram.

Streetcars are passenger vehicles that run on rails embedded in city streets, powered by overhead electric lines. They were the dominant form of urban transit in the early twentieth century before buses and automobiles displaced them. Some cities have preserved or revived streetcar lines: {The streetcar rattled down Canal Street}. Also called trolleys or trams.

A streetlight is a tall lamp post that illuminates public roads and walkways at night. Streetlights line urban streets and highways, providing visibility and safety for drivers and pedestrians: {The streetlight flickered and went out}. They're such standard features of developed areas that their absence signals remoteness or neglect.

Streetlights are lights mounted on poles along roads and sidewalks to illuminate public spaces at night. They're a basic feature of urban infrastructure, switching on automatically at dusk: {The streetlights flickered on as we walked home}. Figuratively, streetlights evoke nighttime urban atmosphere—empty streets, late walks, the boundary between day and night.

Streets is the plural of street, a paved public road in a town or city. The word often suggests urban life and culture: {street food}, {street art}, {street smarts}. To be {on the streets} can mean homeless or working as a prostitute. {The streets} refers to urban neighborhoods, especially poorer ones, and the culture or knowledge gained there: {He learned everything on the streets}. In finance, {the Street} means Wall Street.

Streetwise describes practical knowledge gained from experience in rough urban environments—knowing how to avoid danger, read situations, and navigate social dynamics that don't appear in books. A streetwise person understands how things actually work on the ground: {She was streetwise enough to know which blocks to avoid after dark}. The term often implies savvy that comes from necessity rather than choice.

Strength is the quality of being strong—the capacity to exert force, resist pressure, or endure strain. Physical strength moves heavy objects; mental strength withstands hardship. The word extends to intensity or concentration: {the strength of the coffee}, {the strength of her convictions}. A strength is also a particular asset or advantage: {Math was never my strength}. To {go from strength to strength} is to achieve successive improvements.

Strengths is the plural of strength—qualities or attributes that give power, advantage, or resilience. People identify their strengths and weaknesses in job interviews and self-reflection: {Her strengths include attention to detail and clear communication}. The word also refers to military forces or resources: {We don't have the strengths to hold this position}.

Stress is a condition that results from injury, pressure, or threat (emotional stress, psychological stress, traumatic stress). Stress is also emphasis, such as importance attached to something, or loudness or force given to a syllable or word in speech. To stress a sound is to pronounce it louder or longer. To stress the importance or significance of something is to give it emphasis. To stress a muscle or joint is to put too much pressure or exertion on it.

Stressed describes being under mental or emotional pressure, often from too many demands: {I'm so stressed about the deadline}. In phonetics, a stressed syllable receives emphasis: the first syllable of "apple" is stressed. Materials under physical strain are also stressed: {The stressed beam began to crack}. As slang, stressed spelled backward is desserts—a coincidence people find meaningful.

Stressful describes situations or experiences that cause mental or emotional strain: {a stressful job}, {stressful commute}, {stressful relationship}. The word emerged alongside modern stress psychology—we now routinely label as stressful what earlier generations might have called trying, difficult, or nerve-wracking.

Stretch is about extending something beyond its resting state. You stretch a rubber band, stretch your legs after sitting, stretch the truth by exaggerating. A stretch of road or time is an extended portion: {a lonely stretch of highway}, {a ten-year stretch in prison}. Something is a stretch if it requires effort to accept: {Calling him a genius is a stretch}. Stretchy fabric extends and returns to shape. {I need to stretch before running}.

A stretcher is a portable frame for carrying a sick or injured person, typically with handles at each end so two people can lift it: {Paramedics loaded her onto a stretcher}. The word extends to any frame that stretches something—a canvas stretcher holds fabric taut for painting, a shoe stretcher expands tight footwear. In masonry, a stretcher is a brick laid lengthwise along a wall.

Stretching is the act of extending muscles, limbs, or materials to their full length or beyond their resting state. People stretch before exercise to warm up or after sitting to relieve stiffness: {I do ten minutes of stretching every morning}. Stretching also describes extending something to cover more area or time: {stretching the budget}, {stretching the truth}. The word implies pulling something toward its limits without quite breaking it.

Stretchmarks are the streaky lines that appear on skin when it stretches rapidly—during pregnancy, growth spurts, or significant weight changes. The skin's elastic fibers tear beneath the surface, leaving visible scars that typically start reddish or purple and fade to silvery white over time. Also spelled as two words: stretch marks.

Stricken describes someone or something severely affected by trouble, illness, or misfortune: {a grief-stricken widow}, {poverty-stricken communities}, {stricken with cancer}. The word carries weight—it suggests being struck down, overwhelmed. As the past participle of strike, stricken appears in legal contexts: {stricken from the record}. In everyday speech, struck has largely replaced it except in these affliction-related uses.

Strict means rigidly enforced or closely adhered to. A strict {teacher} tolerates no deviation from rules. A strict {interpretation} of the law allows no flexibility. Strict can describe someone who demands obedience: {Her parents were strict about curfew}. It also means exact or precise: {in the strict sense of the word}. A strict {diet} permits no exceptions.

Stride is a long, decisive step, or the manner of walking characterized by such steps. Someone who strides walks with purpose and confidence, covering ground efficiently. The word extends to progress generally: {The company has made great strides in sustainability}. To hit your stride means to reach your optimal pace or performance level. In stride suggests taking something calmly, without breaking rhythm: {She took the criticism in stride}.

Strife is bitter conflict or discord, especially prolonged antagonism between people or groups. The word suggests deeper hostility than mere disagreement: {marital strife}, {civil strife}, {The region has been torn by ethnic strife for decades}. Strife is somewhat literary—conflict, tension, or trouble often substitute in everyday speech.

Strigolactones are plant hormones that regulate growth and development, particularly branching patterns in shoots and roots. They're released into soil where they signal to beneficial fungi, promoting symbiotic relationships that help plants absorb nutrients. The name comes from *Striga*, a parasitic weed that exploits these chemical signals to locate host plants: {Researchers are studying strigolactones to develop crops resistant to parasitic weeds}.

Strike has myriad meanings arising from the core verb meaning of hit forcefully: She struck him on the jaw. When strike is followed by an adverbial directional phrase, it means to go or set off on a course: We’ll strike out through the jungle. Strike can also refer to a work stoppage: Workers at the plant will strike for higher wages and better safety. A strike is an instance of striking: There was a strike at the university and classes were cancelled. Several lightning strikes were reported in the area.

A strikebreaker is someone who works during a labor strike, either a regular employee who refuses to join the walkout or an outsider hired to replace striking workers. The term carries strong negative connotations among union supporters, who view strikebreakers as undermining collective bargaining power and worker solidarity. The more contemptuous term *scab* is often used instead. {The company brought in strikebreakers to keep the factory running.}

Strikebreakers are workers hired to replace employees who are on strike, or existing employees who cross picket lines to keep working during a labor dispute. The term carries negative connotations from the perspective of striking workers and union supporters, who view strikebreakers as undermining collective bargaining power. Also called scabs.

A strikeout in baseball is when a batter accumulates three strikes and is out. The term extends to any decisive failure: {The product launch was a strikeout}. As a verb phrase, to strike out means to fail completely or, in dating, to be rejected: {I struck out with her at the party}. Also spelled strike-out or strike out.

A striker is someone or something that strikes. In soccer, a striker is a forward position focused on scoring goals: {The striker headed the ball into the net}. In labor disputes, strikers are workers who have walked off the job. A striker can also be the hammer mechanism in a firearm or clock, or the metal plate a door latch engages.

Strikers are workers who refuse to work as a form of protest, typically to pressure employers over wages, conditions, or other grievances: {The strikers formed a picket line outside the factory}. In soccer, a striker is a forward whose primary role is scoring goals. More generally, anyone or anything that strikes—a clock's hammer, a tool for igniting matches.

Strikes connects ideas of hitting, stopping, and sudden action. To strike is to hit forcefully: {Lightning struck the tree}, {He struck her across the face}. Workers strike when they refuse to work as protest: {The nurses went on strike}. A strike in bowling knocks down all pins. In baseball, a strike is a pitch the batter swings at and misses, or one that crosses the plate in the strike zone—three strikes and you're out. To {strike a match} is to ignite it by friction. To {strike a pose} is to assume one dramatically. {That strikes me as odd} means it seems odd. To {strike gold} or {strike it rich} is to find sudden fortune.

Striking describes something that immediately catches attention and makes a strong impression. A striking {resemblance} is one you notice right away; a striking {woman} has features that stand out from the crowd. The word carries positive connotations of distinctiveness rather than mere oddness. As the present participle of strike, it also describes the act of hitting or the state of workers who have walked off the job: {The striking miners refused to negotiate}.

A string is something long, thin, and fairly flexible, like the apron strings used to tie the garment. Strings made of gut, nylon, or metal make the sounds on string instruments, which may be called strings collectively. A string is also a line of continuity, like a performer’s string of hits or the string of characters that make up a password. To string something up is to attach or suspend it with string. To string someone along is to keep them waiting, or to deceive them.

Strings is the plural of string—thin cords or threads. In music, strings refers collectively to instruments played by bowing or plucking: violin, viola, cello, bass. An orchestra's {string section} or simply {the strings} provides harmonic foundation. In computing, a string is a sequence of characters treated as a single unit: {Parse the input string}. To pull strings is to use hidden influence: {She pulled strings to get him the job}. {No strings attached} means without conditions or obligations.

The noun strip is related to stripe and has some overlap in meaning. A strip is something whose greatest dimension is length (landing strip, comic strip, strip mall). A major street is sometimes called a strip. The verb strip is not related to the noun. To strip something (paint, bark, wallpaper, for example) is to remove it. If you strip a person, you remove their clothes. If a person strips, they do the removing themselves.

A stripe is a long narrow band of color or texture contrasting with its surroundings: {a shirt with blue and white stripes}, {the stripes on a zebra}. Stripes can indicate rank—military personnel wear stripes on their sleeves to show grade. By extension, stripe means type or kind: {politicians of every stripe}. The verb means to mark with stripes: {The morning light striped the floor through the blinds}. To {earn one's stripes} is to prove oneself through experience.

Stripes are long narrow bands or lines that differ in color or texture from what surrounds them. They appear on clothing, flags, animals, and surfaces both natural and designed. A tiger has stripes; so does the American flag. In military and other uniformed contexts, stripes are insignia indicating rank: {She earned her stripes after two years of service}. To earn one's stripes more broadly means to prove oneself through effort or experience.

Stripped is the past tense of strip—to remove covering, clothing, or components. A stripped bed has had its sheets removed. A stripped car has been dismantled for parts. Stripped can mean reduced to essentials: {a stripped-down version of the software}. Paint stripper leaves wood stripped of its finish. To be stripped of a title or rank is to have it taken away as punishment.

A stripper is a person who performs striptease—removing clothing to music as entertainment, typically in a club setting. The word also applies to tools and chemicals that remove things: a wire stripper strips insulation from electrical cables, paint stripper dissolves old coatings. {She worked as a stripper to pay for law school.}

Strippers are people who perform striptease—removing clothing to music, typically for entertainment in clubs or at private parties. The term usually refers to women, though male strippers perform for bachelorette parties and similar events. Separately, a stripper is a tool or chemical that removes paint, insulation, or other coatings: {wire strippers}, {paint stripper}.

Stripping is removing an outer layer or covering. You strip paint from furniture, insulation from wire, or bark from a tree. A person strips by removing clothing—which gives the word its association with striptease performances: {She works as a stripper}. In mechanical contexts, stripping means damaging threads so they no longer grip: {He stripped the bolt by overtightening it}.

Strips are long, narrow pieces cut or torn from something larger: {strips of bacon}, {strips of cloth}, {a strip of land along the coast}. To strip is to remove a covering or outer layer—stripping paint, stripping bark, stripping clothes. A strip is also a sequence of drawn panels telling a story (comic strip) or a road lined with businesses (the Vegas Strip). To strip someone of rank or privilege is to take it away forcibly.

A striptease is an erotic performance in which someone gradually removes their clothing, typically to music. The art lies in the tease—the slow reveal rather than immediate nudity. Striptease is associated with burlesque shows and strip clubs. As a verb, to striptease is to perform such an act: {She worked her way through college doing striptease}.

Strive means to make great effort toward a goal, often against difficulty or opposition. The word suggests sustained exertion rather than a single attempt: {She strives for excellence in everything she does}. You can strive to achieve something, strive for a result, or strive against obstacles. The word carries a sense of earnestness and determination—striving implies the goal matters deeply.

Striving is the act of making great effort toward a goal, often against difficulty or opposition. The word emphasizes ongoing exertion rather than achievement: {Despite years of striving, success eluded him}. It carries a sense of earnest, sometimes noble struggle: {the striving of artists for recognition}, {human striving for meaning}.

A strobe is a light that flashes rapidly and repeatedly, used in photography, emergency vehicles, and dance clubs. The flashing creates a distinctive effect where motion appears choppy or frozen. As a verb, to strobe is to flash in this manner: {Emergency lights strobed across the wet pavement}. Short for stroboscope.

Stroganoff is a dish of sautéed beef in a sauce of sour cream, onions, and mushrooms, typically served over egg noodles or rice. Named after a 19th-century Russian aristocratic family, the dish became popular internationally through French and American adaptations. {We're having beef stroganoff for dinner tonight.} Variations using chicken or ground beef are common in home cooking.

The core idea of stroke is verbal, and is related to strike but usually has more gentle connotations (except in the case of the cerebral blockage or hemorrhage that we call a stroke). To stroke an object or animal is to caress it with the hand, often in a caring and repetitive way. Stroke is sometimes used figuratively to mean flatter: He stroked her ego. A stroke is also an act or instance of stroking, typically when it denotes a repetitive movement: Children learn all the major strokes in swimming. You can see individual brush strokes in the photograph.

Strokes is the plural of stroke, covering its many senses. A stroke is a single movement—of a pen, brush, oar, or limb in swimming: {She completed the race in powerful strokes}. A stroke of luck or genius is a sudden instance of it. In medicine, a stroke is a sudden interruption of blood flow to the brain, often causing paralysis or death. To stroke is to caress gently: {He stroked the cat's fur}. In slang, to stroke someone is to flatter them, feeding their ego.

Stroking is the act of moving one's hand gently over a surface, typically with affection or to soothe: {She sat stroking the cat's fur}. The word extends to any repeated, caressing motion. In competitive contexts, stroking refers to the technique of moving oars or paddles through water. Informally, stroking someone's ego means flattering them.

A stroll is a leisurely walk taken for pleasure rather than purpose: {an evening stroll through the park}. To stroll is to walk in this unhurried way, with no particular destination or urgency. Someone who strolls through a task approaches it casually, perhaps too casually: {He strolled through the interview like he already had the job}.

A stroller is a lightweight wheeled chair for pushing a small child: {She folded up the stroller and put it in the trunk}. The word also means one who strolls—someone taking a leisurely walk—though this sense is less common now that the baby carriage dominates usage.

Strollers are wheeled chairs for transporting small children, pushed by a parent or caregiver. The British term is pushchair or pram. Strollers also refers to people who stroll—walk in a leisurely way: {Evening strollers filled the boardwalk}.

The adjective strong overlaps in meaning with sturdy, powerful, and durable, and is the opposite of weak. Strong wind may be damaging. Strong relationships can withstand stresses. Strong support can be relied upon. To characterize a person as strong can refer to physical strength, or the ability to withstand emotional and psychological distress. If you are strong in something, like faith or conviction, those traits are noticeable in you. A strong smell or strong taste is usually a negative characterization, suggesting excess.

Strongarm means using physical force or intimidation to achieve a goal. As a verb, to strongarm someone is to coerce them through threats or violence: {They strongarmed the shopkeeper into paying protection money}. As an adjective, it describes aggressive tactics: {strongarm methods}, {strongarm robbery}. The term implies bullying rather than persuasion—getting compliance through fear rather than agreement.

Stronger is the comparative form of strong—indicating greater strength, intensity, or degree than something else. Physical strength: {She's stronger than her brother}. Intensity of feeling or effect: {The coffee could be stronger}. Resilience: {What doesn't kill you makes you stronger}. Arguments, evidence, or cases can be stronger than alternatives. A stronger economy shows more robust growth.

A stronghold is a fortified place—a castle, fortress, or defensible position: {The rebels retreated to their mountain stronghold}. By extension, it's any area where a particular group, belief, or activity dominates: {a Republican stronghold}, {a stronghold of traditional values}. The word emphasizes both strength and the idea of holding ground against opposition.

A strongman is a performer who demonstrates feats of physical strength—lifting heavy weights, bending metal bars, breaking chains. The term extends to authoritarian political leaders who rule through force and personal power rather than democratic institutions: {The country fell under the grip of a strongman}. Strongman competitions test athletes in events like deadlifts and atlas stones.

Strongmen is the plural of strongman. In its literal sense, strongmen are performers who demonstrate feats of physical strength—lifting heavy objects, bending metal bars, breaking chains. The term also describes authoritarian political leaders who consolidate power through force of personality and suppression of opposition: {The twentieth century produced no shortage of strongmen}. The athletic and political meanings share connotations of dominance and intimidation.

Struck is the past tense and past participle of strike. A clock struck {midnight}. Lightning struck the {tree}. Workers struck for better {wages}. Someone struck by beauty or grief is powerfully affected. To be {struck dumb} is to be rendered speechless. {Struck from the record} means officially removed. A struck {match} has been ignited by friction.

Structure is the way parts are arranged or organized into a whole. A building has physical structure; an essay has logical structure; a molecule has chemical structure. The word implies that arrangement matters—that components relate to each other in purposeful ways. To structure something is to give it organization: {She structured the course around weekly themes}. Structured environments have clear rules; unstructured time is free of them.

Strudel is a pastry made by wrapping thin layers of dough around a filling, then baking. Apple strudel, filled with spiced apples, raisins, and breadcrumbs, is the classic version: {We ordered strudel and coffee at the Viennese café}. Other fillings include cheese, cherries, or savory ingredients. The dough is stretched paper-thin before rolling.
