Struggle is effort against resistance. You struggle to lift something heavy, struggle to understand difficult material, struggle against an opponent. The word implies difficulty and exertion: {She struggled with depression for years}. A struggle is any hard-fought effort: {the struggle for civil rights}, {a power struggle}. To struggle is also to move with difficulty: {He struggled to his feet}.

Struggles are difficult efforts against resistance or opposition. The word captures both the effort and the hardship: {financial struggles}, {the struggles of daily life}. Someone who struggles with addiction fights an ongoing battle. A company struggles to stay afloat. The plural often emphasizes repeated or various difficulties rather than a single contest: {We all have our struggles}.

Struggling describes effort against difficulty or resistance. Someone struggling with a heavy load strains to carry it. A struggling {business} barely survives. You might struggle to {find the right words} or struggle {with addiction}. The word implies ongoing effort without easy success—not yet failed, but not thriving either.

To strum is to sweep the fingers across the strings of a guitar, banjo, or similar instrument, sounding multiple strings at once rather than plucking them individually: {She strummed a few chords while waiting for the others to tune up}. The word suggests casual or rhythmic playing rather than technical precision. A strum is a single instance of this motion, or the sound it produces.

Strumming is brushing the fingers across guitar strings to produce sound, or the sound produced by doing so. The word captures both the action and its acoustic result: {the strumming of an acoustic guitar in the next room}, {She sat strumming while we talked}. Strumming suggests casual or rhythmic playing rather than precise picking of individual strings.

Strut is a proud, confident walk with head high and chest out—the gait of someone showing off or feeling self-important: {He strutted around the office after his promotion}. The word often carries a whiff of arrogance or vanity: {peacocks strutting}, {models strutting down the runway}. To {strut your stuff} is to display your abilities or assets. A strut is also a structural brace that resists compression, as in aircraft wings or automobile suspensions.

Struts are structural supports designed to resist compression—the beams and bars that keep things from collapsing inward. In vehicles, struts are shock-absorbing components in the suspension system. To strut is to walk with exaggerated pride or self-importance, chest out, shoulders back: {He strutted around like he owned the place}. The phrase {strut your stuff} means to display your abilities or assets confidently.

A stub is a short remaining piece left after the main part has been used or removed—the stub of a pencil, a ticket stub, a check stub. These remnants often serve as records or receipts. In computing, a stub is placeholder code that stands in for functionality not yet implemented. To stub your toe is to strike it painfully against something, and to stub out a cigarette is to extinguish it by pressing the burning end against a surface.

Stubble is the short, stiff remnants of something cut close to its base. After harvest, stubble is the stalks left standing in a field. On a face, stubble is the rough growth of beard a day or two after shaving: {He rubbed the stubble on his chin}. Stubble suggests incompleteness—neither cleanly removed nor fully grown.

Stubborn describes someone who refuses to change their mind or course of action, even in the face of good arguments or evidence. The word carries a negative connotation—stubbornness is persistence without flexibility: {She's too stubborn to admit she was wrong}. A stubborn stain or problem resists removal or solution. Stubborn can shade toward positive when it suggests determination against difficult odds: {his stubborn refusal to give up}.

Stubbornness is the quality of refusing to change one's mind, course of action, or position despite pressure, argument, or good reasons to do so. It carries a negative connotation, suggesting unreasonable persistence rather than admirable resolve. {His stubbornness cost him the deal.} A stubborn person digs in their heels; stubbornness is the tendency to do so habitually. The word can sometimes shade into grudging respect when the resistance proves justified.

Stuck is the past tense and past participle of stick, carrying forward its senses of adhesion and fixedness. Something stuck is unable to move: a drawer stuck shut, a car stuck in mud, a person stuck in traffic. Figuratively, to be stuck is to be unable to proceed: {I'm stuck on this math problem}. If you're stuck with something, you're burdened with it unwillingly: {We're stuck with this old couch}. To get stuck in (British) is to begin energetically.

A stud is an upright post in a wall frame, or a projecting knob or peg—shirt studs, tire studs, studs on a leather jacket. In breeding, a stud is a male animal kept for reproduction, especially a stallion; a stud farm raises horses. By extension, stud is slang for a sexually attractive or virile man: {He thinks he's such a stud}. In poker, stud is a variant where some cards are dealt face up.

A student is someone who studies, especially one enrolled in a school or taking lessons. The word applies from kindergarten through graduate school: {She's a third-grade student}, {law students}. Beyond formal education, student describes anyone learning systematically: {a student of human nature}, {a lifelong student of jazz}. A student can also be someone under observation or training: {a student teacher}, {a student driver}.

Students are people engaged in study, typically at a school, college, or university. The word applies broadly to anyone learning a subject, whether formally enrolled in an institution or pursuing knowledge independently: {a student of history}, {a lifelong student of human nature}. In American usage, student covers learners at all levels, while British English often reserves it for those in higher education, using pupil for younger children.

A studio is a workspace for creative or technical work—an artist's studio, a recording studio, a photography studio. In film and television, a studio is both the physical space where productions are shot and the company that makes them: {The studio rejected the script}. A studio apartment is a single room serving as both living and sleeping space, usually with a small kitchen.

Studs are upright posts in a wall frame—the vertical supports to which drywall or paneling attaches. In clothing, studs are decorative metal fasteners or small ornamental buttons, especially on formal shirt fronts. A stud is also a male animal kept for breeding, which extends to slang for a sexually attractive or active man: {He thinks he's such a stud}. Studded means embedded with studs: {a leather jacket studded with metal}, {snow tires with studs}.

Study centers on applying the mind to learn or understand something. You study for an exam, study a foreign language, or study someone's face for clues to their mood. A study is also the product of such effort—a research paper or detailed analysis: {a study on climate change}. In a home, a study is a room devoted to reading and intellectual work. In art, a study is a preliminary sketch exploring composition or technique. To be {a study in contrasts} is to embody opposing qualities.

Stuff is a general, uncountable noun whose closest synonym is things. What stuff refers to is often only made clear by a preceding adjective (cool stuff, fun stuff, weird stuff, crazy stuff). Someone’s stuff may be their personal possessions (get your stuff off the table!) or their personal problems or issues (she’s dealing with relationship stuff). To stuff something is to fill it with a uniform substance, the way you might stuff a pillow. To stuff yourself is to eat too much.

Stuffed describes something filled to capacity. A stuffed animal has soft material inside; a stuffed pepper has rice and meat. After a big meal, you feel stuffed. To get stuffed is British slang for dismissal: {Get stuffed!} In taxidermy, stuffed animals are preserved specimens with their insides replaced. A stuffed shirt is a pompous, self-important person.

Stuffing is material used to fill something. A pillow or teddy bear contains stuffing—soft material that gives it shape and bulk. In cooking, stuffing is a seasoned mixture of bread, vegetables, and herbs packed inside poultry or vegetables before roasting: {The turkey stuffing had chestnuts and sage}. To {knock the stuffing out of} someone is to defeat or demoralize them thoroughly.

Stuffy describes air that feels close, stale, or poorly ventilated: {The room was stuffy after being shut up all winter}. A stuffy nose is blocked by congestion. Of people or atmospheres, stuffy means excessively formal, old-fashioned, or self-important: {a stuffy professor}, {stuffy Victorian attitudes}. The word suggests a lack of freshness—whether of air, ideas, or manner.

To stumble is to trip or lose your footing while walking: {She stumbled on the uneven pavement}. Extended uses follow naturally—to stumble through a speech is to falter or make mistakes, and to stumble upon something is to discover it by accident: {I stumbled across an old photo in the attic}. A stumble is an instance of tripping, or any misstep or blunder.

Stumbled is the past tense of stumble—to trip or lose one's footing without falling completely: {She stumbled on the uneven pavement}. By extension, to stumble is to speak haltingly or make errors: {He stumbled through his presentation}. To {stumble upon} or {stumble across} something is to discover it by accident: {I stumbled on an old photo while cleaning}.

Stumbling is the present participle of stumble—to trip or lose one's footing while walking: {She went stumbling down the dark hallway}. Figuratively, stumbling means faltering or making mistakes: {stumbling through an apology}, {stumbling over his words}. A stumbling {block} is an obstacle that impedes progress.

A stump is what remains of something after the main part has been removed or destroyed—most commonly a tree trunk left in the ground after the tree is cut down, but also the remnant of a limb or tooth. To stump is to baffle or perplex: {That question really stumped me}. In American politics, to stump means to campaign, especially by traveling and giving speeches—from the old practice of using a tree stump as a makeshift platform. {She's been stumping across the Midwest for weeks.}

Stumped means baffled or unable to proceed—stuck without an answer or solution. The image is of being stopped short, like a tree reduced to a stump. {That last question really stumped me.} {The detective was stumped by the lack of evidence.} In cricket, stumped describes a batsman dismissed when the wicket-keeper breaks the stumps while they're out of their crease.

A stumper is a question or problem that defeats you—one you can't answer or solve: {That last clue was a real stumper}. The word comes from the idea of being stumped, left baffled like a tree reduced to its stump. Stumpers appear in quizzes, riddles, and crossword puzzles where difficulty is the point.

Stumps are what remain when something is cut short—the base of a tree after felling, the remnant of a limb after amputation, or the stub of a pencil worn down by use. In cricket, stumps are the three upright posts forming the wicket. To stump is to baffle or perplex: {The riddle stumped everyone}. Politicians stump when they campaign, traveling to give speeches—from the old practice of speaking from tree stumps. {He's out on the stump in Iowa this week.}

To stun is to daze or render senseless, typically by a blow to the head or an electrical shock: {The boxer was stunned by the punch}. Stun guns and stun grenades incapacitate without killing. More commonly, stun means to shock or astonish: {The news stunned everyone}. Something stunning can be either shocking or strikingly beautiful: {a stunning revelation}, {a stunning dress}.

Stung is the past tense and past participle of sting. A bee stung you, or you've been stung before. Beyond the literal pierce of an insect or plant, stung describes sharp emotional hurt: {I was stung by her criticism}. To get stung is also to be cheated or overcharged: {We got stung on the hotel price}.

Stunned describes being dazed or rendered senseless, either literally or figuratively. A blow to the head can leave someone stunned—unable to think clearly or react. More commonly, stunned describes overwhelming shock or surprise: {I was stunned when she announced her resignation}, {The news left us all stunned}. The effect implies momentary paralysis, a failure to process what just happened.

A stunner is someone or something that stuns, most often by being strikingly attractive or impressive. The word applies especially to people whose appearance makes others take notice: {She walked in and everyone agreed she was a stunner}. It can also describe an unexpected event or outcome that leaves people momentarily speechless, like a stunning upset in sports or politics. In British slang, stunner serves as general praise for anything excellent.

Stunning means striking enough to stun—to overwhelm the senses or leave someone momentarily dazed. A stunning {view} takes your breath away. A stunning {upset} shocks observers. A stunning {dress} commands attention. The word applies to both beauty and surprise: {She looked stunning} describes appearance, while {stunning news} describes impact. Something stunning stops you in your tracks.

A stunt is a daring feat performed for show—especially in film, where stunt doubles take physical risks for actors. The word extends to any attention-grabbing action: {a publicity stunt}, {a political stunt}. The implication is often that the act prioritizes spectacle over substance. Separately, to stunt something is to prevent its full growth or development: {Malnutrition stunted the child's growth}. A stunted tree remains small and twisted.

Stunted describes something whose growth has been checked or limited, leaving it smaller or less developed than normal. A stunted tree never reached full height; a stunted economy fails to expand. The word often implies deprivation—lack of nutrients, resources, or opportunity: {Malnutrition left the children physically and mentally stunted}. Figuratively, stunted suggests something held back from reaching its potential: {His emotional development seemed stunted}.

Stunting is showing off, especially by flaunting wealth, style, or success. The term comes from hip-hop culture, where it describes ostentatious displays—expensive cars, jewelry, designer clothes: {He's been stunting on Instagram all week}. Separately, stunting refers to impaired growth or development: {Malnutrition causes stunting in children}.

A stuntman is a person who performs dangerous physical feats in place of an actor during film or television production—falls, fights, car crashes, fire gags. The work requires athletic skill and precise choreography to create the illusion that the star is in peril. {The stuntman doubled for the lead in all the action sequences.} Also: stuntwoman, stunt performer.

Stuntmen are performers who execute dangerous or physically demanding actions in film and television, substituting for actors during scenes involving falls, fights, car crashes, or other hazards. The work requires athletic skill and precise choreography to create the illusion that the star performed the action. {The stuntmen rehearsed the explosion scene for hours.}

Stunts are daring or dangerous feats, especially those performed for entertainment: {movie stunts}, {aerial stunts}. A stunt double performs risky scenes in place of an actor. Extended to attention-getting acts: {a publicity stunt}, {a political stunt}. To stunt is to perform such feats. Separately, to stunt something is to prevent its full growth or development: {Malnutrition stunted the children}.

A stuntwoman is a woman who performs dangerous action sequences in film or television, substituting for actors during risky scenes. Stuntwomen execute falls, fights, car chases, and other physical feats requiring specialized training: {The stuntwoman did all the rooftop jumps}. The role demands athletic skill and precise timing to create convincing action while minimizing actual danger.

Stupid describes a lack of intelligence or good judgment. A stupid person doesn't think clearly; a stupid decision shows poor reasoning. The word ranges from clinical assessment to casual insult: {That was a stupid thing to say}. Stupid also means pointlessly annoying: {This stupid printer won't work}. As a noun, stupid addresses someone directly: {Hey, stupid}.

Stupidity is the quality of being unintelligent or showing poor judgment. It can describe a permanent trait or a momentary lapse: {I can't believe my own stupidity}. A stupidity is also a particular foolish act or idea: {the stupidities of youth}, {bureaucratic stupidities}. The word carries more bite than foolishness—it suggests someone should have known better.

Stupor is a state of near-unconsciousness or severely reduced mental responsiveness, typically caused by shock, drugs, alcohol, or illness. Someone in a stupor may be awake but barely aware of their surroundings: {He sat in a drunken stupor, unable to respond to questions}. The word also describes mental numbness from exhaustion or overwhelming emotion: {The news left her in a stupor}.

Sturdy describes something solidly built and able to withstand stress or rough handling: {sturdy furniture}, {sturdy hiking boots}. Applied to people, it suggests physical robustness or mental resilience: {a sturdy constitution}, {sturdy independence}. The word implies reliability without elegance—functional strength rather than delicacy.

A sturgeon is a large freshwater fish prized for its roe, which becomes caviar. Sturgeons are ancient, bony-plated fish found in rivers and coastal waters of the Northern Hemisphere. They can grow enormous—some species exceed fifteen feet—and live for decades. Overfishing for caviar has made several species endangered.

Stutter is to speak with involuntary repetition or prolongation of sounds, especially initial consonants: {He stuttered badly as a child}. The noun names this speech pattern. Beyond speech, stutter describes any halting, repetitive motion or sound: {The engine stuttered and died}. {The lights stuttered before going out}.

Stuttering is a speech pattern marked by involuntary repetitions, prolongations, or blocks—moments when words won't come out smoothly: {He's been stuttering since childhood}. As an adjective, it describes halting or interrupted motion: {The engine made a stuttering sound before dying}. Figuratively, stuttering progress is uneven and faltering: {The economy's stuttering recovery worried investors}.

A sty is a pen or enclosure for pigs, typically a small, muddy, foul-smelling structure. By extension, any filthy or cluttered space becomes a sty: {Clean up your room—it's a sty}. A sty (also stye) is separately a small, painful swelling on the edge of an eyelid, caused by an infected gland.

Style is the distinctive way something is done, made, or expressed. A writer's style, a style of architecture, a style of dress. Style often suggests elegance or flair: {She has real style}. To style something is to design or arrange it: {He styled her hair for the wedding}. In fashion and design, to style is to create a particular look. A self-styled expert has given themselves that title without official recognition.

A stylist is someone who cultivates or creates style. A hair stylist cuts and arranges hair. A fashion stylist selects clothing and accessories for photo shoots, celebrities, or everyday clients. In writing, a stylist is someone with distinctive prose style: {She's more stylist than storyteller}. The term implies attention to aesthetics and presentation.

A stylus is a pointed instrument for writing or marking. The original stylus scratched letters into wax tablets; modern versions include the needle that reads vinyl record grooves and the pen-shaped tool for touchscreens and graphics tablets. {She tapped the screen with her stylus.} Plural: styli or styluses.

Styrofoam is a genericized trademark for expanded polystyrene foam, the lightweight white material used for disposable cups, takeout containers, and packing materials. It's technically a brand name for a specific type of insulation board, but common usage applies it to any foam plastic: {The coffee came in a styrofoam cup}. The material is notorious for being non-biodegradable. (Capitalized Styrofoam is the trademark.)

Suave describes a man who is smoothly charming, sophisticated, and socially confident—often with an undertone of superficiality or excessive polish. A suave manner suggests elegant ease in social situations: {a suave diplomat}, {He was too suave to be trusted}. The word carries mild suspicion that the charm may be calculated rather than genuine.

Sub is a noun and verb that is usually a shortening of several words that begin s-u-b: a submarine; a submarine sandwich (one on a long roll or bun); a substitute, or to substitute for someone, such as a teacher (we had a sub today, subbing for the coach); and a subscription: I billed her for the magazine sub. The prefix and adjective sub conveys below, inferior, or subordinate. A subwoofer produces low bass frequencies. A sub par performance is not very good, except in golf.

The subconscious is the part of the mind that operates below conscious awareness—thoughts, memories, and impulses that influence behavior without being directly accessible. {Subconsciously, she'd been avoiding him for weeks.} The term is looser than the technical unconscious in psychology, often used interchangeably in everyday speech: {My subconscious must have known something was wrong.}

A subculture is a group within a larger culture that distinguishes itself through shared interests, values, or practices: {punk subculture}, {gaming subculture}, {the drag subculture}. The term implies both belonging to the mainstream and standing apart from it. Members often signal affiliation through style, language, or behavior that outsiders don't fully understand.

Subcultures is the plural of subculture—a group within a larger culture that distinguishes itself through shared interests, values, or practices. Punks, goths, skaters, and gamers form subcultures. The term implies both belonging to the broader society and standing apart from it: {The city's drag scene was a vibrant subculture with its own stars and hierarchies}.

To subdue is to bring under control, typically through force or authority. You might subdue an attacker, an uprising, or a wild animal. The word extends to quieter forms of conquest: subduing your emotions means keeping them in check, and subdued lighting or colors are muted, soft, less intense than usual. A subdued person is quiet and restrained, perhaps because something has taken the fight out of them. {The medication helped subdue her anxiety.}

Subdued describes something quieted, softened, or restrained from its natural intensity. A subdued {voice} is hushed; subdued {lighting} is dim; subdued {colors} are muted. A person who is subdued has been made less lively or assertive, often through defeat, disappointment, or exhaustion: {He seemed subdued after the meeting}. The word implies something held back or tamped down rather than simply absent.

The commonest meaning of the noun subject (stress on first syllable) is similar to topic, something that is the focus of attention or study. In grammar, the subject of a sentence is typically the agent associated with the verb. In a monarchy, a subject is like a citizen. The verb subject (stress on last syllable) means to cause someone or something to have an unpleasant experience: Do not subject the animals to torture.

Subjugation is the act of bringing someone or something under control, typically by force. Nations subjugate conquered peoples; dictators subjugate populations. The word implies domination and the loss of autonomy: {the subjugation of indigenous tribes}, {economic subjugation}. It can extend to abstract things: {the subjugation of emotion to reason}.

Sublime describes something of such excellence or grandeur that it inspires awe—beauty, art, or nature so elevated it transcends ordinary experience: {a sublime sunset over the mountains}, {Mozart's sublime compositions}. The word carries a sense of the overwhelming or transcendent. In chemistry, to sublime is to pass directly from solid to gas without becoming liquid, as dry ice does. The verb also means to elevate or refine something base into something pure or noble. (Capitalized Sublime refers to the text editor or band.)

A submarine is a vessel designed to operate underwater, used by navies for warfare and surveillance, and in civilian contexts for research and exploration. The word also works as an adjective meaning underwater: {submarine cables}, {submarine warfare}. As a verb, to submarine is to undermine or sabotage covertly. A submarine sandwich—a sub—is a long sandwich on a cylindrical roll, named for its shape.

Submarines are vessels designed to operate underwater. Military submarines carry torpedoes and missiles; research submarines explore ocean depths. The word also refers to long sandwiches on oblong rolls—also called hoagies, grinders, or heroes depending on region: {I ordered a meatball submarine for lunch}. As a verb, to submarine is to undermine something covertly, or in baseball, to pitch with an extreme underhand motion.

To submerge is to put or go under water or another liquid: {The submarine submerged beneath the ice}. By extension, anything that gets buried or overwhelmed is submerged: {submerged in debt}, {submerged in work}. A submerged truth lies hidden beneath the surface. To submerge yourself in a subject is to immerse yourself completely in studying it.

Submerged means underwater or covered by liquid: {The submerged wreckage lay on the ocean floor}. By extension, something submerged is hidden or obscured: {submerged tensions}, {submerged memories}. A submerged population or community exists beneath notice, overlooked by mainstream society.

Submission is the act of yielding to authority or control. A wrestler forces an opponent into submission. In BDSM, submission is the consensual role of surrendering power to a dominant partner. Submission also means presenting something for consideration: {The deadline for submissions is Friday}. A legal submission is a formal argument presented to a court.

Submissions are things submitted—documents, proposals, or creative works offered for consideration or judgment. Writers send submissions to publishers, wrestlers force opponents into submission holds, and courts accept legal submissions. The core idea is yielding: you submit work to an editor's judgment, or submit to authority. In BDSM, submission is the consensual surrender of control to a dominant partner.

Submissive describes someone who yields to authority or the will of others, whether by temperament, circumstance, or choice. A submissive {posture} signals deference; a submissive {tone} avoids confrontation. In BDSM contexts, a submissive (or sub) is a person who consensually cedes control to a dominant partner: {She identifies as a submissive}. The word can suggest weakness when applied critically, or willing surrender when applied neutrally.

Submit means to yield to authority, control, or superior force: {The rebels finally submitted}. You submit a document when you hand it over for consideration or judgment: {submit a proposal}, {submit an application}. The word implies accepting another's will or decision—whether voluntarily or under pressure. To submit to an examination is to undergo it. In wrestling and martial arts, a submission forces an opponent to yield.

Subordinate describes something or someone lower in rank, importance, or position: {a subordinate clause}, {subordinate officers}. As a noun, a subordinate is a person who works under another's authority: {She delegated the task to her subordinates}. The verb means to treat as less important or to place under another's control: {He subordinated his own interests to the company's goals}.

Subpar means below an expected or acceptable standard. The word comes from golf, where par is the number of strokes a skilled player should need—so subpar performance in golf is actually good. But outside golf, subpar always means deficient or inadequate: {The service was subpar}, {a subpar effort}. The reversal from golf's meaning is now firmly established.

A subpoena is a legal document compelling someone to appear in court or produce evidence. The word comes from Latin meaning "under penalty"—failure to comply can result in contempt charges. As a verb, to subpoena someone is to serve them with such a document: {The committee subpoenaed the CEO's financial records}.

Subs is the plural of sub, which has several meanings united by the idea of substitution or being underneath. A sub is a substitute—a sub {teacher}, a sub on a sports team. In BDSM, a sub is the submissive partner. A sub is also a submarine or a submarine sandwich. To sub is to serve as a substitute: {I'm subbing for the regular bartender tonight}. In online contexts, subs are subscriptions or subscribers: {The channel just hit a million subs}.

Subscribe means to sign up to receive something regularly—a magazine, streaming service, newsletter, or channel: {I subscribed to the New York Times}. The word carries a sense of ongoing commitment rather than one-time purchase. To subscribe to a belief or theory is to agree with or support it: {I don't subscribe to that view}. In formal contexts, to subscribe is to sign one's name to a document, affirming its contents.

A subscriber is someone who has signed up to receive something regularly—a magazine, streaming service, newsletter, or channel. The word implies ongoing access in exchange for payment or registration: {The channel just hit a million subscribers}. In older usage, a subscriber was one who signed a document or pledged money to a cause.

A subscription is an arrangement to receive something regularly in exchange for payment: a subscription to a magazine, a streaming service, a meal kit. The model has spread from periodicals to software, where you pay monthly rather than buying outright. To subscribe is to sign up for such an arrangement, or more broadly, to agree with a belief or position: {I don't subscribe to that theory}. A subscriber is anyone who subscribes.

Subscriptions are arrangements where you pay regularly to receive something ongoing—a magazine, streaming service, or software access. The model has expanded from newspapers and gym memberships to nearly everything: {I'm canceling half my subscriptions}. On platforms like YouTube, a subscription follows a creator's content, often without payment. The singular subscription works as an attributive noun: {subscription box}, {subscription fee}.

A subsidy is money given by a government or institution to support an industry, business, or activity deemed beneficial: {farm subsidies}, {housing subsidies}. Subsidies reduce costs for producers or consumers, often to keep prices low or maintain domestic production. Critics argue subsidies distort markets; supporters see them as necessary for strategic industries or public goods. The verb is subsidize.

Substance is the physical material something is made of: {a powdery substance}, {a sticky substance}. In law and medicine, substance often means a drug, especially an illegal one: {substance abuse}, {controlled substance}. Substance also refers to meaningful content or significance: {a speech with little substance}, {arguments lacking substance}. A person {of substance} has wealth or importance.

Substantial means considerable in size, amount, or importance: {a substantial raise}, {substantial evidence}. Something substantial has real weight or significance—not trivial or superficial. A substantial meal is filling and satisfying. Substantial can also mean solidly built or materially real: {a substantial brick building}. In law, substantial compliance means meeting the essential requirements even if not every detail.

A substitute takes the place of something or someone else. A substitute teacher fills in for an absent one. Sugar substitutes replace sugar. To substitute is to make such a replacement: {She substituted honey for sugar in the recipe}. In sports, a substitute enters the game for another player. The word implies something secondary or inferior to the original, though not always: {There's no substitute for experience}.

Substitutes are things or people that take the place of others. A substitute teacher fills in for the regular one. Sugar substitutes replace sugar in food and drinks. In sports, a substitute enters the game for another player. The verb substitute means to use one thing in place of another: {You can substitute olive oil for butter in this recipe}. What substitutes for something serves in its stead.

Substitution is the act of replacing one thing with another: {The coach made a substitution in the second half}. In cooking, a substitution swaps one ingredient for another: {Use applesauce as a substitution for oil}. In mathematics and logic, substitution replaces variables with values or expressions. The word emphasizes the exchange itself—something goes out, something equivalent goes in.

Subterfuge is deception used to achieve a goal—a trick or stratagem that conceals one's true intentions. The word implies cunning rather than brute force: {She gained access through subterfuge, posing as a delivery driver}. Subterfuge often carries a negative connotation, suggesting dishonesty rather than clever maneuvering, though the line between the two depends on who's judging.

Subtext is the unspoken meaning beneath what's actually said or written—the implications, emotions, and intentions that lurk under the surface of dialogue or text. When someone says {We should do this again sometime} with flat affect, the subtext might be that they never want to see you again. Writers layer subtext into scenes to create tension or reveal character without spelling everything out. {The conversation was polite, but the subtext was pure hostility.}

A subtitle is secondary text appearing below a title, adding explanation or context: {The book's subtitle clarified its scope}. Subtitles also refer to the text displayed at the bottom of a screen translating or transcribing dialogue in film or television: {I watch foreign films with subtitles}. To subtitle is to provide either kind.

Subtitles are text displayed at the bottom of a screen showing dialogue or narration, typically translating foreign language content or providing accessibility for deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers. They appear synchronized with speech: {Turn on the subtitles—I can't understand the accent}. Unlike closed captions, subtitles usually omit descriptions of sound effects. To subtitle a film is to add such text.

Subtle whispers its many adjectival meanings: fine, delicate, complex, sophisticated, and cunning. Subtle is the opposite of concepts such as overt, obvious, simple, and blunt. A subtle difference is one that is small and perhaps hard to notice, but significant. A subtle effect is one that may only be noticeable in certain conditions. If you are subtle in your behavior, you are thoughtful, careful, and not loud or brash.

Subtlety is the quality of being subtle—fine distinctions, delicate nuances, or understated skill. A wine's subtlety lies in its complex but quiet flavors. The subtleties of a language are the fine points that take years to master. Someone who lacks subtlety is blunt or heavy-handed: {He approached the negotiation with all the subtlety of a sledgehammer}.

To subtract is to take one quantity away from another: {Subtract three from ten and you get seven}. The word extends beyond arithmetic to any removal or reduction: {If you subtract the cost of materials, there's not much profit left}. The opposite of add.

Subtraction is the mathematical operation of taking one quantity away from another—the inverse of addition. The result is called the difference: {Seven minus three equals four}. Beyond arithmetic, subtraction refers to any removal or reduction: {The subtraction of key players weakened the team}.

A suburb is a residential area on the outskirts of a city, typically with lower density than urban centers. Suburbs developed as places where people could own homes with yards while commuting to city jobs. The adjective suburban often carries connotations of middle-class conformity and homogeneity: {suburban sprawl}, {the suburban dream}. The suburbs collectively form a noun: {They moved to the suburbs}.

Suburban describes things related to suburbs—the residential areas surrounding cities. Suburban neighborhoods typically feature single-family homes, lawns, and car-dependent layouts: {suburban sprawl}, {a suburban shopping mall}. The word can carry connotations of middle-class conformity or blandness: {Their tastes were hopelessly suburban}.

Suburbia is the suburbs collectively, or suburban life as a cultural phenomenon. The word often carries connotations of conformity, material comfort, and social homogeneity—the world of tract housing, lawn care, and commuter culture: {She couldn't wait to escape suburbia}. It can be neutral or dismissive depending on context.

Suburbs are the residential areas surrounding a city, typically characterized by lower density, single-family homes, and car-dependent layouts. The singular suburb refers to one such community: {They moved to a suburb of Chicago}. Suburban life carries connotations of middle-class comfort, uniformity, and distance from urban energy—praised for safety and space, criticized for sprawl and blandness.

Subversion is the act of undermining or overthrowing something established—typically a government, institution, or system of authority. The word carries connotations of working from within or below: {The regime accused dissidents of subversion}. In computing, Subversion (often abbreviated SVN) is a version control system for tracking changes in software code.

Subversive describes something that undermines or seeks to overthrow established systems, institutions, or authority—usually through indirect or covert means rather than open confrontation. A subversive {book} challenges accepted ideas; subversive {activities} work to destabilize a government. As a noun, a subversive is a person engaged in such efforts: {The regime arrested suspected subversives}. The word carries different connotations depending on perspective—what authorities call subversive, dissidents may call necessary.

A subway is an underground railway system for urban transit: {I take the subway to work}. In British usage, subway can also mean an underground pedestrian passage. The word combines the sense of beneath (sub-) with way, emphasizing the route running below street level. {The New York subway runs twenty-four hours a day.} (Capitalized Subway is the sandwich chain.)

Subways are underground railway systems for urban transit, or the tunnels and passages that house them. Major cities have subway networks: {Take the subway to Times Square}. In British usage, a subway may simply be an underground pedestrian passage. As a verb, to subway is to travel by subway: {We subwayed downtown}.

Subzero describes temperatures below zero degrees, whether Celsius or Fahrenheit depending on context: {subzero temperatures}, {subzero wind chill}. The term emphasizes extreme cold: {The explorers endured subzero conditions for weeks}. Figuratively, subzero can describe anything icily cold or hostile: {a subzero reception}.

Succeed means to achieve a desired outcome or reach a goal: {She succeeded in getting the promotion}. It also means to come after in sequence or replace: {Elizabeth succeeded her father as monarch}. To succeed to something is to inherit it, especially a title or position. Success is the noun, successful the adjective.

Succeeded is the past tense of succeed. To succeed is to achieve a desired outcome or accomplish a goal: {She succeeded in convincing them to stay}. It also means to follow in sequence or take over a position: {Elizabeth succeeded her father as monarch}. {The calm succeeded the storm}.

Success is the state of having achieved a goal (The team’s success last weekend means they will move on to the playoffs), or the attainment of that which is normally viewed as desirable, such as fame, wealth, or high social standing: His mansion was evidence of the tycoon’s success. Success is the opposite of failure in most contexts.

Successful means achieving a desired outcome or reaching a goal. A successful {business} turns a profit; a successful {surgery} accomplishes what the surgeon intended. The word often implies wealth, status, or recognition: {a successful lawyer}, {a successful author}. But success is relative to the goal—a successful {escape} needs only to get away.

Succession is a sequence of things following one after another: {a succession of bad decisions}, {a succession of rainy days}. It also means the process of inheriting a position or title: {the line of succession to the throne}, {a succession crisis}. In business, succession planning prepares for leadership transitions. The verb is succeed, which also means to achieve success—two different words that merged in English.

A successor is someone or something that follows another in a position, role, or sequence. A CEO names a successor before retiring. A product replaces its predecessor: {The phone's successor featured a better camera}. In monarchies, the successor to the throne inherits the crown. The word implies continuation—the successor takes over what came before.

Succulent describes something juicy and richly flavorful: {a succulent steak}, {succulent peaches}. The word suggests moisture and tenderness, often appearing in food writing. In botany, succulents are plants with thick, fleshy tissues that store water—cacti, aloe, jade plants. These have become popular as low-maintenance houseplants: {She lined her windowsill with succulents}.

Succulents are plants with thick, fleshy leaves or stems that store water, allowing them to survive in arid conditions. Cacti are the most familiar type, but the category includes aloe, jade plants, and many others. They've become popular houseplants because they tolerate neglect: {I can't kill my succulents no matter how rarely I water them}.

To suck is to draw liquid or air into the mouth: {The baby sucked milk from the bottle}. {Suck the juice through a straw}. Suck extends to anything that draws inward: {The vacuum sucked up the dirt}. {The whirlpool sucked the boat under}. In slang, suck means to be bad or disappointing: {This movie sucks}. {Mondays suck}. This sense likely derives from vulgar phrases, but it's become so mainstream many don't register the origin. To suck up is to flatter obsequiously. To suck it up is to endure hardship without complaining.

A sucker is something that sucks—an adhesive organ like those on an octopus's tentacles, a shoot growing from a plant's roots that saps the main plant's energy, or a lollipop (you suck on it): {The octopus gripped with its suckers}. {Remove the suckers from your tomato plants}. {She handed the child a sucker}. A sucker is also a gullible person, easily fooled: {There's a sucker born every minute}. To sucker someone is to deceive them. A {sucker punch} is an unexpected blow. In affectionate slang, sucker refers to any person or thing: {I love the little sucker}.

Suckers is the plural of sucker—adhesive organs, plant shoots, lollipops, or gullible people: {The octopus has suckers on its tentacles}. {Those suckers fell for the scam}. {She bought suckers for the kids}.

Sucks is the third-person verb meaning draws in liquid or air: {The pump sucks water from the well}. {A black hole sucks in everything nearby}. In slang, sucks means is bad or disappointing: {That sucks} is a common expression of sympathy. {This job sucks}. The slang is so mainstream it's hardly vulgar anymore.

Suction is the force created when air or liquid is removed from a space, causing surrounding matter to rush in to fill the vacuum. A vacuum cleaner works by suction; so does drinking through a straw. The verb means to remove by this force: {The surgeon suctioned blood from the wound}. Anything that creates strong pull may be described as having suction: {The mud had such suction I lost my boot}.

Sudden describes something that happens quickly and without warning: a sudden {storm}, a sudden {realization}, a sudden {death}. The emphasis is on unexpectedness rather than mere speed—a sudden change catches you off guard. {All of a sudden} means abruptly or without anticipation: {All of a sudden, the lights went out}.

Suddenly means in an abrupt or unexpected way, without warning or gradual transition: {Suddenly the lights went out}. The word marks a sharp break from what preceded—something happens all at once rather than building up to it. {He suddenly realized he'd left his wallet at home}.

Sudoku is a logic puzzle played on a nine-by-nine grid divided into nine smaller boxes. The goal is to fill each row, column, and box with the digits one through nine, using each digit exactly once. Puzzles begin with some numbers already placed, and solvers deduce the rest through elimination: {I do the sudoku in the morning paper}, {She's addicted to sudoku apps}.

To sue is to bring legal action against someone, seeking compensation or remedy through the courts: {She sued the company for wrongful termination}. The word extends to formal requests: to {sue for peace} is to petition for an end to hostilities. (Capitalized Sue is a given name.)

Suede is leather with a soft, napped surface, made by buffing the inner side of animal hide. The texture is velvety but vulnerable to water and stains: {suede shoes}, {a suede jacket}. As an adjective, it describes the material or its characteristic finish: {suede elbow patches}. The word comes from French for Sweden, where the leather was first produced.

Suffer means to experience something painful or unpleasant—physical pain, emotional distress, or hardship: {She suffered a broken leg in the accident}, {He suffered greatly after the divorce}. It extends to undergoing any negative effect: {The economy suffered during the recession}. In older or formal usage, suffer means to allow or tolerate: {Suffer the little children to come unto me}. To {suffer fools gladly} is to tolerate stupid people patiently—usually said of someone who doesn't.

Suffered is the past tense of suffer, meaning to experience pain, hardship, or something unpleasant: {She suffered a broken leg in the fall}, {He suffered through years of chronic illness}. It can indicate decline or damage: {His reputation suffered after the scandal}. To suffer something is also to tolerate or endure it: {She doesn't suffer fools gladly}.

Suffering is the experience of pain, distress, or hardship—physical or emotional. It encompasses everything from bodily agony to grief, despair, and prolonged misery: {the suffering of refugees}, {years of suffering in silence}. The word often implies endurance over time rather than momentary pain. As an adjective, suffering describes those currently in distress: {the suffering masses}. To suffer is to undergo pain or to tolerate something unwillingly: {She doesn't suffer fools gladly}.

To suffocate is to die or cause death from lack of air—by smothering, choking, or oxygen deprivation. The meaning extends to any overwhelming constriction: {The heat was suffocating}. Figuratively, suffocate describes emotional or creative stifling: {She felt suffocated by her parents' expectations}. {The relationship suffocated him}.

Suffocated is the past tense of suffocate—to die or kill by cutting off air supply. Someone suffocated by a pillow or in a smoke-filled room cannot breathe. The word extends to any overwhelming restriction: {I felt suffocated by their constant attention}. A suffocated relationship or talent has been smothered rather than allowed to breathe.

Suffocating describes the sensation of being unable to breathe, whether from physical obstruction or lack of air: {The smoke was suffocating}. Figuratively, it characterizes anything oppressively restrictive or stifling: {a suffocating relationship}, {suffocating heat}, {the suffocating expectations of her family}. The word emphasizes not just discomfort but the urgent need for escape or relief.

Suffocation is death or near-death from lack of oxygen—whether from blocked airways, smothering, or displacement of breathable air. The word extends to any overwhelming restriction: {The suffocation of living under constant surveillance}. A room can feel like suffocation; so can a relationship. To die by suffocation is to suffocate.

Suffrage is the right to vote in political elections. The term appears most often in historical contexts—the women's suffrage movement fought for decades to secure voting rights for women. Universal suffrage means all adult citizens can vote regardless of property, race, or sex. {The Nineteenth Amendment granted women's suffrage in the United States.}

A suffragette was a woman who campaigned for voting rights, particularly in Britain and the United States in the early twentieth century. The term originally distinguished militants willing to use confrontational tactics—hunger strikes, property destruction, civil disobedience—from more moderate suffragists. {The suffragettes chained themselves to the railings outside Parliament.} Now often used interchangeably with suffragist for any women's suffrage activist of that era.

Suffragettes were women who fought for the right to vote, particularly in Britain and the United States in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The term often implies militant tactics—marches, hunger strikes, civil disobedience—distinguishing suffragettes from the broader suffragist movement. {The suffragettes chained themselves to the railings outside Parliament.}

A suffragist is someone who advocates for extending voting rights, especially to women. The term is most associated with the movement for women's suffrage in the late 19th and early 20th centuries: {The suffragists marched on Washington demanding the vote}. Unlike suffragette, which was often applied dismissively to militant activists, suffragist is the neutral term.

Suffragists were activists who campaigned for voting rights, particularly women's right to vote. The term applies especially to those in the late 19th and early 20th centuries who fought for women's suffrage in Britain and America: {The suffragists marched on Washington}. The more militant British activists were called suffragettes, often by their opponents.

Sugar is the sweet crystalline substance extracted from cane or beets, used to sweeten food and drink: {Add a spoonful of sugar}. {Sugar rots your teeth}. By extension, sugar means sweetness or flattery: {sugar-coated words}. As a term of endearment: {Hey sugar}. As an exclamation, sugar is a euphemism for shit: {Oh sugar, I dropped it}. The substitution lets speakers express frustration without profanity.

Sugarcane is a tall tropical grass cultivated for the sugar in its fibrous stalks. The raw cane is crushed to extract juice, which is processed into table sugar, molasses, and rum. {Miles of sugarcane fields stretched across the plantation}. Also spelled as two words: sugar cane.

To sugarcoat something is to make it more palatable or acceptable, like coating bitter medicine in sugar. The word almost always appears in contexts about softening unpleasant truths: {Don't sugarcoat it—tell me what's really going on}. A sugarcoated version of events omits or downplays the harsh parts.

Sugarcoated describes something made more palatable or appealing, like medicine coated in sugar to mask bitterness. The term usually applies to unpleasant truths or harsh realities presented in softened form: {Give it to me straight—I don't want the sugarcoated version}. A sugarcoated {pill} may be literal; a sugarcoated {lie} makes deception easier to swallow.

Sugarcoating is presenting something unpleasant in a more palatable way—softening bad news, glossing over problems, or making harsh truths easier to accept. Like candy coating on bitter medicine, it makes things go down easier: {Don't sugarcoat it—just tell me what's wrong}. The verb is sugarcoat; the noun describes the practice or the coating itself.

Sugarcoats means makes something unpleasant seem more acceptable or appealing, like coating bitter medicine with sugar. Someone who sugarcoats bad news softens it to spare feelings: {Don't sugarcoat it—just tell me the truth}. The term often carries a negative implication that the speaker is being evasive or dishonest rather than genuinely kind.

A sugarplum is a small round candy, traditionally made of boiled sugar with fruit or nuts inside. The word evokes old-fashioned confections and appears most often in Christmas contexts—{visions of sugarplums} from the famous poem, or the Sugarplum Fairy in *The Nutcracker*. As a term of endearment, sugarplum sounds affectionate but quaint.

Sugarplums are small round candies, traditionally made of boiled sugar with fruit or nuts inside. The word survives mainly through "The Night Before Christmas," where visions of sugarplums dance in children's heads. By extension, sugarplum can mean any enticing fantasy or sweet reward: {Dreams of promotion were the sugarplums that kept her working late}.

Suggest means to put forward an idea for consideration without insisting on it: {I suggest we leave early}. The word implies tentativeness—a suggestion can be declined. Things can suggest without speaking: {The evidence suggests foul play}. A hint or trace of something also suggests: {a dish with just a suggestion of garlic}. To suggest itself is to come to mind naturally: {A solution suggested itself}.

A suggestion is an idea or plan put forward for someone to consider, typically without strong insistence: {I have a suggestion for how we might solve this}. When you make a suggestion, you're offering a possibility rather than giving an order. Suggestion also refers to a slight trace or hint of something: {There was a suggestion of garlic in the sauce}. In psychology, suggestion describes the process by which an idea is implanted in someone's mind, as in hypnotic suggestion.

Suggestive means hinting at something without stating it directly. A suggestive {remark} or {gesture} implies sexual interest without being explicit. More broadly, something suggestive of another thing evokes or calls it to mind: {The architecture was suggestive of ancient Rome}. The word often carries a faintly improper or risqué connotation, especially without a following "of."

A sugya is a unit of discussion in the Talmud—a self-contained passage examining a particular legal or theological question through debate, interpretation, and commentary. Scholars analyze the Talmud sugya by sugya, each one weaving together biblical verses, rabbinic opinions, and dialectical argument: {We spent the whole class on a single sugya about Sabbath boundaries}.

Suicidal describes someone inclined toward or at risk of taking their own life: {She was hospitalized after expressing suicidal thoughts}. Extended uses describe actions recklessly self-destructive or certain to fail disastrously: {Attacking without reinforcements would be suicidal}. The word carries serious weight in clinical contexts but functions as hyperbole in casual speech: {Career suicide}, {political suicide}.

Suicide is the act of intentionally killing oneself. As a verb, to suicide is to take one's own life—though {commit suicide} remains the more common phrasing. The word extends to self-destructive choices: {political suicide}, {career suicide}. A suicide mission has little chance of survival. In football, a suicide squeeze is a risky play where the runner commits before the batter makes contact.

A suit (noun) can, among other things, be a case at law (lawsuit); a set of clothing in which the pieces match (men’s suit); protective clothing for a particular purpose (wetsuit); and any of the four sets of cards (hearts, diamonds, spades, clubs) that share a symbol. The verb suit typically has an impersonal subject and means to be proper, satisfactory, or appropriate: That color really suits you. When you suit yourself, you do what you want to do.

A suitcase is a rectangular piece of luggage with a handle, designed for carrying clothes and personal items while traveling. Traditional suitcases have a hinged lid and clasps or zippers; modern ones often have wheels and an extendable handle. The word distinguishes this portable case from larger trunks or smaller bags. {I packed my suitcase the night before the flight.} A suitcase is sometimes used figuratively to suggest readiness to leave or transient circumstances.

Suite connects to the idea of a set or sequence. A hotel suite is a connected set of rooms. A suite of furniture is a matching set. In music, a suite is a sequence of related pieces, often dance movements. In computing, a software suite is a bundle of related programs: {the Microsoft Office suite}. The word is pronounced like "sweet."

Suites is the plural of suite, a word with meanings unified by the idea of things that go together. A hotel suite is a set of connected rooms. A suite of furniture is a matching collection. In music, a suite is a sequence of related pieces. Software suites bundle related programs: {productivity suites}, {creative suites}. In business, the C-suite refers to top executives—CEO, CFO, and the like.

A suitor is someone who pursues another romantically, especially a man courting a woman with marriage in mind. The word sounds old-fashioned: {She had many suitors in her youth}. In legal and business contexts, a suitor is a party bringing a lawsuit or a company seeking to acquire another: {The hostile suitor raised its bid}.

Suitors is the plural of suitor—someone who pursues another romantically, especially with marriage in mind. The word sounds old-fashioned, evoking a time when courtship was more formal: {She had many suitors but chose none of them}. In legal contexts, a suitor is a party bringing a lawsuit. In business, suitors are companies attempting to acquire another: {The tech startup attracted several suitors}.

Suits are matching jackets and trousers, or jackets and skirts, worn as formal attire: {He owns three suits}. A suit is also a legal action: {filed a suit against the company}. In cards, suits are the four categories—hearts, diamonds, clubs, spades. Informally, suits are business executives or bureaucrats, often dismissively: {The suits decided to cut the budget}. To suit is to be appropriate for or pleasing to: {Does Thursday suit you?} Something that suits you also looks good on you: {That color suits you}.

Sulfur is a yellow nonmetallic chemical element that occurs naturally in volcanic regions and mineral deposits. It has a distinctive sharp smell, most familiar from rotten eggs and struck matches, which comes from hydrogen sulfide and other sulfur compounds. Sulfur has been known since ancient times, when it was called brimstone—the "fire and brimstone" of religious texts refers to burning sulfur. Industrial uses include making sulfuric acid, fertilizers, and vulcanizing rubber.

To sulk is to brood in silence, withdrawing into resentful or petulant mood rather than expressing displeasure openly. Children sulk when they don't get their way; adults sulk after arguments. The noun describes both the mood and the person in it: {She's in a sulk}, {He's such a sulk}. A sulk is passive aggression made visible—the cold shoulder, the averted gaze, the pointed silence.

Sulking is brooding in silence, typically after being offended or not getting one's way. It's a form of passive displeasure—refusing to engage cheerfully while making sure others notice the unhappiness. Children sulk when denied treats; adults sulk after arguments. The behavior suggests wounded pride mixed with a desire for attention or apology. {He spent the afternoon sulking in his room after being told he couldn't go.}

Sulks is a state of silent, resentful withdrawal—what you're in when you retreat into brooding displeasure: {She's been in the sulks all morning}. The phrase {the sulks} treats this moody silence as a condition one falls into, often childishly, after feeling slighted or not getting one's way.

Sulky describes a mood of silent, withdrawn resentment—refusing to engage or be cheerful because of some grievance: {She gave him a sulky look when he canceled their plans}. Children go sulky when denied what they want; adults do too, though less acceptably. A sulky is also a light two-wheeled cart used in harness racing, pulled by a single horse.

Sullen describes a mood of resentful, silent bad temper. A sullen person withdraws into brooding displeasure rather than expressing anger openly: {He gave a sullen shrug and said nothing}. The word suggests hostility held inward—someone who won't engage but makes their unhappiness known. Weather or skies can be sullen when dark and threatening.

Sulphur is the British spelling of sulfur, the yellow chemical element known for its distinctive smell when burned. It occurs naturally in volcanic regions and hot springs, and has been used since ancient times in gunpowder, matches, and medicinal applications. The spelling with -ph- remains common in British English and in traditional contexts like {brimstone and sulphur}, though scientific publications increasingly favor the -f- spelling standardized by international chemistry bodies.

Sultan is a title for a Muslim sovereign, historically ruling with absolute authority over a territory called a sultanate. The Ottoman sultans ruled for centuries. The word carries connotations of supreme power and Eastern opulence: {He surveyed his domain like a sultan}. A few rulers still bear the title today, notably in Brunei and Oman.

Sultry describes weather that is hot and humid—oppressively warm with moisture hanging in the air: {a sultry August afternoon}. The discomfort of such weather extends to a second meaning: sexually attractive in a languid, smoldering way. A sultry voice or glance suggests slow-burning desire rather than overt seduction: {She gave him a sultry look across the room}.

A sum is a total of numbers added together. It is used frequently of money, even when there is no obvious breakdown of it into parts (hefty sum, lump sum). The sum and substance of something is the essence of it. The expression in sum means in summary, or briefly. The verb sum, typically occurring as sum up, means to summarize. When you sum numbers, you add them up.

A summary is a condensed version of something longer—a text, speech, or event—capturing the main points while omitting details. {Here's a summary of what happened}. As an adjective, summary means done quickly without full procedure: {summary judgment}, {summary execution}. The adjective carries a sense of abruptness, sometimes harshness.

Summer is the warmest season of the year, falling between spring and autumn. In the Northern Hemisphere, it runs roughly from June through August; in the Southern Hemisphere, from December through February. Summer carries associations of vacation, leisure, and outdoor activity: {We spent the summer at the lake}. As a verb, to summer somewhere is to spend that season there: {The family summers in Maine}. A summer can also describe years of age in poetic or literary contexts: {a youth of sixteen summers}.

Summertime is the summer season, the warmest months of the year. The word emphasizes the period's distinct quality—long days, warm weather, outdoor activity—rather than calendar dates: {We spend our summertime at the lake}. It carries nostalgic or leisurely connotations that plain "summer" sometimes lacks.

A summit is the highest point of something, typically a mountain: {We reached the summit at dawn}. The word extends to any peak or culmination: {the summit of her career}. A summit is also a high-level meeting between heads of state or other leaders: {an economic summit}, {a climate summit}. To summit is to reach the top: {She summited Everest without supplemental oxygen}.

Summits is the plural of summit—the highest point of a mountain or hill, or figuratively, the peak of achievement: {She reached the summits of her profession}. Summits also names high-level meetings between heads of state or government: {The G7 summits address global economic policy}. The verb form means to reach the top: {He summits mountains for charity}.

To summon is to call someone to appear or come to you, typically with authority: {The judge summoned the witness to testify}. Courts issue summons; employers summon employees to meetings. The word extends to calling forth effort or emotion: {She summoned her courage}. In fantasy contexts, to summon is to conjure a spirit or creature into being.

A summoner is one who summons—calls someone to appear or brings something forth. The word appears most often in fantasy contexts, where a summoner conjures creatures or spirits: {The summoner called forth a demon from the void}. In legal or historical usage, a summoner is an official who issues summonses requiring court appearance.

Summoning is the act of calling forth or ordering someone to appear. A court summons witnesses, a king summons subjects, a wizard summons spirits. The word carries authority—you summon what must obey: {The president is summoning his advisors}. To summon courage or strength is to gather it deliberately: {She summoned the nerve to speak up}.

A summons is an official order requiring someone to appear somewhere, especially in court: {She received a summons for jury duty}. Police issue summonses for minor violations like traffic tickets. The word also describes any authoritative call to appear: {a summons to the principal's office}. To summon is to issue such a call, or more broadly to call forth: {summon courage}, {summon a memory}.

Sumo is a traditional Japanese form of wrestling in which two large competitors attempt to force each other out of a circular ring or to touch the ground with any body part other than the feet. The wrestlers, called rikishi, are typically massive—weight is an advantage, and there are no weight classes. {We watched sumo on television during our trip to Tokyo.} The word also functions as an adjective suggesting exceptional size or heft: {a sumo-sized portion}.

Sums is the plural of sum—totals, amounts, or the results of addition. {The sums don't add up.} A sum can also be an amount of money: {They invested large sums in the project.} In British usage, sums means arithmetic problems: {The children worked on their sums.} To sum up is to summarize: {Let me sum up what we've discussed.}

The sun is the star at the center of our solar system, source of Earth's light and heat. By extension, any star with orbiting planets is a sun. Sunlight, sunshine, and sunny all derive from this central meaning. To sun oneself is to bask in sunlight: {She sunned herself on the deck}. To be {under the sun} is to exist at all: {the greatest thing under the sun}. (Capitalized Sun is also used, especially in astronomical contexts.)

To sunbathe is to sit or lie in the sun, typically to tan the skin or simply enjoy the warmth: {We spent the afternoon sunbathing by the pool}. The activity can be deliberate tanning or casual lounging outdoors. Sunbathing carries associations with leisure, beaches, and summer vacations.
A sunbather is a person who lies or sits in the sun to tan or relax. The term evokes leisure—beach towels, poolside loungers, parks in summer: {Sunbathers lined the shore by midmorning}.

Sunbathing is exposing the body to sunlight, typically while lying still outdoors or by a window. The purpose is usually to tan the skin or simply enjoy the warmth: {She spent the afternoon sunbathing by the pool}. The practice carries health warnings about skin damage and cancer risk.

A sunbeam is a ray of sunlight, especially one visible as a distinct shaft through clouds, trees, or a window: {Sunbeams streamed through the dusty air}. The word carries warm, pleasant associations—children and pets are sometimes affectionately called sunbeams.

Sunbeams are rays or shafts of sunlight, especially when made visible by dust, mist, or clouds: {Sunbeams streamed through the cathedral windows}. The word carries a warm, gentle connotation—sunbeams feel softer than harsh sunlight. Figuratively, someone might be called a sunbeam for bringing brightness or cheer.

Sunburn is skin damage from overexposure to ultraviolet radiation, typically from the sun. The affected area turns red, feels hot and tender, and may later peel. Severe cases cause blistering. As a verb, to sunburn is to suffer this damage: {I sunburned badly at the beach}. The adjective sunburned or sunburnt describes the resulting condition.

Sunburned describes skin that has been damaged by overexposure to the sun's ultraviolet rays, typically red, painful, and sometimes blistered: {I got sunburned at the beach}. The condition ranges from mild redness to severe burns requiring medical attention. Also spelled sunburnt, more common in British English.

A sunburst is a sudden bright gleaming of sunlight, especially when it breaks through clouds or appears dramatically at a particular moment. The word also describes designs, patterns, or objects that radiate outward from a center point like rays of sun—a sunburst {mirror}, sunburst {clock}, or the sunburst pattern on certain guitar bodies. {A sunburst broke through the overcast sky just as the ceremony ended.}

A suncatcher is a small decorative object, usually made of colored glass or crystal, designed to hang in a window where it catches sunlight and casts colored light or rainbow patterns into a room. {The prism suncatcher scattered rainbows across the kitchen wall.}

A sundae is ice cream served with toppings—typically syrup, whipped cream, nuts, and a cherry. The dish is associated with American ice cream parlors and soda fountains: {a hot fudge sundae}, {a banana split sundae}. The spelling distinguishes it from the day of the week, though the connection to Sunday remains debated.

Sundaes is the plural of sundae, a dessert of ice cream topped with sauce, whipped cream, nuts, or other garnishes. The classic sundae features a scoop or two of ice cream drizzled with chocolate or caramel sauce: {We ordered hot fudge sundaes after dinner}. The spelling distinguishes it from the day of the week.

A sundial is a device that tells time by the position of a shadow cast by the sun. A raised element (the gnomon) casts a shadow onto a marked surface, indicating the hour as the sun moves across the sky. Sundials were the primary timekeeping instruments before mechanical clocks: {The garden featured an old stone sundial}.

Sundials are timekeeping devices that use the position of the sun's shadow to indicate the hour. A gnomon—an angled rod or blade—casts a shadow onto a marked dial face as the sun moves across the sky. Once common in gardens and public squares, sundials now serve mainly as decorative objects: {The old sundial in the courtyard still keeps reasonable time on sunny days}.

Sundown is the time when the sun disappears below the horizon—synonymous with sunset but more common in American English. It marks the end of daylight: {We need to finish before sundown}. In Jewish observance, sundown begins the new day, so holidays start at sundown. {Sundown towns} were communities that excluded Black people after dark.

Sunfish names two very different fish. The ocean sunfish is a massive, oddly shaped creature—one of the heaviest bony fish, with a truncated body that looks like a swimming head. Freshwater sunfish are small, colorful North American fish including bluegills, pumpkinseeds, and crappies, popular with casual anglers: {We caught a few sunfish off the dock}.

A sunflower is a tall plant with large yellow-petaled flowers that track the sun across the sky. The flower head contains edible seeds arranged in spiral patterns, harvested for snacking or pressed for cooking oil. {The sunflowers in the field all faced east at dawn.} The bright yellow blooms have become symbols of optimism and summer.

Sunflowers is the plural of sunflower, a tall plant with large yellow-petaled flower heads that track the sun across the sky. The seeds are eaten as snacks or pressed for oil. Van Gogh's *Sunflowers* paintings are among the most recognized works in Western art. {The field was covered in sunflowers.}

Sunglasses are eyeglasses with tinted or polarized lenses that reduce glare and protect the eyes from bright light. They serve both practical and fashionable purposes: {She grabbed her sunglasses before heading to the beach}. Informal shortenings include shades and sunnies.

Sunk is the past participle of sink, describing something that has gone down or fallen to a lower level. A ship that has sunk lies at the bottom of the ocean. Figuratively, if you're sunk, you're in a hopeless situation: {Without that loan, we're sunk}. Sunk costs are expenses already incurred that can't be recovered.

Sunken describes something that has sunk or lies beneath a surface. A sunken ship rests on the ocean floor. Sunken eyes or cheeks appear hollow and recessed, often from illness or exhaustion. Sunken can also mean situated below the surrounding level: {a sunken living room}, {a sunken garden}. The word functions as the past participle of sink in certain constructions, though sunk is more common.

Sunkissed describes skin, hair, or complexion that has been gently bronzed or lightened by sun exposure—suggesting a healthy, natural glow rather than a deep tan: {Her sunkissed cheeks glowed after the beach vacation}. The word evokes warmth and outdoor leisure. It extends to anything touched by sunlight in an appealing way: {sunkissed tomatoes from the garden}. Also spelled sun-kissed.

Sunlight is the light that comes from the sun. It illuminates the earth during daytime hours and provides the energy plants need for photosynthesis. Direct sunlight streams unobstructed from the sun: {The room gets good sunlight in the morning}. Figuratively, sunlight suggests openness and transparency: {Sunlight is the best disinfectant}.

Sunny describes weather with abundant sunlight and few clouds: {a sunny afternoon}, {sunny skies}. By extension, sunny characterizes anything bright, cheerful, or optimistic: {a sunny disposition}, {a sunny outlook on life}. A sunny spot in a garden gets good light. {The sunny side} of something is its positive aspect—or with eggs, cooked on one side only.

Sunrise is the moment when the sun appears above the horizon at the beginning of day, and by extension, the period of light and color surrounding that moment: {We watched the sunrise from the beach}. The word also names the direction where the sun rises—east—though this use is old-fashioned. Figuratively, sunrise suggests beginnings or early stages: {the sunrise of civilization}, {sunrise industries}.

Sunrises is the plural of sunrise—the moment when the sun appears above the horizon, and the atmospheric display that accompanies it. The word often appears in contexts emphasizing repetition or variety: {I've watched a thousand sunrises from this porch}, {Caribbean sunrises are spectacular}.

A sunroof is a panel in the roof of a car that can be opened or removed to let in light and air. Most modern sunroofs slide open mechanically rather than being fully removable. A panoramic sunroof extends over much of the roof. {We opened the sunroof and let the breeze in.}

Sunscreen is a lotion or spray applied to skin to protect against the sun's ultraviolet rays, which cause sunburn and skin damage. The term also describes the protective compounds themselves: {a sunscreen with zinc oxide}. Sunscreen is rated by SPF (sun protection factor)—the higher the number, the longer the protection lasts.

Sunset is the time when the sun drops below the horizon, ending the day. The word also names the colors and light display that often accompany this event: {We watched the sunset from the beach}. Figuratively, sunset describes the final phase of something: {the sunset of his career}. A sunset {clause} or sunset {provision} causes a law or agreement to expire automatically after a set period.

Sunsets is the plural of sunset—the daily event when the sun descends below the horizon, and the period of light and color that accompanies it. Sunsets often feature spectacular displays of orange, pink, and purple: {We watched the sunsets from our balcony every evening}. Figuratively, a sunset marks an ending or decline: {the sunset of an era}. Sunset provisions or sunset clauses cause laws to expire automatically unless renewed.

Sunshine is the light and warmth that comes from the sun, or the condition of receiving it: {Let's move into the sunshine}. By extension, sunshine describes anything bright and cheerful—a sunny disposition, a source of happiness: {You are my sunshine}. As a form of address, sunshine can be affectionate or mildly sarcastic: {Listen here, sunshine}. Sunshine laws require government proceedings to be open to the public, bringing them "into the light."

A suntan is the darkening of skin from exposure to sunlight or artificial ultraviolet rays. People seek suntans for cosmetic reasons, though prolonged sun exposure carries health risks. The verb means to acquire such coloring: {She spent the afternoon suntanning by the pool}. Suntan also describes a light brown color: {suntan pantyhose}.

Sup is a casual greeting, a clipped form of "what's up": {Sup, how's it going?} The word works as both question and acknowledgment—you can say sup without expecting a real answer. As an older, unrelated verb, sup means to eat supper or sip liquid, now mainly literary: {He supped on bread and broth}.

Super means above, over, or beyond the ordinary. As an adjective, it describes something excellent or outstanding: {That concert was super}. As an adverb, it intensifies: {super excited}, {super careful}. As a prefix, super- indicates excess or superiority: supermarket, superhero, supernatural. In American English, a super is the superintendent of an apartment building. In casual speech, super often replaces very: {I'm super tired}.

Superb means excellent or outstanding, often with a sense of grandeur or impressiveness. A superb performance exceeds expectations. A superb view takes your breath away. The word carries more weight than simply good—it suggests something approaching the best of its kind: {The restaurant serves superb seafood}. {She gave a superb presentation}.

A superbug is a strain of bacteria that has developed resistance to multiple antibiotics, making infections difficult or impossible to treat with standard medications. The term emerged as antibiotic overuse accelerated bacterial evolution: {MRSA is one of the most common superbugs in hospitals}. Sometimes used loosely for any particularly virulent or hard-to-kill pathogen.

Superbugs are bacteria or other microorganisms that have developed resistance to multiple antibiotics or other drugs normally used to treat them. The term emerged as antibiotic overuse accelerated bacterial evolution: {MRSA is one of the most feared superbugs in hospitals}.
