Superbugs pose a growing public health threat because standard treatments fail against them, requiring stronger or experimental drugs—if any work at all.

Supercars are high-performance luxury automobiles distinguished by extreme speed, power, and price. The category sits above ordinary sports cars but typically below hypercars in the automotive hierarchy. Supercars feature exotic designs, powerful engines, and limited production runs: {Ferrari and Lamborghini dominate the supercar market}. The term emerged in the 1960s and 70s with vehicles like the Lamborghini Miura.

To supercharge is to increase the power or performance of something, originally by forcing extra air into an engine's combustion chambers using a supercharger. The term now applies broadly to anything given a dramatic boost: {supercharge your morning with cold brew}, {a supercharged immune system}. The figurative use suggests enhancement beyond normal capacity.

Supercharged means enhanced with extra power or intensity. The literal sense refers to engines fitted with a supercharger—a device that forces more air into combustion for greater output. Figuratively, supercharged describes anything amplified beyond normal levels: {a supercharged atmosphere}, {supercharged emotions}, {a supercharged economy}. The word suggests something running at maximum capacity, often with an edge of volatility.

A superfan is a devotee whose enthusiasm far exceeds ordinary fandom. Where casual fans follow from a distance, superfans collect memorabilia, attend every event, know obscure details, and build their identity around the object of devotion—whether a band, sports team, TV series, or celebrity: {The superfans camped outside the stadium overnight}.

Superficial describes what lies on or near the surface. A superficial wound affects only the outer skin. More commonly, superficial means lacking depth or thoroughness: a superficial {analysis}, a superficial {understanding}. A superficial person concerns themselves with appearances rather than substance: {She dismissed him as superficial and vain}. The word carries judgment—superficial knowledge isn't enough when depth matters.

Superfood is a marketing term for foods claimed to have exceptional nutritional benefits—typically fruits, vegetables, or grains dense in vitamins, antioxidants, or other desirable compounds: {Kale and blueberries are popular superfoods}. The term has no scientific or regulatory definition; nutritionists often dismiss it as hype that overpromises what any single food can deliver.

Superglue is a fast-bonding adhesive that creates nearly instant, permanent bonds on contact. The active ingredient, cyanoacrylate, hardens when pressed between surfaces. Superglue works on most materials but notoriously bonds skin to itself or other objects: {I superglued my fingers together}. As a verb, to superglue is to attach with this adhesive.

A superhero is a fictional character with extraordinary powers or abilities who fights evil and protects the innocent—Superman, Spider-Man, Wonder Woman. The term emerged with comic books in the 1930s and now dominates popular entertainment. Superhero can describe anyone who performs remarkable feats: {My mom was a superhero getting us all through that year}. The compound implies powers beyond ordinary heroism.

Superheroes is the plural of superhero—a fictional character with extraordinary powers or abilities who fights evil and protects the innocent. The term emerged from comic books in the 1930s and 1940s with characters like Superman and Batman. Superheroes typically wear distinctive costumes and maintain secret identities: {The movie featured a team of superheroes saving the world}. The word extends metaphorically to real people who perform exceptional feats: {Emergency responders are the real superheroes}.

Superhuman describes abilities or qualities that exceed what seems possible for ordinary humans: {superhuman strength}, {superhuman endurance}. The word suggests something beyond normal human limits without necessarily implying the supernatural—an athlete's superhuman reflexes, a scholar's superhuman memory. As a noun, a superhuman is a being with such extraordinary powers.

A superintendent is a person who oversees or manages something. In American usage, a superintendent often runs a school district, setting policy and administering budgets across multiple schools. A building superintendent ({super} for short) maintains an apartment building and handles repairs. The term applies broadly to anyone with supervisory authority over an operation or institution: {the superintendent of parks}, {the superintendent of police}.

Superior describes something higher in rank, quality, or position: {a superior officer}, {superior craftsmanship}. The word often carries a comparative sense—superior to something else. A superior is also a person of higher rank: {Report to your superior}. Someone with a superior attitude acts condescending or self-important: {She gave me that superior look}. In anatomy, superior means situated above: the superior vena cava. (Capitalized Superior typically refers to Lake Superior.)

Superiority is the state of being better, higher in rank, or greater in quality than others. It can describe objective advantage—{military superiority}, {numerical superiority}—or a subjective attitude of looking down on others: {an air of superiority}, {a superiority complex}. The word often carries a whiff of arrogance when applied to attitudes rather than measurable qualities.

A superman is a person of extraordinary ability or achievement—someone who seems to transcend normal human limitations: {He thinks he's some kind of superman who doesn't need sleep}. The term derives from Nietzsche's philosophical concept of the Übermensch, an ideal superior being who creates his own values beyond conventional morality. In casual use, it often carries irony, applied to men who overestimate their capabilities. (Capitalized Superman is the comic book superhero.)

A supermarket is a large retail store selling food and household goods, organized into aisles where customers select items themselves and pay at checkout counters. The format revolutionized grocery shopping in the mid-20th century, replacing smaller stores where clerks retrieved items for customers. {I need to stop by the supermarket on the way home.}

A supermodel is a fashion model who has achieved exceptional fame and recognition beyond the industry itself, becoming a celebrity in their own right. The term emerged in the late 1980s when models like Naomi Campbell and Cindy Crawford became household names, commanding enormous fees and appearing in mainstream media. {She dreams of becoming a supermodel someday.}

Supermodels are fashion models who have achieved exceptional fame and commercial success, transcending typical modeling work to become celebrities in their own right. The term emerged in the late 1980s and 1990s with figures like Naomi Campbell and Cindy Crawford, who commanded extraordinary fees and appeared not just in fashion spreads but in mainstream media. {The supermodels of the nineties were household names.}

A supermom is a mother who manages to excel at parenting while also succeeding in career, household management, and personal life—seemingly doing it all. The term can be admiring {She's a total supermom, I don't know how she does it} or gently ironic about impossible standards women face. Sometimes hyphenated: super-mom.

Supernatural describes phenomena beyond natural laws or scientific explanation—ghosts, demons, miracles, psychic powers. The supernatural encompasses these forces collectively: {a fascination with the supernatural}. The word often carries skepticism: calling something supernatural implies it violates known physics. In casual use, supernatural can simply mean extraordinary: {supernatural speed}, {supernatural talent}.

A supernova is the explosive death of a star, releasing enormous energy and briefly outshining entire galaxies. The explosion scatters heavy elements into space—the raw material for planets and life. Figuratively, supernova describes spectacular sudden brilliance or a dramatic peak before collapse: {Her career went supernova in the nineties}.

A superpower is a nation with dominant global influence—militarily, economically, and politically. During the Cold War, the term described the United States and Soviet Union. Extended to individuals, a superpower is an extraordinary ability: {Flying is my favorite superpower}. Informally, any exceptional talent qualifies: {Her superpower is remembering names}.

Superpowers are the extraordinary abilities of fictional heroes and villains—flight, invisibility, superhuman strength, telepathy: {Her superpower is controlling the weather}. Figuratively, any exceptional talent or advantage: {His superpower is remembering everyone's name}. In geopolitics, a superpower is a nation with dominant global influence—militarily, economically, and politically. During the Cold War, the term described the United States and Soviet Union.

Supersonic means faster than the speed of sound—about 767 miles per hour at sea level. A supersonic {jet} breaks the sound barrier, producing a sonic boom. The term applies to aircraft, missiles, and projectiles that exceed this threshold: {The Concorde was a supersonic passenger aircraft}. Figuratively, supersonic suggests extreme speed or intensity.

A superspreader is a person who infects an unusually large number of others with a contagious disease—far more than the typical patient. The term gained wide use during COVID-19 but applies to any outbreak where certain individuals drive transmission disproportionately. By extension, superspreader describes events where mass transmission occurs: {The wedding became a superspreader event}.

A superstar is someone who has achieved exceptional fame and success in their field—typically entertainment, sports, or music. The term implies a level above ordinary stardom: not just famous, but commanding massive audiences and cultural influence. {She went from unknown singer to superstar in two years.} The word extends to anyone dominant in their domain: a superstar {salesman}, a superstar {chef}.

Superstars are celebrities or performers who have achieved the highest level of fame and success in their field. The term originated in entertainment—film superstars, rock superstars—but now applies to anyone who dominates their domain: {a tech superstar}, {a superstar athlete}. The word implies not just excellence but widespread recognition and outsized influence. In casual use, superstar can describe anyone exceptional: {You're a superstar for helping me move}.

Superstition is belief in supernatural causation—that certain actions, objects, or circumstances bring good or bad luck independent of any logical connection. Breaking a mirror invites seven years of misfortune; a rabbit's foot brings protection. Superstitions persist even among people who know better: {I'm not superstitious, but I still knock on wood}. The word carries mild dismissiveness—calling a belief superstition implies it's unfounded.

Superstitions are beliefs or practices based on perceived supernatural causation rather than evidence—that breaking a mirror brings bad luck, or that a lucky charm influences outcomes. The word carries a dismissive edge: calling something a superstition implies it's irrational. What counts as superstition often depends on the observer; one culture's religious practice is another's superstition. {He knocked on wood out of superstition.}

Superstitious describes someone who believes in supernatural causation—that broken mirrors bring bad luck, black cats crossing your path portend misfortune, or knocking on wood prevents jinxing yourself. The word carries mild dismissiveness; calling a belief superstitious implies it lacks rational basis: {She's superstitious about the number thirteen}. Athletes are notoriously superstitious about game-day rituals.

A supervillain is an exceptionally powerful or diabolical villain, especially in comic books, action movies, and video games. The term mirrors superhero—both suggest abilities or ambitions beyond ordinary human scale. A supervillain typically has grand schemes for world domination, destruction, or revenge: {Every superhero needs a supervillain}. The word also applies figuratively to real-world figures portrayed as exceptionally malevolent.

Supervillains is the plural of supervillain—a fictional antagonist with extraordinary powers, abilities, or resources, typically opposing a superhero. The term emerged from comic books but extends to any fiction featuring larger-than-life evildoers: {The movie's supervillains plotted world domination}. Informally, supervillain describes someone perceived as exceptionally malevolent or ruthless: {Tech billionaires cast as corporate supervillains}.

To supervise is to oversee work or workers, ensuring tasks are done properly: {She supervises a team of twelve}. The role implies authority and responsibility for outcomes, though not necessarily doing the work yourself. A supervisor watches, directs, and corrects. Children may need supervision—adult oversight to keep them safe or on task.

Supervision is the act of watching over and directing work or workers. A supervisor ensures tasks are done properly and provides guidance when needed. {The project required close supervision}. Without supervision, children or employees may act unsafely or inefficiently. {She completed the internship under the supervision of a senior attorney}.

A supervisor is someone who oversees the work of others, ensuring tasks are completed properly. The role implies authority without full executive power—supervisors typically answer to managers above them while directing workers below. {My supervisor approved the time-off request.} The term appears across contexts from factory floors to academic research, where a thesis supervisor guides a student's work.

A supervolcano is a volcano capable of eruptions thousands of times more powerful than ordinary volcanic events, ejecting enough material to affect global climate. The term typically applies to volcanoes that have produced eruptions of magnitude 8 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index. Yellowstone sits atop one: {Scientists monitor the Yellowstone supervolcano for signs of activity}.

Superwoman is a woman of extraordinary ability, energy, or accomplishment—someone who seems to excel at everything she takes on. The term often describes women who balance demanding careers with family responsibilities: {She's a superwoman, running a company while raising three kids}. The word can be admiring or gently ironic, sometimes acknowledging the impossible standards women face. Capitalized Superwoman is also a DC Comics character.

Supper is an evening meal, though its relationship to dinner varies by region and era. In some traditions, dinner is the midday meal and supper the lighter evening one. Elsewhere, supper is a late-night snack after dinner, or simply a synonym for dinner itself. {What's for supper?} The word tends toward informality and domesticity—supper is what you have at home, not at a restaurant.

Supple describes something that bends easily without breaking—the opposite of stiff or rigid. A supple body moves gracefully and flexibly: {years of yoga kept her supple}. Supple leather is soft and pliable. The word extends to minds and approaches: a supple {intelligence} adapts readily to new situations.

A supplement is something added to complete or enhance something else. Dietary supplements are pills or powders meant to supply nutrients that might be missing from one's diet. A newspaper supplement is an extra section, often focusing on a particular topic. The verb supplement means to add to or complete: {She supplements her income with freelance work}. The underlying idea is always filling a gap or making up for a deficiency.

Supplements are things added to complete or enhance something else. Dietary supplements—vitamins, minerals, herbs—are taken to supplement nutrition from food. A newspaper supplement is an extra section, often on weekends. To supplement income is to add to it: {She supplements her salary with freelance work}. The verb and noun share the same spelling.

Supplies are materials or provisions needed for a particular purpose. The word usually appears in plural: {office supplies}, {medical supplies}, {art supplies}. Military supplies include everything troops need to function—food, ammunition, equipment. School supplies are the pens, notebooks, and folders students bring to class. The singular supply emphasizes quantity available: {a month's supply of food}, {the water supply}.

Supply is about providing what's needed or requested. A store supplies customers with goods; a well supplies water. As a noun, supply is a stock or quantity available: {medical supplies}, {the water supply}, {supply and demand}. In economics, supply meets demand—what's offered versus what's wanted. To be {in short supply} is to be scarce. A supply {chain} is the sequence of steps bringing products from raw materials to consumers.

When one thing supports another, the first bears or holds up the second : Fifty-foot concrete pillars support the bridge’s spans. This core meaning gives rises to an even more common use of support, which is to help or to assist: Very few senators support the bill. This wage is not enough to support a family of four. A support is anything that aids another thing: She was a great support to me in my illness. The Red Cross has been providing support for the affected families.

A supporter is someone who backs a person, cause, or team. Political candidates have supporters; so do charities and football clubs. The word implies ongoing allegiance rather than one-time help: {She's been a supporter of the museum for decades}. A supporter can also be a device that holds something up or in place—an athletic supporter protects the groin.

Supportive describes someone or something that provides encouragement, assistance, or backing. A supportive {friend} offers emotional comfort during hard times. Supportive {evidence} strengthens an argument. The word often appears in relationship contexts: {My parents were incredibly supportive when I changed careers}. A supportive {role} assists rather than leads.

Suppose means to assume something for the sake of argument or consideration: {Suppose we leave early—will that help?} It also means to believe or think, often with less than full certainty: {I suppose you're right}. {I don't suppose you have change for a twenty?} uses polite doubt. To be supposed to do something is to be expected or required to: {You're supposed to call when you arrive}. In the negative, it indicates prohibition: {You're not supposed to park here}.

Supposed works differently depending on stress. With stress on the second syllable, it means assumed or believed to be true, often with doubt: {The supposed benefits never materialized}. {Be supposed to} indicates expectation or obligation: {You're supposed to call when you arrive}. With stress on the first syllable, it's a past tense verb: {I supposed he was telling the truth}.

Supposedly marks a claim as reported rather than verified—what someone says or believes, which the speaker may doubt: {He supposedly finished the project, but I haven't seen it}. The word often carries skepticism or irony, suggesting the reality may differ from what's claimed: {She's supposedly an expert}. Sometimes it simply attributes information to another source without implying doubt.

To suppress is to put down or stop something by force or authority: {suppress a rebellion}, {suppress dissent}. It extends to holding back or restraining: suppress a {laugh}, suppress a {memory}, suppress an {urge}. Information can be suppressed by preventing its publication or circulation. In medicine and biology, to suppress is to inhibit a process: {drugs that suppress the immune system}. The common thread is preventing something from emerging or continuing.

Suppressed describes something that has been held back, restrained, or prevented from appearing. A suppressed {laugh} is one you struggle to contain. Suppressed {evidence} has been deliberately withheld. A suppressed {memory} remains hidden from conscious awareness. A suppressed {immune system} functions below normal capacity. In firearms, a suppressed weapon has a silencer attached to muffle the sound.

Suppression is the act of putting down or preventing something from emerging. Governments suppress dissent; armies suppress rebellions. A person may suppress emotions, keeping them from surfacing: {She suppressed a laugh}. In medicine, suppression refers to blocking a bodily function or symptom. Fire suppression systems prevent flames from spreading. The word suggests forceful restraint—something actively held back that would otherwise express itself.

Supralapsarianism is a Calvinist theological position holding that God's decree to elect some people for salvation and others for damnation logically preceded the decree to permit the Fall of humanity. The opposing view, infralapsarianism, places the election decree after the Fall. The distinction matters for how one understands God's relationship to human sin: {The supralapsarian view makes predestination seem harsher to critics}.

A supremacist believes their group is inherently superior to others and should dominate them. The term appears most often in {white supremacist}, describing those who believe white people are superior to other races, but it applies to any ideology of group dominance: {male supremacist}, {Christian supremacist}. The word carries strong negative connotations—it's a label applied by critics, rarely claimed proudly.

Supremacists are people who believe their group is inherently superior to others and should dominate. The term almost always appears with a modifier indicating which group: {white supremacists}, {male supremacists}, {Christian supremacists}. White supremacist is by far the most common combination, referring to those who believe white people are racially superior and should hold power over other races.

Supremacy is the state of being supreme—highest in rank, power, or authority. It implies dominance over all others in a given domain: {naval supremacy}, {the supremacy of the federal government over the states}. White supremacy is the racist ideology that white people are inherently superior and should dominate society. {They fought for air supremacy over the Pacific}.

Supreme means highest in degree, quality, or authority. A supreme {commander} outranks all others. The {supreme sacrifice} is giving one's life. Supreme {confidence} is total and unwavering. In cooking, supreme refers to a boneless, skinless chicken breast or a citrus segment with membranes removed. {She reigned supreme on the tennis court for a decade.} (Capitalized Supreme usually refers to the Supreme Court.)

Sure expresses certainty or confidence. If you're sure of something, you have no doubt: {I'm sure she said Tuesday}. As an affirmation, sure means yes: {Can you help me? Sure.} This casual use can sound grudging or unenthusiastic compared to stronger affirmatives. Sure also intensifies: {It sure is hot today}. A sure thing is guaranteed to succeed. {Make sure} means verify or ensure.

Surf refers to the waves breaking on a shore, or the foam and spray they produce. To surf is to ride those waves on a board, a sport that requires balance, timing, and a good read of the water. The word extends naturally to other kinds of gliding motion: you surf the Internet by moving through websites, or surf TV channels by flipping through them. {We spent the morning surfing before the wind died down.} Someone who surfs is a surfer.

Surface is the outermost boundary of something—where an object meets the space around it: {the surface of the water}, {a smooth surface}. Extended uses concern what's apparent rather than hidden: {On the surface, everything seemed fine}. To surface is to rise from below: a submarine surfaces, and so does information that was buried. As an adjective, surface describes what's shallow or exterior rather than deep: {surface wounds}, {surface meaning}.

Surfaced is the past tense of surface, meaning to come up to or appear at the top of something—typically water: {The submarine surfaced after twelve hours}. More often figurative: hidden information surfaces when it becomes known, a person surfaces when they reappear after absence, and problems surface when they emerge: {New evidence surfaced during the investigation}.

Surfaces is the plural of surface—the outer boundaries of objects, what you can see and touch. We speak of flat surfaces, rough surfaces, the surface of the earth. Extended: what appears outwardly versus what lies beneath: {On the surface, everything seemed fine}. The verb surfaces means to come up or emerge: {New evidence surfaces}, {She surfaces around noon on weekends}.

A surfboard is a long, narrow board used to ride ocean waves. Surfers paddle out, then stand on the board as a wave carries them toward shore. Surfboards range from short, maneuverable designs to longer boards for stability. The verb means to ride such a board: {We surfboarded all morning}.

Surfboards are long, buoyant boards used for riding ocean waves. The rider paddles out, catches a wave, and stands to ride it toward shore. Surfboards range from short, maneuverable designs to longer boards offering stability. The word works as a verb too: {We surfboarded all morning}, though most surfers just say {surf}.

A surfer is someone who rides ocean waves on a surfboard, standing upright and maneuvering as the wave carries them toward shore. The term extends to anyone who browses casually—an internet surfer, a channel surfer flipping through TV stations. Both senses share the idea of gliding across a surface, moving from one thing to the next.

Surfing is riding ocean waves on a board, balancing as the wave carries you toward shore. The sport requires reading the water, timing your paddle, and popping up at the right moment. Extended to other board sports: {windsurfing}, {kitesurfing}. Channel surfing means flipping rapidly through TV stations. Surfing the web or {surfing the internet} is browsing casually from site to site.

Surge captures a sudden, powerful forward movement or increase. Ocean waves surge against rocks; crowds surge through gates; electricity surges through power lines. The word implies force and momentum—something swelling or rushing beyond normal levels. A surge of emotion overwhelms you; a surge in prices rises sharply. {The team surged ahead in the final quarter.} Medical professionals may describe a surge of patients overwhelming capacity. Surge protectors guard against sudden spikes in electrical current.

A surgeon is a physician who performs operations—cutting into the body to repair, remove, or replace tissue. Surgeons specialize by area: heart surgeons, brain surgeons, orthopedic surgeons. The term extends to other fields requiring precise manual skill: a dental surgeon, a tree surgeon. {The surgeon removed her appendix}.

Surgeons are physicians who perform operations—cutting into the body to repair, remove, or replace tissue. The term distinguishes them from doctors who treat patients primarily through medication or other non-invasive means. Surgeons specialize by body system or procedure type: {a heart surgeon}, {a brain surgeon}, {plastic surgeons}. {Brain surgeon} and {rocket scientist} serve as stock examples of demanding professions: {It's not brain surgery}.

Surgery is medical treatment involving cutting into the body to repair, remove, or replace tissue or organs. A surgery can also mean an instance of such treatment: {She's scheduled for surgery next week}. In British usage, a surgery is also a doctor's office or the hours when a doctor sees patients: {The morning surgery begins at nine}.

Surgical describes what relates to surgery—the branch of medicine involving physical intervention on the body. A surgical {procedure} happens in an operating room; surgical {gloves} are worn by surgeons. Figuratively, surgical means extremely precise and targeted: a surgical {strike} hits only its intended target, and surgical {precision} suggests careful, exact action with minimal collateral effect.

A surname is a family name, the part of a person's name shared with relatives and passed down through generations: {Her surname is Rodriguez}. In most Western cultures, the surname comes last, following given names. To surname someone is to give them a family name, though this verb is rare. Also called a last name or family name.

Surplus is an amount beyond what's needed or used—the excess that remains after requirements are met. A budget surplus means revenues exceeded expenses. Surplus {grain}, surplus {inventory}, surplus {labor}. Military surplus refers to equipment no longer needed by armed forces, often sold to civilians. As an adjective: {surplus funds}, {surplus population}. {We're running a surplus this quarter.}

Surprise captures the feeling when something unexpected happens, whether pleasant or unpleasant. As a noun, it's both the emotion itself and the unexpected thing that triggers it: {What a lovely surprise!} As a verb, to surprise someone is to catch them off guard or present them with something unanticipated. A surprise {party} is one the guest of honor doesn't know about beforehand. If you {take someone by surprise}, you catch them unprepared. Surprise can also modify other nouns to indicate unexpectedness: {a surprise visit}, {surprise ending}.

Surprised describes the feeling when something unexpected happens. You can be pleasantly surprised by a gift or unpleasantly surprised by bad news. The word ranges from mild {I'm surprised you're still here} to intense {She was surprised to find her ex at the party}. To act surprised is to feign the reaction: {Don't act surprised—you knew all along}.

Surprises is the plural of surprise—unexpected events or revelations: {Life is full of surprises}. The verb form means to catch someone off guard or to strike with wonder: {Nothing surprises me anymore}. A surprise can be pleasant or unpleasant; context usually clarifies which: {We're planning a surprise for her birthday}.

Surprising describes something that catches you off guard or defies expectation. A surprising {twist} in a story, a surprising {victory} by an underdog. The word can express mild shock {(That's surprising—I thought she'd already left)} or emphasize degree: {a surprising amount of money}, {surprisingly good coffee}. Not surprising often dismisses the obvious: {It's not surprising he failed, given how little he studied}.

Surreal describes something dreamlike, bizarre, or strangely disconnected from ordinary reality. The word comes from surrealism, an artistic movement that embraced the irrational and unconscious mind. Something surreal feels unreal while happening: {The whole experience was surreal—I kept expecting to wake up}. The word often describes moments when reality feels too strange, too fortunate, or too terrible to process: {Watching the towers fall was surreal}.

Surrealism is a style or approach that features dreamlike, illogical, or bizarre imagery and ideas. The term comes from the formal art movement but applies broadly to anything with that uncanny, reality-bending quality: {The movie had a surrealism that made you question what was real}. (Capitalized Surrealism is the artistic movement.)

A surrealist is an artist or writer associated with surrealism, the early 20th-century movement that sought to express the unconscious mind through dreamlike imagery and irrational juxtapositions. The term also works as an adjective: {surrealist painting}, {surrealist film}. More loosely, surrealist describes anything bizarre or dreamlike: {The meeting descended into surrealist chaos}.

The verb surrender, without an object, describes agreeing to stop fighting or resisting. With an object, to surrender something is to give it to someone who demands or asks for it (surrender your passport). Give up is a synonym for both uses. The noun surrender is an instance of surrendering, and is used to talk about a formal ending of hostilities: We’re studying Lee’s surrender at Appomattox.

Surrogacy is an arrangement where a woman carries and delivers a child for someone else, typically a couple unable to conceive or carry a pregnancy themselves. In traditional surrogacy, the surrogate's own egg is fertilized; in gestational surrogacy, she carries an embryo created from others' genetic material. {They pursued surrogacy after years of failed fertility treatments.} The practice raises complex legal and ethical questions about parenthood, compensation, and bodily autonomy.

A surrogate is a substitute—someone or something that stands in for another. A surrogate {mother} carries a pregnancy for someone else. A surrogate {decision-maker} acts on behalf of someone who cannot. The word often implies an official or designated replacement rather than a casual one: {The vice president served as a surrogate for the candidate on the campaign trail}. Surrogate can also describe the emotional replacement of one thing for another: {Food became a surrogate for affection}.

Surround means to encircle or be positioned on all sides of something: {Police surrounded the building}. The word implies complete enclosure—partial coverage doesn't count as surrounding. Figuratively, people surround themselves with things they choose to keep close: {She surrounded herself with talented advisors}. As a noun, surroundings refers to one's environment or the area around something.

Surrounded is the past tense and past participle of surround, meaning to be on all sides of something or someone. A house {surrounded by trees} has trees encircling it. Police {surrounded the building}. The word often suggests enclosure or entrapment: {surrounded by enemies}. Figuratively, to be {surrounded by love} or {surrounded by uncertainty} is to have that quality present in every direction you turn.

Surroundings are everything in the environment immediately around a person or thing: {She took a moment to absorb her surroundings}. The word emphasizes what's nearby and perceptible rather than the broader landscape or context. You might find yourself in unfamiliar surroundings, or notice how someone's surroundings reflect their personality.

Surveillance is close observation of a person, place, or activity, typically conducted secretly. The term usually implies systematic monitoring by authorities or institutions: {The suspect was under constant surveillance}. Security cameras, wiretaps, and tracking software are common surveillance tools. The word carries connotations of suspicion and power imbalance—those watched rarely consent to or know about the watching.

A survey is a systematic examination or assessment. To survey land is to measure and map it; a surveyor determines boundaries and elevations. To survey a situation is to look it over comprehensively: {She surveyed the damage}. A survey also gathers opinions or data from a sample of people: {The survey found that most voters disapprove}. Survey can stress the breadth of coverage: {a survey of American literature}.

Surveys cover the act of looking over something comprehensively. A surveyor surveys land to measure boundaries and features. A researcher surveys a population by collecting responses to questions: {The survey found that most respondents preferred the new design}. To survey a situation is to assess it broadly: {She surveyed the damage after the storm}. Survey also names the resulting report or study.

Survival is the state of continuing to exist or live, especially through difficult circumstances. A plane crash survivor achieved survival against the odds. The word often implies threat or hardship: {survival of the fittest}, {survival skills}, {survival mode}. It extends to abstractions that persist: {the survival of democracy}, {the survival of ancient customs}. A survival is also something that has persisted from an earlier time: {The folk song is a survival from medieval England}.

A survivalist is someone who prepares for potential catastrophes—natural disasters, economic collapse, societal breakdown—by stockpiling supplies, learning self-sufficiency skills, and often relocating to remote areas. The term can be neutral or carry connotations of paranoia and extremism: {The survivalist had enough canned goods to last three years}. Related to prepper, though survivalist often implies more radical preparation.

Survive means to remain alive through danger, hardship, or adverse conditions. A patient survives surgery; a species survives extinction; a building survives a fire. The word extends to getting through difficult experiences: {I barely survived that meeting}. To survive someone is to outlive them: {She survived her husband by twenty years}. A survivor is one who remains alive, or more broadly, one who perseveres through trauma or adversity.

A survivor is someone who lives through a dangerous or life-threatening event—a plane crash, a disease, a war. The term extends to those who outlive others: {She was the sole survivor of her generation}. Survivor also describes people who have endured trauma, especially sexual assault or abuse, where it emphasizes resilience over victimhood: {a survivor of childhood abuse}. More loosely, survivor characterizes anyone who perseveres through hardship: {She's a survivor—she'll figure it out}.

Survivors are people who continue living after an event that killed others or threatened their own lives. The word applies to those who outlast disasters, accidents, wars, or diseases: {Holocaust survivors}, {cancer survivors}, {the sole survivor of the crash}. It extends to those who endure difficult circumstances: {survivors of abuse}. In legal contexts, survivors are family members who outlive a deceased person, especially regarding inheritance or benefits.

Sus is slang for suspicious or suspect—someone or something that seems untrustworthy or shady: {That guy's acting real sus}, {The whole deal felt sus to me}. The word exploded in popularity through the video game Among Us, where players identify impostors, but it existed in hip-hop and internet slang earlier. Can also function as a noun: {He's a sus}.

Sushi is a Japanese dish consisting of vinegared rice combined with various ingredients, most commonly raw fish or seafood, though vegetable and cooked versions are also popular. The rice is the essential component—the word itself refers to the seasoned rice, not the fish. Common forms include nigiri (hand-pressed rice topped with fish), maki (rolled in seaweed), and sashimi-style presentations. {We grabbed sushi for lunch.} Sushi has become ubiquitous in Western dining, from high-end omakase restaurants to grocery store grab-and-go.

Suspect covers both doubt and the object of doubt. To suspect someone is to believe they may be guilty of something: {Police suspect the husband}. To suspect a fact is to think it likely: {I suspect she's lying}. A suspect is a person under suspicion. As an adjective, suspect means questionable or unreliable: {His motives are suspect}. The adjective stresses the second syllable; the noun stresses the first.

Suspects functions as both verb and noun around the idea of believing something without proof. To suspect is to think someone guilty or something true based on incomplete evidence: {I suspect he's lying}, {She suspected foul play}. A suspect is a person believed to have committed a crime: {Police questioned three suspects}. As an adjective, suspect means questionable or untrustworthy: {His motives are suspect}.

Suspend means to hang from above, leaving something dangling: {A chandelier was suspended from the ceiling}. From this comes the sense of halting temporarily—something left hanging, unresolved: {The game was suspended due to rain}, {They suspended judgment until more facts emerged}. To suspend a person is to temporarily bar them from a position or privilege: {The student was suspended for fighting}. Suspended animation describes a state of biological inactivity. In chemistry, particles suspended in liquid float without dissolving.

Suspended means hanging from above or held in place within a medium: {A chandelier was suspended from the ceiling}, {particles suspended in liquid}. It also means temporarily stopped or put on hold: {The game was suspended due to rain}, {His license has been suspended}. A student who is suspended has been temporarily barred from school as punishment. In all uses, suspended suggests an intermediate state—neither fully active nor permanently ended.

Suspenders are straps worn over the shoulders to hold up trousers, attached at the waistband with clips or buttons. Americans wear suspenders; the British call them braces. In British English, suspenders are the clips on a garter belt that hold up stockings. {He wore red suspenders with his suit.}

Suspenders are straps worn over the shoulders to hold up trousers, attached by clips or buttons at the waistband. Americans wear suspenders; the British call them braces. In British English, suspenders are the clips on a garter belt that hold up stockings. {He snapped his suspenders for emphasis.}

Suspense is anxious uncertainty about an outcome—the feeling of waiting to learn what happens next. Thrillers and horror films generate suspense deliberately: {The suspense was killing me}. A story can {build suspense} or {keep you in suspense}. In legal contexts, something held in suspense is temporarily undecided or inactive.

Suspension is the state of being suspended—held up, paused, or temporarily stopped. A car's suspension is the system of springs and shock absorbers that holds the body above the wheels. In chemistry, a suspension is particles dispersed in liquid without dissolving. A suspension from school or work is a temporary removal as punishment: {He received a three-day suspension for fighting}. Suspension of disbelief is the willingness to accept implausible elements in fiction.

Suspicion is a feeling that something is wrong or that someone has done something bad, without proof: {I have a suspicion he's lying}. It can be a trace or hint: {a suspicion of garlic in the sauce}. To be {under suspicion} is to be suspected of wrongdoing. {Above suspicion} means too trustworthy to doubt. The phrase {on suspicion of} precedes an alleged crime: {arrested on suspicion of murder}.

Suspicions is the plural of suspicion—feelings that something is wrong, likely, or true without proof to confirm it. You might have suspicions about a spouse's fidelity, a coworker's motives, or the cause of a strange noise. {Her suspicions were aroused when he started working late}. To {arouse suspicions} or {raise suspicions} is to make someone wary. {Above suspicion} means beyond doubt of wrongdoing.

Suspicious describes a state of distrust or doubt about someone's motives or honesty: {I'm suspicious of anyone who flatters me that much}. It also describes behavior or circumstances that arouse such doubt: {suspicious activity}, {a suspicious package}. The word works both ways—you can be suspicious of something, or something can look suspicious to others.

Sustainability is the capacity to maintain something over time without depleting resources or causing harm. The term dominates environmental discourse, where it describes practices that meet present needs without compromising future generations: {sustainable agriculture}, {sustainable energy}. A business model has sustainability if it can continue operating profitably. The word often appears in corporate language where its meaning may be vague or aspirational rather than concrete.

In modern usage sustainable has become a label for products and practices that ensure the continued availability of resources, with little or no impact on environmental health: The greatest advocates of sustainable agriculture are often those with the least influence. In contexts where the environment is not implied, sustainable means able to be maintained: Zambia is trying to develop a model of sustainable economic growth.

SUV stands for sport utility vehicle—a large passenger vehicle built on a truck chassis, combining enclosed cabin space with off-road capability. SUVs rose to dominance in American roads through the 1990s and 2000s, valued for their size, high seating position, and cargo capacity. The category now ranges from compact crossovers to full-size models: {They traded in the sedan for an SUV}.

A swab is a small piece of absorbent material on a stick, used for cleaning or collecting samples: {a cotton swab}, {a nasal swab for COVID testing}. In nautical use, a swab is a mop for cleaning decks. To swab is to clean with such an implement: {swab the deck}, {The nurse swabbed my arm with alcohol}.

Swag has branched into several distinct meanings. Originally it referred to a decorative fabric draping in loops, or to stolen goods and plunder. In Australian English, a swag is a bedroll or bundle of belongings carried by a traveler. The word took on new life in hip-hop culture to describe a confident, stylish manner of carrying oneself: {He walked in with serious swag}. More recently, swag refers to promotional merchandise and freebies, especially at corporate events: {The conference swag included tote bags and water bottles}.

Swagger is a bold, self-assured manner of walking or behaving that suggests confidence bordering on arrogance: {He walked in with a swagger}. The word works as both noun and verb—you can have swagger or you can swagger into a room. Extended to style or attitude generally, swagger describes a kind of cocky flair: {The team played with swagger}. Unlike pure arrogance, swagger often carries admiration—it suggests someone who backs up their confidence.

Swainsonine is an indolizidine alkaloid that disrupts glycosylation by inhibiting Golgi alpha-mannosidase II, an enzyme critical for processing glycoproteins. Found in toxic plants like locoweed (Astragalus and Oxytropis), it causes locoism in livestock, marked by neurological symptoms, erratic behavior, weight loss, and reproductive issues. Chronic exposure leads to lysosomal storage disorders due to impaired glycoprotein metabolism. Swainsonine mimics sugars, making it a candidate for chemotherapy and treatments for metabolic disorders. Cattle grazing on locoweed often suffer swainsonine poisoning.

Swallow works as both verb and noun across two unrelated words. The verb means to pass food or drink from mouth to stomach through the throat: {She swallowed the pill with water}. Extended uses involve accepting something difficult: {swallow your pride}, {a hard pill to swallow}, {I can't swallow that excuse}. A swallow is also an act of swallowing or an amount swallowed. Separately, a swallow is a small migratory bird with a forked tail and graceful flight, known for returning to the same nesting sites—hence the famous swallows of Capistrano.

Swallowed is the past tense of swallow—to take something down the throat. Food is chewed and swallowed. Pills are swallowed with water. Figuratively, to swallow something is to accept it without resistance: {She swallowed her pride and apologized}. If you've {swallowed a story}, you've believed something dubious. To be swallowed up is to be engulfed or absorbed completely.

Swallows are small, swift-flying birds with forked tails and pointed wings, known for catching insects in flight. The verb swallow means to pass something down the throat: {She swallowed the pill with water}. Extended meanings include accepting something reluctantly {(hard to swallow)}, suppressing {(swallow your pride)}, or consuming entirely: {The project swallowed our budget}.

A swamp is a wetland with waterlogged soil and standing water, typically featuring trees and dense vegetation. Swamps differ from marshes (grassy) and bogs (acidic, mossy). Figuratively, to swamp is to overwhelm or flood: {We were swamped with orders}. A swamped boat has taken on water. To be {swamped} is to be buried in work or obligations.

Swamped means overwhelmed or flooded, from the image of a boat taking on water. Most often it describes being buried under work or obligations: {I can't meet for lunch—I'm completely swamped this week}. A business can be swamped with orders, a phone line swamped with calls. The word conveys being so overloaded that you're barely staying afloat.

Swamps are wetlands with waterlogged soil and standing water, typically featuring trees and dense vegetation. Unlike marshes, which have grasses, swamps have woody plants—cypress swamps, mangrove swamps. Figuratively, to swamp is to overwhelm or flood: {We were swamped with orders}. A swamped boat has taken on too much water. To be {swamped} is to be buried in obligations.

A swan is a large waterfowl with a long curved neck, typically white plumage, and graceful movement on water. Swans mate for life and have become symbols of elegance, fidelity, and romance. A swan song is a final performance or gesture before death or retirement—from the ancient belief that swans sing beautifully only when dying. To swan about or swan around is to move in an aimless, leisurely, or self-satisfied manner: {She swanned around Europe all summer while we worked}. (Capitalized Swan appears in proper names.)

Swanky describes something stylishly luxurious or ostentatiously fashionable: {a swanky hotel}, {a swanky new car}. The word carries a hint of showing off—swanky places and things are meant to impress. It can also describe people who flaunt their wealth or status: {He got a little swanky after his promotion}.

Swans are large waterfowl with long necks, related to geese and ducks but more elegant in appearance. They mate for life and are associated with grace and beauty. A swan song is a final performance or gesture before death or retirement, from the ancient belief that mute swans sing only once, at death. To swan about is to move idly or aimlessly in a showy manner: {He swanned around Europe all summer}.

A swansong is a final performance, work, or act before retirement or death. The term comes from the ancient belief that swans sing beautifully just before dying—though they don't. A musician's farewell tour, an athlete's last season, a director's final film: {The album was her swansong before she stopped recording}. Also spelled swan song.

Swap is to exchange one thing for another: {Let's swap seats}, {I'll swap you my apple for your cookie}. The noun is the exchange itself: {a fair swap}, {a prisoner swap}. In computing, swap refers to moving data between memory and disk storage. Swap meets are gatherings where people trade goods.

A swarm is a large group of insects moving together, especially bees leaving a hive with a queen to establish a new colony. The word extends to any dense, moving mass: {a swarm of tourists}, {a swarm of drones}. To swarm is to move in such a mass, or for a place to be crowded with activity: {The beach was swarming with people}. To swarm something is to climb it using arms and legs together: {The sailors swarmed up the rigging}.

Swarming describes things moving in large, dense groups—bees swarming from a hive, tourists swarming a landmark, thoughts swarming someone's mind. The image is of many individuals moving together with apparent purpose or agitation. A place swarming with something is crowded or overrun: {The beach was swarming with jellyfish}. Police or military units swarm a location by converging on it from multiple directions at once.

Swarms is the plural of swarm—a large group of insects moving together, especially bees leaving a hive: {Swarms of locusts devastated the crops}. The word extends to any dense, moving crowd: {Swarms of tourists descended on the plaza}. As a verb, swarms means to move in great numbers or to be crowded with: {The beach swarms with people in summer}.

A swashbuckler is a daring, sword-wielding adventurer—the type who swings from chandeliers and duels villains with theatrical flair. The term evokes romantic heroes of adventure fiction: pirates, musketeers, Robin Hood types. Swashbuckling describes this style of action or the genre itself: {a swashbuckling adventure film}, {He fancied himself a swashbuckler}.

Swashbucklers are daring, romantic adventurers—sword-fighting heroes of the kind found in pirate tales and historical adventure stories. The term evokes flamboyant bravery, cape-swirling swordplay, and gallant rescues: {Errol Flynn made his name playing swashbucklers}. By extension, anyone bold and theatrically daring might be called a swashbuckler.

Swashbuckling describes daring, romantic adventure in the style of sword-fighting heroes—think pirates, musketeers, and dashing rogues. The word evokes dramatic sword fights, cape-swirling escapes, and theatrical bravado: {a swashbuckling adventure film}, {the swashbuckling hero rescued the princess}. A swashbuckler is someone who embodies this spirit, whether in fiction or attitude.

A swastika is a cross with arms bent at right angles, all pointing the same direction. The symbol appears in ancient cultures worldwide—Hindu, Buddhist, Native American—typically representing good fortune or cosmic order. But its adoption by Nazi Germany as a symbol of Aryan supremacy has made it, in Western contexts, an emblem of antisemitism and hate: {Someone spray-painted a swastika on the synagogue}.

Swastikas is the plural of swastika, an ancient symbol of intersecting lines bent at right angles. For millennia the swastika appeared across cultures—Hindu, Buddhist, Native American—as a sign of good fortune or sacred geometry. Its adoption by Nazi Germany as the emblem of fascism and genocide has made it, in Western contexts, a symbol of hate and antisemitism: {Vandals spray-painted swastikas on the synagogue}. The symbol retains its original spiritual meanings in parts of Asia.

To swat is to hit with a quick, sharp blow, typically to kill or drive away an insect: {She swatted the fly with a rolled-up newspaper}. The word extends to any quick slapping motion: {He swatted the ball away}. A swat is such a blow: {One swat and the mosquito was gone}. (Capitalized SWAT is a tactical police unit.)

Swatted is the past tense of swat, meaning struck with a quick, sharp blow—typically how one hits a fly or mosquito: {She swatted the bug with a rolled-up magazine}. In baseball, to swat is to hit powerfully: {He swatted a home run}. More recently, swatted describes being targeted by a swatting attack—a malicious prank where someone falsely reports an emergency at a victim's address to trigger an armed police response: {The streamer got swatted during a live broadcast}.

Swatting is making a false emergency report—typically claiming an armed threat or hostage situation—to send police tactical units to an unsuspecting person's address. The term comes from SWAT (Special Weapons and Tactics) teams. Originally targeting online gamers during livestreams, swatting has expanded to harass politicians, journalists, and others. It's a federal crime that has resulted in deaths: {He was arrested for swatting a rival streamer}.

The verb sway has two main meanings. To sway is to move gently back and forth, like branches of a tree when there is wind. To sway someone is to persuade or influence them so that their thinking changes: He attempted to sway voters. The noun sway is rarely an instance of swaying in the first sense, more often a near synonym of power, authority, and dominion. If you hold sway in a place or situation, you have the power to greatly influence what happens.

Swaying is movement back and forth or side to side, typically gentle and rhythmic. Trees sway in wind, dancers sway to music, crowds sway at concerts. The word can describe physical motion or figurative influence: {Her argument was swaying}. To be swaying is to be in the process of this motion: {He stood swaying on the deck of the ship}.

Swear means to make a solemn promise or oath: {I swear to tell the truth}. To swear by something is to vouch for its reliability: {She swears by her morning coffee}. Swear also means to use profane or vulgar language: {He swore when he stubbed his toe}. To be sworn in is to take an official oath, as when entering office. {I could have sworn I left my keys here} expresses confident belief that turns out wrong.

Swearing is the use of profane, obscene, or taboo language—words like *fuck*, *shit*, and *damn*. People swear to express strong emotion, add emphasis, or shock: {The swearing in that movie was excessive}. Swearing also means taking an oath: {the swearing-in of the new president}. These senses connect through the idea of solemn or emphatic speech.

Swears covers the verb in its common senses. To swear is to use profane or offensive language: {He swears like a sailor}. To swear is also to make a solemn promise or oath: {I swear to tell the truth}. You can swear on something sacred or dear: {I swear on my mother's grave}. To {swear by} something is to vouch for its effectiveness: {She swears by that cold remedy}. To {swear off} something is to renounce it: {He swore off drinking}.

Sweat is the ordinary name for perspiration, the liquid secreted from pores to cool the body. It is used emblematically to stand for heat and exertion, as in the expression blood, sweat, and tears. If you say something is no sweat, you mean it is not a worry or problem. A sweat is a time when perspiration is present. To sweat is to produce sweat, or figuratively, to be deeply worried or nervous about something: I’m sweating the upcoming exam.

A sweater is a knitted garment covering the torso and arms, typically pulled over the head. Sweaters provide warmth and range from casual to dressy: {a cable-knit sweater}, {a cashmere sweater}. In British English, the same garment is often called a jumper. A cardigan is a sweater that opens in the front. To sweat something out is unrelated—a sweater in that sense is someone who sweats.

Sweating is the body's production of moisture through the skin, primarily to regulate temperature. The word extends to any process where moisture forms on a surface: {The pipes are sweating}. To sweat something is to worry about it: {Don't sweat the small stuff}. Sweating someone means pressuring them for information or a confession. In cooking, to sweat vegetables is to cook them gently until they release moisture.

Sweatpants are loose, soft trousers made of absorbent fabric, originally designed for athletic warm-ups but now worn casually for comfort or lounging. The elastic waistband and cuffs distinguish them from other casual pants. {I spent Sunday in sweatpants watching movies.} Wearing sweatpants in public signals informality or indifference to appearance.

Sweats is the plural of sweat—perspiration or its instances—but more commonly refers to sweatpants, a sweatshirt, or both together as an outfit: {I spent the whole weekend in sweats}. The garment sense dominates casual speech. {Cold sweats} describes clammy perspiration from fear or illness.

A sweatshirt is a loose, long-sleeved pullover made of thick cotton jersey, typically worn for warmth or exercise. The fabric has a soft, fleecy interior. Unlike a sweater, a sweatshirt is casual and unstructured. A hooded version is a hoodie. {I threw on a sweatshirt before my morning run.}

A sweatshop is a factory or workshop where workers labor under harsh conditions—long hours, low pay, and unsafe environments. The term emerged during industrialization and remains common in discussions of global labor practices: {The company was accused of using overseas sweatshops}. Figuratively, any exploitative workplace may be called a sweatshop.

Sweatshops are factories or workshops where workers labor under harsh conditions—long hours, low wages, poor ventilation, and minimal safety protections. The term emerged in the garment industry but now applies broadly to exploitative manufacturing: {The company faced criticism for using overseas sweatshops}. Sweatshop often appears in discussions of global supply chains and labor rights.

Sweaty describes something covered in or producing sweat: {sweaty palms}, {a sweaty workout}. It can characterize conditions that cause sweating: {a sweaty August afternoon}. Figuratively, sweaty suggests anxious effort or nervous intensity: {sweaty desperation}. In gaming slang, a sweaty player tries excessively hard to win, prioritizing competition over fun.

To sweep is to brush a surface with a broom to clean it. The characteristic of this action extends to wider meanings, as when a mood sweeps the nation (that is, extends to all parts). Things moved by a powerful force are described with sweep (debris swept downstream by the flood, an epidemic sweeping the area). The noun sweep denotes an instance of sweeping; also an instance of something done thoroughly and successfully, like a three-game sweep (that is, three successive victories).

A sweeper is a person or device that sweeps—cleaning floors, streets, or other surfaces by brushing debris away. {The street sweeper comes through every Tuesday morning.} In soccer, a sweeper is a defensive player positioned behind the main line of defenders, responsible for clearing balls that get past teammates. The term extends to anything that moves across an area systematically: a minesweeper clears explosives, and in cricket, a sweep shot sends the ball across the field.

Sweeping describes broad, comprehensive movement or scope. A sweeping {gesture} covers a wide arc. Sweeping {changes} affect everything. A sweeping {victory} is decisive and total. The word suggests something that moves across or encompasses without stopping for particulars: {a sweeping view of the valley}, {sweeping generalizations}. As a noun, sweepings are debris gathered by a broom.

Sweeps is the plural of sweep in its noun senses—a sweeping motion, a comprehensive search or survey, or a chimney sweep. In American broadcasting, sweeps refers to ratings periods when networks measure viewership to set advertising rates: {The networks save their best programming for sweeps}. A sweeps week typically falls in February, May, July, and November.

A sweepstakes is a promotional contest where winners are chosen by chance rather than skill, typically requiring only that participants enter their names. Unlike lotteries, sweepstakes are usually free to enter and are often used by companies to generate publicity or collect customer information. The word, though plural in form, is used as a singular: {I entered a sweepstakes for a new car}. Winners may receive cash, vehicles, vacations, or other prizes.
The adjective sweet is a relative newcomer as an interjection and is popular with younger speakers as an expression of approval and satisfaction.

To sweeten is to make something sweet or sweeter, literally by adding sugar or another sweetener: {sweeten your coffee}, {sweeten the batter}. Figuratively, to sweeten is to make something more attractive or palatable: {They sweetened the deal with a signing bonus}. A person's mood or disposition can sweeten, becoming more pleasant or agreeable.

A sweetener is a substance that adds sweetness to food or drink. Sugar is the traditional sweetener, but the term usually implies an alternative: artificial sweeteners like aspartame, or natural ones like stevia and honey. Figuratively, a sweetener is something added to make a deal more attractive: {They threw in a company car as a sweetener}.

Sweetheart is an affectionate term for a romantic partner or loved one: {How was your day, sweetheart?} It extends to anyone notably kind or accommodating: {She was a sweetheart about rescheduling}. A sweetheart deal is an arrangement offering unusually favorable terms, often implying favoritism or corruption: {The company got a sweetheart contract from the city}.

Sweethearts are people in a romantic relationship, especially young or innocent love: {high school sweethearts}, {childhood sweethearts}. The singular sweetheart is a term of endearment for a romantic partner or, more loosely, anyone you're fond of: {Thanks, sweetheart}. A sweetheart can also be someone especially kind or agreeable: {She's a real sweetheart}. A sweetheart {deal} is an unusually favorable arrangement, often implying improper favoritism.

Sweetie is an affectionate term of address, typically directed at a romantic partner, child, or someone the speaker finds endearing: {Come here, sweetie}. It can sound patronizing when used toward adults who aren't intimates, particularly from men to women. Sweetie also refers to a sweet person or, in British English, a piece of candy.

Sweetness is the quality of tasting sweet—the sensation produced by sugar, honey, and ripe fruit. The word extends to anything pleasant or agreeable: the sweetness of a melody, the sweetness of victory, the sweetness of someone's disposition. {There was a sweetness to her voice that put everyone at ease.} In direct address, sweetness is an affectionate term: {Hey sweetness, how was your day?}

Sweets are candy, confections, or sugary treats. The term is more common in British English, where Americans would say candy: {The children asked for sweets}. Sweets can also refer more broadly to desserts or sweet foods generally: {She has a weakness for sweets}. As a term of endearment, {sweets} addresses someone affectionately.

A sweetshop is a British term for a small retail store that sells candy, chocolates, and other confections. The American equivalent is a candy store. Sweetshops are often associated with childhood nostalgia and may stock traditional sweets alongside modern treats. {The children spent their pocket money at the village sweetshop.}

To sweettalk someone is to use flattery or charm to persuade them: {He sweettalked his way into the VIP section}. The approach is manipulative but not necessarily dishonest—more coaxing than deceiving. As a noun, sweettalk is the flattery itself: {Don't fall for his sweettalk}. Also spelled sweet-talk and sweet talk.

The noun and verb swell have related meanings connected with expanding or growing larger. To swell is to grow larger, especially from injury or infection. When something abstract swells (swelling crowd, swelling population) it increases quickly. A noise that swells becomes louder. Large waves in the ocean, before they crest or break, are called swells. The somewhat old-fashioned adjective swell is used appreciatively, sometimes ironically, for people and things that are agreeable and enjoyable: He’s a really swell guy.

Swelling is the enlargement of a body part, typically caused by fluid accumulation, injury, or inflammation. A swelling is also the raised area itself: {The swelling on her ankle went down after she iced it}. Beyond the physical, swelling describes any gradual increase in size, intensity, or volume—a swelling {crowd}, swelling {music}, or swelling {emotions}. As a participle of swell, it captures the process of becoming larger or more pronounced.

Sweltering describes oppressively hot and humid conditions—the kind of heat that makes you sweat just standing still: {a sweltering August afternoon}, {The apartment was sweltering without air conditioning}. The word emphasizes discomfort more than mere temperature. To swelter is to suffer in such heat.

Swept is the past tense and past participle of sweep. To sweep is to clean a surface with a broom or brush, moving debris away: {She swept the kitchen floor}. The motion extends to anything moving quickly across a space: {His eyes swept the room}, {Fire swept through the building}. A sweeping {victory} or sweeping {changes} are comprehensive and decisive. To be {swept up} in something is to be carried along by it: {They got swept up in the excitement}.

Swerve is a sudden turn or deviation from a straight path. A car swerves to avoid an obstacle; a conversation swerves into unexpected territory. To swerve is to make such a movement: {The driver swerved at the last second}. In slang, to swerve someone is to dodge or avoid them, especially romantically: {She swerved him hard}.

Swerving is turning sharply to one side, usually to avoid something: {The driver swerved to miss the deer}. The word implies sudden, reactive movement rather than planned course changes. Figuratively, to swerve is to deviate from a path or commitment: {He never swerved from his principles}. In slang, swerving someone means deliberately avoiding or rejecting them.

Swift describes rapid movement or action. A swift {current} moves fast; a swift {response} comes without delay. The word often suggests smooth, effortless speed rather than frantic rushing: {The hawk made a swift descent}. A swift is also a small bird known for its fast, agile flight and its habit of spending most of its life airborne. (Capitalized Swift refers to the singer, the writer, or the programming language.)

A swig is a large gulp of liquid, especially an alcoholic drink taken directly from the bottle or container: {He took a swig of whiskey}. The verb means to drink this way: {She swigged her beer and slammed the glass down}. The word suggests casual, enthusiastic drinking rather than refined sipping.

Swim is to move through water by moving the body—arms, legs, fins, or tail. Fish swim naturally; humans learn to swim. The word extends to floating or being immersed: {eyes swimming with tears}, {bacon swimming in grease}. To swim in something is to have an abundance of it. If your head swims, you feel dizzy or disoriented. A swim is a session of swimming: {I went for a swim}.

A swimmer is someone who swims, whether for recreation, exercise, or competition. The word applies broadly—from children splashing in pools to Olympic athletes racing for medals. A strong swimmer handles water confidently; a weak swimmer may struggle. In biology, swimmer can describe any creature that moves through water: {Sea turtles are powerful swimmers}.

Swimming is propelling yourself through water using movements of the limbs. As an activity, it ranges from leisurely recreation to competitive sport to survival skill. The word also works as an adjective: a swimming {pool}, a swimming {hole}. If your head is swimming, you feel dizzy or disoriented. If something is swimming {in} liquid, it's surrounded by plenty of it: {The pancakes were swimming in syrup}.

A swimsuit is a garment worn for swimming or sunbathing. Women's swimsuits range from one-piece designs to bikinis; men's are typically trunks or briefs. The term covers athletic competition wear and casual beachwear alike: {She packed three swimsuits for the vacation}. Also called a bathing suit or swimming costume (British).

To swindle is to cheat someone out of money or property through deception: {They swindled him out of his life savings}. A swindle is an instance of such fraud. The word suggests elaborate schemes rather than simple theft—confidence games, fake investments, fraudulent contracts. A swindler is someone who makes a practice of it.

A swindler is someone who cheats others out of money or property through deception. The word implies deliberate fraud rather than mere dishonesty—a swindler gains trust, then exploits it: {The swindler convinced retirees to invest their savings in a fake company}. Con artist and grifter are near synonyms.

Swindlers are people who cheat others out of money or property through deception. The word implies deliberate fraud rather than opportunistic theft—swindlers gain trust before exploiting it. {The swindlers posed as investment advisors and disappeared with their clients' savings.}

Swindles are acts of fraud or deception for financial gain. A swindle involves tricking someone out of money or property through false promises or manipulation: {The investment scheme was one of the largest swindles in the company's history}. To swindle is to cheat in this way: {He swindled elderly victims out of their life savings}.

Swindling is the act of cheating someone out of money or property through deception or fraud. The word emphasizes deliberate trickery—a swindler gains trust before exploiting it: {He was arrested for swindling elderly investors out of their retirement savings}. Swindling implies a scheme rather than a single dishonest act.

Swine is the formal or technical term for pigs, used especially in agriculture and veterinary contexts: {swine flu}, {swine fever}. The plural is also swine. As an insult, swine means a contemptible person—greedy, cruel, or morally repugnant: {He's an absolute swine}. The insult sounds slightly old-fashioned or British.

Meanings of swing, noun, verb, and adjective, typically involve motion between two extremes or sides (pendulum swing), or in relation to a fixed point, like the way you swing a golf club or a bat, or the way a door swings open. A swing is an instance of swinging, as well as a piece of playground equipment on which children can swing. A mood swing is a sudden change from elation to depression, or vice versa. Swing voters are those whose votes may decide the outcome.

A swinger is someone who swings—on a playground, at a ball, or through life with carefree energy. The word took on specific meaning in the 1960s for people who engage in partner-swapping or group sex, typically married couples who have sex with other couples by mutual arrangement: {They met other swingers at the club}. A swinger can also simply mean someone fashionable or uninhibited.

Swingers are people who engage in recreational partner-swapping or group sex with other couples, typically as part of an organized social scene: {They met other swingers at a club downtown}. The term emerged in the 1960s and 70s alongside the sexual revolution. Outside this context, a swinger is simply someone lively and uninhibited, though this older sense has largely been eclipsed.

Swinging describes rhythmic back-and-forth motion, like a pendulum or a child on a playground swing. In music, swinging refers to the lilting rhythmic feel of jazz: {a swinging big band number}. As slang, swinging means lively and fashionable, especially evoking the 1960s: {swinging London}. It also describes the practice of couples exchanging sexual partners: {a swinging lifestyle}, {swingers' parties}.

Swings is most often the plural of swing, the playground apparatus or the back-and-forth motion it makes. The verb swing covers this movement and extends to punches thrown in an arc, mood changes, and shifts in opinion or fortune: {The election swings on turnout in three counties}. In music, swing is a jazz style with a driving rhythm that makes you want to move. If something is in full swing, it's at peak activity. The phrase swings and roundabouts suggests gains and losses that balance out.

Swipe is a sweeping motion—to strike or move with a broad, quick stroke. You might {swipe at a fly} or {take a swipe at} an opponent, literally or figuratively. To swipe something is also to steal it: {Someone swiped my phone}. On touchscreens, swiping means dragging a finger across the surface to navigate: {swipe right} on a dating app to indicate interest, {swipe left} to pass. To swipe a card is to run it through a reader.

Swirl describes circular or spiral motion—liquid moving in curves, smoke coiling upward, dancers spinning. As a noun, it's the pattern itself: {a swirl of cream in coffee}, {swirls of color}. Things swirl when they move in curving paths or create spiral shapes: {Leaves swirled in the wind}. Figuratively, thoughts or emotions swirl when they feel chaotic or overwhelming: {Rumors swirled around the resignation}.

Swirling describes circular or spiral motion—liquid moving in a vortex, leaves caught in wind, or fog drifting in curling patterns: {She sat swirling the wine in her glass}. The word extends to confused or chaotic movement: {swirling rumors}, {swirling emotions}. Things that swirl seem to move without clear direction, caught up in their own turbulence.

Swish captures the sound of something moving quickly through air or water—a soft, rushing hiss: {the swish of her silk dress}, {windshield wipers swishing back and forth}. In basketball, a swish is a shot that passes through the net without touching the rim. As an adjective, swish means elegantly fashionable, especially in British English: {a swish restaurant}. The word is also dated slang for effeminate or gay, now largely replaced by other terms.

The idea of two things, and movement or change from one to the other, is inherent in most meanings of switch. If you switch allegiances, suppliers, or phones, you abandon one and start with another. If you switch back to something, you return to a thing that you used before. A switch is an act or instance of switching (make the switch!), or a device that enables some kind of switching: light switch, railroad switch. As a concrete noun, a switch is a flexible whip or rod.

A switcharoo is a sudden or sneaky exchange—swapping one thing for another, often to deceive or surprise: {They pulled the old switcharoo and replaced the real diamond with a fake}. The word is playful and informal, typically appearing in phrases like {pull a switcharoo} or {the old switcharoo}.

A switchback is a road or trail that zigzags up a steep slope, each segment reversing direction from the one before: {The hiking trail switchbacked up the mountain}. The design reduces the grade, making ascent manageable for vehicles or hikers. In British usage, a switchback can also mean a roller coaster. As a verb, to switchback is to follow such a winding course.

Switchbacks are sharp zigzag turns in a road or trail, typically on a steep slope where a straight path would be too steep to navigate. Mountain roads and hiking trails use switchbacks to gain elevation gradually: {The trail made a dozen switchbacks before reaching the summit}. The term also applies to roller coasters with similar zigzag patterns.

A switchblade is a knife with a blade that springs open at the press of a button, designed for quick one-handed deployment. The mechanism made switchblades popular in mid-20th-century gang iconography, leading to legal restrictions in many jurisdictions: {He pulled a switchblade from his pocket}. Also called a flick knife in British English.

A switchblade is a knife with a blade that springs open at the push of a button, designed for quick one-handed deployment. The mechanism made them associated with street violence and gang culture, leading to legal restrictions in many jurisdictions. {He pulled a switchblade from his pocket.} Also called a flick knife in British English.

A switcheroo is an unexpected or sneaky exchange, substitution, or reversal—typically one intended to deceive or catch someone off guard. The word is informal and often playful, suggesting a trick or sudden change rather than a straightforward swap. {The old switcheroo} is a common phrase describing a classic bait-and-switch maneuver. {They pulled a switcheroo on us at the last minute.}

Switches are devices that open or close electrical circuits, or redirect flow from one path to another. Light switches control room lighting; railroad switches direct trains between tracks. To switch is to change or exchange: {She switched seats with me}, {He switched careers}. A switch can also be a thin flexible rod for striking—to switch someone is to hit them with one. In BDSM contexts, a switch is someone who alternates between dominant and submissive roles.

A swivel is a coupling that allows connected parts to rotate independently—a swivel chair spins on its base, a swivel lamp adjusts direction.
