To swivel is to turn or pivot: {She swiveled around to face him}. {His head swiveled toward the sound.} The word suggests quick, rotational movement rather than full-body turning.

Swole is slang for muscular, describing someone with visibly developed muscles from weight training: {He's been hitting the gym—dude is swole}. The word comes from swollen, suggesting muscles that have expanded from exercise. It carries an approving tone, often used admiringly or as a goal: {trying to get swole for summer}.

Swollen describes something that has expanded beyond its normal size, typically from fluid accumulation, pressure, or inflammation. A sprained ankle swells; so do rivers after heavy rain. {Her eyes were swollen from crying.} Figuratively, swollen can suggest excess or inflation: {swollen with pride}, {swollen ranks of protesters}. The word is the past participle of swell, though swelled also serves that function.

Swoon is to faint or lose consciousness, typically from overwhelming emotion. The word now appears more often in its figurative sense—to be overwhelmed with delight or admiration: {Fans swooned when he took the stage}, {a swoon-worthy performance}. The noun names the faint itself or the state of rapturous absorption: {She fell into a swoon}.

Swooning is fainting or losing consciousness, typically from strong emotion, heat, or shock. The word now appears more often in its figurative sense—being overwhelmed by romantic attraction or admiration: {Fans were swooning over the lead singer}. The literal faint has become old-fashioned; the metaphorical swoon thrives.

Swoop is a swift, sweeping descent—the motion of a bird diving toward prey or a plane dropping altitude suddenly. The word captures both speed and the curved arc of the movement: {The hawk swooped down on the rabbit}. To swoop in figuratively is to arrive suddenly and take action: {She swooped in and solved the problem}. In {one fell swoop} means all at once, in a single decisive action.

Swooping describes a swift, curving descent or movement—the motion of a bird diving toward prey, or a hand sweeping down to grab something. The word captures both speed and arc: {A hawk came swooping down from the sky}. Figuratively, someone swooping in arrives suddenly and decisively: {She swooped in at the last minute to save the deal}.

Swoosh is both a sound and a movement—the rush of air or liquid passing swiftly: {The curtain swooshed open}, {He heard the swoosh of skis on snow}. The word imitates what it describes. As a noun, it also refers to a curved shape suggesting motion, most notably the Nike logo: {the iconic swoosh}.

A sword is a weapon with a long metal blade and a handle, designed for cutting or thrusting. Swords were primary weapons in warfare and personal combat from ancient times through the Middle Ages, before firearms made them obsolete on battlefields. They remain important in ceremonial contexts, martial arts, and as symbols of authority or honor. To {cross swords} with someone is to engage in conflict or debate. The {sword of Damocles} refers to imminent danger or a precarious situation.

A swordfight is combat between people wielding swords, whether in historical battle, sport, or staged performance. The term extends to any dramatic blade-to-blade confrontation: {The movie's climactic swordfight lasted ten minutes}. Figuratively, a swordfight is any sharp verbal or intellectual clash: {The debate turned into a swordfight over tax policy}.

Swordfights are combat encounters using swords, whether actual battles or staged performances. The word evokes dueling, fencing, or cinematic action sequences: {The movie featured elaborate swordfights}. Figuratively, any sharp verbal or intellectual clash: {The debate devolved into swordfights over policy details}.

A swordfish is a large ocean fish with a long, flat, sword-shaped upper jaw. Prized as a game fish and for its firm, mild flesh, swordfish is commonly served as steaks: {grilled swordfish with lemon butter}. The plural is swordfish or swordfishes.

Swords are bladed weapons with long metal blades and hilts, designed for cutting or thrusting. Before firearms, swords were primary military weapons; now they're ceremonial, collectible, or used in fencing. To {cross swords} is to clash or argue. A {sword of Damocles} is an ever-present threat. {The pen is mightier than the sword} values persuasion over force.

A swordsman is a person skilled in fighting with a sword. The term appears most often in historical contexts, fantasy fiction, and martial arts: {He trained for years to become a master swordsman}. The word typically refers to men, though swordswoman exists for female practitioners.

Swore is the past tense of swear. Someone who swore made an oath or promise: {She swore to tell the truth}. Swore also means used profanity: {He swore when he stubbed his toe}. The past participle is sworn: {They had sworn allegiance}.

Sworn is the past participle of swear, used in contexts involving oaths and solemn declarations. A sworn {statement} or sworn {testimony} is given under oath, with legal consequences for lying. Sworn {enemies} are bound by deep, enduring hostility. A sworn {officer} has taken an official oath of duty. {He was sworn in as president.}

Sycophants are people who flatter others excessively to gain advantage—yes-men, toadies, brownnosers. The word carries strong disapproval: sycophants are insincere, self-serving, and often surround those in power. {The CEO surrounded himself with sycophants who never challenged his decisions.} {She dismissed his compliments as sycophancy.}

A syllable is a unit of spoken language consisting of a single uninterrupted sound, typically containing a vowel with or without surrounding consonants. Words break into syllables: "cat" has one, "kitten" has two, "syllable" has three. Syllables determine rhythm in speech and poetry, and they guide where words can be hyphenated in writing.

Syllables are the basic rhythmic units of spoken language—each one built around a vowel sound, often with consonants attached. Words break naturally into syllables: "cat" has one, "kitten" has two, "syllable" has three. Counting syllables matters for poetry, pronunciation, and teaching children to read. {How many syllables in "banana"?}

A syllabus is an outline of topics to be covered in a course or text. Professors distribute syllabi at the start of a semester detailing readings, assignments, and exam dates: {The syllabus says the final paper is due December 15th}. The plural is syllabi or syllabuses.

Two organisms live in symbiosis when one supplies an essential element to the other, or each supplies an essential element to the other. The organism we call lichens, for example, is actually a fungus and an alga living in symbiosis. People use symbiosis more generally to talk about any relationship in which two things contribute to each other in a way that fosters dependency. The related adjective is symbiotic.

A symbol is something that represents something else by association or convention. A dove symbolizes peace; a skull symbolizes death. Letters are symbols for sounds, and mathematical symbols stand for operations or quantities. The word extends to any object, image, or mark that carries meaning beyond itself: {The ring became a symbol of their commitment}. To symbolize is to serve as or represent through symbols.

Symbolic describes something that represents something else through association or convention rather than literal resemblance. A dove is symbolic of peace; a wedding ring is symbolic of commitment. The symbolic meaning of an act often matters more than its practical effect: {The gesture was purely symbolic}. In logic and mathematics, symbolic refers to the use of symbols rather than words: {symbolic logic}.

Symbolism is the use of symbols to represent ideas, qualities, or concepts beyond their literal meaning. A dove may stand for peace, a skull for death. Writers, artists, and filmmakers employ symbolism to add layers of meaning: {The novel's water imagery carries obvious symbolism about rebirth}. The term also describes the practice of interpreting things symbolically: {Critics have found Christian symbolism throughout the work}. (Capitalized Symbolism is a 19th-century artistic movement.)

Symbols are things that represent something else by association or convention. A dove symbolizes peace; a skull symbolizes death. Letters are symbols for sounds, and numbers are symbols for quantities. National flags, religious icons, and corporate logos all function as symbols. In computing, symbols include characters like @ and #. The verb symbolize means to serve as a symbol for something: {The broken clock symbolized their failed marriage}.

Symmetrical describes something with parts that mirror each other across a dividing line or point. A symmetrical face has features evenly balanced on both sides. Symmetrical can extend beyond physical form to describe balanced arrangements: {a symmetrical argument}, {symmetrical responsibilities}. The shorter form symmetric appears mainly in technical contexts.

Symmetry is balance achieved through corresponding parts—elements that mirror, repeat, or match across a dividing line or central point. A butterfly's wings have bilateral symmetry; a snowflake has radial symmetry. The concept extends beyond geometry: {the symmetry of their relationship}, {a pleasing symmetry between the book's opening and closing chapters}. In physics, symmetry describes invariance under transformation—properties that remain unchanged when a system is rotated, reflected, or shifted.

Sympathetic describes a feeling of understanding and care for someone else's suffering or misfortune: {She was sympathetic when I told her about losing my job}. A sympathetic person is one who tends to show such feelings. The word extends to things that are agreeable or compatible: a sympathetic {portrayal} presents its subject favorably, and sympathetic {characters} in fiction are ones the audience can root for. In anatomy and physiology, the sympathetic nervous system controls involuntary responses like heart rate and digestion, particularly the "fight or flight" response.

Sympathies is most often encountered in expressions of condolence: {Please accept my sympathies on the loss of your father}. The plural suggests multiple feelings or gestures of compassion directed toward someone in grief or hardship. Sympathies can also mean inclinations or loyalties: {Her political sympathies lie with the left}. One's sympathies are where one's support naturally flows.

To sympathize is to share or understand another's feelings, especially their distress or sorrow: {I sympathize with what you're going through}. It can also mean to support or approve of something: {She sympathized with the workers' demands}. Sympathize emphasizes emotional understanding, while empathize suggests more fully inhabiting another's perspective.

A sympathizer supports or agrees with a cause, group, or belief, often without being a formal member. The term frequently carries political weight, suggesting someone who shares the views of a controversial movement: {Nazi sympathizers}, {communist sympathizers}. While it can be neutral—{I'm a sympathizer with the labor movement}—it often implies suspicion or accusation, as if the person's allegiance is hidden or questionable. The British spelling is sympathiser.

Sympathy is fellow feeling—sharing in another's emotions, especially sorrow or hardship. To {have sympathy for} someone is to understand and care about their situation. Sympathy often implies emotional distance: you feel for them rather than with them, distinguishing it from empathy. {My sympathies} expresses condolences. In the plural, sympathies can mean allegiances: {Her sympathies lay with the rebels}. Things in sympathy resonate together: {The strings vibrated in sympathy}.

A symphony is a large-scale orchestral composition, typically in four movements, representing one of classical music's most ambitious forms. The word extends to symphony orchestras—the ensembles that perform such works—and to harmonious combinations generally: {a symphony of colors}, {a symphony of flavors}. Beethoven's symphonies remain touchstones of the form.

A symptom is a sign that something is wrong—typically a physical or mental change indicating disease or disorder: {Fever is a common symptom of infection}. Symptoms are what patients report; doctors distinguish these from signs, which they observe directly. The word extends to any indication of an underlying problem: {Rising crime rates are a symptom of deeper social issues}.

Symptoms are signs that indicate something is wrong, especially with health. A symptom of disease is something the patient experiences—pain, fatigue, nausea—as distinct from clinical signs a doctor observes. The word extends beyond medicine: {Rising prices are a symptom of inflation}. Symptoms point to underlying causes rather than being the problem itself.

A synagogue is a Jewish house of worship and community gathering. Unlike a temple, which historically referred to the central sanctuary in Jerusalem, synagogues serve local congregations for prayer, study, and social functions. The building typically contains a sanctuary with an ark holding Torah scrolls: {The congregation met at the synagogue for Shabbat services}.

Sync is a clipped form of synchronize, used as both noun and verb. To sync devices or files is to update them so they match or coordinate with each other: {Let me sync my calendar with yours}. When things are {in sync}, they're aligned or operating in harmony; {out of sync} means mismatched or poorly timed. The term dominates in computing and electronics but extends to any coordination of timing or content: {The audio wasn't in sync with the video}.

Synchronicity is the occurrence of meaningful coincidences—events that seem connected by significance rather than cause. The term comes from psychology, where it describes moments when inner experience and outer events align in ways that feel purposeful but lack causal explanation: {Meeting her felt like synchronicity—I'd just been thinking about her}. The word often carries a mystical or spiritual connotation, suggesting the universe arranges meaningful patterns.

Synchronize means to cause things to happen or operate at the same time or rate. You synchronize watches so they show identical times. Swimmers synchronize their movements to perform in unison. In technology, to synchronize is to update files or data across devices so they match: {My phone syncs with my laptop automatically}. The shortened form sync dominates casual use.

The syncytiotrophoblast is the outer layer of cells forming the surface of the placenta, in direct contact with maternal blood. Unlike most tissues, it has no cell boundaries—nuclei share a continuous cytoplasm. This multinucleated layer handles nutrient exchange and hormone production, including the hormones detected by pregnancy tests.

A syndicate is a group of individuals or organizations that join together for a common purpose, typically business or criminal. News syndicates distribute content to multiple outlets; crime syndicates coordinate illegal operations across territories. In finance, syndicates of banks share the risk of large loans. To syndicate content is to sell it for publication across multiple platforms: {The column is syndicated in over two hundred newspapers}.

Syndicates is the plural of syndicate—a group organized around a shared purpose, usually business or crime. A crime syndicate coordinates illegal operations across territories. A media syndicate distributes content to multiple outlets. In gambling, a syndicate pools money for larger bets: {The lottery syndicate split the jackpot twelve ways}. As a verb, to syndicate is to distribute widely: {The column is syndicated to newspapers nationwide}.

A syndrome is a group of symptoms that occur together and characterize a particular condition or disease: {chronic fatigue syndrome}, {Down syndrome}. Medical syndromes are named for their discoverers, symptoms, or affected populations. The word extends to any set of characteristics that typically appear together: {empty nest syndrome}, {imposter syndrome}. In casual use, syndrome can describe any recognizable pattern of behavior: {middle child syndrome}.

A synonym is a word with the same or a similar meaning to another word. Synonyms must be the same part of speech. Some synonyms can substitute for each other in a sentence without significantly changing the meaning. More often, each of a set of synonyms has a slightly different connotation. English has a large vocabulary with many sets of synonyms that give writers and speakers the opportunity to create very subtle distinctions in meaning.

Synonyms is the plural of synonym—words that share meaning with other words. Happy and joyful are synonyms; so are big and large. Perfect synonyms are rare; most differ in connotation, register, or context. {Can you think of any synonyms for "angry"?} The concept is fundamental to thesauruses and vocabulary instruction.

Synth is short for synthesizer—an electronic instrument that generates and manipulates sound waves to produce music. Synths dominated 1980s pop and remain central to electronic genres: {The track opens with a pulsing synth}. The word also works as an adjective: {synth-pop}, {synth-heavy}. In science fiction, synth sometimes means a synthetic human or android.

Synthesis is the combining of separate elements into a unified whole. In chemistry, synthesis creates compounds from simpler substances. In philosophy, synthesis resolves thesis and antithesis into a new understanding. More broadly, any work that pulls together diverse sources or ideas performs a synthesis: {Her book is a synthesis of recent scholarship on the topic}. The verb is synthesize.

Synthesiser is the British spelling of synthesizer. An electronic instrument that generates and manipulates sound waves to produce music. Early synthesisers used analog circuits; modern ones are typically digital. The word extends to any device that combines elements into a whole: {a speech synthesiser}. To synthesise is to combine parts into something new.

A synthesizer is an electronic instrument that generates and manipulates sound, typically through keyboards, oscillators, and filters. Musicians use synthesizers to create tones ranging from imitations of acoustic instruments to entirely novel sounds: {The synthesizer dominated 1980s pop music}. Often shortened to synth. Beyond music, any device that combines elements into a unified output may be called a synthesizer.

Synthetic describes something made artificially rather than occurring naturally. Synthetic {fibers} like nylon and polyester are manufactured, unlike cotton or wool. Synthetic {chemicals} are laboratory creations. The word can suggest inferiority to the natural—a synthetic {smile} is fake, not genuine. In philosophy, a synthetic statement combines concepts not inherently connected, requiring evidence beyond the definitions themselves.

A syringe is a device for injecting or withdrawing fluids, typically a tube fitted with a plunger and a hollow needle. Medical syringes deliver medications or draw blood. Other syringes lack needles—a bulb syringe clears an infant's nose, a turkey baster bastes meat. The verb means to wash or spray with a syringe: {The doctor syringed my ears to remove wax}.

Syringes are tube-shaped medical devices with a plunger mechanism, used to inject fluids into or withdraw them from the body. A syringe typically attaches to a hollow needle for penetrating skin. Beyond medicine, syringes appear in cooking for injecting marinades and in crafts for precise glue application. {The nurse prepared the syringes for the vaccination clinic.}

Syrup is a thick, sweet liquid made by dissolving sugar in water or by reducing plant juices. Maple syrup comes from tree sap; corn syrup from processed corn starch. Cough syrup is medicine in a sweetened liquid base. Figuratively, something syrupy is cloyingly sweet or sentimental: {His syrupy compliments made everyone uncomfortable}.

A system is a set of connected parts working together as a whole. The body has systems—circulatory, nervous, digestive. Governments and institutions are systems. A stereo system combines components. {The system} often means established power structures: {fighting the system}, {working within the system}. To {get something out of your system} is to purge an impulse or emotion by indulging it.

Systems is the plural of system—organized sets of connected parts working together. The word often appears in contexts involving infrastructure or procedures: {computer systems}, {healthcare systems}, {systems failure}. In technical fields, systems thinking emphasizes how components interact rather than examining them in isolation. Someone who works in {systems} typically handles technology or organizational processes.

Tab’s numerous and varied meanings must be discerned from context. Online, a tab is a clickable link that opens a separate page, or a separate display page in your browser. The tab key on your keyboard creates an indentation (a tab), or advances to the next available field. That kind of tab is inspired by the physical one, a projecting piece of something that allows you to identify it, close it, or pull it out. A tab at a restaurant or business is a line of credit. If you keep tabs on someone, you monitor their actions and movements. Tab may also be short for tablet when it refers to a pill.

A tabby is a domestic cat with a distinctive coat pattern of stripes, swirls, or spots, typically in gray or brown with darker markings. The tabby pattern is one of the most common in cats, appearing across many breeds. The term can also describe the coat pattern itself: {a tabby coat}, {tabby markings}. Historically, tabby referred to a type of wavy-patterned silk fabric, which likely inspired the cat terminology.

We encounter two kinds of tables daily: the physical kind, forming a horizontal surface resting on legs (dining table) and the tabular kind, consisting of rows and columns filled with information (league table). Most other noun meanings of table are related: table of contents, the table ordered lasagna. The verb table has different usage in U.S. and UK English. Americans use it to mean postpone (table a motion), but in the UK it means present for discussion (table an amendment). If something is on the table, it is negotiable or under consideration.

Tables are flat surfaces raised on legs, used for eating, working, or display. A table of data arranges information in rows and columns: {The report includes tables showing quarterly earnings}. To table something means to postpone discussion (American) or to bring it forward for discussion (British)—opposite meanings that cause confusion. Under the table describes payments made secretly to avoid taxes or scrutiny. To turn the tables is to reverse a situation's advantage.

A tablet is a flat slab or pad used for writing or display—from ancient clay tablets to modern touchscreen devices. A tablet of paper is a pad of sheets bound at one edge. In medicine, a tablet is a compressed disk of medication: {Take two tablets with water}. Tablets of stone suggest permanence: {The rules aren't written on tablets}.

Tabletop is the flat upper surface of a table. As an adjective, it describes games played on a table rather than electronically—{tabletop RPGs}, {tabletop gaming}—distinguishing dice-and-paper or board games from video games. Tabletop also describes small items sized for display on tables: {a tabletop fountain}, {tabletop Christmas tree}.

Tablets is the plural of tablet. A tablet is a flat, portable slab for writing—from ancient clay tablets to modern touchscreen devices. Pharmaceutical tablets are compressed doses of medication: {Take two tablets with water}. A tablet of paper is a pad of sheets bound at one edge. Stone tablets carry inscribed text, most famously the Ten Commandments.

A tabloid is a newspaper with pages roughly half the size of a broadsheet, typically featuring sensational stories, celebrity gossip, and bold headlines. The format has become so associated with its content that tabloid now describes any sensationalized journalism: {tabloid TV}, {tabloid journalism}. British tabloids like the Sun and Daily Mail are cultural institutions. As an adjective, tabloid suggests lurid or oversimplified coverage: {The story got the tabloid treatment}.

Tabloids are newspapers characterized by sensational headlines, celebrity gossip, and scandal-driven coverage rather than serious journalism. The term comes from the smaller page format these papers traditionally used, half the size of broadsheets. {The tabloids had a field day with the politician's affair.} Tabloid as an adjective describes anything with that sensationalist quality: {tabloid journalism}, {tabloid TV}.

Taboo describes something forbidden by social custom or religious law—not illegal, but culturally prohibited. Certain topics are taboo in polite conversation: death, money, sex. Taboo can also be a noun: {There's a strong taboo against speaking ill of the dead}. The word comes from Tongan, entering English through Captain Cook's Pacific voyages. What counts as taboo varies enormously across cultures and eras.

Taboos are prohibitions against certain behaviors, subjects, or words—things society treats as forbidden or unmentionable. Some are universal (incest, cannibalism), others cultural or generational. The word also functions as an adjective: {a taboo subject}, {taboo language}. What's taboo shifts over time; discussing sex was once taboo in ways that seem quaint now, while racial slurs have become more taboo than they were decades ago.

Tabs are small projecting flaps or strips that allow you to grab, open, or organize something: the tab on a soda can, tabs on file folders. To {keep tabs on} someone is to monitor them. A tab is also a bill, especially at a bar: {Put it on my tab}. In computing, tabs are separate pages within a browser window or sections in an interface. The tab key moves the cursor to preset positions. Tab is also short for tablet, especially of drugs: {a tab of acid}.

The commonest kind of tack is a fastener with a sharp end (thumbtack, upholstery tack). In seafaring, tack is the direction of a vessel. If you take or try a new tack, in a boat or elsewhere, you go off in a different direction. Around horses, tack is a shortening of tackle and refers to harnesses, saddles, bridles, and such. To tack something is to attach it with tacks or (in a boat) to sail in a particular direction.

Tackle centers on grabbing and grappling. In football and rugby, a tackle brings an opponent to the ground; the verb means to do this. Extended, to tackle a problem or task is to take it on directly: {Let's tackle the budget first}. Tackle also means equipment for a particular activity—fishing tackle, sailing tackle. In nautical use, tackle refers to rope-and-pulley systems for lifting. A tackle box holds fishing gear.

Tackling is the act of seizing and bringing someone down, especially in football and rugby where it stops an opponent's advance. The word extends to confronting any difficult task or problem head-on: {We spent the weekend tackling the garage cleanup}. In sailing, tackling refers to the system of ropes and pulleys used to hoist and adjust sails. As fishing gear, it covers the equipment needed to catch fish—rods, reels, lines, and lures.

Tacks are small, sharp-pointed nails with flat heads, used to fasten things temporarily or to surfaces like corkboard: {She used tacks to pin the poster to the wall}. In sailing, a tack is a course relative to the wind, or the maneuver of changing that course. Figuratively, to change tack is to shift approach: {When charm failed, he tried a different tack}. To tack something on is to add it as an afterthought. Tack also refers to a horse's harness and saddle equipment.

Tacky describes something cheap-looking, gaudy, or in poor taste: {tacky souvenir shops}, {a tacky outfit}. It can also mean socially inappropriate or classless: {It's tacky to ask how much someone paid for their house}. Separately, tacky means slightly sticky—not fully dry: {Don't touch the paint; it's still tacky}.

A taco is a Mexican dish consisting of a folded or rolled tortilla filled with meat, beans, cheese, vegetables, or other ingredients. The shell may be soft (flour or corn tortilla) or fried crisp. Tacos range from traditional street food to fast-food versions to elaborate restaurant preparations: {We grabbed tacos from the food truck}.

Tacos are a Mexican dish consisting of a folded or rolled tortilla filled with meat, beans, cheese, vegetables, or other ingredients. The shell may be soft (flour or corn tortilla) or crispy (fried corn). Tacos range from authentic street food to heavily Americanized versions with ground beef and shredded cheese: {We're getting tacos for lunch}.

Tact is sensitivity in dealing with others—knowing what to say and what to leave unsaid, how to raise difficult subjects without giving offense. Someone with tact navigates awkward social situations gracefully: {She had the tact to change the subject when he started crying}. Tactful is the adjective; tactless describes someone who lacks this quality.

A tactic is a practical act or method used to accomplish an objective: The police tried a number of tactics to get the man out of the building. When you change tactics, you try a new approach to achieve success, usually because your previous attempt didn’t work. The frequent phrase scare tactics usually means the attempting to frighten people, usually without good reason, in order to evoke a reaction. Tactics has a specific meaning in reference to warfare and is the counterpart of strategy.

Tactical relates to tactics—the specific maneuvers and methods used to achieve an objective, especially in military operations. A tactical {retreat} is a calculated withdrawal, not a defeat. Tactical contrasts with strategic: tactics concern immediate actions, strategy concerns the larger plan. In consumer culture, tactical has become marketing jargon for military-styled gear: tactical {flashlight}, tactical {vest}, tactical {pants}.

Tactics are the specific methods or maneuvers used to achieve an immediate objective, especially in military contexts where they contrast with strategy—the broader plan. A general's strategy might be to cut off supply lines; the tactics are how troops actually do it. The word extends to any calculated moves: {negotiating tactics}, {scare tactics}, {delay tactics}. Someone tactical thinks in terms of immediate advantage rather than long-term goals.
Tad is a very informal word that means a small amount. It is often used in the phrase a tad, where it is interchangeable with a little. Tad is also a nickname for Thaddeus.

Tada is an exclamation accompanying a reveal or flourish, announcing that something impressive or long-awaited has arrived: {Tada! Your new kitchen is finished}. It mimics a trumpet fanfare and often carries playful or ironic overtones—the reveal may be genuinely impressive or deliberately anticlimactic: {I finally cleaned my room. Tada!} Also spelled ta-da.

A tadpole is the larval stage of a frog or toad—the small, aquatic creature with a rounded body and long tail that emerges from the egg before metamorphosing into an adult. Tadpoles breathe through gills and swim by wriggling their tails. The word sometimes describes anything small and tailed, or affectionately, a small child.

Tadpoles are the larval stage of frogs and toads—the small, aquatic creatures with rounded bodies and long tails that hatch from eggs before metamorphosing into adults. They breathe through gills and swim by wriggling their tails: {The pond was full of tadpoles in spring}. Also called pollywogs.

Taekwondo is a Korean martial art emphasizing high kicks, jumping and spinning kicks, and fast footwork. It became an Olympic sport in 2000. Practitioners advance through colored belt ranks, with black belt indicating proficiency. {She earned her black belt in taekwondo at fifteen.}

Taffy is a chewy candy made by boiling sugar and butter, then pulling and stretching the mixture repeatedly until it becomes light and airy. Saltwater taffy, associated with American beach boardwalks, contains no actual seawater. A taffy pull is a social gathering where people stretch the candy together. In British English, the same confection is called toffee.

A tag is a label – a physical one, like a price tag, or an intangible one, like the tags on a blog post that associate it with various subjects. Tags often help to identify things, like a soldier’s dog tags or an online document’s HTML tags. To tag something is to attach a tag to it (physically) or to identify it with tags, as when a social media site invites you to tag your friends. When you tag on something, it’s usually unnecessary or an afterthought: She tagged on an extra paragraph to the essay. The same concept extends to tag along, which conveys accompanying or following another person or people, often without an invitation to do so. A different tag is a children’s game involving chasing and touching.

Tagged means marked or labeled, often with a physical tag or digital label. In social media, to tag someone is to link their name to a post or photo: {She tagged me in a photo from the party}. Graffiti artists tag surfaces with their signature. In children's games, the person who's been touched becomes tagged—now "it."

Tagging is marking or labeling something for identification or categorization. In graffiti culture, tagging means spray-painting one's signature or symbol on surfaces: {The underpass was covered in tagging}. Online, tagging attaches labels to content for organization or alerts others by linking their names: {She keeps tagging me in photos}. In sports, tagging is touching a runner or base to make an out.

A tagline is a memorable phrase associated with a brand, product, or creative work—a slogan designed to stick in the mind: {Nike's tagline is "Just Do It"}. Films often have taglines on promotional materials: {The tagline for Alien was "In space no one can hear you scream"}. The term also applies to a brief identifying phrase in email signatures or online profiles.

Tags are labels attached to things for identification—price tags on merchandise, name tags at conferences, dog tags on soldiers. In computing, tags are keywords or code markers: HTML tags structure web pages, hashtags categorize social media posts. To tag is to attach such a label, or to touch someone in the children's game of tag: {You're it!} To tag along is to follow someone, usually uninvited.

A tail is a projecting body part at the rear of a mammal, reptile, or bird. The meaning is extended to things that look like this (ponytail, tail of an airplane), or things that are in the rear: Join the tail of the line. The reverse side of a coin is called tails. To tail someone is to follow them, especially secretively. If you turn tail, you run away from danger or a threat, usually out of fear. If traffic tails or tails back, it forms a long, slow line. To tail off is to diminish.

A tailgate is the hinged rear door of a truck bed or hatchback that swings down for loading. To tailgate is to drive dangerously close behind another vehicle: {Stop tailgating me!} In American usage, tailgating also means partying in a parking lot before a sporting event, often with food and drinks served from an open tailgate: {We got there early to tailgate before the game}.

Tailgated is the past tense of tailgate. To tailgate is to drive dangerously close behind another vehicle: {The truck tailgated me for three miles}. Tailgate also means to host or attend a parking lot party before a sporting event, with food and drinks served from the back of vehicles: {We tailgated before the game}.

Tailgaters are drivers who follow too closely behind other vehicles, leaving insufficient stopping distance. The term also refers to people who gather in parking lots before sporting events, eating and drinking from the open tailgates of trucks or hatchbacks: {The tailgaters had their grills going hours before kickoff}. Both senses derive from tailgate—the hinged rear door of a vehicle.

Tailgates names the hinged rear doors or panels on trucks, station wagons, and SUVs that swing down or open outward for loading cargo. To tailgate is to follow another vehicle too closely—dangerously close to its tail. The other common meaning involves partying in parking lots before sporting events, often with food and drinks served from an open tailgate: {We tailgated for hours before the game}.

Tailgating has two distinct meanings in American life. On the road, it's driving dangerously close behind another vehicle: {The truck was tailgating me for miles}. At sporting events, it's the opposite—a social gathering in parking lots where people eat and drink from the backs of vehicles before games: {We got there early for tailgating}.

A tailor is a person who makes, alters, or repairs clothing, especially men's suits and formal wear. The verb means to make or adapt something for a particular purpose or person: {The program is tailored to individual needs}. Tailored clothing is fitted and structured rather than loose. {She had the dress tailored to fit perfectly}.

Tailored describes something fitted or customized for a specific purpose or person. A tailored {suit} has been cut and sewn to fit an individual's body precisely. The meaning extends beyond clothing: a tailored {approach}, a tailored {solution}. The word implies careful attention to particular needs rather than one-size-fits-all treatment: {The program was tailored to each student's learning style}.

Tailoring is the craft of making fitted clothing, especially suits and formal garments. A tailor cuts and sews fabric to fit an individual body. By extension, tailoring means customizing anything to fit specific needs or preferences: {The program offers tailoring to individual learning styles}. As an adjective, it describes the fit and construction of garments: {The tailoring on that jacket is impeccable}.

Tailors are craftspeople who make, alter, or repair clothing, especially suits and other fitted garments. The singular tailor also functions as a verb meaning to customize or adapt something for a specific purpose: {The program is tailored to individual needs}. Something tailor-made fits precisely, whether literally or figuratively.

Tails is the reverse side of a coin—the side opposite the head. In a coin flip, you call {heads or tails} before it lands. Tails also refers to a tailcoat or formal evening wear with long back panels: {white tie and tails}. As a verb form, tails means follows closely: {A detective tails the suspect}.

A tailspin is an aircraft's steep, spiraling descent with the tail tracing circles above the nose—a dangerous loss of control. The figurative use dominates: a rapid, uncontrolled decline or deterioration. {The company went into a tailspin after the scandal broke.} {Her life was in a tailspin.} One word or two: tail spin.

Tailspins is the plural of tailspin—an aircraft's steep, spiraling descent with the tail rotating above the nose. The figurative sense dominates: a rapid, uncontrolled decline. {The company went into a tailspin after the scandal}. {Her life has been in tailspins ever since the divorce}. The verb form describes entering such a state: {The news sent him tailspinning}.

A tailwind is a wind blowing in the same direction you're traveling, pushing you along and making movement easier. Pilots and cyclists benefit from tailwinds, which increase speed and reduce fuel or effort. Figuratively, a tailwind is any favorable condition that helps progress: {The economy provided a tailwind for the company's expansion}. Opposite of headwind.

To taint something literally is to pollute it, the way chemicals might taint a water supply. In extended use, to taint someone’s reputation or perception is to affect it negatively with information, perhaps false information. Taint is the result or fact of being tainted; cork taint happens when the cork spoils the taste of the wine. A taint of something is the small but significant presence of a negative factor that diminishes it.

Tainted means contaminated, spoiled, or corrupted. Food becomes tainted when bacteria grow in it. Evidence is tainted when improperly handled. A reputation is tainted by scandal. The word suggests something once pure or acceptable has been compromised: {tainted water}, {tainted money}, {tainted love}. What's tainted isn't necessarily ruined, but its integrity is now in question.

From a fairly specific early meaning—grasp with the hands—take has become a frequent and varied verb. It retains its original meaning and has come to encroach on the territory of get, from which it differs in one important respect: when you get something you simply acquire it, but when you take something it becomes yours by an act of will. Take is also present in phrasal verbs in which the core meaning is not very evident, such as take after, take apart, take in, and take up. In the 20th century, the noun take assumed the meaning of an idea or assessment: What’s your take on the president’s speech?

Takeaway has two clusters of meaning. In British English, a takeaway is food prepared for eating elsewhere, or the establishment that sells it: {Let's get a takeaway tonight}. Americans say takeout. The other sense, common everywhere, is the main point or lesson to be extracted from something: {The key takeaway from the meeting was that we need more data}. What you take away with you—whether food or insight.

Takeaways are the key points or lessons extracted from an experience, presentation, or document: {What are your main takeaways from the meeting?} The word emphasizes what you carry away mentally. In British English, a takeaway is also food purchased to eat elsewhere, or the restaurant that sells it—what Americans call takeout.

A takedown is the act of bringing someone or something down. In wrestling, it's a move that brings an opponent to the mat. Online, it refers to removing content, often for legal reasons: {The video was subject to a copyright takedown}. A takedown can also be a pointed critique or exposé that damages a reputation: {The article was a brutal takedown of the mayor}. As an adjective, takedown describes something designed for easy disassembly: {a takedown rifle}.

Taken is the past participle of take, used in perfect tenses {I have taken the medicine} and as an adjective. Something taken is removed, captured, or occupied: {That seat is taken}. A person who is taken is romantically unavailable: {Sorry, I'm taken}. To be {taken with} someone is to be charmed by them. {Taken aback} means surprised or disconcerted.

Takeoff is the moment an aircraft leaves the ground, or the act of becoming airborne: {We experienced some turbulence shortly after takeoff}. By extension, takeoff describes any rapid start or surge: {the takeoff of her career}. A takeoff is also a humorous imitation or parody: {His takeoff of the president was spot-on}.

Takeout is food prepared at a restaurant for eating elsewhere: {Let's get Chinese takeout}. The word functions as noun or adjective: {a takeout order}, {the takeout counter}. In British English, the equivalent is takeaway. Takeout also describes anything removed or extracted—in bridge, a takeout double asks partner to bid.

A takeover is the act of assuming control over something, especially a company or organization. In business, a takeover occurs when one company acquires another, sometimes against the target's wishes {(a hostile takeover)}. The term extends to any seizure of control: {a military takeover}, {a government takeover of the banks}. As a verb phrase, to {take over} means to assume control or responsibility: {She took over as CEO last month}.

Takeovers is the plural of takeover—an act of assuming control over something. In business, a takeover is acquiring a company, often against its will: {hostile takeovers}, {corporate raiders}. In politics or military contexts, a takeover seizes power: {a military takeover}, {the takeover of the government}. The word implies displacement of previous control.

Takers are people who accept what's offered. If you ask for volunteers and get no takers, nobody stepped forward. The word often appears with modifiers indicating willingness: {Any takers for the last slice?} A taker may also be someone who takes rather than gives—self-interested rather than generous: {The world has givers and takers}.

Takes is the third-person singular of take, covering its vast range: to grasp {she takes his hand}, to require {it takes courage}, to accept {he takes the job}, to consume {she takes her medicine}. As a noun, takes are recorded performances, especially in film: {We need another take}. A take is also an opinion or interpretation: {What's your take on this?} In informal use, takes often refers to hot takes—quick, provocative opinions shared on social media.

Taking is the act of seizing, acquiring, or receiving something. A taking can be a single instance—{the taking of hostages}—or accumulated receipts: {The day's takings exceeded expectations}. In law, a taking is government seizure of private property, with or without compensation. As an adjective, taking is old-fashioned for attractive or captivating: {a taking smile}.

The noun tale is distantly related to the verb tell, and their meanings are connected. A tale most generally is something told; in other words, a story. Modifying adjectives are frequent to specify the kind of story: for example, fairy tale, cautionary tale (one that has a lesson), and tall tale (story with exaggerations). Someone who is telling tales is likely lying or spreading gossip. The tale unfolds is a way of talking about how events develop and change.

Talent is a natural aptitude or ability, especially one that sets a person apart: {She has a talent for languages}, {a raw talent for comedy}. The word often implies something innate rather than learned. Talent also refers collectively to skilled people: {The company is struggling to attract talent}. In entertainment, talent means performers as distinct from crew: {The talent is ready on set}.

Talented describes someone with natural ability or aptitude in a particular area: {a talented musician}, {a talented writer}. The word implies innate gift rather than acquired skill, though the distinction often blurs—talented people usually also work hard. {She's incredibly talented at making people feel comfortable}.

Talents are natural abilities or aptitudes—things someone does well without extensive training: {She has a talent for languages}, {a young man of many talents}. The word often implies gifts worth developing: {Don't waste your talents}. In the ancient world, a talent was a unit of weight and money; the biblical parable of talents (coins entrusted to servants) gave rise to the modern meaning of God-given abilities.

Tales is the plural of tale—stories, especially those involving adventure, imagination, or exaggeration. Fairy tales, tall tales, folk tales. The word carries a slightly old-fashioned or literary flavor compared to stories: {tales of heroism}, {cautionary tales}. To {tell tales} is to gossip or tattle, especially among children: {Don't go telling tales to the teacher}.

A talisman is an object believed to have magical protective powers or to bring good luck to its bearer. Unlike an amulet, which primarily wards off evil, a talisman is thought to actively attract positive outcomes: {He kept his grandfather's ring as a talisman}. The word often appears figuratively for anything that brings confidence or reassurance: {Her morning coffee was a talisman against the day's chaos}.

Talismans is the plural of talisman—objects believed to carry magical properties or bring good luck to their possessor. Unlike amulets, which ward off harm, talismans are thought to attract positive outcomes: {She collected talismans from her travels}. The word extends to anything treated as a good-luck charm: {His grandfather's watch became a talisman he carried to every interview}.

Talk is verbal communication—the act of speaking, especially in conversation. You can {talk to} someone, {talk about} something, or {talk someone into} doing something. Talk also means the subject of conversation: {She's the talk of the town}. As a noun, a talk is a speech or lecture. Talks in the plural usually means negotiations: {peace talks}, {trade talks}. To {talk shop} is to discuss work; to {talk trash} is to insult opponents; to {talk the talk} is to speak convincingly about something you may not actually do.

Talkative describes someone who talks a lot or readily. The word is neutral to mildly critical—a talkative person may be engaging or tiresome depending on context: {She's talkative once you get to know her}. {The wine made him talkative}. A more pointed synonym is chatty; a harsher one is loquacious.

Talking is the act of speaking or having a conversation. It can describe the activity itself {We did a lot of talking on the drive} or function as an adjective for things that speak: a talking {parrot}, a talking {head} on television. {Now you're talking} expresses approval of what someone just said or suggested.

Talks functions as both verb and noun around the idea of verbal communication. As a verb, it's the third-person form of talk: {She talks too much}, {He talks in his sleep}. As a noun, talks are formal discussions or negotiations: {peace talks}, {trade talks}, {The talks broke down after three days}. Talk shows feature talks with guests.

A talkshow is a television or radio program featuring conversations between a host and guests—celebrities, experts, or ordinary people with interesting stories. The format ranges from late-night entertainment {The Tonight Show} to daytime confessionals {talk show therapy} to political roundtables. Also spelled as two words: talk show.

Tall describes height that exceeds the average or expected—a tall building, a tall person. The word applies mainly to things whose vertical dimension dominates: people are tall, but tables are high. A {tall order} is a difficult demand. A {tall tale} is an exaggerated or improbable story. {She's tall for her age.}

A tally is a count or record of items, points, or occurrences: {The final tally showed three hundred votes in favor}. To tally is to count up or to match: {The numbers don't tally}. Originally a notched stick used to record debts or quantities—each notch a mark of what was owed or counted.

A talon is the sharp, hooked claw of a bird of prey—eagles, hawks, owls, and the like. The word emphasizes the gripping, tearing function: {The hawk sank its talons into the rabbit}. Figuratively, talons suggest predatory grasp or control: {escape the talons of debt collectors}. The word rarely applies to other animals' claws.

Talons are the sharp, curved claws of a bird of prey—eagles, hawks, owls, and falcons use them to seize and kill prey. The word emphasizes lethality: ordinary birds have claws, but raptors have talons. Figuratively, talons suggest grasping aggression: {escape the talons of debt collectors}, {in the talons of addiction}.

A tamale is a Mexican dish of seasoned meat, cheese, or other filling wrapped in corn dough (masa), then wrapped in a corn husk or banana leaf and steamed. The wrapping is removed before eating. {We ordered a dozen tamales for the party.} The phrase {hot tamale} can mean an attractive or sexually exciting person.

Tamales are a traditional Mexican dish of seasoned meat, cheese, or other fillings wrapped in corn dough (masa), then wrapped in corn husks or banana leaves and steamed. The word is the plural of tamal, though English speakers often treat tamale as the singular. Tamales are labor-intensive to prepare, typically made in large batches for holidays and celebrations: {We spent all day making tamales for Christmas}.

A tambourine is a shallow hand-held drum with metal discs called jingles set into the rim. Players shake it or strike it with the hand to produce rhythmic sound, making it common in folk music, pop, and religious worship. The tambourine requires no formal training, which makes it the instrument often handed to the least musical person in the room. {She grabbed a tambourine and joined the drum circle.}

Tame describes animals that have been domesticated or trained to live with humans without fear or aggression, the opposite of wild. By extension, tame characterizes anything lacking excitement, danger, or intensity: {The movie was pretty tame compared to the book}. A tame person is docile or submissive, easily controlled. The verb tame means to bring something wild under control, whether an animal, a wilderness, or an unruly situation: {She managed to tame her frizzy hair}.

Taming is the process of making a wild animal docile and accustomed to human contact. The word extends to subduing or bringing under control anything unruly: {taming inflation}, {taming her wild curls}. Shakespeare's *The Taming of the Shrew* uses the word for breaking a woman's independent spirit—a usage now recognized as troubling.

To tamper is to interfere with something in a way that damages, alters, or corrupts it: {Someone tampered with the evidence}, {tamper-proof packaging}. The interference is usually unauthorized and often subtle—tampering implies meddling rather than obvious destruction. {Tampering with a jury} means attempting to influence jurors illegally.

Tampering is interfering with something in an unauthorized or harmful way, typically to alter, damage, or corrupt it. The word implies improper meddling: {evidence tampering}, {tampering with a jury}, {product tampering}. Someone tampering with records is making unauthorized changes; tampering with equipment suggests sabotage or unauthorized modification.

A tampon is a plug of absorbent material inserted into the vagina to absorb menstrual blood. Tampons come in various absorbencies and may include an applicator for insertion. The word extends to any plug used to stop bleeding or absorb fluid in medical contexts: {The surgeon packed the wound with a tampon}.

Tampons are absorbent cylindrical plugs inserted into the vagina to absorb menstrual blood. Made of cotton or similar material, they typically include a string for removal and may come with an applicator for insertion. The word derives from a French term for plug, and the same principle applies in medical contexts where tampons may be used to absorb blood from wounds. {She always keeps tampons in her bag.}

Tan is a yellowish-brown color, like leather or light wood. To tan is to convert animal hide into leather, or to darken skin through sun exposure: {She tans easily}. A tan is sun-darkened skin: {He came back from vacation with a tan}. To tan someone's hide is to beat them—a threat more than a promise: {I'll tan your hide if you do that again}.

Tandem means one behind the other, in a line. A tandem bicycle has two seats arranged this way, with both riders pedaling. The word extends to any arrangement where things or people work together in sequence: {The two departments operated in tandem to process applications}. Working in tandem suggests close coordination and cooperation, whether the parties are literally lined up or simply partnering closely on an effort.

Tang is a sharp, distinctive taste or smell—the {tang of citrus}, the {tang of sea air}. The word suggests something pleasantly biting or piquant rather than merely strong. Tang also names the projection on a knife blade that extends into the handle, securing the two parts together. As a verb, to tang is to give something that sharp quality, or to ring with a clear metallic sound. (Capitalized Tang is the Chinese dynasty.)

A tangent is a line that touches a curve at exactly one point without crossing it—the geometric sense from which all others derive. In trigonometry, the tangent of an angle is the ratio of the opposite side to the adjacent side in a right triangle. Most commonly, tangent appears in {go off on a tangent}, meaning to diverge abruptly from the main topic: {We were discussing the budget, but he went off on a tangent about his vacation}.

Tangents are lines or paths that touch a curve at exactly one point without crossing it—the geometric sense. More commonly, tangents are digressions from a main topic: {She kept going off on tangents during the lecture}. To {go off on a tangent} is to veer suddenly from the subject at hand. In trigonometry, tangent is a ratio of sides in a right triangle, abbreviated tan.

A tangerine is a small citrus fruit with loose, easily peeled orange skin and sweet flesh, closely related to the mandarin orange. The color tangerine is a reddish-orange, named for the fruit: {tangerine lipstick}, {a tangerine sunset}. The name comes from Tangier, Morocco, a major shipping point for the fruit.

Tangerines is the plural of tangerine, a small citrus fruit with loose, easily peeled skin and sweet-tart flesh. Tangerines are smaller and less acidic than oranges, often eaten fresh or sectioned into salads: {She packed tangerines in the kids' lunches}. The name comes from Tangier, the Moroccan port city.

A tangle is a confused mass of intertwined things—hair, cords, vines, fishing line: {She worked a comb through the tangles in her hair}. To tangle is to become knotted or snarled. Figuratively, a tangle is any complicated mess: {a tangle of bureaucratic regulations}. To {tangle with} someone is to get into a confrontation or fight: {I wouldn't tangle with her if I were you}.

Tangled describes something twisted together in a confused mass—hair, cords, fishing line, Christmas lights. The word extends naturally to complicated situations: a tangled {web of lies}, tangled {emotions}, getting tangled {up in legal problems}. To tangle with someone is to get into a fight or argument: {I wouldn't tangle with her if I were you}.

Tangles are twisted, intertwined masses—of hair, string, wires, or branches. The verb means to twist together or become snarled: {My headphones always tangle in my pocket}. Figuratively, a tangle is a confused situation or dispute: {a legal tangle}, {a tangle of competing interests}. To {tangle with} someone is to clash or fight with them.

Tango is a dramatic partner dance that originated in Argentina, characterized by close embrace, intricate footwork, and sudden pauses. The music accompanying this dance is also called tango. In the NATO phonetic alphabet, tango represents the letter T. The phrase {it takes two to tango} means both parties share responsibility for a situation—you can't dance alone.

Tangy describes a sharp, pleasantly acidic taste or smell—the zing of citrus, vinegar, or fermented foods: {a tangy lemon dressing}, {tangy barbecue sauce}. The word suggests flavor that's bright and stimulating rather than sour or off-putting. Something tangy wakes up the palate.

One kind of tank is a container for storage or holding of liquid or gas (septic tank, fish tank). Another tank is a military vehicle designed to deliver and withstand heavy attack. A think tank is a figurative container for thinkers to come up with new ideas. When something tanks, it is always bad news: it fails, falls into a worse condition, loses, or declines rapidly: The economy tanked due to stock manipulation.

Tanked means drunk, usually very drunk: {We got completely tanked at the wedding}. Separately, tanked describes something that failed badly or collapsed: {The stock tanked after the earnings report}, {The movie tanked at the box office}. In gaming, to tank is to absorb damage for teammates, from the armored vehicle's ability to take hits.

A tanker is a ship, truck, or aircraft designed to transport liquids in bulk—typically oil, fuel, or chemicals. Oil tankers move crude across oceans; tanker trucks deliver gasoline to stations. Military tankers refuel other aircraft in flight. The word emphasizes capacity: {The tanker spilled thousands of gallons into the bay}.

Tanking means failing badly or declining rapidly. A stock tanks when it crashes; a movie tanks when it bombs at the box office; a team tanks when it loses badly: {The company's shares tanked after the earnings report}. In gaming and sports, tanking also means deliberately losing or performing poorly, often to gain a strategic advantage like a better draft pick. In video games, tanking refers to a player who absorbs damage to protect teammates—drawing enemy fire while others attack.

Tanks are large armored military vehicles that move on continuous tracks and carry heavy weapons. The word extends to any large container for storing liquids or gases: a fish tank, a gas tank, a septic tank. To tank is to fail badly: {The movie tanked at the box office}. In gaming, a tank is a character designed to absorb damage and protect teammates. To tank up is to fill a vehicle with fuel or, informally, to drink heavily.

A tannery is a facility where animal hides are processed into leather. The work involves treating raw skins with tannins or other chemicals to preserve them and make them supple. Tanneries have historically been located away from population centers because the process produces strong odors: {The tannery district sat downwind from the city}.

Tanning is the process of converting animal hides into leather, traditionally using tannins from tree bark. The word also refers to darkening skin through sun exposure or artificial UV light: {She's at the tanning salon}. Informally, to give someone a tanning is to beat or thrash them soundly.

Tantalising describes something that tempts or teases by offering something desirable but keeping it just out of reach: {a tantalising glimpse of what's to come}, {the tantalising smell of fresh bread}. The word suggests pleasure mixed with frustration—you want what you're being shown but can't quite have it. British spelling of tantalizing.

Tantalized means tormented by the sight of something desirable but just out of reach. The word comes from Tantalus, a figure in Greek myth condemned to stand in water that receded when he tried to drink, beneath fruit that pulled away when he reached. Someone tantalized by an opportunity can see it clearly but cannot quite grasp it: {She was tantalized by the job listing but knew she lacked the qualifications}.

Tantalizing describes something desirable that remains just out of reach, arousing appetite or curiosity without satisfying it. A tantalizing {aroma} drifts from a kitchen you can't enter. A tantalizing {glimpse} reveals enough to make you want more. The word comes from Tantalus, a figure in Greek myth condemned to stand in water beneath fruit trees—both receding whenever he reached for them.

A tantrum is an outburst of anger, frustration, or distress—typically involving crying, screaming, or physical thrashing. The word most often describes children's meltdowns when they don't get what they want: {She threw a tantrum in the grocery store}. Applied to adults, tantrum suggests childish, disproportionate behavior: {He had a tantrum when his flight was delayed}.

Tantrums are outbursts of uncontrolled anger or frustration, typically involving crying, screaming, or physical displays like kicking and throwing things. The word most often describes young children's meltdowns: {She threw a tantrum when we left the playground}. Applied to adults, it suggests childish behavior: {His tantrums at work made everyone uncomfortable}.

Tap centers on light, quick contact. You tap someone on the shoulder or tap your foot impatiently. A tap is such a touch, or the sound it makes: {the tap of rain on the window}. Tap also names a device controlling liquid flow—a faucet or spigot. To tap a resource is to access it: {tap into savings}, {tap a phone line}. A tap in this sense draws something out. In dance, tap involves metal-soled shoes striking the floor rhythmically. To tap someone for a job is to select them: {She was tapped to lead the committee}.

Tapas are small dishes of Spanish origin, served as appetizers or combined to make a meal. The style emphasizes variety and sharing—a table might hold plates of olives, cured ham, fried potatoes, and grilled shrimp. {We ordered a dozen tapas and split everything}. The concept has spread globally, influencing how restaurants serve small plates meant for grazing.

Tapdance is a style of dance in which the performer wears shoes fitted with metal plates that click rhythmically against the floor. The dancer creates percussive patterns with heel and toe strikes: {She tapdanced her way through the audition}. Figuratively, to tapdance is to improvise evasively or perform verbal acrobatics to avoid a direct answer: {He tapdanced around the question about his finances}.

Tapdancing is a style of dance in which the performer wears shoes fitted with metal plates that click rhythmically against the floor. The dancer creates percussive patterns with the feet, essentially becoming both dancer and drummer. Also spelled tap dancing or tap-dancing. To tapdance around something is to avoid addressing it directly: {The senator tapdanced around the question of funding}.

Tape is a narrow strip of material—fabric, paper, plastic, or adhesive-backed film—used for binding, fastening, sealing, or marking: {masking tape}, {duct tape}, {measuring tape}, {police tape}. Magnetic tape once dominated audio and video recording, so tape became shorthand for recordings themselves: {Did you get that on tape?} The verb means to fasten with tape or to record: {Tape the box shut}, {We taped the interview}.

Tapestries is the plural of tapestry—a heavy textile with woven designs, traditionally hung on walls or used as furnishing. Tapestries often depict scenes, figures, or patterns: {The medieval tapestries showed hunting scenes}. Figuratively, tapestry describes anything richly interwoven: {the tapestry of urban life}, {a tapestry of cultures}.

A tapestry is a heavy textile with decorative designs woven into it, traditionally hung on walls. Tapestries were both ornamental and functional in medieval castles, providing insulation and depicting scenes from history or mythology. Figuratively, tapestry describes anything composed of diverse interwoven elements: {the rich tapestry of urban life}, {a tapestry of cultures}.

A tapeworm is a parasitic flatworm that lives in the intestines of humans and other animals. Tapeworms attach to the intestinal wall and absorb nutrients from their host, sometimes growing to remarkable lengths. Infection typically comes from eating undercooked meat containing larvae: {The patient had a tapeworm from eating raw pork}.

Tapeworms is the plural of tapeworm, a parasitic flatworm that lives in the intestines of humans and other animals. Tapeworms attach to the intestinal wall and absorb nutrients from their host, sometimes growing to considerable length. Infection typically comes from eating undercooked meat containing larvae: {The pork was contaminated with tapeworms}.

Tapioca is a starchy substance extracted from cassava root, used as a thickener and in puddings. Tapioca pudding contains small pearls of the starch that become translucent and chewy when cooked: {The tapioca pudding had that distinctive texture she remembered from childhood}. Larger tapioca pearls appear in bubble tea.

Tapped is the past tense of tap, covering all its senses: struck lightly {He tapped me on the shoulder}, accessed a resource {They tapped the maple trees for syrup}, or selected for a role {She was tapped to lead the committee}. In slang, tapped or tapped out means exhausted or depleted: {I'm tapped—can't lend you anything}. To get tapped can mean to be wiretapped or, vulgarly, to have sex.

Tapping is repeated light strikes or touches. You might hear a tapping at the window or feel someone tapping your shoulder. Tapping a resource means drawing from it: {tapping into reserves}, {tapping a phone line}. In dance, tap dancing involves tapping shoes against a hard floor. To tap someone for a position is to select them: {She was tapped to lead the committee}.

A taproom is a bar or room where beer is served on tap, typically attached to or located within a brewery. Unlike traditional bars that stock various brands, taprooms primarily serve beers made on the premises, giving customers direct access to fresh drafts. The term has seen renewed use with the craft beer movement, as small breweries often open taprooms as their main public-facing space. {The new brewery's taproom opens this weekend.}

Taps is the plural of tap—devices controlling liquid flow, light touches or strikes, or acts of tapping. A bartender works the taps. The taps of a dancer's shoes click against the floor. Phone taps are surveillance devices. To be {on tap} is to be available: {We have several candidates on tap for the position}. (Capitalized Taps is the military bugle call.)

A taqueria is a Mexican restaurant or food stand specializing in tacos and related fare—burritos, quesadillas, tortas. The word is Spanish, and taquerias range from street carts to sit-down establishments: {We grabbed lunch at the taqueria on the corner}.

Tar is a thick, dark, sticky substance derived from organic materials like coal, wood, or petroleum. It's used for waterproofing and paving: {The roofers spread hot tar over the surface}. Cigarette tar refers to the residue that accumulates in lungs. To tar someone is to coat them with tar—historically as punishment ({tarred and feathered})—or to damage their reputation: {Don't tar us all with the same brush}. A tar is also old-fashioned slang for a sailor.

A tarantula is a large, hairy spider. The name originally referred to a European wolf spider associated with the Italian city of Taranto, where its bite supposedly caused frenzied dancing (tarantism). Today it typically means the bigger, stockier spiders of the family Theraphosidae, kept as exotic pets and featured in horror films. Despite their fearsome appearance, most tarantulas are relatively harmless to humans.

A target is something at which you aim a weapon or something that you establish as a goal. If you achieve a target, you reach the goal: They met their sales target. Before another noun, target characterizes the goal: target audience, target date. In military contexts, a target is the thing aimed at with the goal of destroying it. As a verb, target means to take aim at something. If an audience is targeted, it is identified as a group to address or win over. If something is on target, it is meeting expectations or is otherwise accurate, valid, and on course.

Targets are things aimed at—literally or figuratively. A target is what you shoot at, what you're trying to hit or reach: {sales targets}, {target audience}, {target date}. To target something is to select it for attention or attack: {The ads target young adults}. A target can also be someone singled out for criticism or harm: {She became a target of online harassment}.

A tariff is a tax on imported goods, charged when they cross a border. Governments use tariffs to generate revenue or protect domestic industries from foreign competition: {The new tariffs on steel raised prices for manufacturers}. Extended from trade, tariff can mean any schedule of rates or charges: {The hotel's tariff includes breakfast}.

Tariffs are taxes imposed on imported goods, making foreign products more expensive relative to domestic ones. Governments use tariffs to protect local industries, raise revenue, or as leverage in trade disputes: {The administration announced new tariffs on steel imports}. Tariff can also mean any schedule of rates or charges: {the hotel's tariff for room service}.

Tarmac is a paved surface, especially at an airport where planes taxi, load, and unload: {The plane sat on the tarmac for two hours}. The word comes from tarmacadam—a road surface of crushed stone bound with tar. Though technically distinct from modern asphalt, tarmac now serves as a general term for any paved runway or apron area.

Tarnish is the dull film that forms on metal surfaces when they react with air or moisture—silver tarnishes to gray or black, copper to green. To tarnish is to lose or cause to lose luster: {The silverware had tarnished over the years}. Figuratively, tarnish means to damage or sully: {The scandal tarnished his reputation}. A tarnish on someone's record is a blemish that diminishes their standing.

Tarnished describes something that has lost its shine or luster, typically through oxidation or exposure: {tarnished silver}, {tarnished brass}. The word extends naturally to reputation or honor that has been damaged or diminished: {His tarnished reputation never fully recovered}. Something tarnished still exists but has lost the brightness it once had.

Tarot is a deck of 78 cards used for fortune-telling and divination. The deck includes 22 major arcana cards depicting archetypal figures like the Fool, the Lovers, and Death, plus 56 minor arcana in four suits. A tarot reading interprets cards drawn or laid out in patterns: {She consulted the tarot before making her decision}. Originally a Renaissance card game, tarot's occult associations developed later.

Tart describes a sharp, acidic taste—the sourness of unripe fruit or lemon: {tart green apples}, {a tart vinaigrette}. Extended to speech or manner, tart means cutting or caustic: {a tart reply}. As a noun, a tart is a small open pastry with fruit or custard filling. In British slang, tart is a mildly offensive term for a promiscuous woman or prostitute. To {tart up} is to dress or decorate gaudily.

Tartan is a pattern of intersecting horizontal and vertical stripes in multiple colors, forming a distinctive plaid. The pattern is strongly associated with Scotland, where specific tartans identify clans, families, or regions: {the Black Watch tartan}, {wearing the family tartan}. Tartan appears on kilts, scarves, and other textiles. The word also describes fabric woven in this pattern.

Tartar has two main meanings. One is the hard deposit that forms on teeth from plaque—what dentists scrape off during cleanings. The other is a fierce or formidable person: {She's a real tartar when crossed}. This sense comes from the Tartars, Central Asian warriors known for their ferocity. Cream of tartar, used in baking, is an unrelated substance—a byproduct of winemaking.

Tarts are small pastries with a filling—fruit, custard, or savory ingredients—in an open-faced shell: {apple tarts}, {jam tarts}. A larger version is simply a tart rather than a pie when it lacks a top crust. Separately, tart means sharp or acidic in taste: {tart cherries}, {a tart lemonade}. By extension, a tart remark is cutting or biting. In British slang, a tart is a promiscuous woman or prostitute, though the word can be used more loosely for any woman dressed provocatively. To {tart up} something is to dress it up gaudily or cheaply.

A taser is a weapon that delivers an electric shock to incapacitate someone, typically used by police for subduing suspects without lethal force. The device fires two small darts connected by wires that deliver a disabling jolt: {The officer drew his taser when the man refused to comply}. As a verb, to taser someone is to shock them with such a device. The lowercase form has become generic for any similar electroshock weapon. (Capitalized Taser is the trademark.)

A task is a piece of work to be done—something assigned or undertaken: {I have a few tasks to complete before lunch}. Tasks are typically discrete and finite, smaller than projects but more substantial than errands. To task someone is to assign them work, often with a sense of burden: {She was tasked with organizing the event}. To {take someone to task} is to criticize or reprimand them.

A taskmaster is someone who assigns work and demands it be done, especially with strict or exacting standards. The word often carries connotations of harshness: {Her new boss was a real taskmaster}. You can be your own taskmaster, holding yourself to rigorous expectations. The term appears in contexts ranging from workplace supervision to self-discipline.

Tasks are pieces of work that need to be done, usually discrete assignments with defined goals or deadlines. The word implies something that has been assigned or accepted as a responsibility: {I have several tasks to complete before the meeting}. To task someone is to assign them work or burden them with responsibility. If you take someone to task, you criticize or reprimand them for a failing.

A tassel is a bunch of threads or cords bound at one end and hanging loose at the other, used as decoration on clothing, curtains, graduation caps, or furniture: {The tassel on his mortarboard swung as he walked across the stage}. Corn produces tassels—the pollen-bearing flowers at the top of the stalk. To tassel is to form or put forth such flowers.

Tassels are decorative bunches of threads or cords bound at one end and hanging loose at the other. They adorn curtains, graduation caps, throw pillows, and clothing: {The scarf had silk tassels at each end}. Tassel also refers to the pollen-bearing flower cluster at the top of a corn plant. As a verb, to tassel is to form or put forth such clusters: {The corn is starting to tassel}.

Taste is the sense that perceives flavor through the tongue—sweet, salty, sour, bitter, savory. A taste is also a small sample: {Just a taste of the soup}. Extended, taste means preference or discernment: {She has expensive taste in clothes}, {That joke was in bad taste}. To taste something is to perceive its flavor or to experience it briefly: {He tasted freedom for the first time}. A taste for something is an inclination toward it: {He developed a taste for adventure}.

Tastebuds are the sensory receptors on the tongue that detect flavor—sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami. The word often appears figuratively for one's sense of taste or flavor preferences: {My tastebuds aren't ready for anything that spicy}. Also spelled as two words: taste buds.

Tasteful describes choices that show good aesthetic judgment and restraint. A tasteful {outfit} is well-coordinated without being showy. Tasteful {décor} suggests elegance and refinement. The word often implies knowing what to leave out—avoiding excess, vulgarity, or ostentation. {The memorial was simple and tasteful.} Tasteful can sound faintly condescending when applied to others' choices.

Tasteless describes something lacking flavor or aesthetic merit. Bland food is tasteless. So is decor that shows no sense of style. The word extends to behavior that offends good judgment or sensitivity: {a tasteless joke about the accident}, {a tasteless display of wealth at the funeral}. What registers as tasteless varies by culture and context.

A tastemaker is someone whose preferences and choices influence what others consider stylish, desirable, or culturally relevant. The term applies to critics, celebrities, influencers, and industry insiders who shape trends in fashion, food, music, art, or design. {Magazine editors were once the primary tastemakers in fashion.} Being a tastemaker implies not just having good taste but having the cultural authority to establish what good taste means for others.

Tastes is the verb form of taste—to perceive flavor or sample something: {She tastes the soup before serving}. More often it appears as a noun plural referring to personal preferences and sensibilities: {His tastes run toward the exotic}.
