The word often appears in set phrases: {the terrors of war}, {the terrors of the deep}. {Night terrors} are episodes of intense fear during sleep, distinct from nightmares. A person who causes trouble, especially a misbehaving child, may be called {a terror}: {Their toddler is an absolute terror}.

A tesla is the SI unit of magnetic flux density, measuring the strength of magnetic fields. One tesla equals one weber per square meter. The unit is used in physics, engineering, and medical imaging—MRI machines typically operate at 1.5 to 3 teslas. {The Earth's magnetic field is about 50 microteslas.} (Capitalized Tesla refers to the inventor or the car company.)

A test is a procedure to evaluate quality, performance, or knowledge: {a math test}, {a blood test}, {a stress test}. To test something is to subject it to such evaluation. Test can also mean challenge: {The climb tested our endurance}. A {test of character} reveals someone's true nature under pressure. To {put something to the test} is to see if it holds up.

A testament is evidence or proof of something: {The building stands as a testament to Victorian architecture}. More formally, a testament is a will—a legal document directing disposition of property after death, which is why the phrase "last will and testament" exists. In religious contexts, the Old Testament and New Testament are the two main divisions of the Christian Bible. (Capitalized Testament refers specifically to biblical divisions.)

Tested describes something that has been examined, tried, or proven through experience. A tested {method} has demonstrated its effectiveness. A tested {friendship} has survived challenges. {Time-tested} means proven reliable over a long period. In medical contexts, tested indicates having undergone examination: {Have you been tested for allergies?} Battle-tested suggests proven under difficult conditions.

A tester is someone or something that tests. A software tester checks programs for bugs. A product tester evaluates goods before release. The word also names devices that perform tests: a circuit tester, a battery tester. In another sense, a tester is a small sample of a product—especially cosmetics or perfume—provided for customers to try before buying.

A testicle is one of the two oval organs in the male scrotum that produce sperm and testosterone. The word is anatomical and neutral, appearing in medical contexts and everyday speech alike: {He was hit in the testicles}. The informal equivalent is ball or balls.

Testicles are the pair of male reproductive glands that produce sperm and testosterone. They hang in the scrotum outside the body. The singular testicle appears in expressions about courage or audacity: {He didn't have the testicle to say it to my face}, though balls is far more common in such contexts.

Testify means to give evidence or bear witness, most formally in a legal setting where a person testifies under oath about what they know or observed. The word extends beyond courtrooms: you can testify to someone's character or testify that a product works as advertised. In religious contexts, to testify is to publicly declare one's faith or share a personal spiritual experience. {Several witnesses testified against the defendant.} {I can testify to her honesty.}

Testifying is giving testimony—making a formal statement, especially under oath in legal proceedings: {She spent three hours testifying before the grand jury}. The word extends to any solemn declaration of truth or belief: {He's been testifying to the power of exercise for years}. In religious contexts, testifying means bearing witness to one's faith or spiritual experiences.

Testimony is a formal statement, especially one given under oath in legal proceedings: {The witness's testimony contradicted the defendant's account}. Beyond courtrooms, testimony refers to any evidence or proof supporting a claim: {His success is testimony to years of hard work}. In religious contexts, testimony means a public declaration of faith or spiritual experience: {She shared her testimony at the revival}.

Testing is the act of examining something to assess its quality, performance, or condition. Students take tests; software undergoes testing before release; doctors order testing to diagnose illness. {We're still in the testing phase}. As an adjective, testing means difficult or challenging: {It's been a testing few weeks}.

Testosterone is the primary male sex hormone, responsible for developing masculine characteristics like facial hair, deeper voice, and muscle mass. Women produce it too, in smaller amounts. Beyond biology, testosterone often stands for aggressive or competitive male behavior: {Too much testosterone in the boardroom}. Low testosterone ({low T}) is marketed as a treatable condition in aging men.

A tether is a rope, chain, or line that fastens something to a fixed point while allowing limited movement: a dog on a tether, a tethered balloon. To tether is to fasten with such a line. Figuratively, to be {at the end of your tether} is to have exhausted your patience or resources. Tethering a phone shares its internet connection with another device.

Tetherball is a playground game in which two players strike a ball attached by a rope to the top of a pole, each trying to wind the rope completely around the pole in their direction. The game requires no court or equipment beyond the pole and ball: {We played tetherball at recess}. The word also names the ball itself.

Tethered means tied or fastened to something, restricted in movement or range. A tethered {goat} can only graze as far as its rope allows. The meaning extends to anything constrained: a phone tethered to a {charger}, a worker tethered to their {desk}. In computing, tethering connects a device to another for internet access: {I tethered my laptop to my phone}.

Tethers are ropes, chains, or similar restraints that secure something while allowing limited movement—a goat tethered to a post, a spacecraft tethered to a station. Figuratively, tethers are any binding connections: {the tethers of responsibility}. To be at the {end of one's tether} is to have exhausted patience or resources. The verb tether means to fasten with such a restraint: {She tethered her horse outside the saloon}.

Tetrahydrobiopterin is a naturally occurring compound that serves as a cofactor for several enzymes in the body, particularly those involved in producing neurotransmitters like dopamine and serotonin. Deficiencies can cause neurological problems and a form of phenylketonuria that doesn't respond to dietary treatment alone. Often abbreviated BH4 in medical contexts.

Tetris is a puzzle video game where players rotate and position falling geometric shapes to complete horizontal lines, which then disappear. The game, created in 1984 by a Soviet programmer, became one of the most popular and recognizable video games ever made. As a verb, to tetris means to fit objects together efficiently in tight spaces: {I tetrised all our luggage into the trunk}.

Text is language in written form. Text can also refer to the specific wording of anything that is printed: Alterations to the text of the document were being proposed right up to the last minute. In the context of computing, text may refer to a particular kind of file in which the information is encoded in ASCII and is readable by nearly any computer without the use of special programs. The relatively recent verb text is used for the activity of sending SMS between small devices, usually mobile phones: I texted you and you never texted me back.

A textbook is a book designed for formal study of a subject, used in schools and universities: {The professor assigned three textbooks for the course}. As an adjective, textbook means perfectly typical or exemplary—exactly as described in instructional materials: {a textbook case of fraud}, {textbook technique}. The adjective often carries slight irony, since real situations rarely match textbook descriptions.

Textbooks are books designed for formal study of a subject, used in schools and universities. They present information systematically, often with exercises and review questions. {The professor assigned three textbooks for the semester.} As an adjective, textbook describes something that perfectly matches established standards or expectations: {a textbook example of poor leadership}, {textbook technique}.

Textiles are woven or knitted fabrics, or the fibers and yarns used to make them. The term covers everything from cotton and silk to synthetic materials like polyester. In industry and commerce, textiles refers broadly to the cloth trade: {She works in textiles}. The textile industry encompasses spinning, weaving, dyeing, and finishing processes.

Texting is sending written messages via mobile phone or messaging app. The term emerged with SMS technology in the 1990s and now covers any typed conversation on a phone: {I was texting my sister when the bus arrived}. Texting while driving is illegal in many places. The noun texting refers to the activity itself: {Too much texting is ruining kids' spelling}.

Texts are written works, especially those studied for their content: religious texts, literary texts, legal texts. A text is also the main body of a book apart from notes or illustrations. In education, a text is a textbook. Most commonly now, texts are messages sent between phones: {I'll send you a text when I get there}. The verb means to send such a message: {She was texting during dinner}.

Texture is how something feels to the touch—smooth, rough, grainy, silky. The word extends to any surface quality perceived through senses: the texture of a painting's brushstrokes, the texture of a voice. In food, texture describes mouthfeel: {The soup needed more texture}. Figuratively, texture means richness or complexity: {The novel has real texture}.

Textures is the plural of texture—the feel or appearance of a surface. A fabric has texture; so does skin, wood, or stone. In music and writing, texture describes the layered quality of sound or prose: {The symphony's rich textures}. In computing, textures are images applied to 3D surfaces to simulate material appearance: {loading high-resolution textures}. As a verb form, textures means to give surface variation: {She textures the clay with her fingertips}.

To thank is to express gratitude: {I thanked her for the gift}. The noun thanks means an expression of gratitude: {Many thanks for your help}. Thanks also serves as an interjection equivalent to "thank you": {Thanks, I appreciate it}. {Thanks to} attributes cause, often sarcastically: {Thanks to the rain, the picnic was ruined}. {No thanks to you} emphasizes someone's lack of help.

Thankful describes feeling or expressing gratitude: {I'm thankful for my health}, {thankful to be alive}. The word often appears around Thanksgiving, when people enumerate blessings. Thankful emphasizes the emotional state of gratitude, while grateful tends toward the response or action that follows: you feel thankful, then act grateful.

Thankless describes tasks or roles that earn no gratitude despite effort: {a thankless job}, {the thankless work of organizing volunteers}. The word implies that appreciation is deserved but withheld. Less commonly, thankless describes a person who fails to show gratitude—ungrateful: {a thankless child}.

Thanks is an expression of gratitude, a casual alternative to "thank you": {Thanks for the ride}, {Thanks, I appreciate it}. The noun form refers to gratitude itself: {She expressed her thanks}. {Thanks to} attributes cause, often sarcastically: {Thanks to you, we missed the train}. {No thanks} declines an offer: {Coffee? No thanks}.

Thanksgiving is the expression of gratitude, especially to God: {a prayer of thanksgiving}, {a thanksgiving service}. The word emphasizes the act of giving thanks rather than simply feeling grateful. {They offered thanksgiving for the safe return of their loved ones.} (Capitalized Thanksgiving is the American and Canadian holiday.)

Thatch is a roof covering made of straw, reeds, or similar plant material layered to shed water. Thatched cottages evoke rural England and preindustrial life. The word extends to any thick, matted covering resembling such a roof: {a thatch of unruly hair}. To thatch is to apply or make such a covering.

Thaw is the process of frozen things becoming unfrozen—ice melting, ground softening, food warming to usable temperature. A spring thaw ends winter's grip. To thaw meat is to bring it from frozen to workable: {Let the chicken thaw overnight in the fridge}. Figuratively, thaw describes warming relations or softening attitudes: {Relations between the two countries began to thaw}. A person who thaws becomes friendlier after initial coldness.

Thawing is the process of warming something frozen until it softens or liquefies. Frozen food thaws before cooking; ice thaws in spring. The word extends to emotional warming: {Relations between the two countries are finally thawing}. A thawing period follows prolonged coldness, whether of temperature or temperament.

Theater is a building where performances are staged or films are shown. More broadly, theater is the art form itself—dramatic performance as a medium: {She studied theater in college}. A theater of war or operations is a region where military action occurs. Theatrics or theatrical behavior treats real life as if it were a stage performance: {His resignation speech was pure theater}.

Theaters are buildings designed for performances—plays, musicals, operas, and other live entertainment. The word extends to movie theaters, where films are shown. Theater also names the art form itself: {She studied theater in college}. A theater of war is a region where military operations occur. In British English, spelled theatre.

Theatre is the British spelling of theater—the art form of staged dramatic performance, or the building where such performances occur. Both spellings work for all senses: a theatre of war, a surgical theatre, theatrical behavior. American English strongly prefers theater; British English uses theatre almost exclusively.

Theatres is the British spelling of theaters—buildings where plays, films, or other performances take place. The word covers everything from grand Victorian playhouses to small cinema screens. Theatre also means the art form itself: {She's devoted her life to the theatre}. A theatre of war is a region where military operations occur. In medicine, an operating theatre is where surgeries are performed.

Theatrical describes what relates to theater or dramatic performance: {theatrical productions}, {theatrical lighting}. More often, it characterizes behavior that seems exaggerated or designed for effect—dramatic in a way that feels performed rather than genuine: {She made a theatrical sigh}. The word can be neutral or critical depending on context. As a noun, theatricals are dramatic performances or, dismissively, overdone displays of emotion.

Theatricality is the quality of being theatrical—dramatic, exaggerated, or designed for effect. The term can be neutral when describing stage performance: {The production embraced its theatricality}. More often it carries a whiff of criticism, suggesting behavior that feels staged or overwrought: {His theatricality made it hard to take his apology seriously}.

Theatrics are dramatic, exaggerated behaviors designed to attract attention or create an emotional effect. The word usually carries a dismissive tone—suggesting the display is excessive or insincere: {Save the theatrics for someone who cares}. Less commonly, theatrics refers neutrally to theatrical techniques or stagecraft: {The play's theatrics were impressive}.

Theft is the act of taking someone else's property without permission or legal right, intending to keep it permanently. The word covers everything from shoplifting to embezzling millions: {He was charged with theft}. Identity theft involves stealing personal information to commit fraud. Unlike robbery, theft doesn't require force or confrontation—it can happen without the victim knowing.

Them is the objective form of they. You use it to refer to two or more people that you have already named so that you don’t have to repeat their name or names: Please give this to Todd and Kim when you see them.

A theme is any identifiable characteristic that can be observed throughout something. A musical theme, for example, might occur multiple times in a work of many movements. A theme can also be a main idea, or an idea closely associated with someone or something: She repeatedly emphasized the themes of dedication and hard work to bring good results. When theme precedes a noun, it is usually to identify something as having an obvious motif, as in a theme party or a theme restaurant. As a verb, theme means provide an ambience to.

Themes are the central ideas or subjects running through a work—the underlying meanings a story, film, or piece of music explores: {The novel's themes include loss and redemption}. In computing, a theme is a preset visual style: {I changed my phone's theme to dark mode}. Theme also works as a verb: {a Vegas casino themed around ancient Egypt}.

A theocracy is a government in which religious authorities hold political power, or in which the state claims to govern according to divine law. The clergy may rule directly, or secular leaders may derive their authority from religious sanction: {Iran is often described as a theocracy}. The term sometimes describes any society where religion dominates public life: {Critics warned the country was sliding toward theocracy}.

Theology is the study of God, gods, or religious belief—the systematic examination of divine nature, religious doctrines, and spiritual questions. Someone studying theology might analyze scripture, debate the problem of evil, or compare how different traditions understand salvation. The word often implies Christian thought specifically, though it applies to any religion's intellectual tradition: {Islamic theology}, {Hindu theology}. A theology can also mean a particular system of religious beliefs: {liberation theology}, {process theology}.

Theoretical concerns ideas, concepts, and abstract reasoning rather than practical application or direct experience. A theoretical physicist works with mathematical models; a theoretical possibility exists in principle but may never occur. The word often implies a gap between thought and reality: {That sounds good in theory, but will it work?} Theoretical knowledge comes from study and reasoning; practical knowledge comes from doing.

Theories is the plural of theory. A theory is an explanation for how or why something works—a framework of ideas meant to account for observed facts. In science, a theory is well-tested and widely accepted: {the theory of evolution}, {quantum theory}. In everyday speech, theory often means speculation or guess: {I have a theory about why she left}. {In theory} means according to principle, if not always in practice.

A theory is an idea that is proposed to explain something. A theory can be very simple (My theory is that she decided to leave him a long time ago) or extremely complex—like the theory of quantum mechanics. In science, researchers propose a theory and then devise experiments that will prove the theory is correct (that it explains the phenomenon), incorrect (fails to explain what happens experimentally), or occasionally incomplete (explains some aspects satisfactorily, but not others).

Therapeutic describes something that heals or promotes health and wellbeing. Medical treatments are therapeutic, but so are activities that restore mental or emotional balance: {I find gardening therapeutic}. A therapeutic conversation helps someone process difficult feelings. The word often implies relief or restoration rather than cure—something that makes you feel better even if it doesn't fix the underlying problem.

A therapist is a person trained to treat physical or mental conditions. Physical therapists work with the body—restoring movement, reducing pain. Psychotherapists and talk therapists treat mental and emotional issues through conversation rather than medication: {I've been seeing a therapist for my anxiety}. The word often stands alone for the psychological kind: {My therapist says I need better boundaries}.

Therapy is treatment intended to heal or relieve a condition, especially through non-surgical means. Physical therapy restores movement after injury. Radiation therapy targets cancer cells. Used alone, therapy often means psychotherapy—talk-based treatment for mental or emotional problems: {I've been in therapy for years}. {She started therapy after the divorce}. Therapeutic describes anything with healing properties or effects.

While it shares pronunciation with another high-frequency word (their), there is so distinct from its sound-alike that even a computer program can pinpoint errors. There can function as four or five parts of speech but it does most of its work as an adverb. Its easiest job is to be the counterpart of here for things that are more remote in space or time from the speaker. Its more sophisticated role is to introduce a sentence that tells you whether or not something exists or is available: There’s a supermarket just around the corner. There isn’t any soup left. As an interjection, the meaning of there depends on context but usually suggests an idea of finality: There! I finally finished my paper. There, there, that’s enough.

Thermals are columns of rising warm air that birds and gliders use to gain altitude without expending energy. Pilots and hawks circle within thermals to climb. The word also refers to thermal underwear—insulating garments worn in cold weather: {I packed thermals for the ski trip}. Both senses connect to heat retention or movement.

A thermometer is an instrument for measuring temperature. The familiar kind uses liquid—mercury or alcohol—that rises or falls in a glass tube marked with a scale. Digital thermometers have largely replaced these in medical and household use. {The thermometer read 102 degrees.}

A thermos is an insulated container that keeps beverages hot or cold for extended periods. The double-walled vacuum design prevents heat transfer, making it useful for coffee, soup, or cold drinks: {She packed a thermos of hot cocoa for the hike}. Originally a trademark, the word has become generic for any vacuum flask. (Capitalized Thermos is the brand name.)

A thermostat is a device that automatically regulates temperature by switching heating or cooling systems on and off. Most thermostats let you set a target temperature: {Set the thermostat to 68}. Programmable thermostats adjust temperatures on a schedule. Figuratively, anything that maintains equilibrium might be called a thermostat: {The Federal Reserve acts as a thermostat for the economy}.

A thesaurus is a word reference book that groups words according to their semantic relations. The most common relation, and the one for which people often consult a thesaurus, is synonymy: words that share a similar meaning, sometimes representing various parts of speech, are grouped together in a thesaurus. Other relations that may be discoverable in a thesaurus include antonymy (opposites), hypernymy and hyponymy (relations between more general and more specific words), and meronymy (relations of parts to wholes).

A thesis is a proposition put forward for consideration or proof. In academic contexts, a thesis is a substantial research paper required for a degree—especially the extended work submitted for a doctorate. The thesis of an essay or argument is its central claim: {Her thesis is that economic factors drove the revolution}. In classical rhetoric and music, thesis also refers to the stressed or downbeat position.

You use they to designate multiple people or things that you have already referred to with a noun or nouns: The students wrote reports about the field trip they went on. In modern speech, they is also often used to refer back to an indefinite singular pronoun such as whoever, someone, or anybody to avoid the problem of appearing to be sexist by using he or she, and to avoid the awkwardness of using he/she: If anyone wants the extra tickets they should call me.

Thick, mainly an adjective, characterizes a dimension from side to side or front to back. A thick book has many pages. After a unit of measure, thick typically specifies a dimension through something solid (walls 15 inches thick). Abstract things described as thick are hard to understand. People described as thick are being called stupid. If air is thick, it is not fresh and may be polluted with something. Generally, thick characterizes abundance and density (thick hair, thick fog, thick forest).

Thicken means to make or become thicker—more dense, more viscous, or less transparent. You thicken gravy with flour. Fog thickens as visibility drops. A plot thickens when complications arise and things get more interesting: {The plot thickens—now her ex-husband is involved}.

A thicket is a dense growth of shrubs, bushes, or small trees—vegetation too tangled to walk through easily. The word extends to any dense tangle: {a thicket of regulations}, {a thicket of legal complications}. Something described as a thicket is difficult to navigate or sort through.

A thief is someone who steals—takes property belonging to others without permission. The word covers everything from petty shoplifters to professional burglars: {The thief made off with her purse}. Figuratively, anything that deprives you of something valuable: {Time is a thief}. Plural: thieves.

Thieves is the plural of thief—people who steal. The word appears in contexts ranging from petty crime to organized robbery: {Thieves broke into the warehouse overnight}. The phrase {thick as thieves} describes people who are very close or conspiratorial, like partners in crime sharing secrets.

The thigh is the upper part of the leg, between the hip and the knee. It contains the body's largest bone (the femur) and some of its most powerful muscles. Thighs appear in cooking as cuts of poultry: {chicken thighs}, {turkey thighs}. The word carries mild erotic charge when referring to human anatomy: {her bare thighs}.

Thighs are the upper portions of the legs, between the hip and the knee. They contain the body's largest muscles and are associated with strength and power in athletics. In cooking, chicken thighs are prized as darker, more flavorful meat than breast portions. The thigh also carries erotic connotations given its proximity to the genitals; showing too much thigh has historically been considered immodest. {She felt the burn in her thighs after climbing the stairs.}

A thimble is a small protective cap worn on the fingertip when sewing, preventing the needle from pricking the skin as you push it through fabric. Thimbles are typically made of metal, plastic, or leather. The word extends to any small cup-shaped fitting, such as a metal ring used in rigging to protect rope from chafing.

Thin, mainly an adjective, is the opposite of thick but it does not have the dimension-specifying functions that thick has. Things that are thin have a narrow or scant dimension from top to bottom, front to back, or side to side (thin layer of snow). Thin air is air at a high altitude, except in the expression out of thin air (where it is meaningless). To thin something is to dilute it, or reduce its density or dimensions.

Thing is the most general singular noun in English; it rarely refers to people but it can refer to any other object, abstraction, matter, case, situation, quality, or characteristic that can also be designated with a noun. In the plural, thing can refer to circumstances in general or to a situation that has been indicated otherwise: How are things? Aunt Nell is trying to get things settled with Uncle Frank’s estate.

A thingamabob is a thing whose name you don't know or can't recall: {Hand me that thingamabob over there}. It belongs to a family of placeholder words—thingamajig, whatchamacallit, doohickey—used when pointing or context makes the referent clear enough. The word sounds playful and slightly old-fashioned.

Thingamajig is a placeholder name for something whose actual name you can't recall or don't know: {Hand me that thingamajig over there}. It belongs to a family of similar nonsense words—thingamabob, whatchamacallit, doohickey—all serving the same function of pointing at an object while admitting you've forgotten what it's called.

Thingamajigs are objects whose names you can't recall or don't know. The word is a playful placeholder, interchangeable with thingamabob, whatchamacallit, or doohickey: {Hand me that thingamajig over there}. It typically refers to small mechanical parts or gadgets whose proper names escape you in the moment.

Thingamebob is a placeholder word for an object whose name you can't recall or don't know: {Hand me that thingamebob over there}. It belongs to a family of similar terms—thingamajig, whatchamacallit, doohickey—all serving the same purpose of filling in when the real word escapes you.

Thingamejig is a placeholder word for something whose name you can't recall or don't know: {Hand me that thingamejig over there}. It belongs to a family of similar terms—thingamabob, whatchamacallit, doohickey—all serving the same purpose of naming the unnamed. The word sounds playful and informal, often accompanied by vague pointing.

Things is the most general noun in English for referring to objects, matters, or circumstances. It can mean physical objects {(Put your things away)}, situations {(Things are getting complicated)}, actions {(I have things to do)}, or abstract matters {(Let me explain a few things)}. The word's vagueness makes it useful when precision isn't needed or possible: {One thing led to another}. Your things are your belongings. {The thing is} introduces an explanation or excuse. To {do your own thing} is to act independently.

Thingy is a placeholder word for something whose name you can't recall or don't bother to specify: {Hand me that thingy over there}, {The thingy on the car is broken}. It's casual and vague, often accompanied by pointing or gesturing. Variants include thingamajig, thingamabob, and whatchamacallit.

It’s all in your mind. Some meanings of think relate to the actual activity of thinking (I’ve thought long and hard about climate change), and others to the products of thinking, such as opinions: I think we should find more alternative fuels. You can also express a plan or intention with think (I think I’ll stay in tonight). Phrasal verbs that use think, such as think up and think through, also refer to mental activity.

A thinker is someone who thinks deeply or carefully, especially about abstract or philosophical matters. The term often implies intellectual seriousness: {one of the great thinkers of the Enlightenment}. More loosely, it describes anyone given to reflection rather than impulse: {She's a thinker, not a doer}.

Thinking is the mental activity of reasoning, considering, or reflecting. It can describe careful thought: {After much thinking, she decided to accept the job}. As an adjective, thinking suggests someone inclined to reason rather than react: {Any thinking person would question that claim}. To put on your {thinking cap} is to concentrate on solving a problem.

Third indicates position three in a sequence—after first and second: {She finished third in the race}. A third is one of three equal parts: {A third of the budget goes to salaries}. In music, a third is an interval spanning three scale degrees. To third something online is to add agreement after someone has already seconded it.

Thirst is the bodily sensation that signals a need for water or other fluids, and by extension, the act of experiencing that sensation: {I worked up a thirst mowing the lawn}. The word extends naturally to any strong desire or craving: a thirst for {knowledge}, a thirst for {revenge}. In contemporary slang, thirst describes obvious or desperate romantic or sexual interest, often displayed publicly on social media. Someone exhibiting such behavior is called thirsty.

Thirsty describes the sensation of needing liquid—the body's signal that it wants water. Extended uses follow naturally: thirsty {soil} absorbs moisture readily; a thirsty {plant} needs watering. To be thirsty for something is to crave it intensely: {thirsty for knowledge}, {thirsty for revenge}. In recent slang, thirsty describes someone who seems desperate for attention or validation, especially romantic or sexual: {He's so thirsty—he comments on all her posts}.

Thirteen is the cardinal number between twelve and fourteen, represented as 13. It holds superstitious significance in Western culture as an unlucky number—hence {Friday the thirteenth}, triskaidekaphobia (fear of thirteen), and buildings that skip from floor 12 to 14. A {baker's dozen} is thirteen, one extra to avoid shortchanging customers.

The thirties are the years from 30 to 39 in a century or a life. {The Great Depression defined the thirties}. Someone in their thirties is between 30 and 39 years old: {She started her business in her early thirties}. The thirties can also refer to temperatures in that range: {Overnight lows will dip into the thirties}.

Thirty is the cardinal number between twenty-nine and thirty-one, equal to three times ten. It often marks a threshold in age or experience: {She's in her thirties}, {over thirty}. In journalism, the symbol "–30–" traditionally signals the end of a story or article.

A thistle is a prickly plant with spiny leaves and purple or pink flower heads, often considered a weed. Thistles grow wild in fields and roadsides across temperate regions. The plant is the national emblem of Scotland. {The field was overrun with thistles.} Thistledown—the fluffy seeds—drifts on the wind.

A thong is a narrow strip of leather or other material, used for fastening or as a lash. The word extends to minimal footwear held on by a strap between the toes—called flip-flops in American English but thongs in Australian. A thong is also underwear or a swimsuit bottom with a narrow back strip that leaves the buttocks exposed: {She wore a thong bikini to the beach}.

Thongs are thin strips of leather or other material used for fastening or as lashes. The word also names two types of footwear and underwear that share a design element: a strap passing between two parts. Thong sandals (flip-flops) have a strap between the big toe and second toe. Thong underwear has a narrow strip of fabric passing between the buttocks: {She wore a thong under the tight dress}.

A thorn is a sharp, pointed projection on a plant stem—a defense against animals that might eat it. Roses, hawthorns, and blackberries bear thorns. Figuratively, a thorn is a persistent source of irritation: {a thorn in my side}. To be {on thorns} is to be anxious or uneasy. A crown of thorns refers to Christ's suffering, and by extension, any painful burden.

Thorns are sharp, woody projections on plant stems—nature's defense against browsing animals. Roses, hawthorns, and blackberries bear thorns. Figuratively, a thorn is a persistent source of irritation: {a thorn in my side}. The phrase {crown of thorns} refers to Christ's crucifixion and, by extension, any painful burden one must bear.

Thorny describes something covered with thorns or sharp projections: {a thorny bush}, {thorny brambles}. The figurative sense dominates in everyday use—a thorny problem or thorny issue is difficult and contentious, full of complications that make it painful to handle: {The committee avoided the thorny question of budget cuts}.

Thorough means complete and careful, with attention to every detail. A thorough {investigation} examines all evidence. A thorough {cleaning} reaches every corner. The word implies not just completion but conscientiousness—doing something thoroughly means doing it right, leaving nothing overlooked or half-done.

A thoroughbred is an animal bred from pure stock, especially a horse of a breed developed for racing. The word suggests superior lineage and quality: {a thoroughbred Arabian}. Figuratively, thoroughbred describes anything of exceptional pedigree or refinement: {a thoroughbred athlete}, {a thoroughbred institution}. As an adjective, it means purebred or first-rate.

Thoroughbreds are horses of a breed developed for racing, known for speed, agility, and spirited temperament. The breed originated in 17th-century England from Arabian stallions crossed with English mares. Extended to mean purebred animals generally, or figuratively, people of exceptional quality or breeding: {She surrounded herself with thoroughbreds—the best minds in the field}.

Thought is mental activity—the process of thinking or what results from it. A thought is an idea, notion, or reflection: {I had a thought about your proposal}. Thought also means consideration: {Give it some thought}. The plural thoughts often means opinions: {What are your thoughts on this?} Thought can suggest intention: {I had no thought of offending you}. Deep in thought describes concentrated mental focus.

Thoughtcrime is holding opinions or beliefs that authority considers unacceptable—crime committed in the mind rather than through action. The term comes from George Orwell's *1984*, where the totalitarian state punishes citizens for private thoughts. Now used to criticize perceived overreach in policing ideas: {Disagreeing with the policy shouldn't be a thoughtcrime}.

Thoughtcrimes are beliefs or opinions treated as punishable offenses—the idea that wrong thinking itself is criminal. The term comes from George Orwell's *1984*, where the totalitarian state prosecutes citizens for unapproved thoughts. Now used critically to describe perceived overreach in policing speech or belief: {Disagreeing with the official narrative has become a thoughtcrime}. Often invoked sarcastically against cancel culture or ideological conformity.

Thoughtful describes someone who considers others' feelings and needs: {It was thoughtful of you to call}. The word also means showing careful consideration or reflection: {a thoughtful essay}, {a thoughtful pause before answering}. A thoughtful expression suggests someone lost in thought. The two senses—considerate toward others and engaged in thinking—often overlap.

Thoughtfulness is the quality of considering others' feelings and needs. A thoughtful person remembers details, anticipates what might help, and acts with care: {Her thoughtfulness in bringing soup when I was sick meant everything}. The word also describes careful, reflective thinking: {The essay showed real thoughtfulness about the problem}. Both senses share attention directed outward—toward people or ideas—rather than hasty self-concern.

Thoughtless describes acting without consideration for others or without thinking ahead. A thoughtless remark hurts someone's feelings unintentionally. A thoughtless decision ignores consequences. The word implies carelessness rather than malice—the person simply didn't pause to think: {It was thoughtless of me not to call}. Thoughtless can also mean empty-headed or vacuous, though this sense is less common.

Thoughts are mental processes—ideas, reflections, or considerations that arise in the mind. The word often implies quiet contemplation: {lost in thought}, {I'll give it some thought}. To {have second thoughts} is to reconsider. To {collect your thoughts} is to organize what you want to say. {A penny for your thoughts} invites someone to share what's on their mind.

A thousand is the number 1,000—ten hundreds or 10³. Beyond counting, thousand often suggests a large but vague quantity: {I've told you a thousand times}. The plural thousands emphasizes magnitude: {Thousands gathered in the square}. As an adjective: {a thousand reasons to stay}.

Thrash means to beat violently or flail about. You might thrash grain to separate it from chaff, thrash an opponent in competition, or thrash around in bed during a nightmare. To {thrash out} a problem is to work through it vigorously until resolved. Thrash is also a fast, aggressive style of heavy metal music characterized by rapid tempos and intense guitar work.

Thrashed is the past tense of thrash, which means to beat violently or move wildly: {The fish thrashed in the net}. To thrash someone in competition is to defeat them decisively: {We got thrashed 7-0}. To {thrash out} a problem is to discuss it thoroughly until reaching resolution. In computing, thrashing describes a system stuck in inefficient cycles, spending more time managing memory than doing useful work.

Thrashing is a severe beating or defeat: {The team took a thrashing in the playoffs}. It also describes violent, uncontrolled movement—a person thrashing in their sleep, a fish thrashing on the deck. In computing, thrashing is when a system spends more time swapping data between memory levels than doing useful work, grinding productivity to a halt.

Thread is a thin strand of material—cotton, silk, or synthetic fiber—used for sewing or weaving. The concept extends to anything long and slender: a thread of {smoke}, a thread of {light}. A thread of conversation or argument is a continuous line of thought running through it. In computing, a thread is a sequence of linked messages in a forum or email chain, or a unit of program execution. To thread is to pass something through a narrow opening: {thread a needle}, {thread your way through the crowd}.

Threadbare describes fabric worn so thin that the threads show through: {a threadbare carpet}, {threadbare jeans}. The word extends to anything overused or exhausted—a threadbare excuse has lost its power through repetition, a threadbare argument no longer convinces. {The same threadbare promises every election cycle.}

Threads are long, thin strands used for sewing or weaving—the basic units of fabric. The word extends to anything similarly thin and continuous: {a thread of smoke}, {threads of a conversation}. To thread is to pass something through a narrow opening: {thread a needle}, {thread your way through a crowd}. In computing, a thread is a sequence of linked messages or a unit of program execution. Slang uses threads to mean clothes: {Nice threads}. (Capitalized Threads is the social media platform.)

A threat is a declaration of intent to harm or punish: {Is that a threat?} It also means anything that poses danger or risk: {the threat of nuclear war}, {a threat to public safety}. Someone or something described as a threat has the potential to cause harm: {He's no threat to anyone}. In sports, a {triple threat} can hurt you multiple ways.

To threaten is to express intention to harm or punish: {He threatened to fire anyone who spoke to the press}. The harm need not be stated explicitly—a threatening gesture or tone conveys menace. Things that threaten pose potential danger: {Rising waters threaten the town}. A threatened species faces possible extinction. Something threatening feels ominous or dangerous: {threatening clouds gathered on the horizon}.

Threatened describes someone or something facing danger or harm. A person may feel threatened by aggression, competition, or challenge to their status: {He felt threatened by her success}. Species are threatened when their populations decline toward extinction—a formal conservation category between vulnerable and endangered. To be threatened is also to have received a threat: {The witness was threatened into silence}.

Threatening describes something that suggests danger, harm, or hostile intent. A threatening {gesture} implies violence. Threatening {skies} promise a storm. A threatening {letter} warns of consequences. The word captures both direct menace—{He made threatening remarks}—and ominous atmosphere, where harm feels imminent even without explicit declaration.

Threats are expressions of intent to cause harm, damage, or punishment if certain conditions aren't met. A threat can be verbal, written, or implied through action: {He made threats against his former employer}. Beyond interpersonal conflict, threat extends to any source of potential danger or harm: {Climate change poses a serious threat to coastal cities}. Something described as a threat may not have made explicit hostile statements but simply represents a risk or challenge to safety, stability, or success.

Three is the cardinal number between two and four, represented by the numeral 3. It appears throughout language in set phrases: {three strikes and you're out}, {third time's the charm}, {good things come in threes}. Three often suggests completeness or pattern—beginning, middle, and end; small, medium, and large. {We have three kids.}

A threesome is a group of three, especially three people engaged in an activity together. The word most commonly refers to sex involving three participants: {They had a threesome}. In golf, a threesome is a group of three players. The word can describe any trio but carries strong sexual connotations in casual use.

A threshold is the strip of wood or stone at the bottom of a doorway—the boundary you cross when entering. From this concrete sense comes the figurative: a threshold is any point of transition or beginning. The {threshold of adulthood}, the {threshold of war}. In technical use, a threshold is the level at which something begins to happen or take effect: {pain threshold}, {tax threshold}, {The noise exceeded the threshold for hearing damage}.

Thresholds is the plural of threshold—the strip of wood or stone at the bottom of a doorway, or more figuratively, a point of entry or beginning: {on the threshold of a new era}. A threshold also marks a boundary where something changes or takes effect: {pain threshold}, {tax threshold}. In science and engineering, thresholds indicate critical values that trigger responses: {The sensor activates when temperature crosses certain thresholds}.

Threw is the past tense of throw. To throw is to propel something through the air with a motion of the arm: {She threw the ball to first base}. Extended uses follow: throwing a party means hosting one, throwing a punch means delivering it, throwing someone off means confusing them. {He threw on his coat and left.}

Thrift is the habit of spending money carefully and avoiding waste. Someone with thrift stretches resources, saves rather than splurges, and finds value in frugality: {Her Depression-era thrift never left her}. A thrift or thrift store sells secondhand goods cheaply: {I found this jacket at a thrift shop for five dollars}.

Thrifting is shopping at thrift stores, secondhand shops, or consignment stores for used clothing, furniture, or household items. The appeal combines bargain-hunting with treasure-hunting—finding quality pieces at low prices: {I spent Saturday thrifting and found a vintage leather jacket for twelve dollars}. The practice has shed its stigma and become fashionable, especially among younger consumers drawn to sustainability and unique style.

A thriftshop is a store selling secondhand goods, typically clothing, furniture, and household items, often run by charitable organizations. Prices are low because inventory comes from donations. Also spelled as two words: thrift shop. {I found a vintage leather jacket at the thriftshop for twelve dollars.}

Thrifty means careful with money and resources, avoiding waste. A thrifty person clips coupons, repairs rather than replaces, and saves for the future. The word carries approval—unlike cheap or stingy, thrifty suggests wisdom rather than miserliness: {My grandmother was thrifty enough to put three kids through college on a teacher's salary}.

A thrill is a sudden wave of excitement or emotion—pleasure, fear, or anticipation: {the thrill of victory}, {a thrill of terror ran through her}. To thrill is to cause this sensation: {The performance thrilled the audience}. A thriller is a suspenseful story designed to produce such feelings. Something thrilling excites intensely: {a thrilling finish to the game}.

Thrilled means extremely pleased or excited, suggesting a rush of emotion: {I'm thrilled you could make it}, {She was thrilled with the results}. The word implies delight that goes beyond ordinary happiness—a physical sensation of excitement. The older sense of thrill as a shiver or tremor of emotion survives in this intensified pleasure.

A thriller is a story, film, or other work designed to create suspense, excitement, and tension. The genre typically involves danger, pursuit, or intrigue—spy thrillers, psychological thrillers, legal thrillers. The term also applies to anything intensely exciting: {The game was a real thriller, decided in the final seconds}. Michael Jackson's 1982 album and its iconic music video made Thriller a cultural touchstone. (Capitalized Thriller typically refers to the Jackson album.)

Thrillers are novels, films, or other narratives designed to create suspense and excitement. The genre emphasizes tension, danger, and plot twists—keeping audiences on edge about what happens next. Thrillers often involve crime, espionage, or pursuit: {She reads legal thrillers}, {a psychological thriller about a stalker}. The category overlaps with mystery and horror but prioritizes sustained tension over puzzle-solving or fear.

Thrilling describes something that produces a sudden, intense wave of excitement or emotion—a physical sensation that seems to shoot through you. A thrilling {movie}, a thrilling {finish}, a thrilling {discovery}. The word suggests being stirred deeply, often with an element of suspense or danger: {It was thrilling to watch her cross the high wire}.

Thrills are intense feelings of excitement or pleasure—the rush you get from a roller coaster, a close game, or a narrow escape. The word works as both noun and verb: a movie {thrills} audiences, or audiences seek {thrills}. A thriller is a suspenseful story designed to produce this effect. {Thrill-seekers} chase experiences that deliver the sensation reliably.

A thrillseeker is someone who pursues excitement through risky or intense activities—skydiving, bungee jumping, extreme sports. The term carries mild judgment, suggesting recklessness or addiction to adrenaline: {He's always been a thrillseeker, never happy unless he's in danger}. Also spelled thrill-seeker.

Thrive means to grow vigorously, flourish, or prosper. Plants thrive in good soil; businesses thrive in favorable markets; children thrive with attention and care. The word suggests not merely surviving but doing exceptionally well: {She thrives under pressure}. Some people or things thrive on what would harm others: {He thrives on chaos}.

Thriving describes a state of vigorous growth, prosperity, or flourishing. A thriving business is succeeding and expanding. A thriving community buzzes with activity and wellbeing. Plants thrive in good soil; people thrive when conditions support their growth: {The kids are thriving at their new school}. To thrive is more than surviving—it implies abundant health or success.

The throat is the passage from the mouth to the stomach and lungs, including the pharynx and larynx. It's where swallowing and breathing happen, and where voice originates—hence {a singer with a beautiful throat}. Throat extends to narrow passages generally: the throat of a bottle, a cave, a funnel. To {cut your own throat} is to act against your interests. To {ram something down someone's throat} is to force acceptance of it.

Throb is a strong, rhythmic pulsation—the kind you feel in your heartbeat or a wound. Pain throbs when it beats in waves: {My head was throbbing}. Engines and music throb with a deep, steady beat. As a noun, a throb is one such pulse: {the throb of the bass}, {a throb of desire}. The word suggests intensity that rises and falls but doesn't stop.

Throbbing describes a rhythmic, pulsing sensation—typically pain that beats in time with the heartbeat: {a throbbing headache}, {My thumb was throbbing where I'd hit it with the hammer}. The word extends to any strong, pulsating quality: {throbbing bass}, {throbbing desire}. As a noun, throbbing is the sensation itself: {I could feel the throbbing in my temples}.

Throbs is the verb form of throb—to pulse or beat with a strong, rhythmic motion. A heart throbs, a wound throbs with pain, music throbs through speakers. The noun throb is a single pulse or beat: {the throb of the engine}, {a throb of desire}. Throb often carries erotic undertones, especially in romance writing: {Her heart throbbed when he entered the room}.

A throne is a ceremonial chair for a monarch or other dignitary, typically ornate and elevated. By extension, throne refers to royal power itself: {The king ascended the throne at age twelve}. To be {on the throne} is to reign. In casual speech, throne is a joking term for a toilet: {He's on the throne}.

Thrones is the plural of throne—a ceremonial chair for a monarch or deity, and by extension, royal power itself: {The prince was next in line for the throne}. In Christian angelology, Thrones are an order of angels. Informally, the throne is a toilet: {He sat on the porcelain throne reading the newspaper}.

Throttle is a device that controls fuel or airflow to an engine, regulating speed and power. To throttle an engine is to adjust this control—{throttle up} to accelerate, {throttle back} to slow down. Throttle also means to choke or strangle someone by squeezing the throat: {He throttled his attacker}. Extended uses describe suppression or restriction: {The government throttled dissent}. Internet providers throttle bandwidth by deliberately slowing connection speeds.

Through‘s core idea involves space combined with movement from one side to another: Did you come through Durango to get here? Through applies metaphorically to time in the same way: All through my childhood I had allergies. Through also indicates the means or agency by which something is done or happens: Through the management’s neglect, the company ended up in bankruptcy. Anyone or anything that completes a process can be said to go through it: The circuit boards pass through hundreds of stages of production.

Throw is mainly a transitive verb for the action of causing an object to move through the air (throw a rock, throw a ball, throw a pass). If you throw a party, you host it. If you throw a fit or tantrum, you indulge in one. If you throw a punch, you deliver a blow. A throw is an instance or the event of throwing, like a free throw in basketball or the javelin throw at a track meet. A throw is also a smallish blanket that is laid over furniture.

Throwaway describes something meant to be discarded after use: a throwaway {camera}, throwaway {razors}. It extends to remarks made casually without much thought: {a throwaway comment that ended up causing controversy}. As a noun, a throwaway is a disposable item, a flyer or handbill, or—in internet slang—an anonymous account created for a single purpose: {I posted from a throwaway so it couldn't be traced back to me}.

A throwback is something that recalls or resembles an earlier time or type. A person with old-fashioned qualities might be called {a throwback to another era}. In biology, a throwback is an organism showing ancestral traits. On social media, throwback labels nostalgic posts, especially photos from one's past: {Throwback Thursday}, {throwback to summer 2019}.

Throwbacks are things that recall or resemble something from an earlier time. A throwback can be a person whose traits seem to belong to a previous generation, a style that evokes a past era, or a genetic reversion to ancestral characteristics. The word often carries nostalgic appeal: {Thursday's throwback jerseys honored the team's 1970s uniforms}. On social media, {Throwback Thursday} invites posting old photos.

A throwdown is a fight, confrontation, or intense competition—often physical but sometimes verbal or artistic. The word suggests a challenge that's been accepted: {There was a throwdown in the parking lot after the game}. In cooking contexts, a throwdown is a competitive cooking challenge: {Bobby Flay's famous throwdowns}. The verb phrase throw down means to issue or accept such a challenge.

Throwing is the act of propelling something through the air with a motion of the arm: {He's been throwing darts all evening}. Beyond physical objects, throwing extends to abstract projections—throwing a {glance}, throwing {shade}, throwing a {party}. To throw oneself into something is to engage with full commitment. Throwing a game or match means losing deliberately.

Thrown is the past participle of throw. Something thrown has been propelled through the air: {a thrown ball}, {a thrown punch}. A thrown rider has been unseated by a horse. A thrown pot has been shaped on a potter's wheel. If you're thrown by something, you're confused or disconcerted: {I was completely thrown by her question}.

Thrust is forceful forward movement or the force that produces it. A rocket's thrust propels it upward; a sword thrust aims to pierce. To thrust is to push with sudden force: {She thrust the letter into his hands}. The thrust of an argument is its central point or driving idea. In fencing, thrust distinguishes a stabbing motion from a cut or slash.

Thrusts is the plural noun and third-person singular verb form of thrust. A thrust is a forceful push or stab, whether physical {the thrust of a sword} or metaphorical {the main thrust of her argument}. The verb describes pushing something forward with sudden force, often with aggressive or sexual connotations. In engineering and physics, thrust refers specifically to the propulsive force generated by an engine or rocket. {The spacecraft's thrusts were precisely timed for orbital insertion.}

Thud is a dull, heavy sound—the kind made when something solid hits a surface without much bounce or resonance: {The book fell to the floor with a thud}. As a verb, to thud is to make or move with such a sound: {Her heart thudded in her chest}. The word itself sounds like what it describes.

A thug is a violent criminal or ruffian—someone who uses brutality and intimidation: {The thugs beat him and took his wallet}. The word often implies someone who does dirty work for others, like enforcers for organized crime. In hip-hop culture, thug was reclaimed as an identity of toughness and survival: {thug life}. The term can carry racial overtones when applied selectively to Black men.

Thugs are violent criminals or intimidating enforcers. The word often implies brutishness over sophistication—thugs use physical force rather than cunning: {The dictator sent his thugs to silence protesters}. In casual use, thug can describe anyone behaving aggressively or menacingly. The phrase {thug life} was popularized by hip-hop culture to describe survival through street toughness.

The thumb is the short, thick digit set apart from the four fingers of the human hand. Its opposability—the ability to touch each fingertip—distinguishes primate hands and enables gripping. To thumb is to turn pages with the thumb, or to hitchhike by signaling with an extended thumb. A {rule of thumb} is a rough practical guideline. To be {under someone's thumb} is to be controlled by them. {All thumbs} describes clumsiness.

A thumbnail is a small image serving as a preview of a larger one—the term comes from its roughly fingernail-sized scale. On websites and apps, thumbnails let users scan many images quickly before clicking to enlarge: {The video's thumbnail caught my eye}. As an adjective, thumbnail means brief or compressed: {a thumbnail sketch}, {a thumbnail biography}.

Thumbnails are small versions of larger images, used for quick browsing before selecting one to view at full size. The term comes from the fingernail of the thumb as a reference for something small. Photo libraries, video platforms, and file browsers display thumbnails so users can scan many images efficiently: {Click any thumbnail to enlarge}. A thumbnail sketch is a quick, rough drawing or summary.

Thumbs is the plural of thumb—the short, thick digit set apart from the other four fingers, enabling the human hand to grip and manipulate objects. To be {all thumbs} is to be clumsy. {Thumbs up} signals approval; {thumbs down} signals rejection, from the gestures Roman crowds allegedly used to decide gladiators' fates. To {twiddle your thumbs} is to wait idly. Someone {under your thumb} is under your control.

Thump is a dull, heavy sound—the kind made when something solid strikes something else without much resonance: {I heard a thump from upstairs}. As a verb, to thump is to strike with force or to make such a sound: {She thumped the table}, {His heart thumped in his chest}. A thumping can be a beating: {They gave him a good thumping}.

Thumping describes something that makes a heavy, dull, rhythmic sound, like a heartbeat or footsteps on stairs. As an adjective, it intensifies to mean impressively large or emphatic: a thumping {majority}, a thumping {headache}, a thumping {great lie}. This emphatic sense is more common in British English. The word can also function as a noun for the sound itself or the act of delivering blows: {The team took a thumping in the finals}.

Thumps is a respiratory condition in horses and other animals, characterized by spasmodic contractions of the diaphragm that produce a thumping sound and visible flank movement. It typically results from electrolyte imbalances after prolonged exertion. In casual use, thumps describes a pounding heartbeat or general sense of anxious agitation: {I had the thumps before my interview}.

Thunder is the loud rumbling or crashing sound that follows lightning, caused by the rapid expansion of air heated by the electrical discharge. By extension, any deep, resonant booming: {the thunder of hooves}, {thunderous applause}. To thunder is to produce such sound, or to speak forcefully: {He thundered his disapproval}. To {steal someone's thunder} is to preempt their moment of glory.

A thunderbird is a powerful spirit in the mythology of many Indigenous North American peoples, typically depicted as a giant bird that creates thunder with its wingbeats and lightning from its eyes. The image appears widely in Pacific Northwest art and totem poles. In automotive history, the Ford Thunderbird was a popular American car produced from 1955 to 2005. Thunderbird is also an email application developed by Mozilla. {The totem pole featured a thunderbird at the top.}

A thunderbolt is a flash of lightning conceived as a bolt or projectile hurled from the sky. In mythology, gods like Zeus and Thor wielded thunderbolts as weapons. The word now usually describes something sudden and shocking: {The news hit like a thunderbolt}. A person or thing that strikes with devastating speed and force can be called a thunderbolt: {He was a thunderbolt on the football field}. (Capitalized Thunderbolt is a brand name for high-speed data connections.)

Thunderbolts are bolts of lightning, especially when imagined as projectiles hurled from the sky. In mythology, gods like Zeus wielded thunderbolts as weapons. The word suggests sudden, devastating force: {The news hit like a thunderbolt}. A thunderbolt can be any shocking revelation or unexpected blow: {Her resignation came as a thunderbolt to the board}.

A thunderclap is a single crash of thunder—the sharp, loud sound that follows lightning. The word emphasizes suddenness and intensity: {The thunderclap made everyone jump}. Figuratively, anything shocking and unexpected can be a thunderclap: {The news hit like a thunderclap}.

Thunderclouds are the dark, towering clouds that produce thunderstorms—technically cumulonimbus clouds heavy with moisture and electrical charge. The word often appears figuratively for signs of impending trouble or anger: {Thunderclouds gathered on her face when she saw the mess}. A {thundercloud of controversy} suggests brewing conflict.

A thunderhead is a towering cumulonimbus cloud with a characteristic anvil-shaped top, signaling an approaching thunderstorm. The term captures both the cloud's dramatic vertical development and its association with violent weather—lightning, heavy rain, and strong winds. {Dark thunderheads gathered on the horizon.}

Thunderheads are towering cumulonimbus clouds that signal approaching thunderstorms. They rise dramatically with flat, anvil-shaped tops and dark bases, often bringing lightning, heavy rain, and sometimes hail. The term captures both their imposing appearance and their association with thunder: {Thunderheads were building on the horizon}.

Thunderous describes sounds that resemble thunder—deep, powerful, and reverberating: {thunderous applause}, {a thunderous boom}. The word emphasizes volume and force rather than mere loudness. A thunderous voice commands attention; thunderous hooves shake the ground. Figuratively, a thunderous expression suggests dark, stormy anger.

A thunderstorm is a storm with lightning, thunder, and usually heavy rain or hail. Thunderstorms form when warm, moist air rises rapidly and creates towering clouds. They range from brief afternoon disturbances to severe systems spawning tornadoes: {The thunderstorm knocked out power for hours}. {We watched the thunderstorm roll in from the west}.

Thunderstorms are storms characterized by lightning and thunder, typically accompanied by heavy rain, strong winds, and sometimes hail. They form when warm, moist air rises rapidly and condenses into cumulonimbus clouds. Thunderstorms range from brief afternoon showers to severe weather events capable of producing tornadoes. {The forecast calls for thunderstorms this evening.}

Thunderstruck means utterly astonished or stunned, as if struck by lightning. The word conveys sudden, overwhelming shock: {She stood thunderstruck when she saw the test results}. It suggests being frozen in place by the force of surprise, unable to react or respond.

Thunk is the past tense of think in nonstandard or dialectal speech: {Who'd have thunk it?} The phrase {who would have thunk} expresses ironic surprise at an obvious or predictable outcome. In computing, a thunk is a subroutine used to inject additional calculation into another subroutine—a piece of code that delays evaluation until needed. The programming sense comes from the sound of something landing, suggesting a chunk of code dropped into place.

Thwack is a sharp, resounding blow or the sound it makes—harder than a tap, flatter than a thud. The word imitates what it describes: {She thwacked the rug with a broom}. As a noun: {the thwack of a paddle against flesh}. It suggests satisfying impact, the kind you feel as much as hear.

To thwart is to prevent someone from accomplishing what they intend: {Her plans were thwarted by bad weather}. The word suggests frustration—not just failure but blocked effort. A thwart is also a seat running crosswise in a boat, from the word's older sense of lying across something.

Thwarted describes plans, efforts, or ambitions that have been blocked or frustrated. Someone whose attempt was thwarted didn't succeed because something or someone stood in the way: {Her thwarted ambitions left her bitter}. A thwarted person feels the frustration of being prevented from achieving what they wanted.

Thwarting is preventing someone from accomplishing what they intend, or blocking a plan from succeeding. The word emphasizes frustration of purpose—someone actively wanted something, and that desire was defeated: {Her hopes of promotion were thwarted by office politics}. Weather can thwart travel plans; vigilance can thwart a robbery.

Thyme is an aromatic herb with small leaves used in cooking, especially in Mediterranean and French cuisines. It pairs well with roasted meats, soups, and stews: {a sprig of fresh thyme}. The word is pronounced like "time," with a silent th.

A tiara is an ornamental semicircular headpiece, typically jeweled, worn by women on formal occasions—especially brides and beauty pageant winners. Unlike a crown, which encircles the head completely, a tiara sits atop the front of the head like a decorative comb. The Pope's tiara, a triple-crowned headdress, is a distinct ceremonial object no longer worn but still symbolizing papal authority.

Tiaras is the plural of tiara, a jeweled ornamental crown worn on the front of the head, typically by women at formal occasions: {The bride wore her grandmother's tiara}. Tiaras are associated with royalty, pageants, and fairy-tale princesses. A child's plastic tiara signals dress-up play or birthday celebrations.

A tick is a small arachnid that attaches to animals and humans to feed on blood, often transmitting diseases like Lyme. Separately, a tick is a light clicking sound, especially from a clock: {the tick of the grandfather clock}. A tick is also a checkmark indicating something is correct or complete; to tick a box is to mark it. If something ticks you off, it annoys you. To tick through a list is to work through it item by item. What makes someone tick is what motivates them: {I never understood what made her tick}.

Ticked means marked with a tick or check mark: {I ticked off the items on my list}. In British usage, ticked often pairs with off to mean annoyed or irritated: {She was really ticked off about the delay}. American English uses ticked the same way, sometimes without the off: {That comment really ticked me}.

A ticker is something that ticks. The heart is the ticker—slang that emphasizes its rhythmic beating. A stock ticker was originally a machine that printed stock prices on paper tape with a ticking sound; now ticker refers to the scrolling display of prices or headlines across a screen: {The news ticker showed breaking developments}. A ticker-tape parade uses shredded paper strips, originally from stock tickers.

A ticket is a tangible or virtual authorization that entitles the holder to a seat at an event or on a means of transportation (concert ticket, train ticket). A ticket may also be evidence of participation in a lottery or raffle. A ticket issued by a legal authority (parking ticket, speeding ticket), on the other hand, compels the recipient to pay a fine or appear in court. To ticket someone is to issue them a ticket.

Tickets are documents or tokens granting admission, passage, or participation: concert {tickets}, plane {tickets}, lottery {tickets}. A traffic ticket is a citation for a violation. {That's the ticket} means that's exactly right. In politics, the ticket is the slate of candidates: {She's running on the Democratic ticket}. To ticket is to issue a citation or to designate: {ticketed for greatness}.

Ticking is a sturdy, tightly woven fabric used to cover mattresses and pillows, traditionally featuring distinctive stripes. The weave is dense enough to contain feathers or stuffing. Separately, ticking is the present participle of tick—the sound a clock makes, or the act of marking items: {I heard the clock ticking}; {She was ticking off names on her list}.

Tickle is a light touch that produces an involuntary twitching sensation, often with laughter: {Stop tickling me!} The sensation itself is also a tickle: {I have a tickle in my throat}. Figuratively, to tickle is to please or amuse: {The idea tickled her fancy}. Something that tickles your curiosity arouses it gently. To be {tickled pink} is to be delighted.

Tickled is the past tense of tickle, meaning to touch lightly in a way that causes involuntary laughter or squirming: {She tickled the baby's feet}. More often, tickled describes being pleased or amused: {I was tickled by the whole situation}. To be {tickled pink} is to be delighted.

Tickles is the verb tickle in action—to touch lightly in a way that produces involuntary laughter or squirming: {She tickles the baby's feet}. Extended uses describe gentle sensations: {The grass tickles my ankles}. To tickle someone's fancy is to appeal to or amuse them. Something that tickles you delights you: {It tickles me that he remembered}.

Tickling is light, repeated touching that produces an involuntary twitching sensation, often with laughter. It works best in sensitive spots—underarms, feet, ribs—and typically requires another person; tickling yourself rarely works. The sensation hovers between pleasure and discomfort: {Stop tickling me!} Something that tickles your fancy appeals to you.

Ticklish describes sensitivity to light touch that produces involuntary laughter or squirming: {She's extremely ticklish on her feet}. The word extends to situations requiring delicate handling—a ticklish subject, a ticklish negotiation. Something ticklish is easily upset or prone to difficulty: {Getting the timing right is a ticklish business}.

Ticks are small arachnids that attach to animals and humans to feed on blood, often transmitting diseases like Lyme. The word also names the rhythmic sounds of a clock or the small marks used for checking items off a list: {Put a tick next to each completed task}. To tick is to make such sounds or marks. What makes someone {tick} is what motivates them. To {tick off} is to annoy, or in British usage, to reprimand.

Tidal describes anything relating to tides—the regular rise and fall of sea levels caused by gravitational pull from the moon and sun. A tidal {pool} forms when the tide recedes. Tidal {waves} are sometimes confused with tsunamis, though technically they're different phenomena. Figuratively, tidal suggests overwhelming force or rhythm: {a tidal wave of emotion}, {tidal shifts in public opinion}.

A tidbit is a small, choice morsel of food, or by extension, a small piece of interesting information: {She shared a few tidbits of gossip}. The word suggests something appetizing but minor—a taste rather than a meal. British English spells it titbit.

Tidbits are small, choice pieces—originally of food, now of anything. A tidbit of gossip is a juicy morsel of information. A tidbit from a meal is a particularly tasty bite. The word suggests something select and appetizing, whether literal or figurative: {She shared a few tidbits about the upcoming merger}. British English spells it titbit.

Tide is the regular rise and fall of sea levels caused by the gravitational pull of the moon and sun. High tide brings water up the shore; low tide exposes what was submerged. The word extends to any powerful flow or shift: {a rising tide of discontent}, {the tide of battle turned}. To tide someone over is to help them through a difficult period: {This loan should tide you over until payday}.

A tidepool is a small, rocky pool of seawater left behind when the tide recedes. These isolated pockets along coastlines harbor diverse marine life—anemones, crabs, starfish, small fish—that must survive until the next tide returns. {We spent the afternoon exploring tidepools along the shore.} Also spelled tide pool.

Tides are the regular rise and fall of sea levels caused by gravitational pull from the moon and sun. High tide and low tide alternate roughly twice daily. The word extends to any powerful, sweeping movement: {a tide of public opinion}, {the tide of history}. To {turn the tide} is to reverse momentum. Something that {tides you over} sustains you temporarily until conditions improve.

Tidiness is the state of being neat and orderly, with things in their proper places. It applies to physical spaces {the tidiness of her desk}, personal appearance, or habits of organization. Someone who values tidiness keeps their environment uncluttered and arranged. The quality suggests care and discipline, though excessive tidiness can imply rigidity.

Tidy means neat, orderly, and well-arranged: {a tidy desk}, {a tidy appearance}. A tidy person keeps things in order. To tidy is to make something neat: {I need to tidy up before guests arrive}. In British usage, a tidy sum or amount is considerable: {She earned a tidy profit on the sale}.

To tie something is to unite it with or connect it to another thing: you can tie a rope to a vehicle or tie performance to pay. To tie a knot is to create the knot using something like string or rope, but to tie the knot is a figurative way to express entering into marriage. When scores are tied, or when you tie the score, the scores are equal. To tie a record is to achieve the same level as that achievement. Among other things, a tie can be an instance of tying in competition (the game ended in a tie), a strip of material worn and tied around the neck (necktie), or a connection between things: The two countries enjoyed close diplomatic ties.

A tiebreaker is a method for determining a winner when competitors are tied. In tennis, a tiebreaker is a special game played when sets are tied at six games each. More broadly, any deciding factor can be called a tiebreaker: {The candidate's experience was the tiebreaker}. Also spelled tie-breaker.

Tied is the past tense of tie, covering all that verb's meanings. Something tied is fastened or bound: {Her hands were tied behind her back}. A tied game or election has equal scores or votes—neither side ahead. To be tied up is to be busy or unavailable: {I'm tied up in meetings all afternoon}. To have your hands tied is to be prevented from acting.

A tier is one of a series of rows or levels arranged one above another, like the tiers of a wedding cake or stadium seating. The word extends naturally to any hierarchical ranking system: {The company offers three tiers of service}. In gaming and competitive contexts, tier often designates quality or power rankings, with top tier meaning the best and bottom tier the worst. As a verb, tier means to arrange in levels or ranks. The adjective tiered describes something with multiple levels: {a tiered pricing structure}.

Tiers are levels or ranks arranged in a hierarchy, each above or below another: {The stadium has three tiers of seating}, {a two-tier pricing system}. The word implies structured gradation—premium tiers offer more than basic ones, upper tiers sit above lower ones. Subscription services commonly use tiers to differentiate access levels. To tier is to arrange in such levels.

Ties are things that bind, fasten, or connect. A tie secures something: you tie your shoes, tie a knot, tie up a package. Railroad ties are crossbeams holding tracks together. Ties are also connections between people—family ties, business ties. In competitions, a tie means equal scores: {The game ended in a tie}. A tie is also a necktie: {He loosened his tie after the meeting}.

A tiff is a minor quarrel or petty disagreement, typically between people who are otherwise close: {They had a tiff over whose turn it was to cook}. The word suggests something brief and not seriously damaging to the relationship—more a spat than a fight. (All caps TIFF is an image file format.)

The tiger is the largest species of cat and generally thought of as a fierce and dangerous animal. Things called tiger that are not large, fierce cats attract the name because of some feature reminiscent of the real thing. A man described as a tiger is probably virile, successful, and strong. The tiger moth, tiger lily, and tiger prawn are all organisms with striped markings like those of a tiger. Tiger stripes are markings of black or another dark color on a lighter color.

Tigers are large striped cats native to Asia, the largest of the wild cat species. The word appears in various figurative uses: a {paper tiger} is something that appears threatening but isn't, while to {have a tiger by the tail} is to be in a situation difficult to control or escape. In sports, numerous teams bear the name Tigers. {The tigers prowled their enclosure.} (Capitalized Tigers typically refers to a specific team.)
