Tight describes something firmly fixed, stretched taut, or fitting closely with little room to spare. A tight {lid} won't come off easily. Tight {jeans} hug the body. A tight {deadline} leaves no margin. Money is tight when funds are scarce. A tight {game} is closely contested. Someone who is tight with money is stingy; someone tight with a friend is close. Tight also means drunk: {He got tight at the party}. In slang, tight means excellent or cool: {That new album is tight}.

Tighten means to make or become tight—to increase tension, reduce slack, or secure more firmly. You tighten a bolt, a belt, or your grip. Muscles tighten with exertion or anxiety. Rules and restrictions tighten when they become stricter: {The government tightened border controls}. To {tighten your belt} is to reduce spending during hard times.

Tightfisted means unwilling to spend or give money—stingy, miserly: {Her tightfisted uncle never tipped more than five percent}. The image is of a fist clenched around coins, refusing to open. The word carries mild disapproval but is less harsh than cheapskate or miser.

Tightknit describes a group whose members are closely connected through strong bonds of loyalty, affection, or shared purpose: {a tightknit family}, {a tightknit community}. The metaphor comes from fabric woven with threads close together, suggesting unity that's hard to penetrate or pull apart. Also spelled tight-knit.

Tightlipped means reluctant to speak, especially about a particular subject. Someone who is tightlipped keeps information to themselves: {Officials remained tightlipped about the investigation}. The image is of lips pressed firmly together, refusing to let words escape. Also spelled tight-lipped.

A tightrope is a rope or wire stretched taut high above the ground, walked by acrobats and circus performers. The word extends naturally to any precarious situation requiring careful balance: {Walking a tightrope between honesty and diplomacy}, {The negotiations were a tightrope act}. To {walk a tightrope} is to navigate a situation where missteps in either direction bring trouble.

Tights are a snug-fitting garment covering the legs and usually the torso up to the waist, made of stretchy material like nylon or spandex. They differ from stockings by being a single piece rather than two separate leg coverings. Dancers and gymnasts wear opaque tights; sheer tights serve as women's hosiery. In British usage, tights covers what Americans call pantyhose.

A tightwad is a person who is excessively reluctant to spend money—stingy beyond what circumstances require. The word is mildly contemptuous: {Don't be such a tightwad; it's her birthday}. A wad is a roll of bills, and a tightwad keeps that wad held tight.

Tightwads are people who are excessively reluctant to spend money. The term carries mild contempt—tightwads aren't just frugal, they're stingy to the point of annoyance: {Those tightwads won't even split the check fairly}. The image is of someone clutching their wad of cash so tightly nothing escapes.

A tiki is a carved wooden or stone figure representing a Polynesian deity or ancestor, typically featuring a stylized human form with large eyes and exaggerated features. The term extends to the mid-20th-century American aesthetic inspired by Pacific Island culture: tiki {bars}, tiki {torches}, tiki {mugs}. This style evokes an idealized tropical escapism with bamboo, thatch, and rum drinks. {The backyard was decorated with tiki torches for the luau.}

A tile is a flat, thin piece of hard material—ceramic, stone, or clay—used to cover surfaces like floors, walls, and roofs. Tiles are laid in patterns, with grout filling the gaps between them. The word extends to similar units: {ceiling tiles}, {carpet tiles}, {Scrabble tiles}. In computing, to tile windows is to arrange them edge-to-edge without overlapping.

Tiles are flat, thin pieces of hard material—ceramic, stone, or plastic—used to cover surfaces like floors, walls, and roofs. They're typically arranged in patterns and fitted together: {bathroom tiles}, {roof tiles}, {subway tiles}. In games, tiles are the playing pieces in Scrabble, mahjong, and dominoes. To tile is to cover with tiles or, in computing, to arrange windows side by side on a screen.
Till is identical in meaning to until. It is used in conversation and in poetry or lyrics where a word of one syllable rather than two is required.

There are two tilts, each represented as a noun and verb. First, to tilt something is to move it out of horizontal. If something tilts, it does this. A tilt is an instance of tilting or the angled state resulting from tilting (tilt of the head). Second, to tilt is to engage in a competition on horseback, using lances or spears against an opponent. This competition is called a tilt. At full tilt refers to doing something as fast as possible.

Tilted describes something inclined or slanted from its usual position: {a tilted picture frame}, {She held her head at a tilted angle}. In gaming and poker slang, tilted means emotionally agitated or frustrated to the point of impaired judgment: {After losing three hands in a row, he was completely tilted}. The gaming sense has spread to general use for being off-balance or rattled.

A timar was a land grant in the Ottoman Empire, given to cavalrymen in exchange for military service rather than rent. The holder (timariot) collected taxes from peasants on the land and was obligated to report for duty with horses and equipment when called. The system supported Ottoman military expansion for centuries before declining in the 17th and 18th centuries.

Timber is wood prepared for use in building or carpentry—logs, beams, planks. Standing trees destined for harvest are also timber: {old-growth timber}, {timber rights}. As an exclamation, "Timber!" warns that a tree is falling. Figuratively, timber suggests raw material or potential: {presidential timber}, {She's starter timber}.

Every language finds ways to divide time into past, present, and future, so it’s no surprise that the word time is itself a high-frequency word. It appeared first in English as a noun and is related to the word tide, which gives us a glimpse into our ancestors’ sense of time. Like many nouns, time has both countable and uncountable meanings. Uncountable time communicates the concept of the continuum in which all things happen (since the beginning of time), or for a slice of the continuum (the time of the colonization). Countable time relates to occasions, events, and specific hours: The times of the meetings have changed. When is the best time for me to call you? Several times I tried to stop her.

A timebomb is an explosive device set to detonate at a predetermined time. Figuratively, any situation likely to become dangerous or disastrous if left unaddressed: {The pension shortfall is a timebomb waiting to explode}. In computing, a timebomb is code designed to trigger at a specific date—whether malicious or a trial software expiration. Also spelled time bomb.

Timed describes something measured, regulated, or constrained by time. A timed {exam} must be completed within a set period. A timed {release} medication dissolves at controlled intervals. To say something was {well-timed} or {poorly timed} is to judge whether the moment was right: {Her announcement was perfectly timed to maximize impact}.

Timeless describes something unaffected by the passage of time—enduring, ageless, or eternally relevant. A timeless {classic} remains appealing across generations. Timeless {beauty} doesn't fade. Timeless {wisdom} applies regardless of era. The word often carries a tone of admiration: {Her style is timeless}. Something timeless transcends its moment of creation.

Timelessness is the quality of being unaffected by time's passage—remaining relevant, beautiful, or true across eras. A work of art achieves timelessness when it speaks to generations beyond its own: {the timelessness of Shakespeare's themes}. The word can also describe moments that feel suspended outside ordinary time: {the timelessness of a summer afternoon}.

A timeline is a visual or conceptual representation of events arranged in chronological order along a line, typically with dates marked to show when things occurred. Timelines help illustrate the sequence and relative spacing of historical events, project milestones, or personal histories. In social media contexts, timeline refers to the stream of posts and updates that appears on a user's feed: {I scrolled through my timeline for an hour}. As a verb, to timeline something means to plot it out chronologically or schedule it across time.

Timelines are chronological representations of events, showing when things happened in relation to each other: {The timeline of the investigation revealed crucial gaps}. Project managers use timelines to track deadlines and milestones. In science fiction and discussions of time travel, timelines are alternate versions of history: {In that timeline, the war never happened}. The singular timeline often refers to the sequence of posts in a social media feed.

Timely means happening at the right moment or without undue delay. A timely {warning} comes soon enough to be useful. A timely {arrival} is neither too early nor too late. {The rain was timely—the crops were about to fail}. Something timely is also relevant to current events: {a timely discussion of election security}.

Timeout is an enforced pause or break. In sports, teams call timeouts to stop the clock and strategize. With children, timeout is a disciplinary measure—a period of isolation to calm down: {Go sit in timeout for five minutes}. In computing, a timeout occurs when a system stops waiting for a response after a set interval: {The connection timed out}. As a verb (usually hyphenated or two words), to time out is to exceed an allowed duration.

Timeouts is the plural of timeout. In sports, a timeout is a brief stoppage of play requested by a team to strategize or rest: {The coach called two timeouts in the final minute}. For children, a timeout is a disciplinary pause—time spent sitting quietly away from activity. In computing, a timeout occurs when a system stops waiting for a response: {The connection failed after repeated timeouts}.

A timer is a device or mechanism that measures time intervals. Kitchen timers count down cooking minutes; athletic timers measure race durations. In computing, timers trigger events after specified delays. Someone who times things—a race official, a coach with a stopwatch—is also a timer: {The timer signaled the end of the round}.
Times is the word we use to express the multiplication symbol. It is interpreted as a preposition: seven times four is 28.

A timeshare is a vacation property arrangement where multiple owners share rights to use a property, typically for designated weeks each year. The concept emerged from resort condominiums: {They bought a timeshare in Hawaii}. Timeshares are notorious for aggressive sales tactics and difficulty reselling: {We sat through a two-hour timeshare presentation to get free tickets}.

A timestamp is a record of when something occurred—a date, time, or both, attached to data or documents. Computers generate timestamps automatically: file creation times, message send times, transaction records. In video, a timestamp marks a specific moment: {Skip to timestamp 3:42}. As a verb, to timestamp is to mark something with its time of occurrence.

A timesuck is an activity, website, or task that consumes far more time than intended or warranted: {Social media is such a timesuck}, {I meant to check one email and fell into a two-hour timesuck}. The word implies the time was wasted or at least unproductive—something that pulls you in and doesn't let go.

A timetable is a schedule showing when events occur, especially for transportation or academic purposes: {Check the train timetable for departures}. School timetables list class periods and subjects. The verb means to schedule: {The meeting is timetabled for Thursday}. In British English, timetable often appears where Americans would say schedule.

A timewarp is a hypothetical distortion in the flow of time, allowing movement between different eras—a staple of science fiction. More commonly, it describes a place or situation that feels stuck in the past: {Walking into that diner was like entering a timewarp}. The Rocky Horror song "Time Warp" names a dance. Also spelled time warp.

A timezone (usually two words: time zone) is a region of the Earth that observes a uniform standard time for legal, commercial, and social purposes. The world is divided into roughly 24 time zones, each offset from Coordinated Universal Time (UTC): {What timezone are you in?} In computing, timezone often refers to a setting that determines how timestamps display: {The server's timezone was set to UTC}.

Timid describes a tendency toward fear or hesitation, especially in social situations or when facing risk. A timid person shrinks from confrontation, avoids bold action, and may be easily startled or intimidated: {She gave a timid wave from across the room}. The word suggests a disposition rather than a momentary state—someone who is timid by nature, not just afraid in the moment.

Timing is the selection or control of when something happens. Good timing means choosing the right moment; bad timing means choosing the wrong one: {His timing was perfect—he asked for a raise right after landing the big account}. In performance, timing is the rhythm and pace of delivery—a comedian's timing determines whether jokes land. In mechanics, timing refers to the synchronization of engine components: {The car runs rough because the timing is off}.

Tin is a chemical element and an abundant, widely used metal. Some things made or formerly made of tin are called tins, especially in British English (where the corresponding American term is can or pan), such as muffin tin, cake tin, or tin of sardines. So-called tin foil is today more likely to be made of aluminum. To tin something, in British English, is to seal it in a tin (or can in American English): We’ll tin tomatoes to use in the winter.

Tinder is dry, flammable material used to start fires—paper, dry leaves, small twigs, or specially prepared substances that catch a spark easily. The word extends metaphorically to anything that could ignite conflict or passion: {The economic crisis was tinder for revolution}. A tinderbox was originally a container for tinder and flint; now it means a volatile situation ready to explode. (Capitalized Tinder is a dating app.)

A tinderbox is a container holding tinder and the implements for striking a flame—historically flint and steel. Before matches, tinderboxes were essential household items. The word now appears almost exclusively in its figurative sense: a volatile situation ready to ignite. A region with ethnic tensions is a tinderbox; so is a relationship on the verge of explosive conflict. {The disputed territory remained a tinderbox for decades.}

Tinfoil is thin, pliable metallic sheeting, originally made of tin but now almost always aluminum. It's used to wrap food for storage or cooking and to line baking pans. The term persists despite the material change, much like we still "dial" phones. In conspiracy culture, a {tinfoil hat} supposedly blocks mind-control signals, making "tinfoil hat" shorthand for paranoid or outlandish beliefs: {That's some real tinfoil-hat thinking}.

Tingle is a prickling or stinging sensation, often from cold, excitement, or restored circulation: {My fingers tingled as they warmed up}. The feeling suggests thousands of tiny pinpricks. Anticipation or strong emotion can make your skin tingle: {The suspense made my spine tingle}. As a noun, it's the sensation itself: {a tingle of excitement}.

Tingles is a prickling or slightly stinging sensation, often pleasant, spreading across the skin or through the body. The word suggests anticipation or excitement: {I get tingles just thinking about it}. ASMR enthusiasts use tingles specifically for the pleasant scalp or spine sensations triggered by certain sounds. As a verb, to tingle is to experience this sensation: {My fingers tingled in the cold}.

Tingling describes a prickling, slightly stinging sensation on the skin, often compared to pins and needles. It can result from physical causes like reduced blood flow when a limb "falls asleep," or from emotional states like excitement or anticipation: {I felt a tingling in my fingers as the announcement approached}. The word functions as both an adjective and a noun, capturing that distinctive electric-like feeling that hovers between pleasant and uncomfortable.

Tingly describes a prickling, slightly electric sensation on the skin or in the body—the feeling of a limb waking up from numbness, or the excited flutter before something happens. It can be physical: {My fingers are tingly from the cold}. Or it can describe anticipatory excitement: {I get tingly just thinking about the concert}.

A tinker is an itinerant mender of pots, pans, and other metal household items—a trade now nearly vanished. The word survives mainly in the verb: to tinker is to make small adjustments or repairs, often amateur or experimental: {He tinkered with the engine all afternoon}. To tinker with something can suggest aimless fiddling rather than serious work: {Congress keeps tinkering with the tax code}.

A tinkerer is someone who makes small adjustments or repairs, often in an experimental or amateur fashion. The word suggests hands-on curiosity rather than formal expertise—someone who opens things up to see how they work, fiddles with mechanisms, or improvises fixes: {He's a tinkerer who spends weekends in the garage rebuilding old radios}. Tinkerer can carry either admiration for resourcefulness or mild dismissal of unsystematic dabbling.

Tinkering is making small adjustments or repairs, often in an experimental or unskilled way. Someone tinkering with an engine tries minor fixes without systematic knowledge. The word suggests puttering—working without a clear plan: {He spent Saturday tinkering in the garage}. Tinkering with a system means making incremental changes rather than overhauling it: {Congress keeps tinkering with the tax code}.

Tinkers is the plural of tinker, an itinerant metalworker who mends pots, pans, and other household items. The word carries associations with wandering and improvisation. To tinker is to fiddle with something, making small adjustments without a systematic plan: {He tinkers with old radios in his garage}. The expression {tinker's damn} (or dam) means something worthless—so cheap even a tinker wouldn't value it.

Tinkle is a light, high-pitched ringing sound, like a small bell or ice cubes in a glass: {the tinkle of wind chimes}. As a verb, to tinkle is to make such sounds. In informal British English, tinkle is a childish or euphemistic word for urination: {I need to go for a tinkle}. To {give someone a tinkle} is to phone them.

Tinsel is thin strips or threads of shiny metallic material used for decoration, especially on Christmas trees. The glittering effect extends figuratively to anything superficially attractive but lacking substance: {the tinsel of Hollywood}, {all that glitters is tinsel}. As an adjective, tinsel describes gaudy showiness: {tinsel dreams of fame}.

A tint is a slight coloring or shade, typically a pale or delicate variation of a color: {a pinkish tint}, {tinted windows}. To tint is to apply such coloring: {She tinted her hair auburn}. A tint can also be a trace or hint of something: {a tint of sadness in her voice}. In color theory, a tint is a color mixed with white, as opposed to a shade (mixed with black).

Tiny means extremely small—smaller than small, approaching the minimum. A tiny {apartment} barely fits its furniture. A tiny {amount} of salt won't affect the recipe much. Tiny often carries affectionate connotations, especially for living things: {a tiny kitten}, {tiny fingers}. The word intensifies well: {a tiny bit}, {the tiniest hint of jealousy}.

Nouns and verbs with different meanings are represented by tip. A tip is a piece of practical information or advice. If you tip someone off, you give them useful information. A tip is also the end of something, like the tip of a knife or the tips of your toes. To tip something is to give it a (sharp) tip. Finally, a tip is an amount of money given in appreciation of service; to tip someone is to provide this.

A tipi is a cone-shaped tent traditionally used by Indigenous peoples of the North American Great Plains, made of animal hides or canvas stretched over wooden poles. The design allows for quick assembly and disassembly, suited to nomadic life following buffalo herds. Also spelled teepee or tepee. {We stayed in a tipi at the campground.}

A tipoff is advance warning or secret information, especially about something illicit: {Police received a tipoff about the drug shipment}. The word also names the opening play in basketball, when the referee tosses the ball and players jump to tap it to teammates. As a verb (tip off), it means to give such warning: {Someone tipped off the press}.

Tipped describes something with a tip or end of a particular kind: {gold-tipped arrows}, {a white-tipped tail}. It also means having received a tip—either gratuity or information: {a well-tipped waiter}, {police tipped off about the raid}. Something tipped has been tilted or overturned: {The canoe tipped and spilled us into the water}.

Tipping is the practice of giving a gratuity for service—at restaurants, hotels, salons, or for deliveries. The custom varies widely by country and context: {Tipping culture in America expects 20 percent}. Tipping also refers to the act of tilting or overturning: {The boat was tipping dangerously}. A tipping {point} is the threshold where change becomes unstoppable.

Tips are pointed ends or summits—the tip of a finger, the tip of an iceberg. More commonly in everyday speech, tips are small sums of money given for service: {She left a generous tip for the waiter}. Tips also means pieces of advice or inside information: {stock tips}, {betting tips}, {helpful tips for new parents}. As a verb, tips means tilts or overturns: {The canoe tips easily}, {He tips his hat in greeting}.

A tipster is someone who provides tips—inside information, predictions, or confidential advice. In gambling contexts, a tipster offers picks on races or games, sometimes for a fee: {The tipster's horse came in last}. In journalism and law enforcement, a tipster supplies leads or confidential information: {An anonymous tipster alerted police to the location}.

Tipsy describes being slightly drunk—enough to feel the effects of alcohol but not severely impaired. The word suggests a pleasant, mildly unsteady state: {She was tipsy after two glasses of wine}. Tipsy carries a lighter connotation than drunk, often implying cheerful looseness rather than serious intoxication.

Tiptoe is the tips of the toes, or the posture of standing on them: {She stood on tiptoe to see over the crowd}. To tiptoe is to walk quietly on the balls of the feet, minimizing sound: {He tiptoed past the sleeping baby}. Figuratively, to tiptoe around something is to approach it cautiously or avoid addressing it directly: {They tiptoed around the subject of money}.

Tiptoeing is walking on the balls of your feet with heels raised, either to move quietly or to reach something high: {She tiptoed past the sleeping baby}. Figuratively, to tiptoe around something is to approach it cautiously, avoiding direct confrontation: {He's been tiptoeing around the issue for weeks}.

Tiptoes are the tips of one's toes, and to tiptoe is to walk on them—quietly, carefully, or to gain height. {She tiptoed past the sleeping baby.} Figuratively, to tiptoe around something is to approach it cautiously, avoiding direct engagement: {He tiptoed around the subject of money.} To be {on tiptoes} is to be in eager anticipation.

A tirade is a long, angry speech of criticism or denunciation. The word suggests sustained verbal attack rather than brief complaint: {She launched into a tirade about the state of modern politics}. Tirades are typically one-sided—the speaker vents while others endure.

Tirades is the plural of tirade, a long, vehement speech expressing criticism, anger, or disapproval. A tirade is typically one-sided and emotionally charged: {She launched into one of her tirades about the neighbors}. Unlike a rant, which may wander, tirades usually maintain focus on a target: {His tirades against the media were legendary}.

Tiramisu is an Italian dessert made of layered espresso-soaked ladyfingers and mascarpone cream, dusted with cocoa powder. The name means "pick me up" in Italian, referring to the caffeine lift. Rich and creamy with a coffee-bitter edge, it became a staple of Italian restaurant menus worldwide in the 1980s and 90s.

Tire connects to ideas of weariness and encirclement. To tire is to lose energy or become fatigued: {The long hike tired us out}. Something that tires you can also bore you: {His constant complaints tire me}. A tire is also the rubber covering around a wheel—spelled tyre in British English. To tire of something is to grow weary of it: {I never tire of watching the sunset}.

Tired describes the state of needing rest or sleep, whether from exertion, lack of sleep, or mental strain: {I'm too tired to think straight}. The word extends to things that have lost freshness or effectiveness—a tired {argument}, a tired {joke}. To be tired of something is to have lost patience or interest: {I'm tired of hearing excuses}. Tires, the rubber rings on wheels, give us a different tired—fitted with tires.

Tireless describes someone or something that continues without fatigue or flagging effort: {a tireless advocate for reform}, {tireless dedication to the cause}. The word emphasizes sustained energy and persistence rather than literal inability to tire. It often carries admiration for someone's commitment: {She was tireless in her pursuit of justice}.

Tires are the rubber coverings fitted around wheels, providing traction and cushioning the ride. Most tires are pneumatic—inflated with air and mounted on rims. {I need to rotate my tires}. {The car skidded on bald tires}. As a verb, tires means to grow weary or cause fatigue: {The long hike tires me out}. {She never tires of that song}.

Tiring describes something that depletes your energy or patience. A tiring {day} leaves you exhausted. A tiring {conversation} wears you out. The word applies equally to physical exertion and mental strain: {The hike was tiring}, {Dealing with bureaucracy is tiring}. What's tiring for one person may not be for another.

Tissue is a soft, thin paper used for wiping or wrapping—facial tissue for noses, tissue paper for gifts. In biology, tissue is a mass of cells forming a structural material: {muscle tissue}, {scar tissue}, {tissue samples}. A {tissue of lies} is an elaborate fabrication, suggesting something woven together. {She handed him a tissue.}

Tissues are soft, thin sheets of absorbent paper used for wiping noses, cleaning surfaces, or other disposable tasks: {She grabbed a tissue to blot her tears}. In biology, tissue is a mass of cells forming a structural material in living organisms: {muscle tissue}, {nerve tissue}. The plural tissues often appears in both contexts.

A titan is someone of extraordinary size, strength, or achievement in their field: {a titan of industry}, {literary titans}. The word evokes immense power and influence, often applied to business leaders, athletes, or creative figures who dominate their domains. The original Titans were primordial Greek gods who preceded the Olympians—their overthrow by Zeus became a symbol for any clash of great powers. (Capitalized Titan is Saturn's largest moon or a member of the mythological race.)

Titanic means enormous in size, strength, or power—suggesting something of mythic proportions. The word comes from the Titans of Greek mythology, primordial deities of immense might. A titanic {struggle} involves forces of extraordinary magnitude. A titanic {effort} pushes human capacity to its limits. {The project required a titanic investment of resources.} (Capitalized Titanic usually refers to the ship.)

Titans are beings of enormous size, strength, or influence. The word derives from Greek mythology's Titans—primordial gods who ruled before the Olympians. In modern use, titans are dominant figures in their fields: {titans of industry}, {tech titans}. The word suggests not just power but a kind of foundational, era-defining importance. (Capitalized Titans may refer to the mythological beings or sports teams.)

The title of a document, presentation, or work of art is its name. When a person holds a title, it is something they have won in competition (a heavyweight title) or that has been given to them on the basis of some quality or distinction they possess (he inherited the title of marquess). In law, title may refer to a section of a long statute (Title IX of the Higher Education Act) or to the right to property as represented by a document: I’ve lost the title to my car. As a verb, titled usually appears as the participle titled and means called a certain thing: an exhibition aptly titled “Lumps and Bumps”.

Titles are names that indicate rank, office, or distinction: {Doctor}, {President}, {Duke}. They precede or follow personal names to show status or achievement. Title also means the name of a creative work—a book, film, or song: {What's the title of that movie?} In property law, title is legal ownership or the document proving it: {The title to the house was in her name}. In sports, a title is a championship: {He's fighting for the heavyweight title}. To title something is to give it a name.

A tizzy is a state of nervous agitation or flustered excitement, usually over something minor: {She got into a tizzy about the seating arrangements}. The word suggests overreaction—being more worked up than the situation warrants. Informal and slightly dated.

A toad is a tailless amphibian similar to a frog but typically stockier, with warty skin and shorter legs adapted for walking rather than hopping. Toads prefer drier habitats than frogs and secrete toxins through their skin. Calling someone a toad suggests they're repulsive or contemptible: {That little toad betrayed us}.

A toadie is a person who flatters and fawns over someone more powerful, hoping to gain favor or advantage. The word implies servile, insincere behavior—agreeing with everything, laughing at bad jokes, running errands without being asked: {He surrounded himself with toadies who never challenged him}. To toadie or toadie up to someone is to behave this way.

Toadies is the plural of toady—a person who flatters and fawns over someone powerful to gain favor. The word suggests servile, sycophantic behavior: {The executive surrounded himself with toadies who never challenged his decisions}. To toady is to behave this way: {She toadied to the boss shamelessly}.

Toads are squat, warty amphibians related to frogs but typically with drier, bumpier skin and shorter legs suited to walking rather than hopping. They're found worldwide and often appear in folklore as ugly or magical creatures. Figuratively, toad describes an unpleasant or repulsive person: {That little toad sold us out}.

A toadstool is a mushroom, especially one that is poisonous or inedible. The word evokes the classic fairy-tale image: a rounded cap on a stem, often red with white spots. There's no scientific distinction between toadstools and mushrooms—the terms overlap—but toadstool carries connotations of danger or folklore: {Don't eat that, it's a toadstool}.

Toadstools are mushrooms, especially poisonous or inedible ones. The word evokes the classic image of a wild mushroom with a rounded cap on a stem—the kind found in forests and fairy tales. There's no scientific distinction between toadstools and mushrooms; the terms reflect folk tradition rather than biology. {Don't eat those toadstools growing in the yard.}

A toady is a person who flatters and fawns over someone in power, hoping to gain favor. The word carries strong contempt—a toady has no dignity or independent judgment, only servile eagerness to please: {He surrounded himself with toadies who agreed with everything he said}. As a verb, to toady is to behave this way: {She toadied to the boss shamelessly}.

Toast is bread browned by heat, typically in a toaster or under a broiler: {buttered toast}, {toast and jam}. To toast is to brown food this way, or to warm oneself: {toasting by the fire}. A toast is also a ritual of raising glasses to honor someone or something: {a toast to the bride and groom}. To be toast is slang for being doomed or finished: {If the boss finds out, you're toast}.

Toasted describes bread or other food browned by dry heat: {toasted bagel}, {toasted almonds}. The verb toast means to brown food this way, or to raise a glass in someone's honor: {Let's toast the happy couple}. A toast is both the browned bread and the celebratory gesture. Informally, toasted means drunk or high: {We got completely toasted last night}.

A toaster is a small kitchen appliance that browns slices of bread by exposing them to radiant heat. Most toasters have slots that hold the bread vertically and a lever or button that lowers it into the heating chamber. {The toast popped up from the toaster.} Toaster ovens are larger countertop appliances that can toast, bake, and broil.

Toasting is heating bread or other food until browned and crisp: {The smell of toasting bagels filled the kitchen}. It also refers to the act of raising glasses in honor of someone or something: {After much toasting, the wedding guests were thoroughly drunk}. In Jamaican music culture, toasting is a style of rhythmic chanting over beats, a precursor to rap.

Toasts is the plural of toast in all its senses. Slices of bread browned by heat: {She made toasts with butter and jam}. Ceremonial drinks honoring someone: {We raised our glasses for toasts to the bride and groom}. The verb form covers both browning bread and drinking in honor: {He toasts his bagel every morning}; {She toasts her colleagues at every company dinner}.

Toasty means pleasantly warm, with a connotation of coziness: {The fire made the cabin nice and toasty}. It suggests warmth that's comfortable rather than excessive—the temperature of being wrapped in a blanket or sitting near a hearth. The word is informal and often affectionate in tone.

Tobacco is a plant whose dried leaves are smoked, chewed, or snuffed for their stimulant effects. The nicotine in tobacco is highly addictive, making it among the most harmful legal substances: {He quit tobacco after thirty years}. Tobacco also refers to the product itself—loose leaf, cigarettes, cigars, or chewing tobacco. The tobacco industry has faced decades of litigation and regulation over health effects.

A toboggan is a long, flat-bottomed sled without runners, traditionally made of thin boards curved up at the front. Used for sliding downhill over snow or ice: {The kids took the toboggan to the steepest hill in the park}. In some American dialects, toboggan also means a knit winter cap—the kind you'd wear while sledding.

Tobogganing is the activity of riding a toboggan—a long, flat-bottomed sled without runners—down snow-covered slopes. The sport ranges from casual recreation to competitive racing on specially constructed chutes: {We went tobogganing in the park after the first big snowfall}.

Toboggans are long, flat-bottomed sleds without runners, designed for sliding downhill over snow or ice. The front curves upward to glide over obstacles. Multiple riders typically sit in a line: {We piled onto the toboggan and flew down the hill}. In some Southern U.S. dialects, a toboggan is a knit winter cap—the kind you'd wear while sledding.

Today is the current day—the one you're in right now: {I have a meeting today}, {today's weather}. It extends to the present time or era: {Today's smartphones are more powerful than yesterday's computers}. As a noun, today names this day: {Today is my birthday}. The adverb yesterday and tomorrow complete the immediate temporal trio.

A toddler is a young child who has learned to walk but hasn't yet mastered the skill—typically between ages one and three. The word captures the unsteady, tottering gait characteristic of this stage: {The toddler wobbled across the room}. By extension, toddler describes products and services aimed at this age group: {toddler bed}, {toddler classes}.

Toddlers are young children who have recently learned to walk, typically between one and three years old. The word captures their unsteady gait—they toddle rather than stride. {The toddlers chased each other around the playground.} The toddler stage is marked by rapid development, tantrums, and the word "no."

A toe is any of the digits at the end of your foot. The part of a sock or shoe that covers your toes is also the toe. Toe also describes the lowest part of something, or something shaped like a toe. From head to toe is a way of saying thoroughly or throughout, suggesting that no part is overlooked. If you’re on your toes, you are alert and ready to act. To toe the line is to obey rules and conform to expectations.

A toehold is a small ledge or crevice just large enough to support the toes when climbing: {She found a toehold in the rock face}. Figuratively, it's any minimal but secure position from which to advance: {The company established a toehold in the Asian market}. In wrestling, a toehold is a hold in which the foot is bent or twisted.

A toenail is the hard protective plate covering the upper surface of a toe, equivalent to a fingernail. In carpentry, to toenail is to drive a nail at an angle through one piece of wood into another: {He toenailed the stud to the floor plate}.

Toenails are the hard, protective plates covering the tips of the toes, equivalent to fingernails on the feet. They grow slowly and require periodic trimming. In carpentry, to toenail is to drive a nail at an angle through one piece of wood into another: {He toenailed the stud to the plate}.

Toes are the digits at the end of the foot—humans have five on each. To toe a line is to stand with toes touching it, hence to comply with rules or expectations: {He refused to toe the party line}. To be {on your toes} is to be alert and ready. To {toe the water} is to test something cautiously. As a verb, to toe is to touch or kick with the toe: {She toed the ball into the goal}.

Toffee is a chewy candy made by boiling sugar and butter together until it caramelizes and hardens. British toffee tends to be softer than American versions, which are often called taffy. {She made a batch of toffee for the holidays}. Someone who {can't do something for toffee} (British) is utterly hopeless at it.

Tofu is a soft, bland food made from coagulated soy milk pressed into blocks. It originated in East Asia and is a staple protein in vegetarian and vegan cooking. Tofu absorbs flavors from marinades and sauces, making it versatile despite its neutral taste: {The stir-fry had crispy tofu with garlic and ginger}. Textures range from silken to extra-firm.

A toga is the loose outer garment worn by citizens of ancient Rome—a single piece of cloth draped over the body and around one shoulder. The toga symbolized Roman citizenship and formal occasions. Today, toga appears mainly in {toga party}, where people wrap themselves in bedsheets in imitation of the ancient garment.

Togas is the plural of toga, the draped outer garment worn by citizens of ancient Rome. The toga was a marker of Roman citizenship and status—different styles indicated social rank. Today, togas appear mainly at costume parties, where bedsheets serve as approximations: {a toga party at the frat house}.

The useful adverb together suggests union of things that can or did exist separately. To put something together is to assemble its parts, or for abstract things, draw connections among them. To work together is to work cooperatively or harmoniously. If you ask whether two people are together, you want to know if they are a couple. If you take two things together, you consider them as one, or closely related. When people come together, they either gather in one place, or unite in a cause.

Togetherness is the feeling of closeness and connection that comes from being with others—family, friends, or community. It emphasizes shared experience and emotional warmth rather than mere physical proximity: {The holidays are about togetherness}. The word often appears in sentimental contexts celebrating bonds between people.

Toggle is a fastener or switch that moves between two positions—a coat toggle pushed through a loop, a light switch flipped on or off. In computing, toggle describes any control that alternates between states with each activation: {Toggle the setting to enable dark mode}. The verb means to switch back and forth: {I keep toggling between tabs}.

Toil is hard, exhausting labor—work that drains and wears you down: {Years of toil in the fields left his hands calloused}. The word carries connotations of drudgery and thanklessness. As a verb, to toil is to work strenuously: {She toiled through the night to finish the report}. To {toil away} emphasizes the grinding persistence of such effort.

A toilet is a fixture for urinating and defecating, consisting of a bowl with a seat and a mechanism for flushing waste away with water. The room containing this fixture is also called a toilet, especially in British English, where Americans more often say bathroom or restroom. Toilet formerly referred to grooming and dressing, which is why toiletries are personal care items like soap and toothpaste. {The toilet's clogged again.} {Where's the nearest public toilet?}

Toiletries are personal care items used for grooming and hygiene—soap, shampoo, toothpaste, deodorant, razors, and the like. The word typically appears when packing for travel or shopping for bathroom supplies: {Don't forget to pack your toiletries}. Hotels often provide basic toiletries for guests.

Toiling is working hard, especially at physically demanding or tedious labor. The word carries connotations of sustained effort and weariness: {farmers toiling in the fields}, {She spent years toiling away at a job she hated}. Toiling suggests not just work but struggle—effort that extracts a cost.

A token is a small object or an idea that in either case symbolically represents something else. Physical tokens may be used like money, to give you access to something. A gift of flowers may be a token of love. Token has many uses in computing, some having to do with authenticating the way computers communicate with each other. The adjective token is often used disparagingly, suggesting that something is done of the sake of appearance: It was a meaningless token gesture.

Tokenism is the practice of making only a symbolic effort toward inclusion—hiring one woman, featuring one minority character—to deflect criticism rather than achieve genuine diversity or equality. The token presence creates an appearance of fairness while leaving existing power structures intact: {The company's single Black executive felt like tokenism rather than progress}.

Tokens are objects or symbols that stand for something else. A subway token grants passage. A token of appreciation represents gratitude. In computing, tokens are the smallest meaningful units that software processes—words, numbers, or symbols parsed from text. As an adjective, token describes minimal or symbolic efforts: a {token gesture}, a {token minority hire}. The phrase {by the same token} means correspondingly or for the same reason.

Told is the past tense of tell. You told someone something when you communicated it to them: {I told you so}, {She told me a secret}. {All told} means in total, counting everything: {There were fifty people all told}. {I told you} often carries a note of vindication—you warned them and were right.

Tolerance is the capacity to accept or endure something, especially opinions or behaviors different from one's own: {religious tolerance}, {tolerance for dissent}. In medicine and pharmacology, tolerance is the body's diminished response to a substance after repeated exposure: {He had built up a tolerance to the painkillers}. Engineering uses tolerance for the allowable deviation from a standard: {manufacturing tolerances}. To have a high or low tolerance for something is to handle more or less of it before reaching your limit: {I have zero tolerance for rudeness}.

Tolerant describes a willingness to accept differences—in beliefs, behaviors, or people—without interference or complaint. A tolerant society allows diverse viewpoints. Tolerant can also mean able to endure or withstand: plants tolerant of {drought}, patients tolerant of {a medication}. The word sometimes carries faint criticism, implying passive acceptance rather than genuine embrace: {He was tolerant of her habits but never quite approved}.

To tolerate something is to allow or endure it without interference, even if you don't approve: {I tolerate his messy habits but I don't like them}. The word implies reluctant acceptance rather than enthusiasm. You might tolerate a noise, a person's behavior, or an opposing viewpoint. In medicine, to tolerate a drug or treatment is to endure it without adverse reaction: {She tolerates the medication well}.

Meanings of toll are split in two groups, each represented by a noun and a verb. First, a toll is an amount collected for some service, such as crossing a bridge. By extension, a toll is the burden resulting from something, like a heavy toll on people who suffer a disaster. A death toll is the number of deaths associated with an adverse event. To toll someone is to charge them a toll. Second, a toll is the sound that a bell makes. When a bell tolls it makes its characteristic sound.

Tolls are fees charged for using a road, bridge, or other passage, or the act of collecting such fees. The verb toll has a separate meaning: to ring a bell slowly and repeatedly, typically to mark a death or solemn occasion. {The church bells tolled for the fallen soldiers.} When something takes its toll, it causes gradual damage or wear: {Years of stress took their toll on his health.} The phrase {for whom the bell tolls} reminds us that every death diminishes the living.

A tomahawk is a light ax traditionally used by Native Americans of eastern North America, with a straight handle and a head that may be stone or metal. The word entered English from Algonquian languages. To tomahawk is to strike or kill with one. In sports, a tomahawk describes an overhead chopping motion: {a tomahawk dunk}, {a tomahawk chop}.

A tomato is the red, fleshy fruit of a vine plant, eaten raw in salads and sandwiches or cooked into sauces. Botanically a fruit, it's treated as a vegetable in cooking. Tomatoes range from small cherry varieties to large beefsteaks. The plural is tomatoes. In dated slang, a tomato was an attractive woman.

Tomatoes is the plural of tomato, the red fruit of a nightshade plant, eaten as a vegetable in salads, sauces, and countless dishes. {She sliced tomatoes for the sandwiches.} In older slang, tomatoes meant attractive women—dated now and likely to sound odd or offensive.

A tomb is a place of burial, especially one that is built rather than simply dug—a vault, chamber, or monument housing the dead. Tombs range from ancient stone structures to elaborate mausoleums: {the tomb of the unknown soldier}, {Egyptian tombs filled with treasures}. Figuratively, any silent, dark, or deathly still place may be called a tomb: {The house was a tomb after everyone left}.

A tomboy is a girl who enjoys activities, clothing, or behaviors traditionally associated with boys—climbing trees, playing rough sports, rejecting dresses. The term carries mild approval or neutrality, suggesting spirited independence rather than transgression: {She was a tomboy who preferred building forts to playing with dolls}. As gender norms shift, the word appears less frequently.

Tomboys are girls who prefer activities, clothes, or behaviors traditionally associated with boys—climbing trees, playing rough sports, rejecting dresses. The term carries less weight than it once did as gender expectations have loosened, but it still describes girls whose energy and interests don't fit conventional feminine molds: {She was a tomboy who spent summers catching frogs and building forts}.

Tombs are burial chambers or vaults for the dead. A tomb may be an underground room, a stone structure above ground, or a carved-out space in rock. The word often suggests something grander than a simple grave: {the pharaoh's tomb}, {a family tomb}. Figuratively, any dark, silent, or confining place: {The house was a tomb after she left}.

A tombstone is a stone marker placed at a grave, typically inscribed with the deceased person's name and dates: {We found our ancestor's tombstone in the old cemetery}. The word extends to anything resembling such a marker in shape or finality. In finance, a tombstone is a print advertisement announcing a completed deal—so called because of its plain, rectangular format listing participants. In computing, tombstone can refer to a placeholder marking deleted data.

Tombstones are stone markers placed at graves, typically inscribed with the deceased's name, birth and death dates, and sometimes an epitaph: {We wandered through the old cemetery reading tombstones}. In finance, a tombstone is a print advertisement announcing a completed deal—the blocky, text-heavy format resembles a grave marker. The verb tombstone means to dive into water feet-first with arms at your sides, body rigid like a tombstone.

A tomcat is an adult male cat, especially one that roams and hasn't been neutered. The word emphasizes the animal's wandering, territorial, and mating behaviors. By extension, a man who tomcats around pursues casual sexual encounters: {He spent his twenties tomcatting through Europe}.

A tome is a large, heavy book, often one volume of a larger work. The word carries connotations of scholarly weight and physical heft: {dusty tomes lined the library shelves}. It's frequently used with gentle irony for any imposing book: {I'm halfway through that tome on Roman history}.

Tomfoolery is foolish or silly behavior, usually harmless but annoying: {Enough tomfoolery—let's get back to work}. The word suggests playful mischief rather than serious misconduct, often used by adults scolding children or by anyone tired of nonsense.

Tomorrow is the day after today. It functions as both noun and adverb: {Tomorrow is my birthday}, {I'll call you tomorrow}. Beyond the literal, tomorrow represents the future generally: {the leaders of tomorrow}, {tomorrow's technology}. The phrase {tomorrow never comes} observes that postponed tasks remain undone, since tomorrow perpetually recedes.

A ton is a unit of weight. In the US, a short ton equals 2,000 pounds; in Britain, a long ton equals 2,240 pounds. A metric ton (or tonne) is 1,000 kilograms. Beyond measurement, ton commonly means a large quantity: {I have a ton of work to do}. {That must have cost a ton.} In British slang, a ton is a hundred, especially £100 or 100 mph.

Tone designates a value on a scale. In music, a tone is a particular pitch. In sound generally, different tones have different uses, like the ring tone on your phone. Different tones of color have slightly different appearances. Tone can also refer to a quality of emotion or intent, like an angry tone in conversation. Muscle tone is the desirable quality of a muscle’s being fit. To tone something is to give it the desired quality or tone.

Tongs are a gripping tool with two arms joined at one end, used to pick up objects without touching them directly. The word is almost always plural, like scissors or pliers. Kitchen tongs lift hot food; fireplace tongs handle burning logs; ice tongs grip slippery blocks. {She used the tongs to flip the steaks on the grill.}

The tongue is an organ in the mouths of humans and most vertebrates. Because of the obligatory involvement of the tongue in producing speech, it is a metonym for language itself: Her mother tongue is Swahili. Several idioms in which tongue features are about speech: hold your tongue, on the tip of one’s tongue, slip of the tongue. Some inanimate objects with an analogous shape or function are also called tongues, like the flap in the middle of a shoe or the clapper of a bell.

Tongues is the plural of tongue—the muscular organ in the mouth used for tasting, swallowing, and speech. Languages are also tongues: {She speaks in foreign tongues}. In religious contexts, {speaking in tongues} refers to glossolalia—uttering sounds or words believed to be divinely inspired, especially in Pentecostal worship: {The congregation spoke in tongues}.

Tonic connects to tension and restoration. In music, the tonic is the first note of a scale—the home base that resolves tension. A tonic is also something that restores vigor or well-being: {The vacation was a tonic for her spirits}. Tonic water is a carbonated mixer with quinine, traditionally paired with gin. In medicine, tonic describes sustained muscle contraction, as in a tonic seizure.

Tonight refers to the present night or the night following the current day. As an adverb, it indicates when something happens: {I'm staying home tonight}. As a noun, it names this particular evening: {Tonight is the night we've been waiting for}. The word assumes shared temporal context between speaker and listener.

Tons is the plural of ton, a unit of weight equal to 2,000 pounds (short ton) or 2,240 pounds (long ton). More commonly, tons is an informal intensifier meaning a great deal: {I have tons of work to do}, {Thanks tons}. The casual usage far outpaces the precise measurement in everyday speech.

Tonsils are masses of tissue at the back of the throat, one on each side, that help fight infection. They're most discussed when inflamed—tonsillitis often afflicted children before tonsillectomies became routine: {The doctor said her tonsils need to come out}. To be {down to the tonsils} in something is to be deeply immersed in it.

Tonsils are two masses of tissue at the back of the throat, part of the immune system's first line of defense against inhaled or swallowed pathogens. They're most famous for becoming infected—tonsillitis was once treated almost routinely by surgical removal: {She had her tonsils out when she was seven}.

The adverb too has two core ideas: one use signifies excess or extremes: this room is too cold. The other idea is conjunctive. Reflecting this, too is almost always used near a conjunction or in a sentence that has a parallel in a previous sentence or clause: We saw the Palmers, and the Tysons were there, too. In this sense, too is a close synonym of also.

Took is the past tense of take. All the meanings of take appear with took in past contexts: {She took the keys}, {He took offense}, {The project took three months}, {They took a walk}. Took sometimes appears where taken would be standard: {I should have took the other road}—this is common in casual speech but considered nonstandard in formal writing.

A tool is an implement used to accomplish a task—hammers, screwdrivers, saws. The meaning extends to anything that serves a purpose: {Language is a tool for communication}. Software tools help users perform specific functions. To tool is to drive casually: {tooling around town}. In slang, a tool is a person easily manipulated or one who's obnoxiously trying too hard—an insult suggesting someone lacks independent thought: {Don't be such a tool}.

A toolbox is a container for storing and transporting tools, typically with compartments or trays for organization. Figuratively, a toolbox is a set of skills, resources, or techniques available for a particular purpose: {We need to expand our diplomatic toolbox}. In computing, a toolbox is a collection of software utilities or a panel of icons representing available functions.

Tools are implements used to accomplish tasks—hammers, saws, wrenches, and the like. The meaning extends to anything that serves as a means to an end: {Language is a tool for communication}. Software applications are tools. In slang, a tool is a person easily manipulated or used by others, or someone obnoxiously dim: {Don't be such a tool}.

Toot is a short blast of sound from a horn, whistle, or similar instrument: {The train gave a toot as it approached the crossing}. To toot is to make such a sound. To {toot your own horn} is to boast or draw attention to your achievements. In slang, a toot can be a snort of cocaine or a drinking spree. On the social media platform Mastodon, a toot is a post—their playful term for what Twitter calls a tweet.

A tooth is one of the hard, bony structures in the mouth used for biting and chewing. Teeth appear throughout nature and machinery wherever something grips or cuts: the teeth of a {comb}, a {saw}, a {gear}. To have a {sweet tooth} is to crave sugary foods. To fight {tooth and nail} is to struggle fiercely. Something with {teeth} has real power to enforce: {The new regulation has no teeth}.

A toothache is pain in or around a tooth, typically caused by decay, infection, or damage to the tooth or gum. The ache can range from mild sensitivity to severe throbbing. {I couldn't sleep because of my toothache.} Toothache has long been a byword for misery—few pains feel as insistent or distracting.

A toothbrush is a small brush with a handle, used to clean teeth. The bristles are typically nylon, mounted on a head small enough to reach all areas of the mouth. Electric toothbrushes rotate or vibrate the head mechanically. {I need to replace my toothbrush.}

Toothless means lacking teeth, whether literally or figuratively. A toothless {smile} comes from an infant or elderly person who has lost their teeth. A toothless {law} or toothless {regulation} lacks enforcement power—all gums, no bite. {The amendment rendered the bill toothless.}

Toothpaste is a paste or gel applied to a toothbrush for cleaning teeth. It typically contains mild abrasives, fluoride, and flavoring. {I'm out of toothpaste}. Figuratively, something that {can't be put back in the tube} refers to information or actions that can't be undone once released.

A toothpick is a small pointed sliver of wood, plastic, or metal used to remove food particles lodged between teeth. Toothpicks also serve as miniature skewers for hors d'oeuvres or to test whether baked goods are done: {Insert a toothpick—if it comes out clean, the cake is ready}.

As a noun or quasi-adjective, top has the connotation of being highest, uppermost, and the opposite of bottom. The use of top with physical things (top of the building) is extended to abstract things to mean most important or prominent (top of the charts, the top earner). Though infrequently applied in temporal contexts, top usually means first: the top of the fourth inning. This cluster of meanings is carried over to the verb top, whose most frequent meaning is be at the top: The song topped the charts for twenty weeks. With physical things, top can mean add or remove a lid or cover.

Topaz is a hard, transparent gemstone, typically yellow or amber but occurring in other colors including blue, pink, and colorless. It ranks 8 on the Mohs hardness scale, making it suitable for jewelry. Topaz is the traditional birthstone for November: {She wore her grandmother's topaz ring}. The word also names the yellowish-brown color of the classic stone.

Topiary is the art of trimming shrubs and trees into ornamental shapes—geometric forms, animals, spirals. The word also refers to the shaped plants themselves: {The garden featured elaborate topiary}. As an adjective, it describes this style of gardening: {topiary hedges}, {topiary animals}.

A topic is a subject of discussion, study, or conversation: {What's the topic of your essay?} Any matter that people consider or talk about is a topic. A topic can be broad or narrow, serious or trivial. Something {off topic} strays from the subject at hand. {Hot topic} suggests a matter of current interest or controversy.

Topless describes a woman whose breasts are exposed, or a place where such exposure occurs: {a topless beach}, {topless dancers}. The word applies almost exclusively to women—a shirtless man is rarely called topless. Topless also describes things lacking a top: {a topless convertible}, {a topless tower}.

Topping is something placed on top of food—cheese on pizza, whipped cream on pie, sprinkles on ice cream: {What toppings do you want on your burger?} In British usage, topping is an old-fashioned adjective meaning excellent or first-rate. To top something is to surpass it, so a topping performance outdoes others.

Toppings are items added on top of a base food—cheese on pizza, sprinkles on ice cream, croutons on salad. The word almost always appears in plural: {What toppings do you want on your burger?} A topping bar lets customers customize their own.

Topple means to fall over or cause to fall, typically from an upright position: {The statue toppled into the square}. The word suggests instability—something top-heavy losing its balance. Figuratively, topple describes the overthrow of those in power: {The revolution toppled the government}. What topples usually seemed secure before it fell.

Toppled is the past tense of topple, meaning to fall or cause to fall from an upright position: {The statue toppled during the earthquake}, {Protesters toppled the monument}. Extended to power structures, topple means to overthrow or bring down: {The scandal toppled the government}, {A coup toppled the regime}.

Topples is the third-person singular of topple, meaning to fall or cause to fall from an upright position, usually by becoming top-heavy or unbalanced: {The stack of books topples over}. Extended to power structures, topples means to overthrow or bring down: {The revolution topples the regime}. What topples doesn't just fall—it tips, loses balance, comes down from a height.

Toppling is the act of falling or causing to fall, usually from an upright position. A stack of books topples when bumped; a statue is toppled by protesters. The word often describes the overthrow of those in power: {the toppling of the regime}, {toppling the dictator}. What topples was typically standing or dominant before its fall.

Topsyturvy means upside down or in complete disorder—everything reversed from its proper position. A room left topsyturvy has been thoroughly ransacked or chaotically rearranged. The word extends to abstract confusion: {The news turned my world topsyturvy}. Often hyphenated as topsy-turvy.

A torana is a ceremonial gateway in Buddhist and Hindu architecture, typically consisting of two posts with one or more crossbars, often elaborately carved with religious imagery. The most famous examples mark entrances to stupas and temple complexes in South and Southeast Asia: {The toranas at Sanchi feature intricate carvings of the Buddha's life}.

A torch is a handheld light source—originally a burning stick or bundle of materials, now typically a battery-powered flashlight in British English. Americans say flashlight; Brits say torch. A blowtorch produces a hot flame for welding or cutting. To torch something is to set it on fire, often deliberately: {Rioters torched the building}. To {carry a torch} for someone is to harbor unrequited love.

A torchbearer carries a torch, literally or figuratively. The term evokes ceremonial processions—Olympic torchbearers relay the flame from Greece to the host city. More often, torchbearer describes someone who leads or champions a cause, movement, or tradition: {She became the torchbearer for criminal justice reform}. The image suggests carrying light forward through darkness.

Torched is the past tense of torch, meaning to set fire to something deliberately: {Someone torched the abandoned warehouse}. The word often implies arson or intentional destruction. Informally, torched can mean defeated badly or criticized harshly: {The critics torched his new film}.

Torches is the plural of torch—a portable light source, traditionally a burning stick or bundle, now often a battery-powered flashlight (the standard British term). People carry torches through darkness, and mobs carry them to express menace. To {carry a torch} for someone is to maintain unrequited love. {The villagers grabbed torches and pitchforks.}

Tore is the past tense of tear, meaning to rip or pull apart: {She tore the letter in half}. It extends to moving with force or speed: {He tore down the street}. To be {torn} between options is to feel pulled in opposite directions.

Torment is intense suffering—physical pain or mental anguish that persists and gnaws. The noun emphasizes prolonged distress: {the torment of chronic illness}, {the torments of jealousy}. As a verb, to torment is to inflict such suffering or to harass persistently: {Stop tormenting your sister}. Children torment each other; guilt torments the conscience. A tormentor is one who causes such suffering.

Tormented describes someone suffering intense anguish—physical, mental, or emotional. A tormented {soul} is wracked by inner demons; a tormented {artist} channels pain into creation. The word suggests ongoing distress rather than a single moment of pain: {He was tormented by guilt for years}. To be tormented is also to be harassed or plagued: {tormented by mosquitoes}, {tormented by doubts}.

Tormenting describes causing severe physical or mental suffering, or the state of being subjected to it. A tormenting {memory} won't leave you alone. A tormenting {itch} demands attention. The word suggests persistent, nagging distress rather than a single blow: {The tormenting uncertainty of waiting for test results kept her awake}.

A tormentor is someone who inflicts suffering on another—physical pain, psychological cruelty, or persistent harassment: {The bully became her daily tormentor}. The word implies ongoing or repeated torment rather than a single act. In theater, tormentors are the curtains or flats at the sides of a stage that mask the wings from the audience.

Torments are sources of severe suffering or anguish, whether physical or mental: {the torments of chronic pain}, {the torments of jealousy}. The word suggests ongoing affliction rather than a single moment of pain. To torment is to inflict such suffering, or to tease and annoy persistently: {Stop tormenting your sister}.

Torn is the past participle of tear, describing something that has been ripped or pulled apart: {a torn shirt}, {torn pages}. Figuratively, torn describes emotional conflict—being pulled in opposing directions: {I'm torn between staying and leaving}. A country can be {torn apart by war}, a family {torn by disagreement}.

A tornado is a violently rotating column of air extending from a thunderstorm to the ground, forming a distinctive funnel shape. Tornadoes can destroy buildings, uproot trees, and hurl debris at deadly speeds. The word extends to any similarly destructive force: {She tore through the office like a tornado}. Tornado Alley refers to the central United States where tornadoes are most frequent.

Tornadoes is the plural of tornado—a violently rotating column of air extending from a thunderstorm to the ground. Tornadoes form when warm, moist air meets cold, dry air, creating powerful updrafts that can spin into funnel clouds. They range from brief, weak twisters to devastating storms that level entire neighborhoods: {The tornadoes that struck the Midwest left thousands homeless}.

A torpedo is a self-propelled underwater missile designed to detonate on impact with a ship or submarine. The weapon revolutionized naval warfare by allowing smaller vessels to threaten larger warships. Extended uses include the torpedo sandwich (a long submarine-style sandwich) and the verb meaning to deliberately sabotage or destroy something: {The scandal torpedoed his chances at reelection}. In older usage, torpedo referred to electric rays that stun prey, which inspired the weapon's name.

Torpedoed means struck or sunk by a torpedo—an underwater explosive projectile: {The submarine torpedoed the cargo ship}. Figuratively, to torpedo something is to destroy or sabotage it decisively: {The scandal torpedoed his campaign}, {Budget cuts torpedoed the project}. The metaphor emphasizes sudden, devastating destruction of plans or efforts.

Torpedoes is the plural of torpedo, a self-propelled underwater weapon designed to detonate on contact with a target: {The submarine fired torpedoes at the convoy}. The verb form means to destroy or wreck, literally or figuratively: {The scandal torpedoed his campaign}. A torpedo can also be a submarine sandwich in some regional American usage.

A torrent is a violent, rushing stream of water—the kind that appears during heavy rain or snowmelt. The word extends to any overwhelming flow: {a torrent of abuse}, {a torrent of emails}. In computing, a torrent is a file shared through peer-to-peer networks, downloaded in fragments from multiple sources simultaneously: {I downloaded the album as a torrent}.

Torrents are rushing streams of water, especially violent ones caused by heavy rain: {Torrents poured down the mountainside}. The word extends to any overwhelming flow: a torrent of {abuse}, a torrent of {words}. In computing, torrents are files shared through BitTorrent protocol, which distributes data across many users: {I downloaded the album from torrents}.

The torso is the trunk of the human body—everything except the head, arms, and legs. In art, a torso is a sculpture of a body without limbs or head, whether by design or because the original broke: {the torso of Apollo}. The word extends to anything truncated or incomplete: {the torso of an unfinished novel}.

Tortellini are small ring-shaped pasta filled with meat, cheese, or vegetables, folded and pinched to form a distinctive navel-like shape. They originate from the Emilia-Romagna region of Italy and are typically served in broth or with cream sauce: {We ordered the tortellini in brodo}. Smaller than tortelloni, which use the same folding technique but come with different fillings.

A tortilla is a thin, flat round of unleavened bread, fundamental to Mexican and Central American cuisine. Corn tortillas are the traditional form; flour tortillas became common in northern Mexico and the American Southwest. Tortillas wrap fillings in tacos, burritos, and enchiladas, or accompany meals as bread. In Spain, a tortilla is something different: a thick omelet typically made with potatoes and onions.

Tortillas are thin, round flatbreads fundamental to Mexican and Central American cuisine. Corn tortillas are made from masa (nixtamalized corn dough); flour tortillas use wheat flour and are more common in northern Mexico and Tex-Mex cooking. Tortillas wrap tacos, burritos, and enchiladas, or accompany meals as edible utensils: {She scooped up beans with a warm tortilla}.

A tortoise is a land-dwelling reptile with a high-domed shell, into which it can retract its head and legs for protection. Tortoises are known for their slow, deliberate movement and exceptional longevity—some species live well over a century. The word often evokes patience or persistence: {slow and steady wins the race}, from Aesop's fable of the tortoise and the hare.

Tortoiseshell is a mottled pattern of brown, amber, and black, originally from the shell of hawksbill sea turtles, historically used for decorative objects like combs and eyeglass frames. Now the term mostly describes cats with this coloring—nearly always female due to genetics—or anything imitating the pattern: {tortoiseshell glasses}, {a tortoiseshell cat}. Also spelled tortoise-shell.

Torture is the deliberate infliction of severe pain or suffering, typically to extract information, punish, or intimidate. Governments torture prisoners; captors torture hostages. The word extends to intense mental anguish: {Waiting for the test results was torture}. As a verb, to torture someone is to subject them to such treatment. Figuratively, anything agonizingly unpleasant may be called torture: {That movie was absolute torture}.

Tortured describes someone who has been subjected to torture, or something marked by intense suffering: {a tortured prisoner}, {a tortured expression}. Extended uses suggest painful strain or excessive complexity: {tortured logic}, {a tortured metaphor}. A tortured artist or soul suffers inner anguish, often romantically portrayed as fuel for creativity.

A torturer is a person who inflicts severe pain on others, typically to extract information, punish, or terrorize. The term applies both to those who torture professionally—interrogators, executioners—and to anyone who causes extreme suffering: {The regime's torturers operated in secret prisons}. Figuratively, anything that causes prolonged anguish can be called a torturer: {Insomnia was his nightly torturer}.

Torturing is the present participle of torture—inflicting severe pain or suffering, typically to extract information, punish, or terrorize. The word extends to causing intense mental anguish: {Stop torturing yourself over what you said}. It also describes prolonged frustration or anticipation: {The suspense was torturing me}.

Toss means to throw something lightly or casually, often with an upward or sideways motion: {She tossed her keys on the counter}. You can toss a salad by mixing it, toss and turn in bed when you can't sleep, or toss back a drink by downing it quickly. To toss something out is to discard it. A coin toss decides matters by chance. In British slang, if you don't give a toss, you don't care at all, and a tosser is a contemptible person.

Tossed is the past tense of toss, meaning thrown lightly or casually: {He tossed the keys onto the counter}. A tossed salad has been mixed by lifting and turning the ingredients. To have {tossed and turned} is to have slept restlessly. In British slang, tossed off means masturbated.

A tot is a very young child, typically a toddler: {The tots played in the sandbox}. The word also means a small amount, especially of liquor: {a tot of rum}. To tot up is to add figures together: {Let me tot up the bill}.

Total emphasizes completeness or entirety—the whole amount with nothing left out. A total of the numbers is their sum. Total {silence} is absolute silence. A car that's totaled is damaged beyond economical repair: {The crash totaled his truck}. To total something up is to add it: {Let me total the bill}. {A total stranger} is someone completely unknown to you.

Totalitarian describes a political system in which the state holds absolute authority over all aspects of public and private life. A totalitarian regime typically features one-party rule, suppression of dissent, state-controlled media, and intrusive surveillance: {totalitarian governments}, {totalitarian control}. The noun totalitarianism names this system of governance. The word emerged in the twentieth century to describe fascist and communist states.

Totalitarianism is a system of government that demands complete control over public and private life, permitting no opposition or independent institutions. The state regulates everything—economy, education, media, family—and typically enforces conformity through surveillance and terror. The term emerged in the twentieth century to describe regimes like Nazi Germany and Stalinist Russia: {Totalitarianism crushes individual liberty in the name of the collective}. Distinguished from mere authoritarianism by its ambition to reshape society entirely rather than simply maintain power.

Totality is the state of being complete or whole—everything included, nothing left out. {The totality of the evidence points to his guilt.} In astronomy, totality is the phase of an eclipse when one celestial body completely obscures another: {We drove six hours to witness two minutes of totality.}

Tote is both a verb and a noun centered on carrying. To tote something is to carry it, especially something bulky or heavy: {She toted her laptop everywhere}. A tote or tote bag is a large, open-topped bag with handles, typically used for carrying everyday items like groceries or books. The word has an informal, practical feel and appears frequently in compounds like {gun-toting} to describe someone who habitually carries a firearm.

A totem is an object—typically an animal or plant—serving as a spiritual emblem for a group, especially among Indigenous peoples of North America. The totem represents ancestral connection and identity. A totem pole is a carved wooden column depicting such figures. Figuratively, anything symbolizing a group's identity or values: {Homeownership became a totem of the American dream}.

Totems are objects—typically animals or plants—that serve as spiritual symbols or emblems for a group, clan, or individual. In Indigenous North American cultures, a totem represents ancestral connection and may be carved into a totem pole. More broadly, totem describes anything treated as a sacred emblem or symbolic representation: {The company logo became a totem of corporate identity}. A personal totem might be an animal one feels spiritually connected to.

Tots are very young children, roughly toddler age—old enough to walk but still small: {The playground was full of tots}. The word is informal and affectionate. Tots also names small pieces of something, especially tater tots—fried cylinders of shredded potato: {We ordered tots with our burgers}. As a verb, tot means to add up, usually with "up": {Let me tot up the bill}.

A toucan is a tropical American bird with brilliantly colored plumage and an enormous, lightweight bill that can be as long as its body. Toucans live in rainforest canopies and nest in tree hollows. The oversized bill, despite its cartoonish appearance, helps the bird reach fruit on branches too thin to support its weight.

Touch has mainly to do with physical sensations that arise because of our sensitive nerve endings. The sense of touch enables us to feel these. When you touch someone or something (literally), a part of your body, usually a hand or finger, contacts them. To touch someone figuratively is to affect their emotions, usually in a positive way. When physical objects touch, they are in contact with each other. A touch can also be a small thing you do to improve something: The scratch in the wood needs a touch up.

A touchdown is a score in American football worth six points, achieved when a player carries or catches the ball in the opponent's end zone. The term comes from rugby, where the ball must literally touch down, though in American football it need only cross the goal line. Extended to any successful completion: {The spacecraft made a safe touchdown on Mars}. In casual speech, touchdown celebrates any win or accomplishment: {Got the promotion—touchdown!}

Touchdowns are scoring plays in American and Canadian football, worth six points, achieved by carrying or catching the ball in the opponent's end zone. The term comes from rugby, where the ball must touch the ground to score—a requirement football dropped but the name kept. Figuratively, a touchdown is any successful completion: {The product launch was a touchdown for the team}.
Touche is an anglicized spelling of touché

Touched describes being emotionally moved or affected: {I was touched by her kindness}. Something that touches you reaches your feelings. Touched also means slightly mentally unstable or eccentric—{touched in the head}—suggesting someone lightly affected by madness.
