In both senses, touched implies contact with something that leaves a mark, whether tender or troubling.

Touches is the plural of touch—physical contacts or light strokes: {a few touches of the brush completed the portrait}. It also names small additions or modifications: {The room needs a few finishing touches}. Someone who {has the touch} possesses a knack or skill. To say someone is {touched} can mean emotionally moved or slightly crazy.
Touching is a participle that works as a preposition, as is the case with many of its synonyms, such as concerning and regarding.

A touchscreen is a display that responds to finger contact, allowing users to interact directly with what's on screen rather than through a keyboard or mouse. Touchscreens dominate smartphones, tablets, and many ATMs and kiosks. The technology has made swiping, tapping, and pinching standard gestures: {The touchscreen on my phone is cracked but still works}.

Touchscreens are display surfaces that detect and respond to finger contact or stylus input, allowing users to interact directly with what they see rather than through a separate keyboard or mouse. The technology transformed mobile phones and tablets into intuitive devices: {She tapped the touchscreen to select her order}. Touchscreens now appear on everything from ATMs to refrigerators.

A touchstone is a standard by which something is judged or evaluated: {Her first novel remains the touchstone against which her later work is measured}. The word comes from a black stone once used to test gold and silver—rubbing metal against it left a streak that revealed the metal's purity. The figurative sense now dominates: a touchstone is any reliable test or benchmark.

Touchstones are standards by which things are judged or evaluated. The original touchstone was a dark stone used to test gold and silver—rubbing the metal against it revealed its purity by the color of the streak. The figurative sense dominates: {Her first novel remains the touchstone for the genre}. A touchstone is something you measure other things against.

Touchy describes someone who takes offense easily or a situation requiring careful handling. A touchy {person} bristles at minor slights; a touchy {subject} risks provoking strong reactions if raised carelessly. {He's touchy about his height.} The word suggests fragility or volatility—something that might go off at a light touch.

Tough describes something difficult to cut, break, or penetrate—tough meat, tough leather, tough skin. Extended to people, tough means able to endure hardship or adversity: {She's tough—she can handle it}. A tough situation is difficult or demanding: {a tough decision}, {tough questions}. Tough can also mean aggressive or uncompromising: {a tough negotiator}, {tough on crime}. As a noun, a tough is a rough, violent person. The informal {tough luck} or {tough shit} dismisses complaints unsympathetically.

Toughness is the quality of being able to withstand hardship, strain, or damage. Physical toughness means durability—a material's toughness determines whether it cracks under stress. Personal toughness implies resilience and determination: {She showed real toughness getting through that year}. Mental toughness is the capacity to perform under pressure without breaking down.

A toupee is a small hairpiece worn to cover a bald spot, typically by men. Unlike a full wig, a toupee covers only part of the head. The word often carries connotations of vanity or unconvincing concealment: {His toupee wasn't fooling anyone}. Also spelled toupée.

Toupees are hairpieces worn to cover baldness, typically by men. The word carries a slight comic or unflattering connotation—a toupee is often something others notice and the wearer hopes they won't: {His toupee shifted in the wind}. Unlike a wig, which covers the whole head, a toupee covers only a bald spot.

A tour is a journey visiting several places in sequence, typically returning to the starting point: a {tour of Europe}, a {concert tour}, a {factory tour}. Military personnel serve a tour of duty—a defined period at a particular post. To tour is to make such a journey: {The band toured for six months}. A tour guide leads visitors through sites of interest.

Touring is traveling from place to place, typically for pleasure, performance, or promotion. A band goes on tour, playing venues across a region: {The band is touring Europe this summer}. Touring can also describe equipment designed for long-distance travel: a touring {bike}, a touring {car}. The emphasis is on movement through multiple locations rather than staying in one spot.

Tourism is the activity of traveling for pleasure, or the industry built around it. Tourists visit places for recreation, culture, or scenery rather than work. The word often implies organized travel with economic impact: {Tourism drives the local economy}. {Mass tourism has changed the character of the old town}.

A tourist is someone who travels to a place for pleasure rather than work or residence. Tourism implies sightseeing, vacationing, and temporary stays: {The city is overrun with tourists in summer}. Tourist carries a faint whiff of superficiality—tourists see the famous sites but miss the authentic experience locals know. {Tourist trap} describes a place that exploits visitors with overpriced goods or manufactured charm.

Tourists are people who travel to places away from home for pleasure, sightseeing, or recreation rather than for work or permanent relocation. The word often carries connotations of outsider status and unfamiliarity with local customs: {The tourists crowded the monument, blocking the view for everyone else}. Locals sometimes use tourist dismissively to suggest someone who doesn't really belong or understand a place. Tourist also functions as an adjective: {tourist trap}, {tourist season}, {tourist visa}.

Touristy describes places, activities, or things that cater heavily to tourists, often implying they've lost authenticity or local character in the process. The word carries a mildly dismissive tone—somewhere locals avoid: {The waterfront is too touristy for my taste}. A touristy shop sells overpriced souvenirs; a touristy restaurant has laminated menus in six languages.

A tournament is a competition involving multiple contestants or teams in a series of games or matches. Tournaments use various formats—single elimination, double elimination, round-robin—to determine a winner. The word originally meant a medieval jousting contest: {knights competing in tournament}. Now it applies to sports, games, and other competitions: {a chess tournament}, {a golf tournament}, {March Madness is the NCAA basketball tournament}.

Tournaments is the plural of tournament—organized competitions with multiple contestants or teams, where winners advance through successive rounds until a champion emerges. The format appears across sports, games, and other competitive activities: {She's played in three tournaments this year}, {The chess tournaments run all weekend}. Medieval jousting tournaments gave the word its competitive flavor.

A tourniquet is a device wrapped tightly around a limb to compress blood vessels and stop severe bleeding. Traditionally an improvised band of cloth twisted with a stick, modern tourniquets use straps and windlass mechanisms. {Apply the tourniquet above the wound}. Emergency responders and soldiers carry them for trauma situations where direct pressure won't control hemorrhage.

Tours are journeys through a series of places, or guided visits around a single place: {a tour of Europe}, {a factory tour}. A band on tour travels from venue to venue performing. A tour of duty is a period of military service in a particular location. The verb means to travel through or visit: {We toured the wine country}. (Capitalized Tours is a city in France.)

To tow is to pull something behind a vehicle or vessel, typically using a rope, chain, or hitch: {The truck towed the broken-down car to the shop}. A tow is the act of being pulled or the vehicle doing the pulling: {We called for a tow}. To {have someone in tow} is to bring them along. Separately, tow is coarse fiber from flax or hemp, or the pale yellowish color of that fiber: {tow-headed} describes someone with very light blond hair.

A towel is an absorbent cloth or paper used for drying wet surfaces—hands, body, dishes, spills. Bath towels are large; hand towels smaller. To {throw in the towel} is to admit defeat, from boxing corners signaling surrender. As a verb, to towel is to dry with one: {He toweled off after the shower}.

Towels are absorbent cloths for drying things—bodies, hands, dishes, surfaces. Bath towels are large; hand towels and dish towels are smaller. Paper towels are disposable sheets for cleaning. To towel is to dry with one: {She toweled off after the shower}. To {throw in the towel} is to admit defeat, from boxing, where a trainer tosses a towel into the ring to stop a fight.

A tower is a tall, narrow structure, either freestanding or part of a larger building: {church tower}, {control tower}, {water tower}. Towers serve as lookouts, defensive positions, or symbols of power. To tower over something is to rise high above it, literally or figuratively: {She towers over her classmates}. An ivory tower is a place of privileged detachment from practical concerns. (Capitalized Tower often refers to the Tower of London.)

Towering describes extreme height, literal or figurative. A towering {skyscraper} dominates the skyline. A towering {figure} in a field commands exceptional influence. Towering {rage} is intense and barely contained. The word emphasizes not just height but impressive or overwhelming scale—something that looms over its surroundings.

Towers is the plural of tower—tall, narrow structures that rise above their surroundings. Church towers hold bells, guard towers offer vantage points, and office towers dominate city skylines. To tower is to rise high or loom over: {She towers over her classmates}. {The debt towers above what they can repay}. Something towering is impressively tall or great: {a towering achievement}.

Towing is pulling a vehicle or object behind another, typically using a rope, chain, or hitch: {The truck was towing a trailer}. Towing services remove disabled or illegally parked vehicles. A tow truck does the towing. In water sports, boats tow skiers, wakeboarders, or inflatable tubes.

The areas of meaning covered by town overlap partly with city and partly with village, while being mostly opposed to country and rural. A town is a settled place with multiple homes and businesses, but not as big as a city. As a general and sometimes uncountable noun, town has the connotation of urban as opposed to rural: When will you be in town? Let’s go out for a night on the town. I’m out of town for a week. If someone leaves town they simply leave the place where they have been, whether it is a town or another type of place. Many compounds in which town comes first are about local government: town hall, town council, town clerk.

A townhouse is a narrow, multi-story dwelling that shares walls with adjacent units, typically in a row of similar structures. The term originally described an urban residence maintained by wealthy families who also owned country estates. In modern real estate, townhouse usually means a unit in a planned development with shared walls but separate entrances: {They bought a three-bedroom townhouse in the suburbs}. Also spelled as two words: town house.

A townie is a permanent resident of a college town who isn't affiliated with the university—distinct from students who come and go. The term often carries mild condescension from students toward locals: {There was tension between townies and frat boys at the bar}. In British English, townie can mean someone from an urban area as opposed to the countryside, or describe unsophisticated city dwellers.

Townies are local residents of a college town who aren't affiliated with the university—the permanent population as distinct from students and faculty. The term often carries mild condescension from students toward locals, or marks a social divide: {There was always tension between townies and frat boys}. In British English, townies are city dwellers as opposed to country people.

Toxic means poisonous—capable of causing harm or death through chemical action: {toxic waste}, {toxic fumes}. The word extends to anything destructive or harmful: a toxic {relationship} damages those in it, a toxic {workplace} breeds dysfunction. In internet culture, toxic describes hostile behavior in online communities: {The comments section turned toxic fast}.

Toxicity is the quality of being poisonous or harmful to living organisms. In its literal sense, it refers to the degree to which a substance can damage cells, tissues, or bodily systems: {The toxicity of the chemical was measured in laboratory rats}. The word has expanded dramatically in popular usage to describe harmful interpersonal dynamics, environments, or behaviors: {The toxicity in that workplace drove everyone to quit}. Someone displaying toxic traits—manipulation, negativity, emotional abuse—contributes to toxicity in relationships or communities.

A toxin is a poisonous substance produced by living organisms—bacteria, plants, animals, or fungi. Snake venom contains toxins, as do certain mushrooms and the bacteria that cause botulism. In casual use, toxin has expanded to mean any harmful substance in the body or environment, whether naturally produced or not: {I'm doing a cleanse to flush out toxins}. This looser usage irritates scientists, who distinguish toxins (biologically produced) from synthetic poisons and pollutants.

Toxins are poisonous substances produced by living organisms—bacteria, plants, fungi, or animals. Snake venom contains toxins. Botulinum toxin causes food poisoning. In popular usage, toxins has expanded beyond biology to mean any harmful substance in the body, especially in wellness contexts: {juice cleanses that claim to flush toxins from your system}. Scientists often find this broader usage imprecise.

A toy is an object for play, especially one designed for children: dolls, blocks, action figures. By extension, toy describes anything small or miniature: a toy {poodle}, a toy {train}. Adults have toys too—gadgets, sports cars, electronics acquired for pleasure rather than necessity. To toy with something is to handle it idly or consider it without commitment: {She toyed with her food}. To toy with someone is to manipulate them, often romantically: {He was just toying with her}.

Toys are objects designed for play, typically for children: dolls, blocks, action figures, stuffed animals. The meaning extends to gadgets or devices treated as playthings: {He loves his new tech toys}. A toy is also something trivial or diminutive: a toy {poodle}, a toy {piano}. To toy with something is to handle it idly or consider it without commitment: {She toyed with the idea of moving abroad}. To toy with someone is to manipulate their emotions carelessly.

Trace connects ideas of following a path and leaving a mark. A trace is a small amount of something, barely detectable: {traces of poison in the water}, {The smile vanished without a trace}. To trace is to follow the course of something: trace a river to its source, trace the history of an idea, trace a missing person. You can also trace by copying lines through transparent paper. A trace element exists in minute quantities. {There was a trace of sadness in her voice.}

A tracer is something that traces—follows, marks, or makes visible. In military use, a tracer is a bullet or shell that leaves a visible trail of light or smoke, allowing the shooter to see its path: {Tracer fire lit up the night sky}. In medicine and science, a tracer is a substance (often radioactive) introduced into a system to track movement or processes: {Doctors used a radioactive tracer to monitor blood flow}. A tracer can also be an inquiry sent to locate missing mail or shipments.

Tracers are bullets or shells containing a pyrotechnic charge that burns during flight, leaving a visible trail to show the path of fire: {Every fifth round was a tracer}. The term extends to any substance used to track movement or flow—radioactive tracers in medical imaging follow blood through the body, dye tracers reveal underground water paths. In graphic design, tracing software converts images to vectors.

Traces are small amounts left behind—marks, signs, or evidence that something existed or passed through. A detective finds traces of blood; a scientist detects traces of chemicals. To trace is to follow such signs back to their source, or to copy by drawing over: {She traced the outline onto tracing paper}. Traces also refers to the straps connecting a draft animal to its harness; to {kick over the traces} is to rebel against restraint.

Tracing is following or reproducing a path. You trace a route on a map, trace the outline of a shape by drawing over it, or trace a phone call to its origin. A tracing is the copy produced—typically a drawing made by placing thin paper over an original and following its lines. In computing, tracing tracks program execution for debugging: {The tracing showed where the code failed}.

The main idea of track is linear, with reference to a path or progress through time or space. Something that moves through space may leave a track or tracks, or it may follow tracks, as a train does. If you keep track of it, you notice where it is or what it is doing in various stages. If you fail in that, you lose track. Something that is on track is proceeding according to expectations. In recording, track may refer to an individual song (a CD with bonus tracks), or to one of several layers of the recording combined with others to compose a whole work (the bass track). #

A tracker is someone or something that follows a trail or monitors movement. Hunters and detectives track prey or suspects; fitness trackers monitor steps and heart rate. In computing, a tracker coordinates file sharing or collects user data across websites. A tracker can also be a type of music software that sequences sounds in a grid pattern.

Trackers are devices or software that monitor location, movement, or activity. A GPS tracker follows a vehicle's position; a fitness tracker counts steps and heart rate. Online trackers are bits of code that follow users across websites, collecting browsing data for advertising. In older usage, trackers were people who followed trails—hunters tracking game or scouts reading footprints. {She put a tracker on her luggage in case it got lost.}

Tracking is following movement or progress over time. You track a package, track your spending, or track an animal through the woods. In education, tracking sorts students into ability groups. In audio and video, tracking refers to alignment—a VCR's tracking adjustment kept the picture from rolling. Website tracking monitors user behavior: {Disable tracking to protect your privacy}. To {lose track} of something is to lose awareness of it.

Tracks are marks left by something passing—footprints, tire impressions, or the parallel rails that guide trains. The verb means to follow such marks: {Police tracked the suspect through the woods}. A track is also a path or course: a {running track}, a {career track}. In music, a track is a single recorded song or an isolated audio channel. To {cover your tracks} is to hide evidence of your actions. To {stop in your tracks} is to halt suddenly. {On the wrong side of the tracks} suggests a rough or poor neighborhood.

A tracksuit is a matching set of casual clothing—typically a zip-up jacket and loose pants—originally designed for athletes to wear while warming up or cooling down. The fabric is usually lightweight and comfortable, often with elastic cuffs. Tracksuits have become everyday casual wear: {He lounged around the house in his tracksuit}.

Traction is the grip between a surface and something moving across it—a tire's traction on wet pavement, a boot's traction on ice. From this physical sense comes the figurative: to {gain traction} is to build momentum or acceptance. {The idea struggled at first but eventually gained traction.} In medicine, traction is a sustained pulling force applied to bones or muscles, often using weights and pulleys to treat fractures or alignment problems.

A tractor is a powerful vehicle designed to pull or push heavy loads, especially farm equipment like plows and trailers. The word comes from a Latin root meaning "to pull." On farms, tractors replaced horses and oxen as the primary source of draft power. The term extends to the cab portion of a tractor-trailer truck, which pulls the cargo container. {He learned to drive a tractor at twelve.}

Tractors are powerful vehicles designed to pull heavy loads or equipment, especially on farms. The word comes from a Latin root meaning "to pull," which connects its agricultural sense—hauling plows, trailers, and implements across fields—to the tractor-trailer rigs that haul freight on highways. In both cases, the tractor provides the pulling power while other equipment does the specialized work.

The main associations with trade, a noun and verb, are with business, work, and goods. In these contexts, it is more broadly used in British than in American English (trade union, the motor trade). The most general noun use is to denote the buying and selling of goods, especially when done internationally. A trade can also be a single business pursued as a livelihood (the plumbing trade), or an instance of exchanging one thing for another (a favorable trade). The verb trade can mean barter or engage in business: They stopped trading in cocoa. If you trade on something, you use it to your advantage.

Tradecraft is the techniques and methods used in espionage—surveillance, dead drops, coded communication, creating cover identities. The term comes from intelligence work but extends to any specialized professional skills: {She learned the tradecraft of investigative journalism}. It implies practical expertise passed down within a profession rather than formal training.

A trademark is a name, symbol, or design that legally identifies a product or company and distinguishes it from competitors: {Nike's swoosh is one of the most recognizable trademarks in the world}. The term extends to any distinctive characteristic: {Hitchcock's cameos became his trademark}. As a verb, to trademark is to register such a mark for legal protection. Informally, trademark describes signature moves or habits: {his trademark smirk}.

Trademarks are words, symbols, or designs that identify products or services as coming from a particular source. Companies register trademarks to prevent competitors from using confusingly similar marks. Some trademarks become so dominant they risk becoming generic terms—aspirin and escalator were once trademarks. As a verb, to trademark is to register such protection: {They trademarked the logo}. Figuratively, something can be someone's trademark—a distinctive characteristic: {His dry wit was his trademark}.

A tradeoff is a situation where gaining something requires giving up something else. Most decisions involve tradeoffs—more money might mean less time, better quality might mean higher cost: {There's always a tradeoff between speed and accuracy}. The word frames choices as balanced exchanges rather than pure gains or losses.

Tradeoffs are exchanges where gaining one thing means losing or sacrificing another. The term implies that choices have costs—you can't have everything: {There are tradeoffs between price and quality}. In economics and engineering, tradeoff analysis weighs competing priorities. The word captures the uncomfortable reality that most decisions involve giving something up. Also spelled trade-offs.

A trader is someone who buys and sells goods or financial instruments. In commerce, traders deal in commodities: {fur traders}, {slave traders}, {traders at the market}. In finance, a trader executes transactions in stocks, bonds, or currencies, often for an institution: {She works as a derivatives trader on Wall Street}. Day traders buy and sell within a single session, trying to profit from short-term price movements.

Trades is the plural of trade—exchanges, transactions, or occupations involving skilled manual work. The trades refers collectively to skilled crafts like plumbing, carpentry, and electrical work: {He went into the trades instead of college}. In finance, trades are buy-and-sell transactions: {The algorithm executed thousands of trades per second}.

Trade winds are the steady winds that blow toward the equator from the northeast in the Northern Hemisphere and from the southeast in the Southern Hemisphere. They're called trade winds because sailing ships relied on them for commercial voyages. The term now appears figuratively for any reliable, favorable conditions: {The trade winds of economic growth have shifted}.

Trading is buying and selling, especially as a business activity. Stock trading, commodities trading, and currency trading all involve exchanging assets for profit. Trading can also mean exchanging things of comparable value: {We spent the afternoon trading stories}. A trading {post} is a remote commercial outpost. Day trading involves buying and selling securities within a single market session.

Tradition is the handing down of customs, beliefs, or practices from generation to generation. A tradition can be any specific custom so transmitted: {a family tradition of Sunday dinners}, {the Western literary tradition}. Tradition often implies unwritten rules or informal expectations rather than codified law: {By tradition, the eldest son inherits the farm}. Something done {by tradition} follows established precedent rather than formal requirement.

Traditional describes practices, beliefs, or customs passed down through generations rather than newly invented. A traditional {wedding} follows established conventions. Traditional {medicine} predates modern scientific approaches. The word often implies continuity with the past: {My family has a traditional Thanksgiving dinner}. Traditional can suggest resistance to change, sometimes approvingly (preserving heritage), sometimes critically (refusing to modernize).

Traditions are customs, beliefs, or practices passed down through generations within a group, family, or culture. They carry a sense of continuity with the past: {holiday traditions}, {family traditions}, {the Western literary tradition}. Tradition can also refer to this process of transmission itself, or to conventional ways of doing things: {bucking tradition}, {steeped in tradition}. Something done {by tradition} follows established custom rather than written rules.

Traffic is the movement of vehicles, people, or goods along routes of transportation, or the collective mass of things moving: {Traffic was backed up for miles}. By extension, traffic refers to the flow of data through communication networks or visitors through a website. The word also denotes illegal or disreputable commerce, particularly in drugs or humans, and as a verb means to engage in such trade: {They were arrested for trafficking weapons}. To traffic in something more generally is to deal in it, often with unsavory connotations.

Trafficked is the past tense of traffic, meaning to trade or deal in something—usually something illegal or morally objectionable. People are trafficked for forced labor or sexual exploitation. Drugs are trafficked across borders. The word carries connotations of illicit commerce: {She was trafficked into the country as a teenager}. Legal trading rarely uses this verb.

Traffickers are people who trade illegally in goods or humans. The word almost always implies criminal activity—drug traffickers move narcotics across borders, human traffickers exploit people for labor or sex. {Authorities arrested several traffickers at the border.} The term carries strong moral condemnation, distinguishing criminal operators from legitimate traders or smugglers of lesser goods.

Trafficking is the illegal trade or movement of people, goods, or substances. Human trafficking involves coercing or deceiving people into forced labor or sexual exploitation. Drug trafficking is the manufacture and distribution of controlled substances: {He was arrested for trafficking cocaine across the border}. The word implies organized criminal activity rather than casual dealing.

Tragedies is the plural of tragedy. A tragedy is a dramatic work depicting a protagonist's downfall, typically through fate or fatal character flaws: {Greek tragedies}, {Shakespearean tragedies}. More broadly, any event causing great suffering or loss: {The earthquake was a tragedy that claimed thousands of lives}. {Personal tragedies shaped her worldview.}

Tragedy originally meant a serious dramatic work depicting the downfall of a noble protagonist through fate or fatal flaw—Greek tragedies, Shakespearean tragedies. The word now more commonly describes any deeply sad event, especially one involving death or suffering: {The fire was a tragedy that claimed six lives}. A small tragedy is a lesser but still lamentable misfortune: {It would be a tragedy to let this opportunity pass}.

Tragic describes something causing or involving great suffering, destruction, or death. A tragic accident claims lives; a tragic flaw brings down a hero. In classical drama, tragedy follows noble characters to catastrophic ends—{Hamlet} and {Oedipus Rex} are tragic plays. In casual speech, tragic often means merely unfortunate or regrettable: {It's tragic that the restaurant closed}. This weakened sense irritates purists but reflects common usage.

A trail is a path through wilderness or rough terrain, typically made by repeated passage: {a hiking trail}, {a nature trail}. Trail extends to any track or trace left behind—a trail of {breadcrumbs}, a paper {trail}, a trail of {destruction}. To trail is to follow behind, either physically or in competition: {Our team trailed by six points}. It also means to drag or let hang loosely: {Her dress trailed on the ground}. A trailing plant grows along surfaces rather than upward.

A trailblazer is someone who creates a new path where none existed—originally through wilderness, now usually through fields of endeavor. The word emphasizes being first: {She was a trailblazer for women in medicine}. A trailblazer doesn't just succeed but opens the way for others to follow.

Trailblazers are people who forge new paths—literally clearing trails through wilderness, or figuratively pioneering in any field. The word emphasizes being first: {She was a trailblazer for women in science}. Trailblazers don't just succeed; they make it easier for others to follow.

Trailblazing means pioneering or innovative—being the first to do something that others will follow. The image is of cutting a path through wilderness for others to use: {her trailblazing work in genetics}, {a trailblazing civil rights leader}. A trailblazer opens new territory, whether literal or figurative.

A trailer is something towed behind a vehicle—a cargo trailer, a camper trailer, a boat trailer. In American English, trailer often means a mobile home: {They lived in a trailer park outside town}. A movie trailer is a short preview shown before features, originally because these clips trailed the main film. As a verb, to trailer is to transport something by trailer: {We trailered the horses to the fairgrounds}.

Trailers are previews shown before feature films, advertising upcoming releases—so called because they originally trailed after the main attraction. The term extends to any short promotional video: {movie trailers}, {game trailers}, {book trailers}. A trailer is also a wheeled vehicle towed behind another: a semi-trailer hauled by a truck, a camping trailer, or a mobile home. In this sense, trailer can carry class connotations: {trailer park}, {trailer trash}. To trailer something is to transport it on a trailer: {We trailered the boat to the lake}.

Trailing describes something that follows behind or hangs down loosely. A trailing {vine} grows along the ground or drapes from a container. In competition, the trailing team is behind in score. Trailing {edge} refers to the rear portion of a moving object, especially an aircraft wing. As a verb form, it captures the action of following: {The detective spent weeks trailing the suspect}.

Trails are paths through wilderness or rough terrain, typically for hiking, biking, or horseback riding: {We hiked the trail to the summit}. A trail is also a track or scent left behind: {The dogs followed the trail}. To trail is to follow behind or drag along: {She trailed her hand in the water}. Something that trails off diminishes gradually: {His voice trailed off}. In competitions, to trail is to be behind: {They trailed by ten points at halftime}.

The most frequent use of train is for the vehicle of rail travel, but that meaning came later; older meanings are still in use. The common theme of all trains is continuity through time or space. The train of a garment is the part that is dragged along behind. A train of thought is a succession of connected ideas. When train comes before another noun it is always in reference to the mode of transportation. The verb train is used mainly as educate, usually for a fixed time period and in a particular skill: train dogs to sniff out bombs, train volunteers in disaster relief. If someone is described as in training, it is often about improvement or mastery of a job or an athletic skill.

Trained describes someone or something that has been taught specific skills or behaviors through practice and instruction. A trained {nurse} has completed professional education. A trained {dog} responds to commands. The word implies readiness for a particular purpose: {trained soldiers}, {trained eyes} that notice what others miss. To be trained on something is to have learned to use it: {She was trained on the new software}.

A trainee is someone receiving training for a job or skill. The word emphasizes the learning stage—a trainee doctor, trainee pilot, or management trainee is not yet qualified to work independently. {The company hired six trainees for the summer program.} Trainee often appears as a modifier: {trainee wages}, {trainee position}.

A trainer is a person or thing that instructs or coaches, with a couple of exceptions. A dog trainer trains dogs. An elliptical trainer is a machine that allows a person to do physical training. A personal trainer is one you employ to help you get fit. A cross trainer is someone who does fitness routines outside of their athletic specialty, or a type of shoe that is designed for a variety of types of exercise. In British English, athletic shoes are called trainers.

Training is the process of teaching skills, knowledge, or behaviors through instruction and practice. It applies to humans learning job skills or academic subjects, athletes building physical conditioning, and animals being taught commands or behaviors. The word works as both noun and adjective: you undergo {training} before starting a new job, or complete a {training program} to earn certification. In machine learning, training refers to the process of feeding data to an algorithm so it learns to recognize patterns or make predictions.

Trains is the plural of train and the third-person singular verb form. A train is a connected series of railroad cars pulled by a locomotive: {The trains run every hour}. Extended uses keep the idea of things in sequence: a train of {thought}, a bridal {train}. To train is to teach skills through practice: {She trains new employees}. Someone who trains prepares physically: {He trains for marathons}.

Trainspotting is the British hobby of watching trains and recording their identification numbers, typically at railway stations or along tracks. Enthusiasts note locomotive types, liveries, and serial numbers in notebooks. The hobby is often mocked as the epitome of harmless but pointless obsession: {He spent his weekend trainspotting at Crewe}. By extension, trainspotting describes any obsessive cataloguing of trivial details: {His knowledge of craft beers borders on trainspotting}. (Capitalized Trainspotting is the novel and film.)

A trainwreck is literally a railroad accident, but the figurative sense dominates: a situation or person in spectacular disarray. A trainwreck unfolds chaotically and often publicly, impossible to look away from: {The interview was a complete trainwreck}, {Her life has been a trainwreck since the divorce}. Also spelled as two words.

Trainwrecks is the plural of trainwreck—literally, a collision or derailment of trains. The figurative sense dominates: a trainwreck is any spectacular disaster or catastrophically dysfunctional situation. A person whose life is chaotic may be called a trainwreck: {She's a complete trainwreck right now}. The appeal of trainwrecks, literal or figurative, is that they're hard to look away from.

A trait is a distinguishing characteristic or quality. People have personality traits like stubbornness or generosity. In genetics, traits are inherited characteristics passed from parents to offspring: {Blue eyes are a recessive trait}. The word often appears when cataloging someone's qualities: {Her best trait is her honesty}.

A traitor is someone who betrays a trust, allegiance, or loyalty—especially one who commits treason against their country. The word carries strong moral condemnation: {Benedict Arnold is America's most famous traitor}. More loosely, traitor describes anyone who abandons a cause or group: {His old fans called him a traitor for going mainstream}.

Traitors is the plural of traitor—people who betray their country, cause, or trust. The word carries strong moral condemnation: {The traitors were executed for giving secrets to the enemy}. In casual use, traitor softens to playful accusation: {You're watching the show without me? Traitor!}

Traits are distinguishing qualities or characteristics. A person's traits might be physical {(tall, red-haired)} or behavioral {(patient, quick-tempered)}. In biology, traits are heritable features passed from parents to offspring: {eye color is a genetic trait}. Character traits describe personality: {Honesty is her best trait}.

Trajectory is the path something follows through space—originally the curve of a projectile like a bullet or thrown ball, governed by gravity and momentum. The word extends to any course of movement or development: {the trajectory of her career}, {the company's upward trajectory}. In physics, trajectory remains technical; in everyday use, it often implies direction and momentum toward some outcome.

A tram is a passenger vehicle that runs on rails through city streets, powered by overhead electric cables. Called a streetcar or trolley in American English, trams are common in European and Australian cities: {We took the tram from the hotel to the old town}. In mining and industry, a tram is a cart or wagon running on tracks.

Tramp has meanings connected to heavy or aimless walking. To tramp is to walk with firm, heavy steps: {We tramped through the snow}. A tramp is also a person without a fixed home who wanders from place to place, often begging—more derogatory than "homeless." The word extends to a cargo ship without a fixed route. In dated slang, tramp is a derogatory term for a promiscuous woman: {They called her a tramp}. A tramp stamp is a tattoo on the lower back, typically on a woman.

Trample is to step heavily on something, crushing or damaging it underfoot: {The crowd trampled the flowers}. People trample grass, crops, or each other in a stampede. Figuratively, to trample someone's rights or feelings is to treat them with brutal disregard: {The new policy tramples civil liberties}. To {trample on} or {trample over} emphasizes the violation.

Trampling is the act of treading heavily on something, crushing or damaging it underfoot. Crowds trample people in stampedes; cattle trample crops. The word often suggests violence or disregard: {trampling on someone's rights}, {trampling over objections}. What gets trampled is harmed by being walked on—literally or figuratively.

A trampoline is a piece of equipment with a taut fabric surface stretched across a frame by springs, used for bouncing. Children jump on backyard trampolines; gymnasts and divers use them for training. The verb means to bounce on one: {We trampolined for hours}. Figuratively, something can trampoline upward—stocks, careers, enthusiasm.

Trampolines is the plural of trampoline—a piece of equipment with a taut, springy surface stretched across a frame, used for bouncing. Children jump on backyard trampolines; gymnasts and acrobats use them for training and performance. {The park had several trampolines for kids to play on.} As a verb, to trampoline is to bounce on one.

Tramps is the plural of tramp—a person who wanders from place to place without a home or regular work. The word carries connotations of poverty and vagrancy: {Tramps slept under the bridge}. In British slang, tramp is a derogatory term for a promiscuous woman. To tramp is to walk heavily or trudge: {We tramped through the snow for hours}.

Trams are rail vehicles that run on tracks through city streets, powered by overhead electric lines. Called streetcars in American English, trams were common urban transport before buses and cars dominated. Some cities have preserved or revived tram systems: {The tram rattled past the old quarter}. In British usage, a tram can also be a cable car or aerial gondola.

A trance is a half-conscious state between sleeping and waking, characterized by reduced awareness of surroundings and diminished responsiveness. Hypnotists induce trances; so do meditation, repetitive rituals, or intense focus. Someone in a trance appears mentally absent: {She stared out the window in a trance}. Trance also names a genre of electronic dance music with repetitive, hypnotic rhythms designed to produce an altered state in listeners.

Tranquil describes a state of calm, peace, and quietness. A tranquil {lake} has still waters; a tranquil {mind} is free from agitation. The word suggests an undisturbed serenity: {We spent a tranquil afternoon on the porch}. Tranquil tends toward the literary—calm and peaceful are more common in everyday speech.

Tranquility is a state of calm, peace, and freedom from disturbance. It suggests stillness both external and internal—a quiet lake has tranquility, as does a mind free from anxiety. {The tranquility of the countryside was a welcome change from city life.} The word often appears in contexts of meditation, nature, or escape from stress.

A tranquilizer is a drug that calms, sedates, or reduces anxiety. Doctors prescribe tranquilizers for anxiety disorders, insomnia, or agitation. Veterinarians use tranquilizer darts to sedate wild animals for capture or medical treatment. The word often carries connotations of being chemically subdued: {They had her so tranquilized she could barely speak}.

Tranquillity is a state of calm and peacefulness, free from disturbance or agitation. The word suggests deep, settled quiet rather than mere absence of noise: {the tranquillity of a mountain lake at dawn}, {She sought tranquillity after years of chaos}. Also spelled tranquility.

A tranquillizer is a drug that calms or sedates. Minor tranquillizers like Valium reduce anxiety; major tranquillizers like Thorazine treat psychosis. The term extends to animal sedation: {The vet used a tranquillizer dart on the bear}. Figuratively, anything that dulls or pacifies: {Television is a tranquillizer for the masses}. Also spelled tranquilizer.

Trans is a prefix meaning across, beyond, or through: {transatlantic}, {transcontinental}, {transform}. In chemistry, it describes molecular arrangements where atoms are on opposite sides. As a standalone adjective, trans is shorthand for transgender—identifying with a gender different from one's sex assigned at birth: {trans rights}, {trans women}, {a trans man}.

A transaction is an exchange between parties—typically a business deal involving goods, services, or money: {The transaction was completed in seconds}. In computing, a transaction is a sequence of operations treated as a single unit that either succeeds completely or fails completely, preventing partial updates. More broadly, any instance of conducting business or affairs: {diplomatic transactions between nations}.

Transatlantic means crossing or spanning the Atlantic Ocean: a transatlantic {flight}, transatlantic {cable}, transatlantic {slave trade}. It also describes relations or communication between Europe and North America: {transatlantic cooperation}, {the transatlantic alliance}. The word often implies the cultural and political ties between the United States and Western Europe.

Transcendence is the state of rising above or going beyond ordinary limits. In philosophy and religion, it describes existence beyond the physical world or beyond human experience: {The mystic sought transcendence through meditation}. More loosely, transcendence suggests surpassing what's normal or expected: {The performance achieved a kind of transcendence}. The adjective is transcendent.

Transcendent means beyond ordinary limits or experience—surpassing the usual. In philosophy and religion, the transcendent exists outside the physical world or human comprehension: {a transcendent God}, {transcendent reality}. More loosely, transcendent describes anything supremely excellent or awe-inspiring: {a transcendent performance}, {transcendent beauty}. The word elevates whatever it modifies above the mundane.

A transcript is a written record of something spoken or recorded. Court reporters produce transcripts of legal proceedings. Students request transcripts—official records of their academic courses and grades. A transcript of a podcast or interview converts speech to text. In biology, a transcript is RNA copied from a DNA template during gene expression.

Transfer is moving something from one place, person, or situation to another. You transfer funds between accounts, transfer to a different school, or transfer a call to another line. A transfer is the act itself or the thing moved: {a wire transfer}, {a bus transfer}. In sports, a transfer is a player who changes teams. Transfer paper or decals allow images to be moved onto surfaces.

Transfixed describes being held motionless by shock, fear, wonder, or intense focus. Someone transfixed by a sight cannot look away; someone transfixed by fear cannot move. The word carries a sense of being pinned in place: {She stood transfixed as the building collapsed}. {The children watched, transfixed, as the magician performed}.

Transform means to change something fundamentally—in form, appearance, nature, or character. A caterpillar transforms into a butterfly. A renovation transforms a space. The word implies thorough change rather than minor adjustment: {The experience transformed her outlook on life}. In mathematics and computing, a transform converts data from one form to another while preserving essential information.

Transformation is a thorough change in form, appearance, or character. A caterpillar undergoes transformation into a butterfly. A city experiences transformation through development. The word implies something more dramatic than mere alteration—a fundamental shift: {Her transformation from shy student to confident leader surprised everyone}. In mathematics, a transformation is an operation that changes a figure's position, size, or shape.

A transformer is a device that changes the voltage of an electrical current—stepping it up or down as needed for different applications. The large metal boxes on utility poles are transformers. In a different sense, a transformer is anything that fundamentally changes something: {She was a transformer of the industry}. In machine learning, a transformer is a neural network architecture that processes sequences by attending to all parts simultaneously, enabling modern large language models. (Capitalized Transformer refers to the toy franchise.)

Transformers are electrical devices that transfer energy between circuits, typically changing voltage levels—stepping power up for transmission or down for household use. The word also names a franchise of toys and media featuring robots that transform into vehicles. In machine learning, a transformer is a neural network architecture that processes sequences by attending to relationships between all elements simultaneously, powering modern language models like GPT. {The transformer blew during the storm.} {Kids played with their Transformers.} {The model uses a transformer architecture.}

Transgender describes a person whose gender identity differs from the sex they were assigned at birth. A transgender woman was designated male at birth but identifies as female; a transgender man, the reverse. Often shortened to trans: {trans rights}, {trans women}. The term emphasizes identity over biology, distinguishing it from older clinical language. Not to be confused with transsexual, which specifically implies medical transition, or with sexual orientation, which is a separate matter.

Transgression is the act of crossing a boundary or violating a rule, law, or moral standard. The word carries a sense of going beyond what is permitted: {His transgressions caught up with him}. It often appears in religious or ethical contexts, where it suggests sin or moral failing: {She sought forgiveness for her transgressions}. The term can also describe any overstepping of limits, from minor social missteps to serious violations.

Transgressions are acts that violate rules, laws, or moral boundaries. The word carries a sense of crossing a line that shouldn't be crossed, whether legal, ethical, or social. Religious contexts often use transgression to mean sin or violation of divine law. In everyday use, transgressions range from minor social missteps to serious offenses: {He apologized for his past transgressions}. The singular transgression and verb transgress share this sense of boundary violation.

Transience is the quality of being temporary or short-lived. The word often carries a melancholic undertone—an awareness that things pass: {the transience of youth}, {the transience of fame}. Buddhist philosophy emphasizes the transience of all phenomena. The adjective is transient.

Transit is movement from one place to another, especially the passage of people or goods through an intermediate point: {goods damaged in transit}, {passengers in transit to connecting flights}. Public transit refers to buses, trains, subways, and other shared transportation systems. In astronomy, a transit occurs when a smaller celestial body passes across a larger one, as when Venus transits the sun.

Transition is movement from one state, condition, or place to another. A {transition to democracy} marks political change. In writing, transitions connect ideas between paragraphs or sections. The verb means to make such a change: {She transitioned from teaching to administration}. In gender contexts, to transition is to align one's physical presentation or body with one's gender identity: {He began transitioning at nineteen}.

Transitioning is the process of moving from one state or condition to another. The word often appears in discussions of gender transition, where a person takes steps—social, medical, or legal—to live as a different gender than the one assigned at birth: {She began transitioning in her thirties}. More broadly, transitioning describes any gradual shift: {The company is transitioning to remote work}.

Transitions are changes or movements from one state, condition, or place to another. The word applies across domains: a political transition moves power from one leader to another, a gender transition involves changing one's outward presentation and often body, and a musical transition bridges two sections of a piece. In writing and speech, transitions are words or phrases that connect ideas and help readers follow the flow of thought. {The transition from college to working life can be jarring.}

To translate is to express meaning from one language in another: {She translated the novel from Russian into English}. The word extends to any conversion between forms or systems: translating ideas into action, translating scientific findings for general audiences. In biology, translation is the process by which genetic code becomes protein. Something that {doesn't translate} fails to carry over meaningfully: {His humor doesn't translate well across cultures}.

Translating is converting words or text from one language to another: {She's translating the novel from Japanese}. The word extends to any conversion between forms or systems: translating ideas into action, translating scientific findings for general audiences. In biology, translating refers to the process by which genetic code directs protein synthesis.

Translation is the process of converting text or speech from one language into another: {The translation from Japanese took three months}. More broadly, translation means converting anything from one form to another: {the translation of ideas into action}. A translation is also the resulting product—a translated work: {Which translation of the Odyssey do you prefer?}

Translations are texts converted from one language into another, or the act of converting them: {The translations from Latin were unreliable}. Translation also means converting between forms or systems more broadly—turning ideas into action, data into insights, or technical jargon into plain speech. {Something was lost in translation} suggests meaning degraded through conversion.

A translator converts text or speech from one language to another. Unlike an interpreter, who works with spoken language in real time, a translator typically works with written material: {The translator spent months on the novel}. The term extends to anyone who explains or mediates between different worlds: {She served as translator between the technical team and management}. In computing, a translator converts code from one programming language to another.

Transmission is the act of sending or passing something from one place or person to another: the transmission of {disease}, {data}, {radio signals}, {cultural values}. In vehicles, the transmission is the mechanism that transfers power from the engine to the wheels, with gears that shift to match speed and load: {automatic transmission}, {manual transmission}. A transmission can also be a specific broadcast: {We interrupt this transmission}.

Transmissions is the plural of transmission, which centers on the idea of sending something from one place to another. A car's transmission transfers power from engine to wheels. Radio and television transmissions carry signals through the air. Disease transmission spreads pathogens between hosts. {The transmissions were intercepted by enemy intelligence.} Data transmissions move information across networks.

A transmitter is a device that sends signals—radio waves, electrical impulses, or other forms of energy—from one point to another. Radio and television stations use transmitters to broadcast programming. In biology, a neurotransmitter is a chemical that carries signals between nerve cells. More loosely, anything that passes something along is a transmitter: {a transmitter of disease}, {a transmitter of cultural values}.

Transparency is the quality of being see-through—glass has transparency, murky water lacks it. The word extends to openness and honesty in communication: {The company promised greater transparency about its hiring practices}. Government transparency means public access to information about decisions and operations. In design, transparency refers to how much background shows through an image or layer.

Transparent describes something you can see through clearly. Glass is transparent; frosted glass is not. The word extends to actions and motives that are easily perceived: {a transparent attempt to change the subject}, {transparent lies}. In positive contexts, transparent suggests openness and honesty: {The company promised transparent accounting practices}. Transparency has become a buzzword for institutional accountability.

Transphobia is fear, hatred, or discrimination directed at transgender people—those whose gender identity differs from the sex assigned at birth. The term covers both overt hostility and subtler forms of prejudice, such as refusing to use a person's preferred pronouns or excluding trans people from spaces matching their gender identity. {She faced transphobia when applying for jobs}. The adjective is transphobic.

Transplant means to move something from one place to another where it will continue to grow or function. A gardener transplants seedlings from pots to the ground. In medicine, a transplant is an organ or tissue surgically moved from one body to another: {heart transplant}, {kidney transplant}. The verb covers both the surgical procedure and the broader sense of relocation: {She transplanted herself from Texas to New York}. A transplant can also be the person who relocated: {He's a California transplant}.

Transplants covers both the medical procedure and the broader act of moving something from one place to another. Surgeons transplant organs like kidneys and hearts from donors to recipients; gardeners transplant seedlings from pots to garden beds. As a noun, a transplant is either the thing moved or a person who has relocated: {She's a New York transplant living in Austin now}. The verb emphasizes uprooting and reestablishing, whether tissue, plants, or people.

Transport means to move something from one place to another: {The truck transports goods across the country}. As a noun, transport is the act of moving or the means of doing so—British English uses transport where American English prefers transportation. In an older sense, transport describes being carried away by strong emotion: {She was transported by joy}. Historically, to transport criminals was to exile them to a penal colony.

Transportation is the movement of people or goods from one place to another, or the systems and vehicles that enable this: {public transportation}, {air transportation}. In historical legal use, transportation meant exile to a penal colony: {The sentence was transportation to Australia}. The word often appears where the simpler "transport" would serve.

A trap is a device that captures something, usually with bait or a lure, and prevents its escape (mouse trap, grease trap, lint trap). A tourist trap does not prevent the escape of tourists, but attempts to keep them engaged. To trap something is to confine or detain it in a trap. If you are trapped in a place, there may not have been a trap involved, but you are not free to leave. Someone who traps for a living captures wild animals for their fur or meat.

A trapdoor is a hinged or sliding door set into a floor, ceiling, or roof, providing access to a space below or above. Trapdoors appear in stages for dramatic entrances and exits, in attics for storage access, and in adventure stories for escapes and surprises. In computing, a trapdoor is a hidden method of bypassing security—a secret way in: {The programmer left a trapdoor in the code}.

Trapdoors are hinged or sliding doors set into floors, ceilings, or roofs, allowing passage between levels or access to concealed spaces. Stage trapdoors let performers appear or vanish dramatically. In computing, a trapdoor is a hidden method of bypassing security: {The programmer left a trapdoor in the code}. Figuratively, trapdoors suggest sudden, unexpected drops or dangers.

A trapeze is a horizontal bar suspended by two ropes, used by acrobats for swinging and aerial gymnastics. The performer hangs from, swings on, or leaps between trapezes—often high above the ground in circus acts. {The flying trapeze act was the highlight of the show.} The word extends to similar suspended apparatus in gymnastics and aerial arts.

Trapped means confined or caught with no way out. A trapped {animal} is stuck in a snare or cage. A trapped {miner} is buried underground. The feeling extends to situations: {I felt trapped in a dead-end job}. Someone trapped in a burning building can't escape. To be trapped is to have your options cut off—physically, emotionally, or circumstantially.

A trapper is someone who catches animals using traps, typically for fur, pest control, or wildlife management. The term evokes frontier life and the fur trade: {French trappers explored the Canadian wilderness}. In modern use, trappers may work professionally removing nuisance animals or recreationally harvesting fur-bearing species like beaver or muskrat.

Trapping is the practice of catching animals in traps, typically for fur, pest control, or wildlife management: {He learned trapping from his grandfather}. The plural trappings refers to outward signs, equipment, or accessories associated with a particular role or status: {all the trappings of success}, {the trappings of royalty}. This sense suggests visible markers that may be more decorative than substantive.

Trappings are the outward signs, accessories, or adornments associated with something—especially with a position, role, or way of life: {the trappings of wealth}, {the trappings of power}, {all the trappings of success}. The word often carries a hint that these are superficial markers rather than the substance itself. Originally, trappings were decorative coverings for horses.

Traps are devices for catching animals or people—snares, pitfalls, or mechanisms that spring shut. The meaning extends to any situation that confines or deceives: {Don't fall into the trap of thinking it'll be easy}. A trap is also a light two-wheeled carriage, a bend in a pipe that holds water to block sewer gases, or the hinged door in a stage floor ({trapdoor}). To trap is to catch or confine. In slang, traps are the trapezius muscles of the upper back: {He's been working on his traps at the gym}.

Trash is waste material to be discarded—garbage, rubbish, refuse. Americans take out the trash; Britons take out the rubbish. The word extends to anything worthless or of poor quality: {That movie was trash}. As an insult, trash demeans people as low-class or contemptible: {white trash}, {trailer trash}. To trash something is to destroy or severely criticize it: {Critics trashed the album}. To {talk trash} is to boast or taunt aggressively, especially in sports.

A trashcan is a container for garbage or refuse, typically a cylindrical bin with a lid. American English uses trashcan; British English prefers dustbin or rubbish bin. The word appears both as one word and two: {trash can}. Figuratively, sending a file to the trashcan means deleting it—the icon on computer desktops mimics the physical object.

Trashed means destroyed, severely damaged, or thrown away as trash: {Vandals trashed the apartment}. {The car was completely trashed}. {She trashed the old letters}. Trashed can also mean harshly criticized: {The critics trashed the movie}. In slang, trashed means extremely drunk or high: {We got trashed on cheap beer}. The connection is to being wrecked, demolished, in no condition to function.

Trashing is harsh criticism or destruction. You can give something a trashing by attacking it verbally: {The film got a trashing from critics}. Physical trashing means wrecking or vandalizing: {Someone trashed the place}. In computing, trashing files means deleting them. The word implies thoroughness—not just damage but demolition.

Trashtalk is boastful or insulting speech aimed at opponents, meant to intimidate or provoke. Common in sports and gaming: {The teams exchanged trashtalk before the match}. As a verb, to trashtalk someone is to taunt or belittle them: {He's been trashtalking me all season}. Also spelled trash talk or trash-talk.

Trashtalking is the practice of insulting or taunting opponents to gain psychological advantage, common in sports and competitive gaming: {The trashtalking between the two fighters intensified at the weigh-in}. It ranges from playful ribbing to genuinely hostile provocation. Also spelled trash-talking or trash talking.

Trashy describes things that are cheap, low-quality, or lacking in taste. A trashy {novel} or trashy {TV show} offers shallow entertainment without artistic merit—though people often enjoy such things as guilty pleasures. When applied to people or their appearance, trashy suggests vulgarity or tackiness: {She thought his gold chains looked trashy}. The word carries class-based connotations, implying something beneath respectable standards.

Trauma is a deeply distressing experience that overwhelms a person's ability to cope. Physical trauma refers to serious bodily injury: {blunt force trauma}, {trauma surgery}. Psychological trauma leaves lasting emotional damage: {childhood trauma}, {generational trauma}. The adjective traumatic applies to both: {a traumatic brain injury}, {a traumatic divorce}. To traumatize is to inflict such harm.

Traumatic describes experiences that cause lasting psychological harm or distress: {a traumatic childhood}, {traumatic memories of the accident}. In medicine, traumatic refers to physical injury: {traumatic brain injury}, {traumatic amputation}. Casually, traumatic gets stretched to describe anything upsetting or unpleasant: {The interview was traumatic}.

To traumatise is to inflict lasting psychological damage, typically through a shocking or distressing experience: {The accident traumatised her for years}. The word can also describe physical injury in medical contexts, though the psychological sense dominates everyday usage. Often used loosely for any upsetting experience: {That movie traumatised me}. British spelling of traumatize.

To traumatize is to cause lasting psychological damage through a deeply distressing experience. The word comes from medicine—physical trauma is severe bodily injury—but now primarily describes emotional wounds: {The accident traumatized her for years}. In casual speech, traumatize is often hyperbolic: {That movie traumatized me} may just mean it was disturbing or unpleasant.

Traumatized describes someone who has experienced psychological damage from a deeply distressing event. A person traumatized by war, abuse, or disaster may suffer lasting effects: nightmares, anxiety, emotional numbness. The word extends to lesser upsets, often hyperbolically: {I'm still traumatized by that job interview}. The spelling traumatised is British.

Travel is a verb meaning to go from one place to another when the distance is relatively far. You do not travel to the store or to work, but you may travel for work—when you go on a business trip to another city, for example. Travel is not normally used for journeys undertaken on foot or on a bicycle. As a noun, travel most commonly designates the activity of going to distant places: After retirement the couple look forward to birding, travel, and volunteer activities.

A traveler is someone who journeys from place to place. The word covers everyone from tourists on vacation to business professionals in transit to wanderers with no fixed destination. {Fellow travelers} originally meant people on the same journey, but came to describe those who sympathize with a cause without formally joining it. Also spelled traveller in British English.

Traveling is moving from place to place, especially over considerable distances: {We spent the summer traveling through Europe}. The word often implies leisure or adventure rather than routine commuting. In basketball, traveling is the violation of moving without dribbling. Also spelled travelling (British English).

A traveller is someone who journeys from place to place—whether for work, pleasure, or necessity. The word often implies extended or repeated travel rather than a single trip: {a seasoned traveller}, {fellow travellers on the train}. In British usage, Traveller (often capitalized) refers to members of traditionally itinerant communities, including Romani people and Irish Travellers. Also spelled traveler.

Travellers is the plural of traveller, people who journey from place to place. In British and Irish English, Travellers (often capitalized) refers specifically to ethnic groups with traditionally nomadic lifestyles, including Irish Travellers and Romani people: {The council established a site for Travellers}. The term can carry prejudicial weight depending on context. This spelling is standard in British English; Americans write travelers.

A travesty is a grotesque or absurd misrepresentation of something, usually something serious or worthy. A trial conducted without proper procedure is {a travesty of justice}. The word carries indignation—calling something a travesty implies it fails so badly at what it should be that the result is insulting or farcical: {The investigation was a travesty from start to finish}.

A trawler is a fishing boat that drags a large net (a trawl) along the sea bottom or through the water to catch fish. The term extends to the crew operating such vessels. Trawler also describes a style of recreational boat with a displacement hull designed for fuel-efficient long-distance cruising rather than speed.

A tray is a flat, shallow container with raised edges, used for carrying, holding, or displaying items. Trays appear in countless contexts: a waiter carries drinks on a serving tray, office workers stack papers in an inbox tray, and airport security requires laptops placed in plastic trays. The word extends to any shallow receptacle that holds things for easy access or organization: {ice cube tray}, {baking tray}, {tray table on an airplane}.

Treacherous describes someone or something that betrays trust or conceals danger. A treacherous {ally} appears loyal but isn't. Treacherous {waters} look calm but hide currents or rocks. The word implies deception—the danger isn't obvious: {The treacherous path gave way beneath him}. Weather, terrain, and people can all be treacherous.

Treachery is betrayal of trust, especially through deception or disloyalty. The word implies someone close—an ally, friend, or subordinate—turning against you while pretending otherwise: {The king's downfall came through treachery, not battle}. Treachery differs from mere betrayal in suggesting cunning and concealment. The adjective is treacherous, which also describes dangerous conditions: {treacherous roads}.

Meanings of tread mostly have to do with contact of something with the ground. To tread in a particular way (lightly, carefully, cautiously) is to walk that way. A path or trail that is trodden has been walked on. When you tread water, however, you are simply trying to stay afloat. The noun tread can refer to the ground-facing surface of a tire or shoe. Tread is also an instance or manner of treading. The part of a stair that you put your foot on is a tread.

A treadmill is a device with a moving belt or platform that allows walking or running in place. Originally powered by human or animal labor to grind grain or pump water, modern treadmills are exercise machines. Figuratively, a treadmill is any exhausting routine that goes nowhere: {the treadmill of daily commuting}, {stuck on the corporate treadmill}.

Treadmills are exercise machines with continuous moving belts for walking or running in place. The name comes from an earlier device—a wheel turned by the stepping motion of prisoners or animals, used to grind grain or pump water. The figurative sense captures any exhausting routine that goes nowhere: {the treadmill of daily commuting}, {stuck on the corporate treadmill}.

Treason is the crime of betraying one's country, typically by waging war against it or aiding its enemies. In the United States, the Constitution defines treason narrowly—levying war or giving aid and comfort to enemies—making it difficult to prosecute. More loosely, treason describes any serious betrayal of trust: {Rooting for the Yankees felt like treason to his Boston family}.

Treasure is wealth stored or accumulated—gold, jewels, precious objects: {buried treasure}, {sunken treasure}. The word extends to anything highly valued: {The library's rare manuscripts are national treasures}. To treasure something is to value it deeply, often with care and protection: {She treasured the letters her grandmother had written}. A treasury holds treasure, whether a government department managing funds or a collection of valued things: {a treasury of folk songs}.

A treasurer is the person responsible for managing an organization's money—receiving funds, making payments, and keeping financial records. Companies, governments, clubs, and other groups typically designate a treasurer to oversee their finances: {She was elected treasurer of the student council}. The role ranges from volunteer bookkeeper to senior corporate officer.

Treasures are valuable things—wealth, jewels, precious objects. The word extends to anything cherished: {childhood treasures}, {national treasures}. A person can be called a treasure as a term of endearment: {You're an absolute treasure}. To treasure something is to value it highly: {I treasure the time we spent together}. What counts as treasure depends on who's counting.

A treasury is a place where wealth is stored or a fund of money available for use. By extension, it refers to any valuable collection: {a treasury of folk songs}, {a treasury of quotations}. The word suggests accumulated riches held in reserve, whether literal money or figurative wealth of knowledge, art, or literature. (Capitalized Treasury refers to a government department.)

To treat is to behave toward someone or handle something in a particular way: {She treats her employees fairly}, {Handle the package carefully—treat it like glass}. To treat an illness is to apply medical care. To treat a substance is to apply a process: {treated lumber}, {chemically treated water}. A treat is something pleasurable, especially food outside the ordinary: {an ice cream treat}, {We're in for a treat}. To treat someone is to pay for their meal or entertainment: {I'll treat you to dinner}. {Trick or treat} is the Halloween greeting demanding candy.

Treaties are formal agreements between nations or other sovereign entities, typically ending wars, establishing borders, or governing trade and diplomacy. A treaty carries the force of international law and usually requires ratification by each party's government: {The treaty was signed but never ratified by the Senate}. In a looser sense, any solemn agreement between parties: {a peace treaty between warring factions}.

Treatment is what you do to something or how you handle it. Medical treatment addresses illness or injury: {The treatment for his condition involved surgery}. Treatment of a subject is how it's covered: {The book's treatment of the Civil War was superficial}. Treatment of people is how you behave toward them: {She complained about her treatment by the staff}. In film, a treatment is a detailed outline of a screenplay before the full script is written.

Treats are pleasurable things given as rewards or indulgences—candy for children, biscuits for dogs, or small luxuries for oneself: {I brought treats for the office}. To treat someone is to provide them with something enjoyable, often at your expense: {Let me treat you to dinner}. A treat can also be an unexpected pleasure: {Seeing her was a real treat}. To treat something is to handle or deal with it in a particular way: {He treated the matter seriously}. Medical treatment addresses illness or injury; chemical treatment processes materials.

A treaty is a formal agreement between nations, typically ending a conflict or establishing terms for cooperation: {The treaty was signed in Paris}. Treaties cover matters like borders, trade, military alliances, and human rights. In the United States, treaties require Senate ratification. The verb is negotiate or ratify, not sign—though signing often makes headlines: {Both sides signed the peace treaty}.

A trebuchet is a medieval siege weapon that uses a counterweight to hurl heavy projectiles—typically large stones—at fortifications. Unlike catapults that rely on tension or torsion, trebuchets generate power through a pivoting arm with a heavy weight on one end and a sling on the other. The design allowed for impressive range and accuracy in breaching castle walls. Modern trebuchets appear mainly in physics demonstrations and pumpkin-chunking competitions.

The woody, towering plants we call trees inspire most of the other things we call tree because they share a characteristic branching, fractal shape. A family tree, for example, may show a pair of ancestors and their many descendants branching off from successive offspring. Anything that bears internal relationships analogous to this kind of inheritance an be called a tree. A tree diagram is one represented as originating at a single node and branching out multiply from there, as branches and twigs do from a trunk.

A treehouse is a small structure built among the branches of a tree, typically as a play space for children. The word evokes childhood adventure and imagination—a private refuge accessible by ladder or rope. Adults sometimes build more elaborate versions as retreats or novelty accommodations: {We stayed in a treehouse rental in Costa Rica}.

Treehouses are structures built among the branches of trees, typically elevated platforms with walls and a roof accessed by ladder or stairs. Most familiar as children's play spaces in backyards, treehouses range from simple wooden platforms to elaborate constructions with multiple rooms and amenities. The word is sometimes spelled as two words: {tree house}. Adults increasingly build treehouses as retreats, guest accommodations, or eco-tourism lodgings, capitalizing on the childhood appeal of living among the branches.

Trees are tall woody plants with a main trunk and branches forming a distinct crown. The term extends to similar structures: a family tree shows lineage, a decision tree maps choices, a directory tree organizes files. To tree an animal is to chase it up a tree: {The dogs treed the raccoon}. {Can't see the forest for the trees} means missing the big picture while focused on details.

The treetop is the uppermost part of a tree—its crown of branches and leaves. Usually plural: {Birds sang in the treetops}. The word evokes height and the forest canopy: {Sunlight filtered through the treetops}.

Trek is a long, difficult journey, especially one made on foot through rugged terrain: {a trek through the Himalayas}. The word implies effort and endurance rather than leisurely travel. More casually, trek describes any tedious journey: {the daily trek to work}, {I had to trek all the way across campus}.

Trekking is long-distance hiking, typically through rugged or remote terrain over multiple days: {We spent two weeks trekking through the Himalayas}. The word suggests more arduous travel than ordinary hiking—carrying gear, camping, and covering significant ground. More casually, trekking describes any effortful journey: {I'm not trekking all the way across town for coffee}.

Treks is the plural of trek, a long and difficult journey, especially on foot: {The refugees made exhausting treks across the mountains}. As a verb form, treks describes habitual or ongoing arduous travel: {She treks to the office every day through heavy traffic}. The word suggests effort and endurance rather than leisure.
