In British English, villa sometimes refers more modestly to a suburban house, particularly Victorian-era semi-detached homes.

Vinaigrette is a salad dressing made by emulsifying oil and vinegar, typically with mustard, garlic, or herbs: {a simple lemon vinaigrette}, {She tossed the greens with vinaigrette}. The ratio is usually three parts oil to one part vinegar. Unlike creamy dressings, vinaigrette is light and tangy.

To vindicate is to clear someone of blame or suspicion, or to prove that something was right or justified. A verdict may vindicate an accused person; later events may vindicate an unpopular decision: {History vindicated her warnings about the financial crisis}. Vindication carries a sense of triumph—not just being proven correct, but being proven correct after doubt or opposition.

Vindicated means proven right or justified after being doubted, accused, or challenged. Someone vindicated has been cleared of blame or shown to have been correct all along: {The new evidence vindicated her completely}. The word carries a sense of satisfaction—vindication often comes after a period of suffering suspicion or criticism: {I felt vindicated when the project succeeded despite everyone's doubts}.

Vindication is the clearing of blame or suspicion, or the demonstration that something previously doubted or criticized was actually correct or justified. When someone achieves vindication, they are shown to have been right all along: {The DNA evidence provided complete vindication for the wrongly convicted man}. The word carries a sense of triumph and relief, suggesting not just proof but also restoration of reputation or honor. {She saw the company's success as vindication of her controversial strategy}.

Vindictive describes someone who seeks revenge or holds grudges with unusual persistence. A vindictive person doesn't just get angry—they nurse resentment and look for opportunities to retaliate: {Her vindictive ex-husband fought for sole custody just to hurt her}. The word implies pettiness or disproportionate response, punishment beyond what the offense warranted.

A vine is a plant with a long, slender stem that trails along the ground or climbs by attaching to supports. Grapevines, ivy, and kudzu are vines. The word extends to any climbing or trailing growth: {Morning glories vined up the trellis}. To {wither on the vine} is to fail before reaching fruition. {Die on the vine} means the same. (Capitalized Vine was a video-sharing platform.)

Vinegar is a sour liquid made by fermenting alcohol, used in cooking, pickling, and cleaning. The sharpness comes from acetic acid. White vinegar is distilled and neutral; other varieties—wine, apple cider, balsamic—carry distinct flavors. Figuratively, vinegar suggests sourness of disposition: {full of piss and vinegar} means feisty and combative, usually said of someone young.

Vines are plants with long, flexible stems that climb or trail along surfaces. Some climb by tendrils or adhesive pads; others sprawl along the ground. Grapes, ivy, and morning glories are vines. The word extends to any climbing or trailing growth: {Vines covered the old stone wall}. Vine also appears in compounds: {grapevine}, {vineyard}.

A vineyard is land planted with grapevines, typically for wine production. The word often evokes images of rolling hillsides in wine country: {We toured vineyards in Napa Valley}. Vineyards may also grow table grapes or raisins. In biblical contexts, the vineyard appears as a symbol of cultivation and stewardship.

Vineyards is the plural of vineyard—land planted with grapevines, typically for wine production. The word often evokes wine country landscapes: {We toured the vineyards of Napa Valley}. Vineyards may refer to the agricultural plots themselves or to wine-producing estates more broadly: {Several local vineyards offer tastings}.

Vintage originally describes wine from a particular year's grape harvest, and by extension, the year itself: {a 1982 vintage}. The word now applies broadly to items from an earlier era, especially clothing, furniture, or cars prized for their age and quality: {vintage dresses}, {a vintage Mustang}. As an adjective, vintage suggests classic excellence or typicality: {vintage Beatles}, {vintage stupidity}. The term usually implies desirability—old enough to be interesting, not so old as to be antique.

Vinyl is a type of plastic, short for polyvinyl chloride (PVC). It appears in flooring, siding, clothing, and countless manufactured goods. Most distinctively, vinyl refers to phonograph records—the format that dominated music distribution before CDs and digital files: {I've been collecting vinyl since college}, {She prefers the warm sound of vinyl}. As an adjective, vinyl describes anything made from this material: {vinyl seats}, {vinyl records}.

A viola is a stringed instrument slightly larger than a violin and tuned a fifth lower, producing a deeper, mellower tone. It holds the alto voice in the string family and is a standard member of orchestras and string quartets. Viola also names a genus of flowering plants that includes violets and pansies, recognized by their distinctive five-petaled blooms. {She switched from violin to viola in high school.}

To violate is to break or fail to comply with a rule, law, agreement, or principle: {The company violated federal regulations}, {violating the terms of the contract}. More seriously, to violate a person is to treat them with disrespect or violence—especially through sexual assault. To violate a sacred space is to desecrate it. The noun violation covers everything from parking tickets to war crimes.

Violated is the past tense of violate, which means to break or fail to respect a rule, agreement, or someone's rights: {He violated the terms of his parole}, {The search violated her constitutional rights}. To violate a person is to assault them sexually. To violate a sacred place is to desecrate it. The word carries strong connotations of transgression against something that should have been protected or honored.

Violating is breaching or transgressing a rule, law, agreement, or boundary. Someone violating a contract fails to honor its terms. Violating someone's privacy means intruding where you have no right. The word often implies a serious breach rather than a minor infraction: {He was arrested for violating parole}. To violate a person, especially sexually, is to assault them—violating in this sense carries connotations of profound harm and desecration.

Violation is the breaking of a rule, law, agreement, or boundary. A traffic violation breaks driving laws. A violation of {privacy} crosses personal boundaries. A violation of {trust} betrays someone's confidence. The word often implies something more serious than mere infraction—violations suggest willful disregard or harm. In sports, a violation is a minor rule break that doesn't rise to a foul.

Violence is physical force that causes damage or harm. Except when the bringer of violence is inanimate (the violence of the storm), violence is usually intentional and viewed negatively. The phrase domestic violence refers to violence in a household, directed against a spouse, parent, or child. Violence is associated with war, terrorism, civil unrest, and crime. The associated adjective is violent.

Violent describes forceful physical action intended to harm, damage, or destroy. A violent {crime} involves physical force against a person. A violent {storm} has destructive intensity. Violent can also describe emotional intensity: {a violent temper}, {violent disagreement}. The word often carries condemnation but can be neutral when describing natural forces or dramatic action: {The car came to a violent stop}.

Violet is a blue-purple color, named after the small flowering plant with petals of that hue. The color sits at the short-wavelength end of the visible spectrum. Violets are modest wildflowers, often associated with humility and faithfulness: {a bouquet of violets}, {shrinking violet}. A {shrinking violet} is someone timid or shy—ironically, since the flowers spread aggressively. (Capitalized Violet is a given name.)

Violets are small flowering plants with heart-shaped leaves and delicate five-petaled blooms, most commonly in shades of purple, blue, or white. The color violet takes its name from these flowers. Wild violets grow in woodlands and gardens across temperate regions, while African violets are popular houseplants despite being unrelated to true violets. {She picked violets from the meadow.} The phrase {shrinking violet} describes someone excessively shy or modest.

A violin is a four-stringed musical instrument played with a bow, the smallest and highest-pitched member of the string family. The player holds it under the chin and draws the bow across the strings or plucks them. Violins anchor orchestral string sections and dominate classical solo repertoire, but appear across genres from folk to jazz. {She's been playing violin since age five.} Fiddle is an informal synonym, especially in folk and country music.

A violinist is a person who plays the violin. The term applies to anyone from beginners to concert soloists, though it often suggests some level of proficiency: {She's been a violinist with the symphony for twelve years}. {The wedding violinist played during the ceremony}.

Violins is the plural of violin, the smallest and highest-pitched member of the string family. An orchestra's violins divide into first and second sections, with first violins typically carrying the melody. The word appears in contexts ranging from classical performance to folk fiddling: {She's been playing violin since age five}. {The violins swelled as the scene reached its climax.}

A viper is a venomous snake, typically with a thick body and hinged fangs that fold against the roof of the mouth. The term covers many species across several continents. Figuratively, a viper is a treacherous or spiteful person: {She turned out to be a viper who betrayed everyone who trusted her}. To {nurse a viper in one's bosom} is to shelter someone who will ultimately harm you.

Vipers are venomous snakes characterized by long, hinged fangs that fold against the roof of the mouth when not in use. The family includes rattlesnakes, copperheads, and adders. Figuratively, a viper is a treacherous or spiteful person—someone who strikes when you least expect it: {She welcomed him into her home, not knowing she was harboring a viper}.

Viral is an adjective connected with the noun virus and refers to viruses in the context of biology and pathology, as in a viral infection or viral replication. With reference to the Internet, viral refers to the rapid spread or popularity of information. Viral marketing, for example, is an attempt to make something known through multiple Internet channels such as email, social media, and advertising on websites. When something such as a video goes viral on the Internet, it becomes extremely popular very fast because people and the media call attention to it.

Virality is the tendency of content to spread rapidly across the internet through sharing. A video, image, or post achieves virality when it gets passed from person to person at exponential rates: {The campaign's virality exceeded anything they'd planned for}. The term derives from how viruses spread—each infected host transmitting to multiple new hosts. Something with high virality has qualities that compel people to share it.

A virgin is a person who has never had sexual intercourse. The word extends to anything untouched or unused: {virgin territory}, {virgin snow}, {virgin olive oil} (from the first pressing). The {Virgin Mary} is central to Christian theology, and {the Virgin} alone often refers to her. Virgin can describe someone inexperienced in any activity: {a political virgin}. (Capitalized Virgin refers to the zodiac sign or the corporate brand.)

Virginity is the state of never having had sexual intercourse. The concept carries heavy cultural and religious weight, traditionally prized in women before marriage: {She lost her virginity on prom night}. The word extends metaphorically to any first experience: {I lost my political virginity volunteering for that campaign}. What counts as "losing" virginity varies by definition and perspective.

Virgins is the plural of virgin—people who have not had sexual intercourse. The word carries weight in religious and cultural contexts where virginity is prized: {The temple was tended by virgins}. It extends to inexperience generally: {political virgins}, {stock market virgins}. As an adjective, virgin describes things untouched or unused: {virgin soil}, {virgin forest}, {virgin olive oil}.

Virtual describes something that exists in effect or essence but not in actual form or fact. A virtual {monopoly} controls a market without being an official one. In computing, virtual refers to things simulated by software rather than existing physically: virtual {memory}, virtual {reality}, virtual {machine}. A virtual {meeting} happens online rather than in person. The word implies the functional equivalent of something without its literal presence.

Virtue is similar to morality in that it is conformity to a high standard of what is right. Aside from a moral context, a virtue is a commendable or beneficial quality: The film has many virtues, but brevity is not one of them. The common phrase by virtue of means because of and is unrelated to the moral meaning of virtue: They claim to be the greenest parking venue by virtue of the solar panels on their roof.

Virtues are qualities considered morally good or admirable—honesty, courage, patience, kindness. The word often appears in contrast to vices: {Prudence is among the classical virtues}. By extension, virtue means any beneficial quality: {the virtue of simplicity}, {the virtues of exercise}. To make a virtue of necessity is to treat an unavoidable situation as if you chose it. {By virtue of} means by means of or because of: {She succeeded by virtue of hard work}.

Virtuosity is exceptional technical skill, especially in the performing arts. A pianist with virtuosity executes impossibly difficult passages with apparent ease. The word implies mastery that goes beyond competence—a dazzling command that itself becomes part of the performance: {The solo was pure virtuosity}. Extended to other domains, it suggests any highly refined expertise: {rhetorical virtuosity}, {athletic virtuosity}.

A virtuoso is someone with exceptional skill in a fine art, especially music: {a violin virtuoso}, {a virtuoso pianist}. The word implies not just technical mastery but dazzling, seemingly effortless performance. As an adjective, virtuoso describes displays of such skill: {a virtuoso performance}, {virtuoso technique}. The term extends beyond music to any field where someone demonstrates exceptional artistry or expertise: {a virtuoso display of diplomacy}. Plural: virtuosos or virtuosi.

Virtuous describes someone who embodies moral excellence—honest, upright, principled. A virtuous person acts rightly even when no one is watching. The word often implies adherence to traditional values: {a virtuous life}, {virtuous conduct}. It can sound slightly old-fashioned or ironic when applied to minor behaviors: {How virtuous of you to recycle}. A virtuous circle is a chain of events where each positive outcome reinforces the next.

A virus is a microscopic infectious agent that replicates only inside living cells—unlike bacteria, viruses cannot survive or reproduce independently. Diseases caused by viruses include the common cold, influenza, and COVID-19. In computing, a virus is malicious code that spreads by copying itself into other programs or files: {My computer caught a virus}. Figuratively, anything that spreads rapidly and harmfully may be called a virus: {Misinformation is a virus}.

Viruses are infectious agents that replicate only inside living cells. In biology, a virus causes disease by hijacking cellular machinery: {the flu virus}, {HIV is a virus}. In computing, a virus is malicious code that spreads by attaching to programs or files: {My computer caught a virus}. Figuratively, ideas or content that spread rapidly are said to {go viral}.

A visa is an official endorsement in a passport permitting entry into or transit through a particular country. Visas may specify duration, purpose, and conditions: tourist visa, work visa, student visa. {Her visa expires next month.} {He applied for a visa to visit his relatives.} To visa a passport is to stamp it with such authorization. (Capitalized VISA is the credit card company.)

Visas is the plural of visa, an official endorsement in a passport permitting entry into or transit through a country: {Her visas were all in order}. The word also serves as a verb form meaning to stamp or mark with a visa: {The consul visas applications on Tuesdays}.

Visceral means felt deep in the body rather than reasoned in the mind. A visceral {reaction} is instinctive and immediate—{a visceral fear}, {a visceral hatred}. The word derives from viscera (internal organs), suggesting emotions experienced in the gut rather than the head. Visceral often describes art or experiences that provoke raw, physical responses: {The film's violence was visceral and unsettling}.

A vise is a clamping tool with two jaws that tighten by means of a screw, used to hold objects firmly while you work on them. Typically mounted to a workbench: {He secured the pipe in the vise before cutting it}. Figuratively, anything that grips tightly: {caught in the vise of debt}. Also spelled vice, especially in British English.

Visibility is the ability to see or be seen, often measured by distance: {Visibility dropped to near zero in the fog}. It extends to prominence or public awareness: {The campaign increased visibility for the cause}. In business and technology, visibility means access to information about status or progress: {We need better visibility into the supply chain}.

Visible means able to be seen. A visible {scar} can be noticed; visible {progress} is apparent to observers. The word extends from physical sight to general perception: {There was no visible improvement in his condition}. Visible often implies prominence or noticeability—a {visible presence} in the community, a {highly visible} public figure. The opposite is invisible.

Vision is the faculty of sight—the ability to see. It extends to what is seen, especially something imagined or supernatural: {She had a vision of her dead grandmother}. Vision also means foresight or the ability to plan wisely for the future: {a leader with vision}, {a vision for the company}. Someone's vision of something is their particular conception of it: {his vision of a just society}. As a modifier, vision suggests idealized seeing: {vision board}, {vision quest}.

Visionaries is the plural of visionary—people with unusual foresight or imagination about what's possible. The term implies seeing what others miss: {Tech visionaries predicted the smartphone revolution}. It carries admiration but can shade into skepticism when the vision seems impractical: {Critics dismissed them as visionaries disconnected from reality}.

A visionary sees possibilities others miss—someone with unusual foresight or imagination about the future. The word can praise genuine insight {a visionary leader who transformed the industry} or dismiss impractical dreaming {His plans were visionary but ignored basic economics}. As an adjective, visionary describes ideas, plans, or thinking characterized by such imagination. Visionary can also mean relating to supernatural visions or apparitions.

Visions is the plural of vision, covering all its senses. Vision is the faculty of sight, but visions are usually mental images—things seen in dreams, trances, or imagination rather than through the eyes. Religious figures receive visions; artists pursue creative visions. {She had visions of success}. {The prophet's visions warned of catastrophe}. A person who {has visions} may be inspired or delusional, depending on who's judging.

To visit is to go somewhere temporarily—to see a person, place, or thing and then leave. You visit friends, visit a doctor, visit a museum. The noun is the instance: {a brief visit}, {a hospital visit}. In American English, to visit with someone is to chat or spend time together: {We visited with the neighbors for an hour}. Figuratively, disasters or misfortunes visit people: {A plague visited the village}.

Visiting describes the act of going to see someone or something, or being somewhere temporarily. A visiting {professor} holds a temporary appointment at a university. Visiting {hours} are the designated times when you can see patients in a hospital or inmates in a prison. {We have visiting relatives this weekend.}

A visitor is someone who comes to a place temporarily—to see a person, tour a location, or conduct business. {We're expecting visitors this weekend.} The word implies impermanence: visitors don't stay. Hospital visitors come during visiting hours. Website visitors browse pages. A visiting professor holds a temporary appointment at an institution other than their own.

A visor is a projecting brim or shield that protects the eyes from sun or glare. On a cap, the visor is the stiff front piece: {She pulled down her visor against the bright light}. In a car, a visor is the hinged panel above the windshield that flips down to block sunlight. On a helmet, a visor is the movable front piece that covers the face.

Vista is a distant view, especially one seen through an opening or along an avenue of trees: {The path opened onto a vista of rolling hills}. The word suggests breadth and depth—a sweeping perspective rather than a glimpse. Figuratively, vista applies to mental prospects: {College opened new vistas for her}. The word carries a slightly elevated tone.

Vistas are expansive views, especially scenic ones seen through an opening or along an avenue: {The trail opened onto stunning mountain vistas}. The word suggests breadth and distance—a vista implies you can see far. Figuratively, vistas are prospects or possibilities that stretch before you: {The discovery opened new vistas for research}.

Visual relates to sight and seeing. A visual {learner} absorbs information best through images. Visual {effects} are what you see on screen. As a noun, a visual is an image or graphic element: {The presentation needs more visuals}. In the plural, visuals often means the imagery in a film or performance: {The visuals were stunning, but the plot was weak}.

Vital means essential to life or continued existence: {vital organs}, {vital signs}. By extension, vital describes anything critically important: {a vital piece of evidence}, {vital to our success}. The word also suggests energetic liveliness—someone with a vital personality is full of vigor and animation. {She remained vital well into her eighties.}

Vitality is the quality of being alive and energetic—physical vigor, mental alertness, or the capacity to thrive. A person with vitality seems full of life: {She had a vitality that lit up the room}. The word extends to organizations, cultures, or economies: {the vitality of the local arts scene}. Vitality suggests not just survival but flourishing.

Vitals are the essential organs that sustain life—heart, lungs, brain. In medical contexts, vitals refers to vital signs: pulse, blood pressure, temperature, respiration rate. A nurse {checks your vitals} during a routine visit. The word extends to anything essential: {protecting the vitals of the organization}. To strike at someone's vitals is to attack what matters most.

A vitamin is an organic compound essential for normal bodily function that must be obtained through diet because the body cannot produce enough of it. Vitamins are identified by letters—A, B, C, D, E, K—with some having numbered subtypes: {B12 deficiency}, {vitamin D3 supplements}. Vitamin can describe anything perceived as healthful or beneficial: {Laughter is a vitamin for the soul}.

Vitamins are organic compounds essential to health that the body cannot produce in sufficient quantities, so they must come from food or supplements. They're identified by letters—A, B, C, D, E, K—with some subdivided by number: B6, B12. {Take your vitamins.} The singular vitamin usually appears with its letter: {vitamin C}, {vitamin D deficiency}.

Vitriol originally named sulfuric acid and related corrosive substances. The figurative sense now dominates: bitter, caustic criticism or hostility. Vitriol suggests language that burns: {The comment section was full of vitriol}. The adjective vitriolic describes speech or writing marked by this caustic quality: {a vitriolic attack on her opponent}.

Vivid describes something intensely clear, bright, or striking to the senses or imagination. Vivid colors are saturated and eye-catching. A vivid memory feels immediate and detailed, as if relived: {I have vivid memories of that summer}. Vivid dreams are unusually realistic or intense. A vivid description makes scenes come alive through sharp, evocative detail.

A vixen is a female fox. The word extends to a sharp-tempered or quarrelsome woman, though this sense has softened—vixen now often suggests a woman who is attractively fierce or sexually bold: {She played the vixen in every role}. The shift from insult to compliment parallels similar reclamations of words for assertive women.

A vlog is a video blog—regular video content posted online, typically documenting personal experiences, opinions, or daily life. The term blends "video" and "blog." Someone who creates vlogs is a vlogger: {She vlogs about her travels}. As a verb, to vlog is to create such content: {He's been vlogging for five years}.

A vlogger is someone who creates video blogs—regular video content posted online, typically on platforms like YouTube. The term combines "video" and "blogger." Vloggers often document daily life, share opinions, or focus on specific interests: {She's a beauty vlogger with millions of subscribers}. The activity is vlogging.

Vlogging is creating video blogs—regular video content documenting one's life, interests, or expertise, typically posted to platforms like YouTube. The term blends "video" and "blogging." A vlogger might share daily routines, travel experiences, product reviews, or commentary: {She's been vlogging about her renovation project}. The format emphasizes personality and direct address to viewers.

Vlogs are video blogs—regular online video content where someone talks directly to the camera about their life, opinions, or activities. The format emphasizes personality and informal delivery over production quality. Vloggers build audiences on platforms like YouTube by posting consistently: {She vlogs about her daily routine}, {travel vlogs}, {beauty vlogs}. The verb vlog means to create such content.

Vocabulary is the stock of words a person knows or that belong to a language, field, or text. A reader's vocabulary grows through exposure; a writer's vocabulary shapes their style. Technical fields have specialized vocabularies: {legal vocabulary}, {medical vocabulary}. The word can also mean a list of terms with definitions, as in a textbook glossary.

Vocal relates to the voice or to speaking out. The vocal cords produce sound; vocal music features singing rather than instruments alone. Someone who is vocal expresses opinions freely and forcefully: {She's been vocal about her opposition to the plan}. As a noun, vocals refers to the singing parts in a song: {The vocals on that track are incredible}.

Vocals are the sung or spoken parts of a musical performance, as distinct from instrumental accompaniment: {The vocals on that track are incredible}. A vocalist is a singer. In recording contexts, vocals often get recorded separately and mixed in later. Lead vocals carry the main melody; backup or backing vocals provide harmony or support.

A vocation is work you feel called to do—originally a divine calling to religious life, now any career pursued with a sense of purpose or personal mission: {Teaching isn't just a job for her; it's a vocation}. The word implies the work suits your nature or talents. Vocational training prepares people for specific trades or occupations.

Vodka is a clear distilled spirit, traditionally made from fermented grains or potatoes. It originated in Eastern Europe and is characterized by its neutral flavor, making it a base for countless cocktails: {vodka tonic}, {vodka martini}, {Bloody Mary}. Vodka is typically around 40% alcohol by volume. {She ordered a vodka on the rocks.}

Vogue is the prevailing fashion or style at a particular time: {Minimalist design is in vogue right now}. Something in vogue is popular and widely adopted; something out of vogue has fallen from favor. The word often carries a hint of transience—what's in vogue today may be passé tomorrow. To vogue is to strike dramatic poses imitating fashion models, a dance style originating in Black and Latino LGBTQ ballroom culture. (Capitalized Vogue is the fashion magazine.)

Vogueing is a stylized form of dance that emerged from Black and Latino gay ballroom culture, characterized by angular poses, dramatic arm movements, and model-like runway walks. Dancers strike poses inspired by fashion photography, often in competitive "voguing battles" at balls: {She was vogueing on the dance floor}. Also spelled voguing.

Voguing is a stylized form of dance originating in Black and Latino gay ballroom culture, characterized by angular poses, dramatic arm movements, and model-like runway walks that mimic fashion magazine poses. Performers "strike a pose" in competitive battles called balls: {She was voguing on the dance floor}. The style gained mainstream visibility through Madonna's 1990 song "Vogue."

Your voice is the audible sound from your mouth, used to produce speech, music, or other sounds. More personally, someone’s voice is their particular way of expressing themselves; a writer who finds her voice settles into her writing style and manner of storytelling. If you have a voice you have the right or opportunity to express yourself about something. In linguistics, a sound that is voiced causes the vocal cords to vibrate. To voice an opinion or concern is to express it in speech or writing.

Voicemail is a system that records telephone messages when the recipient doesn't answer. The term also refers to the messages themselves: {I left you a voicemail}, {Check your voicemail}. It replaced answering machines for most purposes once mobile phones became standard. Also spelled voice mail.

A voiceover is narration or commentary spoken by someone not visible on screen, heard over film, television, or video content. The voice might belong to a character whose thoughts we hear, an omniscient narrator, or an announcer: {The documentary's voiceover was recorded in three languages}. Also spelled voice-over.

Voices is the plural of voice—the sounds people make when speaking or singing, or the distinctive qualities of those sounds: {I could hear voices in the next room}, {The choir blended their voices beautifully}. Voices also names the distinct perspectives or styles in writing: {The novel weaves multiple voices together}. As a verb, voices means expresses: {She voices her concerns at every meeting}.

Void doesn’t look much like vacuum, but if you remember that it is related, you can remember its meanings. A void is an empty place, especially when this results from the removal of everything. To fill a void is to supply some essential thing that is missing. In law, something that is void is not valid or enforceable. Food that is nutritionally void contains nothing the body needs. To void something in law is to declare it invalid.

Voids is the plural of void—empty spaces or gaps, particularly where something is expected or once existed. In construction and manufacturing, voids are unwanted air pockets or hollow spots: {The inspector found voids in the concrete}. In law, voids may refer to contracts declared invalid. As a verb, voids means empties, invalidates, or excretes: {The warranty voids if you remove the seal}; {The patient voids normally}.

Voilà is a French exclamation used in English to call attention to something that has just been accomplished or revealed, often with a flourish. It translates roughly as "there it is" or "there you have it." The word typically accompanies a demonstration, reveal, or completion of a task: {Add a little garnish and—voilà!—dinner is served}. Though properly spelled with a grave accent, the anglicized voila is common, and the playful misspelling viola (the instrument) appears in casual writing.

Volatile describes something liable to change rapidly and unpredictably, usually for the worse. A volatile {situation} could erupt at any moment. A volatile {personality} swings between emotional extremes. Volatile {markets} see dramatic price swings. In chemistry, volatile substances evaporate quickly at normal temperatures—gasoline is highly volatile. The thread connecting these uses is instability: what's volatile won't stay put.

Volatility is the tendency to change rapidly and unpredictably. In chemistry, volatile substances evaporate quickly at room temperature. In temperament, a volatile person is prone to sudden emotional shifts. In finance, volatility measures how much an asset's price fluctuates: {The stock's volatility makes it risky for conservative investors}. High volatility means dramatic swings; low volatility suggests stability.

Volcanic describes anything relating to volcanoes—volcanic eruptions, volcanic rock, volcanic islands formed by undersea eruptions. The word extends to temperaments or situations that are explosive and unpredictable: {His volcanic temper made everyone nervous}. A volcanic personality may erupt suddenly and violently after a period of apparent calm.

A volcano is an opening in the earth's surface where molten rock, ash, and gases escape from below. The term also applies to the mountain or hill formed by accumulated eruptions: {Mount Vesuvius is an active volcano}. Figuratively, a volatile situation may be a volcano waiting to erupt, or someone might {explode like a volcano} when losing their temper.

Volcanoes is the plural of volcano—an opening in the earth's crust through which molten rock, ash, and gases erupt. The word covers both the geological vent and the mountain that forms around it: {The Hawaiian islands were created by volcanoes}. Figuratively, a person or situation described as a volcano is prone to explosive outbursts.

Volcanos is the plural of volcano, a mountain or hill with openings through which molten rock, ash, and gases erupt from beneath Earth's crust. The spelling volcanos and volcanoes are both standard, with volcanoes more common. {Hawaii's volcanos attract millions of tourists each year.}

A volley is a simultaneous discharge of missiles—arrows, bullets, or stones—or a rapid succession of them: {a volley of gunfire}. In tennis and similar sports, a volley is hitting the ball before it bounces: {She won the point with a crisp volley at the net}. The word extends to any burst of things coming at once: {a volley of questions}, {a volley of insults}. To volley is to fire or exchange in rapid succession.

Volleyball is a sport in which two teams separated by a high net try to ground a ball on the opponent's court. Players strike the ball with their hands or arms, passing among teammates before sending it over. The ball itself is also called a volleyball—lighter and softer than a basketball, designed for repeated striking. {We played volleyball on the beach all afternoon.}

Voltage is the force that pushes electrical current through a circuit, measured in volts. Think of it as electrical pressure—higher voltage means more push. {The outlet supplies 120 volts}. In figurative use, voltage suggests intensity or energy: {The debate lacked voltage}.

Volume is the amount of space something occupies or contains: {the volume of water in the tank}, {What's the volume of this box?} It also means amount or quantity more generally: {the sheer volume of email I receive}. Volume is the loudness of sound: {Turn down the volume}. A volume is a book, especially one in a series: {the first volume of his memoirs}, {a leather-bound volume}. The phrase {speaks volumes} means something conveys a great deal without words: {Her silence spoke volumes}.

Volumes is the plural of volume, which measures how much space something occupies or how much a container holds. Volumes also refers to multiple books, especially in a set: {a twelve-volume encyclopedia}, {speaking volumes} about someone's character. The phrase {volumes of} means large quantities: {volumes of data}, {volumes of complaints}. In audio, volume is loudness level.

Voluntary describes actions done by choice rather than compulsion or obligation. A voluntary {confession} comes freely, not under duress. Voluntary {muscles} respond to conscious will, unlike the heart. A voluntary is also a piece of organ music played before, during, or after a church service—traditionally at the organist's discretion. The noun volunteer shares this root of willing participation.

A volunteer is someone who offers their services without being required or paid: {We need volunteers to staff the booth}. Volunteer work is done willingly rather than for compensation. As a verb, to volunteer is to offer oneself or information freely: {She volunteered to help}, {He volunteered that he'd seen them leave together}. Volunteering someone else commits them without asking: {I got volunteered to organize the potluck}.

Volunteering is offering one's time or services without pay, typically for charitable, civic, or community purposes. The word emphasizes the voluntary nature of the work—no one compelled you: {She's been volunteering at the food bank}. Volunteering can also mean putting yourself forward: {I'm not volunteering for that assignment}.

Volunteers are people who offer their services without pay. Someone volunteers by stepping forward willingly: {She volunteered to help at the food bank}. The word implies choice rather than obligation or compensation. To volunteer information is to offer it without being asked: {He volunteered that he'd seen them together}. Volunteer also works as an adjective: a volunteer {army}, volunteer {firefighters}.

Voluntold describes being assigned a task under the guise of volunteering—when someone in authority "asks" in a way that makes refusal impossible. The word blends volunteer and told, capturing the coercion beneath the polite fiction: {I was voluntold to organize the company picnic}. Common in military and corporate settings where "requests" from superiors aren't really optional.

Voluptuous describes full, curvaceous physical beauty, especially a woman's body with ample breasts and hips: {a voluptuous figure}, {voluptuous curves}. The word carries sensual overtones—suggesting pleasure in the flesh rather than mere measurement. It extends to anything richly sensual or luxurious: {voluptuous fabrics}, {voluptuous music}. The connotation is indulgent, even decadent.

Vomit is to expel the contents of the stomach through the mouth—the body's forceful rejection of what it has taken in. The noun is both the act and the expelled matter itself. Figuratively, anything that spews forth uncontrollably vomits: {The volcano vomited ash}. Something disgusting may {make you want to vomit}.

Vomiting is the forceful expulsion of stomach contents through the mouth. The word functions as both a verb form and a noun: {The patient has been vomiting since noon}; {Persistent vomiting can lead to dehydration}. As an adjective, it describes the act in progress: {a vomiting child}.

Voodoo is a religion originating in West Africa and developed in the Caribbean, particularly Haiti, blending African traditions with Catholic elements. It involves belief in spirits, ritual practices, and communication with the dead. In popular culture, voodoo often appears sensationalized—{voodoo dolls}, curses, zombies—bearing little resemblance to actual practice. Figuratively, voodoo describes something mysterious or irrational: {voodoo economics}, {It's not voodoo, it's just math}.

A vortex is a spinning mass of fluid—water, air, or other substance—that draws things toward its center. Whirlpools and tornadoes are vortexes. The word extends to anything that pulls you in irresistibly: {She was drawn into a vortex of debt}. Plural: vortexes or vortices.

A vote is a formal expression of choice in an election or decision: {cast your vote}, {the vote was unanimous}. To vote is to express such a choice: {I voted for the challenger}. Vote extends to any group decision: {Let's vote on where to eat}. The vote can mean the right to participate: {women winning the vote}. {Vote of confidence} signals support; {no-confidence vote} signals the opposite.

A voter is someone who casts a vote in an election or other decision-making process. The term applies both to those actively voting and to those eligible to vote: {registered voters}, {likely voters}, {voter turnout}. Politicians court voters; analysts study them. In contexts like shareholder meetings, voters are those entitled to participate in formal decisions.

Voters are people who cast votes in elections or other decision-making processes. The term usually refers to citizens eligible to participate in political elections: {Voters turned out in record numbers}. It can also describe anyone with voting rights in a particular context—shareholders, committee members, or award panelists. {Swing voters} are those whose preferences shift between parties or candidates.

Votes are expressions of choice in a formal decision-making process—elections, legislative proceedings, or group deliberations. To vote is to cast such an expression: {I voted for the challenger}. The vote can mean either the act of voting or the collective result: {The vote was unanimous}. Figuratively, to vote with your feet is to express disapproval by leaving.

Voting is the act of casting a vote—expressing a choice in an election, poll, or group decision. The term covers both the individual act {I'm voting tomorrow} and the collective process {Voting begins at 7 a.m.}. As a modifier, voting describes things related to this process: voting {booth}, voting {rights}, voting {bloc}.

To vouch for someone or something is to personally guarantee their quality, truth, or reliability: {I can vouch for her honesty}. The word implies putting your own credibility on the line—if you vouch for someone who proves untrustworthy, your reputation suffers too. A voucher is a document that serves as proof of payment or entitlement.

A vow is a solemn promise or commitment, often made formally or before witnesses: {marriage vows}, {monastic vows}, {a vow of silence}. Vows carry more weight than ordinary promises—breaking one suggests moral failure. To vow is to make such a commitment: {She vowed to return}, {He vowed revenge}.

A vowel is a speech sound produced with an open vocal tract—the letters A, E, I, O, U, and sometimes Y represent these sounds in English. Vowels form the core of syllables; every syllable needs at least one. The term also refers to the letters themselves: {The word "rhythm" has no vowels except Y}. Consonants are the contrasting category.

Vowels are the speech sounds produced with an open vocal tract, represented in English by the letters A, E, I, O, U, and sometimes Y. They form the core of syllables and contrast with consonants, which involve some obstruction of airflow. In casual use, vowels often refers just to these letters rather than the sounds themselves: {The word "rhythm" has no vowels except Y}. Learning to identify vowels is among the first tasks in reading instruction.

Vows are solemn promises or pledges, especially those made in formal or sacred contexts. Wedding vows bind couples in marriage; religious vows commit a person to a faith or order. The singular vow works the same way: {She made a vow of silence}. To vow is to make such a promise: {He vowed to return}.

A voyage is a long journey, especially by water or through space: {The voyage across the Atlantic took three weeks}, {the Voyager spacecraft's voyage to the outer planets}. The word carries more weight than trip—it suggests distance, duration, and often discovery or adventure. A maiden voyage is a ship's first journey. To voyage is to make such a journey, though the verb is literary and less common than the noun.

A voyager is a person who makes a voyage—a long journey, especially by sea or through space. The word carries a sense of adventure and discovery beyond ordinary travel: {The voyagers set sail for the New World}. It appears in literary and historical contexts more than everyday speech, suggesting exploration into unknown territory. (Capitalized Voyager refers to NASA spacecraft.)

Voyages are long journeys, especially by sea or through space. The word carries a sense of significant distance and duration—a cruise across the Atlantic is a voyage, while a ferry ride is not. Figuratively, voyages describe any extended journey of discovery: {a voyage of self-discovery}, {voyages into the unknown}. The verb means to make such a journey: {They voyaged across the Pacific}.

A voyeur is someone who derives sexual pleasure from watching others undress or engage in sexual activity, typically without their knowledge. More broadly, voyeur describes anyone who enjoys observing others' private moments or misfortunes: {The media coverage turned us all into voyeurs of their divorce}. The related noun voyeurism covers both the paraphilia and the general tendency toward intrusive watching.

Voyeurism is deriving sexual pleasure from watching others undress, engage in sexual activity, or perform other private acts—typically without their knowledge or consent. The term extends to any fascination with observing others' private lives: {The show appeals to voyeurism, letting viewers peek into strangers' homes}. A voyeur is one who engages in this behavior.

Vroom is the sound of an engine revving or a vehicle accelerating rapidly. It captures the throaty roar of power and speed: {The motorcycle went vroom and disappeared down the highway}. As a verb, to vroom is to make this sound or to move with such noise: {Sports cars vroomed past the finish line}. The word is onomatopoeic and often appears in children's play or enthusiastic descriptions of vehicles.

Vulgar describes what is crude, coarse, or lacking in taste or refinement. Vulgar {language} includes profanity and obscenity. Vulgar {humor} relies on bodily functions or sexual content. A vulgar {display of wealth} is ostentatious and tasteless. The older sense—common or ordinary, belonging to the masses—survives in phrases like {the vulgar tongue} (everyday language versus Latin) but sounds archaic.

Vulgarity is crudeness or coarseness, especially in language, behavior, or taste. The word covers a spectrum from mere tastelessness to outright obscenity: {The comedian's vulgarity alienated half the audience}. A vulgarity is a specific instance—a crude word or act: {He peppered his speech with vulgarities}. The term implies violation of social refinement rather than moral transgression.

Vulnerability is the state of being open to harm, attack, or damage. A security vulnerability is a weakness that can be exploited. Emotional vulnerability means allowing oneself to be seen and potentially hurt: {It takes courage to show vulnerability}. The word often carries positive connotations in psychology—openness to connection requires accepting risk of rejection.

If someone is vulnerable it means they are at risk of some injury, damage, or loss: Homeless people are particularly vulnerable in these frigid temperatures. Vulnerable usually applies to living things, especially people, but inanimate objects can also be called vulnerable: The contractors assured us that the system was not vulnerable to hackers, but they were wrong. In the card game of bridge, vulnerable means subject to certain penalties.

A vulture is a large bird that feeds on carrion—the flesh of dead animals. Vultures circle high in the sky, watching for carcasses below. The word extends to people who prey on the vulnerable or profit from others' misfortune: {Vultures descended on the estate sale before the body was cold}. A {vulture capitalist} buys distressed companies to strip their assets.

Vultures are large birds that feed primarily on carrion—the flesh of dead animals. They circle high on thermal currents, scanning for carcasses below. Figuratively, vultures are people who prey on the vulnerable or dying, eager to profit from others' misfortune: {The vultures were circling before the company even announced layoffs}. {Debt collectors descended like vultures}.

Wacko is informal for a crazy or eccentric person: {Some wacko called the office three times today}. As an adjective, it describes irrational or bizarre behavior: {a wacko conspiracy theory}. The word is dismissive rather than clinical—you might call someone wacko for beliefs you find absurd, not for genuine mental illness.

Wacky means amusingly strange or unconventional, suggesting playful eccentricity rather than genuine oddness: {a wacky sense of humor}, {wacky hijinks}. The word carries a lighthearted tone—something wacky is weird in an entertaining way. Also spelled whacky.

To waddle is to walk with short steps while swaying from side to side, the gait characteristic of ducks and penguins. People waddle when their build or condition makes a normal stride awkward—a heavily pregnant woman, someone carrying too much weight, a toddler in a bulky diaper: {He waddled to the refrigerator in his bathrobe}. The noun is the walk itself: {the penguin's distinctive waddle}.

Waddles is the third-person singular of waddle, to walk with short steps while swaying from side to side, like a duck or penguin. The gait suggests a wide body or awkward movement: {The toddler waddles across the room}. Waddles can also be a noun—multiple instances of waddling: {His waddles grew more pronounced as he tired}.

Waddling is walking with short steps while swaying from side to side, the characteristic gait of ducks and penguins. People waddle when their build or condition makes a smoother stride difficult: {She waddled down the hall in her ninth month of pregnancy}. The word often carries a slightly comic or unflattering tone.

To wade is to walk through water or another substance that offers resistance, typically at a depth that doesn't require swimming: {We waded across the shallow stream}. By extension, to wade through something is to make slow, effortful progress: {I spent the weekend wading through tax documents}. To {wade in} or {wade into} is to enter forcefully or without hesitation, often into a conflict or difficult situation: {She waded into the debate with strong opinions}. (Capitalized Wade is a given name or surname.)

Wading is walking through water or another substance that impedes movement, typically water shallow enough to keep your head above the surface: {wading in the creek}, {wading through the flooded street}. Figuratively, to wade through something is to make slow progress through difficult or tedious material: {wading through a dense legal document}, {wading through hundreds of emails}.

A wafer is a thin, flat, crisp piece of something—typically food. Communion wafers are unleavened bread used in Christian Eucharist. Ice cream sandwiches use wafer cookies. In electronics, a silicon wafer is a thin slice of semiconductor material from which microchips are cut. The word suggests delicacy and precision: {wafer-thin slices of prosciutto}.

Waffle names two unrelated things. The food is a batter cake with a grid pattern, cooked in a hinged iron that gives it characteristic indentations: {Belgian waffles}, {chicken and waffles}. The verb waffle means to speak or write evasively, avoiding commitment: {The candidate waffled on immigration policy}. To waffle is to equivocate, to go back and forth without deciding.

Waffles are crisp, golden cakes made from batter cooked in a hinged iron that imprints a grid of deep pockets—ideal for holding butter and syrup. As a verb, to waffle is to speak or write vaguely, avoiding commitment: {The candidate waffled on the tax question}. In British usage, waffling also means going on at length without saying much.

Waffling is speaking or writing vaguely, avoiding commitment to a clear position. Politicians waffle when they hedge on controversial issues: {She accused him of waffling on immigration}. The word suggests evasiveness or indecision rather than thoughtful nuance. In British usage, waffling also means rambling on pointlessly: {He spent twenty minutes waffling about nothing}.

Wag means to move rapidly back and forth or up and down, typically said of a dog's tail: {The dog wagged its tail when she came home}. Tongues wag when people gossip. A wag is also a witty person given to joking—someone whose tongue wags entertainingly: {He was the office wag, always ready with a quip}.

Wage is payment for work, typically calculated by the hour or day rather than as an annual salary. The plural wages often appears even for a single job: {She earned good wages at the factory}. The minimum wage is the lowest hourly pay legally permitted. To wage is to carry on or conduct, almost always with war or a campaign: {They waged a fierce battle for market share}.

A wager is a bet—something risked on an uncertain outcome: {I'll wager ten dollars he doesn't show up}. The word sounds slightly more formal than bet, appearing often in legal or philosophical contexts: Pascal's wager argues believing in God is the rational choice. To wager is to stake money or reputation on a prediction: {She wagered her career on the project's success}.

Wages are payment for work, typically calculated by the hour or day and paid weekly or biweekly. The term often implies manual or hourly labor, distinguishing it from salary, which suggests professional or administrative positions with annual compensation. {The minimum wage isn't enough to live on.} In a moral or biblical sense, wages are what one earns through actions: {The wages of sin is death.}

Wagging is the back-and-forth movement of something flexible, especially a tail. A dog's wagging tail signals excitement or happiness. Tongues wag when people gossip: {Tongues were wagging about the scandal}. A finger wags in admonishment. The phrase {the tail wagging the dog} describes a situation where a minor part controls the whole.

To waggle is to move with short, quick motions from side to side or up and down—a less vigorous cousin of wiggle. A dog waggles its tail, a golfer waggles the club before swinging, someone waggles their eyebrows suggestively. The noun waggle is an instance of such movement: {Give it a little waggle to see if it's loose}.

A wagon is a four-wheeled vehicle for hauling loads, traditionally pulled by horses or oxen. Children's wagons are small, low carts pulled by a handle. A station wagon is a car with extended cargo space behind the rear seats. To {fall off the wagon} is to resume drinking after a period of abstinence; to be {on the wagon} is to abstain. To {circle the wagons} is to unite defensively against outside threats.

Wagons is the plural of wagon—wheeled vehicles for hauling goods or people. Farm wagons carry hay; station wagons carry families. To {circle the wagons} is to take a defensive posture, from the frontier practice of arranging wagons for protection. To be {on the wagon} is to abstain from alcohol; {off the wagon} means drinking again.

Wags is the plural of wag—a person known for witty or playful humor, someone who makes jokes and clever remarks: {The office wags had a field day with the new dress code}. Wags also functions as the verb form meaning to move back and forth, especially of a tail: {The dog wags its tail whenever she comes home}. The phrase {the tail wags the dog} describes a situation where a minor part controls the whole.

Wail is a prolonged, high-pitched cry of grief, pain, or distress: {The wail of mourners filled the room}. Sirens and wind can wail—any sustained, mournful sound qualifies. To wail is to make such a sound: {The baby wailed through the night}. In slang, to wail on something is to play music with intense energy, or to strike repeatedly.

Wailing is prolonged, loud crying or lamentation—the kind of grieving sound that fills a room or carries across distance. The wailing of mourners, the wailing of sirens, the wailing of a neglected infant. As an adjective, it describes sounds with that quality: {a wailing guitar solo}, {the wailing wind}.

The waist is the narrowest part of the human torso, between the ribs and hips. Clothing fits at or around the waist: {The pants sit high on the waist}. Waist extends to the corresponding part of garments: {The dress has a fitted waist}. A wasp waist is unusually narrow. The waist of a ship or aircraft is its middle section.

A waistcoat is a sleeveless, close-fitting garment worn over a shirt and under a jacket, typically featuring buttons down the front and a V-shaped neckline. The term is standard in British English; Americans usually say vest. Waistcoats appear most often in formal attire—three-piece suits, wedding ensembles, and period costume: {He adjusted his waistcoat before entering the ballroom}.

The waistline is the narrowest part of the human torso, typically just above the navel, where pants and skirts are often fitted. In clothing, a garment's waistline is where the bodice meets the skirt: {The dress has a dropped waistline}. Figuratively, waistline refers to body weight or girth: {I need to watch my waistline}.

Wait is to stay in place or delay action until something happens. You wait for a bus, wait your turn, or wait to see what develops. A wait is the period of delay itself: {It was a long wait}. To {wait on} someone is to serve them, especially at a restaurant, or in some dialects simply to wait for them. {Wait} alone can mean stop or hold on: {Wait, I'm not finished}.

A waiter is a person who serves food and drinks at a restaurant or similar establishment. The term applies regardless of gender, though waitress specifically denotes a woman. {Our waiter recommended the special}. A waiter can also be a tray for serving, or someone who waits: {a waiter in line}.

Waiters are people who serve food and drinks at restaurants, typically taking orders, bringing dishes to tables, and handling payment. The singular waiter traditionally referred to men, with waitress for women, though waiter now often applies regardless of gender. {The waiters were attentive but not intrusive.}

Waiting is the state of staying in place or remaining inactive until something happens. You might be waiting for a bus, waiting to hear back about a job, or waiting for the right moment. A waiting {room} is where people sit until called. A waiting {list} holds names until space opens up. {The waiting is the hardest part.}

A waitlist is a list of people waiting for something not immediately available—a table at a restaurant, admission to a school, a seat on a full flight. To waitlist someone is to add them to such a list: {She was waitlisted at her first-choice college}. Also spelled as two words: wait list.

A waitress is a woman who serves food and drinks in a restaurant or similar establishment. The term has been largely displaced by the gender-neutral *server* in American English, though waitress remains common in casual speech and in countries where gendered job titles persist: {Our waitress recommended the special}.

A waiver is the voluntary surrender of a right or claim. Legal documents called waivers formalize this: {Sign the liability waiver before using the gym}. In sports, placing a player on waivers makes them available for other teams to claim. To waive is the verb: {She waived her right to an attorney}.

Two different words are spelled w-a-k-e. First, to wake is to awaken, or to rouse (yourself or someone else) from sleep or from inattentiveness. To wake is also to attend a corpse before burial; this verb is not much used now, but the noun wake designates the period before burial when you may view a corpse and console the family of the dead person. Second, a wake is the disturbance in water left by the passage of a boat. By extension, the aftereffects of an activity or event are said to be in the wake of it.

Wakeboarding is a water sport in which a rider stands on a short, wide board and is towed behind a motorboat, using the boat's wake to perform jumps and tricks. It combines elements of water skiing, snowboarding, and surfing: {We went wakeboarding at the lake last summer}.

Wakes serves multiple words. Most commonly it's the verb for emerging from sleep or causing someone to emerge: {She wakes at dawn}, {The noise wakes the baby}. To wake to something is to become aware of it. A wake is also the trail of disturbed water behind a moving boat, extended to any aftermath: {in the wake of the scandal}. Separately, a wake is a vigil held beside a body before burial, often with food and drink—an Irish wake being the cultural touchstone.

Walk is the most general verb to describe travel on foot, and the most general noun to describe an instance of this. To walk a dog is to lead it on a walk. To walk a path, street, or trail is to walk on it. To walk the talk is to behave in accordance with stated principles. To walk away from something is to dissociate yourself from it. To walk off with something is to steal it, or take it by being much better than your competition.

Walkabout originally refers to a journey Australian Aboriginal people take through the bush, often for spiritual purposes or to live in traditional ways. The term has spread to mean any extended wandering or period of travel, especially one taken to clear the mind or escape routine: {He went on a walkabout after quitting his job}. In British usage, a walkabout is also when a public figure walks among crowds to greet them informally: {The princess did a walkabout through the market square}.

A walker is someone who walks, often as regular exercise: {She's an early morning walker}. A walker is also a frame device that helps people with mobility difficulties move around—common among the elderly and those recovering from injuries. In American English, a baby walker is a wheeled seat that lets infants scoot around before they can walk independently. (Capitalized Walker is a surname.)

Walkies is British informal, typically used when speaking to a dog about going for a walk: {Who wants to go walkies?} The -ies ending gives it a playful, childlike quality, fitting the way people often speak to pets. It functions as both noun and exclamation.

Walking is the act of moving on foot at a moderate pace, slower than running. The word often serves as an intensifier suggesting a living embodiment: {He's a walking encyclopedia}, {She's a walking disaster}. Walking appears in compounds describing activities done on foot: {walking tour}, {walking stick}, {walking papers} (notice of dismissal). {The walking wounded} are injured but ambulatory.

A walkoff is a game-ending play in baseball—a hit, home run, or other decisive moment that immediately wins the game for the home team: {He hit a walkoff homer in the bottom of the ninth}. The term captures the finality: the losing team simply walks off the field. As an adjective: {walkoff single}, {walkoff grand slam}. The word has spread to other contexts where something ends dramatically and decisively.

A walkout is an act of leaving as protest or refusal to continue. Workers stage a walkout when they leave their jobs collectively, usually over labor disputes: {The union called a walkout after negotiations stalled}. Students or delegates may walk out of meetings or assemblies to signal objection. As a verb phrase, to walk out is to leave abruptly: {She walked out in the middle of the argument}.

Walkouts are acts of leaving as protest or refusal. Workers stage a walkout when they leave their jobs collectively, often as a strike or demonstration: {The teachers' walkout shut down schools across the district}. Students walk out of classes to protest policies. Someone may walk out of a meeting, performance, or relationship when they've had enough: {There were several walkouts during the controversial speech}.

Walks is the third-person singular of walk, meaning to move on foot at a moderate pace. {She walks to work every morning}. As a plural noun, walks are instances of walking or paths designed for walking: {morning walks through the park}, {garden walks}. In baseball, walks are bases on balls—a batter reaching first after four balls: {He led the league in walks}.

A walkthrough is a step-by-step guide explaining how to complete something, especially a video game: {I couldn't beat the final boss without a walkthrough}. The term extends to any guided explanation or demonstration: {The realtor gave us a walkthrough of the property}. As two words, walk through is the verb: {Let me walk through the process with you}.

A wall is a vertical structure in which length is usually the greatest dimension, thickness the least, and height usually intermediate. Walls typically separate one thing from another: room from room, indoors from outdoors, yard from street or moat from castle. Natural or naturally occurring things that have wall characteristics get the same name: a wall of water. Something that presents a seemingly insurmountable obstacle can be called a wall: a wall of silence. In verbal use, wall is usually followed by a particle to describe how something is separated by the use of a wall: wall off the garden, wall in the prisoners.

Wallabies are small to medium-sized marsupials related to kangaroos, native to Australia and New Guinea. They hop on powerful hind legs and carry their young in pouches, but are generally smaller and stockier than their kangaroo cousins: {We spotted several wallabies grazing at dusk}. (Capitalized Wallabies is Australia's national rugby union team.)

A wallaby is a small to medium-sized marsupial native to Australia and New Guinea, resembling a kangaroo but typically smaller. Like kangaroos, wallabies have powerful hind legs for hopping, long tails for balance, and pouches for carrying young. The term covers several dozen species across multiple genera: {We spotted a wallaby grazing near the trail}.

A wallet is a small, flat folding case for carrying paper money, cards, and identification. Traditionally kept in a pocket or purse: {He pulled a twenty from his wallet}. Digital wallets store payment information electronically for online or contactless transactions. To {open your wallet} is to spend money; a {fat wallet} suggests wealth.

A wallflower is a person who remains on the sidelines at a social gathering, especially someone too shy to dance or mingle: {She spent prom as a wallflower, watching from the bleachers}. The term comes from the flowering plant that grows on walls and rocky places. By extension, wallflower describes anything overlooked or undervalued: {The stock was a wallflower until last quarter}.

Wallflowers is the plural of wallflower—a person who stays on the sidelines at social gatherings, especially dances, rather than participating: {She spent prom as a wallflower, watching others dance}. The image is of someone pressed against the wall, too shy or unpopular to join in. Wallflowers are also fragrant garden plants that grow well against walls and in rocky crevices.

Wallop is a forceful blow or the act of delivering one: {He gave the ball a good wallop}. The word suggests impact—something hit hard and decisively. By extension, wallop describes crushing defeats: {The team got walloped 42-7}. As a noun, wallop can mean power or punch: {This chili has some wallop to it}.

Wallow originally describes how pigs and other animals roll in mud or dust—a pleasurable, messy immersion. The meaning extends to humans indulging in something, usually negative: {wallowing in self-pity}, {wallowing in grief}. To wallow in luxury or wealth carries less judgment. A wallow is also the muddy place where animals do this: {a buffalo wallow}.

Wallowing is the present participle of wallow, which means to roll around or lie in something, typically mud, water, or loose material—as pigs famously do. The word extends to emotional states: if you're wallowing in self-pity or misery, you're indulging in that feeling rather than trying to move past it. {She spent the weekend wallowing in sadness after the breakup.} The term usually carries a note of judgment, suggesting excess or lack of effort to improve one's situation.

Wallpaper is decorative paper applied to interior walls, typically sold in rolls and affixed with paste. The patterns and styles of wallpaper mark eras: {That floral wallpaper screams 1970s}. In computing, wallpaper is the background image on a screen. As a verb, to wallpaper is to cover walls—or figuratively, to plaster something everywhere: {They wallpapered the town with flyers}.

Walls are vertical structures that enclose, divide, or support. They define the boundaries of rooms and buildings, separate properties, and hold up roofs. Figuratively, a wall is any barrier that blocks progress or communication: {We kept hitting a wall with the negotiations}. To wall something off is to separate or isolate it. The expression {off the wall} describes something unconventional or outlandish. If you're {up against the wall}, you're in a desperate situation with limited options.

A walnut is the edible nut of a tree in the genus Juglans, encased in a hard, wrinkled shell. The wood of the walnut tree is prized for furniture and gunstocks, valued for its rich brown color and fine grain. Walnut also describes that characteristic dark brown color: {walnut stain}, {walnut finish}.

Walnuts are the edible nuts of the walnut tree, with wrinkled, brain-shaped kernels inside hard, ridged shells. They're used in baking, salads, and snacking. The wood of walnut trees is prized for furniture and gunstocks. In slang, walnuts can refer to testicles, from the resemblance in size and shape.

A walrus is a large Arctic marine mammal with long tusks, whiskers, and blubbery skin. Walruses haul out on ice floes and beaches, using their tusks to pull themselves up. The tusks, actually elongated canine teeth, serve for defense and dominance displays. A walrus mustache is a thick, bushy mustache that droops over the lip.

Walruses is the plural of walrus, a large marine mammal of Arctic waters with prominent tusks, thick whiskers, and blubbery skin. Walruses haul out on ice floes and beaches in groups: {The walruses basked on the rocks}. The word sometimes appears in references to "The Walrus and the Carpenter," Lewis Carroll's nonsense poem.

A waltz is a ballroom dance in triple time, characterized by smooth, gliding movements and a distinctive one-two-three rhythm. The verb means to dance this way, but extends to any easy, confident movement: {She waltzed into the room like she owned it}. To {waltz through} something is to accomplish it effortlessly: {He waltzed through the exam}.

Waltzes is the plural of waltz, a ballroom dance in triple time where couples turn gracefully across the floor: {They danced three waltzes before the band took a break}. As a verb, waltzes means moves with confident ease, often implying casualness bordering on presumption: {He just waltzes in like he owns the place}.

Waltzing is dancing the waltz—a ballroom dance in triple time where partners rotate smoothly across the floor. The term extends to any gliding, effortless movement: {She came waltzing into the room like she owned the place}. To waltz through something is to accomplish it with ease: {He waltzed through the exam}. The phrase often carries a note of presumption or nonchalance.

A wand is a slender rod held in the hand, associated with magic and ritual. Wizards and fairies wave wands to cast spells; conductors use batons that function similarly. The word extends to any slim handheld device: a {curling wand}, a {metal-detecting wand}, a {mascara wand}. To wave a {magic wand} is to solve problems effortlessly—usually invoked to note that no such solution exists.

Wander means to move about without a fixed course or destination, often aimlessly or leisurely. You might wander through a bookstore, or your thoughts might wander during a boring meeting. The word suggests unhurried, undirected movement—physical or mental—that lacks urgency or purpose. {We wandered the streets of the old city for hours.} A wandering eye suggests attention that strays, usually toward attractive people. To wander off is to drift away from a group or topic.

A wanderer is someone who travels from place to place without a fixed destination or home. The word suggests freedom and restlessness rather than aimlessness—a wanderer moves by choice or temperament, not necessity. {He spent his twenties as a wanderer, drifting through Southeast Asia.} The term extends to anything that roams: a wandering eye, a wandering mind.

Wandering describes movement without a fixed destination or purpose. Someone wandering through a city has no particular place to be. The word extends to attention and thought: {My mind kept wandering during the lecture}. A wandering eye notices attractive people despite being in a relationship. Wandering can suggest pleasant aimlessness or troubling lack of focus, depending on context.

Wanderlust is a strong desire to travel and explore the world. The word comes from German and suggests an almost restless urge to wander, stronger than ordinary interest in travel: {After college, wanderlust took her backpacking through Southeast Asia}. Someone with wanderlust feels confined by staying in one place too long.

Wands are slender rods associated with magic or ceremony. A fairy godmother waves a wand; a magician performs tricks with one. The word extends to wand-shaped implements: a mascara wand, a curling wand, a handheld barcode scanner. {She waved her wand and the pumpkin became a carriage.} {The security guard passed a wand over the visitor.}

Wane means to decrease gradually in size, intensity, or power. The moon wanes as it moves from full toward new, its visible portion shrinking nightly. Interest wanes, enthusiasm wanes, influence wanes: {His popularity waned after the scandal}. The noun appears in {on the wane}, meaning in decline. The opposite is wax.

Waning describes something gradually decreasing in size, intensity, or power. The moon wanes as it shrinks from full to new. Interest wanes when enthusiasm fades: {Public support for the project was waning}. Influence, strength, and daylight all wane. The noun wane appears in {on the wane}, meaning in decline.

Wanker is British slang for a contemptible person—literally one who masturbates, but used as a general-purpose insult suggesting someone pathetic, selfish, or obnoxious: {That wanker cut me off in traffic}. The word is common in British speech and packs a punch while remaining less severe than cunt. Americans recognize it from British media but rarely use it naturally.

Wannabe is someone who aspires to be something they're not, often used dismissively: {a wannabe rock star}, {wannabe gangsters hanging around the corner}. The word suggests the person lacks the talent, credentials, or authenticity to become what they're imitating. It works as both noun and adjective: {wannabe influencers flooding social media}. From "want to be."

Wannabes are people who aspire to be something they're not—usually imitating a style, status, or identity they admire but haven't earned: {The club was full of wannabes trying to look like regulars}. The term is dismissive, suggesting the person lacks authenticity or talent. A wannabe rapper writes lyrics but can't flow. A wannabe socialite name-drops but isn't invited.

If you want something, you feel the need or desire for it, or the lack of it. If an inanimate thing wants something, it would benefit from it: That shed wants a coat of paint. The noun want is less common than the noun need, but is used in a very similar way: want is the state of wanting or needing something. If you’re in want, there’s something you want. To satisfy a want is to fulfill it.

Wanted is the past tense and participle of want, but it has developed its own distinct uses. As an adjective, wanted describes someone or something that is desired or sought after: {a wanted man}, {feeling wanted}. In law enforcement contexts, a wanted person is being sought by police in connection with a crime—hence wanted posters. The opposite, unwanted, describes something not desired or welcome: {unwanted attention}, {unwanted pregnancy}.
Wanting is a participle that can be used as a preposition with the same meaning as without to convey that something is deficient: three kittens wanting a home.

War is conflict using weapons between military forces or other groups with arms. Any particular instance of this is also called a war, such as the civil war in Syria or the Crimean War. Governments often use war to describe a campaign whose aim is to stop a particular undesirable thing, such as the war on drugs or the war on poverty. War is also a verb that means engage in war. It appears most often in the participle and gerund warring: Warring factions conducted raids on each other’s camps.

Warbling is singing with trills, quavers, or melodic flourishes. Birds warble; so do humans who sing in a light, wavering style. The word often carries a gentle or whimsical quality: {a robin warbling outside the window}, {She was warbling an old show tune in the kitchen}. It can also suggest amateurish or unsteady singing.

A warchest is a reserve of money set aside for a specific campaign or contest. Originally military funds for actual war, the term now appears almost exclusively in politics and business: {The senator's warchest topped twenty million dollars}. Companies build warchests for acquisitions or to weather downturns. The spelling varies: war chest, warchest.

A ward is someone under the protection or care of another—typically a child placed under a guardian's supervision by a court: {The orphan became a ward of the state}. Ward also means a division or section, especially in a hospital (the maternity ward, the psychiatric ward) or a political district within a city. To ward something off is to deflect or prevent it: {garlic to ward off vampires}, {ward off a cold}. A ward in a lock is a ridge that prevents the wrong key from turning.

A warden is a person responsible for supervision or enforcement within a defined domain. Prison wardens oversee correctional facilities. Game wardens enforce hunting and fishing regulations. Fire wardens monitor for forest fires. Church wardens assist in parish administration. The word suggests official authority over a specific territory or institution: {The warden ordered a lockdown after the incident}.

A wardrobe is a collection of clothing belonging to one person: {She's updating her wardrobe for the new job}. It also means a tall cabinet or closet for storing clothes, common in homes without built-in closets. In theater and film, wardrobe refers to the department responsible for costumes: {The actor went to wardrobe for a fitting}.

A warehouse is a large building for storing goods, materials, or merchandise before distribution or sale. Warehouses are central to supply chains and logistics: {The company leases warehouse space near the port}. As a verb, to warehouse something is to store it in bulk, or more figuratively, to put aside or neglect: {warehousing the elderly in nursing homes}.
