Whatever can also stand in place of a list you don’t complete because the individual things in it are not important: Bring along your beach stuff: towels, sunscreen, whatever. Some people use whatever as an interjection to show a lack of interest or to express exasperation.

Whatshisface is a placeholder for a man's name you can't recall or don't care to specify: {I ran into whatshisface from accounting}. The word treats the forgotten person as unimportant or barely worth naming. Variants include whatsisface and the feminine whatserface or whatsherface.

Wheat is a cereal grain, one of the world's most important food crops. The plant's seeds are ground into flour for bread, pasta, and countless other foods. {Wheat fields} stretch across temperate regions worldwide. To {separate the wheat from the chaff} is to distinguish what's valuable from what's worthless.

A wheel is round, flat, and revolves around an axis, like a steering wheel in a vehicle, or the wheels on which the vehicle moves. Wheels may suggest a large and complex process, like the wheels of justice, or it may be dated slang for a car: That Mustang is a sweet set of wheels. A person described as a wheel is considered to have power and influence; if they have lots of it, they are a big wheel. To wheel is to propel something on wheels. If you wheel around, you turn around quickly.

A wheelbarrow is a small cart with one wheel at the front and two handles at the back, used for carrying loads short distances—typically in gardens, on construction sites, or around farms. The operator lifts the handles and pushes, with the single wheel allowing easy maneuvering through tight spaces. {He loaded the wheelbarrow with mulch and pushed it to the flower beds.}

Wheelbarrows is the plural of wheelbarrow, a small cart with one wheel at the front and two handles at the back, used to transport loads by hand. The single wheel allows maneuvering in tight spaces: {He loaded the wheelbarrows with mulch and wheeled them to the garden beds}. As a verb, to wheelbarrow is to move something using one.

A wheelchair is a chair mounted on wheels, used by people who cannot walk or have difficulty walking. Manual wheelchairs are propelled by the user pushing the wheels or by someone pushing from behind; powered wheelchairs use electric motors. {She's been in a wheelchair since the accident.} Wheelchair also functions as an adjective: {wheelchair access}, {wheelchair basketball}.

Wheelchairs is the plural of wheelchair, a chair mounted on wheels that allows a person with limited mobility to move around. Manual wheelchairs are propelled by the occupant or pushed by someone else; powered wheelchairs run on batteries. {The stadium has seating for wheelchairs}. {She's been in wheelchairs since the accident}.

A wheelhouse is the enclosed area on a ship where the steering wheel and navigation controls are located—the bridge. In baseball, a batter's wheelhouse is the zone where they hit most powerfully: {He got a fastball right in his wheelhouse}. This sense has spread to mean anyone's area of strength or expertise: {Data analysis is really her wheelhouse}.

A wheelie is the act of riding a bicycle, motorcycle, or other wheeled vehicle with the front wheel lifted off the ground, balancing on the rear wheel: {He popped a wheelie and rode half a block}. The maneuver requires shifting weight backward while accelerating. Wheelies range from brief stunts to sustained rides, and appear in BMX tricks, motorcycle shows, and kids showing off.

A wheelie is a maneuver where a wheeled vehicle balances on its rear wheel or wheels while the front lifts off the ground. Cyclists and motorcyclists pop wheelies to show off: {He rode a wheelie down the whole block}. The plural wheelies is standard: {doing wheelies in the parking lot}. In British English, wheelies can also mean wheeled trash bins.

Wheels are the circular components that rotate to allow vehicles and machines to move. The word commonly refers to transportation itself: {Do you have wheels?} means do you have a car. Wheels can be any rotating discs—steering wheels, spinning wheels, roulette wheels. To {wheel} something is to push or roll it. {The wheels are turning} suggests a process is underway. {Wheels within wheels} describes hidden complexity.

A wheeze is a high-pitched whistling sound made while breathing, typically caused by narrowed airways: {The doctor heard a wheeze in her chest}. To wheeze is to breathe with such a sound, often from asthma, illness, or exertion. Figuratively, old machinery may wheeze. In British slang, a wheeze is a clever scheme or joke: {a good wheeze for making money}.

Wheezing is breathing with a whistling or rattling sound, typically caused by obstruction in the airways. It suggests respiratory distress—from asthma, allergies, or exertion: {He was wheezing after climbing the stairs}. Old or poorly maintained machinery may also wheeze: {The ancient furnace wheezed to life}.

When typically relates to time: When will you be back? We lived there when we were kids. When is interchangeable with if in sentences where the main clause states a truism: When you lie you create complications for yourself. The desert blooms when it rains. When may stand for a particular time stated in an earlier clause: They moved in a month ago, since when we have had no peace. Informally, when is used as a noun to designate an unknown time: We haven’t yet settled the when or the where of the meeting.

Where is mainly an adverb but it can be used as a conjunction to introduce a clause that identifies a place, and by extension, a situation, position, direction, or circumstances: Do you know where the library is? I can’t figure out where he’s going with this proposal. Where there’s smoke, there’s fire. Where is sometimes used informally in sentences to introduce a standard subordinate “that” clause after a verb of perception: I heard where they’d decided not to move after all.

Whereabouts asks about location: {Whereabouts did you leave your keys?} More commonly, it functions as a noun meaning a person's or thing's location: {His whereabouts remain unknown}. Despite the plural form, whereabouts takes either singular or plural verbs: {Her whereabouts is/are a mystery}.

Whew is an exclamation expressing relief, exhaustion, or amazement at a narrow escape: {Whew, that was close!} It often accompanies wiping one's brow or exhaling dramatically. The word can also register surprise at intensity or quantity: {Whew, it's hot out there}.

A whiff is a brief smell carried on the air: {I caught a whiff of perfume as she passed}. By extension, a whiff is any slight trace or hint: {a whiff of scandal}, {a whiff of desperation}. In baseball, to whiff is to swing and miss—three whiffs and you've struck out. The verb also means to smell briefly: {He whiffed the milk to check if it had gone bad}.

Whiffs is the plural of whiff—a brief smell or puff of air: {whiffs of perfume}, {whiffs of smoke}. Extended to hints or traces: {whiffs of scandal}, {whiffs of desperation}. In baseball, whiffs are strikeouts, from the batter swinging and missing—cutting through empty air. To get whiffs of something is to detect faint signs of it.

While can introduce several kinds of information having to do with time, contrast, or context. While precedes one of two activities that are happening at the same time: What did you do while I was away? You can also use while to talk about contrast: While experienced hikers find the trail easy, novices may struggle.

A whim is a sudden desire or impulse, typically minor and not carefully considered: {On a whim, she bought tickets to Paris}. Whims are harmless but unpredictable—acting on whim suggests spontaneity rather than planning. Someone subject to frequent whims is whimsical. {His every whim} suggests catering to capricious demands.

A whimper is a soft, high-pitched cry expressing fear, pain, or distress—the sound a frightened dog makes, or a child trying not to cry. To whimper is to make such sounds: {The puppy whimpered at the door}. The word suggests vulnerability and restraint, crying that's held back rather than released. T.S. Eliot's famous line—"not with a bang but a whimper"—captures its sense of quiet, anticlimactic defeat.

Whimpering is making soft, feeble crying sounds that express pain, fear, or distress. Dogs whimper when anxious or seeking attention; humans whimper when overwhelmed but not fully crying. As a noun, it names this sound collectively: {The whimpering from the back seat told us the kids were exhausted}. The word often carries connotations of weakness or helplessness, sometimes used dismissively to describe complaining: {Stop your whimpering and get on with it}.

Whimpers are soft, plaintive cries expressing fear, pain, or distress—the sounds a frightened dog or upset child makes. To whimper is to make such sounds: {The puppy whimpered at the door}. The word suggests weakness or helplessness, sometimes used dismissively: {He went out with a whimper, not a bang}.

Whims are sudden, unpredictable desires or impulses, usually minor and passing: {She bought the hat on a whim}. The word suggests caprice rather than reason—decisions made without planning or justification. Someone ruled by whims is changeable and hard to predict: {His whims kept the staff guessing}. The singular whim appears most often after "on a."

Whimsical describes something playfully fanciful or unpredictable. A whimsical sense of humor delights in the unexpected. Whimsical decorations might feature oddly shaped objects or surreal imagery. The word suggests lighthearted creativity rather than anything serious or practical: {The garden had a whimsical quality, with winding paths and hidden statues}. A whimsical person acts on sudden fancies rather than careful plans.

Whimsy is playful, fanciful, or quirkily imaginative quality—the lighthearted impulse that produces unexpected delights: {The film is full of whimsy}, {a touch of whimsy in her decorating style}. A whimsy is also a specific instance of such fancifulness: {One of her whimsies was naming all her houseplants}. The word suggests charm without seriousness, imagination untethered from practical concerns.

A whine is a high-pitched, drawn-out sound expressing complaint, distress, or pleading. Dogs whine at the door; children whine for treats. The verb means to make this sound or to complain in a petulant, self-pitying way: {Stop whining and do your homework}. Engines and machinery also whine—a thin, sustained pitch suggesting strain. The word carries connotations of weakness or annoyance; nobody respects a whiner.

A whiner is someone who complains persistently in a petulant or self-pitying way. The term carries contempt—whiners aren't seen as having legitimate grievances but as tiresome people who can't stop feeling sorry for themselves: {Nobody wants to work with a whiner}. Children whine; adults who do the same get called whiners.

Whiners are people who complain in a petulant, self-pitying way. The term is dismissive—it characterizes complaints as excessive or unjustified: {The coach had no patience for whiners}. Calling someone a whiner suggests their grievances don't merit serious attention.

Whining is complaining in a high-pitched, drawn-out, irritating tone—the sound children make when they don't get what they want. Adults whine too, though the word carries childish connotations: {Stop whining and do your job}. The adjective whiny describes someone prone to it. Dogs whine with a similar sound, usually signaling distress or desire.

Whiny describes a complaining, fretful tone—the kind of high-pitched, drawn-out voice children use when they want something or feel mistreated. Adults can be whiny too: {Stop being so whiny about the workload}. The word itself carries irritation; calling someone whiny dismisses their complaints as childish or excessive. Also spelled whiney.

A whip is an instrument of punishment or injury, often consisting of a long strap of leather. To whip someone is to beat them with a whip. Both the noun and verb have figurative use: to whip someone is to defeat or tire them. To whip a substance in cooking is to beat it vigorously, incorporating air. When the wind whips something, it is blowing very hard. In politics, a whip is a party official whose job is to ensure voting conformity.

Whiplash is the snapping motion of a whip's tip, or by extension, any sudden back-and-forth jerk. Most commonly it describes a neck injury from rapid acceleration and deceleration—typically in car accidents when the head snaps forward then backward. Figuratively, whiplash describes the disorienting effect of abrupt reversals: {The policy changes gave everyone whiplash}.

Whipped describes something beaten rapidly—cream whipped until fluffy, eggs whipped into foam. A person who has been whipped has been struck with a whip or strap. Figuratively, whipped means exhausted or defeated: {I'm whipped after that hike}. In slang, whipped describes someone excessively devoted to a romantic partner, doing whatever they want: {He's so whipped he canceled poker night}.

Whipping is beating with a whip or similar instrument, whether as punishment, torture, or in certain sexual practices. The term extends to any thorough defeat: {The team took a whipping}. In cooking, whipping means beating rapidly to incorporate air: {whipping cream}. Whipping also describes rapid, lashing motion: {flags whipping in the wind}.

Whips are flexible instruments for striking—a handle with a lash attached, used to drive animals or punish people. The motion extends to anything that moves with similar speed or snap: {The wind whipped through the canyon}. To whip cream or eggs is to beat them vigorously. In politics, a whip is a party official who ensures members vote as directed. Informally, someone's whip is their car: {Nice whip}.

A whir is a soft, rapid buzzing or humming sound, like spinning machinery or beating wings: {the whir of a ceiling fan}, {hummingbird wings whirring}. The verb means to make such a sound or move with one: {The hard drive whirred to life}. Also spelled whirr.

Whirl captures rapid circular motion. Wind whirls leaves; dancers whirl across a floor; thoughts whirl through a confused mind. A whirl is a spinning movement or a rapid succession of events: {a whirl of activity}, {a social whirl}. To {give something a whirl} is to try it out: {I've never played poker, but I'll give it a whirl}.

A whirlpool is a rapidly rotating body of water that forms when currents meet or drain, creating a circular motion that can pull objects toward its center. The word extends to anything that draws you in with similar force: {a whirlpool of emotions}, {caught in a whirlpool of debt}. A whirlpool bath or tub has jets that create swirling water for therapeutic massage. (Capitalized Whirlpool is the appliance brand.)

Whirlpools are circular currents of water that spin around a central point, drawing floating objects toward the center. They form where opposing currents meet or water drains through a narrow passage. The word extends to any situation that pulls things inward: {a whirlpool of debt}, {caught in a whirlpool of emotions}. Whirlpool is also a brand of home appliances.

A whirlwind is a column of air rotating rapidly around a vertical axis, smaller and less destructive than a tornado but powerful enough to lift debris and dust. The word extends naturally to anything that moves with similar speed and chaos: a whirlwind {romance} develops intensely fast, a whirlwind {tour} covers many places in little time. As an adjective, whirlwind characterizes events marked by hurried, dizzying activity. To {reap the whirlwind} is to suffer severe consequences for earlier actions.

A whisk is a kitchen utensil with wire loops used to beat or blend ingredients: {She used a whisk to make the hollandaise}. To whisk is to beat rapidly with such a tool, or to move something quickly and lightly: {He whisked the eggs}, {She whisked the tablecloth away}. To whisk someone off is to take them away swiftly: {They whisked her off to the hospital}.

Whiskers are the long, stiff hairs growing near the mouths of cats, dogs, and other mammals—sensory organs that help animals navigate their environment. On humans, whiskers are facial hair, especially stubble or a partial beard: {He hadn't shaved in days and had a growth of whiskers}. By a whisker means by a tiny margin: {She won by a whisker}. In the plural, whiskers can also mean the hair of a full beard or sideburns.

Whiskers are the long, stiff hairs growing near the mouth of cats, dogs, and other mammals—sensory organs that detect surroundings. On humans, whiskers are facial hair, especially on the cheeks: {He hadn't shaved in days and had quite the whiskers}. Something that wins or loses {by a whisker} does so by the slimmest margin.

Whiskey is a distilled alcoholic spirit made from fermented grain mash—typically barley, corn, rye, or wheat—and aged in wooden barrels. The spelling whiskey is standard in Ireland and the United States, while whisky (without the e) is used in Scotland, Canada, and Japan. Bourbon, Scotch, and rye are all types of whiskey distinguished by grain composition and origin: {a glass of whiskey}, {Irish whiskey}, {Tennessee whiskey}.

Whisky is a distilled spirit made from fermented grain mash—typically barley, corn, rye, or wheat—and aged in wooden barrels. The spelling whisky is standard in Scotland, Canada, and Japan; whiskey (with an e) is preferred in Ireland and the United States. Scotch whisky comes specifically from Scotland. {He ordered a whisky neat.}

A whisper is speech produced without vibrating the vocal cords, creating a soft, breathy sound meant for nearby ears only: {She leaned close and whispered the secret}. Whisper extends to any soft rustling sound: {the whisper of leaves}. A whisper of something is a trace or hint: {not a whisper of scandal}. To whisper is also to spread rumors quietly: {People whispered about the affair for months}.

A whisperer is someone who whispers, but the word now primarily appears in compounds describing people with an uncanny ability to communicate with animals or handle difficult situations: {horse whisperer}, {dog whisperer}, {baby whisperer}. The implication is of gentle, intuitive connection rather than force—someone who calms or persuades through quiet understanding.

Whispering is speaking very softly, using breath rather than full voice. The word extends to any quiet, rustling sound: {the whispering of leaves}, {a whispering breeze}. Whispering also suggests secrecy or gossip—people whisper when they don't want to be overheard: {There's been whispering about layoffs}.

Whispers are soft, hushed utterances made by partially voicing words—breath shaped into speech without full sound. People whisper to avoid being overheard or to convey intimacy: {She leaned close and whispered the secret}. Figuratively, whispers are rumors or hints of information circulating quietly: {whispers of a scandal}, {whispers of dissent}. Things that make soft rustling sounds also whisper: {wind whispering through the trees}.

A whistle is a high-pitched sound made by forcing air through a small opening—pursed lips, a narrow tube, or a specialized device. Birds whistle; so do kettles and referees. To whistle is to produce such a sound: {She whistled for her dog}. A whistle is also the device itself: {The coach blew her whistle}. To {wet your whistle} is to take a drink. To {whistle past the graveyard} is to act brave when afraid. A whistleblower exposes wrongdoing, from the referee's whistle that stops play.

A whistleblower is someone who exposes wrongdoing, fraud, or illegal activity within an organization, typically one they work for or have inside knowledge of. The term evokes the image of a referee blowing a whistle to stop play when rules are violated. Whistleblowers often face retaliation despite legal protections designed to shield them: {The whistleblower leaked documents showing the company had falsified safety reports}. The word can be spelled as one word or hyphenated.

Whistleblowing is reporting wrongdoing within an organization to authorities or the public. A whistleblower exposes fraud, corruption, safety violations, or illegal activity—often at personal risk. The term evokes a referee's whistle stopping play when rules are broken. {The company retaliated against her for whistleblowing}. Laws in many jurisdictions protect whistleblowers from dismissal or harassment.

Whistles are high-pitched sounds made by forcing air through a small opening—pursed lips, a mechanical device, or a narrow gap. A whistle can signal, summon, or express approval or disapproval: {The referee blew the whistle}. To whistle is to produce such a sound, whether from the mouth or from wind through trees. Someone who {whistles past the graveyard} pretends confidence despite fear. To {wet your whistle} is to take a drink. A whistleblower exposes wrongdoing, from the referee's whistle stopping play.

Whistling is producing a clear, high-pitched sound by forcing air through pursed lips or teeth, or through a device like a whistle. People whistle tunes, whistle to get attention, or whistle for a dog. A whistling wind makes a similar sound passing through gaps or over surfaces. {He walked down the street, whistling to himself.} To {whistle past the graveyard} is to act brave while afraid.

White is first and foremost a color adjective for the lightest color, or some would say lack of color and presence of light, like that of snow or clouds. From this core meaning arise many other senses that denote or characterize things that are literally or figuratively white, especially in contrast to things that have a more vivid color. White coffee has milk or cream added to it. People whose skin lacks the significant pigmentation seen in people from tropical regions are usually called white. In general, white can characterize many things that are less obviously colored than other things of the same type: white wine, white sand, white bread. In comparison to something truly white in color, they may not be white at all.

A whiteboard is a smooth, glossy surface for writing with erasable markers—the modern descendant of the chalkboard. Whiteboards dominate offices and classrooms: {Let me sketch this out on the whiteboard}. To whiteboard is to brainstorm or plan using one: {We spent the morning whiteboarding the new feature}. A virtual whiteboard is a digital equivalent for remote collaboration.

Whiteness is the quality or state of being white—the color of snow, milk, or blank paper. It describes both literal color and figurative purity: {the whiteness of fresh linen}, {the whiteness of her teeth}. In contemporary social discourse, whiteness refers to the cultural, social, and political dimensions of being perceived as white, often examined critically: {scholarship on whiteness and privilege}, {interrogating whiteness in American institutions}.

Whitening is the process of making something whiter or lighter in color. The term appears most often in contexts of teeth whitening and skin whitening, where products or procedures reduce discoloration or pigmentation. Whitening agents in laundry detergent brighten fabrics. The word can also describe a natural process: {the whitening of hair with age}.

Whiteout has two main meanings. In weather, a whiteout is a blizzard or fog condition where snow and sky blend together, eliminating the horizon and making navigation dangerous: {The pilot couldn't land in the whiteout}. As an office product, whiteout is correction fluid—white liquid painted over typed errors to allow retyping. The verb means to obscure with either: {The storm whiteout the valley} or {She whiteout the typo}.

Whitewash is a cheap white coating made from lime and water, used to paint walls, fences, and buildings. To whitewash something is to apply this coating. Figuratively, to whitewash is to conceal faults or cover up wrongdoing by making something appear better than it is: {The report whitewashed the company's safety violations}. In sports, a whitewash is a shutout or one-sided victory where the losing side scores nothing.

Whitewashed originally describes something coated with whitewash—a cheap white paint made from lime, used on fences and walls. Figuratively, to whitewash is to cover up wrongdoing or present a sanitized version of events: {The report whitewashed the company's role in the disaster}. More recently, whitewashed describes casting white actors in roles written for or historically belonging to people of color: {Critics called the film whitewashed for its lack of Asian leads}.

Whitewashing literally means applying white paint or lime wash to a surface, typically walls or fences. The figurative sense dominates: to whitewash is to conceal wrongdoing or make something unsavory appear acceptable. {The report whitewashed the company's safety failures.} In media criticism, whitewashing refers to casting white actors in roles written for or historically associated with people of color: {Critics accused the studio of whitewashing the film's Asian characters.}

Whitewater refers to turbulent, foamy water in rivers where the current rushes over rocks or through narrow channels, creating rapids. The term appears most often in recreational contexts: whitewater {rafting}, whitewater {kayaking}. The frothy white appearance comes from air mixed into the churning water. {We spent the weekend on a whitewater trip down the Colorado River.} (Capitalized Whitewater may refer to specific place names or the 1990s political scandal.)

Whittle is to carve or shape wood by cutting small pieces away with a knife, typically as a leisurely pastime rather than serious craftwork. The word extends naturally to any gradual reduction: you can whittle down a list of candidates, whittle away at someone's resolve, or watch savings get whittled to nothing. {He whittled the stick into a rough point.} {Budget cuts have whittled the staff down to a skeleton crew.}

Whittled is the past tense of whittle, meaning to carve or shape wood by cutting away small pieces with a knife: {He whittled a stick into a sharp point}. Figuratively, to whittle something down is to reduce it gradually: {Budget cuts whittled the staff down to a skeleton crew}. {She whittled away at her debt over several years}.

Whittling is the craft of carving wood with a knife, typically shaping small objects by cutting away thin shavings. The activity suggests patient, unhurried work—someone on a porch whittling a stick. Figuratively, to whittle something down is to reduce it gradually: {Budget cuts whittled the program down to almost nothing}.

A whizkid is a young person with exceptional talent or ability, especially in a technical or intellectual field: {a computer whizkid}, {a Wall Street whizkid}. The term combines whiz (someone impressively skilled) with kid, emphasizing youth as part of the marvel. Also spelled whiz kid or whiz-kid.

“Wh” words share functions as pronouns and conjunctions. Who and its inflected forms whom and whose have the distinction of being wh words but starting with an h sound. Who is distinct from that and which in referring to, or having as an antecedent, a person as opposed to a thing: Who was that guy you were with? The people who sold us this house want to buy it back. Group nouns composed of people or agents can be referred to with who: The companies who invested here are regretting it. Many speakers today are not keen on using the grammatically correct objective form whom, so many say, for example, Who did you work for before you got this job?
Whoa was originally and still is a command to an animal such as a horse to stop. In conversation it signals either surprise or dismay at a sudden development or revelation.

A whodunit is a mystery story—novel, film, or play—structured around discovering the identity of a criminal, typically a murderer. The term captures the central question driving the plot: who done it? {She spent the weekend reading a classic whodunit.} The word is informal and slightly playful, often applied to traditional detective fiction in the Agatha Christie mold.

A whodunnit is a mystery story—novel, film, or play—centered on discovering who committed a crime, typically murder. The pleasure lies in piecing together clues alongside the detective: {It's a classic whodunnit with red herrings and a surprise ending}. The spelling whodunit also appears. From "who done it," a nonstandard rendering of "who did it."

Whodunnits are mystery stories—novels, films, or plays—where the central puzzle is discovering who committed a crime, typically a murder. The plot withholds the killer's identity until the end, inviting readers to solve it alongside the detective: {I spent the weekend reading Agatha Christie whodunnits}. Also spelled whodunits.

Whole means complete, entire, with no part removed or missing. A whole {pizza} has all its slices. The whole {truth} holds nothing back. Whole also means undivided: {She swallowed the pill whole}. As a noun, a whole is a complete thing or system: {the whole of Western civilization}, {taken as a whole}. The phrase {on the whole} means generally or all things considered.

Wholesale refers to the sale of goods in large quantities, typically to retailers who then sell to consumers: {They buy wholesale and sell retail}. The wholesale price is lower than retail. Figuratively, wholesale means on a large scale, often indiscriminate: {wholesale slaughter}, {wholesale changes to the organization}. As a verb, to wholesale is to sell in bulk.

Wholesome describes what promotes health or well-being—physical, moral, or emotional. Wholesome {food} is nutritious. A wholesome {environment} supports healthy development. The word often carries connotations of innocence or purity: wholesome {entertainment}, a wholesome {image}. In contemporary usage, wholesome has become internet slang for content that is sweet, heartwarming, or refreshingly decent: {That video of the dad surprising his kid is so wholesome}.

Whoop is a loud cry of excitement, joy, or enthusiasm: {The crowd let out a whoop when the home team scored}. To whoop is to make such a cry: {They whooped and hollered all night}. Whooping cough takes its name from the gasping intake of breath that follows coughing fits. To {whoop it up} is to celebrate noisily. {Not worth a whoop} means worthless.
People say Whoopee! when they are doing or thinking about doing something very exciting.
Whoops is another way to spell oops, the word that people use when something awkward or clumsy happens.

Whoosh captures the sound of something moving swiftly through air—wind, a passing vehicle, flames igniting. As a verb, to whoosh is to move with that rushing sound: {The train whooshed past the platform}. The word is onomatopoeic, imitating what it describes. In internet slang, whoosh indicates a joke flying over someone's head: {Whoosh—you missed the point entirely}.

A whopper is something unusually large or impressive of its kind: {That fish was a whopper}. More commonly, a whopper is an outrageous lie—a falsehood so bold it stands out: {He told some real whoppers about his military service}. The word carries informal, slightly playful connotations in both senses. (Capitalized Whopper is the Burger King sandwich.)

Whoppers are things notably large or outrageous. Most often, a whopper is a blatant lie: {He told some real whoppers about his military service}. The word can also describe anything impressively big: {She caught a whopper of a fish}. Whopper is also a Burger King trademark for their signature hamburger.

Whore is a vulgar term for a prostitute, or more broadly, a promiscuous person—usually a woman, and usually meant as an insult. As a verb, to whore means to work as a prostitute, or to pursue something in a degrading or mercenary way: {He whored himself out for the promotion}. The word appears in compounds like {attention whore}, describing someone who craves notice at any cost.

As an adverb and conjunction, why asks or introduces the reason or explanation for something: Can you explain why you did it? Why do you need to know? As an interjection, why usually draws attention to an observation or question that follows it: Why that rascal, I knew he wouldn’t return the money.

A wick is the cord or strip of material in a candle, lamp, or lighter that draws fuel upward by capillary action to be burned: {The candle's wick sputtered and went out}. To wick is to absorb or draw moisture away—performance fabrics wick sweat from skin. To {get on someone's wick} (British) is to annoy them.

Wicked means evil or morally wrong: {a wicked deed}, {a wicked witch}. It extends to things that are severe or unpleasant: {a wicked storm}, {a wicked hangover}. In informal use, especially originating in New England, wicked serves as an intensifier meaning very or extremely: {That concert was wicked good}. Something can also be wicked in an admiring sense—impressively skillful or cool: {She has a wicked sense of humor}.

Wickedness is the quality of being morally bad or evil. The word carries weight—it suggests deliberate wrongdoing rather than mere mischief: {The wickedness of the regime shocked the world}. In lighter contexts, wickedness can describe playful naughtiness or mischievous behavior: {There was wickedness in her smile}.

Wicker is flexible twigs or thin branches woven together to make furniture, baskets, and other items: {a wicker chair}, {a wicker basket}. The material is usually willow, rattan, or bamboo. Wicker furniture is lightweight and often associated with porches, patios, and casual outdoor living.

Wide describes extent from side to side—the opposite of narrow. A wide {river} spans a great distance across. Wide also means fully open: {eyes wide with surprise}, {the door stood wide open}. Extended uses suggest breadth of scope or range: a wide {variety}, wide {experience}, {wide of the mark}. In sports, a shot that goes wide misses to the side of the target.

A widget is a small mechanical device or component, especially one whose name the speaker doesn't know or can't recall: {Hand me that widget, will you?} In computing, a widget is a small application or interface element—a clock, weather display, or button on a screen. The word often serves as a placeholder in economics and business examples: {If we produce 500 widgets per day...}

A widow is a woman whose spouse has died and who has not remarried. The term carries connotations of loss and solitude: {She was widowed young}. In typesetting, a widow is a short line—often a single word—stranded at the top of a page or column, considered poor form. To widow someone is to make them a widow: {The war widowed thousands}.

Widowed describes someone whose spouse has died and who hasn't remarried. The term applies to both sexes, though widow and widower specify: {She was widowed at thirty-five}. Widowed can also modify the noun: {a widowed father raising three children}. The state implies both loss and a change in social status.

A widower is a man whose spouse has died and who has not remarried. The word parallels widow for women, though widow is sometimes used for both sexes. {He became a widower at sixty-three.} The term emphasizes the ongoing state rather than the moment of loss.

A widowmaker is something dangerously likely to kill, leaving widows behind. The term applies to various hazards: a dead branch hanging precariously in a tree, a particularly lethal type of heart attack affecting the left anterior descending artery, or a steep ski run. In each case, the name carries dark humor about fatal potential: {That loose limb is a widowmaker—stay clear}.

Widowmakers are things notorious for killing men—leaving widows behind. The term applies to various hazards: a dead tree branch liable to fall, a particularly dangerous type of heart attack (blockage of the left anterior descending artery), or any equipment or activity with a reputation for fatal accidents. {That old oak has a widowmaker hanging over the driveway.} The word carries dark humor, acknowledging danger while naming it plainly.

Widows is the plural of widow, a woman whose spouse has died and who hasn't remarried. The term extends beyond marriage: {golf widows} are neglected while partners play, {war widows} lost husbands to combat. In typesetting, a widow is an orphaned line of text stranded at the top of a page or column.

Width is the measurement of something from side to side, as opposed to its length or height. A room's width is typically its shorter horizontal dimension. The word extends to abstract contexts: {the width of his knowledge}, {the width of the political spectrum}. Something can have width in the sense of broadness or scope.

To wield something is to hold and use it, especially a tool or weapon: {She wielded the hammer with precision}, {He wielded a sword}. The word extends to abstract power or influence: {wield authority}, {wield political power}. Wield implies active, skillful control—you don't merely possess something, you deploy it effectively.

Wielding is holding and using something, especially a weapon or tool: {wielding a sword}, {wielding a hammer}. The word extends to abstract power or influence: {wielding authority}, {wielding political clout}. Someone wielding something has it in hand and is actively employing it, not merely possessing it.

A wiener is a frankfurter or hot dog—a cooked sausage of German origin, named for Vienna (Wien in German): {I'll have a wiener with mustard}. In childish or humorous slang, wiener means penis: {The little boy ran around showing everyone his wiener}. A wiener dog is a dachshund, named for its sausage shape. To wiener out (slang) means to back down cowardly.

A wife is a married woman in relation to her spouse. The term implies a legal or formally recognized union, though {work wife} and similar constructions describe close platonic partnerships. {My wife and I are celebrating our anniversary}. The plural is wives. Husband is the corresponding term for a married man.

Wiffleball is a backyard variant of baseball played with a lightweight plastic ball perforated with holes and a thin plastic bat. The holes make the ball curve unpredictably and limit how far it travels, allowing play in small spaces. {We played wiffleball in the driveway until dark.} Also spelled wiffle ball or Wiffle ball, after the trademark.

A wig is a head covering made of real or synthetic hair, worn to disguise baldness, change appearance, or for theatrical costume. Wigs range from natural-looking hairpieces to elaborate period styles. Judges and barristers in British courts still wear formal wigs. To {wig out} is to lose composure or become agitated.

Wiggle is a small, quick side-to-side movement. Worms wiggle, loose teeth wiggle, children wiggle in their seats when restless. To wiggle out of something is to escape through evasive maneuvering: {He wiggled out of his responsibilities}. There's {wiggle room} when flexibility exists for negotiation or adjustment.

Wiggly describes something that moves with small, quick, twisting motions—like a worm or a child who can't sit still: {The puppy's wiggly body made him hard to hold}. It also describes lines or shapes that curve irregularly: {wiggly handwriting}, {a wiggly path through the woods}.

Wigs are artificial coverings of hair worn on the head. People wear wigs to disguise baldness, change their appearance, or as part of a costume. In British courts, judges and barristers still wear traditional white wigs. To wig out is to lose control emotionally—to panic or become extremely agitated: {She wigged out when she saw the bill}.

A wiki is a website that allows users to collaboratively create and edit content directly through their browsers. The term comes from Hawaiian for "quick," reflecting the ease of making changes. Wikipedia is the most famous example, but wikis serve countless organizations for documentation and knowledge sharing. To wiki something can mean to look it up on Wikipedia or to edit a wiki page.

Wild describes things uncontrolled by humans—a wild animal lives free, wild land remains uncultivated, wild plants grow without tending. The meaning extends to unrestrained behavior: a wild party, wild applause, a wild child. Wild can mean reckless or extreme: {a wild guess}, {wild accusations}, {wild with grief}. In cards, a wild card can represent any value the holder chooses. The wilds are remote, uninhabited areas: {the wilds of Alaska}. To go wild is to become excited or lose restraint; to run wild is to grow or act without control.

A wildcard is a playing card that can represent any other card the holder chooses. The meaning extends to anything unpredictable that could change an outcome: {The weather is the wildcard in tomorrow's game}. In computing, a wildcard character (usually * or ?) matches any character or string in a search. In sports, a wildcard is a team or player admitted to a tournament despite not qualifying through standard routes.

A wildcat is any of several small to medium-sized wild felines, distinct from domesticated cats. The word extends to describe anything untamed, risky, or operating outside normal channels: a wildcat {strike} happens without union authorization, wildcat {drilling} explores unproven territory for oil, and a wildcat {scheme} is reckless or unsanctioned. As a verb, to wildcat means to drill speculatively for oil or gas in areas not known to be productive.

Wildcats are undomesticated cats of various species—from the European wildcat to bobcats and lynxes. The word suggests untamed ferocity. A wildcat strike is unauthorized by union leadership, springing up spontaneously. A wildcat oil well is drilled speculatively in unproven territory. As a verb, to wildcat is to drill such exploratory wells: {They spent years wildcatting in west Texas}.

A wildebeest is a large African antelope with a heavy build, curved horns, and a shaggy mane—also called a gnu. Wildebeest are famous for their massive seasonal migrations across the Serengeti, where vast herds cross rivers and plains: {We watched thousands of wildebeest streaming across the savanna}.

Wilderness is land in its natural state, uncultivated and uninhabited by humans. The term implies remoteness and wildness: {They hiked deep into the wilderness}. Figuratively, wilderness describes any confusing or neglected expanse: {a wilderness of bureaucratic regulations}. In politics, to be {in the wilderness} is to be out of power or influence: {The party spent a decade in the wilderness}.

Wildfire is an uncontrolled fire that spreads rapidly through vegetation—forests, grasslands, brush. The word emphasizes speed and destruction: {Wildfires devastated the region}. Figuratively, things that spread like wildfire move with similar speed and intensity: {The rumor spread like wildfire}. The phrase {like wildfire} is far more common than the noun alone.

Wildfires are uncontrolled fires burning through wild vegetation—forests, grasslands, brush. They spread rapidly, driven by wind, drought, and fuel. A single wildfire can consume thousands of acres: {Wildfires have displaced entire communities}. The term also works figuratively for anything that spreads fast and uncontrollably: {The rumor spread like wildfire}.
A wildflower is a flowering plant that grows naturally in an area, without cultivation.

Wildflowers are flowers that grow without cultivation—not planted or tended by humans. The term usually applies to native species that appear in meadows, roadsides, and open spaces: {The hillside was covered in wildflowers each spring}. Wildflower often implies simple beauty and natural abundance, in contrast to cultivated garden varieties.

Wildlife refers to animals living in their natural habitat, not domesticated or tamed by humans. The term typically evokes mammals, birds, and other vertebrates—{deer, bears, and other wildlife}—though it technically includes all wild organisms. Wildlife appears often in conservation contexts: {wildlife preserve}, {wildlife refuge}, {wildlife management}. A {wildlife documentary} films animals in their natural environment.

Wilds refers to remote, uncultivated, or uninhabited regions where nature remains largely untouched by human development. The word appears almost exclusively in the plural and typically follows "the": {They spent a month trekking through the wilds of Alaska}. It often carries connotations of adventure, danger, or escape from civilization. Figuratively, wilds can describe any unfamiliar or chaotic territory: {navigating the wilds of the internet}.

Will tells you what the future holds. The auxiliary verb must combine with a main verb, since English doesn’t have a verb form for future time. Will is used with an infinitive, and it is often shortened to ‘ll at the end of a word: Will you see your Aunt in Chicago? I‘ll try, but she may be too busy. Linked to the future, will also suggests actions considered but not completed, such as those involving expectations, orders, capability, or inclination: He will ace his exam. Less common is will‘s use as a transitive verb, where it is connected with intentions, such as your last testament, or your control over your own mind.

Willful describes someone who insists on having their way, often despite advice or opposition: {a willful child}, {willful disregard for the rules}. The word carries a sense of stubborn determination that may be admirable or frustrating depending on context. In legal use, willful indicates intentional rather than accidental action: {willful negligence}, {willful misconduct}. Also spelled wilful.

The willies are feelings of nervous unease or fear, often triggered by something creepy or unsettling: {That abandoned house gives me the willies}. The word appears almost exclusively in the phrase {the willies} and with verbs like give, get, or have. {Just thinking about spiders gives me the willies.}

Willing means ready or prepared to do something without reluctance: {I'm willing to help if you need me}. It suggests consent or agreement rather than enthusiasm—someone willing isn't necessarily eager, just not opposed. A willing {participant} cooperates voluntarily. Willingly is the adverb: {She willingly admitted her mistake}. To be willing also implies capacity: {God willing}, {if fate is willing}.

A willow is a tree or shrub with slender, flexible branches and narrow leaves, typically growing near water. Willows are known for their graceful, drooping form—the weeping willow being the most recognizable variety. The wood is light and pliable, traditionally used for basket-weaving and cricket bats. {Willows lined the riverbank.} (Capitalized Willow is a given name.)

Willows are trees and shrubs with narrow leaves, slender branches, and a preference for wet ground. The weeping willow, with its drooping branches, is the most familiar variety. Willow wood is light and flexible, traditionally used for cricket bats and wicker baskets. {Willows lined the riverbank.}

Willpower is the mental strength to control impulses, resist temptation, or persist through difficulty. It implies deliberate self-discipline rather than natural ease: {It takes willpower to stick to a diet}, {She summoned the willpower to finish the marathon}. Willpower is often treated as a finite resource that can be depleted or strengthened.

Wills is the third-person singular of will in its volitional sense—what someone desires or intends: {She wills herself to stay calm}. More commonly, wills is the plural of the noun will, meaning either determination {(iron wills)} or legal documents directing the distribution of property after death: {They updated their wills after the grandchildren were born}.

Wilt is what plants do when they droop from lack of water or excessive heat—leaves and stems lose rigidity and sag. The meaning extends to people who flag under pressure or harsh conditions: {She wilted under his questioning}, {The team wilted in the fourth quarter}. Wilt also survives as an archaic second-person singular of "will": {Thou wilt not forsake me}.

Wilted describes something that has lost freshness, drooped, or become limp. Plants wilt when they lack water; their leaves and stems sag. The word extends to people who look exhausted or defeated: {She looked wilted after twelve hours in the heat}. A wilted {salad} has gone soggy. To wilt is to lose vigor under pressure or harsh conditions.

A wimp is a weak, timid, or ineffectual person—someone who lacks courage or physical strength. The word carries contempt: {Don't be such a wimp}. To wimp out is to back down from something challenging out of fear or reluctance: {He wimped out of the bungee jump at the last minute}. Wimpy describes characteristically feeble behavior.

Wimpy describes someone or something lacking strength, courage, or resolve. A wimpy person shrinks from confrontation or physical challenge: {Don't be so wimpy—just ask her out}. The word extends to things that seem weak or inadequate: {a wimpy handshake}, {wimpy coffee}. The tone is mildly contemptuous but often playful.

To win is to be victorious over an opponent (win 5 to 4), to prevail (win an argument), or to come first in a competition (win an election). You can also win (acquire some good thing unexpectedly) on the basis of luck (win at bingo, win the lottery). If you win friends, you succeed in acquiring them. Something that wins favor or wins approval becomes accepted. A win is an instance of winning. A winning streak is a series of these.

A wince is a quick, involuntary flinch or grimace in response to pain, embarrassment, or something unpleasant: {She winced when the needle went in}. The word captures that brief contraction of facial muscles or slight recoil of the body. You might wince at a bad pun, a cringeworthy memory, or watching someone else get hurt.

Winced is the past tense of wince—to flinch or draw back slightly, usually in response to pain, discomfort, or something unpleasant. The reaction is typically involuntary and visible: {She winced when the needle went in}, {He winced at the memory of his mistake}. Wincing can be physical or emotional, but always suggests an instinctive recoil.

Wincing is drawing back or flinching, usually in response to pain, discomfort, or something unpleasant. The movement is quick and involuntary—a visible cringe: {She kept wincing as the nurse cleaned the wound}. Wincing can also be a reaction to embarrassment or awkwardness: {I'm still wincing at what I said to her}.

Wind is two words in contemporary English, both of which have noun and verb forms. The wind that is mainly a noun denotes the natural movement of air in the atmosphere, resulting in a detectable current. This wind (short vowel) typically takes verbs of sound or movement: blow, howl, whip, buffet. The regular related verb wind is mostly used as the participle winded, meaning out of breath. The other wind (long vowel) is mainly an irregular verb that means to change direction—once, frequently, or in a regular circular pattern: The river winds through the countryside. Wind the rope around the post. A winding staircase is one that circles a central point as it ascends.

A windbag is a person who talks too much, especially someone who speaks at length without saying anything substantial. The term suggests someone full of air rather than substance: {Uncle Frank is such a windbag—he talked for an hour and said nothing}. The word carries mild contempt but is more dismissive than truly hostile.

Windbags are people who talk too much, especially in a pompous or boring way. The term evokes someone full of nothing but air: {The meeting dragged on while the usual windbags held forth}. A windbag's defining trait isn't just verbosity but the sense that their words carry less substance than volume.

A windbreaker is a lightweight jacket designed to resist wind and light rain. The fabric is typically thin, synthetic, and uninsulated—meant for mild conditions rather than cold weather. {She packed a windbreaker for the hike.} The term is sometimes capitalized as a trademark, though generic use dominates.

Windburn is skin irritation caused by prolonged exposure to cold, dry wind. The face becomes red, raw, and chapped—similar in appearance to mild sunburn but caused by wind stripping moisture from the skin: {My cheeks were windburned after a day on the slopes}. Common among skiers, sailors, and cyclists.

Windchill is the cooling effect of wind on exposed skin, making air feel colder than the actual temperature. Weather reports give windchill as a temperature: {With the windchill, it feels like twenty below}. The effect results from wind stripping away the thin layer of warm air that normally insulates the body. Also spelled wind chill.

A windchime is a decorative arrangement of suspended pieces—typically tubes, rods, or bells made of metal, wood, bamboo, or glass—that strike against each other when moved by the wind to produce musical or tinkling sounds. Windchimes are hung outdoors on porches, in gardens, or near windows, where breezes can activate them. Some cultures associate them with spiritual significance or use them in feng shui to promote positive energy flow. {The gentle sound of the windchime on the porch was soothing.}

Winded means out of breath, typically from physical exertion: {I was winded after climbing the stairs}. The past tense of wind (to deprive of breath) rather than wind (to turn), it describes the temporary breathlessness that follows running, a blow to the stomach, or sudden effort. A long-winded speaker talks at exhausting length.

A windfall is an unexpected gain or piece of good luck, especially money: {The inheritance was a windfall she hadn't anticipated}. The term comes from fruit blown down by wind—free for the taking without climbing or picking. A windfall {profit} or windfall {tax} relates to gains from circumstances beyond one's control rather than effort or skill.

Winding describes something that twists and turns rather than running straight: a winding {road}, a winding {river}, a winding {staircase}. As a noun, a winding is a turn or curve, or coiled material—especially wire wrapped around a core in electrical devices: {the windings of a motor}. The act of winding something up, as with a clock or thread, also produces windings.

A windmill is a structure with large blades or sails that rotate when wind strikes them, traditionally used to grind grain or pump water. Modern wind turbines generate electricity on the same principle. To {tilt at windmills} is to fight imaginary enemies or futile battles, from Don Quixote's attack on windmills he mistook for giants. As a verb, to windmill is to rotate the arms in wide circles: {She windmilled her arms to keep her balance}.

Windmills are structures that harness wind power through rotating blades or sails. Traditional windmills ground grain or pumped water; modern wind turbines generate electricity. To windmill is to rotate the arms in wide circles: {She windmilled her arms to keep balance}. To {tilt at windmills} is to fight imaginary enemies or pursue hopeless causes, from Don Quixote's mistaking windmills for giants.

A window is an opening in a wall or vehicle that lets in light and air, typically covered with glass. Windows can be opened or closed, and the word extends to any framed view or transparent barrier: {the airplane window}, {a display window}. In computing, a window is a framed area on a screen showing a program or document. Figuratively, a window is a period of opportunity or a means of observing something otherwise hidden: {a window into medieval life}, {the launch window closes at noon}.

Windows are openings in walls or roofs that let in light and air, typically fitted with glass in a frame. The plural covers both literal openings {the windows of the old church} and figurative ones: {windows of opportunity}. In computing, windows are rectangular viewing areas on a screen, allowing multiple programs or documents to be visible at once. (Capitalized Windows is Microsoft's operating system.)

The windowsill is the horizontal ledge at the bottom of a window frame. Inside, windowsills hold plants, decorations, or forgotten objects: {The cat slept on the windowsill}. Outside, they provide a narrow perch and help shed rainwater away from the wall.

Winds functions as both verb and noun. To wind (rhymes with "find") is to follow a curving path: {The road winds through the mountains}. To wind (rhymes with "pinned") is to turn something repeatedly, as when winding a clock or winding thread onto a spool. To wind up is to end in a particular state: {We wound up staying the whole weekend}. The noun winds (always rhymes with "pinned") is the plural of wind—moving air: {Strong winds knocked down power lines}.

A windshield is the large glass panel at the front of a vehicle, protecting occupants from wind, debris, and weather while providing visibility. In British English, the term is windscreen. Windshield extends to protective panels on motorcycles and boats. {A rock cracked the windshield on the highway.}

A windsurfer is a person who rides a sailboard—a surfboard fitted with a mast and sail, propelled across water by wind. The term also refers to the board itself: {She bought a new windsurfer for the summer}. The sport combines elements of surfing and sailing, requiring balance and wind-reading skill.

Windsurfing is a water sport combining elements of surfing and sailing. The rider stands on a board and maneuvers a sail attached to a rotating mast, using wind power to glide across the water. Also called boardsailing or sailboarding. {We went windsurfing off the coast of Maui.}

Windswept describes something exposed to strong, persistent winds. A windswept {moor} or {coastline} is barren and weathered. Hair or clothing that is windswept has been blown into disarray: {She arrived looking windswept from the walk across the parking lot}. The word suggests both exposure and the visual effect of that exposure—bent trees, flattened grass, tousled hair.

Windup is the preparatory motion before a throw or pitch—the arm drawn back, body coiled. By extension, it's any buildup to a main event: {the windup to the announcement}. In British English, a windup is a deliberate tease or joke meant to provoke: {Is this a windup?} As an adjective, windup describes toys or mechanisms powered by a coiled spring: {a windup clock}, {a windup toy}.

Windy describes conditions with strong or persistent wind: {a windy day}, {a windy hilltop}. A windy road has many turns and curves. In British usage especially, windy can mean nervous or frightened. Speech or writing that is windy uses too many words—full of air but lacking substance: {a windy speech that said nothing}.

Wine is an alcoholic beverage made by fermenting grapes or other fruits. Red wines ferment with grape skins; white wines without. The word extends to similar fermented drinks: {rice wine}, {dandelion wine}. To wine someone is to treat them to wine, usually paired with dine: {They wined and dined us all weekend}. Wine also names a deep purplish-red color.

A winery is an establishment where wine is made, from crushing grapes through fermentation to bottling. The term covers operations of all scales, from small family vineyards to industrial facilities. Wineries often include tasting rooms where visitors can sample wines: {We visited three wineries in Napa Valley}.

A wing is either of the pair of appendages on a bird or insect that enables it to fly; by natural extension, the lateral projections on an aircraft are also wings. Though chickens don’t fly much, their wings supply abundant human food. A section of a large building or organization is also called a wing, like the West Wing of the White House or the right wing of a political organization. Something winged has wings. To wing somewhere is to fly there.

Winged means having wings: a winged {insect}, a winged {horse}. The word extends to things that resemble or suggest wings: winged {seeds} that spiral as they fall, the winged {victory} statue. Figuratively, winged can mean swift or elevated: {winged words}, {winged messengers}. In compounds, it often specifies type: {red-winged blackbird}, {broken-winged bird}.

A winger is a player positioned on the wing—the outer edges of the field in soccer, hockey, rugby, and similar sports. Wingers typically attack down the sidelines, delivering crosses or cutting inside toward goal. In political slang, a winger is someone on the extreme end of the spectrum: {a right-winger}, {a left-winger}. The political sense often carries dismissive connotations.

A wingman is a pilot flying beside and behind the leader of a formation, providing support and protection. The term extends to social situations, especially dating: a wingman helps a friend approach potential romantic partners, running interference or talking them up. {I need you to be my wingman tonight.} The role implies loyal backup rather than personal agenda.

Wingmen is the plural of wingman—originally a pilot flying beside and slightly behind a lead aircraft to provide support and protection. The meaning has shifted to social contexts: a wingman helps a friend pursue romantic interests, typically by engaging others in a group or talking up the friend's qualities. {I need you to be my wingman tonight.}

Wingnuts are nuts with two flat projections for gripping, allowing hand-tightening without tools. Figuratively, a wingnut is a person with extreme political views, especially on the right: {The comment section filled with wingnuts ranting about the deep state}. The political sense suggests someone whose thinking has gone off-kilter. Singular: wingnut.

Wings are paired appendages that enable flight in birds, insects, and bats—or the analogous structures on aircraft. The word extends to things that flank a central body: the wings of a building, the wings of a stage (offstage areas), or the wing of a political party (its left or right faction). In sports, a wing is a player positioned near the sideline. Chicken wings, often just called wings, are a popular food item, typically fried and sauced. To wing it is to improvise without preparation: {I hadn't studied, so I just winged it}. To take someone under your wing is to mentor or protect them.

Wingspan is the distance from wingtip to wingtip when wings are fully extended. The term applies to birds, aircraft, and insects: {The albatross has the largest wingspan of any living bird}. For aircraft, wingspan affects lift and maneuverability. The word extends to anything with outstretched lateral reach: {He demonstrated the wingspan of his new desk}.

A wingsuit is a specialized jumpsuit with fabric panels between the arms and legs that create wing-like surfaces, allowing skydivers and BASE jumpers to glide horizontally through the air before deploying a parachute. The suit transforms the human body into an airfoil, dramatically increasing flight time and enabling precise aerial maneuvering. {She flew her wingsuit through the narrow canyon at over 100 miles per hour.}

To wink is to close and open one or both eyes quickly. It differs from blink in being assumed to be intentional, and often in conveying information. A wink is an instance of this. A wink of sleep, used with a negative, is a small amount of sleep. A sly wink suggests secret or implicit information aimed at its recipient. To wink at something, an indiscretion for example, is to ignore the implications of it.

Winking is closing and opening one eye quickly, usually as a signal of shared understanding, flirtation, or playful conspiracy: {She caught him winking at her across the room}. The gesture suggests something unspoken between people—a secret joke, a hint not to take something seriously, or romantic interest. Winking can also be involuntary, as with a nervous tic.

A winner is someone or something that wins—a competition, contest, or conflict. The word extends to anything notably successful: {That recipe is a winner}. In sports, a winning goal or shot is also called a winner: {She hit a backhand winner down the line}. To {pick a winner} is to identify something destined for success, often used ironically when someone has chosen poorly.

Winners are those who win—victors in competitions, conflicts, or pursuits. The word extends beyond contests to anything successful or excellent: {That new restaurant is a real winner}. A lottery winner hits the jackpot; a winner in life achieves happiness or success by whatever measure applies. In casual speech, calling something a winner endorses it: {I think this plan is a winner}.

Winning is achieving victory or success—the opposite of losing. A winning {team}, a winning {strategy}, a winning {lottery ticket}. The word also describes qualities that attract favor or approval: a winning {smile}, a winning {personality}. As a noun, winnings are money or prizes gained from gambling or competition: {She collected her winnings from the poker table}.

Winnings are money or prizes won through gambling, competition, or games of chance: {She collected her winnings from the poker table}, {He spent his lottery winnings on a new car}. The word is almost always plural—a single prize is typically called the winnings rather than a winning. Winnings often implies luck or chance rather than earned income.

A wino is a person, typically homeless or destitute, who drinks cheap wine to excess. The term is dismissive and often contemptuous, reducing a person to their addiction: {Some wino was sleeping on the bench}. It evokes skid row imagery—someone clutching a bottle in a paper bag.

Winter is the coldest season of the year, falling between autumn and spring. In the Northern Hemisphere, it runs roughly from December through February; in the Southern Hemisphere, from June through August. Winter suggests short days, bare trees, and in many regions, snow and ice. Figuratively, winter can mean a period of decline or dormancy: {the winter of one's life}. To winter somewhere is to spend the cold months there: {They winter in Florida}.

Wipe is to clean or dry a surface by rubbing it with something: {She wiped the counter with a cloth}, {He wiped his hands on his jeans}. To wipe something away or off is to remove it by rubbing: {wipe away tears}, {wipe off the dust}. To {wipe out} is to destroy completely or, in surfing and skateboarding, to fall dramatically. To {wipe the slate clean} is to start fresh. A wipe is a single rubbing motion or a disposable moistened cloth for cleaning: {baby wipes}, {disinfecting wipes}.

Wiped is the past tense of wipe—to clean or dry a surface by rubbing: {She wiped the counter}. To wipe something out is to destroy it completely: {The storm wiped out the village}. In slang, wiped means exhausted: {I'm completely wiped after that hike}. To get wiped out can also mean to fall hard, especially in surfing or skateboarding.

Wipeout is a dramatic fall or crash, especially one that sends a surfer tumbling off their board or a skier sprawling across the slopes. The term extends to any spectacular failure or total defeat: {The party suffered a wipeout in the midterm elections}. In finance, a wipeout describes the complete loss of an investment's value. As a verb phrase, wipe out means to destroy completely or exhaust utterly: {The pandemic wiped out small businesses across the country}.

Wipes are disposable cloths, usually pre-moistened, designed for cleaning surfaces or skin. Baby wipes clean infants during diaper changes; disinfectant wipes sanitize countertops and hands. As a verb form, wipes means to clean or dry by rubbing: {She wipes down the table after dinner}. To wipe something out is to destroy or eliminate it completely. If you wipe out while skateboarding or surfing, you fall dramatically.

Wird is a dialectal or archaic spelling of *weird*, surviving mainly in Scottish contexts. The phrase {the Weird Sisters} in Macbeth sometimes appears as {Wird Sisters}, connecting to an older sense of fate or destiny. Outside historical or regional usage, wird is likely a typo for *weird* or *word*.

Wire is a flexible strand of metal with various purposes: binding things, making fences, and carrying electrical current or digital information. The wire is used informally for the finish line of a race, or a deadline or endpoint: The student finished the essay, but went down to the wire. A wire is also a clandestine listening device, or a telegram. To wire something, such as a message or money, to a destination is to send it there electronically. To wire a device is to connect functional wires to it. Wired is sometimes used to distinguish some devices that can also operate wirelessly, like headphones, computer mice, or microphones.

Wired means connected by wires, especially to an electrical system or network: {The house is wired for sound}. Someone who is wired is nervously energetic or overstimulated, often from caffeine or drugs: {I had three espressos and I'm completely wired}. To be wired into something is to be deeply connected to it: {She's wired into the local art scene}. Wired can also mean innately predisposed: {Humans are wired to seek social connection}. (Capitalized Wired is the technology magazine.)

Wireless describes technology that transmits signals without physical cables—through radio waves, infrared, or other electromagnetic means. {The café has free wireless.} As a noun, wireless can mean a wireless network or, in older British usage, a radio: {listening to the wireless}. The term gained new currency with WiFi and mobile technology.

Wires is the plural of wire—thin, flexible strands of metal used to conduct electricity or bind things together. The word often appears in contexts involving electrical systems: {The wires in this old house need replacing}. To {pull wires} or {pull strings} is to exert hidden influence. Someone who is {wired} is nervously energetic or electronically connected. {Cross wires} suggests miscommunication: {We got our wires crossed about the meeting time}.

A wiretap is a concealed listening device placed on a telephone line or other communication channel to secretly monitor conversations. The term comes from the early practice of physically tapping into telegraph and telephone wires. As a verb, to wiretap means to install such a device or conduct such surveillance: {Federal agents wiretapped the suspect's phone for six months}. Wiretapping by law enforcement typically requires a court order, though the word now extends to any covert electronic surveillance of communications.

Wiretapping is secretly monitoring telephone or electronic communications, typically by law enforcement or intelligence agencies. The term comes from physically tapping into telephone wires, though modern surveillance intercepts digital signals: {The FBI obtained a warrant for wiretapping the suspect's phone}. Illegal wiretapping is a crime in most jurisdictions.

Wiretaps are devices or methods for secretly monitoring telephone or electronic communications, typically used by law enforcement or intelligence agencies. The term evokes its origins in physically tapping into telephone wires, though modern surveillance is largely digital. As a verb, to wiretap is to conduct such monitoring: {The FBI wiretapped his phone for six months}. Wiretapping usually requires a court order, making unauthorized wiretaps a serious crime.

Wiring refers to a system of electrical wires and connections that distribute power or signals through a building, vehicle, or device. The term also applies to the act of installing such a system: {The electrician finished wiring the new addition}. Figuratively, wiring describes how something is internally configured or predisposed to function, especially the brain or nervous system: {His wiring makes him naturally optimistic}. Faulty wiring is a common cause of electrical fires.

Wisdom is the quality of having good judgment, deep understanding, and insight gained through experience. It differs from mere knowledge—wisdom involves knowing how to apply what you know: {With age comes wisdom}. Conventional wisdom refers to widely held beliefs, which may or may not be accurate. Wisdom teeth are the third molars, so called because they emerge in early adulthood when a person is supposedly wiser.

Wise is the adjective associated with wisdom; it is roughly opposite to ignorant and shares some meaning with intelligent and prudent. A wise decision or choice brings good results; a wise investment brings a good return; wise words and sayings incorporate useful information. The wise is used collectively to designate people who are wise. Wise can be used disparagingly in some expressions like don’t get wise with me (where it means insolent). To wise up is to become informed or aware.

A wiseass is someone who makes clever, sarcastic, or mocking remarks, often at inappropriate moments. The term is mildly vulgar and usually conveys annoyance with the person's attitude rather than genuine offense. It functions both as a noun {Don't be such a wiseass} and as an adjective {I'm tired of your wiseass comments}. The related wisecrack refers to the kind of remark a wiseass makes.

A wisecrack is a clever, flippant remark—often sarcastic or mocking: {He couldn't resist a wisecrack about her cooking}. The term suggests quick wit deployed for humor rather than substance. To wisecrack is to make such remarks: {She wisecracks her way through meetings}. A wisecracker is someone who does this habitually.

Wisecracking means making clever, flippant remarks—the kind of quick verbal jabs associated with old Hollywood comedies and hard-boiled detectives. A wisecracking sidekick keeps up a steady stream of quips. The word describes both the act and the person: {a wisecracking cabbie}, {She spent the whole dinner wisecracking about her ex}.

Wisecracks are clever, often flippant remarks meant to be funny or show off wit. The word implies speed and sharpness—a wisecrack lands quickly, sometimes at someone's expense: {He couldn't resist making wisecracks during the meeting}. To wisecrack is to make such remarks. A wisecracker is someone known for them.

A wiseguy is a person who makes smart-aleck remarks or acts like a know-it-all: {Don't be a wiseguy}. The term carries mild annoyance rather than genuine hostility. In a separate sense, wiseguy is slang for a member of the Mafia or organized crime—someone who's "wise" to how the underworld operates: {He was a wiseguy in the Gambino family}.

A wish is a desire for something, especially something unlikely or impossible: {I wish I could fly}, {Make a wish and blow out the candles}. To wish is to want something to be true or to happen. You can wish someone well, wish them a happy birthday, or wish them dead. A wish can be a polite request: {It is my wish that you leave}. To get your wish is to have your desire fulfilled.

A wishbone is the forked bone between the neck and breast of a bird, formed by fused collarbones. By tradition, two people each grip one end and pull until it snaps; whoever gets the longer piece may make a wish. The shape gives its name to a football formation and various Y-shaped objects.

Wishbones are the forked bones found in birds, formed by the fusion of the two clavicles. The name comes from a tradition: two people each grip one side of a dried wishbone and pull until it snaps, and whoever ends up with the larger piece supposedly gets their wish granted. The term extends to anything Y-shaped: a {wishbone offense} in football splits receivers wide.

Wishes is the plural of wish—desires or hopes for something, especially things beyond one's immediate power to obtain: {She kept her wishes to herself}. Wishes often appear in greetings and blessings: {best wishes}, {birthday wishes}, {get-well wishes}. To send {warm wishes} is to express goodwill. The verb form means to want or hope: {He wishes he'd studied harder}.

Wishing is wanting something to be true or to happen, often with little expectation of bringing it about. The word carries a sense of longing or hope rather than active pursuit: {wishing for better days}, {wishing you were here}. A wishing well is where people toss coins while making wishes. {Wishing won't make it so.}

A wishlist is a collection of desired items, typically maintained for gift-giving occasions or future purchases. Online retailers let customers save wishlists of products they hope to buy or receive: {I added the book to my wishlist}. The term extends to any set of hoped-for outcomes: {Universal healthcare is at the top of progressives' wishlist}. Also spelled wish list.

Wishlists are lists of desired items, typically maintained on shopping websites or apps. Users add products they want but aren't ready to buy, creating a personal catalog for future reference or to share with gift-givers: {I added it to my wishlist for my birthday}. The term extends beyond commerce to any collection of hoped-for things: {a wishlist of travel destinations}.

A wisp is a thin, delicate strand or streak of something: {a wisp of smoke}, {a wisp of hair}. The word suggests something barely there, on the verge of dissolving. A wisp of a person is slight and frail. Will-o'-the-wisp, a flickering light over marshes, extends to anything elusive or deceptive.

Wisps is the plural of wisp—thin, delicate strands or fragments of something: {wisps of smoke rose from the chimney}, {wisps of hair escaped her braid}. The word suggests lightness and insubstantiality. A {wisp of a girl} is slight and fragile. {Will-o'-the-wisps} are elusive lights over marshes, or by extension, any misleading goal.

Wistful describes a gentle, melancholy longing—usually for something past or unattainable. A wistful expression suggests quiet yearning mixed with sadness: {She gave a wistful smile when she saw the old photographs}. The word carries a soft, reflective quality rather than acute grief: {He grew wistful thinking about his college days}.

Wistfulness is a gentle, melancholy longing, often directed toward something in the past or something unattainable. Unlike sharper forms of sadness, wistfulness has a dreamy, reflective quality—a bittersweet awareness of what was or what might have been. {There was a wistfulness in her voice when she talked about her childhood home.} The feeling often surfaces when contemplating old photographs, revisiting familiar places, or remembering people no longer present.

Wit is quick, clever intelligence—the ability to make sharp, often humorous observations or connections. Someone with wit can turn a phrase memorably: {Her wit kept the dinner party lively}. A witty remark is both clever and amusing. Wit also means mental faculty more broadly, as in {scared out of my wits} or {gather your wits}. To {have your wits about you} is to be alert and ready. {At wit's end} describes exhausted mental resources.

A witch is a person, especially a woman, believed to practice magic or sorcery. In folklore and fairy tales, witches cast spells and brew potions, often depicted as malevolent: {The witch cursed the princess}. Historically, accusations of witchcraft led to persecution and execution. Modern witches may practice Wicca or other nature-based spiritual traditions. The word also serves as an insult for an unpleasant woman: {The old witch next door complained again}. To witch is to bewitch or enchant.

Witchcraft is the practice of magic, especially magic associated with evil or supernatural powers. Historically, accusations of witchcraft led to persecution and execution, particularly of women. The term now encompasses modern pagan practices like Wicca, which adherents don't consider evil: {She's been studying witchcraft for years}.
