Figuratively, witchcraft describes any skill so impressive it seems magical: {Her cooking is pure witchcraft}.

Witches is the plural of witch—people, traditionally women, believed to practice magic or sorcery. In folklore and history, witches were feared as servants of evil; witch hunts and trials led to executions. Modern usage includes practitioners of Wicca and other pagan traditions. Figuratively, witch describes a malicious woman: {The old witch next door complained about everything}.

A witchhunt is a campaign to identify and punish people accused of holding unacceptable views or engaging in subversive activity. The term invokes the historical persecution of alleged witches, when accusations spread through communities and evidence mattered less than suspicion. Modern witchhunts target political enemies, social deviants, or anyone deemed threatening: {The hearings became a witchhunt against suspected communists}. Often spelled as two words: witch hunt.

Witchhunts, also spelled as two words, originally referred to organized campaigns to identify and punish people accused of practicing witchcraft, most notoriously in early modern Europe and colonial America. The term now primarily describes aggressive investigations or persecutions targeting individuals or groups based on flimsy evidence, ideological suspicion, or mass hysteria rather than genuine wrongdoing. {The senator dismissed the ethics inquiry as a political witchhunt.} The word carries connotations of unfairness, mob mentality, and scapegoating.

Witching describes the time or atmosphere associated with supernatural activity, especially magic or sorcery. The {witching hour} is traditionally midnight, when witches and spirits are most active. The word evokes an eerie, magical quality: {a witching moonlit night}. As a verb form, witching means practicing witchcraft or casting spells.

To withdraw is to pull back or remove. You withdraw money from an account, withdraw troops from a position, or withdraw a statement you regret. The reflexive use suggests retreating into oneself: {She withdrew after the argument}. Withdrawal describes the process, and also the physical symptoms when stopping an addictive substance: {heroin withdrawal}.

Withdrawal is the act of removing or taking back. You can make a withdrawal from a bank account, withdraw troops from a battlefield, or withdraw a comment you regret. Withdrawal from a competition or agreement means pulling out. In medicine, withdrawal describes the physical and psychological symptoms that occur when someone stops using an addictive substance: {He went through heroin withdrawal}. The word also describes emotional retreat—becoming less engaged or communicative: {Her withdrawal from family life worried everyone}.

Withdrawals is the plural of withdrawal, the act of taking something back or removing oneself. Bank withdrawals are money taken from an account. Troop withdrawals remove military forces from a region. In medicine, withdrawals refers to the physical and psychological symptoms that occur when someone stops using an addictive substance: {The withdrawals from heroin were brutal}. This sense often appears with a singular verb: {Withdrawals is the hardest part of getting clean}.

Withdrawn describes someone who has pulled back from social contact—quiet, reserved, uncommunicative: {She became increasingly withdrawn after the divorce}. The word suggests emotional retreat rather than mere shyness. As the past participle of withdraw, it also describes things that have been removed or taken back: {withdrawn funds}, {a withdrawn application}.

Withdrew is the past tense of withdraw. To withdraw is to pull back or remove—withdrawing troops from a position, withdrawing money from an account, withdrawing a hand from a flame. One can withdraw from a competition or withdraw support. To withdraw into oneself is to become quiet and uncommunicative: {She withdrew after the argument and wouldn't speak to anyone}.

Wither means to dry up, shrivel, or lose vitality. Plants wither from lack of water; hopes wither from neglect. A withering {look} or withering {criticism} is scornful enough to make someone shrink. The phrase {wither on the vine} describes something that dies from inattention before reaching fruition: {The proposal withered on the vine when no one championed it}.

Withered describes something that has dried up, shriveled, or lost vitality—typically plants or body parts: {withered leaves}, {a withered arm}. The past tense of wither, it often functions as an adjective for things that have decayed through age, disease, or lack of nourishment. Figuratively, it applies to anything that has lost its former strength or promise: {withered hopes}, {a withered reputation}.

Withering describes something that shrivels, weakens, or declines—like plants drying up from lack of water. A withering {glance} or withering {criticism} is devastatingly scornful, causing the recipient to shrink as if scorched: {She fixed him with a withering stare}. Withering {fire} in military contexts is intense enough to destroy enemy forces.

To withhold is to hold back or refuse to give something. You might withhold information, withhold payment, withhold judgment, or withhold affection. The word implies deliberate restraint—keeping something that could be given or released: {The company withheld his final paycheck}. Taxes withheld from a paycheck are deducted before you receive it.

Within has the same meaning as inside but is slightly more formal, and often preferred in writing. It indicates a limit in time, space, or scope: The matter was handled within the department. Be back within an hour. That amount of money is not even within my imagination.

Without is the opposite of with when it means including: a cabin without modern plumbing. In Scottish English, or when it is accompanied by within, it can also mean outside: There are several good accommodation choices both within and without the city.

Withstand means to resist or endure something that threatens, pressures, or challenges. The word typically applies to forces that would otherwise cause damage, defeat, or collapse: {The bridge was built to withstand earthquakes}, {She withstood intense criticism without backing down}. What distinguishes withstand from simply endure is the implication of successful resistance—whatever is withstood does not prevail.

A witness is someone who sees an event firsthand, especially one that may require testimony: {Several witnesses saw the accident}. In legal contexts, a witness gives evidence under oath. To witness something is to observe it: {We witnessed history being made}. A witness can also be someone who signs a document to verify another's signature. Religious usage extends the meaning to one who testifies about faith: {bearing witness to God's love}.

Witnesses is the plural of witness—people who observe events or give testimony. In legal contexts, witnesses appear in court to provide evidence: {The prosecution called three witnesses}. Witnesses also attend ceremonies to verify their occurrence: {We need two witnesses for the marriage license}. The verb witnesses means observes or attests to: {She witnesses the signing of contracts daily}.

Witnessing is observing something happen, especially something significant or noteworthy. The word carries weight beyond casual seeing—you witness accidents, crimes, ceremonies, or historic events. In legal contexts, witnessing means formally observing the signing of a document and adding your own signature to verify it occurred. Religious usage extends this further: witnessing can mean sharing one's faith or testifying to spiritual experiences. {I'll never forget witnessing the birth of my first child.}

Wits are mental faculties—the capacity for thinking, reasoning, and responding quickly. Someone who {lives by their wits} relies on cleverness rather than steady employment. To {gather your wits} is to collect yourself mentally. {Scared out of my wits} means terrified beyond rational thought. A {battle of wits} is a contest of intelligence. To be {at your wit's end} is to have exhausted your mental resources and not know what to do next.

Witty describes someone or something marked by quick, clever humor—the ability to make unexpected verbal connections that amuse: {a witty remark}, {a witty conversationalist}. Wit implies mental sharpness rather than broad comedy; witty observations tend toward the pointed or sardonic. {She's too witty for her own good sometimes.}

Wives is the plural of wife, a woman to whom someone is married. The word appears in contexts ranging from domestic to legal: {Both wives attended the ceremony}, {He outlived three wives}. The phrase {old wives' tale} refers to a superstitious belief passed down through generations, typically by women—now used dismissively for any unfounded popular notion.

A wizard is a person with magical powers, especially a man who practices sorcery in fantasy and folklore: {The wizard cast a powerful spell}. By extension, wizard describes someone with exceptional skill in a particular area: {a financial wizard}, {a wizard with computers}. In software, a wizard is a step-by-step guide that walks users through a complex process. British slang uses wizard as an adjective meaning excellent, though this sounds dated: {That's wizard!}

Wizardry is the art or practice of a wizard—magic, sorcery, enchantment. The word extends readily to any impressive skill that seems almost magical: {Her wizardry with numbers saved the company millions}. Technical wizardry suggests mastery of complex systems: {The film's special-effects wizardry won three Academy Awards}.

Wizards are figures with magical powers, appearing throughout mythology, fantasy literature, and games. A wizard typically masters arcane knowledge and casts spells: {The wizard summoned fire from his staff}. By extension, wizard describes anyone with exceptional skill: {a financial wizard}, {a wizard at computers}. In British slang, wizard means excellent: {That's wizard!}

Wobble describes unsteady movement—a rocking or swaying motion that suggests instability or lack of firm support. A table wobbles when its legs are uneven; a toddler wobbles while learning to walk; a politician wobbles when wavering on a position. The noun wobble is an instance of such movement: {There's a wobble in the front wheel}. Something wobbly is prone to wobbling or currently doing so.

Wobbling is moving unsteadily from side to side, rocking or swaying without firm balance. A top wobbles as it slows down. A table wobbles on uneven legs. The word extends to uncertainty or wavering: {She's still wobbling on whether to accept the job}. A wobbling voice trembles with emotion or weakness.

Wobbly describes something that moves unsteadily from side to side, lacking stability or firmness. A wobbly table rocks on uneven legs; a wobbly toddler hasn't quite mastered walking. The word extends to anything uncertain or unreliable: a wobbly economy, a wobbly argument, or feeling wobbly after standing up too fast. In British slang, to {throw a wobbly} means to have an emotional outburst or tantrum.
Woe is mainly a noun denoting grief, loss, or sorrow. As an interjection it expresses any of these in a somewhat literary way.

Woes are troubles, misfortunes, or sources of grief. The word is the plural of woe, an old term for deep sorrow or distress. Woes often appear in phrases describing categories of difficulty: {financial woes}, {marital woes}, {the team's defensive woes}. The word carries a slightly literary or dramatic flavor.

A wok is a round-bottomed cooking pan with high, sloping sides, used especially in Chinese and Southeast Asian cuisine. The shape allows food to be tossed and stirred quickly over high heat: {She stir-fried the vegetables in a hot wok}. Woks work best on gas burners; flat-bottomed versions exist for electric stoves.

Woke began as African American vernacular for being alert to racial injustice and systemic oppression: {Stay woke}. The term spread through social justice movements to mean aware of broader inequalities. By the late 2010s, critics adopted it dismissively for progressive politics they consider excessive or performative: {woke culture}, {go woke, go broke}. The word now carries opposite connotations depending on who's using it.

Wokeness is awareness of social injustice, particularly regarding race, gender, and systemic inequality. The term emerged from Black American slang where being "woke" meant staying alert to racism and its mechanisms. In contemporary usage, wokeness often carries a negative connotation, deployed by critics to mock what they see as performative or excessive concern with progressive causes: {The company's wokeness felt like marketing rather than genuine commitment}. Defenders use it neutrally or positively to describe heightened social consciousness.

Woks are bowl-shaped cooking pans with high, sloping sides, used especially in Asian cuisine. The shape allows food to be tossed and stirred quickly over high heat, making woks ideal for stir-frying. {She seasoned her new wok before using it.}

A wolf is a large wild canine that hunts in packs, native to wilderness regions of North America, Europe, and Asia. The wolf figures prominently in folklore and idiom: a {wolf in sheep's clothing} is a dangerous person disguised as harmless, and to {cry wolf} is to raise false alarms. To wolf food is to eat it ravenously: {He wolfed down his dinner}. A wolf can also be a man who aggressively pursues women.

A wolfpack is a group of wolves that hunt and live together. The term extends to any coordinated group operating as a unit, especially in military contexts: German U-boats hunting in wolfpacks during World War II. More loosely, wolfpack describes any gang or crew moving together with shared purpose: {a wolfpack of fraternity brothers roaming the bars}.

Wolfsbane is a highly poisonous plant of the genus Aconitum, with hooded purple or blue flowers. The name reflects old beliefs that it could ward off wolves—or kill them. In folklore and fiction, wolfsbane protects against werewolves: {She hung wolfsbane by the door during the full moon}. Also called aconite or monkshood.

A wolverine is a stocky, powerful mammal of northern forests and tundra, the largest land-dwelling member of the weasel family. Despite its modest size, the wolverine is famously fierce and can drive much larger predators from kills. Its thick fur resists frost, making it valuable in cold climates. The animal's reputation for tenacity and ferocity has made it a popular mascot and nickname. (Capitalized Wolverine is the Marvel Comics character.)

Wolves is the plural of wolf—large wild canines that hunt in packs and figure prominently in folklore and idiom. {Wolves howled in the distance}. To {throw someone to the wolves} is to abandon them to hostile forces. A {wolf in sheep's clothing} disguises predatory intentions. {Wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone in 1995}.

Woman designates a female human. The word is derived from an older word related to wife, and man. Unlike man, woman has not developed much use before nouns to designate things that are for women, and the possessive form women’s is still preferred.

Womanhood is the state of being a woman, particularly as distinguished from girlhood: {She had just entered womanhood when she left home}. The term also refers to qualities considered characteristic of women, or to women collectively: {a triumph for womanhood}. Unlike manhood, womanhood rarely implies courage or toughness, reflecting older cultural assumptions about feminine virtues.

A womaniser is a man who pursues casual sexual or romantic relationships with many women, typically without serious commitment. The term carries disapproval, suggesting manipulation or insincerity: {He had a reputation as a womaniser}. Also spelled womanizer.

A womanizer is a man who pursues casual sexual relationships with many women, typically without emotional commitment or regard for their feelings. The term carries disapproval, suggesting manipulative or predatory behavior: {He had a reputation as a womanizer}. The verb womanize describes this pattern of conduct.

Womanizing is pursuing casual sexual relationships with many women, typically by a man who does so habitually and without commitment. The word carries connotations of treating women as conquests: {His womanizing eventually cost him his marriage}. A womanizer is someone known for this behavior.

The womb is the organ in female mammals where offspring develop before birth—the uterus. Figuratively, womb suggests any place of origin or nurturing enclosure: {the womb of civilization}, {safe in the womb of the earth}. To return to the womb is to seek comfort and protection from the outside world.

A wombat is a stocky, burrowing marsupial native to Australia, roughly the size of a medium dog. Wombats are known for their powerful digging claws and backward-facing pouches, which prevent dirt from entering while they burrow. Their cube-shaped droppings, unique among animals, help mark territory without rolling away.

Wombats is the plural of wombat, a stocky burrowing marsupial native to Australia. These sturdy animals dig extensive underground tunnels and are known for producing cube-shaped droppings. {Wombats emerged from their burrows at dusk to graze.}

Women is the plural of woman—adult female humans. The word appears in compounds emphasizing female participation or perspective: {women's rights}, {women's studies}, {women's health}. {The women in my family are all teachers.} Calling a group "women" rather than "ladies" or "girls" is generally the neutral, respectful choice.

Won is the past tense and past participle of win. You won a game, won an argument, won someone's trust. {She won by three points.} {He's won every match this season.} Won also names the currency of North and South Korea.

Wonder is a feeling of amazement and curiosity, often tinged with admiration: {The children gazed at the fireworks in wonder}. It can be the thing that provokes this feeling—the seven wonders of the ancient world, a one-hit wonder. To wonder is to feel curiosity or uncertainty: {I wonder what she meant by that}. {No wonder} means it's not surprising: {No wonder he's tired—he worked all night}. Wonder as an adjective suggests remarkable effectiveness: {wonder drug}, {wonder boy}.

Wonderful describes something that inspires wonder or delight—remarkably good, excellent, or pleasing: {We had a wonderful time}. The word has softened from its original sense of awe-inspiring to general enthusiasm. It works as a warm, sincere compliment: {You've been wonderful}. In sarcastic use, wonderful expresses the opposite: {Oh wonderful, now the car won't start}.

Wondering describes a state of curiosity or contemplation—the mind actively questioning or marveling at something. {I was wondering if you'd like to join us} softens a request into polite inquiry. {She sat wondering what went wrong} shows quiet reflection. A wondering {look} or wondering {tone} conveys visible curiosity or amazement. The word captures the mind in motion, not yet arrived at an answer.

A wonderland is a place of magical beauty, enchantment, or delight—real or imaginary. The word evokes Lewis Carroll's fantastical realm in *Alice's Adventures in Wonderland*, and that dreamlike quality colors most uses: {The garden was a wonderland of exotic flowers}. A winter wonderland is a snow-covered landscape of particular beauty. The term often carries a note of childlike amazement or, sometimes, irony when applied to places that dazzle but may deceive.

Wonders are things that inspire awe, amazement, or admiration—the {seven wonders of the ancient world}, the {wonders of modern medicine}. To wonder is to feel curiosity or uncertainty: {I wonder what she meant by that}. It also means to marvel: {We wondered at the beauty of the canyon}. {No wonder} means it's unsurprising: {No wonder you're tired—you've been up since dawn}. To {work wonders} is to achieve remarkable results.

Wonderstruck means filled with sudden wonder or amazement—stopped in your tracks by something astonishing or beautiful. The word suggests being struck as if by a physical force: {She stood wonderstruck before the northern lights}. It carries a sense of speechless awe, often in response to nature, art, or the unexpected.

A wonk is someone who studies a subject with intense, detail-oriented focus—especially policy or technical matters. The term often appears with a modifier: {a policy wonk}, {a budget wonk}, {a health-care wonk}. It can be mildly dismissive, suggesting someone more interested in arcane details than practical results, but many wonks embrace the label proudly. To wonk out is to dive deep into technical specifics.

Wonky means slightly off, unstable, or not quite right. A wonky table wobbles; a wonky argument doesn't hold together. In British usage especially, something wonky is crooked or askew: {The picture frame looks wonky}. In American political slang, wonky describes someone deeply immersed in policy details—from "policy wonk": {She gave a wonky answer about tax reform}.

A wonton is a small dumpling in Chinese cuisine, made of thin dough wrapped around a filling of seasoned meat or seafood. Wontons are typically boiled and served in soup or fried until crispy: {wonton soup}, {fried wontons}. The word comes from Cantonese, meaning "swallowing clouds"—a reference to their shape floating in broth.

Wontons are Chinese dumplings made of thin dough wrapped around a filling, typically pork or shrimp. They appear in soup, fried as appetizers, or steamed. {The wonton soup came with six plump dumplings}. The wrapper is thinner than most dumpling doughs, giving wontons their delicate, slightly slippery texture.

Woo is to seek someone's favor or affection, especially romantically: {He wooed her with flowers and poetry}. The word extends to courting anyone's approval: politicians woo voters, companies woo investors. Wooing implies deliberate effort to charm or persuade. The adjective is wooing, the past tense wooed.

Wood is the hard, fibrous matter found under the bark of trees and that composes most of their bulk. In this use, it is uncountable. As a count noun and also as a plural, wood or woods designates a growth of trees larger than a copse or grove but usually smaller than a forest: lost in the woods. Different objects fashioned from wood use the same name, such as a golf club or a wooden wind instrument. Before another noun, wood means using it (a wood stove) or made of it (wood flooring). The verb wood has little active use and appears mainly as the participle wooded, meaning covered in trees.

A woodchuck is a stocky North American rodent that burrows in the ground, also called a groundhog. Woodchucks hibernate through winter and emerge in early spring—hence Groundhog Day, when the creature supposedly predicts the season's length. The tongue-twister {How much wood would a woodchuck chuck?} plays on the name, though woodchucks don't actually chuck wood.

Woodchucks are stocky North American rodents that dig extensive burrows and hibernate through winter. Also called groundhogs, they're the subject of the tongue-twister {How much wood would a woodchuck chuck if a woodchuck could chuck wood?} Despite the name, woodchucks don't chuck wood—they're burrowers, not lumberjacks.

A woodcut is a print made from an image carved into a block of wood. The artist cuts away the areas meant to remain blank, leaving raised lines that receive ink and transfer to paper. The technique produces bold, graphic images with distinctive texture: {a medieval woodcut of the plague}, {Japanese woodcuts influenced the Impressionists}. A woodcut is also the block itself or the technique as an art form.

Wooden describes things made of wood: a wooden {chair}, a wooden {fence}. The figurative sense captures the qualities of wood as a material—stiff, inflexible, lacking life. A wooden {performance} is awkward and unnatural. A wooden {expression} shows no emotion. Someone described as wooden seems robotic or unable to convey feeling: {His delivery was wooden and unconvincing}.

A woodpecker is a bird that drills into tree bark with its strong, chisel-like beak, searching for insects or excavating nest cavities. The rapid hammering sound is distinctive: {I heard a woodpecker in the backyard}. Woodpeckers have specialized skulls that absorb the impact of repeated pecking. The name extends to anyone who persists at something with similar determination.

Woodpeckers are birds that drill into tree bark with their strong, chisel-like beaks to find insects or excavate nesting cavities. Their distinctive hammering sound carries through forests. The name applies to the entire family, which includes flickers and sapsuckers. {We watched the woodpeckers work on the dead oak.}

Woods is a forested area, smaller or less wild than a forest proper: {a walk in the woods}, {lost in the woods}. The plural form is standard even for a single tract. To be {out of the woods} is to have passed through danger or difficulty. Woods also refers to wooden golf clubs, now typically made of metal but retaining the name: {She hit a three wood off the fairway}. (Capitalized Woods is a surname.)

A woodshed is a small outbuilding for storing firewood. The verb woodshed, from jazz slang, means to practice an instrument intensively in private—as if retreating to a shed to work on your chops away from others: {He woodshedded for months before the audition}. To {take someone to the woodshed} is to reprimand or punish them severely, from the old practice of administering discipline out of public view.

A woodsman is a man who lives or works in the forest—hunting, trapping, logging, or simply dwelling there. The term suggests skill in wilderness survival and comfort in remote settings: {an experienced woodsman who could track deer for miles}. Woodsman carries a rugged, self-reliant connotation, evoking frontier life or backcountry expertise.

Woodsy describes something suggestive of woods or forests—the smell, atmosphere, or aesthetic of a wooded area. A woodsy {fragrance} evokes pine, cedar, or fallen leaves. A woodsy {cabin} feels rustic and nestled among trees. The word carries warm, naturalistic connotations: {The trail had a pleasant woodsy feel}.

A woodwind is a musical instrument played by blowing air through a tube, traditionally made of wood: flutes, clarinets, oboes, bassoons. The category persists even for metal instruments like the modern flute because the classification reflects how sound is produced—through vibrating air columns—rather than material. {She plays woodwind in the orchestra.}

Woodwork is objects or structures made of wood, especially the interior wooden parts of a building—doors, moldings, window frames, trim. To {come out of the woodwork} is to appear suddenly from obscurity, as insects emerge from cracks in wooden structures: {Critics came out of the woodwork after the announcement}. In British sports, the woodwork is the goalpost or crossbar: {The shot hit the woodwork}.

Woodworking is the craft or activity of making things from wood—furniture, cabinets, decorative objects, or structural elements. It encompasses skills like carving, joinery, and finishing: {She took up woodworking as a hobby}. The term covers everything from hobbyist projects to professional cabinetry.

Woof is the sound a dog makes—a deep, gruff bark: {The dog let out a low woof}. As a verb, to woof is to make this sound. Separately, woof is a weaving term for the horizontal threads that cross the warp on a loom, also called the weft. {The warp and woof of society} means its basic structure or foundation.

Wooing is the act of trying to win someone's romantic affection or favor. A suitor woos by paying attention, giving gifts, making declarations of love, and generally trying to make himself attractive to the object of his desire. The word extends beyond romance to any persistent effort to gain support or approval: {Tech companies are wooing recent graduates with signing bonuses}. The verb woo carries an old-fashioned charm that makes it popular in both sincere and ironic contexts.

Wool is the soft, curly fiber that grows as the coat of sheep and some other animals. Sheared and processed, it becomes yarn and fabric prized for warmth and durability: {a wool sweater}, {pure virgin wool}. The texture extends to similar materials: {steel wool} for scrubbing, {cotton wool} for padding. To {pull the wool over someone's eyes} is to deceive them—as if blocking their vision with a woolly blindfold.

Woolly describes something resembling wool—soft, thick, and often curly or tangled. A woolly {sweater} is made of wool or similar material. Woolly {hair} has a dense, textured quality. Figuratively, woolly thinking or ideas lack clarity and precision: {The proposal was full of woolly promises}. A {woolly mammoth} was the extinct elephant covered in thick fur. Also spelled wooly.

Woozy describes a state of unsteadiness or mental fog—dizzy, lightheaded, slightly nauseated. You might feel woozy from medication, a blow to the head, too much wine, or standing up too fast: {The anesthesia left me woozy for hours}. The word suggests impairment without complete incapacitation.

A word is a unit of language that has independent meaning. A word may have a single, unambiguous meaning (like toxoplasmosis), or it may have so many meanings that context is required to determine which one is meant (like pitch). Word is used to express a promise made or intention stated (I give you my word) or a command (Don’t fire till I give the word). As a verb, word means express in words: Be sure to word the instructions simply so everyone will understand.

Wording is the particular words chosen to express something: {The wording of the contract was ambiguous}. The term implies that different phrasings were possible and this one was selected—or should have been selected more carefully: {Watch your wording}.

Wordless means without words or speech. A wordless {glance} communicates silently. A wordless {song} has no lyrics, only melody. Someone rendered wordless is struck speechless: {The news left her wordless}. The term often emphasizes that meaning passes without verbal expression—wordless {grief}, wordless {understanding}.

Wordplay is clever manipulation of language for humorous or rhetorical effect—puns, double meanings, anagrams, or other linguistic tricks. It exploits the gaps between sound and sense, or the multiple meanings words can carry: {The sign at the optometrist read "Site for Sore Eyes"}. Writers use wordplay to amuse, to sharpen wit, or to pack extra meaning into a phrase.

Words are units of language—spoken sounds or written symbols that carry meaning. A word can be a single morpheme or several joined together. Beyond the linguistic sense, words often means speech or conversation: {Can I have a word with you?} To give your word is to promise. {Words fail me} expresses being overwhelmed beyond speech. In the plural, words can mean lyrics: {She wrote the words; he wrote the music}.

A wordsmith is someone skilled at crafting language—a writer, poet, or anyone who works words with care and precision. The term echoes blacksmith and goldsmith, positioning words as raw material to be shaped: {She's a real wordsmith—every sentence is perfectly balanced}. Often used admiringly, though sometimes with a hint of craft over substance.

Wordsmiths are people skilled at crafting language—writers, poets, lyricists, or anyone who shapes words with care and precision. The term treats language as raw material to be forged: {The team's wordsmiths polished the campaign slogan}. As a verb, to wordsmith is to refine text, often with a hint of excessive fussing: {We spent an hour wordsmithing the press release}.

Wore is the past tense of wear. Something wore thin if it became weakened through use or repetition: {My patience wore thin}. A person who wore something had it on their body: {She wore a red dress to the party}. Time wore on means it passed slowly or tediously.
Whether as noun or verb, work is a frequently used word with many meanings all derived from the core original: activity that requires strength to get something done.

A workaholic is someone who works compulsively and excessively, often to the detriment of their health, relationships, or leisure time. The term, modeled on alcoholic, suggests an addiction to work rather than a mere strong work ethic. Workaholics may feel unable to stop working even when they want to, or they may derive their primary sense of identity and satisfaction from their jobs. {She's such a workaholic that she answers emails at 2 a.m.}

Workaholism is compulsive overwork—an inability to stop working even when it damages health, relationships, or quality of life. Unlike mere dedication, workaholism treats work as an addiction rather than a means to an end: {His workaholism cost him his marriage}. The term parallels alcoholism, suggesting the behavior is pathological rather than admirable.

A workaround is a method for bypassing a problem without actually solving it—a temporary fix that gets things working despite an obstacle. In computing, workarounds address software bugs or limitations until a proper patch arrives: {There's a workaround involving clearing your cache}. The term extends to any improvised solution that sidesteps rather than removes a barrier: {We found a workaround for the zoning restrictions}.

Workarounds are methods for bypassing problems or limitations without actually solving them. A workaround gets you past a bug in software, a gap in policy, or a broken system: {Until they fix the glitch, here's a workaround}. The term implies practicality over elegance—you do what works, not what's ideal.

A workbench is a sturdy table designed for manual work, typically found in workshops, garages, and craft rooms. It provides a stable surface for tasks like woodworking, metalworking, or electronics repair, often featuring vises, clamps, or tool storage. {He spent weekends at his workbench building furniture.} In software development, a workbench is an integrated environment that provides tools for coding, debugging, and testing applications.

A workbook is a book designed for active use by students or learners, typically containing exercises, problems, or questions with space to write answers: {The math workbook had practice problems for each chapter}. In software, a workbook is a file containing multiple spreadsheets, as in Excel. The word emphasizes doing work rather than passive reading.

A workday is a day on which work is done, as opposed to weekends or holidays: {The package will arrive within three workdays}. It also means the portion of a day spent working: {an eight-hour workday}. The adjective workday means ordinary or mundane—the everyday as opposed to the special: {workday concerns}, {workday routine}.

Worked is the past tense and past participle of work, covering all its meanings: performed labor, functioned properly, produced results, or manipulated something. {She worked three jobs to pay for school.} {The medicine finally worked.} {He worked the clay until it was soft.} When describing materials or objects, worked means shaped or processed by human effort: worked {leather}, worked {metal}. If someone is worked up, they're agitated or emotionally aroused.

A worker is someone who works, especially someone employed for wages. The term often implies labor rather than management: {factory workers}, {construction workers}, {essential workers}. In biology, workers are sterile members of insect colonies—bees, ants, termites—that perform tasks for the group. A {hard worker} shows diligence; a {miracle worker} achieves the seemingly impossible.

Workers are people who work—those employed in jobs, especially manual or industrial labor. The term often implies wage earners as distinct from owners or management: {factory workers}, {healthcare workers}, {the rights of workers}. Worker also describes someone's habits: {a hard worker}, {a fast worker}. In insect colonies, workers are sterile females that perform most tasks.

Workflow is the sequence of steps through which a piece of work passes from start to completion. In business contexts, it describes how tasks move between people or departments: {We need to streamline our workflow}. Software tools that manage these sequences are workflow {applications} or workflow {management systems}. The term implies systematic process rather than ad hoc effort.

The workforce is the total pool of people available for or engaged in work. It can refer to a nation's entire working population {women entering the workforce} or to the employees of a particular organization {The company laid off half its workforce}. Workforce implies labor as a collective resource.

A workhorse is a horse used for labor rather than riding or racing—pulling plows, hauling loads. The term extends to any person, machine, or thing that reliably handles heavy or unglamorous work: {The old pickup was a workhorse for twenty years}. A workhorse isn't flashy but gets the job done.

Workhorses are horses bred or used for heavy labor—pulling plows, hauling loads, powering machinery before engines replaced them. The term extends to any person or thing that performs reliably and tirelessly without glamour: {She's the workhorse of the department}, {My old laptop is still a workhorse}. The emphasis is on dependable, unglamorous utility rather than speed or style.

A workhouse was an institution where the destitute were housed and required to work in exchange for food and shelter. Common in Britain and colonial America from the 17th through early 20th centuries, workhouses were deliberately harsh to discourage dependency: {The parish sent her to the workhouse}. The term now evokes Victorian-era poverty and punitive social policy.

Workhouses were institutions in Britain and other countries where the destitute could receive food and shelter in exchange for labor. They were deliberately harsh to discourage all but the most desperate from seeking relief: {Oliver Twist was born in a workhouse}. The system largely ended in the early twentieth century, but workhouse survives as a byword for grim, punitive charity.

Working describes something that functions or operates: a working {engine}, a working {model}. It also means engaged in labor or employment: the working {class}, working {mothers}. A working {knowledge} is practical rather than theoretical—enough to get things done. The workings of something are its inner mechanisms or operations: {the workings of the human mind}. In the plural, workings can be mine shafts or excavations.

Workload is the amount of work assigned to or expected from a person, team, or system over a given period. A heavy workload strains capacity; a light one leaves room for more: {The new hires helped distribute the workload more evenly}. In computing, workload refers to the demands placed on a processor or server.

Workmanship is the quality of work in something made, especially by hand or craft. Good workmanship means skilled, careful execution: {The cabinet showed excellent workmanship}. Poor workmanship means shoddy or careless construction. The word emphasizes how something was made rather than what materials were used or how it was designed.

A workout is a session of physical exercise or training: {I try to get in a workout before work}, {a thirty-minute cardio workout}. The term extends to any strenuous effort that tests capacity: {The exam gave my brain a real workout}. As an adjective, workout modifies related nouns: workout {clothes}, workout {routine}.

Workouts are sessions of physical exercise, typically structured around specific goals like building strength, improving endurance, or losing weight: {I do my workouts in the morning before work}. The term covers everything from gym routines to home exercise videos. A workout can also be any strenuous effort: {That exam was a real workout}.

A workplace is a location where work is performed—an office, factory, construction site, or any setting where people do their jobs. The term often appears in discussions of conditions, safety, or culture: {workplace harassment}, {workplace injury}, {a toxic workplace}. It can also refer abstractly to the professional environment as opposed to home life: {keeping personal problems out of the workplace}.

Works collects several meanings around effort and production. A person's works are their creative output: {the complete works of Shakespeare}. The works of a watch or clock are its internal mechanism. A works (or the works) is an industrial facility: {a steel works}, {a gas works}. To give someone {the works} is to give them everything available—the full treatment, whether pleasant or harsh: {I'll have a hot dog with the works}. To be {in the works} is to be under development.

A worksheet is a page of exercises or problems for students to complete, typically as practice or assessment: {The teacher handed out a math worksheet}. In spreadsheet software, a worksheet is a single page within a workbook—a grid of cells for entering and manipulating data. The term also applies to any form designed for recording information or working through a process.

A workshop is a room or building where things are made or repaired—a carpenter's workshop, an auto repair workshop. The word extends to intensive educational sessions where participants work together on a skill or topic: {a writing workshop}, {a leadership workshop}. As a verb, to workshop something is to develop it through collaborative critique: {We workshopped the script before filming}.

Workshops are sessions where people gather to learn or practice a skill through hands-on activity: {a pottery workshop}, {a writing workshop}. Unlike lectures, workshops emphasize participation—attendees do something rather than just listen. The term also means places where things are made or repaired: {a carpenter's workshop}, {Santa's workshop}.

A workspace is a physical area where someone works—a desk, a section of a room, or an entire office: {She cleared her workspace before starting the project}. In computing, a workspace is a virtual environment containing files, applications, or settings for a particular task or project: {Switch between workspaces to keep your projects organized}. The term emphasizes a dedicated, bounded area for focused work.

A workweek is the number of days or hours that constitute a standard period of employment, typically Monday through Friday in Western countries. The forty-hour workweek became standard in the twentieth century: {She works a compressed workweek—four ten-hour days}. Also spelled as two words: work week.

The noun world encompasses several complete things, most of which are considered big in their own way but not always in relation to each other. The core meaning includes both the physical globe that humans inhabit, earth, and the entire phenomenon of humanity. Smaller worlds are subsets of these. Used attributively, world characterizes something as belonging to or associated with the whole world, as in world class or a world power.

Worldbuilding is the process of constructing an imaginary world, especially for fiction, games, or other creative projects. It encompasses geography, history, cultures, languages, and rules governing how the world operates: {The author spent years on worldbuilding before writing the first chapter}. Good worldbuilding creates internal consistency—magic systems have limits, societies have economies, actions have consequences. The term emerged from fantasy and science fiction but now applies to any elaborate fictional setting.

Worldly describes things concerned with material or earthly matters rather than spiritual ones: {worldly possessions}, {worldly pleasures}. A worldly person is experienced and sophisticated about life, especially regarding social situations and practical affairs: {She's too worldly to fall for that scam}. The word can carry slight disapproval when contrasting secular concerns with religious devotion.

Worlds is the plural of world—the earth, or any planet, realm, or sphere of existence. People speak of other worlds in astronomy, fantasy, and philosophy. Worlds apart means extremely different: {Their tastes are worlds apart}. Something that does you a world of good helps enormously. The best of both worlds combines advantages from two options: {Working from home gives me the best of both worlds}.

A worldview is a comprehensive framework of beliefs, values, and assumptions through which a person or culture interprets reality. It shapes how one understands existence, morality, knowledge, and purpose: {Her scientific worldview left no room for supernatural explanations}. The term often appears in discussions of clashing perspectives: {Their worldviews were incompatible}. From German *Weltanschauung*.

Worldwide means extending or operating throughout the entire world: {a worldwide pandemic}, {worldwide distribution}. As an adverb, it describes something happening across the globe: {The album sold ten million copies worldwide}. The word emphasizes global scale or reach, often in contexts of commerce, communication, or phenomena that cross national boundaries.

A worm is any boneless creature with a tube-like body and no limbs that typically thrives only in a particular environment. Earthworms live in soil. Numerous kinds of parasitic worms live in humans, animals, and plants. Infestation with these is usually referred to as worms. A person characterized as a worm is disparaged as contemptible. A machine part that burrows cylindrically is called a worm. To worm your way is to move or progress in the manner of a worm.

A wormhole is a hypothetical tunnel through spacetime connecting distant points in the universe—a shortcut that would allow instantaneous travel across vast distances. The concept comes from physics but thrives in science fiction: {The ship entered a wormhole and emerged in another galaxy}. The name evokes a worm's path through an apple, boring straight through rather than crawling around the surface.

Wormholes are hypothetical tunnels through spacetime that could connect distant points in the universe—or even different universes. The concept comes from physics, where a wormhole would create a shortcut between two locations that are otherwise impossibly far apart. Science fiction seized on the idea for faster-than-light travel: {The ship jumped through a wormhole to the other side of the galaxy}. Outside physics, wormhole sometimes describes any hidden passage or unexpected connection between things.

Worms are a large group of invertebrates that includes many parasitic species. Worms can also be the larval stage of an insect, such as a mealworm, which is the larval stage of a beetle. The word worm is also used for other creatures with similar characteristics, such as velvet worm, which is a caterpillar-like invertebrate unrelated to other worms.

Wormwood is a bitter aromatic plant, especially *Artemisia absinthium*, used historically in medicine and as the key flavoring in absinthe. The intense bitterness made wormwood a biblical symbol of suffering and divine punishment. Figuratively, wormwood means a source of bitterness or grief: {The betrayal was wormwood to him}.

Worn describes something diminished by use or time. Worn {shoes} show scuffs and thinning soles. A worn {path} has been trodden smooth. Worn {patience} is nearly exhausted. As the past participle of wear, it appears in compounds: {worn-out} (exhausted or used up), {well-worn} (familiar from repetition), {careworn} (showing the effects of anxiety). A person who looks worn appears tired or aged.

Worried describes a state of anxious concern about something uncertain or potentially bad: {I'm worried about the test results}, {She gave me a worried look}. The feeling ranges from mild unease to consuming anxiety. To be worried sick is to be extremely anxious. Something that has you worried troubles your mind: {What's got you so worried?}

Worries are concerns or anxieties that occupy the mind: {She has worries about her son's health}. The plural often suggests a collection of troubles weighing on someone: {He drinks to forget his worries}. As a verb form, worries means to feel or cause anxiety: {Nothing worries her}, {It worries me that he hasn't called}.

Worry is anxious unease about something uncertain or potentially bad. You worry about your health, your children, your future. The verb takes various forms: {I'm worried about the test}, {Don't worry}, {What's worrying you?} To worry something is to disturb or harass it—a dog worries a bone, troubles worry a nation. A worry is a source of anxiety: {Money is my biggest worry}.

A worrywart is someone who worries excessively, especially about unlikely or trivial problems. The term is mildly teasing rather than harsh: {My mother's such a worrywart—she calls if I'm five minutes late}. Worrywarts fret about things others would dismiss.

Worse is the comparative form of bad—something worse is more unpleasant, severe, or inferior than something else: {The pain got worse overnight}, {His cooking is even worse than mine}. As a noun, worse names the inferior condition: {I've seen worse}. To {make matters worse} is to compound a problem. {The worse for wear} describes something damaged or deteriorated. For the {worse} indicates negative change: {Things took a turn for the worse}.

Worship is reverent devotion to a deity or sacred power—the acts of prayer, praise, and ritual that express it: {Sunday worship}, {a place of worship}. The word extends to intense admiration for anything: {hero worship}, {worship of money}. To worship someone is to adore them deeply: {He worships his older sister}. British English doubles the consonant: worshipped, worshipping.

A worshiper is someone who worships—expresses devotion to a deity, reveres a person, or shows intense admiration for something. The word usually appears in religious contexts: {Worshipers filled the mosque for Friday prayers}. Also spelled worshipper.

Worshipers are people engaged in worship—those who attend religious services or express devotion to a deity. The term applies broadly across faiths: {Worshipers gathered at the mosque for Friday prayers}. It can extend to secular devotion: {worshipers of celebrity}, {sun worshipers} on the beach. Also spelled worshippers.

Worshiping is showing reverence or adoration, typically toward a deity: {worshiping at the altar}, {worshiping God}. The word extends to intense admiration of anything: {worshiping celebrities}, {worshiping money}. Also spelled worshipping.

Worst is the superlative of bad—the most bad, the lowest in quality, or the most severe: {That was the worst movie I've ever seen}, {the worst pain of my life}. As a noun, the worst refers to the most unfavorable outcome or condition: {Prepare for the worst}. To worst someone is to defeat them, though this verb sounds old-fashioned. {At worst} means in the most unfavorable interpretation: {At worst, we'll have to start over}.

Worth is the value or usefulness of something: {What's that painting worth?} {It's not worth the trouble}. Worth functions as noun, adjective, and preposition—often interchangeably: {a dollar's worth of gas}, {worth a dollar}, {worth every penny}. To be {worth your while} is to merit your time. {For what it's worth} introduces something that may or may not be useful. Net worth is total assets minus liabilities. Self-worth is one's sense of personal value.

Worthless means having no value, use, or merit. A worthless {investment} produces no return. A worthless {promise} will never be kept. Applied to people, it's a harsh judgment of character or capability: {He called his son worthless}. The word carries more finality than similar terms—not merely low in value, but completely without it.

Worthlessness is the quality of having no value, use, or merit. The word often describes a psychological state—a crushing sense of one's own inadequacy: {Depression filled him with feelings of worthlessness}. It can also describe objective lack of value: {the worthlessness of the currency after hyperinflation}.

Worthwhile means deserving the time, effort, or resources invested: {a worthwhile cause}, {The trip was long but worthwhile}. The word weighs cost against benefit—something worthwhile pays off in satisfaction, knowledge, or results. It often carries moral weight: worthwhile {work}, worthwhile {contribution to society}.

Worthy means deserving or meriting something: {worthy of praise}, {worthy of attention}, {a worthy cause}. It often implies meeting a standard of value or respect: {a worthy opponent}, {a worthy successor}. As a noun, worthy refers to a person of importance or merit, often used with gentle irony: {local worthies gathered at the town hall}. The word can sound slightly formal or old-fashioned in casual speech.

Wound has two pronunciations with different meanings. With the "oo" sound, a wound is an injury where skin or tissue is cut or broken: {a gunshot wound}, {wounds that wouldn't heal}. The verb means to inflict such injury, or to hurt emotionally: {His words wounded her deeply}. With the "ow" sound, wound is the past tense of wind—to coil or turn: {She wound the thread around the spool}, {The road wound through the mountains}.

Wounded describes someone or something that has been injured, typically by a weapon or violence. A wounded {soldier} has sustained physical harm in combat; wounded {pride} or a wounded {ego} extends the meaning to emotional or psychological damage. The wounded, used as a noun, refers collectively to injured people: {Medics tended to the wounded after the attack}. As the past tense of wound, it describes the act of inflicting injury: {The bullet wounded him in the shoulder}.

Wounding describes something that causes injury—physical or emotional. A wounding {blow} damages the body; wounding {words} damage feelings or pride. The term often appears in legal contexts: {wounding with intent}. As a noun, wounding is the act of inflicting such injury: {The wounding occurred during the altercation}.

Wounds are injuries to the body where tissue is cut, torn, or broken—cuts, gashes, punctures, lacerations. The verb means to inflict such injury: {The bullet wounded three bystanders}. Figuratively, wounds are emotional injuries, and to wound someone is to hurt their feelings: {His words wounded her deeply}. Wounds can also be third-person singular: {Time wounds all heels}.

Woven is the past participle of weave—fabric or material created by interlacing threads on a loom: {a tightly woven cloth}, {hand-woven baskets}. The word extends to anything constructed by intertwining: {a woven fence of branches}. Figuratively, elements woven together are skillfully combined: {a narrative woven from multiple storylines}, {lies woven into truth}.
People usually say Wow! for positive reasons such as wonder or astonishment but it is also used to react to a shocking turn of events.

A wraith is a ghost or spectral apparition, especially one seen shortly before or after someone's death. The word carries connotations of something pale, insubstantial, and haunting. Figuratively, a wraith is anyone gaunt or ghostly in appearance: {She had become a wraith after months of illness}. Something wraithlike drifts or moves silently: {Fog hung over the field like a wraith}.

To wrangle is to argue or dispute, especially in a noisy or prolonged way: {They wrangled over the inheritance for months}. In American usage, to wrangle also means to herd or manage livestock, especially horses—a wrangler rounds up animals. By extension, to wrangle something is to obtain or arrange it through persistent effort: {She wrangled an invitation to the party}.

A wrangler is someone who handles or herds animals, especially horses or cattle on a ranch: {The wranglers got the horses saddled before dawn}. The term extends to anyone who manages difficult things or people: a {data wrangler} organizes messy information, a {celebrity wrangler} keeps talent on schedule. To wrangle is to argue or to herd—both involve struggle.

Wrangling is prolonged, contentious argument or dispute: {After months of wrangling, the parties reached a settlement}. The term suggests tedious back-and-forth rather than productive debate. In a separate sense, wrangling refers to herding or managing livestock, especially horses—the work of a wrangler on a ranch or film set.

Wrap means to cover something by winding or folding material around it: {She wrapped the gift in paper}, {He wrapped a scarf around his neck}. The noun is a covering or garment that wraps: a plastic wrap, a body wrap at a spa, a sandwich wrap. In film production, {that's a wrap} signals the end of shooting. To be {wrapped up in} something is to be absorbed by it. To {wrap up} is to conclude: {Let's wrap up this meeting}.

Wrapped is the past tense of wrap—to cover or enclose something by folding material around it: {She wrapped the gift in tissue paper}. To be wrapped up in something is to be deeply absorbed or involved: {He's completely wrapped up in his work}. {Wrapped around her finger} means under someone's control through charm or affection.

A wrapper is an outer covering, especially one that encloses something for protection or presentation: {candy wrappers}, {gift wrapper}. In computing, a wrapper is code that encases other code to make it accessible or compatible with a different system. Someone who wraps things can also be called a wrapper: {She worked as a gift wrapper during the holidays}.

Wrapping is material used to cover or enclose something—paper around a gift, plastic around food, bandages around a wound. The word emphasizes the covering itself rather than the act: {The wrapping was more impressive than the gift inside}. Gift wrapping specifically means decorative paper and ribbons for presents. Wrappings (plural) often suggests discarded packaging: {wrappings strewn across the floor on Christmas morning}.

Wrath is intense, often righteous anger—the kind associated with divine punishment or moral outrage. It carries more weight than simple anger, suggesting fury that demands retribution: {the wrath of God}, {incur someone's wrath}. Wrath appears in formal or literary contexts and in phrases like {grapes of wrath}. The adjective is wrathful.

A wreath is a circular arrangement of flowers, leaves, or branches, often hung on doors during holidays or laid at memorials: {a Christmas wreath}, {They placed a wreath on the grave}. The shape extends to anything ring-like: {wreaths of smoke}. To wreathe is to encircle or surround: {Her face was wreathed in smiles}.

Wreaths is the plural of wreath, a circular arrangement of flowers, leaves, or branches. Wreaths appear on doors during holidays, on graves as memorials, and on winners' heads as symbols of victory. The word also applies to ring-shaped things generally: {wreaths of smoke curled toward the ceiling}.

Wreck describes something ruined or destroyed—a ship broken apart on rocks, a car crumpled in a collision, a building reduced to rubble. The word extends to people in poor condition: {I was a wreck after the divorce}. To wreck is to destroy or severely damage: {The storm wrecked the coastline}. A wreck can also be the remains of destruction: {divers exploring the wreck}.

Wreckage is the scattered remains of something destroyed—a crashed plane, a demolished building, a ruined ship. The word emphasizes destruction and debris: {Rescue workers searched the wreckage for survivors}. Figuratively, wreckage describes what's left after any catastrophic failure: {the wreckage of their marriage}, {the wreckage of his political career}.

Wrecked describes something destroyed or badly damaged—a wrecked {car}, a wrecked {ship}, a wrecked {building}. Extended uses cover anything ruined: a wrecked {marriage}, wrecked {plans}. Informally, wrecked means exhausted or intoxicated: {I was completely wrecked after the marathon}; {We got wrecked at the party last night}.

A wrecker is someone or something that wrecks—destroys or ruins. A wrecker can be a person who demolishes buildings, a vehicle that tows disabled cars, or someone who causes shipwrecks to salvage cargo. Figuratively, a wrecker undermines relationships, plans, or institutions: {He was a wrecker of marriages}. In some contexts, wrecker implies deliberate sabotage.

Wrecking is the act of destroying or severely damaging something. A wrecking {ball} demolishes buildings; a wrecking {crew} tears structures down. The term extends to figurative destruction: wrecking someone's {plans}, wrecking a {marriage}. In nautical history, wrecking meant salvaging cargo from shipwrecks—or luring ships onto rocks to plunder them.

A wren is a small, plump songbird with a short tail often held upright. Wrens are known for their loud, complex songs despite their tiny size. The word appears in compound names for similar small birds: {house wren}, {winter wren}, {Carolina wren}. {A wren was singing from the hedgerow.}

In North American English, a wrench is a tool that works by establishing a firm grip that allows torque to be applied. Various modifiers designate the different types (monkey wrench, Allen wrench, socket wrench). Wrench also designates a forceful and perhaps painful movement; this meaning arises from the original wrench, a verb that means to move, pull, or strain with violent twisting or force. To wrench something away from someone is to take it from them against their will.

Wrens are small, plump songbirds known for their loud, complex songs and cocked tails. Found across much of the world, they tend to be brown and inconspicuous, often darting through underbrush or hopping along fences. The house wren is among the most familiar North American species, nesting readily in backyard birdhouses. {A pair of wrens took up residence in our garden shed.}

Wrestle is to grapple with an opponent, attempting to throw or pin them to the ground. It's both a competitive sport and informal roughhousing: {The boys wrestled on the lawn}. Figuratively, to wrestle with something is to struggle with it mentally or emotionally: {She wrestled with the decision for weeks}. A wrestler wrestles; a match is a wrestling match.

A wrestler is someone who wrestles—either as a sport or in informal physical struggle. In amateur wrestling, competitors grapple on a mat following strict rules about holds and pins. Professional wrestling is theatrical entertainment where outcomes are predetermined but athleticism is real: {His favorite wrestler was always the villain}. The term extends to anyone engaged in difficult struggle: {a wrestler with moral dilemmas}.

Wrestling is a sport or activity in which two opponents grapple, attempting to throw or pin each other to the ground. It exists as both an ancient competitive discipline with formal rules and as informal physical struggle: {The boys were wrestling in the backyard}. Professional wrestling is scripted entertainment combining athletic performance with theatrical storylines. Figuratively, to wrestle with something is to struggle with a difficult problem or decision: {She wrestled with her conscience}.

A wretch is a miserable, unfortunate person—someone in a state of deep distress or degradation: {The poor wretch had lost everything}. The word can express genuine pity or contemptuous dismissal. It also describes someone contemptible or base: {That wretch cheated his own mother}. In older religious contexts, sinners called themselves wretches to express spiritual unworthiness.

Wretched describes a state of deep misery, distress, or poor quality. A wretched person may be profoundly unhappy or living in deplorable conditions: {The refugees lived in wretched circumstances}. The word also expresses strong disapproval or contempt: {That wretched car broke down again}. Someone feeling wretched may be physically ill or emotionally devastated. The tone ranges from genuine sympathy for suffering to exasperated annoyance at something inferior or frustrating.

Wriggle is to twist and turn with short, quick movements, like a worm or a child trying to escape a parent's grip: {The puppy wriggled out of my arms}. By extension, to wriggle out of something is to escape an obligation through evasion or cunning: {He wriggled out of the meeting with a flimsy excuse}. A wriggle is one such twisting movement.

Wriggling describes the twisting, squirming motion of a body or body part, typically in short, quick movements. Worms and snakes wriggle naturally, and children wriggle when restless or trying to escape a parent's grip. The word extends to any situation involving uncomfortable squirming or evasive maneuvering: {He kept wriggling in his seat during the long meeting}. To wriggle out of something is to escape an obligation or uncomfortable situation through clever evasion.

To wring is to squeeze and twist something to force out liquid: {wring out a wet towel}. The motion extends to wringing hands—twisting them together in distress or anxiety. To wring something from someone is to extract it with difficulty: {They wrung a confession from him}. {It wrings my heart} means it causes anguish. A wringer is a device with rollers for squeezing water from laundry; to go through the wringer is to endure a punishing ordeal.

A wringer is a device with two rollers pressed together, used to squeeze water from wet laundry by passing fabric between them. Before electric dryers, wringers were standard equipment on washing machines. The phrase {put through the wringer} means to subject someone to a grueling experience—an ordeal that leaves them wrung out: {The divorce really put him through the wringer}.

A wrinkle is a small ridge or crease in a surface, especially skin. Wrinkles form in fabric when it's crumpled, and in faces as people age. To wrinkle is to form such creases: {She wrinkled her nose in disgust}. Figuratively, a wrinkle is a minor problem or complication: {We need to iron out a few wrinkles before launch}. A wrinkle can also be a clever technique or new angle: {Here's a wrinkle you might not have considered}.

Wrinkles are creases or ridges in a surface that should be smooth. Skin develops wrinkles with age; fabric wrinkles when crushed or folded. To wrinkle is to form such creases: {She wrinkled her nose in disgust}. Figuratively, a wrinkle is a minor problem or complication: {We need to iron out a few wrinkles before launch}. A new wrinkle is a novel twist or development.

The wrist is the joint connecting the hand to the forearm, allowing the hand to bend and rotate. It also refers to the area of the arm just above this joint: {She wore a bracelet on her wrist}. A wrist shot in hockey or lacrosse uses a flicking motion of the wrist rather than a full swing.

Wrists is the plural of wrist, the joint connecting the hand to the forearm. The wrist allows the hand to rotate and flex in multiple directions. Wrists appear in contexts of jewelry {(she wore bangles on both wrists)}, injury {(he broke his wrists in the fall)}, and restraint {(the officer cuffed his wrists behind his back)}. To {slit one's wrists} is a method of suicide.

A wristwatch is a small timepiece worn on a strap or band around the wrist. Before wristwatches became standard in the early twentieth century, watches were carried in pockets. The compound distinguishes from pocket watches and other timepieces: {She glanced at her wristwatch during the meeting}.

Write is to form letters, words, or symbols on a surface—typically with a pen, pencil, or keyboard. The meaning extends to composing text: write a {novel}, write a {song}, write {code}. To write someone is to send them a letter or message: {Write me when you get there}. If something is {written all over your face}, your expression reveals it. The past tense is wrote; the past participle is written.

A writer is someone who writes, especially as an occupation or serious pursuit. The term covers novelists, journalists, screenwriters, poets, and essayists—anyone who produces written work. {She's a writer for the local paper.} Writer often implies literary ambition or professional status, distinguishing the craft from mere recording: {He always wanted to be a writer.}

Writers are people who write, especially those who do so professionally or as a serious pursuit. The term covers novelists, journalists, screenwriters, poets, and anyone who composes text for publication or performance. {She's one of my favorite writers}. Writer can also mean simply the person who wrote something: {The writer of this letter remains anonymous}.

Writhe means to twist and contort the body, typically in response to intense physical sensation—pain, discomfort, or sometimes pleasure. {She writhed in agony on the hospital bed.} The word suggests continuous, involuntary movement rather than a single twist. Figuratively, writhe can describe emotional torment: {He writhed with embarrassment at the memory.} Snakes and worms writhe as their natural mode of movement, which gives the word its squirming, serpentine connotation.

Writhing describes twisting, contorting movements of the body, typically from pain, discomfort, or intense emotion. A person writhes on the ground after being kicked; snakes writhe as they move. The word suggests continuous, uncontrolled motion: {She lay writhing in agony}. Figuratively, someone can writhe with embarrassment or shame—squirming inwardly even if still outwardly.

Writing is the act of forming letters, words, or symbols on a surface—or the result of that act. It covers everything from handwriting to composing text: {Her writing is illegible}, {He's working on his writing}. Writing also means written works collectively: {the writing of James Baldwin}. The phrase {the writing on the wall} refers to an ominous sign of what's to come. As a modifier, writing describes tools or activities: {writing desk}, {writing sample}.

Written is the past participle of write, used with auxiliaries to form perfect tenses: {I have written three letters today}. As an adjective, it describes something set down in words rather than spoken: a written {exam}, written {permission}, a written {statement}. What's written carries weight—it's documented, official, on the record. {The written word} suggests permanence compared to speech.

The adjective and adverb wrong is the opposite of right in multiple senses. It overlaps in meaning with incorrect and false. If something goes wrong, it develops in an undesirable or unworkable way. If you go in the wrong direction, you turn or proceed in a way that will not end well. To be on the wrong side of something brings disadvantage or defeat. If you wrong someone, you treat them immorally or unethically. A wrong is an act of wronging someone.

Wrongdoing is behavior that violates moral or legal standards—misconduct, sin, or crime. The word is broad enough to cover anything from petty dishonesty to serious offenses: {The investigation found no evidence of wrongdoing}. A wrongdoer is someone who commits such acts.

Wronged is the past tense and past participle of wrong, used as a verb meaning to treat someone unjustly or unfairly. When you've been wronged, someone has done you harm or violated your rights in some way. {She felt wronged by the company's decision to pass her over for promotion.} The term often carries a sense of moral injury rather than just practical harm, suggesting the person deserved better treatment than they received.

Wrongs are acts that violate someone's rights or cause unjust harm. The word carries moral weight—wrongs demand acknowledgment or redress: {We must right the wrongs of the past}. To wrong someone is to treat them unfairly or harmfully: {She felt deeply wronged by his betrayal}. Legal wrongs are actionable injuries; personal wrongs may fester without remedy.

Wrongthink is holding opinions or beliefs deemed unacceptable by a dominant group or authority. The term derives from George Orwell's *1984*, where "thoughtcrime" described forbidden ideas. In contemporary use, wrongthink often appears sarcastically to criticize perceived ideological conformity: {Expressing any wrongthink gets you canceled these days}. The word implies that certain views are treated as inherently illegitimate rather than merely incorrect.

Wrote is the past tense of write. Where write covers the present act of putting words on a page or composing text, wrote places that action in the past: {She wrote him a letter}, {He wrote three novels before turning forty}. The word extends to any form of composition: {Who wrote this song?}

Wry describes something twisted or bent to one side, especially a facial expression: a wry {smile}, a wry {grin}. The twist suggests ironic amusement or dry humor—acknowledging life's absurdities without complaint. Wry {humor} is understated and slightly mocking, often self-directed: {He made a wry observation about his own failures}. A wry {comment} finds dark comedy in difficult situations.

Wunderkind is a German borrowing meaning a child prodigy—someone who achieves remarkable success or displays extraordinary talent at an unusually young age. The term applies especially to children who excel in music, chess, mathematics, or other fields requiring exceptional ability. In broader use, wunderkind describes any young person who rises quickly to prominence in their field: {The tech wunderkind sold his first startup at nineteen}. The plural may be either wunderkinder (German) or wunderkinds (English).

A wuss is a weak or timid person—someone who lacks courage or physical toughness. The word carries mild contempt: {Don't be such a wuss}. It often appears when someone backs down from a challenge or complains about minor discomfort. The verb wuss out means to chicken out: {He wussed out at the last minute}.

Xenophobia is fear or hatred of foreigners, foreign cultures, or things perceived as foreign. The term combines Greek roots for "stranger" and "fear," but in practice it describes hostility more than anxiety: {xenophobic immigration policies}, {a campaign fueled by xenophobia}. Unlike racism, which targets specific racial groups, xenophobia focuses on national origin or cultural outsider status—though the two often overlap.

Xoxo represents hugs and kisses, used as an affectionate sign-off in messages and letters. The x's symbolize kisses (lips pursed for a kiss) and the o's represent hugs (arms encircling). Common in informal correspondence between friends, family, or romantic partners: {Talk soon, xoxo}. Often written in all caps or with varying repetition: {XOXO}, {xo}, {xoxoxo}.

X-ray refers to a form of electromagnetic radiation that can pass through solid objects, used in medicine to image bones and internal structures, and in security to scan luggage. As a verb, to x-ray is to examine using this radiation: {They x-rayed my ankle to check for fractures}. In the NATO phonetic alphabet, X-ray represents the letter X.

X-rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation that can pass through soft tissue but not bone or metal, making them useful for medical imaging: {The x-ray showed a fracture}. The term works as noun or verb—you can get an x-ray or x-ray a patient. Airport security x-rays luggage. Also spelled X-rays or x rays.

A xylophone is a percussion instrument consisting of wooden bars arranged like piano keys, struck with mallets to produce tones. Each bar is tuned to a specific pitch, with longer bars sounding lower notes. The xylophone appears in orchestras, marching bands, and children's music education: {She played a simple melody on the xylophone}.

A yacht is a boat used for pleasure rather than commerce or fishing. The term typically implies something larger and more luxurious than a simple sailboat or motorboat: {They spent the summer on a yacht in the Mediterranean}. Yacht can function as a verb meaning to sail or cruise in one, though this use is uncommon. The word carries connotations of wealth and leisure.

Yachting is the activity of sailing or racing yachts—typically for recreation or sport rather than commercial purposes. The term suggests leisure and often wealth, as yachts are expensive vessels: {They spent summers yachting in the Mediterranean}. Yacht racing has been an Olympic sport since 1900.

Yachts is the plural of yacht, a recreational boat or ship used for pleasure cruising or racing rather than commercial purposes. Yachts range from small sailboats to massive luxury vessels with full crews: {The harbor was full of yachts}. The word often connotes wealth: {billionaires and their yachts}.
Yahoo is like wahoo, a cry of excitement and exaltation.

A yak is a large, shaggy-haired ox native to the high plateaus of Tibet and Central Asia, domesticated for milk, meat, and transport. Separately, to yak is to talk at length, often tediously: {She yakked on the phone for hours}. The noun yak means such chatter. Also spelled yack.

Yaks are large, shaggy-haired bovines native to the high plateaus of Central Asia, especially Tibet. They serve as pack animals and sources of milk, meat, and fiber in mountainous regions. As a verb, to yak (also yack) is to talk persistently about trivial matters: {They yakked for hours about nothing}.

Yakuza refers to organized crime syndicates in Japan, or a member of such a group. Similar to the Mafia, yakuza organizations are hierarchical, involved in gambling, extortion, and other illegal enterprises, though they have historically operated semi-openly in Japanese society. The word can be singular or plural: {a yakuza boss}, {the yakuza control this district}.

Yams are starchy, edible tubers grown in tropical regions, with rough brown skin and flesh ranging from white to purple. In American English, yam often refers to orange-fleshed sweet potatoes, though true yams are a different plant entirely: {candied yams at Thanksgiving}. True yams can grow several feet long and are a dietary staple in West Africa and the Caribbean.

To yank is to pull with a sharp, sudden motion: {She yanked the door open}, {He yanked his arm free}. The noun is the pull itself: {Give it a good yank}. The word suggests more force or abruptness than a simple pull. (Capitalized Yank is informal for an American.)

Yanks is the plural of yank, a sharp tug or pull: {He gave the cord several yanks before it started}. As a verb form, it means pulls suddenly: {She yanks the door open every morning}. (Capitalized Yanks is informal for Yankees.)

Yap is a verb and noun for the sharp, high-pitched bark of a small dog, or by extension, annoying chatter from a person who won't shut up. If someone tells you to {quit your yapping}, they want you to stop talking. A yap can also mean a mouth: {Keep your yap shut}. The word captures both the sound and the irritation it produces.

A yard is a piece of ground adjacent to a building, especially the area around a house: {front yard}, {back yard}. In American English, yard typically means any outdoor space belonging to a residence; British English prefers garden. Yard also denotes enclosed areas for specific purposes: {shipyard}, {junkyard}, {rail yard}, {prison yard}. Separately, a yard is a unit of length equal to three feet or about 0.91 meters. On a sailing vessel, a yard is a horizontal pole that supports a sail.

Yards is the plural of yard, a unit of length equal to three feet or about 0.91 meters. The term appears in measurements of fabric, distance, and athletic fields: {She bought three yards of silk}, {a hundred-yard dash}.
