Yards also names enclosed outdoor areas attached to buildings: {front yards}, {back yards}, {prison yards}. In nautical use, yards are horizontal spars supporting sails.

A yardstick is a measuring stick one yard (three feet) long, used for measuring length. Figuratively, a yardstick is any standard of comparison or evaluation: {Profit is not the only yardstick of success}. The figurative sense dominates in contemporary usage.

Yardwork is the labor of maintaining a residential yard—mowing the lawn, raking leaves, trimming hedges, pulling weeds, and similar outdoor chores. The term is American; British English prefers gardening even for basic maintenance. {I spent Saturday doing yardwork.}

Yarn is fiber spun into long strands for knitting, weaving, or crocheting: {a ball of yarn}, {She bought yarn for a sweater}. The verb means to spin fiber into thread. Separately, a yarn is a long, often exaggerated story, especially one involving adventure or tall tales: {He spun a yarn about his days at sea}. To yarn is to tell such stories.

A yawn is an involuntary deep breath with the mouth wide open, typically from drowsiness or boredom. The action is famously contagious—seeing or reading about yawning often triggers one. To yawn is to produce this reflex. Figuratively, a yawn is something tedious: {The movie was a yawn}. A yawning gap or chasm is wide open.

Yawning is the act of opening the mouth wide and inhaling deeply, usually from tiredness or boredom. The gesture is famously contagious—seeing or even reading about yawning can trigger it. Figuratively, yawning describes something wide open: {a yawning chasm}, {a yawning gap between rich and poor}.

Yawns are involuntary gaping breaths, mouth opening wide, typically from tiredness or boredom. The singular yawn extends to anything tedious: {The movie was a total yawn}. As a verb form, yawns describes the action: {She yawns every time he starts talking}. Things that gape open may also yawn: {A chasm yawned before them}.

Yay is an exclamation of enthusiasm, celebration, or approval: {Yay, we won!} It expresses simple delight, often with childlike energy. As an adverb, yay indicates approximate size or amount, usually accompanied by a gesture: {The fish was about yay big}.
Yeah is an informal way of saying yes in all of its uses. It may be considered disrespectful to answer someone in authority with yeah rather than yes.

English gets its smallest time divisions—second, minute, and hour—from French and Latin, but the bigger chunks—day, month, and year—have been around since Old English and have cognates in Germanic languages. Of these six time divisions, year is the most frequently used, and like day it represents an observable phenomenon: the 365¼ days that it takes for the earth to circuit the sun. For the first 500 or so years that people used the word year they knew it only as the complete cycle of seasons. When Copernicus posited the idea of the earth orbiting the sun, the word already in use easily adapted to the more technical definition.

A yearbook is a book published annually by a school or organization documenting the year's events, activities, and members. School yearbooks typically feature student photographs, club activities, sports teams, and memorable moments from the academic year. Students often sign each other's yearbooks with messages: {Will you sign my yearbook?}

Yearbooks are annual publications documenting a year's events, typically produced by schools to chronicle the academic year with photographs of students, faculty, and activities. High school and college yearbooks serve as keepsakes: {We spent hours signing each other's yearbooks}. Organizations and institutions also publish yearbooks as annual reports or reference compilations.

Yearn is to long for something with deep, persistent desire—often something distant, lost, or unattainable. The word carries emotional weight that want and wish lack: {She yearned for her homeland}, {He yearned to see his children again}. Yearning suggests an ache, a pull toward something that feels essential but out of reach.

Yearning is a deep, persistent longing—stronger and more aching than mere wanting. You yearn for things felt as distant or lost: a homeland, a former lover, a life not lived. {She felt a yearning for the simplicity of childhood}. The word suggests emotional weight and duration, a desire that sits heavy rather than passes quickly.

Yearnings are deep, persistent longings—desires that pull at you over time. The word suggests emotional intensity and often impossibility or distance: {yearnings for home}, {unfulfilled yearnings}. Where a wish might be fleeting, yearnings imply sustained ache. The word appears most often in literary or reflective contexts.

Years is the plural of year, a unit of time measuring one complete orbit of Earth around the sun—roughly 365 days. Beyond counting time, years often emphasizes long duration or aging: {It's been years since we talked}, {The stress aged him years}. {Years} can stand alone for an indefinite but substantial period: {I've known her for years}.

Yeast is a microscopic fungus that ferments sugars, producing carbon dioxide and alcohol. This makes it essential for baking bread (where the gas creates rise) and brewing beer and wine (where the alcohol is the point). Yeast also appears as a dietary supplement. Figuratively, yeast is anything that causes ferment or activity: {the yeast of revolution}.

Yeehaw is an exclamation associated with cowboys, rodeos, and the American West—a shout of excitement or exuberance, often while riding a horse or bull. It conveys rowdy enthusiasm and has become shorthand for rural Southern or Western culture, sometimes affectionately, sometimes mockingly: {Yeehaw, let's go!}

Yell is to cry out loudly, usually from strong emotion—fear, anger, excitement, or urgency: {She yelled for help}. Unlike scream, yell doesn't necessarily imply a high pitch. A yell is also such a cry. In American universities, a yell is a coordinated chant led by cheerleaders: {the school fight yell}.

Yelling is speaking or crying out in a loud voice, typically from strong emotion—anger, excitement, fear, or urgency. {Stop yelling at me!} {The fans were yelling for their team}. Yelling can also mean calling to someone at a distance: {She yelled across the yard}.

Yellow is a primary color, the color of lemons, that falls between orange and green on the visible spectrum. It has several associations in English that may not be shared in other languages. Applied to people, yellow suggests cowardice and fear, or it may be used disparagingly and offensively to characterize Asians. Yellow journalism is overly sensational. A yellow light stands for caution and the need to be alert. To yellow is to turn yellow or fade, often the result of aging or exposure to the sun.

Yellowface is the practice of non-Asian actors portraying Asian characters, typically through makeup, prosthetics, and stereotyped mannerisms. The term parallels blackface and carries similar connotations of racist caricature. Historical examples include Mickey Rooney's exaggerated Japanese landlord in *Breakfast at Tiffany's*. The practice is now widely condemned: {The casting of a white actor in yellowface sparked immediate backlash}.

A yellowjacket is a wasp with black and yellow markings, known for its aggressive behavior and painful sting. Unlike honeybees, yellowjackets can sting repeatedly and often nest in the ground or wall cavities. They're particularly aggressive around food in late summer: {The picnic was ruined by yellowjackets}. Also spelled yellow jacket.

A yelp is a short, sharp cry of pain, alarm, or excitement—the kind a dog makes when startled or hurt: {The puppy let out a yelp when I stepped on its tail}. People yelp too, usually involuntarily: {She yelped in surprise}. The verb and noun are interchangeable: you can give a yelp or simply yelp. (Capitalized Yelp is the business review platform.)

Yelps are short, sharp cries—the kind a dog makes when startled or hurt, or a person emits in sudden pain or surprise: {The puppy let out a series of yelps when I stepped on its paw}. To yelp is to make such a sound. The word suggests something involuntary and high-pitched, more startled than sustained.

Yen is a longing or craving, an urge to do or have something: {I have a yen for Chinese food}, {She felt a sudden yen to travel}. The word suggests a persistent but not desperate desire. Separately, yen is the basic monetary unit of Japan, divided into 100 sen. The currency sense appears constantly in financial contexts: {The yen weakened against the dollar}.
Yes is the standard adverb and interjection to signal agreement, understanding, and acceptance. It is also a polite way to acknowledge direct address.

Yessir is an emphatic or deferential form of "yes sir," compressed into a single word. It signals agreement, compliance, or enthusiasm: {Yessir, I'll get right on it}. The tone ranges from genuine respect to casual affirmation to ironic mockery, depending on context. Also spelled yes sir or yessiree.

Yesterday is the day before today. It also refers to the recent past more broadly: {Yesterday's technology is today's landfill}. As an adverb, it means on that day: {I saw her yesterday}. {Born yesterday} suggests naïveté: {I wasn't born yesterday—I know what you're up to}.
Yet introduces a contrasting clause with slightly more emphasis than but does: We asked them repeatedly to quiet down yet they still ignored us.

A yeti is a large, ape-like creature said to inhabit the Himalayan mountains—the "abominable snowman" of Tibetan folklore. Like Bigfoot in North America, the yeti occupies cryptozoology: reported sightings persist despite no confirmed evidence. The word extends to anything elusive or legendary: {Finding good help around here is like hunting for a yeti}.

A yew is an evergreen tree or shrub with dark needles and red berries, known for its longevity and dense, fine-grained wood. Yews are commonly planted in churchyards and cemeteries throughout Britain. The wood was historically prized for making longbows: {English archers drew yew bows at Agincourt}. All parts of the tree except the berry flesh are poisonous.

Yield has many meanings as a verb, most of which involve the idea of producing, or of change of possession. If an experiment or analysis yields results, it produces something that is useful and wanted. An investment that yields a return earns money for the investor. When you yield to someone, you give them precedence, either by letting them go first or letting them have their way. The yield of something is the quantity that it gives back. The yield of a crop is how much is harvested, for example, per acre. The yield of an investment is how much it earns.

Yields means to produce or give forth. A field yields crops, an investment yields returns, a search yields results: {The experiment yielded surprising data}. To yield is also to give way—surrendering to force, pressure, or authority: {She yielded to their demands}. A yield sign requires drivers to give way to other traffic. In finance, yield is the return on an investment, expressed as a percentage: {a bond with a 5% yield}.
Yikes is associated with fear but sometimes in an ironic way, where they thing reacted to is not actually frightening but merely something to be avoided.

Yin is one half of the complementary pair in Chinese philosophy, representing the passive, dark, feminine, and receptive principle of the universe. It exists in dynamic balance with yang, its active, bright, masculine counterpart: {the yin and yang of work and rest}. The familiar circular symbol shows each force containing a seed of the other. By extension, yin describes anything characterized by these qualities—coolness, stillness, shadow, or introspection: {She brought yin energy to the hectic office}.
People say Yippee! when they are doing or thinking about doing something very exciting.

Yodel is a style of singing that rapidly alternates between the normal voice and a high falsetto, producing a distinctive warbling sound. It originated in the Alps as a way for herders to communicate across mountains and valleys. The technique appears in folk music worldwide and occasionally in country and pop: {She learned to yodel from her Swiss grandmother}.

Yodeling is a style of singing that rapidly alternates between the normal voice and a high falsetto, producing a distinctive warbling sound. The technique originated in the Alps, where it served as a way for herders to communicate across mountain valleys. It appears in Swiss and Austrian folk music, American country and western songs, and occasionally pop music: {She learned to yodel from her grandmother}.

Yodelling is a style of singing that involves rapid alternation between the normal chest voice and a high falsetto, producing a distinctive warbling sound. The technique originated in the Alpine regions of Europe, where it served as a way for herders to communicate across mountain valleys. {The yodelling echoed through the hills.}

Yoga is a Hindu spiritual discipline involving breath control, meditation, and physical postures aimed at attaining union with the divine or higher consciousness. In Western usage, yoga usually refers to the physical practice—a series of poses and stretches performed for flexibility, strength, and stress relief: {I do yoga three times a week}. Hot yoga, power yoga, and other variations have proliferated as exercise trends. {She rolled out her yoga mat}.

Yoghurt is a variant spelling of yogurt, the thick, creamy dairy product made by fermenting milk with bacterial cultures. This spelling is more common in British English and in countries influenced by British conventions, while yogurt predominates in American English. The fermentation process gives yoghurt its characteristic tangy flavor and smooth texture. {I picked up some Greek yoghurt at the shop.}

A yogi is a practitioner of yoga, particularly someone devoted to its spiritual and meditative disciplines rather than just physical postures. The term suggests serious commitment: {He lived as a yogi in an ashram for ten years}. In casual use, yogi may describe anyone who practices yoga regularly: {She's become quite the yogi since joining that studio}.

Yogurt is a thick, creamy dairy product made by fermenting milk with bacterial cultures. The fermentation process gives yogurt its characteristic tangy flavor and smooth texture. It can be eaten plain or flavored with fruit, honey, or other additions, and serves as both a standalone food and an ingredient in cooking. Greek yogurt is strained to remove whey, resulting in a thicker consistency and higher protein content.

Yoink is an exclamation accompanying the swift grabbing of something: {Yoink! That's mine now}. The word imitates a cartoonish snatching motion. As a verb, to yoink is to snatch or steal quickly: {Someone yoinked my parking spot}. The tone is playful rather than seriously accusatory.

A yoke is a wooden beam fitted across the necks of two draft animals, binding them together to pull a load. From this concrete meaning comes the figurative sense of something that binds or burdens: {the yoke of oppression}, {throw off the yoke of colonialism}. A yoke also names the fitted upper part of a garment across the shoulders or hips. To yoke is to harness animals together, or to join things in general: {yoked in marriage}, {yoked to a tedious job}. A yoke of oxen is a pair.

The yolk is the yellow part of an egg, surrounded by the white. It provides nutrients for a developing embryo and is the fattier, richer portion when eaten: {She likes her yolks runny}. Yolk extends to any similar substance, especially the oily secretion in sheep's wool.

Yolks are the yellow centers of eggs, surrounded by the white. The yolk contains most of the egg's fat and nutrients, serving as food for a developing embryo. In cooking, yolks provide richness to sauces, custards, and baked goods: {Separate the yolks from the whites}. Figuratively, yolk can mean the essential or central part of something.

A yorishiro is an object capable of attracting spirits and serving as a vessel for them in Japanese Shinto belief. These can be natural objects like trees, rocks, or mountains, or crafted items like mirrors and swords. The concept underlies much of shrine architecture and ritual practice—a sacred tree wrapped in rope or a mirror in a shrine's inner sanctum marks where a deity may dwell or manifest.

You is the only official second person pronoun in English for subjects and objects. Because it stands for both singular and plural, several unofficial plural pronouns exist to overcome ambiguity, such as you all, y’all, youse, you guys, and so forth. You is used both when directly addressing a person or group, or as an informal way of talking about people in general: You never know how many fans might turn up.

Young characterizes both living and inanimate things that are in the early stages of growth, development, or existence. It is the opposite of old in most of its uses. As a noun, young is usually construed as a plural and denotes the offspring of animals.

Yours combines two jobs in one; to take the place of a noun or noun phrase already named, and to indicate that the thing referred to belongs to or is associated with the person you’re speaking to, or with people in general: If my car is still in the shop can I use yours? If you’ve got $5.5 million to spare, this house can be yours.

You use yourself as the object of a verb or preposition to refer a second time to the person you are addressing, or to people in general: Did you injure yourself playing football? Always give yourself extra time for the Friday commute. Yourself and other pronouns that end in –self and –selves are called reflexives because they indicate that the action of a verb is reflected back at the subject of the sentence.

Youth is the period of life between childhood and full adulthood, or the quality of being young. A youth is a young person, especially a young man: {Three youths were arrested outside the stadium}. The youth refers collectively to young people: {the youth of today}. Youth carries connotations of energy, inexperience, and potential: {the enthusiasm of youth}, {misspent youth}. As a modifier, it describes things designed for or involving young people: {youth sports}, {youth culture}, {youth hostel}.

A yoyo is a toy consisting of two connected disks with a string wound around the axle between them. You hold the string's end and let the yoyo drop, then flick your wrist to make it climb back up. The term extends to anything that fluctuates up and down: {yoyo dieting}, {yoyo prices}. To yoyo is to move erratically between states. Calling someone a yoyo means they're foolish or incompetent.
Ick expresses a reaction to something that is repugnant to the senses.

Yucky describes something disgusting or unpleasant—food that tastes bad, textures that repel, situations that feel wrong: {This oatmeal is yucky}. The word is childish or deliberately playful, the kind of thing a toddler says about vegetables or an adult says with ironic exaggeration: {Monday meetings are yucky}.
People say yum or yum-yum in response to something that tastes or looks good.

Yummy means delicious or appealing to the taste: {These cookies are yummy}. The word is informal and slightly childish, often used by or around children. It extends to anything pleasurable or attractive: {That's a yummy shade of pink}. The noun yummy or yummies refers to tasty treats.

Yuppie is a mildly derisive term for a young urban professional—someone in their twenties or thirties with a well-paying white-collar job and conspicuous consumption habits. The word emerged in the 1980s to describe ambitious city dwellers more interested in career advancement and material comfort than social causes: {The neighborhood filled with yuppies and overpriced coffee shops}.

Yuppies is the plural of yuppie, a young urban professional—someone in their twenties or thirties with a well-paying white-collar job and conspicuous consumption habits. The term emerged in the 1980s, often used disparagingly to suggest materialism and self-absorption: {The neighborhood filled up with yuppies and their overpriced coffee shops}.

A yurt is a portable, round tent traditionally used by nomadic peoples of Central Asia. The structure consists of a collapsible wooden frame covered with felt or skins, designed for easy assembly and transport. Modern yurts appear as alternative housing, glamping accommodations, or backyard structures: {We stayed in a yurt in Mongolia}. {The retreat center has yurts for guests}.

Zany describes something or someone amusingly unconventional or wildly comical, often with an element of absurdity or eccentricity. A zany {comedy} features exaggerated silliness; a zany {idea} is entertainingly bizarre. The word carries affection rather than criticism—calling someone zany suggests they're delightfully off-kilter rather than genuinely strange. As a noun, a zany is a comical person, though this use is now rare outside theatrical contexts.

Zap captures the idea of sudden, energetic action—originally the sound of a ray gun or electrical discharge in comic books. To zap something is to destroy or disable it quickly: {The laser zapped the target}. In computing, zap means to delete or erase: {I accidentally zapped the whole folder}. Microwaving food is often called zapping: {Just zap it for thirty seconds}. As a noun, a zap is a jolt or burst of energy. The word conveys speed and decisiveness across all its uses.

Zapped is the past tense of zap, which means to strike or destroy with sudden force or energy—originally the blast of a ray gun in science fiction, now extended to microwaves, electrical shocks, or swift elimination: {I zapped the leftovers}, {The surge zapped my computer}. Zapped also means exhausted: {I'm completely zapped after that meeting}.

Zapping is the act of destroying, killing, or hitting something with sudden force or energy—often suggesting electricity, radiation, or weaponry: {The laser kept zapping the invaders}. In casual use, zapping means changing TV channels rapidly with a remote, or heating something quickly in a microwave: {I'm just zapping some leftovers}. The word carries a sense of speed and decisiveness.

Zeal is a feeling of great enthusiasm, usually about something particular which is expressed in a for prepositional phrase: His zeal for seeking out the truth led him to some very surprising discoveries. If someone does something with zeal, they pursue it very energetically and actively: Young people took to the streets with revolutionary zeal. In most contexts zeal has positive connotations. The related adjective is zealous.

A zealot is someone who pursues a cause with excessive fervor, often to the point of fanaticism. The word implies single-minded devotion that ignores reason or tolerance: {a religious zealot}, {political zealots on both sides}. Unlike mere enthusiasm, zealotry suggests an intensity that others find troubling or dangerous. {She's a zealot about recycling—she'll lecture you for using a plastic straw.}

Zealots are people who pursue a cause with excessive fervor, often to the point of fanaticism. The word implies not just dedication but aggressive advocacy that brooks no compromise: {The anti-smoking zealots succeeded in banning it from all public spaces}. Unlike enthusiasts, zealots tend to alienate others with their intensity. (Capitalized Zealots refers to the ancient Jewish sect.)

A zebra is an African wild horse with distinctive black and white stripes. Each animal's stripe pattern is unique, like a fingerprint. The word appears in various extended uses: a {zebra crossing} (British) is a striped pedestrian crosswalk, and in American sports slang, a zebra is a referee, from the black-and-white striped shirt.

Zebras is the plural of zebra, the African equid with distinctive black-and-white stripes. Each zebra's pattern is unique, like a fingerprint. The word appears in various extended uses: {zebra crossings} are striped pedestrian walkways, and in American sports, {zebras} refers to referees in their black-and-white striped shirts.

Zeitgeist is the spirit or mood of a particular era—the shared attitudes, ideas, and beliefs that define a time. From German, literally "time-spirit." The word captures something broader than fashion or trend: the underlying assumptions and concerns that shape how people think during a period. {Her novel captured the zeitgeist of postwar America.} {Social media is very much part of the current zeitgeist.}

Zemirot are Jewish hymns sung at the Sabbath table, typically between courses of the meal. The songs are traditional, with texts drawn from medieval Hebrew poetry praising God, the Sabbath, and the joy of rest. Different Jewish communities have their own repertoires and melodies. Also spelled zemiros or zmiros. Singular: zemer or zemirah.

Zen describes a state of calm, focused awareness or meditative tranquility: {I felt totally zen after yoga}, {She has this zen approach to chaos}. The adjective suggests being unruffled, present, and accepting—drawing loosely from the Buddhist tradition without necessarily invoking it directly. Often used casually to describe minimalist aesthetics or unflustered attitudes: {His apartment has a very zen vibe}. (Capitalized Zen is the Buddhist tradition.)

Zenith is the point in the sky directly overhead, the highest point the sun or a star reaches in its arc across the sky. By extension, zenith means the peak or pinnacle of anything: {at the zenith of her career}, {the zenith of Roman power}. The opposite is nadir.

A zeppelin is a large rigid airship with a cigar-shaped body, named after its German inventor Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin. The design featured a metal framework containing multiple gas cells, unlike simpler blimps. Zeppelins were used for passenger travel and military bombing in the early twentieth century before the Hindenburg disaster ended the era: {The zeppelin floated silently over the city}. (Capitalized Zeppelin refers to the inventor or the rock band.)

Zeppelins are large rigid airships, named after German Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin, who pioneered their development in the early twentieth century. Unlike blimps, zeppelins have an internal metal framework supporting the gas-filled envelope. They were used for passenger travel and military bombing before the Hindenburg disaster of 1937 effectively ended their era: {The zeppelin floated silently over the city}.

Zero is the notional number 0 between positive and negative integers. On the Celsius scale, it is the temperature at which water freezes. Zero is used figuratively like nothing to characterize the lack or absence of value where it could be expected. A person who is a zero amounts to nothing. A score of zero on a test suggests that no correct responses were given. To zero a device is to set it to a reading of 0, or to reset it to default conditions. To zero in on something is to focus on it directly.

Zest is enthusiastic enjoyment or energy: {She approached the project with zest}. The word also means the outer, colored part of citrus peel, prized for its aromatic oils in cooking: {Add the zest of one lemon}. To zest a fruit is to scrape off this layer. Both senses share an idea of flavor or piquancy—something that adds interest to an experience or dish.

Zesty describes something with a lively, piquant quality—originally referring to food with bright, citrusy, or spicy flavors: {a zesty lemon vinaigrette}. The meaning extends to anything energetic or spirited: {a zesty performance}, {zesty dialogue}. The word derives from zest, the outer peel of citrus fruit, which carries concentrated flavor oils.

Zigzag describes a path or pattern of sharp alternating turns—angling left, then right, then left again. The word works as noun, verb, adjective, and adverb: {a zigzag pattern}, {The road zigzags up the mountain}, {She ran zigzag across the field}. Lightning bolts, mountain switchbacks, and evasive maneuvers all zigzag.

Zigzags are lines or paths that alternate sharply between two directions, forming a series of Z-shaped angles: {The road zigzags up the mountain}. The pattern appears in lightning bolts, decorative borders, and evasive movement. To zigzag is to proceed in this alternating fashion: {The rabbit zigzagged across the field to escape the hawk}.

Zilch means nothing at all—zero, none, nada. It emphasizes complete absence: {I know zilch about cars}, {We got zilch for our trouble}. The word has a slightly comic or dismissive tone, often used when expectations were higher: {After all that work, the payoff was zilch}.

Zillion is an indefinitely large number, used for comic or emphatic effect rather than mathematical precision: {I've told you a zillion times}. Like its cousins bazillion and gazillion, it follows the pattern of actual large numbers (million, billion, trillion) while signaling exaggeration. The adjective zillionth works similarly: {For the zillionth time, clean your room}.

A zillionaire is an extremely wealthy person—richer than a millionaire or billionaire, though the amount is unspecified. The word is informal and often playful or hyperbolic: {He drives that sports car like he's some kind of zillionaire}. Unlike million or billion, zillion has no mathematical value, making zillionaire inherently imprecise and slightly comic.

A zine is a small-circulation, self-published magazine, typically photocopied and stapled, devoted to a niche interest or subculture. Zines emerged from science fiction fandom and punk rock scenes, where fans created their own publications outside mainstream media. The word clips magazine: {She traded zines at the record shop}. Now often applied to any DIY publication, including digital formats.

Zing is a quality of sharp energy or liveliness—a spark that makes something exciting or memorable: {The sauce needs more zing}, {Her presentation had real zing}. As a verb, zing means to move swiftly with a high-pitched sound {Bullets zinged past}, or to deliver a quick, pointed criticism: {He zinged her about the typo in front of everyone}.

A zinger is a quick, sharp remark—often witty, often cutting. It lands with impact, whether as a joke's punchline, a clever comeback, or a pointed criticism: {She delivered a zinger that silenced the whole table}. In casual use, zinger can also mean anything surprising or striking: {The report's final paragraph contained a real zinger}.

Zip represents several unrelated words, including the word for zipper in British English, and in all English dialects, the verb used to mean close with that fastener. In American English and used informally, zip means zero or nothing; it is also short for ZIP code, used by the postal service to sort addresses geographically. Zip is the quality of vigor and energy; to zip along or zip somewhere is to move very fast. Zip is also to compress a file or group of computer files for storage or transmission.

A zipline is a cable stretched between two points at different heights, along which a person rides suspended by a pulley or harness. Ziplines appear at adventure parks and canopy tours, offering the thrill of gliding above treetops or gorges: {We ziplined through the rainforest}. The word also works as a verb for the activity itself.

Ziplines are cables suspended between elevated points, fitted with a pulley and harness that allow a person to glide down by gravity. They appear in adventure parks, canopy tours, and military training. The singular zipline also works as a verb: {We ziplined through the rainforest}.

Ziplining is the recreational activity of riding a suspended cable from a higher point to a lower one, typically harnessed to a pulley that rolls along the line. It originated as a practical means of traversing difficult terrain but has become popular as an adventure sport and tourist attraction, often set up in forests, over canyons, or at resorts. {We went ziplining through the jungle canopy on our vacation.}

A zipper is a fastening device with two rows of interlocking metal or plastic teeth that join or separate when a sliding tab is pulled along them. Zippers close jackets, bags, and pants. To zip is to fasten with a zipper, or to move quickly: {She zipped through the crowd}. {Zip it} means shut up—close your mouth like a zipper.

Zipping describes rapid movement or the action of closing a zipper. A car zips down the highway; you zip up a jacket. In computing, zipping compresses files into a smaller archive format: {I'm zipping these folders before sending them}. The word suggests speed and efficiency—things done quickly and smoothly.

A ziptie is a thin plastic strip with teeth on one side and a ratcheting head that locks when the tail is pulled through, creating a loop that tightens but won't release. Used to bundle cables, secure objects, or improvise restraints. Also called a cable tie or zip tie. {The cops used zipties instead of handcuffs.}

A zit is a pimple—a small inflamed spot on the skin, typically on the face. The word is informal and most associated with teenage acne: {I woke up with a huge zit on my nose}. Zit suggests something temporary and minor rather than a serious skin condition.

Zits is the plural of zit, an informal word for a pimple—a small inflamed spot on the skin, typically on the face. The term is casual and common among younger speakers: {I broke out in zits right before prom}. Zit carries slightly more teenage connotation than pimple.

The zodiac is a band of sky divided into twelve sections, each named for a constellation: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, and so on. In astrology, your zodiac sign corresponds to the sun's position at your birth and supposedly influences personality and fate. {What's your zodiac sign?} A zodiac can also refer to a diagram representing these divisions.

A zombie is a reanimated corpse, a dead body brought back to a semblance of life. The concept originates in Haitian folklore, where zombies were corpses raised by sorcery. Modern usage owes more to horror films, where zombies are shambling, flesh-eating undead that spread their condition through bites. Figuratively, a zombie is someone who moves or acts mechanically, without awareness: {I was a zombie before my morning coffee}. In computing, a zombie is a compromised computer controlled remotely without its owner's knowledge, often used in coordinated attacks.

Zombies is the plural of zombie—reanimated corpses in horror fiction and Caribbean folklore, or people who seem lifeless and mechanical: {The commuters shuffled onto the train like zombies}. In computing, a zombie is a compromised computer controlled remotely without the owner's knowledge, often part of a botnet. {The movie was overrun with zombies by the second act.}

A zone is a geographic or notional space set aside for a purpose. The euro is the accepted currency in the Euro zone; a war zone is the site of a military conflict. Your comfort zone is the state of mind in which you are not stressed. Time zones divide the world into logical divisions for designating clock time. In planning, to zone an area is to designate it for a particular purpose, such as housing, businesses, or industry. To zone out, in slang, is to stop paying attention.

Zones are defined areas or regions, distinguished from surrounding space by some characteristic or purpose. Time zones divide the globe; war zones see combat; comfort zones mark psychological limits. To zone is to divide into designated areas: {The city zoned that land for commercial use}. If you zone out, your attention drifts and you become mentally absent.

A zoo is a facility where wild animals are kept for public viewing, typically in enclosures designed to approximate their natural habitats. Zoos serve purposes of entertainment, education, and conservation. Informally, zoo describes any chaotic scene: {The airport was a zoo during the holidays}.

A zookeeper is a person who cares for animals in a zoo—feeding them, cleaning enclosures, monitoring health, and sometimes training them for enrichment or veterinary procedures. The work combines animal husbandry with public education: {The zookeeper explained the penguin feeding schedule to visitors}.

Zoom means to move quickly or suddenly: {The car zoomed past us}. In photography and film, to zoom is to adjust a lens to make a subject appear closer or farther: {The camera zoomed in on her face}. A zoom lens enables this effect. By extension, zoom describes rapid increase: {Prices zoomed after the shortage}. (Capitalized Zoom is the video conferencing platform.)

Zoomies describes the sudden burst of frantic energy that compels a pet—usually a dog—to sprint in wild circles or figure eights, often for no apparent reason. The term comes from animal behavior (formally called frenetic random activity periods) but has become the standard informal word among pet owners: {The puppy got the zoomies right after her bath}.

Zooming is rapid movement, especially with a humming or buzzing sound: {Cars went zooming past}. In photography and video, zooming means adjusting a lens to make subjects appear closer or farther: {The camera kept zooming in on her face}. On computers and phones, zooming enlarges or shrinks what's displayed on screen. During the pandemic, zooming became shorthand for video calling: {We spent the whole day zooming with clients}.

Zoos are facilities where wild animals are kept for public display, education, and conservation. The singular zoo is short for zoological garden. Modern zoos emphasize species preservation and research alongside entertainment: {The pandas at the zoo just had twins}. Figuratively, any chaotic or crowded place: {The office was a zoo today}.

Zucchini is a variety of summer squash with dark green skin and mild, slightly watery flesh. It's harvested young, when tender, and used in everything from stir-fries to baked goods: {zucchini bread}, {grilled zucchini}. The British call it courgette. Gardeners know it for its prolific yields—a few plants can overwhelm a household.
